## Series title page

# Patrologia Latina, vol. 18

## Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library

Complete, uniform, comprehensive, and economical library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprint of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, carefully corrected by comparison with one another and with various manuscript codices; continually illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes for the individual volumes and for each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject treated; enlarged with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is easy for the reader to discover which Fathers commented on the individual books of Scripture, and in which places of their works they did so.

A most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if the following points are properly weighed: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes and its consistent uniformity throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection itself—unified, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and little works previously scattered here and there, but now gathered for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

### First Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great.

Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of complete series in every branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# Ulfilas

## Bishop of the Goths

Complete works, or surviving fragments of the Gothic version of the Old and New Testaments,

corrected in accordance with the authority of the codices, furnished with a Latin translation, historical and philological prolegomena, and critical and continuous annotation, from the edition of the most learned and erudite H. C. de Gabelentz and J. Loebe. There have also been added a grammar and glossary of the Gothic language, prepared by the same authors, translated from German into Latin, and furnished with historical, geographical, critical, and explanatory notes, translated by F. Tempestini.

Preceded by the complete writings of

Saint Martin of Tours,

Tichonius,

Novatus the Catholic,

the Anonymous,

Aurelius Symmachus,

Maximus the Grammarian,

Mamertinus,

Publius Victor,

collected from the best editions of Gallandius, Margarino de la Bigne, Jacob de la Baune, and Edmond Martene.

## In the year of the Lord 399. Saint Martin, Bishop of Tours

(From Gallandius, Ancient Library of the Fathers, vol. VII.)

[Col. 0009]

# Prolegomena

## I

[Col. 0009A] That the blessed Martin, bishop of the Church of Tours, was distinguished not only by the holiness of his life but also by the excellence of his teaching is sufficiently and brilliantly attested by Sulpicius Severus, who knew him well. For he says:

[Col. 0009D] > “But how great was his seriousness and dignity in speech and conversation! How incisive, how effective, and how ready and capable in resolving questions of Scripture! I call Jesus and our common hope to witness that never from anyone’s mouth have I heard such knowledge, such intelligence, or speech so good and pure. Yet how small a commendation this is among Martin’s virtues—except that it is remarkable that this grace was not lacking even in an uneducated man.”

[Note: Sulpicius Severus, *Life of Blessed Martin*, chapter 25, works, volume I, page 34, Verona edition, 1741.]

And elsewhere:

[Col. 0009B] > “Now, if you turn slightly to the left and enter the Gulf of Achaia, let Corinth know, let Athens know, that Plato in the Academy was not wiser, nor Socrates in prison braver. Happy indeed is Greece, which deserved to hear the Apostle preaching; but by no means were the Gauls abandoned by Christ, since he granted them the gift of possessing Martin.”

[Note: The same author, *Dialogue* III, chapter 17, same volume, page 146.]

Thus far Sulpicius.

## II

[Col. 0009C] Moreover, under the name of so great a Father there circulates a *Confession of the Threefold Unity and One Trinity*, composed in a simple style and in some places rather obscure, perhaps through the ignorance of copyists. Jodocus Clichtoveus was the first to publish it, in 1512, together with other little works of the ancients. Afterwards the same little book is found repeatedly printed anew through the labors of learned men such as Pierre Pithou, Caspar Barthius, Christian Daumius, and others. It has also been printed in most libraries of the Fathers and in collections of the councils.

[Col. 0010A] Combefis writes the following about it:

[Col. 0010C] > “I had copied a sermon on the Holy Trinity, bearing his name [Martin’s], from a manuscript of the late Cardinal Mazarin; but it was so corrupt that it did not seem worth reproducing. This appears to have happened because the antiquarian was unable to copy it successfully from older parchments or wax tablets. Nevertheless, it is that very work which, in my judgment, corresponds with what Severus writes with such emphatic testimony concerning Martin’s learning and eloquence despite his lack of education.”

[Note: Combefis, *Library of the Councils*, volume VIII, page 470, note.]

Combefis was referring to the passages we have just quoted from Sulpicius. The same *Confession* was also published at Utrecht in 1514 from ancient manuscripts by Theodore Pulmannus; Daumius relegated its variant readings to the end of his edition, which appeared at Zwickau in 1677.

## III

[Col. 0010B] But above all, the diligence of Thomas Beauxamis seems worthy of commendation. Having obtained three very ancient codices and carefully collated them, he sent the same little work of the holy bishop of Tours to press at Paris in 1571, provided with a brief commentary and appended to the *Life of Blessed Martin* written by Sulpicius Severus.

[Col. 0010D] Since we have followed this edition, which is much more carefully corrected than the others and is moreover reckoned among the rarer editions, it will be useful to bring forward some material from the same Parisian editor.

[Note: Daumius, preface to the little work *On the Holy Trinity*, page 7; *Literary History of France*, volume I, part II, page 417.] In doing so, he reveals the effort he devoted to this little work and at the same time asserts its integrity and value.

Thus he writes:

[Note: Beauxamis, preface, page 251 and following.]

[Col. 0011A] > “Three volumes were brought to me from different libraries, and the hand itself testified that they were sufficiently ancient. For, when compared with other characters that had been in use a thousand years earlier, they were judged by everyone to be exceedingly similar. When I had obtained these three volumes, a threefold history of Sulpicius Severus was woven together … But when, at the very beginning of each book, I recognized a summary of our faith written by Saint Martin, I was truly astonished that, although Severus had so often come from the presses, no mention whatever had been made of it. Yet, as I suppose, apart from the antiquity of the script, they were deterred by the difficulty of the work itself.

> “For the text was not delimited by periods, commas, or other marks, so that it appeared ambiguous to some, defective to others, and obscure to everyone. Since it comprehends, with the greatest brevity, a matter of the utmost difficulty, who could have extracted anything certain from expressions so unbounded and perplexing? … I therefore judged it worthwhile to restrain the words that were running together with their proper punctuation, as though with bonds, and thus make Saint Martin’s *Confession* readily accessible. And so that nothing would be lacking, I added brief notes, lest the obscurity of any expression should keep the reader in suspense any longer.”

[Col. 0012A] Thereafter our Parisian editor, continuing to explain the excellence of the little work, shows that Saint Martin overthrows in this *Confession* numerous heresies: those of Ebion, Cerinthus, Marcion, Manes, Apollinarius, Arius, Macedonius, and Eunomius. After recounting these matters, he concludes:

> “You see, Christian reader, how concisely our Martin destroys many heresies. For he lived in those times when those who tried either to overthrow the Trinity or to abolish the one divinity were multiplying … Consider how many schisms, factions, and sects arose at the time when he flourished; then you will easily recognize that this statement on the faith of the Trinity and the one divinity was issued not without reason.”

Thus he writes.

[Col. 0011B] If anyone carefully weighs all these matters, he will, in my judgment, certainly conclude that [Col. 0012B] certain learned men wrongly regarded this *Confession* as suspect. It is fortified, in the first place, by the testimony and authority of extremely ancient codices, and is plainly worthy of comparison with the *Exposition of Faith* of Gregory Thaumaturgus.

[Note: See our *Library of the Fathers*, volume III, page 385.]

A few somewhat harsh expressions may be excepted, which might perhaps be attributed to the fault of the copyists.

[Col. 0011]

# Confession of Saint Martin on the Threefold Unity and One Trinity (C, S)*


[Col. 0011C] The merciful Trinity is one divinity. But, so that it may be known through the mystery, the unity is from him who is holy and Spirit;

[Note: “From him,” etc. Another reading: “from him who is the Holy Spirit, from whom,” etc.] from him who is, and the only-begotten, existing in this manner, there is the divine nature, light, and Spirit—of itself, through nature, through the substance of majesty, power, might, and divine light.

[Col. 0011D] One Spirit is in two, and both are in the same thing: the Father in the Son, the Son in the Father, in the Holy Spirit. Thus, in three persons, we confess the body of foreknowledge, which encompasses all things above everything.

[Note: “The body of foreknowledge”—that is, he himself who foreknows all things from eternity, whose foreknowledge is his very substance. —Beaux.]

Therefore we believe in this mystery: that all things arose from things that did not exist. The human mind cannot conceive this mystery, nor can eloquent speech recount it; nor could the volumes of libraries, even if books filled the whole world, render the ineffable divine knowledge speakable. He who is unspeakable can in no way be described or enclosed, whether by a word or by the proper substance of his divinity.

He is the source of divine light, radiance, and the light and nature of his own substance. Let eloquent speech be silent, because language fails before the unspeakable. When the human mind has finished speaking about the divine majesty, then it begins.

[Col. 0012C] No one knows how great divine mercy is except the one who begot him; and no one has discovered the Father’s secrets except the one who, by nature, lost the beginning of his birth.

Therefore let all the gentleness and modesty of the learned turn to the prophet and, relying upon the authority of the Lord, presume to say: “I believed, therefore I spoke” (Psalm 115:10).

But since, through the mystery, the confession is simple, like the foundation of the Church established by apostolic authority, let the following predestination presume to speak: “From now on let no one trouble me. I believe in Christ, and in him crucified.”

For when he confesses the Son of Man, he also confesses the Holy Spirit, since the Mediator is born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. When he confesses the firstborn, it is necessary that he also testify concerning the only-begotten, who is one and alone, without origin.

[Note: “The third person, the Father.” The Father is the third person because the three are one. —The same author. —Another reading: “one and alone, without origin, to be the third person, the Father.”]

[Col. 0012D] He confesses the third person, the Father, existing as divine nature and light. The Spirit, as I have said, who according to the divine nature—as I said above—is one in two, and both are in the same thing: the Father in the Son, the Son in the Father, in the Holy Spirit.

[Note: “In the holy Church.” Another reading: “one in the holy Church.”]

Now and throughout the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

# In the Year of the Lord 399. Tichonius the African

(From Gallandius, *Ancient Library of the Fathers*, vol. VIII.)

[Col. 0013]

# Prolegomena

## I

[Col. 0013A] “Tichonius, an African by nation, was sufficiently learned in the divine writings according to their historical sense, and was not ignorant of secular literature. He was also diligent in ecclesiastical affairs.”

These are the words of Gennadius.

[Note: Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 18.]

[Col. 0013C] Saint Augustine, who knew him well and had read many of his writings, speaks of him frequently. He says that he was “a man endowed with a keen intellect and abundant eloquence, but nevertheless a Donatist.”

[Note: Augustine, *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, book I, chapter 1, works, volume IX, page 11.]

At some point, surrounded by the words of the holy pages, he awoke, and therefore sharpened his pen against his own people. Having undertaken this task, the holy Doctor adds:

[Col. 0013B] > “While Tichonius argued vehemently and at length and stopped the mouths of his opponents with many great and clear testimonies of the holy Scriptures, he did not see what ought consequently to have been seen.”

He says that Tichonius “wrote most invincibly against the Donatists, although he himself was a Donatist; and there he is found to have had a most absurd heart, because he was unwilling to abandon them in every respect.”

[Note: The same author, *On Christian Doctrine*, book III, chapter 30, section 42, volume III, page 57.]

Thus far the holy Doctor.

The author flourished in the same period as Rufinus, according to Gennadius, during the reign of Theodosius and his son.

[Note: Gennadius, cited above.]

[Col. 0014C] On this matter the highly learned Tillemont is precise, as he almost always is.

[Note: Tillemont, *Memoirs of Church History*, volume VI, page 718, note 32, “On the Donatists.”]

## II

Of the works committed to writing by Tichonius, which Gennadius enumerates with sufficient care, one little work alone survives, entitled *On the Seven Rules*:

> “By these rules,” says Saint Augustine, “as though by keys, the hidden things of the divine Scriptures might be opened … When these rules are considered as he sets them out, they contribute no little toward penetrating what is concealed in the divine utterances. Yet not everything written in such a way that it is not readily understood can be found through these rules; there are many other methods as well. This sevenfold number does not encompass them to such an extent that the same author does not explain many obscure matters in which he applies none of these rules, because there is no need.”

After inserting several other remarks, he adds:

[Col. 0014A] > “I thought this ought to be said so that the book itself might be read by diligent students, since it contributes greatly to understanding the Scriptures, and so that no more might be expected from it than it possesses. It must certainly be read with caution, not only because of certain matters in which he erred as a human being, but especially because of those points on which he speaks as a heretical Donatist.”

After recounting these matters, the holy Father examines Tichonius’s same Rules. We have therefore arranged to print Augustine’s treatment of them below, at the end of this volume.

## III

The same Saint Augustine also mentions Tichonius’s work elsewhere. Writing to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, he says:

> “Concerning Tichonius’s seven rules, or keys, as I have often written already, I await your opinion.”

[Note: The same author, Letter 41, section 2, works, volume II, page 88.]

[Col. 0014B] How highly that holy Doctor valued such a work is clear from the fact that, when revising his treatment of the Pauline passage concerning the golden and silver vessels placed in a great house, he changed his former judgment. Previously he had followed the interpretation of Saint Cyprian; afterwards he adopted Tichonius’s interpretation.

[Note: 2 Timothy 2:20.]

[Note: Augustine, *Retractations*, book II, chapter 18.]

> “But I approve more,” he says, “what I later found or noticed in Tichonius: that in both categories certain vessels are to be understood as being for honor—not only the golden and silver ones—and again in both categories certain vessels as being for dishonor—not, of course, only the wooden and earthen ones.”

Thus he writes.

Nor did Cassiodorus and Saint Isidore of Seville judge otherwise concerning the excellence of Tichonius’s Rules. Cassiodorus, speaking of interpreters of divine Scripture who construct modes of expression for the sake of explanation and, by means of varied examples and comparisons, make intelligible what previously remained closed, assigns the first place to Tichonius the Donatist and associates him with Saint Augustine, Hadrian, Eucherius, and Junilius.

[Note: Cassiodorus, *On the Institutions of Divine Literature*, chapter 10.]

Elsewhere he further observes that the same writer discussed the matter more fully and carefully in his books of Rules.

[Col. 0015A] The other, Saint Isidore, is found to have held Tichonius’s seven Rules in such high esteem that he condensed them and inserted them into his own books of the *Sentences*, and listed their author among the Wise.

[Note: Isidore of Seville, *Sentences*, book I, chapter 19.]

## IV

[Col. 0016A] The book of Tichonius’s Rules was first published at Basel in 1569 in Grynaeus’s *Orthodoxographi*. Afterwards it appeared in the first Parisian edition of the *Library of the Fathers* by de la Bigne, in 1575. Moreover, Andreas Schottus published the same work of Tichonius, corrected against manuscript codices, in 1622 in the *Supplement* or *Appendix* to the Cologne *Library of the Fathers*. In this revised form it was subsequently incorporated into the latest Lyons edition.

We have reproduced Schottus’s edition in type, carefully marked the passages of Sacred Scripture, removed the many errors with which the earlier exemplar was full, and enlarged it with several observations.

[Col. 0015]

# The Book of Tichonius the African on the Seven Rules (C)


[Col. 0015B] I considered it necessary, before everything else that seems important to me, to write this little book of Rules and to fashion laws of the secrets, as it were keys and lights. For there are certain mystical rules that possess the innermost recesses of the whole Law and make the treasures of truth invisible to some people.

If the system of these Rules is received without jealousy, as we are sharing it, everything that was closed will be opened and obscure things will be illuminated. Thus, as someone travels through the whole forest of prophecy, led in a certain manner along paths of light by these Rules, he may be guarded from error.

[Col. 0015C] These, then, are the Rules:

1. Concerning the Lord and his body.
2. Concerning the Lord’s bipartite body.
3. Concerning the promises and the Law.
4. Concerning species and genus.
5. Concerning times.
6. Concerning recapitulation.
7. Concerning the devil and his body.

# Rule I. Concerning the Lord and His Body

[Col. 0015D] Scripture speaks of the Lord and his body—that is, the Church (2 Timothy 1:20). Reason alone distinguishes them, by persuading us what applies to each; but because the force of truth is so great, it compels us.

At times one and the same person is addressed, although the distinct functions of two persons teach that he is double. Thus, through Isaiah:

> “He himself bears our sins, suffers for us, and he himself was wounded because of our crimes. God delivered him for our sins,” and so forth (Isaiah 53:4, 6, according to the Septuagint).

The whole Church celebrates these words as applying to the Lord.

But the passage continues and says of the same person:

> “And God wishes to cleanse him from the plague, and God wishes to take the light away from him in his suffering, and to form him with understanding” (ibid., 10–11).

Does he wish to show light to the one whom he delivered for our sins and to form him with understanding, when he himself is the light and wisdom of God—and not to his body?

[Col. 0016B] Therefore it is clear that reason alone can show when the transition is made from the head to the body.

Daniel likewise says that the Lord, a stone cut from the mountain, struck the body of the kingdoms of the world and crushed it into dust. He says that the mountain was formed and filled the whole earth: this was his body.

This is not to be understood, as some say, to the dishonor of the kingdom of God and of Christ’s unconquered inheritance—a claim I make not without pain. The Lord occupied the whole world by his power (Matthew 28:18), and not by the fullness of his body.

They say that the world was filled by that mountain because what was previously permitted only in Zion—namely, to offer sacrifice—became permitted to the Christian everywhere. But if this is so, there was no need to say that the stone became a mountain and that, through growth, it began to fill the world.

[Col. 0016C] For our Lord Christ possessed this glory before the foundation of the world (John 17:2). And although that man was the Son of God, he did not receive all authority in heaven and on earth gradually, like a stone, but at one time.

[Note: “Authority.”]

The stone, however, became a mountain through growth and, as it grew, covered the whole earth. If it had filled the whole earth by power rather than by its body, it would not be comparable to a stone. Power is an intangible thing, whereas a stone is a tangible body.

It is shown not by reason alone that the body grows, not the head; it is also confirmed by apostolic authority:

> “Grow in every respect into him who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body, constructed and joined together through every supporting contact, according to the measure of each individual part, makes the body grow for its own edification” (Ephesians 4:15–16).

And again:

[Col. 0016D] > “You do not hold fast to the head, from whom the whole body, constructed and supplied through its contacts and conjunction, grows with the growth of God” (Colossians 2:19).

Therefore it is not the head—which is the same from its origin—but the body that grows from the head.

Let us return to the matter at hand. It is written concerning the Lord and his body; what applies to each must be distinguished by reason:

[Col. 0017A] > “He has commanded his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways. They will carry you in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone. You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon. Because he hoped in me, I will deliver him; I will protect him, because he has known my name. He called upon me, and I will answer him; I am with him in tribulation. I will deliver him and glorify him. I will fill him with length of days, and I will show him my salvation” (Psalm 90:11–16).

Did God, who commanded the angels to minister to the same person, show his salvation to that person and not to his body?

Again:

> “He placed a diadem upon me like a bridegroom, and adorned me with an ornament like a bride” (Isaiah 61:10, according to the Septuagint).

[Col. 0017B] He spoke of one body consisting of both sexes, bridegroom and bride; but reason recognizes what applies to the Lord and what applies to the Church.

The same Lord says in the Apocalypse:

> “I am bridegroom and bride” (Revelation 18:23).

And again:

> “They went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride” (Matthew 25:1).

Again, Isaiah makes clear by reason what must be distinguished as belonging to the head and what to the body:

[Col. 0017D] > “Thus says the Lord God to my anointed Lord, whose right hand I have held, so that nations may obey him” (Isaiah 45:1–3).

[Note: Instead of *Kyrō* (Κύρῳ), “to Cyrus,” he reads *Kyriō* (Κυρίῳ), “to the Lord.”]

The passage continues and says what can apply only to the body:

> “And I will give you hidden treasures; I will open invisible things to you, so that you may know that I am the Lord, who call you by your name, the God of Israel, for the sake of my servant Jacob and my chosen Israel.”

[Col. 0017C] For the sake of the covenant that he established with the Fathers, God opens to the body of Christ, so that it may know him, the invisible treasures “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man” (1 Corinthians 2:9).

[Col. 0018D] Nor are these treasures revealed to the hardened man who is not in the body of Christ; but God revealed them to the Church through the Holy Spirit, although this too is a work of God’s grace.

[Note: “Hardened.”]

When reason is applied, however, certain things are sometimes seen more easily. There are other passages in which this kind of reasoning is less clear, because the statement fits correctly either the Lord or his body. These can therefore be perceived only by the singular and greater grace of God.

Thus in the Gospel:

> “From now on,” he says, “you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power of God and coming in the clouds of heaven” (Matthew 26:64).

Elsewhere he says:

> “They will not see him coming in the clouds of heaven except on the last day, when all the tribes of the earth will mourn. And then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven” (Matthew 24:30).

Both events must take place. First comes the body—that is, the Church, continually coming in the same invisible glory; then comes the head—that is, the Lord, in manifest glory.

If he had said, “From now on you will see him coming,” the coming of the body alone would have to be understood. But if he had said simply, “You will see,” the coming of the head would be meant.

[Col. 0018A] Now, however, he says, “From now on you will see him coming,” because he comes continually in his body through the birth and glory of similar sufferings. For if those who are born again become members of Christ, and the members constitute the body, it is Christ who comes, since birth is a coming, as it is written:

> “He enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9).

And again:

> “One generation goes, and another generation comes” (Ecclesiastes 1:4).

And again:

> “As you have heard that Antichrist is coming” (1 John 2:18).

Again, concerning the same body:

> “For if the one who comes preaches another Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:4).

Therefore, when the Lord was asked about the sign of his coming, he began to speak of that coming of his which can be imitated by the hostile body through signs and wonders:

> “Be careful,” he says, “that no one deceives you” (Matthew 24:4). “Many will come in my name”—that is, in the name of my body.

But at the final coming of the Lord—that is, at the completion of his entire coming—no one, as some suppose, would die.

But so that these matters may be stated more fully, let us leave them to their proper place.

Nor is it absurd that we wish the entire body to be understood from one member, so that the Son of Man may mean the Church. For the Church—that is, the children of God gathered into one body—has been called the Son of God, has been called one man, and has also been called God, as the Apostle says:

> “Above everything that is called God or that is worshiped” (2 Thessalonians 2:4).

The one who is called God is the Church; what is worshiped is the supreme God. Thus he may sit in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God—that is, as though he were the Church.

It is as though he said: “Let him sit in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were the temple of God.” Or: “Let him sit in God, displaying himself as though he were God.”

Daniel, as we know, intended to obscure this interpretation no less in speaking of the final king:

> “His place will be glorified in the Lord” (Daniel 11:38, according to the Septuagint),

that is, it will be made glorious. [Col. 0018C] He brought forward the Church as though in the place of the Church, in the holy place, through the abomination of desolation, as God—that is, as the Church.

The Lord also calls the whole people bride and sister. The Apostle calls the holy Virgin, and the hostile body, the man of sin.

David calls the whole of Christ the Church:

> “Showing mercies to his Christ, David, and to his offspring forever” (Psalm 17:51).

The Apostle Paul calls the body of Christ “Christ”:

> “For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ” (1 Corinthians 12:12),

that is, the body of Christ, which is the Church.

Again:

> “I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and I complete what is lacking of the afflictions of Christ” (Colossians 1:24),

that is, of the Church.

For nothing was lacking in Christ’s sufferings, since it is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher.

Thus we shall understand the coming of Christ according to the passages in which it occurs.

[Col. 0018B] Likewise, in Exodus, we recognize that all the children of God are one son and that all the firstborn of the Egyptians are one firstborn, as God says:

> “You shall say to Pharaoh: Thus says the Lord: Israel is my firstborn son. I said to you, ‘Let my people go, so that he may serve me.’ But you refused to let him go” (Exodus 4:22).

Whence also:

> “Behold, I will kill your firstborn son.”

[Col. 0019A] David likewise calls the Lord’s vineyard one son:

> “God of hosts, turn back; look down from heaven and see, and visit this vineyard and perfect it, which your right hand planted, and the Son of Man whom you established for yourself” (Psalm 79:15).

The Apostle also calls a son of God the one who has been joined to the Son of God:

[Col. 0019B] > “Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, called as an Apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had previously promised through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined to be the Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of sanctification, through the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 1:1–4).

If he had said “concerning his Son” in order to point out one son through the resurrection of the dead, that would be clear. But he says, “concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined to be the Son of God.”

Our Lord was not predestined to be the Son of God, because he is God and is coequal with the Father; from the moment he was created, he was already this. But the one to whom, according to Luke, he says at his baptism, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7), was formed from the seed of David and joined to the governing Spirit, and became himself the Son of God through the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ.

That is, the seed of David rises again in Christ—not the one of whom David himself says:

> “Thus says the Lord to my Lord” (Psalm 109:1).

And so the two became one flesh: “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14), and flesh became God, because we were born not of blood but of God.

The Apostle says:

[Col. 0019C] > “The two shall be one flesh. This mystery is great, but I am speaking with reference to Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5:31–32).

For God promised one seed to Abraham, so that all who were joined to Christ would be one in Christ, as the Apostle says:

> “All of you are one in Christ Jesus. And if you are one in Christ Jesus, then you are Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise” (Galatians 3:28–29).

There is, however, a distinction between “you are one” and “you are one thing.” Whenever one person is joined to another by will, they are one. Thus the Lord says:

> “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

But whenever two are joined bodily and solidified into one flesh, they are one body.

[Col. 0019D] Thus, in his head, he is the Son of God; and God, in his body, is the Son of Man, who comes each day by being born and grows into the holy temple of God.

For the temple is bipartite. One part of it, although built of great stones, is destroyed, and not one stone will be left upon another.

We must beware of this continual coming until the Church departs from its midst.

# Rule II. Concerning the Lord’s Bipartite Body
The rule concerning the Lord’s bipartite body is much more necessary, and therefore must be examined by us with correspondingly greater care and kept before our eyes throughout all the Scriptures. For just as, as stated above, the relation from the head to the body is perceived by reason alone, so also the return from one part of the body to the other—from the right to the left, or from the left to the right—is made clear in the head mentioned above.

For when he says to one body, “I will open for you invisible treasures, so that you may know that I am God, and I will take you up” (Isa. 45:3), he adds: “But you did not know me, because I am God, and there is no other God besides me, and you did not know me” (ibid., 4–5). Although he is addressing one body, do the words “I will open for you invisible treasures, so that you may know that I am God, for the sake of my servant Jacob” agree with the words “But you did not know me” in one and the same mind? In the same [sense], Jacob did not receive what God promised.

Or do these words not agree in one mind: “But you did not recognize me, and you did not know me”? For “you did not know” is said only to one who already knows. “You did not recognize me,” however, is said to one who, although he was called for the purpose of knowing, and although he visibly belongs to the same body and approaches God with his lips, is nevertheless separated from him in heart. To him he says, “But you did not know me.”

Again: “I will lead the blind along a way they did not know, and they will tread paths they did not know; I will make darkness light for them, and crooked things straight. These are the things I will do, and I will not abandon them. But they themselves turned back” (Isa. 42:16–17). Are those whom he said he would not abandon the same ones who turned back, and not merely a part of them?

Again the Lord says to Jacob: “Do not fear, for I am with you. From the East I will bring your offspring, and from the West I will gather you. I will say to the North, ‘Give them up,’ and to the South, ‘Do not hinder.’ Bring my sons from a distant land and my daughters from the ends of the earth, and all those upon whom my name has been called. For I prepared him for my glory, and I formed him, and I brought forth a blind people, and their eyes are likewise blind, and they have deaf ears” (Isa. 43:5, 8). Are those whom he prepared for his glory the same as the blind and deaf?

Again: “Your fathers first; their rulers committed a crime against me, and your princes profaned my holy things, and I gave Jacob over to destruction and Israel to a curse” (ibid., 25). “Now hear me, my servant Jacob, and Israel whom I chose” (Isa. 44:1). He shows that he had given Jacob over to destruction and Israel to a curse, whom he had not chosen.

Again: “I formed you, my servant; you are mine, Israel; do not forget me. For behold, I have blotted out your crimes like a cloud, and your sins like a mist. Turn back to me, and I will redeem you” (ibid., 21). Did he blot out the sins of one to whom he says, “You are mine,” and reminds him not to forget him, saying, “Turn back to me”? Or are the sins of someone blotted out before he turns back?

Again: “I know that, having been rejected, you will be rejected; for the sake of your name I will show you my dignity, and I will bring my splendid things upon you” (Isa. 48:8–9). Does he show his dignity to one who has been rejected, and bring his splendid things upon him?

Again:

> [Note: [Col. 0019D] LXX, οὐ πρέσβυς, οὐδὲ ἄγγελος. “Not an elder, nor an angel.” “Not an envoy, nor an angel.” And immediately: ἀλλ᾽ αὐτὸς ἔσωσεν αὐτούς. [Col. 0020D] “But he himself saved them.”]

“Not an elder, not an angel, but he himself regarded them because he loved them and spared them. He himself redeemed them, took them up, and exalted them all the days of the age. But they were disobedient and grieved the Holy Spirit” (Isa. 63:9–10, according to the Septuagint). At what time were those whom he exalted throughout all the days of the age disobedient, or did they grieve the Holy Spirit?

Again, God plainly promises firmness and destruction to one body, saying: “Jerusalem, wealthy city, tents that shall not be shaken; the stakes of your tent shall not be moved for ever, and its ropes shall not be broken” (Isa. 33:20–21, according to the Septuagint). And he adds: “Your ropes have been broken, because the mast of your ship could not withstand; they lowered your sails, and he will not raise the signal until it is handed over to destruction” (ibid., 23).

Again, he briefly reveals Christ’s bipartite body: “I am dark and beautiful” (Song 1:4). For far be it from us to suppose that the Church, which has neither “spot nor wrinkle” (Eph. 5:27), and which the Lord cleansed with his own blood, is dark in any part, except in the left-hand part, through which God’s name is blasphemed among the nations. Otherwise she is wholly beautiful, as he says: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no fault in you” (Song 4:7).

Indeed, he states the reason why she is dark and beautiful: “Like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon.” He shows two tents: a royal one and a servile one. Yet both are the offspring of Abraham. For Kedar is the son of Ishmael.

Finally, in another passage, lamenting a long dwelling with this Kedar—that is, with the servant descended from Abraham—the Church cried out: “Alas for me, for my sojourn has been prolonged! I dwelt among the tents of Kedar; my soul has made a very long sojourn. With those who hated peace I was peaceful; when I spoke to them, they fought against me without cause” (Ps. 119:5–7, according to the Septuagint).

I cannot say that the tent of Kedar is outside the Church. For he himself says, “The tent of Kedar and of Solomon”: hence, he says, “I am dark and beautiful.” For the Church is not dark in those who are outside.

By this mystery the Lord, in the Apocalypse, speaks of seven angels—that is, the sevenfold Church—and shows them now as holy and guardians of the commandments, now as those same persons guilty of many crimes and deserving of repentance.

And in the Gospel he reveals one body of overseers, possessing diverse merit, saying: “Blessed is that servant whom his master, when he comes, finds doing so” (Luke 12:43). And concerning the same servant: “But if that wicked servant…”—the Lord “divides him into two parts” (Luke 19:21). I ask: will he divide or cut the whole of him? Finally, he will place not the whole, but a part of him, with the hypocrites (Matt. 24:51). For in one body he shows both.

Accordingly, this body must be understood throughout the Scriptures wherever God says that Israel will perish on account of its merit, or calls his inheritance accursed. For the Apostle argues at length in this way, especially in the Epistle to the Romans: whatever is said about the whole body must be understood as referring to a part.

“To Israel,” he says, “he declares: ‘All day long I stretched out my hands to a disobedient people’” (Rom. 10:21). And to show that this was said of a part, he says: “I ask, then, has God rejected his people? Certainly not. For I myself am an Israelite, of the offspring of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew” (Rom. 11:1–2).

And after teaching how this manner of speech should be understood, by the same kind of expression he shows that one body is both good and evil, saying: “According to the Gospel, they are enemies for your sake; but according to election, beloved for the sake of the fathers” (ibid., 28). Are those who are beloved the same as those who are enemies? Or can both descriptions apply in the same respect?

Thus the Lord, throughout all the Scriptures, testifies that the one body of Abraham’s offspring grows, flourishes, and perishes among all the nations.

## RULE III. Concerning the Promises and the Law

Paul is expounded with reference to Romans and Galatians, and to Isaiah, chapter 48.

Divine authority establishes that no one could ever be justified by works of the Law. By that same authority it is most firmly established that there were people who kept the Law and were justified.

[Col. 0022B] It is written: “Whatever things the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become subject to God. For no flesh is justified in his sight by the law. Through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Rom. III, 19–20). Again: “Sin shall not rule over you. For you are not under the law” (Rom. VI, 4). Again: “We too have believed in Christ, so that we might be justified by faith and not by works of the law” (Gal. II, 16). Again: “For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly have come from the law. But Scripture confined all things under sin, so that the promise might be given to those who believe through faith in Jesus Christ” (Gal. III, 21–22).

But someone may say: “From Christ onward, and below, the law does not justify; nevertheless, in its own time it did justify.” The authority of the apostle Peter answers him. When the Gentiles were being compelled by the brethren to submit to the yoke of the law, he said: “Why do you test God by seeking to place upon the neck of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?” (Acts XV, 10). And the apostle Paul says: “When we were in the flesh, the passions of sins that come through the law were at work in our members, so that they might bear fruit for death” (Rom. VII, 5). Yet, in contrast, the same Apostle says: “According to the righteousness that is from the law, I was preserved blameless” (Phil. III, 6).

And if the authority of so great an Apostle were lacking, what could be said against the testimony of the Lord, who says: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John I, 47)? And even if the Lord had not deigned to give this testimony, who would be so sacrilegious, who so lifted up by the swelling of dullness, as to say that Moses and the Prophets—or all the saints—did not practice righteousness, or were not justified [Col. 0022D]? For Scripture says of Zechariah and his wife: “They were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of God without blame” (Luke I, 6). And the Lord did not come to call the righteous, but sinners (Matt. IX, 13).

But how could the law have justified anyone from sin, when it was given for this very purpose: “The law entered in so that sin might increase” (Rom. V, 20)? We must know and hold firmly to this: the seed of Abraham was never at any time cut off, from Isaac down to the present day. The seed of Abraham, however, is not carnal but spiritual; it is not from the law but from the promise. For there is another, carnal seed, which is from the law, from Mount Sinai—“which is Hagar, bearing children into slavery.” The one who was born carnally from the slave woman; “but the one from the free woman is from the promise” (Gal. IV, 23–24).

That there is no seed of Abraham except what is from faith, the Apostle says: “You understand, then, that those who are from faith—these are the sons of Abraham” (Gal. III, 7). And again: “But you, brothers, are sons of the promise according to Isaac” (Gal. IV, 28). Therefore the seed of Abraham is not from the law but from the promise, which continually proceeds from Isaac. If it is established that the seed of Abraham which is from faith exists, it is established that it was never from the law. For it could not be from the law and from faith. Law and faith are different things. For the law is not from faith but from works, as it is written: “The law is not from faith, but, ‘Whoever does these things shall live by them’” (Gal. III, 12).

Abraham, therefore, always had sons by faith, never by the law. For the promise was not made to Abraham or to his seed through the law—that he should be heir of the world—but through the righteousness of faith. For if those who are from the law are heirs, faith is emptied, and the promise is emptied. For the law produces wrath. Therefore, if neither faith nor the promise made to Abraham can be destroyed, it has remained continuously from its beginning. Nor, when the law was given, was it hindered, so that sons of Abraham according to the promise of faith could be begotten.

For the Apostle says that the law, given four hundred and thirty years later, neither harmed nor destroyed the promise: “For if the inheritance is from the law” [Note: [Col. 0023D] “Inheritance”], “it is no longer from the promise. But God granted it to Abraham through the promise” (Gal. III, 18). And elsewhere: “Is the law, then, against the promises of God? Certainly not!” (Ibid., 21). We see that the law does not pertain to the promises, and that the one never collided with the other, but that each maintained its own order [Col. 0023C]. For just as the law never harmed faith, so faith did not destroy the law. As it is written: “Do we then destroy the law through faith? Certainly not; rather, we establish the law” (Rom. III, 31)—that is, we strengthen it. For they strengthen one another.

Therefore the sons of Abraham are not from the law but from faith through the promise. But it must be asked how those who are said not to have been able to be justified by works of the law, although placed under the law and practicing the law, were justified. It must also be asked why, after the promise of faith—which cannot in any way be destroyed—the law was given, although it is not from faith and no one would be justified by its works, because “all who are from the works of the law are under a curse.” For it is written: “Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things written in the book of the law, to do them” [Col. 0023D] (Gal. III, 10).

Finally, the Apostle, anticipating this question, while asserting that the sons of Abraham had always been sons by God’s gift through faith and not through a law of works, answered himself by speaking in the person of another, saying: “What, then, is the law of works?” (Rom. III, 27). That is: If the sons are from faith, why was the law of works given, when the promise would have been sufficient for begetting the sons of Abraham, and they were to be nourished by faith? For “the righteous one lives by faith” (Rom. I, 17; Gal. III, 11; Heb. X, 30).

Before he had asked himself, “What, then, is the law of works?” he had already said that those who could not be justified by faith were to live in this way: “But since no one is justified before God by the law, ‘the righteous one shall live by faith’” (Gal. III, 11). Moreover, he showed that “he lives by faith” had been spoken through the Prophet, so that it might become clear how those who could not fulfill the law would live.

But what is meant by “the righteous one lives by faith” (Hab. II, 4) is less clear. For no one could live as a righteous person while placed under the law unless he had done the works of the law—and all the works; otherwise he would be accursed. God gave the law and said: “You shall not covet” (Exod. XX, 17; Deut. V, 21). Immediately, taking occasion from the commandment, sin produced every form of coveting. For the passions of sins that come through the law must work in the members of the one who is under the law. Therefore it was given “so that sin might abound” (Rom. V, 20), because “the strength of sin is the law.”

But one who has been sold under sin no longer does the good that he wants, but the evil that he does not want; for in his inner person he agrees with the law. Yet he is overcome by another law in his members and is dragged away captive, nor could he ever be freed except by grace alone through faith. It is a great crime of faithlessness not to have recognized the kind of weapons by which the violence of sin could be defeated; conversely, it is a mark of magnificent faith to have sought and perceived them.

A mind is sacrilegious and thinks wrongly about God if, seeing that the law could in no way be fulfilled by human power and that it was prepared for punishment, it does not understand that there is some remedy of life; if it does not understand that the good God, who knew that the law could not be fulfilled, would not have left another path to life; and that he would not have closed on every side the ways of life against human beings whom he had made for life.

[Col. 0024C] Faith did not tolerate or admit this. But when humanity was oppressed by the weakness of the flesh and the power of sin, God gave illumination. Knowing that the Lord is good and just, and that he had not closed the depths of his compassion against the works of his hands, faith understood that there was a path to life and perceived a remedy for fulfilling the law.

For when God said, “You shall not covet,” he did not reveal how this could come about; rather, he truly and decisively said, “You shall not covet,” since he left it to be discovered. For if he had commanded that the result be sought from him, he would have destroyed both law and faith. Why would he give the law if he promised that the law would be fulfilled in all its works? Or what would be left for faith if, by promising assistance, he anticipated faith?

But now, in the goodness of faith, he gave the law, the minister of death, so that those who love life might see life through faith, and the righteous might live by faith—those who believed that the work of the law could be accomplished not by their own power but by God’s gift. For the law cannot be fulfilled by the flesh; and when it has not been fulfilled, it punishes. What hope, then, does a person have of fulfilling the law and escaping death, except for the help and mercy of God, which faith discovers?

“The flesh is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. VIII, 7, 9). He shows that the Spirit of God and of Christ is one and the same. He further shows that whoever has the Spirit of God is not in the flesh.

Therefore, if the Spirit of God and of Christ is one, the prophets and saints, because they had the Spirit of God, had the Spirit of Christ. If they had the Spirit of God, they were not in the flesh, and they fulfilled the law, because the flesh is hostile to God and is not subject to his law.

Whoever therefore takes refuge in God receives the Spirit of God. Once he has received it, the flesh is put to death; and when the flesh has been put to death, the spiritual person, freed from the law because the law is not laid down for the righteous, can fulfill the law. And again: “If you are led by the Spirit of God, you are not under the law” (Gal. V, 18).

It is therefore clear that our fathers, who had the Spirit of God, were not under the law. As long as a person is in the flesh—that is, does not have the Spirit of God—the law rules over him. But if he gives himself over to grace, he dies to the law, and the law of the Spirit works in him, while the flesh dies, for the flesh cannot be subject to the law of God.

What was taking place then is also taking place now. For the prohibition of coveting has not ceased because we are not under the law; nor has it instead increased. But through faith we hasten toward the grace that has been revealed, taught by the Lord to ask for the work of the law from his mercy and to say: “Your will be done,” and, “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. VI, 10, 13).

But they, through the same faith, were compelled toward what had not yet been revealed, by fear of the death that they saw threatened by the sword prepared by the law, its minister. The law was given until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made, and until he should proclaim faith.

Previously, the law compelled people toward faith, as though faith could not be expressed without the law, in order to seek the grace of God, because sin had no power. Once the law had been given, however, the passions that come through the law worked in our members, pressing us toward sin, so that by necessity they might be driven toward faith, which would implore the grace of God for help in endurance.

We endured the custody of a prison, with the law threatening death and enclosing us on every side with an invincible wall. Its enclosure had only one entrance: grace. Faith stood guard at this entrance, so that no one might escape that prison unless faith opened it; and whoever did not knock at this door would die within the confines of the law.

We endured the law as a pedagogue who compelled us to devote ourselves to faith, who compelled us toward Christ. For the Apostle says that the law was given for this reason: to enclose us in its custody for the faith that was destined to be revealed in Christ, who is the end of the law, through whom all those lived who sought the faith of God’s grace.

“Before faith came,” he says, “we were kept under the law, confined for the faith that was destined to be revealed.” Therefore the law was our pedagogue toward Christ (Gal. III, 24), so that we might be justified by faith. The law, I say, [Note: [Col. 0025D] “Of faith”] was the demonstrator of faith.

But someone may say: If the law was given for the benefit of faith, why was it not given from the beginning of the seed of Abraham, since faith was perpetual? Indeed, it was perpetual. Faith was perpetual, as the mother of the sons of Abraham. The law too was perpetual, through the discernment of good and evil.

But after the promise of the sons of Abraham, when they had multiplied according to the flesh, the seed of Abraham that is not from faith also had to be multiplied. This multiplication could not take place without the assistance of the multiplied law, by which the multitude might, as has already been said, be led toward faith that had not yet been revealed, if necessary.

Thus, by God’s providence, the holy seed was increased and governed, so that through the severity and fear of the law many might be compelled toward faith, and the seed might be supported until the revelation of faith: “The law entered in so that sin might be multiplied.” “Where sin was multiplied,” he says, “grace abounded beyond measure” (Rom. V, 20).

He did not say that grace was born, but that it abounded beyond measure. From the beginning it was given to those fleeing the burdens and domination of the law. It abounded when the law was multiplied, but it overflowed upon all flesh when it was revealed in Christ.

When he came to restore the things in heaven and the things on earth, he proclaimed faith to those who were near and to those who were far away (Isa. LVII, 19; Eph. II, 17)—that is, to the sinners of Israel and to the Gentiles. For the righteous of Israel, who were from faith, were called to the same faith. The same Spirit, the same faith, and the same grace were always given through Christ.

At his coming he granted their fullness to every nation, removing the veil of the law. In manner, not in kind, they differed from the things that were to come. For the seed of Abraham was never otherwise. And if anyone was justified apart from faith, he was not a son of Abraham. For he cannot be called a son of Abraham if he was justified by the law and not, like Abraham, by faith.

The Apostle teaches that the Church has passed from the same image of grace and Spirit into the same image, saying: “We all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of God, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory” (II Cor. III, 18).

He also says that there was glory before the Lord’s passion, and denies that it could have been elicited—that is, expressed, brought forth, or produced—from the law. Hence it is clear that it was from faith.

“Where, then,” he says, “is boasting? It has been excluded. By what law? By that of works? No, but by the law of faith” (Rom. III, 27–28). For what does Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. IV, 3).

We have passed from one glory into the same glory, and that glory was not from the law. If it was from works, it possesses glory, but not before God. For it is impossible to possess any glory without the grace of God. There is one glory, and it has always existed in one and the same manner.

No one has conquered except the one to whom God has granted victory. This is not from the law but from the one who has done it. God makes our adversary weak for faith. Therefore, “Whoever boasts, let him boast in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31).

For if what we conquer is not ours, it is not from works but from faith. Therefore there is nothing of which we may boast as coming from ourselves. For we have nothing that we have not received. If we exist, we exist from God, so that the greatness of the power may be God’s and not ours.

Our entire work is faith. To the extent that faith exists in us, to that extent God works in us. Solomon glorifies God in this matter, saying that continence was not from human beings but was God’s gift: “When I knew that I could not otherwise be continent unless God gave it, and that this itself was wisdom—to know whose gift it was—I approached the Lord and prayed” (Wis. VIII, 21).

Solomon’s judgment must be believed: all who knew that the work of the law had to be fulfilled by God, so that they might have something in which to glory, were justified not by works but by the grace of God. The Apostle says: “So that no flesh might boast in the presence of God” (I Cor. I, 29).

The wicked have no ground for boasting because they did not know God; the righteous have none because they are not their own work but God’s. “God chose,” he says, “the useless and despised things, the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are, so that no flesh might boast in the presence of God. But from him you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, so that, as it is written: ‘Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord’” (Ibid., 28–30).

And again: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves” [Col. 0027B] (Eph. II, 8). “It is God’s gift, not from works, so that no one may boast; for we are his workmanship, created in Christ.”

Thus no flesh can ever be justified by the law—that is, by works—so that every righteous person might have glory from God. There is another reason why no one should boast in God’s presence: God works in his own people in such a way that there is something for him to forgive. For “no one is clean from defilement, not even if his life is but one day” (Job XIV, 4).

David also says: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLII, 2). And Solomon says at the dedication of the temple: “There is no person who has not sinned” (III Kings VIII, 46). And again: “Against you alone have I sinned” (Ps. L, 6).

For who will boast that he has a pure heart? Or who will boast that he is clean from sin? It was not enough to speak of a pure heart—that is, freedom from thoughts—unless no one also boasted that he was clean from sin.

Every victory is granted not from works but by God’s compassion, as it is written: “He crowns you with compassion and mercy” (Ps. CIV, 4). And the mother of the martyrs says to her son: “May I receive you with your brothers through that compassion” (II Macc. VII, 29).

The righteous fulfilled God’s will by desire and effort. They strive and long to serve God, though not under the law. If the law had justified them, all the righteous would have possessed one and the same merit, because it demands equal observance from everyone; otherwise it would produce a curse.

But if merit differed, then each received as much of God’s grace and mercy as he believed would be given to him, transformed from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of God—that is, from the same into the same.

For it is the same thing that faith was given after Christ as that the Holy Spirit was given: all the prophets and righteous persons always lived by the same Spirit. They could not live in any other way than by the Spirit of faith.

“For all who were under the law were killed. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (II Cor. III, 6). Yet the Lord says of this same Spirit: “Unless I go away, he will not come” (John XVI, 7), even though he had already given the same Spirit to the Apostles.

But the Apostle says that the same Spirit existed among the ancients: “Having the same Spirit of faith, as it is written: ‘I believed, and therefore I spoke’” (II Cor. IV, 13). He said that they had the same Spirit of faith—the same Spirit as the one who said, “I believed, and therefore I spoke” (Ps. CXV, 1)—and he confirms this by saying: “We also believe, and therefore we speak.”

By saying, “We also,” he shows that they too believed by the same Spirit of faith. Hence it is clear that the righteous always possessed these things not by the law but by the Spirit of faith.

Whatever comes through the Lord is fullness, of which a part came through him. It is like a child who, although he possesses nothing less than a man, is nevertheless not a man; through growth—not of new members but of the same members—he comes into the fullness of the body and becomes mature, while remaining the same one who had been a child.

In truth, the Holy Spirit was not in everyone before the Lord’s passion, but in those who believed in him while he was present, so that, once he had conquered and perfected all things, those marked by him might be perfected.

For the righteous whom he found here had the Holy Spirit, such as Simeon, Nathanael, Zechariah, Elizabeth, and Anna, the widow, daughter of Phanuel.

The promise is separate from the law; since they are different, they cannot be mixed together. It is not the condition that weakens the promise. Yet we are compelled to speak of things that we cannot hear without the fire of grief.

Some say—for they do not understand the firmness of the promises or the transgression that comes from the law—that God indeed promised Abraham all the nations, but only provided that they preserved the law, while preserving free choice. And if it is useful to expose the dangers of the ignorance of certain righteous people for the sake of salvation, nevertheless, when speaking about almighty God, we must moderate what we say, lest, by reckoning things that should be silent among things to be remembered, we cause foreign words—even if they are not our own—to be heard from our mouth.

Therefore, speaking with trembling, let us leave each person to consider his own dangers. It is clear that God foreknew whether those whom he promised to Abraham would come to be through free choice, or would not. There are only two possibilities: if they would come to be, the question is settled; if they would not, the faithful God would not have promised them.

Or if this had been established with God—that he would give those who had been promised only if they wished to be the promised people—then surely Abraham, his servant and believer, would have said that God, because he is able to do what he has promised, was not deceiving him.

That promise, however, is one that involves no condition. Otherwise the promise is not firm and faith is not complete. For what would remain stable in God’s promise or in Abraham’s faith if what was promised and believed depended upon the will of those who were promised? Thus God promised what belonged to another, and Abraham believed rashly.

Why, moreover, was the promise itself later made a debt, when God said: “All the nations of the earth shall be blessed in you, because you heard my voice and did not spare your beloved son for my sake” (Gen. XXII, 18)?

Nor does God confirm himself a debtor only because of those matters by which it is easy to raise an accusation against Abraham’s merit and free choice. Even after Abraham’s death, he confirms himself to be his debtor and says that, for Abraham’s sake, he will do what he was promising to his son:

“I will be with you and bless you. For I will give this land to you and to your seed, and I will establish my oath which I swore to Abraham your father. I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven, and I will give to you and to your seed all the nations of the earth, because Abraham your father heard my voice” (Gen. XXVI, 3–5).

Behold, Abraham’s debt has been confirmed. For he could not, through free choice, lose after death what he had merited while alive. But the nations did not wish to believe.

What will Abraham do, to whom the debt is owed? How will he receive the debt of his faith and testing, since he had been secure in owing it to God? If he had been told, “I will give what I promised and repay what I swore” (Ibid., 4), but only if the nations should wish to believe, he would not have believed it; rather, he would have awaited a chance occurrence.

If a condition is necessary, it should belong to the laborer, not to the wages. For a laborer can wish to receive or not to receive; wages, however, are not a matter of being paid or not being paid. For all the nations were given to Abraham as the wages of his faith, just as God says: “Your reward is very great” (Gen. XV, 1).

He did not promise because they would become this people, but because they were going to become it. For it was not because of Abraham’s faith that it pleased God that all the nations should be saved; he possessed them not only before Abraham’s faith but before the foundation of the world.

But he sought a faithful person to whom he might give what had been destined to be, and from whom there might be the one for whom he had determined that it would come to pass. Abraham therefore did not merit that they should exist who were destined to exist, whom God had chosen and whom he had foreseen would be conformed to the image of his Son.

In Genesis, Scripture testifies that all the nations were promised to Abraham through God’s foreknowledge, saying: “Abraham shall surely become, and shall become, a great and numerous nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him” (Gen. XXVI, 16).

He also knew that Abraham would instruct his sons and his household after him to keep the ways of the Lord, to practice righteousness and judgment, so that God might bring upon Abraham everything that he had spoken to him.

Yet we also find conditions, such as: “If you will hear me and be willing.” Where are God’s foreknowledge and the firmness of the promise in conditions of this kind? The Apostle also said that the promise was given from faith and not from the law so that the promise might be firm (Rom. IV, 16).

“The law,” he says, “produces wrath; but where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Ibid., 15). Therefore it is from faith, so that, according to grace, the promise might be firm for all the seed.

Rightly he says, “so that the promise might be firm.” For he added that it is not firm under a condition. It is indeed quite foolish to believe that what is said of a divided body applies to the whole body.

Far be it from God to say to those whom he knew would hear him—those whom, before he made them, he knew would persevere in the image of God, and whom he also promised—“If you will hear me” [Col. 0029D].

The condition—that is, the law—was given only to the ungodly and sinners, so that they might either take refuge in grace or be punished more justly if they made it void.

Why give the law to the righteous, for whom the law was not established; who, with God favorable to them, fulfill the law without the law; who serve God; who live according to the image and likeness of God and Christ; who are good willingly?

The one who is under the law, through fear of death, is not such a person. He is merciful neither, and he is not the image of God. He dislikes the law but fears its vengeance, and he cannot fulfill it; he thinks it must be done not by desire but by necessity.

He must be handed over to his own will, so that his will may certainly receive its reward, because he has not united his soul to the will of God. He dislikes what God willed. For the person who is good by necessity is evil by will.

The law is an impediment to the deed, not to the will. The person who would pursue evil if there were no punishment for evil is not joined to God. Nor does the one who groans because he is not doing his own will do the will of God.

He is not merciful who fears being cruel. He is under the law; he is a slave. He does not hate theft but fears the punishment. Yet he must steal when persuaded and overcome—he who is carnal, under the power of sin, and does not have the Spirit of God.

But whoever loves the good is the image of God, lives by the faith of the Lord, and is an heir. He is no longer the son of the slave woman (Gal. IV, 30–31), who received the law in fear, but of the free woman, according to Isaac, who did not receive the spirit of slavery in fear, but the adoption of sons, crying, “Abba, Father” (Rom. VIII, 15).

Whoever loves God does not fear in a servile manner. It is written that servile fear is accompanied by hatred of discipline, whereas sons approach with honor toward their father.

It is one thing to fear because of the law, and another to tremble out of reverence for the fearful majesty of God. People of this kind are like their Father, who is in heaven: when reminded and taught, they love the good and hate evil.

They are without the law; they are free; they themselves are the ones promised. It is not said to them, “If you will hear me”: for can he hear? Would this apply to one whom God had not yet foreseen as hearing?

The righteous, whom God foreknew (Ibid., 29), are in this law. It is said to them also, “If you will hear me,” but for another reason—not because they are able not to hear, but so that they may always be attentive to their salvation and certain of their outcome.

For no one is secure that he belongs to the number of those foreknown, since the Apostle says: “Lest I myself should become disqualified” (I Cor. IX, 27). Therefore this law does not produce wrath for them, but is an exercise of faith by which they continually seek God’s grace, laboring so that what God foresaw in them may be perfected and so that they may have been destined for life through free choice.

Otherwise it is impossible not to hear the one whom God foresaw would hear, promised, and swore to.

The Lord declares in the Gospel to which part the law properly applies, although it is given to one body, when he says to the Apostles: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them. I do not speak of all of you. I know whom I have chosen” (John XIII, 17–18).

This is a strikingly concise statement showing one body and making a separation. For if he had said, “I do not speak of all of you,” or, “I do not speak of all,” he would not have shown one body. But by saying, “I do not speak of all,” he shows that although he did not speak of all, he nevertheless spoke of those others.

It is as though someone were to say, “I did not speak of your whole self”: two bodies are mixed together, as though they were one, and in common one body is praised or rebuked.

Thus in Exodus, when someone contrary to the prohibition went out on the Sabbath to gather manna, God said to Moses: “How long will you refuse to hear my law?” (Exod. XVI, 26), although Moses had always heard it.

What shall we say of that law which plainly seems contrary to the promise? It is written in Isaiah: “If you had listened to me, Israel, your number would have been like the sand of the sea” (Isa. XLVIII, 18).

Behold, Israel is rebuked because through its own fault it did not become like the sand of the sea. It remains to understand that if it does not always listen, it will always remain few in number.

And where is the firmness of the promises? This happens because we first want to understand before believing, and to subject faith to reason. But if we believe that everything will happen precisely as God swore, faith will provide the explanation.

How faithless it is to seek by reason, when we understand that the firmness of the promises is greater than the weakness we suppose! For this saying, “If Israel had listened,” recalls the righteousness of God and confirms the promises: by God’s arrangement some were made for death and others for life.

Therefore he said to those who were present, “If you had listened to me,” so that it might become clear that he promised those who would be like the sand because he foresaw that they would listen.

Before the Lord Christ, when this was said, was the seed of Abraham ever like the sand of the sea? This is easy to prove. First, because he promised this multitude in Christ: “Not to seeds, as of many, but as of one, ‘and to your seed,’ which is Christ” (Gal. III, 16).

Next, because he promised all the nations, which could not happen before Christ. And if, before the Lord, the number of the sons of Israel was like the sand of the sea, it was so together with false brothers who are not sons of Abraham.

For not everyone who is from Abraham is therefore a son of Abraham; nor, because someone is Israel, is he therefore all Israel. The Apostle, when he wished to become anathema for Israel (Rom. IX, 3), whose were the adoption and the covenants, showed that they were not sons of the kind in question, but that he grieved out of affection for his carnal kinship because they did not belong to that number.

It was not that God’s promise had failed. He says: “Yet the word of God has not failed. For not all who are from Israel are Israel, nor, because they are the seed of Abraham, are they all sons; but, ‘In Isaac shall your seed be called’—that is, those who are children of the flesh are not the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as seed” (Ibid., 6–8).

Therefore, in the ancient multitude there was no seed of Abraham except among those who, according to Isaac, were sons of faith and of the promise.

He also introduces this example: “If the number of the sons of Israel should be like the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved”—that is, a small number (Isa. X, 12; Hos. I, 10). And: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have been like Sodom” (Isa. I, 9).

That remnant itself was the seed of Abraham, so that all Judea would not be like Sodom.

Again, when he asserted that God had never abandoned his inheritance, but that just as at the Lord’s coming part of Israel was saved, so it had always been, he says: “What does the divine response say? ‘I have kept for myself seven thousand living men who have not bent the knee before Baal’” (III Kings XVIII, 19; Rom. XI, 4).

“So also at the present time a remnant has been saved according to election.” By saying, “at the present time,” he shows that this had also previously happened in Israel, so that a remnant—that is, a small number—might be saved.

But if neither faith nor reason persuades us that the one who had been promised was the one of whom it was said, “If you had listened to me, Israel, your number would have been like the sand of the sea” (Isa. XLVIII, 18), then Jacob, who was given before he was born, was afterward rejected through free choice.

As Hosea says: “The Lord has a lawsuit against Judah, to punish Jacob; he will repay him according to his ways and according to his deeds” (Hos. XII, 2), because “in the womb he supplanted his brother, and in his struggles he prevailed with God; he prevailed with the angel and became strong” (Gen. XXV, 23; Rom. IX, 10).

But if it is established that the beloved was perfected in Jacob, then the one who prevailed with God in his struggles is not identical with the supplanter; rather, there are two in one body. For this is a figure of the twofold seed of Abraham—that is, of two peoples struggling in the one womb of Mother Church.

One is beloved according to election, through foreknowledge; the other is wicked through the election of his own will. Jacob and Esau are in one body, from one seed. But the fact that two were plainly brought forth is a disclosure of two peoples.

And lest anyone think that the two peoples would be so plainly separated, it was shown that both would be in one body in Jacob, who was both called beloved and represented as the supplanter of his brother.

Thus quantity was expressed in the two, not the quality of their separation. In any case, the two who were separated were shown to be destined to exist in one before they were divided.

And Isaac said: “Your brother came with deceit and took your blessing” (Gen. XXVII, 35). Unless this is a mystical form of speech, briefly showing two in one body, is it not contrary to reason that he should have deceitfully received a blessing intended for his neighbor, when Scripture says: “The one who has not sworn deceitfully to his neighbor shall receive blessing from the Lord” (Ps. XXIII, 4)?

Jacob—that is, the Church—has never come to the blessing without deceit accompanying him, that is, false brothers. But because innocence and deceit come together to the blessing, they are not blessed together; for “let the one who can receive it receive it” (Matt. XIX, 12), and one seed produces according to the quality of the soil.

It is not contrary to this that the evil seems to have supplanted his brother, because he did not say, “In the womb he supplanted Esau,” but “his brother.” Esau, everywhere, is a sign and name of the wicked; Jacob, however, belongs to both groups.

The reason is that the evil part pretends to be Jacob—and certainly under one name—whereas the good part cannot pretend to be Esau. The former name belongs only to the wicked; the latter is divided between both.

In any case, with respect to free choice, neither is all Jacob good nor all Esau evil; rather, each contains both. Thus the seed was shown to be divided from Abraham.

One was born from the slave woman as a figure (Gal. IV, 22), so that it might also be shown that slaves would arise from Abraham, and he departed with his mother.

After he had departed, what is from the free woman was found in the seed of the other: what is from Israel, which received the law on Mount Sinai, which is Hagar, bearing children into slavery.
