There, in the same people, according to Isaac, many sons of the promise were begotten from the free woman—that is, many holy and faithful people.

Thus, after the figures of Israel and Esau had been separated from the believers, everything subsequently came forth in one people. There, from
From the beginning, both Testaments are represented by Hagar and Isaac; but, according to the time, one has lain hidden under the name of the other [Col. 0033A] and continues to lie hidden, because even when the new has been revealed, the old does not cease from begetting. Therefore he did not say, “Hagar, who begets into slavery.” Both, however, must grow together until the harvest.

Just as at that time the new lay hidden under the profession of the Old Testament—that is, grace, which, according to Isaac, would beget from the free woman the children of the promise, which has been revealed in Christ—so now also, while the new prevails, there are not lacking children of slavery, with Hagar begetting them; this will be revealed in Christ.

The Apostle confirms that what was then taking place among the brothers is also now taking place, saying: “But you, brothers, are children of the promise according to Isaac. But just as then the one born according to the flesh persecuted the spiritual one, so also now” (ibid. 28–29). And he necessarily added: “But what does Scripture say? ‘Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman’” [Col. 0033B] (ibid. 30).

What he said—“Just as then he persecuted, so also now”—is not empty. For the Apostle interpreted what “persecuted” means. Scripture says: “Ishmael was playing with Isaac” (Gen. XXI, 9). Were the brothers who proclaimed circumcisions to the Galatians pursuing them openly, rather than through play—that is, without any indication of persecution? Just as, therefore, he called the persecutor by reference to the kind of play, so too he referred to these men who separate the children of God from Christ, as though for the sake of a common benefit—that is, the discipline of the law—and who serve as sons to their mother Hagar.

For there is no other reason why the sons of the devil should creep in to test our freedom, pretend to be brothers, and play in our Paradise as though they were sons of God, except that they glory in the subjugated freedom of the children of God [Col. 0033C]. They will bear judgment, whatever kind they may be, who persecuted every holy person, who killed the prophets, who have always resisted the Holy Spirit: enemies of the cross of Christ, denying Christ in the flesh while they hate his members; the body of sin, the sons of destruction, the ministry of wickedness. They come according to the working of Satan, with every power, signs, and wonders, and with spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. The Lord Christ—whom they persecute in the flesh—will kill them with the breath of his mouth and destroy them by the manifestation of his coming.

For it is time for these things to be spoken, not in ministries, but openly, with the departure drawing near—that is, the revelation of the man of sin—as Lot departs from Sodom. [Note: Col. 0033D: “Mysteries” (*mysteriis*) in place of “ministries” (*ministeriis*).]

## RULE IV. On Species and Genus

Light adduced from Ezekiel, chapters XXVII, XXXII, XXXVI, and XXXVII; Isaiah XIII and XXIV; Jeremiah XXV.

[Col. 0033D]

We speak of figure and genus, not according to the rhetorical power of human wisdom—a power that the one who possessed it more than all others did not employ, lest he should make the cross of Christ empty, if it had needed the aid and adornment of eloquence, as falsehood does. Rather, we speak according to the mysteries of heavenly wisdom, under the instruction of the Holy Spirit. He who established faith as the price of the mystery of truth narrated the genus in the species, concealing it, so that he might take up in the old Jerusalem the whole Church that now exists throughout the world, or, in one member, the whole body, as in Solomon.

But this is no less hidden than the other matters that are concealed not only by the form of the wording but also by manifold narration. Therefore, having called upon God’s grace for assistance, we must labor so that the Spirit may multiply the approaches to reading, and so that the subtle language—which, as an impediment to understanding, inserts the genus into the figure or the figure into the genus—may be recognized with ease, lest the genus be mistaken for the figure. For while he narrates the figure, he passes into the genus in such a way that the transition does not immediately become clear; rather, as he passes over, he places words that apply to both, until little by little he exceeds the bounds of the figure and clarifies the transition, when the things that had begun from the figure fit only the genus. In the same way, he leaves the genus and returns to the figure.

Sometimes, however, he returns from the species to the genus not in the manner stated above. Sometimes he passes over in the manner stated above and returns clearly, with a similar variation of order; or he ends the narration either from species to genus or from genus to species. Sometimes he returns from one to the other more than once, and the whole narration neither exceeds the species nor passes beyond the genus, fitting both. This variety of transition and order requires faith that seeks the grace of God.

Thus the Lord speaks through Ezekiel and joins to the kings who had been captured and dispersed from Jerusalem the coming of the nations; and in the land that our fathers possessed he expresses the world. For the seven nations promised to Abraham are a figure of all the nations.

“The word of the Lord came to me,” he says, “saying: Son of man, the house of Israel dwelt in the land and polluted it by its way and by its idols and sins; their way before my face became like the uncleanness of a menstruating woman. And I poured out my anger upon them, and scattered them among the nations into which they entered, and there they polluted my holy name, while they themselves were saying, ‘These are the people of the Lord, and they have gone out from his land.’ And I spared them for the sake of your holy name, which the house of Israel had polluted among the nations into which they had entered.

“Therefore say to the house of Israel: Thus says the Lord: It is not for your sake that I act, O house of Israel, but for the sake of my holy name, which you have polluted among the nations into whose midst you entered.” Here he begins to join the genus:

“And I will sanctify my great, holy name, which has been polluted among the nations, which you have polluted in their midst; and the nations shall know that I am the Lord, when I am sanctified in you before their eyes. And I will take you from the nations, and gather you from all the lands, and bring you into your own land.”

He plainly exceeds the species:

“And I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your idols; and I will cleanse you. And I will give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. And I will take away the heart of stone from your flesh, and give you a heart of flesh. And I will put my spirit within you, and I will make you walk in my statutes, and observe my judgments, and perform them. And you shall dwell in the land that I gave to your fathers. And you shall be my people, and I shall be your God; and I will cleanse you from all your uncleannesses” (Ezek. XXXVI, 17–28).

He touches upon the species, yet does not leave the genus:

“And I will call for the grain, and multiply it, and I will not bring famine upon you. And I will multiply the fruit of the tree and the produce of the field, so that you may no longer receive the reproach of famine among the nations. And you shall remember your most evil ways and your thoughts that were not good, and you shall hate them before their eyes because of your iniquities and your abominations. It is not for your sake that I act, says the Lord. Let it be known to you; be ashamed and turn back from your ways, O house of Israel.

“Thus says Adonai the Lord: On the day when I cleanse you from all your iniquities, I will cause the cities to be inhabited; and the land of Judah, which had been laid waste by wars and destroyed before the eyes of every passerby, shall be cultivated. And they will say, ‘That land which had been destroyed has become like a garden of delights; and the cities that were deserted, destroyed, and demolished are fortified and inhabited.’ And the nations, all those that are left around you, shall know that I am the Lord. I have built up the demolished places and planted the destroyed ones, because I, the Lord, have spoken and acted” (ibid. 29–38).

The Apostle likewise interprets the entrance of the nations as having been promised in the entrance of Jacob, saying: “Until the fullness of the nations enters, and thus all Israel will be saved, as it is written: He will come from Zion, the one who delivers and removes ungodliness from Jacob” (Rom. XI, 25–26). And by the same kind of expression he returns to the figure, saying: “According to the Gospel, indeed, they are enemies for your sake” [Rom. XI, 28].

Likewise, in Ezekiel he begins with the species, which also applies to the genus, and ends with the genus alone, showing that the land of the fathers is the possession of the world:

“Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will take the whole house of Israel from the midst of the nations into which they entered, and I will gather them from all those who are around them, and bring them into the land of Israel, and there will be one ruler over them. They shall no longer be two nations, nor shall they be divided any longer into two kingdoms, so that they may not again be defiled by their idols. And I will deliver them from all their iniquities, in which they sinned, and I will cleanse them; and they shall be my people, and I, the Lord, will be their God” (Ezek. XXXVII, 21, 23).

He plainly passes into the genus:

“And my servant David shall be ruler in their midst, one shepherd over all. They shall walk in my commandments, observe my judgments, and perform them. And they shall dwell in their own land, which I gave to my servant Jacob, where their fathers dwelt; and they themselves shall dwell in it, and David my servant shall be their ruler forever.

“And I will establish for them a covenant of peace, and it shall be an everlasting covenant with them. And I will place my sanctuaries in their midst forever. My dwelling shall be among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And the nations shall know that I am the Lord who sanctifies them, while my sanctuaries are in their midst, says the Lord” (ibid. 24–28).

There too he inserts the coming of the nations into Israel’s departure from dispersion.

[Col. 0036A]

It is made clear that the wilderness was a species of the deserted people, in which the Church now exists; and that those same wicked people, although they are recalled from the nations together with God’s people into the land of Israel, nevertheless do not belong in the land:

“As I live, says the Lord, if I answer you; and if this has entered your heart, it shall not be as you say: ‘We shall be like the nations and like the tribes of the earth, so that we may serve wood and stone.’ As I live, says the Lord, surely I will rule over you with a strong hand and an exalted arm, and with wrath poured out; I will bring you out from the peoples and gather you from the regions in which you were scattered, with a strong hand and an exalted arm and wrath poured out; and I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face.

“Just as I entered into judgment with your fathers in the wilderness of the land of Egypt, so I will judge you, says the Lord, and bring you under my rod, and bring you into the number [or: into the bonds] of the covenant, and I will select from among you the wicked and the deserters. For I will bring them out from the land of their sojourning, but they shall not enter the land of Israel; and you shall know that I am the Lord” (Ezek. XX, 31, 38).

[Note: [Col. 0035D] In the Vulgate, in Ezekiel XX, 37: “into the bonds of the covenant.”]

Likewise, God promises that captivity abundance upon the mountains of Israel and the multiplication of peoples until the end:

“Because,” he says, “they have taken possession of your land for themselves, dishonoring souls with delight, and have utterly destroyed it as a desolation; therefore prophesy over the land of Israel, and say to the mountains and hills, the ravines and the woods: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I have spoken in my zeal and in my wrath, because you bear the reproach of the nations. Behold, I will raise my hand against the nations that are around you. They shall receive their injury. But you, mountains of Israel, my people, who are drawing near to come, shall eat your grape and your fruit. For behold, I am for you, and you shall be cultivated and sown; and I will multiply upon you the whole house of Israel to the end. The cities shall be inhabited, and the places that were desolate shall be rebuilt” (Ezek. XXXVI, 5, 10).

Likewise, there, as though in the final resurrection, the first is signified:

“He spoke to me,” he says, “saying: Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel. They themselves say: ‘Our bones have become dry; our hope has perished; we have expired.’ Therefore prophesy and say: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will open your tombs, and bring you out of your tombs, and bring you into the land of Israel. And you shall know that I am the Lord, when I open your graves and bring my people out of their tombs. And I will put my spirit within you, and you shall live; and I will place you upon your own land, and you shall know that I am the Lord” (Ezek. XXXVII, 11–14).

Is it not clear that, when we have risen, we shall then know the Lord, and not now, when we rise through baptism? Or will the dead be able to say, “Our bones have become dry” (ibid. 11), so that we should rightly believe that this was promised to the dead?

For God has disclosed what the mystery means, so that it would not remain ambiguous. We believe that no Christian doubts the final resurrection of the flesh. And the Lord, according to John, reveals these resurrections, saying:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life and will not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life. Amen, amen, I say to you: the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live. For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself. And he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John V, 24–27).

He joins to this the final resurrection:

“Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, while those who have done evil will come forth to the resurrection of judgment” (ibid. 28–29).

First he said that the dead who hear will live. Second, that all who are in the tombs will come forth.

[Col. 0037B]

Likewise, that the whole body is signified in one man, God promises in the Book of Kings to David, speaking of Solomon:

“I will raise up his kingdom; he himself will build me a house” (2 Kings VII, 15).

These things agree; but it exceeds the literal sense when it says: “And I will establish his throne forever.” Likewise, in both respects: “I will be his father, and he will be my son. And if his iniquity comes to pass, I will rebuke him with the rod of men and with the scourges of the sons of men; but I will not take my mercy away from him, as I took it away from those from whom I took it away before me, and his house shall become faithful.” Again it exceeds the literal sense: “And his kingdom shall be forever before me, and his house shall become faithful.” Again it exceeds the literal sense: “And his kingdom shall be forever in my sight, and his throne shall be established [Col. 0037C] forever” (ibid., 13, 16).

Now, although what appears in the literal sense to promise Christ’s throne forever, it promises the throne of the Son of Man, and thus the Body of Christ, that is, the Church. For God did not promise Christ that he would reign on David’s account; he had promised him this glory before the foundation of the world. And through Isaiah God says this to Christ: “It will be a great thing for you to be called my servant, to establish the tribes of Jacob, and to turn back Israel’s dispersion. Behold, I have appointed you as a covenant of the race, as a light to the nations, so that you may be for salvation to the end of the earth” (Isa. XLIX, 6).

What is greater than for the Son of God to be called “my servant” and to turn back Israel’s dispersion—or than Israel itself, and heaven and earth, and the visible and invisible things in them, having been made through him? Yet he said that it was great for the one who was mingled with the Son of God from David’s seed. For the whole promise to Abraham and David is that their seed would show mercy to the one to whom all things belong, and would be his fellow-heir forever—not that Christ would reign because of them, since he is the king of all, appointed by the Father.

What shall we say about Solomon? Is he with God, or was he rejected after his idolatry? If we say that he is with God, we shall promise impunity to idol-worshipers. For Scripture does not say that Solomon repented or recovered wisdom. But if we say that he was rejected, God’s word confronts us, saying that he would not even take the earthly kingdom away from Solomon because of David, as it is written in the Book of Kings:

“I will surely tear your kingdom from your hand and give it to your servant. But in your days I will not do this, for the sake of David your father. From the hand of your son I will take it. Yet I will not take away the whole kingdom; I will give one scepter to your son, for the sake of David my servant and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city which I chose” (III Kings XI, 11, 14) [Col. 0038A].

For what benefit would David gain if, because of him, his son were to obtain the earthly kingdom while losing the heavenly one? This makes it clear that Solomon is with God: the earthly kingdom was not taken away from him because of David, as he had also said: “I will rebuke his sins with the rod of men, but I will not take my mercy away from him” (II Kings VII, 14).

But if he was neither rejected, nor do idol-worshipers possess the kingdom of God, it is clear that Solomon was a figure of the divided Church—one whose breadth of heart and wisdom were like the sand of the sea, yet whose idolatry was dreadful. “I will surely tear your kingdom from your hand,” he says, “but in your days I will not do it. From the hand of your son I will take it.” The repeated form, “I will surely tear,” indicates continuous action, just as “blessing I will bless” and “multiplying I will multiply your seed.” For he shows that Solomon would always exist in the son, that is, in his descendants: in the later generations of Solomon God does not take away the kingdom, according to the promises made to the fathers, but corrects it forever, so that he may continually take it away on account of Solomon’s idolatry, while he persists in his sin. Otherwise, how does he tear or not tear the kingdom from Solomon’s hand, if Solomon does not now exist in his sons as either good or evil? [Col. 0038B]

But when he says, “Yet I will not take away the whole kingdom,” he returns to the literal sense, beginning another figure in Solomon’s son and servant.

Likewise, in Joshua, the Lord speaks in such a way as to show what the future Body would be in one man; but in this passage only the evil is in view. “The people sinned,” he says, “and transgressed the covenant which I established with them; they stole from the devoted things and put them in their own vessels” (Josh. VIII, 11)—although only Achar of the tribe of Judah had done this. Understanding that the Body would always be future, Joshua said this when he killed him: “May God destroy you as he has done today” (ibid., 25).

But it is much more necessary to know that all the cities of Israel and of the nations, or the provinces addressed by Scripture, or in which it reports something having occurred, are figures of the Church. Some signify only an evil part, some a good part, and some both. And if there are passages that also appear to apply to the nations outside, nevertheless everything hostile is brought together in the part that is within, just as, when Israel is captive, the return of the nations to God is promised.

For it is impossible for the Law to speak to one who is not in the Law—to speak about him but not to him personally. And whenever it addresses foreigners somewhere without this particular occasion, they must in every respect be understood as being within; for even if what was prophesied happened in a particular case, it is nevertheless the Church. Indeed, the specific feature does not correspond to every figure [Note: [Col. 0037D] Alternatively: “occurs.”]. For Damascus, Tyre, Soor, and many others still exist, although God had said that they would be utterly destroyed and never restored.

That the Church is represented among foreign cities is clearly shown in Ezekiel. When the Lord told him to prophesy the destruction of Theman, which is Esau, and of Dagon, which is the idol of the Philistines, he understood the parable to concern Jerusalem and the temple. “The word of the Lord came to me,” he says, “saying: Son of man, set your face toward Theman, look toward Dagon, prophesy against the forest of Nages. Hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will kindle a fire against you, and it will devour every green tree and every dry tree. The burning flame will not be extinguished, and every face from the south wind to the north will be burned in it, so that all flesh may know that I, the Lord, have kindled it; it will not be extinguished again.” And I said, “No, Lord.” They say to me: “Is this not the parable that is spoken?” (Ezek. XX, 45–49).

“And the word of the Lord came to me,” he says, “saying: Therefore, son of man, prophesy and set your face toward Jerusalem, looking toward their sanctuaries; and you shall prophesy against the land of Israel. Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will draw my sword from its sheath, and I will destroy from you the enemy and the unjust. Thus my sword shall go out from its sheath against all flesh, from the south wind to the north, and all flesh shall know that I am the Lord who brought my sword out from its sheath; it shall not go out again. Set your face,” he says, “toward Theman, and look toward Dagon” (Ezek. XXI, 1–5) [Col. 0039B].

And he interpreted it, saying: “Set your face toward Jerusalem, and look toward their sanctuaries.” And he showed that it referred to all Jerusalem, saying: “I will destroy from you the enemy and the unjust.” Thus he speaks generally: “So my sword shall go out against all flesh, from the south wind to the north.”

He shows that Theman is in Jerusalem, where God destroys it, as well as Dagon and all the abominations of the nations, through David’s son Solomon in his descendants. In this way, the fallen and demolished temples of God, spiritually burned, are cast into the torrent—that is, the world—by Josiah, the son born of David, so that the altar at Bethel may be broken, as it is written: “Altar, altar, thus says the Lord: Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David; Josiah shall be his name” (III Kings XIII, 2).

Nineveh, the city of foreigners, is a figure of the divided Church. But because it would take too long to interpret the reading in order, it will be enough to state what cannot correspond to the literal sense. “Nineveh was a great city,” he says (Jonah III, 3)—so great that, although it was hostile to God, it was the metropolis of the Assyrians, who destroyed Samaria and continually oppressed all Judea. Yet, in the figure of the Church, when Jonah—that is, Christ—preached, it was entirely delivered.

The same Nineveh is described by the following Prophet as destined wholly to perish, to whom the Lord preaches: “The sign of Jonah in the belly of the whale” (Matt. XII, 40; Luke XI, 30). And, as the Prophet himself also shows, that city is not a particular one, he inserts certain things that exceed the limits of the literal sense. “There was no end,” he says, “to its nations,” although it was a city of one nation. And again: “You multiplied your merchants beyond the stars of heaven,” that is, the Church. And again: “Against whom has your wickedness not continually come?” Could the wickedness of one city have come against every human being, or have done so always, unless it was that city which Cain founded by the blood of his brother in the name of his son—that is, of his posterity? [Col. 0040A]

The Prophet teaches even more clearly that Nineveh is the Church. “And he will stretch out his hand toward the north”—that is, toward the people alienated from the Sun, against the south—“and he will destroy the Assyrian” (Zeph. II, 13). And this also: “Nineveh shall be a desolation without water, a desert; and flocks shall feed in its midst, all the beasts of the earth. Chameleons and goats shall lie in its ceilings, and beasts shall cry out in its hollows, and ravens at its gates, because its height was like a cedar. The contemptuous city, which dwells in hope, which says in its heart, ‘I am, and there is no one after me’” (ibid., 13, 15). And again: “How has it become a desolation, a pasture for beasts? Everyone who passes through it will hiss and shake his hands” (ibid., 15).

“O illustrious and redeemed city, dove, which heard the voice but did not receive instruction, which did not trust in the Lord and did not draw near to her Lord! Her princes within her are roaring lions; her judges are wolves of Arabia, leaving nothing until morning. Her prophets are men lifted up by the spirit, contemptuous men. Her priests profane sacred things [Note: [Col. 0039D] Greek βεβηλοῦσι, ‘they profane’], and violate the Law; but the righteous Lord will not do injustice in her temple” (Zeph. III, 1–5).

Egypt likewise is divided. “Behold,” he says, “the Lord sits upon a light cloud and comes into Egypt” (Isa. XIX, 1, 3). [The cloud is the spiritual body after Baptism, and the glory of the Son of Man. For this is the first coming of the Lord, continually coming in his Body, as he says: “From now on you will see him coming in the clouds of heaven.”]

“And the works made by hand in Egypt shall be crushed before him, and their heart shall be weakened within them. Egyptians shall rise against Egyptians, and [Note: [Col. 0040D] Read “he will defeat.”] a man shall defeat his brother and a man his neighbor; city shall fight against city, and nation shall rise against nation” (Matt. XXIV, 30)—that is, Egypt against Egypt, and law against law, namely, through diversity of interpretation under one Law: “And the spirit of the Egyptians shall be troubled within them, and I will scatter their counsels.”

And after he had mixed sometimes the species with the genus, sometimes the genus with the species, he added, saying: “On that day there shall be an altar of the Lord in the land of the Egyptians, and monuments to the Lord at its borders. And it shall be for a sign forever to the Lord in the land of the Egyptians” (Isa. XIX, 19). He did not say, “It will be possible for an altar to exist forever at the borders of Egypt,” but “It shall be.”

Ezekiel shows more plainly that the whole world is Egypt, saying: “O days! For the day of the Lord is near, a day of cloud; it shall be the end of the nations, and a sword shall come upon the Egyptians. And he joins the literal sense: There shall be tumult in Ethiopia, and the wounded shall fall in Egypt, and its foundations shall fall—Persians and Cretans and Lydians and all the mixed peoples—and the sons of my covenant shall fall by the sword in it with them” (Ezek. XXX, 3–5).

This happened when, after the destruction, they went down into Egypt and were killed there by Nebuchadnezzar, according to Jeremiah’s prophecy. But it will also happen generally on the last day, when the sons of the covenant fall together with the Egyptians, living in the manner of the Egyptians.

Likewise, through Ezekiel God threatens the king of Egypt and his multitude, saying that they would be terrifying to the saints, counted among the circumcised. This applies only to those who flatter themselves with circumcision—that is, with sacred rites. “Because he brought his terror upon the land of the living, so that Pharaoh, wounded by the sword, might sleep in the midst of the uncircumcised, and all his multitude with him,” says the Lord.

And there he moves from genus to species: “Thus says the Lord: I will cast you upon the land of many peoples, and I will draw you out in my net, and I will spread you over your fields. I will set over you all the birds of heaven, and I will fill all the beasts of the whole earth with you. I will place your flesh upon the mountains and fill the hills with your blood. The earth shall be watered by what comes forth from you; with your multitude I will fill the mountains with thorns from you. When you are extinguished, I will cover the heavens, darken their stars, cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give its light. All things that shine with light in heaven shall be darkened, and I will bring darkness upon your land,” says the Lord.

He joins the literal sense: “And I will provoke many peoples against you, when I lead your captivity among the nations, into a land which you did not know” (Ezek. XXXII, 4–8).

He exceeds the literal sense: “And many nations shall mourn over you, and their kings shall be stunned in bewilderment when my sword flies over their faces; in their midst it shall be for destruction from the day of your ruin.”

He returns to the literal sense: “For thus says the Lord: The sword of the king of Babylon comes upon you with the swords of mighty men, and I will cast down your strength. All the pestilences from the nations shall be against you, and they shall dishonor Egypt, and all its strength shall be crushed.”

To the genus: “And I will destroy all its cattle beside abundant waters; no human foot shall trouble them again, nor shall the hoof of cattle trample them. Then their waters shall rest, and their rivers shall be like oil,” says the Lord (ibid., 9–14).

Species: “And I will give Egypt over to destruction, and the land shall be desolate with its fullness, and I will scatter all who dwell in it” (ibid., 15).

Genus: “And they shall know that I am the Lord.”

“I will cover the heavens,” he says, “when you are extinguished; I will darken its stars, I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give its light. All things that shine with light in heaven shall be darkened over you, and I will bring darkness upon your land” (Ezek. XXXII, 7–8).

[In the Lord’s Passion there was darkness not only in the land of Egypt, but throughout the whole world. Yet when Egypt was captured, the nations did not become astonished, awaiting their own ruin from the day of its ruin. For it is also written concerning Soor:

“Thus says the Lord to Soor: Will not the islands be shaken from the day of your ruin, amid the groaning of the wounded, while they are being killed by the sword in your midst? And all the princes of the sea shall leave their seats, remove their turbans and their garments, and strip themselves. In bewilderment of mind they shall be stunned and terrified at your destruction; they shall groan over you and take up a lamentation over you and say to you: ‘How has that praiseworthy city been destroyed from the sea, which brought its fear upon all who dwelt in it?’ And the islands shall fear from the day of your ruin” (Ezek. XXVI, 15–18, according to the Septuagint).

“At the sound of your voice your pilots shall tremble with fear; all your rowers, passengers, and helmsmen of the sea shall leave their ships and stand upon the land. They shall howl over you with their voice, cry bitterly over you, put earth upon their heads, and spread ashes beneath themselves. They shall take up a lamentation over you, the lament of the children—a lament for Soor.

“How great a profit you gained from the sea! You satisfied the nations with your abundance, and enriched all the kings of the earth by your trade. But now you are sorrowful in the sea, in the depth of the waters; your merchandise and your whole assembly are in your midst. All your rowers have fallen; all who inhabit the islands have mourned over you, and their rowers have been stunned in bewilderment of mind, and their faces have wept over you. Their merchants among the nations shall hiss at you. You have become destruction; you shall be no more forever,” says the Lord (Ezek. XXVII, 28–36, according to the Septuagint).]

Can the things that have been said apply to one island, or could it alone have enriched all the kings of the earth? But we leave some matters for their appropriate places; although they are stated briefly there, they may be understood.

Tyre is divided, as Isaiah says. After much concerning the species and the genus, he adds this also, saying: “After seventy years Tyre shall be like the song of a prostitute. Take a lyre, a prostitute city, forgotten in playing the lyre well; sing many songs, so that you may be remembered. And after seventy years God will visit Tyre, and she shall again be restored to her former condition” (Isa. XXIII, 15–17).

Is it credible that all the kingdoms of the earth came to Tyre for the purpose of trading? And if they do come, what benefit would there be in predicting to Tyre future commerce with all the kingdoms of the earth, if Tyre is not the Church, in which all the commerce of the earth concerns eternal life?

For what follows shows what its commerce is: “And its trade and its profit shall be holy to the Lord” (Isa. XXIII, 15–17). It is not gathered for them, but for those who dwell in the presence of the Lord. “All its commerce is to eat, drink, and be filled, as a memorial-sign in the presence of the Lord” (ibid., 18).

If, then, its commerce is holy to the Lord, how can it belong to all the kingdoms unless this Tyre exists everywhere? For what follows plainly shows what Tyre is: “Behold, the Lord will corrupt the inhabited world, lay it waste, strip its face bare, scatter those who dwell in it, and the people shall be like the priest” (Isa. XXIV, 1–6).

[Is this not that inhabited world whose commerce is holy to the Lord, where the servant is like the Lord and the maidservant like the mistress?]

“And the buyer shall be like the seller, and the debtor like the creditor, and the lender like the borrower, because the earth shall be utterly corrupted and laid waste. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things. The earth mourned; the inhabited world was bowed down; the heights of the earth mourned. The earth committed an offense because of those who dwell in it, because they transgressed the Law and changed the commands of the eternal covenant. Therefore a curse shall consume the earth, because those who dwell in it have sinned. Therefore those who inhabit the earth shall be poor” (Isa. XXIV, 1–6).

[Can those be the nations whose commerce in all the kingdoms of the earth is to eat, drink, and be filled—not at some particular time, but as a memorial-sign in the presence of the Lord? “And few human beings shall be left. The vine shall mourn; the wine shall mourn. All whose soul rejoices shall groan. The joy of the tambourine shall cease, when the shamelessness and riches of the wicked cease. Will the sound of the saints’ lyre cease? They were confounded; they did not drink pure wine; the wine became bitter for those who drank it. Every city was deserted; all applauded so that they might not enter; howl, you divine ones; everywhere the joy of the earth shall cease, and deserted cities shall be left, and abandoned houses shall perish” (ibid., 6–8).]

All these things shall happen to the earth in the midst of the nations. If every city has been deserted, what are the nations in whose midst these things take place? Even if some of these matters appear obscure, nevertheless they are all spiritual. He calls every spiritually deserted city dead—but that prostitute Tyre, not the Tyre whose commerce is holy throughout the whole world.

In Jerusalem, however, few people shall be left, with the status of those who perish nevertheless preserved. Few shall be left of those whom he calls spiritually dead: those who came to life through remembrance, whom the Ecclesiasticus did not kill, as we read in many places.

But since we must fulfill our purpose, we shall be content with two examples. God threatens fire from the fire of Israel against the king of the Assyrians, that is, against the hostile body, and says to the Syrian—or to the straw—that after a little while they will become fire: “The Lord Sabaoth will send disgrace upon your honor, and a burning fire upon your glory; and Israel the light shall burn, and it shall be fire for you, and it shall sanctify it in the burning flame”—namely, the light of Israel—“and it shall devour the forest like hay. On that day the mountains shall burn; and those who flee shall flee through the precipices, like one fleeing from a burning flame. And those who remain of them shall be counted, and a child shall write them” (Isa. X, 16–19).

“Those who remain,” he says, “of them.” For can the fire that burns fail to burn? [Note: [Col. 0044D] Perhaps “delay,” “remain,” or “not burn.”] But those who survive from among the burned shall become fire.

In Zechariah we read that those whom the Church has not killed return, so that they may turn back to her; but that it kills the others spiritually through torments. For while they stand, it tears out their eyes and causes their flesh to waste away:

“He will dwell in Israel with confidence. And this shall be the slaughter with which God will strike all the peoples who have fought against Israel. Their flesh shall waste away while they stand upon their feet; their eyes shall flow from their sockets, and their tongue shall waste away in their mouth. And on that day there shall be great bewilderment among them, and each person shall seize the hand of his neighbor, and his hand shall be filled with the hand of his neighbor”—that is, the blind leading the blind.

“And Judah shall fight in Jerusalem, and he shall gather the men of all the peoples, and an exceedingly great quantity of gold, silver, and clothing. And this shall be the slaughter of the horses, mules, camels, asses, and all the cattle that are in those camps, according to this slaughter. And whoever is left of all the nations that come against Jerusalem shall go up each year to worship the King, the Lord God Almighty, and to celebrate the feast of booths” (Zech. XVI, 11–16).

Elam belongs to the foreigners. Here he joins the particular to the general and shows that it is divided. “Thus says the Lord: I will break the bow of Nair, the rulers of Elam.” And he exceeds the literal sense: “I will bring four winds from the four corners of heaven, and there shall be no nation that does not come there, which will drive out Elam.”

He returns to the literal sense: “And I will terrify them before their enemies who seek their lives, and I will bring them according to the anger of my wrath, and I will send my sword after them until it consumes them.”

He joins the genus: “And I will set my throne in Elam, and I will destroy from there the king and the mighty. And in the last days I will restore the captivity of Elam,” says the Lord (Jerem. XXV, 35–38, according to the Septuagint; but according to the Vulgate XLIX, 35–39).

Is it to be believed that there was no nation that did not come to conquer Elam, or that the Lord’s throne was there—he whose captivity he reverses—unless Elam is a figure of the Church?

Some figures, however, are solely of the evil side, such as Sodom, as it is written: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom” (Isa. I, 10), and the one that is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, “where also their Lord was crucified” (Rev. XI, 8). From these Sodoms Lot will go out—that is, “departure”—so that the man of sin may be revealed (II Thess. II, 3).

Babylon is a city opposed to Jerusalem. Its part of the whole world is represented in Israel. These things are brought together: “The vision against Babylon,” he says, and he speaks of the holy soldiers of God who will come against the inhabited world: “Take your turn and rejoice in turn with them; do not fear; encourage one another; open your hands, you magistrates, for behold, I command. They have been sanctified and summoned; giants come to appease my wrath, rejoicing together and inflicting injury. The voice of many nations in the mountains, like the voice of many nations, the voice of kings and nations gathered together” (Isa. XIII, 1–4, according to the Septuagint)—when the nation and king of the Medes overthrow Babylon.

He continues and says who these kings are and what Babylon is: “The God Sabaoth has commanded a warlike nation to come from afar, from the highest foundation of heaven. God and his warriors have corrupted the whole inhabited world. Howl, for the day of the Lord is near, and destruction from God will be present. Therefore all hands shall be weakened, and every human soul shall tremble. The envoys shall be troubled and shall suffer pangs; the surrounding walls shall be shaken; each shall be terrified by the other, and their faces shall be changed like flame. For behold, an incurable day of the Lord is coming, a day of indignation and wrath, to make the inhabited world desolate and destroy sinners from it” (ibid., 4–9).

[He speaks of the day of the Lord from the time when he suffered: from the time when the world is spiritually killed by God’s army, while the wicked do not see its light, so that they may be saved. He says: “For the stars of the outer heaven and all its lights shall give light, and its light shall grow dark, and its light shall not endure. And I will inflict evils upon the dead of the earth and their sins upon the unjust; I will destroy the wrongdoing of the wicked and humble the wrongdoing of the proud.”]

“And those who remain”—that is, those whom the soldiers mentioned above have not killed—“shall be more honored than gold that has not touched fire, and a human being shall be more honored than a stone of sapphire. For heaven shall be indignant, and the earth shall be shaken from its foundations because of the stirring of God’s wrath on the day when his indignation is present.”

He joins the literal sense: “And the one who is left shall be like a fleeing doe and like a wandering sheep, and there shall be no one to gather him, so that a person may return to his people and hasten to come to his tribe. For whoever is caught shall be overcome; and if any are gathered, they shall fall by the sword, and their daughters shall fall before their eyes, and their houses shall be plundered, and their wives shall be possessed. Behold, I am raising up the Medes against you, who do not reckon money and have no need of gold” (Isa. XIII, 10–17).

[He subtly inserts the genus: for you are those [Note: [Col. 0045D] Perhaps “these.”] who have no need of gold and silver—unless it is the Ecclesiasticus, who spiritually enjoys life. “The archers shall break the young men, they shall have no mercy on your children, and their eyes shall not spare your grandchildren” (ibid., 18).]

Everything is spiritual, as it is written concerning the same Babylon: “Blessed is he who shall seize you and dash your little ones against the rock” (Ps. CXXXVI, 9). For he did not call the king of the Medes blessed because he conquered Babylon, but the Ecclesiastici, who conquer and dash Babylon’s children against the rock of scandal.

He prevails, as it is written: “Let him who now prevails hold fast until he is removed from the midst” (II Thess. II, 7).

And after much concerning the species and the genus, the conclusion of the passage plainly shows that all are Babylon, and that they are destroyed in the land and mountains—that is, in the Church:

“Thus says the Lord: I will make Babylon a desert, so that hedgehogs may dwell in it; and it shall be reduced to nothing, and I will make it a muddy abyss for destruction. Thus says the Lord Sabaoth: As I have said, so shall it be; and as I have planned, so shall it remain, so that I may destroy the Assyrians in my land and in my mountains. They shall be trampled, and their yoke shall be removed from them, and their glory shall be removed from their shoulders. This is the plan which the Lord has planned for the whole inhabited world, and this is the hand raised over all the nations of the inhabited world. For when the holy God has planned something, who will scatter it? And when that strong hand is raised, who will turn it aside?” (Isa. XIV, 22–27).]

Whenever, after the destruction, he threatens a ruined city with habitation by beasts, he means that unclean spirits will dwell in human beings whom the Holy Spirit has abandoned. For the inhabitants who have been killed cannot feel this insult or this ruin.

“The words,” says Amos, “which he saw concerning Jerusalem,” and he began: “For three impieties of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn it away, because they sawed those who were with child with iron saws” (Amos I, 1–3). And again: “For three impieties of Idumea, and for four, I will not turn it away, because he pursued his brother with the sword” (ibid., 11).

Many other cities of foreigners likewise correspond to the figure of the Church. Wherever he names Idumea, Theman, Bosor, or Seir, he signifies evil brothers. These are the possessions of Esau. By iron saws he means hard and harsh men who cut apart Churches in labor.

Likewise, Jeremiah testifies that all the nations under heaven drink God’s wrath in the city of God and are struck there, saying:

“Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Take from my hand the cup of unmixed wine, and you shall make all the nations to which I send you drink it. They shall vomit and become delirious before the sword which I am sending among them. And I took the cup from the hand of the Lord and made the nations to which the Lord sent me drink it: to Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, and its kings and its rulers, so that they might be made desolate, devastated, and objects of hissing; and to Pharaoh king of Egypt, his servants, his officials, all his people, and all his mixed population; and all the kings of the foreigners, Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and those facing Ashdod; and Edom and Moab and the sons of Ammon; and the king of Tyre and the king of Sidon, and the kings who are across the sea; and Dedan, Theman, and Bosor; and everyone cut off from the face; and all the mixed peoples who dwell in the desert; and all the kings of Elam; and all the kings of the Persians; and all the kings from the south, those far away and those nearby, each one against his brother; and all the kingdoms of the earth that are upon the face of the earth. And you shall say to them:

“‘Thus says the Lord Almighty: Drink, become drunk, vomit, fall, and rise again before the sword which I am sending among you.’

“And to those who refused to receive the cup so as to drink it, you shall say: ‘Thus says the Lord: You shall surely drink. For in the city in which my name has been invoked, upon that city I begin to afflict you; and you shall not be cleansed by purification, because I am summoning the sword against the inhabitants of the earth’” (Jerem. XXV, 15–29).]

“You shall make Jerusalem, the cities of Judah, and its kings and rulers drink it,” he says. Then he says: “And to all the kingdoms of the earth that are upon the face of the earth,” to show that he has passed from the particular—Jerusalem—to the general, in which all the nations of the earth are found, and which God will strike there, as he also interprets it, saying: “For in the city in which my name has been invoked, in that city I begin to afflict you, and you shall not be cleansed by purification.”

Was Jeremiah, while still in the body—the man who had never gone to Egypt from the prison of Judea except under compulsion—really giving, with unmixed wine added to the cup, that drink to all the nations under heaven? Or is he now prophesying through the Church? And if there was a place in the Church then as well as now, it is clear that all the nations to which that Jeremiah speaks are brought together in their principal part.

For if Satan has anything supreme, anything grave, anything on the right in his body, he has mingled it with the heavenly beings, as is the custom of combatants to oppose the strong with the strong. Hence the Apostle says that the saints’ struggle is not against humanity, but against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Eph. VI, 12).

## RULE V. On Times.

The quantity of time in Scripture is frequently mystical through the figure of synecdoche, or through legitimate numbers, which are set forth in many ways and are to be understood according to their context.[Col. 0047A] Synecdoche, moreover, is either the whole from a part or a part from the whole.

By this figure, Israel served four hundred years in Egypt. For God says to Abraham: “Know with certainty that your seed will be a sojourner in a land that is not its own; they will serve them, and they will afflict them for four hundred years” (Gen. XV, 13). But the Book of Exodus says that they were in Egypt for 430 years (Exod. XII, 40). Did Israel not serve for the whole period? We must therefore ask: from what point? This is easy to discover. Scripture says that the people did not begin to serve until after the death of Joseph, all his brothers, and all that generation. “The children of Israel increased and multiplied, and became numerous [Note: [Col. 0047D] They became Cethaei. LXX, Exod. I, 7: χυδαῖοι ἐγένοντο, ‘they became spread abroad’], and they grew exceedingly strong, and the land was filled with them. Then another king arose over Egypt who did not know Joseph, and he said to his people: ‘Behold, the people of the children of Israel are a great multitude, and they are stronger than we are. Come, therefore, let us deal shrewdly with them’” (Exod. I, 7–10).

If the people began to serve after Joseph’s death, and if from the 530 years during which Israel sojourned in Egypt we subtract the eighty years of Joseph’s reign—for he reigned from the age of thirty until 110—then the remaining period of Israel’s servitude will be 340 years, whereas God said 400.[Note: [Col. 0047D] Rather, 430; so that, after subtracting 80, the remaining years are 350. Thus Exodus XII, 40; Josephus, *Antiquities*, book II, chapter 6. [Col. 0048D]] If Israel served throughout the entire period of its sojourning, the number is greater than what God said; if it served from Joseph’s death, according to the testimony of holy Scripture, it is less. It is therefore evident that 100 is a part taken from the whole. For after 300 years, the part remaining is 100 years. That is why he said 400 years.

If, in this entire reckoning of time, one says, for example, “after nine days” or “after nine months,” the first day of the tenth month is intended, as it is written: “In my mother’s womb I was formed, flesh compacted through ten months in blood” (Wis. VI, 2).[Col. 0047C] Just as the first part of any period contains the whole period, so in the final hour the entire day is present; the remainder of a thousand years is a thousand years.

The world’s age consists of six days, that is, 6,000 years. In the remainder of the sixth day, that is, the thousand years, the Lord was born, suffered, and rose again. Likewise, the remaining thousand years are called the thousand years of the first resurrection. For just as the remainder of the sixth day—namely, three hours—is the whole day, one of the three days of the Lord’s burial, so the remainder of the greater sixth day, on which the Church arose, is the whole day, namely, a thousand years.

By this figure, therefore, the three days and three nights are established. Night and day together constitute one period of twenty-four hours, and nights are not added to days except for a definite reason. At other times Scripture counts only days, as when the Apostle is said to have stayed with Peter for fifteen days (Gal. I, 18). Was it necessary to say “as many days and nights”? For it is written: “Evening came and morning came: one day” (Gen. I, 5).

If night and day constitute one period, the final hour of the day contains both the entire day and the night that has passed. Similarly, the final hour of the night contains the entire day and the night that is to come. For an hour is a part of either period.

The hour in which the Lord was buried is part of Friday together with the night that had passed; and the hour of the night in which he rose was part of the approaching day. Otherwise, if neither the past night belongs to the present day nor the following day to the present night, the Lord did not rise by day but by night. For day begins at sunrise, as it is written: “The greater light is the beginning of the day” (ibid., 16).

But the Lord rose before sunrise. For Mark says, “At sunrise” (Matt. XVI, 2)—not after the sun had risen, but while it was rising, that is, moving toward its rising. Luke says, “at dawn” (Luke XXIV, 1). But lest there be uncertainty about this expression, the other Evangelists plainly testify that it was night. Matthew says that the women came to the tomb at night and saw the Lord (Matt. XXVIII, 1); John says, “while it was still dark” (John XX, 1).

If the Lord rose before the sun, that is, before the beginning of the day, that night was part of the day that was beginning to dawn. This also accords with the works of God: the day was not darkened into night, but the night grew bright into day. That night itself was illumined and became day, which is a figure of what was accomplished in Christ. For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts (II Cor. IV, 6); he illumined the darkness, as it is written: “Your darkness shall be like midday” (Isa. LVIII, 10). And: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near; let us walk decently as in the day” (Rom. XIII, 12).

For what is carnal comes first, and afterward what is spiritual. Thus the first day and the last day are a part taken from the whole. Only the middle day was complete, from evening to evening, according to the ordinance and commandment. Thus Moses says: “From evening to evening [Note: [Col. 0048D] I darkened. Read, with the Vulgate, ‘you shall celebrate,’ or, with the Septuagint, ‘you shall keep Sabbath,’ σαββατιεῖτε] you shall keep the Sabbath” (Lev. XXIII, 33).

Some say that the reckoning must begin from the day, because the Lord said “three days and nights,” not “three nights and days.” But this is easily disproved. If the burial began by day and ended at night, or if it ended by day, then it began at night. For if the day is included at both ends, there will be more than one day.

They further say that the past night cannot belong to the day, nor the future day to the night; rather, three separate days and nights must be assigned: the first day being that on which he was crucified, the second consisting of the three remaining hours, and the third being the Sabbath. Thus the Lord’s day would be the fourth.

Those who avoid this evasion agree that the reckoning must begin from the night, but say that nights must be separated from days. They count as the first night the three hours of extraordinary darkness, as the second the Sabbath night, and as the third the night preceding the Lord’s day. Thus there are supposedly three nights but two days: the first day consisting of the three hours after the darkness, and the second being the Sabbath.

But whoever proposes separate days cannot say that the future day was present in the night in which the Lord rose. If he concedes this, he must also concede that the preceding night was present in the remainder of Friday. Although these were extraordinary darkness, the three hours of light nevertheless belonged to the same day, and did not lose their order so as not to be part of their own day and night.

I say nothing of the fact that the three hours of darkness could not constitute a night, since they occurred contrary to the order of God’s creation. Whatever takes place as a sign does not disturb the rational course of the elements.[Col. 0049A] For it was not the case that, because the sun and moon stood still in the days of Joshua (Josh. X, 13) and Hezekiah (IV Kings XX, 10), the sun alone turned back, or that any portion of the course between the sun and moon was mutilated, removed, or added to the day or night, and from that point a new reckoning of times or new moons began—the reckoning that God established through the sun and moon for the days and years of time, as it is written in Genesis (Gen. I, 17).

Much more, then, was nothing disturbed on that day to which three hours of darkness were not added so as to make fifteen. For if we say that the sun was darkened and then the day appeared again, what name shall we give, and what order shall we assign, to that day which is said to have occurred between Friday and the Sabbath? Unless that was the Sabbath, that week had eight days.

Certainly, if the dispute cannot be settled by reasoning, we establish the matter briefly: the three hours of darkness did not belong to the Lord’s burial, because he was still alive. He could not have been in the heart of the earth except from the time when he died or was buried; and this occurred during the three hours of Friday, before the twelfth hour.

For after sunset the Jews were not permitted to bury, since the Preparation was the beginning of the Sabbath, as John says (John XIII, 2; XIX, 42). Therefore, because of the Jews’ Preparation, since the tomb was nearby, they placed Jesus there.

Days are preferred to nights in dignity, not in the order of novelty, just as all firstborn are males, as it is said: “He fathered sons and daughters, and he died” (Gen. V). This is contrary to the law of nature, since all those men would have fathered males first.

For us, however, the whole of time is day. Everything is new; the figures have passed away.

The legitimate numbers are seven, ten, and twelve. The same number also remains the same when multiplied: seventy, or seven hundred, or a number multiplied by itself, such as seven times seven or ten times ten. These numbers signify either perfection, the whole from a part, or a simple total.

They signify perfection, for example, in the seven spirits and the seven churches (Rev. I, 4–11); or where he says: “Seven times a day I praise you” (Ps. CXVIII, 164); or, “He will receive sevenfold in this age” (Matt. XXII; Eccles. XXXV, 13).

Similarly, the number ten is used when another Evangelist says: “He will receive a hundredfold in this age” (Mark X, 30). Daniel comprehended the innumerable multitude of angels, heaven, or the Church by the number ten, saying: “A thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood around him” (Dan. VII, 10). David likewise says: “The chariots of God are ten thousand times ten thousand” (Ps. LXVII, 18). And concerning all time David says: “For a thousand generations” (Ps. CIV, 8).

The number twelve is likewise used of the whole Church, as in the 144,000 and the twelve tribes.[Note: [Col. 0049D] Read 144,000, according to the cited passage of Revelation.] “The twelve tribes of Israel” comprise all the nations, as it is written: “You will sit judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX, 28).

The whole from a part is indicated when a period is defined by legitimate numbers, as in the Apocalypse: “You will have tribulation for ten days” (Rev. IV, 10), although this signifies “until the end.” It would now be tedious to prove that the seventy years in Babylon signify the same period.

Apart from legitimate numbers, Scripture frequently abbreviates any period by whatever number, as when the time mentioned above is called an hour, the Apostle saying: “It is the last hour” (I John II, 18). It is also called a day: “Behold, now is the day [Note: [Col. 0049D] Perhaps *salvation*, or *of salvation*, rather than *salutation*. For in II Cor. VI, 2 we read σωτηρίας, ‘of salvation.’ The same applies at Isaiah XLIX, 8, which the Apostle follows.] of salvation” (II Cor. VI, 2).

An entire year is also proclaimed, as through Isaiah: “To proclaim an acceptable year of the Lord” (Isa. LVI, 2). For not only the year in which the Lord preached was acceptable, but also the year in which he preaches, as it is written: “At an acceptable time I heard you” (Isa. XLIX, 8); and the Apostle interprets it: “Behold, now is the acceptable time” (II Cor. VI, 2).

Finally, he joined the end of this year—that is, of judgment—to the statement, saying: “To proclaim an acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense.” David likewise says: “You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness” (Ps. LXIV, 12).[Col. 0050B]

Sometimes an hour, a day, and months signify a year, as in the Apocalypse: “Prepared for the hour, and day, and month, and year” (Rev. IX, 15), which means three and a half years.

In the same book, months signify years: “It was given power to destroy human beings for five months” (ibid., 5).

Sometimes days, by the number ten, signify 100 days, as in the Apocalypse: “One thousand two hundred and sixty days” (Rev. XI, 3). For 1,260 multiplied by 100 gives 126,000 days, which are 350 years, reckoned in months of thirty days.

In the same place, one month, by the number ten, signifies 100 months: “They will trample the holy city for forty-two months” (ibid., 2). For forty-two times 100 gives 4,200 months, which are 350 years.

Time is either a year or 100 years, as in “a time, times, and half a time” (Dan. VII, 25; XII, 7), which means either three and a half years or 350 years.

Likewise, one day sometimes signifies 100 years, as it is written concerning the Church: “To lie in the city where their Lord was crucified, and after three and a half days” (Rev. XI, 8, 11). And: “The Son of Man must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and rise again after three days” (Matt. XX, 18; Mark X, 33; Luke XVIII, 32). For he rose on the third day.

A generation sometimes signifies 100 years, as the Lord says to Abraham: “But in the fourth generation they will return here” (Gen. XV, 16). In Exodus, however, the statement concerns not the period of servitude but the entire period of sojourning: “In the fifth generation the people came up from Egypt” (Exod. XII, 42), that is, after 430 years.

Likewise, a generation sometimes signifies ten years, as Jeremiah says: “You will be in Babylon for seven generations” (Baruch VI, 2).

That the number three can signify the same as ten is shown more fully in the Gospel. Matthew says that the master’s property was entrusted to three servants (Matt. XXV, 13), whereas Luke says ten (Luke XIX, 13). He reduces the ten to three when he himself says that an account was demanded from three.

Sometimes one day signifies 1,000 years, as it is written: “On the day when you taste from the tree, you shall die” (Gen. II, 17). The first seven days therefore signify 7,000 years.

God worked for six days and rested from all his works on the seventh day, and blessed and sanctified it (ibid., 2–3). But the Lord says: “My Father is working until now” (John V, 17). For just as he worked on this world for six days, so he works on the spiritual world, which is the Church, for 6,000 years, and will cease on the seventh day, which he blessed and made eternal.

This is why, among all the other commandments, the Lord commanded so frequently that we observe and love the Sabbath day. Whoever performs God’s commandments should love God’s Sabbath, that is, the seventh day of eternal rest.

Therefore God urges the people not to enter the gates of Jerusalem carrying a burden on the Sabbath, and threatens the gates, those entering them, and those leaving them, as he commands Jeremiah, saying:

“Go and stand in the gates of the children of your people, through which the kings of Judah enter and leave, and in all the gates of Jerusalem. Say to them: ‘Hear the word of the Lord, you who enter these gates. Thus says the Lord: Guard your souls, and do not carry burdens on the Sabbath day. Do not go out through the gates of Jerusalem, and do not carry burdens from your houses on the Sabbath day, as I commanded your fathers. But they did not listen with their ears, and they stiffened their necks beyond their fathers, so as not to hear me or receive instruction.

“And it shall be, if you listen to me, says the Lord, and do not bring burdens through the gates of this city on the Sabbath day; if you do no work, but sanctify the Sabbath day, then kings and rulers will enter through the gates of this city, sitting on the throne of David. They will ascend in chariots and on horses, they and their rulers, the men of Judah who inhabit Jerusalem. This city will be inhabited forever.

“And they will come from the cities of Judah, from the cities of Jerusalem, from the land of Benjamin, from the plain, and from the land to the south, bringing burnt offerings and incense, manna and frankincense, bringing praise into the house of the Lord.

“But if you do not listen to me, so as to sanctify the Sabbath day, and do not carry burdens or enter through the gates of Jerusalem, I will kindle a fire in its gates, and it will consume the houses of Jerusalem, and it will not be extinguished” (Jerem. XVII, 19–27).

It would have been enough simply to command them not to work on the Sabbaths. Why, then, say: “Do not bring burdens through the gates of Jerusalem”? Or, if it was necessary to specify the kind of work, why say: “Do not bring them through the gates”? For no one was carrying burdens into the city over the walls or across the roofs.

Jerusalem is divided in two, and its gates are divided in two. Through the gates of hell one leaves the holy Jerusalem, and through those same gates one enters the accursed Jerusalem. Those who enter through the gates enter the eternal Jerusalem, like kings in chariots and on horses, sitting on the throne of David, as Isaiah says: “The children of children will bring gifts to God from all the nations, with horses and chariots [Note: [Col. 0051D] In the splendor of many. LXX, Isa. LXVI, 20: ἐν λαμπήναις ἡμιόνων, ‘in the litters of mules.’] in the splendor of many, with canopies, into the holy city” (Isa. LVI, 20).

The gate of the holy city Jerusalem is Christ, together with his deputies, the guardians of the law—those who kill the prophets and stone those sent to them. The gate is the devil, and his deputy is the false apostles, transgressors of the law, who hide the keys of the kingdom of heaven through their profound interpretation.[Col. 0052A] These are the gates that do not overcome the Church, which is founded upon the rock. For “the foundation of God stands,” as it is written: “God knows those who are his” (II Tim. II, 19).

If anyone enters by the commandments of those presiding over the chair of Moses, he enters through Christ. The commandments belong to Christ; he lays down the burden of his sins, and without him no one enters the Sabbath rest.

But if anyone enters not through the commandments but through the deeds of those presiding over the chair of Moses, he is more a child of Gehenna than they are.

And while all those who gathered manna before the Sabbath are at rest, let that person be found with his burden on the Sabbath day, on which manna is not to be gathered nor the burden laid down. For they do not wish to hear the voice of the Son of God crying in the Church and saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matt. XI, 28).

These are the thieves who enter not through the true door but through their own gates into their own Jerusalem. God will kindle a fire in the gates of Jerusalem, and it will burn up its roads, and it will not be extinguished. For the fire that burned the gates of the particular Jerusalem has been extinguished.

The Apostle says that the Sabbath and the other commandments of the law are a figure of what is to come: “Therefore let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a festival, or of a new moon, or of Sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come” (Coloss. II, 16).

In many passages, different events belonging to one period are described separately in appearance, so that they produce two periods, as though following one another in sequence. In reality, both events belong to a single period.

Thus, if Joseph’s fourteen years consist only of seven years of abundance and seven years of famine (Gen. XLI)—that is, the entire period of the Lord’s Passion, in whose figure Joseph was made ruler of Egypt when he was thirty years old—then the seven years of abundance and satiety that belong to us are the same as the remaining seven years of sterility and famine.

During this period the Lord threatens the rich with famine, but promises fullness to the poor. He promises these good things and threatens the evils of two periods that are to come at one time.

The Book of Exodus testifies that Israel was clearly immune from all the plagues of Egypt (Exod. X), and that it had light during the three days of darkness. This is now accomplished spiritually, just as God later threatened the same Pharaoh, saying: “I will bring darkness over your land” (ibid., 2).

Sometimes one period is divided into many parts, each of which is itself the whole period. Thus the year in which Noah was in the ark is divided among all the numbers.

Whenever time is mentioned, however, the number four specifically signifies the period from the Lord’s Passion until the end. Four is used whenever the number is complete, or when the fourth is represented by a part after the third, as in 340 or three and a half. The other numbers—for they must be understood according to their contexts—are signs, not explicit definitions.

The forty days of the Flood therefore signify the whole period. For there are forty years in Egypt, forty years in the wilderness, and forty days of the Lord’s, Moses’, Elijah’s,[Note: [Col. 0052D] “Elijah’s,” correctly, as in III Kings XIX.] and the Church’s fast, during which the Church fasts in the Church—that is, abstains from the pleasures of the dead.

The same forty days during which the Church eats and drinks with the Lord after the resurrection signify the forty years during which the Church was eating and drinking under Solomon, with profound peace everywhere, although the twofold Solomon oppressed them, as the same Church says: “One father oppressed us” (III Kings XII, 30).

For forty days the water remained at its height, and for an equal period it receded, so that, together with the recession of the water, the tenth month—that is, the perfect period—might be completed. But in general it is not the case that something grows strong at one time and then grows weak. For in the period in which it grows strong carnally, it grows weak spiritually, so that its very elevation is its decline, until the period is completed.

Thus the reigning world is placed beneath the feet of the Church, the Son of Man. The forty days, then, discharge the sins of Judah, and the 149 [days] those of Israel—one and the same thing.

The ark rested in the seventh month: the same period. The water continued to recede until the tenth month: the same period. He came out of the ark in the twelfth month (Gen. VII, 14). This is the Lord’s acceptable year of freedom. When it is completed, it will be revealed that the Church has passed through the Flood of the world.

Each part of this year is the same year. It is as if he had said: “He came out of the ark on the fortieth day,” or “in the seventh month,” or “in the tenth.”

## RULE VI. On Recapitulation

These are recapitulations: sections extending from the beginning to the end. Thus, from Adam to Enoch—namely, the translation of the Church—there are seven generations, which constitute the whole period.

Again, from Adam to Noah—namely, the restoration—there are ten generations, which constitute the whole period; and from Noah to Abraham there are ten generations.

The 100 years during which the ark was being built likewise signify the entire period during which the Church is being built and, during that period, is governed while all others perish in the Flood. We leave the fuller investigation of this matter as a path given to the wise.

Since there would otherwise have been no end to interpreting the abundance of Scripture, we have not thought it necessary to pursue each matter individually or remove those things that might perhaps obstruct this understanding, as we hasten toward another subject.

Among the rules by which the Spirit marked out the law so that the path of light might be guarded, he sometimes preserves the seal of recapitulation with such subtlety that it appears to be a continuation of the narrative rather than a recapitulation.

For sometimes he recapitulates in this way: “At that hour, on that day, at that time.” Thus the Lord speaks in the Gospel, saying: “On the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire rained from heaven and destroyed them all” (Gen. XIX, 24). “So will it be in the days of the Son of Man” (Matt. XXIV, 37), when that hour is revealed: “Let the one who is on the roof, with his belongings in the house, not come down to take them; and let the one who is in the field likewise not turn back” (Matt. XIII, 15–16). “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke XVII, 32).

Surely, at the hour when the Lord will be revealed in his coming, must a person not turn back to what belongs to him and remember Lot’s wife? And must he do this only after he has been revealed?

The Lord commanded these things to be observed at the hour when he will be revealed—not only to make the truth more welcome by concealing it from those who seek it, but also to show that the whole period is a day or an hour.

Thus he commanded that these things be observed at that same hour, that is, at that time, but before he is revealed. It is indeed the same hour, but reason enables us to recognize in which part of the hour it occurs.

Sometimes, however, such passages are not recapitulations but likenesses of future events. Thus the Lord says: “When you see what was spoken by Daniel the prophet, then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains” (Matt. XXIV, 15; Dan. IX, 27).

And he brings in the end. What Daniel said is happening in Africa,[Col. 0054A] and the end does not occur at the same time. But because what is to come will occur under the same heading, he said “then,” that is, when the same thing has happened throughout the world: the departure and revelation of the man of sin.

In this manner of expression the Spirit speaks in the Psalms:

“When the Lord restores the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are comforted. Then our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with rejoicing. Then they will say among the nations: ‘The Lord has done great things for them.’ The Lord has done great things for us; we became joyful” (Ps. CXXV, 1–3).

But by saying, “When the Lord turns away the captivity of Zion,” he said, “then they spoke among the nations.”[Note: [Col. 0053D] “To those who mourn,” according to the correction.] “Now he will turn it away,” he says; “then they will speak among the nations.”

For we are the nations whose captivity he has turned away. In the figure of those people, we have their time as our own, saying: “The Lord has done great things for them; the Lord has done great things for us.”

He therefore made their time and ours one time and joined them together by the likeness, saying: “Then they will say among the nations,” that is, when he has done something similar for the nations.

Nor should I pass over the fact that the Spirit intended something else to be understood without mysteries or allegory.

“According to John, many false prophets have gone out into the world. By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that dissolves Jesus and denies that he came in the flesh is not from God; and this is the spirit of Antichrist. You have heard that he is coming, and now he is present in this world” (I John IV, 3).

Does everyone who does not deny that Jesus came in the flesh possess the Spirit of God? Yet he subtly warns that this denial exists in deeds, not in words, and that each person must be understood not from profession but from fruits. He does so throughout the Epistle in which he wrote only about good and evil fruits, using the same manner of expression: “By this we know him, if we keep his commandments” (I John II, 3–4).

But whoever says, “I have known him,” and does not keep his commandments is a liar. Did he say that a brother who does not know God is to be recognized from his profession, and not from his works? And whoever says that he loves God but hates his brother is a liar (I John IV, 20).

If, as he says, he loves God, let him show it by his works; let him cling to God; let him love God in his brother. If he believes that Christ became incarnate, let him cease hating the members of Christ. If he believes that the Word became flesh, what is he persecuting in the flesh—the Word made flesh (John I, 14)? What is he persecuting—the Word in the flesh?

The Lord said: “Whatever you did for one of the least of my brothers who believe in me, you did for me” (Matt. XXV, 40). Let him not do evil to Christ’s flesh, that is, to his servants, because the Lord and the Church are one flesh.

If he believes that a human being exists in this flesh, why does he not love him—or, what is more cruel, why does he hate him? For it is written: “Whoever does not love his brother remains in death” (I John III, 14); and: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (ibid., 14).

He said that there is no other greater or clearer sign by which to recognize Antichrist than that the one who denies Christ in the flesh also hates his brother.

The statement, “Whoever denies Christ in the flesh is not from God” (II John XVII), is like the statement: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (I Cor. XII, 3), although many say, “Lord, Lord,” as he himself testifies: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII, 21).

But here the Apostle said that no one can say “Lord Jesus Christ” except in the Holy Spirit according to conscience, according to the inner person, not according to mere profession. He wished to show that those who say “Lord Jesus” possess nothing less than those who exalt themselves through various kinds of spiritual gifts.

Rather, everyone who believes in the Lord Jesus and proves by his works that he has believed possesses one and the same Spirit. “No one,” he says, “can say ‘Lord Jesus’ except in the Holy Spirit.” “There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord” (ibid., 4–5).
