To dissolve Jesus means not to do what one confesses Jesus did, as the same Lord says: “Whoever dissolves one of these least commandments and teaches people accordingly will be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 20).

What “dissolving” means he makes clear from what follows: “But whoever does them and teaches them accordingly…” The Apostle Paul likewise confirms that this denial consists in deeds, not words: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Tit. I, 16). And again: “Having the appearance of piety but denying its power” (II Tim. III, 5).

In this sense he says that some brothers preach Christ not outwardly but in their hearts. For they preach him outwardly in a holy manner. In the end he agrees with their preaching and commands that they be heard, saying: “What does it matter, whether Christ is proclaimed through pretext or in truth?” (Philipp. I, 18).

Antichrist preaches the Lord Christ not from devotion but from pretext. Aiming elsewhere, he enters through the name of Christ, preparing a way for himself, using Christ’s name to serve his belly and—what is shameful to say—giving the name of holiness and simplicity to such things, affirming through signs and wonders performed in chambers that he is Christ.

The Apostle warns us to avoid such people with salutary caution, saying: “Children, keep yourselves from idols” (I John V, 21).

## RULE VII. On the Devil and His Body

Two passages elucidated: Isaiah, chapter XIV, and Ezekiel, chapter XXVIII.

Concerning the devil and his body, the matter can be understood briefly if what has been said about the Lord and his body is observed here as well. For the transition from the head to the body is recognized by the same method, just as Isaiah says concerning the king of Babylon:

“How has Lucifer fallen from heaven, the morning star? He has been crushed upon the earth who was sent to all the nations? But you said in your heart: ‘I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I shall set my throne; I shall sit upon the high mountain, above the high mountains toward the north; I shall ascend above the clouds; I shall be like the Most High.’ But now you have descended to the underworld, to the foundations of the earth. And those who see you will marvel at you and say: ‘Is this the man who stirs up the earth, shakes kings, and makes the whole inhabited world desolate? He destroyed the city and did not release the captives. All the kings of the nations slept in honor, each in his own house. But you have been cast upon the mountains like a dead man, abominated together with all those who fell by the sword in the deserts and descended to the underworld. How have you come? Just as a garment sprinkled with blood will not be clean, so neither will you be clean, because you destroyed my land and killed my people. You shall not endure forever, evil seed. Prepare; kill your sons, so that the sin of your father may not rise again’” (Isa. XIV, 12, 22).

The king of Babylon signifies all the kings and the whole people, for they are one body. “How,” he says, “has Lucifer fallen from heaven, the morning star, broken upon the earth, who was sent to all the nations? But you said in your heart: ‘I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I shall set my throne.’” The devil promises this to himself. For he cannot hope that, by remaining in heaven, he will be able to ascend there—he who could not resist being cast down. Much less can a human being hope for this; and yet Scripture says of him that he is a man: “This is the man who stirs up the earth.”

But apart from this interpretation—which neither the devil nor a human being can hope to fulfill, namely, that he can ascend into heaven, sit above the stars of God, and become like God—the Scripture itself warns us to seek another meaning. For if he says that he will set his throne in heaven and above the stars of God, how will he sit upon a high mountain, or above the mountains toward the north, or upon the clouds, so as to be like the Most High? The Most High does not have his throne in such places.

By “heaven” he means the Church, as we shall see from the subsequent text. From this heaven the morning star falls. For Lucifer is divided into two parts, just as the Lord says in the Apocalypse concerning himself and his body: “I am the root and offspring of David, the radiant morning star, the bridegroom and the bride” (Apoc. XXII, 16). Likewise there: “To the one who conquers I shall give the morning star” (Apoc. II, 28)—that is, that he may be a morning star like Christ, whom we have received.

Therefore one part of Lucifer—that is, the opposing body, which consists of the devil, the kings, and the people—falls from heaven and is broken upon the earth.

With these rules Wisdom speaks:

“Listen, therefore, O kings, and understand; learn, you judges of the ends of the earth. Give ear, you who rule the multitude and take pride in the crowds of nations, because authority has been given to you by the Lord and power by the Most High, who will examine your works and scrutinize your thoughts. For although you were ministers of his kingdom, you did not judge rightly, nor did you keep the law” (Wis. VI, 2–3).

The king of Babylon, then, is the whole body; but according to the particular passages we understand to which part of the body each statement applies. “Lucifer has fallen from heaven” can apply to the whole body.

“I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I shall set my throne” applies similarly to the head: to the greater ones who think that they should rule over the stars of God—that is, over the saints—although their inferiors rule over them, as it is written: “The greater shall serve the lesser” (Gen. XXV, 23).

To this Esau—that is, to the evil brothers—the Lord speaks through the prophet Obadiah:

“He exalted his dwelling-place, saying in his heart: ‘Who will bring me down to the earth?’ Though you rise high like an eagle and set your nest among the stars, from there I shall bring you down, says the Lord” (Obad. I, 3–4).

“I shall sit upon the high mountain, above the high mountains toward the north; I shall ascend above the clouds; I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 13).

The high mountain is the proud people. The high mountains are each of the individuals who, gathered together, form the mountain—that is, the body of the devil. Scripture says that there are many evil mountains: “The mountains shall be moved into the heart of the sea” (Ps. XLV, 3). Again: “The foundations of the mountains were shaken and moved, because God was angry” (Ps. XVII, 8).

The body of the Lord, that is, the Church, is also called a mountain; and those individuals who make up the Church are called mountains, as it is written: “But I have been established as king by him upon his holy mountain of Zion, proclaiming his decrees” (Ps. II, 6). Again: “I shall destroy the Assyrians in my land and upon my mountains” (Isa. XIV, 25). Again: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness” (Ps. LXXI, 3). Again: “The mountains shall leap like rams, and the hills like lambs of sheep” (Ps. CXIII, 4).

God has his throne upon Mount Zion, upon the mountains of Israel, and upon his holy clouds, which is the Church. It is written: “Let all the earth fear before the face of the Lord, for he rises from the holy clouds” (Ps. XXXII, 8). Again: “I shall command the clouds not to rain upon it” (Isa. V, 6). Again: “A cloud and darkness are around him” (Ps. XCVI, 2).

That he dwells upon Mount Zion he says in this way: “You shall know that I am the Lord your God, dwelling in Zion, my holy mountain” (Ezek. XXXV, 3).

The devil too sits upon a mountain, namely Seir, which is Esau—that is, the evil brothers. God rebukes this mountain through Ezekiel and says that he will make it desolate, in the joy of the whole earth, because it exercises hostility against Israel. It is the mountain; they are the mountains of the north. The devil sits in them and seems to rule over the clouds of heaven.

Thus far he says that he is like the Most High (Isa. XIV, 14). There are two parts in the Church: the south and the north, that is, the southern and northern regions.

In the southern region the Lord dwells. It is written: “Where do you pasture, where do you dwell at midday?” (Song I, 6). But the devil is in the north, as God says to his people: “I shall drive him away from you, from the north, and expel him into a waterless land—that is, among his own people—and I shall destroy his face in the eastern sea and his rear in the western sea,” which means among the first and last peoples (Joel II, 20).

This world has been fashioned in the likeness of the Church. In it the rising sun has no path except through the south—that is, the southern region—and, after traversing the southern region, it passes invisibly to its place of return. So also our Lord God Jesus Christ, the eternal Sun, traverses his own region, and for this reason he calls it the south.

But he does not rise in the north—that is, in the opposing region—as those same people will say when they come to judgment: “The light of righteousness did not shine for us” (Wis. V, 6).

For those who fear the Lord, however, the Sun of righteousness rises, “and healing is in his wings,” as it is written (Mal. IV, 2).

But for the wicked it is night at midday, as it is written: “While they await the light, darkness has come upon them; they walked in a dark night instead of brightness. They will grope like the blind at a wall, and, having no eyes, they will grope and fall at midday as though at midnight” (Isa. LIX, 9–10, according to the Septuagint).

Again: “The sun shall set at midday, and the day of light shall become dark over the earth” (Amos VIII, 9). Again: “Therefore night shall be your vision, and darkness your divination; the sun shall set upon the prophets, and the day of light shall grow dark over them” (Mic. III, 6).

Against this people from the south God threatens, just as he rebukes Tyre through Ezekiel, saying: “The spirit of the south has crushed you” (Ezek. XXVII, 26). For he permits it to crush them, saying: “Rise, O north wind, and come, O south wind; blow through my garden, and let my spices flow” (Song IV, 16).

When the evil spirit rises, the Holy Spirit resists him; he blows through the Lord’s garden, and the spices are drawn forth—that is, the fragrance of sweetness is offered.

Through Ezekiel God says the same thing concerning the remnants of the evil people, whom he is to bring against his own people—the same people being the mystery of the crime:

“Behold, I am against you, Gog, prince of Mosoch and Tubal. I shall gather you and bring you, and I shall place you from the farthest part of the north; and I shall bring you against the mountains of Israel. I shall break your bow from your left hand and your arrows from your right hand, and I shall cast you upon the mountains of Israel” (Ezek. XXXIX, 1–4).

This takes place from the passion of the Lord until the Church departs from the midst of the same mystery of crime—the Church which restrains it, so that wickedness may be revealed in its own time, as the Apostle says:

“And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of iniquity is already at work; only let the one who now restrains restrain, until he is removed from the midst. And then that wicked one will be revealed” (II Thess. II, 6–8).

We read also in Jeremiah that the sinners of Israel gather in the north, when the Lord says:

“Go and read these words toward the north, and say: ‘Return to me, house of Israel,’ says the Lord” (Jer. III, 12).

The south, however, is the Lord’s region, as it is also written in Job: “From the southern region life shall spring forth there” (Job XI, 17).

The north belongs to the devil. Both regions, however, are found throughout the whole world.

“I shall ascend,” he says, “above the clouds; I shall be like the Most High.” But now you shall descend to the underworld, to the foundations of the earth. Those who see you will marvel at you and say: “This is the man who stirs up the earth, shakes kings, and makes the whole inhabited world desolate.”

Does the statement “Those who see you will marvel at you” apply to the devil? Or to the final king, when he descends to the underworld? For when he descends to the underworld, there will be no one to marvel, since the world will have ended.

They will not say: “This is the man who stirred up the earth, the kings, and made the whole inhabited world desolate,” but rather, “who stirs up, shakes, and makes desolate.” For he calls the whole body a man, both in kings and in peoples. When God strikes and casts down to the underworld the proud part of this man, we say:

“This is the man who stirs up the earth, shakes kings—that is, the saints—and makes the whole inhabited world desolate.”

This is the voice of mockers, not of those confirming a fact, as in the statement: “He who destroys the temple and in three days raises it up” (Mark XV, 29).

For he said:

“I shall accomplish strength and wisdom of understanding. I shall remove the boundaries of nations and lay waste their strength; I shall shatter cities and their inhabitants. I shall grasp the whole inhabited world in my hand like a nest, and like abandoned eggs I shall take it away; and there shall be no one who escapes me or resists me” (Isa. X, 13–14).

Can he fulfill what he promises himself? He does indeed make the whole inhabited world desolate—but his own world. He destroyed cities—namely, the cities of his own world.

For the world is divided into two: the movable and the immovable, as in Chronicles:

“Let all the earth be moved before the face of the Lord. For he founded the inhabited world, and it shall not be moved. He did not release the captives” (I Chron. XVI, 30; Ps. XCV, 9).

This can be understood figuratively: he did not grant release to those held captive in any respect, but, considering them to have been seized by enemies, he exercised his entire sovereign power against them.

God rebukes this, saying: “I was angry for a little while, but they added to the evils” (Zech. I, 15).

Nevertheless, these things were done and said as a figure of the general reality, and they are fulfilled spiritually: whenever those who rule afflict their subjects—whether subjected to them for the sake of testing or by merit—without regard for mercy or their common condition; whenever their authority is not enough for them, but they disdain to use it with moderation. God condemns this, saying: “They pursue retribution” (Isa. I, 23). Again: “He stretched out his hand against him in requital” (Ps. LIV, 21).

For it is not enough that he is an enemy; he still desires to avenge himself upon the subject, as it is written: “You pierce all your subjects.” He pretends to hate the Lord, while being both enemy and avenger, and by vengeance—reserved by God for himself alone—he usurps something of holiness.

For it is written: “Vengeance is mine, and I shall repay, says the Lord” (Rom. XII, 19).

“All the kings of the earth slept in honor, each in his own house” (Isa. XIV, 18–19).

He called the saints kings. For not all kings or private persons slept in their own house, as the saints did in the house they chose.

“But you have been cast upon the mountains like a dead man, abominated together with all those who have fallen, pierced by the sword, and descended to the underworld.”

He says to the devil: “You have been cast upon the mountains,” upon which he sits. Finally, he did not say “dead,” but “like a dead man, abominated.” For he still lives, although he himself is slain in his own people by the sword and descends to the underworld.

For just as the Lord said that whatever his own suffer, he suffers himself (Matt. XXV, 40), so also the devil himself is trampled down in his own people. He himself, abominated, is broken, as it is written: “With the diminution of the people comes the destruction of the prince” (Prov. XIV, 28).

The devil is not separated from his man; nor can the man in whom the devil is say: “I shall be like the Most High.” Nor can the devil—this man who stirs up the earth—exist except in a man.

Just as the Lord cannot be called man except in man, so neither can man exist except in Christ. But to whom each statement applies must be observed according to the individual passages.

Again, the statement applies to the body of the devil:

“How have you come? Just as a garment sprinkled with blood is not clean, so neither will you be clean, because you destroyed my land and killed my people. You shall not endure forever, evil seed. Prepare; kill your sons because of the sins of your father, so that they may not rise again” (Isa. XIV, 19–21, according to the Septuagint).

Here he shows that the statement does not apply figuratively to the king of Babylon, who devastated the Lord’s land and killed his people—that is, to Nebuchadnezzar—for he died in purity and lives forever. Rather, he speaks to the body of each particular age, telling it to prepare those whom it has begotten to be killed by the sins of the one who is begotten and addressed.

For the final king can have not sons but brothers. Nor will he be “like a dead man” when he descends to the underworld, but dead.

Through Ezekiel God rebukes the king of Tyre in this way:

“Because your heart was lifted up and you said: ‘I am God; I have dwelt in the habitation of God, in the heart of the sea.’ But you are a man and not God, and you have made your heart like the heart of God. Are you wiser than Daniel? The wise rebuked you by your wisdom. By your wisdom or your knowledge did you acquire for yourself strength, and gold and silver in your treasuries? By your great knowledge and your commerce did you multiply your strength?

“Therefore thus says the Lord: Because you have made your heart like the heart of God, behold, I am bringing foreign plagues upon you from the nations; they shall empty their swords against you and against the beauty of your knowledge. They shall wound your beauty to destruction; they shall cast you down, and you shall die the death of the wounded in the heart of the sea.

“Will you say before those who kill you: ‘I am God’? But you are a man and not God. You shall perish among the multitude of the uncircumcised, in the hands of foreigners, because I have spoken, says the Lord.

“You are the seal of likeness and the crown of beauty. You were in the delights of the paradise of God. You had every precious stone fastened upon you: sardius, topaz, emerald, carbuncle, sapphire, jasper, silver and gold, ligure, agate, amethyst, chrysolite, beryl, and onyx. You filled your treasuries and storehouses with gold.

“With the cherub I placed you upon the holy mountain of God. You were in the midst of fiery stones. You walked without blemish in your days, from the day on which you were created until iniquities were found in you.

“From the abundance of your commerce you filled your storehouses with iniquity and sins; and you were wounded upon the mountain of God. The cherub drove you out from the midst of the fiery stones. Your heart was lifted up within you; your teaching was corrupted together with your beauty.

“Because of the multitude of your sins and the iniquity of your commerce, your holy places were polluted. I shall bring fire out from your midst; it shall devour you. I shall give you as ashes upon your land in the sight of all who see you. All who know you among the nations shall be grieved over you. You have become destruction, and you shall not endure forever” (Ezek. XXVIII, 2–19, according to the Septuagint).

“Because your heart,” he says, “was lifted up, and you said: ‘I am God; I have dwelt in the habitation of God, in the heart of the sea’”—this also applies to the man who says: “I am Christ,” and to the devil who dwells in the heart of the sea—that is, in the people—just as God sits in the hearts of his saints.

The people dwell in the heart of the sea—that is, in the pleasure or grandeur of the world—as God says elsewhere to the same city: “You are exceedingly satisfied and honored in the heart of the sea. In it your rowers brought you far. The spirit of the south crushed you in the heart of the sea of your strength.”

[Note: Read “water” (aqua).]

“But you are a man and not God” (Ezek. XXVII, 25–26).

The devil in a man is also called “man,” just as the Lord said in the Gospel: “An enemy has done this” (Matt. XIII, 28). And he interpreted it, saying: “The one who sows it is the devil” (ibid., 39).

The man of the devil cannot be God. Therefore the statement applies to both: “You are a man and not God.”

“You have made your heart like the heart of God. Are you wiser than Daniel?”

In Daniel the whole body of the Church is signified, since no one can be wiser in the affairs of life than [Daniel; text uncertain], just as he is wiser in his own affairs than the sons of light.

It can also apply figuratively, since Daniel in particular confounds the king of Babylon in the figure: by the prophetic Spirit he prostrated the proud king before the confession of the one God with ecclesiastical majesty; and by confessing his own virtues and heavenly wisdom he overthrew the superstitions of Babylon.

[Note: Above, the word “not” is lacking.]

“The wise did not rebuke you by your wisdom.” For not Daniel alone was wise, but also the three young men, who, by affirming one Lord, confounded the king and his entire kingdom together with its gods, God himself being present. To this day they generally shatter, by the light of truth, both the external and internal Babylon of the same kind.

“By your knowledge or your wisdom did you acquire strength for yourself, and gold and silver in your treasuries? By your great knowledge or your commerce did you multiply your strength for yourself? And your heart was lifted up in your strength.”

The proud and ungrateful think that they can accomplish something by their own strength and become rich by their wisdom, not knowing that it is written: “The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise” (Eccl. IX, 11). Again: “Will the axe boast without the one who cuts with it?” (Isa. X, 15).

Riches do not belong to the prudent, nor favor to the learned. These things are not in our power but are bestowed by God. “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV, 7). Again: “Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom” (Jer. IX, 23).

Therefore thus says the Lord:

“Because you have made your heart like the heart of God, behold, I am bringing foreigners against you, plagues from the nations; they shall empty their swords against you and against the beauty of your knowledge” (Ezek. XXVIII, 7–8).

Although it can apply figuratively to worldly kings, who in their pride allow themselves to be called lords, it also applies generically. For God frequently brings foreigners into the Church and wounds many to death.

He also brings many from the nations through hidden persecution, in order to test his people and kill the wicked by means of their likenesses, as in the case of Mattathias.

“And they shall wound your beauty to destruction.” For they wound some not to destruction but with the hope of healing.

“And they shall cast you down,” that is, they shall humble you. “And you shall die the death of the wounded in the heart of the sea.”

He would not say to one already wounded, “You shall die the death of the wounded,” unless it were because he is not openly wounded and dies, but is himself present in those who are wounded.

“Will you declare, declaring, before those who kill you: ‘I am God’?” That is: Will you terrify those to whom you are handed over, both spiritually and bodily, with titles belonging to the divine race?

“But you are a man and not God; you shall perish in the multitude of the uncircumcised, by the hands of foreigners, because I have spoken, says the Lord.”

Now he has revealed by what kind of claim he says that he is God: he threatens that he will perish in the multitude of the uncircumcised, by the hands of foreigners. This applies only to one who seems circumcised to himself.

For the king of Tyre could fear death alone: whether he would die among the circumcised or with them.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

“Son of man, take up a lamentation over the prince of Tyre and say to him: Thus says the Lord: You are the seal of likeness, and you were in the paradise of God.”

Was paradise made for the devil, so that he himself, having lost paradise, should be rebuked? It was a man who was in the delights of paradise; he is the seal of likeness, having been made according to the likeness of God.

He called him “the seal” for the sake of beauty, just as God promises the Church through Haggai, when brothers wage war against one another:

“I shall shake heaven and earth, the sea and the dry land; I shall overturn chariots and riders. Horses and their riders shall descend, each with a sword against his brother. On that day, says the Lord Almighty, I shall take you, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, my servant, and I shall make you as a seal, because I have chosen you, says the Lord Almighty” (Hag. II, 22–24; Eccl. XLIX, 13).

Zerubbabel signifies the whole body. For nowhere thereafter do we read that Zerubbabel was shaken and came against anyone. He was of the tribe of Judah and, under Darius, was worthy to build Jerusalem. He also founded the house of God figuratively and completed it, as the same Lord says: “The hands of Zerubbabel laid the foundations of this house, and his hands shall complete it” (Zech. IV, 9).

What this seal and crown of beauty are, God promises to the Church in this way:

“Nations shall see your righteousness, and kings your glory; and they shall call you by a new name, which the Lord has named. You shall be a crown of beauty in the hand of the Lord and a diadem of royalty in the hand of your God. You shall no longer be called Forsaken, and your land shall no longer be called Desolate. You shall also be called ‘My Will,’ and your land ‘The Inhabited World’” (Isa. LXII, 2–4).

The man, therefore, is the seal of likeness and the crown of beauty. One part of him remains in the beauty of the divine likeness and in the delights of paradise—that is, in the Church. But over the other part, lest it live forever, a flaming sword is turned between it and the tree of life (Gen. III, 24).

For Adam, as the Apostle says, is a shadow of the future (Rom. V, 14). Thus also these brothers are divided into Cain and Abel.

“Having every precious stone fastened upon you: sardius, topaz, emerald, carbuncle, sapphire, jasper, silver and gold, ligure, agate, amethyst, chrysolite, beryl, and onyx; and you filled your treasuries and storehouses with gold.”

These things apply both to the devil and to man. For these twelve stones, together with gold and silver, and all the treasures, cling to and are assigned to the devil. Indeed, he says: “You have them fastened upon you.” And again: “Your storehouses are in you.”

Just as the body of the Lord is adorned by the saints, so God promises, saying:

“Lift up your eyes all around and see: all your sons have gathered and have come to you. As I live, says the Lord, you shall put all of them on as clothing and place them upon yourself like the adornment of a bride, because your deserted and ruined places, and those that have fallen, will now be too narrow for their inhabitants” (Isa. XLIX, 18–19; LX, 14).

In the Apocalypse the same city is built upon twelve foundation stones (Apoc. XXI, 19–20).

He says “every precious stone” and enumerates twelve, to show perfection in the number twelve. For everything that God made is good (Gen. I, 25).

The devil changed their use, not their nature. All human beings of exceptional understanding and powerful intellect are, according to nature, gold and silver and precious stones; but they belong to the one whose service enables them to enjoy their nature.

For whoever gives himself over to obedience to someone is that person’s servant, whether of sin or of righteousness. Thus the devil too possesses gold and silver and precious stones—not all of them his according to their origin, but his according to his will.

For in Job it is also written to the devil: “All the gold of the sea is under him” (Job XLI, 21).

And the Apostle says that some vessels of gold and silver are for dishonor (II Tim. II, 20). For he did not, as some think, reject all wooden and earthen vessels, since some of them are for honor, as he himself says: “Does not the potter of clay have power to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. IX, 21).

From wood also, one thing is prepared for use and another for sacrilege. From gold and silver—that is, from great and conspicuous things—he said that they were made unclean.

In the Apocalypse too, the prostitute—that is, the opposing body—is adorned with purple, scarlet, gold, silver, and precious stones, holding in her hand a golden cup full of the abominations and impurities of the whole earth (Apoc. XVII, 4).

These, therefore, are the ornaments of the devil: precious stones, by which he imitates the fiery stones; and man has within himself treasures both of crimes and of conspicuous things.

He himself bears his own possessions, by which his resources have bound him like fetters.

Besides those things which are produced for adornment by both sexes of the devil’s body, even those things that are buried have the heart implanted in them. “For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Matt. VI, 21).

The old man and his earth are one body, because he too is earth. Therefore the Apostle defined not only the things that can be committed with the body but also greed as a member of the possessor, saying:

“Put to death, therefore, your members that are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, passion, evil desire, and greed, which is idolatry. Because of these things the wrath of God is coming” (Col. III, 5–6).

“From the day on which you were created, with the cherub I placed you upon the holy mountain of God” (Ezek. XXVIII, 14)—that is, in Christ or the Church.

“You were in the midst of fiery stones,” that is, holy men who, when gathered together, form the mountain of God. Angels, being of another substance, cannot be called stones, because they do not have bodies.

“You walked without blemish in your days, from the day on which you were created, until iniquities were found in you, from the abundance of your commerce” (ibid., 15).

Peter says that the stones are the Church:

“Behold, brothers, as living stones, you are being built together into spiritual houses” (I Pet. II, 5).

God says that this house is fiery and that it burns the evil brothers:

“The house of Jacob shall be fire, and the house of Joseph a flame; but the house of Esau shall be stubble. They shall burn them and consume them, and there shall be no fire-bearer in the house of Esau, for the Lord has spoken” (Obad. 18).

When a man sins, he is cast down from the mountain of God; and there will be no fire-bearer, since he has lost the Spirit, and he will be burned to ashes.

“You sinned, and you were wounded upon the mountain of God; and the cherub drove you out from the midst of the fiery stones.”

[The cherub is the ministry of God, which excluded all the wicked from the Church, but spiritually. For the one who does not have the wedding garment is excluded in this world from the midst of those reclining at the feast. Finally, he is sent into darkness—that is, into hardness of heart—until he descends into the eternal fire. In the world to come no one will be mingled with the choir of the saints who is afterward excluded.]

“Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty; your knowledge was corrupted together with your beauty.”

His knowledge is corrupted who, although knowingly and deliberately, asserts a lie while concealing the truth under the pretense of cultivated wisdom, as the Spirit says:

“When they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became foolish in their thoughts, saying that they were wise” (Rom. I, 21–22).

[The knowledge of those who teach others but do not teach themselves is corrupted. The beauty of one who does not correspond to his own kind by the likeness of his works is corrupted.]

“Because of the multitude of your sins I cast you upon the earth; I gave you to be dishonored in the sight of kings” (Ezek. XXVIII, 18).

The devil too is upon the earth—that is, in man—and man is cast down from the height of the Church to be trampled underfoot, if Jeremiah says:

“He cast down from heaven to earth the glory of Israel, in the sight of kings” (Lam. II, 1).

He means Christians, whose feet trample upon the devil and his man.

[Because of the multitude of your sins and the iniquity of your commerce, your holy places are polluted.]

He seems to have reproached the body of the devil with its principal title: he speaks rather of commerce and treasures, which are spiritual wickedness.

For just as commerce in spiritual righteousness is a treasure, as the Lord says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant” (Matt. XIII, 45), and again: “Store up treasures for yourselves in heaven” (Matt. VI, 20), and again: “He gave his servants his property, so that they might trade with it” (Luke XIX, 13), and again: “The merchants of Carthage—resistentib., etc.” (Ezek. XXVII, 12), and again: “Its commerce and its wages shall be holy to the Lord” (Isa. XXIII, 18), and the Apostle says: “Godliness is great commerce” (I Tim. VI, 6)—so spiritual wickedness is a commerce consisting of a treasure of sins, as the Lord says: “The evil man brings forth evil things from the treasure of his heart” (Matt. XII, 35), and the Apostle: “You are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath” (Rom. II, 5).

“Because of the iniquity,” he says, “of your commerce, your holy places are polluted.”

For whoever does not use God’s holiness rightly makes it his own, just as God says concerning his sabbaths: “My soul hates your sabbaths.”

“I shall bring fire out from your midst; it shall devour you” (Isa. I, 13).

The fire is the Church. When it has departed from the midst of the mystery of crime, then the Lord will rain fire from the Lord, from the Church, as it is written:

“The sun rose over the earth, and Lot entered Zoar; and the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the Lord out of heaven” (Gen. XIX, 23–24).

This is the fire of which he said above:

“The house of Jacob shall be fire, and the house of Esau stubble. They shall burn them and consume them, and there shall be no fire-bearer in the house of Esau” (Obad. 18).

Again in Genesis it is written:

“When God destroyed all the cities round about, God remembered Abraham and brought Lot out from the midst of the overthrow, when God overthrew the cities in which Lot dwelt” (Gen. XIX, 29).

Did Lot not deserve to be saved by his own righteousness, so that Scripture should say, “God remembered Abraham and brought Lot out from the midst of the overthrow”? Or did he dwell in cities, and not in one city, so that it should say, “the cities in which Lot dwelt”?

This is a prophecy of the future departure. Remembering the promise made to Abraham, God cast Lot out from all the cities of the Sodomites, upon which the fire from the fire of the Church will come—the Church that will be led out from their midst.

“And I shall give you as ashes upon your land” (Ezek. XXVIII, 18)—that is, among human beings, or the human beings themselves upon their own land, who were unwilling to be in God’s land.

“In the sight of those who see you”—that is, of those who understand.

Can the devil be seen in a man?

“And all who know you among the nations shall grieve over you” (ibid., 19).

For when the Lord strikes or exposes the wicked, those who were accustomed to rely upon their assistance grieve, because a part of their body has been weakened.

“You have become destruction, and you shall not endure forever.”

[Col. 0065] Augustine examined these Rules of Tyconius in volume III, book III, chapters 30–37, of *On Christian Doctrine*.

## In the Year of the Lord 398. Hilary the Deacon

[Col. 0065]

## Prolegomena

*(From Schoenemann, volume I, p. 306.)*

[Col. 0065C]

### 1. The Life of Hilary the Deacon

He was from Sardinia. He was a deacon of the Roman Church. In that capacity he was sent by Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, to Constantius after the Council of Arles. When he had vigorously defended the cause of Athanasius at the council held at Milan, he was beaten with rods and sent into exile together with Lucifer and Pancratius.

Later he joined Lucifer, but proceeded so far in his rash opinion that he decided that the Arians, those who had communicated with them, and absolutely all who had been contaminated by any heresy had to be baptized again before they could be received into the fellowship of the Catholic Church. For this reason Jerome wittily, though not very accurately, called him the Deucalion of the world.

It was fortunate for the Church at that time that Hilary was only a deacon. Since there was no means of ordaining clergy, scarcely anyone joined him; and thus this teaching of his—which otherwise would have provoked an enormous schism—perished with its author [lacuna].

### 2. His Writings

The writings commonly attributed to Hilary are of very uncertain and doubtful authenticity: namely, the commentary on the Epistles of Paul, customarily published with Ambrose, and the *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, found among Augustine’s works. Oudinus discussed these matters more fully, while arguing that both works should be denied to Hilary, in volume I of *On the Saints of the Church*, pp. 480–491.

[Col. 0065]

## Commentary on the Twelve Epistles of Blessed Paul, Ascribed to Hilary the Deacon

(See this commentary among the spurious works appended to the works of Saint Ambrose, volume XVII of our *Patrology*.)

[Col. 0067]

## Questions on the Old and New Testaments Attributed to Hilary the Deacon

## In an Uncertain Year of the Lord. Novatus the Catholic

[Col. 0067]

# NOVATUS’S TREATISE ON HUMILITY AND OBEDIENCE, AND ON TRAMPLING DOWN PRIDE (C, S)

[Col. 0067A] We speak one way in the Church to secular people, and we ought to speak another way to you. To them we sometimes speak of things that have sound but no power, for, being weak, they take pleasure in the sound of words rather than in the power of God. You, however, in the name of Christ, do not take pleasure in this; rather, you wish to hear the word of salvation, in which you have been called. You have put on these mournful garments in the world, awaiting better ones with God.

You already know and understand this. You have now spent a long time here struggling against the one with whom you must wrestle. Your adversary is not outside but within, in your very inward parts; we have an opponent in our own limbs. For if the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that we do not do the things we wish (Gal. 5:17), you see that this adversary is within.

[Col. 0067B] This adversary, however, is overcome only by humility and love. For our Lord Jesus Christ Himself would not have overcome the devil unless He had humbled Himself; and He was humbled not by necessity but by love. If He had not loved, He would not have become humble. He became humble because of His love for us.

If, then, He who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them (Ps. 145:4), the Lord of all the angels, who created all things, became humble for our sake, why do we refuse humility for our own sake? The way of salvation, therefore, is not open to us unless we are humbled.

When you begin to practice humility, seek it for God’s sake and endure it for the sake of this community. In the community, although you are equals, each person ought to regard the other as superior to himself, even though he is not actually superior. No one does this unless he possesses humility.

The servants of God need no other reward than humility, because humility, when it exists in a person, makes him obedient. Whoever is obedient, or pursues obedience, obeys not human beings but God. For the Lord says: “Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever hears me hears him who sent me” (Luke 10:16).

The abbot is the father; the brothers who follow are patriarchs. Whoever else among you perhaps has a good life, greater continence, more excellent vigils, or better care of his body is also, by virtue of imitation, a father.

Therefore act in this way among yourselves: first, preserve humility, not so that you may appear humble to human beings, but to God. That is true humility which is shown to God, not to human beings. For humility displayed to people is pretense, not humility; and this ought to be entirely foreign to the servants of God.

I do not, of course, think that there are such people among you; but I admonish you lest such a disease creep in.

[Col. 0068B] We are human beings, and we speak to human beings. Therefore you ought first to show humility to your brothers for the sake of imitation, so that humility itself may be founded inwardly in the heart according to God. For when humility has been founded in your heart for God’s sake, then God grants that your brother may understand and imitate your humility. But if humility has not been founded in your heart, God reveals to your brother that your humility is feigned.

This, then, is the first way of salvation: to hold to simple humility for God’s sake, not for human beings; not to please people by it, but to please God.

Let obedience follow humility, and obey one another just as the limbs obey one another. Do the limbs obey by deliberation, and not by natural love? If the foot stumbles, the hand comes to its aid, lest the whole body be injured and fall. As the Apostle says: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (1 Cor. 12:26).

[Col. 0068C] From what source, then, does this arise, except love? If you love one another, there will be no disturbance. Let no one suffer scandals—not on account of food, drink, clothing, vigils, work, the kitchen, or service.

Once you love one another, if someone does something he ought not to do, that love will not allow you to take offense.

Have, then, brothers, humility and obedience, followed by peace, so that you may be children of peace. For love, as the Apostle says, is “the bond of perfection” (Col. 3:14).

When someone possesses humility, he imitates Christ, who became humble for our sake. When someone possesses obedience, he imitates Christ, who became obedient unto death (Phil. 2:8). When someone possesses love, he imitates Christ, because “God is love” (1 John 5:16).

[Col. 0069B] But first strive to conquer your vices within. Let peace first be made in soul and heart with God’s commandment, so that against the habit and weakness of the body there may be two victors: God’s commandment and your consent.

The situation is like this: there is a physician, a sick person, and an illness. If the sick person gives himself over to the illness, the physician is defeated; two become arrayed against one, and the physician is overcome. But if the sick person joins himself to the physician, the illness is defeated.

Christ is the physician; we are the sick; the disease of the illness is the habit of sin.

Whoever has already renounced the world in part, although he lives in the world, should consider where he ought to cling: to the illness or to the physician. If he does not cling to the physician, the physician labors.

Therefore the Gospel cries out to us in the world [Col. 0069C] and says: “Be reconciled with your adversary quickly, while you are with him on the way” (Matt. 5:25). It does not teach us to agree with the adversary, the devil; rather, it teaches us to agree with the adversary that is God’s commandment, which opposes our evils, our habits, and our iniquities.

If we agree, we become reconciled with God’s commandment and receive, as it were, God’s yoke. For this reason the Lord says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, for it is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:28).

[Col. 0069D] See what is so light. Consider, finally, how those who possess something in this world fear that it may be taken away. How they fear losing what they have acquired! In what ways they torment themselves, as though they were carrying anxiety under a very heavy burden!

You, however, have no other labor than to do what the abbot commands. You are already under the yoke; you do not think about where you will live, because you ought not to think about it. There is one who governs you; there is one who cares for you. The concern for food and clothing ought not to belong to you at all.

Whatever the abbot gives, regard it as though God had given it. This is true humility. But perhaps one person has more and another less; regard this also as having been done by God. One person sits at one table and another at another; if the abbot orders it, if he approves it, regard it as though God had commanded it.

Do not question this by saying, “Tomorrow I shall sit there.” Do not make it your habit to impose that necessity upon yourself.

[Col. 0070A] If perhaps there is nothing to be given, or it does not seem appropriate that it should be given, accept it either because there is nothing to give or because it has seemed unwise to give it.

If you preserve these things, brothers, you will certainly possess eternal life.

Do not allow yourselves to be driven by evil words. If perhaps a sick person falls into speaking perversely, restrain him immediately; say at once: “Do not do this; do not, brother—you are sinning.”

For since you are together as one and have one abbot, you ought also to be abbots to one another. Can one man, because he has two eyes and two ears, hear everyone or see everyone? Does he not also need to go out somewhere and attend to something?

Be abbots to one another. And just as you fear the abbot when he is present, fear him also when he is absent, because God is present. Fear and dread this above all: God is always present.

[Col. 0070B] If one man cares for so many, how much more ought all of you to care for one another, lest he find cause for anger, sorrow, offense, or groaning, or think that the labor of so much time will perish.

These things will be able to benefit us only if we possess humility, obedience, and love. There is no other way to God except humility, obedience, and love. He Himself is the way, the truth, and the life.

To suffer, fast for two, three, or four days, and frequently make fasts lasting whole weeks—because of these things brothers become proud, thinking that what they do no one else can do. They consider it extraordinary that another cannot do it. Or someone walks barefoot and thinks that he alone can do this. Or perhaps he does not even drink mixed water [the omitted complement is uncertain]; this is a temporary exercise, since he cannot always do it.

[Col. 0070C] Rather, let him think of humility, piety, love, and obedience. He ought to undertake these practices as a good athlete in order to break the strength of the body and subdue the blood and flesh; but he must not boast about them, lest he lose what he has accomplished.

For that Pharisee who went up into the Temple to pray—were the works he enumerated insignificant? They were immense: to fast twice on the Sabbath, to give tithes of all his possessions to the poor, to commit no fraud, and not to commit adultery—these are no small things. But because he vaunted them in pride, everything he had done became pride (Luke 18:9 ff.).

Therefore David says: “Let not the foot of pride come against me, and let not the hand of sinners move me. There all who practice iniquity have fallen” (Ps. 35:12).

Where did they fall? In the fall of pride. For the devil fell from there; he fell through pride.

Pride, therefore, must not be admitted at all among the servants of God. Whoever now lives differently and has ordered his life better must not be like that Pharisee.

The tax collector, however, humbled, did not dare even to raise his eyes to heaven; and, commended by the Lord’s verdict, he returned to his home more justified than that Pharisee.

We have learned by experience, both from the holy Scriptures and from our brothers, that whoever has held to the way of humility makes progress and does not perish.

# ANONYMOUS AUTHOR WHOSE WORKS WERE PUBLISHED UNDER THE NAME OF SAINT ATHANASIUS

From the works of Saint Athanasius, vol. III.

[Col. 0071]

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING TWO ASCETIC WORKS

For many centuries the following two ascetic exhortations, one addressed to monks and the other to the brides of Christ, have appeared under the name of Athanasius. In the collection of Rules compiled in the eighth century by Benedict of Aniane, both are found bearing the name of Athanasius, although neither admits anything of Athanasius except the name.

Indeed, it is clearer than daylight that they were composed by a Latin writer—an elegant and highly accomplished writer in Latin, especially for that age. The second appears complete in the Acts of the Council of Aachen and is attributed to Athanasius. Hence one may perhaps suspect that it, and likewise the earlier work, which was written in nearly the same style, was marked with Athanasius’s name by its author as a recommendation.

Both little works were published in the Appendix to the Codex of Rules, edited by Lucas Holstenius, in Paris in 1663.

[Col. 0071]

## EXHORTATION TO MONKS (C, S)

[Col. 0071A] If it is permissible to glory in Christ at all, then, having been initiated into principles of this kind, so that your beginning may be perfection, and having flown past the intervening stages toward the true fruit of life and occupied the very summit, you should hold to the full measure of discipline, so that everyone ought to wish to have you as his models and to imitate you rather than think that he can be trained by anyone else.

Yet paternal affection has assigned to me this license of privilege, and the fulfillment of your appeal is something I must embrace. While you listen to me, you have made me bold through your love—not merely willingly, but eagerly.

I lead those who precede me, and, stretched beyond the measure of my ability, I am compelled to lead those whom I desire to follow. I shall therefore proceed along the path of your life, so that, like one who is being instructed in the first elements of letters and treads upon drawn outlines with an imitative stylus, I may trace the figures prefigured in shadows, as you advance toward the hoped-for rewards of your blessed way of life, which must be pursued.

[Col. 0071B] First come care for abstinence, fasting, patience, perseverance in prayer and reading—or, if someone is still without letters, the desire to listen along with the eagerness to learn. These are, as it were, the first toys of infants’ cradles in the knowledge of God, by which a person, warned and instructed, begins to wish to enter the path of his divine origin, while he gradually becomes accustomed to being able to do so.

In teaching these things, I am not speaking of the indiscriminate faith of the common crowd, which is content with the mere confession of almighty God that has been imparted and the instruction in singular innocence that has been instilled, with pardon alone.

Although our Lord, as we read (Rom. 7:6), wishes all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, yet, because not everyone can attain the capacity for preeminent grace, “not all who are from Israel are Israelites” (Gen. 21; Gal. 4). Ishmael, after all, is excluded from participation in his brother’s inheritance, while Jacob and Esau, struggling with one another, burst from the enclosure of one womb.

[Col. 0072A] Or, content with the well of living water, let us prepare ourselves as a holocaust of ourselves, a sacrifice of voluntary offering, desiring and preparing food, and granting to those foremost ones, as the measure of pardon, this judgment: “Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Tim. 4:4).

For us, striving through that labor toward the reward of glory, “it is good not to eat flesh or drink wine.” And again: “Everyone who competes in the contest abstains from everything” (1 Cor. 9:25). They do so in order to receive a perishable crown; we, an imperishable one.

Abstinence is the nurse of continence. Through it, whether unmarried or married, a person more easily submits to the restraints of passion if he is not spurred on by the goads of pleasure. Thus I wish, or command, those who strive toward the highest things to honor it, lest they think that marriage is a crime in others, knowing that it is written: “It is good to marry, better not to marry” (1 Cor. 7:37).

Those who consider this unlawful diminish the reward of their labor. To avoid what is unlawful is the yoke of necessity; to overcome what is permitted is the gift of free choice. To abstain from evils is the reward of discipline; to surpass good things is the freedom of merit, not the end of command. The former is granted by the law within limits; the latter is reserved for the increase of grace.

### 2

There should likewise be no fixed measure of fasting for those who wish to fast, but it should be extended as far as the ability of the one who labors can endure. Apart from Sundays, these fasts should always be solemn observances when they are undertaken as vows.

Preparing himself through these practices, the most blessed Moses made himself worthy of God’s utterances. Through them the threats foretold by Jonah turned the Ninevites once more toward a favorable sentence. Through them the people of Bethulia, shut in by the Assyrian siege and terrified by repeated trials of courage even to the point of surrender, deserved to be delivered from the swelling threats of Holofernes by the steadfast hand of a woman.

[Col. 0072C] Through them Mordecai brought the cruelly proud Haman to the gallows he had prepared for himself, turning the punishment back upon its author. Through them Jesus our Savior, instructed in the human flesh He had assumed, blunted the persuasions of the tempting devil.

Although He could have driven them away by other means, He nevertheless wished to shape the peoples who were to be taught through this example.

Prayer must be pursued so constantly that scarcely any time passes between prayers. For it is written: “Persist in prayers, keeping watch in them” (Matt. 7:18). And again: “Seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matt. 6:19).

Through prayer a sleeping friend is awakened; and although deep sleep has overtaken the entire household, the importunate petitioner nevertheless extorts from him the bread that he asks to have brought out and given to him.

[Col. 0073A] If possible, let only the interval devoted to reading interrupt these prayers. Care concerning this should be placed in the canonical writings—not because we ought to condemn the apocryphal books, especially those unknown to us, but because we think the sequence of the canon sufficient for an ordered knowledge of God. If those writings agree with the canon, they are superfluous; if they disagree, they are to be avoided.

Without devotion to reading no one will be able to remain intent upon the Lord. First, works of this kind draw us away from the fleeting occupations of other activities; and the knowledge conveyed by diverse examples makes us either desire what is good or beware of what is evil.

Otherwise the Apostle Peter would not admonish us, saying: “Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for an account of the word of your hope and faith” (1 Pet. 3:16). And the Apostle says: “We do not cease praying for you, that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding” (Col. 1:9). And again: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom” (Col. 5:16).

[Col. 0073C] In the Old Testament also, inspired speech impressed a similar care for sacred instruction upon human beings. Thus David says: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence. But his delight is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he will meditate day and night” (Ps. 1:1).

And God speaks to Joshua: “This book shall not depart from your hands, and you shall meditate on it day and night” (Josh. 1:8).

Even amid these occupations the slippery thoughts of evil things frequently insinuate themselves. Although such diligence itself directs the mind toward God, it nevertheless makes the mind anxious through the gnawing concern of the world.

### 3

[Col. 0073D] If someone devoted to religious labor frequently and importunately suffers these disturbances, an idle person will certainly never be free of them.

Now that we have arranged the limbs of study, let us increase and complete the growth of conduct.

I think this point should also be mentioned: food should be simple and clothing cheap, since these things were discovered for covering the body, not adorning it; and food is for sustaining the soul rather than overwhelming it.

Dedicated to the practices we have set forth above, let the person put aside all hatred of his enemy. Nor should he be content with this alone: let him exchange hostility for love, temper anger with the bridle of patience, overcome greed by the strong authority of abstinence, and especially fence in his tongue with the guardianship of silence.

Let it not flare up contentiously into quarrels; let it not fall shamelessly into cursing; let it not creep maliciously into slander; let it not slip easily into swearing; let it not feign falsehood; let it not practice cunning in deception; let it not boast arrogantly in self-exaltation.

[Col. 0074A] Rather, observing a time for silence and a time for speech, let him know that every idle word is liable to judgment. For this reason the most blessed David asks that a guard be set over his mouth. The sacred writing of the blessed Paul declares that speech must be seasoned with salt. And the teaching attested by James has shown that no member is so untamable as the tongue.

Let the person who climbs this path therefore be silent, gentle, and kind. Since the affection of charity is considered indissoluble, let him always, with equal zeal, judge another to be better than himself.

By this bridle he restrains envy, which is so often aroused by the judgment of neighboring pride; for, while he seeks the honor that he thinks is owed to him, he incurs the mark of wretched resentment.

Nor does each person first perceive how much this is so when he demands it from human beings: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet. 5:5). When teaching his disciples this practice, Christ declares that the greatest is the one who wishes to be least of all.

If some people honor your brother more generously, do not therefore regard them as less friendly, nor regard him as a rival because of the honor shown to him above you. Rather, judge that the increase of his honor brings increase to you, knowing that it is written: “If one member glories, all the members rejoice with it. Now you are the body of Christ, and members” (1 Cor. 12:26).

[Col. 0074C] For whoever loves one of you ascribes every dignity to God, into whom you have gathered yourselves.

In this there is a pleasing gentle silence; in this a gracious affability is loved. One person is commended by an unformed and innate simplicity, another by learned knowledge. The patience of one in the constancy of fasting is praised; another’s contempt in the strength of abstinence; another’s diligence in the constancy of reading—all according to the diversity of divine gifts.

As it is written: “One and the same Spirit accomplishes all these things, distributing to each one individually as he wills. For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ. For we have all been baptized in one Spirit into one body” (1 Cor. 12:11).

Each of you may claim the sum of all good things for yourselves, provided that no one begins to exalt himself in the matter in which another excels.

[Col. 0074D] But when you bind one another tightly with the bond of charity, do not condemn those outside who are still bound by worldly ties in their secular way of life, knowing that it is written: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged” (Luke 6:37). And again: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master. And he will stand, for God is able to make him stand” (Rom. 14:4).

Rather, by exhortations to kindness and by inviting gentleness, show them the way of truth and clear away the cloud of error, so that no one may begin to be dragged along, but may follow the one who goes before.

### 4

[Col. 0074D] The harsher things must always be bent, lest a curvature weakened by force, before it comes into a circle, strike against a fragment that is breaking apart. For scandals among the common people are often generated here through mockery, when censorial authority is arrogated over the yoke of religion.

Let our life give commands and our tongue persuade, because example carries greater authority, and the gentle formation of conduct instills the desire to imitate it.

Therefore shine in all your conduct as though in a reflecting mirror. Be watchful everywhere and concerned everywhere, lest envy find something, or false rumor inflict something.

Honor reputable women who are truly devoted to religious observance, with a measured degree of respect, so that neither inhuman severity nor lax attentiveness may be present.

Your visits to one another should not be forced but natural—made necessary by a reason, not permitted by superfluity. Let several be received together with several; or, if at some time a number of the other sex is lacking, let either the proven gravity of a particular age, the prominence of the place, or the appropriateness of the time make it honorable, since above all age, time, and solitude must be avoided by you.

[Col. 0075B] This is not because I am permitted to judge otherwise concerning those who have once truly devoted their hearts to God, but so that, out of abundant caution, we may guard against everything that can be imagined as though it could also be believed. Let suspicion born of opportunity perish before it is nourished by tongues.

Not only the credibility of an act, but even the possibility of a lie, must be restrained. Blessed and splendid is the life concerning which falsehood is permitted nothing.

I have not taken up this judgment as a harsh censor; rather, as a gentle admonisher, I have assumed a heavenly command. For the Apostle says: “Being jealous over you with the jealousy of God, I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2), knowing that it is written: “Do not put a stumbling block or an occasion of offense before your brother” (Rom. 14:13); and again: “Be without offense to Jews and Greeks and to the Church of God” (1 Cor. 10:32); and again: “Let not our good be blasphemed” (Rom. 14:16); and again: “Why should my freedom be judged by another’s conscience?” (1 Cor. 10:29); and again: “Let all your things be done honorably” (1 Cor. 14:40); and again: “Commending ourselves to every human conscience before God” (2 Cor. 4:2); and again: “Let us provide what is good not only before God but also before human beings” (Rom. 12:17); and again: “So that the one who opposes may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us” (Tit. 2:8).

[Col. 0075C] Nor am I unaware that the envy of secular malice is always burning to slander religion and fixing the biting tooth of mockery into malicious rumors.

Let the world follow its own nature, provided that it finds nothing in our discipline. Let falsehood be loudly proclaimed according to custom, provided that what is said cannot even appear plausible.

No one ought to disregard the wound of defamation because rumor has always been accustomed to fabricate; rather, he should take greater care, since rumor is also accustomed to compose inventions.

No one should be made secure from fear of slander by the regularity of slander itself. Nor is negligence justified by the fact that anxiety has become a continual matter.

Let there therefore be a safe and watchful guardianship of your modesty and reverence.

Leave the house only when necessary, and rarely—when religious duty has sent you out, or when the needs of sustenance have arranged that you undertake some work.

Abstain from all gifts except those sufficient for daily food and yearly clothing, knowing that it is written: “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (1 Tim. 6:8); and again: “Walk honorably toward those who are outside, and desire nothing from anyone” (1 Thess. 4:12).

[Col. 0076A] Nor, even for the sake of giving alms, should you presume to take anything from anyone beyond what has been mentioned for sustenance, knowing that it is written: “If the will is ready, it is accepted according to what one has, not according to what one does not have” (2 Cor. 8:12).

Thus the divine saying of the Gospel, which tells of a poor widow placing only two small coins among the abundant gifts of the rich, enriched her with magnificent acceptance of her offering. For what is everything cannot be little. No one gave more than the one who kept nothing for herself.

### 5

[Col. 0076A] If these requirements seem too strict to anyone besides you who has attempted to knock at God’s gates, he may relax them according to what his circumstances require, lest someone be bound by a spouse or hindered by children.

Apart from these things, the strict substance of the religious life has many matters that may follow. Let no one think himself rejected, but admitted to the entrance of another calling, as it is written: “Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called” (1 Cor. 7:24).

Yet he must not devote more attentive care to his property than to religion, becoming more occupied with what is perishable, recognizing that those who possess should live “as though they did not possess.”

If a more fortunate nature has freed someone from the fetter of offspring—provided that he understands it—he will have no reason to remain in the world unless he is ignorant of God’s gifts.

Why should he not, by his will to live, release what must be broken by the law of dying, making profit from his lot, so that he may increase virtue from necessity?

Rather, whoever makes great things from small things and precious things from worthless things in his household, making eternal things from perishable ones, is the only person who, after arriving there, can be the everlasting possessor of his inheritance.

[Col. 0076C] If he is not greedy, he ought to despise what must be ended; if he is greedy, he ought to desire things everlasting, knowing that it is written: “Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves neither break in nor steal” (Matt. 19:20).

For one who is not without children, this is an exhortation; for one who is without them, it is a command.

One who practices all these things—appropriate to the times, suited to the persons, filled with examples, seasoned with kindness, attractive in expression, and marked by the gentle integrity of exhortation—can persuade more easily.

For you are not envious of any fruit of all these things, nor are you deprived of them by anyone’s judgment. Certainly you possessed a strong body, an unimpaired age, and unformed minds, while, within the narrow limits permitted by the diversity of the human race, there lay open to you either the practice of trade, or the ambition of military service, or various crafts, or innumerable occupations in worldly affairs by which your resources might be increased.

[Col. 0076D] Finally, there was no lack either of a poor wife, who might prepare the pleasures of life, or of the endearments of children implanted in human feeling.

You have rejected all these things in body and in chaste affections, preserving the pattern of the divine judgment through religious actions, as Scripture says: “Whoever prefers house, wife, or children to me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:27).

Therefore, seeing your examples, let those who have come to pursue this way of life with equal possessions not despair through a narrow assessment of their own merits.

Having been established on this path of life, therefore, dearly beloved sons, devote yourselves and see that the Lord is sweet.

[Col. 0077A] Spend your days and nights in readings and prayers, and remember always me, whom you chose as your teacher even though I am the least formed [or: “abortive”] of all priests in work and knowledge.

“Keep watch, stand firm in the faith, act manfully, be strong. Let all your things be done in love, and the God of peace will be with you” (1 Cor. 16:13).

[Col. 0077]

## EXHORTATION TO THE BRIDE OF CHRIST (C, G, S)*

[Col. 0077A] 1. How great a blessedness in heaven holy virginity possesses, we learn not only from the testimony of the Scriptures but also from the custom of the Church. For we learn that a particular merit belongs to it, whose consecration is special.

Although the whole multitude of believers receives equal gifts of grace and all alike glory in the same sacramental blessings, these women possess something of their own beyond the rest. From that holy and spotless flock of the Church they are chosen by the Holy Spirit, as holier and purer sacrifices, according to the merits of their will, and are offered upon the altar by the supreme priest of God.

Truly worthy of the Lord is the offering of such a precious creature, and no sacrifice is more pleasing to Him than the sacrifice of His own image.

I think the Apostle spoke especially of such women when he said: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Rom. 12:1).

[Col. 0077B] Virginity therefore possesses both what others have and what others do not have. It possesses both a common and a special grace, and rejoices, so to speak, in the privilege of its own consecration.

Ecclesiastical authority also permits us to call virgins brides of Christ, since the Church veils those whom she consecrates to the Lord in the manner of brides. She thereby shows that those who have avoided carnal union will possess spiritual marriage to the greatest degree.

And rightly are those spiritually joined to God through the comparison of marriage who, for love of Him, have rejected human marriages. In them above all is fulfilled the Apostle’s saying: “Whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17).

### 2

[Col. 0077C] Great and immortal, almost beyond bodily nature, is the task of putting luxury to sleep, extinguishing by strength of mind the flame of desire kindled by the torches of youth, and by spiritual effort excluding the force of natural pleasure; to live contrary to the custom of the human race, despise the consolations of spouses, reject the sweetness of children, and count as nothing all the advantages that may belong to the present life for the sake of hope in future blessedness.

These are, as I have said, great and admirable virtues, and not undeservedly are they destined for an immense reward in proportion to the greatness of their labor.

“I shall give,” says the Lord, “to my eunuchs in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters of Israel; I shall give them an everlasting name that shall not perish” (Isa. 56:4).

Concerning these eunuchs the Lord repeats in the Gospel, saying: “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:12).

The labor of chastity is indeed great, but its reward is greater: its guardianship is temporary, but its recompense eternal.

[Col. 0077D] The blessed Apostle John also speaks of these, saying that they follow the Lamb wherever He goes (Rev. 14:4). Understand this as meaning that no place in the heavenly court will be closed to them, and that all the dwelling places of God will be opened to them.

But so that the merit of virginity may shine more clearly, and so that it may be more plainly understood how worthy it is of God, let this be considered: when our Lord and Savior, who is God, deigned to assume humanity for the salvation of the human race, He chose no other than a virginal womb.

And to show that such a state was especially pleasing to Him, and to make known the goodness of chastity to both sexes, He had a virgin for His mother while remaining a virgin Himself. In Himself He offered an example of virginity to men, and in His mother to women.

[Col. 0078B] Thus it might be demonstrated that blessed integrity is possessed in both sexes in the Godhead and has merited from its fullness [the transmitted reading is uncertain]; for whatever was possessed in the Son was wholly present in the mother.

But why do I labor to reveal the excellent and sublime merit of chastity and display the goodness of glorious virginity, when I know that many have already spoken at length on this subject, established its blessedness by the clearest arguments, and shown that no wise person can doubt that the matter demanding the greater labor possesses the greater merit?

Whoever considers chastity to be worthy of no reward or only a small one clearly either does not understand it or does not willingly undertake its labor. For those who either do not possess chastity or are compelled to possess it unwillingly always disparage it.

[Col. 0078C] **3.** Since, then, as briefly as possible, we have shown both the labor and the merit of integrity, lest a thing established by great virtue and destined for an immense reward should be deprived of its fruit, we must keep watch with greater diligence. For the more precious any kind of thing is, the greater the care with which it is guarded. And since there are many things that lack their own excellence unless they are supported by the help of other things—as with honey, which, unless it is preserved in the protection of wax and the cells of the honeycombs, and, to speak more accurately, nourished by them, loses its natural sweetness and cannot subsist by itself; just so with wine, which, unless its vessel is of good quality and is frequently renewed by coating it with pitch, loses the genuine force of its pleasantness—therefore we must take more careful thought, lest virginity too should require other things without which it cannot at all produce fruit; and lest so great a labor should benefit nothing, while what is possessed without the necessary accompanying things is vainly believed to be beneficial.

For, unless I am mistaken, integrity of chastity is preserved for the reward of the heavenly kingdom; and it is sufficiently certain that no one can attain that reward without the merit of eternal life. Scripture testifies that eternal life can be earned only through the observance of all the divine commandments, saying: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. XIX, 17). Therefore no one possesses life except the one who has kept all the commandments of the law; and whoever does not possess life cannot be an heir of the heavenly kingdom, in which not the dead but all who are alive will reign.

Virginity alone, then, will accomplish nothing, though it hopes for the glory of the heavenly kingdom, unless it also possesses that to which perpetual life is promised, through which the reward of the heavenly kingdom is possessed. Before all else, therefore, those who preserve chastity and integrity and hope for its recompense from God’s justice must observe the commandments, lest the labor of glorious chastity and continence be brought to nothing.

No wise and learned person is unaware that virginity stands above a commandment or precept, since the Apostle says: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel” (1 Cor. VII, 25). When, therefore, he gives counsel concerning the preservation of virginity, he does not establish a commandment; rather, he declares that it stands above a commandment or precept. Whoever, then, preserves virginity does more than is commanded. Doing more than one has been ordered will benefit only if one does what has been ordered.

Desiring to fulfill the divine counsel, keep the commandment above all else; wishing to obtain the reward of virginity, embrace the merits of life, so that your chastity may be rewarded. For just as the observance of the commandments bestows life, so, conversely, their transgression produces death. And one who has been consigned to death through transgression cannot hope for the crown of virginity, nor can one appointed to punishment expect the reward of chastity.

**4.** There are three forms by which one enters into possession of the heavenly kingdom. The first is chastity; the second, contempt of the world; the third, justice. Just as, when joined together, these confer great benefit upon those who possess them, so, when separated, they can scarcely be useful, since each is demanded not merely for its own sake but for the sake of the others.

First, therefore, chastity is sought, so that contempt of the world may more easily follow; for the world can be despised more readily by those who are not held by the bonds of marriage. Contempt of the world, in turn, is demanded so that justice may be preserved; yet those entangled in the affairs of secular possessions and worldly pleasures can scarcely fulfill it.

Whoever possesses the first form, chastity, but does not obtain the second, contempt of the world, possesses the first almost without purpose, since he lacks the second, for the sake of which the first was sought. And if he has the first and second but lacks the third, which is justice, he labors in vain, since the first two are sought chiefly for the sake of justice.

For what does it profit to possess chastity for the sake of contempt of the world, yet not possess that for which one has chastity? Or why do you despise the things of the world if you do not preserve justice, for the sake of which it is fitting that you possess both chastity and contempt of the world? For just as the first form exists for the sake of the second, so the first and second exist for the sake of the third; and if the third is absent, neither the first nor the second will be beneficial.

**5.** Perhaps you will say: “Teach me, then, what justice is, so that, once I know it, I may more easily be able to fulfill it.” I shall speak briefly, as I am able, and shall use the simplicity of ordinary words, because the matter with which we are dealing is such that it ought not to be obscured by the more elaborate language of eloquence, but revealed through simpler forms of expression. A matter necessary to all should be explained in language common to all.

Justice, then, is nothing other than not sinning. Not sinning, however, is observing the precepts of the law. The observance of the precepts is maintained in two ways: by doing nothing that is forbidden and by striving to fulfill everything that is commanded.
