This is what is said: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXIII, 15).

Do not suppose that justice consists in this alone, that you do no evil, since failing to do good is also evil, and transgression of the law is committed in both respects. For the one who said, “Turn away from evil,” also said, “Do good.” If you turn away from evil and do not do good, you are a transgressor of the Law, which is fulfilled not only in abhorring evil acts but also in perfecting good works.

You are not commanded merely not to strip the clothed of their garments, but also to clothe the stripped with your own; not merely not to take away his bread from one who has bread, but willingly to share yours with one who has none; not merely not to drive the poor man from his lodging, but to receive into your home the one who has been driven out and has no shelter.

For we have been commanded: “Weep with those who weep” (Rom. XII, 15). How do we weep with them if we do not share in their necessities at all, nor offer them any help in the matters over which they shed tears? God does not seek the useless moisture of our tears; rather, because tears are an indication of grief, he wishes you to feel another’s distress as your own, and to help another as you would wish to be helped if you were in such tribulation, in accordance with this: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them” (Matt. VII, 11).

For to weep with one who weeps and, when you are able, to contribute nothing to the one who weeps is a sign of mockery, not of compassion. Indeed, our Savior wept with Mary and Martha, the sisters of Lazarus, and displayed the feeling of immense mercy by the testimony of his tears; and signs of true compassion were immediately followed by deeds, when Lazarus, for whose sake the tears had been shed, was raised and restored to his sisters. This was truly to weep with those who weep: to remove the occasion of their weeping.

“But,” you will say, “he did this as one who was powerful.” True; but nothing impossible is commanded of you either. The one who did what he could fulfilled everything.

**6.** But, as we had begun to say, it is not enough for a Christian to abstain from evil unless he also performs the duties of good works. This is confirmed above all by the testimony in which the Lord threatens that those who, although they have done no evil, have not done all that is good will be guilty of eternal fire. He says: “Then the King will say to those who are on his left: Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that my Father prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food,” and so forth (Matt. XXV, 41).

He did not say: “Depart from me, accursed ones, because you committed murder, because you committed adultery, or because you committed theft.” They are not condemned and handed over to the punishments of eternal Gehenna because they did evil, but because they had not done good; not because they had committed what was forbidden, but because they were unwilling to fulfill what had been commanded.

Hence one must consider what hope those can have who still do some of the things that are forbidden, when even those who have not done what is commanded are held guilty. Do not flatter yourself in this respect if you have not done certain things, merely because you have done others, since it is written: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all” (Jas. II, 10).

Adam sinned once and died; and do you think yourself alive while repeatedly committing the act whose single perpetration killed another? Or do you think he committed some great crime, for which he was rightly condemned to a harsher punishment? Let us see, then, what he did against the commandment. He ate from the fruit of the tree. What then? Did God punish a human being with death because of the fruit of a tree? Not because of the fruit of the tree, but because of contempt for the commandment. Therefore the issue is not the nature of the sin but the transgression of the commandment.

And the one who told Adam not to eat from the fruit of the tree himself commanded you not to curse, not to lie, not to slander, and not to listen to one who slanders; not to swear at all; not to covet; not to envy; not to be lukewarm; not to be greedy; to return no evil for evil; to love your enemies; to bless those who curse you; to pray for your accusers and persecutors; to offer the other cheek to one who strikes you; not to litigate in a secular court; if someone wishes to take away what is yours, to surrender it gladly; not to admit into your heart the evil of anger, jealousy, or resentment; to flee the crime of avarice; to beware of every evil of pride and boastfulness; and to live humbly and gently according to the example of Christ.

You must avoid the company of the wicked so completely that you do not even eat with fornicators, the greedy, those who curse, the envious, slanderers, drunkards, or the rapacious. If you despise him in any one respect, he will not spare you, even if he spared Adam. Indeed, Adam deserved greater mercy, since he was still inexperienced and newly formed, and had before him no example of anyone who had sinned and died because of his sin. But for you, after so many lessons, after the Law, after the Prophets, after the Gospels, after the Apostles—if you should wish to sin—I do not know how he could show mercy.

**7.** Do you perhaps flatter yourself because of the privilege of virginity? Remember that Adam and Eve sinned while virgins, and that bodily integrity did not benefit them when they sinned. A virgin who sins must be compared with Eve, not with Mary.

We do not deny the remedy of repentance in the present age; but we urge you rather to hope for a reward than to require pardon. It is shameful for those who expect the palm of virginity to ask indulgence for sin, and for those who have castrated themselves even with respect to what is lawful to incur something unlawful.

For it is lawful to enter into marriage. And just as those who, for the love of Christ and the glory of the heavenly kingdom, have rejected marital union are to be praised, so those who, out of a desire for innocence, have not yet been devoted to God and make use of the apostolic remedy are not to be condemned. Therefore, as we have said, those who abandon marriage reject not what is unlawful but what is lawful.

But if such women swear, curse, slander, endure listening to slanderers, return evil for evil, incur the guilt of coveting what belongs to others or of avarice regarding what is their own, harbor the poisons of jealousy or resentment, speak or think anything indecent contrary to legal and apostolic institutions, or go out dressed and adorned with the desire to please the flesh; if they do any of the things that, as is customary, are unlawful, what will it profit them to have rejected what was permitted and to practice what is not permitted?

If you wish what you have rejected as lawful to benefit you, take care not to do any of the things that are unlawful. For it is foolish to fear what is lesser and not fear what is greater, or to fail to avoid what is forbidden if one has avoided what is permitted.

The Apostle says: “The unmarried woman considers the things of the Lord, how she may please God, so that she may be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman considers the things of the world, how she may please her husband” (1 Cor. VII, 34). He says that the married woman pleases her husband by considering the things of the world, whereas the unmarried woman pleases God because she has no concern for the world.

Let the woman who has no husband, yet considers the things of the world, tell me: whom does she desire to please? Will she not begin to be surpassed by the married woman? For the married woman, by considering the things of the world, pleases at least her husband; but the unmarried woman can please neither a husband, whom she does not have, nor God.

**8.** Nor should we pass over in silence what he said: “The unmarried woman considers the things of the Lord, how she may please God, so that she may be holy in body and spirit” (1 Cor. VII, 34). What, then, are the things of the Lord? Let the Apostle say: “Whatever things are holy, whatever things are just, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good repute; if there is any virtue, if there is any praise of discipline” (Ps. IV, 8).

These are the things of the Lord, which holy, true, and apostolic virgins meditate upon and consider day and night without any interruption of time. The kingdom of heaven is the Lord’s; the resurrection of the dead is the Lord’s; immortality is the Lord’s; incorruption is the Lord’s; the splendor of the sun promised to the saints is the Lord’s, as it is written in the Gospel: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII).

The many dwelling places of the saints in heaven are the Lord’s; the thirtieth-, sixtieth-, and hundredfold fruit is the Lord’s. They consider these things, and they consider by what works they might merit the things that are the Lord’s.

The Law of the New and Old Testament is also the Lord’s; in them the holy utterances of his mouth shine forth. If virgins meditate upon these without ceasing, they consider the things that are the Lord’s, and the prophetic word is fulfilled in them: “Eternal foundations upon a solid rock, and the commandments of the Lord in the heart of a holy woman” (Ecclus. XXVI, 24).

It follows: “How you may please God”—God, I say, not human beings—“so that she may be holy in body and spirit” (1 Cor. VII, 34). He did not say, “so that she may be holy in one member,” or “in the body only,” but “in body and spirit.” A member is one part of the body; the body, however, is the structure composed of all the members. When he says “so that she may be holy in body,” he testifies that she must be sanctified in all her members. For the sanctification of the other members will not benefit her if corruption is found in even one. And she will no longer be holy in body, which consists of all the members, if it has been polluted by the defilement of even one.

**9.** But so that what I am saying may become more manifest and clearer, suppose that she has been purified by the sanctification of all her members, and that only her tongue sins by blaspheming or bearing false witness. Will all the other members free the one? Or will the others be judged because of the one?

Therefore, if the sanctification of the other members is of no benefit when there is a fault in one, how much more, when all are corrupted by various sins, will the integrity of one be of no benefit? Hence, I ask you, virgin: do not flatter yourself on your chastity alone, nor place your confidence in the integrity of one member; but, according to the Apostle, preserve the holiness of your body for God alone.

Cleanse your head from every defilement. For it is a crime, after the sanctification of chrism, to soil it with the color or powder of saffron or any other pigment, or to adorn it with gold, gems, or anything of earthly kind, when it already shines with the splendor of heavenly adornment. For the preference of worldly and secular ornament is a great insult to divine grace.

Cleanse your forehead, so that it may blush at human works, not divine ones, and receive that shame which produces not sin but the glory of God, as Scripture says: “There is a shame that leads to sin, and there is a shame that leads to glory” (Ecclus. IV, 25).

Cleanse your neck, so that your hair may not wear golden nets and hanging necklaces, but rather carry those ornaments of which Scripture says: “Let mercy and faithfulness not forsake you; hang them upon your heart as upon your neck” (Prov. III, 3).

Cleanse your eyes by withdrawing them from every form of desire, never turning them away from the poor, and preserving them free from all cosmetics in the sincerity in which they were made by God.

Cleanse your tongue from lying, because “the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. I, 11). Cleanse it from slander, oaths, flattery, and perjury. Do not think that I have put the order backward because I said that the tongue must be cleansed from swearing before perjury. You will more easily avoid perjury if you do not swear at all.

Let this saying be fulfilled in you: “Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit” (Ps. XXXIII). And remember the Apostle’s words: “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. XII, 14). But remember this more frequently: “See that no one repays anyone evil for good, nor curse for curse, but, on the contrary, bless; for to this you were called, that you may inherit a blessing” (1 Pet. III, 9). And also this: “If anyone does not offend in speech, he is perfect” (Jas. III, 2).

For it is impious that those lips with which you confess, pray to, bless, and praise the Lord should be polluted by the filth of any sin. I do not know with what conscience and tongue anyone prays to God with the same tongue by which he lies, curses, or slanders. God hears holy lips, and he quickly grants the prayers uttered by an undefiled tongue.

Cleanse your ears, so that they may give hearing only to holy and truthful words; so that they may never receive obscene, shameful, or worldly speech, nor hear anyone speaking disparagingly of another, in accordance with what is written: “Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to an evil tongue” (Ecclus. XXVIII, 29). Thus you may share in the portion of the one of whom it is said that he was righteous in hearing and seeing—that is, he did not sin either with his ears or with his eyes.

Let your hands not be extended to receive while folded when it comes to giving, nor be prepared to strike, but let them be fully ready for every work of mercy and compassion.

Cleanse your feet, so that they may not travel the broad and spacious way that leads to the splendid and luxurious banquets of the world, but may rather walk the arduous and narrow path that leads to heaven, since it is written: “Make straight paths for your feet” (Isa. LVII, 14).

Recognize that your members were formed by God the creator not for vices but for virtue. When you have cleansed all your limbs from every stain of sin and have been sanctified in your entire body, then understand that chastity will benefit you, and await with complete confidence the palm of virginity.

**10.** I believe that I have explained briefly but fully what it means to be holy in body. Now we must understand what follows, “and in spirit”: namely, that what it is forbidden to do in deed must also be forbidden to conceive in thought.

She is holy both in body and in spirit who sins neither in mind nor in heart, knowing that God is also the examiner of the heart; and therefore she strives to keep her soul, no less than her body, entirely clean from sin, knowing that it is written: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Prov. IV, 23); and again: “The Lord loves holy hearts, but all the blameless are acceptable to him”; and elsewhere: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8).

I believe this is said of those whose conscience reproves them for no guilt of sin. Concerning them, I think John said in his Epistle: “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God, and whatever we ask we shall receive from him” (1 John III, 20).

Do not think that you have escaped the crime of sin if the will is not followed by the deed, since it is written: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 17). Nor should you say, “I thought about it, but I did not carry it out,” because even desiring is wrong.

Hence blessed Peter commanded, saying: “Purifying your souls” (1 Pet. I, 22). If he had known of no defilement of the soul, he would not have desired it to be purified.

We must also consider more carefully and observe that passage in which it is written: “These are they who did not defile themselves with women, for they remained virgins; these follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. XIV, 4). Are they joined to the divine company and traverse all the courts of heaven solely on account of the merit of the integrity of their chastity? Or are there also other qualities by which virginity attains the glory of so great a blessedness?

How can we know this? From what follows, unless I am mistaken, where it is written: “These were purchased from among human beings as firstfruits for God and for the Lamb, and no lie was found in their mouth; for they are without blemish” (ibid. XIV, 5).

You see, then, that those who are said to cling to the Lord’s footsteps are not characterized in one member alone, but are those who, in addition to virginity, have led a life undefiled by every contamination of sin.

For this reason, above all, a virgin rejects marriage: so that, being more secure, she may more easily guard herself from every offense and fulfill all the commandments of the law—something also required of married women. For if she does not marry but nevertheless does the things from which married women too are commanded to remain free, what benefit will it be not to have married?

Although no Christian is permitted to sin, and all who are cleansed by the sanctification of spiritual washing ought to live an undefiled life, so that they may be joined inwardly to the Church, which is described as being without stain, wrinkle, or anything of that kind, nevertheless the virgin must fulfill this all the more, since neither a husband, nor children, nor any other necessity prevents her from carrying out divine Scripture; nor, if she sins, will she be able to defend herself with any excuse.

**11.** O virgin, preserve the commitment appointed for you to a great reward. The virtue of virginity and chastity is glorious before God, provided that it is not weakened by other falls into sin and evil.

Recognize your status; recognize your place; recognize your commitment. You are called the bride of Christ. Take care not to admit anything unworthy of him to whom you appear betrothed; he will quickly write a bill of repudiation if he sees even one adultery in you.

Any woman who is betrothed with the tokens of human engagement immediately asks carefully and diligently from the household members, relatives, friends, and servants of the bridegroom what sort of character the young man has, what he chiefly loves, what he accepts, how he lives, by what habits he governs himself, what foods he uses, and in what things he especially delights and rejoices. Once she has learned these things, she regulates herself in all respects so that her obedience, her joy, her diligence, and her life may accord with the character of her bridegroom.

And you, who have Christ as your bridegroom, ask his household members and friends about the character of your bridegroom, and inquire diligently and attentively in what things he especially delights, what arrangement of clothing he loves in you, and what kind of adornment he desires.

Let his closest associate Peter tell you. He does not permit even married women bodily adornment, as he wrote in his Epistle: “Women likewise, subject to their own husbands, so that if any do not believe the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives, observing your chaste conduct in the fear of God. Let your adornment not be outward, in the braiding of hair, or the wearing of gold, or the elegance of clothing, but the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptibility of a quiet and modest spirit, which is precious in the sight of God” (1 Pet. III, 1 ff.).

Let the other blessed Apostle Paul also tell you. Writing to Timothy, the bishop, he likewise bears witness concerning the discipline of faithful women: “Women likewise, in an adornment of dress, with modesty and sobriety, should adorn themselves, not with curled hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly clothing, but as is fitting for women professing chastity through good conduct” (1 Tim. II, 9).

**12.** But perhaps you will say: “Why did these same Apostles not command these things to virgins?” Because they did not consider it necessary, lest such an admonition to virgins should appear an insult rather than correction. Nor did they ever believe that virgins would be so reckless as to presume upon the bodily and earthly ornaments not even granted to married women.

Indeed, a virgin ought to adorn and arrange herself. For how could she please her bridegroom unless she came forth arranged and adorned? Let her certainly adorn herself, but with inward ornaments; let her be arranged spiritually, not carnally, because God considers in her not the beauty of the body but that of the soul.

Therefore you too, whoever desire your soul to be loved and inhabited by God, arrange it with every diligence and adorn it with spiritual garments. Let nothing disgraceful, nothing foul, appear in it. Let it shine with the gold of justice, sparkle with the gems of holiness, and gleam with the most precious pearl of chastity.

Instead of fine linen and silk, let it be clothed with a tunic of mercy and compassion, according to what is written: “Put on, therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, the inward parts of compassion, kindness, humility,” and so forth (Col. III, 12).

Let it not seek the beauty of white lead or any other pigment, but possess the brightness of innocence and simplicity. Let it have the rose-colored hue of modesty and the purple color of blush and shame. Let it be washed with the heavenly soda of instruction and cleansed by spiritual lamentation. Let no stain of malice, no mark of the devil, remain in it; and lest it ever smell foul with the odor of sin, let it be drenched with the ointment of the sweetest wisdom and knowledge.

**13.** This is the kind of adornment God seeks, and he desires a soul arranged in this way. Remember that you are called God’s daughter, according to the saying: “Hear, O daughter, and see” (Ps. XLIV, 11). And whenever you yourself call God “Father,” you testify that you are God’s daughter.

Therefore, if you are God’s daughter, take care not to do anything unbecoming to God the Father, but conduct yourself in everything as God’s daughter. Observe how the daughters of the nobles of this world conduct themselves, what habits they acquire, and by what disciplines they train themselves. Some possess such modesty, such gravity, and such self-restraint that, out of regard for their human nobility, they surpass the custom of other people; and, lest by their fall they stamp a mark of disgrace upon their honorable parents, they strive in some way to make another nature for themselves among human beings through their way of life.

You too, then, look to your origin, consider your lineage, and recognize the glory of your nobility. Acknowledge that you are not the daughter of a human being but of God, and that you are adorned with the nobility of divine birth. Conduct yourself so that heavenly birth may appear in you and divine nobility shine forth.

Let there be in you a new gravity, admirable honor, astonishing modesty, remarkable patience, a virginal bearing, the habit of true chastity, and speech always modest and uttered at the proper time. Then whoever sees you will marvel and say: “What is this patience of a new gravity among human beings? What modesty of shame? What restraint of honor? What maturity of wisdom? This is not human training, nor mortal discipline. Something heavenly exhales from this earthly body. I think that God dwells in certain human beings.”

And when that person learns that you are Christ’s servant, he will be seized with still greater wonder and will consider what kind of Lord he must be whose servant is such a woman.

**14.** If you wish, then, to be with Christ and to share in Christ, you must live according to Christ’s example. He was so entirely free from every malice and wickedness that he did not even return an injury to his enemies, but rather prayed for them.

Do not consider those souls Christian which, I do not say, hate brothers or sisters, but do not love their neighbors with their whole heart and conscience before God as witness; for Christians, in imitation of Christ, must love even their enemies.

If you desire to share in the company of the saints, cleanse your heart from every thought of malice and wickedness. Let no one deceive you; let no one seduce you with deceitful speech. The heavenly court will receive only the holy, the just, the simple, the innocent, and the pure. Malice has no place with God.

Anyone who desires to reign with Christ must be clean from every wickedness and deceit. Nothing is so contrary to God, nothing so detestable to him, as to hate someone or wish to harm someone; nothing is so approved as to love everyone. Knowing this, the Prophet testifies, saying: “You who love the Lord, hate evil” (Ps. XCVI, 10).

**15.** Take care not to love human glory in any respect, lest your portion also be counted among those to whom it was said: “How can you believe, who seek glory from one another?” (John V, 44). And concerning whom it is said through the Prophet: “Increase evils upon them; increase evils upon the glorious of the earth.” And elsewhere: “Be ashamed of your boasting, of your reproach in the sight of God” (Isa. XLV).

Do not look to those who are virgins of the world, not of Christ; who, forgetful of their commitment and profession, take delight in luxury, delight in wealth, and delight in the nobility of bodily origin.

If they truly believed themselves to be daughters of God, they would never, after divine birth, admire human nobility, nor glory in some honored father. If they understood that they have God as their Father, they would not love nobility of the flesh.

Why do you flatter and indulge yourself in the nobility of your ancestry? In the beginning God made two human beings, from whom the entire forest of the human race descended. Worldly nobility was bestowed not by the equity of nature but by the ambition of desire.

Certainly, through the generation of divine washing we all become equal, and there can be no distinction among those whom a second birth has generated. Through it, the rich and the poor, the free and the slave, the noble and the ignoble become sons of God; earthly nobility is overshadowed by the splendor of heavenly glory and now disappears entirely, since those who previously were unequal in secular honors are clothed equally in the glory of heavenly and divine nobility.

There is now no place for ignobility, nor is anyone degenerate whom the sublimity of divine birth adorns—except among those who do not think that heavenly things should be preferred to human things. Or, if they do think so, how foolish it is for them to prefer themselves in lesser matters to those whom they know to be their equals in greater matters, and to regard as beneath them on earth those whom they believe to be their equals in heaven.

But you, whoever you are—a virgin of Christ, not of the world—flee all the glory of the present life, so that you may obtain the glory promised in the future.

**16.** Avoid words of contention and the causes of hostility; evade occasions of discord and lawsuits as well. For if, according to the Apostle’s teaching, “the servant of the Lord must not quarrel” (2 Tim. II, 24), how much more must this be true of the handmaid of God? The more modest her sex, the more modest her spirit ought to be.

Restrain your tongue from evil speech, and place the bridle of the Law upon your mouth. If you should happen to speak when silence would be sinful, take care not to say anything that may rightly be reproved. A spoken word is a stone cast forth; therefore it must be considered for a long time before it is uttered. Blessed are the lips that never release anything they might later wish to recall.

The speech of a chaste mind ought also to be chaste, always building up those who hear rather than at some time destroying them, according to the Apostle’s command: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but only such as is good for building up in faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Eph. IV, 29).

Precious to God is the tongue that does not know how to construct words apart from divine matters, and holy is the mouth from which heavenly utterances are always brought forth.

Deter slanderers of the absent as malign persons by the authority of Scripture. For the Prophet counts it among the virtues of the perfect person that the malicious person who speaks things unworthy against his neighbor is brought to nothing in the sight of the just. You may not patiently listen to another’s disparagement, since you do not wish your own to be received by others (Ps. LXXIV, 5).

Whatever comes against the Gospel of Christ is unjust, if you allow something to be inflicted upon another that you find troubling when it is done to you by someone else. Always accustom your tongue to speak of good things, and direct your hearing more toward the praise of good people than toward the criticism of evil ones.

See to it that everything you do well, you do for God’s sake, knowing that you will receive from the Lord only such a reward for that deed as you have performed because of fear and love of him.

Strive to be holy rather than to appear holy, because it is useless to be considered what one is not; and it is the guilt of a double sin both not to possess what one is believed to possess and to pretend to possess what one does not have.

**17.** Take greater delight in fasts than in banquets, remembering that widow who did not depart from the temple, serving God with fasts and prayers day and night. And if such a woman was a widow in Judea, what ought a virgin of Christ to be now?

Love the banquet of divine reading more, and desire to be filled with spiritual foods; seek rather those kinds of nourishment by which the soul is refreshed more than the body.

Flee meat and wine as sources of bodily heat and incentives to lust. If ever you use wine, do so only when stomach pain and excessive bodily weakness compel you to it.

Conquer anger; restrain hostility; and whatever it may be that afterward brings repentance for the deed, avoid it as the abhorrence of an impending offense.

The mind that desires to be God’s dwelling must be sufficiently tranquil and quiet, removed from every disturbance of fury. Through the Prophet God testifies and says: “Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI, 3).

Believe that God observes all your deeds and thoughts, and take care not to do or think anything unworthy of the divine eyes.

18. When you desire to celebrate the liturgy, present yourself as though you were about to speak with the Lord. When you recite a psalm, recognize whose words you are reciting; and take greater delight in the compunction of the soul than in the sweetness of a ringing voice [Col. 0089A]. For God approves the tears of one who sings psalms more than the charm of the voice, as the Prophet says: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Ps. 2:11). Where there is fear and trembling, there is not vocal exaltation, but the soul’s mournful and tearful abasement.

Apply diligence to all your actions, because it is written: “Cursed is the one who does the work of the Lord negligently” (Jer. 46:10). Let grace increase in you with the years, and righteousness increase with age; let your faith appear more perfect the older you become, because our Lord Jesus, who left us an example of how to live, advanced not only in bodily age but also in wisdom and spiritual grace before God and human beings (Luke 2:25). Consider every period in which you have not found yourself improved to have been lost.

Preserve the resolve of virginity that you have undertaken [Col. 0089B] all the way to its end, because it is a mark of virtue not merely to have begun but to have brought it to completion, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 22:10). Take care not to give anyone an occasion even for desire, because your bridegroom is a jealous God. For an adulteress against Christ is more guilty [Col. 0090A] than an adulteress against her husband. Hence the Roman Church, doubtless animated by the apostolic spirit of the one whose see it holds, recently established so severe a judgment in this matter that it scarcely considered worthy of penance the woman who had violated a body consecrated to God by lustful defilement.

19. Be, therefore, a pattern of life to all; be an example. In conduct, go before those whom you surpass in the sanctification of chastity. Show yourself a virgin in every respect. Let no corruption be brought against your head, whose body is whole, so that your way of life too may be inviolate.

And since, as we stated at the beginning of the letter, you have been made a sacrifice to God—a sacrifice that certainly imparts its holiness also to others, so that whoever worthily receives something from it may himself share in sanctification—so, through you, as through a divine offering, let the other women also be sanctified [Col. 0090B]. Conduct yourself in every respect among them in such a way that whoever encounters your life either by hearing or by sight may feel the power of sanctification, and may understand that grace is so abundantly transfused into him from your conduct that, while he desires to imitate you, he too may be worthy of God’s sacrifice.

---

## [SUPPLEMENT TO THE WORKS OF SAINT AMBROSE.]

[Col. 0089]

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING SERMONS OF SAINT AMBROSE

These three sermons were entitled to a place among the works of the holy bishop of Milan both by sound reason and by chronological order. Why, then, have they been published somewhat out of sequence in this volume? The principal reason was the great difficulty of tracking them down: the reprinting of the holy Father’s works would have had to be delayed by no fewer than three or four months in order to complete it by their addition. Realizing that such a delay would be intolerable not only to our own diligence but also to the eager wishes of our subscribers, we quickly brought the series of Ambrose’s writings to a close, since it had already become exceedingly rich, and assigned the Sessonian sermons to the following volume. We did so all the more willingly because that volume would serve, as it were, as an appendix to the fourth century.

[Col. 0089]

## PREFACE OF D. LEANDER

[Note: The dedicatory letter that ought to have been placed before this preface was omitted through a typographical error. See it at the end of this volume. EDITOR.]

[Col. 0089C]

## I. The writings of Saint Ambrose have always been held in the highest honor, and many corruptions in them were formerly purged by the Maurists

No learned person is unaware that the Fathers, the supreme pontiffs, the ecumenical councils, and even the heterodox themselves have always held in the highest regard the writings of Saint Ambrose, who in the fourth century occupied the most illustrious episcopal see of Milan [Note: See the selected testimonies of the ancients collected by the Maurists in the preface to the first volume of the works of Saint Ambrose.]. Yet everyone equally knows that many apocryphal works were once included among the writings of this most holy bishop, and that they were so full of defects that they even made some passages entirely alien to Catholic doctrine [Col. 0090C] [Note: Formerly, commentaries on the Pauline Epistles were attributed to Saint Ambrose, and their author certainly expresses something inconsistent with sound doctrine. Indeed, the Benedictine editors write in the preliminary notice to volume IV, appendix, column 30, that their author cannot be defended unless he agreed with Origen that it is in the will of demons to turn back from error. There is also the well-known sore that he maintains that a husband is always permitted, after dismissing his wife on account of adultery, to take another wife, while he denies that a wife separated from an adulterous husband may enter into marriage with another man (hence the canon *Uxor a viro*, 17, cause 32, question 7; the Roman correctors should be consulted concerning it). Nor are the following matters sufficiently sound: he denies that woman was made in the image of God; he denies that bishops hold a rank superior to presbyters or that they are instituted by a different ordination; and he occasionally teaches certain other things less compatible with the common Catholic understanding.].

Accordingly, there were Roman pontiffs who, desiring the writings of a Father so ancient and so deserving of the Church to flourish in praise of sound doctrine, strongly urged learned men to search diligently for and collate manuscripts of the highest quality for the preparation of a new edition. From these, they could select the genuine productions of Ambrose, reject the spurious, and extract the certain teachings of that same bishop. Thus, in accordance with the mandates of the supreme pontiffs Pius IV, Pius V, and Gregory XIII, and through the zeal and labor of Sixtus V, the Roman edition of Ambrose’s works, the most complete of all the others, was brought to light [Col. 0091A] [Note: From the year 1580 to the year 1585.].

But since even that edition contained not a few things that, as the Maurists stated in the preface to the works of the same holy teacher [Note: In the preface, volume I.], were rightly approved neither by heretics nor by orthodox Christians, the Maurists themselves came forward. After undertaking, so to speak, Herculean labors in searching libraries and collating manuscripts, they restored the writings of the bishop of Milan, cleansed of every blemish, to their proper honor by publishing a new edition. In maturity of judgment and abundance of learning, it easily surpassed all the earlier editions [Col. 0091D] [Note: This edition, begun in 1686, was completed in Paris in 1690 in two folio volumes; it was issued again in Venice in four folio volumes in 1748, which is the edition I use. Franciscus Pitterius also had it printed in his Venetian printing house in eight folio volumes in 1781.].

## II. The Maurist edition is enriched by three sermons drawn from the Sessorian manuscript

Now, as for what might further enrich the praised edition, I believe that three previously unpublished sermons have recently been discovered by me on the Sessorian shelves. If learned men will briefly consider either the antiquity of the source from which they derive or the exceedingly useful instruction that will certainly flow from them for the formation of Christian conduct, I trust that they will recognize them as entirely worthy of being eagerly and favorably welcomed by all.

## III. The antiquity and paleography of the Sessorian manuscript

The distinguished source of these sermons is that Nonantulan manuscript, almost square in format and bound with exceedingly thin parchment leaves. Formerly marked with the numbers 60, 90, or 134, it has now been assigned number fifty-five in the new catalogue that I have prepared.

Scholars may recognize its script—which has faded so greatly that many pages are extremely difficult to read and obscure—in the printed specimen found in the Roman edition of Saint Maximus of 1784, plate 1, no. 2, p. 200. The script appears to me to have been written in the seventh century, or at the latest at the beginning of the eighth, belonging to what is called the second Roman period inclining toward the Lombardic [Note: That is, not the script used by the Lombards, a rough people wholly ignorant of letters, but the script used by the Italians during the period when they were subject to the rule of the Lombard kings.], though I would not, with the Most Eminent Besutius, call it sixth-century [Note: The Most Eminent Besutius, a man outstanding in every praise of virtue and intellect, and so learned in both profane and especially sacred archaeology that the members of the Academy of Etruscan Antiquities of the ancient city of Cortona chose him as their principal *Locumon*, left the following note concerning this manuscript on a paper slip dated about 1730: “Codex 134, in folio parchment, of extremely ancient character, perhaps of the sixth century, and certainly, in my judgment, written more than a thousand years ago. It contains several works, including first a sermon of Saint Augustine on Marriage, etc.”].

Its orthography is written with the greatest correctness according to the ancient standard, and is supported by such consistent authority from old manuscripts that it is plainly necessary to return to that more correct method of writing. In this manuscript the character V is never written in this form but always as U; nor is any diphthong used except *ae*, and that without a ligature [Col. 0091D], as is almost invariably the practice in very ancient manuscripts.

The preposition *ad* consistently retains the letter *d* before *c, e, m, n, p, r,* and *s*, and does not assimilate it to the following consonant except in the words *accipio* and *arripio*. The prefix *con-* retains *n* before *l, m, p,* and *r*; and *in-* never drops *n* before *b, m, p,* or *s*, except in the verb *impleo*. Words such as *aput, aliut, illut, istut, jubat,* and so forth—whose spelling generally depended on the ear of the scribe receiving words dictated aloud—are almost always found written in the manuscript in the form just recited. At the same time, it has the good and correct spellings *caelum, condicio, intellego, querella, uincla,* and many others, which I have not left unnoticed in my paleographical notes appended beneath the text.

Moreover, there is no punctuation in the manuscript: no marks of exclamation or interrogation, and no separation of words is visible. There are, however, occasional points, always placed in the middle, and inserted so haphazardly that they increase rather than lessen the ambiguity of the meaning. Letters at the ends of lines are sometimes reduced or joined into a monogram [Col. 0092B]. The scribe uses individual letters or sigla only sparingly, and then those familiar to ancient clerks, such as *Incp, Dns, Ds, ihs, xps, sps, scs, nr.*, for *Incipit, Dominus, Deus, Iesus, Christus, Spiritus, Sanctus,* and *noster*. At the ends of words he also uses *b·* and *q·*, with a point in the middle, for *-bus* and *-que*.

## IV. Why the three Ambrosian sermons contained in this same manuscript are judged to be unpublished

Let no one challenge my assertion that three sermons inscribed in this most ancient manuscript under the name of Saint Ambrose are unpublished. Even if I have said this somewhat incorrectly, I have not said it recklessly, since after applying the greatest care I could, I found them neither among the works of Ambrose published to the present day, nor among the works of Saints Augustine, Maximus, and Fulgentius—which we know in ancient times were mixed together with the Ambrosian writings—nor among the writings of any other holy Fathers [Col. 0092C].

My prior judgment was especially strengthened by the three testimonies from Isaiah—10:33–34 and 11:5—which are read in full in the third sermon [Note: § 10, pp. 27 and 28 (below, columns 136 and 138).]. For Sabatier, in his fragments of the ancient version of the Bible, either reports the passage in Isaiah 10:33–34 only in mutilated form or entirely omits the passage in Isaiah 11:5. Since that author was accustomed to apply every diligence in seeking testimonies to ancient biblical versions, especially among the Fathers, I thought it reasonable to infer that these sermons had in fact still been hidden in manuscripts in Sabatier’s time.

## V. The titles and analysis of these sermons

The first of these sermons is entitled *On Perfection*; the second, on the same subject, bears the title *Against Those Who Say That Property Should Not Be Sold but That Mercy Should Be Practiced from Its Fruits*; while the third is entitled *On Charity, from a Reading of the Holy Apostle Paul, against the Wicked Who Envy the Good* [Col. 0093A].

In the first sermon, after citing several testimonies from Scripture, the author shows that Christians, if they are to attain the highest degree of perfection, must sell all their possessions and distribute the proceeds to the poor. They must entrust themselves so completely to divine providence that, always occupied with meditation on the divine law and always engaged in keeping the commandments, they have no free time in which to think about worldly affairs, to be vainly disturbed by the troubles of this world, or to be deceived by the fleeting hope of earthly riches.

In the second, the author confirms what he had said in the preceding sermon. By setting before his readers Christ’s command and the example of the Apostle Paul, he demonstrates against the detractors of that virtue [Col. 0093B] how glorious, useful, and necessary contempt and renunciation of earthly things are.

Finally, in the third sermon, on the virtue of fraternal charity—which is extended at such length that I would call it a treatise rather than a sermon—the author has combined moral instruction with dogmatic teaching. First, examining the apostolic words of 1 Corinthians 13:1–3, he teaches that none of the various kinds of virtue benefits us without charity, since charity alone embraces all the other virtues and constitutes the completion of the whole of Christian perfection.

Second, turning to the various works of charity, he declares that they consist especially in humility, gentleness, kindness, and simplicity, and sets these qualities before us for contemplation and imitation in the election of David, in the apostolic election, and in the Lord’s example. He attacks with particular force the opposing vices—pride, envy, anger, enmity, and others of the same kind [Col. 0093C].

Meanwhile, as the occasion requires, he speaks of the twofold nature of our Lord Jesus Christ, divine and human, both perfect; of the hypostatic union; and of his baptism, passion, death, and glorious resurrection. He also discusses certain matters concerning the sacrament of baptism and its effects.

## VI. By what indications these three sermons are attributed to Ambrose, bishop of Milan

That these sermons should be attributed to Ambrose himself, bishop of Milan, seems to be demonstrated by very many appropriate indications.

1. Ambrosian expressions frequently occur in them, and many sentences are repeatedly found which unmistakably bear the stamp of Ambrose. I have made this evident several times in the scholia, though it could have been done much more fully and abundantly. Nor does it seem an obstacle or objection that one may sometimes observe in them a more relaxed style than in other treatises of the holy bishop. For, to use the words of the Maurists, “we are not unaware that authors vary their style, and that according to the subject and the occasion it is sometimes raised and sometimes lowered” [Note: [Col. 0093C] In the preface to the books *On the Sacraments*, vol. III.]. Indeed, as they themselves admit together with Gillot, “we know,” they say, “that it is nothing new if a holy doctor changes his style according to the subject, place, time, and persons” [Note: [Col. 0093C] See the admonition prefixed to the work *The Second Apology of David*, and that prefixed to the book *On Tobit*, vol. I.].

To this it may also be added that Ambrose applied his midwife’s hand, so to speak, to his other sermons now extant, when he collected them and arranged them into books; [Note: [Col. 0093C] “The author’s autograph,” says the distinguished Majus in the preface to book XIII *On the Republic*, p. 56 of the 1828 edition, “was generally the freer writing of sheets which Isidore, *Origins* VI, 14, defines as ‘that which is still being corrected and has not yet been reduced into books.’ No one has denied that it was especially Ambrose’s custom to distribute into books the sermons which he had delivered to the people without extensive preparation (*Preface to the Book on the Sacraments*, col. 432, vol. III), after subsequently correcting them.”] whereas our sermons, having remained scattered and separate, have reached us in the form in which they fell from his lips, unpolished through the work of the shorthand writer.

Now, having noted these matters for the benefit of those who are excessively fastidious, I declare that there is absolutely nothing in them that differs from Ambrose’s style, genius, or character. [Note: [Col. 0093C] I admit that in these sermons there are a few expressions which may perhaps offend certain very sensitive philologists, either because the published Ambrosian writings have not hitherto recorded them, or because, in their judgment, they do not bear the mark of good Latin. Such are *demandare* for *valde mandare* (“to command strongly”); *distrahere* for *vendere* (“to sell”); *distractio* for *venditio* (“sale”); *praerogare pretium* or *quantitatem* or *odia* for *ante erogare pretium* or *quantitatem*, or *ante odium in aliquem habere* (“to expend a price or quantity beforehand,” or “to bear hatred toward someone beforehand”), from which comes *praerogatio*; and *similare* for *similem facere* or *assimilare*, constructed with a dative. Yet although these words, in the meaning in which they are used in these sermons, may either not sound entirely good Latin or may so far lack the authority of Ambrose, they nevertheless do not depart from Ambrosian style.

For the same words either already existed in the writings of authors older than Ambrose of Milan, or were found among the ancient jurists. It is therefore not at all surprising that Ambrose used words which were already current in his time; nor was it foreign to his habits to speak in juridical terms. For he himself, as a man trained in forensic practice, frequently used legal expressions in his works according to place and occasion, as may be seen, for example, in vol. II, p. 338, and vol. III, p. 918, and elsewhere.

The jurists’ term *distrahere* for “to sell” was often used by Ulpian in the *Digest*. The same source has *distractio* for “sale” (*Digest* 14.3.5, from the middle, and 2.15.8, around the middle), and *praerogare* for “to expend beforehand” (*Digest*, title “On Location and Conduct,” law *Sed addes*). Thus these were familiar and customary expressions. The verb *distrahere* in a similar sense occurs in Tacitus, *Annals* VI, 17, in Justin IX, 1, and in Suetonius, *Vespasian* XVI; in Suetonius *prerogare* is also found in *Augustus* 53, while *demandare* in the sense of “to command strongly” occurs in *Nero* 35, *Augustus* 10, and *Caesar* 83.

The word *praerogatio* is said to have been first used by Latin lexicographers by Fulgentius, *Mythologies* I, 2, at the beginning. But just as *distractio* could easily be derived from the older *distrahere*, so *praerogatio* could easily be formed from *praerogare*. The verb *similare*, meaning “to make similar” or “to assimilate,” and indeed constructed with a dative, is used by the very ancient translator of Ezra, book IV, chapter 8, p. 44; and the same Saint Ambrose used it more than once in his works.

Thus, from these words, as I have said—whether they were customary in Ambrose’s age or belonged to legal usage—nothing can be established against the authenticity (*γνησιότης*, genuineness) of these sermons. The fact that they are not found in the writings so far attributed to Ambrose, or are not listed among the vocabulary of correct Latin, is no objection. For many expressions occur in the published writings of Ambrose which are found in only one or another book and nowhere else; and many are omitted by Latin lexicographers or are recorded by them with a different meaning.

Thus, for example, in book IV of the *Hexaemeron* III, 10, *perfunctio* occurs for *fruitio* (“enjoyment”); in book II *On Cain and Abel*, *conspersio* for *confusio* (“confusion”); in the first sermon on Psalm CXVIII, p. 13, *colludium* for *collusio* (“collusion”); and, not to prolong the discussion, *lentandum* for *lente morandum* (“for remaining slowly”), and so forth.

Just as it would be the judgment of a madman to assert that each of these celebrated books was not the work of Ambrose because they contain words used nowhere else and not sounding good Latin, so it would be unsound judgment to deny these sermons to the bishop of Milan because they contain a few expressions which so far lack Ambrose’s attested authority and have not been inserted into the dictionaries of the golden age of Latin. Under such a rule, many works would have to be denied to their authors, and scarcely any work, I would say, would remain whose authenticity could not be doubted.

Moreover, that distinguished political work of Cicero recently published by the learned Maius would have to be denied to Cicero, because it contains more than twenty words which appear either in none of Cicero’s other writings or in the lexica. I also observe in passing that the variations of diction with which the writings of the ancients are excessively burdened are often due to the confusion and boldness of copyists. They either took down the words of a preacher or dictating Father, or copied them from a manuscript; and if, because of lack of time, the difficulty of the manuscript, or their own ignorance, they were forced to leave gaps in their tablets, they filled them out in their own words and thus published interpolated writings. The ancient Fathers and all learned men have repeatedly complained of this discretion of excerptors, shorthand writers, and scribes.

An internal argument drawn from expression is therefore of very great value in distinguishing an author’s genuine offspring from spurious works; yet it cannot be used, when other indications are not lacking, to deny an entire work’s authenticity on the basis of one or another unusual word.]

2. And indeed, the fact that in the first sermon Ambrose strongly commends to his hearers the abandonment of all temporal goods and their distribution to the poor is entirely consistent with Ambrose himself, whom history tells us left all his possessions and gave them to the Church or the poor [Note: [Col. 0095D] Paulinus, *Life of Saint Ambrose*, no. 38, and Ambrose himself in Letter 20, p. 8, vol. III, plainly testify to this.]. We know with complete certainty from his published writings that he habitually instructed his people most diligently in such strict principles of Christian ethics [Note: [Col. 0096C] See at least the books entitled *On Abraham* and *On Naboth the Jezreelite*, vol. I; *On the Duties of Ministers*, passim, vol. III; and the *Exposition of Psalm CXVIII*, especially sermon 12, p. 37 ff., vol. II.].

3. It is also clear from the books *On Isaac and the Soul*, *On the Good of Death*, and especially *On Flight from the World*, as well as from the *Exposition of Psalm CXVIII*, that Ambrose made it his settled practice in his sermons to impress with particular care how strongly Christians were bound to flee the vanities and anxieties of the world, so that they might devote themselves more freely, day and night, to sacred reading and to God himself [Note: [Col. 0096C] Vol. I, pp. 418, 458, and 491; and vol. II, from p. 330 onward.]. This is also confirmed by our sermon.

4. The connection between the other sermon and the preceding one is so close that, once the author of one is known, the author of both is known.

5. Even if this connection were absent, the character and coloring of the sentences, as well as the circumstances appropriate to the time, would sufficiently demonstrate that it ought to be attributed to Ambrose. For there is no doubt that Ambrose not only urged in his writings the renunciation of his possessions and their distribution among the poor, but also repeatedly defended the usefulness of this evangelical counsel of perfection and sharply attacked those who opposed it. He left examples of this kind in the Psalms, especially in Psalm CXVIII, and in Letter 58 [Note: [Col. 0096C] Vol. III, col. 1098.].

6. The same must be said of the third sermon, which claims the same author as the other two, as is evident from their sequence. In it Ambrose, who had fallen upon the already corrupted times of the empress Justina, directs his chief efforts toward strengthening his people against the poison of the Arians, who at that time possessed great power in Milan, and toward restoring among them the practice of fraternal charity, which they were abandoning.

There Ambrose, clearly attacking the principal Arian heresies by which Christ’s divinity was assailed, offers, as we indicated above, highly appropriate doctrinal arguments for confirming the divinity of the Word. At the same time he urges his hearers most earnestly not to persecute a brother because of the grace bestowed upon him by divine aid, or acquired through the labors of fasts, the assiduity of prayers, the constancy of vigils, and every kind of virtue [Note: [Col. 0096C] Sermon 3, § 1.]; nor to be disturbed by any plots of the envious or provoked by any offenses [Note: [Col. 0096C] Ibid., §§ 4, 5, 11.]; but, following the Lord’s example, not to fear the hatred of the world [Note: [Col. 0096C] Ibid., § 7]. Thus they were to endure with patient spirit the insults, abuse, and curses inflicted upon them by false brothers and by the rulers of this age—namely, Justina, her courtiers, and the other Arians—so that they might be an example and model of humility and gentleness for all [Note: [Col. 0096C] Ibid., §§ 7, 10.].

All these ideas frequently occur in Ambrose’s works [Note: [Col. 0096D] Ambrose chiefly fought against the Arians in the books *On the Interpellation of Job and David*, book I, 9, and II, 4 and 6, vol. I; in the *Exposition of Psalms* XLIII, XLV, XLVII, XLVIII, and LXI; in the *Exposition of Luke*, vol. II; in the books *On the Mysteries* and *On the Faith*, vol. III; and *On the Holy Spirit* and *On the Incarnation*, vol. IV, as well as elsewhere throughout his works. As for preserving fraternal charity, Ambrosian writings abundantly supply similar ideas—for example, in Psalms XXXVII, 45; XXXVIII, 10 ff.; and CXVIII, sermon 10, pp. 3, 10, 41, and 50; sermon 12, p. 49; and sermon 15, p. 15 ff.; in *Luke* VII, 28 and 59, and VIII, 24, vol. II; book II *On Duties*, from chapter 15 onward; and Letters 41, p. 9, and 63, p. 83, vol. III. These examples among so many are sufficient to cite here.], and they correspond perfectly to those times [Note: [Col. 0096D] Consult Paulinus, *Life of Saint Ambrose*, no. 12 ff., as well as Ambrose’s Letters 20 and 21, vol. V, and, in the same volume, the sermon *On the Basilicas Not to Be Surrendered*, fol. 914.].

7. The mention made in the sermon of the deeds of Elijah also strongly recalls Ambrose. He states that he frequently remembered them in his writings. “We have set forth,” he says in book III, 5 of *On Elijah and Fasting*, “many things about the deeds of Elijah in the frequent discussions of various books” [Note: [Col. 0096D] Vol. I, col. 645.].

8. It is also very well known that Ambrose himself was accustomed to instruct the newly baptized, and that, in order to deter them more effectively from returning to the world to which they had renounced allegiance through baptism, he repeatedly urged them to die forever to the world by renouncing bodily pleasures, desires, and every allure­ment of the world [Note: [Col. 0096D] Book III, 9 of *On the Good of Death*, vol. I, col. 461], and to rise again with Christ in heaven [Col. 0097A]. See on this subject Augustine’s *Confessions*, book VI, chapters 3 and 4, as well as Ambrose’s works *On Flight from the World*, *On Jacob and the Blessed Life*, and *On the Mysteries* [Note: [Col. 0097C].].

Similar statements are found in these Sessorian sermons, which were likewise delivered to those who had already been assigned to heaven by their profession of faith [Note: [Col. 0097C] Sermon 1, § 1, p. 12 (below, cols. 109–112)], and who, already dead through baptism to worldly birth, had been born through grace and ennobled for heaven [Note: [Col. 0097C] Sermon 3, § 10, p. 26 (below, col. 135).].

9. Nor does the fact that in them he invites the faithful to spend the night in vigils and to sing hymns and psalms add nothing toward confirming the attribution of these sermons to Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0097C] Sermon 1, § 5, and sermon 3, § 11, pp. 6 and 30 (below, cols. 116 and 140).]. Nothing is more familiar in his writings than this practice [Note: [Col. 0097C] Thus in book III of the *Hexaemeron*, chapters 1 and 5; book II *On the Interpellation of David*, 6, vol. I; in the preface to Psalm I; in Psalms XLVIII, 23, and CXVIII; sermon 7, p. 25, vol. II; and elsewhere.].

Augustine and Paulinus testify that Ambrose was the first, during the height of Justina’s persecution, to institute vigils and the singing of hymns and psalms in the church according to the custom of the Eastern regions. Augustine says this of his mother, who was then living at Milan, in book IX of the *Confessions*, chapter 12:

> There my mother, your servant, who belonged to him—namely, Ambrose—and held the leading place in solicitude and vigils, lived by prayers.

A little later he continues:

> Then it was instituted that hymns and psalms should be sung according to the custom of the Eastern regions, and from that time it has been retained down to the present, being imitated by many and almost all your flocks, and throughout the other regions of the world.

See also book IX of *The City of God*, chapter 12, col. 162 [Note: [Col. 0097D].].

Paulinus likewise says in the *Life of Ambrose*:

> At this time—namely, when the Arians were attempting to seize the Portian Basilica—antiphons, hymns, and vigils first began to be celebrated in the Milanese Church. The devotion of this celebration has continued to the present day, not only in that Church but throughout almost all the provinces of the West.

[Note: [Col. 0097D] Ibid., no. 13.]

10 and 11. But even if there were no other arguments, two considerations would suffice: first, the very close agreement between the chief points expressed more briefly in these sermons and those treated more fully in the expositions of the Psalms, especially Psalm CXVIII; and second, the same Vulgate text used in them, which is found in the works of Ambrose so far admitted. These alone would suffice to make it certain and beyond dispute that these sermons are Ambrosian.

I frankly admit, however, that in some places certain passages of Sacred Scripture are quoted with different wording. Yet I affirm that this does not in the least harm my position. First, because “from reading the works of Saint Ambrose,” to use the words of Natalis Alexander [Note: [Col. 0097D] *Ecclesiastical History*, fourth century, part I, p. 508, col. 2.], as the Benedictine editors confirm [Note: [Col. 0097D] In the preface to the books *On the Sacraments*, vol. III.], “it is evident that he did not always cite the same passages of Sacred Scripture in the same words.” Second, because in the Sessorian sermons this disagreement is not confirmed except rarely, and only in those passages which Ambrose himself always cited with different wording. Third, because the variations are of such a kind that, far from indicating two different versions, they rather exclude that conclusion.

All these points are especially clear from the various readings appended to the text of our manuscript, so that it would be entirely superfluous and useless to linger over what can be examined directly with one’s own eyes.

12 and 13. Furthermore, I certainly cannot pass over the fact that in these sermons, in accordance with Ambrosian practice, the hearers are never enticed by elaborate introductions, nor is a precise order or artful division maintained. At the same time, I observe that the author repeatedly looks to the works of Saint Basil, whose writings Ambrose certainly tasted beforehand as a source when composing his own books.

Among others, there are the homilies of Saint Basil now published as numbers 7, 8, 20, and 21 [Note: [Col. 0097D] Vol. II of the works of Saint Basil, Paris edition, 1721, pp. 51, 62, 156 ff.], whose subject matter has considerable affinity with these sermons of Ambrose.

14. Who does not know that many of Ambrose’s sermons have been lost? The Maurists certainly record that many works of Ambrose have perished [Note: [Col. 0098C] In the prefaces to volumes III and IV of the works of Saint Ambrose. See also Ceillier, *General History of Sacred and Ecclesiastical Authors*, vol. VII, p. 574 ff.]. Indeed, one may infer that there were many more from the fact that nothing is more certain than that Ambrose preached not only on every Sunday, but also instructed catechumens, candidates for baptism, and the newly baptized in daily sermons at the appointed seasons of the year [Note: [Col. 0098C] This threefold ancient distinction is explained from the Vatican manuscripts by the learned Maius in note 1 to the *Explanation of the Creed* of Saint Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, p. 35 of the Roman edition, 1827.], as we know from his writings [Note: [Col. 0098C] Book I of *On the Mysteries*, vol. III, col. 408], and also from the clearest testimonies of Augustine and Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0098C] Augustine testifies that Ambrose actually preached every Sunday. In book VI of the *Confessions*, chapter 3, he writes: “Every Sunday I used to hear him correctly handling the word of truth before the people.” Concerning the assiduity with which Ambrose taught those preparing for baptism, Paulinus says in his *Life*, no. 38: “He was exceedingly strong in fulfilling divine duties, to such an extent that what he had been accustomed to perform alone for those preparing for baptism, five bishops afterward could scarcely accomplish during the time in which he died.”].

Therefore, let no one begrudge me the discovery of previously unpublished Ambrosian sermons, or accuse me of overconfidence.

15. And indeed, does not the Sessorian manuscript—a miscellaneous codex of the highest quality—make Ambrose the author of these sermons? [Note: [Col. 0098D] In the manuscript, after the name Ambrose, the title “bishop” is omitted. Yet no one should therefore attribute these sermons to another Ambrose distinct from the bishop of Milan. For if the age of the manuscript, the style of the sermons, the ideas, and the character and purpose of their author are taken into account, one must admit that they can be attributed to no one bearing that name except the bishop of Milan. Moreover, in ancient manuscripts copyists often omit titles of holiness and rank, whether from habit or, more likely, from carelessness. In this very manuscript, for example, several works are consistently inscribed simply to Saint Augustine, although they most certainly belong to the bishop of Hippo.], a manuscript which, through the envy of time, concealed these Ambrosian gems for more than a thousand years?

In it, written by a hand contemporary with the age of the manuscript, these three sermons are inscribed under the name of Saint Ambrose. To what man of that name, then, if we do not go beyond the age of the manuscript, shall we attribute them besides the bishop of Milan?

Certainly not to Ambrose, the disciple of Origen and deacon of the Church of Alexandria [Note: [Col. 0099B] See Eusebius, book VI, 18; Epiphanius, *Heresy* 64; and Saint Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 56.]; nor to the one who flourished in the age of Saint Didymus, doctor of that same Church of Alexandria [Note: [Col. 0099B] Compare du Pin and Moreri.]. Neither of them possessed episcopal dignity or preached sermons to the people, which at that time were generally delivered only by bishops. Both wrote in Greek; and our sermons, so far from bearing the flavor of a Latin translation from Greek, wholly exclude it.

Nor should anyone attribute them to Ambrose of Carduc in Gaul. For even if someone were to say that the Sessorian manuscript was his archetype, these sermons could scarcely, if at all, be attributed to Ambrose of Carduc. That Ambrose was raised to the episcopate only after the middle of the eighth century [Note: [Col. 0099B] More about this Ambrose may be read in *Literary History of France*, vol. IV, p. 137 ff., and in Ceillier, the work cited above, vol. VIII, p. 486.]. Yet the manuscript contains these sermons—which clearly can only be the offspring of a bishop—in a codex older than the age of that bishop, written, as I have said, in the seventh century or, at the latest, at the beginning of the eighth.

For the same reason, the opinion of those who maintain that these sermons are the work of Ambrose Autpertus, the monk, should be utterly disregarded [Note: [Col. 0099C] Mabillon relates the deeds of this Ambrose in *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. IV, third century, part II, p. 259 onward. See also Anastasius, p. 1711 ff.]. For apart from the fact that it can be shown with sufficient probability from the author’s character and purpose, his style and manner of writing, and the different biblical version he used, that they are not his work [Note: [Col. 0099C] To demonstrate again that these sermons suit a bishop alone, just as in former times it belonged to bishops alone to instruct catechumens and the newly baptized, I shall not linger over the matter, nor shall I make an equally laborious attempt to show how greatly our sermons differ from Autpertus’s character and purpose, style, and manner of writing. I shall nevertheless hastily review a few points.

Autpertus scarcely ever fails in his writings to praise the monastic rule or to reveal himself as a monk addressing monks. Moreover, anyone who carefully reads Autpertus’s writings will frequently find in them expressions, antitheses, and sometimes nearly entire periods from Saint Augustine, as well as frequent affectionate forms of address such as “dearly beloved brothers,” and other similar expressions familiar to him. Our sermons are so completely alien to all these features that they have scarcely, I would say, a single syllable in common with Autpertus’s writings.

Furthermore, Autpertus used a biblical version which is scarcely anything other than a new Vulgate rendered almost word for word, and is therefore entirely different from the version found in these sermons. This can easily be detected by comparing his version with ours, at least if one consults Martène, vol. IX of the *Amplissima Collectio*, pp. 222, 227, 229, and elsewhere, and the Cologne edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XIII, pp. 480 and 492, where one will find all of Autpertus’s extant writings that have been published.], even if we were to deny them to him, one reason above all would suffice—the same reason by which we judged them inadmissible as the work of the bishop of Carduc.

For even the age of the monk Ambrose, not to include him among the writers who flourished at the end of the ninth century with Trithemius, cannot be placed before approximately the year 760 or extended beyond the year 778. Around the year 760 he began to become renowned for his commentaries on the Apocalypse; and in the year 778, according to the more probable opinion of scholars, he died while traveling to Rome, after having served as abbot of the monastery of Saint Vincent at the Volturnus near Benevento for only two months and twenty-five days, and not peacefully.

It therefore remains either to invent another Ambrose, distinct from those already mentioned and belonging to the first seven centuries of the Church, or to call the authority and antiquity of the manuscript into question. Neither course is acceptable. These sermons must therefore be attributed, on the authority of the Sessorian manuscript, to Ambrose of Milan.

The authority of this manuscript is abundantly demonstrated by eminent authors, who either testify that they held it in the highest esteem or extracted from it new writings both of Saint Augustine and of Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin.

## VII. Authors who used the Sessorian manuscript and spoke of it

Concerning this manuscript, which, as I said above, formerly belonged to the monastery of Nonantola, whence Hilarion Rancatus—who rendered outstanding service both to his order and to the universal Church, and founded the Sessorian Library—brought it to Rome [Note: [Col. 0099D] Concerning this distinguished man, deserving the highest praise of all, Joseph Blanchini, in part II of his *Evangeliary*, while displaying, among much else, specimens of several manuscripts in the Sessorian Library, writes as follows at fol. 593 verso: “At the venerable monastery of Holy Cross in Jerusalem there is an outstanding library, filled with manuscript codices, through the work of the distinguished Hilarion Rancatus of Milan, a Cistercian monk, procurator and general president of his order in Italy during his lifetime. He was exceptionally approved by five supreme pontiffs, Paul V and his successors, for his examination of Syriac books, his Arabic translation of the Bible, and his elucidation of controversies of faith. He lived sixty-nine years and died on 12 April 1663, as Mabillon writes (*Italian Journey*, p. 90). But what chiefly redounds to his praise is,” in almost the words of the cited Mabillon (ibid., vol. II), “that he diligently collected various manuscripts sought out from the monasteries of Italy; through them the said library became famous. From it were recovered that splendid letter of Saint Augustine to Alypius, which is number 29 in the new edition, and several new sermons.” Fumagalli, who carefully wrote and published his Life at Brescia in 1762, may also be consulted concerning this great man. Here, lest I incur the charge of ingratitude, I must not pass over in silence the above-mentioned most eminent Cardinal Joachim Besutius, a man, indeed, as Blanchini says in the same place, no less distinguished by modesty and piety than by exceptional learning. For he too not only increased and enriched the Sessorian Library with an abundance of exceedingly rare books and several most precious codices, but also made the monastery his universal heir and ensured that a librarian was appointed. To the words reported above, Blanchini added: ‘Cistercians now inhabit this place by the office of Pope Sixtus V.’ This is wholly at variance with the truth; for it is established from the series of abbots placed at the end of the history of that monastery, published at Rome in 1750 by Raimund Besutius, that Benedictine-Cistercian monks had already occupied the Sessorian monastery from 1563, under Pope Pius IV.], the illustrious Mabillon writes as follows in his *Italian Museum* [Note: [Col. 0100D] Vol. I, part II, p. 4, § 4.]:

> “In the Roman codex of Holy Cross, which formerly belonged to the monastery of Nonantola and was acquired before the year 800 by Abbot Anselm, there are seventy-three homilies, most of which are found in the Saint Gall exemplar. The author’s name was written on the front of the codex; but, after it had been erased, the name of Saint Ambrose was substituted. The greater part of these homilies are nevertheless by Maximus, although certain others by Jerome and Augustine are inserted under their names.”

Blanchini speaks of this manuscript in no different terms, as does likewise the most recent Roman editor of the works of Saint Maximus, who describes it accurately in his preface [Note: [Col. 0101C] Part I, § 5, pp. 16 ff. (*Our Patrology*, vol. LVII, cols. 17–18 ff.).]:

> “Another of the chief manuscripts I have mentioned is that formerly of the monastery of Nonantola in the territory of Modena, now in the Roman library of the Cistercian monks of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. It is a parchment folio codex, marked XC, as the outer front of the volume shows, although on p. 1 it bears the number CXXXIV. It surpasses the other manuscripts of this library both in antiquity and in the more accurate reading and integrity of its writing; it belongs to the seventh, or at latest the eighth, century of the Church. Its letter forms are Roman, of what is called the second age, inclining slightly toward Lombardic. From p. 129 to 169 it contains sixty items, partly homilies and partly sermons, concerning which the most eminent Cardinal Besutius, in the catalogue of the Library of Holy Cross [Note: [Col. 0101C] Would that this catalogue still existed! It would accurately and learnedly teach us what and how many most precious things had once been in that library. But when foreign armies invaded Italy, the library was plundered in 1809, and this catalogue perished, together with various manuscript codices and many exceedingly rare books, not without great loss to the republic of letters. It is recognized and admitted among scholars that nothing is more useful for adorning, enlarging, and advancing more deeply the study of letters than catalogues of manuscripts lying hidden in libraries. Yet, besides what we have reported above, the following notes concerning this manuscript by the eminent man survive on a slip of paper sewn to the front of the codex itself.]
>
> **COD. 134.**
>
> Contains, p. 1, a sermon of Saint Augustine *On Marriage*; from p. 2, the books of Saint Augustine’s *Confessions*. 2, f. 80, a sermon of Saint Ambrose *On Charity*. 3, f. 81, Saint Jerome’s *Epitaph of Paula*. 4, f. 88, a sermon of Saint Ambrose *On Perfection*. 5, f. 89, the seven Conferences of Cassian, those of Abbot Chaeremon and Abbot Joseph, which in the printed editions are numbers 11 through 17. 6, f. 129, sixty-one sermons of Saint Maximus, which, however, are attributed in this codex to Saint Ambrose. 7, f. 169, a sermon of Saint Augustine on what is written: ‘This is the day which the Lord has made.’ 8, f. 169, a sermon of Saint Jerome on Exodus in Lent. [Col. 0102C] 9, f. 170, a sermon of Saint Augustine to the Candidates and Catechumens; and up to f. 175 other sermons follow which are attributed in this codex to Saint Augustine. 10, f. 175, a sermon of Saint Jerome on Exodus at the Vigil of Easter. 11, f. 177, the Monastic Institutes of Saint Basil, translated by Rufinus. 12, f. 200, a sermon of Saint Augustine *On the Resurrection*. The codex seems to me very ancient, and the sermons of these Fathers should be compared with their published works.”
>
> From these words we infer three things in support of our position: first, that Besutius understood by the name Saint Ambrose one Ambrose of Milan; for he also uses the name simply in no. 6, where he certainly had the bishop of Milan in view; second, that he regarded our sermons as genuine products of the holy doctor, otherwise he would have noted the fact; for what seemed to him spurious or falsely attributed he consistently noted, as in nos. 6 and 9; finally, that he assigned all the sermons exhibited by this manuscript to the Holy Fathers, and thought that some among them were unpublished. For in his final words he refers readers, in order to compare those sermons, to the published works of the Holy Fathers, and not to the writings of others. This catalogue lacks the sermon printed here in second place. Since it is very brief and placed at the foot of the page, it escaped the eminent man’s diligence; at first sight it seems rather a continuation of the first than a second sermon.] declared: ‘I am certain that they have Saint Maximus as their author.’
