That these highly praised men mention no genuine sermon of Ambrose as occurring in the Sessorian manuscript, but wish all those assigned to Ambrose, though by a later hand, to be attributed to Saints Augustine, Jerome, and Maximus, will trouble no one who carefully considers that they are speaking only of the sermons which the codex contains from p. 129 onward, and not of ours, which are contained on the preceding pages and are ascribed to Saint Ambrose in those most clear words, and indeed in the first hand.

At this point I shall not suppress something which, I hope, will be pleasing to scholars: namely, that this very manuscript plainly proves that Mabillon and the praised editor of Saint Maximus did not consult the codex itself accurately in counting the sermons contained in it from the cited p. 129 onward. The former counted them all as seventy-three; the latter, although he recognized sixty as by Saint Maximus, transcribed sixty-two in his preliminary notices [Note: [Col. 0102D] P. 174 ff.]. Each thought it enough to notice the index prefixed to these sermons on the recto of the cited folio, and the same index deceived them both. For, through a duplicated no. 13, seventy-three sermons are numbered in it, although there are in fact seventy-four titles; at the same time sixty-two are attributed to Maximus, although the last of them is numbered 61. Nor did the editor of Saint Maximus err with the index only in the number, but also in the titles. To make this clearer, I have thought it worthwhile to list individually everything contained in this same codex.

## VIII. Contents of the Sessorian Codex

In it, on folio 1 recto, there is indeed a sermon of St. Augustine on Marriage, which begins without a title: “Marriage, at which Christ was both the giver and the guest at table, etc.” It ends: “Therefore those men were dried up and withered; but we have eaten and drunk and been refreshed through Jesus Christ himself, who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.” I have been unable to find this sermon, in which Augustine maintains against the Manichaeans that Christ truly instituted marriage, among the published works. It is clear, moreover, that Augustine preached a sermon on the goodness of marriage from the fragment of it which the Maurists quote from Bede and Florus, vol. V of the works, part II, col. 1519; yet our sermon has no agreement with it. This sermon is read only with difficulty in the codex, both because the characters have faded with age and are covered with dirt, and because the leaf is worn away by decay around its edges.

On folio 2 recto follow the thirteen books of the Confessions of the same St. Augustine, whose title is written at the foot of the verso of folio 1 as follows: “Here begin the books of the Confessions of the same St. Augustine.” This work is not divided into chapters and provides, in comparison with the Maurist edition, a rich harvest of variants for a new printing.

Folio 79 verso: “Here begins a sermon of St. Ambrose on Charity, from a reading of St. Paul the Apostle, against the wicked who envy the good”; this sermon is published here in third place.

Folio 81 recto: St. Jerome’s epitaph of St. Paula, with the heading: “Here begins the epitaph of St. Paula, composed by the blessed presbyter Jerome.” At the end of the same work there is a title for the tomb, written in uncial letters and executed in the form commonly preserved on stone inscriptions. It states that Paula died during the consulship of Honorius Augustus for the sixth time and Aristhenetus—not Arestenius, as it appears in the edition of the works of St. Jerome by Marianus Victor, nor Aristaenetus, as retained by the Paris edition, vol. IV, col. 669, and the Verona edition, vol. I, col. 689.

Folio 88 recto: “Here begins a sermon of St. Ambrose on the Perfect,” which is now brought to light first in the sequence.

On the verso of the same folio: “Here begins another work of the same author, against those who say that property should not be sold, but that mercy should be practiced from its fruits”; this sermon claims the second place among those on these leaves.

Folio 89 recto: John Cassian’s Conferences of the seven Fathers of the Thebaid. At its beginning one reads:

> “Contained in this codex are seven Conferences: that of Abbot Chaeremon, on perfection; another of the same author, on chastity; another of the same, on the protection of God; that of Abbot Nesteros, on spiritual knowledge; another of the same, on divine gifts; that of Abbot Joseph, on friendship; and another of the same, on definition.”

Titles of the chapters are inscribed in each Conference. In the first place there is a preface to Honoratus and Eucherius, although they are not named in the codex. These are the Conferences published as numbers 11–17 in the Roman edition printed for the Apostolic Chamber in 1611.

On folio 129 recto begin the sermons attributed in the first hand to St. Maximus of Turin, in the second hand to St. Ambrose, and again, in a more recent script, restored to St. Maximus. They are preceded by a list of titles in which, as we have already noted, seventy-four titles are counted, while seventy-three are counted under the repeated number 13. From this list Father Bruno, the editor of St. Maximus, excerpted the first sixty-three titles and, as I indicated above, published them on page 174 of his preliminary notes, when discussing the codices he used in preparing his edition.

On folio 177 recto occur the *Institutes for Monks* of St. Basil the Great, published beginning at col. 327 in vol. II of the Paris edition of 1730. In the codex they bear this title:

> “Institutes for monks of St. Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, in Christ. Preface of St. Rufinus the presbyter.”

I am surprised that the distinguished Fontanini, although he had seen this codex, nevertheless failed to notice that Rufinus is called a saint. Another writer would have noted this at the end of his *History of Aquileia*, in the final paragraph of which he recounts Rufinus’s praises and observes that Bolland would write of him as a saint.

Finally, on folio 200 recto, LXXIII, there is a sermon entitled: “Here begins a sermon of St. Augustine on the Resurrection.” This sermon, formerly counted among the writings of St. Fulgentius, the Benedictine editors of Augustine’s works, relying on the authority of this codex and another, removed from Fulgentius and published among Augustine’s genuine works, vol. V, part I, col. 1024.

This sermon is defective in the codex, which has lost two complete leaves. It thereby lost not only the final words of this sermon but also entirely lost another sermon of the same St. Augustine, which would have been number LXXIIII in our codex. Its title still appears in the list on folio 129 recto as follows:

> “Also another sermon of the same author at the beginning of the book, on the verse of the eleventh Psalm: ‘You, Lord, will preserve us and guard us from this generation forever.’”

## IX. Conjectures concerning the Date of the Ambrosian Sermons and the Time at Which They Were Preached

But, having set aside the codex, we must return to the Ambrosian sermons. I cannot leave them before at least touching upon the question of the time at which they were preached. Now that their author is known, their date too has been discovered. Nevertheless, I have no certainty about the year in which they were delivered; and if I may indulge in conjectures—though I wish the judgment concerning them to remain entirely with the reader—I think that they are not much earlier than the year 389.

For since they repeatedly and unmistakably mention both ecclesiastical singing and the psalms, hymns, and vigils—a discipline which St. Ambrose instituted at Milan around the year 386—it cannot be said that these sermons were written before that time.

This conjecture may perhaps also be confirmed by the fact that the third sermon contains much that, as I recall having noted elsewhere, seems especially appropriate to the extremely difficult times of Justina’s persecution. That unpunished harassment by the Arians was suppressed before the year 389, when Valentinian the Younger returned to Milan together with Theodosius after the tyrant Maximus had been killed.

That these three sermons were delivered in the same year is evident from their connection and sequence. It is much less difficult to determine at what season of the year they should be assigned. There can scarcely be any doubt that Ambrose delivered them during the Easter season.

Indeed, when he says in the first sermon that he is addressing those who, by the very profession of their devotion, have already been reckoned near to God and destined for heaven; and more clearly in the third, that he is addressing those who, having rejected the pageants and desires of the world, had made their passage to heaven by a better course, who had been cleansed from every trace of their former contagion through the saving washing of regeneration, and who, having died through baptism to the births of the world, had been ennobled by grace and born for heaven—this seems to indicate that he was speaking to a people who had already received baptism, to which no one was admitted except at the Easter vigil.

One may also add that there the holy teacher speaks very clearly of the ineffable mystery of the Incarnation, which at that time bishops carefully concealed from those who had not yet been baptized; and at the same time explains the effects of the sacrament of baptism already received. He exhorts his hearers not to enter into any future association with the world, to which they had said farewell on the day of redemption—that is, baptism, by which they had been marked with the Holy Spirit—for, having stripped off the old man and died with Christ, they had on that day put on the new man and risen again with him.

If anyone thinks that this cannot be sufficiently established from the context of the first sermon, because the words quoted may suitably be referred to catechumens and candidates for baptism, I shall not oppose him. And if he prefers to assign the first and second sermons to the preceding Lent, during which Ambrose taught catechumens and candidates for baptism in daily addresses, I shall not object.

I am well aware that St. Ambrose particularly exhorted those about to be baptized to despise earthly things; but I know equally well that, after they had received baptism, he confirmed them through new sermons in the same moral instructions which they had already learned from his teaching. In fact, Ambrose delivered the sermons comprising the books *On Flight from the World* and *On Jacob and the Blessed Life*, in which the renunciation of the affairs of this world is chiefly discussed, to the newly baptized, as the learned Maurist editors have wisely demonstrated.

[Note: In the preliminary admonitions.]

## X. On the Teaching of These Sermons

There is no reason for me to praise the sermons now brought to light; they will, as I anticipate, commend themselves to learned and devout readers.

That in the first and especially the second of them Ambrose teaches, in evangelical terms, that Christians must abandon all their possessions, distribute them to the poor for Christ’s sake, and entrust themselves entirely to divine providence should not be understood so strictly that no one may neglect this command without forfeiting eternal salvation. Rather, it must be observed and fulfilled by the person who strives to attain the highest degree of evangelical perfection.

Indeed, no one—whatever modern heterodox writers may babble—who has read at least chapter 11 of book I *On Duties* will deny that this distinction is ancient and is found in the writings of Ambrose. There he says most explicitly:

[Note: Sermon 1, § 4.]

> “Every duty, however, is either intermediate or perfect; and we can prove this equally by the authority of Scripture. For we have in the Gospel that the Lord said: ‘If you wish to enter into eternal life, keep the commandments.’ He said to him: ‘Which ones?’ Jesus said to him: ‘You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; honor your father and mother; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself’ (Matthew 19:17–19). These are intermediate duties, to which something is lacking. Finally, the young man says to him: ‘I have kept all these things from my youth; what do I still lack?’ Jesus says to him: ‘If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me’ (ibid., 20–21) … This, therefore, is the perfect duty.”

Ambrose therefore urges all Christians to fulfill the intermediate commandments, but only those more devoted to perfection to embrace the perfect commandments.

That this is so the same Ambrose declares in the first sermon, saying that “the Lord, wishing to provide for the perfect and complete, decreed that everything they possessed should be sold and expended.”

[Note: Vol. III, col. 13, nos. 36–37.]

The Lord therefore commanded not everyone, but only the perfect and complete, to sell all their resources and distribute them among the poor.

This is sufficient to silence heretics, unbelievers, and pseudo-politicians who, even in our own most wretched age, because of the rigid doctrines of Christian ethics handed down by the Fathers with complete agreement—which they insist must necessarily be extended to all the faithful without any distinction—declare, as falsely as impiously, that our most holy religion is antisocial.

[Note: Barbeyrac and Gibbon thus insult the moral teaching of the holy Fathers. Their errors have recently been revived in a work entitled *On Ancient and Modern Jesuitism: Political Works of M. de Pradt, former Archbishop of Mechlin*, Troyes, Paris edition, 1828. See, if permitted, chapter 5, “On the Modification of the Action of Christianity by Civilization,” pp. 48 ff. This book is filled with many sacrilegious and frivolous opinions, which it is not necessary to refute here at greater length.]

## XI. On the Division and the Editor’s Notes

There is still one matter that I shall touch upon briefly: namely, what I have done in publishing these sermons.

The text of the sermons runs continuously in the codex all the way to the end and therefore displays no division into paragraphs. Nevertheless, since I have seen this practice frequently employed by our predecessors even against the evidence of the codices, I judged that the custom should be retained, especially for the convenience of readers. The reader’s spirit is refreshed, as Augustine says somewhere, by a new heading after weariness on the road, just as the traveler’s spirit is refreshed by a lodging.

Rutilius Claudius Namatianus therefore rightly sang, writing to Victorinus Rufus, in his *Itinerary*:

[Note: Book II, division 4.]

> The frequent milestone, marked with an inscription,  
> Seems to provide intervals of the road for the weary.

I have also appended several scholia to the text of the sermons. Some concern the variants of the codex, its emendation, grammar, and paleography. Others I have supplied so that I might point out, almost with an extended finger, the parallel passages found in Ambrosian writings. Finally, I have not omitted comparative biblical notes, setting them beside the same passages of Sacred Scripture that Ambrose uses in his works published to date, or, where the Ambrosian writings lack them, passages used by other Fathers who were either contemporaries of Ambrose or flourished not long before or after his time.

Thus, from all these internal arguments—namely, the complete agreement with the Ambrosian writings—and from the external arguments, namely the authority and excellence of the codex, everyone may know and regard it as established that these sermons are genuine offspring of Ambrose, bishop of Milan.

But with these preliminary matters stated, let the candid and learned reader judge. For behold, the sermons.

## Three Sermons of St. Ambrose, Bishop of Milan

[Note: It should be observed that the word *Ambrosi* is consistently written in the codex with a single *i*, according to ancient orthography.]

### First Sermon: On the Perfect

#### 1

The heavenly command of our Lord Jesus Christ is recorded in the most sacred Gospel passages:

[Note: Our scribe uses only the diphthong *ae*, which he writes without ligature, in the manner of the ancients. Salmasius, in his letter to Sarravius; Conringius, *Censura diplomatica Lindaviensis*, p. 316; and Casleius, *Bibliotheca Britannica*, vol. V, p. 325, discuss the antiquity of this diphthong at length. We shall follow this orthography in editing the text, lest we deprive the manuscript of its proper appearance; but not in the notes, except when the Sessorian codex is being cited. — Editor.]

> “Sell everything that you possess and give alms” (Luke 12:33).

[Note: The new Latin Vulgate omits *everything* after “Sell”; but Ambrose uses a version of both the Old and New Testaments that differs considerably from ours. Moreover, when Ambrose cites the parallel passage at Matthew 19:21, he consistently adds *everything* after *sell*, although our Vulgate lacks the word there as well. Thus one may read it in book I *On Abraham*, chapter 3, p. 12; *On Naboth the Jezreelite*, chapter 14, p. 58; *On Psalm 118*, sermon 7, § 9; book VII *On Luke*, § 196; and elsewhere.

As for the passage just cited from Luke, it should be observed that it does not occur in the Ambrosian works published thus far. Accordingly, through this testimony and others to be cited below, Ambrose’s version may be enriched—the same version which the distinguished Sabatier collected together with those of the other holy Fathers and assembled with great usefulness and labor in the notes to his *Collection of Ancient Biblical Texts*. Indeed, this most valuable collection is supplemented and enlarged by more than four hundred verses from the extremely ancient Sessorian codex, which, God willing, we shall publish as soon as possible.]

The present sermon contains no ambiguities and leaves nothing uncertain or entangled in obscurity. With clear truth it commands the sale of possessions, and it does not pass over the disbursement of the proceeds.

[Note: The codex has *praetii* with the diphthong, which I would prefer to remove, since grammarians entirely exclude it from this word.]

[Note: *Praerogatio* may derive either from *prae* and *erogatio*, that is, careful expenditure, or rather from the verb *praerogare*, “to do something beforehand,” in accordance with Suetonius, *Augustus* 53, “to cast votes beforehand,” and Ulpian, *Digest* 19.2.19, where he speaks of paying rent in advance. Ambrose in fact repeatedly uses expressions from Ulpian and other jurists, as the Maurists themselves have often reminded us; see at least their notes, vol. II, p. 386, and vol. III, p. 917.

The same may be said of the word *distractio* used above, which is likewise a legal term for “sale”: Ulpian, *Digest* 14.3.5 near the end, and 2.15.8 near the middle.]

[Note: Here is Ambrose’s view of perfection. Following it himself, he renounced all his temporal possessions and either distributed them to the needy or gave them to the Church, as is clear from his Life and shines forth everywhere from his writings. Thus he writes in book I *On the Death of Satyrus*, no. 60: “For this is the highest justice: to sell what you possess and give to the poor. ‘He has distributed; he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever’ (Psalm 111:9). Therefore he left us as stewards, not heirs; for an inheritance is sought for a successor, whereas stewardship is owed to the poor.”

The holy doctor agrees with himself in Letter 7, p. 15, vol. III, where he says: “It is written, Matthew 19:21, not that you should offer half a didrachm, if indeed you wish to be perfect before God, but that you should sell all that is yours and give to the poor.” Compare also book I *On Duties*, chapter 30, § 6; *On Widows*, § 27 ff.; and Letter 26, p. 6, vol. III.]

> “Sell,” he says, “everything that you possess, and give alms.”

[Note: The bishop of Milan frequently commends almsgiving in his sermons, especially in *On Psalm 118*, sermon 8, § 22; sermon 12, § 24; book VIII *On Luke*, §§ 245 ff., vol. II; and Letter 2, § 26, vol. III.]

It does not allow those occupied with heavenly duties to become entangled in the care and burden of worldly possessions; and, since they are already close to God by the very profession of their devotion—or rather united to Christ by the sincerity of their mind—it frees them from the care and anxiety of secular possession.

[Note: The codex has *curam*, an obvious error.]

[Note: Thus the codex preserves the preposition *in*. On these and similar prepositions, which our codex always retains except in a few instances, see Putschius, *Ancient Orthographers*.]

[Note: The codex has *sinceritatem*. The letter *m* is clearly superfluous.]

[Note: The codex has *coniunctus*, but I preferred to write *coniunctos*, since the preceding words—*occupatos* and *proximos*—clearly require the accusative plural. In ancient codices we often find the letters *o* and *u* interchanged and substituted for one another.]

[Note: The codex has *curam sollicitudinemque*. I thought the *m* should be removed from both words, for many other changes would be required if they were retained as they stand in the codex. If anyone prefers to defend the codex’s reading, he should read as follows: “and, already near to God by the very profession of devotion, or rather united to Christ by sincerity of mind, he absolves the care and anxiety of secular possession,” with “the perfect man” understood; that is, he overcomes or conquers it. Ambrose uses *absolvit* in this sense in *On Psalm 37*, § 21, vol. II. Yet the reading I have retained seemed to yield a smoother meaning, with *absolvit* understood as “frees”—that is, God frees him—in the same way that the word is used in *On Psalm 45*, § 17.]

It removes from the world the whole course of your activity and every movement of your thought—you whom it has deigned to assign to heaven.

[Note: Here and below Ambrose, although addressing several people, speaks in the singular, as is his custom. Such examples occur frequently in Ambrosian writings. See book VI *On Flight from the World*, § 33, vol. I, and elsewhere.]

From this comes what he openly commands:

> “Do not worry, saying: ‘What shall we eat, or what shall we wear?’” (Matthew 6:31).

[Note: The codex has *edamus*, but I have written *edemus*, since the codex retains this reading below as well.]

[Note: The second reading, which is not found in the Ambrosian writings in question, appears in St. Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, col. 210; *On Works and Almsgiving*, col. 240; and book III of the *Testimonies*, col. 307. Cyprian adds, with the Vulgate, “or what shall we drink,” which the author of the *Rule for Clerics* in Augustine omits, vol. I, col. 39.]

> “And do not worry about tomorrow” (ibid., 34).

[Note: St. Augustine, the disciple of our Ambrose, whom the Maurists note frequently looked back to his teacher’s writings, cites this passage in book II *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, vol. III, col. 222; in *On Lying*, col. 437; and also in *Against Adimantus*, vol. VIII, col. 115.]

So that what he had commanded might easily be fulfilled once every anxious thought had been removed:

> “Sell,” he says, “everything that you possess, and give alms.”

He cut off every excuse of crafty greed when he ordered that nothing be left for tomorrow, and when he commanded the whole amount of one’s substance to be paid out beforehand.

[Note: See the note above, p. 1, note f—on this page, note b.]

[Note: Recall the annotations above, p. 1, note 2—on this page, note 1—and compare similar passages in *On Psalm 118*, sermon 8, § 9, and sermon 21, § 18, vol. II.]

## II.

But let us return to the preceding discussion [Note: The word *disputatio* frequently has the same meaning in Ambrose as *tractatio*, that is, evangelical exposition or preaching. Thus the Benedictine editors, vol. II, p. 1040, note d.], to shed light upon it [Note: Thus the manuscript, with an ancient and indeed correct spelling, has *conlustranda* for *collustranda*; for lambdacism (λαβδακισμός) was characteristic of Africans, as Isidore testifies, *Origins* I, 32.].

> “Do not worry, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ For the nations [Note: *Natio* is used in a disparaging sense, following Greek usage. See Suidas under the word ἔθνος (*ethnos*).] seek all these things. But your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things [Note: This passage, which is absent from the Ambrosian manuscripts, is cited in this form by Saint Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, col. 210, and *On Works and Almsgiving*, col. 210 [Col. 0113C], though the word “heavenly,” retained in the manuscript of Claromontanus used by Sabatier, is omitted. It should be noted that below, in this same passage, *gentes* is read in place of *nationes*, as it is also found in the author of the *Opus imperfectum on Matthew*, homily 16.]” (ibid., 32).

The thought of distrust destroys within you the faith that professes divine providence; and while you fear [Note: The manuscript reads *metuit*, but *metuis* must be read, as the following second-person verbs—*dubites* . . . *retrahis* . . . *desistas*—plainly show.] that something may be lacking on the following day [Note: Thus the manuscript, perhaps because *d* follows; evidently *t* before *d* was pronounced with one and the same sound among the ancients.], you must doubt the promises. Then you withdraw your hands from righteous works. Thus, held fast by weak-minded anxiety, you cease from good works; and by ceasing from good works, you lose the name of religion and of God. By the very faithlessness [Note: Saint Ambrose frequently uses this word to denote the fault of unbelief. See below, and vol. I, col. 659, no. 41; vol. III, cols. 106 and 961, nos. 82 and 110.] of your weakness you become comparable to unbelieving pagans [Note: The manuscript here and elsewhere in such words preserves *con*.], and incur the detestable name of unbelief and the designation of pagan folly [Note: The manuscript reads *incurrat*, but this is certainly erroneous.].

It belongs to Christians to think of the future with unwavering hope [Note: The holy bishop has substantially similar statements in *On Isaac and the Soul* I, 1; *On David’s Intercession* II, 3, 12, vol. I; *On Psalm 36*, 79, and *On Psalm 37*, 2, vol. II; and Letter 35, 14, vol. III.], whereas it belongs to pagans, in faithlessness and despair, to seek only the present [Note: Compare the passages cited in the Psalms.], as Christ says:

> “Do not worry, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ For the nations seek these things.”

And he added:

> “But your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things.”

## III.

The divine word has taught us that the necessity of our condition [Note: The manuscript has *ci* for *ti*; examples of this kind recur below and are common in ancient manuscripts.] [Note: The manuscript has *necessitatem*; but I have corrected it to *necessitatis*, as the sense seems to require.] cannot be hidden from our heavenly Father [Note: The manuscript has *calestis Patris*, but it had to be corrected to *caelesti Patri*.], and it entrusts to his providence and care the provision of everything for us [Note: Thus the manuscript consistently retains the preposition *ad*]; provided that, clinging to works of righteousness and occupied with seeking the heavenly kingdom, we are not pierced by anxiety over any present troubles [Note: The manuscript reads *conpugnat*, an obvious transposition in place of *conpungat*.] [Note: Ambrose likewise teaches that the perfect are never pierced by disturbances of the world or harassed by worldly desires, in *On Jacob* I, 8, 35; II, 6, 28; *On Cain and Abel* II, 2, 8; *On Flight from the World* IV, 17, vol. I; and *On Duties* I, 38, 200, vol. III.], saying:

> “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you [Note: Augustine has the same wording in Sermon 57, vol. V, col. 337, and *Tractate 122 on John*, vol. III, col. 811, as well as in the author of the *Rule for Clerics*, vol. I, col. 39, though with *these things* added before *all*. Ambrose, however, in *On Cain and Abel* I, 4, 12, vol. I, has: “Seek the kingdom of God, and behold, all things are at hand for you”; in *On Luke* VII, 130, vol. II: “Seek the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you”; but in *On the Exhortation to Virginity* 9, 56, vol. III: “and behold, all things will be supplied to you.” No one should attempt, on the basis of this diversity of readings—which it has not been irrelevant to note here—to undermine the reliability of our Ambrosian text. For, as Natalis Alexander aptly writes (*Ecclesiastical History*, century IV, part I, § 2, p. 503), a reading of Saint Ambrose’s works shows that he did not always quote the same passages of Sacred Scripture in the same words. Indeed, the Maurists say in the preface to *On the Sacraments*, col. 432, vol. III: Since it is beyond doubt that this author of ours spoke without extensive preparation, it should by no means seem surprising if he did not always quote Scripture in its own words, but in those which memory suggested to him at the moment. I am not unaware that Ansaldi held the contrary opinion in his work entitled *On the Authentic Readings of Sacred Scripture among the Holy Fathers*, published at Verona in 1747. Yet unless it is proved that this same Father possessed several authoritative biblical versions at the same time, it is beyond doubt that, if Ansaldi’s prejudice were applied critically to all the Fathers’ writings from beginning to end, scarcely one work would be found that could be called the genuine offspring of that Father, since scarcely one would be found in which he consistently cites the same passages of Sacred Scripture in the same words.]” (ibid., 33).

Those devoted to works of righteousness and piety, and occupied with heavenly exercises, he makes secure and tranquil in every respect, so that you are not diverted from knowledge of the Father, nor drawn away from knowledge of the Only-Begotten, nor cease from the confession of the gift of the Holy Spirit; so that you do not stray from meditation upon the commandment, from hope in the promise, from faith in what has been believed, from love of neighbor, or from perfection in fulfilling the commandment [Note: In a similar sense Ambrose writes in *On Abraham* I, 2, 9, vol. I: “He who follows God is always safe. Therefore we must prefer God to everything: neither regard for one’s homeland, nor affection for parents and children, nor consideration for one’s wife ought to call us back from carrying out the heavenly commandments, because God grants us all these things and is able to preserve what he gives. Compare also II, 5, 21.].

Of this Moses gives instruction (Deut. 6:6–8): the commandment is always to dwell in our heart, always to stand before our eyes, bound by meditation to all our limbs [Note: The manuscript reads *vinculatus*, but I have judged that *vinculatum* should be written, so that it agrees with the neuter *mandatum*.], and always to cling to our senses [Note: Almost the same words occur in *On Psalm 1*, 30, and *On Psalm 117*, Sermon 19, 31 and following; in these passages also the holy teacher uses both the Deuteronomic text cited above and the authority of Moses. See also *On Psalm 36*, 65, vol. II.].

Concerning this David says:

> “Your ordinances, O Lord, will always be my songs [Note: In this passage Ambrose quotes the words in *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 7, 25, omitting only *always in the midst* and *O Lord* at the end. He seems to have added these not as belonging to the scriptural text, but to serve his own argument. The holy bishop wishes us always to devote ourselves to meditation on God’s law and always to delight in his ordinances. Since whose ordinances they are is not apparent from the truncated verse of the Psalm, he naturally added “O Lord.”]” (Ps. 118:54).

And again:

> “His delight is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he will meditate day and night [Note: Ambrose quotes this word for word in *On Psalm 1*, 30, vol. II.]” (Ps. 1:2).

And elsewhere it is written [Note: Thus the manuscript writes it with *b*, as below *recursitat*; this spelling frequently occurs in ancient manuscripts. See Mai, *Cicero’s Ancient Interpreter* XV, 2, on *In Vatinium*, vol. II, p. 185, Roman edition of 1828.]:

> “Let not the book of this law depart from your hand, and you shall meditate upon it day and night [Note: This is the ancient version in Sabatier, except that it has *from your mouth* instead of *from your hand*. But *from your hand* is found in Cassiodorus, *On Psalm 6*, col. 29, and this sermon suggests that Ambrose read it in that form.]” (Josh. 1:8).

Similarly, the Apostle exhorts and instructs Timothy, writing:

> “Meditate on these things; be occupied with them, so that your progress may appear to all [Note: The Vulgate has *may be manifest* instead of *may appear*, and the ancient version in Sabatier and the Ambrosiaster agree with the Vulgate. The Greek text reads φανερὰ ᾖ ἐν πᾶσιν (*phanera ē en pasin*), “may be manifest among all,” though several manuscripts omit ἐν (*en*).]” (1 Tim. 4:15).

## IV.

The will of a religious person, held fast by heavenly laws and occupied day and night with meditation on divine ordinances, has no free time in which to think about the world, care for possessions, adorn urban estates, cultivate the discipline of farming, calculate revenues, or examine expenses [Note: Similar statements are found in *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 13, 7, where, setting David’s perfection before us as an example, he says of him: “His mind was not led away by worldly allurements; he did not burn with the desire to accumulate a patrimony of money; nor did anxiety over extending his boundaries and excluding his neighbor turn back the attention devoted to meditation. Whatever time the day could contain, meditation on the law alone claimed entirely for itself.”].

For if he takes hold of the one, he abandons the other, in accordance with what the Lord’s word promised:

> “No one who has put his hand to the plow”—that is, to heavenly labor and to the sign of the Lord’s cross [Note: I have marked the parentheses with my own signs so that readers may be aware of the parenthesis and not confuse Ambrose’s explanation with the sacred text.] [Note: This means either literally the sign of the cross, which the ancient Christians commonly made at the beginning of every undertaking, as the holy Fathers frequently attest; or perhaps baptism, by which Ambrose’s congregation had recently been initiated or was soon to be initiated. The Maurists believe that Ambrose calls baptism the sacrament of the cross in *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 13, 6, vol. II. See the note there, col. 546, and below. In this passage and elsewhere Ambrose, according to his usual practice, interweaves his words with the words of Sacred Scripture. See at least the cited sermon *On the Basilicas Not to Be Surrendered*, and scattered passages elsewhere.]—“looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God [Note: Ambrose has in *On Psalm 43*, 32, vol. II: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God”; and in *On Luke* VIII, 43: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven.” Thus, if *fit* is read in the first passage instead of *able*, as in the second, with *and* added after *plow*; or if the final words of the second passage, *the kingdom of God*, are substituted for *the kingdom of heaven*, the third reading—our manuscript’s reading—will arise word for word from Ambrose.]” (Luke 9:62).

For one cannot carry out both things: one is opposed to the other in reason, different in truth, and rival in will. The one thinks about the world; the other longs for heaven. The one persists in worldly calculations; the other devotes itself to divine prayers and meditations.

Finally, to confirm my statements by facts and strengthen my argument by deeds, I shall use an example [Note: Ambrose frequently uses examples by which he explains or confirms his position, as may be seen, for example, in *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 8, 26, vol. II, and *On the Mysteries* IX, 50, vol. III.].

If, while you are carrying the divine book in your hands, taking in its letters with your eyes as you read, and committing the divine commandments to your senses [Note: Thus the manuscript reads in place of *commendanti*: in ancient orthography *n* before *m* was pronounced like *m*.], someone should hand you books of accounts or documents concerning acquired property, you must throw aside the book of divine law that you were carrying in your hands [Note: The manuscript has this form, with a clear single *i* through contraction; it is frequent in ancient manuscripts.], in order to receive and read the documents of worldly accounts. And thus it happens that, preferring worldly calculations to the divine books, you become a despiser of the commandment, which repeatedly warns that the book must not be absent from your hands and that meditation upon it must not cease in your heart [Note: The Benedictine editors rightly observe that our holy bishop frequently commended constant reading of Sacred Scripture to the faithful in his sermons, vol. II, col. 474. We have also noted this above; anyone who reads *On Abraham* II, 5, 22, vol. I, and especially *On Psalms 1 and 118*, will find it entirely evident.].

For this reason the Lord, wishing to provide for the perfect and those who have attained completion, judged that everything they possessed should be sold and distributed [Note: “The righteous man sold his possessions,” Ambrose writes in *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 21, 18; “he distributed them to the poor and kept nothing for himself.” Recall the statements above, p. 1, note 2 (col. 111, no. 1).], so that they might not be torn away from love of him by any consideration [Note: Thus the manuscript reads in place of *delectu*. I have retained the reading because it bears the mark of antiquity and occurs very frequently, correctly written in ancient manuscripts of the highest quality. Maius read it in the palimpsest of Cicero’s *On the Republic* I, 35, p. 94, and in the various readings of Cicero’s *Laws* I, 6. He also wisely remarked on the matter in the work cited, II, 32, note a, p. 206: “Before we always attribute such spellings to the discretion of copyists, Aegretius should be read, for he gives the differences among words beginning with *de-* and *di-*,” p. 2267.], or diverted from meditation [Note: While treating this subject, the holy doctor expresses the same idea in *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 10, 29: “Let us therefore learn also to meditate on the law; let us not be diverted by worldly allurements or occupied by impediments, but let us always attend to the law of God. Compare the notes above, p. 4, note 2, and p. 5, note 3 (col. 114, no. 7, and this page, no. 1).].

This is why he forbade even consideration of the necessities of mortals—clothing, food, and drink—and promised that all things would be supplied by himself to those who act accordingly [Note: In explaining Matthew 6:33, Ambrose says something similar in *On Luke* VII, 130, vol. II: “The Lord shows that grace will not be lacking to the faithful either in the present or in the future, provided that those who desire divine things do not seek earthly things. For it is disgraceful for people concerned with the kingdom to worry about food. The king knows how to feed, nourish, and clothe his household.”], so that, as has often already been said, no necessity might hold you back from the work of God; so that no barrenness of the year might disturb you, no scarcity of crops or dryness of the fields torment you, nor the deceptive yields of olive groves and vineyards; and so that losses from dying livestock might not shake you [Note: Compare *On Jacob and the Blessed Life* I, VII, 32, vol. I, and *On Psalm 118*, Sermons 8, 7, and 21, 18, vol. II.].

## V.

Let devotion remain free and unshaken, so that, possessed by love of its God and Lord Christ, it may resound with hymns, devote itself to prayer, and persist in fasting and vigils [Note: See *On Psalm 43*, 23, and *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 7, 25–37, where similar expressions and ideas occur.], and may suitably and appropriately break into that prophetic song:

> “The fig tree will not bear fruit, there will be no growth in the vineyards. The work of the olive will fail; the fields will yield no food. The sheep will be removed from the pasture, and there will be no cattle in the stalls [Note: Cyprian likewise has this in his Letter to Demetrianus, col. 222, except that he reads *fruit* instead of *fruits*, *food* instead of *foodstuff*, and adds *and* twice, namely after *fruit* and before *fields*. Augustine, in the passage cited, also supports Ambrose.]  
> Yet I will rejoice in the Lord and exult in God my Savior [Note: Cyprian has the same wording in the passage cited, as does Augustine in the parallel passage, though both omit *and* after *I will rejoice*]” (Hab. 3:17–18).

The person who, having cast off the burdens of worldly possession—or rather, having distributed them in advance for the poverty of his brothers—is not overwhelmed by impending or present calamities, always rejoices and is glad in the Lord. He is not driven by the demand of tribute and necessity [Note: Ambrose teaches everywhere that the perfect man is not harassed by worldly disturbances, in addition to the places noted above, p. 3, note 5 (col. 113, no. 4), and especially in *On Cain and Abel* II, 2, 8; *On Jacob and the Blessed Life* I, 7, 32, and 8, 35; *On Jacob* II, 6, 28, vol. I; *On Psalm 1*, 34; *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 8, 7, vol. II; and *On Duties* I, 38, 200, vol. III. Ambrose speaks as follows in *On Psalm 38*, 27, where he includes the collection of tribute among the troubles of the world: “Do not be foolishly troubled because of riches; do not be roused from sleep to consider how you may preserve your money or increase your wealth; do not go out at night or keep watch at the judge’s house in order to seize another’s property, bring a lawsuit against a poor man, or fear the tax collector. Such trouble is vain.”], nor by fields of possessions lying barren [Note: Thus the manuscript reads with a single *l*. I have judged that this reading should be retained, since similar forms have appeared to me in ancient and excellent manuscripts.], nor by orchards disfigured through the abandonment of their cultivators. He is not troubled by the savage slaughter of hail [Note: The manuscript reads *caedis*, but this plainly appears to be an error; the sense shows that *caedes* should be written in the nominative. The faulty spelling may have arisen because ancient copyists used *e* and *i* indiscriminately. Thus *sicet* occurs for *secet*, *Menerva* for *Minerva*, and *Magester* for *Magister*, as Fumagallius notes, *Diplomatic Institutions* I, 6, 9, pp. 109 and following. See also Cicero’s ancient interpreter cited by Maius, pp. 107, 123, 134, 144, 147, and elsewhere.], nor by the abundance of rains suspended by a long period of clear weather, nor by the frequent violence of storms [Note: Ambrose speaks in this way of evangelical perfection in the person of the Apostle Peter in *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 8, 7: “Your portion is not dried by drought, dissolved by rain, scorched by cold, or shaken by storm.”], nor by the collapse of roofs, nor does the condition or anxiety of nearby relatives who are suffering or dying torment him; nor the flight of slaves, nor theft.

## VI.

Everything that has been transferred to heaven is secure [Note: Ambrose frequently teaches in his writings that it is through the poor that everything belonging to us is conveyed to the heavenly treasures, or placed in heaven. At least the following passages should be consulted: *On Naboth of Jezreel* XIV, 58, vol. I; *On Duties* II, 28, 140; Sermon *On the Basilicas Not to Be Surrendered*, no. 33; and Letter 38, 7, vol. III.]. Such things are disturbed by no slander, attacked by no lawsuit, and perish through no worldly loss. What has been sent ahead to heaven is preserved under God’s protection, as the Lord Jesus Christ says:

> “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where moth and rust destroy [Note: Here and below special attention should be paid to the word *extermino*, which Saint Ambrose always uses in this passage of Sacred Scripture in place of *demolior*, as in the Vulgate. From this one may infer that either this sermon is a genuine work of Ambrose or at least bears the character of the Ambrosian age. In the fifth century Saint Jerome removed this word from the sacred text. His comment on Matthew 6:16 is as follows: “The word *exterminant*, which through the fault of translators has become common in ecclesiastical writings, signifies something quite different from what is commonly understood: exiles are *exterminated*, for they are sent beyond the boundaries. Therefore, in place of this expression, we should always understand *demoliri*, ‘to destroy.’” Millius writes concerning this word in his prolegomena, p. LI: “Among suitable Latin words we also count obsolete terms, although they are now commonly heard. For words that have become worthless under this name were, when these writings were composed, in daily use among Christians. Such are, for example, *exterminant* in Matthew 6:16 and 19, which Jerome acknowledges as common in ecclesiastical writings, even though he disapproves of it and substitutes the much harsher *demoliri*.”]; and where thieves break in and steal [Note: Ambrose has this word for word in *On the Holy Spirit* I, 16, 182, vol. IV. In *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 8, 8, vol. II, he has: “Do not store up treasure for yourselves on earth”; and in Sermon 12, 2: “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where rust and moth destroy.”].  
> But store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves do not break in and steal [Note: Ambrose similarly has this in *On the Holy Spirit*, II, 183, except that he omits *but* and adds *treasures* after *for yourselves*. He omits the word *treasures* in the cited *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 12, 2, where he reads: “But store up for yourselves in heaven.” In the cited Sermon 8, 8, he differs from himself, writing: “But store up treasure for yourselves in heaven.”]. For where your treasure is, there also will your heart be” [Note: He reads this word for word in *On Jacob and the Blessed Life* II, 5, 23, vol. I, and *On the Holy Spirit* I, in the passage cited.] (Matt. 6:19–21).

Following the example of this commandment, the Apostle Paul most blessedly instructs Timothy concerning what must be commanded to the rich of this age: they are not to be exalted by worldly pomp, but to attain the height of Christian humility; they are not to be deceived by the fleeting hope of worldly riches, but to be invited by the permanence of divine promises [Note: Ambrose frequently condemns worldly pomp and the pride of this age in his writings. In them he also often commends humility to the rich and sets before their eyes how earthly things are to be regarded as nothing in comparison with heavenly things—for example, in *On Abraham*, *On Isaac*, *On the Good of Death*, especially chapters 5, 6, and 7; *On Flight from the World*, especially chapters 1 and 4, vol. I; and in the Psalms, particularly *On Psalm 38*, 36, and *On Psalm 117*, Sermons 4, 25; 5, 27 and 36, vol. II.].

> “Command the rich of this age,” he says, “not to be high-minded, nor to set their hope on the uncertainty of riches, but on the living God, who gives us all things richly for enjoyment [Note: The author of the Letter to Demetrianus, col. 41, Augustine in Letter 30, vol. II, col. 383, and elsewhere in scattered passages, Chromatius of Aquileia in *On Matthew*, col. 988, Sedulius the Irishman in *On 1 Timothy 6*, and others cite this passage in the same form, except that they have *abundantly* instead of *richly*.]; to do good, to be rich in good works, to give readily [Note: Augustine likewise has this in Letter 157, vol. II, col. 554; *On the City of God* I, 10, vol. VII, col. 11; *Against Adimantus*, vol. VIII, col. 143; and elsewhere.], to share, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of true life [Note: Augustine agrees with our Ambrose in Letter 130, col. 382, vol. II, and *Tractate 22 on John*, vol. III, col. 466, as well as in many other passages.]” (1 Tim. 6:17–19) [Note: Thus this sermon ends in the manuscript; let the learned judge whether it is mutilated. Moreover, the Sessorian manuscript offers no indication whatever that the sermon is mutilated; rather, it seems to exclude that possibility, since, without leaving any blank space on the parchment, it immediately presents another sermon, which I am hastening to transcribe.].

# SERMON II  
## Against Those Who Say That Possessions Should Not Be Sold but That Mercy Should Be Practiced from Their Revenues

## I.

The saving commandment of Jesus Christ is:

> “Sell everything that you possess and give alms [Note: See the notes in the first sermon, p. 1, note 1 (col. 109, no. 1).]” (Luke 12:33).

The faith of the Lord and teacher is clear [Note: The worm-eaten parchment preserves only the letters *ma* of this word intact, together with a few upper strokes, from which I interpreted it as *magistri*.]: he commanded not only that possessions be sold [Note: Compare Ulpian, *On Transactions*; Apuleius I; Suetonius, *Vespasian* XVI; Justin IX, 1; Tacitus, *Annals* VI, 17; and recall the earlier statement in note f, p. 1 (col. 111, b).], but also prescribed what should be done with what was sold [Note: Recall the statement at the cited place, note 2 (our col. 111, no. 1).].

But wicked teachers obscure this faith with frivolous and empty words. The Apostle Paul has already condemned them, not as adulterers of the flesh but, what is prior, as adulterators of the divine utterances [Note: This word too is difficult to read in the manuscript, and I write it more conjecturally than confidently, although I know this comparative expression to be familiar to Ambrose.], saying:

> “Peddling the word of God [Note: Irenaeus has this in *Against Heresies* IV, 26, col. 263; Jerome and Bede agree in this passage. The Greek reads καπηλεύοντες τὸν λόγον τοῦ Θεοῦ (*kapēleuontes ton logon tou Theou*), “peddling the word of God.”]” (2 Cor. 2:17).

And again:

> “Do you not know that whoever corrupts the temple of God, God will destroy him? [Note: The opening words, “Do you not know,” have been transferred here from the preceding verse, 1 Cor. 3:16. Augustine, *Against the Manichaeans*, vol. VIII, col. 179, reads the remainder as follows: “Whoever corrupts the temple of God, God will corrupt him.” He adds: “Fearing this word, many Latin translators did not wish to say ‘he will corrupt him,’ but said ‘God will destroy him’; and while not departing from the substance of the matter, they avoided the offensiveness of the word … But they [the Manichaeans] are convicted by the Greek copies, in which it is most clearly written: ‘Whoever corrupts the temple of God, God will corrupt him.’” The Greek text has φθείρει … φθερεῖ (*phtheirei … phtherei*). Apart from Augustine and Hilary, no Latin Father doubles the verb *corrumpet*; most, like our Ambrose, retain *disperdet*—“will destroy”—in the second place.]” (1 Cor. 3:17).

And that saying which Christ recalled in the Gospel while rebuking the Pharisees:

> “You reject the commandments of God in order to establish your traditions [Note: Saint Cyprian likewise has this in Letters 40, 63, 68, and 74, cols. 54, 108, 109, 118, and 139, but in the singular and with *Rejecting a commandment* instead of *Rejecting commandments*. Zeno of Verona has the same in Book I, Treatise 1, col. 12, as does Siricius in Letter 4, except that they read *Rejecting a commandment* for *Rejecting commandments*.]” (Mark 7:9).

## II.

“They say that possession should not be sold, but retained, and that works of mercy should be performed from its revenues.”

What are you concealing under the appearance of a work of mercy—the ardor and desire to possess and retain property [Note: The manuscript has *habende retinendeque*, without the diphthong]? What crime of impiety are you shading beneath the covering of piety? Why do you deprive believers, through subtle persuasion, of the Lord’s commandment, which is itself illustrious in its purity? Why do you deny the religious the heavenly commandment through a contrived and deceptive conversation [Note: Thus the manuscript reads here and below, *conloquium* with a single *l*, according to ancient usage.]? Why, with serpentine counsel, do you close paradise to God’s servants [Note: This expression is familiar to Ambrose. See at least the Sermon *On the Basilicas Not to Be Surrendered*, no. 30, p. 924, vol. III, and passim]—you who not only do not enter yourself, but also hide the keys of the heavenly kingdoms from those who wish to enter? [Note: It is clearly established from many passages in the works of this holy bishop that in Saint Ambrose’s time there were people who strongly opposed the evangelical counsel of poverty and, while professing it, held it in contempt. See at least *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 21, no. 18, where these memorable words occur: “How often are good deeds themselves made into a crime? How often is virtue counted a disgrace? How often is grace itself ungrateful? The righteous man sold his possessions, distributed them to the poor, and kept nothing for himself; yet he is often despised even in the Church because he has ceased to be rich, as it is written: ‘If he were to give all his possessions for love, he would be utterly despised’” (Song 8:7). Ambrose’s Letter 58 also concerns this subject. In it the holy doctor relates that Paulinus and Therasia renounced all their possessions for Christ and distributed them to the poor, and demonstrates by the examples of the patriarchs that what seemed shameful and disgraceful to worldly people was in fact rightly and properly done.].

You are not wiser than Christ, who commanded it to be done, nor better than the Apostle Paul, who carried it out [Note: Ambrose repeatedly sets before his people the examples of the Apostle Paul for imitation, since, as he says in *On Virginity* 20, 130, Paul “challenges by his honor, teaches by his instruction, and invites by his example.”].

As soon as he had been enlightened by grace [Note: Thus the manuscript reads, an excellent and ancient form, *inluminatus*.], he did not yield to flesh and blood amid fearful sufferings [Note: Ambrose here refers to Galatians 1:16]; he did not go up to Jerusalem to seek counsel from the preceding Apostles [Note: He is referring to the cited passage, verse 17], since divine and heavenly converse had instructed him in every proclamation of the faith [Note: See the cited passage, verse 12.]; he did not go to Cilicia [Note: Thus the manuscript reads *petit* for *petiit*, a contraction customary among ancient scribes.] to receive his paternal inheritance in his native city [Note: Paul’s origin in Tarsus of Cilicia is a well-known historical fact.], which he had abandoned for Christ and for the poor [Note: This word at the end of the verse has run together into a monogram, and can scarcely be deciphered from the faded characters.]; nor did he defend the nobility of the Roman race from which he derived his blood [Note: Paul enjoyed the privilege of Roman citizenship, by which the people of Tarsus, who favored the Augustan cause, had been honored by that emperor. Acts 22:27–28.], which he knew had been disgraced by the Lord’s Passion [Note: Namely, because Jesus Christ was crucified by the authority of Roman governors and Roman soldiers.]. Rather, he passed through the region of Arabia [Note: That Paul traveled through Arabia preaching the word of God is clear from Galatians 1:17], so that he might proclaim by faithful preaching to all mortals as saving and divine that venerable name which he had unjustly persecuted, which he had attacked by eloquence and by Pharisaic envy.

Who, then, proves comparable in deeds to Paul, endowed with many triumphs: one who has stripped himself of all the bonds and splendors of the world [Note: Thus the manuscript, in good and ancient orthography, in place of *vinculis*. Cicero too used such syncopated forms, as Cornutus notes, p. 2288], and will rightly be called God’s servant; one who, despite envious detractors, perseveringly persists in fulfilling the commandments of the Lord Christ, who said:

> “Sell everything that you possess and give alms (Luke 12:33); and behold, all things are clean for you [Note: Ambrose reads “And behold, all things are clean for you” in *On Luke* VII, 100, with the same words but in a different order: “and behold, all things are clean for you.”]” (ibid. 11:41).

### III

In the command, the selling-off is enjoined, and distribution of what has been sold is required [Note: [Col. 0121B] See above, note 2, p. 1 (Col. 111, no. 1) and following, where a similar expression occurs in the Ambrosian passage cited from *On the Death of Satyrus* I, 60.]. Purification of mind is promised to the devoted; for those cleansed of defilement, the heavenly kingdom has been prepared [Col. 0121B]. I ask: what more do you seek, or what remains, except that, if servants do not do what is commanded, God should do what he threatens? He also said:

> “If you have not been faithful with unrighteous mammon [Note: [Col. 0121C] “Of mammon,” says Ambrose in the cited passage in Luke, no. 224, “not a just power, but an unjust servitude.”], who will entrust to you what is true [Note: [Col. 0121C] Saint Cyprian similarly has this in *On Works and Almsgiving*, col. 240, and Saint Augustine in *Confessions* V, vol. I, col. 127, except that at the end he has *who will entrust you to yourselves?* in place of *who will entrust to you?* Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* II, 24, col. 169, reads it with the codex.]? And if you have not been faithful with what belongs to another [Note: [Col. 0121C] Saint Ambrose, in this passage, *On Luke* VII, no. 246, writes: “Riches are alien to us, because they are contrary to nature; they are neither born with us nor pass away with us.” In the same place, explaining this testimony, he expounds it in the sense he employs in the sermon. Thus he says, no. 247: “The Jews therefore appear to be convicted both of fraud and of greed. For those who knew that their possessions were alien—for the fruits of the earth were given by the Lord God for common use to all—ought certainly to have shared them with the poor.”] who will entrust to you what is yours [Note: [Col. 0121D] Ambrose, in the cited passage, no. 215, likewise has *who will entrust to you?* at the end, in place of *who will give you?* Let the reader judge whether Saint Ambrose recited these testimonies from memory and altered the final words of both verses, or whether rather the same transposition should be attributed to the copyist’s carelessness.] (Luke XVI, 11–12). And these will go away into eternal burning, but the righteous into eternal life [Note: [Col. 0121D] Saint Cyprian recites this passage literally in the work cited above, and in *Testimonies* II and III, cols. 290, 303. Saint Augustine agrees in *On John* V, vol. III, col. 443, except that he has *they will go* instead of *they will go away.] (Matthew XXV, 46).”

## SERMON III. ON CHARITY

From the reading of Saint Paul the Apostle against the wicked, who envy the good.

### I

Having completed and examined the gifts of perfection [Note: [Col. 0122C] Ambrose here follows his customary practice: when he has already discussed matters in an earlier sermon, he recalls them again after first stating them, usually at the beginning of a sermon. Ambrosian writings furnish abundant examples of this kind. It will suffice, however, to cite the books *On Cain and Abel*, *On the Good of Death*, *On the Flight from the World*, *On Joseph the Patriarch*, *On Widows*, *On the Mysteries*, *On the Incarnation*, and *On the Death of Satyrus*.], let us proceed, as we promised, to the Apostle’s more excellent and loftier proclamations [Note: [Col. 0122C] Saint Ambrose is accustomed not only to cite what he has already explained, but sometimes also to promise what he intends to develop further. See at least *Sermon on Not Surrendering the Basilicas*, no. 24, p. 922, and there, nos. c and t, vol. III, as well as the Prologue to Book II *On the Holy Spirit*, no. 12, vol. IV.] [Note: [Col. 0122C] Ambrose sometimes uses a transition much like this in his writings. See Book I *On David’s Appeals*, 1, 5, vol. I.]: he has declared that neither knowledge of the mysteries, nor loftiness of eloquence, nor generous compassion, nor the sublime merit of faith, nor the brave and fearless steadfastness of martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0122C] Compare Letter 78, 6 and 10, vol. III.] can be of benefit [Note: [Col. 0121B] The codex has *memorarit*; perhaps this is an archaic form for *memoraverit*. I have preferred to read *memoravit* as the sense requires.], if brotherly and sincere charity is lacking.

For what benefit is it to nourish with expense [Note: [Col. 0122B] Whether the particle *si* (“if”) should be added.] one whom you kill with the sword? Or what benefit is it to cherish with whatever nourishment you can provide one whom you pursue with a brigand’s hatred? He is deprived of every duty of compassion who, inflamed by the fires of hatred, persecutes in his brother the favor either conferred by divine assistance [Note: [Col. 0122B] The codex, with correct and ancient reading, does not double the *l*, but incorrectly writes *conlata* instead of *conlatam*.], or acquired through the labors of fasting, the constancy of prayers, the perseverance of vigils, and every kind of virtue [Note: [Col. 0122D] Ambrose likewise wrote in Book IV *On Luke*, no. 46, vol. II: “In vain would you await the help of heavenly mercy if you envy another’s fruits of virtue; for the Lord is a despiser of the envious, and from those who persecute divine benefits in others he turns away the miracles of his power.”].

Charity without mercy is imperfect [Note: [Col. 0122D] Ambrose teaches again that perfect charity is never separated from mercy in Book I *On Repentance*, 11, 52, vol. III, where he says: “You cannot be a neighbor unless you show mercy.” This virtue is also highly commended by the holy teacher in *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 8, 22 and following; Book II *On Luke*, no. 27; Book II, Book I *On Duties*, 11, 38 and following; Book III, 19; and Letter 7, 3, vol. III.], because mercy is a member of the body of charity [Col. 0123A]; whereas mercy without charity is nothing [Note: [Col. 0123C] Recall the statements above, p. 13, note 4 (Col. 122, no. 12).], because every member dies if it has been torn away or cut off from a solid body.

For charity is a certain summit among all the members, holding the citadel [Note: [Col. 0123C] Compare Book II *On Duties*, 14, 66, vol. III.] to which all the duties of the virtues, incorporated [Note: [Col. 0123B] That is, joined, as it is read in Ammianus XVI, 8, and Solinus XXXVII. Ambrose also uses the word *corporatus* to mean “joined” or “admitted into one body” in Book III *On Duties*, 7, 50, vol. III.] and linked, continue [Note: [Col. 0123C] Ambrose says in the cited book *On Duties*, 7, 39: “Charity, then, is first for the commendation of our character. It is good to have a testimony of love. From this faith is born … Likewise, through faith and charity one arrives.” And in Letter 41, 17: “Where there is no love,” he says, “there is no faith” (understand: living faith), “there is no affection.” The holy teacher continues to explain this statement in Letter 78, 9, writing: “Where there is perfect charity, there is every kind of faith; just as where there is perfect charity, there is every kind of hope … It is greater because it embraces both hope and faith.” He also recalls the matter in Book VIII *On Luke*, no. 30, vol. II.], without which the reward of all good things either grows weak or perishes [Note: [Col. 0123B] In the codex, *omnium* is repeated after *bonorum*, and then marked above with dots for deletion.], as the Apostle says:

> “If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have charity, I am one like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal [Note: [Col. 0123C] This wording, which is absent from Ambrosian writings, corresponds neither to the Vulgate nor to the Greek. The Greek has χαλκὸς ἠχῶν (“sounding bronze”), and the Vulgate reads *aes sonans*. This nevertheless confirms what we have already noted elsewhere: Ambrose used a different codex from the Vulgate. It also demonstrates what the Maurist editors pointed out in *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 8, 13, note a, col. 449, vol. II, and elsewhere—namely, that Ambrose’s Greek edition differs in many respects from those now in our possession. There is in fact a certain Greek manuscript in Sabatier that omits ἠχῶν.]. And if I have prophecy, and know all the mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have all faith, so that I move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing [Note: [Col. 0123D] Ambrose has this in *On Psalm 45*, 9, and Book VII *On Luke*, no. 176, vol. II, except that at the end he has *it profits me nothing* instead of *I am nothing*. Perhaps those words have been transferred here in the codex from the following verse. Likewise in Letter 78, 6, though there he reads *if I shall have* instead of *if I have*, in agreement with the Vulgate.]. And if I give away all my possessions, and distribute all that is mine to the poor, and if I hand over my body to be burned, so that I may boast, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing [Note: [Col. 0123D] Ambrose’s disciple Augustine nearly agrees in Sermon 130, vol. V, col. 1349, except for *that I may burn* instead of *to be burned*, and with *so that I may boast* omitted. Saint Pacianus has *to be burned* in Letter 2, p. 308 and following. Saint Jerome alone, in Book III *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*, vol. IV, col. 307, with *that I may burn* removed, reads *so that I may boast*. There he thinks this arose from the similarity, in Greek, between the verbs *I may burn* (καυθήσωμαι, “I may be burned”) and *I may boast* (καυχήσωμαι, “I may boast”). But in fact, Jerome himself observes in his commentary on Isaiah LVIII, vol. III, col. 428, that these two words were once read together in very ancient Greek copies, where he writes: “If the Apostle even hands over his body to martyrdom so that he may burn, or so that he may boast—for both are found in the copies—without the charity of God … he says in vain that he sheds his blood.”]” (1 Corinthians XIII, 1–3).

### II

Charity is the mother of all good things, the beginning of mercy, the origin of compassion, the fountain of kindness [Note: [Col. 0124C] Compare Letter 41, 17, vol. III.] [Col. 0124A], the head [Note: [Col. 0123B] In the codex, *capud* appears instead of *caput*, whereas elsewhere we have seen *illut* and *istut* for *illud* and *istud*.] of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0124C] Ambrose certainly writes this in *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 16, 45, vol. II: “He who loves the commandments of righteousness does what he loves.”], the fulfillment of the law, the perfection of the commandments [Note: [Col. 0124C] Ambrose has similar statements in *On Psalm 118*, Sermons 5, 20, and 16, 44, as well as in Letter 78, 7.]. Without this one virtue, all things either grow weak and collapse [Note: [Col. 0123B] The codex has *conruunt* instead of *corruunt*, an archaic spelling.] or are excluded from the kingdom.

For to have prophetic insight is nothing; to know the mysteries is a small thing; to drive out demons [Note: [Col. 0123B] The codex has *demonas*, a word wholly corrupted by error; *daemones* must be written, as it is written below in this same codex.] is little; and to bring every kind of virtue to perfection is empty if charity is absent.

Therefore the Lord Christ says:

> “Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord [Note: [Col. 0124B] The codex has *Lord* only once. But since in sacred Scripture, whatever version is used, *Lord* is doubled here, I would rather believe that the word was omitted from the codex through the copyist’s carelessness, and I have judged that it should be added.], did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform mighty works? [Note: [Col. 0124C] Ambrose likewise reads this passage in the cited sermon on the psalm, Sermon 20, 47, except that he has *cast out* instead of *excluded*. Saint Cyprian retains *excluded* in *On the Unity of the Church*, p. 199, and in *Testimonies*, col. 314.] Then I will say to them: Depart from me; I do not know you, you who work iniquity [Note: [Col. 0124D] In the cited sermon on the psalm, Sermon 15, 25, Ambrose recites the passage thus: “Depart from me, you who work iniquity,” omitting “I do not know you.” Likewise in Sermon 20, 47, and in *On Psalm 36*, 31, though at the end he adds “I do not know you.” Augustine, in *On Psalm 34*, col. 238, vol. IV, has the same wording as the codex, *I do not know you*, but places those words at the beginning of the verse. Saint Jerome, in his Letter to Damasus, col. 152, vol. IV, reads it word for word with us.]” (Matthew VII, 22–23).

The work of iniquity is for one human being to wish to be preferred to another, for a brother to envy a brother, and for one person not to wish for another what he wishes for himself; and, although we share one natural condition [Note: [Col. 0124D] You will often find a similar statement in Ambrosian writings; compare at least *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 8, 14, vol. II.], to wish one condition [Col. 0124B] to be preferred to another [Note: [Col. 0124D] You will find parallel statements in Saint Ambrose, Book X *On Luke*, no. 50 and following, and Book II *On Duties*, 27, 134, vol. III.].

### III

When the author of our salvation, possessing what belongs to nature and conscious of his divinity, presented himself as mortal to all mortals, and showed himself human to all human beings, and—what is greater—subjected one condition [Note: [Col. 0124B] The codex has *condicione*, but it seemed to me that *condicionem* should be read.] to another [Col. 0125A], he adapted the form of his body to the form of our body [Note: [Col. 0125B] Ambrose, in order to strengthen his people against the poison of the Arians, who in his time possessed great influence at Milan, repeatedly supplied in his sermons doctrinal instruction suited to confirming both the divinity of the Word and his humanity. He suffused all his works with the teaching of this ineffable mystery and treated it at length in *On the Incarnation* and *On the Faith*, as well as in *On Psalm 61*, 5; *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 14, 46; *On Luke* X, 135, vol. II; and Letter 46, 6, vol. III. In these passages, as here, he employs Philippians II, 6 in support of his position.], so that by this sacrament [Note: [Col. 0125C] That is, “mystery”; the holy Fathers used this expression in this sense very familiarly, as did our Ambrose, as can be seen at least in Book XI *On the Blessing of the Patriarchs*, 48, vol. I, and *On Luke* VII, 28, vol. II.] he might make loftiness equal to humility and humility equal to loftiness [Note: [Col. 0125C] Compare, besides the work cited above, *On Psalm 61*, 4; *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 14, 20, vol. II; Book II *On the Faith*, 7, 56; Book V, 109, vol. III; and the *Oration on the Death of Theodosius*, no. 27, vol. IV.]; and so that in this he might complete the Father’s will [Note: [Col. 0125C] You will find the same words in the cited passage, and also in *On Psalm 37*, 5; *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 18, 32; *On Luke* X, 60, vol. II; and Book II *On the Faith*, 7, 52, as well as frequently elsewhere. These matters should be carefully noted, so that we may recognize this sermon as thoroughly Ambrosian. Here Ambrose speaks simultaneously of Christ’s divinity, perfect humanity, bodily mortality, humility, and obedience to the Father, and, while treating these matters, uses Philippians II, 6, exactly as was his usual practice in nearly all the passages cited.], who said:

> “I have not come down from heaven to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me [Note: [Col. 0125C] Ambrose has this in Book II *On the Faith*, vol. III, except that at the beginning he has *For this* instead of *Not*, and places *not* after *heaven*.]” (John VI, 38).

And again:

> “The Son of Man,” he says, “did not come to be served but to serve [Note: [Col. 0125B] This expression was very familiar to Ambrose; you may read it in *On Jacob* VII, 32; *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 7, 29; and *On Luke* VI, 32, and X, 56.]” (Matthew XX, 28).

And easily, when he set aside the loftiness of majesty [Note: [Col. 0125D] Saint Ambrose writes similarly in the Prologue to Book I *On the Holy Spirit*, no. 11, vol. IV, though he does not place *came* after the verb.], he took the form of a servant, as the Apostle says:

> “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard it as plunder [Note: [Col. 0125B] The codex has *rapina*, but *rapinam* must certainly be written. I suspect that the final *a* may have been added by a line for *m*.] to be equal to God [Note: [Col. 0125D] Saint Ambrose recites this passage exactly in *On Joseph the Patriarch*, 3, 14; *The Second Apology of David*, 7, 39, vol. I; *On Psalm 35*, 5, vol. II; and elsewhere.], but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant [Note: [Col. 0125D] Thus literally in the cited passage.]” (Philippians II, 6–7).

And this:

> “Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord [Note: [Col. 0126B] The codex omits the word *Lord* here, as above; we have ventured to double it. See p. 15, note d (Col. 124, no. g).], will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven [Note: [Col. 0125D] The holy teacher is never consistent with himself when he cites this passage in his writings. In *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 11, 40, vol. II, he reads: “Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven”; and immediately above, in the same place: “For not everyone who says, Lord, Lord, will himself enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of God.” But in Book I *On Duties*, 26, 125, vol. III: “For not the one who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does what I say.” Finally, in Book III *On the Holy Spirit*, 17, 130: “Not all who say to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven.”]” (Matthew VII, 21).

### IV

But we cannot do the Father’s will before we first know what that will itself is. The will of God, therefore, according to the Apostle Paul, is “our sanctification [Note: [Col. 0126B] The Vulgate and the Fathers read *your* instead of *our*; but here Ambrose is speaking in sacred language, not quoting the text.].” Through the regeneration of the saving bath [Note: [Col. 0126B] An apostolic expression for baptism (Titus III, 5), which was very familiar to our bishop. Consult Book II *On David’s Appeals*, 4, 14 and 9, 55, vol. I; *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 22, 3, vol. II; and the books *On the Mysteries* and *On the Holy Spirit*, 10, 64, vols. III and IV.] he cleansed us from every appearance of the ancient contagion by this confession of ours, by which we believe that God came in the weakness of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0126B] Compare *On Psalm 61*, 5, vol. II, and recall the statements above (this page, note 1).], by which we confess that he was born of a virgin, by which we do not deny that he was subjected to a condition [Note: [Col. 0126B] Supply *human*. Ambrose uses this word here and there in this sense, for example in *On Luke* X, 129, vol. II, and in the *Sermon against Auxentius*, no. 8, p. 916, vol. III.]—that is, a human condition—by which we exalt Christ crucified, proclaim him buried, and proclaim him raised by the glory of God [Note: [Col. 0126C] Read the passage cited above, p. 16, note 1 (this page, no. 4), and no. 3, where there are similar statements and expressions. These points should be carefully noted, so that it may increasingly be recognized that the author addressed this sermon to the newly baptized. For the Roman books of the liturgical order, which bishops Odilber of Milan, Leidrad of Lyon, Amalarius of Trier, and Theodulf of Orléans wrote on baptism at the command of Charlemagne, clearly show that bishops formerly used these same or similar words for the newly baptized during the handing over of the Creed. To these may now be added another book on baptism, which is preserved in a parchment codex, apparently of the ninth century, in the Sessorian Library. I consider it unpublished and do not hesitate to attribute it to Alcuin. Thus it reads on folio 163 recto: “This is the sum of our faith, dearly beloved; these are the words of the Creed, composed not in the language of human wisdom but according to the reason of true divinity. No one is unfit, no one is unsuitable to understand and preserve them. Here the one and equal power of God the Father and the Son is proclaimed; here the only-begotten Son of God, born of Mary the virgin and of the Holy Spirit according to the flesh, is shown; here his crucifixion and burial, and his resurrection on the third day, are proclaimed,” and so forth.].

Since, then, we see that so great a sanctification has been conferred upon us solely through confession of him, from this we can understand how great a reward may be conferred through imitation of him and through a will either accomplished or understood. Concerning this the Apostle teaches us:

> “That you may know what the will of God is: what is good, pleasing, and perfect [Note: [Col. 0126D] Augustine, in *Confessions* XIII, vol. I, cols. 229 and 236, and elsewhere, consistently cites this passage as follows: “to prove to yourselves what the will of God is, what is good, well-pleasing, and perfect.” Ambrosiaster has in this passage: “that you may prove what the will of God is, what is good, pleasing, and perfect.” Jerome agrees in Book I *Against Jovinianus*, vol. IV, col. 179. Cyprian favors the Vulgate in Letter 77, col. 159, and Sedulius and Bede read it word for word with the Vulgate here. All, however, read *that you may prove* instead of *that you may know*. Greek: Εἰς τὸ δοκιμάζειν ὑμᾶς τί τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ τό ἀγαθόν, καὶ εὐάρεστον, καὶ τέλειον (“that you may discern what the will of God is—what is good, pleasing, and perfect”).]” (Romans XII, 2).

The will of God is love of one’s brother and neighbor: that you may rejoice with your brother, not envy the better person, and prefer the inferior person to yourself [Note: [Col. 0127C] Saint Ambrose often denounces this destructive vice, which penetrates even religious hearts, especially in Book IV *On Luke*, no. 46, and VII, 23, vol. II; Book II *On Duties*, 30, 152, vol.
