III; and Letter 29, 17.]; that you do not admit an offense, that you forgive one already committed; that you precede those who honor you with honor; that you anticipate those who love you with affection [Note: [Col. 0127B] Compare the notes above, p. 6, note b (Col. 115, no. d), and observe here and below that the codex writes *dilectu* instead of *delectu*, a good and ancient reading, as Forcellinius notes concerning this word.]; that you pray for your enemies; that you feed your adversaries [Note: [Col. 0127B] Thus the codex, with an aspirate inserted between two vowels. Since this reading occurs in ancient codices, I do not think it should be disturbed. Cicero’s ancient interpreter, preserved by Mai, provides examples of this variation, vol. II, pp. 32, 54, 82, 84, 90, 102.]; that you do not hate those who persecute you [Note: [Col. 0127C] Similar statements occur in *On Psalm 38*, 10; *On Psalm 118*, Sermons 10, 3 and 41, and 15, 15 and following; *On Luke* VIII, 24, vol. II; and Book I *On Duties*, 48, 244 and following, vol. III.] (Romans XII, 9 and following).

Thus every virtue becomes a glory, an adornment—faith, perfection, mercy, martyrdom, the body burned by flames. Thus we become children of God when in our works we make ourselves like our heavenly Father [Note: [Col. 0127B] *Similamus* means “we make similar” or “we assimilate,” with *nos* understood. Since this verb is generally constructed with the accusative, I would have preferred, against the codex, to write either *adsimilamus* or *caelestis Patris opera similamus* (“we make ourselves like the works of the heavenly Father”). But after examining the ancient interpreter of Ezra, who has in IV Ezra VIII, 44, “You made yourself like the seed of the farmer,” I hesitated over the proposed emendation and judged that the codex reading should be retained.] (Romans VIII, 16–17). Thus we are joined to Christ by hereditary right [Note: [Col. 0127B] Ambrose says in Letter 75, 5, vol. III: “Charity acquires adoption, and adoption acquires inheritance.”], when we bestow good things on the good and the wicked alike, when we either forget an injury [Note: [Col. 0127C] In the codex, *iniuria* is written without the final *e*; perhaps *iniuriam* should be read, with the final *m* omitted by the scribe, or with a letter carrying a line added above it, though scarcely, if at all, visible now.] or forgive in our heart an injury we have retained [Note: [Col. 0127C] Ambrose, explaining Matthew XIX, 21, says again in Book I *On Duties*, 11, 37, vol. III: “And above it is written, where he commands that enemies be loved, that we pray for those who slander and persecute us, and that we bless those who curse us: we must do this if we wish to be perfect, like our Father who is in heaven, who commands his sun to pour its rays upon the good and the wicked and causes the earths of all people to grow fertile with rain and dew, without any distinction.” He has other similar statements in *On Joseph the Patriarch*, 1, 3, vol. I; *On Psalm 37*, 45, vol. II; Letter 63, 83, vol. III; and elsewhere.], when with superior affection we give not only our possessions but ourselves for our friends; thus we shall abound in the Holy Spirit, whose we are, if we are filled with every gentleness that belongs to kindness.

### V

Therefore the Lord Christ warned the Apostles, who were hastening to avenge the inhospitable Samaritans [Note: [Col. 0127D] They had refused to receive Christ as a guest. Luke IX, 53.], saying:

> “Do you not know whose spirit you are? [Note: [Col. 0127D] Ambrose recites this passage word for word in *On Luke* VII, 60, vol. II, and Book I *On Repentance*, 16, 88, vol. III. Ambrose also commends gentleness to his people through the notable authority of this Gospel testimony in the cited passage in *On Luke*.]” (Luke IX, 55).

That is, the spirit of gentleness: the spirit that is removed from every agitation, shaken by no injury, free from every disturbance, supported by tranquility, mild, kind, gentle, and gracious [Note: [Col. 0128C] Ambrose says in *On Psalm 36*, 22, vol. II: “Who are the gentle, if not those whom no goad of dissension harasses, whom anger does not disturb, savagery does not exasperate, and the frenzy of cruelty does not inflame?”].

Elijah saw him [Note: [Col. 0128B] The codex has *videt* (“sees”), but the reading I have written seemed more consonant with the sense, and I ventured to adopt it; the other reading is not wholly absurd. On the interchange of *i* and *e*, recall what was said above, p. 6, note b, and p. 18, note a (Col. 115, no. d, and this page, no. a), and below.] for the third time [Note: [Col. 0128B] The codex consistently has *Helias* with an initial aspirate, as is found in ancient codices.] [Note: [Col. 0128C] Ambrose himself frequently admits that he has discussed the deeds of Elijah in his writings, in *On Elijah and Fasting*, 3, 5: “For we have composed many things about Elijah’s deeds in the frequent speech of various people.” Referring to this passage, the Benedictine editors wisely noted in the preface to volumes III and IV: “If the holy man means nothing other than that the deeds of Elijah are frequently mentioned in his books, scarcely anything will seem to have been lost in this respect.”], as Scripture says [Note: [Col. 0128B] Thus the codex writes *scribtura*, with *b* instead of *p*, just as above we saw *scribtum*, p. 4, note b (Col. 114, no. [lacuna])]:

> “Tomorrow you shall go out and stand before the presence of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0128B] After *before the presence of the Lord*, the codex adds: “and the Lord was not in that spirit.” These words are superfluous; perhaps our copyist inserted them, deceived by the fact that similar words recur below after *in the presence of the Lord*.]; and behold, the Lord will pass by, and behold, a great and powerful wind, shattering mountains and breaking rocks before the presence of the Lord; and the Lord was not in that wind; and after the wind [Note: [Col. 0128B] The codex has *spiritu*, with the final *m* omitted.], an earthquake: and the Lord was not in the earthquake [Note: [Col. 0128D] With the addition of the words *on the mountain* after *the presence of the Lord*, the Greek text favors Ambrose’s reading.]; and after the earthquake, fire; and the Lord was not in the fire [Note: [Col. 0128B] The codex has *igni*.]; and after the fire, the sound of a gentle breeze; and the Lord was in it [Note: [Col. 0128D] The ancient interpreter of Irenaeus, IV, 20, col. 255, reads similarly, as does the Greek, except for *and after the fire*. But both in the cited passage and in the ancient and modern Vulgate, the final words *and the Lord was in it* are omitted. Perhaps Ambrose added them here, not as words flowing from the sacred source, but rather to serve his own argument.]” (3 Kings XIX, 11–12).

But what Elijah was enabled to see through the mystery, the prophet Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0128C] The codex consistently writes *Eseias* instead of *Esaias* or *Isaias*, or rather *Iesaias*. I would scarcely say that this arose from the Greek Ἡσοίας, since in ancient orthography *ai* was read as *ei*, as Fumagallius notes, *Institutiones Diplomaticae* I, p. 1; VI, § 9, p. 103.] clearly learned when the Lord revealed it. He says:

> “Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble, the gentle, and the one who trembles at my words [Note: [Col. 0128D] Ambrose likewise has this in Book IV *Hexaemeron*, 8, 49 and 75, vol. I, except that he has *quiet* instead of *gentle*; but he has *gentle* with the codex in the *Oration on the Death of Theodosius*, no. 33, vol. IV]?” (Isaiah LXVI, 2).

So too that Samuel [Note: [Col. 0128C] The codex has *Samuhel*, with an *h* inserted between the two vowels.], that illustrious priest, Samuel [Note: [Col. 0129B] Thus the codex, with emphasis.], rejects and dismisses at the Lord’s command brothers of the most distinguished appearance, alike in stature and not unequal in virtue; but he anoints David, their brother, subject in humility, weak in gentleness, and gentler in the spirit of tranquility, as king at the Lord’s command [Note: [Col. 0129C] Ambrose often speaks of David’s humility in *On David’s Appeals*, in both of his *Apologies*, in Book I *On Duties*, 6, 21, and 48, 245 and following, and in Letter 51, 7 and following.].

Therefore he himself, having prayed [Note: [Col. 0129B] Thus the codex, with a diphthong, which I reluctantly retained, although this spelling has repeatedly appeared to me in other ancient codices as well.], says:

> “Remember, Lord [Note: [Col. 0129B] I have ventured to add *Lord*, since the sense seems to require it. Because of the copyist’s confusion caused by the following word beginning with *d*, I thought that *Lord* had been omitted here.], David and all his gentleness [Note: [Col. 0129C] Greek: καὶ πάσης τῆς πραότητος αὐτοῦ (“and all his gentleness”); but in the sixth Venetian edition, ταπεινώσεως (“humiliation”).]” (Psalm CXXXI, 1).

This election of God has always remained, and remains still: it attacks and casts down the proud, and cherishes and exalts the humble. This exaltation cannot exist without humiliation [Note: [Col. 0129C] The codex has *humilatione*, certainly incorrectly, unless the *i* was added above and is now blended with the stroke of the *p*; the upper line of this word descends over the *a*.], nor election without rejection [Note: [Col. 0129C] I would prefer to read *are chosen*, but since the codex reading is supported by examples, I have judged that it should be retained. Recall what was said above concerning the word *dilectu*, p. 6, note b, and p. 18, note a (Col. 115, no. d, and 127, no. a).], nor calling without distinction.

And therefore, when weak, despised, and lowly things are loved [Note: [Col. 0129C] Compare *On Psalm 37*, 47, vol. II.], those that are lofty and great are rejected [Note: [Col. 0129C] See *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 18, 34, and elsewhere]; for with God the great are weak, and the weak are great [Note: [Col. 0129C] Thus Ambrose says in the cited passage, Sermon 3, 41: “What is contemptible in this world is precious with God.”].

The Apostle Paul taught this, showing that the calling of believers proceeds from this election:

> “Consider your calling, brothers,” he says, “because not many are wise according to the flesh, not many are strong, not many are noble [Note: [Col. 0129C] The ancient version in Sabatier has *because* instead of *for*, and *powerful* instead of *strong*. Augustine favors this reading in *On John*, codex 349, part II, vol. III, and elsewhere. Irenaeus, however, reads *strong* with our Ambrose in Book II, chapter 19, col. 144.]; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong [Note: [Col. 0129D] Again, Ambrose has in *On Psalm 36*, 7, vol. II: “For God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise.”]; and God chose the ignoble and despised things of this world, the things that are not (namely, the despised things [Note: [Col. 0130B] I judged that these parentheses should be marked here with their own signs, lest the reader confuse Ambrose’s words with those of the sacred text.]), to destroy the things that are (namely, the despised things [Note: [Col. 0129D] Ambrose writes the first words of this verse—“God chose the despised things of this world”—in *On Psalm 118*, Sermon 3, 41; but he twice recites the remainder—“because God chose the things that are not, to destroy the things that are”—in *On Luke* VII, 234, vol. II.], so that no flesh might boast in his presence [Note: [Col. 0129D] The Greek text agrees with Ambrose.]” (1 Corinthians I, 26–29).

[Col. 0130A] **VI.** Therefore let those glory in the world who glory in the flesh; let those glory in the flesh who glory in man—those who are lifted up by the honors of the world, puffed up by riches, and proud of nobility [Note: [Col. 0129D] Ambrose repeats a similar statement in *On Psalm* I, 15; XLVIII, 24; and CXVIII, Sermon 8, 8; Sermon 14, 33; and Sermon 20, 3 and 7, vol. II.]. “But far be it from us to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to us and we to the world [Note: [Col. 0130C] Here Ambrose quotes the passage rhetorically in the plural; it also occurs, however, in the singular, as in the sacred text, in *On the Good of Death* 3, 9; *On Flight from the World* 9, 56, vol. I; *On Psalm* CXVIII, Sermon 8, 5; and *On Luke* III, VI, 34, vol. II; in Letter 78, 10, vol. III; and Book III of *On the Holy Spirit*, 8, 50, vol. IV. Yet in none of these places does he cite this passage in exactly the same words.] (Gal. VI, 14).” We had already lost and cast away the world’s pomp and pleasures when, in a better company, we made our passage to heaven [Note: [Col. 0130C] Compare at least *On the Mysteries* 2, 5.], just as John’s admonition, the teacher of heavenly life, impressed upon us the pattern and image of how to live:

> “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him [Note: [Col. 0130C] Augustine quotes this passage here exactly in Letter 220, col. 814, vol. II. So too Cyprian, *On the Conduct of Virgins*, col. 175; *On the Lord’s Prayer*, col. 208; *On Mortality*, col. 236; and Book III of *Testimonies*, col. 308. Likewise Zeno of Verona, Book I, Tractates 2, 7, and 12, pp. 24, 67, and 90; and the Council of Carthage, canon 491; Ambrose now joins these authorities.]: because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition [Col. 0130B] of the age. This is not from the Father, but from the desire of the age [Note: [Col. 0130D] With the exception of reading “because” in place of “for,” Augustine reads this passage in this way in Book I of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, vol. X, col. 290, and Book VII *Against Julian*, col. 663; so does Cyprian in the passage cited; and Zeno of Verona in the work cited above. Ambrose, however, is not consistent with himself in *On Psalm* CXVIII, Sermon 13, 27, vol. II, where he reads: “Because everything that is in the age is desire of the flesh, desire of the eyes, and boasting of life.”]” (I John II, 15–16).

**VII.** Whoever hates the world does not fear the world’s hatred: by his hatred he himself provoked the world to hate him. Therefore it is not right either to fear or to dread its hatred, if it attempts to attach to you those things which it has judged you to have preferred to itself [Note: [Col. 0130C] The manuscript reads “it has judged you to have preferred to yourself.” I believe that the text has suffered a transposition, and that *te sibi*—“you to itself”—is the preferable reading, if the sense is considered.] [Note: [Col. 0130C] See also *On Psalm* CXVIII, Sermon 22, 21 and following, vol. II.] Thus this worldly hatred, by whose attacks we are torn apart and whose blasphemies make us objects of derision, is neither new nor sudden. We know that it was inflicted long ago upon the Lord Christ [Note: [Col. 0130D] See *On the Faith* no. 94, vol. III.] and his apostles, as the Evangelist says:

> “If they called the master of the household Beelzebub [Note: [Col. 0131B] This is the reading of the manuscript, which I have retained because it is not sufficiently clear to me whether a *b* or an *l* should be added at the end. All the ancient manuscripts cited by Sabatier read *Beelzebul*, with *l*, in this passage, corresponding to the Greek Βεελζεβοὺλ (*Beelzeboul*). Jerome, however, in *On Hebrew Names*, holds that the letter *b*, not *l*, should be read at the end of this word; for, he says, *zebub* means “fly.”] how much more the members of his household [Note: [Col. 0131C] So read both the ancient and the recent Vulgate, in agreement with the Greek.]?” (Matt. X, 25).

And again:

> “If the world hates you, know that it hated me first [Note: [Col. 0131C] The ancient version cited by Sabatier reads: “If the world … because it hated me before,” etc. The Vulgate has: “because it hated me before you.” Cyprian, *Letter to Fortunatus*, p. 268, reads: “because it hated me first.” The Greek reads: Εἰ ὁ κόσμος … γινώσκετε ὅτι ἐμὲ πρῶτον ὑμῶν μεμίσηκεν—“If the world … know that it hated me before you.”]” (John XV, 18).

So also the Apostle says:

> “We have become a spectacle to this world, and to angels, and to men [Note: [Col. 0131C] Ambrose, *On Elijah and Fasting* 21, 79, vol. I, has: “We have become, he says, a spectacle of this world”; and in *On Psalm* XLIII, 33, vol. II: “that we may be a spectacle to this world, and to angels, and to men.” He reads the passage word for word with the manuscript in Letter 63, 71, omitting only “to men”: “For we have become a spectacle to this world and to angels.” The ancient version and the Greek agree with our reading, although the Greek lacks “to this.”]” (I Cor. IV, 9)—that is, to the nations and to false brethren, who under the name of religion transform themselves into angels of light.

Finally, he clearly gathered this together both above and below:

> “Already you are filled; already you have become rich; you reign without us—and would that you did reign, so that we too might reign with you [Note: [Col. 0131D] The ancient version cited by Sabatier reads this way, except that instead of “we might reign with you” it has “we might reign.” Saint Hilary, however, uses the verb *conregnemus*—“we might reign with you”—in *On Psalm* II, 42, col. 49, and LX and LXV, cols. 144 and 197.]” (ibid., 8).

And below:

> “We are fools for Christ, but you are wise in Christ; we are weak, but you are strong [Note: [Col. 0131D] This is the reading of both Vulgates, in agreement with the Greek, but they add at the end: “you are noble, but we are ignoble.”]. Until this hour we are hungry, naked, and buffeted [Note: [Col. 0131B] The manuscript reads *culafizamur* instead of *colaphisamur*. Longus, pp. 2216 and 2222, aptly observes that the letters *u* and *o* were sometimes confused among the Latins, so that they read *u* even when they wrote *o*. Valerianus, pp. 2289 and 2290, and Papirianus, p. 2292, confirm this, as does the distinguished Maius, who preceded me in noting these matters in his orthographical index to Fronto. As for the letter *f*, the Latins plainly wrote it without *ph*. Thus the very diligent and always praiseworthy Maius states in *On the Republic* I, 2, p. 7, note a. Cicero, *Oration* 48, tells us that the letter *ph* was formerly not used by the Latins. Martianus, Book III, chapter on Conjugation, says: “nor will they exclude *f*, when we say *triumfo*, although it comes from the Greeks and is more properly written with *p* and *h*.” The same Maius observes in his paleographical index to Cicero and his interpreter, vol. II of *Classical Authors*, p. 388, col. 2: “*F* for *ph* everywhere; and rightly, as I think. For why would the Latins always have written two letters, *ph*, less conveniently in place of their single letter *f*?” Our manuscript, however, elsewhere consistently uses *ph* when usage requires it. On the letter *z*, see Isidore, *Origins* I, 4, and the ancient orthographers in Putschius.], and are unstable [Note: [Col. 0131D] Ambrose differs in *On Psalm* CXVIII, Sermon 8, 7, vol. II, where he reads: “Until this hour we are hungry, thirsty, naked, struck with blows, and unstable.” He has *colaphisamur*—“we are buffeted”—with the ancient Vulgate cited by Sabatier. Ambrosiaster agrees with them here, as does the Greek κολαφιζόμεθα—“we are buffeted.”]” (that is, we do not resist [Col. 0131B] or defend ourselves [Note: [Col. 0132B] Here and below I have ventured to mark the parenthesis as above.]), “and we labor, working with our own hands. We are cursed, and we bless; we suffer persecution, and we endure [Note: [Col. 0131D] Ambrose uses this wording in *On Psalm* XXVIII, 10; CXVIII, the sermon just cited, vol. II; Book I of *On Duties*, 48, 244, vol. III; and Book II of *On Repentance*, 1, 5, of the same volume.]. When reviled, we entreat [Note: [Col. 0132B] The manuscript consistently has the diphthong. See above, p. 20, note a (col. 129, n. b).]; we have become as the refuse of this world, the scum of all things [Note: [Col. 0132C] The ancient version cited by Sabatier agrees, except that it has “we entreat” in place of “we beseech,” and the Greek does not differ. Ambrose, in *On Psalm* CXVIII, the passage cited, has: “We are blasphemed, and we entreat; we have become as the cleansing of this world, the refuse of all things, until now.”]” (ibid., 10–13).

This is apostolic teaching; this is the mystery of God and Christ; this is the heavenly way of life; this is the spiritual profession. The world does not receive it; hypocrisy [Note: [Col. 0132B] So it is written in the manuscript, with the initial aspiration omitted.] rejects it, as the Apostle says:

> “The natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him [Note: [Col. 0132C] Saint Ambrose quotes this passage here word for word in *On Luke* VII, 148, vol. II, and Book III of *On the Holy Spirit*, 17, 121, vol. IV, except that he has “for it is foolishness to him” instead of “for they are foolishness to him.”]” (I Cor. II, 14).

**VIII.** The fruits of the Spirit are those which the Apostle enumerates, saying:

> “Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, gentleness, faith, meekness [Note: [Col. 0132B] The manuscript has *laenitas* with a diphthong, but we have removed it, since the manuscript itself does not retain it in *lenis*, *lenior*, *lenitas*, and so forth.], self-control, chastity [Note: [Col. 0132C] The holy Doctor, *On Paradise* 13, 64, says: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, modesty, self-control, affection.” In this passage the Roman edition reads “chastity” instead of “affection.” In *On Noah and the Ark* 29, 108, he writes: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness.” But in *On Psalm* XXXVI, 12, vol. II: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, modesty, self-control.” Finally, in Book I of *On the Holy Spirit* 6, 69, he has the wording of *On Noah* cited above, except that he puts peace first; nevertheless, in the same book, XII, 126, vol. IV, he writes the word after joy.]” (Gal. V, 22–23).

And concerning this [Note: [Col. 0132B] The manuscript has *quod*, but the *d* is wholly superfluous. Fumagalli, *Institutiones Diplomaticae* I, ch. 6, §9, p. 102, observes that the ancients quite often added the letter *d* at the end of a word, especially to words ending in *o*. Thus, for example, they wrote *estod*, *malod*, *ceditod*, etc., for *esto*, *malo*, *cedito*, etc.] the same Apostle instructed the church of the Ephesians in his letter [Note: [Col. 0132C] The manuscript reads *Ecclesia*—“church”—but a small stroke has been placed above the letter *a* to represent *m*, which can scarcely be read.], saying [Note: [Col. 0132D] Compare Letter 71, vol. III, in which, at the request of Irenaeus, Ambrose explains the substance of this apostolic letter, col. 1186 and following.]:

> “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed on the day of redemption [Note: [Col. 0132B] Ambrose similarly omits the words “for the day of redemption” at the end in Book III of *On the Holy Spirit*, 8, 48, vol. IV.]” (Eph. IV, 30).

The Spirit is grieved by contrary desires—that is, by the works of the flesh—which, among the other works that lie hidden [Col. 0133A], are these [Note: [Col. 0133B] The Fathers, in complete agreement with the ancient and recent Vulgates, state with the Apostle that the works of the flesh enumerated below are manifest, not hidden; the Greek text likewise reads φανερὰ—“manifest.” Here perhaps the works of the flesh listed are erroneously called “hidden” instead of “manifest.” Alternatively, Ambrose may be understood to say that the works he mentions are themselves manifest, while the others are hidden, so that the sense is: “from the works of the flesh, which, among the other hidden works, are manifest, these are the ones.” One might therefore suppose that the word “manifest” has dropped out, unless one prefers to say that Ambrose calls the works of the flesh he lists “hidden” in comparison with those he omits—such as adultery, sexual impurity, and murder—which reveal themselves more clearly by their own shamefulness. [ [Col. 0134D] The phrasing is wholly unusual. The sense is: “Or it must be said that the works Ambrose mentions are themselves manifest,” and so forth. EDIT.]]:

> “Hostilities, disputes, jealousies, indignations, provocations, angers, quarrels, dissensions, sects [Note: [Col. 0133C] Irenaeus, Book V, chapter 11, col. 305: “hostilities,” he says, “disputes, jealousies, angers, rivalries, resentments, irritations, dissensions, heresies.” Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, col. 209: “hostilities, disputes, rivalries, resentments, provocations, enmities, dissensions, heresies.” Augustine, Letter 29, Book II, col. 50: “hostilities, disputes, rivalries, resentments, dissensions, heresies.” The same holy Father has this wording scattered throughout his works, except in Book II of *On the Sermon on the Mount*, where he adds “sects” to the word “heresies.” Finally, Lucifer of Cagliari, Book II *On Behalf of Athanasius*, col. 282, and Jerome in this passage, omitting “indignations” and “provocations,” have the same wording as Ambrose if “heresies” is read at the end instead of “sects.” The Vulgate retains “sects” with us, from the Greek αἱρέσεις—“heresies” or “sects.”], envies, drunkenness, revelries [Note: [Col. 0133B] The manuscript has *comisationes* instead of *comessationes*, with the consonant *s* not doubled and *i* substituted for *e* after *com-*, as in the Sabatier manuscript Reg. On the interchangeable use of the letters *i* and *e*, see above, p. 6, note b; p. 18, note a; p. 19, note a (col. 115, n. d; 127, n. a; 128, n. f). I have retained the manuscript’s reading, since examples of this kind occur more than once in ancient manuscripts.], that is, those who feast [Note: [Col. 0133C] The Fathers cited in the passage above have this wording verbatim, except for Lucifer of Cagliari, who adds “murders” after “envies.” [Col. 0133D] On this passage Jerome notes in the place cited: “In the Latin manuscripts, adultery, sexual impurity, and murders are also reported as written in this catalogue of vices. But it must be understood that no more than fifteen works of the flesh are named. Twelve are named in this sermon; therefore, if the three reported by Jerome are added, the catalogue will yield fifteen works of the flesh, as he says.”]]” (Gal. V, 20–21).

By these works the Spirit is grieved and offended; he abandons and departs, as Solomon says [Note: [Col. 0133B] So the manuscript reads. Sabatier observes, in his note on Proverbs I, 1, that the ancient manuscripts of Lactantius and Cyprian read *Solomon*. Several manuscripts of the Sessorian collection likewise have this form, including one extremely ancient copy.], [Note: [Col. 0133D] Among Ambrose’s works, for example *On Paradise* I, 6 and XIII, this passage may be counted among those in which the Book of Wisdom is attributed to Solomon, in accordance with the opinion of his time. On this matter see the Maurist annotations on the cited passage of *On Paradise*, as well as Ackermann, *Introduction to the Books of the Sacred Old Testament*, Part II, chapter 7, §245, Vienna edition of 1825, p. 367.]:

> “For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee the deceitful person [Note: [Col. 0133D] This is the reading of the Vulgate, together with Augustine in several places, if the opening is read in this order: “For the Holy Spirit …”]” (Wis. I, 5).

**IX.** “Do not grieve,” the Apostle Paul says, “the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed on the day of redemption” (Eph. IV, 30). The day of redemption is the day on which, redeemed by the gift of saving forgiveness, we are freed from the sentence of death; on which we put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new, who has been created according to God in good works [Note: [Col. 0134B] Ambrose also expounds this apostolic statement in *On Psalm* XXXVIII, 22, vol. II; *On the Instruction of a Virgin* 2, 13, vol. III; and Book II of *On the Holy Spirit*, 7, 65, vol. IV.].

On that day we are also sealed for the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0134B] The author of *On the Sacraments*, preserved among Ambrose’s works, likewise teaches that the baptized person is sealed for the Holy Spirit, Book III, col. 457 and following.], when we are brought to completion through all the sacraments [Note: [Col. 0134B] That is, when through baptism all the mysteries of the Christian religion are opened to us—mysteries from which the profane were formerly excluded—and faith is acquired, by which we believe all the divine mysteries; or rather, when through this sacrament we are made capable of receiving all the other sacraments as well, since it is the gate of the sacraments. Yet Ambrose may also have had the Eucharist in view here, since according to the ancient custom of the Church it was conferred together with baptism and confirmation; this practice still obtains in ecclesiastical discipline for the baptism of adults.], as the Evangelist says:

> “And when Jesus had been baptized, immediately he went up from the water; and behold, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending from heaven like a dove [Note: [Col. 0134B] The manuscript omits the *m* in *columbam*, a customary error.], coming upon him [Note: [Col. 0134C] Hilary agrees in *On Psalm* CXXXVIII, col. 507. The Greek text and the ancient version cited by Sabatier add *to him* before “the heavens” and omit “of God” after “the Spirit.”]” (Matt. III, 16).

The dove is simple in innocence [Note: [Col. 0134C] Ambrose frequently teaches in his writings that simplicity is signified by the dove. More clearly in *On Isaac* 7, 59, vol. I, and in *On Luke* II, 92, where he says: “It was disclosed that heaven opened and the Holy Spirit descended in bodily form like a dove … Let us consider the mystery: why like a dove? For the grace of the washing requires simplicity, so that we may be simple like doves.” He writes similarly in *On the Mysteries* 4, 25, vol. III: “He rightly descended like a dove, to admonish us that we ought to possess the simplicity of the dove.”], or innocent through simplicity: not violent in its cry, not savage in fury [Note: [Col. 0134D] Ambrose also holds that peace must be understood through the mystery of the dove, in *On Isaac*, in *On Luke* at the passage cited, in *On the Mysteries* 3, 11, vol. III, and in Letter 41, 21.], not irascible in conduct [Note: [Col. 0134D] Compare at least *On Psalm* CXVIII, Sermon 12, 18, vol. II.], not hostile in the bitterness of gall [Note: [Col. 0134D] This expression is familiar to Ambrose; it occurs again in *On Paradise* 2, 8, vol. I, and elsewhere].

And therefore, having received the same Spirit who descended in the form of a dove, the Apostle added these words:

> “Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be taken away from you [Note: [Col. 0134D] Saint Cyprian quotes this passage exactly in Book III of *Testimonies*, col. 306.]” (Eph. IV, 31).

Bitterness consists in conceiving hostility, belching forth hatred, vomiting out poisons, slandering one’s neighbors, and spreading deadly things [Note: [Col. 0134B] The manuscript has the diphthong in *laetalia*, a reading also confirmed by examples from ancient manuscripts.], as it is written in Deuteronomy [Note: [Col. 0134B] So the manuscript reads, with the aspiration.]. “Our enemies are senseless [Note: [Col. 0134D] This reading is supported by the ancient version cited by Sabatier, together with Vigilius of Thapsus, Book V of *On the Trinity*, col. 215, though it adds “after our enemies.” The Greek has ἀνόητοι—“senseless” or “foolish.”]:

> “Their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their vine-shoots are from Gomorrah; their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster is bitterness [Note: [Col. 0135C] Ambrose does not use this passage in the same words; in *On Elijah and Fasting* 14, 52, vol. I, he has: “From the vine of Sodom is their wine, and their vine is the vine of Gomorrah; their grape is a grape of gall, their cluster is bitterness in them.”]. Their wine is the poison of dragons [Note: [Col. 0135B] This word is found with the aspiration even in ancient manuscripts.], and the incurable fury of asps [Note: [Col. 0135C] Ambrose has this in the passage cited, if “poison” is placed where he has “fury,” and vice versa].” (Deut. XXXII, 31–33).

And David says:

> “Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they acted deceitfully; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness [Note: [Col. 0135C] The ancient and recent Vulgates have this word for word, together with Augustine and Cassiodorus; our Ambrose now joins them. In the works of Ambrose published thus far, only the opening words had appeared: “Their throat is an open tomb,” in *On Psalm* CXVIII, Sermon 16, 28, vol. II.]” (Ps. XIII, 3).

“Anger,” he says—anger [Note: [Col. 0135B] The manuscript repeats *anger* emphatically]—“is to envy one who is better, to disparage one who is fortunate, and to grieve over the progress of one’s neighbor.” Thus the Prophet says:

> “The sinner will see and be angry; he will gnash his teeth and waste away [Note: [Col. 0135C] Saint Augustine consistently writes “he will gnash his teeth and waste away,” as does the brief Mozarabic text. The Greek has Βρύξει, καὶ τακήσεται—“he will gnash and melt away.”]” (Ps. CXI, 10).

“Indignation,” he says—indignation [Note: [Col. 0135B] Here is another emphatic repetition. Maius says in *On the Republic* I, 47, p. 123, that Moserus’s denial that emphasis can be signified by repetition of a word seems strange to him; and indeed Cicero himself appears to refute it, p. 103]—“is to resent that an inferior is made equal to a superior by the gift of grace, or is placed before him in the rank of spiritual gifts [Note: [Col. 0135C] This appears to refer to the distinction between the wicked and the envious which the holy Doctor uses in Book II of *On Duties*, 30, 152, vol. III: “Sons, flee the wicked; beware of the envious. The difference between the wicked and the envious is this: the wicked delights in his own good, while the envious is tormented by another’s; the former loves evil things, the latter hates good things. Thus the one who wishes himself well is plainly more tolerable than the one who wishes everyone ill.” Ambrose strongly urges that envy, as a kind of wholly incurable disease, is not to be endured but fled. Thus in Letter 29, 17, vol. III: “Flee lands in which there is envy, where there is ambition, where there is contention. For when lands are corrupted by this twice-detestable plague, there is no peace, no love, no order, because nothing is settled justly.”],” while the Apostle says to the Galatians [Note: [Col. 0135B] The manuscript erroneously reads “to the Corinthians.”]:

> “There is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female; but you are all one in Christ Jesus [Note: [Col. 0136C] Ambrose, Book II of *On the Holy Spirit*, 8, 79, has: “You are all one in Christ Jesus.”]” (Gal. III, 28).

[Col. 0135B] **X.** The most blessed Paul teaches in almost all his letters [Note: The manuscript has *epistulis* instead of *epistolis*. See above, p. 22, note 1 b (Col. 151, note c), where I observed that among the ancients the letters *o* and *u* regularly replace one another.] that those summoned to faith from every nation, rank, nobility, age, or sex become one in Christ [Note: Romans X, 12; First Corinthians X, 17; Galatians, the passage cited; and Colossians III, 11.]—through the sacrament of whose Passion the dominion of the world has been dishonored, nobility disfigured, exaltation cast down, humility raised up, what was elevated brought low, what was filthy purified, what lay prostrate erected, and what was dead brought to life [Col. 0136A]. Thus, in Isaiah (Isaiah XI, 4), the hollow places of the valleys are filled [Note: The manuscript has *repletur* (“is filled”), plainly an error for the plural *replentur*.], the heights of the mountains humbled; thus crooked things are straightened and rough places smoothed out. Thus the slopes of every hill, balanced into equality, have been brought down onto the level plain of the fields. Thus the cedars [Note: The manuscript has *caedri*, with the diphthong; this reading is not without the authority of ancient manuscripts.] of Lebanon, reduced in height, grow stout, and the shoots [Note: In the manuscript: *virgultae ... roboratae*, which is itself repeated corruption; *virgulta* is neuter, and therefore the final *e* is excessive in both words.] of young plants [Note: From the earliest times the word *vitulamen* (“planting,” “shoot”) was established among sacred and ecclesiastical writers. Saint Augustine speaks of its origin as follows, *On Christian Doctrine* II, volume III, part I, column 26: “Because *moschos* (μόσχος) in Greek means ‘calf,’ some, not understanding that *moscheumata* (μοσχεύματα) means ‘plantings,’ translated it as *vitulamina*. This error so occupied many manuscripts that it is scarcely found written otherwise; yet the meaning is perfectly clear, since the following words make it plain: ‘For illegitimate plantings will not strike deep roots’ (Wisdom IV, 3). That is more suitably said than *vitulamina*, which walk upon the ground with their feet and do not cling by roots.”] become vigorous and luxuriant. Thus the fierceness of lions [Note: So the manuscript, with the diphthong in *faeritas*; ancient manuscripts quite often present this reading.] having been tamed is joined to goodness, and, rejecting the fat of meat, the lion eats straw with the ox. Thus the wolf, laying aside its rage, grazes the meadows of the fields with the lambs. Thus the bear agrees with the calf, and the kid with the leopard (ibid. XI, 6–7). Thus infants put their hands into the dens of asps and are not harmed [Note: Ambrose also uses these same words of Isaiah in *Hexaemeron* V, 2, 6; *On the Interpellation of Job and David* II, 14; *On Psalm 118*, sermon 6, 17; and *On Luke* VII, 45 and 202, volume II; as well as *On Repentance* I, 13, 65 and 67, and below.]. Thus the diversity of the human race—for concern for oxen does not pertain to God [Note: The holy Doctor refers to the Apostle’s words, First Corinthians IX, 9: “Is God concerned about oxen?”]—will be brought together into one [Note: I have marked this as a parenthesis so that the passage may be clearer]. Thus diversity of birth agrees in unity. Thus rival conditions are made equal, when through baptism they die to the births of the world and through grace are born in heaven to nobility [Note: See *On the Mysteries* 3, 11, and 4, 21, and *On the Holy Spirit* I, 6, 76 ff., where similar expressions and ideas occur. Likewise *On Flight from the World* 11, 54, volume I: “He died once; but he dies for each person who is baptized into Christ’s death, so that we may be buried with him, rise with him, and walk in the newness of his life.” See also *On the Sacraments* III, 1 ff., in Ambrose’s works.], as the prophet Isaiah says:

> “Behold, now the sovereign Lord Sabaoth will disturb the glorious with power; those who are proud will be crushed by insult; they will be humbled, and the exalted will fall by the sword. But Lebanon will fall with its heights [Note: The Greek supports this reading. Where the ancient Vulgate, as printed by Sabatier, has “Lord of powers,” and the new Vulgate has “Lord of hosts,” the Greek has with us, ὁ δεσπότης Κύριος σαβαώθ, “the sovereign Lord Sabaoth.” Instead of “the exalted will be crushed” or “the tall will be cut down,” it reads οἱ ὑψηλοὶ τῇ ὕβρει συντριβήσονται, “the exalted will be crushed by pride.” The remainder reads καὶ οἱ ὑψηλοὶ ταπεινωθήσονται, that is, “and the exalted will be humbled.” Since Sabatier—though extraordinarily diligent in searching the Fathers’ writings for fragments of the ancient biblical version—gives these verses of Isaiah X, 33–34 incompletely, I have established with certainty that this sermon was still hidden in manuscripts at that time. This is further confirmed by the passage from Isaiah XI, 5, to be read below, which entirely escaped Sabatier’s labors.]” (ibid. X, 33–34).”

The divine word frequently compares Mount Lebanon and its cedar-clad summits with the worldly kingdom and its rulers [Note: Ambrose likewise remarks on this in *On Psalm 36*, 77 and 80, volume II; *On the Mysteries* 7, 39; and Letter 70, 7, volume III]. That kingdom and its ministers the Lord Christ cast down and crushed through his Passion. And lest the diversity of the passages trouble us, the same prophet, designating the person of the Lord Christ himself, who would bring all these things to completion, added:

> “A branch will go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will rise from his root [Note: Ambrose has this wording, except that he reads *ex* rather than *de* before *radice*, in *On the Blessing of the Patriarchs* 4, 19, volume I, and in *Luke* II, 24, and III, 8, volume II. He has *ex* in *On the Institution of a Virgin* 9, 59, volume III; but in *On the Holy Spirit* II, 5, 38, he retains *ut*, as in the manuscript. See also, if convenient, *An Apology for the Prophet David*, second book, 8, 43, volume I.]” (ibid. XI, 1).

“Root of David” [Note: This expression is frequent in Ambrose’s writings. You will find it in nearly all the passages just cited and elsewhere throughout his works. Let no one suppose that Ambrose contradicts himself because in one place he reads “the root of the family of the Jews” and here “the root of David”; for it is certain that the holy Doctor refers to David by both expressions. “It is clear,” Ambrose says in *An Apology for the Prophet David* 7, 38, volume I, “that by David the prophet is understood, and by the prophet the prophetic people, namely, the Jews.” In *On the Holy Spirit*, the work cited above, he says: “The root, Jesse, of the patriarchal family of the Jews; namely, David.” Compare the cited *Apology* 4, 27; *Luke* III, 8, volume II; and *On the Faith* V, 8, 105, volume III.] certainly signifies the person from whose seed Christ was born according to the flesh. Bursting forth from the loins of his father Jesse, he extended his human origin as far as the flower of the Lord’s birth.

Finally he added:

> “The Spirit of God will rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength [Col. 0137B], the spirit of knowledge and piety [Note: Ambrose has in *Luke* III, 8: “And the Spirit of the Lord will rest upon him: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding.” The Greek, like our Ambrose, reads Θεοῦ, “of God,” instead of “of the Lord.” Lactantius, *Institutes* IV, 13, column 577; Irenaeus III, chapter 9, column 184, and 17, column 208; and Tertullian, *Against the Jews* 9, column 143, agree with this. Ambrose reproduces the rest of the verse word for word in *On Psalm 118*, sermon 5, 38; *On the Mysteries* 7, 42; and elsewhere.], the spirit of the holy fear of God will fill him [Note: In all the cited passages Ambrose, omitting the other words, reads “the spirit of holy fear.” The holy Doctor seems to join these words to the preceding verse.]” (ibid. 2–3).

And to show more plainly that Christ was to be understood [Note: So the manuscript, in a good and ancient reading, as above, p. 17, note a (Col. 126, note d)], he continues:

> “He will not judge according to glory, nor reprove according to eloquence [Note: Jerome observes that the Septuagint read “according to the word he will reprove” in this passage]; but he will judge with humble judgment, reprove the glorious of the earth, and strike the earth [Note: The manuscript has *terra*, singular.] with the word [Note: The manuscript has *verba*, evidently in error.] of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he will kill the impious [Note: Irenaeus III, chapter 9, column 185, together with Jerome in this passage and the Greek text, supports the Ambrosian reading.]” (ibid. 4);

that is, with the word and the breath of his lips by which he said:

> “The dominion of this world—that is, its mastery [Note: Recall what we said above concerning the parenthesis, note a (Col. 115, note a), and elsewhere—]—will be cast out [Note: The Greek text and the Fathers who cite this passage read *princeps*, “the prince,” at the beginning, instead of *principatus*, “dominion.” At the end Augustine, *Questions on Leviticus* 72, volume III, part I, column 521, has “has been cast out.” The author of *On the Promises*, chapter 2, column 190, has “has been cast down.” Saint Jerome, with the Greek and the Vulgate, has “will be cast out.” A Cambridge manuscript cited by Sabatier has with us “will be cast out.”]” (John XII, 31).

And again:

> “The ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me [Note: This is a Hellenism, which Ambrose also uses below, as you will see in note 41 (the note on p. 8 of this page), when he cites the passage in *On Tobit* IX, 33, and *On Flight from the World* IV, 24.]” (John XIV, 30).

[Note: Ambrose does not always use this testimony in the same words. In *On Abraham* II, 9, 62; *On Isaac* 6, 55; *On Jacob* 5, 24, volume I; and *On Virginity* 17, 108, volume III, he has: “The prince of this world has come, and he will find nothing in me.” In *On Tobit* 9, 33, volume I: “Behold, the prince of this world has come, and he has found nothing of his own in me.” In *On Flight from the World* 4, 23, volume I; *On Psalm 118*, sermon 8, 6; and *Luke* IV, 29: “For the prince of this world has come, and has found nothing in me.” In *On Duties* I, 49, 249: “The prince of this world will come, and will find nothing in me.” Finally, word for word as in the manuscript—“he will find nothing in me”—he reads in *On Flight from the World*, the passage cited, section 24.]

And to display the sacrament of the cross [Note: This expression is familiar to Ambrose. Compare *On Psalm 118*, sermon 13, volume II, and the Maurist note there, as well as *On the Holy Spirit* I, 9, 108, volume IV], he added:

> “He will be girded with righteousness around his loins, and with truth he will wrap his sides” [Note: This verse enlarges Sabatier’s collection of biblical materials. Recall what was said in note 1, p. 27 (Col. 136, note 12).] (Isaiah XI, 5).

“Then,” he says—that is, from that time—

> “the wolf will feed with the lamb, and the leopard will rest with the kid [Note: The manuscript has *aedo* without the *h*, although shortly before we saw that it retained the aspirated form. I did not think the aspiration should be added, since the authority of ancient manuscripts does not oppose this reading.], and the calf, the bull, and the lion will feed together; and a little child will lead them [Note: *On Repentance* I, 13, 67, volume III, closely reproduces this passage as follows: “Then wolves and lambs will feed together.”]”—

that is, a priest, or one innocent through the smallness of his age [Note: So the manuscript, with one *u*. Although this may seem a scribal error, I decided to retain it, moved by the notable authority of ancient manuscripts, which frequently omit one of two *u*’s occurring together,] or supported by the purity of innocence, will govern them.

> “The ox and the bear will feed together [Note: Literally so in the Greek.]”—

and their kind will be one—

> “and the lion and the ox will eat straw [Note: Ambrose in the cited passage of *On Repentance* has: “The lion and the ox will eat straw.”]”—

that is, dry foods—

> “(ibid. 6–7).”

And lest my interpretation [Note: The manuscript consistently has the diphthong, which I have thought should be removed. Recall what was said p. 8, note b (Col. 118, note e).] be judged presumptuous or rash by attentive listeners [Note: Observe here Ambrose’s practice: he never used to flatter his listeners], I shall insert into my interpretations the Apostle Paul’s argument [Col. 0139A] [Note: The holy Doctor frequently explains and confirms his own view in his writings, especially in the Psalms, with the Apostle’s words], who says:

> “Strip off the old man with his deeds [Note: In *An Apology for the Prophet David* 9, 46, volume I, we read: “Stripping off the old man with his deeds,” and similarly in *On Psalm 118*, sermon 3, 22, except that it has *ejus* (“his”) at the end instead of *suis* (“its”). Sermon 10, 17, of the same psalm omits *vos* (“you”), which it retains in *Luke* 4, 58, but again omits in the same work, 8, 44: “So that, stripping off the old man with his deeds.” This reading, without *ut*, agrees with *On the Faith* III; but *On the Faith* V, chapter 16, 176, has: “Stripping off the old man with his deeds.”], and put on the new man, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him [Note: Ambrose cites this passage in *An Apology for the Prophet David*, the work just mentioned, and in *On Psalm 118*, sermon 3, the passage cited. But below, sermon 10 of the same psalm, he has: “And we put on the new man, who is renewed into knowledge,” and so likewise *On the Faith* V, the passage cited—provided that at the beginning one reads *induamus*, “let us put on,” instead of *induimus*, “we put on.” In *On the Faith* III: “And putting on the new according to the image,” and in *Luke* IV, the passage cited: “Put on the new man, who was created according to Christ”; while in VIII, the same passage, he writes simply “clothed with the new man.”]—where there is neither male nor female, Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free; but Christ is all things and in all [Note: Omitting “circumcision and uncircumcision,” which Ambrose retains here along with the Greek, he reproduces the rest word for word in *On the Faith* V, 14, 177. See also *On Psalm 118*, sermon 10, 17; *Luke* I, 5, and II, 47; and Letter 62, 85.]” (Colossians III, 9–11).

He clothes those stripped of the deeds of the old man [Note: Supply “of the old man.”] with the conduct of the new man, who is Christ. He did not allow them to remain naked, but covered them with the garment of honorable conduct [Note: The manuscript has *honeste*, without the diphthong, although the genitive of this word requires it.] and the brightness of good works [Note: The manuscript has *opere*. I added the diphthong and wrote *operae*, so as not to disturb the manuscript reading too much; nevertheless, I thought *operum* should be read.].

> “Put on,” he says, “as God’s chosen, holy [Note: In the Greek, as in the Vulgate, after *sancti* there is also καὶ ἠγαπημένοι, ‘and beloved’], compassion, kindness, humility, patience, gentleness, bearing with one another and forgiving one another, if anyone has a complaint against anyone [Col. 0139B] [Note: The manuscript has *quaerellam*, with the diphthong, which I thought should be removed on the authority of the manuscripts and the grammarians’ prescriptions; but I retained the doubled *l*. This spelling is quite common in ancient manuscripts. The distinguished Mai, commenting on Cicero, *On the Republic* II, 25, p. 194, noted the following concerning the spelling: “*Querella*, with a double *l*, is written almost consistently in ancient manuscripts and even on inscriptions. Yet Caper and Scaurus, pp. 2241 and 2249, forbid doubling the *l* in this word; in view of so many contrary examples, their grammatical rule scarcely deserves attention, especially since Papirianus, p. 2290, attests the somewhat later practice of writing the word with two *l*’s. The spelling *querella* is retained in Spanish, like many other relics of ancient Latin.”], just as the Lord forgave you, so also do you” [Note: Saint Augustine likewise has this in *Tractate 58 on John*, column 662, volume III, except that he reads *adversus* instead of *adversum*.] (ibid. 12–13).”

**XI.** By God’s gift everything has been forgiven us. We shall remain unharmed if we too forgive the offenses of our brothers [Col. 0140A] [Note: Similar words are found in *On Psalm 37*, 45, volume II, and in Letter 61, 9, volume III, where he says: “Let us beware, therefore, lest this happen to us: by not forgiving what is owed to us, we may begin to pay even those debts that have been forgiven us … Let us therefore forgive the little things, since greater things have been forgiven us, and let us understand that we shall be more acceptable to God insofar as we forgive more; for we are more grateful to God insofar as more has been forgiven us.” See also Letter 63, 83.]; if we are joined by the bonds of charity in an inseparable union (ibid. 14 ff.); if we rejoice in the gift of peace through mutual love [Note: Compare *On Psalm 118*, sermon 21, 17, volume II]; if we build ourselves up through divine utterances; if we summon one another to heavenly things with psalms; if we invite one another to what is above with songs [Note: Ambrose frequently invites his people in his sermons to sing psalms, especially in *Hexaemeron* V, 12, 36, volume I, and in the preface to *On Psalm 1*, 9, volume II. There he says that the pious custom of the faithful singing psalms together is a pledge of peace and concord and a great bond of unity. He repeats the same in *On Psalm 43*, 23; *On Psalm 118*, sermon 7, 25; and elsewhere. Here Ambrose seems to be referring to the Apostle’s words in Colossians III, 14–17.]; if everything that we do in action, say in speech, or encompass in thought we accomplish in the fear of God; giving thanks to the Father through the Son, praising God in Christ, and exalting Christ [Note: The manuscript again has “in Christ,” which would make the sense unlikely or at least obscure. The passage therefore appears to suffer some corruption. Perhaps the scribe referred to what he had written shortly before and put *in Christum* (“in Christ”) again instead of *Christum*, as I have thought best to write it and as the sense requires.] in God, so that, comparing heavenly things with heavenly and spiritual things with spiritual, we may resemble one another.

There is no other work than to praise the glory of God with the divine voice, as John says [Note: Ambrose defends the Apocalypse as belonging to John the Evangelist in *On Psalm 1*, 54; *On Psalm 40*, 26; *On Virginity* 14, 86; *On the Incarnation* 10, 114; and elsewhere. He seems in some way to approach the same position here. Yet one should not simply accept M. Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, who attributes the Apocalypse to a presbyter John distinct from the Evangelist, for Millius sufficiently refuted him in the prolegomena to this book, to which I gladly refer learned readers. Compare Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII, chapter 25, p. 309 ff., Valesius’s edition, Turin, 1746, volume I, and p. 749 of the same volume, among the notes of various scholars.]:

> “I saw and heard the voice of many around the throne, and of the living creatures and the elders; and their number was ten times one hundred thousand [Note: The Greek text favors this reading, and Cassiodorus agrees with it in *On Psalm 1*, column 14, adding one word, *magnam*, “a great voice.”], saying with a loud voice: ‘Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and strength and riches and patience and honor and might and glory and blessing [Note: Ambrose’s writings lack this biblical testimony. The Fathers who cite it, however, never reproduce it in exactly the same words; they frequently alter, insert, or remove words and disturb the order of the items. The various ancient versions do not agree among themselves, nor does our Vulgate agree with the Greek.]’ And every creature that is in heaven and on the earth and in the sea, and all things that are in them [Col. 0141A] [Note: The ancient version printed by Sabatier adds “under the earth,” with which the new Vulgate agrees, though not in the same words]” (Revelation V, 11–13).

And again he declares:

> “The angels stood around the throne, and the elders, and the four living creatures. They fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God [Note: The Greek favors the reading of our Ambrose if at the beginning one writes, “And all the angels,”], saying: ‘Blessing, [Col. 0142A] and glory, and wisdom, and thanksgiving, and honor, and power, and strength be to our God forever and ever. Amen [Note: In the ancient and modern versions, *claritas*, “splendor,” occurs instead of *gloria*, “glory.” But Saint Fulgentius retains *gloria* with us in fragment 34 against Fabianus, column 646; so does the Greek text, which at the end, as in the manuscript, adds Ἀμήν, “Amen.”]’” (ibid. VII, 11–12).

**EXPLICIT** [Note: In the manuscript: “…t sermo sci Amb.” The letters of this formula’s first word have been entirely obliterated, and only a brief trace of the final letter *t* remains; I have printed it in its correct form. It was nevertheless not difficult to supply the formula, considering the available space, since *explicit* was the solemn ancient formula for closing books.] **SERMON OF SAINT AMBROSE.**

**In the year of the Lord 384. Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, vir clarissimus, ordinary consul and prefect of the city.**

# PROLEGOMENA

[Col. 0141]

## GUILIELMUS CAVE’S HISTORICAL NOTICE OF AURELIUS SYMMACHUS

[Col. 0141B] Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, born at Rome, senator and prefect of that same city, was especially distinguished in the year 384. He held the consulship in 391. Everywhere he reveals a mind hostile to the Christian religion, above all in the *Relation* concerning the Altar of Victory which he presented to the emperor Valentinian. In it he vigorously and openly argues the cause of the pagans, finding an opponent in Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, who elegantly and forcefully refutes Symmachus’s work.

Nor did Symmachus merely lose his case [Col. 0142B]; shortly afterward, as though guilty of treason, he was placed on a cheap wagon and sent into exile one hundred miles from the city, although Theodosius soon afterward restored him to favor. This *Relation* survives both among the works of Ambrose and among Symmachus’s letters. It was published with the notes of François Juret and Jean Lectius at Geneva in 1598, octavo; with ten added books of miscellanies, at Paris in 1604, quarto; and at Neapoli Nemetum in 1628, octavo, with the notes of Paraeus.

[Col. 0141]

## THE LIFE OF SYMMACHUS FROM THE MOST ANCIENT EDITION

[Col. 0141B] Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, a man of consular rank, lived at nearly the same time as the holy Doctors Jerome and Ambrose and the poets Ausonius, Prudentius, and Claudian. Prosper, in *On Times*, assigns his consulship and that of his colleague Titianus to the year of the Lord 394 [Col. 0141C], which was the final year of the emperor Valentinian the Younger. A letter of Symmachus addressed to him and bearing its own title is indeed preserved, although such an incidental item is otherwise lacking.

Nor are his letters to Ausonius unknown; no one is unaware that Ausonius was a man of the highest distinction who lived at the same time. This is the Symmachus who, in a most brilliant speech, defended the cause of the pagan gods before the divine emperor Theodosius and the Caesars Arcadius and Honorius. Against him several others wrote, but with greater force Saint Ambrose and Aurelius Prudentius in two books: the latter in hexameter verse, the former in prose.

From that very speech one may see how great and how refined was his ability in speaking—so great, indeed, that Angelus Politianus, a man of the most discerning judgment, quite deservedly enrolled him among the great orators of antiquity [Col. 0141D]. One may also learn something from this little book of familiar letters. Since it was commonly attributed to Boethius’s father-in-law, and since there were certain defenders of this error [Col. 0142B] who professed to know all history and, with utterly shameless cunning, had insinuated themselves not only into courts but even into the minds of princes—alas, the times!—I considered their insolent ignorance intolerable. With impartial judgment, restoring the offspring to its parent [Col. 0142C], I demonstrated how empty is the invention of those who fabricate history at will and, contrary even to the evidence of chronology, rearrange the past—as one may also see here.

For that Symmachus, the father-in-law of Boethius, who was killed by Theodoric in the year of the Lord 521, could not have written a letter to Valentinian except either from his cradle or—if we allow the doctrine of rebirth—from the Elysian fields before being born again. But why speak of these mountebanks? My present purpose was to commend Symmachus’s letters to lovers of antiquity and refined literature. Although they may not read them as corrected as he wrote them elegantly, I know that they will be grateful to those who preferred to publish them in this form rather than allow them to perish altogether [Col. 0142D]. For they have not yielded so completely to corruptors that a good portion has not remained intact—enough to make even sharp-nosed readers wrinkle their noses.

[Col. 0143]

# SYMMACHIAN PRAISES

## MACROBIUS, *SATURNALIA* V, chapter 1

“According to Eusebius,” he says, “there are four kinds of style: the copious, in which Cicero reigns; the concise, in which Sallust rules; the dry, attributed to Fronto; and the rich and florid, in which Pliny the Younger once luxuriated, and now our Symmachus, inferior to none of the ancients.”

## AURELIUS PRUDENTIUS, *AGAINST SYMMACHUS*, BOOK I

> O tongue flowing from a marvelous fountain of words,
>
> Glory of Roman eloquence, before which even Tully
>

He cites the custom of the ancients.

## AMMIANUS MARCELLINUS, BOOK XXVII

Symmachus succeeded Apronianus. He deserves to be named among the foremost examples of learning and modesty. Under his administration the most sacred City enjoyed an abundance of leisure and resources greater than usual, and rejoiced in the ambitious and exceptionally strong bridge which he himself built and dedicated amid great civic happiness—only to discover, as the event plainly showed, the ingratitude of the citizens. After several years they burned his splendid house in the Transtiberine district, provoked by the fact that some obscure plebeian had falsely claimed, without any evidence or witness, that he had said: “He would more willingly extinguish limekilns with his own wine than sell wine at the prices being expected.”

## SAINT PROSPER OF AQUITAINE, *ON THE PROMISES OF GOD*, PART III

Symmachus, that man endowed with marvelous eloquence and learning, yet a pagan, informed the Christian emperor, through a speech of praise delivered before the imperial council, that the Altar of Victory should be restored to the Senate, using the subtle skill at which he excelled. The emperor, immediately driving him from the objects of his affection, ordered him to remain on that day, placed upon an unupholstered wagon, at the hundredth milestone.

## GAIUS SOLLIUS APOLLINARIS SIDONIUS, BOOK I, LETTER 1

I shall pursue, with presumptuous footsteps, the rounded style of Quintus Symmachus and the discipline and maturity of Gaius Pliny.

The same author, Book VIII, Letter 10:

You apply to my character enormous titles of praise. But if you had made even some account of our modesty, you ought to have thought of that Symmachian saying: “As true praise adorns, so false praise chastises.”

The same Sidonius to the consul Felix:

> But do not attempt to compare me
>
> With those whom, though myself far inferior,
>
> I admire all the more:
>
> Paulinus, Ampelius, and Symmachus.

## ANONYMOUS

> Symmachus is sparing in words, but profound in mind;
>
> Lavish in meaning, narrow in words; abundant
>
> In mind, but lesser in speech; blessed in fruit, not foliage:
>
> He confines the riches of thought within brevity of speech.

## MAGNUS AURELIUS CASSIODORUS, *VARIAE* II, LETTER 1

You retain, moreover, that splendid saying of the most eloquent Symmachus. I happily contemplate the growth of his virtue, since I postpone praising its beginnings.

## CASSIODORUS, *TRIPARTITE HISTORY* IX, chapter 23

While Valentinian and Theodosius were staying in the city of Rome and celebrating the festivities of Victory, the emperor Theodosius then displayed his kindness toward Symmachus, the former consul. Symmachus was regarded as one of the foremost senators and was remarkable for his mastery of Roman eloquence; many of his books are also found.

He wrote a panegyric of Maximus and recited it. Consequently he later seemed guilty of treason. Fearing death, he fled into a church. But the emperor, being a Christian of the highest perfection and honoring not only the priests of his own faith but also the Novatians, who adhered very closely to the decrees of his faith, granted a favor at the request of Leontius, then bishop of the Roman Novatian Church, and absolved Symmachus from the charge.

When Symmachus had obtained pardon, he wrote to the emperor Theodosius an *Apology*, that is, a book of satisfaction. Thus far Cassiodorus. The same account is also found in Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History* V, chapter 14, and Nicephorus XII, chapter 21.

[Col. 0144D] Verses of Ennodius of Ticinum concerning Ambrose’s letter against Symmachus, regarding the Altar of Victory, when Symmachus, defeated, requested that it be worshiped:

> Victory takes from his friend the palm of eloquence.
>
> It passes to Ambrose; the goddess’s anger favors him more.

## SIGEBERT OF GEMBLOUX, *CHRONICLE*, UNDER THE YEAR OF THE LORD 407

Rhadagaisus the Scythian, coming from Scythia with two hundred thousand Goths, invaded Italy. From this there arose a loud murmur among many blasphemers against Christ. Blaming the times of Christianity, they exalted the former prosperity. Among them Symmachus the orator raged especially; in his writings and letters he also argued for idolatry and for the restoration of the Altar of Victory [Col. 0145A]. Augustine, in his book *The City of God*, and Orosius, in his *History*, stopped the mouths of these barking men by thrusting into them the bone of truth. The poet Prudentius likewise refuted Symmachus’s blasphemies in a brilliant little work in verse.

## JOANNES CUSPINIANUS, IN HIS COMMENTARY ON THE CONSULS

Quintus Symmachus, a man of consular rank and prefect of the City, exceptionally eloquent and learned, the brother of Ausonius, defended the cause of the pagan gods in a brilliant speech before the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian. This speech is inserted in the fifth book of his letters—in this edition, the tenth. Against it Saint Ambrose wrote most vigorously, as did Aurelius Prudentius, who flourished about this time, in two most elegant books of heroic verse.

He also wrote extremely elegant familiar letters, remarkable for their brevity and rounded style, the foremost adherent of Cicero’s Academy. They ought certainly to be read by younger writers in place of the letters of Carolus and Casparinus. The two brightest lights of our age, Pomponius Laetus and Angelus Politianus, praised them greatly. They possess graceful elegance joined to agreeable brevity, and they explain several events of their age. Read, reader, and you will rejoice.

## JACOBUS LECTIUS

Symmachus possessed genuine eloquence, a skillful and penetrating intellect, and an equal gravity and charm of thought. If one considers his words, there is pleasing brevity; but if one searches more deeply into his meaning, there is extensive and multifaceted learning. Add to this a solid and hidden knowledge of civil wisdom. Add the rare integrity of his character under the emperors and the Roman freedom with which he offered legal advice. He is not someone to be handled lightly by administrators of public affairs or jurists, especially counselors or secretaries of great princes.

## JOANNES JACOMOTTUS

> To whom belongs the fragrance of eloquence,
>
> Learned brevity,
>
> Grave dignity of thought,
>
> Wisdom in affairs worthy of princes,
>
> Wit untouched by gall,
>
> To whom the venerable decrees of Latin Themis are pleasing,
>
> And skillful vigor—come here.

[Col. 0146B]

## CASPAR BARTHIUS, *ABLEGATIONES* II, chapter 8

It cannot be said how highly Symmachus’s letters deserve to be valued. Not merely because of that precise brevity, supremely suited to this kind of writing, but because of their political judgments, and in such abundance that from them alone a prudent person could learn how to administer a state with honor and advantage.

There is not one of them that does not breathe the genius of a man experienced in the distinguished administration of public affairs. There is no letter that could not convey an entire doctrine of some political system.

[Col. 0145]

# THE TEN BOOKS OF LETTERS OF QUINTUS AURELIUS SYMMACHUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, ORDINARY CONSUL AND PREFECT OF THE CITY

## BOOK ONE

### LETTER ONE. SYMMACHUS TO HIS FATHER

[Col. 0145C]

So that the interruption of my letters may not be held against me, I prefer to be prompt in the performance of duty rather than sit idle awaiting a long-delayed exchange—especially since words are not to be assigned to parents by the scale or by measure. I should seem unjust if I contended with you on equal terms. For anyone who demands equal service from unequals is reckoned beyond what is fair. Thus your conversation proceeds from generosity, mine from obligation. These considerations, and others of the same kind, very nearly compelled me to omit the additional duty of writing.

Now I must disclose the sequence of our activities; for I am no less willing to give an account of my leisure than of my business. We exchanged Bauli for the Lucrine residence—not because we had grown tired of that lodging, since the longer one visits it, the more one loves it, but because I feared that, if an attachment to Bauli grew upon me, the other places that ought to be visited might displease me. There I offered measured words to Acyndinus, its founder, and to his ancestors, and brought within orderly bounds the license of the paintings that assigns different dress to each figure. I would delay you a little, if I were not afraid that waiting might lessen anticipation. Therefore receive this song, laboriously worked upon a slender thread.

> An Attic cloak covers my father-in-law; a painted toga, my father.  
> He presided over sacred rites; this one pronounced laws for the Quirites.  
> But I wear the military dress that the brooch fastens and bites;  
> among eastern peoples I governed the royal headquarters of Dawn.  
> Yet the painting is silent about the fasces; you, consult the records.

I know that, as soon as you read these lines, you will immediately set your poetic lyre in motion. Do not do so, lest you boast at my expense. I address you, after the example of our own poet, as though under a certain law: let me be permitted to honk among melodious swans. Unless you comply, you will impose silence upon me. Do you wish to test how little I fear you? Here I reveal to you another secret of my delirium, while I am still anxious about the earlier one. Hear the verses relating to the history of Bauli.

> Here the god Alcides drove the cattle into their stall,  
> rescued from the hearth of triple-bodied Geryon.  
> From that time, a later age, corrupting the name, calls  
> the place Bauli, by a hidden indication of its origin.  
> From the god to eminent lords Fortune ran,  
> lest the hero suffer the fame of the place to remain obscure.  
> The fortunate Hortensius, rich in wealth, celebrated this palace,  
> he who stood opposite the Arpinate in eloquence.  
> Here the consul Acyndinus prolonged a brilliant age,  
> as did Orfitus, who gave laws to the descendants of Aeneas.  
> Among these, the youthful ornament, but with the honor of an old man,  
> raised high by twelve fasces, you shine, Symmachus.  
> Yet the leisurely pleasures of Bauli do not yet seek you;  
> let public responsibility keep the young man vigilant through the night.

Of course, you are mocking me because I have spoken of myself somewhat more indulgently than was proper. This is a true and deserved criticism. For all ostentation is not free from the suspicion of falsehood, since whatever is assumed is not thought to be one’s own. Moreover, greedy boasting greatly diminishes modesty. I could say—if some outsider happened to overhear—that these were my verses; I would certainly make it possible for modesty to be forgiven, if praise had proceeded from another. But I see that the little work is not something to regret. Thus the matter, obscure and uncertain, leaves me in doubt whether I should fear the danger to modesty or to glory. To you, therefore, who surpass the rest in prudence, I assign the task of deciding this wish. You yourself will see what use should be made of it. I have chosen, without immodesty, a father who is conscious of both my childishness and my lack of judgment. Farewell.

## Letter II. The Father to Symmachus

[Col. 0147C]

This is a gift by which Campania alone cannot boast; indeed, such a language might be translated at Rome or Athens into the honor of speaking Greek. For what is more polished than the letter of yours that I recently received? What is more delightful than the admixture of verse? I will tell you frankly: it came to an end too quickly for those who wished to read more. If only some portion of their meaning survives—the meaning of those whose portraits we see bearing epigrams inscribed above them! Such successors to their labors will readily praise those who have illuminated the brilliance of the paintings with more beautiful verses.

I too, then, congratulate you, not merely because your belly has been filled with oysters and pelorides, but because your breast has been filled with eloquence. And since you yourself, by beginning, have released my modesty, receive from us as well some recently written encomia of the good men of my age. Since there is nothing for me to do, and, when I have nothing to do, a miserable recollection of my ancestors comes over me, I have found something that we may add to the little books I recently dictated. You know that Terentius—not the comic poet, but that Terentius of Reate, father of Roman learning—embellished his books of the Hebdomads with the addition of epigrams. If fortune allows, we are attempting to imitate him. But of the first pieces I assembled I have meanwhile sent only a few, entreating you by God to correct anything in them that displeases you. There is nothing shameful in that for me. For if anything pleases you in them, the praise is mine; nor do I avoid the association in which I am not ashamed to have such a critic.

### Aradius Rufinus

> First in talent, and first through the gift of Fortune,  
> Rufinus, first among the men of your generation; to you prosperity,  
> and glory, equal to sorrow amid swelling circumstances, were granted.  
> One love to all, and a protection to the fearful.  
> In the time of emperors under whom you flourished, learned  
> either to put spurs to good men or to restrain tyrants with the reins.

### Valerius Proculus

> Among the foremost, whom the glory of their fathers did not burden,  
> we shall place Proculus, distinguished by the beauty of his life and character,  
> never unworthy of the great Poplicolae.  
> He always loved truth, and possessed steadfastness, simplicity,  
> and the worship of the heavenly gods; you could not despise him.  
> And although he will be revered, you will not therefore fear him.

### Anicius Julianus

> Whose wealth, nobility, or such great power  
> did not Anicius alone surpass as he yielded to no one?  
> Keen in intellect, yet equally accommodating to everyone.  
> He was dear in conversation and ready to help;  
> for although rich and elevated by honors, he was greater  
> than those honors and, by his name, filled eternal Rome.

### Petronius Probianus

> Let Fortune boast of others, whom, with no judge,  
> their own license raised to the light of Romulus.  
> You, Probianus, were aided by modesty, fortunate favor,  
> Italian simplicity of character, and skill.  
> Therefore, as a constant acquaintance and guest of the emperors,  
> you deservedly received the rewards of great honors.

### Verinus

> Should I admire your virtue more in arms, Verinus,  
> when, as a commander, you subdued the eastern Armenians with slaughter?  
> Or rather your eloquence, and the charm of your character and life?  
> And—unless when public responsibility called you to official duties—  
> the fact that you happily maintained your life in innocent fields?  
> There is no further work of virtue; for if there were, you would possess it.

I do not know whether I alone shall be able to meet the claims of eighty persons. Therefore we entrust to you epigrams on our father-in-law and uncle. For even Varro’s books are marked with different authors.

## Letter III. Symmachus to His Father

I am filled with the greatest gratitude because I notice that my letters do not seem tasteless to you; and I count it a great gift that this judgment of our letters is held among you. For to be praised by a man who is himself praised is a rare reward of talent.

But just as this gave me joy, so I think that other matter was added in jest: if anything had been coarse in your verses, it was to be polished by the attention of my style. Surely I would be stupid and worthless if I did not realize that my mouth had been smeared with cosmetic. For what can be corrected either by me or, in your case, may be corrected at all? In our age you alone have fashioned the currency of Latin eloquence on Cicero’s anvil. Whatever was graceful among poets, weighty among orators, trustworthy in the annals, or learned among grammarians, you alone have absorbed, the rightful heir of ancient literature.

Do not deceive me with words. I know the force of the proverb: “The pig teaches Minerva.” You are thoroughly versed in epic discipline, no less skilled at blowing the pedestrian trumpet. Do you really say so? Are you equally great in speaking and singing, and will you pretend that I am unworthy of your assistance? You are not acting fairly, nor does false boasting please me.

Meanwhile, if you grant us empty ears to use, I shall tell you what we have been doing in recent days. I was enjoying leisure at Baiae, with no witnesses present. After a report arrived that the sons of Earth were gathering, we took great care lest a plebeian society stain our sober solitude. First I withdrew to Naples, then, after a short interval, to Beneventum.

There I was received with the utmost attention and universal applause, and celebrated with such honor that I was already burdened by the attentions. Assiduity that is not repaid becomes burdensome. Although the city is very large, each of its leading men seemed to me greater than the city itself: lovers of literature and remarkable in character. A large part of them worships God. They vie with one another in exhausting their private wealth for the adornment of the city. For after the earthquake, scarcely anything had been left to them, yet shattered fortunes found their spirits unbroken. Each in his own way strives to perform the work of a good citizen. Night is joined to day in labor.

Hence we were very anxious to leave sooner than I wished, lest those who had devoted themselves to me for so long should be missed from their work, or lest their doubled occupation should distract them. Accordingly, I returned to the Bay of Baiae. For at that time Baiae itself was already silent. From here I send you the service of a greeting and report that, God willing, we shall soon return.
