May fortune favor this promise. Nevertheless, may your indulgence often grant me an address, as though we were going to be absent longer. Farewell.

## Letter IV. Symmachus to His Father

You imitate the zeal of Menippean Varro, but you surpass his talent. For the epigrams that you have recently composed about our countrymen seem to me to shine above the encomia of the Hebdomads; these are equally sober, yet not dull. Those were struck from good metal, but did not know how to be finished on the lathe.

And, unless I am mistaken, you are attempting a harder material. He treated Pythagoras, who first asserted that souls are eternal; Plato, who persuaded men that the gods exist; Aristotle, who reduced the nature of good speaking to an art; poor Curius, yet one who ruled the rich; the stern Catones, the Fabian clan, the glories of the Scipios, and that entire triumphal senate, touching them with restrained praise. You illuminate the ruins of the immediately preceding age. It is difficult to add honor to restricted circumstances.

You also command me to append certain things in verse to your verses. Your Flaccus did not instruct us so in those decrees of the poetic art, of which I remember this to be the beginning: that a horse’s neck should not be joined to a human head. Thus let the obstinacy of the service I have refused displease you, rather than the imprudence of a work I had promised displease me. We shall speak more about this face to face, when we prepare to follow or overtake this letter. Complete what you have begun, and be generous with such skillful eloquence. Just as I deny you the services of my tongue, so I shall lend you my ears. Farewell.

## Letter V. Symmachus to His Father

We are accused of silence even though our greatest care is to fulfill our duty, almost as though there has been no stopping-place among all these regions where we have taken a holiday from this obligation. Yet the pious exacting of conversation truly pleases the spirit. A complaint born of indulgence is sweet. You need only recognize readily that this remonstrance is more dutiful than justified.

Meanwhile, you have been silent about your retreat at Praeneste, of which rumor informed me. How I wish I might unexpectedly steal upon your pleasures! Although the pleasant places of Campania surpass it, it would nevertheless suit me better to spend time with you and temper the summer fragrance with the breezes of that region.

But our household affairs are declining. We must inspect them everywhere—not so that the total of our profits may grow rich, but so that the hope of the estate may be supported by voluntary expenditures. For this has come upon our age: the countryside, which once used to feed us, must now be fed.

But I shall let this go, lest a greeting turned into a complaint diminish the pleasure of duty. Take care of your health, and of more frequent conversation; when we ask this, we earnestly promise the same. Farewell.

## Letter VI. Symmachus to His Father

Those who hope that some gift is to be conferred upon them are usually impatient of delay. But we now see this newly arising among you: that generous men cannot endure delay in giving what belongs to them.

Recently an estate came to you by law, and you legally bestowed it upon me. Your profit ran to my advantage, and you imitated Fortune with a better intention. For what you had taken sorrowfully from the property of a relative, you handed over joyfully.

What is more, you increased this generosity with the most distinguished testimonial. I prefer its honorable distinction to gifts. For one who is helped without praise for his wealth seems to receive a necessary gift rather than a deserved reward.

Therefore I thank your judgment, and give you thanks as greatly as thanks can be given, because you have bestowed both honors upon me. And I pray the gods that we may all enjoy for a long time what you have given in common, and that there may be among us those to whom we may transfer the estate at Ostia according to our own judgment and following your example. Farewell.

## Letter VII. Symmachus to His Father

[Col. 0150C]

We are in good spirits, now that you have begun the journey, mindful of your promise. Haste is needed, so that while the season of the year is warm we may quickly enjoy the blessings of autumn. In these months Campania shines with the richness of its fields and the beauty of its orchards.

Baiae is tempered by infrequent rain and moderate sun; the tables are plentiful because of the aediles, whom you threaten with crowds of friends. But I have no avoidance of an honorable multitude. And if twice as many as you write should arrive, you will have produced a good harvest. There will be no shortage of what they need to drive away hunger. For your companions, being sober men, are concerned with slaughtering the fattened animals only later.

Why do I prolong my speech? I am sending words away and demanding the deed. It is the mark of prudence to seize the opportunity. If anything is taken away by delaying the journey, the delay will be repaid by leisure. Farewell.

## Letter VIII. Symmachus to His Father

For a long time your silent Lucrine waters, your clear Baian waters, Puteoli still famous, and great, silent Bauli have been longing for you. Yet you sit idle at rustic Cora or barren Formiae. At last, if it is worth the effort, hasten along the road and observe better lands, where one rests in deep peace from crowds, and where there is no limit to enjoying holidays.

> Where horned Lyaeus  
> covers the heights with vine,  
> Vulcan in his fiery caverns  
> cooks the middle of the earth.  
>   
> Thetis and her Baian sisters  
> now possess many fish;  
> the water is warm, the sky is cool,  
> while Dione, smiling Amathusian,  
> swims among the dances—  
> mistress of salt and vapor,  
> flower of the stars.

Do I seem to you, as though drunk on excessive luxury, to be out of my mind and, indeed, to have enrolled among the poets? I attach no importance to this kind of literature: I have exercised the power of the place rather than of my own talent. But if I am speaking words of invitation, quicken your pace, so that you too may rejoice in present delights and Fortune may grant us the enjoyment of what we desire. Farewell.

## Letter IX. Symmachus to His Father

[Col. 0151B]

We were afraid that rain might hold you back. But true is that saying which our poet left written: piety has overcome a difficult journey. Therefore we await your arrival on the appointed day. May the gods only ensure that what you have resolved in your mind is obstructed by no excuses. Farewell.

## Letter X. Symmachus to His Father

Is this to be my fortune, that wherever I turn my foot and step, something is offered to me for rebuilding? Now the restoration of the praetorium at Capua is forcing me into heavy expenses. One part is collapsing through neglect; another, repaired long ago with careless haste, provides an unsightly and unsound dwelling. Unless prompt attention comes to its aid, either the expense of money will later accumulate, or the buildings will collapse. For whoever interrupts this work loses everything.

Therefore I have resolved to remove the old age of the buildings. Thus, although we had desired and sought leisure, we have yielded to an expensive undertaking. You have heard what we are doing. In return, let us know the favorable state of your health and affairs, so that this little while which we are preparing to spend in Campania may pass without offense caused by your silence. Farewell.

## Letter XI. Symmachus to His Father

When the birthday of our daughter was already approaching, the gifts you had sent arrived at a most opportune time. They were very dear and important to us all. For when one provides generously for those who are absent, the greater the outlay, the greater the pleasure.

At once we embraced the letter that accompanied the gifts and began waiting for you to write as soon as possible that you were undertaking the journey along the Appian Way. The page announced none of this. I asked the courier whether some sudden event had disturbed the firmness of your decision. He said that the intention was not wavering at all, but that your plans were being delayed until the Formian estate had been equipped with abundant produce and other necessities of this kind.

Then my spirit returned from its distress. I give you my word that nothing will be lacking for a humble table, for service, or for livestock. So that I may not later deny this statement, here is a letter to you in the form of a written bond. Affection guarantees the pledge. For I shall not allow those whom I long to embrace to be deceived. Farewell.

## Letter XII. Symmachus to His Father

[Col. 0152A]

The duty of censors was to inspect the works they had commissioned. You wanted me to manage this task. I have obeyed your command, either because I ought to have been obedient to your word, or because I recognized that the assigned task suited my own enthusiasm.

Receive, then, an account of how far our supervision has advanced the buildings. The stairways have been enriched with the distinction of marble; the upper rooms are covered with inlaid work, executed so lightly that the joinery gives the appearance of solidity. You purchased the columns for no more than if they had come to you as a gift. If my eyes serve me well, I believe they were cut from Bithynian stone.

This is what you ought to know for now. Hereafter we shall add to your knowledge as much as we see being added to the construction. Farewell.

## Letter XIII. Symmachus to Ausonius

[Col. 0152B]

Joy is usually eloquent, and, scorning the confinement of a closed breast, rejoices exuberantly. For you, my friend, fortunate circumstances produced forgetfulness of writing. That could not serve as an example for me, whom the heavenly speech of our lord Gratian filled with good hope and cheerfulness.

Therefore I did not spare myself the effort of addressing you unprompted, both for the sake of duty and for the sake of my joy: the one was suggested by our intimacy, the other by the public prosperity. Now, if you can spare the effort, lend me your mind for a little while.

The first days of January were approaching. We had come in large numbers to the Senate-house very early, before daylight made clear the end of the gloomy night. Then, by chance, a report arrived that the speech of the desired emperor had come late at night—and it was true. For the courier, tired from keeping watch, was standing there.

Before the sky had grown white, we rushed together with lamps burning, to receive the destiny of a new age. Why say more? We received the daylight for which we had still been waiting.

You will ask—for it is better to hear this—what our fathers thought of that speech. Let the nature of events answer you, by what votes the long-desired piety was heard. We know how to embrace our blessings. If you believe me, I am still suffering a kind of rawness from that joy of mine.

Good Nerva, vigorous Trajan, dutiful Antoninus, and blameless Marcus were assisted by an age full of devotion to duty, which then knew no other standards. Here the nature of the emperor is praised; there it is the gift of an earlier age. Why, with the order reversed, should we think these examples belong to the best arts, and those merely vestiges of an earlier age?

May Fortune protect its ancient service, and at least be willing to preserve these delights for the Roman name. May public happiness not be gnawed by any enchantment. You have heard everything, but only tasted it superficially with your lips. The records of our Senate-house will speak to you more fully. When you find several rescripts there, judge how much richer were the wishes of a single mind than the applause it poured forth. Farewell.

## Letter XIV. Symmachus to Ausonius

You ask me for longer letters. This is a sign of genuine affection toward us. But I, conscious of the poverty of my talent, prefer to cultivate Laconic brevity rather than publish the thinness of my childishness in many-paged volumes.

Nor is it surprising that the vein of our eloquence has grown thin, since for a long time you have not nourished it by reading any of your poems or your prose volumes. Why, then, do you demand a generous loan of my conversation, when you have extended no literary credit? Your Mosella, consecrated by you in divine verses, flies through the hands and bosoms of many, but merely glides past our lips. Why, I ask, did you wish me to be excluded from that little book? Did I seem to you unmusical, unable to judge it, or perhaps spiteful, unable to praise it? Thus you diminished either my talent or my character.

Nevertheless, despite your prohibition, I soon penetrated the secrets of that work. I should like to keep silent about what I think; I should like to avenge myself upon you with a silence proportionate to your treatment. But admiration for the writing breaks the force of the injury. For I knew that river long ago, when I was accompanying the standards of the eternal emperors: equal to many, inferior to the greatest.

Now, unexpectedly, you have made it greater than the Egyptian Melon in the dignity of its famous verses, colder than the Scythian Tanais, and clearer than our own popular Fucinus. I would never believe you when you tell great stories about the Mosella’s source and course, unless I knew for certain that you do not lie even in a poem.

Where did you find those shoals of river fish? They are as varied in name as in color; just as they differ in size, so they differ in taste—and you have colored them beyond nature’s gifts with the pigments of your poem. Yet I have often been a guest at your tables, and, while marveling at many other things set before me for eating in the praetorium, I never discovered this kind of fish. When were these fish born for you in the book, when they were not present on the serving dishes?

Do you think I am joking and playing around? May I prove acceptable to the gods in this: I place your poem beside the books of Maro. But I shall now stop, forgetting my own grievance, from clinging to your praises, lest this too add to your glory—that we admire you even while offended.

You may scatter your volumes and always exclude me; we shall nevertheless enjoy your work through the kindness of others. Farewell.

## Letter XV. Symmachus to Ausonius

It had almost happened that I should speak with you in compressed brevity, since there was nothing worthy of remembrance; and when events are lacking, there is no need to indulge in words. But, at an opportune moment, the declamation of our rhetorician Palladius enlarged the page. Since it pleased the foremost men of letters, it ought not to have remained hidden from you.

Therefore, since such a report suited both my duty and your interest, scarcely had the assembly dispersed when, before the reliability of my hearing had been tested, I dictated it while my judgment was still warm.

The new guest of the Athenaeum moved the Latin council by his skill in division, abundance of invention, gravity of thought, and brilliance of language. I speak according to my own judgment: he is as upright in speech as in character. Then our countrymen, who often disagree among themselves about other matters, held a unanimous opinion about his praise.

I firmly believe—and my confidence is not empty—that this is the lineage of rhetoricians. For he is known to possess a breast full of talent. It is not merely his face or complexion that proclaims a descendant worthy of honoring his parents. Nature possesses more certain proofs of sound judgment and good speaking. Heirs are born, not written. What others are taught, he was born with.

I did not think these matters should be kept silent from you, my lord, both because, out of love for you, I regard nothing as too insignificant, and because I am never sorry to know how highly you value me in return. I wish this to be done for Palladius: honorable things should not remain hidden when they deserve to be spoken. Take care of your health; and since you have the opportunity to write, apply your willingness as well. Farewell.

## Letter XVI. Symmachus to Ausonius

I am often pressed by the language of your unanimity to write about the letters you sent me with such devoted care; and, as each one arrived, I immediately answered it with equal conscientiousness, because neither the duty of replying nor the exchange of affection allowed me to remain idle longer.

Now too I declare that I am acting and giving thanks because you do not allow the favorable news to remain hidden from me. I had spoken of these and other matters with you in earlier letters as well. But if the couriers have made you familiar with my conversation, its repetition is not burdensome. I would rather dull your ears by repeating myself than defraud you by keeping silent.

I rejoice at the honor of my brother Hesperius, but I am wounded by his silence. For if his conduct proved him affectionate toward me, he ought by his writing to have anticipated the report, which for a long time, being uncertain, had offered my joy only wavering assurance. He himself ought to have been the messenger of our common good, so that the assertion of a letter would leave no room for uncertain opinion.

But you say that he was restrained by modesty and avoided boasting of his successes. Does anyone blush when he speaks about himself to himself? And why did he refrain from bringing me a matter that he knew justly belonged to both of us?

Yet just as I make these complaints dutifully, so I willingly dismiss them, because it is inconsistent with my love for you to remain silent about what pains me, but it is inconsistent with friendship to exceed the measure of the pain that has been caused. Farewell.

## Letter XVII. Symmachus to Ausonius

Ambrosius, one of the leading men of the provincial court, has been sent by the commonwealth of Sicily to our lords and emperors, equipped with various instructions that seemed directed toward the public good. If you become his supporter, I think that he will obtain from his labor a reward suited to it.

I therefore ask you, either for the sake of the embassy itself or in my name, to look favorably upon this excellent man. He is sufficiently encouraged in spirit to believe that, with your support, his petitions will be advanced by the favorable outcome he seeks. Farewell.

## Letter XVIII. Symmachus to Ausonius

Even if I could celebrate your honor in uninterrupted letters, I would not seem to be performing my duty sufficiently for what the matter requires; far from reproaching you for the effort of constancy. But just as this suits my modesty, so it belongs to your courtesy to sustain our zeal with equal favor.

Notice where the main force of my words is directed. For a long time now you have contributed nothing for us to read. “The care of the praetorium,” you will say, “has wholly emancipated me for itself.” It is true. You possess the highest judgments deservedly. But great Fortune does not burden the greatest powers of your talent.

Therefore devote yourself also to those matters which, although they occupy busy men, bring them no annoyance, and which usually relieve the very annoyances themselves. Farewell.

## Letter XIX. Symmachus to Ausonius

Those who are abandoned by their own confidence take my letters as a means of recommendation. This case is different. For I gave a letter to my brother Potitus on the condition that he himself would commend it. He is no less one of the foremost among your friends than I am. Once he has made you acquainted with his presence, I fear that my excuse may not deserve forgiveness.

But if I have learned your placability through experience, I think that the outcome will be not that you reproach me, who remained behind, by comparing me with another who has come, but that you will receive him all the more warmly on behalf of us both. Farewell.

## Letter XX. Symmachus to Ausonius

I am overflowing with joy that the new year receives you as consul. But haste is now necessary. In a second letter I shall testify more fully to this congratulation upon you. For the moment I must take up another subject.

Patroinus, a man of senatorial rank, was preparing a journey at your summons and thought it would be useful to him to rely upon my testimony. I thought that nothing would be added to him through me; nevertheless, I did not wish to be absent, knowing that your judgment of him could not be increased by my writing, but that something would be taken away from my duty if I remained silent.

There is therefore one thing that I ask and entreat you to do: let him receive the favor due for the labor he has undertaken, in addition to the reward that will come to him from seeing you, meeting you, and receiving your honor. Farewell.

## Letter XXI. Symmachus to Ausonius

Wisely and well did our ancestors, as with their other institutions of that age, place the temples of Honor and Virtue together, joined with twin façades; they devised what we see in you—that the rewards of honor exist where the merits of virtue exist.

But it is on their account that the worship of the Camenae is directed toward the sacred spring, because the path to attaining magistracies is often advanced by letters. These institutions of our ancestors are the evidence of your consulship, to which the gravity of your character and the antiquity of your disciplines have brought the distinction of the curule chair.

Many men hereafter will strive after the liberal arts, genuine praise, and pure learning. Unless we are ignorant that the famous Great One, whose fortune exceeded his hopes, bestowed nothing upon his Stagirite, save that the captive cloak given as so great a gift to Quintus Ennius from Aetolian spoils disgraces Fulvius.

Indeed, neither the younger Africanus for Panaetius, nor Rutilius for Opillus, nor Pyrrhus for Cyneas, nor Mithridates of Pontus for his Metrodorus paid the price of liberal learning. But now the most learned emperor, generous in wealth and honors, has bestowed rewards upon you as though they were interest, and repays beyond the principal of the loan.

In this great joy of mine, with what words can I excuse the fact that I cannot be present? I fear greatly that, if you interpret my excuse badly, you will think my congratulations insufficient. I wished to hurry to your sight, but, exhausted in strength by the illness that has long drained me, I avoided long journeys and difficult lodgings, as well as attacks of cold, the shortening of the days, and whatever other dangers accompany such travel.

If you have regarded me favorably in your heart, I ask you to be fair to me and to judge these explanations kindly. May we perhaps obtain from you the old favor; for now, let us at least struggle free from your offense.

## Letter XXII. Symmachus to Ausonius

I am glad that I am worth more to you than the others, since you are so disposed that you voluntarily look after my interests, do not wait for requests, and follow only the report of my wishes.

I have received four travel permits, extraordinarily convenient for my excursions and returns. May the gods reward you for such great kindness; and since nothing can be added to blessings that are complete and exalted to their utmost, may they wish to keep safe and secure what they have given. Farewell.

## Letter XXIII. Symmachus to Ausonius

After your long silence, I desired longer letters from you no less than I hoped for them. For human circumstances vary in such a way that abundance follows upon deficiency. That expectation held me in vain, since a recent page, brief in length, arrived in my hands from you.

It was sprinkled with Attic wit and fragrant with thyme; but it was too sparing, more suited to wiping away disgust than to satisfying hunger. What if I had asked for sumptuous dinners, a savory banquet, servings of meat, and a feast, while you set before me only second courses and tiny delicacies on a small dish?

Let us recall what the Greek saying has to say about this. “Although,” it says, “we are defended from death by small nourishments, we nevertheless make no progress toward robust health.”

Do you think I shall remain silent about your occupations? You are quaestor, I remember; you are, I know, a participant in royal counsels; add a thousand other responsibilities to these. It has never happened that labor wears down your talent, care bends your generosity, or practical affairs exhaust your eloquence.

If you never separate your daily business from rest, surely you have not indulged in sleep before dawn, so that some time might be granted to your duties. Does the comic poet seem to provide you with too little of an example when he says: “How I wish it were customary to give attention to friends even at night!”

But why do I continue grumbling, poor in speech? I must imitate your recent letter, as I imitate the rest of your character: perhaps, being occupied, you decline longer letters. I rightly infer that this is so. For I see how unwilling you are to read much when you scarcely have leisure to dictate a little. Farewell.

## Letter XXIV. Symmachus to Ausonius

If you have a natural affection for the natural history that Pliny composed, here are some little books for you, whose immediate availability was assured. In them, as I suppose, a careless copyist will displease your wealthy learning by his neglect of accuracy. But the negligence of correction will not be attributed to me. For I preferred to please you by the speed with which I performed my own duty rather than by examining another’s work. Farewell.

## Letter XXV. Symmachus to Ausonius

[Col. 0157A]

Although the praise of children by their parents is generally truthful, it nevertheless suffers some loss of merit because people are thought to observe the favor owed to the persons involved. I therefore ask, uncertain in mind, what words I should now take up concerning Thalassius, your honorable son-in-law.

If I touch sparingly upon the adornments of his character, I shall be judged like an envious man; if I praise him justly, I shall be next-door to a flatterer. I shall therefore imitate the restraint of Sallust’s testimony.

You have a man worthy of you and, through you, of a consular family. Fortune found him greater than his father's rank through its own gifts; the refinement and integrity of his character made him equal to those honors. Farewell.

## Letter XXVI. Symmachus to Ausonius

[Col. 0157B]

I make use of the confidence you have given me. You have long been sparing of letters, but I shall not imitate your example, since I know that, for a man placed upon the watchtower of honors and therefore concerned with varied and important matters, it is not zeal that is lacking so much as opportunity.

For the nature of circumstances is such that what is neglected beyond one’s diligence is said to be deserving of forgiveness. Nevertheless, secure in your affection, as usual, I do not refuse the customary duty. I shall place it among the highest expressions of gratitude and honor if some benefit comes to my friend who will deliver this letter to you, in return for such great devotion toward us. Farewell.

## Letter XXVII. Symmachus to Ausonius

[Col. 0157C]

You ask what I am doing. Day by day I await the kind of letter that your opportunity now promises me and that your affection has always supplied.

I am happy in present circumstances, since I know that no room has been left for my attacker, and, beyond that, I am able to promise you—the thing I have always desired for you—a fortune worthy of you.

Therefore, since circumstances have brought it about that anxious matters have changed, let us receive the fruit of your desired conversation, which may enlarge my spirit and show that, after such a long intimacy, you very much desire me. Farewell.

## Letter XXVIII. Symmachus to Ausonius

You act in accordance with our mutual devotion and the long-standing character of our friendship when you affirm that your honor is within my strength. Your statement agrees with the integrity of your character, and no day will ever accuse you of being unlike such writings. May generous Fortune merely favor your hopes for prosperity.

It is prudent to say little about these matters, lest longer flatteries corrupt the dignity of truth. If you should need to know anything about me, my brother Claudius, devoted to your service and familiar with my interests, will arrange it. Farewell.

## Letter XXIX. Symmachus to Ausonius.

I take no account of the others, the ignoble mob, who counterfeit philosophy by their arrogance and dress. Our age has produced a few—and among them especially my friend Barachus—whose genuine wisdom tended toward antiquity. “Then,” you will say, “would you dare to judge philosophers?” It is permissible to contemplate the virtues of others. For even a great many people untrained in that art admired Phidias’ Olympian Jupiter, Myron’s little cow, and Polyclitus’ Canephorae. The nature of understanding is more generously accessible. Otherwise, splendid works would be approved by very few, if the perception of every good thing did not reach even those unequal to it. Grant me, then, the role of witness concerning Barachus, and embrace the friendship of a prudent man. His examination will soon make you believe me equally readily about everything I know, since you will see that I am not false even in what I do not know. Farewell.

## LETTER XXX. SYMMACHUS TO AUSONIUS

Here you have a rustic scarcely released from urban business; for the sake of our friendship, I wish you to forgive him the fault of delay. It was not avoidance of work that granted me leisure. It is difficult to leave once you have come; indeed, if you wish to contemplate the majesty of our city, you will think you have returned sooner than was proper. But I am not troubled about this, since among your other virtues you possess so accommodating a disposition that you take minor errors in good part. This, however, it is fitting to request more earnestly: let your care in writing to me be as great as the affection with which you honor me. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXI. SYMMACHUS TO AUSONIUS

The writings of your learning gave me sheer joy; I received them while stationed at Capua. In them was a festivity steeped in Ciceronian honey, and praise of my speech that was not so much true as flattering. What, then, should I admire more? Uncertain of my judgment, I hesitate between the adornments of your speech and those of your heart. For you surpass all others in eloquence so completely that one is afraid to write back; yet you approve my efforts so kindly that I want not to remain silent.

If I praise you further, I shall seem to scratch each other’s backs, and to be more an imitator of your address than an examiner of it. Moreover, since you yourself do nothing for the sake of display, it is to be feared that I may praise as affected the qualities that are genuine in you. Yet learn this from me with unquestionable truth: there is no mortal whom I love before you; you have held me bound by honorable affection.

But in one respect you seem excessively bashful to me: you accuse your little book of betraying you. It is easier to suppress glowing embers with one’s mouth than to keep secret a brilliant work. Once a poem has proceeded from you, you have surrendered every right over it. A published speech is a free thing. Are you afraid of the venom of a hostile reader, lest your little book be consumed by the bite of a harsh tooth? For you alone, neither favor has bestowed nor envy taken anything away in this matter. You are praiseworthy in the eyes of every severe and upright judge.

Therefore, henceforth shut out these empty fears and indulge your pen, so that you may often be betrayed. At any rate, assign some didactic or exhortatory poem to my name as well. Put my silence to the test. Although I hope to demonstrate it to you, I do not dare promise it. I know the itch to release a work that has won approval. In a certain way, the first person to proclaim another’s well-spoken words claims a share in the praise.

For that reason, in comedies the writers carried off the highest glory; nevertheless, fame did not fail Roscius, Ambivius, and the other actors. So devote your leisure to such a task, and sustain our hunger with new volumes. But if, wary of boasting, you fear a talkative herald, grant me silence as well, so that I may safely pretend that what you write is ours. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXII. AUSONIUS TO SYMMACHUS

Only now do I understand how honeyed a speech can be, how soothing, and how persuasive its eloquence. You persuaded me that the composition of my letter, which was delivered to you at Capua, was not uncouth. But this lasted no longer than the time in which I read your page, which leads me on, gaping at its flatteries, as though smeared with the juice of nectar.

For when I put the little sheet aside and question myself, it then gives off pure wormwood, and I discover cups smeared with honey. But if, as I often do, I return to your letter, I am again enticed; and that most sweet, that flower-laden breath of your speech vanishes as soon as the reading is laid down, while the weight of the evidence prevents sweetness from being present in it.

This delights me no longer than the glittering veneer of bronze foil, or a painted mist, lasts while it is visible; like the little chameleon, which takes its color from the objects beneath it. I experience one thing from your letter and another from my conscience. And you dare to honor me with the praise of the most eloquent men? You, I say, offer me these words—you who have placed yourself beyond the correction of all. No one shines so brightly that, when compared with you, he does not look filthy.

Who approaches the charm of Aesop, the sophistical conclusions of Socrates, the enthymemes of Demosthenes, the richness of Cicero, or the precision of our Maro? Who so embraces each individual quality that you fill them all? For what else are you than a perfection gathered from every talent of the liberal arts?

My lord, my son Symmachus, I do not fear that these words about you may seem more flattering than true. You tested the honesty of my mind and words when we both lived in the imperial entourage, though of different ages: there you earned, as a recruit, the rewards of old military service, while I, already a veteran, served my apprenticeship. In the entourage I was truthful with you; you should not suppose that, abroad, I compose fables.

In the entourage, I say—that place which opens men’s faces and conceals their minds—you recognized that I was dearer to you than a father, than a friend, and, if anything is dearer than either, dearer than that as well. But let us leave this, lest the recollection seem to approach that fear of Sosia.

What almost escaped notice was the feeling with which you added the request that I send some didactic work or exhortatory discourse. Am I to teach you, when I still need to be taught, if I were of an age to learn? Or am I to stir you, vigorous and alert as you are? By the same effort I would urge the Muses to sing, the seas to pour forth, the breezes to carry, and the fires to burn; and if anything occurs by nature even against our will, I would uselessly spur it on.

One error is enough: that one of my works was published against my will and, by good fortune, fell into the hands of friends. For if the result had been otherwise, you could not have persuaded me that I could please anyone.

Let this be my reply to your letter. I shall summarize the other matters you wish to know; the letter is already long enough. If you think there is anything to ask about us, I commend to you Julianus, a friend of our household. At the same time I ask you, once you have learned the reason for his arrival, to assist the enterprise that you have partly encouraged. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO AUSONIUS

They say that when snails thirst in the dry air and nothing flows down to them from heaven, they live on their own juice. The same has happened to me: deprived of nourishment from your eloquence, I am still sustaining myself on my own dew.

You have deferred the task of writing for a long time, and I fear that perhaps a parent’s affection is closing against us. If my supposition is false, see to it that the care of answering your other affairs takes precedence. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO AUSONIUS

I am engaged in a laborious business, since I persist in addressing you so often while you remain silent. Yet unless I continue pressing you and carving something of a letter out of you, forgetfulness will grow. Whether, then, you judge this diligence of mine dutiful or troublesome, my decision stands: to make its honor renowned through conversation. For there has been no departure from my old love for you.

And rightly so, since nowhere have I devoted myself to friendship with equal success. Therefore I complain of your silence. A more tender affection makes complaint more ready. The spirit of one who cares is soft and sharp to every sensation of pain. If you handle it too carelessly, it quickly withers like a rose; if you hold it too harshly, it is bruised like lilies.

I remember reading that even a facial expression can often injure filial devotion. What would that very strict judge have decided about continuous silence and a deliberately withheld duty of writing? You will weigh this more carefully yourself.

For my part, I made it a scruple to conceal what caused me pain. For just as I remain wholly dependent on your goodwill, so I eagerly await the benefit of your complete devotion. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXV. SYMMACHUS TO AUSONIUS

I spent a long time at leisure in the retreats of Campania and therefore lacked an opportunity for writing. That is why, for a little while, the service of my speech toward you grew cold. But once I set foot again in my homeland, my former diligence in renewing my duty returned.

I therefore offer you the honor due in a greeting, asking both that proper pardon be granted for my earlier silence and that my present attentiveness receive a reciprocal response. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVI. SYMMACHUS TO AUSONIUS

I interrupt your occupations with the constancy of my conversation. I myself am nourished by such a service, and I believe that your journey is refreshed by consolations of this kind. In return I await your letters; I do not demand them. For it is unjust to insist vehemently upon what one hopes for, lest what is voluntary appear extorted.

I certainly congratulate my brother Innocentius that he obtained your friendship before I wrote, since it has become easier for me to commend someone whom you have approved than someone unknown to you. Thus I ask only this favor: that the man who now relies upon his own improvement may be loved all the more for the sake of my testimonial. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVII. SYMMACHUS TO AUSONIUS

They do not praise it without reason: human minds shine in clear weather and grow weak beneath a gathered cloud. My own spirit confirms this by example. For whenever I write to you, a supply of suitable words is available to me, although at other times I lack such a store.

Joy is a talkative thing and displays itself; indeed, there is no precaution against this illness for a large part of humanity. Therefore allow me, most distinguished of all men on earth, to speak at length about what concerns your praises: you exert yourself, from the greatest resources, to watch over my interests, and you persist in friendship with steadfast diligence.

If anyone has been sincerely faithful, I think it is you. Most people display such faithfulness in words but abandon it in deeds; that sort of faithfulness is useful for nothing except talking. I rightly count your advances toward me as a debt upon my account, since I am, and have always been, a matter of great concern to you.

Yet there is something I would like added to this devotion of yours. I do not want you to remember that I once became angry with you. Love nourishes confidence. What is as free as friendship? In the midst of affairs, reproach is generally attached to it without damaging harmony.

Thus it is true that, although I thank you today, I could not conceal what grieved me. Those who flatter continually are empty of trust. But why should I continue uncovering what I want you to forget? Remain toward me as you are, with kindly goodwill; I feel that this is something I should expect from you rather than request. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO AUSONIUS

It is falsely believed that Fortune is ignorant of judgment. In fact, mindful of the past, attentive to the present, and prudent concerning the future, she repays you whatever she has granted to others. She is therefore neither empty nor erratic. Through her, we know that others have received a household as a beginning, while you have received a reward.

“Who,” you will ask, “gave you an indication of our honor?” The renown of fame, which is immediately believed when it reports what is just. Should I have waited for your letter about this, delayed by bashfulness? Not at all, since the heart finds it difficult to be patient with joys.

Thus, as you see, I perform your part, and I have preferred in some fashion to announce what I ought to have learned. But I do not want this haste of my letter to obstruct your service. Pretend not to know what I am now writing, and treat it as a new message, which I shall be glad to hear repeated. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIX. SYMMACHUS TO AUSONIUS

I know that my letters will be delivered to you late, either because of the occupations that will keep you for a while on active duty, or because my brother Gorgonius, an admirer of your virtues, will indulge in a prolonged rest among the Picentes. Whatever the circumstances may be, I did not think that my duty should be set aside.

Perhaps these written words will happen to reach your hands promptly. Nevertheless, insofar as travelers permit, I shall not fail to perform the service of a proper obligation. Farewell.

## LETTER XL. SYMMACHUS TO AUSONIUS

I readily commend to you my friend Sanctus Victor—not as someone new or unknown, but as one already tested by the fidelity and diligence of military service. To this point in his life no fault in his conduct has tarnished him; only the license of Fortune, which sometimes discolors even the best, has for a little while weakened his hopes. The blessedness of the age will restore them completely if you look favorably upon the innocence of this petitioner. Farewell.

## LETTER XLI. SYMMACHUS TO AUSONIUS

I am doing something consistent both with your character and with my own devotion: I am winning the friendship of the best men for a man of outstanding merit. Thus I now deliver to you a candidate for philosophy. His modesty will be evident at first sight; long acquaintance will reveal his other virtues.

I would not want you to love him unless he deserved approval. But if I judge correctly, he will deserve it very soon, and therefore I ask nothing more about him. For he ought not to be bound by my prior judgment, since I await yours.

This, rather, I wish to ask you: continue your diligence toward our man. In making this request, I fear you may think me unjust for asking from you what you are going to grant spontaneously. Farewell.

## LETTER XLII. SYMMACHUS TO AUSONIUS

You compensated for your long silence with a double letter. You gave me two letters at once, embracing my longing with a more generous service. From this I perceived that until now you had lacked not the will but the messenger. Otherwise you could not have deprived me so long of the honor of your conversation.

With good reason, our respect for you increases day by day, and our affection grows by a proper increase. For we see that friendship well placed advances through experience each day. But this aspect should be left without words. I ought not to say what I prefer you to feel.

I have learned from your letters how greatly you desire to be released from your public office, and I confess that I am astonished that you have such distaste for an administration whose favorable fruits are promised by the love of everyone. Is anything more enduring than glory, which adds praise to pleasure? Nevertheless, care will not be lacking to enable you to obtain it. You, for your part, should console your journey with a proper love of the province. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIII. SYMMACHUS TO AUSONIUS

There is an old saying: “Arts are nourished by honor.” The experience of our age has confirmed it. No one known in war or distinguished at home has found his industry deprived of reward. Thus, when fruits are granted to the deserving, hope is prepared for those who follow the same path.

I therefore swell with joy both on behalf of others, whose active lives win them Fortune, and especially on behalf of my brother Julianus, whom I want you to love and whom I trust you will find worthy of approval.

You know, surely, how rare in the dust of the law courts is the union of eloquence and a good heart: either modest talent is cramped by bashfulness, or eloquence grows arrogant through success. In my friend and associate these qualities flourished together in such a way that he neither withered from excessive modesty nor overflowed to the detriment of his bearing. He never corrupted the adornments of his tongue for the sake of reward. Poor in possessions and fortune, he exchanged wealth for integrity and profit for praise.

I gladly place him in your hands—or rather, in your heart. My chief concern is that good men may enrich your friendship. I know that you want the same. Nature always rejoices in equals, and everything similar is familiar to it.

But lest I incur the suspicion of a flatterer through an overlong testimonial, I ask you to judge him yourself by a more careful examination. Once you approve his character, you will have put my judgment to the test. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIV. SYMMACHUS TO AGORIUS PRAETEXTATUS

Your indulgence toward me deserves that I not allow the matters that recently brought me praise to remain hidden from you. I believe that rumor has informed you that, when my father was wearing away the wrong done to his ruined household in the countryside and retirement, the Senate summoned him by frequent votes and finally by sending deputations, honoring him with a new distinction.

As soon as the day first brought him the opportunity to speak before his colleagues, he thanked the Senate in the weighty style of eloquence for which he is known. It was then the Kalends, with which the year begins. Shortly afterward, when I had promised to undertake the advocacy of the son of my friend Trigetius, a candidate for the praetorship, I felt it a religious obligation to discharge, on the occasion of the duty already assigned, a task that I still owed my father—although, as I said, he had already discharged it toward the Senate.

Accordingly, on the fifth day before the Ides of January, I spoke in the most august order. When those words reach your hands, you will infer from your own judgment what the judgments of the others were. Since your examination remains uncertain to me, I thought the opinions of the others should be concealed, lest I seem to pressure you through the prior judgment of so great an order. Farewell.

## LETTER XLV. SYMMACHUS TO AGORIUS PRAETEXTATUS

I have been greatly rejoiced that your health has returned with you into favor. For your safety has always been the chief object of my prayers. Now, if—by the will of the gods—the restoration of your strength has renewed the vigor of your spirit, see to it that your letter is enlarged by many pages.

I hate the parsimony of good words. Brevity in writing is closer to disdain than to duty. I do not want letters dripping from the very edge of your mouth. I ask for those that cannot dry up, those drawn from the innermost spring of your heart.

I remember that Spartan brevity was once considered praiseworthy. But with you I deal according to Roman rules—or, if you prefer, Attic ones—for the Athenians drew such distinction from eloquence that it seems to me the Lacedaemonians assigned their pursuits in the opposite direction out of fear of comparison.

I would like more, but I must prick you in your own manner. At the same time, I must be careful lest too much speech offend you. I therefore bring my practice to an end while obeying yours. From this you understand that I have brought you to such a condition of envy and obligation that you will seem to want me to write little unless you write much in reply. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVI. SYMMACHUS TO AGORIUS PRAETEXTATUS

I could have written a shorter letter, since your brother seemed likely to satisfy you more fully in his own words than I in mine. But honorable duties should be placed among our greater gains, and much leisure among our lesser ones.

Therefore, it is neither necessary for me to remain silent so that the honor of friendship may be credited to me, nor have all matters been entrusted to writing, so that something may remain for him to narrate. Nevertheless, receive the main points and the outlines of the business, so that, once reminded, your brother may explain what was sought in greater detail.

It was agreed among the priests that we should entrust the care of the gods to the custody of the citizens through public service. For the favor of a superior power is lost unless it is maintained by worship. Thus the heavenly honor has been made much more splendid than usual.

You seem to be waiting for everything that remains. My Titianus will serve as your informant; he has been assigned the task of narrating whatever you wish with greater indulgence. If the edict of the emperors is not already known to you, he will explain it as well.

You have also recovered the statues, almost with the same acclamations of the people with which you had lost them. Are you laughing? You may laugh as much as you please. I shall say no more, lest, after briefly revealing the better matters, I seem to linger over the lesser ones. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVII. SYMMACHUS TO AGORIUS PRAETEXTATUS

The explanation for our silence is different, but the result is the same. I am hindered by the care of priestly office; you by the indolence of Baian leisure. Relaxation of spirit makes a person no less inactive than occupation does.

Nor is it surprising if that region claims you wholly for itself, since it is reliably believed that even Hannibal, unconquered in war, surrendered his hands to Campania. Its allure of climate and soil has not been equaled by the Lotos that clings to visitors, Circe’s persuasive cups, or the half-winged girls at the dining couch.

I do not insist that you are spending your holidays in gluttony, nor do I think that you have weakened your virtue through luxury. But while you read for yourself, write for yourself, and, weary of urban affairs, tame your great spirit in solitude, you perform none of the duties of friendship.

Why not seize your pen and pay a reciprocal honor to the affection we feel for you? Unless you prefer to test the authority of the pontiff. We have many matters to deliberate in the college. Who granted you this suspension of public service? You will experience the priest’s right unless you fulfill the friend’s right. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVIII. SYMMACHUS TO AGORIUS PRAETEXTATUS

Good gods, how nothing is safe or certain for human beings! Certainly you had gone to Baiae to lighten your spirit. What eye has bewitched the rest you had planned? Had the shared anxiety over Paulina, then, reached a crisis threatening her life? Or is your fear for her so great that every discomfort of hers is regarded as the equivalent of danger?

Whatever the case, one may imagine what anxieties of day and watches of night you have endured. We are born in such a way that we more often undergo adversity. Pleasures flee, and the enjoyment of every good thing is as brief as its sensation is light. But let these matters be left to the disputations of philosophers.

For now let us encourage a more cheerful state of mind, since the peace of the gods has restored the health of our Paulina to firm ground. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIX. SYMMACHUS TO AGORIUS PRAETEXTATUS

As a citizen born for the common good, you ask what most nearly resembles the truth in the reports concerning these anxious matters. We learned of favorable developments from reliable indications. Thereafter, the suspicion generated by a long silence gave way to anxious rumors.

But I have no concern for opinions of this kind, which circulate without an author. I am deeply distressed that, despite repeated sacrifices and frequent renewals before each authority, the portent at Spoletium has not yet been atoned for in the name of the state.

For Jupiter was scarcely appeased by the eighth slaughter, and the eleventh honor paid to Public Fortune with many kinds of victims was offered in vain. You understand the position in which we are. For now I have decided to summon my colleagues to a meeting. I shall make sure that you learn whether the divine remedies have advanced our cause. Farewell.

## LETTER L. SYMMACHUS TO AGORIUS PRAETEXTATUS

For my part, secure in our friendship and willing to make allowances, I overlook any fault committed against me by someone who loves me. But it is fitting that your character, which lacks nothing for praise, should be deficient in the diligence of duty.

You think that I am complaining because you write nothing, and you prepare to refute the falsehood because you remember having written something. I would be only minimally distressed if you were silent in the way you have been, since you delivered to me and my father one single letter, and that extremely brief.

So we both seem to you worthy of a single page? “It was in your honor,” you will say, “that you were joined with my father.” There are other things that I wish to share with him, or to equal him in. Let love be offered to me in my own name.

Therefore refrain from letters that are like an edict. Let all disdain depart, the source of this concern for brevity. But it is prudent not to speak too long about this, lest the length of my complaint prove more troublesome to you than the shortness of your letter has been to me.

For the rest, I ask the gods that you return to visit us as soon as possible, bringing us full joy. It will be easy to repay the narrowness of your writings with a flood of words. Farewell.

## LETTER LI. SYMMACHUS TO AGORIUS PRAETEXTATUS

We had decided to remain abroad a little longer, but news of our tottering homeland changed our plans, since, amid all these evils, my security seemed discolored. In addition, the administration of the sacred pontificate demands my care and the service required in the appointed month.

My spirit cannot bear, amid such negligence on the part of the priests, to appoint a substitute colleague. Once this may have been a simple delegation of divine affairs. Now, for Romans to be absent from the altars is a kind of canvassing.

How long will Etruria retain you? We already complain that there is something that is being preferred to the citizens for so long. Even if the condition of the countryside is more agreeable, no one can properly enjoy leisure who fears for his absent countrymen. Farewell.

## LETTER LII. SYMMACHUS TO AGORIUS PRAETEXTATUS

I rejoice no less that you approved my speech than that the better part of the human race—the Senate—heard it with favorable esteem. You added the weight of an oath and swore your assent, knowing that the judgments of friends are suspected of partiality. For where friendship is certain, the credibility of praise is less certain.

Therefore, confident in your examination, I pay no attention to the opinions of the others. If you had been present as a listener of such goodwill, I would truly have touched the vault of heaven with my finger, as the saying goes. Perhaps on another occasion we shall have a more welcome opportunity for your presence. For now we enjoy the testimony of your letter; then we shall use the assistance of your favor. Farewell.

## LETTER LIII. SYMMACHUS TO AGORIUS PRAETEXTATUS

You boast of leisure and hunting. This is indeed a pleasant boast, but it was put forward by you more in play than in earnest. For you gladly spend your periods of relaxation and freedom from public business in turning over the books of the ancients.

So you may offer that story to others who did not know you at first meeting. I know the activities to which you devote yourself day and night, and I infer your daily nourishment of intellect from the flavor of the literature you give me.

Unless, perhaps, you have continued with Apollo in the woods, like that Hesiodic shepherd whom the Muses’ family crowned with poetic laurel. For where does this novelty of ideas and antiquity of words in your letters come from, if you are so devoted to knotted nets, feathered scares, keen dogs, and all the business of hunting that you have forgotten better pursuits?

Therefore, when you write, remember to set a limit to your eloquence. Let what you say be rustic and uncultivated, so that you may be believed to be a hunter. Farewell.

## LETTER LIV. SYMMACHUS TO AGORIUS PRAETEXTATUS

You have given great consolation to my grief. As rumor informed you some time ago, wounded by my brother’s death, I am continually tormented by anguish of spirit. Yet amid my present cares I received no slight relief when I learned that you are well, in accordance with our common wishes.

It remains for you to deem such services worthy of frequent attention; you perceive that they bring a kind of medicine to misfortune and mourning. Farewell.

## LETTER LV. SYMMACHUS TO AGORIUS PRAETEXTATUS

I know that what you advise proceeds from brotherly love. But reconciliation requires as its author the person who was the leader in the unjust disagreement, lest he seem to have deserved no blame who, as though he had suffered nothing, seeks to renew friendships he had renounced.

Therefore I do not reject the harmony you offer. Setting Fortune’s circumstances aside, let the person who caused the offense return to friendship. For the sake of our friendship I congratulate you sufficiently; your labor will benefit the public welfare, about which I shall speak more sparingly for now.

For a matter that concerns everyone is never satisfied with a single witness, and it is especially fitting for me to remember your glory in such a way that I not seem to have forgotten your modesty. Farewell.

## LETTER LVI. SYMMACHUS TO PROBUS

Since you are occupied with public business, brief letters lessen the tedium of reading; and the constancy of my duty has exhausted whatever seemed necessary to write. After offering a modest greeting, I necessarily compress this economical letter into brevity.

A declaration of love is one thing, a display of language another; therefore the work of serving you has always been older in my eyes than the work of speaking. We shall seem abundant if we are judged sufficiently diligent. Farewell.

## LETTER LVII. SYMMACHUS TO PROBUS

At present I offer as much as seemed sufficient for honoring our friendship, taking into consideration both your occupations and the haste of the messenger. On another occasion I shall lack neither the use of pardon nor the care required for a longer letter.

May the gods favor our wishes and establish the safety of the state on firm ground! Then my willingness will be more ready both to write what you will gladly receive and to read what you will write back in a mind free from care. Farewell.

## LETTER LVIII. SYMMACHUS TO PROBUS

Keep a fair and patient spirit toward the duty imposed upon you. It often happens that proven virtue is restored to renewed labors.

What of you? Do you think what happened to Gaius Atilius was pleasant—that he exchanged the fasces for the plow and, in the middle of sowing, made the panting oxen stop, like a farmer? Whoever is a man of good character is claimed for the public advantage.

For the moment, put aside those thoughts of your happy leisure. How beautifully I was raising urban works with new gables! Where is our field—that one so fertile in every abundance in autumn, or that one sunny in winter? Or the one that strips the first roses from the earth in spring, or the one that cools itself from grove and spring beneath the summer sun?

But why have I wandered from my subject? While treating your complaints, I have voluntarily suggested things to be missed. Remain as you are, enduring every care, and discharge the service owed to the emperors, who took account more of your merit than of your wishes. Farewell.

## LETTER LIX. SYMMACHUS TO PROBUS

You advise that we cultivate the good of friendship through frequent writing. I approve this exhortation, which invites devotion. And, to speak truthfully, your willingness is an honor to me; for great love demands more.

But when you say that I, being free from public affairs, ought rather to undertake this vigilance, I disagree that it is fair. First, as a man enjoying unrestricted leisure, I do not labor to investigate the movements of messengers; your dignity finds a conveyance for letters unless it creates one.

Furthermore, inactive disuse dulls my talent, while long practice has eased for you the task of speaking. Therefore, the greater your opportunity to write, the more deserving I am of pardon for rarity. Do I seem sufficiently defended by these arguments for the future? I want you to remember that whatever conversation you receive from me is a service, not leisure. Farewell.

## LETTER LX. SYMMACHUS TO PROBUS

I know that you choose men not for their fortunes but for their merits. My friend Romanus still performs courtly duties, as befits an administrator of the sacred treasury. But he has cultivated the instruments of integrity in the exercise of honor.

Therefore that dignity is shared indiscriminately with many, while honesty is equal only with a few. I thought this should be mentioned so that you too may judge him according to his way of life, not according to his military rank.

Put him to the test in the greatest affairs; test him in serious or relaxed circumstances. You will find in him concealed fidelity, open religious devotion, independent prudence, and unservile modesty. I therefore want this to have happened for him, so that the credibility of my testimony may shine forth and a friend of refined integrity may come to you. Farewell.

## LETTER LXI. SYMMACHUS TO PROBUS

You say that you are hindered by many necessities from addressing the dearest of your friends with energy. Let the assertion of a familiar fact cease. For even though we are far away, we feel your cares and vigils through the resources and abundance of our common homeland.

You have therefore changed your duty, not denied it. For it was older for you—and as it should have been—to secure the safety of the citizens than to offer a greeting.

Now, certainly, we both desire and demand your letters, richly stored grain for the expenditure of the coming winter, although I know that this part of the future still does not seem entirely safe to you. Love of country is never secure; however many remedies it seeks, it always thinks that what it feared is about to happen. Farewell.

## LETTER LXII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER CELSINUS TICIANUS

Full of good hope, after you gave me word of your arrival, I add a kind of spur to those who are hastening. For this purpose I appeal to your service: hasten your parents’ efforts by encouraging them. The memory of your benefit will remain with me and will never be silent, if you take care of what has been entrusted to you by your brothers. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER CELSINUS TICIANUS

Let words speak at length when they are being offered on behalf of strangers or outsiders. For me, this service should end when our common brother Saturus receives our letters, which I have sent not as a commendation of him but as an expression of our love toward you. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIV. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER CELSINUS TICIANUS

You may perhaps be surprised that I am commending a bishop to you. The circumstance, not the sect, persuaded me to do this. For Clemens, having performed the duty of a good man, protected Caesarea, his homeland, after securing for it the peace of the greatest rulers.

You had heard by report how much private or public, sacred or profane gold and silver of Mauretania was torn apart by the plundering of the enemy during the barbarian rebellion. It happened at that time that even the fisc’s deposit was seized under the law of war; the leading men of the city, whom flight had left behind, were demanding the treasury’s legal due.

It was a miserable and bitter situation—unless the sadness of the times had moved Clemens to care. I would say that he contributed no less to the reputation of the age than to the safety of the citizens. For what would the treasury gain, apart from unpopularity, if it demanded resources from an impoverished curia?

You have the sequence of events. For what remains, strive to make the breath of your influence fill the sails of their petitions. Farewell.

## LETTER LXV. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER CELSINUS TICIANUS

You ask what we think about those who provoke us. Do not expect the counsel of an angry man. Do not labor to worsen the case of one whom you see already abounding in faults. He himself will provide grounds on which you may not seem to have wished for them. But I have said enough about him.

I turn to what affection leads me to say. You are extraordinarily idle in writing, and you are not afraid that we may bite you on account of your silence. What will winter do, when it delays travel by land and sea? Consider the necessity of your duty and the reciprocal nature of our concern, and seize the diligence that you demand from us in return. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVI. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER CELSINUS TICIANUS

Gelasius, for whom I wish this to have occurred, has taken charge of the imperial household. The office has brought him some distinction, although his character possesses even more honor. He practiced medicine among the foremost men of our age. From this he made a path toward further merits.

For the leading men of the court, whom he had benefited by restoring their health, served as witnesses rather than patrons. May it never happen that you need his medical skill, since the other honors of so holy a man can speak in his favor. Therefore love Gelasius, who has long been pleasing to me and, with me as your guarantor, will please you. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER CELSINUS TICIANUS

I would commend Anysius to you, an admirable man, if he had not entered into my friendship with you as his sponsor. Since, then, my speech can gain nothing for him, I count it a benefit if the affection of your holy spirit grows toward him.

For once the beginnings of love have been anticipated, there remains room for a second favor, so that further increases may be requested. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER CELSINUS TICIANUS
Source/review notes: Raw Terra review retained as complete=false solely for omitted inline anchors. Each anchor was traced by its source epistle to the corresponding English epistle body; mapping is preserved in `native-anchor-mapping.json`.

[Col. 0169C] Rufus, the pontifical treasurer, is pursuing with you the instructions of the college to which, above all others, the responsibility for retaining the Vaganian forest has been entrusted. I ask you to arrange matters so that the assistance of your rank may appear divinely offered, and remember that you are the chief of both priestly offices. Whatever the public authority or private initiative requires, carry it out when requested. The public interest will advance greatly through your favor. You have the substance of my petition. The individual details will either be set out for you in the series of reminders or explained by Rufus; grant him a prompt result, so that, after his temporary detachment, he may resume his office. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIX. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER CELSINUS TICIANUS

[Col. 0169D] My brother Acutianus could have obtained in his own name what he requests, since he is no less familiar to you than to me. Yet it was part of my duty to offer him my voluntary assistance. His desire is also supported by the justice of his petition. For he asks that his brothers, Nichasius and Rogatianus, who are attending to a joint matter, either be referred for adjudication to the governor of Numidia or—what he values more highly—that you, above all, serve as their judge and release them as soon as possible from the burden of litigation. Therefore, if his standing with you is considerable, if his case does not conflict with the laws, and if my intervention inclines the balance of your favor, it is only right to strive that the wish of an excellent man should proceed according to his desire. Farewell.

## LETTER LXX. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER CELSINUS TICIANUS

[Col. 0170A] The petition of our brothers Romanus and Magnillus is just, and I have undertaken to pursue it. They are deeply concerned that the people of the most distinguished woman Euticia should be supported by the protection of the judges. You understand that these are persons to whom this favor should be owed more to their own merit than to my letters. Nor should you be surprised that they themselves did not write concerning the matter, since their respect for me caused them to make use of our recommendation instead. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXI. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER CELSINUS TICIANUS

[Col. 0170B] My undertaking commends Caecilianus, an honorable man who has undertaken the defense of Laurentius of Lavinium. Even if the other distinctions of his life afforded him no means of winning your favor, my intervention ought to secure it for him. Therefore, love a man who is pleasing to me and who conscientiously serves the interests of the city. We shall take your affection as demonstrated if you assist those to whom he has entrusted a family matter. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER CELSINUS TICIANUS

We do not refuse to serve the wishes of friends, so long as we believe what they request to be just—as has now happened in my case. I did not think that Bassus, esteemed by the best men, should be abandoned without my support. Thus, while preserving my own reputation for having trusted good men, a longer passage of time will reveal to you the man’s merit. It is enough for me if his first approach gives him fuller hope. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER CELSINUS TICIANUS

[Col. 0170C] Since the gods have granted you the power to be useful to my friends and intimates, I trust that an ample supply of good hope is ready for the excellent man Romanus, with whom I have long been intimate, through your protection. He is supported by two recommendations, both of which you have long been accustomed to value: the precedence of my testimony and the consciousness of his own merit. For I confidently dare to judge him worthy of your esteem and, to put it briefly, worthy of an acquaintance whose friendship you would not find burdensome. I have observed in him peace of mind and diligence in duty. No one makes use of trust among friends more readily. If you grant any weight to me, I ask you to believe that these things are so. If your mind hesitates, I urge you to examine him. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO AGORIUS PRAETEXTATUS

[Col. 0170D] There is some substance in the complaints of my daughter Fasgamia, which, I confess, has turned out for me as I wished. For unless she had asked for letters that might later be useful to her, there would have been no occasion for me to write. I therefore offer first the greeting that concerns my duty. The rest of the page will concern the case of a most distinguished woman, who complains that some lands have been taken from her by your men. Conscious of your position and merit, I believe that this was done behind your back, with servile audacity; and for that reason I promised my daughter an easy correction, if a private complaint had conveyed to you this kind of injury. I therefore ask you to order the condition of the violated possession to be restored. If there is any dispute, let it be postponed until the presence of our pledge, who, confident in your justice, refuses other judges. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXV. SYMMACHUS TO HESPERIUS

[Col. 0171A] Whenever testimonials are delivered on behalf of men distinguished in military service, it is fitting to make one’s words concise, since there is no need to linger over matters already known. You know that everything done for Caesarius meets with approval. I ought to hope, rather than ask, that you will hold him in esteem. If you seek anything further, we shall include it in another letter. For now I must restrain my verbosity, since it appears that satisfaction has been given both to his wishes, your honor, and my duty. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVI. SYMMACHUS TO HESPERIUS

[Col. 0171B] It is the nature of things that those who stammer speak more; they affect abundance out of embarrassment at their deficiency. This example applies to me, who have great impatience to write although I lack eloquence. Since two men were traveling together, I did not think it consistent with duty that one letter should deal with two opportunities at once. Your judgment will determine whether I should more properly be called talkative or diligent. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVII. SYMMACHUS TO HESPERIUS

[Col. 0171C] To attend to the requests of friends is a service of good character, especially when justice does not oppose their petitions. I shall briefly explain the purpose of this preface. I praise Sabinianus, a most distinguished man, as I praise those whom I honor most highly. I cannot tolerate that, through pressure, the responsibility of guardianship over his brother’s children should be imposed upon him. Two privileges remove the injustice: his advanced age and the number of his children. Although this matter has been recorded in public documents, the stubborn petition still does not withdraw from its declared persistence. Now, since hope in this matter rests upon favorable fortune, I ask you, by the excellence in which you are eminent, to wish the deed done for him; for the favor ought to be granted either to oblige me or to preserve the precedence of law for your own glory. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO HESPERIUS

[Col. 0171D] You alone still surpass the leading men of letters; and I, who am jealous of praise, would wish my eloquence to win your approval. The matter has turned out as I desired: I have the witness I wanted. Now I must exclaim in the voice of the comic youth: “Who is more fortunate than I today, and indeed more full of charm?” Unless, perhaps, your affection for me has compelled your style to show me favor. It often happens that affection softens the severity of judgment, and that we assess the deeds and words of friends with the indulgence with which individuals generally love even their own faults.

But these things would properly be said if the opinion of the best men, who heard my speech, did not support you. This is not because the authority of your judgment needs the agreement of others, but because a judgment from which no one dissents is not open to suspicion. Yet I shall see whether faithfulness or affection wrote that letter. In either case my honor is equally supreme: whether you judge of me so magnificently that you seem to have wished to oblige me, or whether you are so devoted to me that you cannot judge otherwise. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIX. SYMMACHUS TO HESPERIUS

[Col. 0172A] [Col. 0172B] You know, whether by assumption or by experience, how long I have valued your reputation. For that reason I cannot allow anything to happen that would diminish the grace of your actions. My brother Priscianus, who must be reckoned among the foremost in philosophical learning and character, receives the benefits of a salary with the authorization of the senate. A dispute is said to have arisen concerning his allowances. If the goodwill of the best men had previously granted him no advantage, your learning ought to bear fruit for him. For you know that the liberal arts are nourished by honor, and that it is a mark of a flourishing state that rich rewards are paid to professors of the disciplines.

I therefore ask that neither his benefit be diminished by this disturbance nor the authority of the most distinguished order to make its assessment be impaired. It concerns your reputation and glory that you should appear to have questioned the philosopher’s salary in order to confirm rather than deny the benefit. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXX. SYMMACHUS TO HESPERIUS

Here are my second letters to you, while reciprocity is still owed to the first. You may say that the business of travel long hindered your writing, and perhaps you will offer many other excuses. Out of affection for you, I shall not find this pardon burdensome. But out of that same affection I ask that, when you have leisure, the delay of compelled silence be made good by the voluntary performance of duty. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXI. SYMMACHUS TO HESPERIUS

[Col. 0172C] I believe that the most distinguished man Vitalianus asked for my letters more out of regard for my duty than for his own assistance. For since nothing further could be added to win your affection for him personally, he seems to have done only this: to make my service produce a richer reconciliation with you. Accept, therefore, this greeting hastily plucked. If you answer it with greater eloquence, you will expose the meagerness of my talent as an example of your abundance. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXII. SYMMACHUS TO HESPERIUS

[Col. 0172D] I am exceedingly impatient of your silence, which is a form of complaint familiar to those who love. Yet I confess that my desire has been fulfilled by your most recent letter. I therefore thank you and earnestly beg you to indulge frequently in writing. These alone among services never produce weariness through repetition. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO HESPERIUS

It is a sign of devotion that you reproach me for my silence. But I ask you to believe that it was misfortune, not intention, that kept me for so long from the duty of writing. Nor do I think you are unaware of the extent to which fortune has raged against us, since it deprived me of a brother most loving and excellent. Therefore, if the passage of time has taken away something of the feeling of such great grief, customary care will be shown through familiar letters. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO HESPERIUS

[Col. 0173A] Whenever I take up conversations with you, a kind of image of your presence passes before my eyes. For that reason I take greater pleasure in them, since I feel that both the monument of your duty and the evidence of my merit remain vigorous. But so that the diligence of this service toward me may continue more readily, I too have undertaken the care of sending conversation, having often discovered that affection is stirred by the incentive of reciprocal exchange. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXV. SYMMACHUS TO HESPERIUS

[Col. 0173B] At last I have recovered good health, which until now had failed me, and I now share with you the benefit of that condition, although I avoided making you a participant in my former anxiety.
