Yet I know that even during the time when illness restrained my duty, you did not refrain from such a service. It remains for you to reward my attentiveness with reciprocity. For this will both demonstrate your care and provide assistance for my recovery. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXVI. SYMMACHUS TO HESPERIUS

I am uncertain whether this page should now be delivered to you while you are staying at Milan. Yet I thought I would be failing in the trust of friendship if I ceased to return the honor of your letters. Therefore, without hesitation, I entrusted to chance this customary and simple greeting in words. If it comes into your hands, please let the return of your conversation show that my letter has reached you. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXVII. SYMMACHUS TO HESPERIUS

[Col. 0173C] If the opportunity for writing were often available, the will would never be lacking in duty. A clear and certain proof of this is that, as soon as the faithful opportunity provided by our mutual friend shone forth, I gladly undertook the service of writing. For I understood that the letter would be more pleasant to you if it were delivered by a more familiar messenger, who will faithfully convey not only the letter but also an account of my affairs. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO HESPERIUS

[Col. 0173D] I shall never spare myself in obeying your wishes. I know how much you desire my conversation. Therefore I have resolved not to leave anything undone in offering letters and not to await reciprocity, lest I become slower in writing. But just as I feared that it would be a disgrace to me if I remained silent, so I ask you to take care not to incur the blame of a friendship concealed or disavowed. I am fully convinced that you will attend to this, because, considering your talent no less than my own merit, I cannot distrust your affection.

## LETTER LXXXIX. SYMMACHUS TO ANTONIUS

[Col. 0174A] You have long shone for us with the brilliance of an eloquence that was not unknown; but your recent speech, suited to great matters and adapted to the majesty of its subject, has added fresh glory to that which you previously sought through teaching. For, beyond the verbal ornaments with which nature endowed you, you sounded something similar and entirely suited to the ears of the senators, in the gravity of your ideas and the precision of your words.

In short, even those whose Minerva is more stale do not deny that your eloquence belongs more to the curia than to the theater. Yet those who are carried on a loftier tragic buskin and delight in the scaffolding of elaborate constructions have celebrated, with harmonious praise, neither your somber solidity nor your playful charm. These are the seasonings of your speech and heart: you neither bristle with gravity nor luxuriate in elegance, but, fixed and steady through reason, you lay genuine colors over your subject.

I do not want you to await my judgment, lest affection cause me to err. What various talents thought, the matter itself made clear. For there was something in that composition that each person could love and praise according to the quality of his own talent. Therefore continue your fortunate beginnings and rival yourself in everything. For us, as a testimony of devotion, it is enough that we have not been silent about the judgment of the others. Farewell.

## LETTER XC. SYMMACHUS TO ANTONIUS

[Col. 0174B] [Col. 0174C] Although affection has already anticipated me, so that I should not be sparing in my duty toward you, I now pursue the service of writing more eagerly than often before. First, because the departure of our brother Marius ought not to have lacked some provision for his journey. Next, because I thought my letters would have somewhat more recommendation if they were delivered to you by one whom you love with religious devotion and intense affection. It often happens that a cheerful bearer adorns even insignificant matters.

For another reason too the ardor of my zeal has grown: I thought I ought to congratulate you on the praise of such a man, who brings back from the suburban province as much public longing as he has left behind as an example. I shall not call it deceit, since he is incapable of flattery. The fraternal vein is strong in him. And this has made us all the more unable to bear his departure, since we seemed to enjoy both brothers in one person.

I fear prolonging my testimony, lest I be judged to have served his praise more than his modesty. For those whose mind is honorable have a weak brow—that is, little skill in self-praise. From a few words, infer more than I now ought to suggest; I shall not hesitate to write it through another. Farewell.

## LETTER XCI. SYMMACHUS TO ANTONIUS

[Col. 0174D] For some time I was surprised that you were indulging in silence, and the matter greatly increased my pain because I myself was by no means neglecting the observance of writing. As soon as I received your letter, joy entered my mind and complaint departed. Friendship is quickly healed by duty. You had so covered the page with the honey of your most learned mouth that every offense was submerged as though in a cup of Lethe.

I therefore turn my pen and acknowledge the favor, although I had been preparing to reproach you; and I add this request: do not ever persist in leaving letters unwritten. If there should be nothing to write, it will be enough for me to congratulate you on your good health. Farewell.

## LETTER XCII. SYMMACHUS TO ANTONIUS

[Col. 0175A] The contest of duty is a sweet one, and therefore we have rightly both taken care not to be defeated by one another. I congratulate us on being equal not only in the affection of our minds but also in the reciprocity of our letters. Yet from now on I shall see to it that the balance and scales of my devotion outweigh yours, so that it may not appear a kind of collusion in idleness for us always to be judged equal in the balance.

Therefore I shall write more often, provided that the opportunity of travelers is not lacking for the one who desires it. Thus I shall seek the praise of diligence, and I shall urge you, occupied with public duties, to return our conversations with greater regularity. Farewell.

## LETTER XCIII. SYMMACHUS TO ANTONIUS

I ought not to commend the holy Zeno, whom I know to belong to your patronage and friendships. Yet such is his integrity of character that I cannot remain silent about his praises. Therefore I ask you to favor more generously, also at my request, a man deservedly welcomed by all good people for his diligence. In doing so, you will serve both your own reputation, which ought to be celebrated by everyone’s lips, and my intervention, so that he may understand that these letters have benefited him. Farewell.

## LETTER XCIV. SYMMACHUS TO SYAGRIUS

[Col. 0175B] Let the unknown be praised, so that the brilliance of a testimonial may illuminate their merits, which lie hidden. For the present I must refrain from writing in this manner, lest I prove unsuccessful in my undertaking if I support my brother Palladius, a man esteemed by all good people, in eloquence and learning. Moreover, caution is required lest a petition unequal to so great a man fail to match the recipient and diminish the attractiveness of my service.

I therefore lay aside this role, and I want you to be persuaded of this one thing: Palladius’s eloquence deserves that we should grieve that he was denied to the city; his amiability deserves that we should rejoice that he was summoned. Farewell.

## LETTER XCV. SYMMACHUS TO SYAGRIUS

[Col. 0175C] [Col. 0175D] [Col. 0176A] The fact that I sent you no letters when I was assigned to deliver a speech before the assembly of the senators, to be read before the eternal emperors, was not, I know, due to any disdain for you. For in a good and proven friendship, even when duty ceases, judgments remain sufficiently secure. Therefore I avoided returning like for like, fearing that you might think I had repaid with resentment what you had done unwillingly. The condition of accidental silence is altogether different from that of deliberate silence. One and the same thing is neglected, but it matters greatly whether someone omitted it as though occupied or as though invited to do so.

But enough has been said about this. Now, if you love me—or rather because you love me, for I trust that what I offer will be returned—make known before the unconquered emperors my joy that they entrusted divine writings to a human voice; the senate heard their victories from the storehouse of my mouth. Let it come to mind what that day was like when, as though coming from the middle of battle, I first poured welcome news into the ears and hearts of everyone.

Long ago, when the Roman state gained a military victory, the twin Polluxes proclaimed the success of the battle beside the lake of Juturna. For the tradition of the ancient books tells that they sought to announce the victory with panting horses, drenched in sweat and dust, leaving the report of the battle behind them. The same honor has now been granted to me by the sacred judgment. Thus, as much favor as the Castors obtained, so much have the emperors bestowed.

You will pursue this matter on my behalf before the author of the favor, more fully and more elegantly, as your command of language is superior. You have the substance of my wish; if you breathe some recommendation into it, the honor of this present service will be added to the other ornaments of your character. Farewell.

## LETTER XCVI. SYMMACHUS TO SYAGRIUS

You have increased with the reward of praise the zeal that I display in writing speeches. It is an old saying that the arts are nourished by honor. What honor, however, is so complete as the palm of eloquence? Therefore, although I understand that affection for me has led you astray, I shall inscribe the title of your illustrious testimonial with a white pebble, according to the custom of the ancients. For the praise was not bestowed upon me from a starved mouth; rather, the fruit of sound judgment smiled upon me from the storehouse of eloquence.

I fear indulging in words in praise of your testimony, lest we be thought to strive for a reciprocal exchange of favors. Farewell; and, as one devoted to us, persevere in your conscientious observance. Farewell.

## LETTER XCVII. SYMMACHUS TO SYAGRIUS

[Col. 0176B] Since my letters are welcome to you, they will travel more frequently. For I do not trouble myself about your replying, since it seems unjust to demand services that a conscientious mind promises spontaneously. Farewell.

## LETTER XCVIII. SYMMACHUS TO SYAGRIUS

[Col. 0176C] For some time now no honor has been shown me through your letters. I would complain of your silence if I had doubts about your devotion. But since our friendship has been entrusted to experience and weighed by proofs, it is beyond the danger of suspicion. I understand, of course, that your diligence in writing has been restrained by public occupations; nevertheless, I ask you to restore the interrupted service. The favor of the duty you perform will stand with me as though no fault of omission had preceded it. Farewell.

## LETTER XCIX. SYMMACHUS TO SYAGRIUS

Whenever I have to speak in testimony for a friend, I restrain my effort to say more. For where devotion is at work, what need is there of eloquence? I therefore bring you a bare but faithful judgment concerning my friend Pontiganus; unless I had found him worthy of our affection, I certainly would not have entrusted him to yours. His mind is open; his life is directed toward praise. You certainly know that I am never more ready to grant favor than to grant truth. You will confirm the truth of all this when you find even more in him. Farewell.

## LETTER C. SYMMACHUS TO SYAGRIUS

[Col. 0176D] [Col. 0177A] Late consolations renew grief, and therefore we ought to offer one another silence in our misfortunes, lest the wounds of fortune, which in time develop a scar, grow raw when touched at an unsuitable moment. Conversation should instead be turned toward matters that encourage you to care for your health. For every internal pain of the body increases under the injury of winter; and unless you travel during sunny days and in healthful breezes, I greatly fear that neglect will aggravate the condition.

I have now sent you the things that I thought suitable for a remedy, or that experience recommended to us for use, making it the chief of my prayers that you should forestall the need for such remedies by voluntary well-being—or, if any remnants of illness remain, that they should be wiped away by these words. You will give sufficient service to our shared friendship if, without delay, you remove through more favorable news the anxiety that your illness has caused in me. Farewell.

## LETTER CI. SYMMACHUS TO SYAGRIUS

[Col. 0177B] I see, most distinguished consul, how much honor your affection imposes upon me. You order me to come to you and to enjoy in person the happiness of your magistracy. How could I refuse, unless you forgive me in the same spirit of devotion with which you invited me? For what am I to do, uncertain before fortune, when on one side I am hindered by long-established devotion to your honor and on the other by grief for my lost brother? Two different roles are presented to me at once. How can one mouth clothe itself in contrary emotions?

Therefore, with an even mind, grant me pardon for this burden. May the fortunate attend your chair in a joyful procession. May every friend, untouched by fate, be present beneath your auspices. In the meantime, allow me to digest my raw grief through time or reason. Besides, I must console my parents amid our shared mourning; their distress will be doubled if concern for my journey so soon away from home is added to it.

Be ready, then, to forgive. Certainly, if you think I should be blamed for being absent, direct your anger rather at my fortune. It laid its hand upon me; it drew me back against my will. May that same ungovernable goddess, Fortune, not persuade you that I was unwilling to depart. Farewell.

## LETTER CII. SYMMACHUS TO SYAGRIUS

[Col. 0177C] Rumor had reported before your letter that you were staying at Milan, for it does not allow anything concerning distinguished men to remain unknown. But what benefit is it to those who long for you that, though you have arrived so near us, you are denied to us? I bore your distant separation more easily. For the hope of your presence, denied by a great interval, had ceased. Now the ease of your proximity torments our expectation.

Nor can you excuse yourself by citing the intervention of the Alps among your colleagues, since the nearer you are, the more justified is our path to complaint and the worse your case for pardon. But a limit must be imposed upon my grief. At least from now on, let your letters frequent Rome, sweeter than the honey of Hybla or Hymettus. Receiving them delights me with the greatest profit, while paying the debt of replying exhausts me. Farewell.

## LETTER CIII. SYMMACHUS TO SYAGRIUS

[Col. 0178A] Whatever service you have conferred upon those present appears to have been delivered as a duty. We, who were absent from your consulship because of various occupations, have been honored by the distinction of friendship, not by the reward of our presence. I therefore offer you abundant thanks for your consular gift, but even greater thanks in a good spirit. And unless your modesty imposed a limit upon my words, I would wander farther. For that reason my speech will for now be sparing, but my memory will be more expansive. Farewell.

## LETTER CIV. SYMMACHUS TO SYAGRIUS

[Col. 0178B] It is certainly a mark of your virtue to assist all who shine through Palatine service by your protection. But I owe special care to the excellent man Romanus because of the friendship that has grown between us over many years. Therefore, if you grant any weight to my testimony, do not hesitate to believe that he is worthy of your affection and of your rewarding him with the greatest services. Certainly, if you deign to examine him, you will declare that my letters lacked nothing that you will find abundant in his merits. Farewell.

## LETTER CV. SYMMACHUS TO SYAGRIUS

Lest you think it entirely idle, I entrust to your learning a little book as a witness of my vigils, in which I recently secured the favorable votes of the citizens in the senate. You see with what prejudgment I anticipate the severity of your most serious examination. I do not put forward the merit of my style, but the judgment of the order. I share a common case with those who authored it. They will all know either that your judgment of us agrees with theirs or that they themselves have been insulted. Farewell.

## LETTER CVI. SYMMACHUS TO SYAGRIUS

[Col. 0178C] I am thought capable of achieving something through friendships. Hence arises the hope that, through my speech, promises your assistance to the most distinguished man Theophilus. What we wish for his advantage is therefore clear. I ask you to ensure that his confidence in me does not appear to have been disappointed. Farewell.

## LETTER CVII. SYMMACHUS TO SYAGRIUS

Alexander, a most distinguished man who has obtained a provincial governorship, thinks that an increase will be added to his honor if he gains your affection. Therefore he has made me the interpreter of his desire, knowing that my letters have such standing with you that this recommendation will be regarded as equivalent to the strongest testimonial. Farewell.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0177]

## LETTER ONE. SYMMACHUS GREETS HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

[Col. 0177D] This is that Paralius whose accuser, his father, caused him as much danger as he provided him with praise. For a senator cleared through many investigations and, most importantly, by the emperor’s own voice cannot bring a charge against the impious will of his parent, which made his innocence more conspicuous. If you ask to love this man, read the testimony of our emperor, so that you may recognize how fortunate was the outcome for the accused, whom you see acquitted in this way. Farewell.

## LETTER II. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

[Col. 0178D] Let the extravagant antiquity of praise be silent, which has honored Apelles, Zeuxis, and their like—each in the order produced by his age—with the distinction of books. In speaking of Lucillus, my words are more restrained but my faith greater. For what benefit is there in indulging words when the matter itself may be tested? Let your judgment therefore concern him, since you have always been an observer of the liberal arts. For my part, I attest to Lucillus’s pure modesty and integrity. Does he seem to you worthy of your affection, a man whose dignity relies upon me as sponsor, while his skill and learning deserve you yourself as judge? Farewell.

## LETTER III. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

[Col. 0179A] It is a pious and honorable concern to wish to know the affairs of brothers. I shall therefore gladly answer your questions. We reached Capua in heavy rain. After remaining there for three days to lighten the journey, we proceeded in a continuous excursion, first to Terracina and on the following day to Formiae. It may be possible that the provisions of the same estate will keep us there for as many as two days. Meanwhile, after completing what you intend to do at Rome, begin the Appian Way under the favorable protection of the gods, at such a pace that you may follow close behind our footsteps. Farewell.

## LETTER IV. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

[Col. 0179B] I want you to rest and enjoy leisure free from cares. For the honorable man Antonius informed me that the plan for the African embassy had become inactive. The credibility of the report was strengthened by the fact that recent letters from friends had brought similar news concerning this matter. Is there anything else you would wish to know? Indeed, in my opinion, this should have been reported to you first.

When we cast off from Cumae, I reached the Formian shore when the sky was almost whitening, relying more on the strength of the rowers than on the favor of the winds. The sun had already broken through midday; the navigation of the friends whom the smaller vessel carried was slower, whether because the wind opposed them or because of the negligence of the attendants. This is what the circumstances have meanwhile suggested that I write. I shall see to it that, through frequent letters, I deserve from you a similar diligence in duty. Farewell.

## LETTER V. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

[Col. 0179C] We reached Formiae after much of the day had passed. Since we thought you anxious about this, we forestalled your inquiry with a letter. Nor were you more anxious about our voyage than we were apprehensive that you might remain uncertain for a long time. Whatever could have been answered in your letters has therefore already been exhausted by my earlier message.

Now judge how much better our judgment of you was than yours of us. For we observed the magnitude of your anxiety before you sent your letter, since you sent it because you thought that we would not write unless reminded. Farewell.

## LETTER VI. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

[Col. 0179D] Having traversed these shores as well, which extend from Formiae to Anxur, we are not delaying over either the ship or the rowers. But the gods are needed so that this return of ours may find nothing to regret. For it is commonly said that the people are being driven into disturbances by scanty food. Nor is there any hope that abundance can follow upon the present difficulties. Everywhere the year is close to famine. The fleet has been diverted to other routes. Summer has almost departed into autumn.

By Hercules, as I said at the outset, the management of this uncertainty must be entrusted to the gods. Human remedies, long concealed, are now too late. Farewell, and expect better letters if fortune changes the bitterness of our city’s circumstances for the better. Farewell.

## LETTER VII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

[Col. 0180A] [Col. 0180B] At this time I would have judged you especially fortunate, since, removed from the troubles of your native land, you are enjoying leisure—unless I knew that good citizens, and men like you, bear more heavily the misfortunes they do not see. For it is the nature of things that whatever is learned from another is considered harsher and greater.

Add to this that an unblemished mind thinks its innocence diminished if it is absent from the dangers of its own people. I say this not to urge you to return quickly, but so that you may know that amid shared misfortunes there is nothing preferable. For what would you help the state by returning, even though you are the wisest of all? In the first place, there is no room for counsel while the person of those deliberating gives weight to their opinions. When does one resist a superior, or yield to an equal?

Moreover, the present situation requires not wisdom but fortune. We fear a failure of grain, with all those whom Rome had received with open and generous breast driven away. May chance allow us to recover through these remedies. At what hatred of the provinces does that security cost us? Ancestral gods, grant indulgence for the neglected rites! Drive away our miserable famine. May our city recall as soon as possible those whom it reluctantly dismissed.

I do not wish to speak with you at greater length than necessary about our common misfortunes. Take care of your health, and entrust to the gods whatever is beyond human power to manage. Farewell.

## LETTER VIII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

[Col. 0180C] Your first letter was delivered to me so brief and hurried that it seemed to imitate your journey. But, if you believe me, it lacked none of the length I desired. For you compressed into a concise enumeration everything I wished to know about the favorable circumstances of your high position: how strong your health was, how quickly you had arrived, and what serenity you had found in the eternal emperor.

I would dare to say that the page of that letter was richer in facts than in words. For there was much about which I ought to rejoice, although there was little for me to read. Nevertheless, remember henceforth to water even your familiar papers with the abundance of your eloquence. What exhausts you is not the fact that you dispatch the petitions of visitors with tireless speech, or that you articulate the mind and oracles of the revered emperor. Let these be the first things, but not the only ones. For I allow you to devote so much to public service that you take nothing away from my consolations. Farewell.

## LETTER IX. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

[Col. 0180D] Both out of regard for you and out of duty toward me, any opportunity for writing ought to be embraced; how much more so one supplied by a citizen, which I ought not to have allowed to pass. You recognize the man from the seven hills: known at home for the excellence of his family and abroad for the length of his military service. It is unnecessary for me to speak at length on his behalf before you. A recommendation must be offered for those who are unknown. In his case, however, the fact that he is both a Roman and a friend is sufficient to win your favor. Farewell.

## LETTER X. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

[Col. 0181A] Justice indeed requires no support, but the promptness of cases is often assisted by regard for friendships. “What is the point of this?” you will ask. It is that your exceptional dignity may know that the honorable man Carissimus, one of the companions, hopes from the nature of the case to obtain the outcome he desires, but understands that something will yield to his efforts to win the judge’s favor if he is supported by my letters.

I therefore ask you to advance the requests of the man whom I embrace with fraternal affection. I undertook to commend them because, having weighed the character of the petitioner, I presumed them to be just. Farewell.

## LETTER XI

I returned to Rome by the Ides of November—for I thought you would do the same—and now impatiently await your arrival. Indeed, I know that my letters will be delivered to you not far from the city. For the holy Patricius, whom you wished to be the guide and protector of your journey, announced that you would soon be here. May the gods turn everything to good! For the present we have offered only a few words, but we are reserving more for conversation. Farewell.

## LETTER XII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

[Col. 0181B] [Col. 0181C] I have learned that many people are walking about the Forum of the Eternal City after receiving my letters, although I am very much afraid that pretended haste has committed some deception. With good reason I have placed before you copies of my letters, together with the names of the people, for you to reread. In return, report to me for each one either confirmation that the duty was fulfilled or, if it was violated, expose the treachery.

I am no less eager to learn whether you received them all sealed with the ring by which my name is more readily recognized than read. You will judge, after going through the copies, that there was nothing for me to fear from their publication. Nor is there any reason for secrecy between us. With open hearts we mingle pure services. Nothing lies hidden in our conscience that could be concealed by the subterranean devices of written communications.

But it is not right for us to allow our frankness to be mocked. For my diligence must not admit a traitor merely because caution made it unnecessary for me to fear. Farewell.

## LETTER XIII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS.

As I was reviewing in the honor of my style the civil and military praises of our lord Theodosius—for I confess that I have encountered all these matters more often than I have done justice to each of them—I also incorporated his laws concerning the blessings of peace. Just as I knew that these laws had robbed earlier enactments of admiration, so I did not think that they had left equal glory to later ones. But this recent enactment concerning fideicommissa, and concerning the advantages of codicils forever rejected by the excellent emperor, surpasses the brilliance of earlier laws by as much as it is more august for a ruler to set a limit for himself than for his subjects to set one.

And would that private avarice might understand the mind of the proposer and draw its character from the laws! For it is not hidden what he wishes the others voluntarily to do, since he was the first to recoil from the gains he had undertaken. I certainly fear that the greed of the wicked may regard an accidental profit as relevant to its interests, and that the cause of the innocent may become worse if the opportunity for fraud returns only to those restrained neither by law nor by shame. Therefore, since the condition of masters is more restricted, let the remedy of the law confront private desires. The old decrees have long grown cold among criminal men, their force having perished with their authors. As crimes have increased, so much must again be added to the severity of the laws. Otherwise, if the reform of the greater part is abandoned, the emperor alone will have bound himself in vain with harsh enactments—he who has always been good and upright in character. [Col. 0181D] Farewell.

**LETTER XIV. SYMMACHUS TO SYAGRIUS**

I have accepted into my friendship, at your request, my son Aurelianus, who now commands the urban cohorts. Consequently, I did not refuse him the recommendation that he had previously earned from you. For what you yourself have done ought not to seem burdensome to you.

The petition of this most modest young man arose from the misfortune of his father-in-law. He does not defend what the latter did, but wishes his fall to be lifted. Do what you customarily do, out of regard for the petitioner; and if anything is lacking to the requirements of justice, yield it to compassion. Farewell.

**LETTER XV. SYMMACHUS TO SYAGRIUS**

[Col. 0182B]

I have given letters for Marcellus and Romanus, men of the greatest modesty and devoted to you, more for the convenience of friendship than to make an effective recommendation, lest I add anything concerning men whom you have already approved. You know their reserve and their diligent zeal, and you have no doubt about the variety of their services. What room, then, remains for my testimony, when nothing can be added to your judgment of them?

Nevertheless, if they allow a full measure to have something added to it, I ask them to understand that, through my prayers, your favor toward them has increased. Thus they will also credit me with what they would have deserved from you without an advocate. Farewell.

**LETTER XVI. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

[Col. 0182C] If you have not yet learned the praiseworthy character and honorable training of my son Nicasius, accept the richest guarantee: my Promotus, distinguished for virtue and humanity. He has long enjoyed the intimacy of his birth with him, and you may weigh the excellence of the young man by Promotus’ judgment. For it is a sound inference that is drawn from the worth and esteem of one’s friends. My own support has less force, since the standing of the superior person outweighs it. His honor should be respected by having him regarded by you not as someone newly subjected to examination, but as one already approved. Farewell.

**LETTER XVII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

The language of intimacy usually begins with a general greeting. [Col. 0182D] I therefore strive to wish this for you more earnestly than to express it in writing. So, in place of the customary words, I shall embrace matters worth knowing.

Our sons are still staying in their grandmother’s care. Forgive a woman burdened by age and meanwhile deprived of your comfort if she tenaciously retains the second support of her old age and solitude. Nevertheless, we are preparing for one of them the equipment for a journey and for the other a companion in the fellowship of counsel.

I heard with reluctance—or, what is more fitting to say, believed only with difficulty—that travel has become old age’s burden for you, when you possess the blessings of your fatherland and the joys of your children in the favor of the excellent emperor. Therefore cast aside thoughts of Baiae and repose unproductive of virtue. This labor of yours is more joyful than any leisure. I urge us to embrace a lovable service beneath a beloved military command. Farewell.

**LETTER XVIII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**  
*(Join this letter with Letters 34 and 35 of Book V.)*

[Col. 0183A]

May a happy outcome smile upon my wishes for you, so that I may not have to bear heavily the fact that my brother Hephaestion, whom I came to know through you and have approved on his own account, has encountered some bitterness, I know not what. And because contemplation of your virtues causes me to attach to him a matter that carries less weight with you, I turn to prayers and ask you to answer to yourself and to consider your reputation.

Do this for your companionship; do this for your own judgment, so that you may not lack patience if he lacked restraint. I do not want you to seem to satisfy someone recently returned to Rome through contempt for a friend, someone whose complaint among us has increased your glory. Certainly Eusebius, foremost among physicians, whom I entrusted to you and who is well suited to soften grievances, will now be able to season what is bitter. Of his wit I guarantee two things: that neither restraint will be lacking to Hephaestion nor consolation to you. Farewell.

**LETTER XIX. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

Here is our son, whom we have taken away from our own comfort while yielding to your longing. At last, supported by this dear consolation, return to the joy of your former happiness.

But if you accept my view, as soon as the sight of your child has soothed your paternal affection, put useful things before pleasant ones and strive to send the young man to the civil offices. Why should you keep him in camp before your eyes? This is the form of my advice. You yourself will choose what you judge with greater prudence. For the person who judges conditions face to face sees more. What I say is a wish; you must form your judgment about the matters I have set before you. [Col. 0183C] Farewell.

**LETTER XX. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

Come to the aid of loyalty, which does not allow me to remain longer a debtor to the services of friends. My brothers Romanus and Magnillus, most distinguished men, have long bound me to them by the merits of their devotion. Although they do not demand the rewards that lesser fortune usually expects, they nevertheless more sharply and more frequently appeal to my sense of honor.

I would be lying if I claimed that I lacked the time to provide assistance, since my power is measured by the strength of your honor. Please arrange that, through the fulfillment of their honor, they may feel that, on account of the harmony between you and me, whatever is offered to one is owed by both. Farewell.

**LETTER XXI. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

[Col. 0183D]

The requirements of my duty persuaded me to write, since the person who will deliver this letter is such that he expects more from your judgment than from my assistance. I therefore entrust to him, rather than explain in writing, all the matters customarily set out in letters. From him you will learn both what your greatness believes worth knowing about me and what his own circumstances require. Farewell.

**LETTER XXII. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS**

I should long ago have restored the health of my frail body if I had been able to enjoy the salubrity of the countryside. But now the suburban district is unsafe because of brigandage; and therefore it is better to waste away in the leisure of the city than to encounter the dangers of the countryside.

Nevertheless, I feel my health improving through your letters, [Col. 0184A] in which you frequently enumerate the benefits of our lord Theodosius and affirm that your merits are being increased by great rewards. Your tongue will certainly suffice for giving him thanks. For my part, according to the modest measure of my talent, I have paid the tribute of praise to that most excellent man, our partner in wishing well to Flavianus.

But it is also time for you to allow the very man for whom we are indebted to return. How long will you claim the office of a distant province for the sake of your consolation? There is no excuse arising from your wife’s womb, whose expectation has been released by a timely birth. Farewell.

**LETTER XXIII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

I thought that, through so many admonitions and exhortations of mine, some measure of endurance had been added to your mind. Yet you even distress our revered relationships by your journey. [Col. 0184B] But what does this complaint accomplish? Those whose wish is for your return do not tolerate your impatience. They see that a hasty departure among certain rival citizens will win no praise.

Rather, assume constancy and consider what is proper more than what is pleasing—especially since you yourself admit that, in the love of our lord Theodosius, the venerable emperor, you have found the favor of all your dearest children. Farewell.

**LETTER XXIV. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

I detained Simplicius, an agent in affairs, almost at the Flaminian Gate, so that I could dictate to you a few things that ought not to be omitted. Our son Flavianus arrived in Rome the day before the Kalends of March, and soon, under favorable auspices, will begin his journey to Asia. It was fitting that I report this so that the promised hope might wipe away the anxiety you have endured until now over his delay. [Col. 0184C] Farewell.

**LETTER XXV. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

You certainly abound in counsel: prepared for every practical need and trained in the arts of wisdom, you have no need of an adviser. Yet it is proper that you allow my vigilance also to contribute something to your private affairs.

Therefore, if fraternal writing should suggest anything previously considered by both of us, carry it out more confidently, as something approved by two people. If you read anything there that is still new, suppose that you discovered it yourself, since it is being suggested by one who loves you.

I have appended an outline of the matters because I did not wish to embrace them in a letter and thereby incur weariness. It will be your task to weigh what I have intimated. For I have fulfilled my duty in such a way as to leave the judgment to you. Farewell.

**LETTER XXVI. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS**

[Col. 0184D]

Deeply displeased with the solitude of Baiae, I preferred to remain at Puteoli. The healthy habitation of that place pleases us. Afterward, if our wishes proceed with God’s help, we are preparing to make an excursion to Capua, and we assign this entire month of November to various places and cities of Campania. This is the sum of our plan.

But so that our minds may more cheerfully advance what they have resolved, they must be raised by your conversation, since we value nothing more highly than news of your health and prosperity. Yet you will do this spontaneously out of your distinguished sense of duty. Therefore there is no need to apply the goads of exhortation to voluntary services.

Meanwhile, I warmly embrace your promise, my brother, that you will be here. And would that your entire household might accompany you, so that the arrival of all may bring us fuller joy, and so that you may have no reason to return more quickly to your fatherland out of longing for and love of those who remain behind! [Col. 0185A] Farewell.

**LETTER XXVII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

Although rumor has preceded my letter and announced that you have been released from public obligations, I confirm the report in writing so that the assertion may be more reliable. But although you rejoice at your discharge from public affairs, I want you to be protected against uncertainties.

Specifically, when your Acts are being compiled, if you still retain the authority of the vicariate prefecture—which, when you ask for it, will not fail to be granted you on fair terms—let an account of your diligence be set in order. It should be able to show how many animals you lodged, with what equipment you furnished the stations, and how much your care advanced the collection of the fiscal assessments. [Col. 0185B]

This testimony will protect you against all either accidental complaints or deliberate attacks. Farewell.

**LETTER XXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

Argue about plans after the outcome as you wish, and blame me because the prefecture complained that it had been held in contempt. It is easy to accuse someone who has been abandoned without assistance. Therefore I prefer to take upon myself the confession of error, so that I may attack neither friends for negligence nor adversaries for harshness.

It will have been the fault of fortune, not of my conscience, that I seemed defeated, since I had not yet begun to litigate. Yet you also write that one ought to abstain from similar cases. You see [Col. 0185C] how much power belongs to the outcome. You have forgotten my character. For my part, I shall join fear even to my customary reserve and thank your letters, which urge me, after I have laid aside reliance on the law and on friends, to remain silent about every injury. Farewell.

**LETTER XXIX. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

Whoever intervenes on behalf of excellent men seems to assist their advantage no more than he recommends his own judgment. Therefore, in following up in writing the wishes of my brother Maximus, I benefit not so much him as my own reputation.

He is equally distinguished by his life and by his education in the liberal disciplines, second to none of the outstanding philosophers, and therefore most worthy of your friendship. When he has completed the business for which he was sent to you, I ask that you, in the humanity for which you are renowned, support his just requests with substantial assistance. [Col. 0185D] Farewell.

**LETTER XXX. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

You can easily infer what I felt on learning that the Sicilian affair had been wounded, since you know that I am stung even by the injustice of judgments affecting others. Moreover, you reproach me for an imprudent policy because of what has been lost.

You are right. Why did I hope that the insult of the sacred tribunal would be avenged? Why did I presume justice and legitimacy from friends? And to what state have we been reduced? I lost justice while waiting for vengeance.

Now how shall I explain the fact that Probus is judged more merciful because he yielded the retention of my little field, to the prejudice—or perhaps the discredit—of my possession, when the entire inheritance of the little woman was being promised to him? For this alone was the reason for reporting the matter to the prefect of the City: not that the governor of Sicily should pay the penalty for receiving appeals, but that the examiner of the sacred tribunal should avenge his own injury.

Now the matter would be referred back to the case, after my victory, contrary to the decision of the prefecture, to which the opposing party agrees. If the report concerned the outcome of the affair, and if supplementary statements or rebuttals had been offered by the quarreling parties, I ask: what actions will be judged—those which one party brought forward in Sicily after my appeal, to which the acts of tyrannical times have been joined?

Such is the envy directed against me and the criticism pleasing to certain people. Yield to the will of my opponents, and deign to suggest to our unconquered lord and emperor, Theodosius, ever Augustus, that wealth is worth no more to me than reputation. I place the good judgment of the father of the state, my protector, above any patrimony.

If it pleases him that I surrender all my hereditary property, whatever the lord of all things decrees with tranquil authority shall be law for me. [Col. 0186B] Farewell.

**LETTER XXXI. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

I know that you are a friend of justice and that you love me, and I fear that you may undertake some contest on behalf of an absent man’s reputation and turn some hatreds against yourself. I therefore ask you to remain at rest.

Perhaps I shall someday have the opportunity to present the truth before the eternal emperor, our lord Theodosius, [Col. 0186C] whose favor toward me has allowed envy to contrive something for the present. I do not think that my case will have the same condition in good times as it had under the tyrant whose letters, issued at Marcellinus’ suggestion, you know caused my men to be fined. I did not keep silent about this in the defense of my panegyric. Farewell.

**LETTER XXXII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

The man who ought to have delivered your letters to me will deliver mine to you. For we do not have the same excuse for silence, as you do. A many-sided throng of public affairs surrounds you; I, released from every business, wear away a dreary leisure.

What I previously did for the sake of your honor I now take up for my own consolation. My mind is relieved from grief whenever it is directed toward the services of friendship. My withdrawal testifies that I speak from truth, not for glory. For when I was burning with a wound of sorrow, I approached the dwelling of our common mother as though it were some shrine of a saving deity.

Now, by her counsel, my wound has come together into a scar. I heed her admonitions; by her aid I breathe again. Your other revered relations are also present; and what pleases me above all else is that our conversation daily exercises a tender remembrance of you.

For this reason I spent most of the summer within the boundaries of Campania, where your presence is welcome and where the condition of our fatherland is such that those who can be excluded by wicked men must meanwhile remain away as though by our own choice. [Col. 0186D] Farewell.

**LETTER XXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

[Col. 0187A]

The report of our brother, the illustrious vicarius, will disclose the disgracefulness of the crime that has been detected. Therefore it is unnecessary for our speech to recount what is unspeakable in word and hearing.

There is one thing that my petition and the wishes of the others desire: in accordance with your justice, do not allow this to go unpunished. It will be a grave example unless the severe punishment of the perpetrators suppresses the violent audacity of others.

It is reported that Ampelius and certain others, senators from Sardinia, as is alleged, were brought into the charge and that you ordered them to observe the competent court. I now hear that they have been transferred to another tribunal. Therefore, if you remember having judged the matter in this way, I think it proper that you deign to uphold your own decisions. Farewell.

**LETTER XXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

[Col. 0187B]

I supposed that you were preparing your return because the sacred rites of the Mother of the Gods were approaching. You press on with a journey of one day and leave us and your fatherland behind you. Mock the easy indulgence of your friends as you wish; if this injury wounded them, they would at least refrain from writing instead of showing ill will.

But now we soften the departure with services and offer gentle encouragement to your mind, while you place the care of your household above everything. For you remember that you began this letter with the preface: “Nothing at this age should be attended to more carefully than domestic affairs.”

As I contemplate the tenor of your character, I know that it was composed in jest. When would the sublimity of your intellect bend to lesser cares? I therefore think that you are preparing to give this answer to others, who do not know the sacred inner chamber of your mind.

You will satisfy me in one way only: if, setting aside defenses in letters, you yourself return. [Col. 0187C] Farewell.

**LETTER XXXV. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

I too, in writing, embrace the practice of antiquity, and I am exceedingly surprised that a copyist’s error has crept in—the copyist who, accustomed to placing only names before my letters, has altered the simple usage by a novel addition. Yet it will be clear that this happened by chance rather than deliberately if you remember that earlier letters were never sullied by a title of this kind.

Nevertheless, however the matter occurred, I am glad that something new has been offered which might release me from my customary manner of replying. For how long shall we babble words for giving and returning greetings when no other subject is available to the pen?

But in former times even the fathers of the state used to bring public affairs—which are now narrow or nonexistent—into the pages of their friends. Since, turned toward leisure, we have abandoned such matters, we must generally seek seeds of writing that have not been attempted, so as to wear away the tedium of general letters.

I was therefore pleased by the fault that I corrected, and, if I am not mistaken, it also gave you a way to report something unusual. [Col. 0187D] Farewell.

**LETTER XXXVI. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

Has our common father been so pleased that it is necessary for you to be detained longer than I wished? Or do you avoid the people of the city so greatly that, with a pious excuse, you frustrate my expectation? And truly, what is done or said here is something that a good spirit and sincere nature could embrace.

But however these matters stand, if you were in Rome, mutual access between us might perhaps soften them. Now, since I am alone, I experience every offense of circumstances more heavily.

Take one example, from which you may infer the rest. The virgins, the priestesses of the sacred Vestal cult, are planning to dedicate a monument with a statue to our Praetextatus. The pontiffs were consulted. Before considering the reverence due to exalted priesthood, the authority of long experience, or the condition of the present time, they assented—apart from the few who followed me—to the establishment of this honor.

I observed that such services by virgins to men were incompatible with their dignity and that this had never been done in accordance with custom—something that Numa, Metellus, the protector of religious observances, and all the chief pontiffs had never previously deserved. I kept silent about these matters, lest, once reported to rivals of the sacred rites, they create harm, since they judged the innovation.

I merely replied that the example ought to be avoided, lest an affair arising from a respectable beginning should soon, through canvassing, pass to unworthy persons. Not to speak at length, I sent you the very words, approved by good men but perhaps liable to be defeated by numbers, although the form in pontifical decrees is not the same as that in the senate-house. But ignorance will make little of this as well.

If you were present, the sound judgment of the two of us would greatly advance the matter. Therefore, as soon as our common father emerges from the uncertainty of his illness, return to me, so that shared consolations may make the course of life more equitable for us. [Col. 0188B] Farewell.

**LETTER XXXVII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

[Col. 0188C]

I cannot determine what form of writing is most suitable for me. For the intemperance of various rumors has continued so long that I ought neither to deceive those who love me most with falsehoods nor trouble them with truths.

Nevertheless, the hope that always counsels patience in adverse circumstances is secure. And if it brings any advantage, I shall certainly not delay in being the herald of better things. Farewell.

**LETTER XXXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

The arrival of my son Parthenius needs no assistance from the blandishments of recommendations. But I think it will add to his favor that my own speech is joined to his presence.

From him you will learn what has happened in Rome, although rumor has preceded the written account. Great and unexpected events do not allow themselves to remain secret. Our populace is changing for the better, to such an extent that punishment of the seditious is continually demanded and the insolent have already turned their backs.

There is no need for many words. I ought not to detract from anything by narrating it, since I have reserved a full account of events for the messenger who will come to you. [Col. 0188D] Farewell.

**LETTER XXXIX. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

The philosopher Horus, distinguished in life and learning, has long been dear to me as a friend. He counts it among the foremost gifts of fortune if he is joined to the best men.

Therefore, wishing to bring his desire to fulfillment, I ask you to count him, both because of his own merit and in honor of my recommendation, among the foremost and most honorable of your friends. [Col. 0189A] Farewell.

**LETTER XL. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

I congratulate my Ignatius that our diligence toward him is surpassed by your affection. What I wished has happened: I had prefaced my testimony concerning him with greater caution than you have now begun to feel was warranted.

If you wish to know anything about my actions, he will explain it. Such is his virtue and the confidence arising from his intimacy with both of us that he can neither be ignorant of anything concerning me nor conceal anything from you. Farewell.

**LETTER XLI. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

I forestall your voluntary benefits with a request, so that what you grant spontaneously may seem to have been obtained by me, and the goodness of your nature may pass into my favor.

I have ordered Nicagoras, a most distinguished man who has held the fasces in Sicily, to appear in custody. Both the integrity of his life and his fraternal merits recommend him to you. My prayer adds to his privilege: although I hope that your generosity will answer his probity, I earnestly ask that the opportunity of producing him may turn to the advantage of this most holy young man. [Col. 0189B] Farewell.

**LETTER XLII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

I had previously recommended to you the son of Macedonius, a most distinguished man, when he had entered your court under his own name. I believe that this benefited the young man in accordance with my zeal.

But since nothing is enough for parents, and repetition of a petition seems more effective to some people, when asked I renew the request—not that you should show a new benevolence to the advocate, but that you should deign to increase what you have already granted.

In my own name I ask you not to infer from the repeated expression of this desire that I distrust having obtained it from you previously. [Col. 0189C] Farewell.

**LETTER XLIII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

Many people speak favorably of the merits of Sexio, who formerly governed Calabria, and for that reason they asked that he be entrusted to me for recommendation by your support.

It is characteristic of your humanity and customary practice to honor with affection those who are pleasing to others as well. Therefore, if nothing stands in the way of the petitioners’ wish, I ask you to ensure that both my words and the wishes of many benefit Sexio with you. [Col. 0189D] Farewell.

**LETTER XLIV. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

The soldier sent from the praetorian guard produced the Palatine officials accused of the injuries whom your greatness had ordered to be summoned from Bruttium. But since the same case also belonged to the sacred tribunal, my lord, our father, the prefect of the City, claimed the persons and the case for himself by the authority of the law and in reliance on you.

I write this so that you may know that the officer had just grounds for what he did, since he yielded both to your father and to the laws. Farewell.

**LETTER XLV. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

Those who obtain their wishes through the favor of the gods consider it equivalent to gratitude to honor the donors of their blessings in person. Thus my brother Paeonius, secured by the rich gift of your testimonial, hastened to hear from the author of his share of honor. [Col. 0190A]

I would recommend to you an excellent citizen if you could think little of one whom you previously advanced to a higher position. It is therefore unnecessary to use the words ordinarily employed to support those who are departing.

For it is not a vain hope that the merits of the man present will have greater force with you, since you have already regarded the absent man with favor. Farewell.

**LETTER XLVI. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

They say that Socrates, whenever something happened contrary to his wishes or plans, judged the event useful to him. An interpreter secure in his own merit inferred that the things given by chance were better than those desired by the mind.

I follow the example of the wise man and interpret favorably the fact that the number of Saxons, reduced by death, remained within the total decreed for the people’s entertainment, lest anything excessive should be withdrawn from our exhibition. For when could private custody have prevented the impious hands of a desperate race, since the first day of the gladiatorial games saw twenty-nine broken throats without the noose?

I therefore have no concern for a race more wicked than Spartacus’ own. I wish that, if it can be done so easily, this generosity of the emperor might be exchanged for a distribution of Libyan beasts. The common administration will provide men suitable for gladiatorial combat; this is the foremost part of the quaestor’s equipment, so that those selected under contract may be trained by long practice.

I have no doubt that our men, to whom the selection and procurement of bears have long been entrusted, have been conveyed to you in accordance with the calculation of time. [Col. 0190C] But if the greed of the officials in charge of the public couriers delays them, it will be your generosity to release them from the delays by which they are held. Farewell.

**LETTER XLVII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

By the favor of the gods, we reached our destination with a favorable voyage and an easy journey. The appropriate hour for the meal was approaching. When we began to care for our bodies with food, someone hurried up and delivered your dear letters to me, together with the provisions you had caught from the sea, which soon served as our meal.

For we were pleased to indulge our natural appetite after the desired hope had looked favorably upon the rescue of our little one from danger. You have the whole account. Take care of your health and return as soon as possible to your fatherland, which loves you, with the good leave of our father, as I hope; after the solemnity of the purification has soon been completed, you will be restored to him. [Col. 0190D] Farewell.

**LETTER XLVIII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

On the third day before the Nones of October, at first light, I replied to your letters, which, because of the interruption caused by the journey that now keeps us apart, you ought to have received before midday.

But as the writings delivered to me toward evening revealed, the slowness of the courier suspended my duty and my care. Nevertheless, I cannot be angry with this delay. You would have lacked a reason to repeat your message if you had read our reply promptly; I trust that it has now been delivered—unless perhaps some wealthy urban highwayman has once again stolen our letters. May the gods punish them according to their own minds!

Now let us return to the matters you asked about. The fluid that had settled in our little one’s chest and caused a troublesome cough has been considerably reduced. Thus the passages of his throat are clear, and they no longer make any wheezing sound. May the benevolence of the gods establish the progress of his health firmly. Just as we have breathed again after the fear of present circumstances, so we fortify the future with our prayers. [Col. 0191A]

**LETTER XLIX. SYMMACHUS TO SYAGRIUS**

Until now I had been unwilling to write, amid the complaints of our weaknesses, which we avoid reporting. Hence it happened that your greetings anticipated my duty.

After, by divine aid, we began to enjoy the blessing of health, care for conversation returned. Receive, then, these letters—late indeed, but corresponding to your wish and intention. Just as they have been long delayed, so they will repay your longing for them by the better evidence of their arrival. [Col. 0191B] Farewell.

**LETTER L. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

With the gods as our guides, we shall begin our journey to our fatherland, as you already know. But religious duty advised me to make you more certain even of the day. Learn, then, that tomorrow we must retrace our road. And since you are most faithful in keeping promises, make sure that you remember to hasten to the public solemnity. [Col. 0191C] Farewell.

**LETTER LI. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

I had sent a written message earlier, which I presume reached your hands some time ago. Not much time had passed when someone arrived and delivered your letter to me. As I ran my eyes over the page, I discovered that I was being asked about the day appointed for beginning the journey.

But I had anticipated this concern in a spontaneous message. Therefore we have used up our time in replying. What remains except to congratulate us on having kindred minds? For what I presumed you wished to know, I indicated before you asked. Farewell.

**LETTER LII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

The return and journey back to our fatherland, which is always welcome to everyone, has in no way answered our haste as we expected. If you want the reasons, hear them.

First, although we put common interests before domestic ones, no importation increases the grain supply of our city. Hope itself, which ordinarily sustains people’s spirits in adversity, refuses to promise an escape, since the barren year has not even returned the seeds entrusted to the earth.

Next, to speak of a family concern familiar to you, our estate at Ostia is being pressed by a military requisition. We call the laws an empty name. May the gods see the outcome of the case. Meanwhile, what torments us is not fear of loss but the injury done to the state.

The discussion of my colleagues, which had summoned me, gave the eternal emperors the option of appointing men to be sent to Africa. Since the deliberation of the fathers has therefore ceased, we are not summoned. [Col. 0191D] Farewell.

**LETTER LIII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

You are performing the duty of a good brother. But stop reminding one who remembers. We know the ceremonies of the gods and the festivals prescribed by the deity.

Unless perhaps you ask me alone to perform your part, and, as is customary when a religious rite is entrusted to someone else, you impose your office upon me. Enjoy your abundant pleasures. We shall attend to what has been entrusted to us.

But remember, when the holidays have been completed, to make those who worked so hard to be your companions in fasting share in your luxury. [Col. 0192A] Farewell.

**LETTER LIV. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

A remonstrance is welcome when it demands a service. But since I have never displayed an unwilling disposition in writing, I am accused in vain of neglecting our intimacy.

I have the testimony in this matter of your people, who long ago delayed a letter entrusted to them through the fault of the courier. I therefore want the account of the friendship I have preserved to stand firm with you. For it is profoundly unjust to incur the blemish of violated devotion because of another person’s fault. Farewell.

**LETTER LV. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

[Col. 0192B]

We chose a place near the sea in the hope of good health. But we have not yet experienced healthy breezes, since the winds oppose them. Hence the matron’s return to health is slower; if a better day adds anything to her recovery, I shall not delay in reporting the welcome news about her.

As you have deigned to suggest, a heedless adviser mocks your anxious concern for urban affairs. An ineffective measure, harmful to resources, is being attempted at another’s peril, so that, when fear of scarcity has driven the state into straits, greedy selling may increase the profits of the powerful.

Do you think these are men who harm their friends more by their advice than they could have harmed their enemies by their hatred? But since we long ago completed our public service, let us remain silent about the affairs of others. May the gods arrange better things! For it would not be worthy to rejoice if some praise for me arose from another’s error. [Col. 0192C] Farewell.

**LETTER LVI. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

In the greatest matters I have often observed how much devotion and affection you show me. But I also embrace the services of frequent conversation, since they are drawn from the deepest affection; their constancy balances my own devotion toward you on equal scales.

The pleasure is so great that I confess your conversation stimulates me to desire more than it fills me. Such is the order and nature of all things: what delights the human senses cannot offer them satiety.

Therefore, since I cannot be equal to giving and expressing thanks, I do what dishonest debtors customarily do. Still weighed down by another’s money, they wish to bind themselves under a second bond of interest. Thus, although your letters are numerous, I ask—not as an ungrateful man, but as one eager for your gift—that they be more frequent.

It is easy to infer what sort of return in conversation I would promise in my leisure, since, while you are occupied, I impatiently demand such a service from you. [Col. 0192D] Farewell.

**LETTER LVII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS**

I had resolved to remain away from home for a long time and was spending agreeable leisure with our friends at the suburban estate of Arabiana. But since Fortune turns human affairs and plans do not always succeed according to one’s wishes, the prefect’s letters broke up my leisure; they mingled anxious matters with good hope.

More specifically, they requested my presence in ambiguous terms. I shall not delay your expectation. They indicated in writing that the senate was being stirred by the discussion of the colleagues and that an offer was also to be made through more confidential letters.

Nothing was published; nothing was read. The magnitude of the matter requested exceeded the recognized wealth. A vast silence imposed sudden astonishment upon everyone. As the matter advanced further, it was decided to extend the deliberations to another time, so that the absent would not be excluded.

Although I myself said that those in Rome or in the immediate vicinity ought either to be summoned or consulted, in the name of the others, about the proposed contribution, so that they might promise their agreement to the decisions of the order, the deliberations were deferred.

You have the whole matter, and you know well enough what I think of it. Even if the cause is common to you, your being far away nevertheless contributes to my consolation. [Col. 0193A] Farewell.

**LETTER LVIII. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS**

[Col. 0193B]

A little while ago I sent a letter. Now I return an answer, because the former contains what was necessary, while this one contains only a brief greeting.

We are well, as is true. If everything is proceeding favorably for you, share the common good with me in the trustworthiness of your writing. Farewell.

**LETTER LIX. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS**
I was living on a suburban estate adjoining the Appian Way when a messenger brought me your letter here. You know the countryside of which we speak, where I have built a large house on a cramped site. Here we spent a little time in sweet leisure—if anything is sweet without you. Now, for the sake of the Vestal festival, I am returning home, uncertain whether I shall remain [Col. 0193C] with my fellow citizens or withdraw again to the neighboring estate. You must let me know what you decide to do, for surely you have been away longer than is proper. The designation of my candidate summons you to our senate, with the gods’ approval, as soon as possible; you will be an ornament above all others to those who will attend us out of kinship or friendship. Farewell.

## LETTER LX. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

I had wished for an empty plot of land near Naples, adjoining the one I own, on which to build a new house; but you are sharing the Lucellian project with me. And, so that embarrassment may not hold back what you have offered, you deny that the property appears to belong to you, although I confess that it was not mine. Allow me at least to owe you my gratitude. For it is not right that I should recover in bad faith what I can accept in good faith.

You add further inducements [Col. 0193D] calculated to aggravate the builder’s illness: a double colonnade, curved in solid and incorruptible workmanship, extending for many paces in length; the structures I am building are nearby, and the small building project that lies between them can be incorporated. Why do you struggle against my embarrassment? I too am doing what you refuse to do. I am grateful for your gift; but I fear that, when the expense is added, while we strive to rival the old structures with new ones, I may discover that you wish to grant more than I am able to restore. Farewell.

## LETTER LXI. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

As his appearance and hair indicate, Serapas does not claim proficiency in letters; if he had remembered that he lacked it, he would never have assumed an adornment appropriate to philosophers. But let your judgment decide this matter, since you profess knowledge of such things. For my part, I considered it a religious obligation not to refuse one who asked for words. You will therefore do something in keeping with your character if, through assistance and kindness, you help the fortune of this foreigner. Farewell.

## LETTER LXII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

After I had given Gaudentius, your usher, a letter listing the journey I had completed, an *agens in rebus* brought me an official letter consonant with my hopes and desires. Through it I learned clearly that the designation of my consulship ought to be announced to the public. What, then, should I wish for your distinguished spirit, full of joy, except that we may soon enjoy a similar happiness concerning you also? I hope that our lord Theodosius, venerable to all and especially to the good, will grant this through a firm regard for his friends [Col. 0194B]—since it is fitting that the most august patron of our honors should match with dignities those whom he knows to be united in spirit. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

Many things win your affection for my friend Cresconius. First, he delivered the official letter concerning my designation as consul; next, his native Africa, dear to you no less than to me, commends him. Although I ought to have ranked his character first, I preferred to reserve it for your judgment. Receive, then, I ask you, a man known for military service, who believes that he will have reached the summit of happiness if the splendor of your patronage [Col. 0194C] illuminates him. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIV. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

The preparation for the consulship, with its wished-for and happy responsibilities, is occupying me. But, as your letters frequently make clear, your concern for me outweighs my own. You exhort, advise, and compel me to hasten whatever the office of the highest magistracy requires; and although you are the exacting overseer of my diligence, you nevertheless claim everything for your solicitude. Will the longed-for time ever come when, bound by equal duties toward you, I can match that disposition? I hope that soon, with the state flourishing and the rule of our lord Theodosius extended into eternity, your virtues will be rewarded with the fasces and offices. Then I shall need no goad from letters and shall await no monitor. For from you I have learned willingly [Col. 0194D] to undertake whatever must be attended to on behalf of a brother. Farewell.

## LETTER LXV. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

Brilliant merits do not require an endorsement, since virtue, conspicuous by its own light, rejects the assistance of another’s recommendation. Therefore, since my lord and brother Licinius has made himself illustrious by governing the state according to the standards of the ancient discipline, what dignity could private praise add to him? Having made this point first, I wish to join to your exalted spirit a man of the utmost loyalty and diligence toward his friends—not because your judgment is slow or difficult in gathering the abilities and testing the intentions of good men, but lest brief acquaintance and a hasty departure [Col. 0195A] deny you the proper time for examination. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVI. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

If friendship always demands that we assist one another’s affairs through our services, how much greater care is owed to our relatives, whose fortunes and misfortunes are shared with us? And what of the fact that the goodness of a cause often urges us to grant more readily to justice what we owe to our family? This moved me on his behalf no less than kinship did, as you yourself will judge once you have learned the matter from the report of the distinguished Victor. For the matter to become better known, I preferred to attach copies of the official letters, lest I be thought to say anything through favor and confidence. Now, if my wish is dear to you, grant this case the timely security that, even if I were silent, you would extend on behalf of justice.

## LETTER LXVII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

The recommendation contained in my letter would be slight if Leontius’s innocent life did not win him the favor of all good men. Endowed, therefore, with merit of his own, he has no need of the support of an endorsement; nevertheless, I ought not to refrain from this kind of letter, more to satisfy friendship than to provide him any assistance. You need only see, in keeping with the esteem in which you are renowned, that he knows his gratitude to be doubled by my name as well. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

A message suddenly entrusted to someone in haste must necessarily be brief. Therefore, both duty and the limited time require that I discharge toward you the honor of a greeting. I should not demand a return, which I believe will be offered to me even without prompting by a man most faithful to friendship. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIX. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

Just as I cannot remain silent whenever an occasion invites my pen, so, when there is no reason for a longer address, I compress the sequence of the page into brevity. For it is a loquacious abundance that, in ordinary and solemn matters, overflows in a flood of words. I therefore greet you, and in turn ask that you reward me with news of your prosperity. Farewell.

## LETTER LXX. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

It is part of human kindness to bring recommendations to those who ask. In the case of Zenobius, however, the motive for such service is especially strong, since he is my friend, and affection is owed to him rather than merely bestowed upon him. For this reason I wish your patronage to arise. The first thing is that he should be valued because of my support; the second will be that he should please you through his own honorable character. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXI. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

Considering how much affection you deem worthy to show me, I believe these letters will benefit my household member Cyriacus. I ask you to regard his convenience with ready favor. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXII. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

[Col. 0196A]

The most illustrious Honoratus has pleased me above all in the integrity and decency of his life. I believe that you will not regard my judgment with contempt. If this is so, and if your opinion of me is not mistaken, I think that, on the strength of this testimonial, he will approach the intimacy of your splendid unanimity as one who has also been carefully observed and approved by you. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

It is a pleasure to address frequently those whose affection for me I have confirmed by proofs. Receive, then, my letter, which I send gladly because I in turn am nourished by the conversations of your reverence. This should sharpen us toward readier services, since from here the generous interest of a profitable exchange answers you. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

Valentinianus, a protector whom I formerly entrusted and commended to you for the protection of your eminence, is being detained by domestic occupations. He therefore urgently requested that some assignment be obtained for him in the suburban provinces. Accordingly, either exclude from our dignity the service desired by my friend, or obtain him leave by which he may be protected from military censure under this arrangement. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXV. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

[Col. 0196C]

While a notorious case was pending in the prefectural court, Discolius—the man who had brought the charge of theft and had touched many men of our order with accusation—evaded the inquiry, not without bringing discredit upon the judge, after secretly making an agreement with the defendants. An usher sent to investigate this matter will have an easier opportunity to bring back the accuser if he obtains the assistance of the praetorians. It is in the interest of public discipline, and also bears upon the reputation of the investigator, that you order him, after being sought out with the greatest diligence, to be brought back to court under guard, lest suspicion, exposing the senators to rumor, stain their innocence. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVI. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

[Col. 0196D]

Your known and powerful affection for Domitius has spared me the labor of recommending him. For him it will be enough that I say this much: he too is joined to me by an old friendship. I hope that this fact will increase your patronage of him; for the common similarity of our judgment will make him more acceptable to you.

Meanwhile, at the very moment of the games, we are in need of the bears so often promised and so long awaited. We scarcely receive a few cubs, weakened by hunger and toil. As for the lions, there has been no further news; their arrival could ensure that the shortage of bears would be made good by a Libyan encounter. The people’s spontaneous will has reduced to an abundant supply in the storehouses the ounce of bread that had been maliciously and recklessly restored. Everything, therefore, is safe and secure—everything that was rightly gnawing at your mind [Col. 0197A]. If only equal success had eased your quaestorian concerns! Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS
