You contribute both the customary and the unusual to the presentation of our games. You devise everything generously and inventively, so as to win the favor of the people for our quaestor. This has now been demonstrated by the gift of seven Scottish hounds, which Rome admired so greatly on the day of the preliminary display that it thought they had been brought in iron cages. For this reason, and also for all your other gifts, I offer you the greatest thanks I can—although, in the things you bestow so eagerly upon your brothers in proportion to your greatness of spirit, you do not consider yourself to be conferring a benefit but receiving one. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

[Col. 0197B]

Some people delight in economies and profits; I delight in expenditure made for a desired purpose. Thus, eager for civic favor, I am striving to add another form of generosity to the expenses of my son the quaestor, so that we may also bestow five slaves each upon the curule stables of the Eternal City. Since slaves are easily found along the frontier and their price is usually tolerable, I most earnestly ask you to order twenty young men suitable for this business to be purchased through energetic agents. For this purpose I have sent you solidi, with the understanding that it is not their appearance but their age and health that must be selected. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIX. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

[Col. 0197C]

All good qualities are familiar to our brother Andromachus, but above all fidelity, by which he has been awaited by me and wishes to win your judgment as well. Therefore, while seeking you, he undertook a journey burdensome to the weak, forgetting his frailty. This was chiefly possible because of his strength, as the spirit often lightens illness through hope and joy. You can therefore see with what ready and open embrace of friendship he should be received: he preferred his desire for you to his own health. What more need be said? You ought to seek him, even if he were not following you of his own accord. Therefore extend a reverent hand to the man who hastens to you, so that one who knows you to be superior in virtues may feel you equal in fellowship. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXX. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

Titianus, a most devoted man, was commended to me by my brother Hilarius. With what other benefit can I reward him than by introducing him, as a petitioner whom you will not reject, to your holy heart? And now I hope that fortune will yield to my request, since you are so disposed and resolved that you regard it as a mark of favor if a worthy friend comes to you. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXI. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

Our son Symmachus, having completed the office of candidate, offers you quaestorian gifts and shares our other relationships with equal honor. I therefore ask you to deign to accept, in his name, diptychs and *apophoreta* [presentation gifts], since you have contributed many splendid things to his preparations [Col. 0198A]. Moreover, to our lord and prince I sent a gold-mounted diptych, as a diligent—rather than equal—return for his generosity. I also honored the other friends with ivory writing tablets and small silver baskets. I therefore entrust to your power and judgment that the things sent may be presented to each person at the appropriate time. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXII. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

Many people have asked me for a literary recommendation. To some I gave equal favor on the basis of their merits, and to others on the basis of their requests; yet I do not fear that the distinction among citizens is unknown to you, when you recall your common judgment concerning them. You will therefore pardon, in some cases, my embarrassment, which yielded to those who pleaded. You follow what you know to be my differing judgment of each individual.

I think that from these words it can easily be recognized in what rank I place our son, the distinguished man Attalus. For this free and open distinction has safely been entrusted to one who was not forced into taking a side. Therefore, in your name and mine, embrace the friendship of this man who hastens to you, so that the cultivation of good men may bear fruit for him, while the wicked may grieve that they are not loved in the same way. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

For a long time our lord and brother Alipius had wished to see and visit the sacred court. At last a late but joyful opportunity came: you summoned him as consul. He therefore hastened into your presence, eager to repay your benefactions with the services he desired to render and, relying on your holy spirit, to wipe away the cloud of former envy [Col. 0198C]. I believe that this will turn out for him according to his wish. For you will not allow anything to be lacking from his reputation, since you have granted him security in every respect. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

You judged correctly and plausibly that our brother, the distinguished man Titianus, ought to attend your consulship, since equity demanded that he enjoy the fulfillment of his wish. None of us has ever yielded to you in affection; rather, he has always claimed the first place for himself in respect toward you. Therefore he requires no other witness. He knows that he has more standing in your heart than he could obtain through my words. I therefore leave him to his confidence, since nothing could be more complete [Col. 0198D]. I am content to add only this: if he receives any favor, I too am bound to you in his name. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXV. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHER FLAVIANUS

Affection would easily have drawn our brother Elpidius to depart, if concern for his only child had not held him back. There is so much sincerity and sweetness in him that only his closest relationships are preferred to him. I could not refuse your orders concerning a man so highly regarded by me and so closely joined to me, because in such matters the pleasure of yielding is greater for me than that of keeping what I possess. Receive, therefore, one who loves us greatly, with the disposition in which you asked for him. Consider that, in the joy of those who arrive, you ought not to deny to those who remain what you grant to those whom you summon. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXVI. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

I seem to travel with you whenever you introduce your journeys and return journeys through a vivid account. You draw our minds on through your devoted attentiveness and illuminate them with the brilliance of your language, so that whatever your discourse sets forth is, in some fashion, seen by our affection. We therefore hold your health to be secure and continually pray for your safe return. For since we cannot match the love you bear us, we discharge through prayers what we cannot discharge through services.

Greet us, then, my incomparable lord, and graciously illuminate us with these gifts of your mouth and heart, both generally among the others, as you now do, and specially among the most distinguished, as you used to do. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXVII. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

The voice of law and legal principle declares that a contract made in good faith cannot be rescinded. Our brother Elpidius hopes to obtain the implementation of this principle. After the sale of his Spanish estate, the purchaser lays claim to part of it, although everything customary has been duly completed in transferring the possession in its entirety to the new owner. This is the whole substance of the petition, which my words support, but which is aided by his merits. I ask you, in the equity for which you are renowned, either to shame the resisting party’s modesty through a private rebuke, or to break his contumacy through the public authority of a judgment. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

[Col. 0199C]

I am delighted both by the honor with which you have now been advanced and by your constant affection for me. I therefore want you to have no doubt that the common pledges of our care are dear to me, since your merits commend them more strongly than any letters could. It remained only for me to request the constant service of your pen. But it is excessive labor to ask for what is spontaneously good, lest my pen seem to extort what the kindness of your spirit promises. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXIX. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

I had sent you a letter shortly before, but I was not reluctant to repeat the greeting owed to you [Col. 0200A]. For affection observes no limit in its services. Moreover, familiarity with those traveling through required that the page advance with their recommendation appended. I do not ask for a reply, secure in your distinguished spirit, which promises me voluntary conversation without prompting. Farewell.

## LETTER XC. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

You are always the author of immense joys for me. But now you have gone beyond my hopes by honoring me with the friendship of a man whom I plainly desired and sought. I do not infer this from suspicion. For the patrician’s conversation made clear that, under your leadership, his diligence toward me had been stimulated. Through this, another title will rightly be added to your other benefactions, and this title alone could fulfill any degree of greed for favor [Col. 0200B]. Farewell.

## LETTER XCI. SYMMACHUS TO FLAVIANUS

Whenever we are indebted by the benefactions of parents, the bond of obligation must extend to their heirs. The general statement made above concerns my son, a distinguished senator and most eminent man, whose father—illustrious in every respect and remembered by me with exceptional reverence—showed my household the greatest honor and respect. Bound by his services, I wish to repay through his son what I contracted from the father.

Only your magnificence can release me from this debt of gratitude, if it assists his descendants, especially in matters supported by the protection of justice [Col. 0200C]. He complains that his lands have been substantially mutilated contrary to your judgment. This would seem serious and intolerable, unless the agreement of the parties were also being mocked by evasions. For it is less serious to disregard another’s judgment than to differ from one’s own.

It is therefore in your power, in a petition of such clear and plausible character, while preserving the laws and considering equity, to defer something also to my person. My intervention was requested because of weariness with prolonged litigation, not because of distrust in the case. Farewell.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0199]

## LETTER ONE. SYMMACHUS TO JULIANUS RUSTICUS

[Col. 0199D]

After being detained in the countryside until now, once I had returned to my urban residence I found the welcome greeting of your letter. After such prolonged silence, it possessed so much favor and honor among us that the only thing displeasing in it was its brevity. My ears, starved and more than sufficiently thirsty for your splendid eloquence, ought to have been refreshed by a more abundant address.

I too took care to confine the page within narrower limits, so that, my brother, I might bite you with an answering dose of writing. Yet I am so conscious of my barren inexperience that, just as I receive as much pain when I receive brief letters [Col. 0200D], so I grant as much benefit when I answer with few words. Farewell.

## LETTER II. SYMMACHUS TO JULIANUS RUSTICUS

Placed in the countryside, I pay you the customary tribute. For I allow no time to be free of this duty, nor does separation of place lead me into forgetfulness of our intimacy. If you made me more prompt through the spur of reciprocity, I would certainly never restrain my sluggish tongue. Nevertheless, I diligently perform my duty and do not let myself be reproached through your example of cessation. I attribute your silence to the difficulties of public business, because it is enough for my confidence in our friendship that I believe myself loved in return. Farewell.

## LETTER III. SYMMACHUS TO JULIANUS RUSTICUS

An ancient custom has established this practice of writing: those who depart for foreign places claim for themselves the first opportunity to converse with those who are absent. But affection, impatient of delay, has changed the order of writing in deference to friendship. Therefore, breaking the rule of silence, I anticipate your conversation in my haste. I add, as a dutiful greeting, a recommendation of a man who should be numbered among the very best: long ago his parents made him illustrious, the splendor of courtly rank cultivated him, and the most exalted curia did not receive him as a newcomer but welcomed him as one to whom it was owed.

These qualities, however, are to be ranked second in our brother Philippus, both in place and in honor [Col. 0201B], because he possesses more distinction in his character and is more conspicuous for integrity than he boasts in the gifts of fortune. I would say more, if either his modesty allowed it or extended praise suited a letter. I certainly promise you this: when you meet him in person, your excellence will be able to find much that I have left unsaid, but will miss nothing that I have written. Farewell.

## LETTER IV. SYMMACHUS TO JULIANUS RUSTICUS

It is fitting that you frequently demand letters from me, but it is not fitting that you should suspect anything serious from my silence. You have judged that I had forgotten you because I have been silent up to this day. Is either the trustworthiness of my character so obscure or the significance of your merits so slight that such an opinion of me should have had any place? Thus our shared friendship has suffered more injury from your suspicion [Col. 0201C] than from my silence. For it is less blameworthy to abandon a duty from necessity than to judge hastily from inclination.

Do you think to lessen the fault by the customary form of defense? I was away for a long time, spent extended periods of leisure in rural retreat, and lacked messengers. Although these things are generally true, they have been worn down by repetition and have fallen under the suspicion of falsehood. My occupations, far from ordinary, offer nothing trivial: a new marriage-connection has assailed my household affairs, contrary to the laws, the felicity of the times, the agreement of the parents, and the compacts of our ancestors. But I shall restrain myself and dwell no longer on these complaints; the messenger, if he is a friend to truth, will explain them. Thus you will receive a full knowledge of what has happened, while I shall seem to have indicated my excuse rather than my pain. Farewell.

## LETTER V. SYMMACHUS TO JULIANUS RUSTICUS

[Col. 0201D]

Those skilled in rhetorical discipline say that there is no dispute when the rights of the parties are the same. Do you ask for an image of the matter? I set aside the well-worn fictions of judicial exercises and the empty likenesses of legal cases. Even the prolonged duration of our silence is an example of such a matter.

You will charge me with negligence in concealing my duty; this argument will apply to you as well. Since we are equals, then, it is a pleasant game between us that neither should complain against the other. You will obtain the pardon you have granted. But why am I dealing with you on equal terms? My case is already better, since I am the first to atone for the fault of both [Col. 0202A]. I shall see what remedy you will have when you return the conversation.

I have restored to the path of our friendship its accidental stupor, and I do not seek credit for doing so. It is praise enough for me to have dissolved the reproach of silence. Farewell.

## LETTER VI. SYMMACHUS TO JULIANUS RUSTICUS

Reason usually mitigates the sufferings of the mind, but the wound to our fortunes is so great that not even your soothing and persuasive eloquence can cover it with a scar. Perhaps time—or a long day—will eventually blunt the loosened pain, since every evil in time comes to an end. Meanwhile, the words of those who offer consolation grow cold, and a mind deafened by injury does not lend its ears to good counsel.

This is the third bereavement I have suffered among my excellent brothers. After so many miseries, who would not think that I had forgotten how to endure [Col. 0202B]? But the more the event itself has found us weakened, the more deeply I grieve. Now even those things to which long duration had given a numbness grow raw again. For the latest blow reopens the old wounds with pain.

I do not fail to recognize that many examples of unconquered spirit can be cited. Pericles came into the senate after recently losing his children; but the cause of his country compelled him. The philosopher Anaxagoras was not drawn away from his discussions by the grievous news of his son, but entrusted the neglect of his calamity to philosophy. Marcus Horatius, when he learned of the death of his child, ordered the corpse to be carried out; but such constancy was necessary in one who was dedicating the Capitol. You see what my state of mind is; and yet life must be continued. For the love of light given by nature sustains the weakness of grief.

I almost passed over what ought to have been placed among the first matters. I offer you the fullest thanks for assigning our friend Projectus, torn away from your companionship, to be my consolation. From this I understand how great a necessity prevented you from coming. Yet, although I could not see you yourself, I saw your spirit; it was not enough for you to provide a remedy for our misfortune through a letter. You added a kind of embassy whose constant presence might break the force of the evil, because you knew that the consolation of letters ends with their reading.

As we proceed into praise of you, we conclude that you refer your reverence more to conscience than to glory. Let the conversation therefore have an end, although affection for you will never have an end. Farewell.

## LETTER VII. SYMMACHUS TO JULIANUS RUSTICUS

I appoint you judge of my letters. If you have any leisure from public affairs, receive this little speech of mine [Col. 0202D], whose confidence in publication was granted by the favor of the citizens. For hope is often nourished by examples, and we assume that what has already pleased others will please as well. It will now be your part, once you have read it, to answer whether the senate ought to have encouraged me. Certainly I cannot be blamed for having hoped as well from your ears as I straightforwardly trusted the votes of those who came before. Farewell.

## LETTER VIII. SYMMACHUS TO JULIANUS RUSTICUS

As soon as a trustworthy opportunity appeared, I did not delay bringing you news of my return. For I know that you wish to learn everything favorable concerning us. I too have an equal concern to learn joyful and welcome news of your health and activities [Col. 0203A]. Therefore, whenever fortune grants the opportunity, you will deign to fulfill toward us the duties of mutual affection. Farewell.

## LETTER IX. SYMMACHUS TO JULIANUS RUSTICUS

I received your letter, which you sent me after a long silence, with such delight of spirit that I confess I have forgotten my earlier complaint. The kindness of your recent service has made the memory of the previous interruption ancient. Henceforth, if I am dear to you, frequently allow me the service of your writing, to be repaid in turn with conversation and affection. Farewell.

## LETTER X. SYMMACHUS TO NAUCELLIUS

[Col. 0203B]

You expect more extensive letters from me; I am pleased by your judgment. For it is praise of an intellect when abundance is desired. But I would prefer you to dislike an excess of words. What can empty speech do, how can it turn, where can it linger, when it has no substance? I hate long draperies on a small body. That garment is suitable for clothing which does not gather dust and, trailing on the ground, is not trampled. Write something, then, that I can extend in replying, although I am misled by reverence when I dare promise you abundant letters. I shall see what the outcome of your judgment will be. Still, remember that I promised you not a choice but an abundance. Farewell.

## LETTER XI. SYMMACHUS TO NAUCELLIUS

I received your two letters, written, so to speak, by a Nestor-like hand, and I labor to follow their gravity [Col. 0203C]. The practice of our age draws us into the cleverness of plausible speech. Therefore accept more fairly the language of our time, and kindly regard the absence of Attic refinement from this letter. It is fitting that this very confession of fault before you should help secure an easy pardon.

But if you cannot tolerate novelty, take judges from the forum: should pardon of style be sought for me or for you? Believe me, I shall earn more votes—not through fairness and justice, but because more people favor common faults. Thus, as you yourself sometimes say, I alone remain a spectator of the old coinage; the rest are captivated by the soothing of the ears.

Let this agreement therefore stand between us: that I may enjoy taking a model of antiquity from your autograph, while you do not regret bearing the novelty of my writings.

I shall not be silent about the other gift of your little work, in which you translated into Latin from a Greek book the ancient practices of each state. We had taken weapons from the Samnites, insignia from the Etruscans, and laws from the hearth of Lycurgus and Solon. Your labor has now added to these foreign monuments, which themselves no longer know their origins. Now, truly, our state has become the parent of all peoples and can teach each one the antiquities of its own people.

As for the subject matter itself, worthy of praise: with how much gold of language does it glitter? You would not know whether the volume rejoices more in its adornment or in its contents. The rumor concerning my illness did not deceive you at all; but now, if I may say so with your pardon, the harbor of recovery is opening for me.

I gave the boy the copy of your poems to take back; and because the order of the eclogues was confused, I also sent the sequence that I had transcribed [Col. 0204A], so that you might provide both the correction of it and the addition of the other poems you are now composing. Farewell.

## LETTER XII. SYMMACHUS TO NAUCELLIUS

If, as you say, this is your sole reason for practicing your pen—to exclude from me the turn of conversation—then your letters place a high value upon our silence. Take care, therefore, lest the benefit of remaining silent restrain me from writing more powerfully, because if I answer often, perhaps you will relax your diligence, already victorious in what you sought.

Remain, then, in your purpose of constant writing even after my letter, although I would rather obtain your trust than your pages. Those pages are indeed segmented with Ciceronian gold; but more and better things are taken from living friends. Words themselves also flow better from the fountains of the mouth than when they are committed to papyrus texts [Col. 0204B].

Why, then, after struggling free from the decay of prolonged leisure, do you not revisit our Caelius? Enough time has been given to Spoletium, a good city and mother of excellent citizens, although it understands that it cannot capture the men of our curia through familiarity. Farewell.

## LETTER XIII. SYMMACHUS TO NAUCELLIUS

Your attendant brought me two letters. I would be accused of fraud if I had not returned the same number. In both you promised that you would return to Rome, if your years permitted it; you have written the same thing many times. I no longer pay attention to your written promises. To repeat a promise is to contemplate deception.

I know that old men become slow to undertake exertion. But because faults grow with time, you, ungrateful man, must be drawn to me before a longer delay makes pardon more justified [Col. 0204C]. Nestor did not ask release from military service in the third century of his life, nor did Phoenix, the counselor, excuse Achilles by pleading the coldness of his age.

And in any case there is not much distance between us. Spoletium is our suburb. While you mull over your poems, while you compose epigrams for consecrated groves or rivers, your learned reflections deceive your awareness of the exertion. Farewell.

## LETTER XIV. SYMMACHUS TO NAUCELLIUS

I count it as my due that you have announced your intention to adorn your desired return. But I greatly fear that this zeal of yours may be hindered by your refusal to reside here. I ask you to accept this in the good sense, assured of my wishes toward you. I call the gods as witnesses that these houses, one of which you requested [Col. 0204D], were long ago designated by me for guests.

I therefore ask you to lend faith to my oath, although you ought to have believed even merely my intention, and hasten back to your own rooms. The house that previously satisfied you, when you lived and resided there with your children in the ambition of youth, ought not to offend the moderation of old age merely because your sons have been distributed among other houses. Farewell.

## LETTER XV. SYMMACHUS TO NAUCELLIUS

You ask me to answer your letters. This is a declaration of battle. But where can I find, although I am advancing in years, that old and comic quality of mine? Whom are you now imitating from the ancients? Yet the despair of my pen will not defend your wish [Col. 0205A]. What shame is there in being defeated after a confession? This too compelled me to reply: I feared that, by the example of my cessation, I might give you some model of silence. I realized that there would be more deceit in me if your offense imitated one who was silent than if my boldness imitated a superior.

You will judge for yourself how much I have done this out of love for you, against my own modesty. Meanwhile, it is sweet that you are well, although you have added that care is needed lest sudden events overtake our return before your years do. I do not want you to count the years. Confidence in health lies in strength. When you see that strength being expended under the protection of your character, hope that the gods will bring it about that you remain sound in life until the limits assigned to your generation by the definition of the ancients. Farewell.

## LETTER XVI. SYMMACHUS TO NAUCELLIUS

[Col. 0205B]

Perhaps you will blame my prolonged silence. Do not apply this delay to negligence. The continuation of a long journey stood in the way of my pen. At last we reached the Formian shore, which would have been more welcome to me if we could enjoy the pleasure of this place together. But since your years and health do not permit this, I ask at least to be informed through mutual letters how much vigor you have added to your little body. I do not doubt that you possess moderation and the other safeguards by which old age must be preserved. Farewell.

## LETTER XVII. SYMMACHUS TO GREGORIUS
I have plausible grounds for reproaching you, since, after being advanced to pontifical and literary distinction, you gave me no indication of our shared joy. But I do not wish my first letter to be steeped in the gall of reproach, lest bitter words constrict your spirit. Therefore I withdraw my complaints and make this agreement with you: henceforth, take care to show diligence in friendship. Let there be frequent mutual respect for that duty; let exchanges of familiar letters be constant. For silent concord is like hatred. Nature or human ingenuity fashioned the art of letters precisely so that affection might never be mute, and so that, when we are absent, signs of words might perform the service of the tongue. Let this suffice for the present. Henceforth I hope you will give me material for a reply through the favor of your service, not through the pain of irritation. Farewell.

## EPIST. XVIII. SYMMACHUS TO GREGORY

[Col. 0205D]

You certainly abound in nature’s gifts and in the resources of talent; yet it is difficult even for you to clear yourself of the charge of uninterrupted silence. For what can be said, whether truthfully or by way of invention? “Long journeys,” you will say, “kept me away”; but often there was delay, and sometimes arrival. “I devote vigilant attention to public affairs”; but every business is interrupted by intervals of leisure. It remains—what I least wish—that you should confess neglect of friendship. For if you usually abandon your duties, that is occupation; if always, you may regard it as the charge of forgetfulness. If this could be done, I would keep silent about it. You are therefore mocking my patience. Yet you will understand that a fair-minded person must be rewarded at a higher price; and the one whom conscience does not permit us to offend is injured all the more shamefully.

[Col. 0206A] And certainly it was part of your concern to exercise some exchange of familiar words when a speech from your archives was sent to me. For the moment I shall keep you in suspense about it; only later will I give you my public judgment, when you have won my pardon, when you have earned it, and—because I value your letters so highly—when you have written. Farewell.

## EPIST. XIX. SYMMACHUS TO GREGORY

You have broken the long silence, but, by Hercules, only after being driven by frequent obligations. Nevertheless, I feel no less gratitude than if you had sent me a letter of your own accord. I rejoice in my brother Germanius’s delegated authority as though an honor had been added to me. I am also delighted by your favor toward him, as though you yourself had rendered some service, since certain trust assures me that the distinguished man Syagrius has joined him in striving for a good and fruitful undertaking.

[Col. 0206B] I thought I should write this to you so that, as a diligent advocate, you might carry out our gratitude. Farewell.

## EPIST. XX. SYMMACHUS TO GREGORY

You have chosen an easier subject: human speech is more suited to complaint than to gratitude. For this reason, I think, you attacked me for silence, although I am constantly striving to give and return greetings. You did this, in fact, to my pleasure. For the person who counts another’s negligence of duty as a fault promises more prompt service on his own part. Your reproach is a kind of pledge. I shall neither meditate upon your words nor devise arguments. If you have incurred fault by keeping silent, you will be accused only by your own letters. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXI. SYMMACHUS TO GREGORY

I should like to use you as an envoy before the excellent consul to clear and excuse my absence, if I knew that you would first forgive me for it. For when I think of your affection, I fear that, just as you both love me equally, so you may both blame me alike. Who, then, should be appointed defender of my case? Clearly, my fortune—for its acquittal is as just as it is unhappy. For justice does not allow mourners to perform joyful duties; perhaps my sadness would also constrict your cheerfulness, since it is always natural for us to take the state of our minds from the faces of our friends.

[Col. 0206D] Therefore forgive my absence and show favor to it before the excellent man, the consul, whose honor it is ours to glory in and whose fortunate auspices it is ours to attend. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXII. SYMMACHUS TO GREGORY

You possess such an abundance of eloquence that you deserve pardon for your earlier silence through praise of your present eloquence. For what part of your letter lacked either the prudence of invention, the novelty of thought, or the antiquity of diction? Since, then, you do not lack a rich store of resources, I beg you to strive to be approved in moral seriousness just as you are remarkable in speech. The frequency of your letters will accomplish this: it will win you gratitude and also make me more prompt. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXIII. SYMMACHUS TO MARINIANUS

[Col. 0207A]

Here in leisure we are enjoying country life and taking pleasure in autumn in many ways. For after we entrusted the new wines to the jars, after they had flowed forth under foot and press, the Sicyonian berry is crushed in the olive mills, so that the early olive may be softened for use as green oil. Meanwhile the place is kept busy by the search for the lairs of wild beasts, and the uncertain farmer runs about to various tasks. Some creep up ladders to the tops of the trees; most clarify the stored must. Others track the fragrant footprints of boars with the keenness of dogs.

But all this would please you more if you were conducting it with us. The learning of the Scaevolas dulls you while, as an ever-watchful teacher, you instruct others in the records of the courts. So hasten here swiftly, that the tedium of work may be wiped away by the rest of the holidays. Certainly,

[Col. 0207B] if your love for that workhouse is so great, be present energetically, so that you may return more ready for speaking. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXIV. SYMMACHUS TO MARINIANUS

I regard the prosperous flowering of your fortunes as my own gain, since I am so disposed that I do not consider the success of friends external to my own advantages. And truly, how many days are joyful to a person who counts only his own good fortune? The one who feeds upon another’s blessings rejoices more broadly.

With what gratitude, then, do you think I was affected when I learned that the marriage gods had joined you to a mother of a household and had already granted you a son from her in due season? For, since we are kept apart by sea and land, I learned of your marriage no earlier than of your child. Indeed, in a single letter you brought both news of a newly born daughter and a wedding gift.

[Col. 0207C] These blessings came to you separately in time, but they entered my heart together. May divided joys yield to joined ones. The delay has provided me with a richer harvest. I no longer complain that your letters are late. It is a pleasant delay that restores several blessings at once. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXV. SYMMACHUS TO MARINIANUS

I had believed that nothing could be added to a friendship between us that was full and long-established. Yet you found a way by which we might raise your perfect attentiveness to its highest point. For, with kindly confidence, you directed that provision be made for your Ansio, as the winter journey required.

[Col. 0207D] But you, abounding in everything, devised a reason for asking in your eagerness to give a benefit. It is clear enough that by this you have conferred gratitude: for the one who claims something for himself from another’s love receives more. Only in one respect—if I may say so—your friendly claim stumbled: you promise to repay me from Galatia when you have returned to your ancestral hearth.

I would not have wished the constancy of a good deed to descend into these words of anxious modesty. But I shall pass over the slight enchantment of your praised letter. The obligation of such great gratitude does not permit me to be an interpreter in words. Why, however, do we say so much when we are about to send so little? The description of the garments to be delivered to you occupies the second page.

[Col. 0208A] You yourself will judge what you think of their modest quality, since you wanted clothing suited more to winter than to adornment. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXVI. SYMMACHUS TO MARINIANUS

As I see it, secure in writing to me, you neglect the turns of correspondence. For you know that such a fault will go without retaliation. How often have I threatened equal silence if you refrained from letters? Yet affection will overcome me, and I take pleasure in this lie of mine. From this you can understand how steadfastly I love you, since I grow angry so inconsistently. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXVII. SYMMACHUS TO MARINIANUS

The late arrival of my man brought me the letters I had desired, and they gave us a most welcome sign of your good health. If only the ease of travel allowed a more frequent exchange of duty! Farewell.

## EPIST. XXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO MARINIANUS

Your expected letter reached me, making me more ready to return your service. Nor should you wonder that our words will be delivered to you late, since occupations claim some of our time, opportunity is sometimes lacking, and the negligence of letter-carriers often frustrates the service undertaken. Therefore cease measuring our affection by the frequency of our letters, since affection is judged by deeds rather than words. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXIX. SYMMACHUS TO MARINIANUS

You announce something I had already anticipated in hope and expectation: that your first meeting would open to you the friendship of good men. Both your character and their judgment had promised this to us. Honesty, once recognized, readily pleases those who judge virtue.

But this aspect of the matter should be enjoyed by me rather than prolonged. I should prefer to proclaim more broadly—if speech could match the greatness of the matter—that you claim from us clothing suited to your use. Nothing is more sincere than this affection. Know that confidence arising from simple affection is a kind of virtue.

But what worthy return do I make for this purity? Until now we have stood equal in services of devotion. Now, without hesitation, we yield to you. I think it is enough for you, in place of such great gratitude, that you have conquered us into confessing it. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXX. SYMMACHUS TO AMBROSIUS

[Col. 0208D]

You have freely granted many things to my friend Sallustius. Now add what remains, so that I too may be considered to have obtained a share of the benefit. The letter-carrier will convey the additions to his request; I thought it superfluous to pursue them in writing. For the indication of the living voice is more appropriate for communicating matters of business between us. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXXI. SYMMACHUS TO AMBROSIUS

I renew my request on behalf of my friend Sallustius, whom, as you yourself affirmed, you also took into your care some time ago—not because I fear that you might abandon his protection through forgetfulness, since it is characteristic of your constancy faithfully to carry out entrusted commands, but because the fortune of a friend often troubles my diligence, and when people are in difficulty a single recommendation is insufficient. Though I remember this firmly, I remind you again.

The speed of your benefaction will ensure that I need not do the same thing repeatedly. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXXII. SYMMACHUS TO AMBROSIUS

My brothers Dorotheus and Septimius, distinguished men, preferred a single letter from you. But I felt it improper to seize such an advantage, so that both a doubled return of service might accrue to you and each of them might receive the honor of a due testimonial.

For although Dorotheus has been approved, I nevertheless wish him to be commended to you to a greater degree by the privilege of my judgment. I do not doubt that this will happen, since affection is capable of increase whenever it is challenged by merits. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO AMBROSIUS

[Col. 0209B]

Although I suppose that my earlier letter has reached your hands—the one in which I asked you to defend my brother Marcianus from injuries—I nevertheless ought not to refrain from a second petition, so that a repeated prayer might attest the necessity of an excellent man, though entangled in the envy of a tyrannical age.

Therefore I again urge you to defend a friend whose poverty, arising from his integrity, does not allow him to pay the assessments imposed over many years, although imperial clemency has already remitted them for many judges of the same period. The path to obtaining this favor will therefore be easier for you, since the assistance of your merits will be supported by the examples of others. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO AMBROSIUS

[Col. 0209C]

It is almost the measure of an age that my brother Magnillus, who served in Africa with delegated authority and was publicly and privately distinguished by everyone’s testimony, should be delayed there by various obstacles. You know the maturity of our excellent man, as well as the other good qualities by which he also attracted your affection when he governed Liguria. Therefore it would be redundant work for me to praise what you already know.

I earnestly ask you, then, when you have learned from the bearer of the letter the reasons for the delays, to deem it proper to intervene conscientiously on behalf of his return, so that, finally restored to his homeland, he may exchange the hardship of a long absence for the desired peace. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXXV. SYMMACHUS TO AMBROSIUS

[Col. 0209D]

It is customary for those seeking help to take refuge in approved support. One of these is Eusebius, who, having slipped through the error of youth and been condemned by a judgment, implores the well-tested remedy of imperial pardon. But so that its effect might quickly smile upon him, he wished the hope of his petition to be entrusted to your care. Its whole aim is that, through remission of his sentence, he may avert the wound to his reputation. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXXVI. SYMMACHUS TO AMBROSIUS

My son Caecilianus, a most distinguished man who now administers the grain supply of our common fatherland, learned from reliable evidence that his opponent, named Pyratas, or his agent, had drawn hope from your favor.

[Col. 0210A] I told him that you do not usually take monetary lawsuits into your care. Nevertheless, as people are generally prone to needless apprehension, he asked for a letter from me consistent with your holy character. I did not refuse my assistance to one asking for what was easy and just.

The substance of the duty imposed upon me, therefore, is that you should not allow anyone to hope for the protection of your justice against an absent citizen who is also occupied with public responsibilities. There are courts, laws, tribunals, and magistrates for the litigant to use without compromising your conscience. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXXVII. SYMMACHUS TO AMBROSIUS

Diarius, a most distinguished man who rightly holds the highest place among practitioners of medicine, wished his kinsman, who bears the same name, to be entrusted to your patronage through my request.

[Col. 0210B] I willingly satisfied the desire of my very dear friend, so that in one way I might both honor you by conveying greetings and make myself useful to him. Therefore, I beg you, protect him with your assistance as one commended to you, and reward me with a return message. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO HILARIUS

When I gave this letter to you, I was confined to my sickbed; I had indeed been rescued from danger, but was still weak in strength, which from time to time was worn down by uncertain fevers.

Amid these troubles of my illness, however, I entrusted a task to my friends, so that the common pledge might be joined to the consular men after the senators’ consultation. Account was taken of your merits. I consider nothing to have been referred through my favor. I handed the proceedings of the most distinguished order to the honorable man Ticinius.

[Col. 0210C] When they come into your hands, declare that I have satisfied the demands of friendship. For I desire nothing more than to be judged diligent in honorable service. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXXIX. SYMMACHUS TO HILARIUS

The vigor of my health has begun to rise. It is proper that a regular exchange of letters be demanded from me, provided only that confidence in my health remains—a confidence that the harshness of winter generally troubles. For the process of recovery is extremely delicate and weak, and before it can receive medical attention my health awaits the help of a gentler climate, lest you should think that I have prolonged my illness through the art of medicine.

I wish us to break the memory of our troubles with the charm of jesting. But something must now also be said about the excellent young man Repentinus, whose constant presence I have missed. As I think, his modesty denied it to me, although the confidence he derived from you ought to have led him to provide it.

[Col. 0210D] There will nevertheless be better opportunity when he understands that he ought not to have deserted one whom he knew, through your frequent testimony, to have placed his trust in him. Farewell.

## EPIST. XL. SYMMACHUS TO HILARIUS

I am in good health. This ought to be the beginning of a letter, since it is what the reader’s prayers most earnestly desire. I am equally delighted that strength has been restored to you, for recently you gladdened me with news of this kind. I also count among the sum of my joys the fact that you have shown yourself mindful of me through the honor of your recent letter.

I must not remain silent about my gratitude for this, so that you may be encouraged by this invitation to persevere in the service of correspondence. Farewell.

## EPIST. XLI. SYMMACHUS TO HILARIUS

[Col. 0211A]

It is characteristic of your pious and just mind to issue commands. I say this first so that you may know that I both fulfilled and approved what you had ordered concerning the son of the most distinguished man Habemianus.

Your letter of request was therefore superfluous. I ought to have been instructed, not asked. Besides, I had the closest familiarity with him. Thus the favor of friendship was joined to the justice of his petition.

What more need be said? The memoranda of our council, prepared concerning his acquittal, will come into your hands; they will show that the prompt fulfillment of your wishes was granted out of reverence for Bebianus. But for this service I ask you for more frequent letters. Their generosity will be easy for you, given your resources in eloquence; their reception will be precious to me as an expression of our mutual regard.

[Col. 0211B] Farewell.

## EPIST. XLII. SYMMACHUS TO HILARIUS

Once again I bind a debtor of good faith by the interest of letters. Since I have received in return the greeting you recently sent me, I do not allow you to be free from the bond of this service.

This contract will provide me with only one benefit: that the signs of prosperity you receive concerning me may be balanced by the pleasure of your own blessings. Farewell.

## EPIST. XLIII. SYMMACHUS TO SIBURIUS

I count the joys of your fortune among my own assets, and I make you judge of this opinion, since you know my character and consult your own. This was owed to the tender blessings of the age: that a man praised by the public council should be added to its members.

Therefore, since circumstances have turned out according to everyone’s wishes, carry out a service worthy of the judgment of so great a ruler. The expectation of good men presses upon you, and it is always burdensome. For although it looks toward the deserving, it is nevertheless close to danger, since it promises itself even more.

You have an age friendly to virtue, in which, unless every excellent man wins glory, the fault lies with the person, not with the times. You certainly see that the very man who presides over Roman affairs was born for the public good. Good qualities and virtues are carried forward, so to speak, on a favorable course. But your own spirit will explain these matters to you more fully than our pen.

I have performed the duty of a friend and assumed the role of one giving reminders rather than instruction. I hope that very soon you will be considered greater than the expectation—which is great—that people have of you.

[Col. 0211D] Nor would I have received a letter of this kind unless it were clear to me that I was entrusting good words to a well-corrected heart. For the rest, remember, when returning greetings, both to carry out your own duty and to call forth the diligence of mine. Farewell.

## EPIST. XLIV. SYMMACHUS TO SIBURIUS

I yield to your rules, and willingly embrace an **ἀρχαϊσμός**—an archaizing style—in writing. You must nevertheless remember that what the usage of a later age has adopted seems simpler to some.

Do you want our letters to bear bare names in the manner of our ancestors? If you love antiquity so greatly, let us return with equal zeal to the ancient words with which the Salii sing, the augurs consult the birds, and the decemvirs established the Twelve Tables.

[Col. 0212A] These have long since been abandoned, as the succession of the ages changed what earlier generations approved. Or, if we had to write a forensic speech, would we preface it with Jupiter and the foreign gods according to Cato’s law, lest we be charged either with neglect of antiquity or with ignorance? Yet it is better to follow Cicero, who employs beginnings unknown to his ancestors.

But why should I say more about this, when I obey your word and have yielded the field to your wishes? You need not entreat me to write often. The constancy of my letters will remind you of reciprocal duty. Farewell.

## EPIST. XLV. SYMMACHUS TO SIBURIUS

It is true that reputation is swift. But I disagree with the Mantuan, who thinks it should be counted among evils. For what is more splendid than this, when it waters the ears and minds of good people with joyful news?

It is especially welcome to me since it first brought news of your acquittal. I was in the country, sad in spirit because I had lost a parent. There secure report released me from the anxieties I had felt about you. Nor was trust lacking. I immediately believed that what I had learned was true, since I knew it accorded both with your innocence and with the justice of the times.

Your letters also arrived, so witty and graceful that, although the matter was already known, I thought a new joy about you had been announced to me. They contained confidence in a good conscience, together with praise of public justice. For you gave thanks to the great emperors as one acquitted, and complained only about fortune as an innocent man.

But what more? When will you come to Rome? When will you return to the leisure of the city? When will you return to the consolations of reading and writing? I hope soon, since circumstances require that the hardship of your absence commend to you the desire for rest. Farewell.

## EPIST. XLVI. SYMMACHUS TO EUTROPIUS

Things proceed according to my cherished wishes whenever I am allowed to enjoy the knowledge of your well-being through the service of conversation. I consider this sufficiently clear and established in your eyes. For what love would you show me if you were uncertain about me?

If only these writings of yours, as full of honor as they are, were equally frequent! The thirst for good things is grievous, and only constant enjoyment provides its remedy. Therefore make more generous use of the abundance of your letters. For the more they contain that gives me joy,

[Col. 0212D] the more remains for me to desire. Farewell.

## EPIST. XLVII. SYMMACHUS TO EUTROPIUS

Rest free from guilt, and attend to your books with less intensity, now that the revolving days have brought it about that the burdens of the state, wavering under their weight, are supported by the strong and fortunate hand of our lord Gratian.

Do I seem to you to have spoken more **πανηγυρικώτερον**—more panegyrically—than the custom of a letter allows? The nature of the matter is such that the greatest subjects require great openings of the mouth. But we concede these matters, which must be pursued in writing, to you above all, since Minerva is powerful in you.

Let us return to familiar subjects. Good health long disagreed with me. You were alarmed for a little while, I know; set aside your concern: we are well now. What I need is restoration, and if you approve of such a service, it may come to me through the nourishment of your conversation.

[Col. 0213A] Farewell.

## EPIST. XLVIII. SYMMACHUS TO EUTROPIUS

To commend distinguished people is superfluous work: it is like carrying a torch before those already standing in the sun and trying to assist the brightness of day by lighting lamps. Therefore, at present, without delaying over the duty of giving testimony, I devoted my pen to your greeting.

But I should like you also, in my name, to show affection to our brother Posthumianus, a young man of the highest rank, so that he may understand that what might seem a justified omission of his praise has in fact brought him greater honor. Farewell.

## EPIST. XLIX. SYMMACHUS TO EUTROPIUS

[Col. 0213B]

I count it among your serious gifts that you add to my friendship men of distinguished integrity. You do this in keeping with all your other attentiveness toward me, and you never cease to take thought for what may be useful to me.

What if I also give you thanks in the name of my brother Sabinus? Being regarded favorably by you has brought him such an advantage that he seems already approved by everyone. He is entirely worthy of the testimony of such a man; and since you granted it to him in commendation of his character, you may be considered to have provided it also to those by whom he has been commended. Farewell.

## EPIST. L. SYMMACHUS TO EUTROPIUS

When you conveniently returned to Rome, I established myself in a suburban retreat for reading. For a long time we had neglected this pursuit because pressing cares hindered it.

Now, while you—the older part of my friends—are absent, the writings of the ancients perform the service of your conversation. Previously, however, I had exchanged the city for the countryside so that the coolness of Praeneste might break the heat of summer; but the intervention of a personal matter interrupted my leisure.

[Col. 0213C] So now I am reading my way along the road, having laid aside what I was reading. If anything else needs to be known, my Palladius will explain it. I grieve no less that he has been withdrawn from Roman youth than I rejoice that he has been summoned in hope of his own distinction. Farewell.

## EPIST. LI. SYMMACHUS TO EUTROPIUS

I offer abundant thanks for your eagerness, by which you win for me the friendship of every most approved man. But my brother Hyperechius has long since been Roman by education.

[Col. 0213D] Why, then, do you commend our good men to me? Commend to others men unknown to me by acquaintance but like him in character—if, indeed, the rarity of virtues allows you to find one or two of equally distinguished integrity. I shall consider those whom I do not know to have been acquired as friends through your benefaction. You have returned this man to me rather than given him to me. Farewell.

## EPIST. LII. SYMMACHUS TO EUTROPIUS

For the present I am staying at Milan, summoned to attend upon the consular auspices of D. Valentinianus. The chance of my being summoned gave me the opportunity to exercise my pen concerning you.

I gladly embraced it, as the honor owed to friendship required, and convey greetings to you. If I understand correctly, you will repay the devotion of your friends through the frequent practice of reciprocal exchange. Farewell.

## EPIST. LIII. SYMMACHUS TO EUTROPIUS

Musonianus, a most distinguished man and your admirer, learned from a letter recently brought from Asia that his fields adjoining yours were being damaged. When he told me about the matter familiarly, knowing of our friendship, I first advised him not to be led into believing so serious an accusation through the fickleness of his own people.

Afterward, when he asked for a letter, I did not refuse this service, knowing that it accords with mutual attentiveness for us to share matters affecting the integrity of our reputations.

[Col. 0214B] I therefore ask you to receive in good part what I write, and either quickly dispel the deceit involved in the violation of another’s rights, or, if something has been disturbed without your knowledge, order it to be restored. Farewell.

## EPIST. LIV. SYMMACHUS TO RICOMER

It is my custom always to address your excellence. What is yours? To abstain from letters. We do what we usually do: I write, you remain silent.

But I know that in loving friends there is greater constancy in your virtues than willingness to neglect letters. Therefore, secure in your disposition, I do not abandon the respect owed to you in thought and speech, by no means demanding that a return of writings answer mine, since love itself makes the return. Farewell.

## EPIST. LV. SYMMACHUS TO RICOMER

While fostering leisure on my suburban estate, I received your letters. For why should I remain in Rome when you were leaving? The estate that now holds me looks out upon our Tiber along the side where its waters join.

From here I gladly observe what daily harvest is added to the eternal city and what Macedonian supply is added to the Roman granaries. For, as you remember, when Africa failed, famine was almost at the threshold; our most merciful emperor, born for the public welfare, forestalled it by bringing in the resources of foreign soil.

[Col. 0214D] Now the first fleet of many greets our harbor. Now we are filled with security. Now we say that whatever grows anywhere for a good ruler belongs to us.

I write this so that you may announce to the lord of the world the effect of his benefaction and yourself enjoy a share in the common joy. I am preparing shortly to go farther away, but I shall not refrain from writing to you so fully.

Those remaining in the City will take care both to send you my conversation through suitable persons and to deliver to me with equal fidelity whatever you write. Farewell.

## EPIST. LVI. SYMMACHUS TO RICOMER

I could patiently endure your silence, remembering your custom, if a messenger had not recently struck me with news of the illness from which you are suffering. I fear, therefore, that concern rather than your customary abstention may be preventing your exchange of words.

I ask you, then, to relieve my cares, undertaken in brotherly love, through letters or instructions. For although I am eager for letters, I nevertheless count it among my secondary consolations that my spirit, anxious for you, may be lifted by news, if not yet by letters. Farewell.

## EPIST. LVII. SYMMACHUS TO RICOMER

[Col. 0215A]

I freely accuse myself of the fault of silence whenever any interval of days delays the exercise of my duty. For no excuse is available to me if I do not frequently interweave the practice of friendship with public business.

But the same person who avoids the fault of idleness also refrains from being excessively long in writing. For although I know that your mind is in no way liable to irritation, I nevertheless perceive that, according to the nature of one’s cares, a limit must be placed on words. For just as length is welcome to one who longs for it, so brevity cannot displease one who is occupied. Farewell.

## EPIST. LVIII. SYMMACHUS TO RICOMER

I love and admire your virtues. But it has happened that, as a friend, I even envy you. For a while you alone will enjoy my Flavianus.

Let me explain more plainly what I mean. Everything that was best in Rome has moved to you. Your companionship will indeed give you mutual joy. But what consolation will remain for me? He has abandoned me, and you will miss him less, because one man will suffice for you in place of both. Farewell.

## EPIST. LIX. SYMMACHUS TO RICOMER

Someone else might think that the gift discharged by the consul of the previous year has arrived late. I understand that I and the others who live far away have been postponed until this time by the confidence of friendship.

Those whose memory you could not have retained for so long were satisfied immediately. For the man who is generous at once is, in a way, reminded by the insignia of his office itself. The man who returns services after an interval

[Col. 0215C] testifies that he preferred to delay them for those whose forgetfulness a longer passage of time could not conceal.

Let anyone decide whether he thinks himself placed after others in rank or honor. I understand that I have been preferred through pure affection. For a man is not sufficiently a friend if something customary is returned to him at once. More honorable is that security which thinks it no disgrace if something is owed to friends for a long time.

Therefore I should like you to believe that the delay itself was also pleasant to me. This is how I judge and interpret what was long ago conferred upon others according to custom but preserved for us out of affection. Farewell.

## EPIST. LX. SYMMACHUS TO RICOMER

A desired event has offered me a most faithful opportunity to discharge my duty. For my lord and brother Eugenius, after granting me an opportunity to see him, added to it the favor of taking a letter when he was asked.

Through it I offer you a respectful greeting and earnestly beg you not to allow me to remain any longer suspended in your silence. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXI. SYMMACHUS TO RICOMER

Some time ago I had sent replies that testified how welcome to me were the gifts of your most distinguished consulship. But once again, having obtained the company of Eugenius, my most distinguished brother, I doubled my writings, not fearing that repeated speech might cause irritation.

For I measure friendship by my own spirit and believe that it cannot experience satiety with services: however frequent they may be, and however much they resemble one another in succession, they are always received as rare and long desired.

[Col. 0216A] The constancy of your letters will confirm this opinion of mine. It is implanted in good minds that what we eagerly desire to receive in abundance from others, we ourselves should generously bestow. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXII. SYMMACHUS TO RICOMER

When the official messenger had completed his instructions and we reached our destination, he ought not to have departed without a testimonial from us—especially lest you should think that your attention toward me had been misplaced if delayed speech had postponed the repayment of gratitude.

I therefore greet you and already send ahead my request: when we begin retracing our journey to our homeland, decide to provide more abundant assistance for overcoming its difficulties. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXIII. SYMMACHUS TO RICOMER

[Col. 0216B]

I have exchanged the leisure of my homeland for a joyful absence. For, summoned by order of our lord Valentinianus along with many leading men of the most distinguished court, I am enjoying public festivities in place of the quiet of home.

Since report could carry this news to you, it seemed more fitting that I should announce it myself. You will preserve your custom of answering my kindness; for I desire your letters no less than the sight and words of my own people. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXIV. SYMMACHUS TO RICOMER

I leave it to you to estimate how much pleasure your letters have brought me; if I judge correctly, my conversation in turn gives you pleasure. Continue, then, as you have already been pleased to do, both to honor our friendship with devoted affection and to cultivate it through constant conversation.

I shall take care to be your equal in returning the service. For the one who asks services from another also promises frequent application of his own zeal. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXV. SYMMACHUS TO RICOMER

I know that your excellent spirit eagerly awaits, as friendship requires, signs of my well-being and return. Therefore, having returned to my homeland, I satisfied your expectation and inform you that I am proceeding according to my wishes and that I am mindful of the kindness you have shown us.

At the same time I beg you not to hesitate, whenever circumstances permit, to increase through the gift of letters the affection that you have deigned to render to me when present and to promise me when absent.

[Col. 0216D] Farewell.

## EPIST. LXVI. SYMMACHUS TO RICOMER

If you would like to know how great a portion of my heart belongs to my lord Flavianus, embrace the friendship of the man who is approaching, so that you may bind two men.

We are both the same. For the better of us permits me to say this. I would write more if you wished to be asked for a long time to commend the merits of so great a man. Therefore it is enough that you have received signs of my wish.

No effort or solicitation is needed, since it naturally follows that a man resembling you in character is loved by you. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXVII. SYMMACHUS TO RICOMER

It was fitting that my household servant Firmus, who had honorably completed his military service, should be assisted by my testimony, so that he might reach your acquaintance by an easier approach.

Therefore, I beg you, extend a helping hand to one seeking the lawful rewards he is accustomed to receive. Such a privilege is owed to veterans: the dignity of the protectors’ office should be added to them as the price of long service.

This will undoubtedly happen to Firmus if your favor approves the wishes of a man striving toward the customary rewards. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO RICOMER

The proper consideration of your merits demands that I frequently devote my attention to familiar letters, since I have learned that services offered to wise men do not perish.

I therefore perform the service of greeting, which alone testifies to care for the absent. I ask your excellence both to cultivate the good of friendship, as you are accustomed to do, through conversation and to guard it in your mind. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXIX. SYMMACHUS TO RICOMER.

I cannot allow my lord and brother Flavianus, a man eminent in virtues and honors, to be deprived of your justice. In proportion to his honors, I present the case that necessity demands, knowing that matters are said to have been undertaken without your authority, though certain malicious men designated them under the pretext of acting with your support. Hence I have greater confidence that the matter can be severely vindicated, since your own reputation too has been assailed. If you so order, his presentation will set out the nature of the complaint more effectively, because the injury is multifaceted and exceeds the scope of a personal letter. Nor did the illustrious man’s son, himself now one who has completed his term of office, endure lesser wrongs in his proconsular property; [Col. 0217C] these concern the guilt of one man, but the contempt of both.

Therefore, as is your custom, deign to defend—after hearing the allegations of those who protect the interests of absent persons—first reputation, which is precious to every good man; then friendship, the proof of loyalty; and finally the laws, for which you keep watch. Thus may the illustrious man, who through the absence of his family is unaware of their troubles, learn of the benefit of your favor before their grief and complaint reach him. Farewell.

**LETTER LXX. SYMMACHUS TO TYMASIUS**

I am often glad to address your Excellence, although I have received no conversation from you in return. For your sake I spontaneously answer myself that, amid military concerns, there is no room for idle services. [Col. 0217D] And would that the constant frequency of my addresses did not seem to you intrusive. I am almost ready to regard the favor of your letters as returned to me, if I know that what I write does not bring weariness. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXI. SYMMACHUS TO TYMASIUS**

You have encouraged me to write by reporting a reciprocal response. For the nature of things is such that diligence in rendering services grows warm through the reward of reciprocity. Accept, then, my greeting, and gladly embrace at the same time this indication of my well-being; in return, according to my wish and inclination, you will bring me reciprocal joys through similar reports of your actions. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXII. SYMMACHUS TO TYMASIUS**

[Col. 0218A]

I press upon you with frequent letters and do not abandon you in affection. Felix is the intermediary of my communication, a commendable man both in the integrity of his life and in his military service. I would not dare to urge you to take his circumstances into consideration, since your equity can accomplish for him as much as my favor could desire. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO TYMASIUS**

The petition of my lord and brother Stemmatius requires a reminder to you more than an intercessor. For your acquaintance with him is so long-standing that you anticipate our request with your favor; we ought to count the labor of asking as gain. Briefly, then, observe what he seeks. He lost the supports of life—those things usually called possessions when one’s resources are more abundant—through the misfortune of proscription. He entrusts their restoration, in the great joy of the state, especially to your merits. Accept, I beg you, a task full of goodness, and comfort the poverty of my friend, upon whom the misfortune of wretched health has also fallen, by restoring his household resources. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO PROMOTUS**

Nature has heaped many virtues upon you. If anyone should weigh them with more careful judgment, he would not know whether the qualities of your courage or those of your mind are more outstanding. But the emperor, ruler of the human race, is the supporter of the former praise; we must be witnesses of your personal services, though we cannot equal you in our devoted zeal. Yet I am amazed that your affection for me has advanced so far that you flatter me with false praise, when you say that you desire something from the storehouse of my speech. What use to you, amid the din of my hoarse utterances, is the noise of my address? It is indeed characteristic of virtue to apply soothing remedies to the senses during exertion. For the greatest of poets reports that Achilles dissolved the cares of a troubled spirit with his lyre. But we confess our poverty in musical eloquence, and seek nourishment for speech from the writings of those whom both report and your own letters testify to be attached to your entourage. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXV. SYMMACHUS TO PROMOTUS**

The sight of your family will certainly satisfy you with every joy. But I suppose that this happiness can be increased if our conversation too is added to it. For since domestic blessings are dear to you above all else, the care of friends rightly protects the joy nearest to them. Therefore, when your pious relationships have satisfied your longing, let your eyes also turn to our letters; their entire substance is this: that you should know me to be well. For I do not wish to detain you from conversations with your family by a longer page. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXVI. SYMMACHUS TO PROMOTUS**

Two pleasant things happen to me whenever letters are requested from me: that I bestow upon you the honor of a greeting, and that I offer the service of a recommendation to those who ask it. Since, then, our client Paregorius was making preparations to return to Africa and was urgently requesting a letter of this kind, I willingly granted his wish, knowing that, with one who loves me, neither his petition would lack the benefit of success nor my speech prove ineffective. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXVII. SYMMACHUS TO PROMOTUS**

You did not return a response to my earlier letters. But it was my duty to multiply my writings, lest I be deprived of so trustworthy an opportunity—especially since our mutual friend Auxentius thought that something of favor would accrue to him from my letters. I need not recommend him to you for that reason, since you are accustomed to be a witness to his merits with you rather than before others. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO PROMOTUS**

[Col. 0219B]

You impelled me, who was lingering over my letters, to cultivate now, at your prompting, the friendship that I had long been silently desiring. I embrace the goodwill that inaugurates our future intimacy. And although your wish has anticipated mine, I shall strive, as far as I can, not to be surpassed in services. For I see that this part has been reserved for me: that the devotion which, at your urging, has made a beginning should, with my effort, increase. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXIX. SYMMACHUS TO PROMOTUS**

I promptly returned a reciprocal response to your first letters. But because greater service is owed to those who inaugurate a new intimacy, I persist in cultivating our friendship with the gift of a letter, so that you may perceive how well an alliance of spirits is joined with those who know how to repay religion with fuller gratitude. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXX. SYMMACHUS TO PROMOTUS**

I consider myself blessed with many goods whenever I am delighted by the honor and brilliance of your conversation. And, so that I may deserve this, I too do not abandon the diligence of frequent service. Let there therefore stand between us both the faithful sincerity of our spirits and the friendly rivalry of this service. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXXI. SYMMACHUS TO RUFINUS**

I was angry at your silence. But after you gave me news of your brother’s honor, pleasure overcame my displeasure. Matters have returned to such a state that I am thanking the man whom I had been preparing dutifully to rebuke. As for you, remain silent under this request as long as you wish, provided that afterward you redeem the holidays of your pen with good letters.

What a message, like your own wish! No one should have written this except one whom it is clear had wished for it. Yet, besides the joy I gain from your brother’s advancement, you greatly diminish my judgment of you. For you alone seemed to me capable of rejoicing when the rewards of virtue had been restored. But when you say that, after the wicked were excluded, hope was restored to the good, I do not congratulate you on this as something unusual or newly begun. For it is customary for our lord Theodosius to exercise judgment among his own, to select character, and always to weigh each person, new as well as established, without allowing custom to excuse anyone from judgment.

That is why he receives your unblemished character with greater kindness, having examined it severely and carefully. Indeed, he extends his eyes far afield and searches throughout the world for the veins of good men, drawing none more eagerly than those who desire nothing. Thus he recently summoned my Flavianus—and therefore yours—whom modesty would still conceal if distinguished merits had not betrayed him.

This is what joy has dictated to me for the present. Now I ask you to love him as your most devoted brother—or, more truly, as a part of myself—which you will do spontaneously. Love in him his pursuits, and whatever you recognize as akin to your own virtues. Just as I am troubled by being separated from my brother, so it will be a consolation to me if I know that he has truly found a Symmachus in you. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXXII. SYMMACHUS TO RUFINUS**

You are still silent. But my loquacity is not restrained by your example, and I have leisure that is favorable to an abundance of words. For I am in the country, though I am not becoming rustic. From the bank of the Tiber—for the river flows through my estates—I merely watch the heavily laden ships; I am no longer, as before, anxious about the famine of the citizens.

For public fear has been transformed from want into joy, after the venerable father of his country made good Africa’s losses with Macedonian supplies. Now everyone loves him as the god who nourishes the human race. For he allowed the rebellious Africans nothing against Rome. Therefore, from the vantage point of my fields, I count the passage of foreign ships and rejoice that the Roman people’s food supply depends not on the fate of provinces but on the devotion with which you customarily fail to conceal the public good.

I speak more sparingly, deservedly leaving it to your eloquence to insinuate more elegantly, if it so pleases you, what we have recounted in unpolished truth. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO RUFINUS**

[Col. 0220C]

You have, as I judge from your report, completed your journey—the one circumstance that alone supported your silence. Now may the rest afforded by your station restore to us your accustomed practice of writing, both in pen and spirit. Although the facility of your speech, even while you were making your way along the road, could have quenched our thirst with brilliant conversation, let the labor of travel serve to clear you of the charge of silence.

There is now no defense left, since both the eloquence that was not hindered even before remains available and the leisure that was desired has arrived. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO RUFINUS**

I follow you with letters, since I do not abandon you in mind and affection. Nor do I seem to myself to be taking up these consolations too soon, while your recent pleasant presence still flourishes among us. For I perceive that the separation of good people immediately seems prolonged. If, as I suppose, your spirit too has experienced this, let me know through a hastened exchange of writings that you likewise consider this interval of days long. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXXV. SYMMACHUS TO RUFINUS**

Custom and reason demanded that, since I intended to remain at home, I should request from the most august emperor leave from the journey he had ordered me to undertake. I explained the reason for my excuse in letters, which I ask your favor to commend through a gracious approach and a kindly reading. For nothing of mine would please me without the assistance of every good man. I speak of a matter known to all and never to be concealed by me: both friends and rivals know this. Some of them rejoice that their merits have earned them a place with you; others grieve that their wealth has not done so. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXXVI. SYMMACHUS TO RUFINUS**

I understood that it was not without reason that you had long refrained from writing. At last it became clear that the diligence of your services had been halted by impaired eyesight. Thus I, who had been anxious about that silence, confess that I approve your having postponed news of a harsh circumstance until the joy of your recovery, so that I might not first receive anxiety about the trouble that had arisen in you, rather than security that it had been removed.

Now that your health has returned to harmony with you, reward our friendship with more generous pages; otherwise, if they cease, I shall again fear something similar. But enough words on this subject. I rejoice exceedingly that Flavianus, the lord of my heart and your companion, clings to your spirit, to the grief of the wicked. For he often boasts to me of such a friendship. I had foreseen that this would happen, considering the virtues of both, whose likeness produces concord.

Therefore I receive more joy than surprise, and I ask you not to allow any evil eye to affect such friends. He does not need to be asked, since it is not expedient for him to wish anything else. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXXVII. SYMMACHUS TO RUFINUS**

Unknown men may be commended through a lengthy circuit of words. But the merits of Severianus, a man of senatorial rank, verified by the proven record of long military service, require no elaborate testimony. He held the foremost position in governing the cohorts of the urban prefecture and was transferred by law into the senatorial order.

It remains for him, after the dignity of the curia—which is greater than other honors—to offer the provinces a demonstration of his worth. He believes this will happen if, concerning this matter, you readily support him with a letter to my lord the prefect of the City. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO RUFINUS**

You have bitten my silence concerning the death of the citizen Emeritus with the most amusing argument in a letter.
