For what more ingenious device could have been devised to chastise me for suppressing the news than that I, a resident of the Caelian Hill, should learn of Rome through an unsolicited letter? But the recognized seriousness of your judgment imposed a scruple upon me. I feared that such a report might make me seem happy to you.

You know that humanity requires us, toward those whom we have esteemed only slightly and with whom we were previously at odds, to offer at least the reverence of silence in exchange for the grief that death ordinarily inspires. Therefore spare your oblique pen from striking at what I feared would displease your ears. Rather, give thanks to my circumspection, which makes room for your wit. And would that you often write letters in jest that you deny writing seriously!

Why do you use your talent’s resources so sparingly? I fear that hereafter it may be more useful for me to refrain from sending letters. For your next page about me was elicited by your offense at my silence. And so perhaps you will make amends for my fault by not returning my services. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXXIX. SYMMACHUS TO RUFINUS**

I would commend my son Flavianus to you, were he not summoned at your own wish. I shall therefore detract nothing from your kindness. It is sufficient for my young man, as evidence of a grateful disposition toward you, that he does not seek the assistance of his father’s letters. Nevertheless, I think piety requires me also, in his name, to confess that I am bound to you by gratitude. The result will be that you will heap upon him more gifts of your attention, since you have not one debtor in him alone. Farewell.

**LETTER XC. SYMMACHUS TO RUFINUS**

You are often the source of my joy, either its first cause or its only one. Formerly you announced my brother as quaestor, and now as prefect of the praetorium, in your letters. Thus every one of your letters contains some great cause of joy for me. What is more, the very words overflow, and the brilliance of your style bears witness to the liveliness of your spirit.

Since I cannot equal these things with their counterparts, I meet them with a prayer to the gods: may the fortune of the best men always be agreeable to your happiness. Farewell.

**LETTER XCI. SYMMACHUS TO RUFINUS**

For men distinguished by integrity and honor, another person’s speech adds nothing. Those conspicuous by their own light are not helped by borrowed testimonies. What sort of man, and how great, my lord and brother is, is evident. Our talent rightly yields to his praises.

There is nevertheless one thing that I do not think should be passed over: with him I share the closest fellowship of familial duties. This circumstance also commonly commends to you men whose merits are lesser. Hence I judge that your illustrious mind will readily and abundantly show him affection, which both his own distinction and the privilege of my friendship bring him. Farewell.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0221]

**LETTER ONE. SYMMACHUS TO STILICHO**

[Col. 0221D]

I confess that I remained silent for a long time so that your conversation might provide confidence for writing. But when I saw that I had not yet been prompted by any invitation to service, I was the first to burst into words of greeting, asking you most earnestly to deign to imitate this example. Farewell.

**LETTER II. CS. CS.**

My son Flavianus abounds in his own and his father’s influence, sufficient to win the favor of good men. But it is a matter of affection, which I truly owe my child, that, while I see that nothing is lacking from his merits, I should not neglect the duty of a parent. Therefore I do what is superfluous and add a crowning touch to what is already complete.

I believe this will do much to attach my Flavianus to Your Excellence, because you understand that I should count it as a favor that you would have granted him solely on your own judgment. Farewell.

**LETTER III. CS. CS.**

The distinguished Rufinus, who must be counted among the choicest members of our order, was proceeding to render you the services owed to you. He thought that he would be envious of me unless he undertook ours as well. Thus he brings you a greeting to be returned by me—a greeting I would often convey to you if it were easy to find men like him. His message is therefore rare because such an opportunity is rare.

We say nothing about the man himself. Conscious of his own merit, he avoids suspicions of seeking favor; and, coming before your judgment, he does not wish his recommendation to depend more upon a witness than upon a judge. Farewell.

**LETTER IV. SYMMACHUS TO STILICHO**

What the most distinguished order decided, when consulted by sacred command concerning the grief of the Africans and the complaints of the military men, you will learn plainly and openly by inspecting the records of the curia. But because you also ordered me, as a friend, to report the proceedings, I shall not conceal in summary what was decreed.

After the letters and judgments of our lord the emperor Honorius Augustus had been read, and after all the pages containing Gildo’s crimes had been reviewed, an equal movement of the good burst forth. We were therefore consulted in the senate according to ancestral custom—for the authority of a judgment could not have stood in accordance with the regular legal procedure—and with votes devoted to this great cause we gave satisfaction.

After the condemnation of the case, a supplication was added on behalf of the food supply of the Roman people. For we fear that delay at this intermediate stage may harm the grain convoys and give rise to a disturbance among the plebs. What I pronounced will come into your hands. You will find that I both asserted the justice of this action and pleaded the cause of public concord before our lord Arcadius. Farewell.

**LETTER V. SYMMACHUS TO STILICHO**

The man who is proceeding to offer thanks does not require a recommendation. For this reason I took care to spare my son Flavianus, relying on the benefits of your exalted position, this sort of parental trouble. It remains for me to write that his personal gratitude will follow, since nothing is more ready, through your virtues, to restore the fortunes of men.

You had restored his former position, which had been brought low, and it was thought that you had exhausted what could be offered. Now an honorable summons has been added to it, and the authority of your testimony helped it. You find new stages of benefaction and regard love as fickle if it has not received increase. O generosity of a fortunate genius! I do not know what more I could wish for my Flavianus, since by spontaneously anticipating us you make us appear shameless if we still desire anything. Farewell.

**LETTER VI. SYMMACHUS TO STILICHO**

I rejoice that I have obtained the travel permits with which you have deigned, through the virtue in which you excel, to assist my son’s praetorship. It remains for you to crown what you have supplied in accordance with the habit of your magnificent spirit, and to order my retainers, who have been sent to Spain to purchase chariot horses, to pass through immediately, since we are pressed by the time of the coming public games.

I do not dare to ask this of you, but leave it to your judgment whether you should order my desire to be assisted by letters sent to my friends. Farewell.

**LETTER VII. SYMMACHUS TO STILICHO**

I feel myself wholly unequal to giving you thanks for my son Flavianus. Although words are easier than deeds, I cannot equal the greatness of your benefaction in speech. Nor is it only my gratitude, since the honor lost with him has returned to favor. The senate and all good men share in it among themselves. Therefore it is difficult for one person’s speech to compensate for what the affection of so many has brought about.

You will therefore pardon me for saying little about you. Restoring an honor is something greater than bestowing one. Fortune allows the latter to happen; humanity accomplishes the former in opposition to fortune itself. The father of the emperors, received into heaven, had sent ahead other examples of clemency, and had restored to my Flavianus much that had been taken away by misfortune.

One and most important title of goodness remained for the heir, which our lord Honorius added to his father’s benefactions at your urging, interpreting, evidently, that the divine emperor had lacked time, not goodwill. Now, through a similar successor, the works of clemency interrupted by fate have been completed. The gentlest and most august emperor has placed a kind of summit upon the undertakings of his father. In return, I hope that you and those like you will be his advisers in gratitude. For those who counsel the supreme rulers of the empire toward pious and honorable deeds are instruments of a good age.

Our ruler certainly possesses a genius from a divine source and a nature ready for the course of every virtue. But, if I may use an image, even the best helmsmen are helped considerably by the hands of their rowers. Your faithfulness in military service and your affection of kinship make you especially friendly to his reputation. Hence you find ways to win love for him from every direction, and you remind a man occupied with greater matters to look upon private destinies.

Human misfortunes have been turned into flight, and nothing sad has remained in the senate. Honor has been bestowed on some and restored to others. Whatever we individually are is owed to one family. But I shall now keep within the limits of a letter, for I fear that these very words may weary your distinguished modesty, since they cannot equal the return due for your gratitude.

Rather, let those joys reward you which security in your merits produces. I do not wish you to expect from anyone’s words repayment for so great a benefaction. Above all, you know that only the reward of a good conscience can satisfy those who accomplish great things.

Nevertheless, like an immoderate man, I add one request: that you may continually cherish your benefits toward my Flavianus. Farewell.

**LETTER VIII. SYMMACHUS TO STILICHO**

I understand from the delay and hesitation over the divine rescript that something in the petition concerning my son’s praetorship has been judged inappropriate or doubtful. Therefore I owe you another account of my requests.

As for the gift of horses for the birthday of our lord Honorius, the unconquered emperor, although the proper time for that service has passed this year, I think my request could not have been censured. The request for theatrical water and silk garments has also often been granted to others before me, and is therefore supported by precedents.

As for the amphitheatrical spectacle, which I wish to be granted to my son’s public performance because of the capacity of the venue, the rescripts testify that it has not been denied even to the preliminary entertainments of quaestors; nor is it closed to consuls alone by any privilege.

You should know that I initiated this matter some time ago—not so that anything might be added to the consular dignity, which the fortunate office recently adorning your exalted position and formerly owed to you already ennobled—for the chief honor of all does not require such additions; but so that the Roman people, being more eager for this kind of pleasure, should not be constrained by the narrowness of a smaller venue.

For the rest, I do not see what special privilege it possesses, since even the census officials commonly present the games of absent persons there; and we wish to rival their modest scale. I write this so that I may not seem open to accusation of injustice or arrogance if something is denied. But I leave it to your most eminent and ever-revered Sublimity to weigh what you rightly judge appropriate.

For human opinion will judge rashly if I do not obtain what is just, although the spirit of your judgment is accustomed to bestow great things. Farewell.

**LETTER IX. SYMMACHUS TO STILICHO**

When the most distinguished order entrusted me with an embassy to Your Sublime Excellence, both the necessity of my country compelled me to undertake it and the assistance of your exalted position encouraged me. Having therefore reached the court of our lord and emperor Honorius, I did not delay in reporting to Your Magnificence the reason for my arrival.

The hope of this common service depends upon the judgment of your censorship. I therefore ask you, after reading the petitions of the most distinguished order, copies of which I have enclosed, to deign, amid the fortunate actions of your greatness, to inform my expectation by a letter concerning this matter as well. Farewell.

**LETTER X. CS. CS.**

Has forgetfulness of me so seized your exalted mind that you allow me to remain for so long deprived of your conversation? Or do you think that I can calmly tolerate the neglect of a personal service? Come, then, as is customary with your virtues, celebrate our friendship in writing, and at the same time consider how much more abundantly and readily I ought to return care through your letters—a care that I continually display even when you are silent. Farewell.

**LETTER XI. SYMMACHUS TO STILICHO**

I have often sent you letters, which I believe were suppressed. For when would you, a man most faithful to friendship and endowed with so many good qualities of spirit, have denied me the distinction of your service? Let this have been the fault of those whose fidelity failed in delivering pages.

Now a desirable outcome has provided my letters with a guarantor of the old-fashioned virtues. Therefore, through the diligence that the fidelity of a departing messenger promises, I renew toward you the observance of greeting. Your replies will cause me, prompted by reciprocity, to exercise frequently the use of the pen that I resumed late through modesty. Farewell.

**LETTER XII. SYMMACHUS TO STILICHO**

You prolong my consulship through your generosity and, as a public father, summon imperial generosity even for future offices. With what language, then, should I celebrate you, who, conspicuous by right in the height of honors, also furnish the apparatus of praetors? For you consider that the duties even of private persons ought to be appropriate to later generations.

Thus you continually add zeal for doing good to our lord Honorius, emperor of divine stock, and teach the unconquered prince to encourage senatorial modesty through gifts. You alone among all can give him thanks on my behalf, since you were the author of the benefaction before anyone else.

I shall testify to this at my son’s public games, when the course of leopards fills the Roman arena, and when the more justified applause and joyful acclamations will be owed to you. I would go on longer, were it not that your noble modesty, equal to your other virtues, avoids burdens of praise.

I shall therefore be sparing in words while showing deference to your singular modesty. But let your lofty Sublimity hold this fixed: my gratitude, though sparing in speech, overflows in my heart. Farewell.

**LETTER XIII. SYMMACHUS TO STILICHO**

I announce that I have returned to my homeland, though I have not yet recovered my health. But if your arrival smiles upon me, I hope that good health will soon return to harmony with me. Farewell.

**LETTER XIV. SYMMACHUS TO STILICHO**

When we wished to unite our children in a marital bond, our deliberation first consulted Your Magnificence on this matter, so that the auspice of a fortunate undertaking might be received from the public father. God has granted the fulfillment of our nuptial vows.

Now the honor of accepting the wedding gift must be paid to your exalted position both by custom and by affection. We ask you kindly to extend your hand and heart toward accepting this service. Our festivities still desire this summit of joy: that you, who before all others deigned to be the author of the relationship to be joined through our sons, may remain equally its approver. Farewell.

**LETTER XV. SYMMACHUS TO BATHON**

[Col. 0226C]

That suspicion does not apply to you, that you might be thought deliberately negligent of friendship. Your spirit is tenacious of loyalty, and just as you exercise cautious prudence in receiving friendships, so you show firm constancy in retaining them.

Therefore I never supposed that I had been removed from the number of the others to whom, at the beginning of the year, you bestowed the consular gift; and now I believe that more has been conferred upon me than upon the rest. For what a general offering gave to them, a special concern has restored to us.

In this matter I ought not even to be angry with those who wished me to be deprived of the earlier honor. For it could not otherwise have happened that I should deserve what another’s deceit had taken away from me. Your continual favor will therefore remain in my heart, and the memory of your steadfast service will not be weakened by any forgetfulness, whether error or deceit brought this about.

You have taught everyone to think nothing cunningly devised can further destroy friendships that people see growing through their own intrigues. Farewell.

**LETTER XVI. SYMMACHUS TO BATHON**

I count your letters among my chief joys, since they bear witness to a brotherly spirit and interpret true devotion. The more frequently I receive them, the more earnestly and abundantly I desire them. Satiety in good things is difficult, and pleasant things most strongly occupy our spirits when they seem to fill them.

Write, then, more often, as you do, and do not fear that you will find me ungrateful, when you see that I am so desirous both of your affection and of your conversation. Farewell.

**LETTER XVII. SYMMACHUS TO PROTADIUS**

I am indeed too sick at heart and unequal to performing my duties amid such great grief. But fortune will never have so much power over me that, overcome by sorrow, I should conceal your honor. Rather, I make literary consolations remedies for my wound. Although they are weak in proportion to the greatness of my grief, your conversation nevertheless brings me the most effective medicine.

See what I expect: service, if you think fit, owed to friendship and destined to benefit my afflicted spirit. Farewell.

**LETTER XVIII. SYMMACHUS TO PROTADIUS**

[Col. 0227B]

You falsely boast to me of your passion for hunting, since your letters breathe the thyme of eloquence. Do not try to deceive me: leisure and business have different signs. The rustic smells of bitter herbs; the wine-breathing reveler belches; a headache follows one who has swum; you, friends of the Muses, belch forth the flower of Helicon.

What tracking of hares, what birthdays of dogs, what hunting festivals are you inventing for us? Do you think I can be drawn away from the study of books to those pursuits you claim as your own? Not even in my youth, when age allowed it, did I take care to keep Amyclaean or Molossian hounds. How much less do I wish for such things now, as my years incline toward old age!

> After my beard, brighter, fell beneath the shears.

But suppose that I sometimes wish to pursue rustic pleasures. Which of the foremost men of the senate has such abundant freedom that, amid the cares of his country, he can breathe through woodland labor? You recently learned of the grain complaints of the great city. This was followed by a shortage of oil, and the complaint about grain still remains. For this reason, exhausted by these circumstances, we sent men of the curia to petition for remedies; and there is hope that the most clement and divine emperor will respond to the petitions with salutary assistance.

Meanwhile the city resounds with the murmuring of those who suffer. You, my friend, are now hunting and distressing men who are already too anxious by boasting of your pleasures. But how can I believe that so great and remarkable a man as you has leisure to search out the lairs of hares? Why, then, do you ask me for a history in the same letters in which you proclaim the feast days and workdays of your dogs?

True pursuits cannot be concealed. For, unwillingly, you confess amid your playful fictions the disease of reading. I shall go no farther. You ask that the ancient histories of the Gauls be brought into your hands. Turn over the closing books of the writer of Patavium, in which the deeds of Caesar are explained; or, if Livy is inadequate to your desire, take Caesar’s *Ephemeris*, extracted from my little library so that it might be sent to you as a gift.

This will teach you the origins, locations, battles, and everything that existed in the customs or laws of the Gallic provinces. I shall strive, if fortune aids my wish, also to procure Pliny Secundus’s account of the German wars.

Meanwhile, be content with the reliability of the work offered, and with our brother Minervius, the most learned and most kindly judge of my writings—and why should I call him a judge, when I prefer to call him an applauder?—and a companion in reading. Although I know that this need not at all be requested from you. For equal mutual love does not permit a good thing to be divided between you. Farewell.

**LETTER XIX. SYMMACHUS TO PROTADIUS**

We should begin with favorable matters; therefore, in what I may call the preface of my letter, I offer greetings and wishes for your health. Next I append my request. Flavianus, an illustrious man and our common child, long struggling through the hardships of fortune but restored to stability by the benefaction of the divine emperor, has been ordered to pay his father’s solarium payment, with the assessment of prices heavily inflated. His resources are not sufficient for so great a burden.

Therefore, if you have any power, see to it that humane consideration for the times show mercy to the afflicted household; otherwise the property restored through indulgence will be stripped away by a sale to meet the interest. As we hope, the young Augustus will follow his father’s benefactions; just as the succession of the empire reached him from his father, so may the imitation of his goodness do likewise. Farewell.

**LETTER XX. SYMMACHUS TO PROTADIUS**

You brightened my day with a letter that testified that the diligence of our friendship is alive in you. Great pleasure slipped into my heart. Indeed, I had decided to anticipate your service with a letter, if I had learned that you had come to Milan. I had assigned this task to your brother, whose affection for you I would not yield to, so that he might announce your arrival quickly.

But through some collusion, delaying the report, he granted you first place in beginning the greeting. I am not displeased that your brother’s favor takes precedence with you.

Meanwhile I must respond to your inquiry, by which you ask to know through what pursuits we pass our lives. While my son is being initiated into Greek letters, I have once again joined myself to his studies as though I were his equal. Piety commands us to become children again, so that shared labor may introduce the sweetness of letters to our children.

Your affairs are not in the bud but in the fruit; and, as I have learned by report, your most eloquent young man presses upon his father with the nearest steps of eloquence. How fortunate you are, my friend, if you are surpassed! Our instruction is still laboring to create a flower, and a single effort cannot be commanded to produce everything at once. Thus, amid pure anxiety and diligence, the progress of our dear child slowly grows.

Plainly, as I judge, we have satisfied your questions. Now in turn I desire to learn the course of your affairs. It is easy, if you consider me worthy of letters, to send them, since you may use the messengers of your brother who is stationed at court. Farewell.

**LETTER XXI. SYMMACHUS TO PROTADIUS**
After the ruinous famine of our city, when the grain supply had been restored to calm conditions, I had reached the coast of Campania. Just then your close associate Martianus arrived, bringing me your letter as a friend on your behalf. When I read it through with delighted eyes, my appreciation of those celebrated shores increased. For it generally happens that, through fortunate events, the honor and pleasure of places grow and display tokens of affection. No one cultivates friendship more ardently than one who is angered by neglect. I want you to understand this in such a way that the grounds for my duty remain intact: I acknowledge no offense arising from any cooling of my concern for you.

[Col. 0229A] Why, just recently, with our mutual brother as witness—the man whom the magistracy of the city embraces—I sent you a double greeting by letter. Must I also answer for the reliability of travelers? Consider how rare or concealed are men’s journeys over long distances; add the treachery of those who frustrate entrusted messages. I hope you will not accuse an absent man of laziness if you reflect that, both in sending pages and in returning them, an opportunity and a trustworthy messenger belonging to someone else are required.

But why do I strive to establish my diligence toward you by these proofs? I believe our Martianus himself carefully revealed to you how vividly the memory and praise of you live upon my lips and in my heart. As for what you think about my writings or my silence, I do not ask: for speaking to you frequently is less than speaking constantly about you. Why, then, do you ask for writings, which are often poorly entrusted? What is conveyed about an absent man is freer and truer. So, as you wish, glory in the frequency of your pen; I surpass your service in judgment. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXII. SYMMACHUS TO PROTADIUS

A double message from you reached my hands at the same time, while you continue to cultivate our friendship through manifold services. Following your example—for affection is measured by its manner, not by its gift—I return two letters to you: one will be delivered by our brother Eusebius, a part of my heart; this one by Martyrius, a youth of excellent promise. At the same time I ask you to remember to emulate the reliability of this repayment when the interest of frequent pages begins in turn to press upon you. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXIII. SYMMACHUS TO PROTADIUS

[Col. 0229C]

A certain observance had until now held me back from sending the first letter. An old-established custom has ordained that the greeting of those who are separated from their own homes by a long journey should arrive first. I therefore give and owe abundant thanks for having been anticipated by the service through which I learned that, after shaking off your illness, you are in better health; and it has, in a way, reopened my hand for writing. In return I wish you better progress.

For although, in accordance with your character and birth, you have attained the summit of honors, Fortune has not yet restored to you the perfect reward and due recompense. Even if she has bestowed great things upon you, she will never equal your merit. I now return to the customary words by which, fulfilling the duty of greeting according to tradition, I ask for a reciprocal gift. You understand that the minds of writers are spurred on by mutual exchange. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXIV. SYMMACHUS TO PROTADIUS

In the Sallustian records there are letters of Africanus which Jugurtha, after the destruction of Numantia, brought before Micipsa as witnesses to his own distinction. In the presence of our brother Florentinus, I think these should now be committed to the pages word for word, because the two men shone with equal glory in their affairs, and the same honor of testimony appropriately belongs to the excellence of each.

Scipio willingly restored that testimony to the Numidian king; we, though unwilling, yield so great an ornament to you. For it must be admitted that it was out of regard for you that we allowed this man to depart.

[Col. 0230A] As for me, if you ask to be informed of anything concerning our friendship, he will be the index of your inquiries who was the arbiter of my affairs. Believe this much from my letter: that I am well and cherish your diligence, which the reciprocal trust between us promises will be emulated by me. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXV. SYMMACHUS TO PROTADIUS

I longed for your letters when many people were arriving whom I had assumed would bring me your message. But when that hope disappointed my expectation, I even took the initiative in addressing you, so that by the example of my service I might provoke you to a similar concern.

I therefore ask you not to allow the vigor of our friendship to weaken or the duties of friendship to grow cold—duties that I impatiently seek—although I know that your concern for me, even when you refrain from writing, is faithfully preserved in your heart. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXVI. SYMMACHUS TO PROTADIUS

I overflow with the greatest joy when I see that equal honor is not denied to my literary services; and for that reason I am encouraged by the love of exercising my pen. For it is not right that an enthusiasm which equal kindness rewards with a return of favor should grow sluggish.

I would have wished to say more, but your modesty should not be burdened by an excessive excursion of praise. Farewell, and, as you do, preserve our friendship as an example. Although we are unequal in elegance of expression, we shall strive to be equal in steadfast devotion. Farewell again.

## EPIST. XXVII. SYMMACHUS TO PROTADIUS

[Col. 0230C]

You often accuse me of laziness in writing. I do not know what could grieve me more. Omitted speech seems to accuse friendship of neglect; sparing speech, of childish incompetence. Yet I prefer that you reproach my talent rather than my character: as long as I remain mindful of myself, you cannot charge me with forgetting you.

You have also criticized me for joining the greeting I send you to those addressed to your brothers. I am indeed poor in speech and sparing of paper. But you ought not to blame me for embracing them, as is evident. Our curia’s law, however, makes the authority of the greater number prevail with me.

What if I invited all of you together to a convivial meal? Would you refuse to be received on the same couch as your brothers? Nor should you begrudge me if, being creditor of a single letter, I somehow exact from you a profit at triple interest. Nothing is paid to me by each of you on behalf of the other. Or why do you demand that my services be divided when you unite in reproaching me? Farewell.

## EPIST. XXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO PROTADIUS

It is clear to everyone that human talents are ready to find fault. But you, who are counted among rare excellences, should stop pursuing what nature makes easiest and undertake the defense of my long silence, which is supported by many arguments of justice—if you observe that, toward the neighborhood of the Rhine, from which both the excellent emperor and the most powerful magistrate are now absent, none of our people is traveling in the meantime.

Perhaps someone, unknown to me, undertakes so long a journey for a private matter. You have greater opportunity to send people who are departing for Rome. First, because people from every nation gather from all directions at the common capital of the Empire; and then because the most merciful emperor, who resides in that region, is followed by the diverse wishes and needs of all.

And yet, although many causes offer you messengers, you are equally restrained from writing, and you are not assailed by any complaint from us. My confidence makes me certain that I am loved even by one who is silent. Therefore let the confidence of our friendship not depend upon letters. Chance creates the intervals between them. Mutual trust in our care for one another resents the assertion of the tongue.

Besides, you ask for lengthy letters, as though you intended to test how much I have progressed in writing in my gray old age. I have always been like a stream running dry, avoiding broader banks so that studied brevity might conceal my poverty. Now even the heavy years, if anything was trickling from my heart, have drunk it up.

Moreover, there is no subject matter available for extending what we write. You know my leisure, about which it is tedious for either of us to speak at length to the other. Greater affairs suit more words. Let the measure of our speech be the same as that of our fortune.

I would rather, after the manner of the Aborigines, write a greeting of eternal life upon wood or bark. Egypt may have woven volumes of papyrus for libraries and the forum. Let it sometimes be enough to celebrate friendship: if you are well, all is well.

I wish these very exchanges of greetings, which you complain are brief, to remain long between us while we are apart. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXIX. SYMMACHUS TO PROTADIUS

I hope that, as I have learned by report, you are coming to the neighboring region. Perhaps what I have heard is true. Nevertheless, either to be handed to you in person by our brother Minervius or to be sent to your homeland, I entrusted two little speeches of mine to his fidelity.

I ought to be brief in this letter. For the greedy affection with which you will receive those works for reading will be satisfied by them. Yet I warn you not to let the title of one speech alter your opinion of me. For the rejection of the censorship weighs upon us at the outset, if one looks only at the subject of the argument. But once you have read the words, you will return to agreement with my view.

The authority of our entire order preferred this part, which was rejected in the storm of events, lest under a respectable name doors be opened to those accustomed to solicit the offices of arbitrary power. You will find many assertions of usefulness and honor in the body of the speech itself. Our concern desires your judgment on both works. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXX. SYMMACHUS TO PROTADIUS

[Col. 0231D]

You know that silence is a similar fault between us; and therefore blame is unjustly assigned to me for what is common to both of us. Nevertheless I have a defense: the departures of travelers are not known, and you do not remain in the same places, exchanging either Trier, with its civic religious observances, or the five provinces, with the pleasures of leisure.

I have a permanent station at Rome; and now I have an even greater reason for remaining, since the presence of your eminent brother holds me here through his care and delights me through his glory. Thus you could have joined our writings by a single route, which a brother and one equal to his brother might have received. I am glad that you have seen to this, even if late.

Yet when you refrained from writing, I did not think that your diligence toward me had suffered any decline. Such is the confidence of true friendship that it derives an estimation of mutual affection from its own fidelity.

I am tired of saying more in this vein. I therefore pass to that part of your message which seems to touch upon your desire for my speeches. You say that our writings came into your hands through our brother Minervius, who does not abstain from my trifles, driven more by a literary curiosity than by proper enjoyment.

If you have so much leisure that, to dispel boredom, you even seek out some tasteless things, I shall exhibit whatever we have worked upon with the pen, confident of the pardon promised me by your affection.

I almost passed over what I ought to have accused in the foremost place. Has the simple use of our letters really perished, so that you prefer to your pages the embellishments of the present age?

[Col. 0232B] Let us therefore return to unadorned titles of names; and when a greeting is spoken or returned, let us consider that nothing is more honorable or pleasing than our very names. Let my letter certainly serve as an example to you: if you disdain to emulate it, I shall seem marked both by arrogance and by association with the others, whose words are greatly suspect but whose feelings contain no refinement. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXXI. SYMMACHUS TO PROTADIUS

The same consul who had summoned me summoned you to Milan. I hoped that a shared purpose would bring us together. But when illness kept you away, I suffered most bitterly the loss of the joy for which I had waited.

Now, after the consular celebrations have been completed beyond the magnanimity of everyone, I am returning to Rome, where the most eminent magistrate has immediately promised that he will come, with his son-in-law supporting the pledge.

How I wish that, if your health has fully returned, you would compensate by your arrival for the pardon you owe and, by one route, both offer the Senate a voluntary service and pay what you owe the consul. But why should I hope for so much, when it has been useless to hope for lesser things? How long will you prefer the hunt to the toga? Farewell.

## EPIST. XXXII. SYMMACHUS TO PROTADIUS

I wish our debt of affection to grow daily. But I do not wish to owe anything to your letters, which generally reproach me as lazy. Therefore, since your two letters were not returned to me together, I answer them in equal number but in a single dispatch.

We are as well as advancing age, inclining toward old age, permits. We rarely visit the countryside, but our practice of reading is much more regular. You have abundant opportunity both to live in the country and to cultivate learning. That is why you address us so often: all your time is claimed by leisure for intellectual inquiry.

But the boldness of our confidence will not yield to yours. You may draw from the records of the ancients and yourself commit them to pages for learning. Nevertheless, with parched words I shall trouble the writings of the man whom I must read out of affection and judgment, so that I may compensate for the losses of those works which I neglect. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO PROTADIUS

You delight in my letters. I believe it. That is why you often and ardently demand them. But I do not immediately deserve the mark of laziness if I cannot satisfy the greed of your love for me.

Do you think that the memory of friendship slips away through silence? Beware of forming such opinions about hearts whose judgments are eternal. Faith carries great weight, and, bound by a voluntary oath, it does not need the reminder of the pen.

Have I not always written these things to you? Yet you do not abandon your old complaint. What if it is better to remain silent for a long time? Do you not see that the oracles of old have ceased to speak, that no letters are read in the Cumaean cave, that Dodona speaks through its leaves no longer, and that no verse is heard from the Delphic springs?

Permit me, then, as a little man fashioned by Prometheus’s hand, to cease committing to papyrus what has long not been read upon the leaves of prophets. Yet I do not want you to suspect that I have announced silence to you. In writing I shall observe an interval of time as great as the distance between us in place.

You too must overcome your impatience with the reasoning that prevents my letters from being delivered to you every day while you are stationed near the Rhine by our Albula. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO PROTADIUS

The fruits I gather from your letters are indeed great. But they become richer as they pass through the hands of our mutual brothers. Each adds something of his own to your writings. I therefore count as received from you whatever I gather from all their mouths.

But consider again how difficult it is to answer the variety of so many lofty talents. For you are equals, yet not alike. Thus they bring me no less difficulty in returning than sweetness in receiving.

Nature has imposed this law upon all human joys: cares follow pleasures. The first day after the birth of offspring makes parents happy; soon dutiful anxieties drive away that brief grace. Honor is joyful at its beginning; afterward the heat of labors enters the mind. It would take a long time if I continued weaving together similar examples.

I must also consider what it is permissible to say about so great a man. You swore rashly. You complain that letters are committed to perishable paper, yet you have bound yourself by an enormous oath of judgment. Are you making sport of me, imagining that the things I speak to you more casually should be transferred onto stylus tablets or limewood writing boards, lest advancing old age readily destroy writings on papyrus?

The divination of the Marsian seers was indeed impressed upon perishable bark. The Cumaean warnings were recorded on woven linen. You even order my letters to be poured into silken volumes after the manner of the Achaemenids.

Great is the weight of your authority, and I cannot regard as pleasing what you assert under oath. But when I look again at myself, confidence falters and conscience resists the testimony. Thus what the person of the judge makes credible, the distrust of the listener rejects.

You alone, therefore, will remove the uncertainty if you order your love henceforth to speak more sparingly of my praises. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXXV. SYMMACHUS TO MINERVIUS

You stole ahead of my modesty by writing first; I want you to believe that I regard myself as bound to you by this service. But I cannot allow you to seem, so to speak, a new greeter arriving at the house of friendship.

Long ago I received your virtues, equal to those of your brothers, into the possession of my heart. You have also grown into a legitimate share of your father’s inherited intimacy with me, although the fullness of my love has been bestowed upon each of you individually: for although the goods of the spirit are thought to be scattered among many, they nevertheless benefit each person fully and undividedly.

Moreover, since we are fellow soldiers of Palatine eloquence, I extended my right hand to your friendship. Therefore, joined by so many and such great pledges, let us not measure the age of our affection by an apprenticeship in letter-writing. For just as the mind is swifter than letters, so it was earlier to love than to write. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXXVI. SYMMACHUS TO MINERVIUS

After travelers made it publicly known that you had come to Milan, I hoped for your letters shortly afterward. But when my expectation was deceived and no return was made for my hope, I claimed for my work the service I had presumed from you.

My brother Bassus, a distinguished man, also increased my reason for writing. Having been separated from us for a short time, he ought to be transferred by me into your heart. I added another page to be delivered to your brother, if chance should favor your return to your homeland.

He had long before sprinkled us with the flowers of his eloquence and had entrusted to our pleasant leisure the copying of the ancient records of Gaul. It has happened as desired that, through you, both things should be returned to him: the honor of my letter and the fruit of the history he sought. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXXVII. SYMMACHUS TO MINERVIUS

My friend Paulus has long served in the sacred treasury, but you should not judge him by the rank of his service. For by the integrity of his character he surpasses the modesty of his office.

Do not despise the man if you examine the number of his pay grades. His advancement has been slower because of a modesty that causes him to remain beneath the rank his merits deserve. Yet he does not regret having stood for a long time. He has been reserved for your judgment, under which emerging will be the greatest reward for his delay.

Since the integrity of his life and the length of his service support him, it is fitting that, with me as petitioner and you as sponsor, he should reach the rewards due to him. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO MINERVIUS

My friend Gaudentius has taken refuge in the shelter of your patronage, a man worthy of being loved in every respect. He is of senatorial birth; his mind and modesty are nobler than his origin and lineage.

If you do not think my testimony tainted by the cosmetics of favor, accept him as one deserving affection. A long examination of his services will make you judge that I have said too little. Farewell.

## EPIST. XXXIX. SYMMACHUS TO MINERVIUS

Love my lord and son Flavianus as much as you understand me to wish, and, if possible, enter into a contest with me in loving him. I shall rejoice if you win. But I shall consider this proved only when he himself begins to honor you beyond the measure of my diligence.

For if friendship consists in reciprocal services, it will be easy for me to measure your feeling from his. Farewell.

## EPIST. XL. SYMMACHUS TO MINERVIUS

[Col. 0235A]

If you consider how rare innocent men are, you will love my son Desiderius, who should be counted among the choice of the few. You will not think my judgment about him mistaken when he comes under your scrutiny.

In the meantime, I ask that through me the sanctuary of your friendship be opened to him, and that you offer a kindly ear to him as he recounts his just causes. If you give him good counsel, my trust—which has faithfully fulfilled before him his hope of your benevolence—will be vindicated. Farewell.

## EPIST. XLI. SYMMACHUS TO MINERVIUS

In securing the acquittal of our Rusticus, I conveyed my request to you; my son Caecilianus supplied the assistance. It is therefore not consistent with my modesty to seize the gratitude due to another’s labor.

Let us both give him credit for what your care ordered to be done but my health was unable to carry out. Farewell.

## EPIST. XLII. SYMMACHUS TO MINERVIUS

I know what you think of me; but, confident in your judgment, I now refuse to be praised. Rather emulate the silent admiration with which I regard you, because right reverence carries greater weight.

Let us leave verbal flatteries to new friends among themselves. Let reciprocal praises help them along until they attain the confidence of a pact. Let our affection be hidden in the sanctuary of our hearts. The dwelling of the heart itself is concealed. From there, let your care look back upon me.

But it is not my way to give a form to letters. I want you to consider only this: since you are most generous in praise, what I am praised for by you may seem little to me unless I am placed under a greater obligation.

Moreover, I ask why the antiquated practice preserved in our preceding names was absent from the weaving together of the letter. Let others be raised up by titles of grandeur. I reject the designation of magnificence, unless perhaps you think me wicked because I do not offer the same soothing words to your honor. Feigned love is submitted to those words; the cultivation of friendship is sincere.

Let white garments, not robes embroidered with bands, clothe our fidelity. What use is a lofty rank of reverence to me? I would rather be loved by a brother than looked up to. Farewell.

## EPIST. XLIII. SYMMACHUS TO MINERVIUS

My closest friend Eusebius, an old soldier of the private treasury, was for a long time prevented by illness from attending upon you. I ask you not to have him listed among those who remain behind.

But the granting of pardon will not endure unless, having been appeased, you add some benefit to him. I therefore ask that he be ordered to devote his concern to demanding the public debts owed throughout Etruria, so that he may remove the blame of his long absence by some commendable labor. Farewell.

## EPIST. XLIV. SYMMACHUS TO MINERVIUS

A greeting sent by you always creates joy for me, but especially one entrusted to be brought by my friends. It adds things worth seeking in your writings and conveys to my hearing, if anything was missing from my reading, some report about you.

Thus, just now, your man Sebastius, after delivering your letter, when I asked whether you were doing sufficiently according to my wishes, offered me an image of your presence. He will now also tell you what you wish to know about my leisure, for I have remained in the Laurentian woods, clinging to rural quiet.

What else should I pursue more eagerly, as I sometimes restore my failing health, often avoid crowds, and always cherish the innocence of letters? Farewell.

## EPIST. XLV. SYMMACHUS TO MINERVIUS

I have no confidence either in my pen or in my talent. But your kindness provokes my boldness. I have therefore sent two of our little speeches for your learned consideration.

One, concerning the son of Polybius, arose from a recent matter; the other, prepared by me long ago when the issue was being debated in the curia, has now come forth enlarged by more extensive work. Its subject is the rejected censorship, which the authority of the entire Senate at that time drove away.

Do not be surprised that the most dignified order rejected this office. In our speech you will find no trivial reasons for avoiding that power. Farewell.

## EPIST. XLVI. SYMMACHUS TO MINERVIUS

I ought to commend to you men of proven excellence, since it is a special duty to insert them into your friendships. I therefore ask you to receive men easily preeminent in birth and character, and to honor them at their first meeting with intimate familiarity.

The provincial Campanians have entrusted them with a common embassy. The affair abounds in justice; my concern commends the persons. You will observe two reasons for exercising kindness toward them: publicly, the fairness of their petitions; privately, a disinterested advocate intervenes. Farewell.

## EPIST. XLVII. SYMMACHUS TO MINERVIUS

I saw our son Protadius at Rome, and nothing from the adornments of your family was lacking from his recommendation except your letters. When I had asked for them, you, though far away, replied that a journey through Further Gaul had been imposed upon him by his father-in-law.

I did not readily accept the young man’s excuse; I approved the rest of his character. This is enough for his father’s ears, for I do not want testimony based on a brief experience to seem favorable to me.

At the same time I fear that I may diminish your love for your son, who ought not to be helped in your eyes through the support of another’s recommendation. Farewell.

## EPIST. XLVIII. SYMMACHUS TO MINERVIUS

[Col. 0236D]

I extend letters to some people as a courtesy. But these are for my lord and brother Bassus, whose equitable claim is not distinct from his sister's; indeed, it is fortified by the assistance of the law.

For he asks that a rebellious slave be brought to him, yet neither the authority of a divine command nor the vigor of the comes Africanus has been able to reach the man in his investigation. Conscious of his bold crime, he avoided the punishment threatening him by fleeing into hiding.

Since, then, it is said that the honorable comes of Africa has sent you an official letter concerning his deed and wickedness, it will be an act of your justice and kindness, in favor of our family, to invoke divine judgment, so that an innocent household may no longer be terrified by the malicious inventions of a worthless slave. Farewell.

## EPIST. XLIX. SYMMACHUS TO MINERVIUS

[Col. 0237A]

While I was staying at Milan, I performed the service of greeting you; and now, having retraced my journey, I have not denied careful attention to the duty of writing. I suppose you expect me to demand repayment for my letter. That repayment is promised not by my insistence but plainly by your affection. Let those who do not deserve the spirit’s services demand a return from the pen. Farewell.

## EPIST. L. SYMMACHUS TO FLORENTINUS

You long delayed giving me news of your brother’s arrival; I believe you did so so that the honor of your greeting might come first. I recognize this dutiful collusion; yet I believe that I alone call the two of you into a contest of friendly writings.

“You have leisure,” you will say, “and that gives you this confidence in your services.” What of the fact that the honor of the quaestorship and your experience in drafting decrees have cultivated you even more? My condition of private life is shared with him.

Would that the vigilance of the good emperor might also claim his services for itself. It must be endured: both of you may please through devotion, even if both cease writing to me. Farewell.

## EPIST. LI. SYMMACHUS TO FLORENTINUS

I learn from events that you do everything for the welfare of Flavianus, a most distinguished man and my cherished son. From this arises hope, and my spirit rises, that his remaining difficulties may be healed under you as physician.

Having obtained great things through the kindness of the divine emperor, he is still, so to speak, strangled by one knot of misfortune: although a poor man, now severely drained by the impairment of his patrimony, he is ordered to pay the assessed value of his father’s assistance.

Therefore through you and men like you the impending ruin must be removed. Nor is the matter difficult to obtain. For what imperial clemency has remitted to many troubled by the envy directed against them, a much fairer pardon will relax when it is requested in the father’s name.

This concession will also contribute to the glory of the age, if a pious successor adds what was lacking from the emperor’s benefactions. Farewell.

## EPIST. LII. SYMMACHUS TO FLORENTINUS

I cannot express in words how many joys a single day has brought me all at once. I believe you recognize the reason, of which you were the author. For a third honor of your writings raised to its summit the two letters of our mutual brothers.

Thus, since the choice among good things is difficult, I hesitated for a while over which page I should read first; such was my longing for each one individually. Soon I read through them all with an eager sweep, lest I delay my perusal by lingering. Reading them once was not enough, so that repetition might impress anything the first eagerness had passed over.

There was a varied charm of expression in each person’s words, and only in this did the letters differ. For my one hand had dictated them all. I could honestly add greater praise. But although your ears rejoice in the praises of your brothers, your modesty cannot bear a share in the glorious testimony.

It remains for me to answer briefly your request—expressed under the pretext of an invitation from the curia—that I return. We are preparing to return to your sight by the Ides of November, provided circumstances assist our plans.

If the promised day seems late, I do not want the Senate’s embassy to be delayed on my account. It was long ago entrusted to distinguished men and furnished with instructions; it requires no addition either of persons or of petitions. It is fitting, therefore, to stand by what has been arranged, and it is not lawful to overturn by new negotiations what was confirmed by the example of the recent disagreement.

As you write, you yourself saw these matters before me; all the more must we adhere to the decisions commended to me by your authority and to you by our agreement. Farewell.

## EPIST. LIII. SYMMACHUS TO FLORENTINUS

You have risen through your military rank by such labor that you ought to assist the fortunes of my friend Benedictus, whom the injustice of Fortune, though subject to no charge, drove from his position and deprived of his honor.

To win your favor for him, not only his integrity but also my recommendation ought to open the way. For I believe that my letters carry such weight with you that it is permissible to hope for success even if I were asking something difficult.

I thought this should be mentioned so that you might understand what we think about your character and friendship, and how much justice ought either to benefit or to stand beside this man. Farewell.

## EPIST. LIV. SYMMACHUS TO FLORENTINUS

You excuse yourself for having remained silent until now. This fault is shared. For poor health also kept me away from literary exchange for a long time. I suppose you shuddered after reading the bitter news you learned about me.

Return to a happier state of mind: by God’s favor I have recovered my health. Let forgiveness for our literary cessation therefore be easy for both of us. Let us each forgive the other for what both of us have done wrong.

But what are you whispering to me about the meager shipments from Africa? May the present year not imitate the fortune of earlier ones. Providence will, I hope, block the gloomy paths of misfortune by informing sacred ears and correcting the judges whose concern is the importation of grain.

Nor does the season obstruct hope. The sea is still open to proper navigation, and autumn has not yet plunged into winter. Nevertheless, amid all this, I am pleased that you are anxious and, through dutiful fear, anticipate necessity.

A better outcome will reward your care, and the fruit of your praise will make it sweet for you afterward to have been afraid. Farewell.

## EPIST. LV. SYMMACHUS TO FLORENTINUS

[Col. 0238D]

I repay with equal honor the greeting sent to me by you. I wish that the practice of alternating our pens might often come to both of us. But since distance does not allow this to occur according to our common desire, let the principle of patience satisfy us.

Certainly forgiveness for mutual delays ought to be ready between us. You will not excuse yourself with equal ease for the fact that I learned of the marriage of our son Minervius from the report of others rather than from your letters.

Were you afraid that I would miss a coin struck in gold by you? My modesty could have kept silent about the loss of the little gift. Love does not know how to forgive the denial of joy.

And yet, since I am kindly disposed toward my own people, I promise you remission of this offense once you have come before me in writing with news of the grandson who has been born. Farewell.

## EPIST. LVI. HERE ENDS [THE SECTION] TO FLORENTINUS. HERE BEGINS [THE SECTION] TO THE BROTHERS MINERVIUS, PROTADIUS, AND FLORENTINUS JOINTLY

[Col. 0239A]

Both your harmony and my weakness during these days cause me to join you in the greeting of a single page. You will regard this either as reasonable in view of your shared affection or as deserving pardon because of the circumstances.

For you will judge the exhaustion of my strength when a trembling hand has moved to sign this letter. In addition, the dutiful haste of our son Nemesius toward his father and ancestral home has sought more a formal declaration of service from me than a fulfillment of it.

The occasion requires that, after the greeting already given, I bear witness to his flourishing character. But I fear that I may seem to display my own efforts, which would have contributed more to the young man’s cultivation of the liberal arts had a brother’s misfortune not broken the course of two men.

This, however, I can say with the utmost sincerity: his parents’ happiness has indeed been diminished in one respect, but he is able to suffice for the joy of his family in place of both. Farewell.

## EPIST. LVII. SYMMACHUS TO MINERVIUS, PROTADIUS, AND FLORENTINUS

Resume the course of the custom you have until now neglected, with me as the leader of your familial services, since I was the first to break the common silence. I do not ask for letters in proportion to your number, although the love of each individually owes me this exchange.

It is a matter of great indulgence that you repay by alternating compensation the interest which I alone pay out to you. Farewell.

## EPIST. LVIII. SYMMACHUS TO EUPRAXIUS

I receive annual fruits of joy from your letters. Spain pays me this return, these resources. Therefore, when the routes of ships open after winter has been driven away, I commend your pages to the winds; this year, indeed, delivers them frequently, but late.

For autumn was already declining when your people touched the Tiber. This caused them to remain with us because navigation had failed. I therefore advise you, in accordance with your justice, to regard their delay favorably.

Although first, in my name, pardon must be sought for my having neglected the right of choice you gave me concerning four curule horses. I want you to believe that this abstention was not caused by disdain. But since I found none of them eager under the yoke or gentle upon the back, the option, not stirred by their merits, yielded to the circumstances.

It seems timely to solicit your diligence with prayers, so that horses noble in appearance and speed may be prepared for my son’s praetorian office. Twice before we have come into people’s mouths through the distinction of our productions. It seems necessary to satisfy the expectation that has grown through precedent.

Therefore I commend to your affection the cause of our reputation, which for a little while ought to bend your strictness of life and gravity of mind toward the ears of the public. The price will be supplied from home, to be paid at your discretion to the owners of noble four-horse teams. I ask only the care of choosing from your friendship.

The task is easy, since Spain is rich in horse herds and the great number of flocks provides an abundance from which to select. Farewell.

## EPIST. LIX. SYMMACHUS TO EUPRAXIUS

[Col. 0240A]

I am indeed an excessive demander of your conversation. I do not criticize the intervals of silence, but I suspect that something is subtracted from our friendship by the rarity of our exchanges, since I know that the heart is the seat of devotion and that relief from longing proceeds from the mouth.

My earlier letters therefore contained more a longing for your conversation than a correction of your silence. For that reason, you need not labor to prove your love for me: I draw my judgment of your heart from my own, since no truer assessor of another’s love exists than the person who takes his example from his own.

That being established, and since I dislike being verbose about an obvious matter, I announce to you that my son has been designated for the urban praetorship. You understand what this announcement means. Curule horses of distinction must be prepared.

We shall send the price by the coming summer, but the choice should already anticipate necessity: in such matters, extended diligence is highly valuable. Therefore gird yourself to ensure that the second magistracy of my son surpasses the former magnificence of his quaestorship, for which distinguished fame was acquired through you.

For it is truly the greatest and most genuine advancement in reputation whenever later achievements surpass earlier ones. Farewell.

## EPIST. LX. SYMMACHUS TO EUPRAXIUS
[Col. 0240C]

The praetorship of my son, if fortune should favor the undertaking, awaits the coming year. I must prepare the nobility of the curule horses; you must attend to it, so that my money and your care may answer the expectations of the Roman people. You remember that I requested this in frequent letters. Now I should employ words of admonition, not repetition; yet since your goodwill toward us requires no canvassing, my vows nevertheless trouble me so greatly that, like a new petitioner, I thrust anxious appeals upon your ears. For I must surpass the reputation of our precedents, which, after the consular munificence of our house and my son’s quaestorian office, promises nothing mediocre of us. This, then, is the whole substance of my petition: that your diligence make me equal to the glory of the past. My household will promptly pay the prices to be fixed according to your fairness. It will be your service to provide from your own estate, or select from the herds of others, whatever Spain produces of noble stock suited to the curule contest. I do not fear that you will think me pursuing plebeian praise in this matter. [Col. 0240D] For in your wisdom you know that narrow-mindedness does not suit the magistrates of a great city. Your own Tullius also teaches this, censuring luxury in private affairs but approving magnificence in public ones. Therefore, from your abundant resources, help give the Roman year its splendid appearance; you will share in popular favor if, through your generosity to us, a more distinguished reputation comes to us. Farewell.

EPISTLE LXI. SYMMACHUS TO EUPRAXIUS.

Let your Tuentius sleep soundly on either ear. For no great dignity demands anything from a poor man. Poverty itself may perhaps be burdensome to many, yet it carries the privilege of exemption from another’s burden. Add, if you please, to the security of his priesthood the protection of his poverty, and the manifold defenses of a single man. It seems to me that a fortune exhausted by every remedy of exemption is stronger than all such remedies. But I wish you to know that the surveyors of senatorial property will arrive at once, and that Tuentius may hope for a fuller pardon if their investigation confirms the truth of his poverty. Meanwhile, let him safely enjoy his earlier achievements. Nothing will be changed after the judgment rendered on his behalf by the illustrious Felix, provided that careful examination verifies the senator’s straitened circumstances, which he alleged some time ago. Now I must reproach you as a friend: although you passed near us, you thought it a long detour to turn the reins toward us. Spain would have granted Rome’s delay, had Rome been your destination. For she knows how to submit her desires to the parent of all the provinces. Nor is she so stingy as to refuse to show us her own good things. Therefore, deprived of the benefit of your presence, we earnestly request the secondary fruits of friendship: whenever fortune grants the opportunity, let us at least read the man whom we would rather have seen. Farewell.

EPISTLE LXII. SYMMACHUS TO EUPRAXIUS.

Our friendship is on the lips of many, and the fame of your horses has traveled far. Hence the magistrates of every city ask for the assistance of my recommendation, enticed by the reputation of your herds. For this reason the leading men of Antioch, sent to purchase chariots, wished to be helped by the influence of my conversation with you. Grant, I ask, to men who have traveled so far, a proper kindness in the matter of selection and price; let it confirm that those who followed a flattering expectation truly hoped for something from your zeal and from my good offices. Farewell.

EPISTLE LXIII. SYMMACHUS TO EUPRAXIUS.

[Col. 0241C]

Permit me to say this: we do not lack a supply of curule horses, but the delay of the praetorship drives us to desire a more generous gift. Therefore, if—as is customary—the execution of my commission is pleasing to you, I wish four teams of horses from the Laudacian herds, selected by your judgment, to be brought to me as soon as the spring voyage has opened the sea. I shall reimburse, through the agents sent for the purpose, the price indicated in your letter. Although I ought not to promise this, since the trust of friendship requires no written contract. I suppose you wonder why I do not instead ask from your own herds, which surpass the finest Iberian horses in nobility. The city is wearied by the sameness of a uniform spectacle, and I must overcome its satiety by variety. It is only for your diligence to exercise judgment and to match the reputation of your own horses with selections from foreign stables. For when a friend’s business is at stake, you must consider those whom you choose your own as well. Farewell.

EPISTLE LXIV. SYMMACHUS TO EUPRAXIUS.

No one has ever carried one of your letters to you and returned from you empty-handed in the same service; yet you reproach us for our infrequency and even complain that you must take responsibility for our regularity. You do this as lovers do, among whom, even when such attentions overflow, the thirst for them remains great. Nor do you merely ask for letters: you also command that our unpublished little speeches be brought into your hands. This seems to show what judgment you have formed of those you previously received. For no desire advances toward a second installment if the first displeased. I have therefore sent five of the more recent pieces; one of them has already been given confidence by public approval. But even after the verdict of the toga-clad public, I still await your judgment, which I want you to issue under oath, because it is fitting that faith be bound by an oath whenever friendship has come under suspicion of favoritism. Farewell.

EPISTLE LXV. SYMMACHUS TO EUPRAXIUS.

For some time I had been awaiting your letter, uncertain what such a long delay meant. But when you restored to me possession of the service I had desired, my anxiety turned to joy. And indeed nature has arranged things so that complaint over a long-awaited kindness disappears when we obtain what we hoped for. I therefore congratulate you most warmly that the pledge of your devotion to me has been renewed. You will ensure that I am not mistaken in this opinion if you preserve your diligence toward me through constant affection. Farewell.

EPISTLE LXVI. SYMMACHUS TO EUSIGNIUS.

I shall see what the justice of the times, the merit of our case, and your care can accomplish—if, that is, I am dear to you. In my brother Eusebius, a man of illustrious rank, I embrace the hope of moderation preserved toward us, and I honor his integrity in my thoughts and commend it in my speech. Although he does not seek the reward of a good intention, we nevertheless wish to repay an honorable life through your friendship. You will therefore do something as agreeable to my wishes as it is consistent with your character if that most prudent man recognizes that whatever is granted to me he has offered to the favor of all good men. Farewell.

EPISTLE LXVII. SYMMACHUS TO EUSIGNIUS.

It accords with the clemency of the times, and it is familiar to your sacred character, to raise up those in need of help. Hence I have gained confidence to petition you on behalf of our brother Stemmatius, whom envy has long stripped of everything fortune possessed, except the affection of good men. For there can be no doubt what he deserves from every excellent person, since recently he was summoned by the unconquered emperors so that he might not be freed through indulgence; and his sad fate was changed more by honor than by pardon. He was not so much rescued as desired. Hence there is sure hope that our emperor, venerable for his clemency, following the example of a just father and a pious brother, will grant better supports to his fortune, provided that your intercession assists the plea of the impoverished senator. For he asks two things easy to accomplish but great for the glory of the one who grants them: that he be restored to the senate-house by sacred testimonial, and that he be rescued from poverty through the recovery of a modest sum of money. May your favor, and that of the other leading men who urge you, advance this cause; it is in the interest of a good age, to which pious deeds bring perpetual renown. Farewell.

EPISTLE LXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO EUSIGNIUS.

Even if a domestic and friendly petition were absent, public authority could not fail a just desire. For what is more familiar to justice than that the deceiver of my most distinguished and praiseworthy mother should be deprived of the success of his cunning, lest, relying on the assistance of provincial patrons, he mock the interests of others? Their impudence compelled my mother, a matron who avoids litigation, to hasten to the judgment of the praetorian court. The matter at issue is as follows. A very few months ago, that man rented from my mother the granaries at Aquileia, and the property designated “CF.”, whose location was unknown because of the distance of the journey, for a small rent; and he abused them so that, despite the brief period, he is said deliberately to have inflicted damage upon those same places. When she repeatedly summoned him to withdraw from the lease, she was repeatedly thwarted by the man’s contempt and by the intervention of certain people. Now, in need of help, she desires a twofold benefit from your favor. First, that the utterly unscrupulous tenant be expelled from his occupation of the properties. Then, after an assessment has been made of the deterioration, that he acknowledge the expense of proper restoration. Since, therefore, we ask only what is equitable, I believe that your favor will smile upon my petition and my mother’s interests. Farewell.

EPISTLE LXIX. SYMMACHUS TO EUSIGNIUS.

In your customary kindness, you aided our return by sending an apparitor, whom I dismissed after he had advanced toward the upper Apennines, adding the duty of carrying this letter, so that the gratitude I cannot match in deeds might at least be repaid with the honor of words. I hope that the remainder of the journey will be completed without difficulty, with the previously mentioned permission of God. For things that promise the near hope of arrival are less troublesome. Farewell.

EPISTLE LXX. SYMMACHUS TO EUSIGNIUS.

[Col. 0243C]

When I was departing, you deigned to entrust me with a task appropriate to friendship: that I should not remain silent about matters suited to your reputation and actions. Since the case requires it, I am carrying out what was assigned. I see that responsibility for the basilica and bridge has rightly been entrusted to Bonosus, a man of provincial rank: he possesses both the vigilance to limit the complications of the public accounts and the integrity to pursue whatever the investigation discovers. But I fear that the assigned matter may grow cold through evasions, because he has been given someone as his associate in the inquiry who resists him. Therefore I cannot allow you to remain unaware that the matter has reached the point where a great stain may be laid upon public expenditures through a spirit of rivalry. For what does this association mean, especially in an investigation that seems to bind the very investigator himself? Accordingly, correction must be applied only to this aspect, and the entire inquiry must be referred to one person whom you select voluntarily, with the assistance of your staff; thus the lesser officials will be compelled to disclose the reliability of those who supplied or transported the materials. The outcome will show how much your care has provided for the public interest, when, with new expenses restrained, the remaining sum has satisfied the completion of the works. Farewell.

EPISTLE LXXI. SYMMACHUS TO EUSIGNIUS.

I am filled with the greatest joy whenever you write, and especially when your letter contains no bitterness of complaint. Now your style departs from its customary pleasantness. For it falsely accuses a pledge of mine of some injustice, although you have a dispute with it concerning certain boundaries. I therefore suppressed the letter I had sent to him against the law of friendship, lest justified indignation offend one who loves you. His mother had a final dispute in Sicily with your procurator; but it was settled not, as you write, by Venustus, but by another governor. Thus, in both persons, the error of the informer was exposed and removed that resentment from my pledge. In your exceptional modesty, you understand which party most deserves an apology. I say nothing about the present circumstances, which ought to have restrained the writer. Add that financial disputes should not be extended to the detriment of friendships. But why say more? Henceforth I hope to deserve gentler speech from you and, by extending your love even to my people, to gather the constancy of your longstanding regard for me. Farewell.

EPISTLE LXXII. SYMMACHUS TO EUSIGNIUS.

[Col. 0244B]

Frequent experience demonstrates, and the clear proofs of your character testify, that examples of true friendship must be taken from you. No one devotes firmer constancy to the duties of friendship, especially amid such a great mass of public responsibilities, which could blunt another man’s zeal, unless fraternal affection overcame the pressing necessities. I therefore yield the one thing that alone suits modesty to your outstanding devotion, and I humbly acknowledge that I am unequal to returning the favor. Nor do I fear that your diligence will grow sluggish through such praise; rather, I hope that your goodwill—if anything can be added to what is already full—will become more generous, since it is characteristic of good men to heap up their kindly efforts, because it is characteristic of good men to multiply kindly efforts when they perceive that their favors do not perish. Farewell.

EPISTLE LXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO EUSIGNIUS.

[Col. 0244C]

I am doing what courtesy recommends: I am attaching to your friendship men of good character. One of them is Felix, honorable in rank and distinguished by military service. If you show him any affection, it will contribute to my gratitude. Farewell.

EPISTLE LXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO EUSIGNIUS.

I wondered why you, so devoted to friendship, had long abstained from writing letters. But the sequence of your letter revealed that you had avoided becoming the messenger of sad affairs—affairs that neither familial devotion nor our common cause permitted to remain concealed through a longer silence. For it is generally useful to bring into public knowledge whatever one wishes to have corrected, so that, by announcing the danger to come, the concern of all may be moved to take counsel. Thus, under great necessity, you have protested the scarcity that threatens next year. For what hope remains when, in the African provinces, the threshing of grain has not sufficed even for meager sustenance, and the neighboring year awaits seed supplied from other lands? Rightly, therefore, the concern of the provinces has fled for refuge to the providence of the eternal emperors. Meanwhile, while greater relief is sought from them, may your humanity cherish the exhausted and, as though sharing another’s grief, persuade the afflicted that whatever the province has suffered has happened to you yourself. I am well, although my sick spirit is unable to recognize the blessing of health; but, so that I may gain some consolation, I beg you to write more indulgently and invite me to reply by the example of your own regularity. Farewell.

BOOK FIVE.

[Col. 0245]

EPISTLE I. SYMMACHUS TO HIEROPHANTI.

[Col. 0245A]

I am in good health. This should be the beginning of a letter, since it is what readers’ prayers desire most. I am exceedingly glad that you likewise possess the vigor you wished for, for you recently cheered me with this indication. I also count among the chief grounds for gratitude the fact that your frequent use of the familiar style shows you to be most devoted to us. I intend to attribute praise for this to you, so that by this invitation you may be summoned to persevere by the encouragement of a grateful spirit. Farewell.

EPISTLE II. SYMMACHUS TO HIEROPHANTI.

You enrich me with a precious gift whenever you honor our friendship with an indication of your good health. I therefore pray to the gods that they may prosper you in return for such devotion toward us. In return for your written attention, I willingly offer equal diligence, so that you may be more ready for such duties when you see that, with one who remembers what has been written, your gratitude does not go to waste. Farewell.

EPISTLE III. SYMMACHUS TO HIEROPHANTI.

Probatius recently presented me with your letter, and it brought me a great deal of congratulation because I learned from it that everything was going according to your wishes. I need not urge you to do this often, since spontaneous services ought not to be stirred into action by the spur of exhortation. Farewell.

EPISTLE IV. SYMMACHUS TO THEODORUS.
