The frequent agreement of good men concerning your sacred character prompts me to desire your friendship impatiently. For those who are celebrated in everyone’s conversation and distinguished by the renown of their integrity invite even strangers to the habits of their own intimacy. Therefore, if you do not reject these signs of my goodwill, I ask you to return my conversation, so that I may rejoice in the confirmation of my action, although I already possess the assurance of mutual affection. Farewell.

EPISTLE V. SYMMACHUS TO THEODORUS.

You have, I think, recognized the sincerity of my friendship. Hence it happened that, as consul, you summoned me to share your festivities. I ask that these letters be granted the same trust that judged us worthy of your summons. For a long time I remained uncertain in my choice, torn between my longing for you and my concern for my only son. Your honor urged me to depart; his education held out his welcoming hands. At last I followed what you yourself would have done. The one duty belonged to joy, the other to filial affection. Many people’s attentions will surround the curule office of your distinction. For my son, his hope rests in his father alone. Your indulgent spirit toward your own will speak more fully on our behalf. I entrust to it the task of excusing me, since what affection interprets better should not be handled in words. Farewell.

EPISTLE VI. SYMMACHUS TO THEODORUS.

My son Flavianus—your consulship has recalled [lacuna] into the light. I do not know whether I ought to commend him to you, since you were the author of his greatest joy. Preserve, then, I ask, the course of kindness toward him that you have begun, although this should be expected from your constancy more than requested. The trust of voluntary affection does not come under suspicion. Farewell.

EPISTLE VII. SYMMACHUS TO THEODORUS.

You yourself provided me with the bearer of this reply. I confess that I owe you gratitude for two reasons. He set out from you to deliver the letter, and through you he was offered as the one who would bring back the reply. I ask that such exchanges of service remain between us, and that among your other praises the title of continuous devotion toward your friends be counted yours. Farewell.

EPISTLE VIII. SYMMACHUS TO THEODORUS.

[Col. 0246B]

I rejoice that I have received the first fruits of your conversation, and I earnestly ask that religious care not abandon this most courteous beginning. For the cultivation of friendships grows chiefly through such nourishment. When I wrote this, I was in good health. I have therefore entrusted an indication of that fact to your exceptional generosity, so that mutual affection may repay me with knowledge of your well-being. Farewell.

EPISTLE IX. SYMMACHUS TO THEODORUS.

I hesitate to entrust our writings to your eloquence; but I am no less careful not to deny your affection anything of mine. I have therefore sent two little speeches recently published by me. One restrained a candidate aspiring to the urban fasces; [Col. 0246C] the other was prompted by a censorship that had long before been rejected by decree of the senate. But I have extended the judgment I formed when the matter was actually debated into a more substantial work. Nor should you count against me the rejection of an ancient severity. For certain things, splendid in name alone, do great harm in practice and by experience. You will find the grounds of my judgment in the work. Nevertheless, I wish you to approach both pieces with an impartial mind, for the examination of what has been said. I hope the assertion of the speech will deserve that you, too, as a patron of antiquity, extend your hand to the authority of the order. Farewell.

EPISTLE X. SYMMACHUS TO THEODORUS.

How I fear that you may think I am flattering your ears with compliments! Your consulship is such that it seems to have doubled my own. Now the sum of my prayer has advanced to this: may you long enjoy its honors and match the delay of your reward with the length of your life. For a late payment ought to be compensated by prolonged joy. Farewell.

EPISTLE XI. SYMMACHUS TO THEODORUS.

I wondered that your arrival was so late. But once the reason for the delay had been disclosed, and letters announcing that you would soon be here had given their promise, my anxiety turned to joy. Therefore, secure in your lodging, hasten here, and, refreshed by a brief interval of rest at Rome, raise your most auspicious fasces. Our diligence toward you will provide whatever an equipped consul requires. Farewell.

EPISTLE XII. SYMMACHUS TO THEODORUS.

I hoped in vain for consolation from my journey, since the mournful faces of all grant no respite to my troubled spirit. Or has anyone been born with a nature so hard that he can be present amid the anxieties of many without grief? If you admit that this is impossible, believe that I too, among the afflicted, have in some measure lost even the experience of joy. It remains for your letters to provide me with a remedy; I receive them so willingly that no frequency could ever be sufficient. For my part, according to the opportunities that fortune may offer, I shall provide an example of frequent service. You will then know that my letters are welcome to you when I have received yours. [Col. 0247B] Farewell.

EPISTLE XIII. SYMMACHUS TO THEODORUS.

For some time you have written nothing; it would be fair to repay this fault with a corresponding one. But I think that what you regret should not be imitated, and I persuade myself that other causes intervened to delay your duty rather than a sluggish will. Yet I fear that this very courtesy may make your action worse. For when I excuse you on your behalf, I show that I have deserved nothing of the kind. Write, then, more often and more fully, before, with the previously mentioned help of God, we set sail for the Lucanian forests. For what use is there in lingering in nearby regions when, as you see, no letters are delivered, and distance could honorably excuse your silence? Farewell.

EPISTLE XIV. SYMMACHUS TO THEODORUS.

[Col. 0247C]

Your general refuge has been taken away. You cannot introduce that customary and widely used form of defense: that you are still waiting for my letters, so that you may be released from your obligation by a kind of devotion. For a long time my style has given you the auspice, and I do not deny that you have returned the favor; but afterward you ought also to have rivaled our zeal by voluntary service. Do you expect me to assail you with that reproach? Do you not know how to do right unless compelled by misfortune? I shall say no more, and for the future I rely on your diligence; what devotion has made little of, at least my admonition will restore. Farewell.

EPISTLE XV. SYMMACHUS TO THEODORUS.

[Col. 0247D]

Recently, after returning to Rome, I withdrew from my customary writing not so much through idleness as through occupation. Therefore I ask you to accept in good part my explanation of the preceding silence, and to rejoice with me that, by the sacred and divine judgment of our Lord Theodosius, I have been made consul; its manifold preparations require your industry. But once again my wishes and efforts encounter an obstacle: I do not want the period of your honor to be shortened. Therefore I leave it to your judgment that, if you wish to attend the ceremonial duties desired by our house, you may be released from the labor of administration. Farewell.

EPISTLE XVI. SYMMACHUS TO THEODORUS.

I believed that advocacy would be useful to your brother Lampadius, both for his hope of advancement and for the improvement of his character. Hence, after first consulting my lord and brother the prefect, I arranged for him to be sent to the legal forum, especially at a time when he could be trained with your assistance. Therefore accept your pledge and shape it according to the good instructions of fraternal devotion. Farewell.

EPISTLE XVII. SYMMACHUS TO MAGNILLUS.

A letter announcing a return should be brief. For what should you entrust to a page when everything customarily committed to writing ought rather to be disclosed in conversation? This is the purpose of the present letter, which, if the gods favor my wish, we shall soon follow in person. Farewell.

EPISTLE XVIII. SYMMACHUS TO MAGNILLUS.

[Col. 0248B]

You advise me to return, lest a violent incursion disturb the rights of our estate. But I think that your care can advance the matter no less than my presence. I suspect that you are piously exaggerating this alarm while trying to draw me back to Rome. For my part, wearied by this matter—not merely out of love of leisure—I wish to remain away a little longer; and anything attempted with the owner absent and uninformed will be fruitless. Your consultation with the others who care for us will discover the plan for dealing with the matter. Let no one begrudge my repose, since it must be prolonged while the care of good friends performs our duties in our place. Farewell.

EPISTLE XIX. SYMMACHUS TO MAGNILLUS.

I always place you at the foremost point of my affections. With good reason, therefore, I await news of your health with an uncertain mind; if mutual conversation provides it, our return will be hastened by eagerness. Farewell.

EPISTLE XX. SYMMACHUS TO MAGNILLUS.

We desire your arrival above all. You console our longing by sending gifts. I am greatly pleased by what you have sent, but this very service makes us feel the loss of your absence more heavily. From a friend who was present we would receive fuller support and adornment. But now, amid the business of my candidate’s public vows and the preparations for the quaestor’s office, I complain that we are deprived of the companionship of your counsel. Yet, although you are not far away, you do not neglect what must be undertaken. Your urging compelled my people, after the price had been paid, to release the silken garments they had been holding back, as well as the remaining equipment of the ceremonial gifts. I therefore wish you God’s ready favor and a happy return; and I ask that, if fortune grants you the opportunity, you hasten to attend our ceremony. Its pleasure will be greatly increased if you arrive as the longed-for participant in our new joy. Farewell.

EPISTLE XXI. SYMMACHUS TO MAGNILLUS.

The holy Aurelius could have explained anything you wished to know about me without our letters. But since a greeting delivered in bare speech is tedious, I have joined written words to my instructions. I therefore greet you, and at the same time I beg you, in accordance with the memorandum in which I briefly replied concerning what must be prepared for the ceremony, to show, as you customarily do and without compromising your judicial reputation, the care due to a devoted brother; and order our people to provide the proper expenditure for purchasing what the public presentation requires. Farewell.

EPISTLE XXII. SYMMACHUS TO MAGNILLUS.

As I hastened the quaestorian ceremony of our little son, I entrusted our common friend Aurelius with certain things to purchase or arrange. But because he is occupied with public business and various assignments, I have sent Eusebius, a member of my household, specifically so that, through his reminders, your care may be roused to complete everything. Since it seemed tedious to set out all that must be done in a letter, do not be displeased to run through the brief memorandum I have marked, which I think sufficient to stimulate your diligence. For there is no need to add prayers when the will of a friend alone ought to sharpen your zeal. Farewell.

EPISTLE XXIII. SYMMACHUS TO MAGNILLUS.

You will, I trust, acknowledge our Anastasius. You have often seen him at home. This familiarity with him ought to serve him as a recommendation with you, even if it were supported by no conversation. Now I cannot doubt that your care for him will be still greater, since both longstanding acquaintance and recent conversation commend him.

EPISTLE XXIV. SYMMACHUS TO MAGNILLUS.

A familiar opportunity has arisen to bring you news of my health. For I cannot doubt that my letters will be delivered to you by Silvanus, who will present them as part of his devotion to our friendship. This very commendation of the service he has undertaken ought to serve him as a recommendation with you. As for a reply, I do not press you, since mutual affection promises me an exchange of your writings. Farewell.

EPISTLE XXV. SYMMACHUS TO MAGNILLUS.

My mother is well and is being brought to endure the pain. Therefore lay aside this part of your anxieties and turn your mind toward better things. Certainly, if you have any leisure from your own affairs, deign to devote your diligence to ours, so that it may prove worthwhile that, in sending a collector, I have complied with your letters and instructions. Farewell.

EPISTLE XXVI. SYMMACHUS TO MAGNILLUS.

[Col. 0249D]

As you remember, we entrusted Oceanus with many matters to be completed through letters and memoranda; he will not be equal to carrying them out unless he is urged on by your impulse and instructions. When they have advanced to completion with your help, I ask you not to burden me by failing to furnish news through a written account. Farewell.

EPISTLE XXVII. SYMMACHUS TO MAGNILLUS.

The arrival of our friend Numida brought me no ordinary joy. Your conversation doubled that happiness. Thus, affected by two gifts from you, I return my friend to you with a written greeting. Farewell.

EPISTLE XXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO MAGNILLUS.

[Col. 0250A]

It was my duty to anticipate the proper order of writing. You possess the glory of a service performed in haste, since I confess my delay. Certainly I could have alleged something in excuse for the postponement. I still had a great deal of road ahead of me, but I preferred to reassure you that our labor was over. Yet there is no shame in anticipating another through pious zeal. Love, then, one who voluntarily yields to you; this very simplicity ought to win me frequent letters from you. If I do not equal them in number, my confession will once again make that admission a reward for you. Farewell.

EPISTLE XXIX. SYMMACHUS TO MAGNILLUS.

I have entrusted my friend, who is returning to the Bruttii, to a letter of escort, so that I might discharge the duty of greeting you and offer him some form of recommendation. I therefore ask you both to return the courtesy of my letter and to provide him with full protection. Farewell.

EPISTLE XXX. SYMMACHUS TO MAGNILLUS.

You departed from the city only recently. But, believing that some new gift ought to meet one whose longing for you has already grown old, I undertook the duty of writing, without awaiting the proper order or observing the custom that is usually a law among friends: that those who are placed far away should give letters before they receive them. Indeed, every affection is impatient even of a delay that is just and legitimate. I have therefore broken the custom with a devotion greater than if I had wished to preserve it. [Col. 0250C] If this is pleasing to you, repay me with the interest of conversation and show favor to the bearer of such a letter. Just as I could offer him nothing more than a letter, so you will be able to give him nothing more than your favor. Farewell.

EPISTLE XXXI. SYMMACHUS TO MAGNILLUS.

It was not fitting that the relative of the holy philosopher Asclepiades should depart without a letter from me. For his merits demanded that he be entrusted to your patronage as one belonging to the care of an outstanding man. In this matter, I do not think it necessary to employ the ambition of a lengthy speech, since reverence for your parent grants you that kindness without anyone’s petition. Farewell.

EPISTLE XXXII. SYMMACHUS TO MAGNILLUS.

[Col. 0250D]

I am already weary and reluctant to write. For how long shall we imitate the pleasure of living conversation through the image of a pen? Moreover, public prosperity and peace throughout the world urge you to return to your household. In this matter our brother Pontianus will come as a timely inciter, having received this task at the request of good men: to awaken in you, while you linger on account of your wife, the desire to revisit Rome. Farewell.

EPISTLE XXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO MAGNILLUS.

I do not want you to blame the young man for returning late. My distress over Symmachus left me no time for writing and delayed the messenger’s return until there was good hope. Now, because his danger has turned into illness, I have been able to speak of this very matter to you. May divine mercy, which bends pious ears toward the prayers of parents, soon announce to you once again news of my security that will comfort your spirit. Farewell.

EPISTLE XXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO HEPHAESTION.

I did not lack the desire to begin the journey, but a late summons shortened the time available for reaching my destination. Therefore it seemed more respectful to ask pardon than to arrive after the consul’s duties had been completed. Besides this, I sent full letters some time ago to Our Most Clement Lord, the emperor, and to the others who wished me to be present; Festus, an agens in rebus, is still delaying their dispatch through his hesitation to depart. And since I fear that what I wrote may either lie concealed after being suppressed or be corrupted after being altered by rivals, I decided to send all the copies to you, my lord and brother, [Col. 0251B] so that you might review them. It will be a sign of your affection toward me if you write at length concerning the reliability of everything. Let the small documents containing the domestic concerns also be delivered to you; after reviewing them, you will judge what the justice and reputation of the good times require. Farewell.

EPISTLE XXXV. SYMMACHUS TO HEPHAESTION.

Bands of men of letters follow your departure; and just as they customarily seek Athens of Attica or the other gymnasia of the Muses, so, drawn by longing, they accompany you on your journeys. Nor, I think, is the gathering of friends burdensome to you, who abound in the rewards of military service. Therefore nourish the learned with the resources of your rank, and expect that more guests will come to you and remain safe, now that the regular support of sustenance has been withdrawn from the teachers of Roman youth. Farewell.

EPISTLE XXXVI. SYMMACHUS TO HEPHAESTION.

I learned from reading the letters you sent that your spirit had recently been troubled, and I was greatly astonished that a sudden disagreement had arisen among the closest of companions. I begged my lord and brother not to depart from his customary conduct. But I ask you, not only in my name but also in your own, to show patience equal to the other good qualities of your character and to endure all that the condition of travel ordinarily entails. I hope that everything can be softened both through the mediation of my son Flavianus and through the gentle words of Eusebius the Chief Physician. Farewell.

EPISTLE XXXVII. SYMMACHUS TO HEPHAESTION.

[Col. 0251D]

Your letters are girded with Spartan brevity, but they overflow with substance; and although they provoke a complaint about their infrequency, their fullness of service effaces the memory of the intervening delay. If frequent practice exercises them, they will satisfy my longing without the weariness of satiety. But I see what resists your spirit and obstructs your will. Our Eusebius is detaining you with stories and drinking. Once you have returned him to the care of his gardens, I think your spirit, released from idle jests, will turn to serious affairs. Farewell.

EPISTLE XXXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO NEOTERIUS.

I rejoice beyond measure that an ancient debt has been repaid to your merits. For you have long bound the commonwealth to you by your virtues; and, having obtained a ruler of divine fidelity, it secured for itself, in a sense, the consulship that it owed you. I would have hastened with eager joy to the celebration of this event had the slow delivery of the sacred diploma not compressed the intervening days. Winter also intervened, delaying travel with severe cold and short hours of daylight. Nevertheless, my spirit and my joy are with you. I alone must grieve that fortune has denied me so great a happiness. The number of those present will satisfy you, as will the attentions of those who are absent. Farewell.

EPISTLE XXXIX. SYMMACHUS TO NEOTERIUS.

We ought to be of service to friends who desire what is just, especially to our brother Alexander, whom we approve by our judgment and embrace with affection. Although you know that he is not moved by a desire for honors, common modesty nevertheless does not allow him to lack the testimonial of military service, since the emperor Augustus Valentinianus had voluntarily conferred upon him the rank of tribune and notary before the tyrannical invasion. I therefore ask you, with your support, to make him worthy of the privilege of a sacred testimonial. Under so pious a governor, it is easy for the humanity of the age to overcome the misfortunes of men. Farewell.

EPISTLE XL. SYMMACHUS TO NEOTERIUS.

I am accustomed to bear my friends’ departure impatiently. But I believe that those who have left the city and hasten to your presence will come to me. Why, with affection set apart, do I envy those who will be with you? They alone will enjoy the benefits of your presence [Col. 0252C], whose common enjoyment ought to be mine. Nevertheless, whatever the circumstances, I willingly sent our brothers Celsus and Ticianus, men of good character, confident that something from your stories and activities would return to us through their report. I ask in turn that you restore them promptly to the City and to their studies. For if I concealed this request from you, I would seem to have commended their journey not to your reverence but to my own annoyance. Farewell.

## LETTER XLI. SYMMACHUS TO NEOTERIUS

Knowing that you are a man of forgiving disposition, I have undertaken, on behalf of a friend, to ask pardon. For we have not strayed so far from what is right that we could ever suspect you of being moved rashly. The most illustrious Epictetus, having slipped in the manner of advocates [Col. 0252D], while wishing too zealously to please the person whose case he had undertaken, touched upon the holy Sabinus, approved by all good men, in an incautious remark. This incident is believed to have exasperated the feelings of all of you who care for him. Nor was that unreasonable. The governor’s complaint also sharpened the praetorian authorities. What more need be said? Epictetus was deprived of the honor of the forensic gown, although he deserved precedence over many who are protected by firm advocacy. Now that crowd of clients insults the error of one man, which occurred by chance. Your humanity will ensure that this does not continue long. Enough has been done for correction. Now look to your own character. Let the case have earned that punishment; attribute this further step to leniency. I know that the illustrious prefect of the praetorium will promptly yield to these letters of yours as well. Epictetus, vir clarissimus, will also remain indebted to you for his amendment [Col. 0253A]—he whom the impunity granted to great offenders had shortly before rendered inconsiderate. Farewell.

## LETTER XLII. SYMMACHUS TO NEOTERIUS

I am sufficiently pleased that my friend Drinnacius has met with your approval. For I too gain the greatest honor whenever our judgment agrees. He will therefore enjoy the richest fruit of his innocence: dear to me for his honorable services, and approved by you in just dealings. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIII. SYMMACHUS TO NEOTORIUS

One who entrusts his trifles and ravings to a friend ought not fear judgment. For whatever might be censured is commended by the trust with which it is presented. Rightly confident, I sent you the little speech that I recently delivered in the Senate [Col. 0253B]; I think that my lord and our brother Carterius has fully discussed it with you. For he was present as a hearer at our petition. Although we seem to have begun with the favorable votes of the entire order, we nevertheless place the highest value upon your single testimony. Therefore let me know your judgment, and at the same time disclose to one eager to hear what you are doing, so that the pleasure you will derive from my actions may be balanced by your reciprocal communication. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIV. SYMMACHUS TO NEOTERIUS

In a more flattering letter you bite me with a rebuke for neglected service, while I return thanks to you for the conversation I received, although I had thought those conversations more truly friendly which are offered spontaneously [Col. 0253C]; whereas, in answering, one ought rather to repay an obligation than to present a voluntary composition. Yet your latest letter affected me so deeply that I confess I do not know whether you have returned this gift to me or bestowed it. But consider how much pleasure your pages will possess when you offer them without being reminded, since even these are exceedingly welcome to me, though you send them in fulfillment of a debt. Farewell.

## LETTER XLV. SYMMACHUS TO NEOTERIUS

You do what is proper by consoling my leisure with the continual flow of your writings, since from your affection you infer that the gift which has flowed from your most sacred and eloquent mouth must be pleasing. I therefore repay the obligation more as a testimony of gratitude than as an equivalent for the service [Col. 0253D] by which I acknowledge myself bound to you. Yet for that very reason I think myself more deserving of more frequent conversation; and I return you this palm as though defeated by the interest accruing on your letters. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVI. SYMMACHUS TO NEOTERIUS

Rumor had promised that you would come to our common fatherland. I was exulting in the unexpected joy. But when, as the days passed, the report grew cold, I realized that one consolation remained to me: to return to the practice and habit of writing. I therefore perform the duty of offering a greeting, and ask your Excellence to grant me your arrival in place of letters. There is indeed a festive occasion which ought to summon you—the quaestorship of my son [Col. 0254A], to which shared affection invites you and your people. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVII. SYMMACHUS TO FELIX

You write that respect for me flourishes among everyone. I rejoice in such testimony, but I acknowledge that it is through your efforts that my reputation flourishes in this way. You are the promoter of favorable rumor for me; nor do I feel myself indebted to you only for this favor. For even that which, under your direction, proceeded to the advantage of my relatives, although granted in accordance with justice, is nevertheless credited to you. I will not continue at greater length, since verbal reciprocity is impoverished when repaying benefits. At the same time, I am hindered by the cares that the livelihood of a slender estate sets against domestic duties. Hereafter I shall be more talkative with you, when the security restored to the grain supply has revived my zeal [Col. 0254B]. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVIII. SYMMACHUS TO FELIX

To those whom we know and approve, a ready recommendation is owed, so that they may reach the notice of good men with honorable support. Theodulus, a young man of genuine nobility, enjoys the favor of many whose approval is laudable. But he hopes that the difficulties of fortune, which make the course of his life harsh, can be removed through your assistance. I therefore ask you kindly to smile upon his wishes, lest either my testimony be judged to have been treated as worthless or an empty outcome mock his hopes. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIX. SYMMACHUS TO FELIX

[Col. 0254C]

I love your letters, for they always bring me some cause for congratulation. I, however, answer your benefactions with bare words. But, as the matter stands, your excellent mind considers its pages fruitful in themselves, and therefore I persist diligently in this task, knowing that you regard it as worth a great price. Meanwhile I have thanked our lord and prince, and his benevolence toward me, by letter—with words perhaps meager, but rich in feeling. If your outstanding unanimity and the friendship whose fidelity I have tested should convey these thanks through a pleasant and timely reading, I shall not appear ungrateful, since the invincible prince, as I hope, will have approved that he placed such benefits with one who remembers them. Farewell.

## LETTER L. SYMMACHUS TO FELIX

[Col. 0254D]

I rejoice that my kinsman Aurelius has been restored among your dependents—not merely on behalf of the man whose protection a man of the highest rank undertook, but especially on my own behalf, since you treated my testimony as equivalent to a judgment. To this service your favor was increased by your letter, although it contains something capable of offending a lover—for it was passed over too briefly—and while it brings me pleasure, it denies me satisfaction. Such is the nature of good things: one wishes to enjoy them at greater length, and nothing is harder to bear than the swift passage of pleasing speech. Therefore add abundance to your letters, or, if you can, remove their sweetness. Unless you do so, I shall repay your annoyance with the words I usually employ, and with longer pages [Col. 0255A]. Farewell.

## LETTER LI. SYMMACHUS TO FELIX

Your affection urged me to write, while your haste in passing by urged me to say little. Therefore, content with a greeting—which, even if it does not fulfill the obligation, nevertheless bears witness to affection—return in turn something for us to read, and, if necessary, rival my brevity. For although I desire your polished conversation, I do not dare ask you for an abundance of words while conscious of this very narrow page. Farewell.

## LETTER LII. SYMMACHUS TO FELIX

I entrusted to the bearer of judicial letters a page to be delivered to you [Col. 0255B], offering the tribute of friendship in a greeting and at the same time suggesting that the matter concerns my dependent; the report will explain what must be drawn from the tutor’s grasp. I am not laboring to assert justice, whose protection is your chief concern. But I venture to ask only this: that, as soon as possible, imperial rescripts may lend force to judgments already rendered. Farewell.

## LETTER LIII. SYMMACHUS TO FELIX

Our brother Helpidius was summoned by his desire for you no less than by the letter of the consul. Although your affection is promised him by the ancient bond between you, I think that my own request of recommendation will add something as well. Therefore, I ask you, build upon your old diligence with new benefits toward a friend, so that the two may be brought together in full; and grant me this, though perhaps unwillingly—that he may feel that the merits he established with you through his own services have grown through my favor [Col. 0255C]. Farewell.

## LETTER LIV. SYMMACHUS TO FELIX

Whoever neglects a friend’s reputation is unreliable in loyalty. To prevent this fault from rightly being attributed to me, I am concerned for your reputation even when others are injured. By what law, by what public benefit, did an uncertain and unexamined procurator, said to have earned his place among the notaries, induce Eusebius, vir clarissimus, to use a civil petition to drag a possessing matron away from the urban court? In this case, although the supplication confines itself to a private action, the responses of the sacred authorities threaten consequences. I ask you to consider what ought to be obtained from the imperial chamber, whose oracles you proclaim. I speak to you with fraternal concern. The reputation of all rescripts concerns you. What if the memory of the case also calls your fidelity to account?

You remember, as a citizen and colleague, that Ampelius, a man of illustrious and distinguished memory, bought a small house beneath the Clivus Salutis and increased it with costly decoration. Thirty years have whitened the age of his possession. Its original owner was Posthuminus, grandson of Jovius, who acquired this house by succession among the other property of his parent Porphyria. Porphyria never had any business with Theodosius, whose property Eusebius once obtained. Now a procurator from the Column, known to the courts for many such contrivances, assails established rights with petitions; he tastes the judgments of every authority, abandons the outcomes of actions already begun [Col. 0256A], renews their beginnings, and accuses the Roman tribunal. He allows neither the antiquity of the possession, nor the privilege of senatorial rank, nor the standing of the prefecture to remain undisturbed.

A fiscal pretext is smeared onto these attempts, as though for an inquiry into movable property from the estates that Eusebius deserved and that was owed to the imperial house. Where did this diligence lie dormant for so long? Through whose collusion in the records did public losses remain hidden? If the procurator had not brought public torches to his own business, even now so many offices and investigators sought for the treasury would know nothing of it. And indeed it is right that the defense of the imperial house should apply more attentive eyes to what has been entrusted to it. What do movables have in common with an estate? No error of the senses, no interpretation of words can confuse these names. Moreover, Porphyria and Posthuminus are unrelated to the property once proscribed [Col. 0256B]. Much more remote from any contamination by movable property is Ampelius, the purchaser of the house.

What remains except for your equity to judge that the private petition is supported by no foundation, though it is covered with the shadow of sacred reverence? Love of the world and friendship with you compelled me to set these matters down in a letter. I would have made the same things known openly to our illustrious brother Sperchius, following his character, if he had offered me any confidence in him through letters. But I ought not myself to initiate written correspondence of this kind. It will therefore be for Your Greatness to convey to him what we have written. For it is fitting that whatever benefits the reputation of both should be corrected by the agreement of both. Farewell.

## LETTER LV. SYMMACHUS TO SALLUSTIUS

[Col. 0256C]

Do not assess the character of the man whom I commend by the conduct of the others who deal with senatorial affairs. He was not born in a mediocre position or of the lowest station, but, while preserving the honor of his birth through modesty, he safeguards it. For that reason I did not think it improper to pursue with a letter of testimony one whom I know well. Nor should your singular nobility doubt affection for a man whom you see approved with our support. Let this suffice regarding Ammonius. I must not, however, keep silent about my desire for your conversation; the scarcity of your writings has intensified my appetite for them. Farewell.

## LETTER LVI. SYMMACHUS TO SALLUSTIUS

[Col. 0256D]

You have bestowed upon me a more generous service than I had requested. For when I asked you to help my household in acquiring racehorses, you increased the number purchased by four free quadrigas. Of these, the care of the escorts brought eleven horses through alive, while the rest perished not long afterward. Yet fortune did not diminish the gratitude owed to your devotion. For in the gifts of friends, losses caused by accident must not be taken into account; rather, the whole amount that proceeded from the giver must be credited as received. Through your man we have sent you a two-leaved tablet for a candidate and a gift of two pounds of silver, wishing to show that you were not absent in spirit from our public games. Farewell.

## LETTER LVII. SYMMACHUS TO SALLUSTIUS

[Col. 0257A]

Even without being reminded, I would have assisted your interests. That I have taken them into account, my lord and paternal cousin’s son, a vir spectabilis, will not conceal. You should remind him that, both out of his habitual fulfillment of his own wishes and in consideration of my request, he ought to deign to assist your desires. Farewell.

## LETTER LVIII. SYMMACHUS TO PATERNIUS

I could not attend the Senate on the day when the son of Thalassus was exempted from the duties of our rank. But I had strengthened the hope of future action on his behalf among my friends with no slight recommendation; nevertheless, I do not claim for myself the favor of the grant. The justice of the request and your intervention advanced what was desired. My health, long tossed about, has at last returned to calm. I write this so that, increased by joy at my recovery, you may return equal pleasure concerning your own successes [Col. 0257B]. Farewell.

## LETTER LIX. SYMMACHUS TO PATERNIUS

Repetition adds much weight to our first requests. Therefore I repeat my request concerning the provision of hunters, so that repeated letters may more easily urge you to diligence. The day of our public function is approaching. The generosity of a candidate alone is insufficient if it is to be presented with richer arena spectacles. For munificence shown to the undeserving is foolish. I therefore ask you to grant me the best of your hunters, both through the authority of a judge and out of affection for a brother; you will greatly enhance all the preparations that we are making, with spirited expenditure, for the enjoyment of the citizens [Col. 0257C]. Farewell.

## LETTER LX. SYMMACHUS TO PATERNIUS

All who desire relief through your access do not, I think, pursue a fruitless path toward your favor when they rely upon me as their supporter. One of them is my respectable friend Turasius, who attributes the injustice of the suit brought against him to fortune but hopes especially from your assistance for the favor of a good outcome. Protect one who asks for what is just, and extend more widely the fame of your humanity; it will be greatly increased if success comes to Turasius through you. Farewell.

## LETTER LXI. SYMMACHUS TO PATERNIUS

Devotion demanded that I write, especially since a familiar opportunity urged me. For one of your men presented himself to me as a letter-carrier; I realized that it would be the height of impiety to give him no letter. I therefore send you my wish for your good health, and in turn ask that you honor us with signs of your own well-being. Farewell.

## LETTER LXII. SYMMACHUS TO PATERNIUS

The quaestors of our order have never paid the transport tax on their wild beasts. For our ancestors considered it burdensome that those already bearing the obligations of senatorial rank should be charged an excessive expense. Recently, when I was organizing a gladiatorial spectacle, this privilege was extended less in my own name than in that of the Roman people. Now a fiftieth is being demanded from my brother Cynegius, vir clarissimus and a candidate for the quaestorship [Col. 0258A]—a tax that ought to be recognized only by the traders in bears, since they pursue profit. This injustice awaits your regulation. I ask you to resist the greed of the tax collectors and cut back the losses of your colleagues. The matter will increase your favor in two ways if you honor the Senate with this privilege and assist the candidates by granting relief. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIII. SYMMACHUS TO PATERNIUS

The cause of a friend urged me to write. But I must admit that I was more concerned for your reputation. For Minucianus, vir clarissimus, is endangered by a small sum of money. Yet a considerable path to praise will be opened for you if the slander raised, as I hear, by false promissory notes subsides [Col. 0258B]. I am ashamed to say by what tricks the agents of the Italian treasury are growing powerful. It is reported that private names are falsely recited under the appearance of public debt. The weak are immediately overcome by the pressure. But the stronger, when they invoke legal defenses on their behalf, are entangled in criminal interpretations of words, so that, through fear of unpopularity, they submit themselves to suffering loss.

But Minutianus, vir clarissimus, secure in you and in the laws, wishes to avert the threats of the report through examination. Therefore, I ask you to appoint judges whom the imperial choice has placed over the urban authorities. For it is not fitting that a trifling debt and eminent rank should be summoned to a distant hearing. I would proceed further if equity wished to be assisted by many entreaties. The report will make public the nature of the case; although it will protect the error of the investigator, it may sometimes be possible to obtain that he be trusted by you without another disputant. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIV. SYMMACHUS TO PATERNIUS

I ought not to be a boaster of my devotion toward you. Services arising from a sense of duty reject ostentation. Indeed, I received as something equivalent to abundant gratitude the fact that Scipio, vir clarissimus, approached my friendship under your guidance. For seeking the intimacy of good men is the greatest gain. And I hope that he too will be diligent in all our affairs once he learns from his own people what our concern has accomplished for his business. Farewell.

## LETTER LXV. SYMMACHUS TO PATERNIUS

[Col. 0258D]

The quadragesima transport tax (or revenue tax) is wrongly demanded from senatorial candidates, because the functions of our order ought not to be burdened with double disadvantages. I also pointed this out to you some time ago in letters concerning Cynegius, vir clarissimus. Now the same necessity affecting my son Pompeianus, a most illustrious and excellent young man, has required me to repeat the request. I therefore ask you graciously to grant the humanity—which is first among your virtues—to the organizers of our order’s spectacles, and to remove the transport of bears from the greed of the contractors. The gratitude for this benefit will reach both the Senate, which is relieved of burdens, and the people, whose entertainments are granted immunity. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVI. SYMMACHUS TO PATERNIUS

[Col. 0259A]

The relatives of Ampelius, a man of illustrious memory, are being harassed by a private lawsuit. Do not think that our concern for them is moved solely by remembrance of their parent. Even outsiders, and those who never knew the man, are inflamed by the indignity of the case. I shall touch briefly, as I can, upon its main features and essentials.

Ampelius, once one of the leading men of the Senate, whom you learned to know through the fame of his reputation, bought a small house at Rome from Posthumius, vir clarissimus, heir of Porphyria. The origin of the contract is supported by a legitimate period of possession, nearly a century, during which no one challenged it. Recently, however, a certain trickster raised his head under the name of procurator, shaking the old claim of Eusebius, formerly a notary and vir clarissimus, concerning property of the same Theodosius that he once obtained, and to which he falsely claims that this estate belonged [Col. 0259B]. Theodosius and Porphyria had no connection in accounts and no union of property. The matter was begun in the urban court by the claimant and ended when he himself fled.

Again he revives the ashes of the case into flame through a surreptitious petition; and, distrusting justice, he draws the actions of the imperial house to his own side, supposedly for an investigation of movable property that has nothing in common with the estate. Let the governor of the private treasury investigate these matters according to the order of the laws; let the owner of the house be left to his own judge. Thus there are two cases, divided by the names of the things, differing in their actions, unrelated in origin, and separated by the persons involved. Ampelius did not buy movable property, nor did the treasury attack the house. Why does the procurator support another’s invalid claim with public power?

I ask you to communicate these matters to our brother Sperchius, an illustrious man [Col. 0259C]. He is most devoted to equity, and prefers to yield to the common law rather than favor his own authority. For he knows that laws are more powerful than offices. I am confident that once he learns what has been suppressed, he will not fail to correct what has been brought forward. If he asks why I have not written to him about this, please answer that, since no writing relationship had yet been established between us, I feared that from the beginning I might seem to be bringing an accusation. The correction of this case will give me happier material for speaking with him; a return of thanks will inaugurate my letters. I shall no longer wait for him to offer confidence for conversation to one who is hesitating: his justice will encourage every service. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVII. SYMMACHUS TO OLYBIUS AND PROBINUS

[Col. 0259D]

It is the work of youthful energy to rouse wild beasts from their forest lairs and to distinguish liberal studies with woodland pleasure. Thus in former times the tireless Marsian and the brave Sabine possessed strength. May what has been achieved in our own years prosper. In certain birds there is an example of this kindness: their early age in turn carries nourishment to the aging. But my health does not yet permit me to use the flesh of wild animals; nevertheless, the necessity of moderation does not diminish the gratitude I feel for your gift. For although abstinence from using it benefits my health, the honor of the gift has satisfied my spirit. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO OLYBIUS AND PROBINUS

Your full vigor is attested by your pursuit of wild beasts [Col. 0260A]. This is therefore my first reason for rejoicing in you: that you strengthen your health through rustic pleasures. The second degree of joy is that you have earned what the hunt has captured. For just as it is offered to honor the gods to consecrate the antlers of stags and fasten boars’ teeth to doorposts, so the offerings of the forests are dedicated to the observance owed to friends.

Meanwhile, I reject the opinion that treats hunting as a servile occupation. Its author may be approved only for his writing style, for the defects of his character prevent us from seeking from him authority for the conduct of life. I would rather have you go rusticating with Atillus and follow the sport of physical strength than be led by fine words into the practices of idleness. Certainly this labor suits your ages. The recreation of young men should not be distinguished by a gaming board, a ball, or an Attic hoop, nor by Greek wrestling schools, but by vigorous exertion [Col. 0260B] and the joys of innocent daring. For this activity I shall also encourage my own Symmachus, if he grows up, although he is my only child. The time will come when you must renounce this strenuous pursuit because of age. Then the care of hunting may rightly be considered a servile task. For it is a kind of servitude if, when our strength is declining, we refuse to make use of the respite from labor that old age grants us. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIX. SYMMACHUS TO OLYBIUS AND PROBINUS

You have confirmed my longstanding judgment, since you share my view of the charm and healthfulness of the Formian coast. Until now, your passage had sampled only sparingly the benefits of that shore. Now, having learned them more attentively through a longer stay, you have earned the right to love them [Col. 0260C]. As one who longs for you, I am distressed that you live far away, and I show my patience through my longing for you. But if chance should favor my wishes, I hope to spend with you in that bay whatever remains of our lives, so that the place may grant me health, and you pleasure of spirit. Farewell.

## LETTER LXX. SYMMACHUS TO OLYBIUS AND PROBINUS

You have opened the occasion for my writing only late. You ought to have begun the first offerings of correspondence, since one who departs for foreign places should provide the auspices for an exchange of letters. Therefore, released from the obligation of observance, I now return your greeting and promise for the future, if travelers should provide the opportunity, a steady succession of familiar pages, so that it may be clear to you [Col. 0260D] that I was silent not through my fault but because of your delay. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXI. SYMMACHUS TO OLYBIUS AND PROBINUS

I take delight in the constancy of your conversation, and draw abundant joy from that gift. For what could more clearly display either your feelings or consolation for my longing than that, day by day, the observance of your merits grows in my regard? Friendship, when celebrated through services, is never content with a fixed limit. Therefore it is fitting that you become more ready in offering conversation, since you do not prove forgetful in repaying the obligation. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXII. SYMMACHUS TO LICINIUS

The son of my friend Regilianus, himself approved for the sake of his honorable character, presented you some time ago with my letter recommending him. Therefore, since you already know him, he does not require the assistance of a second endorsement. Yet the principle and habit of my devotion required me to write. For although you yourself have long concealed this, it would not be right for me also to abstain from such services. I hope that what is usually granted spontaneously to friendship may at least be credited to my constancy. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO LICINIUS

When I was departing for a place near the City, I ought not to have refrained from writing to you, so that I might discharge the observance owed by ancient custom [Col. 0261B]. For by an old practice it has become customary for those who set out on a journey to offer the first fruits of their writing. Therefore, summoned by the auspices of familiar service, bear witness through continual conversation to the fraternal devotion that you always display toward me in your thoughts. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO LICINIUS

On the eighth day, having overcome many difficulties of travel, I greeted my ancestral home. Immediately, as friendship required, the memory of your instructions came to me. When I was departing, you had charged me to investigate carefully the affairs of the excellent young men Ticianus and Helpidius. Their teacher, a prudent man unfamiliar with flattery, affirmed that they possessed an adequate knowledge of law for virtually all the needs of judicial [Col. 0261C] and forensic service. It is now your task to summon these outstanding young men; hesitation ought not to delay further their character, already prepared for the honors of public service. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXV. SYMMACHUS TO LICINIUS

Those who desire honorable things should be promptly assisted, so that worthy intentions may be advanced even through another’s effort. Therefore I do not permit Felix, a most reverent young man striving for higher things, to lack assistance. When, being mild in character, he recoiled from the disputes of the urban court, he sought to enroll in the more modest practice of advocacy; my own encouragement also animated him. For I promised his good character and purified morals that the assistance of your mind would in no way be lacking. Therefore, once entreated and favorably disposed, receive him not as a deserter from another court but as one seeking a quieter forum [Col. 0261D]. Whatever benefit of good fortune or advantage comes to him through his service, he will owe to you and your kindness. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVI. SYMMACHUS TO LICINIUS

The Emperor’s command entrusted Bonosus, an excellent man, conspicuous after his Palatine military service for the integrity of two administrations, with the inspection of the bridge and the new basilica. He could complete this task through fidelity and vigilance if he alone possessed the authority to conduct such an examination. Now Cyriades, vir clarissimus, a comes and engineer, who previously managed the expenses of both works, has been admitted as a partner in the inspection and, as is often said, has frequently disagreed with Bonosus’ investigation [Col. 0262A]. Hence an inquiry that could be vigorously pursued by one man is delayed by a contrived conflict between the parties.

For this reason the honorable Bonosus fears that he may be exposed to criticism because the outcome of so important a matter still wavers. He therefore asks that, if anyone thinks that Cyriades, vir clarissimus, ought to be the inspector of the same work whose expenses he previously managed, this annoyance may be removed from him. But if Cyriades himself appears suited to the task, let the whole burden of the investigation belong to him alone. Therefore, out of love for the Republic, whose interests you embrace among the first and most important concerns, deign to bring this matter before the most illustrious and distinguished prefect, so that, once the disputes have been removed, the shortfall in such great expenditures may be uncovered. For I hope that, once new expenditures cease, the total amount already spent will suffice for the completion of both works [Col. 0262B]. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVII. SYMMACHUS TO LICINIUS

You have been silent for a long time. But I ought not to imitate such an example. Therefore I have been the first to break into the sphere of service and address you with a devout reminder: the gift of letters, which you ought to have offered spontaneously to our friendship, should at least be discharged when prompted. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS

You ask how I am or what I am doing. I answer your question, which arises from affection. I delight in the quiet of the countryside. It provides me with healthy air and nourishment for reading. Often I feast my eyes on the fields that winter labor cultivates. I greatly rejoice that you enjoy good health and that the memory of our friendship remains in you so abundantly [Col. 0262C]. I have no adequate excuse for my silence. I had nothing to write; and, since you were occupied with hearing cases, I feared that the loquacity of one at leisure might burden you with many additional affairs. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIX. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS

I hope for your presence. For you are not accustomed to abandon your promises. But it is frequently rumored that praetorian letters are obstructing the arrangements already made. Therefore, so that I may not remain long suspended in uncertainty, I wish to be reassured by more recent writings: let me know whether delay will be worthwhile because you are going to come, or whether, if you are being held back, I may be released from the annoyance of waiting. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXX. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS

[Col. 0262D]

I support through letters a common citizen and friend, whose good qualities, because they are known to your judgment, require no assertion. With one who knows him, my speech about him is deservedly easy and brief. Nevertheless, I remind you that he should be loved more strongly for my sake, and that he should understand, from the evidence of increased affection toward him, that my concern with you remains active. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXI. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS

Since I often use unknown opportunities for writing, I think it a breach of friendship if I seem to abstain from writing to those of my household. I have therefore gladly given the most honorable man Acrius, your devotee, a page announcing my good health, adding a respectful greeting [Col. 0263A]. This greeting alone, both when spoken and when returned, fulfills the duties of familiar service. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXII. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS

It is a service full of devotion that you spontaneously anticipate your brother’s wish. Accordingly, our household will soon travel with money to purchase horses, so that from all the quadrigas you have written are for sale, a selection may be made of those superior in speed and distinguished in breed. You must take responsibility for this, so that the reputation of the new games may match our earlier spectacles. Above all, I ask this favor of you: do not weigh the number more heavily than the quality. For since certain hope promises me an abundance of horses from Spain, the horses you promise from nearby must be selected with more assured diligence [Col. 0263B]. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS

The duties of senatorial office arouse our concern for the festivities we desire. The coming year awaits my son’s praetorship, if chance favors what has been said. For the purpose of preparing it, we have entrusted our friends with the task of selecting horses of the highest breed from Spain. Let them experience your support if they ask for any assistance or favor. For it is fitting that, out of our mutual affection, you share with me the matters that require care. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS

[Col. 0263C]

I would myself criticize my silence if I had ever received your letters. Therefore you cannot rebuke in another what you remember having allowed in yourself. Nevertheless, I was the first to break into these services, both to encourage you to take up the practice of writing and to support my friend with the endorsement of my testimony. For his industry and probity are such that he rightly deserves your favor. On his behalf I approach as a petitioner, presuming that our letters will be of great benefit with you. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXV. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS

That you preserve my letters is a sign of your affection; you do not know how to choose what should be copied. But this flattery deceives me. For I am driven toward confidence in writing by the security of pleasing you [Col. 0263D]; nevertheless, whenever I come to my senses, I fear exceedingly that this simplicity may fall upon another reader unlike you. Therefore I would have you keep what we produce without reflection, although the same things may be said to be preserved by my own copyists as well. But they do so through ignorance of critical examination, which you, as a man skilled in the art of Mercury, ought not to do. The kindness of friends knows how to favor mediocre writings; the envy of strangers does not know how to forgive them.

For the rest, I ask you now to come and increase the honor of the festive days by your presence. You surely know the customary festival of Minerva from your school days, just as we generally remember the holidays of childhood even as the years advance. For that day we are preparing a banquet for you, furnished with rustic vegetables, since luxury offends the sober goddess. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXVI. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS

[Col. 0264A]

You lie in wait for my childishness, which I conceal through the modesty of silence. To draw out my replies, you promise that you will come if I agree, although it would be easier for you to do it soon than to promise it. For me, obtaining is pleasant, while hoping is prolonged. Nevertheless, I obey your wish, and I do not fear that you will recklessly repeat in your copyist’s pages the words that I carelessly speak before you. For if anything among these things that I say to you without concern should cause nausea in some reader, it will not be negligence in writing that displeases so much. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXVII. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS

We cannot endure the hardness of our tenants, who, although they have not paid the remaining arrears, also refuse to bear the installment due for the coming year [Col. 0264B]. Therefore I ask you to deign to share responsibility with my man, whom I have sent to collect the dues, and willingly undertake this devout service. It is grievous that we are generous in the public obligations imposed upon our estates, while the agents of the properties are unwilling to return even what they know must be paid each year. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS

I do not allow any time to pass without fulfilling the duty of the holidays. Accordingly, I hastily entrusted the proper words to a letter-carrier who was hurrying; I ask you to undertake the task of returning the obligation, although I would rather rejoice in your return than in the honor of your writing [Col. 0264C]. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXIX. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS.

The reverence and concern owed to friends should not be measured by the sparingness of official duty. Often those eager to write lack the opportunity; yet the memory of friendship does not grow old through a temporary silence. Thus the fact that I have been silent until now should not be attributed to my will: many accidental obstacles have restrained our eagerness. But when a timely opportunity presented itself, I have put into this letter a sign of my intention and affection toward you; I shall make up for my silence hitherto by the frequency of my pages, if you encourage me with some reciprocal stimulus of conversation. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XC. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS

[Col. 0264D]

Concern for my people brought to my attention that your health had again been attacked. Therefore, anxious, I did not delay sending a letter amid uncertainty; divine mercy will ensure that it brings back joyful news about you. It will be your contribution to add the assurance of your health to my leisure. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XCI. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS

In both deeds and letters you discharge the duties of piety. For you extend the support of your favor to my people, and you make me share in the honor of your conversation. I therefore give and shall continue to give thanks, taking care that reciprocity may never be judged unlike our services to one another. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XCII. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS

[Col. 0265A]

When you wrote to my son, you deprived only me of the honor of your pen. I could have wounded you with the retaliation of silence, but I never return contempt equal to the negligence of friends. And would that the letter delivered to my son had contained none of the harshness arising from the settlement of a brotherly obligation. I too would by no means have seemed to myself neglected. Now two things happened together: both the honor of official duty passed me by, and the bitterness shared with my son struck me. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XCIII. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS

We have reached the Formian shore. From here we shall soon proceed to Puteoli. For it is burdensome to confess an eagerness for Baiae under the very ears of the judge. [Col. 0265B] You have the sequence of my plan. Remember yourself the promise by which you pledged that, on account of public affairs, you would be a comfort to my journey abroad. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XCIV. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS

After leaving Rome, following the business of the embassy, I received your letter, in which you promise abundant supplies of grain to our common fatherland. Thus, affected by twofold joy—as a citizen, I rejoice in the public security, and as a brother, I exult as though in the glory of your deed—I urge you with a pious exhortation toward this undertaking, although good will, which arises from character, should not be driven by spurs. I relieved the concern of our fellow citizens by reading aloud your words. For such a praiseworthy and reliable promise ought not to have been kept silent. It remains for a better outcome to attend your pious intention, and for an appropriate distinction in the future to answer to such great labor on behalf of your country. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XCV. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS

I have been sent to Milan by the Fathers to secure the aid of the divine prince, which the concern of our common fatherland demanded. With God’s favor spoken beforehand, prosperous circumstances promise me a swift return. But you will increase the happiness of the present if, through a letter, knowledge of your well-being reaches me. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XCVI. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS

I announce that I have returned to Rome. Would that I could also have been a messenger of my own health, which the hardship of travel and the severity of winter have weakened. But, restored to leisure, I hope for better things. May the divine powers ensure that you yourself are well. For I ought not to ask you to protect my people with your customary favor, since spontaneous services require no encouragement. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XCVII. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS

I would indeed have preferred to obtain your consolation, because letters hold the second place after personal presence in winning favor. The compensation of your writing satisfied my longing for you, and it especially helped my spirit that you announced that you had returned in good health and to good relations with me. I have decided to remain still at Formiae, so that, once autumn’s heats have been moderated, I may withdraw to the suburban estates. For the season does not permit me to enter our common fatherland in sorrow. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XCVIII. SYMMACHUS TO HELPIDIUS

If the circumstances of the time allowed it, I would thrust myself into your wishes even without being asked. In this matter, since you are certain of my state of mind, you do not, I think, require an assertion in words. Now the condition of my fortune excuses us from festive duties to such an extent that it even demands consolation from others. [Col. 0266C] Therefore, since for the moment it is not in my power to attend cheerful gatherings frequently, it will be your task to relieve one who is grieving. “To what does this refer?” you will say. I ask you to allow my brother Florentinus, a most distinguished and most honorable man, to remain attached to my journey abroad. I ask only that you interpret his presence as offering me, through this stay which he grants me, as much pleasure as you would have had from his presence. Farewell.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0265]

## EPISTLE I. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

[Col. 0265C]

In matters that are clear and manifest, nature is a more reliable adviser than rumor. Therefore, amid the narrow sustenance of our fatherland, let us gather praise for the foresight of the past not from the mouth of the multitude, [Col. 0265D] but from a consideration of human character. For late appraisers of benefits must, when scarcity follows upon abundance, recognize the gratitude they had concealed by comparison. Indeed, our populace, previously driven by the efforts of a few into hatred of so great a citizen, openly bears witness to its correction and repentance. But the notorious, stubborn envy of your colleagues does not allow them to confess what truth compels them to judge. Therefore they are afflicted with silent shame, and, like men convicted, cannot express about you what they are compelled to feel. But there is no need to pursue these matters at greater length. It is enough that public testimony has returned to reconcile your reputation. May he only live; and may your consolation lie in the celebrated memory of your father, and paternal renewal in your well-being. Farewell.

## EPISTLE II. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

[Col. 0266D]

Your letter made my day cheerful, and the eagerly awaited message of our household doubled the festivity of the birthday celebration. But after I had finished reading the page, the subscription appended to it furrowed my brow: it indicated that you were being harassed by disputes over Petronia’s property. Nevertheless, I think that, provided your sister Marciana’s promise is not defective, the uncertainty concerning the succession can be removed when you send to my examination the documents of the case, as she herself chose. I have marked below, in an enumeration, which points of the dispute the opposing party is raising, so that your holy unanimity, informed about the objections, may consider how each of you should answer on your own behalf. Farewell.

## EPISTLE III. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

[Col. 0267A]

A preface is necessary when difficult things are being requested; one ought not to solicit favor in matters that are straightforward and easy. Briefly, therefore, and in summary, take note of what favor my brother Fulvius requests from you. With your auspices, he wishes to take in marriage the sister of Pompeianus, formerly a woman of marriageable age, a woman inferior neither in birth nor, perhaps, in property. For I do not count among the adornments of the betrothal the commendable accomplishments of her life and the favorable hopes arising from her friendships with good men. Each person has for himself whatever is regarded as hope and praise. But I attach such importance to the completion of this union that I shall regard it as a great gift if your care assists his wishes. Since, therefore, an honorable undertaking in its beginning and easy in its execution is being requested, I ask you to apply to advancing the matter as much diligence as you infer that I desire. Farewell.

## EPISTLE IV. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

You have doubled, through the harshness of your message, the illness I endure from pain in my right hand. My concern is sharper still because I know that my daughter cannot be persuaded to exercise restraint in food and drink. Anxious, therefore, from a wound of the mind and an illness of the body, I could not postpone writing until I was able to sign the letter; but, by dictating it hastily, I satisfied my anxiety more than my usual practice. First, I beg you to relieve my fear by your reply. Then I beg you, my lady daughter, to avoid what is harmful to your health and to restore, with the help of moderation, the health so often interrupted. For abstaining from harmful things contributes not only to health, but also bears witness to prudence. Farewell.

## EPISTLE V. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

I recalled Severianus, a leading man of the city of Cliternum, from a public complaint, lest his accusation bring any measure of ill will upon our holy friend Severus. I promised, through your common agreement, our distinction, that if there was any dispute between them it could be settled. Therefore I ask you to deign to be an authority to the excellent man Severus for ending the litigation before you. Farewell.

## EPISTLE VI. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

As though still unaware of your affairs, you are setting out formulas for conducting business. But I explained long ago to your unanimity the outcome of both sides of the case, and I believe that what I wrote was delivered into your hands by the soldiers of the vicar. I rightly do not repeat what has already been recounted and ascertained. I had withheld from your knowledge, out of embarrassment at appearing ostentatious, only this further fact: I sent letters to his relatives, so that friends might be informed about the tutor’s frauds. And I think that, if fortune assists the undertaking, something should be decreed by which the offender may be broken.

As for the journey you postponed to the estates nearest the city, although I am most eager for you, I cannot disapprove of it. You allege a pious reason for the delay, and therefore I place the necessity of religious affection before my own desire. I do not know whether, while you delay, some invitation may instead draw us into Campania. But let this be left to the outcome. [Col. 0268A] Meanwhile, let us nurture our mutual longings by writing. The spirit must be softened by consolations whenever what is desired is prolonged. Farewell.

## EPISTLE VII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

Taburnius did not conceal from me that he had been summoned; and perhaps you wonder that my pages made no mention of the matter. But since I had decided to remain at home for many serious and necessary reasons, I judged it useless to bring to you, fruitlessly, matters that had been annulled and concealed. I believe that your holy unanimity is not unaware of what drew me back from my plan of traveling abroad. For you know my weakened health, you contemplate the solitude of my only child, and you have learned of the eruptions of the rivers, almost to the point of fearing a flood. Rumor, I think, has not kept silent among you about the devastation of the Pontine region and the landslides of the mountains either. [Col. 0268B] As a result, the others whom a similar summons had roused also asked leave, except Arcentius and Evangelus: the one was exposed by the vigor of youth, the other by a heedless spirit. I understand that you may be alarmed by the departure of a man who is not your friend. But I advise you to cast off this scruple. For much has also been attended to by my letters, and those who are departing have been given the task of repelling the spiteful attack of a rival. Therefore, free from anxiety, enjoy your leisure, and, as you deign to do, restore me by the constant frequency of your letters. Farewell.

## EPISTLE VIII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

[Col. 0268C]

Your letter was delivered to us while we were staying at Ostia on the seventh day. Immediately, at my request, the illustrious vicar caused a publication of the proceedings to be issued. But your boy left the city without our advice or knowledge, as is characteristic of the insolence of household slaves. It is in your hands whether you will allow this to go unpunished. Meanwhile, the report did not conceal that my daughter was suffering from a renewed illness. The wound of this news has sunk deeply into my heart, and the fear will not be erased unless I receive, through reciprocal writing, assurance of her health. Therefore, I beg you to arrange that security promptly conveyed to me may change my fear. Farewell.

## EPISTLE IX. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

My brother Censorinus is attempting to renew a complaint concerning the boundary of the praetorian estates at Baiae, although he has learned that it was long ago settled between me and the agents of my son Pompeianus. Inspectors were brought in, and they said that our properties were divided by the wall descending from the summit of the mountain between the houses. The new possessor believes that their judgment can be overturned. I therefore ask you, after bringing in our friend Felix and Castor, to deign to be an arbiter of the truth, so that, in the presence of your holiness, the empty undertaking may be suppressed.

Then, once the assertion of the earlier judgment has satisfied my brother Censorinus, only an addition of ten feet beyond his buildings should be permitted for his work and new constructions, so that the boundaries of the parties, the consent recorded in the agreement, and the intervening construction may mark the separation. Farewell.

## EPISTLE X. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

[Col. 0269A]

I hear that we have been asked to perform consular service. My decision, after the labor of the preceding year, is to rest and remain at home. Consider more deeply what you yourself decide, and weigh it wisely. I assume, however, that you—who are said to have been summoned by the authority of a most exalted man—have been selected among the ten, and that your unanimity has deliberately been joined to these matters, so that you may go out to offer thanks on the occasion of the consular duty.

But one must fear that, if you think you ought to make excuses, you may appear offended by obtaining the next rescript. And perhaps, insofar as it is permissible to hope about uncertain matters, this error will be corrected when you arrive safely. I have not discovered that Hispanus was asked. Consider, therefore, the outcome of both alternatives. I shall inform you again if any new knowledge concerning this matter comes to me. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XI. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

When I write many things to you, you answer few, and I am distressed that the beginnings of our instructions remain hot even to my solitude, but soon their progress grows cold through silence. Perhaps you will ask what I now still demand to have reported as evidence of my innocence. I had written that the price of the Capuan house had been settled with the seller. You write nothing about its confirmation.

The restoration and vindication of the Samnite property were ordered. Only later did you inform me that the fields had been emptied of their dowries. Even now I do not know what the required submission has accomplished, and my expectation of it prevents me from going into the countryside. For I fear that, as has often happened, some clandestine intrusion may attempt something. Therefore either inform me what remains to be done to resolve these affairs, or, if matters are secure, open a way for me to take up withdrawal.

I do not object if judgment has been given with some loss to us concerning the coastal spaces in dispute with my brother Censorinus. What remains is that the praetorian properties be divided by the intervening wall, lest, when the indication of the judgment ceases, the neighboring narrow spaces again strive to extend themselves into other boundaries. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

I was delighted by a friend’s letter, which you wished me to read, and I want you to believe that he did not lie about any relaxation of his desire to seize what was not his. The illustrious praetorian judge announced to me the displeasure of the Empress concerning the Senate’s contribution and other remedies for the City; he says that he was distressed by a councillor, because, on the day of the imperial games, when a costly offering was being demanded from us in the Senate who were present, the prefect of the city publicly announced the common contribution to the people.

He suspects that all this has been arranged to destroy the glory of his promises, and, because this pleases those who report it, he turns the ill will solely against me. I answered his heat as best I could while preserving my dignity. And, insofar as the Eastern envoys assert—the very men to whom he himself made my writings known—everyone approved our replies. But, so that he would not remain silent after being defeated by reason and authority, he later sent milder letters containing the same complaint. A copy of all these will be delivered to you, so that you may know amid what storms we are being battered.

As for the matter of your holy unanimity, which the repeated instruction has stirred up, we must use the advice of postponing the settlement, and the portion belonging to your brother must be put up for auction, so that the young man may exaggerate this kind of injury or fulfill his wish. But I wish to know precisely which estates belong in part to the right of your holy brother, lest, through ignorance, the error of an agent touch the bodies of your property rights.

I shall keep your brother in Rome for the time being, since the offering of grain supplies has been extended for twenty days. My daughter, therefore, ought not to take it badly if I delay the animals assigned to her journey. My son Cumazon will tell you the rest, whether you ask him or he volunteers it.

Because of the scarcity of grain, the public discussion concerning the embassy to be sent will be deferred until the return of the most distinguished count. I thought the advice of your holiness salutary. Accordingly, after sending letters to my people, I immediately ordered grain to be transported from our Apulian estate to Campania. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XIII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

The steady succession of the preceding letters has exhausted the task of writing. Now only the general pious greeting remains.
