Indeed, if there were anything else to pursue on the pages, it would more properly be entrusted to the traveler. For now the pen must be indulged, since the person of those departing is not sufficient to receive the instructions. If you consider anything worth knowing, you will learn it more fully from the traveler, without the digression of our conversation. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XIV. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

[Col. 0270C]

I see that you are uncertain whether the punishment of Rufinus was followed also by the confiscation of his property. Proof is available, sealed by imperial orders. Yet, given the deserts of an old-time plunderer, there should have been no doubt that the treasury desires the spoils of the world. And would that the shortage of grain, which no new harvest supplies, did not interrupt such great joy. Moreover, the quality of the food itself produces horror and damages the health of bodies; such nourishment is more burdensome to people than the punishment of fasting.

Amid these circumstances, the people are consoled by hope of the grain offered by the Fathers, and the pious willingness of the nobles preserves the harmony of the city. Now prayers are needed, so that divine assistance may bring in supplies while the safety of the citizens is sustained by private contributions. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XV. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

[Col. 0270D]

The fortune of our common fatherland has been reduced to such straits that extreme measures must be avoided. Therefore I wish to send your brother back to you immediately; deign soon to provide him with the pack animals, and let his haste be assisted by their support. As for my daughter, she ought not to be wearied by travel, as I wrote earlier. After a serious indisposition, her health must be restored by leisure and rest. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XVI. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

I anticipated what fear the rumor of my illness might arouse in you. Since rumor habitually speaks about absent people beyond the truth, it does not even seem to have equaled the magnitude of my danger in reporting it. Therefore, as soon as my health allowed me to form letters, I did not delay easing for you by my pen what I had believed had been spread abroad. And although my earlier message would have been sufficient to moderate your anxiety, a second assurance will nevertheless contribute to establishing security.

Meanwhile, let me know what plan you have begun concerning arranging your return. For I confess that, after the danger to my health, I have become more yielding through affection and can no longer urge you to place your leisure before my desire. Soon, when your brother, as you say, is expected to be present from nearby, he will provide both a happy and a necessary return for you, for the purpose of sharing your fellowship. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XVII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

Friendship is measured by minds, not by years. Therefore do not regard the affection of those whose devotion to you is long-standing as inexperienced. This is directed toward ensuring that you know that Auxentius [Col. 0271B] and Marianus, my sons, most modest young men, are counted among your admirers in the foremost place; and therefore they should not be received as people to be known through a new introduction, but should be honored through the bond and piety of affection.

Now the compulsion of physicians has provided them with a reason for setting out, after they obtained treatment. For they wish to go to Stabiae, so that they may drive away the remnants of a long illness with the milk of herds. But they judge that greater medicine lies in meeting you. Their health, therefore, will be entrusted to you if you add the nourishment of kindness to the remedies of healing herbs. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XVIII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

To our Castor, returning to Campania, we entrusted more extensive instructions concerning domestic matters than we wrote. You will therefore learn more through your ears than through reading. Most of these matters concern the condition of our fatherland, which is suffering severely from a shortage of food. It is dangerous to inhabit it, and impious and cruel to abandon it. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XIX. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

I would have come even while uncertain of my health to my brother Taburnius, whom you wished me to assist, if chance had granted the presence of those whom it was useful for him to meet. Let my spirit, therefore, satisfy your unanimity, even though circumstances denied the effectiveness of my wish. Still weak, but now secure in my recovery, with God’s favor spoken beforehand, I write this; and I rise to greater strength in proportion as nearby hope promises me a more rapid return of your holiness. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XX. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

You had written earlier that my daughter’s health had been restored. Then, in a subsequent letter, you inserted a renewed sting into our anxiety. I am therefore tormented by the more recent message, because adverse reports are more readily believed. I anxiously await your indication of whether the day has brought anything good.

As for the fact that our departure excites you, I recognize in it the state of my own mind. But even now it is better, in response to mutual longing, to advise what is excellent than to begin something that will bring regret through the weakness of affection. Soon, when your brother, as you say, is expected to be present from nearby, he will provide for you both a happy and necessary return, so that you may share your fellowship with one another. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXI. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

The children of my brother Entrecius, an illustrious man, had been summoned by the impatience of paternal love, and the scarcity in the city added reasons for their haste. Therefore they have undertaken their return without waiting for the proper time. Consequently, while navigation is impossible, they will remain for a little while on the shores of Campania. But your kindness will ensure that they do not endure the bitterness of exile. Take my place, therefore, so that those who have now been separated from us by necessity may rejoice that they have found my spirit in you. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

[Col. 0272B]

The disturbance produced by an injury is harsh, but the medicine of patience ought to soften the pain. Nor are you without experience in enduring adversity. For you have learned to bear the blows of fortune frequently. If you were living amid prosperity, happiness would rightly be wounded by unaccustomed misfortunes.

I write this so that you may know that I was surprised that a private lawsuit changed your constancy, which—as I think—was stirred up by the meddler of the Baian shore under the pretext of relatives. But he will receive a different kind of payment. Your case, however, did not lack judicial defense. From one of the two judges an order was obtained that what the agent had devised should not go unpunished; from the other, that your inheritance should be protected.

I shall also warn the lord of the dispute himself, when he has withdrawn from the estate, either to abandon his undertaking or to know that more serious matters will be reported against him. Let this suffice concerning domestic affairs.

As for our fatherland, amid its other evils of grain scarcity, the rivalry surrounding the embassy added a more wicked torch. At first the election joined Posthumianus and Pinianus, two leading men of the court, under such an expression of judgment that the embassy was said to be complete in those two alone. After some days, when the Senate was considering and weighing the instructions of the order, private interests joined Paulinus to them. From this arose a quarrel that proceeded, in my absence, as far as impious fights.

It is shameful to say what accusations and insults the leading senators hurled at one another. But they are said to have regretted that the disputes of the parties had to be settled by my judgment. Fortune will see what end awaits the public cause. Meanwhile, the reputation of the Senate is being torn apart, and the unfortunate men have incurred an additional charge. If the records of what was done come into my hands, you will learn by reading what the modesty of my words refused to explain. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXIII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

I ought to have refrained from writing while my son Decius, an illustrious man, is traveling, since he will tell your holiness more than the text of a page could contain. But I was not reluctant to increase by my pen the pleasure that his fraternal presence will bring. Therefore I offer your unanimity the honor of a greeting, so that the expectation of my arrival may be eased by the gift of my words. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXIV. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

[Col. 0273A]

Sapricius, an accomplished man and a friend of mine, would have deserved the attention of your holy unanimity without an advocate. But because a first conversation recommends strangers, he wished me to open for him, through my agency, an easy path to earning your familiarity. It is therefore fitting that you receive him, who is most eager for you, with immediate affection, and that you not postpone the friendship he requests until it has undergone the tests of long use, but immediately meet the desire of one who is approaching with equal goodwill. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXV. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

My son Zenodotus has not yet come to know you through closer acquaintance, but, with rumor acting as an intermediary, he already welcomes you. For although he is hastening toward Lucania and Bruttium under the compulsion of official honor, he nevertheless eagerly wishes to turn aside from his journey and hasten into your presence. I introduce him into your friendship as an initiator (*mystagogus*), and I take responsibility for his being worthy of your affection.

If, therefore, you attach any value to a parent’s testimony, may his first approach soon find an established piety toward you, and may he immediately experience that openness of your heart which he knows has never been denied to novelty. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXVI. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

I struggled with myself for a long time about sending you our common pledge, but affection prevailed, especially as the prospect of the advancing provisioners grew more encouraging. For a sparing distribution promises the city’s food supplies for twenty days, for the present. Moreover, a second contribution from the most distinguished order promises to add something to security. Nevertheless, even the distribution of meat raised the spirits of the Roman populace.

I therefore ordered the pack animals to return to you, giving thanks that you assisted your brother’s need with suitable support. The choice of the envoys is still wavering. For, in addition to Posthumianus and Pinianus, whom the Senate had recognized from the beginning of their commission, Paulinus is being asserted as a third, and the usefulness of the matter is still being delayed because the parties are divided among their preferences. Once the deadline for confirmation has been received, the full matter will be referred. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXVII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

A more extensive letter is needed when strangers are being commended. But the longstanding familiarity of the most serious and honorable man Justinus with us requires no assistance in winning favor. It is enough, therefore, if you extend to him your customary affection. As for what concerns us, and what was recently indicated to your unanimity in a letter, he himself will now explain orally. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

If anything is secure for a human being, I announce that, after the pain of my internal organs which had suddenly taken me away from you, I have returned to the hope of life. Therefore, if the license of rumor reported anything harsh to you, let oblivion erase it. Above all, I wish it to be secured that you do not hasten back through ill-considered anxiety. But since the situation has turned toward health, deign to satisfy our common longing according to the proper distances of the journey. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXIX. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

An opportunity to tell you of my health must often be sought by me if it is absent, and embraced if it is present—especially at a time when I am anxious about my daughter’s health, which I believe has also been injured by fasting. Therefore release us from fear by reporting favorable news. My steps are still weak. But if reciprocal conversation brings desired news from you, the complaint of my little body will immediately be calmed.

I should not omit adding to this page that a judicial summons expelled Martinianus. Such terror was inflicted upon him because he had so long omitted his journey to Gaul that he had to forestall, by a private journey, the injury of being summoned. An auditor asked, through the intervention of a friend, what we wished to be done concerning Atellanus. I replied that, after the judgment of the priest, I was awaiting only vengeance for the ill will recently contrived. Nevertheless, I left the matters to your discretion.

I therefore ask you, during the delays of the recess, to deign to explain what needs to be done; and at the same time to consider, in opposition to the intervention of so many bishops, what can be obtained rather than what ought to be obtained. For justice and innocence cannot be accorded very much when religious reverence is set against them. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXX. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

After we sent the boy away, much rumor spread that your holiness was to be summoned by sacred letters, [Col. 0274C] so that even the name of a certain Gratianus, who is said to be carrying such writings, is circulating in public speech. Although this still seems uncertain to me, I did not think it should be kept silent. It will belong to the supreme divinity to determine what concerns you and to confirm the proper order of favorable events. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXXI. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

The most illustrious man Principius, distinguished by birth and integrity, requires no recommendation from another, since he also boasts of the testimony of your affection and judgment toward him. I would explain his merits at greater length, were it not a redundant task to repeat what is known to everyone. It will suffice to add this one thing: whatever honor you bestow upon him will reach all good men who love him. [Col. 0274D] Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXXII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

I am staying in a suburban retreat. For I am weary of the annoyances of the city, and I take pleasure in the pleasant renewal provided by a villa suited to autumn. Moreover, the arrival of friends supplies me with the company that alone is judged honorable at Rome.

But the illness of my little granddaughter Galla considerably disturbs the security of our leisure. May divine assistance ensure that you report promptly that she is recovering and doing well. And you, my lady daughter, please take care to inform me day by day how much recovery is being added. This will testify to your pious affection toward me, if you both have attended to her health and conveyed to my knowledge news that will please me. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

If we still entertain any hopes concerning Sicily, they are uncertain. For although Eusebius’s letter announced that the performers for the circus and stage had sailed some time ago, even now rumor keeps their arrival hidden. Therefore it seemed right to request an agent who, after traveling along every shore, might bring back to our ears what he had discovered. Concern for the games has increased since the people, with repeated enthusiasm, demanded a report concerning the securing of the amphitheater and soon obtained the judge’s assent. God’s will will bring it about that, in this matter also, the authority of the divine prince may agree. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

[Col. 0275B]

Your brother, long afflicted in spirit by grief over the loss of his teacher, has begun to lend an ear to those offering consolation; his sorrow has also wounded me severely, apart from the concern that troubles us over choosing a teacher. If you agree, let us request by a joint letter from the illustrious man Adrianus the rhetor Gallus, whom Eusebius had not recently introduced, so that the character of our children, once placed on the path of progress, may not be abandoned.

The character of my future [work], once placed on the path of progress, is abandoned. The labor and expense of the forthcoming production occupy me. For, in arranging the rewards, although I have an ample supply of garments, I discover that some things are still lacking from the equipment. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXXV. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

[Col. 0275C]

As long as matters tossed about by rumor are rashly delayed, enjoy your leisure free from anxiety. If a more recent report brings anything worthy of hearing and supported by credibility, I shall refrain neither from reporting it nor from offering advice. Take this one piece of advice from me before necessity arises: there is no way for you to decline the honor of being summoned.

As for your brother, we have still received no information beyond the instruction. I have put these matters concerning the wedding at Ostia onto the page; the younger son of the illustrious Sallustius summoned us to it. But Rome must immediately be revisited because of the preparations for the games. For these are matters that I must attend to for a long time; if your holiness were present, our common diligence could easily complete them. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXXVI. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

[Col. 0275D]

When sacred letters were delivered to me by an *agens in rebus*, summoning us to the service of the most exalted consul, I saw other letters similarly sent in your name, by which imperial honor summoned you. The same agent also presented the consul’s writings. I therefore advise you to prepare your journey promptly; Hispanus will not accompany you.

Another matter has also arisen that may encourage you. My brother Neoterius, an illustrious man and an admirer of my lord brother, having been asked to undertake the same cause, will provide you consolation and assistance. Therefore I do not want you to hesitate, since you know that the persons of friends were chosen by the authority of the most exalted man, and that these greetings of the divine prince are being conveyed first to you after the uncertainties of fortune. [Col. 0276A]

As for your own business, I willingly undertake before the holy tribune what you had wished to have carried out through my agency. Meanwhile, advance your journey to the Formian shore, and, when the letters delivered to you arrive, hasten more quickly to Rome. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXXVII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS

I put the greeting of health first, since it accords above all with my wish and is owed at the beginning of a letter. Then, my lady daughter, I commend to your care the birthday banquet of your brother. For my man reports that the shores have been deserted through the flight of the sailors. This circumstance compelled me to entrust your holiness with matters of lesser importance.

There is nothing remaining to write about public affairs, except that on Trajan’s Street the collapse of a single apartment block crushed its inhabitants. [Col. 0276B] Popular resentment turned this so strongly against the fortunes of the public carriage that it now has a private driver. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS
Our friend Severus, freed from the public trouble, has returned to the leisure of his homeland. He was soon assisted, in the presence of your brother, the illustrious vicarius, by both a letter from your holiness and the recognition of their longstanding friendship. My concern over the praetorian arrangements is increasing. I write this so that your unanimity may understand that the cooperation of its support is desired. Nor am I an imperious exactor, since I know that my needs must be placed after your convenience. But, if I judge correctly, the respite available during the present month will suffice for your recovery. I have briefly explained the disposition of my own wishes; what needs to be done I leave to your judgment, so that what spontaneous affection chooses may be more praiseworthy for you and more gratifying for me. Farewell.

**LETTER XXXIX. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

I am surprised that the boys whom we sent to your holiness on different days have been delayed; yet we do not abandon the practice of writing, wishing to know how much the restoration of health has progressed. Let the return of your greeting, therefore, promptly satisfy our expectation. Farewell.

**LETTER XL. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

My first pleasure is to ask what state of health you are enjoying; once that is favorable, I shall turn to the other matters which you long ago thought ought to be inquired into. The city is being troubled by grave omens, whose lesser aspects I pass over. Above all, a sorrowful interpretation makes me shudder: on the birthday of Rome, the consul suffectus was thrown from the chariot in which he was riding by the ferocity of the teams that were bearing the triumph. Thus, dressed in the palm-embroidered robe and distinguished by consular attire, he was carried away with a broken leg. The unhappy report has distressed me, and therefore I shall keep this account brief.

Day by day, our honor, your reputation is flourishing more brightly at home and abroad. Of present events, indeed, we ourselves are witnesses. Caecilianus has affirmed the judgments expressed abroad; it would be tedious to enumerate them individually, since everything converges in the fullness of your glory. I wish my daughter, the lady, to be greeted, together with her sweetest grandchildren; she wished us dutifully to remind you that you are engaged in weaving the garments for the presentation of the games. From the following details she will learn what ought to be prepared as a supplement to the praetorian largesse. Farewell.

**LETTER XLI. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

I am distressed in spirit since learning that my daughter is afflicted by her customary pain. I would have wished to begin the journey to you, had not both a heaviness in my head and an unexpected fever kept our Symmachus at home. It is better to say nothing of his bodily complaints, lest your holiness’s anxiety be doubled. Certainly my brother Comazon, who has left the city in longing for you, will explain more fully what we are keeping silent about. I need not ask what you will do spontaneously: restrain the magnitude of our anxieties with happier letters. Farewell.

**LETTER XLII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

[Col. 0277B]

I recently received a letter from Eusebius, in which he reported that our charioteers and some performers had been put aboard ship and, in accordance with my instructions, sent to Campania. Let your holiness therefore order the most diligent investigators to proceed as far as the shore of Salernum, so that they may escort them to Naples after their arrival, or ascertain some indication of their coming.

I also wish our common friend Felix to be advised that, if they have arrived safely in Campania, they should be supplied with grain allowances and expenses and sent to us by continuous passage. For long before the games we must both train them to yoke the horses and win the favor of the populace for their novelty. The substance of my request, then, is this: that the investigation concerning them and the prompt completion of the undertaking be assigned to your men.

**LETTER XLIII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

We tried to preserve the crocodiles displayed in the theatrical spectacle until your presence; but, as the starvation that had wasted them over fifty days continued, they were killed during the subsequent games in the manner of combatants. We shall postpone the arrival of two that are still breathing until you come, although their abstinence from food does not allow us to promise that they can live long. Farewell.

**LETTER XLIV. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

It is excessive labor to remind one who is mindful. But the affairs undertaken for friends do not at all permit us to observe moderation. Therefore I do not cease asking you to carry out energetically the wishes of our common friend Hercules, a most illustrious man. Let the agreement of your relatives act with the zeal of your holy unanimity; for my son Valentinus has stated that he too, having been consulted by Julian’s letter, advised the same things we desire concerning the marriage agreement. Farewell.

**LETTER XLV. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

After learning that you had been shaken by your customary pain, all sense of my other anxieties vanished. For, as Hippocrates says: “Present troubles grow dull if a greater pain has intervened.” I therefore await happier news about you, so that I may return to my former concerns. In this consternation of spirit I pass over the rest as untimely, yet I have enclosed a memorandum which I would like you to consider once your health has been restored to tranquility. Farewell.

**LETTER XLVI. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

You have sent us no letters through our man. Yet I could not imitate the silence of your unanimity, either because the anxiety that you rightly feel for me demanded it, or because genuine affection drives me to the duties of writing. The exchange of replies will show that my action was welcome to you. Farewell.

**LETTER XLVII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

I neither have time to learn about the city’s affairs nor desire to write about them; my mind, occupied by bodily illness, cannot direct its attention to matters belonging to others. I know only this: messengers have lied about the disturbances, and the rumors differ so greatly from the truth that the prefecture has never been celebrated with greater applause. Thus the favor of the order vies with the enthusiasm of the populace for the judge. These reports reach us, if any interval in our sufferings permits us to attend to visitors, in the unanimous account of them all. The letters of your men, who are active in public affairs, should reveal the rest. I shall inquire about other people’s concerns when my own adversities have subsided. Farewell.

**LETTER XLVIII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

With the birthday gift—which common prosperity will lead you to repeat for many years—you have gladdened our spirit and shown your own worth. Your modesty does not allow me to write at length about it. Yet the gratitude retained in my feelings is more abundant than what can be expressed in words. You will learn what concerns the city by reading the accompanying memorandum. You, however, my lady daughter, I earnestly charge, with the devotion that is proper, to take care of supporting your health, so that the security of your well-being may be a pleasure to us all. Farewell.

**LETTER XLIX. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

I used up my writing while your man was returning to Campania. Yet I did not wish your holy and honorable father Severus to depart without a letter from me, both to fulfill the customary greeting and to disclose my judgment, based on my inspection, of the work you are constructing at home. The baths pleased me greatly, both in their arrangement and in their size. In the smaller baths I did not approve of the pool being decorated with paintings rather than mosaic.

The matter reminds me to let you know of Messala’s departure on the night followed by the Nones of March. The other legates will follow shortly. Yet from the conversation of some people I learned that, for the sake of the household by which many of our countrymen are stuffed with delicacies, certain matters have been softened. But my diligence will not be lacking, lest anything be taken away from the senate’s instructions through connivance. Farewell.

**LETTER L. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

I do not refuse to write, but I preferred to reserve for a leisurely face-to-face conversation what I have to tell my son Sibidius. This page, therefore, will serve only as a greeting; its brevity will satisfy your honor without taking anything away from what must be reported to him. Farewell.

**LETTER LI. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

You learned from my earlier letter what I could now reply. I do not regret having returned. We are in possession of good health, and through the diligence of your brother’s teachers his progress is advancing. Only this troubles my spirit: that a long journey separates us from you. But let frequent practice exercise the exchange of letters; among ourselves we shall repair the pleasure of presence. Farewell.

**LETTER LII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

The arrival of our lord and emperor must again be requested. For Theodorus, the illustrious man, having accepted the embassy of the Milanese, is said to be striving to place the desire of the province before the senate’s petitions. The urban prefect wishes your holiness to be associated with this affair, and I think he will send you a letter about it. I therefore urge you, when summoned by his written request, to be so kind as to hurry here before the senate, which will meet on the Ides of June. I think the envoys will be chosen on that very day.

Your household has many matters that you could settle in person on the occasion of the public cause. Moreover, this is a votive embassy, which is likely to be welcome to the ears of those whom we seek to summon. Please do not delay, so that you may regain the reconciliation of your former favor. Farewell.

**LETTER LIII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

Receive Maximus, an old friend but a new agent in public affairs, among the recruits who serve despite his gray hair. From him you will learn what must be done; therefore I must avoid the pleasure of a lengthy letter. Apart from requesting your arrival—which I frequently repeat, and about which I ought already to be silent if longing for you allowed it—I should keep quiet, because requests that achieve nothing produce embarrassment. But my love for you, repeatedly disappointed, nearly urges me to shamelessness. I fear, however, that you promised your return for this reason: so that you might prevent our journey to you. Farewell.

**LETTER LIV. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

We pray for your good health, news of which we hope to receive when the boy returns. For the moment my own health is free from pains, but it requires strengthening, especially as new concerns have been added by the recent offer made by the senate. I am reluctant to go on at greater length, since I already regret having burdened your mind with these matters. Farewell.

**LETTER LV. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

Yesterday I wrote through my man, shaken by fear, after you reported the bitter news about my daughter’s health; and, while awaiting your reply, I am still tormented by uncertainty. I therefore ask to be informed what improvement has come to her for the restoration of her health.

As for present affairs, I had decided to give you no information, lest there return to your ears matters that you had wisely avoided by departing. But since civic affection has brought your concern back to urban affairs, I have briefly run through certain items entered under headings, so that you may learn them without the tedium of reading. Farewell.

**LETTER LVI. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

I believe that by now the earlier letter of my lord the Prefect has been delivered to you. If they have slipped away through some accident or the negligence of the bearer, here is another page from that most subtle man, to which he ordered me to append this message, so that—having been consulted twice—you may explain what your view is concerning the undertaking with which he wishes you to be associated.

For I think you have returned to better health, since you informed me that illness was preventing your return. We would certainly prefer you to promise your return once your health has been restored; but if the complaints of your little body delay the fulfillment of your wish, discharge the expectations of the one who consults you with explicit letters. Farewell.

**LETTER LVII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

In recent days I have satisfied both my attentiveness toward you and your expectation with a great number of letters. This page, however, requires no abundance, since, within the limits of my judgment, I offer your goodwill this sole advice: that the conduct of your Sicilian case be transferred to the praetorian prefect; provided that the offer made to you leaves anything still to be tried. Farewell.

**LETTER LVIII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

After our dear Sibidius returned to Rome, he reported how severe a bodily pain was troubling my daughter; my own spirit is also distressed. I therefore sent a letter without delay, earnestly asking first that she be helped toward health by medical treatment and abstinence from harmful things, and then that the reliability of your reply relieve my anxiety.

After the departure of the legates we ourselves went to the Vatican estate, which adjoins your property; and, if nothing disrupts what has been arranged, we shall enjoy the leisure of the estate until the Kalends of April. The levy of younger men imposed upon the urban households will remain pending until the response of the eternal emperor. You will learn the form of both orders from the enclosed copies.

I sent this because your letters requested it. Otherwise, the sole and exclusive reason for dictating the letter was that definite and friendly news about my daughter’s health should be brought back to us. Farewell.

**LETTER LIX. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

Your earlier letter, followed shortly by another, had given me some hope of your return; the promises of the second have emptied that hope. Thus, after many reasons for refusal, you entrusted the decision to my judgment.

But I, considering first my daughter’s troubled health, which cannot be deprived of the comfort of your presence; then the weakness of your stomach, which you write is unequal to undertaking the journey; then the advice of your paternal friend, who prefers leisure; then the expectation of the illustrious man whom I had long thought would be absent; and, in addition, the interpretations of people who, as you say, suppose that you accepted public office as an opportunity for your own affairs—I return the deliberation you entrusted to me.

For it is unjust that my opinion should become subject to so many contrary questions, and that the credibility of one who gives advice should be bound to uncertain circumstances of the future. Meanwhile, I think the date for settling the matter should be postponed, and I have temporarily refrained from delivering your letter to the magistrate.

First, because it contains mere reverence; then because it placed the reasons for refusal below the magnitude of your devotion; and because I knew that what you had written would be read by many. I therefore wish you, if your desire to decline the labor and journey remains, to reinforce your excuse with greater reverence and more serious complaints. Farewell.

**LETTER LX. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

[Col. 0281B]

Ancient custom made it customary for those departing from home to begin their official correspondence with a letter. But it seemed too long to wait for a letter from your unanimity, whose delay we blame. Therefore, changing our practice, we have burst into this duty.

It remains for you willingly to repay what you ought to have begun, and to exercise your pen in return, as an indication of your health. We ourselves await my lady daughter’s arrival at the Arabian estate; although the reckoning of the solemn days immediately promises that you too, our honor, will be present. Farewell.

**LETTER LXI. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

It is a happy subject to encourage leisure. But such exhortation requires a mind that is its own master. We are prevented from remaining in one place both by the faction of the envious and by the education of our young son, which does not permit us to travel abroad for long. Therefore, as we can, we vary our locations, sometimes by departure and sometimes by return.

This letter is testimony, having recently been sent from a suburban estate; another will follow from our Coranus, if nothing disrupts what has been arranged. It is for you, if you approve, to improve the condition of our absence by frequent letters; if you disapprove, to relieve it. Farewell.

**LETTER LXII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

The legates of our order have returned after all was conducted successfully. The requisition of recruits has subsided, and a concession has been made to us regarding the silver. Yet further advocacy in support of what has been obtained is still hoped for.

Now we shall add domestic matters, friendly to your spirit. We remain in possession of good health. We often vary our stay in the city with a nearby country retreat. Only your absence torments us. But if you come quickly into our presence, we too shall accompany your return to Campania with pleasure. Farewell.

**LETTER LXIII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

I had sent a letter through my man. Immediately Maximus arrived, asking for another; therefore I was not reluctant to double the greeting. Moreover, a recent report concerning the arrival of our lord and emperor required me to remind you of the return that you must hasten, lest your delay forestall the votive embassy, which must now be repeated for the public interest. Farewell.

**LETTER LXIV. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

You had written that you had emptied your bowels with a purgative medicine, so that the inflammation of your eyes might depart along with the rest of the burden. I want to know whether the treatment mentioned was effective, and whether the condition did not require the veins also to be assisted by bloodletting.

A corresponding concern requires you to let me know how much assurance my daughter’s health gives you, so that, once I learn these things as I wish, I may lay aside the sharp edge of my anxieties. I am distressed on other grounds as well when I consider the disturbances of the homeland, which are chiefly provoked by the requisition of services for military use.

We indeed resist with repeated prayers and prolong the day by supplication; and now the miserable offer has reached the price of five pounds of silver. But I fear that, in escaping one matter, the other may strip us of everything. The prefect, who seemed sluggish in conducting the affair, has been replaced by Lampadius, whose character has led people to believe that impossible things could be advanced.

Now I ask you to relieve my anxiety with greater attention to the matter that concerns you. For I am still tormented by uncertainty because of the delay of the little servant who was sent to you some time ago to learn the same things and has not yet returned. Farewell.

**LETTER LXV. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

There is no lack of matters to write about, but my spirit shudders at speaking of harsh things that are painful to remember. Yet I see that the report of urban affairs cannot at all be restrained and, as usually happens, will announce present events in an exaggerated form.

To prevent that, we have separated the matters to be learned in an attached Brief Summary, so that neither the letter bringing you a greeting may derive bitterness from anxious matters, nor the reliability of the written account fail to exclude the license of rumors. But enough about these things.

My daughter’s health weighs more heavily upon me than all the other matters by which my spirit is now embittered. I therefore await your announcement that, with God’s help, everything is pointing toward her recovery. If I learn that her condition is in accordance with my prayer, this portion of comfort will also mitigate the remainder of my anxieties. Farewell.

**LETTER LXVI. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

We were absent from our homeland for only a few days, and the theatrical games demanded our return through the votes of the citizens. Even now, however, we are staying in the suburb along the Ostian road, delaying our return for a while, lest we appear to have waited for the prayers.

Had I wished earlier to act according to the decision of your religious devotion, I would both have avoided the dangers that followed and possessed an expectation of my return that carried greater dignity. But there was one reason for this decision: lest I appear to certain people to have been driven from my position, and lest a modest departure be turned into a mark of cowardice.

Concerning your Sicilian affair, the holy Comazon wrote back, with my agreement as well. That Nectarius is causing trouble concerning our Sicilian business will be shown by the letter that Euscius recently sent. I therefore ask that you restrain in writing this man, who knows nothing of affairs and cherishes his leisure shut up in his room, lest afterward he think differently about Euscius if he defends our cause more forcefully than is just.

I have sent the man’s own letter, so that you may judge from his character the insolence of the attempt—though it is certain that he does not wish to be reproached by us.

In my earlier letters I had asked you to improve the side of my praetorium at Puteoli by which one goes to the baths, by arranging a gentler slope. If the matter has been delayed, I ask you again to do it; if it has been completed, write back so that I may rejoice. Farewell.

**LETTER LXVII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

It is true that no one can obtain everything at once that he desires. How much more splendidly would I have celebrated my birthday if you had been present! At least, prayed-for fortune will grant this in the years to come.

Meanwhile, my lady daughter, I am sufficiently pleased that you have honored me with the finest memorial of your weaving. In it both your love for your father and your matronly industry have shone forth. Thus the women of old are said to have cultivated their lives.

I honor those women and that age barren of luxury, and the loom commanded them to devote their minds to work, because life is lived when temptation has ceased. But for you, neither the proximity of Baiae nor its attractions can take away your care for sober work. You leave the pools to their sweepers and, sitting or walking among the tasks and distaffs of the girls, regard these alone as the delights proper to your sex.

I therefore rightly love you and judge you worthy of your husband, since praise and pleasure alike come to us from his acquired excellence and from your innate virtue. Farewell.

**LETTER LXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

Although, with God’s permission as previously invoked, I hope that we shall soon come into one another’s presence, I ought not to abstain from writing, lest any time be without the duties of friendship. Accept, then, this preliminary greeting, which for the sake of a favorable omen I am still offering you by my pen, but which I shall shortly deliver by voice. Farewell.

**LETTER LXIX. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

You wished to excuse your silence with an elegant explanation. You alleged caution regarding gloomy reports for as long as favorable ones might follow, so that what the interruption of your writing had previously concealed might be revealed through happier indications.

But those matters were not unknown to us through messengers, and these arrived very late indeed. Suspicion that your duty had ceased was increasing the license of rumors. Yet we cannot be angry after the gratitude inspired by your present letter has removed the memory of the former pain.

Only remember to rank care for your pen among your chief and earliest duties, lest recollection of this example again bring greater fears while we suppose that, in awaiting better things, you are once more concealing some adversity. Farewell.

**LETTER LXX. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

I admit that I have long refrained from writing. Nothing arose that we needed to write about. I was receiving happy assurance of your health from the speech of those arriving. At last affection overcame my silence.

We therefore renew our custom of sending greetings, free from every other concern. After our withdrawal to Tibur, we are prolonging a sluggish leisure at Rome. Yet we are not entirely negligent of matters requiring action. At home, the separations of the decayed walls are being repaired, because the original builder preferred haste to solidity, and he considered immediate use more urgent than the security of those who would come after.

You are undertaking new works destined to endure through the ages; indeed, conversation has reported that you have made certain things equal to the works of Lucullus. Yet we shall not yield to you in the magnitude of expenditure. The expense is equal whether one establishes something solid once or repeatedly restores what is falling. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXI. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

Indulge yourselves in luxury, since you overflow with such abundance of land and sea that the wealth of both elements supplies you with lavish nourishment. For us, it is enough that we enjoy a share of everything you possess, and enjoy it so generously that we too abound in sumptuous dishes. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

Having returned to our homeland and household gods, we found certain things that offended us, since our Ostian estate is repeatedly subjected to encroachment. But if your wishes are proceeding favorably, send letters whose joy may wipe away the cloud of the present injury. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

I am tormented by pain in my kidneys. But, lest a more serious report reach your ears, I have briefly indicated the present condition of my health. When happier events follow, I shall, according to my custom, send you a happier page. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

[Col. 0284C]

It was not without reason that we delayed our reply until now: the discussion of the affair and the investigation of the documents required a delay of appropriate length. Once these matters had been completed, we added the reciprocal service of a letter to the other preparations demanded by the case.

We ourselves cannot undertake the journey to you, impeded as we are by many concerns. Yet you will receive more abundant advice concerning the settlement from another relative. Although he does not need an assistant, he will nevertheless deign, because of the empty formalities of the court and the quibbles of old formulas, to await the holy Prosdocius. He will come to you immediately once he has worn away the remnants of ill health through complete recovery. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXV. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

[Col. 0284D]

I had intended to pass by Fundi if I had learned that you had gone to Formiae. Since events turned out otherwise, I decided to divide the journey in order to lessen the labor. It will therefore be in Fortune’s power to make it happen that we are refreshed at our Formian residence by the fifth day before the Kalends of August. This is the intention of our mind; the fulfillment of our wish now lies in the hands of the heavenly powers. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXVI. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

No day passes without my letters. What if you were to return a greeting in turn? Yet I do not regret my diligence, although the honor of reciprocity is neglected. For things done according to custom are pleasing even when freely given.

I am still advancing toward health by a slow path; therefore, uncertain about a further journey, I postpone deciding until I have progressed. My mind eagerly wishes to learn what you yourselves have decided about returning or remaining in the suburbs. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXVII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

I forestalled your inquiry when I realized that you would be anxious because illness had attacked me. Although I had previously written of my own pain that its severity was diminishing, I now announce again, to remove your anxiety—which is always distrustful among those who love one another—that, unless some hostile fortune bewitches what I have said, health is returning to harmony with me.

But the charm of the seashore has not yet penetrated my feelings. Just as a steady step is slowly recovered after the long tossing of the sea, so time is needed for the departure of so great an illness to make room for pleasure. Therefore, for the moment, I derive no sweetness either from the Formian coast or from my building.

But, as I hope, all these things will return with the blessing of good health, and soon, communicated by my pen, they will reach the joy of your spirit. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

When your boy had delivered one letter to me, he settled down as though he were immediately returning to you, so that I might reply at once. But, as I learned, he himself was pressing farther on and used a theatrical trick so that his companion Rusticus might carry our page away.

That man has now returned and received another letter. I imagine you are laughing because, deceived by a slave’s stratagem, I paid double for a single service. For the crafty little servant, having carried one letter, received payment twice. I would go on at greater length if there were more to add.

You are conducting your affairs near the city, amid widespread report, and enjoying an equal leisure. It is your part to enrich those who are far away with what you have learned. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXIX. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

[Col. 0286A]

May this day endure forever—the day, my daughter, that gave you to us. I wish to celebrate it with you through many recurring years, with the joys of the mind and the honors of words, and also to add little gifts that are burdensome to me but pleasing to you.

For now I have sent a linen cloth, whose offering cannot seem insignificant if it is valued more according to the measure of my affection for you than according to its price. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXX. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

I would have wished to celebrate and share with you the birthday of my lady daughter, which we pray may recur through many years, had not the continuous rain stood in the way of my intention.

Nevertheless, we are fulfilling the religious honor owed through a pleasing little gift, asking that the smallness of the offering be increased by the kindness of its reception. Farewell.

**LETTER LXXXI. SYMMACHUS TO THE SONS OF NICOMACHUS**

You have transferred to us all the abundance of the birthday banquet. But one thing was lacking for complete festivity to overflow into our hearts: that we did not consume everything with you. The sight and company of such people often lend distinction even to frugal banquets.

Therefore, for you and for our shared pledge, whose solemn day you have celebrated with devoted diligence, we pray for abundant years and a numerous return to these same festivities. For untroubled happiness befits devoted parents.

At Tibur the air is flattering us; but, in contrast, the mismanagement of the farm stewards aggravates our spirit. The land does not shine with cultivation, a large portion of the produce is owed, and the tenants now have no resources left either to assist the accounts or to maintain the cultivation. Farewell.

**BOOK SEVEN**

[Col. 0285]

**LETTER I. SYMMACHUS TO HIS SON SYMMACHUS**

[Col. 0285C]

Receive eagerly the auspices of your father’s greeting, and henceforth be generous toward us with equal service. At the same time, accept what accords with your wish: the fasces of your praetorship, to be carried forward happily into the year in which, with the will of the gods summoned to our aid, I too may gladly be present.

Rejoice, then, in your desired advancement, and understand that the years of your life and honor have been extended for you: things that are postponed become longer. Do not doubt that Fortune has looked after both of us, so that your magistracy may be aided by your father’s presence and I may enjoy in person the pleasure of your celebrations. Farewell.

**LETTER II. SYMMACHUS TO HIS SON**

As soon as a familiar opportunity gave me the chance to write to you, I did not delay in testifying to my longing for you through a letter, so that, assured of my health, you may care for yours, and then soften my absence through the pleasure of correspondence. Farewell.

**LETTER III. SYMMACHUS TO HIS SON**

[Col. 0286C]

I send a second letter to your beloved self, so that the constancy of my speech may be a consolation to us both. You too, whenever your lord and brother finds the opportunity, should emulate my diligence; may your health give me security and the pleasure of your writings give me delight. Farewell.

**LETTER IV. SYMMACHUS TO HIS SON**

The consular magnificence satisfied the solemnity of the Circus. The most splendid performances and shows are still impending; once these have been completed, as we suppose, before the Nones of February, we shall turn our journey homeward. I write this so that the joy of your affection may be nourished by better hope. Farewell.

**LETTER V. SYMMACHUS TO HIS SON**

I believe that another letter of mine will reach your beloved self first. For the bearers of this letter will follow the returning mules on a slow journey. Yet I could not abstain from the gift of a greeting: I preferred a duty completed late to overflow rather than to be missed through omission.

I have not yet received any letter from your affection. Please make it your chief care to send me this gift. From your own feelings you can measure how much relief the constancy of writing grants to those who are absent. Farewell.

**LETTER VI. SYMMACHUS TO HIS SON**

I recently received the letters from your affection for which I had longed; they revealed both your diligence of spirit and the progress of your talent. Only the brevity of the letter did not at all satisfy a father’s longing. I write this so that you may understand how much pleasure I drew from your speech, since I complain that there was not enough of it. For who would desire satiety except in good things? Henceforth, then, write more indulgently, my light, so that the reader’s mind may be filled by the fuller gift of your pen.

**LETTER VII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS SON**

An additional stretch of days has been added to our journey because of the postponement of the games, which the intervention of rain is delaying. But I want you, assured of my health, to bear this delay gently, and to soften through the constancy of your pen the longing for you that grows in me through the delay. Farewell.

**LETTER VIII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS SON**

I trust that the constancy of my pen can suffice to comfort your spirit. For I add this message to recent writings; its reading will promise you hope of my return, if chance confirms what has been anticipated.

The basis of this expectation is clear: after the magnificent performance of the consular games, only the presentation in the arena still remains. Let your spirit therefore change into joy, and believe that you have obtained what a reasonable conjecture promises. Farewell.

**LETTER IX. SYMMACHUS TO HIS SON**

I rejoice that your letters sparkle with pointed expressions and maxims; for it is fitting that youthful ardor should speak with greater exuberance. But I want you to use the stings of speech in other subjects, while in this kind of writing you should mix something mature and playful—something which I believe your rhetorician also instructs you to do.

For just as in people’s clothing and in every other aspect of life’s cultivation, things suited to place and time are chosen, so the variety of talents ought in familiar letters to imitate a certain negligence, but in forensic writing to shake the weapons of eloquence. But I shall not pursue these matters further. Meanwhile, proceed wherever the impulse of your age and the ardor of your nature drive you.

The chief object of my prayer is that you may enjoy good health and, beyond your years, grow rich in the endowment of literature. Farewell.

**LETTER X. SYMMACHUS TO HIS SON**

As our friend Annius was hurrying past, I could impose upon him only a greeting; but the reading of the letter ought to give you assurance of my health. Be of a happier spirit, then, and hope, my honor, that through frequent writings similar things will come to your knowledge—things in which you will rejoice. Farewell.

**LETTER XI. SYMMACHUS TO HIS SON**

My spirit rises whenever a message from your affection is brought to me. For it both brings assurance of your health and displays the progress of your talent. I therefore urge you to sprinkle me frequently with such little flowers of language. Do not claim any period of silence for yourself while you think that I shall soon be present. Everything will become smoother and easier for my return if your pages stir the spirit of one who is coming back. Farewell.

**LETTER XII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS SON**

The report of your fluctuating health greatly alarmed me, although the same letter also contained assurance of your good health. Therefore, uncertain in spirit, I hasten, praying for divine assistance, so that both my letter and my return may find you in possession of good health. For this fulfillment of a father’s prayer will make my return a delight. Farewell.

**LETTER XIII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS SON**
The variety of reports about my journey delayed me. For while I was investigating your circumstances and marking out the length of the road by inserting days, I finally reached Milan, by way of the distant regions around Ticinum, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March. Now the gracious speech of our lord and emperor has consoled me for my exertion. I also hope that the embassy will soon be brought to the knowledge of the divine emperor, since it is reported that a man exalted above all others, to whom our order has entrusted the leading role in the public cause, will shortly arrive with the strongest forces. I am deeply offended by your silence; and therefore I ask you frequently to relieve the endurance demanded by my absence through your conversation. Farewell.

## LETTER XIV. SYMMACHUS TO HIS SON

Since there was no opportunity to use the couriers, I entrusted the letters for delivery to a private individual. I expect that he will reach you late. Both letters contain the same message: that I entered Milan on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, having been carried around by a long detour, and that, after paying my respects to our lord and emperor, whose speech compensated me for the toil of my journey, I bring before the presence of the man exalted above all others the matters that must be conducted. The assurances of the messengers confirm that he will soon be here, with God’s help. Now, my pride, make it your concern to soothe the anxieties of my absence by the constant activity of your pen. Farewell.

## LETTER XV. SYMMACHUS TO HIS SON

Contemplation of our friendship had given me hope of your arrival. I am nearly ready to believe that I was mistaken in hoping you would voluntarily come into your father’s sight. Since, then, you do not know how to do the right thing without our entreaties, hasten here when asked. And if lofty Tibur has satisfied you, exchange it for the pleasant Laurentine woods; do not fear the warning about the harshness of the countryside. For those who hunt, the sea is before their eyes; the villa is bordered by a well-traveled road. Within it one proceeds to the lairs of wild animals by a level and open approach. Even if these attractions were absent, surely the mutual conversation between us and the generous exchange of letters would surpass Tarentine or Sicilian pleasures. Therefore, if you too extend your hand to this view, add yourself to the number of country-dwellers; and for a little while emulate the Catos and Atilii whom the plow and the plow-handle sent on to the consular axes. Farewell.

## LETTER XVI. SYMMACHUS TO ATTALUS

I am glad that you missed my conversation, but I remove the charge of negligence. For your letter-carrier abandoned the prepared replies after being summoned, as I learned by report, by uncertainty about your health. You recognize, surely, that the causes of my delay are unvarnished and not drawn from some hidden source. I shall go no further, since the assertion of truth is brief. Now I congratulate you on your recovery; once I learned of it after excessive fear, much joy shone forth in my heart. The pleasantness of your letter also offered evidence of returning vigor. For you ask me to supply the remedies of my pen for strengthening your health. This is Bayan festivity. The Lucrine Gulf has infected you with excessive wit. Is there anything in my words that may soothe your ears, anything that may provide medicine for your senses? I believe so, and I agree. For things that are bitter when swallowed are often beneficial to health, and those afflicted by gloomy juices are restored by them. But you are excessively greedy, since, with my Flavian present, you ask for anything at all; in him there are such abundant soothing pleasures that you seem to me to have lingered as though among the Sirens or the Lotus-Eaters. Would that I could join your leisure! I would gather more healthfulness from you than you, who asked me only for letters, desire from me. Farewell.

## LETTER XVII. SYMMACHUS TO ATTALUS

Indeed, I have kept silent all this time in vain while I waited, confident in your promise. At last, in despair of better things, I must return to my customary consolations. Perhaps you are angry at my prolonged silence. It remains only for me to be blamed for a delay that has proved vain in its hope. It is therefore within your authority, concerning the beginning of your journey, to stand by your promises. I shall not regret being content with the relief of the pen. Through this exchange of services, at any rate, I shall either console myself because you are not coming, or earn the result that you will come. Farewell.

## LETTER XVIII. SYMMACHUS TO ATTALUS

Recently returning from the Formian Gulf to my Caelian home, I discovered that you had been away from the house for a long time. I immediately gave our common friend Theophilus, now my companion on the journey, the task both of carrying to you in the Tiburtine countryside news of my return and of conveying words of greeting. You, being inquisitive about my affairs—as though some official inquiry concerning us had been assigned to you—forced him, by questioning him openly, to reveal what I had done abroad. For this was disclosed by your letter, which the excellent Theophilus brought back.

It was a mark of your kindness to investigate the high points and details of my activities: whether frequent travel across land and sea had benefited my health; whether any cultivation had been added to our fields, any polish to our buildings, or any increase to our livestock; what increase had come to our household supplies; whether voluntary moderation had girded the consular table; or whether I had ever exchanged Formiae for a neighboring town or a more distant one. Was it also permissible for you to investigate what the care of my studies had contributed to my pages far from observers? Whether, when I was working on wax tablets, my eyes—usually fixed and standing still—and the signs of pallor had betrayed me? My pen tolerates you as an investigator. You teach friends the paths of suspicion and, if it may be said, hunt down our writings by scent and footprints.

Now I wish to know what literary work you are pursuing in the orchards of Tibur. Rumor has brought me only this: that you recently had a bathhouse constructed for yourself, for which, they say, a single log is enough to supply the proper heat. You yourself have shown that you read authors in both languages during your abundant leisure. Yet I do not ask whether you have also written anything. I see that, inflamed by the glory of awareness of your own work, you wished to learn whether I too had done the same. But now, setting letters aside, I would like you to return—unless, perhaps, the modest expense of your bathhouse urges you not to abandon your habit of frugality. Farewell.

## LETTER XIX. SYMMACHUS TO ATTALUS

You have at once made amends for two offenses against our friendship. For a long time you had been absent from the wit of your letters and had written nothing: what Colchian or Thessalian woman could have relieved these affronts by song or hand? Therefore, in exchange for the soothing of a letter, you will bear the price of pardon. I allow you, free from other concerns, to conduct the wedding celebration of your friend and to make the city of Tibur—which recently carried torches before you—common to Juno and Hercules. I hope you will return to your Caelian home after the wedding festivities. Or, if you still enjoy spending the summer days in your orchards, my indignation must once again be appeased by the honey of your letters. Farewell.

## LETTER XX. SYMMACHUS TO ATTALUS

The villa at Tibur, which has recently come under your ownership, requires an advocate of greater talent. I, however, with my modest command of language, shall honor the place in words as best I can. What beauty there is in the arrangement of the buildings here! What a setting! How broadly, from the height, the view is cast over the plains! I should say that the Orchomenian goddesses frequently occupy these seats, and that they have diligently striven to win you, their master, over to their dwellings. Continue, then, as you are doing, and restore newness to what age has conquered. This is much easier to accomplish than what they say happened to Hesiod, who, after laying aside old age, returned to green years. Meanwhile, congratulate us on our good health; that it may likewise long favor you stands among my prayers. Farewell.

## LETTER XXI. SYMMACHUS TO ATTALUS

After my carriage-driver delivered your letter to me, and the greeting carried from your journey released our respect from its obligation, I was given an opportunity to speak with you frequently while you are away. Therefore I begin with those matters that stand first in your wishes. By God’s peace, my health and that of your only son are flourishing. As far as possible, I avoid the urban crowds in the Vatican countryside. Yet whenever we are summoned to an assembly, I return in obedience to the public council. I know that you want nothing more from us. Only the impulse of your desire to know about our affairs requires an equal knowledge of yours. Farewell.

## LETTER XXII. SYMMACHUS TO ATTALUS

I deliberated at length whether I ought to honor you by awaiting your return at the proper time. For I feared that your haste might be broken by consolations meeting you on the way. But the contrary reasoning resolved this uncertainty and gave me hope that these letters would be like spurs, not reins, for one returning. I deliberately aim at brevity, offering you only a greeting in words, so that the small draught of my speech may be more effective at provoking thirst than at satisfying it. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIII. SYMMACHUS TO ATTALUS

I believe your eyes are looking for me; let your mind have no doubt that I am present. For my care for you travels with me, and I carry you everywhere in the affection of my heart. Nevertheless, I exercise the pleasure of friendship with my pen. If you do the same in return, it will happen that I shall enjoy a long possession of leisure, since you will not deny what could draw me away from it. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIV. SYMMACHUS TO ATTALUS

Having proceeded to the Neapolitan coast, I received your letter ordering us to remain at Baiae until your arrival. The bearer of the letter asserted that your excursion was close on his heels. What could I do, when the same place could not hold me? It seemed more expedient to ask you instead for the favor of continuing our journey to you. For you desired friends, not Baiae—unless, perhaps, you are being drawn there by that gulf of luxury. We shall accompany you if you prefer to return there, although this region has a healthier climate and equal resources. It will be your choice whether we should extend our journey or retrace it. It is my defense that I follow you on your return to the place where I could not wait for you as you arrived. Farewell.

## LETTER XXV. SYMMACHUS TO ATTALUS

If you had answered my letter, you would have relieved the burden on your conscience; now, by your silence, you have assisted ours. For services repaid bring me joy, while services withheld give me victory. And I know that you can do abundantly what you strip from us with much effort. But since you begrudge good words to your readers, and I do not wish to seem to be doing violence to your stinginess, I swallow my loss. Farewell.

## LETTER XXVI. SYMMACHUS TO MACEDONIUS

After the Tiburtine pleasures, I dare to ask you to visit my Lavinate estate; nor am I a prolonged sinner against pious desire. For among friends the condition of requests ought to be such that what is great to those who ask appears easy to those who grant it. Farewell.

## LETTER XXVII. SYMMACHUS TO MACEDONIUS

You are accustomed to assert that you prefer me to yourself. This could be believed if you allowed my son Attalus to come to us. For he is under your authority and he obeys your counsels. I agree that this should happen, but not to the extent that you extend your pontifical authority to our detriment. Is it not enough that you yourself, who are equally desirable, abandon my companionship and begrudge us the society we most desire? In addition, you retain another person as well through the arts of soothing affection; I believe you infer that I will hasten my return if I am deprived of both. But I declare that a monitor is needed to draw back the one who is lingering. For, as you know, I love leisure and feed on tranquility. I therefore prepare you against my slowness: if you already desire the return of your absent friend, allow the brief excursion of the one who is present. Farewell.

## LETTER XXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO MACEDONIUS

Although I was hindered by very serious fevers, I could not deny you the honor of a letter, lest I be judged negligent of my religious duty. Nor was I able to extend the letter into a long series; its brevity is blameless, since it proceeds from the injustice of my illness, not from my will. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIX. SYMMACHUS TO MACEDONIUS

Neither the departure of our brother Proclianus, vir clarissimus, allowed me to remain silent, nor did our affection permit me to moderate my services. Accept, then, the due gift of conversation, and, to make me more ready, frequently undertake the task of offering greetings. Farewell.

## LETTER XXX. SYMMACHUS TO ATTICUS

The leisure of the countryside is indeed a pleasure to me, but I judge your wishes more ancient and more important. Therefore, if fortune should favor the saying, I shall not be absent as spectator and guest at your consular duties. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXI. SYMMACHUS TO ATTICUS

You are trying to draw us from the embrace of Campania by praising the Tiburtine countryside. It is, as you proclaim, dense with cypresses in your estate, rich in springs, and cool because of its mountainous setting. These things would be desirable to me if a longer stay had kept you there. But now, by your hasty return to the city, you have given me some suspicion that you have grown weary of the place. Pleasures often produce satiety. If that is so, I think you have had enough of Formiae, to which you had sent word, since even places preferred to it have displeased you. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXII. SYMMACHUS TO ATTICUS

We are planning to retrace our journey and finally return to your sight, although our sons are without strength and I have been afflicted by the damage caused by fevers. Nevertheless, the effort will be diminished by short intervals of lodging. I hope that the change of places will advance our wishes in some degree. I am glad that I see the care of your diligence, proven by its practice toward me, growing day by day. I would thank you for it at length in words if you did this out of a desire for praise rather than sincere affection. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO ATTICUS

Recently I sent evidence of my health, but you have not yet returned what I might read in return about your prosperity. Nevertheless, I do not regret repeating my dutiful obligation before it has been discharged. Such is your confidence of affection toward us that I consider anything owed by a loving friend already repaid. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO ATTICUS

Having first offered a respectful greeting, I carry out the request of Getulicus, an agent in public affairs, who hopes through me to obtain from you the favor he deserves. It is characteristic of your humanity to embrace a worthy intention and to increase, by adding a new admirer, the number of those who rightly esteem you. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXV. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

You trouble my spirit by recalling the Campanian shore; but for us, too, the Praenestine countryside supplies pleasures no less numerous. Although many people hold the view that the mountains should be placed below the sea, I judge that, for avoiding the heat, wooded places are more suitable than open ones devoted to cultivation. To encourage our departure, you had added that my son Flavian would soon be with you. I have already long been enjoying his presence. From this you understand that my lot is far better. For I have placed the comparison of the two places in the balance, and I have transferred to my own advantage the companionship of my beloved child, in which you chiefly took pride. Therefore you ought to retrace your way to us under changed circumstances, to the point of satiety, after the long use of the resources you have enjoyed. For Campania, while desirable to those who are absent, easily satisfies those who remain there. But I shall say no more about this, lest I seem to announce my weariness to that region which is most pleasing to us, should I come. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVI. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

We have not yet reached the Neapolitan shore to see the citadel of your pleasures. Nevertheless, everything washed by the Tyrrhenian Sea is full of your name. Why say more? You have succeeded to the reputation of Lucullus, and for that reason I am all the more amazed that you can sometimes move on to other places—unless, perhaps, you flee abundance out of distaste and punish satiety by changing locations. But you have been away too long. I think that the desire for abundance has now been reconciled with you by the long duration of frugality. Why, then, do you not advance toward us? Or, if you gladly linger there over our frugality, we must quickly return, since it is not fitting for us to covet another’s pleasures. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVII. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

I am pleased that you are well. But I observe that it is not your true judgment that the Neapolitan coast is preferred to our Formiae. For, to favor your present circumstances, you have changed not your opinion but your words—unless, perhaps, comparison of your possessions makes that place more pleasing to you where the yield is richer. But the regions of nature must be judged by their own merits, not by our gains. And why say much about this? Your stay will show whether you spend your leisure there more willingly, since there is no doubt that you left me unwillingly. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

You seemed to me to be joking when you wrote that you had feared the arms of soldiers meeting you on the road. I believe that you said this so that we would not follow your journey into the distant parts of Campania. For if you yourself, having spent a long time in military camps, have experienced some fear, what bitterness would I, accustomed to the civilian toga, have encountered? But I will not allow your imitated alarm to benefit you by causing delay. The entire Appian Way is free of soldiers, since all those who, with the peace of Africa restored, returned to the service of the divine emperor have been transported elsewhere. Besides, what of the fact that the fatherland, even in difficult circumstances, requires either the aid of good men or their fellowship? Nor does it await our presence only in prosperous times. It is the more praiseworthy duty to share uncertainties with one’s fellow citizens. But already better hope is brightening the mournful face of the city, and its food supply, supported for the moment by the assistance that has been provided, guarantees the arrival of Libyan grain. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIX. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

Chance often disrupts what has been arranged. This has now happened to me: I could not visit the Etruscan vapors for the sake of my health, having been held back by sudden and disorderly circumstances. I therefore impose no delay upon you through me. On the contrary, I urge and ask you to revisit Rome by a hurried journey and to restore to us the pleasure of your presence, which I was unable to enjoy in the suburbs. Farewell.

## LETTER XL. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

Long ago, once you had been released from public cares, you ought to have retraced your journey rather than soften the longing of your friends with the auspices of letters. For if your health is satisfactory, what reason can I give for your remaining longer in Campania? Is it so that you may deprive us, who love you most dearly, of the good qualities we habitually embrace in you? On the contrary, remember the city and us, and while the opportunity of summer invites you, undertake your journey in haste, so that the long losses caused by your absence may finally be repaired by your desired return. Farewell.

## LETTER XLI. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

Where has the faithfulness of your promises gone? You gave the person hoping for your return the relief of letters. We could have been pleased to receive this gift if you had promised nothing greater. Or did you fear that a consular man would be a witness to your pleasures? This precaution accomplished nothing. Though the spectacles were hidden from my eyes, I detect them through my ears. For whenever anyone is offended by our frugality, he sighs that you are away. Thus you are openly missed as an insult to my dinner. The Senate will learn of this; the people will hear it. For I cannot otherwise avenge the just pain caused by your absence. Farewell.

## LETTER XLII. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

The delay must rightly be broken off, and care must be devoted to mutual conversation, lest neglect of writing weaken the memory of our longstanding friendship.
