To make you do this more willingly henceforth, I take the initiative. Here is a letter bringing you a greeting; the rivalry of our service will show that it is a pleasure to your feelings. If this speech also secures for its bearer the benefit of your patronage, I shall accuse the losses caused by my previous silence. For it will be clear that I could have advised more people if I had begun to address you earlier. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIII. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

While I was in the country, recovering my step through the freedom of the open air—a practice whose use has delayed me after my illness—my most intimate friend, prepared to begin his journey, made himself available for my writing. I immediately embraced the friendly fellowship suited to my purpose and did not delay the letter. It would both increase the exchange of our dutiful friendship and open to the traveler the first threshold of acquaintance with you. If you consider the reasons for this letter worthy, may the favor of your conversation come to me, and may he receive the fruit of your affection. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIV. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

I repay the greeting you sent me, although in recent days I have voluntarily cultivated our friendship through the work of my pen; this reminder is not a reproach for your services. My spirit feeds on the pleasure of such diligence. It is therefore your choice whether you wish often to be generous to me in letters—which I desire above all. But if this fruit should at any time be lacking, our conversation will provide me with the same joy of speaking with you. Farewell.

## LETTER XLV. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

This is the one way in which I can be of greatest benefit to my fellow citizens and friends: if, as a guide into the sacred mysteries, I introduce them into your patronage. This is what I now do for Gaudentius, a man of senatorial birth. If you examine his modesty more closely, you will find it equal to his illustrious ancestry. Therefore, once he has been received without delay into your service, let him understand, before the full confidence in himself which examination of his character will soon give him, that my testimony has won him your trust. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVI. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

The exceptional goodness of your character often summons my confidence to make proper requests. There is therefore no need to fear criticism for recommending friends, since you yourself, by the generosity of your wishes, encourage me to this endeavor. I am thus certain that this letter will be welcome, in which I commend Desiderius, a highly distinguished man and my longtime friend. Domestic necessity forced him to interrupt his leisure. He could easily have concealed this loss, if narrow means could admit a great spirit. From him you will hear more fully whatever the brevity of the letter declines to complete. For my part, it is enough to ask on his behalf in general terms. I beg you to undertake the office of doing good, which joins human merits to God, and to gain brighter fruits from his prosperity. For it seems to me that benefits confer more upon the giver. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVII. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

I cannot refrain from writing when my lord and son Flavian is departing to join you, since I ought to accompany him with this travel allowance, nor can I add anything, because your diligence toward him admits no increase. I therefore want you to know that our writing as little as possible about him is not the result of weariness but of confidence presupposed in your mind. Deign always to be toward him what your longstanding friendship promises you will be; the rank of your honor adds to that friendship, so that you should not deny that you can do what you ought to wish for him. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVIII. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

It was through your favor that we obtained the assistance of transport permits, by which members of my household might travel to Spain to purchase Curule horses. I therefore ask you to order those sent for this purpose to move on promptly; the work requires a long time, since the best animals must be selected from each province and more cautious care must bring the process to completion. Moreover, I shall be more deeply indebted to you if you assist their journey with two additional couriers. They will be divided individually, so that from different provinces they may select the choicer animals. After the most illustrious and eminent Count, whatever splendor my son’s praetorian *editio* adds to our household will be owing to your generosity. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIX. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

Your character is the surest harbor against every storm; therefore my sister’s son hastens to you, confident in his hope. The nature of his business expects the aid of the world’s humanity, the quality of which will be disclosed to your virtues by reading his petition. Therefore I ought not to be a lengthy narrator of his injury, since the trustworthiness of his supplication sets out the whole course of his desire. Affection assigns me only this role: to seek the support of your favor for the wife of my beloved child, for whom a grave ruin is being prepared because of her poverty. Farewell.

## LETTER L. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

Out of modesty, I can neither display my joy concerning you nor quickly find another witness to it. It is enough that you measure my affection from your own mind. Yet I must confess the happiness that has transferred the reins of the prefecture to a favorable disposition. Meanwhile, I am filled with no less joy that the prolonged labor of my lord and son Flavian in judging has deserved to enjoy the desired repose. For it was not right that you should be delayed long from this reward, nor that he should be held back from leisure. I write this so that you may know that we give thanks to the eternal emperor for your honor, and that you likewise ought to give thanks for his security. Meanwhile, I ask you to maintain your custom of frequent letters, and not to claim that public duties obstruct private services. For you have been equal to many-sided necessities, and no kind of experience exists whose magnitude or novelty could call you away from the duties owed to friendship. Farewell.

## LETTER LI. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

Perhaps my other recommendations may be interpreted as appeals to your kindness; this one concerns your judgment. For I entrust to your holy heart my brother Severus, a bishop praised by the testimony of people of every sect. Concerning him, neither despair of equaling his merit nor his own modesty allows me to say more. Moreover, I have assumed the role not of a praiser but of a witness, leaving the examination of his character to you. When you have weighed him thoroughly, you will find that I have yielded to his praises rather than failed through negligence. Farewell.

## LETTER LII. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

What worthy return can I make to you for such great care toward me and mine? I truly cannot equal your services, yet I promise that I shall never cease in devotion of mind and affection. Nor do I doubt that for your benefactions you expect only the reward of a good heart. But modesty does not permit me to linger longer in this declaration of gratitude, for you judge that whatever I believe should be rendered is owed to our friendship. Farewell.

## LETTER LIII. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

The recommendation of my writings is small, since the innocent life and long service of Eusebius commend him to all good people. Endowed, then, with merit of his own, he asked not for ambition but for my testimony before you. Nevertheless, I ought not to refrain from this kind of letter, more to satisfy loyalty than to support someone wavering through the favor he receives. This, then, is the sum of my request: may my intention toward him find a corresponding form in your noble heart. Farewell.

## LETTER LIV. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

Since you are perceptive in all matters, you know how much anxiety an embassy contains and how much difficulty accompanies travel. Your affection will make these things light and safe for my lord and son Attalus, who is pursuing the wishes of the Senate. Therefore accept the part of kindness that my request requires and that is suited to your character. Whatever the outcome of your service may be, Attalus will consider himself fortunate to have deserved the care of one superior to him. Farewell.

## LETTER LV. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

You often honor us, as is fitting, with letters. You believe that the bond of our hearts grows old through a certain rust of silence. Perform the duty that accords with brotherly interests and affection. In return, I did not delay in sending you a conversation. Its repayment is this: I still recognize that I am indebted to your affection. For everything is returned through easy reciprocity and compensation. But the contract of friendship and devotion is eternal. Farewell, and persevere in being diligent about writing. We shall supply the consolations of letters, with which you may either soothe your spirit while occupied or return the favor when at leisure. Farewell.

## LETTER LVI. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

Your longstanding humanity urges us not to refuse assistance to those who ask for it. My reason for writing to you on behalf of Theodulus is especially strong, since he is a tenant of my lands and receives care that is owed to him rather than merely granted as a favor. Therefore preserve your customary practice and, as your habit promises, let my prayers move you, so that whatever fault or error he has incurred you may deign to remit in consideration of his merits and my intervention. Farewell.

## LETTER LVII. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

It belongs both to your virtue and to your purpose to welcome all good men; among them Alexander is rightly judged worthy by consideration of his honesty. I have commended him by this friendly letter both for his assistance and because of my affection for you. I earnestly beg you to grant him appropriate favor and to repay me with a conversation in return. Farewell.

## LETTER LVIII. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

I recently sent two short speeches of mine, now published, to the distinguished men Felix and Minervius, endowed with the priesthood of virtue and learning. Since you love me, I also want you to be their reader, provided that you are not offended by mediocre talents. They themselves will provide you with a copy of the volume. For they nourish my reputation so zealously that they do not know how to begrudge me the support of good men. Farewell.

## LETTER LIX. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

Julius, an agent in public affairs, presented me with a sacred letter containing a gift of leopards. The same man also delivered your much-desired page. Therefore, in the first place, I offer you the respect due in a greeting. Next, I ask you to give thanks on my behalf to the author of this wished-for generosity. It will be more pleasing if a timely continuation provides him with a recommendation, and the affability of your speech accomplishes what my modesty could scarcely have completed. For I hope, in proportion to the affection I deserve from you, that I may be able to fulfill most completely the magnitude of our congratulations. Farewell.

## LETTER LX. SYMMACHUS TO DECIUS

It weighed upon my modesty that you had written first. Immediately, your second letter imposed a double debt upon my burdened brow. I fear—and desire—that before I have discharged two contracts, you may grant me a third conversation. For the abundance of speech that prevails in you possesses this impatience: it denies an interval for reciprocity and anticipates services not yet repaid. One path therefore remains to satisfy you: to admit that I am unequal to you in writing, although I do not deny that I am your equal in devotion to friendship. Do not think that I do this defiantly by offering you the diligence of my heart. Otherwise you would love me in vain, unless you allow us at least to be made equal by affection.

Therefore, after this declaration of mine, frequently bestow upon me the gift of your celebrated eloquence; if I am the rarer writer, remember that I have yielded. Should I challenge with my letters the public judgment against a master of royal correspondence? It is ours to inflate pastoral reeds; yours to sound a song upon sacred pipes. Leisure dulls us, while practice exercises you. Unless, perhaps, you think that this freedom from the affairs of private life is more suitable to the frequent writing of letters. You see that rivers do not creep with the same movement from a pond as they hasten from a spring. Everything that is in motion flourishes. Continuity of practice renews its strength. What you might have answered has been taken away from you. Henceforth, since you possess such abundance for writing, make your example provide me with as much ability as my talent has not given me. Farewell.

## LETTER LXI. SYMMACHUS TO PATRICIUS

I had announced that I would be less frequent in writing. What am I to do to friendship, which compels me to lie? I have departed from my purpose, but I believe you approve this kind of deception. Now I would like you to consider how frequent you ought to be, since you have offered greater hope. Was it not you who first hurled the gifts of your speech at me? I respond to them as one extending a blade of grass, while asking pardon. I beg you to stand by your promises and maintain the diligence of what you have begun. I appeal to your faith, since I almost boast that you have made me a liar. Farewell.

## LETTER LXII. SYMMACHUS TO PATRICIUS

Friendship was acquired for this purpose: that mutual advantage might be governed by reciprocal services. The statement made above applies directly to the present matter. For I presume that, through your outstanding distinction, the petition of my brother Callistianus and his wife will not be excluded from the sacred benefit; both the justice of their desire and the customary form of obtaining it support their request. Since, then, nothing obstructs what they ask, bring goodwill to bear in assisting their prayers. Since this quality is innate in you, it lightens the labor of my entreaty. For the man who anxiously asks for what the nature of a generous person spontaneously promises almost wrongs kindness. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIII. SYMMACHUS TO PATRICIUS

I am glad that my Aurelius holds such a place with you that, having been entrusted to you by me, he is returned in turn with your recommendation. You have surpassed our diligence on his behalf, which you order us to increase. Therefore I obey your word. No affection is so complete that it cannot receive increase. You will gladly accept my being away from home and enjoying the leisure of Campania, for you are accustomed to share the good fortune of friends with pleasure. May your military honor bring you favorable rewards; may our life be secure, and yours distinguished. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIV. SYMMACHUS TO PATRICIUS

Martyrius is pursuing the cases of my relatives, and he has earned this letter from me in support of his cause. I ask that he obtain from you the fulfillment of the favor he hopes for. Farewell.

## LETTER LXV. SYMMACHUS TO PATRICIUS

The case of my beloved child will come into your hands, so that a friend may be supported by the laws. But, as the perfidy of guardians is often many-sided, it frequently turns itself toward various devices. I believe that, at least now, they will yield to the sacred oracle, if your equity is celebrated by offering its guidance. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVI. SYMMACHUS TO ALIPIUS

After first offering the honor of a greeting, I attach a familiar prayer to your spirit. For on the lands we possess in Caesarean Mauretania, as commonly happens in the absence of their owners, the misconduct of the provincial governor leaves no remnant of official duty. A complaint often brought before the governor of the province has been treated as insignificant through the judge’s indolence. Therefore, since lesser remedies are of no use, we resort to greater ones. I ask you to bring assistance, lest property exhausted by so many injuries collapse. You owe this both to your reputation and to my friendship, so that you may deign to give particular help to a claim founded on justice. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVII. SYMMACHUS TO ALIPIUS

A person who hopes to come shortly into the sight of his friends usually refrains from writing letters. For me, both that hope of seeing you remains intact and the practice of correspondence creates no weariness. I therefore celebrate your honor by sending a greeting, and meanwhile I do not ask for a reply, since you will soon repay the interest on my pen with the gift of conversation. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO ALPIDIUS

I understand that the diligence I show toward your holy household is already too well known to you. That is why you share joyful news with me and indicate in writing that the health of my wife and daughter is returning to a better condition. I therefore give abundant thanks and pray to the gods that your favorable circumstances may prosper.

For us, the slower arrival of the African ships causes anxiety, as does the scarcity of stored provisions. Accordingly, when summoned to make a contribution, we promised the customary relief for our country. But prayers are needed, so that a prompt fulfillment may answer the voluntary undertaking. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIX. SYMMACHUS TO ALPIDIUS
[Col. 0300C] Those who have recounted ancient affairs have handed down the story that a certain man was summoned for judgment because, having borrowed from a friend a packhorse on loan as far as Aricia, he had passed beyond the steep ascent of the farther hill. This may have been the thrift and carefulness of a poorer age: once he had ridden past the appointed place, he was said to have committed an offense against friendship. I have therefore accepted what your affection was urging upon me; and I am so far from fearing your displeasure that I hope instead to receive the good favor of your trust. For you must approve what you yourself would have done. But why do I set these matters forth as though they had been purged? I am writing from Formianum in sound health; and from there I have sent back the team of horses more exercised than exhausted. I shall keep the mules for a little while. You had given me this choice; if I had rejected it, I would have seemed more willing to use my own judgment in appropriating what was permitted than to yield to yours in what was allowed [Col. 0300D]. Farewell.

## LETTER LXX. SYMMACHUS TO ALIPIUS

When I recall the troubles of the city, I take pleasure in being away; when I contemplate you in thought, I am weary of my absence. Letters therefore provide a middle course of relief. I have sent these to you so that I may both satisfy our friendship and, following your example, receive letters from you in return—for, as you see, there is greater consolation in them. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXI. SYMMACHUS TO ALIPIUS

Your letters provide me with the greatest assistance and support in restoring my health. First, because they testify that you remember me; then, because they bring indications of your prosperity [Col. 0301A]. I therefore confess that my still-weak health is being revived by the constant succession of your writings; and I understand what benefit I shall derive from your presence, when I receive so much healthfulness from letters that report your well-being. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHERS

I write this after setting out for Milan, and from here I offer you the honor of the greeting owed to you. It is fitting that my concern for you should be eased by a report of your loving reciprocity. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHERS

We have arrived, but already regret having done so. For as soon as I touched the soil of the Baian shore, I was immediately seized by pain in my foot [Col. 0301B]. For this reason I dictated only a few words; I shall soon be more expansive in writing if the health I desire looks kindly upon me and your letters in turn call forth a response. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHERS

As we indicated in the preceding letter, our health was stricken at our first arrival, whether by the unhealthy waters or by the change of air. Fortune will decide. Now a better condition has begun gradually to lessen the adversity; but, above all other remedies, it helped that we learned you were well. If you are also asking about the time of our return, we intend, if fortune attends our words, to resume our journey by the Ides of October. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXV. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHERS

[Col. 0301C] I know that my letters are both missed and awaited by you, since it is customary for those departing to begin this kind of offering. I therefore send you an auspicious sign that our greetings are to be maintained between us, having no doubt that, as though a signal had been given, you will not be slow to reply. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVI. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHERS

It is a religious and votive custom that solemn gifts be offered by quaestors-designate to their most distinguished and closest friends. You are rightly counted among that number. I therefore offer you, in the name of my son who has performed the quaestorian office, an ivory diptych and a small silver vessel weighing two pounds; and I earnestly ask that you deem it worthy to receive this mark of honor graciously [Col. 0301D]. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHERS

You may reasonably have inferred that there were certain causes underlying my silence; for how could I have neglected the duties of piety if I had been well? Now, as the pain gradually yields, I could not postpone the duty of greeting you. It will be your responsibility to return the reciprocal favor. Whatever the longed-for day may bring me will provide encouragement for my recovery. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHERS

After I sent out the page that was to carry my greeting to you, the opportunity arose for someone to bring me your letters [Col. 0302A]. At first I rejoiced upon receiving them; but when I learned that our common loved one had taken to bed, I was suddenly overwhelmed by the bitterness of what I read. Yet because the appended words informed me that our son had been restored to health, my spirit returned once more to tranquility. I indicated the state of my own health in earlier writings; there is no need to mention it again, lest repetition in an anxious letter disturb you. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIX. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHERS

A little earlier I sent letters announcing the return of our son Faustus, so that security obtained without delay might lessen the impatience of your longing; but even while he was setting out I was not reluctant to repeat the offering of my greeting. Receive, therefore, a double pleasure: first from his return; then from this fraternal message, in which we tell you that our common children have been restored to health [Col. 0302B]. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXX. SYMMACHUS TO HIS BROTHERS

In recent days I have written frequently; but no amount of constancy can satisfy the heart of one who loves. I think it is sufficient for you to know that we write that we are well, although the common loved one, troubled for a few days by a discharge of blood, diminished the pleasure of our leisure; he has now begun, by divine aid, to emerge into full health. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXI. SYMMACHUS TO MESSALA

Fortune has returned to favor with our fellow citizens, now that the republic has claimed you for itself. [Col. 0302C] My very dear friend Jucundus, therefore, should be counted among those who hope for equity. Already weighed down by a long illness, he had been summoned by your eminent prefecture to appear for the adjudication of a private dispute. It is indeed his prayer to answer the charges before your tribunal. But his health opposes his wish: wounded by a discharge of blood, he refuses the uncertainties of travel. Justice will not be lacking to the opposing petition if the dispute is transferred to your Vicar. This, then, is the whole substance of the request: that, while nothing is lost from the case through a change of venue, removal of the journey may preserve the man’s health. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXII. SYMMACHUS TO MESSALA

I have to prepare and arrange my praetorship, whose presentation has been encouraged by the advancement of your greatness [Col. 0302D]. For my undertaking will make use of my brother’s resources. I therefore ask you to share religiously in my votive duties and to approve the advancement of my business by granting support to my dependents as they travel to distant Spain to purchase carriage horses. It would take too long if I wished to go through in writing everything that must be provided. I have briefly noted the main points in the attached memorandum. It will be open to you to add any favors that the petitioner’s pen has omitted. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO MESSALA

If my earlier letters on behalf of my friend and kindred spirit Jucundus had achieved anything, I would devote my speech more to giving thanks than to renewing petitions [Col. 0303A]. But because repeated attendance in a civil matter increases his weakness, I am now renewing my appeal not for the case but for the health of my dependent. Certainly it ought not to have been difficult to obtain, since an imperial pronouncement has granted him exemption from a long journey. I am surprised that carrying this out should be difficult, since your gentleness is accustomed to provide such things even without the authority of a written reply. I therefore ask even more earnestly that a case often brought before the Vicar’s court in such proceedings be returned there for adjudication; for this is both commanded by the sacred writings and not refused by the humanity of the courts. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO MESSALA

Piety gave me the first reason for writing, so that our friendship might be cultivated through letters. Humanity supplied the second, so that your affection might be won for Thalassus, an excellent man and my dependent [Col. 0303B]. It remains that a reciprocal exchange of your conversation should answer mine, and that the desired outcome should proceed favorably for the one commended. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXV. SYMMACHUS TO MESSALA

Both the nature of my purpose toward you required me to write, and my support ought not to be lacking for the most distinguished and accomplished man Eusebius. I ask that your kindness reward him, since he has deserved well of the best men. For every praiseworthy person desires this one reward for modesty and integrity: to reach, through a sincere recommendation, the intimate friendship of good men and of those like you. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXVI. SYMMACHUS TO MESSALA

[Col. 0303C]

Every recommendation bears witness for friends and offers support to those not yet known. My son Processus, therefore, a most accomplished man, should not be counted among those to whom letters are supplied as a favor; rather, he belongs among those for whom a reciprocal service is paid out of affection. I think it is already clear to you what form of judgment should be observed toward him in friendship, since I commend him without favoritism. It is fitting, therefore, that in your kindness he should find as much as he has placed of merit in my regard. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXVII. SYMMACHUS TO MESSALA

Our friendship ought to help Numida in your eyes. I place him under your support, so that your concern for me may repay the merit he has established among us through honorable services [Col. 0303D]. Judge the man’s character according to my judgment, and in everything his advantage requires, imitate the wish of the one commending him. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO MESSALA

The friendships of parents are rightly transferred to their children, so that affection once begun may, as if by hereditary right, benefit their successors. For this reason I have undertaken to love and protect the son of the once-excellent man Gregorius. I had with his father a faithful bond of hearts; but I wish to share with you the obligation of piety. I therefore ask you to carry out my concern for him in whatever circumstances require. Among the young man’s other wishes, there is one especially notable sign of a generous spirit [Col. 0304A]: he desires to enter your court as an advocate whose birth is not obscure. To him, as I hope, you will provide both instruction through the splendor of your eloquence and support through the goodness of your judgment. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXXIX. SYMMACHUS TO MESSALA

I believe that my letters, sent some time ago, have already reached your hands. In them I stated that my friend Jucundus, although eager to appear before your tribunal, was unable to travel because of his health. His illness grows worse day by day, and therefore I repeat my request, lest a man who deserves pity incur the charge of obstinacy. In truth, humanity will take nothing away from the civil case if the hearing is transferred to your Vicar. Thus the burden will be removed from the sufferer, and the proceeding will reach its proper conclusion. Farewell.

## LETTER XC. SYMMACHUS TO MESSALA

[Col. 0304B]

The outcome has shown that what I hoped for was not undeserved, since you have deigned to provide it; and I could have incurred greater blame if, out of embarrassment, I had kept silent before one who loves me about the needs of our dependent in connection with the praetorship. I therefore rejoice that we are adorned by the frequent proofs of your affection, and I want you to believe that whatever favor our presentation may require will, when I yield to you, be attributed to your benefactions. Farewell.

## LETTER XCI. SYMMACHUS TO MESSALA

You have always held office with the splendor of your life and learning. But now there is a congratulation shared by all good men: a public distinction has also been conferred upon you [Col. 0304C]. I therefore hope that you may enjoy the insignia according to your wishes and, advanced to the summit of glory, equal the greatness of the imperial judgment. Farewell.

## LETTER XCII. SYMMACHUS TO MESSALA

It is my duty to announce that I am well; it is my prayer to learn that you are well. Thus, by reporting my prosperity, I have fulfilled the part of one who loves; you still owe me the joy of learning of your health. Both the favor of the gods and your letters will ensure that it reaches my knowledge in solid truth. Farewell.

## LETTER XCIII. SYMMACHUS TO LONGIMANUS

You share our joys with a friendly spirit and follow with congratulatory writing the restoration of the honor of my son Flavianus [Col. 0304D]. May he always be worthy of happy events. I know, however, that this kindness of your esteem proceeds from the one who made it possible. You are therefore commendably following the instruction of an excellent will. I ask you to maintain the constancy of good circumstances as you have begun; imitate him, and love us. Farewell.

## LETTER XCIV. SYMMACHUS TO LONGIMANUS

The honor of your military service shines through the benefits you bestow. Since the account of your merits places you close to the highest rank, acquire through kindness the distinction of reputation and favor. Nor is there far away someone from whom you may gain such a return. My letters urge you to assist my son Desiderius, a man adorned, apart from fortune, with all the qualities that human care provides [Col. 0305A]. If you favor him, Fortune too will return to favor with him. It remains for you to wish—and, so far as your position and merit permit, to be able—to settle our friend’s readily yielding business by removing the litigation. Farewell.

## LETTER XCV. SYMMACHUS TO LONGIMANUS

You previously deigned to embrace the friendship of my master and son Flavianus. But now an opportunity is given for you to offer him proofs of true intimacy. Summoned to the office of the magnificent consul by the sacred letters of Our Lord, the most august emperor Honorius, he will provide an occasion on which both his merit may become clear to your judgment and your affection for him may shine forth. Meanwhile my intervention performs the part of a parent. There is no doubt how much weight the recommendation of loved ones carries with one who loves his own [Col. 0305B]. This is the whole of my desire: that he may find in your heart a love like mine. Farewell.

## LETTER XCVI. SYMMACHUS TO LONGIMANUS

You urge me to favor Dynamis, in affection for whom I do not yield even to you. He is a man cultivated and adorned with the liberal arts. I therefore gladly defer to your judgment and declare him worthy to be joined to our order. But the distinction of military service must be added to him, so that he may benefit from admission by selection. For imperial enactments have willed that public obligations be remitted only for those whom military honor distinguishes. If you also confer this distinction upon him, adding the allowances of provisions and transport, he will proceed on an easy course to the consular ranks. Thus it lies in your hands to assist both his merit and my efforts with such additions [Col. 0305C].

Meanwhile I am exceedingly surprised that, in the case of the illustrious man Flavianus, my master and son, you considered neither the rank of honor nor the right of friendship. For when your distinguished authority demanded the title of the wine-office that was owed, the matter proceeded as far as condemnation to the statutory fine for neglect of duty. Graciously acknowledge that neither the prefecture nor a man most devoted to you deserved to be touched by such an insult. I therefore ask you to deign henceforth to show him as much respect as it is fitting for you in turn to receive. I, certainly, the parent of both, will not permit any rancor to arise from you; rather, I hope that by dutiful services the grounds of mutual affection between you may increase. Farewell.

## LETTER XCVII. SYMMACHUS TO LONGIMANUS

I received joy from your letters when you informed me that my dependents traveling to Spain had been assisted by your written recommendation [Col. 0305D]. I therefore hold the favor received in my heart and acknowledge it with my lips. Your modesty causes me to speak of this sparingly; you desire affection, not words. Farewell.

## LETTER XCVIII. SYMMACHUS TO LONGIMANUS

I have now received the letters I had long desired, with an extravagant joy of heart. I therefore reply with the reverence and affection that are owed, adding the request that henceforth you deign to repeat the welcome service you freely bestowed. But there is no need to linger over this request. My petition ought not to elicit what your kindness promises of its own accord. Farewell.

## LETTER XCIX. SYMMACHUS TO LONGIMANUS

[Col. 0306A]

I gladly practice the observance of friendship. For I see that you do not deny me a reciprocal care of equal measure. Your affection is a great incentive to diligence. Therefore I cannot reproach you as though it were a favor for what I offer as a duty. You yourself are the author of my services, which you stimulate by the constancy of your writing. Farewell.

## LETTER C. SYMMACHUS TO LONGIMANUS

I perceive what affection you deign to show me in return. But I am greatly surprised that you should suspect my master and son Flavianus, who embraces you with an equal love, of being unequal to your friendship. If, therefore, you think there is any weight in my assertion [Col. 0306B], I ask you to abandon such a belief at my testimony; and, dismissing the whispers of others, preserve a constancy consistent with your holy character and with friendship. Certainly, if some rival’s speech has brought anything to your attention, I ask you to share it with me, so that the bitterness conceived from others’ accusations may be diluted by faithful explanations. Farewell.

## LETTER CI. SYMMACHUS TO LONGIMANUS

I think that for the holy Eusebius it is sufficient as a full recommendation that I declare him approved by me; and therefore I need not labor through many words to win your goodwill for him. I take it as established that your favor will not be lacking to those who have rendered me faithful services. We are well according to our wishes [Col. 0306C], and shall gladly receive letters reporting your good health if you do not withhold them. Farewell.

## LETTER CII. SYMMACHUS TO PETRONIUS AND PATRUINUS

Little needs to be said on behalf of those known and approved. For such letters bear witness to my duty, not to their own merit. I therefore need not labor to commend the merits of my master and son Flavianus to your excellence, since the old friendship between you will turn to happier use. The substance of my message is this: when he returns to his homeland, may he bring back your perpetual affection for himself and a reciprocal greeting for me. Farewell.

## LETTER CIII. SYMMACHUS TO PETRONIUS AND PATRUINUS

I hope that you receive this greeting in full vigor and rejoicing in prosperity [Col. 0306D]. It will be delivered to the excellent man Desiderius, whose blameless life wins him the highest praise. This page is a witness to my duty; it will report much that is good if it draws you, as one inclined toward friendship, to accept him. I do not think that, out of my affection for you, I need strive to have you reply. This is the one concern of my prayer: that the person commended may acquire your favor and return as a praiser of your benefactions; their usefulness will redound to his advantage and my gratitude. Farewell.

## LETTER CIV. SYMMACHUS TO PETRONIUS AND PATRUINUS

I see that the honor of my son Flavianus has lain dormant until now so that a better witness might arise for him. It had fallen under a tyrant’s justice, to be reserved for the judgment of better times [Col. 0307A]. Yet the loss of the prefecture benefited him, because it changed its author. What words, then, will equal so great a favor? I ask you to join us in giving thanks to the eminent man. Since each of us is individually defeated by the greatness of the matter, many praisers are needed, so that their number may fulfill the burden of our obligation. And indeed the lord of my heart, from whom the benefaction proceeded, measures his deed not by another’s words but by the joy of his own conscience; nor is he unaware that what he provides is such as to surpass the hope of repayment. We, nevertheless, shall return a fitting measure of gratitude through the fidelity of friendship and respect; and we offer our hearts as pledges in this matter, with which the free authors of the light are satisfied. For in pious contracts, love is sufficient. Farewell.

## LETTER CV. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

[Col. 0307B]

The mediocrity of my words cannot equal the thanks owed to the most excellent man, Our Lord’s illustrious count. I therefore entrust you with this duty: explain to him more fully the attitude of my mind concerning the transport permits obtained as an aid to the praetorian office; and at the same time deign to strive to secure a swift passage to Spain for those sent on this business. The time for the presentation is approaching, and I fear that the delayed purchase of the carriage horses and the prolonged transport may be compressed by anxious constraints. I have also confidently petitioned the eminent and most distinguished count concerning this matter, assured of success. I further added a reminder, for which I ask you to deign to act as advocate: if the request does not appear burdensome, may he follow my dependents by sending letters to the most powerful men of Spain [Col. 0307C]. Enough has been said. If anything else my friends’ conversation suggests to your ears, I ask you not to hesitate to take it into the care of your holy and faithful heart. Farewell.

## LETTER CVI. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

Mutual affection causes me to delegate to you matters drawn from my own concerns. Since the presentation of my son’s praetorship is approaching, and the illustrious count, most exalted in every virtue, has deigned to assist it with his transport permits, speed must be applied to the purchase of the carriage horses. I therefore ask you not to allow any delay to hold back my dependents, who have been sent to Spain. I wish them to be commended by your letters, so that your merits, impressed upon the minds of the Spaniards, may serve them as support [Col. 0307D]. Farewell.

## LETTER CVII. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

I know the troubles of Julianus, an *agens in rebus*; I approve his birth and grieve over his fortune. For he has long and grievously been exhausted by fatal misfortunes. But I believe that everything will return to harmony with him if he is supported by your patronage and humanity. I shall say no more, since relieving those in need is familiar to your excellent character, and the nature of your mind agrees with this petition of mine. Farewell.

## LETTER CVIII. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

After the agreement of the parties, after the bond of the settlement, and after the records of the arrangements had been submitted in court [Col. 0308A], my son Caecilianus is again being dragged into the uncertainties of litigation. You know the nature of the case; I properly omit setting out in writing what you already know. I ask only this of your holy spirit: with the same strength by which you quieted the struggles, heal this repeated injury, since the broken agreement of the settlement ought to stir your justice more sharply against it. Farewell.

## LETTER CIX. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

The dishonesty of those who reopen matters settled by agreements is evident; through impatience with quiet they exchange the end of a quarrel for a second lawsuit. Consider, therefore, the distress of my son Caecilianus, for whom the peace purchased at the cost of his patrimony could not secure rest [Col. 0308B]. For he is being dragged into distant courts, from which he can easily be rescued if you lend your support. In you and your brother lies the refuge of all whom chance troubles. I need not be prolix in petitioning, since the nature of the case and your justice will draw more favor from you than my intervention can. Farewell.

## LETTER CX. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

Two recent reports have brought me two equally welcome pleasures: that you have advanced through just stages of honor, and that leisure in private life has been granted to my master and son Flavianus. Having accepted this double assurance, I ought to have expected your letters concerning it, which I assumed were delayed through modesty. I therefore leave the measure of my joy to you, since you gather its extent from your affection for us [Col. 0308C]. But to these joys I also wish to join those that you remember were requested long ago concerning the praetorian presentation of my son. I am greatly surprised that the sacred rescript has not yet smiled upon just and customary wishes. Accordingly, in a second letter I again asked that he kindly—as is his custom—order petitions that burden no one but are pleasing to me, and which are supported equally by examples from lower magistracies, to be carried into effect. Yet the beneficence of so great a man, whose pleasure it always is to provide more than hope, should be made more prompt than hope if, as I have often requested, he is urged by your reminders. Farewell.

## LETTER CXI. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

I would say much in praise of my brother Severus if he were seeking your friendship by a new approach or if his talent were suited to commendation. I therefore spare an abundance of words and leave the matter to your judgment, so that the justice of your diligent care may be guided by your own willingness rather than by my letters. Farewell.

## LETTER CXII. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

Since the care of all my people is especially important to you, I presume that intimate friendship with my son Arcentius, a distinguished man whom kinship joins to me, can be opened to him. His moral worth and the antiquity of his family rightly win him this favor. To these particular merits of his my prayers also add an increase to his recommendation, so that I cannot doubt that my testimony will benefit him all the more, together with your judgment [Col. 0309A]. Farewell.

## LETTER CXIII. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

The most distinguished order has sent my master and son Attalus, one of the highest-ranking men, as an envoy to our masters and princes, equipped with various instructions according to custom, which appeared to concern the public good. If you join him as a supporter, I think that his labor will receive an appropriate reward. I therefore ask you, whether on account of the merit of the embassy or in my name, to judge favorably concerning this excellent man; his spirit has been sufficiently strengthened by your support to expect success. Farewell.

## LETTER CXIV. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

Happy are you, who, having completed your honors, enjoy leisure. We live in the open sea of our homeland and are beaten by its waves [Col. 0309B]. My master and son Attalus will explain why I have said this; the hope of seeing your excellence has made the labor of his journey desirable. Farewell.

## LETTER CXV. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

Two things equally pleasing have been brought to me. First, your conversation, which, even if continuous, would not cause weariness. Then came the long-desired arrival of our brother Frumentius. I judged him worthy to be counted among good men even before I had tested his character, on the strength of your recommendation. But when, through closer intercourse, the ornaments of his integrity became clear, I realized that he had been praised less than reason required, out of modesty, lest he seem, through his own praise, to thrust himself into the letters entrusted to him [Col. 0309C]. Through these gifts, therefore, I send you the response you desired, so that you may recognize that I am well according to my wishes and enjoy good health with my family. I think nothing should be added to this matter, since a brotherly congratulation can be fulfilled by the single indication of our well-being. Farewell.

## LETTER CXVI. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

You know, in accordance with the humanity innate in you, what kindness and mercy are owed to little ones deprived of the support of their parents. I do not think I need to employ a long circuit of letters on behalf of the sons of Severus, a man of illustrious memory; unless they are aided by the assistance of good judges, they will be exposed to plunder and injury [Col. 0309D]. Whatever their advantage requires, may your favor not consider it burdensome to provide, so that those abandoned by the support of their family may at least be defended by public assistance. Farewell.

## LETTER CXVII. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

I shall not allow you to be excluded from my conversation, nor shall I be led away from perseverance in writing by imitating your silence. For I know that services are often delayed not through neglect of friendship but because pressing concerns make themselves heard above them. I would have you believe the same, and henceforth undertake to restore this service, which you yourself have long been delaying. I shall then be more ready to provide letters, though even now I do not restrain myself [Col. 0310A], when I receive no reciprocal favor. Farewell.

## LETTER CXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

I am certain that nothing is more welcome to your mind than letters from friends; and therefore I most readily frequent conversations that I know are of great importance to an eminent man. It remains for you, just as kindly as you receive my letters, to send freely reports of your own good health. Farewell.

## LETTER CXIX. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

I take pleasure in addressing you frequently, lest it appear that care for the duties of friendship has grown cold in me. For this reason I wish you health in my prayers and declare it in my letters, asking that, if ever the use of the pen ceases for a longer interval, you attribute the cause of the silence to occupations, not to lack of will or laziness [Col. 0310B]. Farewell.

## LETTER CXX. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

Athanasius, a man of clarissimus rank, has received the hardship of his journey with justified grief. For the marriage promised to him and secured by a bond of pledges in the presence of us as arbiters is being denied. I would enlarge upon the odium of this act if words were not smaller than the facts. He himself will explain more fully to you what assistance he seeks. I need not ask that he be helped by your aid, since both your affection promises this to him and a case fortified by the laws commends it. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXI. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

[Col. 0310C]

I know that it belongs to the proof of friendship that I make you a participant in our difficulty by sharing my religious obligation with you. Receive, therefore, I ask, a straightforward commission, which, out of mutual diligence, you ought to undertake even without being asked. As many bears as possible are being brought from Italy for the presentation of our office; we wish them to be made available promptly for use. Deign, therefore, to protect their passage through your zeal and diligence, and at the same time provide guards, lest greed convert them through fraud. Above all, delays must be broken, because the approaching day of the function allows no postponement for assembling the preparations. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXII. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

I approve your modesty. But it ought not to have been a loss to me while what I hoped for awaited fulfillment [Col. 0310D]. Certainly now, after the result has put an end to the silence, a more frequent pen should repair my loss. There is another way by which you can make up for all your writings: in giving thanks to my lord the consul for his benefaction, take our place, with that affection by which you claim for yourself the joys of your friends. Yet, as I know, you will follow the joy of one who is absent with more brilliant words, both because of the greatness of your talent and without the embarrassment of flattery. Add, if you please, what you already retain as a previous request: that the purchase of other Libyan animals may be granted me by sacred authority. Once this has been obtained, I shall regard it as the gift of all my acquisitions. I do not labor to repeat what concerns my young man, since you remember it freely. For I understand that the need for me to petition is being removed when things not expected are more gladly provided by an eminent and magnificent man. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

In my excellent and very dear friend Perrocius there is Roman simplicity. I say nothing of the fact that he is ennobled by long military service and an irreproachable life. Examination of his character makes all his other qualities seem lesser. Your unanimity has not previously known him; let it receive him by following my judgment. If he now needs to be seen by you, I ask that the honor of my testimony win for him an increase of affection among you. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

We ought to be of use to the children of our friends; even if I myself did not know this, I would have learned it from your example and imitation [Col. 0311B]. The man who will deliver this letter to you belongs to that principle. He serves in the military office of the records; he will have sufficient assistance and good fortune if he proves worthy of reaching the patronage of your most splendid household. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXV. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

I began to love Athanasius, distinguished in the liberal arts, with greater security after I learned your judgment of him. For it is a great advantage to have pleased a wise man. I therefore refrain from recommending him, lest I bring forward something less than what I believe you already think. The part of my message that is easier to state is this: love in him the hope that you have given, and add completion to the benefit you have begun. If some circumstance should frustrate it [Col. 0311C], see to it, I ask, by providing something greater, that the loss of his earlier hope may benefit him. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXVI. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

I am not bringing forward a new or unattempted request, but one that you will recognize as having already been placed before your ears. With paternal affection I defend the daughters of Rufinus, a man of illustrious memory and former urban prefect; through you, who are charged with the care of the republic, I wish their anxieties to be protected. I therefore approach as a petitioner, so that whatever the needs of their distinguished but unfortunate household require, they may deserve to obtain through an easy petition. They have property in Apulia, not so much extensive in income as substantial in assessment. Unless it is supported by the aid of good judges, it will collapse, exhausted by public burdens [Col. 0311D]. It therefore awaits relief from your assistance. You will also make me your debtor in gratitude if, as a merciful defender, you raise a household overcome by a heavy burden. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXVII. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

Your judgments have made me more ready to defend Herennius, an admirable man. Selection gives great pleasure, and hoped-for support calls the spirit forth. But it is not my place to display in writing what our concern has contributed to advancing the case. The man we helped will tell you these things, and the outcome itself will testify to our services. Everything that the plunder had scattered has been investigated and brought to light. Thus Herennius will recover by law the succession owed to him, though it is bitter to a father’s feelings [Col. 0312A]. I now thank you and continue to thank you for your opinion of me; and I hope that our confidence among the best men will endure—the confidence whose proofs you have begun to receive. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

My love for you strives with all its resources to add each day to the esteem in which good men hold you. Far from allowing your old friends to be diminished by the wickedness of accusations, I count among them the most distinguished man Scipio, who, also with me as witness, praises your virtues and laments that he has been deprived of your affection by rivals. Yet it does not seem credible to me that the stability of your mind could have been altered by false rumors, since a man conscious of his life ought to judge that slanderous speech has no power over him [Col. 0312B]. I therefore urge and beg you to spurn whatever lies have been insinuated, and to claim this honor for your merits, so that you may understand that everyone judges you to be what you are. Let no one transfer to you the seeds of his own hatred. For it has long been a kind of strategy, used to nourish the strength of one’s own discord, to stir fear of those more powerful. I shall go no further, since the wisdom of your character promises me success in my petition. I think it will answer my letters to this extent: that you will not so much have forgiven Scipio as have believed that you had heard nothing asserted against him. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXIX. SYMMACHUS TO SIBIDIUS

I do not want you to measure my concern for you by this letter. The words of those who offer greetings are few, but their prayers are extensive. Let me therefore imitate toward you the economy of religious observances by which the rights of friendship are conferred, and let a pious duty be paid in a brief page, as with a small coin [Col. 0312C]. Devotion does not require a long excursion. But I prescribe limits to your pen: whatever you write about yourself will be more than enough for me, provided it is joyful. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXX. SYMMACHUS TO SIBIDIUS

My spirit is sick so long as I lack the certain assurance that you have entered the harbor of health. I want you to satisfy this expectation. I do not wish a literary courtesy to be rendered to me as an honor, but relief from great anxiety. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXI. SYMMACHUS TO SIBIDIUS

You will never make me, by keeping silent, adopt an equal disposition through imitation. For I consider not what is owed to a temporary circumstance but what is owed to enduring friendship. And since I am a strict judge of my own duty, I believe that your concern is interrupted more often by accident than by weariness. But lest a lengthy interruption of conversation compel one who loves you to fear neglect, I ask you steadily to practice the duties of intimacy. For how can I know that what I offer is welcome if you refuse what I request in return? Farewell.

# BOOK EIGHT

[Col. 0313]

## LETTER I

[Col. 0313A]

I know that your mind is not usually changed by any height of honor. For whatever distinction accrues to those who have deserved well seems to you rather something discharged than something bestowed. And therefore I confess that I marvel and am astonished that you, endowed with such virtue and humanity, have for some time abstained from honoring me with the gift of letters. Although I suppose this has happened more because of the pressure of affairs than by your will, I nevertheless do not cease to ask that frequent conversation may show your judgment mindful of me. Farewell.

## LETTER II. SYMMACHUS TO ALMACHIUS

A manifold and varied gift has indeed been presented to me by you; but I noticed that modesty was responsible for your refusal to take full credit for the outcome of the woodland hunt. You boast that the hare was caught by your tracking, but assert that the boar fell to servile hands. Or did the beast’s ferocity seem unworthy of being claimed as your own distinction? But you will laugh at these words, spoken in jest.

Now attend to the other matters about which you inquire concerning me. I have decided to remain at Capua for a few more days; thereafter, by changing among neighboring places, to prolong this entire month; and then, if the gods favor my intention, I shall be able to retrace the Appian Way despite the unpleasant approach of winter. Farewell.

## LETTER III. SYMMACHUS TO FRUCTIANUS

Troubled for a long time by your letters, I shall remain distressed until I learn favorable news about you. I therefore wish to know how much either the physicians’ treatment or your abstinence has advanced you toward recovery. As for myself, now restored to good health, I have decided, with fortune’s support, to revisit my homeland before the labors of travel are increased by the advance of mature winter. Farewell.

## LETTER IV. SYMMACHUS TO LOLLIANUS

You gave me your first letter voluntarily; your second ought to be elicited by my concern. Receive, then, this greeting, which I promise to repay in kind, and likewise, when your reply comes, to make my response equal to it. Farewell.

## LETTER V. SYMMACHUS TO PRISCILLIANUS

Your letters would be welcome to me even if they contained nothing about my services and praises in Africa. For just as they brought me some distinction, so they gave you joy in accordance with our mutual friendship. This is why you sent your letter with delight. An exultant spirit takes pride and cannot refrain from displaying itself. May the kindness of the gods therefore reward such great affection toward us. Indeed, since I myself consider that I am not worthy to repay it, in place of my gratitude I wish for you the favor of heavenly protection. Farewell.

## LETTER VI. SYMMACHUS TO SEVERUS

Your letters have always been welcome, but now they wounded the mind of the reader when they revealed that you were being worn down by the long duration of your illness. I ask that the good gods, guardians of blessings, apply healing hands to your health, lest the prolonged affliction of an excellent senator make it seem that the heavenly powers care for nothing—a view from which I dissent—and I presume that you will promptly be restored to firm health by the aid of the powers that bring healing, provided that you yourself struggle through adversity with a spirit full of hope and joyful thoughts. Farewell.

## LETTER VII. SYMMACHUS TO CAPREOLUS

When Euscius was approaching, I hoped for a letter from you, but chance disappointed my confidence. Nevertheless, I could not imitate your silence; hence I am performing an unowed act of address, so that you, who ought to have been the leader in this duty, may be urged to diligence by the necessity of setting an example. Farewell.

## LETTER VIII. SYMMACHUS TO EUSEBIUS

[Col. 0314B]

It may have been due to your modesty that until now you have brought us no word of greeting. Now take the confidence which I offer as an invitation to intimacy, and prove by the constancy of your conversation that my letters have been welcome. Farewell.

## LETTER IX. SYMMACHUS TO MARTIANUS

By taking the initiative in writing, I challenge your confidence. Enter, therefore, without apprehension upon the path of our intimacy. The reciprocal performance of your duty will cause the friendship begun by me to grow strong. Farewell.

## LETTER X. SYMMACHUS TO IRENAEUS

I imagine that you were waiting for my letter so that, challenged to reciprocal duties, you might break forth. Take, then, the conversation whose example you are to follow. Henceforth I shall be more diligent in writing, if reciprocity answers our beginning. Farewell.

## LETTER XI. SYMMACHUS TO [lacuna]

The affection of my mind for you is not to be measured by letters. Devotion is contained in the faithfulness of the heart; rivalry often lurks in verbal courtesies. Therefore, if I seem to you less frequent in writing, do not suppose that anything has been taken away from my love. It often happens that people close to you neither inform me of their departure nor ask for reciprocal pages. But there is no need to speak at greater length about this, since a brief and concise defense is enough for one who loves.

I turn to matters that are of mutual concern. I rejoiced at the report of your health, and I return news that will make you glad. For the vigor of my own body, too, has begun to rise again after infirm health. Farewell.

## LETTER XII. SYMMACHUS TO PACATUS

I do not think that I appear negligent either in sending or in repaying letters to you. Therefore, although I remember that our courtesies have flowed to you in recent days, I have nevertheless taken care to discharge the debt with the proper interest of conversation as well. But if this practice should ever cease for a brief interval, I would like you to consider that regard for friendships does not grow cold. Devotion is to be measured more by the faithfulness of the heart than by the display of words. Farewell.

## LETTER XIII. SYMMACHUS TO APOLLODORUS

I suppose that the report has reached you which announced that you have been released not only from the burden of office but also from the burden of cares. If so, I shall now be a confirmer of the good you once desired. My health and that of my son are secure through divine aid. Both our prayers and your merits will ensure that you enjoy strong health and a happy return. Farewell.

## LETTER XIV. SYMMACHUS TO CAECILIANUS AND PROBINUS

I am filled with joy since I learned that you are well and that, amid the hardships of affairs, you remember our friendship. But when will it happen that the losses caused by your silence are repaired by the consolations of letters? I would have wished you to be present among the first at my praetorian ceremonies and to lend distinction to our common festivities. But I must endure having the business of the Senate put before me. Thus in the words above there is more a declaration of longing than a complaint about separation. The favor of the heavenly powers will ensure that, once freed from your duties to your homeland, you return by a happy journey to the solemn celebration of our games. Farewell.

## LETTER XV. SYMMACHUS TO ALLEVIUS

Conversation that is returned comes from obligation; conversation offered voluntarily comes from generosity. The second role has been left to me, since your pen anticipated my writings. Now, having repaid your greeting in turn, I ask for your assistance and attention in the matters which Castor has suggested should be advanced for our use and benefit. Farewell.

## LETTER XVI. SYMMACHUS TO CARTERIUS

I am grateful that my testimony was not doubted and that Auxentius, our son, a most distinguished young man, was received into your family; I count this to my credit. By this act our friendship enters into the closer obligations of trust. Longer experience will show that, once you have recognized more of his good qualities, you must admit that my endorsement of his merits remained within the bounds of truth. Farewell.

## LETTER XVII. SYMMACHUS TO RUFINUS

After the provincial case had run its course and, by the necessary appeal, reached the judge of the sacred tribunal, I was pleased by your faithfulness and diligence; and I attributed the outcome of the case to fortune, not to the advocate’s ignorance, but to the judge’s preference. I therefore urge you to place confidence in my friendship and, content for the moment with my endorsement, to protect our household—which is assailed by many injustices—through the service of your forensic skill. Just as we freely declare our gratitude in a bare and simple address, so, if fortune assists, we shall strive to be equal in returning the favor. Farewell.

## LETTER XVIII. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

You are surprised that I am in the countryside. But I am more justly astonished that you have returned to our common homeland, abandoning the leisure of the country, unless the repeated lawsuit has brought you a reason for returning. Otherwise, since your mind is eager for quiet, you would prefer to remain occupied with rural affairs. For me, suburban life, while I suffer from an ailment of the feet, is more a consolation than a pleasure. The sensation of a grievous illness admits no enjoyment. But I hope that, if the divine powers look with favor upon my innocence, I shall also be healed by the attention of the courts. Either my return to Rome or your excursion to the estate where I am now staying will be welcome and easy. Farewell.

## LETTER XIX. SYMMACHUS TO PATRUINUS

I prefer you yourself to the soothing devices of words. You, by contrast, make up for the delays of absence with letters. What if the fertility of your crops had answered you, or abundant harvests had smiled upon you? You would spend every season in the leisure of the countryside, paying no heed to your homeland’s hunger while lingering on your estates. Or are you helped only by bird-catching, part of which you have given me? But even here, where you are stationed, you could indulge generously in the delights of the table. For you would have at hand both provisions bought in the delicatessen market and produce carried in from your suburban estate.

And what of the fact that you pretend that your wife is being tossed about by illness? If you speak truth about her health, solitude is not appropriate to her. Rome has more resources for health and a greater number of physicians. Take care, then, lest you incur another kind of suspicion if you wear out a wife besieged by illness in an empty retreat and an unsafe exile. Farewell.

## LETTER XX

More than in other seasons I delight in summer—not because the sun’s longer course extends the daylight hours, nor because our affairs and resources grow rich with new grain, but because frequent traffic, traveling under calm sailing conditions, regularly brings me your desired letters. For what can be offered that is more delightful to the mind, or more suited to the duty of friendship, than for me to experience you as one who loves me through the practice of frequent conversation? Therefore, while the season of the year invites us and while the sea is passable, let us gather, as though for winter, certain provisions and nourishment for our mutual affection.

When I wrote this, my health was proceeding according to my wishes, evidently aided by your prayers. For I think that our wishes succeed for no other reason than through the judgment and love of Carthage. Farewell.

## LETTER XXI. SYMMACHUS TO LUCILLUS

I used to think, wrongly, that you were indulging in leisure; but you exercise your mind through reading and your body through work. Your writings show this, as do the gifts carved by your pen and the spoils won by the hunt.

I must traverse the Flaminian Way, summoned to the new fasces of a noble consul. If only your return would precede my preparations for departure! I would believe myself assisted by a very generous traveling allowance. But since a long journey separates us, and neither delay for me nor haste for you is convenient, this page will serve in place of a meeting.

With the gods’ permission invoked beforehand, my praetor Symmachus will soon receive the urban tribunal. I wish his festival to be attended by the most distinguished of his friends, among whom you are numbered. Grant him that favor even though you will be far away on those same days. What is offered to the absent is more welcome. Farewell.

## LETTER XXII. SYMMACHUS TO ANDRONICUS

[Col. 0317A]

The Cecropian Muse blooms upon your lips; my tongue is Latin. Do not expect equal gifts from my pen. In letters we are defeated; in love we compete. I would rightly have replied if you had brought only a letter. But you, as a diligent friend, have brought to our library the riches of your poems. What worthy return can I, myself of slender eloquence and impoverished talent, make to you?

I shall submit to public admiration what you sent to be read. Although an unequal praiser, I shall make public a work worthy of the age. This will detract nothing from the glory of your work. For we know that Homer too has been praised by dissimilar voices. The fame of great men would lack renown if it were not content even with lesser witnesses.

But why do I prolong this, when your modesty demands brevity? Take care of your health. And if you add anything to your pen, share it with me, a mediocre judge but not an ungrateful reader. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIII. SYMMACHUS TO MARCIANUS

I pray to the gods that the health which I presently enjoy may likewise be granted to you and yours. It seems to me that I have fully embraced what should be said in this opening: my prayer for your health, and my joy in my own. But you do not allow letters to be brief. What, then, will be the subject of a longer page? If you wish, I shall continue with where I am and what I have been doing, for friendship is especially curious about such matters.

The beginning of my pleasures lies in the Formian Gulf, where a city is said once to have been inhabited by the people of the Laestrygonians. We read that they obeyed their bellies and appetites to the point of incurring the odium of savagery. I spent several days on that shore, but sparingly in pleasures, persuaded to remain by the healthfulness of the climate and the coolness of the waters.

My children arrived, for whose sake I had set out from our city. Once those whom I desired were present, there was no reason to undertake a further journey. Thereafter, at their direction, I explored the coast lying between Formiae and the shores of Cumae. Now, by mutual invitations, we move either to Bauli or to the Gauranian estate of Nichomachus.

Friends continually flock to me in abundance. Do not suppose that I am behaving frivolously amid such beauty of place and abundance of resources. Everywhere we live a consular life, and at Lake Lucrinus we are serious. There is no singing on the boats, no gluttony at banquets, no frequenting of the baths, and no provocative swimming by young men. You should know that places themselves bear no guilt for luxury. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIV. SYMMACHUS TO MAXIMINIANUS

There is no difference between you and your excellent father, either in substance or in affection. Therefore you could also accept as addressed to yourself the letter which I sent out of respect for him, since you share in everything that concerns him. But now you must be honored by us in your own name as well.

Moreover, I took care lest, when one of you replied, I should be charged with returning a gift to two people at once. Brevity nevertheless suits this page, since I have selected what deserved to be reported. Therefore you will keep this address as a witness to our affection for you.

But it is fitting that you be expansive in replying. The conditions are not equal: what I have repeated was addressed to both of you, whereas each of us must undertake an individual labor. It is difficult to fill two channels from one spring; doubled sources flow abundantly into a single channel. Farewell.

## LETTER XXV. SYMMACHUS TO ALBINUS

I suppose you imagine that I have been surrounded by the charms of Campania and negligent until now in writing to you. These places do not have the sort of fortune that allows pleasures to bury serious concerns. Everything resounds with unusual necessities, and delights have yielded to burdens. Thus I have found business instead of leisure.

Nor can I easily turn my mind back to these duties of friendship. Nevertheless, I promise this to your reverence: I shall value you above my letters. I am eager to retrace my journey to you as soon as possible. For the same reason that prevented me from writing compels me to return. Farewell.

## LETTER XXVI. SYMMACHUS TO GREGORIUS

I sent a letter to your father, with which you could have been content. For, since the two of you have one mind, the same devotion will satisfy you both. But I feared imitation, lest one of you should reply to me in the place and voice of both. Therefore, as is customary in honoring the gods, I add a gift to the sacrifice—brief, I admit, and one you would have wished to be longer. But in what is added, measure is not sought.

Return abundance to my brevity yourself; for those who do not need to duplicate their addresses ought to extend their familiar pages. Farewell.

## LETTER XXVII. SYMMACHUS TO CENSORINUS

With a ready and eager hand I seized your letters when they were offered to me, anticipating that I would learn good news. But as I ran through the account of your losses, the pleasure was followed by distress. Those adversities which you endured along with many others, in accordance with human nature, possess some consolation from being shared. But I think this blow of piratical plunder, which harsh fortune inflicted on you personally, has struck more deeply, because it has no companion and has doubled your pain.

Against such accidents the mind must be armed with virtue and reason, and hope of better things must also be adopted. Things that have often tottered have returned to stability. Nothing is eternal for human beings. Frequent changes roll over mortal affairs, and the flight of everything is everywhere visible. I have touched upon these matters briefly, since your learning will suggest more to you.

Now I reply to the matters you wished me to know. As soon as possible I am eager to visit Naples at the request of your fellow citizens; there I shall devote two days to the honor of the revered city. Then, if the gods assist my well-laid plans, we shall seek venerable Rome and our home by way of Capua.

Meanwhile, if I should have the pleasure of seeing and conversing with you, I shall be filled to satiety with joy. But if some greater necessity denies us access to you, I would like you, once the cloud of cares has been cleared away, wisely to recover that cheerfulness of spirit which our meeting could have diligently restored to you. Farewell.

## LETTER XXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO ROMANUS

[Col. 0319A]

I know that you remember that I too was struck by the same grief over our friend; but now the exchange of conversation ought to be a consolation to us. I am therefore writing so that you will be compelled to reply and return from mournful thoughts to the duties owed to the living. If a religious obligation prevented you from writing first, you will not be so irreverent as to refrain when challenged. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIX. SYMMACHUS TO SALVIUS

In the letters recently delivered to me I saw the devout joy of your heart on our behalf, and I clearly recognized what pleasure you derive from the prosperity of friends. I love you more readily, therefore, after observing this prayer of a good mind.

Although I myself have returned thanks for the favor of your writings to the most excellent man, the master of my heart, in honor of your brother Flavianus, I nevertheless ask you to be willing also to affirm the magnitude of my gratitude to the author of so great a benefaction. Farewell.

## LETTER XXX. SYMMACHUS TO JOVIUS

It served the public interest that greater responsibilities should be entrusted to you. Therefore my testimony of joy should not be too expansive, lest suspicion of flattery disfigure the truth of my judgment. I hope, then, that the course of the office you have undertaken will smile upon you. Although I cannot doubt that your integrity will not change and that your good abilities will be stimulated more successfully by the incentive of rewards. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXI. SYMMACHUS TO EUDOXIUS

[Col. 0319C]

I leaped for joy at the honor of your friendship when I received your letter. But when our Annius informed me how uncertain your health was, joy flowed into serious concern. I see that the damage to your health has been added to a journey which is itself almost a disease.

What nevertheless consoles my anxiety is that moderation is familiar to you, that wisdom is your kin, and that your spirit grows greater in adversity—qualities that usually restore bodily strength and the clear sky of vigor. I therefore hope to learn more joyful news about you and am already preparing my ears for happy reports. Justice, which looks favorably upon the devout, will ensure that, after this misfortune has quickly passed, the prosperity of your life will be extended for a long time. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXII. SYMMACHUS TO URBICUS

[Col. 0319D]

As custom requires, you ought to have taken the initiative in writing when the return of the household courier reminded you of this diligence. But since either forgetfulness or preoccupation has deprived us of the desired gift of your devotion, I assume the initiative. Henceforth I shall judge from the variety or abundance of your notes whether you have been absent from beginning your letters by choice or rather by necessity. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO JUSTINIANUS

I know that I was slow in writing. I deliberately postponed taking up my pen while restoring the strength weakened by the journey, so that a page similar to your eager wish for good news about me might be delivered to you. Let the delay, then, be compensated by the best possible news.

Certainly I say that this is the law of letters among friends: by their constancy they test the spirits of their recipients, while by their goodness they delight mine. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO EUSEBIUS

I would have preferred to write to you earlier; but when many people are traveling back and forth, the writer’s judgment must select a trustworthy opportunity. You have received the reason for my slower service. If it has satisfied your mind, please take care that your replies, entrusted to suitable messengers, also reach me. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXV. SYMMACHUS TO JOHN
