That I am writing to you late is evidence of a steadfast friendship, whose memory is proved by repeated duties at intervals. I interpret your silence in the same way. Although I seek the honor of your pen, confident in your loyalty I do not doubt even your silent affection.

But I fear that this view may encourage you to neglect writing and, secure in my judgment, to omit these duties of friendship. I therefore urge and ask you to consider instead that side which makes constancy welcome, not the side that promises pardon for infrequency. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVI. SYMMACHUS TO QUINTILIANUS

We write this as a sign of my love for you and so that you yourself may be challenged to reply by my example. Since, then, I have fulfilled my part in devotion, I expect you also to perform the repayment of reciprocity. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVII. SYMMACHUS TO CHRYSOCOMAS

Recently returned to my household gods, I still turn my mind and thoughts toward you. Thus I compensate with that mental pleasure the delight which I have hitherto enjoyed face to face from your conversation. If mutual care should answer it, and the writing of your friendship has conferred such great favor upon me, how much more will a reply confer when returned? Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO ROMULUS

The health of our mutual dear one is secure, and the studies entrusted to my concern are progressing. You may also be confident of my health, and in response to such news discharge your concern for me by similar replies about yourself. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIX. SYMMACHUS TO [lacuna]

You cannot complain of my silence, since until now you have given me nothing in writing. But if you are waiting for a similar initiative from my pen, take as your example the conscientious duty which you ought to imitate. Henceforth I shall be more ready to exercise my pen, if you encourage me with the fruit of reciprocal conversation. Farewell.

## LETTER XL. SYMMACHUS TO AVENTIUS

I approved your withdrawal even in silence. Since, because of the discord, you could not attend the final rites for your son-in-law, you seemed, by that mournful departure, to have satisfied your duty of affection. As for myself, I completed at home the three-day observance owed to an excellent citizen, not seeking popularity but reflecting upon the vicissitudes of human fortune. For what is more reasonable than to grant a colleague what you would at some time wish good men to offer you? Farewell.

## LETTER XLI. SYMMACHUS TO ANTIOCHUS

You have only just entered upon the threshold of office, yet you are wishing far too soon for the arrival of your successor. I recognize an impatience suited to Greek delicacies; I wish that you would disguise it throughout the whole year and remember that you have migrated into the three Romulean tribes. For what worthy of complaint have you suffered? The insults of military service have not yet struck you; you have not yet fled from troops of women with torn clothing; as a client seeking an audience, you have not yet kept a sleepless vigil before the doors of high officials—and already, with delicate distaste, you reject the magistracy? Change your attitude, if you are able, and endure it for a year or even two.

## LETTER XLII. SYMMACHUS TO [lacuna]

A plausible reason [lacuna] For who, traveling directly to Sicily, can return my conversation to one engaged in distant pursuits? But I shall stop. Hold fast to this: my concern for you ought not to be measured by the number of letters. Diligence toward friends remains constant, but the scarcity of opportunities distinguishes the writings. But I think enough has been said about this.

Now your elegance of talent and the subtlety of your inventions must be praised. For you have discovered a new kind of mosaic, one unattempted by those before you, which even our rusticity will try to attach as decoration to our chambers if, whether on panels or tiles, we take from you an example of a work conceived beforehand. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIII. SYMMACHUS TO CALLISTIANUS

Among the other inheritances to be desired from deceased parents, the succession of friendships should also be sought. Perhaps the inheritance of intimacy should be pursued with even stronger zeal, because fortune bestows material possessions, whereas affection is joined by judgment.

I therefore wish the connection propagated from your family to grow stronger between us more readily. It is entirely consonant with nature that duties begun by you and approved by me should grow together. Henceforth be generous in conversation; you will not lack my concern, which will reward you with the reciprocity of writing. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIV. SYMMACHUS TO PASTINATUS

I may rightly compare your letters with the fruits of the fields. Just as their yield does not disappoint the due season, so the annual conversation of your graciousness does not deceive our expectation. Its delivery to me by our people has now satisfied me. Having read your pages, I rejoice that you are well and delighted by the honor of your address. Nor do I think I shall be judged unequal in replying. Divine favor will ensure that a long life multiplies these exchanges of duty between us. Farewell.

## LETTER XLV. SYMMACHUS TO PIERIUS

The annual debt of your conversation has, in a manner, been paid to me. These replies will also provide you with your customary joy concerning us. Because of the great distance between us, we cannot send them frequently, but we offer them faithfully at fixed times. Let this practice remain, and let mutual confidence between us be stored up as a kind of sign of our health. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVI. SYMMACHUS TO STRATEGIUS

You act toward me with the longing of one who loves, asking me to return; for my own mind, eager for you, has been demanding this for a long time. But impaired health resists my desire. A harmful fluid that has entered my joints still keeps me confined to my bed and is scarcely reduced by the dryness of the seaside climate.

Therefore grant to recovery the time that I had claimed for pleasure. Yet you maintain that, amid such an abundance of good things, nothing has been as pleasant since my departure. But I think that you are deceived by affectionate devotion, because judgment is rare in one who loves.

Indeed, I know what you think of me, and not from this letter alone. It is almost the case, however, that I ought to thank my absence, since it has provided me with a written certificate of your testimony. But I shall let this pass.

I shall not delay your expectation once my strength has been restored. But since this is a long way off for one who is diligent, after seeing what we possess nearby I shall hasten my return. For I hope that my health will gain as much from seeing you as it could be expected to gain from leisure. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVII. SYMMACHUS TO VALERIUS

I would like to announce that my son’s illness has been calmed, but fabrications are of no use to the anxious. Nevertheless, I dare to hope for better things. For, by God’s favor, the reduction of his fevers has begun to approach confidence in his recovery. I thank you for your concern on our behalf, and I pray to the heavenly power that a return of every prosperity may answer the concern which you show toward your friends. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVIII. SYMMACHUS TO MAXIMILIANUS

You are accustomed to being expansive in writing, in keeping with the powers of your talent. After courtly honor called you into military readiness, you too tighten your words and imitate the lightly armed rorarii. What am I to do, a garrulous old man whose measure of speech is prescribed by a young man?

An old-man’s fault, talkativeness, drags us along; but your example intervenes, and I infer that your ears are wearied by the brevity of your pen. For meanwhile I must not violate the form of your page. I shall nevertheless wait to see whether, if I reply at greater length, you demand abundance from me. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIX. SYMMACHUS TO VITALIS

For a long time, conscious of my middling eloquence, I hesitated to reply to the health and beauty of your letters. But devotion broke through my fear. I preferred to displease by my pen rather than by arrogance. Whatever this may be that the page contains, I ask you to judge it kindly and to lower yourself to the mediocrity of my writings, lest my duty be blunted while imitation is despaired of. Farewell.

## LETTER L. SYMMACHUS TO JOVIUS

For a long time I have not earned a reciprocal letter from you in response to the letter I sent; nevertheless, preserving my purpose, I renew the honor of writing. I believe that repetition may now obtain the response which was denied to my first service. Farewell.

## LETTER LI. SYMMACHUS TO MAXIMILIANUS

The infrequency of your letters nearly asserts that my constancy in writing is a burden to you. For you are unusually sparing in conversation. But I defend the constancy of my diligence and am not drawn away from my purpose by argument. It will be in your power either to increase this disposition of my mind by silence or to remove it by letters. Farewell.

## LETTER LII

You understand how much your absence grieves me. For this reason you write to me through my son that necessity has been imposed upon you, so that you may clear yourself by pleading public business. One of two things, then, must be done in accordance with your devotion: either send an abundance of deer and boars, or return more quickly into the sight of your friend. No justice supports an adequate excuse if you deny both the hunt to him and consolation to me. Farewell.

## LETTER LIII. SYMMACHUS TO LEPORIUS

I return the conversation owed to you. For some time our mutual friend has shown me an equal honor of writing; after carefully observing his modesty and integrity, I approved him as worthy of your love. Farewell.

## LETTER LIV. SYMMACHUS TO MARCIANUS

I imagine that my letters seem late to you. But if you count the days of the journey, the calculation will dispel the delay. In addition, a bodily pain caused by my usual ailment intervened, interrupting the familiar duties. Now that rest has been restored to my labor and health, I do not delay the words of greeting, expecting to receive the reward of my service in your reply. Farewell.

## LETTER LV. SYMMACHUS TO MAXIMILIANUS

[Col. 0323D]

If you know my attitude toward you well, you cannot doubt that the poor condition of my health has until now prevented me from sending repeated letters. Having cleared myself on this point, I send you a greeting-bearing page which will testify that I am well.

***

After my health removed the excuse for silence, I had learned from my son’s assertion that you would come to Campania. This was why I abstained from writing. But while either urban concerns or pleasures detain you, our expectation has nearly incurred the blame of silence. I therefore perform my duty toward you by sending a greeting, and leave you to choose whether you prefer to grant me your arrival or to discharge your debt with a reply. Farewell.

## LETTER LVI. SYMMACHUS TO ROMANUS

[Col. 0324A]

I observe the ancient custom by which those who have departed from home begin with letters, and I announce that I am well. It follows from obligation that you should repay the friendly gift sent by me with a friendly reply. Farewell.

## LETTER LVII. SYMMACHUS TO VALERIUS

I summon my son Romulus; you are keeping him back. I claim for myself the role of a father toward him; you exercise the right of a relative by marriage. By voluntary promise he owes me his presence, but you retain him with the hope of sharing your journey. Yet since your arrival too is announced, the delay is a profitable assessment which promises me both men in place of one.

I therefore yield to your wishes and do not deny you patience for a few days. I also offer excessive congratulations to your brother Romulus, whose companionship we both claim through a pious and friendly rivalry. Farewell.

## LETTER LVIII. SYMMACHUS TO MARCIANUS

My son, by the good favor of God, is out of danger, but he suffers a loss of strength almost amounting to illness. He has decided to return, gradually dividing the journey into shorter stages. I too have contracted the contagion from my household. I believe the harm was caused by night watches, whose effect was slight at the time but made itself known afterward.

Nevertheless, I strive to suppress the advancing illness through care and moderation. Therefore, with the heavenly powers summoned to our aid, we are preparing to begin the journey. I would return thanks for your kindness toward us if love would allow itself to be nourished by the praise that it hopes for and owes in return. Farewell.

## LETTER LIX. SYMMACHUS TO ROMANUS

I had wished to be frequent in writing and had promised that this should be expected; but the health of my son, which remained uncertain for a long time, commanded me to desist from such duties. As soon as he began to emerge with the assistance of the powers that bring healing, the practice of writing immediately followed his recovery of security. Receive, then, with pleasure this greeting, which, if desired fortune assists, we shall soon follow in person. Farewell.

## LETTER LX. SYMMACHUS TO SERVIUS

As I understand, you are waiting for my letter, as though you yourself ought not to be the leader in the duty of friendship. Perhaps you invoke custom as an excuse, since most people are persuaded that the initiative in greeting should be taken by those who have departed. I release you either through respect for custom or under the law of laziness. It will be enough for my complete satisfaction if, although reluctant to take the initiative in writing, you at least follow my example. Farewell.

## LETTER LXI. SYMMACHUS TO HIS FRIENDS IN ROME

We are advancing on the road to Capua. Perhaps you suspect that the length of the journey will bring about the customary forgetfulness of the duty I owe you. For there is a common proverb that, once Malea has been sailed around, the memory of those left at home is erased. But wherever I set foot, concern for my friends accompanies me. Hope, then, that the honor of this duty toward you will remain, if fortune consents to your wishes. Farewell.

## LETTER LXII. SYMMACHUS TO ROMULUS

I am not uncertain of the opinion that my letters are awaited. For I suffer an equal impatience of longing for yours. There is therefore one reason for our correspondence: that I may earn yours. As with the drinking of springs, the thirst is greater because the flavor is sweeter. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIII. SYMMACHUS TO LAMPADIUS

When I last departed from the city, you had asked me, if I wished to open the path of writing to you, to begin my letter first. I am satisfying your wish, which embraces respect for ancient custom. Freed, then, from this obligation, break forth into the duties of a familiar pen and share with me whatever you have accomplished for the public good in administering the city’s protection.

But let a writer’s modesty take nothing away from the truth, lest the letter’s modesty diminish my pleasure. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIV. SYMMACHUS TO DIONYSIUS

The good men had been offended that you had departed prematurely. Fortune regretted its error, and restored you to us with equal haste. But what benefit does a friend’s return bring to one who is absent? Console this misfortune with frequent letters. Write also what the responsibility entrusted to you at Rome has permitted you to do, so that, when a more generous day has promised me the hope of seeing your excellence, I too may enjoy at greater length the leisure scarcely snatched after urban troubles. Farewell.

## LETTER LXV. SYMMACHUS TO LAMPADIUS

By giving proof of the city’s tranquillity, you have prolonged the time in which I can, in a manner, claim leisure. For the calm of the citizens—achieved through your counsels, by which the common people were reduced to the shame of repentance—allows me to remain away for a long time.

Now, therefore, after the flight of all cares, I shall be able to extend what I may call rich holidays for myself. Although I ought not to give my mind uncertain instructions, since I am conscious of the tender affection I feel for you and of that longing by which I love my homeland above all the pleasures of life. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVI. SYMMACHUS TO HERCULIUS

[Col. 0325D]

I would thank you profusely, since, although you had only recently departed from us, you anticipated me by sending your greetings, unless my hope of a greater favor claimed this expression of gratitude for itself. For they say that you yourself are going to be present; and, on this account, I confess that I owe you a pledge as a token of greater gratitude. Nevertheless, I should like your letters to lend credibility to the good I hope for, so that I, who take pleasure in such an expectation, may rejoice all the more in the security of its confirmation. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVII. SYMMACHUS TO DYNAMIUS

You long for my letters out of affection, but our common son makes me seem infrequent, since he does not send replies. Yet let it suffice to have said this briefly, lest our defense become a burden to his modesty. For now I offer you the honor of a greeting, and I do not demand what you will do spontaneously: that you address us in return. Both the devotion of your heart and your established practice promise me this exchange. Farewell.

## LETTER LXVIII. SYMMACHUS TO TICIANUS

I gladly received the letters I had desired from you; but knowledge of your actions, of which Euscius was both witness and narrator, brought me a still greater pleasure. I therefore urge and advise you not to abandon what you have begun well, and to pursue the reward of praise through honorable conduct. I would add a request concerning my own affairs if there were someone else to address; but since you voluntarily do what my speech might have asked, I omit the role of commendation. For whatever is presumed upon the confidence of friendship has greater grace when it is performed spontaneously. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIX. SYMMACHUS TO VALERIANUS

You say that you are living in the country, and are fostering your still-unripe old age by training vines or grafting trees. Your letter does not sound like this—unless, perhaps, your Gaul has returned from Helicon. You move one set of furrows with your pen and plant another set of rows. But I, since you wish to know about my affairs, am languishing in leisure and study in the dwelling-place of Latian eloquence. May the gods grant growth to my little boy in years. He himself, with the permission previously granted by Fortune, has summoned me to share his studies. Meanwhile, spur my idleness with frequent letters. For after the bitter disasters of my speeches, this one form of writing alone remains that can draw me back to the practice of composition. Farewell.

## LETTER LXX. SYMMACHUS TO ROMANUS

Only now do I overflow with pleasure, because you have announced that you are free from cares. Until now, the distress of your affairs had been gnawing at me. Therefore I pray to the gods who guard our welfare that your pages may never darken a troubled mind. Meanwhile, such letters deserve an answering recompense. So in turn accept something from me in which you may rejoice. We are in good health, and we are planning to return to the vicinity of Rome. May Fortune’s kindness allow this exchange to continue between us, so that prosperous letters may be answered with corresponding replies. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXI. TO MANY PERSONS, INVITING THEM

With the favor of the Divinity previously invoked, my son Symmachus will assume the fasces of the urban praetorship on the Kalends of January. We ask that his office be honored by your presence, requested through a shared petition. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXII. SIMILIS

With the honor of the Divinity first invoked, my son Symmachus will receive the magistracy of the urban praetorship on the Kalends of January. I ask that your presence lend distinction to our festivities. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIII. SYMMACHUS TO MARCIANUS

[Col. 0327A]

You ought not to blame me for my silence: amid adversity, the practice of the customary services of friendship is neglected. But since there is hope that my Symmachus will gradually recover good health, my courage returns to the duties of friendship, so that, if my silence had caused you any fear, the security of my conversation may set you free from it. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXIV. SYMMACHUS TO ANCHIUS

[Col. 0328A]

I am certain that you consider nothing more important than my letters. I too hold the same opinion regarding the pleasure of your conversation. I have rightly taken up the duty of friendship. If you return it with equal measure, my devotion will be sharpened by the stimulus of your loyalty. Farewell.

# BOOK NINE

[Col. 0327]

## LETTER ONE. SYMMACHUS TO PALLADIUS

[Col. 0327A]

If the memory of our old friendship endures and has not been weakened by any forgetfulness, I believe that you will gladly receive my letters, which I have sent in confidence in our mutual affection. I shall owe you much gratitude if a reciprocal response answers my service. Now I wish you to be petitioned on behalf of my friend Benedictus, whom Fortune rather than guilt has deprived of military rank and honor: please smile upon the innocent man as his supporter, and do not allow him alone to be excluded from the public prosperity that has flowed equally to all.

For it is in the interest of the glory of these most serene times that, just as the breath of heaven and the light of day are common to all who live and are established in this life, so all people’s prayers and actions may feel the clemency of our most exalted emperor. Farewell.

## LETTER TWO. SYMMACHUS TO JAMBLICUS

Most people enjoy gathering precious things from every part of the world. I take pleasure in admitting men devoted to wisdom into the possession of friendship; and those who have experienced you have long testified that you are foremost among them. Above all, our intimate friend Eudoxius, approved by everyone and a careful judge of good men, has learned, after coming to know your virtues more closely, to praise others who strive equally toward honorable things, while attributing to them a desire for learning and for a virtuous life, but to you their perfection.

Thus, invited by the agreement of public reputation and by the testimony of the best witnesses, I extend to you the hand of my friendship. At the same time I hope that a letter brought from you may declare the harmony of your will and obtain the reciprocal devotion we owe one another. Farewell.

## LETTER THREE. SYMMACHUS TO ZENODORUS

Euscius’s commendation must be renewed with you, not begun. For when you were serving at Rome, summoned at my request to support him, you gladly accepted the role of benevolence. It is therefore time for you to assist my interests in the matter of Euscius, whose modesty will attend to our affairs in such a way that it detracts nothing from the reputation of the judge. Farewell.

## LETTER FOUR. SYMMACHUS TO DIONYSIUS

For a long time the reputation of both your character and your medical skill has commended you to me. Therefore, encouraged by praise in both respects, I extend the hand of my friendship and spontaneously invite you into the trust of our intimacy. You will have no small proof of my judgment in the fact that I have appointed you as instructor in the medical art for those whom we have sent to be educated.

[Col. 0328A]

Therefore repay me with a pledge of mutual good will, and accept for instruction in the practice of healing those whom, with Euscius presenting them to you, we entrust both to your loyalty and to your honor. Farewell.

## LETTER FIVE. SYMMACHUS TO AUXENTIUS

[Col. 0328B]

I add to the friendships begun between us when you were serving at Rome the service of writing, so that this pledge of duty offered to you in your absence may demonstrate the loyalty of my feelings. A reciprocal exchange of letters will privately testify to your devotion toward us, while publicly your care in the courts on behalf of Euscius will do so. Farewell.

## LETTER SIX. SYMMACHUS [NAME LOST]

Those who act for absent proprietors and to whom distant property is entrusted live as though released from the laws, since, being far away, they encounter no fear of their masters. Judicial severity is therefore needed to ensure that they pay what has been assigned to their leases.

I ask you, then, to deign to assist the recommendations of my notary, whom I have charged with presenting certain matters to the praetorian office and extracting what is owed from the liable slaves; and please do not refuse to take upon yourself the responsibility that corresponds to my concern. Farewell.

## LETTER SEVEN. SYMMACHUS TO CARTERIUS

On behalf of my son Auxentius, I have undertaken toward you the devotion of a father, the ambition of a suitor, and the trust of a witness. If the authority of such important matters carries any weight with you, I ask you to admit into your family a young man adorned with every virtue of character and every gift of Fortune.

I pledge myself to you as guarantor in all the matters that parental concern ordinarily weighs, although I know that future sons-in-law are judged by their character. Yet, in addition to the adornments of nature, this young man’s wealth also contributes to his honor. I could speak at greater length, but truth does not wish to be supported by words.

Therefore, if I do not seem to you an empty advocate, judge the man on the basis of my testimony, and deign to promise him marriage with your daughter—him whom I gladly number among my pledges. I would have you believe that, when the vows have advanced through my intervention, you, who are being asked, will possess no less gratitude than the man whom I am committing to you. Farewell.

## LETTER EIGHT. SYMMACHUS TO POMPEIANUS

You cannot accuse my silence of being prolonged, since you have learned that I have until now been in the sacred retinue. Having recently returned from it, I now perform the honor of sending my greeting. The reciprocity of our relationship will show that you have gladly received my page.

Meanwhile, I commend to you the bearer of this letter. It will benefit me if you show some favor to his petition. Farewell.

## LETTER NINE. SYMMACHUS TO VINCENTIUS

I approve of men who desire to belong to your patronage. For it is a kind of spark of wisdom to attach oneself to the lights of virtue. Therefore I do not delay commending the praiseworthy intention of my friend Zenodorus, and, like a guide into the mysteries, I introduce him into the sanctuary of your household.

Please ensure that both my devotion and his wish receive a prompt response in the form of success. Farewell.

## LETTER TEN. SYMMACHUS TO LEPORIUS

Wounded grievously by Fortune’s weapon, I now for the first time commit the words of a sorrowful letter to writing. I ought not to have abstained from my duty for long, since no length of time can erase the pain of so great a wound.

I therefore greet you, and at the same time readily commend to your care my very dear friend Sylvanus. He has undertaken the burdensome necessity of traveling in order to restore my patrimony, and he is all the more worthy of every good man’s support because we see no designation of persons expressed in any edicts. Yet officials and record-keepers are free to protect some people from expense while imposing an undue burden on others.

Please examine this matter with regard both to our interests and to your reputation. The officials responsible for the tax assessment are demanding from my men the levy of a recruit, producing no public documents whatever to support this. I therefore have a not unjust suspicion that, to excuse themselves or their associates, they have also subjected our men through a false registration.

It is therefore appropriate that a full instruction be made known to the provincials, either by edict or by your written order, lest the unrestricted and uncontrolled exaction of the record-keepers and city officials provide them with an opportunity for profit. Farewell.

## LETTER ELEVEN. SYMMACHUS TO MARCELLUS

Since your intervention can and ought to take the place of my presence, I am surprised that our affairs are so often burdened by the recommendations of Amazonius. Therefore perform, I beg you, the duties appropriate to friendship, so that, protected by your assistance, the property may both be rescued from harassment and provide us with some advantage.

Among the other matters that he reported, he earnestly begged that you separate Ursus, whom he says has long been subject to our household together with his family, from every public summons, so that he may more easily secure what has been granted [reading uncertain]. But a greater assistance will arise from the favor of your judgment, since his case is not lacking in justice.

For, as the facts have shown, he was ensnared by imprudent caution and ought not to suffer the penalty of rustic simplicity. Farewell.

## LETTER TWELVE. SYMMACHUS TO PERPETUUS

The ceremonial undertaking of my household calls for your assistance. Shortly, if divine favor supports our hopes, my son will perform the urban praetorship, for which the nobility of his chariot horses must be prepared.

If concern for absent friends has any influence with you, I ask that from all the herds with which Spain is endowed you carefully select horses distinguished by breed and speed. My friends, sent there for this purpose, will purchase them at a fair determination of price.

Your kindness will remain perpetually in my memory if you devote to this undertaking the care that mutual loyalty promises. Farewell.

## LETTER THIRTEEN. SYMMACHUS TO VALERINUS

I see that there is a contest of ingenuity between us in a matter that reason, friendship, and time ought to have erased. I therefore put an end to our mutual reproaches, lest the most bitter exchanges of letters continue without limit.

The gift of the entire Livian work that I promised is still delayed by the care required for its correction. But I ask you to send a carrier for the promised gift, since my praetorian preparations have scattered my people across distant places. Farewell.

## LETTER FOURTEEN. SYMMACHUS TO APOLLODORUS

You rightly assume that I share your cares, which, even without being reminded, I would claim as my own because of our friendship. A part of your concern is therefore to be diminished by the arrival of my daughter, whom Rome recently received and will send into your presence once she has refreshed herself by taking a rest along the way.

Meanwhile, the straits of the grain-storekeepers do not allow me to remain silent with you about the rapid transport of provisions for our common homeland. I therefore ask you to order the grain officials to be pressed with all the vigor of which you are capable. The security of Rome will add greatly to your glory. Farewell.

## LETTER FIFTEEN. SYMMACHUS TO GEMINIANUS

I preserve my customary practice and observe the devout regulations I have established toward my friends. Therefore, after first offering you the honor of a greeting, I ask for a reciprocal reply from you; and, if you remember my instructions, I urge you to deign to reassure me about the preparations for the praetorian office.

My concern increases day by day, since the performance draws near, and I am surprised that nothing has been delivered concerning the clothing and animals that my people were formerly supposed to purchase through you at your valuation and determination of price.

Because I am anxious about the delay, I have sent my notary, who, in obedience to your instructions and orders, is to accept all the things that must be transported and urge our agents to pay the prices you have established, lest they seem to have avoided your presence until now through lack of money.

Finally, perform the duties of loyalty, so that your example of diligence may rouse us to a reciprocal exchange of services. Farewell.

## LETTER SIXTEEN. SYMMACHUS TO SAPIDIANUS

Leontius, an agent in public affairs, approved by all good men both for the honor of his life and for his military experience, has also won my approval through his constant devotion. He is therefore rightly numbered among my friends and intimates.

I place him in your hands, asking you to imitate the example of my affection toward him—which I presume you will diligently do. Meanwhile, I cease sending frequent reminders about the animals to be prepared for the arrangements of the games, since by that promise you have relieved me of this concern.

Nevertheless, I have assigned Leontius the duty of reminding you. You will deign to lend him an ear if, when you yourself are handling public and more important matters, he brings this request to your attention in a private word. Farewell.

## LETTER SEVENTEEN. SYMMACHUS TO VENUSTUS

You have placed before my eyes the entire arrangement of my praetorian office and a kind of picture of the work of the craftsmen: the layout, so fully opened up, has marked out what is still rising and what has already been completed.

I shall therefore temporarily refrain from accusing my people of sluggishness, since they have stalled in the same constructions and the sweetness of your page is soothing me. Nevertheless, I want you to chastise the tardiness of our architect in your speech as he retraces the road to Capua, so that you may exercise my anger in my place and he may infer from your rebuke how much harm he must fear from my indignation if he does not attend to what has been entrusted to him. Farewell.

## LETTER EIGHTEEN. SYMMACHUS TO POMPEIA

A welcome opportunity has arisen for me to offer you the courtesy of a greeting. Since, on account of my son’s praetorship, we were sending our household members to Spain and had entrusted them with the purchase of chariot horses, it was fitting to show you the cultivation of a letter and at the same time add a request: deign to select the most distinguished horses from your herds, for our agents to purchase at a fair assessment.

I therefore ask that, if any memory of my household remains with you, you deign, with the greatest readiness and generosity, to grant a request easy for you to fulfill but pleasant and highly honorable for me. Farewell.

## LETTER NINETEEN. SYMMACHUS TO FABIANUS

A welcome cause brings me back into your friendship, although, on account of the distinction of your family and your character, I would have sought your intimacy in any case. My son’s praetorship, with Fortune’s help, must be equipped with chariot horses. Some time ago, through my people, [lacuna] the herds of your livestock [lacuna]

## LETTER TWENTY. SYMMACHUS TO BASSUS

After first offering the honor of a greeting, I append a necessary request. The performance of our son’s office is approaching, and the nobility of his chariot horses must be prepared. Therefore we have sent highly trustworthy men to Spain with ample funds, so that they may purchase noble teams after the most careful selection.

But because we fear that the intervention of winter may prevent the horses from being transported, I ask you, if necessity requires it, to order that fodder be supplied to them on your property for three or four winter months, according to their number, so that they may arrive without hardship when mild weather begins.

Moreover, I ask you to arrange assistance for my men in purchasing horses, if their search should discover any distinguished at Arles in speed and breed. The opportunity for a nearby purchase must be embraced if chance offers something exceptional.

The memory of your kindness will remain permanently with me if, as I hope, brotherly care benefits our ceremonial performance. Farewell.

## LETTER TWENTY-ONE. SYMMACHUS TO THE VICARIUS OF SPAIN

We are being pressed by senatorial performances, whose requirements call for the purchase of chariot horses. For this reason I have sent my closest associates to Spain, so that they may purchase teams from the nobility of every herd.

To carry out these instructions I ask for your support, and I declare that I shall be bound to you by the greatest favor if your authority advances a matter easy for you to accomplish. Farewell.

## LETTER TWENTY-TWO. SYMMACHUS TO AURELIUS

I believe you have learned that our household is preparing for the games that, with God’s help, my son’s praetorship requires. I am therefore about to send some of my people to Spain to purchase chariot teams from the nobility of every herd.

Even now I appeal to your care on behalf of those passing through, so that both speed of passage and the provision of travel permits may be granted them. For the present I have given you this preliminary indication as circumstances permit. But you will provide more, either through arrangements made by your own diligence or through information learned from their recommendations. Farewell.

## LETTER TWENTY-THREE. SYMMACHUS TO MARCELLUS

Another of my letters seeks you throughout Spain. For, because of the extent of your household affairs, I had assumed that you were living there. Once greater certainty informed me that you were enjoying leisure in your ancestral home, I thanked the error that had enabled me to address you again.

Yet this repetition, although it ought to satisfy your feelings, is not sufficient for mine. I would wish to honor our friendship continually through your letters, just as I have never concealed that I cherish it constantly in my mind.

I append a request. My son’s praetorian performance, with Fortune’s help, has long been commended to your understanding and is now approaching. It prompts me to ask you to bring noble teams into the contest, selecting the best from many herds.

My confidence should not be harmed by the fact that you have exchanged Spain for a distant residence, though I have called upon you to assist in the purchase of horses. Help us only by letter. I hope that the delegation of this care to you will be effective for us with your friends. Farewell.

## LETTER TWENTY-FOUR. SYMMACHUS TO BASSUS

I derive great pleasure whenever I receive the gift of your conversation. For your letters are a sign both of health and of affection. I am also delighted that you promise to be here shortly.

So that you may hasten your return all the more, I announce that my son will assume the praetorian fasces at the beginning of the year, if divine favor smiles upon us. I have written to you more fully about this matter through my associates, to whom we entrusted the purchase of Spanish horses.

But since the opportunity advises it, I now renew my request as well. If bad winter weather should delay their return, I ask you to order that they be kept in your estates for a few months and then depart from there to us at the beginning of spring.

Meanwhile, concern for your men has been removed: both my presence and my judicial protection defend them. I have warned the man bringing the lawsuit that the matter concerns me and that they will not lack the assistance of my action. I have no doubt that your distinguished men have also reported this to you. Farewell.

## LETTER TWENTY-FIVE. SYMMACHUS TO VINCENTIUS

I perform my duty whenever I honor you with the courtesy of a greeting. Nor do I conceal my thanks that the return of your letters frequently repays me in turn. But this should not be prolonged, since the claims of good friendship reject self-display.

Now I wish to obtain this from you: deign to assist by letter and by an official order the care of my men, whom I have instructed to purchase chariot teams from Spain for the preparations of the praetorian performance.

I also ask you to confirm by letter the travel permits that the illustrious Theodorus issued for the draught horses, so that, when the judge has changed, the authority of this favor may not lapse. I would seek your favor concerning these matters with excessive entreaty, but simplicity is more effective with modest ears, and modesty more readily grants what is requested with confidence.

Nevertheless, I would have you understand that, although I am sparing now in asking, I shall be abundant in giving thanks after my request has been granted. Farewell.

## LETTER TWENTY-SIX. SYMMACHUS TO VALERIUS

It pleases me that you often blame me for negligence in writing to you. For it is a sign of your affection that you desire in return what you offer. And yet your intention of concealing [lacuna] had promised.

I confess that I was saddened by the boast of a fruitless favor—something neither fitting for you nor expected by me. Therefore, lest an ingenuous modesty write back something similar, I preferred to suppress our mutual pain. For among absent friends, the alternating contest of letters often advances toward hatred.

Now I return to the practice of simple writing, more grateful for your good will than guilty of misfortune. I ask you to stop considering my friendship, which has imposed no burden upon you, harmful. Farewell.

## LETTER TWENTY-SEVEN. SYMMACHUS TO ALEXANDER

You cannot justly blame my silence toward you if you consider your own. Indeed, perhaps you have more reason to feel shame in this matter, since, while often sending letters to Rome on business, you have passed over the duties of friendship toward us.

My men, however, were compelled to pass through Aquileia solely because of the purchase of wild animals. The forgetfulness of a single opportunity does not deserve as much resentment as the contempt for me displayed by your people during their constant journeys has brought upon you in the form of ill repute.

But let forgiveness be granted to both of us, although our negligence is unequal. Hereafter, restore the duty you omitted yourself, and provide us through the same people with an opportunity to send replies. For it is difficult for me to investigate those departing from here. The service of my pen will again cease unless your associates undertake to return our letters to you. Farewell.

## LETTER TWENTY-EIGHT. SYMMACHUS TO MAXIMUS

I never supposed that you would pursue wild animals in hunting and spend the winter months exploring the icy slopes of the Apennines, judging by your health; for you seemed more friendly to letters than to exertions.

One of these two activities, long unknown to me in your case, was revealed by your woodland gift; the other, almost believed already, was confirmed by the cultivation of your pages. Therefore you will be numbered among the companions of Apollo and Diana, a follower of both, although, as your writings testify, you are more pleased by the glory of the hunting art.

When you described wandering through snowy valleys, you danced verbally beyond the proper restraint of a letter—clearly delighted by the difficulty and still warmed by the outcome of your mountain labor. Meanwhile, it would have been enough to send the spoils of the Apennines. The additional details concerning your heart might have become tiresome, had affection for you not removed satiety. Farewell.

## LETTER TWENTY-NINE. SYMMACHUS TO VARUS

While you are relieving the hardships of the provincials and extending a helping hand to those in distress, a more serious calamity has overtaken Apulia. On the basis of an empty reputation for fertility, grain is being demanded from it—grain that must be taken away from the province and will not be useful to the state.

For when the year is already turning toward winter, how can such great crops be ripened? If, therefore, you have the opportunity to advance quickly on your journey toward Campania, let me know, so that I may wait for you briefly. Or, if a more important reason changes your promise, immediately disclose that fact to me, so that our Symmachus, who has spent a long time relaxing on the shores of Formiae, may quickly return with me to our studies. Farewell.

## LETTER THIRTY. SYMMACHUS TO LEO

I do indeed wish you to abound so greatly in the resources of your household wealth that you can purchase rich estates. But I would rather that you direct your eye and your desire toward new purchases without harming or injuring your friends.

For I purchased the Postumian estate in the most legitimate manner from its oldest possessor, without any mention of your partnership. Now, for the first time, at your urging, I am being asked to withdraw from a possession that has almost grown old in my keeping.

Its price is not so moderate that purchasing it would be a pleasure. Therefore, although I could oppose you by law and resist the desire of the person whose affairs are at issue, I nevertheless make it possible for you to pay to my man Euscius, who knows the full amount, the silver that we gave the seller—if, indeed, you prefer to purchase our property rather than release your own from the bond of obligation. Farewell.

## LETTER THIRTY-ONE. SYMMACHUS TO CARTERIUS

What ought to have been defended on behalf of your father-in-law, whose complaint wounded you, you appropriately fulfilled by turning against Epictetus. He is excluded from the courts and has paid the price for his ill-considered tongue. And, if you believe me, he has been corrected by a retaliation proportionate to his insult.

Now, considering your character and disposition, turn your will toward merciful forgiveness. You know the often-unforeseen slips of advocates; and when you adorned the tribunals, first as a defender and later as an examiner of disputes, you usually resisted the errors of such advocacy.

But since some people whose crimes are secure have gained prominence through the silence of my friend Epictetus, I ask you not to allow an unfortunate man rather than an innocent one to be mocked for long. Our distinguished common brother will do whatever he learns that you wish. He will also be ready to restore to him the privilege of pleading, if he receives an indication of your will.

[Col. 0335A]

Only apply a kindly mind to my letters; and, as a friend of the toga, in whose praise you have shone above others, remove the stain from the honorable order and, when asked, forgive a man who was insufficiently cautious. Farewell.

## LETTER THIRTY-TWO. SYMMACHUS TO JANUARIUS

Formerly, when I presided over the tribunals, you used to commend young men of the forum to my judgments. Now, with the roles reversed, I have undertaken this duty and introduce candidates for advocacy to your instruction.

In this matter you must follow my example, so that with the same devotion with which I frequently admitted those presented by you, you may receive those whom I produce as their advocate. Farewell.

## LETTER THIRTY-THREE

I love followers of literature—not because I have any kinship with such pursuits, but because the profession of the liberal arts, like beauty situated even in another body, gives pleasure.

It was therefore appropriate that I should follow Valentinianus, whom I came to know at our first meeting, with the service of my pages, so that my speech might open the first door to him with you, while his life and learning might win him a fuller friendship. Farewell.

## LETTER THIRTY-FOUR

The care shown to the children of friends is a devout duty, especially when intimacy bestowed upon their elders is increased by the merits of their descendants.

The preceding statement applies directly to this matter. For I did not esteem Lampadius, a most illustrious man, solely for his own sake—as is the fleeting and fragile affection of many—but rather contemplate with extended love those born from him and relying upon their father’s good qualities.

[Col. 0335C]

I place them in your hands to be defended from every injustice. I ask that, if circumstances require it, you carry out my role as a just arbiter. Obtaining this favor will greatly advance your praise and my gratitude. Farewell.

## LETTER THIRTY-FIVE. SYMMACHUS [NAME LOST]

Through hesitation in writing, we have lost many reciprocal services between us. I shall not allow our shared fault to be prolonged. Therefore I take upon myself the first duties of this devout service; and, even if you delay returning my words, I shall not change my intention.

The interval before your reply will be a matter for your deliberation. Only remember that a swift return of gratitude displays goodwill, while a late one displays necessity. I think I have said enough about restoring the exchange of letters.

Moreover, your speech owes the bearer, Probus, some benefit. He is my intimate friend and worthy of your patronage. If you look upon him with a kindly expression, he will rejoice that his fortunes have grown. Farewell.

## LETTER THIRTY-SIX. SYMMACHUS [NAME LOST]

Even if you remain silent and pretend not to answer my greeting, you will never drive me away from my devout duty. At some point I shall forge a way to make you abandon this obstinacy.

Meanwhile, though your confidence in me has not yet been restored, I boldly undertake this service. I wish to commend to you the bearer of this letter: a young man of exacting seriousness, long approved by me through honorable proofs, and not unknown—if I judge correctly—to your judgment. Secure in his life and in his long military service, he has never avoided the scrutiny of his superiors.

[Col. 0336A]

But even if you know the man only moderately well, it is not right, if you attach any value to our friendship, that after my testimony he should approach you as though he were a new friend. Farewell.

## LETTER THIRTY-SEVEN. SYMMACHUS [NAME LOST]

I remain anxious in spirit until I receive news of your health. For, while your strength was still weak, you added the burden of a journey, and I cannot be satisfied with the reports of travelers about this, since deeper affection treats the uncertainties of rumor as falsehood.

I therefore long for letters whose reliability may bring me certain reassurance about you. If you wish to know anything about my own actions, you will learn it from the bearer of this letter. He is very close to us because of the integrity of his life and, with me as his witness, worthy to be carefully admitted among the cultivated members of your household. Farewell.

## LETTER THIRTY-EIGHT. SYMMACHUS [NAME LOST]

Antistianus, a man of our order, pleased me long ago by the uprightness of his life and was dear to me for his honorable services. The character of his present request shows that I make this assertion from truth rather than to gain his favor.

For, after serving for a long time in the defense of his homeland, he desires only to reach the safe harbor of private tranquility. This would make him worthy of your support even if my words did not intervene. In accordance with your virtue, you are accustomed to love those who desire leisure and do not know how to canvass for favor.

Therefore, asked and entreated by my letters, deign to grant the desired rest to one who longs to enjoy it. A replacement will not be lacking, since your choice can easily select from the many leading men a man equal in loyalty and diligence. Farewell.

## LETTER THIRTY-NINE. SYMMACHUS [NAME LOST]

My brother Nicias, who must be numbered among the foremost philosophers, has awakened in me a desire for your friendship, after informing me by letter that you have promised your daughter to him in a faithful agreement.

This is evidence that sound judgment resides in you, and therefore that all good men ought spontaneously to seek your intimacy. For such a choice declares a worthy mind.

I therefore spur your excellent intention and urge you, with the help of the gods, to acquire as soon as possible a most praiseworthy son-in-law. His addition to your family will both win you the favor of many and add the distinction of an alliance. Farewell.

## LETTER FORTY

[Col. 0336D]

The principle of justice must always be taken seriously. But in the case of noble and reputable persons there ought to be greater moderation, so that judgment may be recognized in the exercise of discretion.

I say this by way of introduction in order to commend my intervention through its general character. The nature of the request is as follows.

The fields of my sister Italica, an illustrious woman, have been deprived of cultivators and exhausted by the burden of public obligations; they must be restored through judicial authority. I promised her this assistance on the basis of the fairness of your character. For one may confidently presume good intentions in good men.

Therefore, if you value me, fulfill the pledge I have made, and readily grant whatever is suitable to the affairs and interests of the absent matron, charging to my gratitude whatever favor you devote to her. Farewell.

## LETTER FORTY-ONE

[Col. 0337A]

I ought not to have remained silent while one who is yours was traveling, since the relationship that will arise between you persuades me that equal care should be shown by me to both of you.

Therefore I send you a greeting in writing, and I urge you to make the most devoted Ticianus, who is also my very dear friend, as soon as possible the recipient of the connection already proposed. Farewell.

## LETTER FORTY-TWO

The fruit of labor is to please the better sort and to earn the palm of approval through diligence and integrity. Therefore my son, Benignus, a most illustrious man, having carried out the administration of the grain supply with vigilant attention and clean hands, expects from you only the reward of just affection.

The weakness of his body bears witness to his sleepless cares. For he brought back from Sardinia nothing except a good conscience and poor health; and he imported into the granaries only as much grain as the year’s fortune had granted that province.

No adverse rumor has arisen against him, no complaint; his actions are always ready to be examined. The richest reward for all this would be for him to be considered worthy of your friendship.

This seems to me an easy request to obtain, since you must take pleasure in the integrity of those whose selection did not deceive you. Farewell.

## LETTER FORTY-THREE

The question that recalls the fulfillment of agreements is one of devotion rather than envy. Therefore I do not wish you to think that it was reported to me as a fault that you are delaying, through hesitation, the marriage you promised between your daughter and my very dear friend Herculius.

But he wished me to join the others whom he knows to have been either assistants or witnesses in obtaining the marriage from you, so that the vows long held in suspense might be hastened by the intervention of a new advocate.

I therefore ask that the stability of your promises remain firm, and that a change of intention not disfigure senatorial good faith. Let my additional petition on his behalf also benefit the agreement that has been made. You will not deny it without insult, since you ought readily to grant us even what has not been requested.

Certainly, his modesty and his dignity in the Roman forum are such that, to the extent that you have granted him favor, you will receive an equal measure of distinction from your son-in-law. I would pursue his abundant praises and the adornments of his life if you seemed to be admitting an unknown man. But since the condition already accepted clearly proves to you that his qualities are good, I ought not to prolong the praise of one whom the pledge of the agreement you have undertaken indicates to be already approved by you. Farewell.

## LETTER FORTY-FOUR. SYMMACHUS [NAME LOST]

Disarius, a professor of medicine, had followed your father, a man of holy memory and distinction, into Gaul in the hope of greater advantage. And because he had resolved to attach himself to him, he sent some of his property on ahead to Aquitania. Now, deprived of so great a man by his death, contrary to the wishes of everyone, he desires to return to his own people, as his parent testifies. Please assist the young man’s pious wish; and order that the things which, in keeping with your innate character, you have diligently promised to return to him be sent back without delay, lest, in addition to the wound of lost hope, the injury of prolonged exile be inflicted upon him. Farewell.

## EPIST. XLV. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

[Col. 0338A]

Your letter reached me while I was relaxing on the Campanian shores. I imagine you have learned by report or reading how great is the beauty of this region. Your letter surpassed the pleasures set before me. Rejecting, therefore, everything else that the charm of the place offered, I devoted my whole mind to rereading the page until I knew it by heart. Would that you had dictated more. Yet for me, what was often repeated amounted to many things. Henceforth, be more sparing in bringing forth what arises from the abundance of your talent, lest your voluntary frugality force even me, whose style is poor, into narrow limits. For the rest, we again place Aurelius in your hands—not because the earlier recommendation was ineffective, but so that repetition may also attest both his merit and our concern for him. [Col. 0338B] Farewell.

## EPIST. XLVI. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

Whoever asks us for a letter of recommendation renders a favor which he thinks he is receiving. For the cultivation of friendship is older in my estimation than their obtaining protection. Repay, therefore, the reward of this ready service to the man who brings you the letter, and honor him according to the modesty of his circumstances. It is within your power to dignify me also with the honor of reciprocal service. For I do not conduct an interest-bearing business in words, so as to summon you to repay a debt. It would be serious to subject you to the laws of obligation, when you have often surpassed me in voluntary services. Farewell.

## EPIST. XLVII. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

[Col. 0338C]

I do not doubt that you take care of good men. For your character must rejoice in the companionship of similar virtues. If, therefore, you grant me anything, I ask you to embrace the friendship of my master and son Flavianus, whom I recommend not only with a parent’s fidelity but also as a witness. You will find in him a mind worthy of your affection and of better fortune, although the greatness of a sacred benefaction has come to meet his misfortunes and a summons has been added to complete the act of kindness. Therefore it is only right that your familiarity should not abandon one whom imperial support has favored. Farewell.

## EPIST. XLVIII. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

To the children of our friends we ought to transfer our care, lest our loyalty seem to have died with the man. The memory of Petronius, therefore, a former consul whose home was near Ariminum, requires me to defend his sons with inherited affection. Their house has been decreed for military lodging; and unless public authority comes to their aid, they will suffer utter ruin. If you attach any value to my intervention, order by threatening letters to the magistrates and councils of Ariminum that the lodgers be kept away from it and that the ancient security of the little boys’ household be restored. Those who are abandoned by their parents are ordered to be under the protection of the judge. Farewell.

## EPIST. XLIX. SYMMACHUS TO JUSTUS

Severus, an honorable man, has enlisted me as an assistant in his hope and desire. Since I judged his request worthy, I could not refuse the letter he sought. The substance of his request is this: that you promise the marriage of your daughter to his son. He assures me that obtaining this will be easy because the parties are evenly matched, and that you are compatible both in honor and in means. I therefore await a response from you declaring that my testimony has had influence with you . . . . Farewell.

## EPIST. L. SYMMACHUS TO CAECILIANUS

You certainly know, together with my most distinguished friends, how much Lucillus, once a painter, added to the adornment of my house. His son, placed far away by nature and necessity, is now being unjustly harassed, since a dispute has arisen between a certain Numerarius and Opinator, formerly the tenant of the aforesaid proprietor, who is turning the accounts of earlier periods into losses for Lucillus. I ask for what is just, not for a favor; although, through my intervention, an addition of goodwill and zeal is also owed. First and foremost, I ask that the house of this most prudent man, who lives far away in the service of public offices and councils, be kept secure. Next, if there is any dispute between them, let it be settled by your examination, lest, when the matter is reserved for another judge, a renewed injury arise for Lucillus’ son. Farewell.

## EPIST. LI. SYMMACHUS TO APOLLODORIUS

Quintus and Felix, municipal councilors of Hippo, obtained this letter from me through the intervention of distinguished men. For I was bound to judge the men’s integrity by their witnesses. It therefore concerns friendship that the hopes of those who believed me powerful enough to obtain their request should not appear to have been deceived. Accordingly, if their advantage requires anything, add kindness to justice. I believe they will ask for such things as would disgrace neither the request of the intermediary nor the judgment of the one who grants it. Farewell.

## EPIST. LII. SYMMACHUS TO MAXIMILIANUS

I inform you that I am well, and I wish that favorable circumstances attend you. After this, I ask you to do, out of spontaneous kindness, what you would have done anyway: send the lessee of my Sicilian property, as he returns to the province, swiftly on his way to his destination.

## EPIST. LIII. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

There can be no weariness with constant writing. I therefore perform my duty by sending greetings, and at the same time I urge and entreat you not to disdain caring for my men. They should receive not only confidence, if circumstances require them to offer advice, but also the necessary summons. For such is the nature of slaves: they refuse to approach those who would benefit them while they fear that their own fault will be discovered. Farewell.

## EPIST. LIV. SYMMACHUS TO POEMENIUS

The losses inflicted by fortune must be kept silent, lest a late consolation tear open the scar of past grief. I would therefore more rightly discuss with you the highly distinguished character—or rather the fruitful harvest of praises—of our son Nemesius. You have a man worthy of being counted among those blessed with a numerous offspring; I return him to you in person, which I would have wished to do in both ways. [Col. 0340A] You will judge, from the refinement of his character and learning, how much the delay of his studies might have added to him, had our fear not taken account of his father’s longing. Farewell.

## EPIST. LV. SYMMACHUS TO EUSEBIUS

I would pursue at length the merits of our mutual friend Eusebius, were you not already more aware than I of his integrity and military service. Now, anxious about his position, after learning that it had been called into question, he hastened to support his claims by reading a public document, not by verbal assertion. In this matter you are ordered by us to be both a supporter of the litigant and a witness to his claims. Your friendship has promised us the former, and your loyalty guarantees the latter. For you remember that he was transferred some time ago to the school of the Gallic palace. We believe that you kept silent about this in his absence so that the suggestion might not be thought to arise from favor. Now you will support the truth with greater confidence, once you have heard the claims of the man who is present. Farewell.

## EPIST. LVI. SYMMACHUS TO GEMINANUS

When Felix said that he was a cultivator of your household and asked, through friends acting as intermediaries, for the favor of my recommendation, I did not deny him a familiar letter, in which I take first place by sending you greetings. Next, I pursue the request already received, which, if the aforesaid man is not yet known to you, should grant him access to your patronage, and, if he is already known, increase it. Farewell.

## EPIST. LVII. SYMMACHUS TO QUINTILIANUS

[Col. 0340C]

It is my custom to support those whom I know and approve well, and to consider not the persons of men but the merits of their lives. Since, therefore, our domestic Assellus has completed his years of military service in the urban camps without reproach, I ask that, admitted to your patronage, he may rejoice that my protection has benefited him and that yours has been added to it. Farewell.

## EPIST. LVIII. SYMMACHUS TO CAECILIANUS

I do not refuse to intervene on behalf of just obligations. For it is malicious to reject an opportunity for favor in matters whose equity, by its very nature, commends the request. Antiquity decreed for the people of Formiae, as a relief from poverty, a fixed quantity of oil from Africa. They ask you to maintain a custom preserved through long ages; to it the kindness of the one who grants it should add speed. Farewell.

## EPIST. LIX. SYMMACHUS TO JOVIUS

As a ready recommender, I introduce my friend Eusebius—not as someone new or unknown, but as one already proven by loyalty and long military service. No fault in his conduct has darkened him to this time; rather, his absence, which conceals the merits of many when they lack the testimony of those present, is said to have brought his position into an uncertain condition of fortune. Yet I hope that the singular fairness of your mind will not allow misfortune to prevail against the precedence of his years of service. My exhortation, therefore, and his own confidence alike look to your judgment. I ask that, once you have examined the case, you confirm the justice of his earlier service, providing both us, his friends, with security and his colleagues with the honorable companionship of retaining an excellent man. Farewell.

## EPIST. LX. SYMMACHUS TO PROBINUS

To all who provide an occasion for writing, I return a certain reward in the form of a recommendation. Now I wish this to be done for the excellent Petrucius, whom I know asked for this letter not so much for his own recommendation as out of regard for my service; I thought his assistance should be repaid in turn. He requested a letter so that I might commend him to you more earnestly. I, on the contrary, confess that I wrote for the reason that he might become more acceptable to you. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXI. SYMMACHUS TO PACATUS

[Col. 0341B]

I can scarcely be persuaded to believe that my letters, repeated so often, have brought Leontius no relief. For if our frequent intervention had possessed no force, my support, so often disappointed, would have ceased to hope. Since, then, I doubt the truth of this complaint, I wish to discover to which side my doubt should most properly be directed. It is therefore in your hands whether I should henceforth continue my custom of writing, or whether, even by continued silence, I should take care of our modesty. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXII. SYMMACHUS TO ROMULUS

You commend your common pledge with paternal affection. But a life worthy of approval wins the goodwill and affection of good men more effectively for him. You have a young man whose flourishing qualities should bring you joy, although I know that fathers are miserly in their wishes and consider no good in their children complete when compared with their greater longing and desire. Perhaps you think your spirit should be made glad by a sweet report rather than by a trustworthy one. But when divine favor has granted you his return, you will recognize in his merits the truth of my testimony. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXIII. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

An old custom has established the practice that those who have left home should give the first signal of reciprocal correspondence. But, impatient of a long wait, I could not observe the order. I therefore offer you the honor of my style first. Next I append my request, whose form is this: that you not fail to assist Laurentianus, our domestic servant, with your support, since the usefulness of my household requires it. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXIV. SYMMACHUS TO PACATUS

You ought to have encouraged me. But I am now reluctant to prolong this complaint. I therefore turn my speech to the recommendation of my most devoted friend Olympius, and I earnestly ask you to admit him confidently into the inner chambers of your friendship, on the strength of my testimony. You will find in him the virtues of character which the circumspection of your judgment is accustomed to choose. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXV. SYMMACHUS TO ALLEVIUS

The line I have sent will testify what the dimensions of the wheels of the vehicle should be. It remains for the entire cart to be constructed skillfully and with strong joints. If part of the price is needed for this work, I will order whatever sum you write should be paid. The kindness of your gifts should be more moderate. Religious devotion is measured by the spirit rather than by presents. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXVI. SYMMACHUS TO SAECULARIS

The prices of the abandoned properties are being demanded in confused disorder. For neither the judgments [lacuna] will you establish a certain measure of future labor: the most exalted prefecture firmly and definitively holds that there is no merit of his such as ought to be substituted for your high office.

## EPIST. LXVII. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

[Col. 0342B]

I rejoice both in the tranquility of the province and in the praise of your vigor. I claim nothing for my own instruction, since everything that pertains to glory is owed rather to your character. Go forward, then, under the auspices of your first honor, and direct your happy efforts toward more abundant glory, so that you may open for yourself the door to higher ranks and illuminate the Roman name by the distinction of your administration. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXVIII. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

I am accustomed to seek the friendship of the best before all others. Now the decline of my fortune has caused me to be anticipated. The slowness must therefore be forgiven—not negligence, but my grief—and our familiarity, which you have auspiciously initiated, should be joined under a favorable sign. Although you have surpassed me in the order and distinction of service, you will nevertheless not judge me inactive in the future, so that the union of our hearts, which began at your invitation, may be strengthened by frequent letters from me. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXIX. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

I would rather obtain your return than your letters. Yet consolations also have their place whenever we are deprived of what we desire. I fear, however, that you are prolonging your absence from the city for too long. For your elaborate defense of your delay threatens this to us. I therefore wish you to know that no explanations of delay seem justified to those who long for you. Whatever excuse you yourself bring will, as they say, be poured into deaf ears. For the moment I send this from the fourth milestone of the Latin Way, soon to seek the Laurentian estate. It is characteristic of mourners to dispel the cares of the mind by changing place. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXX. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

I would have accused you of silence, had I not seen you in your brother. He alone displayed to me both the satisfaction of service and an image of your presence. For I recognized in him all the good qualities which I formerly approved in you. I therefore love the vein of your family. Even those among them whom we have not yet come to know already seem praiseworthy to us by the distinction of their excellent stock. What remains for me now is that customary demand for letters. I do not think it should be wholly omitted, lest you take less care of what you suppose is not missed; nor should it be pressed too strongly, lest continual remonstrance deprive your spontaneous service of its grace. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXXI. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

Although I was about to retrace my journey and immediately take my equal with me into the countryside, I would not allow even this brief interval to be empty of letters. First, so that by an exchange of conversation I might match the service of your writing. Next, so that I might be understood to repay, with a return of gratitude, the friendship I had sought. Finally, so that, by announcing my arrival, I might obtain from you a little time to remain, if you had soon intended to leave. For these reasons, I sent the letter ahead like an advance guard, while I myself was coming. But the chief reason for my not remaining silent was that you had first expressed the wish to establish our friendship. It was therefore my duty to take care lest, by concealing my response, I incur the blame of disdain. Indeed, I would always prefer friendships to be begun through my own efforts; so far am I from receiving with reluctance or negligence the gift of offered devotion. I therefore thank you for your goodwill, and I will take care by my services that you understand that I could have been anticipated in the order of writing, but not in earnestness of feeling. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXXII. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

As history tells us, Alexander was stung by bitter envy because fortune had granted the bravest Achilles of his age Homer as his herald. But my spirit swells with joy because you have adorned the favorable outcomes of the state with equally fitting language. As a result, even to our eyes, though we live far away, some image of your achievements was presented. I congratulate, therefore, your fortune, which has placed you as a spectator of favorable events, and your eloquence, which has answered the magnitude of such affairs with the dignity of its expression. May the heavenly will ensure that the well-stocked storehouse of your tongue never lacks material for such reports. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXXIII. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

Before receiving your letter, I was anxiously concerned whether you had reached your destination after completing your journey safely. But when I learned that the labor of the journey had diminished nothing of your health, my spirit returned to itself. Divine favor will ensure that, just as we learned of your absence with longing, so we may rejoice at your return. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXXIV. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

[Col. 0343D]

You promise your friendly assistance to our publications. I understand that the effect of your goodwill could have answered my letters, had the prosperity of the province prolonged the period of your office. But although, having laid aside the reins of the state, you cannot set a date for fulfilling your promise, I nevertheless confess that you have bound me to you by gratitude as though you had fulfilled my hopes. For a mind is bound by the wish of one who favors it, not by the outcome of the matter. Meanwhile I overflow with joy that your reputation flourishes in every respect and that I share in the praise you have earned. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXXV. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

You have blessed our senate-house and the Roman Forum, from which Sicily had feared to draw its magistrates because of memories of earlier times. Come, then, to us, where you are awaited, and to them, where you are desired. And I presume you should regard it as something to your credit if the province has benefited from the imitation of what came before. For the one who leaves an example is the author of the good things that follow. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXXVI. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

I silently complained to myself about your silence, but your recent conversation has soothed my friendly irritation. Let us therefore return to our old practice and cultivate our mutual diligence with devoted greetings. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXXVII. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

Your writings give me the greatest pleasure. But if you had wished to remain a little longer in Rome, your presence would have brought us much more than your gracious conversation. Nevertheless, I bear with equanimity the fact that you preferred love of your homeland to our longing. And I hope that, for the sake of seeing your son, who is now being educated in the liberal studies, you will more often grant me the opportunity to see you. Meanwhile, while we are apart, you must make writing a frequent practice, so that my style too may be challenged to reciprocate. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXXVIII. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

I imagine you are surprised that, while the wound inflicted by my fortune is still raw, I have broken my silence. These are my consolations; on these I feed and am refreshed, although I consider greater those which are returned to me from your heart and speech. But I do not want you to demand longer letters from me for the time being. The truces granted by grief are brief, and the evils that have been concealed for a little while soon return to wretched thoughts. Let your speech, therefore, overflow instead; it will preserve for you the praise of a friendship maintained and bring me consolation in my present distress. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXXIX. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

Would that a better cause had detained you; we would then easily endure the losses caused by your absence. Nevertheless, you have mitigated my longing with the consolation of letters. You will be so kind as to send them frequently if some domestic necessity has still imposed a delay upon you. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXXX. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

[Col. 0344D]

I rejoice both in the affection of your holy spirit and in the constancy of your conversation. I do not even consider it a lesser benefit that you grant me suitable opportunities for writing to you. For I hope that my pages can be returned to you by those whom your judgment selects as bearers of this service. Indeed, whatever you deem it appropriate to entrust to me for the sake of our mutual friendship, I willingly undertake to carry out whenever those whom you support with a recommendation require my assistance. But if anything is accomplished too carelessly or too late, it ought to be attributed to the neglect of those who fail in the duty of reminding. For the things you yourself usually delegate are so just and honorable that the execution of worthy letters ought to be desirable to me in either respect. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXXXI. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

[Col. 0345A]

I confess that I had long desired your letters, and their arrival fully satisfied my expectation. But my chief joy was that you announced you were acting according to your wish. Next came the pledge you gave of your arrival. And since I presume that you rejoice in reciprocal news about me, I inform you that, after the immense dangers which I alone endured amid the disturbance of our common homeland, I have returned to a favorable condition. It remains for the joy we hope for to complete our prosperity—something you promised me would happen with your return. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXXXII. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

I would gladly honor your fruits in writing if I were able. Now, beset by pains throughout all my limbs, I leave aside the praise of your woods. Your frequent kindness will ensure that on many other occasions we celebrate the good things of the Phaeacians transferred to the Marsi. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXXXIII. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

I was relaxing in the countryside with my parents, to shut out the heat of the torrid summer with the coolness of my lodging at Praeneste. Your letters found me there, and at first I received them happily, expecting a more favorable report. For until that moment you had brightened me with no gift of conversation.
