But when I carefully reviewed all the troubles you had endured through the agency of the Po, I accused your native river, whose turbulent channels and treacherous current you had experienced; I credited the gods, and Good Fortune, with the grace of your preservation. Therefore I was pleased by the service of the conversation you had finally supplied, whose long interruption I could have reproached amid your favorable circumstances. It happened, by the devotion that was owed, that I learned of your deliverance before I learned of your danger. Therefore this care will remain with the gods who protect you: that they may continually linger over you with their benefactions and grant you, in return for your merits, a long span of life, so that old age may diminish none of your strength. Meanwhile, since a welcome retreat and sweet repose embrace you, please take up the care of speaking with us more often. You will add somewhat to the restoration of your body if you lighten your solitude either by sending letters or by receiving them in return. Certainly nothing will be more important to us than reading you, since for the present we cannot hear the charms of your speech. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXXXIV. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

As our comic poet says, “I never meet you without departing from you more learned”; I may rightly say the same of your letters, which are sometimes enriched with many witty sayings, and more often with verses. Thus your letters now, breathing Platonic nectar, have given me what a great gift! For unless you had found me tested in the liberal arts, you would never have thought me worthy of being entrusted to the Attic Muses. Therefore frequently gird yourself for work of this kind, and diligently persevere in the care of friendship, since the exchange of our services commends this task to you. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXXXV. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

[Col. 0346A]

It is a sign of friendly goodwill that, after obtaining the highest consulship, you granted me knowledge and participation in so great a joy. Therefore the rich praise of this gift is yours in my eyes, since you are so confident of my feelings that you know we can rejoice in your prosperity. Moreover, was it not also a consular duty to spread more widely the news of his honor? Joys enjoyed by few are narrow. You also made the benefaction of the eternal ruler more celebrated and more splendid, since, on the occasion of such a letter, you appeared to give thanks to him before many people for the gracious manner in which services are regarded. Make sure that you continue this gratitude by writing frequently. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXXXVI. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

[Col. 0346B]

You have made me the recipient of the welcome news. For I confess that this is the nature of true friendship: that we rejoice mutually in our advantages. I therefore congratulate you both on account of our friendship and on the reputation of the age, which the fairness of a recent judgment has vindicated for eternal glory. You fulfilled the duty of an excellent citizen, with much effort and unremitting anxiety. But I do not want you to regret it. Virtue shines in more difficult affairs, disdains an easy downward path, and strives toward the steep height of praise with the greatest exertion. Add to this that you are prominent with the bravest ruler and enjoy the public good without satiety; this not only compensates for your labor but also commends it. And what of the fact that, in a case where you struggled uncertainly against the power of fortune, you owe none of us any thanks for your victory? I would say more, but I seem to have said enough for the present. Now, if you have the opportunity, I would rather that you return at once. If anything delays you, please reply. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXXXVII. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

You have the highest praise and solid gratitude from me, since by cultivating friendship you seek to honor us with your letters. But the part of your letter that assigned me praise for eloquence, however pleasing it may be, is nevertheless less than true. I do not dare to write, “You lie and deceive when you praise me in this way,” but rather, “I know that love has deceived you.” You, a man of the highest rank in speaking, whose speech possesses patrician dignity—do you call anyone eloquent? Therefore spare words that flatter, that are covered with cosmetics, and that are composed to win favor. It may suit our friendship for you to wish me to seem such to others; yet it is not consistent with my modesty for you to persuade me that I am such in my own eyes. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXXXVIII. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

Long ago the reputation of your learning made you desirable to me; but I delayed writing for a long time out of modesty, lest I should seem to be courting someone placed at court. This disorder is so frequently affected that men concerned with their reputation blush on behalf of other people’s faults. The cause of my hesitation has now been removed, since you honored me first with a greeting. I will enter, kindly invited, through the open doors of your friendship, and I will plan to compensate for the modest delays of my silence with more frequent pages. Only receive with good will the service of an impoverished tongue, and for a little while lower the judgment of the imperial master. You indicated that you had read some of my writings. I ask for the same patience. I will not be new to you, nor will I fear an inexperienced judge. You have learned to endure all my writings. Familiarity has also grown between us, making you a more equitable judge of me. For friendship is gracious: through affection it changes a severe examination into gentler sentiments.

What if, having laid aside my fear of my poor talent, I promise you frequent letters? See then—when may you expect more from a fuller storehouse? I must admit this as a friend: I seek draughts of Gallic eloquence, not because Latin eloquence has departed from these seven hills, but because an old pupil of the Garonne once infused the principles of rhetoric into my heart. Through my teacher I have a proper kinship with your schools. Whatever there is in me—which I know is very little—I owe to your sky. Water us, then, again from those Camenae who first gave me the milk of the liberal arts. And if anything in my writings has offended you, either protect the former listener of your countryman by your silence, or instruct him again yourself. Farewell.

## EPIST. LXXXIX. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

I accuse your letters, which, in my credulity, I thought would provide a remedy for my longing for you. But, having passed before my eyes, they brought forward torches burning more fiercely. For they overflowed with the abundant honey of eloquence, which I grieve you have carried away with you. Thus, stirred by the flavor of a brief reading, I received a more bitter sense of loss. Amid this, another thought occurred to me: it would be more bitter if you remained silent. Therefore the harsher condition has turned me toward choosing the former one. I ask you, then, to write. But make the intervals between your letters shorter. Let them come to me more often and imitate conversation in your presence. We shall constantly enjoy that aspect in which you are better. And if you add some work requiring greater length, care, and elaboration, it will almost seem that you are pleading not only in Rome but also in our Athenaeum, with the grace you customarily display. Farewell.

## EPIST. XC. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

I am glad that I have returned to your care. But the most distinguished young man Asterius is responsible for this good deed, so suddenly accomplished; in order to prepare a recommendation, he obtained from you at last the writing of a letter. To his friendship, although we discovered it long ago, we have added diligent attention of mind in recognition of his recent merit. But I will not allow you to continue waiting for reminders, and to devote your efforts to the use of others rather than to paying the devoted debt owed to the affection between us. I do not begrudge those who ask for your testimony or support. But the cause of friendship is stronger than that of favor. Set petitionary letters after legitimate ones: let affection attend to these more frequently, and let kindness occasionally provide those. Farewell.

## EPIST. XCI. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

I ought not to have waited for your letters to inform me of the honor you received. I therefore anticipate your modesty with congratulations, and I wish that continued good fortune may increase the rank lawfully granted to your merits. It remains for you to sharpen the diligence of our friendship through constant writing and to compensate for your absences with services. For the truly great man is made greater by his advancement when his eminence bows toward a share of honor. Farewell.

## EPIST. XCII. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

I am accused in vain of dissimulation and silence, since, with Jupiter as my witness, I have not abandoned the diligence owed to you. But I think the fault of my people caused the writings sent to you to remain undelivered. I ask, therefore, that my feelings toward you not be judged by the infrequency of my letters. For affection is often imitated by services. The sincerity of friendship, however, demands the trust of the heart more than the blandishments of speech. Farewell.

## EPIST. XCIII. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

We have joined our pledges. It therefore seems fitting that those whom we have had as companions in the gathering should also be honored with the gift of the sportula. We have accordingly sent you two solidi to be offered—a small gift if it is valued by its price, but a religious offering if it is weighed by the love of the giver. Farewell.

## EPIST. XCIV. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

Certain report had promised that you would come to Rome. We had conceived with great joy the hope of seeing your excellence. But an unexpected change in the news indicated that, at the pious summons of our master and ruler, you are returning to your votive observances. I therefore make up, with the honor of my style, the service of greeting you which I had hoped to offer in person; and I ask you to return the favor in such a way as to suggest that you miss frequent conversation with me, if the first one has shown that it pleased you. Farewell.

## EPIST. XCV. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

You have supplied a reason for the long silence of both of us. For I too confess that until now I restrained myself from the duty of writing. Defended by your explanation, I do not labor to dissolve in letters what is shared between us. Now that everything has been restored to a tranquil condition, let us resume our interrupted efforts with competing diligence. Only then will it be proved that time was responsible for the long rest of our writing, if, with opportunity restored, frequent conversation repairs our mutual care. [Col. 0348D]

## EPIST. XCVI. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

Although you have abstained from letters, I ought not to imitate your example. I therefore complete the generous greeting, and I do not doubt that at least the services which you had begun will be returned to me. Farewell.

## EPIST. XCVII. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

Envy commonly obstructs the good, and now it has stolen from me the joy I had hoped to find in your presence. Thus far it has directed its strength toward damaging our common desire. I shall therefore be content if it has merely deprived me of the expectation of your arrival. May it allow you yourself to remain safe and finally return to favor with both of us. It will be equivalent to a benefaction if I obtain the pleasure of knowing that you are safe. Farewell.

## EPIST. XCVIII. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

Having received news of my arrival, which report could not conceal from you, I waited for you either to write first or, what would be more welcome, to come in person to Formiae. But since either your dissimulation or your business has denied me both, I gladly take your part myself and ask you either to grant me your excursion here or, if something prevents you, at least to reply with a written greeting.

## EPIST. XCIX. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

[Col. 0349B]

I love your letters, but I await your presence, which the reckoning of the days promises me. The hope of your arrival does not allow me to write more. But what we now take away from the letter, we shall repay in conversation face to face. Farewell.

## EPIST. C. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

I am grateful that you kindly devote your most ready efforts to my affairs and testify that you remember me by writing frequently. Hence it happens that our care responds to your services. I therefore gladly return your conversation. And although you willingly apply yourself to helping my men, I nevertheless add the encouragement of a request, so that the services you offer voluntarily may increase when prompted. Farewell.

## EPIST. CI. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

[Col. 0349C]

Your complaint about the infrequency of my letters is more dutiful than just. For although it proceeds from affection, it nevertheless lacks fairness. Now, however, having completed my journey, I promise that I will repair by frequent letters the losses incurred in past services.

## EPIST. CII. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

While you ask for a benefaction, you have conferred one. For I have gained more from your friendship than you have from my defense. I will therefore claim no credit for my kindness, since I owe a great deal to yours. Yet this sort of gift can still be increased by frequent writing, so that goodwill may strengthen our familiarity, which necessity now seems to have begun. Farewell.

## EPIST. CIII. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

[Col. 0349D]

The incorporated members of our common homeland must be assisted with all our strength, especially the contractors of the saltworks, who operate by supplying fuel for the baths. Most people are indebted to them; and unless judicial authority compels payment, the sequence of their difficulties will provoke a public complaint. I therefore ask that, among the other things which Rome expects from your zeal, you also claim this part of diligence for yourself.

## EPIST. CIV. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

We admit that what we have sent is small, but a parent’s honor is measured by devotion rather than by the size of the gift. Yet this very modest offering will bring you greater gratitude if your devotion accepts it, sampled by me for your use. Farewell.

## EPIST. CV. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

The contractors of the saltworks, who serve the splendor and usefulness of our common homeland, must be assisted. Therefore, when you have heard their complaints, you will kindly grant justice to those who approach you—justice useful to the city and consistent with your character. Farewell.

## EPIST. CVI. SYMMACHUS . . . . .

For our sons, joined in marriage with God’s help, we have sent you, in two solidi, a wedding gift. If you receive it with ready graciousness, you will demonstrate that all celebrations among friends are held in common. Farewell.

## LETTER CVII. SYMMACHUS …

I would have wished you also to be present at my son’s wedding among his closest friends. But since your distant absence denied me the service I desired, I sent a gift of two solidi, so that I might testify through this votive offering that your memory remains alive with me. It is indeed a small present if its value is judged by its price; but a religious offering if it is valued by the affection behind it. Farewell.

## LETTER CVIII. SYMMACHUS …

Everything circulated without an author is uncertain. [Col. 0350C] But I do not allow rumor to say anything against the reputation of a sacred virgin. Therefore the duty of a pontiff and the trust of a senator remind me to bring forward what is known. You are said to wish to withdraw from the Vestal secrecy before the years prescribed by law. I do not yet believe the rumor, but I await a statement from your own lips, which may either acknowledge or reject the uncertainty of the report. Farewell.

## LETTER CIX. SYMMACHUS …

At last you have deigned to make me certain about your actions; after reading and considering them, I rejoiced at the standing of your life and innocence in the eyes of Justus. I see that the others have been lacking in diligence when replying; may you deign to encourage them to return the favor, so that, prompted by reciprocity, I may understand that my letters will not afterward become objects of the same disdain. [Col. 0350D] Farewell.

## LETTER CX. SYMMACHUS …

You must consider the judgment of others, whom it is fitting to pass judgment on the Fathers. The poverty of my talent marvels even at small things. Therefore I would have you believe that no honor accrues to you from my testimony. For although it is an old saying that to be praised by a praised man is itself praise, our mediocrity nevertheless does little to advance the splendor of your reputation. But since your will must be obeyed, I shall, as ordered, explain what certain people think of your speeches.

You are almost to be blamed for begrudging our age the fame of Ciceronian style. You will reply that you have devoted all your effort to composing history. [Col. 0351A] Forgive my greed if I desire both. With equal polish and gravity you have refined both senatorial proceedings and the monuments of Roman affairs, so that I may plainly pronounce you, in the Homeric expression *περιδέξιον*—that is, “skilled with both hands,” or “equally adept.” Continue, then, I beg you, and strive to leave posterity this endowment, so that the qualities once pleasing when divided among individual authors may now be praised as united in you. Farewell.

## LETTER CXI. SYMMACHUS …

We ought to count springs and the difficulty of conducting water among the labors of Hercules … … now Neapolis has received [it] after changing its location. Hence, after a short interval of days, I shall not delay crossing to Capua for the sake of your desire.

## LETTER CXII. SYMMACHUS …

[Col. 0351B]

When the time of the December Kalends was already approaching, a letter was delivered to me saying that you had deserved the annual consular robe. I would have you believe that my state of mind shone with great joy at this news. First, because nature has arranged it so that everyone judges an honor conferred upon himself to be deserved when the recipient has proved worthy of receiving it. Next, because an honor long rare and exceedingly difficult for the toga and the senatorial order at last falls to a man of the highest standing in public affairs. Finally, because by your ready summons you have joined our friendship, which had not yet been initiated by other services.

Do you see how credible are the causes of my joy? But I fear you may not believe them sufficiently, since, when summoned, I offer excuses—although a reasonable explanation cannot offend a wise man. For how could I, summoned to the first auspices of your fasces, penetrate the distant regions of Gaul within a few days? Consider the preparations for the journey, the hindrance of winter, the breakdown of the public transport system, and the shortness of the winter daylight. Would not my effort have been fruitless before the January Kalends, or my arrival afterward more disgraceful? [Col. 0351C]

I beg you to pronounce upon these matters with an even temper, and deign to be a good arbiter of our friendship. Interpret in that spirit the arguments I rightly offer in response to your request, and do not abandon your purpose. For a man is believed to have summoned another kindly only when he is not offended by an excuse. Farewell.

## LETTER CXIII. SYMMACHUS …

You have bound me to you by very many services, and although I have not yet repaid your earlier kindnesses, I now ask for another debt. The most distinguished consul ordered me to attend the auspices of his office, and your appeal was added to his letter. This is honorable to one who is coming, but exceedingly burdensome to one who must make excuses. Yet your fairness will lighten my embarrassment through the truth of the matter.

Strive to appease him, to whom the sorrowful event concerning my brother offers excuse for me. For it is disgraceful and impossible to approach joyful gatherings with a stunned mind and mournful face. I recognize what fortune demands: he acts too stubbornly against it who, after receiving a wound, immediately pretends not to be miserable. If our grounds are just, necessary, and true, see to it, I beg you, that he forgive my absence with as ready a pardon as your good will urged me to proceed. Farewell.

## LETTER CXIV. SYMMACHUS …

[Col. 0352A]

Caecilius the comic poet was right: “Man is a god to man, if he knows his duty.” I would apply this saying to you, who have shown vigilant care for our affairs. Hence remembrance dwells in my heart and praise upon my lips. Nor does the glory of your deed and devotion flourish only in the present; as my mind foresees, it will endure for ages.

A longer speech of thanks would even now be appropriate, if I did not fear that I might seem thereby to have discharged all at once what I owe. He is impatient of a benefit received who hastens to free himself from his obligation; nor does he seem to accept reciprocal service as a friend if he is embarrassed by delaying gratitude. My own disposition is different. I hasten to repay a loan of money; I wish for a long time to remain indebted for services. [Col. 0352B] Farewell.

## LETTER CXV. SYMMACHUS …

You advise me to endure with an even temper either the wicked acts of rivals or the shameful decrees of the ungrateful. The quality of your counsel accords with our zeal and character. No one’s wickedness, however violent, is so great that it deserves to move me.

Should I take this ill, knowing that the monuments of the Marcelli were destroyed when Verres was praetor, and that no envious hands spared even the trophies of Marius? The reward and meaning of virtue lie in conscience alone. I pay no attention to statues and the false public inscriptions upon them. Those who have fallen from men’s minds deceive the eyes of provincials.

If I were to desire any honor from public testimony, I ought to be content with your judgment and that of men like you—either following the example of the lyre-players, who, indignant at the crowd of seated spectators, summoned song for themselves and the Muses; or following the philosopher Heraclitus, who considered the highest praise to be pleasing one person, provided that the person who approved was the best.

Therefore be confident in our patience, and congratulate me that I alone torment the hearts of the envious, while those to whom statues have been granted in one way or another have nothing to arouse envy. Farewell.

## LETTER CXVI. SYMMACHUS …

I am as well as my ailing mind permits. Would that the laws were equally sound with me; their health is usually corrupted by the very people entrusted with caring for them. I shall not go further, since my brother Buleforus can disclose this riddle. As my friendship is dear to him, so my complaint is known to him. Once he has made you aware of my distress, I trust that, with such an assistant, the laws will return to our courts. Farewell.

## LETTER CXVII. SYMMACHUS …

Previously you had reproached me concerning the bears with which my son’s quaestorship did not make use. I was stung by the reminder of a failed favor, about which you ought not to have reproached a friend who had not received the benefit. Yet you now also demand payment, as our excellent common brother Brotadius alleges, for something neither hoped for nor delivered.

It pleases me more, if you believe me, that the agreement has moved from embarrassment to money. For it is less burdensome to appear a debtor than ungrateful. It is therefore your choice to set a price on the bears that, as you say, were lost in a shipwreck during bad weather. You have it in your power to determine how much you should value my good will in a fruitless undertaking.

Let our friendship only endure, and let fortune have no power over it. I place the sum against the loss; I shall not deduct my money on account of the misfortunes of your ship. Farewell.

## LETTER CXVIII. SYMMACHUS …

The most distinguished Senate has admitted your guest Faustinus into its membership. Such is the longstanding authority of your recommendation among us that delaying what you wish would amount to an injury. Let him therefore credit your efforts with the favor of the entire order. For just as he owes the attainment of his dignity to the sacred benefit, so he owes the speed of our decree to you. Farewell.

## LETTER CXIX. SYMMACHUS …

[Col. 0353B]

Most of us believed that you would come to Milan at the consul’s summons; some claimed that you had remained in Gaul. Amid these differing opinions, I was uncertain where the quaestorian gifts should be sent. After the arrival of your people gave me an opportunity to discharge my duty, I entrusted the customary delivery of the gifts to Clarentius, whose loyalty I had tested.

As I judge, you will not reject the offering of a diptych and an *aphoreticum*. For it is not burdensome to your modesty to accept customary and votive gifts. Since these are offered as tokens of friendship, it belongs to the acknowledgment of affection that the recipient’s mind should recognize that they are owed to him. Farewell.

## LETTER CXX. SYMMACHUS …

[Col. 0353C]

When I often passed through Ariminum, I learned from your example to honor friends with small gifts. Therefore, instructed by your example, I repay what necessity requires rather than offer what is superfluous. Unless you receive these with ready graciousness, you will seem to mark my generosity by the gifts you have accepted so many times. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXI. SYMMACHUS …

You entrusted me with a ready and easy task, in which I do not claim that my effort has cost you anything. As soon as your letter and my speech approached the distinguished Faustus, so that he might summon for examination the man from Epirus about whom you are disputing, he in no way opposed your request. I therefore hope that, at his summons, the man whom your friendly dispute may adjudge to one of you will soon be present.

But enough words on this matter. I ask you to enrich us from time to time with the honor of your writings, and not to abandon, when friendship urges you, what you have now done because circumstances required it. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXII. SYMMACHUS …

I had indeed expected your justice to support the sincere actions of my brother Magnillus. But after hearing the trustworthy account that the speech of those arriving made known to us all, I greatly rejoiced that fortune had provided him with a fair judge.

I therefore give you thanks for my friend’s security, whose wholly innocent life you have confirmed by the testimony of your judgment. And I hope that, through your consideration, the remaining traces of his misfortune will soon be removed. Thus I approach you as a petitioner, so that you may more readily take up the role of your inborn justice. I shall always remember so great a benefit, if the man whom you have deigned consistently to clear is at last granted complete security. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXIII. SYMMACHUS …

Previously I derived the greatest pleasure from your letters; now you steep the mind of your reader in lamentable complaint. Where is that conviction which, through nature’s gift and the reading of the ancients, fortified you against every weapon of fortune? Assume the patience worthy of a man, and cease mourning what cannot be changed.

Everything ought to seem lighter to you after your criminal son-in-law. Why, however, do you devote yourself to lethargy and idleness, and, neglecting your patrimony, nourish your grief in leisure? Take care of what remains of your property, which the criminal invader left exhausted and torn apart, lest, amid the present necessities of the state, you be unable to support what you recover—things you had previously neglected and despised. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXIV. SYMMACHUS …

Although you may admit that you were compelled to write, I nevertheless credit you with having honored me with the distinction of your style no less than if you had done so willingly. But you may see who was the author of so great a gift. From that letter I received not merely the honor of pleasure but also practical benefit.

For I learned that the security of the city was being strengthened by the grain supply. I also learned that Faustus, as soon as he first heard your case, had shown himself a fair judge, and that, when your arguments were brought forward, the validity of the documents had been established. For I think that the other matters you indicate as having followed were extracted against his will; and we ought to hope that in the remaining issues he will be the kind of judge whom his initial examination revealed to you.

Nevertheless, to encourage the justice which I believe is owed to your merits, I sent him a friendly letter, which you may place in his hands if circumstances require. The condition of the times permits no other kind of remedy to be applied.

But I want you to know—and, for the sake of our friendship, you ought to perceive this voluntarily—that my concern for you does not need a reminder; yet nothing more can be done than for our request to win you the goodwill of the disputant. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXV. SYMMACHUS …

[Col. 0354D]

We are preparing the praetorian games, whose decoration requires foreign animals, so that the Roman spectacle may shine in a new guise. I therefore wish, through your efforts, to have addax antelopes and pygarg antelopes supplied to me, since the neighboring frontier provides you with an abundance of them.

Deign, I beg you, to bind our friendship with a votive pledge. I shall not be unequal to returning the favor if your own needs should require anything. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXVI. SYMMACHUS …

I had long been promising myself hope of your arrival. Yet even now you ask me for an exchange of letters and in a certain way threaten a prolonged absence. [Col. 0355A] For what does your request for mutual consolation mean if your return is already being prepared?

If my advice has any place with you, I recommend that you revisit the city, to which both civic affection and your quaestorian responsibilities summon you. Although its preparations possess the resources of a wealthy man, they nevertheless require the diligence of a candidate. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXVII. SYMMACHUS …

We recognized the feeling you return to us in the sequence of your recent letters; but we regret the rarity of this service. Therefore we urge you frequently to undertake this token of a familiar duty.

Your petition concerning the inheritance of Gaius M. V. Aerius seemed neither to me nor to the others who care for you to be well founded. For what has been left by right and law cannot be alienated through a petition for special favor. Our common friend Valentinianus discovered this to be so; he labored greatly to extract something, if it could be done. But, with justice opposing him, the result of his effort deserted him.

Therefore, if you believe anything I say, remove from yourself the odium of the petition; I also wish that your associate be persuaded to do the same. I prefer your reputation to remain intact rather than that such a petition be charged against you. You will recognize that I offer this advice with friendly and kindly concern for you, in return for the mutual diligence we owe one another. For you understand that I ought to care for nothing more than the reputation of our friends. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXVIII. SYMMACHUS …

In accordance with the custom and practice of our ancestors, an investigation by our college has discovered the incest of Primigenia, formerly chief Vestal at Alba. The proceedings testify that this became clear from the confessions both of the woman who violated sacred chastity and of Maximus, with whom she committed the unspeakable crime.

It remains for the severity of the laws to be exercised against those who polluted the public ceremonies by their abominable crime. You have been assigned this action by the example of recent times. Therefore, considering the public interest and the laws, deign suitably to punish this offense, which has been most severely avenged throughout all generations down to the present day. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXIX. SYMMACHUS …

Following the examples of the recent age, our college has brought a charge before our most distinguished and excellent brother, the urban prefect, against Primigenia, the defiled virgin who supervised the Alban sacred rites. But since his letter advances plausible arguments—that it is not lawful for the walls of the Eternal City to admit one guilty of so great a crime, and that he himself cannot travel to distant places, whereas a crime ought to be expiated where it was committed—we have judged it necessary to approach the neighboring authority to whom the laws of the provinces have been entrusted.

That authority must exercise against Primigenia, who stained the secrets of the public ceremonies, and against her corrupter Maximus, who did not in fact deny the outrage, the severity always applied in such cases. Deign, therefore, after considering the confessions that disclosed the tragedy of the unspeakable crime, to avenge the injury done to our most chaste age by the punishments of the accused. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXX. SYMMACHUS …

[Col. 0356A]

This is a suitable time to test what devotion you show toward our friendship. For the most merciful emperors have conferred the ordinary consulship. Therefore I urgently request your care in providing everything that the spectacle requires.

My men will supply the purchase money for the various items. In this matter alone I desire your zeal and care: order that what has been bought at fair prices be transported in advance as soon as possible. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXI. SYMMACHUS …

Before those who ought to care for the reputation of the times, I do not keep silent about what is just, confident and secure that no one’s efforts will harm the laws.

Because of the remaining wine-chest levy, which earlier emperors ordered many prefects to exact, and which is known to have been paid for the most part into the imperial treasury, the estate of my father-in-law Orfitus, once prefect and dead fifteen years ago without any demand under this heading, is now being pursued. This is being done under the pretext of a letter in which the deified Constantius ordered him to restore whatever had been shown to have been spent on public works, threatening him and his office—as usually happens—with a penalty if appropriate care were lacking in the collection.

But he himself did not neglect the task entrusted to him, and the emperors who followed transferred to later judges what the prefecture had undertaken. The illustrious Valentinianus, a prince memorable throughout every age, and the deified Gratianus confirmed this in sacred letters; it is not proper to depart from their decision.

Moreover, although crimes are usually brought to an end by death, in this one case, contrary to the best customs of the emperor, unexpected losses are extended to posterity, and something is designated as still wholly outstanding even though part has been paid and part, as is established, was extracted by the provincial governors.

When I had received the divine commands concerning this matter, I ought not to conceal the truth, since they were granting a hearing under the law to men who had neither established their case in the inquiry nor obtained a copy of the report. There was also a stronger ground: my wife, long since emancipated, did not claim possession of the property after her father’s death and therefore asserted by rescript that she was not liable.

I therefore sent, under cover of a report, the records of the proceedings, hoping that, with the help of your devotion, this new precedent might also be removed—especially in a case that does not legally involve us. [Col. 0356D]

Let those truly liable under this heading be held responsible. An old declaration by Campani, the consular governor, still exists; so do the records prepared before Etruscus, the governor, which show that the collection of the remaining sums was promised. Spare the innocent, lest an unprecedented procedure be extended against all who administer the state.

Such justice accords with your age, whose reputation ought to be adorned by your counsels. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXII. SYMMACHUS …

A petition merits the support of your eminent spirit. With God’s help, the praetorship awaits our house. In it, both the examples of others and my own eagerness urge me to display crocodiles and many foreign animals to our fellow citizens.

Therefore deign kindly to take my friend Cyriacus into your care, so that he may advance the arrangements already indicated. You will have in the future a debtor who will not forget so great a favor. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXIII. SYMMACHUS …

What you write is the product of voluntary kindness; its lateness is the product of your many concerns. We, however, testify that the devotion owed to your merits is accompanied by the leisure of constant writing.

Order our Euscius, who is besieged by domestic affairs, [Col. 0357A] to be led into your service, and entrust to him, in a spirit of familiarity, the matters you have brought to my attention concerning the preparation of the games. [Col. 0358A]

## LETTER CXXXIV. SYMMACHUS …

I owe you a gift for my consulship, for our friendship, and for your honor. I have sent it to you in the amount of one solidus, asking you to receive with a kindly spirit this small portion of my customary duty. Farewell.

# BOOK TEN

## LETTER ONE. SYMMACHUS TO THE ELDER THEODOSIUS

[Col. 0357A]

Although I know that modesty is akin to virtue, I nevertheless desired in the letters of your Highness an abundance appropriate to the glory of your greatest achievements. First, because friendship demanded that you not fear a blemish of boastfulness in the eyes of one who loves you. Then, because you are equally ready in hand and speech, you ought to have endowed the trustworthiness of your deeds with the honor of your language.

Now you send me back to public reputation and order me to lend my ear to rumors, although the dignity of so great an undertaking requires an equal witness. But because you are secure in my disposition, you have entrusted your merit to the public voice, content with truth instead of praise.

Thus Africa has recovered from its illness, truly through the healing counsel of invincible emperors, whose remedy you were. For those skilled in medicine, once long practice has advanced them to mastery and made them veterans of their art, usually give orders concerning their patients and assist treatment with prescriptions while their hands are at rest.

Your victory, therefore, is the glory of the age. I would speak about it more openly and generously if I were not yielding to your extraordinary modesty, and if I were not taking great care lest, having been recently praised by Your Excellence, I might seem to be returning a favor that had been lent to me—that is, to use the saying, “to scratch mules in return.”

So that I may not appear too close to that proverb, I touch upon the praises of your virtues with restrained speech, leaving it to your distinguished conscience to decide what you yourself deserve, under whose leadership a province friendly to me breathes again, and what I owe you, whose reputation, with such a witness, will never succumb to envy. Farewell.

## LETTER TWO. SYMMACHUS TO GRATIANUS AUGUSTUS

I know that affection for which you usually honor the highest men led you to appoint me as a reader of your sacred address. But when I understand that speech to surpass in every respect all the other writings heard by the Senate in these circumstances, I also judge that I have been esteemed more highly than the rest.

For just as in great enterprises, so in great comedies, carefully chosen actors are employed. Publius Pollio did not receive the same honor in presenting plays as Ambivius, nor did Aesopus and Roscius enjoy equal fame.

Therefore, excellent emperors, I embrace as divinely offered what you have wisely decided concerning me. Your praise, Lord Gratianus, is my duty, since you are so disposed that, when you heal the state, you summon the service of my voice.

You restored the public disturbances among us to tranquility. We all came very close to perishing: such a vast outrage had been planned by those who had seized the highest powers through evil practices. That fierce Maximinus, swollen with success, a clinger to judicial business, slow to decide cases, ready for quarrels … [Col. 0358A]

At the same time, your affairs returned to tranquility. These blessings, although the necessity of your honor brought them about, nevertheless helped my spirit as though doubled. But this report does not yet satisfy us, who fear worse things, so long as the calculation of the stored grain extends into another harvest.

Therefore make me aware of what each day brings into the granaries, so that the pleasure of my leisure may increase together with the resources of my country. Farewell.

## LETTER THREE. SYMMACHUS …

You order me to attend the opening ceremonies of the quaestorian spectacle on the sixth day before the Kalends of November. I received the letter summoning me two days before the appointed time, near Neapolis. As you see, the long distance of the journey and the proximity of the day of the function excuse my absence. But, with the gods’ help, I shall make up my obligation of service through many spectacles of yours.

For now, I ask you to show yourself readily disposed to grant pardon. It is not right that, at such expense to me, blame should also be added. Farewell.

## LETTER FOUR. SYMMACHUS …

It is my purpose and character to care for the reputation of those whom I love. Affinity urges me to show you still greater favor. For this reason I cannot endure hearing it reported to the Senate by the recorders of the attendants that you allow magistrates of the Roman people to be absent, or that it is charged to your injury that the functions of the fatherland are abandoned by those bound to perform them.

Although I presume this has been falsely brought to the public ears, I nevertheless perform a parent’s duty by offering a warning, and I beg you to add to the other praises of your administration this further distinction, about which we are concerned.

For it is a serious matter that, while a man of noble family presides over the highest tribunals in Africa, some of his colleagues decline their Roman duties, and that an almost empty year for those who produce the games should generate envy in place of consular eminence.

Let those who abandon their duties at least hear with how little expense the praetor Aedesius produced the urban games in the previous year, and learn from his example what honor and relief should be granted to the magistrates of the present. Farewell.

## LETTER FIVE. SYMMACHUS …

My mind longs to take part in your vows, but the condition of my body refuses a long journey. For, as leisure is fertile ground for illnesses, pain in my feet has once again bound me while I indulge in the quiet of the countryside. Therefore, I beg you, grant a just remission to my service, and meanwhile allow me to be absent from the wedding celebrations of your household, so that, once healed a little later, I may join in the bonds. Farewell.

## LETTER SIX. SYMMACHUS …

Friends do not usually have to ask pardon anxiously. Therefore I am brief: while I was resting in the countryside, my customary ailment of one foot crept upon me. Accordingly, I ask leave from the duty that I desired to perform. May the gods who preside over auspices grant me the opportunity to attend the wedding vows of your family in restored health. Farewell.

## LETTER SEVEN. SYMMACHUS …

My brother Rabilianus, distinguished by birth and affection, lamented the bitterness of the wrong done to him in a private complaint to me. For he asserts that his agent was punished without anyone having named him; and although he ought to have obtained vengeance from you, which he had requested while you were staying at Rome, he discovered that the injury to his household had been increased.

I think this happened through forgetfulness. For how could you order what you had disapproved when present? Therefore, as a parent I warn you: do not think that increasing what he has suffered is a form of conscientiousness.

Certainly, if equity is absent from your judgments, explain the reason to me in a friendly manner, remembering that a governor ought to undertake the defense of absent masters. Farewell.

## LETTER EIGHT. SYMMACHUS

I would have found pleasure in receiving your writings. For friendship rejoices in reciprocal services. But would that the diligence of my people had fulfilled the pledge of your promise. Although you wrote that they had departed to pay the rent, they have lost a small portion of their revenues; nor were they ashamed, amid such a fruitful year, to accumulate a mass of debts.

Therefore deign to take up the care of our interests and compel the debtors to pay. For what benefit is it that they are assisted by your zeal and favors, when our advantage feels nothing of it? Farewell.

## LETTER NINE. SYMMACHUS …

After the customary greeting—since it is usual to place it before the letter, so that vows may precede the sequence of familiar writings—I cannot remain silent before you that the work at the Cajetana Forma is languishing. Unless your presence gives the undertaking a spur, I fear that the summer opportunity for bringing the work to completion will be lost.

I therefore leave it to your authority to decide what should be done about this. It is enough for me, in matters relevant to your praise, to have fulfilled the role of a friend offering advice. Farewell.

## LETTER TEN. SYMMACHUS …

I rejoice most abundantly that you are taking care that my son’s spectacle be equipped with numerous bears. I would have sent the prices at once, had the severity of winter not prevented their transport. But shortly afterward, when the mildness of spring has softened the difficulties of travel, the purchase of the wild animals will be arranged, for which you promised to establish a fair price.

[Col. 0360A] Meanwhile I thank you and acknowledge my thanks to you, and I declare that I have been challenged to increase our friendship, although you willingly deign to recognize that honorable benefits do not perish among the grateful. Farewell.

## LETTER ELEVEN. SYMMACHUS …

Through our common friend Gaudentius I sent the little petition of my relative Valentinus, a matter certainly relevant to my trust and conscience. For when his brother Proserius was under the pressure of extreme illness, he earnestly begged me, both in person and by letter, to obtain through the easy authority of a rescript that his daughter might be joined in marriage to her brother’s son—something that well-known examples show has been granted to many.

Therefore I cannot refuse assistance to a pious supplication, since the will of my dying relative has bound my trust to this marriage, as the letter attached to the petition makes clear.

Deign, therefore, to help bring about this pious desire, at least to the extent that, if anyone attempts to disturb the paternal command, he may be frightened by the threat of infamy. Once the benefit of the rescript has been obtained, let a man of tested loyalty deliver it. Farewell.

## LETTER TWELVE. SYMMACHUS …

A common cause deserves your assistance. For whatever pertains to senatorial duties must be accomplished through shared effort and united zeal. Therefore, with the authority appropriate to your position, support the interests and accounts belonging to the most distinguished curia.

You will gain much praise from this matter if the payment demanded from those liable restores the duties of our order, which it has long been evident are wavering. Farewell.

## LETTER THIRTEEN. SYMMACHUS …

Fortune favors our spectacle, since it has chosen to bring you to the administration of Apulia. Use the present opportunity, therefore, and in connection with the praetorship of our house—at which bears will shortly be brought safely from overseas—establish suitable supports, so that this further addition may be joined to your earlier services. Farewell.

## LETTER FOURTEEN. SYMMACHUS …

I am delighted by your diligence and judicial vigor. But the poverty—or rather destitution—of the Forminian order is incapable even of corrective treatment. For just as bodies weakened by a prolonged illness cannot endure harsher medicine, so a curia reduced by numbers and poverty is extinguished by excessive severity of correction.

Therefore willingly accept the advice of a parent, who does not defend the fault of the order but asks for moderation in correction. Regard must be had for the public revenues, and the restoration of the summer bath must be weighed against the resources of the state, so that, if anything remains over from the other expenses, it may be devoted to the cost of the work.

More time must also be granted for the restoration, lest a hurried repair diminish its strength. Nothing is taken from your glory by this delay. For the fault of the old curia does not reach the present judge.

I could add more, but since consideration of all matters flourishes in your wisdom, I shall avoid being more prolix and remain content with one warning: we must take great care that your arrival bring relief rather than burden to orders already partly exhausted. [Col. 0361A]

## LETTER FIFTEEN. SYMMACHUS …

If we were asking for a new favor concerning the purchase of bears, a longer approach would be necessary. But since promises are merely being repeated, it is more appropriate to remind you than to ask you.

The substance of this letter, therefore, is that you should not hesitate to assist my men, to whom we have already entrusted the purchase of the wild animals, so that the spectacle we are preparing for my son, with God’s blessing, may be equipped through your assistance and my expense. Farewell.

## LETTER SIXTEEN. SYMMACHUS …

[Col. 0361B]

Suessa is the homeland of honorable citizens, so that I may rightly say that even men of the lowest fortune ought to be judged free from plebeian vices. I therefore wish you to believe that no one from that city would have come forward amid the tumult of the courts unless a bitter assault had compelled him; my letters will not speak of it.

For the public voice will support their grief more forcefully than a private one could. Through me they seek only to deserve the convenience of a hearing. Whatever must be done quickly for the despoiled and harassed, your favor and the rule of law will provide. Farewell.

## LETTER SEVENTEEN. SYMMACHUS …

The public office commends the allegations of the people of Suessa to you; private compassion commends them to me. Therefore they ask judicial vigor from you, and words from me.

I accordingly perform my part, and I ask you as a friend, after hearing the lamentations of the unfortunate, to be moved in that direction which is friendly both to justice and to compassion. Farewell.

## LETTER EIGHTEEN. SYMMACHUS …

The first reason for writing is to offer the honor of a greeting. The second is to approach your proven modesty with a just petition. For many members of my household have escaped by flight and are hiding in the places bordering on you. After hearing the allegations of my agent, I ask you to restore them.

It accords with your character and our friendship both to show consideration and to deny refuge to servile wickedness. Farewell.

## LETTER NINETEEN. SYMMACHUS …

[Col. 0361D]

After receiving your letter from the Sicilian strait, and being prompted to undertake the return service, I announce that I have been greeted by good fortune and wish the same to be available to you.

Next, I remind you about the preparations for our spectacle, although a devoted mind requires no second reminder. Above all the creatures required by Roman spectacles, the theatrical production demands crocodiles. I hold your faithful promise concerning them; its fulfillment will be easy if the efforts of your support are aided by the men specially sent to attend to the matter. Farewell.

## LETTER TWENTY. SYMMACHUS …

[Col. 0362A]

Reliable reports affirm that several bears from Dalmatia will shortly be coming for the preparations of our household. We must privately arrange their transport with vehicles already organized. Your diligence, tested by experience, promises me completion of this task. I therefore ask you to undertake this responsibility immediately … … … … … … … … …

## LETTER TWENTY-ONE. SYMMACHUS …
. . . expiated it with the capital punishment and tears of all. Now one human being shines upon another. The Senate retains its ancient standing. It is a pleasure to live; one does not regret having been born, and everything looks toward well-being. Poverty is no longer a danger to anyone. The state has returned to its former age, and its enfeebled spirits have changed, since you spoke words calling it to virtue. With equal vigilance, we see provision made for the grain supply to be brought more generously toward satisfying the city; abundant purification [or: refining] should boil away the debasement of the [Flandae] coinage; henceforth no observer will tilt the scales through any increase of provincial gold. I could pursue a thousand other matters which, remembering your glory and forgetting my own childishness, would reveal me as I am. For no prudent and humane person has corrupted oracles with words. Therefore let your divine mind, young Augustus, glory of the Roman name, ride forth in the chariot of its own eloquence; we, in offering thanks, creep along the ground, more suited to the comic slipper than to the tragic buskin, since eloquence has begun to be a matter of state. For, so far as I know, you have granted the Muses rooms in the palace and sumptuous support—a deed that may prosper for you and your piety, since you make no account of arrogance and leisure, the vices of greater fortune. It is enough for my well-being that you are well. The happiness sought by the public vow will ensure that, as great as your clemency’s desire to give back, so great may be the abundance available for advancing public business.

## EPISTLE XXII. TO THE LORD VALENTINIAN, EVER-AUGUSTUS, SYMMACHUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

To me, tranquil and long since withdrawn from the desire for office, you voluntarily granted the prefecture, coveted by many. I give thanks for the will of so many good emperors toward me. But I understand how much greater the anxiety of a magistracy is when it comes by judgment than when it comes by favor. The former, given as a reward for merit, must match the hope placed in it; the latter, obtained as a benefaction, is free from the danger of having to make good that expectation, lord emperor. Who, then, will make me equal to this burden? Clearly, your clemency, whose concern it is that I not be thought rashly chosen. For my conscience it is enough that I did not seek public responsibility. What sort of man I shall prove to be lies in the hands of time. Good magistrates are made by the favor of emperors, and the virtues of judges always flow from your character. Make everyone understand that, if the governors should lack unimpaired vigor and a just conscience, this is the fault of the man, not of the age. I am not excessive in my request when I commend my office to those who bestowed it. How much, after all, do I owe in thanks to your divinity? Make the state, too, grateful to you on my behalf.

## EPISTLE XXIII. TO THE LORD THEODOSIUS, EVER-AUGUSTUS, SYMMACHUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

For some time now, as circumstances show, the hearings of your divinity have looked favorably upon me. Otherwise, when emperors grant nothing rashly, I would not have appeared among the foremost—or first of all. I therefore seem to have been reserved until now for the state, which, when it summoned your majesty’s care to the distant regions of the empire, found in you, lord emperor, judgments already considered. It is right, then, that I give thanks to your eternity for the single honor I have received. You have often made men prefects, and will continue to do so for an immeasurable age, but men whom persistent service and experience have introduced. Me, a man long of proconsular rank and for a long time yielding to the ways of the powerful, you preferred to appoint to office before I could expect it. Now I ask and entreat you to support your action with perpetual favor. It is pleasant to preside over citizens, but difficult to please them. For even among acquaintances, constancy is often harsh. What of the fact that it frequently happens that some, through long experience of power, no longer recognize my office? Those who gave it will not abandon it. I shall strive, as far as I can, to ensure that the earlier reputation you had of me does not appear to have deceived your clemency: it will belong to your divinity to defend the common cause. For in the case of good magistrates, the reputation of the age seeks greater glory than the judgments of judges.

## EPISTLE XXIV. TO THE LORD THEODOSIUS, EVER-AUGUSTUS, SYMMACHUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

What we would not have kept silent before the divine emperor, brother of your clemency, if the Roman state still enjoyed him, I bring to the guardians of his reputation, with that devotion by which your prefect ought to put loyalty before flattery, lord emperor. It was falsely believed that the height of urban power would be elevated by the use of a foreign and ostentatious vehicle. This consideration alone then persuaded his kindly mind that the ancient magistracy should be carried in lavish pomp. A sober office rejects such an honor and is never ashamed of itself. If we suffer anything to be added to it, we admit that it has hitherto been lacking. Thus the eyes of the city seek the noble simplicity of a private vehicle, and the Roman people regard as degenerate a prefecture that has dragged along later examples. Far be it that the governor of a free—and indeed devoted—city should be driven in like another Salmoneus. We have no use for foreign marvels. Your Rome does not tolerate an incentive to arrogance, mindful, surely, of the good ancestors whom the pride of the Tarquins and Camillus’ own chariot offended. For white quadrigae brought that great man a grievous exile. Publicola lowered the consul’s axe before the assembly of the citizens and broke the summit of his own honor in order to raise the city’s liberty. Let us therefore be judged by character rather than by insignia. We do not condemn the new benefaction, but prefer the good old ways. Remove the vehicle whose decoration is more splendid; we prefer the one whose use is more ancient.

## EPISTLE XXV. TO THE LORD THEODOSIUS, EVER-AUGUSTUS, SYMMACHUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

Among the principal matters of public concern, it was often arranged that philosophical teachers should be summoned from Attica for the education of the nobility. Thus public law and authority admitted some of them for the use of our city, lord emperor. Now the kindness of your age has voluntarily assigned to the Roman schools a leading figure in wisdom: Celsus, son of Achetimus (whom the memory of letters agrees to have been comparable to Aristotle), promises to teach our youth the liberal arts, seeking no profit from his profession. He is therefore worthy to be enrolled in the highest order, so that we may reward a mind free from the vices of avarice with the prize of rank.

There are noble precedents for this, which prudent imitation may follow. For the Athenian council honored both Carneades of Cyrene and the Carthaginian Clitomachus with membership; in the same way they granted citizenship to Zaleucus, founder of the Locrian laws. It is therefore worthy of your eternal divinity to assign Celsus—laudable in birth, learning, and intention—to the nobility as a pledge of distinction, with consular precedence, so that we may not appear to have sought his expense more than his teaching, and so that we may not incur the charge of avarice by requesting public services from one who promises instruction without payment.

## EPISTLE XXVI. TO THE LORDS THEODOSIUS AND ARCADIUS, EVER-AUGUSTI, SYMMACHUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

The Roman people await exceptional benefits from your divinity, lord emperors. But it now asks back, as though they were owed, what your eternity voluntarily promised—not because it distrusts that these things will be granted (for nowhere is hope greater than in the promise of good emperors), but lest it seem to hope disdainfully for what has been offered unless it demands it insistently. Your clemency is therefore asked, after the subsidies your generosity will provide for our sustenance, also to furnish chariot and theatrical entertainments for the Circus and Pompey’s theater. For urban joy takes pleasure in these things, and you awakened its desire by your promise. Every day people await messengers who will confirm that the promised gifts are approaching the city. The fame of charioteers and horses is spreading; every vehicle and every ship is said to have brought theatrical performers. Yet it is love for your perpetuity, not desire for spectacles, that sharpens the people’s longing. Give what is requested for now, so that there may be room for the other things you will grant without end.

## EPISTLE XXVII. TO THE LORDS THEODOSIUS AND ARCADIUS, EVER-AUGUSTI, SYMMACHUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

Antiquity devoted the Kalends, the auspices of the year, when the cycle of the months begins anew, to the giving of New Year’s gifts, lord emperors. You anticipate the custom by the speed of your generosity, considering a liberality that is offered at its appointed times to be late. Happy, by Hercules, is the age in which emperors cannot long restrain what they must give, while they hesitate to demand what is owed them. What, then, should I praise first, what above all? The ready and swift generosity of your divinity, or your mindful care for those who are absent, or the fact that you have increased the sacred gift by the honor of your words? I shall say what is true: your clemency took care that, as though placed in your presence, I might enjoy the emperors’ conversations and reverence your august faces in the gifts themselves. When will it be granted me to receive from you joys expressed and alive? How great is the goodness of truth, whose appearance and image are marvelous!

I therefore give and possess my thanks—and, since I am not equal to repaying them, I delegate my obligation to the heavenly powers, so that the gods may repay on my behalf what I cannot repay. (See Seneca, *On Benefits*, Book IV, chapter 11; and note the use of the verb *delegare*, “to delegate.”) I delegate it to the virtues: may they reward your clemency with worthy advancement. We honor you, we love you—something which you know to be superior to all things—because you govern the state beneficially in order to deserve this alone.

## EPISTLE XXVIII. TO THE LORDS THEODOSIUS AND ARCADIUS, EVER-AUGUSTI, SYMMACHUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

There are fixed times for all the benefits which a stronger fortune bestows upon those beneath it, lord emperors. Only laws that advance the common good never suffer decline. The revered order gives thanks to your divine enactments, also in the name of posterity, to whom the state will be handed down improved.

For when disgraceful display had burdened senatorial functions with heavy expenses, you restored the old health both to our conduct and to our expenditures: so that either a modest edition would not disgrace colleagues unequal in means, or reckless extravagance would not, through shame, harm those who attempted things beyond their resources. Through the salutary effect of the same policy, the ancient form of expressing opinions has also been restored: so that the highest place in decision-making would be granted not by the fortune of wealth but by the nature of the offices; and so that the assent of the others would follow, even unwillingly, whatever the more fortunate senator had decided before them all.

We therefore believe that, once these abuses have been removed, the virtues have returned to their own kingdom. Economy will be maintained in public entertainments, order in the Senate; wealth, always weak in good times, will not put itself on display. It remains for the Augustan law to confirm, once the senatorial decree is known, what your serenity has entrusted to the Fathers for deliberation. With no one dissenting, the Senate has determined what limit should be set, once or repeatedly, to the moderation applicable to the staging of public entertainments; what should be assigned to gladiatorial shows and what limits on expenditure suit theatrical games; what freedom the expenditure of the present may claim and what loss the obstinacy of absentees ought to suffer.

When your eternity, venerable, ordered these matters to be determined by the Senate, it immediately commanded them to be referred back to you, so that decisions pleasing to all might be secured by an immortal law. We have obeyed your commands. Let us await the oracle by which you will beneficially, as is familiar to your divinity, confirm the decrees of the Fathers—with an added threat of punishment if at any time influence should corrupt any of the provisions that, by heavenly counsel, you have enacted for the dignity of the order.

## EPISTLE XXIX. TO THE LORDS THEODOSIUS AND ARCADIUS, EVER-AUGUSTI, SYMMACHUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

To give thanks for the city of Rome in response to your benefactions is as proper an act of duty as it is an audacious act of presumption. For words are not equal to great things, and no speech can fill the role of the Roman people, lord emperors. But because in such matters the consideration is more one of desire than of talent, I do not fear the reputation of inadequacy, so long as I avoid being called ungrateful toward the City, which heaven and the stars have received into their care. You heap upon it the good things of the whole world, and you believe that what Rome has sought is especially an addition to your own glory.

We have received the secure assurance of the ancient privilege: for under your rule it is established that whatever nature produces or human industry shapes anywhere that is noble belongs to the Roman people. Indeed, you have also given posterity an outstanding example. Future generations will know that public pleasures flow abundantly only when palaces do not demand them. This is the mark of a self-controlled spirit: to deny oneself what is offered to others, and to place the joy of others before one’s own consolations. Such conduct befits good emperors. The fruit of ears and eyes is fleeting; that of generosity is eternal.

Others might have reserved these gifts for their own triumphs, so that, once crowned with laurel, the Pompeian stage might resound for new performers; so that Indian beasts might precede the chariot of captive tetrarchs; so that a long line of horses might be led like nations. Your triumph will receive the Arsacids bound behind their backs and the treasures of conquered Babylon. Affected display does not enter great minds. You do not know how to postpone what must be given: whatever the service of nations offers is immediately public property.

Rightly the Senate and people celebrate you with their voices, venerate you with devotion, and embrace you with love. Believe me, you possess the hidden chambers of every heart—the places where affection for children and parents dwells. And because every reward, when offered to your benefactions, is too small, the most distinguished order found a beloved return by which to prove its gratitude. It consecrated in equestrian statues, among the ancient names, the ancestor of your family and stock, once an African and British commander, who fathered the most fortunate star and one auspicious to the empire. Thus are honored those whose children are born for the public good.

The imperial people, filled with pledges of your generosity, readily yielded to love for you. When it learned, at my announcement, that gifts from the public fathers were at hand, it poured out through every gate and rushed toward the distance, each person judging himself happier than the rest if he were first to see your gifts. I pass over the fact that, although imperial gifts are usually awaited, these arrived unannounced.

I pass over that day when the procession preceded the royal elephants through the crowded ranks of noble horses. I prefer to describe the roar of the Murcia Valley and that distribution of four-horse chariots in which the man to whom the urn soon granted the choice was no more or less fortunate than the one whom the lot had placed last. How often did the first envy the one who followed? Choice is uncertain when judgments are made among equals.

Nor should you think that this kind of pleasure appears small to the Martial people, for whom the marriage of neighboring circuses supplied the delights of the races; to whom the highest honor seemed to be to carry jubilant riders on the backs of horses and to be borne in triumphal chariots—when Victory, familiar to the Romulean race, would reward your clemency in accordance with everyone’s wish.

You have made the hoary City revel, restored to its first joy, to that springtime of a once-flourishing age. I now dare hope for still greater things. You will also send a royal fleet to increase the nourishment of your devoted people with grain supplies. The Senate, mingled with the people, will receive it at the mouths of the Tiber. They will venerate as sacred the ships that have carried the fortunate cargoes of Egyptian grain.

These are not greedy prayers, but ones awakened by the humanity of the age. Confidence comes from precedent. By receiving great things, we anticipate greater ones. Now read the auspicious votes of the Senate and people. I know that more is present in their hearts than can be expressed in words; nevertheless, accept certain first offerings of public love toward you. If what has been said so far is small, attribute it to the marvels of your gifts. For the magnitude of astonishment has left little room for the many rounds of applause.

## EPISTLE XXX. TO THE LORDS THEODOSIUS AND ARCADIUS, EVER-AUGUSTI, SYMMACHUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

I would rather have been an announcer of joyful events, lord emperors; but the demands of public duty imposed upon me the necessity of delivering sad news. Your Praetextatus, adorned with honors, champion of ancient integrity, has been taken from us by envious death—a man endowed with every virtue at home and abroad. It is too difficult to appoint someone like him in his place, for your eternity as well, which knows how to choose the best. Thus he left behind the deepest longing for him in the state and great grief among grateful citizens.

As soon as the bitter rumor about him spread through Rome, the people refused the customary pleasures of the theater. By many acclamations it testified to his illustrious memory and bitterly reproached the envy of fortune for having taken from it the benefaction of renowned emperors. He fulfilled the law of nature; but we, as companions of his spirit and of your judgment, have been confounded by such grief that we ask for relief in retirement. I am silent about the rest, which does not allow me to bear the prefecture patiently. This single loss of a colleague is sufficient justification for obtaining leave.

Let others love perpetual authority. For me, the highest fruit of happiness would be to come into the presence of your divinity and behold the stars of your kindness. This is the one thing, above all that you have granted, that I desire. It is a simple request and does not seek a path toward office. It has become sufficiently clear that I desire nothing else, since as a suppliant I have fled from magistracy.

## EPISTLE XXXI. TO THE LORD VALENTINIAN, EVER-AUGUSTUS, SYMMACHUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

Although I think my letter has been anticipated by messengers or rumor—for what can be swifter than fame, lord emperor?—I nevertheless cannot, compelled by the demands of public duty, remain silent about the death of this illustrious man while the grief is still raw. Fate has snatched away Vettius Praetextatus, equal to the men of old in every virtue, amid the profound lamentation of his country, to which he had brought distinguished glory. I pass over his praises and fitting encomia in the shock of my spirit. There is no place for anyone’s testimony when the glory of his life is attested by your clemency’s judgments and the grief of all has made his death renowned.

## EPISTLE XXXII. TO THE LORDS THEODOSIUS AND ARCADIUS, EVER-AUGUSTI, SYMMACHUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

Although Vettius Praetextatus has been released by the law of nature, he nevertheless lives on in everyone’s memory and affection. In this one respect he punishes envy: death contributed so much to his glory that envy must even envy this fortune, lord emperors.

For, in addition to the Roman people’s unprecedented grief, the Senate, impatient at its own loss, seeks consolation in honoring his virtue and begs your divinity to ensure that the lasting endurance of statues will present this remarkable man of our age to the eyes of posterity—not because he desired earthly rewards, since even when he lived as a human being he trampled bodily pleasures as fleeting things, but because imitation is stimulated by the honors bestowed upon good men, and emulating virtue is nourished by the example of another’s honor.

For this reason, even in the rough ages of old, the very best citizens were represented by hand and art and sent into lasting memory. Would that the ease of flatterers had not later diminished anything from this distinction! Although things sought by unequal skill are not equal. It is therefore fitting that he who lives in everyone’s heart should be on the lips of many.

He was always greater than his offices: temperate toward others, severe toward himself; approachable without contempt, revered without terror. If any advantage of succession came to him, it soon returned to the nearest testators. No prosperity broke him; he never laughed at another’s misfortunes; he knew nothing of disgraceful generosity. He was a man whom honor always followed unwillingly, and each person nearby entrusted his own limits to his fairness.

I would wish to say more about him, and I would owe more about him, but all must be reserved for the testimony of your clemency. For praise proceeding from heavenly judgment is more illustrious. Therefore, as patrons of integrity, present the good men of your age for future generations also to see. Certainly this is the Praetextatus whom you justly made consul, so that the calendars, mindful of him, might extend his celebrated name. For the benefit of others, repair the losses that are fatal. Let the reward depart with the man, but let the judgment remain after the man. Prove that misfortune has no power against glory. For what he earned from his fellow citizens is unique; what he lost is shared by many.

## EPISTLE XXXIII. TO THE LORD THEODOSIUS, EVER-AUGUSTUS, SYMMACHUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

If the merits of your divine clemency are considered, no riches that nature supplies or fortune conveys will equal the gratitude of our love toward you, lord emperor. But, in my view, the public judgment concerning a good emperor should not be measured by gifts. Nevertheless, the Senate, ready to obey, eagerly undertakes every duty by which affection may be shown, and prays your saving divinity to understand, in this offering—which has added something to those made previously—that care has been taken lest we appear to be less capable under your rule.

For to your divine parents a smaller sum was decreed for each on the occasion of their ten-year anniversaries. It is also reported that your divine brother was honored with more modest generosity when he completed the third five-year period of imperial rule. Now our devotion has grown in love for you. For the devoted order has promised sixteen hundred pounds of gold for the ten-year anniversaries of your reign, to be contributed according to urban weights—that is, tested by a more generous standard of the scales.

If the Senate had possessed strength equal to its spirit, you would know that its wealth lies in its public love for your perpetuity. But it preferred to please your clemency by the reliability of payment rather than by the magnitude of a faithless promise. Further, under a novice emperor, a sound measure of generosity is a vow to give often. Far be it from us to impose upon a good emperor more than we can provide. The generosity of those who love does not exhaust the strength of those who offer it.

Therefore, gladly accept now the subsidies decreed for the sacred treasury, and reserve for the future progress of your reign the hope of similar services.

## EPISTLE XXXIV. TO THE LORD VALENTINIAN, EVER-AUGUSTUS, SYMMACHUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

Public necessities have this characteristic: they often persuade us to attempt the impossible, lord emperor. But caution is needed, lest the difficulty of the matter produce only resentment through an unsuccessful outcome—resentment which no one should avoid more than a young emperor, whose favor ought to grow with his age.

Therefore, as I considered both the reputation of your divinity and the difficulty of the matter, I hesitated to summon the incorporated merchants, members of the eternal City, to the contribution of horses that you ordered by letter, lest a public complaint anticipate the liberation granted by your clemency. The matter remains open; it still awaits the soundness of more careful deliberation. Grant justice to what you remit to unpopularity.

The precedents for what we are avoiding come from the past. Your clemency’s father, a participant in heaven, when he had attempted to assign a small duty to this class of men, was moved by the freedom of the people and refrained. And certainly that matter involved the interests of only a few; it called more for the administration of public money than for the expense of contributing it. Yet, attentive to his own glory, so that he would not order anything against the will of those concerned, and as a most diligent and serious emperor, he forgave the hoped-for benefit as a popular ruler.

Nor should your eternity think that this near-divine man rashly abandoned his undertaking. He knew that the burdens of so great a city were sustained by the service of these corporations. One of them transports wool-bearing livestock; another gathers cattle for the people’s food; the duty of others concerns pork; one group carries wood to be burned in the baths. Some apply skilled hands to august works; through others accidental fires are kept at bay. It would be tedious to enumerate the taverns, bakery services, carriers of grain and oil, and many others who serve their native city in this fashion.

In sum, it is clear that the ancient privilege costs the Romans a great deal. By continual service they purchased the name of immunity.
