If unusual demands are added, perhaps the customary services will cease. We therefore place before you the example of your father’s clemency. I have preferred the oracle which you, his pious successor, should imitate. I ask and entreat you not to rank among other cities the people whom you, in triumph, have often honored. Better fortune will provide whatever military practice demands. Your necessity will be calmed by the merit of humanity.

## EPISTLE XXXV. TO THE LORDS VALENTINIAN, THEODOSIUS, AND ARCADIUS, EVER-AUGUSTI, SYMMACHUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

Almost from the founding of the Martial City, the custom of New Year’s gifts has grown, under the authority of King Tatius, who first received sprigs from a fortunate tree in the grove of Strenua as auspices of the new year, lord emperors. The name itself indicates that these gifts suit vigorous men because of their virtue; and therefore such an insignia is owed to you, whose divine mind awaits testimony to your vigilance more than an omen.

Receive, then, defenders of public safety, these little gifts ceremonially fashioned in gold—not because you rejoice in the honor of precious metal, but so that our devotion may testify to the prosperity of the fortunate age. We offer a first taste of goods well acquired to good emperors. Accept openly expressed service from judges who condemn hidden prices.

Rightly we offer you ceremonial cups, together with five solidi each, as offerings to divinities of integrity—gifts that burden neither your modesty nor our resources. May such a custom of duty remain around us, and may the recurring years continually renew the honor of your clemency. The prefecture will gladly perform the ceremonial office of presenting New Year’s gifts to vigorous men.

## EPISTLE XXXVI. TO THE LORD THEODOSIUS, EVER-AUGUSTUS, SYMMACHUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

I freely acknowledge what I know your clemency can answer. I accepted the appeal more out of modesty than by right, without an existing judgment, lest I be thought offended by the objection of a free, though premature, utterance, lord emperor.

For when litigation concerning the right to a will was being conducted between the next of kin of Emphasius, vir clarissimus, and the appointed heirs, who had long enjoyed possession by the benefit of the praetor, and when they impatiently demanded a judgment concerning possession, although intestate succession did not belong to them, since it was shown to have been granted to the named heirs according to the will, Priscianus and Polemonianus appealed upon notification that the matter had been postponed.

When an explanation was sought from them, they testified that others had prompted their speech, as the records attached to the letter will show. Nor was official action lacking to propose a penalty for prejudicing the case. But it was appropriate for a judge of your age to reserve the force of the constitution for the sacred imperial pronouncement, since the petitioners alleged that a stranger’s urging had driven them into an incautious appeal.

## EPISTLE XXXVII. TO THE LORD THEODOSIUS, EVER-AUGUSTUS, SYMMACHUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

My loyalty is owed to the love of your age and to care for the state, lest I conceal matters that require correction, lord emperor. Since the whole administration of civil affairs belongs to the urban prefecture, certain departments are entrusted to subordinate offices. Industrious private citizens ought to be appointed to govern them, so that each person may advance his assigned duty with unimpaired competence.

The public service now expects such men from the judgment of your divinity. But I do not wish to blame those presently in office, since it is enough for my concern if you entrust the internal offices to better men. The weight of all affairs rests upon my shoulders, while the others have withdrawn—men whom the multiple occupations of your clemency have not had the opportunity to test. The prosperity of the age possesses worthier men. The vein of good men is abundant. You will provide better for our city in the future if you choose unwilling men.

## EPISTLE XXXVIII. TO THE LORD THEODOSIUS, EVER-AUGUSTUS, SYMMACHUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

Your prosperity, lord emperor, promises the eternal City an abundance of its customary food supply. But we must be secure through reality rather than hope, which will easily be achieved if your clemency’s care also attends to this matter. For, as summer advances and very little grain is transported from the African regions, we are touched by no idle fear that the grain supply may be driven into severe straits.

Therefore I ask and entreat the salutary protection of your perpetuity that the African governors and the notary to whom your eternity has entrusted the grain transports disregard the harsher letters, and that vigorous men be sent for this business, who, while navigation remains manageable, may provide the customary loads for the nourishment of the City. This is worthy of your age and of your divine virtues: to place the security of the Roman people among your foremost and primary concerns. Fully laden ships will arrive on the desired courses, and a frequent, heavily loaded fleet will enter the Roman harbors, if the favorable support of your divinity gives them assistance.

## EPISTLE XXXIX. TO THE LORD THEODOSIUS, EVER-AUGUSTUS, SYMMACHUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

The conclusion of old disputes is difficult. A matter handled through many judgments becomes entangled through the variety of actions, the movement of those conducting the inquiry, and changes of persons, lord emperor. This is what I now encountered when I heard an old struggle between Gaudentius, guardian of the distinguished woman Martiana, and Liberius, agent of her aunt, also named Martiana while she lived.

At the very threshold of the inquiry, when the agency entrusted by the elder Martiana, daughter of C. F., was said to be invalid because it had previously been assigned to a certain principal, we found that actions had been transferred back to the lady and that rights had again been transferred to Liberius through the praetorian records. We recognized the objection concerning the void agency. Then the opposing party’s defense denied that the person whose agency was not preserved by the earlier proceedings could maintain standing.

Against this, they argued that a prior reading of the mandate had first been required and that the benefit of restoration had been granted to the agent between the parties. The dispute lingered over this point longer than it should have. But because the earlier judge, as a just defender, had restored the course of time—which could not be obtained through the agents—and because the agency was read as having been bound by the praetor’s judgment, this objection too fell silent.

Another issue followed: it was said that Martiana’s death had extinguished the mandate. Against this, the venerable enactment of Julian ordered that the duties of agents begun while the owners of the cases were alive should continue. Therefore, since Liberius had obtained both restoration while Martiana was alive and the agreement of the opposing party concerning the valuation of the property, we pronounced that the mandate had not perished.

Then, when the petitioner hastened, under the constitution of your divinity, to be put into possession of the maternal estate in order to secure the debt, because the opposing party, though summoned, had refused to make the valuation of the property, it was answered that the validity of the petition first had to be examined. I admitted what seemed reasonable.

When access was therefore granted for argument about the petitions, the defender of C. F. Martiana thought he detected a falsehood in the petitioner’s supplication: the petitioner had said that, by the will of her mother Prisca, her granddaughters born from Placidianus had received the inheritance, but he did not prove that all the granddaughters had been made heirs by her. It was answered that the petition concerned only those whom their grandmother had instituted as heirs, and that there had never been any mention of all of them, but only of those to whom the succession had been transferred.

At this point the curator’s selected advocate began to demand that the petitioner declare from which titles the proposed actions descended. Then, appearing on the claim of Placidianus, vir clarissimus, who was the father of the adult woman, he replied that the actions arose on account of excessive donations. He asserted that the supplement of the shares was sought from the heir of Placidia, to whom her sister Martiana had succeeded.

The opposing party refuted this only to the extent of saying that the younger Martiana, daughter of C. F., had acquired not only the succession of her father Placidianus but also that of her sister Placidia in specified shares, and yet that no mention of Placidia was contained in the sequence of the petitions.

But since the allegation of the other party maintained that it was pursuing the matter under the designated titles of the actions, and that Martiana, daughter of C. F., possessed the property at issue in a specified share, and since it showed by the petitions that her name had been included together with the designation of the causes, my deliberation as judge remained suspended. One side asserted that Placidia’s name ought to have been added to the supplication; the other denied that anything remained to be sought after the designation of the property and of the person who currently enjoyed possession of the corporate bodies.

A more compelling reason was added to my hesitation: the law orders that within four months the possessor must be bound to the petitioner for the valuation of the property; but, as the records will show, the time allowed by the agreement seemed far too short for valuing property belonging to outsiders. Therefore, moved by these ambiguities, I reserved all matters for distinction by the oracle of your divinity. For in doubtful matters there is one salutary course: every matter should be referred to the divine or to those close to God.

The attached pages contain the allegations of the parties and their supplements. When your majesty’s justice has weighed them, I ask that you set boundaries to this painstaking litigation by an absolute decision.

## EPISTLE XL. TO THE LORD THEODOSIUS, EVER-AUGUSTUS, SYMMACHUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

[Col. 0372C]

When your clemency had remembered that the expense of making a *carruca* had been decreed from the sacred treasury, you judged that its silver should be restored to the public storehouses, lord emperor. But a trustworthy examination established that the material used for the vehicle’s decoration had been taken from other accounts. My illustrious predecessor, Anthemius Bassus, is also said to have reported the matter to your perpetuity.

Therefore the equity of your age ordered me to submit what had been examined and discovered. Since the treasury did not possess the necessary funds at the proper time, silver was supplied for the ordered work from the quaestor’s chest, from the stores of the pattern-office as well, and furthermore from the thrift of the bankers. If the *carruca* had remained in use, its repayment would rightly have been demanded from the imperial treasuries. But now that the novelty of the carriage has been removed, each party claims what it deposited. We do not think it difficult to obtain what is requested from the fathers of the laws.

I ask you to give a response worthy of the times, so that the most illustrious and distinguished count of the sacred largesses may know that what he drew without a gap in the imperial treasury from another’s contribution must be refunded under public accounts and to private persons.

## EPISTLE XLI. TO THE LORDS THEODOSIUS AND ARCADIUS, EVER-AUGUSTI, SYMMACHUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY
I know indeed that, through the fault of human nature, integrity is subject to envy. But I am amazed that the plots of rivals have advanced so far that an innocent man’s reputation should be attacked by a crude lie, most revered emperors. For what would they not dare, and what would they leave unattempted, who have fabricated a tale of shrines in the citadel of the world supposedly vindicated against the injuries of Christian law? I believe the author of that theatrical production wept when he pretended that men had been dragged from the inner sanctuaries of the Church to torture, and when he described bishops being led in chains from distant and neighboring cities. For he could not have compelled your serene clemency, without these sophistries, to summon the people by sacred edict, so that with letters harsher than is customary for your piety they might accuse the prefect whom you elected without intrigue.

Let that man, whoever he is, now give an account of his deception—the man who, under cover of a legitimate investigation, for which you ordered me to inquire into the worship of the despoiled walls, claims that tragic interrogations concerning ministers of the Catholic religion were conducted. Let him answer the letter of Bishop Damasus, in which he denied that any followers of that same religion had suffered insult. I do not make much of the responses of my office; it was precisely for this reason that the truth of the matter was sought, lest some event escape the memory of the investigator. Let credence be given to the bishop of the law which is alleged to have been injured. Let credence be given to the prefect who, reminded of your perpetual edict, is astonished that something credited on the spot should be alleged to have occurred which Rome does not know to have been done.

I pass over the insult to the prefecture and to my conscience, since the accusation has advanced so far as to touch even you, the authors of my honor, with a certain reproach. For those who stain judges of the highest rank appear to be attacking the facility of sacred testimony. Long ago the divine father of Your Divinity honored me with exceptional distinction: he was the singular judge of merit, whose authority you received together with his character. Follow your father’s judgment; protect your own. May we who earned the prefecture without intrigue lay it down without offense.

I am thought to have abused the recommendations of the excellent man and meritorious servant of the state, the prefect of the praetorian guard, Praetextatus. But what if, despite that decree which he plausibly obtained, no investigation at all had yet been undertaken by me? I foresaw what rivals might suspect and therefore entrusted the sacred orders, sealed by the prefectural office, to their proper execution. Nor did this conjecture deceive me: I am accused of having rigorously carried out something which I am not convicted of having begun.

I have appended all these matters, set forth in the official records. I add only this: may Your Perpetuity absolve me from the necessity of the investigation whose authority you ordered to be referred to the imperial archives. For if such men were permitted to attack me while an order was in force, what will they not be permitted to do when the letters have been withdrawn? Indeed, since the honorable bishop denies that any of his people are being held either in prison or in chains, and the office gives the same report, I do not know whom in particular you ordered to be released. The laws do hold men guilty of various crimes, but, as I have discovered, they are strangers to the mysteries of Christian law.

I await with devotion what Your Perpetuity shall decide, and I ask that you blunt the deception which disturbed the repose of your divine heart and compelled the care of the revered emperor to resort to the necessity of an edict. Envy has fortified me: once its falsehood has been exposed, it will have no place thereafter in sacred ears. If, however, the murmur of detractors should again contribute anything, I desire judgment. Those who cannot prove me guilty will discover me steadfast under imperial scrutiny.

**LETTER XLII. To the Ever-August Emperors Theodosius and Arcadius. Symmachus, Prefect of the City**

A dispute recently arose concerning the tribuneship of the wine market, and it gave me cause to consult the arbiters of the laws, revered emperor. The prefect insisted that the office assigned to him should be allotted to him. An old man excused himself from resigning the honor, relying on a law that had fixed definite terms for such appointments. Following the custom preserved through long usage, I admitted the man who put forward the recent benefaction of Your Majesty. But so that, if circumstances should ever require it thereafter, hesitation might be removed from the judgment by an authoritative ruling, I have decided to consult the sacred oracle of Your Divinity: whether it is lawful for new tribunes to be postponed while the law is observed, or whether it is preferable that the old ones should be removed through devotion.

**LETTER XLIII. To the Ever-August Emperor Theodosius. Symmachus, Prefect of the City**

One consolation for my injuries has been granted by the course of events, revered emperor: that the excellent and illustrious Count Hesperius, ever devoted to your clemency and to the public welfare, was sent to Rome. For if I did not have him as a witness to the insults I suffered, who would doubt that the prefecture which surpasses the others at Rome had done something disorderly in the exercise of its authority? Since he is always a friend to truth and cherishes the reputation of good times, if Your Perpetuity grants him the opportunity, he will not be silent about the contempt shown for the laws and for the age.

For my part, I shall recount a few matters as I can, briefly revisiting the causes which, as I believe, provoked these plots against me. When, in accordance with the diligence that ought to belong to all judges, an account was sought of the public silver contributed by the tax assessors for the provision of gifts, it was discovered among the other frauds that certain men, although released from their obligations, had not paid the expense owed to the state. To conceal the deception, they contributed from someone else’s silver an equal amount to the assessors, charging it under false headings—what two men ought to have contributed.

When these most distinguished men voluntarily repaid the amount without adding to the expense, I consulted the Senate according to ancient custom, asking what the authority of the fathers indicated in a common matter. After several opinions had been expressed, the assent of that revered order approved my action.

After some days, when the excellent and distinguished vicarius came to Rome, Celsus, an advocate of my court and his associate—the associate of the man who had repaid the debt—sought protection against me and against the most distinguished prefect of the grain supply from the vicariate court. I had brought a civil action against his mother in a public case concerning the gift made by her grandson, while preserving the reply by which it was asserted that the estate of Candidatus was being retained. The prefect of the grain supply, however, was said merely to have demanded verbally from the excellent baker the public grain which Celsus had rescued with the hands of his officials.

Your Perpetuity must now judge the insult to the prefecture: its advocate, having suffered nothing, obtained the assistance of a second court.

Since these events did not at all shake my patience, something further was added which I cannot conceal. When the vicariate authority had come forth to the common secretariat to examine the records of Bassus, prefect of the City, someone—I do not know who—submitted a petition to the vicarius complaining of collusion or injustice on the part of my office. The complaint was that Memorius, a litigant whom Bassus had ordered to be taken to the African courts for the payment of a debt, had been carried away by ship, although both my distinguished predecessor Aventius and I had petitioned by written submissions that he not be sent there.

The excellent and distinguished vicarius immediately ordered him to appear, as the subscription to the petition shows. When we had both taken our seats and I had learned the sequence of the complaints from its recitation, I advised that the man who was present should enter to prove the vicariate court. His office then replied that the man who ought to have been summoned for examination by the order of his judge was absent. What should be judged of this I leave to the wise.

He was summoned once and again by the herald’s voice, yet the man did not come when called. Then, with no one assisting him, the urban office began to insist that he had been transported to Africa, where he could accuse the distinguished Bassus of a crime. It was submitted that the judgment had been obeyed; although Bassus had issued it after the parties’ struggle, the appeal did not remove it.

At this point Fulgentius, an excellent man, tribune and notary, asserted that he had summoned the assistants of the urban court so that Memorius would not sail. When he was asked whether Memorius had brought any accusation concerning these crimes against him, he said that his complaints were contained in the pages of his petitions—I believe because he did not dare to pretend that he wished to be an accuser. The assistant of the urban office replied that, through Felix, he had been ordered by the distinguished Fulgentius to have Memorius taken to Africa in accordance with the judgment.

We therefore decided that Felix should be detained, so that it might become clear whether he had acted as messenger of that order. Meanwhile the distinguished vicarius, although others were present whom we could have heard in the case of Bassus, abandoned the entire proceeding because of Memorius’ absence, an absence which could easily be remedied by recalling him from the African provinces. I do not know whether he did so at the command of those who had flocked there to be heard. I departed after promising to report the matter.

Felix, who had been ordered to be detained in the common interest, was seized in the execution of his office. When he sought from me the protection of a guard, and requested one nomenclator so that he might walk safely through the peaceful city, he was violently seized behind the prefectural carriage, by order of Fulgentius, by Gaudentius and Victor, agents in public affairs, together with Boniface, a palace official who had hitherto served in the urban office, and was taken to the house of the man whose orders he was to be examined about.

Fulgentius, the excellent man, thinking that being regarded as the author of my insult would expose him to hatred, hastened to the circus secretariat, wishing to give an account there of his unlawful act. He said that he had feared that, through the instigation of the office, Felix might be suborned.

Most august emperors, I believe you expect that the prefect, secure both in your judgment and in his own innocence, should be said to have adopted some severity. I admit it, and do not regret it: I restrained my feelings while hoping for certain vengeance from you. I ordered Felix to be handed over to sureties unknown to Fulgentius. What more lenient or milder decision could have been made?

Then he went out as though he were going to furnish a guarantee. But when the chief of his office had gone once and again to his house and could not bend the man’s obstinacy, he brought back an empty bond, by which he had postponed Felix’s return to the following day through a guarantee. He keeps at home a witness whom he knew was to be heard against him.

I also bear this insult with patience. Use the accusation as you wish, as is proper. I knew that the judges’ case is stronger when reserved for the masters of the facts. We expected Felix to be returned the next day with the office properly prepared. But on the following morning, as the records will show, he was taken away to be handed over to the vicariate authority, contrary to the assurance given.

When the chief of the office learned this, he hurried out accompanied by a few men. He detained Felix in a crowded place in the City, but did not rescue him. Thus Fulgentius, who pretends that he had been beaten, resisted the laws with a stronger hand.

Meanwhile Felix was taken away by soldiers of the vicariate authority. And when the chief of my office was heard in the presence of the Roman people, I see what judgment Your Perpetuity ought to have formed concerning this act.

I shall preserve the order of events. Under examination by another investigator, the litigant admitted that no order had been given by my attendants against Fulgentius. At Fulgentius’ command he was then brought by the heads of both offices to the common secretariat, where I had summoned all the senior officials to make an offering. Nothing had been discovered that could implicate the prefecture.

Then Fulgentius, driven by consciousness of his deed, complained that he had been beaten. But this part of the matter was soon cleared by the response of Felix himself and of the most devoted chief of the office. Nevertheless I did not deny his complaint a hearing, admitting the distinguished and eminent vicarius as a fellow investigator, should he wish to assemble the names of plebeian witnesses who were to be produced.

He promised to do so—I believe so that, through delay, my pain might either be softened by satisfaction or he himself might again contrive other plots. But, as the facts show, after the suborned man who had submitted a petition to the vicariate authority privately confessed the affair at home, Fulgentius dared to ask him that his attendants, whom he had ordered detained in prison because of the litigant’s departure, should not be subjected to insult.

After this, again usurping public authority and neglecting the judgment, conscious of his bold deed, he fled in order to forestall the prefecture’s just complaints, unaware—as the facts demonstrate—that the fathers of the human race are moved more by justice than by envy.

That these events occurred in this way and were not fabricated by any device will be confirmed by the attached dossier. In it Your Perpetuity will find that the prefecture, which you entrusted to me with a pure judgment, contrived nothing even for the purpose of public discipline’s vengeance, although every insult was endured which all good men assume ought to be punished in accordance with the vigor of the age.

For this hope and confidence weakened the right of the authority entrusted to me, so that the authors of my honor might defend with proper severity both the public dignity and the insult to their judgment.

**LETTER XLIV. To the Ever-August Lord Theodosius. Symmachus, Prefect of the City**

Every few months, the Senate’s written proceedings and the acts of the people are sent to Your Perpetuities. They will be able to indicate what Praetextatus, a man of exalted and illustrious memory, communicated either to the most distinguished order or to the people devoted to you, for the commendation of your age, revered emperor.

But because you specifically commanded by sacred letters that, if anything had been done by him at Rome in these assemblies, excerpts should be handed to the agent in public affairs, I have sent everything in obedience to your heavenly orders: everything which, in his presence, the sanction of your revered counsels defined and the authority of the fathers approved. I have also appended what he said to the people in order to summon everyone to love the good times.

As for the judgment of the citizens concerning his virtue and innocence, which they gave on the final day, I specifically reported it to the distinguished and eminent master of offices, with copies of the records appended—although, together with the other things customarily sent by public conveyance, it must all reach the knowledge of Your Serenity again.

**LETTER XLV. To the Ever-August Emperor Theodosius. Symmachus, Prefect of the City**

Cyriades, an excellent man, count and professor of mechanics, has now produced your divine rescript, revered emperor. In it Your Perpetuity had ordered that he should clear himself of certain men’s accusations and in turn press charges against anyone whom he accused of fraud.

When he had begun to accuse the excellent Auxentius under examination by my predecessor, and the matter came before my court, Auxentius, an excellent man, reproached him over the excessive expense of the basilica and bridge. Cyriades, a man of equal rank, thought that he should retaliate with a counter-accusation.

It therefore seemed appropriate that a trustworthy inspection should assess the construction of both works. I entrusted the matter to men who, in my judgment, were sufficiently conscientious. Although Cyriades almost refused, I decided to appoint to the assessment of the work masters of the building trade whom he considered more impartial toward his adversary. Nevertheless, the care and administration of the work already begun remained with Auxentius, since Your Perpetuity had not yet changed his office by appointing a successor.

After several days had passed, while the examination of the work was still pending, the office assigned to Auxentius informed me through a notary that the distinguished man had abandoned responsibility for the places entrusted to him, and that, at the very beginning of summer—when the progress of the construction ought to have been rising—nothing was being advanced.

But since the flight of a senator did not seem something to be believed rashly, I ordered that the matter be investigated with greater diligence. For a long time he could not be found anywhere. When he was ordered to appear before the sacred retinue of Your Divinity, he fled.

Meanwhile Cyriades, the excellent count and engineer, seeing that my decision had been frustrated by his departure, was deeply anxious lest his adversary contrive something against the absent man. He therefore requested that I submit both the report of my excellent predecessor and the present records to Your Perpetuity, deeply anxious lest his adversary contrive anything against the absent man. I could not deny him a hearing, since by the same route I wished, through your divine command, to learn what should be done concerning the assessment of the expenses incurred by the expenditure of both parties. For it is the concern of my office not to remain silent about the loss of public money.

The records appended to the letter will establish its reliability. When these have been read aloud and have reached the sacred ears of Your Perpetuity, I earnestly and humbly ask that the uncertainty of my mind be instructed by an imperial reply.

**LETTER XLVI. To the Ever-August Emperors Theodosius and Arcadius. Symmachus, Excellent Man, Prefect of the City**

It is certain that your clemency, out of love for good faith and devotion to truth, often recalls matters already examined for renewed scrutiny, most revered emperors. But since Auxentius, an excellent man, and Cyriades, count and engineer of equal rank, disagree with each other in a certain dispute, some derogation is made from the judgments of earlier judges.

Long ago the excellent and illustrious Anthemius Bassus, after inspecting the work of the new bridge, signed the records, assigning blame or negligence to the individual parties; and his successor is said to have examined the same places again.

Then, when they avoided renewed examination before me under the rescript which the excellent Cyriades had obtained, and when, although both were present, I had decided that an investigation should examine both the expenses and the construction, the excellent Auxentius suddenly abandoned the judgment.

As I was preparing to send a report concerning his conduct, which the interruption of the work required, I again received other decrees of Your Divinity, by which you joined the excellent and eminent vicarius to my investigation, so that, with both of us presiding, the alleged defects of the bridge might be examined.

There was no failure to obey your orders. Accordingly, with the excellent tribune and notary Aphrodisius also present, to whom responsibility for the new works had been assigned after the excellent Auxentius, an inquiry was held into those who had laid the foundations of the same bridge.

It was thereby established that a short and distinct section, begun at the beginning of winter, had collapsed under the force of the river. The builders assessed the expense of this at twenty solidi. But the collapse of that section, since it was still separated from the rest of the structure, appears to have caused no damage to the parts farther away; Cyriades, the excellent man, promises that it can easily be repaired.

After this, inspection of another place discovered a gaping joint in the stones. Cyriades, the count and engineer, reported that it had been placed in accordance with his own advice and technical judgment, so that the gaps would later be closed when the liquid material was poured in at the necessary expense.

Although he ought to have done this, he is said instead to have sought to claim the credit for his successor’s industry, so that the gaps might be closed with bundles of hay and rushes, to the discredit of the original builder. When he supported this by reading the records, the craftsman who had carried out the underwater work did not deny the act, but asserted that this remedy had been provided as part of the ordinary practice of the work, not to dishonor the excellent Cyriades.

Then, disturbed by the divergence of the replies, we restrained him as contradicting the earlier evidence. But he said that Cyriades had long been a source of fear to him. This does not seem credible, since the investigator of that period reached the truth through a searching examination.

Meanwhile the excellent Cyriades reported that the work could easily be repaired and that its stability, as had been asserted, had not been weakened even by a third winter. He himself also disclosed through indications certain matters concerning the buildings of the excellent Auxentius and the appropriation of an excessive amount of gold.

It seemed appropriate to attach these matters to the pages of the records, so that Your Perpetuity, having patiently heard everything in order, might deign to provide how, with the rivalry of the disputants restrained, both the integrity of the expenses and the soundness of the work may be secured.

**LETTER XLVII. To the Ever-August Emperor Theodosius. Symmachus, Prefect of the City**

Just as I revere the sanctions of Your Divinity, so I continually observe the most salutary decrees of your divine father. For what did he establish that could abandon the public interest?

Among the measures he introduced for the public good, he also gave practitioners of medicine an order of succession, should the fortune of death leave any position vacant. That law provided that the senior members of the same profession should judge the knowledge of the newcomers. The age, they assert, has preserved this arrangement by following it, revered emperor.

Now Joannes, an excellent man, is attempting to obtain not the rank which the divine enactments assigned to substitutes, but the rank immediately below the highest, relying on the privilege of palace service and on the special grant by which he obtained the position of Epictetus, chief physician, who at that time was still alive.

But since the law and custom required that the leading members of the same profession be summoned for examination, the entire college of physicians was brought into the judgment. Its most prominent members, not daring to decide between reverence for the law and respect for the new benefaction, had decided to assign to Joannes the vacant post which he could have held if, at the time when he was assigned to palace service, he had been added to the number of the chief physicians.

When the duties of palace rank were demanded from him, so that by producing his codicils he might show what order among the chief physicians belonged to him, he asserted that even the documents of his dignity had been taken from him through domestic plunder.

A large part of the physicians, however, supported by the divine law, produced the examples of those who had passed from the Palace into this rank while preserving the order of succession. Therefore, troubled by these ambiguities, and daring neither to break the sanction of your divine father nor to oppose the special commands, I have left the substance of the matter to the divine judgment of Your Divinity, with the allegations of the parties appended, awaiting what the imperial deliberation shall establish. It alone has the right to judge concerning divine enactments.

**LETTER XLVIII. To the Ever-August Emperor Theodosius. Symmachus, Prefect of the City**

I understand what just emperors may censure. For in cases where a reform of substance is sought, appeals ought not to be received. But I deliberately admitted the appeal now brought, so that both the indignity of the seizure and the manner of the judgment might reach the scrutiny of Your Clemency, revered emperor.

Scirtius, an excellent man, repeatedly complained that a portion of the Caesarian estate had been taken from him. When he had obtained restoration of the status he had lost, the heirs of Theseus, who were resisting, were brought forward against him.

Then Artemisius, agent of Olibrius, an excellent and illustrious man, opposed the execution, as he himself acknowledged. When I ordered the inhabitants of the place to appear so that the state of the possession might be thoroughly examined, those who were being led there were seized, in defiance of the laws, by the official Ruffinus, who was carrying out the orders.

The records will identify the authors of this uncivil act. Meanwhile I postponed judicial punishment and again assigned the matter to the office, ordering it to summon the necessary persons.

Then, when the principals of the distinguished household and the others had withdrawn, heirs were substituted to oppose Theseus—only one being produced, who asserted that he was the deceased man’s freedman. When asked where the inhabitants of the estates had gone, he replied that some had hidden, while Scirtius’ slaves had been transferred to the urban estate belonging to the excellent and illustrious Olibrius.

I pass over the remainder of what Theseus’ freedman said, although this objection does not apply to him, since he had received the benefit of freedom from the father of the minors.

With these matters established, the Praenestines, in whose territory the Caesarian possession lies, were produced after the attendants had been sent for them. Only then did Olibrius’ excellent and eminent procurator appear. The defender of the minors also attended.

Finally, when the courts compelled him to answer, a contest between Scirtius and the two parties was proposed, although the advocacy of the distinguished household and that of Theseus’ successors appeared to disagree in some respect.

The matter proceeded to an investigation of possession, which, after being debated through the various conflicts of the parties, lawfully passed to the questioning of witnesses. I ordered the curiales to be admonished individually, according to custom, by name and rank. I sought replies from each and then asked for the rightful possessors of the places. After that I inquired who had paid the annual obligations or the assessments.

When all the testimony proceeded in Scirtius’ favor, and it was established that he had held the possession with Theseus, I investigated when and by whom he had been dispossessed. They generally agreed that it was about the second or third month before, when men of the distinguished and illustrious household had expelled him.

After hearing the testimony of the leading men, I again admitted the defenders, who argued against one another. The questions and answers were communicated to the parties.

There Tarpeius, the excellent man and procurator of Olibrius, asserted that six unciae of Theseus’ estates had been acquired by Olibrius at Theseus’ death. Scirtius, on the other hand, did not deny the six unciae which the minors retained even with his consent, nor did he say that it mattered to him whether the agents of the distinguished household or the heirs of Theseus enjoyed that same portion.

Then, after the actions had been joined, they began to press Scirtius with the claim that, in accordance with the mandate of C. F. Faciana, he had returned six unciae to Theseus by letter and had voluntarily bestowed six others upon Theseus’ children.

In reply, Scirtius said in private letters that the amount had been transferred to Theseus or to the children by way of gifts, at Theseus’ request, so that the reliability of the records might strengthen the benefaction.

Indeed, since the later records testify that six unciae of the estate had been transferred to them jointly and indivisibly, we understood that the donor’s portion had been retained. For why would he give something jointly and indivisibly if nothing remained for him to retain?

But when I said that this concerned the question of ownership, the defenders read a constitution which grants judges the power, but does not impose the necessity, whenever they judge possession arising from succession, to decide at once, if circumstances require it, also concerning the right of ownership.

In consequence, they confessed that they preferred to proceed to another issue. Moreover, Scirtius alone did not appear to be pressed by the question of ownership, since the opposing parties themselves also disagreed with one another to some extent concerning this portion.

Therefore I judged the possession in accordance with Scirtius’ documents and the testimony of the principal witnesses, confirming his adversaries in the retention and legal right to the six unciae. I reserved the principal case, without prejudice to the parties’ allegations, for a future examination.

I then issued a copy of the judgment, when the eminent man’s procurator immediately requested its publication. Scirtius then produced sanctions by which he sought to show that appeals have no place in a reform of substance.

On the following day, the distinguished and illustrious procurator and the defender of the minors, who had been thought to disagree in court, indicated their agreement by joining their appeals.

This is the entire substance of the struggle. Now the outcome of the litigation awaits the oracle of Your Divinity. I have appended the records and the supplementary submissions of both parties; instructed by these, may Your Perpetuity deign, by the example of one case, to provide security for all.

**LETTER XLIX. To the Ever-August Emperor Theodosius. Symmachus, Excellent Man, Prefect of the City**

[Col. 0381B]

The body of collectors is responsible for selling solidi, which public usage frequently requires; the wine treasury supplies them with a fixed price. To this class of men, weakened by the small profit of the assessment, the divine brother of Your Divinity established that an amount should be contributed for each solidus equal to what the fairness of that time demanded, revered emperor.

But as the extraordinary rise in the value of gold gradually increased, the force of the divine remedy was broken. Since a solidus is valued at a higher amount in the marketplace for goods sold, the money-changers pay lower prices.

They therefore petition Your Perpetuity, in proportion to present conditions, for an increase in the most just assessment, since they can no longer bear the burden of such a great charge. This is the cause of their complaint, which the reliability of the records will more fully explain to your divine senses.

If you judge the type of petition reasonable, I ask that an order of your gentleness also convey a salutary remedy to this group.

**LETTER L. To the Ever-August Emperor Theodosius. Symmachus, Prefect of the City**

The palace officials responsible for sacred payments, Amicus and Castor, while pursuing public revenues, summoned the heirs of Postumianus, an excellent man, before my court along with the other names which they were prosecuting through legal action, revered emperor.

Lucian, who had previously handled the senator’s assessment, advised that only that household was liable for the payments of gifts. One part of the debt was said to press upon Lolliana, another equally upon Cattianilla and Severella.

Meanwhile, after the name of Lolliana, C. F., had been set aside—the collection binding her for six unciae—a dispute arose among those whom responsibility for payment burdened according to each quarter of the property.

After the hearing had generally been adjourned to a later date, the matter was brought to the point at which the treasury’s advocates demanded that the distinguished persons provide assurances guaranteeing completion of the payments in successive installments, while the written defense of Cattianilla and Severella was sent to the imperial fiscal department.

For this was an old question, frequently debated in the investigations of the prefecture, and it had reached the judgment of your renowned and ever-revered father. Consulted through a petition of Juventius, prefect of the City, of distinguished and illustrious memory, he marked in part of a rescript that it was established that the gifts due from Cattianilla and Severella, distinguished women, had been paid at the appropriate times.

This has until now made me ready and inclined to demand proof of the assessments, since the emperor’s assertion appeared stronger than all the assurances.

It is for Your Clemency to judge concerning his replies, which will endure in perpetual honor. We are accustomed to venerate divine oracles rather than interpret them.

The records are at hand, and the parties’ supplementary submissions continue to be presented. It is right that human hesitation should be informed by the judgment of Your Majesty.

**LETTER LI. To the Ever-August Emperor Theodosius. Symmachus, Prefect of the City**

It is characteristic and closely related to savage character to arm one’s spirit with the example of impunity, revered emperor. For why should someone despair of a second escape who has evaded the snares of an earlier crime?

The preceding judgment is relevant to the present case, since Valerianus, an excellent man, who is said to have an estate in Epirus, is moved neither by the reverence due to rescripts, nor by the severity of the laws, nor by the good faith of agreements, nor by respect for judgments.

First ordered to be summoned before the praetorian court, he evaded the force of the rescript of the highest authority through a petition of the excellent Junior. Then, summoned by proconsular edicts, he frustrated the laws by the same device.

For when he was pressed by both a civil action and a criminal accusation, he uncivilly resisted the established orders, as the attendants of the prefecture of the City recorded, some in notarial documents and others in reports. One of them informed the agent in public affairs, after the death of the person to whom execution of the sacred order belonged, that he had suffered serious insults from Valerianus.

Moved, therefore, by the indignity of such complaints, and seeing that the judgments might again be mocked if I adopted any more severe measure, I thought it best to reserve the authority to decide this case for Your Perpetuity. For you alone have the legal power to correct offenses committed by a person of the highest rank.

The truth is explained by the consistent records of events. Nevertheless, the attendant who returned to the Senate and reported the senator’s defiance and servile assaults will be present, when circumstances require it, with his reports.

I ask your eternal clemency, after weighing everything with your customary fairness, not to allow the frustrator of so many judges to wander any farther.

**LETTER LII. To the Ever-August Emperor Theodosius. Symmachus, Prefect of the City**

[Col. 0382D]

It is difficult for a case to be good when its action is transferred to the law through the desperation of another. The facts proved this fully, revered emperor.

For Theodorus, as he asserted, having been appointed procurator by a certain Anania in a matter concerning his property, brought a certain Flavianus to court by announcing a lawsuit, when Cuprasius, a most distinguished and upright man, presided over the urban tribunals. But he failed to observe the appointed day and allowed the lawful period of the case to lapse.

After a long interval, when he sought restoration from me and I had brought the parties together for the necessary examination, a prescription arose after many allegations, which the courts rejected as invalid. It asserted that the periods ought to have been renewed after the death of the possessor.

For it was established that not only Flavianus, who had first accepted the question brought before the law, but also his successor had completed the course of life.

In addition, a reading was introduced which, as the evidence appears to show, declared that renewal had been granted only to the heir of the petitioner. Although this was asserted in words, it was not supported by the enactments and was overturned by the reading of a contrary law.

Following therefore the clear statutes, not annulled by any imperial replies, I judged that the proceedings should cease, since a lawsuit announced against one person could not, after the time limits had expired, bind another person.

Then, when petitions of appeal and renewal were submitted, the judgment was suspended. Your Perpetuity will assess its merit after reading the records and the connected rebuttals.

I ought not to be prolix in reporting, since the case had already been rejected by the laws almost at the very threshold of the proceedings.

**LETTER LIII. To the Ever-August Emperor Theodosius. Symmachus, Prefect of the City**

[Col. 0383B]

In cases of appeal, I would rather infringe the law of authority than endure the uncertainties of interpretations—especially when conscious that the judgment was not unjust, and that it will gain some distinction if strengthened by the pronouncement of your Eternity, Lord Emperor. Accordingly, I admitted the appeal rashly made by Constantius Suarius, after I had restored, on the basis of a rescript from your Divinity, the status that he had taken away from Theodosius in his absence. For your Clemency, moved by petitions and complaints, ordered a brief inquiry into whether, after Theodosius had been placed outside the conflict and then appealed lest he lose his property, Constantius had thereby acquired possession of the persons concerned. Having therefore cited the divine instruction, I initially reserved the examination of the entire matter to the presence of Your Illustriousness’s vicar, although it had been specifically entrusted to me by the delegation of Your Serenity. For this case appeared to be connected with the other appeals that had been denied admission under my predecessor, Your Illustriousness, who had appointed another examiner together with me.

Then, when you retained for your own examination that part which belonged to the judge of that period, separating it from the inquiry into the appeal, and when I no longer had a fellow participant in the judgment, I heard, in obedience to the rescript, the complaint concerning the disturbance of possession. Since it was clear that Theodosius had not been present at the judgment in which he complained that his powers had been taken away, and since Constantius exposed no falsehoods in his petitions, I carried out the heavenly judgment concerning the supplicant’s brother and heir, restoring the status that was clearly defended immediately afterward by the appeal that was brought. This was so even though the subordinate official under examination stated that the petitions published by Theodosius had remained in his possession.

Nevertheless, obeying the imperial commands, I ordered that the reliability of the earlier proceedings be sent to the Augustan archives. From this arose the appeal, whose justice or contumacy will be weighed by the sacred judgment. Meanwhile, mindful of the constitution, I ordered the movable property and its revenues to be sequestered, so that exploitation during the intervening period might not abuse what was not lawfully due. Faithful documents of all the proceedings have been joined, as usual, to the report together with the parties’ supplements, so that you may finally grant a stable conclusion, by your divine decision, to a case long tossed about.

**LETTER LIV. To the Ever-August Lords Theodosius and Arcadius, Symmachus, Vir Clarissimus, Prefect of the City**

[Col. 0384A]

All of us who are advanced to the highest ranks of honor by the judgment or favor of your Clemency ought to strive with the greatest zeal to protect the reputation of our age by the truth of our representations, Lord Emperor. For what means of repaying the favor shown by princes will Fortune find unequal to the benefits, if it abandons the loyalty that alone fortifies the empire?

As I contemplated, therefore, the rescript of your Divinity by which you directed that the debts owed to the wine treasury be recovered from the prefect in whose tenure they were said to have been incurred, I could not remain silent about what accords with the justice of your reign. First, I confess my astonishment that, while your heavenly gentleness is occupied with the affairs of the whole world, letters of the deified Constantius were represented to you in such a way that a conditional threat was treated as though it were a debt. Second, I am astonished that, through some omission, the part of the rescript that concerned the office was passed over, so that the person of the judge, as though he were of lesser standing, might be oppressed by the impunity of his own attendants. Third, the sum of solidi that the inquiry and report of my illustrious predecessor proved to have been paid for the most part is now demanded from the treasury as though it were both due and untouched.

Therefore, amid the many matters that occupy your attention, some points must be treated briefly. The inquiry of the prefecture, the letters of the examiners, and the writings of my predecessor, Your Illustriousness, all showed that 11,446 solidi had entered the sacred treasuries from the year following the consulship of Sergius and Nigrinianus. In the midst of so much substantial evidence, I could not violate by silence the loyalty I owe to your Clemency—especially since I observed that your Divinity had acted with its customary caution: you did not sign the rescript with the name of a judge, and you judged that the person who was to be summoned was still alive.

For how could your Clemency have extended the force of an old threat against a dead man, when even the punishment for serious offenses is discharged by the end of life? Indeed, the terror contained in the letters of the deified prince could not have compelled even a living man. You often threaten your subjects with severe measures, more in order to sharpen their diligence than to harm them. This too your deified father, who will live forever in the minds and speech of all, established by a pious law: he deprived even a sentence issued under threat of any effect or enforcement.

The condition that the deified Constantius added to his letters was undermined by many events that became known later. While that same emperor was still ruling the world, the collection was transferred to Tertullus, the memorable prefect of the City; if it had depended on the power of a single man, it might have remained attached to the person of the earlier judge. Not long afterward, responsibility for this charge fell upon Clytholius Maximus, then holding equal rank. Under the rule of your deified father, who guided Roman laws and destinies, the task was entrusted to prefects and examiners, and the collection of the public debt was assigned in turn to successive administrators.

Most recently, your deified brother made Basil himself liable, appointing over him one who spared no persons among the judges; he made the principal secretaries of the urban office, whose diligence had ensured collection through successive administrations, liable either to pay the debt or to render an account. Thus the inquiry conducted both by Your Illustriousness and by the most distinguished Anicius Bassus, as well as by Aventius, a respectable man, repeatedly discovered that the greater part of the debt had been paid; it also found the undertaking of the provincial judges, who declared that, if the urban office ceased its efforts, they themselves could make good the full amount of this charge.

When these matters are compared with the laws, your Eternity will pronounce that the undertaking was real but the threat merely terror. Moreover, it is reported that the recent dispatch of attendants to compel the provincial judges created hope that the debts would be recovered. It is not my part to pursue uncertain rumors concerning reputation. Your divine Majesty will discover why this collection has lacked continual attention.

For this operation targets my father-in-law, the man of most illustrious memory, Orfitus; and Your Illustriousness and the illustrious master of offices have entered his heirs in their letters, although the modesty of your sacred oracle expressed no name. What, then, should I think of the treatment of a man who lived for nearly fifteen years with greater honors than resources? Is a threat often read, always disregarded, and then buried by subsequent decrees—one that neither the imperial law admits nor the payment of a large part has left standing—to be revived against a dead man, although it was never applied against the living?

Or should I think that this is done to insult me, and that the sequence of so many statutes of such authority, the recent instruction of the deified Gratian, the diligence of the examiners, the inquiries of the prefects, and the reliability of the report are to be wounded by new representations? I call God, guardian of your Divinity, as witness that I consider no one worthy of such an injury.

You granted me this prefecture in peace, without any personal favoritism. If envy happens to trouble anyone, or if I have not yielded to someone’s wishes because of my devotion to the commonwealth, let him consider that private hatreds must not be exercised against the laws. Finally, let whoever he is recognize that neither I nor my heirs entered into succession to the man of most illustrious and distinguished memory, Orfitus, whether by legal right or by acceptance of his property.

I therefore ask that no fraud be prepared against either the law or innocence, to the insult of your judgment. When have proceedings conducted among others harmed people who were absent and ignorant of them? Who has ever received a sentence of your Divinity without being heard? When has a threat ever been extended to heirs? Certainly, to speak of the case itself—which, with your favor toward me and my relations, concerns me under no legal right—the greater part of the debt is shown to have been paid; the remainder lies against clearly identified names.

For what purpose are debtors to be freed by diligence in collection, while innocent persons are entangled? I therefore appeal to the justice implanted in your divine minds: do not allow people ignorant of the matter and strangers to their father’s inheritance to be harassed by an inappropriate summons contrary to the determination of the deified Gratian, contrary to the rescripts of so many princes who ordered the prefects to recover the debts, and contrary to the report that demonstrated that the larger sum had been paid while stating, according to the letters of the governors, that the remainder was to be extracted from those liable.

Nor, pious Emperor, should you introduce the unprecedented example that the succession of nobles who have governed the commonwealth should not pass safely to their children. This precedent will restrain many, and, as I think, more justly, those who may have abused your provinces. But the descendants of the man of illustrious memory, Orfitus, sought nothing from him except the distinction of their lineage.

This representation is nevertheless an injury to me. No one succeeded to his frequently exhausted poverty by testament, nor did any of us succeed through acceptance of his property. Hence your Clemency understands that I am troubled not by fear for a family case, which is protected by the laws, but by concern for the times, lest useless envy should return only to the detriment of the innocence of your treasury.

These points have been stated only briefly, so that adjournment should not delay the matter entrusted to me, and they concern only the share sought on behalf of my wife Rusticiana, a most distinguished woman. Her sister, whose resources are much narrower, has been ordered to come from distant Etruria. We all pray your saving Divinity that the unexpected ruin of a senatorial house may not be thought able to discharge what has already been returned for the greater part from so many provinces, but which difficult collection is still laboriously exacting.

This condition will harm many who have governed the commonwealth. For it would not be right that a single family should be crushed by a novel precedent. I therefore ask you to deign to hear the proceedings that confirm the truth of the report and to review the laws, whose severity you have often moderated, in your Clemency, through decrees issued by your governors.

**LETTER LV. To the Ever-August Lord Theodosius, Symmachus, Prefect of the City**

Your prosperity promises the Roman people inexhaustible supplies, Lord Emperor. Yet the caution of the judges continues to require attention, so that diligence may secure what better fortune promises. The daily supply of grain is readily available; only the supply of oil, brought in too sparingly to sustain the populace, causes concern.

Your Illustriousness, the prefect of the grain supply and a diligent executor of his responsibilities in the most exalted praetorian prefecture, recently reported this matter, as he himself states, sending the customary brief reports that disclosed the shortages in the storehouses. But as the deficiency grows more serious, concern for the homeland could not remain silent before your Clemency, since its hopes and resources are increased by the favor of good princes.

We therefore all humbly ask—if you await petitions, although you anticipate everyone’s prayers with your benefactions—that your divine utterance promptly urge the African judges to bring this commodity into the Roman storehouses. Speed is necessary before prolonged distribution exhausts what remains. Add this favor, therefore, to the others you are accustomed to provide, so that all the blessings of the age may flow together in equal abundance.

**LETTER LVI. To the Ever-August Lord Theodosius, Symmachus, Prefect of the City**

Day and night I am anxious to advance the commands of your divine Clemency through prompt obedience. For it is not permissible that decrees favorable to justice and the laws be postponed through lengthy adjournment, Lord Emperor. Care must therefore be taken lest delay introduced by others into the execution of your instructions disfigure my reputation.

When your Eternity recently entrusted me with judgment concerning Macedonius, who had deserved ill of the commonwealth, and likewise concerning Ammianus, I learned from the testimony of the protectores that Ammianus had been consumed by illness when he was in the vicinity of the City. Various reports are circulating about Macedonius, whom the vigilance of the guards ought long ago to have brought before me.

I therefore ask your gentleness that delay contracted through another’s diligence or negligence not be held against me. At the same time, I beg that your venerable Eternity distinguish what must be sought separately, in case the care of those pursuing him has handed the designated defendant over to my jurisdiction.

**LETTER LVII. To the Ever-August Lord Theodosius, Symmachus, Prefect of the City**

You alone among all people can rescue the expenses of the Eternal City from a shortage of funds, Lord Emperor. The subordinate authorities of your Majesty are capable of applying remedies only to moderate difficulties; they are overwhelmed by the weight of major matters.

We therefore hasten to you, saving Divinity, and implore generous assistance for the Roman people’s treasury, to which the provinces assigned for taxation have for a long time contributed none of their customary revenues. There is consequently good reason to fear that, as support ceases, necessary services will be abandoned—services that until now have been sustained by impoverished persons, as they complain, at the expense of others.

Moreover, when the venerable order was consulted and could not itself remedy the distressed situation, it sought the assistance of your Eternity. An account has been drawn up of the taxes that were supposed to bring in supplies from Spain and Alexandria. The office has also arranged the appropriate headings of expenditure.

I ask that, after willingly examining all the connected materials, you swiftly provide a remedy for the public interest. Since the circumstances are urgent, the regular payment of expenditure cannot be denied. Therefore, as you customarily do, favorably extend assistance; and you who bring new benefits to the Roman people’s pious minds, preserve the old ones as well. Deign to grant your City both what past neglect has suspended and what future use awaits, with favorable success.

**LETTER LVIII. To the Ever-August Lord Theodosius, Symmachus, Prefect of the City**

In matters concluded by time and judgment, it is right to end the excursion of a lengthy speech, lest extended verbosity burden the salutary acts of your Divinity and loquacity without relevance to the facts become wearisome, Lord Emperor.

When a case involving violence was being heard before the judgment of the governor of Apulia, between Marcellus, who complained that he had been dispossessed, on the one side, and Venantius the strator and his sister Batrachia, as he himself confirms, on the other, the defendants rashly brought an appeal because the provincial examiner, after sending letters to the vicariate authority, retained the inquiry he had undertaken.

The judge of the sacred court was then consulted by the governor concerning the appeal. He imposed a preliminary fine upon the appellants, and charged the petitioner himself with the offense, together with execution of the penalty. After this, certain proceedings took place through the parties’ concealments, so that the completed judgment would be prolonged.

For my distinguished predecessor, when he learned that the fine had been collected—a preliminary appeal having acknowledged it by decree of the sacred court—decided that the criminal case ought to be transferred to him. I followed the same course and summoned the parties for examination. But since the time for restoration had elapsed, and since the treasury had either awaited or received the penalty for the appeal, while the declaration of Venantius and Batrachia concerning the violence, together with the capital condemnation of certain persons, had also brought the matter to an end, I pronounced that the inquiry belonged to the sacred court.

I further judged that Venantius, whom Your Illustriousness and the illustrious master of offices had ordered to be produced, should be returned to Decentius, the agent in affairs, under whose escort he had come. But since Marcellus had accused Venantius the strator of unlawful and usurped military service—for, as the proceedings showed, although enrolled among the decurions, he had crossed over to the palace camp contrary to the laws—I ought not to suppress the accusation. In a matter exceeding the scope of my examination, your Eternity should judge with greater authority according to the very laws that you protect.

**LETTER LIX. To the Ever-August Lord Theodosius, Symmachus, Prefect of the City**

It often happens, through the logic or the fortune of cases, that in disputes one party relies upon equity and the other upon strict law. When human judgment falters, the examiner’s deliberation has recourse to the oracle of your Clemency, Lord Emperor. The character of the present case likewise demands this.

Musa, having reached legal age, complained that Syntrophius had been admitted to a share of her father’s property. The curator Acholius had fraudulently brought him in as though he were her adult brother. Musa obtained complete restoration through the support of the law. But after being drawn through many appeals and various judgments, she was unable to pursue the actions she had initiated within the limits of the proper time.

As the circumstances required, she restored the benefit she had lost by means of a petition for restoration. Yet the same woman’s misfortune was deprived even of the kindness of a rescript. For, after the course of four months had been delayed, the examiner allowed her to fall outside the final day of the time that had been granted; and when his successor arrived, he deprived her of authority after issuing an interdict.

Afterward, when she wished to repair the unhappy lapse of the case by restoration, she was rejected through reliance upon the Constantinian law, which denied any extension beyond the specially granted periods. An appeal was then brought against the judgment. When the matter came before the sacred court, the same constitution was again produced by Faustinus, heir of the curator Acholius. The procurator to whom Musa had entrusted her actions proved that the case had fallen outside the time through no fault of his own.

He also produced the enactments of your divine parents, the deified emperors, which, among other exceptions, grant restoration to litigants if a case lapses through the examiner. Since, therefore, the Constantinian law—which removes restoration after specially granted periods—does not exclude this case of an examiner’s failure to act, and since the more recent enactments of the deified emperors have provided restoration for all cases if they are abandoned by a judge, I could not incline readily to either side.

Instead, I reserved the outcome of this carefully contested dispute to the august arbiters of the laws, which is the one remedy appropriate to uncertain circumstances. I appended all the proceedings in the customary manner, so that their reading might establish the truth of my representation.

**LETTER LX. To the Ever-August Lord Theodosius, Symmachus, Prefect of the City**

The disputes of cities and peoples, being greater than those of private individuals, must be judged by a more august authority, Lord Emperor. It was therefore appropriate that I reserve for the judgment of your Majesty the case of the people of Puteoli and Terracina, which, after the examination of the governor of Campania, passed by appeal to the sacred court; for I perceived that it was balanced on an equal scale.

The matter at issue is as follows. The deified Constantine granted the municipal citizens of Puteoli 150,000 modii for the nourishment of the city. This amount was reduced by half when the deified Constans was governing the commonwealth. After him, Constantius, likewise received among the gods, granted the people of Puteoli an additional 25,000 modii of grain after a petition had been submitted. Thus the same people came to receive 100,000 modii for their sustenance.

But when the deified Julian was governing the commonwealth, Lupus, who presided over Campania with consular authority, observed the distress of the people of Terracina. The towns that had long ago been assigned subsidies were contributing nothing, and he feared that a city which supplied the Roman people with wood for the public baths and lime for the repair of the walls might collapse, exhausted by a sudden deficiency. He therefore assigned to the use of Terracina 5,700 modii deducted from the municipal citizens of Puteoli, and reported the measure as established and defined by the most exalted praetorian court.

Mamertinus at that time held the honor of the prefecture. Although he confirmed the arrangement, he nevertheless sought an imperial decision. He received no reply, because the ruler of the empire was then occupied by the Persian war. From that point the distribution continued for several years, until a delegation from Capua approached the deified and renowned Gratian, the brother of your Divinity, lamenting only its own losses. It obtained from him the restoration to all cities of the quantity of grain that Cerealis had taken from many cities of the Roman commonwealth.

On the occasion of the rescript, however, when the provincial supply had recovered only the 38,000 modii that had been added to the storehouses of the Eternal City, the municipal citizens of Puteoli also refused the 5,700 modii to the people of Terracina.

When this case came before the provincial court, Your Illustriousness, without considering the amount preserved by the rescript of the deified emperor, decreed in a general judgment that everything should be returned to the people of Puteoli. But after the appeal, the sacred court’s examination perceived that the quantity of grain restored to the Campanians had been decreed from the 5,700 modii that the city of Terracina had received for the needs of the Eternal City.

Since the divine rescript remained in force, the court could neither confirm the subsidies that the people of Terracina were receiving by the judgment of Lupus and the confirmation of the prefect Mamertinus—for no authority of a sacred reply existed—nor remove them from the city, lest a people obligated to the interests of the Eternal City should lack its just benefits.

Therefore, as is customary in doubtful matters, we hasten to the salutary judgment of your Clemency, although the defense of Puteoli, after the promised report, thought that an appeal would be futile. The reliability of the proceedings is at hand and can strengthen your Eternity. I ask and beseech you to grant at last a stable remedy to a matter that has been wavering for many years.

**LETTER LXI. [Note: See the two letters that Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, wrote against this letter of Symmachus in volume XVII of our Patrology, columns 961–972. Editor.] To the Ever-August Lords Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, Symmachus, Prefect of the City**

[Col. 0390A]

When the most exalted Senate, forever your own, recognized the vices that had been subdued by the laws and saw the reputation of recent times cleansed by pious princes, it followed the authority of a good age, disgorged its long-suppressed grief, and once again ordered me to be the ambassador of its complaints.

Wicked men had for this reason denied the divine prince a hearing: justice would not be absent, Lords Emperors. I therefore perform a double office: as your prefect, I pursue the public proceedings; as the citizens’ ambassador, I commend their instructions. There is no disagreement here between our wills, because people have ceased to believe that they can advance through the zeal of courtiers if they disagree with them.

To be loved, honored, and cherished is greater than imperial power. Who could tolerate private quarrels harming the commonwealth? The Senate rightly pursues those who have placed their own power above the reputation of the prince. Our labor, however, keeps watch on behalf of your Clemency.

For whom does it serve better that we defend the institutions of our ancestors and the laws and destinies of our homeland than the glory of your age? That glory is greatest when you understand that nothing is permitted to you contrary to the custom of your ancestors. We therefore seek the restoration of the status of the religions, which long benefited the commonwealth.

Let the opinions of the emperors of both religious parties be counted: the one nearest to our time honored the ceremonies of the fathers; the more recent did not remove them. If the religion of former times does not establish an example, let the restraint of recent times do so. Who is so intimate with the barbarians that he does not seek the altar of Victory?

We are cautious about the future and avoid the omens of grim events. Let honor be restored to the name that has been denied to the divinity. Your Eternity owes much to Victory and will yet owe her more. Let those reject this power who have gained nothing from it. Do not abandon the patroness who is the friend of your triumphs. This power is desired by all. Let no one refuse to honor what he professes to wish for.

If there were no just reason to avoid this omen, at least it would have been fitting to refrain from removing the ornaments of the Senate-house. Grant, I beg you, that what we received as children we may leave to our descendants in old age. The love of custom is great. The deed of the deified Constans rightly did not last long. You ought to avoid all the examples that you soon learned to set aside. We care for the lasting reputation of your Divinity, lest a future age find anything that needs correction.

Upon what laws and words of yours shall we swear? By what religious scruple shall a false mind be terrified from lying in testimony? Everything, indeed, is full of God, and no place is safe for the treacherous. Yet the presence of religion has great power to intensify fear of wrongdoing.

That altar safeguards the concord of all; that altar brings together the trust of individuals. Nothing gives greater authority to our decisions than the fact that the entire order decrees as though under oath. Will the sacred seat therefore be exposed to perjuries, and will the renowned princes who are protected by the public oath judge this acceptable?

But it is said that the deified Constantius did the same. Let us rather imitate the other deeds of that prince. He would have undertaken nothing of this kind if someone before him had gone astray. The lapse of a predecessor corrects the successor, and amendment arises from criticism of an earlier example.

Perhaps that father of your Clemency did not guard against unpopularity in a matter that was still new. Can the same defense apply to us if we imitate what our own mind disapproves? Let your Eternity accept other deeds of that same prince and make them more worthy of use.

He took nothing away from the privileges of the sacred virgins; he decreed priesthoods for nobles; he did not deny expenditures for Roman ceremonies. Following the joyful Senate through all the streets of the Eternal City, he saw the shrines with a tranquil face, read the names of the gods inscribed upon the pediments, asked about the origins of the temples, and admired their founders.

Although he himself followed other religions, he preserved these for the empire. Each person has his own custom and his own rite. The divine mind has distributed different guardians among all cities. As souls are assigned to those who are born, so tutelary spirits are assigned at birth to peoples.

Utility also contributes, and it is what most strongly establishes the gods for human beings.
