Since the whole rational explanation lies hidden, where can knowledge of the divine come more appropriately than from the memory and evidence of past successes? If long duration gives authority to a religion, then faith maintained through so many centuries must be preserved, and we must follow ancestors who followed their own ancestors successfully.

Let us now imagine Rome standing before us and addressing you in these words:

“Best of princes, fathers of your country, respect my years, to which pious ritual has brought me, so that I may use the ceremonies of my ancestors; I do not regret them. Let me live according to my custom, for I am free. This worship brought the world under my laws; these sacred rites drove Hannibal from my walls and the Senones from the Capitol. Was I preserved for this purpose, to be criticized in my old age? I shall see what sort of thing it is that is thought necessary to establish. Yet correction in old age is both late and insulting.

“Therefore we ask peace from the ancestral gods and the gods who dwell within the land. It is right that whatever all worship should be regarded as one. We all behold the same stars; the sky is common to us all; the same universe surrounds us. What difference does it make by what wisdom each person seeks the truth? One road cannot reach so great a secret. But this is a debate for leisure. Now we offer prayers, not arguments.

“How much benefit has been gained for your sacred treasury by removing the prerogative of the Vestal Virgins? Under the most generous emperors, what the most frugal provided is denied. The only honor in that allowance is the stipend of chastity. Just as their fillets adorn their heads, so it is regarded as a distinction that they have been exempt from public duties. They seek, so to speak, only the bare name of immunity, since their poverty protects them from expense.

“Thus those who take something away from their property contribute more to their praise; for virginity dedicated to the public welfare gains in merit when it lacks reward. Let such savings be absent from the purity of your treasury. Let the treasury of good princes grow not through the losses of priests but through the spoils of enemies. Does any profit compensate for unpopularity?

“And because avarice does not belong to your character, those from whom ancient supports have been removed are all the more pitiable. Under emperors who abstain from what belongs to others and resist greed, what is taken away causes only injury to the person who loses it; it does not awaken desire in the one who takes it.

“The treasury also retains lands left by testament to the virgins and their attendants by the will of those who have died. I beg you, priests of justice, to restore private succession to your City’s sacred institutions. Let them make their wills without fear, and let them know that under non-avaricious princes what they have written remains secure. Let this happiness of the human race delight you.

“This example in the present case has begun to trouble the dying. Do Roman religions not come under Roman laws? What name shall be given to the confiscation of property that no law and no circumstance has made liable to forfeiture? Freedmen receive legacies; slaves are not denied the legitimate benefits of wills. Only noble virgins and ministers of the rites ordained by fate are excluded from estates acquired by inheritance.

“What benefit is there in dedicating a chaste body to the public welfare, supporting the eternity of the empire with heavenly protections, attaching friendly virtues to your arms and wings, offering effective prayers on behalf of all, and yet not possessing rights equally with all? Thus slavery rendered to human beings is better than this.

“We injure the commonwealth, which never benefits from ingratitude. Let no one think that I am defending only the cause of religion. From such crimes have all the misfortunes of the human race arisen.

“The law had honored the Vestal Virgins and the ministers of the gods with modest maintenance and just privileges. The integrity of this provision lasted until the degenerate money-changers converted the sustenance of sacred chastity into payment for lowly porters. Public famine followed, and the sickly harvest disappointed the hopes of all the provinces.

“These are not faults of the soil. We blame neither the south winds nor rust; mildew did not harm the crops, nor did wild oats destroy the grain. The year dried up because of sacrilege. For everything denied to religious institutions had to perish for everyone.

“Certainly, if there is some example of this evil, let us attribute such famine to the cycles of the years. A harsh atmosphere compressed this barrenness. Life is prolonged on wild shrubs, and once again the poverty of the rural people has driven them to the oak trees of Dodona.

“What comparable suffering did our ancestors endure when public honor fed the ministers of religion? When was the oak shaken for human use? When were the roots of plants torn up? When did mutual fertility abandon the alternating needs of the regions, while the grain supply was shared by the people and the sacred virgins?

“The produce of the earth commended the nourishment of the priests; it was more a remedy than a largesse. Is there any doubt that what was once given for the abundance of all has now been claimed by the poverty of all?

“Someone may say that public expenditure has been denied to the expenses of an alien religion. May such a judgment be far from good princes: what has been assigned from the common stock to certain persons ought not to appear to belong to the treasury. For since the commonwealth consists of individuals, what proceeds from it becomes again the property of individuals.

“You govern everything, but preserve what belongs to each person; justice has greater force with you than license. Consider your own generosity: would you wish these things to be regarded as public property, when you transferred them to others? Once savings have been granted to the honor of the City, they cease to belong to those who grant them; what was originally a benefit becomes, through use and time, a debt.

“Someone attempts to instill an empty fear in your divine mind if he claims that you should feel the obligation of those who made the grants, unless you have incurred the unpopularity of those who remove them. May the hidden protections of every religious tradition favor your Clemency, and may those above all that once helped your ancestors defend you and be honored by us.

“We seek the religious order that preserved the empire for the deified father of your throne and supplied legitimate heirs to the fortunate prince. That aged deified emperor looks down from the starry citadel upon the tears of the priests and believes himself blamed for violating a custom that he himself gladly preserved.

“Grant also to your deified brother the correction of another’s counsel. Conceal the deed that he did not know had displeased the Senate; for it is clear that the delegation was excluded precisely so that the public judgment should not reach him. It is a matter of preserving the reputation of earlier times that you should not hesitate to abolish what must be recognized as not having been the prince’s own decision.”

**LETTER LXII. To the Ever-August Lord Theodosius, Symmachus, Prefect of the City**
It is certain and clear that nothing is so closely allied to the laws as your decrees, Lord Emperor. Yet the wrongful interpretation of executors, while favoring petitioners, for the most part corrupts orders. Your brother, received into heaven, had determined that, when Martianus, formerly protector of Aggaria, had claimed certain property as ownerless, if the inheritance had neither a designated nor a legitimate successor, it should be granted nakedly to the imperial treasury as its owner; and that then, after the matter had been reported through the accountant of the imperial patrimony, the petitioner should await what your sacred Humanity might grant him.

It is now nearly the second year in which, through the defenders and accountants of the most august imperial household, and despite the solemn justice of the imperial rescript, the designated heirs have been worn down, although the sixth year is already being counted from the reading of the will. Most recently, the fortune of the case encountered an impassable reef in a disgraceful investigation. For when, before the most perfect accountant Bassianus, proceedings were first brought against the informer concerning the property in accordance with the sacred enactments, the prescribed rule was trampled underfoot by a novel act of audacity. Thereafter, when the reading publicly established the validity of the will lawfully executed, an empty accusation was brought: that the signatories had received some legacy or other under the same will. Imperial documents were also added, by which the support of a certain person was removed—a person who was said to have assisted his cause by his testimony—[Col. 0393D] as though it were plausible that a modest honor, with which the deceased had sprinkled the subscribers out of friendship, could abolish a legitimate judicial determination.

For if we lived under such laws, we would make better use of hostile signatories, whose resentment would demand no act of humanity from the testator. It pains me to say that among five solidi, the principal legacy was that of a subscriber. For the others received rather an honorable remembrance than a monetary gain. Thus either I was the heir of extreme poverty, if it is thought that a small honor wounded the reliability of a legitimate judgment; or, if the hereditary estate is considered more substantial, the brief sum of the legacy is free from suspicion. Who does not call upon his closest friends to sign when his final arrangements are being made? What wonder, then, [Col. 0394A] if the person who deserved to be called in, having been present before his eyes, should also deserve some memorial of affection?

I cannot tolerate a signatory to whom a large portion of the property is conveyed. For even if he is enriched with an undivided conscience, he is not enriched with untainted modesty. But these slight pledges are left either as a token of affection or out of the testator’s sense of propriety. Nothing has been taken away from this practice by the new laws. This custom remains, and, so long as we preserve the laws, it will always remain. Only one accountant has emerged since human memory began who would introduce an example of a new kind of judgment.

From this arose an appeal. When the matter had entered the sacred tribunal by decree and also under your law, an empty invention was again proposed in order to evade the judgment: it was said that an inquiry delegated by the distinguished official, the count of private affairs, was an examination belonging to the accountant, and that therefore the case ought again to be transferred to the judgment of that same official. Yet since the entire question, arising from the petitions of Martianus, formerly protector, and from the generosity of your Clemency, belonged by appeal to the sacred tribunal, especially in view of the recent sanction which, under ancient law, assigned such indiscriminate appeals to the tribunal that acts in the place of the emperors—

Having therefore examined everything, I pronounced that the property was not subject to the rescript: for the eternal justice of your Divinity had determined that, if an inheritance lacked designated or legitimate successors, the treasury should be admitted; but Marcellus, Bizias, and Heliodorus had taken possession of these assets in accordance with the deceased’s wishes. Now the venerable defender of the imperial household has suspended my judgment by an unprecedented appeal. But since he suggested that no example of an investigative proceeding in this matter existed, I nevertheless willingly admitted the submission, summarized everything in my report, and appended the documentary record of the proceedings, presuming that what I had judged according to the laws and in keeping with the reputation of the age would please benevolent emperors.

## Letter LXIII. Symmachus, Prefect of the City, to Theodosius, Ever-August

Petronianus, formerly a soldier of the urban cohorts, advanced to the rank of cornicularius through the long duration of blameless service. In accordance with the custom and practice of our ancestors, he thereby earned testimony to his military diligence—a distinction which the judgments of others, too, have conferred after an honorable course of service, Lord Emperor. It is therefore worthy of the divine felicity of your age that, if the kindly face of your Perpetuity smiles upon him, a solemn privilege should adorn his completed service without offense.

## Letter LXIV. Symmachus, Prefect of the City, to Theodosius, Ever-August

I am concerned that those who agree in spirit and dignity should enjoy mutual honor. It is therefore fitting, Lord Emperor, that the decree of the senate concerning the invincible brothers of your Divinity should reach them, if your Clemency approves, through your introduction.

Their ancestor and parent, as I remember having written some time ago to Your Excellency and Illustrious Master of Offices, was honored with equestrian statues, which the venerable order decreed for him in remembrance of the African and British wars. The purpose was plainly that, alongside the just titles of earlier commanders, the devotion of those presently serving you might be encouraged.

## Letter LXV. Symmachus, Prefect of the City, to Theodosius, Ever-August

[Col. 0395A]

When the lessees of the saltworks had been reduced from a very large number to a few and could no longer bear the burden of the public necessity, they submitted a petition and obtained the privilege that those who had previously been enrolled and excused should be restored, and that they should promptly receive proper reinforcements from other corporations or from vacant positions, Lord Emperor.

Accordingly, having cited a divine order, when they discovered that many had previously been protected in their association through the intervention of Macedonius, they obtained a report concerning their protections. For it is the exclusive right of your Clemency to rescind rescripts improperly obtained. Then, as the shortage pressed, they began to summon the shipowners, who were likewise liable to the function of supplying timber, to an equal responsibility, so that the concern of both corporations might recognize a common and undivided obligation. But the shipowners preferred to surrender certain men from their own turmae rather than enter into partnership in so great a burden.

Thus it happened that, with the consent of the parties concerned, certain men were joined to the lessees. Now the public interest demands your Perpetuity’s firm decision that, through surreptitious petitions, the reinforcements of an established corporation not be stripped away. I have appended the record of the proceedings to my report, both concerning those whom the intervention of Macedonius had released and concerning the proceedings completed while I was presiding—proceedings in which, without regard for anyone’s dignity, the will of the shipowners assigned certain men to the lessees.

It will now belong to your sacred Divinity both to invalidate the recommendations of those whom it is shown that influence freed and to close the avenue of petition to those whom the assent of their own corporation assigned.

## Letter LXVI. Symmachus, Prefect of the City, to Theodosius, Ever-August

[Col. 0395C]

In accordance with duty and custom, I bring to the attention of your Perpetuity the names of the magistrates to whom the most illustrious order, at the time of their designation, entrusted various functions, Lord Emperor, so that the imperial administration may receive information about those appointed to discharge offices or assume the fasces. Joined to these are those whom recent elevation added to your senate.

I ought not to be prolix in such matters, since the reliability of a public decree demands rather the presentation of the record than the eloquence of a lengthy reporter.

## Letter LXVII. Symmachus, Prefect of the City, to Theodosius, Ever-August

[Col. 0395D]

Even if ancient practice had not established a procedure or order for sending brief statements of the census to your Clemency, Lord Emperor, the diligence of a good age would nevertheless demand the reliable fulfillment of the public instruction. For it is fitting that rulers and fathers of the human race should be informed what the admission of new senators adds to the venerable order, and what an exemption removes.

A quarterly statement will provide your Perpetuity with a reliable account of these matters. I have solemnly obtained it from the census office and appended it to the pages of my report, so that your Majesty may learn how many colleagues have entered the most distinguished curia, and what increase a new registration has given to the senatorial census or what an old exemption has cut away.

## Letter LXVIII. Symmachus, Prefect of the City, to Theodosius, Ever-August

[Col. 0396A]

The fame of your wars does not conceal their glorious outcomes, but the proof of victory that is confirmed by the eyes is greater, Lord Emperor. Some time ago the Roman People had learned by report of the funerals of the slaughtered Sarmatians. Now the joy of the messengers has been confirmed by the triumphal spectacle.

We are no longer inferior to the examples of antiquity. We saw what we admire: a chained column of the conquered nation being led in, and those faces, formerly savage, transformed by pitiable pallor. In the middle of the arena stood the people who had previously been an object of terror and were now subjected to entertainment; hands accustomed to the weapons of their nation held gladiatorial instruments.

How fortunate was the commander of this war who, relying on the auspices of your divine Clemency, utterly destroyed some of the enemy for the security of the provinces and preserved others for the joy of the martial populace. Your judgments rightly answer to him; he is deservedly celebrated often in imperial letters. For such devotion could find no worthier herald.

May the use of laurels be frequent and easy for you, and may the courage of the soldiers seize those who may have raised impious audacity against the Roman name, while the city’s arena weighs them. May you continually bestow these things upon your devoted citizens as tributes of your valor.

## Letter LXIX. Symmachus, Prefect of the City, to Theodosius, Ever-August

The duties of every authority are clearly defined. It is the particular business of the urban prefecture to protect the rights of senators, Lord Emperor. Therefore, compelled by the necessity of my office, I could not fail to attend to the allegations of distinguished men who were demanding what was just.

Eusebius, a palatine official, had been ordered to exact a number of slaves from them and to reopen the inquiry into the property of Catulus, a man of illustrious memory, although it had been concluded by sacred judgments and rescripts. This aroused the complaints of the leading men, who had long enjoyed their share.

The case therefore came before the laws, at the wish of the executor, whom contradiction was repelling. The sanctions of your Divinity were invoked—those which forbade the transfer of senatorial disputes from the urban court to foreign tribunals. But when I asserted that the slaves were not subject to the same privilege as those whose petitions your Perpetuity had assigned to a particular judge, the reply was that a subtle petition had attacked the fortunes of distinguished persons.

Meanwhile, while Donatus was present, joined by sacred rescript to the other offenders, I asked, as is customary, whether another person had been placed under the same name, what his condition was, and whether he himself had petitioned concerning the judgment of Catulus. He then declared that he was the slave of the distinguished man Hilarianus and firmly asserted that he had had no part in the petition which he was said to have submitted with the others. Thus the reliability of the petition seemed to waver even as to its author.

Another submission, full of law and reason, was added: after repeated hearings and numerous rescripts issued in response to reports, those who had petitioned again contrary to the prohibition had incurred the penalty of the law. For judgments existed which, when an appeal had attempted to suspend them, the deified father of your Clemency, consulted through a report, had used to bring the matter to an end.

The treasury had shared in that victory, receiving, as was asserted, a fixed portion of the profits from the property of Catulus, a man of illustrious memory. Since, then, the senators’ allegation rested upon rescripts and laws, they preferred to disclose their case to your justice through me rather than vindicate it by legitimate judgment, confident that you would preserve the decrees both because of the necessity of the law and out of reverence for your deified father.

Accordingly, they delivered the slaves in good faith. Equity in these times, as we presume, will not permit them to be heard after the completion of the proceedings, to the prejudice of those who were absent.

## Letter LXX. Symmachus, Prefect of the City, to Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, Ever-August Emperors

You know better than anyone what legal condition belongs to an indictment, founders of public law, Lords Emperors. For provision has been made that no one should rashly rush into danger for another’s life unless he first bound himself by a pledge to undergo the same penalty.

Acting according to these provisions of the laws, Africanus, an agent in affairs, formally brought an accusation and charged Companus and Hyginus, distinguished men, with the crime of violence. Immediately, as severity required, military custody surrounded the accused, without regard to their dignity.

But when the parties appeared before the court, and the hearing had proceeded through much struggle among the advocates, it overflowed more with speeches than with proofs. Since the case was being drawn out through a long sequence of words, we summoned the leading men of the city of Aricia, whom the accuser had called forth as accomplices, to participate in the inquiry, and asked them about the order of events.

Everyone agreed in asserting that no disturbance had been fabricated. Then, to evade the judgment, the presence of a certain person began to be demanded—a person whom the indictment did not hold. At last the matter reached the point where the parties on Africanus’ side sought, in despair, to abandon the accusation.

It remained that, since the crime had not been proved, the penalty feared by the accused would pass to the accuser. But since Africanus’ military service as well as his heedless youth moved me, I preferred to reserve judgment concerning him to your Clemency. For magistrates are in one position: their judgments appear corrupt if they are more lenient than the laws; the power of sovereign rulers is in another position, and it is fitting for them to bend the sharpness of strict law.

I appended the record of the proceedings to my report and also joined the supplementary submissions of the parties. I ask your most august Perpetuity, after weighing everything, to order what should be followed.

## Letter LXXI. Symmachus, Prefect of the City, to the Emperor Honorius, Ever-August

It is not fitting for me to remain silent about anything that happens in the City, in view of the duty of service that I always offer to your Majesty. When Bishop Zosimus had long been suffering from a serious illness, to such an extent that he was frequently reported dead, it happened that he died on the second day after my arrival.

Immediately, as had been agreed, I addressed the people and admonished them that everything should be concluded through the peaceful deliberation of the clergy, and that popular disturbance should not involve itself in arranging affairs. For it was certain that, in choosing a bishop, the judgment of Almighty God had to be awaited, Lord Emperors Honorius and Theodosius, pious, fortunate, renowned conquerors, Ever-August.

I also admonished the organized bodies, issued warnings to the officials, and deterred the leading men of the districts, so that no one would attempt to disturb the peace of your City. This was observed in such a way [Col. 0398A] that everything was concluded without uproar.

But when the holy man Eulalius had been brought by the people and clergy to the Lateran Church for the funeral rites of the former bishop, he remained there for two days with a very large crowd and with several priests, so that the customary day might be awaited on which he could be solemnly ordained.

While matters stood thus, several priests suddenly hurried with Boniface, a priest of the same rank, to the church of Theodora, having gathered the people there; and after deliberation had taken place, they began to propose ordaining him bishop. When I learned this, I summoned all the priests who were there together to come to me. Sitting with the distinguished tribune Serenianus, I admonished them not to permit anything rash to be done, or anything contrary to the order of sacred law or to customary practice.

But they resisted with such obstinacy that they did not hesitate in the least to do whatever they had been forbidden. For they even decided that the priest Boniface should be ordained in the church of Marcellus, and proceeded with him to the basilica of Saint Peter.

Since it belongs to your Piety to give judgment in this matter, I immediately thought that, in accordance with the concern appropriate to my office, I should consult your Majesty, so that whatever your Piety should decree might clearly instruct the matter by the command of your Divinity, etc.

Dated the fourth day before the Kalends of January.

## Letter LXXII. The Emperor Honorius Augustus to Symmachus, Prefect of the City (C)

After reviewing all the proceedings, it became entirely clear from the report of Your Sublimity that, in the ordination of the venerable priest, the insolence of a few had attempted to violate the ancient peace. For, after the departure of the venerable Zosimus, when a multitude had gathered by common judgment and acclaimed the suitability of Eulalius to be installed in the proper order, and when the confirmation of the successor had preserved in every respect the requirements of the rule of Catholic discipline, we are profoundly amazed that some should have hastened to ordain another while disregarding the solemn occasion.

It is right that our gentleness should properly rise up to chastise their act, unless we decide that they should be admitted to pardon on this sole ground: that, quickly recognizing their own fall, they have returned to seek the support of supplication and ask to be forgiven because, as they complain, they acted under compulsion.

Let Your Sublimity therefore know, by the present authority of our Clemency, that our will and purpose concerning Eulalius, the bishop and guardian of sacred law, are in agreement. The appropriate number of ordainers, the solemnity of the lawful time, and the suitability of the place have rightly conferred upon him the dignity of the venerable name.

Since it is clear that Boniface lacked all these things, we have judged that our decision was needlessly awaited, since those who had presumed to act appear to have condemned their own deed by the petitions they have submitted.

Accordingly, with the order made definitive and the extraordinary presumption removed, we decree that Boniface be immediately forbidden from entering the City under the prohibition imposed. It will be to his credit, out of modesty, if he obeys the heavenly decrees and departs voluntarily; if he resists more stubbornly, we order him to be expelled against his will.

Your Sublimity, Symmachus, dearest and most beloved father, shall also order the instigators of the plebeian sedition and their associates to be detained and suitably punished, so that this rashly undertaken act may not pass [Col. 0399A] unpunished.

For this purpose it has pleased our gentleness to send Aphrodisius, a distinguished tribune and notary, so that, in his presence, what we have decreed may be carried out more quickly, in order that the peace of the people not be disturbed and that the whole community may peacefully honor him whom, according to ancient custom, the observed mysteries of sacred law have received.

Dated on the third day before the Nones of January, at Ravenna.

## Letter LXXIII. Symmachus, Prefect of the City, to the Emperor Honorius, Ever-August

As soon as the sacred message of your Piety, by its speed, anticipated the people’s expectation, it removed everything that the diversity of opinions had appropriated concerning the election of the bishops, and at the outset cut away by divine providence what, through the delay of an unskilled multitude and the growth of competing loyalties, would have been more difficult to remove, Lord Emperor.

For this reason I hastened immediately, in the service required of me, to fulfill what had been commanded. And—something that must be credited to the felicity of your Clemency—a matter of unprecedented character, of the greatest contention and struggle, was brought to an end, as it had begun, without any admonition of the people, and with the peace of the entire multitude preserved under your Clemency.

For at the time when the sacred authority reached me, on the very day on which the holy solemnity was to be celebrated, I immediately sent the chief secretary and summoned Boniface to come to me and acknowledge what had been commanded, so that he might abstain from the procession which he had learned was forbidden to him.

He disregarded the summons, proceeded onward, and handed over to the people the man whom I had named to be flogged. When this was reported, after conferring with the distinguished tribune Serenianus, I sent both the sacred documents and a detachment of officials to Saint Paul’s, where he had assembled, for the sake of precaution, so that the gathered crowd would not rashly do anything injurious to the public authority in defiance of the commands.

But he allowed neither to take place. Since he wished to return to the City together with the people, both his associates and the apparitors immediately met him at the gates to prevent him, as had been decreed, from entering your City. Yet he thought that these too should be disregarded and entered forcibly. At a certain part of the City, several people came out to meet him and drove him back; he was not permitted to carry out what he intended.

When the crowd accompanying him saw this, it dispersed without any disturbance. He himself was led outside the walls and remains not far from the City. But, lest he should secretly enter the City by night, hurry to the church, and again stir up the people’s zeal, after common deliberation and in accordance with the concern appropriate to my office, I arranged for four associates and apparitors to watch there without injury to him, while awaiting what your Piety would decree, so that the peace hitherto preserved might continue.

As for Eulalius, the venerable bishop, who on that day was celebrating the solemn rites at the basilica of the holy apostle Peter with almost the entire multitude, as soon as the commands of your Piety were published, the whole city rejoiced.

I therefore thought that the things which the Roman people, in their public joy, testified with varied acclamations while giving thanks to your Majesty should be published, and I included everything in my report, so that your Piety might recognize with what peace the whole City had corrected what had been wrongly admitted through the rashness of a few, and with what gratitude it had received what your Clemency, guided by divine judgment and reverence for the religion that must be preserved, had thought should be decreed and established forever for the peace of the Roman people.

Dated on the sixth day before the Ides of January.

## Letter LXXIV. The Priests on Boniface’s Behalf, Reporting in a Letter or Petition with Firm Confidence What Had Happened, Since They Knew the Emperor Had Been Deceived by the Report (C)

We ask your Clemency, most pious and merciful Emperors Honorius and Theodosius, Ever-August, after the departure of the holy Pope Zosimus of the Catholic Church of the City of Rome. As custom required and the discipline of religion itself dictated, several of us priests gathered together to deliberate by common judgment concerning the appointment of a successor.

But because the archdeacon Eulalius, having almost all the entrances blocked, was holding the Lateran Church with deacons, a very few priests, and a disturbed crowd of the populace, while impiously disregarding the funeral rites of the chief priest, we hurried to the same church on the following day, where it had previously been decided by everyone that we should meet after consultation.

There, having taken counsel with the Christian people, we elected the man whom God commanded. For we asserted that the venerable Boniface, an old priest, most learned in the law, proven in good conduct, and—what honored him most—unwilling, had been consecrated in accordance with the divine institution, by the acclamation of the entire people and the consent of the better citizens.

It is established that the blessing was celebrated at the proper time, with approximately seventy priests subscribing and nine bishops from different provinces standing by. Everything required by the solemnity had first been celebrated.

But the aforesaid Eulalius—who had earlier been formally summoned by many through three of our fellow priests not to presume to undertake anything rashly, contrary to the knowledge of the senior clergy—having ensnared a very few priests, maltreated and committed to various forms of custody those who had come with letters to prevent him, and having also brought with the others the bishop of Ostia, who is known to have been summoned when nearly dead—for his old age and illness testify that he was dragged there against his will—burst through ambition into a place not owed to him, with the order of religion neglected.

He then began to defend his act through men ignorant of discipline and improperly informed about religion, thinking that he could obscure the divine judgment by human disturbances.

And since it is clear that your Clemency was deceived by a false report, so that you might sanction something injurious to the divine will—for whatever the election of so many confirms is divine—we ask your Piety to order the earlier decisions removed, and to require Eulalius, who has intruded into another’s place, to be brought to the presence of your Serenity together with his instigators.

For we declare that the holy Pope Boniface will appear with our priests. Leaving their individual titles, all the priests will be present to proclaim their will—that is, the judgment of God.

Let your Clemency also order all those whom the case binds to be present, and let those unwilling to come be expelled from the City, so that they may not avoid being brought before you.

When the uncertain matter begins to be investigated, you will find that it is abhorrent to all divine laws and may even be displeasing to human ones. For this result we shall offer your eternal rule the greatest and fullest thanks.

## Letter LXXV. The Emperor Honorius, Ever-August, to Symmachus, Prefect of the City

After Your Sublimity’s report had been brought to the ears of our gentleness, the delegation of the priests placed before us a matter requiring no superficial deliberation. Therefore, setting ambiguity aside, it is fitting to examine the faithful order of events directly and, with many judges present, to approve which side the order omitted from the proceedings condemns and which side the order preserved supports. Thus, after weighing the character of both acts together, we may rightly uphold one and ensure that the other, undertaken rashly, does not remain in force, Symmachus, dearest and most beloved father.

For this reason, Your Illustrious and Exalted Greatness shall, by the authority of this present decree, suspend everything decreed above, without establishing prejudice against anyone in the meantime, and shall summon both Boniface and Eulalius, most religious men, with worthy insistence, so that they do not delay presenting themselves in the city of Ravenna by the sixth day before the Ides of February.

All and each of those who were responsible for either ordination shall be admonished not to be absent after setting aside excuses. Each shall defend his own conduct toward the other by producing the documents of ecclesiastical institution, and, having cleared himself, shall prove that the other has offended more seriously against Catholic law through his presumed and undeserved election.

If either neglects to appear for judgment concerning his status, he shall receive the judgment he deserves—understanding, surely, that he acted thoughtlessly, indeed unlawfully, since he does not dare defend his actions in person.

We have also summoned by letters of our Serenity a suitable number of priests from different provinces, so that, after the matter has been brought into doubt, the discussion of the many may be resolved before us.

Since everything has been reserved intact for the future judgment, no one ought to flatter himself concerning what has already taken place. The example of the present judgment will also teach what must be observed in such matters in the future.

Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, through Aphtonius.

## Letter LXXVI. Symmachus, Prefect of the City, to the Emperor Honorius, Ever-August

When the distinguished Aphtonius, decurion of your sacred palace, had come to the venerable City with the heavenly command, I hastened in every way to render obedience to the orders of your Divinity.

For immediately, after the nobles had been assembled, the sacred order was published, and a summons was sent to the religious men Boniface and Eulalius, Lord Emperor. I also ordered their clerics to be admonished, so that, with your Piety conducting the inquiry, nothing should be lacking to the future examination.

I have therefore appended all these matters below, gathered into the sequence of the proceedings, for a complete account.

But after each side of the people had been agitated by separate disturbances, I summoned the individuals with an admonition not to assemble at a single church and, contrary to what was permitted, for the crowd to fight among itself. But this seemed to them, I believe, suspicious: I had thought that peace should be urged upon men who wished to disturb the City.

For this reason both sides most slanderously believed that they should appeal by formal protests, so that they might excuse their error through fabricated lies. To ensure that none of this should remain hidden from your Clemency, I sent the very submissions they had offered, inserted into the official record, so that they could not complain that anything had been suppressed.

It remains for your Clemency not to allow your servants’ absence to be attacked by the partisanship of either side. Having always been approved by your Majesty through pure service, your servant believed that he ought, as was proper, to abstain both from opposition to and from favor toward either party.

Dated on the eighth day before the Kalends of February.

## Letter LXXVII. The Emperor Honorius Augustus to Symmachus, Prefect of the City (C)

The judgment of matters requiring great deliberation must not be hasty, nor should decisions that are sanctioned for perpetual observance be issued rashly. Often, after disputes between factions, an inquiry concerning the bishops of the eternal City has been entrusted to the examination of priests.

But so that nothing hasty might be produced by the speed of judgment, our Clemency has reserved the matter to its own discretion. Since, however, the proximity of the holy days required the presence of a bishop, and since it is not lawful in the most sacred City to celebrate, especially the days of Easter, without a priest, let Your Illustrious Magnificence, Symmachus, dearest and most beloved father, know that we have chosen Achilleus, who is known to be free from the favor of either party, to perform the sacred mysteries in accordance with the observance.

After the feast days have passed, we shall consider at a more mature council, through the judgment of the priests, what must be preserved.

We admonish you, once the leaders of the districts have been summoned, to provide for public discipline and peace. Order the commands of our decrees to be disclosed to them, so that no one may dare to stir up any disturbance or sedition. If anyone seeks such a thing through insane persuasion, he should know that punishment will be exacted not only from those discovered in the disturbance but also from the leaders of the districts.

For we know that public peace is easily preserved when the desires and fomentations of those who incite disturbances have ceased.

## Letter LXXVIII. Symmachus, Prefect of the City, to the Ever-Illustrious, In Every Respect Magnificent, Deservedly Exalted Constantius

Whatever happens suddenly, when no one expects it, cannot be attributed to the fault of the judge, and unsettles a people ignorant of reason through an unforeseen novelty.

The religious man Eulalius entered the City at midday on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, without my knowledge. I thought that he had brought some order with him. But that same day, toward evening, the bishop of Spoleto sent a letter warning me that he had been ordered to celebrate in the City on the holy day of Easter the sacred rites that had reached him.

I had previously known nothing of this order, Lord Ever-Illustrious, in every respect Magnificent, Deservedly Exalted and Most High Patron. When the arrival of Saint Eulalius became known to me, I immediately thought that the commands of the invincible prince had to be obeyed.

Meanwhile, however, on the appointed day Saint Achilleus entered the City, and a popular disturbance arose, so that on one side an armed crowd, equipped with swords and weapons, gathered at the forum in military dress.

When I had summoned the nobles and proceeded in order, after consultation, to calm the people by addressing them for the sake of the City’s peace, they first came to the assembly. Then, when Saint Achilleus’ presence was awaited so that he might publish what had been commanded, he could not come because the crowd resisted.

When both I and the distinguished vicar, driven by the urgency of the people, had entered the Forum of Vespasian to urge peace upon the multitude of both sides, suddenly armed slaves attacked with weapons and stones—and some also with swords—the people belonging to Eulalius’ party, who had assembled unarmed to learn what had been commanded concerning the bishop of Spoleto.

They wounded them so severely—those who had come prepared against the unprepared—that they even seemed intent on attacking me and the distinguished vicar, while in their seditious fury they admitted no reason at all. Unless divine power had been present to rescue us, and unless we had escaped by a more secluded route and avoided the blows of stones and the attack of the conspiring crowd, we could scarcely have got away.

It is established that the greater part of these men were slaves, some of whom have been recognized and detained and must be examined.

I therefore hastened to report to Your Excellence what belonged to my office, so that, once the events had been investigated, Your Greatness might determine a definite conclusion.

Since Saint Eulalius had entered the City, and the bishop of Spoleto had followed on the third day, while no orders from your Powers had been delivered to me for me to follow, a disturbance of the entire populace arose—a populace enraged against itself and endangering the judges.

Unless you order by a swift reply, before the venerable day of Easter, what is to be done, the people threaten to fight one another, since each side believes that the other must be excluded from the Lateran basilica.

Therefore, lest anything adverse occur—which may the felicity of Your Sublimity avert—I ask you to decree by an explicit order that the dangerous obstinacy of this frenzied contention be excluded.

Dated on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.

## Letter LXXIX. Constantius to Symmachus, Prefect of the City (C)

So that we may learn each matter with certainty and so that the instigators of the factions may not escape the notice of a reliable messenger and inspector, we have sent our chancellor Vitulus, so that he may convey the address of the Lord, the invincible prince, and his judgment to Your Exaltedness and to the people with swift dispatch.

We also admonish you that whatever is contained in the sacred authorities must not be violated by any rashness, and that what has been commanded must be carried out promptly and insistently. Otherwise the Clemency of the Augusti, now recognizing what it has delayed, will not hesitate to correct it by the force of its Majesty.

## Letter LXXX. The Emperor Honorius Augustus to Symmachus, Prefect of the City

[Col. 0403D]

While our clemency, eager to restore peace, had devised this kind of counsel for healing the error of the first disturbance—namely, that until an absolute decision concerning the confirmation of the urban priesthood should be issued, each of the two men on whose account the earlier tumult had arisen should be separated from residence in the Most Sacred City and remain awaiting the future judgment, with the period of confinement clearly specified for either one—we cannot calmly overlook that, contrary to the beginnings of our clemency, a public war was all but declared against them, so that they might be crushed; and that Eulalius, who transgressed the commands, was its instigator, since he did not permit himself to remain away even briefly, in accordance with the sequence of the instructions.

[Col. 0404A] Symmachus, dearest parent.

Let Your Sublimity know that we established this so that both the salutary earlier order of the command and the measured decree of the synod should be observed. We judge that this cannot otherwise be done unless Eulalius is pressed with every force, so that, departing from the City with all speed, he may not by his presence offer incitement to the insolent populace, nor become the cause of death to the innocent. He must have no doubt that, if he persists in this obstinate presumption, not only has a judgment already been pronounced concerning his position, but one concerning the danger to his safety must also be issued. For guilt now deserves no pardon when, having been warned, it is not avoided. He will have no excuse from claiming that he is being held back by the populace against his will.

If anyone from the number of the clergy should judge that communion ought to be given to Eulalius while the judgment is pending, let him know that he too is to be condemned by the same sentence.

As for laymen who, after our prohibition, should think that Eulalius’s communion ought to be sought, let them know that they will undergo the punishment of proscription if they occupy an honorable station, while slaves will suffer capital punishment; nor are their masters to be rescued from this danger. Let the leading men of the districts know that, unless they have subdued and restrained the spirit of the undisciplined populace, they will be seized and handed over to the final judgment.

The bishop of Spoleto, however, as had previously been determined, shall complete the order of the festive solemnity during the holy days of Easter. We decree that the Lateran church shall be open to him alone for celebrating the sacred mysteries, while the others who attempt such a thing are to be driven away. We further admonish that the aforesaid priest of the city of Spoleto must be received in the latter’s place, in order to complete the order of the sacred mysteries.

Throughout all the titular churches and places [Col. 0404C] regularly frequented by large gatherings, let these things that we have established be publicly announced, so that it may be clear to everyone both that we have not wished to perpetrate anything disorderly and that we are still awaiting the restoration of what has been disturbed.

Let Your Sublimity know that the chief secretary and the rest of the office that assists your actions will suffer not only the expense of a very severe fine but also capital punishment, unless it hastens to provide, through strenuous effort, an effective fulfillment of the measures of our clemency.

Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of April, at Ravenna.

## LETTER LXXXI. SYMMACHUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY, TO CONSTANTIUS, ALWAYS ILLUSTRIOUS, MAGNIFICENT IN ALL THINGS, RIGHTLY SUBLIME AND EXALTED

As soon as the sacred commands of our invincible lord and emperor [Col. 0404D] had been delivered, I immediately rendered the obedience that was required, as had been agreed. But Eulalius, with the same obstinacy with which he had entered the City without the sacred command, likewise refused with equal pertinacity to leave, although compelled to do so by every authority.

For during the evening hours, on the very day on which the command was delivered, he is acknowledged to have learned through the Urban office what the invincible emperor had ordered, most illustrious, most sacred, magnificent, rightly sublime and exalted lord and patron. After it was read, he stated that he would consider it more carefully, but, though repeatedly urged, he did not take care to leave.

On the following day, after once again being warned through the entire staff, even during the night hours, he gathered a crowd and rashly believed that the Lateran basilica should be invaded. [Col. 0405A] After consultation with the leading men, orders were issued to all the offices that he should be expelled. The distinguished vicar had also decided to go to the same basilica, but at first he was unable to approach it because of excessive fear.

For my part, although I had sent both the armed officials and the entire office, I could not go there, lest some rival should bring religious odium upon me. Nevertheless, with Your Excellency’s authority preserved, when numerous armed officials and the leading men of the districts who serve the imperial commands rushed in, Eulalius was driven from that church, expelled from the City, and, with officials assigned to him, sent to the place where he had been ordered to reside.

I also ordered that the religious man, the holy bishop Achilleus, should celebrate quietly what had been commanded, after Eulalius had been expelled, without any disturbance of the populace, out of reverence for the holy days. For I placed officials on guard at the Lateran basilica, so that it might not be handed over to anyone else.

Several clerics of Eulalius’s party, instigators of the sedition, have also been arrested, and I await instructions concerning what is to be ordered about them. Since I have thought it right to report to Your Excellencies everything that has meanwhile taken place, whatever may be reported in the following days for the peace of the City, which Your Felicity governs, I shall communicate separately, in accordance with the truth and sequence of events, with better evidence.

## LETTER LXXXII. THE EMPEROR HONORIUS AUGUSTUS TO SYMMACHUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY (C)

Our serenity acted with exceptional moderation, lest presumption find an opportunity. For the judgment of the venerable priests was deferred to the judgment of God, so that whatever religion and whatever truth required might be decided by calm deliberation, without any disturbance.

But the text of the report has shown that, through Eulalius’s usurpation against the decision of the venerable synod, many unlawful acts were committed there. By supplying the populace with a cause for fury through his presence, he wished to destroy everything that our moderation preserves.

For when, by our arrangement and by the decision of the bishops, whose greater number had assembled in the synod, and with the agreement and declaration of the parties, it had been determined that anyone who entered the City to incite the people would thereby know himself to be specially condemned, he forgot himself and demonstrated by his present action what kind of beginning he appeared to have made.

Since, therefore, it is clear that he was rightly expelled from the City after so many offenses, and since the judgment of our clemency and of the bishops appeared to have established that he ought not to approach it, let Your Sublimity know, dearest and most beloved parent Symmachus, that we have determined that the venerable man Boniface, bishop—whose moderation we rightly judged should be joined with our authority—ought to enter the City, so that under his guidance reverence for the religious law may be fulfilled with firm moderation.

Given on the third day before the Nones of April; received on the Ides of April.

## LETTER LXXXIII. SYMMACHUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY, TO THE LORD HONORIUS, ALWAYS AUGUSTUS

[Col. 0406B] Whatever is done with God as its author is rightly confirmed by the divine judgment of Your Piety. Recently, when the sacred authority of Your Clemency had been issued to me, your servant, as though all uncertainty had been removed, Your Majesty strengthened the priesthood of the venerable bishop Boniface.

What had been commanded proved so pleasing to everyone that both the most distinguished order and the Roman people approved it, my lord emperor. For when the heavenly statutes had been recited by me to the people and published in edicts displayed out of affection, such fervor and joy arose throughout the entire City that everyone, in fitting thanksgiving, testified that religion had been restored and security of peace provided.

After a two-day interval, therefore, the aforementioned venerable bishop entered the City, with the entire populace rushing to meet him, just as [Col. 0406C] Your Serenity had ordained; nor did the services of my office in any way fail. No disagreement now remains among the people, and all have accepted the will of God and of Your Majesty.

With the factions therefore ceasing, everyone began to think as Your command, prompted by God, had established. Through the acclamations set out below, the Roman people expressed the reasons for their joy and do not cease each day to give thanks to Your Serenity. Your foresight, just as it protects the peace of the world, has restored quiet to the City and concord to the people.

# IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 399. MAXIMUS THE GRAMMARIAN

[Col. 0405]

## GUILIELM CAVE’S NOTICE ON MAXIMUS

[Col. 0405D] Maximus, an African by nation and a citizen of Madaura (which was a town in Africa proper, between Numidia and Getulia), a grammarian by profession and a friend of Saint Augustine, flourished toward the end of this century, around the year 399.

A pagan passionately devoted to the zeal of his religion, he wrote a letter to Augustine in which he defended the worship of his gods. He says that he confesses one supreme God, without beginning and without offspring by nature, and that he invokes His powers, diffused throughout the structure of the world, under many names. “Thus,” he says, “while we pursue, in separate prayers, what are in a sense certain members of Him, we appear in fact to worship Him in His entirety.”

He then attacks the Christians: partly because they claimed as their own the God whom they asserted they saw in hidden places; partly because, abandoning the temples and neglecting the spirits of their ancestors, they foolishly frequented the tombs of dead men. Hence he ridicules certain martyrs distinguished by Punic names—Mygdon or Miggin, Sana, Lucita, and above all the arch-martyr Namphanion.

It is not easy to conjecture whom Namphanion denotes here, nor do I remember that anyone has attempted it. If it is permissible to conjecture in an obscure matter, I should think that no one other than Christ our Lord is meant: partly because he is called the arch-martyr, that is, one who suffered for the religion he established in a manner more eminent than the other martyrs; partly because, while one deity or another is preferred to this or that other deity, Maximus says: “The Christians, outrageously, preferred Him to the immortal gods”; and finally because, according to Augustine’s interpretation [Col. 0407B] in his reply, Namphanion in the Punic language means nothing other than “a man of good foot,” that is, one whose arrival brings some good fortune—just as we usually say that a person “entered with the right foot” when some prosperity followed his entrance.

This fits our Lord exceedingly well: He came into the world with the wished-for foot and went about doing good (εὐεργετῶν). Of Him, above all, that prophetic saying was spoken: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who proclaims peace, who announces good things, who proclaims salvation!”

I am not unaware that, in the Roman Martyrology, the memory of Saint Namphanion the martyr and his companions is celebrated on July 4. He strengthened them for the struggle and led them forward to the crown, and they suffered at Malaura in Africa. But who does not see that all these details have been taken from these very letters? Indeed, the most illustrious Baronius expressly admits this in his notes.

Maximus concludes with the customary formula: “May the gods preserve you—those through whom we, all mortals whom the earth sustains, venerate and worship, in harmonious disagreement and in a thousand ways, both them and their common Father and the Father of all mortals.”

Augustine, replying to him in the following letter, sharply rebukes the man and shows that, if he wished to indulge in mockery, Augustine could answer him in kind; but he seriously urges him to approach the subject seriously, declaring himself ready to debate these matters in a manner worthy of the argument.

He closes the letter with these words: “So that this may not escape you and draw you unawares into sacrilegious abuse, know that the Catholic Christians, whose church has also been established in your town, worship no dead person, nor do they adore as a deity anything that has been made and created by God, but the one God Himself, who made and created all things.”

The time at which these letters were written is uncertain. The most recent editors assign them to the year 390, when the worship of idols was prohibited by the subsequent imperial law. But no argument can be drawn from this, since imperial constitutions on this subject were issued not only then but in almost every succeeding year, as may be seen in the Theodosian Code—namely, in the years 392, 395, and 396; in 399 four constitutions, two of which specifically concern Africa; and again in 408, to say nothing of later years.

These letters are found in the latest edition as numbers 16 and 17, and in the common editions as numbers 43 and 44.

[Col. 0407]

## MAXIMUS’S LETTER TO SAINT AUGUSTINE

See this letter among Augustine’s letters, under number 16, volume XXXIII of our *Patrology*, column 81. —Editor

# IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 362. MAMERTINUS

[Col. 0407]

## ON THE AUTHOR OF THE PANEGYRIC AND THE TIME AND PLACE OF ITS DELIVERY

[Col. 0407C] Mamertinus, made consul by Julian Augustus, gives thanks to the emperor in this speech. It was delivered in the year of Christ 362, when, as appears from the official lists, he held the consulship with Nevitta as his colleague.

Who this Mamertinus was, or from what homeland he came, has nowhere, so far as I know, been recorded. I would readily suppose that he came from Messana; for the people of Messana were called Mamertines because they had received the Mamertines as guests.

He is mentioned in various places by Ammianus, in Book VI, Book XXI, and Book XXIII. He also speaks of himself more than once in this *Panegyric*. From all these passages it is clear that Mamertinus was prefect of the treasury, then prefect of the praetorium for Illyricum, in whose administration he was acquitted of a charge of embezzlement, and finally was made consul by Julian.

Whether this Mamertinus was the same man to whom the second and third panegyrics addressed to Maximian are attributed, I would not wish to affirm, as may be observed concerning those panegyrics, because seventy years separate their period from the time of this panegyric; nor would I dare altogether to deny it, since when he delivered this speech he appears to have been extremely old, as is clear from *Panegyric* 17: “From my earliest years, from childhood onward to this gray-haired age, I have burned with love for the consulship.”

[Col. 0407]

## SUMMARY OF THE PANEGYRIC

### In the Exordium

[Col. 0407C]

He explains why, although he had received the prefecture of the treasury and had not yet given thanks to the emperor Julian, he now undertakes to do so as consul. In his earlier dignities, the emperor could appear to have taken account either of his own advantage or of the public interest; in conferring the consulship, however, he had regard only to the dignity of the man upon whom it was bestowed.

### Division

In the first part of this speech he enumerates the emperor’s virtues; in the second he gives thanks for the consulship he has received.

**First part.** He briefly touches on Julian’s victories, the recovery of Gaul through his valor, and the near-subjugation of all the barbarian world, section 3. He again discusses Gaul, rescued both from barbarian devastation and from the tyranny and greed of the judges under whom it had been placed; the Germans destroyed, justice restored, and morals corrected by the example of Julian’s virtues, section 4. All these things wonderfully alienated Constantius from Julian, section 5. Julian suddenly appears in the middle of Illyricum, victorious here and everywhere, section 6. He travels along the Danube by ship, causing such terror among the barbarians that they beg for mercy, section 7. He fights and conquers as far as the Adriatic, the Tyrrhenian Sea, and the Maeotian Sea; restores Nicopolis; and restores Eleusis and other cities of Macedonia, Illyricum, and the Peloponnese, section 9. Patient in military labor, he is content with camp food, section 12. Harsh toward himself and easy toward others, sparing toward himself and generous toward others, section 11. Chaste, constantly in the camps, section 13. Thus, after traversing Thrace through his victories, he considers how to relieve the City’s shortage of grain, section 14.

**Second part.** He magnifies the emperor’s favor toward himself: he received the consulship without deserving it; although there was a great abundance of good men; although he sought a lesser magistracy; without gifts or the labor of canvassing; and although he was of modest means and inexperienced in canvassing, he could never have achieved his wish, section 15. In the same year he was honored with responsibility for the public treasury, the prefecture, and the consulship, section 22.

He returns to commemorating the emperor’s virtues: his zeal in fostering literature and restoring the arts, section 23; his diligence in winning everyone’s affection, section 25; his prudence in choosing friends [Col. 0410B] and his loyalty toward them, section 26; his modesty at the highest summit of honors; his clemency in pardoning injuries, section 27; and, above all, his exceptional humanity toward himself and his colleague.

### At the End

Finally, he promises that he will never be forgetful of the favor received from so great an emperor, section 31.

[Col. 0409]

# MAMERTINUS’S THANKSGIVING SPEECH TO JULIAN AUGUSTUS

[Col. 0409C] **I.** Although I know that you, emperor, and all those [Col. 0409D] who share in your counsels may wonder

**Note:** Those who are your advisers. that I have only now begun to give thanks, as though your favors toward me began with the consulship, nevertheless I shall confess

**Note:** Mamertinus had already received from Julian Augustus the prefecture of the treasury and had already been prefect of the praetorium for Illyricum, when the consulship was added as, so to speak, the culmination of so many honors. Hence below, section 21: “Since he sees me honored three times in one year for the very small merit of my innocence.” that, conscious of my ability—which I regret—I would even now have preferred

**Note:** Because I am conscious of the poverty of my talent, which troubles me. to remain silent, and to confine the joy that burst forth from this office within the consciousness of an inward happiness.

But whether our hesitation or our purpose was overcome by the benefits heaped and piled together into one, they reduced me to such a dilemma of necessity [Col. 0410D] that

**Note:** The straits of necessity. I would have to accept either the reputation of being inarticulate or that of being ungrateful. I preferred that eloquence rather than piety and duty toward you should be lacking.

And indeed, in the honors with which you had previously dignified me, there appeared to be less reason for giving thanks. For when you wished me to administer the public treasury—

**Note:** That is, the public money deposited in the temple of Saturn. Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 49, and Dio, Book LV, add that prefects of the treasury were first instituted by Augustus.

—when you were seeking a man courageous in the face of money, independent in the face of offenses, steadfast in the face of envy—you chose me because I appeared to you to be such a man.

**Note:** Truly, or falsely? I do not know. Ammianus, Book XXVII, relates that Mamertinus was accused of embezzlement by Avitianus. You did so at a time when the exhausted provinces, partly through barbarian plunder and partly through the no less destructive than disgraceful robberies of their governors, were openly calling for the emperor’s aid; and when soldiers, often treated as a joke in earlier times, were demanding their current pay. In whatever way I appeared to bear the burden, I seemed to repay the honor with the burden.

But when you appointed me prefect of the praetorium and entrusted to my loyalty and protection provinces that had deserved so well of you, your judgment bestowed an immense favor. [Col. 0411A] Yet in that matter I seemed to have served not only myself, whom you had invested with so great a prefecture, but also, in some measure, your own affairs.

**Note:** Before the time of Constantine, the prefect of the praetorium was so called who was in charge of the soldiers whom the emperor had selected for his personal protection. But after the praetorian cohorts stirred up disturbances on behalf of Maxentius, this dignity was completely abolished by Constantine after the tyrant had been killed. When the Roman world was divided into four parts, or dioceses, four prefects of the praetorium were appointed to preside over them individually: one was called prefect of the praetorium of Gaul, another of Italy, a third of Illyricum, and a fourth of the East. Ammianus, Book XXII, says that Mamertinus was prefect of the praetorium for Illyricum.

**II.** In conferring the consulship, by setting aside your own advantages, you considered only my dignity. For in administrative offices labor is joined to honor; in the consulship honor is received without labor. In the former, if you rejoice, you may seem ambitious; in the latter, unless you openly and publicly rejoice, you are ungrateful.

Moreover, this very city [Col. 0411C]—Constantinople, called by a new name, though once named Byzantium—and this most august temple of public counsel demand the service of this speech. This city, bearing a new name but possessing the most ancient nobility, is your fatherland.

**Note:** Julian Augustus was born at Constantinople in the year of Christ 331, on the eighth day before the Ides of November.

Here you were first born; here you rose like a certain saving star for the human race.

These citizens and fellow countrymen of yours do not permit me to remain silent, nor do they allow anyone else to assume the duty of speaking to you and about you on the most auspicious day [Col. 0411C] than one endowed

**Note:** The Kalends of January, on which Mamertinus entered upon the consulship together with his colleague Nevitta.

with the most distinguished magistracy. with the most distinguished magistracy. They think—and rightly—that the name of consul adds something to the splendor of your praises. For the dignity of the praises is increased by the honor of the one who praises.

And although, most excellent emperor, I ought to give you thanks by public judgment and in the public name, I shall now pass over most of what you accomplished at home and abroad for the supreme interests of the state, so that the speech may reach as quickly as possible what properly belongs to it.

**Note:** Very swiftly.

**III.** Shall I now proceed to recall as though they were new and unheard-of achievements the recovery through your valor of Gaul [Col. 0411C], and the subjugation of all barbarian peoples [Col. 0411D]—especially the Franks and all the Germans—

**Note:** Gaul was rescued from the barbarians, whom Constantius Augustus had summoned against Magnentius; when they found themselves of no use for that purpose, they ravaged Gaul. Sozomen, Book V, chapter 2. Julian says that they had already taken almost forty-five towns.

—achievements celebrated in this part of the Roman Empire with such glorious renown that they deserved to arouse the envy of the emperor your brother?

**Note:** Constantius Augustus, whom Julian calls his brother, either because they were cousins—that is, had the same grandfather, Constantius—or because Julian had married Helena, Constantius’s sister.

For what else alienated from you the mind of your imperial colleague [Col. 0411D] than the splendor of your glory?

**Note:** Constantius. I call immortal God to witness; I call my conscience, sacred to me in place of a deity, to witness

**Note:** And in the place of a god. that I would have spoken firmly on many matters in this City concerning the acts conceived and undertaken harshly and impiously against the best of emperors [Col. 0412A], if the deified Constantius still frequented gatherings of men.

**Note:** If Constantius were still alive. He had, however, died the year before, on the third day before the Nones of October, near Tarsus, while setting out against the Persians.

I certainly would not have failed in the duty of a free citizen and good senator: I would have refuted and proved that the reasons for his hatred of you were precisely those that ought to have inflamed love and served as pledges of loyalty.

**Note:** That is, they should have bound you to love and loyalty.

**IV.** Once, the most flourishing and ancient cities were held by barbarians [Col. 0412C].

**Note:** Forty-five, if we believe Julian, leaving aside the smaller forts and castles. The rest of Gaul was laid waste and left uncultivated by barbarian ravages and incursions. That celebrated nobility of the Gauls had either been killed by the sword or was serving under cruel masters. Other cities, which intervening distances had separated from the devastation of the barbarians, were held by wicked robbers under the name of judges. Freeborn bodies [Col. 0412C] were subjected to unworthy tortures; no one was free from injury, no one untouched by insult, except the man who had softened the robber’s cruelty with money [Col. 0411D], so that people already longed for the barbarians and the wretched preferred the fate of captives.

**Note:** Add *suberant* or *lacerabantur*; the latter word is suspected by Livincius to have dropped out. Or read, with Acidalius, *ingenui indignis oneribus correpti*—“freeborn men seized by unworthy burdens.”

In this condition our emperor found Gaul. He had very little labor or danger against the enemy:

**Note:** At the battle on the plains of Argentoratum, where Julian with few soldiers utterly routed the seven most powerful kings of all Germany with their very numerous army. Six thousand barbarians were killed, as is commonly said, or sixty thousand, according to Zosimus; the Frankish king Chnodomarius was captured and taken to Constantius with an innumerable multitude of prisoners.

— in a single battle all Germany was destroyed [Col. 0412C]; the war was finished in one engagement. But the reform of morals, the correction of judgments, and the difficult and dangerous task of struggle required much effort.

**Note:** An arduous task.

For the more wicked a man was, the more hostile he was to Caesar’s interests. Seeking remedies for his new crime in order to avoid the penalties of the laws, and unable to defend his criminal acts, he heaped unpopularity upon the avenger of justice [Col. 0412D].

**Note:** He stirred up hostility against this champion of equity.

**Note:** He heaped unpopularity upon this defender of equity.

And when the conduct and institutions of the holy prince removed the license for false opinions and accusations, through a clever art of doing harm they concealed the cruelty of their accusations beneath titles of praise [Col. 0412D].

**Note:** They disguised it under the appearance of praise.

**Note:** They praised Julian as though out of affection, but in reality to provoke Constantius. No kind of detraction is more malicious.

In every gathering they spread these claims as though out of goodwill: “Julian conquered Alamannia; Julian raised the cities of Gaul from ashes and ruins. Those provinces, besieged, conquered, and ravaged with sword and fire, are happier than the towns that Constantius possesses without an enemy.” [Col. 0412C]

**Note:** Ammianus makes this assertion about Julian.

“He spends every summer in the camps and every winter in the courts.” Thus his years were divided so that he either subdued barbarians or restored laws to citizens, constantly professing a struggle either against the enemy or against vices.

**V.** These words were more powerful than every insult for inflaming hatred. For if they had attempted to fabricate any crimes, they would easily have been refuted by the very brilliance of praise and glory. They discovered a kind of accusation that no one could refute.

But what, I ask you, do you think our prince ought to have done? Should he have handed Roman cities over to the enemy, lest he offend his brother’s feelings? Should he have allowed the strongest and most useful provinces of the state to be harassed and plundered before his eyes, lest the Augustus hear anything he did not wish to hear? Should he not merely have loosened the reins on the crimes of administrators but even have spurred them on, lest dissimilarity of character produce discord between the emperors?

They say that a noble youth of Etruria [Col. 0413C], when he aroused the love of many women because of the exceptional beauty of his appearance, wounded his own face in order to obliterate his beauty.

**Note:** His name was Spurinna, as I find written in the margin of the Viennese edition. Valerius Maximus recounts the story at length in Book IV, chapter 5.

But it was easy for a young man who preferred the beauty of character to the dignity of the body to discolor his fair complexion and disfigure the radiance of his face with deeply impressed scars [Col. 0413C].

**Note:** A word used by Cellius for “to disfigure.”

Was Julian supposed to do something of this sort against the love of his citizens? He could not even have done so—unless perhaps we think that the forms of virtues are patient of wounds.

Surely he could have cast a shadow over the brightness of equity, erased from temperance the purple of holy modesty [Col. 0413D],

**Note:** The blush of chaste modesty.

— pierced the neck of courage with unworthy wounds, and torn out the eyes of foresight!

**Note:** Read with Lipsius, “the neck of courage”; for, as he says in Book III of the *Epistles*, question 24, “in the neck are the power of endurance and the meeting of the sinews.” Mamertinus above, section 5: “unless perhaps we think that the forms of virtues are patient of wounds.”

Moreover, unless that youth had inflicted a severe hand upon his own features [Col. 0413C], time and delay, with the succession of advancing age [Col. 0413D], would soon have destroyed all that bodily bloom.

**Note:** What if we read with Acidalius: “Days and no long delay, through the succession of age.”

But in our emperor’s virtues, the longer his life, the more excellent his beauty.

**Note:** “But in his virtues.” —Acidalius.

**VI.** I pass over all the barbarian peoples roused to arms against the defender of Roman liberty [Col. 0413D], and the peoples recently conquered [Col. 0413D] by Constantius and his great son Constantine and freed from the incursions of the Franks, who, uncertain whether to submit their necks to the yoke recently imposed, had been stirred by wicked goads into renewed madness.

**Note:** Driven into a new frenzy.

All these things finally overcame the steadfast and immovable patience of the greatest prince. [Col. 0414A] Thus, when he had crushed rebellious Alamannia in the very act of its attempt—

**Note:** That is, when he believed that Constantius was on the point of invading Gaul.

—he who shortly before had traversed with a victorious army regions, rivers, and mountains whose names had not even been heard,

**Note:** He had led his victorious army across regions, rivers, and mountains not even known by name.

— flying over the farthest kingdoms of savage peoples and trampling upon the heads of kings—he suddenly appeared in the middle of Illyricum.

We saw his fortunate companions on the journey standing amazed, and the peoples of the cities hesitating to believe what they saw. I imagine that the peoples who received the Palladium as it fell from heaven were no more dismayed [Col. 0413D].

**Note:** It was a statue of Pallas, which, at the time when the altar and temple of Minerva were being built, was said to have fallen from heaven and to have placed itself in the temple. Since fate had decreed that Troy would remain unharmed as long as the statue was preserved within its walls, Diomedes and Ulysses removed the fateful image. Not long afterward, deprived of this protective deity, the Greeks overthrew Troy after its ten-year siege. *Aeneid* II, 163.

Young girls, boys, women, trembling old women, and tottering old men [Col. 0414D] looked upon the emperor

**Note:** Perhaps the final word, *attoniti* (“stunned”), should be inserted here.

— with great, stunned terror as he ran a long way beneath the weight of heavy armor. His breathing showed the effort of haste [Col. 0414D] without any sign that he felt fatigue;

**Note:** So that he seemed not to feel weariness.

— streams of sweat poured more thickly down his vigorous neck; and amid the roughness of the dust that weighed upon his beard and hair [Col. 0414B], his eyes shone with star-like fire.

**Note:** With beard and hair roughened by dust, and his eyes blazing with heavenly fire.
