The magnitude of the miracle overwhelmed the voices of those who rejoiced. The customary services of praise ceased before a sight that deserved more praise than they could offer.

**VII.** Mere haste would indeed have sufficed for the expedition and the matters immediately at hand, but it is not enough for our prince to serve the state in only one way. He undertakes many things at once: his spirit has never been wearied by any labor.

**Note:** The writers of Julian’s life, especially Ammianus, testify that Julian was exceptionally patient in military labor.

In order at one and the same time both to settle the condition of the most loyal provinces and to strike terror into all the barbarian world by bringing the threat nearer, he decided to travel along the Danube by ship for its entire length.

O holy divinity! What a spectacle that voyage presented,

**Note:** Below, section 28: “There, O holy divinity! while all rejoiced—by what mouth, by what voice?” he says, “Hail, most distinguished consul!”

— when the right bank of the famous river was lined continuously by people of both sexes and every rank, armed and unarmed, while on the left the barbarian world knelt in miserable supplication!

All the cities that inhabit the Danube were visited; the decrees of all were heard; their condition was relieved [Col. 0414D], and their fortunes restored [Col. 0414D].

**Note:** Their resources were increased. Pardon was granted to innumerable barbarians, and the gift of peace was bestowed.

**Note:** Perhaps to the Quadi and Saxons, whom Julian destroyed through the agency of a certain deserter named Charietto and admitted to peace on the condition that they would never bear arms against the Romans.

Whoever observes that hurried journey will think that the emperor did nothing but travel; whoever considers the multitude of his accomplishments will not believe that he hurried.

**VIII.** O eloquent Greece, powerful in speech! You alone have been able to magnify the deeds of all your princes; you alone have stretched the glories of achievements to the abundance of words.

You raised a single ship to the heavens on account of the theft of the golden fleece and the abduction of a maiden, and consecrated it among the stars [Col. 0415C].

**Note:** It was called the Argo; hence the Argonauts were so named, for they sailed in it to Colchis to carry away the golden fleece. Virgil, *Eclogue* IV, 34:

> Then there will be another Tiphys, and another Argo  
> To carry chosen heroes.

I am reluctant to recount all that the poets relate about it—for example, that it was prophetic and was consecrated in heaven, and so forth.

**Note:** This refers to Medea.

You [begin to speak of] the boy [Triptolemus]. Ovid, *Tristia*, Book III, elegy 8:

> Now, therefore, I would wish to mount Triptolemus’s chariot.

[source text ends mid-note]

He sent the raw seed into unknown soil.

[Note: You boasted that Triptolemus, the inventor of sowing, flying in a chariot drawn by winged dragons, scattered seed over the earth. This is a familiar story from all the poets.]

What would you make of Julian’s small craft and liburnian ships, if you devoted yourself to writing and celebrating the deeds of our emperor? They take nothing away from anyone, nor do they ravage hospitable cities; rather, they freely bestow exemptions, privileges, and money upon all peoples. With what dignity would you describe a fleet flying by oars and winds along the course of a mighty river, and then our prince, elevated upon the lofty stern—not scattering grain over fields of one kind or another, but distributing good hopes, freedom, and wealth among Roman towns, while on the other side sowing upon barbarian soil the terrors of war, panic, flight, and fear?

### IX

How remarkable, then, was it that, while still sailing on the Hister [Note: The river Hister, or Danube.], you extended your benefactions as far as the Adriatic, the Tyrrhenian, and the Maeotian seas? At that very time, the Dalmatians [Note: Peoples of Illyria along the Adriatic coast.] and the Epirotes [Note: Peoples of Greece on the Ionian Sea, whose region is now called Albania.]—relieved of the exorbitant prices of horses and crushed by the intolerable burden of tribute, reduced to the last extremity [Note: Reduced to the utmost straits.] [Note: A metaphor drawn from the game of draughts, in which one particular piece, called the *regillus*, is kept motionless on its line and cannot be moved except in the final crisis. When someone is said to have been brought into the greatest difficulty, he is therefore said to have been “reduced to the *incitae*.” The *incitae* were lines beyond which the pieces could not be moved. So Erasmus. Plautus often uses this proverb.]—by your foresight, emperor, not only cast off their miseries but also recovered [Note: They regained.] an ample and prosperous fortune.

The city of Nicopolis [Note: Founded at Actium by Augustus in memory of his victory there.]—which the deified Augustus had built as a monument to the victory at Actium, in the likeness of a trophy—had almost entirely collapsed into a ruin deserving of tears. The houses of the nobles were battered, the fora roofless, and everything was long since filled with squalor and dust, the aqueducts having fallen into disrepair. The public games, customarily attended every five years, had been suspended by a mournful *justitium* [Note: A suspension of legal proceedings, as though the administration of justice had been interrupted on account of some public mourning. Livy: “The dictator declares a *justitium*, orders the shops throughout the city to be closed, and forbids anyone to conduct private business.” *Justitium* is also sometimes used for a thirty-day suspension of the collection of money.], a disgraceful cessation.

Athens [Note: A city situated on the river Ilissus, in that part of Achaea called Attica; the head of all Greece and the mother of every discipline. Today, Setines.], itself the teacher and inventor of the liberal arts, had lost all public and private adornment. Eleusis [Note: A coastal town of Attica, between Megara and the harbor of Piraeus at Athens.] had fallen into a pitiable ruin. But it would take far too long to enumerate all the cities restored by the emperor’s aid [Note: Reformed or restored.]. It is enough to know that all the cities of Macedonia [Note: The celebrated region of Greece between the Aegean and Adriatic seas, now defined by narrower boundaries than in former times.], Illyricum, and the Peloponnese [Note: The Greek peninsula, now called the Morea, famous for Lacedaemon.] stood firm, their walls suddenly renewed, their youth restored by one or two letters from the great emperor [Note: Their walls were suddenly restored, making them secure.]. Water gushed forth everywhere: places that shortly before appeared dry and gasping with thirst were now washed, cleansed, and drenched. Fora, promenades, and gymnasia were thronged with joyful and rejoicing crowds; ancient festivals were celebrated, and new ones consecrated in honor of the prince.

### X

If some mortal, lifted by a cloud to a heavenly watchtower, had shortly before seen everything mournful—towns half destroyed, walls deserted, the native inhabitants reduced to solitude, and a crowd of exiles—and if he were now set down again upon that same height and looked down upon everything flourishing, fields planted, cities crowded, water flowing into the towns, not merely private houses but public buildings rising in magnificent splendor [Note: This means not merely private dwellings, but public buildings as well. Likewise below, section 19: “not even men, but little women,” that is, not merely men.], rich harvests according to the fertility of the lands, vintage yields surpassing the farmers’ hopes, steep hills and deep valleys, and the broad plains filled with the sounds of bleating, neighing, and lowing [Note: For “wide fields,” as in Virgil’s “narrow ways,” and similar expressions.], he would certainly marvel that everything had been changed so quickly. He would leap down from the clouds and eagerly abandon the neighborhood of heaven in order to enjoy your lands, emperor.

But what is more astonishing than this: that no one, amid such an abundance of resources, felt any loss; that money was drawn forth by the emperor for every purpose; and that, in a kind of reversal, tribute was paid to the provinces [Note: That is, wealth flowed from the imperial treasury back to the peoples from whom it had previously flowed in.], so that riches flowed from the place to which they had formerly converged from everywhere? One might well ask from whom you receive, emperor, since you distribute so generously to everyone. Yet anyone who has understood the principles and practice of your life will easily discover the source of this abundance. Your frugality, Augustus, provides you with the greatest revenue: whatever others squandered on extravagant desires is now all reserved for public uses.

### XI

Until now, the sole advantage of imperial power was thought to be that an emperor differed from the other citizens not by brave deeds or the splendor of glory, but by the magnitude of his expenditure [Note: That he differed from them.]. Hence the huge masses of foundations needed for enormous buildings [Note: Enormous building works. Cicero, *Pro Milone*, section 53: “On that estate, because of those insane substructures, nearly a thousand men could easily be employed.” And section 85: “The shrines which he had overwhelmed with the insane masses of his foundations.”], and the immense crowds of courtiers, easily exceeded the expenditure of legions.

Indeed, the Roman people felt the elaborate extravagance of banquets and dinners; the most carefully selected dishes were valued not by their taste but by their difficulty of acquisition: marvelous birds, fish from distant seas, fruit out of season, summer snow, and winter roses [Note: As is said by Capitolinus to have occurred at the banquet of the emperor Lucius Verus.]. Your spirit, victorious over every pleasure, rejected all these things. Painted veneers of marble and ceilings roofed with solid gold are not to be compared with the lot of one who spends most of the year lying on bare earth, covered only by the sky; nor the throngs of servants trained to provide delicacies with one who has so little that needs to be provided; nor the time spent feasting with one who more often takes a fixed ration of food simply to meet the needs of the human body, rejoicing in military fare and an attendant close at hand and a chance cup [Note: The laws did not allow one to disdain even a chance turf—that is, something readily at hand. Those who praise Julian’s abstinence and moderation praise it wonderfully even while sharply criticizing his other faults.].

### XII

Yet amid all this I cannot sufficiently marvel that, while you are so severely frugal toward yourself, you are so liberal and indulgent toward your fellow citizens; that you undertake the harshest labors for yourself so that we may enjoy a life of leisure. For we observe that those who pursue a life removed from pleasures are difficult and morose: they are little happy themselves, but make others even sadder, and turn private households into places of mourning and anxiety.

But the most holy emperor takes the greatest pains that we should live according to our dignity, that we should abound in comforts, and that we should pass our lives chastely but cheerfully. Other princes have been made harsh by labor and slack by idleness, and serious emperors have always lacked popularity [Note: Those who make themselves difficult to approach.], while common affairs have lacked diligence [Note: Popular or concerned with the people.] [Note: Acidalius reads *comibus*, “courteous.” Either reading may be chosen.]. No one who was burdensome to himself ever made himself so accessible to others that he did not restrain them by his own example.

Our emperor grants himself no indulgence and imposes no trouble or labor upon others. He provides everyone with leisure by undertaking his own business; he is generous in dispensing wealth but sparing of cares [Note: He gives wealth with a generous hand but anxiety sparingly. Since it is the most difficult task, he prefers to carry it out himself rather than command others to do it.]; he chooses to perform the most laborious duties himself rather than order others to perform them.

### XIII

Many, after the kings had been expelled, desired sole command of the entire commonwealth [Note: They ardently wished to rule the whole state alone.]. Those who remember know the names of the men who, raging within their own country, paid the penalties for aspiring to kingship [Note: This alludes to Livy’s account of Manlius Capitolinus, book VI, chapter 20. Convicted of aspiring to power, he was thrown headlong from the Tarpeian Rock. His house was also demolished, and a law was added forbidding any patrician thereafter to live on the citadel or in the Capitol. A decree of the Manlian family likewise provided that no one thereafter should be called Marcus Manlius.].

I pass over the ancients who were hurled from the rock, whose goods were confiscated, whose houses were torn down [Note: They were demolished by law, as Juretus suspects.], and whose names were forbidden to their descendants [Note: More precisely, their praenomina; for from that time there were people called Manlii, but plainly no one called Marcus Manlius.]. Our own age, too, has produced not a few madmen driven senseless by this frenzy, who rushed upon the sword because of their blind desire to rule.

If God were to restore such men to life for a little while and address them—“You, for example, Nepotianus” [Note: According to Tristan’s coin, Flavius Nepotianus Constantinus; according to Goltz and Occon, Flavius Popilius Nepotianus. He was born of Eutropia, the sister of Constantine the Great, and Popilius Nepotianus, a former consul. After invading the city and the imperial power at the same time that Magnentius’s army was defeated, he was in turn destroyed and killed by Maxentius.] “and you, Sylvanus” [Note: Sylvanus was born in Gaul, the son of Bonitus, a Frank distinguished in war. After defecting from the rebel Magnentius to Constantius, he was consequently appointed master of the infantry. At last he assumed the purple at Cologne. He did so from necessity rather than from a desire for tyranny: suspected of aspiring to imperial power, he had been marked for death by Constantius, though he did not escape it, for he was overwhelmed by Constantius’s troops in that same city. Ammianus, book IV; Aurelius Victor.]—you sought imperial power through hostile swords and imminent deaths. But now power to reign is freely offered you, on the same terms on which Julian reigns: you must keep watch day and night for the leisure of all; though you are called masters, you must serve the freedom of the citizens; you must engage in battle more often than in dining; you must take nothing from anyone and instead give generously to everyone; you must show favor to no one and act savagely toward no one; throughout the whole world, the reputation of no virgin may be violated; let there be a bed even without illicit pleasures, but with lawful ones [Note: Others read “and legitimate.”], purer than the beds of the Vestals” [Note: The Vestal virgins, devoted to the rites of Vesta and the guardianship of the perpetual fire, were first instituted by Numa Pompilius. Ovid, *Tristia*, book IV, elegy 2:

“Who preserve  
the chaste hearths  
in perpetual virginity.”]

“Let them endure on their uncovered heads, in summer, the dust of Alamannia, and in winter, the frost of Thrace.” Surely the delicate ears of such men could not endure the very burden of these words. Terrified by such great responsibilities, weary not only of imperial power but of life itself, they would hasten to return to some lower underworld. For they would see that just rule is troubled by labors, cares, and sleeplessness—whose pleasant and attractive appearance they had admired without seeing the hardships of its duties.

### XIV

When, therefore, after completing a journey amid outstanding duties, we had reached the borders of Thrace, and the army’s supplies had been arranged in haste, he turned his attention toward the Roman city, which was without grain. Any other man would have been deterred from attempting to bring relief by the gravest famine and the most distressing danger to the state. But through the contributions of the provinces, the revenues of his own patrimony, and grain purchased everywhere, he refilled the already starving City until it possessed abundant and overflowing supplies.

Someone may ask: how could so much be accomplished in so short a time? And rightly so. But our emperor adds to his time whatever he takes away from his leisure. He assigns nothing to sleep, nothing to banquets, nothing to idleness; he deprives himself even of the use of the natural necessities required for life [Note: He cuts down his use of the things necessary for life.]; he devotes himself entirely to the public welfare.

Thus his reign will seem already of great age to those who measure Julian’s time not by the number of days or months but by the multitude of his works and the number of things accomplished. While the food of the Roman people and the army’s supplies were in his hands, in the midst of the anxiety involved in procuring grain, a message arrived that many ships laden with African wheat had passed along the Achaean coast [Note: Achaea, also called Greece, is bounded by sea on one side and by Thessaly and Epirus on the other. Achaea in the narrower sense was the region of the Peloponnese between Corinth and Patras.] and sped on to Constantinople [Note: A city situated on the Thracian Bosporus and the capital of Thrace. Formerly Byzantium.].

Everyone was disturbed and angry with those responsible for guarding the coast. We went to the emperor, each of us complaining on his own behalf that, through the negligence of the authorities, so much grain had been lost. But the great emperor, smiling serenely, said that no mistake had been made, and that the grain intended for this city had not been lost. We thought that remark expressed his familiar love for his country, while an ambiguity in his words concealed a betrayal of what was to come. Even then, his divine mind, conscious of the future happiness, foresaw its outcome.

### XV

Within a few days, after the state had been restored to a new and flourishing condition, his sacred mind turned toward the honors and adornments of magistracies. In the assembly of his sacred breast, the consulship began to be considered [Note: This is how someone who deliberates with himself about some matter is said to hold an assembly within himself, weighing the considerations on both sides. Thus Plautus, *Epidicus*, scene 2, act 1:

“Now I shall summon the senate in the heart of my counsels.”

Likewise in *Mostellaria*:

“While I summon the senate of counsel within my heart.”]

He alone knows what he pursued, and whatever plans his divinity delights to formulate. I was chosen first among all the men of the Roman Empire, while he enhanced my honor with a colleague illustrious in military distinctions [Note: Flavius Nevitta, whom Ammianus, book XXII, says had marked Constantine excessively as the first promoter of the debasement of barbarian worth.].

Thanks to you, thanks, emperor, if you believed me worthy; and many more thanks, emperor, if you loved me so greatly that you made me consul even though I was unworthy. I know that the highest honors are usually conferred upon men of little merit because better candidates are lacking, but I am not afraid that any ill-wisher will claim this happened in my consulship. If anyone spitefully asserts this, the very timing disproves him. It is enough to say against him that Rome was already obeying our prince.

What of the fact that, when I expected nothing beyond an increase in honor—for the modesty of my hopes did not extend beyond the prefecture—a messenger was brought to me announcing that I had been made consul without expense, which for a long time had been available only to a few; without labor, which had never been so; and without solicitation, which had been available to no one?

### XVI

Who does not know how many labors candidates once undertook, even when honors were entrusted to the votes of the Roman people? They had to learn the names of all the tribes, greet the people one by one [Note: That is, each individual person had to be greeted. Acidalius reads “all, and even individually,” and so forth. The old manuscript, however, has: “the names of all had to be learned; all, tribe by tribe, and even individually, had to be greeted.”], grasp the hands of passers-by, and smile at everyone. They had to simulate familiarity not only with the lowest people but also with strangers, and undertake many other things for the sake of office that otherwise would not befit a man worthy of honor.

Hence the famous saying of Crassus when he was seeking the consulship and happened to be walking through the streets of Rome with his father-in-law Scaevola. In the presence of that most dignified and severe man, he did not dare flatter the people, stroke those he met, or practice the arts of canvassing. “Please, Mucius,” he said, “step away for a little while, and do not imagine that your company gives me distinction. You are obstructing my advancement; with you watching, I cannot behave foolishly” [Note: Taken from Cicero, *On the Orator*, book I, section 112: “Indeed, when I was seeking office,” and so forth.].

But I earned no one’s favor through shameful flattery; I did nothing foolish and undertook nothing that I would have been unwilling for Mucius to witness. I did not solicit even a single member of the people; nor did I approach you yourself, emperor, whom it is glorious to address and to whom it is full of dignity to offer prayers—not even with a word. This divine gift from you flowed spontaneously into my family.

### XVII

I shall confess everything to you, great emperor, and safely open before you all the hidden chambers of my mind [Note: The secrets of my heart.]. I never desired power over the lives of citizens, nor provinces. But because the commonwealth seemed also to require my assistance, to the extent of my ability [Note: That is, according to my strength. Tacitus, *Life of Agricola*: “As though you were granting the prince—namely Domitian—your share of innocence.” Although this expression, so far as I know, does not occur in Cicero, it is not unlike Cicero’s phrase in *Pro Sestio*: “Those who defend this to the best of their ability are the optimates.”], I did not shrink from office when called to it, lest I be thought idle.

I neither sought public business through canvassing nor refused it through cowardice or sloth; rather, from my earliest years, from childhood [Note: Mamertinus was therefore an old man when he delivered this speech.], right up to these gray hairs, I have burned with love for the consulship [Note: I must also confess this second matter to you.].

While the state was in the power of other emperors, I long cherished an empty desire without the consolation of hope. For what madness would it have been for me to aspire to this title, lacking resources and ignorant of the art of canvassing [Note: Since I had neither the means nor the skill to canvass.]? But first, when you were Caesar, you rekindled the flame of my desire, already languishing, with the breath of good hope. When I saw you, Augustus, as a marvelous observer of innocence and virtue, I then said to myself: “Claudius Mamertinus, you have not lived this long in vain. You have a suitable judge of your loyalty and diligence. Remember that your fortunes are in great danger. It will be known that you did not deserve the consulship if this emperor does not confer it upon you.”

### XVIII

You have, Augustus, the betrayal of my silence and the matter that I concealed from you through a silence of no short duration [Note: This explains my silence and the matter that I had long kept hidden by silence.]. Yet I have not revealed everything. I no longer wish to carry any secret with me; I shall empty out every hidden chamber of my heart.

If you had held back your kindness and added some artifice to that generosity toward me, contrary to your usual character [Note: That is, if you had suspended your benevolence—an expression extremely common among good writers, meaning “if you had delayed granting it.”], perhaps I would have asked. But do you think it a small favor, emperor, that you spared me the danger of asking? I mean a danger, most holy emperor, if you had hesitated to grant it, if you had postponed it for the future: what would have become of me after rejection? Even in the lightest favors that are requested and not obtained, friendship is dissolved. For the love by which friendship is held together [Note: The affection by which friendship is sustained.] is stained in both parties. One thinks that he is not loved because he did not grant the request; the other supposes that he is hated because he did not obtain it.

Nor would I have seemed to have become consul freely if I had purchased the honor with prayers. I would have undertaken, after spending the better part of my life, a miserable and laborious apprenticeship in begging. For I do not think it more burdensome to spend money than to pour out prayers. Indeed, in making purchases we all see people draw out gold and silver with great confidence and high spirits, trusting that they will be repaid [Note: That is, trusting that they will receive compensation.]; but those who plead with prayers are humble and downcast, scarcely uttering their words with hesitation and stammering. They lower not only their speech but their entire bodies, sinking to their knees. In short, to speak as I feel: the man who accepts prayers sells a favor at the highest price.

### XIX

But if I had been made consul in the centuriate assembly, would I have seemed more gloriously declared consul by the votes of the entire people? Not at all. Even in those ancient times, the Campus was disgraced by the canvassing of many. The crimes of the vote distributors are well known, as are the tricks of the ballot boxes [Note: Ausonius has something similar in his panegyric to Gratian: “I, emperor Augustus, consul by your gift, did not endure the barriers, the Campus, the votes, the ballots, or the ballot boxes.”], as well as the hands of hired gangs purchased for violence and sedition.

Nor can anything be carefully considered amid a confused multitude of ignorant people [Note: That anything can be deliberate or carefully weighed.]. Since good men are rare and the mob of the wicked is immense, and since numbers and crowds prevail in the Campus, it is clear beyond doubt that the man who obtains office through the votes of the people is the one approved by the majority—that is, by the worse men. Hence our ancestors came to see Gabinii designated and Catones rejected [Note: Or perhaps “Vatinii,” as Lipsius observes, *Epistles*, book III, letter 24. Cato was passed over in the candidacy for the consulship in favor of Vatinius, not Gabinius. Seneca relates the same story in *That No Injury Can Be Done to the Wise Man*, as well as in *On Divine Providence*, and Valerius Maximus, book VII, chapter 5.].

But let these ancient examples recall how office was sought shortly before [Note: Let them bring to mind.]. Scarcely a few appeared to whom office was awarded for their virtues, even though the reward for their diligence and integrity came slowly to those very men. The rest frequented every depraved courtier, and whenever someone seemed especially favored by the emperor through the most shameful arts, they sought to purchase him through constant attentions and to capture him with gifts.

They canvassed not only men but little women; and not women alone but eunuchs as well, whom either nature’s origin or bodily mutilation had separated from both sexes, as though they were exiles from human society. Thus those splendid names of antiquity flattered every most sordid and disgraceful man in the imperial retinue [Note: Lucretius uses this word in book V: “They flatter with the braying of their voice”; and Ausonius in his *Gratiarum Actio* to Gratian: “I did not flatter the centuries.”].

When such men were sent into the provinces, they plundered both sacred and profane property, preparing their road to the consulship with money. Thus there was no longer any devotion to the liberal arts.

### XX

Military service was rejected by nearly every nobleman as sordid and unworthy of a free man. The knowledge of civil law, which had elevated the Manlii [Note: He means Titus Manlius, whom Valerius Maximus, book V, chapter 8, reports to have been highly skilled in civil law and pontifical sacred law. Acidalius reads *Manilii* instead of *Manlios*. Manilius, after transferring himself from military service to forensic life, wrote three books on civil law.], the Scaevolae [Note: Publius Mucius Scaevola was consul with Lucius Calpurnius Piso in 617 from the founding of the City, and was pontifex maximus. Plutarch, in *Sulla*, says that he wrote ten books on civil law. His son, Quintus Mucius Scaevola, was the first to arrange civil law systematically into eighteen books; he had many distinguished pupils, and Cicero says that he learned much from him. Cicero’s Crassus called him the most eloquent of jurists and the most learned jurist among orators. There was also another Quintus Mucius Scaevola, the Augur, whom Cicero introduces speaking in *On Friendship* and from whom he professes to have learned civil law. He was Laelius’s son-in-law and Crassus’s father-in-law.], and Servii [Note: Publius Servius Sulpicius, who was consul in 703 from the founding of the City. He was a great imitator of Quintus Mucius Scaevola, who inspired him to study civil law with these words: “It is disgraceful for a patrician pleading cases to be ignorant of the law in which he is engaged.” He was the first to apply dialectic to law and began to treat it systematically. He was Cicero’s closest friend. Cicero erected a bronze standing statue of him on the Rostra after his death, when Cicero had been sent by the Senate to Mutina to use his eloquence to placate Antony. He is often mentioned in Cicero.] to the highest rank of dignity, was called the craft of freedmen [Note: It was customary among the Romans for candidates for office to win the support of voters through money and gifts. Those who distributed money tribe by tribe were called *divisores*.].

Our nobles rejected oratory, a task of great labor and little practical use, wishing to appear unwilling to do what they had been unable to attain. And indeed it was considered madness to undertake so much labor and so many sleepless nights to acquire something whose use did not contribute to the adornment of practical life.

Thus every effort was devoted to amassing money.

[Note: Juvenal, *Satires* 3.143:

“As much money as each man keeps in his chest,  
so much faith does he possess.”]

The better a man was, the wealthier he was thought to be. Then came a pitiable endurance of servitude and a remarkable cunning in flattery. The thresholds of court ministers were worn down every day. At the doors of those who served the desires of the emperor, one might see three men of patrician birth [Note: Read *cernuos*, “bowed down,” as Lipsius observes, *Epistles*, book III, letter 24.] who were deterred from such disgrace neither by rain, nor frost, nor the bitterness of the insult itself. Bowed down and prostrate, they could scarcely lift their heads above the knees of those whom they were imploring. In the end, they earned honors not through the judgment or goodwill of the proud, but through pity.

### XXI

But now, whoever desires provinces, tribuneships, prefectures, or consulships need not seek money by fair means or foul, nor diminish his freedom by becoming a despicable caller. The more ready he is for servitude, the more unworthy of honor he will be judged [Note: Bongarsius and Gruter read “will be judged”; this is also the reading in the Viennese edition.].

There is now another kind of person in the friendship of our prince—rough, as these city-dwellers think, not particularly polished, somewhat rustic. He resists the flattery of flatterers and recoils from touching another man’s money as though it were a harmful substance. He places his greatest wealth in the safety of the state and the glorious praise of his emperor.

The emperor himself is fortified by immense and divine foresight against every enticement and trap of flatterers [Note: Acidalius reads “with great and enduring foresight.”]. For what danger can come to him from the disguised poisons of flatterers, when he is burdened even by true praise and gives it a reluctant hearing [Note: There is no reason to fear that he will allow himself to be captured by the false words of flatterers, since he scarcely lends his ears even to genuine praise.]?

But the method of seeking honors is now much easier. Whoever wishes to obtain office, I say, should disregard gold and silver; he need not visit the houses of the powerful from door to door, nor embrace anyone’s feet or knees. Let him take as his companions only justice, courage, temperance, and prudence—companions freely available and easy to obtain. The great emperor himself will come to him and urge him to undertake public service.

While he is at leisure and occupied with other matters, provinces, prefectures, the fasces, the curule chair, and all the insignia of magistracies will be carried to him [Note: The twelve rods carried before the consul by the lictors.]. For what promise concerning honor could a man of true and perfect virtue not confidently make to himself, when he sees me honored three times in a single year for so small a measure of innocence [Note: The three magistracies of Mamertinus were mentioned at the beginning of this speech.]?

### XXII

Has any god ever given a single field multiple harvests in one year? Has anyone ever reaped more than once in a single summer from the same fallow field [Note: A *novale* is land that rests and is sown in alternate years, as in Virgil, *Georgics* 1.71: “The same fallows to rest in alternate years.” Here the word is used simply for land.]? Has anyone ever gathered a triple vintage in one autumn from a single vineyard? Certainly one winter produces only one olive harvest [Note: A term used by Cato, Varro, and Columella for the season in which olives are gathered.].

But in the benefactions of our prince, multiplied fertility is no miracle. To say nothing of the other excellent men who reaped an abundance of honors from one autumn to the next, I certainly have enjoyed the third harvest of a single year: the consulship.

First came the entrusted guardianship of all the treasuries and the administration of distributions. The prefecture occupies the second place among the fruits of my honors. Added to these—enough by itself to defeat anyone’s greed—came the third yield of your benefactions, the consulship.

Then, when a field is exhausted and reduced to barrenness by constant harvests, the later generosity of our emperor surpasses the earlier. It does not become sterile through giving birth, but is made fertile by alternating yields. It was a wholly new and unexpected accumulation of honors. The courses of the stars had not yet changed their position when the prince was already setting in motion the course of another dignity; the sun was still shining from the region of those same constellations, and Augustus had already passed beyond the third insignia of my magistracy.

Tell me: would you not have thought someone greedy for empty glory and inflamed with conspicuous ambition if he had desired for himself as much at once as Augustus bestowed upon me at a single time?

### XXIII

They say that just men inhabit lands in the Ocean called the Fortunate Isles [Note: These islands are frequently mentioned by the poets. Horace, *Epodes* 16:

“Let us seek the blessed fields,  
the rich islands,  
where the untilled earth gives back  
Ceres every year,  
and the unpruned vine  
continually flourishes,”

and so forth.]. There, grain grows from untilled soil, hills are clothed with vines that have sprung up by chance, trees are spontaneously weighed down with fruit, and vegetables are common in place of grass.

How small are such gifts, if you consider that God is their author? We too, though we do not cultivate our fields with our own hands, have such things growing without labor. How much happier is our condition, how much greater our blessedness! Not wheat ears [Note: From the nominative *spicum*, used by Cicero in *Aratus*: “bearing a splendid ear.”], not worthless clusters of grapes, but wealth and riches are poured upon those who do no labor; provinces, prefectures, fasces, and magistracies spring up spontaneously.

You, you, I say, great emperor, have brought back to the commonwealth virtues that had gone into exile and been banished, as though by a restoration of civil rights [Note: Those who return to the same place, or to the same threshold, from which they had departed, return by *postliminium*.]. You have kindled the studies of literature, already extinguished [Note: A word Tacitus uses more than once in the sense of “inflamed.”]. You have freed philosophy—until recently suspect, and not merely stripped of its honors but accused and put on trial—not merely by a judicial decision, but by placing it upon a royal throne, clothed in purple and crowned with gold and jewels [Note: Likewise Pacatus, *Panegyric on Theodosius*, section 16: “You not only called friendship within the palace, but received it upon the throne, clothed in purple and crowned with gold and jewels.”].

It is now permissible to raise our gaze to heaven and contemplate the stars with untroubled eyes, though shortly before we seemed, like cattle and four-footed animals, to fix our trembling eyes upon the ground. For who would have dared to watch the rising of a star, or its setting? Not even farmers, whose work must be regulated by the movement of the heavenly signs, examined the omens of the weather. The sailors themselves, who guide their nocturnal courses by the stars, refrained from using the names of the constellations. In short, on land and sea we lived not according to celestial reason but by chance and at random.

## XXIV

Therefore, Emperor, it is no wonder that so great and so genuine a love for you burns in the hearts of the citizens. For I do not think that, since human beings were born, anyone has ever been loved with such ardor by the human race. The affections of other kings and emperors were exceedingly rare and never lasting. They dwelt only on the surface of men’s hearts, aroused by sudden and favorable fortune, not bound to them by admiration for their virtues. [Note: That is, in the innermost part of the breast, so that it is contrasted with what follows shortly afterward: “But our affection is fastened in the deepest recesses of the mind.” The word *animus* that follows appears to have been rightly removed by Acidalius.]

But our affection is the result of true and certain judgment: our spirit is fastened in the deepest recesses of the mind, mingled and united with life, and destined to live on with the immortal mind even after our bodies have been dissolved by death. Thus the weapons, and the young men with swords and spears, are not a guard for your person but a kind of solemn adornment of imperial majesty. For what need have you of them, when you are enclosed by the strongest wall of civic affection? Should you fear the senate-house, when you have not only restored the senate’s ancient dignity but also added a very large measure of new honor? [Note: The place where public affairs were conducted.] Or is the people to be feared—people for whom you are the provider of their provisions, the protector of their lives, and the author of their freedom? [Note: Julian had sustained Rome, afflicted by prolonged wars and famine, by supplying it with provisions.]

For why should I speak of the soldiers? Two or three pairs of friends are generally brought forward from ancient memory. [Note: The friendship of Theseus and Pirithous, Damon and Pythias, and Gaius Laelius and Scipio Africanus is well known. See many further examples of this kind scattered throughout the authors.] I deny that anyone has ever been loved by a single friend more than you, Emperor, are loved—not only by your counts and tribunes, but by all the legions, cavalry and infantry alike, and even by the common soldiers. [Note: Of the three orders of counts introduced by Constantine; what was appropriate to each according to its rank; and of the provincial counts, the count of the imperial household, the count of largesses, and so forth. See Gruter, *On the Offices of the Augustan Household*.] [Note: A *gregarius miles* is one of the common herd, collected hastily from all quarters.]

Therefore, as far as you are concerned, you could now remove all weapons from the guard assigned to you—but when can you persuade the soldiers of this? The vigilance of loyal men is anxious. [Note: Because of the person whom one loves greatly, one is exceedingly fearful.] The greatest love is joined to the greatest fear. It is not enough for us that you have secured the result that no one wishes to harm you, unless we also ensure that no one is able to do so.

## XXV

Some other princes have had a devoted and affectionate retinue, but in a different manner. First, because, being ignorant and uncultivated, they selected the most uneducated men for their counsels, plainly so that their own wisdom might stand out somewhat above their common people. Thus, when every man of the lowest sort had gained honors and riches, they loved their own advantages and the vices of their princes. Everyone of the best character was driven far away from them, since integrity was suspect and hated; and the more honorable a man was, [Note: The more troublesome a witness to the disgraceful things they were doing, and the more unwelcome an observer, he was avoided.] the more unwelcome a judge of their disgraceful acts, the more carefully he was shunned.

But you, Augustus, once every kind of foolishness has been removed, seek out every man who is best and most learned. If someone excels in military virtues and renown in warfare, he is counted among your friends; whoever excels in oratory or in knowledge of civil law is invited of his own accord into your intimacy. Whoever has ever shown himself upright and energetic in the administration of the state is admitted to share in its offices. In governing the provinces, you choose not the most intimate of your associates but the most upright. All are enriched by you with money, made wealthy with riches, and honored with distinctions.

## XXVI

You protect friendships altogether with the loyalty of a private citizen and the resources of an emperor—the first guarantee of perpetual and steadfast goodwill, the surest proof of virtue, and its chief reality. [Note: Perhaps the sense is: “Have I heard that anyone has maliciously suspected him of himself?” This is how Livineius seems to understand it.] Have I ever heard that you held anyone under suspicion in your heart? No one has been deceived by affected flatteries; no one by a false promise. Who does not know the cheerful harshness of other emperors, and their laughter-filled cruelty? [Note: That is, cruelty which he concealed beneath loud laughter or an outburst of mirth. Domitian is meant: whenever he had resolved to rage against someone, he concealed his anger beneath a composed face prepared for laughter and jokes.] Their innate cruelty was concealed by a contrived appearance of joy.

There is a remarkable harmony between the mind and speech of our prince. He knows that lying is not merely a vice of a low and petty spirit but a servile vice. [Note: This is taken from Plutarch, *On the Education of Children*: “To lie is slavish.”] And rightly so: since either poverty or fear makes men liars, an emperor who lies does not understand the greatness of his own fortune.

Who, I ask you, has supplied more abundant evidence of loyalty and constancy? All those whom he admitted into his intimacy as a private citizen he treats with the same affection as emperor. No one has been removed from his rank; no one has been barred from access; the doors of the palace have been closed to no one. He regards them all as good men. In receiving friends he is an excellent judge. If some wicked men must be tolerated, he remains an unchanged friend despite the faults of his intimates. [Note: “Does he love?” Unless this has that meaning, it signifies what *habet* means among the Greeks, namely “holds” or “retains.”]

## XXVII

But do favorable circumstances change men’s dispositions? If they have not yet changed our prince, when will they? Whose good fortune has ever been more divine? A short while ago, in the devastated provinces of Gaul, [Note: Acidalius reads: “in the provinces of Gaul that had been torn apart.”] he was attacked by deadly enemies with open arms and hidden ambushes; within a few months, by the gift of heaven, he became ruler of Libya, Europe, and Asia. What greater rewards of the gods, or more abundant gifts of Fortune, shall we expect?

See whether, elated by prosperity, he has changed anything in the gentleness and moderation of his former life. He has changed—plainly, he has changed. For, having become more civil, he has blunted the envy directed against prosperity. Who would not regard as an indication of a mind brought to calm even that moment when, once the state had been freed from fear of a terrible war, we all rose up in exultant joy?

But the emperor, although he saw that the safety of the state had been prolonged through heavenly assistance, both grieved over the human condition and, granting pardon for offenses, assumed the role of a brother. Though he knew that his life had been attacked by the arms of the man whose death he adorned, [Note: Rittershusius reads: “whose life he knew had been attacked.”] he honored his death and afterward himself paid the proper rites. In both memory and forgetfulness he was remarkable: he forgot that the man was an enemy, but remembered that he was the heir of the empire. [Note: He forgot that he had been an enemy, but remembered that he was the heir to that empire.]

## XXVIII

But why should I seek further evidence of a mild and gentle spirit? This very day—this very day, I say—has provided sufficiently clear proofs of a civil disposition.

My colleague and I were afraid that the great emperor might do something too eagerly out of his zeal for humanity. Accordingly, at the first light of morning we went to the palace. Our arrival was announced to the prince, who at that moment was perhaps attending to those who came to pay their respects. [Note: It was customary among the Romans for eminent men, or those who stood above others in power, to be saluted during the first and second hours of the morning. Martial, Book IV, epigram 8:

> “The first hour wears out those who come to greet you, and the second as well.”]

Immediately he leapt from his throne as though he had been given advance notice, [Note: That is, having been anticipated, as in Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.105:

> “I anticipated everything and had already gone through it all in my mind.”]

with an anxious and busy expression—such as my own might have been if I had arrived late to meet the prince. With difficulty he cleared aside the crowds of people who were preceding us, striving to come as far as possible to meet us. There, by holy divinity, while everyone rejoiced, with what expression and in what voice did he say: “Hail, most illustrious consul!”

He deigned to kiss me with lips consecrated by divine utterances, and gave me his right hand—that hand, an immortal pledge of virtue and loyalty. [Note: Were the consuls honored with this title, as Joannes Savaro observes concerning epigram 9 of Book I of Apollinaris Sidonius? Or was it because Mamertinus had reached the consulship through his own virtue? For Cicero says in *For Roscius of Ameria* 85: “He seems to me most eminent who has reached a higher position through his own virtue.”]

The poets tell of that highest god, who restrains all things by his power and governs divine and human affairs under perpetual dominion, who, when he looks down upon the earth, changes the uncertainty of storms by the expression of his face, [Note: Or “by his breath,” although the expression “the appearance of the mouth” is also found in Lucan.] makes the world tremble at his nod, drives away storms by his cheerfulness, scatters the clouds, and pours bright calm across the world.

## XXIX

That this is so, we were able to experience shortly beforehand with our own eyes. [Note: The people burst into what joy while you smiled upon your consuls.] Into what an outpouring of joy did the people expand when you smiled upon your consuls? We saw the astonished faces of those who marveled, the varied postures of those who rejoiced, and the different movements of their bodies. Their unrestrained freedom in praising you poured forth unarticulated cries. The crowd danced with repeated leaps. Excessive joy made them forget dignity and gravity. That tossing of their togas, that exultation of their bodies, was produced in people who scarcely knew what they were doing. Their unrestrained rejoicing overcame all the people’s modesty and all their reverence for you.

“Hail, most illustrious consul.”

“I am indeed well, Emperor, and I shall continue to be well. For the outcome of this wish cannot be uncertain, since he who bids me be well has already made me so.” [Note: For the success of this wish cannot be doubtful.]

“Most illustrious consul.”

“I am indeed both a consul and a most illustrious consul. For who was ever a more illustrious consul than I, whom the consulship you bestowed elevates and glorifies, and whom the greatness that you confer ennobles?” [Note: “Elevates.” The word is found in Ennius and Nonius.]

After the auspicious conversations of the first salutation, he asks what we might wish to do in virtue of the consulship, intending to fulfill his senatorial duty if we wished to go to the tribunal, summon an assembly, or mount the Rostra. [Note: The various duties of consuls included going to the tribunal, convening an assembly, mounting the Rostra, and presenting senatorial resolutions in the senate-house. This may be seen frequently in the writers of Roman history.]

But the solemn business of that day led us to the senate-house. Accordingly, he immediately offers himself as our companion and, clothed in the bordered toga, walks on with both sides of the consulship covered by its purple-edged garment, differing little from his own magistrates either in dress or in color.

## XXX

It may perhaps seem superfluous to repeat what you yourselves saw. For what has been witnessed by the eyes is not sought from the ears. Yet these things must be entrusted to writing, inserted into monuments, and transmitted to future generations—miracles scarcely credible in the ages to come.

Almost within the very doors of the imperial palace, he ordered the consular litters to be brought in. When, out of deference to his honor and majesty, we refused that seat of the highest dignity, he almost placed us upon it with his own hands, then began to walk on foot before us, mingled with the ranks of the toga-clad citizens. He moderated his pace almost at the nod of a lictor and at the command of an attendant.

Will anyone believe this who shortly before witnessed the haughtiness of men clothed in purple—men who bestowed such honor upon their own people only so that they might not despise those who were without honor? Will anyone believe that, after so long a time, that ancient freedom of the earliest ages has been restored to the state?

For my part, I do not think that the consulship of Lucius Brutus and Publius Valerius, who first ruled their fellow citizens with annual power after the kings had been expelled, should be preferred to ours. [Note: I refrain from relating here what the writers of Roman history recount at length about those first Roman consuls.] Both acted for the public good; both were beneficial to the safety of the Roman state; both were distinguished at the beginnings of its advantages. Yet each possesses something special. They received consular power through the people; we received it back through Julian. In their year liberty arose; in ours it was restored.

## XXXI

But, most holy Emperor, let whatever you do justly, moderately, and civilly be a wonder to others if they wish; it cannot be one to me, since I know that you are free and absolved from all human vices, [Note: I shall observe at the end of Julian’s life that this was not so.] that you burn only with love of immortality, and that you direct all your resources and thoughts toward the eternal memory of posterity, serving above all those judges who, in future ages, will judge your deeds without hatred or favor. No one who knows that people will always speak about him can conceive anything base or mean.

Now, if I should seem to you, Emperor, to have employed a speech too limited and not commensurate with your merits, I beg and beseech you to attribute this rather to my nature than to the magnitude of your benefits. No one since human beings were born has ever received greater rewards from kings and emperors; no one has had a heavier burden placed upon him.

I will not deny that prefectures and consulships have been conferred upon many, but for them, after immense labors, the honor was restored as something almost owed. For me, although I have already attained the honor, it is only now necessary to labor so that I may deserve it. With the order of time reversed and the exchange of offices altered, I must now strive to be judged worthy of the reward, although I have already received the reward.

O grievous burden of your swift benevolence! I fear that I may not be able to express clearly the sequence of my difficulties. It is easier, Emperor, through good qualities to deserve becoming consul than, through diligence and labor, to bring it about that one appears to have deserved it once one has become consul.

## XXXII

Far be it from us, Augustus, and may holy divinity avert such an omen, that you should expect anyone among mortals to repay your benefaction! Nevertheless, since this is the only return that such great fortune can receive, or that can be bestowed by us in recompense for your benefactions, I shall honor the immortality of your gifts with everlasting services.

All my work and all my leisure shall be devoted to adorning and celebrating your achievements. Nor shall the gratitude and goodwill of my living self be shown only while I remain alive and vigorous; even when my soul has departed, the monuments of your benefaction toward me will endure. [Note: In the Putean edition it reads: “when my soul has departed from me.” I have deleted the two words with Acidalius. Other editions read: “when my soul has departed from me.”] [Note: This passage is plainly taken from Cicero’s speech *After His Return to the Quirites*, near the end.]

In expressing my gratitude, most holy Emperor, I promise you this, and shall always fulfill it: in offering counsel, I shall not lack truth; in undertaking dangers, if circumstances require it, I shall not lack courage; in giving my opinion frankly, I shall not lack loyalty; in opposing, for the sake of the state and of you, the wishes of men, I shall not lack freedom; in enduring labors, I shall not lack diligence; and in increasing the advantages of your empire, I shall not lack the goodwill of a grateful heart.

Throughout my entire life I shall strive, labor, and accomplish this: that the honors you have bestowed upon me may appear not to have been conferred upon just anyone because necessity required it, but to have been rightly placed and appropriately assigned because it was fitting.

# APPENDIX

## LIFE OF FLAVIUS CLAUDIUS JULIANUS

[Col. 0429]

In the year 1084 from the founding of the City, A.D. 331, the twenty-sixth year of the reign of the Emperor Constantine the Great.

Flavius Claudius Julianus, surnamed the Apostate because, after gaining power, he most shamefully abandoned the Christian religion which he had professed as a young man, was born at Constantinople on the eighth day before the Ides of November. His father was Constantius, the brother of Constantine the Great; his mother was Basilina, a most noble Christian woman and the second wife of Constantius. His mother died a few months afterward. (Julian, *Misopogon*.)

[Col. 0430D]

In the year 1090 from the founding of the City, A.D. 337, the first year of the reign of Constantine, Constantius, and Constans Augusti.

Constantius, his brother Hannibalianus, and Dalmatius Caesar, the son of their brother Dalmatius—men whom Constantine the Great had honored with purple and gold clothing and the title of nobility—were overwhelmed in a military uprising, either at the instigation of Constantius Augustus or, at any rate, with his connivance: either so that he might rule more securely, or so that he might avenge upon them the poison which he suspected had been administered to his father Constantine.

Only Julian and his sole brother Gallus, then both twelve years old, barely escaped the same fate. Gallus escaped because, owing to his uncertain and almost failing health, he was thought unlikely to live long; Julian because he was still a child. For, as the date of his death indicates, he had not yet much exceeded five years of age.

In the year 1092 from the founding of the City, A.D. 339, the third year of the reign of Constantine, Constantius, and Constans Augusti.

The following year, when certain men were using the names of Julian and Gallus to stir up rebellions, both were taken away to Cappadocia and educated at Macellum—a place near Mount Argaeus, not far from Caesarea, and thoroughly royal—in the liberal arts and the knowledge of sacred writings. In this retreat they were kept under the strictest guard for six entire years, as he reports. [Note: Julian, letter to the Senate and People of Athens.] No one had access to them, yet they made such progress that, after becoming clerics, they publicly read the ecclesiastical books to the people.

While both of them were erecting a basilica to the martyr Saint Mamas at their own expense—Gallus to display his piety, Julian to display his impiety, that is, to conceal from Constantius the Christian religion which he had already renounced in his heart—it happened that, while Gallus’s work advanced, Julian’s building was destroyed by an earthquake. When this was reported to Constantius, he regarded it as an ominous sign of their piety and was violently angry with both of them. (Gregory of Nazianzus, oration; Sozomen; Zonaras; Cedrenus; and others.)

In the year 1098 from the founding of the City, A.D. 345, the ninth year of the reign of Constantius and Constans Augusti.

After the anger of Constantius, who was unsuccessfully engaged in the Pontic expedition, had somewhat cooled, Gallus was sent to Ephesus, where considerable property had been left to him by his ancestors. Julian was summoned to the public schools at Constantinople. In that light of the whole world he made such progress over the course of approximately three years under the instruction of Nicocles, the Lacedaemonian grammarian, and Ecebolius the sophist, that he was openly said to be fit to govern the empire.

Constantius, disturbed by this and fearing that the occasion might provoke some disturbance in the empire’s principal city, ordered Julian to move away as quickly as possible.

In the year 1101 from the founding of the City, A.D. 348, the twelfth year of the reign of Constantius and Constans Augusti.

While Constantius Augustus was occupied against the Persians, Julian was entrusted for education at Nicomedia to Eusebius, bishop of that city and his Arian relative. He had been forbidden to attach himself to the sophist Libanius, an exceptionally fierce defender of pagan superstition. At first, however, Julian secretly devoted himself entirely to reading Libanius’s books; then, emboldened by this reading and increasingly eager for superstition, he went openly to him.

Jamblichus and Maximus, distinguished magicians, immediately came to him. They so beguiled Julian’s already excessively inclined mind with their deceptions that he never left their side. He was especially delighted with Maximus because Maximus had inspired him with hope of imperial power.

This was reported to Constantius. When Julian learned of it, caught between fear and hope, he had his head shaved to signify that his mind was alien to imperial power, pretended to lead a monastic life, and was appointed a reader in the church at Nicomedia.

In the year 1104 from the founding of the City, A.D. 351, the fifteenth year of the reign of Constantius Augustus.

Julian’s brother Gallus became Caesar on the Ides of March and was called Constantius Gallus. Along with the entire prefecture of the East, Constantius’s sister Constantia was given to him as wife.

Meanwhile, as Julian was increasingly drawn toward summoning demons and apparitions, examining the entrails of beasts, and other occult practices of diviners, he left Nicomedia and traveled through the remaining parts of Asia, seeking men skilled in magic, who were rumored to be numerous there. First he visited Ionia, then twice within two months he visited Phrygia, although completely weakened by an illness contracted from the strain of travel, and finally he hurried through Greece, as he himself says in his letter to Themistius.

In the year 1106 from the founding of the City, A.D. 353, the seventeenth year of the reign of Constantius Augustus.

This year Gallus was summoned to Italy by Constantius through a certain Domitian, either because he was suspected of aspiring to imperial power or because of the massacres committed at Antioch. Domitian himself was killed by Gallus’s soldiers because he had addressed Gallus too arrogantly, and Gallus came to Italy.

Constantius also suspected Julian of still burning with desire for imperial power—either because Gallus, on his way to the East, had turned aside to Nicomedia in order, as Socrates says, to see Julian secretly, or because Julian, when moving to Asia, had passed through Constantinople so that he might see his brother Gallus there, as Ammianus says. In any event, Constantius ordered him to be kept under guard there.

But when Julian saw that he could escape from the hands of his guards, he changed his location from time to time and escaped. So Socrates reports.

In the year 1107 from the founding of the City, A.D. 354, the eighteenth year of the reign of Constantius Augustus.

After Gallus’s wife Constantia had died of a fever in Bithynia, and Gallus himself had been killed in Illyricum on the island of Flanona, as Ammianus says, Julian, fearing a similar fate, hastened to Milan, where Constantius was staying after returning from Germany under a treaty with the Alamanni.

While hiding in a suburb—or, as others maintain, at Novocomum—he obtained through the intercession of the Empress Eusebia permission to speak with the emperor and made a complete defense of himself. He therefore returned home victorious, and indeed was honorably escorted by Eusebia. But when that journey was obstructed by some unknown accident, he was sent back to Greece, which all interpreted as an exile. (Julian, letter to Themistius and letter to the Senate and People of Athens.)

Julian himself regarded this as a favor received from Eusebia, whether, as he said, for the sake of his studies, or rather because he wished to communicate about his affairs with the priests and impostors of that region. (Gregory of Nazianzus, first oration against Julian; Sozomen.)

Gregory of Nazianzus, having seen Julian at Athens, said: “What sort of evil is the Roman world nourishing?” He was not a false prophet.

In the year 1108 from the founding of the City, A.D. 355, the nineteenth year of the reign of Constantius Augustus and the twenty-fourth year of Julian’s age.

When the barbarians summoned by Constantius against Magnentius and Britannio were ravaging Gaul—and, according to Ammianus, had occupied more than forty-five towns—Constantius, judging it insufficiently safe to withdraw from Italy, recalled Julian from Athens, where he was living as a philosopher, and made him Caesar on the eighth day before the Ides of November.

At the same time, to strengthen Julian’s loyalty, Constantius gave him his sister Helena in marriage a few days later. He sent Julian in command of the transalpine provinces, either to carry the emperor’s image into Gaul, as Julian himself says, or rather to fight against the barbarians.

Accordingly, with only 360 soldiers, as he himself says in his letter to the Senate and People of Athens, and with authority over them such that he could do nothing without the advice of the commanders, he departed on the Kalends of December. He was escorted by Augustus as far as a place marked by two columns, situated between Laumellum and Ticinum. From there he proceeded by the direct roads toward Taurini.

There he heard the report that Cologne had been freed from a stubborn barbarian siege but had been extensively destroyed, and he recognized how much danger he had incurred by accepting this province. He himself repeatedly said that he had achieved nothing more than dying amid greater burdens, recalling that Homeric line concerning the day on which he assumed the purple:

> “Purple death seized him, and mighty Fate.”

From there he advanced to Vienne on the Rhône and was received with a great gathering and acclamation from all the peoples. Then an old woman deprived of sight, asking who had entered and learning that it was Julian Caesar, exclaimed that he would restore the temples of the gods. (Ammianus.) The truth of this prophecy was confirmed not long afterward by events, when, having become emperor, he professed paganism openly—not at night and in secret, but after publicly renouncing the Christian religion.

In the year 1109 from the founding of the City, A.D. 356, the twentieth year of the reign of Constantius Augustus and the twenty-fifth year of Julian’s age.

Constantius returned to the city as though in triumph. Julian, who was consul that year, spent the winter at Vienne and then marched against the barbarians. First, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, he reached Augustodunum with only the cataphracts and ballistarii, and suddenly seized Autissiodorum and Tricasses.

From there, passing through Rheims—where he was expected by Marcellus, the successor of Ursicinus, and indeed by Ursicinus himself with the entire army—he hastened to Decempagi and the Rhine. There he recovered Brotomagus, today Brumath in Alsace; Tabernae; Alison; Nemetae, or Speyer; Vangiones, today Worms; and Mainz.

With no one thereafter offering resistance, he recovered Cologne, which, as Ammianus and Julian in his letter to the Senate and People of Athens say, had been occupied by the barbarians less than ten months earlier, around the end of September, and forced the terrified Franks to seek peace.

Julian, delighted by these beginnings of victory, passed through Trier and wintered at Sens, then a strategically advantageous town. (Ammianus.) There, as he himself says in his letter to the Senate and People of Athens, he defeated with only a few soldiers a very powerful army after a month-long siege, while no aid was sent to him by Marcellus, the master of cavalry.

Marcellus was summoned to Milan, where Constantius was staying, to give an account of his conduct; he was removed from command and sent into exile at Sardica, which was his native place. The same letter to the Senate and People of Athens reports this.

In the year 1110 from the founding of the City, A.D. 357, the twenty-first year of the reign of Constantius Augustus and the twenty-sixth year of Julian’s age.

While Julian, consul for the second time, was preparing himself against the Germans, Lyons was invaded by them, though they were expelled not long afterward. He also restored the Three Taverns, a fort near Argentoratum at the foot of the Vosges that had recently been destroyed.

In a single great and extremely difficult battle on the fields of Argentoratum, he defeated seven of the most powerful kings of all Germany: Chonodomarius, Vestralpus, Urius, Ursicinus, Serapio, Suomarius, and Hortarius. (Ammianus.)

Julian sent many captives to Constantius, who was struck by their appearance and size. Six thousand Alamannic bodies—not sixty thousand, as Zosimus incorrectly says—were counted lying prostrate on the field, and immeasurable heaps of the dead were carried along by the river’s waters. On Julian’s side, 247 were lost.

The Frankish king Chonodomarius was captured in battle, according to Victor, or, according to Ammianus, treacherously at a banquet. He was presented to Julian, thrown to the ground, and, begging for mercy, was afterward sent after a few days to the emperor Constantius’s court, as Constantius was conveniently returning from the Quadi and Sarmatians, the peoples dwelling along the Danube. He was immediately sent to Rome and, as Julian adds in his letter to Athens, wasted away from a lethargic illness in the camp on the Caelian Hill.

Victorious once more, Julian came to the Three Taverns and Mainz, ravaged the peoples beyond the Rhine, forced them to seek peace at the autumnal equinox, drove the Franks back from the Meuse, and finally wintered at Paris.

In the year 1111 from the founding of the City, A.D. 358, the twenty-second year of the reign of Constantius Augustus and the twenty-seventh year of Julian’s age.

Around the month of July, Julian terrified and received into submission the Salii, Frisians, Chattuarii, Chamavi, and Bructeri, who had established settlements for themselves on Roman soil and were ravaging it. He assigned lands to them and restored the forts destroyed along the Meuse. (Ammianus.)

In the year 1112 from the founding of the City, A.D. 359, the twenty-third year of the reign of Constantius Augustus and the twenty-eighth year of Julian’s age.

Julian again marched against the Alamanni, crossing the Rhine near Mainz, while the enemy guarded the crossing point in vain. He compelled the kings Macrianus, Hariobaudus, and Vadomarius to seek terms of peace.

Here granaries were established for supplying the soldiers who guarded the Rhine.

In the year 1113 from the founding of the City, A.D. 360, the twenty-fourth year of the reign of Constantius Augustus and the twenty-ninth year of Julian’s age.

Julian was holding his third consulship when Constantius, jealous of his glory, recalled through the tribune and notary Decentius the Heruli, Batavians, Celts, and other auxiliary troops, intending to use them against the Persians.

But those troops—whether out of hatred for Constantius, love for Julian, or deliberate design, or because they rejected service overseas—proclaimed Julian Augustus at Paris against his will, as he himself says.

He immediately sent envoys to Constantius at Constantinople with letters in which he explained his conduct. Constantius received them arrogantly at Caesarea in Cappadocia.

Julian therefore went to the Meuse crossing and then overwhelmed the Chattuarii, who were ravaging the farthest parts of Gaul and were secure because they believed themselves protected by the difficulty of access to the terrain. He forced them to seek peace.

He then wintered at Vienne and celebrated the fifth anniversary of his accession. There his wife Helena died, and her body was sent to Rome.

Meanwhile, Julian, no longer trusting that Constantius would ever be reconciled, resolved to seize the whole empire by open warfare. Accordingly, he sent letters to various cities urging them to remain loyal to him, and went into Pannonia to fight against Constantius.

In the year 1114 from the founding of the City, A.D. 361, the twenty-fifth year of the reign of Constantius Augustus and the thirtieth year of Julian’s age.

Constantius Augustus died near Tarsus on the third day before the Nones of October while on the Persian expedition. Julian, after again defeating the Alamanni and putting Gaul in order, proceeded directly to Constantinople. Of Constantius’s principal officials and friends he punished some with death and others with exile.

He recalled the exiled bishops and, so that they might afflict one another with mutual disputes, allowed each to follow whichever sect he preferred. He publicly renounced the Christian religion and attacked it no less cruelly than cunningly. He reopened and restored the temples of the pagans, and himself was consecrated to profane rites as Pontifex Maximus.

In the year 1115 from the founding of the City, A.D. 362, the first year of Julian’s reign and the thirty-first year of his age.

Embassies arrived at Julian from every direction. He himself, setting out against the Persians, passed through Nicomedia and wintered at Antioch.

There, mocked by the Antiochenes—and especially angered by the insults they hurled at his beard, which was longer than it should have been—he first became angry; then, in a satirical pamphlet full of jokes which he titled *Misopogon*, that is, “Beard-Hater,” he attacked them. Throughout it, however, he appears by constant irony to accuse not their luxury and softness but himself, because he was unable to imitate them.

The consul Mamertinus delivered a speech of thanksgiving to the emperor for the consulship which he held that year with Nevita.

Julian sent Athanasius into exile at the request of the Arians. He attacked Christian teachers of the liberal arts so severely that Prohaeresius, although expressly exempted by the edict, as well as Musonius and Marius Victorinus, abandoned their schools.

But he honored with the highest distinctions Themistius the philosopher, Libanius the sophist, Oribasius, a certain physician from Pergamum, Maximus the Cynic, Ecebolius the sophist, and others who professed impious paganism.

In the year 1116 from the founding of the City, A.D. 363, the second year of Julian’s reign and the thirty-second year of his age.

Julian, consul for the fourth time, having taken as his colleague Sallustius, who was most closely associated with him in the worship of idols, spent the winter at Antioch and departed from there on the day before the Nones of March.

He crossed the Euphrates on the seventh day before the Ides of April and, after capturing several cities along the way, reached Ctesiphon. There, when a battle had begun, he was pierced by an arrow amid the confused crowd on the sixth day before the Kalends of July.

By whom he was wounded is uncertain: whether by a Persian deserter, as Victor’s epitome says; by one of his own men, as Ammianus says; by a Christian, as Libanius records; by the demon himself, as Callistus, Julian’s attendant, relates—Callistus having composed Julian’s deeds in heroic verse; by angels, as Gregory of Nazianzus reports; or finally by the martyr Mercury, as Damascus asserts on the authority of Helladius, to whom Nicephorus adds the martyr Artemius as his companion.

“Certainly,” says Gregory of Nazianzus, “Julian received a wound salutary to the whole world; and by this death he made offering to all those whom he had killed with the utmost cruelty.”

As soon as he felt himself wounded by the mortal blow, he threw the blood he had caught in his full hand toward heaven and said: “You have conquered, Galilean”—for so he mockingly called Christ. Thus Theodoret reports it. “Be satisfied, Nazarene.” Thus Nicephorus.

He was immediately carried back to the camp, his side gaping more widely from the deep wound and the swelling obstructing the passage of the breath through his veins. After drinking the cold water he requested, he died at midnight in the thirty-second year of his age, having ruled for one year and approximately seven months after the death of Constantius. This is Ammianus’s account.

His body, however, was carried to Tarsus in Cilicia and buried there amid the great mockery of the people toward the dead, if we believe Ammianus. But if Gregory of Nazianzus is to be believed, the earth itself, which Julian had polluted with his crimes, shook him off and he was thrown into the sea.

He possessed an outstanding and attractive but frivolous and crafty character, corrupted by vain superstition concerning the gods and by magical arts. He affected a kind of philosophical gravity and was always surrounded by a crowd of sophists. He was talkative, given to scurrilous wit, and excessively subservient to popular approval.

He was so superstitious that he treated even the philosopher Jamblichus, whom he called Mercury, as though he were the protecting god of Nicomedia. In every branch of literature, however, he was exceedingly cultivated and especially skilled in the Greek language. He was generous, contemptuous of wealth, luxury, and pleasures, outstanding in the arts of war and peace, patient of labor and hunger, fortunate and just—except toward Christians, whom he persecuted with every kind of cruelty—and extraordinarily fond of literature and of literary men, unless they happened to be Christians.

## PUBLIUS VICTOR

[Col. 0435]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE DESCRIPTION OF THE CITY OF ROME
[Col. 0435B] It is very well known from Suetonius, *Life of Augustus*, chapter 30, from Pliny, Tacitus, and others, that the city of Rome was divided by Augustus into fourteen districts, which a later age began to call, under a corrupted name, *rioni*. The same is attested by an inscription that can still be seen at Rome beneath the portico of the Palace of the Conservators, composed in these words:

“ To the Emperor Caesar Trajan Hadrian Augustus, son of the divine Trajan Parthicus, grandson of the divine Nerva, Pontifex Maximus, invested with tribunician power for the twentieth time, acclaimed emperor twice, consul three times, father of his country: the masters of the districts of the city’s fourteen regions.”

[Col. 0435C] We possess a brief description of these districts, composed under the emperors Valentinian and Valens, whose authors are believed to have been Sextus Rufus and Publius Victor. Onufrius Panvinius, Famianus Nardinus, and others enlarged and illustrated their work more fully. Short works attributed to Rufus and Victor have been published more than once; most recently Graevius also included them in volume III of the *Roman Antiquities*. Yet none of them has reached us complete and cleansed of corruptions.

In addition, Guido Pancirolo prefixed to his excellent commentary on the *Notitia Dignitatum* of both empires, part 2, another description of the city of Rome. Its author, whether Victor or someone else, appears to have flourished under the emperors Honorius or Valentinian III. There we find the same material [Col. 0435D] that is read in Rufus’s and Victor’s description, sometimes more, sometimes less, and occasionally different.

This latter work, as though it were something new, was reprinted in 1651 by Philippus Labbe, priest of the Society of Jesus.
