Two copies of it, both extremely ancient, [Col. 0436B] among the manuscripts of the richest of all the Vatican libraries, were discovered and transcribed by Father Joseph Blanchinius of Verona, priest of the Roman Oratory and nephew on his father’s side of the celebrated Francis Blanchinius, who has already acquired great fame for himself through books published on sacred learning.

When, out of affection for me, he presented the same work to me, I wished to make it public here, since it might perhaps be of some use to lovers of Roman scholarship. I have also appended the description published by Pancirolo and Labbe, so that the reader may have before him at a single glance the variant readings occurring in the two copies.

Although the Labbean edition rightly claims the more honorable place, and although the Vatican copy is by no means free from errors, it may nevertheless happen that the scholar who investigates the magnificent ornaments of the eternal city may derive some light [Col. 0436C] even from the wording of that manuscript.

Nor can I conceal that, in this very work, I too found the opinion of those confirmed who suppose that the *insulae* situated in the City were houses separated from the others by some intervening space. Yet when I see before my eyes, on the one hand, forty-six thousand six hundred and two *insulae* throughout the City and, on the other, one thousand seven hundred and ninety houses, as the description records, I am compelled to doubt greatly whether the opinion of those men should be preferred who think that *insulae* were what we call the private dwellings of the people, most of them rented, separated from their neighbors only by walls, while the name “houses” was applied to what we now call palaces.

For why would those ancient describers have omitted the people’s adjoining houses—the principal part, surely, of that immense city—while counting only buildings separated from one another by some intervening space? Certainly forty-six thousand six hundred and two *insulae*, together with temples, palaces, theaters, amphitheaters, baths, circuses, granaries, schools, and so forth, constituted an excessively vast and enormous city. I add no more.

[Col. 0437]

# DESCRIPTION OF THE CITY OF ROME

## From the edition of Father Philippus Labbe, of the Society of Jesus, 1651

# DESCRIPTION OF THE CITY OF ROME, ONCE DESOLATED BUT NOW RESTORED TO GREATER GLORY UNDER THE MOST PIOUS IMPERIAL GOVERNMENT

By an uncertain author who lived under Honorius or Valentinian III.

[Col. 0437A]

## REGION I

The Capena Gate. It contains the temple of Honor and Virtue; the Camenae; the Lake of Prometheus; the Baths of Torquatus and Vespasian; the Severan and Commodian Baths; the Area of Apollo, the Area of Hope, and the Area of Gallus; the Glassmakers’ Street; the Bakers’ Area; Caesar’s changing-station; [Col. 0437B] the Baths of Bolanus and Mamertinus; the Area of Carsura; the Baths of Abascantus and Antiochianus; the temple of Mars, Minerva, and Tempestas; the Almo River; the arch of the divine Verus Parthicus, and of the divine Trajan, and of Drusus.

Ten streets. Ten shrines. Forty-eight district-masters. Two curators. Three thousand two hundred and fifty *insulae*. Thirteen granaries. Eighty-six baths. Eighty-four pools. [Col. 0437C] Twenty bakeries. It contains 12,219 feet.

## REGION II

The Caelimontium. It contains the temple of Claudius; the Great Market; the wolf-keepers; the Cave of the Cyclops; the cohorts of the watch; the Foreign Camp; the Head of Africa; the sacred tree; the house of Philippus and the Vectilian house; the Morning School and the Gallic School; the spoliarium; [Col. 0437D] the infirmary; the armory; the Golden Mica.

Seven streets. Seven shrines. Forty-eight district-masters. Two curators. Three thousand six hundred *insulae*. [Col. 0439A] One hundred and twenty-four houses. Fourteen granaries. Eighty-two baths. Sixty-two pools. Twelve bakeries. It contains 12,200 feet.

## REGION III

Isis and Serapis. It contains the Mint; the amphitheater, which holds 87,000 spectators; the Morning School and the Dacian School; the house of Bryttius; the most imposing stage equipment; the Shepherd’s Pool; the school of the quaestors and of the corpse-bearers; [Col. 0439B] the Baths of Trajan and Titus; the Portico of Livia; the Camp of the Misenian fleet.

Twelve streets. Twelve shrines. Forty-nine district-masters. Two curators. Two thousand seven hundred and fifty-seven *insulae*. Sixty houses. Fourteen granaries. Eighty baths. Sixty-five pools. Sixteen bakeries. It contains 12,340 feet.

[Col. 0439C]

## REGION IV

The Temple of Peace. It contains the apsidal portico; the Area of Vulcan; the Golden Trumpet; Apollo Sandaliarius; the temple of Tellus; the Chartarian Granaries; the Jorarian Beam; the Colossus, one hundred feet high. On its head it has seven rays, each twenty-two and a half feet long; the sweating Meta; the temple of Roma and Venus; the temple of Jupiter Stator; the Sacred Way; [Col. 0439D] the Constantinian Basilica; the Temple of Faustina; the Basilica of Paul; the Transitorium Forum; the Subura; the Baths of Daphnis.

Eight streets. Forty-eight district-masters. Two curators. Two thousand seven hundred and fifty-seven *insulae*. Eighty-eight houses. Eighteen granaries. Seventy-five baths. [Col. 0441A] Seventy-eight pools. Twelve bakeries. It contains 13,000 feet.

## REGION V

The Esquiliae. It contains the Pool of Orpheus; the Livian Market; the Nymphaeum of the divine Alexander; two cohorts of the watch; Hercules Syllanus; the Pallantian Gardens; the military amphitheater; the Viminal Field beneath the embankment; Minerva Medica; Isis Patricia.

Fifteen streets. [Col. 0441B] Forty-eight district-masters. Two curators. Three thousand eight hundred and fifty *insulae*. One hundred and eighty houses. Twenty-three granaries. Seventy-five baths. Seventy-four pools. Fifteen bakeries. It contains 15,600 feet.

## REGION VI

The High Road. It contains the temple of Salus and Serapis; the temple of Flora; the ancient Capitol; [Col. 0441C] the lead statue of Mamurius; the temple of Quirinus; the Punic apple; the Sallustian Gardens; the Flavian family; the Baths of Diocletian and Constantine; ten shops; the white hens; the Area of Candidus; three cohorts of the watch.

Seventeen streets. Seventeen shrines. Eighteen district-masters. Two curators. [Col. 0441D] Three thousand four hundred and three *insulae*. One hundred and forty-six houses. Seventeen granaries. Seventy-five baths. Seventy-three pools. Sixteen bakeries. It contains 15,700 feet.

## REGION VII

The Broad Way. It contains the Pool of Ganymede; seven cohorts of the watch; the New Arch; the Nymphaeum of Jupiter; the Goat Shrine; [Col. 0443A] the Field of Agrippa; the Temple of the Sun and its camp; the Portico of Gypsianus and Constantine; two new temples of Hope and Fortune; the horse of Tiridates, king of the Armenians; the Swine Forum; the Largian Gardens; the Tame Animals; the Pierced Stone.

Fifteen streets. Fifteen shrines. Forty-eight district-masters. Two curators. Three thousand eight hundred and five *insulae*. One hundred and twenty houses. [Col. 0443B] Twenty-five granaries. Seventy-five baths. Seventy-six pools. Fifteen bakeries. It contains 15,700 feet.

## REGION VIII

The Roman Forum and the Great Forum. It contains the Rostra; the golden Genius of the Roman People and the horse of Constantine; the Little Senate; the Atrium of Minerva; the Forums of Caesar, Augustus, Nerva, and Trajan; the Temple of the divine Trajan and the spiral column, 128½ feet high, with 1,805 steps inside and forty-five windows; [Col. 0443C] six cohorts of the watch; the Argentarian Basilica; the Temple of Concord; the Navel of Rome; the Temple of Saturn and Vespasian; the Capitol; the Golden Milestone; the temple of Julia, the Castors, and Vesta; the Germanic and Agrippian Granaries; a water basin containing four *scauri* beneath the temple.

[Col. 0443D] The Atrium of Cacus; the Unguentary Street; the Greek Tribunal; the Pearl Portico; the Herb Market with its elephant.

Thirty-four streets. Twenty-nine shrines. Forty-eight district-masters. Two curators. Three thousand eight hundred and eighty *insulae*. One hundred and thirty houses. Eighteen granaries. Eighty-three baths. One hundred and twenty pools. [Col. 0445A] Twenty bakeries. It contains 13,067 feet.

## REGION IX

The Flaminius Circus. It contains four faction stables; the temple of Hercules; the Portico of Philippus; the two Minucian structures, the old and the grain market; the Crypt of Balbus; four theaters, especially that of Balbus, which holds 30,085 spectators; the Field of Mars; the Trigarium; [Col. 0445B] the Kneeling Storks; the Pantheon; the Basilicas of Matidia and Marciana; the Temple of the divine Antoninus and the spiral column, 175½ feet high, with 203 steps inside and fifty-six windows; the Hadrianium; the Alexandrian and Agrippan Baths; the Portico of the Argonauts and of Meleager; the Iseum and Serapeum; the Felicula Island.

Thirty-five streets. [Col. 0445C] Thirty-five shrines. Thirty-five district-masters. Two curators. Two thousand seven hundred and seventy-four *insulae*. One hundred and forty houses. Twenty-two granaries. Sixty-three baths. Sixty-three pools. Twenty bakeries. It contains 32,500 feet.

## REGION X

The Palatine. It contains the hut of Romulus; the temple of the Mother of the Gods and of Apollo Rhamnusius; the Five-Gated Building; [Col. 0445D] the Augustan and Tiberian Houses; the temple of Jupiter Victor; the house of Dio; the Old Curia; Fortune Looking Backward; the Septizonium of the divine Severus; Germanician Victory; the Lupercal.

Twenty streets. Twenty shrines. Forty-eight district-masters. Two curators. Two thousand six hundred and forty-three *insulae*. Eighty-eight houses. [Col. 0447A] Forty-eight granaries. Fourteen baths. Eighty-nine pools. Twenty bakeries. It contains 11,600 feet.

## REGION XI

The Circus Maximus, which holds 485,000 spectators. It contains twelve gates; the Temple of Mercury; the temple of Dis Pater; Ceres; the Threefold Gate; Apollo Who Looks Toward Heaven; Hercules Olivarius; [Col. 0447B] the Velabrum; the Arch of the divine Constantine.

Eighteen streets. Nineteen shrines. Forty-eight district-masters. Two curators. Two thousand six hundred *insulae*. Eighty-nine houses. Sixteen granaries. Fifteen baths. Twenty pools. Fifteen bakeries. It contains 11,500 feet.

## REGION XII

The Public Fishpond. It contains the Radicarian Area; the New Way; Fortune Mammosa; Isis Athenodoria; the temple of Bona Dea Subsaxana; the Dolphin Statue; the Antonine Baths; seven Parthian houses; the Wool-workers’ Field; the house of Chilo; four cohorts of the watch; the house of Cornificius; Hadrian’s private property.

Fourteen streets. Seventeen shrines. [Col. 0447D] Forty-eight district-masters. Two curators. Two thousand four hundred and eighty-seven *insulae*. One hundred and fourteen houses. Seventeen granaries. Sixty-three baths. Eighty-one pools. Twenty bakeries. It contains 12,000 feet.

## REGION XIII

The Aventine. It contains the temple of Diana and Minerva; three Nymphaea; [Col. 0449A] the Varian and Decian Baths; the Little Jar; the Golden Map; the Plane-tree Grove; the Granaries of Galba; the Bean Portico; the School of Cassius; the Bakers’ Forum.

Seventeen streets. Seventeen shrines. Forty-eight district-masters. Two curators. Two thousand four hundred and eighty-seven *insulae*. One hundred and thirty houses. Twenty-five granaries. [Col. 0449B] Sixty-four baths. Eighty-eight pools. Twenty bakeries. It contains 209,000 feet.

## REGION XIV

Across the Tiber. It contains the Gaianum and Vaticanum; the Phrygianum; five naval-battle basins; the Domitian Gardens; the Baths of Ampelides, Priscus, and Diana Molinis; the Janiculum; the Valerian Statue; seven cohorts of the watch; the Head of the Gorgon; [Col. 0449C] the Temple of Fors Fortuna; the Septimian Area; the Reclining Hercules; the Brytian and Codetan Fields; the Gardens of Geta; the Camp of the Chair-bearers.

Seventy-eight streets. Forty-eight district-masters. Seventy-eight shrines. Three curators. Four thousand four hundred and five *insulae*. One hundred and fifty houses. Twenty-two granaries. [Col. 0449D] Eighty-six baths. One hundred and eighty pools. Twenty-three bakeries. It contains 33,488 feet.

Twenty-nine libraries. Of these, two are especially notable: the Palatine and the Ulpian.

# FIVE OBELISKS

One in the Circus Maximus, 88½ feet high. One in the Vatican, 71 feet high. One in the Field of Mars, 82½ feet high. [Col. 0451A] Two in the Mausoleum of Augustus, each 82½ feet high.

# SEVEN BRIDGES

The Aelian, Aurelia, Mulvian, Sublician, Fabrician, Cestian, and Probian.

# SEVEN HILLS

The Caelian, Aventine, Tarpeian, Palatine, [Col. 0451B] Esquiline, Vatican, and Janiculan.

# EIGHT FIELDS

The Viminal, Agrippa’s, Martian, Codetan, Octavian, Cattle, Wool-workers’, and Brytian.

# ELEVEN FORUMS

The Roman, Great, [Col. 0451C] Caesar’s, Augustus’s, Nerva’s, Trajan’s, Ahenobarbus’s, Cattle, Swine, Bakers’, Gauls’, and Rustic.

# TEN BASILICAS

The Julian, Ulpian, Paul’s, Neptune’s, [Col. 0451D] Matidian, Marcian, Bascellarian, Floscellarian, Sicinian, and Constantinian.

# ELEVEN BATHS

The Trajanic, Titian, Agrippan, Syran, Commodian, Severan, Alexandrian, [Col. 0453A] Antonine, Decian, Diocletian, and Constantinian.

# NINETEEN AQUEDUCTS

The Trajanic, Anio, Alsian, Claudian, Marcian, Herculean, Julian, Augustan, Appian, [Col. 0453B] Alsietine, Setine, Ciminian, Aurelian, Damnata, Virgo, Tepulan, Severan, Antonine, and Alexandrian.

# TWENTY-NINE ROADS

The Trajanic, Appian, Latin, Lavican, [Col. 0453C] Praenestine, Tiburtine, Nomentan, Salarian, Flaminian, Aemilian, Clodian, Valerian, Aurelian, Campanian, Ostian, Portuensian, Janiculan, Laurentine, Ardeatine, [Col. 0453D] Setine, Quintian, Cassian, Gallic, Cornelian, Triumphal, Patinarian, Asinarian, Ciminian, and Tiberine.

# SUMMARY OF THESE ITEMS

Two Capitols. Two circuses. Two amphitheaters. [Col. 0455A] Two colossi. Two spiral columns. Two markets. Three theaters. Four schools. Five naval-battle basins. Fifteen Nymphaea. Twenty-three great horses. Eighty gilded statues. Eighty-four ivory statues. Thirty-six marble arches. Thirty-seven gates. Four hundred and twenty-four streets. Four hundred and twenty-four shrines. Six hundred and seventy-two district-masters. [Col. 0455B] Twenty-four curators. Throughout the city, 46,602 *insulae*. 1,780 houses. 856 baths. 1,352 pools. 254 bakeries. Forty-five brothels. Forty-four public latrines. Ten praetorian cohorts. Four urban cohorts. Seven cohorts of the watch, with fourteen watch-stations. Two common standards. The camp of the foreign salt-fish cavalry—

End of the description of Rome.

Two Capitols. Two circuses. Two amphitheaters. [Col. 0456A] Two colossi. Two spiral columns. Three theaters. Four schools. Five naval-battle basins. Fifteen Nymphaea. Twenty-two great horses. Eighty golden statues. Seventy-four ivory statues. Thirty-seven marble arches. Thirty-seven gates. Four hundred and twenty-three streets. Four hundred and twenty-three shrines. Seven hundred and seventy-two district-masters. [Col. 0456B] Twenty-eight curators. One hundred and forty-four public latrines, that is, *sicessos*. Ten praetorian cohorts. Four urban cohorts. Seven cohorts of the watch, whose watch-stations number fourteen. Two common standards. The camps of the foreign cavalry, the *singulares*, the Ravennates, the chair-bearers, the *silagarii*, the Misenian troops, [Col. 0456C] the letter-carriers, and the victimarii. Throughout the city, 2,300 oil tables.

The end.

# AT THE END OF THE FOURTH CENTURY: ULFILAS, BISHOP OF THE MOESO-GOTHS

[Col. 0455]

# EDITOR’S NOTICE

If anyone should ask why we have delayed so long in publishing Ulfilas, let him receive this answer: we did not wish to reproduce the works of this author, commendable on so many grounds, except from an edition of the highest quality and one easily preferable to all others. The beginnings of that edition were being worked out in Germany when, in chronological order, we had already reached the end of the fourth century.

This edition, to which the final hand was put only a few months ago, consists of three parts. The first presents the text of Ulfilas’s translation, preceded by Prolegomena in which everything pertaining either to the author’s life or to the published and manuscript codices is investigated; it is accompanied and continuously supplemented by a Latin interpretation and notes explaining variant readings as well as the conjectures of the authors.

[Col. 0457] The second part consists of a critical Grammar, which treats with the greatest erudition both the general theories of the Gothic language and the difficulties of Ulfilas’s text.

The third part contains two lexica: one Gothic–Latin, in which the individual words of Ulfilas’s language are explained or also discussed; the other Greek–Gothic, from which it is easy to discover how great a wealth of synonyms the Gothic language possesses.

But since the Grammar and lexica had been written in German, it was necessary to clothe them in Latin. Here a difficult task and labor presented itself, and no easy path opened before us; rather, the way was bristling with innumerable rough places. Among these, the chief were the extremely narrow interval of the allotted time, which it was altogether forbidden to exceed, and the repeated fact that the character of German words is utterly inaccessible to the Latin language.

Whatever the case may be, we have willingly and conscientiously accomplished whatever lay within our powers. At least the translation does not lack the most desirable of all qualities, namely *ἀκρίβεια* (*akribeia*), or, as they say, fidelity; nor does the translator lack the hope of winning the reader’s favor and pardon for the defects of his little work.

[Col. 0457]

# DEDICATORY LETTER

## THE EDITORS TO MAXIMILIAN, HEIR TO THE BAVARIAN KINGDOM
# Dedication

Most illustrious Prince,

We have ventured to adorn this work with your name, moved by no other feeling than the deepest reverence. For who has proved a more distinguished patron of these studies, or who else has kindled, enlarged, and adorned them with more splendid generosity? We therefore did not fear that you would be displeased with our efforts. You had resolved to send other learned men to investigate that celebrated treasure of the Uppsala library before news of this plan had reached us; and we might perhaps have seemed to impede your desire to give a new proof of a truly royal spirit by going there ourselves. Rather, we were persuaded that we would win the approval of so exalted and magnificent a prince for our studies, and so resolved to dedicate this little work to you. We humbly ask that you may be pleased to regard it with favor.

We have collected, according to our abilities, whatever was readily available. But what acclamations, what praises from the entire learned world, what congratulations will greet you if your emissaries, assisted by royal munificence, return from Gaul and Spain—lands once occupied by the Goths—with the long-desired treasures, rescued from the hidden recesses of monasteries as though from prolonged captivity, and bring them into your august halls! Encouraged by this hope, if our little book, most exalted and gracious Prince, readily gains access to you, we shall consider ourselves to have received the greatest possible reward.

Most devoted to your most exalted name,

H. C. de Gabelentz  
J. Loebe

[Col. 0459]

# PROLEGOMENA

## Ulfilas

[Note: [Col. 0461] Besides *Ulphilas* (Οὐλφίλας), Ulfilas’s name is written in various ways by the authors: Urfilas, Urfilus, Gulfilas, Hulfilas, Gilfulas, Galfilas, Ulphias, Gulfias, Gudila, Gudillas, Unila. Hispanic writers have admitted the greatest number of these corruptions; see Essberg, *Ulfil.* 1. Without doubt it should most correctly be written *Vulfila*, since this is commended by the character of the Gothic language (see Grimm I, 57 ff.); the word is a diminutive noun derived from *vulfs* (“wolf”), properly meaning “little wolf”; see Massmann, *Skeir.*, p. 97.]

[Col. 0461] Whether Ulfilas was by birth a Cappadocian, originally from the village of Sadagolthina, whose parents Philostorgius [Note: [Col. 0461] *Ecclesiastical History* 2.5; compare Aschbach, *Geschichte der Westgothen*, p. 31, note 63.] relates to have been carried away from their home into Europe by their Gothic conquerors during the Goths’ invasion of Cappadocia toward the end of the third century, or whether, as the testimony of the other writers indicates, he was born to parents who were themselves Gothic, we shall for the present leave undecided, since this seems to have little bearing on our subject. For, apart from the other authorities, Philostorgius himself relates that Ulfilas was born and brought up among the Goths about the year 318, that after passing through the remaining ecclesiastical ranks he became bishop of this people in the year 348 [Note: [Col. 0461] Compare the booklet discovered by Knust in Paris and described and published by Waitz, *Ueber das Leben und die Lehre des Ulfila*, Hanover 1840, 4to.], namely, of those Goths who were called the “Lesser Goths” and lived in Lower Moesia, between the Danube and Mount Haemus [Note: [Col. 0461] Jordanes, *De rebus Geticis*, p. 135, Lindenbrog edition.].

To these Goths, who had allowed themselves to be imbued with the teaching of the Christian religion, by a teacher and at a time unknown to us, Ulfilas succeeded Theophilus—who was the first bishop under the emperor Constantine the Great [Note: [Col. 0461] Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History* 9.32; Nicephorus Callistus 9.44; Cassiodorus, *Historia ecclesiastica tripartita* 5.38; Essberg, cited work, p. 8; Aschbach, cited work, p. 29.]—Ulfilas succeeded as their bishop of sacred things about the year 355 [Note: [Col. 0461] Since Philostorgius regarded Ulfilas as the first bishop of the Goths, it is not surprising that he wrote that Ulfilas was a contemporary of Constantine the Great; compare Benzel’s preface, p. XXXI. In Scholz’s *Novum Testamentum*, vol. I, preface, p. CXXIX, Ulfilas is said to have translated the Bible in the fifth century, undoubtedly through a printer’s error.]. They had in him not only a highly skilled interpreter of the Gospel and an exhorter of proven virtue, but they especially praise him for this greatest service to his fellow citizens: that he translated the sacred books into their language [Note: [Col. 0461] Socrates 4.33; Sozomen 6.37; Nicephorus 11.48; Cassiodorus 8.13; Jordanes, p. 106; see Essberg, p. 12; Knittel, p. 442 ff.; Castillion, *Specimen*, preface, p. XI.].

At Constantinople, however, to which city he had already gone in the year 360 and which he revisited in 388 for the purpose of defending the faith of his people, despised and condemned as it was, he fell ill and died [Note: [Col. 0462] See the work cited above (note 3), pp. 34 ff. The same booklet, p. 17, also contains the confession of faith that Ulfilas made as he lay dying.]

[Col. 0462] Of the ancient writers who attribute the Gothic translation of the Sacred Scriptures to Ulfilas, some say generally that this was done, without naming which books he translated or omitted; others write that he translated the whole collection [Note: [Col. 0462] Among others, Isidore of Seville, *Chronicon*, under the year 5576 of the era: “Then Wulfila translated both Testaments into his own language.”], as Philostorgius himself does—although he excepts the Books of Kings and gives as the reason for this that, since those books contain mention of very many wars, Ulfilas feared that his fellow citizens, whom he ought rather to restrain from the pursuit of war, might be led by the authority of Sacred Scripture to become still more fierce and warlike [Note: [Col. 0462] In the same work: “Urfilas translated all the Scriptures into the language of the Goths, except indeed the Books of Kings, since they contain the history of wars, while the nation was war-loving and needed rather a bridle for its impulse toward battle, not something that would spur it on toward these things.”].

Learned men have rejected and dismissed this opinion of Philostorgius as ridiculous. Even if, in other matters that he relates about Ulfilas, he should prove to be an unreliable authority and could be accused of many falsehoods because of his attachment to the Arian party, nevertheless, since in this matter he had no reason to lie, his statement seems to have been rejected more from a desire to disparage than from sound judgment. For what interest, I ask, could the Arian Cappadocians have had in whether Ulfilas included the Books of Kings in his translation or not? Unless everything deceives us, the learned men who deny Philostorgius all credibility in these matters condemn him rashly. Their chief error is that they fail to distinguish carefully between the matter itself—which is supported by weaker arguments—and those arguments [Note: [Col. 0462] Knittel, pp. 443 ff., thought that Philostorgius could be refuted on the grounds that Theodatus, king of the Goths, had quoted testimony from the Books of Kings in a certain letter. Knittel says that Gothic nobles and kings would not have done this if Ulfilas, whose counsels and sayings were regarded among the Goths as oracles, had wished to prevent the Goths from reading the Books of Kings. But the good man, who should have remembered that Cassiodorus, not Theodatus, wrote that letter, ought also to have remembered that the lifetimes of Ulfilas and Theodatus were separated by two centuries. During that interval the books omitted by Ulfilas could have been translated by others. We learn especially from Jordanes that the alleged reason is improbable: he says, p. 135, that those same Goths among whom Ulfilas was bishop were indeed a numerous people, but poor and weak, possessing nothing in abundance except herds of various kinds, flocks, pastures, and forests of timber.].

Since we do not accept the reason Philostorgius gives for the omission of those books, we regard no one as a more credible witness in this matter than Philostorgius himself, who was Ulfilas’s contemporary. Whether he knew, or had learned by report, that the Books of Kings were absent from the Gothic version, he wished to attach some reason to their omission, without caring whether it was true or not. There is therefore nothing to prevent us from believing that Ulfilas did not translate the Books of Kings [Note: [Col. 0463] Compare Castillion, *Excursus ad Philippenses*, p. 65.]. As for why he did not translate them, we confess that we do not know, but suspect that Ulfilas lacked either the strength or the time to complete so vast a work. If he translated the greater part of the Bible, that very fact deserves the greatest admiration, since, besides this undertaking, he had many duties to perform at home and also had to undertake embassies to Constantinople on behalf of his fellow citizens [Note: [Col. 0463] See Essberg, pp. 13–14; Zahn, *Einleitung*, p. 20.].

That the entire body of the sacred books had been translated into the Gothic language is now confirmed by many arguments, although formerly it was believed on the authority of writers who were ignorant of these matters and merely repeated what they had heard. For, besides the Gospels, which were previously the only books known, fragments of Paul’s Epistles and portions of the Old Testament books Ezra and Nehemiah have been discovered in our own time. From this we infer that Gothic theologians did not leave the remaining books of the Old Testament untouched. For what could have moved them to translate books of such meager content, contributing nothing to faith or worship, while omitting others so outstanding and weighty?

Moreover, we find traces even of books whose fragments have not yet been discovered preserved in other surviving materials. In *Skeireins*, p. 37, the second and third verses of Psalm 53 are quoted:

> *saei fraþjai aiþþau sokjai guþ. allai usvandidedun. samana unbrukjai vaur þun*

that is:

> “who understands or seeks God; all have turned aside; together they have become useless.”

Then, in the margin of Codex A, Ephesians 4:8 is followed by the words *psalmo ...*, by which the scribe wished to indicate that this passage had been taken from the Book of Psalms (68:19). It is therefore rightly inferred, beyond doubt, that the Psalms had been translated into Gothic [Note: [Col. 0464] Compare Massmann, *Skeireins*, p. 88.]. Certainly, the author of that exposition cited all the New Testament passages from our version; nor do we doubt that he did the same whenever he quotes passages from the remaining books of the Bible.

From the same exposition of the Gospel of John we also learn that the Gothic version included the Books of Moses. For on pp. 41 ff., although the actual words are not given, the sense of Numbers 19:2–9 is rendered:

> *vasuh þan jah frauja þo ahmeinon anafilhands daupein. eiþan garaihtaba varþ bi sviknein sokeins gavagida. unte vitoþ þize unfaurveisane missadede ainaizos vitoþ raidida azgon kalbons gabrannidaizos utana bibaurgeinais. afaruh þan þo ïn vato vairpandans hrain jah hyssopon jah vullai raudai ufartrusnjandans. svasve gadob þans ufarmiton munandans*

that is:

> “But the Lord also commended this spiritual baptism; therefore the question concerning purification was rightly raised. For the law prescribed, for these involuntary sins, one law: the ashes of a heifer burned outside the enclosure; thereafter, casting these into pure water and covering them with hyssop and red wool, as befitted those who were minded to be proud.”

[Note: [Col. 0464] Massmann’s argument that the Goth quoted this from the Epistle to the Hebrews, cited work, pp. 65 ff., has not convinced us.]

The translation of those books is known much more clearly from another codex preserved at Vienna [Note: [Col. 0463] *Membr. Salisb.*, no. 140, formerly Salisb. LXXI.]. Besides runic signs, it contains many Gothic words and letters representing numerals. Wilhelm Grimm, a man exceptionally learned in Germanic letters, was the first to observe that most of the latter were drawn from Genesis, chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 0463] See *Wiener Jahrbücher* XLIII, pp. 15 ff.]. They are as follows:

- verse 3: `sl` = 230 (Vulgate 130);
- verse 5: `[Gothic 900] l` = 930;
- verse 7: `wz` = 707 (Vulgate 807);
- verse 8: `[Gothic 900] ib` = 912;
- verse 13: `wm` = 740 (Vulgate 840).

It follows from this that the scribe had before his eyes a codex containing the Gothic translation of the Old Testament, from which he copied these figures.

It therefore seems that all the sacred books were translated into Gothic, although no traces have yet appeared of certain books of the New Testament—for example, the Acts of the Apostles, the Catholic Epistles, and the Apocalypse of John. Whether the missing books lie hidden in the darkness of monasteries or buried among obliterated manuscripts, or whether they perished altogether in the destruction of libraries, who can guess?

But whether Ulfilas himself completed that translation is another question. Above we indicated why we should not deny that he completed the whole work. Yet when tradition had spread throughout antiquity that he had translated the Bible into the Gothic language, it could easily have happened that the work begun under his auspices and perhaps on his authority, and completed by other learned men in those portions that he himself had not finished, came to be attributed entirely to him.

If we may use conjecture amid such great obscurity, a certain Selinas seems to have been the person who, apart from Ulfilas, devoted himself most earnestly to translating the Bible. Ulfilas had him as his secretary and successor in the episcopate [Note: [Col. 0463] See Sozomen 7.17; Nicephorus Callistus 12.30.]. Since he knew both his native and the Greek language, he could readily have completed, for the benefit of his church, the work begun, received, or undertaken by his predecessor [Note: [Col. 0464] Compare Castillion, *Specimen*, preface, pp. X ff.: “It is easy to believe that the Gothic Bible was written by Selinas at Ulfilas’s dictation and, in accordance with his function as scribe, divided and corrected.”].

Many testimonies are also found among writers to the existence not only of the completed Gothic translation but also of its preservation through the centuries, especially from the time when a large part of the Goths, abandoning their settlements along the Ister, crossed the Alps under the leadership of Theodoric and held Italy in occupation. Since the Goths lived and ruled there, it is not surprising that throughout the regions of that land—certainly in those where the royal seat was located—they spoke the Gothic language and used Gothic Bibles in their churches.

[Col. 0465] It seems that the short discourse placed at the end of the Brixian codex was composed at that time. In it, interpreters of the Sacred Scriptures are warned to take care lest the reader should think that one thing is expressed in the Greek language and another in the Latin or Gothic language [Note: [Col. 0465] See Garbellus in Blanchini, *Evangeliorum quadruplex*, prolegomena, pp. 7 ff. These words, badly written and copied even more badly, seemed to Semler to belong to a preface placed before a comparison of the Gothic version with the Latin and Greek texts; see that venerable scholar’s *Versuch einer Erläuterung einer alten Spur einer gothischen Uebersetzung*, Halle 1764, 4to.].

From this we learn that the Gothic interpretation not only existed in Italy and other lands held by the Goths at a later period, but also possessed authority equal to that of the Latin version. A second testimony concerning the Gothic version is found in Walafrid Strabo, a writer of the ninth century, who says that monuments of the Gothic Bible were still possessed by some people in his time [Note: [Col. 0465] *De rebus ecclesiasticis*, chapter 7.]. His testimony carries all the greater weight because, as provost of the monastery of Reichenau, he lived almost on the border of the regions that had once been inhabited by both Gothic peoples.

Afterward, for six centuries, no one mentioned the Gothic Bible, unless someone merely repeated what he had read in ancient writers, and nowhere did a trace of books containing that version appear. In the sixteenth century, however, a single codex was discovered in the library of the monastery of Werden, founded in Belgic Gaul on the Ruhr.

Antonio Morillon [Note: [Col. 0465] Although Ihre correctly called the first discoverer of Ulfilas’s version Morillon in his dissertation on the language of the Silver Codex, written and published in 1754, he shortly afterward, in another work on the Silver Codex published in 1759, less correctly called him Arnold Mercator; see Zahn, *Einleitung*, pp. 39 ff. It has also been asked whether this was the Silver Codex or another manuscript. Ihre, *Ulfilas illustratus*, p. 98, denies that it was the Silver Codex, chiefly because Morillon used writing abbreviations that are not found in the Silver Codex, at least not in the passages he copied [Col. 0466]; and also because he displayed letter-forms that the Silver Codex does not recognize at all. Others have demonstrated that he had no other manuscript than the Silver Codex before his eyes; see Zahn, cited work.]—who served as secretary to Antonio Perrenot, Cardinal Granvelle—came upon the codex while examining the manuscripts of that library. He immediately recognized that it contained Ulfilas’s version, and copied from it the Lord’s Prayer together with several other passages. Maximilian, Antonio’s brother, communicated these copies to Goropius Becanus, who inserted them into his *Gotodanica* [Note: [Col. 0466] See Goropius, *Origines Antuerpenses*, book VII, pp. 739 ff., 750.].

Shortly afterward, Gruterus published in his *Thesaurus inscriptionum* several verses excerpted from the same codex by Arnold Mercator [Note: [Col. 0466] Pp. 147 ff.]. All the fragments preserved in that codex were published much later, in 1665, through the work of Francis Junius, and subsequently many times.

For a long time, however, students of the Gothic language complained bitterly that so little remained of this translation of the whole of Sacred Scripture, and that what did survive consisted only of fragments of the Gospels, insufficient to unravel and remove the difficulties of interpretation. Then, in the preceding century, Knittel, archdeacon of the metropolitan church at Wolfenbüttel, discovered in the codex of the Wolfenbüttel library fragments of Paul’s Epistle to the Romans.

A still greater stroke of fortune—through which we obtained fragments of the Gothic Bible, not complete in every part but far more extensive, nevertheless, from many books of the New Testament—was reserved for the learned men of our own century. In the Milanese library, Angelo Mai and Carlo Ottavio Castillionaeus discovered palimpsest codices. When those learned men examined the earlier writing more carefully, it became clear that it contained fragments of Ulfilas’s version of the Gospel of Matthew; of Paul’s Epistle to the Romans; of more extensive portions than Knittel had already discovered from both Epistles to the Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, both Epistles to the Thessalonians, and the Pastoral Epistles to Timothy, Titus, and Philemon; and, in addition, fragments of the Old Testament books Ezra and Nehemiah. Those fragments were first published by the two scholars jointly, and afterward by Castillionaeus alone, beginning in the nineteenth year of the present century.

But learned men had long since raised the question whether what were regarded as fragments of Ulfilas’s, or the Gothic, version were truly Gothic, or whether they belonged to another version prepared for the use of some other barbarian nation. Among others, La Croze denied that they were Gothic and attempted to prove that the language of our version was Frankish [Note: [Col. 0466] See La Croze’s letter to John Chamberlayne in *Thesaurus epistolarum*, vol. III, pp. 92 ff.].

The question is as hackneyed and nearly proverbial as the arguments with which La Croze tried to establish his opinion are inept and weak. First, he says that the codex of our version was discovered not in the regions where the Goths lived but where the Franks lived; second, that some of the forms of these letters more closely resemble the ancient Frankish manner of writing; third, that certain letters are Latin, and could not have been known to the Goths living in Moesia; and finally, that among the letters of this language there are four new ones, unlike both Greek and Latin forms, three of which correspond to letters reformed by Chilperic, king of the Franks. Who could fail to see that arguments scarcely worthy of refutation have thereby already been refuted?

It is therefore astonishing that this perverse mode of argument could persuade, among others, Wetstein, a man of great acumen, to support the opinion [Note: [Col. 0466] See Zahn, *Einleitung*, p. 27.] [Note: [Col. 0466] Wetstein, *Prolegomena in Novum Testamentum*, pp. 304 ff., Semler edition.]. Ihre demonstrated better than anyone else how cold and inadequate La Croze’s arguments were, in his dissertation on the language of the Silver Codex published in 1754 [Note: [Col. 0466] See *Ulfilas illustratus*, pp. 259 ff.], and wiser men had long since rejected that nonsense [Note: [Col. 0466] Semler, in his comments on Wetstein’s *Prolegomena*, p. 305—although we are surprised that shortly afterward, on p. 308, he calls our interpreter “Frankish-Gothic”—compare Zahn, *Einleitung*, pp. 26 ff.; Aschbach, cited work, pp. 36 ff.].

[Col. 0467] Since they could not even make it seem probable that our Bible was Frankish, its truly Gothic character is now confirmed by the strongest arguments.

It is established that, besides the translation of the Bible, two monuments concerning Gothic letters have been preserved. One of them consists of four Gothic subscriptions placed beneath a Latin-written record of a sale [Note: [Col. 0467] See Zahn, *Einleitung*, pp. 76 ff. Grimm suspects that these were written at the beginning of the sixth century, *Grammatik*, preface, p. XLVII, earlier edition.]. One of them reads as follows:

> *ïk merila bokareis handau meinai ufmelida jah andnemum skilliggans .j. jah faurþis þairh kavtsjon jah miþ diakuna alamoda unsaramma jah miþ gahlaibim unsaraim andnemum skilliggans .rk. vairþ þize saive*

that is:

> “I, Merila, the scribe, subscribed with my own hand, and we received sixty solidi; and previously, by surety and together with our deacon Alamodus and our colleagues, we received one hundred and twenty solidi, the price of these lakes.”

The other, a similar record, contains one Gothic subscription, which runs approximately as follows:

> *ïk gudilub diakun þo frabauhta. boka fram mis gavaurhta þus diakun alamoda. fidvor unkjana (?) hugsis kaballarja jah killiggans .rlg. andnam jah ufmelida*

that is:

> “I, Gudilub the deacon, have sold these things; I made the document for you, deacon Alamodus; I received four ounces of the estate of Caballaria and one hundred and thirty-three solidi, and I subscribed.”

[Note: [Col. 0467] Massmann, *Die gothischen Urkunden von Neapel und Arezzo*, Vienna 1838, p. 18, incorrectly joins *frabauhta boka* as *frabauhtaboka*—it should have been *frabauhtiboka*—and his interpretation of this monument cannot therefore be accepted.]

The first of these documents is preserved at Naples and is accordingly called the Neapolitan document; the other was formerly at Arezzo [Note: [Col. 0467] Massmann, cited work, p. X, intends to publish that inscription, together with the others, in a more accurately corrected form and in a separate booklet for the benefit of scholarship.], and is therefore called the Aretine document. Both, however, reached their later repositories from Ravenna, where they were written.

What other language, then, can that language be which those witnesses use except Gothic, since under Theodoric Ravenna was the seat of no Germanic people other than the Goths, and since in the other records written in Latin those witnesses are expressly called priests of the Gothic church? And since the language of these documents is the same as that of our version, to what other people than the Goths can this version be attributed?

There is an additional argument, and a very powerful one. At the end of one of the Ambrosian codices [Note: [Col. 0467] S. 36, upper part, which Castillionaeus marked with the letter A in his edition and which we likewise designate by that letter.], containing fragments of Paul’s Epistles, a calendar has been added [Note: [Col. 0468] See Castillion, *Specimen*, pp. 26 ff.]. In it, feast days and holy days, somewhat different from the usual ones, are recorded. A fragment of this calendar begins as follows:

> *.kg. þize ana gutþiudai managaize marytre jah friþareikeis*

that is:

> “XXIII [understand: the day] of these, in the Gothic nation, of many martyrs and of Fritharicus.”

[Note: [Col. 0468] Castillion published *madagrize* incorrectly and, through a scribal error, *friþareikeikeis*, with the syllable *kei* wrongly duplicated; see the note on Matthew 11:16.]

From this it is clearer than daylight that this calendar was composed for the *gutica*, that is, Gothic nation, and therefore written in no language other than Gothic. Since here too we have the same language as in our version, all doubts [Col. 0468] concerning the genuinely Gothic origin of the version circulated under the name Gothic collapse [Note: [Col. 0468] Compare Aschbach, cited work, p. 38.]. Finally, let this argument also be added: there is a passage in this version from which it is understood that the translator was an Arian. It is universally acknowledged that, apart from the Goths, no other Germanic people adhered to that sect.

If these arguments have been correctly presented, there can no longer be any doubt that this language is Germanic. Those who have wished to call it *theodisc*—German—are asserting the same thing under a different name. For if the Goths themselves were Germanic by nation, as is confirmed by the testimony of ancient writers, both inhabitants and outsiders, then their language must also have belonged to the Germanic languages.

For the rest, we do not ask whether this speech should be called Ostrogothic, Visigothic, or Moesogothic. We are convinced that all Goths had the same language—a point we shall demonstrate elsewhere—and the same translation of the Bible.

It remains for us to speak about the integrity of Ulfilas’s version. Some, doubting whether our version was truly Ulfilas’s, have asked whether it should instead be attributed to other theologians of a later period.

The first among these was Hickes [Note: [Col. 0468] See *Institutiones grammaticae Anglo-Saxonicae et Moeso-Gothicae*.]. What especially offended this learned man was that our fragments agreed with the Latin manuscripts, although a Goth living in Moesia could scarcely have had access to such manuscripts and must undoubtedly have used a Greek copy of the Bible. He was also troubled by the fact that no traces of Arianism now appeared, although such traces ought to have been conspicuous if the version were rightly attributed to Ulfilas, since Ulfilas and his Goths followed the Arian heresy [Note: [Col. 0468] Compare Heupel, cited work, p. 11; Essberg, p. 13; Knittel, p. 449; Manson, *Geschichte der Ostgothen*, p. 9; Aschbach, cited work, pp. 29 ff., compare pp. 222 ff.; Massmann, *Skeireins*, pp. 69 ff.; Castillion, *Excursus ad Philippenses* 2:16, pp. 63 ff., compare *Specimen*, preface, pp. XIII ff.].

But we shall demonstrate below that our version was not drawn from Latin books; nor do we understand why Arian opinions must necessarily be present in it. For neither the time when Ulfilas converted from the Catholic faith to the Arians nor the time when he translated the Sacred Scriptures is known. Perhaps he completed his translation before he fell into that heresy. Or—and this is much more probable—the Goths at the beginning do not seem to have pursued the finer points of faith and confession with such strictness that they would have inserted into the Bible doctrines that they did not find in the original.

Furthermore, among the fragments contained in the Silver Codex, no passage is found on which Arians differed from the Orthodox. Zahn [Note: [Col. 0468] *Einleitung*, p. 37.] wished to examine two passages in particular for clarification of the matter: the beginning of the Gospel of John and Romans 9:5. We now possess one of these:

> *xristus saei ïst ufar allaim guþ þiuþiþs ï aivam*

“Christ, who is over all, God blessed forever.”

If anyone should infer from this that the Goths or the translator were not Arians, he would be proceeding too hastily. For although learned men have shown that it is not necessary here to understand *guþ* as referring to Christ, it must be kept in mind that the Arians denied not Christ’s divinity but Christ’s identity, as it were, with God the Father. Thus even the strictest follower of Arius could have written in precisely this way, like the author of the frequently cited exposition [Note: [Col. 0469] *Skeireins*, p. 46, line 13.]:

> *ainabaura sunau guþs guþ visandin*

“to the only-begotten Son of God, being God.”

Nor does the long-desired passage at 1 Timothy 3:16 settle the question, where Christ is also said to be *guþ gabairhtiþs vas ïn leika* [Note: [Col. 0469] According to Castillionaeus, this statement about 1 Timothy 3:16 is false; see the note on that passage itself. After the book edited by Waitz became known, there is especially no longer any doubt that the Goths were Arians. See Waitz, pp. 40 ff., 56.].

Nor can we sufficiently express our astonishment that Castillionaeus cited Colossians 1:16 in order to free the Gothic version from the charge of heterodoxy.

There is only one passage, already identified by Castillionaeus, from which the Arianism of our translator can be clearly recognized. For at Philippians 2:6 we read:

> *ïn xristau ïesu. saei ïn guþaskaunein visands ni vulva rahnida visan sik galeiko guþa.*

“in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the likeness of God, did not consider it robbery to be like God.”

Massmann, *Skeireins*, p. 73, who had failed to distinguish *samaleiks* and *galeiks* correctly, denied that Arianism was proved by this passage. Castillionaeus, however, discussed it admirably in the appendix to his Epistle to the Philippians, pp. 63 ff., and demonstrated that it provides evidence that the Gothic translator placed the Arian doctrine into the text by substituting likeness for equality.

Knittel, on the other hand, in arguing that our version was Ulfilas’s own, does not conduct his case any more successfully [Note: [Col. 0469] Pp. 444 ff.]. When he says that it must be Ulfilas’s because writers mention the translation of the sacred books of no one but Ulfilas, he failed to consider how little force there is in arguments drawn from the silence of writers. If we possessed accounts of Gothic ecclesiastical affairs written by the Goths themselves, or if these matters had been narrated in detail in other histories of the Goths, silence concerning a revised translation would be noteworthy. But since no such mention is found, we understand from this that later translators did not undertake the work publicly or at any fixed time, but proceeded from then on in such a way that different portions were altered by different people.

In truth, it is difficult either to affirm or to deny that the fragments preserved to our time belong to the version which Ulfilas composed according to the testimony of the writers. The authority of that version in the Gothic church was great. This is shown both by the authority Ulfilas enjoyed among his people and by the fact that historians mention no one else’s work in translating the Bible. But if that authority was so great, what reason would anyone have had to undertake a new translation of the Sacred Scriptures?

Yet although we deny that the entire version was reproduced, we do not deny that, as time passed, certain changes were made here and there. This could have been recognized from the Silver Codex if the condition and character of its individual parts had been examined more carefully: several recensions had existed. Ignorance of this fact led Marshall into error, when, because of the astonishing antiquity of the Silver Codex, he judged that this version could be none other than Ulfilas’s most ancient version [Note: [Col. 0469] *Observationes* in Junius, p. 388.]. Now that many portions of the Epistles and some passages of the Gospels can be compared twice in different codices, the matter is understood even more clearly.

Those recensions, however, certainly derived from one source, apparently Ulfilas’s version. They were altered by learned men of a later age, either when they found that Ulfilas’s version did not correspond sufficiently accurately to the Greek text, or when they discovered other readings in their own books than those possessed by Ulfilas.

It is not difficult to see that this happened; but no one will easily say which readings in those passages were originally written by Ulfilas and which were altered, added, or omitted by others. It is unfortunate that Heynatius, who boasts that he recognized certain additions from the differing character of the language [Note: [Col. 0469] Compare Zahn, *Einleitung*, p. 36.], did not disclose the signs by which he recognized them.

Having stated these general points about the language and the author of our version, we proceed to investigate the method by which it was composed, from which its principal usefulness in emending passages of Sacred Scripture will become clear.

First, however, we must speak of the source from which the Gothic translator drew. No one formerly doubted that Ulfilas composed his translation from Greek books; this is already attested by the author of the *Martyrdom of Nicetas* [Note: [Col. 0469] In Simeon Metaphrastes’ *Acts of Saint Nicetas* (*Acta Sanctorum*, September, vol. V, p. 41, Antwerp edition), he says: “Ulfila, having transferred our sacred and divinely inspired Scripture from Greek into the Gothic language.” Cf. Jerome’s letter written to Sunnias and Fritela, in which he says that the Goths used Greek copies of Sacred Scripture.], and after him by Sixtus of Siena [Note: [Col. 0470] *Bibliotheca*, IV, p. 390, Cologne edition: “Ulfilas, the first Goth, transmitted all the divine Scriptures as translated by him from Greek into the Gothic language.”].

We do not know how this information reached those men—whether the report had spread among the ancients, or whether they inferred it from the fact that Ulfilas had lived in Moesia and, through contact with the people of Constantinople, had acquired knowledge of the Greek language, and therefore had also employed Greek books to complete his work. Nevertheless, the testimony of that earlier writer, on account of its antiquity, does not seem altogether contemptible.

Whoever sides with those who maintain that Ulfilas followed Greek books [Note: [Col. 0470] With Usher, in Junius’ *Glossary*, p. 16; cf. Mareshall, p. 389 ff.; Benzelius, Preface, p. VI; Lye, p. XXXVI; Ihre, *Ulfilas Illustratus*, p. 268; Knittel, p. 445; Zahn, *Introduction*, p. 28 ff.], must rely not only on the authority of writers—an authority which in such matters is generally not sufficiently persuasive—but also on arguments drawn from a comparison of our version with the Greek text, by which the point is demonstrated.

Of the many available examples we present the following few. For the Gothic translator not only faithfully preserves the order of words in which the Greeks led the way—except where the character of the Gothic language requires another order [Col. 0471], as in placing the negative next to the verb of the clause, cf. John XIV, 11; Luke VIII, 12; in positioning certain particles either at the beginning or immediately after the beginning of the clause, as *ïþ*, which, unlike δέ, the Greek particle corresponding to the Gothic one, is placed first in the clause; or where some other, unknown linguistic reason requires a different order, as when the pronoun precedes the noun, *þata andbahti* = τὴν διακονίαν ταύτην—he also conformed his speech in very many respects to the Greek.

To this seem to belong the use of the dual number, which Ulfilas nevertheless employs more often than it occurs in the Greek text, and almost always where two persons are indicated; then the figure called attraction; the frequent use of participles, adapted to Greek models; the misuse of the demonstrative pronoun to perform the functions of the Greek article; and many other features, which our grammar will teach readers.

Yet despite this, there were men entirely unacquainted with the Gothic language and its character who, comparing individual Gothic words with Greek ones, thought they had observed Ulfilas departing from the Greek text and agreeing with the Latin books. They assigned such weight to this observation that, while denying that he had drawn from a Greek source, they undertook to prove that he had instead followed Latin books. Wetstein, above all, pursued this argument [Note: [Col. 0471] *Prolegomena to the New Testament*, p. 114 ff., earlier edition.]; but the arguments he brought forward as proofs were so weak that not only did others arise who attempted to refute them [Note: [Col. 0471] See Bengel’s *Apparatus of the New Testament*, p. 408 f.], but he himself, after reconsidering the matter, returned to a more judicious view and concluded that our version generally expresses the Greek text, though it often follows the Italian version after abandoning the Greek [Note: [Col. 0471] *Ibid.*, p. 358, Semler’s edition.].

No one but the blind or the quarrelsome will deny that there are passages from which it may be recognized that numerous words and verses found only in Latin books have been incorporated into our version, and that it contains readings which, while departing from the Greek, agree with the Latin.

First, many additions are found which the Greek manuscripts entirely reject but the Latin manuscripts recognize [Note: [Col. 0471] Cf. Zahn, *Introduction*, p. 32 f.]. These include:

- Matthew X, 29, *viljan*—Latin *voluntate*, “by the will”;
- Mark XIV, 65, *gabaurjaba*—*cum voluntate*, “willingly”;
- Luke I, 3, *jah ahmin veihamma*—*et Spiritui sancto*, “and to the Holy Spirit”;
- Luke IX, 2, *allans*—*omnes*, “all”;
- Luke IX, 43: *qaþ paitrus, frauja duwe weis ni mahtedum usdreiban þamma. ïþ ïesus qaþ, þata kuni ni usgaggiþ nibai in bidom jah ïn fastubnja*—with slight alterations, the Corbie and Cologne manuscripts read: “Peter said to him, ‘Lord, why were we unable to cast it out?’ And he said to them, ‘This kind will be cast out only by prayers and fastings’”;
- Luke IX, 50, *ni ainhun auk ïst manne saei ni gavaurkjai maht ïn namin meinamma*—“for no one is there who does not perform a mighty deed in my name”;
- Luke XV, 31, *wast jah*—*fuisti et*, “you were, and…”;
- Luke XIX, 22, *jah lata*—*et piger*, “and lazy.”

All these, omitted by the Greek manuscripts, are found with the Gothic in the Cologne, Corbie, Brixian, and Reggio manuscripts, or in other Latin copies.

Next, there are very many passages in which Latin readings have been substituted for Greek ones. To prove this, Zahn, in his *Introduction*, p. 32, rather inappropriately cites Luke V, 3 and John VII, 9. In the former passage he supposes that the Goth, together with the Brixian manuscript, read *jussit* (*ἐκέλευσε*) instead of the Greek *ἠρώτησε*; in the latter, that for *εἰπὼν ἔμεινε* he read *dixit cum esset*. The matter will be fully clarified for anyone who examines the following passages:

- Mark VII, 3, *ufta*, “often,” is adapted not to the Greek πυγμῇ but to the reading *crebro* found in certain Latin copies;
- Luke IX, 20: where the Greek has τὸν Χριστὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, the Goth has *þu ïs xristus sunus guþs*, “you are Christ, the Son of God,” agreeing with the Reggio and Brixian manuscripts, which read *tu es Christus, filius Dei*;
- Luke V, 10, *siud nutans*, “you shall be,” does not render the Greek ἔσῃ ζωγρῶν, “you shall be catching [men],” but rather corresponds to the Brixian reading *eritis captores*, “you shall be captors”;
- Luke II, 14, *godis viljins*, “of good will”: who would maintain that the Goth rendered the Greek εὐδοκία or εὐδοκίας by these words, rather than the Latin manuscripts’ *bonae voluntatis*, “of good will”?
- Luke I, 29, *ïnnagahtai* unquestionably follows the Latin manuscripts, which read *introitu*, “at the entrance,” in place of the Greek λόγῳ;
- and likewise in the Epistles:
  - 2 Corinthians V, 10: where the Greek has διά, the Gothic *svesona* corresponds to the Latin *proprios*, “one’s own,” which seem to presuppose a reading ἴδια;
  - 2 Corinthians XII, 17: *ïbai þairh wana*—the Vulgate *numquid per aliquem*, “surely not through anyone,” whereas the Greek has τινα ὧν = δι’ αὐτοῦ;
  - Philippians IV, 8: *veih*, “holy,” agrees with the Latin *sancta*, while the Greek has ἁγνά, “pure”;
  - 1 Corinthians I, 18, *þandei*, “because,” agrees with the Latin *dum*, while the Greek has πλήν or πλὴν ὅτι.

Thus, in 2 Corinthians VIII, 19, the Goth renders the Greek χειροτονηθείς by *gateviþs*, which we suspect had before it the Latin *ordinatus*, “appointed”; the Gothic word, derived from *tevi*, “order,” is much closer to the Latin than to the Greek. Likewise, in Philippians IV, 6, where the Greek ἐν παντὶ τῇ προσευχῇ is translated by *ïn allai bidai*, “in every prayer,” one might suppose that the Gothic translator followed not the Greek words but the Latin *in omni oratione*, incorrectly understanding the phrase *in omni*, “in every,” as a unit standing by itself (*in allem*) and attaching it to the following word [Note: [Col. 0471] Wetstein, p. 306, attempts to support his view that our version was composed from Latin books by saying that whenever the Latin translator rendered the Greek words inaccurately or incorrectly, the Goth likewise translated them in the same way. But the readings in most of the passages he criticizes—Matthew VI, 11, 16, 27; IX, 38; Mark I, 38—are correct and agree with the Greek, or at least contain renderings properly suited to the Gothic understanding. Conversely, in other places the Goth, without following the Latin books, translated less correctly on his own initiative; see, among others, Luke I, 5 and 8, where the Greek ἐφημερία was rendered by the Latins much more accurately as *vicem*, “course” or “turn,” whereas the Goth rendered it by *afar* and *kuni*. Nor does Semler, in his remarks on Wetstein, p. 308, establish with stronger arguments that the Epistle to the Romans was translated from a Latin codex. The passages he adduces either prove nothing or were wrongly read or explained by Knittel. Thus, at Romans XI, 34, the Goth used *ïmma*, the dative, for the Greek αὐτοῦ because in his language the dative is regularly placed with nouns in the place of the genitive; and what Latin version has *ei* or *illi* in such a way that the Goth could be said to have followed it? At Romans XII, 3, *guþs* (“of God”) is found in no Latin version, while many Greek manuscripts add it. At Romans XII, 19, we have said that Knittel read the passage incorrectly. At Romans XIV, 9, *qivaim—dauþaim*, “the living—the dead,” the words are transposed not only in the Latin manuscripts but also in the Greek ones.].

Although these traces have been pointed out, we nevertheless maintain that our version was derived from Greek books. We refer readers to what we said above generally about the character of this version, and add the following observations.

The Goth regularly uses the participle of the substantive verbs εἶναι and ὑπάρχειν where the Latins, because they lack an equivalent participle, employ either a relative pronoun or some conjunction to paraphrase it. He faithfully renders certain Greek particles omitted by the Latins, for example ἄν in Luke IX, 46; X, 13; XVII, 6; John IX, 41; Romans IX, 29, and περ in Luke XVIII, 14 and 2 Corinthians VIII, 7. In many passages he does not have the Latin readings that differ from the Greek, but agrees with the Greek; thus at Luke I, 10, where none of the Latin manuscripts reads προσδεχόμενον, “expecting.” At the end of the Lord’s Prayer the Goth has the doxology together with the Greek manuscripts, whereas scarcely any Latin manuscript acknowledges it. And why should we cite further examples, when almost everything, with only a few exceptions, plainly testifies that it was drawn from Greek?

When learned men therefore discovered in Ulfilas’ version, in several places, readings from Latin manuscripts, some judged that he had consulted books in both languages [Note: [Col. 0473] Benzelius, Preface, p. XXXIII: “The version was made from no source other than the authentic Greek, though not without consulting a Latin translator, whoever he may have been”; cf. Bengel, *Defense of the New Testament*, p. 27; Semler on Wetstein, p. 309; Grimm, *W. J.*, LXX, p. 47.], while others thought that the Gothic version had later been revised by other theologians in accordance with Latin books [Note: [Col. 0473] Wetstein, p. 306, Semler’s edition; Ihre, *Ulfilas Illustratus*, p. 268; Zahn, *Introduction*, p. 31 ff.; Castillion, *Specimen*, Preface, p. XX; cf. the same author on Ephesians II, 3 and Galatians IV, 18.].

The former opinion seems scarcely deserving of approval. For even if we do not ask, with Wetstein, whether Ulfilas knew the Latin language, or, with Hickes and La Croze, whether Latin was common in Moesia and Latin copies of Sacred Scripture had been brought there [Note: [Col. 0473] Cf. Ihre, *Ulfilas Illustratus*, p. 260, 269.], nevertheless, since the light of the Gospel had shone upon the Goths from the Greek world, it could not have been otherwise than that the Gothic teachers who had received their instruction from the Greeks and had taken part in the councils of Greek Christians should have known the Greek language. It follows that there is no reason why the first translator of the Bible should have resorted to Latin books; and if he truly knew that language, his knowledge of it was certainly no more readily available to him than his knowledge of Greek.

We know that in the Middle Ages theologians suffered from such ignorance of Greek that, whenever Sacred Scripture had to be used, they resorted to Latin books, as our Luther did before he began to study Greek. But to infer from this that in that earlier age Latin was also easier for foreigners to understand than Greek, and that Latin books were used in explaining difficult passages, seems hazardous.

And if he truly possessed Latin books, why did he consult them in so few passages and neglect them in so many others, where, because of the difficulties of interpretation, he translated either less correctly or altogether wrongly?

The other opinion is much more probable: namely, that the version was composed in Moesia from Greek books and was subsequently altered and interpolated in Italy by other Gothic theologians according to the tenor and standard of Latin books.

Nor should Griesbach be followed [Note: [Col. 0473] In a letter addressed to Zahn; see Zahn, *Introduction*, p. 34.]. He denied that the Gothic version had any relationship to the Latin versions and preferred to suppose that whatever elements it seemed to have taken from them had either been added by chance, independently by both the Goth and the Latins, or, where agreement existed, had been derived by both versions from the same source—for example, interpretations, glosses, additions from parallel passages, and other matters of that kind [Note: [Col. 0473] The passages interpolated from parallels are the following: Matthew (III, 11), XXVII, 42 (58); Mark II, 22; X, 4; XIV, 47; XV, 21, 37, 40; XVI, 1, 2; Luke IV, 33; VI, 4; IX, 43, 50; John XV, 2; Galatians V, 20; Colossians III, 8; cf. Mill’s *Prolegomena*, p. 742 ff.].

This second opinion—leaving the first aside—was ingeniously conceived. But if the learned man had been able to compare the Epistles now published, and had seen even errors pass from the Latin into the Gothic version, he would undoubtedly have judged otherwise. For example, at Ephesians II, 3, The word *viljans* (“wills”) stands in the text, with *lustuns* (“desires”) placed in the margin. From where could that reading have come except from a Latin codex in which words of similar sound had been confused?

Nor is the opinion we approve as ridiculous as it seemed to Richard Simon [Note: [Col. 0474] *Critical History of the Versions of the New Testament*, p. 222], provided that one does not think of the Vulgate as the version to which our translation was conformed.

The Goths did not use the Vulgate as it is now called. This is known not only because it came into general use much later, but also because the Gothic version of both the New and the Old Testament agrees scarcely at all with it [Note: [Col. 0474] Cf. Knittel, p. 376; Zahn, p. 32. As one of many other passages, we now cite 1 Timothy III, 6, the celebrated passage in which the Gothic, together with the Greek manuscripts, reads θεός, “God,” omitted by the Vulgate. For the Old Testament, cf. the numbers from Genesis cited above, p. XI, which differ greatly from the Vulgate.]. Rather, it agrees more frequently with that ancient version which Sabatier collected from various manuscripts and published under that name together with the Vulgate, and more frequently also with the Brixian manuscript published by Blanchini. But the Goth agrees with none of these books so closely that he can be said to have followed one or another of them in preference to the rest.

The matter seems to have been as follows. After leaving the banks of the Ister, the Goths carried their Bible with them into Italy, just as it had been translated by Ulfilas—or perhaps completed by someone else wherever anything was lacking. Once settled there, after learning the language of the Romans and seeing that the Latin copies of Sacred Scripture which came into their hands differed from their own interpretation and were often fuller, they corrected and altered their books according to those examples. They either exchanged individual Gothic words from the ancient version for other words, whether more customary or more suitable for expressing the sense, or supplied passages that seemed incomplete.

As a result, not only are readings from Latin books found in the version that had been made from Greek manuscripts [Note: [Col. 0474] See above, pp. 465–466], but those portions of Sacred Scripture preserved in two Gothic copies also display traces of two recensions: one older and more closely adapted to the Greek text, the other more recent, corrected, altered, and interpolated in many places. Yet those who reread and revised it carefully placed the readings of the ancient books reverently in the margin of their copies, and later scribes either reproduced these annotations or even increased them with others [Col. 0475].

Thus, after more carefully comparing among themselves those fragments contained only in the *Codex Argenteus*, we think we have discovered that some belong to the more recent recension and others to the older one. To the former class we refer especially the striking difference between the Gospel of Luke and the other Gospels: its more frequent agreement with Latin books, its divergent spellings of individual words [Note: [Col. 0475] In this Gospel, *d* is very frequently written instead of *þ* in endings, especially in the third-person singular and second-person plural: I, 13, *gabairid* for *gabairiþ*; 17, *fauraqimid*; 32, 35; V, 36, 37; VI, 45; II, 12; V, 10, 24, 30, 34; VI, 2, 24, 25, 31, 32, 34, 46; III, 14; VI, 27, 28, 33, 35, 36, 37, 38; III, 4; V, 4; VI, 23, 27, 35, 37; VI, 3.

In the neuter form of the past participle: II, 12, *galagid*; 23; IV, 10, 17; VI, 48; cf. XV, 16, *sad*, and VII, 46, *haubid* for *saþ* and *haubiþ*.

In the third-person singular past of first-conjugation verbs: *bad*, VIII, 31; XV, 28; *anabaud*, V, 14; VIII, 29, 55; *faurbaud*, V, 14; VIII, 56; *mid* in compound verbs.

Thus, in masculine endings before the letter *s*: *stads*, XIV, 22; *faheds*, I, 14; II, 10; XV, 7; *hundafads*, VII, 6; and in participles *mikilids*, IV, 15; *gahrainids*, IV, 27; *gamanvids*, VI, 40.

Then *b* for *f*, as in IV, 3, *hlaibs*; *n* for *g* before palatal letters; *ng*, *nk*, *nq* for *gg*, *gk*, *gq*; see the note on Luke XIV, 31. This spelling system, which is also found in the Arezzo document, seems to bear the imprint of Latin.

*usraisjan*, VIII, 24, for *urraisjan*; doubled letters are written simply: *fulnan* for *fullnan*, see II, 21; *fauragagjins* and *fauragagjan*, VIII, 3; XVI, 1, for *fauragaggjan*.

Moreover, vowels are exchanged with other vowels and diphthongs: *ei* with *e*: II, 10, *faheid*, 15, *ïohannein*; VIII, 32, *anasaisleip*; IX, 13, *manas seidai*, for *fahed*, *ïohannen*, *anasaislep*, *manasedai*; cf. the note on III, 5; likewise *qeins*, I, 5; XVII, 32; *duthei*, VII, 7; *visseis*, XIX, 22.

*e* with *ei*: II, 37, *blotande*; 43, *miþþane*; X, 5, *þane*; XIX, 37, *þoze*, for *blotandei*, *miþþanei*, *þanei*, *þozei*; cf. the note on X, 5.

Again *e* with *ei*: *andbahtededun*, VIII, 3; *svekunþs*, VIII, 17; *aggele*, IX, 26; XV, 10, for *andbahtidedun*, *svikunþs*, *aggile*.

*i* with *e*: *galagidideina*, V, 18; VI, 11; *qimi*, VII, 3, for *galagidedeina* and *qemi*; see the note on VIII, 56.

*au* with *u*, see the note on Mark VII, 32; *u* with *au*, see the note on Luke I, 54; *o* with *u*: III, 26, *ïodins*; XVI, 8, *sunjos*, for *ïudins*—see verse 30—and *sunjus*. Other examples are noted under IV, 13.

The omission of the letter *j* from certain forms of the verb *visan* also belongs here: IX, 12, *sium*; V, 10, *siud*; IX, 41, *siau*; VIII, 25 and XIV, 31, *siai*.

The following also seem to be evidence of a double recension in Luke: at IX, 34, before the marginal reading *at ïm ïn milhmam atgaggandam*, the word *jah* is read. We said that it is superfluous here; perhaps *jah* does not belong to the text but is the glossator’s word, indicating that the reading *at ïm ïn m. a.* was also found. Similarly, at XVII, 6, *aiþþau jus jabai* must be explained. The words seem first to have been written in the margin and to have belonged to *jubai*, while the glossator wished to say: “*jabai* or (*i.e.*, *aiþþau*), with the pronoun *jus* added.” Thus the true reading of the passage is: *jabai* (or *jus jabai*) *habaidedeiþ galaubein sve kaurno sinapis. qiþeiþ du bainabagma*—“if you had faith like a mustard seed, you would say to this mulberry tree…”].

In addition, the Gospel of Luke contains forms of words and verbs that occur either never or only very rarely in the other Gospels [Note: [Col. 0475] Verb forms peculiar to this Gospel alone in the *Codex Argenteus* include: *auhmists*, III, 2; IV, 29; XIX, 47, for *auhumists*; *ïba*, XVII, 9, for *ïbai*; *unhulþa* for *unhulþo*, IV, 35; VIII, 29, 33; IX, 42—although it is also read at Matthew XXV, 41, that passage being from the Ambrosian manuscript; VI, 40, *laisaris* for *laisareis*; I, 23, *andbahteis* for *andbahtjis*, see the passage; IX, 39, *hropjiþ* for *hropeiþ*, cf. Grimm I, 847; XIX, 12, *gaggida* for *ïddja*; *bai* for *bajoþs*, I, 6, 7; V, 7; VI, 39; VII, 42; *nauhþan* for *nauhþanuh*, I, 15; VIII, 49; IX, 42—in a negative sentence also John VI, 17.

The number of those words which are found either nowhere else in the Gospels or only extremely rarely is so great that they can scarcely all be listed; we therefore refer readers to the Glossary. It will suffice to give one or two examples: in Luke one finds *airus* for *aggilus*, *flodus* for *awa*, *naus* for *dauþs*, *manaseds* for *managei*, *gaujans* for *bisitands*, *gatvo* and *fauradauri* for *plapjo* (*platjo*), *unhails* for *siuks*, *namnjan* for *haitan*, *skeinan* for *liuhtjan*, *þiuþspillon* for *vailamerjan*, *magus* for *þiumagus*, and many simple verbs in place of compounds, such as *sviltan*, *aistan*, and *qistjan*. We omit other examples because they are also peculiar to this Gospel in the Greek text.

We add here, from the syntactical observations, this feature above all: in this Gospel the article is also placed after the noun; see III, 8, *us stainam þaim*; XVII, 17, *taihun þai*; XX, 15, *aurtjam þaim*. This construction occurs very frequently in the Epistles, but elsewhere in the Gospels only at John VII, 8.].

There is also the different meaning of familiar words [Note: [Col. 0476] For example, *aftra*, τὰ ὀπίσω, “the things behind,” Luke IX, 62; *gaþrafteins*, ἄφεσις, “release” or “forgiveness,” Luke IV, 19; *fraletan*, ἀποστέλλειν, “to send,” likewise IV, 19; *fragiþan*, ἀθετεῖν, “to reject,” VII, 30, in the passage under discussion.], and the many variant readings and glosses written in the margin [Note: [Col. 0476] Variant readings: V, 28, text *ïddja*—margin *laistida*; VI, 27, *fijandam*—*hatjandam*; VI, 40, *gamanvids*—*ustauhans*; VII, 32, *gaunodedum*—*hufum*; VIII, 27, *unhulþons*—*skohsla*; IX, 34, *qemun ïn þamma milhmin*—*jah at ïm ïn milhmin atgaggandam*; XVI, 13, *faihuþraihna*—*mammonim*.

Glosses: III, 14, text *valdaiþ*—margin *ganohidai sijaiþ*; VI, 49, *flodus*—*awa*; IX, 13, *manaseidai*—*managein*. It is extremely difficult, however, to distinguish with certainty between genuine variant readings and glosses.], whether added by the correctors themselves or by scribes comparing other copies. Some of these have been brought into the text [Note: [Col. 0476] These are far fewer than those Zahn enumerated in his *Introduction*, p. 34; and Castillion wrongly includes here 1 Corinthians XII, 15; 2 Corinthians X, 16; Galatians V, 4; and Colossians II, 32, concerning which passages we have spoken in the notes. But beyond all doubt, at Luke II, 2, one of the phrases *at visandin kindina syriais* and *raginondin saurim* arose from a gloss, since *at visandin kindina syriais* means the same as *raginondin saurim*; likewise at V, 35, concerning the second *jah*; at XIV, 32, concerning *jabai nist mahteigs*; at XVII, 6, concerning *jabai*; at 1 Corinthians XV, 6, concerning *fifhundam*; and at Colossians III, 12, concerning *armahairtein*. Cf. also the note on Luke XIX, 7.], as the correcting hands clearly indicate.

To this may be added the fact that in the Vienna manuscript mentioned above a few Gothic words are cited in comparison with forms from the more recent Germanic language. Among these, which were undoubtedly taken from the Gospel of Luke, are readings of the titles and of another passage that differ from the *Codex Argenteus* [Note: [Col. 0476] It reads *aivaggeljo þairh lokan* (“Gospel according to Luke”); since our manuscript reads *lukan*, it is evident that the former was taken from another copy. Likewise, *vaurþun afar þo* (“it came to pass after these [words]”), which certainly belongs to Luke IX, 28, is found in our manuscript with *þan* added: *vaurþun þan afar þo*—understand *vaurda*, “words.”].

Traces of two recensions are also found in the Gospel of Mark. In it several features of the language are recognized, either shared with Luke or departing from all the others [Note: [Col. 0476] For example, although with Matthew the article is usually added to the formula *sunus mans* (“son of man”)—Matthew IX, 6; X, 23; XI, 19—in Mark it is omitted at II, 10; VIII, 31, 38; IX, 9, 12, 31; X, 33, 45; XIII, 26; XIV, 41, as it is also generally omitted in Luke.], and variant readings have been written in the margin [Note: [Col. 0476] I, 6, text *haiþivisk*—margin *vilþi*; I, 11, [Col. 0477] *ïn þozei vaila galeikaida*—*þukei vilda*; V, 4, *gatamjan*—*gabindan*; XII, 24, *mela*—*bokos*.]. Its text, like Luke’s, also appears to have been interpolated from the other Gospels on many occasions [Note: [Col. 0477] See Note 5, column 473.].

What learned scholars have discovered from these indications concerning Luke and Mark must also be posited for Matthew and John, as other Gothic books prove. For in the Ambrosian manuscripts fragments of Matthew’s Gospel are read in which there are differences from the text of the *Codex Argenteus* [Note: [Col. 0477] XXVI, 72: *cod. Arg.* *afaiaik*—*cod. Ambr.* *laugnida*; XXVI, 75: *afaikis*—*ïnvidis*; XXVII, 1: *runa*—*garuni*; in the same passage: *gudjans*—*þai gudjans*.].

Furthermore, in that theological work written on the Gospel of John, the *Skeireins*, most passages from this Gospel are cited, and it is apparent from them that the author of that work had a text differing from ours [Note: [Col. 0477] John VI, 11: *cod. Arg.* *gaþ du siponjam*—*Skeir.* *qaþ siponjam*; in the same verse *þei*—*ei*; VI, 13, *fimf*—*þaim ·e·*; shortly afterward, *hlaibam þaim barizeinam*—*hlaibam barizeinam*; in the same verse, *þaim matjandam*—*at þaim matjandam*; VII, 46, *andhofun*—*andhofun þan*; VII, 48, *fareisaie*—*þize fareisaie*. We omit the fact that at VII, 47 *siuþ* is written for *sijuþ*, and at VI, 9 *tvans* for *·b·*.
