For the rest, the following features are nearly unique to the text of John: *dahþe* for *duþe*—which is also read at VI, 65 and VIII, 47—or *duþþe*, see the Glossary under *þata*; the extremely frequent use of the particles *þaruh* and *þanuh* for the Greek δὲ and καὶ, see the Glossary under the respective entries; the enclitic *uh* and the relative *ïze* for rendering Greek participles, see the Glossary under *-uh* and the grammar where participles are discussed; the use of the particle *ïth* in adversative sentences where the Greek text has no corresponding word, see the note on John VI, 58; and the use of *ïþ* for the conditional Greek εἴ, which John shares with Luke.].

In view of these divergences, it is recognized that they are only minor and that neither the character nor the uniformity of the earlier translation was lost through that revision. We for our part do not dare decide whether the Epistles had already been translated for the Goths on the banks of the Danube, or only later in Italy, although we can think of nothing that would have prevented this from happening. The fragments, however, that have survived to our age may be assigned to a later period from the fact that they not only agree for the most part with the Italian manuscripts, but also contain new forms (see the note on 1 Thessalonians IV, 14), new syntactical usages (see the note on Colossians IV, 10), and many of the peculiarities indicated above.

The disagreement of the manuscripts further indicates that two recensions of these Epistles existed.

[Note: [Col. 0477] Castillion, in his note on 1 Timothy II, 6, denies that the twofold recension of the Epistles is contained in codices A and B, because codex A generally agrees with codex B. Certainly there are passages where both codices have the same reading, although anyone who carefully examines the passages cited by Castillion will see that their number ought to be considerably reduced. But who, being intelligent and judicious, would deny that there are also passages—and not “very few,” as Castillion says—in which they differ? We have called these divergences of reading traces of a double recension or revision, not of an entirely new translation, as Castillion seems not to have understood. Nor did Castillion persuade us so easily that we had been mistaken, as Massmann did in MGA 1840, p. 137.]

Of the older recension, so far as it survives, we have printed the text continuously (codex Carolinus and codex B); the other, whose variants we have appended in the notes (codex A), appears to be more recent. For the two codices mentioned above have no marginal notes—at least none that indicate variant readings or glosses—

[Note: [Col. 0477] The margin of codex B contains isolated numerical letters, together with the word *laiktjo*, by which the former indicate chapters and the latter ecclesiastical readings. See below concerning these. As for the reading *sihv* in 1 Corinthians XV, 57, Castillion did not even himself approve his conjecture that it signified verse 218, nor have we been able to determine the meaning of those letters, unless perhaps someone, considering the sense of the verse in which it is said that God has given us victory through Jesus Christ, should conjecture that the letters are Latin, standing for *si. h. v.* = *signo hoc vinces*, “by this sign you will conquer,” so that the Gothic theologian may have wished to indicate that the citizens, using this token, would win victory over their enemies, whether external or internal.]

—in the other, however, the more recent character is evident, unless from the various readings inserted in the margin—

[Note: [Col. 0477] Romans IX, 13: in the text *fijaida*—in the margin *andvaih* (?); X, 7: *ïup*—*rjo* (in this fragment we suspect that not an adverb but a verb lies beneath *ïup*, for *ustiuhan*, perhaps *usfarjon*); 1 Corinthians IX, 9: *ni faurmuljais auhsau þriskaidai*—*ni faurvaipjais munþ auhsau þriskandin*; verse 19: *gageigaidedjau*—*gastaistaldjau*; verse 21: *gageiggau*—*gavandidedjau*; verse 22: *waiva*—*vaila*; X, 30: *andnima*—*brukja*; XIII, 3: *ei gabrannjaidau*—*ei wopau*; verse 5: *ni sokeiþ sein ain*—*ni ïnaljanoþ sein ain*; XV, 33: *riurjand*—*fravardjand*; 2 Corinthians I, 8: *afsvaggvidai veseima*—*skamaidedeima*; II, 11: *galiginondau*—*gafaihondau*; verse 15: *fraqistnandam*—*fralusnandam*; III, 14: *afdaubnodedun*—*gablindnodedun*; V, 12: *uskannjaima*—*anafilhaima*; XII, 7: *hnuþo*—*gairu*; XII, 15: *laþaleiko*—*gabaurjaba*; Galatians II, 5: *gastandai*—*þairhvisai*; verse 6: *andsitaiþ*—*nimiþ*; verse 8: *gatavida*—*vaurhta*; IV, 3: *uf stabim fairwaus*—*uf tugglam*; verse 13: *siukein*—*unmatht*; verse 21: *niu hauseiþ*—*niu ussuggvuþ*; VI, 3: *fraþjamarzeins ïst*—*sik silban uslutonds ïst*; Ephesians I, 9: *bi viljan saei fauragaleikaida ïmma*—*ana leikainai þoei garaidida ïn ïmma*; verse 14: *gafreideinais*—*ganistais*; II, 3: *viljans*—*lustuns*; ibid.: *vistai barna hatizis*—*us sateinai urrugkai*; II, 10: *godaim*—*þiuþeigaim*; III, 10: *filufaihu*—*managnandei managei* (?). Most of these notes contain interpretations, others corrections according to the Greek text (1 Corinthians XIII, 3; Galatians II, 6; Ephesians I, 9), or according to Latin versions (Galatians IV, 21; Ephesians II, 3), or readings of codex B (2 Corinthians I, 8; XII, 15).]

—or certainly from the exceedingly frequent correction of readings according to the Greek text—

[Note: [Col. 0478] 1 Corinthians XVI, 2: codex B *taujai* (“let him make”)—codex A *lagjai*, in agreement with all Greek manuscripts, *τιθέτω* (“let him put”); 2 Corinthians I, 8: *skamaidedeima uns* (“we should be in despair”)—*afsvaggvidai veseima* (“we should be perplexed”), which is closer to the Greek *ἐξαπορηθῆναι*; II, 19: *vailamerjada* (“is evangelized”)—*merjada* (“is preached”), in agreement with all Greek manuscripts, *κηρυχθείς* (“having been preached”); II, 13: *ïmma ei* (“to him that”)—*ïm* (“to them”), in agreement with all Greek manuscripts, *αὐτοῖς* (“to them”); III, 3: *svikunþ* (“manifest”)—*svikunþai* (“manifest”), in agreement with all Greek manuscripts, *φανερούμενοι* (“being made manifest”); III, 9: *us vulþau* (“from glory”)—*ïn vulþau* (“in glory”), in agreement with all Greek manuscripts, *(ἐν δόξῃ)*; VIII, 19: *miþ gasinþam* (“with companions”)—*miþgasinþa* (“a companion”), in agreement with all Greek manuscripts, *συνέκδημος* (“fellow traveler”); verse 20: *bivandjandam* (“those who avoid”)—*bivandjandans* (“avoiding”), in agreement with all Greek manuscripts, *στελλόμενοι* (“being restrained”); verse 22: *filaus mais* (“much more”)—*filu* (“much”), in agreement with all Greek manuscripts, *πολύ* (“much”); XIII, 5: *ïbai num* (*μῆτι, ἄρα*, “surely, then?”)—*nibai* (“unless”), in agreement with most Greek manuscripts, *εἰ μήτι* (“unless indeed”); Ephesians I, 22: *all* (“all,” neuter singular)—*alla* (“all things”), *πάντα*; II, 2: *aivis* (“of the age”)—*fairwaus* (“of the world”), in agreement with all Greek manuscripts, *κόσμου* (“of the world”); II, 5: *sijum* (“we are”)—*sijuþ* (“you are”), in agreement with all Greek manuscripts, *ἐστέ* (“you are”); conversely, IV, 25 and IV, 28: *ak* (“but”)—*ïþ* (“but, truly”), in agreement with all Greek manuscripts, *δέ* (“but”); IV, 30: *þammei* (“in which”)—*ïn þammei* (“in which”), in agreement with all Greek manuscripts, *ἐν ᾧ* (“in which”).]

—can be recognized as more recent. Many other divergences between the two codices are arranged in such a way that each followed a different Greek text, while codex A chiefly follows those whose Italian origin is certain:

2 Corinthians II, 12: codex B *ïn aivaggeljon* (*εἰς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον*, “for the Gospel”)—codices A *ïn aivaggeljons* (*διὰ τὸ εὐαγγέλιον*, “because of the Gospel”); verse 16: *dauþaus* (*θανάτου*, “of death”)—*us dauþau* (*ἐκ θανάτου*, “from death”); III, 9: *andbahti* (*διακονία*, “ministry”)—*andbahtja* (*διακονίᾳ*, “in ministry”); V, 12: *hairtin* (*καρδίᾳ*, “in the heart”)—*ïn hairtin* (*ἐν καρδίᾳ*, “in the heart”); VII, 3: *gasviltan* (*ἀποθανεῖν*, “to die”)—*miþgasviltan* (*συναποθανεῖν*, “to die with”); Ephesians I, 19: *ïn uns* (*εἰς ἡμᾶς*, “toward us”)—*ïn ïzvis* (*εἰς ὑμᾶς*, “toward you”); Philippians III, 13: *ni þau* (*οὐκ [ἄρα]*, “not, therefore”)—*ni nauh* (*οὔπω*, “not yet”).

Only very rarely does the authority of the Greek manuscripts fail the readings of codex A. Thus, in 2 Corinthians VII, 9 it reads *vahtai* instead of *ïn vaihtai*, although all Greek manuscripts recognize the preposition *ἐν* (“in”); likewise, in IX, 2 it has *wopam* (“we boast”) instead of *wopa* (“I boast”), though neither the Greek nor the Latin witnesses have this reading; in XIII, 7 it reads *ungakusanai* (“rejected”)—with only codex Lincolnianus, so far as we know—in place of *gakusanai* (*δόκιμοι*, “approved”); finally, in Colossians III, 1 it offers *þar* (“there”) instead of *þarei* (“where”), which all codices require (*οὗ*). We suspect that this was inserted through a copyist’s error.

The remaining divergences do not present a different meaning or text, but differences of interpretation. Thus, in 2 Corinthians VII, 8, codex B has *auk*, codex A *unte*; IX, 2: *gavagida*—*usvagida*; Galatians II, 6: *vulþris*—*vulþrais*; VI, 1: *atsaiwands*—*andsaiwands*; Ephesians I, 14: *ïzei*—*saei*; III, 10: *managfalþo*—*filufaihu*; III, 19: *du*—*ïn*; VI, 11: *diabulaus*—*unhulpins*; VI, 18: *vakandans*—*duvakandans*; Colossians III, 5: *vinnon*—*vinna*.

This is also shown by the distinctive spelling frequently encountered. To this category we refer the frequent use of assimilation, whereby a final *h* is changed into the same initial letter as that of the following word. This figure occurs more rarely in the Gospels—at least in those contained in the Silver Codex—and is found there only before *þ*—

[Note: [Col. 0479] The forms written *jan-ni* in Matthew XXV, 42 and *jassa* in XXVI, 2 are from the Ambrosian codex.]

—and more rarely also in codex B, whereas in codex A it is used before all liquids and medial consonants—

[Note: [Col. 0479] Apart from the fact that this change is admitted before *þ*, it also occurs before liquids: *l*, 2 Corinthians I, 8 (elsewhere VII, 8), Ephesians III, 18; *m*, Philippians III, 17; *n*, 1 Corinthians X, 20; 2 Corinthians I, 18–19; III, 13; V, 12; VIII, 5; Philippians III, 3, and elsewhere; *r*, 2 Corinthians VIII, 10, compare the note on IV, 6; *s*, 1 Corinthians V, 8; 2 Corinthians II, 2; VIII, 15; VII, 3; Philippians IV, 2. Before medial consonants: *b*, 1 Corinthians X, 21; 2 Corinthians VII, 15; IX, 4; *g*, 2 Corinthians II, 7; V, 5, 18; VIII, 23; Ephesians IV, 24; *d*, 2 Corinthians II, 16. Indeed, before the voiceless letter *k* he uses assimilation in 1 Corinthians VII, 16.]

—then the use of simple vowels in endings in place of diphthongs—

[Note: [Col. 0479] Thus *i* for *ei*: 2 Corinthians XIII, 3 *siukiþ*, Galatians VI, 3 *þugkiþ*, for *siukeiþ*, *þugkeiþ*; *e* for *ei*: 2 Corinthians V, 21; VIII, 16; Galatians VI, 13; Ephesians II, 16; Philippians II, 26 *ïze* and *þize* for *ïzei* and *þizei*. Conversely, in medial forms he prefers fuller sounds, for he writes in 2 Corinthians I, 12 *usmeitum*; Galatians III, 19 *þizeiei*; 2 Corinthians IV, 7 *tykeikus*, for *usmetum*, *þizeei*, *tykekus*.]

—the omission of more weakly sounded letters at the ends of words—

[Note: [Col. 0479] 2 Corinthians XIII, 5 *þau*; XII, 2–3; Ephesians II, 12 *ïnu* for *þauh* and *ïnuh*.]

—and the avoidance of certain kinds of hiatus by inserting the letter *j*—

[Note: [Col. 0479] For example, where the word *friaþva* occurs, he writes *ija* for *ia*, namely *frijaþva* throughout; *iai*—*ijai* in *sijai*, Philippians IV, 5 and Colossians IV, 6; *aiï*—*aiji* in *saijiþ*, 2 Corinthians IX, 6 and Galatians VI, 7–8; *eiha*—*eijha* in *freijhals*, 2 Corinthians III, 17, and in many other passages. Conversely, *iu*, for which *iju* used formerly to be written, is especially restored in codex A, in *sium* and *siuþ*, 2 Corinthians II, 17; III, 3; VI, 16; XIII, 9; Ephesians II, 8, 10; IV, 1; Philippians III, 3.]

When all these features are considered together—and this abundance can easily be increased by many other examples—it is clearly shown that the Gothic language, previously rough, rustic, and unformed, was diverted from its uncorrupted integrity and softened toward the usage of a foreign language by those who undertook anew the Gothic translation of the sacred books.

There remain the fragments of the Old Testament, few indeed, but sufficient to justify the firmest conjecture that most of its books had certainly been translated into Gothic. For we have shown above that it is scarcely credible that books of less serious content were handed down by the Goths in their native language while the more important books were not; rather, without doubt, a translation of the remaining books also existed. This translation, however, appears to belong to the period after the Goths had established settlements in Italy. For since it did not flow from a Hebrew manuscript but from the translation of the Septuagint, specifically from that which was the source of the Complutensian edition—as can easily be recognized by comparing the Gothic with the Complutensian text—

[Note: [Col. 0480] See Ezra II, 31, where it adds *anþaris*, generally omitted, in agreement with the Complutensian text (*ἑτέρου*, “of another”); verse 39: *þusundi iz*—*χίλιοι δεκαεπτά* (“one thousand seventeen”), following the Complutensian reading instead of *χίλιοι ἑπτά* (“one thousand seven”). In Nehemiah V, 13, at the beginning, in agreement with the Complutensian text, it adds *jah* (*καίγε*, “and indeed”); likewise in verse 14, after *artarksairksaus* (*Ἀρθασασθά*, “Artaxerxes”), it has *þiudanis* (*βασιλεῖ*, “to the king”), and there *καὶ ἐγώ* (“and I”) instead of *ἐγώ* (“I”), except that, with the words transposed, it reads *ïk jah* (“I also”). Shortly afterward, where the common text reads *βίαν αὐτῶν οὐκ ἔφαγον καὶ τὰς βίας τὰς πρώτας ἃς πρὸ ἐμοῦ ἐβάρυναν ἐπ’ αὐτούς* (“I did not eat their provisions, and the earlier provisions which had been imposed upon them before me”), the Gothic, with the Complutensian text, reads *ἄρτον τῆς ἡγεμονίας μου οὐκ ἐφάγομεν, οἱ δὲ ἄρχοντες οἱ ἔμπροσθέν μου ἐβάρυναν ἐπὶ τὸν λαόν* (“we did not eat the bread of my governorship, but the rulers who preceded me laid burdens upon the people”), translating: *hlaif fauramaþleis meinis ni matidedum. ïþ fauramaþljos þaiei vesum faura mis kauridedun þo managein*. In verse 15, in place of *δίδραχμα* (“didrachmas”), it reads, with the Complutensian text, *σίκλους* (“shekels,” *sikle*); and in place of *ἐκτετιναγμένοι αὐτῶν ἐξουσιάζονται* (“their extortioners rule over them”), with the same book it has *παιδάρια αὐτῶν ἐκυρίευσαν* (“their servants ruled over them”), translating *skalkos ïze fraujinodedun* (“their servants ruled over them”), and so forth. The editors of the *Specimen* have already indicated the agreement of the Gothic text with the Complutensian, though they have not done so in every passage where the Gothic agrees with that book.]

—and since it is established that the Complutensian edition was compiled from Italian manuscripts—

[Note: [Col. 0480] See the letter prefixed to the Complutensian edition, addressed to Pope Leo X.]

—it follows that the Gothic translation also, at least our fragments, was drawn from Italian books and made in Italy.

To the arguments by which we proved above that our translation underwent most of its changes in Italy, the following, still more certain, may be added. After the headings of the individual books appears *dustodeiþ* or *anastodeiþ*, that is, “it begins”—

[Note: [Col. 0480] See the Gospels of Mark and Luke; the Second Epistle to the Corinthians; the Epistles to the Ephesians and to the Second Thessalonians; the First Epistle to Timothy, at this passage; and the Epistle to Titus. The Epistle to the Galatians begins abruptly, as does the Second Epistle to Timothy, since codex A has neither headings nor subscriptions. The remaining Gospels and Epistles are *ἀκέφαλα*, “without a heading.”]

—a formula found in none of the Greek manuscripts, but in most Latin ones—

[Note: [Col. 0480] Compare Wetstein, at the cited place, p. 305.]

—and at the end of the Epistles *ustauh*, that is, “it is complete”—

[Note: [Col. 0480] See the Epistles to the Romans, both Epistles to the Corinthians, and those to the Galatians, Ephesians, Colossians, and the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians. As for the fact that we have translated the Gothic *ustauh* by the Latin word *explicit*, “it is complete,” the more correct expression would have been *perfecit*, “he completed it”; compare Grimm, *W. J.*, p. 34.]

—is added, either with a brief indication of the church to whose Christians the Apostle wrote the Epistle—

[Note: [Col. 0480] This is usually the case in codex B.]

—or with the place from which he sent it—

[Note: [Col. 0480] This is the case in codex A, which also often has two subscriptions joined together.]

Since it is universally acknowledged that these subscriptions were first made by Euthalius, bishop of Alexandria, only in the middle of the fifth century—

[Note: [Col. 0480] Euthalius completed this work in the year 458. See Mill, *Prolegomena*, pp. 940 and 944. We learn from Jerome’s Letter 28.4, moreover, that the custom of placing *explicit* at the end of books was already practiced by the Romans in the fourth century.]

—and since at that time Ulfilas was no longer alive, the Visigoths were no longer dwelling in their ancient settlements on the Danube, and the Ostrogoths, after rebelling upon Attila’s death and preparing to seek new settlements, do not appear to have been occupied with such matters—at what other time, then, unless after they had occupied Italy and, if the same is to be said of the remaining Goths, Gaul, could their books have received these headings and subscriptions?

The fact that the Goths also transferred from Latin books into their Bible the index of ecclesiastical readings, an addition introduced at the same time as the subscriptions—

[Note: [Col. 0481] See Mill, *Prolegomena*, p. 941.]

—is demonstrated by their designation *laiktjo*. For if the Goths had taken those sections from Greek books, they would have formed a word derived from *siggvan* (*ἀναγινώσκειν*, “to read”), corresponding to the Greek *ἀνάγνωσις* (“reading”); but instead they used a purely Latin word—

[Note: [Col. 0481] These readings are written in the margin of codex B, specifically at 1 Corinthians XV, 58; 2 Corinthians III, 4; V, 11; VIII, 1; IX, 1; XI, 29 (of which five readings Euthalius recognizes only four); Galatians V, 2 and 25; Ephesians V, 1 and 5; Philippians I, 21; III, 1; IV, 1; 1 Thessalonians III, 1; and Philemon 12.]

—namely, a term that clearly shows their Latin source.

Apart from this division according to readings, another division according to chapters appears in both codices, though it is different in each. Those divisions that occur only in codex B agree for the most part with the Euthalian divisions; those additionally found in codices A and B agree with no other division of the books.

[Note: [Col. 0481] In the Epistle to the Romans, no divisions appear to be marked, except in codex Carolinus at XII, 1, *i*, and XIII, 1, *e*. In the First Epistle to the Corinthians, codex A has at XI, 3, *h* (8); at XIV, 26, *ie* (15); and at XV, 58, *iz* (17). It also has at XI, 25, *e* (5), which Castillion considers an indication of the Euthalian division; compare Knittel, p. 384. In the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, codex B has at I, 3, *a* (1); I, 15, *b* (2); II, 12, *g* (3); IV, 1, *e* (5); IV, 7, *q* (6); V, 12, *z* (7); VII, 4, *h* (8); VIII, 1, *þ* (9); IX, 3, *i* (10); XI, 21, *ia* (11). Castillion says that the letter *d* (4), at II, 1, 3, was omitted or had disappeared in such a way that he found no trace of it. The first Euthalian section, however, is placed at I, 1; the eighth at VII, 2; the tenth at X, 1; and the eleventh at XI, 1. In codex A only two sections are noted: at V, 11, *d* (4), and VIII, 1, *q* (6), neither of which agrees with the Greek divisions at all. In the Epistle to the Galatians codex B has at II, 11, *g* (3); IV, 21, *þ* (9); V, 13, *ia* (11); and VI, 11, *ib* (12), with several omissions; codex A has at III, 27, *g* (3), and IV, 13, *d* (4). The Epistle to the Ephesians has in codex A at II, 1, *a* (1). The First Epistle to the Thessalonians has in codex B at II, 17, *b* (2), and III, 11, *g* (3). The Second has at II, 6, *e* (5), and II, 16, *q* (6). The First Epistle to Timothy has at II, 1, *d* (4); V, 3, *ia* (11); and VI, 11, *iz* (17). The Second has at II, 14, *e* (5), and IV, 1, *h* (8).]

For the sake of mentioning this at the present point, the Gospels in the Silver Codex are divided according to canons not unlike those of Eusebius—

[Note: [Col. 0481] Lye first appended these canons to Benzelius’s edition. The passages where they depart from the Eusebian canons are as follows:

In the Gospel of Matthew: section *md*, VI, 9, corresponding to Eusebius VI, 14; *mq*, VI, 20, corresponding to VI, 19; *ne*, VII, 15, corresponding to VII, 13; *nþ*, VII, 19, corresponding to VII, 21; *jþ*, VIII, 22, corresponding to VIII, 23; *[Gothic 90]d*, X, 33, corresponding to X, 32; *rq*, XI, 16, corresponding to XI, 14; *rz*, XI, 18, corresponding to XI, 15; *tme*, XXVII, 51, corresponding to XXVII, 52.

In the Gospel of Mark: section *b*, I, 4, corresponding to Eusebius I, 3; *g*, I, 6, corresponding to I, 4; *þ*, I, 14, corresponding to I, 15; *ka*, II, 13, corresponding to II, 14; *kþ*, III, 13, corresponding to III, 14; *mq*, IV, 34, corresponding to IV, 35; *mz*, IV, 35, corresponding to IV, 36; *nq*, VI, 12, corresponding to VI, 13; *nh*, VI, 15, corresponding to VI, 16; *j*, VI, 18, corresponding to VI, 21; *jþ*, VI, 54, corresponding to VI, 53; *ud*, VII, 30, corresponding to VII, 31; *uq*, VII, 37, corresponding to VIII, 1; *pg*, VIII, 29, corresponding to VIII, 30; *[Gothic 90]d*, IX, 33, corresponding to IX, 32; *ra*, IX, 49, corresponding to IX, 44; *rb*, IX, 50, corresponding to IX, 49; *rih*, XI, 3, corresponding to XI, 4; *rl*, XII, 12, corresponding to XII, 13; *rnþ*, XIV, 8, corresponding to XIV, 7; *rpe*, XIV, 50, corresponding to XIV, 49; *r[Gothic 90]q*, XIV, 68, corresponding to XIV, 69; *r[Gothic 90]þ*, XV, 1, corresponding to XV, 2; *s*, XV, 2, corresponding to XV, 3; *sa*, XV, 3, corresponding to XV, 4; *sþ*, XV, 20, corresponding to XV, 21.

In the Gospel of Luke: section *b*, I, 35, corresponding to II, 6; *g*, I, 36, corresponding to II, 8; *i*, III, 15, corresponding to III, 16; *ia*, III, 16, corresponding to III, 17; *ib*, III, 17, corresponding to III, 19; *lb*, V, 10, corresponding to V, 11; *mh*, VI, 21, corresponding to VI, 22; *na*, VI, 26, corresponding to VI, 25; *jþ*, VII, 18, corresponding to VII, 19; *uh*, VIII, 11, corresponding to VIII, 12; *rpz*, XV, 3, corresponding to XV, 4; *r[Gothic 90]*, XV, 11, corresponding to XV, 12; *r[Gothic 90]b*, XVI, 13, corresponding to XVI, 14; *r[Gothic 90]þ*, XVII, 3, corresponding to XVII, 4; *sq*, XVII, 24, corresponding to XVII, 25; *siq*, XVIII, 14, corresponding to XVIII, 15; *ska*, XVIII, 27, corresponding to XVIII, 29; *ske*, XVIII, 43, corresponding to XIX, 1; *slg*, XIX, 35, corresponding to XIX, 32; *sld*, XIX, 37, corresponding to XIX, 36; *slq*, XIX, 40, corresponding to XIX, 41.

In the Gospel of John: section *nq*, VI, 35, corresponding to VI, 37; *jg*, VI, 48, corresponding to VI, 49; *jd*, VI, 49, corresponding to VI, 50; *ua*, VI, 63, corresponding to VI, 64; *ub*, VI, 64, corresponding to VI, 65; *ug*, VI, 65, corresponding to VI, 66; *[Gothic 90]a*, X, 15, corresponding to X, 16; *[Gothic 90]b*, X, 16, corresponding to X, 17; *[Gothic 90]g*, X, 39, corresponding to X, 40; *rh*, XII, 27, corresponding to XII, 28; *rkq*, XIII, 36, corresponding to XIII, 37; *rlb*, XIV, 25, corresponding to XIV, 26; *rlz*, XV, 16, corresponding to XV, 17; *rlh*, XV, 17, corresponding to XV, 18; *rmd*, XV, 23, corresponding to XV, 24; *rme*, XV, 24, corresponding to XV, 25; *rmq*, XVI, 2, corresponding to XVI, 1; *rmz*, XVI, 4, corresponding to XVI, 5; *rmþ*, XVI, 15, corresponding to XVI, 16; *rne*, XVII, 25, corresponding to XVII, 26; *rjþ*, XVIII, 19, corresponding to XVIII, 18; *ruz*, XVIII, 28, corresponding to XVIII, 29; *ruþ*, XVIII, 35, corresponding to XVIII, 34; *r[Gothic 90]*, XIX, 6, corresponding to XIX, 7.

Moreover, the copyist sometimes omitted writing the canons in the codex. They are missing at Matthew VII, 15, *nq*; VII, 17, *nh*; XXVII, 51, *tmd*; XXVII, 62, *tna*; Mark XVI, 11, *sld*, and 12, *sle*; Luke IV, 24, *ka*; VI, 6, *mb*; VII, 11, *jz*; IX, 37, *[Gothic 90]þ*; X, 1 through 10, 29, where thereafter the numbers of five sections, from *rz* through *rib*, are absent; X, 29, *rkb*; XVI, 13, *r[Gothic 90]a*; XVII, 7, *sa*; John XV, 23, *rmg*.]

—but it cannot be stated with certainty whether these were added by the first translator or by others.

After having discussed the sources from which the Gothic version now in our possession was composed, there follows a second question: the manner in which Ulfilas performed the task of translator. Once this question has been settled, it will be possible to understand what new benefit the textual criticism of the New Testament derives from it.

Almost everyone agrees that Ulfilas, following the authority of the Greek text with the utmost scrupulousness, rendered it word for word. But many have conceived of this slavish fidelity as so extreme and superstitious that it remains uncertain whether it ought to be condemned rather than praised. For when those who say that he followed the Greek so closely that he even uses passive forms for Greek middle forms, which he misunderstood, what else are they doing but accusing the Goth of ignorance of Greek and indeed of his own language? Yet these same people say at one moment that the Goth forgot to imitate the Greek text more accurately, and at another that he abandoned Greek authority whenever the euphony or the genius of the Gothic language required it—

[Note: [Col. 0482] See Zahn on Luke XIX, 31 and *Einleitung*, p. 30, 2.]

If, however, he translated from the Greek in such a way that he also observed the laws of his own language, who would maintain that he translated slavishly, when the only thing deserving praise in him would be his fidelity?

Nor is it true, as other learned men say—

[Note: [Col. 0482] For example, Castillion, *Specimen*, preface, p. XX. We now suppose that this excellent man, instructed by much use of and familiarity with Ulfilas, would think differently, just as he himself does not praise those who rendered the sense literally, which Aschbach did at the cited place, p. 35.]

—that Ulfilas translated his Greek exemplar in precisely the same words, rendered obscure things obscurely, left ambiguities ambiguous, and preserved Greek syntax and word order, so that in his book we have a Greek text clothed in Gothic vocabulary but entirely devoid of northern idioms.

It is not only intrinsically incredible that a wise man should have so deprived himself of his own judgment as to produce a translation of the sacred books arranged in such a way that those who read his words would neither understand them nor derive any benefit from them, when his aim was precisely that his fellow citizens should be instructed and strengthened by the Christian teaching to be drawn from the Scriptures—

[Col. 0483]

—but it can also be demonstrated very easily that the Goth used the resources of his own language and observed its laws so carefully that he can be said to have produced a genuinely Gothic translation, not a Greek text dressed in Gothic words—

[Note: [Col. 0483] See Grimm’s learned discussion of this matter, as is his custom, *Grammar*, preface, p. XLVI of the first edition.]

For he neither places the article except where Gothic speech permits it, nor imitates the Greek usage of joining a singular verb to a neuter plural subject. He uses the dual number more often than Greek does, and very frequently employs datives in place of genitives dependent on nouns (compare the note on John VIII, 34). He does not make the predicate agree with the subject in case, but renders it by adding the preposition *du*. Content with two verbal tenses, he introduces no new forms either to render the future or to distinguish past times. He reckons periods of time not by years but by spans of winters (see the notes on Matthew IX, 20 and Luke II, 42), and not by new moons but by full moons (see the note on Colossians II, 16).

And who could enumerate how often he transposes words—not only the negation, about which we have spoken above, but other words as well? For example, in Matthew alone:

VII, 24: *vaurda meina*, Greek *μοῦ τοὺς λόγους* (“my words”);

VII, 24: *jainamma razna*, Greek *οἰκίᾳ ἐκείνῃ* (“that house”); likewise VIII, 13 and IX, 26;

VIII, 3: *þata þrustfill ïs*, Greek *αὐτοῦ ἡ λέπρα* (“his leprosy”);

VIII, 8: *uf hrot mein*, Greek *μοῦ ὑπὸ στέγην* (“under my roof”);

IX, 6: *þana ligr þeinana*, Greek *σοῦ τὴν κλίνην* (“your bed”);

IX, 27: *ïesua jainþro*, Greek *ἐκεῖθεν τῷ Ἰησοῦ* (“to Jesus from there”);

XI, 10: *sa ïst auk*, Greek *οὗτος γάρ ἐστι* (“for this is he”);

XXVII, 45: *varth rigis*, Greek *σκότος ἐγένετο* (“darkness came”);

XXVII, 46: *weila niundon*, Greek *ἐννάτην ὥραν* (“the ninth hour”).

How often he adds certain words without following any authority, for example in Matthew V, 17, *ïk* (“I”); verse 19, *sah* (“this”), corresponding to the preceding *saei* (“who”); VIII, 26, *ïesus* (“Jesus”), which is also added by the Syriac and Vulgate versions; IX, 17, *biþeh þan* (“afterward then”); X, 28, *þatainei* (“only”), which, apart from Tertullian, *Against the Gnostics*, p. 829 [our *Patrologia*, vol. II, col. 139], although in another passage with the sense “those who kill only the body,” is found in no manuscript; XI, 23, *eis* (“you”); XXVII, 15, *warjanoh* (“or whom”).

How often he omits words, as in the same Gospel, XXV, 43, *ἤμην* (“I was”); XXVII, 16, *λεγόμενον* (“called”).

How often he admits expansions of things and concepts, on which see the notes on Matthew IX, 8 and 23; compare the note on 1 Corinthians IX, 25.

How often he renders the same frequently repeated Greek word by different Gothic words, as in Matthew:

V, 23–24: *aibr*, *giba* for *δῶρον* (“gift”);

VI, 2 and 5: *andnemun*, *haband* for *ἀπέχουσι* (“they have received”);

VI, 1 and 2: *laun*, *mizdon* for *μισθόν* (“reward”);

VI, 19–20: *hlifand*, *stiland* for *κλέπτουσι* (“steal”);

VI, 27–28: *maurnan*, *saurgan* for *μεριμνᾶν* (“be anxious”);

VII, 13: *ïnngaggan*, *ïnngaleiþan* for *εἰσέρχεσθαι* (“enter”);

VII, 17–18: *gods*, *þiuþeigs* for *ἀγαθός* (“good”);

VII, 24 and 26: *vair*, *manna* for *ἀνήρ* (“man”);

IX, 17: *niujata*, *juggata* for *νέον* (“new”);

IX, 32–33: *bauds*, *dumbs* for *κωφός* (“mute”);

XXVI, 70 and 72: *laugnida*, *afaiaik* for *ἠρνήσατο* (“denied”).

Compare Mareshall, p. 472 ff.; Massmann, *B. A.* 1834, p. 962.

From all these examples—not only those found in Matthew but also those in the other Gospels and in the Epistles—it is evident that Ulfilas did not absurdly imitate Greek, but faithfully preserved the character of the Gothic language and its modes of expression.

Nor in that other recension, which we said above was made at a later period and elaborated in a style corresponding more accurately to the Greek, did the peculiarities of the Gothic language so completely disappear that it could be regarded as a Greek text clothed in Gothic words.

[Col. 0484]

Those who consider these matters will recognize that Ulfilas, insofar as understanding permitted, scrupulously followed the traces of the Greek; but whenever the character of his language required it, he disregarded Greek authority while nevertheless rendering the sense correctly and accurately.

There are indeed passages where he appears to have translated less accurately. This happens to almost all translators of foreign languages: they either depart from the author’s meaning in individual words, fail to grasp his thought, or lack sufficient knowledge of the customs and institutions of other peoples. Nor do we intend to absolve Ulfilas from this fault, although he was exceptionally well versed in the Greek language and carried out his work with outstanding skill.

He did not know that the Jewish priests had been arranged in classes, each of which performed the sacred service in its own assigned week. Therefore *ἐφημερία* (“course of service”) in Luke I, 5 and 8 should not have been translated either by *afar* (“after,” that is, “posterity,” “descendants”) or by *kuni* (“kind,” “nation,” “family”). Nor do we approve his rendering in Matthew V, 26 of *ἔσχατος* (“last”) by *minnista* (“smallest”); in Mark I, 4 of *ἄφεσις* (“release,” “forgiveness”) by *aflageins* (“deposit”); in Luke VI, 44 of *τρυγᾶν* (“to gather grapes”) by *trudan* (“to tread”); or in 2 Corinthians XI, 20 of *ἐπαίρεσθαι* (“to exalt oneself”) by *ïn arbaidai briggan* (“to bring into slavery”). Compare Castillion on Colossians II, 23. In these passages he neglected to investigate more carefully the meaning of individual words. The same thing happened to him in rendering certain particles; see the notes on 1 Corinthians IV, 5 and VII, 17, and 2 Corinthians XI, 16.

Here belong those passages in which he lacked a deeper knowledge of the Greek language. Thus in John VIII, 25 he translated *τὴν ἀρχήν* (“in the first place,” or “absolutely”) incorrectly; a fault also committed by several Latin translators. Or he changed the order of the words according to the ordinary rules correctly enough, but with damage to the sense; see the note on John XIV, 11. Or he rendered Greek words easy to explain more freely than was suitable for conveying their meaning. Such passages include 1 Corinthians XII, 15; see the note on that passage.

In Romans XI, 24, where *κατὰ φύσιν* (“according to nature”) and *παρὰ φύσιν* (“contrary to nature”) are contrasted, he not only failed to render the opposition but distorted the sense of the first statement. For instead of *us vistai þis vilþeis alevabagmis*, “from the nature of this wild olive tree,” which should correspond to the Greek *ἐκ τῆς κατὰ φύσιν ἀγριελαίου* (“from the naturally wild olive tree”), he ought to have written *us þamma (bi) vistai—alevabagma*, “from the natural condition of the olive tree.”

Where, because of the lack of forms by which Greek verbal tenses could be expressed more precisely, he could not render the Greek accurately, he is not deserving of blame. Yet even in 1 Corinthians XVI, 3, for *δοκιμάσητε* (“you may approve”), he could have used the present *gakiusiþ* rather than the past *gakusuþ*; and in John V, 45, where he rendered the participle *κατηγορῶν* (“accusing”) by a relative circumlocution, he could more correctly have used the present *vroheiþ* rather than *vrohida*.

However many passages may be added to these in which Ulfilas suffered something human—

[Note: [Col. 0484] See the notes on Mark XII, 13; Luke XVI, 16; XVII, 22; and 1 Thessalonians V, 23.]

—their number is nevertheless so small and the faults so slight in so great a work that his translation must be regarded as the best. We have pointed out these passages especially for this reason: so that no one may suppose that the Goth was there following a variant Greek reading.

Furthermore, it often happened that, deceived in his own manuscript by the similarity of writing—whether of individual letters or of abbreviations for words—

[Col. 0485]

he translated differently from the Greek text as it now stands. We shall not discuss here the passages Mark VII, 3; 2 Corinthians V, 10; and Philippians IV, 8. For in those places not only the Latin translators but also other writers read *πυκνά* (“frequently,” or something similar), *ἴδια* (“one’s own”), and *ἅγια* (“holy”) instead of *πυγμῇ* (“with the fist”), *διά* (“through”), and *ἁγνά* (“pure”), so that it appears that such a textual variation existed in some manuscripts.

For the same reason, 2 Corinthians I, 24 should not be brought into this category. For it was not the Goth alone who read *χάριτος* (“grace”) instead of *χαρᾶς* (“joy”); codices 37 and 71 and the Armenian version do so as well. The Goth agrees very frequently with that earlier codex.

Rather, we cite Mark IX, 18, where he read *ῥίπτει* (“throws down”) instead of *ῥήσσει* (“tears”), and 1 Thessalonians V, 14, where he has *ἀνέχεσθε* (“bear with”) instead of *ἀντέχεσθε* (“hold fast to”). There are, however, some witnesses that agree with the Gothic reading in these passages: in the former, manuscript 12 according to Mill; in the latter, manuscript 74 according to Griesbach. But agreement with those books is either absent elsewhere or so rare that it appears that they coincide here by chance, and that the same thing happened to their copyists as happened to the Goth.

We take the same position concerning Luke I, 10, where both the Goth and the scribes of codex 131 and lectionary 44 falsely read *προσδεχόμενον* (“expecting”) instead of *προσευχόμενον* (“praying”).

That he read falsely is much clearer in Luke VII, 25, where all Greek manuscripts have *τρυφῇ* (“luxury,” “delicacy”), whereas he translated as though he had found *τροφῇ* (“food”) written there—*fodeinai*, as in Matthew VI, 25–26; Luke V, 16; Ephesians V, 29; and *Skeireins* 50, 14.

Likewise, in John XVI, 6, since he wrote *gadaubida* (“he hardened”), he must be regarded as having read *πεπώρωκεν* (“he hardened”) instead of *πεπλήρωκεν* (“he filled”), for which the Gothic is *usfullida*.

Mareshall and Benzelius are also justified in thinking that in Mark X, 22 Ulfilas read *χρήματα* (“money”) instead of *κτήματα* (“possessions”), and in Matthew XXVII, 52 *κειμένων* (“lying there”) instead of *κεκοιμημένων* (“those who had fallen asleep”) through a similar error; see the notes on those passages.

With no less suitable arguments we seem to have shown, in the note on Mark X, 24, that the Goth translated *πεποιθότας* (“those who trust”) as though it were *πεποθηκότας* (“those who have desired”). Likewise, in Mark XV, 29, we have seen that he did not correctly distinguish the prepositions *παρά* (“beside,” “from”) and *πρό* (“before”) in compounds, unless, rather, the copyist introduced the error into the codex.

It does not seem unlikely that in Luke XIX, 2 the translator, carried away by haste, read *ὑπέστρεψεν* (“he returned”) as *ὑποστρέψαι* (“to return”), and in Luke XVIII, 35 *προσαιτῶν* (“begging”) as *προσαιτεῖν* (“to beg”); and then that in 2 Corinthians III, 7 he confused *ἐνδόξῃ* (“glorious”) with *ἐνδόξη* and in Luke VIII, 53 *ἰδόντες* (“having seen”) with *εἰδότες* (“knowing”).

As for Luke III, 14, we now regret having approved Mareshall’s conjecture that Ulfilas perhaps read *ἄρχετε* or *ἄρχεσθε* (“rule,” “begin”) instead of *ἀρκεῖσθε* (“be content”), because no verb compounded with *valdan* (“to rule”) contains that *ἄρχειν*; and *ganohidai sijaiþ* (“be satisfied”) written in the margin appears to be a gloss rather than a variant reading.

But the fact that in Mark XV, 24 and Luke XV, 8 *τίς* (“who?”) is found interchanged with *τις* (“someone”); in 1 Corinthians X, 17 and Philippians I, 16 *οἱ* (“those who”) with *οἵ* (“who”; compare Luke VIII, 14); and in Galatians II, 17 *ἆρα* (“then?”) with *ἄρα* (“therefore”)—this resulted solely from the translator’s negligence. It could happen more easily because accents and breathings were formerly omitted.

In these passages also one must beware of supposing that the Goth has rendered a variant of the Greek text.

It remains to speak also of those passages in which Ulfilas seems to have committed errors contrary to the laws of his own language. [Col. 0486] Chief among these are passages where, forgetting the construction required by the character of the Gothic language, he followed the Greek alone and translated rather carelessly. Thus, at Luke 1:9, *hlauts ïmma urrann du saljan atgaggands* (“the lot for him went out to offer incense, entering”) occurs instead of *atgaggandin* (“when he entered”), because the Greek has ἔλαχε τοῦ θυμιᾶσαι εἰσελθών (“he was chosen by lot to offer incense, having entered”). At 1 Corinthians 7:10ff., he wrote *þaim liugom haftam anabiuda qenai—jah aban* instead of *abin*; the Goth did so on account of the Greek γυναῖκα—καὶ ἄνδρα (“wife—and husband”). At Luke 16:18 he rendered *wazuh saei afletands—jah liugands* instead of *afletiþ jah liugaiþ*. Since he was going to render the Greek participles ἀπολύων καὶ γαμῶν (“divorcing and marrying”) by a relative clause, after placing the relative pronoun he also added the participles in place of the verbs themselves. See also what we noted on Colossians 2:14 and 3:5, and compare Luke 9:13, *maizo fimf hlaibam jah fiskos tvai* (“more than five loaves and two fishes”): since, in place of the Greek ἢ πέντε ἄρτοι (“or five loaves”), he had used the dative ordinarily employed after a comparative, he ought to have continued with *fiskam tvaim* (“two fishes” in the dative); but, forgetting his construction, he follows the Greeks, who correctly have ἰχθύες δύο (“two fishes”), and himself incorrectly continues with the nominative. Likewise, at Matthew 8:15, perhaps he ought more correctly to have written *heitons* (“fevers”) instead of *heito* (“fever”), which he uses in agreement with the Greek, on account of the preceding *heitom* (“fevers”).

There are other passages that may be brought under this heading but that have something with which they can be defended, such as John 6:63, *þo vaurda. þoei ïk rodida ïzvis. ahma ïst jah libains ïst* (“these words, which I spoke to you: spirit is, and life is”). Here the Gothic *ïst* (“is”) seems to refer not to the subject *vaurda* (“words”), but to the predicates *ahma* and *libains* (“spirit” and “life”), to which it is attached. Thus also the Latin manuscripts of Cambridge and Corbie translated the passage. More often, however, he went wrong by attaching to nouns adjectival forms that do not agree with their gender. We have collected these passages under Nehemiah 6:16.

No one has yet denied that the greatest benefit from comparison with our translation arises for the restoration of the integrity of the Greek text. Although we have enumerated not a few passages in which Ulfilas departed from the Greek, whether through error or deliberately, and although there are very many others in which the character of the Gothic language diverted him from a more exact imitation of the Greek, we nevertheless do not hesitate to assign our version the first place, because he not only rendered the Greek with the utmost fidelity, but also because no other language is more closely related to Greek, and none is better suited to reproduce the Greek text as though in a mirror, than Gothic.

There have indeed been those who preferred the Syriac version. [Note: [Col. 0485] See Heupelius, *l. l.* 4, a, who, influenced by the authority of Franzius, who was unaware of the excellence of the Gothic version, seems to have made this claim.] But if we consider the cloud of variant readings introduced by scholars expert in the Syriac language, [Note: [Col. 0486] See Scholzius, *I. prolegg.*, p. CXXIff.] and compare it with the very small number found in the Gothic version, it will appear that the Syriac is superior to it in nothing except age.

Anyone who wishes to judge correctly the worth of a given version must possess such knowledge of the language in which it was written that he can properly distinguish which readings in it are variants and which are properties of the language. Those who undertook a comparison of the Greek text with the Ulfilan version without this knowledge could not help but carry out the task with less than satisfactory success. Zahnius admits that at the beginning his lack of expertise prevented him from noting all the readings that differed from the Greek; but after he had begun to become more proficient, death took him away before he could complete the work.

As for the variants that Griesbach, omitting several already supplied by Mill, [Note: [Col. 0487A] Zahnius considers this more deserving of praise than of blame, *Einleit.*, p. 33. [ [Col. 0488A] The passages marked by Griesbachius.]] had noted from the imperfect editions of Junius and Knittel, Schulzius, who prepared the Griesbachian edition anew, increased their number by using Zahnius’s poor version. Yet it is impossible to understand the principle on which he acted, since, while adding a few new readings, he omitted hundreds.

Lest we seem to be making an unfair accusation, let us indicate from several chapters of John’s Gospel which variant readings he silently passed over. We shall, however, omit passages in which the Gothic reading agrees with no other book, whether the Goth altered, shortened, or added something arbitrarily or because of the natural difference between the languages. For example:

- John 10:21: *mag unhulþo* (“a demon is able”) for the Greek δαιμόνων δύναται (“demons are able”), although Scholzius notes that this is also read in manuscript 235;
- 10:25, where αὐτοῖς (“to them”) is omitted;
- 11:4, where, in place of Ἰησοῦς (“Jesus”), he has *ïs* (which may be a scribal error, a copyist writing *ïs* instead of *is*);
- 11:6, where οὖν (“therefore”) is omitted;
- 11:25, where αὐτῇ (“to her”) is omitted;
- 11:34, *lagidedun* (“they placed”) instead of τεθείκατε (“have you placed”);
- 12:6, where he places *ïna* (“it”) in one position and the Greek in another;
- 12:9, where he adds *ïesus* (“Jesus”);
- 12:28, where he places *namo þeinata* (“your name”) for σοῦ τὸ ὄνομα (“your name”);
- 12:43, where he places *mais* (“more”) in one passage.

There are very many other passages where he either made a false observation—for example, at 10:16, where he says that the Goth read αὐλή (“courtyard”) instead of ποίμνη (“flock”); see our note on this passage—or where his authority ought to have been removed. Thus, at 10:18, he ought to have recognized that the Gothic authority had to be rejected, for, as we proved at that passage, it was not ἀλλ’—ἐμαυτοῦ (“but—from myself”) that the Goth omitted, but ἐμοῦ—αὐτήν (“of me—it”), which had dropped out through scribal negligence. At 10:36 he absurdly adds that the Goth omitted the article τοῦ (“the”)—as though Ulfilas had ever placed it before the word θεός (“God”)! At 11:4 he says that αὕτη (“this”) is absent from the Goth, although it has plainly been translated by the word *þo*; through this error the learned man went astray in innumerable passages. At 11:9 and 12:20 he says that the Goth omitted ἐκ (“from”), although the Goth generally omits that preposition after partitive words such as πολλοί (“many”), τινές (“some”), and the like. At 11:33 he says that the Goth agrees with manuscript D and other Latin manuscripts; rather, it agrees with certain Latin manuscripts cited by Sabatier, which read: “the Jews who had come [or were] with her, weeping.”

Nor did he append the Gothic authority to other readings that he records. Thus, at 10:39 he does not note that the Goth, together with other manuscripts, omits οὖν (“therefore”), although immediately afterward he says that in the Goth πάλιν (“again”) is placed after αὐτόν (“him”). Likewise, at 10:41 and 42 he does not note that the Goth reads ἐποίησε σημεῖον (“performed a sign”) and εἰς αὐτὸν ἐκεῖ (“there toward him”) together with the other witnesses. At 11:21, ὁ ἀδελφός μου (“my brother”) is placed after ἀπέθανε (ἐτεθνήκει) (“died [had died]”); at 11:29 δέ (“but”) is added; at 12:6 τοῦτο δὲ εἶπε (“but he said this”) is read; and likewise at 12:26 ἐμοί τις διακονῇ (“if anyone serves me”). The failure to indicate the Gothic agreement with other Greek books is all the more striking because elsewhere the Gothic version is included among the authorities, as at 10:10; 10:16—although it may also be questioned whether this was rightly done, for even if the Goth had read γενήσεται (“will become”), he could not have written otherwise—10:29, 30, 39; 11:17, 30, 32, 46. At the last passage we fear that he may have falsely noted that the Goth read ὅ (“which,” singular neuter) instead of ἅ (“which,” plural neuter), for the Goth often uses the singular neuter in place of the plural. At 12:17 and 37 it was superfluous to cite the Goth: since he says both *galaubjan ïmma* and *du ïmma* indiscriminately, it cannot be determined with certainty whether εἰς αὐτόν (“toward him”) or αὐτῷ (“to him”) was read. But these examples are sufficient.

Scholzius, the most recent editor of the New Testament, added nothing to Schulzius’s additions. For the most part, without troubling himself to determine whether they were false or sound, he was led by Schulzius’s authority and incorporated them into his own commentary; he also omitted some, no one knows with what purpose or for what reason.

Since it seemed to be the duty of a careful critic to note all discrepancies between the Greek text and the Gothic version, we did so, as Michaelis advised, [Note: [Col. 0488A] *Einleitung in die göttlichen Schriften*, p. 279.] except for those arising not from a different reading but from the distinct character of the two languages. Thus, for example, the genitive plural occurs after *alls*, *was*, *sums*, and *ainshun* in place of the same case of those words themselves:

- Matthew 7:17, *all bagme* (“every one of the trees”)—πᾶν δένδρον (“every tree”);
- 5:46, *wo mizdono* (“what reward”)—τίνα μισθόν (“what reward”);
- John 12:20, *sumai þiudo* (“some of the gentiles”)—τινὲς Ἕλληνες (“some Greeks”);
- Mark 6:5, *ni ainohun mahte* (“not one of the powers”)—οὐδεμίαν δύναμιν (“no power”).

Likewise, the circumlocution of the infinitive with a preposition and article:

- Matthew 27:12, *miþþanei vrohiþs vas* (“while he was being accused”)—ἐν τῷ κατηγορεῖσθαι αὐτόν (“while he was being accused”);
- 27:57, *þan seiþu varþ* (“when it became late”)—ὀψίας γενομένης (“when evening had come”).

Likewise, the passive infinitive:

- Mark 10:45, *at andbahtjam* (“for service”)—διακονηθῆναι (“to be served”);

see also the notes on 8:31 and 15:9. The use of the past tense in narrative where the Greek has the present—see the notes on Matthew 8:20 and Luke 3:11—and many other such features, which it would take too long to enumerate, are not variant readings. With the help of a deeper knowledge of the Gothic language, they are not particularly difficult to identify.

There are indeed passages where one may be uncertain which reading the Goth followed because the same Gothic form corresponds to two Greek forms. Thus, at Galatians 6:2, *usfulleiþ* could represent both ἀναπληρώσατε (“fulfill”) and ἀναπληρώσετε (“you will fulfill”); at 1 Corinthians 15:49, *bairaima* could render both φορέσομεν (“we shall bear”) and φορέσωμεν (“let us bear”); compare the note on Luke 5:30. Or different Greek particles may not have been sufficiently carefully distinguished by the Goth, such as δέ and γάρ (“but” and “for”), δέ and καί (“but” and “and”), or καί and οὖν (“and” and “therefore”). In such cases it will be preferable to say that the Goth followed those manuscripts with which he generally agrees.

But those readings that are genuinely variants must be noted all the more carefully, because the Gothic version, which agrees with none of the surviving ancient books so consistently that it can be said to have been derived from that one source alone, must itself be treated as a manuscript. For although in many passages of the Gospels it agrees with manuscript D, and in the Epistles with manuscripts DEFG, [Note: [Col. 0488A] The manuscripts designated by Griesbachius.] it cannot be maintained that the Goth followed D in the Gospels or those manuscripts in the Epistles, because there are quite a few passages in which he departs from their authority. This is also why the Gothic version, since it must be counted among the mixed witnesses, ought not to have been assigned by scholars solely to the Byzantine or Constantinopolitan recension.

Thus:

- Matthew 5:46: manuscript D has τελῶναι (“tax collectors”), while the Goth has *thiudo* (ἐθνικοί, “gentiles”);
- 6:1: D has δικαιοσύνην (“righteousness”), while the Goth has *armaion* (ἐλεημοσύνην, “almsgiving”);
- 6:4: D has αὐτός (“he himself”), which the Goth omits;
- 6:13: D omits the doxology, which the Goth includes;

and there are very many other examples.

The same occurs in the Epistles:

- Romans 8:34: DEFG have καί (“and”) after ὅς (“who”), while the Goth, with other witnesses, omits it;
- 9:18: they read οὖν μοι (“therefore to me”), while the Goth, with others, has *mis nu* (μοι οὖν, “to me therefore”);
- 9:23: they have καί (“and”), which the Goth omits;
- 9:26: αὐτοί (“they themselves”), omitted by them, is added by the Goth;
- 9:32: they have ὡς (“as”), which the Goth, with others, omits;
- 15:11: they read ἐπαινέσατε (“praise”), while the Goth, with others, has ἐπαινέτωσαν (“let them praise”);

and similarly in many other places.

Having made these preliminary remarks, in which we ask for the fairness and indulgence of our judges regarding matters either argued less correctly or touched upon only cursorily and briefly, we shall finally speak of the manuscripts containing the Gothic version and of the editions prepared by learned men before our own.

The Codex Argenteus holds the foremost place both in age and in importance. [Note: [Col. 0489C] For a fuller discussion of this manuscript, see Ihre, in his dissertation on the Codex Argenteus of 1769 (*Ulfil. illustrat.*, p. 184ff.), and in the preface to the same work, p. 3ff.; then Zahnius, *Einleitung*, p. 37ff.] It was discovered in the sixteenth century in the monastery at Werden and, toward the end of that same century, [Note: [Col. 0489C] Learned men who suppose that the manuscript was taken to Prague during the Thirty Years’ War have been unable to produce adequate evidence for their claim. That it had already been removed from its original location in the sixteenth century is shown by the book of Richard Streinius, counselor to Emperor Rudolf II and superintendent of the palace of Archduke Matthias, entitled *Apologia oder Schutzred uber des durchleuchtigsten Hauses Osterreich von weiland Kaiser Friderich I demselben anno 1156 erthailten ansechlichen Privilegio*. In that work, after saying that Otfrid had used *wamba*, an obscene word, for “belly,” the author adds: “that this word is also found in the Gothic Gospel book, of which His Imperial Majesty possesses the original,” that is, that this word also occurs in the Gothic Gospel, whose genuine exemplar is preserved, and so forth. Since Streinius died in 1601, it is beyond doubt that the Codex Argenteus—undoubtedly the same manuscript that he had before his eyes—had already reached Prague in the sixteenth century. The learned Schmeller most courteously communicated this observation to us.] was first brought to Prague. Later, in 1648, Count Königsmarck sent it to Stockholm among his spoils; in 1655 it went from there to the Netherlands with Isaac Vossius, although we do not know whether this occurred at the will of Queen Christina or of Vossius himself. It is universally agreed that Count de la Gardie subsequently redeemed it at great cost, [Note: [Col. 0489D] Zahnius, *Einleit.*, p. 44f., records the differing opinions of scholars regarding the price paid by de la Gardie. Two of these accounts are correct: according to one, he bought it for six hundred thalers—meaning Swedish imperial thalers—and according to the other, for four hundred—meaning Swedish imperial copper thalers. Each sum, in fact, amounts to two hundred of our thalers.] adorned it with a silver binding, and donated it to the library of the University of Uppsala.

This manuscript was written in silver and gold letters on purple parchment, in quarto format, toward the end of the fifth or the beginning of the sixth century, when the Goths were living in Italy. [Note: [Col. 0490C] Ihre was the first to venture to assert that the letters were stamped or burned into the parchment, and Schönmeierus and Adelungius followed him. But Zahnius has already shown very well that the arguments Ihre offers as proofs are rather feeble. Since we are tired of recalling such nonsense, we ask only how, if the principles of the art of printing—since it is clear that these learned men had that art in mind—were already known at that time, the art could again have been consigned to such a long oblivion; and, further, why the scribe drew double lines, when, had he struck off types, not even one line would have been necessary.]

It is demonstrated by its quaternional division that the manuscript originally consisted of 320 leaves. When it was discovered, 188 remained; in recent times an impious hand removed at least eleven of them. [Note: [Col. 0490D] When this theft, first discovered by us and, by I know not what authority, publicized in newspapers throughout almost every country, became known, an Englishman who had collated the manuscript was accused. But neither are we the accusers, nor is the name of the Englishman known to us—someone who read the manuscript with the intention of making some use of it. It is remarkable, however, that Italians have openly declared that another manuscript containing the Gothic Gospels was taken from Naples to England; see Castill., *Specim.*, Preface, p. V.]

Thus, in our books we have the following portions derived from the Codex Argenteus:

- Matthew 5:15–6:23; 7:12–10:1; 10:23–11:23, including the leaf mutilated on one side at verses 13–23; 26:70–27:19; 27:42–65;
- Mark 1:1–6:30; 6:53–12:38; 13:16–29; 14:4–16; 14:41–15:12;
- Luke 1:1–10:30; 14:9–16:24; 17:3–20:46;
- John 5:45–11:47; 12:1–49; 13:11–19:13.

The following passages are now also missing from the manuscript: Mark 1:13–37; 2:15–3:7; 5:42–7:33; and, unless we are altogether mistaken, Matthew 27:54 to the end.

The Gospels in the Codex Argenteus did not follow the order preserved by our editions, but this order: Matthew, John, Luke, Mark. Although this cannot be learned from the distorted order in which the individual leaves are now scattered, it can be learned both from the order in which they appear in the arches painted beneath the text (see Plate I) and from the numeral letters written on the individual quires. The following survive:

- *g* (3) on folio 14, beginning at Matthew 9:27;
- *ie*–*k* (15–20) on folio 33, John 7:16–2; folio 101, John 8:57; folio 87 [Note: [Col. 0490D] At Ihre, *Ulfil. illustr.*, p. 87, “187” is incorrectly printed.] , John 11:22; folio 79, John 13:11; folio 73, John 16:14; folio 117, John 19:4;
- *kb* (22), *kd*–*kz* (24–27), *l* and *la* (30 and 31), the quires containing the text of Luke;
- *le* (35), *lq* (36), *lh* (38), *lþ* (39), and *m* (40), in which quires the Gospel of Mark is written.

Above the text of each leaf, on the left, appears *þairh* (that is, κατά, “according to”), followed by *aivaggeljo* (“Gospel”); on the right appears the name of the Evangelist: *matþaiu*, *ïohannen*, *lukan*, or *marku*. These inscriptions are in a later hand and are poorly written. Beneath them comes the text, written on each leaf in twenty lines. At the bottom of the leaf are the arches mentioned above, in which parallel passages from the other Gospels are indicated in letters written in gold. In the margins are numeral letters indicating the canons or sections (see Plate I), as well as variant readings and glosses, written in very different styles. Some are extremely elegant, such as those at Luke 6:49, 7:32, and 9:13; others are poorly formed, such as that at Luke 6:27; others imitate the shape and color of the letters in the inscriptions; some have retained their silver brilliance, such as those at Mark 1:6 and 11; while the color of others has become so black that it is scarcely possible to tell whether they were ever silver. Other additions, written in ink and in Latin, in a later period, are also found. Their writer wished to indicate the numbers of the chapters, the subject of individual verses or chapters, passages omitted by the Goth (see the note on John 7:52), the meaning of words—these explanations are written above the Gothic words themselves—and, at the bottom of the pages, what is missing from the following passages and after how many leaves the continuation is to be found. An incompetent hand also altered the text in several places with silver ink, but in miserable lettering, introducing different forms of words; see the notes on Matthew 9:24 and Mark 4:7.

We shall discuss more fully matters concerning the manner of writing, abbreviations, errors, and other things of this kind in the Gothic palaeography to be added to our grammar. For the rest, the greater part of the leaves has been preserved so that the writing can easily be read. There are, however, verses and even individual leaves whose letters have been erased so thoroughly, for whatever reason, that they look as though wiped away with a sponge, and nothing of the letters can be discerned except under suitable illumination, or even when that illumination is slightly withdrawn. In other places the pigments of the letters have eaten into the parchment so deeply that individual letters and words have disappeared, and what was written can be inferred only from the holes left behind. Elsewhere the letters on the reverse page have penetrated so strongly and become so entangled with the strokes of the writing on the facing page that they must be carefully distinguished if one wishes to avoid error.

Many of the leaves have changed their purple color and taken on a pink, violet, or brown hue; the silver letters have for the most part turned livid or rust-colored. Nevertheless, there is no reason to fear that this manuscript will perish altogether, since the people of Uppsala preserve it with such care that we may reasonably hope it will also reach posterity.

The Codex Carolinus [Note: [Col. 0491D] See Knittelius, p. 316ff.] is a palimpsest containing, on four leaves, portions of the version of the Epistle to the Romans, overwritten by the *Etymologies* of Isidore of Seville. It was discovered by Knittel in 1756 in the Wolfenbüttel library. The parchment is of larger format, and the letters closely resemble those of the Codex Argenteus (see Plates II and V). In Knittel’s opinion, it was written in Italy at approximately the same time as the Codex Argenteus. It was formerly taken to the monastery of Weissenburg, [Note: [Col. 0491D] That this manuscript belonged to the monastery of Bobbio in Liguria, from which the palimpsests of the Ambrosian Library also came, was shown in letters sent to Angelo Mai by the celebrated Niebuhr. Another manuscript in the Vatican Library, containing fragments of Gothic homilies (*Skeireins*), also belonged to Bobbio; see Castillionaeus, *Addenda ad epistolam Corinth. alteram*, p. 83. It therefore appears that Adelungius was mistaken in suspecting that the Codex Carolinus was written in Spain, the seat of the Visigoths.] then sent, together with a number of other books, to Mainz for sale. There it was purchased by Heinrich Julius von Blum and taken to Prague; finally, during the reign of Anton Ulrich, it reached Wolfenbüttel in 1690, where it is preserved today.

It contains:

- folio 277: Romans 11:33–12:5;
- folio 256: 12:17–13:5;
- folio 255: 14:9–20;
- folio 280: 15:3–13.

The pages are divided into two parts. On the left is the Gothic text, written in twenty-seven very uneven lines; on the right is a Latin version, which agrees neither with the Vulgate nor with the Gothic text.

There are five Ambrosian manuscripts. They are parchment palimpsests brought to Milan from the monastery of Bobbio, situated in Liguria. Castillionaeus proved that all of them were written during the period when the Goths ruled Italy. [Note: [Col. 0492D] See Castill., *Specim.*, Preface, p. IVff., XVff.]

Among them, Codex A (S 36, upper text; see Plates II and III), in quarto format, now contains homilies of Gregory the Great on Ezekiel. Beneath them lie fragments of the Epistle to the Romans:

- 6:23–8:10; 8:34–11:1; 11:11–33; 12:8–14:5; 16:21 to the end;
- First Corinthians 1:12–25; 4:2–12; 5:3–6:1; 7:5–28; 8:9–9:9; 9:19–10:4; 10:15–11:6; 11:21–31; 12:10–22; 13:1–12; 14:20–27; 15:1–35; 15:46–16:11; 16:23 to the end;
- Second Corinthians 1:8–4:10; 5:1–9:7; 12:1 to the end;
- Galatians 1:22–2:8; 2:17–3:6; 3:28–4:23; 5:17 to the end;
- Ephesians 1:1–2:20; 3:9–5:3; 5:17–29; 6:9–19;
- Philippians 2:26–4:7;
- Colossians 1:10–29; 2:10–3:8; 4:4–13;
- First Thessalonians 5:22 to the end;
- Second Thessalonians 1:1–2:4; 3:7 to the end;
- First Timothy 1:1–9, 18–4:8; 5:4–6:13;
- Second Timothy 1:1–18; 2:21–4:16;
- Titus 1:9–2:1;
- Philemon 1:23.

The inscriptions placed in the upper part of the pages—*du kaurinþium*, *du aifaisium*, and others—have for the most part perished through mutilation of the parchment. In the margins are variant readings and glosses (see note 6, cols. 477–478), written in smaller, slanting letters than those of the text.

Castillionaeus judges that the writing in the manuscript is not by one and the same scribe: one part was written by a more skilled hand, the other by a rougher one. Although the letters are generally not difficult to read, several leaves are so scraped or washed away that he scarcely hopes anyone will ever be able to decipher the Gothic writing. The order of the leaves has also been completely disturbed by the person who overwrote the manuscript.

Codex B (S 45, upper text; see Plates II and IV), in the same format as A, contains Jerome’s commentary on Isaiah, written over the Gothic version of:

- First Corinthians 15:48 to the end;
- the whole of Second Corinthians;
- Galatians 1:1–2:17; 4:19 to the end;
- Ephesians 1:1–4:6; 4:17–5:11; 6:8 to the end;
- Philippians 1:14–2:8; 2:22–4:17;
- Colossians 1:6–29; 2:11 to the end;
- First Thessalonians 2:10 to the end;
- Second Thessalonians 1:1–5; 2:16 to the end;
- First Timothy 1:1–3:5; 4:1–5:10; 5:21–6:16;
- Second Timothy 1:5–4:11;
- Titus 1:1, 10.

The form of the letters is not inelegant, but it seems to display a certain haste. Because of the more recent writing superimposed upon it, the Ulfilan text can often be made out only with difficulty. The order of the leaves is disturbed in the same way as in Codex A.

In third place is the manuscript that we have called Ambrosian. It consists of only four small-format pages of a manuscript containing a Latin version of the Gospels (I 61, upper text; see Plate II, II). Beneath this is written a fragment of the Gothic interpretation of the Gospel of Matthew, belonging to the portion that is now largely missing from the Codex Argenteus. From it we gain Matthew 25:38–26:3 and 26:65–70; thereafter, once the Codex Argenteus has begun at this verse, it continues with that manuscript through 27:1. The script is large and more closely approaches that of the Codex Argenteus than do the other Ambrosian manuscripts (see Plate II, II).

There remain three leaves of a manuscript (G 82, upper text), in which a Latin commentary on the Books of Kings is written. For his own use, the scribe reused manuscripts of the plays of Plautus, the tragedies of Seneca, and the Ulfilan interpretation of Nehemiah and Ezra. Four pages preserve Nehemiah 5:13–18; 6:14–7:3; two preserve Ezra 2:8–12. A specimen of the letters is reproduced in Plate II, I.

Finally, in fifth place, we place the manuscript containing the *Skeireins*. One part is preserved at Rome in the Vatican Library, with Frontinus written over it (manuscript no. 5750, quarto parchment); the other is in Milan (Ambrosian Codex E 147, quarto parchment), on which the Council of Chalcedon has been written over the Gothic text. See Massmann’s learned and extensive discussion of it, *Skeir.*, p. 55ff.

We have mentioned it here for the following reason: from it we derived John 1:29; 3:3–5, 23–26, 29–32; 5:21–23, 35–38, and also several other passages that are found in the Codex Argenteus as well. We have indicated their variants in the notes.

We have already mentioned above that Antonius Morillon was the first to restore the memory of the Ulfilan version. After him, a certain Derrer copied the entire Codex Argenteus. This copy was purchased by Count de la Gardie together with the Codex Argenteus and transported to Uppsala, but in 1702 it was burned along with the house and books of Olaus Rudbeck.

Francis Junius prepared the first edition of Ulfilas, drawn from the Codex Argenteus and Derrer’s copy.

> **[Note: [Col. 0493C]]** Four very ancient versions of the four Gospels of Our Lord Jesus Christ, namely Gothic and Anglo-Saxon; the former is now published for the first time from the celebrated Codex Argenteus by Francis Junius. A Gothic glossary is also included. Dordrecht, 1665 (Amsterdam, 1684), 2 vols., quarto.

That edition, however, is so full of errors that it now has scarcely any usefulness. Moreover, Junius added much for which no trace appears in the manuscript, while omitting passages that even today can be read without difficulty.

The observations of Thomas Marshall, an Englishman, added to the first volume from page 385 onward, deserve much praise.

The edition of Georg Stiernhielm, Swedish military councillor and president of the Stockholm College of Antiquities, turned out no better. It repeated Junius’s edition, correcting it in very few places and making it considerably more corrupt in many others.

> **[Note: [Col. 0493C]]** The Holy Gospels of Our Lord Jesus Christ, translated into Gothic from the Greek by Ulfilas, bishop of the Goths in Moesia, around the year 360 after the birth of Christ, now published together with parallel Swedish-Gothic, Norse—or Icelandic—and Latin Vulgate versions. Stockholm, 1671, quarto. See Ebert, *Allgemeines bibliographisches Lexikon*, II, p. 991.

With much greater care, Eric Benzelius, archbishop of Uppsala, and, after his death, Edward Lye, an Englishman, published Ulfilas.

> **[Note: [Col. 0493D]]** The Gothic version of the Sacred Gospels, corrected and supplemented from the Codex Argenteus, with a Latin translation and notes, edited by E. Benzelius; E. Lye added his own observations and prefixed a Gothic grammar. Oxford, 1750, quarto.

Benzelius not only corrected many readings of Junius and Stiernhielm, but was also the first to judge most accurately the differences and agreements of our version with the Greek text. Only one thing was lacking: he was unable to provide all the passages that had faded or were difficult to read.

John Ihre, councillor of the Royal Chancellery and professor at the University of Uppsala, undertook that task. He arranged for the entire work to be copied from Stiernhielm’s edition and inserted into that copy corrections drawn from the Codex Argenteus itself.

> **[Note: [Col. 0493D]]** This copy eventually came into the possession of Heinatius, a professor at Frankfurt, and was consequently called the “Heinatius manuscript.” Zahn later used it in consultation.

In this undertaking he displayed such diligence, judgment, and expertise that only someone who has seen the Codex Argenteus with his own eyes can adequately appreciate it.

What Ihre had extracted from the manuscript and gathered from other sources in preparation for a new edition of Ulfilas, but was prevented by death from completing himself, was published by A. F. Büsching, director of the Berlin Gymnasium.

> **[Note: [Col. 0493D]]** The writings of John Ihre illustrating the Ulfilan version and the Moeso-Gothic language, corrected by the learned author himself and enlarged with new additions, now collected and published together with other writings on the same subject by A. F. Büsching. Berlin, 1773, quarto. The appendix to this book also contains John Gordon’s, an Edinburgh jurist’s, *Specimen of Critical Observations on the Ancient Gothic Version of the Gospels*, full of excellent observations. It is regrettable that we have no more from this man, who was so skilled in the Gothic language and possessed such exceptionally refined judgment.

Many years later, what had not fallen to Ihre’s lot—namely, to publish Ulfilas in its entirety—fell to J. Chr. Zahn, a Saxon clergyman.

> **[Note: [Col. 0494D]]** *Ulfilas’s Gothic Bible Translation according to Ihre’s Text, Worked Out with a Grammatical and Literal Latin Translation, Together with a Grammar and Glossary, Compiled by F. K. Fulda, the Glossary Revised by W. F. H. Reinwald, etc., Published by J. Chr. Zahn.* Weissenfels, 1805, quarto.

Zahn not only enlarged the text with fragments of the Epistle to the Romans discovered by Knittel,

> **[Note: [Col. 0494D]]** *The Gothic Version of Ulfilas of Several Chapters of Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, Extracted from the Erasure of a Rewritten Manuscript Preserved in the Ducal Library at Wolfenbüttel, etc., Brought to Light, Commented upon, and Published by F. A. Knittel.* 1762, quarto. If Ebert says, in the place cited above, p. 992, that this edition contains a text read and recovered with the greatest accuracy, then he either praised it undeservedly or judged too confidently concerning a matter of which he had insufficient knowledge. Knittel correctly read those passages in the manuscript that are easy to read; in the somewhat more difficult passages he often went wrong. The peculiarities of the Gothic language, moreover, were entirely unknown to him.

Zahn also used, with great care and the utmost fidelity, Ihre’s corrections, supplements, and notes. Insofar as he could, he produced a text that was as corrected and complete as possible, except in those passages where Ihre himself had neglected to examine the Codex Argenteus more carefully.

Since this had happened in numerous places, Zahn was either led into error or was unable to correct mistakes that Ihre had failed to notice. It was also to be wished that Zahn had possessed a greater command of the Gothic language and a more subtle judgment. For, apart from what he owed to Marshall, Gordon, and Ihre, the notes he appended to the text are meager and inept, and for the most part also false.

After Zahn, no one published the Ulfilan fragments in their entirety. The surviving portions of Matthew’s Gospel, however, were published twice, by S. Henshall, an English schoolmaster, and J. A. Schmeller, lecturer in German at the University of Munich.

> **[Note: [Col. 0495C]]** One of these men published a booklet entitled *The Gothic Gospel of St. Matthew from the Codex Argenteus of the Fourth Century, with the Corresponding English or Saxon from the Durham Book of the Eighth Century, etc.*, by S. Henshall. London, 1807, octavo. He contributed nothing to the correction of the text; indeed, he badly disfigured it through false separations or combinations of words. The notes appended to the text are so perverse and inept that they do not deserve mention. Schmeller published Matthew’s fragments much better in the following booklet: *The Version of the Gospel according to Matthew in Ninth-Century Frankish, and also the Gothic Version of the Fourth Century, insofar as it survives.* Stuttgart, 1827, octavo. For this highly learned man published the text, taken from Zahn’s edition, as accurately corrected as possible, and was also the first to enlarge the fragments with those discovered in the Ambrosian Codex.

Since a new edition of Ulfilas appeared necessary both because of the defects of the earlier editions and because they did not contain the fragments recently discovered by Mai and published by Castillioneus,

> **[Note: [Col. 0495D]]** *Specimen of the Unpublished Portions of Ulfilas, Discovered by Angelo Mai in the Ambrosian Palimpsests, Published through the Joint Efforts of Mai and C. O. Castillioneus.* Milan, 1819, quarto.  
> *The Gothic Version of the Second Epistle of the Apostle Paul to the Corinthians, etc.*, published by C. O. Castillioneus. Milan, 1829.  
> *The Surviving Portions of the Gothic Version of the Epistles of the Apostle Paul to the Romans, First Corinthians, and Ephesians, etc.*, published by C. O. Castillioneus. Milan, 1834.  
> *The Surviving Portions of the Gothic Version of the Epistles of the Apostle Paul to the Galatians, Philippians, Colossians, and First Thessalonians, etc.*, published by C. O. Castillioneus. Milan, 1835.  
> *The Surviving Portions of the Gothic Version of the Epistles of the Apostle Paul to the Second Thessalonians, Timothy, Titus, and Philemon, etc.*, published by C. O. Castillioneus. Milan, 1839.

> **[Note: [Col. 0496D]]** Among other things, the extent to which the defects of those editions led the most learned men of our age into error may best be seen from Graff’s dissertation on the weak declension of the German language, filled with much learning and published in the second volume of the *New Journal of the Berlin Society of Scholars*, etc., from p. 1 onward. For he established many rules derived from false readings; once he has learned the true readings, although he will not regret having done so, he will himself understand that the passages he now cited as proofs do not prove what he intended.

—and since those whom we had heard would prepare such an edition either delayed too long or abandoned the undertaking, we ourselves turned to this work. We resolved not only to collect all the fragments of the Ulfilan version but also to publish them more accurately than had yet been done.

For, as we read and reread the material carefully, we found many things both in the one part of the text corrected by Zahn from Ihre’s notes and in the remainder drawn by Knittel and Castillioneus from the manuscripts that could not withstand critical examination when weighed in the balance. It seemed that no remedy could be found for them except through repeated inspection and reexamination of the manuscripts.

Accordingly, we traveled to Uppsala and Wolfenbüttel and, thanks to the exceptional courtesy and generosity of the custodians of the libraries—whose conduct deserves the highest praise—obtained permission to read and examine the Codex Argenteus and the Codex Carolinus at leisure, from beginning to end, and to determine whether the defects we noticed were attributable to the negligence of the scribes or to the carelessness of the editors.

In collating both manuscripts, our expectation was, if not exceeded, certainly not disappointed. How many readings formerly doubtful we have now freed from suspicion, and how many corrupt readings we have corrected, anyone who reads our notes will see for himself.

The Ambrosian manuscripts required examination still more urgently than those, although Massmann had partly inspected them again. Since we ourselves were unable to do this, we approached Castillioneus with a request that he compare with the manuscript writing our conjectures, which we had substituted for doubtful and plainly false readings. He undertook this task not only with the greatest readiness and exceptionally generous goodwill, but also carried it out with such diligence and accuracy that the text of the Epistles, insofar as it survives, which we have published in a much more corrected form than his own edition, must rightly be attributed in great part to Castillioneus’s efforts as well.

[Col. 0496B] In preparing our edition, we proceeded as follows. We reproduced the true readings of the manuscripts—those of the Codex Argenteus in the Gospels and those of Codex B in the Epistles—with the utmost fidelity, rather than the readings presented by the editions. We excepted only those readings that were plainly false; these we corrected according to the rules of the language.
