Doubtful readings, and those whose correction was not immediately evident, we left untouched.

In the spelling of words, since we wished to preserve the integrity of the Gothic letters, we followed this rule: we did not write *th*, *ch*, *wh*, or *qu*, but used simply þ—the form of the Icelandic letter, already introduced by other scholars—x, w, and q, and, for w, the simple form v. Finally, we separated the words with punctuation marks, more frequently indeed than they appear in the manuscripts, but with such marks as seemed useful for clarifying the sense.

To the text thus established we added a Latin translation—not one like Zahn’s, which, by considering only the Gothic words, violated the usage of the Latin language—but one that observed the rules of Latin and rendered each Gothic word with a Latin word. In this undertaking, insofar as possible, we followed the Vulgate.

Finally, we added a critical apparatus. First, we listed the errors of the earlier editions, which seemed not to be omitted now because they belonged to the history of the Gothic text and made it possible to determine with what care or negligence the manuscripts had been used by the critics.

Next, we indicated readings that were rightly suspect, defended those that had been rashly called into question, and subjected to judgment the reasons for corrections or explanations proposed by others. Nor did we omit to point out cases in which the Goth had handled the interpretation less correctly, had violated the usage of his own language, or had read the Greek incorrectly.

We then noted the frequent disagreements between our text and the standard Greek text. By the standard Greek text we mean the text provided by Griesbach’s edition; in addition to the variants printed there, we also consulted Mill and Matthaei.

Finally, we added variants found either in the other manuscript or written in the margins, so that everything occurring in the texts of other editions would be represented: notes, observations, and attempts by others at explanation that seemed useful; all additions found in the Gothic books; glosses; variant readings; and differences between the Gothic and Greek texts.

To enable us to be more concise, we used the abbreviations that we deliberately placed at the beginning of these prolegomena.

[Col. 0497]

## [VERSION OF THE BIBLE]

## GOSPELS

### AIVAGGELJO þAIRH MATþAIU  
### The Gospel according to Matthew
[Note: Col. 0497] “But I baptize you in water; yet he who comes after me is mightier than I, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy, bending down, to loosen; but he baptizes you in the Holy Spirit.”

[Note: Col. 0497] We have added this verse, and V.8, which are not found in Codex Argenteus, from the book edited by Massmann under the title *Skeireins aivaggeljons þairh ïohannen* (“Explanation of the Gospel through John”). This first verse is cited in *Sk.* p. 14 (42). — *ïn daupja* corresponds to Greek *παρὰ* in all witnesses; the Gothic then omits *εἰς μετάνοιαν*, which the Greek likewise omits in the parallel passages (Mark 1:8; Luke 3:16; John 1:26). The same words are lacking at Matthew 9:13 and Mark 2:17, both in Gothic and in certain Greek witnesses. — *ïk*: the second “I” is absent from all Greek witnesses. — *anahneivands*, “bending down,” absent from all Greek witnesses, appears to have been added from Mark 1:7 (cf. note on XXVII.42). — *andbindau—ïs*: “loosen the strap of his sandal”; all Greek witnesses have *τὰ ὑποδήματα βαστάσαι*, “carry his sandals.” — *þan*, “but,” is absent from all Greek witnesses. — *veihamma*: Ulfilas, together with the editions, omits *καὶ πυρί*, “and with fire.”

“But I baptize you in water; but he who came after me is mightier than I, so that I am not worthy, bending down, to loosen the strap of his sandal. He baptizes you in the Holy Spirit.”

[Note: Col. 0497] “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”

Castiglione, p. 24; it is now repeated in *Sk.* p. 26 (48). — *audagai*: the words *auk þan qaþ* (“for then he said”) follow; they were inserted by the author of this work so that the words of Holy Scripture might cohere with their context.

“…but upon a lampstand; and it gives light to all those in the house.”

[Note: Col. 0497] This is the beginning of the material preserved in Codex Argenteus. — *lukarnastaþan*: J. St. has *lukarnastaþin*; [Col. 0498] H. adds *div.* — *liuteiþ*: whether this, or *liugeiþ*, as the editions print, was written in Codex Argenteus cannot now be distinguished. We have preferred *liuteiþ* with G. (*Ulfilas illustratus*, appendix, p. 50), who seems rightly to judge it an error of the copyist for *liuhteiþ* (1 Cor. 4:5); see v. 16, *liuhtjai*, and add 2 Cor. 4:4, *liuhtjai*, and v. 6, *liuhtida*. Individual letters were frequently omitted through copyists’ negligence: Mark 15:38 *als* for *alhs*; Luke 6:12 *þairvakands* for *þairhvakands*; Luke 6:17 and 8:4 *hiuma* for *hiuhma*; John 6:12 *drausnos* for *drauhsnos*. — *þamma*: H. adds *þamna*.

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. …but upon a lampstand, and it gives light to all in the house. So let your light shine before people, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

[Note: Col. 0497] “So may your light shine in the presence of people, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

[Note: Col. 0498] *liuhtjai*: H. adds *liughtjai*.

“Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish but to fulfil.”

[Note: Col. 0498] *ïk*, “I,” is absent from all Greek witnesses; B. adds *ni*, “not.” — *ei ïk qemjau*: J. St. adds *ei qam*.

“Do not suppose that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I came not to abolish, but to fulfil. For truly I tell you: until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the Law, until all comes to pass.”

[Note: Col. 0497] “For truly I tell you: until heaven and earth passes away, one iota or one stroke shall not pass from the Law, until all comes to pass.”

[Note: Col. 0498] *jah*: H. adds *jau*. — *allata vairþiþ*: J. St. and B. add *alla gavairþiþ*; H. adds *alla tavairþiþ*.

“But whoever now abolishes one of these least commandments and teaches people thus will be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does and teaches thus will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”

[Note: Col. 0498] *sah*: Z. originally has *sa*; otherwise it is absent from all Greek witnesses. — *þiudangardjai*: H. adds *div.* — *sva*: the second “thus” is absent from the Greek.

“For I tell you that unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall certainly not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

[Note: Col. 0498] *ni þau*: the editions add *jet*. — *ïzvaraizos garaihteins* corresponds to the Greek; Ulfilas, however, omits *πλεῖον*, “more.”

“You have heard that it was said to the people of old: ‘You shall not murder’; but whoever murders shall be liable to judgment.”

“But I tell you that everyone angry with his brother without cause shall be liable to judgment; whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca!’ shall be liable to the council; and whoever says, ‘Fool!’ shall be liable to the Gehenna of fire.”

[Note: Col. 0499] *skula*: Schm. adds *scula* before it.

“If, then, you bring your *aibr* [‘offering?’] to the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you—”

[Note: Col. 0499] *jabai*: H. regularly adds *gabai*. — *aibr*: thus Codex Argenteus; neither Ihre’s conjecture *bair* nor Zahn’s *libr* deserves acceptance, since neither has manuscript authority. Nor is *giba* persuasive, because the text has *þein*, not *þeina*, which *giba* requires. Grimm likewise retained *aibr*, of uncertain origin and sense, at I, 44 ff.; later DM., p. 25, and Gr. I, 43 (3rd ed.), conjectured *tibr*. Ettmüller also considered that reading necessary (*HLZ*, 1838, no. 224, in his review of our edition); but see the Glossary, s.v. *Aibr*.

“—leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother; then come and offer your gift.”

[Note: Col. 0499] *andvairþja*: H. adds *andvirþja*. — *gasibjon*: “be reconciled”; all Greek witnesses have *διαλλάγηθι*. — *atbair*: H. adds *div.*

“Be well disposed toward your adversary promptly, while you are on the way with him, lest the adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be cast into prison.”

[Note: Col. 0499] *atgibai þuk* corresponds to all Greek witnesses.

“Truly I tell you: you shall not come out from there until you have paid the smallest coin.”

[Note: Col. 0499] *minnistan*, “smallest,” whereas all Greek witnesses have *ἔσχατον*, “last”; accordingly Sch. suspects that Ulfilas read *ἐλάχιστον*. Perhaps the Goth translated incorrectly, as indeed happened to him more than once.

“You have heard that it was said: ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I tell you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”

“If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it away from you; for it is better for you that one of your members perish and not your whole body fall into Gehenna.”

[Note: Col. 0499] *þata*: J. St. adds *þana*. — *usstagg*: Schm. adds *afstagg*; Grimm, II, 190*, correctly observed that the reading of Codex Argenteus is erroneous for *usstigg*. In the codex an *a* has been erased, perhaps indicating correction. — *gadriusai*: Z., preface p. XIV, absurdly contends that the Goth read *πέσῃ*, “fall,” for *βληθῇ*, “be cast,” treating Ulfilas as an exceptionally literal translator of Greek words; compare VI.2, *andnemum*, “they received,” for *ἀπέχουσι*, and other cases.

“And if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it away from you; for it is better for you that one of your members perish and not your whole body fall into Gehenna.”

[Note: Col. 0499] *þeinaize*: St. adds *þeinlize*. — *gadriusai*: H. omits *driusai*.

“It was also said: ‘Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce.’”

[Note: Col. 0499] *qiþanuh þan*: J. St. and Hz., almost everywhere, add [Col. 0500] *qiþan uhþan*. For *uh* is an enclitic, not a proclitic, particle; see the Grammar. Z. likewise makes this error in very many passages. — *wazuh*: Codex Argenteus has *wa || wazuh*. Thus syllables written at the end of a preceding line were often repeated at the beginning of the following line; see Luke 1:65 and John 9:41. — *qen*: Ulfilas omits *αὐτοῦ*, together with Codex 6, as Scholz observes.

“But I tell you that everyone who dismisses his wife, except on account of adultery, makes her commit adultery; and he who marries a dismissed woman commits adultery.”

[Note: Col. 0500] *sa ïze*: F. omits *sa ïzei*; Hz., after correction, has *saïze*. Z. correctly divides it here and at VII.15, but at Mark 9:1 adds *jct.*

“Again, you have heard that it was said to the people of old: ‘You shall not swear falsely, but fulfil your oaths to the Lord.’”

[Note: Col. 0500] *ni ufarsvarais*: J. St., B., and H. add *niu farsvarais*. — *usgibais*: St. adds *usgibas*. — *fraujin*: in Codex Argenteus, except in passages where God or Jesus is not being spoken of (Matt. 6:24; 27:63; Luke 16:13; John 15:15), this word is always written with the abbreviation *fin*—likewise *fins*, *fan*, for *fraujins*, *fraujan*. J. St., B., and H. interpreted it as *fanin*; Gordon, p. 51, first restored the correct full form.

“But I tell you: do not swear at all; neither by heaven, for it is God’s throne; nor by earth, for it is his footstool; nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King; nor shall you swear by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black.”

[Note: Col. 0500] *guþs*: editions have *goþs*, H. *jþ*. The editions consistently use *goþ*, *goþis*, etc.; Maresch., p. 408, Gordon, p. 52 ff., and I[h]re rightly direct that *guþ*, *guþs* be written; see John 10:34, where *guda* occurs without abbreviation. Castiglione likewise always correctly prints this in his edition of the Epistles. — *þiudanis*: H. adds *þiudanins*. — *gataujan*: H. adds *gataugan*, as also at V.47.

“Let your word, then, be: ‘Yes, yes; no, no.’ But what exceeds this is from evil.”

[Note: Col. 0500] *sijaiþþan*: J. has *sij aiþþan*; B. separates it; Z. has *sijaiþ þan*; II. *sijai þau*; Schm. *sijaiþþan*. No interpreter has understood the true character of the form. Z. believes it to be compounded from *sijai* and *uþþan* or *aþþan*, though such contraction with *aþþan* is unheard of; there is some truth in the other view. Schm. seems to mark by a full stop that something is missing. The matter is this: the enclitic particle *uh*, with a connective force, is joined at the beginning of clauses to verbs. If the word to which it is joined ends in a long vowel or diphthong, the particle’s *u* is lost to avoid hiatus: thus here *sijaih* for *sijaiuh*, as *viljauh*, *sumaih*, *þaih* for *viljau-uh*, *sumai-uh*, *þai-uh*. If the final vowel is short, that vowel is dropped and the full particle *uh* is added: John 6:64 *vissuh*, Luke 7:6 *ïddjuh*, for *vissa-uh*, *ïddja-uh*. The *h* is then often assimilated to a following consonant; compare *janni* (XXV.42), *jag-gabairaidau* (John 3:4), *jas-sa* (Matt. 26:71), *nis-sijai* (Luke 20:16), and especially *sumaiþ-þan* (Matt. 26:67; John 11:46), *þaiþ-þan* (Rom. 12:4). The formation is frequent in the Epistles; see Massmann, *Sk.*, p. 60.

“You have heard that it was said: ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ But I tell you not to resist evil at all; rather, if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, turn the other to him also.”

[Note: Col. 0501] *allis*, “at all,” absent from all Greek witnesses; only Ptolemy, cited by Epiphanius, *Haeres.* 33.6, has *ὅλως*, according to Mill. — *unseljin*: H. has *unselgin*. — *taihsvon*: H. has *taishvon*.

“To one wishing to sue you and take your cloak, permit him your tunic also.”

[Note: Col. 0501] *staua*: St. has *stava*.

“And if anyone compels you for one mile, go with him two. Give to him who asks you, and do not turn away from him who wishes to borrow from you.”

[Note: Col. 0501] *jah*: St. has *jak*.

“You have heard that it was said: ‘Love your neighbour and hate your enemy.’”

[Note: Col. 0501] *fiais*: St. has *filis*. — *newundjan*: H. adds *div.*

“But I tell you: love your enemies, bless those persecuting you, do good to those hating you, and pray for those afflicting you.”

[Note: Col. 0501] Griesbach and Mill are mistaken in thinking that the Goth omitted *καὶ διωκόντων ὑμᾶς*, “and [those] persecuting you,” for he rendered it by *jah vrikandans ïzvis*. Rather, he read in his manuscript and translated accordingly: *ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν, εὐλογεῖτε τοὺς διώκοντας ὑμᾶς, καλῶς ποιεῖτε τοῖς μισοῦσιν ὑμᾶς καὶ προσεύχεσθε ὑπὲρ τῶν ἐπηρεαζόντων ὑμᾶς*: “Love your enemies, bless those who persecute you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who abuse you.” Thus there is no need either to give *vrikan* a new sense rejected by its etymology, or, with Rw., to conjecture *fraqiþandans* for *vrikandans*; cf. Luke 3:14.

“…that you may become sons of your Father who is in heaven; for he causes his sun to rise upon evil and good, and sends rain upon just and unjust.”

[Note: Col. 0502] *ana*, the third “upon,” is absent from all Greek witnesses.

“For if you love those loving you only, what reward have you? Do not even the Gentiles do the same?”

[Note: Col. 0502] *ainans*, “only,” absent from all Greek witnesses. — *þiudo*, “Gentiles,” where Greek has *τελῶναι*, “tax collectors.”

“And if you greet only your friends, what more do you do? Do not even the carriers do the same?”

[Note: Col. 0502] *frijonds*, “friends,” where Greek has *ἀδελφούς*, “brothers.” — *taujiþ*: H. has *taugiþ*, as at v. 36 and frequently elsewhere. — *motarjos*, “tax collectors,” where Greek has *ἐθνικοί*, “Gentiles.” — *þata samo*, “the same,” where Greek has *οὕτω*, “thus.”

“Be, therefore, perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.”

[Note: Col. 0502] *fullatojai*: H. adds *div.* in both places. — *atta*: H. has *attah*. — *ïzvar*: Z. adds *zvar*.

“Take heed not to perform your beneficence before people in order to be seen by them; otherwise you have no reward from your Father in heaven.”

[Note: Col. 0502] *armaion*: St. has *armajon*; Greek has *δικαιοσύνην*, “righteousness.” — *andvairþja*: St. has *andvairþia*, H. *andvairþga*.

“When, then, you perform beneficence, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in synagogues and streets, that they may be praised by people. Truly I tell you: they have received their reward.”

[Note: Col. 0502] *ei*: H. omits it. — *hauhjaindau fram*: H. has *hauhjainda ufram*. — *andnemun*: H. adds *div.*, as frequently.

“But when you perform beneficence, let not your left hand know what your right hand does, that your beneficence may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you openly.”

[Note: Col. 0502] *sijai*: Z. has *siai*. — *þeina*: Greek places it before *so*. — first *fulhsnja*: Codex Argenteus has *fulhsja*. — second *fulhsnja*: Ulfilas omits *αὐτός*, together with the manuscripts and versions.

“And when you pray, do not be as the hypocrites; for they love to pray standing in synagogues and at the street-corners, in order that they may be observed by people. Truly I tell you: they have their reward.”

[Note: Col. 0502] *bidjaiþ—sijaiþ*, “when you pray—be”; Greek *προσεύχῃ—ἔσῃ*. — second *jah*: Ulfilas omits Greek *ἐν*. — *plapjo*: because this word occurs in no Germanic language, Ulfilas seems to have borrowed it from Greek *πλατεῖα*; accordingly we think it should be written *platjo*.

“But you, when you pray, go into your chamber; and, having shut your door, pray to your Father in secret. And your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you openly.”

[Note: Col. 0502] *galukands*: J. St. has *galaukands*. Zahn’s conjecture *paurdai* for *haurdai* is unnecessary; see 2 Cor. 2:12.

“But when praying, do not use many words, as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard because of their many words.”

[Note: Col. 0503] *bidjandansuþ-þan*: editions have *bidjandans uþ-þan*.

“Do not, therefore, become like them; for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.”

[Note: Col. 0503] *jus*, “you,” is absent from all Greek witnesses; H. has *gus*, as often, with *g* for *j*. — *faurþizei*: H. adds *div.*

“Pray, therefore, in this way: Our Father, you in heaven, hallowed be your name. May your kingdom come. May your will be done, as in heaven, also upon earth. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us that in which we are debtors, as we also forgive our debtors. And do not bring us into temptation, but deliver us from evil. For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory for ever. Amen.”

[Note: Col. 0503] The Lord’s Prayer has often, but incorrectly, been repeated in books of varied subject matter—for example, in the anonymous book on the letters and language of the Getae, edited by Bonaventura Vulcanius; in Graeter’s *Bragur*, I, p. 110; and in Adelung’s *Mithridates*, II, p. 182. — *þu*, “you,” where Greek has *ὁ*, “the”; see Luke 6:20. — *sinteinan*: the word, whose sense seemed obscure to Adelung, I, is to be compared with *seiteins*, 2 Cor. 11:28 = *ὁ καθ᾽ ἡμέραν*, “daily”; it therefore means “daily.” — *himma daga*: editions add *j t.* — *unte—amen*: absent from Greek.

“For if you forgive people their offences, your Father above the heavens will forgive you also; but if you do not forgive people their offences, neither will your Father forgive your offences.”

[Note: Col. 0503] *ni þau*: editions add *jet*, for *þau* belongs to *afletiþ*.

“But when you fast, do not become gloomy like the hypocrites; for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear to people as fasting. Truly I tell you: they have received their reward.”

[Note: Col. 0503] *svasve*: Z. has *sve*. — *fravardjand*: J. St. has *fravaurdjand*, H. *fravardjana*. — *gasaiwaindau*: J. St. has *gasaiwandau*.

“But you, when fasting, anoint your head and wash your face, that you may not appear to people as fasting, but to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.”

[Note: Col. 0503] *haubiþ þein*, “your head,” corresponds to all Greek witnesses.

“Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves neither break in nor steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart is also.”

[Note: Col. 0503] *huzdjaiþ*: St. has *husdjaiþ*.

“The lamp of the body is the eye. If, then, your eye is sound, your whole body shall be full of light; but if your eye is evil, your whole body shall be dark. If, then, the light in you is darkness, how great is that darkness!”

“No one can serve two masters; for if he hates one, he will love the other; or he will be subject to one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and Mammon.”

[Note: Col. 0503] *unte jabai*, “for if,” whereas all Greek witnesses have *ἢ γάρ*, “or for”; therefore Ulfilas is thought to have read *εἰ γάρ*, and the sense is: “for if he hates one, he also loves the other.” In the parallel passage, Luke 16:13, the Gothic likewise differs from Greek; see the note there. — *fijaiþ ainana* corresponds to all Greek witnesses. — *ufhauseiþ*, “is subject to,” whereas all Greek witnesses have *ἀνθέξεται*; Ulfilas may have read *ὑποτάξεται*, to which *ufhausjan* corresponds at Luke 2:51; 10:17, 20; Romans 13:1. — *ïþ*, “but,” where Greek has *καί*, “and”; Gothic *ïþ* is used in adversative clauses elsewhere as well (Mark 10:42; 15:15; cf. 15:31).

“Therefore I tell you: do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or drink; nor about your body, what you will wear. Is not life more than food, and the body than clothing?”

[Note: Col. 0504] *matjaiþ*: Z. has *maþjaiþ*.

“Look at the birds of heaven: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your Father above the heavens feeds them. Are you not much more valuable than they?”

[Note: Col. 0504] *nih*: Z. omits it. — *sneiþand*: J. St. and B. have *sneiand*; Bü. II, *sneidhand*. — *maisve aþrizans*: so Codex Argenteus reads, though the letters are scarcely legible; H. has *mais veaþrizans*. Interpreters, correctly judging the codex reading corrupt, have proposed various conjectures: Gordon, p. 54, *mais vairþizans*; Z., *mais sveraiþans*, apparently approved by Schm. and Wackernagel, *Deutsches Lesebuch*, I, preface p. XXIII. Rw., *Glossary*, p. 77, defends the received reading but admits that he does not know what *maisve* is; Z., *Glossary*, p. 178, rightly denies that it is a Gothic form. There can be no doubt that this monstrous reading arose from a copyist’s negligence; and since conjectural correction is required, none easier or truer can be found than Gordon’s. Although Z. doubts whether *mais* may be joined with a comparative, Greeks and Latins use *μᾶλλον* and *potius* with a comparative, as do Icelanders; see the editors’ Glossary, s.v. *Heldr*. The Goths themselves permit such pleonasms: see 2 Cor. 8:22, *mais usdaudozan*. In this passage the Vulgate too has *magis pluris*.

“Which of you, by being anxious, can add one cubit to his stature?”

[Note: Col. 0505] *vahstu*: J. St. has *vahstm*. — *seinana aleina*: thus Codex Argenteus; editions have *seinan alleina*.

“And concerning clothing, why are you anxious? Consider the flowers of the field, how they grow: they neither labour nor spin. Yet I tell you that not even Solomon, in all his glory, clothed himself like one of these.”

[Note: Col. 0505] *saurgaiþ*: J. St., B., and H. have *saurjaiþ*. — *vulþau*: J. St. has *vulþu*.

“And if God so clothes the grass of the field, which exists today and, on the morrow [Gothic *gistradagis*, literally ‘yesterday’], is thrown into the furnace, how much more you, of little faith?”

[Note: Col. 0505] *jah*: J. St. prefixes *jabai*. — *gistradagis*: Greek *αὔριον*, “tomorrow.” The word *gistra*, whose root in all related dialects means not “tomorrow” but “yesterday,” seems to have been used through the translator’s error. If anyone wishes, in defence of the reading and to clear Ulfilas of blame, to compare the Bohemian *zegtra*, “tomorrow,” let him recall 1 Cor. 15:32, where *αὔριον* is rendered *du maurgina*. — *waiva mais*: “how much more,” Greek *οὐ πολλῷ μᾶλλον*.

“Do not, then, be anxious, saying: ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ For the Gentiles seek all these things; but your Father above the heavens knows that you need—”

[Note: Col. 0505] *we*: J. St. has *wa*. — *all auk*: H. has *alla uk*.

“[lacuna] people [do] for you; likewise you too do to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets.”

“Enter through the narrow gate. For broad is the gate and spacious the road leading to destruction, and many are those entering through it. How narrow is the gate and constricted the road leading to life, and few are those who find it!”

[Note: Col. 0506] *vigs*: H. has *vigis*. Codex Argenteus has *vigss*; the first *s* was deleted by a perpendicular stroke added by a later hand, which scholars took for the letter *i*. We do not deny, however, that this corrector—whose ignorance of Gothic is evident elsewhere—thought that *vigis* ought to be read. — *ïnngaleiþ*: J. St. and B. have *ïngaleiþ*.

“Beware, nevertheless, of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s garments but inwardly are ravening wolves.”

[Note: Col. 0505] *sveþauh*: J. St. has *sveþau*; that form occurs nowhere, whereas *þau* compounded with *sve* is always written with added *h*, that is, *uh*. The older spelling *sveþau* at II.22 and 24 was incorrect. — *liugnapraufetum*: St. adds *div.* — *þaim ïzei*: J. St. and Hz. add *jct.*; see V.32.

“By their fruits you shall know them. Are grapes gathered from thorns, or figs from thistles? Thus every good tree produces good fruit, but the bad tree produces bad fruit. A good tree cannot produce bad fruit, nor a bad tree good fruit. Every tree not producing good fruit is cut down and cast into the fire. Therefore by their fruits you shall know them.”

[Note: Col. 0506] *gataujiþ*: Z. has *gataujit*.

“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter into the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father in heaven. Many shall say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name do mighty deeds?’ And then I shall confess to them: ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you workers of iniquity.’”

[Note: Col. 0506] *unsibjana*: G. and LM. have already maintained that this form is corrupt. Instead of Gordon’s conjecture *unsibjata*, we suspect that *unsibja* should be read; *sawazuh nu saei*, etc. For ordinary Gothic usage indeed requires *sawazuh*; see X.32; cf. Mark 9:37; 10:11 and other passages. (Although one also finds Matt. 7:26 *jah wazuh saei*—John 6:45 [source ends incomplete].

Therefore, whoever—). N is used instead of S, and vice versa, in other passages as well; see Mark 6:2; compare the note on Luke 3:14.]

“I never knew you. Depart from me, you workers of lawlessness.” Therefore everyone who hears my words and does these things—I will compare him to a prudent man who built his house upon rock. [Note: [Col. 0505] “And the rain fell down, and the waters came, and the winds blew, and they rushed against that house, and it did not fall, for it had been founded upon rock.”] [Note: [Col. 0506] *vaurda meina* (“my words”): according to the Greek in all these passages and in verse 26; otherwise Ulfilas has Greek *toútous* (“these”) in both places, as do the manuscripts.]

And it did not fall, because it had been founded upon rock. And the rain fell down, and the waters came, and the winds blew, and they rushed against that house, and it did not fall. [Col. 0507] [Note: [Col. 0507] “And everyone who hears my words and does not do these things is like a foolish man, who built his house upon sand.”] [Note: [Col. 0507] *vaurda meina*: see the note on verse 24.]

And it did not fall, because it had been founded upon rock. And everyone who hears my words and does not do them is like a foolish man, who built his house upon sand. And the rain fell down, and the waters came, and the winds blew, and they rushed against that house, and it fell, and its ruin was great. [Note: [Col. 0507] *jainamma razna* (“that house”): according to the Greek in all these passages.—*drus*: J. and St. add *draus*.]

And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these words, that the crowds were astonished at his teaching. [Note: [Col. 0507] “For he was teaching them as one having authority, and not as the scribes.”] [Note: [Col. 0507] *ïesus*: J., B., and H. add *ïaisus*; St. adds *jaisus*; the Codex Argenteus always has *is*. The first to discover the correct reading was Maresh (see Junius, p. 405), after whom it was commended by Gordon (see *Ulfilas illustratus*, appendix), p. 52, and by Z. on Matthew 8:7. Compare Castillon on Ezra 2:36.—*biabridedun*: this form, in place of which Z. wished to substitute *bibairdedun* (rather, *bibairidedun*!), is proved correct by *abrs* in Luke 15:14 and *abraba* in Matthew 27:54.]

And Jesus finished these words. The crowds were astonished at his teaching, for he was teaching them as one having authority and not as the scribes. [Note: [Col. 0507] “And when he came down from the mountain, many crowds followed him.”] [Note: [Col. 0507] *ïumjons*: J., St., and B. II add *ïunjons*; Z. adds *jumjons*.]

When he had come down from the mountain, many crowds followed him. And behold, a man having leprosy came running, bowed before him, and said: “Lord, if you wish, you can cleanse me.” [Note: [Col. 0507] “And stretching out his hand, he touched him, saying: ‘I will; be cleansed!’ And immediately his leprous skin was cleansed.”] [Note: [Col. 0507] *ïmma*: Ulfilas has *Iēsus* instead.] [Note: [Col. 0507] *qiþands* (“saying”): St. adds *qitands*.—*þata—ïs*: according to the Greek in all the manuscripts: “his leprosy.”]

And he said: “Lord, if you wish, you can cleanse me.” And stretching out his hand, he touched him, saying: “I will; be cleansed!” And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. [Note: [Col. 0507] “And Jesus said to him: ‘See that you tell no one, but go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.’”] [Note: [Col. 0507] *jah*: St. adds *ïah*, as often elsewhere.—*mann*: J. [Col. 0508] St. and B. add *man*.]

“I will; be cleansed.” And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. And Jesus said to him: “See that you tell no one, but go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses commanded for a testimony to them.” [Note: [Col. 0507] “After this, when he entered Capernaum, a centurion approached him, beseeching him.”] [Note: [Col. 0508] *ufaruh þan þata*: “but after this”; Greek *dé*.]

After this, when he entered Capernaum, a centurion approached him, beseeching him and saying: “Lord, my servant lies at home, paralyzed and suffering terribly.” [Note: [Col. 0507] “And Jesus said to him: ‘I will come and heal him.’”]

And the centurion answered and said: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant will be healed.” [Note: [Col. 0508] *mein*: according to the Greek in all the manuscripts, before *uf*.]

For I too am a man, having soldiers under my authority, and I say to this one, “Go,” and he goes; and to another, “Come,” and he comes; and to my servant, “Do this,” and he does it. [Note: [Col. 0507] “And Jesus, hearing this, marvelled and said to those who followed him: ‘Truly I say to you, I have not found such faith in Israel.’”] [Note: [Col. 0508] *habands—meinamma*: “having under my authority”; Greek *hypò exousían échōn hyp’ emautón*.]

And Jesus, hearing this, marvelled and said to those who followed him: “Truly I say to you, I have not found such faith in Israel.” [Note: [Col. 0507] “But I say to you that many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.”] [Note: [Col. 0508] *aþþan*: J. and St. add *aþþau*.—*saggqa*: J. and St. add *saitqa*.—*ïakoba*: Schm. adds *ïacoba*.]

But I say to you that many from east and west will come and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. But the sons of the kingdom will be cast out into the outermost darkness. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. [Note: [Col. 0507] “And Jesus said to this centurion: ‘Go; as you have believed, so let it be for you.’ And his servant was healed at that hour.”] [Note: [Col. 0508] *jainai weilai*: according to the Greek in all the manuscripts.]

And there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. And Jesus said to the centurion: “Go, and as you have believed, so let it be for you.” And his servant was healed in that hour. [Note: [Col. 0507] “And when Jesus came into Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying with a fever.”] [Note: [Col. 0508] *jah*: follows the preceding participle, as also in John 6:45 and often elsewhere.]

And Jesus came into Peter’s house and saw his mother-in-law lying with a fever. And he touched her hand, and the fever left her. And she arose and ministered to him. [Note: [Col. 0507] “And when evening came, they brought him many demon-possessed persons, and he cast out the spirits by a word and healed all who were ill.”] [Note: [Col. 0508] *ïmma*: “to him,” Greek *autoîs*.]

And when evening had come, they brought to him many demon-possessed persons, and he cast out the demons with a word and healed all who were ill. [Note: [Col. 0507] “In order that what had been written through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: ‘He took our infirmities and bore our diseases.’”] [Note: [Col. 0508] *at andanahtja*: J. and St. add *ict.*; H. adds *at ande nahtja*.]

So that what had been written through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: “He took our infirmities and bore our diseases.” [Note: [Col. 0508] *usnam*: if Ulfilas read Greek *anélabe* in his manuscript, as Sch. maintains, he would have written *andnam* (see Luke 9:51). Moreover, *usbairan* follows for the simple Greek *bastázein*.—*sauhtins*: B. II adds *sautins*.]

He cast out the spirits with a word and healed all who were ill, so that what had been written through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: “He took our infirmities and bore our diseases.” [Note: [Col. 0509] “But Jesus, seeing many crowds around him, ordered the disciples to go across the sea.”] [Note: [Col. 0509] *siponjans*: “disciples,” omitted by the Greek in all the manuscripts; Ulfilas agrees with the versions.]

But Jesus, seeing many crowds around him, ordered the disciples to go across the sea. And a certain scribe approached and said to him: “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.” [Note: [Col. 0509] *atgaggands*: H. adds *atgangands*.]

And a certain scribe approached and said to him: “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.” [Note: [Col. 0509] “And Jesus said to him: ‘Foxes have dens and the birds of heaven nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.’”] [Note: [Col. 0509] *qaþ*: “he said,” according to the Greek in all the manuscripts, *légei*; thus Ulfilas almost always uses the past tense in narrative instead of the Greek historical present.—*sein anahnaivjai*: J. and St. add *seinana hnaivjai*; otherwise *sein*, “his,” is omitted by the Greek in all the manuscripts.]

The scribe said to him: “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.” And Jesus said to him: “Foxes have dens and birds of heaven nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” [Note: [Col. 0509] “And another of his disciples said to him: ‘Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father.’”]

But another of his disciples said to him: “Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father.” And Jesus said to him: “Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead.” [Note: [Col. 0509] “And when he entered the boat, his disciples followed him.”]

And when he entered the boat, his disciples followed him. And behold, a great disturbance arose in the sea, so that the boat was covered by the waves; but he was sleeping. [Note: [Col. 0509] *saislep*: J. and St. add an obelus.]

And his disciples approached and woke him, saying: “Lord, save us! We are perishing!” [Note: [Col. 0509] *ïs*: “his,” omitted by the Greek.]

And the disciples approached and woke him, saying: “Lord, save us! We are perishing!” And Jesus said to them: “Why are you afraid, you of little faith?” Then he arose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and a great calm came about. [Note: [Col. 0509] *ïesus*: omitted by the Greek in all the manuscripts; Ulfilas agrees with the versions.—*wa*: J. adds *wl*.]

And Jesus said to them: “Why are you afraid, you of little faith?” Then he arose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and a great calm came about. But the men marvelled, saying: “What sort of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?” [Note: [Col. 0509] *wileiks*: H. adds an obelus.—*sa ei*: the editors add *jct.*]

And the men marvelled, saying: “What sort of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?” And when he came across the sea into the region of the Gergesenes, two demon-possessed men met him, coming out from the tombs, exceedingly violent, so that no one could pass along that road. [Note: [Col. 0509] *gairgaisaine*: one would expect *gairgaisene*, for Ulfilas normally renders Greek eta by *e*, not by *ai*; certainly he does so only rarely, as in Ezra 2:31 *aillam* (*Ēlám*), Luke 10:13 and 9:10 *baiþsaïda* (*Bēthsaida*), Luke 1:17 *hailias* (*Ēlías*), Mark 6:17 *hairodias* (*Hērōdiás*), and *neikaudaimus* (*Nikódēmos*), although elsewhere the forms *beþsaida*, *helias*, *herodias*, and *neikaudemus* occur.]

And behold, they cried out, saying: “What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come here before the appointed time to torment us?” [Note: [Col. 0509] *sunau*: H. adds *sundu*.]

When he came across the sea into the region of the Gergesenes, two demon-possessed men met him, running out from the tombs, exceedingly fierce, so that no one could pass along that road. And behold, they cried out, saying: “What have we to do with you and with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come here before the appointed time to torment us?”

Now a considerable distance away from them there was a large herd of pigs grazing. [Note: [Col. 0509] *haldana*: Lye, *Grammar*, p. 50, wrongly conjectured *haldanda* (rather *haldandei*), and Z. improperly supports him here and on Luke 8:32. For Ih. had already correctly observed that *haldan* means “to pasture” (see verse 33), not “to be pastured”; see also Mark 5:11.]

And the demons begged him, saying: “If you cast us out, permit us to go into that herd of pigs.” [Note: [Col. 0509] *qiþandans*: Schm., who was troubled by the masculine form, seems not to know that this is a construction by *synthesis*, see 9:33, Luke 9:11, and very often.—*uslaubei uns galeiþan*: “permit us to go,” Greek *apósteilon hēmâs*. Z. and Schm. add *uslaubai*.]

And he said to them: “Go!” And they came out and went into the herd of pigs. And behold, the whole herd rushed down the precipice into the sea, and they perished in the waters. [Note: [Col. 0510] *hairda sveine*: “herd of pigs,” Greek *toùs choírous*.—*hairda*: the second occurrence; Ulfilas omits the Greek article *tōn choírōn*, which he certainly read in his manuscript. See the note on such omissions at Luke 15:24 and 1 Timothy 6:6.—*and driuson*: J., St., and H. add *jct*.]

And he said to them: “Go!” And they came out and went into the herd of pigs. And behold, the whole herd rushed down the precipice into the sea, and they perished in the waters. But those who had been pasturing them fled, and going into the city they reported everything concerning the demon-possessed men. [Note: [Col. 0509] “And behold, the whole city came out to meet Jesus, and when they saw him they begged him to leave their borders.”] [Note: [Col. 0510] *gaitaihun in baurg*: according to the Greek in all the manuscripts. Sch., following Z., translates “in the village”; but *baurg* may also be an accusative.—*bi*: “concerning,” not “because of”; Ulfilas agrees with the manuscripts in reading Greek *katá*.]

And the whole city came out to meet Jesus, and when they saw him they begged him to leave their borders. And he went up into a boat, crossed over, and came into his own city. [Note: [Col. 0509] “Then they brought to him a paralytic lying on a bed, and when Jesus saw their faith he said to the paralytic: ‘Take courage, little son; your sins are forgiven!’”] [Note: [Col. 0510] *þan usatberun*: the Greek has *kaì idoù prosépheron*. Sch., following Z., translates *þan* as “then,” supposing that Ulfilas had read Greek *tóte*; wrongly, for *þan* in that sense never stands at the beginning of sentences (see Matthew 7:23; 9:15; Mark 13:21, 26, and elsewhere), but *þanuh* does (Matthew 8:26; 9:6; 14:29, and elsewhere). Although Ulfilas renders Greek *kaì idoú* in Matthew 27:51 by *jah þan*, he seems not to have read *idoú* in his manuscript here; it is also absent from Codex E in Mi. and from several versions in Sch. Since, however, Ulfilas renders Greek *kaì prosphérein* in Mark 10:13 by *þanuh atberun*, and elsewhere usually renders *prosphérein* by *atbairan*, it seems that *þanuh atberun* ought to be written here too. Moreover, since Jesus had entered the city (see verse 1), and the sick man did not need to be carried before the city, *usatbairan* (“carry out”) does not give a suitable sense.]

He crossed over in a boat and came into his own city. Then they brought to him a paralytic lying on a bed. And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic: “Take courage, little son; your sins are forgiven.” [Col. 0511] [Note: [Col. 0511] “Then some of their scribes said within themselves: ‘This man blasphemes.’”] [Note: [Col. 0511] “And Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said: ‘Why do you think evil in your hearts?’”] [Note: [Col. 0511] *vitands*: “knowing,” Greek *idṓn*.—*hairtam*: St. adds *har am*.]

Then some of the scribes said within themselves: “This man blasphemes.” And Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” [Note: [Col. 0511] “For which is easier, to say: ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say: ‘Rise and go’?”] [Note: [Col. 0511] *waþar*: Z. adds *watar*.—*ïst raihtis*: according to the Greek in all the manuscripts; Griesbach incorrectly notes that *gár* is absent from the Gothic.—*þus*: “to you,” Greek *sou*.]

But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said: “Why do you think evil in your hearts? For which is easier, to say: ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say: ‘Rise and go’?” [Note: [Col. 0511] “But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, then he said to the paralytic: ‘Rise, take up your bed, and go into your house.’”] [Note: [Col. 0511] *afleitan*: *leitan* is used here instead of the more frequent *letan*, as in Mark 15:9; Luke 2:29 and 16:18.—*þeinana*: according to the Greek in all the manuscripts, before *þana*.]

“But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—then he said to the paralytic: “Rise, take up your bed, and go into your house.” [Note: [Col. 0511] “And he rose and went into his house.”] [Note: [Col. 0511] *seinana*: St. adds *seinada*.]

And he rose and went into his house. When the crowds saw this, they were afraid, marvelled, and glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings. [Note: [Col. 0511] *ohtedun sildaleikjandans*: according to Maresh, Ulfilas combined both Greek readings, *ethaúmasan* (“they marvelled”) and *ephobḗthēsan* (“they were afraid”). B. holds that our reading arose from a gloss inserted into the text; but neither explanation will satisfy an attentive reader. Unless Ulfilas read *ephobḗthēsan thaυmásantes* (“they were afraid, having marvelled”; compare Luke 8:25), one must consider some enlargement of meaning, of the kind Ulfilas frequently employs. See Mark 1:27, *afslauþnodedun sildaleikjandans* (“they were utterly astonished, marvelling”), where B. likewise wrongly judges *sildaleikjandans* to have arisen from a gloss; Mark 2:12, *hauhidedun mikiljandans* (“they glorified, magnifying”), and compare Mark 2:4, Matthew 9:23 and 26:72. John 13:36 has *andhafjands qaþ*. On similar enlargement of meaning, see the note on 1 Corinthians 9:25.—*valdufni*: J. and St. add *valaufni*.]

And he rose and went into his house. When the crowds saw this, they were afraid, marvelled, and glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings. [Note: [Col. 0511] “And as Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man sitting at the tax office, called Matthew, and said to him: ‘Follow me.’ And he rose and followed him.”] [Note: [Col. 0511] *maþþaiu*: used here instead of *matþaiu* (Mark 3:18), as also in Luke 6:15.]

And as Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man sitting at the tax office, called Matthew, and said to him: “Follow me.” And he rose and followed him. [Note: [Col. 0511] “And it came to pass, when he reclined in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and reclined with Jesus and his disciples.”]

And it came to pass, when he reclined in the house, that many tax collectors and sinners came and reclined with Jesus and his disciples. [Note: [Col. 0511] “And the Pharisees, seeing this, said to his disciples: ‘Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?’”]

And the Pharisees, seeing this, said to his disciples: “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” [Note: [Col. 0511] “But Jesus, hearing this, said to them: ‘Those who are well do not need a physician, but those who have illness.’”] [Note: [Col. 0511] “But go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice’; for I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”] [Note: [Col. 0511] *wa*: Z. adds *sva*.]

But Jesus, hearing this, said to them: “Those who are well do not need a physician, but those who are ill. Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice’; for I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”

Then the disciples of John approached, saying: “Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, while your disciples do not fast?” [Note: [Col. 0511] *atïddjedun*: Ulfilas has *auto* in place of Greek *autō*.—*fastam*: J. and St. add *fastaim*.]

Then the disciples of John approached, saying: “Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, while your disciples do not fast?” [Note: [Col. 0511] “And Jesus said to them: ‘Can the sons of the bridegroom mourn while the bridegroom is with them? But days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast.’”] [Note: [Col. 0511] *atgaggand*: Codex Argenteus adds *atgaggand*.—*þan*: J. and St. add *þam*.]

And Jesus said to them: “Can the sons of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them? But days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast.” [Note: [Col. 0511] “No one puts a piece of rough cloth onto an old garment; for it tears away the fullness from that garment, and the tear becomes worse.”] [Note: [Col. 0511] *du plata*: J., St., and B. II add *jct.*; the preposition *du* is placed before the predicate of the clause, as in Mark 11:17 and 12:10, and elsewhere.]

But no one puts a piece of rough cloth onto an old garment, for it tears away its fullness from the garment, and the tear becomes worse. [Note: [Col. 0512] *fanan þarihis ana*: Codex Argenteus has an *i* written above (*þarihis*); J. and St. add *fananþa rihis*; B. has *fanan þarhis*; Gordon (*Ulfilas illustratus*, appendix, p. 56) conjectures *fanan þarhisana ana*, disregarding the superscript *i*; Schm. conjectured *þarihis* or *anþaris*, but the learned man should have indicated what the new word meant, or in what sense he wished *anþar* to be understood here. A reader of the Greek text sees that *autoû* stands after *plḗrōma*, as all manuscripts and versions have it, but that it is missing in Gothic. What prevents us from supposing that *ïs* was attached, by the person who wrote the Codex Argenteus, to the word *þarih*, although he did not know where it belonged? If that *ïs*, removed from *þarihis*, is placed after *fullon*, and the syllable *ana*, which was certainly omitted because of the following *ana*, is added to the remaining *þarih*, we obtain a suitable reading: *þarihana ana snagan—fullon ïs af þamma*, and so forth. In any event, Ulfilas seems to have borrowed *þarihs* from the Greek adjective *trachýs*, which means “unworked, rough,” see the *Etymologicum Magnum*, p. 714, line 24.]

No one puts a piece of rough cloth onto an old garment, for it tears away its fullness from the garment, and the tear becomes worse. Nor do they pour new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wineskins burst, and then both the wine spills out and the wineskins are destroyed. Rather, they pour new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved. [Note: [Col. 0511] “While he was saying these things to them, behold, a certain ruler came and bowed before him, saying: ‘My daughter has just died; but come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live.’”] [Note: [Col. 0512] *biþeh þan*: “then afterwards,” omitted by the Greek in all the manuscripts. Schm. hesitates, and Z., with B., suspects that *þan* is a gloss on *biþeh*, although it ought then to be *þanuh* (see the note on 9:2). Such pleonasms, however, are exceedingly common: *auk raihtis*, *auk allis*, *þan auk*, *ïþ þan*, *aþþan sveþauh*, and so forth. On closer consideration, it seems rather that only *biþeh* is redundant, while *þaniah* means “also,” as in 1 Timothy 5:25.]

But while he was saying these things to them, behold, a certain ruler came and bowed before him, saying: “My daughter has just died; but come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live.” [Col. 0513] [Note: [Col. 0513] “And Jesus arose and went after him, together with his disciples.”]

And Jesus rose and went after him, together with his disciples. [Note: [Col. 0513] “And behold, a woman suffering from a flow of blood for twelve winters approached from behind and touched the fringe of his garment.”] [Note: [Col. 0513] *vintruns*: “winters”; the Greek has *étē* (“years”) throughout. This way of reckoning time by winters is characteristic of Germanic peoples, not by years.—*ïb*: so the Codex Argenteus and J. and B.; St. and Z. omit the numeral XII.]

And behold, a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve winters, approaching from behind, touched the fringe of his garment. [Note: [Col. 0513] “For she said within herself: ‘If I only touch his garment, I shall be healed.’”] [Note: [Col. 0513] *jabai*: Z. adds an obelus.—*þatainei*: H. adds an obelus.—*vastjai*: J. and St. add *vastjan*.]

For she said within herself: “If I only touch his garment, I shall be healed.” For she said to herself: “If I only touch his garment, I shall be healed.” But Jesus, turning and seeing her, said: “Take courage, daughter; your faith has healed you.” And the woman was healed from that hour. [Note: [Col. 0513] “And Jesus came into the house of the ruler and saw the flute players and the crowd making a tumult.”] [Note: [Col. 0513] *svigljans*: J. adds *svilgjans*.—*jah haurnjans haurnjandans*: “and the trumpet players sounding trumpets,” according to the Greek in all the manuscripts. B., with Zahn, suspects that this is a gloss on *svigljans*, but *sviglja* means “flute player,” compare Matthew 2:17 and Luke 7:32, where *svigljan* means “to play the flute”; *haurnja* means “trumpeter,” compare Matthew 6:2, where *haurnjan* means “to sound a trumpet.” Rather, one should see in these words, as in Luke 2:29 *fraujinond frauja*, an enlargement of the idea, similar to the one noted at 9:8.]

And Jesus came into the house of the ruler and saw the flute players and the trumpet players sounding trumpets, and the crowd making a tumult. [Note: [Col. 0513] “He said to them: ‘Go away! For the girl has not died, but is sleeping.’ And they laughed at him.”] [Note: [Col. 0513] *slepiþ*: this is how it is read in the Codex Argenteus, as also in Mark 4:27 and 38; nor did the same impious and ignorant hand change it in Mark 5:39 or Luke 9:32. J. corrupted *slepiþ* into *saepiþ* (compare the note on Mark 4:7), a form that is altogether non-Gothic, since neither *ae*, nor *eu*, nor *ui* are Gothic diphthongs. See Ih. *Ulfilas illustratus*, p. 15; and we are surprised that Rw., *Glossary*, p. 143, ventured to defend that monstrosity. The alteration seems to have been made by some Scandinavian, who compared Icelandic *sofa* and Swedish *sofva*, and our form, but not Anglo-Saxon *slapan* or English *slepp*. In any case, Bopp’s *Comparative Grammar* I, p. 84 and following, compare p. 19, shows that both forms derive from the same root.]

And Jesus came into the house of the ruler and saw the flute players, the trumpet players sounding trumpets, and the crowd making a tumult. He said to them: “Go away! For the girl has not died, but is sleeping.” And they laughed at him. [Note: [Col. 0513] “Then, when the crowd had been put outside, he entered, took her hand, and the girl arose.”] [Note: [Col. 0514] *þanuh þan*: the editors translate this incorrectly as “when”; compare the note on 9:2. For *þanuh* is demonstrative, and is also read in 1 Corinthians 15:54. Instead of *þanuh þan*, Mark 8:20 has *aþþan þan*, and 1 Corinthians 15:28 has *þanuh biþe*.]

Then, when the crowd had been put outside, he entered, took her hand, and the girl arose. [Note: [Col. 0513] “And this report went out into all that land.”] [Note: [Col. 0514] *jaina airþa*: according to the Greek in all the manuscripts.]

And the girl arose. And the report of this went out into all that land. [Note: [Col. 0513] “And as Jesus went away from there, two blind men followed him, crying out and saying: ‘Have mercy on us, Son of David!’”] [Note: [Col. 0514] *ïesua jainþro*: according to the Greek in all the manuscripts.]

And as Jesus went away from there, two blind men followed him, crying out and saying: “Have mercy on us, Son of David!” [Note: [Col. 0513] “And when he came into the house, the blind men approached him, and Jesus said to them: ‘Do you believe that I can do this?’ They said to him: ‘Yes, Lord!’”] [Note: [Col. 0514] *gaulaubjats*: so in the Codex Argenteus and in Schm.; J., St., B., and Hz. omit *u* and have *galaubjats*. They were unfamiliar with the purely Gothic usage of placing *u*, the interrogative particle, between the prefix *ga* and the verb itself; so in Luke 18:8 *biugitai*, John 9:35 *gaulaubeis*, and likewise with another verb inserted between them in Mark 8:23 *gau wa sewi*. Compare John 5:46 *gaþau laubidedeiþ*, and the note on Mark 9:44.]

And when he came into the house, the blind men approached him, and Jesus said to them: “Do you believe that I can do this?” They said to him: “Yes, Lord!” Then he touched their eyes, saying: “According to your faith, let it be for you.” [Note: [Col. 0513] “And their eyes were opened, and Jesus sternly charged them, saying: ‘See that no one knows.’”]

And their eyes were opened, and Jesus sternly charged them, saying: “See that no one knows.” [Note: [Col. 0514] *qiþands*: St. adds *qiþans*.]

But when they went out, they spread his fame throughout all that land. [Note: [Col. 0513] “And when they had gone out, behold, they brought him a mute man possessed by a demon.”] [Note: [Col. 0514] *ut*: “outside,” omitted by the Greek in all the manuscripts.—*usïddjedun eis*: according to the Greek in all the manuscripts.]

And when they had gone out, behold, they brought him a mute man possessed by a demon. And when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke, and the crowds marvelled, saying: “Such a thing has never been seen in Israel.” [Note: [Col. 0513] *usdribans*: Z. and Schm. hesitate; it is a figure of *synthesis*, compare the note on 8:31. Grimm, *Deutsche Mythologie*, p. 555, thinks that *unhulþo* should be read instead of *unhulþa*, but see the *Glossary*, s.v.—*ni aiv*: J. and St. add *ni ïn aiva*.—*sva uskunþ*: according to the Greek.—*ïsraela*: J., St., and B. II add *ïsraelan*.]

And when they had gone out, behold, they brought him a mute man possessed by a demon. And when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke, and the crowds marvelled, saying: “Such a thing has never been seen in Israel.” But the Pharisees said: “By the ruler of the demons he casts out demons.” [Note: [Col. 0514] *fauramaþlja*: J., St., and B. add *faurabaþaja*.]

But the Pharisees said: “By the ruler of the demons he casts out demons.” [Note: [Col. 0513] “And Jesus went around all the cities and villages, teaching in their assemblies and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every infirmity.”] [Note: [Col. 0514] *gaqumþim*: J. and St. add *gaqumþin*.]

And Jesus went around all the cities and villages, teaching in their assemblies, proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every infirmity. [Note: [Col. 0513] “And when he saw the crowds, he had compassion on them, because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep not having a shepherd.”]

And when Jesus saw the crowds, he had compassion on them, because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep not having a shepherd. [Note: [Col. 0513] “Then he said to his disciples: ‘The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the workers are few.’”]

Then he said to his disciples: “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the workers are few.” [Note: [Col. 0513] “Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send workers into his harvest.”]

Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send workers into his harvest. [Note: [Col. 0515] “And calling the twelve disciples to him—[lacuna]”]

And calling the twelve disciples to him—[lacuna] [Note: [Col. 0515] “—from this city flee into another; for truly I say to you, you will not finish the cities of Israel until the Son of Man comes.”] [Note: [Col. 0515] *þliuhaiþ*: II adds *þluhaiþ*.—*anþara*: Ulfilas agrees with Codex k and the versions in reading Greek *hetéran eis tḕn*.]

From this city flee into another. For truly I say to you, you will not finish the cities of Israel until the Son of Man comes. [Note: [Col. 0515] “A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his lord.”] [Note: [Col. 0515] *seinamma*: Z. adds *sainamma*.]

A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his lord. [Note: [Col. 0515] “It is enough for the disciple to become like his teacher, and the servant like his lord. If they called the master of the household Beelzebul, how much more his household members.”] [Note: [Col. 0515] *siponi*: this is correct, for *ganah* normally takes an accusative with it; see also 2 Corinthians 12:9.—*baiailzaibul*: J. and St. add *baiailzabul*.—*ïnnakundans*: H. adds *ïnnarundans*.]

For the Son of Man is coming. A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his lord. It is enough for the disciple to become like his teacher and the servant like his lord. If they called the master of the household Beelzebul, how much more his household members.

Therefore do not fear them, for nothing is covered that will not be uncovered, nor hidden that will not be known. [Note: [Col. 0515] *ni nunu*: J., St., B., Hz., and H. add *ninu nu*.—*ni vaiht*: Z. adds *nivaith*.]

Therefore do not fear them, for nothing is covered that will not be uncovered, nor hidden that will not be known. What I say to you in darkness, say in the light; and what you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the housetops. [Note: [Col. 0515] “And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear the one who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.”] [Note: [Col. 0515] *þatainei*: “only,” according to the Greek in all the manuscripts.—*saivalai*: the preposition is present; Hz. omits *saivala*.]

What I say to you in darkness, say in the light; and what you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the housetops. And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear the one who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.

What you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the housetops. And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear the one who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna. [Note: [Col. 0515] “Are not two sparrows bought for an assarion? And not one of them falls to the ground without the will of your Father.”] [Note: [Col. 0515] *bugjanda*: “are bought,” according to the Greek in all the manuscripts, *pōleîtai*, which would be *frabugjanda*.—*viljan*: “will,” while the Greek in all the manuscripts omits the word.]

Are not two sparrows bought for an assarion? And not one of them falls to the ground without the will of your Father. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. [Note: [Col. 0515] *tagla*: H. adds *tagal*.]

Are not two sparrows bought for an assarion? And not one of them falls to the ground without the will of your Father. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. [Note: [Col. 0515] “Therefore do not fear; you are worth more than many sparrows.”] [Note: [Col. 0515] *ni nunu*: J. and St. add *jct.*; B. and H. add *ninu nu*. See verse 26.—*managaim*: J. adds *managain*.]

Therefore do not fear; you are worth more than many sparrows. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Do not fear; you are worth more than many sparrows. [Note: [Col. 0515] “Therefore everyone who confesses me in the presence—”]

[lacuna] of men, I too will confess him in the presence of my Father who is in heaven. [Note: [Col. 0515] *sawazuh*: Z. omits it; various readings. — *andhaita*: II adds *adhaita*.] You are better. Therefore, whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess him before my Father who is in heaven. [Note: [Col. 0515] “But whoever denies me before men, I too deny him before my Father who is in heaven.”] [Note: [Col. 0515] *þiswanoh*: Z. omits it. — *ina*: Greek places it before *jah ïk*.]

But whoever denies me before men, I too will deny him before my Father who is in heaven. [Note: [Col. 0515] “Do not suppose that I came to bring peace upon earth; I did not come to bring peace, but a sword.”] Do not suppose that I came to bring peace upon earth. I did not come to bring peace, but a sword. [Note: [Col. 0515] “For I came to divide a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.”] For I came to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. [Note: [Col. 0515] “And the enemies of a man are his own household.”] [Note: [Col. 0515] “Whoever loves father or mother above me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me.”] And a man’s enemies are those of his own household. Whoever loves father or mother above me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me. [Note: [Col. 0515] “And whoever does not take his cross and follow after me is not worthy of me.”]

And whoever does not take his cross and follow after me is not worthy of me. [Note: [Col. 0515] “Whoever finds his life loses it; and whoever loses his life for my sake finds it.”] Whoever finds his life loses it, and whoever loses his life for my sake finds it.

[Note: [Col. 0515] “Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.”] Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. [Note: [Col. 0515] “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet receives a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man receives a righteous man’s reward.”] Whoever receives a prophet in a prophet’s name receives a prophet’s reward, and whoever receives a righteous man in a righteous man’s name receives a righteous man’s reward. [Note: [Col. 0515] “And whoever gives one of these least ones only a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple, truly I say to you, he will not lose his reward.”] [Note: [Col. 0515] *minnistane*: “of the least”; Greek μικρῶν (*mikron*). Sch. errs in saying that Ulfilas read, with manuscript 157, τῶν μικρῶν τούτων τῶν ἐλαχίστων (*tōn mikrōn toutōn tōn elachistōn*, “of these least little ones”).] And whoever gives one of these least ones a cup of cold water merely in the name of a disciple—truly I say to you, he shall not lose his reward.

[Note: [Col. 0515] “And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished commanding his twelve disciples, that he departed from there to teach and preach in their cities.”] [Note: [Col. 0516] *biþe*: Z. adds *biþ*.] And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished giving commands to his twelve disciples, that he went away from there to teach and preach in their cities.

[Note: [Col. 0515] “But John, hearing in prison of the works of Christ, sent word through his disciples and said to him:”] [Note: [Col. 0515] *bi*: B., in order to correspond to the Greek δύο (*duo*, “two”), thinks that this reading was written in place of *b*, that this letter denotes two, and that the Goths pronounced it *bi*. Maresh., in Jun. p. 403, and Ih., *Ulfilas illustratus*, p. 135, explain it as “through” and think that Ulfilas read διά (*dia*), with certain manuscripts and versions. Z. conjectured that ·b· *bi* had been written. Z.’s and B.’s conjectures alike offend against linguistic usage: *ïnsandjan* is not construed with the dative, and *bi* does not mean “from” or “of” in this sense. Although the opinion of Maresh. and Ih. seems to us by far the most persuasive, we admit that we have found *bi* in this meaning (“through”) nowhere else. For in Galatians II.1, where Greek διά is rendered by *bi*, it has a temporal meaning and cannot be compared with our passage. Nor does Ettmüller’s solution help if he joins *bi siponjam* with *qaþ*: even then *bi* must mean “through,” which it does not mean, while *qiþan bi ainana* means “to speak concerning someone.”] But John, hearing in prison the works of Christ, sending through his disciples, said to him: [Note: [Col. 0515–0517] “Are you the one who is coming, or should we expect another?”] Are you the one who is to come, or should we await another?

[Note: [Col. 0517] “Jesus answered and said to them: Go and report to John what you hear and see:”] And Jesus answered and said to them: Go, report to John what you hear and see: [Note: [Col. 0517] “The blind see and the lame walk; lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear; the dead rise and the poor are evangelized.”] [Note: [Col. 0517] *ussaiwand*: St. adds *assaiwand*. — *þrutsfillai*: St. adds *þrustfillai*. — *jah*: omitted by the third Greek witness.] The blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, and the poor receive the good news. [Note: [Col. 0517] “And blessed is everyone who is not offended by me.”] And blessed is everyone who is not offended by me.

[Note: [Col. 0517] “While these were departing, Jesus began to say to the crowds concerning John: What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?”] [Note: [Col. 0517] *þan afgaggandam*: J. St. add *þana fargaggandam*; in the Codex Argenteus, certain letters, perhaps *ar*, had been written between *af* and *gaggandam*, but after their rightful erasure a lacuna remained. — *usïddjeduþ*: St. adds *usïddjedut*.] While these were departing, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John: What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?

[Note: [Col. 0517] “But what did you go out to see? A man clothed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses.”] [Note: [Col. 0517] *þaiei*: J. St. add *þaei*.] But what did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses. [Note: [Col. 0517] “But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Certainly, I say to you—and more than a prophet.”] [Note: [Col. 0517] *jai*: St. adds *ïah*. — *managizo*: J. St. B. H. omit *managiza*. — *praufetau*: H. adds *praufetan*.] But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I say to you, and more than a prophet.

[Note: [Col. 0517] “For this is he of whom it is written: Behold, I send my angel before you, who prepares your way before you.”] [Note: [Col. 0517] *ïst auk*: supported by all Greek witnesses. In Gothic *auk* very frequently stands after the first two words of a sentence; see the Glossary. — *meinana*: J. St. add *meinna*, H. *meina*. — *faura*: B. adds *frura*.] For this is he of whom it is written: “Behold, I send my messenger before you, who will prepare your way before you.”

[Note: [Col. 0517] “Truly I say to you: among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen; but the one least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.”] Truly I say to you: among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen; but the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.

[Note: [Col. 0517] “From the days of John this Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and violent persons seize it.”] [Note: [Col. 0517] *fravilvand*: J. St. add *fravilvan*.] From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven is violently assailed, and violent persons seize it. [Note: [Col. 0517] “For all the prophets and the law prophesied until John; and if you are willing to receive it, this is Elijah who was to come.”] For all the prophets and the law prophesied until John. And if you are willing to receive it, this is Elijah who was to come. [Note: [Col. 0517] “Let the one who has ears to hear, hear.”] Let the one who has ears to hear, hear.

[Note: [Col. 0517] This page of the Codex Argenteus, containing these ten verses, is torn away through nearly half its extent. Had Schmeller known this, he would not have stated that the letters on this page had faded so greatly that they could scarcely be read; see the plate in Ih., *Ulfilas illustratus*, p. 189. Ih. first ventured to supply from Luke VII.32 ff. and X.13 ff. what had perished of the Gothic words. Z. and H. followed him, as did Schm. for the most part. Since verse 15 is preserved complete in J. and St., as are other things now missing, one might conjecture that in their time the tear had not gaped so widely. But whoever knows their practice of supplying Gothic from Greek will attach little weight to that opinion.]

[Note: [Col. 0517] *ausona*: in this word the letter *s* is entirely illegible, and only the lower part of *u* remains. — *gahausjai*: the syllable *ga* is not legible in the Codex Argenteus; Schm. therefore did not edit it with sufficient accuracy.]

[Note: [Col. 0517–0518] “To whom, then, shall I compare this generation? It is like children seated in the marketplace, calling to others,”] [Note: [Col. 0517–0518] *wamma*: the editions read *we*; the reading printed here was conjectured by Schm. The conjecture is commended not only by the sense—for the question is not to what thing (*we*), but to what person (*wamma*), this generation is like; compare Luke VI.47, *wazuh sa gaggands du mis — wamma galeiks ïst?* (“Everyone who comes to me—whom is he like?”). Yet *we* is not false, as appears from the parallel Luke VII.31. It is also commended because *we* does not fill the available space. — *kuni*: J. St. B. add *kunni*. J. St. have text from *þata* to *anþaran*, indeed *anþaran* for *anþarans*. In the Codex Argenteus part of a *þ* is plainly visible where J. St. printed *v*. Syntax requires *anþarans*; compare Luke VII.32. It seems likely that a copyist wrote *anþaranþarans*, an error of a kind frequently found elsewhere: Luke VI.17; John IX.41; XII.47; XIII.13; compare the note on Matthew V.31. Ulfilas, with the manuscripts and versions, read ἑτέροις (*heterois*, “others”); Z. and Schm. wrongly repeated the addition *frijonds seinans* made by Ih. It translates ἑταίροις αὐτῶν (*hetaireis autōn*, “their companions”), which some Greek manuscripts read in place of τοῖς ἑτέροις (*tois heterois*, “the others”); nor would the space contain so many letters. — *garunsai*: since some manuscripts read ἀγορᾷ (*agorāi*) and others ἀγοραῖς (*agorais*), one may also read *garunsim*. — *jah*: H. adds *jai*.] To whom, then, shall I compare this generation? It is like children seated in the marketplace, calling to others,

[Note: [Col. 0517] “and saying: We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we mourned, and you did not lament.”] [Note: [Col. 0518] These verses are complete in J. St. — *hufum*: the *ïzvis* which J. St. Ih. Z. and Schm. add after *hufum* must be deleted, because the torn portion of the page cannot contain so many letters; most Greek manuscripts likewise omit ὑμῖν (*hymin*, “for you”). — *nih matjands*: Ih. Z. omit *ni matjands*. — *unhulþon*: the Codex Argenteus reads *unhulþ..*, not *unhul..*, as Schm. prints.] saying: “We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we mourned, and you did not lament.”

[Note: [Col. 0517] “For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say: He has a demon.”] John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say: “He has a demon.” [Note: [Col. 0517] “The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say: Behold, a gluttonous man and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners; and wisdom was justified by her children.”] [Note: [Col. 0518] *afdrugkja*: J. St. preserve the whole verse except *afdrugkja*, for which they read *afd . . .*; but in the Codex Argenteus only *a* remains. Ih.’s restoration is correctly supported by 1 Corinthians V.11. — *frijonds*: H. adds *frijands*.] The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say: “Behold, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.” And wisdom was justified by her children.

[Note: [Col. 0517–0519] “Then he began to reproach the cities in which most of his mighty works had been done, because they did not repent.”] [Note: [Col. 0518] The whole passage is found in J. St. — *þanuh*: St. Z. add *tanuh*. — *ni*: J. St. add *nih*. — *ïdreigodedun*: perhaps *gavandidedun* should be restored, as the variation in Luke XVII.3 f. suggests. — *sik*: J. St. B. omit it.] Then he began to reproach the cities in which most of his mighty works had been done, because they did not repent.

[Note: [Col. 0519] “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done among you had been done in the territory of Tyre and Sidon, they would perhaps long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes.”] [Note: [Col. 0519] *kaurazein*: Ib. Z. add *horazein*; see Luke X.13. B. H. had already given the correct reading. — *beþsaïdan*: or, if preferred, *beþsaeidan*; see John XII.21. — *vaurþeina—vaurþanons*: B. adds *in tyrai jah seidonai vaurþeina . . . laudai mahteis þos vaurþanons*; Ih. Z. H. Schm. add *vaurþeina ïn tyrai jah seidonai svelauda mahte svasve þos vaurþanons*. The word *landa* is clearly legible in the Codex Argenteus. Although it is absent from Greek, it must be retained, because otherwise the reading cannot be restored. The Greek witnesses otherwise agree. Of *þa* in *vaurþanons*, only portions of the letters survive. — *airis þau*: Schm. adds *jet*. — *azgon*: J. St. B. Ih., p. 236, n. 2, omit *azgom*. — *idreigodedeina*: it would more correctly be written *gaïdreigodedeina*, as at Luke X.13.] Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done among you had been done in the land of Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago perhaps have repented in sackcloth and ashes.

[Note: [Col. 0519] “Nevertheless I say to you: it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you.”] [Note: [Col. 0519] *sveþauh*: thus the Codex Argenteus; J. St. Ih. Z. H. Schm. add *sveþau*; see the note on VII.15. — *tyrim*: H. adds *turim*; J. St. after *ïzvis* add *þatei*. — *sutizo*: Ih. II. add *suþizo*. — *ïzvis*: J. St. at the end omit *þus*.] Nevertheless, I say to you: it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you.

[Note: [Col. 0519] “And you, Capernaum—will you be exalted to heaven? You will go down to hell. For if the mighty works done among you had been done in Sodom, it would perhaps have remained until this day.”] [Note: [Col. 0519–0520] *dalaþ und halja*: Ih. H. Z. Schm. add *und halja dalaþa*; but *dalaþa* means “below” (Mark XIV.66), not “downward,” which is *dalaþ*. — *unte jabai*: J. St. add *þatei ei*. Yet *ei*, and not *jabai*, is used for Greek εἰ (*ei*, “if”) except in interrogative clauses: Mark XI.13; XV.44; Philippians III.11. Ih. Z. Schm. rightly give *unte ïþ*; H. has *unþe ïþ*, though this does not fill the verse. — *saudaumjam*: J. St. add *saudaumjan*. — *matheis*: Ih. Z. H. Schm. add *þos*. Neither does the space contain so many letters nor is there any trace of the word, though elsewhere every descender is visible. — *ïzvis*: [Col. 0520] “for you”; all Greek witnesses read σοί (*soi*, “for you”). — *eis*: “they”; all Greek witnesses omit it.] And you, Capernaum, you have been exalted to heaven; you shall go down to hell. For if the mighty works done among you had been done in Sodom, it might have remained until this day.

[Note: [Col. 0519] “Nevertheless I say to you that it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for you.”] [Note: [Col. 0520] *sveþauh*: J. St. add *sveþau*; Z. Schm. add *sve þau*; see the note on VII.15.] Nevertheless, I say to you that it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for you.

[Note: [Col. 0519] “At that time, answering—”] [Note: [Col. 0520] *andhaf*: thus far the Codex Argenteus; J. St. supplied from their own materials the complete form *andhafjands*, followed by Z.] At that time, answering—[source boundary].

[Note: [Col. 0519] “When, then, did we see you as a stranger and invite you in, or naked and clothe you?”] [Note: [Col. 0520] “Beginning of chapter 26, verse 3. This fragment, not found in the Codex Argenteus, was discovered by Angelo Mai and Castiglione in an Ambrosian manuscript and published in *Specimen Ulphilae partium ineditarum*, p. 8 f.”] When, then, did we see you as a stranger and invite you in, or naked and clothe you? [Note: [Col. 0519] “When did we see you sick or in prison and come to you?”] When did we see you sick or in prison and come to you?

[Note: [Col. 0519] “And the king answering says to them: Truly I say to you: inasmuch as you did it to one of these least brothers of mine, you did it to me.”] [Note: [Col. 0520] *jah þan ei*: “even indeed as,” German *gesetzt auch dass*; Cast. adds *jah þanei*; compare Luke V.24. All Greek witnesses read ἐφ’ ὅσον (*eph’ hoson*, “insofar as”). The Goth, following Greek more closely, omitted the accusative of the thing, “something”; likewise in verse 45. — *minnistane*: in Greek it follows *meinaize*. — *meinaize*: Cast. adds *meinaze*.] And the king, answering, says to them: Truly I say to you: inasmuch as you did it to one of these least brothers of mine, you did it to me.

[Note: [Col. 0519] “Then he says also to those on the left: Go away from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.”] Then he says also to those on the left: Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. [Note: [Col. 0519] “For I was hungry and you gave me nothing to eat; I was thirsty and you gave me nothing to drink.”] For I was hungry and you gave me nothing to eat; I was thirsty and you gave me nothing to drink.
