[Note: [Col. 0519] “I was a stranger and you did not invite me in; naked and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison and you did not visit me.”] [Note: [Col. 0520] *gasts*: Ulfilas omits ἤμην (*ēmēn*, “I was”).] I was a stranger and you did not invite me in; naked and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison and you did not visit me.

[Note: [Col. 0519] “Then they too answer, saying: Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty, or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and fail to minister to you?”] Then they too answer, saying: Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty, or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and fail to minister to you? [Note: [Col. 0519] “Then he answers them, saying: Truly I say to you: inasmuch as you did not do it to one of these least ones, you did not do it to me.”] [Note: [Col. 0520] *jah þan ei*: see the note on verse 40. — *leitilane*: “the little ones”; all Greek witnesses have ἐλαχίστων (*elachistōn*, “least ones”).] Then he answers them, saying: Truly I say to you: inasmuch as you did not do it to one of these little ones, you did not do it to me.

[Note: [Col. 0519] “And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”] And they will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 0519] “And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished all these words, that he said to his disciples:”] And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished all these words, that he said to his disciples: [Note: [Col. 0519] “You know that after two days the Passover comes, and the Son of Man is handed over to be crucified.”] You know that after two days the Passover comes, and the Son of Man is handed over to be crucified.

[Note: [Col. 0519] “Then—”] [Note: [Col. 0520] These passages are contained in the same manuscript mentioned at XXV.38; the Codex Argenteus contains of these matters only what follows from verse 70 of chapter XXVI.]

[Note: [Col. 0520] *sai nu gahausideduþ*: Cast. adds *saikgga hausideduþ*, Schm. *sai gahausideduþ*. We had long since reached the true reading by conjecture when Mssm. also noted, in Sk., p. 182, that it is read in the Ambrosian manuscript. We are surprised that Grimm, a man of such sound judgment, attempted to defend the monstrous form *saikgga* in G. III.12.]

Then—do we still need witnesses? Behold, now you have heard the blasphemy. [Note: [Col. 0521] “Do we still need witnesses? Behold, now you have heard the blasphemy.”] What do you think? But they answered and said: He is deserving of death.

[Note: [Col. 0521] “Then they spat in his face and struck him with their fists; others struck him with the palms of their hands, saying:”] Then they spat in his face and struck him with their fists; others struck him with the palms of their hands, saying: [Note: [Col. 0521] “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is the one who struck you?”] Prophesy to us, Christ: who is the one who struck you?

[Note: [Col. 0521] “But Peter was seated outside in the courtyard, and one maidservant came to him, saying: You too were with Jesus the Galilean.”] [Note: [Col. 0521] *uta sat*: “sat outside”; misled by Cast.’s version, Sch. wrongly says that Gothic has ἔξωθεν (*exōthen*, “outside”) after ἐκάθητο (*ekathēto*, “he sat”).] But Peter was seated outside in the courtyard, and one maidservant came to him, saying: You too were with Jesus the Galilean.

[Note: [Col. 0521] “But he denied it before them all, saying: I do not know what you are saying.”] [Note: [Col. 0521] *þaim*: “them”; Gothic therefore does not reject αὐτῶν (*autōn*, “of them”), as Sch. notes. — *wa qiþis*: the fragment of the Codex Argenteus begins with these words.] But he denied it before them all, saying: I do not know what you are saying.

[Note: [Col. 0521] “But as he was going out into the gateway, another saw him and said to those there: This man too was with Jesus the Nazarene.”] [Note: [Col. 0521] *jah sa*: the Ambrosian manuscript has *jas-sa*; see the note on V.37.] But as he went out into the gateway, another saw him and said to those there: This man too was with Jesus the Nazarene.

[Note: [Col. 0521] “And again he denied it with an oath, swearing: I do not know the man.”] [Note: [Col. 0521] *afaiaik*: J. St. add *afaiair*; the Ambrosian manuscript has *laugnida*, which has the same meaning. — *svarands*: “swearing,” omitted by all Greek witnesses. B. seems to think it a gloss on *miþ aiþa*, but both manuscripts have it, and such abundance of expression is not unusual; compare Mark I.6 *vaurda qiþan* (“to speak a word”), IV.3 *saian fraiva* (“to sow seed”), VI.9 *gaskohs suljom* (“sandals on feet”), I.40 *knivam knussjands* (“kneeling on the knees”); compare the note on Matthew IX.8.] And again he denied it with an oath, swearing: I do not know the man.

[Note: [Col. 0521] “After a little while, those standing by came and said to Peter: Truly, you also are one of them, for your speech betrays you.”] [Note: [Col. 0521] *standandans*: the Ambrosian manuscript adds *standans*. — *paitrau*: the Ambrosian manuscript has *du paitrau*, but the addition *du* has been erased. — *bi sunjai*: J. St. B. Z. H. add the usual abbreviation.] After a little while those standing by came and said to Peter: Truly, you also are one of them, for your speech betrays you.

[Note: [Col. 0521] “Then he began to curse and swear that he did not know the man; and immediately a cock crowed.”] Then he began to curse and swear that he did not know the man; and immediately a cock crowed. [Note: [Col. 0521] “And Peter remembered the word of Jesus spoken to him: Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times; and he went out and wept bitterly.”] [Note: [Col. 0521] *qiþanis*: “spoken”; all Greek witnesses have εἰρηκότος (*eirēkotos*), as at Mark XV.28, *þata gamelido þata qiþano* (“the written thing, the spoken thing”) = ἡ γραφὴ ἡ λέγουσα (*hē graphē hē legousa*, “the Scripture which says”). — *afaikis*: the Ambrosian manuscript has *ïnvidis*, with the same meaning.] And Peter remembered the word of Jesus spoken to him: Before a cock crows, you will deny me three times. And he went out and wept bitterly.

[Note: [Col. 0521] “When morning came, all the priests and the elders of the people took counsel concerning Jesus, in order to put him to death.”] [Note: [Col. 0521–0522] *at maurgin*: J. St. add the usual abbreviation; B. adds *at maurgan*. — *vaurþanana*: lh. conjectures *vaurþanamma*, but both manuscripts have the accusative. *maurgin*, from nominative *maurgins*, must likewise be taken as accusative. The preposition *at* is indeed rarely construed with the accusative, but is so here and also at Mark XII.2 and Luke II.41. — *runa*: Ambrosian *garuni*. — *gudjans*: the Ambrosian manuscript adds *t* and the article *þai*. — *jah þai*: the Ambrosian fragment extends to this point.] When morning came, all the priests and elders of the people took counsel concerning Jesus, in order to put him to death.

# THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK BEGINS

[Col. 0525]

[Note: In the title, **anastodeiþ** (“begins”) is found in all Greek manuscripts; likewise in the title of Luke.]

[Col. 0525] **[Note:]** The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.

**[Note:]** As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: “Behold, I send my angel before you, who prepares your way before you.”

**[Note:]** *faura þus*: “before you,” omitted in the Greek. *Anastodeins aivanggeljons ïesuis xristaus sunaus guþs*: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, Son of God. *sve gameliþ ïst ïn esaï ïn praufetau*: As it is written in Isaiah the prophet. Behold.

**[Note:]** “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God!”

**[Note:]** *guþs unsaris*: “of our God”; the Greek has “of him.”

“I send my angel before you, who will prepare your way before you. The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Make ready the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God.”

**[Note:]** John was baptizing in the wilderness and proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.

**[Note:]** *aflageinai*: Thus the manuscript of Argenteus clearly reads it; J. St. and B. add *aflateinai*, which Z. has unjustly rejected.

“John was baptizing in the wilderness and proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. Make ready the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God.”

**[Note:]** And all the land of Judea and the inhabitants of Jerusalem went out to him, and all were baptized by him in the water of the Jordan, confessing their sins.

**[Note:]** *usïddjedun*: “they went out.” Either Ulfilas read the Greek *exeporeuonto*, or he constructed the word *land* in a collective sense, according to Gothic usage.  
*allai*: The Greek places this after *ïairusaulymeis*.

“They went out to him—all the land of Judea and the people of Jerusalem—and were all baptized by him in the water of the Jordan, confessing their sins.”

**[Note:]** John was clothed in camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist, and he ate locusts and wild honey.

**[Note:]** *haiþivisk*: The manuscript of Argenteus has *vilþi* in the margin, meaning the same; see Romans 11:17, 24.

“John was clothed in camel’s hair and had a leather belt around his waist; he ate locusts and wild honey.”

**[Note:]** And he proclaimed, saying: “After me comes one stronger than I, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to stoop down and untie.”

**[Note:]** *sa*: “this one,” omitted in the Greek.  
*þizei*: J. St. adds *þize*.  
*ïk*: “I,” omitted in the Greek.  
*anahneivands*: St. adds *anahneivauds*.

“He comes after me, stronger than I. I am not worthy to stoop down and untie the strap of his sandal.”

**[Note:]** But I baptize you in water; he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit.

**[Note:]** *aþþan*: See the note at 9:12.

“But I baptize you in water; he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit. The one who comes after me, of whom I am not worthy to stoop down and untie the strap of his sandal.”

[Col. 0527] **[Note:]** And it happened in those days that Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan.

**[Note:]** *ïohanne*: J. St. adds *ïohannes*.

“John baptized you in water, but he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit.”

Now it happened in those days that Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan.

**[Note:]** And immediately, as he came up from the water, he saw the heavens opened and the Spirit descending upon him like a dove.

**[Note:]** *usluknans*: LH, in *Ulfilas illustratus*, p. 155, says that the form *usluknandans* appears to have been written, but Z., rightly doubtful on this point in his *Grammar*, p. 55, preferred to take it as a passive participle of *uslukan*. According to grammatical rules, however, the form ought to have been *uslukanans*. We must therefore suppose either that the scribe erred in writing *usluknans* for *uslukanans*—as Grimm, *Grammar* 4.26, and Ettmüller maintain—or that *usluknans* belongs to the adjective *uslukns*; compare Luke 6:35, *usvenans*, from *usvens*.

“And immediately, coming up from the water, he saw the heavens opened and the Spirit descending upon him like a dove.”

**[Note:]** And a voice came from heaven: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased.”

**[Note:]** *qam*: “came,” as in all Greek manuscripts; the Greek has *egeneto*. Compare John 6:25.  
*ïn þuzei vaila galeikaida*: The manuscript of Argenteus has in the margin *þukei vilda*—“the one whom I desired.”

“And the voice came from heaven: ‘You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased.’”

**[Note:]** And immediately the Spirit drove him into the wilderness.

**[Note:]** *suns sai*: “Immediately, behold.” Since no Greek manuscript has any trace of *sai* here—and it is entirely contrary to the sense—while several have *eutheōs* instead of the common *euthys*, and our text normally renders *eutheōs* by *sunsaiv* (3:6; 5:29 and following; 6:25; 10:52), *sunsaiv* must certainly be read here as well.

“You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased.” And immediately, behold, the Spirit drove him into the wilderness.

**[Note:]** And he was in that wilderness forty days, tempted by Satan; he was with the wild animals, and angels ministered to him.

**[Note:]** *diuzam*: The editors add *dihzam*. The reading in the manuscript of Argenteus was undoubtedly correct, but it cannot now be established with certainty, because this passage was written on one of the leaves which an impious hand removed from the manuscript. *Diuzam* was first reached by Grimm through conjecture (*I* 606), and he repeated it after rejecting it (*II* 266; *III* 359), having been reminded of 1 Corinthians 15:32.

“And he was in that wilderness forty days, tempted by Satan; he was with the wild animals, and angels ministered to him.”

**[Note:]** But after John had been handed over, Jesus came into Galilee proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom of God.

**[Note:]** *atgibans*: J. St. adds *atihdans*.

“But after John had been handed over, Jesus came into Galilee proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom of God.”

**[Note:]** He said that the time had been fulfilled, the kingdom of God had drawn near; repent and believe in the gospel.

**[Note:]** *qiþands*: Before this word Ulfilas, with the manuscripts, omits the Greek *kai*.

“The kingdom of God has been fulfilled and has drawn near. Repent and believe in the gospel.”

**[Note:]** And as he was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew, Simon’s brother, casting a net into the sea; for they were fishermen.

**[Note:]** *jah warbonds*: Ulfilas’ manuscripts seem to have read the Greek *kai paragōn*; see 2:14.  
*andraian*: St. adds *andrajan*.  
*þis seimonis*: “of this Simon,” omitted in the Greek.  
*fiskjans*: St. adds *fiskians*.

“Repent and believe in the gospel.” And as he was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew, Simon’s brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen.

**[Note:]** And Jesus said to them: “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of human beings.”

**[Note:]** *ïgqis*: J. St. adds *ïgvis*; Maresh is correct, p. 414.

“And Jesus said to them: ‘Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of human beings.’”

**[Note:]** And immediately they left their nets and followed him.

“And immediately they left their nets and followed him.”

**[Note:]** And going on a little farther, he saw James, the son of Zebedee, and John, his brother, who were also in the boat preparing their nets.

**[Note:]** *jainþro ïnngaggands*: This agrees with all Greek manuscripts. J. St. adds *ïngaggands*.  
*framis leitil*: J. and Z. add *framisleitl*; St. and B. add *framisleita*. Z., here and in *Versuch*, p. 86, adds *fram ïs leitil*. What was written in the manuscript of Argenteus is unknown, nor did LH record it; today it cannot be established because this leaf was torn from the manuscript. Grimm, *III* 591, compare 97, correctly takes *framis* as an adverbial comparative, meaning “farther,” and corresponding to Greek *pro-* in compound verbs, as in Romans 13:12, *framis galaiþ* = “he advanced.” But when he says that *leitl* is a shorter form of *leitil*, it seems more correct to us to suppose that *leitl* arose from *leitil* through scribal negligence.  
*zaibaidaiaus*: St. adds *zaibaidajaus*.  
*ïohanne*: J. St. adds *ïohannes*.

“And going on a little farther, he saw James, the son of Zebedee, and John, his brother, in the boat preparing their nets.”

**[Note:]** And immediately he called them; and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired servants and followed him.

“And immediately he called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired servants and followed him.”

**[Note:]** And they entered Capernaum; and immediately, on the Sabbath, he entered the synagogue and taught them.

**[Note:]** *synagogen*: Z. adds *syn gogin*.  
*ïns*: “them,” omitted in the Greek.

“And they entered Capernaum. Immediately, on the Sabbath, he entered the synagogue and taught them.”

**[Note:]** And they were astonished at his teaching, for he was teaching them as one having authority and not as the scribes.

“They were astonished at his teaching, for he was teaching them as one having authority and not as the scribes.”

**[Note:]** And in their synagogue there was a man with an unclean spirit, and he cried out.

“And in their synagogue there was a man with an unclean spirit, and he cried out.”

**[Note:]** He said: “Stop! What have we to do with you, Jesus Nazarene? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God.”

**[Note:]** *nazorenai*: Gothic consistently has this form, although the Greek has either *Nazērēnos* or *Nazōraios*; compare 14:67 and 16:6.  
*þu*: “you,” omitted in the Greek.

“And he cried out, saying: ‘Stop! What have we to do with you, Jesus Nazarene? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God.’”

**[Note:]** And Jesus rebuked him, saying: “Be silent and come out of him, unclean spirit.”

**[Note:]** *ahma unhrainja*: “unclean spirit,” omitted in all Greek manuscripts except Codex D.

“And Jesus rebuked him, saying: ‘Be silent and come out of him, unclean spirit.’”

**[Note:]** And the unclean spirit convulsed him and, crying out with a loud voice, came out of him.

“And the unclean spirit convulsed him and, crying out with a loud voice, came out of him.”

**[Note:]** And they were all amazed, so that they debated among themselves, saying: “What is this? What is this new teaching? For with authority he even commands the unclean spirits, and they obey him.”

**[Note:]** *afslauþnodedun*: B. adds *afslauþnodeaun*. Ulfilas adds *sildaleikjandans*, “being astonished,” which all the Greek manuscripts omit; see the note at Matthew 9:8 and 1 Corinthians 4:25.  
*laiseino*: See the note at 6:2.

“And they were all amazed, so that they debated among themselves, saying: ‘What is this? What is this new teaching? With authority he commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him.’”

[Col. 0529] **[Note:]** And his fame immediately spread throughout all the surrounding region of Galilee.

“And immediately his fame spread throughout all the surrounding region of Galilee.”

**[Note:]** And immediately, leaving the synagogue, they entered the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John.

**[Note:]** *ïohannen*: J. St. adds *ïohannes*.

“And immediately, leaving the synagogue, they entered the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John.”

**[Note:]** Simon’s mother-in-law was lying sick with a fever, and immediately they told him about her.

“Simon’s mother-in-law was lying sick with a fever, and immediately they told him about her.”

**[Note:]** And approaching, he raised her up, taking her by the hand; and the fever left her immediately, and she ministered to them.

“And approaching, he raised her up, taking her by the hand; and the fever left her immediately, and she ministered to them.”

**[Note:]** And when evening came, after the sun had set, they brought to him all who were ill and those possessed by demons.

**[Note:]** *gasaggq sauïl*: This is correctly read by LH in *Ulfilas illustratus*, pp. 113–114. J. St. add *gasag ju sa uïl*; B. and Hz. add *gasaggq sau ïl*.

“When evening came, after the sun had set, they brought to him all who were ill and those possessed by demons.”

**[Note:]** And the whole city was gathered at the door.

“And the whole city was gathered at the door.”

**[Note:]** And he healed many who were ill with various diseases, and cast out many demons; and he did not permit the demons to speak, because they knew him.

**[Note:]** *usvarp*: J. St. adds *usvairp*.

“And he healed many who were ill with various diseases, and cast out many demons; and he did not permit the demons to speak, because they knew him.”

**[Note:]** And rising very early, while it was still dark, he went out and departed to a deserted place, and there he prayed.

**[Note:]** *air uhtvon*: Z. conjectures *airuh tvon* rashly. The common reading is confirmed by the occurrence of the same word in related languages; see Schmid, *Schwäbisches Wörterbuch*, p. 8, and Graff, *Althochdeutscher Sprachschatz* I, p. 138. Ulfilas, with the manuscripts and versions, omits the Greek *lian*.

“And rising before dawn, while it was still dark, he went out and went to a deserted place, and there he prayed.”

**[Note:]** And Simon and those who were with him followed him.

“And Simon and those who were with him followed him.”

**[Note:]** And when they found him, they said to him: “Everyone is looking for you.”

**[Note:]** *þuk sokjand*: This agrees with the Greek.

“And when they found him, they said to him: ‘Everyone is looking for you.’”

**[Note:]** And he said to them: “Let us go elsewhere, to the neighboring villages and towns, so that I may preach there also; for that is why I came.”

**[Note:]** *bisunjane*: “around, nearby.” Ulfilas, together with Codex D, seems to have read the Greek *engys*.  
*haimom jah baurgim*: “villages and towns,” corresponding to the Greek *kōmopoleis*. J. St., B., and Hz. add *haimon*; see LH, *Ulfilas illustratus*, p. 229.

“And he said to them: ‘Let us go elsewhere, to the neighboring villages and towns, so that I may preach there also; for that is why I came.’”

**[Note:]** And he was preaching in their synagogues throughout all Galilee and casting out demons.

**[Note:]** *ïn synagogim*: “in the synagogues”; the Greek has “into the synagogues.”

“And he was preaching in their synagogues throughout all Galilee and casting out demons.”

**[Note:]** And a leper came to him, entreating him, kneeling before him, and saying to him: “If you will, you can cleanse me.”

**[Note:]** *knussjands*: Ulfilas, with the manuscripts, omits the Greek pronoun “him.”

“And a leper came to him, entreating him, kneeling before him, and saying to him: ‘If you will, you can cleanse me.’”

**[Note:]** But Jesus, moved with compassion, stretched out his hand, touched him, and said to him: “I will; be cleansed.”

**[Note:]** *seina*: “his,” omitted in all Greek manuscripts except one, Codex D, according to Maresh, p. 418.

“But Jesus, moved with compassion, stretched out his hand, touched him, and said to him: ‘I will; be cleansed.’”

**[Note:]** And when he had said this, the leprosy immediately left him, and he was cleansed.

**[Note:]** *þata*: “this,” omitted in all Greek manuscripts.  
*ïesus*: Since all Greek manuscripts at this place and at Luke 6:12; 8:10; John 18:1 have the demonstrative pronoun (*autos* or *ho*), it may be suspected that *ïs* should be read here, for which a scribe could easily have written *ïesus*. Perhaps the same correction should be made at 2:25, where, apart from the Syriac and Armenian versions, no manuscript has *ïesus*. J. St. and Luc. at Luke, place B, nevertheless preferred *ïesus*, following all the Greek manuscripts.

“Jesus, moved with compassion, stretched out his hand, touched him, and said to him: ‘I will; be cleansed.’ And immediately the leprosy left him, and he was cleansed.”

The matter cannot, however, be denied that there are places where such an error is less readily supposed—for example Mark 5:22, where *iuis* (that is, *ïesuis*) appears, while all the Greek manuscripts consistently have *autou*. It is still more difficult to decide about Mark 6:55: the reading *ei ïs vesi* corresponds to the Latin versions; if *ei ïesus vesi* were read, it would agree better with Codex D and with those versions with which Gothic commonly agrees elsewhere. I have not wished to accept Benzel’s judgment that Ulfilas read *ekeinos* for *ekei*. To settle the matter here, we add that at Mark 1:45 and Luke 5:34, editors have wrongly replaced *ïs*—which the manuscript of Argenteus has, together with all Greek manuscripts—with *ïesus*, against the authority of the manuscript. The same is true of Mark 2:15, where all editors have done this.

**[Note:]** *þata þrutsfill*: All Greek manuscripts except one from Mi. place this after *ïmma*.

**[Note:]** And he sternly warned him and immediately sent him away.

**[Note:]** And he said to him: “See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded as a testimony to them.”

**[Note:]** *mannhun*: Z. adds *manhun*.  
*gudjin*: Griesbach rashly contends that Ulfilas read *archierei*, “high priest,” instead of *hierei*, “priest.” Ulfilas uses *gudja* and *auhumists gudja* interchangeably, and one cannot for that reason infer, at 2:26, that he read the simple *hiereōs* in his manuscript, as the same scholar did.

“And he sent him away and said to him: ‘See that you say nothing to anyone; but go, show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded as a testimony to them.’”

**[Note:]** But he went out and began to proclaim and spread the word widely, so that he could no longer openly enter a city; he remained outside in deserted places, and they came to him from everywhere.

**[Note:]** *iþ ïs*: See the note at 1:42.

“But he went out and began to proclaim and spread the word widely, so that Jesus could no longer openly enter a city; he remained outside in deserted places, and they came to him from everywhere.”

**[Note:]** And again, after some days, he entered Capernaum, and it was heard that he was in the house.

**[Note:]** *galaiþ aftra*: This agrees with the Greek.  
*gafrehun*: “they learned, discovered”; all Greek manuscripts have *ēkousthē*, “it was heard.”  
*ïn garda*: “in the house”; the Greek has “into a house.”

“And again, after some days, he entered Capernaum, and it was heard that he was in the house.”

**[Note:]** And immediately many gathered, so that there was no longer room—not even at the door—and he spoke the word to them.

**[Note:]** *at daura*: Ulfilas, together with manuscripts 28 and 131, has the Greek equivalent of “at the door.”  
*gamostedun*: *gamotan* means “to have room, to be contained”; see John 8:37 and 2 Corinthians 7:2.

“And immediately many gathered, so that there was no longer room—not even at the door—and he spoke the word to them.”

“And they came to him, bringing a paralytic carried by four men.”

**[Note:]** *fidvorim*: The manuscript of Argenteus and the editors add *fidvorin*.

**[Note:]** And since they could not bring him near because of the crowd, they uncovered the roof where Jesus was; and having dug through it, they lowered the pallet on which the paralytic was lying.

*lag*: All Greek manuscripts place this after *usliþa*.

“And since they could not bring him near because of the crowd, they uncovered the roof where Jesus was; and having dug through it, they lowered the pallet on which the paralytic was lying.”

**[Note:]** Seeing their faith, Jesus said to the paralytic: “Child, your sins are forgiven you.”

**[Note:]** *þus—þeinos*: “to you—your”; the Greek manuscripts have *sou* and *soi*, as does the Gothic version at verse 9.

“Seeing their faith, Jesus said to the paralytic: ‘Child, your sins are forgiven you.’”

**[Note:]** Some of the scribes were sitting there and reasoning in their hearts.

“Some of the scribes were sitting there and reasoning in their hearts.”

**[Note:]** “Why does this man speak blasphemies in this way? Who can forgive sins except one—God?”

“And they were reasoning in their hearts: ‘Why does this man speak blasphemies in this way? Who can forgive sins except one—God?’”

**[Note:]** And immediately Jesus, knowing in his spirit that they were reasoning in this way within themselves, said to them: “Why are you reasoning about this in your hearts?”

**[Note:]** *mitoþ þata*: This agrees with all Greek manuscripts.

“And immediately Jesus, knowing in his spirit that they were reasoning in this way within themselves, said to them: ‘Why are you reasoning about this in your hearts?’”

**[Note:]** Which is easier: to say to this paralytic, “Your sins are forgiven,” or to say, “Rise, take up your pallet, and walk”?

**[Note:]** *afletanda*: The manuscript of Argenteus adds *afleþanda*.  
*þus—þeinos*: See the note at verse 5.  
*jah*: “and,” omitted in the Greek.  
*þeinata*: All Greek manuscripts place this before *þata*.

“Which is easier: to say to this paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise, take up your pallet, and walk’?”

**[Note:]** But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—he said to the paralytic:

**[Note:]** “I say to you, rise, take up your pallet, and go to your house.”

**[Note:]** *nimuh*: Some say that Ulfilas omitted the Greek *kai*, “and,” but they are mistaken, not knowing that the particle *-uh* has a connective force; thus at 14:13 *qaþuh* = “and he says.” *Nimuh* stands for *jah nim*, “and take,” as stated at verse 9; the Goth is accustomed to vary his expression.

“And so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the paralytic—“I say to you, rise, take up your pallet, and go to your house.”

**[Note:]** And he rose immediately, took up the pallet, and went out before them all, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying: “We have never seen anything like this.”

**[Note:]** *hauhidedun mikiljandans*: See the note at Matthew 9:8. St. additionally has *haubidedun*.  
*þatei*: St. adds *þaþei*.  
*gasewum*: J. St., together with the manuscript of Argenteus, has *gasewun*, which corresponds neither to the Greek nor to the sense. In the manuscript the form is *gasewu*, evidently a scribal error.

“And he rose immediately, took up the pallet, and went out before them all, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying: ‘We have never seen anything like this.’”

**[Note:]** And he went out again beside the sea; and all the crowd came to him, and he taught them.

**[Note:]** *galaiþ*: St. adds *gelaiþ*.  
*jah all—ïmma*: This clause does not occur in the text of the manuscript of Argenteus but appears in the margin. J. St. and B. add: “and all the crowd went out to him.” In the manuscript, the letters *ns* of *manageins* were separated, beginning a new verse; they took them for *us*. Mixing the correct reading with this false one, the compiler of the Hz. manuscript produced: “and all the crowd went out.” 

“And he went out again beside the sea; and all the crowd came to him, and he taught them.”

*balgins*: The second editor, J. St., adds *baljins*; they likewise soon afterward add *baljeis*.  
*giutand*: “They pour”; all Greek manuscripts have the impersonal expression *blēteon*, “it must be put in,” while Ulfilas has the form found in Luke 5:38, where some manuscripts have *ballousi*, “they pour.”

*faurlageinais*: J. St. adds *fauralageinais*; see Luke 6:4.

**[Note:]** *hailidedi*: All Greek manuscripts place this after *daga*; J. St. additionally adds *jau*, “whether,” following Luke 6:7, and Ulfilas, with the manuscripts, omits the Greek pronoun “him.”

“And they watched him to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they might accuse him.”

**[Note:]** *ïn*: “in,” as in the Greek.

“And he said to them: ‘Is it permitted on the Sabbaths to do good or to do evil, to save a life or to destroy it?’ But they were silent.”

**[Note:]** *ustaig*: This is the form in the manuscript of Argenteus; the editors have *usstaig*, which is more correct, but in compound verbs the second *s* is often omitted by scribes. Compare Matthew 27:51, *diskritnoda*; Luke 8:55, *ustoþ*; 14:14, *ustassai*; see Massmann, *Sk.* p. 59. The same occurs when one verb ends in *s* and the next begins with *s*; see the note at Mark 10:45 and 16:1.

[Col. 0535] **[Note:]** And to have authority to heal diseases and cast out demons.

“And to have authority to heal diseases and cast out demons.”

**[Note:]** And he gave Simon the name Peter.

**[Note:]** *paitrus*: According to grammatical rules, it should have been written *paitru*, in the accusative case; see Luke 1:13, *haitais namo ïs ïohannen*, “you shall call his name John,” and compare Matthew 9:9. Ettmüller ought not to have doubted this. What Grimm says in *Grammar* 4.622 is correct concerning *haltan* and *vopjan*, but not concerning *namjan*. Nor do we doubt that when Graff, in *Göttingische Gelehrte Anzeigen* 1836, p. 1792, says, “After the words *namnjan* the nominative is always constructed,” he was thinking of the passive construction. We have correctly noted that *paitrus* is confirmed also by the parallel passage at Luke 6:14: “whom he also named Peter.” Furthermore, at verse 17, instead of *ïakobau* and *ïohanne* as datives, we preferred *jakobu* and *johannem* as accusatives, because the sense requires it. We did not consider that these datives might depend on *gasatida*, since *jah gasatida ïm* follows. If Ettmüller’s view of this passage is correct, we cannot avoid saying that Ulfilas paid too little attention to the sense.

“And he gave Simon the name Peter.”

**[Note:]** And James, the son of Zebedee, and John, the brother of James; and he gave them the name Boanerges, which means “sons of thunder.”

“And he appointed the twelve to be with him, to send them out to preach, and to have authority to heal diseases and cast out demons. And he gave Simon the name Peter; and James, the son of Zebedee, and John, the brother of James—he gave them the name Boanerges, which means ‘sons of thunder.’”
ïakobau---ïohanne] The two datives have nothing on which they can depend; the sense requires that they be joined as accusatives to the verb *gavaurhta*. Otherwise, instead of *ïohanne*, J. St. has *ïohannes*.

He gave Simon the name Peter. And James, the son of Zebedee, and John, the brother of James, and he gave them the name Boanerges, that is, “sons of thunder.” And Andrew and Philip and Bartholomew and Matthew and Thomas and James, the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus and Simon, the Cananaean,

[Note: [Col. 0535] And Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him.]

matþaiu] St. has *matþaju*.

kananeiten] St. Z. has *kananeiþen*.

gave them the name Boanerges, that is, “sons of thunder.” And Andrew and Philip and Bartholomew and

[Note: [Col. 0535] and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him.]

Matthew and Thomas and James, the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus and Simon, the Cananaean, and Judas Iscariot,

[Note: [Col. 0535] And they went into the house, and the crowd gathered together, so that they could not even eat bread.]

atïddjedun] St. has *atïddiedun*. Likewise *gaïddia* for *gaïddja*, *matian* for *matjan*, and frequently elsewhere. Otherwise, Ulfila omits Greek *πάλιν* and *αὐτοῦς*.

entered the house. And the crowd gathered, so that they were not even able to eat bread. When those associated with him heard of it, they went out to seize him, for they said that he was beside himself.

fram---anþarai] “from—others,” Greek *οἱ παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ*.

usgaisiþs] Grimm, *Grammatik* IV, 26, considers that *usgeisiþs* should be emended; see the Glossary under *Geisan*.

And the scribes who came from Jerusalem said that he has Beelzebul, and that by the chief of demons he casts out these demons.

ïairusaulymai] J. adds *ïairusaulyma*.

And, calling them to him in parables, he said to them: How can Satan cast out Satan?

gajukom] J. St. adds *gajukon*.

waiva] So the Codex Argenteus; not *weaiva*, as B. says he reads there.

And if a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand; and if a house is divided against itself, that house cannot stand. And if Satan has risen up against himself and has been divided, he cannot stand, but has an end.

satana usstoþ] The editions add *satanaus stoþ*. *Satanaus* is never used in the nominative, but *satana* occurs at J. XIII, 27; II Corinthians XI, 14; or *satanas* at Mark III, 23.

gastandan] J. St. B. add *standan*.

ak] St. adds *ah*.

. . . saiwands] The editions add *gasaiwands*. Ih. notes that he read *gaisaiwands* in the Codex Argenteus; but the learned man is mistaken. What preceded *saiwands* can indeed be conjectured, but cannot be stated with certainty, because the parchment is perforated at this point and only a perpendicular line remains. Ih. takes this for the letter *i*. But we fear that the *ga* added by conjecture is intended merely to fill the space. Since Ulfila often renders Greek *καί* at the beginning of sentences by *jah—þan* (see III, 6, 31; Luke VI, 6; and elsewhere), without doubt one should read *jah saiwands þan*, and it should be assumed that the Goth read, with the manuscripts, *καὶ ἰδών*. The remaining line, however, is the latter part of the letter *h*.

The editors’ reading is false, because the abstract form *unhrainjai*, which they posit, cannot occur here with the article; nor does *usgaleiþan* (“to go out”) correspond to the Greek *εἰσελθεῖν*, nor is this compound found anywhere else. The reading we have supplied agrees with the Gothic language and is sufficiently confirmed by the parallel passages Matthew VIII, 32 and Luke VIII, 33, where *galiþun* is read. Although this emendation of ours was also approved by Ettmüller and is so certain that every competent reader ought to agree with it, Graff, *Althochdeutsche Sprachschatz* V, 36, nevertheless rejected it—and who would believe it?—and retains the defective reading of the editions (see also Bopp, *Vocalism*, p. 102); nor does it seem to him that *usgaliþun* here distorts the sense. No one, surely, will begrudge him that opinion!
