And King Herod heard—for his name had become well known—and he said: “John the baptizer has risen from the dead; therefore these powers are at work in him.” [Note: [Col. 0545] “And King Herod heard…”] [Note: [Col. 0545] “*duþþe*”: So far from supposing that Ulfilas omitted Greek καί, we believe that *duþþe*—for *duh þe*, and that for *du uh þe*—was spoken instead of *jah duþe*; see L. XIV, 21, and compare the notes at II, 11 and J. XVIII, 26.]

But others said: “He is Elijah”; and others said: “He is a prophet, like one of the prophets.” [Note: [Col. 0545] “*þatei*”: the primary manuscript; St adds *þatai*.]

But when Herod heard, he said: “John, whom I beheaded—this is he; he has risen from the dead.” [Note: [Col. 0545] “And Herod heard…”] [Note: [Col. 0545] “*ïohanne*”: J and St add *ïohannes*. — “*sa ïst sah*”: “he is the one,” Greek οὗτος. — “*sah*”: St adds *jah*.]

For Herod himself had sent and seized John and bound him in prison because of Herodias, the wife of Philip, his brother, because he had married her. [Note: [Col. 0545] “For Herod…”] [Note: [Col. 0545] “*hairodiadins*”: see the note at M. VIII, 28. — “*broþrs*”: J and St add *broþr*.]

For John had said to Herod: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.” [Note: [Col. 0545] “For John said to Herod…”]

But Herodias plotted against him and wanted to kill him, but she could not. [Note: [Col. 0545] “But Herodias plotted…”] [Note: [Col. 0546] “*herodianai svor*”: This reading of the Codex Argenteus, which all the editors have reproduced, is undoubtedly corrupt. B. and L. already suspected that *saisvor* should be read instead of *svor*; L. most correctly says that, by comparison with the Anglo-Saxon verb *syrvan*, the verb must be *sveran*, from which that preterite is derived; compare *taitok* from *tekan* and similar forms. The syllable *sai* that we require is concealed in the final part of the monstrous form *herodianai*, while the letters *s* and *n* are frequently interchanged in Gothic manuscripts, as we have seen in verse 2 of this chapter; add what was noted at M. VII, 23. Once the syllable *sai* is removed, *herodia* remains. The final *s* of this word was omitted by the scribe because it was also the initial letter of the following verb. See the note at III, 13 for how often this occurs.]

The woman Herodias was plotting against him and wanted to kill him, but she could not, because Herod feared John, knowing him to be a righteous and holy man; he protected him, and when he heard him, he did many things and gladly listened to him. [Note: [Col. 0545] “For Herod feared John…”] [Note: [Col. 0546] “*herodis*”: J and St add *herodes*.]

And when an opportune day came, when Herod, on the occasion of his birthday, held a banquet for his nobles, the tribunes, and the leading men of Galilee, [Note: [Col. 0545] “And when an opportune day came…”] [Note: [Col. 0545] “And when Herod’s birthday came…”] and when the daughter of Herodias entered and danced and pleased Herod and those reclining with him, the king said to the girl: “Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you.” [Note: [Col. 0546] “*dauhtar*”: According to the sense, as Ib. explains (Ulfilas illustratus, p. 238), this is either an unusual dative form or a scribal error for *dauhtr*. Since accusatives used absolutely are also found at M. VI, 3, we believe the reading of the Codex Argenteus is correct. Otherwise Ulfilas, together with the manuscripts, has αὐτῆς.]

And he swore to her: “Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half my kingdom.” [Note: [Col. 0546] “*bidjais mik*”: according to the Greek.]

But she went out and said to her mother: “What shall I ask?” And she said: “The head of John the baptizer.” [Note: [Col. 0545] “But she went out…”] [Note: [Col. 0546] “*ïohannis*”: St adds *johannis*, as also in verse 25.]

And immediately she entered quickly before the king and asked, saying: “I want you to give me at once on a platter the head of John the baptizer.” [Col. 0547] [Note: [Col. 0545] “And entering immediately…”] [Note: [Col. 0546] “*gibais*”: Ulfilas, together with the manuscripts, has Greek ἐξαυτῆς. — “*ïohannis*”: see the note at verse 24.]

And she went out and said to her mother: “What shall I ask?” But she said: “The head of John the baptizer.” And immediately she went in haste to the king and asked, saying: “I want you to give me on a platter the head of John the baptizer.” [Note: [Col. 0545] “And entering immediately…”]

And the king became sad because of the oaths and because of those reclining with him; he did not want to reject her. [Note: [Col. 0547] “And this king became sad…”] [Note: [Col. 0547] “*ïn*”: “because of,” according to the Greek.]

And immediately the king sent a guard and ordered him to bring his head. And he went and beheaded him in the prison, [Note: [Col. 0547] “And immediately this king, sending a guard…”] [Note: [Col. 0547] “*ïnsandjands*”: J and St add *ïnsandjans*. — “*spaikulatur*”: St adds *spaiculatur*. — “*afmaimait*”: St adds *afmaimat*.] and brought his head on a platter and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother. [Note: [Col. 0547] “And he brought his head…”] [Note: [Col. 0547] “*þizai*”: J and St have *þize*.]

And when his disciples heard, they came and took his body and placed it in a tomb.

And the apostles came to Jesus and told him everything, including all that they had done. [Note: [Col. 0547] “And the apostles came…”] [Note: [Col. 0547] “*gaïddjedun*”: see the note at III, 20.] [lacuna] And they landed. [Note: [Col. 0547] “And they landed.”]

And as they were going out of the boat, immediately recognizing him, [Note: [Col. 0547] “And as they went out of the boat…”] they ran through the whole region and began carrying the sick on beds wherever they heard that he was. [Note: [Col. 0547] “And running through the whole region…”] [Note: [Col. 0547] “*badjam*”: St adds *badiam*. — “*bairan*”: Ulfilas, together with Codex φ, seems to have read φέρειν instead of περιφέρειν. — “*ïs*”: see the note at I, 42.]

And wherever he entered villages or cities or settlements, they laid the sick in the marketplaces and begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment; and as many as touched him were healed. [Note: [Col. 0547] “And wherever he entered…”] [Note: [Col. 0547] “*ïn*”: secondary witnesses have *m*; according to the Greek. — “*gagga*”: “street” or “marketplace”; Ulfilas seems, instead of Greek ἀγοραῖς, to have read πλατείαις or πλατείᾳ, as in the Latin versions; compare XI, 4.]

And the Pharisees and some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem gathered around him. [Note: [Col. 0547] “And the Pharisees gathered around him…”] And when they saw some of his disciples eating bread with common hands—that is, unwashed hands— [Note: [Col. 0547] “And seeing some of his disciples…”] [Note: [Col. 0547] “*gamainjaim*”: St adds *gamainiaim*. — “*unþvahanaim*”: J and St add *unþvaihanaim*.]

But the Pharisees and all the Jews, unless they wash their hands frequently, do not eat, holding to the tradition of their elders. [Note: [Col. 0547] “But the Pharisees and all the Jews…”] [Note: [Col. 0547] “*ïþ*”: “but,” though the Greek has γάρ; likewise J. VI, 6 and often. — “*ufta*”: “frequently”; Ulfilas, together with the Latin versions, seems to have read πυκνά; see L. V, 33.]

And when they return from the marketplace, unless they wash, they do not eat; and there are many other things they have received for observance: washings of cups, pitchers, kettles, and couches.

Then the Pharisees and scribes asked him: “Why do your disciples not walk according to what the elders handed down, but eat bread with unwashed hands?” [Note: [Col. 0547] “Then the Pharisees and scribes asked him…”] [Note: [Col. 0547] “*þaþroh*”: J and St add *þaþro*. — “*þan*”: “but,” according to all Greek manuscripts. — “*unþvahanaim*”: “unwashed,” Greek κοιναῖς.]

But he answered and said to them: “Isaiah prophesied well about you hypocrites, as it is written: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart keeps itself far from me.’” [Note: [Col. 0547] “But he answered…”] [Note: [Col. 0548] “*hairto*”: St adds *hairþo*.]

“In vain they honor me, teaching doctrines that are human commandments.” [Note: [Col. 0547] “But in vain they honor me…”] [Note: [Col. 0548] “*mik blotand*”: according to the Greek.]

For you abandon God’s commandment and hold to human tradition: washings of pitchers and cups, and you do many other similar things. [Note: [Col. 0547] “For you abandon…”] [Note: [Col. 0548] “*raihtis*”: “for”; Griesbach incorrectly notes that Gothic omits Greek γάρ. — “*svaleikata*”: J and St add *div*.]

And he said to them: “You set aside God’s commandment well, so that you may establish your own tradition.” [Note: [Col. 0547] “And he said to them…”] [Note: [Col. 0548] “*fastaiþ*”: St adds *fastaih*.]

For Moses said: “Honor your father and your mother,” and “Whoever speaks evil of father or mother shall surely die.” [Note: [Col. 0547] “For Moses indeed said…”] [Note: [Col. 0548] “*sverai*”: Hz. adds *sveran*. — “*seinamma* and *seinai*”: “his” and “her,” according to all Greek manuscripts; J, St, and B add *seina* instead of *seinai*.]

But you say: “If a man says to his father or mother, ‘Whatever benefit you might receive from me is *kaurban*’”—that is, a gift— [Note: [Col. 0547] “But you say…”] [Note: [Col. 0548] “*seinamma*”: “his,” according to all Greek manuscripts. — “*þiswah þatei*”: J and St add *þiswa þatei*.]

then you no longer allow him to do anything for his father or mother, [Note: [Col. 0547] “And you do not permit him…”] [Note: [Col. 0548] “*ni*”: “not,” while most Greek manuscripts have οὐκέτι.] nullifying the word of God by this commandment of yours, which you have handed down. And you do many similar things.” (See the following page.) [Note: [Col. 0548] “*þizai—þoei*”: J and St leave a lacuna. The reading we supplied was first adopted by B. and afterward by Ih.; whether correctly cannot be said, because this leaf is one of those stolen. — “*anabusnai*”: “tradition”; it appears that Ulfilas read Greek ἐντολῇ or ἐντάλματι (see verses 7 and 9), whereas all Greek manuscripts have παραδόσει, which in other passages is usually rendered *anafilhs* (verse 3); see, however, 1 Cor. XI, 2. — “*galeik*”: J and St incorrectly add *anþar*, which not even the Greek has here. — “*taujiþ*”: St adds *tavjiþ*.]

And summoning the whole crowd, he said to them: “Hear me, all of you, and understand: nothing exists outside a person that, entering into him, can defile him; but what comes out of a person is what defiles the person.” [Note: [Col. 0549] “And summoning the whole crowd…”] [Note: [Col. 0549] “Nothing entering from outside a person…”] [Note: [Col. 0549] “*ni vaihts*”: J, St, and B have *ni vaiht*, and that is more correct, since *vaihts* is used in this way only as a predicate: J. VIII, 54, *so hauheins meina ni vaihts ïst* (“this my glory is nothing”); 1 Cor. X, 20, *ni þatei þo galiugaguda vaihts sijaina* (“not that the idol should be anything”); VII, 19, *þata bimait ni vaihts ïst* (“circumcision is nothing”), where *ni vaiht*, added by an ignorant scribe, must be removed from the text; XIII, 2, *jabai friaþva ni habau, ni vaihts ïm* (“if I do not have love, I am nothing”). — “*utaþro*”: J, St, and B add *uzaþro*. — “*þatei magi*”: J, St, and B add *þata* before *mag*. — “*utgaggando—mannan*”: J, St, and B omit *usgaggando af ïmma*; J and St add *ïna*. Apart from this, instead of *us mann* (“from a person”), the Greek has ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ.]

And calling all the crowd to him, he said: “Listen to me, all of you, and understand. Nothing from outside enters a person that can defile him, but what comes out of a person is what defiles the person.”

“If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.” [Note: [Col. 0549] “If anyone has ears…”] [Note: [Col. 0549] “*hausjandona*”: see the note at IV, 9.]

And when he entered the house away from the crowd, his disciples asked him about this parable. [Note: [Col. 0549] “And when he entered the house…”] [Note: [Col. 0549] “*us—verse 19 usgagg*”: J, St, and B mark a lacuna. The readings now present are due to Ihrio, who says that these verses were extremely difficult to read; nevertheless, he often erred.]

And he said to them: “Are you also so without understanding? Do you not understand that everything entering a person from outside cannot defile him, because it does not enter his heart, but his belly, and goes out into the latrine, cleansing all foods?” [Note: [Col. 0549] “And he said to them…”] [Note: [Col. 0549] “*jah*”: secondary witness Z adds *ïah*. — “*unvitans*”: Codex Argenteus, according to Ih., adds *ïnvitans*. Ih. vainly tries to defend this reading, although he prefers *unvitans*. *unvits* also occurs at 2 Cor. XI, 19, 23; XII, 6, 11; compare *unviti* at Mark VII, 22. Z silently placed *unvitans* in the text. — “*þaumei*”: “because,” see the note at Phil. II, 24. — “*ïnngaggando*”: Ih. and Z add *ïngaggando*; Ih. wrongly says that *ïst* must also be supplied.]

And he said: “What comes out of a person is what defiles the person. For from within, out of the human heart, evil thoughts come out: fornications, adulteries, murders, [Note: [Col. 0549] “But he said that what comes out of a person…”] thefts, greed, wickedness, deceit, indecency, an evil eye, blasphemies, arrogance, folly; [Note: [Col. 0549] “For from within the hearts of people…”] [Note: [Col. 0549] “*aglaitei*”: Griesbach incorrectly treats this as plural, but we fear that his note belongs to the word *βλασφημία*, since there is uncertainty about *vajamereins*: whether it is the plural nominative of *vajamerei* or the singular. Although *vajamerei* must be written at J. X, 33, two forms of the same noun are nevertheless found, such as *veitvodei* and *veitvodeins*, *sviknei* and *svikneins*, *hrainei* and *hraineins*. And at Eph. IV, 31 *vajamereins* is again written, where none of the Greek manuscripts recognizes the plural βλασφημίας.]

all these evils come out from within and defile the person.” [Note: [Col. 0549] “All these evils come out from within…”] [Note: [Col. 0550] “*þo alla*”: according to the Greek.]

And rising from there, he went into the region of Tyre and Sidon; and entering a house, he did not want anyone to know it, yet he could not remain hidden. [Note: [Col. 0549] “And rising from there…”] [Note: [Col. 0550] “*usstandands*”: St adds *ustandands*.]

For a woman, having heard about him—whose daughter had an unclean spirit—came and fell at his feet. [Note: [Col. 0549] “For a woman hearing about him…”] [Note: [Col. 0550] “*gahausjandei*, etc.”: Griesbach is wrong to say that Ulfilas read ἀλλ᾽ εὐθὺς ἀκούσασα γυνή, since the text follows the commonly received reading. — “*dauhtar*”: Ulfilas, together with the manuscripts, has αὐτῆς. — “*fotum*”: Codex Argenteus (?) and the editions; Hz. adds *fotun*.]

And he could not be hidden. For when she heard about him, the woman came, whose daughter had an unclean spirit. [Note: [Col. 0549] “But this woman was a gentile, Syrophoenician by birth…”] [Note: [Col. 0550] “*saurinifynikiska*”: J and St add *sauraifyniska*; B has *sauraifynikiska*, perhaps correctly. — “*usvaurpi*”: J and St add a sign of division. — “*dauhtr*”: J adds *dauhtar*, St *dauþar*, Z *dauþr*.]

And she came and fell at his feet. Now the woman was a gentile, Syrophoenician by birth, and she begged him to cast the demon out of her daughter.

And Jesus said to her: “Let the children first be satisfied, for it is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs.” [Note: [Col. 0549] “But Jesus said to her…”]

But she answered and said to him: “Yes, Lord; for even the dogs under the table eat from the children’s crumbs.” [Note: [Col. 0549] “But she answered…”] [Note: [Col. 0550] “*ïmma*”: “to him,” according to all Greek manuscripts.]

And he said to her: “Because of this word, go; the demon has gone out of your daughter.” [Note: [Col. 0549] “And he said to her…”]

And when she went into her house, she found the demon gone out, and the daughter lying on the bed.

And again departing from the region of Tyre and Sidon, he came to the Sea of Galilee, between the borders of the Decapolis. [Note: [Col. 0549] “And again departing from the borders…”] [Note: [Col. 0550] “*markom*”: the primary manuscript; J and St add *markon*. — “*miþ tveihnaim*”: J adds a sign of division; St adds *miþtveihnam*.]

And they brought him a deaf man who could scarcely speak, and begged him to lay his hand upon him. [Col. 0551] [Note: [Col. 0549] “And they brought to him a deaf mute…”] [Note: [Col. 0550] “*handau*”: for *handu*. The interchange of accusative and dative endings is more frequent in proper names and rarer in common nouns; thus at L. IX, 27, *þiudinassau* occurs for *þiudinassu*, see Mark IX, 1; 1 Cor. II, 26, *dauþau* for *dauþu*. For *hairau*, read in the Codex Ambrosianus at Rom. XIII, 4, the Codex Carolinus correctly has *hairu*. Likewise at L. IV, 3, *sunaus*, verse 5 *diabulaus*, and Eph. V, 5 *skalkinassaus* are written for *diabulus*, *sunus*, and *skalkinassus*; compare the note at L. I, 54.]

And taking him away from the crowd privately, he put his fingers into his ears, and spitting, touched his tongue; and looking up toward heaven, he sighed and said to him: “Ephphatha,” which means, “Be opened.” [Note: [Col. 0551] “And taking him away from the crowd…”] [Note: [Col. 0551] “*spevanas*”: thus the Codex Argenteus; the editions have *speivands*, which is more correct, or certainly more common.]

And immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was loosened, and he spoke correctly. [Note: [Col. 0551] “And immediately his ears were opened…”]

And he commanded them that they should tell no one; but the more he commanded them, the more abundantly they proclaimed it. [Note: [Col. 0551] “And he commanded them…”] [Note: [Col. 0551] “*wan filu*”: Ulfilas has Greek δέ. — “*mais þamma*”: “the more this,” according to all Greek manuscripts, μᾶλλον περισσότερον. — “*eis*”: “they,” according to the Greek.]

And they were exceedingly astonished, saying: “He has done everything well; he makes the deaf hear and the mute speak!”

In those days, when there was again a very large crowd and they had nothing to eat, he summoned his disciples and said to them: [Note: [Col. 0551] “In those days…”] [Note: [Col. 0551] “*þan*”: “but,” according to all Greek manuscripts. — “*aftra*”: “again,” according to the Greek; otherwise Ulfilas seems to have read παμπόλλου instead of the simple πολλοῦ, rendering it with *filu managai*. — “*siponjans*”: Ulfilas, together with the manuscripts, has αὑτοῦ.]

“I have compassion on this crowd, because they have already remained with me three days and have nothing to eat. And if I send them away fasting to their homes, they will collapse on the road; for some of them have come from far away.” [Note: [Col. 0551] “I have compassion on this crowd…”] [Note: [Col. 0551] “*dagans*”: “days,” in the accusative, Greek ἡμέρᾳ; compare IX, 21. — “*haband*”: Z adds *hahand*.]

And his disciples answered him: “From where could anyone satisfy these people with bread in the wilderness?” [Note: [Col. 0551] “And his disciples answered him…”] [Note: [Col. 0551] “*was*”: Ulfilas, together with the manuscripts and the versions, has Greek ὧδε.]

And he asked them: “How many loaves do you have?” And they said: “Seven.”

And he commanded the crowd to recline on the ground. And taking the seven loaves and giving thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before them; and they set them before the crowd. [Note: [Col. 0551] “And he commanded the crowd…”] [Note: [Col. 0551] “*þizai*”: J and St add *þze*. — “*jah*”: the third *and*, according to the Greek. — “*aviliudonds*”: St adds *aviliudons*.]

And they had a few fish; and blessing them, he said that these too should be set before them. [Note: [Col. 0551] “And they had a few fish…”] [Note: [Col. 0551] “*þans*”: the primary manuscript has “these,” according to the Greek.]

And they ate and were satisfied, and they took up the remaining fragments: seven baskets. [Note: [Col. 0551] “And they ate…”] And there were about four thousand who ate, and he dismissed them. [Note: [Col. 0551] “And there were about four thousand…”] [Note: [Col. 0551] “*fralailot*”: St adds *ralailot*.]

And immediately he entered the boat with his disciples and came to the region of Magadan. [Note: [Col. 0551] “And he immediately entered the boat…”] [Note: [Col. 0552] “*galaiþ sunsaiv*”: according to the Greek. — “*magdalan*”: Greek Δαλμανουθά.]

And the Pharisees went out and began to argue with him, seeking from him a sign from heaven and testing him. [Note: [Col. 0551] “And the Pharisees went out…”]

And sighing deeply in his spirit, he said: “Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly I say to you, if a sign is given to this generation—” [Note: [Col. 0551] “And sighing in his spirit…”] [Note: [Col. 0552] “*kuni*”: J and St add *kun*. — “*gibaidau*”: J and St add *gibaidi*; B has *gabaid*. The ending *-au* has completely disappeared from the Codex Argenteus.]

And leaving them, he entered the boat again and departed across the sea.

And they forgot to take bread, and they had no more than one loaf with them in the boat.

And he commanded them, saying: “See that you beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.” [Note: [Col. 0551] “And he commanded them…”] [Note: [Col. 0552] “*ei*”: “that,” according to all Greek manuscripts.]

And they reasoned among themselves, saying: “It is because we have no bread.” [Note: [Col. 0551] “And they forgot…”]

Knowing this, Jesus said to them: “Why are you reasoning that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Do you have your heart hardened? [Note: [Col. 0551] “And Jesus, knowing it…”] [Note: [Col. 0552] “*unte*”: secondary witness; “because,” Greek ἔτι. Ulfilas, together with Codex 106 cited by Griesbach, read ὅτι, as B. already observed.]

Having eyes, do you not see? And having ears, do you not hear? And do you not remember, [Note: [Col. 0551] “Having eyes…”] when I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of fragments did you take up?” They said to him: “Twelve.”

“And when I broke the seven loaves for the four thousand, how many baskets full of fragments did you take up?” And they said: “Seven.” [Note: [Col. 0551] “When I broke the five loaves…”] [Note: [Col. 0552] “*hlaibans*”: “loaves,” according to the Greek. — “*usnemuþ*”: J and St add *usnemiþ*.]

And he said to them: “How do you not yet understand?” [Note: [Col. 0551] “And he said to them…”] [Note: [Col. 0552] “*ni nauh*”: “not yet,” Greek οὐ; compare the note at IV, 40. J, St, and B also add a sign of division.]

And they came to Bethsaida. [See the following page.] [Col. 0553] And they brought a blind man to him and begged him to touch him. [Note: [Col. 0551] “And they came to Bethsaida…”] [Note: [Col. 0553] “*qemun*”: “they came,” while the Greek has ἔρχεται. — “*beþaniïn*”: Greek Βηθσαϊδάν.]

And taking the hand of the blind man, he led him outside the village; and spitting on his eyes and laying his hands upon him, he asked him whether he saw anything. [Note: [Col. 0553] “And taking the hand of this blind man…”] [Note: [Col. 0553] “*seinos*”: “his,” Greek αὐτῷ. — “*gau*”: see the note at M. IX, 28.]

And looking up, he said: “I see people, because I see them like trees walking.” [Note: [Col. 0553] “And looking up, he said…”] [Note: [Col. 0553] “*þatei*”: “that,” according to the Greek. — “*gasaiwa*”: secondary witness; “I see,” according to the Greek.]

Then again he placed his hands upon his eyes, and he made him look up; and he was restored, and he saw everything clearly. [Note: [Col. 0553] “Then again he placed his hands…”] [Note: [Col. 0553] “*aftra*”: “again,” used for ἀπό in the compound verb ἀποκατεστάθη; likewise IX, 12, *aftra gaboteiþ* = ἀποκατεστᾷ; compare L. XIV, 12, *aftra haitaina* = ἀντικαλέσωσι.]

And he sent him to his house, saying: “Do not enter the village, and do not tell anyone in the village.” [Note: [Col. 0553] “And he sent him to his house…”] [Note: [Col. 0553] “*mannhun qiþais*”: according to the Greek. — “*þamma*”: J and St add *þammah*.]

And Jesus and his disciples went out into the villages of Caesarea Philippi; and on the way he asked his disciples, saying to them: “Whom …”

“[They] say that the people are?” [Note: [Col. 0553] *usïddja*: St. adds *ussïddja*.] And again he was restored and saw all things clearly. He sent him to his house, saying: “Do not enter the village, and do not tell anyone in the village.” And Jesus and his disciples went out into the villages of Caesarea Philippi; and on the way he asked his disciples, saying to them: “Whom do people say that I am?” [Note: [Col. 0553] “But they answered: John the Baptist; others, Elijah; and some, one of the prophets.”] And they answered him: “John the Baptist; others, Elijah; and still others, one of the prophets.” [Note: [Col. 0553] “*þan*”: St. adds *þain*.] And he said to them: “But whom do you say that I am?” Peter, answering, said to him: “You are Christ.” And he strictly charged them not to tell anyone about him. And he began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer much, and must be rejected by the elders, the chief priests, and the scribes, and be killed and rise again after three days. [Note: [Col. 0553] “*skulds ïst*”: Z. is mistaken in glossing this as *skal*, saying that it is an error. Ulfilas uses this verb to render the Greek passive infinitive, which Gothic entirely lacks; thus Luke 9:44, *skulds ïst atgiban* (“he is about to be delivered,” Greek *μέλλει παραδίδοσθαι*); John 12:34, *ushauhjan* (“to be lifted up,” *ὑψωθῆναι*); 1 Corinthians 5:10, *ataugjan* (“to be revealed,” *φανερωθῆναι*). Compare *mahtana visan* at Mark 14:5; John 3:4; 10:35. — *usstandan*: St. adds *ustandan*.]

And he spoke this word openly. Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him. [Note: [Col. 0553] “And taking him aside, Peter began to rebuke him.”] But he turned and, seeing his disciples, rebuked Peter, saying: “Go behind me, Satan, because you do not understand the things of God, but the things of men.” [Note: [Col. 0553] “But turning and seeing his disciples, he rebuked Peter, saying: Go behind me, Satan! For you do not know the things of God, but the things of men.”] And calling the crowd together with his disciples, he said to them: “Whoever wishes to follow after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” [Note: [Col. 0553] “*saivalai seinai*”: according to the Greek. — “*ïn*”: according to the Greek, “on account of,” or simply the Greek preposition.] For whoever wishes to save his life will lose it; but whoever loses his life for my sake and for the sake of this gospel will save it. [Note: [Col. 0554] “*saivalai seinai*”: according to the Greek.] For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and harms his own life? [Note: [Col. 0553] “*boteiþ*”: St. adds *boþeiþ*. — “*allana*”: J. and St. add *allama*.] Or what price can a man give as ransom for his life? For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels. [Note: [Col. 0554] “*vaurde meinaize*”: according to the Greek throughout. — “*seinis*”: St. adds *seinins*.]

And he said to them: “Truly I say to you, there are some of those standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God coming in power.” [Note: [Col. 0553] “And he said to them: Truly I say to you, there are some of those standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God coming in power.”] [Note: [Col. 0554] “*þai ïze*”: the editors add *jct.*; see the note at Mark 5:32.]

And after six days Jesus took Peter, James, and John and led them up onto a high mountain, apart by themselves, and he was transformed before them. [Note: [Col. 0553] “And after six days Jesus takes Peter and James and John and leads them up onto a high mountain, privately, alone, and he was transformed before them.] And his garments became shining, exceedingly white like snow, such as no fuller on earth can whiten them.” [Note: [Col. 0554] “*glitmunjandeins*”: J., St., and B. add *glitmunjande sva*. — “*weitos*”: Ulfilas, together with the versions, apparently read the Greek *λίαν*. — “*snaivs*”: St. adds *snaiys*. — “*vullareis*”: J., St., and B. add *vuslareis*.]

And Elijah appeared to them with Moses, and they were speaking with Jesus. [Note: [Col. 0553] “And Elijah was seen by them with Moses, and they were speaking with Jesus.”] [Note: [Col. 0554] “*varþ*”: St. adds *qarþ*.] Peter answered and said to Jesus: “Rabbi, it is good for us to be here; let us make three shelters, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” [Note: [Col. 0555] “*ainana helijin*”: according to the Greek throughout.]

For he did not know what he was saying, for they were terrified. And a cloud came, overshadowing them, and a voice came from the cloud: “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.” And suddenly, looking around, they no longer saw anyone except Jesus alone with them. [Note: [Col. 0555] “*ni þanaseiþs*”: St. and Z. add *jct.* — “*ainohun*”: thus the Argenteus manuscript, instead of *ainnohun*; likewise Luke 8:51 and John 5:22.]

As they were coming down from the mountain, he commanded them not to tell anyone what they had seen, except when the Son of Man had risen from the dead. [Note: [Col. 0555] “*manhun*”: J., St., and B. add *manhun*. — “*þatei*”: St. adds *þetei*.] And they kept this saying among themselves, asking what “rising from the dead” meant. And they asked him, saying: “Why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?” [Note: [Col. 0555] “*faurþis*”: J. and St. add *div*.]

But he answered them: “Elijah indeed, when he comes first, restores all things; and how is it written concerning the Son of Man, that he must suffer much and be despised?” [Note: [Col. 0555] “*helias*”: J. and St. omit *helia*. — “*sveþauh*”: Sch. translates this with “however” together with Z.; but although it renders the Greek *δέ* at Matthew 7:15, there it has a sense that it cannot have in our passage. It should rather be considered to correspond to the Greek *μέν*. See Mark 10:39 and Philippians 3:1; and although Sch. says that Mark almost nowhere uses the particle *μέν*, Ulfilas reads it here and at Mark 1:8, where he translates it by *aþþan*; see Titus 1:15. — “*aftra gaboteiþ*”: the editors add *jct.*; see the note at Mark 8:25.]

“But I say to you that Elijah has already come, and they did to him whatever they wished, just as it is written about him.” [Note: [Col. 0555] “But I say to you that Elijah has already come, and they did to him as much as they wished, just as it is written about him.”] And coming to the disciples, he saw a great crowd around them and scribes disputing with them. [Note: [Col. 0555] “*filu manageins*”: according to the Greek throughout.] And immediately the whole crowd, seeing him, was astonished and, running up, greeted him. [Note: [Col. 0555] “*gasaiwandans*”: “seeing”; Ulfilas seems to have read the Greek *ἰδόντες*. Griesbach argues more boldly that Gothic often writes by *synesis*, even when the Greek does not agree.]

And he asked the scribes: “What are you seeking with them?” [Note: [Col. 0555] “*þans bokarjans*”: “the scribes”; the Greek has “them.”] One from the crowd answered and said: “Teacher, I brought my son to you, who has a mute spirit.” [Note: [Col. 0555] “And one from the crowd answered.”] And wherever it seizes him, it throws him down; he foams, gnashes his teeth, and dries up. I told your disciples to cast it out, but they could not. [Note: [Col. 0556] “*gavairpiþ*”: “it throws him down”; the Greek is *ῥήσσει*, as in codex 12 apud Mi. — “*usdreibeina ïna*”: according to the Greek throughout; otherwise *usdreibeina* should be *usdribeina*. See Grimm I, 844.]

He answered them: “O unbelieving generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you? Bring him to me.” [Note: [Col. 0556] “*ïk*”: the editors add *ïesus*; see the note at Mark 1:42. — “*kuni*”: J. and St. add *kunni*. — “*þulau*”: J. and St., together with B., read *þuldu*; likewise at Luke 8:15 they add *þuldinai* instead of *þulainai*.] And they brought him to him. When the spirit saw him, it immediately convulsed him; and falling on the ground, he rolled about foaming. [Note: [Col. 0556] “*valvnoda*”: J. and St. add *valvinoda*; the Argenteus, B., Hz., and Z. add *valvisoda*. Neither reading can be proved. An intransitive verb is required, which should derive from the primitive *valvjan* as *valvnan*; compare *afwapnan*, *gafullnan*, and *gahailnan*, derived from *afwapjan*, *gafulljan*, and *gahailjan*. Verbs ending in *-inon* are formed from nouns: *fraujinon*, *reikinon*, and *gudjinon* from *frauja*, *reiks*, and *gudja*. No Gothic verb has the ending *-ison*. — “*waþjands*”: J. and St. add *kawjands*.]

And he asked his father: “How long has it been since this happened to him?” He said: “From childhood. It has often thrown him into fire and water, to destroy him. But if you can do anything, help us, having mercy on us.” [Note: [Col. 0556] “*jabai*”: Ulfilas apparently read the Greek *τί*.] Jesus said to him: “If you can believe: all things are possible to the one who believes.” Immediately the father of the child cried out with tears and said: “I believe; help my unbelief.” [Note: [Col. 0556] “*samaþ rann*”: the editors add *jct.*; likewise at 1 Corinthians 5:4 *samaþ gaggandam*, and at 1 Corinthians 7:5 *samaþ gavandjaiþ* should be written thus. — “*þu*”: see the note at Mark 6:9.]

When Jesus saw that the crowd was running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it: “You mute and deaf spirit, I command you: come out of him and never enter him again.” [Note: [Col. 0556] “*ïna*”: “him,” according to the Greek.] And crying out and convulsing him violently, it came out; and he became like one dead, so that many said: “He has died.” [Note: [Col. 0555] “And crying out and violently convulsing him, it came out, and he became as one dead, so that many said that he had died.”] But Jesus took him by the hand, raised him, and he stood up. [Note: [Col. 0557] “But Jesus, taking him by the hand, raised him, and he stood up.”]

When he had entered the house, his disciples asked him privately: “Why could we not cast it out?” [Note: [Col. 0557] “*galeiþandan*”: St. adds *galeitandan*. — “*duwe*”: “why,” Greek *ὅτι*. — “*mahtedum*”: J., St., and B. add *mahtedun*, as does the Argenteus manuscript.] And he said to them: “This kind cannot come out by anything except prayer and fasting.” [Note: [Col. 0557] “And he said to them: This kind cannot come out in any way except by prayer and fasting.”] And leaving there, they went through Galilee, and he did not want anyone to know. [Note: [Col. 0557] “And leaving there, they went through Galilee, and he did not want anyone to know.”] For he taught his disciples and said to them: “The Son of Man is delivered into the hands of men; they will kill him, and after he has been killed, he will rise on the third day.” But they did not understand the saying and were afraid to ask him. [Note: [Col. 0557] “*froþun*”: J. and St. add *frodun*.]

And he came to Capernaum. When he was in the house, he asked them: “What were you discussing with one another on the way?” [Note: [Col. 0557] “*qumans*”: thus correctly in the Argenteus manuscript; the editors add *qumands*.] They kept silent, for on the way they had argued with one another about who was the greatest. [Note: [Col. 0557] “*misso*”: Ulfilas, according to the Greek *γάρ*. — “*andrunnun*”: Ulfilas, the codex, and the versions, according to the Greek *ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ*. — “*maists vesi*”: “would be greatest,” Greek *μείζων*; otherwise Ulfilas agrees with no Greek manuscript; compare Mark 4:32.]

And sitting down, he called the Twelve and said to them: “If anyone wishes to be first, he shall be last of all and servant of all.” [Note: [Col. 0557] “*atvopida*”: St. adds *otvopida*.] And taking a child, he placed it among them; and taking it in his arms, he said to them: “Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me; and whoever receives me does not receive me, but the one who sent me.” [Note: [Col. 0557] “*ana*”: Ulfilas, together with the manuscripts, apparently read *ἐν* instead of *ἐπί*; Sch. argues rashly otherwise.]

John answered him, saying: “Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, who does not follow us, and we forbade him, because he does not follow us.” [Note: [Col. 0557] “*ïn*”: “in,” according to the Greek. — “*saei—unsis*”: “who—not us,” according to the Greek; otherwise, instead of *laisteiþ*, St. adds *laisteih*.] But Jesus said: “Do not forbid him, for no one who performs a mighty deed in my name can immediately speak evil of me. Whoever is not against us is for us.” [Note: [Col. 0557] “For whoever is not against you is for you.”]

“For whoever gives you a cup of water to drink in my name, because you belong to Christ, truly I say to you, he will not lose his reward.” [Note: [Col. 0557] “*meinamma*”: “my,” according to the Greek. — “*ei*”: “that,” according to the Greek. — “*mizdon*”: St. adds *misdon*.]

“And whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it is better for him that a millstone turned by an ass be hung around his neck and that he be thrown into the sea.” [Note: [Col. 0558] “*asiluqairnus*”: J. and St. add *div.*; since *asiluquairnus* properly means a millstone moved by an ass, Ulfilas undoubtedly read the Greek *μύλος ὀνικός* together with the manuscripts and versions. — “*balsaggan*”: this is indeed the reading of the Argenteus and the editions, except St., who has *halsaggan* in the text but *balsaggan* in the glossary. We greatly doubt whether this reading is correct, since the meaning of the word cannot be determined either from Gothic or from related languages. We offer *halsaggan* as a certain conjecture: *hals* occurs for Greek *τράχηλος* at Luke 15:20; see Grimm III, 399, and compare Schmid, *Schwäbisches Wörterbuch*, s.v. *Anke*, and Graff, *Althochdeutscher Sprachschatz* I, 345. That the letters *h* and *b* are exchanged elsewhere too is indicated by Ih. at Luke 6:40. — “*fravaurpans*”: J. and St. add *fravairpans*.]

“For everyone will be salted with fire, and every sacrifice will be salted with salt.” [Note: [Col. 0559] “*hunsle*”: St. adds *hunse*.] “Salt is good; but if the salt becomes saltless, with what will you season it? Have salt in yourselves and be at peace with one another.” [Note: [Col. 0559] “*we*”: Ulfilas, together with the manuscripts, apparently read the Greek *αὐτό*; — “*supuda*”: for *supoda*, see Grimm I, 40 and 855; likewise Luke 20:18 *gakrotuda*; compare Mark 11:32 *uhtedun* for *ohtedun* and the observations at Luke 4:13. Ulfilas appears to have read *ἀρτύσεται* or *ἀρτυθήσεται* with the manuscripts rather than *ἀρτύσετε*.]

And rising from there, he came into the regions of Judea beyond the Jordan. Crowds again gathered around him, and as was his custom, he again taught them. [Note: [Col. 0559] “*hindar*”: the Greek has *διὰ τοῦ πέραν*. If Ulfilas had read *hindar* with the accusative, he would have used it with the accusative; for *ïaurdanau* is not, as interpreters maintain, an accusative but a dative. *Hindar* with the dative indicates not the place toward which Jesus was going, but where the regions of Judea were to which he came (*πέραν*). Thus John 3:26, *saei vas miþ þus hindar ïaurdanau* (“who was with you beyond the Jordan,” *πέραν*); Mark 6:22, *stoþ hindar marein* (“stood beyond the sea”); verse 25, *bigetun ïna hindar marein* (“they found him beyond the sea”). That the Goths used *hindar* with the dative was hitherto unknown to scholars; see also Romans 14:5, *hindar daga* (“beyond the days”).]

And the Pharisees approached and asked him whether it was lawful for a man to dismiss his wife, testing him. [Note: [Col. 0559] “And the Pharisees, coming to him, asked him: Is it lawful for a man to dismiss his wife, testing him?”] But he answered them: “What did Moses command you?” [Note: [Col. 0559] “*qaþ*”: Ulfilas has the Greek *αὐτοῖς*.] They said: “Moses permitted us to write a bill of divorce and dismiss her.” [Note: [Col. 0559] “*unsis*”: “to us,” according to the Greek throughout; added from Matthew 19:8.]

Jesus answered and said to them: “Because of the hardness of your hearts he wrote you this commandment.” [Note: [Col. 0559] “*þo*”: “this”; Sch. therefore falsely notes that Ulfilas omitted the Greek *ταύτην*. This scholar made such errors hundreds of times.] “But from the beginning of creation God made them male and female.” [Note: [Col. 0559] “*gatavida*”: Ulfilas, together with the manuscripts and versions, has the Greek *αὐτούς*.] “For this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother,” [Note: [Col. 0559] “*seinai*”: the Greek is complete throughout; compare Mark 7:10 and following. The verse ends with *καί*. — *αὐτοῦ* is found with Ulfilas, the manuscripts, B., and c. apud Mi.; but it may perhaps be attributed to a copyist’s error, whose eye slipped from the first *seinai* to the second; compare the note at Romans 9:15.] “and the two shall become one body,” so that they are no longer two but one body. [Note: [Col. 0560] “*leika samin*”: J., St., and B. add *leikas ain*; otherwise *samin* (“the same”) corresponds to the Greek *μία*, as at Luke 17:34, and at Ephesians 2:14 *sama* without the article has this meaning. — “*leik ain*”: according to the Greek.] Therefore what God has joined together, let no man separate. [Note: [Col. 0560] “*þamma*”: “this,” according to the Greek throughout.]

And in the house his disciples again asked him about this matter; and he said to them: “Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery with her.” [Note: [Col. 0560] “*wazuh*”: St. adds *wasuh*.] “And if a wife leaves her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.” [Note: [Col. 0560] “*horinoþ*”: St. adds *horinnoþ*.]

Then they brought children to him so that he might touch them; but his disciples rebuked those who were bringing them. [Note: [Col. 0560] “*attaitoki*”: J. and St. add *attaitok*. — “*ïs*”: “his,” according to the Greek. — “*bairandam*”: together with the following verse’s *dugasaiwands*. Since this compound verb occurs nowhere else and does not seem well suited to the Greek *ἰδών*, it is suspect. On the other hand, for *προσφέρειν* not the simple *bairan* but the compound *dubairan* would be expected. Perhaps one should read: *bairandam du. gasaiwands*, etc. Prepositions placed after adverbs as their equivalents are not uncommon: Mark 8:6 *atlagjan faur*; 8:23 *atlagjan ana*; 11:7 *galagidedun ana*; Luke 8:44 *atgaggan du*; 19:4 *biþragjan faur*; 28 *gaggan fram*; compare Matthew 9:15; Mark 5:40 and 15:43. It should also be noted that in the Argenteus manuscript these two verses are not separated by a point, as also happens elsewhere.]

And if a woman leaves her husband and marries another, she commits adultery. Then they brought children to him so that he might touch them. But when the disciples saw those bringing them, they rebuked them. Jesus, seeing this, was indignant and said to them: “Let the children come to me, and do not forbid them, for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.” [Note: [Col. 0559] “*barna*”: J. and St. add *barn*. — “*jah*”: according to the Greek, “and.” — “*þize*”: “of such as these”; the Greek has *τῶν τοιούτων* throughout. Ulfilas either read *τούτων* instead of *τοιούτων*, or omitted *τοιούτων* by mistake because of the similarity of the preceding word.]

“Truly I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child will not enter it.” And embracing them, he laid his hands on them and blessed them. [Note: [Col. 0559] “And embracing them, laying his hands on them, he blessed them.”]

As he was setting out on the road, someone ran up, knelt before him, and asked him: “Good teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” [Note: [Col. 0560] “*knussjands*”: St. adds *knussjads*; Ulfilas and the versions have the Greek *αὐτόν*. — “*qiþands*”: “saying,” according to the Greek.] Jesus said to him: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one—God.” [Note: [Col. 0560] “*þeina*”: “your,” according to the Greek.]

“You know the commandments: ‘Do not commit adultery; do not kill; do not steal; do not bear false witness; do not defraud; honor your father and your mother.’” [Note: [Col. 0560] “*þeina*”: “your,” according to the Greek.] He answered and said to him: “Teacher, I have kept all these things from my youth.” [Col. 0561] Jesus, looking at him, loved him and said to him: “You lack one thing: go, sell whatever you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me, taking up the cross.” [Note: [Col. 0561] “*himinam*”: “in heaven,” according to the Greek throughout, except for one manuscript, E apud Mi., which agrees with Ulfilas.]

But he, troubled by this saying, went away sorrowful, for he had many possessions. [Note: [Col. 0561] “*faihu*”: “possessions,” according to the Greek throughout, *κτήματα*. Maresh. p. 434 reasonably suspects that Ulfilas read *χρήματα*, since Gothic regularly uses *faihu* for that Greek word; see the following verses and Luke 18:24.]

Jesus, looking around, said to his disciples: “See how difficult it is for those who have riches to enter the kingdom of God.” [Note: [Col. 0561] “*sai*”: “behold,” according to the Greek throughout. — “*faiho*”: an unusual form instead of *faihu*; see the note at Luke 4:13.] The disciples were astonished at his words. Jesus answered again and said to them: “Children, how difficult it is for those desirous of riches to enter the kingdom of God.” [Note: [Col. 0561] “*ïm*”: J. and St. add *ïn*. — “*hunjandam*”: thus in the Argenteus manuscript and the editions. Ih. notes that the manuscript is so obscure here that it cannot be determined with certainty whether *hunjandam* or *hugjandam* should be read; but he is mistaken, for nothing is missing except *n* between *a* and *d*, which was lost through damage to the parchment. There is another point to which the interpreter should attend: the editors translate *hunjan* as “to trust,” certainly because the Greek has *πεποιθότας*. But to trust in something is Gothic *trauan* with the dative or with *du* (Luke 18:9; 2 Corinthians 1:9). Since *afar* is added in our passage, and this preposition indicates application, desire, or longing for a thing, the verb *hunjan* must contain the meaning “to desire, to long for” (compare Anglo-Saxon *hongian*, English *hone*). Thus *hunjan afar wa* means “to desire something, to be desirous or eager for something.” Once this is established, it is impossible that Ulfilas read *πεποιθότας*; rather, through some error he must have read *πεποθηκότας*. Careful readers will find similar errors often; compare the notes at Luke 3:14; 7:25; John 16:6; and 2 Corinthians 1:24.]

They were even more astonished, saying among themselves: “Who then can be saved?” [Note: [Col. 0561] “But they were even more astonished, saying among themselves: Who can be saved?”] Jesus, looking at them, said: “With men it is impossible, but not with God; for all things are possible with God.” [Note: [Col. 0562] “*ïnsaiwands*”: Ulfilas, together with the manuscripts, has the Greek *δέ*. — “*akei*”: “but,” found throughout the Greek before *ni*, as the sense appears to require. — “*ïst*”: “is,” according to the Greek.]

Peter began to say to him: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you.” [Note: [Col. 0562] “*þan*”: “then,” according to the Greek.] Jesus answered and said: “Truly I say to you, no one has left house, brothers, sisters, mother, father, wife, children, or fields for my sake and for the sake of this gospel [Note: [Col. 0562] “*ïm*”: “to them,” according to the Greek throughout. — “*aflailoti*”: the Argenteus adds *aflailoloti*. — “*broþruns*”: Ulfilas has the Greek *ἢ ἀδελφάς*. — “*aiþþau aiþein*”: the Greek comes after *attan*, for which the Argenteus and the editions add *attin*. — “*haimoþlja*”: thus in the Argenteus manuscript here and in the following verse; the correct reading was long ago reached by conjecture by Z., *Gloss.* p. 178, and Grimm II, 257.] who will not receive a hundredfold now, in this time, houses, brothers, sisters, mothers, children, and fields, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life.” [Note: [Col. 0562] “*saei*”: St. adds *sai*; some argue more boldly that Ulfilas read *ὅς* instead of *ὃς ἄν*. — “*jah attan*”: “and father,” according to the Greek. — “*aiþein*”: “mothers,” Greek *μητέρας*. — “*haimoþlja*”: see the note at verse 29. — “*vrakom*”: perhaps [the supplied source breaks off here].]

The reading should be **vrakjom**. See IV, 17; Romans VIII, 35; for from the verb *vrakjan* one cannot form *vraka*, but *vrakja*, while from *vrekun*, the preterite of *vrikan*, comes *vrekei* (Corinthians II, XII, 10). On the genuine form *vraka*, see the note on Galatians VI, 12.]

[Note: [Col. 0561] Of this gospel. Whoever does not receive a hundredfold now, in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and father and mother and children and fields, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life.]

[Note: [Col. 0561] But many who are first will be last, and the last first.]

[Note: [Col. 0561] They were on the road, going up to Jerusalem; and Jesus was going ahead of them. They were astonished, and those who followed became afraid. Taking the Twelve aside again, he began to tell them what was going to happen to him.]

[Note: [Col. 0562] *ïairusaulymai*: J. St. B. omit *ïairausaulymai*, as it appears in the following verse. — *jah*: originally; Ulfila has ὃ ἦν, “which was.” — *gadaban*: correctly so; compare *gadof ïst*, Titus II, 1; *Skeir.* p. 38, 5; 11, 40, 14; 42, 3.]

But many who are first will be last, and the last first. They were on the road, going to Jerusalem, and Jesus was going ahead of them.. They were astonished, and, following, became afraid.

[Note: [Col. 0561] “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death.”]

[Note: [Col. 0562] *ïairusaulyma*: see the note on verse 32. — *dauþau*: Ulfila has ὃ καὶ παραδώσουσιν αὐτὸν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν, “and they will hand him over to the Gentiles,” a clause found in all Greek manuscripts; in the Argenteus codex no trace of it appears.]

And taking the Twelve aside again, he began to tell them what was going to happen to him: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes; they will condemn him to death, mock him, flog him, spit upon him, kill him, and on the third day he will rise.”

[Note: [Col. 0561] “And they will mock him and flog him and spit upon him and kill him, and on the third day he will rise.”]

[Note: [Col. 0562] *usstandiþ*: St. adds *ustandiþ*.]

[Col. 0563] And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, approached him and said: “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you.”

[Note: [Col. 0563] *þuk*: “you,” as in the Greek.]

[Col. 0563] But he said to them: “What do you want me to do for you?”

[Col. 0563] And they said to him: “Grant us that we may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory.”

[Note: [Col. 0563] *ugkis*: in verse 35 it is *uggkis*. Likewise the forms *drigkan* and *driggkan*, *þagkjan* and *þaggkjan*, *þugkjan* and *þuggkjan*, and others vary. — *sitaiva*: Ih. suspects that *sitaima* should be read, which Z. rashly admitted into the text; Grimm, I, 840, considers it a dual form, as it also seems to us.]

“Teacher, we ask you to do this for us.” But Jesus said to them: “You do not know what you are asking. Can you drink the cup that I drink and receive the baptism with which I am baptized, so that you may be baptized?”

[Note: [Col. 0563] “But Jesus said to them: You do not know what you are asking. Can you drink the cup that I drink and receive the baptism with which I am baptized, so that you may be baptized?”]

[Note: [Col. 0563] *vituts*: J. St. B. add *vituþs*. — *magutsu driggkan*: J. St. omits *maguts driggkan*; B. conjectured *maguts udrigqkan*. L. Ih. Z. rightly observe that *u-* is an interrogative suffix. — *ïk*: originally; St. adds *ïh*. — *ei daupjaindau*: so Ulfila, since Gothic has no passive infinitive of the kind one would expect; likewise John III, 4, *ïbai mag aftra galeiþan jah gabairaidau*, “can he perhaps enter again and be born?” See the note on VIII, 31.]

“One at your right hand and one at your left, may we sit in your glory.” But Jesus said to them: “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink and receive the baptism with which I am baptized?”

And they said to him: “We are able.” But Jesus said to them: “You will indeed drink the cup that I drink, and you will receive the baptism with which I am baptized.”

[Note: [Col. 0563] “They said to him: We are able. But Jesus said to them: You will indeed drink the cup that I drink and receive the baptism with which I am baptized.”]

[Note: [Col. 0563] *magu*: so the Argenteus codex; the editions add *magum*. *Magu* is a dual form; compare *siju*, John X, 30; XVII, 22. — *daupjada*: Gothic has βαπτισθήσεσθε, “you will be baptized,” through a scribal error; see the note on Romans IX, 15.]

But to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant, but it belongs to those for whom it has been prepared.

[Note: [Col. 0563] “But to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant, but it belongs to those for whom it has been prepared.”]

[Note: [Col. 0563] *aiþþau*: “or,” Greek καί.]

And when the ten heard this, they began to be indignant at James and John.

[Note: [Col. 0563] “And when the ten heard this, they began to be indignant at James and John.”]

But Jesus called them and said to them: “You know that those who are considered rulers of the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them.”

[Note: [Col. 0563] “But Jesus called them and said to them: You know that those who are considered rulers of the nations rule over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them.”]

[Note: [Col. 0563] *þatei*: Z. proposes two conjectures to restore the genuine reading. Either he prefers to read *þuggkjands* for *þuggkjand*, a shorter form (?) for *þuggkjandans*; or *þaiei* for *þatei*, a reading which would have some appearance of truth if all Greek manuscripts did not read ὅτι, “that,” which is also required by the sense. Moreover, the *t* of *þatei* is distinctly written in the Argenteus codex. We think it safer to suppose that the scribe, who made many errors in this sheet, omitted *þaiei* after *þatei*. Compare the notes on Luke X, 5, and Corinthians I, XII, 22. — *þuggkjand*: Z. omits *þugkjand*. — *ïþ*: see the note on Matthew VI, 24.]

It is not so among you. Rather, whoever wishes to become great among you must be your servant; and whoever wishes to be first among you must be the servant of all.

[Note: [Col. 0563] “And whoever wishes to become first among you must be servant to all.”]

[Note: [Col. 0563] *frumists*: the Argenteus codex; J. St. add *frumist*. Z. rightly observes that the *s* was omitted because of the same letter in the following word; likewise in verse 45 and XVI, 1. See Massmann, *Skeireins*, p. 59.]

[Note: [Col. 0563] “For the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many.”]

[Note: [Col. 0564] *al andbahtjam*: B. Hz. and Grimm, I, 855, add a conjecture; J. St. add *atandbahtjan*. Z. conjectured *at andbahtnan*, since *at* is nowhere else found attached to an infinitive. We do not understand what Grimm decided concerning this passage. Ulfila uses a circumlocution for the passive infinitive, which the Gothic language entirely lacks (see the notes on VIII, 31; X, 38; XV, 9). Thus the expression is *at andbahtjam*, from *andbahti*, “service, office,” meaning “for services to be rendered to him”; compare Corinthians I, XVI, 15.]

[Note: [Col. 0563] “For the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many.”]

[Note: [Col. 0564] *faur managans saun*: agrees with all Greek manuscripts. Elsewhere the Argenteus codex, J. St., and B. add *managan*; see the note on verse 44 and compare Matthew XXVII, 51; Mark III, 13; Corinthians II, III, 2; IV, 5. It should also be noted that in *Skeireins*, p. 37, 9, where *saun*, or rather *ussaunei*, occurs again, the second *s* was likewise omitted through a similar error (*usaunein*).]

Let him be your servant. And whoever wishes to become first among you must be servant of all.. For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many.

[Note: [Col. 0564] *jainþro*: “from there,” Greek ἀπὸ Ἱεριχώ. — *miþ*: “with,” Greek καί. — *teimaiaus barteimaiaus*: J. St. omit *timaiaus bartimaiaus*.]

[Note: [Col. 0563] “And many rebuked him, telling him to be silent; but he cried out much more: Son of David, have mercy on me!”]

[Note: [Col. 0564] *ïesu*: the Greek has αὐτῷ, “him,” and after *laistida*, “he followed,” it has the same pronoun.]

[Note: [Col. 0564] *vesun*: J. adds *vemun*; St. omits *qemun*. — *ïairusalem*: J. St. add *ïairusaleim*. — *beþsfagein*: Greek Βηθφαγή. — *biþaniïn*: elsewhere *beþania*; see verses 11 and 12.]

And they went to Jerusalem. Entering the temple, Jesus began to drive out those who were selling and buying in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves.

[Note: [Col. 0565] “And he did not permit anyone to carry a vessel through the temple.”]

[Note: [Col. 0566] *þairhberi*: J. St. add *þairhbeki*.]

And Jesus answered and said to them: “Have faith in God.”

[Note: [Col. 0567] *ïzvis*: “to you,” according to the Greek.]

[Note: [Col. 0567] “And they went again to Jerusalem; and while he was walking in the temple, the chief priests, scribes, and elders came to him.”]

And they said to him: “By what authority are you doing these things? And who gave you this authority to do these things?”

[Note: [Col. 0567] *taujis*: the second occurrence; St. adds *þaujis*.]

But if we say, “From human beings,” they feared the crowd, for everyone held that John was truly a prophet.

[Note: [Col. 0567] *ak*: Ulfila, with the manuscripts, has ἐάν, “if.” — *uhtedun*: for *ohtedun*, “they feared”; see the note on IX, 50. — *alakjo*: “altogether,” according to all Greek manuscripts, likewise Luke IV, 22.]

[Note: [Col. 0567] *du ïesua*: so the Argenteus codex (*iua*); J. St. B. add *du ïna*; Z. omits *du ïmma*. — *andhafjands ïesus*: agrees with the Greek. — *ïzvis qiþa*: agrees with all Greek manuscripts.]

And he began to speak to them in parables:: “A man planted a vineyard, enclosed it with a hedge, dug a pit beneath the winepress, built a tower, entrusted it to laborers, and went away into a foreign land..”

[Note: [Col. 0567] “And he began to speak to them in parables: A man planted a vineyard, enclosed it with a hedge, dug a pit beneath the winepress, built a tower, leased it to laborers, and went away into a foreign land.”]

[Note: [Col. 0567] *veinagard*: J. St. add *veingard*. — *manna*: St. adds *mannna*. — *bisatida*: J. St. omit *atlagida*. In the Argenteus codex nothing can be read except *satida*; the letters written before it have disappeared. Nevertheless scholars have probably conjectured correctly in supplying what we have printed. — *ïna*: originally “him”; Greek manuscripts have the pronoun. — *dal*: J. St. mark a lacuna; B. adds a plus sign; Z. gives *dal-*, suspecting that *dalg* was written, relying, unless we are mistaken, on Luke VI, 39. But in that passage it is unquestionably *dal gadriusand*, not *dalga driusand*, that should be read. Ih. long ago restored the passage correctly, observing that there is no trace of a lacuna after *dal* and that, except where the parchment is partly mutilated, what has been printed can be read without difficulty. *Dal uf mesa* (B. Ih. add *ufmesa*), as Z. rightly interprets it, signifies a pit or vessel placed beneath the winepress.]

[Note: [Col. 0567] “And he sent to the laborers at the proper time a servant, so that he might receive from the laborers some of the fruit of this vineyard.”]

[Note: [Col. 0568] *at*: Z. omits it in favor of *af*; see the note on XV, 45.]

The lord of the vineyard will come, destroy those laborers, and give the vineyard to others.

And they sought to seize him, but feared the crowd. For they understood that he had spoken the parable against them. So they left him and went away.

And they sent to him some of the Pharisees and Herodians, so that they might catch him in his words.

[Note: [Col. 0569] *sumai*: “some,” according to all Greek manuscripts, τινάς.]

And coming, they said to him: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and care for no one; for you do not look at the face of human beings, but teach the way of God in truth. Is it lawful to pay the tribute to Caesar, or not? Should we pay, or should we not pay?”

[Note: [Col. 0569] “And coming, they said to him: Teacher, we know that you are truthful and do not care about anyone; for you do not look at the face of human beings, but teach the way of God in truth. Is it lawful to pay the tribute to Caesar, or not?”]

[Note: [Col. 0569] *saiwis*: J. St. B. add *saiwais*. — *laiseis*: Z. adds *laisis*. — *giban kaisara*: agrees with the Greek. — *þau*: J. St. add *þan*. — *gibaima*: Ulfila, codex 225, and the versions have ἢ μὴ δῶμεν, “or shall we not pay,” and connect *gibaima* with the preceding *þau niu*, “or not.”]

But they came and said to him: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and do not care for anyone; for you do not look at the face of human beings, but teach the way of God in truth. Is it lawful to pay the tribute to Caesar, or not?”

[Note: [Col. 0569] “But Jesus, seeing their deceit, said to them: Why are you testing me? Bring me a denarius, that I may see it.”]

[Note: [Col. 0569] *ïesus*: so the Argenteus codex; J. St. Hz. Z. add *ïs*. — *gasaiwands*: “seeing,” Greek εἰδώς, likewise XII, 28. — *wa mik*: J. St. add *wa me*, and B. *Iac*.]

“But Jesus, seeing their deceit, said to them: “Why are you testing me? Bring me a denarius, that I may see it.” They brought it, and he said to them: “Whose image and inscription is this?” They said to him: “Caesar’s.”.”

to my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet.” David himself, therefore, calls him Lord; and how is he his son?

> [Col. 0571] *raihtis*: “therefore,” Greek manuscripts universally οὖν. Either Ulfilas or the scribe seems to have written it through an error induced by the beginning of the preceding verse, for *raihtis* is nowhere else used for οὖν.—*fraujan*: J., St., B. read *fraujin* (“Lord”); in the Codex Argenteus it can no longer be read.—*ïmma sunus*: supported by the Greek manuscripts universally.—*alla*: “whole,” Greek manuscripts universally πολύς.

“—his garment.”

“But woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days. But pray that your flight may not occur in winter. For those days will be such affliction as has not been from the beginning of creation, which God created, until now, and will not be. And unless the Lord had shortened those days, no flesh would be saved; but for the sake of the elect whom he chose, he shortened the days.

“And then, if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ,’ or ‘Look, there,’ do not believe it. For false Christs and false prophets will arise and give signs and wonders, to deceive, if possible, even the elect. But you, take heed: look, I have foretold all things to you.

“But in those days, after that affliction, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars of heaven will be falling, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken. And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory. And then he will send his angels and gather his elect from the four winds, from the end of the earth to the end of heaven.

“But learn the parable from the fig tree: when its branch has now become tender and puts forth leaves, you know that summer is near. So you also, when you see these things happening, know that it is near—[lacuna]—this ointment was [destroyed?].”

And wherever he enters, say to the master of the house: ‘The teacher says: Where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ And he will show you a large upper room, furnished and ready; prepare for us there.”

And immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the Twelve, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests, scribes, and elders. Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying: “Whomever I kiss, he is the one. Seize him and lead him away securely.” And when he came, he immediately approached him and said: “Rabbi, Rabbi!” and kissed him. But they laid hands on him and seized him.

But one of those standing by drew a sword, struck the servant of the chief priest, and cut off his right ear. And Jesus answered and said to them: “Have you come out as against a malefactor, with swords and clubs, to seize me? Day by day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But let the Scriptures be fulfilled.” And all abandoned him and fled.

And a certain young man followed him, clothed in a linen cloth over his naked body; and the young men seized him. But he left the linen cloth and fled from them naked.

And they led Jesus to the chief priest, and all the chief priests, elders, and scribes assembled with him. And Peter followed him from afar, until he came into the court of the chief priest; and he sat with the servants and warmed himself by the fire.

But the chief priests and the whole council sought testimony against Jesus in order to put him to death, and found none. For many bore false witness against him, but their testimonies were not consistent. And some arose and bore false witness against him, saying: “We heard him saying, ‘I will destroy this temple made with hands, and in three days I will build another not made with hands.’” Yet not even so was their testimony consistent.

And the chief priest, standing in their midst, questioned Jesus, saying: “Do you answer nothing? What do these testify against you?” But he kept silent and answered nothing. Again the chief priest questioned him and said to him: “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?” But Jesus said: “I am. And you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of power and coming with the clouds of heaven.”

Then the chief priest tore his garments and said: “Why do we still need witnesses? You have heard his blasphemy. What do you think?” And all condemned him as deserving death. And some began to spit upon his face, to cover his face, and to strike him with blows, saying to him: “Prophesy!” And the attendants struck him with the palms of their hands.

> [Col. 0573] Immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests, scribes, and elders.

> [Col. 0573–0574] *atuh þan gaf*: B., Z. read *at uhþan gaf*. J. and St. already correctly printed the reading, whom Z. criticizes unjustly; that learned man was evidently unaware of the enclitic nature of the particle *-uh*, [Col. 0574] and especially did not remember passages such as 16:8, *dizuh þan sat*, since *s* is changed into the related *z* only within words or compounds. Moreover, between prepositions and verbs compounded with them, this *-uh* is rather often placed: Luke 17:7 *anuhkumbei* (for *anakumbei-uh*); 18:38 *ubuhvopida* (for *ufvopida-uh*); John 7:32; 11:41; 16:28; 17:1; Ephesians 4:9. Compounds are also separated by other inserted particles: Luke 20:25 *us nu gibeiþ*; John 6:22 *miþ ni qam*. Both forms occur in our passage; likewise 1 Corinthians 14:23 *atuþ-þan gaggand*, 15:15 *biþ-þan gitanda*, Ephesians 4:23 *anuþ-þan niujaiþ*; compare the note on Matthew 9:28.—*ïm*: “to them,” while the Greek manuscripts universally have αὐτὸν—αὐτοῖς.

And Pilate asked him: “Are you the king of the Jews?” But he answered and said to him: “You say so.” And the chief priests accused him of many things. Now at every feast he released for them one prisoner whom they requested. And there was one called Barabbas, bound with those who had made an insurrection with him, who had committed murder in the uprising. And the whole crowd came out and began to ask him to do as he had always done for them.

But Pilate answered them, saying: “Do you wish me to release to you the king of the Jews?” For he knew that the chief priests had handed him over out of envy. But the chief priests stirred up the crowd so that he might rather release Barabbas to them.

And Pilate again answered and said to them: “What then do you wish me to do with him whom you call king of the Jews?” But they again cried out: “Crucify him!” And Pilate said to them: “Why? What evil has he done?” But they cried out all the more: “Crucify him!”

> [Col. 0577] And Pilate asked him: “Are you king of the Jews?” But he, answering, said to him: “You say so.”

> [Col. 0577] *ïudaie*: St. reads *jadaje*.

> [Col. 0577] And the chief priests accused him greatly.

> [Col. 0577] But Pilate again asked him, saying: “Do you answer nothing? See how many things they testify against you.”

> [Col. 0577] But Jesus answered no more, so that Pilate wondered.

> [Col. 0577] *ni*: Ulfilas omits οὐδέν (“nothing”).

> [Col. 0577] But at every feast he released to them one prisoner, whom they asked for.

> [Col. 0577] *warjoh*: B. reads *warja*; Codex Argenteus, J., St., and Z. read *warjo*. The same error recurs in Skeireins 43.16, where *warjano* is read for *warjanoh*; compare Luke 8, where *ainvarjamma* is read for *ainvarjammeh*, or rather for *ainwarjanoh*. The enclitic *-h*—that is, *-uh*; compare the note on Matthew 5:37—must be added, because without it the interrogative pronoun remains, which the sense here does not permit (Grimm III, 29). In the parallel Matthew 27:15, *warjanoh* is read, a masculine form that itself troubles the attentive reader, since *dulþs* is feminine in gender (Luke 2:42; John 6:4).

> [Col. 0577] There was one named Barabbas, bound with those who had made an insurrection with him, who had committed murder in the uprising.

> [Col. 0577] And the whole crowd, coming up, began to request that he should do as he always had done for them.

> [Col. 0577] *usgaggandei*: “coming up,” Greek ἀναβοήσας.—*alla*: “the whole,” absent from the Greek.

> [Col. 0577] But Pilate answered them, saying: “Do you wish that I release to you this king of the Jews?”

> [Col. 0577–0578] *vileidu fraleitan*: J., St. delete *vileid ei fraleitau*; B. reads *vileid fraleitam*; Z., with Ih. and F., reads *vileidu fraleitau*. The Codex Argenteus reading which we have given is altogether sound. The *u* in *vileidu* was certainly written, although it can now scarcely be detected; and without doubt we should miss this enclitic, since it serves to mark a question. Further, though the Goth ordinarily uses *ei* (“that”) after *viljan* (15:12; Luke 18:41), he also uses the infinitive with an accusative (Mark 10:36; Luke 19:14). Finally, no one who remembers that Gothic entirely lacks a passive infinitive will be surprised that Ulfilas employed *fraleitan* for the passive; see the note on 10:45. A similar case here is Luke 1:62, *waiva vildedi haitan* (“what he wished to be called”), compare Mark 9:45, 47; Luke 3:7, 12; and 2 Corinthians 5:20, where δεόμεθα—καταλλάγητε τῷ θεῷ is rendered by the Goth, as here, *bidjam gagavairþnan guþa* [Col. 0578], “we ask to be reconciled to God”; similarly Matthew 5:24, *gagg gasibjon*—ὕπαγε διαλλάγηθι.

> [Col. 0577] For he knew that the chief priests had delivered him up through envy.

> [Col. 0577] But Pilate again answered and said to them: “What then do you wish that I do with him whom you call king of the Jews?”

> [Col. 0578] *þana*: an article very rarely added to proper names—Luke 6:11; John 5:36 (for Mark 1:16 and Luke 3:1 are different cases)—is used with a certain force, meaning: “that man of whom such grave things are said.”—*ïþ*, the second occurrence: see the note on Matthew 6:24.—*ïesu atgaf*: supported by all Greek manuscripts.

But the soldiers led him inside the courtyard, that is, the praetorium; and they summoned the whole cohort. They clothed him in purple and put upon him a crown of thorns which they had woven. And they began to salute him: “Hail, king of the Jews!” They struck his head with a reed, spat upon him, and, kneeling, did him homage.

And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple and clothed him in his own garments. Then they led him out to crucify him. And they compelled a certain man, Simon of Cyrene, coming from the field, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross.

And they brought him to the place Golgotha, which, translated, means “Place of a Skull.” And they gave him wine mingled with myrrh to drink, but he did not take it. And they crucified him and divided his garments, casting lots over them, what each should take.

Now it was the third hour, and they crucified him. And the inscription of his charge was written above: “THE KING OF THE JEWS.” And with him they crucified two malefactors, one on his right and one on his left.

And the Scripture was fulfilled which said: “And he was numbered with the lawless.” And those passing by reviled him, shaking their heads and saying: “Ah! You who destroy the temple and build it in three days, save yourself and come down from the cross!”

Likewise the chief priests, mocking him among themselves with the scribes, said: “He saved others, but he cannot save himself. Let the Christ, the king of Israel, now come down from the cross, so that we may see and believe.” And those crucified with him reproached him.

And when the sixth hour came, darkness fell over all the earth until the ninth hour. And at the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice: “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which, translated, means: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

And some of those standing by, hearing it, said: “Look, he calls Elijah.” And one ran, filled a sponge with vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave him drink, saying: “Let us see whether Elijah comes to take him down.”

But Jesus again uttered a loud cry and expired. And the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom.

> [Col. 0577] But the soldiers led him inside the courtyard, which is the praetorium, and summoned the entire cohort.

> [Col. 0578] *ïnnana gardis*: the editions read *ïnn anagardis*. That reading is objectionable not only in respect of composition, since neither does *anagards* adequately render the meaning of Greek αὐλή (“courtyard,” or the front part of a house), whereas simple *gards* corresponds to that Greek word—see 14:54—but also because a genitive follows the adverb *ïnn*. If a genitive is required after adverbs of this kind, the Goths use forms such as *utana*, *hindana*; compare Graff, *Althochdeutsche Präpositionen*, p. 10. By analogy with these, one should say *ïnnana*; see 2 Corinthians 7:5. These considerations make it more reasonable to maintain that Ulfilas read ἔσω than Griesbach’s claim that the Goth found εἰς in his manuscript.

> [Col. 0577] And they clothed him in purple and, weaving a crown of thorns, put it upon him.

[Col. 0581] [Note: [Col. 0581] But Pilate was astonished that he had already died; and summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he had already died.]

[[Note: [Col. 0581] *at*] F., at this place and at Mark 12:2, without any authority, writes *af*.

[Note: [Col. 0581] *ïs*] “he,” with all the Greek witnesses..—*þan*] “but,” with all the Greek witnesses. Since the particles *jah þan*, expressing a single idea, are not ordinarily separated by the insertion of another verb, we think that an error lies in *þan*, and that *þana* should be read. This, however, could by no means have been mutilated into *þan* for the sake of euphony, as learned men suppose while producing examples that prove nothing.—*juþan*] “already,” secondarily; Greek *πάλαι*.]

[[Note: [Col. 0581] And as the Sabbath day was impending, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might come and anoint him.].]

[Note: [Col. 0581] *ïnvisandins*] The Codex Argenteus, J. St., and B. add *ïnvisandin*; the *s* is omitted because of the following identical letter. See 10:45; compare the note on 3:13. Moreover, instead of Greek *διαγενομένου σαββάτου* (“when the Sabbath had passed”), the Gothic has “when the day was at hand,”,” and seems to agree with Luke 23:56 and 24:1; see the note on verse 2. The genitives are not absolute, as they are called, but properly indicate time, as in the following verse. Thus *ïnvisandins sabbate dagis* (“with the Sabbath day preceding”) is opposed to *þis dagis afar sabbate* (“on the day after the Sabbath”). The preceding Sabbath day, mentioned above at 15:42 as “the first of the Sabbaths,” was so called because both the preceding Sabbath and the following one were festival days; the Sabbath itself lay between them.]

[Note: [Col. 0581] And very early on the day after the Sabbath, they came to the tomb, at sunrise.]

[Note: [Col. 0581] *þis—sabbate*] “on the following day after the Sabbath” (more strictly, “on the day after the Sabbath”; German *am Nachtag des Sabbats*, French *le lendemain du sabbat*), Greek *τῆς μιᾶς σαββάτων* (“the first [day] of the week”), in place of *þis afar dagis*. See Luke 7:11. In place of *afar sabbate*, perhaps *jct. afar sabbate* should be read, just as in certain former regions of Germany Tuesday (*Dienstag*, French *mardi*) was called *aftermontag* (“after-Monday,” literally French *après lundi*); see Grimm, *DRA*, p. 820. Moreover, as we have already indicated above, Ulfila, differing from all the Greek witnesses, follows Luke’s narrative. The Gothic should be understood thus: on the day preceding the Sabbath itself, the women bought spices (on the Sabbath itself they rested, Luke 23:56); on the day after the Sabbath (which is “one of the Sabbaths” in Greek), they hastened to the tomb.—*atïddjedun*] The Codex Argenteus adds *atïddedun*.—*at urrinandin*] J. St. Z. add *jct*.]

Do not be afraid. You are seeking Jesus the Nazarene, the crucified one. He is not here; he has risen. Behold the place where they laid him.

[Note: [Col. 0581] But go and tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you into Galilee; there you will see him, just as he told you.]

[Note: [Col. 0582] *faurbigaggiþ*] J. St. B. reject *fauratgaggiþ*.—*ïzvis*] Secondarily; J. St. add *ïna ïs* (“him he”), but Maresh. read this way, p. 441.]
