### Editorial and textual notes

[Col. 0591] “And it was announced to him by this Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he saw the Lord’s Christ.”

[Col. 0591] “And he came in the Spirit into this temple, and while they brought in this infant Jesus, so that they might do with him according to the custom of the law.”

[Col. 0591] “And he took him into his arms and blessed God and said.”

[Col. 0592] *ïna*: “him”; understand Jesus. In the Greek, αὐτό refers to the child, as also at I, 59; compare the note on Mark XIV, 46.

[Col. 0591] “Now release your servant, Lord and Master, according to your word in peace.”

[Col. 0592] *fraleitais*: Hertz has *fraletais*; see the note on Matthew IX, 6.

[Col. 0592] *fraujinond frauja*: B has *frauja* as a gloss inserted into the text, and Ih and Z agree with him. Mareshall, p. 447, however, defends the reading much more correctly. Gothic uses this fullness of expression either to convey the solemn meaning of the word δεσπότης, “master,” or as an amplification of the matter, as at Matthew IX, 23, *haurnjans haurnjandans*; compare the note on Matthew IX, 8.

[Col. 0591] “For my eyes have seen your salvation.”

[Col. 0591] “Which you prepared in the presence of all peoples.”

[Col. 0591] “A light for revelation to the nations and a glory for your people Israel.”

[Col. 0591] “And Joseph and his mother were amazed at what was said about him.”

[Col. 0592] *ïosef—ïs*: “Joseph and his mother”; the Greek has ὁ πατὴρ αὐτοῦ καὶ ἡ μήτηρ, “his father and mother.”

[Col. 0591] “And Simeon blessed him and said to Mary, his mother: Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel and for a sign of opposition.”

[Col. 0592] *ïna*: “him”; nearly all Greek manuscripts have αὐτούς, “them.”

[Col. 0591] “And your own soul a sword will pierce, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.”

[Col. 0593] *framaldra*: J and St add a division of the word.

[Col. 0593] *soh*: Ulfila seems to have read καὶ αὕτη, “and she”; see the note on verse 37.

[Col. 0593] *jera*: the Greek has the phrase before *miþ*, “with.”

[Col. 0593] “And this widow was eighty-four years old. She did not depart far from the temple, serving with fastings and prayers, worshiping the Lord night and day.”

[Col. 0593] *viduvo*: the manuscripts of Ulfila apparently read ὡς or ἕως, “as” or “until.”

[Col. 0593] *soh*: “she”; all Greek manuscripts have ἥ. In verse 38 *soh* corresponds to καὶ αὕτη, “and she”; see the note on John XVIII, 26. J and St omit *so*.

[Col. 0593] *blotande*: so the Argenteus manuscript; the editors print *blotandei*, the more frequent form. See the note on X, 5.

[Col. 0593] *fraujan*: “the Lord”; omitted by all Greek manuscripts.

[Col. 0593] “At this very hour she stood by, gave thanks to the Lord, and spoke about him to all who were awaiting the consolation of Jerusalem.”

[Col. 0593] *soh*: see the note on verse 37.

[Col. 0593] *ïn allaim*: “among all”; all Greek manuscripts have πᾶσι, “to all.” J omits *ïn*.

[Col. 0593] “And when they had completed everything according to the law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own city, Nazareth.”

[Col. 0593] *allata*: the manuscripts of Ulfila have τὰ, “the things”; *bi vitoda*, “according to the law,” therefore belongs with *ustauhun*, “they completed.”

[Col. 0593] “But this child grew and became strong, filled with the Spirit and wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him.”

[Col. 0593] *ahmins—handugeins*: “filled with the Spirit and wisdom”; the Greek has πνεύματι πληρούμενον σοφίας.

[Col. 0593] *fullnands*: St omits *fulnands*.

[Col. 0593] “And his parents went each year to Jerusalem for the feast of Passover.”

[Col. 0593] “And when he was twelve winters old, and they had gone up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast.”

[Col. 0593–0594] *tvalib vintruns*: “twelve winters”; the Greek has ἐτῶν δώδεκα, “twelve years,” as we have translated. Lye had already indicated this on p. LXV; compare Matthew IX, 20. The Argenteus manuscript and the editions add *tvalib vintrus*. Ih and Hertz have *tvalibvintrus* and appear to have taken it as an adjective; compare Luke VIII, 42. Grimm, Grammar II, 950, reads *tvalibvintruns* and repeats this at IV, 652, because, if our division of those words were correct, one would have to say *tvalibins vintruns*. But such an accusative, which Zahn already wished to adopt at John VI, 70, is found nowhere and will not be found. In any case, the synecdoche by which winters are used for years in estimating age—part for the whole—is common to Icelanders and Goths.

[Col. 0593] *þan*: “but”; omitted by all Greek manuscripts. See the note on XVI, 23.

[Col. 0593] “And when they had completed these days, as they returned, Jesus the child remained in Jerusalem, and Joseph and his mother did not know it.”

[Col. 0594] *miþþane*: so the Argenteus manuscript and the editions, for *miþþanei*; see the note on X, 5.

[Col. 0594] *aftra*: “again”; omitted by all Greek manuscripts.

[Col. 0594] *vissedun*: “they knew”; the Greek has ἔγνω, “he knew.” The Argenteus manuscript adds *visedun*. Since this spelling occurs only here, we thought it safer to place the regular form in the text.

[Col. 0593] “Supposing him to be among their companions, they traveled a day’s journey and sought him among their relatives and acquaintances.”

[Col. 0594] *hugjandona*: Ulfila omits δέ, “but.”

[Col. 0594] *ïna*: “him”; placed before *ïn* by the principal Greek manuscripts.

[Col. 0594] *ïn*: the third occurrence of “in”; omitted by the Greek manuscripts.

[Col. 0593] “And when they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem seeking him.”

[Col. 0594] *ïna*: “him”; omitted by the Greek manuscripts.

[Col. 0593] “And after three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and questioning them.”

[Col. 0594] *alh*: the Argenteus manuscript adds *allh*; see the note on Galatians V, 15.

[Col. 0593] “And all who heard him were astonished at his understanding and his answers.”

[Col. 0594] *ïs*: “his”; J and St add *ïna*, “them.”

[Col. 0593] “And when they saw him, they were amazed, and his mother said these things to him: Child, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I, grieving, have sought you.”

[Col. 0594] *qaþ*: the Greek places this after *ïs*, “his.”

[Col. 0593] “And he said to them: Why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I had to be in the things of my Father?”

[Col. 0594] *skulda*: “I had to”; all Greek manuscripts have δεῖ, the present tense, “it is necessary.”

[Col. 0593] “And they did not understand this word that he spoke to them.”

[Col. 0593] “And he went with them, came to Nazareth, and was obedient to them; and his mother kept all these words in her heart.”

[Col. 0594] *þo vaurda*: the Greek places this after *alla*, “all.”

[Col. 0593] “And Jesus advanced in wisdom, stature, and grace with God and men.”

[Col. 0593–0595] “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governing Judaea, and Herod was tetrarch of this Galilee; and Philip, his brother, was tetrarch of this Ituraea and of the region of Trachonitis, and Lysanias was tetrarch of Abilene.”

[Col. 0594] *fimftataihundin*: J, St, and B add *fimftaihundin*. In the Argenteus manuscript the omitted syllable *ta* is written above the line.

[Col. 0594–0595] *fidurraginja—herodeis*: J, St, and B omit *herodis*; Z has *herodei*, the dative. *fidurraginja* is derived from the nominative *fidurragineis* or *fidurragini* and means “tetrarchy,” not “tetrarch.” This is shown by the following genitives, *filippaus* and *lysaniaus*, and is why we printed *herodeis*, since a similar dative form, *herodei*, is no longer found. In the Argenteus manuscript we could not determine what was written after *herodei*, although a trace of some writing remains. Finally, *fidurraginja* is a dative corresponding to the nominative *fidurragineis*—*ragineis* at Mark XV, 43; Romans XI, 34; Skeireins 52, 11—which we preferred to restore as *fidurragini*, because common nouns more often designate both a person and his office, function, or craft. Among other examples are *fauramaþleis*, “ruler,” at Matthew IX, 34, and *fauramaþli*, “government,” at Nehemiah V, 14, unless the nominative *fauramaþli* is established by analogy with *fauragaggi*, “administration,” at Luke XVI, 2; *airus*, “legate,” at Luke VII, 24, and “legation” at XIV, 32; and *gaman*, “companion,” at Luke V, 7, but “companionship” at 2 Corinthians XIII, 13. See also the note on Luke XIX, 23. The verb *staua* has a different history.

[Col. 0595] “Under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John, son of Zachariah, in the wilderness.”

[Col. 0595] *auhmistam gudjam*: “the high priests”; the Greek has ἀρχιερέως, “high priest.” J, St, and B omit *auhumistam* in favor of *auhmistam*.

[Col. 0595] *ïohannen*: St adds *johannem*.

[Col. 0595] “And he came through all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.”

[Col. 0595] “As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet, who says: The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.”

[Col. 0595] “Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; the crooked shall become straight, and the rough ways smooth.”

[Col. 0595] *dalei*: a plural genitive instead of the usual *dale*. Compare *fareisaiei* at V, 32—this should be restored at Skeireins 52, 9—*ïudaiei* at John XI, 45 and XII, 11, *gardei* at Luke X, 5, and *þizei* at Mark XIV, 69 and following, and *ïzei* at John VII, 50. See Grimm I, 36.

[Col. 0595] *þata*: J and St add *þana*.

[Col. 0595] *usdrusteis*: J and B add *usþrusteis*.

[Col. 0595] “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God.”

[Col. 0595] “And he said to the crowds who came out to be baptized by him: Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from this coming wrath?”

[Col. 0595] *akran*: “fruit”; the Greek has καρπούς, “fruits.”

[Col. 0595] “Therefore produce fruit worthy of repentance, and do not begin to say among yourselves: We have Abraham as our father. For I tell you that God can raise up children for Abraham from these stones.”

[Col. 0595] “But already the axe lies at the roots of the trees. Therefore every tree that does not produce good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.”

[Col. 0595] *ju*: Ulfila’s manuscripts, codex D, and the versions omit καί, “and.”

[Col. 0595] “And the crowds asked him, saying: What, then, shall we do?”

[Col. 0595] *an*: J and St add *þan*. In interrogative sentences *an* corresponds to Greek καί at Luke X, 29; XVIII, 26; and John IX, 36; John XVIII, 37, *an nuh*, corresponds to οὐκοῦν, “then, surely.”

[Col. 0595] “And he answered and said: Let the one who has two tunics give to the one who has none; and let the one who has food do likewise.”

[Col. 0595] *qaþ*: “he said.” Those who claim that Ulfila read ἔλεγε, “he was saying,” instead of λέγει, “he says,” in his manuscript are mistaken; in narrative Gothic normally uses the preterite, as we noted at Matthew VIII, 20. Ulfila’s manuscripts omit αὐτοῖς, “to them.”

[Col. 0595] “Tax collectors also came to be baptized and said to him: Teacher, what shall we do?”

[Col. 0596] *þan*: Ulfila omits καί, “and”; compare Mark XV, 40.

[Col. 0595] “Then he said to them: Exact nothing beyond what has been appointed for you.”

[Col. 0595] “Soldiers also asked him, saying: And what shall we do? And he said to them: Do violence to no one, accuse no one falsely, and be content with your wages.”

[Col. 0596] *þa*: “they”; Ulfila, with the manuscripts, seems to have read οἱ, “those.”

[Col. 0596] *ni mannanhun anamahtjaid*: “do not extort anyone.” Since this does not agree with the Greek manuscripts, which have μηδὲ συκοφαντήσητε, “nor accuse anyone falsely,” it is very likely that Ulfila, with his manuscripts, read μηδένα ἀδικήσητε, “wrong no one,” but placed it here, and then omitted μηδὲ συκοφαντήσητε entirely; compare the note on Matthew V, 44. Alternatively, since *afholon* at Luke XIX, 8 means συκοφαντεῖν, “to accuse falsely,” perhaps he read συκοφαντήσητε for διασείσητε, “extort.” The former explanation appears more probable. J and St print *anamahtjaiþ* against the authority of the Argenteus manuscript, which has *anamahtjaid*. Compare Mareshall on this passage.

[Col. 0596] *valdaiþ*: “be content” or “be satisfied”; all Greek manuscripts have ἀρκεῖσθε. The gloss in the Argenteus manuscript, *ganohidai sijaiþ*, “let there be enough for you,” renders the meaning well. See Skeireins 49, 20, *managai ganohjands ïns vailaviznai*, “satisfying them abundantly with food”; compare John XIV, 8 and 2 Corinthians XII, 9. According to Mareshall’s ingenious conjecture, Ulfila may have read ἄρχετε, “rule,” instead of ἀρκεῖσθε, perhaps owing to a faulty exemplar. See Prolegomena, col. 485.

[Col. 0596] *annom*: this word has created many difficulties for scholars. Ihrius, in *Ulfilas Illustratus*, pp. 292 and following, defended the reading; Z. wished, incorrectly, to change it to *launom*; Schmid, *Schwäbisches Wörterbuch*, p. 99, preferred *asnom*, which is much better; compare *asneis*, “day-laborer,” and *misθιος*, “hireling.” The same word occurs again with the same meaning at 1 Corinthians IX, 7.

[Col. 0595] “While all the people were expecting, and all were thinking in their hearts about John, whether he might perhaps be the Christ.”

[Col. 0596] *at venjandein*: J, St, and Z add a division.

[Col. 0596] *allai*: “all”; the Greek manuscripts have “the whole.”

[Col. 0596] *ïohannein*: so written instead of *ïohannen* in this one place; compare the note on III, 5.

[Col. 0596] *niu*: J adds *uiu*.

[Col. 0595] “John answered everyone, saying: I indeed baptize you with water, but one stronger than I is coming, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loosen. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.”

[Col. 0596] *þan*: “but”; omitted by all Greek manuscripts.

[Col. 0596] *ïzvis*: placed after *daupja*, “I baptize you,” in all Greek manuscripts.

[Col. 0596] *ïk*: the second occurrence of “I”; omitted by all Greek manuscripts.

[Col. 0597] “He has his winnowing shovel in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing floor and gather the grain into his granary; but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.”

[Col. 0597] *jah*: at the end; St adds *jak*.

[Col. 0597] *bansta*: J and St add the final *n*.

[Col. 0597] *unwapnandin*: see the note on Mark IV, 7.

[Col. 0597] “And with many other exhortations he proclaimed the good news to the people.”

[Col. 0597] *þan*: it is uncertain whether Ulfila omitted μέν, “indeed,” or οὖν, “therefore,” since *þan* can represent either. It corresponds especially to οὖν in the Gospels; μέν, opposed to *ïþ* (δέ), occurs only at 1 Corinthians IV, 10.

[Col. 0597] “But Herod the tetrarch, reproved by him concerning Herodias, the wife of his brother, and concerning all the evil things that Herod had done.”

[Col. 0597] “He added this also to everything and shut John up in prison.”

[Col. 0597] *ïohannen*: B adds *ïoaannen*.

[Col. 0597] “And it happened, when he had baptized all the people, and Jesus had been baptized and was praying, that heaven was opened.”

[Col. 0597] *daupida—managein*: “he baptized—the crowd.” On the basis of all Greek manuscripts one would expect *daupjada alla managei*, “he baptized all the crowd,” which would also suit the sense better than Ulfila’s wording.

[Col. 0597] *alla*: J and St add *allama*.

[Col. 0597] *managein*: St adds *mitoþim*.

[Col. 0597] *ïesu*: see the note on Mark X, 50.

[Col. 0597] *ufdaupdamma jah bidjandin*: J and St add forms meaning “when he had been baptized and was praying.”

[Col. 0597] “And the Holy Spirit descended upon him in bodily form, like a dove, and a voice came from heaven, saying: You are my beloved Son; in you I have been well pleased.”

[Col. 0597] “And Jesus himself was about thirty years old when he began his ministry, being regarded as the son of Joseph, son of Heli.”

[Col. 0597–0598] *uf gakunþai*: J, St, B, and Ih add a conjectural form. There is no need for Lye’s conjecture *us gabaurþai*, nor for Mareshall’s *uf gagunþai*, which Ih wished to change to *uf gagunnai*. B correctly interprets the codex reading as “under public manifestation,” and Ulfila read ἀρχόμενος, “beginning,” supplying the ellipsis according to his own construction. Ulfila’s manuscripts have ὤν, “being.” St adds *sylei*. The Greek places *sunus*, “son,” after *vas*, “was.” *sunaus*, “of the son,” corresponds to the Greek τοῦ; the versions likewise preserve this form in the following passages.

[Col. 0597] “Son of Mattathias, son of Levi, son of Melchi, son of Janna, son of Joseph.”

[Col. 0598] *laivveis*: St adds *laiveis*; likewise in verse 29.

[Col. 0598] *jannins*: St adds *ïannis*, and Z has *ïannins*.

[Col. 0598] *ïosefis*: St adds *ïosephis*, likewise in verses 26 and 30.

[Col. 0597] “Son of Mattathias, son of Amos, son of Naum, son of Esli, son of Nagge.”

[Col. 0598] *aizleimis*: the Greek has Ἐσλί.

[Col. 0597] “Son of Maath, son of Mattathias, son of Semein, son of Joseph, son of Joda.”

[Col. 0597] “Son of Jonam, son of Rhesa, son of Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, son of Neri.”

[Col. 0598] *ïohannins*: St adds *ïohannis*, since *ïohannins* is derived from the nominative *ïohanna*; likewise in verse 30.

[Col. 0597] “Son of Melchi, son of Addi, son of Cosam, son of Elmadam, son of Er.”

[Col. 0598] *airmodamis*: the Greek has Ἐλμωδάμ.

[Col. 0597] “Son of Joshua, son of Eliezer, son of Jorim, son of Mattathias, son of Levi.”

[Col. 0597] “Son of Simeon, son of Judah, son of Joseph, son of Jonam, son of Eliakim.”

[Col. 0597] “Son of Melea, son of Menna, son of Mattatha, son of Nathan, son of David.”

[Col. 0598] *maila anis*: Z adds *malaianis*. The Greek manuscripts, however, have Μελεᾶ.

[Col. 0598] *sunaus*: at its third occurrence St has *sunans*, as also in verse 36.

[Col. 0597] “Son of Jesse, son of Obed, son of Boaz, son of Salmon, son of Nahshon.”

[Col. 0597] “Son of Amminadab, son of Admin, son of Arni, son of Hezron, son of Perez, son of Judah.”

[Col. 0598] *aizoris*: all Greek manuscripts have Ἐσρώμ.

[Col. 0597] “Son of Jacob, son of Isaac, son of Abraham, son of Terah, son of Nahor.”

[Col. 0598] *ïakobis*: St adds *ïacobis*.

[Col. 0597] “Son of Serug, son of Reu, son of Peleg, son of Eber, son of Shelah.”

[Col. 0598] *sairokis*: St adds *saikoris*.

[Col. 0598] *falaigis*: the Greek has Φαλέκ.

[Col. 0597] “Son of Cainan, son of Arphaxad, son of Shem, son of Noah, son of Lamech.”

[Col. 0597] “Son of Methuselah, son of Enoch, son of Jared, son of Mahalaleel, son of Cainan.”

[Col. 0598] *ïaredis*: one would expect *ïaraidis*, since Gothic *ai* normally corresponds to Greek η; compare *tairtius* for *tertius*.

[Col. 0598] *maleilaielis*: J and St add *maleiaielis*.

[Col. 0597] “Son of Enos, son of Seth, son of Adam, son of God.”

[Col. 0597] “But Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, turned back from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness.”

[Col. 0598] *ïn authidai*: “in the wilderness”; the Greek has εἰς τὴν ἔρημον.

[Col. 0597] “For forty days he was tempted by the devil; and he ate nothing during those days, and when they were completed he was hungry.”

[Col. 0599] *at ustauhanaim*: J and St add a conjectural reading.

[Col. 0599] *þaim dagam*: “during those days”; all Greek manuscripts have αὐτῶν, “of them.”

[Col. 0599] “And the devil said to him: If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread.”

[Col. 0599] *diabulus*: J, St, and B omit the final *s* in favor of *diabulaus*.

[Col. 0599] *sunaus*: so the Argenteus manuscript, St, B, and Z, instead of *sunus*; see the note on Mark VII, 32.

[Col. 0599] “And Jesus answered him, saying: It is written that man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.”

[Col. 0599] “And the devil led him up onto a high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of this world in a moment of time.”

[Col. 0599] *diabulaus*: so the Argenteus manuscript, J, St, and B, instead of the usual *diabulus*; see the note on verse 3.

[Col. 0599] “And the devil said to him: To you I will give all this authority and their glory, because it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whomever I wish.”

[Col. 0599] *sa*: J and St add it.

[Col. 0599] *þize*: “of these”; omitted by all Greek manuscripts, which rather have ταύτην, “this.”

[Col. 0599] *þei*: this passage is noteworthy, because it shows that Grimm was mistaken at III, 19, 5 in teaching that *þei* was a contracted form of *þatei*, the neuter relative pronoun. Here it refers to the masculine *þiswammeh*, “whomever,” and one would expect *þammei*. Rather, *þei* is contracted from *þatei*, the relative particle, equivalent to *ei* and often used in place of a relative pronoun; compare the note on Luke I, 20. Thus at Mark XI, 23 we read *þiswazuh ei* for *þiswazuh saei* (Mark IV, 25), and frequently elsewhere.

[Col. 0599] “He showed him all the kingdoms of this world in a moment of time.”

[Col. 0599] “And the devil said to him: To you I will give this authority over all these things and their glory, because it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whomever I wish.”

[Col. 0599] “Therefore, if you worship me in my presence, all of it will be yours.”

[Col. 0599] *mik*: “me”; omitted by all Greek manuscripts. B thinks, not very correctly, that it may be a gloss, since *ïnveitan* is not intransitive in the sense in which the Greek προσκυνεῖν, “to worship,” is used.

[Col. 0599] *ïesus qaþ*: parallel to all Greek manuscripts except codex 11 in Mill.

[Col. 0599] *ïnveitais*: the Greek places this before *fraujan*, “the Lord.”

[Col. 0599] “And Jesus answered him and said: It is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve.”

[Col. 0599] “Then he led him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him: If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here.”

[Col. 0599] *vairþ*: J and St add *vairpi*.

[Col. 0599] “For it is written that he will command his angels concerning you, to preserve you.”

[Col. 0599] *handum*: J and St add *handun*.

[Col. 0599] *þuk ufhaband*: parallel to all Greek manuscripts.

[Col. 0599] *gastagqjais bi*: J adds *gastagujaisei*; B has *gastagqjaisei*.

[Col. 0599] “And that they will hold you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone.”

[Col. 0599] “And Jesus answered and said to him: It is said, You shall not tempt the Lord your God.”

[Col. 0599] “And when the devil had completed every temptation, he departed from him until the appointed time.”

[Col. 0600] *fraistobnjo*: J and St have *fraistubnjo*, the more frequent form; compare Matthew VI, 13 and Luke VIII, 13, but also Luke VII, 12, XVII, 13, XX, 12, and Mark X, 23. The forms vary between *faiho*, *ushofun*, *vundon*, and *faihu*; see the note on Mark IX, 50.

[Col. 0599] *diabulus*: J adds *diabolus*, and St has *daibolaus*.

[Col. 0599] “And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through all the surrounding region.”

[Col. 0599] “And he taught in their assemblies, being glorified by all.”

[Col. 0599] “And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and entered according to his custom on the Sabbath day into the synagogue, and stood up to read the book.”

[Col. 0600] *bi biuhtja*: St adds a conjectural reading.

[Col. 0600] *bokos*: “the book”; omitted by all Greek manuscripts.

[Col. 0599] “And the book of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him, and when he had opened the book, he found the place where it was written.”

[Col. 0600] *praufetus*: see the note on I, 54.

[Col. 0599] “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor; he has sent me to heal the brokenhearted.”

[Col. 0600] *du ganasjan—hairtin*: “to heal—the heart”; omitted by the Greek manuscripts.

[Col. 0600] *gamalvidans*: Wachter, *Glossarium Germanicum*, under *Malmen*, emends this to *gamalmidans*. The emendation is more attractive than convincing, since from *malan* (Luke XVII, 35) comes *malvjan*. Compare the other verbs ending in *-vjan*: *balvjan*, *bandvjan*, *valvjan*, *skadvjan*.

[Col. 0599] “To proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind, to set the broken free in consolation, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.”

[Col. 0600] *frahunþanaim*: J and St add a division, *frahun þanais*. Z’s conjecture *frabunþanaim*, or at least *frabundanaim*, is now accepted by no one; compare Romans VII, 23; 2 Corinthians X, 5; and Philemon 23.

[Col. 0600] *gaþrafstein*: “consolation”; all Greek manuscripts have ἄφεσις, “release.”

[Col. 0599] “And he folded up the book, gave it back to the attendant, and sat down; and the eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed upon him.”

[Col. 0600] *jah*: the second occurrence of “and”; omitted by all Greek manuscripts except codex X in Mill.

[Col. 0600] *þizai*: St adds a conjectural form.

[Col. 0600] *vesun*: the Greek places this after *augona*, “eyes.”

[Col. 0599] “And he began to say to them: Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your ears.”

[Col. 0600] *dugann*: the editions add *dugan*. In the Argenteus manuscript it cannot be determined whether the liquid was doubled, but the space appears too narrow to contain *nn*.

[Col. 0599–0601] “And all bore witness to him and were amazed at these words of grace proceeding from his mouth, and they said: Is this not Joseph’s son?”

[Col. 0600] *alakjo*: see the note on Mark XI, 32.

[Col. 0601] “And he said to them: Surely you will say to me this proverb: Physician, heal yourself. Whatever we have heard was done in Capernaum, do also here in your homeland.”

[Col. 0601] *þo*: “this”; those who say that Ulfila omitted ταύτην, “this,” are mistaken.

[Col. 0601] *þu*: “you”; omitted by all Greek manuscripts.

[Col. 0601] “And they said: Is this not Joseph’s son?”

[Col. 0601] “And he said to them: Surely you will say to me this proverb: Physician, heal yourself. Whatever we have heard was done in Capernaum, do also here in your homeland.”

[Col. 0601] “And he said: Amen, I tell you that no prophet is accepted in his homeland.”
ïzvis] Greek, after *qiþa*.

[Note: [Col. 0601] “Truly I say to you, there were many widows in the days of Elijah in Israel, when the heavens were shut up for three years and six months, when a great famine came over the whole land.”]

[Note: [Col. 0601] *þatei*] “that,” according to the Greek. — *dagam*] J. St. + *daga*. — *ïsraela*] J. + *ïsrael*. — *jeram þrim*] J. St. B. + *jeran þrin*.]

Then he said: “Amen, I say to you, no prophet is acceptable in his homeland. But in truth I say to you, there were many widows in the days of Elijah in Israel, when the heavens were shut up for three years and six months, so that a great famine arose throughout the whole earth. And Elijah was sent to none of them, except to a widow at Sarepta of Sidon.”

And there were many lepers under the prophet Elisha in Israel, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.

[Note: [Col. 0601] *haileisaiu*] Thus in the Argenteus manuscript; J. St. + *haileisand*, Hickes conjectures + *haileisaia*, B. Z. + *haileisaim*. — *naiman*] that is, Νεμάν or Ναιμάν; but since the Greek manuscripts variously read Νεεμάν or Ναιεμάν, perhaps *naiaiman* should be read, as in *gaiainna* (γέεννα), *baiailzaibul* (Βεελζεβούλ). Compare, however, *ïsak* for *ïsaak* (Ισαάκ).]

And all those in the synagogue, hearing this, were filled with anger. They rose up and drove him outside the city and led him to the brow of the mountain on which their city had been built, in order to throw him down from there.

[Note: [Col. 0601] *ut us*] J. St. B. + *utun*. — *þaþro*] “from here,” according to the Greek.]

And all in the synagogue were enraged when they heard this. Rising, they drove him outside the city and brought him to the brow of the mountain on which their city had been built, to cast him down. But he, passing through the midst of them, went away.

[Note: [Col. 0601] “But he, passing through the midst of them, went away.”]

And he went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee, and was teaching them on the Sabbaths.

[Note: [Col. 0601] “And he went to Capernaum, a city of Galilee, and was teaching them on the Sabbaths.”]

And they were astonished at his teaching, because his word was with authority.

[Note: [Col. 0601] “And they were astonished at his teaching, because his word was with authority.”]

And in this synagogue there was a man who had an unclean demonic spirit, and he cried out:

[Note: [Col. 0602] *unhrainjana*] “unclean.” It refers to *ahman* (“spirit,” πνεῦμα); Gothic agrees here with codex D (ἀκάθαρτον), whereas the other Greek manuscripts have ἀκαθάρτου, which should be joined with δαιμονίου (*unhulþons*). — *ufhropida*] Ulfilas agrees with codex 33 cited by Griesbach, with φωνῇ μεγάλῃ; compare Mark 1:23.]

“Leave us alone! What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God.”

[Note: [Col. 0601] “And Jesus rebuked him, saying: Be silent and come out from him! And the demon, throwing him into the midst, came out from him, without harming him in any way.”]

[Note: [Col. 0602] *nazorenu*] See the note on Mark 1:24.]

And Jesus rebuked him, saying: “Be silent, and come out from him.” And the unclean spirit, throwing him into the midst, came out from him without injuring him at all.

And amazement came upon them all, and they spoke to one another, saying: “What is this word, that with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out?”

[Note: [Col. 0601] “And it came to pass that all were astonished and spoke to one another, saying: What is this word, that with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out?”]

And a report about him went out into every place of the surrounding region.

[Note: [Col. 0601] “And rising from the synagogue, he went into Simon’s house; Simon’s mother-in-law was held by a great fever, and they asked him about her.”]

And he rose from the synagogue and went into Simon’s house. Simon’s mother-in-law was afflicted with a severe fever, and they entreated him concerning her. Standing over her, he rebuked the fever, and it left her. Immediately she rose and ministered to them.

[Note: [Col. 0601] “And when the sun had set, all who had sick people suffering from various diseases brought them to him; but he laid his hands on each one of them and healed them.”]

When the sun had set, all those who had sick people with various diseases brought them to him. He laid his hands on each one of them and healed them.

[Note: [Col. 0602] *sagq*] J. St. + *sagu*. — *ainwarjammeh*] J. St. + *ainwarjaneh*, Hz. + *ainwarjameh*.]

And demons also came out from many, crying out and saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of God.” But rebuking them, he did not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0601] *xristus*] “Christ,” according to the Greek. — *ïm*] “to them,” according to the Greek manuscripts generally. — *silban*] “himself,” according to the Greek manuscripts generally; but Ulfilas seems to have intended this word to render the Greek article.]

They brought them to him. But he laid his hand on each one of them and healed them.

And when day came, he went out and went to a deserted place. The crowds sought him, came to him, and held him so that he would not go away from them.

[Note: [Col. 0602] *afliþi*] J. St. + *galaiþ*.]

And he rebuked them and did not allow them to speak, because they themselves knew him to be Christ.

After this, when it was day, he went out and went to a deserted place. The crowds sought him, came to him, and held him so that he would not depart from them.

[Note: [Col. 0601] “Then he said to them: I must also announce the good news of the kingdom of God to these other cities.” [Col. 0603] “For this is why I was sent.”]

[Note: [Col. 0602] *skal bi*] J. St. + *skulda*.]

He said to them: “I must also proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to the other cities, for this is why I was sent.”

[Col. 0603]

And he was preaching in the synagogues of Galilee.

[Note: [Col. 0603] “And it came to pass, while the crowd pressed upon him to hear the word of God, that he himself was standing beside the lake of Gennesaret.”]

And it came to pass, while the crowd pressed upon him to hear the word of God, that he himself was standing beside the lake of Gennesaret. He saw two boats standing by the lake, but the fishermen had gone away from them and were washing their nets.

[Note: [Col. 0603] “And he entered one of these boats, which was Simon’s; he ordered him to put out a little from the shore, and sitting down he taught the crowds from the boat.”]

[Note: [Col. 0603] *galaiþ*] “He embarked,” according to the Greek, ἐμβάς. — *aftiuhan*] The Greek comes after *staþa*.]

And he entered one of the boats, which was Simon’s, and ordered him to put out a little from the shore. He sat down and taught the crowds from the boat.

When he had ceased speaking, he said to Simon: “Put out into the deep and lower your nets for a catch.”

[Note: [Col. 0603] *brigg*] St. + *bring*. — *athahid*] J. St. + *athaihid*; Griesbach incorrectly notes that Ulfilas read χαλάσωμεν.]

And Simon answered and said to him: “Teacher, having labored all night, we caught nothing; but at your word I will lower the net.”

[Note: [Col. 0603] *þairharbaidjandans*] J. St. B. + division; compare VI, 12, *naht þairhvakands* (“keeping watch through the night”); 1 Corinthians 10:1, *marein þairhïddjedun* (“they passed through the sea”). — *nemum*] St. + *nemun*. — *vairpam*] “we lower,” Greek χαλάσω.]

Putting out into the deep, they lowered their net for a catch. And Simon answered and said to him: “Teacher—”

[Note: [Col. 0603] “And doing this, they enclosed a great multitude of fish, so that their nets were breaking.”]

[Note: [Col. 0603] *sve—ïze*] “so that their nets were breaking,” Greek διεῤῥήγνυτο δὲ τὸ δίκτυον αὐτῶν. Gothic agrees with codex D; but we do not know whether αὐτῶν, omitted in Griesbach’s apparatus, is found there.]

Though they had labored all night, they caught nothing; but at your word we lower the net. And they signaled to their companions who were in the other boat to come and help them. They came and filled both boats, so that they were sinking.

[Note: [Col. 0603] *þoei*] J. St. B. + *þaei*; Ih. conjectured *þaiei* here, but Ulfilas’s reading in the Argenteus manuscript is defended because it is credible that people of both sexes were engaged in the fishing. Gothic could not write otherwise here, since *gaman* is neuter; compare 2 Corinthians 8:23, *gaman mein* (“my companion”). — *sugqun*] Ulfilas omits αὐτά.]

Simon Peter, seeing this, fell at Jesus’ knees, saying: “I beg you, depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord.”

[Note: [Col. 0603] *bidja þuk*] “I beg you,” according to the Greek.]

For amazement had seized him and all who were with him because of the catch of fish which they had taken. Likewise also James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were Simon’s companions.

[Note: [Col. 0603] *zaibaidaiaus*] J. + *zabaidaiaus*. — *þaiei*] J. St. B. [Col. 0604] + *þatei*, likewise in verse 29. — *fram himma nu*] Z. rightly observes that *fram himma* is sufficient to render the Greek ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν (John 13:9; 14:7), but is seriously mistaken in claiming that *fram nu* can also be used; prepositions are not joined to adverbs unless a demonstrative pronoun is added. Compare 2 Corinthians 5:16, *fram þamma nu*; 8:13, *ïn þamma nu mela*. Moreover, we learn from Luke 1:48 and *Skeireins* 43.17, *und hita nu*, that the reading of the Argenteus manuscript is correct. — *siud nutans*] “you are catchers,” Greek ἔσῃ ζωγρῶν; Zahn’s edition has “you will be catchers.”]

And Jesus said to Simon: “Do not be afraid. From now on you will be catching people.”

And it came to pass on one of those days, while he was teaching, that Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there, having come together from all the villages of Galilee and Judea and Jerusalem. And the power of the Lord was present to heal them.

[Note: [Col. 0606] *þan*] St. + *tan*. — *plat*] J. St. + *naat*. — *aiþþau*] St. + *aihþau*. — *gatimid*] Ulfilas, with the Greek manuscripts, has ἐπίβλημα.]

St. Z. add a conjunction. — *jah—baurge*] “and the other cities,” omitted by all the Greek manuscripts; without doubt these words stood in the margin of the manuscript which had ἄλλων πόλεων instead of Ἱερουσαλὴμ—Σιδῶνος, and the scribe who copied the Argenteus manuscript brought them into the text.].]

who had come to hear him and to be healed of their diseases; and those who were troubled by unclean spirits were healed.

[Note: [Col. 0609] “And the whole crowd sought to touch him, because power went out from him and healed them all.”]

And the whole crowd sought to touch him, because power went out from him and healed them all. And all those who were afflicted by unclean spirits were healed.

[Note: [Col. 0609] “And raising his eyes toward his disciples, he said: Blessed are you poor in spirit, for yours is the kingdom of heaven.”]

And he, raising his eyes toward his disciples, said: “Blessed are you poor in spirit, for yours is the kingdom of heaven.”

[Note: [Col. 0609] *siponjam seinaim*] J. St. + *siponje seinai*, B. + *siponje seinaize*. What was written in the Argenteus manuscript can no longer be determined; we have supplied the form found in Ih., since the construction requires the preposition *du*. — *jus*] “you,” Greek οἱ. Ulfilas often adds the personal pronoun as a vocative where Greek uses the article. Compare Matthew 6:11, *atta unsar þu ïn himinam*; 7:23; Mark 9:25; Luke 4:23; 6:25; Ephesians 6:9. He rarely imitates Greek usage: Mark 15:29 and following, *o sa gatairands þo alh nasei þuk!* (“O you who destroy this temple, save yourself!”), or Luke 9:41, *o kuni!* (“O generation!”). More often he omits the pronoun, as in Mark 10:47; Luke 7:54; John 19:3; or the interjection, as in Romans 9:20, *manna!* (“O man!”). — *ahmin*] “in spirit,” according to the Greek; J. St. adds *nu*. — *himine*] “of heaven,” according to all the Greek manuscripts, θεοῦ.]

Blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh.

[Note: [Col. 0609] *fin.*] J. St. place a lacuna sign after *ufhlohjanda*, but nothing is added in the Argenteus manuscript. Those scholars were misled because the scribe wrote nothing at the end of the line, while the letters that seem to be present have bled through from the reverse side of the page.]

[Note: [Col. 0609] *sijuþ*] Hz. omits +. — *fijand*] J. St. + *fijond*. — *jah*] The printed edition; Ulfilas omits the Greek ὅταν.]

[Note: [Col. 0609] *laikid*] J. St. B. + *laikod*. — *himinam*] “in heaven,” Greek οὐρανῷ. — *praufetum*] Thus in the Argenteus manuscript; J. St. B. + *praufetun*.]

But woe to you who are rich, for you already have your consolation.

[Note: [Col. 0610] *ju*] “already,” according to all the Greek manuscripts; J. St. omits + *nu*. — *gaþlaiht*] J. + *gaþrafst*, St. + *gaþod*, and instead, in the glossary p. 56, + *gadaliþ*. Z. ineptly proposes *laþon*, which scarcely gives an acceptable sense here; the Argenteus manuscript has the form printed by B. Compare also 2 Corinthians 1:3 and following; 7:4, 7.]

Woe to you who are full now, for you will hunger. Woe to you who laugh now, for you will begin to mourn and weep..

[Note: [Col. 0610] *sadans*] St. + *sandans*. — *nu*] The printed edition: “now,” according to the Greek. — *duginnid*] “you begin,” according to all the Greek manuscripts. Ulfilas used it to indicate future time; where his language lacked the corresponding tense, he usually employed the present, but sometimes compensated for this deficiency by a periphrasis, adding to *duginnan* (“begin”) the verbs *haban* (“have”), *skulan* (“owe, be obliged”), *munan* (“think, intend”), or *sik skaftjan* (“prepare oneself”).]

[Note: [Col. 0609] *allai*] “all,” according to the Greek.]

For their fathers did the same to the false prophets. But I say to you who hear: Love those who hate you, do good to those who hate you..

Bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you.

To the one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also; and from the one who takes your cloak, do not withhold your tunic also.

[Note: [Col. 0610] *ïimma*] “to him,” according to the Greek.]

Bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you.

[Note: [Col. 0609] But to everyone who asks you, give; and from the one who takes what is yours, do not demand it back.]

And just as you wish people to do to you, you also do the same to them.

[Note: [Col. 0609] And as you wish people to do to you, do the same to them.]

[Note: [Col. 0609] But if you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them.]

[Note: [Col. 0610] *aþþan* = “and,” Greek καί throughout.]

[Note: [Col. 0609] And if you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners do the same.]

And if you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what credit is that to you? For even sinners lend to sinners, so that they may receive an equal return.

[Note: [Col. 0609] And if you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what credit is that to you? For even sinners lend to sinners, so that they may receive an equal return.]

[Note: [Col. 0610] *þaimei*; J, St, and B read *þammei*.]

But love your enemies, do good and lend, expecting nothing in return; and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for he is kind toward the ungrateful and the wicked.

[Note: [Col. 0609] But love your enemies, do good and lend, expecting nothing in return; and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for he is kind toward the ungrateful and the wicked.]

[Note: [Col. 0610] *ïzvarans*: Ulfila has *ïzvar*, Greek καί. *jah*: the third hand and Z add *ja*. *unfagram*: J and St add *unfairam*.]

Be compassionate, just as your Father also is compassionate.

[Note: [Col. 0609] Be compassionate, just as your Father also is compassionate.]

[Note: [Col. 0610] *vairþaid*: Ulfila and the manuscripts have *vairþai*, corresponding to Greek οὖν. *svasve*: the Argenteus manuscript adds *svave*. *ïzvar*: J and St add *ïzvara*.]

[Note: [Col. 0611] *ei*: “so that,” Greek καί; see the note on John XVI, 17.]

Give, and it will be given to you: a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing, will be put into your lap. For with the measure with which you measure, it will be measured to you.

[Note: [Col. 0611] Give, and it will be given to you: a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing, will be put into your lap. For with the measure with which you measure, it will be measured to you.]

[Note: [Col. 0611] *jah*: the second hand has “and”; the Greek has καί. *ufarfulla*: “overfull.” The Greek πεπιεσμένον is not adequately represented by the Gothic word; B. suspects that Ulfila read περισσόν. *gibada*: “it will be given”; all Greek manuscripts have δώσουσιν; compare verse 44. *mitid*: so also B.’s conjecture, approved by Ih. in his note to Hz.; we have adopted it. [Note: [Col. 0611] *þan*: St adds *tan*. *ïm*: J and St add *ïn*. *dal gadriusand*: the editions print *dalga driusand*; see the note on Mark XII, 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0611] *gamanvids*: J and St add *gaustaujane manvids*; B adds *ga ustaujane manvids*. [Note: [Col. 0611] *gaumeis*: the second hand; J and St add *gaumjeis*.]

How can you say to your brother, “Brother, let me remove this splinter from your eye,” while you yourself do not see the beam in your own eye? Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see clearly how to remove the splinter from your brother’s eye.

[Note: [Col. 0611] Or how can you say to your brother, “Brother, let me remove this splinter from your eye,” while you yourself do not see the beam in your own eye? Hypocrite, first remove this beam from your own eye, and then you will see clearly how to remove this splinter from your brother’s eye.]

[Note: [Col. 0611] *ïk*: “I,” as in all Greek manuscripts.]

For no good tree produces bad fruit, nor does a bad tree produce good fruit. For every tree is known by its own fruit. For figs are not gathered from thorns, nor are grapes harvested from a thornbush.

[Note: [Col. 0611] For no good tree produces bad fruit, nor does a bad tree produce good fruit. For every tree is known by its own fruit. For figs are not gathered from thorns, nor are grapes harvested from a thornbush.]

[Note: [Col. 0611] *lisanda—trudanda*: “are gathered—are harvested”; all Greek manuscripts have συλλέγουσιν—τρυγῶσιν; compare verse 38. The Gothic *trudan*, “to tread,” “to trample” (X, 19; VIII, 5), does not at all correspond to Greek τρυγᾶν, “to reap” or “to harvest grapes.” If someone should say that Ulfila considered the sense rather than the words, then *us aiwatundjai* does not seem suitably applied. We count this passage among those in which he did not adequately understand the meaning of the Greek words; see the note on I, 5. *veinabasja*: “grapes,” plural; Greek σταφυλήν. J adds *veinabasjan*, and St *vainabasjan*.]

[Note: [Col. 0612] *usbairid*: the first hand; St adds *nsbairid*.]

[Note: [Col. 0612] *vaurda meina*: corresponds to all the Greek manuscripts. *galeiks ïst*: corresponds to all the Greek manuscripts.]

Everyone who comes to me, hears my words, and does them—I will show you whom he resembles. He resembles a man building a house, who dug deep, laid a foundation on rock; and when a flood came, the water broke against that house and could not shake it, because it had been founded on the rock.

[Note: [Col. 0611] Everyone who comes to me, hears my words, and does them—I will show you whom he resembles.]

[Note: [Col. 0611] He resembles a man building a house, who dug deep, laid a foundation on rock; and when a flood came, the water broke against that house and could not shake it, because it had been founded on this rock.]

[Note: [Col. 0612] *at garunjon*: J adds *atarunjan*; St *at garunjan*; B *atgarunjan*. *bistagq awa*: J has *bistagun awa*; St *bistaguna wa*. *ana*: the second hand; J and St add *and*.]

But the one who hears and does not act is like a man building a house on the ground without a foundation. When the flood struck it, it immediately collapsed, and the ruin of that house was great.

[Note: [Col. 0611] But the one who hears and does not act is like a man building a house on the ground without a foundation. When the flood struck it, it immediately collapsed, and the ruin of that house was great.]

[Note: [Col. 0612] *þatei*: If it is taken as a relative or causal particle, the sense becomes wholly confused. All Greek manuscripts have ᾗ, referring to οἰκία and depending on προσέρρηξεν. If the Goth intended to reproduce the Greek reading word for word, he should have written *bi þammei*, for the preposition *bi*, or *du*, or *viþra*, is usually joined with the verb *stigqan* (Matthew VII, 25, 27; Luke IV, 11; XIV, 31; Romans IX, 32). If *þatei* refers to *razn*, as the sense requires, Ulfila altered the construction, as he often did, though here rather boldly. *bistagq*: J and St add *bistagun*. *flodus*: J, St, and B add *awaflodus*; the Argenteus manuscript has *awa* (“river”) in the margin. Those learned men have introduced the gloss into the text. *gadraus*: We suspect that Ulfila read, with the Greek, συνέπεσε.]

And when he had finished all these words in the hearing of the people, he went into Capernaum.

[Note: [Col. 0611] And when he had finished all these words in the hearing of the people, he went into Capernaum.]

A centurion’s servant, who was ill and near death, was dear to him.

[Note: [Col. 0611] A certain centurion’s servant was ill and near death, and he was dear to him.]

[Note: [Col. 0613] *svultavairþja*: Z adds *div*; J, St, and B have *svulta vairþid*. *svultavairþja* means “turning toward death,” that is, “approaching death” (Grimm II, 577). The Greek ἤμελλε τελευτᾶν has a concrete form preceded by an abstract one, a feature at which a careful reader may take offense.]

When he heard about Jesus, he sent Jewish elders to him, asking him to come and heal his servant.

[Note: [Col. 0613] When he heard about Jesus, he sent Jewish elders to him, asking him to come and heal his servant.]

[Note: [Col. 0613] *qimi*: so the Argenteus manuscript; Hz adds *qemi*; see the note on VIII, 56.]

But when they came to Jesus, they earnestly entreated him, saying that he was worthy for him to do this for him, because he loves our nation and built the synagogue for us.

[Note: [Col. 0613] Those who came to Jesus earnestly entreated him, saying that he was worthy for him to do this for him.]

[Note: [Col. 0613] *fragibis*: J, St, and B add *frambis*.]

So Jesus went with them. And when he was no longer far from the house, the centurion sent friends to him, saying, “Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof. For this reason I did not consider myself worthy to come to you; but say the word, and my servant will be healed.”

[Note: [Col. 0613] He loves our nation and built the synagogue for us.]

[Note: [Col. 0613] But Jesus went with them; and when he was no longer far from the house, this centurion sent friends to him, saying, “Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.”]

[Note: [Col. 0613] Therefore I did not consider myself worthy to come to you, but say the word, and this servant of mine will be healed.]

For I too am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, “Go,” and he goes, and to another, “Come here,” and he comes, and to my servant, “Do this,” and he does it.

[Note: [Col. 0613] For I too am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, “Go,” and he goes, and to another, “Come here,” and he comes, and to my servant, “Do this,” and he does it.]

[Note: [Col. 0613] *mis silbin*: J and B add an abbreviation, also found in verse 49; St has *missisbin*. *her*: “here,” as in all Greek manuscripts.]

When Jesus heard this, he marveled at him and, turning to the crowd following him, said, “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.”

[Note: [Col. 0613] When Jesus heard this, he marveled at him and, turning to the crowd following him, said, “Amen I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.”]

[Note: [Col. 0613] *amen*: “amen,” as in the Greek.]

And those who had been sent returned to the house and found the sick servant well.

[Note: [Col. 0613] And those who had been sent returned to the house and found the sick servant well.]

And it happened on the following day that he went into a town called Nain. His disciples and a large crowd went with him.

[Note: [Col. 0613] And it happened on the following day that he went into a town called Nain, and his disciples and a very large crowd went with him.]

[Note: [Col. 0613] *afar daga*: St and Z add an abbreviation. *naen*: In the Argenteus manuscript it appears to be written *maen*; all Greek manuscripts have Ναΐν.]

When he came near the gate of the town, behold, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother; she herself was a widow, and a large crowd of the town was with her.

[Note: [Col. 0613] When he came near the gate of this town, behold, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother; she herself was a widow, and a large crowd of this town was with her.]

[Note: [Col. 0613] *vidovo*: see the note on IV, 13. *managei*: J and St add *managai*. *si silbo*: “she herself,” Greek αὕτη. *ganoha*: Ulfila and the manuscripts have *ganoha*, corresponding to Greek ἦν.]

When the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, “Do not weep.”

[Note: [Col. 0613] When the Lord Jesus saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, “Do not weep.”]

[Note: [Col. 0613] *frauja ïesus*: “the Lord Jesus.” Some Greek manuscripts have κύριος, others Ἰησοῦς; Ulfila and manuscript 225 combine both.]

He came up and touched the bier; the bearers stood still. And he said, “Young man, I say to you, arise!”

[Note: [Col. 0613] He came up and touched the bier; the bearers stood still. And he said, “Young man, I say to you, arise!”]

[Note: [Col. 0613] *dugann*: St adds *dugan*.]

And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and he gave him back to his mother.

[Note: [Col. 0613] And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and he gave him back to his mother.]

But fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying, “A great prophet has arisen among us,” and, “God has visited his people.”

[Note: [Col. 0613] Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying, “A great prophet has arisen among us,” and, “God has visited his people.”]

[Note: [Col. 0614] *allans agis*: corresponds to all the Greek manuscripts. *mikilidedun*: J, St, and B add *mikelidedun*. *qiþandans*: Ih. notes here that the Goth neglected to place the little stroke, the sign of *n*, over the final syllable; but the learned man is mistaken, for the stroke is clearly drawn above it. *seinaizos*: St adds *seinazos*.]

And this report about him went out through all Judea and all the surrounding region.

[Note: [Col. 0613] And this report about him went out through all Judea and all the surrounding region.]

Then John’s disciples reported to him about all these things. And John, calling two of his disciples, sent them to Jesus, saying, “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?”

[Note: [Col. 0613] John’s disciples reported to him about all these things.]

[Note: [Col. 0613] And John, calling two of his disciples, sent them to Jesus, saying, “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?”]

[Note: [Col. 0614] *tvans*: Ulfila, manuscript D, and the versions have τινάς. *ïns*: “them,” as in all the Greek manuscripts.]

So they came to him and said, “John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, ‘Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?’”

[Note: [Col. 0613] When these men came to him, they said, “John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, ‘Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?’”]

[Note: [Col. 0614] *venjaima*: St adds *venjaina*.]

At that very hour he healed many of diseases, afflictions, and evil spirits, and to many blind people he gave sight.

[Note: [Col. 0613] At that hour he healed many of diseases and afflictions and evil spirits, and to many blind people he gave sight.]

[Note: [Col. 0614] *ahmane ubilaize*: St adds *ahmanum*. B.’s conjecture *ahmam ubilaim* is unnecessary, for verbs meaning “to heal” and “to make well” are constructed both with the genitive (Luke V, 15; VI, 18; VIII, 2) and with the preposition *af* (Mark V, 29, 34). The passages in which Ulfila changes the construction are these: IV, 25, *galuknoda himins du jeram þrim jah menoþs saihs*; Mark I, 6, *vas gavasiþs taglam jah gairda*; compare the note on 2 Corinthians XII, 21.]

And Jesus answered and said to them, “Go and report to John what you have seen and heard: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, and the poor receive good news.”

[Note: [Col. 0613] And Jesus answered and said to them, “Go and report to John what you have seen and heard: the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, and the poor receive good news.”]

[Note: [Col. 0614] *gateihats*: Z adds *gataihats*.]

Blessed is anyone who does not take offense at me.

[Note: [Col. 0615] And blessed is everyone who does not take offense at me.]

When John’s messengers had departed, he began to speak to the crowd about John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see—a reed shaken by the wind?

[Note: [Col. 0615] When these messengers of John had departed, he began to speak to the crowd about John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see—a reed shaken by the wind?”]

[Note: [Col. 0615] *at galeiþandam*: St and Z add an abbreviation; J adds *afgaleiþandam*.]

But what did you go out to see—a man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those in splendid clothing and living in luxury are in royal palaces.

[Note: [Col. 0615] But what did you go out to see—a man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those in splendid clothing and living in luxury are in royal palaces.]

[Note: [Col. 0615] *vulþagaim*: J, St, and B add *vulþanaim*. *fodeinai*: “food.” Ulfila apparently read τροφῇ instead of τρυφῇ, as Maresh. and B. correctly observed. Unless someone supposes that *fodeinai* is to be supplied from the preceding *vulþagaim*, so that *fodeins vulþaga* (“luxurious food”) corresponds to Greek τρυφή, this explanation seems too artificial. *þiudangardjom*: J and St add *þiudangardja*; B adds *þiudangardjan*—apparently the manuscript was written with *-on* instead of *-om*.]

[Note: [Col. 0615] But what did you go out to see—a prophet? Yes, I tell you, and one greater than a prophet.]

[Note: [Col. 0615] *jai*: J and St add *jah*. *praufetu*: second hand; see the note on I, 54.]

[Note: [Col. 0615] This is the one about whom it is written: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you.”]

[Note: [Col. 0615] *þanei*: J adds *þamei*.]

For I tell you, among those born of women no prophet is greater than John; yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.

[Note: [Col. 0615] For I tell you, among those born of women no prophet is greater than John the Baptist; yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.]

[Note: [Col. 0615] *baurim*: J and St add *bauran*. *nist*: J and B add *ni ïst*. *ïmma*: the preposition *et* is prefixed, as in all Greek manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0615] And all the people who heard, including the tax collectors, acknowledged God’s righteousness, having been baptized with John’s baptism.]

[Note: [Col. 0615] *gahausjandei*: J and St omit *gahausjandans*. *garaihtana domidedun guþ*: J and St have *garaihta ...*; these words and what follows have completely disappeared from the Argenteus manuscript.]

But the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected God’s purpose for themselves, not having been baptized by him.

[Note: [Col. 0615] But the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected God’s purpose for themselves, not having been baptized by him.]

[Note: [Col. 0616] *frageþun ana*: J and St add *frakunþ ...*; B, Hz, and Z have *frajeþun and*. We printed *fraqeþun*, which is required by the analogy of the language, since *jeþun* can arise neither from *jaþan* (B., marginal note) nor from *jaiþan* (Z.), and no trace of the letter *j* appears in the Argenteus manuscript, where it would be written below the line. The verb *fraqiþan*, properly meaning “to curse” (Matthew XXV, 41; Mark XI, 21, and elsewhere), here takes on the meaning “to despise” or “to reject” (elsewhere *ufbrikan*, Mark VI, 26). The reading *and*, which some adopt instead of *ana* because it gives a sense foreign to this passage, cannot be approved; nor should *ana*, which the marginal hand had previously conjectured, be rejected merely because of Benzelius’ authority, since it can no longer be clearly recognized in the Argenteus manuscript. To render the Greek εἰς ἑαυτούς (“against themselves,” “to their own detriment”), nothing is more suitable than *ana sik*; compare Matthew XXVII, 13; Mark III, 26; XIV, 55; John XVIII, 29; 2 Corinthians X, 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0615] To what, then, shall I compare the people of this generation, and what are they like?]

[Note: [Col. 0616] At the beginning of the verse J and St add *qaþ þan frauja* (“then the Lord said”); some Greek manuscripts likewise add it, but the Argenteus manuscript does not recognize it.]

[Note: [Col. 0615] They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, saying, “We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we mourned, and you did not weep.”]

[Note: [Col. 0616] *seina misso*: the editions add an abbreviation. *sviglodedum*: J and St add *svigalodedum*. *gaunodedum*: the Argenteus manuscript has the marginal synonym *hufum*, from Matthew XI, 17.]

[Note: [Col. 0615] For John the Baptist has come, neither eating bread nor drinking wine, and you say, “He has a demon.”]

[Note: [Col. 0616] *nih*: the second hand; J and St omit *ni*.]

The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, “Behold, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.”

[Note: [Col. 0615] The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, “Behold, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.”]

[Note: [Col. 0616] *afetja*: J and B add *afetei*.]

Yet wisdom has been vindicated by all her children.

[Note: [Col. 0615] Yet wisdom has been vindicated by all her children.]

[Note: [Col. 0616] *seinaim*: J adds *seinama*; St *seinamma*.]

[Note: [Col. 0615] One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him; and he entered the Pharisee’s house and reclined.]

[Note: [Col. 0616] *ïna sums*: corresponds to all the Greek manuscripts.]

And behold, a woman in that town, who was a sinner, learned that he was reclining in the Pharisee’s house. She brought an alabaster jar of perfume and, standing behind him at his feet, weeping, began to wet his feet with her tears; she wiped them with the hair of her head, kissed his feet, and anointed them with the perfume.

[Note: [Col. 0615] Then, behold, a woman in that town, who was a sinner, learned that he was reclining in the Pharisee’s house, and brought an alabaster jar of perfume.]

[Note: [Col. 0616] *sei*: J, St, and B add *so*. *jah*: “and,” as in the Greek; J and St add *sah*. *ïn razna*: J has *ïn gard*; St *and gard*. *þis fareisaiaus briggandei*: J and St add *fareisaie brinjandei*, omitting the final part of the verse. *alabalstraun*: B adds *alabaastraum*; all Greek manuscripts have ἀλάβαστρον.]

[Note: [Col. 0615] She stood behind him at his feet, weeping; she began to wet his feet with her tears, wiped them with the hair of her head, kissed his feet, and anointed them with the perfume.]

[Note: [Col. 0616] *aftaro*: Greek has “before,” *faura*. From *fotum* through *fravaurhta* in verse 39, J and St have a lacuna. Nearly all traces of the individual letters in the Argenteus manuscript have disappeared.]

[Note: [Col. 0615] When the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he spoke to himself, saying, “If this man were a prophet, he would certainly know who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him—for she is a sinner.”]

[Note: [Col. 0617] *fareisaius*: so the Argenteus manuscript; Hz and Z add *fareisaiaus*. *sis*: B omits *ïn sis*. *ains*: “alone,” as in all Greek manuscripts. *ufkunþedi*: so the Argenteus manuscript and the second hand in Hz; B’s marginal hand has *ufkunþeda*. *tekiþ ïmma*: B adds *sik attekiþ*.]

[Note: [Col. 0617] Jesus answered Peter: “Simon, I have something to say to you.” But he said, “Teacher, speak.”]

[Note: [Col. 0617] *paitrau*: “Peter”; all Greek manuscripts have αὐτόν, which is why J printed *ïmma*. St omits *paitru*; otherwise Gothic agrees with Brix.]

[Note: [Col. 0617] There were two debtors to a certain creditor: one owed five hundred denarii, but the other fifty.]

[Note: [Col. 0617] *dulgis skulans*: B and Z add an abbreviation; see Grimm II, 598–599. J and St add *dulgiskulans*. *dulgahaitjin*: J and B add *duliahaitjin*.]

[Note: [Col. 0617] Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both. Which of them, then, will love him more?]

[Note: [Col. 0617] *þan*: Ulfila has the Greek αὐτῶν. *þana*: J and St add *þama*; the Greek has ὅτι, while Ulfila has it after *gavenja*.]

[Note: [Col. 0617] Simon answered, “I suppose the one whom he forgave more.” Then he said to him, “You have judged rightly.”]

[Note: [Col. 0617] And turning toward this woman, he said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? When I entered your house, you gave me no water for my feet; but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair.”]

[Note: [Col. 0617] *qaþ*: all Greek manuscripts place it after *seimona*. *atgaggandin*: “entering,” all Greek manuscripts have εἰσῆλθον. *mis*: “to me,” as in all Greek manuscripts. *seinaim*: “with her own,” as in all Greek manuscripts.]
