[Note: [Col. 0639] “Which would fall to me”: so the Argenteus manuscript; J., St., and B. add *so undrinnandein*, for which L. much more correctly conjectured *þo undrinnandein*; lh. and Z. add *sei undrinnai mis*.]

And he divided his property between them.

[Note: [Col. 0639] “And after not many days the younger son gathered everything together and went away into a distant land, and there squandered his property, living recklessly.”]

The younger son took everything belonging to him and went away into a distant land, and there squandered his property, living riotously.

[Note: [Col. 0639] “Into a land existing far away”: see the note at XIX, 12.]

He divided his property among them. And after not many days the younger son gathered everything together and went away into a distant land, and there squandered his property, living recklessly.

[Note: [Col. 0639] “But when he had spent everything, a great famine arose throughout that land, and he began to be in need.”]

[Note: [Col. 0639] “Entirely needy”: so the Argenteus manuscript; J. and St. add *allaþarba*, which Z. wrongly approves, or thinks that *allþarba*—which is no better—should be read; see Grim. II. 627.]

And when he had spent everything, a great famine arose throughout that land, and he began to be in need. He went away into a distant land and there attached himself to one of the citizens. He sent him into his fields to pasture swine.

[Note: [Col. 0639] “And going, he attached himself to one of the citizens of that region, and he sent him into his field to pasture swine.”]

[Note: [Col. 0639] “Of the city”: J. adds *baurjane*.—“Of that region”: corresponding to the Greek throughout.—“Of the field”: *haiþjos* means “of the field,” a genitive indicating the place to which he was sent; likewise Mk. IV, 35 and L. XIX, 12; see Grim. III. 127.]

And when he had spent everything, a great famine arose throughout that region.. He went and attached himself to one of the citizens of that region, who sent him into his field to pasture swine.

[Note: [Col. 0639] “And he desired to eat the pods that the swine ate, and no one gave him any.”]

[Note: [Col. 0639] “To eat”: St. adds *jct.*; otherwise Ulfilas, with the manuscripts and versions, seems to have read χορτασθῆναι (“to be filled”).—“To him”: all Greek manuscripts have it after *gave*.]

He attached himself to one of the citizens of that region. He sent him into his field to pasture swine, and he desired to eat the pods that the swine ate, but no one gave him any.

[Note: [Col. 0639] “He came to himself and said: How many of my father’s hired servants have an abundance of bread, while I am perishing here from hunger!”]

[Note: [Col. 0639] “Coming … to himself”: corresponding to the Greek throughout.—“Abundance”: St. adds *ufaraslau*.—“Here”: Ulfilas, with the manuscripts, has ὧδε (“here”).]

He desired to eat the pods that the swine ate, but no one gave him any. Coming to himself, he said:

[Note: [Col. 0639] “I will arise and go to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you.”]

[Note: [Col. 0639] “Against me”: see the note at M. XXVII, 4.—“In”: St. adds *ïs*.]

“Some hired servants of my father have more than enough bread, but I am dying here of hunger. I will arise and go to my father and say to him:

[Note: [Col. 0639] “I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants.”]

[Note: [Col. 0639] “Now”: Ulfilas either substituted it for καί (“and”), which most manuscripts have in this place, as at Mk. IX, 13 and below at verse 21, and therefore should not be said with Griesbach to have omitted καί; or, if he did not read καί, he added pleonastically the adverb *þanaseiþs*, as at L. XVI, 2 he added the adverb *þanamais*. For *ju ni* instead of the usual *þanaseiþs ni* corresponding to Greek οὐκέτι (“no longer”), see Rom. VII, 17, 20; Eph. II, 19; Philem. 16.]

“I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants.”

[Note: [Col. 0639] “And rising, he came to his father; while he was still far away, his father saw him, was moved with compassion, and ran, fell upon his neck, and kissed him.”]

[Note: [Col. 0639] “And he said to him, this son: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son.”]

[Note: [Col. 0639] “Now”: see the note at verse 19.—“To be called”: J. adds *haitaudau*.]

“I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.” But his father, while he was still far away, saw him and had compassion, and running, fell upon his neck and kissed him.

[Note: [Col. 0639] “And this father said to his servants: Quickly bring the first robe and clothe him, and put a ring on his hand and shoes on his feet.”]

[Note: [Col. 0639] “Father”: St. adds *arta*.—“To his own”: J. and St. add *seiname*.]

And the son said to him: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son.”

[Col. 0640]

[Note: [Col. 0640] “Quickly bring”: J. and B. add *suns tobrigg*; otherwise *sprauto* corresponds to the Greek and *bringiþ* to *briggiþ*; see the note at XIV, 31.—“Ring”: J. adds *friggragulþ*; St. adds *fingragulþ*.]

But the father said to his servants: “Quickly bring the first robe and clothe him, and put a ring on his hand and shoes on his feet.”

[Note: [Col. 0639] “And bringing this fattened calf, slaughter it, and let us eat and celebrate.”]

And put a ring on his hand and shoes on his feet. Bring the fattened calf, slaughter it, and let us eat and celebrate.

[Note: [Col. 0639] “For this son of mine was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found.”]

[Note: [Col. 0640] “He became”: St. adds *varþa*.—“To be”: J., St., and B. add *vailavisan*, an addition that seems required by the sense; but they did not know that *visan* here is not the substantive verb but means “to feast,” and belongs to the class of forms explained by Grim. I. 842, X. The *vaila* added at verse 23, however, is omitted here by Ulfilas, as he often does, so that when one of two compound verbs follows closely, he does not repeat the particle; see L. XIX, 5, *dalaþ atsteig*, and verse 6, simply *atstaig*, although both render καταβαίνειν. We collected other examples of this kind at 1 Tim. VI, 6.]

For this son of mine was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found. And they began to feast.

[Note: [Col. 0639] “Now his older son was in the field, and coming, he approached the house and heard songs and dances.”]

[Note: [Col. 0640] “Older”: J., St., and B. have a lacuna here.—“Field”: J. adds *lande*, B. *landa*.—“And”: Ulfilas has ὡς (“when”).—“Coming … near”: J., St., and B. add *miþþanei gavandida sik jah atïddja newa*.—“And”: the second *and* occurs in all Greek manuscripts.—“Songs”: from here to verse 27, J., St., and B. have a lacuna; these difficult words have nevertheless been correctly recovered by Ih. from the Argenteus manuscript.]

Now his older son was in the field. When he came and drew near the house, he heard songs and dancing. And he called one of the servants and asked what this was.

[Note: [Col. 0639] “And calling one of the servants, he asked what this was.”]

[Note: [Col. 0639] “Then he said to him: Your brother has come, and your father has slaughtered this fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.”]

[Note: [Col. 0640] “He slaughtered”: so the Argenteus manuscript; Hz., in the first hand, has *afsnaiþ*. Z. and Wackernagel are therefore mistaken in saying that *afsnaiþ* is the reading of the Argenteus manuscript.]

And there was dancing and a pipe. One of the servants asked what this was. He said to him: “Your brother has come, and your father has slaughtered this fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.”

[Note: [Col. 0639] “Then he became angry and did not wish to enter, but his father went out and pleaded with him.”]

[Note: [Col. 0640] “But”: “but” in Greek οὖν (“therefore”), whereas Ulfilas, with the manuscripts, has δέ (“but”); see the note at 1 Cor. XV, 11.—“Out”: “outside,” as in all Greek manuscripts; see M. IX, 32.]

But he became angry and did not wish to enter. His father went out and pleaded with him. Then he answered his father:

[Col. 0641]

[Note: [Col. 0641] “Behold, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your commandment; yet you never gave me a young goat so that I might feast with my friends.”]

[Note: [Col. 0641] “There”: St. omits *þanuh*.—“I served”: “I served,” Greek δουλεύω (“I serve”) throughout.—“I might feast”: Ulfilas appears to have read ἀριστήσω (“I may dine”) instead of εὐφρανθῶ (“I may rejoice”), with manuscript D; Griesbach argues this too boldly.]

But he became angry and did not wish to enter. His father went out and pleaded with him. Then he answered his father: “Behold, for so many years I have served you, and I have never transgressed your commandment; yet you never gave me a young goat so that I might feast with my friends.

[Note: [Col. 0641] “But when this son of yours, who devoured your property with prostitutes, came, you slaughtered for him this fattened calf.”]

[Note: [Col. 0641] “Ate”: the scribe incorrectly wrote *fret* for *frat*, as Grim. correctly judged at I. 844; Wackernagel follows him.]

“But when this son of yours, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, came, you slaughtered for him this fattened calf.” But he said to him:

[Note: [Col. 0641] “Child, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.”]

[Note: [Col. 0641] “You were and are”: all Greek manuscripts have only εἶ (“you are”); Ulfilas, with the Latin versions, has *vast jah is*.—“All”: J. and St. add *alla*.]

But he said to him: “Child, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But it was necessary to feast and rejoice,

[Note: [Col. 0641] “It was necessary to feast and rejoice, because your brother was dead and has come to life again, and was lost and has been found.”]

[Note: [Col. 0641] “To feast”: J., St., and B. add *jct.*; otherwise Ulfilas has δέ (“but”).—“I rejoice”: J. adds *fajinon*.—“Brother”: Ulfilas, with the manuscripts, has οὗτος (“this one”).—“Was lost”: Ulfilas, with the manuscripts, has ἦν (“was”).]

because your brother was dead and has come to life again, and was lost and has been found.”

[Note: [Col. 0641] “He said also to his disciples: A certain rich man had a steward, and this man was accused before him of wasting his property.”]

[Note: [Col. 0641] “Then”: Ulfilas, with the manuscripts and versions, has καί (“and”).—“Who”: St. adds *saie*.—“Had”: J. and St. add *aihida*.—“To manage”: so the Argenteus manuscript and J.; St., B., Ih., and Z. omit the second *g*, giving the more usual form; see the following verses and VIII, 3.—“He was wasting his property”: J., St., and B. add *distahidudi aigan*.]

And he said to his disciples: “There was a certain rich man who had a steward, and this man was accused before him of wasting his property.”

[Note: [Col. 0641] “And calling him, he said to him: What is this I hear about you? Give an account of your stewardship, for you can no longer be steward.”]

[Note: [Col. 0641] “Hear”: St. adds *hausjah*.—“Of your stewardship”: St. omits the second *g*.—“Now”: J. and St. add *jct.*; see the note at XV, 19.]

He said to his disciples: “A certain rich man had a steward, and this man was accused before him of wasting his property. And calling him, he said to him: ‘What is this I hear about you? Give an account of your stewardship, for you can no longer be steward.’”

[Note: [Col. 0641] “Then this steward said to himself: What shall I do, since my master is taking the stewardship away from me? I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg.”]

[Note: [Col. 0641] “Steward”: J. adds *fauragaggji*.—“I cannot”: St. adds *nim ag*.]

Then the steward said to himself: “What shall I do, since my master is taking the stewardship away from me? I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg.”.”

[Note: [Col. 0641] “I have decided what I will do, so that, when I am removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses.”]

[Note: [Col. 0641] “If perhaps”: J. and St. add *eiþan*; otherwise *þau* (ἄν) is found in all Greek manuscripts, as in the Gothic text itself at verse 9.]

“I cannot dig, and I am ashamed to beg. I have decided what I will do, so that, when I am removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses.”

[Note: [Col. 0641] “And calling each one of his master’s debtors, he said to the first: How much do you owe my master?”]

[Note: [Col. 0641] “You owe”: St. adds *shalt*.]

And he called each of his master’s debtors and said to the first: “How much do you owe my master?”

[Note: [Col. 0641] “He said: A hundred measures of oil. And he said to him: Take your written account, sit down quickly, and write fifty.”]

[Note: [Col. 0641] ““Hundred”: so the Argenteus manuscript here and in the following verse; B., Hu., and Z. have *taihuntehund* in both places; see the note at XV, 4..—“Written accounts”: St. adds *hokos*.—“Fifty”: so the Argenteus manuscript; J., B., and Z. omit the second *f*.]

And he said to the first: “How much do you owe my master?” He said: “A hundred measures of oil.” And he said to him: “Take your written account, sit down quickly, and write fifty.”

[Note: [Col. 0641] “Then he said to another: And how much do you owe? He said: A hundred measures of wheat. And he said to him: Take your written account and write eighty.”]

[Note: [Col. 0642] “Ninety”: see the note at verse 6.]

Then he said to another: “And how much do you owe?” He said: “A hundred measures of wheat.” And he said to him: “Take your written account and write eighty.”

[Note: [Col. 0641] “And the master praised this unrighteous steward, because he acted prudently; for the sons of this age are more prudent than the sons of light in their own generation.”]

[Note: [Col. 0642] “Sons”: for *sunjus*; see the note at IV, 13.]

And the master praised this steward of unrighteousness, because he acted prudently. For the sons of this age are more prudent than the sons of light in their own generation.

[Note: [Col. 0641] “And I say to you: Make friends for yourselves from the wealth of unrighteousness, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings.”]

And I say to you: Make friends for yourselves from the wealth of unrighteousness, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings..

[Note: [Col. 0641] “Whoever is faithful in very little is also faithful in much; and whoever is unfaithful in very little is also unfaithful in much.”]

For the sons of this age are more prudent than the sons of light in their own generation. And I say to you: Make friends for yourselves from the wealth of unrighteousness, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings..

[Note: [Col. 0642] “Faithful”: J. and St. add *triggva*.—“In very little”: from this word to the end of the verse J. and St. have a lacuna, although the passage is complete in the Argenteus manuscript and contains nothing that makes the reading difficult. For *leitilamma*, all Greek manuscripts have ἐλαχίστῳ (“the least”).—“He who … is unfaithful”: B. omits *saei … ïst untriggvs*.]

Whoever is faithful in very little is also faithful in much, and whoever is unfaithful in very little is also unfaithful in much.

[Note: [Col. 0641] “Therefore, if you have not been faithful in unrighteous wealth, who will entrust the true wealth to you?”]

[Note: [Col. 0642] “Wealth”: B. adds *frihuþraihna*, likewise at verse 13.]

And if you have not been faithful in unrighteous wealth, who will entrust the true wealth to you?

[Note: [Col. 0641] “And if you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?”]

And if you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?

[Note: [Col. 0641] “No servant can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will cling to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and wealth.”]

[Note: [Col. 0642] “And otherwise”: from here to the end of the verse J. and St. have a lacuna; B. omits *aiþþau*. The form *andizuh*, clearly the reading of the Argenteus manuscript, is a verb of uncertain origin and meaning (Grim. III, 15). All Greek manuscripts have ἢ γάρ (“or for”), which Ulfilas rendered in the parallel passage M. VI, 24 by *unte jabai* (“for if”); from this it may be conjectured that *andizuh* means “on the contrary, otherwise.”—“Or otherwise”: B. adds *aiþau*.—“And he despises”: this seems to be written in the Argenteus manuscript, but cannot be stated with certainty because the letters are very faded; B. conjectured *and…*, and himself added *andnimiþ*.—“But”: B. omits *jah*, following the Greek, which has καί (“and”).—“Wealth”: see the note at verse 11; in the margin of cod. d. Arg., *mammonim*.]

No servant can serve two masters.. Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will cling to one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and wealth.

[Col. 0643]

[Note: [Col. 0643] “Now all these things the Pharisees also heard, who were lovers of money, and they mocked him.”]

[Note: [Col. 0643] “Pharisees”: B. adds *fareisaies*.—“They mocked”: thus the Argenteus manuscript and the editions, without doubt with an added syllable; Grim. I. 848 thinks that, instead of *bimaminidedun*, we should write *bimamidedun*.]

The Pharisees also heard all these things, being lovers of money, and they mocked him. He said to them:

[Note: [Col. 0643] “You are those who justify yourselves in the sight of men, but God knows your hearts; for what is high among men is an abomination in the sight of God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0643] “Hearts”: J., St., and B. add *hairtana*.—“High”: all Greek manuscripts place it after “among men.”—“Is an abomination”: J. adds *andset*.]

““You are those who justify yourselves in the sight of men, but God knows your hearts, for what is high among men is an abomination in the sight of God.”.

[Note: [Col. 0643] “The law and the prophets lasted until John; from then on the kingdom of God is proclaimed, and everyone is compelled to enter it.”]

[Note: [Col. 0643] “Is compelled”: Ulfilas did not understand the Greek words meaning “they use force toward it”—that is, he seems to have taken βιάζεται as a passive middle verb, which disturbs the sense. Nor does *nauþjan* suitably correspond to Greek βιάζεσθαι; rather, *anamahtjan* corresponds to it (M. XI, 12), while *nauþjan* = ἀναγκάζειν, L. XIV, 23; cf. Skeir. 38, 2.]

The law and the prophets lasted until John. From then on the kingdom of God is proclaimed, and everyone is compelled to enter it.

[Note: [Col. 0643] “It is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of the law to fall.”]

[Note: [Col. 0643] “But”: St. omits *jah*.—“A stroke to fall”: J., St., and B. add *vruta driusan*.]

Yet it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of the law to fall.

[Note: [Col. 0643] “Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and everyone who marries a woman divorced by her husband commits adultery.”]

[Note: [Col. 0643] “His”: St. adds *saina*.—“Divorced”: Ulfilas, with the manuscripts and versions, has ἀπὸ ἀνδρός (“from her husband”).]

Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and everyone who marries a woman divorced by her husband commits adultery.

[Note: [Col. 0643] “A certain rich man was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day.”]

[Note: [Col. 0643] “Fine linen”: J. adds *byssaum*.—The third “and” is found in all Greek manuscripts.—“Feasting splendidly”: the editions add *jct.*; see the note at XV, 32.—“Every day”: the editions add *jct.*]

And a certain rich man was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day.

[Note: [Col. 0643] “But a certain poor man named Lazarus was laid at his gate, full of sores.”]

[Note: [Col. 0643] “Named”: “called,” as in all Greek manuscripts.—“He”: “who,” in all Greek manuscripts; see the note at John XVIII, 26.—“Full”: J. and St. add *fuls*.]

And a certain poor man named Lazarus was laid at his gate, full of sores. The rich man was dressed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day.

[Note: [Col. 0643] “And he desired to eat from the crumbs falling from the table of this rich man; but even the dogs, coming, licked his sores.”]

[Note: [Col. 0643] “To eat”: J., St., and B. add *saþnan*.—“They licked”: J. adds *bilaigvodedun*; Ulfilas, with the manuscripts, appears to have read ἐπέλειχον instead of ἀπέλειχον.]

But the poor man desired to eat from the crumbs falling from the table of the rich man, and even the dogs, coming, licked his sores.

[Note: [Col. 0643] “It happened that this poor man died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom; the rich man also died and was buried.”]

[Note: [Col. 0643] “To carry”: Ulfilas has αὐτόν (“him”).]

A certain poor man named Lazarus was laid at his gate, full of sores, and he desired to eat from the crumbs falling from the table of the rich man; even the dogs, coming, licked his sores. It happened that the poor man died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom; the rich man also died and was buried.

[Note: [Col. 0643] “And in Hades, lifting up his eyes, being in torments, he saw Abraham from far away and Lazarus in his bosom.”]

[Note: [Col. 0643] “Then”: so the Argenteus manuscript; B., lh., and Z. add *þana*. All Greek manuscripts have it. Ulfilas sometimes adds this particle in the apodosis after preceding temporal particles or participles; see L. II, 42.—“Lazarus”: J. and St. add *lazarum*; B. omits *lazaru*.]

The rich man died and was buried. Then, in Hades, lifting up his eyes while in torments, he saw Abraham far away and Lazarus in his bosom.

[Note: [Col. 0643] “And he cried out—”]

And he cried out—[lacuna]

[Note: [Col. 0643] “If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he turns back, forgive him.”]

[Note: [Col. 0644] “If”: It cannot be stated with certainty whether Ulfilas omitted δέ (“but”), as Griesbach claims, because some words are missing in the Argenteus manuscript before *jabai*, the last of which seems to have been *ïþ*. It is usual for Ulfilas to say *ïþ jabai* = ἐὰν δέ, εἰ δέ (“but if”).—“Sins against you”: Ulfilas, with the manuscripts and versions, has εἴς σε (“against you”).—“Repents”: J. adds *ïdreijo*.]

If your brother sins against you, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him..”

[Note: [Col. 0643] “And if seven times in the day he sins against you, and seven times in the day he turns back, saying, ‘I repent,’ you shall forgive him.”]

[Note: [Col. 0644] “Seven times”: J., St., and B. add *jct.*—“You shall forgive”: J. omits *afletais*.]

And if he sins against you seven times in the day, and seven times in the day turns back, saying, “I repent,” you shall forgive him.

[Note: [Col. 0643] “And the apostles said to the Lord: Increase our faith.”]

And he said to his disciples: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, perhaps you would say to this mulberry tree, ‘Uproot yourself and plant yourself in the sea,’ and it would perhaps obey you.”

[Note: [Col. 0644] “Or if you said”: “or if you should say,” Greek ἐλέγετε ἄν. Our reading distorts the sense; a particle expressing the Greek ἄν is required. Since that particle is *aiþþau* (M. XI, 23; John XIV, 2, 7, 28; XV, 19; XVIII, 36), *jabai* must have been placed in the margin by someone who thought that ἄν, rather than ἐάν, had been used and wished to indicate that it should be rendered by *jabai*. It was subsequently brought into the text by the scribe and must now be removed; the reading should be: *aiþþau jus qiþeiþ*. *Jus* (“you”) is omitted by all Greek manuscripts, but is likewise added in a similar passage at John XIV, 28: *jabai frijodedeiþ mik. aiþþau jus faginodedeiþ*. Concerning *qiþeiþ* for *qeþeiþ*, see the note at VIII, 56.—“Would obey”: St. adds *andhauseidei*.]

And the apostles said to the Lord: “Increase our faith.” The Lord said: “If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, perhaps you would say to this mulberry tree, ‘Uproot yourself from your roots and plant yourself in the sea,’ and it would obey you.”

[Note: [Col. 0643] “But which of you, having a servant plowing or tending sheep, when he returns from the field, will say to him immediately: Come here and recline?”]

[Note: [Col. 0644] “Plowing”: J. and St. add *ariandam*.—“Tending”: J. and St. add *haldandam*.—“Returning”: J. and B. add *qimandim*.—“Come here and recline”: J. and B. add *hindarleiþa nuh kumbei*; St. has *hindarlei þanuh kumbei*. L. discovered the true reading long ago; see the note at Mk. XIV, 44.]

And which of you, having a servant plowing or tending sheep, when he returns from the field, will say to him immediately: “Come here and recline”?

[Note: [Col. 0645] “Will he not rather say to him: Prepare what I shall eat tonight, gird yourself, and serve me while I eat and drink; and afterward you shall eat and drink?”]

[Note: [Col. 0645] “Shall I eat at night”: the editions add *jct.*; otherwise B. conjectured *waduh nahtmatjau*, and L.’s *wa du nahtmatjan* is no better.]

Or will he not say to him: “Prepare my meal, gird yourself, and serve me while I eat and drink; and afterward you shall eat and drink”?

[Note: [Col. 0645] “Does he thank that servant because he did what was commanded? I do not think so.”]

[Note: [Col. 0645] “Whether”: so the Argenteus manuscript, for the usual *ïbai*; cf. Grim. III. 284.—“Do you think that you thank”: so the Argenteus manuscript; J. and St. add *þankjus fairhaitei*, B. has *þankþ usfairhaitiþ*, and lh. has *þankþ usfairhaitis*. The passage, which seemed difficult to interpreters, was correctly established by Zahn. It corresponds to the Greek words; Ulfilas wished to render the middle ἔχει (ἔχῃ) by adding the pronoun *þus*. For this reason neither *þau*, conjectured by Z., nor *þis*, proposed by Rw., is admissible here. See M. V, 42 *leiwan sis* (δανείσασθαι), Mk. II, 6 *þagkjan sis* (διαλογίζεσθαι), and John IX, 22; Tit. I, 14 *afwandjan sis* (ἀποστρέφεσθαι). Concerning *þank* written for *þagk*, see the note at XIV, 31.]

Does he thank that servant because he did what was commanded? I do not think so.

[Note: [Col. 0645] “So you also, when you have done all these things commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants, because we have done what we were obliged to do.”]

So you also, when you have done all the things commanded you, say: “We are unprofitable servants, because we have done what we were obliged to do.”

[Note: [Col. 0645] “And it happened, while he was going to Jerusalem, that he passed through the midst of Samaria and Galilee.”]

And it happened, while he was going to Jerusalem, that he passed through the midst of Samaria and Galilee.

[Note: [Col. 0645] “And as he was entering a certain village, ten leprous men met him, and they stood far away.”]

[Note: [Col. 0645] “They”: J. and St. add *þai*; concerning *þaih* for *þaiei*, see the note at John XVIII, 26.]

And as he was entering a certain village, ten leprous men met him, and they stood far away. And they raised their voices, saying: “Jesus, teacher, have mercy on us!”

[Note: [Col. 0645] “And they raised their voices, saying: Jesus, teacher, have mercy on us.”]

[Note: [Col. 0645] “They raised”: so the Argenteus manuscript, for *ushofun*; see the note at IV, 13.]

And when he saw them, he said to them: “Go and show yourselves to the priests.” And it happened that, while they were going, they were cleansed.

[Note: [Col. 0645] “And observing, he said to them: Go and show yourselves to the priests. And it happened that, while they went, they were cleansed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0645] “To the priests”: J. and B. add *gudjan*.]

The men stood far away. They raised their voices, saying: “Jesus, teacher, have mercy on us.” And when he saw them, he said to them: “Go and show yourselves to the priests.” And it happened that, while they went, they were cleansed.

[Note: [Col. 0645] “But one of them, seeing that he had been made clean, turned back, glorifying God with a loud voice,”]

[Note: [Col. 0645] “He became clean”: “He was purified,” corresponding to Greek ἰάθη (“he was healed”); Ulfilas, with the manuscripts and versions, appears to have read ἐκαθαρίσθη (“he was cleansed”), cf. V, 13; M. VIII, 3; XI, 5.]

But one of them, seeing that he had been made clean, turned back, glorifying God with a loud voice, and fell on his face at his feet, giving him thanks. And he was a Samaritan.

[Note: [Col. 0645] “And he fell on his face before his feet, giving him thanks; and this man was a Samaritan.”]

[Note: [Col. 0645] “This”: B. falsely notes that Ulfilas omitted καί (“and”); see the note at John XVIII, 26.]

And he fell on his face at his feet, giving him thanks. And he was a Samaritan.

[Note: [Col. 0645] “And Jesus, answering, said: Were not these ten made clean? But where are the nine?”]

[Note: [Col. 0646] “These”: originally “these,” with Ulfilas and the Greek manuscripts, which read οὗτοι and place it after δέκα (“ten”); or, if preferred, transpose *taihun þai* and read *þai taihun*; see the notes at IX, 35, and XIV, 28.]

And Jesus, answering, said: “Were not these ten made clean? But where are the nine?”

[Note: [Col. 0645] “Were none found turning back to give glory to God except this foreigner?”]

And the nine were not found, turning back to give glory to God, except this foreigner.

[Note: [Col. 0645] “And he said to him: Arise, go; your faith has saved you.”]

[Note: [Col. 0646] “Arising”: J. adds *usstandans*; St. and Z. omit the second *s*.]

And he said to him: “Arise, go; your faith has saved you.”

[Note: [Col. 0645] “And being questioned by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them and said: The kingdom of God does not come with observation.”]

[Note: [Col. 0646] “Questioned”: J. and St. add *fraihands*.—“He answered”: J., St., and B. add *andhaf*.]

And when he was questioned by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them and said: “The kingdom of God does not come with observation.”

[Note: [Col. 0645] “Nor do they say: Behold, here! or: Behold, there! For behold, the kingdom of God is within you.”]

[Note: [Col. 0646] “Saying”: St. adds *qiþands*.]

Nor do they say: “Behold, here!” or “Behold, there!” For behold, the kingdom of God is within you.

[Note: [Col. 0645] “And he said to his disciples: The days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it.”]

[Note: [Col. 0646] “But”: “at,” corresponding to Greek throughout.—“Of these”: “of these,” as in Greek.—“Sons”: the Argenteus manuscript has *sunus*, for which Z. rashly admitted Benzelius’s conjecture *sunaus*. Ulfilas undoubtedly misunderstood the passage and translated it incorrectly. Ettmüller correctly judged *sununs*: it is written because of the following *mans* instead of *sunu*; cf. 1 Cor. VI, 16 and our *Beiträge zur Textberichtigung … der Skeireins* (“Contributions to the correction of the text … of the Skeireins”), p. 53. Perhaps likewise at Skeir. p. 48, 7, *attins veitvodeins* should be read instead of *atteins veitvodeins*.]

And he said to his disciples: “The days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it.”

[Note: [Col. 0645] “And they will say to you: Behold, here! or: Behold, there! Do not go away or follow them.”]

And they will say to you: “Behold, here!” or “Behold, there!” Do not go away, and do not follow them.

[Note: [Col. 0645] “For as lightning, flashing from one place under heaven to another place under heaven, shines, so will the Son of Man be in his day.”]

For just as lightning, flashing from one place under heaven to another place under heaven, shines, so will the Son of Man be in his day.

[Note: [Col. 0645] “But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.”]

[Note: [Col. 0646] “Many things to endure”: J. and St. add *managai þulan*.]

But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.

[Note: [Col. 0645] “And as it happened in the days of Noah, so will it also be in the days of the Son of Man.”]

[Note: [Col. 0646] “Noah”: all Greek manuscripts have Νῶε; Goths often append consonants to proper names ending in a vowel; we shall note this at 2 Cor. VI, 15.]

And as it happened in the days of Noah, so will it also be in the days of the Son of Man.

[Note: [Col. 0645] “They ate and drank; they took wives and were given in marriage, until the day Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all.”]

[Note: [Col. 0646] “And”: supplied as a second *and*, as in all Greek manuscripts.]

They ate and drank, took wives and were given in marriage, until the day Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all.

[Note: [Col. 0645] “Likewise, as it happened in the days of Lot: they ate and drank, bought and sold, planted and built.”]

[Note: [Col. 0646] “Lot”: all Greek manuscripts have Λώτ, with a single consonant.—The second and third “and” occur in all Greek manuscripts.]

Likewise, as it happened in the days of Lot: they ate and drank, bought and sold, planted and built.
all. Likewise, just as it happened in the days of Lot: they ate and drank, bought and sold, planted and built. But on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, it rained sulfur and fire from heaven and destroyed them all. [Col. 0647] [Note: [Col. 0647] But on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, it rained sulfur and fire from heaven and destroyed them all.] [Note: [Col. 0647] “sulfur and fire”: according to the Greek.]

They planted and built. But on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, sulfur and fire rained from heaven and destroyed them all. So it will be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed. [Note: [Col. 0647] “on that—which”: see the note at I, 20.] [Note: [Col. 0647] On that day, whoever is on the housetop, with his belongings in the house, must not go down to take them; and whoever is in the field likewise must not turn back.] [Note: [Col. 0647] “let him descend”: J. and St. add “let him come.”]

Remember Lot’s wife. [Note: [Col. 0647] Remember Lot’s wife.]

Whoever seeks to preserve his life will destroy it, and whoever destroys it for my sake will preserve it. [Note: [Col. 0647] “for my sake”: “on account of me,” according to the Greek. “He will preserve”: J. and St. add “will make alive”; by this they seem to have wished to render the Greek reading ζωοποιήσει or ζωογονήσει. But since most manuscripts read σώσει, we have no doubt that Wulfila followed them.]

Likewise, I tell you, in that night there will be two on one bed: one will be taken and the other will be left. [Note: [Col. 0647] “that”: “which,” according to the Greek; Wulfila’s manuscripts, as in Mi., apparently have another reading. “Two will be”: according to the Greek. “Together”: J. and St. add “one”; from here to the end of the verse the manuscripts have the same lacuna.]

Two will be grinding together: one will be taken and the other will be left. [Note: [Col. 0647] “Two … grinding”: J. and St. add “two … grinding.” “Together”: J. has a lacuna; St. adds it.]

And they answered and said to him, “Where, Lord?” But he said to them, “Where the body is, there the eagles will gather.” [Note: [Col. 0647] The beginning of this verse (“two will be”) is found in J.; in St. there is a lacuna marker. In the Argenteus manuscript no trace of writing appears, for Wulfila’s Gothic, like the Greek, omits the entire verse.] [Note: [Col. 0647] And they answered and said to him, “Where, Lord?” But he said to them, “Where the body is, there the eagles will gather.”] [Note: [Col. 0647] “to them”: J. has a mark indicating omission, followed by “to them.” “There”: J. and St. add “there also.” “That place”: J. and St. add “there.” “They gather”: J. and St. add “coming,” and from there to the end of the verse they have a lacuna.]

And he also told them a parable, because they ought always to pray and not become discouraged, saying: “There was a judge in a certain city who did not fear God and did not respect man.” [Note: [Col. 0647] “They ought”: J. and St. add “we ought.” “Discouraged”: the editors add a different reading, but, misled by their authority and because the letters g and t are not easily distinguished, Castillio also printed the divergent form in II Corinthians IV, 1 and 16. After being alerted by Ephesians III, 13 and Galatians VI, 9, where the reading we have given is perfectly clear, and after reexamining the manuscripts, he corrected that error.] [Note: [Col. 0647] “There was a certain one”: according to all the Greek manuscripts.]

There was also a widow in that city, and she came to him, saying, “Avenge me against my adversary.” [Note: [Col. 0647] “But there was also a widow in that city, and she came to him, saying, ‘Avenge me against my adversary.’”] [Note: [Col. 0648] “There was—but a widow”: “there was—but a widow,” according to all the Greek manuscripts, χήρα δὲ ἦν.]

But he was unwilling for a long time. Afterward he said to himself, “Although I do not fear God and do not respect man, nevertheless, because this widow troubles me, I will avenge her, so that she may not finally come and weary me.” [Note: [Col. 0647] “But because this widow troubles me, I will avenge her, so that she may not come continually and weary me.”] [Note: [Col. 0648] “But”: γέ in all the Greek manuscripts, for which Wulfila seems to have read δέ. “She may weary”: St. adds a variant form. “Whether until”: J. and St. add “whether not in.” “She may trouble”: J. and St. add another variant.]

And the Lord said, “Hear what the unjust judge says. And will God not avenge his elect, who cry to him day and night, although he is patient with them? [Note: [Col. 0647] “Will God not avenge his elect, who cry to him day and night, and is he patient with them?”] [Note: [Col. 0648] “Days … nights”: “days … nights,” according to all the Greek manuscripts; St. adds a variant for “nights.” “Is”: according to all the Greek manuscripts.]

I tell you that he will avenge them quickly. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?” [Note: [Col. 0647] “But I tell you that he will avenge them suddenly; nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?”] [Note: [Col. 0648] “Nevertheless”: “but,” according to all the Greek manuscripts. “Even so”: for the Greek πλήν; see the note at XIX, 27. “Will he find”: this is the reading of the Argenteus manuscript; J., St., and B. add a different form. The Argenteus form should not be taken as evidence that Wulfila omitted the Greek interrogative ἆρα; he rendered that particle interrogatively by adding the vowel u.]

He also told this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and despised others: “Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.” [Note: [Col. 0647] “He said to certain people who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and despised the others, this parable.”] [Note: [Col. 0648] “Then”: Wulfila’s manuscripts have the Greek καί.]

The Pharisee stood by himself and prayed this: “God, I thank you that I am not like these other men—robbers, unjust, adulterers—or like this tax collector. I fast twice each week and give a tenth of everything I possess.” [Note: [Col. 0647] “I fast twice in the week and give a tenth of everything I possess.”] [Note: [Col. 0648] “And”: “and,” according to all the Greek manuscripts. “A tenth part of everything”: this is the reading of the Argenteus; the editors add “giving a tenth of everything.”]

But the tax collector, standing far off, did not even want to lift his eyes toward heaven, but struck his breast, saying, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” [Note: [Col. 0647] “And this tax collector, standing far away, did not even wish to lift his eyes to heaven, but struck his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner.’”] [Note: [Col. 0648] “His”: “his,” according to all the Greek manuscripts. “To lift up”: the Greek follows “heaven.”]

I tell you, this man went down to his house declared more righteous than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but whoever humbles himself will be exalted. [Note: [Col. 0649] “His own self”: both forms occur; J. and St. add the reflexive form.]

They also brought infants to him so that he might touch them. When the disciples saw this, they rebuked them. But Jesus called them and said, “Let the children come to me, and do not hinder them, for of such is the kingdom of God.” [Note: [Col. 0649] “They brought children to him so that he might touch them; but when the disciples saw them, they rebuked them.”] [Note: [Col. 0649] “Jesus, calling them, said: ‘Allow these children to come to me, and do not hinder them, for of such is the kingdom of God.’”] [Note: [Col. 0649] “To go”: St. adds a variant spelling. “Kingdom”: St. adds a variant form.]

Amen, I tell you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child will not enter it. [Note: [Col. 0649] “Like”: St. adds a variant form.]

And one of the rulers questioned him, saying, “Good teacher, what must I do to become an heir of eternal life?” [Note: [Col. 0649] “A certain one”: according to all the Greek manuscripts.]

Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one—God. You know the commandments: ‘Do not commit adultery; do not kill; do not steal; do not bear false witness; honor your father and mother.’” [Note: [Col. 0649] “The false witness”: St. adds another form. “Your mother”: Wulfila’s manuscripts have the Greek σοῦ, “your.”]

He said, “I have kept all these things from my youth.” [Note: [Col. 0649] “But he said: ‘I have observed all this from my youth.’”]

When Jesus heard this, he said to him, “You still lack one thing: sell everything you have and distribute it to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.” [Note: [Col. 0649] “But when Jesus heard this, he said to him: ‘You still lack one thing; sell everything you have and distribute it to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven, and come, follow me.’”] [Note: [Col. 0649] “To follow”: “follow,” according to all the Greek manuscripts.]

Having heard this, he became sad, for he was very rich. [Note: [Col. 0649] “But when he heard this, he became sad, for he was very rich.”]

When Jesus saw him become sad, he said, “How difficult it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom of God!” [Note: [Col. 0649] “But when Jesus saw him become sad, he said: ‘How difficult it is for those who have possessions to enter the kingdom of God!’”] [Note: [Col. 0649] “With difficulty”: St. adds a variant.]

For it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God. [Note: [Col. 0649] “Camel”: St. adds another form. “To pass through”: the Argenteus has a divergent spelling; Wulfila’s manuscripts read διελθεῖν, “to pass through,” instead of the customary εἰσελθεῖν, “to enter.” “Than”: St. adds a variant.]

Those who heard this said, “Then who can be saved?” [Note: [Col. 0649] “But those who heard this said: ‘Who can be saved?’”] [Note: [Col. 0649] “Who was able”: J. and St. add a variant.]

But he said, “What is impossible with men is possible with God.” [Note: [Col. 0649] “But he said: ‘This is impossible among men, but possible with God.’”]

Then Peter said, “Look, we have left everything and followed you.” [Note: [Col. 0649] “But Peter said: ‘Look, we have left everything and followed you.’”]

He said to them, “Amen, I tell you, there is no one who has left house, or parents, or brothers, or wife, or children for the sake of the kingdom of God, [Note: [Col. 0649] “Whoever does not receive many times as much in this present time and in the age to come eternal life.”] [Note: [Col. 0650] “Manyfold”: St. adds another form.]

who will not receive many times as much in this time and in the age to come eternal life.” [Note: [Col. 0649] “And taking the Twelve, he said to them: ‘Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything written through the prophets about the Son of Man will be fulfilled.’”] [Note: [Col. 0650] “About the Son”: “about the Son,” with the Greek dative τῷ υἱῷ, which belongs to τελεσθήσεται, “will be fulfilled”; Wulfila’s manuscripts read περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ, “concerning the Son,” which depends on γεγραμμένα, “the things written.”]

For he will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, insulted, and spat upon; they will scourge him and kill him, and on the third day he will rise. [Note: [Col. 0649] “He will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, insulted, and spat upon, and they will scourge him and kill him, and on the third day he will rise.”] [Note: [Col. 0650] “Scourging”: St. adds a variant. “On the third day”: according to the Greek.]

But they understood none of these things; this saying was hidden from them, and they did not know what was said. [Note: [Col. 0649] “And they understood nothing of this, and this word was hidden from them, and they did not know these sayings.”]

And it happened, when he came near Jericho, that a certain blind man sat beside the road begging. [Note: [Col. 0649] “While he was near Jericho, a certain blind man sat beside the road begging.”] [Note: [Col. 0650] “To beg”: “to beg,” according to all the Greek manuscripts, προσαιτῶν. This is also the participial form used in J. IX, 8, “who sat begging”; thus one might suspect that Wulfila read προσαιτεῖν in those earlier passages. Below, at XIX, 48, some manuscripts read ἀκούειν, “to hear,” instead of ἀκούων, “hearing”; Wulfila has “to hear.”]

When he heard the crowd passing by, he asked what this was. [Note: [Col. 0649] “Hearing the crowd passing by, he asked what this was.”] [Note: [Col. 0650] “Passing by”: instead of διαπορευομένου, Wulfila seems to have read παραπορευομένου, as do Codex D and the versions; see Mark II, 20.]

They told him that Jesus the Nazarene was passing by. [Note: [Col. 0649] “They told him that Jesus the Nazarene was passing by.”]

He cried out, saying, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” [Col. 0651] [Note: [Col. 0650] “Passing through”: Z. adds a variant.] [Note: [Col. 0649] “But he cried out, saying: ‘Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!’”] [Note: [Col. 0651] “But these who were going ahead rebuked him, so that he would be silent; but he cried out all the more: ‘Son of David, have mercy on me!’”] [Note: [Col. 0650] “But he”: “but he,” according to all the Greek manuscripts, καί. “Him”: J., St., and B. add “to him.” “Son”: instead of the customary vocative form sunau, “son,” as in I Corinthians XV, 15, John XIX, 5, Matthew XXVI, 28, where the forms differ from the usual vocatives; see the note at Luke I, 54.]

He asked what this was. They told him that Jesus the Nazarene was passing by. But he cried out, [Col. 0651] saying, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me.” And those who went ahead rebuked him, so that he would be silent. But he cried out much more, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” [Note: [Col. 0651] “Him”: J., St., and B. add “to him.”]

Jesus stood and commanded that he be brought to him. When he came near him, he questioned him, [Note: [Col. 0651] “But Jesus, standing, commanded that he be brought to him; and when he had come near him, he questioned him.”] [Note: [Col. 0651] “To him”: “to him,” according to all the Greek manuscripts; for αὐτοῦ, as they read it, belongs to ἐγγίσσαντος, “having come near.”]

saying, “What do you want me to do for you?” But he said, “Lord, that I may see.” [Note: [Col. 0651] “He cried out even much more, ‘Son of David, have mercy on me.’ Jesus stood and commanded him to be brought to him. When he had come near him, he asked him, saying: ‘What do you want me to do for you?’ But he said: ‘Lord, that I may see.’”]

And Jesus said to him, “See; your faith has saved you.” [Note: [Col. 0651] “And Jesus said to him: ‘See; your faith has saved you.’”]

Immediately he saw and followed him, giving thanks to God; and all the people, seeing this, gave praise to God. [Note: [Col. 0651] “And immediately he saw and followed him, giving thanks to God, and all the crowd, seeing this, gave praise to God.”]

And he entered and passed through Jericho. [Note: [Col. 0651] “Jericho”: J. and St. add a variant.]

And behold, a man named Zacchaeus was there; he was chief of the tax collectors and was rich. [Note: [Col. 0651] “A man named Zacchaeus”: the Argenteus reads as printed; J. adds “a man called Zacchaeus”; St. adds the same; B. omits “man.” “This”: perhaps Wulfila, with Codex D and the versions, read οὗτος, “this,” instead of the usual καὶ αὐτός, “and he”; see the note at John XVIII, 26. B. omits “and this,” while J. and St. have a lacuna through “tax collector.” “And”: finally, Wulfila’s manuscripts have the Greek οὗτος, “this.” “Rich”: J., St., and B. omit the form.]

He sought to see who Jesus was, but he could not because of the crowd, since he was short in stature. [Note: [Col. 0651] “Short in stature”: J., St., and B. add a variant.]

So he ran ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, because he was about to pass that way. [Note: [Col. 0651] “And running ahead, he climbed a fig tree to see him, for he was about to pass through that way.”] [Note: [Col. 0651] “Running ahead”: St. adds a variant. Instead of the customary προδραμών, Wulfila’s manuscripts seem to have read προσδραμών; the prefix bi- is closer in sense to the preposition πρός than to πρό. “He climbed ahead”: J., St., and B. add “before he climbed.” “He”: “he,” according to all the Greek manuscripts.]

When Jesus came to that place, he looked up and saw him and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay in your house.” [Note: [Col. 0651] “And when he came to this place, Jesus looked up and saw him and said to him: ‘Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must be in your house.’”] [Note: [Col. 0651] “Up”: J., St., and B. add or omit the relevant form. “To Zacchaeus”: J. and St. add the dative form; see the note at XVIII, 38. “Come down”: J. adds “go down.” “For in”: J. adds “and.” Griesbach incorrectly notes that Wulfila omitted γάρ, “for,” since it is rendered by auk, “for.”]

He hurried down and received him joyfully. [Note: [Col. 0651] “And he hurried down and received him with joy.”] [Note: [Col. 0651] “He came down”: J. adds “he went down.”]

When everyone saw this, they murmured, saying, “He has gone in to lodge with a sinful man.” [Note: [Col. 0651] “And when everyone saw this, they murmured, saying that he had gone into the house of a sinful man to lodge.”] [Note: [Col. 0651–0652] “To lodge”: an unusual construction, since the preposition du is followed by a genitive, with which it is not normally joined. The passage appears corrupt; the expression “in the house” is both indicated and superfluous. Z. preferred either to delete du or, with “in the house” omitted, to read “to lodge with a sinful man.” If one may suppose that a gloss had entered the text—examples of this are not uncommon—a glossator may have added “in the house” to explain the construction “to lodge with a sinful man.” Such an ellipsis is familiar in Greek and is not foreign to Gothic; see the note at VIII, 49. If everything transmitted is genuine, the word order must certainly be changed to: “a sinful man went into the house to lodge”; compare the note at Matthew IX, 16. We hesitate to agree with Zahn, who thinks that du can be connected with “went.” “Of a sinful man”: J. and St. add a different form.]

Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Look, Lord, I will give half of my possessions to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.” [Note: [Col. 0651] “But Zacchaeus, standing, said to the Lord: ‘Look, Lord, I will give half of my possessions to the poor, and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.’”] [Note: [Col. 0652] “Zacchaeus”: J. adds another spelling. “Look”: J. and St. add “look, look.” “Fourfold repayment”: according to all the Greek manuscripts.]

Then Jesus said to him, “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and save the lost.” [Note: [Col. 0651] “But Jesus said to him: ‘Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham.’”] [Note: [Col. 0652] “And”: St. adds a variant. “The lost”: “the lost,” according to all the Greek manuscripts, τὸ ἀπολωλός.]

While they were listening to this, he added and told a parable, because he was near Jerusalem and they supposed that the kingdom of God would immediately appear. [Note: [Col. 0651] “While they were hearing this, he added and told a parable, because he was near Jerusalem and it seemed to them that the kingdom of God would immediately be revealed.”] [Note: [Col. 0652] “While they were listening”: J., St., and B. add a different form. “Jerusalem was”: according to all the Greek manuscripts.]

He said, “A certain nobleman went into a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself and to return.” [Note: [Col. 0651] “He said: ‘A certain nobleman went into a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself and return.’”] [Note: [Col. 0652] “A certain one”: St. adds “immediately.” “Country”: the Greek εἰς χώραν μακράν, “into a distant country,” which above, at XV, 12, he rendered fully by “into a far country.” “To receive”: St. adds another form. “He returned”: “to return,” according to all the Greek manuscripts, ὑποστρέψαι.]

He called ten of his servants and gave them ten portions, saying to them, “Trade until I come.” [Note: [Col. 0651] “Calling his ten servants, he gave them ten portions and said to them: ‘Trade until I come.’”] [Note: [Col. 0652] “I”: “I,” according to all the Greek manuscripts.]

But his citizens hated him and sent an ambassador after him, saying, “We do not want this man to reign over us.” [Note: [Col. 0651–0653] “But his citizens hated him and sent a messenger after him, saying: ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’”] [Note: [Col. 0652] From the word “there” through the end of verse 23 J. and St. have a lacuna, which B. and lh. supplied. In the present condition of the Argenteus, nothing can be read clearly through verse 20 except letters transmitted from the reverse page.] [Note: [Col. 0652] “That one”: B. has a lacuna.]

And it happened that, when he returned after receiving the kingdom, he commanded those servants to whom he had given the silver to be called to him, so that he might know what each had done. [Note: [Col. 0653] “And it happened, when he returned after receiving the kingdom, that he commanded those servants to whom he had given the silver to be called to him, so that he might know what each had done.”] [Note: [Col. 0653] “Himself”: B. adds a form; “to himself”: B. has a lacuna. “Silver”: B. adds a variant. “Whatever each”: “what each,” according to the Greek τίς τί (τι). “Had done”: B. gives an incomplete form.]

The first came, saying, “Lord, your mina has made ten minas.” [Note: [Col. 0653] “The first came, saying: ‘Lord, your mina has made ten minas.’”] [Note: [Col. 0653] “Which”: B. adds a form.]

He said to him, “Well done, good servant. Because you were faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.” [Note: [Col. 0653] “And he said to him: ‘Well done, good servant, because you were faithful in a little; you shall have authority over ten cities.’”] [Note: [Col. 0653] “Because”: B. has a lacuna. “In a little”: Ih., followed by Büsch., adds a form; the Greek manuscripts all have ἐλαχίστῳ, “in the least.” “You were faithful”: according to all the Greek manuscripts. “May you be”: B. has a lacuna. “Ten”: B. adds another form.]

The second came, saying, “Lord, your mina has made five minas.” [Note: [Col. 0653] “And another came, saying: ‘Lord, your mina has made five minas.’”] [Note: [Col. 0653] “It made”: B. adds “it produced.” “Five”: Hz. adds a form, as also in verse 19.]

And he said to him, “You too shall be over five cities.” [Note: [Col. 0653] “And he said also to this one: ‘You too shall be over five cities.’”] [Note: [Col. 0653] “Over”: B. omits it; see Luke II, 8. “Five”: see the note at verse 18.]

And another came, saying, “Lord, look, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a cloth. [Note: [Col. 0653] “And a certain one came, saying: ‘Lord, look, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a cloth.’”] [Note: [Col. 0653] “A certain one”: B. has “another,” which better suits the Greek text, since nowhere else does Wulfila use sums, “a certain one,” for ἕτερος, “another,” except at XIV, 20. “Laid away”: Z. has “I laid it away,” which, according to Ih., was written in the Argenteus; we rejected it because it disturbs the sense and is supported by no Greek authority. B. places lacuna marks from here to the end of the verse.]

For I was afraid of you, because you are a harsh man: you take what you did not deposit and reap what you did not sow.” [Note: [Col. 0653] “For I feared you, because you are a harsh man: you take what you did not place and reap what you did not sow.”] [Note: [Col. 0653] “In the cloth”: the Argenteus has this form; the editors propose a different reading. “And”: a scribe suggests that Wulfila, with the versions, may have read καί, “and,” instead of δέ, “but”; this is more plausible than certain. “A harsh man”: according to all the Greek manuscripts.]

He said to him, “I judge you from your own mouth, wicked servant. You knew that I am a harsh man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow. [Note: [Col. 0653] “And he said to him: ‘From your own mouth I judge you, wicked and lazy servant! You knew that I am a harsh man, taking what I did not place and reaping what I did not sow.’”] [Note: [Col. 0653] “And”: a conjecture that Wulfila, with the versions, read καί rather than δέ is more attractive than convincing; jah, “and,” very often renders δέ. “And lazy”: “and lazy,” according to all the Greek manuscripts. “You knew”: instead of “you would have known”; see the Prolegomena.]

Why, then, did you not put my silver in the bank? When I came, I would have collected it with interest.” [Note: [Col. 0653] “And why did you not deposit this silver of mine with the money-changers, so that when I came I might collect it with interest?”] [Note: [Col. 0653–0654] “With the money-changers”: literally, “to the money-changers,” corresponding to the Greek ἐπὶ τράπεζαν; compare I Corinthians X, 25, and the note at Luke III, 1. “And”: in the second occurrence, Wulfila has the Greek ἐγώ, “I.”]

And he said to those standing by, “Take the mina from him and give it to the one who has the ten minas.” [Note: [Col. 0653] “And he said to those standing by: ‘Take this mina from him and give it to the one who has the ten portions.’”] [Note: [Col. 0654] “To those standing by”: Z. adds a variant.]

They said to him, “Lord, he has ten minas.” [Note: [Col. 0653] “And they said to him: ‘Lord, he has ten portions.’”]

“For I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him. [Note: [Col. 0653] “For I tell you that to everyone who has, more is given, but from the one who does not have, even what he has is taken away from him.”]

But those enemies of mine—those who did not want me to reign over them—bring them here and kill them before me.” [Note: [Col. 0653] “But as for those enemies of mine who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and kill them before me.”] [Note: [Col. 0654] “But”: “but,” according to all the Greek manuscripts; B. suspects that “even so” entered the text from the margin. After saying this, he went on, going up to Jerusalem. [Note: [Col. 0653] “And after saying this, he went on, going up to Jerusalem.”] [Note: [Col. 0653] “Those who”: J. and St. add “those who.”]

And it happened, when he drew near Bethphage and Bethany, at the mountain called the Mount of Olives, that he sent two of his disciples, [Note: [Col. 0653] “And it happened, when he was near Bethphage and Bethany, at the mountain called the Mount of Olives, that he sent two of his disciples.”] [Note: [Col. 0654] “From”: this is the reading of the Argenteus and of J. and St.; B., Hz., and Z. have “at,” which the sense seems to require, but the manuscript reading can be defended, since Latin too says that something is near something else.]

saying, “Go into the village opposite you. When you enter it, you will find a colt tied up, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it. And if anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ say this to him: ‘The Lord needs it.’” [Note: [Col. 0653] “And if anyone asks you: ‘Why are you untying it?’ say this to him: ‘The Lord desires it.’”] [Note: [Col. 0654] “To you”: the Argenteus has this form instead of the expected form; see the note at XIV, 31. Those who had been sent went and found it just as he had told them. [Note: [Col. 0653] “Those who had been sent went and found it just as he had told them.”]

They said, “The Lord needs it.” [Note: [Col. 0653] “But they said: ‘The Lord has need of it.’”]

As he went, they spread their garments on the road. [Note: [Col. 0655] “As he went, they spread their garments on the road.”]

When he was already near the descent of the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began joyfully to praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works they had seen, [Note: [Col. 0655] “When he was already near the descent of the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began, rejoicing, to praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works they had seen.”] [Note: [Col. 0654] “Olive trees”: J. and St. add a variant. “All”: J. and St. leave a lacuna; B. adds “all these.” The adverb “all” normally occurs with “all,” but here functions as an adjective meaning ἅπας, “the whole”; compare below verse 48 and Luke VI, 5, “the whole multitude of the fish.” “Which they saw”: J. and St. add “which they saw”; see the note at X, 5.]

saying, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! and they will level you to the ground, you and your children within you, and they will not leave one stone upon another in you, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.” [Note: [Col. 0655] “And they will level you and your children within you to the ground, and they will not leave one stone upon another in you, because you did not recognize this time of your visitation.”]

[Col. 0657]

[Note: [Col. 0656] *gebeina*: St. adds *gebena*.]

[Note: [Col. 0657] “But when they saw him, these gardeners reasoned among themselves, saying: ‘This is the heir; let us kill him, so that the inheritance may become ours.’”]

When they saw him, the tenants considered among themselves, saying: “This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may become ours.” And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him.

And when they heard this, they said: “May it not be so!”

What, then, will the owner of the vineyard do to them? He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.

“Show me a coin. Whose image and inscription does it have?” They answered: “Caesar’s.”

[Note: [Col. 0657] “But he said to them: ‘Then give back these things to Caesar, to Caesar, and these things to God, to God.’”]

[Note: [Col. 0658] *andavaurde*: “answers”; all Greek witnesses have ἀποκρίσει. J. St. additionally have *andvaurde*.]

Some of the Sadducees, who say that there is no resurrection, approached him and questioned him: “Teacher, Moses wrote for us: If someone’s brother dies, having a wife, and he dies childless, his brother is to take that wife and raise up offspring for his brother.”

[Note: [Col. 0658] *ïs*: J. St. B. omit it.]

Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife and died childless.

Then the second took that wife, and he died childless.

And the third took her, likewise; and likewise all seven, and they left no children and died.

[Note: [Col. 0657] “And another took this wife, and he died childless.”]

[Note: [Col. 0657] “And a third took this one in the same way; likewise also all seven, and they left no children and died.”]

[Note: [Col. 0658] *spedista*: “last”; all Greek witnesses have ὕστερον (“afterward”). Ulfilas, with the manuscripts, omits δέ (“but”).]

[Note: [Col. 0658] *nu*: all Greek witnesses place it before *usstassai*.—*vaïrþiþ*: Sch. argues rashly that the Gothic translator read ἔσται.]

[Note: [Col. 0659] “But those who are considered worthy to attain that age and the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage.”]

[Note: [Col. 0659] *þaiei*: J. St. add *þatei*.—*usstassais*: St. adds *usstassai*.]

“For they cannot die any more, because they are equal to the angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection.”

The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage, but those who are worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage. For they cannot die any more, because they are equal to the angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 0659] “For they can no longer die, since they are equal to the angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection.”]

“But that the dead are raised, Moses also indicated at the bush, when he says: ‘I saw the Lord, the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob.’”

St. B. add *saei*. [Note: [Col. 0659] “But Moses also indicated that the dead are raised, at the bush, as he says: ‘I saw the Lord God of Abraham and the God”]

[Note: [Col. 0659] “of Isaac and the God of Jacob.”]

[Note: [Col. 0659] “For God is not God of the dead but of the living; for all live to him.”]

For he is not the God of the dead but of the living, for all live to him.

[Note: [Col. 0659] “And some of the scribes answered and said: ‘Teacher, you have spoken well.’”]

[Note: [Col. 0659] “Nor did they dare any longer to question him about anything.”]

But he said to them: “How do they say that the Christ is David’s son?”

[Note: [Col. 0659] “And he himself, David, says in the book of Psalms: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand.’”]

David himself says in the book of Psalms: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.’”

[Note: [Col. 0659] *ïk*: “I”; all Greek witnesses have it.]

[Note: [Col. 0659] “David calls him Lord, and how is he his son?”]

David calls him Lord, and how, then, is he his son?

[Note: [Col. 0659] *daveid*: Ulfilas omits οὖν.—*ïna fraujan*: according to the Greek.]

[Note: [Col. 0659] “He calls him Lord.”]

[Col. 0659]

When all the crowd was listening, he said to his disciples:

[Note: [Col. 0659] “While all the crowd was listening, he said to his disciples:”]

[Note: [Col. 0660] *at gahausjandein*: Z. adds *jct*.]

“Beware of these scribes, who desire to walk about in white garments—”

[Note: [Col. 0659] “Beware of these scribes who desire to walk about in white garments—”]

[Note: [Col. 0660] *weitaim*: “in white garments,” unquestionably *vastjom* (στολαῖς, XV, 22; Mark XVI, 5), as Ihre rightly saw; it immediately followed. There is no trace in the Greek of any verb corresponding to *weitaim*, and it is unclear from where Ulfilas obtained it. Ihre notes that white garments, as indicating a certain grandeur, honor, and majesty, apparently pleased the Jewish scribes, who assumed that their dignity acquired an additional measure of reverence from their dress.]

# THE GOSPEL THROUGH JOHN

[Note: [Col. 0659] The fragments that we have added from chapter one, chapter three, and chapter five through verse 38 are preserved in a commentary on the Gospel according to John, written in the Gothic language. Massmann, a professor at Munich, recently collected its fragments from Vatican and Ambrosian codices and published them under the title *Skeireins aivaggeljons þairh ïohannen*.]

[Col. 0659]

[Note: [Col. 0659] “Behold, this is the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of this world.” — [Note: [Col. 0659] Skeireins, p. 4 (37). **ïst* = “is,” omitted in all Greek copies..]

[Note: [Col. 0659] “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless one is born from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0659] Skeireins, p. 7 (39).]

Behold, this is the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of this world.—Amen, amen, I say to you: unless he is born from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God.—How is a man able to be born when he is an adult? Can he perhaps enter again into his mother’s womb and be born?

[Note: [Col. 0659] Skeireins, pp. 8 (39) and again 9 (40). *manna* is correctly read thus on p. 9; in the other passage *ma* has been added, for the scribe omitted writing the second part of this word on the following line. — *gabairan alþeis visands*: thus on p. 8 in all copies; on p. 9, *gabairan* follows *visands*. — *aftra galeiþan*: Massmann, pp. 39 and 40, adds *jct.* — *jag*: p. 9 has *jah*; see the note on Mark V, 37.]

Unless one is born from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God.—How is a man able to be born when he is an adult?

[Note: [Col. 0659] “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless one is born of water and Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0660] Skeireins, p. 9 (40).]

Can he enter again into his mother’s womb and be born?—Amen, amen, I say to you: unless one is born of water and Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.

[Note: [Col. 0659] “There were many waters there; therefore they came and were baptized.”]

[Note: [Col. 0660] Skeireins, p. 11 (41). *naga vesun*: Massmann conjectured *managa vatna gavesun*. But since *gavisan* does not mean “to be” but “to remain, dwell” (*μένειν*, John VIII, 27), and all Greek copies read “many waters” (*ὕδατα πολλά*), it seems preferable to complete the text as *vatna managa vesun*. — *— *jainar*: Massmann, p. 41, omits it.].]

I say to you: unless one is born of water and Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.—There were many waters there.

[Note: [Col. 0659] “John had not yet been put into prison.”]

[Note: [Col. 0660] Skeireins, p. 11 (41). *nauhþanuh*: Massmann adds *div.*; otherwise the Gothic has no equivalent of the Greek γάρ. — *galagiþs vas*: so in all Greek copies.]

[Note: [Col. 0659] “Then a dispute arose between John’s disciples and the Jews concerning purification.”]

[Note: [Col. 0660] Skeireins, p. 11 ff. (41). *þan*: the manuscript, if it is truly written so, adds *þau*. — *ïudaium*: “of the Jews,” Greek Ἰουδαίου.]

They were there, and therefore they came and were baptized. John had not yet been put into prison. Then a dispute arose between John’s disciples and the Jews concerning purification.

[Note: [Col. 0659] “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you bore witness—behold, he baptizes, and everyone is going to him.”]

[Note: [Col. 0660] Skeireins, p. 15 (43). *jaurdanau*: see the note on Mark X, 1.]

Then a dispute arose among John’s disciples with the Jews concerning purification.—Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you bore witness: behold, he baptizes, and everyone is going to him.

[Note: [Col. 0661] “Therefore this joy of mine has been fulfilled.”]

[Note: [Col. 0661] Skeireins, p. 15 (43).]

He who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you bore witness: behold, he baptizes, and everyone is going to him.—Therefore this joy of mine has been fulfilled.

[Note: [Col. 0661] Skeireins, p. 15 (43).]

[Note: [Col. 0661] “He must increase, but I must decrease.”]

[Note: [Col. 0661] Skeireins, p. 15 (43), twice, and p. 23 (47).]

He must increase, but I must decrease.

[Note: [Col. 0661] “He who comes from above is above all; he who comes from heaven is above all.”]

[Note: [Col. 0661] Skeireins, pp. 16–17 (43–44). *ïst*: the material that follows this word down to Greek λαλεῖ (“speaks”) is not translated word for word in the Gothic commentary. It is written there: *sik airþakundana jah us airþai rodjandan*, that is, “understanding himself as earthly and speaking from the earth.” These are the interpreter’s words, quoted incompletely. According to the Greek, the text should have been: “he who exists from the earth” (*sa visands us airþai*; I, *sa airþakunda*), “is from the earth and speaks from the earth.”]

He who comes from above is above all. He who comes from heaven is above all.—My joy has been fulfilled; he must increase, but I must decrease.

[Note: [Col. 0661] “What he has seen and heard, this he bears witness to, and no one receives his testimony.”]

[Note: [Col. 0661] Skeireins, p. 17 (44). *veitvodida* stands for *veitvodiþa*. It might be taken as a passive participle, as Massmann thinks, but the received reading does not allow this because of the following *ïs*, which would then have to mean “from him” or “by him.”]

He who comes from above is above all. What he has seen and heard, this he bears witness to, and no one receives his testimony.

[Note: [Col. 0661] “For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to those whom he wishes.”]

[Note: [Col. 0661] Skeireins, p. 20 (45).]

He who comes from heaven is above all. What he has seen and heard, this he bears witness to, and no one receives his testimony.—For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to those whom he wishes.

[Note: [Col. 0661] “Nor does the Father judge anyone, but he has given all judgment to the Son.”]

[Note: [Col. 0661] Skeireins, p. 20 (45). *ainohun*: this is how the Ambrosian manuscript reads; Massmann emended it to *ainnohun*. See the note on Mark IX, 8.]

For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to those whom he wishes. Nor does the Father judge anyone, but he has given all judgment to the Son.

[Note: [Col. 0661] “So that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.”]

[Note: [Col. 0661] Skeireins, pp. 21–22 (46).]

So that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father..

[Note: [Col. 0661] “He was the burning and shining lamp, but you wanted to rejoice for a while in his light.”]

[Note: [Col. 0661] Skeireins, p. 23 (47).]

He was the burning and shining lamp, but you wanted to rejoice for a while in his light.

[Note: [Col. 0661] “But I have testimony greater than John’s. For the works that the Father gave me to accomplish—these works that I do—bear witness concerning me that the Father sent me.”]

[Note: [Col. 0661] Skeireins, pp. 23–24 (47). *þamma*: concerning the use of the article before proper names, see the note on Mark XV, 15. — *— *ïk*: the second *ego* (“I”), omitted in all Greek copies.].]

But I have testimony greater than John’s. For the works that the Father gave me to accomplish—these works that I do—bear witness concerning me that the Father sent me.

[Note: [Col. 0661] “And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness concerning me. You have never heard his voice, nor have you seen his form.”]

[Note: [Col. 0661] Skeireins, pp. 25–26 (48), and Specimen, p. 24. *sandida*: this is correctly written in the Ambrosian manuscript; the Specimen adds *sanda*. — *wanhun gahausideduþ*: as in the Greek. — *gasewuþ*: the Ambrosian manuscript has *gas.*, while the Specimen adds *gasaiwiþ*. Massmann has now found the correct reading; see him at p. 26.]

The works that the Father gave me to accomplish—these works that I do—bear witness concerning me that the Father sent me. And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness concerning me. You have never heard his voice, nor have you seen his form.

[Note: [Col. 0661] “And you do not have his word dwelling in you, because you do not believe the one whom he sent.”]

[Note: [Col. 0662] Skeireins, p. 26 (48), and Specimen, p. 24.]

And you do not have his word dwelling in you, because you do not believe the one whom he sent.

[Note: [Col. 0661] “I would accuse you before the Father; there is one who accuses you—Moses, in whom you place your hope.”]

[Note: [Col. 0662] Here begin the portions of the Gospel of John that survive in the Argenteus manuscript. — *du*: the first manuscript; J. St. B. adds *bi*. — *vrohida*: “accused.” Ulfilas uses the preterite less correctly instead of the present; all Greek copies have a participle, whose meaning he has not properly understood and has therefore translated the words incorrectly.]

I would accuse you before the Father. There is one who accuses you—Moses, in whom you place your hope.

[Note: [Col. 0661] “For if you believed Moses, you would also believe me, for he wrote about me.”]

[Note: [Col. 0662] *mose galaubidedeiþ*: as in all Greek copies. — *ga-þaulaubidedeiþ*: J. adds *jaþau galaubidedeiþ*; St. adds *jaþan galaubidedeiþ*; B. adds *ga þau galaubidedeiþ*. See also the note on Mark IX, 28. — *mik auk*: as in the Greek.]

For if you believed Moses, you would also believe me, for he wrote about me.

[Note: [Col. 0661] “But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?”]

[Note: [Col. 0662] *galaubjaiþ*: we do not wish to argue with B. that Ulfilas read the Greek πιστεύσητε with the subjunctive, since he very frequently rendered the Greek future by his subjunctive.]

If you believe Moses, you would also believe me, for he wrote about me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?

[Note: [Col. 0661] “After this Jesus went across the Sea of Galilee, that is, of Tiberias.”]

[Note: [Col. 0662] *þata*: St. adds *þaþa*. — *jah*: “and,” as in the Greek. — *tibairiade*: J. and St. add *tiberiade*.]

But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words? After this Jesus went across the sea of Galilee, that is, of Tiberias.

[Note: [Col. 0661] “And a large crowd followed him, because they saw the signs that he performed on the sick.”]

And a large crowd followed him, because they saw the signs that he performed on the sick.

[Note: [Col. 0661] “Jesus went up onto the mountain, and there he sat with his disciples.”]

[Note: [Col. 0661] “Now Passover, the feast of the Jews, was near.”]

A large crowd followed him, because they saw the signs that he performed on the sick. Jesus went up onto the mountain, and there he sat with his disciples. Now Passover, the feast of the Jews, was near.

[Note: [Col. 0661] “Then Jesus lifted up his eyes and saw that a large crowd was coming to him, and he said to Philip: From where shall we buy bread, so that these people may eat?”]

[Note: [Col. 0662] *augona ïesus*: as in the Greek. — *manageins filu*: as in all Greek copies. — *qaþuh*: “and he said”; see the note on John XVIII, 26; compare the notes on Mark II, 11 and 1 Corinthians XVI, 13.]

Jesus went up onto the mountain, and there he sat with his disciples. Now Passover, the feast of the Jews, was near. Then Jesus lifted up his eyes and saw that a large crowd was coming to him, and he said to Philip: From where shall we buy bread, so that these people may eat?

[Note: [Col. 0661] “But he said this to test him, for he himself knew what he was going to do.”]

But he said this to test him, for he himself knew what he was going to do.

[Note: [Col. 0661] “Philip answered him: Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for them, so that each might receive a little.”]

[Note: [Col. 0662] *nimai*: all Greek copies place this after *leitil* (“a little”); otherwise the Ulfilas manuscripts have neither the Greek αὐτῶν nor τί.]

Philip answered him: Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for them, so that each might receive a little.

[Note: [Col. 0661] “One of his disciples, Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, said to him:”]

[Note: [Col. 0662] *qaþ*: Ulfilas has no equivalent of the Greek αὐτῷ. — *siponje*: B. adds *sinonje*. — *paitraus seimonaus*: as in all Greek copies.]
