One of his disciples, Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, said to him: There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish; but what are these for so many?

[Note: [Col. 0661] “Jesus said: Make the people sit down. Now there was much grass in that place, and the men sat down, about five thousand in number.”]

[Note: [Col. 0662] These verses are also found, for the most part, in Skeireins, pp. 27 ff. (49–50).]

[Note: [Col. 0663] *ïesus qaþ*: as in all Greek copies. — *vasun—þusundjos*: the Skeireins gives the sense rather than the individual words as follows: “But they made this multitude sit down on much grass existing in that place, five thousand men.”]

There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish; but what are these for so many? Jesus said: Make the people sit down. Now there was much grass in that place, and they sat down, about five thousand men.

[Note: [Col. 0663] “Jesus took the loaves and, after giving thanks, distributed them to those who were seated; likewise also of the fish, as much as they wished.”]

[Note: [Col. 0662] These verses are also found, for the most part, in Skeireins, pp. 27 ff. (49–50). *gadailida*: the Ulfilas manuscripts have no equivalent of the Greek τοῖς μαθηταῖς, οἱ δὲ μαθηταί.]

He had five barley loaves and two fish, but what are these for so many? Jesus said: Make the people sit down. There was much grass in that place, and they sat down, about five thousand men. Jesus then took the loaves and, after giving thanks, distributed them to those who were seated; likewise also of the fish, as much as they wished.

[Note: [Col. 0663] “When they were satisfied, he said to his disciples: Gather up the remaining fragments, so that nothing may be lost.”]

[Note: [Col. 0662] These verses are also found, for the most part, in Skeireins, pp. 27 ff. (49–50). *du*: absent in Skeireins. — *drauhsnos*: Skeireins has *drausnos*; see the note on Matthew V, 15. — *þei*: Skeireins has *ei*.]

He then distributed the loaves and fish to those who were seated, as much as they wished. When they were satisfied, he said to his disciples: Gather up the remaining fragments, so that nothing may be lost.

[Note: [Col. 0663] “So they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves, which remained for those who had eaten.”]

[Note: [Col. 0662] These verses are also found, for the most part, in Skeireins, pp. 27 ff. (49–50).]

[Note: [Col. 0663] *fimf*: Skeireins has *þaim ·e·*, a reading that greatly pleases us compared with the reading of the Argenteus manuscript, since an article is almost always added when nouns are repeated. — *þaim*: the first manuscript has “to them”; Skeireins has no equivalent. — *barizeinam*: Skeireins adds “and two fish,” which no Greek manuscript recognizes. — *aflifnoda*: correctly so in Skeireins; the Argenteus manuscript has *aflif . . . a*, with the missing part unreadable because the parchment is damaged there. The editors incorrectly supplied *aflifnanda*. — *þaim*: the second occurrence; Skeireins has *at þaim*.]

Then they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves, which remained for those who had eaten.

[Note: [Col. 0663] “When the people saw the sign that Jesus had performed, they said: This is truly the prophet, the one coming into the world.”]

The people, seeing what sign Jesus had performed, said: This is truly the prophet, the one coming into the world.

[Note: [Col. 0663] “But Jesus, knowing that they intended to come and seize him in order to make him king, withdrew again to the mountain by himself.”]

[Note: [Col. 0663] *vilvan*: Ulfilas has no equivalent of the Greek αὐτόν.]

The people, seeing what sign Jesus had performed, said: This is truly the prophet, the one coming into the world. But Jesus, knowing that they intended to come and seize him in order to make him king, withdrew again to the mountain by himself.

[Note: [Col. 0663] “When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea.”]

But Jesus, knowing that they intended to come and seize him in order to make him king, withdrew again to the mountain by himself. When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea.

[Note: [Col. 0663] “They got into a boat and went across the sea to Capernaum. Darkness had already come, and Jesus had not yet come to them.”]

[Note: [Col. 0664] *ïddjedunuh ufar*: J. adds *ïddjedun uh ufar*; St. adds *ïddjedun uhufar*. — *nauhþan*: “still,” whereas the Greek has οὔπω; Ulfilas and the Greek manuscripts read this way, compare III, 24 and VII, 39.]

The disciples went down to the sea. They got into a boat and went across the sea to Capernaum. Darkness had already come, and Jesus had not yet come to them.

[Note: [Col. 0663] “The sea was stirred up because a strong wind was blowing.”]

[Note: [Col. 0664] *ïþ*: “but,” whereas all Greek copies have τε; Ulfilas perhaps read δέ; see the note on Luke XVIII, 5. — *marei*: J. and St. add *marein*.]

Darkness had already come, and Jesus had not yet come to them. The sea was stirred up because a strong wind was blowing.

[Note: [Col. 0663] “When they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were afraid.”]

[Note: [Col. 0664] *·k· jah ·e·*: St. and Hz. add “about.”]

The sea was stirred up because a strong wind was blowing. When they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were afraid.

[Note: [Col. 0663] “Then he said: It is I; do not be afraid.”]

[Note: [Col. 0664] *qaþ*: Ulfilas has no equivalent of the Greek αὐτοῖς.]

Then they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were afraid. Then he said: It is I; do not be afraid.

[Note: [Col. 0663] “Then they wanted to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat came to the land to which they were going.”]

[Note: [Col. 0664] *ïna niman*: as in the Greek. — *eis*: “they,” with no equivalent in all Greek copies.]

Then they wanted to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat came to the land to which they were going.

[Note: [Col. 0663] “The next day the crowd that stood on the other side of the sea saw that there had been no other boat there except one, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples alone had gone away.”]

[Note: [Col. 0664] *daga*: “day,” with no equivalent in all Greek copies. — *sewun*: “they saw,” although the Greek has ἰδών (“having seen”); Ulfilas and the copies have εἶδον (“they saw”). — *alja*: J. and St. add *usja*. — *miþ ni qam*: see the note on Mark XIV, 44.]

The next day the crowd that stood on the other side of the sea saw that there had been no other boat there except one, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples alone had gone away..

[Note: [Col. 0663] “Other boats came from Tiberias, near the place where they had eaten the bread over which the Lord had given thanks.”]

[Note: [Col. 0664] *skipa qemun*: as in the Greek. — *ana þammei*: “in which.” Ulfilas uses this to express what are called genitive absolutes; compare VII, 14.]

The next day the crowd that stood on the other side of the sea saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples. They got into the boats and came to Capernaum, seeking Jesus. Other boats came from Tiberias, near the place where they had eaten the bread over which the Lord had given thanks.

[Note: [Col. 0663] “When the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they got into the boats and came to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.”]

[Note: [Col. 0664] *gastigun*: Ulfilas and the copies have no equivalent of the Greek αὐτοί.]

When the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they got into the boats and came to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.

[Note: [Col. 0663] “They found him on the other side of the sea and said to him: Rabbi, when did you come here?”]

[Note: [Col. 0664] *qeþunuh*: J. and St. add a division mark.]

The disciples had gone away by boat, and other boats came from Tiberias, near the place where they had eaten the bread over which the Lord had given thanks. When the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they got into the boats and came to Capernaum, seeking Jesus. They found him on the other side of the sea and said to him: Rabbi, when did you come here?

[Note: [Col. 0663] “Jesus answered them and said: Amen, amen, I say to you: you seek me, not because you saw signs and wonders, but because you ate of those loaves and were satisfied.”]

[Note: [Col. 0664] *jah fauratanja*: “and wonders,” with no equivalent in the Greek.]

They found him on the other side of the sea and said to him: Rabbi, when did you come here? Jesus answered them and said: Amen, amen, I say to you: you seek me, not because you saw signs and wonders, but because you ate of those loaves and were satisfied.

[Note: [Col. 0663] “Work not for this perishable food, but for the food that remains for eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you; for God the Father has sealed him.”]

[Note: [Col. 0664] *aiveinon*: J. and St. add *aiveinan*; Z. adds *aivainon*. — *gibiþ ïzvis*: as in the Greek.]

You seek me, not because you saw signs and wonders, but because you ate of those loaves and were satisfied. Work not for this perishable food, but for the food that remains for eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you; for God the Father has sealed him.

[Note: [Col. 0663] “Then they said to him: What shall we do, so that we may perform the works of God?”]

[Note: [Col. 0664] *vaurstva*: the Argenteus manuscript adds *vaursva*.]

Work not for this perishable food, but for the food that remains for eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you; for God the Father has sealed him. Then they said to him: What shall we do, so that we may perform the works of God?

[Note: [Col. 0663] “Jesus answered and said to them: This is the work of God, that you believe in the one whom he sent.”]

Jesus answered and said to them: This is the work of God, that you believe in the one whom he sent.

[Col. 0665]

[Note: [Col. 0665] “They said to him: What sign do you perform, then, so that we may see and believe you? What do you work?”]

[Note: [Col. 0665] *qeþun*: Ulfilas and his copies have no equivalent of οὖν (“then”); and earlier also, contrary to what Griesbach mistakenly notes, they do not contain the other word that the Greek places after τί, for this has been rendered by *aþþan*.]

This is the work of God, that you believe in the one whom he sent. They said to him: What sign do you perform, then, so that we may see and believe you? What do you work?

[Note: [Col. 0665] “Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness, as it is written: He gave them bread from heaven to eat.”]

They said to him: What sign do you perform, then, so that we may see and believe you?? What do you work? Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness, as it is written: He gave them bread from heaven to eat.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “Then Jesus said to them: Amen, amen, I say to you: Moses did not give you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven.”]

[Note: [Col. 0665] *— *gaf*: the second occurrence, “gave,” whereas all Greek copies have δίδωσι (“gives”);”); the same occurs in verse 37. See the note on Luke X, 19.]

Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness, as it is written: He gave them bread from heaven to eat. Then Jesus said to them: Amen, amen, I say to you: Moses did not give you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “For the bread of God is the one who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.”]

[Note: [Col. 0665] *gaf libain*: as in the Greek.]

Then Jesus said to them: Amen, amen, I say to you: Moses did not give you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is the one who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “Then they said to him: Lord, always give us this bread.”]

The bread of God is the one who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world. Then they said to him: Lord, always give us this bread.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “And Jesus said to them: I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me will not hunger, and whoever believes in me will never thirst.”]

And Jesus said to them: I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me will not hunger, and whoever believes in me will never thirst.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “But I told you that you have seen me and do not believe.”]

[Note: [Col. 0665] *þatei*: Ulfilas and the copies have no equivalent of the Greek καί.]

I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me will not hunger, and whoever believes in me will never thirst. But I told you that you have seen me and do not believe.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will certainly not cast out.”]

[Note: [Col. 0665] *gaf*: see the note on verse 32. — *gaggandan*: St. adds *gaggandin*.]

But I told you that you have seen me and do not believe. Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will certainly not cast out.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of the one who sent me.”]

Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will certainly not cast out. For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of the one who sent me.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “And this is the will of the one who sent me: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.”]

[Note: [Col. 0665] This verse is absent from the Argenteus manuscript, perhaps through the same scribal error by which it was omitted in manuscript 157 cited by Griesbach. This could easily have happened because this verse and the following one have the same beginning and the same ending. Compare Luke XVII, 36.]

And this is the will of the one who sent me: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “And this is the will of the one who sent me: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.”]

[Note: [Col. 0665] *vilja*: the Argenteus manuscript, Hz., and the editions add *viljan*. We do not deny that the noun θέλημα (“will”) could be rendered in Gothic by *viljan* (“to will”), but we deny that a subjective genitive can be joined with it. Lye had already reached the received reading by conjecture, and Ih. approved it. Compare also 1 Corinthians XVI, 7, where manuscript A erroneously reads *venjan* for *venja*, while manuscript B has the correct *venja*.]

Not that I should do my own will, but the will of the one who sent me. And this is the will of the one who sent me: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “The Jews therefore grumbled about him because he said: I am the bread that came down from heaven.”]

The Jews therefore grumbled about him, because he said: I am the bread that came down from heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “And they said: Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then does he now say: I have come down from heaven?”]

And they said: Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then does he now say: I have come down from heaven?

[Note: [Col. 0665] “Jesus answered and said to them: Do not grumble among yourselves.”]

[Note: [Col. 0666] *þan*: “but,” with no equivalent in the Greek.]

And they said: Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then does he now say: I have come down from heaven? Jesus answered and said to them: Do not grumble among yourselves.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him, and I will raise him up on the last day.”]

He is the one who came down from heaven. Jesus then answered and said to them: Do not grumble among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him, and I will raise him up on the last day.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “It is written in the prophets: And they shall all be taught by God. Everyone who hears from the Father and learns comes to me.”]

[Note: [Col. 0666] *nu*: “now,” with no equivalent in the Greek.]

It is written in the prophets: And they shall all be taught by God. Everyone who hears from the Father and learns comes to me.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “Not that anyone has seen the Father, except the one who is from the Father; he has seen the Father.”]

[Note: [Col. 0666] *sewi was*: no equivalent in the Greek. — *attin*: “the Father,” whereas all Greek copies have θεοῦ (“God”).]

It is written in the prophets: And they shall all be taught by God. Everyone who hears from the Father and learns comes to me—not that anyone has seen the Father, except the one who is from the Father; he has seen the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever believes in me has eternal life.”]

Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever believes in me has eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “I am the bread of life.”]

[Note: [Col. 0666] *libainais*: St. adds *labainais*, as in verse 63.]

I am the bread of life.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness and died.”]

Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever believes in me has eternal life. I am the bread of life. Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness and died.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that whoever eats of it may not die.”]

[Note: [Col. 0666] *ei—gadauþnai*: “so that whoever eats of it may not die.” All Greek copies have ἵνα τις ἐξ αὐτοῦ φάγῃ καὶ μὴ ἀποθάνῃ (“so that someone may eat of it and may not die”); the Greek conjunction καί (“and”) is omitted by the Gothic, the Vulgate of Cologne, and the Latin Fathers.]

Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness and died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that whoever eats of it may not die.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever; and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world.”]

[Note: [Col. 0666] *libanda sa*: J., St., and B. add *libandans*. — *jabai*: Z. adds *jah*.]

This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that whoever eats of it may not die. I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever; and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “The Jews therefore argued with one another, saying: How can this man give us his flesh to eat?”]

[Note: [Col. 0666] *leik giban*: as in the Greek.]

The Jews therefore argued with one another, saying: How can this man give us his flesh to eat?

[Note: [Col. 0665] “Then Jesus said to them: Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you do not have life in yourselves.”]

[Note: [Col. 0666] *driggkaiþ*: J. has *drigkaiþ*. This verb is more often written with one *g*, but in the Gospel of John it is always written with doubled *g*; see the note on Mark X, 37.]

Then Jesus said to them: Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you do not have life in yourselves.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.”]

[Note: [Col. 0666] *driggkiþ*: St. adds *dringkiþ*. — *ïn*: “in,” with no equivalent in the Greek.]

Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you do not have life in yourselves. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.

[Note: [Col. 0665] “For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.”]

[Col. 0667]

For whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day. For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.

[Note: [Col. 0667] “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.”]

[Note: [Col. 0667] “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will also live because of me.”]

Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him. As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will also live because of me.

[Note: [Col. 0667] “This is the bread that came down from heaven—not as your fathers ate manna and died; whoever eats this bread will live forever.”]

[Note: [Col. 0667] *manna*: “manna,” with no equivalent in the Greek. — *ïþ*: “but.” Ulfilas frequently adds this particle in John in adversative statements contrary to the Greek usage, as in VII, 8, 23, 29; VIII, 15, 23, and elsewhere.]

As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will also live because of me. This is the bread that came down from heaven—not as your fathers ate manna and died; whoever eats this bread will live forever.

[Note: [Col. 0667] “He said this while teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum.”]

[Note: [Col. 0667] *synagoge*: Z. adds *synanoge*. — *kafarnaum*: St. adds *kafarnum*.]

He said this while teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum.

[Note: [Col. 0667] “Many of his disciples, when they heard this, said: This is a hard saying; who can hear it?”]

He said this while teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum. Many of his disciples, when they heard this, said: This is a hard saying; who can hear it?

[Note: [Col. 0667] “But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them: Does this offend you?”]

But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them: Does this offend you?

[Note: [Col. 0667] “What, then, if you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?”]

But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them: Does this offend you? What, then, if you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?

[Note: [Col. 0667] “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words that I have spoken to you are Spirit and life.”]

[Note: [Col. 0667] *liban taujiþ*: the editions add *jct.* — *rodida*: “I have spoken,” Greek λαλῶ. — *libains*: see the note on verse 48.]

What, then, if you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before? It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words that I have spoken to you are Spirit and life.

[Note: [Col. 0667] “But there are some among you who do not believe.” For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who betrayed him..]

[Note: [Col. 0667] *galeiveiþ*: J. and St. remove *g*.]

The words that I have spoken to you are Spirit and life. But there are some among you who do not believe. For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him.

[Note: [Col. 0667] “And he said: For this reason I told you that no one can come to me unless it has been granted him by my Father.”]

From the beginning Jesus knew who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him. And he said: For this reason I told you that no one can come to me unless it has been granted him by my Father.

[Note: [Col. 0667] “From that time many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him.”]

[Note: [Col. 0667] *mela*: “time,” with no equivalent in the Greek; compare the note on verse 22.]

From that time many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him.

[Note: [Col. 0667] “Then Jesus said to the Twelve: Do you also want to go away?”]

[Note: [Col. 0667] *jah*: St. adds *jaþ*.]

From that time many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him. Then Jesus said to the Twelve: Do you also want to go away?

[Note: [Col. 0667] “Then Simon Peter answered him: Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.”]

[Note: [Col. 0667] *þanuh*: “then,” with no equivalent in the Greek.]

Then Jesus said to the Twelve: Do you also want to go away? Simon Peter answered him: Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 0667] “And we have believed and have come to know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0667] *xristus sunus*: “Christ, the Son,” whereas the Greek has ἅγιος (“holy”). — *libandins*: [Col. 0668] “living,” with no equivalent in the Greek.]

Simon Peter answered him: Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life. And we have believed and have come to know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God.

[Note: [Col. 0667] “Jesus answered them: Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?”]

Jesus answered them: Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?

[Note: [Col. 0667] “Now he was speaking of Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot; for he was going to betray him, being one of the Twelve.”]

He was speaking of Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot; for he was going to betray him, being one of the Twelve.

[Note: [Col. 0667] “After this Jesus walked in Galilee, for he did not want to walk in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him.”]

After this Jesus walked in Galilee. For he did not want to go into Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him.

[Note: [Col. 0667] “Now the Jewish feast, the Feast of Booths, was near.”]

[Note: [Col. 0667] “Then his brothers said to him: Leave here and go into Judea, so that your disciples also may see the works that you do.”]

Now the Jewish feast, the Feast of Booths, was near. Then his brothers said to him: Leave here and go into Judea, so that your disciples also may see the works that you do.

[Note: [Col. 0668] *siponjos*: Ulfilas has no equivalent of the Greek σοῦ. — *þu*: “you,” with no equivalent in the Greek.]

[Note: [Col. 0667] “For no one does anything in secret while seeking to be known openly. If you do these things, reveal yourself to the world.”]

His brothers said to him: Leave here and go into Judea, so that your disciples also may see the works that you do. For no one does anything in secret while seeking to be known openly. If you do these things, reveal yourself to the world.

[Note: [Col. 0667] “For even his brothers did not believe in him.”]

[Note: [Col. 0667] “Then Jesus said to them: My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready.”]

[Note: [Col. 0668] *ni nauh*: the editions add *jct.*, as in verse 8 and frequently elsewhere.]

For even his brothers did not believe in him. Then Jesus said to them: My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready.

[Note: [Col. 0667] “The world cannot hate you, but it hates me, because I testify concerning it that its works are evil.”]

[Note: [Col. 0668] *ïns*: “them,” whereas all Greek copies have αὐτοῦ (“of him”); Ulfilas uses it by syntactical attraction in place of *ïja*.].]

The world cannot hate you, but it hates me, because I testify concerning it that its works are evil.

[Note: [Col. 0667] “Go up to this feast yourselves; I am not yet going up to this feast, because my time has not yet been fulfilled.”]

[Note: [Col. 0668] **ïþ*: “but,” omitted in all Greek copies; see the note on VI, 58.. — *meinata mel*: as in the Greek.]

The world cannot hate you, but it hates me, because I testify concerning it that its works are evil. You go up to this feast yourselves; I am not yet going up to this feast, because my time has not yet been fulfilled.

[Note: [Col. 0667] “After saying these things to them, he remained in Galilee.”]

[Note: [Col. 0668] *þan—visands*: “he said—being,” whereas all Greek copies have εἰπών—ἔμεινεν (“having said—he remained”); Ulfilas and the Brixian manuscript agree in reading “he said while being.” Z. is not quite correct in saying this.]

You go up to this feast yourselves; I am not yet going up to this feast, because my time has not yet been fulfilled. After saying these things to them, he remained in Galilee.

[Note: [Col. 0667] “But when his brothers had gone up, then he also went up to the feast, not publicly, but as if in secret.”]

But when his brothers had gone up, then he also went up to the feast, not publicly, but as if in secret.

[Note: [Col. 0667] “The Jews therefore sought him at the feast and said: Where is he?”]

But when his brothers had gone up, then he also went up to the feast, not publicly, but as if in secret. The Jews therefore sought him at the feast and said: Where is he?

[Note: [Col. 0667] “And there was much murmuring about him among the crowd. Some said: He is good; others said: No, but he misleads the crowd.”]

[Note: [Col. 0668] *mikila*: Ulfilas has no equivalent of περὶ αὐτοῦ (“about him”).]

The Jews therefore sought him at the feast and said: Where is he? And there was much murmuring about him among the crowd. Some said: He is good; others said: No, but he misleads the crowd.

[Note: [Col. 0667] “Yet no one spoke boldly about him because of fear of the Jews.”]

[Note: [Col. 0668] *nih þan*: J., St., and Z. add *jct.*]

And there was much murmuring about him among the crowd. Some said: He is good; others said: No, but he misleads the crowd. Yet no one spoke boldly about him because of fear of the Jews.

[Col. 0669]

[Note: [Col. 0669] “But in the middle of the feast Jesus went up into the temple and taught.”]

[Note: [Col. 0669] *midjai*: thus in the Argenteus manuscript; B. adds *midja*. — *dulþ usstaig*: J. adds *dulþus staig*. The dative form *dulþ* instead of *dulþai* is noteworthy (verse 11; XII, 20; compare VII, 37 and Luke II, 42). Anyone who takes *dulþ* as an accusative and, with B., reads *midja* must consider that *ana* with the accusative has another meaning; see Luke XVII, 4, *ana dag*, that is, “for a day.” In the present passage, however, the dative is required to indicate the time during which something occurred; compare John VI, 23.]

But in the middle of the feast Jesus went up into the temple and taught.

[Note: [Col. 0669] “And the crowds were amazed, saying: How does this man know letters, although he has not been taught?”]

[Note: [Col. 0669] *manageins*: “the crowds,” whereas all Greek copies have Ἰουδαῖοι (“Jews”).]

But in the middle of the feast Jesus went up into the temple and taught, and the crowds were amazed, saying: How does this man know letters, although he has not been taught?

And he taught. And the crowds were astonished, saying, “How does this man know letters, though he has not been taught?” [Note: [Col. 0669] But Jesus answered and said: “This teaching of mine is not mine, but that of him who sent me.”] [Note: [Col. 0669] “Then”: Ulfilas, with codex o according to Mi., reads Greek *αὐτοῖς* (“to them”).]

Jesus then answered and said:

“My teaching is not mine, but belongs to the one who sent me. If anyone wishes to do his will, he will recognize concerning this teaching whether it is from God, or whether I speak from myself. Whoever speaks from himself seeks his own glory; but whoever seeks the glory of the one who sent him is genuine, and there is no injustice in him.” [Note: *ufkunnaiþ*: although Ulfilas’s illustrated manuscript, pp. 158 and 160, and this passage and verse 51 would favor reading *ufkunnai* (“recognize”), the editor seems not to have known that *ufkunnan* follows two different patterns of inflection. “I”: J. St. B. add *ik*.] “Did not Moses give you the law? Yet none of you observes this commandment. Why do you seek to kill me?”

The crowd answered and said, “You have a demon. Who is seeking to kill you?” [Note: “The crowd answered and said: You have a demon; who is seeking to kill you?”]

Jesus answered and said to them, “I performed one work, and you are all astonished.”

“For this reason Moses gave you circumcision—not because it is from Moses, but from the fathers—and you circumcise a man on the Sabbath. If a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath so that the law of Moses may not be broken, why are you angry with me because I made an entire man well on the Sabbath?” [Note: *þata*: because Ulfilas adds the article to the noun *vitoþ* (“law”), he seems to have read Greek *οὗτος* (“this”) in his manuscript; yet no trace of it is found in any Greek manuscript. “But”: Greek manuscripts universally read *ïþ*. “Entire”: J. St. add *allama*.] “Do not judge by appearance, but judge with righteous judgment.” [Note: *staua*: J. St. add *stava*.]

Some of the inhabitants of Jerusalem therefore said, “Is this not the man whom they are seeking to kill?” [Note: *þize*: St. deletes *þizei*.] “And look, he speaks openly, and they say nothing to him. Can it be that the rulers have truly recognized that this is truly the Christ?” [Note: *vaiht*: St. adds *vaiþt*. “In truth”: the second hand; Greek manuscripts read “in truth.”]

“But we know where this man is from. Yet when the Christ comes, no one knows where he is from.” Jesus therefore cried out in the temple while teaching and said:

“You know me, and you know where I am from. I have not come from myself, but the one who sent me is genuine, whom you do not know. I know him, because I am from him, and he sent me.” [Note: *ïþ*: “but”; Greek manuscripts read *ïþ*; see the note at VI, 58.]

They therefore sought to seize him, but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come. [Note: *uslagida*: J. deletes *lagida*.]

But many of the crowd believed in him and said, “When the Christ comes, will he perhaps perform more signs than this man has performed?” [Note: *qeþun*: Ulfilas’s manuscript and certain copies read Greek *ὅτι* (“that”). “Whether indeed”: J. St. Z. and Grimm (III, 284) add this form; but we very much doubt whether this combination of particles is correct. *ei* does occur in interrogative sentences, but then it is neither enclitic nor to be attached to other words. Since *ïbai* alone is sufficient to express the sense of Greek *μήτι* (“surely not?”), *ei* is superfluous here, while a word rendering Greek *ὅτι* is lacking above. Perhaps *ei* was placed here through a scribal error and should have stood after *qeþun*; compare the note at Matthew IX, 16. “Signs”: Ulfilas’s manuscript and certain copies read Greek *τούτων* (“of these”).]

The Pharisees heard the crowd murmuring these things about him, and the Pharisees and the chief priests sent attendants to seize him. [Note: *þan*: “then”; Greek manuscripts read *þan*. *ïnuhsanaidedun*: concerning the insertion of *uh* between the parts of a compound verb, see the note at Mark XIV, 44. As for the use of this enclitic in place of Greek *καί* (“and”), compare the note at Mark II, 11. *andbahtans*: Greek places this after “chief priests.”]

Then Jesus said, “I am with you for only a little while, and then I go to the one who sent me. You will seek me and not find me, and where I am you cannot come.” [Note: “Little”: J. St. add *leitil*. “Then”: Greek manuscripts universally read “then.”]

The Jews therefore said among themselves, “Where does this man intend to go, that we shall not find him? Surely he does not intend to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks?” [Note: “Intend”: St. adds *shuli*. “Greeks”: J. St. add *þiudos*.]

“What is the meaning of this saying that he spoke: ‘You will seek me and not find me, and where I am you cannot come’?” [Note: *maguþ*: J. St. add *majup*.]

On the last and greatest day of the feast Jesus stood and cried out, saying, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” [Note: “This great feast”: *dulþais*; “last”: Greek manuscripts read *ἐσχάτῃ* (“last”).]

He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive, for the Holy Spirit had not yet come upon them, because Jesus had not yet been glorified. [Note: *sa*: “this”; Greek manuscripts universally read “this.” “Upon them”: Greek manuscripts read “upon them.”]

When the crowd heard these words, some said, “This is truly the prophet.” [Note: “These words”: Greek *τὸν λόγον* (“the word”); Ulfilas’s manuscript and certain copies agree with those that read *τῶν λόγων τούτων* (“these words”).] Others said, “This is the Christ.” Others said, “Surely the Christ does not come from Galilee?” [Note: *sumaih*: “others” or “others, however”; Ulfilas may have read Greek *οἱ δέ* (“but others”). “This”: the Argenteus manuscript has *þu*, apparently an unintelligible pronoun. B. conjectured *þau*, a conjecture repeated by Ih. If Ulfilas had used bare *ïbai*, no one would find anything missing, since Greek *μὴ γάρ* in 1 Corinthians XI, 22 is rendered by Gothic *ïbai* alone with the same meaning. But since *þu* has been added and the sense does not tolerate it, an emendation is needed. We have not been able to determine which of the scholars’ conjectures is more probable; compare 1 Corinthians XV, 29 and following.]

Did not the Scripture say that the Christ comes from the offspring of David and from Bethlehem, the village where David was? The crowd therefore became divided over him. Some of them wanted to seize him, but no one laid hands on him. [Note: These verses are also read for the most part in the *Skeireins*, pp. 31 and following (51 and following). “They wanted”: Greek manuscripts have the corresponding form; *ni*: St. adds *nih*.]

The attendants therefore went to the chief priests and Pharisees, and they said to them, “Why did you not bring him?” [Note: These verses are also read for the most part in the *Skeireins*, pp. 31 and following (51 and following). “Chief”: Z. adds *auhumistan*.]

The attendants answered, “No man has ever spoken as this man speaks.” [Note: These verses are also read for the most part in the *Skeireins*, pp. 31 and following (51 and following). *andhofun*: the *Skeireins* and certain copies add *þan* (“then”). *andbahtos*: the *Skeireins* omits this and adds *qiþandans þatei* (“saying that”), which no Greek manuscript recognizes; compare the note at Matthew V, 8. *aiv*: Ulfilas’s manuscript and copy 7 read Greek *οὕτως* (“thus”).]

The Pharisees answered them, “Have you also been deceived?” [Note: These verses are also read for the most part in the *Skeireins*, pp. 31 and following (51 and following). “Are”: the *Skeireins* has *siuþ*.]

“Has any one of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed in him?” [Note: These verses are also read for the most part in the *Skeireins*, pp. 31 and following (51 and following). “Look, perhaps”: “look, perhaps” corresponds to Greek *μή* (“surely not?”). “Or”: Z. adds *aiþþan*; the *Skeireins* adds *þize* (“of these”).]

“But this crowd, which does not know the law, is accursed.” [Note: These verses are also read for the most part in the *Skeireins*, pp. 31 and following (51 and following). “This”: Z. adds *sa*.]

Nicodemus—he who had previously come to him at night, being one of them—said to them, [Note: These verses are also read for the most part in the *Skeireins*, pp. 31 and following (51 and following). “To him”: Greek places this after “night.” “Of whom”: J. St. delete *ïze*.]

“Does our law judge a man unless it first hears him and learns what he does?” [Note: These verses are also read for the most part in the *Skeireins*, pp. 31 and following (51 and following). “Man”: J. St. add *manna*. “Previously”: Greek places this after “him.” “Recognize”: see the note at verse 17.]

They answered and said to him, “Are you also from Galilee? Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee.” [Note: These verses are also read for the most part in the *Skeireins*, pp. 31 and following (51 and following). “And they said”: “and they said” occurs in the *Skeireins* as *qiþandans* (“saying”), with the words that follow, *du ïmma*, omitted, contrary to the authority of all Greek manuscripts. “Arise”: after this verb J. St. add *jah* (“and”) and then place a lacuna sign. In the Argenteus manuscript, however, there is neither the word *jah* nor any indication of an omission. Gothic, like many manuscripts and versions, omits the final verse of this chapter and the passage about the adulterous woman (VIII, 1–11). A later hand therefore added the following at VIII, 12: “Chapter VIII of John. Again Jesus spoke to them, saying: I am the light of the world.” The beginning of the chapter omitted here, as well as the preceding words, is: “And each went to his own house.”]

Then Jesus spoke to them again, saying, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.” [Note: “Again”: Ulfilas’s manuscripts and versions read Greek *οὖν* (“therefore”). “To them”: Greek places this after “Jesus.”]

The Pharisees therefore said to him, “You testify about yourself; your testimony is not true.” Jesus answered and said to them, “Even if I testify about myself, my testimony is true, because I know where I came from and where I am going. But you do not know where I come from or where I am going. You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one. Yet if I do judge, my judgment is true, because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.” [Note: *ïþ*: “but”; Greek manuscripts universally read *ïþ*; see the note at VI, 58. *aþþan*: Ulfilas’s manuscripts and copies read Greek *δέ* (“but”); *aþþan* means Greek *καί* (“and”), as at Luke VI, 32.]

“And in your law it is written that the testimony of two men is true. I am the one who testifies about myself, and the one who sent me, the Father, testifies about me.” [Note: “The Father”: *atta*.]

They therefore said to him, “Where is this father of yours?” Jesus answered, “You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would also know my Father.” [Note: *nih*: St. deletes *ni*. “And thus”: J. adds *jah*; St. adds *jah þan*; Greek manuscripts universally place *þau* after *kunþedeiþ*.]

He spoke these words in the treasury while teaching in the temple, and no one seized him, because his hour had not yet come. [Note: “These words”: the Gothic text reads *þo vaurda* (“the words”); “treasury”: *gazaufylakio*.]

Then Jesus said to them again, “I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sin. Where I am going, you cannot come.” [Note: “Yet he had not come”: *naunþanuh ni qam weila*; “again”: Greek manuscripts have *οὖν* (“therefore”).]

The Jews therefore said, “Surely he is not going to kill himself, since he says, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come’?” [Note: “Kill himself”: the Gothic phrase is *nibai usqimai sis silbin* (“lest he kill himself”).]

He said to them, “You are from below; I am from above. You are from this world; I am not from this world. I told you that you will die in your sins, for if you do not believe that I am he, you will die in your sins.” [Note: *ïesus*: Greek manuscripts universally read “Jesus.” *ïþ*: “but”; Greek manuscripts universally read *ïþ*; see the note at VI, 58. *þaim*: second hand; St. adds *þain*. *ïupaþro*: Z. regularly adds *jupaþro*.]

Then they said to him, “Who are you?” Jesus said to them, “The beginning—the very thing I am also speaking to you.” [Note: *anastodeins*: Greek manuscripts universally read *τὴν ἀρχήν*. Since this plainly means “from the beginning,” while Ulfilas translates it as though Jesus answered that he himself was “the beginning,” he undoubtedly erred, together with the Latin versions and Fathers who understood *τὴν ἀρχήν* in the same way; see Griesbach.]

“I have much to say about you and to judge, but the one who sent me is true, and what I heard from him I speak in this world.” [Note: *rodja*: “I speak”; Greek manuscripts appear to have read *λαλῶ* rather than *λέγω*, since Gothic *rodjan* usually corresponds to the former verb; the same is true in verse 45.]

They did not understand that he was speaking to them about the Father. Jesus therefore said to them, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and that I do nothing from myself, but speak just as my Father taught me. And the one who sent me is with me; the Father has not left me alone, because I always do what pleases him.” [Note: “When you lift up”: *ushauheiþ*. “Father”: *atta*.]

As he spoke these things, many believed in him. Jesus therefore said to the Jews who had believed in him, “If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” [Note: *gastandiþ*: St. adds *gastandit*.]

They answered him, “We are Abraham’s offspring and have never been enslaved to anyone. How can you say, ‘You will become free’?” Jesus answered them, “Amen, amen, I say to you, everyone who commits sin is a slave to sin. But the slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. If therefore the Son makes you free, you are truly free.” [Note: *fravaurhtai*: B. and Z. delete *fravaurhtais*. The dative dependent on nouns is extremely common; see, among many passages, Mark II, 28: *frauja ïst sa sunus mans jah þamma sabbato* (“the Son of Man is lord also of the Sabbath”), and compare the note at John IX, 28.]

“I know that you are Abraham’s offspring, but you seek to kill me because my word finds no place in you. What I have seen with my Father I speak, and what you have heard from your father you do.” [Note: *gasaw*: St. adds *gasah*. *jus*: Ulfilas’s manuscripts and copies read Greek *οὖν* (“therefore”).]

They answered and said to him, “Our father is Abraham.” Jesus said to them, “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham. But now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth that I heard from God. Abraham did not do this. You do the works of your father.”

They said to him, “We were not born of fornication; we have one Father, God.” Jesus said to them, “If God were your Father, you would love me, for I came forth from God and came here. For I did not come from myself, but he sent me.” [Note: *urrann*: Z. adds *urran*. *ni*: Greek manuscripts universally omit “not.” The presence of this particle is especially objectionable after *nih*, since Gothic generally does not imitate the Greek practice of multiplying negations; here no Greek manuscript has two negations. Ulfilas does this several times; see below IX, 33; XVI, 24; Matthew XXVII, 14; Mark VII, 12; Luke IX, 36. A comparable case is the formula *ni þanaseiþsni* = Greek *οὐκέτι* (“no longer”) at John XVI, 21 and 2 Corinthians V, 16.]

“Why do you not understand my speech? Because you cannot hear my word. You are from your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of this father of yours. He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks falsehood, he speaks from his own nature, because he is a liar and the father of it.” [Note: *manamaurþrja*: thus the Argenteus manuscript; the editions add *mannamaurþrja*. Compare *manaseds*.]

“But because I speak the truth, you do not believe me. Which of you convicts me of sin? If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me? Whoever is from God hears God’s words. For this reason you do not hear, because you are not from God.” [Note: *rodida*: “I have spoken”; Greek manuscripts universally read *λαλῶ* (“I speak”); see the note at verse 26, and compare the note at Luke X, 19. *duwe*: Ulfilas’s manuscripts and copies read Greek *ὑμεῖς* (“you”).]

The Jews answered and said to him, “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” [Note: *þan*: “but”; Greek manuscripts read *þan*. *qiþam*: St. adds *qiþan*.]

Jesus answered, “I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you dishonor me. I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges.” [Note: *ïk*: Ulfilas’s manuscripts and copies read Greek *δή* (“indeed”).]

“Amen, amen, I say to you, if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.” [Note: *aiva dage*: St. adds *jct.*; thus also verse 52 with J. Otherwise Greek manuscripts universally read *dage* (“of days”) here and in the following verse.]

Then the Jews said to him, “Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham died, and the prophets died, yet you say, ‘If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death.’” [Note: *mein vaurd*: parallel to all Greek manuscripts. *aiva dage*: see the note at verse 51. *dauþau*: see the note at Luke IX, 27.]

“Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? The prophets also died. Whom do you make yourself?” [Note: *þu*: “you”; Greek manuscripts read “you.”]

Jesus answered, “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, whom you say is our God. Yet you have not known him, but I know him. And if I said that I did not know him, I would be like you, a liar. But I know him and keep his word.” [Note: *unsar*: “our”; Greek reads “your.” *kunnjau*: J. St. B. add *kunjau*.]

“Abraham your father rejoiced that he would see my day; he saw it and was glad.” [Note: *sifaida*: “rejoiced.”]

The Jews therefore said to him, “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” Jesus said to them, “Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am.” [Note: *ïm*: J. St. add *ïmma*.]

Then they picked up stones to throw at him. But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple, passing through their midst, and went away in this manner. [Note: *þan*: “then”; Greek manuscripts universally read “then.” *usleiþands—sva*: “going away—thus”; Greek manuscripts read “and passing through their midst, he went away.”]

As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. His disciples therefore asked him, saying, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” [Note: *sau þau*: J. St. add *sa uþþau* (“this one or”). *blinds*: thus the Argenteus manuscript; Hz. adds *blins*.]

Jesus answered, “Neither did this man sin, nor his parents; but it was so that the works of God might be revealed in him.” [Note: The Gothic has *sa fravaurhta*, “this sinner,” but the sense requires “he sinned.”]

“I must work the works of the one who sent me while it is day. Night is coming, when no one can work. While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” [Note: *þa..ei*: the editions add *þatei*. What was written in the Argenteus manuscript cannot be determined because part of the parchment has been damaged between *þa* and *ei*. There is room for approximately two letters; after *a* there appears to be a trace of *d*, and before *e* a trace of *m*, *n*, or something similar. Although we cannot affirm that *þatei* or *þarei*, the conjectures proposed by Z., are correct—neither fills the space exactly, and neither corresponds adequately to Greek *ὅτε* (“when”)—we have found nothing in the entire Gothic vocabulary worth restoring. The one conjecture that can be proposed with some probability is *þandei*, for which the scribe may have written *þadnei* by carelessly transposing the letters, just as he wrote *gaggast* for *gaggats* at Mark XIV, 13. “No one”: St. adds *meinamma*.]

After saying this, he spat on the ground and made clay from the spittle, and he smeared the clay on the eyes of the blind man. [Note: *ïmma*: Greek manuscripts read *ei* (“on him”). “On the eyes”: Greek manuscripts universally place these words after *fani* (“clay”). “Blind”: J. St. add *blindis*.]

And he said to him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam”—which is translated “Sent.” He went, washed, and came back seeing. [Note: *þvahan*: “to wash”; Greek manuscripts universally read the middle imperative *νίψαι* (“wash yourself”). Thus Gothic often renders one asyndetically attached imperative by an infinitive; compare Matthew V, 24, *gagg gasibjon*; Mark I, 44; and Luke XVIII, 22. *galaiþ*: Ulfilas’s manuscripts and copies read Greek *οὖν* (“therefore”).]

The neighbors and those who had previously seen him as a beggar said, “Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?” [Note: *ïs*: “he”; Greek manuscripts universally read “he.”]

Some said, “This is he”; others said, “He resembles him.” But he said, “I am he.” [Note: *sumaih*: “others”; J. St. add *sumai*. *ïþ*: “but”; Greek manuscripts read “but.”]

They therefore said to him, “How were your eyes opened?” [Note: *þo*: J. St. B. omit the particle, perhaps because it is written above in the Argenteus manuscript; but the first hand wrote it.]

He answered, “The man called Jesus made clay, smeared my eyes, and said to me, ‘Go and wash in the pool of Siloam.’ So I went, washed, and received my sight.” [Note: *afþvahan*: “to wash”; Greek has *καὶ νίψαι* (“and wash”), after “Siloam.” Ulfilas agrees with the manuscripts that place *νίψαι* after *ὕπαγε* (“go”); see the note at verse 7. *ïn þata svumfsl siloamis*: “in this pool of Siloam”; Greek *εἰς τὸν Σιλωάμ*. *ïk*: “I”; Greek manuscripts universally read “I.”]

They said to him, “Where is he?” But he said, “I do not know.” [Note: *ïþ ïs*: “but he”; Greek manuscripts universally read “but he.”]

They brought to the Pharisees the man who had formerly been blind. [Note: *gatiuhand*: St. adds *gatjuhand*. *saei*: Ulfilas has Greek *ποτέ* (“formerly”).]

Now it was the Sabbath when Jesus made the clay and opened his eyes. The Pharisees again asked him how he had received his sight. And he said to them, “He put clay on my eyes; I washed, and I see.” [Note: *fareisaieis*: thus the Argenteus manuscript; J. St. Hz. add *fareisaeis*. *jah*: “also”; Greek manuscripts universally read “also.”]

Some of the Pharisees therefore said, “This man is not from God, because he does not observe the Sabbath.” Others said, “How can a sinful man perform such signs…”.
to do? And disagreement arose among them.] [Note: [Col. 0678] *sumai*] Greek manuscripts universally place it after *fareisaie*.

He washed and saw. Then some of the Pharisees said, “This man is not from God, because he does not observe the Sabbath day.” Others said, “How can a sinful man perform such signs?” And there was disagreement among them. [Note: [Col. 0677] They said again to the man who had formerly been blind, “What do you say about him, since he opened your eyes?” But he said, “He is a prophet.”] [Note: [Col. 0678] *faurþis*] “formerly”; Ulfilas’ codex 11, according to Miller, reads Greek ποτέ.

They said again to the formerly blind man, “What do you say about him, since he opened your eyes?” [Note: [Col. 0677] The Jews did not believe concerning him that he had been blind and had received sight, until they summoned his parents, this man who now saw.] [Note: [Col. 0678] *ïs*] “he”; so all the Greek manuscripts.

But he said, “He is a prophet.” Then the Jews did not believe about him that he had been blind and had received sight, until they summoned his parents, the parents of the one who had received sight. And they questioned them, saying, “Is this your son, whom you say was born blind? How does he now see?” [Note: [Col. 0677] His parents answered them and said, “We know that this is our son and that he was born blind;] [Note: [Col. 0678] *þan*] “but”; the Greek manuscripts have δέ, while other witnesses of Ulfilas have δέ or οὖν; since *þan* corresponds to both particles, it cannot be determined with certainty which was read.]

“but how he now sees, we do not know, nor do we know who opened his eyes. He is of age; ask him. He will speak for himself.” [Note: [Col. 0677] His parents said this because they feared the Jews, for the Jews had already agreed that if anyone confessed him to be Christ, he should be expelled from the synagogue.] [Note: [Col. 0678] *utana synagogais*] “outside the synagogue”; J. and St. add *jct.* [Note: [Col. 0678] *vairþai*] so in the Argenteus codex; J. and B. have *varþai*.

His parents said this because they feared the Jews; for the Jews had already agreed among themselves that, if anyone confessed him to be Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue. Therefore his parents said, “He is of age; ask him.”

They summoned the man a second time, the one who had been blind, and said to him, “Give glory to God! We know that this man is a sinner.” [Note: [Col. 0677] They summoned again the man who had been blind and said to him, “Give glory to God! We know that this man is a sinner.”]

He answered, “Whether he is a sinner, I do not know. One thing I know: I was blind, but now I see.” [Note: [Col. 0677] Then he answered, “If he is a sinner, I do not know that; one thing I know, that I was blind, but now I see.”] [Note: [Col. 0679] *jains*] Ulfilas and the other codices have “and he said.” [Note: [Col. 0679] *ïk*] “I”; all the Greek manuscripts. [Note: [Col. 0679] *þat-ain*] “this one thing”; all the Greek manuscripts have ἕν. It is written *þatain* instead of *þata ain*. Do not confuse it with *þatainei*, which is merely an adverb; *þat-ain* functions as a substantive. [Note: [Col. 0679] *vas ïþ*] “I was, but”; the Greek has ὤν, while the Gothic codices have ἤμην καί.

?”]

Then they said again, “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?” He answered them, “I already told you, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?” [Note: [Col. 0679] He answered them, “I have already told you, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?”]

Then they mocked him and said, “You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses.” [Note: [Col. 0679] *þanuh*] “then”; so the Greek. [Note: [Col. 0679] *moses*] Editors take this as a genitive form; elsewhere it is *mosezis* (see VII, 23; Mark XII, 26; Luke II, 22; 1 Corinthians IX, 9; 2 Corinthians III, 7). But since the Goths ordinarily say “to be someone’s disciple,” not “to be a disciple of someone,” either Ulfilas uses *moses* as a dative, or the copyist mistakenly wrote *moses* for *mose* (V, 46; VII, 22; Mark IX, 4; Luke IX, 33, and elsewhere). [Note: [Col. 0679] *siponjos sijum*] “we are disciples”; all the Greek manuscripts have the corresponding form.]

“We know that God spoke to Moses; but as for this man, we do not know where he is from.” [Note: [Col. 0679] The man answered and said to them, “In this indeed is something marvelous: that you do not know where he is from, and yet he opened my eyes.”] [Note: [Col. 0679] *auk*] This particle is noteworthy in its unusual position. Since it ordinarily follows one or more words of the sentence, it is here placed at the beginning; so also at Mark XII, 25; compare the discussion of *raihtis* at Romans X, 18.]

The man answered and said to them, “In this indeed is something marvelous: that you do not know where he is from, and yet he opened my eyes. We know that God does not hear sinners; but if anyone is devout and does his will, he hears him.” [Note: [Col. 0679] *guþ fravaurhtaim*] “God [does not hear] sinners”; corresponding to the Greek in all manuscripts.]

“From the beginning it has never been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.” [Note: [Col. 0679] *mahtedi*] St. adds *maþedi*.

They answered and said to him, “You were born entirely in sins, and you teach us?” And they cast him out. [Note: [Col. 0679] They answered him, “You were born wholly in sins, and you teach us?” And they expelled him.]

Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and when he found him he said to him, “Do you believe in the Son of God?” [Note: [Col. 0679] *gaulaubeis*] So in the Argenteus codex; the editors add *galaubeis*; see Matthew IX, 28.]

He answered and said, “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?” [Note: [Col. 0679] *an*] An interrogative particle corresponding to the Greek καί placed before the pronoun in the question; see Luke III, 10. In other places Gothic also uses *jah*, “also,” for this, as at Mark X, 26; Luke III, 14; 2 Corinthians II, 2.]

Jesus said to him, “You have seen him, and the one speaking with you is he.” But he said, “I believe, Lord,” and worshiped him. [Note: [Col. 0679] But he said, “I believe, Lord,” and he worshiped him.].]

And Jesus said, “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.” [Note: [Col. 0680] *þamma*] “this one.” Sch. wrongly counts Ulfilas among those who omit τοῦτον.]

Some of the Pharisees who were with him heard this and said to him, “Are we also blind?” [Note: [Col. 0679] Jesus said to them, “If you were blind, you would have no sin; but now you say, ‘We see’; therefore your sin remains.”] [Note: [Col. 0680] *qiþiþ*] The Argenteus codex has *qi\ qiþiþ*; the copyist often erred by repeating the same syllables on different lines; see the notes on Matthew V, 31; Luke I, 65; John VII, 45. The same thing happened more than once even on the same line; see the notes on XII, 47; XIII, 13; Mark X, 29; Luke VI, 17; compare 2 Corinthians X, 12. [Note: [Col. 0680] *eiþan*] This is correctly printed by J. and the editors, and by Grimm III, 282; it corresponds to the simple particle οὖν or ὥστε. Castillion and Massmann therefore printed *ei þan* separately at 1 Corinthians II, 27 and in Skeireins 41, 21; 43, 3; 46, 14; 47, 6, but incorrectly.]

Jesus said to them, “If you were blind, you would not have sin; but now you say, ‘We see’; therefore your sin remains.”

“Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever does not enter through the door into the sheepfold, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber.” [Note: [Col. 0679] “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever does not enter through the door into the sheepfold, but climbs in elsewhere, is a thief and a robber.”] [Note: [Col. 0680] *daur*] St. adds *dauk*, as in the following verse.

“But the one who enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep.” [Note: [Col. 0680] *daur*] See the note on verse 1.

“To him the doorkeeper opens, and the sheep hear his voice; he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.” [Note: [Col. 0679] “The doorkeeper opens to him, and these sheep hear his voice; he calls these own sheep by name and leads them out.”] [Note: [Col. 0680] *stibnai*] J. and St. add *stibna*.

“When he has brought out his own sheep, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, because they know his voice.” [Note: [Col. 0679] “And when he leads out his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, because they know his voice.”] [Note: [Col. 0680] *svesona*] Ulfilas has the Greek πρόβατα, “sheep.”

“They will not follow a stranger, but will flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers.” [Note: [Col. 0679] “But they do not follow a stranger; rather, they flee from him, because they do not know the voice of these strangers.”]

Jesus spoke this parable to them, but they did not understand what it was that he had said to them. [Note: [Col. 0679] “Jesus spoke this parable to them, but they did not understand what it was that he said to them.”]

Then Jesus said to them again, “Amen, amen, I say to you: I am the door of the sheep. All, as many as came, are thieves and robbers; but the sheep did not listen to them.” [Note: [Col. 0680] *ïm*] A secondary reading; J. adds *am*. [Note: [Col. 0679] “All who came before me are thieves and robbers; but the sheep did not listen to them.”].”] [Note: [Col. 0680] *sve*] Ulfilas and certain codices have the Greek πρὸ ἐμοῦ, “before me.”]

“I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will enter and go out and find pasture.” [Note: [Col. 0681] “I am this door; through me, if anyone enters, he will be safe, and he will enter and go out and find pasture.”] [Note: [Col. 0681] *ïnngaggiþ*] A secondary reading; St. adds *ïngaggiþ*.

“A thief comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy; but I came so that they may have life and have it more abundantly.” [Note: [Col. 0681] *ïþ*] “but”; the Greek, as at VI, 58.

“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” [Note: [Col. 0681] *faur*] J. and St. add *faura*, as also in verse 15.

“The hired man, who is not the shepherd and whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees; and the wolf seizes them and scatters the sheep.” [Note: [Col. 0681] “But the hired man flees, because he is a hired man and does not care about the sheep.”] [Note: [Col. 0681] *þliuþiþ*] St. adds *tliuhiþ*.

“[Note: [Col. 0681] *kar-ïst*]*] By elision for *kara ïst*; compare XII, 6. Likewise *þat-ïst*, *þat-ain*, and *nist* stand for *þata ïst*, *þata ain*, and *ni ïst*. Ulfilas often uses *kara* alone, omitting the substantive verb; see Matthew XXVII, 4; Mark IV, 38; XII, 14.]

“I am the good shepherd, and I know my own, and my own know me,” [Note: [Col. 0681] “I am the good shepherd, and I know mine, and these mine know me.”] [Note: [Col. 0681] *kunnun—meina*] “know—mine”; the Greek is γιγνώσκομαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἐμῶν, “I am known by my own”; otherwise J. and St. add *kunnon*.

“just as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep.” [Note: [Col. 0681] “As the Father knows me and I know the Father, and I lay down my life for these sheep.”] [Note: [Col. 0681] *faur*] See the note on verse 11.

“And I have other sheep, which are not of this fold; these too I must bring, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock and one shepherd.” [Note: [Col. 0681] “And I have other sheep that are not of this sheepfold, and these I must lead; they hear my voice and become one flock, one shepherd.”] [Note: [Col. 0681] *þis avistris*] So in the Argenteus codex; J. adds *þiza vistris*, St. *þisa vistris*. [Note: [Col. 0681] *ain aveþi*] J. and St., with B.’s approval, add *aina veþi*. *Aveþi*, already shown by Lh. to be correct, is now confirmed by 1 Corinthians IX, 7; this also proves Schulz wrong when he says that Ulfilas read αὐλή, “fold,” instead of ποίμνη, “flock.” There too *aveþi* means “flock.”]

“For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life so that I may take it up again.” [Note: [Col. 0681] “Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life so that I may take it up again.”]

“No one takes it from me by himself; I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. I received this command from my Father.” [Note: [Col. 0681] “No one takes it from me by himself; I have authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again. I received this command from my Father.”] [Note: [Col. 0681] *mis silbin*] “by myself.” It would be natural to think that Ulfilas and the other codices omitted ἀλλ’ ἐμαυτοῦ, “but of myself”; yet *mis silbin* shows that this is not so, since it corresponds to the Greek ἐμαυτοῦ, not ἐμοῦ. Nor would *mis silbin* by itself yield a satisfactory sense. Rather, the copyist should be thought to have skipped from *þo af mis* to *þo af mis silbin*, omitting *af mis* in “not from me, but I lay it down” (ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ, ἀλλ’ ἐγὼ τίθημι αὐτήν); see the note on Romans IX, 15. Z. came very close to the truth. The lacuna marked by St. after *þo* has no trace in the Argenteus codex. [Note: [Col. 0682] *at*] J., St., and B. add *bi*.

“For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life so that I may take it up again. No one takes it from me by himself; I have authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again. This command I received from my Father.”

Again disagreement arose among the Jews because of these words. [Note: [Col. 0681] “Many of them said, ‘He has a demon and is insane. Why do you listen to him?’”] [Note: [Col. 0682] *qeþunuh*] “and they said”; the Greek is ἔλεγον δέ. Although, in agreement with the Latin versions, Ulfilas could have read καί, to which *-uh* aptly corresponds, the evidence of the codices makes it seem that he read οὖν; see XVI, 18, where *qeþunuh* corresponds to ἔλεγον οὖν.]

Some of them said, “These words are not those of one who has a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?” [Note: [Col. 0681] “Some said, ‘These words are not those of one who has a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?’”] [Note: [Col. 0682] *mag unhulþo*] Corresponds to the Greek in all manuscripts except codex 235.

There was then a renewal in Jerusalem, and it was winter. [Note: [Col. 0681] “There was a feast of renewal in Jerusalem, and it was winter.”] [Note: [Col. 0682] *ubizvai*] The Argenteus codex, by a later hand, adds *ubizali*.

Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s portico. [Note: [Col. 0681] “And Jesus was walking in the temple in Solomon’s portico.”]

Then the Jews surrounded him and said to him, “How long will you keep our soul in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us openly.” [Note: [Col. 0681] “Then the Jews surrounded him and said to him, ‘How long will you keep our soul in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us openly.’”]

Jesus answered, “I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name, these testify about me.” [Note: [Col. 0681] “Jesus answered, ‘I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name testify about me.’”] [Note: [Col. 0682] *andhof*] Ulfilas has the Greek αὐτοῖς, “to them.”

“But you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep, as I told you.” [Note: [Col. 0681] “But you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep, as I told you.”]

“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” [Note: [Col. 0681] “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.”] [Note: [Col. 0682] *meinai*] B. adds *meina*.

“And I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, and no one will snatch them from my hand.” [Note: [Col. 0681] “And I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them from my hand.”]

““What my Father gave me is greater than all, and no one can snatch them from the hand of my Father.” [Note: [Col. 0682] *þatei—maizo*]*] “which—greater”; the Greek has ὅς—μείζων. Gothic codex L and the Latin Fathers and Vulgate have the corresponding reading. [Note: [Col. 0682] *ni aiv*] J., St., and B. add *jct.*; otherwise *aiv*, “ever,” is found in all the Greek manuscripts. [Note: [Col. 0682] *þo*] “them”; so the Greek.]

“I and the Father are one.” [Note: [Col. 0682] *meins*] “my”; so the Greek. [Note: [Col. 0682] *siju*] So in the Argenteus codex; the editions have *sijum*. It is the first-person dual number required by the sense, as below at XVII, 22; compare the note on Mark X, 39; see Grimm I, 840, 1.]

Again the Jews took up stones to throw at him. [Note: [Col. 0683] “Again the Jews took up stones in order to throw them at him.”] [Note: [Col. 0682] *nemun*] Ulfilas and the other codices have the Greek οὖν, “then.”]

Jesus answered them, “I have shown you many good works from my Father. For which of these works are you stoning me?” [Note: [Col. 0683] “Jesus answered them, ‘I have shown you many good works from my Father. For which of these works are you stoning me?’”] [Note: [Col. 0683] *ïm*] J., St., and B. add *him*.

The Jews answered him, “We are not stoning you for a good work, but for blasphemy, and because you, being a man, make yourself God.” [Note: [Col. 0683] *ïudaieis*] Ulfilas and the codex have the Greek λέγοντες, “saying.”

Jesus answered them, “Is it not written in your law, ‘I said, You are gods’?” [Note: [Col. 0683] “Jesus answered them, ‘Is it not written in your law: I said, You are gods?’”]

“If he called them gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be annulled—” [Note: [Col. 0683] *þaimei*] J. and St. add *þammei*.

“then concerning the one whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, do you say, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” [Note: [Col. 0683] *vajamerjau*] “I blaspheme”; the Greek is βλασφημεῖς, “you blaspheme,” in Ulfilas and the codex cited by Mi.]

““Unless I do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, even if you do not believe me, believe the works, so that you may know and believe that the Father is in me and I am in him.” [Note: [Col. 0683] *niba*]*] Do not expect *jabai ni*, “if not”; Gothic elsewhere regularly renders the Greek εἰ οὐ in this way; see Mark XI, 26; Luke XVI, 11 and following; 1 Corinthians XV, 13; XVI, 32; or *þande ni* at John V, 47. *Niba* corresponds to εἰ μή, “unless.”] [Note: [Col. 0683] *niba mis*] “unless me”; all the Greek manuscripts have κἄν μοι μή (οὐ). [Note: [Col. 0683] *þaim vaurstvam galaubjaiþ*] Hertz adds *galaubjaiþ*; St. adds *ufkunnaiþ*.]

Again they sought to seize him, but he escaped from their hands. [Note: [Col. 0683] “They sought again to seize him, and he went out from their hands.”] [Note: [Col. 0683] *sokidedun*] Ulfilas and the codex have the Greek οὖν, “then.” [Note: [Col. 0683] *ïna aftra*] Corresponds to the Greek. [Note: [Col. 0683] *handum*] “hands”; all the Greek manuscripts except codex q cited by Mi. have the singular χειρός.]

And he went away again across the Jordan, to the place where John had first been baptizing, and he remained there. [Note: [Col. 0683] *þarei*] St. adds *þatei*. [Note: [Col. 0683] *jainar*] St. adds *jainak*.

Many came to him and said, “John performed no sign, but everything John said about this man was true.” [Note: [Col. 0683] *ïohannes*] The first form; Ulfilas and the other codices have the Greek μέν, “indeed.” [Note: [Col. 0683] *gatavida taikne*] Corresponds to the Greek.]

And many believed in him there. [Note: [Col. 0683] *galaubidedun*] St. adds *galaubitedun*. [Note: [Col. 0683] *jainar*] The Greek places it before *du*, “to.”

There was a certain sick man, Lazarus of Bethany, from the village of Mary and Martha, her sister. [Note: [Col. 0683] *beþanias*] See the note on Matthew XXVII, 57. [Note: [Col. 0684] *svistrs*] St. adds *svisttrs*.

It was Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair; her brother Lazarus was sick. [Note: [Col. 0683] “Mary was the one who anointed the Lord with perfume and wiped his feet with her hair; her brother Lazarus was sick.”] [Note: [Col. 0684] *fraujan*] J., St., and B. add *fraujin*.

Then his sisters sent to him, saying, “Lord, behold, the one whom you love is sick.”.” [Note: [Col. 0684] *ïs*] “his”; so the Greek.]

But when Jesus heard it, he said, “This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.” [Note: [Col. 0683] “But when he heard it, he said, ‘This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.’”] [Note: [Col. 0684] *ïs*] “he”; so the Argenteus codex and the editions, while all the Greek manuscripts have Ἰησοῦς, “Jesus.” See the note on Mark I, 42. [Note: [Col. 0684] *so*] “this”; Sch. wrongly observes that Ulfilas omits αὕτη, “this.” [Note: [Col. 0684] *þairh þata*] “through this”; all the Greek manuscripts have δι’ αὐτῆς, understood as “through this sickness.” One might expect *þairh þo*, understood as “through the sickness,” but Gothic refers it to the sense of the whole sentence.]

Now Jesus loved Martha, her sister, and Lazarus. [Note: [Col. 0683] “Jesus loved Martha, her sister, and Lazarus.”]

When he heard that he was sick, then he remained in the place where he was for two days. [Note: [Col. 0684] *sve*] Ulfilas has the Greek οὖν, “then.” [Note: [Col. 0684] *þan*] St. adds *þans*.

Then, after this, he said to the disciples, “Let us go again into Judea.” [Note: [Col. 0683] “Then after this he said to the disciples, ‘Let us go again into Judea.’”]

The disciples said to him, “Rabbi, the Jews were just seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?” [Note: [Col. 0684] *þai*] St. omits it.

Jesus answered, “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world.” [Note: [Col. 0683] “Jesus answered, ‘Are there not twelve hours of the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world.’”] [Note: [Col. 0684] *ïn dag*] “in the day”; all the Greek manuscripts have ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ, which in Gothic would be *ïn daga*; see Romans XIII, 13; compare the note on Ephesians VI, 18.]

“But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.” [Note: [Col. 0683] “But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.”]

He said this, and after this he said to them, “Lazarus, our friend, has fallen asleep, but let us go to awaken him.” [Note: [Col. 0683] “He said this, and after this he said to them, ‘Lazarus, our friend, has fallen asleep, but let us go to awaken him.’”] [Note: [Col. 0684] *gaggam*] “let us go”; all the Greek manuscripts have πορεύομαι, “I go.” Elsewhere *gaggam* generally corresponds to the Greek ἄγωμεν, “let us go.”]

Then his disciples said, “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover.” [Note: [Col. 0683] “Then his disciples said, ‘Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will become well.’”] [Note: [Col. 0684] *slepiþ*] See the note on Matthew IX, 24.

But Jesus was speaking about his death, while they thought that he was speaking about ordinary sleep. [Note: [Col. 0685] “But Jesus spoke about his death, while they thought that he was speaking about sleep.”] [Note: [Col. 0685] *ïs*] A secondary reading; “he,” as in all the Greek manuscripts. [Note: [Col. 0685] *bi slep*] “about sleep”; all the Greek manuscripts have περὶ τῆς κοιμήσεως τοῦ ὕπνου, “about the sleep of sleep.” A later hand in the Argenteus codex absurdly changed *slep* to *saeun*; see the note on Matthew IX, 24.]

Then Jesus said to them plainly, “Lazarus has died,” [Note: [Col. 0685] “Then Jesus said to them plainly, ‘Lazarus has died.’”] “and I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe, because I was not there; but let us go to him.”

Then Thomas, who is called Didymus, said to his fellow disciples, “Let us also go, so that we may die with him.” [Note: [Col. 0685] “Then Thomas, who is called Didymus, said to his fellow disciples, ‘Let us also go, so that we may die with him.’”] [Note: [Col. 0685] *seinaim*] “his”; so the Greek.

When Jesus came, he found that he had already been four days in the tomb. [Note: [Col. 0685] *juþan*] The Greek places it after “days.”

Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away. [Note: [Col. 0685] *ïairusaulymiam*] So in the Argenteus codex, B., and Z.; J. and St. add *pro ïairusaulymim*; J. and St. add *ïairusaulmiam*.

Many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother. [Note: [Col. 0685] “Many Jews had gathered around Martha and Mary in order to console them concerning their brother.”] [Note: [Col. 0685] *gaqemun bi*] “had gathered around”; some Greek manuscripts have ἐληλύθεισαν πρὸς τὰς περί, others ἐληλύθεισαν πρός. Ulfilas seems to have followed neither, but to have read συνεληλύθεισαν περί, “had gathered around,” or else he did not correctly understand the Greek sense.]

Martha, as soon as she heard that Jesus was coming, went to meet him; but Mary sat in the house. [Note: [Col. 0685] “But Martha, as soon as she heard that Jesus had come, went to meet him; Mary, however, sat in the house.”] [Note: [Col. 0685] *garda*] Ulfilas and the other codices have καί, “and.” [Note: [Col. 0686] *greitai*] Hertz omits it.

Then Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.” [Note: [Col. 0685] “Then Martha said to Jesus, ‘Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.’”] [Note: [Col. 0685] *ïesua*] St. adds *ïaisuna*. [Note: [Col. 0685] *gadauþnodedi*] St. adds *gadauþnodedei*. [Note: [Col. 0685] *broþar meins*] The Greek places it before “not.”]

“But even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.” [Note: [Col. 0685] “But even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God gives you.”]

Jesus said to her, “Your brother will rise.” [Note: [Col. 0685] “Jesus said to her, ‘Your brother will rise.’”]
