It is feminine, as in all related languages (Grimm III, 463), and belongs to nouns preserving the nominative form in the genitive (Grimm I, 610, 2). Here it is the genitive customarily called partitive; so XI, 28, *þis hlaibis matjai*, and J. VI, 26 and 50. In all these passages, including this one, Greek adds ἐκ.] Or do only I and Barnabas lack authority not to work? Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not eat milk from the flock?

[Note: [Col. 0735] “Do I say these things according to a human being, or does not the Law also say them?”] [Note: [Col. 0735] *mannan*: thus manuscript A; Cast. reads *manna*.] [Note: [Col. 0735] *aiþþau*: Gothic omits οὐχί; by omitting that particle it has dealt badly with the sense. There are manuscripts which omit it too, but they have εἰ, “if,” in its place.] Do I say these things according to a human being, or does not the Law also say them?

[Note: [Col. 0735] “For it is written in the Law of Moses: ‘You shall not muzzle an ox while threshing’; is it not because of oxen—”] [Note: [Col. 0735] *vitoda*: Greek places it after *mosezis*.] [Note: [Col. 0735] *þriskaidai*: Cast. asserts that this is written in manuscript A. First, however, it wrongly has a passive form for an active; secondly, if a passive could be admitted, another participial form, *þruskans* (see Grimm II, 40 and III, 431), would be necessary; finally, because *auhsus*, “ox,” is masculine, the adjective ought to be of the same gender. In sum, *þriskandin* should be written. In the margin of manuscript A traces of a variant reading are visible: “.. s munþ a..þr..,” [Col. 0736] which Cast. thinks should be completed from I Tim. V, 18: *ni faurvaipjais munþ auhsau þriskandin*, “you shall not muzzle the mouth of an ox while it is threshing.” Since Cast. omitted *-andin* because of an erasure in the parchment, we have supplied it.] [Note: [Col. 0736] *þatei*: “that”; omitted in Greek throughout.] [Note: [Col. 0736] *auhsum*: thus manuscript A; Cast. reads *auhsun*.] For it is written in the Law of Moses: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing.” Is it not because he is concerned about oxen—[lacuna]

[Note: [Col. 0735] “—that I might gain the more.”] [Note: [Col. 0736] *gageigaidedjau*: manuscript A’s margin has *gastaistaldjau*, “that I might acquire/possess.”]—that I might gain the more.

[Note: [Col. 0735] “And I became to the Jews as a Jew, that I might gain Jews; to those under law as under law, though I myself was not under law but under grace, that I might gain those under law.”] [Note: [Col. 0736] *gageigaidedjau*: manuscript A and Cast. have *gageigaidau*.] [Note: [Col. 0736] *ak uf anstai*: “but under grace,” omitted in Greek throughout; Gothic agrees with Augustine, according to Mill.] [Note: [Col. 0736] *gageiggaidedjau*: thus manuscript A, as in vv. 21 and 22.] And I became to Jews as a Jew, that I might gain Jews; to those under law as under law, though I myself was not under law but under grace, that I might gain those under law.

[Note: [Col. 0735] “To those without law as without law, though not without God’s law, but in Christ’s law, that I might gain those without law.”] [Note: [Col. 0736] *vitodis laus*: Cast. omits it in *jct.*] [Note: [Col. 0736] *ïn vitoþ*: “into the law”; *ïn vitoda*, “in the law,” ought to have been said.] [Note: [Col. 0736] *gageiggau*: manuscript A’s margin has *gavandidedjau*, “that I might convert.”] To those without law as without law, though not without God’s law but in Christ’s law, that I might gain those without law.

[Note: [Col. 0735] “I became weak to the weak, that I might gain the weak; I became all things to all, that I might perhaps save some.”] [Note: [Col. 0736] *waiva*: perhaps; Greek throughout has πάντως, “altogether/by all means.” The marginal reading *vaila*, “well,” does not answer the Greek word more suitably. The translator of *waiva* undoubtedly read πῶς, “how,” in his manuscript for πάντως; compare Rom. II, 14.] I became weak to the weak, that I might gain the weak. I became all things to all, that I might perhaps save some.

[Note: [Col. 0735] “But I do this for the Gospel’s sake, that I may become a sharer in it.”] I do this for the Gospel’s sake, that I may become a sharer in it.

[Note: [Col. 0735] “Do you not know that those running in a stadium all run, but one receives the prize? Run thus, that you may attain it.”] [Note: [Col. 0736] *spraud*: thus manuscript A, by transposition of letters for *spaurd*; see J. VI, 19; XI, 18.] [Note: [Col. 0736] *allai*: Gothic omits μέν, “indeed.”] Do you not know that those running in a stadium all run, but one receives the prize? Run thus, that you may attain it.

[Note: [Col. 0735] “But everyone who competes restrains himself in all things; they indeed do so to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one.”] [Note: [Col. 0736] *haifstjan sniviþ*: “strives in contest”; Greek throughout has ἀγωνιζόμενος. Ulfilas similarly uses a fuller mode of expression at J. XII, 18, *ïddjedun gamotjan*, “they went to meet,” for ὑπήντησεν; XIII, 38, *afaikis kunnan*, “you will know denial,” for ἀπαρνήσῃ; and at Mc. XII, 4, *gaaiviskodedun jah haubiþ vundan brahtedun*, “they treated shamefully and brought back with a wounded head,” for ἐκεφαλαίωσαν. Below, XV, 10, *arbaidida jah usaivida*, “I laboured and toiled,” for ἐκοπίασα; Phil. III, 16, *ei samo hugjaima jah samo fraþjaima*, “that we may think and understand the same,” for τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν. Compare the notes on M. IX, 8 and 23.] [Note: [Col. 0736] *gaþarbiþ*: Grimm IV, 31 suspects that *gaþarbaiþ* should be read, and we cannot but agree; compare I Tim. IV, 3.] [Note: [Col. 0736] *eis*: Gothic, with the manuscripts, has οὖν, “therefore.”] But everyone who strives in contest restrains himself in all things. They indeed do so to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one.

[Note: [Col. 0735] “But I run thus, not toward an uncertain goal; I fight thus, not as [Col. 0737] one beating the air.”] [Note: [Col. 0736] *rinna*: Gothic omits ὡς, “as.”] [Note: [Col. 0736] *ni sve*: corresponding to Greek throughout.] But I now run thus, not toward an uncertain goal; I fight thus, not as one beating the air.

[Col. 0737] [Note: [Col. 0737] “but I discipline my body and enslave it, lest, after preaching to others, I myself become rejected.”] [Note: [Col. 0737] *leik mein*: corresponding to Greek throughout.] [Note: [Col. 0737] *vlizja*: Greek throughout places it before *leik*.] But I discipline my body and enslave it, lest, after preaching to others, I myself become rejected.

[Note: [Col. 0737] “I do not wish you, brothers, to be ignorant that our fathers all were under the cloud and all passed through the sea.”] [Note: [Col. 0737] *viljau*: Gothic omits γάρ, “for.”] I do not wish you, brothers, to be ignorant that our fathers all were under the cloud and all passed through the sea.

[Note: [Col. 0737] “And all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.”] [Note: [Col. 0737] “And all ate the same spiritual food.”] And all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food,

[Note: [Col. 0737] “and all drank the same spiritual drink—”] [Note: [Col. 0737] *jah*: Gothic, with codex 2 in Mill, omits πάντες, “all.”] and all drank the same spiritual drink—[lacuna]

[Note: [Col. 0737] “—I speak to sensible persons; judge for yourselves what I say.”] [Note: [Col. 0737] *..daim*: a fragment of the word *frodaim*, “to sensible persons,” correctly supplied by Cast.]—I speak to sensible persons; judge for yourselves what I say.

[Note: [Col. 0737] “The cup of blessing which we bless—is it not a communion in the Lord’s blood? It interpreted παρὰ τοῦτο, although that expression nevertheless has a definite meaning, as though τὸ σῶμα, “the body,” had to be supplied, and begins the question only with *nist*. [Col. 0743–0744] **þau [fif hundam] taihun tevjam**] Castiglione adds *þan*. No one can doubt that the gloss here has been introduced into the text. Since Gothic, imitating the indefinite Greek number πεντακοσίοις, rendered it by *taihun tevjam*, that is, “ten companies” or “ten divisions” (compare verse 23 below, where *teva* = τάγμα), the glossator, translating πεντακοσίοις literally or explaining *taihun tevjam*, added *fifhundam*, “five hundred,” in the margin. This gloss was later inserted into the text by the copyist of manuscript A. Mssm., writing *fif hundamtahiun-tevjam* and using the form *tevis* (“regular”; *Skeireins* Glossary, p. 166), confesses that we do not know what he intended—unless perhaps he meant ordinary disciples, that is, persons duly admitted to the number of disciples. Otherwise, what do those who are baptized for the dead accomplish, if the dead do not rise at all? Why, then, are they baptized for them? [Note: [Col. 0745] “Why, then, are we in danger every hour?”] [Note: [Col. 0746] *daupjandans*: an active form here receives a somewhat passive sense, “having themselves baptized,” as in the immediately following *daupjand*; cf. Mark 7:4, where *daupjan* means “to be baptized,” “to wash oneself”; similarly Galatians 5:2, *bimaitiþ*, “you have yourselves circumcised.”—*þau*: this and the following verse answer the Greek *καί* used in the question.]

Why, then, are we in danger every hour? Daily I die, by the boast I have in Christ Jesus our Lord. [Note: [Col. 0745] “I die every day because of your glory, brothers, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord.”] [Note: [Col. 0746] *gasviltandans*: “dying,” Greek *ἀποθνήσκω*.—*ïn*: “because of,” Greek *νή*.—*broþrjus*: “brothers,” as in the Greek witness.]

If, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what benefit is it to me? If the dead do not rise, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” [Note: [Col. 0745] “Do not be deceived: evil conversations corrupt good morals.”] [Note: [Col. 0746] *riurjand*: Codex A has in the margin *fravardjand* (“they destroy”); this is how *fravaurdjand* should be read, rather than the form *fravaurkjand*, which Cast. printed incorrectly from a place he says was entirely obliterated; see II, IV, 16; VII, 2.]

Do not be deceived. Evil company corrupts good morals. Wake up properly and do not sin. Some have no knowledge of God; I say this to your shame. [Note: [Col. 0745] “Be rightly sober and do not sin; for some have ignorance of God. I speak this to your shame.”] [Note: [Col. 0746] *unkunþi*: Gothic, corresponding to the Greek *γάρ* (“for”).]

But someone says: “How are the dead raised? [lacuna] spiritual.” [Note: [Col. 0747] “—spiritual.”] [Note: [Col. 0747] “This first man is from the earth, dusty; this second man is the Lord from heaven.”] [Note: [Col. 0747] *fruma*: thus Codex A; Cast. adds *frums*.] The first man was from the earth, made of dust; the second man was the Lord from heaven.. As was the man of dust, so also are those of dust; and as is the heavenly man, so also are those who are heavenly. [Note: [Col. 0747] “As is the man of dust, so also are those of dust; and as is the heavenly man, so also are those who are heavenly.”] [Note: [Col. 0747] *muldeinans*: Gothic, with Codex I according to Mi., corresponding to the Greek *καί* (“also”).—*wileiks*: the second witness; Codex B begins here.]

And just as we have borne the image of the earthly, so let us also bear the image of the heavenly. [Note: [Col. 0747] “And just as we have borne the image of the earthly, so let us also bear the image of the heavenly.”] [Note: [Col. 0747] *manleikan*: thus Codex B; Codex A has *mannleikan*.—*sva*: “so,” as Codex A and all the Greek witnesses.]

Now this I say, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does corruption inherit incorruption. [Note: [Col. 0747] “For this I say, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does corruption inherit incorruption.”]

Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall not all die, but we shall all be changed. [Note: [Col. 0747] “Behold, I tell you a mystery: for we shall not all die, but we shall all be changed.”]

In an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed. [Note: [Col. 0747] “In an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet; for the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.”]

For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality. [Note: [Col. 0747] “For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality.”] [Note: [Col. 0747] *ïst auk*: “for it is”; so Codex A.]

When this corruptible body has put on incorruption and this mortal body has put on immortality, then the word that is written will come to pass: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.” [Note: [Col. 0747] “When this mortal body has put on immortality, then this word that is written comes to pass: Death has been swallowed up in victory.”] [Note: [Col. 0747] *þanuþ—undivanein*: Codex B has this reading; otherwise Codex A, together with the other witnesses, has the Greek *τὸ φθαρτὸν … καί*. On this omission see the note on Romans 9:15; on *þanuþþan*, see the note on Matthew 9:25; and on *gavasjada*, see the note on John 13:35.—*ufsaggqiþs*: Codex A has *ufsagqiþs*.]

“Where is your sting, O death? Where is your victory, O Hades?” [Note: [Col. 0747] “Where is your sting, O death? Where is your victory, O Hades?”] [Note: [Col. 0747] *ïst*: “is,” in both witnesses and all the Greek manuscripts.—*gazds*: all the Greek witnesses place it after *dauþu* (“death”); likewise shortly afterward *sigis* (“victory”) follows *halja* (“Hades”).—*dauþu*: instead of *dauþau*; see the note on Luke 18:38.]

The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. [Note: [Col. 0747] “The sting of death is sin, but the power of sin is the law.”]

But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. [Note: [Col. 0747] “Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.”] [Note: [Col. 0747] *aviliuþ*: Codex A has *aviliud*.—*ïzei*: Codex A has *ïze*; compare the note on Luke 3:5.—*xristu*: Codex A has *xristau*; concerning this variation see the note on Mark 7:32. Codex B, in the margin, has *sihv*, whose significance neither Cast. nor we have been able to determine; see nevertheless the Prolegomena, p. +.]

Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not in vain in the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0747] *nu*: see the note on XIV, 22.—*vairþaiþ*: Codex A has *vairþiþ* (“become”).]

Now concerning the collection for the saints: as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also must do. [Note: [Col. 0747] “Now concerning the collection for the saints: as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also must do.”] [Note: [Col. 0747] *galatiais*: Codex A has *galatie* (“of the Galatians”).]

On the first day of every week, let each of you set something aside privately, considering what he wishes, so that collections will not take place when I come.. [Note: [Col. 0747] “On the first day of every week, let each of you set aside privately, storing up whatever he wishes, so that there will be no collection when I come.”] [Note: [Col. 0747] *taujai*: Codex A has *lagjai* (“let him place”).—*huhjands*: thus the codices and Cast. for *huzdjands* (“storing up,” Greek *θησαυρίζων*).—*vairþai*: Cast. adds *vairþli*.]

And when I arrive, I will send those whom you approve by letters to carry your gift to Jerusalem. [Note: [Col. 0747] “And when I come, those whom you approve I will send by letters to carry your gift to Jerusalem.”]

But if it is worthwhile for me to go, they will go with me. [Note: [Col. 0747] “And if it is worthwhile for me to go, they will go with me.”] [Note: [Col. 0748] *mis vairþ*: so in all the Greek witnesses; otherwise Gothic *jah* corresponds to the *καί* in *κἀμέ* (“and me”); compare the note on X, 33.—*galeiþand*: all the Greek witnesses place it after *mis* (“with me”).]

But I will come to you after passing through Macedonia—for I am passing through Macedonia—and perhaps I will remain with you, or even spend the winter, so that you may send me wherever I may go. [Note: [Col. 0747] “But I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia; for I am passing through Macedonia.”] [Note: [Col. 0748] *auk*: Codex B has the Greek witness.]

For I do not want to see you now merely in passing, since I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits. [Note: [Col. 0747] “For I do not want to see you now merely in passing, since I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits.”] [Note: [Col. 0748] *vaitei*: Cast. adds *div*. This learned man did not sufficiently grasp the meaning of the word, for he thinks that *ni* has been omitted so as to produce the sense “I do not know whether,” whereas it seems to have been spoken elliptically in the sense “God knows whether,” that is, “perhaps”; compare John 18:35 and the particle *vainei*.—*þiswaduh*: Cast. adds *bis div*.—*þe*: Codex A has *þei*; compare the note on Luke 10:5.—*ïk*: “I,” as in all the Greek witnesses.]

I will remain in Ephesus until Pentecost, for a great and effective door has opened to me, and there are many adversaries. [Note: [Col. 0747] “But I will remain in Ephesus until Pentecost, for a great and effective door has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.”] [Note: [Col. 0748] *venja*: Codex A adds *venjan*.—*wo weilo*: corresponding to the Greek; Gothic, together with Codices 2 and 7 according to Mi.]

If Timothy comes, see that he is without fear among you, for he is doing the work of the Lord just as I am. [Note: [Col. 0747] “If Timothy comes, see that he is without fear among you, for he is doing the work of the Lord just as I am.”] [Note: [Col. 0748] *saiwaiþ*: Codex A has *saiwiþ* (“see”).—*unagands*: Codex A adds *unagans*; compare the note on Mark 12:24.]

Therefore let no one despise him. Send him on his way in peace, so that he may come to me; for I am awaiting him with the brothers. [Note: [Col. 0747] “Let no one despise him, but send him on his way in peace, so that he may come to me; for I am awaiting him with the brothers.”] [Note: [Col. 0748] *washun*: Gothic, with the Greek witness *οὖν* (“therefore”).—*ïþ*: from here through the end of verse 22, the corresponding material is absent from Codex A.]

Now concerning our brother Apollos: I urged him strongly to come to you with the brothers, but he was not at all willing to come now. He will come when he has an opportunity. [Note: [Col. 0747] “Now concerning Apollos, this brother: I inform you that I urged him strongly to come to you with the brothers, but perhaps it was not his will to come now. He will come when he has an opportunity.”] [Note: [Col. 0748] *bandvja ïzvis þatei*: “I inform you that,” as in the Greek witness.—*ïna bad*: corresponding to all the Greek witnesses.—*ïs*: “he,” as in all the Greek witnesses.]

Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act courageously, be strong. [Note: [Col. 0749] “Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act courageously, be strong.”] [Note: [Col. 0749] *standaiduh*: “stand firm.” The Gothic, not imitating the Greek asyndeton, joins these imperatives by attaching the particle *uh*, just as above in XI, 23 (*nimiþ matjiþ*); compare Mark 2:11 and John 18:26. Likewise Matthew 27:65 has *gaggiþ vitaiduh* (“go, secure it”).]

Let all that is yours be done in love.. [Note: [Col. 0749] “Let everything you do be done in love.”] [Note: [Col. 0749] *vairþai*: Cast. adds *vairþa*.]

I urge you, brothers—you know the household of Stephanas, that it is the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have appointed themselves for service to the saints. [Note: [Col. 0749] “I urge you, brothers: you know the household of Stephanas, that they are the firstfruits of Achaia and have appointed themselves for service to the saints.”] [Note: [Col. 0749] *bidja*: Gothic, with the Greek witness *δέ* (“but”).—*sind*: “are,” as in all the Greek witnesses, *ἐστί*. Here Gothic already uses a plural verb with the collective noun, whereas the Greek does so only later.—*akaije*: see the note on II, I, 1.]

Submit yourselves also to such people and to everyone who works and labors with them. [Note: [Col. 0749] “So that you also may now submit yourselves to such people and to all these workers and laborers.”] [Note: [Col. 0749] *nu*: “therefore,” as in all the Greek witnesses.]

I rejoice at the arrival of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, because they have supplied what was lacking on your part. [Note: [Col. 0749] “But I rejoice at the arrival of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, because they have supplied what was lacking on your part.”]

For they have refreshed my spirit and yours. Therefore acknowledge such people. [Note: [Col. 0749] “For they have refreshed both my spirit and yours. Therefore acknowledge such people.”] [Note: [Col. 0749] *jah*: the first witness has “and,” corresponding to the Greek.—*ïzvara*: either a scribal error or Cast.’s error for *ïzvarana*. It cannot be taken as the genitive plural in the Greek manner, since the usage of the Gothic language does not permit this.]

The churches of Asia greet you. Aquila and Prisca greet you warmly in the Lord, together with the church in their house, where I also stay. [Note: [Col. 0749] “The churches of Asia greet you; Aquila and Prisca greet you warmly in the Lord, together with the church in their house, where I also stay.”] [Note: [Col. 0750] *goleiþ*: “greets,” corresponding to the Greek *ἀσπάζονται*, except in Codex G according to Mi.—*priska*: Greek *πρίσκιλλα*.—*at—salja*: “with whom I stay,” as in the Greek witness.]

Greet one another with a holy kiss.. [Note: [Col. 0749] “Greet one another with a holy kiss.”] [Note: [Col. 0750] At the beginning, Gothic corresponds to the Greek *ἀσπάζονται … πάντες* (“all greet”).]

The greeting is in my own hand—Paul’s. If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed. Maranatha. [Note: [Col. 0749] “My greeting in the hand of Paul. If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed. Maranatha.”] [Note: [Col. 0750] *xristu*: Gothic corresponds to the Greek *ἤτω* (“let him be”).]

My love is with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen. [Note: [Col. 0749] “The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you.”] [Note: [Col. 0750] *ïesuis*: Gothic, with the codex, corresponds to the Greek *Χριστοῦ*. Subscription: the second codex.]

To the Corinthians, First; it ends. [Note: [Col. 0749] “To the Corinthians, First; it ends”: Gothic, with the other codices, including D, F, and G.—“To the Corinthians, first … Philippi”: the codices with which the Gothic usually agrees add various other statements concerning these matters. Concerning the form *frume*—thus it is read in Codex A, not *fruma*, as Cast. incorrectly printed—in place of *frumei*, see the note on Luke 10:5. *silbons*, since it refers to *apaustaulaus*, is a solecism in place of *silbins*.—*sve … asiai*: “as … Asia,” as in all the Greek witnesses.] [Note: [Col. 0749] “My love is with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen.”]

*.

[The First Epistle] to the Corinthians ends.

The First [Epistle] to the Corinthians was written from Philippi, as some have said; but it seems more likely, according to the apostle’s own testimony, to have been written from Asia.

] Anathema. Maranatha. The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen.

To the Corinthians, First, ended. The First [Epistle] to the Corinthians was written from Philippi, as some have said; but it seems more likely, according to the apostle’s own testimony, to have been written from Asia.

**TO THE CORINTHIANS, SECOND, BEGINS.** [Note: [Col. 0749]

This epistle is contained in its entirety in codex B, and for the most part also in codex A.

**Superscription.** *kaurinþaium*: thus here and in the subscription of this epistle, in place of *kaurinþium*, as Cast. correctly noted already; in codex A, where that name occurs, it is written with *i*, and likewise in codex B at VI.11 *kaurinþius* is more correctly written. *kaurinþaius* should not be compared with *ïudaius*, *nazoraius*, and other names based on *-aius*, because Greek forms (Ἰουδαῖος, Ναζοραῖος) preceded those forms. — *anþara*: Gothic, common to the codices; Greek ἐπιστολή (“epistle”). — *dustodeiþ*: “begins,” in all Greek witnesses. In place of *dustodeiþ*, *anastodeiþ* is read in the superscriptions of the Gospels of Mark and Luke and of the Epistle to the Ephesians.]

[Col. 0749]

[Note: [Col. 0749] Paul, apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Timothy the brother, to the church of God which is in Corinth, together with all the saints who are throughout Achaia;] Paul, apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Timothy the brother, to the church of God which is in Corinth, together with all the saints who are throughout all Achaia. [Note: [Col. 0750] “All”: all Greek witnesses place this after “saints.” “Achaia”: codex B thus has *akaijai* for *akajai*; see IX, 2. Likewise at I, XVI, 15, *akaije* is read for *akaje*; see below, XI, 10.]

[Note: [Col. 0749] Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ;] Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0751] Blessed be God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation,] Blessed be God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation,

[Note: [Col. 0751] who comforted us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those in every affliction through the consolation by which we ourselves have been comforted by God.] who comforted us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those in every affliction through that consolation by which we ourselves have been comforted by God.

[Note: [Col. 0751] For just as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so also through Christ our consolation abounds greatly.] [Note: [Col. 0751] *jah* (“also”) is prefixed in all Greek witnesses.] For just as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so also through Christ our consolation abounds greatly.

[Note: [Col. 0751] But whether we are afflicted, it is for your consolation and salvation, effective in endurance of those same sufferings which we too suffer; and our hope for you is firm; or whether we are comforted, it is for your consolation and salvation,] [Note: [Col. 0751] “Whether we are comforted … salvation”: the Greek places “and salvation” before “which is effective.” *Jaþþe gaþrafstjanda. — naseinais*: the Greek has, before *þizos vaurstveigons*, “and salvation.”] But whether we are afflicted, it is for your consolation and salvation, effective in endurance of those same sufferings which we too suffer; and our hope for you is firm; or whether we are comforted, it is for your consolation and salvation,

[Note: [Col. 0751] knowing that, just as you are partners in the sufferings, so also you will become partners in the consolation;] [Note: [Col. 0751] “You are”: all Greek witnesses place this before “endurance”; otherwise Gothic lacks the Greek *οὕτω* (“so”). “You will become”: this is absent from all Greek witnesses.] knowing that, just as you are partners in the sufferings, so also you will become partners in the consolation.

[Note: [Col. 0751] For we do not wish you, brothers, to be ignorant concerning this affliction which happened to us in Asia; for we were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we despaired even of living.] [Note: [Col. 0751] “Ignorant”: literally, “being unknowing,” with *visan* understood. “So that … living”: from this point through IV, 10, *unsaramma* (“our”) is also found in codex A. Codex A reads: *svasve afsvaggvidai veseima jal-liban*, “so that we were uncertain even to live”; “yet another reading is indicated in the margin thus … *maide* … and again lower down in the same margin, *skamaidedeima*.” Castiglione.] For we do not wish you, brothers, to be ignorant concerning this affliction which happened to us in Asia; for we were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we despaired even of living.

[Note: [Col. 0751] But we ourselves had within ourselves the sentence of death, so that we might not be trusting in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead,] [Note: [Col. 0751] “We might be trusting”: supported by all Greek witnesses.] But we ourselves had within ourselves the sentence of death, so that we might not be trusting in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead,

[Note: [Col. 0751] who delivered us from such deaths and delivers us; in whom we have hoped that he will deliver us.] [Note: [Col. 0751] “From such deaths”: Greek, *τηλικούτου θανάτου*, “from so great a death.” “Delivered us”: absent from all Greek witnesses. “That”: Gothic has Greek *καὶ ἔτι*, “and still.”] who delivered us from such deaths and delivers us; in whom we have hoped that he will deliver us.

[Note: [Col. 0751] You also helping us on our behalf by prayer, so that, from many persons, the gift bestowed upon us may be gratefully acknowledged on our behalf through many.] [Note: [Col. 0751] “In the presence of many”: Greek, *ἐκ πολλῶν προσώπων*, “from many faces/persons.”] You also help us on our behalf by prayer, so that, from many persons, the gift bestowed upon us may be gratefully acknowledged on our behalf through many.

[Note: [Col. 0751] For our boast is this: the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and the sincerity of God—not in fleshly wisdom, but in the grace of God—we have conducted ourselves in the world, and especially toward you.] [Note: [Col. 0751] *Hlutrein*: thus manuscripts I and II; at II, 17, *hlutriþai*; VII, 11, *hlutrans*. Castiglione adds *hautrein, hautriþai, hautrans*. *Usmetum*: codex A has *usmeitum*.] For our boast is this: the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and the sincerity of God—not in fleshly wisdom, but in the grace of God—we have conducted ourselves in the world, and especially toward you.

[Note: [Col. 0751] For we write nothing else to you than what you read or also recognize; and I hope that you will recognize it to the end,] [Note: [Col. 0751–0752] “Other than”: Greek *ἀλλ᾽ ἤ* (“but rather”); compare Mark IX, 8, where the variant *ἀλλ᾽ ἤ* also occurs for *ἀλλά*. “And”: Gothic, with the manuscripts, has Greek *καί*.] For we write nothing else to you than what you read or also recognize; and I hope that you will recognize it to the end,

[Note: [Col. 0751] just as you have recognized us in part: that we are your boast, just as you also are ours, on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.] [Note: [Col. 0752] “Just as”: in place of Gothic *jah* (“also”). “Christ”: absent in codex A, with the Greek.] just as you have recognized us in part: that we are your boast, just as you also are ours, on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0751] And in this confidence I intended first to come to you, so that you might have a second grace,] [Note: [Col. 0752] “First … you”: the Greek has this word order.] And in this confidence I intended first to come to you, so that you might have a second grace,

[Note: [Col. 0751] and through you to go into Macedonia, and again from Macedonia to come to you, and from you to be sent onward into Judaea.] [Note: [Col. 0752] “And through”: codex A reads *jaþ-þairh*. “Macedonia”: codex A reads *makaidonja* here, again at II, 13 shortly below, and at VII, 5, *makaidonjai*. We do not think this variation arose, as Castiglione supposed, because the Greeks supposedly wrote both Μακηδονία and Μακεδονία, of which codex B rendered one as *makidonja*—because η was pronounced as *i* in Ulfilas’s time—and codex A the other as *makaidonja*. The Greeks did not use these forms indiscriminately; Μακηδονία occurs among poets alone, where required by metrical considerations. Rather, *makidonja* seems the more anomalous form, and nothing is readily comparable except *aggiljus* and *aggeljus* (ἄγγελοι, “angels”).] and through you to go into Macedonia, and again from Macedonia to come to you, and from you to be sent onward into Judaea.

[Note: [Col. 0751] When therefore I had this intention, did I perhaps use levity? Or do I plan what I plan according to the flesh, so that with me there should be “yes, yes” and “no, no”?] [Note: [Col. 0752] “No”: codex A, with all Greek witnesses, has *ni*. “And no”: codex A has *jan-ne*.] When therefore I had this intention, did I perhaps use levity? Or do I plan what I plan according to the flesh, so that with me there should be “yes, yes” and “no, no”?

[Note: [Col. 0751] But God is faithful: our word to you is not “yes and no”;] [Note: [Col. 0752] “Is not”: Greek, *οὐκ ἐγένετο*, “did not come to be.” “And no”: codex A has *jan-ne*.] But God is faithful: our word to you is not “yes and no”;

[Note: [Col. 0751–0753] for the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was proclaimed among you through us—through me and Silvanus and Timothy—did not become “yes and no,” but became “yes” in him.] [Note: [Col. 0752] “Was proclaimed”: codex A reads *merjada*. “Timothy”: codex B correctly has *teimauþaiu*; codex A adds a letter. “Nor”: codex A has *ni*. “And no”: codex A has the fuller form.] for the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was proclaimed among you through us—through me and Silvanus and Timothy—did not become “yes and no,” but became “yes” in him.

[Note: [Col. 0753] For however many promises of God there are, in him is the “yes”; therefore also through him is the “Amen” to God for glory through us.] [Note: [Col. 0753] “For”: Gothic omits Greek γάρ. “Therefore … him”: Greek has *καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ*, “and in him”; otherwise codex A reads *jaþ-þairh* for *jah þairh*.] For however many promises of God there are, in him is the “yes”; therefore also through him is the “Amen” to God for glory through us.

[Note: [Col. 0753] But he who establishes us with you in Christ and anoints us is God;] [Note: [Col. 0753] “Us”: codex A has *uns*. “Anointing”: codex A adds *salbonsd*.] But he who establishes us with you in Christ and anoints us is God;

[Note: [Col. 0753] and who seals us and gives the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts.] [Note: [Col. 0753] “Spirit”: all Greek witnesses have *πνεύματος* (“of the Spirit”), dependent on *vadi* (“pledge”); Mill reports that Latin Fathers follow the same reading.] and who seals us and gives the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts.

[Note: [Col. 0753] But I call God as witness against my soul, that, sparing you, I came no more to Corinth;] But I call God as witness against my soul, that, sparing you, I came no more to Corinth;

[Note: [Col. 0753] not that we lord it over your faith, but we are fellow-workers for your grace; for you stand firm in faith.] [Note: [Col. 0753] “Lord it over”: codex A correctly reads *fraujinoma*; codex B adds *fraujoma*. “Grace”: the Latin has *gratiae* (“grace”), while the Greek has χαρᾶς (“joy”); Gothic agrees with manuscripts 37 and 71, which read χάριτος (“grace”).] not that we lord it over your faith, but we are fellow-workers for your grace; for you stand firm in faith.

[Note: [Col. 0753] But I determined this very thing within myself: not to come again to you in sorrow.] [Note: [Col. 0753] “This very thing within myself”: Greek *ἐμαυτῷ τοῦτο*; not only is the word order different, but the Gothic translator must be noted as having translated as though he read τὸ αὐτό, that is, *τοῦτο αὐτὸ ἐμοί*. “To come”: the Greek places it after “to you.”] But I determined this very thing within myself: not to come again to you in sorrow.

[Note: [Col. 0753] For if I make you sorrowful, who then is the one who makes me glad, except the one made sorrowful by me?] [Note: [Col. 0753] *Nibai*: codex A has *niba*.] For if I make you sorrowful, who then is the one who makes me glad, except the one made sorrowful by me?

[Note: [Col. 0753] And I wrote this very thing to you, so that, when I came, I might not have sorrow from those over whom I ought to rejoice, being confident about you all that my joy is that of all of you.] [Note: [Col. 0753] “And this”: codex A has *jaþ-þata*. “This very thing”: the Greek places it after “you.” “Joy”: codex A has *faheþs*.] And I wrote this very thing to you, so that, when I came, I might not have sorrow from those over whom I ought to rejoice, being confident about you all that my joy is that of all of you.

[Note: [Col. 0753] But out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you through many tears, not that you might be sorrowful, but that you might know the love which I have in abundance toward you.] [Note: [Col. 0753] “But that”: Castiglione adds *jct.*; otherwise *ei* occurs after *friaþva* (“love”) in all Greek witnesses. “Love”: codex A has *frijaþva*.] But out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you through many tears, not that you might be sorrowful, but that you might know the love which I have in abundance toward you.

[Note: [Col. 0753] But if anyone has caused sorrow, he has caused sorrow not to me, but in part, that I may not burden all of you.] But if anyone has caused sorrow, he has caused sorrow not to me, but in part, that I may not burden all of you.

[Note: [Col. 0753] This rebuke from the majority is sufficient for such a person,] This rebuke from the majority is sufficient for such a person,

[Note: [Col. 0753] so that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up by excessive sorrow.] [Note: [Col. 0753] “You rather”: according to the Greek. “And comfort”: codex A has *jag-gaþlaihan*.] so that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up by excessive sorrow.

[Note: [Col. 0753] Therefore I urge you to confirm your love toward him.] [Note: [Col. 0753] *Ïnuh þis*: codex A has *ïnuþ-þis*.] Therefore I urge you to confirm your love toward him.

[Note: [Col. 0753] For this reason I wrote, that I might know the proof of you: whether you are obedient in all things.] [Note: [Col. 0753] “For this reason”: Gothic omits Greek γὰρ καί. “Whether you are”: Greek has εἰ ἐστέ, with ἐστέ after “obedient”; Gothic commonly renders εἰ in indirect questions in this way; see Matthew XXVII, 49; Mark X, 11; XV, 36.] For this reason I wrote, that I might know the proof of you: whether you are obedient in all things.

[Note: [Col. 0753] But to whom you grant anything, I also grant; for I too, if I have granted anything, have granted it for your sake in the presence of Christ,] [Note: [Col. 0753] “Grant”: according to the Greek, the verb comes before *jabai* (“if”); otherwise Gothic, with Tertullian, has ὅ (ᾧ), and codex A twice reads *fragaf*, “I granted.”] But to whom you grant anything, I also grant; for I too, if I have granted anything, have granted it for your sake in the presence of Christ,

[Note: [Col. 0753] so that we may not be defrauded by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.] [Note: [Col. 0754] “Not ignorant … his”: absent from the Greek. *Galiginondau*: Grimm, *W. J.* XLVI, p. 193, says that *ligan* means “to set out” and “to lie in wait.” Yet, remembering what we taught at Mark IX, 20—that forms ending in *-inon* refer not to verbs but nouns—we still doubt whether that learned man has seen rightly. Moreover, according to the Greek text, πλεονεκτεῖν requires a verb meaning not “to lie in wait,” but “to deceive” or “to make one’s own.” *Galiuginondau* seemed better suited to this meaning; but since Castiglione denies that it is read in either codex, we have ventured another emendation: perhaps *gaaiginondau* should be read. Although the word occurs nowhere else, it may properly be derived from *aigin* (“possession”), and is related to our *eignen*; scarcely any word would answer Greek πλεονεκτεῖν better. This is also indicated by the gloss in codex A, *gafaihondau*, derived from *faihu* (“wealth”) and meaning the same as *bifaihondau* (πλεονεκτεῖν; see VII, 2; XII, 17–18; 1 Thessalonians IV, 6). The distinction of the letters *a* and *l* in the Gothic codices, especially in the palimpsests, is extremely difficult. *Unvitandans ... ïs* agrees with all Greek witnesses.] so that we may not be defrauded by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.

[Note: [Col. 0753] But when I came to Troas for the gospel of Christ, and a door had been opened to me in the Lord, I had no rest for my spirit, because I did not find Titus my brother;] [Note: [Col. 0754] “Gospel”: codex A has *aivaggeljons*, with Greek witnesses that read διὰ τὸ εὐαγγέλιον, “because of the gospel.”] But when I came to Troas for the gospel of Christ, and a door had been opened to me in the Lord, I had no rest for my spirit, because I did not find Titus my brother;

[Note: [Col. 0753] but, taking leave of him, I went into Macedonia.] [Note: [Col. 0754] “Taking leave of him”: codex A reads *tvisstandans ïm* (“taking leave of them”), agreeing with all Greek witnesses; compare Galatians V, 20, where *tvisstassei* has double *s* in codex B and single *s* in codex A. “Macedonia”: see the note on I, 16.] but, taking leave of him, I went into Macedonia.

[Note: [Col. 0753] But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and manifests through us in every place the fragrance of his knowledge;] [Note: [Col. 0754] “Thanks”: codex A has *aviliuþ*. “Manifesting”: codex A has *gabairhjandin*; compare Titus I, 3, *atbairhida*. “Through us”: codex A, with all Greek witnesses, places this before “in.”] But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and manifests through us in every place the fragrance of his knowledge;

[Note: [Col. 0753–0755] for we are the sweet fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing:] [Note: [Col. 0754–0755] “Christ”: codex A omits *xristaus* and adds *voþi* (“sweet, pleasant”); Castiglione had formerly misunderstood it as a preposition. Since εὐωδία must be translated “sweet fragrance,” whereas *dauns* means “odour” generally, Gothic rendered εὐ- by adding the adjective *voþi*; compare Ephesians V, 3, *du daunai voþjai*, “for a sweet fragrance.” “Perishing”: codex A’s margin has *fralusnandam*.] for we are the sweet fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing:

[Note: [Col. 0755] to some, indeed, an odour of death unto death; but to others, an odour from life unto life. And who is sufficient for these things?] [Note: [Col. 0755] “Indeed”: absent in codex A. “Of death”: codex A, with manuscripts, has *us dauþau*, “from death.” “From life”: Greek ζωῆς, “from life.” “And to”: codex A has *jad-du*.] to some, indeed, an odour of death unto death; but to others, an odour from life unto life. And who is sufficient for these things?

[Note: [Col. 0755] For we are not like certain persons who adulterate the word of God, but out of sincerity, and as from God, before God, in Christ, we speak.] [Note: [Col. 0755] “We are”: codex A has *sium*. “Like”: codex B omits it. “Certain persons”: Greek has either πολλοί (“many”) or λοιποί (“the rest”). “But”: Gothic, with the manuscripts, has ὡς (“as”). “Sincerity”: see I, 12.] For we are not like certain persons who adulterate the word of God, but out of sincerity, and as from God, before God, in Christ, we speak.

[Note: [Col. 0755] Are we beginning again to commend ourselves? Or do we need, like certain persons, letters of recommendation to you or letters of recommendation from you?] Are we beginning again to commend ourselves? Or do we need, like certain persons, letters of recommendation to you or letters of recommendation from you?

[Note: [Col. 0755] You are our letter, written in our hearts, known and read by all people.] [Note: [Col. 0755] “You are”: codex B has *jusijuþ*, as at Galatians II, 8, *vaurstveigatavida*, and codex A below at IV, 5, *unskalkans*; compare Mark X, 44.] You are our letter, written in our hearts, known and read by all people.

[Note: [Col. 0755] It is manifest that you are a letter of Christ, administered by us, written within not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of fleshly hearts.] [Note: [Col. 0755–0756] “Manifest”: codex A has *svikunþai* (“manifest [plural]”), accommodated to the Greek; the received reading displays a construction peculiar to the Germanic languages; see Mark VI, 3. “You are”: codex A has *siuþ*. “Ink”: there is great disagreement over what the codices actually contain. Castiglione himself had printed *svartizaai*, but has now informed us that it should be corrected to *svartizla*. Massmann, *Bairische Annalen* (1834), p. 325, says that one codex has *svartizai*, the other *vartizla*; in the *Skeireins*, p. 182, he says that *svartizlai*—perhaps in codex B—is read. From these reports, if we may make a conjecture, codex A appears to have *svartizla*, codex B *svartizlai*. Grimm, after conjecturing *svartizai* or *svartizvai* in *W. J.* XLVI, p. 203, also proposed *svartizlai* in *Grammar* III, 526. “Hearts”: Greek has καρδίας.] It is manifest that you are a letter of Christ, administered by us, written within not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of fleshly hearts.

[Note: [Col. 0755] But such confidence we have through Christ toward God,] But such confidence we have through Christ toward God,

[Note: [Col. 0755] not that we are sufficient to think anything from ourselves, as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God,] [Note: [Col. 0756] “From ourselves”: the Greek places this before “to think.” “As from ourselves”: codex A adds this; see Romans IX, 15. “Is”: absent from all Greek witnesses.] not that we are sufficient to think anything from ourselves, as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God,

[Note: [Col. 0755] who also made us sufficient ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.] who also made us sufficient ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

[Note: [Col. 0755] But if the ministry of death, in letters engraved upon stones, came in glory, so that the children of Israel could not gaze upon the face of Moses because of the glory of his face, which was passing away,] [Note: [Col. 0756] “Glorious”: Greek omits ἐν δόξῃ (“in glory”); unless the Gothic translator varied the expression in his usual manner, he seems to have read ἔνδοξη. “They could”: codex A reads *mahtedeina*; codex B and Castiglione have *mahtede*, for which see Galatians IV, 5 and Matthew V, 31. “To gaze”: all Greek witnesses place it before “sons.”] But if the ministry of death, in letters engraved upon stones, came in glory, so that the children of Israel could not gaze upon the face of Moses because of the glory of his face, which was passing away,

[Note: [Col. 0755] how shall not rather the ministry of the Spirit be in glory?] [Note: [Col. 0756] *Nei*, in place of *niu* or *ni*, occurs only here and is suspect.] how shall not rather the ministry of the Spirit be in glory?

[Note: [Col. 0755] For if the ministry of condemnation is glory, much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory.] [Note: [Col. 0756] “Ministry”: codex A has *andbahtja* (“in the ministry”), with Greek τῇ διακονίᾳ. “From”: codex A and the manuscripts have *ïn*, “in.”] For if the ministry of condemnation is glory, much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory.

[Note: [Col. 0755] For that which was made glorious has not been made glorious in this respect, because of the surpassing glory;] [Note: [Col. 0756] At the beginning, Gothic omits καί (“and”).] For that which was made glorious has not been made glorious in this respect, because of the surpassing glory;

[Note: [Col. 0755] for if that which was passing away was through glory, much more that which remains is in glory.] for if that which was passing away was through glory, much more that which remains is in glory.

[Note: [Col. 0755] Therefore, having such hope, we use great boldness,] Therefore, having such hope, we use great boldness,

[Note: [Col. 0755] and not as Moses put a veil upon his face, so that the children of Israel might not gaze upon the end of that which was passing away.] [Note: [Col. 0756] “And not”: codex A has *jan-ni*. “Moses”: codex A has *mosez*. “His face”: Gothic has Greek ἑαυτοῦ.] and not as Moses put a veil upon his face, so that the children of Israel might not gaze upon the end of that which was passing away.

[Note: [Col. 0755] But their minds were hardened; for until this day the same veil remains at the reading of the old covenant, not being unveiled, because it is abolished in Christ.] [Note: [Col. 0756] *Afdaubnodedun*: in the margin codex A has *gablindnodedun*, “were blinded.” “That”: Castiglione adds *þaþa*.] But their minds were hardened; for until this day the same veil remains at the reading of the old covenant, not being unveiled, because it is abolished in Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0755] But until this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies upon their heart;] [Note: [Col. 0756] “Day”: absent from all Greek witnesses except codex c as cited by Mill. “Lies”: all Greek witnesses place it after “their.”] But until this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies upon their heart;

[Note: [Col. 0755] but whenever it turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.] but whenever it turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.

[Note: [Col. 0755] But the Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.] [Note: [Col. 0756] “Freedom”: codex A has *freijhals*. “Is”: the second *est* is absent from all Greek witnesses.] But the Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.

[Note: [Col. 0755–0757] But we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as from the Spirit of the Lord.] [Note: [Col. 0756–0757] *Frisaht*: Castiglione adds *frisath*; on the accusative used in Greek fashion, see John XI, 44. “Spirit”: codex A correctly has *ahmin*; codex B adds *ahmins*.] But we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as from the Spirit of the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0757] Therefore, having this ministry, as we have received mercy, we do not become faint-hearted,] [Note: [Col. 0757] “Ministry”: codex A has *andbahtei*. “We become”: codex A has *vairþam* (“we become”), with almost all Greek witnesses; the reading of codex B agrees with the Latin Fathers. *Usgrudjans*: thus the codices; Castiglione adds *ustrudjans*, as in verse 16; see Luke XVIII, 1.] Therefore, having this ministry, as we have received mercy, we do not become faint-hearted,

[Note: [Col. 0757] but we have renounced the hidden things of shame, not walking in craftiness, nor falsifying the word of God; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every conscience of men before God.] [Note: [Col. 0757] “Nor”: codex A has *ni*.] but we have renounced the hidden things of shame, not walking in craftiness, nor falsifying the word of God; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every conscience of men before God.

[Note: [Col. 0757] But if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing,] [Note: [Col. 0757] “If”: Gothic, with the manuscripts, has καί (“also”).] But if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing,

[Note: [Col. 0757] among whom God has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age, so that the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ—who is the image of the invisible God—may not shine upon them.] [Note: [Col. 0757] A point occurs after *guþ* (“God”), to show that this word is to be separated from what follows, so that τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου (“of this age”) refers not to θεός (“God”) but to ἀπίστων (“the unbelieving”); all those who wrote against the Manichaeans and Marcionites maintain the same interpretation. “Upon them”: absent from the Greek. *Liuhadein*: thus codex B and Castiglione. Unless—as at VIII, 8—the final *s* has dropped through the same scribal error, it must be taken either as an accusative, “that God may not kindle the light of the gospel,” or as a dative, “that God may not shine with the light of the gospel”; we can scarcely believe it to be the neuter of the adjective *liuhadeins* (Matthew VI, 22). Codex A reads *liuhadeins*; do not consider this a nominative, for substantives in *-eins*, formed from verbs, are rather to be understood as the genitive of *liuhadei*—the only form to be posited—formed from *liuhaþ*. This genitive depends, so to speak, upon *ni* (“not”); compare Matthew IX, 36, *ni habandona hairdeis*; Mark XII, 19, *barne ni bileiþai*; Luke II, *ni vas ïm rumis*. “Invisible”: absent in codex A, with the Greek.] among whom God has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age, so that the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ—who is the image of the invisible God—may not shine upon them.

[Note: [Col. 0757] For we proclaim not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.] [Note: [Col. 0757] “Jesus Christ”: in all Greek witnesses this phrase precedes “Lord.” “Your servants”: see III, 2.] For we proclaim not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.

[Note: [Col. 0757] For God, who said, “Out of darkness let light shine,” is he who also shone in our hearts, for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.] [Note: [Col. 0757–0758] *Ur-riqiza*: the codices thus read it for *us riqiza*, a kind of consonantal assimilation otherwise found only in verbal composition. “Also”: absent in all Greek witnesses; Gothic agrees with the Armenian version.] For God, who said, “Out of darkness let light shine,” is he who also shone in our hearts, for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0757] But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing greatness of the power may be of God and not from us.] [Note: [Col. 0758] “Having”: Greek has ἔχομεν, “we have.” “May be of power”: supported by all Greek witnesses.] But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing greatness of the power may be of God and not from us.

[Note: [Col. 0757] In every affliction, but not hard pressed; at a loss, but not terrified;] In every affliction, but not hard pressed; at a loss, but not terrified;

[Note: [Col. 0757] persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed;] persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed;

[Note: [Col. 0757] always the death of the Lord Jesus in our body—manifested may be.] [Note: [Col. 0758] “Of the Lord”: absent from the Greek. “Our body”: absent from the Greek. After this word two pages are missing in codex A, containing the Gothic text from here to V, 1. The scribe of codex B, misled by the repetition of *leika unsaramma* (“our body”) in the same verse, omitted the words by which Gothic rendered Greek περιφέροντες ἵνα καὶ ἡ ζωὴ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἐν τῷ σώματι ἡμῶν, “carrying about, so that also the life of Jesus in our body”; see Romans IX, 15.] always the death of the Lord Jesus in our body [lacuna] may be manifested.

[Note: [Col. 0757] For we who live are always handed over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our corruptible body.] [Note: [Col. 0758] “Always”: Gothic omits Greek γάρ.] For we who live are always handed over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our corruptible body.

[Note: [Col. 0757] Thus now death works in us, but life in you.] [Note: [Col. 0758] “Now”: absent from all Greek witnesses.] Thus now death works in us, but life in you.

[Note: [Col. 0757] But having the same spirit of faith according to what is written, “I believed, therefore I spoke,” we also believe, and therefore we also speak,] [Note: [Col. 0758] “And”: Gothic prefixes “also,” which is absent from the Greek.] But having the same spirit of faith according to what is written, “I believed, therefore I spoke,” we also believe, and therefore we also speak,

[Note: [Col. 0757] knowing that he who raises the Lord will also raise us through Jesus and present us with you.] [Note: [Col. 0758] “The Lord”: Gothic omits “Jesus,” which the Greek has.] knowing that he who raises the Lord will also raise us through Jesus and present us with you.

[Note: [Col. 0757] For all things are for your sake, so that grace, increasing through many, may abound in thanksgiving to the glory of God.] For all things are for your sake, so that grace, increasing through many, may abound in thanksgiving to the glory of God.

[Note: [Col. 0757] Therefore we do not become faint-hearted; but even if our outward person is being destroyed, nevertheless our inward person is renewed day by day.] [Note: [Col. 0758] *Usgrudjans*: see verse 1. *Aþþan* here means ἀλλά (“but”). Grimm, *Grammar* III, 275, incorrectly teaches that neither *ïþ* nor *aþþan* may stand for ἀλλά; yet it does so here, below at II, 6, and doubtless at I, IX, 2, where Castiglione already suspected *aþþan* should be read for *aiþþau*. Following *jabai* or *þauhjabai* (“if,” “even if”), it means “yet” or “nevertheless.” *Ïnnuma* is certainly the manuscript reading, as at Romans VII, 22 and Ephesians III, 16; see Colossians I, 29. Castiglione printed *ïnnuna*, for which Grimm proposed *ïnnana* in *W. J.*, p. 187.] Therefore we do not become faint-hearted; but even if our outward person is being destroyed, nevertheless our inward person is renewed day by day.

[Note: [Col. 0757–0759] For this present, momentary and light affliction of ours works for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure,] [Note: [Col. 0758–0759] “Momentary and”: absent in the Greek. “Light”: codex B has *weiht*; Grimm, *W. J.*, pp. 212 ff., conjectured *leiht*, supported by I, 17, where *leihts* = ἐλαφρία (“lightness”). “Beyond all measure”: Gothic, with manuscripts f and g cited by Mill, has εἰς ὑπερβολήν. “An eternal weight of glory”: all Greek witnesses have αἰώνιον βάρος δόξης.] For this present, momentary and light affliction of ours works for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure,

[Note: [Col. 0759] while we look not at the things seen, but at those not seen; for the things seen are perishable, but the things not seen eternal.] [Note: [Col. 0759] “Looking”: Gothic omits ἡμῶν (“us”), perhaps because of the preceding *unsis*, to which the participle refers. “Are”: the verb is absent from all Greek witnesses.] while we look not at the things seen, but at those not seen; for the things seen are perishable, but the things not seen eternal.

[Note: [Col. 0759] For we know that if our earthly house of this tent is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.] [Note: [Col. 0759] “Earthly”: codex B has *airþeina*; Castiglione adds *airteina*. It should be noted that the masculine noun *gards* (“house”) here takes a feminine adjective; see Nehemiah VI, 16. “That”: absent from the Greek; see John XIII, 29. “From”: codex A begins here.] For we know that if our earthly house of this tent is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.

[Note: [Col. 0759] For indeed in this we groan, desiring to be clothed over with our dwelling from heaven,] For indeed in this we groan, desiring to be clothed over with our dwelling from heaven,

[Note: [Col. 0759] if indeed, even when clothed, we shall not be found naked.] [Note: [Col. 0759] “And”: this conjunction is absent from codex A.] if indeed, even when clothed, we shall not be found naked.

[Note: [Col. 0759] For indeed, while we are in this tent, we groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed, so that the mortal may be swallowed up by—] For indeed, while we are in this tent, we groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed, so that the mortal may be swallowed up by—
[Col. 0759] May live. He who also prepared us for this very thing is God, who also gave us the pledge of the Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0759] *jah*] “also,” as in the Greek throughout; Codex A has *jag*.

[Note: [Col. 0759] *ahman*] “Spirit,” Greek throughout: πνεύματος.

Now, always confident and knowing that, while we are present in the body, we are absent from the Lord—for we walk by faith, not by sight—we are confident and prefer rather to leave the body and be at home with the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0759] *anahaimjaim*] Dative. Castillion appears to have objected to it, and Grimm, *W. J. l. l.*, p. 188, judges it corrupt; it is nevertheless correct, for it depends on *valjam*, namely *unsis*: “we desire for ourselves.”

Therefore, whether at home or away, we make it our aim to please him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive the things proper to the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil.

[Note: [Col. 0760] *svesona*] “proper,” Greek throughout διά (“through”); Gothic, with the versions, has read ἴδια (“proper things”).

Knowing therefore the fear of the Lord, we persuade people; but we are known to God. I hope, moreover, that we are known also in your consciences.

[Note: [Col. 0760] *svikunþans*] “known,” as though *venjam* had previously been written; after *venja*, *svikunþana* was to be expected.

We are not again commending ourselves to you, but giving you an occasion for boasting on our behalf, so that you may have an answer for those who boast in outward appearance and not in heart.

[Note: [Col. 0760] *ei*] “so that”; Greek throughout has γάρ (“for”), in place of which Gothic, with the manuscripts, has ὁ γάρ (“for”).

[Note: [Col. 0760] *uskannjaima*] Codex A, in the margin, has *anafilhaima*, of the same meaning.

[Note: [Col. 0760] *ans*] The second hand of Codex A has *unsis*.

[Note: [Col. 0760] *jah ni*] Codex A has *jan-ni*, adding, with the manuscripts, *ïn*.

For whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you. For the love of Christ constrains us, judging this: one died for all; therefore all died. And he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them.

[Note: [Col. 0760] *þatei*] Gothic, with the manuscripts, has εἰ (“if”).

[Note: [Col. 0760] *sis*] Codex A omits it.

[Note: [Col. 0760] *libaina*] Thus Codex A; Codex B adds *libainai*.

Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh; and even if we knew Christ according to the flesh, now we no longer know him thus.

[Note: [Col. 0760] *jabai*] Gothic, with the manuscripts, has καί (“and”).

[Note: [Col. 0760] *ni þanaseiþs ni*] See the note on John XVI, 21.

[Note: [Col. 0760] *ïna*] “him,” omitted by Codex A, with the Greek throughout.

Thus, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new. But all things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation: namely, that God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning their transgressions against them, and placing in us the word of reconciliation.

[Note: [Col. 0760] *unsis*] Gothic has ἑαυτῷ (“to himself”). Perhaps *unsis sis*, or *uns sis*, had been written; see the following verse, and compare Romans IX, 15 and Second Corinthians III, 2.

[Note: [Col. 0760] *þairh*] Gothic, with the manuscripts, has Ἰησοῦ (“Jesus”).

[Note: [Col. 0760] *jah*] Codex A has *jag*.

[Note: [Col. 0760] *uns*] Codex A has *unsis*.

[Note: [Col. 0761] *bidjam*] Codex A, with the manuscripts, has *bidjandans*, “entreating.”

[Note: [Col. 0761] *gagavairþnan*] “to be reconciled,” Greek καταλλάγητε; compare Matthew V, 24.

[Note: [Col. 0761] *ïzei*] Codex A has *ïze*.

[Note: [Col. 0761] *gatavida fravaurht*] “made sin,” as in the Greek throughout.

[Note: [Col. 0761] *jah*] Codex A has *jaþ*.

[Note: [Col. 0761] *bidjandans*] “entreating,” Greek παρακαλοῦμεν.

[Note: [Col. 0761] *mela—qiþiþ*] As in the Greek throughout, unless perhaps these words should be transposed; compare Luke IX, 36.

[Note: [Col. 0761] *andanem*] Correctly so in Codex A; Codex B adds *andnem*.

[Note: [Col. 0761] *þannu*] “indeed,” omitted by Codex A, with the Greek throughout.

[Note: [Col. 0761] *unsar*] “our,” omitted in Greek.

[Note: [Col. 0761] *lausqiþrein*] “fastings,” Greek throughout νηστείαις.

in purity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in unhypocritical love; in the word of truth, in the power of God, through the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and the left; through glory and dishonour, through evil report and good report; as deceivers and true; as unknown and yet well known; as dying, and behold, we live; as disciplined, and not put to death; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet enriching many; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.

[Note: [Col. 0761] *friaþvai*] Codex A has *frijaþvai*.

[Note: [Col. 0761] The beginning adds *jah* (“and”) in Codex A.]

[Note: [Col. 0761] *waïht aihandans*] Thus the manuscripts, as Grimm, *W. J. l. l.*, p. 188, had long ago conjectured; Castillion adds *waïhtai handans*.

Our mouth is opened to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged.

[Note: [Col. 0761] *munþ*] For *munþs*, as in Luke I, 64; VI, 45.

[Note: [Col. 0761] *urrumnoda*] Thus Codex A; Codex B has *usrumnoda*. Castillion adds *usrumnada*, because the final part of the word cannot clearly be read in the codex. Below, in verse 13, the same codex correctly has *urrumnaiþ*; see Luke VIII, 24.

[Note: [Col. 0761] *jus*] “you,” omitted in Greek throughout.

Do not become unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement, moreover, has Christ with Belial? Or what share has a believer with an unbeliever?

[Note: [Col. 0761] *miþ*] The first *miþ*: “with,” Greek throughout καί.

[Note: [Col. 0761] *aiþþau*] “or,” Greek δέ.

[Note: [Col. 0761] *wouh þan*] Codex A has *wouþ-þan*, likewise in the following verse.

[Note: [Col. 0762] *bailiama*] The form *bailiam* for Greek Βελιάρ or Βελίαλ (“Belial”), rejected by Castillion because it lacks all etymological authority, can, in our judgment, be defended. If Gothic read Βελία, as Latin authors have it, it could pronounce *bailiam* by adding *m*, especially when an ending beginning with a vowel was added. Thus it wrote *aizleimis* and *salamis* for τοῦ Ἐσλί (“of Esli”) and Σαλά (“Sala”), and *nauelis* for τοῦ Νῶε (“of Noah”). Whether it would have written the nominatives *bailiam*, *aizleim*, and *salam* is doubtful.

Or what agreement has the temple of God with idols? For you are the temple of the living God, as God says: “I will dwell among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.”

[Note: [Col. 0762] *wouh þan*] See verse 15.

[Note: [Col. 0762] *alhs*] First, “temple.” The symmetry of the expression requires the dative *alh*, and there is no doubt that Gothic wrote this; the scribe, deceived by the formula *alhs guþs* in what follows, wrote *alhs* here also.

[Note: [Col. 0762] *sijuþ*] Codex A has *siuþ*.

[Note: [Col. 0762] *auk*] “for,” Greek καθώς (“as”).

[Note: [Col. 0762] *ïnna gagga*] Castillion adds a conjectural sign. The particle *ïnna* is not compounded with verbs; nor, because it signifies rest rather than motion (see I, V, 12), can it here be compounded with *gaggan*. The apostle says that he will walk about and dwell among them.

“Therefore come out from their midst, and be separate,” says the Lord; “and do not touch what is unclean, and I will receive you. And I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me,” says the Lord Almighty.

[Note: [Col. 0762] *ïnuh þis*] Codex A has *ïnuþ-þis*.

Having therefore these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.

[Note: [Col. 0762] *habandans nu*] Omitted in Greek throughout.

[Note: [Col. 0762] *bisauleino*] Correctly so in Codex A; Codex B, through transposition of *s* and *l*, incorrectly has *bilauseino*. Compare *bisauljan*, Titus I, 15, and *bisaulnan*, John XVIII, 28.

[Col. 0763] Make room for us: we have wronged no one, corrupted no one, defrauded no one. I do not say this to condemn you; for I have already said that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.

[Note: [Col. 0763] *sijuþ*] Correctly so in Codex A; Codex B has the senseless *sijum*.

[Note: [Col. 0763] *gasviltan*] Codex A has *miþgasviltan*, “to die together” (συναποθανεῖν). Both readings are supported by Greek manuscripts.

[Note: [Col. 0763] *jah samana liban*] Codex A has *jassamana* with an addition, followed by *libam*; Castillion conjectures *samana liban*. See Mark IX, 25.

[Note: [Col. 0763] *managons*] “much,” omitted in Greek throughout.

[Note: [Col. 0763] *makidonjai*] Codex A has *makaidonjai*; see I, 16.

[Note: [Col. 0763] *gaþlaihands*] Correctly so in Codex A; Codex B adds *gaþlaihans*. See Mark XII, 24.

[Note: [Col. 0763] *ïzvarana*] One would expect *ïzvara*, referring to *gaunoþa*. Grimm, *W. J. l. l.*, p. 193, regards *ïzvarana* as correct and *gaunoþa* as a scribal error for *gaunoþ*. We consider it one of the solecisms discussed at Nehemiah VI, 16.

[Note: [Col. 0763] *varþ*] “came to be,” omitted in Greek throughout.

For if I grieved you by that letter, I do not regret it; and even if I did regret it—for I see that that letter, although only briefly, grieved you—

[Note: [Col. 0764] *jabai*] Gothic, with Codex C as cited by Mi., has καί.

[Note: [Col. 0764] *þaim*] Omitted in Codex A.

[Note: [Col. 0764] *jah jabai*] Greek throughout has εἰ καί. This formula in this word-order also occurs at XII, 11; at Luke XVIII, 4, however, *jabai jah* is read.

[Note: [Col. 0764] *gasaiwa auk*] Codex A has *unte gasaiwa*: “for I see.”

[Note: [Col. 0764] *dulleitilai*] Codex A has *du leitilai*. The received reading, as Castillion observed, stands for *duh leitilai* (see First Corinthians VII, 16), containing the particle *-uh*. Although at John XVIII, 26 we denied that enclitic *uh* could signify καί (“and”), passages in which καί (“and”) is joined with εἰ (“if”) are exceptions. There Gothic either omits *jah* altogether or puts it before *jabai*. Thus it appears that in these passages Gothic did not attach an emphatic force to καί. Moreover, *leitilai*, “a little,” is omitted in Greek throughout and is not added at John V, 35 or Philemon 15; but *Skeireins*, p. 47, l. 3, has *du leitilamma mela*.

now I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved unto repentance. For you were grieved according to God, so that you might suffer no loss in anything through us. For godly sorrow produces repentance unto a salvation not to be regretted; but the sorrow of the world produces death.

[Note: [Col. 0764] *saurgaideduþ*] Correctly so in Codex A; Codex B adds *saurgideduþ*.

[Note: [Col. 0764] *ïn*] Omitted by Codex A.

[Note: [Col. 0764] *so*] Omitted by Codex A.

[Note: [Col. 0764] *gatulgidai*] Codex A has *gatulgida*, referring it to *ïdreiga*, whereas *gatulgidai* should refer to *ganistai*.

[Note: [Col. 0764] *saiw*] Codex A adds *saiwa*: “I see.”

[Note: [Col. 0764] *hlutrans*] Thus the manuscripts; Castillion adds *hautrans*. See I, 12.

[Note: [Col. 0764] *visan*] Gothic, with the manuscripts, has ἐν.

[Note: [Col. 0764] *jabai*] Gothic omits καί (“and”).

[Note: [Col. 0764] *melida*] Gothic omits ὑμῖν (“you”).

[Note: [Col. 0764] *sium*] Codex A has *sijum*.

[Note: [Col. 0766] *ïzei*] Codex A has *ïze*.

[Note: [Col. 0766] *faur ïzvis*] Omitted by Codex B.

[Note: [Col. 0766] *silba viljands*] Castillion adds a conjectural sign.

[Note: [Col. 0766] *þizei*] Codex A adds *þizai*.

[Note: [Col. 0766] *ïn*] “in,” Greek throughout ἐν.

[Note: [Col. 0766] *and*] “through.” Castillion, *Add.*, p. 68, says that Codex B appears to have *and*, while Codex A appears to have *ana*; but *and* alone is correct.

[Note: [Col. 0767] *filaus mais*] On this fullness of expression, see Matthew VI, 26; Codex A has *filu*.

As for the ministry for the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you. For I know your readiness, of which I boast about you to the Macedonians: “Achaia has been prepared since last year”; and your zeal has stirred up the greater number of them.

[Note: [Col. 0767] *aþþan*] Gothic renders either μέν (“on the one hand”) or γάρ (“for”) by *aþþan*. It is more likely, however, that it omitted μέν: γάρ (“for”) is read in all the manuscripts with which Gothic elsewhere tends to agree; and δέ (“but”) in verse 3, set against μέν, is again translated *aþþan*. No passage is known in which μέν—δέ (“on the one hand—but”) is rendered *aþþan—aþþan*; rather, one or the other Greek particle corresponds to it. Gothic also often omits μέν; compare XI, 4.

[Col. 0768]

[Note: [Col. 0768] *wopa*] Codex A has *wopam*, “we boast.”

[Note: [Col. 0768] *makidonnim*] Thus Codex B for *makidonim*; see Galatians V, 15.

[Note: [Col. 0768] *gavagida*] Codex A has *usvagida*, with the same meaning.

[Note: [Col. 0768] *ïzei*] “of them,” omitted by Codex A, with the Greek throughout.

I have sent the brothers ahead so that our boasting about you might not prove empty in this respect, and so that, as I said, you might be prepared.

But if Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we—not to say you—would be put to shame in this confidence of boasting.

[Note: [Col. 0768] *jah bigitand*] Codex A has *jab-bigitand*.

[Note: [Col. 0768] *unmanvjans*] Codex A adds *unmanvjands*; see Luke X, 2.

[Note: [Col. 0768] *gaaiviskondau*] Codex A adds *gaaiviskonda*.

[Note: [Col. 0768] *qiþau*] “I should say,” Greek λέγωμεν.

[Note: [Col. 0768] *þizos wolftuljos*] “of this boasting,” as in Greek and Codex A; Codex A omits *þizos*.

Therefore I considered it necessary to urge the brothers to go to you and prepare beforehand—the surviving Gothic text breaks off after *þana*.

[Note: [Col. 0767] I therefore thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go to you and prepare beforehand this promised blessing of yours, so that it may be ready as a blessing and not as an exaction.]

[Note: [Col. 0768] *jah ni*] Codex A has *jan-ni*.

The one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows with blessing will also reap with blessing. [Note: [Col. 0767] But this: whoever sows from parsimony will also reap from parsimony, and whoever sows in blessing will also reap from blessing.] [Note: [Col. 0768] *saïiþ*: dual; Codex A has *saijiþ*.—*us gaþagkja*: dual; Castillion has added *jct.*—*þiuþeinai*: “in blessing,” Greek εὐλογίαις (*in blessings*); moreover, for the first Greek ἐπί, the Gothic and certain codices seem to have read ἐν; concerning the second, it is not sufficiently clear whether he read ἐπί or ἐξ.]

And this: whoever sows from parsimony will also reap from parsimony, and whoever sows in blessing will also reap from blessing. Each one, just as he has determined in his heart—not from grief or necessity, for God loves a cheerful giver. [Note: [Col. 0767] Each one, just as he has predetermined in his heart, not from sorrow or necessity, for God loves a cheerful giver.] [Note: [Col. 0768] *nauþai*: from here through *andhulei* at XII.1, the text is absent in Codex A.—*giband*: Castillion, saying that this is a false form in place of *gibandan*, is mistaken; see Grimm I, 1017.]

And God is able to make every grace abound toward you, so that, always having all sufficiency in everything, you may abound in every good work. As it is written: “He distributed; he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever.” [Note: [Col. 0767] As it is written: “He dispersed; he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever.”] [Note: [Col. 0768] *usvaurhts*: Codex B has *usvaurts*; see the note at Matthew V.15.]
