You will be enriched in every respect, in all generosity, which produces thanksgiving to God through us. [Note: [Col. 0767] In every enrichment, in all simplicity, which works through us as thanksgiving to God.] [Col. 0769] For the ministry of this service is not only filling the needs of the saints, but is also increasing through many thanksgivings to God. [Note: [Col. 0769] For the ministry of this gift is not only filling the poverty of these saints, but also increasing through many graces to God.]

Through the testing of this ministry, glorifying God for the obedience of your confession to the gospel of Christ and for the simplicity of your fellowship with them and with all, and through their prayer for you, they long for you because of the surpassing grace of God in you. [Note: [Col. 0769] Through the testing of this ministry, glorifying God in the obedience of your confession to the gospel of Christ and in the simplicity of your sharing with them and with all, and through their prayer for you, desiring you because of the abundance of God’s grace in you.] [Note: [Col. 0769] *ïn*: the second hand; “in” in the complete Greek text.]

Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift. [Note: [Col. 0769] Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift.] [Note: [Col. 0769] *aviliud*: most codices have the Gothic equivalent of Greek δέ (*but*).—*unusspillodons*: Codex B has *unusspillidons*; see Romans XI.33; we have observed at Luke I.23 that scribes sometimes falsely wrote *i* for *o*.]

But I myself, Paul, appeal to you by the gentleness and mildness of Christ—I who, when present, am humble among you, but when absent, am confident toward you. [Note: [Col. 0769] But I myself, Paul, beg you by the gentleness and mildness of Christ—I who in person am humble among you, but otherwise am confident toward you.] [Note: [Col. 0769] *ïk silba*: “I myself,” as in the complete Greek text.—*ïm*: “am,” as in the complete Greek text.—*aljar visands*: Castillion has added *jct.*; so in verse 11.]

And I ask that, when present, I may not be confident with the confidence with which I intend to dare against some who think that we walk according to the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0769] But I ask that I may not, when present, be confident with the confidence with which I think I shall dare against some who regard us as walking according to the flesh.] [Note: [Col. 0769] *bidjam*: Codex B has *bidjan*, which would correspond to the Greek; if *bidja* (“I ask”) were read.—*gatrauau*: Codex B has *gatraiau*. Castillion thought that *ai* had been written for *au* to avoid doubling the same diphthong; we very much doubt that this defense will commend itself to scholars.]

For although we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0769] For although we walk in the flesh, we do not fight according to the flesh.] For the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly, but powerful through God for the overthrow of strongholds. [Note: [Col. 0769] The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of fortifications.] [Note: [Col. 0769] *unsaris drauhtinassaus*: absent from the complete Greek text.]

We overthrow arguments and every lofty thing raised against the knowledge of God, and we take every thought captive into the obedience of Christ. [Note: [Col. 0769] Overthrowing arguments and every exalted thing against the knowledge of God, and taking every mind captive and leading it into the obedience of Christ.] [Note: [Col. 0769] *jah*: “and,” third; the complete Greek text has καί.—*tiuhandans*: “leading,” Greek.]

And we are ready to punish every disobedience when your obedience has been fulfilled. [Note: [Col. 0769] And being prepared to avenge every disobedience when your obedience has been completed.]

Do you look at what is before your eyes? If anyone trusts in himself that he belongs to Christ, let him consider this again within himself: that just as he belongs to Christ, so also do we. [Note: [Col. 0769] Do you see these things in person? If anyone is confident that he himself is Christ’s, let him consider again within himself that, just as he is Christ’s, so also are we.]

And even if I boast somewhat more about our authority, which the Lord gave us for building up and not for destroying you, I shall not be ashamed. [Note: [Col. 0769] But even if we boast somewhat more about our authority, which the Lord gave us for your building up and not for your destruction, we are not ashamed.] [Note: [Col. 0769] *sveþauh jabai*: “indeed, if,” corresponding to ἐάν τε, although the Gothic seems to have omitted καί; *sveþauh* serves to render enclitics elsewhere as well; see Romans VIII.9, where *sveþauh jabai* = εἴπερ. In place of *sveþauh*, *raihtis* is more often used in this sense; see the note at VIII.7.—Greek τε is generally not expressed in Gothic; see the note at Luke II.16.—*wa managizo*: “somewhat more,” with *gaaiviskonda*: “we shall be ashamed,” in the complete Greek text.]

So that we may not seem to be terrifying you through letters. [Note: [Col. 0769] So that we may not seem to terrify you through letters.] [Note: [Col. 0770] *þugkjaima*: “we may seem,” Greek δόξω.—*þlahsjandans*: “terrifying,” Greek ἐκφοβεῖν.]

“For the letters,” they say, “are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible.” [Note: [Col. 0769] For they say that the letters are weighty and powerful, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech despised.] [Note: [Col. 0770] *qiþand*: “they say,” Greek φησίν, as in all the Greek witnesses; Gothic and the Vulgate.—*sind*: “are,” as in all the Greek witnesses.—*qums*: so Codex B; Castillion has added *quma*.]

Let such a person consider this: whatever we are in word through letters when absent, such we shall also be in deed when present. [Note: [Col. 0769] Let such a person consider that, whatever we are in word through letters while absent, such we shall also be in deed when present.] [Note: [Col. 0770] *aljar visandans*: see the note at verse 1.]

For we do not dare to judge ourselves or compare ourselves with those who commend themselves; but they, measuring themselves by themselves and comparing themselves with themselves, do not understand. [Note: [Col. 0769] For we do not dare to judge ourselves or compare ourselves with those who commend themselves; but those who measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves do not understand.] [Note: [Col. 0770] *unsis silbans*: “ourselves,” as in the complete Greek text.—*du þaim*: “to those,” as in the complete Greek text.—*sik*: Codex B has *sik sik*; the same word is often repeated erroneously by scribal negligence, as above at VI.3 *ei ei*, below at XII.6 *aiþþau aiþþau*; see also the note at John IX.41. Even several words are found repeated through scribal negligence, as at Ephesians VI.9, where *jah jus fraujans* is written twice in Codex A.]

But we—according to the measure of the rule which God measured out to us, a measure extending even to you. [Note: [Col. 0769] But we, according to the measure of the rule which God measured out to us, a measure reaching even to you.] [Note: [Col. 0770] *veis*: at the beginning of the verse, the words corresponding to the Greek οὐχὶ εἰς τὰ ἄμετρα καυχησόμεθα (“shall we not boast beyond measure?”) are absent. While copying, the scribe omitted an entire line; afterward, seeing that the sense could not stand at all, he added *veis* (“we”) above the line; see also the note at IV.10.—*fairrinnandein*: “extending to,” Greek ἐφικέσθαι.]

For we do not stretch ourselves beyond you, as though we did not reach you; for we have reached even you in the gospel of Christ. [Note: [Col. 0769] For, unlike those who do not reach as far as you, we extend ourselves abundantly; for we have reached even you in the gospel of Christ.]

Not boasting beyond measure in the labors of others, but having hope, as your faith grows in you, that we shall be enlarged according to our rule in abundance. [Note: [Col. 0771] Not boasting in the labors of others, but having hope that, as your faith grows in you, we shall be enlarged according to our rule toward abundance.] [Note: [Col. 0771] *habam*: “we have,” Greek ἔχοντες.]

So that we may preach the gospel beyond you, not boasting in what has already been prepared through the labors of others. [Note: [Col. 0771] So as to preach the gospel beyond you, not boasting about what has been prepared through the labors of others.] [Note: [Col. 0771] *ufairjaina*: this is printed with Castillion’s and Junius’s *jct.*; perhaps it should more correctly be written *ufar jaina*, as at XI.5 *ufar mikil* (ὑπερλίαν).—*arbaidim*: “labors,” Greek κανόνι, which now appears to have come here from the preceding verse.]

But “the one who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0771] But the one who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.] For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends. [Note: [Col. 0771] For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.] [Note: [Col. 0771] *gakusans*: Codex B has *gakusands*; see the note at Luke X.2.]

Would that you would bear with a little of my foolishness—but indeed, bear with me. [Note: [Col. 0771] Would that you would endure a little of my foolishness; but indeed, endure me.] [Note: [Col. 0771] *meinaizos—unfrodeins*: “my foolishness,” Greek μου—ἀφροσύνῃ, and *wa* “what,” Greek τι.]

For I am jealous over you with God’s jealousy, since I betrothed you to one man, as a pure virgin, to present you to Christ. [Note: [Col. 0771] For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God, since I betrothed you to one man, a pure girl, to present you to Christ.] [Note: [Col. 0771] *aljanonds*: “being jealous,” Greek ζηλῶ, in all Greek witnesses and the Gothic and Latin versions.—*du usgaban*: Castillion has added *jct.*; without doubt, in place of *usgaban*, which Castillion says can clearly be read in the codex, *usgiban* should be read; see Romans XII.1.]

But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your minds may somehow be corrupted from the simplicity and purity that are in Christ. [Note: [Col. 0771] But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, your minds may be corrupted from this simplicity and purity in Christ.] [Note: [Col. 0771] *seinai*: the Gothic and codices have οὕτω, “thus.”—*jah sviknein*: “and purity,” as in the Greek witnesses.]

For if the one who comes preaches another Jesus whom we did not preach, or you receive another spirit which you did not receive, or another gospel which you did not accept, you put up with it well enough. [Note: [Col. 0771] If the one who comes preaches another Jesus whom we did not preach, or you receive another spirit which you did not receive, or another gospel which you did not accept, you bear with it well.] [Note: [Col. 0771] *jabai*: the Gothic has μέν, “indeed.”—*veis*: “we,” as in all the Greek witnesses.—*ahman*: Codex B has *ahma*; Castillion has already placed the true reading in the text, as shortly afterward *aivaggeljon* instead of Codex B’s false reading *aivaggeljo*.—*nemuþ*: present, “you receive,” Greek λαμβάνετε; the past translation does not suit us, but this appears to have been written by the scribe rather than by the translator, whose eye wandered to the following occurrence of the same verb.]

For I think that I am not inferior in anything to those “super-apostles.” [Note: [Col. 0771] For I think that I do nothing less than those who are apostles above measure.] [Note: [Col. 0771] *visandam*: “existing,” as in all the Greek witnesses.—*apaustaulum*: Codex B has *apauslum*; see the note at John XVIII.15.]

Even if I am untrained in speech, I am not so in knowledge; but in every way we have made this evident among all and toward you. [Note: [Col. 0771] I am untrained in speech, but not in knowledge; nevertheless, in every way I have manifested myself in all things to you.] [Note: [Col. 0772] *jabai*: Gothic has δέ καί, “but also.”—*ïm*: “am,” as in all the Greek witnesses.—*gabairhtida*: “I manifested,” namely “myself,” Greek φανερωθέντες; perhaps *gabairhtidai* (“having been manifested”) should be read.]

Or did I commit a sin by humbling myself, so that you might be exalted, because I preached the gospel of God to you without payment? [Note: [Col. 0771] Or did I commit a sin by humbling myself, so that you might be exalted, because I preached the gospel of God to you without payment?] [Note: [Col. 0772] *ïbai*: “or,” as in all the Greek witnesses; Gothic and the Vulgate.]

I robbed other churches, receiving support for your ministry, and while present with you and in need, I was not a burden to anyone. [Note: [Col. 0771] I despoiled other churches, receiving provisions for your ministry, and while I was with you and in need, I was not a burden to anyone.] [Note: [Col. 0772] *ïzvis*: “you,” which Codex B has, seems to us false; through the same error the scribe of Codex A wrote *þe* instead of *jaþþe* at 5.9. Grimm thought the codex reading not entirely contemptible, but Castillion has now restored *ïzvis* to the text.—*ainnohun kaurida*: “I burdened anyone,” corresponding to the complete Greek text.]

For the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my needs; and in everything I kept myself from being burdensome to you, and I will keep myself so. [Note: [Col. 0771] For the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my needs; and in everything I kept myself from burdening you, and I will keep myself so.] [Note: [Col. 0772] *ïn allaim unkaureinom*: “in everything without burdens.” Castillion and Grimm, treating *unkaureinom* as an adverb, are mistaken. Even if it be admitted that it could be an adverb, its form seems unusual to Castillion, nor could Grimm support it with another example. The construction of the words is also opposed to this: since *ïn allaim* represents Greek ἐν παντί, Gothic never uses it in this way, it must be connected with *unkaureinom*, the dative plural; compare Grimm I.605. The complete Greek text has ἀβαρῆ, which is not a neuter standing absolutely, but masculine and referring to the following ἐμαυτόν.]

As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia. Why? [Note: [Col. 0771] The truth of Christ is in me, because this boasting is not obstructed in me in the land of Achaia; for what reason?] Because I do not love you? God knows. [Note: [Col. 0771] Because I do not love you? God knows.] [Note: [Col. 0771] *fraujins*: Gothic and the codices have ἡμῶν, “our.”—*sa*: Gothic has ὤν, “being.”]

But what I do, I will also continue to do, so that I may cut off the opportunity of those who desire an opportunity, so that in what they boast they may be found just like us. [Note: [Col. 0771] But what I do and will do is so that I may cut off the opportunity of those who desire an opportunity, so that in what they boast they may be found as we are.]

For such people are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. [Note: [Col. 0771] For such people are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ.] And it is no wonder, for Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light. [Note: [Col. 0771] And it is not a great wonder, for Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light.] [Note: [Col. 0772] *nist*: “it is not,” Greek οὐ; so also in verse 15.—*aggillau*: Codex B has this form instead of *aggilau*; see the note at Galatians V.15.]

Therefore it is no great thing if his ministers also disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness. Their end will be according to their works. [Note: [Col. 0771] It is not a great thing, then, if his ministers also disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness, whose end will be according to their works.] [Note: [Col. 0772] *nist*: see the note at verse 14.—*mikil*: the Gothic and codices have Greek οὖν, “therefore,” at [Col. 0773].—*jabai*: the Gothic and Codex 9, according to Mill, have Greek καί, “also.”—*bi*: because a gap in the parchment has produced a lacuna at this point, Castillion supplied this little word by conjecture.]

Again I say: let no one think that I am foolish; but if not, at least accept me as foolish, so that I too may boast a little. [Note: [Col. 0773] Again I say, so that no one may think me foolish; otherwise, receive me indeed as foolish, so that I too may boast a little.] [Note: [Col. 0773] *unfrondana*: preliminary; Gothic has εἶναι, “to be”; see the note at Romans XV.8.—*vaila þau*: “well indeed,” Greek οὖν. Although it has a concessive force, *vaila þau* seems poorly suited to the Greek. If the reading is genuine, the Goth apparently misunderstood κἄν and took it for καὶ ἄν, apparently meaning our “yet, indeed, at least” (French *encore, mais bien, au moins*); compare Luke XVI.4. Even so, *vaila* is idle unless it is regarded as a synonym added to *þau*. We lack passages that establish such usage. *vaila* has a somewhat similar meaning in the margin of Codex A at 1 Corinthians IX.12, where it represents πάντως.]

What I am saying, I am not saying according to the Lord, but as in foolishness, in this matter of boasting. [Note: [Col. 0773] What I am saying, I am not saying according to the Lord, but as in foolishness, in this substance of this boasting.]

Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast. [Note: [Col. 0773] Because many boast according to the flesh, I too boast.] For you gladly put up with the foolish, being wise yourselves. [Note: [Col. 0773] For you willingly endure the ignorant, being wise yourselves.]

For you tolerate it if someone enslaves you, if someone devours you, if someone takes from you, if someone exalts himself, if someone strikes you in the face. [Note: [Col. 0773] You endure it if someone enslaves you, if someone devours you, if someone takes from you, if someone leads you into labor, if someone strikes you in the face.] [Note: [Col. 0773] *usþulaiþ*: Gothic has γάρ, “for.”—*ïn arbaidai briggiþ*: “leads into labor.” Although this circumlocution does not correspond word-for-word to Greek ἐπαίρεται, no one will persuade us that the Goth perhaps read ἐπηρεάζει. No Greek witness reads that verb here, and, even if it did, the Gothic words would not adequately express its meaning.]

I speak with shame, as though we had been weak; but in whatever anyone dares—in foolishness I speak—I dare also. [Note: [Col. 0773] I speak according to dishonor, as though we had been weak; but in whatever anyone dares, I speak in foolishness; I dare also.] [Note: [Col. 0773] *we*: unless written by scribal error in place of *wa*, this pronoun, which Gothic often adds against the authority of the Greek (see XII.6 and 18), should be judged to stand for Greek ἄν. Apart from *weh* (“only,” Galatians VI.12; Philippians I.27), however, this particle is found nowhere else, nor does Gothic usually render ἄν after relative pronouns.]

They are Hebrews? So am I. They are Israelites? So am I. They are Abraham’s offspring? So am I. [Note: [Col. 0773] They are Hebrews? So am I. They are Israelites? So am I. They are Abraham’s seed? So am I.]

They are ministers of Christ—as though beside myself I speak—I am more. [Note: [Col. 0773] They are ministers of Christ—as one untrained I speak—I am more.] In more labors, more abundantly in prisons, in beatings beyond measure, often in deaths. [Note: [Col. 0773] In more labors, in prisons abundantly, in beatings abundantly, often in deaths.] [Note: [Col. 0774] *svasve*: “as,” as in the complete Greek text and the Gothic and Vulgate.—*karkarom—slahim*: the complete Greek text and the Gothic and Vulgate.]

From the Jews I received five times forty less one. [Note: [Col. 0773] From the Jews I received five times forty lashes less one.] Three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; three times I suffered shipwreck; I spent a night and a day in the depths of the sea. [Note: [Col. 0773] Three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; three times I made a journey from a ship; night and day I was in the depth of the sea.] [Note: [Col. 0774] *mareins*: “of the sea,” as in all the Greek witnesses and the Gothic and Vulgate.]

Often on journeys: dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my people, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers. [Note: [Col. 0773] Often on journeys, in dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my race, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the desert, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers.]

In labors and hardships, in many sleepless nights, in hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold and nakedness. [Note: [Col. 0773] In afflictions and labors, often in vigils, in hunger and thirst, often in fasts, in cold and nakedness.] [Note: [Col. 0774] At the beginning, the Gothic and codices have ἐν, “in.”—*aglom—arbaidim*: “afflictions—labors,” as in the complete Greek text, which has the singular number for κόπῳ—μόχθῳ.—*naqadein*: so Codex B; Castillion has added *naqadin*.]

Besides these things, there is the daily pressure upon me: concern for all the churches. [Note: [Col. 0773] In addition to these things, my labor is continual, my concern for all the churches.] [Note: [Col. 0774] *meina*: “my,” second; as in the complete Greek text.—*seiteina*: so Codex B instead of *sinteina* (Matthew VI.11). Grimm, *W. J.* p. 202, judges *seiteins* to be a corrupt reading, because the Gothic language does not permit the elision of the consonant *n*.]

Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn? [Note: [Col. 0773] Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is troubled, and I do not burn?] [Note: [Col. 0774] *tundnau*: so Codex B; Castillion has added *tundvjau*.]

If I must boast, I will boast of the things belonging to my weakness. [Note: [Col. 0773] If boasting is necessary, I will boast of the things of my weakness.]

The God and Father of the Lord Jesus knows—he who is blessed forever—that I am not lying. [Note: [Col. 0773] God and the Father of the Lord Jesus knows, he who is blessed forever, that I do not lie.] [Note: [Col. 0774] *fraujins*: Gothic and the codices have ἡμῶν, “our.”—*sa*: Gothic has ὤν, “being.”]

In Damascus, the governor under King Aretas guarded the city of the Damascenes, wishing to seize me. [Note: [Col. 0773] In Damascus, the governor of the people under King Aretas guarded the city of Damascus, wishing to seize me.] [Note: [Col. 0774] *baurg damaskai*: “city of the Damascenes,” Greek Δαμασκηνῶν πόλιν. Castillion, not knowing that *damaskai* was an adjectival form, preferred to read *damaskaie*.]

And through a window I was lowered in a basket through the wall, and I escaped his hands. [Note: [Col. 0773] And through a window, in a basket, I was lowered through the wall and escaped his hands.] [Note: [Col. 0774] *handuns*: Codex B has *handus*.]

It is necessary to boast, although it is not advantageous; for I will come to visions and revelations of the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0773] It is necessary to boast, but it is not advantageous; for I also come to visions and revelations of the Lord.] [Note: [Col. 0774] *woþan—ïst*: “it is necessary to boast,” Greek καυχᾶσθαι δὴ οὐ συμφέρει μοι; for this, the Gothic, the versions, and Syriac appear to have read καυχᾶσθαι δεῖ, ἀλλ’ οὐ συμφέρει. The text of Codex A continues *andhuleinins*.]

I know a man in Christ fourteen years ago—whether in the body, I do not know, or outside the body, I do not know; God knows—that such a one was caught up to the third heaven. [Note: [Col. 0773] I know a man in Christ fourteen years ago, whether in the body, I do not know, or outside the body, I do not know; God knows; such a one was caught up to the third heaven.] [Note: [Col. 0774] *fidvortaihune*: Codex B has *vidvortaihune*, Codex A *id*. The remarkable construction of the numeral, which Castillion had previously confirmed elsewhere, at Galatians II.1, has now been printed there according to the true reading of the codex, *bi fidvortaihun jera*. Therefore here too, after deleting the final *e*, one should read *fidvortaihun*. Grimm’s attempt to make *fidvortaihune* an accusative of some neuter plural is consequently futile.—*ïnuh*: Codex A has *ïnu*, as in the following verse.]

And I know that such a man—whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows—was caught up into paradise and heard ineffable words which a human being is not permitted to speak. [Note: [Col. 0775] And I know such a man, whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows, who was caught up into paradise and heard ineffable words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak.]

About such a one I will boast; but about myself I will boast nothing except in my weaknesses. [Note: [Col. 0775] About such a person I boast, but about myself I boast nothing except in my weaknesses.] [Note: [Col. 0775] *vaht*: “anything,” as in the complete Greek text.]

For if I wish to boast, I shall not be foolish, for I speak the truth; but I refrain, so that no one may think more of me than what he sees or hears from me. [Note: [Col. 0775] *wa*: “what,” omitted in the complete Greek text.—*saiwiþ*: the Gothic, with Codices 6 and 9 according to Mill, has Greek με.—*aiþþau*: Codex A has *aiþþau aiþþau*; see the note at X.12.] [Note: [Col. 0775] But if I wish to boast, I shall not be ignorant, for I speak the truth; yet I refrain, lest anyone think something about me beyond what he sees or hears.]

And because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, so that I might not be exalted, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to strike me, so that I might not become arrogant. [Note: [Col. 0775] And according to the abundance of the revelations, so that I might not be exalted, a thorn was given to my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me, so that I might not become proud.] [Note: [Col. 0775] *hnuto*: Codex A has *hnuþo* and in the margin *gairu*.—*meinamma*: “my,” as in all the Greek witnesses.]

Three times I appealed to the Lord concerning this, that it might depart from me; and he said to me: [Note: [Col. 0775] Three times I appealed to the Lord, that it might depart from me; and he said to me:] [Note: [Col. 0775] *fraujan*: so Codex A; Codex B has *frauja*.]

“My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast more gladly in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell upon me. [Note: [Col. 0775] My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weaknesses. Therefore I will boast very gladly in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell upon me.] [Note: [Col. 0775] *mahts*: the Gothic and codices have μοῦ, “my.”—*siukeim*: “in weaknesses”; Codex A, with all the Greek witnesses, has *siukein*, “in weakness.”]

Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in insults, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses, for Christ; for when I am weak, then I am powerful. [Note: [Col. 0775] In which I take pleasure: in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ; for when I am weak, then I am powerful.] [Note: [Col. 0775] *þreihslam*: so Codex A; Codex B has *þleihslam*—for that is what is written, not *þleihsham*, where Castillion, in his note on this passage, does not say *þleihsam*, as Massmann says at *Skeir* p.182. We have now preferred the reading of Codex A because it has the verb *þreihan*, by which it can be supported, whereas *þleihst* lacks all support. Grimm likewise, in the cited passage p.187, thinks the reading of Codex B arose from scribal error.]

I have become foolish; you compelled me. For I ought to have been commended by you, since I was in no way inferior to those super-apostles, even if I am nothing. [Note: [Col. 0775] I have become foolish in boasting; you compelled me. Yet I ought to have been commended by you, for I was in no way inferior to those who are apostles above measure, even though I am nothing.] [Note: [Col. 0775] *woþands*: “boasting,” Greek.—*jah jabai*: corresponding to the complete Greek text; see the note at VII.8.]

The signs of an apostle were indeed performed among you with all endurance: signs, wonders, and mighty deeds. [Note: [Col. 0775] Moreover, the signs of an apostle were performed among you in all endurance, in signs, wonders, and powers.] [Note: [Col. 0775] *aiþþau sveþauh*: “moreover indeed,” so both codices; the Greek has only μέν, “indeed,” so *aiþþau* is excessive. Some codices read otherwise, but none of those readings is suited to Gothic *aiþþau*. If the Goth had read ἀλλ’ ἤ with some others, he would certainly have written *alja*; see the note at I.13. Castillion, also offended by the codex reading, conjectured *aþþan sveþauh*, by which Greek πλήν is translated, Luke XIX.37, Philippians III.26; compare Romans IX.6. Although it does not exactly agree with the Greek words, it does not overturn the sense. The combination *aiþþau sveþauh* is found nowhere else.—*apaustaulaus*: Codex A has *apaustaulus*; concerning this variation, see the note at Luke I.54.—*þulainai*: Gothic and the codices have ἐν, “in.”]

For what is it in which you were inferior to the other churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong. [Note: [Col. 0775] For what is it in which you were inferior to the other churches, except that I myself did not burden you?] [Note: [Col. 0776] *þize*: see the note at Luke X.5.—*ïk silba*: “I myself,” as in all the Greek witnesses.]

Behold, this is the third time I am ready to come to you, and I will not burden you; for I do not seek your possessions, but you. For children ought not to store up wealth for their parents, but parents for their children. [Note: [Col. 0775] Behold, this is the third time I am ready to come to you and will not burden you, for I do not seek what belongs to you, but you; children are not obliged to gather wealth for their parents, but parents for their children.] [Note: [Col. 0776] *jah ni*: Codex A has *jan-ni*.]

And I will very gladly spend and be spent for your souls, even if, loving you more abundantly, I am loved less. [Note: [Col. 0775] But I will gladly spend and be spent for your souls, although, loving you abundantly, I am loved less.] [Note: [Col. 0776] *gabaurjaba*: Codex A has *laþaleiko*; the marginal reading is that of Codex B.—*sveþauh ei*: “even though,” Greek εἰ καί.—*minz*: Codex A has *mins*.]

But let it be so: I did not burden you; yet, being crafty, I caught you by deceit. [Note: [Col. 0775] But behold, I did not burden you; nevertheless, being perhaps crafty, I caught you by deceit.] [Note: [Col. 0776] *aþþan sai nu*: “but behold now,” as though the Goth had read νυνὶ δέ; see VIII.22 and the note at Romans VII.6. Since all the Greek witnesses read ἔστω δέ, perhaps *siai* (*sijai*) should be written; Grimm also judges so, *Grammar* III.247. *nu* has no equivalent in the complete Greek text.—*aufto*: “perhaps,” as in all the Greek witnesses.]

Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? [Note: [Col. 0775] Did I deceive you through anyone of those whom I sent to you?] [Note: [Col. 0776] *þairh wana*: “through someone,” Greek τινα δι’ αὐτοῦ, as in the Gothic and Vulgate.]

I appealed to Titus and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not walk in the same spirit? Did we not follow the same footsteps? [Note: [Col. 0775] I appealed to Titus and sent the brother with him. Did Titus deceive you? Did we not walk in the same spirit? Did we not follow the same footsteps?] [Note: [Col. 0776] *ïmma*: “with him,” as in all the Greek witnesses except Codex d according to Mill.—*wa*: Gothic adds this against the authority of the Greek, or perhaps read μὴ τι rather than μήτι.—*laistim*: Codex B has *laustim*; see *Skeir* 40.19; 45.9.]

Again, do you think that we defend ourselves against you? In the presence of God, in … [source ends] [Note: [Col. 0777] Do you think again that we are defending ourselves before you? We speak before God in Christ; and all this, beloved, is for your building up.] [Note: [Col. 0777] *þugkeiþ*: correctly so in Codex A; Codex B has *þukeiþ*.—*sunjoma*: correctly so in Codex A; Codex B has *sunjodama*. [Note: [Col. 0777] For I fear that, when I come, I may perhaps not find you such as I wish, and that I may be found by you such as you do not wish me to be—perhaps anger, jealousy, hostility, quarrels, slanders, whisperings, deceptions, swellings, seditions.] [Note: [Col. 0777] *mik*: “me,” as in all the Greek witnesses.—*aljan*: “jealousy,” Greek ζῆλοι, as at Galatians V.20.—*haifsteis*: Codex B has *hafsteis*; see Romans XIII.13 and *Skeir* 44.22 and following.—*bifaiha ufsvalleinos*: Codex B has *bifaiha*; we added the form from Codex A. The first of these words—which Castillion correctly supplied with an initial *b*, faded in the codex—is omitted by all the Greek witnesses; the second is acknowledged by all. Concerning *bifaiha*, note that here it is the neuter form *bifaih*, whereas elsewhere it is usually *bifaiho*.]

Christ speaking. But all this, beloved, is for your edification. For I fear lest perhaps, when I come again, I may find you not such as I wish, and I may be found by you such as you do not wish me to be: lest perhaps there be strife, jealousy, anger, contentions, slanderings, whisperings, conceits, disturbances.

[Note: [Col. 0777] “Lest, when I come again, God humble me among you, and I mourn many of those who have sinned before and have not repented of the impurity which they committed, of fornication, and of licentiousness.”]

[Note: “God”: all the Greek witnesses place it after *gahaunjai*; moreover, the Gothic agrees with the manuscripts in omitting *mou* (“my”) and the immediately preceding *me*.—“And not”: codex A has *jan-ni*.—“Those who committed”: all Greek witnesses omit this after *aglaitja*; later the Gothic omits *kai* (“and”).—“Impurity”: thus codex A; codex B has *aglaiteino*, for which Massmann’s conjecture *aglaiteinom* cannot be approved, since the nominative form is not *aglaiteins* but *aglaitei* (Mark 7:22; Eph. 4:19; cf. 2 Cor. 4:4). If *aglaitein* had been written, we should have the correct reading; but there is now no place for the genitive.]

Lest, when I come again, God humble me among you, and I mourn many of those who have sinned before and have not repented of the impurity which they committed, and of fornication and licentiousness.

[Note: [Col. 0777] “This is the third time that I am coming to you: at the mouth of two witnesses and three every word shall stand.”]

[Note: “And three”: codex A, *jaþ-þrije*.—“Shall stand”: codex A, *gastandiþ* (“stands”).]

This is the third time that I am coming to you: “At the mouth of two witnesses and three every word shall stand.”

[Note: [Col. 0777] “I have said beforehand and I say beforehand again, as when present the second time, and now, being absent, I write to those who have sinned before and to all the others, that if I come again I shall not spare.”]

[Note: “Again”: omitted by all Greek witnesses; the Gothic agrees with the Armenian version.—“I write”: omitted by the Greek.]

I have said beforehand and I say beforehand again, as when present the second time, and now, being absent, I write to those who have sinned before and to all the others, that if I come again I shall not spare.

[Note: [Col. 0777] “For you seek proof of Christ speaking in me, who is not weak among you, but is mighty among you.”]

[Note: “You seek this”: thus rightly codex A and Castiglione; codex B has *sokeiþis*; see 2 Cor. 3:2.—“Among you”: all Greek witnesses place it before “does not.”—“Is weak”: codex A, *siukiþ*.]

For you seek proof of Christ speaking in me, who is not weak among you, but is mighty among you.

[Note: [Col. 0777] “But if he was crucified from weakness, yet he lives by the power of God; for we also are weak in him, yet we shall live with him by the power of God among you.”]

[Note: [Col. 0778] “If”: codex A, with the Greek, adds *jah* (“also”).—“For”: codex A, with the Greek, adds *veis* (“we”).]

For although he was crucified from weakness, yet he lives by the power of God; for we also are weak in him, yet we shall live with him by the power of God among you.

[Note: [Col. 0777] “Test yourselves whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves. Or do you not know yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you? Unless indeed you are rejected.”]

[Note: [Col. 0778] “Among you”: the first occurrence is omitted by codex A.—“Test yourselves”: thus codex A; codex B has *fragiþ*. We judged, with Grimm, *W. J.*, p. 210, that the former reading is to be preferred, because not only is the form *fragan* unheard of, but, even if it were Gothic, it would not yield the sense conveyed by the Greek text.—“Be”: Castiglione adds *sigaidu*.—“Yet”: codex A, *þau*.—“You”: the third occurrence is omitted by codex B.—“Unless”: codex A, *nibai* (“unless”).]

Test yourselves whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves. Or do you not know yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you? Unless indeed you are rejected.

[Note: [Col. 0777] “But I hope that you will know that we are not rejected.”]

[Note: [Col. 0778] “That … may”: codex A reverses the order: *þatei* … *ei*.—“We are”: codex A, *sium*.]

But I hope that you will know that we are not rejected.

[Note: [Col. 0777] “But I pray to God that you may do nothing evil—not that we may appear approved, but that you may do what is good, even though we may appear rejected.”]

[Note: [Col. 0778] “Anything … do”: corresponding to all Greek witnesses; the Gothic agrees with the Vulgate.—“Rejected”: codex A has *ungakusanai* (“rejected”), with the Lincoln codex cited by Mill.—“But that”: Castiglione adds *jct.*—“That we”: “that we,” all Greek witnesses: *hēmeis de hōs*, followed by codex A, which reads *ïþ veis sve* (“but we as”).—“May appear”: the Greek has *ōmen* (“we may be”).]

But we pray to God that you may do nothing evil—not that we may appear approved, but that you may do what is good, even though we may appear rejected.

[Note: [Col. 0777] “For we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth.”]

[Note: [Col. 0778] “We can”: thus the codices; Castiglione adds *mageim*.]

For we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth.

[Note: [Col. 0777] “But we rejoice when we are weak and you are strong; and this also we pray for: your perfection.”]

[Note: [Col. 0778] “May be”: codex A, *siuþ*.]

But we rejoice when we are weak and you are strong; and this also we pray for: your perfection.

[Note: [Col. 0777] “Therefore I write these things while absent, so that when present I may not act harshly, according to the authority which the Lord gave me for edification and not for destruction.”]

[Note: [Col. 0778] “Harshly”: codex A, *hardaba*; both forms are correct, just as both *glaggvaba* and *glaggvuba* are used.—“The Lord”: omitted by the Greek after “to me.”—“And not”: codex A, *jan-ni*.]

Therefore I write these things while absent, so that when present I may not act harshly, according to the authority which the Lord gave me for edification and not for destruction.

[Note: [Col. 0777–0779] “For the rest, brethren, rejoice; be perfected, be encouraged, think the same thing, be makers of peace; and the God of peace and love shall be with you.”]

[Note: [Col. 0778] “This”: see 1 Cor. 1:16.—“Be perfected”: omitted by codex B; we have supplied it from codex A. For the rest, brethren, rejoice; be perfected, be encouraged, think the same thing, be makers of peace; and the God of peace and love shall be with you.

[Note: [Col. 0779] “Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you.”]

[Note: “Holy love”: corresponding to the Greek.]

Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you.

[Note: [Col. 0779] “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit, be with all of you. Amen.”]

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit, be with all of you. Amen.

To the Corinthians, the Second Epistle ends. To the Corinthians II was written from Philippi in Macedonia.

Subscription: *du—ustauh*: omitted in all the Greek manuscripts; moreover, in place of [Col. 0780] *kaurinþaium anþara*, codex A has *kaurinþium ·b·*. “The Second [Epistle] to the Corinthians ends. To Corinthians II: it was written from Philippi in Macedonia.”

**TO THE GALATIANS.** [Note: [Col. 0779] Heading: The Epistle begins abruptly, without a title. CAST.]

[Col. 0779]

[Note: [Col. 0781] For if I rebuild what I destroyed, I establish myself as a transgressor.] [Note: [Col. 0782] *missataujandan*] Codex A and Cast. add *missataujandin*.] For if I rebuild what I destroyed, I establish myself as a transgressor. [Note: [Col. 0781] For through the law I died to the law, that I might live to God,] For through the law I died to the law, that I might live to God.

And the life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.] [Note: [Col. 0782] *nu*] “Now,” omitted by all Greek manuscripts. — *sunus*] Thus codex A and Cast. for *sunaus*; see Luke I.54.] I was crucified with Christ; yet I live, no longer I, but Christ lives in me. [Note: [Col. 0781] I do not set aside the grace of God; for if righteousness is through the law, then indeed Christ died in vain.] [Note: [Col. 0782] *aiþþau jah*] “Then indeed,” Greek ἄρα; thus *aiþþau* also occurs in the second member of conditional sentences followed by the indicative at 1 Cor. IX.2, where the Greek has ἀλλάγε; cf. 2 Cor. IV.16.] I do not set aside the grace of God; for if righteousness is through the law, then indeed Christ died in vain.

[Col. 0783] [Note: [Col. 0783] O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you not to obey the truth? You before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified among you?] [Note: [Col. 0783] *sunjai ni ufhausjan*] “Not to obey the truth,” omitted by the Greek.] O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you not to obey the truth—you before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly set forth as crucified among you? [Note: [Col. 0783] Did you suffer so much in vain? If indeed it was in vain.] [Note: [Col. 0783] *aþþan jabai*] “If indeed,” Greek εἴγε; thus the particle γε is translated by *aþþan*; cf. [Note: [Col. 0783] Just as Abraham also believed God. ———] [Note: [Col. 0783] *jah*] “Also,” omitted by the Greek.] Just as Abraham also believed God. ———

[Note: [Col. 0783] For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.] For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ. John X.30; XVII.22.] There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female; for you all are one in Christ Jesus. [Note: [Col. 0783] And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promises.] [Note: [Col. 0783] *gahaitam*] “Promises,” while all Greek manuscripts have ἐπαγγελίαν. — *arbjans*] Codex A adds *abrjans*.] And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promises.

[Note: [Col. 0783] But I say: for as long as the heir is a child, he differs in no respect from a slave, though he is lord of all,] But I say: as long as the heir is a child, he differs in no way from a slave, though he is lord of all, [Note: [Col. 0783] but he is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by his father.] [Note: [Col. 0783] So also we, when we were children, were enslaved under the elements of this world.] [Note: [Col. 0783] *uf—fairwaus*] In the margin of codex A: *uf tugglam* (“under the stars”); these words should be considered a gloss rather than a variant reading, for Augustine with other Fathers understands “the elements of the world” here as the heavenly bodies. [Note: [Col. 0783] But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law,] But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law, [Note: [Col. 0783] that he might redeem those under the law, that they might receive adoption as sons.] [Note: [Col. 0783] *usbauhtedi ei*] Cast. has *usbauhtidedi ei*. But since Cast. admits that the final two letters are uncertain, perhaps he wrote *usbauhtide* for *usbauhtedi*; cf. Luke XIV.29. — *sunive sibja*] Cast. adds *jct.*] that he might redeem those under the law, so that they might receive the status of sons. [Note: [Col. 0783] And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, “Abba, Father!”] [Note: [Col. 0783] *jus*] “You,” omitted by the Greek. — *guþs*] “Of God,” omitted by the Greek. — *ïzvara*] [Col. 0784] “Your,” while the Greek has ἡμῶν (“our”).] And because you are sons of God, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying: “Abba, Father!” [Note: [Col. 0783] Therefore you are no longer a slave, but a son; and if a son, an heir of God through Christ.] [Note: [Col. 0784] *skalks*] Gothic omits ἀλλ᾽ υἱός (“but a son”); Cast. already saw that this omission was due to the scribe’s fault; but he is mistaken in saying that the scribe omitted εἰ δὲ υἱός.] Therefore you are no longer a slave, but a son, and an heir of God through Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0783] But then, not knowing God, you served those which by nature are not gods;] [Note: [Col. 0784] *vistai ni*] Beside the Greek. — *skalkinodeduþ*] All Greek manuscripts place this before *þaim*; Gothic agrees with the Vulgate.] But then, not knowing God, you served those which by nature are not gods. [Note: [Col. 0783] But now, behold, knowing God—or rather, being known by God—how have you turned again to these weak and miserable elements, to which you wish again anew to be enslaved?] [Note: [Col. 0784] *ïþ nu sai*] See on Rom. VII.6.] But now, behold, knowing God—or rather being known by God—how have you turned again to the weak and miserable elements, to which you wish anew to be enslaved? [Note: [Col. 0783] You observe days and months and seasons and years!] [Note: [Col. 0784] *melam*] Since all Greek manuscripts read καιρούς in the plural, Cast., though unable to determine whether *melam* or *mela* was read because of an erasure in the parchment, ought not to have doubted that his edition was correct.] You observe days, months, seasons, and years! [Note: [Col. 0783] I fear for you, lest I have laboured among you in vain.] [Note: [Col. 0784] *arbaididedjau*] Codex A and Cast. have *arbaidedidjau*; see on John XVIII.36.] I fear for you, lest I have laboured among you in vain.

[Note: [Col. 0783] Become as I am, for I also became as you are, brothers. I beseech you: you have done me no wrong.] [Note: [Col. 0784] *aþþan*] “But,” omitted by all Greek manuscripts.] Become as I am, for I also am as you are, brothers. I beseech you: you have done me no wrong. [Note: [Col. 0783] You know that through weakness of the flesh I preached the gospel to you at the first,] [Note: [Col. 0784] *vituþ*] Gothic agrees with manuscripts omitting δέ. — *siukein*] Marginal reading in codex A: *unmaht* (“weakness”).] You know that through weakness of the flesh I preached the gospel to you at first; [Note: [Col. 0783] and you did not despise or reject my trial in my flesh, but received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.] [Note: [Col. 0784] *fraistubnjai*] Gothic agrees with manuscripts omitting μου (“my”).] and you did not despise or reject the trial in my flesh, but received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus. [Note: [Col. 0783] What then was your blessedness? For I testify to you that, if it had been possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me.] [Note: [Col. 0784] *vas nu*] Beside the Greek. — *vesi*] “It were,” omitted by all Greek manuscripts.] What then was your blessedness? For I testify to you that, if possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me. [Note: [Col. 0783] So then, have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?] [Col. 0785] [Note: [Col. 0784] *ïþ nu sve*] “So then,” Greek ὥστε.] So then, have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?

[Col. 0785] [Note: [Col. 0785] They are zealous for you, not honourably; rather, they want to exclude you, so that you may be zealous for them.] They are zealous for you, not honourably; rather, they want to exclude you, so that you may be zealous for them. [Note: [Col. 0785] But it is good to be zealous in what is good always, and not only when I am present with you.] [Note: [Col. 0785] *ïst*] “Is,” omitted by all Greek manuscripts.] But it is good to be zealous in what is good always, and not only when I am present with you. [Note: [Col. 0785] My little children, for whom I travail again until Christ is formed in you,] [Note: [Col. 0785] *þanzei*] Codex B continues. — *gabairhtjaidau*] “May be manifested”; all Greek manuscripts have μορφωθῇ, but Gothic, according to Cast., with the Ethiopic version, read φανερωθῇ. In the margin of codex A several words are written, which Cast., after much effort, could read approximately as: *d . . . . . laudjai gafrisah..naim*, and which he completed as *du laudjai gafrisahtnaim*. But first, he ought not to have called it a gloss: it is a variant reading, by which the scribe, or someone else, wished to translate the Greek μορφωθῇ literally. Nor do we approve his proposed completion, not only because it has no good sense, but also because in that case the marginal mark ought to stand after *ïzvis*, while it is correctly drawn above *gabairhtjaidau*. Finally, Castiglione’s interpretation, “deformed to excess,” even of his own reading, is wholly false. The matter seems rather to stand thus: whoever wished to translate μορφοῦσθαι had to use words conveying “be brought into a form,” and did so by writing *du ludjai gaf risahtnai ïn (ïzvis)*, i.e. “may he be conformed to an appearance in (you),” namely Christ. *Ludja*, whose proper meaning is πρόσωπον (“face,” Matt. VI.17), and whose synonym *vlits* is used at Phil. II.7 also for μορφή, may itself likewise be used for Greek μορφή. A bolder editor might even conjecture *skaunjai* instead of *ludjai*, since Gothic uses *guþaskaunei* and *ïbnaskaunis* at Phil. II.6 and III.21 for θεοῦ μορφή and σύμμορφος. Nothing supports *laudjai*; certainly it now has no place if Cast., with Grimm III.46, holds that suffix *-lauds* has a quantitative sense. — *xristaus*] Thus codex B; codex A and Cast. have *xristus*. On this variation between the codices, see Mark VII.32.] My little children, for whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you—[Note: [Col. 0785] but I wished to come to you now and change my tone, for I am perplexed about you.] but I wished to come to you now and change my tone, for I am perplexed about you.

[Note: [Col. 0785] Tell me, you who wish to be under the law: do you not hear the law?] [Note: [Col. 0785] *niu hauseiþ*] In the margin of codex A: *niu ussuggvuþ* (“have you not read?”), agreeing with the versions, οὐκ ἀναγινώσκετε.] Tell me, you who wish to be under the law: do you not hear the law? [Note: [Col. 0785] For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman.] [Note: [Col. 0785] *aihta sununs*] Beside the Greek.] For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman. [Note: [Col. 0785] But the one by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the one by the free woman was born through the promise.] [Note: [Col. 0786] *leika*] Codex A ends. — *gahaita*] It is not a plural, as Cast. thinks, for then *gahaitam* would be required; see III.29. Rather, it is a singular dative, which all Greek manuscripts also have.] But the one by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the one by the free woman was born through promise.

[Note: [Col. 0785] These things are allegorical; for these are the two covenants: one, indeed, from Mount Sinai, bearing children into slavery, which is Hagar.] [Note: [Col. 0786] *aljaleikaidos*] Thus codex B. Since it means “otherwise pleasing,” while the sense requires “spoken allegorically,” *aljaleikodos* would be expected.] These things are spoken allegorically; for they are the two covenants: one from Mount Sinai, bearing children into slavery, which is Hagar. [Note: [Col. 0785] Mount Sinai is in Arabia, adjoining the present Jerusalem; but she is enslaved with her children.] [Note: [Col. 0786] Beginning:] Gothic agrees with the manuscripts in omitting τὸ γὰρ Ἄγαρ. — *gamarko*] “Adjoining”; Greek συστοιχεῖ δέ. — *ïþ*] Cast. read *guþ* (i.e. *gþ*), because the space seemed to him larger than should occur between *ï* and *þ*. But since he himself admits that the upper stroke of the letter *g* is faint and uncertain, and since the sense absolutely excludes *guþ*, while *ïþ* is necessary to translate γάρ, we do not doubt that the manuscript has what we have printed. — *seinaim burnam*] Beside the Greek.] Now Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, adjoining the present Jerusalem; but she is enslaved with her children. [Note: [Col. 0785] But the Jerusalem above is free; she is our mother.] But the Jerusalem above is free; she is our mother.

[Note: [Col. 0785] For it is written: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail; for the children of the desolate woman are many more than those of her who has a husband.”] [Note: [Col. 0786] *anþjons*] Thus codex B; Cast. has *auþjos*. — *þau*] Thus codex B; Cast. has *þan*.] For it is written: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail; for the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband.” [Note: [Col. 0785] But we, brothers, are children according to the promise made to Isaac.] [Note: [Col. 0786] *bi ïsakis gahaita*] “According to the promise to Isaac,” i.e. the promise made to Isaac; all Greek manuscripts have κατὰ Ἰσαὰκ ἐπαγγελίας, governed by the following τέκνα.] But we, brothers, are children according to the promise made to Isaac. [Note: [Col. 0785] But as then the one born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the Spirit, so also now.] [Note: [Col. 0786] *þan svasve*] Beside the Greek. — *swah jah*] Thus in the codex, with either *jah* or enclitic *-h* apparently superfluous; see John XVIII.26; cf., however, below at VI.7, *þatuh jah*.] But as then the one born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the Spirit, so also now.

[Note: [Col. 0785] By the freedom with which Christ made us free, stand firm, therefore, and do not again submit to a yoke of slavery.] [Note: [Col. 0786] *þammei freihalsa*] “By the freedom by which,” Greek τῇ ἐλευθερίᾳ ᾗ; cf. [Note: [Col. 0785] Behold, I Paul say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you.] [Note: [Col. 0786] *bimaitiþ*] “You are circumcised,” i.e. you have yourselves circumcised; see on 1 Cor. XV.29.] Behold, I Paul say to you: if you are circumcised, Christ is of no benefit to you. Mark XV.6.] And I testify again to every circumcised man that he is obliged to perform the whole law. [Note: [Col. 0785] You are severed from Christ, you who declare yourselves righteous in the law; you have fallen from grace.] [Note: [Col. 0786] *garaihtans qiþiþ ïzvis*] After saying that Gothic translates “you are justified” as “the righteous,” Cast. then translated it “Christ speaks to you,” added that *qiþiþ ïzvis* is absent from all Greek, Latin, and other versions, and considered the words a gloss introduced into the text. We are surprised that this learned man did not see how aptly Gothic renders δικαιοῦσθε by *garaihtans qiþiþ ïzvis*, i.e. “you declare yourselves righteous”; cf. *garaihtana gateihan* = δικαιοῦν, Luke XVIII.14.] You are severed from Christ, you who declare yourselves righteous in the law; you have fallen away from grace. [Col. 0787] [Note: [Col. 0787] But we through the Spirit, by faith, await the hope of righteousness.] But we through the Spirit, by faith, await the hope of righteousness. [Note: [Col. 0787] For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any power, but faith working through love.] [Note: [Col. 0787] *xristu*] For *xristau*; see Luke I.54.] For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any power, but faith working through love.

[Note: [Col. 0787] You were running well. Who hindered you from obeying the truth?] You were running well. Who hindered you from obeying the truth? [Note: [Col. 0787] This persuasion is not from him who calls you.] [Note: [Col. 0787] *gakunds*] Cast. printed *gaku(nd)s*; rather he should have printed *gak(un)ds*, for the letters *un* do not appear in the codex. Yet there is no doubt that he rightly restored the faded letters, although *gakunds* occurs nowhere else. — *laþondin*] Codex B and Cast. have *laþodin*. — *ïst*] “Is,” omitted by all Greek manuscripts.] This persuasion is not from him who calls you. [Note: [Col. 0787] A little leaven corrupts the whole lump.] [Note: [Col. 0787] *beistis*] Codex B and Cast. have *beitis*. — *distairiþ*] “Is corrupted”; Greek ζυμοῖ. Gothic, with the codices and Vulgate, seems to have read δολοῖ; ζυμοῖ should have been rendered by *gabeisteiþ*; see 1 Cor. V.6.] A little leaven corrupts the whole lump. [Note: [Col. 0787] I have confidence in you in the Lord that you will think nothing otherwise; but the one troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.] [Note: [Col. 0787] *sa*] The second “he,” omitted by the Greek. — *bairaiþ*] Thus codex B and Cast. for *bairai*; see 1 Thess. IV.14.] I have confidence in you in the Lord that you will think nothing otherwise; but the one troubling you will bear judgment, whoever he may be.

[Note: [Col. 0787] But I, brothers, if I still preach circumcision, why am I still persecuted? Then the offence of the cross has indeed been removed.] [Note: [Col. 0787] *bimait*] Gothic, with the manuscripts, has ἔτι (“still”). — *þanamais*] Cast. adds *div.* — *gatauran*] Thus codex B and Cast. for *gataurana*, unless it is a solecism; many such have been noted at Neh. VI.16; cf. Eph. III.10.] But I, brothers, if I still preach circumcision, why am I still persecuted? Then indeed the stumbling-block of the cross has been removed. [Note: [Col. 0787] Would that those troubling you would even cut themselves off!] Would that those troubling you would even cut themselves off!

[Note: [Col. 0787] For you, brothers, were called to freedom; only do not make this freedom an occasion for the flesh, but through love of the Spirit serve one another.] [Note: [Col. 0787] *leikís*] “Of the flesh,” Greek σαρκί. — *taujaiþ*] “You make,” omitted by all Greek manuscripts except codex G (δῶτε) and the Vulgate (*detis*). — *ahmins*] “Of the Spirit,” omitted by the Greek.] For you, brothers, were called to freedom; only do not make freedom an occasion for the flesh, but through love of the Spirit serve one another. [Note: [Col. 0787] For the entire law is fulfilled in you in one word: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself.”] [Note: [Col. 0787] *ïn ïzvis*] “In you,” omitted by the Greek.] For the whole law is fulfilled in you in one saying: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself.” [Note: [Col. 0787] But if you bite and devour one another, beware lest you be consumed by one another.] [Note: [Col. 0787] *fairrinoþ*] “You devour”; all Greek manuscripts have κατεσθίετε. Gothic agrees with the versions and Latin Fathers. Moreover, *fairinoþ* would be a more correct spelling than *fairrinoþ*; but scribes often wrongly double liquid consonants, as in 1 Cor. VII.18 *kannt*; 2 Cor. IX.2 *makidonnim*; Phil. IV.15 *ainnohun*; 2 Cor. X.14 *aggillau*; Luke II.46 *allh*; 1 Thess. V.8 *nasseinais*. Nor is the contrary more correct, for elsewhere one liquid is omitted, especially in *fullnan*; see Luke II.21.] But if you bite and devour one another, beware lest you be consumed by one another.

[Note: [Col. 0787] But I say: walk by the Spirit, and do not fulfil the desire of the flesh.] [Note: [Col. 0788] *ei*] “That,” omitted by all Greek manuscripts.] But I say: walk by the Spirit, and do not fulfil the desire of the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0787] For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; these oppose one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish.] [Note: [Col. 0788] *ïþ*] Codex A continues.] For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; these oppose one another, so that you do not do the things you wish. [Note: [Col. 0787] But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.] But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.

[Note: [Col. 0787] Now the works of the flesh are manifest: adultery, fornication, impurity, licentiousness,] [Note: [Col. 0788] *horinassus*] “Adultery,” omitted by the Greek.] Now the works of the flesh are manifest: adultery, fornication, impurity, licentiousness, [Note: [Col. 0787] idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, anger, quarrels, dissensions, slanders, heresies,] [Note: [Col. 0788] *aljan*] “Jealousy,” Greek ζῆλοι; thus at 2 Cor. XII.20. — *tvisstasseis*] Thus codex B; codex A has *tvistasseis*; cf. Mark III.13 and 2 Cor. III.2. — *birodeinos*] “Slanders,” omitted by the Greek; Gothic appears to have imported it here from the parallel passage, 2 Cor. XII.20.] idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, anger, quarrels, dissensions, slanders, heresies, [Note: [Col. 0787] envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these; I warn you beforehand, as I warned you before, that those doing such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God.] [Note: [Col. 0788] *drugkaneins*] Thus the codices; also at Rom. XIII.13, where Cast.

*dragkameim* we had edited; on re-examining the manuscript we are informed that *drugkaneim* is written; for the scribe had written *dragkaneim*, but, having recognized the error, himself changed *a* to *u*. Castiglione, *Addenda*, p. 65.—*faurqiþa*] thus the manuscripts and Castiglione, with + in place of *fauraqiþa* (“I foretell”).—*ju*] “also,” Greek manuscripts all have καί.—*svaleik taujandans*] thus codex A; codex B, according to Castiglione, has *svaleik tataujandans*, but we suspect that either *svaleikata taujandans* or *svaleik gataujandans* is written.]

Fornication, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, anger, contentions, dissensions, factions, heresies, envyings, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these; concerning which I foretell you, as I also foretold, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.

[Note: [Col. 0787] But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, faithfulness,]

[Note: [Col. 0788] *friaþva*] thus codex B; codex A and Castiglione, *frijaþva*.—*faheþs*] codex A, *faheds*.—*sviknei*] “chastity,” absent from the Greek.]

But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy,

[Note: [Col. 0787] gentleness, self-control, chastity; against such things there is no law.]

peace, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control, chastity. Against such things there is no law.

[Note: [Col. 0787] But those who belong to Christ crucify their own flesh with its passions and desires.]

[Note: [Col. 0788] *sein*] “their own,” absent from the Greek.]

But those who are Christ’s have crucified their own flesh with passions and desires. If we live by the Spirit,

[Note: [Col. 0787] If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit.]

let us also walk by the Spirit. Let us not become vainglorious, provoking one another, envying one another.

[Col. 0789]

[Note: [Col. 0789] Brothers, if a person is detected in any sin, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you too be tempted.]

[Note: [Col. 0789] *jabai*] Gothic, with the manuscripts; without καί.—*atsaiwands*] “giving attention to”; codex A, *andsaiwands* (“looking back”), each of which readings has something to recommend it.—*ïbai*] thus codex B; codex A and Castiglione, *ïba*; compare 2 Corinthians 2:2.]

Brothers, if a person is overtaken in some transgression, you who are spiritual restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you too be tempted.

[Note: [Col. 0789] Bear one another’s burdens, and thus fulfil the law of Christ.]

Bear one another’s burdens, and thus fulfil the law of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0789] But if anyone supposes himself to be something, being nothing, he deceives himself.]

[Note: [Col. 0789] *þugkeiþ*] thus codex B; codex A and Castiglione, *þugkiþ*; compare 2 Corinthians 13:3.—*wa visan*] absent from all Greek manuscripts.—*vaiht*] here and in verse 15 in place of *vaihts*; see on Mark 7:15.—*sis—ïst*] in the margin codex A has a variant reading which Castiglione, indistinctly, reads thus: *sic silban uslutonds ïst* (“he is deceiving himself”); compare Titus 1:10, where *lutonds* = φρεναπάτης.]

For if anyone thinks himself to be something, being nothing, he deceives himself.

[Note: [Col. 0789] But let each person test his own work; then he will have ground for glorying in himself alone, and not in another.]

[Note: [Col. 0789] *silbin*] Gothic, with the versions; without μόνον.—*woftulja*] Castiglione, thinking it to be plural in number and translating “grounds for glorying,” is mistaken; for it is clear that *woftuli* is feminine, not neuter.—*ni*] codex A omits +.]

But let each person test his own work, and then he will have cause for glorying in himself and not in another.

[Note: [Col. 0789] For each person bears his own load.]

[Note: [Col. 0789] *baurþein*] thus codex B; codex A, *baurein*; moreover, *bairiþ*, not *bauriþ*, is correctly read in codex A, as Castiglione printed in his note.]

For each person will bear his own load.

[Note: [Col. 0789] Let the one who is instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs.]

[Note: [Col. 0789] *godaim*] Castiglione thought that *ïs* (“his”) had been added in codex A, but because of an erasure in the parchment he could not determine this clearly.]

But let the one instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs.

[Note: [Col. 0789] Do not be deceived: God is not mocked; for whatever a person sows, this he will also reap.]

[Note: [Col. 0790] *manna*] all Greek manuscripts place it after *saiïþ*.—*saiïþ þatuh*] codex A and Castiglione, *saijiþ þata*.]

Do not be led astray: God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that will he also reap.

[Note: [Col. 0789] For the one who sows in his own flesh will also reap destruction from the flesh; but the one who sows in the Spirit will also reap eternal life from the Spirit.]

[Note: [Col. 0790] *saiïþ*] both codex A and Castiglione have *saijiþ*.—*jah*] in both places, “also,” absent from the Greek; in the earlier occurrence Gothic agrees with the Vulgate.]

For the one who sows in his own flesh will from the flesh also reap destruction; but the one who sows in the Spirit will from the Spirit also reap eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 0789] But in doing good let us not become weary, for in due season we shall reap if we do not grow faint.]

[Note: [Col. 0790] *sneiþam*] codex A adds *sneiþa* (“I reap”).]

But let us not grow weary in doing good; for in our own season we shall reap, if we do not lose heart.

[Note: [Col. 0789] Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith.]

Therefore, while we have time, let us work what is good toward all, especially toward those who share our faith.

[Note: [Col. 0789] See with what kind of letters I have written to you with my own hand.]

[Note: [Col. 0790] *ïzvis*] codex A and Castiglione place it after *gameliaa*; all Greek manuscripts place it before *bokom*.]

See with what kind of letters I have written to you with my own hand.

[Note: [Col. 0789] As many as wish to please themselves in the flesh compel you to be circumcised, only in order that they may not suffer persecution for the cross of Christ.]

[Note: [Col. 0790] *ei weh*] “only in order that,” absent from all Greek manuscripts; compare Philippians 1:27.—*vrakja*] codex A and Castiglione, *vraka*; if this reading is genuine, it confirms *vrakom* in Mark 10:30, concerning which we once doubted whether it was correct.]

As many as wish to please themselves in the flesh compel you to be circumcised, only in order that they may not suffer persecution for Christ’s cross.

[Note: [Col. 0789] For not even those who are circumcised themselves keep the law; rather, they wish you to be circumcised so that they may glory in your flesh.]

[Note: [Col. 0790] *nih*] codex A and Castiglione, *niþ*.—*sveþauh*] “indeed,” absent from the Greek.—*ïzei*] codex A and Castiglione, *ïze*.—*sind*] Gothic omits Greek αὐτοί.]

For not even those who are circumcised themselves keep the law; but they wish you to be circumcised, that they may boast in your flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0789] But far be it from me to glory in anything except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.]

[Note: [Col. 0790] *ïn ni vaihtai*] “in nothing whatsoever,” absent from all Greek manuscripts.—*fairwaus*] thus codex B; codex A and Castiglione, *fairwus*; see on Mark 7:32.]

But may it never be mine to boast in anything except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.

[Note: [Col. 0789] For neither circumcision is anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation,]

[Note: [Col. 0790] *unte*] Gothic, with the manuscripts, omits ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.—*vaiht*] see on verse 3.]

For neither circumcision is anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.

[Note: [Col. 0789] and as many as have followed this rule, peace be upon them and mercy, and upon the Israel of God.]

And upon as many as walk by this rule, peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God.

[Note: [Col. 0789] Henceforth let no one cause me trouble, for I bear the marks of our Lord Jesus Christ in my body.]

[Note: [Col. 0790] *mis*] all Greek manuscripts place it before *ni*.—*unsaris*] “our,” from all Greek manuscripts; compare 1 Corinthians 7:16.—*xristaus*] “Christ,” absent from the Greek. The subscription is absent from all Greek manuscripts.]

Henceforth let no one cause me trouble; for I—the marks of the Lord [fragment ends].

[Note: [Col. 0789] The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.]

To the Galatians ends.

…of our Lord Jesus Christ I bear in my body. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brethren. Amen.

To the Galatians ends.

THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE EPHESIANS begins. [Note: [Col. 0791] We have supplied the inscription, which is absent from codex B, from codex A. — *aipistaule pavlaus*] equivalent to the Greek. — *anastodiþ*] “begins,” omitted by all Greek manuscripts. Moreover, since Castiglione, *Specimen*, p. 35, says that he reads the sigla A. F. above the inscription, it appears that between these letters an I has been lost through an erasure in the parchment, and that AIF was written, by which letters the scribe intended to display the title of the epistle, adorned with some sort of decorative design; see Plate II.]

[Note: [Col. 0795] To me, the least of all these saints, this grace was given: to preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ,] [Note: [Col. 0795] *undarleijin*] Thus Codex B. Massmann, *B*, *A*, p. 1038, conjectured *undarleikin*, a conjecture which pleases us greatly more than Grimm’s proposal, *undarlegjin* (“lying beneath”), in *Wiener Jahrbücher der Literatur* 70, p. 48; for Grimm himself observes that the meaning of the word lies in *undar* (“under”), compare 4:9, *undaraists*, a superlative form, like Greek κατώτατος (“lowest”), formed from an adverb. —[*þize*] “of these,” absent from the Greek.—[*unfairlaistidon*] This conjecture of Massmann, there indicated, is confirmed by renewed examination of the codex; Castiglione adds *unfairrastidon*.] To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given: to proclaim among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, [Note: [Col. 0795] and to enlighten all people as to what is the administration of this mystery, hidden from the ages in God, who created all things,] [Note: [Col. 0795] *ïn*] Codex A continues here.] and to enlighten all people as to what is the administration of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things, [Note: [Col. 0795] so that now, through the church, the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms.] [Note: [Col. 0796] *kanniþ*] Since it must be referred either to *handugei* (“wisdom”) or to the preceding *runa* (“mystery”), *kannida* should have been written, as below, 4:7, *gibana ïst ansts* (“grace was given”); but just as here, so also in Galatians 5:11 *gatauran ïst marzeins* is written for *gataurana*; compare Nehemiah 6:16.—[*managfalþo*] Codex A has *filufaihu*, and in the margin *managna . . .*; this should not, with Castiglione, be completed as *managnando*, but as *managnandei managei*, “of manifold multitude,” i.e. from *undans*, “multitude.” What the glossator intended to explain is uncertain, unless perhaps two readings—*managnandei handugei* and *managei handugeins*—have been combined. If our conjecture is correct, *managei* is here used for *managduþs* (“abundance”), though elsewhere it signifies a countable multitude. From the reading of Codex A, moreover, we say that Grimm, I.722, did not quite rightly suppose the concrete form of adjectives ending in *-us* to agree with that of adjectives ending in *-is*; according to that doctrine *filufaihjo* ought now to have been written. [Col. 0799]

[*usvalugidai*] Grimm, in the cited passage, p. 48, prefers by plausible conjecture *usvalvidai*; nevertheless, we note that the published reading is confirmed by renewed examination of Codex A.—[*ïn*], first occurrence: “in,” absent from all Greek manuscripts.—[*wammeh*] By an obvious scribal error, the word corresponding to Greek ἀνέμῳ, “wind,” has fallen out. Castiglione judges this to be *luftau*, which, because it begins like the following *liuteis*, might easily have been omitted by the scribe; Grimm more correctly supplies *vinda*, the word by which the Goth usually renders Greek ἄνεμος, or *vinde*, a plural genitive dependent on *wammeh*.—[*liuteis*] Thus Codex A according to Castiglione; but even if that form could be defended under Castiglione’s theory—which we deny—the sense certainly does not permit the genitive. Rather, *liutein* should be read: “in every [wind or winds] of teaching, in the wickedness of people.” We have observed at Matthew 7:23 that *n* and *s* are often interchanged in the codices. Moreover, moving *ïn* from its position and placing it before *liutein*, as Grimm wishes, does not seem necessary to us, because prepositions may stand with the first item, be omitted with the second, and need be repeated only with the third; see Matthew 8:9 and Mark 6:56.—[*filudeisein du listeigon usvandjai*] This conjecture of ours is confirmed by the evidence of Codex A; Castiglione adds *filudeiseinai listeigo us vandjai*, a published reading which Grimm, in the cited passage, p. 49, almost entirely approved, though by that approval he has not now demonstrated the subtlety of his judgment. First, *filudeiseinai* is not a true but a false form; see 2 Corinthians 2:3 and compare 2 Corinthians 4:4. Next, *us vandjai*, which he says represents πρὸς μεθοδείαν, “toward contrivance,” would mean something else if the reading were genuine. Finally, if *listeigo* were correctly read, it would not have been inserted idly or as a gloss equivalent to *us vandjai*; rather, *listeigon*, an adjective placed with *usvandjai*, yields the sense of μεθοδεία, “crafty scheming,”

[Col. 0800]

compare below, 6:11, where *lists* = μεθοδεία.] so that we may no longer be children, tossed about and carried away by every wind of teaching, by human deceitfulness, in craftiness toward the cunning contrivance of error.

Therefore take up the whole armour of God, so that you may be able to withstand on the evil day and, having accomplished everything, to stand.

[Note: [Col. 0803] Stand therefore, having girded your loins with truth and having put on the breastplate of righteousness.]

[Note: [Col. 0803] *hupins*] “Loins”; all Greek manuscripts: *ὀσφύν*. Moreover, whether Castiglione and Grimm, in the cited places, correctly took *brunjon* as an accusative is very doubtful. For Gothic, along with Greek, does indeed commonly put in the accusative the part in which something is done, but not the thing by which something is done. We take it as a dative, although the Vulgate followed the Greek, because the verbs for putting on and clothing are always construed with the dative of the thing when an accusative of the person is added or the verb is passive; see further 1 Thessalonians V, 8: *gahamodai brunjon jah hilma*, “having put on a breastplate and helmet.”]

Massmann, *Skeireins*, p. 73, errs in treating *galeiks* and *samaleiks* as synonyms, though they differ in meaning: the former corresponds to Greek ὅμοιος (“similar”), the latter to ἴσος (“equal”). This is one of those places where the Gothic relative particle *ei*, when the Greek uses only the conjunction ὅτι (“that”), is preceded by a demonstrative pronoun governed by the verb of the principal clause. Thus *gatraua þammei* stands for *gatraua þamma ei*: “I trust in that which—,” German *darauf dass* (“upon the fact that”). So Luke XV.6, *faginoþ miþ mis þammei bigat* (“rejoice with me, in that I have found,” Greek ὅτι εὗρον, “that I found”); Mark IV.38, *niu kara þuk þizei fraqistnam* (“do you not care that we perish?”—literally, “concerning that we perish,” Greek ὅτι ἀπολλύμεθα, “that we perish”); likewise Mark VII.18; XVI.4; John VI.5.]
