[Note: Col. 0845] *garda valdan*] Castiglione and Massmann, p. 212, supply *j[.....].*; likewise we ourselves formerly ought to have written *garda valdands* in Matt. 10:25 and Luke 14:21. For the compound must be *gardivaldands*, as are *matibalgs*, *gastigods*, *frastisibja*, *drauhtivitoþ*, *andilaus*—not *andalaus*, as codex A has above at I, 4.

[Note: Col. 0845] “. . . widows, let [the household] minister to them, and let not the church be burdened, so that it may assist those who are truly . . . . . . .”

[Note: Col. 0845] *andbahtjai*] Castiglione doubts whether this or *andstaldai* should be read; but *andstaldan* takes a person in the accusative after it, and a thing in the dative; see 2 Cor. 9:10; Gal. 3:5; 1 Tim. 1:4.

“I wish, therefore, that younger women should marry, bear children, manage households [lacuna] let [the church] assist widows [lacuna].”

[Note: Col. 0845] “. . . in word and teaching.”

[Note: Col. 0845] *laiseinai*] Castiglione prints *ïn laiseinai*. But since no Greek manuscript has ἐν (“in”), and Castiglione could not read it in the codex but inserted it solely because the passage seemed to him to have a gap, we have omitted it.

[Note: Col. 0845] “For Scripture says: ‘You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain’; and, ‘The worker is worthy of his wages.’”

[Note: Col. 0845] *qaþ*] “said”; all Greek manuscripts have λέγει, “says.”—*vaurtsva*] Massmann, p. 126, dislikes this and prefers *vaurstvja*, denying that *unvaurstvons*, occurring above in verse 13, can be used as evidence. Certainly that word cannot, nor can *allavaurstvans* at Col. 4:12; but just as we now have *vaurstva*, so in very many passages *gavaurstva* (συνεργός, “fellow-worker,” ὁ συνεργῶν, “the one who works with”) occurs; nor have we been troubled by that form.

“[lacuna] in word and teaching. For Scripture says: ‘You shall not muzzle the mouth of an ox treading grain,’ and, ‘The worker is worthy of his wages.’”

[Note: Col. 0845] “Do not receive an accusation against an elder except before two or three witnesses.”

[Note: Col. 0845] *ïn andvairþja*] Castiglione could make out nothing beyond the letters “. . . rþ . . .”; wrongly he wrote *bi* instead of *ïn*, an error also noted by Massmann, p. 134. Moreover, if the Gothic writer really wrote this, he departs too greatly from the authority of the Greeks, nor would he approach them more closely if Castiglione’s conjecture *ana munþa* were more probable. Perhaps *bi veitvodiþai* (“on the testimony”) should be written.—*tvadje*] Thus Castiglione printed it instead of *tvaddje*, since he thought the place could not contain a double *d*.

“Against an elder do not receive an accusation except before two or three witnesses.”

[Note: Col. 0845] “But rebuke those who sin before all, that the rest also may have fear.”

[Note: Col. 0846] *ïþ*] “but,” omitted by the Greek.

“But rebuke those who sin before all, that the others also may have fear.”

[Note: Col. 0845] “I testify before God and our Lord Jesus Christ and these elect angels that you observe this without prejudice, doing nothing according to inclination.”

[Note: Col. 0846] *unsaris*] “our,” omitted by all Greek manuscripts except manuscript 9 in Mill.—*viljahalþein*] Codex B continues.

“I testify before God and our Lord Jesus Christ and the elect angels, that you observe this without prejudice, doing nothing according to partiality.”

[Note: Col. 0845] “Lay hands quickly on no one, nor share in the sins of others.”

[Note: Col. 0846] *mannhun*] Castiglione, from codex B, adds *manhun*; codex A is erased; see Mark 1:44.

“Lay hands hastily on no one, nor become a participant in another’s sins.”

[Note: Col. 0845] “Keep yourself pure. No longer drink only water, but use a little wine because of your stomach and your frequent infirmities.”

[Note: Col. 0846] *qiþaus*] Codex B margin: *suqnis* (“illness”).—*þizo ufta—þeinaizo*] Thus the codices, although almost all the writing has been erased; Massmann also thinks this should be read, p. 133. Castiglione supplies *þize ufte—þeinaize*.

“Keep yourself pure. No longer drink water only, but use a little wine because of your stomach and your frequent ailments.”

[Note: Col. 0845] “The sins of some people are manifest, going beforehand to judgment; but in some persons they also follow after.”

[Note: Col. 0846] *sumaize*] second occurrence: codex A has *sumaizeh*; moreover the Gothic reads τινῶν (“of some”) with the Colbert manuscript cited by Mill, instead of τισί (“to some”).

“The sins of some people are plainly visible, going before them to judgment; but those of others also follow afterward.”

[Note: Col. 0845] “Likewise also good works are manifest, and those which are otherwise cannot be hidden.”

[Note: Col. 0846] *þan*] “but,” omitted by all Greek manuscripts except the manuscript cited by Mill.

“Likewise also good works are manifest; and those which are otherwise cannot be hidden.”

[Note: Col. 0845] “Let as many servants as are under the yoke regard their own masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be blasphemed.”

[Note: Col. 0846] *jukuzjai*] Massmann, p. 136, wishes to ascertain whether this is really read thus, because in Gal. 5:1 the same case is *jukuzja*. But that learned man is mistaken: in that passage *jukuzja* is accusative, whereas in ours *jukuzjai* is dative; both correctly derive from the form *jukuzi*.—*fraujins*] “of the Lord,” where the Greek has θεοῦ, “of God.”

“Let as many as are servants under the yoke consider their own masters worthy of all honor, so that the name of the Lord and the teaching may not be spoken against.”

[Note: Col. 0845] “But those who have believing masters, let them not despise them because they are brethren, but rather serve them, because they are believers and beloved, partakers of the benefit. Teach and exhort these things.”

“But those who have believing masters, let them not despise them because they are brethren, but serve them the more, because they are believers and beloved, partakers of the benefit. Teach and exhort these things.”

[Note: Col. 0845] “If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to these sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the teaching which is according to godliness:”

[Note: Col. 0846] *atgaggai*] “may assent”; codex A has *atgaggiþ* (“assents”).—*laiseinai*] Castiglione supplies *laisenai*, but himself corrects it on p. 72.

“Teach and exhort these things. If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to teaching according to godliness—”

[Note: Col. 0845] “But he is proud, knowing nothing, but [Col. 0847] sick concerning disputes and word-contentions, from which arise envy, murders, strife, revilings, evil suspicions,”

[Note: Col. 0846] *ïþ*] “but,” omitted by all Greek manuscripts; the Gothic agrees with the Latin versions and Fathers.—*hauhþuhts*] “proud,” where all Greek manuscripts have τετύφωται, “he is puffed up.”—*maurþra*] “murders,” omitted by all Greek manuscripts and not read in codex A. For although a trace of the letter *a* appears and there seems to be some space, it does not suffice for the whole word; Castiglione thinks that this letter was written mistakenly by the scribe and erased by him. It is, moreover, beyond doubt that *maurþra* in codex B arose because some read φόνοι (“murders”) in place of φθόνοι (“envies”); the translator either adopted both readings, or a scribe inserted one from the margin. Compare Eph. 2:3.—*haifsteis*] Thus correctly codex A; codex B has *haifteis*.

“—but is proud, knowing nothing, but sick over controversies and verbal disputes, from which arise envy, murders, strife, revilings, evil suspicions,”

[Col. 0847]

[Note: Col. 0847] “contentions of people corrupted in mind, from whom the truth has been hidden, who suppose that godliness is gain.”

[Note: Col. 0847] *ahin*] Gothic omits καί, “and.”—*gatarniþ*] Thus codex B, instead of *gatarnida*; compare Nehemiah 6:16. There is no reason to suspect, as Castiglione does, a scribal error for *gatairniþ*—indeed *gataurniþ*. For *gatarnan* is excellent if compared with *tarnjan* and *tarnen*, “to hide,” words used by Germans of the Upper and Middle Ages; see Glossary V, “Tarnjan.”—*gagudein*] Codex B omits this with the Greek ἀφίστασο ἀπὸ τῶν τοιούτων (“withdraw from such persons”). In codex A these words seem to have been written, but because of later writing Castiglione could identify nothing but the letter *þ*.

“And verbal disputes, from which arise envy, murders, strife, revilings, evil suspicions, contentions of people corrupted in mind, from whom truth is hidden, supposing godliness to be a means of gain.”

[Note: Col. 0847] “But godliness with contentment is great gain;”

[Note: Col. 0847] *gavaurki*] In the immediately preceding verse stood *faihugavaurki* (“gain through wealth”). Concerning this Gothic practice—when two compound words immediately follow one another, not to repeat the particle in the second, but to use a simple form—we have already spoken at Luke 15:24. We now add these examples:

Rom. 15:4: *sva filu auk sve fauragameliþ varþ, du unsarai laiseinai gameliþ varþ*—“For whatever things were written beforehand were written for our instruction” (ὅσα γὰρ προεγράφη, εἰς τὴν ἡμετέραν διδασκαλίαν προεγράφη).

Rom. 12:1–2: *vaila galeikaidana—galeikaiþ* (“acceptable—acceptable,” εὐάρεστον—εὐάρεστον).

1 Cor. 15:48–49: *sa ufarhiminakunda—þis himinakundins* (“the heavenly one—of the heavenly one,” ὁ ἐπουράνιος—τοῦ ἐπουρανίου).

2 Thess. 3:15: *svasve—sve* (“as—as,” ὡς—ὡς).

John 9:31: *andhauseiþ—hauseiþ* (“he hears—hears,” ἀκούει—ἀκούει); 13:14: *usþvoh—þvahan* (“I washed—to wash,” ἔνιψα—νίπτειν); 17:25: *ufkunþa—kunþa* (“knew—knew,” ἔγνω—ἔγνων).

Therefore at 2 Tim. 3:4, φιλἡδονοι μᾶλλον ἢ φιλόθεοι (“lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God”), the Gothic translates thus: *frijondans viljan seinana mais þau guþ*—“loving their own will rather than God.” Similarly Matt. 8:32: *hairda sveine—hairda* (“the herd of swine—the herd,” τὴν ἀγέλην τῶν χοίρων—ἡ ἀγέλη τῶν χοίρων). Compare John 10:31: *nemun stainans ei vaurpeina*—“they took stones in order that they might throw [them]” (that is, *stainam*, λιθάσωσι, “that they might stone him”) at him.

Rarely the simple form precedes and the compound follows: 1 Cor. 4:7: *namt—andnamt* (“you received—you received,” ἔλαβες—ἔλαβες); 2 Cor. 3:2–3: *gamelida—ïnna gamelida* (“written—written within,” Greek twice ἐγγεγραμμένη).

[Note: Col. 0847] “For we brought nothing into this world; indeed, it is evident that we are able to carry nothing out.”

[Note: Col. 0847] *bi sunjai*] “indeed, truly” (ἀληθές); the Greek has δῆλον, “evident.”

“But godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into this world; truly, neither are we able to carry anything out.”

[Note: Col. 0847] “But having food and clothing, let us be content with these.”

[Note: Col. 0847] *usfodein—gaskadvein*] “food—clothing,” Greek διατροφὰς—σκεπάσματα.

“But having food and clothing, with these let us be content.”

[Note: Col. 0847] “But those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and the devil’s snare, and into many useless and harmful desires, which sink people into destruction and perdition.”

[Note: Col. 0848] *hlamma*] Castiglione and Massmann, p. 202, wrongly take this as a dative; Massmann makes its nominative *hlams*—thus! The construction both here and above at III, 7 clearly shows it to be accusative. But it is uncertain whether the form itself, *hlamm*, is neuter—in which case the Goth uses a plural—or *hlamma* feminine. For related-language words see Graff IV, 557; Grimm II, 33.—*unhulþins*] “of the devil,” omitted in the Greek.—*unnutjans*] “useless,” where the Greek has ἀνοήτους (“foolish”); the Gothic follows manuscripts and versions reading ἀνονήτους (“unprofitable”).—*saggqjand*] Codex A has *sagqjand*.

“But those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and the devil’s snare, and into many useless and harmful desires, which sink people into destruction and perdition.”

[Note: Col. 0847] “For the root of all evils is covetousness, which some, desiring it, have been led away from the faith and have pierced themselves through with many pains.”

[Note: Col. 0848] *vaurts*] Gothic omits γάρ (“for”); but the scribe may have omitted it through the following *allaize* (“of all”), compare Rom. 9:15.—*faihugeiro*] Massmann, p. 139, thinks *faihugeironi* should be read, as at Col. 3:5. On the contrary, we think that at Col. 3:5 *faihugeironi* should be changed to *faihugeiron* on the evidence of our passage; for the form must be feminine, as the pronoun *sei* in that passage and *þizozei* in this one show.—*gaþivaidedun*] “have pierced themselves through”; all Greek manuscripts have περιέπειραν.

“For the root of all evils is love of money, which some, desiring it, have been led away from the faith and have pierced themselves through with many pains.”

[Note: Col. 0847] “But you indeed, man of God, flee these things; but pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, patience, gentleness.”

[Note: Col. 0848] *jai*] “indeed,” omitted by all Greek manuscripts; see Rom. 9:18, 20.—*friaþva*] Codex A has *frijaþva*.

“But you indeed, man of God, flee these things; but pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, patience, gentleness.”

[Note: Col. 0847] “Fight the good fight of faith; lay hold on eternal life, to which you were called and confessed the good confession before many witnesses.”

[Note: Col. 0848] *libain aiveinon*] “eternal life,” corresponding to all Greek manuscripts.

“Fight the good fight of faith; lay hold of eternal life, to which you were called and confessed the good confession before many witnesses.”

[Note: Col. 0847] “I command you before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who witnessed under Pontius Pilate the good confession,”

[Note: Col. 0848] *anabiuda*] Gothic omits “you,” together with the manuscripts cited by Mill.—*andvairþja*] Codex A ends.—*paunteau*] Castiglione affirms that this is unquestionably read in codex B. We expected either *pauntiau*, as written at Matt. 27:2 and Luke 3:1, or *pauntjau*. The codex reading could be tolerated if that man’s Greek name were Ποντεῖος; but since he is called Πόντιος, the scribe undoubtedly wrote *-eau* wrongly for *-jau*. By scribal carelessness *e* and *j* are also interchanged in 2 Cor. 8:20 and Nehemiah 6:18.

“I command before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who witnessed before Pontius Pilate the good confession,”

[Note: Col. 0847] “that you keep the commandment spotless, irreproachable, until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ,”

[Note: Col. 0848] *qum*] Thus codex B; Castiglione supplies *quma*.

“Keep the commandment spotless, irreproachable, until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ,”

[Note: Col. 0847] “which, in his own times, the blessed and only Mighty One will show—the King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule,”

[Note: Col. 0848] *ïn*] “in,” omitted by all Greek manuscripts.—*taikneiþ*] Thus codex B; Castiglione supplies *taikniþ*.—*jah*] the second “and,” omitted by all Greek manuscripts.

“Which in his own times the blessed and only Mighty One will reveal, the King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule,”

[Note: Col. 0847] “who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no one among men has seen, nor can see . . . . .”

[Note: Col. 0848] *jah*] “and,” omitted by the Greek.—*manne ni ainskun*] “no one among men,” corresponding to all Greek manuscripts.

“He alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no one among human beings has seen, nor may see . . .”

## The Second [Epistle] to Timothy.

> **Inscription.** In Codex A no inscription is found; in Codex B the beginning through verse 5 is missing. We have therefore supplied the inscription conjecturally.

[Col. 0849]

[Col. 0849]

Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, according to the promise of this life in Christ Jesus.

[Note: *gahaitam*: “promises”; all Greek manuscripts have “promise” (*epangelian*).]

To Timothy, beloved child: grace, mercy, peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

I give thanks to my God, whom I serve from my forefathers in a pure conscience, as I have unceasing remembrance of you in my prayers night and day.

[Note: *aviliudo*: Castillion reads also *aviliuao*. — *meinamma*: “my,” absent from the Greek. — *unsveibando*: Castillion thinks that Gothic here uses the neuter, like the Greeks, namely *adialeipton*, “unceasing”; but the learned man did not observe that *adialeipton* is not neuter but feminine, and refers to *mneian*, “remembrance.” Gothic uses the neuter because *gaminþi* is of that gender. If it did not refer to *gaminþi*, one would have to say *unsveibands aviliudo*, as in Ephesians 1:16; compare 1 Thessalonians 5:17, *unsveibandans bidjaiþ*, “pray unceasingly.” Taking this opportunity, we note that at 1 Thessalonians 2:13 one should write *unsveibandans*, not *unsveibandanei*, which we had printed on Castillion’s authority; Castillion, re-examining the manuscript, found this reading, which we had long before reached by conjecture. — *þuk*: thus Codex A; Castillion adds *þus*.]

Longing to see you, remembering your tears, so that I may be filled with joy—

[Note: *tagre þeinaize*: Castillion wrongly printed *þeinaize tagre* from a completely corrupt place.]

—receiving remembrance of the unfeigned faith which is in you, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice; and I am persuaded that it is in you also.

[Note: *lauïdja*: thus Codex A; we prefer *lauïdjai*. Moreover, the Goth seems to have read Λοϊδί rather than Λωϊδί, since Greek *o* is usually rendered in Gothic by *au*, although *au* is also used for Greek omega: *adauneikam*, Ἀδωνικάμ, Ezra 2:13; *dauriþaius*, Δωρι- or Δωρόθεος, Gothic Calendar; *nauel*, Νῶε, Luke 17:27; *praitauira*, πραιτώριον, John 18:33; *trauada*, Τρωάς, 2 Corinthians 2:12 and 2 Timothy 4:14; *trakauneitidus*, Τρακωνίτις, Luke 3:1. — *aivneika*: Codex B begins with the final two letters of this word, but the scribe wrote *ra* wrongly instead of *ka*. We prefer *aivneikai*. — *aþþan*: Castillion adds *þan*, since *þan*, if it means δέ, “but,” does not occur at the beginning of a sentence; Castillion himself thinks *aþþan* should be read. [Col. 0850] Before *þan* there is in both manuscripts a blank space for two letters.]

For this reason I remind you to rekindle the grace of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands.

[Note: *analagein*: thus Codex B; Codex A has *lagein*. So at 1 Timothy 5:22, where the Goth translates χεῖρας ἐπιτιθέναι, “to lay hands,” by the simple *lagjan handuns*.]

For God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power and love and sobriety.

[Note: *friaþvos*: Codex A has *frijaþvos*.]

Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord Jesus, nor of me, his prisoner; but suffer hardship with the gospel according to the power of God,

[Note: *nunu*: Codex A adds *nu*. Between *nu* and *nunu* in prohibitions this is the difference: *nunu* follows the negation itself—Matthew 10:26 and 31, “do not fear them”; Romans 14:15, “do not by your food destroy that person”; 14:20, “do not for food’s sake destroy the work of God.” But *nu* has the verb placed between itself and the negation: Matthew 6:8, “do not therefore be like them”; 6:31, “therefore do not be anxious, saying”; Romans 14:13, “let us therefore no longer judge one another”; Ephesians 5:7, “therefore do not become partners with them”; Colossians 2:16, “therefore let no one judge you in food.” — *ïesuis*: absent from the Greek; manuscripts which have it add “Christ.”]

—who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before eternal ages,

[Note: *laþondins*: Codex A has *lapondins uns*, “calling us,” together with the Aldine edition cited by Mill.]

but now made manifest through the appearing of our Savior Jesus Christ, who indeed abolished death but brought life and incorruption to light through the gospel.

[Note: *dauþau*: thus Codex B for *dauþu*; Codex A is obliterated; see 1 Timothy 1:16. — *aivaggeljon*: thus, we hope, Codex A, which is worn away here; Codex B has *aivaggejon*.]

For this gospel I was appointed preacher, apostle, and teacher of the nations. For this reason I also suffer these things; but I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to guard that which has been entrusted to me until that day.

[Note: *þammei*, in place of *þatei* (ὅτι, “that”): see Philippians 2:24. Add Mark 16:4, “they noticed that the stone had been rolled away”; Luke 17:15, “seeing that he had been healed.” Luke 10:20 also says, “Do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you; but rejoice because…” (ἐν τούτῳ μὴ χαίρετε, ὅτι τὰ πνεύματα ὑμῖν ὑποτάσσεται, χαίρετε δὲ ὅτι κτλ.). — *ïn jainana dag*: Codex B and Castillion add *ïn jainamma dag*. In Codex B it appears that *daga* was written; after the scribe had deleted the final *a* because of the sense, he neglected to correct the preceding pronoun.]

Hold the pattern of sound words which you heard from me, in faith and love in Christ Jesus.

[Col. 0851]

[Note: *habands*: “holding”; Greek ἔχε, “hold”; Gothic agrees with the German manuscript cited by Mill. — *friaþvai*: Codex A has *frijaþvai*. Between *friaþvai* and *ïn* Codex A has an empty space in which the article *þizai* (“the,” τῇ) seems to have been written; Codex B omits it altogether.]

Guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us.

[Note: *bauïþ*: see Romans 7:18.]

You know that all who are in Asia turned away from me; among them are Phygelus and Hermogenes.

[Note: *vaist*: Codex B and Castillion add *vaits*; Codex A is effaced. Scribes often transpose letters carelessly; compare Mark 14:13. Moreover, Gothic omits τοῦτο, “this,” unless perhaps the scribe carelessly omitted *þata* because of the following *þatei*; the same happened at 1 Timothy 1:9. — *þizei*: “of whom,” thus Codex B; Codex A remains obliterated. The Greek ὧν ought to have been rendered *þizeei*, and we do not doubt that the translator wrote this; the scribe, through carelessness, wrote the double *e* only once. See 2 Timothy 2:17. — *fygailus*: Greek Φύγελλος. — *airmogaineis*: the Goth pronounced Ἑρμογένης without the rough breathing; similarly below, at 2 Timothy 2:17, *ymainaius*, whereas at 1 Timothy 1:20 he correctly wrote *hymainaius*. Note also that the short Greek *o* in this proper name is rendered by long Gothic *o*; compare Philippians 4:2.]

May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chains.

[Note: *garda*: thus Codex B; Castillion adds *gardin*.]

Rather, when he came to Rome, he diligently sought me and found me.

[Note: *usdaudo*: “diligently”; Greek σπουδαιότερον.]

May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day; and you know very well how much he served me at Ephesus.

[Note: *frauja ïmma*: “may the Lord grant him”; absent from all Greek manuscripts. — *mais*: “more.” This adverb in its present position wholly disturbs the sense. Since a little below *vaila*, the positive form, occurs for comparative βέλτιον, “better,” we think that *mais*, wrongly placed by the scribe, should stand before or after *vaila*. Codex A is so effaced here that Castillion is wholly uncertain where this page ends; it continues only at last at 2 Timothy 2:21.]

You therefore, my beloved child, be strengthened in this grace which is in Christ Jesus.

[Note: *vailso*: “beloved,” absent from all Greek manuscripts.]

And the things which you heard from me through many testimonies—the words of God—commit these to faithful persons, who will be competent to teach others also.

[Note: *veitvodja vaurda guþs*: “testimonies, words of God”; the Greek manuscripts have only μαρτύρων, “witnesses.” As Castillion correctly observed, the Goth seems rather to have read μαρτυρίων, “testimonies.” *Vaurda guþs*, “words of God,” which are entirely superfluous, were undoubtedly inserted here by a scribe from the margin, where a glossator had placed them; on this see our notes on 1 Corinthians 15:6 and the Prolegomena. Castillion adds *jct. veitvodjavaurda*. Massmann, in the cited place, pp. 211–212, writes it sometimes joined and sometimes separated; when he separates it, *veitvodja* seems to be an adjective. But if that is so, what becomes of *guþs*, a most idle addition? — *triggvaim mannam*: Codex B has *triggvaimannam*; see 2 Thessalonians 3:17.]

Suffer hardship, then, as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.

[Note: *xristaus ïesuis*: supported by the Greek.]

No one serving as a soldier entangles himself in the affairs of this life, so that he may please the one under whom he serves.

[Note: *fraujin*: “lord”; some Greek manuscripts omit it, while others read τῷ θεῷ, “God.” The Goth read τῷ κυρίῳ, “the Lord,” in his book. — *gavaurkjam þizos aldais*: “the affairs of this life,” absent from all Greek manuscripts. — *galeikai þammei drauhtinoþ*: “may please the one under whom he serves”; absent from all Greek manuscripts, τῷ στρατολογήσαντι ἀρέσῃ.]

And if anyone competes, he is not crowned unless he competes lawfully.

The laboring cultivator of the soil ought to receive the fruits first.

[Note: *arbaidjands*: Codex B adds *arbaidjans*; see 1 Timothy 1:3. — *airþos vaurstvja*: “cultivator of the soil”; Greek γεωργός, “farmer,” is absent from all Greek manuscripts. If Castillion says that the Goths had no name for a farmer because they were uncultivated and followed cattle, Massmann, cited pp. 219 ff., refutes him excellently and vigorously vindicates our forefathers’ knowledge of agriculture. Yet the Goth should not have called a farmer by the barbarous words *bauman* or *akraman*, since *vaurstvja* was available and means γεωργός at Mark 12:1, Luke 20:9, and John 15:1.]

Understand what I say; for the Lord will give you understanding in all things.

[Note: *gibiþ*: “gives”; Greek δῴη, “may he give.” Gothic, with the manuscripts, read δώσει, “will give.” — *us allaim*: “from all things”; Greek ἐν πᾶσιν, “in all things.”]

Remember Christ Jesus, raised from the dead, of David’s seed, according to my gospel,

[Note: *xristu ïesu*: absent from all Greek manuscripts.]

for which I suffer hardship, even to chains, as an evildoer; but the word of God is not bound.

For this reason I endure all things for the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory.

This is a faithful saying: if we died with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him; if we deny him, he too will deny us; if we do not believe, he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself.

[Note: *jabai*: Gothic lacks γάρ, “for.” — *afaikan*: Gothic, with the manuscripts, lacks γάρ.]

Remind them of these things, charging them before the Lord not to contend over words, since it is useful for nothing except the overthrow of those who hear.

[Col. 0853]

[Note: *vaurdam—hausjondam*: “over words—those who hear.” The Goth followed the sense more than the words of the Greek text, translating as though he had read λογομαχεῖν (γὰρ) εἰς οὐδὲν χρήσιμον εἰ μὴ ἐπὶ κτλ., “to contend over words—for nothing useful, unless for…” *Hausjondam* is not incorrectly written for *hausjandam*, as Castillion thinks; see Luke 5:15.]

Be diligent to present yourself approved to God, a worker unashamed, rightly directing the word of truth.

[Note: *gakusanana*: thus Codex B; Castillion has *gakiusanana*.]

But avoid these foolish, profane empty speeches, for they advance greatly toward ungodliness.

[Note: *dvalona, usveihona*: “foolish, profane”; the Greek has only βεβήλους, “profane.” — *lausavaurdja*: Massmann, cited p. 126, hesitates because 1 Timothy 1:6 has *lausavaurdei*, but both forms are correct. Here *lausavaurdja* derives from *lausavaurdi*, as also *andavaurdi* at Luke 2:47 and John 19:9, and *gavaurdi* at 1 Corinthians 15:33; *lausavaurdei* is formed like *aglaitivaurdei*, Colossians 3:8; *dvalavaurdei*, Ephesians 5:4; and *filuvaurdei*, Matthew 6:8. — *unte—afgudein*: “for—toward ungodliness.” Castillion, as is often his way, speaks here unfairly—indeed maliciously—of the capacities of the Gothic language and entirely missed the sense. The preposition ἐπί, “toward,” was not omitted by the Goth but rendered by *du* and placed with *afgudein*. Even if it had truly been absent, Castillion should not have said that it could be rendered by *unte*, “for,” as Massmann already observed, cited p. 134. Nor can *und filu* be said here, for this phrase, unless joined with *mais*, does not occur before a comparative; see Luke 18:39; 2 Corinthians 3:9; Philippians 1:23.]

And their word spreads like a festering sore; among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus,

[Note: *gund vuliþ*: Castillion adds *gun svuliþ*; Codex B has *gun.. vuliþ*, with the letter between *n* and *v* entirely erased. Since *gunt*, *kund* among the ancient Germans, and *gund* among the Anglo-Saxons, mean “pus, matter” (Graff IV, 219), and since Gothic has no *svulan* whereas *vulan* is already found at Romans 12:11, we have no doubt that our reading is certain. Massmann, who conjectured *guns vuliþ* (p. 201), and Grimm, who preferred *gunds vuliþ* (Grammar I, 564, 3rd ed.), came very close to the correct reading. — *vesun*: “were”; Greek ἐστί, “is,” is absent. Likewise, with two singular subjects the plural verb occurs at Luke 2:43, “Joseph and his mother knew,” Greek ἔγνω Ἰωσὴφ καὶ ἡ μήτηρ. — *ymainaius*: see 1:15. Castillion printed *ymainaïus*, saying that the manuscript seems to have not merely two but three dots over the *i*. But neither do the scribes of these codices write points in the middle of words [Col. 0854], nor do Goths divide the sound *ai* in pronouncing these endings of proper names. Perhaps those points are accidental stains on the parchment; compare Massmann, *Skeireins*, p. 17.]

who have strayed concerning the truth, saying that the resurrection has already happened, and have overturned the faith of some.

[Note: *sunja*: Codex B and Castillion add *sunjai*, which would be quite unsuitable: they did not err “according to the truth” (κατὰ τὴν ἀλήθειαν), but “concerning the truth” (περὶ τὴν ἀλήθειαν). The manuscript reading arose from the ending of the following verb, *usvissai*; see *Skeireins*, p. 33, line 10, *miþ baitreins þvairheins* for *baitrein*; compare 2 Corinthians 3:18, Codex B *af fraujins ahmins* for *ahmin*; *Skeireins* 40:20, *du daupeinais garehsnais* for *garehsnai*, where the scribe was misled by the preceding ending. — *galaubein—usvaltidedun*: “faith—overturned”; absent from all Greek manuscripts.]

But the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: “The Lord knows those who are his,” and, “Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.”

In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay; and some are for honor, others for dishonor.

[Note: *sverain—unsverain*: Massmann rightly says (p. 132) that this manuscript reading is erroneous and that one must read either *sverainai—unsverainai* or *sverein—unsverein*. One must not think here of the accusative after *du*, on the model of Colossians 4:10 and 13.]

If anyone cleanses himself from these, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work.

[Note: *gaveihaiþ*: Gothic lacks καί, “also.” — *du*: Codex A continues.]

But flee youthful desires; instead pursue righteousness, faith, love, peace, with those who call upon the Lord in prayer from a pure heart.

[Note: *friaþva*: Codex A has *frijaþva*. — *bidai anahaitandam*: “calling upon in prayer”; Greek has only ἐπικαλουμένων, “calling upon”; similarly Romans 10:13; compare 1 Thessalonians 4:1. — *fraujan*: correctly so in Codex A; in Codex B I doubt whether I read *frauja*, which would be a scribal error. Castillion.]

But avoid foolish and unlearned questions, knowing that they produce disputes.

The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, apt to teach, patient,

in gentleness teaching those who oppose, perhaps God may grant them repentance leading to knowledge of the truth,

[Note: *andstandandans*: “opponents”; Greek ἀντιδιατιθεμένους, “those opposing themselves.” The Goth, with the manuscripts, read ἀντικειμένους, “those who oppose”; see 1 Timothy 1:10; Galatians 5:17; 2 Thessalonians 2:4. — *niu wan*: Castillion thinks that Luke 4:11, *wan ni*—indeed, *ei wan ni*—has the same meaning as *niu wan* here. We do not think so; rather, the Goth understood very well the differing sense in the two passages, as his different translations prove.]

and that they may recover their senses out of the devil’s snare, having been captured by him to be led after his will.

[Note: *usskavjaindau*: thus Codex B; Codex A has *usskarjaindau*. With Castillion we prefer the reading of Codex B, because at 1 Corinthians 15:34 the Goth renders ἐκνήφειν, “come to sobriety,” by *usskavjan sik*, and at 1 Thessalonians 5:8 renders νήφωμεν, “let us be sober,” by *usskavai sijaima*. We would accept Codex A’s reading, which greatly pleases Massmann (pp. 138, 203), and which, citing Old Saxon *scerian*, he explains as “to order, arrange,” if mention of some arrangement or adornment “out of the devil’s snares” suited the sense here. For a passive form with *sik* used actively, see 1 Corinthians 15:33, *ni afairzjaindau*: “do not be deceived!” — “Take care that you do not deceive yourselves!” — *fram þammei gafahanai tiuhanda*: “having been captured by whom they are led”; Greek has ἐζωγρημένοι ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ, “captured by him.” Codex A has *habanda*, “are held,” for *tiuhanda*, “being led.” — *afar*: “after”; Greek εἰς, “unto.”]

[Col. 0855]

But know this: in the last days difficult times will come.

[Note: *jera*: “years”; all Greek manuscripts have καιροί, “times.”]

For people will become lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, proud, abusive, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, ungodly,

[Note: *jah*: “and”; Greek γάρ, “for.” — *friondans*: Codex A has *frijondans* and in the margin *seinaigairnai*, incorrectly for *seinagairnai*; the same codex has Titus 1:10 *lausaivaurdai* for *lausavaurdai*. This error arose from the following endings. Or, since the scribe of the same codex wrongly wrote 1 Timothy 1:4 *andalausaize* for *andilausaize*, we are almost led to suspect that he sometimes wrote words as the speech of the common people pronounced them indistinctly. It should in any case be written separately, *seina gairnai*, because verbs are not compounded with pronouns. — *hauhhairtai*: Codex B adds *hauhairtai*. — *unairknai*: Codex A has *unairknans*.]

without natural affection, irreconcilable, without love, slanderers, without self-control, savage, hostile to what is good,

[Note: *unhunslagai, unmildjai*: “irreconcilable, without love”; absent from the Greek. — *unmanariggvai*: Codex A adds *unmanarigvai*.]

traitors, reckless, puffed up, loving their own will more than God,

[Note: *frijondans viljan seinana*: “loving their own will”; Greek φιλήδονοι, “lovers of pleasure.” Castillion thinks it probable that, following Latin versions, the Goth read “will” in place of “pleasure”; compare Ephesians 2:3. — *þau*: Castillion adds *þan*.]

having a form of godliness, but denying its power. Avoid them also.

[Note: *jah þans*: Codex A has *jaþ-þans*.]

For among these are those who creep into houses and lead captive little women burdened with sins, led by various desires,

[Note: *þaiei*: correctly so in Codex A; Codex B and Castillion have *þoei*, “which.” — *du lustum*: “to desires”; Greek has only ἐπιθυμίαις, “desires,” in the instrumental case. Codex A has *luslustum* for *lustum*; compare John 9:41.]

always teaching themselves, yet never able to come to the knowledge of truth.

[Note: *ni*: “not”; Codex A, with all Greek manuscripts, has *jan-ni*, καὶ μή, “and not.”]

Now just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these also oppose the truth: people corrupted in mind, rejected concerning faith.

[Note: *þamma—ei*: see Luke 1:20 and Colossians 1:9; compare Romans 9:20 and Luke 10:5. — *jannis*: Codex A has *nnes*. — *mambres*: Greek Ἰαμβρῆς.]

But they shall not advance further, for their folly will become manifest to all, as that of those men also became manifest.

[Note: *svikunþ*: Codex A has in the margin *gatarhiþ*, “notorious.” — *jah*: “also”; absent from Codex B, but written above the line in Codex A.]

But you have followed my teaching, manner of life, purpose, faith, long-suffering, love, patience,

[Note: *galaista ïs*: Castillion and Massmann (p. 138) print *galaistais*, which they think was wrongly written by both scribes for *galaistjais*. But what, we ask, would a subjunctive mean here in this construction, when the Greek text has the perfect tense? Our reading is supported by Galatians 6:16, “as many as walk according to this rule,” ὅσοι τῷ κανόνι τούτῳ στοιχήσουσι; Mark 1:36, “they pursued him,” καὶ κατεδίωξαν αὐτόν. Codex A’s margin has *galaisides* for *galaistides*, “you followed.” — *laiseinai meinai*: “my teaching,” absent from all Greek manuscripts. — *sidau*: “manner of life,” absent from the Greek. — *friaþvai*: Codex A has *frijaþvai*.]

persecutions and sufferings—such as happened to me at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra; such persecutions I endured, and out of them all the Lord delivered me.

[Note: *lystros*: since this dative form is not Gothic, the translator seems to have used the Greek form, as he is acknowledged by all to have done often: *ïairusaulymon*, *gazaufylakio*, *þoman*, and elsewhere. He wrote *o* for Greek οι, because this vowel is wholly lacking in Gothic; thus Βέροια in the Gothic Calendar is rendered *bairauja*. — *vrakos*: Codex A has *vrakjos*; compare Galatians 6:12. — *usþulida*: both codices have this for *usþulaida*.]

Indeed, all who wish to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecutions.

But evil people and impostors will advance to worse things, going astray and leading others astray.

[Note: *du vairsizin*: Codex A’s margin has *du ubelamma*, wrongly for *ubilamma*; see Luke 8:17: “toward evil.” — *airzjai jah airzjandans*: “going astray and leading others astray”; absent from all Greek manuscripts. Gothic agrees with the Vulgate.]

But you, for your part, remain in the things in which you were taught and which were entrusted to you, knowing from whom you received them,

[Note: *framvairpis*: “for your part,” not “steadfast,” as Castillion interprets; absent from all Greek manuscripts. — *jah*: thus Codex B. Castillion could not determine whether Codex A read *jan* or *jau*.]

and that from childhood you have known the sacred books, which are able to instruct you for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.

[Note: *usfratvjan*: thus the codices, for *usfraþjan* or *usfraþvjan*, as Castillion thinks.]

Every book divinely inspired is also useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in righteousness,

[Col. 0857]

[Note: *garaihteinai—garaihtein*: Castillion wishes it to be observed that *garaihteins* in this verse corresponds both to Greek ἐπανόρθωσις, “correction,” and δικαιοσύνη, “righteousness.” But he is mistaken: *garaihteinai*, in a transitive sense, derives from *garaihteins*; *garaihtein*, in an intransitive sense, derives from *garaihtei*.]

so that the person of God may be complete, prepared for every good work.

[Note: *manna guþs*: “person of God”; absent from all Greek manuscripts. Gothic agrees with the Vulgate.]

I charge you before God and Christ Jesus the Lord, who is to judge the living and the dead, by his appearing and his kingdom:

[Note: *fraujins*: “Lord”; absent from the Greek. — *xristaus ïesuis*: supported by the Greek. — *bi*: Greek has καί, “and.” — *qum*: Massmann thinks (p. 204) that this is a dative produced by elision, an extraordinary conjecture for which there is no need: *bi* is used in this way with the accusative elsewhere as well. — *ïs*: the first hand; Gothic lacks καί.]

Preach the word; stand ready in season and out of season; reprove, exhort, rebuke with all patience and teaching.

[Note: *stand*: Codex A has *ïnstand*. — *uhteigo*: correctly thus in Codex A; Codex B has *ohteigo*; compare Luke 4:13. — *gaþlaih gawotei*: “exhort, rebuke”; absent from the Greek.]

For the time will come when they will not endure sound teaching, but, according to their own desires, will heap up teachers for themselves, seeking teachers who tickle their hearing.

[Note: *vairþiþ*: Gothic lacks γάρ, “for.” — *dragand sis*: “heap up for themselves”; absent from the Greek. Codex A has *gadragand*, “heap together.” — *suþjondans*: Codex A has *suþjandans*; compare 2 Timothy 2:14. Here the Goth follows the sense more than the words: *suþjondans* is an accusative referring to *laisarjans*, “teachers,” and should be interpreted, “they seek teachers who delight their ears.”]

They will turn their hearing away from the truth, and turn themselves aside to fables.

[Note: The beginning of the Gothic lacks καί, “and.”]

But you, be sober in all things; suffer hardship; perform the work of an evangelist; fulfill your ministry.

But I am already being poured out as an offering, and the time of my departure is at hand.

[Note: *disvissais*: “departure”; Codex A’s margin has *gamalteinais*, “dissolution.”]

I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course; I have kept the faith.

But henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day; and not to me only, but also to all who love his appearing.

[Note: *þaþro þan*: “but henceforth”; Codex A has *þaþroh*.]

Thereafter.—**vaiþs garaihteins**] “crown of righteousness,” corresponding to all the Greek manuscripts.—**raihta**] Codex A has *garaihta*, which is much more frequent; compare, however, Romans IX.33.

“For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have completed the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give to me on that day.”

[Note: Col. 0857] “Make haste to come to me quickly;”

[Note: Col. 0857] “for Demas has forsaken me, having loved the present age, and has gone to Thessalonica; Crispus to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia;”

[Note: Col. 0858] **jah**] Codex A has *jag*.—**krispus**] Thus Codex B, with the Syriac; Codex A has *kreskus*, with the Greek.—**teitus du dalmatiai**] “Titus to Dalmatia”; omitted by Codex B.

“But not for me only, but also for all those who love his coming. Make haste to come to me quickly. For Demas has forsaken me, loving the present age, and has gone to Thessalonica; Crispus to Galatia; Titus to Dalmatia.”

[Note: Col. 0857] “Luke alone is with me; take Mark and bring him with yourself, for he is useful to me for ministry.”

[Note: Col. 0858] **miþ mis ains**] “alone with me,” corresponding to the Greek.—**andbahtja**] Codex B ends here.

“Luke alone is with me. Taking Mark, bring him with yourself, for he is useful to me for ministry.”

[Note: Col. 0857] “But I sent Tychicus to Ephesus.”

“To Dalmatia. But I sent Tychicus to Ephesus.”

[Note: Col. 0857] “The cloak which I left at Troas with Carpus, when you come bring it, and the books, especially the parchments.”

[Note: Col. 0858] **hakul**] Thus in Codex A; Massmann discovered it by conjecture, *l. l.* p. 127 ff.; Castiglione has *hakga*.

“The cloak which I left at Troas with Carpus—when you come, bring it—and the books, especially the parchments.”

[Note: Col. 0857] “Alexander the coppersmith did me many evils; may the Lord repay him according to his works;”

[Note: Col. 0858] **alaiksandrus**] Codex A has *alaiaiksandrus*; concerning this erroneous repetition of syllables see on John IX.41.—**usgildiþ**] “he will repay” (*ἀποδώσει*); the Greek has *ἀποδῴη*, “may he repay.”

“Alexander the coppersmith inflicted many evils upon me. The Lord will repay him according to his works.”

[Note: Col. 0857] “Whom you too must beware of, for he greatly opposed our words.”

“Of whom you too beware, for he greatly opposed our words.”

[Note: Col. 0857] “At my first defence no man stood by me, but all forsook me; may it not be reckoned [against them]—”

[Note: Col. 0858] **miþvas**] Codex A has *miþvasa*.—**ni**] Gothic either omitted *αὐτοῖς* (“to them”), or found it after *λογισθείη* (“may it be reckoned”) in its exemplar, although it is so read in none of the manuscripts now available.

“At my first defence no man stood by me, but all forsook me. May it not be reckoned . . . [lacuna]”

## To Titus

[Note: Col. 0857]

Fragments of this epistle as far as I.10 are found in codex B, and I.9—II.1 in codex A; they have already been published in *Specimen of Unpublished Portions of Ulfilas*, Milan, 1819, p. 18 ff. [Col. 0858]

Superscription, “To Titus”] Of this word nothing survives in the codex except the first letter. Castalio; compare the Prolegomena.]

[Col. 0857]

[Note: Col. 0857: “Paul, servant of God, but apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God’s chosen ones and the knowledge of truth which accords with godliness,”] Paul, servant of God but apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God’s elect and the knowledge of truth [Note: Col. 0857: “unto the hope of eternal life, which the God who does not lie promised before eternal times,”] which accords with godliness, unto the hope of eternal life, which the God who does not lie promised before eternal ages. [Col. 0859]

[Note: Col. 0859: “but made manifest at the proper time his word in the preaching which was entrusted to me according to the command of God our Saviour,”]

[Note: Col. 0859: *atbairhtida*] Thus codex B; the *Specimen* has *atbairhida*.—*mela svesamma*: “at the proper time,” Greek in all witnesses: καιροῖς ἰδίοις.]

But he made manifest his word at the proper time in the proclamation entrusted to me according to the command of God our Saviour [Note: Col. 0859: “to Titus, beloved son according to the common faith: grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Saviour.”]

[Note: Col. 0859: *valisin*] Thus codex B; the *Specimen* has *validin*, for this means “desired” (see 2 Cor. V.8; Phil. I.22), whereas γνήσιος is translated by *valis*; see Phil. IV.3; 1 Tim. I.2; compare 2 Tim. II.1; Col. III.12.—*galaubeinai*: thus codex B; the *Specimen* has *galaubeinais*.—*jah*: before it, Greek has ἔλεος, “mercy.”—*xristau iesu*: Greek, κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, “the Lord Jesus Christ.”]

of our God. To Titus, beloved son according to the common faith: grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Saviour.

[Note: Col. 0859: “For this reason I left you in Crete: that you might correct what was lacking and appoint elders in every city, as I directed you.”]

[Note: Col. 0859: *þizozei vaihtais*] “For this reason”; Greek in all witnesses: τούτου.—*in þize ei*: “that”; Greek in all witnesses: ἵνα. Castalio has *jct. þizeei*; likewise in Neh. V.18 *in þize ei* should not be written separately.—*vanata*: thus codex B; the *Specimen* has *van[an]*.—*and*: thus codex B; the *Specimen* has *ana*.—*praizbytairein*: “elders,” Greek in all witnesses πρεσβυτέρους; Gothic agrees with the Latin.]

For this reason I left you in Crete, that you might set right what was lacking and appoint elders in every city, as I directed you.

[Note: Col. 0859: “If anyone is blameless, husband of one wife, having faithful children, not accused of debauchery or insubordination.”]

[Note: Col. 0859: *ungafairinonds*] See the note on 1 Tim. III.2.]

If anyone is blameless, husband of one wife, having believing children, not accused of dissipation or insubordination.

[Note: Col. 0859: “For a bishop must be blameless as God’s steward: not arrogant, not boastful, not quick-tempered, not given to wine, not violent, not greedy for shameful gain;”]

[Note: Col. 0859: *ni bihaitja*] “Not boastful”; omitted by all Greek witnesses. The *Specimen* has *ni bihatgja*. Nor does *bihaitja* mean “quarrelsome,” as Castalio translates it in *Specimen*, p. 30, nor “quick-tempered” (ὀργίλος), as Massmann explains it in the glossary to the *Skeireins*, p. 137; rather, it means ἀλαζών, “a braggart, boaster”; see 2 Tim. III.2. From that parallel passage this *ni bihaitja* appears to have been brought here.]

For a bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward: not proud, not boastful, not violent-tempered, not [Note: Col. 0859: “but hospitable, kind, sober, just, holy, self-controlled,”]

[Note: Col. 0859: *gaþaurbs*] Thus codex B; Castalio has *gataurbs*, the *Specimen* *gaþair[d]s*.]

a drunkard, not a striker, not greedy for shameful gain; but hospitable, kindly, prudent, just, holy, self-controlled;

[Note: Col. 0859: “holding fast the faithful word according to the teaching, so that he may be able both to encourage by sound teaching and to refute those who contradict it.”]

[Note: Col. 0859: *vaurdis*] Codex A begins here.—*vaurdis triggvis*: “faithful word,” agreeing with all Greek witnesses. Instead of *triggvis*, the correct reading of codex B, codex A has *triggvs* and the *Specimen* *traiggvs*.]

holding to the faithful word according to the teaching, that he may be able both to exhort by sound teaching and to refute those who oppose it.

[Note: Col. 0859: “For there are many insubordinate persons, empty talkers, and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision,”]

[Note: Col. 0859: *managai*] Gothic agrees with the manuscripts which omit καί, “and.”—*lausavaurdai*] [Col. 0860] Codex A has *lausaivaudai*; see 2 Tim. III.2. Moreover, Gothic omits καί.—*þishun*: codex B ends.]

For there are many insubordinate persons, empty talkers, deceivers, especially those of the circumcision,

[Note: Col. 0859: “whom one must refute; they overturn whole households, teaching what they ought not for the sake of shameful gain.”]

[Note: Col. 0860: *gardins allans*] “Whole households,” agreeing with all Greek witnesses.]

whom one must rebuke, since they overturn whole households, teaching what is not proper for the sake of gain.

[Note: Col. 0859: “For one of them, their own prophet, said: ‘Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies.’”]

[Note: Col. 0860: *auk*] “For”; absent from Greek. Gothic either read γάρ with codex d cited by Mill, or δέ with codices F and G; thus *auk* stands for Greek δέ in Rom. VIII.10; 1 Cor. X.20; XV.50; compare *auk jah* for δὲ καί in 1 Cor. I.16; 2 Cor. XIII.9.—*kretes*: thus the codex, for *kreteis*; compare Luke X.5 and 2 Thess. III.17.—*biarja*: thus codex A; the *Specimen* has *unbiarja*; compare Grimm, *Grammar* I.39, 3rd ed. Since all agree that these words form a heroic verse, which the apostle Paul took from the seer Epimenides (see Blomfield on Callimachus, *Hymn to Zeus*, 8), Massmann, at the cited place, p. 224, also tried to force the Gothic words into such a verse. He produced this:

> kretos (thus!) | sintei- | no [ga]- | liugnjans | ubila | biar- | ja.

By my faith, what a very beautiful verse!]

For one of them, their own prophet, said: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies.”

[Note: Col. 0859: “This testimony is true. For this reason rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith,”]

[Note: Col. 0860: *ist*] In all Greek witnesses it stands before *sunjeina*, “true.”—*wassaba*] Thus Castalio now prints it, whereas the *Specimen* had *þrussaba*, because the first two letters in the codex have been worn away. The adverb *wassaba* is supported by the noun *wassei*, “severity” (ἀποτομία), Rom. XI.22; but *þrussaba* has nothing to establish it.]

This testimony is true. For this reason rebuke them severely, that they may be sound in the faith,

[Note: Col. 0859: “not giving heed to Jewish myths and commandments of people who turn themselves away from the truth.”]

[Note: Col. 0860: *spilli*] Thus codex A for *spille*; see Rom. VII.5; Grimm I.36.—*afvandjandane sis sunja*] *sis* is not superfluous, as Castalio thinks. Rather, as Massmann rightly observes at the cited place, p. 125, by adding *sis* the Goth renders the middle voice.]

not giving heed to Jewish myths and commandments of people turning themselves away from the truth.

[Note: Col. 0859: “But to the pure all things are pure; yet to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure, but both their mind and conscience are defiled.”]

But to the pure all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure; rather, both their mind and conscience are defiled.

[Note: Col. 0859: “They profess to know God, but deny him by their works, being abominable, unbelieving, and rejected for every good work.”]

[Note: Col. 0860: *uskusanai*] Codex A has in the margin *ungakusanai*, which also answers to Greek ἀδόκιμος, “rejected”; see 2 Cor. XIII.5 ff.]

They profess to know God, but deny him by their works, being abominable and unbelieving, rejected for every good work.

[Note: Col. 0859: “But you, speak what is fitting for sound teaching------”]

But you, speak what is fitting for sound teaching------

## To Philemon

[Note: Col. 0861]

What survives of this epistle is contained in codex A alone.]

[Col. 0861]

[Note: Col. 0861: “---but now useful to you and to me.”]

[Note: Col. 0861: *þanuh*] Castalio thinks that the Goth read οὖν, “therefore,” for ὅν, “whom”; but this conjecture is unnecessary. *þanuh* is used for *þanei*, as often; see John VIII.26, to which add Luke XVI.20; XVII.12.—*insandida*: “I sent,” Greek ἀνέπεμψα.]

[Note: Col. 0861: “I have sent him back; but receive him—that is, my own heart;”]

[Note: Col. 0861: *meinos brusts*] “My own heart”; codex A has in the margin *meina h[air]þra*, meaning the same. Castalio correctly restored the letters *air*, cut away with part of the parchment; see 2 Cor. VI.12.]

---but now useful to you and to me. Therefore I have sent him back; receive him—that is, my own heart.

[Note: Col. 0861: “I wished to keep him with me, so that in your place he might minister to me in the chains of the gospel.”]

I wished to keep him with me, that in your place he might minister to me in the bonds of the gospel.

[Note: Col. 0861: “But I wished to do nothing without your consent, so that your good deed might not be as if by compulsion but voluntarily.”]

[Note: Col. 0861: *þiuþ þein sijai*] Codex A and Castalio have *þiuþeinssijai*: in one case *þ* has been omitted because of the same following letter (see Mark X.44), and in another *s* has been incorrectly doubled.—*us lustum*] Codex A has in the margin *gabaurjaba*, “willingly,” which often stands for ἡδέως, “gladly”; see Mark VI.20; XII.37; XIV.65; 2 Cor. IX.15.]

But I wished to do nothing without your consent, that your good deed might not be as if under compulsion but voluntarily.

[Note: Col. 0861: “For perhaps he was separated for a time for this reason, that you might receive him back for ever,”]

For perhaps he departed for a time for this reason, that you might receive him back for ever;

[Note: Col. 0861: “no longer as a slave, but more than a slave—a beloved brother, especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord?”]

no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother—especially to me, but much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.

[Note: Col. 0861: “If, then, you regard me as a partner, receive him as you would me.”]

If, then, you regard me as a partner, receive him as you would me.

[Note: Col. 0861: “But if he has wronged you in any way, or owes you anything, charge this to me.”]

[Note: Col. 0861: “I, Paul, have written it with my own hand: I will repay it—not to say to you that you yourself also owe me your very self.”]

[Note: Col. 0861: *þuk silban mis skula ist*] It should be noted that, with *skula ist*, just as we still speak today, the accusative is used, as though this were a transitive verb. But in Rom. XIII.8, *ni ainummehun vaihtais skulans sijaiþ*, “owe no one anything,” the thing owed is put in the genitive. For accusatives similarly used, compare Grimm, *Grammar* IV.755 ff.]

But if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge this to me. I, Paul, have written it with my own hand: I will repay it—not to tell you that you yourself owe me your very self.

[Note: Col. 0861: “Yes, brother, may I have joy of you in the Lord; refresh my heart in Christ.”]

Yes, brother, may I have joy of you in the Lord; refresh my heart in Christ.

[Note: Col. 0861: “Confident of your obedience, I wrote to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say.”]

Confident of your obedience, I wrote to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say.

[Note: Col. 0861: “And at the same time prepare lodging for me; for I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you.”]

[Note: Col. 0862: *bijandzuþ-*] From what word this is derived, and what it truly means, remains doubtful. Castalio, *Specimen*, p. 31, compares Anglo-Saxon *bigeondan*, English *beyond*, and translates it “furthermore.” Grimm, *Grammar* II.127 note, derives it from *bijan*—that is, “to pass by, cross, proceed”—and considers it an anomalous genitive of a participle, used adverbially and meaning likewise “further, furthermore.” If *bijands* is truly a participle, as we do not doubt, it may also be nominative—whereas Grimm takes it for a genitive or plural accusative—and be referred to the subject of the sentence in this sense: “proceeding, adding, prepare lodging for me.” Thus the Goth uses participles for Greek adverbs: 1 Cor. XVI.10, *ei taimauþaius unagands sijai at izwis*, “that Timothy may be with you without fear,” Greek ἀφόβως γένηται; 1 Thess. II.13, *weis aviliudom guþa unsveibandans*—thus the codex reads, instead of the published *unsveibandane*—Greek ἀδιαλείπτως, “unceasingly”; likewise V.17. But elsewhere ἅμα, “at the same time,” which Greek has here, is rendered in Gothic by *samana*, Ps. LIII.3; Col. IV.3; 1 Thess. V.10, or by *suns*, “immediately,” 1 Thess. IV.17.]

And furthermore, prepare lodging for me; for I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you.

[Note: Col. 0861: “Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you------”]

Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you------

## Fragments of the Old Testament

[Col. 0863]

### I. Fragment of the Psalms

[Note: Col. 0863]

Psalms. If the Goths had the remaining books of the Old Testament translated into their own language (see Prolegomena, col. 463), it may certainly be supposed that a translation of the Book of Psalms (*bokos psalmo*, Luke XX.42; compare Eph. IV.8, margin of codex A) was also available to them—especially since the Gothic priests Sunja and Frithila are reported to have devoted their labour to it (Massmann, *Skeireins*, p. 88 note). We now possess fragments of that translation of the Psalms. For the rendering of passages quoted from it in the New Testament was derived not from the Book of Psalms itself, but from the Greek New-Testament text; see Eph. IV.8, where the Goth says with the Apostle: “Having ascended on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to men,” whereas Ps. LXVIII.19 says: “Having ascended on high, you led captivity captive; you received gifts among mankind.” Likewise John XIII.18: “He who ate bread with me lifted up his heel against me,” where Ulfilas, departing from both the Hebrew and the Septuagint (Ps. XLI.10), drew from the Greek text of the Evangelist. Luke XX.42 [Col. 0864]: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet,” where the Evangelist agrees word for word with the Septuagint (Ps. CX.1). For it is certain that the Gothic translation of the Old Testament was made not from a Hebrew manuscript, but from the Greek translation, especially from that form of the text contained in the Complutensian edition, or from the Latin Vulgate, a version which issued from the same source as the Complutensian text; see Prolegomena, col. 479. Evidence for this view may also be drawn from our fragment of Ps. LIII.2–3, published from the *Skeireins*, p. 37; for, differing from the Hebrew words, it agrees with the Septuagint. Nothing needs to be noted on the individual words of this fragment, except that Massmann, p. 37, in following the Greek version more closely, translated less accurately “understanding—seeking” instead of “let him understand—let him seek.”]

[Col. 0863]

[Note: Col. 0863: “. . . who understands or seeks God.”]

[Note: Col. 0863: “All turned aside; together they became useless.”]

. . . who understands or seeks God. All turned aside; together they became useless.

[Note: Col. 0863: Ezra. Castiglione most generously entrusted to us for publication the verses hitherto unpublished. Concerning the condition of the codex he writes: “It is remarkable that on this little page the numbers frequently differ from the Greek text, whereas on the page already published they often agree. It may indeed sometimes have happened that I read wrongly; but I can scarcely believe that this happened to me more than once or twice, since I took the greatest care in reading. The same must be said of the spelling of names and of the fact that the Goth, in place of Greek υἱοί (*sunjus*, ‘sons’), also uses the genitive *sunive* and *vairos*, ‘men’; these readings are certainly very secure. Yet I do not wish to conceal that the entire page has been rewritten (compare Prolegomena, p. 493), so that lines of later writing have been laid over the earlier lines, and no part of the latter appears clearly.” Verses 28–42 have already been published in the *Specimen*, p. 2.]
