### III. Fragment of the Book of Nehemiah

[Note: Col. 0867]

Nehemiah. This fragment was published in the *Specimen*, pp. 4–6.]

[Col. 0867]

… and the whole assembly said, “Amen,” and praised the Lord; and all this people carried out this word.

[Note: [Col. 0867] *alla gamainþs*] Shortly afterward the Gothic has *alla so managei* (“the whole multitude”); this placement of the article after *alls* is more frequent (Grimm IV, 391); nevertheless see Mark XI.18, *alla managei*. Grimm IV, 515. — *tavidedun*: “they did,” whereas the Septuagint, Vulgate, and Hebrew have “he did”; thus the Gothic translator customarily uses a plural verb after collective nouns; see Grimm IV, 191. — *þata vaurd—managei*: so in all books; otherwise *alla* (“all”) is omitted by all.]

… and the whole assembly said, “Amen,” and praised the Lord; and all the multitude carried out this word.

[Note: [Col. 0867] “And from the day on which he commanded me to be their governor in Judah, from the twentieth year unto the thirty-second year of King Artaxerxes—twelve years—I and my brothers did not eat the bread of my governorship.”]

[Note: [Col. 0867] *jah*] First occurrence: “and”; omitted by the Septuagint. Gothic agrees with the Complutensian text (*καίγε*, “indeed also”). — *þamma daga ei*: see on Luke I.20. — *ei veisjau fauramaþleis*: Castillionaeus adds *ei veisi du fauramaþleis*; see Loebe, *Beiträge zur Textberichtigung der Skeireins*, p. 35. Moreover, the Septuagint writes *εἶναι εἰς ἄρχοντα* (“to be as ruler”), which in Gothic is *visan du fauramaþlja*; see Col. IV.11, *þatei vesun mis du gaþrafsteinai* (“who were to me for comfort”). On account of this difference, and because after *anabiudan* (“to command”) it places *ei* in place of the infinitive supplied by the Greek—and which the Gothic translator, along with the Greeks, customarily employs after this verb everywhere else—there can scarcely be doubt that the Gothic translator rendered the Vulgate here: *ut essem dux*, “that I might be leader.” — *ïn ïudaia*: “in Judah”; all the books have *ἐν γῇ Ἰούδα* (“in the land of Judah”), which would be *ïn ïudaialand* in Gothic; see Mark I.5; cf. Luke III.1. — *und*: the Septuagint and Hebrew have *καὶ ἕως* (“and until”); Gothic agrees with the Vulgate. — *anþar*: Castillionaeus adds *·b·n·[is]*; he now says that this appears to have been written in the codex as we have printed it; certainly it cannot be written otherwise. — *artarksairksaus*: Septuagint and Hebrew, *Ἀρθασασθά*; Gothic agrees with the Vulgate. — *þiudanis*: “of the king”; omitted by the Septuagint; Gothic agrees with the Complutensian text. — *·i·b· jera*: “twelve years,” alike in all books. — *hlaif—matitedum*: “bread—we ate”; Septuagint: *βίαν αὐτῶν οὐκ ἔφαγον* (“I did not eat their exaction”); Gothic agrees with the Complutensian: *ἄρτον τῆς ἡγεμονίας μου οὐκ ἐφάγομεν* (“we did not eat the bread of my governorship”).]

And from the day when he commanded me to be their governor in Judah, from the twentieth year until the thirty-second year of King Artaxerxes—twelve years—I and my brothers did not eat the bread of my governorship.

[Note: [Col. 0867] “But the governors who had been before me burdened this people, and took from them bread and wine, and moreover forty silver shekels; and their servants exercised lordship over this people. But I did not do so, because of the fear of God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0867] *ïþ—managein*: “but—the people”; Septuagint: *καὶ τὰς βίας τὰς πρώτας, αἳ πρὸ ἐμοῦ ἐβάρυναν ἐπ’ αὐτούς* (“and the former exactions, which before me weighed upon them”). Gothic agrees with the Complutensian: *οἱ δὲ ἄρχοντες οἱ ἔμπροσθέν μου ἐβάρυναν ἐπὶ τὸν λαόν* (“but the governors before me burdened the people”). — *hlaibans—vein*: “bread—wine”; Septuagint and Vulgate have *ἐν ἄρτοις—ἐν οἴνῳ*, evidently translating the Hebrew word for word; Gothic translates correctly. — *jah nauhþanuh*: “and moreover”; Greek *ἔσχατον*. — *sikle*: “shekels”; Septuagint *δίδραχμα* (“didrachms”); Gothic agrees with the Complutensian *σίκλους* (“shekels”). — *skalkos—fraujinodedun*: “the servants exercised lordship”; Septuagint: *ἐκτετιναγμένοι—ἐξουσιάζονται*; Gothic agrees with the Complutensian [Col. 0868]: *τὰ παιδάρια—ἐκυρίευσαν*. — *guþs*: “of God”; thus Gothic with Septuagint and Vulgate, although the Complutensian has *κυρίου*, “of the Lord.”]

But the governors who were before me burdened the people and took from them bread and wine, and moreover forty silver shekels; and their servants exercised lordship over that people. But I did not do so because of the fear of God.

[Note: [Col. 0867] “And I did not prevent the work of this wall, nor acquire land; and my servants and all these who were assembled were at this work.”]

[Note: [Col. 0868] *vaurstv—svinþida*: “work—I did not prevent,” Gothic, disregarding the authority of the Complutensian text (*ἐν ἔργῳ τοῦ τείχους τούτων ἐκράτησα*, “in the work of this wall I obtained possession of these things”) and of the Vulgate (“rather, I built in the work of the wall”), comes closer to the Septuagint, which translates: *ἐν ἔργῳ τοῦ τείχους τούτων οὐκ ἐκράτησα* (“in the work of this wall I did not lay hold of these things”). — *jah*: first occurrence, “and”; omitted by the Septuagint. Gothic agrees with the Vulgate and Hebrew. — *jah þivos meinai*: “and my servants”; omitted by the Septuagint. Gothic agrees with the Complutensian, but omits *ἐκεῖ* (“there,” Gothic *jainar*) after *galisanans* (“assembled”), which all have; and with Septuagint and Vulgate it reads *ἐπί* (“at”) instead of *διά* (“through”).]

And I did not prevent the work of this wall, nor did I acquire land; and my servants and all who had been assembled were at this work.

[Note: [Col. 0867] “And one hundred and fifty Jews and governors, and those who came to us from the nations round about us, were maintained at my table.”]

[Note: [Col. 0868] *jah þai fauramaþljos*: “and the governors”; omitted by the Septuagint. Gothic agrees with the Complutensian, but beyond this authority, after *·r·* inserts *jah* (“and”) with the Septuagint. — *þai*: second occurrence, “those”; omitted by all Greek and Latin books. — *andnumanai veisun*: “were maintained”; omitted by Septuagint and Hebrew; cf. the Vulgate, which adds *quae erant* (“who were”).]

And the Jews, and the governors, one hundred and fifty men, and those coming to us from the nations around us, were maintained at my table.

[Note: [Col. 0867] “And what was consumed each day was one ox, six choice rams, and a goat prepared for me; and every ten days I provided wine for all this multitude [and for all this people]; and in addition to all this I did not demand the bread [Col. 0869] of my governorship, lest I burden this people in these labours …”]

[Note: [Col. 0868] *vas fraquman*: “was consumed”; Gothic agrees neither with Greek and Hebrew (*γινόμενον*, “being prepared”) nor with the Vulgate (*parabatur*, “was prepared”). — *wizuh*: “each”; all have *μίαν* (“one”), *ainis*, but the Gothic translator renders well. — *·a·*: Gothic agrees with Hebrew; *καί* (“and”) is omitted. — *gavalida ·q·*: alike in all books. — *gaitsa*: thus the codex, according to Castillionaeus; one would expect *gaitja*. — *dagans*: Gothic omits *ἐν πᾶσι* (“in all”), but inserts *allai* before *þizai filusnai* and *gaf* (“I gave”) before *vein*, contrary to all authorities, except that the Vulgate below adds *tribuebam* (“I supplied”). — *filusnai*: thus the codex; Castillionaeus adds *filussiai*. Since what follows, *jah allai þizai managein* (“and for all this people”), occurs in no other book, there is no doubt that two readings have become mixed in the text: one (*filusnai*, “multitude,” Greek *πλήθει*) is more suited to the Greek text, where it refers to the abundance of wine being discussed; the other (*managein*, “people”) better accords with the way in which the translator understood the author’s meaning. It would be more correct to read *all ïn þizai filusnai*. — *jah allamma þo alla hlaif*: Castillionaeus printed it thus, but the reading is certainly false. For first, what does *allamma* mean, and to which word of the text does it correspond? Secondly, *hlaifs* (“bread”) is masculine, not feminine. Further, when the article is joined with *alls* (“all”), it stands either after *alls*, or, if it precedes, *alls* is placed after the noun; see Grimm IV, 515 ff. Finally, if the printed reading were true, the translator would have rendered what is in Greek (*καὶ σὺν τούτοις*, “and with these things”) and in the Vulgate (*insuper et*, “moreover also”) very carelessly—indeed, without sense. Moreover, the codex has not *allamma* but *alla* [Col. 0869; in Migne, *m* is printed above *alla* to represent the manuscript reading], which seemed to Castillionaeus to be an abbreviation for *allamma*. If we consider the Vulgate text, which the Gothic translator follows more than once in disregard of Greek authority, much else is absent in the Gothic, including *insuper et* (*καὶ σὺν τούτοις*); yet we can readily restore it by writing, in place of the solecistic printed reading, *jah alla miþ þaim jah* (“and all things, with these also”). — *hlaif*: “bread”; Septuagint *ἄρτους* (“breads”); Gothic agrees with the Complutensian. — *fauramaþleis meinis*: “of my governorship”; Septuagint *τῆς βίας* (“of the exaction”); Gothic agrees with the Complutensian *τῆς ἡγεμονίας μου* (“of my governorship”). — *ïn þize—vaurstvam*: “because of these things—labours”; the Gothic translator follows the author’s sense more than his words, yet comes closer to the Greek (*ὅτι βαρεῖα ἡ δουλεία ἐπὶ τὸν λαὸν τοῦτον*, “because the servitude lay heavily upon this people”) than to the Vulgate (“for the people was greatly impoverished”). On writing *þize ei* separately, see on Titus I.5.]

At my table they were maintained. And what was consumed each day was one ox, six choice sheep, and a goat prepared for me. And every ten days I provided wine for all this multitude, and for all this people; and besides all this I did not demand the bread of my governorship, because I did not burden the people in these labours …

[Note: [Col. 0869] “(Of the prophe)ts who intimidated me.”]

[Note: [Col. 0869] *… te*: Castillionaeus correctly supplies *prafete*, “prophets.” — *prafstidedun*: if this truly is written so in the codex, the translator completely reverses the author’s meaning. For Noadiah and the other prophets did not comfort or encourage Nehemiah—which is what *þrafstidedun* means—but rather devoted every effort to preventing his plan of building the wall; they were therefore *φοβερίζοντες*, “frightening/intimidating.” In Gothic this is *þlahsidedun*; see 2 Corinthians X.9: *eï ni þugkjaima sve þlahsjandans ïzvis þairh bokos* (“that we may not seem to be frightening you through letters”), Greek *ἐκφοβεῖν ὑμᾶς*.]

… of the prophets who encouraged me [but perhaps: “intimidated me”].

[Note: [Col. 0869] “And this wall was completed on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty-two days; and it came to pass, when all our enemies heard it, that all these nations around us feared, and fear fell greatly in their eyes, and they knew that this work had been completed by our God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0869] *daga*: “day”; omitted by Septuagint and Hebrew; Gothic agrees with the Vulgate. — *menoþs ailulis*: Castillionaeus printed *men …*, because he could not read the following letters owing to a tear in the parchment. We have supplied the words from the Greek text (*Ἐλούλ μηνός*, “of the month Elul”), or rather from the Vulgate, which gives the words in transposed order, *mensis Elul*. — *dage jah ·b·*: alike in all books.]

… the labours … of the prophets who encouraged me. And the wall was completed … on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty-two days. And it happened, when all our enemies heard it, that all the nations around us feared, and great fear fell into their ears, and they knew that this work had been completed by our God.

[Note: [Col. 0869] *allai*: this is the reading required; Castillionaeus adds *allans*, though apart from *all …* nothing can be made out. Grimm’s less successful conjecture (IV, 516), that the Gothic translator read *πάντας* and that this accusative depends upon *hausidedun* (“heard”), is therefore unnecessary. Moreover, all books have *allai* before *fiands* (“enemies”). — *jah*: second occurrence, “and”; noteworthy is the construction which it shares with the Septuagint, without support from the Vulgate. Thus *jah* is often placed in the apodosis; cf. on Matthew VIII.14. — *ausona*: “ears”; Septuagint and Hebrew have *ὀφθαλμοῖς*, “eyes”; therefore Castillionaeus considers *ausona* a scribal error for *augona*, “eyes.” — *abraba*: Septuagint and Hebrew place it after *agis*, “fear.” — *ufkunþidun*: thus the codex for the usual *ufkunþedun*; see on Luke VIII.56. — *usfulliþs*: thus the codex, as Massmann noted, *Skeireins*, p. 182; Castillionaeus adds *usfullþs*. The codex reading is troublesome because *usfulliþs*, masculine, relates to *vaurstv* (“work”), which is neuter. But this occurs often, especially when the predicate precedes. Galatians II.16: *vairþiþ garaihts ainhun leike* (“no flesh is justified”); *Skeireins* 40.14: *naudiþaurfts vas jah gadob—anþar* (“there was need and it was fitting—another”), with neuter gender. Otherwise a neuter predicate relates to feminine nouns: Galatians V.11, *gatauran ist marzeins* (“the offence is removed”); Ephesians III.10, *kanniþ vesi—sohandugei* (“that wisdom may be made known”); or a masculine predicate is used, especially when the substantives end in *-s*, as in Romans VII.8 and 11, *lev nimands fravaurhts* (“sin, having taken occasion”). What is read in *Skeireins* 49.17, *visandin vaihtai*, should be *visandein*, as we noted on 1 Timothy I.4. Not only participles, but also adjectives and possessive pronouns often differ in gender from their nouns; this matter will be discussed in the Grammar.]

[Note: [Col. 0869] “And in those days many of the Jewish nobles sent letters to Tobiah, and letters from Tobiah came to them.”]

[Note: [Col. 0870] *managai—ïm*: “many—to them.” Gothic differs both from the Greek—*ἀπὸ πολλῶν ἐντίμων Ἰούδα ἐπιστολαὶ ἐπορεύοντο πρὸς Τωβίαν καὶ αἱ Τωβία ἤρχοντο πρὸς αὐτούς* (“letters from many Jewish nobles went to Tobiah, and Tobiah’s letters came to them”)—and from the Vulgate (“many letters of the Jewish nobles were sent to Tobiah, and from Tobiah came to them”), but in concise and elegant language it captures the author’s thought excellently.]

And in those days many Jewish nobles sent letters to Tobiah, and Tobiah sent letters to them.

[Note: [Col. 0869] “For many in Judah were bound to him by oath, because he was son-in-law to Shecaniah son of Arah; and Johanan his son had taken as wife the daughter of Meshullam son of Berechiah.”]

[Note: [Col. 0870] *ufaiþjai*: Castillionaeus printed *ufaiþeai*, which Grimm, *Grammar* I.59 (3rd ed.), thinks should be understood as *ufaiþiai*; but even so that reading is not correct, for whence should *ufaiþiai* arise? Our reading is commended both by the integrity of its form and by the frequent scribal interchange of *j* and *e*; cf. on 1 Timothy VI.13. Moreover, Castillionaeus himself now acknowledges that it is doubtful whether *ufaiþeai* or *ufaiþjai* is written. — *aieirins*: Greek *Ἠραέ*, Vulgate *Area*; perhaps Gothic read with the Vulgate and wrote *aireiïns*, through a false transposition of letters; cf. on John XVIII.36. It also reads *ïoanan* with the Vulgate, whereas Greek has *Ἰωνάν*.]

For many in Judah were bound to him by oath, because he was son-in-law of Shecaniah son of Arah; and Johanan his son took the daughter of Meshullam son of Berechiah as wife.

[Note: [Col. 0869] “They also spoke before me of matters pertaining to him, and reported my words to him; and Tobiah sent letters to intimidate me.”]

[Note: [Col. 0870] *du ïmma—*: Castillionaeus printed only *du* and says that the passage is so thoroughly obliterated that the words afterward written cannot be read, though it appears that words should be supplied that mean *τὰ συμφέροντα αὐτῷ* (“things advantageous to him”), as found in the Complutensian text. Later Massmann, *Skeireins*, p. 182, read *ïmma* after *du*, but could not explain the remainder. Since this is so, and *du ïmma* must depend upon an obliterated verb, that verb cannot have the meaning of Greek *συμφέρειν* (“to be advantageous”), because with expressions such as *dugan* (“to avail”) and *batizo visan* (“to be better”) Gothic does not ordinarily join the preposition *du*—the case is otherwise in 2 Timothy II.14, *du vaihtai ni daug* (“it is profitable for nothing”). It must rather bear a less definite sense, for example “to pertain,” and may itself be *fairrinnan*, which the Goths construe with *du*; Ephesians V.4. Thus the Gothic differs somewhat from the Complutensian (*καίγε τὰ συμφέροντα αὐτῷ ἔλεγεν*, “and indeed they spoke the things advantageous to him”) and the Vulgate (“but they also praised him”), and comes closer to the Septuagint (*καὶ τοὺς λόγους αὐτοῦ ἦσαν λέγοντες*, “and they were speaking his words”); but it often stands midway between the two texts; cf. on V.16. — *ogjan*: thus the codex; Castillionaeus adds *otjan*.]

… they spoke before me of matters pertaining to him, and reported my words to him; and Tobiah sent letters to intimidate me.

[Note: [Col. 0869] “And it came to pass, when this wall had been built, that I set up the doors, and the gatekeepers, singers, and Levites were appointed.”]

And it came to pass, when the wall had been built, that I set up the doors, and gatekeepers and singers [Col. 0871] and Levites were appointed.

[Note: [Col. 0871] “And I commanded Hanani my brother, and Hananiah, governor of the city of Jerusalem—for he was a faithful man and feared the Lord more than many—”]

[Note: [Col. 0871] *broþr*: thus the codex; Castillionaeus adds *broþri*. — *ïairusalems*: “of Jerusalem”; Greek *ἐν Ἱερουσαλήμ*, “in Jerusalem.” — *vas*: “he was”; all books have *ὡς* (“as”), although among the Greek witnesses some read *ἦν* (“he was”). — *ufar*: “more than”; Septuagint *παρά*; Gothic agrees with the Complutensian *ὑπέρ*.]

And I commanded Hanani, my brother, and Hananiah, governor of the city of Jerusalem, because he was a faithful man and feared the Lord more than many.

And I said to them, “Let not the gates of Jerusalem be opened until the sun rises …”

[Col. 0871]

# OTHER FRAGMENTS OF THE GOTHIC LANGUAGE

[Col. 0871]

# EDITOR’S NOTICE

(Partly excerpted from the Preface to the Glossary.)

[Col. 0871] Besides Ulfilas’s translation, there survive two monuments which, though their authorship is uncertain, nevertheless bear an unmistakably Gothic character: namely, the *Skeireins* and the Gothic Calendar. Since the text of the former, restored and corrected by Massmann (cf. *Jenaer Allgemeine Literaturzeitung*, 1835, no. 61; Loebe, *Beyträge zur Textberichtigung und Erklärung der Skeireins*, Altenburg, 1839), and that of the latter are found only in the *Specimen of the Unpublished Portions of Ulfilas*, we judged it most suitable to our purpose to append both below. Further, in order to make investigation easier, we have indicated in the margin of the text of the *Skeireins* the pages and columns of the codex, according to Massmann’s recension, in Roman numerals and letters; these indications are also used in the glossary. We have marked, in Arabic numerals, the pages of the same text as edited and restored by Massmann; these numbers have likewise already been used in the notes to Ulfilas’s text. Variant readings of manuscripts are denoted by C; those of editions by M (Massmann) and Cast. (Castillionaeus).

# I. THE *SKEIREINS*

[Note: [Col. 0871] Numbers and letters in square brackets are printed in the left margin in Migne.]

[I, a] …who understands or seeks God. “All have turned aside together; they have become unprofitable.” [37] [Note: [Col. 0871] Read *staua* (“pillar”)?] Yet for this purpose the common Saviour of all came: to cleanse all from sins, not by a righteousness equal or similar to ours, but by being righteousness himself, so that, offering himself for us as a sacrifice well pleasing to God, he might accomplish the reconciliation of humankind. [Note: [Col. 0871] C reads *usaunein*.] Therefore John, seeing that he who was to come after him was the Lord, declared truly: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.”

He was able also, upon taking human flesh, by that divine authority to redeem all from the devil’s power. But, knowing that such a manifestation of power had necessarily to be preceded by the firm establishment of righteousness, [38] he brought about humanity’s salvation by necessity. For if the devil had not, from the beginning, compelled human beings, but had deceived them and by falsehood induced them to transgress the commandment, it was fitting that the Lord, coming in divine might and authority, should redeem them and necessarily turn them back to good. For it did not seem consistent with righteousness to transgress the commandment which he had formerly established from the beginning by righteousness. Rather, it was fitting that the devil, who had persuaded them by his own will to transgress God’s commandment, should in turn be compelled by his own will to become the Saviour’s servant [d] and acknowledge the evil of his former deception; and that truth, when made known, should restore them to their original, unshaken standing in God.

For this purpose he also took human flesh, so that he might become for us the teacher of that righteousness which leads to God. For he had to teach us conformity to himself, call humankind back through words and works, and become the undefiled exemplar of the Gospel. But in this course of the law [I, a] he did not accomplish this. … [Note: [Col. 0872] M reads *gavandein ai …*] … [lacuna] … becoming, indeed, by faith before him bold at the time of the righteous suffering [39] of the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0872] M reads *leik is*.] After the suffering, he revealed himself to Joseph, making himself known, lest he should abandon himself to anxious reflection.

[Col. 0873] Yet the Saviour, while still setting forth the beginning, showed him the way leading upward into God’s kingdom, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless one is born from above, he cannot [b] see the kingdom of God.”

By “from above,” therefore, he means the other birth, holy and heavenly, through the washing of regeneration. But Nicodemus, still untaught and not understanding what he had first heard from the Teacher, replied: “How can a human being, being old, be born? Can he enter again into his mother’s womb [40] and be born?” [Note: [Col. 0873] M reads *aftragaleiþan* (“go back again”).] Still ignorant and not understanding the spiritual birth, while thinking of the bodily birth from the womb, he fell into doubt. Therefore he said: “How can a human being, being old, be born? Can he enter again into his mother’s womb and be born?”

But the Saviour, observing his present judgment and explaining that he had the capacity to grow in faith, addressed him as one still ignorant: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless one is born of water and Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” For it was necessary and fitting to receive cleansing through baptism. A human being, constituted from different elements, consists of a rational soul and body, and has an appearance distinct from the spirit. Therefore, following this pattern, he named two things corresponding to the two elements of baptismal cleansing: visible water [III, a] and invisible Spirit, so that the visible … [lacuna] … were not there. [Note: [Col. 0873] M reads “… they were not”; M omits “there.”] There [41] they came and were baptized; for John had not yet been cast into prison.

[Note: [Col. 0873] M reads *nauh þanuh* (“yet, still”).] By saying this, the Evangelist showed that the controversy concerning him had only recently arisen through Herod’s imprisonment. But before that, because both baptized according to two dispensations and each commended his own baptism, they began to dispute among themselves, [b] [Note: [Col. 0873] C perhaps, and M, read *undrunnun*] some not knowing which ought to be regarded as greater. Hence arose a dispute between John’s disciples and a Jew concerning purification. [Note: [Col. 0873] C and M perhaps read *þau*; M reads *inþizei*.] In that purification, bodily cleanness was prescribed by custom and purity before God was commanded. Yet they were not to employ Jewish washings and repeated baptisms for removing defilements; rather, hearing John, the forerunner of the Gospel, they were to understand that the Lord also appointed spiritual baptism. [Note: [Col. 0874] Read perhaps *sinteinom*, “repeated.”] Therefore the dispute concerning purification was rightly brought to an end.

For the law [c] prescribed that a spotless red heifer, having been slaughtered, should be burned outside the camp. [Note: [Col. 0874] M omits “one law.”] Then, after sprinkling with water, hyssop, and scarlet wool, they were purified, as was fitting for those intending to be purified. [Note: [Col. 0874] C reads *munandane*.]

But John preached a baptism of repentance and promised forgiveness of sins to those who simply turned back. The Lord’s baptism gives forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Holy Spirit, and grants that they become true citizens of the kingdom. [Note: [Col. 0874] M reads “the Lord’s.”] Thus John’s baptism lies in the middle between the two, surpassing the bodily cleansing prescribed by the righteous law, but falling short of the Gospel’s baptism. [Note: [Col. 0874] C reads *minizei*, “less.”] Therefore he clearly teaches us, saying: [Note: [Col. 0874] M reads “teaches, declares.”] “But I baptize you in water; he who comes after me is mightier than I, whose sandal-thong I am not worthy, stooping down, to unfasten. He [IV, a] will baptize you in the Holy Spirit.” [Note: [Col. 0874] C and M perhaps read *gaggida* for “coming”; see supplement to p. 33.]

Concerning purification, then … “Now my joy has been fulfilled. He [43] must increase, but I must decrease.” Therefore, when his disciples, seeking the Jews concerning purification, said among themselves, [Note: [Col. 0874] C reads *sokjandans*, “seeking.”] “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you bore witness—behold, he baptizes, and all go to him,” they still did not understand concerning the Saviour. [Note: [Col. 0874] M reads *inuh þis*.] Therefore he taught them, [b] saying: “He must increase, but I must decrease.”

John’s teaching concerning him was useful only for a short time, and prepared the souls of those baptized to receive the Gospel proclamation. But the Lord’s teaching, beginning from Judaea, spread through the whole world and grows further, now also drawing every person to the knowledge of God and thereby becoming manifest. [Note: [Col. 0874] C and M read *alamanne*, “all people”; M reads *und* for “and.”] He made known the greatness of the Lord’s glory, saying: “He who comes from above is above all.”

He did not state this merely because he is above all, [44 c] but also because he showed the greatness of his power by speaking of one who is heavenly and comes from above; whereas the one who is earthly and speaks from the earth belongs to earthly and verbal existence. Among human beings there was one who might be holy or a prophet, even while proclaiming righteousness; nevertheless, being from earth, he spoke out of earthly and verbal existence. [Note: [Col. 0874] M reads *inþizei*.] But he who came from heaven, even though he seemed to be in flesh, is above all; and what he saw and heard, [d] that he testifies. Yet no one receives his testimony.

Nevertheless, although he came from heaven to earth in human reconciliation, [Col. 0875] he was not merely earthly, nor did he speak from earth, but proclaimed the heavenly revelation which he had seen and heard from the Father. [Note: [Col. 0875] C reads *anairþai*; M, *ana airþa*; M reads *þehaldis*, “merely”; C reads *þai* for “earth.”] The objections made against John, therefore, were not intended merely to make known the Lord’s greatness, but to refute and overthrow the godless error of Sabellius and Marcellus. [Note: [Col. 0875] M reads *markaillaus*.] They declared Father and Son to be one. But [V, a] the other—the holy … [lacuna] … awaits honour from the Father in every work of the one dispensation. [45] [Note: [Col. 0875] Something such as “he says one” or “he says the other” is missing.]

What follows distinguishes the one who loves from the other who is loved, and the one who indicates another from the other made equal in works. [Note: [Col. 0875] C reads *frijondan* for “beloved,” and has the compounded reading *taiknjandanþaranuh*.] Knowing the present error, he wished them to be corrected by the twofold manifestation of Father and Son, and not to speak confusedly. Therefore, using a clear expression, he said: “For as the Father raises the dead and makes them live, so also the Son makes live those whom he wills.” Thus, being alike in will and power to the one who first raises the dead, and asserting the unbelievers’ rash presumption, he said: “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” [Note: [Col. 0875] C reads *ainohun*.]

Sabellius’s assertion that they are one and the same has assumed different force from the expressions “judges” and “does not judge.” [46 c] How can the same one have power both to judge and not to judge? The distinction does not arise merely from the naming of two different manifestations, but still more from the evidence of the works: the one truly judges no one, but gives the Son authority of judgment; and the Son, receiving honour from the Father and doing all judgment according to his will, acts so that all may honour the Son as they honour the Father.

We all, therefore, must confess, on the basis of such a clear declaration, the honour due to the unbegotten God, and recognize the only-begotten Son of God as God. [Note: [Col. 0875] Read perhaps *gakunnan*, “recognize”; compare Galatians 2:5.] Thus, believing, we may render to both the honour that is due. [Note: [Col. 0875] C and M read *waþaramma*, “to both”; M reads *vairþida*, “due honour.”] For the saying, “that all may honour the Son as they honour [d] the Father,” teaches us to render not identical but like honour. [Note: [Col. 0875] C reads *svasverand*.] The Saviour himself, praying to the Father concerning the disciples, said: “That you may love them as you love me.” He means not identical love but like love, as the expression demonstrates. Likewise … [Note: [Col. 0876] Perhaps *haidau*?] [VI, a] [lacuna] … thereby necessarily exposed the error of that one. [Note: [Col. 0876] Read perhaps *silba*, “himself.”] He himself says: “He must increase, [47] but I must decrease.”

When they seemed for a short time to believe John on hearing him, afterwards they made no great profession concerning him. [Note: [Col. 0876] The manuscript is illegible here; perhaps *atsewun*, “they showed themselves.”] Yet he commends them properly, saying: “He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing for a while to rejoice in his light. But I have testimony greater than John’s. For the works which the Father gave me to do—the works which I do—testify concerning me, that the Father sent me.”

For testimony borne in human words seems liable to doubt to those who do not know its truth. [Note: [Col. 0876] M reads *þuhta*; the codex is very faded here.] But the Father’s testimony through my works exceeds every human testimony. John, who testified to you, could make you know without fear. For every human word can be interpreted in another sense. [Note: [Col. 0876] Read perhaps *sunja*, “truth.”] But holy works, [c] being indisputable, [Note: [Col. 0876] M reads *unandsokana*.] revealing plainly the judgment of their doer, [48] demonstrate that he was sent from the Father in heaven. Therefore he says: “And the Father who sent me has himself testified concerning me.” [Note: [Col. 0876] Castillion reads *sanda*, “sent.”]

The Father testified concerning him in different ways and at different times: sometimes through prophetic words, sometimes through a voice from heaven, sometimes through signs. But because the hearts of unbelievers had become harder concerning these things which had occurred, he rightly added: “You have never heard his voice or seen his form, and you do not have his word abiding in you, because you do not believe him whom he sent.” [Note: [Col. 0876] C has a defective reading; Castillion supplies *gasaiwiþ*, “you have seen.”] For blame cannot be assigned to those who have seen. Some heard his voice; others saw his form. Blessed, too, are those pure in heart, as he said, [VII, a] for they shall see God. Thus, as it were, through … [lacuna] … the power [49] of the Lord, who knows, and their acknowledgment of his authority.

Not only [inherited source boundary], but Andrew also, who said, “There is one little boy here, who has five barley loaves and two fish,” made a similar acknowledgment. [Note: [Col. 0876] M reads *fimf*, “five.”] Philip likewise declared it, thinking little of the matter and not recognizing the Teacher’s worth, when he said: “But what are these [b] for so many?” The Lord answered him without mockery: “Make the men recline.” Since there was much grass in that place, they made the multitude recline: five thousand men, besides women and children, as though reclining for a great supper, having no other food than the five loaves and two fish. [Note: [Col. 0877] C and M read *visandin*, “being.”] Taking them and blessing them, he multiplied them; and, satisfying so many, he gave them not only enough for their need but much more.

After the multitude had eaten, twelve baskets full of the remaining fragments of bread were found. [Note: [Col. 0877] M reads *tvalif*, “twelve.”] Likewise, there was as much fish as they wished. He displayed the [lacuna] miracle of his own power not only in the loaves but also in the fish. For he made them become as many as he considered fitting: sufficient that each person might receive as much as he wished. [Note: [Col. 0877] M reads *gahabaida ize*, “he made them have”; C is illegible. C and M perhaps read *ainwarjamma*, “to each one.”] Nor did he allow this abundance to become deficient in anything; rather, even after that abundance, he filled the disciples more fully and instructed others to observe that he was the same one who fed their fathers in the wilderness for forty years. [Note: [Col. 0877] M reads *fidvortiguns*, “forty.”]

Then, when they had been satisfied, he said to his disciples: “Gather the remaining fragments, lest anything be lost.” They gathered them and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves and two fish that remained from the … [VIII, a] [lacuna] … they laid hands upon him. [Note: [Col. 0877] M omits “then.”] For by his holy power he invisibly restrained their evil, while they were still deliberating and did not dare to rise against him. Then the officers went to the chief priests and Pharisees. They said to them: “Why [51] have you not brought him?” [Note: [Col. 0877] M reads *du we*, “why.”] The officers answered: “Never has any human being spoken as this man speaks.”

But their reply to the accusation was stronger than the sentence directed against that unbelief. For they answered those who reproached them because they had not brought him, not defending the evil conduct of their accusers, but judging the Lord’s teaching, openly revealed before all people, to be much more worthy. [Note: [Col. 0877] M reads *silkaleikjandans*.] But those others, unable through hatred to endure their own arrogance, answered them, [c] saying: “Have you also been deceived? [Note: [Col. 0877] M reads *si(j)uþ*.] Behold, has any ruler [52] or Pharisee believed in him? But this multitude, which does not know the law, is accursed.”

Yet they spoke with bitter perversity, intending by a lie to make it appear that no ruler or Pharisee had believed in him. Nicodemus, who had come to him by night and boldly pleaded the truth before them, said: “Does our law judge a person?” [Note: [Col. 0878] M reads *neikaudemau*, “we came at night.”] When they said that no ruler or Pharisee had believed in him, they did not know that the righteous Pharisee—indeed, a ruler, a member of the Jewish council—had risen from among those called accursed, believed in the Lord, and spoken before them in defence against their evil judgment. [Note: [Col. 0878] C perhaps reads *raihits*, “righteous”; C perhaps reads *ainhun*, “any.”] But, unable to endure that defence, they answered him: “Are you also from Galilee? Search and see that …” [Source ends incomplete.]

# GRAMMAR OF THE GOTHIC LANGUAGE, RENDERED FROM GERMAN INTO LATIN BY F. TEMPESTINI

## PREFACE

Before undertaking this grammar, we have thought it worthwhile briefly to explain its basis and character.

With respect to the arrangement of the work, we were obliged to seek an independent path in syntax, a field hitherto unexplored. In attempting, however, to follow a didactic order, our attention has occasionally relaxed; accordingly, we reasonably hope that the index of subjects and words placed at the end of the work will be a great aid to those for whom our arrangement is not yet familiar.

In the first three chapters, which treat writing and pronunciation, together with the inflection and formation of words, we have indeed followed the customary order with regard to form. But with regard to substance, the attentive reader will readily observe that here also, as in syntax, fortified by our own investigations and following our own path, we have departed from the common doctrine. Whether, and to what extent, we have rightly done so, the candid reader will judge.

Although, in preparing this work, we have chiefly kept before our eyes the principle that the grammar of every language should be restricted so as to explain the language from the language itself, and should take particular care neither to follow any preconceived system nor impose upon the language to be explained forms belonging to another—even a cognate—language, we have nevertheless not been so bound by this principle that we have failed constantly to invoke, especially in syntax, the Greek text, the foundation of Gothic literature. For the distinctive character of Gothic emerges more clearly from this comparison.

Whenever we occasionally mention an earlier and a later language, by the latter we mean the one indicated in the prolegomena to the text, col. 473.

Since, moreover, in preparing this work we have repeatedly had occasion to supply and correct omissions and errors which had crept into both the glossary [Note: [Col. 0879] In the German edition the glossary was published before the grammar. Translator.] and the text with its translation, we think that we shall perform a welcome service by collecting these corrections here and referring the reader to the grammar through page-indicating numbers.

# INTRODUCTION

[Col. 0881]

§ 1. The Gothic language (*gutiska razda*) [Note: [Col. 0881] *Razda* is the Gothic word denoting a people’s speech, like Greek γλῶσσα, “language,” and λαλιά, “speech,” French *langage*. But *tuggo* denotes the instrument of speech, the tongue (*la langue*), Mark 7:33, 35; Luke 1:64; and *maþleins* denotes the word or speech which people speak (λαλιά), John 8:43; see *Gr. Gr.* I, 1 (third edition).] is the common language of the eastern Germans, designated collectively by the name Goths.

[Note: [Col. 0882] Material enclosed in French quotation marks («—») is less important and concerns learned readers rather than beginners. A person approaching this grammar wholly unprepared may, if desired, pass it over, returning to it after becoming sufficiently familiar with the rest. Translator.]

«The native name of the Goths is *Guthos*—not *Gutans*, as Zeuss writes in *Die Deutschen*, p. 134—as appears in the Gothic Calendar, where *gutþiuda* means the Gothic people. The Greeks called them Γόθοι, with an aspirated dental, or rather Γότθοι, with a doubled consonant; the Romans called them *Gothi*, without doubling, always shortening the vowel *o* in verse. Thus in Gruter, *Inscriptions* 161, 2, where metre requires the vowel to be long, one reads, “Who was able to subdue the fierce minds of the Goths” [Arnoldus Mercator], instead of *Gothorum*.

The forms *Gotti* and *Gotticus*, however, used in the *History of the Emperors* by Coelius Spartianus (*Antoninus Caracalla* 10 and *Antoninus Geta* 6), do not derive from Greek. The old and original spelling of this name is still found in an ancient Latin writing which, from very many characteristics, is conjectured to have been written by a Goth himself: namely, in the marginal gloss of the Paris codex containing the Acts of the Council of Aquileia, published by Waitz, where p. 13 has *lingua gotica*; and in a Neapolitan document dating approximately to the middle of the sixth century, where *ecclesia gotica* is written.

The genuine spelling has been preserved in Old High German, for eighth-century glosses have *Guti* and *Gudi*; see Graff, *Althochdeutschen Sprachschatz* IV, 173 ff. Among chroniclers of the same century, moreover, the part of southern Gaul occupied by the Goths bears the names *Gutiae* and *Goziae*; see Zeuss, *Die Deutschen*, 420. Of the same stock are Tacitus’s *Gotones* and *Gothones* (*Annals* 2.62; *Germania* 40), Pliny’s *Gutones* (*Natural History* 4.14; 37.2), and Ptolemy’s Γύθωνες, “Gythones.”

As for Strabo’s Βούτονες, “Boutones,” 7.1, it would be too bold to emend this to Γούτονες, “Goutones,” on account of the quantity of the vowel *o*. Yet *Gutones* certainly correspond to *Gutos* (*Guti*) in the same way as *Burgundiones* correspond to *Burgundi*. Zeuss is mistaken when, in the cited passage, p. 134, arranging chronologically the names found in Greek and Latin authors, he thinks that *Goths* derives from *Gutones*, and that Greek Γότθοι derives from *Gutþiuda*.

The Goths are also frequently called Getae, or this people is alluded to; see Zeuss, cited passage, p. 403. Jornandes did likewise: himself a Goth, he entitled his people’s history *On the Origin and Deeds of the Getic Nation*. Hence in later times the name “Getic language” was applied to Gothic, as may be found in Bonaventura Vulcanius; compare § 2. The names Γουταί—commonly but incorrectly written Γοῦται—in Ptolemy and Γαυτοί in Procopius, *Gothic War* 2.15, belong not to the continental Goths but to Scandinavia; Zeuss perceptively discusses them in the cited passage, pp. 158 and 511; compare § 3.

Whoever wishes to know what *Gutos* means must first compare it with both Gothic *guþ*, “God,” and *gods*, “good,” and with the Caucasian terms *gots*, *kodji*, *katsi*, “human beings.” Castillion follows the latter derivation in his preface to 2 Corinthians, p. X. The older Scandinavian scholars interpret their Goths (*Gotnar*) as wanderers, travellers, and men; see *Edda Sæmundar* I, 41, 530 b, correctly deriving the name from *gautr*, “a shrewd man.” Whoever finally wishes to compare the name with *giota* will find an explanation in the “womb of nations,” or “workshop of peoples,” as Jornandes calls Scandinavia, p. 83 of Lindenbrog’s edition.

For our continental Goths, however, a derivation from *giutan, gaut, gutun, gutans*, “to pour,” could hardly be maintained, since it cannot be proved that *giutan* also means “to beget” or “to create,” as Zeuss maintains in the cited passage, p. 134. We therefore gladly confess, in conclusion, that we do not know at all what the name of the Goths means.

«Grimm rightly observed (*Grammar* XLV, first edition) that the language under discussion is incorrectly called Moeso-Gothic. If Ulfilas, who was probably the first to write in Gothic, or at least whose writings are the oldest surviving monuments—see §§ 6 and 11—lived among Goths inhabiting Moesia, those Goths, though they had earlier separated from their other brethren, certainly shared a common language with them. Indeed, the Gothic documents surviving to us, produced in Italy under Ostrogothic rule, are entirely written in the same language as the biblical translations. If the Ostrogoths spoke this same language, then so also did the Visigoths, part of whom inhabited Moesia. Our language was thus common to all Goths; compare § 4.» 

§ 2. The Gothic language belongs to the Indo-Germanic stock, and among the languages of the Germanic family it is that which supplies the oldest monuments; thus, unquestionably the first of all to be written, it has come down to us preserved in its purity.

«In modern times attempts have been made abroad—that is, outside Germany—to prove that the Goths did not belong to the Germanic stock. Among others, Stephen Horvat, in *Tudományos Gyütemény*, 1834, fourth fascicle, considers them a people both allied to and ancestral to the Huns, Polovtsians, [Note: [Col. 0883] Polovtsians or Polovtzes—that is, “hunters” in Russian idiom—are the people commonly called Cossacks (*les Cosaques*), who are of Slavic origin. Translator.] Cumans, [Note: [Col. 0883–0884] Cumans (*les Comans*), also called Kumyks or Koumyks, are of Tartar origin and inhabit the Caucasus. Translator.] and others. But the learned man was mistaken, deceived by the Arabic name *Guss* for *Us* or *Uz*, [Note: [Col. 0884] In the German edition the glossary precedes the grammar; in ours it has been placed after it. Translator.] who are probably the same as the Cumans.

The Goths would also be assigned to another stock if they were believed identical with the Getae; see § 1. But in fact the Goths have nothing in common with the Getae except that, living as neighbours on the two banks of the lower Danube, they sometimes lived intermixed. In any event, the Germanic origin of the Goths is established by both ethnography and linguistics, and is no longer questioned by anyone.»

§ 3. Among Germanic languages, Gothic stands nearest to Germanic, and next nearest to Old High German, though it has more in common with the Scandinavian idioms. Unlike Old High German, however, which produced Middle and New High German, Gothic had no descendant.

“Although we do not retract the principle set out in the preface to the glossary [Note: [Col. 0884] In the German edition the glossary precedes the grammar; in ours it has been placed after it. Translator], and although it is not our intention here to examine and display the relations of the Gothic language to Sanskrit and the other related languages of Asia, Bopp’s remark (Conjugationssystem, [Col. 0884] p. X) is especially pertinent: ‘I believe I am reading Sanskrit when I read the venerable Ulfilas; his language stands, so to speak, midway between Sanskrit and German.’ That is: I think I read Sanskrit when reading the venerable Ulfilas; for his language stands between Sanskrit and German. Moreover, without exaggeration, Bopp’s statement (Vergleichende Grammatik I, p. 115**; II, preface p. VII ff.) is wholly true and especially worthy of notice in marking Gothic’s affinity with the other languages of the Germanic family: ‘Gothic is the true point of departure and illumination, the true foundation-pillar of German grammar—the Germanic Sanskrit.’ That is, Gothic is the true source of light and explanation, and the pivot of German grammar; in a word, Sanskrit in Germanic form.

Castiglione offers a strange alternative concerning Gothic’s relation to the other Germanic languages. Having read a note of Fulda which asserts that Gothic is not exclusively the foundation of any one of the Germanic languages, he does not hesitate to illustrate his opinion thus (II Corinthians, preface p. IV ff.): ‘Either the same happened with the Gothic language as later with Latin: although it became, as it were, the mother and source of several related languages, and although many Latin words became obsolete in them, it is still visible in each of them through countless remaining traces; or, conversely, it may be thought that, when the Germanic Gothic people occupied a great part of Europe and were divided among several peoples, the intermingling of dialects made the Gothic language mixed.’

Yet it is evident, and nobody will deny, that Gothic, High German, Icelandic, and so forth—each now a distinct language—ultimately spring from one common stock. We maintain only that Gothic arose earlier than the others, although much concerning that origin escapes us. For if it were true—as was for a long time believed on the authority of Jordanes, and is still believed among the Swedes from patriotic feeling (Geijer, History of Sweden, German translation by Leffler, I, 10 ff.)—that the Goths of the continent were identical with those of Scandinavia (against this see Zeuss, pp. 403, 437; Grimm, preface to Wuk Stephanowitsch’s Servian grammar, p. XXIV*), then the closest and most numerous relationships between the northern languages and Gothic would doubtless be known. But this is not so; Gothic has its greatest affinity with High German. That affinity appears especially in vowel gradation, particularly in vocalization and the resemblance of inflectional forms; there is, further, a certain relation between Gothic and the Scandinavian languages in the shifting-out of vowels (*déplacement*), Gr. Gr. LI [1st ed.], I, 8, 9 [3rd ed.].

Had anything, or anything more substantial, survived from the other East Germanic languages—those of the Lombards, Heruli, Rugians [Note: [Col. 0884] The original inhabitants of Farther Pomerania. Translator], Thuringians, Marcomanni, and Quadi [Col. 0885] [Note: [Col. 0885] Inhabitants of Moravia, the borders of Silesia, Upper Hungary, and that part of Austria lying between the Danube and the Morava. [Col. 0886] Translator] (French, *les Quades*)—we should probably find in them the connecting link between Gothic and Old High German. The same must be said of the other languages of the Germanic family.”

## § 4. Nothing certain can be determined concerning the dialects of Gothic.

“Neither in certain double forms, such as *aglaitei* and *aglaiti*, nor in some variant spellings, such as *gaþarhjan* for *gatarhjan*, should one properly seek traces of dialect, as Castiglione argues in the preface to II Corinthians, p. VI, and at Galatians II, 11. In the first case, if the form differs, a difference of meaning may be conceived; in the second, it is a scribe’s error, since elsewhere too he frequently substitutes *t* for *þ*. Indeed, even if a definite dialectal difference were detected in these or similar cases, no benefit could arise from it for us, since we do not know to which dialect this or that feature belongs.

“Grimm (Gr. I, 2 [3rd ed.]) considers the languages of the Gepids, Vandals, Heruli, and perhaps Bastarnae [Note: [Col. 0886] Living near Dacia. Translator] akin to Gothic. Procopius explicitly says (*On the Vandalic War* I, 2) that the Visigoths, Vandals, and Gepids had ‘one speech, called Gothic’ (*phōnē mia, gothikē legomenē*). But Procopius’ belief that the Vandals were of the same stock as the Goths is certainly a mere conjecture, one which Zeuss (p. 441) and Grimm himself refuse to accept, since the Vandalic names transmitted to us plainly exhibit a conspicuous difference from Gothic. If, trusting this phrase *gothikē legomenē*, one could conclude that it was the language called Gothic at Constantinople, its identity with our Gothic would be asserted rashly. Certainly Gothic priests were teachers of the Vandals (cf. Zeuss, p. 453**); but it does not follow that the two peoples had the same language. Nor should one infer this, with Castiglione (on Philippians, p. 65), from Salvian’s vehement attacks on the Arianism of Goths and Vandals (cited by Massmann, *Skeireins*, p. 109), or from the writers’ silence about a Vandalic translation of the Bible, and conclude that the Vandals used the Gothic version.”

## § 5. The treasury of the Gothic language also contains no small number of foreign riches; their admission is readily explained by the fact that the Goths were dependent upon neighbouring peoples, though upon different peoples at different times, in their social, political, and religious order.

“Castiglione certainly exaggerates when he says (II Corinthians, preface p. IV): ‘Hardly one or two words remain in Gothic for which a related word cannot be found either in the newer German dialects or at least in the remnants of the older ones.’ On the contrary, there are quite a number of Gothic words for which no related forms can be found throughout the entire range of Germanic dialects, so far as we know; see the preface to the glossary. There are indeed certain Gothic words lost in the remains of the Germanic languages which are explained from Indic languages (see Bopp, *Conjugationssystem*, p. X), and which Sanskrit especially has supplied to Germanic idioms. But there are many more which the Goths drew from an external source; cf. Grimm, Gr. I, 9 [3rd ed.].

We have already mentioned Slavic and Lithuanian words in the preface to the glossary. With regard to Finnish, these are indeed the words which Ihre (*Ulfilas illustratus*, p. 266) rightly called Scythian, and which deserve still more investigation today because their relation to Germanic has been established. Some of these, then, remain the same in both languages, as Gothic *paida*, Finnish *païta* (since *p* occurs mute in Gothic words); and Grimm, in Hofer’s periodical on linguistic studies I, 10 ff., presents many other correspondences with Gothic; that scholar assumes that one language or the other borrowed from the other. Namely:

| Gothic | Finnish |
|---|---|
| *maþa* | *mato* |
| *marei* | *meri* |
| *namo* | *nimi* |
| *meki* | *miekka* |
| *mulda* | *multa* |
| *ahana* | *akana* |
| *runa* | *runo* (‘poem’) |
| *gulþ* | *kulta* |
| *aiþei* | *äeti* |
| *dauhtar* | *tytti* |

To these might be added:

| Gothic | Finnish |
|---|---|
| *sama* | *sama* |
| *manags* | *moni* |
| *mitaþ* | *mitta* |
| *hansa* | *kansa* |
| *audag* | *autuas* |
| *miton* | *miettiä* |
| *aggvu* | *angen* |
| *vasti* | *waatet* |
| *waþo* | *wahto* |
| *auþja* | *autia* |
| *kiusan* | *kiusata* |
| *vald-ufni* | *walta* |
| *hlaibs* | *leibä* |

Cf. Castiglione on II Timothy I, 5.

“According to Jordanes (p. 90, Lindenbrog edition), the Goths borrowed from the Huns only proper names. The Roman influence on Gothic was much smaller, though it is readily explained by the extension of Latin throughout Moesia; it would seem greater if Gothic writings composed when the Goths inhabited northern Italy and the Roman provinces of Gaul and Spain had come down to us. Gothic borrowed or admitted from Latin: *militon* (‘to serve as a soldier’), *kavtsjo* (‘surety, caution’), *laiktjo* (‘reading’), *assarjus* (‘as’), *aurali* (‘oral, neck-cloth’), *faskia* (‘band, bandage’), *kaisar* (‘Caesar’), *karkara* (‘prison’), *kapillon* (‘hair’), *lukarn* (‘lamp’), *kumbjan* (‘to lie down’), *pund* (‘pound’), and so forth.

The Goths living on the Danube experienced a greater Greek influence, since they always remained allied with the capital of the Greek Empire, from which they received Christianity and from the Greek source of which they took their translation of the Bible [Col. 0887]. Thus they borrowed from Greek, for example: *markreitus* (*margaritēs*, ‘pearl’), *pistikeins* (*pistikos*, ‘genuine’), *spyreida* (*spyris*, ‘basket’), *aipistaule* (*epistolē*, ‘letter’), *ackklesjo* (*ekklēsia*, ‘assembly, church’), *paurpaura* (*porphyra*, ‘purple’), *drakma* (*drachmē*, ‘drachma’), *smyrn* (*smyrrhon*, ‘myrrh’), *saban* (*sabanon*, ‘burial-cloth’), *apaustaulus* (*apostolos*, ‘apostle’), etc. But how easily one may be deceived by pressing similarity of words too far is apparent from Castiglione’s note on I Corinthians XIII, 1. There he discusses *klismoklis* and emphatically maintains that it is of Greek origin, although it is certain that this was never numbered among the known instruments of the Greeks.

“No foreign influence appears, however, in the forms of inflection. It cannot be called influence when proper names, drawn from a foreign source, often have a foreign or foreign-imitating inflection, while native words experience nothing comparable. Foreigners did not influence syntax in any way either—or at least this was universally accepted before the question arose whether Ulfilas’ translation was slavishly made from Greek; see the prolegomena to Ulfilas. Yet the Hellenisms we recognize are also adapted to the character of Gothic, since they occur elsewhere even without Greek prompting, as, for example, attraction; on this see the syntax.”

## § 6. What Gothic literature has reached us is only scanty and poor; apart from fragments of the biblical translation and what is known as the *Skeireins*, only certain trifling remnants survive.

“That which properly constitutes literature appeared among all peoples before literature itself: namely poems and songs. That the same was so among the Goths is clear from the native words they used for these things. A song (*ōdē*) is here called *saggvs* (Ephesians V, 19; Colossians III, 16), from *siggvan* (‘to sing,’ *adein*); and a poem, *liuþ*, from *liuþan* (Romans XV, 9), also used for *psallein* (‘to sing psalms’). Besides these general designations, there are certain specific names: for ‘hymn,’ *hazeins* (*hymnos*: Ephesians V, 19; Colossians III, 16). In *naiteins* (cf. Old Lithuanian *neizjan*, Gf. II, 1128), which in Mark II, 7; III, 28; and Luke V, 23 renders *blasphēmia*, one may readily recognize the Germanic stem expressing an ironical and declamatory poem—perhaps called *neiþ* among the Goths, as in Old Norse *nið*; cf. Gf. II, 1031. Religious songs had no special vocabulary, or at least the biblical translators borrowed Greek *psalma* (Luke XX, 42) or *psalmo* (I Corinthians XIV, 26; Ephesians IV, 8 margin; V, 19; Colossians III, 16), though they could have used *liuþ* for *psalmos* as well. On maxims, see below. A riddle was called *frisahts* (I Corinthians XIII, 12); a likeness, *gajuko* (see glossary, s.v.); tales, parables, and narratives, *spill* (see glossary, s.v.).

We conclude that songs existed among the Goths not merely from their having special names, but also from Jordanes’ explicit testimony. He calls them both songs (*cantiones*, p. 93, Lind. edition) and poems (*carmina*, p. 83), and further affirms that there were historical and heroic songs in which were celebrated, for example, the Goths’ departure from Scandinavia to the continent, the subjugation of the Vandals, and their passage through Scythia to the Black Sea (p. 83); indeed, ‘the deeds of Ethesparma, Hanala, Fridigern, Vidicula, and others held in great repute by this people—men whom wondrous antiquity scarcely boasts to have had as heroes’ (p. 86). Of the rhythm of these poems we know absolutely nothing. They were probably iterative, like the songs of the other Germanic peoples; but it is certain that they were not cast in the heroic Greek metre, as Massmann unhappily conjectured from the verse cited in Titus I, 12. Nor were they committed to writing, but, as among other Germanic peoples, were handed down orally by particular singers.

The Gothic name of these singers escapes us. For they cannot be called *liuþarjos*, the word by which the singing Levites (*adontes*) of the Hebrews are rendered in Ezra II, 41 and Nehemiah VII, 1: the Hebrews sang in our manner, whereas the Germans sang rather in a recitative manner, accompanied by the modulation of the lyre (Jordanes, p. 86). To sing in that manner in Gothic is *siggvan*, and the compound *ussiggvan*, that is, ‘to recite’ (*anaginōskein*); hence *saggvjans* would be a more suitable name for such singers.

The reason why Gothic poems were not written down is easy to understand. In early times this was not customary; and even if the Goths possessed writing before Ulfilas’ age (see § 11), it is difficult to believe that it was readily available and suitable for poems. When they did possess a suitable script, Maecenases were lacking; nor could they readily devote themselves to letters except when, enjoying political tranquillity, they had also recovered their ancestral customs and a love of their own literature. Add that among the Goths writing was long reserved to priests alone; priests first used it in defending and spreading religion, and consequently could not have devoted themselves to poetry even had they wished.

“Many, relying on a passage of Jordanes, also believed that the early Goths had written laws. This passage, notable also from another standpoint, reads as follows (Lind., p. 93): ‘Diceneus instructed them, the Goths, in nearly every branch of philosophy. He taught them ethics, in order to restrain their barbarous customs; imparting physics, he caused them to live naturally according to their own laws, which they still call, when written down, *bellagines*; instructing them in logic, he made them experienced in reasoning above other nations; showing them practice, he commanded them to live in good deeds; demonstrating theory, he taught them to contemplate the twelve signs, the courses of the planets through them, and all astronomy, etc. He chose their wisest men and, instructing them in theology, persuaded them to worship certain divinities and shrines.’

Although it is certain that the Gothic nation was not philosophically educated in the manner that this passage of Jordanes, full of unseemly and disorderly learning, would persuade us, it nevertheless follows that the Goths were not uncultivated, but variously instructed in human and divine, terrestrial and celestial matters. Now, when we compare neighbouring or remote nations that had the same institutions, we find a certain collection of maxims: the Indians had the *Puranas*; the Greeks, the *Gnomic* poetry and Hesiod’s *Works and Days*; the Scandinavians, a rich and poetic body of maxims (see Dietrich, *Altnordisches Lesebuch*, preface XXXIII); and so did the Germans. Therefore we ought to find a similar body of maxims among the Goths, and the passage of Jordanes cited above probably alludes to this. For it mentions a body of maxims committed to writing and designated by the name *Bellagines*. But what are these *Bellagines*, or more correctly *Bilagînes* (or *Bilageineis*)?

Almost everyone took them for genuine laws and, as Jordanes implies, for a Gothic law-code. Hence some supposed that written monuments existed before Ulfilas; others doubted the authenticity of this code (cf. Manso, *Geschichte der Ostgothen*, p. 91i), and rightly so, since the Visigoths did not possess a law-code until Euric’s reign, that is, the fifth century (Aschbach, *Geschichte der Westgothen*, p. 157). But the context, if examined, does not justify this interpretation at all. There is clearly a lacuna here. For whatever laws or enactments may be imagined, no philosopher teaching physics ever promulgated civil laws; and these are assigned here to physics, which deals only with the investigation of nature and the essence of things. Thus the genuinely philosophical science of polity—the ordering of civil life—is missing from the text. It is therefore easy to see that the basis of the error lies in *naturaliter* (‘naturally’), and that the sentence may originally have run something like this: ‘teaching physics, he caused them to learn the nature of things; teaching polity, [he caused them to live] naturally,’ etc.

Nor need these laws be understood as positive laws. On the contrary, it may properly be supposed that they are merely the natural principles of equity by which civil life is ordered. We might also suspect incantatory and conjurational formulas—such as antiquity has transmitted to us from Greeks, Scandinavians, and Germans—in the word *cantiones* following the cited passage of Jordanes, unless the context suggested that the word *cantio* is restricted to the less common meaning ‘song.’

“Concerning the translation of the Bible, begun by Ulfilas about the fourth century and continued by another, unless perhaps by Ulfilas himself, the question has already been addressed above in the prolegomena to the Ulfilan text. But concerning the *Skeireins*, that other major fragment of Gothic literature edited by Massmann—its date, whether it is a translation or an original writing, and finally by what Gothic teacher it was composed—everything remains uncertain; cf. Löbe, *Textberichtigung der Skeireins*, Altenburg, 1839.

Ulfilas also wrote several other translations and theological treatises, as is established beyond doubt from documents only recently consulted and published by Waitz (*Ueber das Leben und die Lehre des Ulfila*, Hanover, 1840). For there it is said (p. 14): ‘He himself [Ulfilas] left behind, in three languages—Greek, Latin, and Gothic [Col. 0890]—several treatises and many interpretations for the profit and edification of those who desired them, for his own everlasting remembrance and reward.’ To an earlier period belong the historical work of Ablavius and geographical writings—or rather, an itinerary of all Germany—composed by Athanaritus, Hildebald, and Markomir in the sixth century, and very frequently cited by the Ravenna geographer (see Grimm, Gr. XLVI [1st ed.]).

Neither the Gothic Calendar nor Gothic subscriptions to certain documents written in Latin in Italy (see preface to the Gothic glossary) should be assigned to the domain of literature, though otherwise of great importance to us; still less should the spurious items which Massmann, after much labour, gathered from a source far too unreliable and published in Haupt’s periodical, *Alterthum* I, 294 ff., under the title ‘Gothic Minor Pieces’; cf. § 7.”

## § 7. Gothic flourished only briefly. In Moesia it disappears for us as the native Goths themselves disappeared amid the flood of new peoples rushing into the Danubian regions; in the western lands, where Ostrogoths and Visigoths supplanted the Goths, it probably perished before the people itself, through the influence of Latin.

“Gothic was elevated into a literary language, or at least its writing was first established, in Moesia, where Ulfilas devised the script (see § 11) and began the Bible translation. Gothic flourished there even after Ulfilas’ death in 383, as is apparent from Tertullian’s [Note: [Col. 0889] How this serious error slipped into the otherwise so careful German edition, we do not know at all. The learned editors did not fail to know that no letter of Tertullian, who in any case died about 216, was ever cited, even the slightest one. Thus this is merely a slip of the pen: intending to write JEROME, he mistakenly wrote TERTULLIAN. [Col. 0890] Translator] letter written about 403. This letter (Jerome’s works, vol. I, Epistle CVI; *Patrologia*, vol. XXII, Migne edition; Letters II, p. 626, Paris edition) contains Jerome’s reply to the Gothic priests Sunnias and Fretela, who asked him about several passages of the Old Testament; they certainly used not merely oral instruction but some written work.

Indeed, as late as the ninth century, among the Goths of the lower Danube, as Walafrid Strabo was told by missionaries, the divine offices were recited in Gothic: ‘The Goths,’ he says (*De rebus ecclesiasticis* 7), ‘who are also Getae, at the time when they were brought to faith in Christ, while dwelling in Greek provinces, had our language—that is, theodisc [German]—and, as histories attest, scholars of that nation later translated the divine books into the idiom of their own speech. Monuments of these are still possessed by some. And we have learned from the report of faithful brethren that certain Scythian peoples, especially the inhabitants of Tomis, still recite the divine offices in that same speech.’

But when Olaus Rudbeck (*Atlantica* III, 210) relates that even in his own time, in the seventeenth century, traces of Gothic speech remained in many places in Wallachia, this must be assigned to the fables with which his work abounds. Indeed, even if it were true, as he affirms, that he himself saw a certain man sent from those regions as envoy to the King of Sweden who read Ulfilas in Gothic, it would still be wrong to conclude that Gothic then existed in Wallachia. Castiglione (II Corinthians, p. 83) could indeed explain such traces of Gothic in that region through Saxon settlers of Transylvania; but who would believe that a Saxon could read Ulfilas in that manner, when Gothic script and language were unknown to him?

“The Goths never imposed their language upon the peoples they subdued, allowing them to retain their laws, ancestral customs, and language. Such was the Ostrogoths’ practice in Italy. We leave undecided whether Manso touched the point when he said (*Geschichte des ostgothischen Reichs*, p. 135) that the Goths understood that they could only learn and receive from Roman laws and speech—for this learned man thinks astonishingly poorly of Gothic, arguing with the vulgar that it was not yet sufficiently developed to express the necessary concepts of civil life. But in fact Gothic could in no way be introduced among the Italians. Particular cases must be explained by particular causes when certain Romans spoke Gothic (cf. Cassiodorus VIII, 21). Conversely, this new region, urban in its customs, rich in products, and singular in pleasures, so seduced Gothic minds and weakened their national character that Theodoric himself earnestly urged his people to attend Roman schools.

That the Goths spoke Gothic in Italy is proved both by the inscriptions of the Neapolitan and Aretine documents and by the separate courts of Goths and Italians (on which Glöden expressed his view in *Das römische Recht im ostgothischen Reiche*, Jena, 1843). It is highly probable that all the extant remains of Gothic speech were brought from Italy; cf. Castiglione, *Specimen* IV and II Corinthians, p. 83; W. Grimm, *Jahrbücher der Literatur* XLIII, 29.

“The Visigoths did not proceed further in abusing victory after invading Gaul and Spain; as in sacred matters, so in secular matters they showed themselves tolerant. The Goths themselves retained their customs, laws, and language for two hundred years, until under Reccared’s reign (601) they became Romans. Wishing Goths and Romans subject to him to become one people and one nation, he devoted himself entirely to carrying out this policy under clerical influence. He therefore enacted a law applicable to both; but since Roman subjects were far more numerous, that law had to be drafted in Latin, so that Latin became the language of the state. Devoted to the Christian faith, he ordered the divine offices to be celebrated in Latin, so that Latin thereafter became the language of that Church. He gave Latin names to his courtiers, so that the court language too became Latin (cf. Aschbach, *Geschichte der Westgothen*, p. 230 ff.). After these changes, could the written language of Gothic survive?

Certainly, in the final period of Gothic rule [Col. 0892], the language appears gradually to have fallen from the people’s speech. Apart from a very few Germanic words introduced into Spanish (cf. preface to the Gothic glossary), only a few words from the rustic dialect of Spain—now perhaps not unreasonably called Germanic, from Old German *gau* ‘country district,’ *gauer* ‘countryman’—are explained from Germanic: *ledro*, ‘left,’ Gothic *hleidumea*, from the stem *hleid-, led-*; *mundo*, ‘face,’ Gothic *munþs*, ‘mouth’; perhaps also *godo*, ‘right,’ Gothic *god*, ‘good’ (as elsewhere an expression meaning ‘right side’ also signifies ‘good’); *navio*, ‘body, corpse,’ Gothic *naus*, ‘ship’; *anclas*, ‘hands,’ Gothic *agga*, ‘joint, limb,’ cf. English *ankle*, Low German *enkel*.

One must not proceed further in these investigations, since several other apparently Germanic words are nevertheless of Romance origin: *asas*, ‘ears,’ certainly Gothic *ausa*, but Spanish *asa*, ‘ear’; *meter*, ‘to eat,’ certainly Gothic *matjan*, but Spanish *meter*, ‘to put in’; *bufar*, ‘to cry out, call,’ certainly Gothic *vopjan*, but Spanish *bufar*, ‘to bellow’; *navio* itself might be Spanish *navio*, ‘ship’; cf. *Vocabulario de Germania an den Romances de Germania*, published by Juan Hidalgo, Madrid, 1779.

We cannot establish with any certainty that any Gothic writing which has reached us was composed in Spain. Whoever maintained that the Codex Carolinus and the fragments of the Old Testament were composed there, relying on the fact that the former is inscribed with Isidore of Seville’s *Origins* and the latter agree with the text of the Complutensian Bible, would be defending an intolerable opinion. Yet neither should Lembke (*Geschichte Spaniens* I, 245) be heard when he says that no trace remains from which it can be inferred that anything was written in Gothic in Spain; on this see Massmann in Haupt’s *Zeitschrift* I, 378. Moreover, when Gothic books are mentioned, this does not mean that they were written in Gothic, but that they belonged as ritual books to the Gothic office—that is, to the general liturgy introduced by the Council of Toledo into the Gothic Church of Spain and Septimania (Aschbach, p. 350).

“At Constantinople, where toward the end of the fourth and beginning of the fifth century a school was opened through Chrysostom’s care for teaching Goths in Gothic (see Massmann, *Skeireins*, p. 91), Gothic speech is often mentioned. Even in the tenth century a certain *Gotthikon* is still mentioned in Constantine Porphyrogenitus, *De caeremoniis aulae Byzantinae* I, 83. This *Gotthikon* was not properly a song but a kind of game or spectacle—explicitly called ‘playing the Gothic’ (*paizein to gothikon*)—introduced on the ninth day of the Twelve Nights during a banquet in the imperial palace by the Blues and Greens.

There were two camps, with two Goths on each side. Clothed in hairy garments and their faces covered with masks, they bore a shield in the left hand and a staff in the right. The song accompanying the spectacle was performed alternately, partly in Greek by choristers and partly in barbarian speech by those dressed as Goths. The latter, opening the game amid the noise of shields struck with staffs, shouted loudly: ‘*tul, tul!*’ Then, completing the game with circular motion and again withdrawing to either side, accompanied by panduras [Note: [Col. 0893] A kind of instrument. Translator], they recited:

> “Gauzas; bonas; bēkēdias; hagia; gaudentes; helkēbonides; enkertys; hagia; bona; hōra; toutou; bantes; bona amore; episkyantes; idesalbātous; nana; deous; deous; sebakiba; nana; daimonogyngybele; gybilous; gybelares; nana; gybilous; gybelares; nana; tou gegdema; de toulbele; nikato touldo; nana.”

Greek words then followed, after which these barbarian words again succeeded:

> “iber; eberiem; tou ingeroua; gergerethrō; nana; sikadiase peretoures.”

We have cited these words only to this end: that it may be plain to everyone that this song—for the words are undoubtedly those of a song—is not Gothic, and that its author, whether on his own initiative or another’s, seems to have blunted, so to speak, the supposed Gothic character of these words when he asserts that the Goths say ‘the Gothic things which are these’ (*ta Gothika hatina esti tauta*).

But the name of the Goths is conspicuous here. Whence, then, could Goths have come into this context, when since Justinian’s age they had already yielded to other Germanic peoples in the Constantinopolitan Empire and the emperors’ court? Were these people called Goths, or rather Jutes [Note: [Col. 0893] Ancient inhabitants of Denmark. Translator], inhabitants of Lower Germany who, under the emperors, served as Varangians and attended the court? At least George Codinus, *De officiis aulae Constantinopolitanae*, p. 90, reports that these Varangians customarily congratulated Caesar on the first day of the new year ‘in their ancestral language, that is, English’ (*kata tēn patrion glōssan autōn, ēgoun Inglisti*).

The game or spectacle called Gothic agrees completely with the Swedish *Julbock* and the *Schoduvellopen* of the inhabitants of Lower Germany (High German *Schauteufellaufen*, French *la course au diable*), explained by Du Cange under *Cervula* and called *Jottici* by certain medieval writers. Reiske, however, wrongly calls it a Gothic game in his note on Constantine Porphyrogenitus, p. 112, Leipzig. The only word in this *Gotthikon* which has a Germanic flavour is *ampaato*, by which the Byzantine choristers urged the Goths to begin the dance. It could be derived in Gothic from *andbahtjan*, but in the form *ampaato* it agrees better with North Germanic *ambaht*, etc.; see the Gothic glossary. Nor should it be omitted that the *gounas* (*gunna*, fur garments) worn by the Goths belong to Lower Germany, Saxony, and are preserved in English *gown*, ‘robe’; see Reiz, cited work, p. 113. Massmann too could find nothing Gothic in this *Gotthikon* (Haupt’s *Zeitschrift* I, 366 ff.); and it would be excessively far-fetched to derive *jul* from *tul*.

“Gothic survived longest, if travellers are to be believed, in the Tauric Chersonese (French, *Crimée*), where the Tetraxite Goths lived. According to Procopius (*On the Gothic War* IV, 4, 5), this was first recognized by the Brabantine Franciscan William of Rubruck, who travelled through the region in 1253. His sole report—‘among whom there were many Goths, whose language is Teutonic’—has been greatly distorted by interpreters; see Massmann, cited work, p. 351. Something more certain occurs in Josaphat Barbaro [Col. 0894], who was sent by the Venetians as ambassador to the city of Azov in 1436: ‘The Goths speak in German, and I know this because, having a German servant with me, they spoke together and understood one another quite reasonably well, just as a Friulian and a Florentine would understand one another.’ That is, the Goths used German speech; I learned this because, while I had a German servant with me, he was understood when speaking with them, and vice versa, almost as if a Friulian and a Florentine were conversing with each other (in Ramusio II, 97).

Busbecq, who, while living in Constantinople as imperial ambassador in 1557–64, had met two men sent there from the Crimea, gives in the fourth letter of his Turkish embassy, p. 2577 (Frankfurt edition, 1595), a list of words which are undoubtedly Germanic and for the most part wholly Gothic: *Plut*, German *Blut*, ‘blood’; *stul*, German *Stuhl*, ‘chair’; *hus*, German *Haus*, ‘house’; *wingart*, German *Weinberg*, ‘vineyard’; *reghen*, German *Regen*, ‘rain’; *bruder*, German *Bruder*, ‘brother’; *schwester*, German *Schwester*, ‘sister’; *alt*, German *alt*, ‘old, aged’; *salt*, German *Salz*, ‘salt’; *fisct*, German *Fisch*, ‘fish’; *handa*, German *Hand*, ‘hand’; *brunna*, German *Brunnen*, ‘well’; *schwalt*, ‘death’; see Massmann, cited work, pp. 357 ff. But the name of the Goths seems to have vanished by degrees, and today no traces of this language are found; see Pallas, *Voyages dans les gouvernements méridionaux de l’empire de Russie*, II, 396 ff.; cf. Zeuss, *Die Deutschen*, pp. 432 ff.; Castiglione, *Specimen*, XXIII ff.”

## § 8. Although Gothic died out for us at an early date, and only the very fewest fragments of its literature have reached us, what survives nevertheless abundantly suffices for us to acquire a most complete knowledge of the language. From these remains, once we know its vocabulary, formation, and conspicuous ease of translation into other idioms, we can construct a grammatical system. Moreover, no one fails to see that Gothic grammar accords especially with the grammar of the Germans.
