“The Goths were not a rude and barbarous people, as they and the other Germans were formerly reputed to be—and are still reputed today—has already been demonstrated by Grimm (Grammar, XLVI [1st ed.]); nor were they sluggish in developing their language, as the editors of the Milan specimen have already admitted, asserting on p. XII that “in Ulfilas’s age the speech of the Goths had already attained such a degree that it could compete with the more cultivated languages.” Yet they subsequently forgot this admission so completely that Mai, in the preface to the eighth volume of the new collection of ancient writers, again mentions the “barbarism of the Gothic language”; and Castiglione, in his notes on the Pauline epistles edited by him, more than once charges it, as a “rude language,” with weakness and imperfection, indeed once asserts (on 2 Timothy 2:16) that in Gothic there is “a usage, though absurd in itself, nevertheless not infrequent among Gothic writers, as belonging to a language still rude.” So difficult is it for one who belongs to a foreign people to judge our German language rightly. [Note: [Col. 0894] German. Translator.] [Col. 0895] Nor can it be laid to the charge of the Gothic language that it lacks certain verbal forms enjoyed by other languages, since it supplies them so remarkably by constructions; still less that it has not produced proper words for things and ideas wholly unknown to the people; compare the preface to the Gothic glossary. If, therefore, the language lacks, or is poor in, words designating maritime things, this is not as surprising as it would have been if the people had travelled by sea and been accustomed to it; rather, it is fresh evidence that the ancient reports concerning the Goths’ migration from Scandinavia and their seafaring are mere inventions and fables (see above, § 1). For how could the Goths have failed to form *skipabruka*, just as the northern peoples have *skipbrot, skibbrud, skeppsbrote*, if they had previously known the thing? Moreover, could anyone find it surprising that the Goths have no word for “grandchild,” expressing it by *barne barna*? For in the ancient languages it is expressed in no other way: Old Norse *barnabörn*, Danish *boerneboern*, Swedish *barnbarn*, Old High German *chindeschind, chindo chind*; likewise in later High German *kindeskinder* and related languages. Indeed, even in Homer no proper word is given for “grandchild,” but it is expressed equivalently: παίδων παῖδες, “children of children.” Now Manso (Ostgothen, 135), from the fact that the Gothic language suffers from a scarcity of words belonging to civil life, infers that the Goths did not establish a firm footing in Italy. But this alone can be inferred: that the Goths, a people accustomed to upright morals and subject to an easy rule, did not possess a language capable of expressing Roman licence and vices, and the almost innumerable dignities and indignities of offices of every kind. Besides, what certainly cannot be denied is that, if the language of the Lombards was still suited to forming almost innumerable names for offices, why should Gothic not have possessed the same capacity?

The Gothic language excels especially in being exceedingly rich in synonyms; in being able to form words expressing wholly new things and ideas; in possessing complete inflectional forms and consequently enjoying that freedom of transposing words by which—since prose writers possess the boldness of Saxon and northern poets (Grimm, Grammar IV, 552; compare II, 920)—Gothic poets, at least in this respect, are scarcely to be regretted; in having an orthography so fixed that nothing is left to the writer’s discretion; and finally in allowing the writings of a foreign literature, indeed abstract thoughts, to be rendered into it with the greatest ease (Grimm, Grammar XLVI [1st ed.]; our Prolegomena to Ulfilas). Hence what Ihre says, Glossarium Suigothicum I, 29—“the Gothic language is so cultivated and well-ordered that in elegance it yields nothing to any language, not even Greek or Latin”—is true as regards its principle; and as regards its development, it might have become true had the language lived longer.

Whether the Gothic language is in fact so easy to learn as Mai and Castiglione once asserted (Specimen VI: “nor is the Ulfilan language very difficult, nor will anyone, even without a teacher, fail to acquire its first knowledge in a short time” [Col. 0896]) depends upon the greater or lesser knowledge one wishes to acquire. Yet be well assured of this: more than an elementary knowledge is necessary before anyone can judge the Gothic language soundly.

§ 9. The grammatical observations on the Gothic language written either by earlier or by recent scholars have been collected by Massmann (in Haupt’s *Zeitschrift für deutsches Alterthum* I, 298 ff.); while the grammars published since the age of Junius through special study of the Ulfilan text have been listed, with his own judgments, by Zahn (*Einleitung zum Ulfilas*, p. 61 ff.). The first grammar not unworthy of the name was written by Fulda; but the first body of sound doctrine will be found in Grimm’s German Grammar.

“We know of no native Gothic grammarians; moreover, the language had too short a life to incur the danger of corruption, the more usual cause of native grammars. A Gothic alphabet and certain rules for determining the pronunciation of some sounds are first found in the Vienna manuscript (Membran. Salisb. no. 140, formerly Salisb. 71, fol. 20), first published by Wilhelm Grimm (*Jahrbücher für Literatur*, vol. 43, p. 5 ff.); on this see Massmann, cited work, p. 296 ff.

“Then a small work was published by Bonaventura Vulcanius, by an anonymous author, bearing the title: *On the Letters and Language of the Getae or Goths*; appended to it is a *Short Commentary on the Gothic Language*, Leiden, 1597. See Massmann, cited work, p. 311 ff. It contains several excerpts from the text and observations on certain letters and on the correct pronunciation of certain vowels; the same is also to be found in Gruter’s inscriptions.

“G. Hickes, *Grammatical Institutions of Anglo-Saxon and Moeso-Gothic*, Oxford, 1689, quarto; the first part contains the same author’s *Thesaurus of the Ancient Northern Languages*, a work republished, Oxford, 1705, 2 folio vols.

“Lambert ten Kate, *Gemeenschap tussen de Gottische Spracke en de Nederduistsche* [Relationship between the Gothic Language and Low German], Amsterdam, 1710, quarto.

“Edward Lye, *Gothic Grammar*, in the preface to which the Gothic translation of the Holy Gospels was introduced by its editor, Benzelius, Oxford, 1750, quarto, pp. 39–62. A summary of this grammar is Owen Manning’s *Anglo-Saxon (and) Moeso-Gothic Grammar*, whose first volume contains Lye’s Saxon- and Gothic-Latin Dictionary, edited by Manning himself, London, 1772, 2 folio vols.

“Fr. Karl Fulda, *Ulfilanische Sprachlehre* [Ulfilan Grammar], in vol. 2 of Zahn’s edition of Ulfilas, pp. 1–62.

“J. Grimm, *Deutsche Grammatik*, Göttingen, 1819, 2nd edition, 4 vols.; likewise 1822–37; 3rd edition, vol. 1, 1840.

“For the teaching of pronunciation and forms, F. Bopp’s *Vergleichende Grammatik* [Comparative Grammar], Berlin, 1833–42, 4 parts, should be noted.

“Among monographs the following deserve commendation:

“Joh. von Ihre, *De verbis Moesogothorum* [On Moeso-Gothic Verbs], in Büsching’s collection of writers illustrating the Ulfilan translation [Col. 0897] and the Moeso-Gothic language, Berlin, 1773, quarto, pp. 149–71.

“By the same author, *De nominibus substantivis et adjectivis Moesogothorum* [On Moeso-Gothic Substantives and Adjectives], 1769, ibid., pp. 221–56.

[Col. 0898] “Alb. Wellmann, *Das Gothische adjectivum* [The Gothic Adjective], Stettin, 1835.

“Ad. Ziemann, *Gothisch-hochdeutsche Wortlehre* [Gothic–High German Lexicology], Quedlinburg, 1834.

# CHAPTER ONE. ON WRITING AND PRONUNCIATION.

[Col. 0897]

## A. ON WRITING.

§ 10. The Gothic language has twenty-five letters (*bokos*), as follows:

[Gothic a] a; [Gothic b] b; [Gothic g] g; [Gothic d] d; [Gothic e] e; [Gothic q] q; [Gothic z] z; [Gothic h] h; [Gothic dh] dh (þ); [Gothic i] i; [Gothic k] k; [Gothic l] l; [Gothic m] m; [Gothic n] n; [Gothic j] j; [Gothic u] u; [Gothic p] p; [Gothic r] r; [Gothic s] s; [Gothic t] t; [Gothic v] v; [Gothic f] f; [Gothic x] x; [Gothic w] w; [Gothic o] o.

“§ 11. Note 1.—The invention of the Gothic script is attributed to Ulfilas. Philostorgius (*Ecclesiastical History* 2.5) calls him “εὑρετὴν γραμμάτων οἰκείων,” “inventor of a script of their own,” and Socrates (*Ecclesiastical History* 4.32) states that “γράμματα ἐφεῦρε γοτθικά,” “he devised Gothic letters,” a statement afterwards repeated by many others (see Waitz, *Leben des Ulfilas*, p. 51). It was indeed believed, on the testimony of Jordanes, that because the *Bilagines* had been written (see § 6), the art of writing too had been known and practised among the Goths before Ulfilas; and Italian scholars find it scarcely credible that a language endowed with the powerful qualities which Ulfilas displays in his works should have lacked writing. But if this reasoning were valid, then, since Castiglione afterwards (on Philippians 1:18), because the Gothic language requires a future tense and leaves too much to the interpreter’s carelessness in translating the passive, rejected it as rude and barbarous, it might be legitimately concluded that even in Ulfilas’s age the Goths still possessed no script. But the principle that a language’s organic perfection depends on writing rests on no foundation (compare W. Grimm, *Deutsche Runen*, p. 45). On the contrary, W. Grimm shows with great force of argument that already in the biblical translation the concepts of writing, reading, letter, book, shelf, and so forth are denoted by native terms; see § 18. Waitz indeed (cited work, p. 53) carries the art of writing among the Goths back before Ulfilas; but he maintains that the letters then in use were not those introduced by Ulfilas, but runes. This conclusion should be accepted without hesitation, since it admirably explains the apparent contradiction between records written before Ulfilas and the script invented by Ulfilas—facts of which, historically speaking, there is no reason to doubt.

“Now the table shows that Gothic letters, with scarcely any exceptions, correspond exactly to Greek and Latin ones, so that Ulfilas did nothing other than adapt these to the Gothic language. But here the question arises: since most letters of the Gothic alphabet agree with Greek and Latin, which of these alphabets did Ulfilas make his own? And to what other alphabet should be assigned those letters which agree with neither Greek nor Latin, whether in shape or in value? By universal agreement this alphabet is the runic one, already known among the Goths before Ulfilas’s age. As to the first question, Ihre (*Dissertation on the Silver Codex and Moeso-Gothic Literature*) and W. Grimm (cited work, p. 28 ff.), unwilling to admit that the Gothic alphabet had been arbitrarily selected from several others, assert that it had already before Ulfilas been drawn from the same source as Greek and Latin. Against this view it weighs not only that, according to certain tradition, Ulfilas invented the Gothic script, but also that the characters themselves agree with Latin and Greek so closely that one cannot suppose an independent and original form for them. Moreover, what is this primitive alphabet, parent at once of Gothic, Greek, and Latin? Ihre calls it Pelasgian, an alphabet wholly unknown to us. W. Grimm offers none; yet the correspondence of Gothic letters with Greek and Latin is so irresistible that he was compelled to admit that the Graeco-Latin alphabet had again influenced Gothic through contact of peoples. Once this is admitted, the question returns; it is not solved. But Waitz (cited work, p. 51 ff.) and Bäumlein (*Untersuchungen über die Entstehung des gothischen Alphabets*, p. 97 ff.) have touched the true point: they regard the Greek alphabet as the model of the Gothic, although Ulfilas will have borrowed some characters from Latin and, we must admit, from runes. This was also Jacob Grimm’s opinion when, in the preface to Vuk Stefanović’s Serbian grammar, p. X, he says: “Ulfilas based his work upon the Greek and Latin alphabet, adding runic or arbitrary signs for the special sounds of the Gothic language”; that is, Ulfilas constructed his work from the Greek and Latin alphabet, with certain signs taken from the runic alphabet or chosen arbitrarily, so that the peculiar sounds of Gothic might be represented in writing. But the learned man seems recently to have adopted the opposite opinion, saying (*Deutsche Grammatik* I, 25 [3rd ed.]): “Greek and Latin letters have been inserted among runic ones in the Gothic alphabet.”

[Col. 0899] “Now if anyone considers the Gothic letters without partisan bias, he will be convinced that the following belong to the Greek alphabet: [Gothic a], [Gothic b], [Gothic g], [Gothic e], [Gothic z], [Gothic i], [Gothic k], [Gothic l], [Gothic m], [Gothic n], [Gothic p], [Gothic t], [Gothic v], [Gothic o], [Gothic x]; and the following to the Latin: [Gothic d], [Gothic q], [Gothic h], [Gothic r], [Gothic s], [Gothic f]. Yet several of the former are Latin as well, namely [Gothic a], [Gothic b], [Gothic e], [Gothic i], [Gothic k], [Gothic n], [Gothic t]. Finally, the following properly belong to Gothic, if not in form then at least in value: [Gothic dh] and [Gothic w], derived from Greek Ψ and Θ; [Gothic j] and [Gothic u], from Latin G and n. If this last letter did not correspond less closely to the shape of cursive Latin *n*, it could be foreign or perhaps native (see § 12). Nothing, then, remains to be assigned to the runic alphabet. Many have objected to the assertion that Ulfilas selected certain signs at will. Yet one may reasonably suppose that he wished above all for the sounds of his language to correspond as closely as possible to foreign signs; then, since certain characters did not correspond to their sounds and other languages lacked certain sounds peculiar to Gothic, he could legitimately borrow these signs as he pleased. In this he should be praised rather than blamed. Simonides and Epicharmus likewise made efforts to find characters suitable to definite sounds for the Greek alphabet; the emperor Claudius did so for Latin (see Schneider, *Formenlehre der lateinischen Sprache* I, 4 ff.); Chilperic did so for the Frankish alphabet (Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks* V.45); and Cyril especially derived the Slavonic alphabet from Greek.

“When Gothic script is mentioned even after the time of the Goths, one should not suppose that it is the script used in Gothic writings. For in Spain “Gothic” was the name given to a script elsewhere called Toledan, mixed from Gothic and Latin letters; it was adopted by the Franks (Aschbach, *Geschichte der Westgothen*, pp. 353 f.) and abolished by the Council of León in 1091. Likewise, in Italy runic signs were improperly called Gothic; see Massmann, *Skeireins*, p. XV, and Haupt’s *Zeitschrift für deutsches Alterthum* I, 377. But that Gothic script was preserved in Italy, and that the Brescia inscription on the first plate in the *Specimen of Unpublished Portions of Ulfilas* was written in this same script, cannot be firmly asserted on the basis of this sole surviving monument; compare Grimm, *Jahrbücher der Literatur* XLIII, 21.”

§ 12. Note 2.—As regards the form, appearance, and value of the letters, we must first note the erroneous conjecture of Mai (*Specimen*, XVI), namely that Ulfilas invented a majuscule and a minuscule alphabet. Certainly, in manuscripts letters are larger or smaller according to the place which they occupy: thus the beginnings of chapters and verses are written in larger letters, but smaller ones are used where text is written in the margin beyond the defined line. But both kinds of letter are of the same type. With better reason—and perhaps this was Mai’s own meaning—Massmann (*Die gothischen Urkunden von Neapel und Arezzo*, p. 6 ff.) distinguished an upright, formal script used for manuscript codices, books, and inscriptions, from another, sloping and cursive script for everyday purposes. The former, says the learned author, differs from the latter in that certain letters, even when fully formed, [Col. 0900] permit broader pen-strokes, whereas in cursive writing they are traced with a slighter outline. This must be said, besides [Gothic a] and [Gothic d], of [Gothic dh]. The glosses and annotations in manuscript codices are also written in this cursive script; see the plate in Massmann’s *Skeireins*, except those occurring in the Codex Argenteus, which are written in upright, formal but smaller—though often beautiful—letters distinct from the script of the text. Only a few, such as those on Luke 6:27 and 16:13, exhibit cursive writing; from this it is evident that they were written either at a different time or by a different hand.

“As to the differing appearance which certain letters display in different codices, formerly nothing certain could be conjectured, because facsimiles were lacking and only mere drawings, often inaccurate, were available. But facsimiles of all the codices have now been made: of the Milanese manuscripts by Mai and Castiglione; of the Viennese by W. Grimm; of the *Skeireins* and the Neapolitan document by Massmann; and of the Argenteus and Carolinus codices by ourselves, from which we have prepared the accompanying table.

“Now let the following observations be made concerning certain letters:

“[Gothic d]. See below, § 13.

“[Gothic q] is neither the Greek koppa, as W. Grimm held (see § 13), nor the runic *koen* (), as Lye XXXIX maintains—which agrees with it only in later Latin-derived forms—but Latin *q*. Nor may it be transcribed *qv*, perhaps on the basis of the analogy of the other dialects (Grimm, Grammar I, 3), since the Gothic language nowhere has the double sound *kw*, which Ulfilas renders *kv* even in *Akvila*.

“[Gothic dh]. Lye (*Gothic Grammar*, XXIX) conjectured without foundation that [Gothic dh] had arisen from combined T and H, so that it was properly , and finally became [Gothic dh]; or from two [Gothic d] placed opposite each other (). Nor is it more true that this letter originated from a semicircle crossed by a transverse line (W. Grimm, *Runen*, 44); for its two horns are formed with divergent points (see table). Another form of this letter exists, in which the horns are joined at the upper part, making it resemble Greek Φ (W. Grimm, *Wiener Jahrbücher* XLIII, 5). Nor does Gothic [Gothic dh] agree in shape with the runic sign (W. Grimm, *Runen*, 44; J. Grimm, Grammar I, 3), although in manuscripts written in Latin script that sign is used for [Gothic dh]. [Gothic dh] is in form identical with Greek Ψ (*ps*); but Ulfilas does not use it for *ps*, rendering the double consonant by a double sign. Since he found in neither the Greek nor the Latin alphabet a character corresponding to Gothic *dh*, he adapted it to this sound. On Visigothic coins Gothic [Gothic dh] occurs for Greek Θ in CINDASVIN[Gothic w]VS and [Gothic r][Gothic e]CC[Gothic e]SVIN[Gothic w]VS (see Aschbach, 360), because probably among these later Goths the pure sound *dh* had gradually disappeared, and *th*, and then, with aspiration removed, *t*, had taken its place, as the terminations of these names also show. Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths, must have subscribed his edicts [Gothic dh][Gothic e][Gothic o][Gothic d] (or [Gothic w][Gothic e]O[Gothic d]), [Col. 0901] for the Anonymous Valesianus in Muratori (*Antiquitates Italicae* II, 305) expressly says: “Theodoric was illiterate, and so dull of understanding that during ten years of his reign he could by no means learn the four letters of the signature to his edict. For this reason he ordered a perforated gold plate to be made, bearing the four letters of the king, TH[Gothic e]OD; whenever he wished to sign, the plate was laid upon the document, the pen was drawn through it, and his signature alone appeared.” But since these words state that the king signed with only four letters, whereas TH[Gothic e]OD consists of five, Reiske, in his edition of Constantine’s *De caerimoniis aulae Byzantinae*, p. 140, Leipzig, conjectured rather unhappily that something else should be read in place of TH[Gothic e]OD, perhaps LEGI. From this Massmann’s question, *Skeireins*, preface p. X**, whether Theodoric’s seal contained Gothic writing, is readily resolved.

“[Gothic i] and I must be distinguished in this respect: the former is used at the beginning, the latter in the middle and at the end of a word; see § 17.

“[Gothic j] is Latin G. The scribe of the Vienna codex (see § 9) has and uses both [Gothic j] and Γ for the same letter, yet with this difference: the former, Latin character has the soft value *j*, the latter, Greek character the hard value *G*. Then, in order to establish the pronunciation of unknown Gothic sounds, he adduces words of known pronunciation, *genuit* and *Gabriel*, intending, as it were, to say: where the pronunciation is softer, as in *genuit*, use Gothic [Gothic j]; where it is harder, as in *Gabriel*, use Γ. W. Grimm and Massmann understood the matter in the same way. The former, in the Vienna *Jahrbücher*, p. 13, and the latter, in Haupt’s *Zeitschrift*, p. 299, state that this example *genuit* sheds no light upon the matter, and that they would prefer a word beginning with J, such as perhaps *judaius*. It should also be observed in passing that Lye, p. XXXIX, wrongly took [Gothic j] for Greek ι because Gothic *ïskarjotes* corresponds to Greek Ἰσκαριώτης, “Iscariot”; and that Ihre, p. 202 (Büsching edition), declared it should be pronounced with a soft sibilant sound—probably because, in making this conjecture, he had before his eyes ξ, occupying the same position in the Greek alphabet as [Gothic j] in the Gothic.

“[Gothic u], if it is not derived from Latin *n*, would be a proper sign of the Gothic alphabet. But no one can reasonably deny that it is more similar to runic *Ur* () than that they should not be called one and the same, as Lye, p. XXXIX, Grimm, *Runen*, 43, and Waitz, cited work, p. 52, have preceded us in saying. Moreover, its distinct pronunciation explains why Graeco-Latin O was not selected for the sound *u*: Latin U, used as a vowel, was not yet distinguished from consonantal V.

“[Gothic s], in its older form, is Latin *s*. The form closely approaching Greek C first occurs in later script tending toward cursive; see Massmann, *Skeireins*, [Gothic x], where the angular form also appears; see Vienna *Jahrbücher*, p. 9.

“[Gothic v] is neither Anglo-Saxon þ (Lye XL), from whose form it differs greatly, nor runic (Grimm, *Runen*, 44), but Greek Y (Grimm, Grammar I, 42, 57; Waitz, 52).

“[Gothic f] is Latin F. Grimm indeed (*Runen*, 41) regards it as Aeolic digamma; but against this stands the fact that the latter has a pronunciation different from Gothic *f*, [Col. 0902] and Ulfilas knows that pronunciation otherwise, using *v* wherever Greek words ought to be pronounced with digamma. If Ulfilas had borrowed no sign from the Latin alphabet, Gothic [Gothic f] would more readily be considered runic, since it would be unknown why he did not choose Greek Φ for the sound F, when he always transcribes Greek φ with this sign; for example, *Filippus*, Φίλιππος; *Fygailus*, Φύγελλος; *Filemon*, Φυλήμων; *Nymfa*, Νυμφᾶ, etc.

“[Gothic w]. Although all agree that this sign belongs to an unknown alphabet, and Waitz at least maintains that it is not Greek, yet, since we have already established that Ulfilas used Greek letters to which no sound in his language corresponded in order to designate other sounds peculiar to Gothic, nothing prevents us from saying that [Gothic w] is not a sign proper to the Goths, but simply Greek Θ. Moreover, everyone sees that Ulfilas interchanged Greek Ψ and Θ in his alphabet: that is, he substituted Gothic [Gothic dh] for Greek Θ, and Gothic [Gothic w] for Greek Ψ.

“[Gothic o], according to W. Grimm (*Runen*, 43), is runic; but this *oedil* () of the Vienna codex (*Wiener Jahrbücher*) belongs, like the others, to a script luxuriant in strokes, which cannot be proposed as a model. Besides, the Danish sound () agrees least of all with Gothic (o). Thus [Gothic o], as Lye XXXIX and Waitz 52 suggest, is rather Greek Ω. An O altogether similar to this sign also occurs in an inscription reproduced by Grotefend, *Altitalien* V, plate II, 4.”

“§ 13. Note 3.—To these twenty-five letters must be added two episemata, namely:

“1) [Gothic 90]. Although this sign appears nowhere as a letter, but only as a numeral in the Codex Argenteus, Ihre (p. 205, Büsching edition) nonetheless regards it as a genuine letter and argues that, just as its form agrees with the Russian character having the value *tsk* (*tsch*), so its sound-value agrees too. But against this is the fact that Ulfilas never rendered a double sound by a single sign, and that the compound sound *tsk* appears nowhere in the whole Gothic script. Although Ihre’s conjecture had already been rejected by Zahn, in notes prefixed to the Gothic alphabet in Fulda’s Gothic grammar, as a mere fabrication, W. Grimm renewed the attack upon it (*Wiener Jahrbücher*, p. 7), though in another way, again recognizing in this sign a letter, namely one having the value *dh*. But that sound corresponds to [Gothic dh], as will be shown below (§ 50). Jacob Grimm too (*Wiener Jahrbücher*, p. 40) did not dislike the idea that [Gothic 90] was a letter; but that learned man denied that this letter necessarily belonged to the Gothic alphabet, assigning it to the alphabet from which the latter arose. He compares Slavonic, but maintains that this letter is not dental but guttural. However these matters stand, the sign now under discussion is not a Gothic letter but only a numerical mark, having the value 90: the Greek koppa; see Schneider, *Formenlehre* I, 322; Matthiä, *Griechische Grammatik* I, 22; Buttmann, *Griechische Grammatik* I, 12. Hence W. Grimm rather unhappily equated Gothic [Gothic q] with Greek koppa, whereas it properly corresponds to Latin *q*. Moreover, nobody can deny that [Gothic q] and [Gothic 90] correspond to one another in the same manner as Greek kappa and koppa. There is also, according to Grimm (*Wiener Jahrbücher*, pp. 7 and 41), another form of [Gothic d], which, when its loop is extended higher while inclining outwards and its stem is drawn more to the left, becomes , and was confused with our [Gothic 90]. Thus it is given this appearance in the Vienna codex and on the Visigothic coin where GON[Gothic e]MAR is read for *Gondemar* (see Aschbach, 359). But this sign has nothing in common with the episemon [Gothic 90].

“2) [Gothic 900]. This sign does not occur in Ulfilas’s translation of the New Testament; but at 2 Ezra 36, where the number 900 is expressed by the numeral word *niunhunda*, Castiglione (*Specimen*, p. 2) rightly conjectured that it is doubtful whether the Goths had a special sign for the number 900, since it is not found in the Vatican alphabet (*Wiener Jahrbücher*, p. 4). It first appeared as a numeral sign in the numerical series of the Vienna codex, which W. Grimm (*Wiener Jahrbücher*, pp. 16 f.) reasonably conjectured to have been excerpted from the first book of Moses; compare the Prolegomena, col. 464. (Massmann, in Haupt’s *Zeitschrift*, p. 303, states that he recognized it in Ezekiel and the books of Maccabees.) Moreover, this sign is the Greek sampi; see Buttmann, *Griechische Grammatik* I, 12; II, 378; Matthiä, *Griechische Grammatik* I, 22 f.; Böckh, *Staatshaushaltung der Athener* I, 386. In this form, probably taken from the Greek alphabet, it already occurs in Ihre’s table (p. 200, Büsching edition) and in the Greek alphabet of the Vienna codex.

“Now it is remarkable that Ulfilas, after borrowing the two episemata mentioned above from the Greeks, did not also adopt a third, namely *bau* or *vau*, having the value 6 and the form S (compare Ihre, p. 210, Büsching edition); but substituted his own *q* in place of this sign, in order to denote the sixth number. From this it is evident that Ulfilas exercised discretion in composing the alphabet.”

§ 14. Note 4.—With respect to numerical value, the Gothic letters and episemata have the following values:

[Gothic a] 1; [Gothic b] 2; [Gothic g] 3; [Gothic d] 4; [Gothic e] 5; [Gothic q] 6; [Gothic z] 7; [Gothic h] 8; [Gothic dh] 9; [Gothic i] 10; [Gothic k] 20; [Gothic l] 30; [Gothic m] 40; [Gothic n] 50; [Gothic j] 60; [Gothic u] 70; [Gothic p] 80; [Gothic 90] 90; [Gothic r] 100; [Gothic s] 200; [Gothic t] 300; [Gothic v] 400; [Gothic f] 500; [Gothic x] 600; [Gothic w] 700; [Gothic o] 800; [Gothic 900] 900.

“These numerical values are known from various passages of the biblical translation, the *Skeireins*, and documents, in which numbers are denoted by letters: thus, *a* (1), Nehemiah 5:18; *b* (2), John 6:9; *Skeireins* VII, d; *g* (3), 2 Ezra 35; *e* (5), John 6:9; *Skeireins* VII, a, d; *q* (6), Nehemiah 5:18; *h* (8), 2 Ezra 16; *i* (10), Nehemiah 5:18; *ib* (12), Matthew 9:20; *Skeireins* VII, c, d; *id* (14), 2 Corinthians 12;? Codex A; [Col. 0904] *iz* (17), 2 Ezra 39; *k* (20), John 6:19; *l* (30), Mark 4:8; *m* (40), *Skeireins* VII, d; Nehemiah 5:15; *me* (45), 2 Ezra 8; *n* (50), Nehemiah 5:17; *nb* (52), 2 Ezra 29; *j* (60), Mark 4:8; Neapolitan document; *jq* (66), 2 Ezra 14; *ug* (73), 2 Ezra 36; *ud* (74), 2 Ezra 40; [Gothic 90]*e* (95), 2 Ezra 20; [Gothic r] (100), Mark 4:8; *rib* (112), 2 Ezra 18; *rk* (120), Neapolitan document; *rkb* (122), 2 Ezra 27; *rkg* (123), 2 Ezra 21; *rkh* (128), 2 Ezra 23; *rlg* (133), Arezzo document; *rmq* (146), 2 Ezra 22; *rnq* (156), 2 Ezra 30; *rnh* (158), 2 Ezra 24; *skg* (223), 2 Ezra 19; *smz* (247), 2 Ezra 38; *snd* (254), 2 Ezra 31; *t* (300), John 12:5; *tk* (320), 2 Ezra 32; *tlg* (333), 2 Ezra 17; *tme* (345), 2 Ezra 34; *vnd* (454), 2 Ezra 15; *xib* (612), 2 Ezra 26; *xkg* (623), 2 Ezra 11; *xl* (630), 2 Ezra 35; *xmb* (642), 2 Ezra 10; *xjq* (666), 2 Ezra 13; *wke* (725), 2 Ezra 33; *wmg* (743), 2 Ezra 25; *wj* (760), 2 Ezra 13; *wuq* (776), 2 Ezra 12. They are further known from the fragment of the Gothic Calendar, in which the numbers from 1 to 30 occur (see preface to the Gothic glossary); from the marginal numbers marking sections of codices—with the additional fact that in the margin of the Codex Argenteus parallel passages of the other Gospels are also indicated; see Castiglione, *Specimen*, XIX, on 2 Corinthians 1:3, and especially our Prolegomena to Ulfilas; and finally from the catchwords (French *réclames* or signatures) by which the numbers of gatherings are indicated in manuscripts, Massmann, *Skeireins*, 57. It should also be noted that at 1 Corinthians 14:26 the scribe wrote [Gothic a] above a word which he had first written incorrectly, and [Gothic b] above the word which should have preceded it; see Castiglione on this passage. Likewise, the alphabet of the Vatican codex (*Wiener Jahrbücher*, p. 4) contains the numbers placed beside the letters down to [Gothic r], with [Gothic 900] altogether absent at the end.

“In order that numeral letters may be distinguished from others: (a) a line or  is drawn over them, in the same manner as in Greek codices (see Bast, *Commentarius palaeographicus*, p. 850 in Schäfer’s edition of Gregorius Corinthius), and then the diacritical points of ï are absent—for example, 5, 10, 100, etc.; sometimes it is drawn beneath them, as in Viljarith’s signature in the Neapolitan document. (b) In addition, a point is placed before and after the letter, more commonly only one point; for example, 2, 40, 12, etc. In the Neapolitan document, however, there are two, for example in the signatures of Sunjafrithas: 60, 120. In place of points Viljarith uses (c) small hooks: , as Gudileb also does in the Arezzo document: . Similar hooks enclose the catchwords (French *réclames* or signatures): ; see Massmann, *Skeireins*, 57. Ufitahari marks individual letters of a two-digit number in this manner: , and Viljarith separates them by a point: ; in which case observe also a sort of small stroke placed beneath each letter. From the different methods of indicating numbers in the Vienna codex (*Wiener Jahrbücher*, p. 11), it is evident that they must be assigned to different sources. The first series is as follows: 130), (807), (840), (912); and W. Grimm, p. 16, proved that they were excerpted from Genesis. The later series, however, has an overline: (60), (30), (590), (70), (890).

«§ 15. Note 5.—“The numerical value of the letters also indicates their order in the alphabet [Col. 0905]; this order is the same as that in which the letters were set out in §10. This arrangement is found in the so-called Vatican alphabet of §14, in another alphabet in Vienna manuscript no. 140, fol. 20b (Wien. Jahrb. 5 ff.), and there beside the Gothic-written runic alphabet, which, however, proceeds no farther than u (Wien. Jahrb. 1 ff.); in the same order Ihre arranged the Gothic letters in the table on p. 200 of Büsching’s edition. On the model of the Latin alphabet—which was later also imitated in the North in arranging the runic alphabet—the Gothic alphabet is arranged in another series of the Vienna manuscript:

[Gothic a], [Gothic b], [Gothic g], [Gothic d], [Gothic e], [Gothic f], [Gothic j], [Gothic h], [Gothic i], [Gothic k], [Gothic l], [Gothic m], [Gothic n], [Gothic u], [Gothic p], [Gothic q], [Gothic r], [Gothic s], [Gothic t], [Gothic v], [Gothic o], [Gothic x], [Gothic w], [Gothic dh].

Since the letters [Gothic w] and [Gothic dh] were of unknown origin to the scribe, he relegated them to the end; as for [Gothic o], it appears to have been treated as w. Hickes, p. 1, arranged the signs distinctive of Gothic arbitrarily:

[Gothic a], [Gothic b], [Gothic g], [Gothic d], [Gothic e], [Gothic f], [Gothic j], [Gothic h], [Gothic i], [Gothic k], [Gothic l], [Gothic m], [Gothic n], [Gothic o], [Gothic p], [Gothic w], [Gothic k], [Gothic s], [Gothic t], [Gothic dh], [Gothic u], [Gothic q], [Gothic v], [Gothic x], [Gothic z].

This order was followed also by Lye, p. XXXIX, and Zahn at the beginning of the Fulda grammar, with the observation, however, that the latter placed episemon [Gothic 90] between [Gothic w] and [Gothic k]. Massmann, on the other hand, employed an entirely peculiar order in the glossary to the *Skeireins*, namely:

[Gothic a], [Gothic b], [Gothic d], [Gothic e], [Gothic f], [Gothic g], [Gothic h], [Gothic w], [Gothic i], [Gothic j], [Gothic k], [Gothic l], [Gothic m], [Gothic n], [Gothic o], [Gothic p], [Gothic q], [Gothic r], [Gothic s], [Gothic t], [Gothic dh], [Gothic u], ([Gothic x]), [Gothic v], ([Gothic z]).”  

«§ 16. Note 6.—The names of the Gothic letters have not come down to us, since the language was not treated by native grammarians. Only one name occurs in the Bible translation, namely *jota*, Matthew V.18, and this too is Greek. That [Gothic b] is additionally called *bi* is merely Benzelius’s conjecture on Matthew II.2; nor does Ihre, p. 210 of Büsching’s edition, have a better basis for asserting that [Gothic q] is called *bau* or *vau*, or Lye, p. XXXIX, for calling [Gothic k] *chon*. The Vienna alphabet indeed (Wien. Jahrb. 5 ff.) gives a name for each letter, namely:

[Gothic a] *aza*; [Gothic b] *bercna*; [Gothic g] *geuua*; [Gothic d] *daaz*; [Gothic e] *eyz*; [Gothic f] *fe*; [Gothic j] *gaar*; [Gothic h] *haal*; [Gothic i] *iiz*; [Gothic k] *chozma*; [Gothic l] *laaz*; [Gothic m] *manna*; [Gothic n] *noicz*; [Gothic u] *uraz*; [Gothic p] *pertra*; [Gothic q] *quetra*; [Gothic r] *reda*; [Gothic s] *sugil*; [Gothic t] *tyz*; [Gothic v] *uuinne*; [Gothic o] *utal*; [Gothic x] *enguz*; [Gothic z] *ezec*; [Gothic w] *uuaer*; [Gothic dh] *thyth*.

But how strange and obscure are the forms of these names! For even if they all agreed with W. Grimm (Wien. Jahrb. p. 19), we could never admit his conjecture that these names have a Gothic character, still less say with him that their scribe knew the Gothic language. Jacob Grimm (ibid., p. 41) seeks in the Slavic language a means of elucidating these difficult names; and although some of them seem strange and unprecedented to him, he nevertheless does not hesitate to assert that they in fact designate Gothic letters. But who would find it even probable that the names of Gothic letters, several centuries after the language had died out, had been preserved by tradition until the time when they were written [Col. 0906A]? In any event, whatever may be thought and judged on this matter, it is certain that these names have been so greatly corrupted that they no longer even possess a Gothic appearance; neither J. Grimm himself nor Massmann (in Haupt’s *Zeitschrift*, p. 301), despite their most ingenious inventions, has conjectured anything correct. Nothing safer can be said of these names than that they still display a Germanic element; compare Waitz, p. 52, note 3.”  

§ 17. Note 7.—With regard to reading signs, the following points must be noted:

“1) Diacritical signs. These consist solely of dots placed over initial ï; see Lye, XXXIX; Mai, *Spec.* XX. This most common notation is wholly peculiar to the Gothic language. For although two dots placed over i appear in Greek manuscripts of the later period, their use is so particular that in some they occur only over an i at the beginning of a word, in others over a different i, and in still others serve as a diaeretic dot; see Bast, *Commentatio palaeographica*, p. 718 ff. In Lye’s judgment, in accordance with the character of the Gothic language, ì is dotted in several biblical manuscripts—for example in the Alexandrinus, Cantabrigiensis, Colbertinus, and so forth—yet without any consistent practice.

“The absence of the dot in *akaikus*, *gaius*, *ïudaivisks* proves that the Goths treated *ai* as a single sound, whereas the Greeks always pronounced it separately, as it is still written Ἀχαϊκός, Γάϊος, ἰουδαϊκός. We therefore carefully corrected in this edition the formerly incorrect spelling *gaïus*, Romans XVI.23; 1 Corinthians I.14. Castiglione writes *ymainaïus*, 2 Timothy II.17, without justification, because i bore three dots above it; yet, according to 1 Timothy I.19, *ymenaius* must be read.

“A diaeretic dot would be expected in *au*, where these vowels are uttered as two sounds, for example in *laudeikaia*, Colossians IV.13, 15, 16; corresponding to Greek Λαοδικεία, it must be read *la-u-deikaia*.

“2) Signs of punctuation. It may be taken as a rule that a single point denotes lesser, and a double point greater, pauses; Lye, p. XL; Ihre, p. 193 of Büsching’s edition; Castiglione, *Spec.* XIX; Massmann, *Skeir.* p. 58. Yet this punctuation is not applied consistently, since these signs are often used without necessity and even contrary to the sense. After major pauses a blank space is left (Massmann, p. 57), whereas otherwise words follow one another with no interval; or a new line is begun, in which case a mark is drawn above the initial letters, which are capitals, in the Codex Argenteus or the Carolingian manuscript. A minor punctuation mark occurs as an explanatory indication at 2 Corinthians IV.4, where *ïn þaimei guþ. þis aiwis* is read: by this point the scribe indicated that *guþ þis aiwis* is not to be read together.

“3) A word to be written over two lines is divided not according to principles of etymology, but arbitrarily and according to available space (Massmann, *Skeir.* 58 f.). Only very rarely is the division of a word marked by a special sign (a division mark, equivalent to the French *trait-d’union*). Thus none occurs in the Codex Argenteus. In the *Skeireins*, Castiglione, upon re-examining the manuscript [Col. 0907], observed in one place, III.a (fol. 25a, line 1), the sign - placed at the end of the preceding line (as is customary among us), thus: *jai-nar*. In other places, however, the same sign is used for the same purpose not at the end of the preceding line but at the beginning of the following one; see Castiglione on 1 Timothy I.1, where *ve-nais* is written.

“And another sign occurs at Colossians IV.7, which Castiglione describes as a double large reversed comma.”

“If this last sign is inverted, it occurs in Philippians IV.12, resembling one comma placed beneath another, to indicate that a syllable which the scribe had omitted in writing and restored above the line must be inserted: a sign of insertion. In its place, in *Skeir.* IV.d, a sign is prefixed for enclosing a word.

“4) The signs by which passages quoted are distinguished from the text (antilambda; French *guillemets*) are either simple hooks () or double ones (), placed in the margin before each line containing the quoted text; Ihre, p. 190 of Büsching’s edition; Massmann, *Skeir.* 58. In the latter fashion, passages from poets cited or intermingled with the text are marked in Greek manuscripts; see Bast, *Comment. palaeogr.* p. 859. In the *Skeireins*, where a simple antilambda is used, a mark is also added to the first line, and an inverted sign to the last. In *Skeireins* VIII.c, where a verse is quoted incompletely, a simple hook is also placed at the end of the line at which the verse is interrupted.

“5) Signs of abbreviation. Now,

a) some are used for particular letters, namely an inverted sign for *n*, and another for *m*; Ihre, p. 191 f.; Massmann, *Skeir.* 58. These signs are chiefly used at the end of a line, where there was no room for those letters; but they are also placed in the middle, as in Mark VIII.43, *gavadjands*, and *Skeir.* VI.a, *miznan*.

[Note: [Col. 0907] Double-click on the ornament icon which follows to view this character as it appears in Migne.]

“As to their position, they are more commonly written above the vowel after which the omitted letter is to be read; more rarely, at the end of a line, after the letter itself. These signs have also not infrequently either been neglected by the scribe or erased in the manuscripts, whence it has often happened that forms were altered; see on Matthew XXVII.7; Mark II.12; Luke VII.25.

“b) Other signs indicate that a word is written in abbreviated form, namely, more commonly [sign omitted in supplied text], or [sign omitted in supplied text], the latter also being used in Greek manuscripts; see Schäfer and Bast on Gregory of Corinth, pp. 116, 295, 785 f., 815. More rarely, a hook is placed before and after the abbreviated word, as [Gothic l][Gothic k][Gothic n]

[Note: [Col. 0907] Double-click on the ornament icon which follows to view these characters as they appear in Migne.]

in the Neapolitan document, for *diakaun*. The words *guþ*, *ïesus*, *xristus*, and *frauja* are regularly abbreviated; see Gordon, *Specimen animadversionum criticarum in priscam evangeliorum versionem Gothicam*, p. 52 in Büsching; Knittel, *Ulfilae versio epistolae Pauli ad Romanos*, p. 321; Castiglione, *Spec.* p. XIX; Massmann, *Skeireins*, p. 58; specifically in the forms *gþ, gþs, gþa; is, iuis, iua, iu; xs, xaus, xau, xu; fa, fins, fin, fan*.

Finally, *ïesus* is not abbreviated when it is the name not of Christ but of other men, as at Colossians IV.11; Ezra II.36, 40.

«§ 18. Note 8.—Before alphabetic writing had been invented, the Goths probably used the runic script, which the other Germans also employed. They probably called it *runic* from Gothic *runos*, which, although in the Bible translation it now means μυστήριον, “mystery,” is also used for βουλή, “counsel,” and συμβούλιον, “council” (see glossary); likewise Anglo-Saxon *run* has all these meanings. The strokes of letters (*elementa*) are called in Gothic *stabeis* (στοιχεῖα, “elements”; compare Galatians IV.3, 9; Colossians II.20); the various little strokes, hooks, dots, and horns are *vritos* (κεραῖαι, “small strokes,” Luke XVI.17), *strikos* (κεραῖαι, Matthew V.18), and *stikos* (στιγμαί, “points”; compare Luke IV.15).

“They called writing *boka*, or, more commonly, in the plural *bokos*. A letter and a testimonial charter, in the Neapolitan document, have no other name than *boka*, elsewhere plural *bokos*; likewise a document of indebtedness or betrothal (γράμματα, “documents,” Luke XVI.6, 7). A bond is *vadjabokos* (χειρόγραφον, Colossians II.14); a bill of divorce (ἀποστάσιον, Mark XIX.4; Matthew V.31) is *bokos afsateinais* or *bokos afstassais*, a designation also used for an epistle (ἐπιστολή); see the glossary, s.v. The word for book (βίβλος, βιβλίον) is treated there as well. In the Christian sense—that is, denoting the book of books, the Scriptures (γραφαί)—it is designated by the same word, *boka*, *bokos*. Finally, *boka* corresponds to “letter,” Greek γράμμα and γράμματα, and Latin *littera*, *litterae* (Romans VII.6; 2 Corinthians III.6; especially Galatians VI.11); and *bokos* is used for learning, knowledge of the Scriptures [Col. 0910] (John VII.15). Accordingly, the learned men of the Scriptures among the Jews (γραμματεῖς) bear the name *bokarjos* (see glossary, s.v.), which properly means “scribe”; see the Neapolitan document. For “epistle” (ἐπιστολή), the translator of the Pauline epistles employed Greek *aipistaule* (see glossary, s.v.), in the sense of apostolic letters. *Sigljo*, “seal” (σφραγίς), and *sigljan, gasigljan*, “to seal” (σφραγίζειν), are peculiar to the Gothic language (see glossary, s.vv.).

“Besides *bokos*, denoting a written work, especially sacred Scripture, there occur also *mela* (Mark XII.24; Luke IV.21; John V.47) and *gameleins* (John VII.38, 42; 2 Corinthians III.7; 1 Timothy V.18), or more often *þata gamelido* (see glossary, s.v.), the past participle of *gameljan*, which, like the simple *meljan*, means ‘to write’ (γράφειν). Hence *ufmeljan*, ‘to subscribe,’ and *ufarmeljan*, ‘to inscribe’ (ἐπιγράφειν; see there), with *ufarmeli* or *ufarmeleins*, ‘inscription’ (ἐπιγραφή; see there).

“Concerning the material upon which the Goths first wrote, we know nothing certain. The claim that they used tree bark for this purpose and derived the name *boka* from the name of a tree, just as Latin *liber* was derived, rests on mere conjecture. Later, after intercourse with the Greeks had begun, they used parchment, or at least received for it the name *maimbrana* (2 Timothy IV.13), copied from Greek μεμβράνα. All Gothic manuscript codices which have survived to us are written on parchment; among them the Codex Argenteus stands out, written on red parchment in silver and gold letters; see *Prolegomena*, col. 489 ff. The Neapolitan document is indeed written on papyrus, but it is not wholly Gothic. They must early have bound leaves together into a book, since *spildos* (πινακίδια, πλάκες, “tablets,” Luke I.63; 2 Corinthians III.3) already occurs in the Bible translation.

“As for the instrument used in writing, it was a black pen, *svartisl* or *svartisla* (μέλαν, ‘black ink’; glossary, s.v.), probably a reed, *raus*, like the other kinds of reed (κάλαμος); see glossary, s.v. Both are Gothic words. To read and to recite, *siggvan* and *ussiggvan*, are the same word as that meaning song or the declamation of popular songs; hence ‘reading’ (ἀνάγνωσις, 1 Timothy IV.13) is rendered *saggvs*.”  

## B. ON PRONUNCIATION

[Col. 0909]

§ 19. Although it is almost impossible to determine with complete certainty the pronunciation of an extinct language, certain indications nevertheless remain; when these are weighed, we may reach the fleeting sounds clothed in the signs of writing. The particular indications afforded by the Gothic language are as follows:

1. the character of the letters, insofar as they derive from a language not unknown to us;
2. the spelling of foreign words and proper names;
3. letters interchanged with one another, whether this occurs by rule or through scribal error; and finally,
4. the analogy of related languages.

Although below we intend, with the aid of these indications, to reconstruct the sounds of the Gothic language, it is not irrelevant to observe that we shall use the fourth indication—the analogy of related languages—only with the greatest caution, and for several reasons. Gothic, like a dead branch of the Germanic stock, survives in no part of the related languages [Col. 0911], nor can it be compared with any language of its own age, since the languages of the Lombards, Vandals, Burgundians, and the rest have likewise perished. Even Old High German, which is the nearest of all to Gothic, neither derives from it so directly that it can be called its offspring, nor is so close to it in age that it can be called its contemporary. Thus, in investigating Gothic sounds by analogy with Old German [Col. 0912], greater caution is needed because the system proper to that language is more confused, and even the most expert scholars are to this day uncertain and divided more sharply into opposing views. Even apart from these unwelcome circumstances, one always acts imprudently in attempting to compare the sounds of one language with those of a related language, since even languages most closely related often differ greatly in their sounds.

## I. ON THE VOWELS

[Col. 0911]

§ 20. The Gothic language has five simple vowels: *a, e, i, u, o*; and four diphthongs: *ai, au, ei, iu*.

“Note.—A sixth vowel, *y*, occurs only in foreign words and does not properly belong to the Gothic language; see §27.”

§ 21. Vowels are either short or long; long vowels are equivalent to two short ones and are ordinarily short vowels either lengthened or doubled. Hence short vowels must be regarded as primary.

Among the simple vowels there are three short ones, *a, i, u*, upon which the entire vocalic system rests and from which the remaining vowels and diphthongs are formed. Of these three short vowels, *a* is the primary vowel, descending through weakening on one side to *u*, on the other to *i*. *E* and *o* are only long, and must indeed be regarded as long forms of *a*, since *e* approaches *i* more closely and *o* approaches *u* more closely. The long forms of *i* and *u* are either *i* and *u* again, or the diphthongs *ei* and *iu*; while *a*, joined with *i* and *u*, forms the diphthongs *ai* and *au*.

These latter diphthongs, however, are not to be regarded as composed of two vowels: rather, they are vowels intermediate between *a* and *i*, and between *a* and *o*, and consequently have no necessary reason to become long; indeed, they are often in fact short. But *ei* and *iu* are true diphthongs, that is, formed from two originally short vowels, and are therefore only long. Once these points are established, the entire Gothic vowel system develops in such a way that its simplicity and regularity become manifest.

## A

§ 22. 1) It is certain that the vowel *a* is primary in Gothic, not only because it is the predominant vowel in inflections and is weakened into *i* or *u* only according to fixed laws (§32.4), but also because in transcriptions of foreign words it generally occurs as short *a*, used especially for Latin *e* and Greek ε; for example: *karkara*, Latin *carcer*; *lukarn*, Latin *lucerna*; *kafarnaum*, Καπερναούμ; *beþlahaim*, Βηθλεέμ.

2) No vowel is more frequent in use than *a*; it can therefore occupy any position in a word, and may stand before or after any consonant. Thus:

a) At the beginning: *aba, agis, adam, aqizi, azets, aha, aþþan, ak, alls, ammo, ana, ajukduþs, apaustaulus, ara, asans, atta, avo, af, axaja, awa*, etc.

b) In the middle: *badi, blandan, brakja, gaggan, glaggvuba, gras, dags, dragk, qaþ, qrammiþa, zakkaius, haban, hlas, hramjan, þagkjan, þlahsjan, þragjan, þvahan, kalds, niuklahs, land, manna, namo, jah, papa, plats, praggan, rahnjan, sakan, tagl, valdan, fastan, was; graban, lagjan, vadi, þlaqus, razda, faheds, laþon, staks, malan, sama, fani, bajoþs, skapjan, þarba, vas, mats, skavjan, hafjan, zaxxaius, saw*, etc.

c) At the end: *giba, liga, bida, sigqa, batiza, slaha, qiþa, leika, vaila, ïmma, ïna, alja, vairpa, skura, lisa, maita, speiva, hlifa, pasxa, leiwa*, etc.

3) Except in the cases mentioned above, *a* occurs only rarely in Gothic words, apart from compounds, before or after vowels with which it does not contract into a diphthong. If it does happen, it occurs only before *u* (§29, note 1) and after *i, ei, ai, au*: *fiaþva, friaþva*, in which case the hiatus is avoided by inserting *j* (see §34.4); *keian, feian; laian, saian, vaian; trauan, bauan*.

“Note 1.—In foreign words other combinations can indeed arise, such as *baiþlaem* (alongside which *beþlahaim* also occurs), *baiþsaïda, kaeinan, aiddua*. But the Goth avoids *aa*, either by inserting *h*, as in *aharon*, Ἀαρών; *abraham*, Ἀβραάμ; *nahasson*, Ναασσών; *mahaþ*, Μαάθ; or by writing only one a, as in *ïsak*, Ἰσαάκ. Yet *aa* is found at the end: *gabaa*, Ezra II.25; compare *sainnaïns* from *sainnaa*, II.35. Apart from these two examples in Ezra, which are at least justified by the Greek, there are other forms occurring also in Ezra but corruptly: II.11 *babaavis*; II.21 *baaaiþlaem*; II.25 *kareiaþiaareim*; II.28 *aai*, certainly a scribal error, or at least to be read *a-ai*.”

4) Except for the examples cited above, Gothic *a* constantly corresponds to Greek α, and consequently must have had its pronunciation; for example: *abba*, ἀββᾶ; *abjaþar*, Ἀβιάθαρ; *agar*, Ἄγαρ; *adam*, Ἀδάμ; *adauneikam*, Ἀδωνικάμ; *addin*, Ἀδδίν; *akaja*, Ἀχαΐα; *alfaius*, Ἀλφαῖος; *ameinadab*, Ἀμιναδάβ; *andraias*, Ἀνδρέας; *annas*, Ἄννας; *arkippus*, Ἄρχιππος; *asgad*, Ἀσγάδ; *assaum*, Ἀσούμ; *ater*, Ἀτήρ; *gaulgauþa*, Γολγοθᾶ; *damasko*, Δαμασκός; *kefas*, Κηφᾶς; *seina*, Σινᾶ.

[Col. 0913] 5) Although *a* is used for both long and short Greek α, in Gothic it is only short, whether it belongs to a root or a formative syllable. This is apparent both from the formation of the second conjugation and from the representation of *a* by *o*—a representation made by the people, not by the translator—in *rumoneis* for *Romani*; see below, 7).

6) While retaining its shortness, *a* can also become acute, which happens especially before liquids, *s, z,* and *h*. The reason is that the liquid, *s*, and *z* are either redundantly doubled, as in *nasseinais*, 1 Thessalonians V.8; *ïasson* (Ἰάσων), Romans XVI.21; *lazzarus* (Λάζαρος), Luke XVI.23; *kannt*, 1 Corinthians VII.16; or, conversely, simplified, so that a single liquid is used where etymologically a double one would be expected, as in *branjan*, John XV.6 (from *brinnan*); compare §55, notes 1 and 2. This happens especially when, through composition, the stress moves beyond the syllable in question; for example: *alaþárba* (from *alls*), *manamaúrþrja* (from *manna*). Before *h*, *a* becomes acute especially in the word *jah*, when h assimilates to the following consonant (§56).

“Note 2.—The doubling of d in *gaddarenus* for Γαδαρηνός may arise from a similar principle; see glossary, s.v.

“Note 3.—For weakened *a*, see §32.4.”

7) The long vowel corresponding to *a* is *o*. Thus *a* not only often becomes *o*, but *o* is generally used where a long *a* would be expected. The form *rumoneis* for *Romani* has already been mentioned above in 5). Other examples in which *a* changes to *o*, and where no proper vowel alternation (§32.2) can be supposed, are: *gahobains* from *haban*, *ganohs* from *nahan*, *abtaudogs*, *fidurdogs* from *dags*. In other cases, such as *soþ* from *saþs*, *bota* from *bats*, vowel alternation may be explained by a verb that has perhaps fallen out of use (*saþan, soþ*; *hatan, bot*).

That in inflection too *o* corresponds to long *a* is evident from *gibos* from *giba*, *vigos* from *vigs* (stem *VIGA*), as contrasted with *gasteis* from *gasts* (stem *GASTI*); and conversely from the genitive *hairtane* from *hairtona*, in which *o*, because of a following long *e*, again falls into its corresponding short *a*. The forms *warjanoh, warjatoh, warjoh*, which occur in place of *warjana-uh*, etc., are not to be explained as resulting from contraction of *a-u* into *o*, since elsewhere *a* is elided before *uh*. Rather, it may be conjectured either that the originally long vowel of the ending could have been preserved before the enclitic particle, as in *ainohun* from *aina* and *hun*, *ainnohun* from *ainana* (syncopated *ainna*) and *hun* (and perhaps also *weilohun* from *weila* and *hun*); or that the enclitic, which was early and regularly added to these words, influenced the vowel of the ending by attracting the stress, whereas in later times, when that influence ceased, the short vowel of the ending was finally elided.

“Note 4.—For *e* regarded as the other long vowel corresponding to *a*, see §25.4.”

## I

§ 23. 1) After *a*, vowel *i* occurs most frequently, although it is found more often in the middle than at the beginning or end of a word:

[Col. 0914]

a) At the beginning: *ïakob, ïbai, ïggqis, ïdveit, ïesus, ïzei, ïþ, ïk, ïm, ïn, ïja, ïs, ïlan, ïftuma, ïohannes*.

b) In the middle: *bida, blinds, brinno, giba, glitmunjan, grids, digrei, drigkan, qiþan, hilpan, hlifan, hnivans, hrisjan, þivi, þriskan, kilþei, klismo, kniva, krispus, ligan, miþ, niman, saijiþ, pistikeins, plinsjan, priska, rimis, sijis, skildus, skritnan, slindan, smiþa, snivan, spillon, stiks, striks, svibls, timrja, triva, tvis* [lacuna], *vinds, vlits, vrikan, finþan, frijei, wileiks; siai, siau, libains, gibla, stibna, trigo, ligrs, svignjan, siggvan, sigqan, sidus, bidjan, fidvor, riqis, þize, mizdo, andavizn, vlizjan, nih, aggviþa, niþjis, viþra, mikils, stikls, svikns, andtilon, silba, milds, filhan, vilþeis, filleins, usfilma, vilja, hilpan, sviltan, gilstr, qiman, himma, simle, mimz, trimpan, fimf, blinds, minznan, gasinþa, vinja, þinsan, kintus, frijon, skip, vipja, ganipnan, hiri, hirjiþ, vis, trisgan, vrisqan, fisks, klismjan, vissa, lists, hulistr, sitan, sitls, þivi, sifan, hliftus, lifnan*.

c) At the end: *arbi, aigi*, John VI.40; *fauragaggi, vadi, bandi, aqizi, þvohi*, 1 Timothy V.10; *aveþi, meki, aurali, nemi*, Mark XII.2; *fani, hropi, wilftri, usvissi, nati, hivi, sewi*, Mark VIII.23.

2) In simple Gothic words it is only rarely placed after vowels with which it does not form a diphthong, and then only after *ai* and *au*: *saiïþ*, 2 Corinthians IX.6; *tauï, sauïl, stauïda*.

“Note 1.—When two i’s meet, either both are changed into *ei*, or the first becomes *j* (§34.3).”

3) In transcribed foreign words, i commonly corresponds to Greek ι, whether accented or unaccented: *ïaeirus*, Ἰάειρος; *ïairaimias*, Ἱερεμίας; *ïairiko*, Ἱεριχώ; *aivxaristia*, εὐχαριστία; *þymiama*, θυμίαμα; *gabriel*, Γαβριήλ; *diabulus*, διάβολος; *didimus*, Δίδυμος; *krispus*, Κρίσπος; *lukius*, Λούκιος; *makeibis*, Μαγεβίς; *nikaudemus*, Νικόδημος; *siloam*, Σιλωάμ.

“Note 2.—Sometimes i is also used:

a) for Greek η (compare Castiglione on 2 Corinthians I.16): *aunisimus*, Ὀνήσιμος; *baiþil*, Βαιθήλ; *jannis*, Ἰαννῆς; *abeileni*, Ἀβιληνή; *filippisius*, Φιλιππήσιος; *biþania*, Βηθανία;

b) exceptionally, for Greek υ: *didimus*, Δίδυμος (in *akvíla* for Ἀκύλας, however, the Latin form seems rather to have been the model);

c) for Greek ε: *andrias*, Gothic Calendar; *zauraubabil*, Ζοροβάβελ; *aggilus*, ἄγγελος; *makidonja*, Μακεδονία;

d) for Greek ει: *antiaukia*, Ἀντιοχεία;

e) for Greek χ: *ïareim*, Χαρίμ.”

4) Like *a*, i is originally short; but since in pronunciation it closely approaches *ei* and *e*, it sometimes performs the role of a long vowel. It is therefore used:

a) for *ei* in: *digan*, Romans IX.20; *ufarassiþ*, 1 Timothy I.14; *þagkiþ*, Galatians VI.3; *visandin* (for *visandein*), 1 Timothy I.4; *Skeir.* VII.6; *laisaris*, Luke VI.40; *silubrins*, Matthew XXVII.3; *gabigs*, Matthew XXVII.57 and often; compare on Galatians VI.3; especially in proper names, such as *ananias*, Nehemiah VII.2; *ïairiko*, Mark X.46; *bainiamein*, Philippians III.5 at this passage; *ïsraelites*, Romans IX.4;

b) for *e*: *spidists*, 1 Timothy IV.1; *azitizo*, Mark X.25; *svigniþa*, Luke I.44; *birusjos*, II.41; *snivun*, Mark VI.53; *nimeina*, Luke VI.34; *qimi*, VII.3; *qiþeina*, VIII.56; IX.21; *qiþeiþ*, XVII.6; *usdribeina*, IX.40; *galagidideina*, V.18; *tavidideina*, VI.11; [Col. 0915] *ufkunþidun*, Nehemiah VI.16; *fravaurhti*, Romans VII.5; *spilli*, Titus I.14; *herodis*, Luke IX.7; *ïohannis*, Mark VI.14. On Gothic coins *Reccaredus* and *Reccaridus* are interchanged; see Aschbach, *Westg.* 358.

“Note 3.—The same interchange is observable among the Latins; and just as e belongs to their earlier and rustic speech, whereas i belongs to their later and urban speech (compare Schneider, *Lateinische Formenlehre*), so the same appears to have been the case among the Goths.

“Note 4.—But where i is long, breaking (§32.5), which is otherwise commonly applied before certain consonants, can have no place. Hence *bi rusjos* (instead of *berusjos*); *hiri* is contracted from *her*; *nih* from *ni-uh*.”

5) **Ei** is the long form of *i*, as is demonstrated either by the transcription of Greek words (§ 30, 2 b) or by the doctrine of inflectional forms (§§ 64, 5; 128). Yet, because of their affinity, *i* and *ei* are often used interchangeably, as was shown above under 4), and will be shown more fully below in § 30, 3).

6) *I* changes: a) by breaking into *ai* (§ 32, 5); b) before a vowel, into *j* (§ 34, 3).

## U

### § 24

1) **U**, the third short vowel of the Gothic vowel triad, occurs less frequently than *i*, and indeed not equally in all combinations of consonants. At the beginning of a word it is almost exclusively confined to particles and pronouns; at the end, apart from certain particles and neuter nouns, it is used only in a few inflections.

a) At the beginning: *ubizva, ubils, ugkis, uhteigs, ulbandus, und, undar, undaurns, uns, unte, us, ut, uf, ufar, ufjo, ufta*;

b) In the middle: *bugjan, brusts, gulþ, usgrudja, dugan, drus, qums, hugjan, hlutrs, hnuto, hruk, þus, þrutsfill, kukjan, knussjan, krusts, lustus, munan, nuta, jus, puggs, runs, sulja, skulan, snutrs, stubjus, svultavairþja, tulgus, intrusgjan, vulan, vruggo, fuls, frums, fairwus; lubains, silubr, bugum, juggs, fugls, ludja, suqon, suqns, jukuzi, anabuzns, huzd, huhrus, þuhtus, guþ, mukamodei, fula, fulls, hulþs, mulda, numans, andanumts, svumsl, runa, brunna, afgrundiþa, kunþi, brunjo, hups, skura, hus, andhruskan, barusnjan, kustus, luton, hufum, luftus*;

c) At the end: *du, þu, ju, nu, ïnu, faihu, gairu, handu, aggva, siju*.

2) In transcribing foreign words, *u* is regularly used for Greek ου, and sometimes for *o*, especially in endings. Thus it stands:

a) for Greek ου in: *fanuel* Φανουήλ (*Phanuel*), *ïairusalem* Ἱερουσαλήμ (*Jerusalem*), *ïesus* Ἰησοῦς (*Jesus*), *ïdumaia* Ἰδουμαία (*Idumaea*), *ïturaia* Ἰτουραία (*Ituraea*), *ïudas* Ἰούδας (*Judas*), *ïudaia* Ἰουδαία (*Judaea*), *kusa* Χουζᾶ (*Chuza*), *lukas* Λουκᾶς (*Luke*), *maþusal* Μαθουσαλά (*Methuselah*), *naum* Νοούμ (*Nahum*), *odueia* Ὠδουίας (*Oduiah*);

b) for Greek ο in: *paintekuste* πεντηκοστή (*Pentecost*), *aipistule*, Neh. VI, 17, 19, ἐπιστολή (*letter*), *puntius* Πόντιος (*Pontius*), *ïairusaulyma* Ἱεροσόλυμα (*Jerusalem*), *laudeikaia* Λαοδικεία (*Laodicea*), *diakun* διάκονος (*deacon*), *diabulus* διάβολος (*devil*), *apaustaulus* ἀπόστολος (*apostle*), *barþulomaius* Βαρθολομαῖος (*Bartholomew*); and in proper names ending in ος, such as *paitrus* Πέτρος (*Peter*), [Col. 0916] *pavlus* Παῦλος (*Paul*), *filippus* Φίλιππος (*Philip*), *alaiksandrus* Ἀλέξανδρος (*Alexander*), *akajus* Ἀχαιός (*Achaean*). This ending prevails so strongly that it is sometimes used even for Greek ης, as in *praufetus* προφήτης (*prophet*), *kreskus* Κρήσκης (*Crescens*), *skyþus* Σκύθης (*Scythian*).

> **Note 1.—** *U* is also written for *o* in Latin words: *pund* for *pondus*, *kustanteinus* for *Constantinus*, just as *u* transcribes the Greek and Latin *o* of Gothic names.

> **Note 2.—** Only exceptionally is it also used for Greek ω and υ: *ïuse* Ἰωσῆ (*Joses*), *spaikulatur* σπεκουλάτωρ (*executioner*), *rumoneis* Ῥωμαῖοι (*Romans*), *paurpura* πορφύρα (*purple*), *saur* Σύρος (*Syrian*), *tukeikus* Τυχικός (*Tychicus*). *ïakubos*, Luke IX, 54, is a scribal error for *ïakobus*.

3) *U* is short and long; indeed, it is long primitively, not accidentally, as when *i* is used in place of *ei* and *e*. That *u* is in fact long is demonstrated by the following reasons:

a) For it frequently alternates with *o*: either *u* stands for *o*, as in *krotuda*, Luke XX, 18, *supuda*, Mark IX, 50, *uhtedun*, Mark XI, 32, and in Greek words such as *ïuse*, etc. (see Note 2); or *o* is written for *u*, as in *aljakons*, Eph. II, 19, *lauhmoni*, Luke XVII, 24; II Thess. I, 8, *vidovo*, Luke VII, 12, *faiho*, Mark X, 23, *fraistobnjo*, Luke IV, 13, *ushofon*, XVII, 13, *sunjos*, Luke XVI, 8, *vondon*, Luke XX, 12, *ohteigo*, II Tim. IV, 2, *ainomehun*, Luke VIII, 43, and in Greek words such as *ïodas*, etc. (see § 26, 2 c). In the same way, on coins *Gundemar* and *Gondemar*, *Rodericus* and *Rudericus*, alternate; see Aschbach, *Westg.* p. 362.

b) Since short *u* is regularly broken before *h* and *r*, it must therefore be considered long in the following cases: *juhiza, þuhta,* and *huhrus*, from *juggs, þugkjan,* and *huggrjan* (in which, besides position, etymology also proves that *u* is long); *bruhta* from *brukjan* (as *bauhta* from *bugjan*); *-uh, nuh, uhteigs, uhtvo, spaikulatur* [for Greek ω], *skura, urreisan, urrinnan*, etc.

c) Long *u* is also required in *hrukjan*, on account of the third-person singular present indicative *hrukeiþ*, John XIII, 38 (§ 128), and in *lukan*, because here it corresponds to the unquestionably long *iu* in *siukan, liusan, biudan*, and similar words.

> **Note 3.—** In cases other than those given above, it can only with difficulty be decided whether *u* should be considered long; it is nevertheless probably so in *mul, fuls, hus, rums, bruþs, dubo, stubjus, runa, þusundi, dugan, vulan*.

4) The pronunciation of *u* may be compared with the *u* of the Germans, but with this difference: it seems to approach *o* more closely. This at least explains why it so frequently alternates with *o* (§ 26, 4) and *au* (§ 29, 3).

5) *U* undergoes alternations similar to those of *i*; it therefore changes: a) before *r* and *h*, by breaking, into *au* (§ 32, 5); b) before a vowel, into *v* (§ 35, 3).

## E

### § 25

1) **E** is always long; in Gothic words it occupies only medial and final position, occurring generally less frequently than *i* and *u*:

a) In the middle: *berun, blesan, gebun, gredus, qens, heþjo,* [Col. 0917] *hleþra, þevis, kelikn, letan, megs, nemun, jer, garedan, sels, skevjan, slepan, speds, svegnjan, teva, vesun, vrekei, fera, flekan, fret; vegs, unleds, gafehaba, garehsns, neþla, meki, mel, qemun, mena, vepna, ferja, mes, andasets, lev, newa*;

b) At the end: *ne, þe, we, sve, simle, svare, unte, þande, hidre, jaindre, wadre, bisunjane*, and in the genitive plural, *fiske, vaurde*, etc.

c) But *e* is never preceded by other vowels, except *i*, with which it forms the diphthong *ei*.

2) In transcribed foreign words, it regularly corresponds to Greek η: *esav* Ἠσαῦ (*Esau*), *ïesus* Ἰησοῦς (*Jesus*), *ïairusalem* Ἱηρουσαλήμ (*Jerusalem*), *ïsrael* Ἰσραήλ (*Israel*), *kaidmeiel* Καδμιήλ (*Kadmiel*), *ïosef* Ἰωσήφ (*Joseph*), *ïoses* Ἰωσῆ (*Joses*), *kefas* Κηφᾶς (*Cephas*), *kreta* Κρήτη (*Crete*), *nazorenus* Ναζωρηνός (*Nazarene*), *gaddarenus* Γαδαρηνός (*Gadarene*), *gainnesaraiþ* Γεννησαρέτ (*Gennesaret*).

> **Note.—** Exceptionally, however, it stands: a) for ι, in *naen* Ναίν (*Nain*), *tykekus*, Col. IV, 7, Τυχικός (*Tychicus*); b) for ε, in *ïared* Ἰαρέδ (*Jared*), *tertius* Τέρτιος (*Tertius*), *baiþlaem* Βεθλαέμ (*Bethlehem*); c) for αι, Latin *ae*, in *kreks* Γραικός, *Graecus* (“Greek”).

3) It has already been noted above (§ 23, Note 2) that *e* often alternates with *i*. Besides the examples cited there, in which *i* stands for *e*, there are also quite a few in which, conversely, *e* seems to stand for *i* or *ei*.

a) For *i*: *svekunþ*, Luke VIII, 17; *weleiks*, I, 29; *seneigs*, I Tim. V, 1, 2; *aggeljus*, Rom. VIII, 38; *ubels*, II Tim. III, 13; *filegri*, Luke XIX, 46; *drebi*, Mark V, 10; *andbahtededun*, Luke VIII, 17.

b) For *ei*: *vehs*, Mark VIII, 26, 27; *lekeis*, Mark II, 17 and often; *lekinon*, Luke X, 9; *hleþra*, John VII, 2; *skereins*, I Cor. XIV, 26; *spevan*, Mark VII, 33; *ne*, *Skeir.* I, c; *frume*, subscription to I Corinthians; *anavilje*, Phil. IV, 5; *ake*, Gal. II, 14; *þe*, I Cor. XVI, 6; *þataine*, *Skeir.* I, 6; *miþþane*, Luke II, 43; *þane*, X, 5; *þoze*, XIX, 37; *þize*, I Cor. VIII, 11; II Cor. XII, 13; *ïze*, Matt. V, 32 and often; *blotande*, Luke II, 37; *qenes*, Eph. V, 22, 24; *kretes*, Tit. I, 12; *visses*, Luke XIX, 22; *aipistaulem*, II Thess. II, 17.

c) For *ai*, see § 28, 3.

4) In very many cases *e* seems to be a long form of *a*, just as Greek η is long *a*. Thus *wammeh, warjammeh, ainummehun* are written instead of *wamma-uh, warjamma-uh, ainamma-hun*. These examples are explained only by the fact that the longer form, with primitive *e*, was retained before the enclitic particle, whereas elsewhere it was shortened to *a*; or by the fact that here too, as we conjectured above (§ 22, 7), the primitive enclitic lengthened the vowel of the ending. Likewise, the plurals *gebun, nemun*, with lengthened *a*, must be derived from the singulars *gaf, nam*. The second-person singular preterite ending of the second conjugation, *des*, must also be explained in a similar manner, once it is admitted that in this ending the preterite may perhaps have become confused with the stem of the word: namely, *dad, dast, dad, dedum, deduþ, dedun*. In the singular it would have discarded its *d* (*t*), and only in the second person would have resumed its vowel, long by position, with *a* and *e* interchanged: *dast, das, des*. See § 127. It may indeed be suspected that *fret* in Luke XV, 30 arose from *fra-at*; but it would be safer to conjecture that this is not for *fraet* (for what Gothic verb [Col. 0918] ends in *e* in the singular preterite indicative?), but is a scribal error for *frat*.

5) *E* may have been pronounced like Latin *e*, or like German *e* in *See, Meer* (French *e fermé et allongé*, “closed and lengthened e”); but, later approaching *i* more closely, it gave rise to its frequent interchange with *i* and *ei*.

## O

### § 26

1) **O** occurs more frequently than *e*, but is found only very rarely at the beginning of words, most frequently in the middle and at the end.

a) At the beginning: only *ogan, ogjan* (*o*);

b) In the middle: *boka, bloþ, broþar, gods, doms, hoha, ufhlohjan, hrot, þroþjan, þvoh, knoda, kroton, lofa, mota, nota, rodjan, sokjan, skohs, sloh, snorjo, stoma, svogatjan, ubiltojis, tvos, vopjan, vrohjan, fotus, flodus, froþs, wota; gahobains, fidurdogs, mods, fodjan, fodr, ganohjan, skohsl, rohsns, hroþeigs, vokains, vokrs, holon, stols, goljan, bloma, fon, stojan, wopan, hropjan, hors, los, blostreis, botan, gadof, woftuli*;

c) At the end: *o, þo, so, wo, lailo, saiso, vaivo, spillo, holo, airino, luto, aglo, sunno, brunjo, augo, auso, hairto, vato*, etc.; and the genitive plurals *gibo, tuggono, manageino*, etc.

2) It is commonly used for Greek ω, more rarely for ο and ου.

a) For ω, it is employed in: *ainok* Ἐνώχ (*Enoch*), *ainos* Ἐνώς (*Enosh*), *ammo* Ἀμώς (*Amos*), *anaþoþ* Ἀναθώθ (*Anathoth*), *apaullo* Ἀπολλώς (*Apollos*), *asmoþ* Αζμώθ (*Azmoth*), *beroþ* Βηρώθ (*Beeroth*), *zelotes* ζηλωτής (*Zealot*), *lod* Λώτ (*Lot*), *mammona* μαμμωνᾶς (*Mammon*), *nahasson* Ναασσών (*Nahshon*), *nakor* Ναχώρ (*Nahor*), *ïasson* Ἰάσων (*Jason*), *sabaoþ* Σαβαώθ (*Sabaoth*), *seimon* Σίμων (*Simon*).

b) For ο: *makidonja* Μακεδονία (*Macedonia*), *antiokja*, Gal. II, 11, Ἀντιοχεία (*Antioch*), *aiodia* εὐοδία (*Euodia*), *airmogaineis* Ἑρμογένης (*Hermogenes*), *barþulomaius*, Luke VI, 14, Βαρθολομαῖος (*Bartholomew*), *diakon* διάκονος (*deacon*), *daimonareis* δαιμονιζόμενος (*demon-possessed*).

c) For ου: *ïodas*, Luke III, 26, Ἰούδας (*Judas*), *lokas* Λουκᾶς (*Luke*), *sairok* Σερούχ (*Serug*).

3) *O* appears to permit no *i*, and generally no vowel, after it; but when such a case arises, it changes rather into *au*, or, where the words are foreign, causes *h* to be introduced. Thus: *stauïda, staua* from *stojan*; *tauï*, genitive *tojis*; *lauïdja* Λωίς (*Lois*), *nauel* Νῶε (*Noah*), *trauada* Τρωάς (*Troas*), *ïohannes* Ἰωάννης (*John*), *ïohanna* Ἰωάννα (*Joanna*). On this principle, the word *alþjanoïne*, occurring in the Gothic Calendar, is rightly judged to be spurious.

> **Note 1.—** In *ïoanan*, Neh. VI, 18, for Ἰωνάν (*Johanan*), the first *a* is certainly a scribal error. In *siloam*, John IX, 7, for Σιλωάμ (*Siloam*), the diphthong *ao* is to be pronounced in the Greek manner; finally, in *ailoe*, Mark XV, 34, for ἐλωί (*Eloi*), *oe* has been introduced in place of the unusual *oi*. To avoid *oi*, II Tim. III, 11 also has *lystros* for Greek Λύστροις (*at Lystra*); compare, however, § 96.

4) We have already said above (§ 24, 3) that this vowel frequently alternates with *u*. It also sometimes changes into *au*, though for a less evident reason. This happens when, as noted above, another vowel follows, or when two consonants—that is, *ht*—follow, so that it would, against its nature, become acute. Thus, from *slahan, sloh* comes the verbal noun *slauhts*; from *NAHAN, NOH*, the anomalous *nah, nauhta*, whence again *ganauha* and, in a seemingly more regular form, *ganohs*.

[Col. 0919]

> **Note 2.—** Conversely, *tojis* seems to be used alongside *taujan* without necessity, unless it is explained by comparison with *stojan, stauïda*. But no reason is evident why *dauhnan* became *dobnan*. Perhaps, despite their related meaning, they should be separated etymologically, and *dobnam* should rather be referred to *dumbnan* (perhaps for *dubnan*?) (§ 38, 3).

5) On regarding *o* as a long form of *a*, see what we said above (§ 22, 7).

## Y

### § 27

**Y**, as a vowel, occurs only in Greek words, in which it regularly represents Greek υ; for example: *ymainaius, hymainaius* Ὑμέναιος (*Hymenaeus*), *skyþus* Σκύθης (*Scythian*), *tykeikus* Τυχικός (*Tychicus*), *tyra* Τύρος (*Tyre*), *syria* Συρία (*Syria*), *nymfa* Νυμφᾶ (*Nymphas*), *fygailus* Φύγελλος (*Phygelus*), *symaion* Συμεών (*Simeon*), *synagoge* Συναγωγή (*synagogue*), *syntyke* Συντύχη (*Syntyche*), *kyreinaius* Κυρηναῖος (*Cyrenian*), *ïairusaulyma* Ἱεροσόλυμα (*Jerusalem*), *þymiama* θυμίαμα (*incense*), *praizbytaireis* πρεσβύτερος (*elder*), *spyreida* σπυρίς (*basket*), *byssus* βυσσός (*fine linen*), *smyrn* σμύῤῥον (*myrrh*), *hyssopo* ὕσσωπος (*hyssop*), *martyr* μάρτυρ (*witness, martyr*), *lysanius* Λυσάνιος (*Lysanias*).

> **Note 1.—** It is written for Greek οι in *sauraufynikiska* (for this, rather than *saurinifynikiska*, is the correct reading), συροφοίνισσα (*Syrophoenician woman*).

> **Note 2.—** Sometimes *u* and *au* are also used in its place: thus *tukeikus*, Eph. VI, 21, alongside *tykeikus*; and *saura*, Gal. I, 21, and *sauraufynikiska*, mentioned in Note 1, alongside *syria*.

## AI

### § 28

1) When the letters *a* and *i* are joined, they form a simple sound in Gothic, occurring frequently at the beginning, middle, and end of words:

a) At the beginning: *aiaik, aiauk, aibr, aigan, aiz, aihts, aiþei, aikan, ains, airþa, aistan, aivs, aiwatundi*;

b) In the middle: *bairan, braids, gairnei, dails, draibjan, qainon, haitan, hlaiv, hnaivjan, hrains, þaih, þlaihan, faihuþraihns, þvairhs, laisjan, gamains, naiteins, jains, paida, raidjan, saivala, skaidan, slaihts, smairþr, snaivs, spaiskuldrs, stains, svairban, tains, vaihts, vlaiton, vraiqs, fairguni, fraiv, wairnei; vaian, armaio, gahlaiba, bilaigon, garaids, haiza, haihs, fraihnan, vaihsta, garaihts, svaihra, haiþi, maiþms, laikon, hails, haims, vainei, saijiþ, vaips, tairan, wairban, bairgahei, vairdus, fairzna, þairh, vairþan, þairko, stairno, vairpan, fairra, vairsiza, hairto, fairwus, laisjan, maitan, baitrs, saivs, haifsts, saiwan*;

c) At the end: *bai, þai, jai, jabai, ïbai, nibai, sai, tvai, vai, gibai, anstai, allai, qiþai*, etc.

2) In Greek words and proper names, it represents both ε and αι. It is therefore written:

a) for ε in: *aibair* Ἐβέρ (*Eber*), *aizaikeia* Ἐζεκία (*Hezekiah*), *aizleim* Ἐσλί (*Esli*), *aikklesjo* ἐκκλησία (*church*), *aileiaizair* Ἐλιέζερ (*Eliezer*), *aileisabaiþ* Ἐλισάβετ (*Elizabeth*), *aimmeira* Ἐμμήρ (*Immer*), *baiailzaibul* Βεελζεβούλ (*Beelzebul*), *baineiamein* Βενιαμίν (*Benjamin*), *bauanairgais* βοανεργές (*Boanerges*), *spaikulatur* σπεκουλάτωρ (*executioner*), *gainnesaraiþ* Γεννησαρέτ (*Gennesaret*), *þaiaufeilus* Θεόφιλος (*Theophilus*), *ïaireiko* Ἱεριχώ (*Jericho*), *ïairaimias* Ἱερεμίας (*Jeremiah*), *kaidron* Κεδρών (*Kidron*), *hairaisis* αἵρεσις (*sect, heresy*);

b) for αι in: *zaibaidaius* Ζεβεδαῖος (*Zebedee*), *zakkaius* Ζακχαῖος (*Zacchaeus*), *kyreinaius* Κυρηναῖος (*Cyrenian*), *ïudaius* Ἰουδαῖος (*Jew*), *ymainaius* Ὑμέναιος (*Hymenaeus*), *haileisaius* Ἐλισσαῖος (*Elisha*), *haibraius* [Col. 0920] Ἑβραῖος (*Hebrew*), *þaddaius* Θαδδαῖος (*Thaddaeus*), *ïdumaia* Ἰδουμαία (*Idumaea*), *ïturaia* Ἰτουραία (*Ituraea*), *kaisar* Καῖσαρ (*Caesar*), *ïaissais* Ἰεσσαί (*Jesse*), *praitoriaun* πραιτώριον (*praetorium*).

> **Note 1.—** It is also used for separate αι in *ïudaivisks* ἰουδαϊκός (*Judaic*), *akaikus* ἀχαϊκός (*Achaean*), *gaius* Γάϊος (*Gaius*; see above § 17, 1), but not in *baiþsaïdan*, Luke X, 13, Βηθσαϊδά (*Bethsaida*), or *esaïas*, Matt. VIII, 17, Ἠσαΐας (*Isaiah*). In these, as the forms *beþsaeidan, esaeias* prove, *i* must be considered long.

> **Note 2.—** For εε, *ai* is simply written in *naiman* Νεεμάν (*Naaman*), although the Gothic ear was by no means averse to doubled *ai*, since *aiaik, gaiainna,* and *baiailzaibul* occur elsewhere.

> **Note 3.—** Greek ευ is transcribed in Gothic by *aiv* (before a vowel also by *aivv*): *aivaggeljo* εὐαγγέλιον (*gospel*), *aivlaugia* εὐλογία (*blessing*), *aivxaristia* εὐχαριστία (*thanksgiving*), *aivva* Εὐα (*Eve*), *laivveis* Λευίς (*Levi*).

> **Note 4.—** Exceptionally, *ai* is used: a) for Greek η in *gairgaisainus* Γεργεσηνός (*Gergesene*), *aillam* Ἠλάμ (*Elam*), *baiþsaïdan* Βηθσαϊδά (*Bethsaida*), *hailias*, Luke I, 17, Ἡλίας (*Elijah*), *hairodias*, Mark VI, 17, Ἡρωδίας (*Herodias*), *neikaudaimus*, *Skeir.* VIII, c, Νικόδημος (*Nicodemus*), *klaimaintus*, Phil. IV, 3, Κλημης (*Clement*); b) for Greek ι in *kaurainþaius* Κορίνθιος (*Corinthian*), and perhaps *aai* Ἁΐ (*Ai*); c) for Greek ει in *laudeikaia* Λαοδικεία (*Laodicea*); d) for Greek εὐ in *aiodia* εὐοδία (*Euodia*); e) for Greek α in *kaidmeiel* Καδμιήλ (*Kadmiel*), *baidsaiïïdan*, Luke IX, 10, Βηθσαϊδά (*Bethsaida*), *akaijus*, I Cor. XVI, 15, Ἀχαιός (*Achaean*), *akaija*, II Cor. I, 1, Ἀχαία (*Achaia*), where the equally usual forms *akajus, akaja* prove that the *ai* is separate.

3) *Ai* seems to have changed into *e* in *tehund* from *taihun*, also written consistently *taihund*, Luke XVI, 6, 7. For the same relation is present here as where *ai* is written for Greek η; moreover, this interchange can be explained by similarity of sound. The same similarity explains why the scribe of Codex A erroneously wrote *þizai*, II Cor. VIII, 18, for *þizei*; this will be admitted all the more readily because of the greater affinity between *ai* and *e*, and because *þizei* and *þize* in fact often alternate.

4) That *ai* is both long and short could already be inferred from its serving to transcribe both Greek ε and long αι.
