But in Gothic words it is much harder to determine where it is long and where short, because even in endings *ai* corresponds sometimes to a short, sometimes to a long vowel. Thus the feminine singular dative *gibai, anstai* corresponds on the one hand to the plurals *gibom, anstim*, and on the other to the masculine *fiska, balga*; or the preterite *habaida* runs parallel on the one hand with *sokida*, on the other with *spilloda*. Likewise, although in the ablaut series *steigan, staig* corresponds to *driusan, draus*, it remains uncertain whether *ai* and *au* should be long by the pattern of the present, or short by the pattern of the plurals *stigum, drusum*. It is still more difficult to determine the quantity of this diphthong in the root syllable, since comparison with related languages is of less service, because a firm law can be established only from a great many similar cases; and what is conjectured of one might be conjectured of all. This, however, is certain: *ai* is short where it is derived by breaking from *i* (§ 32, 5).

5) In any event, *ai* has the same sound as German ä, or as open *e* in *Berg, Feld, Recht* (French [Col. 0921] *e ouvert* in *excès, procès*). That this was the pronunciation of *ai*, at least in certain cases, was asserted already by the ancient grammarians in the Vienna manuscript (see *Wiener Jahrbücher*, XLIII, 11), and has always generally been observed; for in what other way could the sound of Greek ε have been represented? But the further question is whether, besides this pronunciation, there was not another, closer to German *ai*, so that to distinguish these two pronunciations they marked one by *aí*, the other by *ái*. The authority of the following arguments moves us to admit this distinction:

a) *Aí* arises from *i* by breaking and is short, whereas *ái* is a diphthong and is long;

b) *Aí* and *ái* correspond to different vowels in the transcription of foreign words; therefore they themselves must differ from one another;

c) *Ai* is used for both Greek ε and αι; it is therefore pronounced *aí* in the former case, *ái* in the latter;

d) In the comparative *maiza* (from *mah* and *iza*) it is still clear how *ai* arose from *a* and *i*;

e) *Ai* sometimes changes into *aj*; therefore both vowels must have been heard in pronunciation.

But, to speak truly, these arguments are not unassailable, nor is that distinction in any way demonstrated by the monuments of the Gothic language; it serves more to confuse than to elucidate the doctrine of Gothic sounds, which is in itself simple and regular. It is first necessary, therefore, to resort to some composition or conjunction in order to explain the varying pronunciation of *ai*, since it could with equal right have been pronounced *e, e* and *ai, ai*. Moreover, in the Vienna manuscript (see *Wiener Jahrbücher*, XLIII, 11), the pronunciation of the word *libaida* is established by citing *libeda*, with this explicit addition: “the diphthong *ai* for long *e*.” As to the analogy of neighbouring languages, it cannot be introduced here, since Gothic is the oldest known of all languages of the Germanic stock; consequently every conjecture based on the later language, namely Old German, which is corrupted in many ways and whose sound-system is neither consistent nor determinate, would be of only moderate assistance.

Now, if *ai* corresponds in turn to Greek ε and αι, you should not conclude from this that the Gothic diphthong had a double sound; rather, you may legitimately assert only that the ancient Greeks—at least those contemporary with Ulfilas—pronounced αι, like modern Greeks, as ε. This fact, generally accepted by almost all modern philologists, is further confirmed by the circumstance that Γραικός, *Graecus* (“Greek”), is transcribed in Gothic as *kreks*. It is no less certain that *maiza* derives from the root *MAH* and the comparative ending *iza* than that *ai* in a few cases changes into *aj*; but from this circumstance arises an etymological, not a phonetic, value. Indeed, to illustrate our point by a related example: just as the fact that *tauï*, despite the preterite *tavida*, forms the genitive *tojis*, reveals the etymon *TIVAN, TAU* (root *TAV*), but not its sound—except that *au* is akin to *o*—so *maiza* could be composed from *ma-iza* without the two elements having necessarily to be separated in pronunciation. The same is true in Sanskrit, in which *a* and *i* are, by a constant rule, merged into *e*.

As for *ai* changing into *aj*, it must also be noted that this occurs only in *aiv, ajukduþ, vai, vaja* (not, however, in *bai, bajoþs* from *BA*). The Gothic language as transmitted to us can almost in no way explain these formations; and, like *maiza*, they must undoubtedly be assigned to those earlier times of the language when etymological consciousness had not yet become dulled. If, then, no arguments establish that *ai* must be divided into two different sounds, the question is how the Goth, whose language presents so regular and simple a sound-system, could have distinguished with such certainty and precision sounds such as *i, ei, e*, which pass remarkably one into another, that in almost all cases, despite the fluctuation in spelling in certain manuscripts, it is easy to infer the correct form with certainty. How could a Goth have denoted by one and the same sign sounds exhibiting so great a difference as *e* and *aí*, *o* and *au*? But if he had no distinction between *aí* and *ái*, if he was entirely unfamiliar with every accentual differentiation, and if no necessity otherwise requires such a divergence, anyone attempting to introduce it would assuredly distort the Gothic language.

Moreover, *ai* and *au* are in the same condition. Since we shall prove still more confidently that *au* was always pronounced like open *o*, and that every distinction between *aú* and *áu* must be rejected, this will furnish a further argument against the distinction between *aí* and *ái*. The same conclusion follows from false consequences: for *aí* (*aú*) ought regularly to be used before *r* and *h* (and *w*), yet very many words have *ái* (*áu*) before those consonants, while others employ different accents in different forms. This fluctuation is especially apparent in such cases as *gatáih* and *gataíhum, áihta* and *aíhtron, sái* and *saíwan, dráusna* and *draúhsna*.

## AU

### § 29

1) **Au**, as a simple sound, occurs as frequently as *ai*; it can occupy any position in a word and combine with any consonants:

a) At the beginning: *audags, augo, auhuma, auhsa, auþs, aukan, aurali, aurtja, auso, aufto*;

b) In the middle: *bauan, blauþjan, bnauan, gaunon, dauþus, drausjan, haubiþ, hlauts, dishnaupnan, þaurnus, þlauhs, þraut, kaurn, kraust, laun, maurgins, nauþs, rauds, sauhts, skaudaraip, afslauþjan, spaurds, staua, gataura, trausti, vaurd, gaufaurs, flautan, frauja, waurbun; trauan, trauaida, sauïl, galaubeins, usbaugjan, sauds, nauh, dauhts, bauþs, galauk, sauls, gaumjan, dauns, taujan, raupjan, faura, þaurbun, saurga, baurd, vaurhta, faurhts, vaurþum, maurþr, staurknan, vaurms, haurn, gabaurjoþus, þaurp, staurran, þaursus, raurstv, vaurts, þaurfta, raus, lausjan*;

c) At the end: *dau, þau, jau, snau, ahtau, sunau*, etc.

> **Note 1.—** Cases in which *a* and *u* belong to separate syllables are not to be included here, such as *gau*, Matt. IX, 28; Mark VIII, 22; *sau*, John IX, 2, 19; *svau*, 18, 22; *wauh*, I Cor. IV, 7; *gaunledjan*.

2) In transcribed Greek words it is regularly written for ο; for example: *bauaus* Βοὸζ (*Boaz*), *barþaulaumaius* Βαρθολομαῖος (*Bartholomew*), *diakaunus* διάκονος (*deacon*), *eikaunio* Ἰκόνιον (*Iconium*), *zauraubabil* Ζοροβάβελ (*Zerubbabel*), *ïaurdanus* Ἰόρδανος (*Jordan*), *Kaurazein* Χοραζίν (*Chorazin*), *nicaudemus* Νικόδημος (*Nicodemus*), *pauntius* Πόντιος (*Pontius*), *praufetus* προφήτης (*prophet*), *saudauma* Σόδομα (*Sodom*), *saulaumon* Σολομῶν (*Solomon*), *aunisimus* Ὀνήσιμος (*Onesimus*), *apaustaulus* ἀπόστολος (*apostle*), *bairauja* Βέροϊα (*Beroea*).

> **Note 2.—** Exceptionally it is written: a) for Greek ου: *saillaum* Σελλούμ (*Shallum*), *maisaullam* Μεσουλάμ (*Meshullam*), *rabbaunei* ῥαββουνί (*Rabbouni*), *banauï* Βανουί (*Bannui*), *nabau* (? genitive *nabavis*) Ναβού (*Nabu*), *assaum* Ἀσούμ (*Assum*); b) for Greek ω: *praitauria*, John XVIII, 33; XIX, 9, πραιτώριον (*praetorium*), *dauriþaius* Δωρόθεος (*Dorotheus*), *trakauneitidus* Τραχωνῖτις (*Trachonitis*), *adauneikam* Ἀδωνικάμ (*Adonikam*); compare § 26, 2 b; c) for Greek υ: *saur* Σύρος (*Syrian*), *paurpaura*, Luke XVI, 19, πορφύρα (*purple*); d) for Greek α: *kaurbanaun* κορβανᾶν (*corban*).

3) *Au* frequently alternates with *u*, not only in proper names but especially in the endings of nouns in *-us*: for example, *fairwaus*, Gal. VI, 14, for *fairwus*; *sunaus*, Luke IV, 3, for *sunus*; *barteimaiaus*, Mark X, 46, for *barteimaius*; *dauþau*, John VIII, 52; I Cor. XI, 26; II Tim. I, 10, for *dauþu*; compare Mark VII, 32; I Tim. I, 16. Conversely, *sunus*, Eph. IV, 13; Gal. II, 20, occurs for *sunaus*; *apaustaulus*, II Cor. XII, 12, in this passage, for *apaustaulaus*; *xristu*, Gal. V, 6; Eph. V, 24, for *xristau*; *teimauþaiu*, I Thess. III, 6, for *teimauþaiau*; compare Luke I, 54. In the vocative of every declension, *u* and *au* are used so indiscriminately that it is difficult to determine which vowel is regular; compare Luke XVIII, 38. Failing to recognize this interchange of *au* and *u*, Castiglione has here imagined just as many scribal errors—for example, at Phil. III, 8, 19; compare III, 5; I Thess. III, 6; I Tim. I, 16.

> **Note 3.—** On *au* changed into *o*, see § 26, 4.

4) With respect to quantity, *au* exhibits the closest analogy with *ai*: like it, it is short and long, although in some cases this quantity cannot be determined with certainty. But where it arises from *u* by breaking (§ 32, 5), it must always be considered short.

5) In all cases *au* has the same sound as open *o* in the German words *Korn, Holz, doch*.

For *au*, too, a double pronunciation has been imagined, corresponding partly to *o*, partly to *au*; and by using two marks, *aú* was assigned to the former and *áu* to the latter; compare *aí* and *ái* (§ 28, 5). But against this opinion it must be said that a different pronunciation cannot be inferred from different quantity, nor can any conjecture whatever in favour of the most ancient and likewise purest Gothic language be drawn from dialects far later and in part already extinct. Nor would this distinction of *au* be established from Gothic itself nearly so well as the distinction of *ai*: for that diphthong corresponds in transcribed foreign words both to Greek ε and to Greek αι, whereas this one is regularly used only for Greek ο and never corresponds either to Greek αυ or Latin *au*. These diphthongs are always transcribed in Gothic by *av*: [Col. 0924] for example, *ragav* Ῥαγαῦ (*Ragau*), *esav* Ἠσαῦ (*Esau*), *pavlus* Παῦλος (*Paul*), *daveid* Δαυίδ (*David*), *kavtsjo*—not *kautsjo*, Grimm III, 559—*cautio* (“caution”). But in place of *avgustus* Αὔγουστος (*Augustus*), where the concurrence of *v* and *g* might have offended the Gothic ear, Luke II, 1 has not *augustus* but *agustus*.

Indeed, even in Gothic words *au* alternates with *o* according to fixed rules (§ 26, 4); and this latter vowel, not *au*, can explain the frequent interchange of *au* with *u*, whose phonetic affinity with *o* we indicated above (§ 24, 4). But it is objected that *áu* also changes into *av*, for example *taujan, tavida; MAUJA, mavi*. This objection is merely specious, as is clear from the fact that *tojis* corresponds to *taujan*, and *tauï* to *tavida*; thus here too we are compelled to distinguish etymology from sound, and to recognize in Gothic the same relation as in Sanskrit, where *a* and *u* likewise merge into *ô*, which is again resolved into *av*.

## EI

### § 30

1) **Ei** is of the same nature as *ai* and *au*, though it occurs at the beginning only very rarely:

a) At the beginning: only in *ei, eis, eisarn*;
b) Medially: beidan, bleiþs, usgeisnan, greipan, deigan, dreiban, qeins, heito, hleibjan, hneivan, þeihan, þreihan, keinan, galeiþan, meina, neiþ, peikabagms, reiks, seiþu, skeinan, sleiþa, smeitan, sneiþan, speivan, steigan, svein, gateihan, tveihnai, veihs, andavleizns, ïnfeinan, freidjan, weits; sveiban, gageigan, hleiduma, veihnan, þeihs, leihts, þreihsl, leiþus, hleiþra, leik, weila, skeima, lein, undarleija, veipan, reiran, skeirs, veis, leitils, fairveitl, heivafrauja, tveifls, leiwan;

c) At the end: nei, þei, sei, þatei, aiþei, gabei, managei, etc.; and the imperatives sokei, lagei, etc.

2) It is used indiscriminately for Greek ει and ι, whether the latter bears an accent or not, and whether it is short or long.

a) For ει: ïaeirus Ἰάειρος, ïoreim Ἰωρείμ, aileia keim Ἐλιακείμ, Samareites Σαμαρείτης, helei Ἡλεί;

b) for accented ι: addeín Ἀδδί, aizleim Ἐσλί, mailkein Μελχί, saimaiein Σεμεί, rabbei ῥαββί, kumei κουμί, helei Ἡλί, daveid Δαυίδ, baineiamein Βενιαμίν, aizaikeia Ἐζεκία, ananeias Ἀνανίας, barakeias Βαραχίας, heleias Ἡλίας, seimon Σίμων, aivneika Εὐνίκη, þaissalauneika Θεσσαλονίκη, teitus Τίτος, areistarkus Ἀρίσταρχος, peilatus Πίλατος;

c) for unaccented ι: aipafraudeitus Ἐπαφρόδιτος, eikaunio Ἰκόνιον, adauneikam Ἀδονικάμ, abeileni Ἀβιληνή, aileiaizair Ἐλιέζερ, aileisabaiþ Ἐλισάβετ, ameinadab Ἀμιναδάβ, areimaþaia Ἀριμαθαία, kaeinan Καϊνάν, galeilaia Γαλιλαία, taleiþa Ταλιθά, teimaius Τιμαῖος, teimauþaius Τιμόθεος, þaiaufeilus Θεόφιλος, iaireiko (eiaireiko, Ezra II.34) Ἱεριχώ, tykeikus Τυχικός, teibairius Τιβέριος.

> **Note 1.** It is sometimes also used for η (whose pronunciation, already in Ulfilas’ age, was approaching ῖ very closely): aimmeira Ἐμμήρ, kyreinaius Κυρηναῖος, [Col. 0925] aþeineis Ἀθῆναι, nazoreinus Ναζωρηνός, obeid Ὠβήδ, eiram Ἠράμ, airmogaineis Ἑρμογένης, auneiseifaurus Ὀνησίφορος, paraskaivein, Matthew XXVII.62, παρασκευήν (“preparation”); drakmein, Luke XV.9, δραχμήν (“drachma”), see at this passage. Exceptionally, it stands for ε: makeibis Μαγεβίς.

3) *Ei* is frequently interchanged with *e*, so that not only does *e* stand for *ei* (§ 23.6), but conversely *ei* is also used for *e*: leitan, Matthew IX.6; Mark XV.9 and often; greitan, Mark XIV.72; Luke VII.38 and often; qeins, Luke I.5; II.5; faheiþs, Luke VIII.13; manaseiþs, Luke IX.13 and often; speidiza, Matthew XXVII.64; bireiks, 1 Corinthians XV.30; leivjan, John VI.64; teikan, Colossians II.21; amasaisleip, Luke VIII.23; usmeitum, 2 Corinthians I.12, at this passage; veiseis, John XI.32; veisun, Nehemiah V.15; VI.17; veisjau, Nehemiah V.14; dalei, Luke III.5; fareisaiei, V.33; ïudaiei, John XI.45; XII.11; gardei, Luke X.5; þizeiei, Philippians III.19; ïzei, John VII.50; 2 Corinthians IX.2, 14; þizei, Mark XIV.69; Luke XIV.15; John VII.50; 2 Corinthians IV.18; Galatians II.10; 2 Timothy II.14; þizeiei, Galatians III.19; hidrei, Luke IX.41; þandei, Luke I.34 and often; svarei, 2 Corinthians VI.1; iohannein, Luke III.15; visseis, Luke XIX.22.

> **Note 2.** *Ei* is sometimes also used for *i*: kunnei, John XVII.23; dreibeina, Mark IX.18; greteiþ, Romans IX.27; flauteiþ, 1 Corinthians XIII.4; siukeiþ, 2 Corinthians XIII.3; baireiþ, Galatians VI.5.

4) Although *ei* sometimes stands where, in accordance with the Greek, a short *i* would be expected, it nevertheless always remains long. For in genuine Gothic words it appears either as the long form of *i* or as formed from *ii*: thus in the plural *gasteis* from GASTI, as *vigos* from VIGA; and in the subjunctive *vandeiþ* for *vandi-iþ*. Etymologically, *ei* is of the same status as *ji*: for example, *lagjiþ* and *vandeiþ*, *harjis* and *hairdeis*, *gavairþjis* and *gavairþeis*; see on Luke I.23. Yet it would wrongly be asserted that in these cases *ei* arose from *ji*.

The difference between the two is readily apparent from the quantity of the preceding syllable. When this radical syllable is short [Col. 0926], *ji* is introduced for strengthening, as in *harjis, lagjiþ*. When the syllable is long, however—either because it needs no such strengthening, or because it precedes a derivative syllable incompatible with it—*ei* is used, as in *haïrdeis, vandeiþ, sokeiþ, mikileiþ, laisareis*.

5) *Ei* is pronounced as *e* and *i*, whose pronunciation was sufficiently distinct that they are not confused, but not sufficiently so that the ear separates them. This is demonstrated not only by the fact that etymologically *ei* represents *i* or *ii*, but also because it is frequently interchanged with *e* and *i*, and is regularly used for Greek ι.

## IU

§ 31. 1) *Iu*, the last of the Gothic vowels, has a more restricted use than the others. It occurs only in radical syllables, and is found neither in derivative syllables (except for the sole and consequently doubtful *uhtiug*, 1 Corinthians XVI.12) nor in the transcription of foreign words. Its use will be apparent from the following examples:

a) Initially: ïumjo, ïup, ïusiza, ïusila;

b) Medially: biudan, giutan, dius, driusan, gaqiujan, hiufan, hliuþ, dishniupan, þiuþ, þliuhan, kiusan, kriustan, liubs, niutan, jiuka, gariuds, siujan, afskiuban, sliupan, sniumjan, stiurjan, tiuhan, frius; þîubs, driugan, þiuda, diuza, liuhaþ, hiuhma, liuhtjan, niuhsjan, liuþon, siuks, jiuleis, hliuma, niun, niujis, diups, riurs, fraliusan, liuta;

c) Finally: triu, kniu, þiu.

> **Note.** In *niu* (from *ni-u*), *sium* (for *sijum*), and *siuþ* (for *sijuþ*), *iu* is not a diphthong but consists of two syllables. The same applies in foreign words, such as ïudas Ἰούδας and filippisius Φιλιππήσιος; accordingly, here too it is interchanged with *ju*: judas, John XII.4.

2) Etymologically, *iu* is the long form of *u*, just as *ei* is the long form of *i*. This is especially clear from comparing the ablaut classes of the two sounds. It is likewise evident in the plural nouns of masculine and feminine gender whose radical form ends in *u*, since here analogy with other nouns requires *i* to be lengthened, as the following comparison shows:

[Col. 0925] 3) *Iu* seems to have been a sound peculiar to Gothic. Its pronunciation is all the more difficult to conjecture because it does not occur in the transcription of foreign words. At least it is certain that this vowel did not have the same sound as German *ü* or French *u*, since it never serves to transcribe Greek υ. It was probably something blended from the two sounds *i* and *u*. Hence, in Gothic proper names occurring in Latin authors, it is transcribed *eo*, for example Theodoricus (*þiudareiks*). This also explains why it changes, on the one hand, into *iv*, and on the other into *ju*.

Its change into *iv* occurs in *kniu*, genitive *knivis*; *triu*, genitive *trivis*; [Col. 0926] *þius*, genitive *þivis*; *qius*, plural *qivai*. Its change into *ju* occurs in the plurals *sunjus, handjus*, etc., since here, as we said above in 2), analogy with other declensions requires the *u* of the radical form to be lengthened. But in the genitive *sunive*, *i* is again assumed; hence *u* changes into *v*.

§ 32. Now that the series of Gothic vowels has been completed, it remains for us briefly to describe certain modifications to which either all vowels generally, or at least most of them, are subject. These modifications are: lengthening, shortening, ablaut, weakening, breaking, apocope, syncope, hiatus, and contraction.

1) **Lengthening** is the transition of a short vowel into its corresponding [Col. 0927] long vowel: *a* into *o* (§ 22.7), *i* into *ei* (§ 23.6), and *u* into *iu* (§ 31.2).

2) **Shortening** of a vowel is caused by a following consonant. The liquids especially, as well as *s, z, h,* and *f*, regularly require the preceding vowel to be shortened when one or more consonants follow in the same syllable: for example, balgs, allai, malmo, valdan, halbs, hals, salt, milds, filleins, hilms, hilpan, dulgs, fulls, mulda, vamba, mammo, svimmam, trimpan, dumbs, andanumts, laggs, band, dragk, fanþ, manna, ansts, briggan, drigkan, sigqan, vinds, vinnan, gaminþi, juggs, bistugqs, mundrei, kunnan, kunþs, vargs, arms, þarbs, vardja, varþ, bairgan, svairban, vairdus, vairþs, fairra, fairzna, baurgs, þaurfts, vaurd, vaurts, maurþr, wass, asts, ïst, fisks, brusts, razn, andavizn, anabuzns, mahts, raihts, sauhts, hafts, gifts, skufts.

> **Note 1.** A vowel is not shortened when the consonant following a liquid belongs, not to the same radical syllable, but to the ending: for example, *smals, fuls, sums, vans, muns, gaurs, valjan, gramjan, sunja, harjis, gabaurjaba, gataurnan*.

> **Note 2.** In very many cases the letters *l, m, n, r,* and *s* seem, in and of themselves, to induce shortening. Thus they may be doubled in writing without necessity, or used singly where etymology would demand doubling (§ 55, notes 1–2).

3) **Ablaut** [Note: Since, so far as I can see, no fully equivalent Latin term corresponds to the German word *Ablaut*, and since I wished to avoid a periphrasis, which is always inconvenient for translation, I have preferred to coin a new term. Accordingly, throughout the course of this work, reader, understand *absonantia* to mean the transition of a vowel or sound into another. Translator.] consists in the vowel of the radical syllable changing into another according to fixed rules, either by derivation or by word formation. There are certain ablaut series containing two, three, or even four different vowels. They will occur especially, and be treated more fully, in connection with the formation of strong conjugation (§ 117, f, g) and of words (§§ 139, 143). Here it is enough to extract from these classes the principal ones in respect of sound, giving the following classes:

In the first, second, and third classes the pure radical vowel *a* predominates; in the fourth, *i*; in the fifth, *u*; while in the sixth, the most imperfect of all, *a* appears again, in which the latent long radical *o* seems to be shortened by ablaut. This raises the question whether this class does not display a secondary formation of roots from the second [Col. 0928] and third classes: for example, *ganoh* is derived from *nahan*, itself belonging to a lost verb of the first class (§ 26.4); or *vrohjan* should be referred to some *vrakan, vrok*, derived from *vrikan, vrak*. The fact that many verbs belonging to this class take *j* in the present—that is, are weakly conjugated—also supports this relationship.

A further, though rarer, ablaut class is closely related to the sixth:

**Class 7a:** *ai, e — o — o — ai, e*, occurring only in reduplicated verbs (§ 126). In this class *e* appears to be primitive in the present. Although it does not remain before other vowels (§ 25.1.c), in verbs whose radical syllable ends in a vowel it changes into *ai*, which is akin to it in sound, in precisely the same manner as, in similar cases (§ 26.3), *au* represents *o*.

> **Note 1.** That the first three classes are very closely related is evident at first sight. In them we have seen the triad of Gothic vowels unfold; hence, because of the predominating *a*, we have not without reason assigned them first place as primitive classes. In the fourth and fifth classes, which also have the closest affinity with one another, *a* is wholly absent; *i* appears only in the former and *u* only in the latter, their ablaut being effected either by lengthening (*ei, iu*) or by breaking (*ai, au*). Since lengthening and breaking presuppose a more extensive development of a simple system of sounds, we have consequently regarded these classes as later; and we have assigned the sixth the last place, immediately after them, either because it is derived from the first or because it is the most recent, or at least the most imperfect.

> **Note 2.** Although ablaut appears especially in the formation of strong conjugation, there are nevertheless some cases in which it plainly cannot be referred to that conjugation: such as *dogs* from *dag*, *hobains* from *haban*, and *ganohs* from *nahan*. All these are formed on the analogy of the sixth class, although a verb *dagan, dog* or *haban, hob* seems both strange and inadmissible (for the conjectured NAHAN, NOH, see § 26.4). Another example of irregular ablaut is supplied by *briggan, brahta*. Suggesting the first class, it points to a perhaps conjectural primitive *brigan, brag*, from which, by introduction of a nasal—as in *standan, stoþ* or *þagkjan, þahta*—a new present arose; and, by a broader formation of the preterite, also occurring in certain other verbs (compare *mag, mahta; og, ohta*, etc.), a new preterite with weak inflection arose.

4) The effect which ablaut has upon the vowel of the radical syllable, weakening also has upon the vowel of the formative syllable. Only the vowel *a* is subject to this modification, changing under its influence into *i* or *u*. Weakening depends both upon the nature of the consonant [Col. 0929] preceding or following the vowel and upon the addition of a longer formative syllable; it is also used in forming both declensional and conjugational forms. Its use can be regulated by the following rules:

a) *A* is weakened into *i*:

aa) Before dentals and sibilants: for example, in the declension of VIGA, genitive *vigis* (§ 64.4); in the conjugation *lagja, lagjis, lagjiþ, lagjam, lagjiþ, lagjand*, participle *lagiþs* (§ 113);

bb) when a formative syllable is followed by another containing *a*. Thus the dative *hanin* from the root HANAN is to be explained (§ 88.4), although it has changed its *a*, the characteristic of the dative; for it is held to have passed through the forms *hanana, hanina* in arriving at *hanin*. The same explanation perhaps applies to *i* before nominal endings *þa, lo*, etc.: for example, *daubiþa* from DAUBA, *kauriþa* from KAURA, *svikniþa* from SVIKNA, *barnilo* from BARNA. In these forms *i* seems to incline all the more toward dentals because, though one says *magula* from MAGU, one does not say *agluþa, manvuþa* from AGLU, MANVU, but *agliþa, manviþa*.

b) Final *a* is weakened into *u* when, in conjugation, the *a* of the radical syllable changes into *u*: thus in the preterite plural *bundun, bunduþ, bundun*, alongside *bindam, bindiþ, bindand*. Since this kind of weakening occurs even in verbs which do not have *u* as their vowel of alternation in the preterite plural, it may rightly be concluded that this form is primitive and very ancient. Peculiar is the weakening in *ainummehun* for *ainammahun*, where it seems to have been attracted by the length of the following syllable.

5) **Breaking** is the change of *i* and *u* into *ai* and *au*. It follows partly from the rules of ablaut (see above, 3), and partly from the regressive influence of the preceding consonants *r, h,* and *w*; and it occurs in every case in which *i* and *u* are in fact long. Breaking therefore has a real effect upon ablaut itself, since wherever *i* or *u* ought to occur under its rules, *ai* or *au* is used. Hence the following new ablaut classes:

6) **Apocope** is the removal of a vowel from the end of a word. Such are, in declension, the datives *hanin, vatin* for *hanana, vatina*; compounds with enclitic *uh*, such as *þammuh, anþaranuh*, for *þamma-uh, anþarana-uh*; and also *þat-ïst, kar-ïst, nist, nibai*, for *þata ïst, kara ïst, ni ïst, ni ïbai*.

7) **Syncope** is the removal of a vowel situated between two consonants. This occurs in declension in *vatna, namna*, together with *hairtona* (§ 90, note), and in *ainnohun* for *ainanahun* (§ 111, β); in conjugation, however, in the preterite *bruhta* for *brukida*, *þahta* for *þagkida*, etc. (§ 128, note 4).

8) **Hiatus** is the concurrence of two vowels belonging to different syllables, as in *gaarman, wauh, laudeikaia, fiaþva, ïesus, saian, bauan*, etc. We have already shown above (§§ 25.1.c; 26.3) that certain hiatuses cannot occur. Others the Goth moderates either by introducing *j* after *i*, whence *fijaþva* for *fiaþva*, *sijum* for *sium*, etc.; or by changing *i* and *u* into their corresponding semivowels, whence *sunjus* for *sunius*, *sunive* for *suniue*, *mavi* for *maui*, etc.; or finally by inserting *h* (§ 22, note 1).

9) **Contraction** is the reduction of two concurrent vowels to one, as in *sokeiþ* for *sokiiþ*, or in *fret* (if this reading is genuine) for *fraat*.

## II. CONCERNING THE CONSONANTS

[Col. 0929]

[Col. 0929] § 33. Consonants are divided into semivowels (*j, v*), liquids (*l, m, n, r*), mutes (*g, h, k, x, q, w, b, f, p, d, þ, t*), and sibilants (*s, z*).

Semivowels occupy an intermediate position between vowels and consonants, since *j* corresponds to *i*, and *v* to *u*, and they are often interchanged with them. Closest to the semivowels are the liquids, themselves possessing something vocalic, since they have resonance in themselves and one of them, *r*, has retained a trace of the pure nature of vowels. The mutes are again divided into three classes: gutturals (*g, h, k, x, q, w*), labials (*b, f, p*), and linguals (*d, þ, t*); and they are either medial (*b, d, g*), aspirated (*f, þ, h*), or finally tenuis (*p, t, k*). The remaining gutturals occur partly only in foreign words (*x*) and are partly distinctive sounds (*q, w*), in the production of which several speech-organs seem to cooperate. Finally, the sibilants belong to the class of linguals, into which they may change according to fixed laws of sound. Thus the entire system of Gothic consonants may be arranged as follows:

1. Semivowels: *j, v*  
2. Liquids: *l, m, n, r*  
4. Sibilants: *s, z*.

## 1. CONCERNING THE SEMIVOWELS

### J

§ 34. 1) *J* occurs only at the beginning of syllables and words, never at the end or before a consonant: for example, jabai, jains, jau, jer, jiuka, juggs, vajamereins, bajoþs, saijiþ, taujan, fijands, undarleija (?), niujis, stojan, galaubjan, lagjan, daddjan, [Col. 0931] hazjan, saggqjan, vaihjo, fraþjan, vrakja, anaviljei, qemjau (Matthew V.17; X.34), sunjus, namnjan, afwapjan, warjis, laisjan, laistjan, aurtja, hnaivjan, ufjo, newjan.

> **Note.** It is found at the end of a syllable in only one word, namely *freijhals*, 2 Corinthians III.17; Galatians II.4, where the reading *freihals* is undoubtedly preferable.

2) *J* is used for Greek ι (Latin *i*), whether enclosed between two vowels, following a consonant, or placed initially: for example, kajafa Καϊάφας, akaja Ἀχαία, abjaþar Ἀβιάθαρ, ïskarjotes, John XIV.22, Ἰσκαριώτης, marja Μαρία, antiokja Ἀντιοχεία, laiktjo “reading,” kavtsjo “caution,” jaeirus Ἰάειρος, janna Ἰαννά, jannis Ἰαννῆς, jaurdanus Ἰόρδανος, judas, John XII.4, Ἰούδας, justus Ιοῦστος, jota ἰῶτο.

> **Note 1.** In these cases it is frequently interchanged with *i*, which is more regular in ïskariotes, ïaeirus, ïaurdanus, ïudas.

3) *J* arises from *i* when a vowel follows in the formative syllable: thus *laisarjos* for *laisarios*, *sunjus* for *sunius*, *þiujos* for *þivios* (from *þivi*, root ÞIUJA, in which *v*, after introduction of *j*, is again resolved into *u*), *maujos* for *mavios* (from *mavi*, root MAUJA), *tojis* from *taui*, *lagjiþ* for *lagiiþ*, *harjis* for *hariis*.

> **Note 2.** For the rule according to which *ii* changes sometimes into *ji*, sometimes into *ei* (*sokeiþ* for *sokiiþ*, *hairdeis* for *hairdiis*), see § 20.4.

> **Note 3.** But *i* cannot change into *j* when it belongs to the root of the word, as in *siai, sium, friaþva, fiands, þius, saian, vaian*; or in foreign words, such as *asia, arabia, kileikia, galatia, dalmatia, aivlaugia, aifaisius, filippisius*. The exceptions are *ajukduþ* from *aivs* and *vaja* from *vai*.

4) To avoid hiatus, *j* is inserted where another vowel follows the semi-radical *i* (*ai*): as in *sijai, sijum, saijiþ*, Mark IV.14, *frijaþva, fijands*; see § 32.8, and compare Prolegomena, col. 479, note 5.

5) The Gothic *j* seems to have had the same sound as German *j*, but sharper than English *y*. With its pronunciation approaching *g*, it is distinguished from *iu*. Though otherwise quite similar, these differ in genuine Gothic words such that one may not write ïuggs, sunius for juggs, sunjus, or juþ, jumjo for ïup, ïumjo. This pronunciation of *j* was also what the writer intended to define in codex membranaceus Salisburgensis no. 140 (*Wiener Jahrbücher*, XLIII, 11), when he said: “where *genuit* is said, *j* is written; where *gabriel*, they write *g*”; compare above § 12, letter J.

### V

§ 35. 1) *V* occurs at the beginning, middle, and end of words; initially it can be prefixed to vowels and also to *l* and *r*:

a) Initially: valjan, vens, vindan, vulþus, vokrs, vlits, vrikan, etc.;

b) Medially: slavan, favai, mavi, gavi, havi, tavida, hnaivjan, aivs, snaivs, saivs, saivala, waiva, sitaiva, Mark X.37, skevjan, levjan, speivan, hneivan, heivafrauja, kniva, snivan, þivadv, þivi, sunive, lasivs, viduvo, etc.;

c) Finally: aiv, hlaiv, snaiv, saiv, lev, gaidv, þivadv, [Col. 0932] vaurstv; the preterites hnaiv, spaiv, valv; and the imperatives hneiv, speiv, vilv.

> **Note 1.** On *v* used as *y*, see above § 27.

2) It is used for Greek υ after a vowel: pavlus Παῦλος, esav Ἠσαῦ, daveid Δαυίδ; compare kavtsjo, Latin *cautio*; paraskaive παρασκευή, aivlaugia εὐλογία, aivneika Εὐνίκη, aivxaristia εὐχαριστία, εὐαγγέλιον (“good news, Gospel”).

> **Note 2.** In this case it is sometimes doubled: aivva Εὖα, laivveis Λευίς, laivveitus Λευίτης; compare Schneider, *Latin Forms* I, 367. Likewise, *Livvigild* inscribed on Gothic coins (see Aschbach, *Westg.* 357) may have been understood as *Leovigild* or *Livigild*. Sometimes it is omitted: aiodia εὐοδία, agustus Αὔγουστος. But *Akvila* seems to derive less from Greek Ἀκύλας than from Latin *aquila*. Elsewhere Latin *v* is transcribed in Gothic by *b* (§ 46.2).

3) *V* arises from *u* placed between two vowels: for example, *mavi* from MAUJA, *havi* from HAUJA, *stravida* from *straujan*, *tavida* from *taujan*, *triva* from *triu*, *kniva* from *kniu*, *þivi* from *þius*, *navis* from *naus*, *sunive* for *suniue*. But it changes back into *u* when the following vowel is absent, as in *snivan*, preterite *snau*.

> **Note 3.** In a similar way *fidur-* is formed from *fidvor*, *tuz-* from *tvis-*. In *spai-skuldrs* from *speivan, spaiv*, *v* has entirely disappeared.

> **Note 4.** Nevertheless, *u* placed between two vowels does not everywhere change into *v*: for example, tauï, stauïda, trauan, bauan, etc.

4) Gothic *v* seems to correspond to German *w* and English *v*. But it must have differed from Latin *v*, since Latin *v* is transcribed in Gothic by *b*, as we indicated above in note 2; conversely, Gothic *v* is expressed in Latin writings by *vv* (for example, in the names VVillienant, VViliarit), and on coins by *w* (Wittiza, Wittiges). Moreover, from the scribal error *vidvor* for *fidvor*, 2 Corinthians XII.2, one could scarcely infer an affinity between *v* and *f*.

## 2. CONCERNING THE LIQUIDS

### L

§ 36. 1) *L* occurs frequently at the beginning, middle, and end of words:

a) Initially: laggs, laisjan, laus, lev, leik, ligan, liuhaþ, lustus, lofa, etc.;

b) Medially: halja, hails, sauls, sels, weila, skilja, jiuleis, fula, holon, etc.;

c) Finally: skal, dail, mel, til, etc.

2) It constantly corresponds to Greek λ and has its pronunciation: for example, lysanius Λυσάνιος, abeileni Ἀβιληνή, baiailzaibul Βεελζεβούλ, gabriel Γαβριήλ. It is sometimes inserted redundantly, as in alabalstraun ἀλάβαστρον, nauel Νωέ.

### M

§ 37. 1) *M* occurs in every position in a word:

a) Initially: manags, maiz, maurgins, megs, meins, minz, mulda, mota, etc.;

b) Medially: namo, haims, gaumjan, andanems, skeima, himins, ïumja, rums, stoma, etc.;

c) Finally: qam, nam, manageim, nim, sum, qinom, etc.

[Col. 0933] 2) It is used for Greek μ, to which it corresponds entirely in pronunciation: for example, moses Μωσῆς, hymainaius Ὑμέναιος, naum Ναούμ. It is sometimes also redundantly placed at the end of words: for example, mariam Μαρία—unless the Goth read Μαριάμ in his codex; compare bailiam, 2 Corinthians VI.15, whereas the Greek has Βελίαλ, Βελίαρ, or Βελίαν.

### N

§ 38. 1) *N* can occupy the same positions as *m*, but occurs more frequently:

a) Initially: naqaþs, naiteins, nauh, newa, neiþ, niman, niun, nuta, nota, etc.;

b) Medially: vaninassus, sainjan, ussauneins, mena, keinan, ïna, runa, etc.;

c) Finally: man, gamain, laun, ven, sein, namin, siun, ainshun, fon, etc.

> **Note.** Before gutturals, *g* is substituted for *n*, in Greek fashion (see § 40.5).

2) *N* corresponds completely to Greek ν: for example, naggai Ναγγαί, ananeias Ἀνανίας, aharon Ἀαρών. It is also sometimes added redundantly at the end of a word, as in nerin Νηρί, mailkein Μελχί.

3) *N*, together with its substitute *g*, which before labials also becomes *m*, is sometimes inserted in order to produce a short radical syllable: thus in *standan*, preterite *stoþ*; *þagkjan*, preterite *þahta*; *þugkjan*, preterite *þuhta*; *briggan*, preterite *brahta*. Conversely, it is sometimes absent where the preceding vowel is either long by position or changes into its corresponding long form: as in *kustanteinus* “Constantine,” *seiteins* for *sinteins*, and *dobnan* for *dumbnan*.

### R

§ 39. 1) *R* also occurs frequently in every position in a word:

a) Initially: raþjo, raihts, rauds, redan, reisan, rimis, riurs, rums, rodjan, etc.;

b) Medially: faran, vairilo, dauro, sveran, reiro, hiri, riurei, skura, horinon, etc.;

c) Finally: bar, vair, daur, skeir, stiur, for, etc.

> **Note 1.** We have already said above (§ 32.5) that *r*, when placed before short *i* and *u*, causes them to be broken.

2) In foreign words it corresponds to Greek ρ, and seems to have had its pronunciation: for example, raibaikka Ῥεβέκκα, markus Μάρκος, zauraubabil Ζοροβάβελ, aileiaizair Ἐλιέζερ. In artarksairksus (Artaxerxes) it is inserted redundantly; in airmodam (Ἐλμωδάμ) it is incorrectly used for λ.

3) The vocalic nature of this letter (*r*), evident in other languages of the same stock and especially in Sanskrit, must not be overlooked in Gothic. Hence the declension of certain nouns—namely those expressing a relationship of kinship, such as *broþar, dauhtar*—corresponds exactly to that of other words. This is plainly apparent from the following comparison of the two declensions, with the proviso that, in order to avoid all ambiguity, we have thought it necessary to signify vocalic R by *r*, weakened R by *r*, and long R by *r*.

For recognizing the complete analogy of the two declensions, it must be considered:

a) That *a* in the nominative and accusative singular (*broþar*) is a euphonic vowel, introduced because vocalic R (corresponding to consonantal *r*) is absent;

b) That the plural declension shows that vocalic R was changed into *u* under stress; hence they always used *ru* for *r*, and *rju* for *r* (for *riu*, § 31.3). In the genitive singular, however, where a consonant likewise follows vocalic R, it indeed does not change into *u*, because in the declension of other words that case requires the vowel to be weakened; but the vowel at least disappears altogether.

> **Note 2.** To the vocalic nature of *r* must also be attributed the fact that this consonant permits most of the other consonants to precede it initially—namely *v, g, h, k, q, (x), b, f, p, d, þ, t*, and the double consonants *sk, sp,* and *st*—with only *j* and *w*, the linguals, and the sibilants excepted.

## 5. CONCERNING THE MUTES

### CONCERNING THE GUTTURALS: G

§ 40. 1) *G* can occur at the beginning, middle, and end of words, and initially before *l* and *r*:

a) Initially: gabeigs, gairnjan, gaurs, gebi, geigan, gilþa, gintan, guþ, gods, glitmunjan, gretan, etc.;

b) Medially: magan, laigon, augo, megs, steigan, ligan, liugan, bugjan, ogan, etc.;

c) Finally: mag, daig, bang, veg, steig, etc.

2) It regularly corresponds to Greek γ: for example, Gabriel Γαβριήλ, gaulgauþa Γολγοθᾶ, agar Ἄγαρ, magdalene Μαγδαληνή, asgad Ἀσγάδ, fygailus Φύγελλος, synagoge συναγωγή, falaig Φάλεγ (thus Ulfilas reads at Luke III.35, with several codices, Φάλεγ rather than Φάλεκ).

3) At the end of a syllable it frequently changes into *h*: thus *vaih* from *veigan*, *mahta* from *magan*, *bauhta* from *bugjan*, *brahta* from *briggan*, *aihta* from *aigan*, *gahts* from *gaggan*. It is also sometimes interchanged with *h*, as in *aigands* and *aihands*, 2 Corinthians VI.10; *aigum* and *aihum*, John XIX.7; *aih* and *aig*, 1 Corinthians VII.13; or it arises from *h*, as in *fulgins* from *filhan*. *G* also becomes *k* in *gadik* from *deigan*.

4) In pronunciation, Gothic *g* seems to have had the same sound as German *g*: that is, like lenis *k* at the beginning of a syllable, but at the end something guttural, very similar to German *ch*; compare § 34.5.

5) Before another guttural it assumes a nasal sound, corresponding to Greek γ: for example, aggelus ἄγγελος, naggai Ναγγαί; likewise in Gothic words *briggan, siggvan, þagkjan, ïgqis*, etc. Before *k* or *q* it is frequently doubled: as in *driggkan, þaggkjan, uggkis*, [Col. 0935] *þuggjan, siggqan, stiggqan, ïggqis*. This doubling appears erroneous in *geiggan*, 1 Corinthians IX.20, for *geigan*, since no guttural follows. Conversely, a single *g* sometimes stands for a double one: *fauragagja*, Luke VIII.3; XVI.1, for *fauragaggja*; *unmanarigvai*, 2 Timothy III.3, codex A, for *unmariggvai*; *hugridai*, 1 Corinthians IV.11, for *huggridai*; *qaagvein*, Skeireins I.c, for *gaaggvein*.

In derived words, however, this nasal *g* disappears, whether compensated or not (compare what was said of *n* in § 38): hence *juhiza* from *juggs*, *huhrus* from *hugrjan*, *gahts* from *gaggan*, *brahta* from *briggan*, *þahta* from *þagkjan*, *þuhta* from *þugkjan*.

> **Note.** In place of nasal *g*, *n* is sometimes erroneously written in Luke: for example, þankeiþ, Luke XIV.31; bringiþ, XV.22; þank, XVII.9; ïnqis, XIX.31. This must undoubtedly be attributed to Roman influence, during which our text of Luke may have been revised. Among the Romans, Accius likewise writes *aggelus* for *angelus*; see Varro in Priscian, p. 37.

### H

§ 41. 1) *H* also occurs in every position in a word, and may occur initially before *l, n,* and *r*:

a) Initially: haban, haitan, haubiþ, her, heito, himins, hiuhma, huljan, holon, hlaþan, hnaivjan, hnrains;

b) Medially: fahan, þlaihan, fauho, þeihan, liuhaþ, hoha;

c) Finally: frah, jah, gataih, þauh, nauh, hauh, tauh, tiuh, -uh, skoh.

> **Note 1.** We noted above (§ 32.5) that it does not occur before short *i* and *u* without causing them to be broken.

2) It corresponds to the Greek rough breathing, e.g. hyssopo “hyssop,” ὕσσωπος; hymainaius “Hymenaeus,” Ὑμέναιος; haibraius “Hebrew,” Ἑβραῖος; herodes “Herod,” Ἡρώδης, etc. It is also found redundantly: helias “Elijah,” Ἠλίας; haileisaius “Elisha,” Ἐλισσαῖος. On the other hand, it is more often omitted, as in airmogaineis “Hermogenes,” Ἑρμογένης; ymainaius “Hymenaeus,” Ὑμέναιος; ïairaimias “Jeremiah,” Ἱερεμίας; ïairusalem “Jerusalem,” Ἱερουσαλήμ; ïairaupaulis “Hierapolis,” Ἱεράπολις; ïaireiko “Jericho,” Ἱεριχώ; osanna “hosanna,” ὡσαννά; aai “Ai,” Ἁΐ. This omission is more easily explained because the Greeks did not write the breathing. It also occurs on coins in ERMENEGILD instead of HERMENEGILD; see Aschbach, *Westg.* 358.

“Note 2.—We have already indicated above (§ 26, 3) that h is inserted between two vowels in foreign words.

“Note 3.—On its origin from g and k, see §§ 40, 3 and 42, 3; and on its interchange with g, see § 40, 3.”

3) H, when placed before other consonants or at the end of a word, is sometimes lost; e.g. liuteiþ, Matt. V, 15, instead of liuhteiþ; hiuma, Luke VI, 17; VIII, 4, instead of hiuhma; drausnos, John VI, 12, instead of drauhsnos; usvaurts, 2 Cor. IX, 9, instead of usvaurhts; warjo, Mark XV, 6, instead of warjoh; warjano, *Skeir.* IV, 6, instead of warjanoh; wamme, Gal. V, 3, instead of wammeh; al, Mark XV, 38; 2 Thess. II, 4, instead of alh; þairvakands, Luke VI, 12, instead of þairhvakands; hauhairts, 2 Tim. III, 2, instead of hauhhairts. This omission is regular in vaurstv from vaurhts, and gatvo from gahts.

[Col. 0936] 4) In respect of pronunciation, it appears to have differed according as h occurs before a vowel, before a consonant, or at the end of a word. Before a vowel it may have corresponded to the Greek rough breathing—that is, to breath itself; before a consonant, however, it corresponds to Germanic *ch*, the guttural sound being clearly heard in initial hl, hn, hr and in final ht, hs. Finally, at the end of words it was perhaps less audible; h serves chiefly to sharpen the preceding vowel, and consequently is either readily assimilated to a following consonant (§ 56) or omitted (see above, 3).

## K

§ 42. 1) K may be initial, medial, or final; when initial it can be combined with l, n, and r.

a) At the beginning: kalds, kaupon, kelikn, keinan, kintus, kiusan, kustus, klismo, kniu, krusts;

b) In the middle: akran, laikan, aukan, tekan, peika, rikan, siukei, lukan, vokains;

c) At the end: gasak, mik, sik, þuk, gajuk, taitok, auk, siuk.

2) In proper names and foreign words it normally corresponds: a) to Latin c and Greek κ, with the latter agreeing in pronunciation; e.g. lukarn “lamp,” *lucerna*; karkara “prison,” *carcer*; kavtsjo “surety,” *cautio*; laiktjo “reading,” *lectio*; kaisar “Caesar,” Καῖσαρ; kefas “Cephas,” Κηφᾶς; kileikia “Cilicia,” Κιλικία; krispus “Crispus,” Κρίσπος; ïsak “Isaac,” Ἰσαάκ; ïskarjotes “Iscariot,” Ἰσκαριώτης; lucas “Luke,” Λουκᾶς. Sometimes it also corresponds b) to Greek γ: makeibis “Magebis,” Μαγεβίς; kreks “Greek,” γραϊκός, *Graecus*; markreitus “pearl,” μαργαρίτα. Finally, more often, c) to Greek χ: kaurazein “Chorazin,” χοραζίν; kafairi “Chephirah,” Χαφιρά; kusa “Chuza,” Χουζᾶ; ïaireiko “Jericho,” Ἱεριχώ; antiaukia “Antioch,” Ἀντιοχεία; akaja “Achaia,” Ἀχαΐα; trakauneitidus “Trachonitis,” Τραχωνῖτις; tykeikus “Tychicus,” Τυχικός; zakarias “Zechariah,” Ζαχαρίας; saikaineias “Shecaniah,” Σεχενίας; taitrarkes “tetrarch,” τετράρχης; areistarkus “Aristarchus,” Ἀρίσταρχος; arkaggilus “archangel,” ἀρχάγγελος; arkippus “Archippus,” Ἄρχιππος; paska “Passover,” πάσχα; mailkein “Melchi,” Μελχί; malkus “Malchus,” Μάλχος; makmas “Michmash,” Μαχμάς; drakma “drachma,” δραχμή; zakkaius “Zacchaeus,” Ζααχαῖος [sic]; ainok “Enoch,” Ἐνώχ; sairok “Serug,” Σερούχ; lamaik “Lamech,” Λάμεχ.

3) Preceded by t, it changes into h; e.g. bruhta from brukjan, þahta from þagkjan, þuhta from þugkjan, sahts from sakan, sauhts from siukan, vahtvo from vakan.

“Note.—When combined with s, ks serves only to reproduce Greek ξ: arfaksad ‘Arphaxad,’ Ἀρφαξάδ; artarkserkses ‘Artaxerxes,’ Ἀρταξέρξης.”

## X

§ 43. X occurs only in Greek words and proper names, in which it corresponds to χ; e.g. xristus “Christ,” Χριστός; pasxa “Passover,” πάσχα; zaxarias “Zechariah,” Ζαχαρίας; axaja “Achaia,” Ἀχαΐα. It is also doubled for κχ in zaxxaius “Zacchou,” Ζαχκού. In all these words, however, except xristus, it alternates with k, the sound of which it seems to have had among the Goths. For if Greek χ had been simply aspirated for them, no reason would be apparent why, at least in some cases, they did not express it by h, the equivalent of an aspirate, and perhaps write arhippus as gatarhiþs, malhus as alh, or hristus as hrisjan.

## Q

§ 44. 1) Q occurs at the beginning, middle, and end of words:

[Col. 0937] a) At the beginning: qam, qainon, qens, qiþan, qinjan, qums; preceding a consonant, it is found only in the doubtful qrammiþa;

b) In the middle: þlaqus, vraiqo, suqon, etc.;

c) At the end: sagq, bistugq, etc.

2) Among foreign words it occurs only in qartus, Greek Κούαρτος, Latin *Quartus*; thus it stands for Latin *qu*. But since in akvila it is written kv, q appears to have had the same pronunciation.

## W

§ 45. 1) W occurs at the beginning, middle, and end of words, though rather rarely; when initial, however, it never precedes a consonant:

a) At the beginning: was, wairban, waurbun, we, weila, wilftri, wopan;

b) In the middle: saiwan, leiwan, arwazna, newa;

c) At the end: new, and the preterites saw, laiw, together with the imperatives saiw, leiw.

“Note.—It never follows short i and u without causing them to be broken; compare § 32, 5 on this matter.”

2) It is not found in foreign words, and therefore its pronunciation is very difficult to determine. Etymologically it corresponds to the combinations hv and wh in cognate languages. Hickes takes it as cv or hv; Ihre as qh. Yet that it was a simple sound for the Goth is clear from the fact that he assigned one sign to it, but not to other combinations of letters, such as hl, hn, hr. Moreover, hv occurs even in compound words, as ubuhvopida, Luke XVIII, 38, þairhvakands, VI, 12, without changing into w.

## b. LABIALS

## B

§ 46. 1) B occurs frequently at the beginning, both before vowels and before the liquids l, n, r, and also in the middle; at the end, however, only after the liquids l and m, and rarely after r or vowels:

a) At the beginning: balgs, bai, bauan, berusjos, bida, biuds, bugjan, boka, bliggvan, bnauan, brikan;

b) In the middle: haban, gahlaiba, raubon, gebun, hleibjan, liban, þiubi, dubo, drobnan;

c) At the end: halb, dumb, bisvarb (hence svarf in the glossary must be corrected to svarb), tvalib, Luke II, 42; VIII, 1; hlaib, Mark VII, 27; Luke IV, 4 and often; grob, Luke VI, 48.

2) It regularly stands for Greek β; e.g. barbarus “barbarian,” βάρβαρος; beþania “Bethany,” Βηθανία; byssus “fine linen,” βυσσός; gabaa “Gabaah,” Γαβαά; abba “father,” ἀββᾶ; abraham “Abraham,” Ἀβραάμ; maimbrana “membrane,” μεμβράνα; nabav “Nabou,” Ναβού; ïakob “Jacob,” Ἰακώβ. It also stands for Greek ου where Latin v corresponds: silbanus “Silvanus,” Σιλουανός, *Silvanus*; naubaimbair “November.”

3) At the end of a word and before t it regularly changes into f; conversely f, when followed by a vowel, changes into b; e.g. hlaif, hlaifs from HLAIBA; laufs from LAUBA; gif, gaf, gaft from giban; hafts from haban; svaif from sveiban; skauf from skiuban; þarf, þaurfta from þarban; grof from graban; conversely, asabis from asaf; tvalibim from tvalif; ubuh from uf; abu from af. Even at the end of a word f changes into b, e.g. hlaibs, Luke IV, 3; hlaib, tvalib, grob (see above, 1c); likewise in the ending ubni-ufni.

“Note.—In timbrjan instead of timrjan, b has been inserted for euphony.”

4) The pronunciation of b seems to have been somewhat weaker and to have approached Latin v more closely, since it was used for the latter.

## F

§ 47. 1) F occurs at the beginning, middle, and end; at the beginning it can also be combined with l and r:

a) At the beginning: fana, fairwus, faura, fera, feian, fidvor, fulls, fodjan, flekan, flodus, flautan, flahto, fraþi, etc.;

b) In the middle: afar, hafjan, sifan, hiufan, ufar, lofa;

c) At the end: the hlaif, gif, gaf, etc. cited above, and in addition af, uf, fimf, tvalif.

2) In foreign words it corresponds to Greek φ; e.g. falaig “Peleg,” Φάλεγ; fanuel “Phanuel,” Φανουήλ; filippus “Philip,” Φίλιππος; filetus “Philetus,” Φιλητός; faurtunatus “Fortunatus,” Φουρτούνατος; fareisaius “Pharisee,” Φαρισαῖος; fygailus “Phygelus,” Φύγελλος; aipafraudeitus “Epaphroditus,” Ἐπαφρόδιτος; arfaksad “Arphaxad,” Ἀρφαξάδ; nymfa “Nymphas,” Νυμφᾶς; kajafa “Caiaphas,” Καϊάφας; ïosef “Joseph,” Ἰωσήφ. Exceptionally it also corresponds to π in kafarnaum “Capernaum,” Καπερναούμ.

3) We have already noted above (§ 46, 3) that f arises from b and changes into b; concerning its derivation from p, see § 48. In svumfsl from svimman it has been inserted for euphony.

4) Hence it may be inferred that f was pronounced more weakly, like bh, and not like ph, as likewise appears in the class of linguals, and perhaps also of gutturals, where aspirates seem to approach the mediae more closely than the tenues. Yet that Gothic f did not wholly agree with Greek φ may be inferred from the fact that the Goth took the occasion to borrow for it a special sign from the Latin alphabet. See § 12, col. 901.

## P

§ 48. 1) P occurs only rarely, perhaps never at the beginning of a genuine Gothic word; it occurs more often in the middle and at the end:

a) At the beginning: paida, peikabagms, puggs, pund, plapja, plats, plinsjan, praggan;

b) In the middle: skapan, kaupon, slepan, veipan, nipnan, diupiþa, supon, wopan;

c) At the end: raip, saislep, skip, iup, hup, wop.

2) In proper names and foreign words it corresponds to Greek π, whose sound it has; e.g. parakletus “Paraclete,” παράκλητος; paintekuste “Pentecost,” πεντεκοστή; pauntius “Pontius,” Πόντιος; peilatus “Pilate,” Πιλάτος; praufetus “prophet,” προφήτης; aipafras “Epaphras,” Ἐπαφρᾶς; apaustaulus “apostle,” ἀπόστολος; karpus “Carpus,” Κάρπος; spaikulatur “executioner,” σπεκουλάτωρ. Exceptionally it also represents φ in paurpura “purple,” πορφύρα, and ps represents ψ in psalma “psalm,” ψαλμός.

3) Before t it sometimes changes into f; e.g. gaskafts from skapjan, woftuli from wopan. Probably to these must be added the second persons of the preterite indicative skoft, waiwoft, saisleft, varft, etc., although proof is lacking. Grefts is much less to be referred to greipan than to Old High German *grafo*, Low German *grebe*; see Graff, *Alth. Sprachsch.* IV, pp. 312 ff.

## c. LINGUALS

## D

[Col. 0939]

§ 49. 1) D is frequently used at the beginning, middle, and end; initially it permits r and v after it:

a) At the beginning: dags, dails, dauþus, deds, deigan, digrei, diups, dulþs, doms, dragan, driusan, drobnan, dvals;

b) In the middle: badi, paida, daudjan, garedaba, beidan, bida, liudan, gudja, flodus;

c) At the end: very many neuters, accusatives, and preterites, such as sad, god, braid, stad, bad, etc.

2) It normally corresponds to Greek δ; e.g. daveid “David,” Δαυίδ; diakaunus “deacon,” διάκονος; didimus “Didymus,” Δίδυμος; drakma “drachma,” δραχμή; andraias “Andrew,” Ἀνδρέας; beþsaeidan “Bethsaida,” Βηθσαϊδά; arfaksad “Arphaxad,” Ἀρφαξάδ; asgad “Asgad,” Ἀσγάδ; þaddaius “Thaddaeus,” Θαδδαῖος; saddukaius “Sadducee,” Σαδδουκαῖος. Rarely it corresponds to Greek θ: baidsaiïdan, Luke IX, 10, Βηθσαϊδά; lod “Lot,” Λώθ (for which Ulfilas probably read Λώτ).

3) At the end of a word and before nominative s it frequently alternates with þ; e.g. faheds and faheþs, milads and mitaþs, manaseds and manaseþs, sads and saþs, stads and staþs, fads and faþs, aviliud and aviliuþ, juggalaud, Luke VII, 14, and juggalauþ, Mark XVI, 5; bad and baþ, baud and bauþ, wad and waþ; especially in Luke, in the endings of the third person singular, the second person plural, and the past participle: drigkid, Luke I, 15, and drigkiþ, John VI, 54; libaid, Luke IV, 4, and libaiþ, Matt. IX, 18; frijod, Luke VII, 42, and frijoþ, VII, 5; rodeid, VI, 45, and rodeiþ, V, 21; manveid, III, 4, and manveiþ, Mark I, 3; siud, Luke V, 10, and siuþ, 2 Cor. III, 3; magud, Luke V, 34, and maguþ, Mark XIV, 7; gamelid, Luke IV, 4, and gameliþ, Matt. II, 10; gamanvids, Luke VI, 40, and gamanviþs, 2 Tim. III, 17; compare the Prolegomena, col. 475, note 1.

This interchange rarely occurs in the middle of a word, as in unfrodans, Gal. III, 1, and unfroþans, III, 3; compare midïddjedun, Luke VII, 11, for miþïddjedun.

“Note.—On d changing into þ, see § 50, 4; into s, § 52, 4; into z, § 53, 4.”

4) After n it is sometimes lost, as in the active participle (§ 116, note 2); compare banvida, Luke XX, 37. In the same way, the third person plural in the preterite, originally ending in nd, as in the present, later first lost d. In the anomalous sind (for sijund), d still remains; compare § 134, 4.

5) D seems to have had the same sound as Greek δ and Old High German d. Nor should one rightly infer a harsher pronunciation of this letter from the scribal error mad, Rom. XII, 20, for mat.

## Þ

§ 50. 1) Þ occurs frequently in every position of a word; initially it may also be followed by l, r, or v:

a) At the beginning: þata, þairh, þauh, þevis, þeihan, þizei, þiuda, þugkjan, þo, þlaqus, þliuhan, þragjan, þreis, þroþjan, þvastiþa;

b) In the middle: waþar, aiþei, dauþus, heþjo, seiþu, qiþan, þiuþeigs, bruþs, broþar;

c) At the end: apart from the cases in which it alternates with d [Col. 0940] (§ 49, 3), ïþ, miþ, guþ, bloþ, qaþ, froþ, stoþ, varþ, hanþ, fanþ, etc.

2) In Greek words and proper names it regularly stands for θ: þaddaïus “Thaddaeus,” Θαδδαῖος; þaiaufeilus “Theophilus,” Θεόφιλος; þymiama “incense,” θυμίαμα; þomas “Thomas,” Θωμᾶς; naþan “Nathan,” Ναθάν; sabakþani “sabachthani,” σαβαχθανί; salaþiel “Shealtiel,” Σαλαθιήλ; maþusal “Methuselah,” Μαθουσαλά; kaurinþo “Corinth,” Κόρινθος; mahaþ “Maath,” Μαάθ; sabaoþ “Sabaoth,” Σαβαώθ; nazaraiþ “Nazareth,” Ναζαρέθ. Rarely it stands for τ: aleisabeiþ “Elizabeth,” Ἐλισάβετ; gannesaraiþ “Gennesaret,” Γεννησαρέτ; and when doubled it stands for τθ: maþþaius “Matthew,” Ματθαῖος.

3) It frequently alternates with d (§ 49, 3), and sometimes also with t; e.g. hnuto for hnuþo, teimumauþaius for teimauþaius, fratvjan for fraþvjan (?), usbloþains, 2 Cor. VIII, 4, for usbloteins, bloþan for blotan, unsahþaba, 1 Tim. III, 16, for unsahtaba, gaþarhiþs, Gal. II, 11, for gatarhiþs, afleþanda, Mark II, 9, for afletanda.

4) It regularly arises from d when that would otherwise occur at the end of a word or before s; e.g. faþs from FADI, staþs from STADI, aviliuþ from AVILIUDA, liuhaþ from LIUHADA, naqaþs from NAQADA, and in past participles such as habaiþs from HABAIDA, sokiþs from SOKIDA, spilloþs from SPILLODA. It also occurs in the preterite of *kunnan* instead of d: kunþa for kunnda. Conversely, d remains after other liquids in such anomalous verbs: skulda from skulan, munda from munan.

5) Conversely, where a vowel follows, it returns again to d—not only in inflection, as faheþs, genitive fahedais; staþs, genitive stadis; sokiþs, feminine sokida—but also before the enclitics u and uh; e.g. vitudu, John XIII, 12, from vituþ; sijaidu, 2 Cor. II, 9, from sijaiþ; vileidu, Mark XV, 9, from vileiþ; qiþiduh, Mark XVI, 7, from qiþiþ; vairþaiduh, Eph. IV, 32, from vairþaiþ; standaiduh, 1 Cor. XVI, 13, from standaiþ, etc.

“Note.—On þ changing into s, see § 52, 4.”

6) Þ probably had to be pronounced as an aspirated d. It is indeed commonly regarded as th, but wrongly: on the one hand it only very rarely, and perhaps through scribal error, alternates with t; on the other, it regularly and very frequently changes into d. Moreover, if this letter had wholly agreed with Greek θ, Ulfilas would undoubtedly have kept that character for it rather than selecting another at will. In any event, it is equally wrong to write the sound of þ either as th or as dh, since neither t nor d joined with h corresponds at all to þ; e.g. athaitan, not aþaitan; andhausjan, not anþausjan.

## T

§ 51. 1) T occurs frequently in all positions of a word; initially it also occurs before r and v:

a) At the beginning: tagr, taihun, taujan, tekan, teihan, timrja, tiuhan, tunþus, trauan, triu, tvai, tveifls;

b) In the middle: lata, haitan, sprauto, gretan, beitan, miton, giutan, luton, gaigrotun;

c) At the end: at, mat, plat, vait, hlaut, fralet, usmet, andabeit, vit, hrot, etc.

2) In foreign words and proper names it is used for Greek τ and Latin t, with which it otherwise wholly agrees; e.g. taleiþa “Talitha,” ταλιθά; teimaius “Timaeus,” Τιμαῖος; tykeikus “Tychicus,” Τυχικός; galatia “Galatia,” Γαλατία; ïturaia “Ituraea,” Ἰτουραία; kananeites “Canaanite,” Κανανίτης; kreta “Crete,” Κρήτη; laiktjo “reading,” *lectio*; lystra “Lystra,” Λύστρα; matþat “Matthat,” Ματθάτ; mattaþius “Mattathias,” Ματταθίας.

3) It is used for d and þ before a following mute or sibilant: namely, in the preterite of anomalous verbs—aihta, mahta, ohta, brahta, þahta, þuhta, bauhta, þaurfte, mosta—instead of aih-da, mah-da, etc.; in word formations hliftus, þuhtus, kustus as compared with vratodus, auhjodus; aihts, andabauhts, gifts, usdrusts as compared with gabaurþs, gaqumþs, etc. Alongside gaqumþs (from qiman) has intruded andanumts (from niman), where audanumþs would be expected.

4) On the change of this letter into the sibilants s and z, see §§ 52, 4; 53, 4.

## 4. SIBILANTS

## S

§ 52. 1) S, especially initial s, is the most frequent of all consonants. At the beginning of words it readily combines with k, kr, l, m, n, p, pr, t, tr, and v:

a) At the beginning: sama, sair, sauïl, sels, seins, sibun, siuks, sunus, sokjan, skaidan, skreitan, slahan, smairþr, snorjo, spillon, sprauto, staþs, straujan, svers;

b) In the middle: vasjan, laiseins, hausjon, mesa, veison, visan, driusan, þusundi;

c) At the end: hlas, urrais, raus, sves, veis, vis, hus, los.

2) It regularly stands for Greek ς; e.g. samaria “Samaria,” Σαμαρία; symaion “Symeon,” Συμεών; saimaiein “Semei,” Σεμεΐ; seimon “Simon,” Σίμων; saulaumon “Solomon,” Σολομών; susanna “Susanna,” Σουσάννα; ïoses “Joses,” Ἰωσῆ; ïsrael “Israel,” Ἰσραήλ; kaisar “Caesar,” καῖσαρ; mambres “Mambres,” Μαμβρῆς; markus “Mark,” Μάρκος; paitrus “Peter,” Πέτρος, etc. It sometimes also stands for Greek ζ: kusa “Chuza,” Ξουζᾶ; asmoþ “Azmoth,” Ἀζμώθ.

3) S placed between two vowels or liquids changes into z, namely:

a) In compounds: uzon from us-anan; uzeta from us-itan; especially before the enclitics u, uh, and ei: vileizu, Luke IX, 54; uzu, Gal. III, 2, 5; uzuh, Luke VI, 45 and often; dizuh, Mark XVI, 8; wazuh, wanzuh, wizuh, warjizuh, andizuh, veizuh, juzuh, 1 Cor. IV, 10; þizuh, þanzuh, maizuh, Gal. IV, 9; filippauzuh, Luke III, 1; þizei, þozei, þanzei, ïzei, þuzei, juzei, ïzvizei. Irregularly, also in bijandzuh, Philem. 22; conversely, not in vasuh, Matt. VIII, 30 and often; sumansuh, Mark XII, 5; bidjandansuh, Matt. VI, 7.

b) In inflections: hatiza, Luke III, 7, from hatis; riqiza, Luke I, 79; riqizis, Rom. XIII, 12, from riqis; anza, Luke VI, 41, 42, from ans; haizam, John XVIII, 3, from hais? Also in proper names: bauauzis from bauaus; ïaissaizis from ïaissais; ïosezis from ïoses; mosezis from moses. But not in agisa, Luke II, 9, from agis; rimisa, 2 Thess. III, 12, from rimis.

c) In formations: hatizon from hatis; riqizeins, riqizjan from riqis; minznan from mins; maiza from mais.

“Note 1.—On its frequent interchange with z, see § 53, 3.”

4) It arises from d, þ, and t, namely:

a) In inflections, when another dental immediately follows:

aa) In the second person singular preterite of strong verbs: anabaust, Luke XIV, 22, for anabaudt from biudan; qast, [Col. 0942] Mark XII, 32, for qaþt from qiþan; varst, John IX, 34, for varþt from vairþan; bilaist, Matt. XXVII, 46, for bilaiþt from bileiþan; ufsnaist, Luke XV, 30, for ufsnaiþt from ufsneiþan; gastost, Rom. II, 20, for gastoþt from gastandan; haibaist, 1 Tim. VI, 12, for haihaitt from haitan.

“Note 2.—Saisost, Luke XIX, 21, for saisot from saian, is plainly redundant; perhaps the analogy of gastost influenced it. Something similar is also found in the formation of blostreis from blotan, unless blosreis is the original form, in which an euphonic t was introduced to connect the letters s and r more easily.”

bb) In the preterite of the irregular verbs motan, kaupatjan, and vitan, which attach the preterite ending da directly to the root (as skulda from skulan, vilda from viljan, munda from munan). Here d of the ending changes into t because of the preceding t (compare § 51, 3), and then the first t changes into s: mot-da, motta, mosta; kaupat-da, kaupatta, kaupasta. In vitan the change extends further, since the latter t is assimilated to the preceding s: vit-da, vitta, vista, vissa.

b) In formations, especially where a dental of verbal nouns is followed by another dental as an element in word formation; in that case both become s. Thus stass from standan (root STAþ), qiss from qiþan, viss from vidan, just as kunþs from kunnan, qumþs from qiman, aihts from aigan, gifts from giban, etc. Vissei from vitan is exactly parallel to baurþei from bairan, whereas staþþs, qiþþs, vidþs, vitþei must be regarded as the original form, from which the present form was derived after the two dentals had changed into sibilants and the ending s had been dropped. A still wider change of dental into sibilant before n occurs in forming anabusns from anabiudan, usbeisns from usbeidan. Perhaps garehsns likewise arose from garaihtjan in the same way?

5) As regards pronunciation, s must have been sharp and opposed to z, which is used when a sibilant is to be pronounced more weakly.

## Z

§ 53. 1) Initial z occurs in no Gothic words; final z only rarely and solely in place of s; medial z, however, occurs more often:

a) As a radical element in aqizi, azets, hazjan, vizon, etc.;

b) In inflections: namely, aa) in the genitive of adjectives and pronouns, such as godaizos, godaize, þizos, þize, etc.; bb) in the second person singular passive, haitaza, sokjaza;

c) In forming comparatives: batiza, minniza, juhiza, framaldroza, etc.;

d) It also arises from s, as will be said below under 3;

e) Finally, for s: minz, riqiz; also mimz, aiz for mims, ais.

2) In Greek words and proper names it represents ζ; e.g. zaibaidaius “Zebedee,” Ζεβεδαῖος; zauraubabil “Zerubbabel,” Ζοροβάβελ; zelotes “zealot,” ζηλωτής; aizaikeia “Hezekiah,” Ἐζεκία; aileiaizair “Eliezer,” Ἐλιέζερ; baiailzeibul “Beelzebul,” Βεελζεβούλ; kaurazein “Chorazin,” Χοραζίν; lazarus “Lazarus,” Λάζαρος; azymus “unleavened,” ἄζυμος; nazaraiþ “Nazareth,” Ναζαρέθ. Sometimes it also represents ς: praizbytaireis “elder,” πρεσβύτερος; aizleim “Esli,” Ἐσλί; aizor “Esrom,” Ἐσρώρ.

3) It frequently alternates with s; e.g. riqiz, Matt. VI, 23; John XII, 35; Eph. V, 8, for riqis; minz, [Col. 0943] 2 Cor. XII, 15, for mins; saizlep, John XI, 11, compared with 1 Cor. XV, 6, for saislep; mosez, 2 Cor. III, 13, codex A, for moses; ïosez, Matt. XXVII, 50, is a scribal error for ïosezis; anabuzns, Mark XII, 28, for anabusns, is only Stiernhielm’s false reading and must be removed from the glossary. But the reverse substitution of s for z is nowhere proved.

4) Z, like s, arises from dentals, especially before n: vleizns, vlizjan from vleitan.

5) Z seems to have been pronounced as a weak s. For although it stands for Greek ζ, it cannot have had its sound, equivalent to ds, since Ulfilas elsewhere rendered this by ds, or at least not by a simple letter; and it is clear from its phonetic relation that z is merely a weaker s. Moreover, since in lazzarus a doubled z must be understood as a simple sound s, not as the double sound ds, it follows that even in proper names z may have had a weaker sound—whether Greek ζ in Ulfilas’s age actually had this sound, or whether its harsher sound was so difficult for the Goth to pronounce that he substituted for it the better-known Gothic z.
