§ 55. The other kind of linked consonants is gemination, that is, repetition of the same letter. In genuine Gothic words, except for the nasal gg, only liquids, dentals, and sibilants are doubled, as follows:

a) Liquids: LL: alls, hallus, ufsvalleins, fill, spillon, vulla, fulls; MM: vamm, svamm, stamms, dammjan, mammo, hlamm, and in the dative endings þamma, anþaramma, ïmma, himma, ainummehun; NN: manna, anno, kannjan, rannjan, ïnna, kinnus, brinnan, vinnan, spinnan, duginnan, aflinnan, rinnan, minniza, sunno, brunna, munnan, kunnan, runnun, etc.; RR: fairra, qairrus, andstaurran;

b) Dentals: DD: daddjan, vaddjus, tvaddje, ïddja; þþ: aþþan, aiþþau; TT: atta, skatts;

c) Sibilants: SS: wass, ungatass, usstass, gaviss, gaqiss, misso, missa-, vissa, knussjan, and the ending -assus.

“Note 1.—These letters are also often doubled redundantly; e.g. allh, Luke II, 46; aggillau, 2 Cor. XI, 14; kannt, 1 Cor. VII, 18; ainnohun, Phil. IV, 15; fairrinoþ, Gal. V, 15; nasseinais, 1 Thess. V, 8; perhaps also ïddveit, 1 Tim. III, 7 (see Castill. on this passage), especially in proper names: aillam ‘Adam,’ Ἠδάμ; maisaullam ‘Meshullam,’ Μεσουλάμ; ammo ‘Amos,’ Ἀμώς; makidonnim, 2 Cor. IX, 12; sainnaa ‘Senaah,’ Σεναά; aiddua ‘Jedaiah,’ Ἰεδουά; gaddarenus ‘Gadarene,’ Γαδαρηνός; (lyddomaeis? ‘Lodadid?’ Λοδαδίδ); lazzarus, Luke XVI, 23, ‘Lazarus,’ Λάζαρος; assaum ‘Assum,’ Ἀσούμ; ïasson ‘Jason,’ Ἰάσων; see on Gal. V, 15.

“Note 2.—Conversely, a simple consonant is sometimes used where a double one would be expected: fulnan, Luke II, 21; Eph. III, 19; frakuni, Rom. XIV, 3, [Col. 0946] manhun, 1 Tim. V, 22; visedun, Luke II, 43; compare the note on Mark III, 13; X, 45; tvadje, 1 Tim. V, 19.

“Note 3.—With regard to the remaining consonants, they are not doubled except in proper names and foreign words, e.g.: laivvi, aivva, abba, rabbi, filippus, aiffaþa, aikklesjo, zaxxaius; sakkus and smakka are certainly not genuinely Gothic words, and vippja at John XIX. 2 is a scribal error for vipja.

A certain doubling is produced by assimilation, whereby the final consonant of a word or word-element coalesces with the initial consonant of the following one. Especially subject to this are the τὸ h [the h] of the particles nih, jah, uh, and the τὸ s [the s] of the preposition us, e.g.: niþ-þan, jas-sa, jan-ni, vasuþ-þan, ur-reisan, etc. More examples will be found in the glossary under these words.

§ 56. We have already noted, under the individual consonants, their transitions into others; these transitions are therefore of three kinds:

1. The transition of a tenuis and a media into an aspirate, as follows: g and k into h, b and p into f, d into þ.

2. The transition of an aspirate into a media, as follows: h into g, f into b, þ into d.

3. The transition of dentals into sibilants; that is, d, þ, t into s and z.

§ 57. The following affections of consonants should also be observed:

1. Paragoge, by which a liquid is added at the end of a word; it occurs only in foreign proper names, e.g.: mariam Μαρία [Mary], nauel Νῶε [Noah], nerin Νηρί [Neri], mailkein Μεχλί [Mechli].

2. Epenthesis, by which a consonant is inserted in the middle of a word, and which in several cases serves euphony; e.g. swumfsl John IX. 11 instead of svumsl; timbrjan, Luke XIV. 28, 30, instead of timrjan; compare inserted j, § 34.4.

3. Metathesis, by which a consonant is moved from its place, as in marytr in the Gothic calendar instead of martyr. But sprauds, 1 Cor. IX. 24, instead of spaurds, and þvalh, Skeireins II.6, instead of þvahl, must certainly be ascribed to scribal errors, since the genuine forms spaurds and þvahl occur elsewhere.

4. Elision, by which a consonant is dropped for euphony, e.g. fimtiguns, Luke XVI.6, for fimftiguns.

## CHAPTER TWO. INFLECTION OF WORDS.

[Col. 0945]

### A. DECLENSION.

[Col. 0945] § 58. The Gothic language has nine parts of speech: substantive, adjective, numeral, pronoun, verb, adverb, preposition, conjunction, interjection. The last four, since they do not undergo inflection, are called [Col. 0946] indeclinable; the others, inflectable. Of the latter, however, the first four are declined, while the last—that is, the verb—is conjugated.

## I. THE SUBSTANTIVE.

[Col. 0945]

§ 59. In the Gothic language three genders are assigned to substantives: namely masculine, neuter, and feminine. Indeed, this grammatical gender more often corresponds to the gender [Col. 0946] of nature or sex, e.g. atta, masculine, “father”; aiþei, feminine, “mother”; haubiþ, neuter, “head.” Yet this rule does not admit of no exceptions; rather, [Col. 0947] there are many words denoting inanimate things, qualities, arts, or dispositions of mind, etc., which have been assigned masculine or feminine gender through a personification common to all languages: thus bagms, masculine, “tree”; airþa, feminine, “earth”; doms, masculine, “judgment”; muns, masculine, “opinion”; gahugds, feminine, “thought”; vens, feminine, “hope”; etc.

Conversely, there are certain words signifying persons which bear the gender of things—that is, the neuter—either because their gender was intended to remain indefinite, as in barn, τὸ παιδίον, “child, infant,” and gaman, ὁ πλησίος, “neighbour”; or because persons were intended, contemptuously, to be reduced to the class of things, as in þevis, neuter, “slave,” and gaskalki, neuter, “fellow-servant.” There is another, common gender for words which express animate beings of either gender or sex and are consequently used as masculine or feminine, as asilus, masculine “ass,” feminine “she-ass.” Such cases occur only rarely, since ordinarily the form changes when the gender changes: thus svaihra, masculine “father-in-law,” svaihro, feminine “mother-in-law”; þius, masculine “servant,” þivi, feminine “maidservant”; magus, masculine “boy,” mavi (instead of magvi? Grimm III, 336), feminine “girl.” These matters will be developed more fully elsewhere, when word-formation is discussed (§ 142 ff.). Here it is sufficient, with reference to declension, to say that the neuter always forms its accusative like its nominative, and that the feminine prefers fuller vowels in inflection. In certain words, however, different endings are assigned to each gender, so that it is more or less difficult to determine what gender such words possess. These endings are as follows:

§ 60. Substantives have two numbers: singular and plural. The dual, which occurs in the pronoun and verb, occurs nowhere in substantives.

§ 61. Each number has five cases: nominative, vocative, accusative, dative, and genitive. The instrumental case is indeed not found in substantives, but it has left certain traces in the pronoun (see §§ 108, 110). Moreover, if Gothic nouns, as we shall say below, are arranged in various declensions according to the form of their cases, this diversity consists less in a change of wholly different endings than in the diversity of the radical or derivative syllables preceding the ending, and in the influence of the latter upon the former. Hence, from the following characteristics, the cases of both numbers and of all declensions may generally be recognized.

The nominative ends in a vowel or in -s, with the neuter also ending in other consonants; the singular vocative agrees with the nominative, except that the s peculiar to the latter is dropped; the singular accusative generally presents the bare root of the word; the singular dative originally ends in a; the singular genitive in s. Likewise, the masculine and feminine plural nominative and vocative end in s, the neuter in a; the plural accusative in s or ns, the neuter in a; the plural dative in m; and the plural genitive in one of the long vowels e or o. The following table exhibits all these endings:

§ 62. In distinguishing the various declensions, the theme or root of the word must first be observed. By root we understand that form of the substantive which, although perhaps in itself has no indication of any case and does not generally exist as such in the language, nevertheless serves so fundamentally for forming cases, developing the declension, and forming the word, that not only all existing forms of declension, but also forms derived from existing words, can be reduced to it. In the course of this work we have marked this radical form with uncial letters.

§ 63. Declension is divided into two parts, which earlier scholars, from a name closely connected with the adjective, [Col. 0949] called abstract and concrete or emphatic, while modern scholars call them the strong and weak forms. But both designations are mistaken: the former because it considers meaning rather than form and, moreover, is of scarcely any value for substantives; the latter because it rests upon an erroneous view of the form of the two declensions. In truth, the two declensions differ from one another not because the so-called weak declension results from the accidental addition of formative n at the beginning of the declension, but because the radical form in one ends in a vowel and in the other in a consonant. We have therefore, we hope with better justification, called them the vocalic and consonantal declensions.

[Note: [Col. 0949] *Vocalic, consonantal*: new terms devised to convey a new idea. The editor.]

The latter, namely the consonantal, comprises those words whose radical form ends in n belonging to the formative syllable (compare Bopp, *Comparative Grammar*, § 125, p. 149); this letter, however, belongs to the formation of the word, not to its inflection. But since here we have to deal only with the latter, the word must be considered in that form alone in which it is joined to the case-endings.

## A. VOCALIC DECLENSION.

§ 64. Vocalic declension essentially consists in this: the radical form of words belonging to it ends in a vowel. Now only three vowels occur at the end of the radical form, a, i, and u; these undergo various modifications in declension, being weakened, lengthened, or even in some cases wholly dropped: a very frequently, i only rarely, but u never. The following rules serve for forming the cases of the vocalic declension:

1. The singular nominative in the masculine and feminine adds s to the radical form; the vowel, if it is u, remains unchanged; if i, it is dropped; and if finally a, it is either dropped or weakened to i. The feminine alone preserves the latter form, without taking the ending n. The neuter behaves like the masculine, except that it does not take the ending s.

2. The singular accusative and vocative agree with the nominative after the final s has been dropped.

3. The singular dative is formed by attaching a to the ending. Hence, in words whose radical form ends in a, it agrees with that form; but if it ends in i, this vowel is displaced by a in the masculine, while in the feminine it is broken, a producing the same breaking in the radical vowel u.

4. The singular genitive takes the ending s with the vowel already present. This vowel appears originally to have been a; in masculine and neuter radical forms in a and i it was weakened to i, while in the feminine, which takes fuller-sounding endings, it was blended with the final vowel into o and ai. If the radical vowel is u, breaking follows and au results.

5. The masculine and feminine plural nominative and vocative take the ending s, and the radical vowel is lengthened [Col. 0950] (a to o, i to ei, u to ju instead of iu); the neuter takes the ending a.

6. The plural accusative, which in the neuter agrees with the nominative, attaches to the radical form in masculine and feminine the ending ns; in the feminine, however, where this form ends in -a, s alone is used, the radical vowel being lengthened, so that here too the accusative agrees with the nominative.

7. The plural dative constantly adds m to the radical form; where the radical vowel is a, however, this vowel is lengthened again to o in the feminine alone.

8. Finally, the plural genitive has the ending e; in the feminine alone, and where the radical form ends in a, it causes that vowel to be lengthened.

Furthermore, it should be observed that, where j or v preceding the radical vowel must be dropped, it is changed into the related vowel i or u according to the rules of sound (§§ 34.3; 35.3).

§ 65. Vocalic declension itself is subdivided into three classes according as the radical form ends in one of the three vowels a, i, or u. Moreover, j or v placed before the final vowel, as well as the gender of the substantive, affects the vowel, so that the following table includes all possible cases of this declension:

But these cases occur complete only with radical vowel a; with the other two they have many gaps. Thus it is a rule subject to no exceptions that consonants j and v cannot precede their related vowels i and u, the forms ji and vu nowhere otherwise occurring. Furthermore, in declining words vocalic r is also introduced as a fourth radical vowel (see the discussion of sounds, § 39.3), and it likewise claims its place in vocalic declension.

## FIRST VOCALIC DECLENSION. Radical vowel a.

### a. Masculine.

The following are thus declined: aiþs “oath,” asts “branch,” bagms “tree,” andbahts “servant” (plural andbahtos, not andbahteis, as has erroneously entered the glossary), dags “day,” himins “heaven,” hlaifs “bread,” hunds “dog,” hors “adulterer,” þiubs “thief,” þiudans “king,” kreks “Greek,” [Col. 0951] laufs “leaf,” ligrs “bed,” sitls “seat,” skalks “servant,” skatts “silver coin,” skilliggs “denarius,” stains “stone,” stols “seat,” tains “twig,” dauravards “doorkeeper,” vigs “way,” vinds “wind,” vulfs “wolf,” figgrs “finger,” fugls “bird.”

“Note 1.—For many words which cannot occur in the plural because of their meaning, or whose plural nominative, accusative, or dative is not found at least in the extant monuments, it remains doubtful whether their radical form ends in a or i. Such are akrs “field,” biuds “table,” gadiliggs “cousin,” gazds “rod,” daigs “dough,” doms “judgment,” qums “coming,” hakuls (not hakul, as given in the glossary) “cloak,” hlains “hill,” hlauts “lot,” þagks “grace,” þlauhs “flight,” faihuþraihns “riches,” katils “kettle,” kindins “governor,” maiþms “gift,” maurgins “morning,” megs “son-in-law,” munþs “mouth,” run “course,” saivs “sea,” snaivs “snow,” stikls “cup,” striks “stroke of a line,” vaurms “worm,” vigans “war,” vaips “crown,” vlits “face,” vrits “erasure,” vraks “persecutor.”

[Col. 0951] According to the pattern of hairdeis are declined words in which either a derivative syllable or a long radical syllable precedes the syllable of the ending, such as andeis “end,” aurkeis “vessel,” asneis “servant,” beruseis, plural berusjos, “elders,” guþblostreis “despiser of God,” fauramaþleis “chief,” silbasiuneis “eyewitness,” faurstasseis “chief,” vitodafasteis “expert in the law,” waiteis “grain”; bokareis “scribe,” laisareis “teacher,” liuþareis “singer,” motareis “tax collector,” sokareis “searcher,” vullareis “fuller,” ragineis “counsellor,” siponeis “disciple.”

## ANOMALIES OF VOCALIC DECLENSION.

§ 85. Certain classes of words also belong to vocalic declension which, although in some cases they lose their vocalic nature and clearly suggest a consonantal root, nevertheless in other cases, especially in compounds, retain features by which their radical form is recognized as truly vocalic; consequently, it would be improper to regard them as species of consonantal declension.

### a. Masculine.

The following substantives derived from active participles are thus declined: daupjands “baptizer,” hatands “hater,” merjands “preacher,” nasjands “saviour,” bisitands “neighbour,” talzjands “teacher,” allvaldands “almighty,” fraveitands “avenger,” fijands “enemy, foe,” frijonds “friend,” fraujinonds “ruler,” midumonds “mediator.”

“Note.—To this declension also belongs menoþs ‘month,’ from which the following cases may be demonstrated: singular nominative menoþs, Luke I.36; dative menoþ, Luke I.26; genitive menoþs, Nehemiah VI.15; plural accusative menoþs, Luke I.24, 56; dative menoþum, Gal. IV.10. Hence vocative and accusative singular menoþ, and plural genitive menoþe, must be assumed.”

### b. Feminine.

The following are thus declined: alhs “temple,” brusts “breast,” dulþs “feast,” mitaþs “measure,” miluks “milk,” nahts “night,” spaurds “race-course,” vaihts “thing, affair.”

“Note.—Dulþs and vaihts are also regularly declined: genitive dulþais, vaihtais, etc. Nahts has plural dative nahtam, Mark V.5.”

## B. CONSONANTAL DECLENSION.

§ 88. In certain respects the consonantal declension is to be observed as follows:

1. The singular nominative drops the final n of the radical form.

2. The singular vocative is like the nominative.

3. The singular accusative exhibits the bare radical form, except in the neuter, which, according to a rule admitting no exceptions, has its accusative identical with the nominative.

4. The singular dative has lost the a proper to this case, which, however, was formerly present, as is evident from the preceding vowel of the formative syllable, weakened into i.

5. The singular genitive joins s directly to the radical form, with the a of the formative syllable weakened to i.

6. The masculine and feminine plural nominative prefixes s to the radical form; the neuter uses a instead, with the vowel of the formative syllable lengthened.

7. The plural vocative and accusative always agree with the nominative.

8. The plural dative ends in m, the n of the radical form being dropped.

9. The plural genitive adds e to the radical form in masculine and neuter, o in feminine.

### a. Masculine.

The following are thus declined: halsagga “neck,” aha “understanding,” ahma “spirit,” amsa “shoulder,” ara “eagle,” atta “father,” blinda “blind man,” bloma “flower,” brunna “well,” broþrahan, plural only, “brothers,” fauragagga “chief, president,” galga “cross,” garda “stable,” gibla “pinnacle,” guma “man,” gadaila “participant,” gadauka “guest,” drakma “drachma,” drobna “sedition,” hiuhma “crowd,” gahlaiba “companion,” hliuma “ear, hearing,” unhulþa “evil one (spirit),” hoha “plough,” uzeta “manger,” galaista “companion,” manleika “image,” galeika “fellow-member,” usliþa “paralytic,” liuta “hypocrite,” lofa “withered hand,” magula “little one,” maimbrana “parchment,” malma “sand,” mela “measure,” mena “moon,” milhma “people,” ganauha “sufficiency,” nuta “captor,” nota “stern,” gajuka “companion,” garazna “neighbour,” sinista “last-born,” gasinþa “companion,” skula “debtor,” skuggva “mirror,” smakka “fig,” snaga “garment,” sunna “sun,” sparva “sparrow,” spilla “preacher,” spyreida “basket,” gataura “cleft,” vaihsta “corner,” gavaurstva [Col. 0961] “fellow-worker,” veiha “presbyter,” fana “cloth,” fula “fulness”; and formations in -ja: aurtja “gardener,” arbja “heir,” baurgja “citizen,” bandja “captive,” fauragaggja “steward,” ïngardja “inhabitant,” gauja “settler,” gudja “priest,” vaidedja “evildoer,” afdrugkja, veindrugkja “drunkard,” bihaitja “quarrelsome person,” dulgahaitja “creditor,” haurnja “trumpeter,” hlija “tent,” afetja “eater,” kasja “potter,” manamaurþrja “murderer,” newundja “neighbour,” arbinumja “heir,” unkja “ounce,” gasinþja “companion,” skattja “money-changer,” skilja “executioner,” sviglja “flute-player,” timrja “carpenter,” vaurstvja “worker,” vardja “guardian,” vilja “will,” faskja “band,” fiskja “fisherman,” frauja “lord.”

> **Note.**—*Namo* “name” and *vato* “water,” like the masculine *auhsa* and *aba* (§ 89, note 2), drop the formative syllable *a* in the plural: nominative and accusative *namna*, Mark III.17; Luke X.20; Philippians IV.3; dative *vatnam*, Matthew VIII.32; Luke VIII.25.

### c. Feminine

They are declined as follows: *aglo* “affliction,” *azgo* “ashes,” *anno* “wages,” *armaio* “alms,” *avo* “grandmother,” *bandvo* “sign,” *brinno* “fever,” *gatvo* “way,” *faihugeiro* “avarice,” *dauro* “door,” *hraivadubo* “turtledove,” *driuso* “precipice,” *qino* “woman,” *haiþno* “heathen woman,” *heito* “fever,” *hnuto* “scourge,” *unhulþo* “malignant one,” *þaho* “clay,” *þeiwo* “thunder,” *ïnilo* “excuse,” *kalbo* “heifer,” *klismo* “cymbal,” *ïnkilþo* “pregnant, with child,” *broþralubo* “love of one’s neighbour,” *gamarko* “neighbourhood,” *mammo* “flesh,” *gamaitano* “circumcision,” *malo* “moth,” *mavilo* “girl,” *mizdo* “reward,” *gajuko* “likeness,” *uthvo* “morning,” *garazno* “neighbouring woman,” *reiro* “trembling,” *vinþiskauro* “winnowing-shovel,” *sunno* “sun,” *stairno* “star,” *stairo* “barrenness,” *svaihro* “mother-in-law,” *trigo* “mourning,” *vairilo* “lip,” *vahtvo* “guard,” *dauravardo* “door-keeping,” *viko* “week,” [Col. 0962] *vinno* “pain,” *vruggo* “snare,” *fauho* “fox,” *usfarþo* “departure,” *fullo* “fulness,” *waþo* “foam”; likewise formations in *-jo*: *arbjo* “female heir,” *brunjo* “breastplate,” *ïddaljo* “precipice,” *heþjo* “bed,” *ïumjo* “multitude,” *kalkjo* “concubine,” *mitadjo* “measure,” *niþjo* “sister,” *raþjo* “number,” *garunjo* “flow of water,” *sakjo* “quarrel,” *snorjo* “daughter-in-law,” *tainjo* “basket,” *gatimrjo* “building,” *vaihjo* “fight.”

## ANOMALOUS FORMS

### § 93.

Since anomalous forms belonging to the several declensions have already been placed in their respective locations, there remain here only those which, belonging to no declension in particular, are irregular chiefly in being defective—that is, in lacking certain ordinary cases, which they partly supply by borrowing cases from another root-form. Such words are:

1. *Manna*, “man,” which forms its cases both from the root [Col. 0963] *MANNA* and from the root *MAN*, in the following manner:

2. In the same way, *fon*, neuter “fire,” occurring only in the singular, derives its cases from the roots *FONA* and *FUNAN*:

3. *Fadrein*, which, although in form singular neuter, is used in the nominative and accusative as a masculine plural; for example, *þai fadrein*, John IX.20; *þans fadrein*, IX.18. In place of its other cases, the regular plural *fadreina* (2 Corinthians XII.14) seems more commonly to be used; for example, *fadreinam*, Colossians III.20; 2 Timothy III.2. Hence one may ask whether *fadrein*, as it is written in the glossary, is properly indeclinable, or should rather be regarded as defective.

## DECLENSION OF PROPER AND FOREIGN NAMES

### § 94.

The declension of these names and words requires particular examination. For although the Goth at times retained untouched the foreign form of Greek words, at other times he also attempted to inflect them after the manner of Gothic words; hence it would be wrong to disregard their departure from the customary form. They are now arranged according to Gothic declensions, as follows.

### A. VOCALIC DECLENSION

#### 1. Root vowel *a*

##### a. Masculine

**α. Root form *-a*.**

A very large number of foreign words follow this form, such as *abjaþar, aibair, abraham, adam, bailiam, bauaus, daveid, ïakob, ïsak, ïsrael, ïosef, kaisar, lod, moses, saulaumon, seimon, siloam, fanuel*, etc.; with this distinction, however, that they do not add *s* in the nominative. The same must be said of the Gothic name *viljariþ* in the Neapolitan document.

**β. Root form *-ja*.**

*Laivveis, lyddomaeis, (mailkeis*, Luke III.24), *naitofateis, praizbytaireis, saudaumeis.*

##### b. Feminine

Not a few foreign names and words are declined in this way, such as *akaja, antiaukia, asia, galatia, dalmatia, ïairusaulyma, kileikia, lauïdja, makidona* or *makidonja, paurpura, seidona, syria, trauada, tyra, filippa*, etc. Yet in the genitive they take the ending *-ais* instead of *-os*; for example, *asiais*, 1 Corinthians XVI.19; *kileikiais*, Galatians I.21. The more regular *ïairusaulymos* occurs at Luke II.38. *Synagoge*, on the other hand, though otherwise declined consonantally, has the genitive *synagogais* at Luke VIII.41 [Col. 0964] and John IX.21; but the dative *lauïdja*, 2 Timothy I.5, is a copyist’s error for *lauïdjai*.

#### 2. Root vowel *i*: Masculine

Only gentilic names are declined in this way, such as *saur* “Syrian,” dative plural *saurim*, Luke II.2, especially in the plural: *makidoneis, rumoneis, seidoneis, saudaumeis* (Luke XVII.29), *galateis, ïairusaulymeis*. Some also have the Greek ending *-es* in the nominative singular: *ïsraeleites, samareites, ïairusaulymeites*.

#### 3. Root vowel *u*: Masculine

A very large number of words belong here, such as *aggilus, aipiskaupus, aifaisius, akajus, alfaius, apaustaulus, barþaulaumaius, gaddarenus, gairgaisainus, galatius, galeilaius, zaibaidaius, zakkaius, haibraius, ïakobus, ïaurdanus, ïudaius, kaurinþius, nikaudemus, paitrus, pavlus, peilatus, saddukaius, seimonus, teibairius, teimauþaius, teitus, fareisaius, filippisius*, etc. It should, however, be observed that they form the nominative plural in *-eis* and the genitive plural in *-e*; for example, *apaustauleis, apaustaule; ïudaieis, ïudaie*—except only those ending in *-ius* in the singular, such as *aifaisius, kaurinþius, filippisius*, which have the same sound in the nominative plural. There is also a nominative plural *aggiljus*, Mark XII.25; Luke II.15; Romans VIII.38, alongside *aggileis*, Mark I.13. Some likewise take *-es* instead of *-us* in the nominative singular, as *praufetes*, Mark VI.15; XI.32, *ïskariotes*, John XII.4; by this new ending they join the above-mentioned *ïsraeleites, samareites,* and *ïairusaulymeites*. The dative *ïohannau*, Luke IX.9, is likewise formed from *ïohannes*.

> **Note.**—The following belong to the vocalic declension, although they conform to no particular form: *ano*, genitive *anos*; *helei*, genitive *heleis*; *naggai*, genitive *naggais*; *herodes*, dative *heroda*, genitive *herodes* or *herodis*; *ïohannes*, accusative *ïohannen* (*ïohanna*, Mark I.19), dative *ïohanne, ïohannen,* and *ïohannau*, Luke IX.9, genitive *ïohannes* or *ïohannis*. Probably *taitrarkes, jannes, mambres,* and *airmogaineis* should be declined similarly.

### B. CONSONANTAL DECLENSION

#### a. Masculine

### § 95.

The names to be assigned here—*abia, aimmeira, barakeia, helia, þymiama, kajafa, kusa, papa, resa, satana*, etc.—are declined entirely regularly, with this sole exception: many, after the Greek fashion, take *s* in the nominative singular, as *aipafras, andraias, annas, barnabas, esaeias, zakarias, helias, þomas, ïairaimias, ïudas, lukas, tobeias, satanas*, etc. The Gothic name *sunjaifriþas* behaves in the same way.

Very many feminine forms are likewise declined according to this declension, such as *aiodia, beþania, gaiainna, maria, marþa, samaria, sarra*, and probably many others, such as *aivva, raibaikka, priska, susanna, saudauma*, etc. Similarly, the accusative plural *aipistulans*, Nehemiah VI.17, 19, occurs from *aipistule*. From the dative *herodiadein* (for *herodiadin*?) in Luke III.19 and the genitive *herodiadins* in Mark VI.17, 22, one may infer a nominative [Col. 0965] *herodiada*, though *herodias* appears to have been the more customary form in its place; see on Mark VI.19.

#### b. Feminine

**α. Root form *-on*.**

*Damasko, eikaunio, kaurinþo, aifaiso, ïaireiko, psalmo, aikklesjo, skaurpjo, laiktjo, kavtsjo.*

**β. Root form *-ein*.**

*Beþsfagei, aipiskaupei, praizbytairei.* Some words having the Greek ending *-e* form their remaining cases in accordance with this declension: thus *synagoge*, accusative *synagogein*, Luke VI.6; VII.5, dative *synagogein*, Luke IV.16, 20; *aipistaule*, accusative *aipistaulein*, Romans XVI.22, dative *aipistaulein*, 1 Corinthians V.9, dative plural *aipistaulem* (instead of *aipistauleim*), 2 Thessalonians III.17; *paraskaive*, accusative *paraskaivein*, Matthew XXVII.62; *syntyke*, accusative *syntykein*, Philippians IV.2. In the same way the datives *daikapaulein*, Mark V.20, and *ïairaupaulein*, Colossians IV.13, derive from *daikapaulis* and *ïairaupolis*.

> **Note 1.**—*Synagoge* forms other cases irregularly: genitive singular *synagogais*, Luke VIII.41; John IX.22; dative plural *synagogim*, Mark I.39; Luke IV.44.

> **Note 2.**—Some masculines whose nominative ends in *-n* are declined like feminines of this declension: *symaion*, genitive *symaions*, Luke III.30; *aharon*, genitive *aharons*, Luke I.5; *ammon*, genitive *ammons*, Luke III.25; *apaullon* (*apaullo*?), accusative *apaullon*, 1 Corinthians XVI.12, dative *apaullon*, IV.6, genitive *apaullons*, I.12; *addein* (*addei*?), genitive *addeins*, Luke III.28; *mailkein* (*mailkei*?), genitive *mailkeins*, III.28; *nerin*, genitive *nerins*, III.27. Perhaps *ïoanan* and *naiman* as well.

> **Note 3.**—*Ïairusalem* is likewise declined in the same manner: accusative *ïairusalem*, Luke II.22; dative *ïairusalem*, Mark XI.1; genitive *ïairusalems*, Nehemiah VII.2, 3.

### § 96.

In some cases, however, the Goth retained the Greek declension:

Singular nominative: besides the names cited above in *-as*, [Col. 0966] *-es*, and *-e*, one must also include *magdalene, salome; praufeteis* (προφῆτις, “prophetess”); *herodias*.

Accusative: *Iudaian*, Luke II.4; John VII; *zeloten*, Luke VI.15; *ïskarioten*, Mark III.19; Luke VI.16; *kananeiten*, Mark III.18; *ïohannen*, Matthew XI.7; Mark V.37; *paintekunsten*, 1 Corinthians XVI.8; *synagogen*, Mark I.21; and perhaps also the forms mentioned above with *ei* in place of *e* (cf. § 30, 3), *aipistaulein, paraskaivein, synagogein, syntykein*; *byssaun*, Luke XVI.19; *teitaun*, 2 Corinthians II.13; VIII.6; *alabalstraun*, Luke VII.37; *praitoriaun*, Mark XV.16; John XVIII.28; cf. *kaurbanaun*, Matthew XXVII.6; *seimona*, Mark III.18; XV.21.

Dative: *aivneika*, 2 Timothy I.15; *arabia*, Galatians IV.25; *idumaia*, Mark III.8; *ïudaia*, Luke III.1; 2 Corinthians I.16; *ïaurdane*, Mark I.5, 9; *ïohanne*, Matthew XI.4, 11; *mose*, Mark IX.4, 5; *magdalene*, Mark XVI.9 (and perhaps also *synagogei*, John XII.42, in place of *synagoge*); *gazaufilakio*, John VIII.20; *faraoni*, Romans IX.17.

Genitive: *Areimaþaias*, Matthew XXVII.57; Mark XV.43; *beþanias*, John XI.1; *galeilaias*, Mark I.9, 28; *ïudaias*, Mark X.1; Luke I.5; *ïturaias*, Luke III.1; *kaisarias*, Mark VIII.27; *daikapaulaios*, Mark VII.31; *synagogeis*, Luke VIII.41 (unless *synagogais* should be read here).

Plural nominative: *Israelitai*, Romans IX.4; *kretes*, Titus I.12; *hairaiseis*, Galatians V.20.

Accusative: *aromata*, Mark XVI.1.

Dative: *lystros*, 2 Timothy III.11 (unless perhaps *lystron* should be read, since elsewhere the Goth, except for *aþeineis*, 1 Thessalonians III.1, never uses a city-name solely as a plural).

> **Note.**—Certain names taken chiefly from Hebrew are, in Gothic as in Greek, indeclinable; for example: *aai, abeilem, aileisabeþ, beþlaihaim, gainnesaraiþ, ïuse, kafarnaum, nazaraiþ, sabbato, sion*; likewise words drawn from a Hebrew or Greek source: *aiffaþa, amen, anaþaima, kaidron, kaurban, laigaion, manna, maran aþa, paska, raka, taleiþa kumei, osanna*, etc.

## II. THE ADJECTIVE

(Cf. Welman, *Das gothische Adjectivum*, Stettin, 1835.)

[Col. 0965]

### § 97.

In the declension of the adjective, almost the same matters require consideration as in that of the substantive. First, there is a threefold development corresponding to the three genders; it is then subdivided into vocalic and consonantal declension; and finally it undergoes various modifications according as its root-form ends in one of the three vowels *a, i*, or *u*. You should observe, however, that adjectives in *i* correspond not so much to substantives possessing a similar root [Col. 0966] (§ 75 ff.) as to substantives in *a* preceded by *i* (§§ 67, 70, 73), so that perhaps the root-form *-ja* would with better reason be assigned to them. Otherwise, the adjective has cases and number just as does the substantive. Now, with reference to nominative endings, the following general table is drawn up.

### A. VOCALIC DECLENSION

[Col. 0967]

### § 98. 1. Root form *-a*: *GODA*

The following are declined in this manner: *abrs* “strong,” *agls* “ugly,” *ïnahs* “prudent,” *unairkns* “impious,” *framaldrs* “advanced in age,” *alls* “all,” *arms* “wretched,” *bairhts* “manifest,” *baikrs* “bitter,” *bauþs* “mute,” *biuhts* “accustomed,” *blinds* “blind,” *braids* “broad,” *gaurs* “sad,” *afguds* “impious,” *gaguds* “pious,” *gods* “good,” *-dogs* “-day-old,” *-duanus* “-day-old”;

*daubs* “dull,” *usdauds* “solicitous,” *diups* “deep,” *dumbs* “mute,” *dvals* “foolish,” *gadobs* “beautiful,” *lausquiþrs* “fasting,” *hafts* “affected,” *haihs* “one-eyed,” *-hairts* “-hearted”;

> **[Col. 0967]** For example, *arma-hairts* “merciful.” Translator.

*ushaists* “poor,” *halbs* “half,” *halks* “wretched,” *halts* “lame,” *hauhs* “high,” *hauns* “lowly,” *hanfs* “weak”;

> **[Col. 0968]** Properly, “having only one hand.” Translator.

*hulþs* “gracious,” *hlutrs* “pure,” *gaþaurbs* “modest,” *þaurfts* “necessary,” *þarbs* “necessary,” *þarihs* “unkempt, new,” *hauhþuhts, mikilþuhts* “proud,” *þvairhs* “angry,” *ïbns* “simple,” *ïbuks* “backward,” *kalds* “cold,” *niuklahs* “newborn,” *aljakuns* “foreign,” etc.; *airþakunds* “earthly,” etc.; *kunþs* “known,” etc.; *laggs* “long,” *samalauds* “equal, like,” etc.; *lasivs* “weak,” *lats* “lazy,” *unleds* “poor,” *galeiks* “like,” etc.; *fralets* “freed,” *liubs* “beloved,” *galaubs, galubs* “precious,” etc.; *galings* “mistaken,” *liuts* “a dissembler,” *uslukns* “opened,” *lustusams* “desired,” *mahts* “possible,” *gamaids* “weak, powerless,” *untilamalsks* “presumptuous,” *friaþvamilds* “pious,” *naqaþs* “naked,” *ganohs* “sufficient,” *andaneiþs* “adversary,” *andanems* “acceptable,” *juggs* “young,” *garaids* “appointed,” *raihts* “straight,” *rauds* “red,” *unmanariggvs* “unaccustomed,” *rums* “spacious,” *gariuds* “modest,” *urrugks* “rejected,” *saþs* “sated,” *unandsoks* “unassailable,” *siuks* “sick,” *skulds* “owing,” *gaskohs* “shod,” *slaihts* “smooth,” *smals* “small,” *snutrs* “wise,” *aglaitgastalds* “pursuing shameful gain,” *stamms* “mute,” *svarts* “black,” *svers* “honoured,” *svikns* “innocent,” *svinþs* “strong,” *tils* “fitting,” *untals* “foolish,” *triggvs* “faithful,” *unvahs* “irreproachable,” *anavairþs* “future,” *andvairþs* “present,” *viþravairþs* “opposed,” *vairþs* “worthy,” *vans* “lacking, deficient,” *lausavaurds* “vain-speaking,” etc.; *handuvaurhts* “made by hand,” etc.; *gavaurts* “rooted,” *vars* “sober,” *veihs* “holy,” *vilvs* “rapacious,” *gavamms* “unclean,” *unvamms* “spotless,” *ïnvinds* “perverse,” *unvits* “ignorant,” *fullavits* “perfect,” *vulþrs* “more powerful,” [Col. 0968] *vunds* “wounded,” *vods* “mad,” *fagrs* “useful,” *-falþs* “-fold”;

> **[Col. 0968]** For example, *ainfalþs* “single, simple,” etc. Translator.

*faurhts* “timid,” *gafaurs* “disposed,” *unfaurs* “talkative,” *þrutsfills* “leprous,” *fulls* “full,” *froþs* “wise,” *faihufriks* “avaricious,” *gawairbs* “joinable,” etc.; *weihts* “light,” *unweils* “continuous,” *weits* “white”; *ahmeins* “spiritual,” *airþeins* “earthly,” *aiveins* “eternal,” *barizeins* “barley-made,” *gulþeins* “golden,” *eisarneins* “iron,” *þaurneins* “thorny,” *leikeins* “bodily,” *galaubeins* “faithful,” *liuhadeins* “bright,” *muldeins* “dusty,” *pistikeins* “pistic,” *riqizeins* “dark,” *seiteins* “daily,” *silubreins* “silver,” *staineins* “stone,” *triveins* “wooden,” *filleins* “of skin”; *unaivisks* “unconfused,” *barnisks* “childish,” *gudisks* “divine,” *haiþivisks* “woodland,” *mannisks* “human,” *funisks* “fiery”; *ansteigs* “gracious,” *usbeisneigs* “long-suffering,” *gabeigs* “rich,” *hroþeigs* “victorious,” *þiuþeigs* “good,” *laiseigs* “fit to teach,” *listeigs* “crafty,” *mahteigs* “powerful,” *andanemeigs* “caring,” *uhteigs* “idle,” *sineigs* “old,” *gavairþeigs* “peaceful,” *vaurstveigs* “effective,” *gavizneigs* “joyful,” *audags* “blessed,” *gredags* “hungry,” *unhunslags* “not libating,” *manags* “many,” *modags* “angry,” *vulþags* “noble”; *unbarnahs* “bereft of children,” *stainahs* “stony,” *vainahs* “wretched,” *vaurdahs* “literal”; *handugs* “wise,” *uhtiugs* “idle”; *leitils* “small,” *mikils* “great,” *ubils* “evil”; *unfairins, usfairins* “blameless,” *fulgins* “hidden”; *samasaivals* “of one mind”; *skaþuls* “harmful”; *ainakls* “only, abandoned.”

> **Note 1.**—Adjectives whose root ends in *s* drop the ending *s* in the masculine nominative singular, like substantives: *gaqiss* “agreeing,” *hlas* “joyful,” *laus* “empty,” *sves* “particular,” *ungatass* “disorderly,” *usviss* “vain,” *hindarveis* “deceitful,” etc.; *unvis* “uncertain.”

> **Note 2.**—It is doubtful whether, when the root ends in *v*, this *v*, following *i* and *a*, is changed into *u* in the masculine and neuter nominative singular, as happens with substantives, and whether *qius, faus, usskaus*, or *qivs, favs, usskavs*, as the glossary presents them, should be read. The *v* of the derivative syllable, however, remains unchanged in *lasivs*, 2 Corinthians X.10.

> **Note 3.**—When *r* precedes, the root *s* remains in the masculine nominative singular; for example, *svers, vars, gaurs*, except, however, *anþar*, “other.”

> **Note 4.**—The vocative occurs only rarely in the vocalic form, and only in the singular: masculine *bauþs*, Mark IX.25; feminine *audahafta*, Luke I.28. Otherwise the consonantal form is chiefly used.

> **Note 5.**—The neuter singular nominative and accusative form in *-ata* is used interchangeably with the apocopated form; for example, nominative *allata*, Matthew V.18, 30; *veihata*, Romans VII.12; accusative *daubata*, Mark VIII.17; *mikilata*, Mark XIV.15; *vairþata*, Luke III.8; *juggata*, Mark II.22; *svaleikata*, Matthew IX.8; *hauhata*, Luke IV.5; alongside *all*, Matthew VII.19; Philippians III.8; *mikil*, Mark IV.39, 41; *wirþ*, 1 Corinthians XVI.4; *jugg*, Luke V.39; *svaleik*, Luke IX.9; *hauh*, Mark IX.2.

### § 99. 2. Root form *-i*: *SUTI* “gentle,” *HRAINI* “pure,” *NIVI* “new,” *VILþI* “wild”

[Col. 0969]

In this declension there is greater difficulty concerning the form of the nominative singular, from which the accusative and genitive are partly derived, since it does not occur sufficiently often for a general rule concerning it to be safely established. Be that as it may, the following observations may be made:

1. **Masculine:**

   a. The original form seems to have been in *-is*, from which the other cases are produced both by subtraction and by lengthening. This form now occurs only in *airknis* “holy” and *sutis* “gentle,” 1 Timothy III.3 (*navis* “dead,” Romans VII.8). It may indeed be present in *airzis* “false,” *analaugnis* “hidden,” *unnutis* “useless,” *vailameris* “praiseworthy,” etc.; but *airzeis, analaugns, unnuts,* and *vailamers* may also have been used instead.

   b. Final *i* is absent in *hrains* “clean,” Matthew VIII.3; *aljakuns* “foreign,” Romans XI.24; *gamains* “a partaker,” Romans XI.17; *gafaurs* “modest,” 1 Timothy III.2; *andanems* “accepted,” Luke IV.24; *bruks* “useful,” 2 Timothy IV.11 (*bleiþs* “kind,” Luke VI.36; Titus I.8); likewise where a long vowel or diphthong precedes in the root: *auþs* “deserted,” *riurs* “corruptible,” *sels* “good,” *skeirs* “manifest,” *voþs* “acceptable,” *vailamers* “praiseworthy,” *anasiuns* “visible,” *analaugns* “hidden,” *andasets* “abominable,” *skauns* “beautiful,” *ufaiþs* “sworn,” *bireks* “in danger,” *anahaims* “domestic,” *afhaims* “foreign,” *sleiþs* “harsh,” *kaurs* “heavy,” *unqeþs* “ineffable,” *speds* “slow,” *alevs* “olive,” *usgruds* “sluggish,” *reiks* “king, ruler.”

   c. But *i* is expanded to *ei* in *alþeis* “old,” John III.4, and *vilþeis* “wild,” Romans XI.17. This also occurs when two consonants precede, the first of which is a liquid: *fairneis* “old,” *airzeis* “false,” *mildeis* “soft, tender,” *ïngardeis* “an inhabitant.” The same ending was probably used, as in substantives, where a short formative syllable precedes; for example, *framaþeis* “foreign,” though no evidence exists for this. Finally, it is doubtful whether one should say *dauþubleis* or *dauþublis*, “mortal.”

   d. When the root ends in a vowel, *j* is inserted between that vowel and the ending, as in *niujis* “new,” 1 Corinthians V.7; *ubillojis* “evil-doing”; *fullatojis* “perfect”; or, when the root-vowel is *i*, this and the ending’s *i* merge into *ei*, as in *freis* “free,” 1 Corinthians VII.21, 22. *Undarleijis* “lowest” is to be understood in the same way as *niujis*, provided the reading at Ephesians III.8 is genuine.

   e. Likewise, when the root syllable is short and ends in a consonant, the same *j* is placed before the ending, as in *sakjis* “quarrelsome,” 1 Timothy III.3 (unless this is a substantive), *warjis* “who,” Luke IX.46; and likewise in *aljis* “other,” *grindafraþjis* “faint-hearted,” *samafraþjis* “like-minded,” *unkarjis* “careless,” *unsibjis* “wicked,” *gaviljis* “willing,” *midjis* “middle.”

2. **Neuter:**

   a. Adjectives which drop *i* in the masculine commonly suppress it also in the neuter; for example, *hrain*, Matthew VIII.3; *analaugn*, Mark IV.22; *unsel*, Matthew VI.23; *audaset*, Luke XVI.15; *gamain*, Romans XIV.14; *andanem*, Luke IV.19; *bruk*, 2 Timothy II.21. Yet *vailameri*, Philippians IV.8, also occurs, from which a masculine *vailameris* may be inferred. *Anasium*, *Skeir.* II.d, according to the recent investigations of Castiglione, is a false reading, to be corrected to *anasiun*.

   b. Those ending in *-eis* in the masculine form the neuter in *-i*, as *vilþi*, Mark I.6, in this passage.

   c. Finally, those having a short root syllable or a vowel-final root probably possess only the full form *-jata*, as *niujata*, Matthew IX.17.

3. **Feminine:**

   a. Those which drop *i* in the masculine and neuter have, at least in the examples presently available, a feminine agreeing with the masculine: *sels*, 1 Corinthians XIII.4; *skeirs*, *Skeir.* IV.b; *bruks*, 1 Timothy IV.8; *Skeir.* IV.b. The form *voþi*, 2 Corinthians II.15, formed after the pattern of substantives, is unique and perhaps arose through a copyist’s negligence. Be that as it may, a masculine *voþis* must be assumed, to which feminine *voþi* relates in the same manner as neuter *vailameri* to *vailameris*. As for *navis*, Romans VII.8, it is evidently irregularly construed, just as *nimands* (for *nimandei*) is in the same passage.

   b. Other adjectives of this declension probably had the ending *-ja*, though this is certain only for *niuja*, John XIII.34; accusative *gavilja*, 1 Corinthians VII.12; and *frija*, Romans VII.3.

> **Note.**—The declension of certain words is indeterminate: *airknis*, 1 Timothy III.3; *unairknai*, 2 Timothy III.2; *unmildjai*, 2 Timothy III.3; *friaþvamildai*, Romans XII.10.

### § 100. 3. Root form *-u*: *HARDU*, “hard”

It occurs only in the masculine, feminine, and neuter nominative singular, and in the neuter accusative singular; the remaining cases are formed from the root-form *i*, as follows:

They are declined in this way: *aggvus* “narrow,” *aglus* “difficult,” *laushandus* “empty-handed,” *hnasqus* “tender,” *þlaqus* “delicate,” *qairrus* “gentle,” *manvus* “ready,” *tulgus* “firm,” *filufaihus* “varied,” *þaursus* “dry.”

### B. CONSONANTAL DECLENSION

### § 101. Root form *-a*

Adjectives whose root-form has *i* or *u* are declined in this way, with the addition that *j* is placed before the ending; for example, *niuja, niujo, niujo; hardja, hardjo, hardjo*.

Very many adjectives occur only in the consonantal form; for example, *usfairina, unfairina* “blameless,” *usvena* “hoping,” *usfilma* “terrified,” *ushaista* “poor,” *alaþarba* “needy, destitute,” *unvita* “ignorant,” *fullavita* “perfect,” *ïngardja* “an inhabitant,” *usgrudja* “sluggish,” *unkarja* “careless,” *svultavairþja* “near death, dying.”

> **Note.**—From *ainaha* “only,” the feminine *ainoho* is irregularly formed.

## INTENSIVE DEGREES OF ADJECTIVES

### § 102.

How the intensive degrees of adjectives are formed will be explained when word formation is discussed (see § 151); for the present, only their declension is to be set forth.

1. The comparative is always declined consonantally: in the masculine and neuter after the manner of adjectives of the first declension, but in the feminine with the ending *-ei*, like the substantives *managei*, etc., according to the following paradigm:

The old comparatives (§ 151) in *-uma*, such as *auhuma* “higher,” *aftuma* “last” (*hinduma* “hindmost”), *hleiduma* “left,” *ïftuma* “following,” *ïnnuma* “innermost” (*speduma* “last”), *fruma* “former, first,” have only the consonantal form and likewise form the feminine with the ending *-ei*: for example, *fruma*, neuter *frumo*, feminine *frumei*, etc.

2. The superlative, which has the ending *-ist*, may be declined either vocalically or consonantally, and is declined throughout after the pattern of adjectives of the first declension.

## DECLENSION OF PARTICIPLES

### § 103.

Participles are indeed classed with adjectives on account of their form; but, since they display certain peculiarities in declension, it is necessary to mention them here.

There are two participles, active and passive; the passive, moreover, has two forms, according as it belongs to a verb of the first or of the two later conjugations. Except for the masculine singular nominative and vocative, the active participle occurs only with consonantal declension; the passive participle occurs declined both vocalically and consonantally. Further observe that the active participle forms the feminine by adding the ending *-ei*, after the pattern of comparatives (§ 102.1).

1. **ACTIVE PARTICIPLE**

2. **PASSIVE PARTICIPLE**

   a. **FIRST CONJUGATION**

   b. **LATER CONJUGATION**

which are declined entirely after the manner of adjectives.

### a. Cardinals

### § 104.

The first three cardinal numbers are completely declinable; the others up to nineteen are declined only in the genitive, or, when used substantivally, in the dative. Of the tens from twenty to sixty, all have their cases; the rest remain indeclinable, while hundreds and thousands are again declinable.

### b. Ordinals

### § 105.

Ordinal numbers are declined consonantally, except “second,” *anþar*, neuter *anþar*, feminine *anþara*. Of the rest only these occur: “first,” *fruma*, neuter *frumo*, feminine *frumei* (see § 102.2), of which there is also the superlative *frumists*, declined either vocalically or consonantally [Col. 0975] after the pattern of other superlatives; “third,” *þridja*; “sixth,” *saihsta*; “eighth,” *ahtuda*; “ninth,” *niunda*; “tenth,” *taihunda*; “fifteenth,” *fimftataihunda*. “Fourth,” however, would probably be *fidurta*, “fifth” *fimfta*, “seventh” *sibunda*, etc.

### c. Distributives

*Tveihnai*, “two apiece,” is declined vocalically. Evidence for the remaining distributives is lacking.

### d. Multiplicatives

[Col. 0976]

The multiplicatives *ainfalþs* “single, simple,” *fidurfalþs* “fourfold,” etc., are declined after the pattern of other adjectives; on their formation see § 168.

### e. Iteratives

For the expressed iteratives *ainamma* “once,” *tvaim sinþam* “twice,” etc., see Syntax.

## IV. THE PRONOUN

[Col. 0975]

### A. PERSONAL PRONOUNS

### § 106.

Personal pronouns have no gender, except in the third person, which has, alongside the genderless reflexive, another form with gender. Moreover, the personal pronoun has, besides singular and plural number, a dual, which has become obsolete in substantives and adjectives.

#### aa. PRONOUN WITHOUT GENDER

> **Note 1.**—In place of *ugkis*, the apocopated form *ugk*, Ephesians VI.22, also occurs, unless—what is most probable—the copyist, misled by resemblance because of the following *ïst*, omitted the *is*.

> **Note 2.**—For the writing of *uggkis, iggqis* in place of *ugkis, igqis*, see § 40.5; concerning the reading *inqis*, Luke XIX.31, see also the note in the same place.

> **Note 3.**—The reflexive forms serve not merely for the singular, but also for the dual and plural.

> **Note 4.**—The distinct forms *uns* and *unsis* appear to differ in that *unsis* is the primitive form, serving for two cases, and was subsequently shortened to *uns*, especially in the accusative; either because that case, even in substantives and adjectives, is shorter than the dative, or for some other reason.

#### bb. PRONOUN WITH GENDER

### § 107.

Possessives derive their form from the genitive of the personal pronouns (§ 152) and, like adjectives, though only vocalically, are declined.

### § 109.

The relative is formed from the particles *ïzei* and *ei*. The former is placed independently after substantives or demonstratives; the latter, however, is appended as an enclitic to personal pronouns (*ïkei*, 1 Corinthians XV.9; 2 Corinthians X.1; 1 Timothy I.15; *þuei*, Romans XIV.4; *þuzei*, Mark I.11; Luke III.22; *þukei*, Mark I.11 margin; *juzei*, Luke XVI.15; 2 Corinthians VIII.10; Galatians V.4; Ephesians II.13, 17; 1 Thessalonians II.13; *ïzvizei*, Galatians III.1) and to the demonstrative. § 110. α. *was*: who?

“Note 1.—This pronoun has the instrumental form *we* at Matthew V.47; VI.25, 31; Mark IV.30; IX.50; Luke VII.31, etc.

*Warjis*, neuter *warjata*, feminine *warja* (Mark XII.28), is declined throughout according to the pattern of *niujis* (§ 99); for example: masculine singular accusative *warjana*, John XIII.22; dative *warjamma*, Mark XII.23; genitive *warjis*, Luke XX.33; plural nominative *warjai*, John VI.64; accusative *warjans*, John XIII.18; neuter singular genitive *warjis*, John X.32.

## B. ON CONJUGATION

[Col. 0979]

(See Gräfe, *On Strong and Weak Conjugation*, in the St Petersburg *Bulletin scientifique*, 1837, no. 15.)

§ 113. In conjugation, person, number, mood, tense, and voice must be considered.

There are three persons and three numbers; for besides singular and plural, the verb also has a dual, to which, however, the third person does not belong (see § 187.2). The endings of the persons in the present originally appear to have been as follows: singular: 1. *-a*, 2. *-is*, 3. *-iþ*; dual: 1. *-os*, 2. *-ats*; plural: 1. *-am*, 2. *-iþ*, 3. *-and*.

These still occur in the earlier (primitive) conjugation, though in the later one they have undergone various changes caused by the preceding vowel of the root (§ 127). The preterite, originally formed by vowel alternation or reduplication, has no personal ending in the first and third persons singular; but *-t* is affixed in the second singular, *-u* in the first dual, *-uts* in the second dual, and finally *-um*, *-uþ*, *-un* in the first, second, and third plural. We have already observed above (§ 32.4a) that the *i* of the second and third singular persons and of the second plural person had been weakened from *a*.

There are three moods of the verb: indicative, conjunctive (subjunctive), and imperative. To these must be added, as nominal forms, the infinitive and participle; the latter, by its form and meaning, is to be assigned among the adjectives (§ 103).

[Col. 0980] There are only two tenses: present and preterite. Whether a distinctive later form of the subjunctive is concealed in *bairaiþ*, Galatians V.10, *svignjaiþ*, Colossians III.15, and *tiuhaiþ*, I Thessalonians IV.14, is uncertain; see concerning this § 182, note 7, and § 186, note 4.

Finally, verbs have three voices: active, passive, and middle. The passive is incomplete, and the middle occurs only in certain fragments.

§ 114. As meanings differ, so does the method of formation. There are three conjugations: strong, weak, and mixed; for example: *vakan*, “to wake,” *vakjan*, “to awaken,” *vaknan*, “to become awake”; *ganahan*, “to suffice,” *ganohjan*, “to make sufficient,” *ganohnan*, “to be fulfilled”; *þairsan*, “to dry,” *þaursjan*, “to make dry,” *þaursnan*, “to become dry.” The root-form of the first, or strong, conjugation ends in a consonant; that of the second, or weak, conjugation in a vowel; and that of the third, or mixed, conjugation in an *n* belonging to the formative suffix.

Verbs of the first conjugation generally have an intransitive meaning; upon passing into the second, they become transitive: for example, *sitan*, “to sit,” *satjan*, “to set”; *ligan*, “to lie,” *lagjan*, “to lay”; *vindan*, “to wind itself,” *vandjan*, “to wind, turn”; *sigqan* (*siggqan*), “to sink,” *sagqjan*, “to immerse”; *brinnan*, “to burn,” *branjan*, “to burn [something]”; *nisan*, “to be healed,” *nasjan*, “to heal”; *hneivan*, “to incline,” *hnaivjan*, “to humble”; *reisan*, “to rise,” [Col. 0981] *raisjan*, “to raise”; *driusan*, “to fall,” *drausjan*, “to cast down”; *urrinnan*, “to go out,” *urranjan*, “to cause to arise.”

In the third conjugation, however, the transitive or active meanings of the first and second conjugations become neuter and acquire a passive sense: for example, *bindan*, “to bind,” *bundnan*, “to be bound”; *giutan*, “to pour,” *gutnan*, “to flow”; *dishniupan*, “to break apart,” *dishnaupnan*, “to be broken apart”; *þairsan*, “to dry,” *þaursnan*, “to become dry”; *fraliusan*, “to lose,” *fralusnan*, “to perish”; *lukan*, “to shut,” *luknan*, “to be opened”; *disskreitan*, “to rend,” *disskritnan*, “to be rent”; *gatairan*, “to destroy,” *gataurnan*, “to be destroyed”; *skaidan*, “to separate,” *skaidnan*, “to be separated”; *aukan*, “to increase,” *auknan*, “to grow”; *blindjan*, “to blind,” *blindnan*, “to be blinded”; *gabigjan*, “to enrich,” *gabignan*, “to be rich”; *dauþjan*, “to kill,” *dauþnan*, “to die”; *drobjan*, “to disturb,” *drobnan*, “to be shaken”; *fraqistjan*, “to destroy,” *fraqistnan*, “to perish”; *gaqiujan*, “to make alive,” *gaqiunan*, “to be made alive”; *gahaftjan*, “to bind,” *gahaftnan*, “to be bound, adhere”; *hailjan*, “to heal,” *hailnan*, “to be healed”; *ufarhafjan*, “to exalt,” *ufarhafnan*, “to be exalted, become proud”; *þlahsjan*, “to terrify,” *þlahsnan*, “to be troubled”; *mikiljan*, “to magnify,” *mikilnan*, “to glory”; *afslauþjan*, “to terrify,” *afslauþnan*, “to be terrified”; *svinþjan*, “to strengthen,” *svinþnan*, “to be strengthened”; *gagavairþjan*, “to reconcile,” *gagavairþnan*, “to be reconciled”; *veihan*, “to sanctify,” *veihnan*, “to be sanctified”; *fulljan*, “to fill,” *fullnan*, “to be filled.”

§ 115. The three conjugations differ especially in forming the preterite. In the first it is formed by vowel alternation and reduplication; in the second and third by a characteristic ending appended to the verbal root and still recognizable as derived from the independent strong verb (§ 127). The second and third conjugations differ from each other in that the present in the second is formed weakly—that is, by a vowel placed before the ending—whereas in the third it is formed strongly, as in the first—that is, by an ending immediately attached to a verbal root ending in a consonant. The same difference also occurs in the imperative: in the first and third conjugations it ends consonantally, but in the second vocalically.

From the powerful influence which vowel alternation exercises throughout the Gothic language, it must be concluded that the alternational, that is, the first conjugation is the most ancient and by far the primitive one. Reduplication also appears to have prevailed from earliest times; yet, where vowel alternation sufficed to distinguish the tenses, it could fall out of use, and in the language as now preserved be employed together with vowel alternation only exceptionally. Later, as the character of the language permitted, the second and third conjugations arose partly from nominal roots and partly, with the aid of vowel alternation, from verbs of the first conjugation.

§ 116. A general table follows, displaying the forms of conjugation at one view.

“a) That the first person present indicative is found in the following examples: α) from strong verbs, *galeiþos*, John XIV.23; *bidjos*, Mark X.37; β) from weak verbs, *taujos*, John XIV.23; *habos*, I Corinthians IX.6;

“b) That the first person present subjunctive is known only through the strong form *sitaiva*, Mark X.37. Hence, from comparison with subjunctives of both conjugations elsewhere, it must be concluded that it existed in weak forms such as *sokjaiva*, *habaiva*, *spillova*;

“c) That the first person preterite indicative does not in fact occur; but the first person present indicative of certain anomalous verbs whose present has the form of the strong preterite (§ 134), for example *siju*, John X.30; XVII.22; *magu*, Mark X.30, permits us confidently to posit strong verbs *qeþu*, *bundu*, *galiþu*, etc., and weak verbs *sokidedu*, *habaidedu*, *spillodedu*;

“d) That the first person preterite subjunctive likewise occurs nowhere; but by analogy with the present subjunctive, in which, while the second person ends in *-aits*, the first ends in *-aiva*, it is probable that here too, while the second person ended in *-eits*, the first ended in *-eiva*;

“e) That the second person present indicative is: α) in strong verbs, *bigitats*, Mark XI.2; Luke XIX.30; *drigkats*, Mark X. [Col. 0983] 39; *andbindats*, Luke XIX.33; *bidjats*, Mark X.38; β) in weak verbs, *taujats*, Mark XI.3, 5; *galaubjats*, Matthew IX.28;

“f) That the second person present subjunctive can be inferred only from the strong form *qiþaits*, Mark XI.3; XIV.14; Luke XIX.31; but from comparison of the present subjunctives of the strong and weak conjugations it may legitimately be maintained that *habaits*, *sokjaits*, and *spillots* also existed. Further observe:

“g) The second person imperative: α) of strong verbs, *gateihats*, Luke VII.22; *saiwats*, Matthew IX.30; *gaggats*, Mark XI.2; XIV.13; Luke XIX.30. Hence *attiuhats* or *attiuhaits* must be read for *attiuhits*, Mark XI.2; β) of weak verbs, only the example *hirjats*, Mark I.17, is found;

“h) The second person preterite indicative: α) of strong verbs, *gasewuts*, Luke VII.22, compare *vituts* and *maguts*, Mark X.38; β) of weak verbs, *gahausideduts*, Luke VII.22.

“i) The second person preterite subjunctive is not in fact found, but must be inferred from the form *vileits*. Evidence is lacking for the third conjugation; nevertheless, the following rule may be established: it is inflected strongly in the present, but weakly in the preterite.

[Col. 0984] “Note 4.—The form of the first person plural imperative is confirmed by the following examples: a) of strong verbs: *drigkam*, I Corinthians XV.32; *usvairpam*, Romans XIII.12; *usqimam*, Mark XII.7; *usleiþam*, Mark IV.35; *galeiþam*, Luke VIII.22; *aflaham*, Luke XX.14; *gaggam*, Mark I.38; XIV.42; John XI.16; XIV.31; *visam*, Luke XV.23; b) of weak verbs: *vaurkjam*, Galatians VI.10, compare Mark IX.5; *hrainjam*, II Corinthians VII.1; *gavasjam*, Romans XIII.12; *dulþjam*, I Corinthians V.8; *matjam*, XV.32.”

## I. ACTIVE

[Col. 0983]

### FIRST CONJUGATION

#### a. VOWEL-ALTERNATING (WITHOUT REDUPLICATION)

§ 117. From the different kinds of vowel alternation arise the following subdivisions of the first conjugation:

“Note 1.—In the first three classes the dominant root vowel is *a*; in the fourth, *i*; in the fifth, *u*. The first three are distinguished in this respect: in verbs of the first class two consonants, the former of which is a liquid or *s*, follow the root vowel; in verbs of the second class a single liquid follows it; and in verbs of the third class a mute, sibilant, or semivowel. Moreover, the second and third classes appear to be irregular forms of the first, which must be regarded as primitive, for: 1) in those classes whose root vowel is *i* or *u*, the vowel of the passive participle corresponds to the vowel of the plural preterite; the same, therefore, must be expected of the root vowel *a*; 2) the first class consists of verbs in which two consonants follow the root vowel, and therefore any alteration of the vowel, whether by weakening or lengthening, demanded by the laws of vowel alternation, was at least as little possible as could be; 3) several very ancient verbs which in the present have the strong preterite form, from which they again form a weak preterite (§ 133.2), follow the first class of vowel alternation, although they take only a single consonant after the root vowel; for example, *skal, skulun*, from *SKILAN*; *man, munun*, from *MINAN*. Thus similarly *stal, stulun* (instead of [Col. 0984] *stelun*) from *stilan*, etc., must originally have existed.

“Note 2.—That in all these classes of vowel alternation *i* and *u* before *r*, *h*, and *w* are broken into *ai* and *au*, see § 32.5.”

Thus, for example: present *hlahja*, imperative *hlahei*, active participle *hlahjands*.”

#### b. REDUPLICATING

§ 124. Reduplication consists in doubling before *ai* the initial consonant of the verbal root; for example, *hahan*, preterite *haihah*; *saltan*, preterite *saisalt*. But if the initial element is a vowel, reduplication is accomplished merely by prefixing *ai*, for example *aukan*, preterite *aiauk*. If there are two or more consonants, only the first is doubled, for example *fraisan*, preterite *faifrais*, except for consonant clusters *sk*, *st* (and *sp*), for example *skaidan*, preterite *skaiskaid*. Reduplicating verbs are divided into two classes, according as they are formed with or without vowel alternation. Only verbs having either *e* as their root vowel or *ai* serving in its place (§ 32.3) belong to the latter class. Hence the following table is drawn up.

“Note.—If *flauteiþ*, I Corinthians XIII.4, is really to be read, it is used in place of *flautiþ* (§ 30, note 2); but perhaps *flautaiþ* should be read more correctly, in which case it would belong to the second conjugation (*haban*).”

“Note.—From *saian* occurs the second person singular preterite indicative *saisost*, Luke XIX.21. *Saijiþ*, Mark IV.14, is used only for euphony (§ 34.4) in place of *saiïþ*, II Corinthians IX.6.”

### SECOND CONJUGATION

§ 127. In the second, weak or vocalic conjugation, there are three different forms, according as the root-form of the verb ends in *i*, *ai*, or *o*.

In forming the present, root *i* before a vowel either becomes *j* or contracts with a following *i* into *ei*; [Col. 0990] *ai*, however, before a vowel ending disappears, unless that vowel is *i*, which is dropped after *ai*. Conversely, after *o* all vowels of the ending disappear, so that *o* remains unchanged in all endings.

The preterite is formed from the root compounded with the preterite of the strong verb *didan, dad, dedun* (from which *deds* has arisen); compare § 25.4. This verb is still clearly evident in the indicative dual and plural and throughout the subjunctive. In the singular indicative alone, which properly ought to sound *-dad, -dast, -dad*, the final consonant is dropped; and in the second person, so that the quantity of the vowel previously long by position, but shortened by this loss, might probably be compensated, the long plural vowel *e* is introduced in place of short *a*: *-da, -des, -da*.

#### 1. ROOT-FORM IN *-i*

§ 128. Here there is a certain distinction in forming the present and imperative. Where a long root syllable or a short derivative syllable precedes, the *i* of the root-form contracts with the *i* of the ending into *ei*; but where a short root syllable precedes, it is lengthened in such a way that the *i* of the root-form changes into *j*. Moreover, the same transition to *j* occurs in order to avoid hiatus.

##### a. *sokjan*, to seek. b. *lagjan*, to lay. Indicative.

In other respects they are inflected regularly: that is, the present like the preterite of the first conjugation, and the preterite like the syncopated preterite of the second conjugation (§ 128, note 4); for example:

Nor is the plural imperative better established, since the forms *ogeiþ*, Matthew X.26; *kunneiþ*, Mark XIII.29; John XV.18; *gamuneiþ*, John XV.20, may with equal right be referred to the subjunctive; compare § 186.

2. To the verbs mentioned above, and specifically to the fourth ablaut class, also belongs *viljan*, “to wish,” preterite *vilda*. It has, however, the peculiarity that it lacks a present indicative, the place of which is supplied by the subjunctive:

# CHAPTER THREE. ON THE FORMATION OF WORDS

[Col. 1001]

§ 136. We call the root the primary material from which a word is formed. Yet a root nowhere occurs in the language as it has been transmitted to us; only the stem, sprung from the root, occurs, and from this, with formative and inflectional elements added, the word comes into being. The root, therefore, is something abstract; the stem, something concrete. Their forms, nevertheless, may sometimes coincide.

Without a single exception, roots are monosyllabic. But because several sounds may combine to form one syllable, roots, with regard to their ending, are called vocalic or consonantal.

1) Vocalic roots are:

a) Either a simple vowel, as *i* (the root of the pronoun *ïs*), *u* (the interrogative particle);

b) Or a consonant and a vowel, as *þa* (the root of the pronoun *þata*), *hi* (the root of the pronoun *his*), and the verbal roots *lai, vai, sai, bau, stau, kei*, etc.

> **Note.**—The primitive vowel *a* is too general in value to constitute a root by itself; rather, it is probably restricted to something more particular either by weakening (to *i* or *u*) or by lengthening (to *o*), etc., or it acquires radical force when strengthened by a consonant.

2) Consonantal roots consist of either one or two consonants, and are:

a) A vowel and a consonant, as in the verbal roots *aik, auk, al, an, at*;

b) A vowel between two consonants, for example: *hah, bar, mait, skaid, sniþ, stig, skrit, band, varp, halp, svalt, sland*, etc.

§ 137. Considered in relation to the stems to which they give rise, roots are of four kinds:

a) Verbal, as in the roots cited above, *lai, aik, hah*, etc.;

b) Nominal, as *aiz, ast, bloþ*, etc.;

c) Pronominal, as *i, þa, hi*, etc.;

d) Particles, as *ak, and, bi, du*, etc.

> **Note.**—That the root of all words is a verb is by no means proved in the Gothic language. On the contrary, there are not a few words which seem, either in form or in meaning, to resist derivation from a verbal root. It is indeed true that a sentence cannot be understood without a verb; but there is a difference between a verbal idea and the verb itself. For the connection inherent in a verb—the union of a copula with the idea of an action—is itself already a certain advance in speech, and therefore presupposes something earlier; indeed, in several other languages it has not yet been achieved. We admittedly concede that, from a higher point of view, the opinion that individual words and individual nouns proceed from the verb is not without foundation; but we believe that the grammarian must refrain from this opinion and attend only to the linguistic material as it occurs. Therefore, prompted by this truth, we shall confine ourselves to elucidating the Gothic [Col. 1002] language through itself. Nor is there reason to divide roots into verbal and pronominal (Bopp, *Vergleichende Grammatik*, p. 105), since the former divide again into verbal and nominal, and the latter into pronominal and particle roots, and thus correspond exactly to this division.

§ 138. In verbal roots the vowel is for the most part regularly altered (ablaut, § 32.3). Now, as stated there, the following ablaut classes occur:

One might expect that in all these ablaut classes the radical vowel would always be found in the same position. But, upon closer examination, this is not so. For if, for example, one always takes the vowel of the present as radical, then in the first three ablaut classes one can scarcely explain how *a* and *u* could have arisen from *i*. If, on the contrary, one always seeks the root in the singular preterite, the breaking found in the fourth and fifth classes will oppose this. Therefore the following principle may be established: in each ablaut class, the vowel must be regarded as radical from which the others are derived in the most straightforward way according to the known laws of sounds. On this basis, the vowel of the singular preterite in the first three classes, and the vowel of the passive participle in the remaining classes, must be regarded as radical.

§ 139. We have already mentioned above (§ 119 ff.) the verbs belonging to the different ablaut classes. But there are also many other stems which, exhibiting the same ablaut relation, must likewise be assigned to strong verbs, although they no longer occur in the language as it has reached us. The following, then, belong here:

1) *Svillan*, “to swell”; *ufsvalleins*, “swelling”;—*hilþan*, “to be gracious”; *haldis*, “kindly disposed”; *viljahalþei*, “goodwill”; *hulþs*, “kind, propitious”;—*vilþan*, “to be wild, strong (?)”; *vilþeis*, “wild”; *valdan*, “to rule”; *vulþus*, “glory”;—*vimman*, “to defile”; *gavamms*, “unclean”; *anavammjan*, “to blame”;—*svimman*, “to swim”; *svumsl*, “a plank”;—*ïnnan*, “to favour”; *anno*, “a yearly wage”; *ansts*, “grace”;—*grindan*, “to grind, crush”; *grindafraþjis*, “faint-hearted”; *grundus*, “ground, earth”;—*tindan*, “to burn”; *tandjan*, “to kindle”; *tundnan*, “to be kindled”;—*sinþan*, “to go”; *sinþ*, “a going, step, journey”; *gasinþa*, “a travelling companion”; *sandjan*, “to send”;—*vriggan*, “to twist, encircle”; [Col. 1003] *vruggo*, “a snare”;—*þigkan*, “to think”; *þagks*, “thanksgiving”; *þagkjan*, “to think”; *þugkjan*, “to seem”;—*sviggvan*, “to sway”; *afsvaggvjan*, “to shake”;—*vairdan*, “to care for”; *vairdus*, “a host”; *vards*, “a guard”; *fravardjan*, “to corrupt”;—*vairman*, “to become warm”; *varms*, “warm”; *vaurms*, “a worm”;—*flaihtan*, “to twist”; *flahto*, “a torque.”

> **Note.**—Regarding some of these stems, the question arises whether, despite the ablaut to which they are subject, they should indeed be referred to those lost strong verbs, or whether one should rather believe that ablaut has sometimes also entered domains other than verbal roots (§ 32.3, note 2), since the idea seems to approach a nominal rather than a verbal root; for example, *qinan, knivan, dagan*.

> **Note 2.**—Other words cannot be derived according to the rules of ablaut and therefore resist an origin from a strong verb. Such are especially names of heavenly bodies, as *sunna, mena, stairno*; of elements and natural phenomena, as *airþa, vato, fon, vinds, rign*; of animals, as *fauho, auhsa, lamb, viþrus, ulbandus, asilus, fugls, ara, dubo, ahaks, hana, sparva*; of plants and their parts, as *triu, bagms, aurts, gras, þaurnus, asts, tains, vaurts, laufs, akran, basi, peika, smakka*; of bodily members, as *haubiþ, auso, augo, munþs, tunþus, tuggo, hals, arms, brusts, vamba, fotus*, etc., although some other words belonging to this class may perhaps also be referred to a verbal root, such as *hunds* and *handus* to *hinþan*, *vulfs* to *vilvan* (?), and the like.

§ 140. Thus, in grammar, as in plants, the root is the part hidden from sight from which the word grows; the stem, however, emerges visibly from the root in order to form a concrete word. Now the stem of a word too, if we separate it from its formative element, always appears in monosyllabic form; but if we consider the word relative to its inflectional element—that is, if we separate only this element—the stem may be derivative, enriched by a formative addition, and consequently polysyllabic. Thus, for example, *nam* is the root and *nim* the stem of *niman*; but *numt* (with the formative addition *t*, § 148) is the stem of *numts*, and *nemeig* (with the formative addition *eig*, § 150, ζ) the stem of *nemeigs*.

> **Note.**—The stem differs from the fundamental form in that the latter is already enriched by a formative element. Hence the radical form must be treated in discussing the inflection of words, but the stem in discussing formation. Thus, for example, *nam* is the root, *numt* the stem, and finally *NUMPTI* the fundamental form of *numts*.

§ 141. If we consider the formation of words only externally, we shall see that it is produced either by simple addition of the termination proper to each class of words, with or without ablaut—for example, *niman, nems* from the root *nam*—or by the composition of two or more stems, as *afniman, arbinumja, miþgarda* [Col. 1005] *vaddjus*. But if we consider this same formation internally, that is, in view of the word’s proper meaning, it will be seen to divide into four classes: nominal, pronominal, verbal, and adverbial. Formative elements are always immediately joined to the stem, and inflectional elements are then appended to them. Moreover, a formative element is either a simple consonant (as *t* in *numts*) or a complete syllable (as *eig* in *nemeigs*). Where a further formative addition is affixed to an already derived word, several formative syllables may follow one another, as in *skalkinassus* from *skalks*.

# A. NOMINAL FORMATION

[Col. 1005]

## I. NOUN

§ 142. Although gender has some influence upon the meaning of a word (§ 59), here that influence is for the most part so confused and its laws so little known that, in considering word-formation, only secondary attention may be given to it. Where gender rests upon a distinction of natural sex, as in *niþjis*, “male kinsman,” *niþjo*, “female kinswoman”; *garazna*, “neighbour, next”; *garazno*, “female neighbour”; *þius*, “male servant”; *þivi*, “female servant,” this is always evident from the meaning and does indeed bear upon word-formation. But where this natural distinction is lacking, it is now impossible safely to compare the meanings displayed by the various grammatical genders in word-formation. Although one may say in general that the masculine signifies rather the concrete, while the feminine and neuter signify rather the abstract, as well as an action and its object, this general distinction is nevertheless too vague and subject to too many exceptions for a division according to the three genders to offer any advantage in explaining nominal formation. For this reason, it would perhaps be preferable first to set out the derived form and then to introduce the division by gender.

§ 143. 1) Derivation without a **FORMATIVE ELEMENT**.

a) From verbs of the strong conjugation:

aa) From the present only very few words are derived, and these almost exclusively in the first ablaut class; for example, masculine *bairgs* (from *bairgan*); neuter *sinþ* (from *sinþan*), *anafilh* (from *filhan*), *gild* (from *gildan*), *gavairþi* (from *vairþan*); feminine *gabinda, gabindi* (from *bindan*), *gairda* (from *gairdan*), *vinna* (from *vinnan*). To the second ablaut class belongs only feminine *skilja* (from *skilan*); to the fourth, neuter *andabeit* (from *beitan*), *ïdveit* (from *veitan*); to the fifth, neuter *galiug* (from *liugan*).

bb) From the singular preterite: α) masculine *gards* (from *gairdan*), *þagks* (from *þigkan*), *sagqs* (from *sigqan*), *saggvs* (from *siggvan*); neuter *draggk* (from *drigkan*), *gaþrask* (from *þriskan*), *vamm* (from *vimman*), *gaþagki* (from *þigkan*); feminine *bandi* (from *bindan*), *usvandi* (from *vindan*), *þarba* (from *þairban*), *flahta* (from *flaihtan*); β) feminine *skalja* (from *skilan*); γ) masculine *vraks* (from *vrikan*); neuter *vadi* (from *vidan*); feminine *staks* (from *stikan*), *vraka, vrakja* (from *vrikan*), *brakja* (from *brikan*); δ) masculine *daigs* (from *deigan*), *vaips* (from *veipan*); feminine *laiba* (from *leiban*), *staiga* (from *steigen*); ε) feminine *laudja* (from *liudan*); ζ) neuter *soþ* (from *saþan*); feminine *bota* (from *batan*), *groba* (from *graban*).

cc) From the plural preterite, only some words of the second and third classes are certainly derived: masculine *vegs* (from *vigan*); neuter *andanem* (from *niman*), *andaset* [Col. 1006] (from *sitan*), *tevi* (from *tivan*); feminine *teva* (from *tivan*), *kunaveda* (from *vidan*).

dd) From the passive participle: α) feminine *baurgs* (from *bairgan*), *hunþs* (from *hinþan*), *vunns* (from *vinnan*), *gabundi* (from *bindan*); β) masculine *baur, gabaur* (from *bairan*), *qums* (from *qiman*), *muns* (from *minan*), *runs* (from *rinnan*); neuter *bistugq* (from *stigqan*), *gabaur* (from *bairan*); feminine *usvaurpa* (from *vairpan*), *sulja* (from *silan*), *gabruka* (from *brikan*); γ) masculine *þius* (from *þivan*), *stiks* (from *stikan*); neuter *bifaih* (from *faihan*); feminine *bida* (from *bidjan*), *giba* (from *giban*); δ) masculine *vlits* (from *vleitan*); neuter *gadik* (from *deigan*?); feminine *vipja* (from *veipan*); ε) masculine *drus* (from *driusan*); neuter *usluk* (from *lukan*); feminine *þlauhs* (from *þliuhan*), *krusts* (from *kriustan*), *skura* (from *skiuran*), *ludja* (from *liudan*); ζ) masculine *gaggs* (from *gaggan*), *slahs* (from *slahan*), *andastaþjis* (from *standan*), *sakjis* (from *sakan*); neuter *fraþi* (from *fraþjan*), *fauragaggi* (from *gaggan*); feminine *staþs* (from *standan*), *graba* (from *graban*); η) masculine *grets* (from *gretan*); neuter *aflet* (from *letan*).

ee) From verbs simply reduplicating without ablaut: masculine *laiks* (from *laikan*), *sleps* (from *slepan*); neuter *faurhah* (from *hahan*), *gafah* (from *fahan*), *andstald* (from *staldan*), *bimait* (from *maitan*); feminine *haiti* (from *haitan*).

b) From verbs of the weak conjugation: masculine *fauramaþleis* (from *maþljan*), *vitodafasteis* (from *fastan*), *huhrus* (from *huggrjan*); neuter *andaugi* (from *augjan*), *fauramaþli* (from *maþljan*), *ufarmeli* (from *meljan*), *tauï* (from *taujan*), *hropi* (probably neuter, from *hropjan*), *gavaurki* (from *vaurkjan*); feminine *vrohs* (from *vrohjan*), *liuga* (from *liugan*).

c) From nouns are derived:

aa) Masculines denoting one who holds an office or practises an art, as *hairdeis* (from *hairda*), *ragineis* (from *ragin*), *silbasiuneis* (from *siun*), *faurstasseis* (from *stass*).

bb) Neuters, either formed by composition from other already derived words, as *ataþni* (from *aþn*), *fauradauri* (from *daur*), *andalauni* (from *laun*), *andanahti* (from *nahts*), *garuni* (from *runa*), *andvairþi* (from *vairþs*, “price”), *andavaurdi* (from *vaurd*), *faurafilli* (from *fill*); or formed as concrete nouns from personal nouns, as *andbahti* (from *andbahts*), *þiubi* (from *þiubs*), *reiki* (from *reiks*), *gaskalki*, “fellow servant” (see § 191, I.1, from *skalks*), *veitvodi* (from *veitvods*).

cc) Feminines formed in the same way as the neuters, that is, by composition: *þiudangardi* (from *gards*); also to denote natural gender: *varda* (from *vards*), *þivi* (from *þius*); or with a somewhat altered meaning: *daïla* (from *dails*).

d) Finally, from adjectives:

aa) Masculines: only *dauþus* (from *dauþs*).

bb) Neuters: *sildaleik* (from *leiks*), *azeti* (from *azets*), [Col. 1007] *biuhti* (from *biuhts*), *unhaili* (from *hails*), *unledi* (from *unleds*), *galeiki* (from *galeiks*), *manvi* (from *manvus*), *gariudi* (from *gariuds*), *unsuti* (from *sutis*), *andvairþi* (from *andvairþs*), *unviti* (from *unvits*), *usvissi* (from *usviss*).

cc) Feminines: *halba* (from *halbs*), *triggva* (from *triggvs*), *sibja* (from *sibjis*), *sunja* (from *sunjis*).

§ 144. 2) Derivation with a **FORMATIVE ELEMENT**.

a) With semivowels:

aa) Derivatives with *J*, where this arises from *i*, are mentioned in the preceding section; others nowhere occur.

bb) Derivatives with simple *V* are scarcely found; rather, a dental seems everywhere to have been inserted before the semivowel, as in feminine *fijaþva* (from *fijan*), *frijaþva* (from *frijon*), *saliþvos* (from *saljan*); neuter *þivadv* (from *þivan*), *vaurstv* (instead of *vaurht-dv*? See § 52.4, from *vaurkjan*). In the same way must be explained words whose origin is otherwise obscure, such as feminine *ubizva* and neuter *gaidv*.
