Feminine *bandva* is undoubtedly used for *band-dva* (especially if it belongs to *bindan*). Of the same kind are words in which the *n* of the second declension is added, as masculine *vaurstva, vaurstvja*; feminine *bandvo, vahtvo* (from *vakan*), *unvaurstvo, gatvo* (instead of *gahtvo*? from *gaggan*), and also *uktvo*. A dental is likewise inserted in the masculine word of obscure origin *nidva*, except for the sole *bidagva*, unless perhaps this is used for primitive *bidag-dva* for euphony. *Viduvo*, however, certainly derives from Latin, and its *v* is present only to avoid hiatus.

§ 145. b) With liquids:

aa) Masculine and neuter derivatives with simple *L* signify an instrument by which, or a place in which, something is done: masculine *sitls* (from *sitan*), *stikls* (from *stikan*), *stols* (from *standan*?); neuter *þvahl* (from *þvahan*), *fairveitl* (from *veitan*); feminine *ïusila* (from *ïus*).

Sometimes another formative element is placed before or after this *L*, producing the following combinations:

*SL*: neuter *þreihsl* (from *þreihan*), *svumsl* (from *svimman*), *hunsl* (from *hinþan*?), *skohsl, svartizl*.

*þL*: neuter *haimoþli* (from *haims*); compare feminine *woftuli* (from *wopan*).

*L-N* forms diminutives: masculine *magula* (from *magus*); compare the proper names *merila, vulfila*; neuter *barnilo* (from *barn*). In place of *qiþlo*, *Skeireins* V.d, *qiþano* (*qiþao*) should be read more correctly; compare Mark XV.28. *Mavilo* (from *mavi*); compare *ïnilo, vairilo*.

> **Note.**—The word *manauli* cannot be assigned, with regard to formation, to any of the classes described above, and is therefore suspect. Thus perhaps, with Massmann, *Phil.* II.8, *manludjai* (compare *manleika*) should be read in place of *manaulja*. Of more obscure origin are the masculines *hakuls* (not *hakul*, as the glossary gives) and *asilus*.

bb) Derivation with *M* occurs only in masculine *barms* (from *bairan*); but the combination *M-N* occurs more frequently: masculine *ahma* (from *ahan*?), *malma* (from *malan*), *hliuma* (from *hlivan*?), *stoma, bloma, milhma, hiuhma*; neuter *aldomo* (from *alþan*); feminine *miduma* (from *midja*), *lauhmuni* (from *liuhan*), *glitmuni* (from *gleitan*).

cc) *N* is the most frequently employed of all formative elements [Col. 1008] for strengthening words, especially nouns, in which it seems to have the same meaning as in forming the infinitive and the preterite participle of strong verbs. The following must therefore be considered:

α) Nouns of the second declension whose *n* has disappeared in the nominative singular. Among them:

αα) Masculines, with only a few exceptions, denote persons distinguished by an office or quality. With respect to derivation, they include:

ααα) Those derived from other nouns, as *gadaila* (from *dails*), *gahlaiba* (from *hlaibs*), *galaista* (from *laists*), *usliþa* (from *liþus*), *gajuka* (from *juk*), *garazna* (from *razn*), *gasinþa, gasinþja* (from *sinþ*), *spilla* (from *spill*), *staua* (from feminine *staua*), *aurtja* (from *aurts*), *arbja* (from *arbi*), *baurgja* (from *baurgs*), *ïngardja* (from *gards*), *gauja* (from *gavi*), *gudja* (from *guþ*), *vaidedja* (from *deds*), *haurnja* (from *haurn*), *kasja* (from *kas*), *mana maurþrja* (from *maurþr*), *skattja* (from *skatts*), *vardja* (from *vards*), *liugnja* (from *liugn*).

βββ) Those originating from adjectives: *unhulpa* (from *hulþs*), *þarba* (from *þarbs*), *veiha* (from *veihs*), *galeika* (from *galeiks*), *gamainja* (from *gamains*).

γγγ) Those derived from verbs: *fauragagga, fauragaggja* (from *gaggan*), *liuta* (from *liutan*), *nuta* (from *niutan*), *skula* (from *skulan*), *ufarsvara* (from *svaran*), *bandja* (from *bindan*), *afdrugkja* (from *drigkan*), *bihaitja* (from *haitan*), *afetja* (from *ïtan*), *arbinumja* (from *niman*), *skilja* (from *skilan*?), *sviglja* (from *sviglon*), *timrja* (from *timrjan*).

> **Note.**—The following have a concrete meaning: *garda* (from *gards*), *mela* (from *mel*), *lukarnastaþa* (from *staþs*), *ganauha* (from *ganauhan*), *uzeta* (unless it is the neuter *[uzets]*, from *ïtan*), *gataura* (from *tairan*), *vilja* (from *viljan*), *drobna* (from *drobnan*).

ββ) Only a few neuters occur in this class: *kaurno* (from *kaurn*), *gajuko* (from *juk*), *sigljo* (from *sigljan*); and the peculiarly formed *armaio* (from *arman*).

γγ) Feminines of this class end:

ααα) In *ein*: these are for the most part derived from adjectives and denote a quality, as *gaaggvei* (from *aggvus*), *aglaitei* (from *aglaits*), *airzei* (from *airzis*), *audagei* (from *audags*), *bairhtei* (from *bairhts*), etc. (see § 92). Derivatives from participles also belong here: *undivanei* (from *divans*), *drugkanei* (from *drugkans*).

Those arising from verbs signify an action or condition with the secondary idea of longer duration or more frequent repetition: *unagei* (from *agan*), *hropei* (from *hropjan*), *vajamerei* (from *merjan*), *ustauhei* (from *tiuhan*), *vrekei* (from *vrikan*), *gabei* (from *giban*), *baurei* (from *bairan*).

Those originating from nouns likewise denote a habit, condition, or state: *afgudei* (from *guþ*), *usbeisnei* (from *usbeisns*), *oglaitivaurdei* (from *vaurd*), *vaurstvei* (from *vaurstv*), *veitvodei* (from *veitvods*), *unbeistei* (from *beists*), *liuhadei* (from *liuhaþ*), *frumadei* (from *frumaþ*?), *magaþei* (from *magaþs*), *aipiskaupei* (from *aipiskaupus*), *apaustaulei* (from *apaustaulus*), *praizbytairei* (from *praizbytaireis*).

βββ) In *on*: closely related are certain words which, derived from masculines, denote natural gender: *unhulþo* (from *unhulþa*), *garazno* (from *garazna*), [Col. 1009] *svaihro* (from *svaihra*), *dauravardo* (from *vards*), *haiþno* (from *haiþna*?), *gamarko* (from *gamarka*?), *arbjo* (from *arbja*), *niþjo* (from *niþjis*), *kalkjo* (from *kalkja*?). Others denote things: *dauro* (from *daur*), *driuso* (from *driusan*), *malo* (from *malan*), *rinno* (from *rinnan*), *vinþiskauro* (from *skiuran*), *vruggo* (from *vriggan*), *flahto* (from *flaihtan*), *waþo* (from *waþjan*), *tainjo* (from *tains*), *ïddaljo* (from *dal*), *mitadjo* (from *mitaþs*), *garunjo* (from *rinnan*). Finally, others are abstract: *gajuko* (from *juk*), *fullo* (from *fulls*), *gariudjo* (from *gariuds*), *brinno* (from *brinnan*), *faihugeiro* (from *geiran*), *broþrulubo* (from *liuban*), *reiro* (from *reiran*), *vinno* (from *vinnan*), *raþjo* (from *raþjan*), *sakjo* (from *sakan*), *vaihjo* (from *veihan*), *gatimrjo* (from *timrjan*).

β) Moreover, further words are formed with simple *N*, namely:

αα) With it immediately affixed to the stem: masculine *faihuþraihns* (from *þreihan*), *andavleizns* (from *vleitan*); neuter *barn* (from *bairan*), *liugn* (from *liugan*), *andavizn* (from *vizon*); feminine *usbeisns* (from *beidan*), *anabusns* (from *biudan*), *sokns* (from *sokan*), *vailavizns* (from *vizon*); compare *garehsns, rohsns*.

ββ) With the euphonic vowel *A*: masculine *þiudans* (from *þiuda*), *vigans* (from *veihan*); neuter *akran* (from *akrs*?), *aljan* (from *alan*?); feminine *asans*.

γγ) With *I*: masculine *kindins, maurgins*; neuter *aigin* (from *aigan*); feminine *fairina* (from *fairan*).

δδ) With *U*: neuter *faihugairuni* (from *geiran*), *fairguni*.

εε) With *EI, AI,* and *O*: very many feminines derived from verbs of the second conjugation are thus formed, as *balveins* (from *balvjan*), *goleins* (from *goljan*), *dauþeins* (from *dauþjan*), *daupeins* (from *daupjan*), *afdomeins* (from *domjan*), *qisteins* (from *qistjan*), *hazeins* (from *hazjan*); *bauains* (from *bauan*), *þulains* (from *þulan*), *leikains* (from *leikan*), *libains* (from *liban*), *trauains* (from *trauan*); *aihtrons* (from *aihtron*), *laþons* (from *laþon*), *mitons* (from *miton*), *salbons* (from *salbon*), etc. Moreover, all nouns having this ending must be referred to verbs of the second conjugation, even ones no longer occurring; thus, for example, *ahmateins* to *ahmatjan*, *gahobains* to *gahoban*, *vanains* to *vanan*. In place of *usbloteins*, II Corinthians VIII.4, *usblotains*, from *blotan* (not *blotjan*), should more properly be read.

γ) With other consonants the following combinations result:

*SN, ZN*: neuter *fulhsni* (from *filhan*); feminine *hlaivasna* (from *hlaiv*), *filusna* (from *filu*); compare *drauhsna, arwazna, fairzna*.

*BN, FN*: neuter *vitubni* (from *vitan*), *fastubni* (from *fastan*), *valdufni* (from *valdan*); feminine *fraistubni* (from *fraisan*), *vundufni* (from *vundon*).

dd) R: words formed with this element are
α) Masculines, namely:

αα) Most of the words in *reis* derived from verbs and denoting an agent, among which the following should be noted: *laisareis* (from *laisjan*), *liuþareis* (from *liuþon*), *sokareis* (from *sokjan*), *blostreis* (from *blotan*), *bokareis* (from *boka*), *motareis* (from *mota*), *vullareis* (from *vulla*). As regards their meaning, the observations set out above under cc) α) αα) apply to them, with the addition that they are formed in this manner more rarely [Col. 1010] and probably only at a later period.

ββ) Words in *AR* of more obscure origin, denoting various relations of kinship, such as *fadar*, *broþar*; corresponding to these are the feminines *svistar*, *dauhtar*.

γγ) In addition, *ligrs* (from *ligan*) and *spaiskuldrs*.

β) Neuters: *vaggari* (from *vagga*?), *galigri* (from *ligan*), *filigri* (from *filhan*), in which the insertion of *i* for euphony should especially be noted, unless it stands for *filhigri* with the formative syllable *gri*.

γ) Feminines: besides the aforementioned *svistar*, *dauhtar*, also *vulþrs* (if the reading of manuscript A at Gal. II.6 is genuine, from *vulþus*), *saldra* (from *sildan*?). As for the words *mundrei*, *digrei*, belonging to the formative element *N*, they come from the adjectives *mundrs*, *digrs*, and consequently are not to be assigned here.

Connected with other consonants, it occurs only in the cluster *STR*: neuter *gilstr* (from *gilþan*), *avistr* (from *avi*), *navistr* (from *naus*), *hulistr* (from *huljan*).

§ 146. c) With gutturals:

The gutturals play only an insignificant role in the formation of substantives. Only the following require mention:

aa) The masculine ending *IGG* occurs only in the words *gadiliggs* and *skilliggs*.

bb) The masculine *broþrahans*, belonging to the second declension, appears, like *ainaha*, to have adjectival force.

cc) Similarly, the feminine *ïdreiga* (from *ïdr*) is to be referred to the adjective *ïdreigs*.

dd) The neuters *aiviski*, *barniski* are more directly formed from adjectives in *-isks*; likewise, the masculine *atisks* (or neuter *atisk*) seems to have borrowed its form from an adjective of this kind.

ee) The derivation of *miluks* and *ahaks* is unknown.

§ 147. d) With labials:

They do not occur in the formation of words, except for the neuters and feminines in *ubni*, *ufni* mentioned above (§ 145, cc, γ).

§ 148. e) With dentals and sibilants:

The class of dentals and sibilants is the one most suited to the formation of liquid substantives. In most cases *þ* appears to be the dental which properly constitutes the formative element; on this assumption, the *d*, *t*, and *s* occurring in other forms would arise from *þ* according to the known phonetic laws (§§ 49, 50, 52). Nor should it be overlooked that the formation of these substantives agrees with that of the passive participle of the second conjugation. This might all the more suggest a corresponding affinity of meaning between the two forms, since, where a word is derived from a verb of the first conjugation, the vowel of the passive participle is employed. Most substantives of this formation also denote efficacy, the very act of an operation, whereas others, derived without a formative element (§ 143 a), rather designate the object of the operation. The formations belonging here may be arranged as follows:

aa) Those having primitive *þ*, whether joined to the stem of the word through a vowel or attached directly to it; in the latter case it changes, for euphony, into *d*, *t*, or *s*:

α) Masculines: *gabaurjoþus* (from *gabauris*), *manniskodus* (from *mannisks*), *auhjodus* (from *auhjon*), *vratodus* (from *vraton*), *skildus* (from *skilan*), *kustus* (from *kiusan*), *vahstus* (from *vashjan*), *þuhtus* (from *þugkjan*), *hliftus* (from *hlifan*).

β) Neuters: *liuhaþ* (from *liuhan*), *vitoþ* (from *veitan*), *fulliþ* (from *fulls*), *miliþ* (from *milan*?), *beist* (from *beitan*); *aveþi* (from *avi*), *kunþi* (from *kunnan*), *gaminþi* (from *minan*), *gavairþi* (from *vairan*?).

γ) Feminines:

αα) According to the second vocalic declension, chiefly verbals denoting an operation: *mitaþs* (from *mitan*), *magaþs* (from *magus*), *astaþs*; *arbaiþs*, *fulleiþs* (from *fulls*), *faheþs* (from *fahs*); *gaqumþs* (from *qiman*), *gakunþs* (from *kunnan*), *gamainþs* (from *gamains*), *gabaurþs* (from *bairan*), *gataurþs* (from *tairan*); *anaminds*, *gamunds* (from *minan*), *gakunds* (from *kunnan*), *gafaurds* (from *fairan*), *gahugds* (from *hugjan*); *aihts* (from *aigan*), *andabauhts* (from *bugjan*), *ïnnagahts* (from *gaggan*), *gaþlaihts* (from *þlaihan*), *mahts* (from *magan*), *gasahts* (from *sakan*), *sauhts* (from *siukan*), *slauhts* (from *slahan*), *ustauhts* (from *tiuhan*), *usvaurhts* (from *vaurkjan*), *usdrusts* (from *driusan*), *lists* (from *leisan*), *fralusts* (from *liusan*), *ganists* (from *nisan*), *urrists* (from *reisan*), *usvahsts* (from *vahsjan*), *vists* (from *visan*), *fragifts* (from *giban*), *andahafts* (from *hafjan*), *þaurfts* (from *þaurban*), *gaskafts* (from *skapjan*), *andanumts* (from *niman*); *anaqiss* (from *qiþan*), *afstass* (from *standan*), *gaviss* (from *vidan*).

ββ) With the ending *iþa*, derived from adjectives and denoting a particular quality: *aggviþa* (from *aggvus*), *agliþa* (from *agls*), *airziþa* (from *airzis*), *airkniþa* (from *airknis*), *gauriþa* (from *gaurs*), *daubiþa* (from *daubs*), *diupiþa* (from *diups*), *dvaliþa* (from *dvals*), *qrammiþa* (from *qramms*), *armahairtiþa* (from *armahairts*), *hauhiþa* (from *hauhs*), *hlutriþa* (from *hlutrs*), *unhrainiþa* (from *hrains*), *þvastiþa* (from *þvasts*), *kauriþa* (from *kaurs*), *manviþa* (from *manvus*), *mildiþa* (from *milds*), *niujiþa* (from *niujis*), *garaihtiþa* (from *raihts*), *sveriþa* (from *svers*), *svikniþa* (from *svikns*), *tulgiþa* (from *tulgus*), *veihiþa* (from *veihs*), *ïnvindiþa* (from *ïnvinds*), *fairniþa* (from *fairnis*), *auþida* (from *auþs*), *vairþida* (from *vairþs*). A few also seem to arise from substantives [Col. 1012] and verbs: *afgrundiþa* (from *grundus*), *veitvodiþa* (from *veitvods*), *meriþa* (from *merjan*), *svegniþa* (from *svegnjan*), *varjiþa* (from *vargjan*), collective *gaunoþa* (from *gaunon*). To this class also belong *junda* (in place of *juggiþa*? from *juggs*), *skanda* (in place of *skamiþa*? from *skaman*), and *mulda* (from *milan*).

> Note 1.—In some of these substantives a later formation has arisen through *n* of the consonantal declension, as *mitadjo* (from *mitaþ*), *baurþei* (from *baurþs*), *þaurstei* (from *þaursts*?), *usfarþo* (from *farþs*?); hence they belong under § 145, cc, α, γγ.

bb) Those having primitive *T*: neuters *stiviti*, *aglaiti*; feminine *vasti* (from *vasjan*). To this group, moreover, are to be assigned:

cc) Formations with *ST*: neuters *hauhisti*, *frumisti* (derived from superlatives), *trausti* (from *trauan*); feminines *ansts* (from *ïnnan*), *brunsts* (from *brinnan*), *gramsts* (from *gramjan*), *bansts* (for *bandsts*, from *bindan*).

dd) Formations with *ND*: feminines *hulundi* (from *huls*), *frijondi* (from *frijon*); collective feminine *þusundi* and masculine of the second declension *newundja* (from *new*).

ee) Formations with primitive *S* (*Z*): masculine *urruns* (from *rinnan*); neuters *agis* (from *agan*), *hatis* (from *hatan*), *skaþis* (from *skaþjan*), *gadikis* (from *deigan*), *þevis* (from *þivan*), collectives *riqis*, *sigis*, *rimis* (*baris*); feminines *garuns* (from *rinnan*), *jukuzi* (from *juk*), *aqizi*.

> Note 2.—In the masculine *beruseis*, *s* was inserted instead of *r* so that two *r*s might not immediately follow each other, producing *berureîs*, as in *laisareîs* (§ 145, dd α).

ff) Formations with *SS*: the masculines belonging to this class are for the most part derived from verbs and denote an action or condition: *gudjinassus* (from *gudjinon*), *drauhtinassus* (from *drauhtinon*), *horinassus* (from *horinon*), *kalkinassus* (from *kalkinon*), *leikinassus* (from *leikinon*), *skalkinassus* (from *skalkinon*), *fraujinassus* (from *fraujinon*), *þiudinassus* (from *þiudanon*), *blotinassus* (from *blotan*), *vaninassus* (from *vans*), *ïbnassus* (from *ïbns*), *ufarassus* (from *ufar*).

## II. THE ADJECTIVE

[Col. 1011]

§ 149. 1) There are likewise very many adjectives which are derived from substantives and verbs without a formative element, the ending being simply added to the stem; namely:

a) From verbs of the first conjugation:

aa) From the present: *vilvs* (from *vilvan*), *invinds* (from *vindan*), *gawairbs* (from *wairban*), *tils* (from *tilan*), *diups* (from *diupan*), *liubs* (from *liuban*), *galiugs* (from *liugan*), *liuts* (from *liutan*), *siuks* (from *siukan*), probably also *gaqiss* (from *qiþan*), *bats* (from *batan*), *saþs* (from *saþan*), *grindafraþjis* (from *fraþjan*), *aglaitgastalds* (from *staldan*), *fralets* (from *letan*).

bb) From the singular preterite: *þarbs* (from *þairban*), *gavamms* (from *vimman*), *untals* (from *tilan*), *hnaivs* (from *hneivan*), *galaubs* (from *liuban*), *laus* (from *liusan*), *gadobs* (from *daban*), *ganohs* (from *nahan*), *unandsoks* (from *sakan*), *froþs* (from *fraþjan*).

[Col. 1012]

cc) From the plural preterite: *andanems* (from *niman*), *gatems* (from *timan*), *bireks* (from *rikan*), *gafehs* (from *faihan*), *andasets* (from *sitan*), *unqeþis* (from *qiþan*); probably also *hulþs* (from *hilþan*), *þaursus* (from *þairsan*), *gaþaurbs* (from *þairban*), *unvits* (from *veitan*), *galubs* (from *liuban*), *unnutis* (from *niutan*).

dd) None are certainly derived from the passive participle.

b) From verbs of the second conjugation: *usskavs* (from *skavjan*), *gaviljis* (from *viljan*), *vailamers* (from *merjan*), *ubiltogis* (from *taujan*).

> Note.—Some adjectives, such as *garaids* (from *raidjan*), *gamaids* (from *maidjan*), *gavaurts* (from *vaurtjan*?), *uslukns* (from *uslukan*), by virtue of their form and meaning, seem to be apocopated participles.

c) From substantives: *alevis* (from *alev*), *alþeis* (from *alþs*), *navis* (from *naus*), *reiks* (from *reiks*), *rums* (from *rums*), *sleiþis* (from *sleiþa*), *sves* (from *sves*), *vairþs* (from *vairþs*); especially [Col. 1013] in compounds: *ïnahs* (from *aha*), *ufaiþs* (from *aiþs*), *ïngardis* (from *gards*), *afguds* (from *guþ*), *anahaims* (from *haims*), *unkarja* (from *kara*), *andaneiþs* (from *neiþ*), *anasiuns* (from *siun*), *gaskohs* (from *skoh*), *gavaurts* (from *vaurts*), *usvena* (from *vens*), *unweils* (from *weila*), *armahairts*, *hauhhairts* (from *hairts*), *laushandus* (from *handus*), *aljakuns* (from *kuni*), *samasaivals* (from *saivala*), *filufaihus* (from *faihu*), *þrutsfills* (from *fill*); and, with phonetic divergence, *dags* (from *dags*).

§ 150. 2) With a formative element:

a) With *V*: only *lasivs*, of obscure origin, belongs here.

b) With *L*: *slahals* (from *slahan*), unless it should be divided *sla-hals* instead of *slah-hals*; see the glossary under this word; *leitils*, *mikils*, *ubils*; *skaþuls* (from *skaþan*), *veinuls*? see the glossary under this word; and further, in clusters:

*BL*: *dauþublis* (from *dauþus*).

*KL*: *ainakls* (from *ains*).

> Note.—*Undarleija*, Eph. III.8, is suspect; or, if correct, it existed before composition.

c) With *M*: here belong the old comparative endings: *auhuma*, *aftuma*, *hinduma*, *hleiduma*, *ïnnuma*, *ïftuma*, *speduma*, (*miduma*), *fruma*.

d) With *N*: *gairns* (from *geiran*), *analaugns* (from *liugan*), *uslukns* (from *lukan*); *fairins* (from *fairan*), *fulgins* (from *filhan*); and especially adjectives in *-ein*, ordinarily denoting material: *airþeins*, *barizeins*, *gulþeins*, *eisarneins*, *þaurneins*, *leikeins*, *liuhadeins*, *muldeins*, *riqizeins*, *silubreins*, *staineins*, *triveins*, *filleins*; and, with a more metaphorical meaning: *aiveins*, *qimeins*, *gumeins*, *galaubeins*, *pistikeins*, *siuteins*, *sunjeins*. The formative *GG* occurs only in *unveniggs* (from *vens*), unless the formative syllable here belongs to the adverb (§ 163, b, α).

e) With *R*: *framaldrs* (from *alþs*), *lausqiþrs* (from *qiþus*), *vulþrs* (from *vulþus*), *fagrs* (from *faihan*), *baitrs* (from *beitan*), *hlutrs*, *digrs* (?), *mundrs* (?).

f) With *G* (*H*): *audugs* (from *aud*), *unhunslags* (from *hunsl*), *manags* (from *man*), *modags* (from *mods*), *vulþags* (from *vulþus*), *gredags* (from *gredus*), *bidags* (conjectured from *bidagva*, from *bida*), *unbarnahs* (from *barn*), *stainahs* (from *stains*), *vainahs* (from *veinan*?), *vaurdahs* (from *vaurd*), *ainaha* (from *ains*), *broþrahs* (conjectured from *broþrahans*, from *broþar*), *handugs* (from *handus*), *valugs* (whence *valugjan*), *uhtiugs* (from *uht*); especially in the form *-eig*, which perhaps corresponds with *eigan* (whence *aigan*) and likewise has the meaning “having something,” as *ansteigs*, “having grace” (from *ansts*), *usbeisneigs*, “having patience” (from *usbeisnei*), *gabeigs*, “having riches” (from *gabei*); likewise *hroþeigs*, *þiuþeigs*, *laiseigs*, *listeigs*, *mahteigs*, *andanemeigs*, *uhteigs*, *sineigs*, *gavairþeigs*, *vaurstveigs*, *vitodeigs*, *gavizneigs*.

g) *K*. This letter occurs only in the cluster *SK*, which closely corresponds in form and meaning to the German ending *-isch*: *aivisks*, *barnisks*, *gudisks*, [Col. 1014] *þiudisks*, *mannisks*, *funisks*, *haiþivisks*, *ïudaivisks*, *sauraufynikisks*. Does *malsks* also belong here?

h) With *þ* (*D*, *T*): *kunþs* (from *kunnan*), *kunds* (from *kuni*), *skulds* (from *skulan*), *unatgahts* (from *gaggan*), *mahts* (from *magan*), *hauhþuhts* (from *þugkjan*), *handuvaurhts* (from *vaurkjan*), *hafts* (from *haban*), *þaurfts* (from *þaurban*), *haists* (from *haitan*?); and with an euphonic vowel: *naqaþs*, *framaþeis* (from *fram*), *bajoþs* (from *bai*).

i) With *S*: only *valîs* (from *valjan*).

§ 150. 3) Another mode of formation is comparison, by which various degrees of form and meaning arise.

a) The comparative is regularly formed by *z*, preceded by *i* or *o*. No fixed rule determines which of these vowels is to be selected, except that *o* occurs only in adjectives having *a* as their fundamental vowel; for example: *airiza*, *azetiza*, *hauhiza*, *managiza*, *raþiza*, *speidiza*, *faviza*, *vulþriza*, *ïusiza*, *þaurftiza*, *alþiza* (from *alþeis*), *hardiza* (from *hardus*); *framaldroza*, *frodoza*, *garaihtoza*, *svinþoza*, *hlasoza*, *usdaudoza*, *handugoza*, *svikunþoza*, *sniumundoza*, *aljaleikoza* (to be inferred from the adverbs *sniumundos* and *aljaleikos*).

b) The superlative is regularly formed by *st*, likewise preceded by *i* or *o*: *hauhists*, *smalists*, *spedists*, *managists*, *reikists*; *armosts*, *lasivosts*.

> Note 1.—From the preceding examples it is to be inferred that the vowel of the formative syllable corresponds in the comparative and superlative. Thus, on the one hand, the comparatives *smaliza*, *reikiza*, *armoza*, *lasivoza* may be compared, and on the other the superlatives *airists*, *azetists*, *framaldrosts*, *frodosts*, etc.

> Note 2.—The following adjectives derive their comparative and superlative from other roots:

> Note 3.—From *juggs*, with the nasal rejected (§ 40, 5), are formed the comparative *juhiza* and the superlative *juhists*.

> Note 4.—A peculiar form of the superlative is *undaraists*, from which a comparative *undaraiza* must be assumed.

> Note 5.—The forms mentioned in § 150, c), which by their nature lack positives, are comparatives: namely *auhuma*, *aftuma*, *hleiduma*, *ïnnuma*, *ïftuma*, (*miduma*), *fruma*. That these forms, regarded by earlier scholars as superlatives, are in fact comparatives will be shown in the syntax (§ 198, b). From them are formed the superlatives *auhumists*, *aftumists*, *frumists*, *hindumists*, and *spedumists*; from the latter two, the comparative forms *hinduma* and *speduma* must be assumed.

## B. PRONOMINAL FORMATION

[Col. 1013]

[Col. 1013] § 152. In forming pronouns by derivation, the Gothic language suffers from a distinctive poverty, [Col. 1014] since the entire work of formation revolves around only two stems, namely the personal and the interrogative. Other relations, expressed by particles or by a certain kind of composition, will be treated below (§ 170).

1) The personal pronouns form possessives from the genitive, whose ending is exchanged for the ending of adjectives of the first declension, as follows:

2) The interrogative pronoun *wa, was* means generally “what, who,” without specific determination; hence a twofold interrogative pronoun is formed: *waþar*, “which of two, which one?” and *warjis*, “which of many, who?” This latter form is of obscure origin; the former also occurs in *anþar*, “other.”

## C. VERBAL FORMATION

(Jacobi, *Beiträge zur deutschen Grammatik*, p. 131 ff.)

[Col. 1015]

## I. FIRST CONJUGATION

[Col. 1015]

§ 153. Since we have regarded the first conjugation, because of the laws of vowel alternation to which it is subject, as both primitive and radical, it would generally be vain to seek an earlier derivation of these verbs. Nevertheless, there are cases in which this inquiry is not without value.

a) For we observed above (§ 32, 3) that verbs belonging to the sixth ablaut class seem to be later derived from the second and third classes. Although in most verbs the evidence has now disappeared, since individual radical verbs may have perished and been displaced by the later forms derived from them, some traces still remain. Thus, alongside *malan, mol*, there occurs a certain *milan, mal*, to which *miliþ, mel, mulda* were referred above (§ 139, 2). Likewise, alongside *svaran* (“to make heavy,” “to confirm,” “to swear”), there is *svairan, svar*, “to be heavy,” from which *svare*, “with difficulty, in vain,” and *svers*, “heavy, honoured,” must be derived. Accordingly, alongside *vrikan, vrak*, a *vrakan, vrok* must be assumed, from which *vrohjan* may be formed. Finally, alongside *faran, for*, *fairan, far* also occurs, although the meanings of the two do not agree correspondingly.

b) It may likewise be concluded from their form alone that other verbs of this kind are in fact derived, although the derivation is hidden—especially those whose root consists of two consonants, such as *þairsan*, *þriskan*, *vahsjan*, *kriustan*, etc. But it would be vain to search the whole Gothic language for a simple root; it survives only in a few cases. Thus *alþan*, “to grow old,” seems to be later formed from *alan*, “to nourish,” and *þinsan*, “to draw, extend,” from *þinan*, “to be extended.” Perhaps in a similar way *vairdan*, “to defend,” is to be derived from *vairan*, “to remain,” and *vahsjan*, “to grow,” from *vakan*, “to be awake.”

## II. SECOND CONJUGATION

§ 154. So far as their origin can be traced back, verbs of the second conjugation in *-jan* are for the most part derived from verbs of the first conjugation, adjectives, or substantives. In all of them the fundamental meaning appears to be “making”; for example, *lagjan*, “to cause to lie” (“to lay”), from *ligan*; *varmjan*, “to make warm,” from *varms*; *huzdjan*, “to make treasure” (“to treasure up”), from *huzd*. Indeed, in most of these verbs the meaning is more or less weakened or is to be taken only metaphorically. Those derived especially from substantives mean not so much that the object denoted by the substantive is to be made, as that something is to be done with it; thus the objective sense passes into an instrumental one, as in *haurnjan*, “to sound a trumpet”; *klismjan*, “to sound or ring with a cymbal”; *tinnire*, “to ring”; *ufarhleiþrjan*, “to cover with a tent, cover over”; *ganagljan*, “to fasten with a nail”; *stainjan*, “to overwhelm with stones, to stone.” Only rarely does this transitive meaning become intransitive, namely “to become” or “to exist,” as in *andbahtjan* (properly “to perform service”), “to be a minister”; *sipunjan*, “to be a disciple”; *riqizjan*, “to be dark”; *faurhtjan*, “to be timid.”

a) Those derived from verbs of the first conjugation generally take the vowel of the singular preterite; only a few have the vowel of the passive participle. They are therefore derived:

aa) From the singular preterite:

1. *vammjan* (from *vimman*), *brannjan* (from *brinnan*), *rannjan* (from *rinnan*), *sandjan* (from *sinþan*), *tandjan* (from *tindan*), *vandjan* (from *vindan*), *dragkjan* (from *drigkan*), *þagkjan* (from *þigkan*), *sagqjan* (from *sigqan*), *stagqjan* (from *stigqan*), *svaggvjan* (from *sviggvan*), *þarbjan* (from *þairban*), *fravardjan* (from *vairdan*?).

2. *ufþanjan* (from *þinan*), *tamjan* (from *timan*).

3. *daujan* (from *divan*), *taujan* (from *tivan*), *lagjan* (from *ligan*), *vagjan* (from *vigan*), *rakjan* (from *rikan*), *vrakjan* (from *vrikan*), *fahjan* (from *faihan*), *atjan* (from *ïtan*), *satjan* (from *sitan*), *nasjan* (from *nisan*).

4. *hnaivjan* (from *hneivan*), *draibjan* (from *dreiban*), *vaibjan* (from *veiban*), *vaipjan* (from *veipan*), *baidjan* (from *beidan*), *gaisjan* (from *geisan*), *laisjan* (from *leisan*), *raisjan* (from *reisan*).

5. *gaumjan* (from *giuman*?), *laubjan* (from *liuban*), *daupjan* (from *diupan*), *slaupjan* (from *sliupan*), *drausjan* (from *driusan*), *lausjan* (from *liusan*), *kausjan* (from *kiusan*).

6. *goljan* (from *galan*?), *ogjan* (from *agan*), *sokjan* (from *sakan*), *rodjan* (from *raþjan*?), *stodjan* (from *standan*), *soþjan* (from *saþan*), *botjan* (from *batan*).

bb) From the passive participle:

1. *þaursjan* (from *þairsan*), *þugkjan* (from *þigkan*), *trusgjan* (from *trisgan*).

2. *huljan* (from *hilan*).

6. *aljan* (from *alan*), *farjan* (from *faran*), *agjan* (from *agan*), *vakjan* (from *vakan*), *batjan* (from *batan*).

b) The following are derived from adjectives:

aa) Of the first declension: *biabrjan* (from *abrs*), *usagljan* (from *agls*), *bairhtjan* (from *bairhts*), *balþjan* (from *balþs*), *balvjan* (from *balvs*), *blindjan* (from *blinds*), *usbraidjan* (from *braids*), *gairnjan* (from *gairns*), *gaurjan* (from *gaurs*), *daubjan* (from *daubs*), *usdaudjan* (from *usdauds*), *dauþjan* (from *dauþs*), *gadiupjan* (from *diups*), *gaqiujan* (from *qius*), *haftjan* (from *hafts*), *hailjan* (from *hails*), *hauhjan* (from *hauhs*), *haunjan* [Col. 1017] (from *hauns*), *þvastjan* (from *þvasts*), *ïbnjan* (from *ïbns*), *kaurjan* (from *kaurs*), *latjan* (from *lats*), *gaunledjan* (from *unleds*), *sildaleikjan* (from *sildaleiks*), *maidjan* (from *maids*), *raidjan* (from *raids*), *garaihtjan* (from *garaihts*), *svinþjan* (from *svinþs*), *varmjan* (from *varms*), *varjan* (from *vars*), *veisjan* (from *veis*), *fahrjan* (from *fagrs*), *faurhtjan* (from *faurhts*), *fulljan* (from *fulls*), *audagjan* (from *audags*), *managjan* (from *manags*), *gabigjan* (from *gabeigs*), *valugjan* (from *valugs*?), *mikiljan* (from *mikils*).

bb) Of the second declension: *airzjan* (from *airzis*), *augjan* (from *augs*), *bleiþjan* (from *bleiþs*), *hrainjan* (from *hrains*), *laugnjan* (from *laugnis*), *gamainjan* (from *gamains*), *skeirjan* (from *skeirs*), *stiurjan* (from *stiurs*), *svinþjan* (from *svinþs*), *framaþjan* (from *framaþeis*).

cc) Of the third declension: *gaaggvjan* (from *aggvus*), *gahardjan* (from *hardus*), *manvjan* (from *manvus*), *tulgjan* (from *tulgus*).

> Note.—*Newjan* also belongs here, although not the adjective *news*, but only the adverb *new*, occurs. Many others likewise show an origin from adjectives that have disappeared, for example *gailjan* (from *gails*), *liuhtjan* (from *liuhts*), *natjan* (from *nats*), etc.

c) The following are derived from substantives:

aa) With a more or less clear sense of making: *aivaggeljan* (from *aivaggeli*), *arbaidjan* (from *arbaiþs*), *bandvjan* (from *bandvo*), *gabeistjan* (from *beists*), *glitmunjan* (from *glitmuni*), *dailjan* (from *dails*), *dulþjan* (from *dulþs*), *domjan* (from *doms*), *huzdjan* (from *huzd*), *hunsljan* (from *hunsl*), *hrukjan* (from *hruk*), *levjan* (from *lev*), *anamahtjan* (from *mahts*), *maþljan* (from *maþl*), *meljan* (from *mel*), *nauþjan* (from *nauþs*), *ufarassjan* (from *ufarassus*), *rignjan* (from *rign*), *skaftjan* (from *skafts*), *sleiþjan* (from *sleiþa*), *gasuljan* (from *sulja*), *stojan* (from *staua*), *lagrjan* (from *tagr*), *taiknjan* (from *taikns*), *gatevjan* (from *teva*), *gagavairþjan* (from *gavairþi*), *andvaurdjan* (from *vaurd*), *venjan* (from *vens*), *gafrisahtjan* (from *frisahts*), *wotjan* (from *wota*), *faihugeironjan* (from *faihugeiro*), *ahjan* (from *aha*), *hugjan* (from *hugs*), *miþlitjan* (from *lita*), *tveifljan* (from *tveifls*), *þiuþjan* (from *þiuþ*), *vargjan* (from *vargs*), *vaifairwjan* (from *fairwus*), *usaivjan* (from *aivs*).

bb) With an instrumental meaning: *haurnjan*, “to sound a trumpet” (from *haurn*); *klismjan*, “to sound or ring with a cymbal” (from *klismo*); *ufarhleiþrjan*, “to cover with a tent” (from *hleiþra*); *ganagljan*, “to fasten with a nail” (from *nagls*); *ïnsailjan*, “to ensnare” (from *sail*); *stainjan*, “to overwhelm with stones” (from *stains*); *laistjan*, “to follow in tracks” (from *laists*); *faurmuljan*, “to bind the mouth” (from *mul*); *matjan*, “to eat” (from *mats*).

cc) With the meaning “to exist” or “to become”: *andbahtjan*, “to be a minister” (from *andbahts*); *praufetjan*, “to be a prophet” (from *praufetes*); *sipunjan*, “to be a disciple” (from *siponeis*); *riqizjan*, “to become dark” (from *riqiz*).

§ 155. A formative element is only rarely inserted between stem and ending; only the following examples occur:

*V*: *malvjan* (from *malan*), *usfraþvjan* (from *fraþjan*), *skadvjan* (from *skadus*).

*M*: *sniumjan* (from *snivan*), *tarmjan* (from *tairan*?).

*N*: In *namnjan* (from *namo*), *n* belongs to the stem. The obscure *bimaminjan* would belong here, unless perhaps, according to Massmann’s judicious conjecture, at Luke XVI.14 [Col. 1018] *binamnidedun* should be read instead of *bimamindedum*; compare *birodjam*, of the same meaning.

*AT*: *lauhatjan* (from *liuhan*), *svogatjan* (from *svogjan*), *ahmatjan* (from *ahma*), *kaupatjan*.

*Z*: *talzjan* (from *tilan*), *vlizjan* (from *vlits*).

*SS*: *knussjan* (from *kniu*).

§ 156. 2) Of verbs in *-on*, whose ending likewise is usually attached directly to the stem, most are derived from substantives and only a few from verbs.

a) From verbs of the first conjugation: *miton* (from *mitan*), *bifaihon* (from *faihan*), *ufarmunnon* (from *munan*), *vlaiton* (from *vleitan*), *warbon* (from *wairban*), *luton* (from *liutan*). It is uncertain whether *trudon* is derived from a verb of the second conjugation in *-an*, or whether both are derived from a lost strong verb *triudan*.

b) From adjectives: *ushulon* (from *huls*), *ïdreigon* (from *ïdreigs*), *galeikon* (from *galeiks*), *mundon* (from *munds*?), *vundon* (from *vunds*), *gatilon* (from *tils*), *gaveison* (from *veis*); *aiviskon* (from *aivisks*), *ïudaiviskon* (from *ïudaivisks*); *gasibjon* (from *sibjis*), *sungon* (from *sunjis*).

c) From substantives, especially those whose fundamental vowel is *a*: *aviliudon* (from *aviliud*), *hamon* (from *hams*), *karon* (from *kara*), *liuþon* (from *liuþ*), *gapaidon* (from *paida*), *spillon* (from *spill*), *vairþon* (from *vairþs*), *fiskon* (from *fisks*), *gavadjon* (from *vadi*), *gasmiþon* (from *smiþa*), *friþon* (from *friþa*?), *aljanon* (from *aljan*), *þiudanon* (from *þiudans*), *midumon* (from *miduma*), *paurpuron* (from *paurpura*), *hatizon* (from *hatis*), *navistron* (from *navistr*); sometimes also from substantives with the fundamental vowel *u*: *gredon* (from *gredus*), *luston* (from *lustus*), *sidon* (from *sidus*).

§ 157. Among those derived with an expanded stem, note:

a) Those which, with inserted formative syllable *-in*, are derived from personal substantives: *skalkinon* (from *skalks*), *horinon* (from *hors*), *drauhtinon* (from *gadrauhts*), *reikinon* (from *reiks*), *leikinon* (from *leikeis*), *airinon* (from *airus*), *gudjinon* (from *gudja*), *fraujinon* (from *frauja*). But in those derived from names of things—*aiginon* (from *aigin*), *raginon* (from *ragin*), *faginon* (from *fagin*?), *fairinon* (from *fairina*)—the derivative syllable *-in* belongs to the substantive; consequently, they correspond to the verbs just listed through accidental coincidence rather than intrinsic affinity.

b) Those formed with *-is*: only *valvison* belongs here, provided that the reading at Mark IX.20 is genuine. But if it is compared with *hatizon* from *hatis*, mentioned above (§ 156, c), one must not unreasonably posit a lost substantive *valvis*; consequently, several other verbs of this kind must be assigned to the present class, such as *agison* (from *agis*), *sigison* (from *sigis*).

c) Those with *-m*: *dvalmon* (from *dvals*).

§ 158. 3) Verbs in *-an*, which, with only a few exceptions, are likewise attached directly to the stem.

a) From verbs of the first conjugation: *þivan* (from *þivan*), *boljan* (from *batan*), *valdan* (from *vildan*), *faian*, *fijan* (from *feian*), *luban* (from *liuban*). Also belonging here are verbs which, although originating from anomalous verbs, are nevertheless regularly inflected: *kunnan*, *munnan*, and *vitan*.

b) From adjectives, with the meaning of holding or treating as—e.g. *veihan*, “to regard as holy” (from *veihs*), [Col. 1019] *sveran*, “to regard as precious” (from *svers*), *arman*, “to regard as poor, to pity” (from *arms*), and also *leikan* (from *leiks*).

c) From substantives, namely only from feminines of the first declension with fundamental vowel *a*: *liugan* (from *liuga*), *jiukan* (from *jiuka*), *saurgan* (from *saurga*), *weilan* (from *weila*).

§ 159. Of verbs originating from expanded stems of the second conjugation, only those formed by means of the syllable *an* occur: *gaainanan* (from *ains*) and *gastoþanan* (from *standan*).

## III. THIRD CONJUGATION

§ 160. All verbs of this conjugation are to be referred to verbs of the first or second conjugation; where such verbs no longer exist, they can readily be supplied.

a) From verbs of the first conjugation they are regularly formed by means of the vowel of the passive participle, which appears highly appropriate to the passive meaning. In certain verbs belonging to the fourth ablaut class, however, the present vowel is preferred, namely in *usgeisnan*, *ïnfeinan*, and *keinan*. In *dishnaupnan*, assigned to the fourth class, the singular preterite vowel has indeed been inserted, unless a *dishnaupjan* is to be assumed as an intermediate form; compare *ganohnan*, belonging to the sixth class, alongside which the second-conjugation verb *ganohjan* still occurs. They are derived as follows:

aa) From the strong first conjugation: *bundnan* (from *bindan*), *tundnan* (from *tindan*), *gaþaursnan* (from *þairsan*).

[Col. 1020]

bb) From the second: *aftaurnan* (from *tairan*).

cc) From the fourth: *lifnan* (from *leiban*), *disskritnan* (from *skreitan*), *usgeisnan* (from *geisan*), *keinan* (from *keian*), *ïnfeinan* (from *feian*).

dd) From the fifth: *usgutnan* (from *giutan*), *usluknan* (from *lukan*), *fralusnan* (from *fraliusan*); *dishnaupnan* (from *dishniupan*).

ee) From the sixth: *batnan* (from *batan*), *vaknan* (from *vakan*), *hafnan* (from *hafjan*).

ff) From the seventh: *gaskaidnan* (from *skaidan*), *auknan* (from *aukan*).

gg) From the eighth: *andletnan* (from *letan*).

§ 161. b) Among verbs of the second conjugation, only those ending in *-jan* form verbs of the third conjugation: *blindnan* (from *blindjan*), *gabignan* (from *gabigjan*), *daubnan* (from *daubjan*), *dauþnan* (from *dauþjan*), *dumbnan* (from *dumbjan*?), *drobnan* (from *drobjan*), *fraqistnan* (from *fraqistjan*), *gaqiunan* (from *gaqiujan*), *ushauhnan* (from *ushauhjan*), *gahaftnan* (from *gahaftjan*), *hailnan* (from *hailjan*), *gaþlahsnan* (from *þlahsjan*), *managnan* (from *managjan*), *mikilnan* (from *mikiljan*), *minznan* (from *minzjan*?), *ganipnan* (from *ganipjan*?), *ganohnan* (from *ganohjan*), *urrumnan* (from *urrumjan*?), *afslauþnan* (from *afslauþjan*), *gastaurknan* (from *gastaurkjan*?), *svinþnan* (from *svinþjan*), *gagavairpnan* (from *gagavairpjan*), *fullnan* (from *fulljan*), *afwapnan* (from *afwapjan*). Only *veihnan* (from *veihan*) is excepted here.

## D. ADVERBIAL FORMATION

[Col. 1019]

§ 162. With respect to formation, adverbs are divided into adverbs of manner, place, and time. Here, however, we do not discuss those formed either by composition, for example with the particles *-uh*, *-ei*, *-hun*, or periphrastically through genuine substantives or adjectives, with or without a preposition; the former will be treated under compounds, the latter in syntax.

## I. ADVERBS OF MANNER

§ 163. 1) Adverbs derived from adjectives are most commonly formed with *ba* attached to the base form.

a) From adjectives of the first declension: *abraba*, *azetaba*, *bairhtaba*, *baitraba*, *balþaba*, *gabigaba*, *gagudaba*, *hauhaba*, *svikunþaba*, *mikilaba*, *ubilaba*, *raihtaba*, *garaihtaba*, *garedaba*, *unsahtaba*, *sviknaba*, *ungatassaba*, *gatilaba*, *triggvaba*, *vairþaba*, *unvairþaba*, *veihaba*, *ainfalþaba*, *gafehaba*, *frodaba*, *wassaba*; also from participles: *unfairinodaba*.

b) From adjectives of the second declension. Here one must again distinguish whether the radical syllable preceding the ending is long or short. In the former case the adverbial ending is *iba*, in the latter *jaba*: thus *arniba*, *andaugiba*, *analaugniba*, *unanasiuniba*, *usstiuriba*, *gatemiba*, but *gabaurjaba*, *sunjaba*.

c) From adjectives of the third declension: *agluba*, *glaggvuba*, *harduba*, *manvuba*.

> Note 1.—Here *u* sometimes changes into *a*, as in *glaggvaba*, Luke XV.8, and *hardaba*, 2 Cor. XIII.10, manuscript A.

> Note 2.—Although the interrogative adverb *waiva?*, “how?”, belongs here by reason of its meaning, it is doubtful whether it should also be assigned here on formal grounds. Yet, since above (§ 46, 4) we showed that *b* and *v* are phonetically related, it would not be impossible if *waiva* stood in place of *waiba*. Be this as it may, this way of considering it seems preferable to the opinion according to which the adverb arose from a composition of *we* and *aiva*. Moreover, corresponding to this *waiva*, derived from the interrogative pronoun *wa*, is *sva*, formed from the demonstrative *sa*, which is to be understood as *s-va* and in which no composition with *aiva* is to be assumed. Besides, the ending of each is similar in origin and in meaning. The relative *sve* seems to be made from *sva* combined with the relative particle *ei*; or perhaps it differs from the conjunction *svaei* only by contraction.

2) Another common form, which is not confined to adverbs derived from adjectives, is *o*. It sometimes occurs together with the form *ba*, as *andaugjo* alongside *andaugiba*, *glaggvo* (if we have correctly conjectured it in the glossary under this word) alongside *glaggvaba*. It is uncertain, however, whether all adjectives admit this double adverbial ending, some rather preferring one form to another. Thus, the form with *o* belongs exclusively to those adjectives furnished with a derivative syllable, except only the formative syllable *il*, which has, from earliest times, become in some measure fused with the stem (*mikils*, *ubils*).

a) From adjectives of the first declension: *analeiko*, [Col. 1021] *anþarleiko*, *galeiko*, *laþaleiko*, *samaleiko*, *vairaleiko*, *sinteino*, *þiudisko*, *ïudaivisko*, *uhteigo*, *unuhteigo*, *vitodeigo*, probably also *usdaudo*, *ussindo*, *sundro*, *sniumundo*, *unveniggo*; the last two at least could hardly be derived from the verbs *sniumjan*, *venjan*.

b) From adjectives of the second declension: *andaugjo*, and also *arvjo*, *þiubjo*, *gahahjo*, *allandjo*; and further the numeral *þridjo*, “for the third time,” from *þridja*, “third.”

c) From adjectives of the third declension: *glaggvo* (*gaaggvo*).

d) The following do not appear to be referable to adjectives: *aufto*, *ufjo*, *misso*, *sprauto*.

3) Adverbs derived from comparatives and superlatives employ the simple stem of the comparative or superlative without a vocalic ending, except that they change comparative *z* into *s*:

a) Comparatives: *hauhis* (from *hauhiza*), *vulþris* (from *vulþriza*), *andvairþis* (from *andvairþiza*), *framvairþis* (from *framvairþiza*), *mais* (from *maiza*). Of the same formation are comparatives derived immediately from adverbs: *airis* (from *air*), *andis* (from *and*), *newis* (from *new*), *framis* (from *fram*), *faurþis* (from *faurþ*?), *haldis* (from *halþ*?), *halis* (from *hal*?), *sniumundos* (from *sniumundo*), *aljaleikos* (from *aljaleiko*?).

> Note 1.—The adverbs *allis* and *raihtis*, coming very close to simple particles, seem indeed to belong here in form. But, since *alls* contains no notion of comparison and the comparative of *raihts* is *raihtoza*, no comparative is to be assumed in these adverbs.

> “Note 2.—Some adverbs belonging here present a syncopated form, with the *i* preceding *s* expelled: *mins* (from *minniza*), *vairs* (from *vairsiza*), and likewise *seiþs* (from the positive *seiþu*), *jaindvairþs* (cf. *andvairþis, framvairþis*), *suns, anaks*.
>
> “Note 3.—The form *filaus*, derived from the adverb *filu*, is used before comparatives; since it cannot be regarded as a genitive used before an adverb, perhaps a comparative should here be assumed, and *filaus* taken as standing for *filos*.”

b) Superlatives: *maist* (from *maists*), *frumist* (from *frumists*).

4) Besides the three preceding classes of adverbs, there are also a few others which, though of doubtful origin, must nevertheless be referred here, namely:

a) With *is*: the already mentioned *allis, raihtis*;

b) With *e*: *sve, svare*;

c) With *u*: *filu, seipu*;

d) With *a*: *sunja*.

## II. Adverbs of Place

[Col. 1022]

§ 164. The adverbs belonging here are for the most part formed either from pronominal stems or from other particles, only a few being referable to nominal roots. They are divided into three classes, according as they signify existence in a place, motion toward a place, or motion from a place.

1) To designate the place in which something is or occurs, the following adverbs serve:

a) With the ending *a*: *afta*, behind; *faura*, before; *dalaþa*, below; *ïupa*, above; *uta*, outside; *ïnna*, within, inside; *fairra*, far away; *newa*, near; and the adverbs occurring only in compounds, *anda*, opposite, and *unþa*, at a distance. Likewise *alja*, outside (properly “in another direction”), must also be referred here;

b) With the ending *r, ar*: *war*, where; *þar*, here; *her*, there; *jainar*, yonder; *aljar*, elsewhere; compare the prepositions *hindar*, behind, after; *ufar*, over; *undar*, under; *afar*, after.

c) From some of these adverbs others are formed with the ending *o*, with their sense slightly altered: *ufaro*, above, upwards; *undaro*, beneath; *aftaro*, behind, after.

d) With the ending *na* added, the preceding adverbs have the same sense, but with the additional feature that they sometimes express motion from a place: *aftana*, behind; *utana*, from outside; *ïnnana*, from within; *ïupana*, from above; *hindana*, behind, after; *samana*, together, collectively.

2) Motion toward a place is indicated either by a simple consonant-final stem—*faur, ïup, ut, ïnn, new*—or by the endings:

a) *þ* (D): *waþ*, whither; *jaind*, thither; *þad*, hither (surviving only in the compound *þadei*, “whither”); *aljaþ*, elsewhere; *dalaþ*, hither below; *samaþ*, together (with motion); to which ending, sometimes also

b) *re* is attached, with the same meaning remaining: *wadre*, whither; *jaindre*, thither; *hidre*, hither.

3) Finally, motion from a place is indicated by the ending *þro*: *waþro*, whence; *þaþro*, hence; *jainþro*, thence; *utaþro*, from outside; *ïnnaþro*, from within; *ïupaþro*, from above; *dalaþro*, from below; *fairraþro*, from afar; *aljaþro*, from elsewhere; *allaþro*, from every side.

> “Note.—*bisunjane*, ‘around,’ could not be placed in any of these classes, its formation and origin being alike obscure. In form it appears to be a plural genitive, or at least corresponds to one both in sense and in the constructions in which it occurs; for example, Mark III.34, *bisaiwan bisunjane*, ‘to look around’; Nehemiah V.17; VI.16, *þai bisunjane unsis*, ‘those around us.’”

## III. Adverbs of Time

[Col. 1023]

§ 165. The Gothic language has particular difficulty in forming these adverbs. Apart from a few primitive words, such as *nu*, now; *ju*, already; *air*, early, others are chiefly expressed periphrastically: *himma daga*, today; *du maurgina*, in the morning; *gistradagis* (not properly an adverb, but the genitive of *gistradags*), yesterday. Only a few points need be noted here:

a) From the pronominal stems *WA, þA, SUMA*, with *n* added, are formed the temporal adverbs: *wan*, when; *þan*, then; *suman*, once, formerly;

b) Certain others, for the most part of obscure origin, take the ending *e* or *a*: *þande*, while; *unte*, until; *simle*, formerly; *ufta*, often; *aftra*, again.

# E. Formation by Composition

[Col. 1023]

§ 166. Proper composition consists in joining two words together in such a way that the first part of the word can no longer have a distinct inflection. Where this is not the case, the composition is improper. Composition differs from derivation in that derivation attaches to a word an element which of itself and in itself lacks meaning—or whose meaning has at least escaped us—whereas composition consists of parts meaningful in themselves. Compounds may, moreover, be formed not only from derivatives but also from words previously compounded; the latter are called double compounds, for example: *miþgardavaddjus, ufarhiminakunds, galiugabroþar, gabaurþivaurd, untilamalsks, unhanduvaurhts, ïnnatgaggan*. There is also this further difference: in composition the first part of the word is more important, whereas in derivation the latter part is more important. Accordingly, in treating composition, we shall arrange it in three classes, according as the first part is nominal, pronominal, or a particle.

> “Note 1.—Whether verbal composition occurs in Gothic cannot be established with certainty. *Slahals*, if indeed it is a compound (§ 150, b), can be derived both from *slahan* and from *slahs*. The same must be said of *vinþiskauro* (from *vinþjan*), *spaiskuldrs* (from *speivan*), and *þiuþiqiss* (from *þiuþjan*). Likewise, *laþaleiko* appears to be derived from the adjective *laþs* rather than immediately from the verb *laþon*. Other examples can scarcely be found.
>
> “Note 2.—Hybrid words occur nowhere in the Gothic language. For in such words as *motastaþs, smakkabagms*, it is uncertain to what language the first part belongs; while *afarsabbatus, galiugaxristus,* and *galiugaapaustaulus* have borrowed their latter part from Hebrew, they have nevertheless been granted semantic citizenship (the printed Latin wording is uncertain).”

## I. Nominal Composition

[Col. 1023]

### I. Nouns

§ 167. Nominal composition is subject to this general rule: the first part of a compound is simply used in its basic form. Only in some rarer cases is a consonant-final apocopated form preferred; this indeed regularly corresponds to the accusative, though it must not be regarded as an accusative. No reason can be assigned why the full forms *gudalaus, gudafaurhts, veinatriu, veinagards, lausavaurds* occur alongside *gudhus, guþblostreis, veindrugkja, laushandus, lausqiþrs*, etc. In any case, one must carefully avoid taking the former for datives; for, if this could be said of words of the first declension, it could in no way be said of words of the second or third vocalic declension, the meaning itself being opposed to it in most cases. The only exceptions to the rule given above are words whose stem ends in a vowel, as in *þiumagus, niuklahs, freihals*, or is polysyllabic, as in *sigislaun, þiudangardi, mikilþuhts, ubiltojis*, where the shorter form may have been chosen instead of the longer *sigisalaun, þiudanagardi*, etc., for the sake of euphony. With anomalous nouns, either the simple stem is used, for example *bruþfaþs, manleika*; or the full form in *a*, as *nahtamats, manaseþs*; or finally a form in *a* that presents the appearance of a genitive, as *baurgsvaddjus, þrutsfill*. Words of consonantal declension reject their *n* in composition, the long vowel remaining but changing into its corresponding short vowel, thus: *vaihstastains* from *VAIHSTAN*, *augadaura* from *AUGAN*, *qinakunds* from *QINON*, *marisaivs* from *MAREIN*.

Nouns are compounded with nouns, adjectives, participles, and only rarely with particles.

The following are examples of compound nouns with nouns, adjectives, and participles:

a) Vocalic declension:

aa) With basic vowel *a*: *vigadeina* (from *vigs*), *figgragulþ* (from *figgrs*), *kaisaragild* (from *kaisar*), *himinakunds* (from *himins*), *gilstrameleins* (from *gilstr*), *alevabagms* (from *alev*), *veinabasi, veinatains, veinatriu, veinagards* (from *vein*), *eisarnabandi* (from *eisarn*), *vitodafasteis, vitodalaisareis, vitodalaus* (from *vitoþ*), *liugnapraufetus, liugnavaurds* (from *liugn*), *lukarnastaþa* (from *lukarn*), *dauravards* [Col. 1025] (from *daur*), *launavargs* (from *laun*), *vaurdajiuka* (from *vaurd*), *guþaskaunei, gudalaus, gudafaurhts* (from *guþ*), *akranalaus* (from *akran*), *bloþarinnands* (from *bloþ*), *hleþrastakeins* (from *hleiþra*), *motastaþs* (from *mota*), *stauastols* (from *staua*), *weilawairbs* (from *weila*), *friaþvamilds* (from *friaþva*).

> “Note 1.—In nouns whose basic form ends in *-ja*, one must again distinguish whether a derivational syllable, or a long or short stem syllable, precedes; for in the former case the apocopated form in *i*, and in the latter the full form *-ja*, is used in composition: *andilaus* from *andeis* (theme *ANDJA*), *þusundifaþs* from *þusundi* (theme *ÞUSUNDJA*), *arbinumja* from *arbi* (theme *ARBJA*), *fraþjamarzeins* from *fraþi* (theme *FRAÞJA*), *vadjabokos* from *vadi* (theme *VADJA*), *lubjaleisei* from *lubja?* (theme *LUBJA*).”

bb) With basic vowel *i*: *matibalgs* (from *mats*), *drauhtivitoþ* (from *drauhts*), *gastigods* (from *gasts*), *naudibandi, naudiþaurfts* (from *nauþs*), *gabaurþivaurd* (from *gabaurþs*), *aurftigards* (from *aurts?*).

cc) With basic vowel *u*: *asiluqairnus* (from *asilus*), *fotubandi, fotubaurd* (from *fotus*), *grunduvaddjus* (from *grundus*), *qiþuhafts* (from *qiþus*), *lustusams* (from *lustus*), *faihuþraihns, faihugairnei, faihuskula, faihufrikei, faihugavaurki* (from *faihu*), *handuvaurhts* (from *handus*).

dd) With basic vowel *r*: *broþrulubo* or *broþralubo* (from *broþar*).

> “Note 2.—The following occur with the final vowel of the basic form rejected: *guþblostreîs, gudhus, halsagga, veindrugkja, gutþiuda, þiumagus, sigislaun, þiudangardi*. Although the formation of *midjungards* is obscure, it is nevertheless probable that it is formed from some lost *midjun* or *midjuns*. What we have entered in the glossary as *þiuþspillon* should more appropriately be divided as *þiuþ spillon*; compare *þiuþ taujan*, Mark III.4; Luke VI.9, 33, 35.
>
> “Note 4.—Although nouns are not compounded with verbs, verbs can nevertheless be derived from compound nouns, as *þuthaurnjan* from *þuthaurn*, *faihugeironjan* from *faihugeiro*.
>
> “Note 3.—The sole examples of a noun compounded with a participle are *mannahun* and *weilohun*.”

ee) Anomalous forms: the few examples occurring have been mentioned above; to these must certainly be added *bruþfaþs, nahtamats, baurgsvaddjus*. Likewise *manleika, manaseþs, manamaurþrja*, derived from *manna*, may be referred here, since the theme *MAN* (§ 93, 1) underlies them; the analogy of *baurgsvaddjus* supports *þrutsfïll*.

b) Consonantal declension: *vaihstastains* (from *vaihsta*), *smakkabagms* (from *smakka*), *viljahalþei* (from *vilja*), *gumakunds* (from *guma*), *miþgardavaddjus* (from *miþgarda?*), [Col. 1026] *augadauro* (from *augo*), *qinakunds* (from *qino*), *marisaivs* (from *marei*), *aglaitivaurdei* (from *aglaitei*).

### II. Adjectives

§ 168. The same in general must be said of compound adjectives as of nouns. Compounds with verbs do occur, but only compounds of *fulls*: *fullafahjan, fullafraþjan, fullaveisjan*.

The following are examples of adjectives compounded with nouns, adjectives, and participles:

a) With basic vowel *a*: *armahairtei* (from *arms*), *juggalauþs* (from *juggs*), *laggamodei* (from *laggs*), *mukamodei* (from *muks?*), *þrasabalþei* (from *þras?*), *balvavesei* (from *balvs?*), *dvalavaurdei* (from *dvals*), *lausavaurdi, lausavaurdei, lausavaurds* (from *laus*), *godakunds* (from *gods*), *fullatojis, fullavits* (from *fulls*), *ïbnaleiks, ïbnaskauns* (from *ïbns*), *liubaleiks* (from *liubs*), *untilamalsks* (from *tils*), *allavaurstva, alaþarba, alamans* (from *alls*).

b) With basic vowel *i*: here probably occurs the same distinction noted above in nouns (§ 167, note 1), though only the following examples occur: *midjasveipains* (from *midja*), *aljakuns, aljaleiks, aljaleikoþs* (from *aljis*), *hrainjahairts* (from *hrains*).

c) Examples with basic vowel *u* are lacking.

> “Note.—The following are found with the final vowel of the basic form rejected: *allbrunsts, allsverei, allvaldands, allandis* (from *alls*), *hauhþuhts, hauhhairts, hauhhairtei* (from *hauhs*), *laushandus, lausqiþrs, lausqiþre* (from *laus*), *aglaitgastalds* (from *aglaits*), *anþarleiks* (from *anþar*), *managfalþs* (from *manags*), *ubilvaurds, ubiltojis* (from *ubils*), *mikilþuhts* (from *mikils*), *niuklahs* (from *niujis*), *freihals* (from *freis*).”

### III. Numerals

§ 169. a) Fully inflected numerals, when compounded, are subject to the same rules as nouns and adjectives; thus they are used in the vowel-final basic form: *ainabaur* (from *ains*), *hundafaþs* (from *hund*), *þusundifaþs* (from *þusundi*), and also in apocopated form: *ainwarjizuh, ainwaþaruh*. Numerals denoting tens and hundreds, such as *tvaitigjus, þreistigjus, tvahunda, þrijahunda*, like *ainshun*, are not properly compounds, since both parts—or even the first—are inflected (§ 166).

b) Defective or scarcely inflected numerals, however, appear to remain unaltered in composition: *fidvortigjus, fimftigjus, fimfhunda, saihstigjus, ahtaudogs, niuhunda*; yet alongside *fidvor* an apocopated form *fidur* also occurs: *fidurdogs, fidurragineis*.

c) Multiplicatives are formed with *falþs*, preceded by an apocopated form of the numeral: *ainfalþs, tvafalþs* (?), *þreifalþs* (?), *fidurfalþs, taihuntaihundfalþs*, etc.

## II. Pronominal Composition

[Col. 1025]

§ 170. Pronominal composition is either proper or improper. The former occurs only in forming adjectives from the pronouns *sama* and *silba*: *samaleiks, samakuns, samalauds, samasaivals, samafraþjis*, [Col. 1026] *samaqiss, silbasiunis, silbavileis, silbaviljands*. On the irregular *seinaigairns*, see the note on 2 Timothy III.2. Improperly, however, adjectives are formed with the help of the particles *ei, uh,* and *hun*.

[Col. 1027]

a) With *ei*: *ïkei, þuei, ïzei, saei*, etc. (§ 109); compare the particles *þadei, þarei, þaþroei, svaei, akei, sunsei, miþþanei*, etc.;

b) With *uh*: *sah, wazuh, warjizuh, waþaruh* (§§ 108, 111); compare the particles *þanuh, þaruh, þiswaruh, þiswaduh*;

c) With *hun*: *washun*; compare the already mentioned *mannahun, weilohun, ainshun*, and the particles *þishun, wan*—

[Col. 1028]

Also conspicuous are improperly compounded words formed with the pronoun *sa, so, þata* and some of its cases: nominative *sawazuh, þatïst, þatain, þatainei*; genitive *þiswazuh, þiswaduh, þishun*; dative (instrumental) *þehaldis*. Finally, *welauds* and *weleiks* are likewise compounded from the instrumental case of the interrogative pronoun.

## III. Composition of Particles

[Col. 1027]

§ 171. Since particles can neither be inflected nor changed, they are mostly used unaltered in composition and contribute little to this section on word formation. On the other hand, words composed from particles are almost innumerable and therefore cannot be omitted here. Particles may be combined with every part of speech; and composition with adverbs must be distinguished from composition with prepositions.

### I. Adverbs

*Vaila*: *vailaqiss, vailavizns, vailamerjan*.  
*Vai* (*vaja*): *vaidedja, vaifairwjan, vajamerjan, vajamereins*.  
*Missa*: *missadeds, missaqiss, missaleiks, missataujands*.  
*Filu*: *filudeisei, filuvaurdei, filufaihus, filugalaubs, filuvaurdjan*.  
*Suns*: *sunsaiv, sunsei*.  
*Halis*: *halisaiv*.  
*þan* (*þana*): *þanamais, þanaseiþs*.  
*Sva*: *svalauds, svaleiks*; compare the correlatives *welauds, weleiks* (§ 170).  
*Inn*: *ïnngaggan, ïnnvairpan, ïnnatbairan, ïnnatgaggan, ïnnattiuhan, ïnngaleiþan, ïnnufsliupan, miþïnngaleiþan*.  
*Inna*: *ïnnakunds, ïnnagahts*.  
*Ut*: *utbairan, utgaggan*.  
*Faura*: *fauragaggan, fauraqiþan, fauraqiman, fauragahaitan, fauragateihan, fauragaggja, fauradauri, fauramaþleis*.  
*Anda*: *andabauhts, andabeit, andahait, andahafts, andaþahts, andalauni, andanahti, andanem, andanumts, andastaþjis, andastaua, andavaurd, andavaurdi, andavizn, andavleizns, andaneiþs, andanems, andanemeigs, andasets*.  
*Unþa*: *unþaþliuhan*.  
*Tvis, tuz*: *tvisstandan, tuzverjan*.

### II. Prepositions

§ 172. Among the prepositions we have also included certain particles which occur only in composition, such as *fair, fra, fri, ga, dis, ïd, un*. Here, however, we shall arrange only a few examples, referring the reader for the others to the glossary, in which the individual compounds are listed under each particle.

*Ana*: *anabiudan, anaïnsakan, anamahts, anavairþs, analeiko*.  
*And*: *andbindan, andtilon, andbahts, andvairþs, andaugjo*.  
*At*: *ataugjan, atgaraihtjan, atgaggs*.  
*Af*: *afaikan, afletan, afgrundiþa, afguds, afgastoþans*.  
*Afar*: *afargaggan, afarlaistjan, afardags*.  
*Bi*: *bimaitan, bivindan, bibaurgeins, bifaiho, bireiks, biþe*, and also *biwe*, Luke I.18.  
*Ga*: *ganisan, gateihan, gahaitan, gamunan, gagahaftjan, gagaleikon, gagamainjan, gagatilon, gagavairþjan, gagavairþnan, gadaila, galaubeins, gaguds, gafulgins, gahahjo, gatemiba*.  
*Dis*: *distairan, dishaban, distaheins, disviss*.  
*Du*: *duginnan, dustodjan, duatgaggan, duatsnivan, duatrinnan, dugavindan, duþe, duwe*.  
*Hindar*: *hindarleiþan, hindarveisei, hindarveis*.  
*þairh*: *þairharbaidjan, þairhsaiwan, þairhgaleikon*.  
*Id*: *ïdveitjan, ïdveit, ïddaljo*.  
*In*: *ïnagjan, ïnsandjan, ïngaleikon, ïnsahts, ïnvinds*.  
*Inu*: does not form compounds.  
*Miþ*: *miþniman, miþanakumbjan, miþgatiuhan, miþushramjan, miþïnsandjan, miþfrahunþans, miþgaleikonds, miþvissei, miþgasinþa*.  
*Un*: *unverjan, unkunnands, unþvahans, ungalaubjands, unandsakans, unbilaistiþs, unusspilloþs, unfairlaistiþs, unufbrikands, unagei, ungalaubeins, unbimait, unhails, unandsoks, unatgahts, ungatass, unhindarveis, unfaurveis, unveniggo, unanasiuniba*.  
*Und*: *undgreipan, undredan, undrinnan*.  
*Undar*: does not form compounds.  
*Us*: *usbeidan, urreisan, usgasaiwan, usvahsans, usstass, usvaurhts, ussindo*.  
*Uf*: *ufbrikan, ufhropjan, ufhauseins, ufkunþi*.  
*Ufar*: *ufarhafjan, ufarmeleins, ufarfulls, ufarhiminakunds*.  
*Viþra*: *viþragaggan, viþragamotjan, viþravairþs*.  
*Fair*: *fairaihan, fairhaitan, fairveitl*.  
*Faur*: *faurbiudan, faurbigaggan, faurbauhts*.  
*Faura*: see § 171.  
*Fra*: *frabugjan, fragifts, fralets*.  
*Fram*: *framgahts, framaldrs, framvigis, framvairþis*.  
*Fri*: *frisahts*.

§ 173. From the preceding paragraphs it is certainly clear how great is the Gothic language’s capacity for forming words. Yet, on comparing Ulfilas’s version with the Greek text, it will become evident that this capacity had its limits, and that the character of the language did not always permit the Goth to translate into his own language certain Greek formations or compounds. Therefore, while we acknowledge that the Gothic language ought, as far as possible, to be developed from itself, it is neither irrelevant nor useless to our proposed purpose to delineate here, by a negative method as well, the limits of Gothic word formation. Once these are known, the linguistic monuments will be better understood. Following the same arrangement in this respect, let us consider:

1) Formation by derivation:

a) Of nouns. From the abundance of forms available for forming nouns derived from verbs and nouns, which we have discussed above (§ 142 ff.), one would scarcely believe that the Gothic translation of even a single Greek word was impossible.

> “Thus, if the Goth renders Colossians II.22, *τὰ ἀποχρήσει* (‘the things for use’; the printed Greek is contextually incomplete), by *þairh þatei ïs brukjaidau*; Matthew VI.12, *τὰ ὀφειλήματα ἡμῶν* (‘our debts’), by *þatei skulans sijaima*; Colossians I.24, *παθήματά μου* (‘my sufferings’), by *þoei vinna*; 1 Timothy IV.15, *σοῦ ἡ προκοπή* (‘your progress’), by *þatei þeihais þu*—just as in Colossians I.10 he renders *εἰς πᾶσαν ἀρέσκειαν* (‘unto all pleasing’) by *ïn allamma þatei galeikai*, Mark VII.5, 8 *παράδοσις* (‘tradition’) by *þatei anafulhun*, and Luke VI.7 *κατηγορία* (‘accusation’) by *til du vrohjan*—this must be attributed solely to a more perfect translation or to a closer grasp of the character of Gothic, although in other places he employs the verbal nouns *leikains, anafilh,* and *vrohs* with the same meaning.”

b) Of adjectives. Greek verbal adjectives in *-τος* (“-able,” “-ed”) are generally rendered by the participle; see § 190, 3.

c) Of verbs. Here the Gothic language especially yields to Greek. Verbs particularly in *-εύω, -άζω, -ίζω, -όω,* and *-έω* had to be rendered periphrastically in Gothic.

aa) Verbs in *-εύω* and *-έω*:

> “Indeed, *αἰχμαλωτεύειν* (‘to take captive’) is rendered by *ushinþan*; *ἀγρεύειν* (‘to catch’) by *ganiutan*; *βασιλεύειν* (‘to reign’) by *þiudanon*; *θεραπεύειν* (‘to heal, serve’) by *hailjan, leikinon*; *ἱερατεύειν* (‘to serve as priest’) by *gudjinon*; *δουλεύειν* (‘to be enslaved, serve’) by *skalkinon*; *πτωχεύειν* (‘to be poor’) by *gaunledjan sik*, etc. But in very many other cases these verbs must be paraphrased, for example: *ἀληθεύειν* (‘to speak or act truly’), by *sunja gateihan* or *taujan*; *θριαμβεύειν* (‘to triumph’) by *hroþeigana ustaiknjan*; *γυμνητεύειν* (‘to be naked’) by *naqads visan*; *ἡγεμονεύειν* (‘to govern’) by *kindins visan* (also *raginon*); *κινδυνεύειν* (‘to be in danger’) by *bireks visan*; *εἰρηνεύειν* (‘to live in peace’) by *gavairþeigs visan*, *gavairþi haban* or *taujan*; *πρωτεύειν* (‘to hold first place’) by *framadein haban*; *διανυκτερεύειν* (‘to spend the night’) by *naht þairhvakan*.
>
> “Similarly, *ἀρκεῖν* (‘to suffice’) by *ganohs visan*; *ἀσθενεῖν* (‘to be weak’) by *siuks visan*; *δυνατεῖν* (‘to be able’) by *mahteigs visan*; *ἐνδημεῖν* (‘to be at home’) by *anahaims visan*; *εὐκαιρεῖν* (‘to have leisure’) by *uhtiugs visan*; *συνευδοκεῖν* (‘to approve together’) by *gaviljis visan*; *ψευδομαρτυρεῖν* (‘to bear false witness’) by *galiugaveitvods visan*; *παρακολουθεῖν* (‘to follow closely’) by *galaista visan*; *φθονεῖν* (‘to envy’) by *ïn neiþa visan*; *ὠφελεῖν* (‘to benefit’) by *du botai visan*; *ἐκκακεῖν* (‘to lose heart’) by *vairþan usgrudja*; *πλουτεῖν* (‘to be rich’) by *gabigs vairþan*; *κληρονομεῖν* (‘to inherit’) by *arbja vairþan*; *ἐλαττονεῖν* (‘to diminish’) by *favizo haban*; *ὑστερεῖν* (‘to lack’) by *minz haban*; *ὑστερεῖσθαι* (‘to suffer want’) by *þarbos þulan*; *δειπνεῖν* (‘to dine’) by *du naht matjan*.”

bb) Verbs in *-άζω*:

> “Alongside *ἁγιάζειν* (‘to sanctify’), rendered by *veihan*; *ἀγοράζειν* (‘to buy’) by *bugjan*; *ἀτιμάζειν* (‘to dishonour’) by *unsveran*; *αὐγάζειν* (‘to shine upon’) by *liuhtjan*; *ἑτοιμάζειν* (‘to prepare’) by *manvjan*; *ἑορτάζειν* (‘to celebrate a feast’) by *dulþjan*, etc., there are also *νηπιάζειν* (‘to be childish’) by *barnisks visan*; *ὁμοιάζειν* (‘to be like’) by *galeiks visan*; *σχολάζειν* (‘to be at leisure’) by *uhteigs visan*; *παραχειμάζειν* (‘to winter’) by *vintru visan*; *πλεονάζειν* (‘to abound’) by *managizo haban*; *λιθάζειν* (‘to stone’) by *stainan afvairþan* (and also *stainjan*).”

[Col. 1030]

cc) Verbs in *-ίζω*:

> “Alongside *ἀναθεματίζειν* (‘to curse’) rendered by *afaikan*; *ἀφανίζειν* (‘to destroy’) by *fravardjan*; *βασανίζειν* (‘to torment’) by *balvjan*; *βυθίζειν* (‘to sink’) by *sagqjan*; *ἐγκεντρίζειν* (‘to graft in’) by *ïntrisgan*; *σαλπίζειν* (‘to sound a trumpet’) by *haurnjan*, etc., there occur *ἐγγίζειν* (‘to draw near’) by *newa visan* (and also *newjan, atnewjan*); *ἐθίζειν* (‘to accustom’) by *biuhts visan*; *δαιμονίζεσθαι* (‘to be demon-possessed’) by *vods visan*, *unhulþons haban*; *ὀργίζεσθαι* (‘to be angry’) by *þvairhs visan*; *ἀπελπίζειν* (‘to despair’) by *usvena vairþan*; *ἀνδρίζεσθαι* (‘to act manfully’) by *vairaleiko taujan*; *παροργίζειν* (‘to provoke to anger’) by *briggan ïn þvairhein*; *ψωμίζειν* (‘to feed’) by *mat giban*; *ῥαπίζειν* (‘to strike with the palm’) by *lofam slahan*; *ῥαβδίζειν* (‘to beat with rods’) by *usbliggvan vandum*; *ἀποκεφαλίζειν* (‘to behead’) by *haubiþ afmaitan*; *ἐδαφίζειν* (‘to dash to the ground’) by *airþai gaïbnjan*; *ἐναγκαλίζεσθαι* (‘to take into one’s arms’) by *ana armins niman*; *εὐαγγελίζεσθαι* (‘to proclaim good news’) by *aivaggeljan merjan*.”

dd) Verbs in *-όω*:

> “Alongside *βεβαιοῦν* (‘to establish’) rendered by *gaþvastjan, gatulgjan*; *δουλοῦν* (‘to enslave’) by *gaþivan*; *δηλοῦν* (‘to make manifest’) by *bandvjan, gakannjan*; *θανατοῦν* (‘to put to death’) by *gadauþjan*; *ἐπιδιορθοῦν* (‘to set right further’) by *atgaraihtjan*; *ζημιοῦν* (‘to cause loss’) by *gasleiþjan*; (*μορφοῦν*, ‘to form,’ by *gabairhtjan*); *ὁμοιοῦν* (‘to make like’) by *galeikon*; *τελειοῦν* (‘to perfect’) by *usfulljan, ustiuhan*; *νεκροῦν* (‘to put to death’) by *dauþjan*, etc., there occur *δολοῦν* (‘to deceive’) by *galiug taujan*; *ἀξιοῦν* (‘to deem worthy’) and *ἱκανοῦν* (‘to make sufficient’) by *vairþana briggan*; *ἐλευθεροῦν* (‘to set free’) by *frijana briggan*; *κεφαλαιοῦν* (‘to sum up’) by *briggan haubiþ vundan* (likewise *ἑλκοῦν*, ‘to make ulcerous,’ by *banjo fullana briggan*; compare Luke XVI.20); *παραζηλοῦν* (‘to provoke to jealousy’) by *ïn aljan briggan*; *δικαιοῦν* (‘to justify’) by *garaihtana domjan, qiþan, gateihan* (and also *garaihtjan, gasunjon*); *ἐκριζοῦν* (‘to root out’) by *uslausjan us vaurtim*; *ἀποδεκατοῦν* (‘to tithe’) by *afdailjan taihundon tail*; *χαριτοῦν* (‘to endow with grace’) by *ansteigs visan*; *κληροῦσθαι* (‘to receive an allotted inheritance’) by *hlauts gasatiþs visan*.”

ee) Other periphrases with *visan, vairþan, haban*, etc., are these:

> “*Διαφέρειν* (‘to differ, excel’) by *vulþris visan, batiza visan*; *ἱλάσκεσθαι* (‘to be propitious’) by *hulþs visan*; *νήφειν* (‘to be sober’) by *andaþahts, usskavs, vars visan*; *πεινῇν* (‘to hunger’) by *gredags visan* (also *gredon*); *πικραίνεσθαι* (‘to become bitter’) by *baitrs visan*; *προσοφείλειν* (‘to owe besides’) by *skula visan*; *συνήδεσθαι* (‘to rejoice with’) by *gavizneigs visan*; *ὑγιαίνειν* (‘to be healthy’) by *hails visan*; *συμφάναι* (‘to agree’) by *gaqiss visan*; *φρεναπατᾷν* (‘to deceive the mind’) by *fraþjamarzeins visan*; *προκεῖσθαι* (‘to lie before’) by *ïn gagreftai visan*; *καταδιώκειν* (‘to pursue’) by *galaista vairþan*; *πλήττεσθαι* (‘to be struck’) by *usfilma vairþan*; *κερδαίνειν* (‘to gain’) by *du gavaurkja haban*; *ἐπαίρεσθαι* (‘to be exalted’) by *ïn arbaidai briggan*; *ἀνήκειν* (‘to be fitting’) by *du þaurftai fairrinnan*; compare *σπαταλᾷν* (‘to live luxuriously’) by *vizon ïn azetjam*.”
>
> “Note.—Verbs derived from comparatives appear in general not to have been expressible by the Goth. The sole exception is *minznan*; elsewhere occur *managizo haban* (*πλεονάζειν*, ‘to abound’), *favizo haban* (*ἐλαττόνειν*, ‘to diminish’), *minz haban* (*ὑστεροῦν*, ‘to lack’), *batiza visan* (*διαφέρειν*, ‘to excel’), *ufarassau ganohjan* (*περισσεύειν*, ‘to abound exceedingly’).”

2) Formation by composition:

a) Of nouns. Here again a distinction must be made according to the relation of the first part of the compound to the second.

aa) In adjectival relation:

> “*Ἀγριέλαιος* (‘wild olive tree’), *vilþeis alevabagms*; *καλλιέλαιος* (‘cultivated olive tree’), *gods alevabagms*; *κενοδοξία* (‘vain glory’), *lausa hauheins* (also *lausavaurdi, armahairtei*, and similar expressions); *εὐωδία* (‘sweet fragrance’), *daun voþi*; *ταπεινοφροσύνη* (‘humility’), *hauneins gahugdais*; *ἀρχιτελώνης* (‘chief tax collector’), *fauramaþleis motarje*; *ἀρχιερεύς* (‘high priest’), *auhumists gudja*, etc.; *ἀρχισυνάγωγος* (‘ruler of the synagogue’), *fauramaþleis synagogeis*.”

bb) In genitival relation:

> “*Τεχνογονία* (‘childbearing’), *barne gabaurþs*; *υἱοθεσία* (‘adoption as sons’), *sunive gadeds*; *νομοθεσία* (‘legislation’), *vitodis garaideins*; *γεωργός* (‘husbandman’), *airþos vaurstvja*; *εἰδωλολατρεία* (‘idolatry’), *galiugagude skalkinassus*; *εἰδωλολάτρης* (‘idolater’), *galiugam skalkinonds*; *εἰδωλόθυτον* (‘a thing sacrificed to an idol’), *þatei galiugam saljada*; [Col. 1031] *ἐθνάρχης* (‘ruler of a people’), *fauramaþleis þiudo*; *κοσμοκράτωρ* (‘ruler of the world’), *sa fairwu habands*; *ἀνδραποδιστής* (‘enslaver of men’), *mannans gaþivands*; *ἀνδροφόνος* (‘murderer’), *mannans maurþrjands*; *πατραλῴης* (‘father-slayer’), *attan bliggvands*; *μητραλῴης* (‘mother-slayer’), *aiþein bliggvands*; *ὀφθαλμοδουλεία* (‘eye-service’), *ïn augam skalkinon*; *θεοσέβεια* (‘reverence for God’), *guþ blotan*. Compare *εἰδωλεῖον* (‘idol-temple’), *galiuge staþs* (with *lukarnastaþs*); *γενέσια* (‘birthday celebration’), *mel gabaurþais* (with *gabaurþivaurd*); *ῥάπισμα* (‘a blow with the palm’), *slahs lofin*; *πέδη* (‘fetter’), *eisarn bi fotuns gabugan* (and also *fotubandi*).”

cc) In prepositional relation:

> “*Ὑπολήνιον* (‘wine-vat beneath the press’), *dal uf mesa*; *περίχωρος* (‘the surrounding region’), *þata bisunjane land*; *προαύλιον* (‘forecourt’), *faur gard*; *ἐπαύριον* (‘the following day’), *ïftuma dags*.”

dd) In correlative relation:

> “*Νυχθήμερον* (‘night and day’), *naht jah dag*.”

b) Of adjectives.

aa) Although the Goth renders alpha privative either through *un-* or through *-laus*, there are nevertheless some cases in which he prefers paraphrase.

> “Thus *ἀμεταμέλητος* (‘irrevocable, not to be repented of’), Romans XI.29, *ïnu ïdreiga*; *ἀφιλάργυρος* (‘not fond of money’), 1 Timothy III.3, *ni faihufriks*; *ἄνομος* (‘without law’), 1 Corinthians IX.21, *vitodis laus* (though *vitodalaus* is also used elsewhere).”

bb) Certain adjectives formed from prepositions and nouns, and having the same meaning as the nouns mentioned above under 2(a)(cc), appear not to have been capable of translation by the Goth:

> “Thus he says *faur marein* for *παράλιος* (‘by the sea’), Luke VI.17; *uf vaira* for *ὕπανδρος* (‘subject to a husband’), Romans VII.2; *us synagogein usvaurpans* for *ἀποσυνάγωγος* (‘expelled from the synagogue’), John XII.42; compare *ïn heitom* for *πυρέσσουσα* (‘feverish’), Matthew VIII.14; *aljar visands* for *ἀπών* (‘absent’), 2 Corinthians X.1, 11.”

cc) The following are examples of other paraphrases:

> “*Θεοδίδακτος* (‘taught by God’), *at guþa uslaisiþs*; *θεόπνευστος* (‘God-breathed’), *gudiskaizos ahmateinais*; *ὀλιγόπιστος* (‘of little faith’), *leitil galaubjands*; *φιλήδονος* (‘loving pleasure’), [Col. 1032] *frijonds viljan seinana*; *ἰσάγγελος* (‘equal to angels’), *ïbna aggilum*; *δευτερόπρωτος* (‘second-first’), *anþar fruma*.”

c) Of verbs.

aa) Alpha privative in verbs is indeed sometimes rendered by *un-* (§ 172; compare the glossary under that heading), but is generally paraphrased:

> “*Ἀγνοεῖν* (‘not to know’), *ni vitan*; *ἀπειθεῖν, ἀπιστεῖν* (‘to disobey, disbelieve’), *ni galaubjan*; *ἀδυνατεῖν* (‘to be unable’), *unmahteigs visan*; *ἀμελεῖν* (‘to be unconcerned’), *unkarja visan*; *ἀσταθεῖν* (‘to be unstable’), *ungastoþans visan*; *ἀτακτεῖν* (‘to act disorderly’), *ungateviþs visan*; *ἀστοχεῖν* (‘to miss the mark’), *afairziþs visan*; *ἀσθενεῖν* (‘to be weak’), *siuks visan* (*unhails visan*); *ἀθυμεῖν* (‘to lose courage’), *ïn unlustau visan*; *ἀχρειοῦσθαι* (‘to become useless’), *unbruks vairþan*; *ἀκαιρεῖσθαι* (‘to be untimely’), *analatiþs vairþan*; *ἀθετεῖν* (‘to set aside’), *vanana gataujan*.”

bb) Where, however, the first part of the compound has an adverbial relation, the Goth chiefly employs paraphrase:

> “*Ὀρθοτομεῖν* (‘to cut straight’), *raihtaba raidjan*; *ὀρθοποδεῖν* (‘to walk uprightly’), *raihtaba gaggan*; *ὑψηλοφρονεῖν* (‘to think highly’), *hauhaba hugjan*; *ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν* (‘to teach differently’), *aljaleikos laisjan*; *ὑπερφρονεῖν* (‘to think beyond measure’), *mais fraþjan*; *ἀγαθοποιεῖν* (‘to do good’), *þiuþ taujan*; *κακοποιεῖν* (‘to do evil’), *unþiuþ taujan*; *ψευδομαρτυρεῖν* (‘to bear false witness’), *galiug veitvodjan*.”

cc) The same is true where an objective relation occurs:

> “*Καρποφορεῖν* (‘to bear fruit’), *akran bairan*; *ξενοδοχεῖν* (‘to receive strangers’), *gastins andniman*; *τεκνογονεῖν* (‘to bear children’), *barna bairan*; *τεκνοτροφεῖν* (‘to rear children’), *barna fodjan*; *ὑδροποτεῖν* (‘to drink water’), *vato drigkan*; *ζωγρεῖν* (‘to take alive’) *gafahanana tiuhan* or *haban*; *οἰκοδεσποτεῖν* (‘to rule a household’), *garda valdan*; *ναυαγεῖν* (‘to suffer shipwreck’), *usfarþon gataujan us skipa*; *θηριομαχεῖν* (‘to fight with beasts’), *du diuzam veihan*; *λογομαχεῖν* (‘to contend about words’), *vaurdam veihan*; *λιθοβολεῖν* (‘to stone’), *stainam vairpan*; *ζωοποιεῖν* (‘to make alive’), *liban taujan*. Compare *ἀνακλίνειν* (‘to recline’) *gavaurkjan anakumbjan*; *αὐξῆσαι* (‘to cause to grow’) *vahsjan gataujan*; *κατακαλύπτεσθαι* (‘to cover oneself’) *gahuljan haubiþ sein*, 1 Corinthians XI.6.

# Chapter Four. On the Connection of Words, or Syntax

[Col. 1031]

§ 174. Up to this point we have considered words in themselves and in isolation; but words, rather meaningless in themselves, have in speech the purpose of placing a thought before the eyes, if one may so speak, and of binding human minds together through mutual communication. They cannot, however, attain this purpose unless they are clothed in a definite form and arranged in a definite order. It remains for us, therefore, now that the other matters have been completed, to teach those properties which words must possess in order to signify one thought or another.
