A thought expressed in words is called a sentence. Every sentence necessarily presents something which is predicated—the predicate—and an object of which it is predicated—the subject. Now the predicate either resides in a verb or is expressed by a distinct word; in the former case the idea of the predicate lies in the verbal stem, and only exceptionally in the inflectional element. Since the subject can likewise be included in the same inflectional element of the verb, a single verb can form an entire sentence. The adjuncts of the subject are indicated by the attribute; those of the predicate, by the object. What form each word in a sentence ought to assume follows partly from their mutual relation and partly from their dependence (government); moreover, the order in which the individual words ought to be arranged is determined both, and especially, by their own nature, and in certain cases by their force. Finally, according as either the subject or the predicate is one and the same, or manifold and diverse, the sentence becomes simple or compound.

§ 175. A grammar properly ought to aim at elucidating and explaining a language from itself, and especially, in syntax, to show how the people who spoke that language were able to express their thoughts, governed by the laws of understanding yet still allowing scope to choice. Such, therefore, ought to be a grammar of the Gothic language. But since its monuments—probably all that have come down to us—consist for the most part merely of translations, indeed from Greek, and are far from genuine compositions, it becomes necessary, in explaining Gothic syntax, to compare Gothic with Greek. This comparison will first show how the Goth was able, despite the relative poverty of his own forms and the corresponding lack of derivative words expressing finer distinctions of discourse, nevertheless to render well and equivalently the sentences of a language whose certain parts of speech and derived words are far richer in forms and number (as the verb and conjunction are); and also how free he was in combining words, although closely following his model, and how restrained he was where he departed from it (cf. § 8).

## A. THE PARTS OF THE SENTENCE IN RELATION TO SYNTAX

[Col. 1033]

# I. THE VERB

## I. VOICE

[Col. 1033]

§ 176. I. ACTIVE. 1) Both intransitive and transitive verbs employ the active form: John 7:37, *stoþ Iesus jah hropida qiþands. jabai wans þaursjai, gaggai du mis jah driggkai. saei galaubeiþ du mis, svasve qaþ gameleins, awos us wambai is rinnand watins libandins*—“Jesus stood and cried out, saying: ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as Scripture has said, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly’”; Eph. 4:20, *ni sva ganemuþ Xristu, jabai sveþauh ina hausideduþ—ei aflagjaiþ þana fairnjan mannan*—“you have not so learned Christ, if indeed you have heard him—that you should put off the old man.”

2) The active is often used for the Greek middle; see § 178, 2, b.

3) Quite a few verbs also exhibit a passive meaning in the active; see § 177, note 3; or they require a particular connection and construction; see note 4 there.

4) The Goth frequently renders Greek intransitive verbs as reflexives. Here it should be noted that the reflexive pronoun is normally placed after the verb; but where a determining word precedes the verb, the pronoun may be placed between the two. Thus: μεταβαίνειν, “to depart,” Matt. 11:1, and ἐμβατεύειν, Col. 2:18, by *ushafjan sik*, “to raise oneself,” German *sich erheben* (“to rise”), French *s’en aller* (“to go away”); θαρσεῖν, “to take courage,” Matt. 9:2 and elsewhere, *þrafstjan sik*, “to comfort oneself,” German *sich getrösten* (“to take comfort”), French *se confier* (“to trust”); ἐκνήφειν, “to awake, to be sober-minded,” 1 Cor. 15:34, *usskavjan sik*, “to preserve oneself,” German *sich bewahren* (“to preserve oneself”), French *se garder* (“to keep oneself”); ὑποστρέφειν, “to return,” Mark 4:12; Luke 1:56; 10:17, *gavandjan sik*, “to turn oneself around,” German *sich umwenden* (“to turn around”), French *s’en retourner* (“to return”); μετανοεῖν, “to repent,” Luke 17:3; 2 Cor. 7:8, *idreigon sik*, “to repent oneself,” German *sich reuen* (“to repent”), French *se repentir* (“to repent”); μέλλειν, “to be about to be,” John 12:4, *skaftjan*, German *sich anschicken* (“to set oneself about something”), French *se préparer* (“to prepare oneself”); πτωχεύειν, “to become poor,” 2 Cor. 8:9, *gaunledjan sik*, German *entledigen* (“to divest oneself”), French *se dépouiller* (“to strip oneself”); ἐγγίζειν, “to approach,” Luke 15:1; Mark 1:15; Luke 10:11, *newjan sik* and *atnewjan sik*, German *sich nähern* (“to draw near”), French *s’approcher* (“to approach”); ἀπέχειν, “to be distant,” Mark 7:6, *fairra haban sik*, German *sich fern halten* (“to keep oneself at a distance”), French *se tenir de loin, s’éloigner* (“to keep far off, to move away”); ἄλλως ἔχειν, “to be otherwise disposed,” literally “to conduct oneself otherwise,” 1 Tim. 5:25, *aljaleikos sik haban*, German *sich anders verhalten* (“to behave otherwise”), French *se conduire autrement* (“to conduct oneself otherwise”); ἐπιμένειν, “to remain,” Rom. 11:23, *gatulgjan sik*, German *sich befestigen* (“to establish oneself”), French *s’affermir* (“to become firm”); μανθάνειν, “to learn,” Phil. 4:9, *galaisjan sik*, German *sich belehren* (“to instruct oneself”), French *s’instruire* (“to educate oneself”); προσκαρτερεῖν, “to adhere,” Col. 4:2, *haftjan sik*, German *sich anhängen* (“to attach oneself”), French *s’attacher* (“to attach oneself”).

> **Note.**—Sometimes, even when *sik* is omitted, these verbs remain intransitive. Thus: *gavandjan*, “to return” [Col. 1034] (ἐπιστρέφειν), John 12:40; 2 Cor. 3:16; Gal. 4:9; *galaisjan*, “to learn” (μανθάνειν), 1 Tim. 5:4, Codex B; *haftjan*, “to adhere” (προσκαρτερεῖν), Rom. 12:12; *andrinnan*, “to dispute” (διαλέγεσθαι), Mark 9:34. Indeed, the following seem to occur more commonly without *sik*: *gagaggan* and *gaqiman*, “to assemble” (συνάγεσθαι); *atnewjan*, “to approach” (ἐγγίζειν); and *idreigon*, “to repent”; see the glossary, under these words. In other passages the reflexive must be supplied from what precedes; thus, *Skeireins* VII, a, *andþaggkjands*, from *andþaggkjandins sik*.

§ 177. II. PASSIVE. 1) Gothic alone among the Germanic languages possesses a passive. Yet it has been inferred that the passive had already almost become extinct in that language, because it has far fewer forms than the active (see § 132). This inference, however, is not confirmed by the surviving monuments, since the passive occurs in every one of them, without a single exception; nor is it used merely to translate the Greek passive, but also to express thoughts rendered actively in Greek (see note 5), and to supply Greek ellipses, as at Rom. 12:19, etc.

The passive occurs, for example: Matt. 7:16, *ibai lisanda af þaurnum veinabasja*, “are grapes gathered from thorns?”; v. 19, *all bagme ni taujandane akran god usmaitada jah in fon atlagjada*, “every tree not producing good fruit is cut down and cast into fire” (ἐκκόπτεται—βάλλεται); v. 26, *galeikoda, mann dvalamma*, “shall be likened to a foolish man” (ὁμοιωθήσεται); Matt. 8:12; 10:26, *ni waiht ist gahuliþ, þatei ni andhuljaidau*, “there is nothing hidden that shall not be revealed, known” (γνωσθήσεται); 10:29; 11:5, 6, 12; 26:2; 27:17; Mark 2:5, 20; 3:24, 28; 4:12, 15, 17, 21, 22, 29, 31, 32; 9:31, 49, 50; 10:33, 38, *magutsu daupeinai, þizaiei ik daupjada, ei daupjaindau*—“can you [receive] the baptism with which I am baptized, so that you may be baptized?” (βαπτίζομαι—δύνασθε βαπτισθῆναι); 11:17; 13:25; 14:9, 41; Luke 1:15, 20, 32, 60, *haitaidau Iohannes*, “he shall be called John” (κληθήσεται); 1:61, 76, *þu barnilo praufetus hauhistins haitaza*, “you, child, shall be called prophet of the Highest” (κληθήσῃ); 2:4, 23, 35; 3:5, 9; 5:20, *afleitanda þus fravaurhteis þeinos*, “your sins are forgiven” (ἀφέωνται); 5:23, 35, 38; 6:37, 38, 44; 7:22, 23, 47; 8:12, 17, 18, 50; 10:15; 14:10, 11, 14, 34; 15:19, *ni im wairþs, ei haitaidau sunus þeins*, “I am not worthy to be called your son” (κληθῆναι); 16:4, 16; 17:30, 34, 35; 18:14, 31, 32; 19:26, 29; 20:18; John 3:3, 4, 5; 7:23; 9:7; 11:4; 12:23, 31, 32; 14:13, 21; 15:6; 16:1, 32; Rom. 7:2, 3; 8:36, *in þuk gadauþjanda all dagis*, “for your sake we are put to death all day long” (θανατύμεθα); 9:7, 8, 17, 19 (see note 5); 9:26, 33; 10:10, 15; 11:19, 22, 23, 24, 35; [Col. 1035] 12:19, 21, *ni gajiukaizau*, “do not be overcome” (μὴ νικῶ); 13:9; 14:10, 15, 16; 1 Cor. 1:17; 4:2, 3; 7:22; 8:10; 10:25, 27, 29, 30; 11:6; 13:3, 5, 8; 14:24; 15:9, 12, 15—where “we are found” must be restored in the translation in place of “they are found”—26, 33, 51; 2 Cor. 1:6, 11, 19; 2:11, *ei ni gaaiginondau* or *gafaihondau*, “lest we be defrauded” (πλεονεκτηθῶμεν), where “that we be deceived” must be read in the translation in place of “that you be deceived”; 3:14, 15, 16, 18; 4:11, 16; 5:1, 3, 4; 6:3, 12; 7:9; 9:4; 10:8; 11:7, 10, 12, 29; 12:9, 15, 20; Gal. 1:6, *afvandjanda*, “you are being turned away” (μετατίθεσθε); 2:17; 4:19; 5:11, 12, 15, 18; 6:1, 7; Eph. 3:15; 4:31; 5:3; 6:19; Phil. 1:18, 20; 2:5; 3:9; Col. 2:22; 4:16; 1 Thess. 3:3; 4:17; 5:23, 27; 2 Thess. 3:1, 2; 1 Tim. 1:19; 3:10; 4:5, 10; 5:9, 16; 6:1; 2 Tim. 2:5, 26; 3:6; 4:6; Philem. 22; Neh. 7:3; *Skeireins* VII, a; VIII, c.

2) The Goth can also construct in the passive verbs which govern the dative. For example, *fraqiman*: Mark 5:26, *qino fraqimandei allamma seinamma*, “a woman who had spent all that she possessed,” and elsewhere; hence *fragimada*, 2 Cor. 12:15; Gal. 5:15. Likewise *fraþjan*: Luke 2:50, *ni froþun þamma waurda*, “they did not understand the saying,” and elsewhere; hence Phil. 2:5, *þata fraþjaidau*, “let this be understood.”

3) Besides the passive form, there is a distinct class of verbs with passive meaning: namely, verbs of the third conjugation, for example *andbundnan*, “to be loosed”; *usgutnan*, “to be poured out”; *gahailnan*, “to be healed”; *usmernan*, “to be reported,” etc.; see § 131.

> **Note 1.**—The passive frequently occurs alongside third-conjugation verbs derived from the same stem, and there is no distinction of meaning between them. Thus: *vaurda meina usfulljanda in mela seinamma*, “my words shall be fulfilled in their time,” Luke 1:20, alongside *usfullnoda þata gamelido*, “that which had been spoken was fulfilled,” Matt. 8:17; *ushauhjada sunus guþs þairh þata*, “the Son of God may be glorified through it,” John 11:4, alongside *ushauhniþ namo fraujins*, “the Lord’s name is glorified,” 2 Thess. 1:12; *ni uslukaindau daurons*, “let not the doors be shut,” Neh. 7:3, alongside *haurds mis usluknoda*, “a door was opened to me,” 1 Cor. 16:9; *all gaveihada*, “everything is sanctified,” 1 Tim. 4:5, alongside *veihnai namo þein*, “hallowed be your name,” Matt. 6:9. So *afdauþjada*, Mark 7:10, alongside *gadauþnan*; *fraletada*, Luke 6:32, alongside *andletnan*; *merjada*, 1 Cor. 15:12, alongside *usmernan*; *gatairada*, John 7:23, alongside *gataurnan*; *mikiljada*, Phil. 1:20, alongside *mikilnan*.

> Likewise with intransitives from the same stem: *ganasjada* (“is saved,” σώζεται), Luke 8:50, alongside *ganisan* (“to be saved,” σώζεσθαι); *gabrannjada* (“is burned,” καίoμαι), 1 Cor. 13:3, alongside *brinnan* (“to burn,” καίεσθαι); *gadrausjada*, “is cast down” (καταβιβάζεται), Luke 10:15, alongside *gadriusiþ*, “is cast” (βάλλεται), Matt. 5:29; *ufsaggqiþs varþ*, “was swallowed up” (κατεπόθη), “death,” 1 Cor. 15:54, alongside *gasiggqai*, “may be swallowed up” (καταποθῇ), “the like,” 2 Cor. 2:7. In this latter case, however, the distinct forms are more often differentiated by distinct meanings than in the former: *galagjada*, “is cast, is led” (βάλλεται), Matt. 5:25, but *ligiþ*, “has been cast, lies” (βέβληται), Matt. 8:6; *hnaivjada*, “is humbled” (ταπεινοῦται), Luke 14:11, but *hneivan*, “to incline” (κλίνειν), Luke 9:12.

4) The Goth also translates the Greek passive by corresponding intransitives, a practice often justified by the meaning. Thus Greek ὑποτάττεσθαι, “to be subject,” and πείθεσθαι, “to be persuaded,” are rendered by *ufhausjan*, “to obey”; [Col. 1036] μιμνήσκεσθαι, “to remember,” by *gamunan*, “to think”; λυπεῖσθαι, “to be affected by grief,” by *saurgan*, “to care”; ἵστασθαι, “to stand,” by *standan*, “to stand.” Hence also Mark 3:5, *gastoþ aftra so hanaus*, “the hand was restored” (ἀποκατεστάθη); Luke 6:11; βυθίζεσθαι, “to be submerged,” by *siggqan*, “to sink” (Luke 5:7); καυματίζεσθαι, “to be scorched,” by *ufbrinnan*, “to burn” (Mark 4:6); ἐκλύεσθαι, “to faint,” by *ufligan*, “to fail” (Mark 8:3); μηκύνεσθαι, “to be lengthened,” by *liudan*, “to grow”; ἐκπλήττεσθαι, “to be astonished,” by *sildaleikjan*, “to marvel”; προσορμίζεσθαι, “to be brought to shore,” by *duatsnivan*, “to put in”; καταβιβάζεσθαι, “to be cast down,” by *dalaþ galeiþan*, “to go down into the depths” (Matt. 11:23), etc.

5) The Greek passive is sometimes understood as reflexive and translated accordingly: *gakunnan sik* for ὑποτάττεσθαι, “to subject oneself,” 1 Cor. 15:28; *gafilhan sik* for κρύπτεσθαι, “to hide oneself,” John 8:59; 12:36; *ushafjan sik* for αἴρεσθαι, “to raise oneself,” Mark 11:23; *inmaidjan sik* for μεταμορφοῦσθαι, “to transform oneself,” Mark 9:2; *gavandjan sik* for ἐπιστρέφεσθαι, “to turn back,” Matt. 9:22; Mark 5:30; *gahaftjan sik* for κολλᾶσθαι, “to attach oneself,” Luke 15:15; *ataugjan sik* for ὁρᾶσθαι, φαίνεσθαι, “to appear, be seen,” 1 Cor. 15:7; Luke 9:8 and elsewhere; *afskaidan sik* for ἀφορίζεσθαι, “to separate oneself,” 2 Cor. 6:17; *uslausjan sik us vaurtim* for ἐκριζοῦσθαι, “to be uprooted,” Luke 17:6; *ussatjan sik* for φυτεύεσθαι, “to be planted,” Luke 17:6; *afgiban sik* for χωρίζεσθαι, “to depart,” Philem. 15; *galisan sik* for συνάγεσθαι, “to gather oneself,” Mark 4:1; Luke 17:37; *gasleiþjan sik* for ζημιοῦσθαι, “to harm oneself,” Mark 8:36; cf. *vairpan sis* for βάλλεσθαι, “to cast oneself,” Mark 2:23.

> **Note 2.**—Some of these verbs are also used without the reflexive pronoun: Gal. 2:5, *gakunþedum*, “we yielded” (εἴξαμεν); 1 Tim. 1:6, *usvandidedun*, “they turned aside” (ἐξετράπησαν); John 12:40, *gavandidedun*, “they turned back” (ἐπεστράφησαν); 2 Cor. 11:6, *gabairhtida me*, “I made myself manifest” (ἐφανερώθην). For if this were a past participle, as the Greek text’s φανερωθέντες otherwise suggests, there would be no reason in the context for use of the consonantal form, unless one supposes that the genuine form was *gabairhtidai*, from which the final *i* was deleted because of the immediately following *i*. At least the reflexive *gabairhtjan* also occurs at Luke 1:79. At Luke 9:25, *gasleijands sik silban*, “harming himself,” *sis silbin* must be supplied from the preceding context; cf. § 178, note 3, and § 176, note.

> **Note 3.**—Some verbs have passive as well as reflexive meaning even in the active, especially *daupjan*: “to wash, be washed, wash oneself” (βαπτίσαι, βαπτίσασθαι, βαπτισθῆναι). Matt. 3:11: *izwis daupja*, “I baptize you” (ὑμᾶς βαπτίζω); Mark 7:4, *niba daupjand, ni matjand*, “unless they wash, they do not eat” (ἐὰν μὴ βαπτίσωνται). Luke 3:21, *biþe daupida*, “when [Jesus] was baptized” (ἐν τῷ βαπτισθῆναι). Yet a passive of this verb also occurs: Mark 10:38, *daupeinai þizaiei ik daupjada ei daupjaindau*, “with the baptism with which I am baptized, that you may be baptized.” Similarly *binaitan*: “to circumcise, be circumcised, circumcise oneself” (περιτέμνειν, περιτέμνεσθαι). Although its passive participle *bimaitans* is found, βαπτιζόμενος at 1 Cor. 15:29 is rendered actively as *daup jands*.

> **Note 4.**—The active is commonly used instead of the passive in the infinitive:  
> a) where a purpose is indicated: Luke 5:15, *garunnun leikinon fram imma*, “they ran together to be healed by him” (ἰαθῆναι); Luke 2:1 and 5, *urrann gameljan—anameljan*, “a decree went out to register—to be enrolled” (ἀπογράφεσθαι); 2 Thess. 1:10, *qimiþ ushauhjan*, “he comes to be glorified” (ἐνδοξασθῆναι). Here *sik* may also occur: Luke 6:17, *qemun hailjan sik*, “they came to be healed” (ἰαθῆναι); and in a somewhat more particular manner, 2 Cor. 1:16, *vilda fram izwis gasandjan mik*, “I wished to be sent on by you” (προπεμφθῆναι).  
> b) Once, by a substantive periphrasis: Mark 10:45, *qam at andbahtjam*, “he came for service,” that is, to perform his ministry (ἦλθε διακονηθῆναι).  
> c) In Germanic fashion after verbs of commanding, willing, and giving: Matt. 27:64, *hait vitan hlaiva*, “he commanded the tomb to be guarded” (ἀσφαλισθῆναι); Mark 5:43; 10:49; Luke 18:40; 19:15; Luke 8:15, *anabaud izai giban mat*, “he commanded food to be given her” (δοθῆναι); Mark 6:27; Luke 1:62, *waiva vildedi haitan þata barn*, “what they wished the child to be called” (καλεῖσθαι); Matt. 26:1, *sunus mans atgibada du ushramjan*, “the Son of Man is given up to be crucified” (εἰς τὸ σταυρωθῆναι).  
> d) With *skulds wisan*, “to be necessary,” and *mahts wisan*, “to be possible,” which contain a passive idea: Mark 8:31, *sunus mans skulds ist uskiusan fram þaim sinistam*, “the Son of Man must be rejected by the elders” (δεῖ ... ἀποδοκιμασθῆναι); Luke 9:44, *sunus mans skulds ist atgiban*, “the Son of Man is about to be delivered up” (μέλλει παραδίδοσθαι); Luke 19:11, *skulda vas þiudangardi guþs gasvikunþjan*, “the kingdom of God was bound to be manifested”; John 12:34; 2 Cor. 5:10; 12:11; Mark 14:5, *maht vas þatabalsan frabugjan*, “this ointment could have been sold” (ἠδύνατο ... πραθῆναι); Luke 8:43, *qino ni mahtavas galeikinon*, “the woman could not be healed” (οὐκ ἴσχυσεν θεραπευθῆναι); John 3:4, *waiva mahts ist manna gabairan*, “how can a man be born?” (δύναται γεννηθῆναι); John 10:35; 1 Tim. 5:25.

b) A sentence expressed passively is not infrequently changed into an active one, so that the sense becomes more concrete.

a) Rom. 10:10, *hairto galaubeiþ*, “the heart believes,” for Greek καρδίᾳ πιστεύεται, “it is believed with the heart”; Mark 2:1, *gafrehun þatei in garda ist*, “they learned that he was in the house,” for ἠκούσθη ὅτι εἰς οἶκόν ἐστιν, “it was heard that he was in the house”; Luke 9:17, *unte qeþun sumai*, “for some said,” for διὰ τὸ λέγεσθαι ὑπό τινων, “because it was said by some”; Mark 5:4, *unte galausida af sis þos naudibandjos jah þo ana fotum eisarna gabrak*, “for he had broken the chains from himself and shattered the iron fetters on his feet,” for διὰ τὸ διεσπάσθαι ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ τὰς ἁλύσεις καὶ τὰς πέδας συντετρῖφθαι; Mark 2:2, *wein juggata in balgins niujans giutand*, “they pour new wine into new wineskins,” for οἶνον νέον εἰς ἀσκοὺς καινοὺς βλητέον, “new wine must be put into new wineskins”; Luke 4:43, *mik insandida*, namely God, “sent me,” for ἀπέσταλμαι, namely ὑπὸ Θεοῦ, “I have been sent by God”; John 10:14, *kunnun mik þo meina*, “my own know me,” for γινώσκομαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἐμῶν, “I am known by my own”—or rather, as the manuscripts read, γιγνώσκουσί με τὰ ἐμά, “my own know me.”

b) Gal. 6:12, *vrakja galgins Xristaus ni vinnand*, “they do not suffer persecution for Christ’s cross,” for σταυρῷ τοῦ Χριστοῦ οὐ διώκονται, “they are persecuted for Christ’s cross”; 1 Tim. 5:10, *aglons vinnan*, “to undergo afflictions,” for θλίβεσθαι, “to be afflicted”; cf. Phil. 4:12; Luke 1:11, *varþ in siunai aggilus*, “an angel came into view,” for ὤφθη ἄγγελος, “an angel was seen”; Luke 16:21, *gairnida sat itan*, “he desired to sit and eat,” for ἐπεθύμει χορτασθῆναι, “he desired to be filled”; Luke 20:6, *triggvaba galaubjand allai*, “all firmly believe,” for πεπεισμένος ἐστι πᾶς ὁ λαός, “all the people are convinced.” Quite a few of these verbs belong to the middle voice: Gal. 5:4, *in witoda garaihtans qiþiþ izwis*, “you declare yourselves righteous in the law,” for δικαιοῦσθε; 1 Cor. 11:6, *qino gahuljai haubiþ sein*, “let a woman veil her head,” for κατακαλυπτέσθω; Luke 9:25, *þaurft gataujan sis*, or 1 Cor. 13:3, *bota sis taujan*, for ὠφελεῖσθαι, “to benefit oneself.”

[Col. 1038]

> **Note 5.**—Conversely, the Goth sometimes presents passively a sentence expressed actively, again in order to make the sense concrete: Rom. 9:19, *wa nu faianda*, “why are we still blamed?”—for *vituperamur* must be read in the translation instead of *vituperant*—Greek τί ἔτι μέμφεται, namely, “why does God still blame us?”; Luke 6:38, *mitads goda gibada*, “a good measure will be given,” for μέτρον καλὸν δώσουσι, “they will give a good measure”; v. 44 and Matt. 7:16, *ni us þaurnum lisanda smakkans nih þan us aiwatundjai trudanda veinabasja*, “figs are not gathered from thorns, nor grapes harvested from a bramble,” for οὐκ ἐξ ἀκανθῶν συλλέγουσι σῦκα—τρυγῶσι σταφυλάς, “they do not gather figs from thorns—nor harvest grapes”; John 16:21, *biþe gabauran ist barn*, “when a child is born,” for ὅταν γεννήσῃ, namely γυνή, τὸ παιδίον, “when the woman bears the child”; John 15:6 is translated in the Gothic manner favoured by the translator: *galisada jah in fon galagjand jah inbrannjada*, “it is gathered, and they cast it into fire, and it is burned,” for συνάγουσι—βάλλουσι—καίεται.
>
> So with intransitives: Mark 7:10, *dauþau afdauþjaidau*, “let him be put to death” (θανὰτῳ τελευτάτω, “let him die by death”); Luke 6:21, *ufhlohjanda*, “you shall rejoice,” for γελάσετε, “you shall laugh”; 2 Tim. 2:26, *usskavjaindau*, “that they may recover themselves,” for ἀνανήψωσι; Mark 9:42, *galagjada asiluqairnus ana halsaggan*, “a millstone is placed upon his neck,” for περίκειται λίθος μυλικὸς περὶ τὸν τράχηλον, “a millstone lies about his neck”; John 11:38, *hulundi staina ufarlagida vas*, “a stone had been laid over the cave,” for λίθος ἐπέκειτο ἐπὶ τῷ σπηλαίῳ; cf. Mark 4:29, *biþe atgibada akran*, “when the grain gives itself up,” for ὅταν παραδῷ, namely ἑαυτόν, ὁ καρπός, “when the fruit gives itself up.”

> **Note 6.**—Very many passive participles become adjectives; see § 190, 5.

§ 178. III. MIDDLE. The middle occurs only very rarely. Its unquestionable examples are: *atsteigadau* (καταβάτω), “let him come down,” Matt. 27:42; Mark 15:32; *lausjadau* (ῥυσάσθω), “let him deliver himself,” Matt. 27:43; *ufkunnanda* (γνώσονται), “they shall know,” John 13:35; *vaurkjada* (κατεργάζεται), “works,” 2 Cor. 4:17; *ustiuhada* (κατεργάζεται), “works,” 7:10. *Gavasjada* indeed (ἐνδύσηται), 1 Cor. 15:54, could be considered passive, since nothing prevents *undivanein* from being dative—“is clothed with immortality”; but both sense and context suggest that it should be regarded as middle. It may be doubtful whether *liugada* and *liuganda*, said of a woman in Mark 10:12; 12:25; Luke 17:27; 20:34, 35; 1 Cor. 7:28, are passive, “to be married,” or middle, “to marry”; *liugandau*, 1 Cor. 7:9, appears to decide the question in favour of the passive.

> **Note 1.**—*Faianda*, which others had previously offered as a middle, fails at Rom. 9:19; see above, § 177, note 5. Conversely, Matt. 11:12, *anamahtjada*, and Luke 16:16, *nauþjada* (βιάζεται), might be counted among examples of the middle—at least the latter, since in Greek it is only middle. But the Goth did not rightly understand this passage (“each person uses force upon himself”) and treated βιάζεται as passive (“is compelled,” etc.; hence *in izai*). If *sunjodana*, 2 Cor. 12:19, Codex B, actually stood for ἀπολογούμεθα, then a middle would have to be acknowledged there; but Codex A more correctly has *sunjoma*. The syllable *da*, however, lost here, is preserved in other places: namely John 14:31, *frijoda*, “loved,” where neither is the preterite required (ἀγαπῶ) nor does it fit. We should therefore be inclined to regard *frijoda* as middle, were it not, in view of the aforementioned *sunjodama*, highly probable [Col. 1039] that this word belonged to the exemplar, in which the syllable *da* perhaps contained some critical annotation, and subsequently slipped in incongruously into the text.

> **Note 2.**—Others have already rightly observed that these passages in which the middle occurs do not present passives substituted by the translator through misunderstanding Greek middle forms. For some correspond to Greek actives, while others are Greek forms not to be regarded as passives. Thus, at least, our translators, who showed themselves knowledgeable in Greek, intelligently distinguished those middles. To these arguments add that the middle and passive differ at least in the subjunctive—middle *-adau, -andau*, passive *-aidau, -aindau*—and further that, from the occurrence twice, indeed in otherwise diverse parallel passages, of this καταβάτω, it is evident that they were not simply translated by the translator. Be that as it may, the Gothic middle, as it appears to us here, is an equally unexplained voice. In fact it is almost always used for the Greek middle. As regards *atsteigadau*, if we may state our view, it either has a double meaning—transitive “to lower” and intransitive “to descend,” so that the middle means “to lower oneself”—or, as frequently happens through composition, *steigan* acquired transitive meaning; cf. *gagaggan*. But the middle of *liugan* is conspicuous and valuable for Germanic antiquities, since it confirms that girls did not come into marriage at the arbitrary will of parents or at masters’ pleasure, like objects, but themselves chose their husbands or were freely married by those who loved them.

2) Elsewhere the Greek middle is translated into Gothic:

a) By a reflexive; cf. § 176, 4:

aa) With *sis*: δανείσασθαι, *leiwan sis*, “to lend for oneself,” Matt. 5:43; ἀπεκδύεσθαι, *afslaupjan sis*, “to strip oneself,” Col. 3:9; χάριν ἔχεσθαι, *þagk sis fairhaitan*, “to acknowledge thanks for oneself,” Luke 17:9; ἀγοράζεσθαι, *bugjan sis*, “to buy for oneself,” Luke 9:12; φοβεῖσθαι, *ogan sis*, “to fear for oneself,” Matt. 10:26 and elsewhere; διαλογίζεσθαι, *þagkjan sis*, “to deliberate with oneself,” Luke 1:29. But *ogan* and *þagkjan* also occur simply; see the glossary under these words.

bb) With *sik*: περιβάλλεσθαι, *gavasjan sik*, “to clothe oneself,” Matt. 6:29; ἐνδύεσθαι, *gahamon sik*, “to put on oneself,” Eph. 6:11; Col. 3:12; ἀπεκδύεσθαι, *andhamon sik*, “to strip oneself,” Col. 2:15; ἐμπλέκεσθαι, *dugavindan sik*, “to entangle oneself,” 2 Tim. 2:4; μετασχηματίζεσθαι, *gagaleikon sik*, “to transform oneself,” 2 Cor. 11:13; συναναμίγνυσθαι, *blandan sik*, “to associate oneself,” 2 Thess. 3:14; ἀπέχεσθαι, *afhaban sik*, “to abstain,” 1 Thess. 5:22; ἐγκρατεύεσθαι, *gahaban sik*, “to restrain oneself,” 1 Cor. 7:9, and *sik gaþarban*, “to exercise oneself,” 9:25; χωρίζεσθαι, *skaidan sik*, “to separate oneself,” 1 Cor. 7:15; διαχωρίζεσθαι, *afskaidan sik*, “to separate oneself,” Luke 9:33; ὑπεραίρεσθαι, *ufarhafjan sik*, “to exalt oneself,” 2 Thess. 2:4; ἐπεκτείνεσθαι, *sik ufþanjan*, “to stretch oneself forward,” Phil. 3:14; ἀπάγχεσθαι, *ushahan sik*, “to hang oneself,” Matt. 27:5; ἐντρέπεσθαι, *gavandjan sik*, “to turn oneself,” 2 Tim. 4:2; *gaskaman sik*, “to be ashamed,” 2 Thess. 3:14; αἰσχύνεσθαι, *skaman sik*, “to be ashamed,” Luke 16:3 and elsewhere; ἐπανέρχεσθαι, *atvandjan sik*, “to return,” Luke 19:15; συνέρχεσθαι, *gagaggan sik*, “to come together,” Mark 3:40; συνάγεσθαι, *gaqiman sik*, “to assemble,” Matt. 27:6; Mark 2:2; διαλέγεσθαι, *sik andrinnan*, “to dispute with oneself,” *Skeireins* III, a; ταπεινοῦσθαι, *haunjan sik*, “to humble oneself,” Phil. 4:12; σκύλλεσθαι, *draibjan sik*, “to trouble oneself,” Luke 7:6; ἐνδυναμοῦσθαι, *insvinþjan sik*, “to strengthen oneself,” Eph. 6:10; θερμαίνεσθαι, *varmjan sik*, “to warm oneself,” Mark 14:54; John 18:18; μεθύσκεσθαι, *anadrigkan sik*, “to intoxicate oneself,” Eph. 5:18; ἐπαναπαύεσθαι, *gaweilan sik*, “to rest oneself,” Luke 10:6; ἀπολογεῖσθαι, *sunjon sik*, “to defend oneself,” 2 Cor. 12:19.

cc) So that the possessive pronoun refers to the dependent noun: 1 Cor. 11:6, *jabai agl ist qinon du kapillon aiþþau skaban, gahuljai haubiþ sein*—“if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her veil her head”; Greek κατακαλυπτέσθαι, French *elle se voile la tête* (“she veils herself at the head”), instead of *elle voile sa tête* (“she veils her head”).

> **Note 3.**—Sometimes *sik* is also omitted; but then it is usually used with the same verb immediately preceding: 1 Cor. 5:11, *blandan*, “to associate,” namely *izwis*, from v. 9, *blandan izwis*; Matt. 6:31, *we vasjaima*, “wherewith we may clothe [ourselves],” namely *uns*, from v. 29, *gavasida sik*. In 1 Cor. 7:15, *skaidai*, “let [her] depart” (χωριζέσθω), *skaidiþ sik* immediately precedes; whereas in v. 10, *skaidan* (χωρισθῆναι) is indeed used absolutely. Thus Rom. 13:12, *gavasjam*, “let us clothe ourselves” (ἐνδυσώμεθα); Eph. 4:24; Col. 3:11, *gahamoþ*, “clothe yourselves” (ἐνδύσασθε).

b) By the simple active: thus *andhaitan* means equally ὁμολογεῖν, “to confess,” and ἐξομολογεῖσθαι, “to confess openly”; *athaitan*, καλεῖν, “to call,” and προσκαλεῖσθαι, “to call to oneself”; *gahaitan*, συγκαλεῖν, “to summon together” (Mark 15:16), and συγκαλεῖσθαι, “to summon together for oneself” (Luke 9:1); *afniman*, ἀφαιρεῖν, “to take away” (Luke 1:25), and ἀφαιρεῖσθαι, “to take away for oneself” (Luke 16:3); *gasigljan*, σφραγίζειν, “to seal” (John 6:27), and *sigljan*, σφραγίζεσθαι, “to be sealed” (2 Cor. 1:22); *ataugjan*, δεῖξαι, “to show” (Luke 4:5 and elsewhere), and ἐνδείξασθαι, “to show for oneself” (Eph. 2:7); *ganimam*, παραλαμβάνειν, “to take along” (Mark 5:40), and συλλαμβάνεσθαι, “to conceive” (Luke 1:31); *gafastan*, διαφυλάττειν, “to guard carefully” (Luke 4:10), and φυλάττεσθαι, “to guard oneself” (Mark 10:20); *lagjan*, τιθέναι, “to place” (Matt. 27:60 and elsewhere), and τίθεσθαι, “to place for oneself” (Luke 1:60); *taujan*, ποιεῖν, “to do” (Matt. 5:46 and elsewhere), and ποιεῖσθαι, “to do for oneself” (Luke 5:33).

Likewise, middle and deponent verbs: ῥύεσθαι, *lausjan*, “to deliver”; ἀγαλλιᾶσθαι, *svegnjan*, “to rejoice”; ἀπωθεῖσθαι, *afskiuban*, “to reject”; παῤῥησιάζεσθαι, *gadaursjan*, “to speak boldly”; περιποιεῖσθαι, *fairvaurkjan*, “to acquire”—although at 1 Tim. 3:13 ἑαυτοῖς is not once translated; διαστέλλεσθαι, *anabiudan*, “to charge”; ἐναγκαλίζεσθαι, *gaþlaihan*, “to take in one’s arms”; ἐκλέγεσθαι, *gavaljan*, “to choose”; ἐπαγγέλλεσθαι, *gahaitan*, “to promise”; εὐαγγελίζεσθαι, *spillon* and *vailamerjan*, “to proclaim good news”; παύεσθαι, *gananþjan* and *anaslavan*, “to cease,” etc.

c) Rarely by the passive, as Gal. 3:27, *Xristau gahamodai sijuþ*, “you have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Χριστὸν ἐνεδύσασθε); more frequently, however, in the participle: ἐνδυσάμενος, *gavasiþs*, “having clothed oneself,” 2 Cor. 5:3; *gapaidoþs*, “having put on,” Eph. 6:14; *gahamoþs*, “having clothed oneself,” 1 Thess. 5:8; περιζωσάμενος, *bigaurdans*, “having girded oneself,” Luke 17:8; *ufgaurdans*, “having girded oneself,” Eph. 6:14.

## II. TENSE

§ 179. In Gothic the active has two tenses, namely the present and the preterite; but the passive and middle have only the present. The passive preterite is expressed periphrastically with the aid of *visan*, “to be,” or *vairþan*, “to become” (§ 181). A future proper is lacking; but what is presented as certain in the future is expressed by the present indicative, and what is presented as uncertain by the present subjunctive. There are also certain auxiliaries for expressing it periphrastically (§ 182).

§ 180. I. The PRESENT is used:

1) When speaking of a present action; of an action begun earlier but still continuing or not yet completed; and likewise of an action universally or generally understood. Hence it is used of customs and habits and in proverbs: Rom. 7:1, *witoþ fraujinoþ mann, sva lagga weila sve libaiþ*—“the law rules over a person as long as he lives” (κυριεύει—ζῇ); 1 Cor. 16:19, *goljand izwis aikklesjons Asiais, goleiþ izwis Akvila jah Priska, at þaimei jah salja*—“the churches of Asia greet you; Aquila and Priscilla greet you, with whom I also lodge” (ἀσπάζονται—ξενίζεται); 2 Cor. 13:9, *faginom, þan weis siukam, iþ jus svinþai sijuþ*—“we rejoice when we are weak and you are strong” (χαίρομεν—ἀσθενῶμεν—ἦτε); Mark 10:38, *magutsu driggkan stikl, þanei ik driggka*—“can you drink the cup which I drink?” (δύνασθε—πίνω); Mark 3:32, *aiþei þeina jah broþrjus þeinai jah svistrjos þeinos uta sokjand þuk*—“your mother and your brothers and sisters outside seek you” (ζητοῦσι); John 11:9, *tvalif sind weilos dagis, jabai was gaggiþ in dag, ni gastiggqiþ, unte liuhaþ þis fairwaus gasaiwiþ*—“are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world”; Mark 7:4, *Iudaieis niba ufta þvahand, ni matjand*—“the Jews do not eat unless they wash often” (βαπτίσωνται—ἐσθίουσι); Mark 4:29, *biþe gibada akran, insandeiþ gilþa*—“when the grain yields, he immediately sends forth the sickle” (ἀποστέλλει); 2 Cor. 9:7, *hlasana giband frijoþ guþ*—“God loves a cheerful giver” (ἀγαπᾷ).

2) For the future; see § 182, 1.

3) For more vivid narration—then called the historical present—sometimes where the Greek exemplar precedes: Luke 8:49, *nauhþan imma rodjandin gaggiþ sums manne*, “while he is still speaking, a certain man comes” (ἔρχεται); John 6:19, *þaruh farjandans swe spaurde k jah e aiþþau l gasaiwand Iesus*, “when they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia, they see Jesus” (θεωροῦσιν); 9:13, *gatiuhand ina du Fareisaium þana saei vas blinds*, “they bring to the Pharisees the man who had been blind” (ἄγουσιν); 11:38, *þanuh Iesus gaggiþ du hlaiva*, “therefore Jesus comes to the tomb” (ἔρχεται); 11:11, *þo qaþ jah afar þata qiþiþ du im*, “he said this, and after this he says to them” (εἶπε—λέγει).

The Goth uses it similarly, even without the Greek precedent, together with present and preterite: John 12:22, *gaggiþ Filippus jah qiþiþ du Andraiin jah aftra Andreas jah Filippus qeþun du Iesua*—“Philip comes and tells Andrew, and Andrew and Philip again tell Jesus”; Mark 5:15, *jah atiddjedun du Iesua jah gasaiwand þana vodan sitandan*—“and they come to Jesus and see the demoniac sitting”; v. 22, *jah sai qimiþ ains þize synagogafade jah gadraus du fotum Iesuis*—“and behold, one of the rulers of the synagogue comes and falls at Jesus’ feet”; v. 40, *Iesus ganimiþ allan þis barnis jah aiþein jah þans miþ sis jah galiþ inn*—“Jesus takes the child’s father and mother and those with him, and enters in” (παραλαμβάνει—εἰσπορεύεται).

More commonly, however, the preterite is used for the Greeks’ historical present: Matt. 8:4, *jah qah imma*, “and he said to him” (λέγει); 8:7; 8:20, 26; 26:71; Mark 1:12, *ahma ustauh ina in auþida*, “the Spirit drove him into the wilderness” (ἐκβάλλει); v. 21, *jah galiþun in Kafarnaum*, “and they entered Capernaum” (εἰσπορεύονται); 1:30, 37, 38, 40; 2:3, 4, 5, 10, 17, 18; 3:13, 20, 31; 4:36, 38; 5:19, 35; 6:1, 30; 7:1, 32; 10:49; 16:4; Luke 16:7; 19:22; John 6:5, 20; 9:17; 11:29; 13:24; 18:28; 19:9, 10.

4) Often for the Greek perfect:

a) When the Goth renders its present sense by a corresponding verb. Thus he translates Mark 4:29, παρέστηκεν ὁ θερισμός, “the harvest has arrived,” by *atist asans*, “it is at hand”; 2 Tim. 4:6, καιρὸς τῆς ἐμῆς ἀναλύσεως ἐφέστηκε, “the time of my departure has arrived,” by *mel meinai zos disvissais atist*, “the time of my dissolution is at hand”; Luke 8:20, ἡ μήτηρ σου καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοί σου ἑστήκασιν ἔξω, “your mother and brothers are standing outside,” by *aiþei þeina jah broþrjus þeinai standand uta*; 1 Cor. 15:1; Rom. 9:19, βουλήματι αὐτοῦ τίς ἀνθέστηκεν, “who has resisted his will?” by *viljan is was andstandiþ*, “who resists his will?”—for *andstandiþ* must be read in place of *andstandi*, the scribe having omitted *þ* because of the immediately following *þ*, as at 2 Cor. 13:3; cf. the note on 2 Cor. 3:2; Rom. 8:38, πέπεισμαι, “I am persuaded,” by *gatraua*, “I believe”; 14:14, οἶδα καὶ πέπεισμαι, “I know and am persuaded,” by *wait jah gatraua*, “I know and believe.” Similarly 2 Cor. 10:7; Gal. 5:10; Phil. 1:14; 2 Thess. 3:4, πέποιθα, equivalent to πέπεισμαι, likewise by *gatraua*. John 8:55, ἐγνώκατε, “you have known,” by *kunnuþ*, “you know”; 1 Tim. 5:8, τὴν πίστιν ἤρνηται, “he has denied the faith,” by *galaubein inwidiþ*, “he denies the faith.”

Conversely, the Goth renders Mark 8:3, μακρόθεν ἥκουσι, “they have come from afar,” by *fairraþro qemun*, “they came from afar”; Luke 15:27; John 8:42 and elsewhere; 11:28, ὁ διδάσκαλος πάρεστι, “the teacher is present,” by *laisareis qam*, “the teacher came”; Matt. 6:2, ἀπέχουσι τὸν μισθὸν αὐτῶν, “they have their reward,” by *andnemun mizdon seina*, “they received their reward”; Gal. 4:20, ἀποροῦμαι, “I am perplexed,” by *afslautiþs im*, “I am perplexed” (perfect); Phil. 1:17, κεῖμαι, “I lie,” by *gasatiþs im*, “I have been placed.”

> “Note 1.—But the Gothic translator fails, in rendering a Greek perfect by a Gothic present, at 2 Tim. III.15 and John VI.42, where he translates οἶδας (*you know*) and οἴδαμεν (*we know*) by *kunþes* (*you know*) and *kunþedum* (*we know*); Rom. XI.20 ἕστηκας (*you stand*) and 2 Cor. I.24 ἑστήκατε (*you stand*) by *gastost* (*you stood*) and *gastoþuþ* (*you stood*); and Rom. XIII.2 ἀνθέστηκε (*he opposes*) by *andstoþ* (*he opposed*).”

b) Where a past action, but one continuing in its consequences, is represented: John V.45, εἰς Μωσῆν ὑμεῖς ἠλπίκατε (*you have placed your hope in Moses, and still place it*) is translated by *du mose jus veneiþ* (*you hope in Moses*); V.37, ὁ πέμψας με πατὴρ αὐτὸς μεμαρτύρηκε περὶ ἐμοῦ (*the Father who sent me has borne witness concerning me, and his testimony still stands*) by *saei sandida mik atta sah veitvodeiþ bi mik* (*the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me*). Hence the Gothic translator also renders XIV.7, γινώσκετε τὸν πατέρα μου καὶ ἑωράκατε (*you know my Father and have seen him, and still see him in me*) by *kunnuþ attan meinana jah gasaiwiþ* (*you know my Father and see him*); and Jesus’ reply at Matt. IX.2, 5; Mark II.5, 9; Luke VII.47, 48, ἀφέωνταί σοι αἱ ἁμαρτίαι σου (*your sins have been forgiven, and remain forgiven*) likewise by *fraletanda þus fravaurhteis þeinos* (*your sins are forgiven to you*). Rom. VII.2, ἐὰν ἀποθάνῃ ὁ ἀνήρ, κατήργηται ἡ γυνὴ ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου τοῦ ἀνδρός (*if the husband dies, the wife has been, and remains, released from the law of her husband*) is rendered by *jabai gasviltiþ aba, galausjada qens af þamma vitoda abins* (*if the husband dies, the wife is released from her husband’s law*).

5) In indirect discourse, and also in subordinate clauses, most commonly where the Greek has preceded: Mark X.47: *gahausjands þatei iesus sa nazaraius ist* (*hearing that Jesus the Nazarene is*, ἐστί); John VI.24, *gasaw managei þatei iesus nist jainar* (*the crowd saw that Jesus is not there*, οὐκ ἔστι); Rom. XI.32, *galauk guþ allans in ungalaubeinai, ei allans gaarmai* (*God shut up all in unbelief, that he may have mercy upon all*, ἐλεήσῃ); *Skeireins* V.a, *gasok, ei galaisjaina sik* (*he sought that he might teach himself*). And contrary to the Greek: Luke V.26, *fullai vaurþun agisis qiþandans, þatei gasaiwam vulþaga himma dago* (*they were filled with fear, saying, “We have seen marvellous things today”*, εἴδομεν); John IX.32, *fram aiwa ni gahausiþ vas, þatei uslukiþ augona blindamma* (*from eternity it has not been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a blind man*, ἀνέῳξεν). Conversely, 1 Thess. III.4, *fauraqeþum izvis þatei anavairþ vas uns du winnon agliþos* (*we told you beforehand that we were about to suffer affliction*, μέλλομεν).

> “Note 2.—But where the translator in other passages explains a Greek present by a preterite, this arises because he understands his text in a particular, though not always judicious, way: John VI.32, *atta meins gaf* [Col. 1043] (*my Father gives*, δίδωσι) *izvis hlaif* (*you bread*); 37, *all þatei gaf mis atta, du mis qimiþ* (*all that the Father gives me comes to me*, δίδωσι); VIII.45, *þatei sunja rodida, ni galaubeiþ mis* (*because I spoke the truth, you do not believe me*, λέγω); XIV.31, *ak ei ufkunnai so manaseþs, þatei ik frijoda attan meinana—urreisiþ* (*but that the world may know that I loved my Father—arise*; see §179, note 1); XIX.4, *attiuha izvis ina ut, ei viteiþ, þatei in imma ni ainhun fairino bigat* (*I bring him out to you, that you may know that I found no fault in him*, εὑρίσκω); 1 Tim. V.18, *qaþ gameleins* (*the Scripture said*, λέγει); 2 Tim. II.17, *vaurd ize sve gund vuliþ, þizeei vesun ymainaius jah filetus* (*their word spread like gangrene, among whom were Hymenaeus and Philetus*, ἐστίν); 2 Cor. I.4, *gaþrafstjam þans in allaim aglom þairh þo gaþlaiht, þizaiei gaþrafstidai sijum silbans fram guþa* (*we comfort those in every affliction through the comfort by which we were ourselves comforted by God*, παρακαλούμεθα); Eph. II.22, *in þammei jah jus miþgatimridai sijuþ du bauainai guþa* (*in whom you too are being built together into a dwelling-place of God*, συνοικοδομεῖσθε).

> This occurs especially in defining time: that is, where the Gothic translator prefers, instead of the point of time up to which something happens, to represent the time from which the matter has occurred. Mark VIII.2, *infeinoda du þizai managein, unte ju dagans þrins miþ mis vesun jah ni haband wa matjaina* (*I had compassion on the crowd, because they have been with me three days and have nothing to eat*, σπλαγχνίζομαι; Greek προσμένουσι); Luke XV.29, *sva filu jere skalkinoda þus jah ni wanhun anabusn þeina ufariddja* (*for so many years I served you and never transgressed your command*, δουλεύω; παρέλθον); John XIV.9, *svalaud melis miþ izvis vas jah ni ufkunþes mik* (*I was with you so long, and you have not known me*, εἰμί; ἔγνωκας).”

## §181. II. THE PRETERITE

The preterite is used:

### 1) For the Greek imperfect

a) Mark I.13, *andbahtidedun*, “they ministered,” διηκόνουν; 21, *laisida*, “he taught,” ἐδίδασκε; 30, *svaihro seimonis lag*, “Simon’s mother-in-law lay,” κατέκειτο, in a fever; 35, Jesus *jaina baþ*, “prayed there,” προσηύχετο; XI.8, some *astans maimaitun*, “cut branches,” ἔκοπτον, from the trees and *stravidedun*, “spread them,” ἐστρώννυον, on the road.

b) The passive imperfect is translated by the preterite participle, aided by the preterite of *visan*, “to be”: Mark I.5, *daupidai vesun*, “they were baptized,” ἐβαπτίζοντο, all of them; John III.23; Luke I.65, *in allai bairgahein iudaias merida vesun alla þo vaurda*, “all these words were discussed throughout all the hill-country of Judaea,” διελαλεῖτο; XXIII.3, *svaei sunus munds vas iosefis*, “as was supposed, the son of Joseph,” ἐνομίζετο; IV.1, *iesus tauhans vas in ahmin in auþidai*, “Jesus was being led by the Spirit into the wilderness,” ἤγετο; VII.12; VIII.27, 29, 37; XVI.19; XVII.27; John VI.18; Rom. VII.6; 1 Cor. XI.23; Neh. V.18. Once, Mark VI.3, occurs *gamarzidai vaurþun*, “they were offended,” ἐσκανδαλίζοντο, by him.

### 2) For the perfect

a) Matt. IX.22, *galaubeins þeina ganasida þuk*, “your faith saved you,” σέσωκέ σε; Mark V.34; I.38, *gaggam du þaim bisunjane haimom jah baurgim, ei jah jainar merjau, unte duþe qam*, “let us go into the neighbouring villages and towns, that I may preach there too; for that purpose I came,” ἐξελήλυθα; VII.29, *usiddja unhulþo us dauhtr þeinai*, “the demon has gone out from your daughter,” ἐξελήλυθεν; XI.2, *bigitats fulan gabundanana, ana þammei nauh ainshun manne ni sat*, “you will find a colt tied, upon which no person has yet sat,” κεκάθικε; XIII.23, *fauragataih izvis allata*, “I have told you all things beforehand,” προείρηκα; XIV.42, *sa levjands mik atnewida*, “the one betraying me has drawn near,” ἤγγικε; and so forth; Luke VII.16, *praufetus mikils urrais*, “a great prophet has arisen,” ἐγήγερται; 2 Cor. XV.12 [as printed].

John III.29, *faheds meina usfullnoda*, “my joy has been made complete,” πεπλήρωται; XII.27, *saivala meina gadrobnoda*, “my soul has been troubled,” τετάρακται; Mark XI.21, *smakkabagms gaþaursnoda*, “the fig-tree has withered,” ἐξήρανται; 1 Cor. XVI.9, *haurds mis usluknoda*, “a door has been opened to me,” ἀνέῳγε; 2 Cor. VI.11.

b) The passive perfect is expressed transitively:

aa) Ordinarily by the preterite participle and the present [Col. 1044] of *visan*: Matt. X.30, *izvara tagla haubidis alla garaþana sind*, “all the hairs of your head are numbered,” ἠριθμημέναι εἰσί; Matt. XI.10, *bi þanei gameliþ ist*, “of whom it is written,” namely in Scripture, γέγραπται; Mark I.2; VII.6; XI.17; Luke II.23; III.4; IV.4; X.26; Rom. VIII.36; 2 Cor. VIII.14; Luke IV.12, *giþan ist ni fraisais fraujan*, “it is said, ‘You shall not tempt the Lord,’” namely in Scripture, εἴρηται; Mark IV.11, *izvis atgiban ist kunnan runa*, “to you it has been given to know the mystery,” δέδοται; Luke IV.6; VIII.10; John VII.8, *meinata mel ni nauh usfulliþ ist*, “my time has not yet been fulfilled,” πεπλήρωται; 47, *ibai jah jus afairzidai sijuþ*, “perhaps you too have been led astray,” πεπλάνησθε; XVII.10; XVIII.37; Rom. VII.2; XIII.1; 1 Cor. I.13; IV.4; VII.14, 27; 2 Cor. VII.4, 13; IX.2, 3; Gal. V.4; VI.14; Phil. III.12; IV.12; Col. I.16; IV.3; Tit. I.15.

But the substantive verb is only rarely placed before the participle, and then only where it is drawn forward by a negation or, with the Greek preceding, is put first: John VI.65, *nibai ist atgiban*, “unless it has been given”; VIII.41, *ni sijum gabauranai*, “we have not been born”; XII.14, *svasve ist gameliþ*, “as it is written”; XVI.24, *bidjaiþ ei faheþs izvara sijai usfullida*, “ask, that your joy may be made full,” ᾖ πεπληρωμένη; XVII.23, *ik in im jah þu in mis, ei sijaina ustauhanai*, “I in them and you in me, that they may be made perfect,” ὦσι τετελειωμένοι; 2 Cor. IV.3, *jabai ist gahulida*, “if it is veiled,” ἐστι κεκαλυμμένον; 1 Cor. VII.15, *nist gaþivaiþs*, “is not enslaved”; 2 Tim. II.9, *nist gabundan*, “is not bound.”

bb) More rarely, by the preterite participle and the preterite of *visan* or *vairþan*: Mark X.40, *þata du sitan af taihsvon meinai aiþþau af hleidumein nist mein du giban alja þaimei manviþ vas*, “to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to give, except to those for whom it had been prepared,” ἡτοίμασται; Gal. II.7, *þai þugkjandans ni vaiht anainsokun ak þata viþravairþo gasaiwandans, þatei gatrauaida vas mis aivaggeljo*, “those who were thought to be something added nothing to me; but, on the contrary, seeing that the Gospel had been entrusted to me,” πεπίστευμαι; IV.23; Mark IX.42. Mark III.26, *jabai satana usstoþ ana sik silban jah gadailiþs varþ, ni mag gastandan*, “if Satan rose up against himself and was divided, he cannot stand,” μεμέρισται; John XVI.11, *parakletus gasakiþ þo manaseþ bi staua, þatei sa reiks þis fairwaus afdomiþs varþ*, “the Comforter shall convict the world concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has been judged,” κέκριται; 2 Cor. VII.11; Gal. II.23.

Once Gothic employs *haban*, “to have,” with a preterite participle referring to the object, in the Latin manner: 1 Tim. IV.2, *afstandand sumai atsaiwandans laiseino unhulþono gatandida habandane svesa miþvissein*, “some shall depart, giving heed to teachings of demons, having their own conscience branded,” literally, “having [it] branded”; Greek κεκαυτηριασμένων τὴν συνείδησιν, “having their conscience cauterized.” Likewise, the preterite more strictly determined by *faura*, “before,” is to be noted: Luke XIV.24, *ni ainshun manne jainaize þize faura haitanane*, “not one of those men previously invited,” for τῶν κεκλημένων. Elsewhere the simple participle suffices, e.g. *gabaurans*, “born,” for γεγεννημένος, John IX.32.

Just as in indirect discourse the present is to be understood in place of the preterite according to the sense (§180.5), so too the perfect is used in place of the pluperfect: Mark XVI.4, *gaumidedun þammei afvalviþs ist sa stains*, “they noticed that the stone had been rolled away,” ἀποκεκύλισται.

### 3) For the pluperfect

a) Mark XIV.44, *atgaf sa levjands im bandvon*, “the betrayer had given them a sign,” δεδώκει; XV.7, *in auhjodau maurþr gatavidedun*, “they had committed murder in the insurrection,” πεποιήκεισαν; 10, *in neiþis atgebun ina þai gudjans*, “the chief priests had delivered him up out of envy,” παραδεδώκεισαν; XVI.9, *usvarp sibun unhulþons*, “he had cast out seven demons,” ἐκβεβλήκει; Luke VIII.2, 29, 35, 38; John VI.17; VII.30; VIII.20; XI.13, 19, 30; XIV.7; *Skeireins* VII.d [Col. 1045], *gasaw jag—gahausida*, “he had seen and heard.” Gothic translates ἐκάθητο, Mark X.46, and εἱστήκει, John VII.37; XVIII.5, 16, 18, as simple preterites according to their sense, “he sat,” “he stood,” by *sat* and *stoþ*.

b) The passive pluperfect is everywhere paraphrased with the preterite participle and the preterite of *visan*: Matt. VII.25, *razn gasuliþ vas ana staina*, “the house had been founded upon a rock,” τεθεμελίωτο; Luke VI.48; Luke IV.29, *ana fairgunja baurgs gatimrida vas*, “the city had been built upon a hill,” ᾠκοδόμητο; XVI.20, *lazarus atvaurpans vas du daura*, “Lazarus had been cast at the gate,” ἐβέβλητο; John XI.44, *vlits is auralja bibundans*, “his face was wrapped round,” scilicet *vas*, περιεδέδετο; XIX.11, *ni aihtedeis valdufnje ainhun ana mik, nih vesi þus atgiban iupaþro*, “you would have no authority at all over me unless it had been given you from above,” ἦν δεδομένον. John IX.22, συνετέθειντο is used in a middle sense, which Ulfilas rendered by *gaqeþun sis*, “they had agreed among themselves.”

### 4) For the aorist

a) Matt. V.28, *wazuh saei saiwiþ qinon du luston izos, ju gahorinoda izai*, “whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her,” ἐμοίχευσεν; VII.22, *niu þeinamma namin praufetidedum jah þeinamma namin unhulþons usvaurpum jah þeinamma namin mahtins mikilos gatavidedum*, “did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons in your name, and perform mighty works in your name?” προεφητεύσαμεν, ἐξεβάλομεν, ἐποιήσαμεν; and so forth.

b) For the passive aorist Gothic uses the preterite participle:

aa) With the preterite of *vairþan*, “to become”: Matt. XI.19, *usvaurhta gadomida varþ handugei*, “wisdom was justified by works,” ἐδικαιώθη; XXVII.8, *duþþe haitans varþ akrs jains akrs bloþis*, “therefore that field was called the Field of Blood,” ἐκλήθη; 3, *iesus du stauai gatauhans varþ*, “Jesus was brought to judgment,” κατεκρίθη; Mark II.27, *sabbato in mans varþ gaskapans*, “the Sabbath was made for man,” ἐκτίσθη; IX.4, *ataugiþs varþ im helias miþ mose*, “Elijah appeared to them with Moses,” ὤφθη; XVI.11, *hausjandans þatei libaiþ jah gasaiwans varþ, ni galaubidedun*, “hearing that he lived and had been seen, they did not believe,” ἐθεάθη; Luke VII.35; VIII.5, 20; IX.36; XV.24, 32; XVI.1; XVII.14, 18; John IX.2, 19, 20, 34; XII.38; XV.18; XVI.21; XVII.12; Rom. VII.4, 6, 10; XI.17, 24 (*usmitans jah intrusgans varþ*, “was cut off and grafted in”); XV.4; 1 Cor. I.13; VII.18; XV.54; 2 Cor. IV.1; VII.14; XII.4, 12; Eph. I.13; III.8; Phil. III.12; Col. I.16, 26; 2 Thess. II.3; 1 Tim. I.16; II.13, 14 (*varþ uslutoþs*, “was deceived”); III.16; IV.14; VI.10; Neh. VI.15, 16 (*varþ usfulliþs*, “was completed”); VII.1.

bb) With the preterite of *visan*, as also in paraphrasing the imperfect and pluperfect: Mark I.9, *qam iesus fram nazaraiþ jah daupiþs vas*, “Jesus came from Nazareth and was baptized,” ἐβαπτίσθη; XV.15, *peilatus iesus atgaf, ei ushramiþs vesi*, “Pilate delivered Jesus up, that he might be crucified,” σταυρωθῇ; 28, *miþ unsibjaim rahniþs vas*, “he was numbered with transgressors,” ἐλογίσθη; Luke II.18, *svasve rodiþ vas du im*, “as had been spoken to them,” ἐλαλήθη; IV.26, *insandiþs vas helias in saraipta*, “Elijah was sent to Sarepta,” ἐπέμφθη; 27, *ni ainshun ize gahrainiþs vas alja naiman*, “not one of them was cleansed except Naaman,” ἐκαθαρίσθη; John VII.39, *iesus nauhþanuh ni hauhiþs vas*, “Jesus had not yet been glorified,” ἐδοξάσθη; IX.32; XII.5, 16; XVIII.36; 1 Cor. I.13; VII.20, 21, 24; X.2; XV.4; 2 Cor. I.8; VII.7, 9; XI.25, 33; XIII.4; Gal. II.3; III.1, 27; Eph. I.11; III.3, 10; Col. III.15; 1 Thess. III.1; 1 Tim. I.13; Neh. V.17.

cc) With the present of *visan*, as also in paraphrasing the perfect: Matt. V.21, *hausideduþ þatei qiþan ist þaim airizam*, “you have heard that it was said to the ancients,” ἐρρέθη; Luke II.11, [Col. 1046] *spillo izvis faheid mikila, sei vairþiþ allai managein, þatei gabaurans ist izvis nasjands*, “I bring you good news of great joy, which shall be for all the people: a Saviour has been born for you,” ἐτέχθη; X.20, *faginod in þammei namna izvara gamelida sind in himinam*, “rejoice that your names have been written in heaven,” ἐγράφη; 22, *all mis atgiban ist fram attin*, “all things have been delivered to me by my Father,” παρεδόθη; John XIII.32, *jabai guþ hauhiþs ist in imma, jah guþ hauheiþ ina*, “if God has been glorified in him, God will also glorify him,” ἐδοξάσθη; XV.8; XVI.21, where *gabauran ist barn*, “a child has been born,” is translated passively for γυνὴ γεννήσῃ, “a woman bears a child”; Rom. IX.12; 1 Cor. V.7; VII.34; XII.13; XV.5, 6; subscription; 2 Cor. XII.7; subscription; Gal. II.17; V.13; Eph. III.5; IV.1, 4, 7, 21, 30; Phil. I.29; III.8; 1 Thess. III.7; 2 Thess. I.10; 1 Tim. II.7; VI.12; 2 Tim. I.11; Tit. I.3. Mark III.21, *qeþun þatei usgaisiþs ist*, “they said that he was beside himself,” ἐξέστη, is so expressed because of indirect discourse; compare above, §180.5.

> “Note.—It is difficult to determine where each of these three methods of paraphrase is to be employed, since their difference appears to be individual. From various passages in which these differing methods are used promiscuously, such as John XIII.31, *nu gasveraids varþ sunus mans jah guþ hauhiþs ist in imma*, ‘now the Son of Man was glorified, and God has been glorified in him,’ it is evident that *varþ* denotes an historical occurrence, whereas *ist* denotes an enduring and efficaciously continuing occurrence. Moreover, this passage, among others, proves how deeply the translator grasped the sense of his exemplar and penetrated it. In 1 Cor. VII.22, *saei haitans ist* and *saei haitada* are used indiscriminately for κληθείς, ‘having been called.’”

### 5) For the present

See §180.4 and Note 2.

## §182. III. THE FUTURE

Gothic has no special form for the future; the Greek future is frequently translated either by the present or by paraphrase.

### 1) Thus the present is regularly used for the Greek future, namely

a) The present indicative: Matt. V.8: μακάριοι οἱ καθαροὶ τῇ καρδίᾳ, ὅτι αὐτοὶ τὸν Θεὸν ὄψονται, “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God,” *audagai þai hrainjahairtans, unte þai guþ gasaiwand*; Mark VIII.37, τί δώσει ἄνθρωπος ἀντάλλαγμα τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ, “what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?” *wa giviþ manna inmaidein saivalos seinaizos*; Luke XIX.44, ἥξουσιν ἡμέραι ἐπὶ σὲ καὶ περιβαλοῦσιν οἱ ἐχθροί σου χάρακά σοι καὶ περικυκλώσουσί σε καὶ συνέξουσί σε πάντοθεν, καὶ ἐδαφιοῦσί σε καὶ οὐκ ἀφήσουσιν ἐν σοὶ λίθον ἐπὶ λίθῳ, “days shall come upon you, and your enemies shall cast up a rampart about you, surround you, hem you in on every side, dash you to the ground, and leave not one stone upon another in you,” *qim and dagos anaþus jah bigraband fijands þeinai grabai þuk jah bistandand þuk jah bivaibjand þuk allaþro jah airþai þuk gaibnjand jah ni letand in þus stain ana staina*; Rom. IX.25, καλέσω τὸν οὐ λαόν μου λαόν μου, “I shall call ‘my people’ those who were not my people,” *haita þo ni managein meina managein meina*; Matt. XI.23, *kafarnaum þu und himin ushauhida dalaþ und halja galeiþis*, “Capernaum, you who have been exalted to heaven, shall be brought down to Hades,” καταβιβασθήσῃ; John XVI.20, *amen qiþa izvis, þei greitiþ jah gaunoþ ith manaseþs faginoþ*, “truly I say to you, you shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice,” κλαύσετε καὶ θρηνήσετε; χαρήσεται; 2 Tim. II.11, *jabai miþgadauþnodedum jah miþlibam, jabai gaþulam jah miþþiudanom*, “if we died with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him,” συζήσομεν; συμβασιλεύσομεν; 2 Cor. XII.15, *gabaurjaba fraqima jah fraqimada faur saivalos izvaros*, “I shall gladly spend and be utterly spent for your souls,” δαπανήσω καὶ ἐκδαπανηθήσομαι; Rom. XI.22, *jabai þairhvisis in selein, aththan jah þu usmaitaza*, “if you continue in kindness, otherwise you also shall be cut off,” ἐκκοπήσῃ; Mark X.33, *sunus mans usgibada þaim ufargudjam*, “the Son of Man shall be delivered to the chief priests,” παραδοθήσεται; 1 Cor. XV.51, *allai inmaidjanda*, “we shall all be changed,” ἀλλαγησόμεθα; Mark XIII.25, *mahteis þos in himinam gavagjanda*, “the powers in the heavens shall be shaken,” σαλευθήσονται; and so forth.

b) The present subjunctive, regularly in subjunctive clauses, questions, and wherever the future closely approaches an imperative: Mark IX.19, *o kuni ungalaubjando, und wa at izvis sijau, und wa þulau izvis*, “O unbelieving generation, how long must I be with you? How long must I endure you?” ἔσομαι; ἀνέξομαι; Luke IV.8, *fraujan invitais jah imma ainamma fullafahjais*, “you shall worship the Lord and serve him alone,” προσκυνήσεις; λατρεύσεις—“I must serve”; John VIII.22, *nibai usqimai sis silbin*, “will he kill himself?” ἀποκτενεῖ; VI.68, *frauja du wamma galeiþaima*, “Lord, to whom shall we go?” ἀπελευσόμεθα—“must or can we go?”; Luke XIX.31, *jabai was igqis fraihnai, duwe andbindiþ, sva qiþaits du imma*, “if anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ thus you shall say to him,” ἐρεῖτε—“he can or must say”; Philem. 22, *venja ei þairh bidos izvaros fragibaidau izvis*, “I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you,” χαρισθήσομαι; Mark VIII.12, *amen qipa izvis, jabai gibaidau kunja þamma taikne*, “truly I say to you, no sign shall be given to this generation,” δοθήσεται; Matt. VI.7, *þugkeiþ im ei in filuvaurdein seinai andhausjaindau*, “they think that through their many words they shall be heard,” εἰσακουσθήσονται. Likewise Matt. V.33, 39, 41; X.26; Mark III.27; X.7; XI.13; XII.9; XVI.13; Luke I.13, 31, 60; III.10, 12; IV.8, 12; VI.42; VIII.17; X.6; XVI.3; XVII.4; XVIII.8; XX.15; John V.47; VII.31, 35; IX.21; XV.20; XVI.26; Rom. VIII.35; XI.14, 19, 21, 35; 1 Cor. VII.16; XI.22; 2 Cor. IX.19; XI.30; XIII.1; Gal. V.12; VI.4; 1 Thess. III.3; 1 Tim. III.5; Neh. VII.3.

In indirect questions and indirect discourse the present subjunctive is used where the verb of the principal clause stands in the preterite: Mark III.2, *vitaidedun imma, hailidedi sabbato daga*, “they watched him, whether he would heal on the Sabbath,” θεραπεύσει; Luke VI.7; Mark XI.18, *sokidedun waiwa imma usqistideina*, “they sought how they might destroy him,” ἀπολέσουσιν. Accordingly John V.45, *þatei ik vrohidedjau izvis*, “that I may accuse you,” μὴ δοκεῖτε, is not to be explained in this way.

> “Note 1.—Frequently the indicative or subjunctive is used differently merely because of a variant reading; thus at 2 Cor. XIII.1. In the sentence ἐπὶ στόματος δύο μαρτύρων καὶ τριῶν σταθήσεται πᾶν ῥῆμα, ‘every word shall be established upon the mouth of two or three witnesses,’ Codex B translates the future by the subjunctive *gastandei*, whereas Codex A translates it by the indicative *gastandiþ*. Yet sometimes Gothic also uses indicative or subjunctive at will in the same sentence: Mark IX.39, *ni mannahun ist, saei taujiþ maht in namin meinamma jah magi ubilvaurdjan mis*, ‘there is no one who shall perform a miracle in my name and shall be able to speak evil of me,’ ποιήσει; δυνήσεται; Luke I.31, *sai ganimis in kilþein jah gabairis sunu jah haitais namo is iesus*, ‘behold, you shall conceive in the womb, bear a son, and call his name Jesus,’ συλλήψῃ; τέξῃ; καλέσεις; John XV.20, *jabai mik vrekun jah izvis vrikand, jabai mein vaurd fastaidedeina jah izvar fastaina*, ‘if they persecuted me, they shall persecute you also; if they kept my word, they shall keep yours also,’ διώξουσι; τηρήσουσι; Rom. XI.14, *andbahti mein mikilja, ei waiwa in aljana brigga leik mein jah ganasjau sumans us im*, ‘I magnify my ministry, if somehow I may provoke my flesh to jealousy and save some from them,’ παραζηλώσω; σώσω; 2 Cor. IX.10, *sa andstaldands fraiva þana saiandan jah hlaiba du mata andstaldiþ jah managjai fraiv izvar jah vahsjan gataujai akrana usvaurhtais izvaraizos*, ‘he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food shall supply and multiply your seed and increase the fruits of your righteousness,’ χορηγήσει; πληθυνεῖ; αὐξήσει; compare 2).”

> “Note 2.—Since Gothic renders the future by the subjunctive when it approaches an imperative, it translates it in the same way where it is accompanied by negation (οὐ with the future): Matt. V.21, *ni maurþrjais*, ‘you shall not murder,’ οὐ φονεύσεις; 33, *ni ufarsvarais*, ‘you shall not swear falsely,’ οὐκ ἐπιορκήσεις; Luke IV.12; Rom. VII.7; XIII.9; 1 Cor. IX.9; 2 Cor. V.3.”

> “Note 3.—Conversely, the aorist subjunctive with οὐ μή, which carries a future sense, is normally rendered by the Gothic present indicative (compare §183): Matt. V.18, *und þatei usleiþiþ himins jah airþa, jota ains aiththau ains striks ni usleiþiþ af vitoda*, ‘until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the law,’ οὐ μὴ παρέλθῃ; 20, *qipa izvis þatei nibai managizo vairþiþ izvaraizos garaihteins þau þize bokarje, ni þau qimiþ in þiudangardjai himine*, ‘I say to you that unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes, you shall by no means enter the kingdom of heaven,’ οὐ μὴ εἰσέλθητε; 25, *qiþa þus, ni usgaggis jainþro, unte usgibis þana minnistan kintu*, ‘I say to you, you shall by no means come out from there until you have paid the last coin,’ οὐ μὴ ἐξέλθῃς; Matt. X.42; Luke I.15; IX.27; X.19; XVIII.17; John VI.35, 37; VIII.51; X.5, 28; XIII.38; 1 Cor. VIII.13; Gal. IV.30; 1 Thess. IV.15; V.3.

> The subjunctive, however, occurs only rarely: Luke XVIII.7, *ith guþ niu gavrikai þans gavalidans seinans*, ‘and shall not God vindicate his elect?’ οὐ μὴ ποιήσῃ; John XVIII.11, *stikl þanei gaf mis atta, niu drigkau þana*, ‘the cup which the Father gave me—shall I not drink it?’ οὐ μὴ πίω; VIII.52, *jabai was mein vaurd fastai, ni kausjai dauþau*, ‘if anyone keeps my word, he shall by no means taste death,’ οὐ μὴ γεύσηται; Gal. V.16.”

### 2) At times, however, Gothic prefers paraphrase; in that case it uses certain verbs corresponding to Greek μέλλειν and ἔχειν, such as *skulan*, “to be obliged,” *munan*, “to intend,” *skaftjan sik*, “to prepare oneself,” especially *skulan duginnan*, “to begin to be obliged,” and *haban*, “to have,” with an infinitive: Luke I.66, *galagidedun þo vaurda in hairtin seinamma qiþandans, wa skuli þata barn vairþan*, “they laid up these words in their heart, saying, ‘What then will this child become?’” ἔσται; VI.25, *vai izvis jus hlahjandans nu, unte gaunon jah gretan duginnid*, “woe to you who now laugh, because you shall begin to mourn and weep,” πενθήσετε καὶ κλαύσετε; John XII.26, *þarei ik im, þaruh sa andbahts meins visan habaiþ*, “where I am, there my servant shall also be,” ἔσται.

This paraphrase is especially used where present and future, standing in immediate sequence, are to be distinguished: Phil. I.18, *fagino jah faginon duginna*, “I rejoice and shall rejoice,” χαίρω καὶ χαρήσομαι; 2 Cor. XI.12, *tauja jah taujan haba*, “what I do, I shall also do,” ποιῶ καὶ ποιήσω; 2 Thess. III.4, *taujiþ jah taujan habaiþ*, “you do, and shall do,” ποιεῖτε καὶ ποιήσετε. In this case the subjunctive and indicative are also exchanged: John V.47, *þande jainis melam ni galaubeiþ, waiwa meinaim vaurdam galaubjaiþ*, “if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?” πιστεύετε; πιστεύσετε; 1 Cor. XI.22, *wa qiþau izvis, hazjau izvis, in þamma ni hazja*, “what shall I say to you? Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you,” ἐπαινέσω; ἐπαινῶ. Or a compound with *ga-* is used for the future: Luke XVII.8, *bigaurdans andbahtei mis, unte matja jah drigka, jah biþe gamatjis jah gadrigkais þu*, “gird yourself and serve me until I eat and drink, and afterward you shall eat and drink,” φάγω καὶ πίω; φάγεσαι καὶ πίεσαι; John XVI.16, *leitil nauh jah ni saiwiþ mik jah aftra leitil jah gasaiwiþ mik*, “a little while and you no longer see me, and again a little while and you shall see me,” θεωρεῖτε; ὄψεσθε; XVI.19; Rom. IX.15, *gaarma þanei arma, jah gableiþja*, “I shall have mercy on whom I have mercy, and shall pity”—where *þanei bleiþja*, “whom I pity,” must be supplied for οἰκτείρω, not *gaþleiþja*, as is asserted in the note on this passage.

> “Note 4.—When passages such as Matt. V.8; Mark XIII.26; XIV.62; XVI.7; Luke III.6; XVII.21; John XI.40 are examined, in which ὄψομαι, ‘I shall see,’ is always rendered by *gasaiwan*, whereas present *saiwan* means ‘to see,’ it might be conjectured that Gothic intended to express the future sense by the compound. Yet although forms with *ga-* are often found in that way, simple forms also occur in translating the future; for example, δώσω, ‘I shall give,’ is always rendered by *giba*: see Mark VIII.37; XII.9; XIII.22, 24; Luke I.32; IV.6; XVI.12; XX.16; John VI.27; XI.22; XIII.26; XIV.16; XVI.23; 2 Tim. II.7.”

> “Note 5.—Moreover, the indicative is used indiscriminately for the Greek present and future: John XIV.12, *saei galaubeid mis þo vaurstva, þoei ik tauja, jah is taujiþ jah maizona þaim taujiþ*, ‘he who believes in me, the works which I do he too shall do, and greater than these shall he do,’ ποιῶ; ποιήσει; 2 Tim. II.12, *jabai afaikam jah is afaikiþ uns*, ‘if we deny him, he also shall deny us,’ ἀρνούμεθα; ἀρνήσεται; Luke IV.6, *þus giba þata valdufni þize allata, unte mis atgiban ist jah þiswammeh þau viljau giba þata*, ‘I shall give you all this authority, because it has been given to me, and I give it to whomever I will,’ δώσω; δίδωμι; 2 Cor. XI.18, *wopand jah ik wopa*, ‘they boast, and I too shall boast,’ καυχῶνται κἀγὼ καυχήσομαι; compare 2 Cor. I.10, *izei us svaleikaim dauþum uns galausida jah galauseiþ, du þammei venidedum ei galauseiþ*, ‘who delivered us from so great deaths and delivers us, in whom we hoped that he will also deliver us,’ ῥύεται; ῥύσεται; 13, *ni alja meljam izvis alja þoei ufkunnaiþ, aththan venja ei und andi ufkunnaiþ*, ‘we write to you nothing other than what you recognize, and I hope that you will recognize it to the end,’ ἐπιγινώσκετε; ἐπιγνώσεσθε. John XIII.32 is difficult to understand: *guþ hauheiþ ina in sis jah suns hauhida ina*, ‘God glorifies him in himself and immediately glorified him,’ although the Greek text has the future twice.”

> “Note 6.—As for the future of the substantive verb (ἔσομαι), it is expressed: a) by the present indicative and subjunctive of *visan*: Matt. XXVII.64, *ist so speidizei airziþa vairsizei þizai frumein*, ‘the last deception shall be worse than the first,’ ἔσται; Mark VI.11, *amen qiþa izvis, sutizo ist saudaumjam aiththau gaumaurjam þau þizai baurg*, ‘truly I say to you, it shall be more tolerable for Sodom or Gomorrah than for that city,’ ἔσται; Luke V.10; XIV.10; John VIII.36; XIV.17; Matt. V.48, *sijaiþ nu jus fullatojai svasve atta izvar fullatojis ist*, ‘you therefore shall be perfect, as your Father is perfect,’ ἔσεσθε; Mark IX.19, *und wa at izvis sijau*, ‘how long shall I be with you?’ ἔσομαι; 35, *jabai was vili frumists visan, sijai allaize aftumists*, ‘if anyone wishes to be first, he shall be last of all,’ ἔσται; X.8, 43; Luke I.20, 34; IX.41; XVII.31; XVIII.13; John VIII.55; 2 Cor. XII.6; 2 Tim. II.2; b) by the indicative of *vairþan*, “to become”: Matt. V.21, *saei maurþreiþ, skula vairþiþ stauai*, ‘whoever murders shall be liable to judgment,’ ἔσται; V.22; VIII.12, *jainar vairþiþ grets jah krusts tunþive*, ‘there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth,’ ἔσται; XI.22, 24. In the parallel passage at Matt. VI.11, while there ἔσται is rendered *ist*, here it is rendered *vairþiþ*; Mark X.31, *managai vairþand frumans aftumans jah aftumans frumans*, ‘many who are first shall be last, and the last first,’ ἔσονται; XII.7, 23; XIII.19; Luke I.14, 33; and so forth. More rarely, by the bare subjunctive of *vairþan*: Luke VI.40, *gamanvids warjizuh vairþai sve laisaris is*, ‘everyone fully trained shall be like his teacher,’ ἔσται; 2 Cor. III.7, 8, *jabai andbahti dauþaus varþ vulþag—waiva nei mais andbahti ahmins vairþai in vulþau*, ‘if the ministry of death came in glory—how much more shall the ministry of the Spirit be in glory.’

> Hence, in paraphrase by *visan* and *vairþan*, each is used for the future: Luke I.37, ἀδυνατήσει, *unmahteigs ist*, ‘shall be impossible’; Rom. VIII.39, δυνήσεται, *mahteiga ist*, ‘shall be able’; Luke X.25, κληρονομήσω, *arbja vairþa*, ‘shall inherit’; Gal. V.21; Col. III.4, φανερωθήσεσθε, *bairhtai vairþiþ*, ‘you shall be manifested’; John XI.12, σωθήσεται, *hails vairþiþ*, ‘he shall be saved’; XVI.20, λυπηθήσεσθε, *saurgandans vairþiþ*, ‘you shall grieve’; Phil. I.20, αἰσχυνθήσομαι, *gaaiviskoþs vairþa*, ‘I shall be put to shame’; Luke VI.25, πεινάσετε, *gredagai vairþiþ*, ‘you shall hunger’; 1 Tim. VI.8, *habandans usfodein jah gaskadvein þaimuh ganohidai sijaima*, ‘having food and covering, with these we shall be content,’ ἀρκεσθησόμεθα; Luke XVIII.18, *wa taujands libainais aiveinons arbja vairþau?*, ‘what must I do to inherit eternal life?’ κληρονομήσω. Sometimes *ist* and *vairþiþ* seem to distinguish Greek ἐστί and ἔσται, as Matt. VI.22, *jabai augo þein ainfalþ ist, allata leik þein liuhadein vairþiþ*, ‘if your eye is sound, your whole body shall be full of light,’ ἐστί; ἔσται; yet immediately before, verse 21, *þarei ist huzd izvar, þaruh ist jah hairto izvar*, ‘where your treasure is, there your heart shall be also,’ has *ist* for both ἔστι and ἔσται.

> “Note 7.—The forms *bairaiþ* and *tiuhaiþ* in Gal. V.10, *sa drobjands izvis sa bairaiþ vargiþa*, ‘the one troubling you shall bear judgment,’ βαστάσει, and 1 Thess. IV.14, *guþ þans þaiei anasaislepun þairh iesu tiuhaiþ miþ imma*, ‘God shall bring with him those who fell asleep through Jesus,’ ἄξει, are conspicuous. If the Greek future had been translated by the indicative, they would be *bairiþ* and *tiuhiþ*; if by the subjunctive, *bairai* and *tiuhai*. Those who maintain that there is scribal error in these passages should not be heard, for that is wholly improbable, since elsewhere also, at Col. III.15, this form occurs for the third time, indeed for the imperative; see §186, Note 4. Here, as must be said regarding the passages in Thessalonians, it is a later form of the subjunctive.”

## §183. IV. THE FUTURE PERFECT

Gothic also translates the future perfect by the present, normally by the present indicative (see on 2 Thess. I.10): Matt. V.20, *nibai managizo vairþiþ izvaraizos garaihteins, ni þau qimiþ in þiudangardjai himine*, “unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven,” περισσεύσῃ; 21, *saei maurþreiþ, skula vairþiþ stauai*, “whoever murders shall be liable to judgment,” φονεύσῃ; 22, 26, *ni usgaggis jainþro unte usgibis þana minnistan kintu*, “you shall not come out from there until you have paid the last coin,” ἀποδῷς; Mark II.20, *þan afnimada af im sa bruþfaþs, jah þan fastand*, “when the bridegroom shall have been taken away from them, then they shall fast,” ἀπαρθῇ; John XIII.38, *hana ni hrukeiþ, unte þu mik afaikis kunnan þrim sinþam*, “the cock shall not crow until you have denied knowing me three times,” ἀπαρνήσῃ; 1 Cor. XVI.5, *qima at izvis, þan makindonja usleiþa*, “I shall come to you when I have passed through Macedonia,” διέλθω.

But indicative and subjunctive are exchanged: Matt. V.19, *saei nu gatairiþ aina anabuzne þizo minnistono jah laisjai sva mans, sah minnista haitada in þiudangardjai himine, ith saei taujiþ jah laisjai sva, sah mikils haitada in þiudangardjai himine*, “whoever breaks one of the least of these commandments and teaches people so shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does and teaches them shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven,” λύσῃ; διδάξῃ; ποιήσῃ καὶ διδάξῃ; Mark III.27, *ni manna mag kasa svinþis galeiþands in gard is vilvan, niba faurþis þana svinþan gabindiþ jah þana gard is disvilvai*, “no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man; then he shall plunder his house,” δήσῃ—διαρπάσῃ. Gothic evidently sought to establish some distinction in Matt. V.31 and 32: *qiþan ist þatei wazuh saei afletai qen, gibai izai ufstasseis bokos. Ith ik qiþa izvis þatei wazuh saei afletiþ qen seina, taujiþ þo horinon*: “it has been said, ‘Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce’; but I say to you that whoever dismisses his wife makes her commit adultery,” ἀπολύσῃ in both cases.

## III. CONCERNING MOOD

## §184. I. THE INDICATIVE

The indicative is used to express what actually exists, or what is affirmed to exist.

### 1) In simple sentences

a) Mark XVI.6, *iesus nist her, urrais*: “Jesus is not here; he has risen.”

b) In a direct question: Gal. III.1, *was izvis afhugida?* “Who bewitched you?” John XIII.36, *frauja wad gaggis?* “Lord, where are you going?”

> “Note 1.—The subjunctive also occurs in direct questions; see §185.I.f.

> Note 2.—The verbs ‘to be obliged,’ ‘to be fitting’ (German *sollen*), and ‘to wish’ are, in Greek and Latin fashion, put in the preterite indicative where Germans employ the subjunctive: 2 Cor. II.9, *þata silbo gamelida izvis, ei qimands saurga ni haban, fram þaimei skulda faginon*, ‘for this very reason I wrote to you, so that when I came I might not have sorrow from those of whom I ought to rejoice’—ἔδει, German *ich hätte sollen*, ‘I ought to have’; XII.11, *ik skulds vas fram izvis gakannjan*, ‘I ought to have been commended by you’—ὤφειλον, German *ich hätte sollen*; Gal. IV.19ff., *barnilona meina, þanzei aftra fita, unte gabairhtjaidau xristus in izvis, aththan vilda qimam at izvis*, ‘my little children, for whom I labour again until Christ be formed in you, but I would have wished to come to you’—ἤθελον, German *ich hätte mögen*, ‘I should have liked’; unless Gothic here understood a narrative imperfect, as also in 2 Cor. I.15; Philem. 13, and especially the aorist in Philem. 14, must be understood. Yet sometimes the subjunctive is used, as at 1 Cor. V.10: *ni blandaiþ izvis horam—unte skuldedeiþ þan us þamma fairwau usgaggan*, ‘not at all with the sexually immoral—otherwise you would have to leave the world,’ ὠφείλετε, ‘you would be obliged.’ The verb ‘to wish’ (*viljan*) wholly lacks a present in Gothic and has only the subjunctive (*viljau*); see §134.2.”

### 2) In compound sentences, namely

a) In hypothetical sentences: 1 Cor. XV.16, *jabai dauþans ni urreisand, nih xristus urrais*: “if the dead are not raised, neither has Christ been raised.”

b) After temporal particles.

c) In indirect questions: John IX.21, *waiva nu saiwiþ, ni vitum*: “how he now sees, we do not know.”

d) In indirect discourse: Luke VIII.47, *gasaiwandei so qino, þatei ni galaugnida*: “when the woman saw that she had not escaped notice.”

For a fuller account of these cases, and of how especially in a), c), and d) the subjunctive is very frequently employed, see below in the discussion of compound sentences.

## §185. THE SUBJUNCTIVE

The subjunctive signifies possibility. In simple sentences, moreover, a possibility may be expressed:
a) As something desired (optative): Rom. XV.5, *guþ gibai* (“may God give,” δώῃ) *ïzvis þata samo fraþjan ïn ïzvis misso* (“to you to think the same thing among yourselves”); 2 Thess. III.16; 2 Tim. I.16, 18, *guþ fulljai* (“may God fulfil,” πληρώσαι) *ïzvis allaizos fahedais* (“you with every joy”); 2 Cor. VII.2, *gamoteima ïn ïzvis* (“may we find room in you”), a point which Gothic expressed much more subtly than the Greek *χωρήσατε ἡμᾶς* (“make room for us”); 2 Thess. II.17, *guþ gaþrafstjai* (“may God comfort,” παρακαλέσαι) *hairtona izvara jah gatulgjai* (“your hearts and establish [you],” στηρίξαι) *ïn allaim vaurstvam godaim* (“in every good work”); III.5, *frauja garaihtjai* (“may the Lord direct,” κατευθύναι) *hairtona ïzvara ïn friaþvai guþs* (“your hearts into the love of God”); 1 Thess. III.11–12, *frauja managjai* (“may the Lord increase,” πλεονάσαι) *jah ganohnan gataujai* (“and make abound,” περισσεύσαι) *friaþvai* (“in love”); V.23, *guþ gaveihai* (“may God sanctify,” ἁγιάσαι) *ïzvis jah saivala jah leik unfairinona gafastaidau* (“may [your] spirit and soul and body be kept blameless,” τηρηθείη); Philem.20, *ïk þeina niutau* (“may I have benefit from you,” ὀναίμην) *in fraujin* (“in the Lord”).

With *vainei* (“would that,” ὄφελον), Gal. V.12: *vainei jah usmaitaindau þaidrobjandans ïzvis* (“would that those troubling you might even cut themselves off,” ὄφελον ἀποκόψονται). But when the Greek uses the past indicative, Gothic employs the past subjunctive: 1 Cor. IV.8, *ïnu uns þiudanodeduþ jah vainei þiudanodedeiþ* (“now you have begun to reign without us—and would that you had reigned,” ὄφελον ἐβασιλεύσατε); 2 Cor. XI.1, *vainei usþulaidedeiþ meinaizos leitil unfrodeins* (“would that you had endured a little folly from me,” ὄφελον ἠνείχεσθε). The formula *ni sijai* (“may it not be,” μὴ γένοιτο) also belongs here: Luke XX.16; Rom. VII.7.

b) As something conceded and humbly uttered (permissive): Luke I.38, Mary said: *sai þivi fraujins, vairþai mis bi vaurda þeinamma* (“behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it happen to me according to your word,” γένοιτο); II.29, Simeon said: *nu fraleitais skalk þeinana ïn gavairþja* (“now you dismiss your servant in peace,” ἀπολύεις).

c) As something willed. Here belongs the first person plural, by which a speaker exhorts a multitude: [Col. 1052] “let us see,” German *lasst uns!* See below, §186.4.

d) As something obligatory. Here especially belongs the third person, which Gothic uses in place of the immediate imperative; see below, §186.3.

e) Generally, as something whose existence depends upon the future; hence the subjunctive is often used for the future itself; see above, §182.1(b).

f) Very frequently in questions, especially where Greek has the future: 1 Tim. III.5, *jabai was seinamma garda fauragaggan ni mag, waiva aikklesjon guþs gakarai* (“if someone cannot manage his own household, how will he care for God’s church?” ἐπιμελήσεται); see above, §182.1(b). Worth noting are passages such as Mark XII.14: *skuldu ïst kaisaragild giban kairsara þau niu gibaima* (“is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or shall we not give it?”); John III.4: *ïbai mag manna alþeis visands ïn vamba aiþeins seinaizos aftra galeiþan jah gabairaidau* (“can a man, being old, enter again into his mother’s womb and be born?”).

> **Note.**—In Luke XIX.8, *halbata aiginis meinis gadailjau unledaim* (“I give half of my possessions to the poor”), the presence of a subjunctive is not to be inferred either from the Greek *δίδωμι* (“I give”) or from the sense, which the sentence alone permits. It is more probable that only *gudailja* is legitimate; the scribe, misled by the identical letter at the beginning of the following word, copied its *u* twice.

2) The subjunctive after temporal, causal, conditional, and explanatory particles will be treated under compound sentences.

## §186. III. THE IMPERATIVE EXPRESSES NECESSITY

1) This mood indeed has a form of its own; but Gothic frequently renders it by the subjunctive as well. For the Greek aorist imperative it regularly uses the imperative form when an act is commanded for immediate performance; for the Greek present imperative, however, it uses the subjunctive form when what is commanded is to be done only in the future. Negation with the infinitive is rendered by *ni* (“not”): 1 Cor.
