XI.24, *nimiþ matjiþ* (“take, eat,” λάβετε φάγετε), *þata ïst leik mein, þata vaurkjaiþ du meinai gamundai* (“this is my body; do this in remembrance of me,” ποιεῖτε); John XVII.11, *atta veiha, fastai ïns ïn namin þeinamma* (“Holy Father, keep them in your name,” τήρησον); 1 Tim. V.23, *þuk silban sviknana fastais* (“keep yourself pure,” τήρει); Mark X.14, *letiþ þo barna gaggan du mis* (“allow the children to come to me,” ἄφετε); XI.25, *þan standaiþ bidjandans, afletaiþ jabai wa habaiþ viþra wana* (“when you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone,” ἀφίετε); Matt. VI.11, *hlaif unsarana þana sinteinan gif uns* (“give us this day our daily bread,” δός); V.42, *þamma bidjandin þuk gibais* (“give to the one asking you,” δίδου); Philem.12, *þu ïna andnim* (“receive him,” προσλαβοῦ); 1 Tim. V.19, *ni andnimais niba ïn andvairþja veitvode* (“do not receive [an accusation] except in the presence of witnesses,” παραδέχου); John XI.39, *afnimiþ þana stain* (“take away the stone,” ἄρατε); Luke IX.3, *ni vaiht nimaiþ ïn vig* (“take nothing for the journey,” αἴρετε); X.2, *bidjiþ fraujan* (“ask the Lord,” δεήθητε); Matt. VI.9, *sva nu bidjaiþ* (“therefore pray thus,” προσεύχεσθε); John XIII.27, *þatei taujis, tavei sprauto* (“what you are doing, do quickly,” ποίησον); Rom. XIII.4, *þiuþ taujais jah habais hazein us þamma* (“do good, and you will have praise from it,” ποίει); John VI.10, *vaurkeiþ þans mans anakumbjan* (“make the men recline,” ποιήσατε); 27, *vaurkjaiþ ni þana mat þana fralusanan* (“work not for the food that perishes,” ἐργάζεσθε); 1 Cor. VII.21, *þauhjabai freis magt vairþan, mais brukei* (“but if you are able to become free, use it rather,” χρῆσαι); 1 Tim. V.23, *ni drigkais þanamais vato, ak veinis leitil brukjais* (“drink water no longer, but use a little wine,” μὴ ὑδροπότει; χρῶ); 2 Cor. VI.17, *usgaggiþ us midumai ïze* (“come out from among them,” ἐξέλθετε); Luke IX.4, *þar saljiþ jah þaþroh usgaggaiþ* (“remain there and depart from there,” ἐξέρχεσθε); XV.22, *sprauto [Col. 1053] briggiþ vastja* (“quickly bring out a garment,” ἐξενέγκατε); X.4, *ni briggaiþ pugg* (“do not carry a purse,” βαστάζετε), etc.

> **Note 1.**—Conversely, the Gothic imperative often corresponds to the Greek present imperative; and, though more rarely, the subjunctive is used for the Greek aorist imperative: Matt. VII.23, *afleiþiþ fairra mis* (“depart from me,” ἀποχωρεῖτε); Rom. XI.20, *jabai gredo fijand þeinana, mat gif ïmma, ïþ jabai þaursjai, dragkei ïna* (“if your enemy is hungry, give him food; if he thirsts, give him drink,” ψώμιζε; πότιζε); Matt. VIII.9, *qiþa du þamma qïm, jah qimiþ* (“I say to one, ‘Come,’ and he comes,” ἔρχου); Luke VII.13, *ni gret* (“do not weep,” κλαῖε); Rom. XI.20, *ni ïn matis gatair vaurstv guþs* (“do not destroy God’s work for the sake of food,” κατάλυε); 1 Tim. IV.11, *anabiud þata jah laisei* (“command these things and teach them,” παράγγελλε—δίδασκε); Matt. VIII.22, *laistei afar mis* (“follow me,” ἀκολούθει); Mark V.36, *ni faurhtei* (“do not fear,” φοβοῦ); Luke I.13, *ni ogs þus* (“do not fear,” φοβοῦ); Matt. X.26, *ni ogeiþ* (“do not fear,” μὴ φοβεῖσθε), etc.—Matt. VII.13, *ïnngaggaiþ þairh aggvu daur* (“enter through the narrow gate,” εἰσέλθετε); Eph. VI.17, *hilm naseinais nimaiþ* (“take the helmet of salvation,” δέξασθε), Col. IV.10; John XV.4, *visaiþ ïn mis jah ïk ïn ïzvis* (“remain in me, and I in you,” μείνατε); Col. IV.16, *þan ussiggvaidau at ïzvis so aipistaule, taujaiþ ei jah ïn laudekaion ussiggvaidau jah þoei ïst us laudeikaion jus ussiggvaid* (“when the letter has been read among you, arrange that it also be read in Laodicea, and that you read that from Laodicea,” ποιήσατε; ἀναγνῶτε); Matt. X.27; Mark VI.11; XIV.15; John X.38; 1 Cor. XVI.11.

> **Note 2.**—In different passages Gothic translated differently. *Gibiþ* (“give”), which regularly renders *δότε* (“give!”) in Luke IX.13; XV.22; XIX.24; Rom. XII.19, is also found at Eph. IV.27, *ni gibiþ staþ unhulþin* (“do not give place to the devil”), for *δίδοτε* (“give”); but Codex A more correctly has *nih gibaiþ* (“and do not give”), as in Luke VI.38, *gibaid jah gibada ïzvis* (“give, and it shall be given to you,” δίδοτε). *Atbair* (“bring”), Matt. VIII.4, regularly renders *προσένεγκε* (“bring near”), but in 2 Tim. II.13 it renders *φέρε* (“bring”). *Gaþlaih* (“exhort”), 2 Tim. IV.2, renders *παρακάλεσον* (“exhort”), but in 1 Tim. V.1 it also renders *παρακάλει* (“keep exhorting”). *Κρίνατε* (“judge”) is translated in John XVIII.31 by *stojiþ* (“judge”), and in Rom. XIV.13 by *stojaiþ* (“let us judge”); *μὴ κρίνετε* (“do not judge”), Luke VI.37, by *ni stojiþ*, and John VII.24 by *ni stojaiþ*. *Εἴπατε* (“say”) is regularly *qiþiþ* (“say”) in Mark XVI.7; Luke X.9; XX.3, but also *qiþaiþ* in Matt. X.37; Luke X.10; Col. IV.17. *Λέγετε* (“say”), Luke X.5, is *qiþaiþ*, but Gal. IV.21 also has *qiþiþ*. *Ἀσπάσασθε* (“greet”) is *goleiþ* in 1 Cor. XVI.20; Col. IV.15, but *goljaiþ* in 2 Cor. XIII.12; 1 Thess. V.26. *Καλεῖ* (“invite”), Luke XIV.13, is *hait* (“invite”), and *μὴ φώνει* (“do not invite”), XIV.12, *ni haitais*. *Φέρετε* (“bring”) in Mark IX.19; XII.15 is *bairiþ*; but *βαστάζετε* (“bear”) in Gal. VI.2 is *bairaiþ*. *Βλέπετε*, *ὁρᾶτε*, and *θεωρεῖτε* (“see,” “look,” “observe”) are ordinarily rendered *saiwiþ* (“look”): Mark IV.23; XII.38; Luke VIII.18; John XII.19; 1 Cor. X.18; Gal. V.15; Eph. III.2; 1 Thess. V.15; but 1 Cor. XVI.10 also has *saiwaiþ*. The common exhortative formula is the imperative *gagg, gaggiþ* (“come,” “go”) for *ἔλθε*, *πορεύου*, *πορεύθητι*, *ὕπαγε* (“come,” “go,” “go on your way”), etc. Yet Matt. V.41 has *gaggais*, and Eph. V.2, 8; Col. IV.5 have *gaggaiþ*.

2) The second person of the imperative:

a) Matt. V.24, *aflet jainar þo giba þeina* (“leave your gift there,” ἄφες); John VII.3, *usleiþ þaþro* (“go away from here,” μετάβηθι); Luke IV.9, *vairp þuk þaþro dalaþ* (“throw yourself down from here,” βάλε); Mark IX.43, *jabai marzjai handus þeina, afmait þo* (“if your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off,” ἀπόκοψον); XIV.13, *gaggats afar þamma* (“follow him,” ἀκολουθήσατε); Luke V.4, *brigg ana diupiþa jah athahid þo natja ïzvara du fiskon* (“put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch,” ἐπανάγαγε; χαλάσατε); Mark XIV.44, *þammei kukjau, sa ïst, greipiþ þana jah tiuhiþ* (“the one whom I kiss—that is he; seize him and lead him away,” κρατήσατε; ἀγάγετε); Luke XVII.6, *uslausei þuk us vaurtim [Col. 1054] jah ussatei þuk ïn marein* (“be uprooted and planted in the sea,” ἐκριζώθητι; φυτεύθητι); 2 Cor. VI.17, *afskaidiþ ïzvis* (“separate yourselves,” ἀφορίσθητε); 13, *þata samo andalauni urrumnaiþ jah jus* (“in the same recompense, be enlarged also, you,” πλατύνθητε); Matt. VIII.3, *vairþ hrains* (“be clean,” καθαρίσθητι); Mark V.12, *ïnsandei unsis ïn þo sveina* (“send us into the swine,” πέμψον); Luke IV.35, *afdobn* (“be silent,” φιμώθητι), etc.

b) The second person of the subjunctive: Rom. XIII.6, *gilstra ustiuhaiþ* (“pay taxes,” τελεῖτε); 1 Tim. VI.11, *ïþ þu þata þliuhais, ïþ laitsjais garaihtein* (“but you, flee these things and pursue righteousness,” φεῦγε; δίωκε); 1 Cor. IX.24, *sva rinnaiþ, ei garinnaiþ* (“run thus, that you may obtain [the prize],” τρέχετε); 1 Thess. V.21–22, *all uskiusaiþ, þatei goþ sijai, gahabaiþ, af allamma vaihte ubilaizo afhabaiþ ïzvis* (“test everything; hold fast what is good; abstain from every evil thing,” δοκιμάζετε; κατέχετε; ἀπέχεσθε); Eph. V.18, *ni anadrigkaiþ ïzvis veina* (“do not intoxicate yourselves with wine,” μεθύσκεσθε); Phil. I.27, *vairþaba aivaggeljons usmitaiþ* (“conduct yourselves worthily of the Gospel,” πολιτεύεσθε); 1 Cor. XVI.13, *vakaiþ, standaiduh ïn galaubeinai, vairaleiko taujaiþ, gaþvastidai sijaiþ* (“be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act manfully, be strong,” γρηγορεῖτε; στήκετε; ἀνδρίζεσθε; κραταιοῦσθε); 2 Cor. VI.17, *unhrainjamma ni attekaiþ* (“do not touch what is unclean,” ἅπτεσθε); Col. III.9, *ni liugaiþ* (“do not lie,” ψεύδεσθε); Luke X.7, *ni faraiþ us garda ïn gard* (“do not move from house to house,” μεταβαίνετε), etc.

c) Thus the subjunctive is always used for *μὴ* with an aorist subjunctive in imperative sense: Luke XVII.23, *qiþand ïzvis: sai her aiþþau sai jainar, ni galeiþaiþ nih laistjaiþ* (“when they say to you, ‘Behold, here!’ or ‘Behold, there!’ do not go away or follow,” μὴ ἀπέλθητε μηδὲ διώξητε); 1 Tim. V.1, *seneigana ni andbeitais* (“do not rebuke an older man,” μὴ ἐπιπλήξῃς); Matt. V.36, *ni svarais* (“do not swear,” μὴ ὀμόσῃς); Col. II.21, *ni teikais, ni atsnarpjais, ni kausjais, þatei all ïst du riurein* (“do not handle, do not taste, do not touch—things all destined to perish”); Mark XIII.21, *ni galaubjaiþ* (“do not believe”); Matt. V.17; VI.2, 7, 19; X.34; Mark V.7; Luke X.4; XVII.23; 2 Tim. I.8, etc.

> **Note 3.**—The Goths have no special form for a softened command, that is, for entreaty; in its place they use the present subjunctive, for example, “do not rage,” *ni hlifais*; see above, §182, note 2.

3) The third person of the imperative always agrees with the third person of the subjunctive: Matt. V.16, *lïuhtjai liuhaþ ïzvar ïn andvairþja manne* (“let your light shine before men,” λαμψάτω); 31, *saei afletai qen, gibai ïzai afstassais bokos* (“he who divorces a wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce,” δότω); 37, *sijai vaurd ïzvar ja ja, ne ne* (“let your word be ‘yes, yes,’ ‘no, no,’” ἔστω); VI.3, *ni viti hleidumei þeina, wa taujiþ taihsvo þeina* (“let not your left hand know what your right hand does,” γνώτω); VI.10, *qimai þiudinassus þeins* (“let your kingdom come,” ἐλθέτω); VIII.13, *svasve galaubides, vairþai þus* (“as you have believed, let it be done for you,” γενηθήτω); Mark VIII.34, *saei vili afar mis laistjan, ïnvidai sik silban jah nimai galgan seinana jah laistjai mik* (“let him who wishes to follow me deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me,” ἀπαρνησάσθω; ἀράτω; ἀκολουθείτω); Rom. XIV.3, *sa matjands þamma ni maljandin ni frakunni, ïþ sa ni matjands þana matjandan ni stojai* (“let not the eater despise the non-eater, and let not the non-eater judge the eater,” ἐξουθενείτω; κρινέτω); Eph. V.8, *ni manna ïzvis uslusto lausaim vaurdam* (“let no one deceive you with empty words,” ἀπατάτω), etc.; Eph. V.22, *qeneis seinaim abnam ufhausjaina* (“let wives submit themselves to their own husbands,” ὑποταττέσθωσαν); 1 Tim. III.12, *diakaunjus sijaina ainaizos qenais abans* (“let deacons be husbands of one wife,” ἔστωσαν); V.4, *galaisjaina sik svesana gard barusnjan* (“let them learn first to show devotion to their own household,” μανθανέτωσαν); III.10; VI.2; John XIV.27.—Matt. VI.9, *veihnai namo þein* (“let your name be hallowed,” ἁγιασθήτω); John XIV.1, *ni ïndrobnai izvar hairto* (“let not your heart be troubled,” ταραττέσθω); 27, *ni ïndrobnaina ïzvara hairtona nih faurhtjaina* (“let not your hearts be troubled, nor let them be afraid”); Mark VII.10, *saei ubil qiþai attin seinamma, dauþau afdauþjaidau* (“let him who speaks evil of father or mother surely die,” τελευτάτω); Rom. XIV.16, *ni vajamerjaindau [Col. 1055] unsar þiuþ* (“let not our good be spoken evil of,” βλασφημείσθω); 1 Cor. VII.9, *jabai ni gahabaina sik, liugandau* (“if they cannot restrain themselves, let them marry,” γαμησάτωσαν); XI.6, *jabai ni huljai sik qens, skabaidau* (“if a woman does not cover herself, let her be shorn,” κειράσθω); XV.33; Eph. IV.31; V.3; Phil. II.5; 1 Tim. III.10; V.9, 16; 2 Tim. II.26.

> **Note 4.**—At Col. III.15, *gavairþi guþs svignjaiþ ïn hairtam ïzvaraim* (“let the peace of God rule in your hearts,” βραβευέτω), one should read *svignjai*. *Svignjaiþ* must either be attributed to scribal negligence or be written for *svingjai*, as stated above, §182, note 7.

4) The first person plural, used for exhortation (“let us do,” etc.), has a special form corresponding to the indicative: Mark IV.35, *usleiþam jainis stadis* (“let us cross to the other side,” διέλθωμεν); Luke VIII.22; Mark IX.5, *vaurkjam hlijans þrins* (“let us make three tents,” ποιήσωμεν); Gal. VI.10; Mark XII.7, *hirjiþ usqimam ïmma* (“come, let us kill him,” ἀποκτείνωμεν); XIV.42, *urreisiþ gaggam* (“arise, let us go,” ἄγωμεν); I.38; John XI.7, 11, 15; XIV.31; Gal. V.25; Luke XV.23, *matjandans stiur alidana visam vaila* (“let us eat the fattened calf and rejoice,” εὐφρανθῶμεν); XX.14, *sa ïst sa arbinumja, afslaham ïna* (“this is the heir; let us kill him,” ἀποκτείνωμεν); Rom. X.12, *usvairpam vaurstvam riqizis ïþ gavasjam sarvam liuhadis* (“let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armour of light,” ἀποθώμεθα; ἐνδυσώμεθα); 1 Cor. V.8, *dulþjam ni in beista fairnjamma* (“let us keep the feast, not with old leaven,” ἑορτάζωμεν); XV.32, *matjam jah drigkam* (“let us eat and drink,” φάγωμεν καὶ πίωμεν); 2 Cor. VII.1, *hrainjam unsis af allamma bisauleino* (“let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement,” καθαρίσωμεν).

The subjunctive is also frequently used for this person: Luke IX.33, in the parallel passage to Mark IX.5, *gavaurkjaima hleiþros þrins* (“let us make three tents,” ποιήσωμεν); II.15, *þairhgaggaima und beþlahaim jah saiwaima vaurd þata vaurþano* (“let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened,” διέλθωμεν; ἴδωμεν); Rom. XIV.13, *ni uns misso stojaima* (“let us not judge one another,” κρίνωμεν); 19, *þoei gavairþjis sind laistjaima* (“let us pursue the things that make for peace,” διώκωμεν); 1 Cor. XV.49, *svasve berum manleikan þis airþeinins, sva bairaima jah frisaht þis himinakundins* (“as we have borne the image of the earthly man, let us also bear that of the heavenly,” φορέσωμεν); 2 Cor. III.12, *habandans nu svaleika ven managaizos balþeins brukjaima* (“having such hope, let us use great boldness,” χρώμεθα); IV.1, *ni vairþaima usgrudjans* (“let us not become discouraged,” γενώμεθα); Gal. V.26; VI.9; Phil. III.15, *sva managai sve sijaima fullavitans þata hugjaima* (“as many as are mature, let us think this,” φρονῶμεν); 1 Thess. V.6, *ni slepaima sve þai anþarai ak vakaima jah varai sijaima* (“let us not sleep like the others, but let us keep awake and be sober,” καθεύδωμεν; γρηγορῶμεν; νήφωμεν); 8, *unskavai sijaima* (“let us be sober,” νήφωμεν).

> **Note 5.**—Imperatives belonging to a lost verb, corresponding to Greek *δεῦρο, δεῦτε* (“come! come, all of you!”), are *hiri* (German *hier du*, “here, you”), *hirjats* (German *hier ihr beide*, “here, you two”), and *hirjiþ* (German *hier ihr*, “here, you [plural]”); see the glossary under these words.

> **Note 6.**—When two imperatives immediately follow one another, either: (a) they are joined by *jah* (“and”): John XI.34, *hiri jah saiw* (“come and see”); Luke V.23, *urreis jah gagg* (“arise and go”); XVIII.22; or (b) by *-uh* (“and”): Matt. XXVII.65, *gaggiþ vitaiduh* (“go and make it secure”); Mark II.11; XVI.7; or (c) they are juxtaposed without a conjunction: Matt. VIII.4, *gagg þuk silban ataugei* (“go, show yourself”); IX.13, *gaggaiþ ganimiþ* (“go, learn”); Mark X.21, *gagg sva filu swe habais frabugei jah gif* (“go, sell all that you have and give”); XII.7, *hirjiþ usqimam* (“come, let us kill”); or (d) the two imperatives are changed into a subjunctive construction: Mark I.44, parallel to Matt. VIII.4, *gagg þuk silban ataugjan*, literally “go, to show yourself” (Greek *ὕπαγε σεαυτὸν δεῖξον*, “go, show yourself”); Matt. V.24; [Col. 1056] Mark X.21; Luke XVIII.22; John IX.7, 11; Mark VIII.15, *saiwiþ ei atsaiwaiþ*, “see, that you may look out,” literally “look, that you may foresee” (Greek *ὁρᾶτε· βλέπετε*, “see; beware”); Matt. XXVII.49, *let ei saivam* (“leave [him], that we may see,” ἄφες· ἴδωμεν); Matt. IX.30, *saiwats ei manna ni viti* (“see that no one knows,” ὁρᾶτε, μηδεὶς γινωσκέτω). Hence Gal. V.6, *qiþa ei gaggaiþ* (“I say: walk,” λέγω· περιπατεῖτε); compare 2 Thess. III.1, *þata anþar ei bidjaiþ* (“finally, pray”).

## IV. PERSON AND NUMBER

### §187. I. PERSON

1) There are three persons in the singular and plural, but only two in the dual, namely the first and second; see below, II.

2) The verbs possessing only a third person and called impersonal are these: *rigneiþ*, “it rains,” Luke XVII.29; but in Matt. V.45 it is used personally: *(atta ïzvar) rigneiþ ana garaihtans jah ana ïnvindans* (“[your Father] rains upon the righteous and the unrighteous”). Moreover, no special words designate natural phenomena: “it grows late” is *seiþu vairþiþ* (“evening comes”), Matt. XXVII.57; John VI.16.

Verbs signifying natural necessities, “one is hungry” and “one is thirsty,” are sometimes used impersonally: John VI.35, *þana gaggandan du mis ni huggreiþ jah þana galaubjandan du mis ni þaurseiþ* (“the one coming to me shall not hunger, and the one believing in me shall not thirst”); Rom. XII.20, *jabai gredo fijand þeinana … ïþ jabai þaursjai* (“if your enemy hungers … and if he thirsts”); John VII.37, *jabai wans þaursjai* (“if anyone thirsts”). In Greek these verbs are personal, as are *huggriþs* (“hungry”) and *þaursiþs* (“thirsty”), 1 Cor. IV.11, or *afþaursiþs (visan)* (“to be thirsty”), Matt. XXV.42. Conversely, “to become hungry” is personal only under the form *gredags vairþan* (“to become hungry”); see the glossary under that word.

Other impersonals are *vairþiþ*, “it happens,” Mark II.23; Luke IV.36; VI.1; XVI.22; 2 Cor. VII.7; and *boteiþ*, “there is need,” Mark VIII.36. Both are also used personally. *Gadabiþ*, “it suits, is fitting,” Mark X.32; *Skeireins* III.c; its personal form is *gadobs visan*, “to be suitable.” *Þugkeiþ*, “it seems,” Matt. VI.7; Luke XIX.11; 2 Cor. XII.19, is personal in Greek, as it is elsewhere in Gothic; compare Mark X.42; Luke VIII.18; John XVI.2; the subscription to 1 Corinthians, etc. *Binah*, “it is necessary,” 2 Cor. XII.1, is also personal in 1 Cor. X.23; *ganah*, “it is sufficient,” Matt. X.25, is personal in John XIV.8; 2 Cor. II.6; XII.9. The impersonals of other languages—“it is necessary” (*δεῖ*), “one repents,” “one is ashamed,” “one pities,” *μέλει* (“it concerns”)—are personal in Gothic: *skulan* (“to have to”), *ïdreigon sik* (“to repent”), *skaman sik* (“to be ashamed”), *arman* (“to pity”), *karon* (“to care for”); *karïst* alone is impersonal.

### II. NUMBER

There are three numbers: singular, plural, and dual. Gothic uses the dual in its own manner, where it occurs neither in the Greek text, in the first person active, nor elsewhere in the New Testament. But it uses it only in direct speech, not in narrative; this explains why the dual occurs only in the first and second persons, while the plural is used for the third person, who is spoken about: John X.30, *ïk jah atta meins ain siju* (“I and my Father are one”); XVII.22, *vulþu þanei gaft mis, gaf ïm, ei sijaina ain svave vit ain siju* (“the glory which you gave me I gave them, that they may be one as we two, I and the Father, are one”); XIV.23, *jabai was mik frijoþ jah vaurd mein fastaiþ, jah atta meins frijoþ ïna jah du ïmma galeiþos jah saliþvos at ïmma gataujos* (“if anyone loves me and keeps my word, my Father will love him, and we two will come to him and make our dwelling with him”); 1 Cor. IX.6, *ïk jah barnabas ni habos valdufni du ni vaurkjan* (“do Barnabas and I alone not have authority not to work?”).

Matt. IX.28–30: *duatïddjedun ïesua þai blindans* (“the two blind men came to Jesus”) *jah qad ïm ïesus: gaulaubjats þatei magjau þata taujan?* (“and Jesus said to them: do you two believe that I am able to do this?”) [Col. 1057] *qeþun du ïmma: jai, frauja … jah ïnagida ïns ïesus qiþands: saiwats ei manna ni viti ïþ eis usmeridedun ïna* (“they said to him: yes, Lord … and Jesus sternly charged them, saying: see that no one knows; but they spread word of him abroad”); Mark I.16–17: *warbonds ïesus faur marein gasaw seimonu jah andraian vairpandans nati in marein. vesun auk fiskjans. jah qaþ ïm: hirjats afar mis!* (“walking beside the sea, Jesus saw Simon and Andrew casting a net into the sea; for they were fishermen. And he said to them: come, both of you, after me!”); XI.2–4: *ïesus ïnsandida tvans siponje jah qaþ du ïm: gaggats ïn haim jah bigitats fulan andbindandans ïna attiuhits* (“Jesus sent two disciples and said to them: go, both of you, into the village, and you will find a colt tied; untie it and lead it”), concerning this erroneous form see above, §116, note 3; *ja jabai was ïggqis qiþai: duwe þata taujats? qiþaits, þatei frauja þis gairneiþ. galiþun þan jah bigetun fulan* (“and if anyone says to you, ‘Why are you two doing this?’ say, ‘The Lord has need of it.’ They went and found the colt”); Luke XIX.30–33; Luke VII.22: *ïesus qaþ du ïm* (“Jesus said to them,” namely to John’s two messengers), *gaggandans gateihats ïohannen, þatei gasewuts jah gahausideduts* (“go and report to John what you two have seen and heard”).

In the passage richest in examples of the dual, Mark X.35–39: *athabaidedun sik du ïmma ïaakobus jah ïohannes qiþandans: laisari, vileima ei þatei þuk bidjos, taujais unsis* (“James and John came up to him, saying: Teacher, we two wish you to do for us whatever we ask”); *ïþ ïs qaþ ïm: wa vileits taujan mik ïgqis?* (“but he said to them: what do you two wish me to do for you?”); *ïþ eis qeþun: fragif ugkis ei—sitaiva in vulþau þeinamma* (“and they said: grant us that we two may sit in your glory”); *ïþ ïesus qaþ du ïm: ni vituts wis bidjats, magutsu driggkan stikl, þanei ïk driggka jah daupeinai, þizaiei ïk daupjada ei daupjaindau?* (“Jesus said to them: you two do not know what you ask. Are you two able to drink the cup which I drink, and to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?”); *ïþ eis qeþun: magu! ïþ ïesus qaþ: sveþauh þana stikl, þanei ïk driggka, driggkats jah þizai daupeinai, þizaiei ïk daupjada …* (“and they said: we are able. Jesus said: nevertheless, the cup which I drink, you two shall drink; and with the baptism with which I am baptized …”).

First, it is clear that the passive has no dual, since *daupjaindau*, used for *βαπτισθήσεσθε* (“you shall be baptized”), ought to be *daupjainda*. Secondly, the plural *vileima* is absent, for which one would expect *vileiva*. The plural is also occasionally used for the dual: Mark XIV.13–15, *ïnsandida tvans siponje qaþuh du ïm: gaggats ïn þo baurg jah gamoteiþ ïgqis manna kas vatins bairands, gaggats afar þamma jah þadei ïnngaleiþai qiþaits: war sind saliþvos? jah sa ïzvis taikneiþ kelikn jah jainar manvjaiþ unsis* (“he sent two disciples and said to them: go, both of you, into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you; follow him, and wherever he enters say: ‘Where is the guest room?’ And he will show you an upper room; prepare there for us”); Luke XIX.31 and 33, in the same question, has once *duwe andbindiþ* (“why are you two untying [it]?”), then *duwe andbindats*. The plural alone is also used although two people are meant: Luke II.48–49, *sa atta þeins jah ïk sokidedum þuk. jah qap du ïm: wa þatei sokideduþ mik. niu visseduþ þatei ïn þaim attins meinis skulda visan?* (“your father and I have been seeking you. And he said to them: why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s affairs?”). In the former case the translator seems to have acted arbitrarily; in the latter, to have been less attentive and less strictly conformed to the Greek text.

## V. INFINITIVE AND PARTICIPLE

### §188

The infinitive and participle stand midway between verb and noun. They have this in common with the verb: they express the idea of an action and are capable of governing; but they differ from it because their form is not verbal inflection but an independent derivation; see §§145 cc), 148. Therefore they do not contain the copula within themselves and cannot be referred to a subject. In meaning, however, they agree with nouns.

### §189. I. THE INFINITIVE

The infinitive presents the abstract idea of the verb and therefore is by nature a substantive: for example, *ogan*, “to fear,” hence “fear”; *viljan*, “to will,” hence “will,” French *le vouloir*, “the willing”; *frijon*, “to love,” hence “love.”

1) Gothic has only one infinitive, namely the present active. Accordingly, because another is lacking, [Col. 1058] it also renders Greek past infinitives by that same form: Luke I.9, *θυμιᾶσαι* (“to burn incense”) by *saljan* (“to offer”); 57, *τεκεῖν* (“to bear”) by *bairan* (“to bear”); IV.10, *διαφυλάξαι* (“to guard”) by *gafastan* (“to preserve”); Rom. XIII.11, *ἐγερθῆναι* (“to be raised”) by *urreisan* (“to arise”); 2 Cor. X.2, *τολμῆσαι* (“to dare”) by *gadaursan* (“to dare”); Phil. III.11, *κατειληφέναι* (“to have attained”) by *gafahan* (“to attain”), etc. But when Gothic must paraphrase the infinitive by a conjunction, it observes the relation of time: 2 Cor. II.12, *ni habaida gaweilain ahmin meinamma, in þammei ni bigat teitaun* (“I had no rest for my spirit because I did not find Titus,” τῷ μὴ εὑρεῖν, “in not finding”); VIII.5, *ni svasve venidedum, ak sik silbans atgebun, svaei bedeima* (“not as we expected, but they gave themselves, so that we might entreat,” ὥστε παρακαλέσαι, “so as to entreat”). Yet X.2 is also correct in sense: *bidjam ei ni andvairþs gatrauan* (“I ask that, when present, I may not be bold,” τὸ θαῤῥῆσαι, “to be bold”).

2) Passive infinitives are rendered:

a) Frequently by the active infinitive; see §177, note 4.

b) By paraphrase with auxiliary verbs: Luke IX.22, *skal sunus mans uskusans fram sinistam vairþan* (“the Son of Man must become rejected by the elders,” ἀποδοκιμασθῆναι, “to be rejected”); subscription to 1 Corinthians, *du kaurinþium frumei þugkeiþ melida visan us asiai* (“to the Corinthians, first [letter], thought to have been written from Asia,” γεγράφθαι, “to have been written”); 2 Cor. V.11, *venja svikunþans visan uns* (“we hope to have been made manifest,” πεφανερῶσθαι, “to have been manifested”).

c) By a conjunctive resolution: Mark V.3–4, *ni manna mahta ïna gabindan, unte ïs ufta naudibandjom eisarneinaim gabundans vas* (“no one was able to bind him, because he had often been bound with iron fetters,” διὰ τὸ δεδέσθαι, “because of having been bound”); Luke II.3, *ïddjedun allai, ei melidai veseina warjizuh in seinai baurg* (“all went in order that each might be registered in his own city,” ἀπογράφεσθαι, “to be registered”).

3) Because of its substantive nature, the infinitive is used:

a) Also for Greek substantives, and conversely; see §193.1.

b) As the subject of a sentence (§§207.2 and 209.4), but more commonly after verbs as the object of a simple sentence.

c) Where purpose and intention are expressed, it ordinarily takes the preposition *du* (“to, for”), which explains why even in modern German *legen* is distinguished from *zu legen* (“to lay”); see below under compound sentences.

> **Note.**—*Du* may be separated from its infinitive by words serving to define it or dependent upon it: Rom. VII.5, *du akran bairan* (“to bear fruit”); XI.11, *du ïn aljana briggan* (“to bring [them] into jealousy”); 1 Cor. VIII.10, *du galiugagudam gasaliþ matjan* (“to eat sacrificial food in an idol-temple”); Phil. IV.10, *du faur mik fraþjan* (“to care for me”); 2 Thess. I.5, *du vairþans briggan ïzvis* (“for you to be accounted worthy”); II.2, *du ni sprauto vagjan* (“not to be quickly shaken”); *Skeireins* II.c, *du garehsn daupeinais andniman* (“to receive remission through baptism”).

### §190. II. THE PARTICIPLE

The participle is by nature an adjective. There are two participles in the Gothic verb: the present participle, active, and the past participle, passive. Each has three endings for the three genders and, for the most part, two forms, vocalic and consonantal (§103).

1) All verbs of active inflection form an active participle, including those ending in *-nan* with passive meaning. For the distinction between consonantal and vocalic declension in the masculine singular, see §196. The active participle, properly bearing present meaning, is also used for the past participle: Eph. III.9, *κτίσαντα* (“having created”): *qaskapiandin* (“creating”); 1 Tim. I.12, *ἐνδυναμώσαντι* (“having strengthened”)—*θέμενος* (“having appointed”): [Col. 1059] *ïnsvinþjandin* (“strengthening”)—*gasatjands* (“appointing”); IV.3, *ἐπεγνωκόσι* (“those who have known”): *ufkunnandam* (“to those knowing”); Rom. VII.4, *ἐγερθείς* (“having been raised”): *urreisands* (“rising”); 2 Cor. XII.21, *ἐλθόντα* (“having come”): *qimanda* (“coming”), *προημαρτηκότων* (“of those who had sinned before”): *faurafravaurkjandane* (“of those sinning beforehand”), *μετανοησάντων* (“of those who repented”): *ïdreigondane* (“of those repenting”); John XII.37, *πεποιηκότος* (“having done”): *gataujandin* (“doing”); 1 Thess. IV.13, *κεκοιμημένοι* (“those who have fallen asleep”): *þai anaslepandans* (“those sleeping”), etc. Only in circumlocutions with *vairpan* (“to become”) can a genuine past participle occur, as *usvena vaurþans* (“having become despairing”), Eph. IV.19, for *ἀπηλπικώς* (“having become without hope”).

2) Passive participles have different endings according as they derive from a strong or weak verb (§103). For the syntactical distinction between consonantal and vocalic declension, see §196. The passive participle, properly having past meaning, is sometimes used also for the present: 2 Cor. VII.5, *θλιβόμενοι* (“being afflicted”): *anapragganai* (“afflicted”); 1 Cor. XI.24, *τὸ κλώμενον* (“that which is broken”): *þata gabrukano* (“that which has been broken”); Matt. VI.30, *βαλλόμενοι* (“being cast”): *galagiþ* (“cast”), etc.

3) By its nature, the participle often corresponds to a Greek adjective, and conversely: *fairinonds* (“accusing, slanderous”) for *διάβολος* (“slanderous, devilish”), 2 Tim. III.3; *galaubjands* (“believing”) for *πιστός* (“faithful, believing”), 2 Cor. VI.15; *ungalaubjands* (“unbelieving”) for *ἄπιστος* (“unbelieving”), Mark IX.19; *leitil galaubjands* (“little-believing”) for *ὀλιγόπιστος* (“of little faith”), Matt. VI.30; *ufsliupands* (“having crept in”) for *παρείσακτος* (“secretly introduced”), Gal. II.4; *viljands* (“willing”) for *αὐθαίρετος* (“voluntary”), 2 Cor. VIII.17; *unwapnands* (“unquenchable”) for *ἄσβεστος* (“unquenchable”), Mark IX.43; *airzjands* (“leading astray”) for *πλάνος* (“deceiving”), 2 Cor. VI.8; *ufhausjands* (“obeying”) for *ὑπήκοος* (“obedient”), Phil. II.8; *usþulands* (“enduring”) for *ἀνεξίκακος* (“patient in suffering”), 2 Tim. II.24; *bleiþjands* (“merciful”) for *οἰκτίρμων* (“compassionate”), Luke VI.36, together with *bleiþs* (“merciful”); *unliugands* (“not lying”) for *ἀψευδής* (“truthful”), Tit. I.2; *flautands* (“boasting vainly”) for *κενόδοξος* (“vainglorious”), Gal. V.26; *gamainjands* (“sharing”) for *κοινωνός* (“participant”), 1 Cor. X.18; *unufbrikands* (“not causing offence”) for *ἀπρόσκοπος* (“without offence”), X.32; *sik frijonds* (“self-loving”) for *φίλαυτος* (“lover of self”), 2 Tim. III.2. Further, very many compounds in *φιλ-* (“loving”) are rendered by *frijonds* (“loving”): *sik ungahabands* (“not self-controlled”) for *ἀκρατής* (“without self-control”), 2 Tim. III.3.

The passive participle further stands for verbal adjectives in *-τός*: *andhuliþs* (“uncovered”) for *ἀκατακάλυπτος* (“uncovered”), 1 Cor. XI.8; *ungavagids* (“unmoved”) for *ἀμετακίνητος* (“immovable”), 1 Cor. XV.58; *gavaliþs* (“chosen”) for *ἐκλεκτός* (“chosen”), Mark XIII.20; *ungafairinoþs* (“unaccused”) for *ἀνέγκλητος* (“unaccused”) and *ἀνεπίληπτος* (“irreproachable”), 1 Tim. III.10; V.7; *aliþs* (“fattened”) for *σιτευτός* (“fattened”), Luke XV.23; *unbi-* and *unfairlaistiþs* (“unsearchable”) for *ἀνεξιχνίαστος* (“untraceable”), Rom. XI.33; Eph. III.8; *laisiþs* (“taught”) for *διδακτός* (“taught”), John VI.45; *miþfrahunþans* (“taken captive with”) for *συναιχμάλωτος* (“fellow-captive”), Col. IV.10; *fraqiþans* (“accursed”) for *ἐπικατάρατος* (“under a curse”), John VII.49; *þiuþiþs* (“blessed”) for *εὐλόγητος* (“blessed”), Eph. I.3; *galaþoþs* (“called”) for *κλητός* (“called”), 1 Cor. I.24; *unusspilloþs* (“inexpressible”) for *ἀνεκδιήγητος* (“indescribable”), 2 Cor. IX.15; *niuja satiþs* (“newly planted”) for *νεόφυτος* (“newly planted; novice”), 1 Tim. III.6; *gatulgiþs* (“not to be repented of”) for *ἀμεταμέλητος* (“irrevocable”), 2 Cor. VII.10; *ga-* and *vailagaleikaiþs* (“well-pleasing”) for *εὐάρεστος* (“acceptable”), Rom. XII.1; Col. III.12.

It also stands for adjectives: *unsaltans* (“unsalted”) for *ἄναλος* (“saltless”), Mark IX.50; *usagiþs* (“terrified”) for *ἔκφοβος* (“terrified”), IX.6; *ganaiviþs* (“humbled”) for *ταπεινός* (“humble”), Luke I.52; *digans* (“earthen”) for *ὀστράκινος* (“made of clay”), 2 Tim. II.20; *us synagogein usvaurpans* (“cast out of the synagogue”) for *ἀποσυνάγωγος* (“expelled from the synagogue”), John XII.42; *ustauhans* (“complete”) for *τέλειος* (“perfect”) and *ἄρτιος* (“complete”), Rom. XII.2; 2 Tim. III.17; *gakusans* (“approved”) for *δόκιμος* (“approved”), 1 Cor. IX.27; *ungakusans* and *uskusans* (“unapproved,” “rejected”) for *ἀδόκιμος* (“unapproved”), 2 Cor. XIII.5; Tit. I.16; *unbeistjoþs* (“unleavened”) for *ἄζυμος* (“unleavened”), 1 Cor. V.7; *unqeniþs* (“unmarried”) for *ἄγαμος* (“unmarried”), 1 Cor. VII.8; *gatulgiþs* (“established”) for *ἑδραῖος* (“steadfast”) and *βέβαιος* (“firm”), Col. I.23; 2 Cor. I.6.

Conversely, Gothic adjectives correspond to Greek participles: *hails* (“healthy”) to *ὑγιαίνων* (“being well”), Luke V.31, and *ἰσχύων* (“being strong”), Matt. IX.12; *unhails* (“unwell”) to *ἀσθενῶν* (“being weak”), Luke IX.2, and *κακῶς ἔχων* (“being ill”), V.31; *siuks* (“sick”) to [Col. 1060] *ἀσθενῶν* (“being weak”), Mark VI.56; *unmahteigs* (“weak”) to *ἀσθενῶν*, Rom. XIV.1; *gredags* (“hungry”) to *πεινῶν* (“hungering”), Luke I.53; *qius* (“living”) to *ζῶν* (“living”), Mark XII.27; *qiþuhafta* (“pregnant”) to *ἐκ γαστρὶ ἔχουσα* (“having [a child] in the womb”), Mark XIII.17; *þarbs* (“needy”) to *χρείαν ἔχων* (“having need”), Luke IX.11; *fravaurhts* (“sinful”) to *ἁμαρτάνων* (“sinning”), 1 Tim. V.20; *gabigs* (“rich”) to *πλουτῶν* (“being rich”), Rom. X.12; *anavairþs* (“about to come”) to *μέλλων* (“being about to”), Luke III.7, and *ἐρχόμενος* (“coming”), Mark X.30; *andvairþs* (“present”) to *παρών* (“being present”), 1 Cor. V.3, and *ἐνεστώς* (“being present”), Rom. VIII.38; *anahaims* (“at home”) to *ἐνδημῶν* (“being at home”), 2 Cor. V.9; *afhaims* (“away from home”) to *ἐκδημῶν* (“being away from home”), 2 Cor. V.6; *unvita* (“mad”) to *παραφρονῶν* (“being out of one’s mind”), 2 Cor. XI.23; *samafraþjis* (“of one mind”) to *τὸ ἕν φρονῶν* (“thinking the one thing”), Phil. II.2; *auhuma* (“higher”) to *ὑπερέχων* (“surpassing”), II.3; *vans* (“lacking”) to *λείπων* (“lacking”), Tit. I.5; *usvena* (“without hope”) to *ἀπελπίζων* (“despairing”), Luke VI.35; *mahteigs* (“able”) to *δυνάμενος* (“being able”), Eph. III.20; *vaurstveigs* (“effective”) to *ἐνεργούμενος* (“working”), 2 Cor. I.6; *ïnkilþo* (“with child”) to *συνειληφυῖα* (“having conceived”), Luke I.36; *framaldrs* (“advanced in years”) to *προβεβηκώς* (“having advanced”), Luke I.7; *naus* (“dead”) to *τεθνηκώς* (“having died”), Luke VII.12; *dauþs* (“dead”) to *τεθνηκώς*, John XI.44; *riurs* (“perishing”) to *φθειρόμενος* (“being corrupted”), IV.22; *gaurs* (“grieved”) to *συλλυπούμενος* (“grieving with”), Mark III.5; *uslukns* (“opened”) to *σχιζόμενος* (“being split open”), Mark I.10; *vods* (“demon-possessed”) to *δαιμονιζόμενος* (“being demonized”), V.15; *ushaista* (“lacking”) to *ὑστερηθείς* (“having suffered want”), 2 Cor. XI.8; *þvairhs* (“angry”) to *ὀργισθείς* (“having become angry”), Luke XIV.22; and especially to the perfect: *aïnakls* (“solitary”) to *μεμονωμένος* (“having been left alone”), 1 Tim. V.5; *anstai audahafts* (“endowed with grace”) to *κεχαριτωμένος* (“having been favoured with grace”), Luke I.28; *valis* (“chosen”) and *liubs* (“beloved”) to *ἠγαπημένος* (“having been loved”), Col. III.12; Rom. IX.25; *daubs* (“hardened”) to *πεπωρωμένος* (“having been hardened”), Mark VIII.17; *þaursus* (“withered”) to *ἐξηραμμένος* (“having been dried up”), Mark XI.20; *gaskohs* (“shod”) to *ὑποδεδεμένος* (“having been shod”), Mark VI.9; *usliþa* (“paralysed”) to *παραλελυμένος* (“having been paralysed”), Luke V.18; *saþs* (“sated; adorned”) to *ἐκπεπλησμένος* (“having been filled”) and *κεκοσμημένος* (“having been adorned”), Luke VI.25; 1 Cor. IV.8; *gamaids* (“broken”) to *τεθραυσμένος* (“having been broken”), Luke IV.19; *banjo fulls* (“full of sores”) to *ἡλκωμένος* (“having been ulcerated”), XVI.20; *ufarfulls* (“pressed down”) to *πεπιεσμένος* (“having been pressed”), VI.38; *garaids* (“arranged”) to *διατεταγμένος* (“having been appointed”), III.13; *ïnvinds* (“perverted”) to *διεστραμμένος* (“having been perverted”), IX.41; *gafulgins* (“hidden”) to *κεκρυμμένος* (“having been hidden”), Luke XVIII.34; *veihs* (“sanctified”) to *ἡγιασμένος* (“having been sanctified”), John XVII.19; *framaþeis* (“alienated”) to *ἀπηλλοτριωμένος* (“having been alienated”), Eph. II.12; *riqizeins* (“darkened”) to *ἐσκοτισμένος* (“having been darkened”), IV.18; *funisks* (“fiery”) to *πεπυρωμένος* (“having been set on fire”), VI.16.

4) That participles are adjectival in nature is further proved by the fact that they can be compounded with the prefix *un-*, although verbs do not admit this composition: *unagands, unbairands, unhabands, unkunnands, unliugands, unrodjands, unbaurans, unbeistjoþs, undivans, unqeniþs, unþvahans, unliugaiþs*, etc.; see Glossary V, *Un-*.

5) As adjectives, participles are also used substantively, especially with the article; see §195. Thus they are sometimes used in place of Greek substantives, and conversely; see §193.2, to which the substantive forms in *-nds* should likewise be referred; see §193, note.

b) On the participle used temporally, conjunctively, causally, etc., and also on its paraphrase by *saei* and a finite verb, see the discussion of the compound sentence.

> **Note.**—The passive participles of certain intransitive verbs have an active meaning: Mark 1:33 *garunnans*, “having assembled”; 9:33 *qumans*, “coming”; John 6:51; 3:31; Mark 7:30 *usgaggans*, “going out”; John 9:21 *usvahsans*, “grown up”; 2 Timothy 2:8 *urrisans*, “rising”; 1 Timothy 4:7 *usalþans*, “old.” In distinguishing them, the scribe has often erroneously copied *-ans* for *-ands*, as in 1 Timothy 1:3 *galeiþans* for *galeiþands*; see §116, note 2. Rarely, however, the active and passive participles have the same meaning, as in Titus 1:6, 7 *ungafairinands* [Col. 1061] and *ungafairinoþs*, both used for Greek *anénklētos*, “irreproachable.”  
>
> The case is otherwise at Matthew 26:75, where the Gothic renders Greek “Peter remembered the word of Jesus, who had said to him” (*ἐμνήσθη ὁ Πέτρος τοῦ ῥήματος Ἰησοῦ εἰρηκότος αὐτῷ*) by *gamunda paitrus vaurdis ïesuis qiþanis du sis*. It refers *qiþanis* to *vaurdis* [Col. 1062] (“the word of Jesus, which was spoken to him”), whereas it ought to have referred it to *ïesuis* (“who had said to him”). Still less suitably, in Mark 15:28, Greek “the Scripture saying” (*ἐπληρώθη ἡ γραφὴ ἡ λέγουσα*)—with an active participle—has in the translation been changed in the same manner into a passive: *usfullnoda þata gamelido þata qiþano*.

## II. Noun

[Col. 1061]

## I. Substantive

### §191. A. Common Noun. I. Gender

1) In the Gothic language the neuter gender is also a natural gender, since it excludes neither masculine nor feminine (as its name indicates), but embraces and unites both. The neuter occurs not only as the proper gender of certain substantives, listed below under a) and aa), but also in certain constructions: that is, when a pronoun or numeral serves as subject and refers jointly to a masculine and a feminine, it is put in the neuter; see §209.3. The masculine gender, however, is primary and belongs to agents, whereas the feminine is especially reserved for derived words and for words capable of gender variation.

a) Natural gender.

aa) The neuter, in the sense stated above—that is, as containing masculine and feminine together—is the gender of the name of God, *guþ*. Although it may have been used as masculine at a later period under the influence of Christian religion, it is at least originally neuter. Nor should attention be paid to the special word *gud*, reserved for false gods because of the plural *guda* in John 10:34–35, since Galatians 4:8 also has *guþa*. It signifies divinity—not merely its idea or conception, but divinity presented as both god and goddess; this confirms the polytheism of the Goths. In the same manner they conceived *skohsl*, “a demon,” as of either gender.

Furthermore, *barn*, “child/son” (*téknon*), and the diminutive *barnilo*, “little child” (*tekníon, teknídion*); *fadrein*, “parents” (father and mother); *gaman*, “companion”; and *þevis*, “servant” (male or female servant), are neuter. By contrast, *frasts*, “boy,” is masculine, although in 2 Corinthians 6:13 it should not be referred exclusively to males; and *manna*, “human being,” is masculine because a male is chiefly envisaged.

bb) The following occur as masculines with corresponding feminines: *vair*, rarely *guma*, “man”—*qino*, “woman”; *juggalauþs*, “young man”—*magaþs*, “virgin”; *magus*, “boy”—*mavi*, “girl”; *magula*, “little boy”—*mavilo*, “little girl”; *aba*, “man”—*qens*, “woman”; *atta*, and (only at the beginning of Galatians 4:6) *fadar*, “father”—*aiþei*, “mother”; *sunus*, “son”—*dauhtar*, “daughter”; *broþar*, “brother”—*svistar*, “sister”; *megs*, “son-in-law”—*bruþs*, “daughter-in-law”; *svaihra*, “father-in-law”—*svaihro*, “mother-in-law”; *bruþfaþs*, “bridegroom”; *niþjis*, “male relative” (*syngenēs*)—*niþjo*, “female relative.” The feminine *avo*, “grandmother,” presupposes a masculine *ava*, “grandfather”; likewise, from *viduvo*, “widow,” one must grammatically infer *viduva*, “widower.”

cc) Without corresponding feminines, the following names of persons occur as masculines—those engaged in an office, service, occupation, and so forth: *reiks*, ruler; *kindins*, prefect of a city; *þiudans*, king; *frauja*, lord; [Col. 1062] *fauramaþleis*, chief; *andbahts*, minister; *skalks*, slave; *asneis*, hired laborer; *hairdeis*, shepherd; *aurtja*, gardener; *kasja*, potter; *gadrauhts*, soldier; *hundafaþs* and *þusundifaþs*, centurion; and so forth; *veiha*, presbyter; *staua*, judge; *sakjis*, combatant; *andastaþjis*, adversary; *veitvods*, witness; *bokareis*, scribe; *airus*, messenger; *vairdus*, merchant; *gasts*, guest; *gadauka*, resident alien; *gahlaiba*, companion or associate; *gadaila*, participant; *gasinþa*, travelling companion; *galaista*, guide; *liuta*, hypocrite; *þiubs* and *hliftus*, robber; *hors*, adulterer, with the corresponding feminine *kalkjo*, adulteress; *naus*, murderer; *liuþareis*, singer; *vullareis*, keeper; *laisareis*, teacher; and the other words in *-eis*; see §67.

dd) In addition to the substantives listed under bb), the following still occur as variable in gender: *þius*, “male slave,” with corresponding feminine *þivi*, “female slave, maidservant”; *dauravards*, “doorkeeper,” with feminine *dauravarda* and *dauravardo*, “female doorkeeper”; *vaurstva* and *gavaurstva*, “worker, fellow-worker”—the feminine *vaurstvo*, “female worker,” must be inferred from *unvaurstvo* in 1 Timothy 5:13; *arbja*, “male heir”—*arbjo*, “female heir”; *garazna*, “male neighbour”—*garazno*, “female neighbour”; *praufetus*, “prophet”—*praufeteis*, “prophetess.” In *unhulþa*, “wicked man”—*unhulþo*, “wicked woman,” the feminine appears to have existed originally; see the glossary under that word.

The neuter *gajuko*, “companion,” in Philippians 4:7, alongside masculine *gajuka*, and *gaskalki*, “fellow-servant,” in Colossians 1:7; 4:7, alongside *skalks*, seem to carry a diminutive force, but one of friendship and affection after Greek and Latin usage. Likewise, neuter *þevis* in Colossians 3:22; 4:1, alongside *þius*. Conversely, neuter *gumein*, from adjective *gumeins*, in 2 Timothy 3:6, is also diminutive, but in a bad sense. The same applies to *qinein* in Mark 10:6: it is used for male and female, though not in an unfavourable sense; but *fadrein* can scarcely be referred to this category, much less *gaitein* in Luke 15:29, since these cannot be applied to an animal.

ee) Abstract or collective words, such as “people,” “army,” “church,” and the like, are all feminine: *þiuda*, people; *hansa*, crowd; *filusna* and *managei*, multitude; *ïumjo*, baggage; *gamainþs*, church; *vriþus* and *haird*, army. But *hiuhma*, “multitude,” is masculine, while *tevi*, “crowd,” and *aveþi*, “naval force,” are neuter.

ff) Among names of animals, the generic neuters are *dius* and the obscure *biari*, “animal,” as well as *faihu*, “livestock”; among specific terms, only *lamb*, “lamb,” and *svein*, “pig.” Masculine generic terms are *fugls*, bird; *fisks*, fish; *vaurms*, worm; and specific terms are *stiur*, boar; *auhsus* and *auhsa*, ox; *viþrus*, he-goat; *gaits*, male goat; *fula*, foal; *asilus*, ass; *hunds*, dog; *vulfs*, wolf; *ulbandus*, elephant (camel); *ahaks*, dove; *ara*, eagle; *hana*, cock; *sparva*, sparrow; *nadrs*, viper; and perhaps *maþa*, worm. Feminines are *fauho*, fox; *kalbo*, heifer; *gaitei*, she-goat; *hraivadubo*, turtledove; *þramstei*, lizard; and *malo*, moth.

[Col. 1063]

b) Grammatical gender. Here we must say how the gender of inanimate objects was determined. The reason usually escapes us, since the period in which it was established is too remote. Only some objects still display within themselves the origin of their gender—namely, mythology. Therefore, where evidence from the language itself is lacking or insufficiently known, we shall have recourse to the religions and myths of northern peoples in explaining their gender.

aa) In nearly the same way is explained the gender of the names denoting the sun and moon. Yet there is this striking difference between the classical and Germanic peoples: the former made the sun masculine and the moon feminine, whereas the latter followed the reverse course. Thus the Goths made *sunno*, “sun,” feminine and *mena*, “moon,” masculine, because in the mythology of those peoples the moon, Mani, is the son of Mundilfaeri, while the sun, Sol, is his daughter and Glenr’s bride.

The Goth has, indeed, also a masculine form *sunna* and a neuter *sauïl* for “sun”; but besides the fact that feminine *sunno* is more common (Matthew 5:45; Luke 4:40; Ephesians 4:26; Nehemiah 7:3), the other two forms occur only in Mark (*sunnin urrinnandin*, 4:6; 16:2; *gasaggq sauïl*, 1:32; *sauïl riqizeiþ*, 13:24), and Greek and Latin masculine usage probably influenced them. As to the differing roots, *sunno* may be called the older and *sauïl* the newer name, if one credits the Edda (*Alvíssmál* 16.1–2): *sol heiter med mönnum, en sunna med goþom*, “It is called *Sol* among men, but *Sunna* among gods.” Moreover, the Greeks too held that names for objects current among the gods were older than those used among men; see Goettling on Hesiod, *Theogony* 831.

In the old northern language *Sol* is likewise feminine; but Gothic *sauïl*, a neuter form, may stand between *sunno* and *sunna* as a natural neuter—that is, as embracing masculine and feminine; see above, 1). *Tuggl*, “heavenly body,” neuter, and *stairno*, “star,” feminine, are likewise not grounded in natural gender.

bb) Mythology also explains feminine *nahts*, “night,” and masculine *dags*, “day,” since in northern myths Nott is the daughter of Nörvi and bore a son, Dagr, by Dellingr. But *andanahti*, “evening,” just as the other temporal designations *mel* and *þeihs*, “time,” and *jer* and *ataþni*, “year,” is neuter, as an abstract idea. Whether *aþns* is masculine or *aþn* neuter is uncertain; nor do feminine *uhtvo*, “morning,” feminine *viko*, “week,” masculine *aivs*, and feminine *ajukduþs* (*aiōn*, “age”) have anything by which they may be explained.

Nott had another daughter by Anar, namely Jördh, Odin’s bride; hence feminine *airþa*, “earth.” But *himins*, “heaven,” is masculine, for what mythological reason I do not know. Hel was the daughter of Loki; hence feminine *halja*, “hell.” Her brothers—fire, air, and sea—are masculine in Gothic, or at least *luftus*, “air,” and *saivs*, “sea” (for *marei*, “sea,” is feminine). Masculine fire appears in *auhns*, “furnace,” which, when compared with Agni, the Indian god of fire, seems to have retained traces of him. Yet among these elements the neuters are [Col. 1064] *fon*, “fire,” and *vato*, “water.”

The following are explained from mythology as masculine: *vintrus*, “winter”; *vinds*, “wind” (but *vis*, “whirlwind,” is neuter); and probably also *menoþs*, “month,” and *maurgins*, “morning.” Further, *snaivs*, “snow” (*rign*, “rain,” however, is neuter); also *vegs*, “wave”; *flodus*, “river” (but *awa* is feminine); and *brunna*, “spring.” The difficult word *milhma*, “cloud,” occurring only in Gothic, is explained in this way. No trace has, indeed, survived of a god of thunder and lightning; at least, its phenomena are rendered in Gothic as *lauhmuni*, “lightning,” and *þeiwo*, “thunder,” both feminine.

cc) With plant names there is now no relation to persons; perhaps only their greenness (masculine) or dryness (neuter) is considered. At any rate, *bagms*, “tree,” is masculine, as are *asts*, “branch”; *valus* and *vandus*, “rod”; *tains*, “stalk”; *laufs*, “leaf”; *bloma*, “flower”; and *þaurnus*, “thorn-bush.” Only *waurts*, “root,” is feminine. Conversely, the following are neuter: *triu*, which is not merely the generic name of all larger trees, but corresponds exactly to Greek *dóry*, and, like German *Stock* (thus German *Weinstock*, Gothic *veinatriu*), ordinarily denotes dry timber (*xýlon*, Mark 16:42, 48); *fraiv*, “seed”; *basi*, “berry”; *akran*, “fruit” (masculine *smakka*, “fig,” is a foreign word); *ahs*, “ear of grain”; *kaurn*, “grain” and the other cereals, except masculine *vaiteis*, “wheat”; *kaurno*, “grain of wheat”; *raus*, “reed”; *gras*, “grass” in general; *legumen*; and *havi*, “hay.” But *ahana*, “chaff,” is feminine. Of the names of particular plants, *vigadeino*, “thistle,” and *aiwatundi*, “thorns,” are feminine; *sinaps*, “mustard,” and *svamms*, “mushroom,” masculine.

dd) Finally, in the inorganic realm all relation to persons disappears, and gender can no longer be determined from meaning. Only metals are neuter in gender: *gulþ*, gold; *silubr*, silver; *eisarn*, iron; *aiz*, bronze. Of other materials, *salt*, salt, is neuter; *stains*, stone; *hallus*, rock; *malma*, sand; *stubjus*, ashes; and *svibls*, sulphur, are masculine; *þaho*, clay, and *mulda*, ashes, feminine.

As to geographical names, *land*, “land,” and *gavi*, “district,” are neuter; *fera*, “place,” and *marka*, “boundary,” feminine; *fairguni*, “mountain,” is neuter, *hlains*, “hill,” masculine. Whether “valley” is *dal* (neuter) or *dals* (masculine) is uncertain; *driuso*, “slope,” and *ïddaljo*, “descent,” are feminine. *Vigs*, “way,” is masculine; but it is uncertain whether “journey” is *gaggs* (masculine) or *gagg* (neuter). *Staiga*, “step,” is feminine; “height” is *filegri* (neuter) or *hulundi* (feminine). The city, *baurgs*, and village or locality, *haims*, are feminine, but *veihs* is neuter.

> **Note.**—But the gender of the other classes of objects is much more difficult to determine. Thus:
>
> 1) Of the parts of the animal body in general: body, *leik*, and blood, *bloþ*, are neuter; flesh, *mammo* (*sárx*), feminine, and *mimz* (*kréas*, edible flesh, etc.), neuter; fat, *smairþr*, neuter; wool, *vulla*, feminine; hair, *tagl*, and *skuft* (a head of hair), neuter; limb, *liþus*, masculine; head, *haubiþ*, neuter; skull, *wairnei*, feminine; face, *ludja*—that is, the part of the head bare of hair; see Matthew 6:17—feminine; *vlits* and *andavleizns*, “face,” masculine. [Col. 1065] These three words signify “face” insofar as they are distinguished from one another. The abstract terms *andvairþi* and *andaugi*, “face, front part as opposed to the rear,” are neuter.
>
> Eye, *augo*, together with the tears flowing from it, *tagr*, and the eyelashes or brows guarding it, *braw*, is neuter (unless at 1 Corinthians 15:52 *brawai* should be read instead of *brawa*, and the word itself is *brawa*, feminine). So too ear, *auso*, is neuter. Cheek, *kinnus*, is feminine; mouth, *munþs*, masculine; the mouth of animals is probably called *mul* and is neuter (compare 1 Corinthians 9:9 *faurmuljan auhsau*, “to muzzle an ox”). Lip, *vairilo*, and tongue, *tuggo*, are feminine; tooth, *tunþus*; neck, *hals*; nape, *halsagga*; shoulder, *amsa* (or *ahsa*); and arm, *arms*, masculine. Hand, *handus*, however, is feminine; but a dead hand, *lofa*, and finger, *figgrs*, are again masculine. Bosom, *barms*, is masculine, but breast, *brusts*, feminine; it also translates “inward parts,” although there is additionally a neuter plural noun, *hairþra*. Heart, *hairts*, is neuter; thigh, *hups*, masculine; stomach (*koilía, stómakhos*), *qiþus*, masculine, but belly (*koilía, gastḗr*), *vamba*, feminine; knee, *kniu*, neuter; foot, *fotus*, masculine; heel, *fairzna*, feminine.
>
> 2) Of human products:
>
> a) Dwelling and what pertains to it. A house, and what is within it, is in Gothic *gards*, masculine (hence this word is also used of a household); *hus*, “dwelling,” is neuter; as is *razn*, which appears to denote a house originally consisting only of a superimposed roof or made of wooden construction (thus Anglo-Saxon *raesen* is a board or boarded roof), and is therefore used of a built house. A smaller house or hut is *hleiþra*, feminine. Finally, a house insofar as it is lodging is *saliþvos*, feminine plural. Temple, *alhs*, is masculine, but *gudhus* neuter.
>
> Wall, *vaddjus*, is feminine, as are foundation and middle wall, *grundu* and *miþgardavaddjus*; corner-stone, *vaihstastains*, masculine; gable or pinnacle, *gibla*, masculine; roof, *hrot*, neuter; that with which it is covered—tile or brick—*skalja*, feminine; beam, *ans*, masculine; column, *sauls*, likewise feminine; stake, *gairu*, neuter (?); and *hnuto*, feminine. Door, *haurds*, is feminine, and *daur*, neuter; the feminine plural *daurons* alone signifies double doors. Window is *augadauro*, neuter. Hall, *rohsns*; chamber, *ubizva*; and bedroom, *heþjo*, are feminine; upper room (*anṓgeon*) or tower (*pýrgos*), *kelikn*, is neuter.
>
> Secondary buildings: barn, *bansts*, masculine; threshing-floor, *gaþrask*, neuter; stable, *garda*, masculine, and specifically sheepfold, *avistr*, neuter; millstone, *qairnus*, masculine. Greek *agrós* is translated variously in Gothic: *haiþi*, “open country, field,” feminine, in contrast to town; *haimoþli*, neuter, as an object of possession; *akrs*, masculine, with reference to its purpose; *atisks*, masculine or *atisk*, neuter, especially when sown. Pasture, *vinja*, is feminine; garden, *vagg*, neuter, or *vaggs*, masculine; olive-grove, *aurtigards*, and vineyard, *veinagards*, masculine; hedge, *faþa*; ditch, *graba* and *groba*, feminine. Outside the house, street is *fauradauri*, neuter, which also denotes a road; otherwise *gaggs*, masculine (? *gagg*, neuter), *plapja* and *gatvo*, feminine. Market-place, *maþls*, is masculine. Cemetery, *hlaivasnos*, is feminine plural; tomb, *aurahi*, feminine, or *hlaiv*, neuter.
>
> b) Clothing (*gavaseins* or *vastjos*, both feminine, though the latter plural) is made from linen, *lein*, neuter. Cloth is called *fana*, masculine, or *plats*, neuter. The generic term for clothing was feminine *vasti*, embracing three kinds: the toga (French *le vêtement de dessous*, “the undergarment”), *paida*, feminine, of foreign origin; tunic (French *le vêtement de dessus*, “the outer garment”), *snaga*, masculine; and cloak, *hakuls*, masculine. The toga was held by a belt, *gairda*, feminine; the hem of the toga was *skauts*, masculine. Sandals, plural feminine *suljos*, or shoes, *skoh* or *gaskoh*, neuter (? *skohs*, masculine), were fitted to the feet and fastened with shoe-straps, *skaudaraip*, neuter. Among women’s ornaments was the veil, *hulistr*, neuter.
>
> c) Among household furnishings and implements are: bed, *ligrs*, masculine, *badi*, neuter; cushion, *vaggari*, neuter; seat, *sitls*, and chair, *stols*, masculine; table, *biuds*, masculine; footstool, *fotubaurd*, neuter; curtain, *faurhah*, neuter; mirror, *skuggva*, masculine; lamp, *lukarn*, neuter; lampstand, *lukarnastaþa*, masculine; torch, *hais*, neuter. A vessel in general, especially an earthenware one, is *kas*, neuter; urn, *aurkeis*; cup, *stikls*; and kettle, *katils*, masculine. Chest, *arka*, is feminine; skin-bag, *balgs*, and sack, *sakkus*, masculine, as is the foreign word *spyreida*, “basket”; whereas native *snorjo*, a basket made of bark or cords, and *tainjo*, a basket woven from twigs, are feminine. So likewise noose, *hlamma* and *vruggo*; bond, *bandi*; and fetter, *kunaveda*. But scourge, *gazds*, and cross, *galga*, are masculine. Also feminine are needle, *neþla*; axe, *aqizi*; sickle, *gilþa*; and winnowing fan, *vinþiskauro*; but plough, *hoha*, is masculine, and net, *nati*, neuter. Ship, *skip*, is likewise neuter, but its stern, *nota*, is masculine.
>
> d) Arms (*sarva* and *vepna*, both neuter plural) are: helmet, *hilms*; shield, *skildus*; and sword, *hairus*, masculine. Probably *mekeis* (masculine) should also be read instead of *meki* (neuter), since it is masculine in the neighbouring languages. Corselet, *brunjo*, and missile, *arwazna*, are feminine; a spear, originating from an iron-shod pole, is called *triu*; see Mark 14:43.
>
> e) Coins, measures, and so forth: the silver coin in general, and specifically the *mna*, is *skatts*, masculine. Of smaller coins, only *skilliggs* is exclusively Gothic; the others—*drakma*, drachma; *kintus*, denarius; and *assarjus*, as—are of foreign origin and all masculine. *Mela*, “measure,” is likewise masculine; but *aleina*, “cubit,” feminine, and *pund*, “pound,” neuter.
>
> f) Food, *mats*, is masculine, and drink, *dragk*, neuter. Bread, *hlaifs*, is masculine; dough, *daigs*, likewise masculine, but leaven, *beist*, neuter. For flesh see above, 1). Oil, *alev*; honey, *miliþ*; and wine, *vein*, are neuter; strong drink, *leiþus*, and vinegar, *akeits*, masculine; milk, *miluks*, feminine.

3) Very many words which signify an art, office, business, or condition also designate the persons engaged in that art, office, and so forth; for example: *airus*, “embassy” and “ambassador”; *gaman*, “fellowship” and “companion”; *fidurragineis*, “tetrarchy” and “tetrarch” (compare Luke 3:1). Luke 9:52: *ïesus insandida airuns faura sis*, “Jesus sent messengers before himself,” for Greek *angéloi*, “messengers”; 14:32: *ïnsandjands airu bidjiþ gavairþjis*, “sending an embassy, he seeks terms,” for Greek *presbeían*, “an embassy”; 2 Corinthians 13:13: *gaman ahmins veihis miþ ïzvis*, “the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you,” for *koinōnía*, “fellowship”; Philemon 17: *jabai mik habais du gamana andnim þana sve mik*, “if you hold me as a partner, receive him as me,” for *koinonón*, “partner”; Luke 3:1: *raginondin puntiau peilatau iudaia jah fidurraginja þis galeilaias herodeis filippauzuh þan fidurraginja þis ïturaias*, “while Pontius Pilate governed Judea, and Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, and Philip was tetrarch of Iturea”; Romans 11:34: *was ïmma ragineis vas?*, “who has been his counsellor?” for *sýmboulos*, “counsellor.”

For other meanings, however, another form is given: *fauramaþleis* (*árchōn*, ruler) and *fauramaþli* (*hēgemonía*, rule); *fauragaggja* (*oikonómos*, steward) and *fauragaggi* (*oikonomía*, stewardship); *praizbytaireis* (*presbýteros*, elder) and *praisbytairei*, “presbyterate.”

### §192. II. On Number

1) It should be noted that the following are pluralia tantum: *berusjos*, elders; *broþrahans*, brothers (*adelphoí*); *brusts*, breast, inward parts; *hairþra*, inward parts; *bokos*, letters, epistle; *sarva* and *vepna*, arms; *vegos*, waves; *daurons* (double doors), door, doors; *saliþvos*, lodging; *hlaivasnos*, cemetery; *veinatriva*, vineyard; *laubos*, foliage. Conversely, the Goth renders Greek concrete plurals by abstract singulars, as *skufts*, “head of hair,” for *tríkhes*, “hairs.”

Expressions which Greek seeks to put only in the plural, Gothic converts to the singular without any occasion for doing so. Thus Matthew 8:11, Greek “many will come from east and west” (*polloì apò anatolôn kaì dysmôn*), that is, from eastern and western regions, is rendered: *managai fram urrunsa jah saggqa qimand*, “many shall come from east and west.” At John 10:22 *ïnniujiþa*, “the feast of renewal/restoration,” stands for Greek *tà enkaínia*, “the Dedication”; and in Mark 6:21 *mel gabaurþais*, “the day of birth,” for *tà genésia*, “birthday festivities.” Greek *tà euṓnyma* and *tà dexiá*—all that is on the left and right, that is, the left and right side—are translated only in the singular at Mark 10:37 and elsewhere: “the left” and “the right,” with *fera*, “side,” also added.

John 13:12, Greek “he took his garments” (*élabe tà himátia autoû*), is rendered in Gothic *nam vastjos seinos*, although *vastja seina* would have sufficed; but in that case *vastjos* means “clothing” (*himatismós, éndyma*; Luke 7:25; 1 Timothy 2:9; Matthew 6:25, 28). Greek words occurring both in singular and plural, *kólpos* and *kólpoi*, “bosom,” and *ouranós* and *ouranoí*, “heaven,” are likewise rendered by differing numbers in Gothic: *barms* (Luke 16:22) and *barmeis* (v. 23); *himins* (Matthew 5:16) and *himinos* (v. 18, etc.). Many other words occur more frequently in the plural, though they are not pluralia tantum; for example, *aviliuda*, “thanks, thanksgivings,” for Greek *eucharistías*; see 1 Timothy 4:3.

2) Words of abstract meaning can also be put in the plural: Luke 1:6 *garaihteins*, properly “righteousnesses,” here legal ordinances (*dikaiṓmata*); especially in Second Corinthians: 1:3 *bleiþeins*, “mercies” (*oiktirmoí*); 1:10 *dauþjus*, “deaths,” and 11:23 *dauþineis*, “dangers of death” (*thánatoi*); 5:11 *miþvisseins*, “consciences” (*syneidḗseis*); 7:5 *agisa*, “fears” (*phóboi*); 8:14 *þarbos*, “deficiencies”—not a concrete word, but Greek abstract plural *hystérēma*; 11:27 *lausqiþreins*, “fastings,” that is, times during which one must fast (*nēsteîai*). Likewise, 1 Corinthians 7:19 *fastubnja anabusne*, “observance of commandments” (*tḗrēsis entolôn*), must be taken as a plural [Col. 1068]; see §70, since formation in *-bnja* is improbable; §145 cc) γ).

From the Gothic construction it is explained if 2 Corinthians 1:3 reads *guþ allaizo gaþlaihte*, “God of all consolations,” that is, “of every consolation” (*theòs pásēs paraklḗseōs*); 4:2 *ïn allaim miþvisseim*, “to every conscience” (*pròs pâsan syneídēsin*); 6:14 *wo gamainduþe*, “what fellowships?”—that is, “what fellowship?” (*tís koinōnía*); see below §§205 and 215, note 1. At Matthew 8:14, to be sure, *lag ïn heitom*, “she lay in fevers,” stands; but singular *ïn heiton* should probably be read instead, since not only the following *aflailot ïza so heito*, “the fever left her,” agrees with it, but also the parallel Mark 1:29, where *lag ïn brinnon*, “she lay in a fever,” occurs.

3) When a concrete expression is used instead of an abstract one, the former takes plural form. Ulfilas renders *synodía*, “journeying company,” in Luke 2:44 by *gasinþans*, “travelling companions, travellers”; *oîkos*, “household,” in 1 Corinthians 1:16 by *gadaukans*, “resident members”; *trápeza*, “money-changers’ table,” in Luke 19:23 by *skattjans*, “money-changers”; *mákellon*, “meat market,” in 1 Corinthians 10:25 by *skiljans*, “butchers”; *akrobystía*, “uncircumcision,” in Ephesians 2:11 by *unbimaitanai*, “the uncircumcised.” Hence also participles and adjectives: *tò apolōlós*, “that which is lost,” Luke 19:10, by *þai fralusanans*, “the lost”; *tò ídion*, “one’s own,” John 15:19, by *svesai*, “one’s own people.” Likewise John 6:37, *pân hó*, “everything which,” by *all þatei*; indeed, even Greek *presbýteroi*, “elders,” in 1 Timothy 5:19 and Titus 1:5 by *praizbytairei*, “presbyterate.”

### §193

Greek and Gothic often correspond to one another in the following ways:

1) Infinitives and substantives: *siuns*, “sight,” for *tò blépein*, “seeing”; *mats*, “food,” Luke 8:55, for *phageîn*, “eating”; *anaqal*, “quietness,” 1 Thessalonians 4:11, for *hēsycházein*, “to be quiet”; *liugos*, “marriage,” 1 Timothy 4:3, for *gameîn*, “to marry.” Conversely: *afslauþnan*, “to be astonished,” Luke 4:36, for *thámbos*, “astonishment”; *guþ blotan*, “to worship God,” 1 Timothy 2:10, for *theosébeia*, “godliness”; *lausjan*, “to release,” 1 Corinthians 7:27, for *lýsis*, “release”; *du fiskon*, “for fishing,” Luke 5:4, for *eis ágran*, “for a catch”; *viþragamotjan*, “to oppose,” John 12:13; and *du gamotjan*, “for meeting,” 1 Thessalonians 4:17, for *eis hypántēsin*, “for meeting”; *fastan jah bidjan*, “to fast and pray,” 1 Corinthians 7:5, for *nēsteía kaì proseukhḗ*, “fasting and prayer.”

2) Participles and substantives: Luke 2:27 *biuhti*, “custom,” for *tò eithisménon*, “what is customary” (unless the Goth here read *tò éthos* with D, as in 1:9; 2:42); 4:16 *tò eiōthós*, “what was customary”; 4:5 *midjungards*, “the inhabited world,” for *hē oikouménē*; 8:3 *aigin*, “possessions,” for *tà hypárkhonta*; 14:33; 16:1; 19:8; *aihts*, “property,” for *tà hypárkhonta*, 1 Corinthians 13:3; Philippians 3:8 *ufarassus*, “superiority,” for *tò hypérékhon*, “what surpasses”; Matthew 8:16 *daimonareis*, “demoniac,” for *daimonizómenos, daimonistheís*, Luke 8:36, etc.; 2 Esdras 41 *liuþareis*, “singer,” for *ho áidōn*, “the singer”; Luke 20:17 *timrjans*, “builders,” for *hoi oikodomoûntes*, “those building,” etc.

Likewise, Luke 1:27; 2:5, Greek “a virgin betrothed” (*parthénos memnēsteuménē*) is rendered *magaþ ïn fragiftim*, “a virgin in betrothal.” Luke 3:23, Greek “Jesus was about thirty years old when beginning” (*ēn Iēsoûs hōseì etôn triákonta archómenos*) is rendered *vas ïesus sve jere þrigetigive uf gakunþai*, “Jesus was about thirty years old at his manifestation”—that is, as a teacher, as Euthymius likewise explains: “when beginning his manifestation to the people, that is, his teaching” (*ἀρχόμενος τῆς εἰς τὸν λαὸν ἀναδείξεως αὐτοῦ ἤτοι τῆς διδασκαλίας*).

Conversely: *usguldan*, “repaid,” Luke 14:12, for *antapódoma*, “repayment”; *galeikaiþ*, “that which gives pleasure,” Luke 10:21, for *eudokía*, “pleasure” [Col. 1069]. Hence Galatians 2:15, Greek “we Jews by nature” (*hēmeîs phýsei Ioudaîoi*) is rendered *veis ïudaieis visandans*, “we who are Jews”; Romans 11:24 *parà phýsin*, “contrary to nature,” by *aljakuns visands*, “being of another kind”; 1 Corinthians 7:6 *toûto légō katà syngnṓmēn*, “I say this by concession,” by *þata giþa gakunnands*, “I say this conceding”; 16:7 *en paródō ideîn*, “to see in passing,” by *þairhleiþands saiwan*, “to see while passing”; 1 Timothy 3:4 “to have children in submission” (*tékna ékhein en hypotagêi*) by *barna haban ufhausjandona*, “to have obedient children”; 2 Thessalonians 3:8 “in labor and toil” (*en kópōi kaì mókhthōi*) by *vinnands arbaidai*, “working with toil.”

> **Note.**—Along with the substantives in *-nds* treated in §85, which are properly participles but have their own declension, present participles too are used as substantives. But then one can distinguish whether they are properly substantives or participles only when they do not occur either in the nominative singular or in the dative plural: 2 Corinthians 9:7 *hlasana giband*, “a cheerful giver” (*dótēs*), *frijoþ guþ*, “God loves”; Luke 5:5 *qaþ du ïmma: talzjand*, “he said to him: Master” (*epistáta*); Luke 1:47 *svegneid ahma meins guþa nasjand meinamma*, “my spirit rejoiced in God my Saviour” (*sōtêri*); Titus 1:3 *bi anabusnai nasjandis unsaris*, “according to the command of our Saviour”; Luke 1:58 *hausidedun bisitands*, “the neighbours heard” (*períoikoi*); 4:14 *gavi bisitande*, “the surrounding district” (*hē períkhōros*); 7:17 *usïddja þata vaurd and alla ïudaia jah and allans bisitands*, “this report went out into all Judea and throughout all the surrounding region” (*perikhṓrous*).
>
> So too *fijands* (*ekhthrós*, enemy) and *frijonds* (*phílos*, friend); see the glossary. *Fraujinonds* (*despótēs*, master)—not *fraujinond*, as at Luke 2:29—is to be understood adjectivally, and consequently *fraujinonds* should be read; see Mark 9:25 *ahma þu unrodjands*, “you speechless spirit.” Participles are, for example, *airzjands* (*plános*), “deceiver,” because 2 Corinthians 6:8 has *airzjandans*; likewise *lutonds* (*phrenapátēs*), Titus 1:10; *galeikonds* (*mimētḗs*), 1 Thessalonians 2:24; *hatands* (*ekhthrós*), Luke 6:27. Uncertain are 2 Corinthians 6:18 *allvaldands* (*pantokrátōr*, Almighty); 1 Timothy 2:5 *midumonds* (*mesítēs*, mediator); 1 Timothy 2:7 *merjands* (*kḗryx*, herald); 2 Timothy 1:11; Mark 14:7 *drobjands* (*stasiastḗs*, insurgent).
>
> A second indication by which a participle can be recognized is that it is followed by the case governed by its verb: Ephesians 5:1 *galeikondans guþa*, “imitators of God”; Matthew 10:25 *sa garda valdands*, “master of the house” (*oikodespótēs*); Ephesians 6:12 *sa fairwu habands*, “ruler of the world” (*kosmokrátōr*). Many have a double form, such as *daupjands*, “Baptist” (*baptistḗs*): in accusative *daupjand* (Mark 8:28) it is a substantive, but in genitive *daupjandins* and dative *daupjandin* (Matthew 11:11–12, etc.) it is a participle. That these participles are also used substantively is evident from their connection with possessives, as in 1 Corinthians 2:1 *galeikondans meinai*, “my imitators.” Therefore *fraveitands allaize*, “avenger of all” (*ékdikos*), 1 Thessalonians 4:6, may also be a participle.

3) Adjectives and substantives: see §196.II.d.

4) Participles, adjectives, numerals, adverbs, and so forth are used substantively; see §§195.IV; 196; 197.

### §194. B. Proper Noun

1) On the forms of proper names, see §94 ff.

2) City names that are pluralia tantum in Greek are not always translated as such in Gothic. Thus Athens is indeed *aþeineis* in 1 Thessalonians 3:2 because of Greek *Athênai*, and probably likewise *lystros* in 2 Timothy 3:11 for *Lýstrois*, from *Lýstra*. But conversely Greek *Phílippoi* in the subscriptions to 1 and 2 Corinthians is translated in the singular, namely *filippa* (Matthew 5:35, etc.); singular *Hierosólyma* by *ïairusaulyma*; see [Col. 1070] Glossary under both words; likewise *saudauma* and *gaumaurra* in Romans 9:29, which must be taken as feminine singulars.

3) For names of cities and regions, names of peoples are frequently used: Luke 10:12 *qiþa izvis þatei saudaumjam sutizo vairþiþ þau þizai baurg*, “I tell you that it shall be more tolerable for the Sodomites than for that city,” for Greek *Sodomois*, “for Sodom”; 2 Corinthians 11:10 Greek *en klímasi tês Akhaías*, “in the regions of Achaia,” Gothic *ïn landa akaje*, “in the land of the Achaeans.” But at 11:32 occurs *baurgs damaska*, “the city Damascus,” for Greek *Damaskēnôn pólis*, “city of the Damascenes,” so that an adjective stands for a genitive. Finally, in place of these names a compound or apposition is used, as *ïudaialand*, “Judea-land,” in Mark 1:5 for “the land of Judea” (*Ioudaía chṓra*).

### §195

When a substantive denotes an object previously known or immediately specified, it receives the article.

I. Now an object may be known from the context, from itself, or because it is presented as previously known.

1) An object may be known from the context:

a) Namely, when mention has been made of it above: Matthew 5:25 *sijais vaila hugjands andastauïn þeinamma*, “be well disposed toward your adversary” (without the article): *ïbai wan atgibai þuk sa andastaua stauïn jah sa staua þuk gibai andbahta*, “lest perhaps the adversary deliver you to the judge, and the judge deliver you to the officer.” Matthew 8:8 *sa hundafaþs*, “the centurion,” namely the person indicated in v. 6, “said”; v. 15 *aflailot ïja so heito*, “the fever left her,” while v. 14 has *ligandein ïn heitom*, “lying in fevers.” Likewise Mark 1:31 *so brinno*, “the fever,” because of *ïn brinnon*, “in fever,” in v. 29.

Matthew 8:24 *þata skip gahuliþ varþ*, “the boat was covered,” in view of the preceding *ïnnatgaggandin ïn skip*, “entering into a boat,” in v. 23. Matthew 9:15: *ïbai magun sunjus bruþfadis qainon und þata weilos þei miþ ïm ïst bruþfaþs. ïþ atgaggand dagos, þan afnimada af ïm sa bruþfaþs, jah þan fastand*: “Can the sons of the bridechamber mourn while the bridegroom is with them? But days shall come when the bridegroom will be taken from them, and then they shall fast”; compare Mark 2:20. Matthew 9:22 *ganas so qino*, “the woman was healed,” namely the woman with an issue of blood mentioned beforehand in v. 20. Verse 28: *duatïddjedun ïmma þai blindans*, “the blind men came to him,” namely the two blind men mentioned in v. 27. Matthew 27:11 *ïesus stoþ faura kindina jah frah ïna so kindins*, “Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor questioned him.” Mark 1:42 *þata þrutsfill aflaiþ*, “the leprosy departed,” because v. 40 has *þrutsfill habands*, “having leprosy.” Likewise 2:22; 3:5; 4:7, 27, 39; 5:33; etc.; see Glossary V, *þata* 1) a) α).
b) When this term has not indeed been mentioned previously, but is related to another as a synonym, or as genus to species or vice versa: Matt. IX.24 *ni gasvalt so mavi* [“the girl has not died”], referring to v. 18, *þatei dauhtar meina gasvalt* [“my daughter has died”]; likewise Mark V.39, *þata barn ni gadauþnoda* [“the child has not died”], referring to v. 23; Matt. IX.33, *rodida sa dumba* [“the mute man spoke”], while v. 32 has *manna bauds* [“a mute man”]; Luke VII.20, *þai vairos qeþun* [“the men said”], namely the two disciples of v. 19 whom John sent; in v. 24 they are called *þai airjus* [“the messengers”]; IV.35, *sa unhulþa urrann* [“the unclean spirit went out”], in place of *ahma unhulþons unhrains* [“an unclean spirit”] in v. 33; likewise IX.42 and earlier v. 39; IX.33, *þai unhulþans galiþun* [“the demons went out”], in place of v. 27, *habaida unhulþons* [“he had demons”], and v. 36, *ganas sa daimonareis* [“the demoniac was healed”], who is the same man, *saei habaida unhulþons* [“who had demons”]; X.20, *þai ahmans ïzvis ufhausjand* [“the spirits subject to you”], referring to v. 17, *unhulþons ufhausjand unsis* [“the demons are subject to us”]; XX.10, *þai aurtjans ïn sandidedun* [“he sent them into the vineyard”], whereas in v. 9 they are generically called *vaurstvjans* [“laborers”]. For other examples see Glossary V, *þata*, 1) a) β).

c) When this word derives from the same root as the preceding one (being a conjugated verb), or has a similar meaning; Mark XII.7, *sa ïst sa arbinumja. hirjiþ usqimam ïmma jah unsar vairþiþ þata arbi* [“This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours”]; Luke XX.14; Mark XIV.56, *managai galiug veitvodidedun ana ïna jah samaleikos þos veitvodiþos ni vesun* [“many bore false witness against him, and their testimonies were not alike”]; 1 Cor. VII.18–19, *miþ faurafillja galaþoþs varþ was, ni bimaitai. þata bimait ni vaihts ïst* [“Was anyone called while circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised. Circumcision is nothing”]; Luke VI.49, *bistagq flodus jah suns gadraus jah varþ so usvalteins þis raznis mikila* [“the flood struck it, and immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great”]. For other examples see Glossary V, *þata*, 1) a) γ).

2) An object already known may be presupposed, for example:

a) When persons or things are designated in such a way that, although the noun is appellative, it nevertheless indicates nothing but what is known; as in the Gospels: *þai bokarjos*, Mark I.22, “the scribes”; *þai fareisaieis*, Mark V.7, “the Pharisees”; *þai gudjans*, Matt. XXVII.6, “the priests,” that is, the Jewish chief priests; *þai sinistans*, Mark VII.5, “the elders”; likewise *þai fauramaþljos*, Neh. V.17, “the chief men”; *þai siponjos*, Matt. XXVII.64, “the disciples,” that is, Jesus’ disciples; *so managei*, Matt. IX.25 etc., “the multitude,” that is, the great crowd of people which followed or gathered when the teacher taught or acted; likewise *so filusna*, *Skeireins* VII.b–c, “the multitude.” For other examples see Glossary V, *þata*, f).

b) Proper names do not require the article; but *þai ïudaieis* [“the Jews”] sometimes occurs, as John VII.1, 35; VIII.48, 52, 57; X.31, 33; XI.36. In these passages the question is not of the whole Jewish nation, but only of those present on specific occasions. For other examples of the article placed before proper names, see Glossary V, *þata*, 2).

c) Other objects belonging to biblical history or Christian matters take the article in an emphatic sense: *so baurgs*, Mark II.19, “the city,” that is, Jerusalem; *so alhs*, Mark XV.29, “the temple,” namely that in Jerusalem; *so dulþs*, John XII.20, “the feast,” namely Passover; *sa sunus*, John VI.40, “the Son,” namely of God; *so xristus*, Mark XV.32, “the Anointed One,” that is, the awaited, promised Christ, etc. Here, however, it must be remembered that both *sa sunus mans* and simply *sunus mans* [“the Son of Man” / “son of man”] occur, but not *sunus guþs* [“Son of God”]; see Glossary V, *þata*, f) α). *þata vaurd*, Luke I.2 and Rom. X.10, is “the word of God,” namely the Gospel (as also Mark VIII.35 has *so aivaggeljo*, “the gospel”); *so vailamereins*, 1 Cor. I.21, “the preaching of Christ”; *so laþons*, 2 Thess. I.11, “the calling to salvation”; *so usstass*, Luke XX.33, “the resurrection of the dead”; *þos anabusnins*, Mark X.19; Luke XVIII.20, “the Mosaic legislation.” The article is likewise demonstrative in *sa fairwus*, “this world,” and *so manaseþs*, “this world”; see Glossary V, *þata*, f) γ). Add also *so libains*, “this life,” Mark IV.19; Luke VIII.14; *so alds*, “this age,” 2 Tim. II.4; *þata þeihs*, “this present time,” Rom. XIII.11; *þata mel*, “this time,” Col. IV.5; 1 Thess. V.1.

II. An object may be determined:

1) By all kinds of attributes (§ 215), such as:

a) Adjectives and participles: Matt. XXVII.61, *vas jainar marja magdalene jah so anþara marja* [“Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there”]; v. 64, *ïst so speidizei airziþa vairvizei þizai frumein* [“the last error is worse than the first”]; Luke III.7, *was gataiknida ïzvis þliuhan faura þamma anavairþin hatiza* [“Who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?”]; Rom. VII.17, *ni ïk vaurkja þata ak so bauandei ïn mis fravaurhts* [“it is no longer I who do it, but the sin dwelling in me”]; 2 Cor. XI.5, *man ni vaihtai mik minnizo gataujan þaim ufar mikil visandam apaustaulum* [“I consider myself in no way inferior to the exceedingly great apostles”]; Eph. II.11, *þiudos simle vesuþ namnidans unbimaitanai fram þizai namnidon bimait* [“you Gentiles, who were formerly called ‘uncircumcision’ by that which is called ‘circumcision’”]. For other examples see Glossary V, *þata*, c) α) and b).

b) Adverbs or prepositional expressions which take the place of adjectives: 2 Tim. IV.10, *demas mis bilaiþ frijonds þo nu ald* [“Demas has forsaken me, loving the present age”]; Gal. IV.26, *so ïupa ïairusalem frija ïst* [“the Jerusalem above is free”]; Mark I.38, *gaggam du þaim bisunjane haimom* [“let us go to the neighboring villages”]; Col. II.14, *afsvairbands þos ana uns vadjabokos* [“having blotted out the handwriting against us”]; *Skeireins* III.b, *so bi guþ hrainei anabudana vas* [“the purity commanded by God”]. For other examples see Glossary V, *þata*, γ) and δ).

c) Genitives or possessive pronouns: 1 Cor.
