I.16, *ïk daupida þans staifanaus gadaukans* [“I baptized the household of Stephanas”]; v. 18, *þata vaurd galgins þaim fralusnandam dvaliþa ïst* [“the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing”]; Phil. III.18, *qiþa þans fijands galgins xristaus* [“I speak of the enemies of Christ’s cross”]; *Skeireins* IV.a, *so faheds meina usfullnoda* [“my joy has been fulfilled”]; John VIII.13, *so veitvodiþa þeina nist sunjeina* [“your testimony is not true”]; Matt. V.47, *goleiþ þans frijonds ïzvarans* [“you greet your friends”]; Luke VII.1, *usfullida alla þo vaurda seina* [“he completed all his words”]; Matt. X.25, *jabai garda valdand baiailzaibul haihaitun, und wan filu mais þans innakundans ïs* [“if they have called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more those of his household!”]; IX.4, *vitands ïesus þos mitonins ïze* [“Jesus, knowing their thoughts”]. For other examples see Glossary V, *þata*, ε), ζ), η).

2) By *alls* [“all”], and also by *jains* [“that”]: Luke IX.2, *ïnsandida ïns gahailjan allans þans unhailans* [“he sent them to heal all the sick”]; 1 Cor. XVI.16, *ufhausjaiþ allaim þaim gavaurstvam* [“be subject to all such fellow-workers”]; Neh. V.13, *gatavidedun þata vaurd alla so managei* [“all the multitude performed this word”]; Luke IX.25, *wo allis þaurfte gataujiþ sis manna gageigands þo manased alla* [“what profit is it to a man if he gains the whole world?”]; Matt. VIII.28, *ni mahta manna usleiþan þairh þana vig jainana* [“no one was able to pass by that way”]. For other examples see Glossary V, *þata*, θ) and ι).

3) By following relative clauses: Mark II.4, *ïnsailidedun þata badi, ana þammei lag sa usliþa* [“they lowered the bed on which the paralytic lay”]; X.39, *sveþauh þana stikl, þanei ïk driggka, driggkats jah þizai daupeinai, þizaiei ïk daupjada* [“you shall indeed drink the cup which I drink, and be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized”]; XII.23, *ïn þizai usstassai, þan usstandand, warjamma ïze vairþiþ qens?* [“in the resurrection, when they rise, whose wife will she be?”]; etc. See Glossary V, *þata*, b).

4) Where such a relative clause can readily be conceived: Matt. VIII.27, *þai mans sildaleikidedun* [“the men were astonished”], namely, the men accompanying him in the boat; Mark VI.14, *vaurkjand þos mahteis ïn ïmma* [“the powers are at work in him”], that is, the power of which the narrative speaks, or which people believed belonged to one raised from the dead; John XII.3, *ïþ sa gards fulls varþ daunais* [“the house was filled with the fragrance”], namely, the house in which Jesus was; XIX.2, *þai gadrauhteis usvundun vippja* [“the soldiers wove a crown”], namely, the soldiers whom Pilate had ordered to bind Jesus. For other examples see Glossary V, *þata*, d).

III. Where an apposition is placed after a noun for determination or explanation, it takes the article: Matt. XXVI.71, *ïesua þamma nazoraiau* [“Jesus the Nazarene”]; XXVII.26, *marja so magdalene* [“Mary Magdalene”]; John VI.4, *pasxa so dulþs ïudaie* [“Passover, the feast of the Jews”]; XII.4, *ïudas seimonis sa ïskariotes* [“Judas, Simon’s Iscariot”]; XVIII.1, *rinnon þo kaidron* [“the brook Kidron”]; Luke II.43, *ïesus sa magus* [“Jesus, the boy”]; IX.7, *herodes sa taitrarkes* [“Herod the tetrarch”]; Mark VI.14, *ïohannes sa daupjands* [“John the Baptist”]; and other participles and also adjectives, see § 196, II, 2) b).—Matt. XXVII.56, *marja so ïakobis* [“Mary, mother of James”]; John VII.23, *vitoþ þata mosezis* [“the law of Moses”]; Mark III.18, *ïakobu þana alfaiaus* [“James of Alphaeus”]; VI.1, *marein þo galeilaie* [“Mary of Galilee”].

> **Note.**—In all the examples cited above, however, the article may also be absent, especially in case II.1.b): Rom. VII.2 simply has *uf vaira qens* [“a wife bound to a husband”], just as 2 Cor. VII.10 in Codex A reads *bi guþ saurga* [“godly sorrow”]. In case III too the article is often absent: Matt. XXVII.61, *marja magdalene*; Luke IV.34, *ïesu nazorenu*; John VI.71, *ïudan seimonis iskariotu*; and regularly *esaïas praufetus* [“Isaiah the prophet”], *alaiksandrus aizasmiþa* [“Alexander the coppersmith”], *teibairius kaisar* [“Tiberius Caesar”], *kustanteinus þiudans* [“King Constantine”], etc.: Matt. XXVII.2, 9; Mark I.2; John XII.38; Luke I.5; II.36; III.1; IV.27; 2 Cor. XI.32; 2 Tim. IV.14; Calendar.

IV. With the aid of the article, the following perform the function of a substantive:

1) Numerals: Mark VI.7, *ïesus athaihait þans tvalif* [“Jesus called the twelve”], namely the disciples, as Matt. X.1 states; Luke X.17, *gavandidedun sik þai sibuntehund miþ fahedai* [“the seventy returned with joy”]; Mark X.41, *þai taihun dugunnun unverjan bi ïakobu jah ïohannen* [“the ten began to be indignant concerning James and John”]. For other examples see Glossary V, *þata*, c).

2) Adverbs, prepositional formulas, and clauses: Matt. XXVI.71, *qaþ du þaim jainar* [“she said to those there”], i.e. to those standing there; 1 Cor. V.12, *niu þans ïnna jus stojiþ, ïþ þans uta guþ stojiþ* [“do you not judge those within, while God judges those without?”]; John VIII.23, *jus us þaim dalaþro sijuþ, ïþ ïk us þaim ïupaþro ïm* [“you are from below, but I am from above”]; Mark IV.11; Phil. III.14; 1 Tim. III.7; 2 Cor. I.17, *nist af mis þata ja ja jah þata ne ne* [“with me there is not ‘yes, yes’ and ‘no, no’”]; V.16, *fram þamma nu ni ainnohun kunnum* [“from now on we know no one [in this way]”].—Mark III.8, *laistidedun afar ïmma þai bi tyra* [“those from the region of Tyre followed him”]; IV.10, *frehun ïna þai bi ïna* [“those around him asked him”]; Luke V.9, *sildaleik dishabaida ïna jah allans þans miþ ïmma* [“astonishment seized him and all those with him”], that is, his companions; Tit. I.10, *sind managai ungawairbai þishun þai us bimaita* [“there are many unruly talkers, those of the circumcision”]; 2 Cor. X.7, *þo bi andvairþja saiwiþ* [“you look at things before your face”]; XI.28, *ïnuh þo afar þata arbaiþs meïna sinteina* [“besides the things apart from these, my daily burden”]; Luke XVII.21, *lauhmoni lauhatjandei us þamma uf himina ïn þata uf himina skeiniþ* [“as lightning flashing from one part of heaven shines to the other part of heaven”].—Mark IX.10, *wa ïst þata us dauþaim usstandan?* [“what is this ‘rising from the dead’?”]; XII.33, *þata du frijon newundjan sve sik silban managizo ïst allaim þaim allbrunstim* [“to love one’s neighbor as oneself is more than all whole burnt offerings”]; Rom. XIII.9, *þata ni horinos, ni maurþrjais, ni hlifais, nih faihugeironjais ïn þamma vaurda usfulljada þamma frijos newundjan þeinana sve þuk silban* [“‘You shall not commit adultery, murder, steal, or covet’ is fulfilled in this word: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’”]. For other examples see Glossary V, *þata*, d), e), g).

3) Also, after the Greek manner, the neuter plural article (*þo*) with a genitive is used substantively: Mark XII.17, *usgibiþ þo kaisaris kaisara jah þo guþs guþa* [“render to Caesar the things belonging to Caesar, and to God the things belonging to God”]; Luke II.49, *ïn þaim attins meinis skulda visan* [“I must be in my Father’s affairs”]; Phil. II.4, *ni þo seina warjizuh mitondans ak jah þo anþaraize warjizuh* [“not each looking to his own things, but also each to the things of others”]. For other examples see Glossary V, *þata*, f).

V. When several substantives are joined copulatively or adversatively:

a) The article is repeated before each, especially when they differ in gender or number: Mark VII.5, *frehun ïna þai fareisaieis jah þai bokarjos* [“the Pharisees and the scribes asked him”]; XII.13, *wis ïst sa manleika jah so ufarmeleins?* [“What is the image and the inscription?”]; III.33, *wo ïst so aiþei meina aiþþau þai broþrjus meinai?* [“Who is my mother, or my brothers?”]; Phil. III.2, *saiwiþ þans hundans, saiwiþ þans ubilans vaurstvjans, saiwiþ þo gamaitanon* [“beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers, beware of the mutilation”]; 1 Cor. XIV.22, *razdos du bandvai sind ni þaim galaubjandam ak þaim ungalaubjandam* [“tongues are for a sign not to believers but to unbelievers”]; and so ordinarily.

b) Or it need be placed only once: John VI.27, *vaurkjaiþ ni þana mat þana fralusanan ak mat þana visandan du libainai aiveinon* [“work not for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life”]; Matt. XXVII.12, *vrohiþs vas ïesus fram þaim gudjam jah sinistam* [“Jesus was accused by the chief priests and elders”]; John VII.48, *sai jau ainshun þize reike galaubidedi ïmma aiþþau fareisaie* [“Has any one of the rulers or Pharisees believed in him?”]. In *Skeireins* VIII.c, where this passage is cited, it reads *þize fareisaie*, with the article repeated. Mark XIV.43, *qam ïudas jah miþ ïmma managei fram þaim auhumistam gudjam jah bokarjam jah sinistam* [“Judas came, and with him a crowd from the chief priests, scribes, and elders”]; Matt. XXVII.12; Mark X.33; XI.27; XII.33; XIV.54; Luke V.21; VI.7; IX.16; XIX.47; XX.1, 19; John VII.45; XI.25, etc.—Matt. VII.14, *wan aggvu þata daur jah þraihans vigs sa brigganda* [“narrow is the gate and constricted the way that leads”]; Luke VIII.51, *ïesus ni fralailot ainohun ïnngaggan alja þana attan þizos maujos jah aiþein* [“Jesus allowed no one to enter except the girl’s father and mother”]; 1 Cor. VII.8, *qiþa þaim unqenidam jah viduvom* [“I say to the unmarried and to widows”]; John XIV.6, *ïk ïm sa vigs jah sunja jah libains* [“I am the way, the truth, and the life”]; 2 Cor. X.10, *þos bokos kaurjos sind jah svinþos, ïþ qums leikis lasivs jah vaurd frakunþ* [“his letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible”].

c) Sometimes the article is placed only before the later substantive, being absent before the earlier: Luke VIII.24, *gasok vinda jah þamma vega vatins* [“he rebuked the wind and the raging of the water”]; Matt. XXVII.1; Mark XIV.54. But where a third substantive follows, the article is either again omitted or used: Neh. V.17, *ïudaieis jah þai fauramaþljos ·r· jah ·n· gumane jah þai qimandans at unsis ana biuda meinamma andnumanai veisun* [“the Jews, the chief men, one hundred and fifty men, and those who came to us from the nations around us ate at my table”]; John XVIII.12, *þaruh hansa jah sa þusundifaþs jah andbahtos ïudaie undgripun ïesu* [“therefore the cohort, the commander, and the officers of the Jews seized Jesus”]. The following passages, however, have a distinctive construction: Mark VIII.31, *sunus mans uskiusan skulds ïst fram þaim sinistam jah þaim auhumistam gudjam jah bokarjam* [“the Son of Man must be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes”]; XIV.53, *garunnun auhumistans gudjans allai jah þai sinistans jah bokarjos* [“all the chief priests, elders, and scribes assembled”]; Luke XIX.47, *þai auhumistans gudjans jah bokarjos sokidedun ïna usqistjan jah þai frumistans manageins* [“the chief priests and scribes sought to destroy him, and so did the leading men of the people”].

VI. At the beginning of a sentence, particles and other such modifiers may be introduced between the article and the substantive: John VI.33, *so auk hlaifs guþs ïst* [“for the bread of God is”]; XVIII.55, *sah þan siponeis vas kunþs þamma gudjin* [“but the disciple was known to the high priest”]; Rom. X.1, *sa raihtis vilja meinis hairtins* [“the desire of my heart indeed …”].—Matt. IX.12, *þaurbun lekeis þai unhaili habandans* [“those who are ill need a physician”]; Rom. VIII.5, *þai bi leika visandans* [“those who are according to the flesh”]; 1 Cor. V.3, *þana þata sva gataujandan* [“the one who has done this thing”].

## 2. THE ADJECTIVE

(Graff, “On the German Weak Declension,” in *New Yearbooks of the Berlin Society for the German Language*, II, 1, 1 ff.)

### § 196

What is most important in discussing adjectives consists especially in determining precisely the difference between vocalic (strong) and consonantal (weak) declensions. Their essential distinction is this: the vocalic declension denotes what is indeterminate, general, and abstract, whereas the consonantal denotes what is determinate, individual, and concrete. Yet it is groundlessly asserted that the consonantal form is later than the vocalic and developed only subsequently. Those also err who think that this form consists merely of the addition of the article, since the article is attached to the adjective only incidentally, namely in order to designate what has previously been mentioned (cf. § 195, I.1.a). It would be much more correct to say that this form contains within itself the article—which did not exist at all in the ancient languages, but first appeared explicitly at the period to which our Gothic monuments belong. However this may be, the same rule also applies to the passive participle; the active participle, on the other hand, has only the consonantal form, except in the masculine.

I. **THE VOCALIC FORM**, in the positive and superlative degrees:

a) Both attributively: Rom. VII.24, *vainans ïk manna*, “wretched man that I am”; Mark XVI.5, *juggalauþ bivaibidana vastjai weitai*, “a young man clothed in a white garment”; *Skeireins* III.c, *vitoþ raidida azgon kalbons gabrannidaizos* [“the law prescribed a burnt offering of a heifer”], a dark-colored cow, to be burned outside the camp; then, *þo ïn vato vairpandans hrain jah vulla raudai ufartrusnjandans* [“sprinkling with pure water and red wool”]; VI.b, *ïohannes manniskaim vaurdam veitvodida* [“John prophesied in human words”]; VIII.a, *ïst magula ains her, saei habaiþ ·e· hlaibans barizeinans*, “there is one boy here who has five barley loaves”; Matt. III.11, *sah daupeiþ ïn ahmin veihamma*, “he will baptize in the Holy Spirit”; VII.17, *all bagme godaize akrana goda gataujiþ*, “every good tree produces good fruit”; 2 Thess. II.16, *guþ atgaf gaþlaih aiveina jah ven goda ïn anstai*, “God gave eternal comfort and good hope through grace”; and predicatively: Rom. VII.12, *vitoþ veihata jah anabusns veiha jah garaihta jah þiuþeiga*, “the law is holy, and the commandment holy, righteous, and good”; 1 Cor. IV.11, *veis dvalai ïþ jus frodai*, “we are foolish, but you are wise”; Luke X.23, *audaga sind augona*, “blessed are the eyes”; John IX.39, *þai saiwandans blindai vairþand*, “those who see become blind”; Luke VII.10, *bigetun þana siukan skalk hailana*, “they found the sick servant well”; Mark I.3, *raihtos vaurkeiþ staigos guþs unsaris*, “make straight the paths of our God”; *Skeireins* IV.c, *ïohannes ïesu himinakundana jah ïupaþro qumana qaþ*, “John called Jesus heavenly and coming from above.”

b) Always in the words *fulls* “full,” *halbs* “half,” *alls* “all,” *ganohs* “many,” *midjis* “middle,” *svaleiks* “such,” *ains* “one,” *anþar* “other,” *sums* “some,” and in possessive pronouns: Eph. IV.13, *garinnam du vaira fullamma*, “that we may attain to a full-grown man”; Gothic Calendar, *batvins bilaifs aikklesjons fullaizos*, “the relics of the Catholic Church”; Mark VI.23, *þiswah þei bidjais mik, giba þus und halba þiudangardja meina*, “whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom”; Neh. VI.16, *hausidedun fiands unsarai allai jah ohtedun allos þiudos*, “all our enemies heard and all the nations feared”; Mark X.46, *usïddja miþ managein ganohai*, “he went out with a great multitude”; John XVII.3, *ei kunneina þuk ainana sunja guþ*, “that they may know you, the only true God”; Mark II.7, *was mag afletan fravaurhtins niba ains guþ*, “who can forgive sins except one God?”; v. 26, *hlaibans faurlageinais ni skuld ïst matjan niba ainaim gudjam*, “it is not lawful to eat the bread of offering except for the priests alone”; *Skeireins* VII.c, *ni ana þaim hlaibam ainaim mahtais filusna ustaiknida*, “the multitude was not fed by those loaves alone”; Mark IX.36, *gasatida barn ïn midjaim ïm*, “he set a child among them”; John VII.14, *ana midjai dulþ usstaig ïesus ïn alh*, “in the middle of the feast Jesus went up into the temple”; Matt. IX.8, *guþ gaf valdufni svaleikata mannam*, “God gave such authority to men”; Mark VI.2, *mahteis svaleikos þairh handuns ïs vairþand*, “such powers are done through his hands”; 2 Cor. VIII.4, *sa qimanda anþarana ïesu mereiþ*, “the one who comes proclaims another Jesus”; v. 8, *anþaros aikklesjons birauboda*, “I robbed other churches”; Mark XIV.51, *ains sums juggalauþs laistida afar ïmma*, “a certain young man followed him.” Even when these words are substantivally used, the vocalic form remains: Matt. V.18, *allata*, “everything”; VIII.33, *gataihun all bi þans daimonarjans*, “they reported everything concerning the demoniacs”; Mark I.27, *sildaleikidedun allai*, “all were amazed”; *Skeireins* VI.d, *sumai jah stibna ïs gahausidedun, sumai þan ïs siun sewun*, “some heard his voice, but others saw his appearance”; Luke IX.19, *anþarai qiþand þuk heleian, sumai þan þatei profetus usstoþ*, “some say that you are Elijah, but others that one of the prophets has arisen”; Mark XIV.60, *usstoþ sa auhumista gudja ïn midjaim*, “the chief priest stood up among them.” Indeed, this remains so even after the article: Matt. XXVII.49, *þai anþarai qeþun*, “the others said”; 1 Cor. IX.5; John XVIII.16, *sa siponeis anþar*, “the other disciple”; Matt. V.39; 2 Cor. X.11, *þata þagkjai sa svaleiks*, “let such a one think this”; 1 Cor. VII.15, *nist gaþivaids broþar aiþþau svistar ïn þaim svaleikaim*, “a brother or sister is not enslaved in such cases”; 2 Cor. XII.2; Gal. V.21, 23; VI.1; 2 Cor. XI.13, *þai svaleikai galiugaapaustauleis*, “such false apostles”; 1 Cor. XII.12, *liþjus allai us leika þamma ainamma*, “all the members are of the one body”; v. 19, *sind þo alla ains liþus*, “but they are all one member”; Luke XV.32, *þata mein þein ïst*, “this brother of yours.” Hence the Goth renders the formula τὸ λοιπόν (“for the rest,” “henceforth”) by *þata anþar*, 1 Cor. I.16; 2 Cor. XIII.11; Eph. VI.10, etc.

> **Note 1.**—*Allans* in the consonantal form instead of *allai* occurs falsely only at Neh. VI.16; see the note on that passage.

II. **THE CONSONANTAL FORM.** This form is used when the adjective refers to a determinate object, that is, in the concrete sense expressed in Greek by the article, and with ordinal words. Moreover, in the Gothic view, a fundamental determination is present in comparisons; consequently comparatives take this form alone, where a comparison or adversative statement may also be conceived. Likewise, where adjectives are used substantively for persons or individuals, they ordinarily take the consonantal form, and always do so in the vocative.

1) Without the article:

a) Determinate, when the Greek text has the article: Matt. XXVII.62, *ïftumin daga gaqemum auhumistans gudjans* (οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς), “on the next day the chief priests assembled”; but John XVIII.13, *annas vas auhumists veiha* (ἀρχιερεύς), “Annas was high priest that year”; John VII.37, *ïn spedistin daga dulþais stoþ ïesus* (ἐν τῇ ἐσχάτῃ ἡμέρᾳ), “on the last day of the feast Jesus stood”; Mark III.11, *ahmans unhrainjans drusun du ïmma* (τὰ πνεύματα τὰ ἀκάθαρτα), “the unclean spirits fell before him”; John XVIII.10, *afmaimait ïmma auso taihsvo* (τὸ ὠτίον τὸ δεξιόν), “he cut off his right ear”—whereas the parallel Mark XIV.47 has *auso þata taihsvo*, with the article added; see below, 2)b); Matt. V.30, *jabai taihsvo þeina handus marzjai þuk* (ἡ δεξιά σου χείρ), “if your right hand causes you to stumble”; v. 39, *jabai was þuk stautai bi þaihsvon þeina kinnu* (τὴν δεξιάν σου σιαγόνα), “if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also”; 2 Cor. VI.7, *ïn mahtai guþs þairh vepna garaihteins taihsvona jah hleidumona* (τῶν ὅπλων … τῶν δεξιῶν καὶ ἀριστερῶν), “in the power of God, through the weapons of righteousness, on the right and on the left”; 1 Cor. XVI.19, *goleiþ ïzvis priska miþ ïngardjon seinai aikklesjon* (τῇ κατ᾽ οἶκον), “Prisca, with the church in her house, greets you”; 2 Cor. IV.4, *xristus ïst frisahts guþs ungasaiwanins* (τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ἀοράτου), “Christ is the image of the invisible God.” Accordingly in Col. I.15 *ungasaiwanis* must be read in place of *ungasaiwanis*; nevertheless compare Note 5(c). *Skeireins* III.b, *ni þanaseiþs judaiviskom ufarranneineinim brukjand*, “not using Jewish purifications,” that is, purifications instituted in the Mosaic law; Mark XI.1, *newa vesun at fairgunja alevjin* (τὸ ὄρος τῶν ἐλαιῶν), “they were near the Mount of Olives”—that is, the mount of olives near Jerusalem, whereas a mountain planted with olive trees generally would be called *fairguni alevi*; John V.35, *jains vas lukarn brinnando jah liuhtjando* (ὁ καιόμενος), “that man was the burning and shining lamp.” Indeed, the consonantal form is also used where the Greek text lacks the article, as in *libains aiveino* (ζωὴ αἰώνιος), “eternal life,” in contrast to earthly life: Mark X.17, 30; Luke X.25; XVIII.18, 30; John VI.27, 40, 47, 54, 68; X.28; XII.25; XVII.2; Rom. VI.23; Gal. VI.8; 1 Tim. I.16; VI.12; Tit. I.2; Matt. XXV.46, where it is also contrasted with *balveins aiveino*, “eternal punishment,” just as 2 Thess. I.9 has *fralusts aiveino*, “eternal destruction.” Elsewhere, however, the strong (vocalic) form is used, for example *vulþus aiveins*, “eternal glory,” 2 Cor. IV.17; 2 Tim. II.10, 11.

b) Comparative: Matt. IX.16, *vairsiza gataura vairþiþ* (χεῖρον), “the rent becomes worse”; Luke I.18, *qens meina fram aldrozei ïn dagam seinaim* (προβεβηκυῖα), “my wife is advanced in years”; XVI.8, *þai sunjus þis aivis frodazans sunum liuhadis sind*, “the children of this age are wiser than the children of light”; 1 Cor. IX.19, *ei managizans gageigaidedjau*, “that I might gain more”; 2 Cor. VIII.17, *usdaudoza visands galaiþ du ïzvis*, “being more earnest, he went to you”; Gal. IV.1, *arbinumja niuklahs ni und vaiht ïusiza ïst skalka*, “the heir, while a child, differs in nothing from a slave”; *Skeireins* VI.c, *hardizo þize ungalaubjandane varþ hairto*, “the heart became harder than that of the unbelievers”; Luke V.39, *vein fairni batizo ïst*, “the old wine is better”; XVIII.14, *alïddja motareis garaihtoza gataihans du garda seinamma þau jains*, “the tax collector went down to his house more justified than that man.”

Partly from the form they take, partly from their meaning, the following must be regarded as comparatives: *auhuma*, “higher, upper”; *aftuma*, “later”; *fruma*, “earlier”; *innuma*, “inner”; *hleiduma*, “left,” in contrast to the right; *ïftuma*, “following,” presupposing a preceding day; and finally *fairna*, “former,” which belongs here by reason of its meaning and occurs only in the consonantal form. Here the Goth is generally almost more exact than the Greek: Phil. III.3, *anþar anþarana munands sis auhuman* (ὑπερέχοντα), “each considering the other superior to himself”; Mark X.31, *managei vairþand frumans aftumans jah aftumans frumans*, “many who are first will be last, and the last first.” The Greek text has πρῶτοι and ἔσχατοι, though the comparative sense is apparent from the two terms contrasted. Hence *fruma* and *frumei* are used in the heading of the First Epistle to Timothy and in the subscriptions of the First Epistle to the Corinthians and the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians, because there are two epistles. Likewise, in the Gothic Calendar, November is called *fruma ïuleis*, “the first Yule,” because there is another month of Yule. Consequently the Goth renders not only the comparative πρότερος by *fruma*, Gal. IV.13; Eph. IV.22, but also—and correctly—the superlative πρῶτος: Matt. XXVII.64, where the former error corresponds to the latter; John XV.18, “before you”; 1 Cor. XV.47, where *þo fruma manna* corresponds to *anþar*; 1 Tim. II.13, where Eve is contrasted with Adam as created earlier. 2 Cor. IV.16, *sa ïnnuma manna*, ὁ ἔσωθεν ἄνθρωπος, “the inward man,” is set in opposition to the *sa utana manna*, “outward man,” to be supplied; Rom. VII.22; Eph. III.16; Matt. VI.3, *ni viti hleidumei þeina, wa taujiþ taihsvo þeina*, “let not your left hand know what your right hand does”; 2 Cor. VI.7, etc.; Matt. XXVII.62, *ïftumin daga*, τῇ ἐπαύριον, “on the following day,” opposed to the preceding day; likewise Mark XI.12; John VI.22; XII.12. Hence the consonantal form also stands in the expression *af* or *fram fairnin jera*, 2 Cor. VIII.10; IX.2, ἀπὸ πέρυσι, “from the previous year.”

> **Note 2.**—From these comparative forms arise the superlatives *auhumists*, *aftumists*, and *frumists*; and from *hindumists* and *spedumists* may be inferred the forms *hinduma*, “later,” in opposition to an earlier one, and *speduma*, “more recent,” in opposition to a more mature one.

c) Ordinal numerals—except *frumists* and *anþar*, which are not derived from cardinals: Mark IX.31, *usqistiþs þridjin daga usstandiþ* (τῇ τρίτῃ), “having been killed, he shall rise on the third day”; Luke IX.22; XVIII.33; 1 Cor. XV.4; Mark XV.25, *vasuh þan weila þridjo* (τρίτῃ), “it was then the third hour”; 2 Cor. XII.2, *fravulvans und þridjan himin*, “caught up to the third heaven”; Matt. XXVII.45, *fram saihston weilai varþ riqis ufar allai airþai und weila niundon* (ἕκτης … ἐννάτης), “from the sixth hour darkness came over all the earth until the ninth hour”; Matt. XXVII.46, *bi weila niundon ufhropida ïesus*, “about the ninth hour Jesus cried out”; Mark XV.33, *biþe varþ weila saihsto, riqis varþ*, “when the sixth hour came, darkness came”; Luke I.26, *ïn menoþ saihstin ïnsandiþs vas aggilus gabriel* (τῷ ἕκτῳ), “in the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent”; I.36, *jah sa menoþs saihsta ïst ïzai*, “and this is the sixth month for her”; I.59, *varþ ïn daga ahtudin qemun bimaitan þata barn* (τῇ ὀγδόῃ), “on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child”; XVIII.12, *afdailja taihundon dail, þize gastalda*, “I give a tenth of all that I acquire”; III.1, *ïn jera fimtataihundin þiudinassaus teibairiaus varþ vaurd guþs at ïohannen*, “in the fifteenth year of Tiberius’ reign the word of God came to John.”

d) Substantively: *blinda*, “a blind man,” Mark X.46 (ὁ τυφλός); VIII.22 (τυφλός); hence also *blinda sums*, “a certain blind man,” Luke XVIII.45; *tvai blindans*, “two blind men,” Matt. IX.27. But Matt. XI.5 has *blindai ussaïwand*, “the blind receive sight”: the adjective is indeed used substantively, but does not refer to certain blind persons, rather to blind people generally. 1 Cor. XV.29, *wa vaurkjand þai daupjandans faur dauþans* (τῶν νεκρῶν), “what will those who are baptized for the dead do, if the dead do not rise at all?”—that is, the dead who died without baptism and for whom baptism is performed. Compare, conversely, Matt. VIII.22; in the formula *us dauþaim urreisan*, “to rise from the dead,” Matt. XI.5; XXVII.64; Mark VI.14, 16, etc., concerning the resurrection of the dead. Hence *þarbans*, John XII.5 (πτωχοί), means “the poor,” i.e. beggars; but *unleds*, which has the same meaning (πτωχός, ὁ πένης), occurs only in the vocalic form: Matt. XI.5; Luke XVI.20; XVIII.22; 2 Cor. IX.9. Likewise, in the neuter, *nih andvairþo nih anavairþo*, Rom. VIII.38, “neither things present nor things to come” (οὔτε ἐνεστῶτα οὔτε μέλλοντα); and where neuters correspond to Greek substantives: Luke IV.29, *brahtedun ïna und auhmisto þis fairgunjis* (ἕως [τῆς] ὀφρύος), “they brought him to the brow of the hill”; Rom. XIII.7, *usgibiþ nu allaim skuldo* (τὰς ὀφειλάς), “render therefore to all their dues”; compare Eph. IV.9, *undaraisto airþos* (τὰ κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς), “the lower parts of the earth.”

Accordingly, very many adjectives also occur in the consonantal form when they serve as predicates or are used absolutely: Mark VII.18, *jah jus unvitans sijuþ* (ἄσύνετοι), “are you also without understanding?”—not “unknowing,” but “lacking understanding”; 2 Cor. XII.6, 11; Phil. III.15, *sijum fullavitans*, “let us be mature”; Col. I.28; IV.12; Gal. III.3, *sva unfroþans sijuþ* (ἀνόητοι), “are you so foolish?” Conversely, 2 Cor. XI.16 has *qiþa ïbai was mik muni unfrodana*, “I say, lest anyone think me foolish”; Eph. V.17, *ni vairþaiþ unfrodai, ak fraþjandans*, “do not become foolish, but understanding.” Mark XII.3, *ïnsandidedun ïna laushandjan*, “they sent him away empty-handed”; 1 Tim. III.6, *niuja satiþs* (νεόφυτος), “a recent convert”; Luke VII.2, *skalks siukands svultavairþja*, “a servant, being sick, was about to die”; Mark IV.15, *gahausjand unkarjans* (ἀμελοῦντες), “hearing heedlessly”; Luke VI.35, *leiwaid ni vaihtais usvenans* (ἀπελπίζοντες), “lend, expecting nothing”; 2 Cor. XI.8, *ushaista* (ὑστερηθείς), “being in need, I burdened no one”; v. 23, *svasve unvita qiþa* (παραφρονῶν), “I speak as one out of his mind.” Hence, with *vairþan* and *visan*, to paraphrase Greek verbs: *usfilma vairþan* (ἐκπλήττεσθαι), “to be astonished,” Mark I.22; Luke IX.43; *alaþarba vairþan* (ὑστερεῖσθαι), “to be in need,” Luke IV.14; *vairþan usgrudja*, “to become weary,” Luke XVIII.1, etc.; *visan unkarja* (ἀμελεῖν), “to be negligent,” 1 Tim. IV.14; *gamainja visan* (κοινωνεῖν), “to share,” V.22; *unvita visan* (ἀγνοεῖν), “to be ignorant,” 1 Cor. X.1; *gavilja visan* (συνευδοκεῖν), “to consent,” VII.13—where v. 12 should read *gaviljo* rather than *gavilja*.

> **Note 3.**—Very many words have a different form according to their different meaning. For example, *ïbns* means “level”: Luke VI.17, *gastoþ ana stada ïbnamma*, “he stood on a level place.” But *ïbna* means “equal”: Luke XX.36, *ïbnans aggilum sind*, “they are equal to angels”; *Skeireins* I.a, *qam nasjands ni ïbna nih galeiks unsarai garaihtein ak silba garaihtei visands*, “the Savior came, not equal or like to our righteousness, but himself being righteousness”; V.d, *ni ïbnon ak galeika sveriþa usgiban sunau uns laiseiþ*, “he teaches us to render not equal but like recompense to a son.”

e) In the vocative: Luke XIX.17, *vaila goda skalk!* “Well done, good servant!”; John XVII.25, *atta garaihta!* “Righteous Father!”; v. 11, *atta veiha!* “Holy Father!”; Mark X.17, *laisari þiuþeiga!* “Good teacher!”; Luke XVIII.18; XIX.22, *unselja skalk jah lata!* “wicked and lazy servant!”; Mark I.25, *ahma unhrainja!* “unclean spirit!”; V.8; 1 Cor. XV.58, *broþrjus meinai liubans!* “my beloved brothers!”; Gal. III.1, *o unfrodans galateis!* “O foolish Galatians!”; Luke IX.41, *o kuni ungalaubjando!* “O unbelieving generation!”; 2 Cor. VII.1, *liubans, hrainjam unsis!* “beloved, let us cleanse ourselves!”; Matt. V.22, *saei qiþiþ dvala! skula vairþiþ ïn gaiainnan*, “whoever says, ‘Fool!’ shall be liable to Gehenna.”

> **Note 4.**—The following are not to be regarded as exceptions: Mark IX.25, *þu ahma þu unrodjands jah bauþs, ïk þus anabiuda!* “You mute and deaf spirit, I command you!”; XV.29, *o sa gatairands þo alh jah bi þrins dagans gatimrjands þo, nasei þuk silban* [“O you who destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself!”]. Here the nominative, not the vocative, stands in accordance with Greek usage. But Luke I.28 is conspicuous: *fagino anstai audahafta, frauja miþ þus, þiuþido þu ïn qinom* [“Hail, favored one; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women”], where one would expect *audahafto*. In the same way the participle *þiuþida* (masculine) and *þiuþido*, “blessed [feminine]!”, is used. Likewise Mark XI.9–10; Luke XIX.38; John XII.13; but Mark XV.18 reads *hails þiudan ïudaie*, “Hail, king of the Jews!”

> **Note 5.**—The rules under a) and b) are seldom departed from:
>
> a) An adjective lacking the article sometimes takes the weak form: Col. I.7, *aipafras ïst triggva faur ïzvis andbahts ïesuis*, “Epaphras is for you a faithful minister of Jesus,” although this formula elsewhere always occurs with the article (*sa triggva andbahts*; see below, 2)a). The two forms are interchanged in Rom. IX.2: *saurga mis ist mikila* (vocalic) *jah unweilo* (consonantal, ἀδιάλειπτος), “I have great and unceasing grief”; Matt. V.19, *saei laisjai sva mans sah minnista haitada. ïþ saei taujiþ jah laisjai sva sah mikils haitada*, “whoever teaches thus shall be called least; but whoever does and teaches thus shall be called great.”
>
> b) A strong Gothic form is used where the Greek adjective has the article: John X.11, *ïk ïm hairdja gods* (ὁ καλός), “I am the good shepherd”; 2 Thess. I.5, *taikn garaihtaizos stauos guþs* (τῆς δικαίας), “a token of the righteous judgment of God”—whereas John VII.24, τὴν δικαίαν κρίσιν, is regularly translated *þo garaihton staua*; Col. III.10, *gahamoþ niujamma* (τὸν νέον), “having put on the new [man]”; Luke I.70, *rodida þairh munþ veihaize þize fram anastodeinai aive praufete seinaize* [“he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old”], where *veihaize* deserves notice if, as is probable, it is used substantively.
>
> c) Adjectives in a substantival sense also take and use the vocalic form: Mark VII.32, *berun du ïmma baudana*, “they brought to him a deaf man”; XVI.5, *gasewun juggalauþ sitandan ïn taihsvai* (ἐν τοῖς δεξιοῖς), “they saw a young man sitting on the right”; III.27, *ni manna mag kasa svinþis vilvan* (τοῦ ἰσχυροῦ), “no one can plunder a strong man’s goods”; Luke XV.7, *faheds vairþiþ ïn himina ïn ainis fravaurhtis ïdreigondins þau ïn niuntehundis jah niune garaihtaize*, “there is joy in heaven over one repentant sinner rather than over ninety-nine righteous persons”; Rom. XIV.1, *unmahteigana galaubeinai andnimaiþ* (τὸν ἀσθενοῦντα), “receive one weak in faith”; Luke V.31, *ni þaurbun hailai leikeis ak þai unhailans* (οἱ ὐγιαίνοντες), “those who are well do not need a physician, but the sick do”; Mark IV.5, *anþar gadraus ana stainahamma* (τὸ πετρῶδες), “another seed fell upon rocky ground.”

2) With the article—which is naturally joined to the adjective—*sa* is everywhere used for οὗτος, “this.”
a) This article, moreover, is indeed placed immediately adjacent, but not for the sake of the adjective; rather, according to the rule, it refers to the noun (see § 195, 1). This occurs when the noun is repeated or in some manner determined, for example by a genitive, a possessive pronoun, etc.; further, when it bears an emphatic or special sense, and in certain formulas. Mark 14:54, 55: *qam in garda þis auhumistins gudjins* (“[he came] into the court of the high priest”)—*iþ þai auhumistans gudjans* (“but the chief priests”) *sokidedun ana Iesus veitvodiþa* (“sought testimony against Jesus”); in v. 53 he is first called merely *du auhumistin gudjin*—*auhumistans gudjans* (“to the high priest”—“the chief priests”), in which case the latter is always used with the article in vv. 60, 61, 63; 15:1; likewise John 18:19, owing to vv. 14 ff. At times *þai auhumistans gudjans* likewise occurs with the article (John 11:47), because it denotes the Jewish high priests.

Luke 5:37: *distairid þata niujo vein þans balgins* (“the new wine bursts the skins”), after *vein niujata* (“new wine”); v. 39: *þata fairnjo* (“the old [wine]”) *batizo ist* (“is better”), after *ainshun drigkandane fairni [vein] ni suns vili jugg* (“no one, having drunk old [wine], immediately wants new”); see v. 36. Luke 7:10: *bigetun þana siukan skalk hailana* (“they found the sick servant well”), see v. 2; 8:15: *þata ana þizai godon airþai* (“that on the good soil”), see v. 8. In Mark 4:20, instead, there is *ana airþai þizai godon* (“on the good soil”); see below, b).

John 10:11: *ik im hairdeis gods, hairdeis sa goda saivala seina lagjiþ faur lamba* (“I am the good shepherd; the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep”); 17:2–3: *gibai im libain aiveinon. soh þan ist so aiveino libains* (“that he may give eternal life. And this is eternal life”); 19:5: *usiddja Iesus bairands þana þaurneinan vaip jah þo paurpurodon vastja* (“Jesus came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe”), see v. 2.

Mark 12:20–21: *sibun broþrahans wesum ja sa fruma* (“there were seven brothers; the first”), namely *broþar*, “brother,” from *broþrahans*—*jah anþar* (“and the second”)—*jah sa þridja* (“and the third”), namely *broþar*; Luke 20:29–31. Matthew 27:64: *hait nu vitan hlaiva und þana þridjan dag* (“therefore command the tomb to be guarded until the third day”), v. 63 having *þrins dagans* (“three days”). 1 Corinthians 15:48: *vileiks sa muldeina* (“such as is the earthly [man]”), so also *þai muldeinans* (“the earthly [men]”), with v. 47 preceding, *muldeins* (“earthly”); likewise *sa ufarhiminakunda* (“the heavenly [man]”) and v. 49 *þis airþeinins* (“of the earthly [man]”).

Matthew 7:17: *sa ubila bagms akrana ubila taujiþ* (“the bad tree produces bad fruit”), because *all bagme* (“every tree”) precedes. 1 Corinthians 5:7: *ushraineiþ þata fairnjo beist* (“clean out the old leaven”), see v. 6. John 7:24: *þo garaihton staua stojaiþ* (“judge with righteous judgment”), after *ni stojaiþ* (“do not judge”). 1 Timothy 1:10: *þizai hailon laiseinai andstandan* (“opposing sound teaching”), because of *vitodalaisarjos* (“teachers of the law”) in v. 7, or *god ist witoþ* (“the law is good”) in v. 8.

*Skeireins* II, b: *iupaþro qaþ þo veihon jah himinakundon gabaurþ anþara þairh þrahl usþulan* (“he spoke above of the other, holy and heavenly birth through the womb’s suffering”), because *iupaþro gabairada* (“the birth mentioned above”) precedes; ibid.: *þoleikeinon us vambai munands gabaurþ* (“likewise, remembering the birth from the womb”), because *in vamba aiþeins aftra galeiþan jag-gabairaidau* (“to return again into his mother’s womb and be born”) precedes.

Matthew 11:20: *in baurgim vaurþun þos managistons mahteis is* (“in the cities his very many mighty works were done”), because of *is*; see § 195, II, c. *Skeireins* II, d: *nasjands þana anavair þan dom is gasaw* (“the Saviour saw the judgment that was to come”); III, 6: *frauja þo ahmeinon anafalh daupein* (“the Lord commanded the spiritual baptism”). Ephesians 1:6: *ansteigs was uns in þamma hubin sunau seinamma* (“he bestowed grace upon us in his beloved Son”), because of the possessive pronoun. Matthew 5:35: *Iairusaulyma baurgs ist þis mikilins þiudanis* (“Jerusalem is the city of the great king”), i.e. the king of the Jews; 27:53: *innatiddjedun in þo veihon baurg* (“they entered the holy city”), since *baurgs* means “chief city.”

Matthew 5:26: *ni usgaggis jainþro, unte usgibis þana minnistan kintu* (“you shall not come out from there until you have paid the last penny”); and John 6:44: *urraisja ina in þamma spedistin daga* (“I shall raise him on the last day”) are formulaic expressions. Elsewhere *in spedistin daga* occurs without the article (John 7:37). Luke 19:30: *gaggats in þo wiþrawairþon haim* (“go into the village opposite”) is said demonstratively; elsewhere there is *haim þo wiþrawairþon* (“the village opposite”), see b). Likewise *sa haitana* (“the one called”) in Mark 15:7, because it presents a person already known. The article is also combined with the passive participle, as in Luke 1:1: *insaht bi þos gafullawiseidons in uns waihtins* (“an account concerning the things fulfilled among us”). Correspondingly, Luke 15:4 has *gaggiþ afar þamma fralusanin*, “he goes after the lost [one],” namely the sheep, because above one reads *fraliusands ainamma lamba* (“one lost sheep”).

In the later period, when *sa* had become an article, the translators of the epistles first employed it in such a way that, following the Greek, it was not referred back to a noun previously expressed: 1 Corinthians 7:26: *man nu þata goþ wisan in þizos andwairþons þaurftais* (“I consider this to be good because of the present necessity”); 8:11: *sa unmahteiga ana þeinamma witubnja broþar* (“the weak brother is destroyed by your knowledge”); 11:25: *sa stikls so niujo triggwa ist* (“this cup is the new covenant”). 2 Corinthians 3:14: *anakunnains þizos fairnjons triggws* (“the reading of the old covenant”); 8:2: *þata diupo unledi* (“their deep poverty”) *ize usmanagnoda du gabein ainfalþeins ize* (“overflowed into the wealth of their generosity”).

Ephesians 2:4: *guþ gabeigs wisands in armahairtein in þizos managons frijaþwos* (“God, being rich in mercy, because of his great love”), *in þizaiei frijoda uns* (“with which he loved us”); here, however, the article may be regarded as required by the following relative, see § 195, II, 3. Ephesians 3:10: *so managfalþo handugei guþs* (“the manifold wisdom of God”); 3:19: *þo ufarassau mikilon þis kunþjis frijaþwa* (“the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge”); 4:24: *gahamoþ þamma niujin mann* (“put on the new man”); 4:30: *þana weihan ahman guþs* (“the Holy Spirit of God”); 6:21: *Tukeikus sa liuba broþar jah triggwa andbahts* (“Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful servant”); likewise Colossians 4:7, 9, and Colossians 1:7: *Aipafrin þamma liubin gaskalkja* (“Epaphras, the beloved fellow-servant”). Ephesians 4:22: *aflagjaiþ bi frumin usmeta þana fairnjan mannan, þana riurjan bi lustum* (“put off, with respect to the former manner of life, the old man, who is corrupt according to lusts”); Colossians 3:9; 4:15: *goleiþ Nymfan jah þo ingardjon is aikklesjon* (“greet Nympha and the church in her house”), whereas in 1 Corinthians 16:19 the article is absent. 1 Timothy 1:11: *wutþus þis audagins guþs* (“the gospel of the blessed God”); 1:18: *driugais in þaim þata godo drauhtiwitoþ* (“that you may wage the good warfare in them”). *Skeireins* II, d: *twos ganamnida waihts, jah þata raihtis anasiunjo wato jah þana andaþahtan ahman* (“two named things: both the water visibly present and the spiritual meaning”). Ephesians 3:8: *wailamerjan þo unfairlaistidon gabein* (“to proclaim the unsearchable wealth”).

b) Conversely, the adjective immediately draws the article to itself when it follows the noun or stands as an apposition [Col. 1082]: Matthew 5:29, *augo þata taihswo* (“your right eye”); 6:11, *hlaif þana sinteinan* (“daily bread”); 8:12, *riqis þata hindumisto* (“the outer darkness”); Mark 1:26, *ahma sa unhrainja* (“the unclean spirit”); 1:27; 5:13; 9:25; Luke 8:29; Mark 1:27, *so laiseino so niujo* (“the new teaching”); 4:20, *airþai þizai godon* (“the good soil”); 5:7, *guþs þis hauhistins* (“God Most High”); 8:38, *aggilum þaim weiham* (“the holy angels”); 9:7, *sunus meins sa liuba* (“my beloved Son”); Luke 3:22; 9:35; 20:13; 10:30, *in aiwa þamma anawairþin* (“in the age to come”); 11:2, *in haim þo wiþrawairþon* (“in the village opposite”); 14:58, *alh þo handuwaurhton* (“the sanctuary made with hands”); Luke 3:22, *ahma sa weiha* (“the Holy Spirit”); 3:26; John 7:39; 14:26; Ephesians 1:13; Luke 6:6, *handus is so taihswo* (“his right hand”); 7:47, *fravaurhteis þos managons* (“her many sins”); John 6:13, *hlaibam þaim barizeinam* (“the barley loaves”); 6:32, *hlaif þana sunjeinan* (“the true bread”); 7:37, *in spedistin daga þamma mikilin dulþais* (“on the last, great day of the feast”); 15:1, *weinatriu þata sunjeino* (“the true vine”); 2 Corinthians 1:6, *þreihanda in naseinais þizos waurstweigons* (“suffering for the consolation which you endure”); 11:32, *atta sa þiuþeiga* (“Aretas the king”); Ephesians 3:9, *fauragaggi runos þizos gafulginons* (“the dispensation of the mystery hidden from ages”); Colossians 4:14, *leikeis sa liuba* (“Luke the beloved physician”).

Matthew 7:13: *wigs sa brigganda* (“the broad way”); John 6:14: *praufetus sa qimanda* (“the prophet who is coming”); 6:51: *hlaifs sa libanda* (“the living bread”); 15:25: *waurd þata gamelido* (“the word written”); Mark 4:15: *waurd þata insaiano* (“the word sown”); Luke 2:15: *waurd þata waurþano* (“the thing that has happened”); Matthew 11:21, *mahteis þos waurþanons* (“the mighty works that were done”); 11:23; 27:44, *þai waidedjans þai miþushramidans* (“the robbers crucified with him”); Mark 6:2, *so handugeino so gibano* (“the wisdom given”); Luke 6:15, *Seimon þana haitunan Zeloten* (“Simon called the Zealot”); 15:6, *lamb þata fralusano* (“the lost sheep”); John 6:27, *þana mat þana fralusanan* (“the food that perishes”); 2 Corinthians 1:8, *aglon þo waurþanon* (“the affliction which happened”); 8:1, *anst þo gibanon* (“the grace given”); Galatians 2:9; Ephesians 3:7, *bi gibai anstais guþs þizai gibanon mis* (“according to the gift of God’s grace given to me”); Matthew 25:41, *in fon þata aiweino þata manwido* (“into the eternal fire prepared”); Ephesians 4:22, *þamma niujin mann þamma gaskapanin* (“the new man created”); Colossians 3:10. Yet before an adjective the article may also be omitted when it is already placed before the noun: Ephesians 6:13, *in þamma daga ubilin* (“in the evil day”).

c) The article is likewise regularly used where adjectives and participles are employed substantively.

aa) First, in the manner discussed under 2) a): Matthew 9:27–28, *laistidedun afar imma twai blindans* (“two blind men followed him”)—*qimandin þan in garda duatiddjedun imma þai blindans* (“when he came into the house, the blind men came to him”); Matthew 8:22–23, *berun du imma blindan* (“they brought to him a blind man”)—*fairgreipands handu þis blindins ustauh ina* (“taking the blind man’s hand, he led him out”); Mark 3:27, *kasa swinþis wilwan, niba faurþis þana swinþan bindiþ* (“to plunder the strong man’s goods, unless he first binds the strong man”); John 10:5, *framaþjana ni laistjand, unte ni kunnun þize framaþjane stibna* (“they do not follow a stranger, because they do not know the stranger’s voice”).

Luke 16:10: *sa in leitilamma untriggwa* (“he who is unfaithful in a little”), because *saei triggws ist* (“he who is faithful”) precedes; v. 22: *warþ þan gaswiltan þamma unledin* (“the poor man died”)—*gaswalt jah sa gabeiga* (“and the rich man also died”), see vv. 19–20. Matthew 9:33: *rodida sa dumba* (“the mute man spoke”), *mannabauds* (“a dumb man”) being synonymous in v. 32. Mark 5:15: *gasaiwand þana wodan sitandan* (“they saw the possessed man sitting”), the demoniac having previously been mentioned. Mark 15:32: *þai miþushramidans imma* (“those crucified with him”), v. 27 having *jah miþ imma ushramidedun twans waidedjans* (“and with him they crucified two robbers”).

John 12:5–6: *duwe ni fradailiþ ist þarbam* (“why was it not sold for the poor?”), *þata qaþ ni þeei ina þize þarbane kara wesi* (“he said this not because he cared for the poor”). 1 Corinthians 1:19: *fraqistja snutrein þize snutrane jah frodein þize frodane uskiusa* (“I will destroy the wisdom of the wise and reject the understanding of the prudent”); and also:

bb) Although the word has not previously been mentioned, in imitation of Greek usage and model: Matthew 5:8, *audagai þai hrainjahairtans* (“blessed are the pure in heart”); 5:21, *hausideduþ þatei qiþan ist þai mairizam: ni maurþrjais* (“you have heard that it was said to the men of old: You shall not murder”); 5:39, *ik qiþa izwis ni anstandan allis þamma unseljin* (“I say to you, do not resist the evil one”); John 17:15; Matthew 25:46, *þai garaihtans in libain aiweinon* (“the righteous into eternal life”); Mark 10:42, *þai mikilans ize gawaldand im* (“their great ones exercise authority over them”); 13:17, *wai þaim qi þuhaftom* (“woe to those who are pregnant”); 14:61, *þu is Xristus, sa sunus þis þiuþeigins* (“are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?”).

Luke 1:24: *kann þuk, was þu is sa weiha guþs* (“I know you, who you are: the Holy One of God”); 4:34; 6:24, *wai izwis þaim gabeigam* (“woe to you rich people”); 2 Corinthians 13:12, *goljand izwis þai weihans allai* (“all the saints greet you”); Ephesians 1:1; 3:18, etc. John 11:39: *swistar þis dauþins* (“the sister of the dead man”); 11:44; 12:1. Luke 1:49: *gatavida mis mikilein sa mahteiga* (“the Mighty One has done great things for me”); Ephesians 3:20. 1 Corinthians 5:10: *ni blandaiþ izwis þaim faihufrikam jah wilwam* (“do not associate with the covetous and robbers”); Luke 6:35: *gods ist þaim unfagram jah unseljam* (“he is kind to the ungrateful and evil”); 1 Corinthians 8:9: *[waldufni izwar bistugq] wairþai þaim unmahteigam* (“[let this authority of yours not become] a stumbling block to the weak”); v. 11; 9:22; 9:21: *warþ þaim witodalausam swe witodalaus* (“I became as lawless to those without the law”); likewise 10:33: *ni sokja þatei mis bruk sijai ak þatei þaim managam* (“not seeking what is profitable for myself, but what is profitable for the many”); v. 17; 5:13: *usnimiþ þana ubilan* (“remove the wicked man”); Galatians 2:10: *þize unledane gamunan* (“remember the poor”); John 13:29; Galatians 4:27: *managa barna þizos auþjons* (“many are the children of the desolate woman”); 6:1: *jus þai ahmeinans gaþwastjaiþ þana swaleikana* (“you who are spiritual, restore such a one”); Nehemiah 6:17: *managai wesun þize reikjane Iudaie, þaiei sandidedun aipistulans* (“many Jewish nobles were sending letters”); *Skeireins* V, a: *þize anawair þane airzein* (“of the things present, a proof”); Matthew 11:11: *sa minniza in þiudangardjai himine maiza imma ist* (“the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he”).

Similarly in the neuter: Matthew 5:37: *þata managizo þaim us þamma ubilin ist* (“what is more than these is from the evil one”); Luke 3:5: *wairþiþ þata wraiqo du raihtamma* (“the crooked things shall become straight”); 16:11: *þata sunjeino was izwis galaubeiþ* (“who will entrust to you the true [riches]?”); v. 12: *in þamma framaþjin triggwai* (“if you have not been faithful in that which is another’s”); v. 15: *þata hauho in mannam* (“that which is highly esteemed among men”); 18:27: *þata unmahteigo* (“the impossible things”); Romans 8:3; 9:22: *þata mahteigo* (“that which is possible”); John 16:13: *þata anawairþo gateihiþ izwis* (“he will declare to you the things to come”); Colossians 2:17; Romans 7:13: *þata þiuþeigo warþ mis dauþus?* (“did that which is good become death to me?”); 9:25: *haita, þo unliubona liubona* (“I shall call the unloved beloved”).

> **Note [Col. 1083].** According to the Greek text, *þo liubon*, “the beloved” (τὴν ἠγαπημένην), ought to occur here, since it is very obscure to what noun this neuter plural is to be referred. This consonantal form in the predicate is unusual; it ought to be vocalic, *liuba*, as in 1 Corinthians 9:22, *was þaim unmahteigam swe unmahteigs* (“I became as weak to the weak”); 14:25. Moreover, this feminine may be compared with Philippians 3:2, where the Gothic renders βλέπετε τὴν κατατομήν by *saiwiþ þo gamaitanon* (“see the mutilated [thing]”). Should not a feminine noun, such as *managein* (“multitude”) or something similar, be supplied here?

1 Corinthians 14:25: *þo analaugnjona hairtins is swikunþa wairþand* (“the secrets of his heart are made manifest”); 15:53: *skuld*—for thus, rather than *skula*, it must be read—*ist þata riurjo gahamon unriurein jah þata diwano gahamon undiwanein* (“this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality”); 2 Corinthians 3:10: *þata wulþago* (“that which is glorious”); 5:17: *þo alþjona* (“the old things”); 13:7: *þata godo* (“what is good”); Galatians 6:9; 2:7: *þata wiþrawairþo* (“the contrary”); 5:21: *þata galeiko* (“such things”); Ephesians 6:12: *þo ahmeirona* (“the spiritual forces”).

[Col. 1084] cc) Active participle: Romans 8:37: *jiukam þairh þana frijondan uns* (“we are more than conquerors through him who loves us”); 9:20: *ibai qiþiþ gadikis du þamma digandin: wa mik gatawides swa?* (“will the thing formed say to him who forms it: Why did you make me thus?”); Ephesians 1:23: *fullo þis alla in allaim usfulljandins* (“the fullness of him who fills all things in all”).

Matthew 7:14: *fawai sind þai bigitandans wig* (“few are those who find the way”); 27:54: *hundafaþs jah þai miþ imma witandans Iesua ohtedun* (“the centurion and those with him guarding Jesus were afraid”); Mark 10:23: *agluba þai faihu gahabandans in þiudangardja guþs galeiþand* (“how difficult it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God”); Romans 8:4: *garaihtei witodis usfulljada in uns þaim ni bi leika gaggandam* (“that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us who do not walk according to the flesh”); 10:15: *skaunjai fotjus þize spillondane gawairþi, þize spillondane þiuþ* (“how beautiful are the feet of those proclaiming peace, of those proclaiming good things”); 12:14: *þiuþjaiþ þans wrikandans izwis* (“bless those persecuting you”).

Thus the present participle assumes the consonantal form in every case except the nominative singular, which takes the vocalic form: Matthew 7:21, *inngaleiþiþ in þiudangardja himine sa taujands wiljan guþs* (“the one doing the will of God shall enter the kingdom of heaven”); 10:40: *sa andnimands izwis andnimiþ mik* (“he who receives you receives me”); Mark 4:3: *urrann sa saiands saian fraiwa* (“the sower went out to sow seed”); 14:42: *sa lewjands mik atnewida* (“he who betrays me is at hand”); Luke 3:11; 6:49; John 8:47; Romans 9:33; 11:26; 12:8; 13:2; 14:3; 15:12; 1 Corinthians 7:15; 2 Corinthians 4:14; 9:10; 10:17; Galatians 5:10; 1 Thessalonians 3:5. The consonantal form occurs only in *sa qimanda* (“he who comes”) in Mark 11:9; Luke 7:19, 20; 19:38; John 12:13; 2 Corinthians 11:4. Accordingly, John 3:31 (*Skeireins* IV, b) may have had *qimanda* in place of *sa iupaþro qimands*; this undoubtedly also occurs with *sa gagganda* in Matthew 3:11 (*Skeireins* III, d), and with *sa inngaggands* in John 10:2. The feminine, on the contrary, always has the consonantal form, ending here in *-ei*: Luke 1:45, *so galaubjandei* (“she who believed”); Galatians 4:27, *so ni fitandei* (“she who has not borne”).

dd) Passive participle: John 6:51, *so qumana* (“the [bread] that came down”); 2 Corinthians 7:12, *melida ni in þis anamahtjandins, ni in þis anamahtidins* (“I wrote not for the sake of him who did wrong, nor for the sake of him who suffered wrong”); Mark 4:16, 18, *þai saianans* (“those sown”); 13:27, *þans gawalidans* (“the elect”); Luke 6:18, *þai anahabaidans* (“those troubled”); 7:10, *þai insandidans* (“those who had been sent”); 1 Corinthians 7:8, *þaim unqenidam* (“the unmarried”); Colossians 4:10, *sa miþfrahunþana* (“the fellow-prisoner”); Philemon 23.

In the neuter: Mark 7:18, *þata utaþro inngaggando in mannan ni mag ina gamainjan* (“what enters a person from outside cannot defile him”); 7:20, *þata us mann usgaggando gamaineiþ mannan* (“what comes out of a person defiles the person”); Luke 8:14, *þata in þaurnuns gadriusando* (“that which falls among thorns”); 1 Timothy 5:15, *swikunþa sind þo aljaleikos sik habandona* (“they have already turned aside after Satan”); Matthew 8:17: *ei usfullnodedi þata gamelido þairh Esaiian* (“that what was spoken through Isaiah might be fulfilled”); 27:9: *usfullnoda þata qiþano þairh Iairaimian* (“what was spoken through Jeremiah was fulfilled”); Luke 1:45: *ustauhts þize rodidane* (“a fulfillment of the things spoken”); Mark 5:14: *þata waurþano* (“what had happened”); Matthew 27:54: *þo waurþanona* (“the things that had happened”); Luke 17:10: *þo anabudanona* (“the things commanded”); John 12:6: *þata innwaurpano* (“that which was cast in”); 2 Corinthians 4:18: *þo gasaiwanona* (“the things seen”). For other examples of participles, see Glossary V, *þata*, 3) b).

> **Note 6.** It was formerly believed, on the basis of false readings, that the vocalic form is also sometimes used here: namely Luke 20:13, *sunu meinana þana liubana*; 1 Corinthians 15:47, *sa frums manna*; Mark 5:13 [Col. 1085], *ahmans þai unhrainjai*. But the corrected forms *liuban* (according to the more correct division of the word), *fruma* (according to the manuscript reading), and *unhrainjans* (also according to the manuscript) are now accepted by everyone, except Graff alone, who would not allow himself to be persuaded regarding the final correction and proposed another method of emendation in *Sprachsch.* V, 36. Moreover Romans 11:24 reads *þis wilþeis alewabagmis* (“this wild olive-tree”), which I would not emend—perhaps altered to *wilþeins*, although the true form would be *wilþjins*; further, *Skeireins* I, c, *þata gadob* (of which a consonantal form does not appear to have existed), and Romans 10:11, *qiþiþ auk þata gameliþ* (“for the Scripture says”), for which *þata gamelido* could scarcely have been written.

> **Note 7.** Although the Goth seems to imitate Greek usage in employing the neuter plural of adjectives and participles to denote abstractions—2 Corinthians 8:21, *garedandans goda* (“providing good things,” καλά); 5:17, *þo alþjona* (“the old things,” τὰ ἀρχαῖα) *usliþun, sai waurþun niuja alla* (“have passed away; behold, all things have become new”), τὰ πάντα, “all things”; likewise *alla* and *þo alla*, see § 205 V, 1; 2 Corinthians 4:18, *ni fairweitjands þisei gasaiwanane ak þizei ungasaiwanane, unte þo gasaiwanona riurja sind iþ þo ungasaiwanona aiweina* (“not looking at the things seen, but at the things unseen; for the things seen are temporary, but the things unseen eternal”), τὰ βλεπόμενα—τὰ μὴ βλεπόμενα, “visible—invisible”—yet he also uses the singular, in the Germanic manner: Galatians 5:21, *waurstwa leikis sind horinassus, kalkinassus—jah þata galeiko þaim* (“the works of the flesh are fornications, uncleannesses—and things like these”), German *das Gleiche*, Greek τὰ ὅμοια, “similar things”; Luke 17:25, *skal manag gaþulan* (“he must suffer much”), German *Viel*, Greek πολλά, “many things”; Mark 4:34, *sundro siponjam seinaim andband allata* (“privately he explained everything to his disciples”), German *Alles*, Greek πάντα, “all things”; 13:23; Luke 2:39; 2 Corinthians 7:14; Mark 7:8: *daupeinins aurkje jah stikle jah anþar galeik swaleikata manag taujiþ* (“washings of cups and pots, and you do many other similar things”), Greek ἄλλα παρόμοια τοιαῦτα πολλά; Luke 6:30: *af þamma nimandin þein ni lausei* (“from him who takes what is yours, do not demand it back”), τὰ σά; Mark 7:15: *þata utgaggando us mann þata ist þata gamainjando mannan* (“what comes out of a person is what defiles the person”).

## § 197. I. THE COMPARATIVE

1) The comparative always takes the consonantal form; see § 196, II, 1) b).

2) Instead of the comparative, *mais*, “more,” is not infrequently used with the positive: Mark 9:42, *goþ ist imma mais* (“it is better for him”), καλὸν—μᾶλλον; *Skeireins* I, c: *gadob was mais þans ufhausjandans diabulau gaqissans wairþan nasjandis laiseinai* (“it was more fitting that the devil, though he had exalted himself, should be brought into subjection to the Saviour’s teaching”); compare Galatians 4:12: *managa barna þizos auþjons mais þai þizos aigandeins aban* (“the desolate woman has more children than she who has a husband”).

> **Note 1.** Indeed *mais*, used intensively, is combined with the comparative itself: Matthew 6:26, *niu jus mais wulþrizans sijuþ þaim?* (“are you not much more valuable than they?”), μᾶλλον διαφέρετε.

> **Note [Col. 1085].** We have stated at Matthew 6:26 and Galatians 2:6 that this reading is to be preferred to the customary one; it was conjectured by Schmeller (*Gloss. Hell.*, under *uhta*), though later, and by Halbersma.

2 Corinthians 8:22: *broþar gakausidedum filaus mais usdaudozan* (“we have sent the brother, proved much more diligent”), simply πολὺ σπουδαιότερον; Philippians 1:23: *lustu haba miþ Xristau wisan, und filu mais batizo ist* (“I desire to be with Christ, and this is far better”), μᾶλλον κρεῖσσον. Conversely, Mark 5:26 says: *ni waihtai botida mais wairs habaida*: “having been healed in no respect, but rather growing worse.” Moreover Ulfilas slightly avoids pleonasm, since he renders Matthew 5:20, περισσεύει ἡ δικαιοσύνη ὑμῶν πλεῖον τῶν γραμματέων, by *managizo wairþiþ garaihteins izwaraizos þai þize bokarje* (“your righteousness must become more abundant than that of the scribes”).

[Col. 1086] 3) Modifiers of the comparative are *filu*, *filaus*, *und filu*, “much”; *wan*, *wan filu*, *und wan filu*, “how much”; *þamma*, “so much”; *þe*, “so”: Mark 10:49, *is filu mais hropida* (“he cried out much more”); 1 Corinthians 12:22, *iggqara ni þarf ak mais filu þoei þugkjand liþiwe leikis lasiwostai wisan* (“much rather, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary”); *Skeireins* VII, d; Luke 18:39, *is und filu mais hropida* (“he cried out still more”); 2 Corinthians 3:9; Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 7:13, *ana gaþrafsteinai unsarai filaus mais faginodedum* (“we rejoiced much more at our consolation”); 8:22.

*Skeireins* III, d: *ist daupeins Iohannes ana midumai twaddje ligandei, ufarþeihandei raihtis witodis hrainein iþ minnizei filaus aiwaggeljons daupeinai* (“John’s baptism stands midway between the two: surpassing the cleansing of the righteous law, yet far inferior to the baptism of the Gospel”); V, c; VII, c. Romans 11:12: *wan mais fullo ize?* (“how much more their fullness?”); 2 Timothy 1:18: *wan filu mais in Aifaison andbahtida mis, waila þu kant* (“how much he served me in Ephesus, you know very well”); Romans 11:24; Matthew 10:25: *jabai garda waldand Baialzaibul haihaitun, und wan filu mais þans innakundans is?* (“if they called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more those of his household?”); Mark 7:36: *wan filu is im anabauþ, mais þamma eis meridedun* (“the more he commanded them, the more they proclaimed it”); *Skeireins* IV, d: *þauhjabai us himina ana airþai in manne garehsnais qam, akei ni þe haldis airþeins was nih us airþai rodjands* (“although he came from heaven to earth in human form, he was nevertheless not merely earthly, nor did he speak from the earth”).

4) “Than” after a comparative is expressed by *þau*, or by the dative of the noun compared; see below, § 250. “More than” (ὑπέρ, παρά) is translated by the preposition *ufar* with the accusative: Matthew 10:37: *saei frijoþ attan aiþþau aiþein ufar mik nist meina wairþs* (“he who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me”). For other examples, see the Glossary under this word. Yet the Goth sometimes omits this manner of expression peculiar to the exemplar, using the dative customary to him: Luke 16:8: *þai sunjus þis aiwis frodozans sunum liuhadis sind* (“the children of this age are wiser than the children of light”), φρονιμότεροι ὑπὲρ τοὺς υἱούς.

> **Note 2.** When a comparative is used absolutely, either a second clause with “than” must be supplied from the context, or it must be translated using certain qualifying words, such as “than usual,” “than is fitting,” perhaps, and the like: Philippians 2:28: *sniumundos insandida Aipafraudeitu ei gasaiwandans ina aftra faginoþ jah ik hlasoza sijau* (“I sent Epaphroditus more promptly, so that, seeing him again, you may rejoice and I may be less sorrowful”), σπουδαιοτέρως, “more quickly than usual or than was fitting”; ἀλυπότερος, “perhaps more cheerful.” But in this case the Goth often uses the positive in place of the Greek comparative: 2 Timothy 1:18, *waila þu kant*, “you know well,” Greek βέλτιον, “better [than I need tell you]”; τάχιον, “more quickly,” John 13:27; and 1 Timothy 3:14 is rendered by *sprauto*, “quickly, soon.” Yet he follows the Greek when ἤ follows a positive bearing emphatic meaning: Mark 9:43: *goþ þus ist haufamma in libain galeiþan þai twos handuns habandin galeiþan in gaiainnan* (“it is better for you to enter life maimed than, having two hands, to go into Gehenna”).

## II. THE SUPERLATIVE

1) The superlative assumes both vocalic and consonantal forms, which differ here from one another in the same way as in the positive; see § 196.

2) The Goth distinguishes comparative and superlative more accurately and strictly than Greek; hence he often uses the comparative for the Greek superlative and conversely. Besides the comparatives *fruma* (“first”) and *aftuma* (“last”) cited in § 196, II, 1) b), the following belong here: [Col. 1087] Matthew 27:64: *ist so speidizei airziþa wairsizei þizai frumein* (“the latter error will be worse than the first”), ἡ ἐσχάτη; Mark 9:34: *du sis misso andrunnun, warjis maists wesi* (“they disputed with one another who was greatest”), μέιζων; Luke 9:46; Mark 4:31–32: *kaurno sipawis minnist allaize fraiwe ist, jah þan saiada, urrinniþ jah wairþiþ allaize grase maist* (“the grain of mustard seed is the least of all seeds, and when it has been sown, it springs up and becomes the greatest of all plants”), μικρότερον—μείζων; Luke 9:48: *sa minnista wisands in allaim sa wairþiþ mikils* (“he who is least among you all is great”), μικρότερος; Matthew 8:12: *uswairpanda in riqis þata hindumisto* (“cast out into the outer darkness”), ἐξώτερον; 1 Corinthians 15:19: *jabai in þizai libainai ainai in Xristau wenjandans sijum, armostai sium allaize manne* (“if in this life only we have hoped in Christ, we are of all people most miserable”), ἐλεεινότεροι; Luke 20:32: *spedista allaize gadauþnoda jah so qens* (“last of all the woman also died”), ὕστερον; 1 Timothy 4:1: *ahma swikunþaba qiþiþ þatei in spedistaim dagam afstandand sumai* (“the Spirit expressly says that in later days some will depart”), ὑστέροις. In all these places, down to Mark 4:32, Luther also employed the superlative.

> **Note 1.** The superlative is paraphrased with *filu*: 2 Corinthians 12:9, *filu gabaurjaba nu mais wopa in siukeim meinaim* (“most gladly, therefore, I will rather boast in my weaknesses”), ἥδιστα.

> **Note 2.** More than once the positive is introduced in place of the superlative: Luke 16:10, *saei triggws ist in leitilamma, jah in managamma triggws ist* (“he who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much”), ἐλαχίστῳ; probably in order to make the expression more concise; likewise 19:17.

## 3. THE NUMERAL

### § 198. I.

Words that denote numerical quantity generally, such as *manags*, “much,” *leitils*, “little,” *faws*, “few,” *halbs*, “half,” and *alls*, “all,” are adjectives and must be treated as adjectives; see § 196. Nouns signifying a definite number of objects, such as “dozen” (French *une douzaine*, German *Dutzend*), “sixty” in the sense of a set (French *une soixantaine*, German *Schock*), etc., occur nowhere in our fragments, except *tewi*, “fifty” (French *une cinquantaine*); see on 1 Corinthians 15:6.

## II. CARDINAL NUMBERS

1) On their inflection, see § 104.

2) Cardinal numbers are very frequently expressed by numeral signs; see § 14. Words and numeral signs are also often combined.

3) The words and signs composing a compound number are arranged so that the greater number comes first and the lesser follows. Moreover, between tens and units, and generally between the final two numbers, as also where hundreds and tens are joined, *jah*, “and,” is inserted; this conjunction is by no means necessary in numerical notation, especially for the greater numbers. Nine (and perhaps eight as well) with a decade is expressed by the immediately higher decade, less one or two (*ainamma* or *twaim wans*): Ezra 2:9–10, *sunjus Zaxxaiaus ·w· j·; sunjus Banauis ·x· m· b·*; 2:36, *niunhunda ·u· g·*; Nehemiah 6:15, *·n· dage jah ·b·*; Luke 2:37, *ahtautehund jah fidwor*; 15:4, *niuntehund jah niun*; Ezra 2:16, *niuntehund jah ·h·*; Nehemiah 5:17, *·r· jah ·n·*; Ezra [Col. 1088] 2:12, *þusundi ·w· u· q·*; 2:37, *þusundi ·n· b·*; 2:39, *þusundi ·g·*; 2:15, *twa þusundja ·j· q·*; Mark 5:13, *twos þusundjos*.

> **Note [Col. 1087].** On the differing genders of *þusundja* and *þusundjos*, see on Ezra 2:15.

Ezra 2:35, *·g· þusundjos ·k· l·*; John 6:10, *fimf þusundjos* (“five thousand”); 2 Corinthians 11:24, *fram Iudaium fidwortiguns ainamma wanans nam* (“from the Jews I received forty less one”), that is, 40 − 1 = 39.

> **Note 1.** Nehemiah 6:15, *·e· jah ·k·*, and Galatians 2:1 in Codex B (*quatuordicem*, “fourteen”) are unusual Gothic instances suggestive of modern German usage; in its place Codex A has the more correct reading at 2 Corinthians 12:2.

4) Numeral words may either precede or follow their noun: Matthew 6:24, *ni manna mag twaim fraujam skalkinon* (“no one can serve two masters”); Luke 9:31, *wairōs twai miþrodidedun imma* (“two men were speaking with him”).

5) Cardinal numbers are either used:

a) Adjectivally, as Matthew 8:19, *ains bokareis* (“one scribe”); Mark 6:9, *ni wasjaiþ twaim paidom* (“do not put on two tunics”); 27:63, *afar þrins dagans urreisa* (“after three days I shall rise”); John 11:17, *juþan fidwor dagans habaida in hlaiva* (“he had already been in the tomb four days”); Luke 8:2, *usiddjedun unhulþons sibun* (“seven demons had gone out”); 17:12, *taihun þrutsfillai mans* (“ten leprous men”); Mark 8:9, *wesun swe fidwor þusundjos* (“there were about four thousand”), etc.;

b) Or they take a partitive genitive after them: Luke 5:17, *warþ in ainamma dage* (“it happened on one of the days”); Matthew 5:19; Mark 8:28, etc.; Mark 11:1, *insandida twans siponje* (“he sent two of the disciples”); John 6:19, *farjan swe spaurde ·k· jah ·e·* (“having rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia”); Matthew 27:3, *þrinstiguns silubrinaize* (“thirty pieces of silver”); *Skeireins* VII, d, *in auþidai ·m· jere attans fodida* (“in the wilderness he fed the fathers forty years”); John 8:57, *fimftiguns jere nauh ni habais* (“you are not yet fifty years old”); Luke 15:4, *taihuntehund lambe* (“a hundred sheep”); John 6:7, *twaimhundam skatte hlaibos ni ganohai sind* (“two hundred denarii worth of bread are not sufficient”); Luke 7:41, *ains skulda skatte fimfhunda* (“one owed five hundred denarii”); 9:14, *wesun swe fimf þusundjos waire* (“there were about five thousand men”); 14:31, *miþ taihun þusundjom—miþ twaimtigum þusundjo* (“with ten thousand—with twenty thousand”).

## III. ORDINAL NUMBERS

1) They always occur in the consonantal form; see § 196, II, 1) c).

2) In Nehemiah they are also written by numeral signs: 5:14, *fram jera ·k· und jer ·l·* (“from the twentieth year to the thirty-second year”); 6:15, *ustauhana warþ so baurgswaddjus ·e· jah ·k· daga menoþs Ailulis* (“the city wall was completed on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul”).

> **Note 2.** Regarding the first two numerals, the following should be observed:

> a) The form *ainaha*, feminine *ainoho*, derived from *ains*, corresponds to German *einig, einzig* and Latin *unicus*, “only, sole,” and is always inflected consonantally: *sunus ainaha* (“an only son,” Luke 7:12; 9:38) and *dauhtar ainoho* (“an only daughter,” 8:42).

> b) “One,” εἷς, when used not numerically but solely to indicate the identity of two persons or things as one, is Gothic *sama*, “the same”: Mark 10:8, *sijaina þo twō du leika samin* (“the two shall become one flesh”); Luke 17:34, *þizai naht twai wairþand ana ligrā samin* (“on that night two shall be on one bed”); Ephesians 2:14, *gatawida þo ba du samin* (“he made the two one”). Hence Ephesians 6:9 also has *im jah izwis sama frauja ist* (“the same Lord is theirs and yours”), where Greek has ὁ κύριος with the article.

> c) “Both,” likewise referring to two, has two Gothic forms, *bai* and *bajoþs*. They differ as Latin *uterque* and *utrique*: *bai* is used when only two objects are in question and they are regarded or conceived as mutually connected and united into one; *bajoþs*, where objects of different kinds or two parties are concerned. The Goth observes this distinction strictly, although the Greek text has ἀμφότεροι in both cases. Luke 1:6: *wesun garaihta ba* (“both were righteous”), namely Zacharias and Elizabeth; likewise v. 7; 5:7: *gafullidedun ba þo skipa* (“they filled both boats”); 6:39: *ibai mag blinds blindana tiuhan; niu bai in dal gadriusand?* (“can a blind man lead a blind man? Will not both fall into a pit?”); 7:41: *ains skulda skatte fimfhunda, iþ anþar fimftiguns. 42 ni habandam þan, waþro usgebeina, baim fragaf* (“one owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both”), i.e. both debtors, in contrast to the creditor; Ephesians 2:14: *gatawida þo ba du samin* (“he made the two one”); v. 16: *gafriþoda þans bans in ainamma leika guþa* (“he reconciled both in one body to God”).

> Conversely, Matthew 9:17 and Luke 5:38: *giutand wein juggata in balgins niujans jah bajoþum gabairgada* (“new wine is put into new skins, and both are preserved”), namely the wine and the skins; Ephesians 2:17–18: *gawairþi izwis juzei fairra jah gawairþi þaim izei newa unte þairh ina habam atgagg bajoþs du attin* (“he preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near, because through him we both have access to the Father”), namely you and us as distinct parties; *Skeireins* II, d: *twos ganamnida waihts swesā bajoþum du daupeinais garehsnai* (“two named things, both for the preparation of baptism”), namely body and soul; III, a: *bajoþum daupjandam jah ainwaþarammeh seina anafilhandam daupein miþ sis misso sik adrunnun sumai* (“both baptizing and each prescribing his own baptism, they had certain differences between themselves”), namely John and Christ, who are here opposed with respect to baptism.

> d) For the use of *ains* and *anþar* in coordinated clauses (*ains—anþar*, *anþar—anþar*, etc.: “one—the other,” etc.), see the discussion of compound sentences.

## IV. DISTRIBUTIVE NUMBERS

Except *tweihnai*, “two each” (ἀνὰ δύο), distributives do not occur in Gothic; they are paraphrased by *wazuh* and *warjizuh*, “each,” and by *bi* (κατά): Luke 9:3, *ni waiht nimaiþ in wig, nih tweihnos paidos* (“take nothing for the journey, not even two tunics each”); Mark 7:31, *qam at marein Galeilaie miþ tweihnaim markom* (“he came to the Sea of Galilee through the midst of the borders”), ἀνὰ μέσον τῶν ὁρίων; Mark 6:7, *dugann Iesus þans twalif insandjan twans wazuh* (“Jesus began to send the twelve out two by two”), ἀνὰ δύο; Luke 10:1; 9:14, *gawaurkeiþ im anakumbjan kubituns ana warjanoh fimftiguns* (“make them recline in groups of fifty each”), “fifty by fifty,” ἀνὰ πεντήκοντα; compare Matthew 27:15; Mark 15:6; 1 Corinthians 14:27: *jaþþe razdai was rodjai, bi twans aiþþau maist þrins* (“if anyone speaks in a tongue, [let it be] by two, or at most by three”), κατὰ δύο. “One by one” (καθ’ εἷς) is *ainwarjizuh* in Romans 12:5.

## V. MULTIPLICATIVES AND PROPORTIONALS

*Ainfalþs*, “single”; *fidurfalþs*, “fourfold”; *taihuntaihundfalþs*, “hundredfold”; *managfalþs*, “manifold,” etc., are to be treated as adjectives.

## VI. ITERATIVES

“Once,” “twice,” etc., which in other languages are expressed by adverbs, are rendered in Gothic as “one time,” “two times,” etc.: 2 Corinthians 11:24–25: *fram Iudaium fimf sinþam nam, þrim sinþam wandum usbluggwans was, ainamma sinþa stainiþs was* (“from the Jews I received [lashes] five times; three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned”); Mark 14:72: *anþaramma sinþa hana wopida. jah gamunda Paitrus þata waurd swe qaþ imma Iesus, þatei faurþize hana hrukjai twaim sinþam, inwiais mik þrim sinþam* (“a second time the cock crowed. And Peter remembered the word as Jesus had said to him: Before the cock crows twice, you will deny me three times”); Luke 17:4: *jabai sibun sinþam ana dag frawaurkjai du þus jah sibun sinþam ana dag gawandjai sik* (“if seven times in a day he sins against you and seven times in a day turns back to you”).

With ordinals, *prima*, “the first time,” *secunda*, “the second time,” *tertia*, “the third time,” the neuter accusative is used: 2 Corinthians 12:14: *sai þridjo þata manwus im qiman* (“behold, for the third time I am ready to come”), τρίτον. Compare *frumist*, “firstly,” and *þata anþar*, “for the rest; moreover.”

## 4. THE PRONOUN

### A. THE PERSONAL PRONOUN

## § 199.

1) The personal pronouns are: for the first person, *ik*, “I,” *weis*, “we”; for the second, *þu*, “you,” *jus*, “you [plural]”; for the third, which varies by gender, *is*, “he,” *si*, “she,” plural *eis*, “they”; *sa*, “this,” *so*, “this [feminine],” plural *þai*, “these”; and the reflexive pronoun *sik*, “himself, herself, itself, themselves.”

> **Note 1.** *Is* is identical with Greek αὐτὸς, ὁ, French *il*, “he,” but cannot be used adjectivally for “this” or “that.” *Sa*, however, corresponds to Greek αὐτὸς and οὗτος and is therefore also adjectival. On the distinction between these pronouns, see § 202, I.

2) When a personal pronoun is the subject, it is not ordinarily expressed, because it is already implicitly contained in the verbal ending. Nevertheless, it is explicitly present:

a) With first- and second-person pronouns when they carry some emphasis, especially when set in contrast with another: John 6:20: *ohtedun sis, þaruh qaþ Iesus: ik im, ni ogeiþ izwis* (“they were afraid. Then Jesus said: It is I; do not be afraid”); Luke 10:24: *managai praufeteis jah þiudanos wildedun saiwan, þatei jus saiwiþ* (“many prophets and kings desired to see what you see”); John 15:3: *jus hrainjai sijuþ* (“you are clean”), that is, you do not need to be cleansed; 2 Corinthians 5:21: *Xristus faur uns gatawida frawaurht, ei weis wairþeima garaihtei guþs* (“[God] made Christ sin for us, so that we might become God’s righteousness”); 1 Corinthians 1:23: *aþþan ik weitwod guþ anahaita ana meinai saiwalai* (“but I call God as witness upon my soul”); Luke 1:18: *ik im sineigs jah qens meina framaldrozei in dagam seinaim* (“I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in her days”); Matthew 3:11: *aþþan ik in watin izwis daupja, iþ sa afar mis gagganda swinþoza mis ist* (“I baptize you in water, but he who comes after me is stronger than I”).

Matthew 5:21–22: *hausideduþ þatei qiþan ist þaim airizam: ni maurþjais. aþþan ik qiþa izwis—* (“you have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall not murder. But I say to you—”); 6:12: *aflet uns þatei skulans sijaima, swaswe jah weis afletam þaim skulam unsaraim* (“forgive us what we owe, as we also forgive our debtors”); likewise, with preceding *jah*, 10:32–33; 2 Corinthians 1:6. John 8:15: *jus bi leika stojaiþ, iþ ik ni stoja ainnohun* (“you judge according to the flesh; I judge no one”); v. 21: *þadei ik gagga, jus ni maguþ qiman* (“where I am going, you cannot come”); v. 23: *jus us þaim dalaþro sijuþ, iþ ik us þaim iupaþro im* (“you are from below, but I am from above”); 2 Corinthians 13:9: *faginom, þan weis siukam, iþ jus swinþai sijuþ* (“we rejoice when we are weak and you are strong”); 1 Corinthians 5:12: *niu þans inna jus stojaiþ, iþ þans uta guþ stojiþ* (“do you not judge those within, while God judges those outside?”); 7:12: *þaim anþaraim ik qiþa, ni frauja* (“to the rest I say, not the Lord”); Romans 11:18: *ni þu þo waurts bairis ak so waurts bairiþ þuk* (“it is not you who bear the root, but the root bears you”); Galatians 2:10: *nu ni þanaseiþs ik, iþ libaiþ in mis Xristus* (“it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me”).

In these and many other cases the Goth uses the personal pronoun following the Greek, whose example he likewise follows in what follows: 2 Corinthians 1:4: *ei mageima weis gaþrafstjan* (“so that we may be able to comfort”); Ephesians 1:4, 12, 18; 4:22. More rarely the pronoun is used absolutely, as Matthew 5:17: *ni hugjaiþ ei ik qemjau* (“do not suppose that I came”), although it is not otherwise required, since 10:34 simply reads, with the pronoun omitted, *ni agjaiþ þatei qemjau* (“do not think that I came”). Conversely, the Goth frequently introduces
b) The pronoun of the third person, where the Greek does not use it [Col. 1091]: Matt. 11:23, *jabai ïn saudaumjam vaurþeina mahteis þos vaurþanons in ïzvis, aiþþau eis veseina* (“if the miracles which were done among you had been done in Sodom, they would have remained,” ἔμειναν) until this day; Mark 15:44, *peilatus sildaleikida, ei ïs juþan gasvalt* (“Pilate wondered whether he had already died,” τέθνηκε); 1 Cor. 16:12, *ïna bad, ei ïs qemi* (“I urged him that he should come,” ἔλθῃ) to you; especially often in Luke (1:63; 7:15; 14:14; 18:38) and John (6:21; 9:8, 12, 18; 11:13; 14:17; 18:28, 40). At John 18:38 the pronoun is also present where the subject nevertheless follows: *ïþ eis qeþun du ïmma ïudaieis*, “but the Jews said to him”; see on that passage.
