“Note 2.—After a participial construction dependent on a verb (and consequently not absolute), placed at the beginning of the sentence before its verb, the pronoun—indeed redundant, but following the Greek—is repeated in an oblique case: Eph. 2:5, *visandans uns dauþans fravaurhtim miþgaqivida uns xristau*, “when we were dead through transgressions, he made us alive together with Christ”; Matt. 26:71, *usgaggandan ïna ïn daur gasaw ïna anþara þivi*, “as he went out into the gateway, another maid saw him”; Mark 5:18, *ïnngaggandan ïna ïn skip baþ ïna saei vas vods*, “as he entered the boat, the man who had been possessed begged him”; 9:28, *galeiþandan ïna ïn gard siponjos ïs frehun ïna*, “when he went into the house, his disciples asked him”; Mark 9:9, *dalaþ atgaggandam ïm af fairgunja anabaud ïm*, “as they came down from the mountain, he charged them”; Matt. 8:5, *ïnnutgaggandinïmma ïn kafarnaum duatïddja ïmma hundafaþs*, “as he entered Capernaum, a centurion came to him”; 23, *innatgaggandin ïmma ïn skip afarïddjedun ïmma siponjos ïs*, “as he entered the boat, his disciples followed him”; 28; Mark 5:2; Luke 6:29; 17:12; John 8:30; 12:37.

“The earlier pronoun, however, is absent from the participial construction and is placed only after the verb in Matt. 9:28: *qimandin ïn garda duatïddjedun ïmma þai blindans*, ‘when he came into the house, the blind men came to him.’ The participial construction appears more absolute where the verb is construed with a preposition placed before the repeated pronoun: Matt. 9:27, *warbondin ïesua jainþro laistidedun afar ïmma tvai blindans*, ‘when Jesus departed thence, two blind men followed after him’; 8:1, *dalaþ atgaggandin ïmma af fairgunja laistidedun afar ïmma iumjons managos*, ‘when he came down from the mountain, great crowds followed him’; 27:19, *sitandin ïmma ana stauastola insandida du ïmma qens*, ‘while he sat on the judgment-seat, his wife sent to him’; Mark 5:21; 11:27; Luke 7:6; *Skeireins* IV.a. Elsewhere the preposition must stand even before the participial construction, as in Luke 19:26: *af þamma unhabandin jah þatei habaiþ afnimada af ïmma*, ‘from him who does not have, even what he has shall be taken from him.’ Likewise after a relative: Mark 4:25, *þiswammeh saei habaiþ, gibada ïmma*, ‘for to him who has, it shall be given.’ Compare §202, note 4.

“Note 3.—When, after Greek impersonals, a pronoun follows in a subordinate clause, the Goth omits this personal pronoun where he uses a personal verb in place of the impersonal. He does the same when, in order to express an infinitive clause, he uses a finite verb instead of an infinitive: Luke 17:15, *skal ... manag gaþulan*, ‘he must suffer much’ (French *il doit*, German *er muss*, Greek δεῖ αὐτόν, ‘it is necessary for him’); 19:11, *bi þatei newa ïairusalem vas* (‘because Jerusalem was near,’ διὰ τὸ … αὐτὸν εἶναι); 15, *biþe atvandida sik* (‘when he returned,’ ἐν τῷ ἐπανελθεῖν αὐτόν); John 12:18, *hausidedun ei gatavidedi þo taikn*, ‘they heard that he had performed the sign’ (accusative with infinitive: αὐτὸν πεποιηκέναι); Eph. 4:17, *veitvodja ïn fraujin ei þanaseiþs ni gaggaiþ*, ‘I testify in the Lord that you should no longer walk’ (accusative with infinitive: ὑμᾶς περιπατεῖν); 2 Cor. 8:6, *svaei bedeima teitaun*, ‘so that we urged Titus’ (εἰς τὸ παρακαλέσαι ἡμᾶς).

“The pronoun is rarely placed after the verb: Luke 18:35, *miþþanei newa vas ïs ïaireikon*, ‘as he was approaching Jericho.’ Yet the translator of the Epistle to the Ephesians frequently has it in this manner: Eph. 1:12, *ei sïjaima veis du hazeinai*, ‘that we should be to the praise’ (εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἡμᾶς); 18; 4:22. But in 1:4 Codex A omits *veis*, according to the ordinary usage of the language.

“Note 4.—A substantive, occupying the place of a third-person pronoun, is repeated: 1 Cor. 7:12, *jabai was broþar qen aigi ungalaubjandein jah so gavilja ïst bauan miþ ïmma, ni afletai þo qen*, ‘if a brother has an unbelieving wife and she is willing to live with him, let him not put away the wife’ (this woman; all Greek manuscripts have αὐτήν); likewise v. 13, *ni afletai þana aban*, ‘let her not put away the husband’ (this man; Greek αὐτόν). Here perhaps the translator read τὸν ἄνδρα with certain manuscripts, and thus, for the sake of parallelism, also used *þo qen* rather than *ïja* in the preceding clause.”

3) A second-person pronoun is placed before the address, or also as an apposition to it: Luke 4:23, *pu leiki hailei þuk silban*, “you, physician, heal yourself”; 1 Cor. 7:16, *wa nu kannt, þu qinon*, “for how do you know, woman?” (γύναι); Eph. 5:25, *jus vairos frijoþ qenins ïzvaros*, “you husbands, love your wives” (οἱ ἄνδρες); 6:9, *jus fraujans þata samo taujaiþ*, “you masters, do the same” (οἱ κύριοι; with our punctuation slightly altered it should be read: “and you, masters”); Col. 3:18, *jus qinons ufhausjaiþ vairam ïzvaraim*, “you wives, submit yourselves to your husbands”; 21; 4:1; Gal. 4:21, *giþiþ mis jus uf vitoda viljandans visan þata vitoþ niu hauseiþ*, “tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not hear the law?” (οἱ … θέλοντες); Matt. 25:41, *gaggaiþ fairra mis jus fraqiþanans*, “depart from me, you accursed” (οἱ κατηραμένοι); Luke 6:25, *vai ïzvis jus sadans nu*, “woe to you, you who are now full” (οἱ ἐμπεπλησμένοι).—Mark 9:25, *þu ahma þu unrodjands ïk þus anabiuda usgagg*, “you dumb spirit, I command you: come out”; Luke 10:15, *jah þu kafarnaum þu und himin ushauhido gadrausjaza*, “and you, Capernaum, exalted unto heaven, shall be brought down” (καὶ σὺ Κ. ἡ ἕως οὐρανοῦ ὑψωθεῖσα); Matt. 6:9, *atta unsar þu ïn himinam*, “our Father, you who are in the heavens” (ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς).

“Note 5.—Likewise, the first-person pronoun is placed in apposition in place of the article: Phil. 3:3, *veis sijum bimait veis ahmin guþa skalkinondans*, ‘we are the circumcision, we who serve by the Spirit of God’ (οἱ … λατρεύοντες).”

4) The third-person pronoun *ïs* and the reflexive differ as follows when used as an object:

a) The reflexive refers to the subject of the sentence, whereas *ïs* refers to the object or to something named outside the sentence: Matt. 6:29, *nih saulaumon gavasida sik sve ains þize blomane*, “not even Solomon clothed himself like one of these flowers”; 8:32, *run gavaurhtedun sis alla so hairda*, “the swine rushed headlong, all together”; 27:53, *qinos laistidedun afar ïesua andbahtjandeins ïmma*, “women followed Jesus, ministering to him”; 6:8, *vait atta ïzvar þizei jus þaurbuþ, faur þizei jus bidjaiþ ïna*, “your Father knows what you need before you ask him”; 27:43, *trauaida du guþa, lausjaidau zu ïna*, “he trusted in God; let him deliver him”—that is, God; 8:2, *manna þrutsfill habands ïnvait ïna*, “a leprous man worshipped him”—namely Jesus; 7:24, *saei hauseiþ vaurda meina jah taujïþ þo, galeiko ïn a vaira frodamma*, “whoever hears my words and does them, I will compare him to a wise man”; 5:39, *jabai was þuk stautai bi taihsvon þeina kinnu, vandei ïmma jah þo anþara*, “if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him also the other”; Mark 2:19, *qaþ ïm ïesus ïbai magun sunjus bruþfadis, und þatei miþ ïm ïst bruþfaþs, fastan, sva lagga veila sve miþ sis haband bruþfad, aþþan atgaggand dagos, þan afnimada af ïm sa bruþfaþs*, “Jesus said to them: Can the sons of the bridechamber fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with themselves, they cannot fast; but days will come when the bridegroom shall be taken from them”; John 13:32, *guþ hauheiþ ïna ïn sis jah sunus hauhida ïna*, “God glorifies him—the Son—in himself, and the Son glorifies him—God.”

The same principle applies to a participle in an oblique case with the article, not as though it were expanded into “with him who,” with the object becoming the subject [Col. 1093], but as a simple object, *sik* referring to the subject of the sentence: Mark 2:26, *daveid hlaibans faurlageinais matida jah gaf þaim miþ sis visandam*, “David ate the loaves of presentation and gave them to those who were with him”—that is, with David; Luke 6:4; 32, *jah þai fravaurhtans frijond þans frijondans sik*, “and sinners love those who love them”: not, indeed, those loving themselves, but loving sinners, who constitute the subject; 7:9, *ïesus du þizai afarlaistjandein sis managein qaþ*, “Jesus said to the crowd following him”; 14:12, *qaþ þamma haitandin sik*, “he said to the man who had invited him”; Mark 5:30; Luke 14:31; 18:7; John 7:18; 8:31; 13:16; Rom. 10:12. Hence also Matt. 26:75, *gamunda paitrus vaurdis qiþanis du sis*, “Peter remembered the word spoken to him [Peter].” But where *sik* forms a reflexive expression with the verb, it also refers to the object: Mark 14:67, *þivi gasaw paitru varmjandan sik*, “the maid saw Peter warming himself”; Titus 1:14, *ni atsaiwandans judaiviskaize spilli jah anabusne manne afvandjandane sis sunja*, “not attending to Jewish myths and commandments of men who turn themselves away from the truth.”

b) The same is to be said of the accusative with infinitive, whether it refers to a similar subject: John 7:4, *ni manna ïn analaugnein wa taujiþ jah sokeiþ sik uskunþana visan*, “no one does anything in secret while seeking himself to be publicly known”; Phil. 2:6, *xristus ïn guþaskaunein visands ni vulva rahnida visan sïk galeiko guþa*, “Christ, existing in the form of God, did not regard being equal with God as robbery”; *Skeireins* VIII.a, *ni uslaubida faur mel sik gahaban*, “he did not permit himself to be lifted up before the time”; Luke 6:18, *qemun hausjan ïmma jah hailjan sik sauhte seinaizo*, “they came to hear him and to be healed from their diseases.” Or it may refer to a different subject: Mark 3:14, *ïesus gavaurhta tvalif du visan miþ sis*, “Jesus appointed twelve to be with him”; 5:37, *ïesus ni fralailot ainnohun ïze miþ sis afargaggan*, “Jesus allowed no one of them to go with him”; Luke 8:37, *bedun ïna allai gaujans galeiþan fairra sis*, “all the people begged him to depart from them”; 19:27, *fijands meinai ni vildedun mik þiudanon ufar sis*, “my enemies did not want me to reign over them”; 3:7, *qaþ du þaim atgaggandeim manageim daupjan fram sis*, “he said to the crowds coming to be baptized by him.”

c) In a subordinate clause *sik* refers to the subject of that clause: Mark 2:8, *ufkunnands ïesus ahmin seinamma, þatei sva þai mitodedun sis, qaþ þu ïm*, “Jesus, knowing in his spirit that they were reasoning thus within themselves, said to them”; particularly in clauses expressing intention or purpose: Luke 9:12, *fralet þo managein, ei galeiþandans ïn þos bisunjane haimos bugjaina sis matins*, “dismiss the crowd, so that, going into the surrounding villages, they may procure food for themselves”; John 17:13, *nu du þus gagga jah þata rodja ïn manasedai, ei habaina fahed meina usfullida ïn sis*, “but now I come to you, and I speak these things in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves”; 2 Cor. 5:15, *xristus faur allans gasvalt, ei þai libandans libaina þamma faur sik gasviltandin*, “Christ died for all, so that those who live might live for him who died for them”; 2 Thess. 3:14, *ni blandaiþ ïzvis miþ ïmma, ei gaskamai sik*, “do not associate with him, that he may be ashamed.” Conversely, *ïs* refers to the subject of the principal clause: Matt. 8:27, *wileiks ïst sa, ei jah vindos jah marei ufhausjand ïmma*, “what kind of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?”; Luke 8:32, *bedun ïna, ei uslaubidedi im ïn þo galeiþan*, “they begged him to permit them to enter into them”; John 6:64, *vissa ïesus, was ïst, saei galeiveiþ ïna*, “Jesus knew who it was that did not believe him.”

5) On the formation of reflexive verbs by means of *sik*, and on the frequent expression by it of passive and middle meanings, see §§176.4; 177.5; 178.2; and on the placement of the reflexive pronoun immediately next to the verb, see §176.4.

## § 200. I. The reciprocal pronoun, “one another”

1) It is formed from the personal pronoun and the indeclinable word *misso*: Rom. 14:13, *ni þanamais nu uns misso stojaima*, “let us therefore no longer judge one another” (ἀλλήλους); 19, *laistjaima þoei timreinais sind ïn uns misso*, “let us pursue the things that make for mutual edification”; 1 Cor. 7:5, “[lacuna] *izvara misso*,” “one another of you”; Mark 9:33, *wa ïn viga miþ izvis misso mitodeduþ?*, “what were you discussing among yourselves on the way?”; 50; John 6:43; 13:14, 35; 16:19; Rom. 15:5; Gal. 5:13, 15; Eph. 4:32; 5:21; John 13:34, *frijoþ ïzvis misso*, “love one another” (accusative); 15:12, 17; Rom. 12:10, 16; 15:7; 1 Cor. 16:20; 2 Cor. 13:12; Eph. 4:2; Col. 3:9, 13; 1 Thess. 3:12; 4:9, 18; 5:11; 2 Thess. 1:3; Luke 7:32, *vopjandans seina misso*, “calling to one another”; Gal. 5:17, *þo sis misso andstandand*, “these opposing one another”; Mark 1:27, *sokidedun miþ sis misso*, “they questioned among themselves”; 8:16; 15:31; Luke 20:5, 14; John 6:52; *Skeireins* III.a; Mark 4:41, *qeþun du sis misso*, “they said to one another”; 9:10, 34; 10:26; 11:31; 12:7; 16:3; Luke 2:15; 4:36; 6:11; 8:25; John 7:35; 12:19; 13:22; 16:17.

“Note 1.—*Misso* occurs alone, without a personal pronoun, only in Gal. 5:26: *ni vairþaima flautandans misso ushaitandans, misso ïn neiþa visandans*, ‘let us not become vainglorious, challenging one another, envying one another’—with *uns*, ‘us,’ understood in the first instance and *unsis*, ‘us,’ in the second; and Rom. 13:8, *misso frijoþ*, ‘love one another,’ with *ïzvis*, ‘you,’ understood.

“Note 2.—*Sik misso* is sometimes also used in place of the reflexive; see Note 6.

“Note 3.—On *misso* with a possessive pronoun, see §201.4.”

2) “One another” is expressed in Gothic by *anþar anþaris*: Eph. 4:25, *sijuþ anþar anþaris liþus*, “you are members one of another” (ἀλλήλων); Phil. 2:3, *ïn allai hauheinai gahugdais anþar anþarana munands sis auhuman*, “in all humility, deeming one another superior to yourselves” (ἀλλήλους ἡγησάμενοι ὑπερέχοντας ἑαυτῶν). Hence the mutilated passage Rom. 12:5 is to be restored thus: *aþþan ainwarjizuh anþar anþaris liþus*, “but each [is] a member one of another”; and Matt. 11:16 must likewise have contained *anþar anþaris*; see §239.1.

## II. *Silba* (αὐτός), “self”

In form, since it is declined only consonantally, and in meaning, *silba* must be regarded substantivally. It is used:

1) Ordinarily without a pronoun as subject: “I myself,” 1 Cor. 9:27, *ibai anþaraim merjands silba uskusans vairþau*, “lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be disqualified”; 20; Phil. 2:24. “We ourselves”: 2 Cor. 1:4, *gaþrafstidai sijum silbans fram guþa*, “we ourselves are comforted by God”; 9; Gal. 2:27. “You yourself”: Luke 6:42, *waiva magt qiþan—silba ïn augin þeinamma anza ni gaumjands*, “how can you say—while yourself not noticing the beam in your own eye?” “You yourselves”: 1 Thess. 3:3, *silbans viteiþ*, “you yourselves know”; 5:2; 2 Thess. 3:7. “He himself”: Luke 1:17, *silba fauraqimiþ ïn andvairþja guþs*, “he himself will go before the face of God”; 23; 5:37; 6:3; John 6:6; 9:21; 12:24; Eph. 4:11; *Skeireins* I.a. “They themselves”: Luke 17:13, *silbans ushofon stibna*, “they themselves raised their voice.” As object: “him himself,” John 9:24, *vilban fraihniþ*, “question him.”

Nevertheless, the personal pronoun may also be added as subject; in that case *silba* usually follows the pronoun: 2 Cor. 10:1, *aþþan ïk silba pavlus bidja ïzvis*, “but I myself, Paul, beseech you”; 12:13; 2 Thess. 1:4, *veis silbans ïn ïsvis wopam*, “we ourselves boast among you”; Luke 5:1, *ïs silba vas standands newa saiva*, “he himself was standing by the lake”; 1 Cor. 15:28; Luke 7:12, *si silbo vas vidovo*, “she herself was a widow.” Thus also with a relative: Matt. 27:57, *ïosef, saei jah silba siponida ïesua*, “Joseph, who himself had also become a disciple of Jesus”; Mark 15:43.

This position is regularly occupied in the formula *þata silbo*, corresponding either to Greek αὐτὸ τοῦτο or τοῦτο αὐτό: Gal. 2:10, *usdaudida þata silbo taujan*, “they asked that we should do this very thing”; 2 Cor. 2:3, *þata silbo gamelida ïzvis*, “I wrote this very thing to you”; compare Rom. 13:6. The reciprocal differs, however, in meaning: Rom. 7:25, *silba ïk skalkino vitoda guþs*, “I myself”—that is, “I” emphatically expressed—“serve the law of God”; 9:3. But at 1 Thess. 4:9, *silbans jus at guþa uslaisidai sijuþ*, “you yourselves are taught by God” [Col. 1095], the emphasis rests on *silbans*, and *jus* could have been omitted. *Skeireins* VI.a: *sve silba ïs qiþiþ*, “as he himself says”; this, as we conjecture with Castiglione’s agreement, is the reading of the manuscript in place of *sama ïs*, published by Massmann.

2) When *silba* accompanies a substantive, the latter should properly be regarded as an apposition; *silba* then always precedes it: Mark 12:36, *silba auk daveid qaþ*, “for David himself said”; 37; Luke 20:42; 3:23, *jah silba vas ïesus sve jere þrijetigive*, “and Jesus himself was about thirty years old”; John 16:27, *ak silba atta frijoþ ïzvis*, “for the Father himself loves you”; subscription to 1 Cor.: *du kaurinþium frumei þugkeiþ bi silbins apaustaulaus ïnsahtai melida visan us asiai*, “To the Corinthians: it seems to have been first written through Silvanus the apostle, [and] sent from Asia” [the syntax is uncertain as printed]; 2 Cor. 7:11, *saiw auk silbo þata bi guþ saurgan ïzvis welauda gatavida ïzvis usdaudein*, “for behold, this very thing—your godly sorrow—what diligence it produced in you!”; 11:14, *silba satana gagaleikoþ sik aggilau liuhadis*, “Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light”; Eph. 2:20, *at visandin auhumistin vaihstastaina silbin xristau ïesu*, “Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone”; 1 Thess. 3:11; 4:16; 5:23; 2 Thess. 2:16; 3:16; *Skeireins* V.d. Luke 4:41 has *vissedun silban xristu ïna visan*, “they knew him to be Christ,” for τὸν Χριστόν; and Mark 4:28, *silbo auk airþa akran bairiþ*, does not mean “the earth itself bears fruit,” but “the earth bears fruit of itself, spontaneously.”

3) When *silba* is added to a personal pronoun to form a reflexive, it follows it: “to myself” (ἐμαυτῷ, ἑαυτῷ), Luke 7:8, *haba uf mis silbin gadrauhtins*, “I have under myself soldiers”; John 7:17, 28; 8:28, 42; 10:18; 12:49; 14:3, 10; 1 Cor. 4:4; “myself” (ἐμαυτόν, ἑαυτόν), Luke 7:7, *ni mik silban vair þana rahnida at þus qiman*, “I did not consider myself worthy to come to you”; John 8:14, 18, 54; 14:21; 17:19; 1 Cor. 4:3; 7:7; 2 Cor. 11:7, 9; 12:5; Gal. 2:18; Phil. 3:13. “To ourselves” (ἑαυτοῖς), 2 Cor. 1:9, *ïn uns silbam andahaft dauþaus habaidedum*, “we had the sentence of death in ourselves”; 3:5. “Ourselves” (ἑαυτούς), 2 Cor. 3:1, *duginnam aftra uns silbans anafilhan*, “do we begin again to commend ourselves?”; 4:2, 5; 10:12; *unsis silbans*, 2 Thess. 3:9. “To yourself” (σεαυτῷ), John 17:5, *hauhei mik at þus silbin*, “glorify me with yourself”; 18:34; 1 Thess. 4:16. “Yourself” (σεαυτόν, ἑαυτόν), Matt. 8:4, *gagg þuk silban ataugei gudjin*, “go, show yourself to the priest”; Mark 1:44; 12:31; 15:30; Luke 4:23; 5:14; 10:27; John 7:4; 8:13, 53; 14:22; Rom. 13:9; Gal. 5:14; 6:1; 1 Tim. 4:16; 2 Tim. 2:15; Philem. 19. “To yourselves” (ἑαυτοῖς), John 6:53, *ni habaiþ libain ïn ïzvis silbam*, “you do not have life in yourselves”; Rom. 11:25; 12:16; 1 Cor. 5:13. “Yourselves” (ἑαυτούς), Luke 16:15, *garaihtans domeiþ ïzvis silbans ïn andvairþja manne*, “you justify yourselves before men”; Rom. 12:19; Col. 3:16. “To himself/herself/itself” (singular ἑαυτῷ), Mark 5:30, *ïesus ufkunþa ïn sis silbin þo us sis maht usgaggandein*, “Jesus, knowing in himself that power had gone forth from him”; Luke 9:25; 18:4; John 6:61; 7:18; 8:22; 11:38; 15:4; 16:13; 1 Cor. 11:29; 16:2; 2 Cor. 10:7; Gal. 6:3, 4; Eph. 2:15, 16. “Himself/herself/itself” (singular ἑαυτόν), Mark 3:26, *satana usstoþ ana sik silban*, “Satan rose up against himself”; 8:34; 15:31; Luke 9:23; 14:11; 18:14; John 11:33; 19:7, 12; Rom. 14:14 (*sik silbo*, neuter); 1 Cor. 11:28; 2 Cor. 10:7, 18; Gal. 1:4; 2:20; Eph. 5:2, 25, 28; Phil. 2:7, 8; 1 Tim. 2:8; 2 Tim. 2:13. “To themselves” (plural ἑαυτοῖς), Matt. 9:3, *sumai þize bokarje qeþun ïn sis silbam*, “some of the scribes said within themselves”; Luke 7:49; 2 Cor. 5:15; 10:12. “Themselves” (plural ἑαυτούς), 2 Cor. [Col. 1096] 8:5, *sik silbans atgebun frumist fraujin*, “they gave themselves first to the Lord”; Eph. 4:19; 1 Tim. 6:10.

“Note 4.—*Silba* departs from its ordinary position after the personal pronoun when it is not construed in the same case as the pronoun, but as a subject, after the pattern of Latin *se* or *sibi ipse*: Luke 18:9, *qaþ du sumaim, þaiei silbans trauaidedun sis*, ‘he spoke to some who trusted in themselves’ (πεποιθότας ἐφ’ ἑαυτοῖς: ‘trusting in themselves’), ‘that they were righteous’; Rom. 13:2, *þai andstandandans silbans sis vargiþa nimand*, ‘those who resist shall receive judgment for themselves’ (ἑαυτοῖς, ‘to themselves’). Thus in 2 Cor. 2:1, *gastauïda þata silba at mis* (ἔκρινα ἐμαυτῷ τοῦτο, ‘I determined this with myself’) must be read instead of the unintelligible *þata silbo*.

“The ambiguous plural form *silbans* is also used in the nominative, as is clear from its position in 1 Cor. 11:31: *jabai silbans uns stauïdedeina*, ‘if we ourselves judged ourselves,’ not [lacuna] is used. Compare 2 Cor. 13:5, *ïzvis silbans fraisiþ, sijaidu ïn galaubeinai. silbans ïzvis kauseiþ*, ‘test yourselves, whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves’; Eph. 5:27, *xristus sik silban atgaf faur aikklesjon, ei ustauhi silba sis vulþaga aikklesjon*, ‘Christ gave himself for the church, that he might present to himself a glorious church.’

“Note 5.—The personal pronoun is elliptically omitted only in Col. 3:13: *þulandans ïzvis misso jah fragibandans silbans*, ‘bearing with one another and forgiving yourselves [one another]’; here the preceding *ïzvis* must also be supplied. Compare §§176, note; 177, note 2; 178, note 3.

“Note 6.—Conversely, *silba* is often omitted and the simple personal pronoun remains reflexive: Luke 16:9, *taujaiþ ïzvis frijonds*, ‘make friends for yourselves’ (ἑαυτοῖς); 17:14, *gaggandans ataugeiþ ïzvis gudjam*, ‘go, show yourselves to the priests’ (ἑαυτούς); John 12:8, *unledans sinteino habaiþ miþ ïzvis*, ‘you always have the poor with you’ (ἑαυτῶν); 2 Cor. 7:11; John 12:32, *alla at þinsa du mis*, ‘I will draw all to myself’ (ἐμαυτόν); Rom. 14:12, *warjizuh unsara fram sis raþjon usgibiþ guþa*, ‘each of us shall give an account of himself to God’ (ἑαυτοῦ); 2 Cor. 4:5, *merjam uns skalkans ïzvarans*, ‘we proclaim ourselves your servants’ (ἑαυτούς)—here, and in 10:12, *silbans* is to be supplied from the preceding words; compare Note 5; 6:4.

“Note 7.—In Mark and John the reciprocal is sometimes used for the Greek reflexive: Mark 1:27, *sokidedun miþ sis misso*, ‘they questioned among themselves’ (πρὸς ἑαυτούς); 9:10, *þata vaurd habaidedun du sis misso sokjandans*, ‘they kept the saying to themselves, debating it’; 11:31, *þahtedun du sis misso qiþandans*, ‘they reasoned among themselves, saying’; 16:3; John 7:35; 12:19.

“Note 8.—On *silba* joined with a possessive pronoun, see §201.4.”

## III. *Sama* (ὁ αὐτός), “the same”

*Sama* occurs only in the consonantal declension, whether because it was originally a substantive or because it denotes the identity of a known object already mentioned. It is therefore very often joined to the demonstrative/article: *sa sama* (French *ce même, le même*), “this same, the same.” It is used:

1) Substantivally: *Skeireins* VII.d, *gamaudida gaumjan, þatei ïs vas sa sama, saei ïn auþidai ·m· jere attans ïze fodida*, “he recalled that he was the same one who fed their fathers in the wilderness for forty years”; V.b, *ïþ ains jah sa sama vesi*, “but [that] the Father and the Son are one and the same”; *waiva stojan jah ni stojan sa sama mahtedi*, “how can the same power stand and not stand?” 1 Cor. 11:5, *woh qinono bidjandei aiþþau praufetjandei andhulidamma haubida gaaiviskoþ haubiþ sein, ain auk ïst jah þata samo þizai biskabanon*, “every woman praying or prophesying with her head uncovered dishonours her head, for it is one and the same as the woman who has been shaven” [Col. 1097]; Matt. 5:46, *niu jah þai þiudo þata samo taujand?*, “do not even the Gentiles do the same?” Likewise Matt. 27:44; Mark 10:10; Luke 6:33; Rom. 12:16; 15:5; Eph. 6:9; Phil. 2:2; 3:1 (*þosamona*, plural); 4:2 (where “the same” should be read instead of “himself” in our translation); 1 Thess. 2:14. Also *samo* simply, without the demonstrative: 2 Cor. 13:11, *samo fraþjaiþ*, “think the same thing” (τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖτε); Phil. 3:16, *gasnevum, ei samo hugjaima jah samo fraþjaima*, “let us walk according to the same rule and think the same thing.”

2) Adjectivally. In this case it should be noted that, if another adjective is also added to the substantive, it too assumes the consonantal form: Luke 2:8, *hairdjos vesun ïn þamma samin landa þairhvakandans*, “there were shepherds in that same region, keeping watch”; 6:38, *þizai samon mitadjon, þizaiei mitid, mitada ïzvis*, “with the same measure with which you measure, it shall be measured to you”; Rom. 9:21, *habaiþ kasja valdufni þahons us þamma samin daiga sum du galaubamma taujan sumuþ-þan du ungalaubamma kasa*, “does not the potter have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honour and another for dishonour?”; 12:4, *allai ni þata samo tauï habaud*, “all the members do not have the same function”; 1 Cor. 10:3, *allai þana saman mat ahmeinan matidedun jah þata samo dragk ahmeino drugkun*, “all ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink”; 2 Cor. 1:6, *þreihanda ïn naseinais þizos vaurstveigons ïn stivitja þizo samono þulaine, þozei jah veis vinnam*, “whether we are afflicted, it is for your consolation and salvation, effective in the endurance of the same sufferings which we also suffer”; 3:14 (where “the same” should be read instead of “himself” in our translation); 18; 4:13; 6:13; 8:16; 12:18; Phil. 1:30; 2:2; 1 Cor. 12:11, *þata all vaurkeiþ ains jah sa sama ahma*, “all these things are effected by one and the same Spirit.” *Sama* without the article occurs rarely: Rom. 10:12, *ni ïst gaskaideins ïudaiaus jah krekis, sama auk frauja allaize*, “there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, for the same Lord is Lord of all”; Phil. 3:16, *samon gaggan garaideinai*, “to walk by the same rule.”

“Note 9.—That *sama* is also used for εἷς, ‘one,’ where it denotes a whole arisen or formed from two objects, etc., see §198, note 2(b).”

# B. THE POSSESSIVE PRONOUN

## §201. 1) Possessive pronouns of the first and second persons

*Meins*, “my” (ὁ μου, ἐμός); *unsar*, “our” (ὁ ἡμῶν, ἡμέτερος); *þeins*, “thy” (ὁ σου, σός); *ïzvar*, “your” (ὁ ὑμῶν, ὑμέτερος); and *ïggqar*, “of you both” (ὁ ὑμῶν), agree as adjectives with their substantive in gender, number, and case. Although they normally follow their substantives, they may precede them where they convey emphasis: Matt. 9:18, *dauhtar meina nu gasvalt*, “my daughter has just died”; 27:46, *guþ meins, guþ meins, duwe mis bilaist*, “my God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”; Mark 9:24, *hilp meinaizos ungalaubeinais*, “help my unbelief”; Luke 1:46–47, *mikileid saivala meina fraujan jah svigneid ahma meins du guþa nasjand meinamma*, “my soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Saviour”; Neh. 5:14, *ïk jah broþrjus meinai hlaif fauramaþleis meinis ni matidedum*, “I and my brothers have not eaten the bread allotted to the governor”; Matt. 5:30, *jabai taihsvo þeina handus þuk marzjai*, “if your right hand causes you to stumble”; 6:6, *ïþ þu þan bidjais, gagg ïn heþjon þeina jah galukands haurdai þeinai bidei du attin þeinamma jah atta þeins usgibiþ þus*, “but when you pray, go into your chamber, shut your door, pray to your Father, and your Father shall reward you”; Mark 3:32–33, *aiþei þeina jah broþrjus þeinai jah svistrjus þeinos uta sokjand þuk*, “your mother, your brothers, and your sisters are outside seeking you”; 12:30, *frijos fraujan guþ þeinana us allamma hairtin þeinamma jah us allai saivalai þeinai*, “love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul”; Luke 1:44, *sunsei varþ stibna goleinais þeinaizos ïn ausam meinaim lailaik þata barn ïn vambai meinai*, “as soon as the sound of your greeting came into my ears, the child leaped in my womb”; 20:42–43, *qaþ frauja du fraujin meinamma: sit af taihsvon meinai, unte ïk galagja fijands þeinans fotubaurd fotive þeinaize*, “the Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet”; John 8:54, *ïst atta meins, saei hauheiþ mik, þanei jus qiþiþ, þatei guþ unsar ïst*, “it is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say, ‘He is our God’”; Rom. 15:4, *du unsarai laiseinai gameliþ varþ*, “it was written for our instruction”; 2 Cor. 8:23, *traua ïn ïzvis, jaþþe bi teitu, saei ïst gaman mein jah gavaurstva ïn ïzvis, jaþþe broþrjus unsarai apaustauleis aikklesjono*, “whether concerning Titus, who is my partner and fellow-worker among you, or our brothers, apostles of the churches”; 7:4, *ufarfulliþs ïm fahedais ïn allaizos managons aglons unsaraizos*, “I am overflowing with joy in all our affliction”; 8:24, *ustaiknein friaþvos ïzvaraizos jah unsaraizos woftuljos*, “the proof of your love and of our boasting”; Matt. 5:16, *ei gasaiwaina ïzvara goda vaurstva*, “that they may see your good works”; 10:30, *ïzvara jah tagla haubidis alla garaþana sind*, “even all the hairs of your head are numbered”; Phil. 2:25, *þarb munda aipafraudeitu broþar jah gavaurstvan meinana ïþ ïzvarana apaustaulu sandjan du ïzvis*, “I considered it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother and fellow-worker and your apostle”; 2 Cor. 1:14, *woftuli ïzvara sijum svasve jah jus unsara ïn daga fraujins*, “we are your boast, just as you are ours, on the day of the Lord”; Matt. 9:29, *bi galaubeinai ïggqarai vairþai ïggqis*, “according to your faith, let it be done to you both.”

2) The possessive pronoun of the third person:

a) It is *seins*, “his, her, its, their own” (ὁ ἑαυτοῦ, ἑαυτῶν, αὐτοῦ, αὐτῶν, ἴδιος), or the genitive of the personal pronoun, *ïs, ïs, ïzos, ïze, ïzo*, “his, her, their” (αὐτοῦ, αὐτῶν). Now *seins* refers to the subject of the sentence, while the genitive of *ïs* refers to something named outside the sentence or to the object of that sentence. As regards position, *seins* is placed relative to its substantive in the same manner described above under 1; nevertheless, it normally precedes where it corresponds to Greek ἴδιος, “one’s own”: Matt. 5:45, *guþ sunnon seina urranneiþ ana ubilans jah godans*, “God makes his sun rise upon evil and good”; 10:24, *nist siponeis ufar laisarja nih skalks ufar fraujin seinamma*, “a disciple is not above his teacher, nor a slave above his master”; Luke 1:8, *miþþanei gudjinoda ïs ïn vikon kunjis seinis, hlauts ïmma urrann du saljan*, “while he performed priestly service in the order of his own division, the lot fell to him to offer [incense]”; 3:17, *habaiþ vinþis kauron in handau seinai jah gahraineiþ gaþrask sein jah briggiþ kaurn in bansta seinamma*, “he has a winnowing shovel in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing-floor and gather the grain into his barn”; Eph. 5:28, *vairos skulun frijon seinos qenins sve leika seina*, “husbands ought to love their own wives as their own bodies”; Rom. 10:3, *seina garaihtein sokjandans stiurjan garaihtein guþs ni ufhausidedun*, “seeking to establish their own righteousness, they did not submit to God’s righteousness”; Mark 8:23, *ïesus ustauh blindan jah speivands ïn augonaïs atlagida ana handuns seinos*, “Jesus led the blind man out and, spitting into his eyes, laid his hands upon him”: *αὐτοῦ* first means the blind man’s eyes, but then Jesus’ own hands; John 11:2, *marja salboda fraujan balsana jah bisvarb fotuns ïs skufta seinamma*, “Mary anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet”—the master’s—with her own hair; Matt. 6:14, *afletiþ mannam missadedins ïze*, “forgive people their trespasses”; 7:16, *bi akranam ïze ufkunnaiþ ïns*, “by their fruits you shall know them”; 26:65, *gahausïdeduþ þo vajamerein ïs*, “you have heard his blasphemy”—that is, Christ’s; John 11:1, *vas sums siuks lazarus af beþanias us haimai marjins jah marþins svistrs ïzos*, “there was a certain sick man, Lazarus of Bethany, from the village of Mary and her sister Martha.”

b) The same applies to this pronoun in a complex sentence. *Seins* is not, as in Latin, joined with different subjects by referring in a subordinate sentence to the subject of the principal sentence: Luke 5:15, *garunnun hiuhmans managai leikinon fram ïmma sauhte seinaizo*, “great crowds came together to hear and to be healed of their diseases”; Matt. 6:5, *qiþa ïzvis, þatei haband mizdon seina*, “I tell you that they have their reward”; 7, *þugkeiþ ïm, ei ïn filuvaurdein seinai andhausjaindau*, “they think that through their many words they shall be heard”; 9:38, *bidjiþ fraujan asanais ei ussandjai vaurstvjans ïn asan seina*, “ask the Lord of the harvest to send workers into his harvest”; 1 Cor. 7:11, *anabiuda qenai fairra abin ni skaidan. ïþ jabai gaskaidnai, visan unliugaidai aiþþau du abin seinamma aftra gagavairþjan*, “I command the wife not to separate from her husband; but if she separates, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband”; Matt. 7:24, *wazuh saei hauseiþ vaurda meina jah taujiþ þo, galeiko ïna vaira frodamma, saei gatimrida razn sein ana staina*, “whoever hears these words of mine and does them, I will compare him to a wise man who built his house upon the rock”; Luke 1:20, *ni galaubides vaurdam meinaim, þoei usfulljanda in mela seinamma*, “you did not believe my words, which shall be fulfilled in their time”; 1:23, *varþ biþe usfullnodedun dagos andbahteis ïs, galaiþ du garda seinamma*, “when the days of his service, that is, Zechariah’s, were completed, Zechariah went to his own house”; 41, *varþ sve hausida aileisabaiþ golein mariïns, lailaik barn ïn qiþau ïzos*, “when Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the child leaped in her womb”; Matt. 7:28, *varþ þan ustauh ïesus þo vaurda, biabridedun manageins ana laiseinai ïs*, “when Jesus had finished these sayings, the crowds were astonished at his teaching”; 8:34, *alla so baurgs usïddja viþra ïesu jah bedun ïna, ei usliþi hindar markos ïze*, “the whole city went out to meet Jesus and begged him to depart from their territory”; Mark 7:26, *qino baþ ïesu, ei unhulþon usvaurpi us dauhtr ïzos*, “the woman begged Jesus to cast the demon out of her daughter”; Matt. 10:35, *qam skaidan mannan viþra attan ïs jah dauhtar viþra aiþein ïzos jah bruþ viþra svaihron ïzos*, “I came to divide a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law”; Mark 12:19, *moses gamelida unsis, þatei jabai wis broþar gadauþnai jah bileiþai qenai jah barne ni bileiþai, ei nimai broþar ïs þo ïs jah ussatjai barna broþr seinamma*, “Moses wrote for us: if a man’s brother dies, leaves a wife, and leaves no child, his brother shall take the wife and raise up offspring for his brother”; John 11:19, *managai gaqemun bi marþan jah marjan, ei gaþrafstidedeina ïjos bi þana broþar ïzo*, “many came to Martha and Mary to comfort them concerning their brother”; Matt. 11:20, *dugann ïdveitjan baurgim, ïn þaimei vaurþun þos managistons mahteis ïs*, “he began to reproach the cities in which his greatest mighty works had occurred”; John 8:55, *kann ïna jah vaurd ïs fasta*, “I know him and keep his word”; Matt. 8:14, *qimands ïesus ïn garda paitraus jah gasaw svaihronïs ligandein ïn heitom jah attaitok handau ïzos*, “Jesus came into Peter’s house, saw his mother-in-law lying feverish, and touched her hand.”

“Note 1.—Exceptions to this rule are only rare. Moreover, *seins* is correctly used in place of *ïs*: Mark 5:17, *dugunnun bidjan ïna galeiþan hindar markos seinos*, ‘they began to beg him to depart from their territory’; 1 Thess. 3:12–13, *ïzvis frauja ganohnan gataujai friaþvai ïn ïzvis misso, du tulgjan hairtona izvara unfairinona ïn veihiþai faura guþa ïn quma fraujins unsaris ïesuis xristaus miþ allaim þaim veiham seinaim*, ‘may the Lord make you abound in love among yourselves, in order to establish your hearts blameless in holiness before God at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints,’ where ‘at the coming of Christ’ must be understood as ‘when Christ comes.’

“Conversely, *ïs* is incorrectly introduced in place of *seins*: 2 Thess. 1:10, *qimiþ ushauhjan ïn þaim veiham ïs*, ‘when he comes to be glorified in his saints’; 1 Tim. 5:18, *vairþs sa vaurstva mizdons ïs*, ‘the worker is worthy of his reward.’”

c) Hence it legitimately follows that, where in a coordinate or comparative sentence a pronoun is joined to the latter subject while referring to the former, that pronoun is expressed by *ïs*: Matt. 10:25, *ganah siponi ei vairþai sve laisareis ïs jah skalks sve frauja ïs*, “it is enough for the disciple to become like his teacher, and the slave like his master”; 6:40, *nist siponeis ufar laisari seinana, ïþ gamanvids warjizuh vairþai sve laisaris ïs*, “a disciple is not above his own teacher, but everyone fully trained shall be like his teacher”; Luke 1:5, *vas gudja namin zakarias us afar jah abijins jah qeins ïs us dauhtrum aharons*, “there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah, and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron”; 1 Cor. 10:26, *fraujins ïst airþa jah fullo ïzos*, “the earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness.” Hence *seins* does not occur in the nominative.

3) The Goth sometimes uses a possessive in place of the article because it is more definite; in this case the possessive always follows its substantive: John 4:31, *ïk frijoda attan meinana*, “I loved the Father” (τὸν πατέρα); 2 Cor. 12:7; Gal. 6:17, *stakins fraujins unsaris ïesuis xristaus ana leika baira*, “I bear on my body the marks of the Lord Jesus Christ” (τοῦ κυρίου); 1 Cor. 7:16, *wa kannt, guma, þatei qen þeina ganasjais*, “how do you know, husband, whether you will save the wife?” (τὴν γυναῖκα); Phil. 1:25, *visa jah þaihvisa at allaim ïzvis du ïzvarai framgahtai jah fahedai galaubeinais ïzvaraizos*, “I know that I shall remain with you all for your progress and joy in the faith” (τῆς πίστεως); Col. 3:19; especially *seins*: Matt. 8:20, *suus mans ni habaiþ, war haubiþ sein anahnaivjai*, “the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (τὴν κεφαλήν); Mark 1:41; 7:10–11; Luke 7:44 (*tagram seinaim*, “with [her] tears”); 10:21, 23; 18:13; 2 Cor. 8:4; Col. 2:14; 2 Thess. 1:11.

“Note 2.—The possessive is omitted only rarely: Matt. 5:31, *wazuh saei afletiþ qen, gibai ïzai afstassais bokos*, ‘whoever puts away a wife, let him give her a bill of divorce’ (τὴν γυναῖκα αὑτοῦ, ‘his wife’); John 7:3, *gagg ïn ïudaian, ei jah þai siponjos saiwaina vaurstva þeina*, ‘go into Judea, that your disciples also may see your works’ (οἱ μαθηταί σου).”

4) When *silba* is joined to a possessive pronoun, it is put in the genitive, agreeing in gender and number with the word to which the possessive itself refers. This *silba*, and likewise reciprocal *misso*, follow the possessive: Luke 2:35, *þeina silbons saivala þairhgaggiþ hairus*, “a sword shall pierce your own soul” (σοῦ αὐτῆς τὴν ψυχήν); 14:26, *jabai was gaggiþ du mis jah ni fijaiþ attan seinana jah aiþein-nanhuþ—þan seina silbins saivala, ni mag meins siponeis visan*, “if anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother … and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple”; Gal. 6:4, *vaurstv sein silbins kiusai warjizuh*, “let each examine his own work”; Eph. 5:28, *sein silbins leik frijoþ, saei seina qen frijoþ*, “he loves his own body who loves his wife”; Gal. 6:2, *izvaros misso kauriþos bairaiþ*, “bear one another’s burdens.”

“Note 3.—Only once does 1 Cor. 10:29 occur: *þuhtu qiþa ni silbins ak anþaris*, ‘I mean not your own conscience, but that of another’; here *þeina* or *ïzvarana* is missing before *silbins*.”

5) The substantive to which the possessive belongs may also receive the article: Matt. 9:6, *nim þana ligr þeinana*, “take up your bed”; 14, *þai siponjos þeinai ni fastand*, “your disciples do not fast”; Mark 2:18, *þai þeinai siponjos ni fastand*, “your disciples do not fast”; Matt. 6:12, *afletam þaim skulam unsaraim*, “we forgive our debtors”; 2 Cor. 3:5, *so vairþida unsara us guþa ïst*, “our sufficiency is from God”; Matt. 5:47, *duwe miþ motarjam matjiþ sa laisareis ïzvar*, “if you eat with tax collectors, [what do] your teachers [do?]”; Luke 5:4, *athahid þo natja ïzvara du fiskon*, “let down your nets for a catch”; 2 Cor. 4:16, *sautana unsar manna fravardjada*, “our outward man is perishing”; Matt. 5:47; 9:11; Mark 2:9, 11; 3:5; 5:34; 7:9, 13; 13:18; Luke 2:48; 5:14; 6:35; 9:41; 10:11; 15:30; 19:20, 39, 42; John 8:13, 19, 44; 9:19; 16:20, 22; 18:35; 19:7; 1 Cor. 15:14, 17; Col. 1:7.

b) Possessives are also used, in the manner of adjectives, in singular and plural, with or without the article, concretely and abstractly, like substantives: Mark 6:21, *herodis mela gabaurþais nahtamat vaurhta þaim maistam seinaize*, “Herod, on the day of his birthday, made a banquet for his nobles” (τοῖς μεγιστᾶσιν αὑτοῦ); Mark 5:19, *gagg du garda þeinamma du þeinaim*, “go home to your own people” (τοὺς σούς); John 8:44, *þan diabaulus rodeiþ liugn, us seinamma rodeiþ*, “when the devil speaks a lie, he speaks from his own [resources]” (ἐκ τῶν ἰδίων); 16:14, *ahma sunjos us meinamma nimiþ jah gateihiþ ïzvis*, “the Spirit of truth shall take from what is mine and declare it to you” (ἐκ τοῦ ἐμοῦ); 1 Cor. 10:24, *ni ainshun sein sokjai ak anþaris warjizuh*, “let no one seek his own [advantage], but that of another”; 13:5, *friaþva ni sokeiþ sein ain*, “love does not seek its own [interests]”; Mark 5:26, *qens fraqam allamma seinamma*, “the woman had spent all that she possessed” (τὰ παρ’ αὐτῆς πάντα); Luke 15:31, *all þata mein þein ïst*, “all that is mine is yours”; John 17:10, *meina alla þeina sind jah þeina meina*, “all things that are mine are yours, and yours are mine”; Phil. 2:4, *ni þo seina warjizuh mitondans ak jah þo anþaraize*, “each looking not to his own interests, but also to those of others.”

[Col. 1101]

# C. DEMONSTRATIVES

## §202. I. *Sa, so, þata*: “this, that”

*Sa, so, þata*—“this, that”—refers to an object near the speaker. It is used substantivally and adjectivally.

1) When it takes the place of a substantive, it corresponds to Greek αὐτός, and:

a) In the first case it usually differs from *ïs*, just as perhaps in German strong and stressed *der* differs from weaker and unstressed *er*, or as French *lui* differs from *il*: Matt. 5:8, *andagai þai hrainjahairtans, unte þai guþ gasaiwand*, “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (αὐτοί; German *die*, French *eux*); 25:44, *andhafjand jah þai qiþandans*, “then they too shall answer, saying”; Mark 12:6, *snauhþanuh ainana sunu aigand liubana sis ïnsandida jah þana du ïm*, “having still one beloved son, he sent him also to them” (with *þana*, like German stressed *den*); Luke 9:35, *sa ïst sunus meins sa liuba, þamma hausjaiþ*, “this is my beloved Son; listen to him” (German stressed *den*); John 6:50, *sa ïst hlaifs, saei us himina atstaig, ei saei þis matjai ni gadauþnai*, “this is the bread that came down from heaven, so that whoever eats of it may not die.” For further examples see the glossary under *V. þata*.
b) Where αὐτός refers twice to the same substantive, the first is expressed by ïs, which, by reason of its substantive nature, appropriately takes the place of the substantive; the latter, conversely, by sa. Thus in all parallel passages one reads: saei bigitiþ saivala seina, fraqisteiþ ïzai, juh saei fraqisteiþ saivalai seinai in meina, bigitiþ þo, “he who finds his life shall lose it, and he who loses his life for my sake shall find it,” Matt. X.39; Mark VIII.35; Luke IX.24; XVII.33. Matt. VI.26: atta ïzvar fodeiþ ïns, niu jus mais vulþrizans sijuþ þaim? “your Father feeds them; are you not of more value than they?” Luke IV.41: gasakands ïm ni lailot þos rodjan, “rebuking them, he did not permit them to speak.” John XVI.4: þata rodida ïzvis, ei biþe qimai so weila ïze, gamuneiþ þize, “I have told you this, so that, when their hour comes, you may remember them.”

Yet sa is also repeated twice: Matt. XXVII.6–7: ni skuld ïst lagjan þans [skattans] ïn kaurbanaun—usbauhtedum us þaim þana akr kasjins, “it is not lawful to put them [the coins] into the treasury—they bought with them the potter’s field”; Mark VIII.7. Likewise ïs too is used twice: Mark IX.14: gesaw filu manageins bi ïns [siponjans] jah bokarjans sokjandans miþ ïm, “he saw a great crowd around them [the disciples], and scribes disputing with them”; 15.

Where αὐτός occurs three times, ïs—sa—sa is to be used, as in Mark I.30–31: svaihra simonis lag ïn brinnon, jah suns qeþun ïmma bi ïja, jah duatgaggands urraisida þo—jah aflailot þo so brinno, “Simon’s mother-in-law lay sick with fever, and immediately they told him about her; and, coming to her, he raised her up—and the fever left her”; John X.28–29. Yet sa is used three times in Mark XII.21–23; John X.18. But if the first αὐτός is emphatic, sa precedes and ïs follows (sa—ïs): Mark IX.25: usgagg us þamma jah þanaseiþs ni galeiþais ïn ïna, “come out of him, and enter into him no more”; XIV.6; Col. II.14.

c) Where it refers to a relative: Mark XIV.44: þammei kukja, sa ïst, greipiþ þana, “he whom I kiss, that is he: seize him”; John XIV.10: atta, saei ïn mis ïst, sa taujiþ þo vaurstva, “the Father who is in me, he performs the works”; 21; XVIII.11; Phil. IV.3.

d) Sa is especially placed at the end of a sentence, so that it may end fully and emphatically: Matt. VI.8: ni galeikoþ nu þaim, “therefore do not be like them”; VII.13–14: braid daur jah managai sind ïnngaleiþandans þairh þata. þraihans vigs sa brigganda ïn libainai jah favai sind þai bigitandans þana, “broad is the gate, and many are those entering through it. Narrow is the way leading to life, and few are those finding it”; 24: wazuh saei hauseiþ vaurda meina jah taujiþ þo, galeiko ïna vaira frodamma, “everyone who hears my words and does them, I compare him to a wise man”; Mark VI.3; IX.28; X.14; XII.17; XIV.5; XV.29 (absent from the Greek); Luke VI.47; XVIII.16; XIX.23; John V.36; X.3, 17; XII.7; XIII.17; XVII.10; XVIII.38; Rom. XIII.3; Eph. V.25; Col. III.7, 19; 1 Tim. IV.16, etc.

[Col. 1102]

e) Always in the expressions afar þata, “after that,” ïn þis, “because of this,” etc.; see the glossary under *Afar* and *In*.

f) It is also, and distinctively, used for οὗτος, more rarely for ἐκεῖνος: Matt. V.37: þata managizo þaim (τούτων) us þamma ubilin ïst, “what is more than these is from evil”; VI.32: all þata (ταῦτα) þiudos sokjand, “the nations seek all these things”; IX.3: sumai bokarje qeþun: sa (οὗτος) vajamereiþ, “some scribes said: this man blasphemes”; Mark X.15: þata utgaggando us mann þata (ἐκεῖνα) ïst þata gamainjando mannam, “what proceeds from a man, those things are what defile the man”; XII.4: jah þana (κἀκεῖνον) stainam vairpandans gaaiviskodedun, “and him also they stoned and wounded.” For other examples see the glossary under þata.

g) Where joined to a relative (sa saei, sa ïze), it is equivalent to Latin *(is) qui*, Greek ὅς; see §203, 2) and 3).

> Note 1.—It also sometimes means “this very same” (αὐτός οὗτος), indeed only in the formula du þamma, “to this,” 2 Cor. V.5; Eph. VI.18. But whether the passage Mark XIV.10, where it stands for ὁ τοιοῦτος, is corrupt is doubtful, since elsewhere sa svaleiks is read. As for the few cases in which it is used instead of a relative—Luke IX.31: vairos tvai miþrodidedun ïmma, þaiei vesun moses jah helias. þai gasaiwanans ïn vulþau qeþun urruns ïs, “two men spoke with him, who were Moses and Elijah. They, appearing in glory, spoke of his departure”; 2 Tim. I.5: þizei ïst fygailus jah airmogaineis, “among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes”; Phil. III.19: þize guþ vamba ïst, “whose god is their belly”—they are not intrinsically clear, since the Goth does not always employ the corresponding relative where the Greek uses a relative.

> Note 2.—Jah sa is translated both “and this,” that is, “and indeed” (καὶ οὗτος): Phil. I.28: ïst ïm ustaikneins fralustais ïþ ïzvis ganistais, jah þata fram guþa, “it is to them a sign of destruction, but to you of salvation—and this from God”; and likewise “and he too” (καὶ αὐτός): Mark I.19: gasaw ïakobu jah ïohanne jah þans ïn skipa manvjandans natja, “he saw James and John, and them in the boat mending nets”; Luke I.36; XIX.9. In place of jah sa there also occurs jah ïs: John XVII.19: fram ïm ïk veiha mik silban; ei sijaina jah eis veihai ïn sunjai, “for them I sanctify myself, that they too may be sanctified in truth.”

2) As an adjective it means:

a) “This” (οὗτος ὁ): Matt. VII.28: ustauh ïesus þo vaurda (τοὺς λόγους τούτους), “Jesus finished these sayings”; X.42: gadragkeiþ ainana þize minnistane (τῶν μικρῶν τούτων) stiklo kaldis vatins, “gives one of these least ones a cup of cold water to drink”; XI.16: wamma nu galeiko þata kuni (τὴν γενεὰν ταύτην), “to what then shall I compare this generation?” Other examples are found in the glossary under þata.

b) Rarely “this very” (αὐτὸς ὁ): Luke II.38: þizai weilaï (αὐτῇ τῇ ὥρᾳ) anna atstandandei andhaihait fraujin, “at that very hour Anna, coming forward, gave thanks to the Lord”; VII.21; X.7, 21; XX.19; John V.36; or “this—self” (ὁ—αὐτός): John XIV.11: ïn þize vaurstve (διὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτά) galaubeiþ, “believe because of the works themselves”; or “that” (ἐκεῖνος ὁ): Matt. XXVII.19: ni vaiht þus jah þamma garaihtin (τῷ δικαίῳ ἐκείνῳ), “have nothing to do with that righteous man”; Luke XX.18; John XVIII.13.

> Note 3.—Since οὗτος in the Greek text commonly follows its substantive, the Goth likewise sometimes places his demonstrative after it: Matt. IX.26: usïddja meriþo so (ἡ φήμη αὕτη) and alla jaina airþa, “that report went out into all that land”; Luke III.8: guþ mag us stainam þaim (τῶν λίθων τούτων) urraisjan barna abrahama, “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham”; IV.21: usfullnodedun mela þo (ἡ γραφὴ αὕτη), “this scripture has been fulfilled today”; 2 Cor. I.12: woftuli unsara so (ἡ καύχησις ἡμῶν αὕτη) ïst veitvodei miþvisseins unsaraizos, “this boasting of ours is the testimony of our conscience.” Other examples see the glossary under þata.
>
> Moreover, out of a mere love of variation, the Goth says: Mark VIII.12: wa þata kuni (ἡ γενεὰ αὕτη) taikn [Col. 1103] sokeiþ, amen qiþa ïsvis: jabai gibaidau kunja þamma (τῇ γενεᾷ ταύτῃ) taikne, “why does this generation seek a sign? Truly I say to you: if a sign shall be given to this generation …”

> Note 4.—The demonstrative frequently follows the relative clause, e.g. 1 Cor. VII.20: warjizuh ïn laþonai, þizaiei laþoþs vas, in þizai sijai, “let each remain in the calling in which he was called”; 24: warjizuh ïn þammei galaþoþs vas, ïn þamma gastandai, “let each remain with God in that in which he was called.”

3) This pronoun, whether adjective or substantive, is used as an article; see §195.

II. Sah, soh, þatuh is nothing other than the preceding pronoun with the enclitic -uh added. Now, from the various meanings of this enclitic, sah signifies:

1) In a connective sense (-que):

a) “And this,” “this however” (καὶ αὐτός, καὶ οὗτος, ὁ δέ): Luke XVII.15: ains þize gavandida sik—sah (et hic, καὶ αὐτός) vas samareites, “one of them returned—and he was a Samaritan”; John XIV.8: augei unsis þana attan. þatuh (hocque, Greek merely καί) ganah unsis, “show us the Father; and this will suffice us”; Luke II.38; Matt. XXVII.44: þatuh (τὸ δέ) samo jah þai vaidedjans, “and likewise the robbers”; 2 Thess. III.12: þaimuh (τοῖς δέ) svaleikaim anabiudam ei seinana hlaib matjaina, “but such persons we command to eat their own bread.” Likewise John X.2: sa ïnngaggands þairh daur hairdeis ïst lambe, þammuh (eique, Greek merely τούτῳ) dauravards uslukiþ, “he who enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep; to him the doorkeeper opens.”

b) “Who” (ὅς): Luke II.37: anna vas viduvo, soh (ἥ) ni afiddja fairra alh, “Anna was a widow, who did not depart from the temple”; XVI.20: unleds sums vas namin haitans lazarus, sah (ὅς) atvaurpans vas du daura, “there was a certain poor man named Lazarus, who was laid at the gate”; XVII.12: gamotidedun ïmma taihun þrutsfillai mans, þaih (οἵ) gastoþun fairraþro, “ten leprous men met him, who stood at a distance”; 1 Cor. XV.1; Philem. 12. Hence John XVIII.26: qaþ sums þize skalke þis maistins gudjins, sah niþjis vas, “one of the servants of the high priest, who was a kinsman”; Greek συγγενὴς ὤν. Relevant here are constructions such as Matt. XXVII.57: qam manna gabigs af areimaþaias. þizuh namo [and this man’s, or whose, name] ïosef, “there came a rich man from Arimathea, whose name was Joseph”; compare Mark VI.16.

2) With emphatic force (-ce), “this very one,” especially:

a) Where the relative to which it refers precedes: Matt. V.19: saei nu gatairiþ aina anabusne þizo minnistono jah laisjai sva mans, sah—“this very one,” German emphatic *der*, though the pronoun is absent from the Greek text, having been introduced by the Goth for the sake of parallelism—minnista haitada ïn þiudangardjai himine; ïþ saei taujiþ jah laisjai sva, sah (οὗτος) mikils haitada ïn etc., “whoever therefore breaks one of the least of these commandments and teaches people so, this very one shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does and teaches them, this very one shall be called great in …”; Mark XII.10; Luke IX.26; XX.17; John V.37–38; X.1; XII.49; Gal. VI.7; Phil. III.7; *Skeireins* VI.d. Also where a participle with the article (“he who”) precedes: *Skeireins* I.c: gadob nu vas mais þans svesamma viljin ufhausjandans diabulau du ufargaggan anabusn guþs þanzuh aftra svesamma viljin gaqissans vairþan nasjandis laiseinai, “it was fitting rather that he who of his own will exalted the devil to transgress God’s command should, again by his own will, be made subject to the teaching of the Saviour.” Hence Mark XII.10 and Luke XX.17: stains þammei usvaurpan þai timrjans, sah varþ du haubida vaihstins (ὃν λίθον—οὗτος), “the stone which the builders rejected, this became the head of the corner.”

b) Where, after an inserted parenthesis, the discourse continues. For then sah, soh, and especially þatuh, with a following þan, are joined through assimilation as þatuþ-þan: Matt. III.11: sa afar mis gagganda svinþoza mis ïst, þizei ïk ni ïm vairþs ei andbindau skaudaraip skohis ïs; sah þan (αὐτός) ïzvis daupeiþ ïn ahmin, “he who comes after me is mightier than I, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to untie; he himself shall baptize you in the Spirit”; XXVII.58; Mark III.11; XVI.6; Luke II.37, beginning; III.16; John VII.9; VIII.40; XII.6; XIII.28; XVI.33; John VIII.35; Rom. XII.4; 1 Cor. VII.6; 2 Cor. I.17 (τοῦτο οὖν); IV.15 (τὰ γάρ); IX.16; XII.19; Eph. IV.9; 1 Thess. IV.5; 1 Tim. II.3; *Skeireins* II.b; III.a; V.a; VIII.a, c. Parentheses are also formed in this manner: Luke II.1–2: urrann gagrefts gameljan allana midjungard. soh þan (αὕτη) gilstrameleins frumista varþ, “a decree went out to register the whole world. This registration was the first”; John VI.6: þatuh þan (τοῦτο δέ) qaþ fraisands ïna, “but he said this, testing him”; VII.39; XVIII.10, 15; 1 Cor. IX.23.

c) What or whom sah demonstrates is placed afterwards: John VI.40: þatuh þan (τοῦτο δέ) ïst vilja guþs; ei wazuh saiwiþ sunu jah galaubeiþ du ïmma, “and this is the will of God: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him …”; XVII.3: soh þan (αὕτη δέ) ïst so aiveino libains, ei kunneina þuk, “and this is eternal life: that they may know you”; *Skeireins* I.c: þatuh vesi viþra þata gadob, ei frauja þana galausidedi, “and this would be contrary to what was fitting: that the Lord should redeem him”; compare 2 Cor. XIII.9: þizuh (τοῦτο δέ) auk jah bidjam, ïzvaraizos ustauhtais, “and this also we pray: your perfection.”

d) Sah occurs as a simple demonstrative only in 1 Tim. VI.8: habandans usfodein jah gaskadvein, þaimuh ganohidai sijaima, “having food and covering, with these let us be content”; IV.16.

III. His, “this,” is used only in reference to time present to the speaker. Otherwise it is employed adjectivally and substantively, and is defective, occurring only in the singular accusative (masculine hina and neuter hita) and dative himma:

a) Adjectivally: und hina dag, “unto this present day,” Matt. XI.23; XXVII.8; 2 Cor. III.14–15; himma daga, “on this day, today,” Matt. VI.11, 30; Luke II.11; IV.21; V.26; XIX.5, 9; fram himma nu, “from this moment,” Luke I.48; V.10; und hita nu, “up to this instant,” *Skeireins* IV.b.

b) Substantively: fram himma, “from this [day, moment],” John XIII.19; XIV.7; und hita, “until this [moment, this day],” Matt. XI.12; Mark XIII.19; John XVI.24; 1 Cor. XV.6.

IV. Jains, jaina, jain (jainata), “that, that one” (ἐκεῖνος), refers to an object remote from the speaker: Luke XVIII.14: atïddja sa garaihtoza gataihans du garda seinamma þau raihtis jains, “this man went down to his house justified rather than that one”; John III.30: jains skal vahsjan ïþ ïk minznan, “that one must increase, but I must decrease.” It is used:

a) Substantively, as in the two examples quoted above, though rarely in the first Gospels (only Mark XII.5; Luke IX.34; XVIII.14; XX.11), but frequently in John (apart from the passages cited under b), in the *Skeireins*, and in most passages of the Epistles; see the glossary under this word.

b) Adjectivally, commonly preceding its substantive: John XVI.23: ïn jainamma daga mik ni fraihniþ vaihtais, “on that day you will ask me nothing”; 26; XVIII.17: qaþ jaina þivi, “that maid said.” It follows its substantive only in Luke (II.1: in dagans jainans, “in those days”; IV.2; XV.14; XVII.9; XX.1) and Nehemiah VI.17. If an attribute is also present, the pronoun either precedes the substantive: Matt. IX.26: alla jaina airþa, “all that land”; or follows it: IX.31: allai airþai jainai, “through all that land”; Luke XIX.27: fijands meinans jainans, “those enemies of mine.”

But when the substantive has an article, the pronoun regularly follows: Matt. VII.25: vindos bistugqun bi þamma razna jainamma, “the winds beat upon that house”; VIII.28; IX.22; Mark III.24–25; VI.11; XIII.19; Luke IX.5; XVIII.3; 2 Cor. VII.8. It precedes only—following the Greek—in Mark XII.7: jainai þai vaurstvjans, “those husbandmen,” and 1 Cor. X.28: jainis þis bandvjandins, “that one who informed you.”

V. PRONOMINAL ADJECTIVES.

1) Svalauds, “so great” (τοσοῦτος): Matt. VIII.10: ni ïn ïsraela svalauda galaubein bigat, “I have not found such great faith in Israel”; *Skeireins* IV.6: svalauda mikilduþais maht, “power of such greatness.” The neuter is also used substantively with a partitive: John XIV.9: svalaud melis (τοσοῦτον χρόνον) miþ ïzvis vas, “I have been with you so long a time.”

2) Svaleiks, “such” (τοιοῦτος): Matt. IX.8: mikilidedun guþ þana gibandan valdufni svaleikata mannam, “they glorified God, who had given such authority to men”; John IX.16: waiva mag manna fravaurhts svaleikos taiknins taujan, “how can a sinful man perform such signs?” etc.; see the glossary. It is also often used substantively, though retaining its vocalic form (see §196 I.b): 1 Cor. V.11: þamma svaleikamma ni miþmatjaiþ, “with such a person do not even eat”; Luke XVIII.16: þize svaleikaize ïst þiudangardi guþs, “of such persons is the kingdom of God”; IX.9: was ïst sa, bi þanei ïk hausja svaleik (τοιαῦτα), “who is this, about whom I hear such things?”; 1 Cor. VII.28: aglon leikis gastaldand þo svaleika (οἱ τοιοῦτοι), “such persons shall have tribulation in the flesh.”

## D. THE RELATIVE

§203. The relative pronoun is formed by the organic combination of the relative particle ei and the demonstrative pronoun sa: saei, soei or sei, þatei (§109); it corresponds without distinction to Greek ὅστις, ὅσπερ, ὅς ἄν, and ὁ with a participle. It is used:

a) Adjectivally, “who, which, that”; in this case the substantive precedes or also follows, but then the demonstrative is sometimes repeated: Matt. VIII.4: atbair giba, þoei (ὅ) anabauþ moses, “offer the gift which Moses commanded”; X.26: ni vaiht ïst gahuliþ, þatei (ὅ) ni andhuljaidau, “nothing is hidden that shall not be revealed”; XI.20: dugann ïdveitjan baurgim, ïn þaimei (αἷς) vaurþun mahteis, “he began to reproach the cities in which his mighty works had been done”; Mark X.29–30: ni washun ïst, saei (ὅς) aflailoti gard—saei (ὃς ἄν) ni andnimai ·r· falþ, “there is no one who has left a house … who shall not receive a hundredfold”; XV.6: and dulþ warjoh fralailot peilatus ïudaium ainana bandjan, þanei (ὅνπερ) bedun, “at every feast Pilate released to the Jews one prisoner whom they requested”; Luke I.20: ni galaubides vaurdam meinaim, þoei (οἵτινες) usfulljanda, “you did not believe my words, which shall be fulfilled”; John I.29: sa ïst viþrus guþs, saei afnimiþ (ὁ αἴρων) fravaurht þizos manasedais, “this is the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world”; XII.49: saei mik sandida atta, sah mis anabusn atgaf, “the Father who sent me, he gave me commandment.” Other examples see the glossary under þatei, 1) a).

b) Substantively: “he who,” “that which,” “what,” or simply “who, which, that”: Rom. VII.15: þatei (ὅ) vaurkja, ni fraþja, unte ni þatei (ὅ) viljau tauja; ak þatei (ὅ) hatja, þata tauja, “what I do, I do not understand; for I do not do what I wish, but what I hate, that I do”; X.14: waiva bidjand, þammei (cui, εἰς ὅν) ni galaubidedun, aiþþau waiva galaubjand, þammei (quem, ὅν) ni hausidedun? “How shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how shall they believe him of whom they have not heard?” John VIII.25: þu was ïs? jah qaþ du ïm ïesus: anastodeins þatei (ὅ, τι) jah rodja du ïzvis, “Who are you? And Jesus said to them: Precisely what I am also telling you”; Gal. I.23: saei vrak (ὁ διώκων) uns simle, nu mereiþ galaubein, “he who formerly persecuted us now preaches the faith”; Matt. V.19: saei (ὃς ἐάν) nu gatairiþ aina anabusne þizo minnistono, sah minnista haitada ïn þiudangardjai himine, “whoever breaks one of the least commandments, this one shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven”; 1 Cor. XVI.2: warjizuh fram sis silbin taujai huhjands þatei (ὅ, τι ἄν) vili, “let each set aside by himself, storing up whatever he may prosper in.” Other examples see the glossary under this word, b) and c).

> Note 1.—Saei is also sometimes used for other relatives: for ὅσος after alls: Luke XVIII.12: afdailja taihundon dail allis þize (ὅσα) gastalda, “I give a tenth of all that I possess”; [Col. 1106] 22; John X.41; XVI.15; XVII.7; and probably Rom. IX.7 also belongs here, where nih allai þaiei is to be construed; compare the note on that passage. Indeed, it stands for οἷος in Phil. I.30: þo samon haifst habaiþ, þoei (οἷον) gasaiwiþ ïn mis, “having the same conflict such as you see in me”; for εἴ τις in Eph. IV.29: ainhun vaurde ubilaize us munþa ïzvaramma ni usgaggai, ak þaiei (εἴ τις) goþ sijai du timreinai, “let no evil word proceed from your mouth, but if any be good for edification”; John III.3: niba saei (ἐὰν μή τις) gabairada ïupaþro, ni mag gasaiwan þiudangardja guþs, “unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God”; 5; XV.6; for τίς in indirect questions: John VI.6: vissa þatei (τί) habaida taujan, “he knew what he would do”; Eph. V.10; for a demonstrative closely connected with what precedes: Matt. XXVII.46: ufhropida: helei, helei, lima sabakþani, þatei ïst (τοῦτ᾽ ἐστι) guþ meins, etc., “he cried out: ‘Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani,’ that is, ‘My God,’ etc.”; 2 Cor. XII.8; Titus I.5; Eph. III.1; see the notes on these passages; or for οὗτος γάρ in Eph. V.6: ni manna ïzvis uslusto lausaim vaurdam, þairh þoei (διὰ ταῦτα γάρ) qimiþ hatis guþs, “let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes.”

2) Where the relative pronoun refers to a personal pronoun of the first or second person, it takes the forms ïkei, þuei, juzei (veizei never occurs): 1 Cor. XV.9: ïk ïm sa smalista apaustaule, ïkei (ὅς) ni ïm vairþs ei haitaidau apaustaulus, “I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle”; Rom. XIV.4: þu was ïs, þuei stojis (ὁ κρίνων) framaþjana skalk, “who are you, judging another’s servant?”; Luke XVI.15: jus sijuþ, juzei garaihtans domeiþ (οἱ δικαιοῦντες) ïzvis silbans, “you are those who justify yourselves”; Mark I.11: þu ïs sunus meins sa liuba, ïn þuzei (ᾧ) vaila galeikada, “you are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,” in place of which the marginal variant is þukei (ὅν) vilda, “whom I loved”; Gal. III.1: ïzvisei (οἷς) faura augam xristus faurameliþs vas, ïn ïzvis ushramiþs, “before whose eyes Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified.” Other examples see above, §109. Sometimes the personal pronoun is absent at first: Gal. V.4: lausai sijuþ af xristaus, jazei (οἵτινες) ïn vitoda garaihtans qiþiþ ïzvis, “you have been severed from Christ, you who seek justification in the law”; 1 Tim. I.12–13: aviliuda xristau, unte galaubjandan mik gahugida gasatjands ïn andbahtja, ïkei faura vas, “I thank Christ, because he deemed me faithful, appointing me to ministry—I who formerly was a blasphemer.” Once this idiom is understood, it is no longer surprising that sa saei is used in mixed passages for οὗτος ὅς, Luke V.21; for ἐάν τις, John XIII.20; Rom. VIII.5; XI.22; etc.

3) In place of the relative pronoun occur:

a) Sah, “and he,” see §202 II, 1) a).

b) In the nominative, relative particles:

aa) Ise and—always in John and in Second Corinthians—ïzei, comparable with Neo-German *so*, and closely related to the demonstrative: Matt. VII.15: atsaiwiþ faura liugnapraufetum þaim ïzei (οἵτινες) qimand at ïzvis ïn vastjom lambe, “beware of the false prophets who come to you in sheep’s clothing”; Mark IX.1; John XI.37: niu mahta sa ïzei uslauk (οὗτος ὁ ἀνοίξας) augona þamma blindin, gataujan ei jah sa ni gadauþnodedi, “could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have caused this man not to die?”; 2 Cor. V.21: þana ïzei ni kunþa (τὸν μὴ γνόντα) fravaurht faur uns gatavida fravaurht, “him who knew no sin he made sin for us”; 1 Cor. XV.27; Gal. VI.13; 1 Tim. I.16; Eph. II.17: gavairhti þaim ïzei (τοῖς) newa scilicet sind, “he preached peace to those who are near.”

These particles refer to substantives which readily admit them immediately after themselves: John VIII.40: sokeiþ mik usqiman, mannan ïzei (ὅς) sunja ïzvis rodida, “you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth”; XII.4; XV.26; 2 Cor. I.10; VIII.16; Gal. I.1, 4; Eph. I.3, 14. Only rarely, however, is the particle separated from the word to which it refers: Eph. IV.15: vahsjaima ïn ïna þo alla, ïze ïst haubiþ, xristus, “may we grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ”; [Col. 1107] 2 Cor. III.5–6: so vairþida unsara us guþa ïst, ïzei etc., “our sufficiency is from God, who etc.”; Luke VIII.13: þai ana þamma staina [scilicet þai sind] ïze etc., “those upon the rock [that is, those are] who etc.”

bb) Ei, which may also be regarded as a temporal or explanatory particle (“when,” “that,” “because”): Luke I.20: sijais þahands und þana dag ei vairþai þata, “you shall be silent until the day when this happens,” ἄχρι ἧς ἡμέρας (und þanei dag), where the Goth resolves an attraction frequently occurring in Greek; likewise XVII.30; Col. I.9; Neh. V.14; 2 Tim. III.8: þamma haidau ei (ὃν τρόπον, properly þammei haidau) jannis jah mambres andstoþun moseza, sva jah þai andstandand sunjai, “in the manner in which Jannes and Mambres opposed Moses, so these also oppose the truth”; Rom. IX.20: þu was ïs, ei andvaurdjais (ὁ ἀνταποκρινόμενος, for þu ei andvaurdjais) guþa, “who are you, answering back to God?”

> Note 2.—The relative pronoun is also variously expressed in the following passages: Matt. V.32: wazuh saei (ὃς ἄν) afletiþ qen seina ïnu fairina kalkinassaus, taujiþ þo horinon, jah sa ïze (ὃς ἄν) afsatida liugaiþ, horinoþ, “everyone who dismisses his wife except on account of fornication makes her commit adultery, and he who marries a divorced woman commits adultery”; Luke VIII.13–15: þai ana þamma staina sind ïze (οἵ) miþ fahedai andnimand þata vaurd—þata ïn þaurnuns gadriusando þai sind, þaiei—þata ana þizai godon arþai þai sind þai ïze—, “those upon the rock are those who receive the word with joy—those falling among thorns are those who—those upon the good soil are those who—.”

## E. INTERROGATIVES

§204. I. Was, wo, wa is substantive: “who, what” (τίς, τί). In direct and indirect questions it asks generally, without reference to another object, and never occurs in the plural. That, besides the masculine and neuter dative wamma, the instrumental we also exists, see §110, note 1. 1 Cor. IV.7: was (τίς) þuk ussokeiþ, vauþ-þan habais, þatei ni namt, aiþþau jabai andnamt, wa wopis, sve ni nemeis? “Who distinguishes you? And what do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” Luke X.29: was ïst mis newundja? “Who is my neighbour?” IV.34: kann þuk, was ïs, “I know you, who you are”; Mark V.9: wa namo þein? “What is your name?” III.33: wo ïst so aiþei meina aiþþau þai broþrjus meinai? “Who are my mother or my brothers?” XII.16: wis ïst sa manleika jah so ufarmeleins? “Whose is this image and inscription?” VI.24: wis bidjau? “What shall we ask?” Luke VI.47: wazuh sa hausjands vaurda meina jah taujands þo, ataugja ïzvis, wamma galeiks ïst, “everyone who hears my words and does them—I shall show you to whom he is like”; Matt. VI.31: wa matjam, aiþþau wa drigkam aiþþau we [wherewith] vasjaima? “What shall we eat, or what shall we drink, or wherewith shall we be clothed?” Mark VIII.27: wana mik qiþand mans visan? “Whom do people say that I am?” Rom. IX.19: viljin ïs was andstandiþ? “Who has resisted his will?” Other examples see the glossary under Was, 1).

> Note 1.—Where was must be taken adjectivally, its substantive must be partitive; itself being in the singular, it agrees in gender with the substantive: Luke IX.55: niu vituþ, wis ahmane [“of what spirit,” for “what spirit,” οἵου πνεύματος] sijuþ; Matt. V.46: wo mizdono [“of what reward,” for “what reward,” τίνα μισθόν] habaiþ; Mark I.27; VI.2; Luke IX.25; John XVIII.29; Rom. XIII.9; 1 Cor. VII.5; XV.2; XVI.7; 2 Cor. VI.14 ff.; 1 Thess. III.9: wa aviliude (τίνα εὐχαριστίαν) magum usgildan fraujin? “What thanksgiving can we render to the Lord?” Mark XI.28: ïn wamma valdufnje þata taujis? “By what authority do you do these things?”; 29; Luke XX.2. Only Luke XV.4 reads was manna ïzvara aigands taihuntehund lambe, etc., “what man of you, having a hundred sheep,” compare §205, note 1.
>
> Note 2.—In resolving prepositional expressions with the article, wa is sometimes used for a relative: Phil. II.23: gasaiwa wa bi mik ïst (τὰ περὶ ἐμέ), “I shall see what concerns me”; 28; Eph. VI.21–22.

II. Warjis, warja, warjata, “which?” (τίς), is used:

a) Either in the plural: John VI.64: vissa ïesus, warjai (τίνες) sind þai ni galaubjandans jah was (τίς) ïst saei galeiveiþ ïna, “Jesus knew which persons they were who did not believe, and who it was that would betray him”; XIII.18: ïk vait, warjans (οὕς) gavalida, “I know whom I have chosen.” If, in 1 Thess. IV.2, vituþ warjos anabusnins atgebum ïzvis is falsely read in place of waizos, this form, if corrected in itself, would still be erroneous in the passage, since warjis occurs here only as an adjective;

b) Or in opposition to waþar; see III.

aa) Joined with a superlative: Mark IX.34: du sis misso andrunnun, warjis (τίς) maists vesi, “they disputed among themselves which of them should be greatest”; Luke IX.46; Mark XII.28: warja (ποία) ïst allaizo anabusne frumista, “which is the first of all commandments?”; or

bb) Referred to a number or a definite object: Mark XII.23: warjamma ïze [namely, of those seven men] vairþiþ qens, “of which of them shall she be wife?”; Luke XX.33; John XIII.22: sewun du sis misso þai siponjos þagkjandans, bi warjana [namely, of these twelve] qeþi, “the disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke”; X.32: managa goda vaurstva ataugida ïzvis, ïn warjis þize vaurstve (διὰ ποῖον αὐτῶν ἔργων) staineiþ mik? “I have shown you many good works; for which of these works do you stone me?”

> Note 3.—If the question was ïzvara in Matt. VI.27; Luke XIV.28; John VIII.46 is incorrect when addressed to a multitude, warjis ïzvara ought to be expected in Luke XVII.7, where the question is addressed to the apostles: “which of you, having a servant,” etc. Yet the translator seems to have understood that the Lord’s address did not depend on what preceded, nor was it directed only to the apostles, but to the multitude; see §204, I.

III. Waþar, “which of two,” is used in relation to two and with a comparative: *Skeireins* III.a: miþ sis misso sik andrunnun sumai ni kunnandans waþar [Christ or John, namely] skuldedi maiza, “some disputed among themselves, not knowing which ought to be greater”; Luke VII.42: waþar (τίς) þize [of the two debtors] mais ïna frijoþ, “which of them will love him more?”; Matt. IX.5: waþar (τί) ïst azetizo qiþan: afletanda þus fravaurhteis þau qiþan: urreis jah gagg? “Which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’?”; Mark II.9; Luke V.23.

> Note 4.—Waþar occurs only in the nominative singular; hence Matt. XXVII.17 reads: wana vileiþ ei fraletau ïzvis, barabban wau ïesu? “Whom do you wish me to release to you, Barabbas or Jesus?” If John IX.2 reads was (τίς) fravaurhta, sau þau fadrein ïs? “Who sinned, this man or his parents?” rather than waþar, this probably arises because, owing to the plural idea of fadrein, waþar could not be used.

IV. Adjectival pronouns:

1) Wileiks, “of what kind?” (ποῖος, ποταπός, πηλίκος): Mark IV.30: we galeikom þiudangardja guþs aiþþau ïn wileikai (ποίᾳ) gajukon gabairam þo? “With what shall we compare the kingdom of God, or in what kind of parable shall we set it forth?” John XII.33: bandvida wileikamma (ποίῳ) dauþau skulda gadauþnan, “indicating by what kind of death he was to die”; Luke I.29: þahta sis weleika (ποταπή) vesi so goleins, “she considered what manner of greeting this might be”; Gal. VI.11: sai wileikaim (πηλίκοις) bokom ïz vis gamelida, “see with what large letters I have written to you.” Other examples see the glossary under Wileiks.

2) Welauds, “how great?” (πόσος): 2 Cor. VII.11: saiw þata bi guþ saurgan ïzvis welauda gatavida ïzvis usdaudein, “see what great earnestness this godly sorrow has produced in you.”

3) Adjectival pronouns formed from wan:

a) Wan manags, wan filu, “how many?” (πόσος): Mark VIII.5: wan managans habaiþ hlaibans? “How many loaves do you have?”; XIX.20; Matt. XXVII.13: niu hauseis, wan filu ana þuk veitvodjand, “do you not hear how many things they testify against you?”; VI.23; Mark XV.4; Luke XV.17; XVI.5.

b) Wan laggs, “how long?” (πόσος): Mark IX.21: wan lagg mel ïst, ei þata warþ ïmma? “How long is it since this happened to him?”

## F. INDEFINITES

§205. I. Was, wo, wa, “someone, something,” affirmatively, is used only substantively: Mark VIII.4: waþro þans mag was (τίς) gasoþjan, “whence can anyone satisfy these people?”; XI.25: afletaiþ, jabai wa habaiþ viþra wana, “forgive, if you have anything against anyone”; Luke XIX.8: jabai wis wa aþholoda, fidurfalþ fragilda, “if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore fourfold”; John XIV.14: jabai wis bidjiþ mik ïn namin meinamma, ïk tauja, “if you ask me anything in my name, I will do it”; 2 Cor. XII.6: freidja, ïbai was ïn mis wa muni, “I refrain, lest anyone think anything of me”; XIII.8: ni magum wa viþra sunja, “we can do nothing against the truth”; 1 Thess. V.15: saiwiþ ïbai was ubil ana ubilamma vamma usgildai, “see that no one repays evil for evil to anyone”; 2 Thess. III.8: ni arvjo hlaib matidedum at wamma ak vinnandans arbaidai vaurkjondans, ei ni kauridedeima wana ïzvara, “we did not eat anyone’s bread without payment, but worked with labour and toil, so that we might not burden any of you”; Matt. V.39: jabai was (ὅστις) þuk stautai bi taihsvon þeina kinnu, vandei ïmma jah þo anþara, “if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also”; 2 Tim. II.5: jabai haifsteiþ was, ni veipada, niba a vitodeigo brikiþ, “if anyone competes, he is not crowned unless he competes lawfully.” Other examples see the glossary under Was.

> Note 1.—The indefinite adjectival τις is expressed in the same manner as the interrogative; see §204, note 1: Phil. II.1: wa gaþrafsteino (τις παράκλησις)—wo gaþlaihte—wo gamainduþe, “if there is any encouragement—any comfort—any fellowship”; IV.8; 1 Tim. V.4; 1 Cor. XVI.7: wo weilo (χρόνον τινά), “for some time”; VII.5; Rom. XIII.9: wo anþaraizo anabusne, “any other commandment”; Gal. VI.1: ïn wizai missadede, “in some transgression”; Col. II.23: sveriþo wizai, “some severity” (where in our translation *honorum*, “of honours,” should be read as *honore*, “honour”).
>
> Hence the neuter adjective is joined where, nevertheless, in Latin fashion it attracts the singular genitive to itself: “something good.” Mark IV.22: nih allis ïst wa fulginis (τι κρυπτόν), “nor is there anything hidden”; Rom. IX.11: nauhþannh ni gabauranai vesun, aiþþau tavidedeina wa þiuþis aiþþau unþiuþis (τι ἀγαθὸν ἢ κακόν), “not yet having been born, nor having done anything good or bad.” Only was anþar (τις ἄλλος), “someone else,” could be said in Phil. III.4; and the expression μικρόν τι is rendered in Gothic at 2 Cor. XI.1, 16 by leitil wa, “a little something.” It is only apparently adjectival in 1 Cor. VII.12: jabai was broþar qen aigi ungalaubjandein, “if any brother has an unbelieving wife”; for the Goths do not say, as Latins do, “if any king,” but “if anyone who is a king,” so that the passage just cited must be explained: “if anyone who is our brother”; likewise 1 Cor. V.11 emphatically reads jabai was broþar namniþs, “if anyone called a brother”; compare XIV.24. But if 2 Cor. V.17, εἴ τις ἐν Χριστῷ καινὴ κτίσις, “if anyone is in Christ, [there is] a new creation,” is rendered jabai wo ïn xristau niuja gaskafts, the feminine is either incorrectly read for was or was employed by the translator because of the gender of τῆς κτίσεως: “if any [creation], namely a new creation, is in Christ”; for wo cannot in any way refer to niuja gaskafts, “if any new creation is.”

II. Mannahun, washun, and ainshun, ainohun, ainhun occur only with negation and, with its aid, mean at once “nobody” and “none.” As to the negation, it is either placed before these words or, by license, joined to the verb; washun alone almost always has the negation immediately preceding it. These terms differ as follows: ni mannahun (“no man,” used especially by Mark) and ni washun (“nobody”) are substantives—both corresponding to Greek οὐδείς, μηδείς, οὐ—τις, “anyone”—but are rarely found in cases other than the nominative, so much so that ni washun, which occurs in Luke, is supplied in parallel passages by ainshun (see note 6). Moreover, ni washun appears only in the masculine nominative, while mannahun occurs in other cases too. Add ni vaihts or ni vaiht, “nothing, not at all,” corresponding to neuter οὐδέν, μηδέν, οὐ—τι; whereas ni ainshun is substantive (“none,” οὐδείς, μηδείς, οὐδὲ εἷς) and occurs in every singular case and gender.

1) Mark IX.39: ni mannahun ïst, saei taujiþ maht ïn namin meinamma, “there is no one who performs a miracle in my name”; XII.14: ni kara þuk manshun, “you care for no person”; I.44: saiw ei mannhun ni qiþais vaiht, “see that you tell no one anything”; VIII.26; IX.9; XVI.8; 1 Tim.
