V.22; Luke III.14: ni mannanhun holoþ, “do not extort from anyone”; X.4.

Matt. IX.16: ni washun lagjiþ du plata fanan þarih … ana snagan fairnjana, “no one puts a patch of new cloth … onto an old garment”; Mark X.18: ni washun þiuþeigs alja ains guþ, “no one is good except one, God”; 29: ni washun ïst, saei aflailoti gard ïn meina, saei ni adnimai ·r· falþ, “there is no one who has left a house for my sake who shall not receive a hundredfold”; Luke X.22: ni washun kann, was ïst sunus, alja atta, “no one knows who the Son is except the Father”; John X.18: ni washun nimiþ saivala meina af mis, “no one takes my life from me”; 1 Cor. XVI.11: ni washun ïmma frakunni, “let no one despise him”; Col. II.18: ni washun ïzvis gajiukai, “let no one rob you [of the prize].”—John X.28: ni fravilviþ washun lamba meina us handan meinai, “no one shall snatch my sheep out of my hand.”

Matt. X.26: ni vaiht ïst gahuliþ, þatei ni andhuljaidau, “nothing is hidden which shall not be revealed”; Mark V.26: qens manag gaþulandei fram managaim lekjam jah ni vaihtai botida atïddja du ïesua, “a woman, having suffered much from many physicians and having received no benefit, came to Jesus”; VI.8: faurbauþ ïm ei vaiht ni nemeina ïn vig, “he commanded them to take nothing for the journey.” Other examples see the glossary under Vaihts.

2) John XIV.6: ïk ïm sa vigs jah sunja jah libains, ainshun ni qimiþ at attin niba þaïrh mik, “I am the way and the truth and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me”; Mark XII.35: ainshun þanaseiþs ni gadaursta ïna fraihnan, “after that no one dared question him”; John VI.65: ni ainshun mag qiman at mis, “no one can come to me”; Rom. XIII.8: ni ainummehun vaihtais skulans sijaiþ, “owe no one anything”; John V.22: ni stojiþ ainohun, “he judges no one”; Luke IV.26: ni du ainaihun þizo ïnsandiþs vas helias alja ïn saraipta, “Elijah was sent to none of them except to Sarepta.” For further examples see the glossary under Ainshun.

> Note 2.—Here too the adjective “any” is expressed like “who?” (was; note 1): Mark XI.2: bigitats fulan, ana þammei nauh ainshun manne ni (οὐδεὶς ἀνθρώπων) sat, “you will find a colt upon which no human being has yet sat”; Luke XIX.30: ana þammei ni ainshun aiv manne sat, “upon which no one has ever sat”; Luke IV.24: ni ainshun praufete (οὐδεὶς προφήτης) andanems ïst ïn gabaurþai seinai, “no prophet is accepted in his own country”; IX.50; XVI.13; Mark VI.5: ni mahta jainar ainohun mahte (οὐδεμίαν δύναμιν) gataujan, “he could do no miracle there”; John X.41: ïohannes gatavida taikne ni ainohun (σημεῖον οὐδέν), “John performed no sign”; XVI.29; XVIII.28; XIX.4; Luke X.19; Phil. IV.15; Matt. XXVII.14: ni andhof ïmma viþra ni ainhun vaurde (οὐδὲ ἕν ῥῆμα), “he answered him not even one word”; Luke I.37: nist unmahteig guþa ainhun vaurde (πᾶν ῥῆμα), “with God no word is impossible”; John XIX.11: ni aihtedeis valdufnje ainhun (ἐξουσίαν οὐδεμίαν) ana mik, nih vesi þus at giban ïupaþro, “you would have no authority at all over me unless it had been given you from above.” Hence 2 Cor. VI.3: ni ainhun þannu ïn vaihtai gibandans bistuggqei (μηδεμίαν προσκοπήν), ei ni anavammjaidau andbahti unsar, “giving no occasion of stumbling in anything, so that our ministry may not be blamed.” In our notes on that passage we wrongly explained this bistuggqei from the reading of Codex A, bistuggq, as though the ei of Codex B’s bistuggqei were an erroneous repetition of the following ei. For the construction requires a genitive, and bistuggqei is in the genitive, standing for bistuggqe (see §30, 3); but in Codex A this ending was carelessly omitted by the scribe because of the following ei. Finally, ainshun itself proves that bistuggq must be neuter, and consequently the gender must be changed in the glossary under that word.
>
> Just as Phil. III.4 has was anþar (“someone else”; note 1), John XV.24 also has anþar ainshun ni (οὐδεὶς ἄλλος), “no other person.” 1 Thess. IV.12, ni ainishun wis þaurbeiþ, “in need of nothing from anyone,” probably reflects the Vulgate’s *nullius aliquid*, “anything of no one,” except that wis must be understood partitively; “not [needing] anything of anyone,” while the Vulgate’s “anything of no one” conflicts with the sense. 2 Tim. II.4, ni ainshun drauhtinonds (οὐδεὶς στρατευόμενος), does not mean “no one serving as a soldier,” but “not one who serves as a soldier”; compare note 1, in whose place John XIII.28 employs the genitive: þatuh þan ni vissa ainshun þize anakumbjandane, “and no one of those reclining [at table] knew this.”

“Note 3.—From the gloss at 1 Cor. X.19, *ni þatei þo galiugaguda vaihts sijaina*, to the words *ni þatei þo galiugaguda wa sijaina* (for this is merely a gloss to be resolved into the text), a distinction may be established between *wa* and *vaiht*: *wa*, namely, means “something,” whether it refers to something existent or not; *vaihts*, on the other hand, denotes a thing that exists and is actually present. In negative sentences *vaiht* is always substituted for *wa*: Gal. VI.3, *þugkeiþ wa visan ni vaiht visands*, “he thinks himself to be something, while being nothing”; v. 15, *nih bimait vaiht ist, nih faurafilli*, “neither circumcision is anything, nor uncircumcision.”

“Note 4.—Besides *ni mannahun*, there also occurs the substantive *ni nanna*, ‘no one’: Matt. VI.24, *ni manna* (οὐδείς, “no one”) *mag tvaim fraujam skalkinon*, “no one can serve two masters”; VIII.4, *saiw ei mann ni* (μηδενί, “to no one”) *qiþais*, “see that you tell no one”; v. 28, *ni mahta manna* (μή τις, “no one”) *usleiþan þairh þana vig*, “no one was able to pass by that way.” For other examples see the glossary under *Manna*.

“Note 5.—*Ainshun* is also used where an interrogative word occurs in the sentence and a negative reply is expected (*num*, ‘whether perhaps’); for example, *jau*, ‘whether perhaps’: John VII.48, *sai jau ainshun þize reike galaubidedi imma*, “Behold, has perhaps one of the rulers believed in him?”

“Note 6.—That *washun*, whether subsequently supplied or supplied by others making corrections as *ainshun*, is evident from the parallel passages; compare Matt. IX.16; Mark X.18, 29; and Luke V.36; XVIII.19, 29.”

III. *Sums, suma, sum*, “a certain one” (τις), is used substantivally, like *ainshun*, with this addition: it also occurs in the plural, “certain persons”: Luke VIII.46, *taitok mis sums*, “someone touched me”; Mark IX.38, *sewum sumana in þeinamma namin usdreibandan unhulþons*, “we saw someone casting out demons in your name”; XIV.57, *sumai usstandandans galiug veitvodidedun*, “certain persons who stood up bore false witness”; 2 Tim. II.18, *galaubein sumaize usvaltidedun*, “they overthrew the faith of certain persons”; 1 Tim. I.3, *faurbiudais sumaim, ei anþarleiko ni laisjaina*, “you should charge certain persons not to teach differently”; 2 Thess. III.11, *hausjam sumans wairbandans in izvis ungatassaba*, “we hear that certain persons among you are living disorderly.” For other examples see the glossary under *Sums*. It is also joined with *ains*: Mark XIV.47, *ains sums* (εἷς τις, “a certain one”) *þize andstandandane*, “one of those standing by”; XIV.51.

“Note 7.—A partitive naturally follows plural *sums*: Matt. IX.3, *sumai þize bokarje*, “certain of the scribes”; Mark XII.13, *sumai þize fareisaie*, “certain of the Pharisees”; Rom. XI.17, *sumai þize aste*, “some of the branches,” etc. In the singular too, like other indefinites, it admits a partitive: Mark XV.21, *sumana manne*, that is, τινὰ ἄνδρα, “a certain man”; John XVIII.22, *sums andbahte*, “one attendant”; Luke XVIII.18, *sums reike* (τις ἄρχων, “a certain ruler”); XV.15, *sums baurgjane*, “a certain citizen”; XV.11, *manne sums*, “a certain man”; VII.2, *hundafade sumis skalsks*, “the slave of a certain centurion”; Mark V.25, *qinono suma*, “a certain woman.”

Of the indefinites, *sums* alone is taken adjectivally, agreeing in case with its governing noun, namely when it is joined with *ains*: Mark XIV.51, *ains sums juggalauþs*, “a certain young man”; or when an adjective in vocalic form is used substantivally: John XI.1, *sums siuks*, “a certain sick man.” This is frequent in Luke; apart from Roman influence, it probably arose because there it seems ordinarily to be postponed: Luke VII.41, *dulgahaitjin sumamma*, “to a certain creditor”; VIII.27, *vair sums*, “a certain man”; XIV.16, *manna sums*, “a certain man”; XV.8, *suma qino*, “a certain woman”; X.25, *vitodafasteis sums*, “a certain lawyer”; XVIII.2, *staua sums in sumai baurg*, “a certain judge in a certain city”; XVIII.35, *blinda sums*, “a certain blind man”; XVI.20, *unleds sums*, “a certain poor man”; XIX.12, *manna sums godakunds*, “a certain nobleman.”

“Note 8.—For the use of the indefinite *sums* in coordinated sentences (*sums—sumsuh*, ‘one—the other’; ‘some—others’), see below where the compound sentence is treated.”

IV. *Wazuh, warjizuh,* and *waþaruh*, “each,” differ in this: *wazuh*, “every one,” represents totality (πᾶς, “all”), and hence very often means “every”; it is commonly more strictly determined by following relatives. But *warjizuh*, “each one” (individual persons), denotes a part taken from a whole, some persons from a multitude (ἕκαστος, “each”), whether that multitude is actually mentioned or merely to be conceived. Otherwise, *wazuh* and *warjizuh* are sometimes used indiscriminately. As for *waþaruh*, it refers to two (ἑκάτερος, “each of two”; “either”; “both”). To express the singular more distinctly, *warjizuh* and *waþaruh* also receive *ains* before them (Note 10); and the former is not construed with a plural according to *synesis* (§209.3). Mark IX.49, *wazuh* (πᾶς, “every one”) *funin saltada*, “every one shall be salted with fire”; Luke XVI.16, *þiudangardi guþs vailamerjada jah wazuh in izai nauþjada*, “the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone presses into it”; Matt. VII.24, *wazuh saei* (πᾶς ὅστις, “everyone who”) *hauseiþ vaurda jah taujiþ þo, galeiko ina vaira frodamma*, “everyone who hears these words and does them: I shall liken him to a prudent man”; Rom. X.13, *wazuh saei* (πᾶς ὃς ἄν, “whoever”) *anahaitiþ bidai namo fraujins ganisiþ*, “whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved”; Matt. V.28, *wazuh saei saiwiþ* (πᾶς ὁ βλέπων, “everyone who looks”) *qinon du luston izos, ju gahorinoda izai*, “everyone who looks upon a woman with desire has already committed adultery with her”; Rom. X.11, *wazuh sa galaubjands du imma ni gaaiviskoda*, “everyone believing in him shall not be put to shame.”

Luke II.3, *iddjedun allai, ei melidai veseina warjizuh in seinai baurg*, “all went to be enrolled, each (ἕκαστος), each one of all, in his own city”; IX.14, *gavaurkeiþ im anakumbjan kubituns ana warjanoh fimftiguns*, “make them recline in companies of about fifty each”; Rom. XIV.12, *warjizuh unsara fram sis raþjon usgibiþ guþa*, “each of us shall give account of himself to God”; John XVI.32, *qimiþ weila ei distahjada warjizuh* (σκορπισθῆτε ἕκαστος, “you shall be scattered, each one,” namely, each of you) *du seina jah mik ainana bileiþiþ*, “the hour is coming when you shall each be scattered to his own place and leave me alone”; 1 Cor. IV.5, *hazeins vairþiþ warjammeh*—“praise shall come to each one,” namely, of you—*fram guþa*, “from God”; Luke VI.40, *gamanvids warjizuh* (πᾶς, “every one”) *vair þai sve laisaris is*, “every one fully trained shall be as his teacher.”

[Col. 1113] *Skeireins* V.d, *sveriþa waþaramme … gibaima bi vairþidai*, “we shall render honour due to each,” namely, to father and son.

[Note: [Col. 1113] Even in the manuscript, re-examined by Castiglione, *waþaramma* is read; this is incorrect, since an interrogative word has no meaning here. *Waþarammeh* ought properly to be written.]

In this single place only does *waþaruh* occur. For occurrences of *wazuh* and *warjizuh* in other examples, see the glossary under those words.

“Note 9.—*Wazuh* and *warjizuh* admit a partitive after them: Luke II.23, *wazuh gumakundaize* (πᾶν ἄρσεν, “every male”) *uslukands qiþu veihs fraujins haitada*, “every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord”; 1 Cor. XI.5, *woh qinono* (πᾶσα γυνή, “every woman”) *bidjandei aiþþau praufetjandei andhulidamma haubida gaaiviskoþ haubiþ sein*, “every woman praying or prophesying with uncovered head dishonours her head”; XV.30, *duwe bireikjai sijum weilo woh* (πᾶσαν ὥραν, “every hour”), “why are we in danger every hour?”; Gal. V.3, *veitvodja wammeh manne bimaitanaize* (παντὶ ἀνθρώπῳ περιτεμνομένῳ, “to every man being circumcised”), *þatei skula ist all vitoþ taujan*, “I testify that he is bound to perform the whole law”; Luke VI.30, *wammeh bidjandane* (παντὶ τῷ αἰτοῦντι, “to everyone asking”) *þuk qif*, “give to him who asks you.” Luke VI.44, *warjizuh bagme* (ἕκαστον δένδρον, “each tree”) *us svesamma akrana uskunþs ist*, “each tree is known by its own fruit”; *Skeireins* VI.b, *warjatoh vaurde at mannam in mundai maht ist anþarleikein inmaidjan*, “it is possible to understand each word in a man’s mouth differently.”

[Note: [Col. 1113] For thus, on comparison with Castiglione, it is quite clearly to be read in the manuscript, instead of Massmann’s *sunau* and our own conjecture *sunjai*.]

Eph. IV.16, *in mitaþ ainis warjoh fero usvahst leikis taujiþ*, “by the measure of each part the body makes growth.” Here the Goth, departing from the Greek ἑνὸς ἑκάστου μέρους, “of each individual part,” translated as though he had read ἑνὸς ἕκαστον μέρος, “of one, each part”; therefore in our translation “each” must be read in place of “of each.” Luke XIX.26, *warjammeh habandane* (παντὶ τῷ ἔχοντι, “to everyone having”) *gibada*, “to everyone who has, it shall be given.”

“In a similar case these indefinites also take adjectives used only substantivally, and substantives denoting a temporal determination, such as year, hour, feast, and so forth: Matt. V.22, *wazuh modags*, “everyone who is angry”; Neh. V.18, *vas fraquman dagis wizuh* (μίαν ἡμέραν, “one day”), “the provision of one day was …”; Mark XIV.49, *daga wammeh* (καθ’ ἡμέραν, “every day”), “daily”; Luke XVI.19; XIX.47; 1 Cor. XV.31; Luke II.14, *jera wammeh* (κατ’ ἔτος, “year by year”); Luke IX.23, *dag wanoh* (καθ’ ἡμέραν, “daily”); Matt. XXVII.15, *and dulþ warjanoh*, “at every feast”; Mark XV.6.

“*Wazuh* and *warjizuh*, when numeral words are added, form distributives; see §198.III.

“Note 10.—When the relatives *saei, izei, ei,* or *þei* follow *wazuh*, *sa* or *þis* is prefixed to it, the latter especially to render Greek ἄν. Thus: Matt. X.32–33, *sawazuh saei* (πᾶς ὅστις, “everyone who”) *andhaitiþ mis in andvairþja manna, andhaita jah ik imma in andvairþja attins meinis; iþ þiswanoh saei* (ὅστις ἄν, “whoever”) *afaikiþ mik—afaika jah ik ina*, “everyone who confesses me before men, I also shall confess him before my Father; but whoever denies me, I also shall deny him”; Mark XI.23, *þiswazuh ei* (ὃς ἄν, “whoever”) *qiþai … vairþiþ imma þiswah þei* (ὃ ἐάν, “whatever”) *qiþiþ*, “whoever says … whatever he says shall happen to him”; v. 24, *allata þiswah þei* (πάντα ὅσα ἄν, “whatever things”) *bidjandans sokeiþ, vairþiþ izvis*, “whatever you ask in prayer, shall be yours”; John XVI.2, *qimiþ weila ei sawazuh izei usqimiþ* (πᾶς ὁ ἀποκτείνας, “everyone who kills”) *izvis, þuggkeiþ hunsla saljan guþa*, “the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he offers service to God.” Yet John XVI.15 also reads, *þatawah þei* (ὅ, τι ἄν, “whatever”) *bidjaiþ attan, gibaiþ izvis*, “whatever you ask of the Father, he will give you.” For other examples see the glossary under this word.

“But conversely, to express a closer union emphatically, *ain* is prefixed to *warjizuh* and *waþaruh* also [Col. 1114] (εἷς ἕκαστος, ‘each individual’): 2 Thess. I.3, *managniþ friaþva ainwarjizuh* (ἑνὸς ἑκάστου, ‘of each individual’) *allaize izvara in izvis misso*, ‘the love of each one of you toward one another increases’; Luke XVI.5, *athaitands ainwarjanoh* (ἕνα ἕκαστον, ‘each one’) *faihuskulane qaþ þamma frumistin*, ‘calling each one of his master’s debtors, he said to the first’; IV.40, *ainwarjammeh* (ἑνὶ ἑκάστῳ, ‘to each one’) *ize handuns analagjands gahailida ins*, ‘laying hands upon each of them, he healed them’; 1 Cor. XII.18, *guþ gasatida liþuns ainwarjanoh* (ἓν ἕκαστον, ‘each one’) *ize in leika svasve vilda*, ‘God placed the members, each one of them, in the body as he wished’; *Skeireins* VII.c, *svaei ainwarjano sva filu sve vilda andniman is gatavida*, ‘he made each one capable of receiving as much as he wished.’

[Note: [Col. 1114] For thus it is read in the manuscript, as Castiglione informed us, instead of *ainwarjanoh*, which we had conjectured, and *ainwarjamma*, as Massmann read.]

But there is a mixed construction in 1 Cor. VII.17: *ni ei warjammeh svasve gadailida guþ, ainwarjatoh svasve galaþoda guþ, sva gaggai*, “let each one walk as God apportioned to him, as God called each one.”

[Note: [Col. 1114] According to Castiglione, Addenda p. 66, *ainwarjatoh* must be read, not *ainwarjizoh*, as we admitted in our edition following the same Castiglione’s text; the neuter is not used here, since the reference is alike to husband and wife.]

1 Thess. V.11, *þrafsteiþ izvis misso jah timrjaiþ ainwarjizuh anþar anþarana* (εἷς τὸν ἕνα, “each one the other”), “comfort one another and edify each other.” *Skeireins* III.a, *at bajoþum daupjandam jah ainwaþarammeh seina anafilhandam daupein, miþ sis misso sik andrunnun*, “while both were baptizing and committing baptism to each other, they ran against one another.”

“For *ainwarjizuh* used also as a distributive, see §198.III.”

V. *Alls, alla, all*, “all” (πᾶς), is construed in three ways, like the indefinite “anyone”:

1. Substantivally, but only in the plural, “all persons”: Mark V.20, *allai* (πάντες, “all”) *sildaleikidedun*, “all were amazed”; XIV.64, *eis allai gadomidedun ina skulan visan dauþau*, “they all condemned him as deserving death”; *Skeireins* I.a, *iesus qam gamains allaize nasjands; allaize fravaurhtins afhrainjan*, “Jesus came for the salvation of all, to cleanse all from sins”; Eph. IV.7, *guþ atta allaize ist ufar allaim jah and allans jah in allaim uns*, “God, the Father of all, is above all, through all, and in us all,” etc.

Mark IX.12, *helias qimands aftra gaboteiþ alla*, “Elijah, when he comes, restores all things”; for in this way the neuter plural is often used (πάντα or τὰ πάντα, “all things”), after Greek usage: Luke II.20; III.20; John XVII.7; XVIII.4; Rom. XI.36; 1 Cor. XV.27; 2 Cor. V.17, 18; Eph. I.11, 23; III.9; Phil. III.21; Col. I.16, 20; III.11. The neuter singular is also used, after Germanic usage: Matt. VIII.33, *gataihun in baurg all* (πάντα, “all things”), “they reported everything in the city”; Luke XVIII.12, 22; John XIV.26; 1 Cor. IX.22, *allaim vas all*, “I became all things to all”; v. 25; 2 Cor. II.9; Eph. I.22; Phil. III.8; Col. IV.7; 1 Tim. II.1. Or the full form *allata* is used: Matt. V.18, *allata vairþiþ*, “all things shall come to pass”; Mark IV.11, 34; Luke II.39 (ἅπαντα, “all things”); XIV.17; XV.13; XVIII.28; John XIV.26; Eph. IV.10; VI.21; also with the article, *þo alla*: Luke XVI.14; 1 Cor. XII.19; Col. III.8; *þata all*, 2 Cor. XII.19; *þata allata*, John XV.21; 2 Cor. IV.15.

2. Adjectivally:

a. To mean “all” in the plural, agreeing in case with the substantive: Matt. XXVII.1, *runa nemun allai gudjans*, “all the priests took counsel”; Mark IV.32, *kaurno sinapis vairþiþ allaize grase maist*, “a grain of mustard becomes the greatest of all herbs”; 1 Cor. XV.7, *ataugida sik apaustaulum allaim*, “he appeared to all the apostles”; Luke III.3, *qam and allans gaujans*, “he came into all the region”; Matt. VIII.16, *allans þans ubil habandans ganasida*, “he healed all those afflicted”; Luke II.31, *nasein þeina manvides in andvairþja allaizo manageino*, “your salvation, prepared before all peoples”; I.6, *vesun ba gaggandona in allaim anabusnim jah garaihteim fraujins unvaha*, “they both walked blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord”; Matt. IX.35, *bitauh baurgs allos jah haimos*, “he went about through all cities and villages”; Luke I.48, *audagjand mik alla kunja*, “all generations shall call me blessed”; Matt. V.15; Mark I.32; VII.3, 23; Luke I.6, 65, 66, 71; II.19; III.19; IV.5, 37; V.9; VI.26; XVII.2, 10; XIX.37; Rom. X.4, 12; XII.17; 1 Cor. XV.19; 2 Cor. I.1, 3, 4; III.2; IV.2; VIII.18; XI.9; Gal. I.2; Eph. I.18, 21; III.21; IV.6; VI.18; Col. II.13; 2 Thess. III.6.

b. To mean “each” in the singular, especially in the neuter, with a following plural partitive substantive: *Skeireins* V.a, *at allamma vaurtstve ainaizos anabusnais beidiþ*, “he awaits every work of a single commandment”; Luke III.6, *gasaiwiþ all leike* (πᾶσα σάρξ, “all flesh”) *nasein guþs*, “all flesh shall see the salvation of God”; IV.4, *ni bi hlaib ainana libaid manna ak bi all vaurde* (παντὶ ῥήματι, “by every word”) *guþs*, “man shall not live by bread alone but by every word of God”; 2 Cor. XIII.1; Rom. XIV.11, *mis all knive* (πᾶν γόνυ, “every knee”) *biugiþ*, “every knee shall bow to me”; 2 Cor. X.5, *frahinþan all fraþje* (πᾶν νόημα, “every thought”), “bringing every thought captive”; Luke III.5, *all dalei* (πᾶσα φάραγξ, “every valley”) *usfulljada jah all fairgunje jah hlaine* (πᾶν ὄρος καὶ βουνός, “every mountain and hill”) *gahnaivjada*, “every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill made low”; 2 Cor. IX.8, *ufarassjaiþ in allamma vaurstve godaize* (πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθόν, “every good work”), “abound in every good work”; Col. I.10; 1 Tim. V.10; 2 Tim. II.21; III.17.

Col. I.28, *vulþu gateiham talzjandans all manne* (πάντα ἄνθρωπον, “every person”) *jah laisjandans all manne*, “whom we proclaim, admonishing every person and teaching every person”; *Skeireins* IV.b; Phil. IV.7, *ufarist all ahane* (πάντα νοῦν, “every understanding”), “surpassing all understanding”; Matt. VII.17, *all bagme godaize* (πᾶν δένδρον ἀγαθόν, “every good tree”) *akrana goda gataujiþ*, “every good tree produces good fruits”; v. 19, *all bagme ni taujandane akran god usmaitada*, “every tree not producing good fruit is cut down”; John XV.2, *all taine unbairandane akran goþ usnimiþ ita*, “every branch not bearing fruit he takes away.”

Luke IV.13, *ustauh all fraistobnjo* (πάντα πειρασμόν, “every temptation”) *diabulus*, “the devil had ended every temptation”; V.17, *vesun gaqumanai us allamma haimo* (πάσης κώμης, “every village”), “they had come from every village”; X.1, *insandida ins tvans wanzuh in all baurge jah stade* (πᾶσαν πόλιν καὶ τόπον, “every city and place”), “he sent them two by two into every city and place”; Rom. XIII.1, *all saivalo* (πᾶσα ψυχή, “every soul”) *valdufnjam ufarvisandam ufhausjai*, “let every soul be subject to governing authorities”; 2 Cor. VII.1, *hrainjam unsis af allamma bisauleino* (παντὸς μολυσμοῦ, “every defilement”), “let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement”; X.6, *manvuba habaiþ du fraveitan all ufarhauseino* (πᾶσαν παρακοήν, “every disobedience”), “being ready to punish every disobedience”; 2 Tim. III.16, *all boko* (πᾶσα γραφή, “every scripture”); Mark III.28, *allata afletada þata fravaurhte* (πάντα … τὰ ἁμαρτήματα, “all … sins”) *sunum manne*, “all sins shall be forgiven to the children of men.”

“Note 11.—In this latter case a partitive substantive in the singular occurs only rarely: Mark II.13, *all manageins* (πᾶς ὁ ὄχλος, “the whole crowd”) *iddjedun du imma*, “the whole crowd went to him”; 1 Tim. IV.4, *all gaskaftais* (πᾶν κτίσμα, “every creature”) *guþs goþ*, “every creature of God is good”; 2 Cor. X.5, *gatairan all hauhiþos ushafanaizos* (πᾶν ὕψωμα ἐπαιρόμενον, “every lofty thing raised up”) *viþra kunþi guþs*, “destroying every lofty thing raised against the knowledge of God.” And only once does *alla razdo* occur, Rom. XIV.11, *alls* agreeing in gender with the substantive, after the manner of the other indefinites. Perhaps also in 2 Thess. III.6, *gaskaidiþ izvis af allamma broþre wairbandane ungatassaba*, “separate yourselves from every brother living disorderly,” this *allamma* should be taken as masculine; though, since *all manne* is found, it may also be neuter.

“Note 12.—In view of its meaning (ὅλος, πᾶς, ‘whole,’ ‘all’), *alls* has the pure character of an adjective (see glossary under *Alls*, 2). Hence, also in the Pauline epistles—where Greek and Latin probably influenced the Gothic language—it often occurs in the sense ‘every’: 2 Cor. VIII.7, *in allamma managniþ, galaubeinai jah vaurda jah kunþja jah in allai usdaudein* (πάσῃ σπουδῇ, “in all diligence”), “in all zeal, faith, speech, knowledge, and every earnestness”; XII.12, *taikneis apaustaulaus gatavidos vaurþun in isvis in allai þulainai* (πάσῃ ὑπομονῇ, “in all endurance”), “the signs of an apostle were performed among you in all endurance”; Eph. I.3, *guþ gaþiuþida uns in allai þiu þeinai ahmeinai*, “God has blessed us in every spiritual blessing”; Phil. I.20; II.29; IV.6; Col. I.9, 11, 15; III.16; 1 Thess. III.7; 2 Thess. I.11; 1 Tim. I.16.”

## B. ON THE SIMPLE SENTENCE

[Col. 1115]

## SUBJECT, PREDICATE, COPULA

§206. The subject and verb are united in the particular verbal form when the speaking person (first person) speaks of himself, or addresses another person present (second person), or speaks of an absent third person, provided that this person has already been mentioned: Matt. XXVII.63, “that deceiver said: *urreisa*, ‘I rise’”; V.17, *qam*, “I came”; 1 Tim. IV.10, *arbaidjam jah idveitjanda*, “we labour and are reproached”; Luke X.28, *raihtaba andhoft, þata tavei jah libais*, “you answered rightly; do this and you shall live”; 2 Cor. I.24, *galaubeinai gasto þuþ stetistis*, “you stand firm in faith”; Mark V.39, *wa auhjoþ jah gretiþ?*, “why do you make a tumult and weep?”; XIV.42, *urreisiþ, gaggam!*, “rise, let us go!”; Matt. XXVI.75, *usgaggands ut gaigrot*, “having gone out, he wept,” namely Peter; Luke XX.36, *ni gasviltan þanaseiþs magun, sunjus auk guþs sind*, “neither can they die any more, for they are sons of God”—that is, those who have attained eternal life—“they are.”

§207. I. A subject requiring a particular noun is always put in the nominative and is expressed:

1. By pronouns of the first and second persons when they are contrasted with one another or are to be uttered emphatically [Col. 1116]; see §199.2.a. It is also frequently expressed by the pronoun of the third person where Greek employs a simple verb; see the same section, b.

2. In the third person, where the subject has not yet been named, or where one discourse is interrupted by another. A subject can in general be a substantive; a pronoun taking the place of a substantive; an adjective; a numeral; a participle; an infinitive; a prepositional phrase with the article; indeed, even a whole sentence. Moreover, the verb agrees with its subject in number, except in the case of a collective, as stated in §209.3. As to position, the subject is not confined to any particular place: Luke IV.40, *sunno sagq*, “the sun set”; Rom. VII.3, *gasviltiþ vair*, “the husband dies”; Luke IX.10, *apaustauleis usspillodedun*, “the apostles related”; Matt. IX.3, *sa vajamereiþ*, “this man blasphemes”; Luke IX.8, *sumai qeþun: helias ataugida sik*, “some said: Elijah has appeared”; XVII.34, *tvai vairþand ana ligra samin*, “two shall be on one bed together”; I.14, *managai faginond*, “many rejoiced”; VII.22, *blindai ussaiwand, haltai gaggand, þrutsfillai gahrainjanda, baudai gahausjand, naveis urreisand, unledai vailamerjanda*, “the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, the poor receive the gospel”; VIII.34, *þai haldandans gaþlauhun*, “those keeping [the herd] fled”; Rom. VII.18, *viljan atligiþ mis*, “the willing is present with me”; Mark IV.10, *frehun þai bi ina*, “they asked him concerning it”; Luke IX.17, *ushafan varþ þatei aflifnoda im gabruko*, “there was taken up what remained to them of fragments.”

§208. 1. Sometimes the subject of the third-person plural is lacking; but then some general subject, such as “men,” must be supplied, or the expression must be rendered by a passive in Latin (French *on*, German *man*): Mark I.45, *iesus ana auþjaim stadim vas jah iddjedun du imma allaþro*, “Jesus was in deserted places, and they came to him from all quarters”—that is, people came, “there was coming”; V.35, *nauhþanuh imma rodjandin qemun fram þamma synagogafada*, “while he was still speaking, people came from the ruler of the synagogue”; X.13, *atberun du imma barna*, “they brought children to him”; Luke XVII.27, *etun jah drugkun*, “they ate and drank,” namely people in the time of Noah; Mark II.22, *vein juggata in balgins niujans giutand*, “new wine [is] put into new wineskins”: people pour it; it is poured; Greek βλητέον, “it must be put,” “wine must be poured.”

For this ellipsis, borrowed from Greek, often to be rendered by changing the active into the passive, see §177, Note 5. In John XVI.17, *qeþun us þaim siponjaim est sumai*, “some of his disciples said,” must be understood.

But the subject of the third-person singular is omitted only rarely: 2 Cor. VI.2, *mela qiþiþ andanemjamma andhausida þus*, “he says: ‘At an acceptable time I heard you’”: God speaks, namely through the prophets, or the Holy Scripture speaks. Conversely, in X.10, *þos bokos qiþand kaurjos sind*, “the letters, they say, are weighty,” the plural means “people say” (“it is said”); it corresponds to and is equivalent to Greek φησί, “he says.” The Goth also imitated the Greek construction in which a substantive of the same root as the verb is to be supplied as subject (Matthiä, Greek Grammar §295): 1 Cor. XV.52, *þuthaurneiþ* (σαλπίσει), “it shall sound,” namely *þuthaurnja*, “the trumpet.”

2. Where a demonstrative, interrogative, or relative pronoun is the subject, it need not agree with the predicate in gender; rather, after the usual German practice, it may be put in the neuter, just as Germans say *das ist mein Vater*, and French *c’est mon père*, that is, “this is my father”: Mark VI.3, *niu þata* (οὗτος, “this [man]”) *ist sa timrja?*, “is this not the carpenter?”; John VI.40, *þatuh-þan ist vilja þis sandjandins mik*, “this is the will of him who sent me”; Luke II.12, *þata izvis taikns*, “this [shall be] a sign to you”; VIII.11, *þata* (αὕτη, “this [feminine]”) *ist gajuko*, “this is the parable”; John XV.12, *þata* (αὕτη) *ist anabusns meina*, “this is my commandment”; 1 Cor. IX.3, *meina andahafts þat-ist*, “this is my defence”; Eph. I.18, *wa* (τίς or τί, “what?”) *ist vens laþonais is? wa ufarassus mikileins mahtais*, “what is the hope of his calling? what the surpassing greatness of his power?”; 1 Thess. II.19, *wa* (τίς, “what?”) *ist unsara vens*, “what is our hope?”; Phil. I.28, *þatei* (ἥτις, “which”) *ist im ustaikneins fralustais*, “which is to them a sign of destruction.” Yet Mark IX.7 reads *sa ist sunus meins sa liuba*, “this is my beloved Son,” and Tit. I.13, *so ist veitvodei sunjeina*, “this testimony is true.”

3. When pronouns and *ba*, serving as subject, designate two persons of different gender, they are put in the neuter; compare §191.I.1: Luke II.6, *þo* (Greek αὐτοί, namely Joseph and Mary) *vesun jainar*, “they were there”; II.50, *ija* (αὐτοί) *ni froþun þamma vaurda*, “they did not understand the saying”; 1 Cor. VII.28, *aglon leikis gastaldand þo svaleika* (οἱ τοιοῦτοι, namely man and virgin) *du leika samin*, “such persons shall have affliction in the flesh”; compare §209.4.b and Luke II.44, 45, 48; VIII.20; Mark III.31. But where two persons of the same gender are joined, the subject properly agrees with them in gender: Luke VI.39, *bai*—namely blind persons—*in dal gadriusand*, “both shall fall into a pit”; John XI.19, *gaþrafstidedun ijos*—namely Martha and Mary—“they comforted them.”

4. The infinitive is often the subject; see also Mark X.24; Luke VI.4; XVIII.25; John XVIII.31; [Col. 1118] 1 Cor. V.12; VII.9, 26; Gal. IV.18; Phil. I.21, 22; 1 Tim. II.10. Sometimes *du* is joined to the infinitive: Mark X.40, *þata du sitan af taihsvon meinai aiþþau af hleidumein nist mein du giban* (δοῦναι, “to give”), “to sit on my right or left is not mine to give”; 1 Cor. XI.6, *agl ist qinon du kapillon aiþþau skaban* (τὸ κείρασθαι ἢ ξυρᾶσθαι, “to have the hair cut or to be shaved”), “it is shameful for a woman to have her hair cut or be shaved”; Phil. I.24, *du visan* (τὸ ἐπιμένειν, “to remain”) *in leika þaurftizo in izvara*, “to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake.” The article also occurs: Mark XII.33, *þata du frijon* (τὸ ἀγαπᾷν, “to love”) *guþ managizo ist allaim þaim allbrunstim*, “to love God is greater than all burnt offerings.”

Between *waþar ist azetizo qiþan …* (Matt. IX.5; Luke V.23), “which is easier to say …?” and *waþar ist azetizo du qiþan …* (Mark II.9), “which is easier: to say …?”, the following difference seems to exist: the former means “what is easier to say …?”, whereas the latter means “what is easier: to say …?”

Where an infinitive clause is the subject, its own subject is put in the accusative: 2 Cor. VII.11, *þata bi guþ saurgan izvis welauda gatavida izvis usdaudein*, “godly sorrow produced in you what earnestness”; Luke XVI.17, *azetizo ist himin jah airþa hindarleiþan þau vitodis ainana vrigadriusan*, “it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of the law to fail.”

§209. II. When the PREDICATE is a noun, it must be joined to the subject by a copula. Now every class of word that can be a subject (§207) can also be used as predicate. But whatever it may be, the predicate always agrees with the subject; that is, it takes the same inflection.

1. Where a substantive is predicate, it ought to agree with the subject in gender and number, although some exceptions occur in gender and very frequent exceptions in number: Luke XX.14, *sa ist sa arbinumja*, “this is the heir”; I.19, *ik im gabriel*, “I am Gabriel”; IX.9, *was ist sa?*, “who is this?”; V.10, *fram himma nu manne siud nutans*, “from now on you shall be catching men.” John XIV.6, *ik im vigs jah sunja jah libains*, “I am the way, the truth, and the life”; *Skeireins* I.a, *nasjands silba garaihtei vas*, “the Saviour himself was righteousness”; Rom. XI.15, *was andanumts nibai libains us dauþaim*, “what shall their receiving be but life from the dead?”

[In our translation, “who” must be read instead of “what.”]

Eph. I.23, *aikklesjo ist leik is*, “the church is his body”; Rom. VII.7, *vitoþ fravaurhts ist?*, “is the law sin?”; John VI.63, *þo vaurda ahma ist*, “the words are spirit”; Rom. XIII.3, *þai reiks ni sind agis godamma vaurstva*, “rulers are not a terror to good work”; 1 Cor. X.19, *þo galiugaguda sind wa?*, “are idols anything?”; John XVII.11, *þai sijaina ain sve vit*, “that they may be one as we [are]”; 1 Cor. XV.28, *guþ ist alla in allaim*, “God is all in all”; Rom. IX.7; 1 Cor. X.17; 2 Cor. II.15; VIII.23; Phil. III.3.

The predicate may also take the article: John VI.48, *ik im sa hlaifs libainais*, “I am the bread of life”; VII.40, *sa ist sa praufetus*, “this is the prophet”; X.9, *ik im þata daur*, “I am the door,” etc.; see the glossary under *þata*, II.6.

2. When an adjective, participle, or numeral is predicate, it must agree with the subject in gender, number, and case. Further, an infinitive and a sentence are regarded as neuter. For the difference between consonantal and vocalic adjective forms, see §196: Luke I.23, *zakarias vas dumbs*, “Zechariah was dumb”; John XI.39, *ju fuls ist, fidurdogs auk ist*, “he already stinks, for it is the fourth day”; Luke I.7, *vas aileisabaiþ stairo*, “Elizabeth was barren”; v. 29, *weleika ist so goleins*, “what sort of greeting is this?”; Rom. VII.14, *vitoþ ahmein ist*, “the law is spiritual”; 1 Tim. I.8, *god ist vitoþ*, “the law is good”; II.3, *þatuþ-þan ist god jah andanem*, “this is good and acceptable”; Luke XV.31, *all þata mein þein ist*, “all that is mine is yours”; Rom. XI.33, *unbilaistidai sind vigos guþs*, “the ways of God are unsearchable”; XIII.1, *þo valdufnja fram guþa gasatida sind*, “the authorities are ordained by God”; Luke I.20, *sijais þahands jah ni magands rodjan*, “you shall be silent and unable to speak”; VIII.40, *vesun allai beidandans is*, “all were waiting for him”; 1 Tim. IV.15, *þatei þeihais þu* (ἡ προκοπή σου, “your progress”) *svikunþ sijai*, “that your progress may be evident”; Phil. I.29, *izvis fragiban ist du xristau galaubjan*, “to you it has been granted to believe in Christ.”

Luke IV.32, *in valdufnja varþ vaurd is*, “his word was with authority”; 2 Cor. I.5, *ufar filu ist gaþrafsteins*, “the consolation is exceedingly abundant”; Luke IX.55, *wis ahmane sijuþ*, “you are of what spirit.”

“Note 1.—Sometimes predicates, when adjectives or participles, do not agree with their subject in gender. Thus Gal. V.11, *gatauran ist marzeins galgins*, “the offence of the cross has ceased”; Eph. III.10, *kanniþ vesi … handugei guþs*, “that the wisdom of God might be made known”; Rom. XI.33, *unusspilloda sind stauos guþs*, “the judgments of God are inscrutable”; Neh. V.18, *vas fraquman dagis wizuh stiur ·a· lamba gavalida ·q·*, “the provision of one day was one ox and six choice sheep”; 1 Cor. XII.22, *þaiei þugkjand liþive leikis lasivostai visan, þaurfta sind*, “those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary.” In almost every case the Goth imitated these anomalies from the Greek text. Especially conspicuous are 1 Tim. III.16, *unsahtaba mikils ist gagudeins runa*, “great is the mystery of godliness”; Gal. II.16, *vairþiþ garaihts ainhun leike*, “no flesh is justified”; Neh. VI.16, *varþ usfulliþs þata vaurd*, “the work was completed”; *Skeireins* II.c, *naudiþaurfts vas jah gadob vistai—anþar*, “needful was also the provision of food—another [thing]”; *Skeireins* VI.c, *missaleiks jah in missaleikaim melam attins bi ina varþ veitvodeins*, “the Father’s testimony concerning him was manifold and at various times.” But passages such as Eph. III.6, *sind þiudos gaarbjans jah galeikans*, “the Gentiles are fellow-heirs and fellow-members,” do not belong here, because substantives are included in the predicate.”

3. Collectives do not strictly follow this rule of agreement, but can be construed according to *synesis*, that is, not according to the meaning indicated by their form, but according to the sense which they contain: Mark III.32, *setun bi ina managei*, “a crowd was sitting around him”—that is, many people; John XII.18, *iddjedun gamotjan imma managei*, “a crowd went to meet him”; Matt. XI.18, *alla managei sildaleikidedun*, “the whole crowd was amazed”; Mark II.13, *all manageins iddjedun*, “the whole crowd went”; III.7, *filu manageins*—“a great multitude,” that is, many people—*laistidedun afar imma*, “followed him”; 1 Cor. XVI.15, *gards staifanaus sind*—Greek ἐστίν, “is”—*anastodeins akaje*, “the household of Stephanas are the firstfruits of Achaia”; Matt. VIII.32, *run gavaurhtedun alla so hairda*, “the whole herd rushed”; Phil. II.4, *ni þo seina warjizuh mitondans*, “not each considering his own things”; Luke I.10, *alls hiuhma vas beidandans*, “the whole multitude of the people was praying”; John VII.49, *so managei fragiþanai sind*, “this crowd is accursed”; Mark XV.1, *alla so gafaurds gabindandans iesu brahtedun ina at peilatau*, “the whole council, having bound Jesus, brought him to Pilate.” A certain *synesis* is also present where 2 Tim. III.16 says: *all boko gudiskaizos ahmateinais jah þaurftos du laiseinai*, “all Scripture is divinely inspired and profitable for teaching.”

Conversely, however, one also finds: Luke V.1, *managei anatramp*, “the crowd pressed upon [him]”; XX.6, *alla so managei afvairpiþ*, “the whole people will stone us”; Neh. V.13, *qaþ alla gamainþs*, “the whole congregation said,” etc. And *warjizuh* is generally so construed, although Greek ἕκαστος, “each,” often stands with the plural; the reason is to be sought in the meaning of this word; see §205.IV. Yet here the Goth mixes singular and plural in his own fashion: John I.20, *andhof*—singular—*so managei jah qeþun*—plural—“the crowd answered and said.”

“Note 2.—The Greek construction by which a singular verb is used where the subject is neuter plural is wholly foreign to the Gothic language. Thus Luke I.65 says, *in allai bairgahein iudaias merida vesun alla þo vaurda*, ‘all these words were reported throughout all the hill-country of Judaea,’ where Greek has διελαλεῖτο πάντα τὰ ῥήματα ταῦτα, ‘all these sayings was being discussed’; John X.27, *lamba meina stibnai meinas hausjand*, ‘my sheep hear my voice,’ where Greek has πρόβατα … ἀκούει; and so always.”

4. When several subjects are joined by copulative or adversative particles, observe:

a. Since they form a plural, they require the verb to be put in the plural—naturally where an actual plural is present among them: Matt. VIII.27, *vindos jah marei gahausjand imma*, “winds and sea obey him”; Mark I.5, *usiddjedun all iudaialand jah iairusaulymeis*, “all Judaea and Jerusalem went out”; v. 36. But this is also so where all the subjects are singular: John XII.22, *andraias jah filippus qeþun*, “Andrew and Philip said”; 1 Cor. XV.50, *leik jah bloþ þiudinassu guþs ganiman ni magun*, “flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God”; 2 Tim. II.17, *þizeei vesun*—Greek ἦν, singular—*ymainaius jah filetus*, “of whom are Hymenaeus and Philetus”; Luke II.43, *ni vissedun*—Greek ἔγνω, singular—*iosef jah aiþei is*, “Joseph and his mother did not know.” If the subjects are of different persons, the first person takes precedence over the second and third: John X.30, *ik jah atta ain siju*, “I and the Father are one”; 1 Cor. IX.6, *jah barnabas ni habos valdufni?*, “do Barnabas and I alone not have authority?”

Yet these subjects also permit a singular verb: Mark XII.6, *wis ist sa manleika jah so ufarmeleins*, “there is one beloved son”; Luke I.14, *vairþiþ þus faheds jah svegniþa*, “there shall be joy and gladness for you”; Mark VIII.12, *jainar vairþiþ grets jah krusts tunþive*, “there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth”; 1 Cor. XVI.19, *goleiþ izvis akvila jah priska*, “Aquila and Prisca greet you”; Matt. VI.19, *malo jah nidva fravardeiþ*, “moth and rust destroy”; 1 Thess. III.11; 2 Thess. II.16, 17; Luke I.64, *usluknoda munþs is suns jah tuggo*, “his mouth was immediately opened, and his tongue.” Indeed, this occurs even where a plural is among the subjects, provided the verb is far removed from that plural: Luke III.5, *vairþiþ þata vraiqo du raihtamma jah usdrusteis du vigam slaihtaim*, “the crooked shall become straight and the rough places smooth ways”; Rom. IX.4, *þizeei ist frastisibja jah vulþus jah vitodis garaideins jah triggvos jah skarkinassus jah gahaita*, “whose are the adoption, glory, covenants, giving of the law, service, promises”; Eph. V.3, *horinassus jah allos unhrainiþos aiþþau faihufrikei nih namnjaidau in izvis*, “fornication and every uncleanness or covetousness must not even be named among you.” But when one subject is joined to another by *miþ*, “with,” the verb remains singular: Mark IX.4, *ataugiþs varþ in helias miþ mose*, “Elijah appeared with Moses.”

b. When an adjective or participle is predicate, it agrees in gender with the subjects when these are of the same gender; but where they are of different genders, the predicate is neuter, indeed without exception even when living beings are concerned; see §208.3: Matt. XXVII.61, *vas jainar marja magdalene jah so anþara magdalene sitandeins*, “Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were sitting there”; Tit. I.15, *bisaulida sind aha jah miþvissei*, “both mind and conscience are defiled”; 1 Thess. V.23, *saivala jah leik unfairinona gafastaidau*, “may soul and body be preserved blameless”; Luke II.33, *vas iosef jah aiþei is sildaleikjandona*, “Joseph and his mother were marvelling.” Or the predicate is referred to the nearer subject: 1 Cor. VII.15, *nist gaþivaids broþar aiþþau svistar*, “a brother or sister is not enslaved”; Rom. VIII.38, *nih dauþus nih aggeljus nih reikja ni mahteis nih andwairþo nih anawairþo nih hauhiþa nih diupiþa nih gaskafts anþara mahteiga ist uns afskaidan*, “neither death nor angels nor rulers nor powers nor things present nor things to come nor height nor depth nor any other creature is able to separate us.”

5. In place of a predicate in the nominative, the Goth often uses *du* with the dative, whether following Greek or of his own choice: Mark X.8, *gumein jah qinein sijaina du leika samin* (εἰς σάρκα μίαν, “into one flesh”), *svasve þanaseiþs ni sind tva ak leik ain* (σὰρξ μία, “one flesh”), “man and wife shall be one flesh; so then they are no longer two, but one flesh”; 1 Cor. XIV.22, *razdos du bandvai sind*, “tongues are for a sign”; Col. IV.11, *þai vesun mis du gaþrafsteinai*, “they have been a comfort to me”; Gal. V.2, *xristus izvis nist du botai* (οὐδὲν ὠφελήσει, “will profit nothing”), “Christ will be of no benefit to you”; [Col. 1121] 1 Tim. IV.4, *all gaskaftais guþs goþ jah ni vaiht du usvaurpai* (ἀπόβλητον, “rejected”), “every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected”; compare §211.1.

Or an adverb is used as predicate in place of an adjective: Luke XV.20, *nauhþanuh fairra visandan gasaw ina atta*, “while he was still far away, his father saw him”; XIX.37, *iesus newa vas at iddaljin*, “Jesus was near the descent”; *Skeireins* III.b, *so garehsns newa andja vas*, “the revelation was near its end”; 1 Cor. XV.14, *jabai xristus ni urrais, svare þan jas-so mereins unsara jah so galaubeins lausa*, “if Christ has not risen, then our preaching is empty and your faith vain”; v. 17; Phil. II.6, *ni vulva rahnida visan sik galeiko* (ἴσα, “equal [things]”) *guþa*, “he did not consider equality with God a prize to be grasped.”

§210. III. The COPULA is sometimes omitted:

a. Most commonly in the third-person singular (*ist*, “is”): Matt. VII.13, *braid daur jah rums vigs*, “broad [is] the gate and wide [is] the way”; Mark V.9, *wa namo þein?*, “what [is] your name?”; Luke I.28, *frauja miþ þus*, “the Lord [is] with you”; II.49, *wa þatei sokideduþ mik*, “why [is it] that you sought me?”—for *wa ist þatei* (Mark II.16), “what is it that …?”; Luke VI.23; Rom. VII.12; 2 Cor. VI.2, 14; 2 Thess. III.3, etc.; after a relative: Eph. IV.6, *ains atta allaize, saei in allaim uns*, “one Father of all, who [is] in us all”; see the note on Rom. XII.2; in the formulae *niu kara* and *wa kara*, “does it not concern [you]?” and “what concern [is it]?”: Mark IV.38; XII.14; Matt. XXVII.4.

b. In the subjunctive (*sijai*, “may be”): Rom. XI.36, *imma vulþus du aivam!*, “to him [be] glory for ever!”; 1 Cor. XVI.22, *anaþaima!*, “anathema!”; 2 Cor. VIII.13, 16; XIII.13; Eph. I.3.

c. In the preterite (*vas*, “was”): Matt. XXVII.57, *þizuh namo iosef*, “Joseph by name”; Luke I.27; VII.12, *jah si silbo viduvo*, “and she herself [was] a widow”; VII.2, *skalks siukands svultavairþja*, “a slave, sick and at the point of death”; John XI.44, *vlits is auralja bibundans* (περιεδέδετο, “had been bound around”), “his face [was] bound around with a cloth”; Mark X.1, *sve biuhts* (ὡς εἰώθει, “as was his custom”; compare Matt. XXVII.15, *biuhts vas*).

d. In the third-person plural (*sind*, “are”): Luke X.2, *asans managa iþ vaurstvjans favai*, “the harvest [is] plentiful, but the workers [are] few”; Matt. X.36; Luke XVII.17; Rom. XI.36; 2 Cor. X.4, *vepna unsaris drauhtinassaus ni leikeina ak mahteiga*, “the weapons of our warfare [are] not fleshly but powerful.”

e. In the first-person singular (*im*, “am”): Rom. VII.24, *vainans ik manna*, “wretched [am] I, a man!”; John X.38, *in mis atta jah ik in imma*, “the Father [is] in me and I [am] in him.”

f. In the second-person plural (*sijuþ*, “you are”): Eph. II.17, *merida gavairþi izvis juzei fairra*—namely *sijuþ*, “you are”—*jah þaim izei newa*—namely *sind*, “they are”—“peace [to] you who are far off and [to] those who are near”; Luke VI.20, 21; John XIV.20.

g. In the second-person singular subjunctive (imperative *sijais*, “be”) only in the formula *hails* (χαῖρε, “hail!”): Mark XV.18; John XIX.3.

h. In the infinitive in the formula *ni viljau izvis unvitans vel unveisans* (οὐ θέλω ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν, “I do not wish you to be ignorant”): 1 Cor. X.1; 2 Cor. I.8; 1 Thess. IV.13; compare the note on Rom. XI.25.

Likewise in copulative sentences where the copula occurs in the preceding sentence: Phil. IV.12, *sads vairþan jah gredags*, “to be full and to be hungry”; Matt. XXV.43, *afþaursiþs vas, janni dragkideduþ mik; gasts*—namely *vas*, “I was”—*janni galaþodeduþ mik; naqaþs, janni gavasideduþ mik; siuks janni gaveisodeduþ meina*, “I was thirsty, and you gave me no drink; a stranger, and you did not receive me; naked, and you did not clothe me; sick, and you did not visit me”; Luke XVII.31, *jainamma daga saei sijai ana hrota jah kasa is in razna, ni atsteigai dalaþ niman þo; jah saei ana haiþjai, ni gavandjai sik*, “on that day, whoever is on the roof and his goods are in the house must not come down to take them; likewise, whoever is in the field must not turn back”; I.18, *ik im sineigs jah qens meina*—namely *ist*, “is”—*framaldrozei*, “I am old and my wife is advanced in years”; XVIII.11, *ni im svasve þai anþarai*—namely *sind*, “are”—“I am not like the other persons.”

The Goth also often supplies the copula where Greek omits it: 2 Cor. 3:5 *so vairþida unsara us guþa ist* (“our sufficiency is from God”); 4:18; 10:10; Eph. 3:18; likewise in the formula [Col. 1122] εἰ δυνατόν, *jabai mahteig sijai* (“if it be possible”), Mark 13:22; *jabai mahteig wesi*, Gal. 4:15.

## § 211

1) The verbs “to become,” “to remain,” “to appear,” etc., take in the nominative as predicate that which someone or something is said to become, remain, or appear; accordingly they are called predicate verbs: Luke 4:3 *ïesus gredags varþ* (“Jesus became hungry”); 1:24 *inkilþo varþ aileisabaiþ* (“Elizabeth became pregnant”); Mark 12:7 *unsar vairþiþ þata arbi* (“that inheritance shall become ours”); 1 Cor. 14:25 *þo analaugnona hairtins svikunþa vairþand* (“the hidden things of the heart become manifest”); Mark 13:19 *vairþand þai dagos jainai aglo svaleika sve ni vas svaleika* (“those days shall become an affliction such as there has not been”); 2 Cor. 5:21 *xristus faur uns gatavida fravaurht, ei veis vaurþeima garaihtei guþs* (“Christ was made sin for us, so that we might become God’s righteousness”).

—2 Cor. 3:14 *hulistr visiþ unandhuliþ* (“the veil remains unrevealed”); 2 Tim. 2:13 *jains triggvs visiþ* (“he remains faithful”); 1 Cor. 7:10–11 *anabiuda qenai fairra abin ni skaidan; ïþ jabai gaskaidnai, visan unliugaidai* (“I command the wife not to separate from her husband; but if she has separated, to remain unmarried”). The dative refers to *qenai* (“the wife”), and in our translation “remain” must be read in place of “be.”

—2 Cor. 13:7 *bidja du guþa, ei ni vaiht ubilis taujaiþ. ni ei veis gakusanai þugkjaima ak ei jus þata godo taujaiþ, ei veis ungakusanai þugkjaima* (“we pray to God that you may do nothing evil—not in order that we may appear approved, but that you may do what is good, though we should appear unapproved”).

Just as with *visan* (§ 209, 5), so with *vairþan*, *du* with the dative is sometimes joined in place of the predicate nominative: Mark 12:10 *stains, þammei usvaurpun þai timrjans, varþ du haubida vaihstins* (“the stone which the builders rejected became the head of the corner,” εἰς κεφαλήν); Luke 3:5 *vairþiþ þata vraiqo du raihtamma jah usdrusteis du vigam slaihtaim* (“the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places smooth ways,” εἰς εὐθεῖαν, εἰς ὁδοὺς λείας); John 16:20; 2 Cor. 6:18; *Skeireins* VIII, b.

2) As for verbs which in the active take, besides an object, a predicate in the accusative—such as “to name,” “to hold,” “to choose,” and so forth—and which in the passive take this same predicate in the nominative, see § 220, note 2.

## § 212

1) Where the person commanded to do something is expressly named, that person is put in the vocative; adjectives joined with it always take the consonantal form; see § 196, II, 1 e): Luke 19:5 *zakkaiu, dalaþ atsteig* (“Zacchaeus, come down quickly”); 18:13 *guþ, hulþs sijais* (“God, be merciful”); 7:14 *juggalauþ, du þus qiþa, urreis!* (“Young man, I say to you, arise!”); Col. 3:19–20 *vairos, frijoþ qenins ïzvaros. barna, ufhausjaiþ fadreinam* (“Husbands, love your wives. Children, obey your parents”); Mark 15:18 *hails þiudan ïudaie* (“Hail, king of the Jews”); Rom. 15:10 *sifaiþ, þiudos, miþ managein ïs* (“Rejoice, nations, with his people”); Luke 1:13 *ni ogs þus, zakkaria* (“Do not fear, Zechariah”); Mark 5:18 *usgagg, ahma unhrainja* (“Come out, unclean spirit”); 1 Tim. 6:11 *ïþ þu jai, manna guþs. þata þliuhais* (“But you, O man of God, flee these things”); 2 Tim. 2:1 *þu nu, barn mein valiso, ïnsvinþei þuk* (“You therefore, my beloved child, strengthen yourself”); Rom. 11:19 *ni ïzvis silbans gavrikandans, liubans, ak gibiþ staþ þvairhein* (“Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath”); 2 Cor. 7:1 *þo habandans nu gahaita, liubans, hrainjam unsis* (“Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves”).

2) The vocative is also introduced into discourse in the manner of an interjection: Luke 7:40 *seimon, skal þus wa qiþan* (“Simon, I have something to say to you”); Rom. 10:16 *frauja, was galaubida hauseinai unsarai* (“Lord, who has believed our report?”); Philem. 20 *jai, broþar, ïk þeina niutau* (“Yes, brother, let me have benefit from you”); Rom. 9:20 *þannu uu jai, manna, þu was ïs, ei andvaurdjais guþa?* (“But indeed, O man, who are you to answer back to God?”); Gal. 6:18 *ansts fraujins miþ ahmin ïzvaramma, broþrjus* (“The grace of the Lord be with your spirit, brothers”); 4:19 *ïm andvairþs at ïzvis, barnilona meina* (“I am present with you, my little children”); Luke 18:18 *laisari þiuþeiga, wa taujands libainais aiveinons arbja vairþau* (“Good teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?”) [Col. 1123]; 1 Tim. 1:18 *þo anabusn anafilha þus, barnilo þeimauþaiu* (“I entrust this charge to you, my child Timothy”); Rom. 11:33 *diupiþa gabeins handugeins jah vitubnjis guþs, waiva unusspilloda sind stauos ïs* (“O depth of God’s riches, wisdom, and knowledge—how unsearchable are his judgments!”).

Sometimes the interjection *o* is also placed before the vocative: Luke 9:41 *o kuni ungalaubjando, und wa þulau ïzvis* (“O unbelieving generation, how long shall I endure you?”); Gal. 3:1 *o unfrodans galateis, was ïzvis afhugida* (“O foolish Galatians, who bewitched you?”).

> **Note 1.** Sometimes the pronoun of the second person is also placed before the vocative; see § 199, 3.
>
> **Note 2.** Sometimes the nominative is used instead of the vocative: John 19:3 *hails þiudans ïudaie* (“Hail, king of the Jews”), where the parallel passage, Mark 15:18 (*hails þiudan ïndaie*, βασιλεὺ), has the vocative. But at Luke 18:38, *ïesus, sunu daveidis, armai mik mendose* (“Jesus, son of David, have mercy on me”), the doubled *s* in *mendose* seems to arise from the following same letter in *sunu*; consequently *ïesu* should be read, as is also found at 4:34; 8:28; Mark 10:47. Mark 15:29 is consistent with this: *o sa gatairands* (“O you who destroy,” ὁ καταλύων) *þo alh—nasei þuk silbun* (“the temple—save yourself”).
>
> **Note 3.** The following two passages deserve notice: Luke 1:28 *fagino, anstai andahafta* (“Rejoice, you who have obtained grace”), because of its vocalic form; and 2 Thess. 2:1 *bidjam ïzvis broþruns*, where *broþruns* is construed: “we entreat you, brothers” (accusative), instead of “we entreat you, O brothers” (*broþrjus*).

## NEGATION

### § 213

1) Where it is affirmed that a predicate does not belong to a subject, the sentence is negative. The Goth has only one word of negation, *ni*, whether for positive negation (οὐ) or hypothetical negation (μή).

> **Note:** [Col. 1123] Οὐ negates simply and positively: πρῶτον μὲν οὖν οὐκ ἀθυμητέον, “first, then, one must not lose heart” (Demosthenes); but μή negates conditionally [Col. 1124] and hypothetically: δέδοικα μὴ πολλ` ἄγαν εἰρημέν` ἦ, “I fear that far too much may already have been said” (Sophocles). Translator.

This negation is placed before the negated word. But when this word is the copula itself, the negation, where the individual members of the sentence are explicitly expressed, is placed before the copula and in the third person singular combines with it as *nist*; or, where predicate and copula are contained in one verb, it is prefixed to that verb: Matt. 3:11 *ni ïm vairþs ei andbindau skaudaraip skohis ïs* (“I am not worthy to unfasten the strap of his shoes”); 10:37 *saei frijoþ attan aiþþau aiþein ufar mik, nist meina vairþs* (“he who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me”); Luke 8:17 *ni auk ïst analaugn, þatei svikunþ ni vairþai* (“for there is nothing hidden that shall not become manifest,” οὐ φανερὸν γενήσεται); 2 Cor. 11:14 *nist sildaleik* (“it is not remarkable,” οὐ θαυμαστὸν); Matt. 6:24 *ni maguþ guþa skalkinon jah mammonin* (“you cannot serve God and Mammon”); 8:20 *sunus mans ni habaiþ, war haubiþ sein anahnaivjai* (“the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head”); 9:36 *vesun sve lamba ni habandona hairdeis* (“they were like sheep having no shepherd”); Matt. 10:28 *ni ogeiþ izvis þans usqimandans leika* (“do not fear those who kill the body,” μή); 5:21 *ni maurþrjais* (“you shall not murder,” οὐ φονεύσεις); 18 *ains striks ni usleiþiþ af vitoda, unte allata vairþiþ* (“not one stroke shall pass from the law until all comes to pass,” οὐ μὴ παρέλθῃ). For other examples, see Glossary V, *Ni*, a.

Thus, where a verb is paraphrased, the negation is attached to it and not to its object; for example, Eph. 5:4 οὐκ ἀνῆκεν, *du þaurftai ni fairrinnand* (“not fitting”). Indeed, in compounds the negation is inserted between particles and the verb: John 6:22 *miþ ni qam siponjam* (“he did not go in together with the disciples,” οὐ συνεισῆλθε); 10:1 *saei ïnn ni atgaggiþ* (“he who does not enter in,” ὁ μὴ εἰσερχόμενος). [Col. 1124] This intimate affinity of the particle with the verb is why, in negative subordinate sentences with ἵνα μή in the Greek text, the negation is separated from the conjunction and placed with the verb: Mark 3:12 *filu andbait ïns, ei ïna ni gasvikunþidedeina* (“he strictly charged them that they should not make him known,” ἵνα μὴ αὐτόν—); John 6:12 *galisiþ þos aflifnandeins drauhsnos, þei vaihtai ni fraqistnai* (“gather the fragments that remain, so that nothing may be lost,” ἵνα μή τι); 12:35; 2 Cor. 2:1, 3; Phil. 2:27.

> **Note 1.** The negation is not separated from the verb except by conjunctions connecting two parts of a sentence, such as *þan* and *auk*: 1 Cor. 12:21 *niþ—þan mag*; Mark 9:6 *ni auk vissa*; 11:13 *ni auk vas mel*; see Glossary. Yet *ni magt auk* also occurs, Luke 16:2; *ni viljau auk*, 1 Cor. 16:7; *ni manna auk*, John 7:4. But *þau* always intervenes between negation and verb, because it belongs to the expression corresponding to Greek ἄν: Mark 13:20 *ni frauja gamaurgidedi þans dagans, ni þauh ganesi ainhun leike*; Matt. 5:20; Mark 10:15; John 9:41; 11:21, 52; 18:30. In the last passage, *ni þau veis atgebeima*, the personal pronoun is additionally placed between the negation and verb; whereas, conversely, 2 Cor. 11:4 has *veis ni meridedum*. When *nu* (οὖν) follows the negation, it is doubled (*nunu*): Matt. 10:26 *ni nunu ogeiþ ïzvis ïns* (“therefore do not fear them”); v. 31; Rom. 14:15, 20. But where separated from the negation it remains simple: Matt. 6:8 *ni galeikoþ nu þaim*; v. 31; Rom. 14:13; Eph. 5:7; Col. 2:16.

2) Since very many Greek verbs, generally and especially in the past passive tenses, are rendered in Gothic with the auxiliaries *visan* and *vairþan*, the negation, according to the position it occupies, follows this rule: where the construction consists of these verbs and an adjective, the negation is more commonly placed before the copula; but where it consists of a participle, the negation precedes the participle, because the Goth apparently judged the intimate connection of auxiliary and participle—which cannot stand by itself—to be more necessary. Hence he says: Luke 18:1 *ni vairþan usgrudjans* (“not to lose heart,” μὴ ἐκκακεῖν); Gal. 2:16 *ni vairþiþ garaihts* (“is not justified,” οὐ δικαιοῦται); Col. 3:19 *ni sijaiþ baitrai* (“do not be bitter,” μὴ πικραίνεσθε); 2 Cor. 3:10 *ni vas vulþag* (“has not been glorified,” οὐ δεδόξασται). Conversely: Luke 17:18 *ni bigitanai vaurþun* (“they were not found,” οὐχ εὑρέθησαν), as though *bigitanai-vaurþun*; 2 Cor. 7:14 *ni ganiviskoþs varþ* (“I was not put to shame,” οὐ κατησχύνθην); 12:2 *ni frabauht vas* (“was not caught up,” οὐκ ἐπράθη); Rom. 9:11 *ni gabauranai vesun* (“they had not been born,” οὐκ ἐγεννήθησαν). Hence also *ni skuld visan* (“must not be”), *ni maht visan* (“cannot be”), *ni kunþ visan* (“is not known”); see the Glossary for examples and others.

> **Note 2.** A few departures from this rule occur in John and the Pauline epistles: John 6:7 *ni ganohai sind* (“are not sufficient,” οὐκ ἀρκοῦσι); 2 Cor. 12:1 *ni batizo ïst* (“is not advantageous,” οὐ συμφέρει); 1 Tim. 2:14 *ni varþ uslutoþs* (“was not deceived,” οὐκ ἠπατήθη); 2 Cor. 2:11 *ni sijum unvitandans* (“we are not ignorant”); John 8:41 *nisijum gabauranai* (“we have not been born”).

3) The negation of certain words is formed:

a) As in Greek by the privative α, so in Gothic by derivation; namely:

aa) By the prefixed particle *un-* in a negative sense. [Col. 1125] This kind of negation is compounded not only with adjectives and nouns (see Glossary under the word), but also very frequently with participles. Thus, on the one hand, the Goth renders many Greek adjectives and verbal forms made with privative α by participles compounded with *un-*—ἄλαλος, *unrodjands* (“speechless”); ἄφοβος, *unagands* (“fearless”); ἀψευδής, *unliugands* (“truthful”); ἄπιστος, *ungalaubjands* (“unbelieving”); ἀκρατής, *ungahabands* (“without self-control”); ἀδιάλειπτος, *unsveibands* (“uninterrupted”); ἀσύνετος, *unfraþjands* (“unintelligent”); ἀχειροποίητος, *unhanduvaurhts* (“not made by hands”), etc. On the other hand, Greek participles with negation are expressed by such compounds: μὴ φέρων, *unbairands* (“not bearing”), John 15:2; οὐ τίκτουσα, *unbairandei* (“not bearing children”), Gal. 4:27; μὴ ἔχων, *unhabands* (“not having”), Luke 3:11; μὴ βλέπων, *unsaiwands* (“not seeing”), John 9:39; οὐ παυόμενος, *unsveibands* (“not ceasing”), Eph. 1:16; μὴ βλεπόμενος, *ungasaiwans* (“not seen”), 2 Cor. 4:4, 18; μὴ ἀνακαλυπτόμενος, *unandhuliþs* (“not revealed”), 3:14; μὴ μεμαθηκώς, *unuslaisiþs* (“not taught”), John 7:15; *unandsakans*, “irrefutable,” *Skeireins* VI, c.

> **Note 3.** Of verbs, we know only *unverjan* and *unsveran* to be formed with *un-*; for *gaunledjan* and *unþiuþjan* derive from *unleds* and *unþiuþ*. Thus, while the Goth uses *unvitands* for ἀγνοῶν (“ignorant”), and *ungalaubjands* for ἄπιστος and ἀπειθής (“unbelieving,” “disobedient”), he renders ἀγνοεῖν by *ni vitan* (“not to know”), Rom. 7:1, and ἀπιστεῖν and ἀπειθεῖν by *ni galaubjan* (“not to believe”), Mark 16:11; Rom. 11:30–31; 2 Tim. 2:13. Hence it is apparent that there is no distinction between *ni* and *un-*.

bb) By the suffix *-laus* in a privative sense, namely, in nouns: *akranalaus*, “fruitless” (ἄκαρπος); *andilaus*, “endless” (ἀπέρατος); *gudalaus*, “without God, ungodly” (ἄθεος); *vitodalaus*, “without law” (ἄνομος).

b) By the preposition *ïnuh*, “without,” as *ïuuh mitad*, “without measure” (ἄμετρος).

c) By *ni*, with the negation always preceding the negated word: Mark 5:3 *ni naudibandjom eisarneinaim manna mahta gabindan* (“no one was able to bind him even with chains”); Luke 20:7–8 *andhofun, ei ni vissedeina; jah ïesus qaþ du ïm: ni ïk ïzvis qiþa* (“they answered that they did not know; and Jesus said to them: neither do I tell you”); John 14:22 *ïudas ni sa ïskariotes* (“Judas, not Iscariot”); *Skeireins* VI, a *afar ni filu* (“after not much”); 1 Cor. 5:6 *ni goda woftuli* (“not good leaven”); Mark 12:34 *ni fairra ïs* (“he is not far”); Rom. 13:13 *garedaba gaggaima ni gabauram jah drugkaneim, ni ligram jah aglaitjam* (“let us walk decently, not in revelry and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and debauchery”).

Especially in antithesis: Mark 10:27 *fram mannam unmahteig ïst, ni fram guþa* (“with people it is impossible, but not with God”); Matt. 9:13 *armahairtiþa wiljau jah ni hunsl* (“I desire mercy and not sacrifice”); Mark 9:37 *ni mik andnimiþ ak þana sandjandan mik* (“he receives not me but him who sent me”). For other examples see Glossary under a and b.

d) Gothic has no special words for the negative notions “no one,” “nothing,” “none,” “never,” “not yet” (οὔπω), and so forth, but expresses them through affirmative words with *ni* added. Yet for this reason *ni* need not be placed before these words; it may also precede the verb. The Goth observes only that, in a subordinate sentence, the negation precedes the verb: 1 Tim. 5:22 *handuns sprauto ni mannhun lagjais* (“lay hands suddenly on no one,” μηδενί); Mark 8:30 *faurbauþ ïm, ei mannhun ni qeþeina* (“he charged them that they should tell no one,” μηδενί); Matt. 6:24 *ni manna mag tvaim fraujam skalkinon* (“no one can serve two masters,” οὐδεὶς); John 15:13 *maizein þizai friaþvai manna ni habaiþ* (“no one has greater love than this,” οὐδείς); John 10:28 *ni fravilviþ ainshun þo us handau* (“no one shall snatch them out of [Col. 1126] the hand,” οὐ—τις); Mark 10:18 *ni washun þiuþeigs alja ais guþ* (“no one is good except God alone,” οὐδείς); Matt. 10:26 *ni vaiht gahuliþ ist, þatei ni andhuljaidau* (“nothing is hidden that shall not be revealed,” οὐδέν); John 7:26 *waiht du imma ni qiþand* (“they say nothing to him,” οὐδέν); 19:4 *ïn ïmma ni ainohon fairino bigat* (“I find in him no guilt,” οὐδεμίαν), but conversely 18:38 *ainohun fairino ni bigita ïn þamma* (“I find no guilt in him”); likewise Luke 19:30 *fulan, ana þammei ni ainshun aiv manne sat* (“a colt on which no one had ever sat”) and Mark 11:2 *ana þammei nauh ainshun manne ni sat* (“on which no one had yet sat”); Matt. 7:23 *ni wanhun kunþa ïzvis* (“I never knew you,” οὐδέποτε); John 6:35 *þana galaubjandan du mis ni þaurseiþ wanhun* (“whoever believes in me shall never thirst,” οὐ—πώποτε); Matt. 9:33 *ni aiv sva uskunþ vas ïn ïsraela* (“never had anything like this appeared in Israel”); Mark 2:12 *allai hauhidedun guþ qipandans þatei aiv sva ni gasewum* (“all glorified God, saying: ‘We have never seen anything like this,’” οὐδέποτε οὕτως); John 14:19 *so manaseds mik ni þanaseiþs saiwiþ* (“the world sees me no longer,” οὐκέτι); Luke 15:19 *þanaseiþs ni ïm vairþs ei haitaidau sunus þeins* (“I am no longer worthy to be called your son”); Mark 15:5 *þanamais ni andhof* (“he answered nothing further,” οὐκέτι); Eph. 2:19 *ju ni gasteis sijuþ* (“you are no longer strangers,” οὐκέτι); Mark 4:40 *ni nauh habaiþ galaubein* (“have you not yet faith?” οὔπω); John 8:57 *fimftiguns jere nauh ni habais* (“you are not yet fifty years old,” οὔπω); 7:30 *nauhþanuh ni atïddja weila ïs* (“his hour had not yet come”). For further examples see Glossary, b.

4) In Gothic two negations placed in the same sentence never cancel one another; on the contrary, besides the general negation of the sentence there is also a particular one in the negative pronouns *ni waiht* and *ni ainshun*: Mark 7:12 *ni fraleiþ ïna ni waiht taujan* (“you no longer permit him to do anything,” οὐκ … οὐδέν); 15:4 *niu andhafjis ni waiht* (“do you answer nothing?” οὐκ … οὐδέν); Luke 9:36 *mann ni gataihun ni waiht, þizei gaserwun* (“they told no one anything of what they had seen,” οὐδενί … οὐδέν); 20:40 *niþ-þan þanaseiþs gadaurstedun fraihnan ïna ni waihtais* (“they no longer dared ask him anything,” οὐκέτι … οὐδέν); John 9:33; 15:5; 16:24; John 5:22 *nih þan atta ni stojiþ ainohun* (“for neither does the Father judge anyone,” οὐδέ … οὐδένα); Matt. 27:14 *ni andhof ïmma viþra ni ainhun vaurde* (“he answered him not even one word,” οὐκ … οὐδέ); Mark 3:20 *svasve ni mahtedun nih hlaif matjan* (“so that they could not even eat bread,” μή … μηδέ); Luke 18:13 *ni vilda nih augona seina ushafjan* (“he was unwilling even to lift his eyes,” οὐ … οὐδέ).

In the passages cited above, the Goth shares the two negations with Greek. Yet he uses them even where Greek does not precede: John 8:42 *fram guþa qam, nih þan auk fram mis silbin ni qam* (“I came from God; for neither did I come of myself,” οὐδέ … ἐλήλυθα); 16:21 *biþe gabauran ïst barn, ni þanaseiþs ni gaman þizos aglons faura fahedai* (“when the child has been born, she no longer remembers the anguish because of joy,” οὐκέτι μνημονεύει); 2 Cor. 5:16 *nu ni þanaseiþs ni kunnum ïna* (“now we no longer know him,” οὐκέτι γινώσκομεν), whereas above *ni ainnohun kunnum* simply stands; Gal. 6:14 *mis ni sijai wopan ïn ni waihtai niba ïn galgin fraujins* (“may it not be for me to boast in anything except the cross of the Lord”), while *ïn ni waihtai* is wholly absent from the Greek text. Or he uses only one negation where Greek uses two: Mark 1:44 *saiw ei mann ni qiþais waiht* (“see that you say nothing to anyone,” μηδενί … μηδέν); 12:14 *ni kara þuk manshun* (“you care for no one,” οὐ … οὐδενός); 54 *ainshun þanaseiþs ni gadaursta ïna fraihnan* (“after that no one dared ask him,” οὐδεὶς οὐκέτι); 14:60 *niu andhafjis waiht* (“do you answer nothing?” οὐκ … οὐδέν); 16:8 *ni qeþun mannhun waiht* (“they said nothing to anyone,” οὐδενὶ οὐδέν); Luke 4:2; 8:43, 51; John 6:63; 12:19; 14:30; 16:23; 19:11; Rom. 13:8. In 2 Cor. 11:8, because the construction *ni ainnohun kaurida* differed from the Greek οὐ κατενάρκησα οὐδενός, it was unnecessary to double the negation.

[Col. 1127] 5) On continued negation (“neither—nor”), see the discussion of the compound sentence.

## INTERROGATION

### § 214

When a speaker inquires about something, this is done by asking a question. Questions are generally put in the indicative, but in the subjunctive only concerning the future. Otherwise, the words of a sentence do not change their order in interrogation. Now the following types of question must be distinguished:

1) A positively framed question, which:

a) Is expressed without an interrogative word: John 16:31 *nu galaubeiþ?* (“Do you now believe?”); 1 Cor. 1:13 *disdailiþs ïst xristus?* (“Is Christ divided?”); Luke 7:44 *gasaiwis þo qinon?* (“Do you see this woman?”); Matt. 27:11 *þu ïs þiudans ïudaie?* (“Are you the king of the Jews?”); 2 Cor. 10:7 *þo bi andvairþja saiwiþ?* (“Do you look at what is before your face?”); Gal. 4:10 *dagam vitaiþ jah menoþum jah melam?* (“Do you observe days, months, seasons?”); 3:3 *sva unfroþans sijuþ? anastodjandans ahmin nu leika ustiuhiþ? sva filu gavunnuþ svare?* (“Are you so foolish? Having begun in the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh? Have you suffered so much in vain?”); Rom. 7:13 *þata nu þiuþeigo mis varþ dauþus?* (“Did that which is good then become death to me?”).

b) Is indicated by the enclitic *-u*. It is attached to the first word of the interrogative sentence; and where that word is compound, it is introduced after the compounding syllable. In prepositions and compound nouns it is added to the preposition: Mark 10:38 *magutsu driggkan stikl, þanei ïk driggka?* (“Can you drink the cup which I drink?”); John 13:12 *vitudu, wa gatavida ïzvis?* (“Do you know what I have done to you?”); 18:39 *vileidu nu ei fraletau ïzvis þana þiudan ïudaie?* (“Do you wish, then, that I release to you the king of the Jews?”); Luke 9:54 *frauja, vileizu ei qiþaima fon atgaggai us himina?* (“Lord, do you wish us to command fire to come down from heaven?”); John 18:22 *svau andhafjis þamma reikistin gudjin?* (“Do you answer the high priest in this manner?”); Matt. 9:28 *gaulaubjats þatei magjau þata taujan?* (“Do you believe that I am able to do this?”); John 9:35 *þu gaulaubeis du sunau guþs?* (“Do you believe in the Son of God?”); Luke 18:8 *sunus mans qimands, biugitai galaubein?* (“When the Son of Man comes, will he find faith?”); John 18:34 *abu þus silbin þu þata qiþis?* (“Do you say this of yourself?”). For other examples, see Glossary V, *-u*.

c) Where a question is asked concerning something previously mentioned, *an* (καί, οὖν) is prefixed to the interrogative; this particle occurs as Old German *eno, inu*, and still in modern popular German as *en, enne*: Luke 10:29 *an was ïst mis newundja* (“And who is my neighbor?”); 18:26 *an was mag ganisan* (“And who can be saved?”); John 9:36 *an was ïst, frauja, ei galaubjau du ïmma?* (“And who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?”); Luke 3:10 *an wa taujaima?* (“What then shall we do?”); John 18:37 *an nuh þiudans ïs þu?* (“So then, are you a king?”).

2) A negatively framed question, which:

a) Is expressed by bare *ni* with the indicative, or *ne* (*nei*) with the subjunctive: Luke 17:18 *þai niun war? ni bigitanai vaurþun gavandjandans giban vulþa guþa?* (“Were not the ten found who returned to give glory to God?”); Mark 12:10 *nih þata gamelido ussuggvuþ* (“Have you not even read this scripture?”); *Skeireins* I, c *ne auk þuhtedi þau ïn garaihteins gaaggvein ufargaggan þo garehsn?* (“For did it not seem fitting to go beyond the course of righteousness?”); 2 Cor. [Col. 1128] 3:8 *waiva nei mais andbahti ahmins vairþai ïn vulþau* (“how shall the ministry of the Spirit not rather be in glory?”).

b) Is expressed by *niu*, where an affirmative answer is expected from one asking negatively, or is already suggested by the question: Mark 14:60 *niu andhafjis waiht?* (“Do you answer nothing?”); Luke 4:22 *niu sa ïst sunus ïosefis?* (“Is this not Joseph’s son?”); John 18:25 *niu jah þu þize siponje þis ïs?* (“Are you not also one of his disciples?”); 18:11 *niu drigkau stikl?* (“Shall I not drink the cup?”). For other examples see Glossary V, *Niu*.

c) Is expressed by *ïbai* (“perhaps? surely not?”), where a negative answer is expected, or where something negative, unheard of, and the like is to be expressed interrogatively: Matt. 9:15 *ïbai magun sunjus bruþfadis qainon und þata weilos þei miþ ïm ïst bruþfads?* (“Can the sons of the bridechamber mourn while the bridegroom is with them?”); 7:16 *ïbai lisanda af þaurnum veinabasja?* (“Does one gather grapes from thorns?”); John 9:27 *ïbai jah jus vileiþ þamma siponjos vairþan?* (“Do you perhaps also wish to become his disciples?”); 40 *ïbai jah veis blindai sijum?* (“Are we perhaps also blind?”). The distinction between *ïbai* and *niu* is especially clear from Luke 6:39: *ïbai mag blinds blindana tiuhan? niu bai ïn dal gadriusand?* (“Can a blind person lead a blind person? Will they not both fall into a pit?”). For other examples see Glossary V, *Ibai*.

Where a second negation follows *ïbai* (*ïbai ni*, μή οὐ, “perhaps not?”), that negation belongs to the verb, and an affirmative answer is expected: Rom. 10:18 *ïbai ni hausidedun? ïbai ïsrael ni fanþ?* (“Have they not heard? Did Israel not know?”); 1 Cor. 9:4 *ïbai ni habam valdufni matjan jah driggkan?* (“Do we not have authority to eat and drink?”); 9:5; 11:22.

Conversely, *nibai* and the subjunctive are used where the question is ironic and bitter: “Surely not, perhaps!” John 7:35 *nibai ïn distahein þiudo skuli gaggan* (“Surely he is not about to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks?”); 8:22 *nibai usqimai sis silbin?* (“Surely he will not kill himself?”).

3) On interrogative pronouns and adverbs, see §§ 164, 3 and 204.

4) On double questions, see the discussion of the compound sentence.

5) The particles *ja*, “yes” (certainly); *jai*, “yes, indeed”; and *ne*, “no,” furnish simple answers; see Matt. 5:37; 9:28; 2 Cor. 1:17 ff.; Luke 1:60; John 7:12. Yet because these particles probably are not customary in Greek, they do not often occur in this capacity, but are joined with the interrogative verb; or the verb alone is used; or an answer is otherwise expressed. Thus John 18:25: *niu jah þu þize siponje þis ïs? ïþ ïs afaiaik jah qaþ: ne, ni ïm* (“Are you not also one of his disciples? But he denied it and said: ‘No, I am not’”; Greek simply οὐκ εἰμί); 11:27 *galaubeis þata? qaþ ïmma: jai, frauja, ïk galaubida* (“Do you believe this? She said to him: ‘Yes, Lord, I have believed’”); 18:17 *ïbai jah þu þize siponje ïs þis mans? ïþ ïs qaþ: ni ïm* (“Are you perhaps also one of this man’s disciples? But he said: ‘I am not,’” οὐκ εἰμι); Rom. 11:1 *ïbai afskauf guþ managein seinamma? nis-sijai* (“Has God rejected his people? Certainly not,” μή γένοιτο); Matt. 27:11 *frah ïna kindins: þu ïs þiudans ïudaie? ïþ ïesus qaþ þu ïmma: þu qiþis* (“The governor asked him: ‘Are you the king of the Jews?’ But Jesus said to him: ‘You say so,’” σὺ λέγεις); John 18:37 *qaþ ïmma peilatus: an nuh þiudans ïs þu? andhafjands ïesus: þu qiþis ei þiudans ïm ïk* (“Pilate said to him: ‘So then, are you a king?’ Jesus answered: ‘You say that I am a king.’”).

## ATTRIBUTIVE RELATION, OR THE ATTRIBUTE

[Col. 1127]

[Col. 1127] § 215. When a simple sentence is expanded, this expansion consists in a closer determination of its subject and, if it is a substantive, of its predicate by some word; this word is called an attribute. An attribute may be:

[Col. 1128] I. A concordant noun, namely:

1) An adjective or participle, which must always agree with the word determined in gender, number, and case. Here two matters require attention: first, the distinction between the [Col. 1129] consonantal and vocalic forms of these attributes; second, their position. In respect to the latter, observe that attributes commonly follow the word determined, but precede where they bear the emphasis. On both matters see § 196. As to the fact that a superlative does not agree with the substantive but takes a partitive with it, see § 216, 1 b bb.

2) A numeral; see § 198.

3) A pronoun; see § 199 ff.

> **Note 1.** Since numerals, including indefinite numerals, frequently depart from the rule of agreement because of their substantive character—namely, by drawing the substantive into the partitive—see §§ 198, II, 5 b and 205. For the same construction of *alls* when it means “each,” see § 205, V; but when it means “all, whole,” it is used adjectivally and agrees with its substantive; see § 196, note 12.
>
> **Note 2.** On whether a possessive pronoun precedes or follows its substantive, see § 201. The construction where an adjective and possessive pronoun or numeral refer to a substantive is free and most often follows the Greek: Luke 1:72 *gamunan triggvos veihaizos seinaizos* (“to remember his holy covenant”); 1 Cor. 15:58 *broþrjus meinai liubans* (“my beloved brothers”); 2 Cor. 11:28; 2 Tim. 2:1; Luke 7:35 *barnam seinaim allaim* (“by all her children”); 7:1 *alla þo vaurda seina* (“all his words”); 8:43; Eph. 1:6 *ïn þamma liubin sunau seinamma* (“in his beloved Son”); Phil. 4:3 *anþaraim gavaurstvam seinaim* (“his fellow-workers”); 1 Cor. 16:19 *miþ ïngardjon seinai aikklesjon* (“with the church in their house”); 2 Tim. 4:16; *Skeireins* VII, a *hlaibans barizeinans* (“barley loaves”).
>
> **Note 3.** Where an attribute refers to several substantives of the same gender and number, it is stated only once: Phil. 1:25 *du ïzvarai framgahtai jah fahedai* (“for your progress and joy”); Luke 1:6 *ïn allaim anabusnim jah garaihteim* (“in all commandments and ordinances”). Where it refers to two substantives, it is used in the plural: Phil. 1:20 *bi usbeisnai jah venai meinaim* (“according to my expectation and hope”). But a construction such as Matt. 9:35 *baurgs allos jah haimos* (“all cities and villages”) is rare.
