If the substantives are of different gender, or even number, their respective attributes agree separately: *Skeireins* V, b *svesamma viljin jah svesai mahtai* (“by his own will and his own power”); Matt. 7:10 *sverai attan þeinana jah aiþein þeina* (“your father and your mother”); Luke 8:10 *aiþei meina jah broþrjus meinai* (“my mother and my brothers”); Mark 3:32–33; 6:4; 10:7. Yet in such cases an attribute is sometimes stated only once, where the substantives agree in number; then it is joined to the first: Mark 3:5 *broþar meins jah svistar jah aiþei* (“my brother and sister and mother”); 1 Thess. 2:12 *seinai þiudaugardjai jah vulþau* (“his own kingdom and glory”); *Skeireins* I, c *mahtai gudiskai jah valdufnja* (“divine power and authority”).
>
> Where several attributes connected copulatively or adversatively refer to a substantive, they precede that substantive: *Skeireins* II, b *þo veihon jah himina kundon gabaurþ* (“the holy and heavenly birth”); V, c *ni ïbnon ak galeika sveriþa* (“not equal but like punishment”); but also in the same passage *ni ïbnaleika friaþva ak galeika* (“not equal love but like”), with the attributes separated.

[Col. 1130]

> **Note 4.** Adverbs are also used attributively in place of adjectives, especially *filu*, “much, many”: Luke 5:6 *galukun managein fiske filu* (“they caught a great multitude of fish”). It also occurs substantively: Luke 9:37 *gamotida ïmma manageins filu* (“a great multitude met him”), as does *leitil*, “little”: 1 Tim. 5:23 *veinis leitil brukjais* (“use a little wine,” οἴνῳ ὀλίγῳ); compare § 216, 1 b. If *Skeireins* III, b *sinteino daupeinim brukjan* is correctly emended, it too belongs here, since from the context *sinteino* cannot refer to *brukjan*.
>
> **Note 5.** Adjectives of place, time, size, quantity, and the like are joined to substantives as attributes, in the classical manner, where Germans and French would use an adverb: Luke 2:46 *sat ïn midjaim laisarjam* (“he sat among the teachers,” literally “in the midst of teachers”; German *mitten unter*, French *au milieu des docteurs*); John 7:14 *ana midjai dulþ usstaig ïesus ïn alh* (“Jesus went up into the temple in the middle of the feast”); Mark 2:7 *was mag afletan fravaurhtins niba ains guþ* (“who can forgive sins except God alone?”; German *Gott allein*); Luke 4:4 *ni bi hlaib ainana libaid manna* (“a human being shall not live by bread alone”); 1 Tim. 1:16 *ïn mis frumistamma ataugida ïesus alla usbeisnein* (“in me, the foremost, Jesus displayed all patience”); 2:13 *adam fruma gadigans varþ* (“Adam was formed first”); Philem. 15 *afgaf sik du weilai, ei aiveinana ïna andnimais* (“he was separated for an hour, so that you might receive him forever”), etc. Yet Luke 8:7 reads *sum gadraus ïn midumaï þaurnive* (“some fell into the midst of thorns”).
>
> **Note 6.** Sometimes a substantive is also the attribute of another substantive, though this properly belongs to apposition: Luke 4:26 *qino viduvo* (“a widow woman”); *Skeireins* V, d *ainabaur sunus* (“only-begotten son”); Mark 1:5 *ïudaia land* (“the land of Judea”); Luke 3:1 *trakauneitidaus landis* (“the region of Trachonitis”); John 12:3 *balsan nardus* (“nard ointment”); Luke 2:41 *dulþ paska* (“the feast of Passover”).
>
> **Note 7.** Where participles serve as attributes, they may often be translated by relative, copulative, causal, hypothetical, or temporal particles and made into a proper clause; if negative, by particles containing negation: Matt. 8:9 *ïk manna ïm habands uf valdufnja meinamma gadrauhtins* (“I am a man who has soldiers under my authority”); Luke 20:29 *sa frumista nimands qen gadauþnoda unbarnahs* (“the first, who took a wife, died childless”); Matt. 8:10 *gahausjands ïesus sildaleikida* (“when Jesus heard this, he marvelled”); 1 Thess. 3:5 *duþþe jah ïk ju ni usþulands ïnsandida du ufkunnan galaubein ïzvara* (“therefore, because I could no longer endure it, I sent to learn of your faith”); Rom. 7:3 *jabai gasviltiþ vair, qens frija ïst þis vitodis, ei ni sijai horinondei vaurþana abin anþaramma* (“if her husband dies, the wife is free from that law, so that she shall not be called an adulteress if she becomes another man’s wife”); Luke 18:7 *guþ niu gavrikai þans gavalidans seinans þans vopjandans du sis dagam jah nahtam* (“shall not God avenge his elect, although they cry to him day and night,” or “who cry to him”); 4:35 *sa unhulþa urrann af ïmma ni waihtai gaskaþjands ïmma* (“the demon came out from him, doing him no harm”; French *sans lui faire de mal*).

## § 216. II. THE GENITIVE

1) The subjective genitive.

> **Note:** [Col. 1129] The subjective or active genitive is so called when the word placed in the genitive is the subject of the affection expressed by the governing word; for example, “the providence of God,” that is, the providence exercised by God. Translator.

a) It expresses origin, cause, the immediately more specific determination in general, the possessor, author, and so on: Luke 4:4 *vaurd guþs* (“word of God”); 3:6 *naseins guþs* (“salvation of God”); 14:17 *bokos esaeiïns* (“a book of Isaiah”); 19:30 *fula asilaus* (“a colt of an ass”); 2:24 [Col. 1131] *tvos juggons ahake* (“two young pigeons”); 20:17 *haubid vaihstins* (“head of the corner”); 3:9 *vaurteis bagme* (“roots of trees”); John 12:13 *astos peikabagme* (“branches of palm trees”); Luke 18:6 *staua ïnvindiþos* (“a judge of injustice”); 8:14 *saurgos þizos libainais* (“cares of this life”); 9:51 *dagos andanumtais* (“days of his being received up”); 4:8 *gard seimonis* (“Simon’s house”); 16:21 *biuds þis gabigins* (“the rich man’s table”); 20:20 *valdufni kindinis* (“the governor’s authority”); 10:2 *frauju asanais* (“lord of the harvest”).

b) The partitive:

aa) In part joined to indefinite and numeral words; see § 215, note 1.

bb) In part joined to superlatives: Mark 4:31 *minnist allaize fraive* (“the smallest of all seeds”); 32 *allaize grase maist* (“greatest of all herbs”); 12:28 *allaizo anabusne frumista* (“first of all commandments”; also v. 29, *frumista allaizo anabusns*); 1 Cor. 15:9 *sa smalista apaustaule* (“the least of the apostles”), etc.

cc) In part joined to other substantives, and also to pronouns and neuter adjectives functioning substantively: Luke 5:6 *galukun managein fiske* (“they caught a multitude of fish”); Mark 5:11 *vas jaïnar hairda sveine haldana* (“there was a herd of swine feeding there”); Luke 14:19 *juka auhsne usbauhta fimf* (“I bought five yoke of oxen”); 2:24 *gajuk hraivadubono* (“a pair of turtledoves”); 16:7 *taihuntaihund mitade kaurnis* (“a hundred measures of grain”); John 12:3 *pund balsamis* (“a pound of ointment”); Neh. 5:15 *nemun silubris sikle ·m·* (“they took forty shekels of silver”); Mark 14:13 *kas vatins* (“a jar of water”); Matt. 10:42 *stikls kaldis vatins* (“a cup of cold water”); Luke 7:37 *alabastraun balsanis* (“an alabaster flask of ointment”); Luke 4:5 *stiks melis* (“an instant of time”); 2:44 *dagis vigs* (“a day’s journey”); *Skeireins* VII, c *ni waiht mikilis* (“nothing great”); 1 Cor. 5:6 *leitil beistis* (“a little leaven”); compare § 215, note 4.

c) Gothic has imitated Latin in constructions in which the attribute requires, in order to have full sense, an additional adjective or numeral: 2 Tim. 3:16 *all boko gudiskaizos ahmateinais* (“every scripture divinely inspired,” θεόπνευστος, “inspired by God”). Further, Luke 8:42 *dauhtar vas ïmma vintrive tvalibe* (“he had a daughter about twelve years old”); 2:37 *viduvo jere ·o· jah ·d·* (“a widow of eighty-four years”).

2) The objective genitive.

> **Note:** [Col. 1131] The objective or passive genitive is so called when the word placed in the genitive is the object of the affection expressed by the governing word; for example, “love of God,” that is, love in which God is loved, love directed toward God. Translator.

This category also includes the passive: Mark 1:14 *aivaggeljo þiudangardjos* (“the gospel of the kingdom of heaven”); 2 Cor. 5:19 *vaurd gafriþonais* (“word of reconciliation”); Mark 1:28 *meriþa ïs* (“his report,” concerning him); Luke 3:3 *daupeins ïdreigos* (“baptism of repentance,” unto repentance); Mark 6:7 *valdufni ahmane unhrainjaize* (“authority over unclean spirits”); 2 Cor. 10:5 *ufarhauseins xristaus* (“obedience to Christ”); Rom. 10:2 *aljan guþs* (“zeal for God”).

Luke 5:9 *gafah þize fiske* (“the catch of those fishes”); 5:10 *nutans manne* (“fishers of people”); 10:25 *arbja libainais aiveinons* (“heir of eternal life”); 3:3 *aflet fravaurhte* (“forgiveness of sins”); Mark 11:22 *galaubeins guþs* (“faith in God”); John 7:13 *agis iudaie* (“fear of the Jews,” felt toward the Jews); Luke 16:2 *raþjo fauragaggjis* (“an account of the stewardship,” concerning the stewardship); 2 Cor. 10:5 *kunþi guþs* (“knowledge of God,” concerning God); Rom. 8:35 *friaþva xristaus* (“love for Christ”); 2 Tim. 1:5 *gamaudeins galaubeinais* (“remembrance of faith”).

> **Note:** [Col. 1131] All these genitives can in fact be turned into the passive: fishes are caught; God is believed in; the Jews are feared; etc. Translator.
>
> **Note 1.** [Col. 1132] Although this note concerns Germans alone, we have translated it in full, both because we did not wish to deprive the Gothic grammar of even the smallest part and because we believed that we might render a not unwelcome service to those who enjoy comparison of languages. Translator. In place of a substantive and attributive [Col. 1132] genitive, Germans often use a compound: Mark 11:17 *razn bido*, and Luke 19:45 *gards bido*, German *Bethaus* (“house of prayer”); Mark 15:22 *wairneins staþs*, German *Schädelstätte* (“place of a skull,” the place of Calvary); 4:31 *kaurno sinapis*, German *Senfkorn* (“grain of mustard”); 5:25 *runs bloþis*, German *Blutfluss* (“flow of blood”); Luke 19:37 *fairguni alevabagme*, German *Oel(-baum-)berg* (“mount of olive trees”); Matt. 26:75 *hanins hruk*, German *Hahnenruf* (“cock-crow”); 1 Cor. 15:52 *braw augins*, German *Augenblick* (“blink of an eye”).

“Very many Greek compounds are paraphrased in Gothic in this way: Gal. V, 20, *eidōlolatreia*, *galiugagude skalkinassus*, ‘service of idols’ (German *Götzendienst*, “idolatrous service”); Eph. I, 5, *huiothesia*, *sunive gadeds*, ‘adoption as sons’; II Tim. II, 6, *geōrgos*, *airþos vaurstvja*, ‘worker of the earth, farmer’ (German *Erdarbeiter, Landbauer*); Matt. V, 31, *apostasion*, *aftassais bokos*, ‘document of divorce’ (German *Scheidebrief*, “bill of divorce”); II Cor. XI, 32, *ethnarchēs*, *fauramaþleis þiudos*, ‘ruler of a people’; Luke VII, 41, *chreopheiletēs*, *dulgis skula*, ‘debtor,’ for which the compound *faihuskula* also occurs.

“Note 2.—At times the Goth likewise renders an attributive adjective by a substantive in the genitive: II Cor. III, 1, *systatikē epistolē*, ‘a letter of recommendation’ (German *Empfehlungsbrief*), *bokos anafilhis*, ‘letter of recommendation’ (German *Brief der Empfehlung*); Luke III, 22, *sōmatikō eidei*, ‘in bodily form,’ *leikís siunai*, ‘in the form of a body’; I Tim. IV, 7, *graōdeis mythoi*, ‘old-womanish tales,’ *usalþanaizo spilla*, ‘tales of old women’; II Cor. III, 10, *hyperballousa doxa*, ‘surpassing glory,’ *ufarassus vulþaus*, ‘surpassingness of glory’; and similarly *hyperballōn*, “surpassing,” always in II Cor. IX, 14; Eph. I, 19; II, 7. Conversely, *hēmisy tēs basileias*, “half the kingdom,” Mark VI, 23, is rendered *halba þiudangardi*, ‘half of the kingdom’ (although Luke XIX, 8 has *halbata aiginis*, ‘half of possessions’); Luke I, 78, *splanchna eleous*, ‘bowels of mercy,’ *ïnfeinandei armahairtei*, ‘inward affection of mercy’; John XII, 43, *doxa tōn anthrōpōn*, ‘glory of men,’ *hauhei manniska*, ‘human praise,’ alongside *hauhei guþs*, ‘praise of God.’

“Note 3.—Several genitives may also depend upon one another: I Tim. IV, 15, *analageins handive praisbytaireis*, ‘laying-on of the hands of the presbyter’; Rom. XI, 33, *diupiþa gabeins handugeins jah vitubnjis guþs*, ‘depth of the riches, wisdom, and knowledge of God,’ etc.

“Note 4.—The possessive is often likewise expressed in Gothic by the dative; see §227, note, and compare §230, note.

“Note 5.—The genitive regularly follows the word which governs it. In Gothic, however, it may also be placed before it, but only where Greek itself employed this construction, whether in juxtaposition or in composition; see Notes 1 and 2, and Luke II, 44, *dagis vigs*, ‘day’s journey’; III, 2, *zaxariïns sunus*, ‘Zechariah’s son’; John VIII, 17, *tvaddje manne veitvodiþa*, ‘the testimony of two men’; X, 5, *þize framaþjane stibna*, ‘the voice of strangers’; XVIII, 3, *fareisaie andbahtos*, ‘the officers of the Pharisees’; 10, *þis auhumistins gudjins skalks*, ‘the servant of the high priest’; Rom. IX, 9, *gahaitis vaurd*, ‘word of promise’; XIII, 2, *guþs garaideins*, ‘God’s ordinance’; 4, *guþs andbahts*, ‘God’s servant.’ This construction is especially used in the *Skeireins*, probably through Roman influence, [Col. 1133] for example, on its very first folio: *a dauþaus staua*—‘the place of death’; *allaize nasjands, allaize fravaurhtins*—‘saviour of all, of all transgression’; *þizos manasedais ussaunein*—‘the appearance of humanity’; *b mans leik*—‘the body of man’; *diabulaus anamahtai*—‘the devil’s violence’; *garaihteins garehsns*—‘the proclamation of righteousness’; *c garaihteins gaaggvei*—‘the path of righteousness’; *nasjandins laiseinai*—‘the Saviour’s teaching’; *d sunjos kunþi*—‘the knowledge of truth’; *vitodis gaaggveinai*—‘the way of the law,’ etc.

“Note 6.—Instead of a partitive [genitive], the preposition *us*, ‘out of, among,’ is also used: Matt. XXVII, 48, *ains us ïns*, ‘one of them’; Mark IX, 17, *ains us þizai managein*, ‘one of the multitude’; John XVI, 5, *ainshun us ïzvis*, ‘none of you’; XVII, 12, *ainshun us ïm*, ‘none of them’; Rom. XI, 14, *sumans us ïm*, ‘some of them’; John XII, 42, *us þaim reikam managai*, ‘many among the rulers.’ Once *af*, ‘from,’ also occurs: I Tim. I, 6, *af þaimei sumai*, ‘some of whom’ (*hōn*).

Note 7.—Sometimes, following Greek, the governing word of the genitive is omitted: (a) where the governing substantives are supplied by the article, discussed in §195, IV, 3); (b) where, with the word ‘son’ omitted, the simple article is used: Mark I, 19, *gasaw ïakobu þana zaibaidaiaus*, ‘he saw James, [the son] of Zebedee’; II, 14; III, 17, 18; Luke VI, 15; likewise without the article in John VI, 71, *ïudas seimonis*, ‘Judas [son] of Simon,’ and Luke VI, 16, *ïudan ïakobaus*, ‘Judas [son] of James’; (c) where the word ‘house’ is understood, as in Luke XIX, 7, *du fravaurhtis mans … galaiþ ïn gard*, ‘he went into the house of a sinful man’ (*para hamartōlō andri*), *ïn gard*, ‘into a house,’ explaining *du* in the text; (d) where the region is in the genitive after the name of the city situated within it: Mark I, 9, *ïesus qam fram nazaraiþ galeilaias*, ‘Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee’; Luke IV, 26, *ïnsandiþs vas ïn saraipta seidonais*, ‘he was sent to Zarephath of Sidon’; subscription to II Corinthians, codex A, *us filippai makidonais*, ‘from Philippi of Macedonia’; likewise John XII, 21, *atïddjedun du filippau þamma fram beþsaïda galeilaie*, ‘they came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee.’ Here *baurg*, ‘city,’ is probably to be supplied, just as Luke IV, 31 explicitly has *ïn kafarnaum baurg galeilaias*, ‘into Capernaum, a city of Galilee.’”

## §217. III. APPOSITION

1) Apposition—that is, a noun placed beside a substantive or pronoun in order to define it more closely—always agrees with the noun defined in case, and ordinarily also in number. It follows the word to be explained in the normal manner, and often then receives the article. In Gothic speech, however, it sometimes also takes before the word the position which it regularly has in German:

Luke II, 11, *gabaurans ïst ïzvis nasjands, saei ist xristus frauja*, “there has been born to you a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord”; I, 5, *ïn dagam herodes þiudanis ïudaias*, “in the days of Herod, king of Judaea”; III, 1, *ïn jera fimftataihundin þiudinassaus teibairiaus kaisaris*, “in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar”; IV, 17, *bokos eisaeiïns praufetus*, “the book of Isaiah the prophet”; II Tim. IV, 14, *alaiksandrus aizasmiþa*, “Alexander the coppersmith”; Luke II, 36, *vas anna praufeteis, dauhtar fanuelis*, “there was Anna, a prophetess, daughter of Phanuel”; *Calendarium*, *kustanteinus þiudanis … dags*, namely, “the day of Constantine the king”; ibid., *dauriþaius aipiskaupaus*, “Dorithaeus the bishop”; Luke I, 24, *ïnkilþo varþ aileisabaiþ, qens ïs*, “Elizabeth, his wife, conceived”; III, 1, *fidurraginja þis galeilaias herodeis filippauzuh þan broþrs ïs*, “Herod Philip, his brother, tetrarch of Galilee”; [Col. 1134] IV, 41, *ïesus sunus guþs*, “Jesus, Son of God”; 31, *galaiþ ïn kafarnaum, baurg galeilaias*, “he went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee”; I, 47, *svegneid ahma meins du gaþa, nasjand unsaramma*, “my spirit rejoiced in God, our Saviour”; 54, *hleibida ïsraela, þiumagu seinamma*, “he has helped Israel, his servant”; Col. IV, 10, *goleiþ ïzvis markus, gadilligs barnabins*, “Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, greets you”; II Cor. VIII, 23, *broþrjus unsarai, apaustauleis aikklesjono, vulþus xristaus*, “our brethren, apostles of the churches, the glory of Christ”; Luke XVIII, 13, *guþ hulþs sijais mis fravaurhtamma*, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner”; Matt. XXVII, 56, *maria so magdalene*, “Mary the Magdalene”; Luke III, 19, *herodes sa taitrarkes*, “Herod the tetrarch”; IV, 27, *naiman sa saur*, “Naaman the leper”; John XII, 4, *ïudas simonis sa ïskariotes*, “Judas, son of Simon, the Iscariot”; VI, 4, *pasxa so dulþs ïudaie*, “the Passover, the feast of the Jews”; Luke VII, 20, *ïohannes sa daupjands*, “John the Baptist”; Matt. XXVII, 3, *ïudas sa galevjands*, “Judas the betrayer”; Mark V, 8, *ïesu sunau guþs þis hauhistins*, “Jesus, Son of God Most High”; II, 15, *þai mans þai hairdjos qeþun du sis*, “those men, the scribes, said among themselves”; VI, 24, *vai ïzvis þaim gabeigam*, “woe to you, the rich”; Rom. XI, 13, *ïzvis qiþa þaim þiudom*, “I speak to you, the Gentiles.”

Mark VI, 14, *þiudans herodes*, “King Herod”; Luke II, 1, *kaisar agustus*, “Caesar Augustus”; I, 26, *aggilus gabriel*, “the angel Gabriel”; II, 4, *baurgs nazaraiþ*, “the city Nazareth”; V, 1, *saivs gainnesaraiþ*, “the lake Gennesaret”; *Documentum Aretinum*, *hugsis kaballarja*, “Hucgis the horseman”; Luke I, 13, *qens þeina aileisabaiþ gabairid sunu*, “your wife Elizabeth will bear a son”; II, 32, *vulþu managein þeinai israela*, “a glory of your people Israel”; Mark X, 47, *sunau daveidis ïesu!*, “Jesus, Son of David!”; John VII, 2, *dulþs ïudaie so hleþrastakeins*, “the Jewish feast of Tabernacles.”

Mark VI, 16, *þammei ïk haubiþ afmaimait, ïohanne, sa ïst sah urrais us dauþaim*, “John, whom I beheaded—this is he who has risen from the dead”; Luke IX, 17, *ushafan varþ þatei aflifnoda ïm gabruko, tainjons tvalif*, “what remained over to them of fragments was taken up: twelve baskets”; Phil. IV, 13, *all mag ïn þamma ïnsvinþjandin mik, xristau*, “I can do all things in Christ who strengthens me”; Mark V, 11, *vas jainar hairda sveine haldana, ïn þamma fairgunja*, “there was there a herd of swine feeding on the mountain.”

2) An apposition referring to two or more connected objects is put in the plural: Luke IX, 54, *gasaiwandans siþonjos ïs, ïakobus jab ïohannes, qeþun*, “when his disciples, James and John, saw it, they said”; V, 10, *sildaleik dishabaida ïakobau jah ïohannen, sununs zaibaidaiaus*, “likewise also James and John, the sons of Zebedee.”

“Note 1.—Instead of a simple apposition, a relative clause or participle is used: Luke VIII, 41, *qam vair þizei namo ïaeirus*, “a man came whose name was Jairus” (with *vas*, ‘was,’ understood); VIII, 2, *marja sei haitana vas magdalene*, “Mary, who was called Magdalene”; VII, 11, *ïddja ïn baurg namnida naen*, “he went into a city called Nain”; IX, 10, *afïddja ana staþ auþjana baurgs namnidaizos baitsaiïdan*, “he withdrew into a desert place belonging to a city called Bethsaida”; XIX, 2, *guma namin haitans zakkaius*, “a man named Zacchaeus”; and simply with *namin*, ‘by name’: Mark V, 22, *qimiþ ains þize synagogafade namin jaeirus*, “one of the rulers of the synagogue, named Jairus, comes”; Luke I, 5; V, 27.

“Note 2.—The case in which an individual is called by two names, both of which take the same case, is also to be included here: Luke V, 8, *seimon paitrus draus du knivam ïesuis*, “Simon Peter fell at Jesus’ knees”; III, 1, *raginondin pauntiau peilatau ïudaia*, “Pontius Pilate governing Judaea”; Eph. I, 1, *pavlus apaustaulus xristaus ïesuis*, “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus.” Matt. XXVII, 61 also has *maria magdalene* for *so magdalene*, “the Magdalene.””

## III. OBJECTIVE RELATION, OR RELATION TO THE OBJECT

[Col. 1133]

[Col. 1133] §218. That about which the action of the subject is concerned is the object. Now an object may be either a noun or a verb. Yet this designation is given not only to that to which an action is related mediately or immediately [Col. 1134] (accusative, dative, genitive), but also to that with which or through which the action is performed (instrumental); further, to the cause or ground on account of which or from which it is done (causal), and likewise to the manner in which or into which the subject [Col. 1135] acts (modal); finally, place, time, and measure of action may all fall under the object. The cases by which the various relations of subject to object are expressed are called oblique cases, in contrast to the direct case, which is the case of the subject. Since Gothic does not possess forms for marking all relations, it was necessary for several of them to be indicated by the same cases. It also possesses special words, pre-eminent among them the prepositions, both to compensate for this poverty of cases and, especially, to represent with precision the finer degrees of those relations. Which case is to be chosen depends upon the verb; hence government is ascribed to the verb, while dependence belongs to the case: the verb governs, but the case is governed. The verbal object is generally put in the infinitive, but sometimes also in the participle.

### 1. NOMINAL OBJECT

### A. ACCUSATIVE

§219. The object to which the action of the subject is most directly related is put in the accusative; most transitive verbs govern this case. Action is either physical or metaphysical.

1) The transitives denoting physical action and governing the accusative are arranged, according to our fundamental division, as follows:

a) Strong-stem verbs, a few weak verbs in *-an* and *-on*, and several anomalous verbs: *aigan*, possess (Luke IX, 58, *fauhons grobos aigun jah fuglos himinis sitlans*, “foxes have holes and birds of heaven nests”); *haban*, have; *gahaban*, retain; *afhaban*, withhold; *dishaban*, hold fast, occupy; *skulan*, owe, be obliged; *letan*, namely in the pregnant senses of allowing (Mark V, 19), dismissing (Mark XI, 6), allowing in the sense of French *laisser faire*, “letting be done” (Mark XIV, 6; John XII, 7), uttering (Mark XV, 37, *stibna mikila*, “a loud voice”), leaving, French *laisser debout*, “leave standing” (Luke XIX, 44); *afletan*, leave. Thus at Luke V, 11 one must read *afleitandans* rather than *afleiþandans*, since the latter means “failing” and is always intransitive. *Fahan* and *gafahan*, seize; *ushinþan* and *frahinþan*, seize; *undgreipan* and *fairgreipan*, grasp; *gajukan*, fight; *gageigan*, gain.

*Giban*, give; *atgiban*, give, assign; *fragiban*, give, grant; *afgiban*, depart; *usgiban*, render; *ana-* and *biaukan*, add; *niman*, take, seize; *andniman*, receive; *atniman*, take up, receive; *afniman*, take away; *ganiman*, assume; *disniman*, retain; *usniman*, take away; *franiman*, receive; *vilvan* and *fravilvan*, snatch; *disvilvan*, seize; *biraubon*, steal.

*Bairan*, bear; *atbairan*, bring, offer; *ïnnatbairan*, bring in; *þairhbairan*, carry across; *us-* and *utbairan*, take away, carry out; *frabairan*, bear; *briggan*, lead; *tiuhan*, draw, lead; *attiuhan*, bring to; *ïnnattiuhan*, bring in; *aftiuhan*, lead back; *bitiuhan*, lead around; *gatiuhan*, lead away; *ustiuhan*, lead out; *atþinsan*, draw toward; *dreiban*, drive; *usdreiban*, drive out (with accusative and dative; see §229, 1); *vairpan* and *gavairpan*, throw; *at-* and *usvairpan*, throw, cast out (the latter [Col. 1136] with accusative and dative; see §229, 1); *vrikan* and *gavrikan*, pursue; *þreihan*, press.

*Saian*, sow; *sneiþan*, reap; *galisan*, gather; *rikan*, heap up; *giutan*, pour; *þvahan* and *usþvahan*, wash; *hrainjan* and *gahrainjan*, cleanse; *afhrainjan*, purify (*fravaurhtins*, “transgressions,” *Skeireins* I, a); *afsvairban*, erase; *salbon* and *gasalbon*, anoint; *drigkan*, drink; *fraïtan*, devour.

*Gaskapjan*, create; *bairan* and *gabairan*, bear, give birth to; *liugan* and *galiugan*, take [a wife], marry.

*Filhan* and *gafilhan*, hide, bury; *affilhan*, hide; *usfilhan*, bury; *anafilhan*, leave; *galukan*, shut; *uslukan*, open; *usgraban*, dig out; *bigraban*, dig around; *ushulon*, cut out; *falþan*, fold; *bindan* and *gabindan*, bind; *andbindan*, unbind, loose; *bivindan*, wrap around; *gavindan*, gather; *skaidan*, divide; *brikan*, break; *gabrikan*, break in pieces, break (especially *klan*, “break,” whence Gothic *hlaibans*, “break bread”); *dishniupan*, break apart (Luke VIII, 29, *bandjos*, “bonds”); *disskreitan*, tear; *distairan*, tear apart; *gatairan*, dissolve, destroy; *usstiggan*, erase, pluck out; *ufsneiþan*, cut up, sacrifice; *maitan*, *af-* and *usmaitan*, cut off; *bimaitan*, circumcise; *slahan*, strike; *afslahan*, strike, slay; *stautan*, strike; *bliggvan* and *usbliggvan*, strike; *gavundon*, wound; *holon*, defraud; *kriustan*, gnash or creak (French *presser l’un contre l’autre*, “press one against another”; *tunþans*, “teeth,” to gnash, Mark IX, 18).

b) Very many verbs which become transitive by composition, such as: *bistandan*, stand around (Luke XIX, 43); *dissitan*, take hold of; *bisitan*, dwell around (Luke I, 65); *birinnan*, surround (John X, 24); *disdriusan*, seize (Luke I, 12); *anaqiman*, come upon (“come-over,” Luke II, 9); *biqiman*, come upon (I Thess. V, 3, where *biqimiþ* must be read in place of *blissoþ*); *bitiuhan*, go round, traverse (Matt. IX, 35; Mark VI, 6, a region, from the intransitive *tiuhan*, journey, go); *biwairban*, go around, stand around, surround (Luke VIII, 45); *þairhhleiþan*, pass through, go through—(Luke XVIII, 43); *þairhgaggan*, pass through; *ufargaggan*, pass by (Luke XV, 29, *anabusn*, “a command”); *viþragaggan*, go to meet (John XI, 20); *bispeivan*, spit upon (Mark XV, 19; Luke XVIII, 32; simple *speivan* is construed with *ana*); *biskeinan*, shine around, illuminate (Luke II, 9); *bilaigon*, lick (Luke XVI, 21); *gátilon*, suffer, endure (II Tim. II, 10).

c) Derived verbs in *-jan* having a factitive meaning:

aa) From verbs: *satjan* and *gasatjan*, set, place (French *faire asseoir*, “make sit”); *atsatjan*, put beside; *afsatjan*, remove; *bisatjan*, surround, besiege; *miþsatjan*, transpose; *ussatjan*, impose, arrange; *lagjan* and *galagjan*, cast, place (“cause to lie”); *at-* and *analagjan*, lay upon, impose; *aflagjan*, put down; *uslagjan*, place; *faurlagjan*, set before.

*Sandjan*, send (French *faire aller*, “make go”); *ïnsandjan*, send; *gasandjan*, lead away; *ussandjan*, cast out, send away; *draibjan*, compel; *usdraibjan*, drive out; *ushafjan*, lift up; *ufarhafjan*, exalt; *athafjan*, take down; [Col. 1137] *raisjan*, rouse, awaken; *urraisjan*, raise, awaken; *hnaivjan* and *gahnaivjan*, humble; *ufhnaivjan*, subject; *anahnaivjan*, incline, recline (of one sleeping: recline one’s head); *ufrakjan*, stretch out; *ufþanjan*, extend; *urranjan*, cause to arise; *vandjan* and *gavandjan*, turn; *atvandjan*, turn back, convert; *afvandjan*, turn away; *bivandjan*, turn around, avoid, escape; *ïnvandjan*, pervert; *af-* and *ushrisjan*, shake, cause to tremble; *usvaltjan*, roll up; *atvalvjan*, wrap round; *afvalvjan*, roll down; *faurvalvjan*, block beforehand—that is, roll, for example, a stone before the door of a tomb; *ga-* and *afdrausjan*, cast down, throw down; *vagjan* and *gavagjan*, move, agitate; *ïn-* and *usvagjan*, shake, disturb; *drobjan*, trouble, disturb; *tahjan*, tear; *distahjan*, tear apart; *gastagqjan*, strike against (the foot, Luke IV, 11).

*Gadragkjan*, refresh with drink; *gasoþjan*, satisfy; *daupjan*, baptize, immerse; *ufdaupjan*, plunge under; *bugjan*, sell; *usbugjan*, buy; *frabugjan*, sell (to which the instrumental case is also added; see §240, 3); *huljan* and *gahuljan*, cover; *dishuljan*, conceal, cover; *andhuljan*, reveal; *tandjan*, kindle; *ïntandjan*, set on fire; *raupjan*, pluck out; *afwapjan*, choke, extinguish.

*Taujan* and *gataujan*, make; *vaurkjan* and *gavaurkjan*, work, perform, make; *fairvaurkjan*, accomplish; *baidjan* and *gabaidjan*, compel; *nasjan* and *ganasjan*, make whole, heal.

bb) From nouns, namely:

α) From adjectives, which then lie as predicates in the verb: *míkíljan* (from *mikils*, “great”), magnify, enlarge; *gamaurgjan* (from *MAURGS?*; compare Gf. II, 851), shorten; *blauþjan* and *gablauþjan* (from *BLAUþS*, “weak, dull”; compare Gf. III, 251), weaken, diminish, efface; *hauhjan* and *ushauhjan* (from *hauhs*, “high”), exalt, make high; *haunjan* and *gahaunjan*, lower; *gatamjan* (from *TAMS*, “tamed, gentle”), tame, domesticate; *gamainjan*, make common, share, communicate; *manvjan* and *gamanvjan*, prepare; *gahrainjan*, purify; *hailjan* and *gahailjan*, make whole; *lausjan* and *galausjan*, loose, free; *uslausjan*, empty, free; *afdauþjan*, kill; *fulljan* and *gafulljan*, fill; *usfulljan*, fill completely; *natjan* and *ganatjan*, water; *tulgjan* and *gatulgjan*, strengthen, fortify; *gaþvastjan*, fortify; *gaïbnjan*, make equal; *gahardjan*, harden; *gablindjan*, blind; *maidjan*, corrupt; *ïnmaidjan*, change; *garaihtjan*, make right, set straight.

β) From substantives, which are here instrumentals: *nauþjan* (from *nauþs*, “necessity, compulsion”), obtain by compulsion, compel; *taiknjan* (from *taikns*, “sign”), indicate, show by a sign; *ustaiknjan*, explain, designate; *bandvjan*, make a sign, signify; *faurvaipjan* (from *vaips*, “crown, garland, bond”), surround with a crown, crown, bind; *ganagljan*, fasten with a nail; *gasleiþjan*, injure with damage; *gabotjan*, repair with good; *laistjan* and *galaistjan*, follow; *sigljan* and *gasigljan*, seal; *faursigljan*, mark with a seal; *insailjan*, ensnare; *kaupatjan*, strike with the fist; *fodjan*, nourish, feed; *matjan*, cause to eat; *vasjan* and *gavasjan*, clothe, [Col. 1138] put on; *andvasjan*, unclothe, strip; *fravardjan*, corrupt; *disvinþjan*, shatter; *levjan* and *galevjan*, hand over; *ushramjan*, crucify; *disdailjan*, divide, apportion; *afdailjan*, divide; *anamahtjan*, use force against; *timrjan* and *gatimrjan*, build; *siujan*, sew.

2) Transitive verbs which signify metaphysical action, including verbs of sense, feeling, and speech:

*Hausjan* and *gahausjan*, hear; *saiwan* and *gasaiwan*, see, behold.

*Miton*, think, consider; *biþagkjan*, think, suppose; *domjan* and *gadomjan*, judge, distinguish; sometimes *gamunan*, think (see §238, Note 4); *gakaran*, care for, provide for; *fauragaredan*, predestine; *kunnan*, know (Luke I, 34; XVI, 15); *gakunnan*, recognize; *ufkunnan*, know, understand; *vitan*, know; *biniuhsjan*, investigate; *andhruskan*, inquire into; *fraisan*, test; *sokjan*, seek; *ussokjan*, seek out.

*Venjan*, hope, expect (something); *usbeidan*, await (someone); *ogan*, fear, be afraid of—; *vinnan* and *gavinnan*, suffer; *þulan*, bear, endure; *usþulan*, endure.

*Aistan* and *gaaistan*, esteem, venerate; *sveran*, honour; *unsveran*, dishonour; *andvitan*, defame; *fastan* and *gafastan*, consider, behold; *ïnveitan*, worship; *blotan*, worship with sacrifices; *veihan* and *gaveihan*, sanctify; *ïdveitjan*, reproach (see §229, 1); *bilaikan*, dance; *bihlahjan*, laugh at; *gaaiviskon*, disapprove.

*Frijon*, love; *arman* and *gaarman*, pity; *hatan* (Rom. VII, 15) and *fijan*, hate; *gaurjan*, grieve; *marzjan* and *gamarzjan*, cause offence; *airzjan*, lead astray; *afhugjan*, blind; *tveifljan*, doubt (*Skeireins* VI, b); *hahan*, hold suspended, keep in anxious suspense (John X, 24); *ïnaljanon*, provoke to jealousy; *usluton*, deceive; *andstaurran*, murmur; *fraveitan*, vindicate, avenge.

*Laisjan*, teach—especially knowledge, *didaskein*; *talzjan*, educate, instruct, train—especially doctrine of life, *paideuein, nouthetein*; *ussiggvan*, choose; *usqiþan*, explain, unfold by elucidation; *merjan*, notice; *spillon* and *gaspillon*, tell, expound; *fraihnan*, ask; *invidan* and *afaikan*, deny; *bisvaran*, affirm, swear; *bidjan*, pray; *namnjan*, name; *haitan* (*kalein*), call, name (see §220, 2), cry aloud; *anahaitan*, call aloud (see §229, 2); *athaitan*, call to; *gahaitan*, call out, acknowledge; *fairhaitan*, acknowledge; *anabiudan*, command, order, prescribe (Matt. VIII, 4, *atbair giba þoei anabauþ moses*, “offer the gift which Moses commanded”; Mark I, 44; Luke V, 14); *vopjan*, cry (*phōnein, boan*); *atvopjan*, call to; *laþon* and *galaþon*, call, summon; *gavaljan*, choose; *goljan*, greet; *hazjan*, praise; *andbeitan*, blame; *gasakan*, impute, accuse (see §229, 2); *vajamerjan*, slander; *þiuþjan* and *gaþiuþjan*, bless (see §229, 1); *þrafstjan* and *gaþrafstjan*, comfort; *anaþrafstjan*, refresh, strengthen; *fullaveisjan*, convince, rebuke; *bairhtjan*, *at-* and *gabairhtjan*, reveal, make manifest; *gasvikunþjan*, make manifest; *vrohjan*, accuse; *stojan* and [Col. 1139] *gastojan*, judge; *afdomjan*, condemn; *meljan* and *gameljan*, write.

3) The impersonals *huggreiþ* and *gredoþ*, “is hungry,” and *þaurseiþ*, “is thirsty,” also govern the accusative of the person: John VI, 35, *þana gaggandan du mis ni huggreiþ … jah þana galaubjandan du mis ni þaurseiþ*, “he who comes to me shall not hunger … and he who believes in me shall never thirst”; Rom. XII, 20, *jabai gredo fijand þeinana, mat gif ïmma; iþ jabai þaursjai, dragkei ïna*, “if your enemy is hungry, give him food; but if he is thirsty, give him drink.” With *karïst*, “it concerns, troubles” (see §238, 3, note), the accusative of the person and the genitive of the thing are likewise used; see §238, 3.

4) For verbs which, in addition to their accusative, govern a dative or genitive, see §§227, 237, 238.

§220. A second accusative—which, besides the accusative of the object, indicates the result of the action, or is placed as a predicate of the object and in German is rendered by *als*, “as,” *für*, “for,” or *zu*, “to” [Note: [Col. 1139] In Latin it is sometimes expressed in this way, sometimes by a simple accusative. Translator.]—is likewise expressed by the simple accusative. It is governed by verbs:

1) Of making, calling, illustrating, placing, showing, taking, giving, etc.: John VIII, 53, *wana þuk sïlban taujis þu?*, “Whom do you make yourself?”; XIX, 7, *sik silban guþs sunu gatavida*, “he made himself Son of God”; Mark I, 3, *raihtos vaurkeiþ staigos guþs*, “make straight the paths of God”; Rom. IX, 24, *kasa armaions guþ laþoda uns*, “God called us vessels of mercy”; Col. I, 22, *gafriþodai sijuþ in leika þairh dauþu du atsatjan ïzvis veihans jah unvammans*, “you have been reconciled in the body through death, in order to present you holy and blameless”; II Cor. II, 14, *guþa aviliud þamma ustaiknjandin hroþeigans uns in xristau*, “thanks be to God, who manifests through us the fragrance of his knowledge in Christ”; Phil. IV, 14, *vaila gatavideduþ gamainja briggandans meina aglon*, “you did well by sharing in my affliction”; II Tim. II, 15, *usdaudei þuk silban gakusana usgiban guþa, vaurstvjan unaiviskana*, “present yourself approved to God, a workman unashamed”; Luke XX, 43, *galagja fijands þeinans fotubaurd fotive þeinaize*, “I will make your enemies a footstool for your feet”; I, 53, *gabignandans ïnsandida lausans*, “he sent the rich away empty”; XX, 10; VII, 10, *bigetun þana siukan skalk hailana*, “they found the sick servant well”; Matt. XXV, 38, *wan þuk sewum gast?*, “when did we see you a stranger?”; Luke XVIII, 24; X, 18, *gasaw satana sve lauhmunja driusandan us himina*, “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven”; Philem. 15, *aufto duþe atgaf sik du weilai, ei aiveinana ïna andnimais*, “perhaps he departed for a while in order that you might receive him forever”; Luke XV, 27; John XIV, 18, *ni leta ïzvis viduvairnans*, “I will not leave you orphaned”; I Tim. V, 23, *þuk silban sviknana fastais*, “keep yourself steadfast”; II Cor. XI, 16, *sve unfrodana nimiþ mik*, “receive me as foolish”; I, 23, *veitvod guþ anahaita ana meinai saivalai*, “I call God as witness upon my soul”; I, 22, *guþ gibiþ vadi ahman ïn hairtona unsara*, “God gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts”; Eph. IV, 11; I Tim. II, 6; Eph. V, 2, *xristus atgaf sik silban faur uns hunsl jah sauþ*, “Christ gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice”; I Cor. IX, 5, *habam valdufni svistar qinon bitiuhan*, “we have authority to take along a sister as wife”; Luke III, 8, *attan aigum abraham*, “we have Abraham as father”; X, 18, *habai mik faurqiþanana*, “consider me condemned”; Phil. II, 29; III, 17.

2) Of calling, naming, etc.: Luke VI, 13, *ïesus gavalida us ïm tvalib, þanzei jah apaustauluns namnida, seimona, þanei jah namnida paitru*, “Jesus chose twelve from them, whom he also named apostles—Simon, whom he also named Peter”; I, 3, *haitais namo ïs ïohannen*, “his name shall be John”; 31, 59; XX, 44; Rom. IX, 25; Mark X, 18, *wa mik qiþis þiuþeigana?*, “why do you call me good?”; XII, 37; *Skeireins* IV, c; John IX, 22, *jabai was ïesu andhaihaiti xristu, utana synagogais vairþai*, “if anyone confessed Jesus as Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue.”

3) Of holding, having, reckoning, etc.: Luke VII, 7, *ni mik silban vairþana rahnida at þus qiman*, “I did not consider myself worthy to come to you”; [Col. 1140] I Tim. VI, 1; II Cor. XI, 16, *aftra qiþa, ïbai was mik muni unfrodana*, “again I say: lest anyone think me foolish”; Phil. II, 3; I Tim. I, 12, *galaubjandan mik gahugida gasatjands ïn andbahtja*, “he considered me faithful, appointing me to service”; Luke VII, 29, *motarjos garaihtana domidedun guþ*, “the tax collectors declared God righteous”; John XVII, 3, *so ïst so aiveino libains, ei kunneina þuk ainana sunja guþ*, “this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God.”

“Note 1.—Just as with *visan* and *vairþan* (§209, 5), a predicate or result [of an action] is sometimes expressed by *du*, ‘to,’ so it is also with the verbs under nos. 1 and 2: John X, 33, *stainjam þuk, þatei taujis þuk silban du guþa*, “we stone you because you make yourself God”; Mark XI, 17, *jus gatavideduþ razn mein du filigrja vaidedjane*, “you made my house into a den of robbers”; Eph. II, 15, *tvans gaskop ïn sis silbin du ainamma niujamma mann*, “he created the two in himself into one new man”; Neh. VI, 18, *tobeias nam dauhtar maisaullamis du qenai*, “Tobiah took the daughter of Meshullam as wife”; Mark XII, 23, *sibun aihtedun þo du qenai*, “the seven had her as wife”; Philem. 17, *nu mik habais du gamana*, “therefore receive me as a partner.” For other examples, see Glossary V, *Du*, b).

“Note 2.—Just as the above-mentioned verbs, when in the active, govern a double accusative, so, when constructed in the passive, they admit a double nominative: Luke VIII, 2, *marja, sei haitana vas magdalene*, “Mary, who was called Magdalene”; I, 32, *sunus þeins vairþiþ mikils jah sunus hauhistins haitada*, “your son will be great and will be called Son of the Highest”; II, 21, *haitan vas namo ïs ïesus*, “his name was called Jesus”; Eph. I, 11, *ïn xristau hlauts gasatidai vesum*, “in Christ we were appointed as an inheritance”; Luke IX, 36, *bigitans varþ ïesus ains*, “Jesus was found alone”; II Cor. XIII, 7, *ni vaiht ubilis taujaiþ, ni ei veis gakusanai þugkjaima, ak ei jus þata godo taujaiþ*, “that you may do no evil—not that we may appear approved, but that you may do what is good.” But *sve*, “as,” may also be introduced before the second nominative: Rom. VIII, 36, *rahnidai vesum sve lamba slauhtais*, “we were reckoned as sheep for slaughter.” Where the passive is constructed in the participle, and indeed in the accusative, the predicate is correspondingly put in the accusative: Matt. IX, 9, *ïesus gasaw mannan sitandan at motai maþþaiu haitanana*, “Jesus saw a man sitting at the tax-office, called Matthew.”

“Note 3.—The so-called case of title is excepted from this rule: after *vopjan*, ‘call,’ the title given to someone is put in the nominative: John XIII, 13, *jus vopeid mik laisareis jah frauja*, “you call me Teacher and Lord.” Likewise Mark III, 16 has *gasatida seimona namo paitrus*, “he gave Simon the name Peter.”

4) The double accusative expressing person and thing occurs only rarely in Gothic; only examples such as the following can be affirmed: Mark X, 35, *vileima, ei þatei þuk bidjos, taujais uggkis*, “we desire that whatever we ask you, you may do for us,” just as German would say *was wir dich bitten*, and French *ce que nous vous demandons*. Most probably also in John XIV, 26, *ïzvis laiseiþ allata*, “he will teach you all things,” *ïzvis* is accusative, since *laisjan* is constructed similarly in German too (see, for example, Old High German, Gf. II, 256). Very rarely John XVII, 26 has *frijaþva þoei frijodes mik*, “the love with which you loved me”; but elsewhere in constructions of this kind Gothic uses the instrumental case, as Mark X, 38, *daupeinai þizaiei ïk daupjada*, “the baptism with which I am baptized” (see Luke VII, 29); Mark IX, 41, *gadragkjai ïzvis stikla*, “give you to drink with a cup”; XV, 17, *gavasidedun ïna paurpurai*, “they clothed him with purple”; or else another construction, [Col. 1141] such as “ask someone about something” (genitive), Mark IV, 10; “remind someone of something” (genitive), John XIV, 26; “charge someone concerning [something]” (*ïn* with dative or *bi* with dative), I Thess. V, 27, etc.

In Mark XII, 4, *haubiþ vundan brahtedun*, “they brought [him] wounded in the head,” the construction is to be understood as having *vundan*, “wounded,” for its object and *haubiþ* as “in respect of the head” (French *à la tête*, “in the head”), although the consonantal form of *vundan* is difficult to explain here. The *Heliand*, 149, 1, moreover, says in the German fashion: *he ward an that hobid vund*, “he was wounded in the head.” The accusative *haubiþ* is otherwise elucidated by passages in which the accusative is constructed with passive forms that govern an accusative in the active: John XI, 44, *urrann sa dauþa gabundans handuns jah fotuns faskjam*, “the dead man came out, bound hand and foot with grave-cloths”; Eph. VI, 14, *standaiþ ufgaurdanai hupins ïzvarans sunjai*, “stand with your loins girded with truth”; just as German says *die Hände und Füsse gebunden, die Hüften gegürtet*, “the hands and feet bound, the loins girded,” and French *pieds et mains liés, les reins ceints*, “feet and hands bound, loins girded”; compare Luke IV, 18, *blind siun*, “blind in sight”; Phil. III, 5, *bimait ahtaudogs*, “circumcised on the eighth day.” II Cor. III, 18, *þo samon frisaht ïngaleikonda*, “being transformed into the same image,” however, agrees wholly with Greek.

“Note 4.—But here the modal [case] is also used; see §243; or the construction is changed: Gal. II, 7, *pepisteumai to euangelion*, “I have been entrusted with the gospel,” is in Gothic *gatrauaida vas mis aivaggeljo*, “the gospel was entrusted to me”; likewise Titus I, 3. Or I Tim. IV, 2, *kekautēriasmenoi tēn idian syneidēsin*, “having their own conscience seared,” is in Gothic *gatandida habandans svesa miþvissein*, “having their own conscience branded.”

§221. Accusatives are indeed often used absolutely, but only pronominal neuters occur as such accusatives: I Cor. X, 33, *ïk allaim all leika*, “I please all men in all things”; Eph. IV, 15, *vahsjaima ïn ïna þo alla*, “let us grow in him in all things”; II Cor. XII, 18, *ïbai wa bifaihoda ïzvis teitus?*, “did Titus exploit you in anything?”; I Tim. I, 10; Gal. IV, 12, *ni vaiht mis gaskoþuþ*, “you have done me no wrong in anything.” Here belongs the interrogative *wa* (*ti*), “what?”: Matt. VI, 28; VIII, 26, etc.; further *þata anþar* (*to loipon*), “for the rest, henceforth,” I Cor. I, 16; II Cor. XIII, 11, etc.; *þata andaneiþo* (*tounantion*), “on the contrary,” II Cor. II, 7. Sometimes *ïn* with the dative is used instead of the absolute accusative: Eph. VI, 13, *maguþ in allamma usvaurkjandans standan*, “having accomplished all things, you may stand”; or the simple dative: Luke IV, 25, *ni vaihtai gaskaþjands ïmma*, “doing him no harm in anything.”

§222. For the accusative determining place, time, and manner, see §§246, 249, 250.

### B. DATIVE

(Silber, *Essay on the Gothic Dative*. Naumburg, 1845.)

§223. The dative indicates the respect in which two objects are externally and incidentally connected; the close relation in which a subject finds itself or seeks to find itself; the object upon which it indirectly exerts, or desires to exert, its efficacy; indeed, the object which it directly enjoys or seeks to enjoy. In brief, it expresses both the simultaneous and incidental proximity and pertinence of two objects; hence arise relations partly of similarity and community, partly of superiority and inferiority; and finally, the relation of an object to the effects of an agent is expressed in the dative case. The object expressed by the dative is most often a person. [Col. 1142] Nevertheless, Gothic retains not a few traces allowing dative and accusative to be regarded as cases signifying direct or indirect objects of action: partly in form, because, for example, the forms of both cases are identical in the plural of the substantive pronoun (*ïzvis*, *uns*, *unsis*), and in the singular of vocalic anomalous nouns (§§86, 87) and of feminine consonantal declension (§§91, 92), and because in the third vocalic declension they begin interchangeably in *-an* and *-u* (compare §29, 3); partly in meaning, because very many verbs can govern either case with the same meaning.

§224. 1) The more corporeal the relation, the more a verb governing the dative indicates something external. First, *sves visan*, belong to, be proper to (*Skeireins* II, d); then *ïbna visan*, be like (Luke XX, 36, *ïbnans aggilum sind*, “they are equal to angels”); *gaïbnjan*, liken (Luke XIX, 44, *airþai þuk gaïbnjand*, “leveling you with the ground”); *galeïks visan*, be similar (*Skeireins* I, a, *ni ïbnih galeiks unsarai garaihtein ak silba garaihtei vas*, “he was not like our righteousness in equality, but was righteousness itself”); *galeikon*, conform (Rom. XII, 2, *ni galeikoþ ïzvis þamma aiva*, “do not conform yourselves to this age”); compare (Matt. VII, 24, *galeiko ïna vaira frodamma*, “I shall compare him to a wise man”); imitate (Matt. VI, 8, *ni galeikoþ þaim*, “do not be like them”); here also belongs *sa sama*, “the same, thus, just as” (I Cor. XI, 5, *ain ïst jah þata samo þizai biskabanon*, “it is one and the same as she who has been shaved”).

*Gamains vairþan*, become a participant (Rom. XI, 17, *gamains þizai vaurtsai jah smairþra alevabagmis varst*, “you became a participant in the root and richness of the olive tree”); *gamainjan*, share in (I Cor. X, 18, *niu þai matjandans hunsla gamainjandans hunslastada sind*, “are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar?”); *gamotjan*, meet (Matt. VIII, 28, etc.); *afarlaistjan*, follow (Luke VII, 9; I, 3; I Tim. V, 10), while *laistjan* and *galaistjan* govern the accusative; see §219, 1) c) bb) β; *haftjan*, adhere to (Rom. XII, 9, 12; I Tim. III, 8); *gahaftjan sik*, attach oneself (Luke XV, 15, *gahaftida sik ainamma baurgjane*, “he attached himself to a citizen”); *gahaftnan*, adhere to (Luke X, 11); *andtilon*, adhere to (Luke XVI, 13), accommodate oneself (*Skeireins* VII, a); *gabundans visan*, be joined to (I Cor. VII, 27; Rom. VII, 2); *gavadjon*, betroth (II Cor. XI, 2); *liugan*, marry, said of a woman (Mark X, 12, etc.; §178, 1); *blandan*, mix with (I Cor. V, 9, *ni blandaiþ ïzvis horam*, “do not associate with fornicators”); *gahorinon*, commit adultery with (Matt. V, 28, *wazuh saei saiwiþ qinon du luston ïzos ja gahorinoda ïzai*, “everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her”).

Likewise in the contrary sense: *galausiþs visan*, be separated, loosed (I Cor. VII, 27, *galausiþs ïs qenai*, “are you loosed from a wife?”); *skaidan*, separate, divide (Mark X, 9); *usvandjan sik*, depart, turn away (Matt. V, 42); *afskiuban*, drive away (Rom. XI, 1, *ïbai afskauf guþ managein seinamma*, “has God cast away his people?”; I Tim. I, 19); *afstandan*, stand apart, depart, fall away (II Cor. IV, 2, *afstoþum þaim analaugnjam aiviskjis*, “we have renounced the hidden things of shame”; I Tim. IV, 1, *afstandand sumai galaubeinai*, “some will depart from the faith”); *tvisstandan*, separate oneself, take leave (II Cor. II, 13, *tvistandands ïmma galaiþ ïn makidonja*, “having taken leave of them, he went into Macedonia”).

“Note 1.—Several of these verbs are also construed differently: II Thess. III, 14, *ni blandaiþ ïzvis miþ ïmma*, “do not associate with him”; Mark X, 11, *saei afletiþ qen seina [Col. 1143] jah liugaiþ anþara, horinoþ du þizai*, “whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery against her”; Rom. VII, 2, *jabai gasviltiþ aba, galausjada qens af þamma vitoda*, “if the husband dies, the wife is released from the law”; Matt. X, 35, *qam skaidan mannan viþra attan*, “I came to divide a man against his father”; Luke IV, 13, *diabulus afstoþ fairra ïmma*, “the devil departed from him for a time”; II Cor. XII, 8, *fraujan baþ ei afstoþi af mis*, “I besought the Lord that it might depart from me”; II Tim. II, 19. For *laus visan*, *lausjan*, and *galausjan*, see §237, 4) and Note 2. After active *liugan*, said of a man taking a wife, the accusative is used.”

*Vitan*, keep watch (Luke II, 8, *hairdjos vesun vitandans hairdai*, “shepherds were keeping watch by night”; Matt. XXVII, 64, *hait vitan þamma hlaiva*, “command that the tomb be guarded,” etc.); *bairgan*, preserve, keep safe (John XII, 25, *saei fiaiþ saivala seina ïn þamma fairwau, ïn libainai aiveinon bairgiþ ïzai*, “he who hates his life in this world will preserve it for eternal life”); in the contrary sense: *fraliusan*, lose (Luke XV, 8, *saei fraliusiþ drakmin ainamma, sokeiþ unte bigitiþ*, “when she loses one drachma, she seeks until she finds it,” etc. in the same chapter); *fraqiman*, expend (Luke VIII, 43, *ïn lekjans fraqam allamma aigina seinamma*, “she had spent all her property on physicians”), lose, destroy (Luke IX, 54, *qiþaima, fon atgaggai us himina jah fraqimai ïm?*, “shall we say that fire come down from heaven and destroy them?”); *fravisan*, destroy (Luke XV, 14); *biniman*, take away (Matt. XXVII, 64, *ïbai aufto siponjos ïs binimaina ïmma*, “lest perhaps his disciples take him away from them”);

Tekan, to touch (Luke 8:45, 46 *was sa tekands mis? taitok mis sums*, “Who was touching me? Someone touched me”); more solemnly, attekan (Matt. 8:3 *attaitok imma*; 9:21 *jabai atteka vastjai is, ganisa*, “if I touch his garment, I shall be healed,” etc.); gaþlaihan, to embrace (Mark 10:16 *gaþlaihands barnam þiuþida im*; 2 Cor. 7:6); kukjan, to kiss (Luke 7:45 *ni kukides mis*, “you did not kiss me”; 38 *kukida fotum is*, “she kissed his feet”).

2) But the more spiritual the relation is, the more a verb governing the dative indicates something intimate: gateihan, to show; praufetjan, to prophesy; qiþan, to say, and rodjan, to speak (both also frequently construed with *du*, §246, 3 b); andqiþan, to report (Luke 9:61), to address (Luke 8:19); anabiudan and faurbiudan, to command, enjoin; wotjan and gawotjan, to rebuke; laian, to mock (John 9:28); ubil vaurdjan, to revile (Mark 9:39); ubil qiþan, to curse (Mark 7:10); vaila qiþan, to praise, bless (Luke 6:26); gaþlaihan, to console; uslaubjan, to permit.

Gaumjan, to attend to (1 Tim. 4:13 *gaumei saggva boko*), to observe (John 9:1 *þairhleiþands gaumida mann blindamma*, “as he passed by, he observed a blind man”); maurnan, to be anxious; fraþjan, to understand (Mark 9:32 *ni froþun þamma vaurda*, “they did not understand the saying,” etc.); andhausjan, to hear (2 Cor. 6:2 *andhausida þus*, “I heard you”); hausjan, to hear (Mark 9:7 *sa ist sunus meins, þamma hausjaiþ*, “this is my Son; hear him”; John 12:46, etc.; cf. §238); ufhausjan, to hear; galaubjan, to believe; trauan, to believe; frakunnan, to despise (1 Tim. 4:12 *ni manna þeinai jundai frakunni*, “let no one despise your youth”; John 12:48; Matt. 6:24); ufbrikan, to despise (Luke 10:16); ufarmunnon, to forget (Phil. 2:30; 3:14).

Siponjan, to be a disciple (Matt. 27:57 *silba siponida iesua*, “he himself was a disciple of Jesus”); andbahtjan, to minister (*διακονεῖν*); skalkinon, to serve (*δουλεύειν*); drauhtinon, to perform military service, to be a soldier (2 Tim. 2:4); raginon, to govern (*ἡγεμονεύειν*, Luke 2:2); fraujinon, to preside, rule (*κυριεύειν*, Rom. 7:1 etc.; also construed with *faura* in 1 Tim. 2:12); reikinon, to rule (*ἄρχειν*, Mark 10:42; John 14:30); valdan, to govern (1 Tim. 5:14); gavaldan, to exercise dominion over (Mark 10:42); fauragaggan, to provide for, manage (1 Tim. 3:4, 12).

Vailahugjan, to be well-disposed (Matt. 5:25); hulþs visan, to be gracious (Luke 18:13); gods visan, to be good (Luke 6:35; 9:33); svers visan, to be beloved (Luke 7:2); vaila galeikan, to please (Rom. 14:18); modags visan, to be angry (Matt. 5:22); hatizon, to be angry (John 7:23); vailataujan, to do good (Mark 14:7); hleibjan, to help (Luke 1:54); gaskaþjan, to harm, act unjustly; balvjan, to torment, afflict grievously (Mark 5:7; Luke 8:28); gafriþon, to reconcile (2 Cor. 5:19 *guþ vas in xristau manaseþ gafriþonds sis*, “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself”); gagavairþnan, to be reconciled (2 Cor. 5:20 *bidjam faur xristu gagavairþnan guþa*, “we beseech you on Christ’s behalf: be reconciled to God”); gasibjon, to reconcile oneself (Matt. 5:24 *gagg gasibjon broþr þeinamma*, “go, be reconciled to your brother”); gaqiss visan, to agree (Rom. 7:16); gadobs visan, to be fitting (Titus 2:1, etc.); and, in the contrary sense: andvaurdjan, to contradict (Rom. 9:20); andstandan, to resist (Matt. 5:39); andveihan or andvaihjan, to oppose (Rom. 7:23).

> **Note 2.—** That the Goth also uses personally in the passive verbs which govern the dative has already been observed in §177, 2; but sometimes he also uses them impersonally, in Roman fashion, as when he renders “I am spared” by Matt. 9:17 *bajoþum bairgada*; cf. §234.

## §225

A relation of belonging between two objects, expressed through vairþan, “to become,” and visan, “to be (assigned as a lot),” is indicated by the dative. The former object may sometimes be translated in Latin by *possess*, the latter by *have*, the subject becoming dative: Matt. 5:22 *saei qiþiþ broþr seinamma raka! skula vairþiþ gaqumþai*, “whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca!’ shall be liable to judgment”; Mark 12:13 *warjamma (τίνος) ize vairþiþ qens?*, “whose wife shall she be?”; Luke 19:9 *himma daga naseins þamma garda varþ*, “this day salvation has come to this house”; Rom. 9:9 *vairþiþ sarrin (τῇ Σάρρᾳ) sunus*, “Sarah had a son”; 7:3 *qens vairþiþ vaira anþaramma (ἀνδρὶ ἑτέρῳ)*, “the woman becomes another man’s wife”; 4; 11:25 *daubei sumata israela varþ*, “partial blindness befell Israel”; 2 Cor. 6:16 *eis vairþand mis managei*, “they shall be my people”; Mark 9:21 *wan lagg mel ist, ei þata varþ imma?*, “How long has this been happening to him?”—Luke 8:42 *dauhtar ainoho vas imma*, “he had an only daughter”; 9:38; cf. 7:12; Mark 12:37 *waþro imma sunus ist*, “how is he his son?”; Luke 20:44; Mark 6:2 *waþro þamma þata (ist)*, “whence does this come to him?”; Luke 2:14 *vulþus in hauhistjam guþa (sijai)!*, “glory be to God in the highest!”; 1 Tim. 1:17; Luke 10:5 *gavairþi þamma garda (sijai)!*, “peace be to this house!”; 19:34 *fraujin þaurfts þis ist*, “the Lord has need of it”; 7:41 *tvai dulgis skulans vesun dulgahaitjin ainamma*, “two debtors belonged to one creditor”; Rom. 9:2 *saurga mis ist mikila*, “great sorrow is mine”; 2 Cor. 7:4 *managa mis trauains du izvis (ist)*, “great is my confidence toward you”; 2 Thess. 3:2 *nist allaim (πάντων) galaubeins*, “faith does not belong to all.” The formula *wa mis* or *uns jah þus?*, “what [is that] to me, or to us and you?” belongs here; §255, 2.

## §226

With nouns that agree, either in root or meaning, with the verbs listed in §224, the dative is frequently joined in place of the genitive used by Greek: Rom. 11:34 *was imma (αὐτοῦ) ragineis vas?*, “who has known his mind?”; Mark 2:28 *frauja ist sa sunus mans jah þamma sabbato (τοῦ σ[αββάτου])*, “the Son of Man is lord also of the Sabbath”; 9:35 *jabai wasvili frumists visan, sijai allaim (πάντων) andbahts*, “if anyone wishes to be first, let him be servant of all”; 10:44—“slave of all”; John 9:27, 28 *jah jus vileiþ þamma (αὐτοῦ) siponjos vairþan … þu is siponeis þamma*, “do you also wish to become his disciples? … you are that man’s disciple”; Luke 10:29 *was ist mis (μου) newundja?*, “who is my neighbour?”; John 19:12 *ni ist frijonds kaisara (Καίσαρος)*, “he is not Caesar’s friend”; 1 Tim. 5:22 *ni gamainja siais fravaurhtim*, “do not share in sins”; 2 Tim. 3:10 *galaista is laiseinai meinai*, “you have followed my teaching”; Luke 5:10 *vesun gadailans seimona*, “they were Simon’s partners”; 1 Cor. 10:20; 2 Cor. 6:14, 15 *ni vairþaiþ gajukans ungalaubjandam, unte wo dailo garaihtein miþ ungaraihtein, aiþþau wo gamainduþe liuhada miþ riqiza, vouh þan samaqisse xristau miþ bailiama, aiþþau wo daile galaubjandin miþ ungalaubjandin?*, “do not become unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what share has righteousness with unrighteousness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement, then, has Christ with Belial? Or what share has a believer with an unbeliever?”

Likewise John 18:13 has *sa vas svaihra kajafin (τοῦ Καϊάφα)*, “he was Caiaphas’s father-in-law”; and the dative and genitive are used indiscriminately: Mark 6:3 *niu þata ist sa timrja sa sunus marjins iþ broþar iakoba jah iuse jah iudins jah seimonis*, “is this not the carpenter, Mary’s son and the brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon?”, although Greek uses the genitive throughout. Cf. §§230 note and 227 note.

## §227

Several of the verbs mentioned in §§224 and 219 govern an accusative of the thing and a dative of the person. Such are verbs of giving, leaving, handing over (anafilhan), granting (fragiban), promising (fairhaitan), betraying (galevjan), owing (skulan), bringing (atbairan), bringing back (gavandjan), laying on (lagjan [Mark 7:32 has accusative *handau* for *haudu*], galagjan, analagjan), burdening (dragan), preparing (manvjan); forbidding (varjan), taking, striking (afmaitan), cutting off (afslahan), leading out (afslauþjan); showing (taiknjan, ataugjan), reporting (insakan), making known (gakannjan), revealing (andhuljan), explaining (andbindan), raising up, lifting (ussakan), answering (andhafjan), speaking or narrating (merjan, spillon), proclaiming or preaching the Gospel (vailamerjan), and writing (gameljan).

> **Note.—** The Goth frequently employs this construction also where Greek uses a genitive dependent on a noun: Mark 7:33 *lagida figgrans in ausona imma (αὐτοῦ)*, “he put his fingers into his ears”; Greek: “he put his fingers into his ear”; 5:30 *was mis (μου) taitok vastjom?*, “who touched my garments?”; Luke 1:76 *manvei vigans imma (αὐτοῦ)*, “prepare his ways”; 4:20 *allaim (πάντων) vesun augona fairveitjandona du imma*, “the eyes of all were fixed on him”; John 9:32 *was uslukiþ augona blindamma gabauranamma (τυφλοῦ γεγεννημένου)*, “that he opened the eyes of one born blind”; 10:21; 18:10 *paitrus afmaimait imma (αὐτοῦ) auso taihsvo*, “Peter cut off his right ear”; 19:2 *vippja galagidedun imma (αὐτοῦ) ana haubid*, “they placed a crown upon his head”; 12:3 *marja gasalboda fotuns iesua (τοῦ Ἰησοῦ)*, “Mary anointed Jesus’ feet”; 2 Tim. 5:10 *veihaim (ἁγίων) fotuns þvoh*, “she washed the saints’ feet.” But John 13:12 has *usþvoh fotuns ize*, “he washed their feet,” just as Luke 1:27 has *þizei namo iosef vas*, “whose name was Joseph,” contrary to the Greek (*ᾧ ὄνομα ἦν*, “to whom the name was”). Cf. §230 note.

## §228

Verbs compounded with prepositions governing the dative themselves govern the dative, especially those compounded with *miþ*, “with”: miþushramjan (Matt. 27:44 *þai miþushramidans imma*; Gal. 2:20), “to be crucified with”; miþanakumbjan (Mark 2:15 *motarjos miþanakumbidedun iesua*; Luke 14:10), “to recline at table with”; miþsokjan (Mark 8:11 *dugunnun miþsokjan imma*), “to dispute with”; miþgaggan (Mark 15:41 *managos miþiddjedun imma*; Luke 7:11; 14:25), “to go with”; miþfaginon (Luke 1:58), “to rejoice with”; miþrodjan (Luke 9:30), “to speak with”; miþstandan (Luke 9:32), “to stand with”; miþmatjan (Luke 15:2; 1 Cor. 5:11), “to eat with”; miþgavisan (Rom. 12:16), “to be of the same mind with”; miþþiudanon (1 Cor. 4:8), “to reign with”; miþskalkinon (Phil. 2:22), “to serve with”; miþsandjan (2 Cor. 8:18; 12:18), “to send with”; miþlitjan (Gal. 2:13), “to dissemble with”; miþgaqiujan (Eph. 2:5), “to make alive with”; miþurreisan (Col. 3:1), “to rise with.”

More rarely, verbs compounded with other prepositions do so: atstandan (Mark 14:47), atligan (Rom. 7:18), atvisan (Rom. 7:21), attiuhan (Luke 19:35). Indeed, the dative is also used after nouns compounded with prepositions: *miþfrahunþans*, “fellow-prisoner,” Col. 4:10; Philem. 23; *miþgasinþa*, “fellow-traveller,” 2 Cor. 8:19, codex A; *usstass*, “resurrection,” 1 Cor. 15:12 (*usstass dauþaim*, “resurrection of the dead”).

> **Note.—** This construction, which the Goth imitated from Greek, occurs only very rarely in the earlier part of the translation, but frequently in the later part, namely in Luke and the Epistles; there even where Greek does not lead the way (as Phil. 2:22). Originally the preposition was separated from the verb and placed before the noun: Mark 5:37 *miþ mis afargaggan* (*συνακολουθῆσαι αὐτῷ*), “to follow with me”; 8:2 *miþ mis vesun* (*προσμένουσί μοι*), “they have remained with me”; 9:14 *sokjan miþ imma* (*συζητεῖν αὐτῷ*), “to dispute with him”; 9:4 *rodjan miþ iesua* (*συλλαλεῖν τῷ Ἰησοῦ*), “to speak with Jesus.” Likewise Luke 15:6 *faginoþ miþ mis* (*συγχαρῆτέ μοι*), “rejoice with me”; 2 Cor. 8:22 *insandidedun miþ im* (*συνέπεμψαν αὐτοῖς*), “they sent [him] with them.”

## §229

Some verbs govern both the accusative and the dative. This occurs:

1) Without a change of meaning:

Usqiman, “to kill,” with dative: Matt. 10:28 *ni ogeiþ izvis þans usqimandans leika þatainei iþ saivalai ni magandans usqiman*, “do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul”; Mark 3:6; 6:19; 9:31; Luke 8:33; John 7:25; 8:22, 37; 18:32; 1 Thess. 2:15. With accusative: Mark 12:5 *sumans usqimandans*, “killing some”; John 7:1, 19, 20; 8:40. John 16:2 is uncertain.

Fraqistjan, “to destroy, lose,” with dative: Matt. 10:28 *ogeiþ þana magandan jah saivalai jah leika fraqistjan*, “fear him who can destroy both soul and body”; 39; Mark 8:35; Luke 17:29; Rom. 14:15; likewise simple qistjan, Luke 9:56. With accusative: Luke 17:27 *midjasveipains fraqistida allans*, “the flood destroyed them all.” Mark 1:24 and Luke 4:34 are uncertain.

Usvairpan, “to cast out, expel,” with dative: Mark 3:22 (*unhulþom*, “demons”); 9:47 (*augin*, “eye”); 12:10 (*staina*, “stone”); Rom. 13:12 (*vaurstvam*, “works”); Gal. 4:30 (*þiujai*, “slave-woman”). With accusative: Mark 7:22 (*unhulþons*, “demons”); 3:15; 7:26; 11:15 (*þans frabugjandans*, “those buying and selling”).

Usdreiban, “to cast out,” with dative: Mark 5:10 (*im*, “them”); Luke 9:40, 43. With accusative: Mark 9:18 (*ina*, “him”).

Ufarskadvjan, “to overshadow,” with dative: Mark 9:7 (*milhma im*, “a cloud [overshadowed] them”); Luke 1:35 (*mahts hauhistins þus*, “the power of the Most High [will overshadow] you”). With accusative: Luke 9:34 (*milhma ins*, “a cloud [overshadowed] them”).

Þiuþjan, “to bless,” with dative: Mark 10:16; Luke 1:29; 2:28, 34. With accusative: Luke 1:64; 2:34; 6:28; Rom. 12:14.

Idveitjan, “to reproach,” with dative: Matt. 11:20 (*baurgim*, “the cities”); 27:44 (*imma*, “him”); Mark 15:32. With accusative: Rom. 15:3 (*þuk*, “you”).

2) With a changed meaning:

Andhaitan, with dative, “to acknowledge someone as teacher, to acknowledge a doctrine, to profess oneself his disciple”: Matt. 10:32 *saei andhaitiþ mis … andhaita jah imma*, “whoever acknowledges me … I also will acknowledge him”; 1 Tim. 6:12 *andhaihaist þamma godin andhaita*, “you confessed the good confession”; Matt. 7:23 *andhaita im, þatei ni wanhun kunþa izvis*, “I shall declare to them: I never knew you”; Luke 2:38 *andhaihait fraujin*, “she confessed the Lord”; 10:21. With accusative, “to declare, proclaim, confess someone as something”: Skeireins V, a *tva andvairþja attins jah sunaus andhaitan*, “to confess the two persons of Father and Son”; John 9:22 *jabai was ina andhaihaiti xristu*, “if anyone confessed him as Christ”; Rom. 10:9.

Anahaitan, with dative, “to cry out against, to call out in reproach”: Skeireins VIII, b *andhofun jainaim anahaitandam im, in þizei ni attauhun ina, ni andsitandans jainaize unselein þize anahaitandane im*, “they answered those who were crying out against them, because they did not understand him, not opposing the wickedness of those who were crying out against them.” With accusative, “to invoke”: 2 Cor. 1:23 *veitvod guþ anahaita*, “I call God as witness.”

Gasakan, with dative, “to rebuke”: Matt. 8:26 *gasok vindam jah marein*, “he rebuked the winds and the sea”; Mark 4:39; Luke 4:39, 41; 8:24; 9:55; 17:3. With accusative, “to convict, reprove”: John 8:46 *was izvara gasakiþ mik bi fravaurht?*, “which of you convicts me of sin?”; 16:8; 1 Tim. 5:20; Titus 1:9, 11, 13.

Uskiusan, with dative, “to reject, cast away”: Luke 20:17 *stains þammei uskusun timrjans*, “the stone which the builders rejected”; 4:29 *uskusun imma*, “they cast him out.” With accusative, “to test, approve”: 1 Thess. 5:21 *all uskiusaiþ*, “test everything.”

Fullafahjan, with dative, “to satisfy, please, serve”: Mark 15:15 *peilatus vilda þizai managein fullafahjan*, “Pilate wished to satisfy the crowd”; Luke 4:8 *guþa ainamma fullafahjais*, “you shall serve God alone.” With accusative, “to satisfy, convince”: Skeireins VII, d *iesus siponjans fullafahida*, “Jesus satisfied the disciples.”

Varjan, with dative, “to forbid”: Mark 9:38, 39 *sewum sumana in, þeinamma namin usdreibandan unhulþons jah varidedum imma; iþ iesus qaþ: ni varjiþ imma*, “we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we forbade him; but Jesus said: do not forbid him”; Luke 9:49. With accusative, “to hold back, restrain, keep away”: Mark 10:14 *letiþ þo barna gaggan du mis jah ni varjiþ þo*, “allow the children to come to me and do not prevent them”; Luke 18:16. In Luke 9:26, *þamma nimandin af þus vastja jah paida ni varjais*, “from one taking your coat, do not withhold [your] cloak,” *paida* depends on *nimandin*.

Bileiþan, with dative, “to leave, forsake”: Matt. 27:46 *duwe mis bilaist*, “why have you forsaken me?”; Mark 10:7; 12:19 (*bilaiþ qenai*, “leaves a wife”), 20, 21, 22; 14:52 (*bilaiþ þamma leika*, “leaving the linen cloth”); 15:34; Luke 5:28; John 10:12; 16:28; 2 Tim. 4:10, 16. With accusative, “to leave behind” [French *laisser là*]: Luke 15:4 *niu bileiþiþ þo niuntehund jah niun lamba ana auþidai*, “does he not leave the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness?”; 2 Tim. 4:13 *hakul bilaiþ in trauadai*, “I left the cloak at Troas”; John 14:27 *gavairþi bileiþa izvis*, “I leave peace with you.” Hence in Rom. 9:29, *frauja sabaoþ bilaiþ unsis fraiva*, “the Lord of Sabaoth left us a seed,” the striking double dative is plain; but it could not be explained if *unsis* were regarded as an accusative. Accusative and dative are sometimes used interchangeably: John 8:29 *ni bilaiþ mis ainamma atta*, “the Father has not left me alone,” and 16:32 *mik ainana bileiþiþ*, “you will leave me alone.”

> **Note.—** For verbs governing the dative and genitive, see §236 note.

## §230

1) Besides the dative expressing a certain activity of the subject, there is another dative, called the dative of advantage and disadvantage. By it advantage or disadvantage, joy, honour, and the like are attributed to an object, generally a person.

> **Note: [Col. 1147]** Germans and French render this dative by *für*, *pour*, *à*, *sur*, *pro*, *in*, etc. The translator.

Mark 8:19 *fimf hlaibans gabrak fimf þusundjom*, “I broke five loaves for five thousand [people]”; Luke 3:8 *guþ mag us stainam urraisjan barna abrahama*, “God is able from these stones to raise children for Abraham”; 9:13 *bugjaima allai þizai manasedai matins*, “shall we buy food for all this multitude?”; 33 *gavaurkjaima hleiþros þrins, aina þus jah aina mose jah aina helijin*, “let us make three tents: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah”; 10:11 *fotuns unsarans afhrisjam izvis*, “we wipe our feet off upon you” [French *sur vous*]; 15:30 *ufsnaist imma stiur þana alidan*, “you killed the fattened calf for him”; 20:38 *allai imma liband*, “all live for him”; John 18:37 *qam in þamma fairwau ei veitvodjau sunjai*, “I came into the world in order to bear witness to the truth”; Rom. 7:4 *afdauþidai vaurþuþ vitoda*, “[you] were made dead to the law, which no longer rules over you”—*ei akran bairaima guþa*, “that we might bear fruit for God’s honour and joy”; 21 *bigita nu vitoþ viljandin mis goþ taujan*, “I find, then, the law [present] for me when I wish to do good”; 8:1 *ni vaiht vargiþos þaim in xristau*, “there is no condemnation for those in Christ”; 11:27 *so im fram mis triggva*, “this is my covenant for them from me”; 13:3 *reiks ni sind agis godamma vaurstva ak ubilamma*, “rulers are not a terror to good work but to evil”; 1 Cor. 4:9 *fairveitl vaurþum þizai manasedai*, “we have become a spectacle for the world”; 9:2 *jabai anþaraim ni im apaustaulus aiþþau izvis im*, “if I am not an apostle to others, at least I am to you”; 11:29 *saei matjiþ jah drigkiþ unvair þaba, staua sis silbin matjiþ*, “whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment for himself”; 16:1 *gabaur þata þaim veiham*, “the collection for the saints”; 2 Cor. 2:6 *ganah þamma svaleikamma andabeit*, “this punishment is sufficient for such a person” (where the dative does not depend on *ganah*, which governs the accusative); 12:7 *atgibana ist mis hnuto leika meinamma*, “a thorn was given to me in my flesh”; 14 *ni skulun barna fadreinam huzdjan, ak fadreina barnam*, “children ought not to store up for parents, but parents for children”; Gal. 6:14 *þairh xristu mis fairwus ushramiþs ist jah ik fairwau*, “through Christ the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world”; Phil. 1:27 *samana arbaidjaiþ galaubeinai aivaggeljons*, “strive together for the faith of the Gospel.”

> **Note.—** The Goth also sometimes employs the dative of advantage after nouns where Greek uses the genitive, especially the objective genitive: Luke 2:32 *liuhad du andhuleinai þiudom* (*ἐθνῶν*), “a light for revelation to the nations”; 2 Cor. 4:15 *aviliud ufarassjai du vulþau guþa* (*θεοῦ*), “that grace may abound to the glory of God”; 11:28 *saurga meina allaim aikkesjom* (*πασῶν ἐκκλησιῶν*), “my concern for all the churches”; 1 Tim. 4:12 *frisahts sijais þaim galaubjandam* (*τῶν πιστῶν*), “be an example to believers”; 1:16; Rom. 11:12 *missadeds ize gabei fairwau jah vanins ize gabei þiudom*, “their trespass, riches for the world, and their loss, riches for the nations” (but v. 15 has *fairwaus*, “of the world”). Conversely, Luke 1:45 employs the genitive *vairþiþ ustauhts þize rodidane*, “there shall be fulfilment of the things spoken,” for *τελείωσις τοῖς λελαλημένοις*; cf. §227 note.

2) Cases belonging here are those in which, with a construction faintly suggesting a middle sense, a dative of the personal pronoun is added to the verb to indicate the action’s relation to the subject: Matt. 27:4 *fravaurhta mis* (*ἥμαρτον*), “I have sinned”; Luke 15:18; Mark 8:15 *atsaiwiþ izvis* (*βλέπετε*), “look to yourselves,” i.e. beware; Luke 17:9 *ibai þagk þus fairhaitis* (*χάριν ἔχει*), “does he thank you?”; Phil. 3:17 *mundoþ izvis* (*σκοπεῖτε*) *þans sva gaggandans*, “mark for yourselves those who so walk”; Matt. 10:26 *ogan sis* (*φοβεῖσθαι*), “fear for themselves”; Mark 14:41; Luke 19:21; John 9:22; 12:15; and probably also Mark 16:6 *ni faurhteiþ izvis*, “do not be afraid,” where this must be treated as dative; cf. §178, 2 aa); Luke 9:12 *bugjaina sis* (*εὕρωσι*) *matins*, “that they may find food for themselves”; 18:11 *sis (πρὸς ἑαυτόν) þo bad*, “he prayed to himself”; 16:6 *nim þus bokos* (*σοῦ τὸ γράμμα*), “take your bill.”

> **§231. Note 1.—** Purpose is expressed in Gothic not by the dative but by the preposition *du* with dative and *in* with accusative; see §246, 3 a and b.
>
> **Note 2.—** Whether the Goth imitated the Greek construction whereby the dative is joined with passives in place of *ὑπό* with the genitive (*fram* with the dative; see §245, note 3) cannot be decided with certainty. In favour of an affirmative answer one may cite Matt. 6:1, *atsaiwiþ armaion izvara ni taujan in andvairþja manne du saiwan im* (*θεαθῆναι αὐτοῖς*), “take heed not to do your alms before people in order to be seen by them,” and v. 5, *in gaqumþim bidjand ei gaumjaindau mannam*, “praying in the assemblies so that they may be seen by people.” Yet from the latter passage, where *gaumjaindau* corresponds to Greek *φανῶσι*, “they may appear,” and is intransitive, one may conclude that *saiwan* also has the intransitive meaning “to appear, be seen,” as in 1 Cor. 15:6 *gasaiwans ist managizam þau fifhundam*, “he appeared to more than five hundred.” Thus also in v. 5 and in 1 Tim. 3:16 *ataugids ist* must, as regards meaning, necessarily be translated “he was seen, he appeared” [French *il s'est montré*], where in fact *kefin*, “in flesh,” and *aggilum*, “to angels,” are construed in the dative.
>
> John 6:13 and Luke 9:17, *þatei aflifnoda þaim matjandam*, “that which remained over for those eating,” come closest with difficulty to a passive meaning. *Qiþan ist þaim airizam*, Matt. 5:21, is plainly translated “it was said to the elders.” Because in Rom. 7:10 *bigitana varþ mis anabusns* does not mean “the commandment was found by me,” but “the commandment became known to me,” it might also be supposed in 2 Cor. 12:20 that *og ibai aufto bigitaidau izvis svaleiks sve ni vileiþ mik*, “lest perhaps I should be found by you other than you wish,” has *izvis* in the sense “for you, on your account,” unless its opposition to *bigitau izvis* made the interpretation “I shall be found by you” more probable. But Mark 11:17 *razn mein razn bido haitada allaim þiudom* is translated “my house is called a house of prayer for all nations” (cf. Tobit 3:11 and 1 Macc. 7:37).

## §232

That the dative is also used to determine place, time, and measure—including the dative after comparatives—and also instrument, manner, and cause, will be seen below, §239 ff.

# C. THE GENITIVE

## §233

The genitive indicates the close and necessary connection of two objects, and also the existence of one in, under, or from another; hence it is properly causal (see §239, 1). We have already spoken of the genitive dependent on nouns, numerals, neuter adjectives, pronouns, and also superlatives, when discussing the attributive relation of the sentence (§216). Thus, leaving aside its causal relation elsewhere (§329), we must now consider the partitive and possessive genitive insofar as it is governed by verbs and adjectives.

## §234

The possessive relation—by which belonging to something or existence from something is expressed—is indicated:

1) Simply by visan, “to be”: 1 Cor. 10:26 *fraujins ist airþa*, “the earth belongs to the Lord”; Luke 20:33 *warjis þize vairþiþ qens?*, “whose wife shall she be?”—as the future of *to be*, *ἔσται*; Mark 9:41 *xristaus sijuþ*, “you belong to Christ”; Rom. 8:9; 1 Cor. 1:12; 2 Cor. 10:7; 1 Thess. 5:5 *ni siuþ nahts ni riqizis*, “you are not of night or darkness”; Mark 10:14 *þize ist þiudangardi guþs*, “the kingdom of God belongs to such”; Luke 18:16; 5:3 *skip vas seimonis*, “the boat belonged to Simon”; 9:55 *niu vituþ wis ahmane sijuþ?*, “do you not know of what spirit you are?”; John 15:19 *jabai þis fairwaus veseiþ*, “if you were of this world,” i.e. *if you were of the world* (*ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου*); 18:37 *wazuh saei ist sunjos (ἐκ τῆς ἀληθείας) hauseiþ stibnos meinaizos*, “everyone who is of the truth hears my voice”; 10:16 *lamba ni sind þis avistris (ἐκ τῆς αὐλῆς)*, “the sheep are not of this fold”; Rom. 9:16 *gaarman ni viljandins, ni rinnandins ak armandins guþs (ist)*, “therefore [it depends] not on one willing or running, but on God who shows mercy.”

> **Note 1.—** Hence 1 Cor. 15:23 *þai xristaus*, “those who are Christ’s,” i.e. those belonging to Christ; and this is especially so with the neuter: Mark 12:17 *þo kaisaris*, “the things of Caesar”; 8:33; Luke 2:49; 2 Cor. 11:30 (see above §195, IV, 3).
>
> **Note 2.—** More boldly, Rom. 14:19, *τὰ τῆς εἰρήνης*—*τὰ τῆς οἰκοδομῆς*, “the things of peace—the things of edification,” is rendered in Gothic by *þoei gavairþjis sind laistjaima jah þoei timreinais sind in uns misso*, which does not mean “what pertains to peace and edification,” but “what serves peace and mutual edification.”
>
> **Note 3.—** In place of *þis fairwaus visan*, “to be of this world,” John 15:19 has *us þamma fairwau visan*, “to be from the world.”

2) By sves visan, “to be one’s own, belong to,” and veihs visan, “to be holy”: John 10:12 *hairdeis þizei ni sind lamba svesa, bileiþiþ lambam*, “the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, leaves the sheep”; Luke 2:23 *wazuh gamakundaize uslukands qiþa veihs fraujins (κυρίῳ) haitada*, “every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord.”

3) Also belonging here are skula visan, “to be liable,” and vairþs visan, “to be worthy”: Matt. 26:66 *skula dauþaus ist*, “he is liable to death”; Mark 3:29 *skula ist aiveinaizos fravaurhtais*, “he is liable to eternal sin”; Matt. 10:37 *saei frijoþ attan ufar mik, nist meina vairþs*, “whoever loves father more than me is not worthy of me”; Luke 10:7 *vairþs ist vaurstvja mizdons*, “the worker is worthy of his wages”; Phil. 1:27; 1 Tim. 1:15; 4:9. Hence vairþana briggan, “to make worthy”: 2 Thess. 1:11 *izvis vairþans briggai þizos laþonais guþ*, “may God make you worthy of this calling.”
