4) The genitive is also governed by verbs that signify the opposite of possession: laus visan, “to be released”; freis visan, “to be free”; framaþeis visan, “to be far removed.” Hence also frijana briggan, “to set free”; gahrainjan, “to purify”; leikinon and gahailjan, “to heal”; hailjan sik, “to be healed.” Here also belongs afholon, with the genitive of the defrauded person and accusative of the thing of which he is defrauded: 1 Cor. 9:21 *ni visands vitodis laus guþs*, “not being free from God’s law”; Rom. 7:3 *frija ist þis vitodis*, “she is free from the law”; Eph. 4:18 *þiudos gaggand framaþjai libainais (visandans)*, “the nations being alienated from the life”; 2:12; Rom. 8:2 *vitoþ ahmins frijana brahta mik vitodis fravaurhtais*, “the law of the Spirit has set me free from the law of sin”; 2 Tim. 2:21 *jabai was gahrainjai sik þize, vairþiþ kas gaveihaiþ*, “if anyone cleanses himself from these things, he shall be a vessel for honour”; Luke 5:15 *garunnun hiuhmans managai leikinon fram imma sauhte*, “many crowds came to be healed by him of sickness”; 8:2; 6:18 *qemun hailjan sik sauhte*, “they came to be healed of disease”; Luke 19:8 *jabai wis wa afholoda, fidurfalþ fragilda*, “if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.”

> **Note 4.—** In the fragmentary passage 1 Cor. 7:5, the Gothic verb corresponding to Greek *ἀποστερεῖν*, “to defraud,” is constructed in the same manner, with *izvara misso*, “one another,” as object, although the verb itself there is anamahtjan. This verb, used for *ἀποστερεῖν* in Mark 10:19, is used without distinction, or indeed governs the accusative in Luke 3:14. In 1 Tim. 6:5, for the sake of clarification, the Goth paraphrases *ἀποστερημένοι ἀληθείας*, “having been deprived of truth,” as *af þammei gatarnida ist sunja*, “from whom truth has been taken away.”
>
> **Note 5.—** The verbs cited above are also construed with *af* and the dative: Gal. 5:4 *lausai sijuþ af xristau*, “you have been severed from Christ”; 2 Cor. 7:1 *hrainjam unsis af allamma bisauleino*, “let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement.” In Luke 7:21, genitive and *af* are used indiscriminately: *gahailida managans af sauhtim, af slahim jah ahmane ubilaize*, “he healed many of diseases, afflictions, and evil spirits.” Galausjan is always construed with *us* (see glossary, s.v.), but lausjan with *af* (Matt. 6:13); *galausiþs im*, “I am freed,” also occurs with dative, §224, 1.

## §235

The partitive relation occurs when the action of the subject does not extend to the whole object but only to some part of it. Germans express this either by *aus*, by omission of the article, or by *von*; Goths, however, by the genitive.

> **Note: [Col. 1151]** We French also use the genitive: *Cette génération demande des signes; afin qu'on lui donnât des fruits de sa vigne*, “This generation asks for signs; so that fruits from his vineyard might be given to him,” etc. The translator.

Mark 8:12 *jabai gibaidau kunja þamma taikne*, “[whether] a sign shall be given to this generation”; Luke 20:10 *insandida du aurtjam skalk, ei akranis (ἀπὸ τοῦ καρποῦ) þis veinagardis gebeina imma*, “he sent a servant to the tenants, that they might give him of the fruit of the vineyard”; Mark 12:2—*ei at vaurstvjam nemi akranis þis veinagardis*, “that he might receive from the tenants some fruit of the vineyard”; John 6:11 *gadailida þize fiske (ἐκ τῶν ὀψαρίων) sva filu sve vildedun*, “he distributed some of the fish as much as they wished”; 26 *matideduþ þize hlaibe (ἐκ τῶν ἄρτων)*, “you ate of the loaves”; 50, 51; 1 Cor. 11:28 *sva þis hlaibis (ἐκ τοῦ ἄρτου) matjai jah þis stiklis (ἐκ τοῦ ποτηρίου) drigkai*, “so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup.”

Especially with haban, “to have,” and visan, “to be,” accompanied by negation: Matt. 9:36 *lamba ni habandona hairdeis (ποιμένα)*, “sheep not having a shepherd”; Mark 4:5 *ni habaida diupaizos airþos (γῆν)*, “it did not have depth of earth”; John 9:41 *iþ blindai veiseiþ, ni habaidedeiþ fravaurhtais (ἁμαρτίαν)*, “if you were blind, you would not have sin”; Luke 1:7 *ni vas im barne (τέκνον)*, “they had no child”; 2:7 *ni vas im rumis (τόπος) in stada*, “there was no place for them in the lodging.” Hence also Mark 12:19 *barne ni bilaiþ*, “he leaves no child,” and Luke 20:31 *ni biliþun barne*, “they left no children.”

Here belongs visan, “to be one among several”: Matt. 26:73 *jah þu þize is*, “you too are one of them”; Mark 14:69; John 10:26; 18:17; 1 Tim. 1:19; 2 Tim. 1:15. Thus *þai þiudo*, “those belonging to the Gentiles,” “the Gentiles’ people,” in Matt. 5:46; 6:7, is to be explained.

> **Note.—** Nevertheless the accusative also frequently occurs here: 1 Cor. 9:7 *was satjiþ veinatriva jah akran þize ni matjai*, “who plants a vineyard and does not eat its fruit?”, because [the translator] read *τὸν καρπόν*, “the fruit,” in place of *ἐκ τοῦ καρποῦ*, “of the fruit.” Although Mark 2:23 and Luke 6:1 have *τίλλειν τοὺς στάχυας*, “to pluck the ears,” nevertheless not *ahse* but *ahsa* ought to have been written. Add Mark 4:5 *ni habaida airþa managa*, “it did not have much earth”; Luke 8:6 *ni habaida qrammiþa*, “it did not have moisture”; Mark 4:6 *ni habaida vaurtins*, “it had no root”; Luke 8:13; John 15:22 *ni qemjau jah rodidedjau du im, fravaurht ni habaidedeina*, “if I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have had sin.”
>
> Where genitive singular and accusative plural are identical in form, it remains uncertain which case is to be taken. Thus John 15:22 *inilons ni haband*, “they have no excuse”: elsewhere, in comparison with Greek *πρόφασιν*, *inilons* should indeed be considered a genitive; but because of the preceding *fravaurht ni haband*, it must be viewed as an accusative. Cf. v. 33 *in þamma fairwau aglons habaid*, “in the world you have tribulation,” where the plural also corresponds to Greek singular *θλίψιν*. In John 16:14, 15, *us* is used: *us meinamma (ἐκ τοῦ ἐμοῦ) nimiþ*, “he will take from what is mine.”

## §236

Here must be included verbs of sharing, touching, attaining, using, and so forth: 1 Cor. 10:21 *ni maguþ biudis fraujins fairaihan (μετέχειν) jah biudis skohsle*, “you cannot partake of the Lord’s table and the table of demons”; 2 Tim. 2:6 *arbaidjands airþos vaurstja skal frumist akrane andniman (μεταλαμβάνειν)*, “the labouring husbandman must first receive of the fruits.”

Luke 20:20 *ei gafaifaheina is vaurde (ἐπιλάβωνται αὐτοῦ λόγων)*, “that they might lay hold of his words”; 26; Mark 14:51 *gripun is (κρατοῦσιν αὐτόν)*, “they seized him”; 1 Cor. 7:5 *ei ni fraisai izvara (πειράζῃ ὑμᾶς) satana*, “that Satan may not tempt you.”

1 Cor. 10:17 *allai ainis hlaibis jah ainis stiklis brukjam*, “we all partake of one bread and one cup”; 2 Cor. 3:12 *habandans svaleika ven managaizos balþeins brukjaima*, “having such hope, we use great boldness”; 1 Cor. 1:17; 1 Tim. 1:8; Skeireins V, a. Hence in the passive, Col. 2:22 *þairh þatei is brukjaidau*, “through their use”; cf. §224, note 2. Luke 20:35 *vairþai sind jainis aivis niutan jah usstassais us dauþaim*, “are judged worthy to attain that age and the resurrection from the dead”; Philem. 20 *broþar, ik þeina niutau in fraujin*, “brother, let me have benefit from you in the Lord”; Mark 9:1 *sind sumai þai ize ni kausjand dauþaus (θανάτου)*, “there are some who shall not taste death”; Luke 14:24 *kauseiþ þis nahtamatis (δείπνου)*, “[none] shall taste of my supper.”

> **Note.—** Several of these verbs also govern dative or accusative: John 7:32 *ei gafaifaheina ina*, “that they might seize him”; Mark 14:44 *greipiþ þana*, “seize him”; cf. 46; Skeireins III, b *ni þanaseiþs iudaiviskom ufarranneinim jah sinteino daupeinim brukjan usdaudjaina*, “not merely through Jewish observances and continual washings to use [them] for cleansing.” In 1 Tim. 5:23 *veinis leitil brukjais*, “use a little wine,” *veinis* appears to be a partitive genitive dependent on *leitil*, while brukjan governs the accusative; but in 1 Cor. 10:30 *anstai* is modal, although it must be added that the translator misunderstood *χάρις*, “grace,” since *þagka*, “thanks,” ought to have been used. Luke 9:27 and John 8:52 have *kausjan dauþau*, “to taste death,” whereas kausjan in the sense “to test” governs the accusative; see Luke 14:19; 2 Cor. 13:3. Fraisan, “to tempt, test,” likewise is ordinarily construed with the accusative: Mark 8:11; 10:2; 12:15; Luke 20:23; John 6:6; 2 Cor. 13:5.

## §237

Moreover, fulls, “full”; fulls vairþan and fullnan, “to become full”; fulljan, “to fill”; gasoþjan, “to satisfy, fill”; sad itan, “to eat one’s fill”; and, in the contrary sense, þarbs, “in need”; þaurban and vans visan, “to lack”; þaurfts ist and van ist, “there is need” (with the dative of the person who needs): Mark 8:19 *wan managos tainjons fullos gabruko usnemuþ?*, “how many baskets full of fragments did you take up?”; Luke 4:1 *ahmins veihins fulls*, “full of the Holy Spirit”; 16:20 *banjo fulls*, “full of sores”; 5:12; John 12:3 *gards fulls varþ daunais*, “the house was filled with the fragrance”; Luke 4:28 *fullai vaurþun allai modis*, “all were filled with wrath”; 5:26; 6:11; Luke 2:40 *barn svinþnoda ahmins fullnands jah handugeins*, “the child grew strong, being filled with spirit and wisdom”; 1:41, 67; 2 Tim. 1:4 *fahedais usfullnam*, “filled with joy”; Rom. 15:13 *guþ fulljai izvis allaizos fahedais*, “may God fill you with all joy”; John 6:13 *gafullidedun tvalib tainjons gabruko*, “they filled twelve baskets with fragments”; 2 Cor. 7:4 *usfulliþs im gaþlaihtais, ufarfulliþs im fahedais*, “I am filled with consolation, overflowing with joy”; Matt. 27:48; Mark 15:36; Luke 1:15; Col. 1:9; 2 Thess. 1:11; Luke 1:53 *gredagans gasoþida þiuþe*, “he filled the hungry with good things”; 15:16 *gairnida sad itan haurne*, “he desired to fill himself with the husks”; 16:21.

Luke 9:11 *þans þarbans leikinassaus gahailida*, “he healed those needing healing”; Matt. 6:8 *vait atta izvar þizei þaurbuþ*, “your Father knows what you need”; 1 Cor. 12:21 *þeina ni þarf*, “I have no need of you”; 22; 1 Tim. 4:3 *gaþarban mate*, “to abstain from foods”; Matt. 9:12; Mark 2:17; Luke 15:7; John 13:29; 2 Cor. 3:1; 1 Thess. 4:12; 2 Cor. 12:13 *wa ist, þize vanai veseiþ*, “what is it in which you were inferior?”; Mark 10:21 *ainis þpus van ist*, “one thing you lack”; Luke 18:22; Luke 19:34 *fraujin þaurfts þis ist*, “the Lord has need of it.”

> **Note 1.—** In 1 Cor. 9:25 we read *allis sik gaþarbiþ*, which might be rendered “he restrains himself in everything” [French *s'abstient de tout*]; yet here *allis* perhaps means “altogether,” just as Greek *πάντα*, “altogether,” and *allis* itself in Matt. 5:34 and 1 Cor. 15:20.
>
> **Note 2.—** An instrumental is also joined to gasoþjan: Mark 8:4 *waþro þans mag was gasoþjan hlaibam ana auþidai?*, “whence can anyone satisfy these people with bread in the wilderness?”

## §238

The genitive is also assigned to very many verbs that denote a mental operation in the same relation, namely:

1) Luston, “to desire”; gairnjan, “to long for”: Matt. 5:28 *saiwan qinon du luston izos*, “to look at a woman in order to desire her”; Mark 11:3 *frauja þis gairneiþ*, “the Lord needs it”; Luke 19:31; 2 Cor. 9:14; Phil. 2:26; 1 Tim. 3:1; 6:10.

2) Bidjan, “to ask”; fraihnan, “to inquire”; beidan, “to await”: Matt. 27:58 *iosef baþ þis leikis iesuis*, “Joseph asked for the body of Jesus”; Mark 6:24; 10:38; Luke 14:32; John 14:14; 16:23; 1 Cor. 1:22; 2 Cor. 13:9; Mark 4:10 *frehun ina þizos gajukons*, “they asked him about the parable”; 11:29 *fraihna izvis ainis vaurdis*, “I will ask you one question”; Luke 20:40; John 16:23; 18:21; Matt. 11:3 *anþaris beidaima*, “shall we await another?”—hence Luther in his version: *sollen wir eines Andern warten* (“shall we wait for another?”); Mark 15:43 *iosef vas beidands þiudangardjos guþs*, “Joseph was waiting for the kingdom of God”; Luke 1:21; 2:25; Gal. 5:5; Skeireins V, a.

> **Note 1.—** With bidjan, the neuter pronoun also occurs in the accusative; see §220, 4 a.

3) Karist, and simply kara, “it concerns, troubles” [with accusative of the person].

> **Note: [Col. 1153]** Karist is an impersonal verb (§219, 3) with no Latin equivalent; in German it is rendered *es kümmert*, “it troubles,” and in French *il inquiète*, “it concerns/troubles.” The translator.

Unkarja visan, “to be negligent”; gaveison, “to be anxious, troubled”; fairveitjan, “to be concerned with, attend to”; atsaiwan, “to direct attention to, beware”; bisaiwan, “to attend to”; hausjan, “to hear, give ear to”: John 10:13 *ni karist asni þize lambe*, “the sheep do not concern him”; 12:6; Mark 12:14 *vitum þatei ni kara þuk manshun*, “we know that you are not concerned about anyone”; 1 Tim. 4:14 *ni unkarja sijais þizos anstais*, “do not neglect the gift”; Matt. 25:43 *ni gaveisodeduþ meina*, “you did not care for me”; Luke 1:78; 7:16; 2 Cor. 4:18 *ni fairveitjan þize gasaiwanane ak þize ungasaiwanane*, “not attending to the things seen, but to the things unseen”; 1 Tim. 1:4 *faurbiudais ei ni atsaiwaina spille jah gabaurþivaurde andilausaize*, “command [them] not to attend to myths and endless genealogies”; 4:1; Titus 1:14; Mark 8:15 *saiwiþ ei atsaiwiþ izvis þis beistis fareisaie*, “see that you beware of the leaven of the Pharisees”; Rom. 12:17 *bisaiwiþ godis in andvairþja manne allaize*, “provide what is good in the sight of all people”; Luke 2:47 *hausjandans is ana frodein is usgeisnodedun*, “all who heard him were astonished at his understanding”; John 7:40 *managai hausjandans þize vaurde*, “many, hearing the saying”; 10:16 *lamba hausjand stibnos meinaizos*, “sheep hearing my voice”; 18:37; 19:13.

> **Note 2.—** Gakaran, “to care for, administer,” governs the accusative: 1 Tim. 3:5 *jabai was seinamma garda fauragaggan ni mag, waiva aikklesjon guþs gakarai?*, “if anyone cannot manage his own household, how will he care for God’s church?” Atsaiwan in the sense “to attend to, look after, care for” also governs the accusative: Gal. 6:1 *atsaiwands þuk silban ibai jah þu fraisaizau*, “watching yourself lest you too be tempted”; or it is construed with *du*: 1 Tim. 4:16 *atsaiw du þus silbin jah du laiseinai*, “pay attention to yourself and to the teaching.” But meaning “beware,” it is used with *faura* and the dative: Matt. 7:15 *atsaiwiþ faura liugnapraufetum*, “beware of false prophets”; Luke 20:46. Bisaiwan, “to notice, perceive,” governs the accusative: Luke 20:23 *bisaiwands ize unselein iesus qaþ du im*, “perceiving their wickedness, Jesus said to them.” In the question Matt. 27:4 *wa kara unsis*, “what [is it] to us?”, *wa* is not to be taken as a genitive, but a genitive must be supplied. Hausjan ordinarily takes the accusative (Matt. 7:24 etc., §219, 2), but in the sense “to give ear to” it takes the dative (§224, 2).

4) **Hilpan** and **gahilpan**, “to help,” **freidjan**, “to spare”: Mark 9:22 *hilp unsara*, “help us”; 24 *hilp meinaizos ungalaubeinais*, “help my unbelief”; [Col. 1154] Luke 5:7; 2 Corinthians 6:2; 2 Corinthians 1:23 *freidjands ïzvara þanaseiþs ni qam ïn kaurinþon*, “sparing you, I did not come to Corinth.”

“Note 3.—Yet with *freidjan* the accusative is commonly used: Romans 11:21 *guþ þans us gabaurþai astans ni freidida, ïbai aufto ni þuk freidjai*, ‘God did not spare the natural branches; perhaps he will not spare you either’; 1 Corinthians 7:28 *ïzvis freidja*, ‘I spare you.’”

5) **Gamaudjan**, “to remind, instruct,” takes an accusative of the person; **gamunan**, “to remember”; **andþaggkjan sik**, “to reflect, consider”: John 14:26 *parakletus gamaudeiþ ïzvis allis, þatei qaþ du ïzvis*, “the Paraclete will remind you of everything which I told you”; 2 Timothy 2:14 *gamaudei þizei*, “remind them of these things”;“ Matthew 26:75 *gamunda paitrus vaurdis iesuis qiþanis du sis*, “Peter remembered the word of Jesus, spoken to him”; Luke 1:54, 72; 17:32; John 15:20; 16:4; 2 Timothy 1:4; *Skeireins* VII, a: *andþaggkjands sik ïs valdufneis---vairþidos laisareis andþaggkjands*, “considering his authority—he became a teacher, reflecting.”

“Note 4.—*Gamunan* also frequently governs the accusative: Mark 14:72 *gamunda paitrus þata vaurd, sve qaþ ïmma ïesus*, ‘Peter remembered the word, as Jesus said to him’; 1 Corinthians 11:2; 15:1–2; 2 Corinthians 7:15; 2 Timothy 2:8. But *ufarmunnon*, ‘to forget,’ governs the dative; see § 224, 2.”

“Note 5.—Moreover, and probably also, verbs of experiencing, knowing, and the like are construed with the genitive, as may be inferred from Romans 11:25, where after *ni viljau ïzvis þizos runos* [‘I do not wish you to be ignorant of this mystery’] *unveisans* is probably to be understood; see on that passage.”

## D. THE CAUSAL [CASE]

§ 239. The causal object supplies the ground and cause of an action or disposition. The Gothic language has not developed a special case for this purpose; rather, according as a more or less intimate cause is to be expressed, it uses the genitive, the dative, or prepositions.

1) The genitive as causal is used with **skaman sik**, “to be ashamed”: Mark 8:38 *saei skamaiþ sik meina jah vaurde meinaize, jah sunus mans skamaiþ sik ïs*, “whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man also will be ashamed of him”; Luke 9:26; 2 Timothy 1:8, 16; with **sildaleikjan sik**, “to marvel at”; Luke 20:26 *sildaleikjandans andavaurde ïs gaþahaidedun*, “marvelling at his answer, they fell silent”; with **vopjan**, “to cry out”: Luke 7:32 *galeikai sind barnam þaim ïn garunsai sitandam jah vopjandam sei na misso*, “they are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another” [Note: [Col. 1154] See the note at the foot of the volume.].

The causal construction also explains the reading of Codex B, disputed by us, at 2 Corinthians 12:21: *ni qaino managans þize faura fravaurkjandane jah ni ïdreigondane ana unhrainiþai, horinassau jah aglaiteino*, “lest many of those who previously sinned and have not repented of the impurity, sexual immorality, and licentiousness …” Here the construction changes, a simple case being used after the preposition *ana*, which often elsewhere indicates a causal relation; see below, 3(b). Likewise Luke 7:21. In Galatians 6:12, *vrakja galgins xristaus vinnan*, “to suffer persecution because of Christ’s cross,” the genitive depends on *vrakja*: it is an objective genitive—“the persecution of Christ’s cross,” that is, persecution on account of the cross; Greek: “on account of the cross” (*σταυρῷ*).

2) The dative as causal occurs with **faginon**, “to rejoice”: 1 Corinthians 13:6 *ni faginoþ ïnvindiþai*, “it does not rejoice in unrighteousness”; Luke 10:20. Otherwise, though still causal, it occurs in Romans 12:11 *venai faginon*, “rejoicing in hope”; compare 2 Corinthians 1:15 *þizai trauainai vilda faurþis qiman at ïzvis*, “because of this confidence I wished to come to you first”; Romans [Col. 1155] 7:22 *gavizneigs ïm vitoda guþs*, “I delight in God’s law”; 11:20 *ungalaubeinai usbruknodedun*, “they were broken off because of unbelief”; 30 *gaarmidai vaurþuþ þizai ïze ungalaubeinai*, “you received mercy because of their unbelief”; 1 Timothy 6:8 *þaim ganohidai sijaima*, “let us be content with these things”; compare Luke 3:14 *valdaiþ annom ïzvaraim*, “be content with your pay”; Mark 1:34 *gahailida managans ubil habandans missaleikaim sauhtim*, “he healed many who were afflicted with various diseases”; Luke 4:40; 15:17 *huhrau fraqistna*, “perishing from hunger”; 2 Corinthians 9:2 *vait gairnein ïzvara, þizaiei fram ïzvis wopa*, “I know your zeal, on account of which I boast of you”; 11:30.

3) Among prepositions having causal force, the following should be noted:

a) Above all, **ïn** with the genitive: “because of, on account of, toward, for the sake of”: Matthew 27:18 *ïn neiþis atgebun ïna*, “they delivered him up out of envy”; Mark 6:17 *herodes gaband ïohannen ïn hairodiadins*, “Herod had bound John on account of Herodias”; and so forth. It occurs particularly after *faginon* (1 Corinthians 16:17), *sildaleikjan* (Mark 11:18), *gauriþs vairþan* (Mark 6:26), *gaurs* (Mark 3:5), *hazjan* (Luke 2:20), *wopan* (2 Thessalonians 1:4), etc.; see the glossary under **In C**. Hence the expressions *ïn þis*, “because of this,” and *ïn þizei*, “consequently.” More rarely *ïn* is construed with the dative, as in 2 Corinthians 12:5 *faur mik silban ni vaiht wopa niba ïn unmahtim meinaim*, “on my own behalf I will not boast, except in my weaknesses.”

b) **Ana** with the dative: “upon, in”; also after *faginon* (2 Corinthians 7:13), *sildaleikjan* (Mark 12:17), and further after *usfilma vairþan* (Mark 1:22), *usgeisnan* (Luke 2:47), *ïdreigon* (2 Corinthians 12:21), etc.; see the glossary, **Ana 4(b)**. Hence the expression *ana þammei*, “therefore.”

c) **Us**, “out of, through”: 2 Corinthians 13:4 *ushramiþs vas us siukein akei libaiþ us mahtai guþs*, “he was crucified through weakness, but he lives through the power of God”; Galatians 2:16 *ni vairþiþ garaihts us vaurstvam vitodis ainhun leike*, “no flesh is justified by works of the law”; etc.; see the glossary, **Us 3**.

d) **Bi** with the accusative: “because of, in, concerning,” especially after *sildaleikjan* (Luke 2:8), *gretan* (Luke 19:14), *saurgan* (Matthew 6:28), *þulan* (2 Timothy 2:10), *unverjan* (Mark 10:41), etc.; see the glossary, **Bi A 4(f)**. More rarely it takes the dative: 1 Corinthians 10:27 *ni vaiht andsitan bi gahugdai*, “asking no questions on account of conscience”; Luke 1:29 *gaþlahsnoda bi ïnnagahtai ïs*, “she was troubled concerning his saying”; 2 Corinthians 12:7.

e) **Faura** with the dative: “before, in the presence of”: Luke 19:3 *ni mahta ïesu gasaiwan faura managein*, “he could not see Jesus because of the crowd”; John 12:42 *faura fareisaium ni andhaihaitun*, “because of the Pharisees they did not confess.”

f) **Fram**, “from, beyond, because of,” after *faginon* (2 Corinthians 2:3), *gaþrafstjan* (1 Thessalonians 3:7), *aviliudon* (1 Timothy 2:1–2), *wopan* (2 Corinthians 9:2), etc.; see the glossary, **Fram 3(b) bb**.

“Note.—Where *þairh* is used causally, as in Luke 1:78; Ephesians 5:6; Colossians 3:6, the translator seems to have erred over the Greek *διά*, confusing *διά* construed with the accusative in these passages with *διά* construed with the genitive.”

## E. THE INSTRUMENTAL [CASE]

§ 240. Apart from certain traces in pronouns (*þe*, § 108, note 2; *we*, § 110, note 1; and [Bopp, *Comparative Grammar*, p. 189] *sve*), the instrumental form—which indicates the material with which, or the means through which, a thing is produced or accomplished—has entirely disappeared from Gothic, and is everywhere replaced by the dative.

1) Philemon 19 *ïk gamelida meinai handau*, “I have written with my own hand”; John 18:22 *slah lo fin*, “he struck [him] with the palm,” a blow (*ῥάπισμα*); 12:40 *gaumjan augam jah fraþjan hairtin*, “to see with the eyes and understand with the heart”; Matthew 27:59 *ïosef bivand leik ïesuis sabana hrainjamma*, “Joseph wrapped Jesus’ body in clean linen”; Luke 7:38 *qino dugann natjan fotuns ïesuis tagram jah skufta haubidis seinis bisvarb*, “a woman began to wet Jesus’ feet with tears and wiped them with the hair of her head”; John 11:2 *marja salboda fraujan balsana*, “Mary anointed the Lord with ointment”; Luke 8:16 *ni manna dishuljiþ lukarn kasa*, “no one covers a lamp with a vessel”; Mark 5:5 *bliggvan sik stainam*, “to cut oneself with stones”; 2 Corinthians 11:25 *vandum usbluggvans vas*, “I was beaten with rods”; 9:10 *sa andstaldands fraiva þana saiandan jah hlaiba du mata andstaldiþ*, “he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply [them]”; 1 Corinthians 9:7 *was drauhtinoþ svesaim annom wan?*, “who serves as a soldier at his own expense?”; Matthew 8:16 *usvarp ahmans vaurda*, “he cast out spirits with a word”; Mark 7:13 *blauþeiþ vaurd guþs þizai anabusnai ïzvarai*, “you nullify God’s word by your tradition”; 2 Corinthians 4:2 *bairhtein sunjos ustaiknjam uns silbans*, “by the manifestation of the truth we commend ourselves”; 8:9 *ïesus gaunledida sik, ei jus þamma ïs unledja gabeigai vairþaiþ*, “Jesus became poor, so that through his poverty you might become rich”; Matthew 7:22; Mark 10:42; 12:4; Luke 6:1; Romans 11:11; 10:13; 14:15; 2 Corinthians 1:11; Colossians 2:13; 2 Timothy 2:14; Titus 1:16; *Skeireins* I, d; III, c; etc.

2) Especially with verbs of clothing, which in Greek convey the sense “to put on, to surround” (*περιβάλλεσθαι, ἀμφιβάλλεσθαι*) and are construed with the accusative: Mark 15:20 *gavasidedun ïna vastjom svesaim*, “they clothed him in his own garments”; Matthew 6:31 *ni maurnaiþ we vasjaima*, “do not be anxious, ‘What shall we wear?’”; 25; Romans 13:12 *gavasjam sarvam liuhadis*, “let us put on the weapons of light”; Mark 1:6 *vas ïohannes gavasiþs taglam ulbandaus*, “John was clothed in camel’s hair”; Ephesians 4:24 *gahamoþ þamma niujin mann*, “put on the new man”; 6:11 *gahamoþ ïzvis sarvam guþs*, “put on God’s whole armor”; 1 Thessalonians 5:8 *gahamodai sijaima brunjon galaubeinais jah hilma*, “let us be clothed with the breastplate of faith and [with] a helmet”; Matthew 11:8; Romans 13:14; Galatians 3:27; Colossians 3:10, 12. Hence also Ephesians 6:14 *standaiþ ufgaurdanai hupins sunjai jah gapaidodai brunjon garaihteins*, “stand, girded about the loins with truth and clothed with the breastplate of righteousness.” Similarly **andvasjan**, “to strip off”: Mark 15:20 *andvasidedun ïna þizai paurpaurai*, “they stripped him of the purple,” though it ought to be regarded as construed in the same way as **afslaupjan**—that is, with an accusative of the thing and a dative of the person: Colossians 3:9 *ni liugaiþ ïzvis misso afslaupjandans ïzvis þana fairnjan mannan*, “do not lie to one another, having stripped off from yourselves the old man.”

3) Moreover, Gothic frequently uses the instrumental where Greek uses another construction: Mark 11:15 *sitlans þize frabugjandane ahakim usvaltida*, “he overturned the seats of those selling doves,” Greek *περιστεράς*; 12:1 *bisatida ïna faþom*, “he enclosed it with a hedge,” Greek *περιέθηκε φραγμόν*; Luke 19:43 *bigraband fijands grabaiþuk*, “your enemies will surround you with a palisade,” Greek *περιβαλοῦσι χάρακά σοι*; Matthew 6:6 *galukands* (namely, *heþjon*) *haurdai þeinai*, “having shut your door,” Greek *κλείσας τὴν θύραν σου*; 27:60 *faurvalvjands steina mikilamma daurons galaiþ*, “having rolled a great stone against the door, he departed,” Greek *προσκυλίσας λίθον μέγαν τῇ θύρᾳ*; John 11:38 *hulundi staina ufarlagida vas*, “a stone lay upon the cave,” Greek *λίθος ἐπέκειτο ἐπὶ σπηλαίῳ*.

To this class belong many instances in which a dative instrumental is joined to **vairpan**, “to cast,” and its compounds: Matthew 27:5 *atvairpands þaim silubram ïn alh aflaiþ*, “having cast the silver into the temple, he departed,” Greek *τὰ ἀργύρια*; Mark 10:50 *afvairpands vastjai seinai qam at ïesua*, “having cast off his garment, he came to Jesus,” Greek *τὸ ἱμάτιον*; 4:26 *manna vairpiþ fraiva ana airþa*, “a man casts seed upon the earth,” Greek *σπόρον*; 15:24 *vaurpun hlauta ana vastjos*, “they cast lots for the garments,” Greek *κλῆρον*. Hence also Mark 11:8 *managaî vastjom stravidedun ana viga*, “many spread garments on the road”; Luke 19:36.

Luke 17:29 also belongs here: *rignida svibla jah funin*, “it rained sulphur and fire,” just as in Latin, *sanguine pluit*, “it rains blood.”

“Note.—The instrumental is used redundantly: Mark 1:4 *knivam knussjands*, ‘cutting with knives’; 1:6 *vaurda* [Col. 1157] *qiþan*, ‘to speak a word’—Greek *λόγῳ εἰπεῖν*, Matthew 8:8 *λόγον εἰπεῖν*; 4:3 *saian fraiva*, ‘to sow seed’; 6:9 *gaskohs suljom*, ‘sandals on the feet’; 7:10 *dauþau afdauþjaidau*, ‘let him be put to death by death.’”

4) The instrumental is also expressed by the following prepositions:

a) Above all by **þairh** with the accusative (*διά* with the genitive), “through, by”: Mark 6:2 *mahteis þairh handuns ïs vairþand*, “powers are wrought through his hands”; *Skeireins* VI, c *attins bi ïna varþ veitvodeins suman þairh praufete vaurda, sumanuh þan þairh stibna us himina, sumanuh þan þairh taiknins*, “the Father bore witness concerning him, sometimes through the words of a prophet, sometimes through a voice from heaven, and sometimes through signs”; 2 Timothy 1:6 *ansts guþs ïst ïn þus þairh analagein handive meinaizo*, “the grace of God is in you through the laying on of my hands.” For other examples see the glossary, **þairh 2(a)**. This preposition especially denotes a personal instrument, that is, the person through whom something is done: 2 Corinthians 9:11 *ainfalþei vaurkeiþ þairh uns aivxaristian guþa*, “generosity works through us thanksgiving to God”; Colossians 1:16 *alla þairh ïna gaskapana sind*, “all things were created through him”; see the same place, b.

b) By **ïn** with the dative: Mark 11:28 *ïn wamma valdufnje þata taujis?*, “by what authority do you do this?”; Romans 10:9 *andhaitan in munþa*, “to confess with the mouth”; Luke 7:25 *ïn hnasqjaim vastjom gavasiþs*, “clothed in soft garments.” Hence, dative and preposition being used interchangeably: Luke 3:16 *ïk ïzvis vatin daupja, ïþ gaggiþ svinþoza mis, sah ïzvis daupeiþ ïn ahmin veihamma jah funin*, “I baptize you with water, but one stronger than I is coming; he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.” It is used also where a person is the instrument: 1 Corinthians 15:22 *ïn adama allai gadauþnand, ïn xristau allai gaqiunand*, “in Adam all die; in Christ all are made alive”; see the glossary, **In B 3(c)**.

c) By **us** with the dative after verbs of buying and selling: Luke 16:9 *taujan sis frijonds us faihuþraihna ïnvindiþos*, “make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth”; Matthew 27:7 *usbugjam akr us þaim skattam*, “let us buy a field with that money”; Luke 8:3.

d) Rarely by **miþ**: Matthew 26:72 *miþ aiþa svor*, “he swore with an oath.”

## F. THE MODAL [CASE]

§ 241. The modal indicates the manner or mode in which something occurs or is effected. Since it often approaches the instrumental too closely, it differs from it only in normally having an attributive element. It is therefore expressed by the dative. Yet, though the special form has disappeared entirely from the language, it may perhaps be thought to have been preserved in adverbial forms in *-aba* and *-o*, since the proper function of an adverb is to determine the manner and mode of an action or disposition. Thus the Goth sometimes uses the modal in place of an adverb, and an adverb in place of the modal.

1) 2 Timothy 3:8 *þamma haidau ei jannis jah mambres andstoþun moseza, sva jah þaî andstandand sunjai*, “in the manner in which Jannes and Mambres opposed Moses, so these also oppose the truth”; 2 Corinthians 12:16 *visands listeigs hindarveisein ïzvis nam*, “being crafty, I caught you by guile”; 1:8 *ufarassau kauridai vesum*, “we were burdened beyond measure”; 1 Timothy 1:8, Codex A, *god ïst vitoþ, jabai was ïs vitoda brukeiþ*, “the law is good if one uses the law lawfully”; Luke 1:74 *unagein skalkinon*, “that we might serve without fear.”

Mark 4:33 *svaleikaim managaim gajukom rodida du ïm þata vaurd*, “with many such parables he spoke the word to them”; 2 Corinthians 3:18 *veis andhulidamma andvairþja vulþu fraujins þairhsaiwam*, “we all, with unveiled face, behold the glory of the Lord”; 1 Corinthians 11:5; Romans 15:6 *gaviljai ainamma munþa hauhjaiþ guþ*, “that with one mind and one mouth you may glorify God”; Matthew 27:46 *uf hropida ïesus stibnai mikilai*, “Jesus cried out with a loud voice”; 50; Mark 5:7; Luke 1:42; Luke 2:9 *ohtedun agisa mikilamma*, “they feared with great fear,” Greek *φόβον μέγαν*—whereas Mark 4:41 has, under Greek influence, *agis mikil*; [Col. 1158] *Skeireins* I, c: *þatuh vesi viþra þata gadob, ei frauja qimands mahtai gudiskai jah valdufnja þana galausidedi, gadob vas mais þans svesamma viljin ufhausjandans diabulau þanzuh aftra svesamma viljin gaqissans vairþan nasjandis laiseimai*, “yet this was contrary to what was fitting: that the Lord, coming with divine power and authority, should redeem him. It was more fitting that, obeying the devil of his own will, he should again, of his own will, be restored to the Saviour’s saving teaching”;“ John 18:32 *wileikamma dauþau skulda gasviltan*, “he was destined to die by what sort of death”; 2 Corinthians 12:18 *niu þamma samin ahmin ïddjedum, niu þaim samam laistim?*, “did we not walk in the same spirit, [and] in the same footsteps?”; Luke 6:38 *þizai samon mitadjon, þizaiei mitid, mitada ïzvis*, “with the same measure with which you measure, it will be measured to you.”

2) The prepositions used to designate the modal are:

a) Especially **miþ**: Mark 4:16 *miþ fahedai nimand vaurd*, “they receive the word with joy”; Ephesians 4:2 *miþ allai hauheinai jah qairrein, miþ usbeisnai usþulaiþ ïzvis misso*, “with all humility and gentleness, with patience bearing with one another”; Mark 13:26 *gasaiwand sunu mans qimandan miþ mahtai managai jah vulþau*, “they will see the Son of Man coming with great power and glory”; Luke 17:15 *gavandida sik miþ stibnai mikilai ushauhjands guþ*, “he returned, glorifying God with a loud voice.” For other examples, see the glossary, **Miþ 2(b), β and γ**.

b) **Ïn** with the dative: Mark 3:23 *ïn gajukom qaþ du ïm*, “he spoke to them in parables”; Ephesians 5:19 *fullnaiþ ïn ahmin rodjandans ïzvis ïn psalmon jah hazeinim jah saggvim ahmeinaim*, “be filled with the Spirit, speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs”; Mark 9:1 *gasaiwand þiudinassu guþs qumanana ïn mahtai*, “they will see the kingdom of God come in power”; Romans 9:22 *guþ usbeidiþ ïn managai laggamodein bi kasam þvairheins*, “God endured with much patience the vessels of wrath.” For other examples see the glossary, **In B 3(b)**.

c) **Us**: 2 Corinthians 9:6 *saei saiïþ us gaþagkja, us gaþagkja jah sneiþiþ, jah saei saiïþ ïn þiuþeinai, us þiuþeinai jah sneiþiþ*, “the one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows in blessing will also reap in blessing”; 2 Timothy 2:22 *anahaitan fraujan us hrainjamma hairtin*, “call upon the Lord from a pure heart”; Philemon 14 *ïnu þein ragin ni vaiht vilda taujan, ei ni svasve bi nauþ þiuþ þein sijai ak us lustum*, “without your consent I wished to do nothing, so that your good deed might not be as if compelled, but voluntary.” For fuller treatment see the glossary, **Us 3(b)**.

d) **Bi** with the dative: “according to, in the manner of” (*κατά* with the accusative), in the phrases *bi biuhtja*, “according to custom” (Luke 1:9); *bi sunjai*, “truly” (*ἀληθῶς*, Matthew 26:73); *bi nauþai*, “under compulsion” (Philemon 14); *bi vitoda*, “according to the law” (Luke 2:22); *bi gavaleinai*, “according to election” (Romans 9:11); *bi mahtai*, “according to ability” (2 Corinthians 8:3); *bi ïnsahtai*, “according to insight” (*Skeireins* V, b); etc.; see the glossary, **Bi B 3(f)**.

§ 242. Examples of adverbs indicating the modality of an action are these: Nehemiah 6:16 *atdraus agis ïn ausona ïze abraba*, “fear fell greatly upon their ears,” Greek *σφόδρα*; *Skeireins* III, d *ïohannes bairhtaba uns laiseiþ qiþands*, “John clearly teaches us, saying”; Matthew 26:75 *paitrus usgaggands ut gaigrot baitraba*, “Peter went out and wept bitterly,” Greek *πικρῶς*; Mark 6:20 *herodes gabaurjaba ïohanne andhausida*, “Herod listened gladly to John,” Greek *ἡδέως*; 1 Thessalonians 2:10 *veitvods guþs waiva veihaba jah garaihtaba jah unfairinodaba ïzvis þaim galaubjandam vesum*, “God is witness how devoutly, righteously, and blamelessly we behaved toward you believers”; Mark 14:11 *ïudas sokida, waiva gatilaba ïna galevidedi*, “Judas sought how he might conveniently deliver him up”; John 18:23 *ubilaba rodida*, “I have spoken wrongly”; Titus 1:13 *gasak ïns wasslaba*, “rebuke them sharply”; John 7:13 *balþaba rodida*, “he spoke openly,” Greek *ἐν παρρησίᾳ*; Mark 14:44 *grepiþ þana jah tiuhiþ arniba*, “seize him and lead him away securely”; 10:23 *waiva agluba þai faiho gahabandans ïn þiudangardja guþs galeiþand?*, “how difficult it is for those possessing wealth to enter the kingdom of God!”; Matthew 8:6 *þiumagus meins ligiþ ïn garda usliþa harduba balviþs*, “my servant lies at home, paralyzed and grievously tormented”; 2 Corinthians 10:6 *manvuba habaiþ du fraveitan all ufarhauseino*, “being ready to punish every disobedience.”

John 15:25 *fijaidedun mik arvjo*, “they hated me without cause,” Greek *δωρεάν*; 7:10 *galaiþ ïn þo dulþ ni andaugjo ak sve analaugniba*, “he went up secretly, not openly, but as it were in concealment”; [Col. 1159] Luke 7:4 *bedun ïesu usdaudo*, “they pleaded with Jesus earnestly”; John 18:20 *ïk andaugjo rodida, jah þiubjo ni rodida vaiht*, “I spoke openly, and said nothing in secret”; Luke 1:3 *galeikaida mis fram anastodeinai allaim glaggvuba afarlaistjandin gahahjo þus meljan*, “it also seemed good to me, after tracing everything carefully from the beginning, to write it to you in orderly fashion”; Mark 6:25 *atgaggandei sunsaiv sniumundo du þamma þiudana baþ*, “coming in immediately with haste, she asked the king.”

Luke 14:10 *usgagg hauhis*, “go up higher”; Romans 13:11 *nu newis ïst naseins unsara þau þan galaubidedum*, “now our salvation is nearer than when we believed”; Galatians 2:6 *ni vaiht mis vulþris ïst*, “it makes no difference to me”; Philippians 2:28 *sniumundos ïnsandida ïna*, “I sent him more eagerly”; 1 Corinthians 14:27 *was rodjai bi tvans aiþþau maist þrins*, “let [them] speak by two, or at most three.” For other adverbs see § 163 and the examples in the glossary under the relevant entries.

“Note 1.—In place of an adverb there is sometimes supplied:

a) A modal corresponding to an adverb, either in the simple case or more closely defined by a preposition; see § 241, 1 and 3(c), (d). Or adverbs and the modal are used together equally: 2 Thessalonians 3:6 *wairban ungatassaba jah ni bi anafilham*, ‘walking disorderly and not according to the commandment.’

b) A qualification of the predicate: 1 Thessalonians 2:13 *aviliudom guþa unsveibandans*, ‘we give thanks to God without ceasing’ (*ἀδιαλείπτως*); 5:17; John 6:66 *managai galiþun siponje ïs ïbukai*, ‘many of his disciples went back,’ Greek *εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω*; Luke 17:31 *saei ïst ana haiþjai, ni gavandjai sik ïbukana*, ‘whoever is on the housetop, let him not turn back’; 1 Timothy 2:13 *adam fruma gadigans varþ, þaþroh aivva*, ‘Adam was formed first, then Eve’; compare § 215, note 5.”

“Note 2.—For the use of prepositions as adverbs, see § 251, note 4.”

§ 243. To this class should be assigned instances where the dative signifies the object in which, to which, an event or action is directed and exercised, or in which the basis of a given disposition is found—answering the questions “in what?,” “with respect to what?,” or “according to what?”: Colossians 3:22 *ufhausjaiþ bi all leika fraujam*, “obey masters in all things according to the flesh”; Ephesians 6:15 *gaskohai fotum ïn manviþai aivaggeljons*, “having your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel”; Galatians 1:22 *vas unkunþs vlita aikkesjom*, “I was unknown by face to the churches”; Philippians 2:7 *xristus manaulja bigitans varþ sve manna*, “Christ was found in appearance as a man”; Luke 1:80 *barn svinþnoda ahmin*, “the child grew strong in spirit”; 6:20 *audagai jus unledans ahmin*, “blessed are you poor in spirit”; Ephesians 4:23 *ananiujaiþ ahmin*, “be renewed in spirit”—where in our translation *renew yourselves in spirit* must be read; Mark 8:36 *wa boteiþ mannan, jabai gageigaiþ þana fairwu allana jah gasleiþeiþ sik saivalai seinai*, “what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world and forfeits his own soul?”; Luke 4:18 *ganasjan þans gamalvidans hairtin*, “to heal those broken in heart”; 1 Timothy 6:5 *usbalþeins fravardidaize manne ahin*, “persons corrupted in mind”; 2 Timothy 3:8 *mannans fravaur þanai ahin*, “persons corrupted in mind”; 1 Corinthians 14:20 *fraþjam fullaveisai sijaiþ*, “be mature in understanding”; Ephesians 4:18 *riqizeins gahugdai visan*, “darkened in understanding.”

“Note 1.—Here too the preposition *bi* with the dative is often used: Matthew 7:16 *bi akranam ïze ufkunnaiþ ïns*, ‘by their fruits you will know them’; *Skeireins* V, a *bi þamma galaisjand sik tva andvairþja altins jah sunaus andhaitan*, ‘from this they learn to confess the two persons of the Father and the Son’; see the glossary, **Bi 3(a)**.”

Luke 2:52 *ïesus þaih frodein jah vahstau jah anstai*, “Jesus increased in wisdom, stature, and favor”; *Skeireins* IV, c *ïohannes vistai manna vas*, “John was a man in manner of life”; Mark 7:26 *vas qino haiþno saurinifynikiska gabaurþai*, “the woman was a Greek, Syrophoenician by birth”; [Col. 1160] John 6:10 *anakumbidedun vairos raþjon svasve fimf þusundjos*, “the men reclined, about five thousand in number”; Mark 5:22 *qimiþ ains þize synagogafade namin ïaeirus*, “one of the rulers of the synagogue came, named Jairus.”

“Note 2.—For the fact that the accusative is also used here in Greek fashion and under the influence of the text, see § 220, 4.”

## G. DETERMINATION OF PLACE

§ 244. The relation of an object to place is threefold: it either is and exists in the place itself, comes away from a place, or moves toward a place. Now, except for a few general forms used to indicate whither one goes, Gothic possesses no special case by which it expresses even existence in a place, that is, the locative. It makes up for this deficiency by prepositions or by adverbs used as prepositions.

### I. In answer to the question WHERE?

1) Here one must especially consider adverbs which themselves designate place: 1 Corinthians 5:12 *wa mik jah þans uta stojan, niu þans ïnna jus stojiþ?*, “what have I to do with judging those outside? Do you not judge those within?”; Philippians 2:14 *þaim afta ufarmunno, iþ duþaim faura mik ufþanja*, “forgetting the things behind, but stretching forward toward those before [me]”; Colossians 3:1 *þoei ïupa sind sokeiþ*, “seek the things above”; Mark 14:66 *vas paitrus ïn rohsnai dalaþa*, “Peter was below in the courtyard”; Ephesians 2:13 *jus juzei simle vesuþ fairra, vaurþuþ newa ïn bloþa xristaus*, “you who were once far off have become near in Christ’s blood”; John 11:38 *hulundi staina ufarlagida vas ufaro*, “a stone lay upon the cave above.” Likewise *aljar*, “elsewhere”; *war*, “where?”; *þar*, “there”; *þarei*, “where”; *her*, “here”; *jainar*, “there”; see the glossary under these entries.

2) Prepositions and adverbs which take an object in order to define the place more precisely. Namely, for indicating the relation:

a) “In” (answering “where?”), **ïn** with the dative is principally used: Matthew 10:32 *atta meins, saei ïn himinam ïst*, “my Father who is in heaven”; 8:6 *þiumagus meins ligiþ ïn garda*, “my servant lies in the house”; 2 Corinthians 1:8 *aglo unsara so vaur þano uns ïn asiai*, “our affliction which came upon us in Asia”; 1 Corinthians 1:1 *aikklesjo guþs so visandei ïn kaurinþon*, “the church of God which is in Corinth”; Romans 7:18 *ni bauïþ ïn mis, þat-ïst ïn leika meinamma þiuþ*, “no good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh”; Luke 3:4 *gameliþ ïst ïn bokom vaurde esaeiïns*, “it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah.” Hence also, to express existence among or in the midst of: Matthew 8:10 *ni ïn israela svelauda galaubein bigat*, “not even in Israel have I found such faith”; 11:11 *ni urrais ïn baurim qinono maiza ïohanne*, “among those born of women none greater than John has arisen”; 27:56 *ïn ïm vas marja*, “Mary was among them.” For other examples see the glossary, **In B 1**.

Existence upon a place is added to existence in a place, and is rendered by **ana** with the dative: Mark 1:45 *uta ana auþjaim stadim vas*, “he was outside in deserted places”; 4:31 *kaurno sinapis minnist allaize fraive ïst þize ana airþai*, “a grain of mustard is the smallest of all seeds upon the earth”; 2:25 *ahma veihs vas ana ïmma*, “a holy spirit was in him”; see the glossary, **Ana B 1**.

“In the midst of,” “among,” is Gothic **miþ**: Mark 7:31 *qam at marein galeilaie miþ þveihnaim markom daikapaulaios*, “he came to the Sea of Galilee through the borders of Decapolis, between the two boundaries.”

The opposite of existence in a place, namely absence from a place, is expressed by **utana** with the genitive: *Skeireins* III, b *vitoþ garaidida azgon kalbons gabrannidaizos utana bibaurgeinais*, “the law prescribed that the ashes of the burnt calves [be placed] outside the camp.”

b) “Beside, at” is expressed by **at** with the dative: Matthew 9:9 *ïesus gasaw mannan sitandan at motai*, “Jesus saw a man sitting at the toll-place”; 5:2 *tva skipa standandona at þamma saiva*, “two boats standing by the sea”; 1 Corinthians [Col. 1161] 16:6 *at ïzvis vaitei salja*, “perhaps I shall remain with you”; etc.; see the glossary, **At B 1**.

**Bi** with the dative is rarely used, since *undgreipan bi handau*, “to take by the hand” (Mark 5:41; 9:27), is already a figurative expression. In a more proper sense it is used after verbs of swearing and praying, as Matthew 5:34–36; 5:7; 2 Corinthians 10:1.

The relation of proximity is expressed by **newa** with the dative: John 11:18 *vas beþania newa ïairusaulymiam*, “Bethany was near Jerusalem”; Romans 10:8 *newa þus þata vaurd ïst*, “the word is near you.” But “near, before” is expressed by **faur** with the accusative: Mark 10:46 *blinda sat faur vig du aihtron*, “a blind man sat by the way begging”; Luke 18:35.

Existence “with” someone—the relation of community—also belongs to existence “at,” the relation of proximity. Although this relation is not local because of the person with whom one is in communion, it is always rendered by **miþ** with the dative: Matthew 26:69 *jah þu vast miþ ïesua*, “you too were with Jesus”; Luke 2:36 *anna libaida miþ abin jera sibun*, “Anna had lived with a husband seven years”; Matthew 5:41 *jabai was þuk ananauþjai rasta aina, gaggais miþ ïmma tvos*, “if anyone compels you one mile, go with him two.” For other examples see the glossary, **Miþ I 1**. But when this relation of communion is understood in a metaphysical sense, namely that of assistance or discourse, **du** is ordinarily used, especially § 246, 3(b).

The opposite, “without,” is rendered by **ïnuh** with the accusative: John 15:5 *ïnuh mik ni maguþ taujan ni vaiht*, “without me you can do nothing”; Romans 10:14 *waiva hausjand ïnu merjandan*, “how will they hear without a preacher?”; etc.; see the glossary under **Inuh**.

c) “Before, in the presence of” is expressed by **faura** with the dative: Romans 14:10 *allai gasatjanda faura stauastola xristaus*, “all will stand before Christ’s judgment-seat”; Matthew 11:10 *aggilus gamanveiþ vig þeinana faura þus*, “the angel will prepare your way before you”; see the glossary, **Faura A(a)**.

The opposite, “after, behind,” is expressed by **afar** with the dative: Luke 9:23 *jabai was vili afar mis gaggan, afaikai sik silban*, “if anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself”; 19:14 *baurgjans ïnsandidedun airu afar ïmma*, “his citizens sent an embassy after him.” Both prepositions are also used in a metaphysical sense.

d) “Across,” Greek *πέραν*, is Gothic **hindar**, which nevertheless wholly corresponds to German *hinter*: John 3:26 *rabbei, saei vas miþ þus hindar jaurdanau, sa daupeiþ*, “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan is baptizing”; 6:22 *managei stoþ hindar marein*, “the crowd stood on the other side of the sea”; see the glossary, **Hindar II 1**.

e) “Above, upon” is rendered by **ufar** with the dative: Matthew 27:25 *varþ riqiz ufar allai airþai*, “darkness came over all the earth”; 6:14 *atta izvar sa ufar himinam*, “your Father who is in heaven”; or by **ufaro** with the genitive: Luke 10:19 *gaf ïzvis valdufni trudan ufaro vaurme jah skaurpjono*, “he gave you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions.” Elsewhere it is also used figuratively: Ephesians 1:21 *guþ gasatida ïesu ïn taihsvon seinai ïn himinam ufaro allaize reikje jah valdufnje jah mahte*, “God seated Jesus at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every rule, authority, and power”; likewise **ufaro** with the dative: Luke 19:19 *þu sijais ufaro fimf baurgim*, “you shall be over five cities”; see the glossary under **Ufar**.

The opposite, “under, beneath,” is rendered by **uf** with the dative: Mark 4:32 *magun uf skadau bagmis fuglos himinis gabauan*, “the birds of heaven can dwell under the shade of its branches”; 1 Corinthians 10:1 *attans unsarai uf milhmin vesun*, “our fathers were under the cloud”; see the glossary, **Uf B 1**; or by **undaro** with the dative: Mark 6:11 *mulda undaro fotum*, “dust under your feet”; 7:28 *hundos undaro biuda*, “the dogs under the table.” There is, moreover, this difference between *uf* and *undar*: *uf* indicates that an object is subject to another, larger object and is covered and protected by it; *undar* shows that an object is indeed placed beneath another, but so that each protects and covers the other. Besides, *uf*, like *ufar*, can be used metaphorically, as Galatians 4:21 *ufvitoda visan*, “to be under the law”; etc.; see the glossary.

f) “Opposite, against” is rendered by **viþra** with the accusative: Mark 4:1 *managei viþra marein ana staþa vas*, “a great crowd was on the shore opposite the sea”; 15 *þaï viþra vig*, “those beside the road”; 1 Corinthians 13:12 *andvairþi viþra andvairþi*, “face to face”; Luke 1:73 *guþ aiþ svor viþra abrahama*, “God swore an oath to Abraham”—a form properly of the dative, probably to be corrected to *abraham*, since final *-a* has doubtless intruded because of the initial *a* of the following word; or by **andvairþis** with the dative: Matthew 27:61 *vas jainar marja magdalene jah so anþara marja sitandeins andvairþis hlaiva*, “Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb.”

§ 245. II. In answer to the question WHENCE?

1) Here belong adverbs of place: Mark 5:27 *qens atgaggandei ïn managein aftana attaitok vastjai ïesuis*, “a woman, coming through the crowd from behind, touched Jesus’ garment”; in the parallel passages Matthew 9:20 and Luke 8:44, *aftaro* occurs instead; John 8:23 *jus us þaim dalaþro sijuþ, ïþ ïk us þaim ïupaþro ïm*, “you are from below, but I am from above,” together with *ïupana*, which has the more temporal sense “anew” (Galatians 4:9); Mark 7:21 *ïnnaþro us hairtin, manne mitoneis ubilos usgaggand*, “from within, out of the human heart, evil thoughts proceed”; 18 *all þata utraþro ïnngaggando ïn mannan ni mag ïna gamainjan*, “nothing entering a person from outside can defile him”; 2 Corinthians 7:5 *utana vaihjons, ïnnana agisa*, “without, conflicts; within, fears”; Matthew 27:55 *vesun jainar qinons managos fairraþro saiwandeins*, “there were many women there, watching from afar.” Likewise *aljaþro*, “from elsewhere”; *waþro*, “whence?”; *þaþro*, “thence”; *jainþro*, “from there”; *allaþro*, “from every side”; see the glossary under these entries.

2) Among prepositions and adverbs note:

a) To designate movement from a place:

aa) **Af** with the dative, properly indicating movement from a higher place: Luke 16:21 *gairnida saþ ïtan drauhsno þizo driusandeino af biuda þis gabeigins*, “he desired to eat the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table”; Matthew 7:16 *ïbai lisanda af þaurnum veinabasja?*, “do they gather grapes from thorns?”; Luke 6:29 *þamma nimandin af þus vastja jah paida ni varjais*, “from the one taking your cloak do not withhold even your tunic”; Mark 15:21 *undgripun seimona kyreinaiu qimandan af akra*, “they seized Simon of Cyrene coming from the field”; 16:8 *usgaggandeins af þamma hlaiva gaþlauhun*, “going out from the tomb, they fled”; Philippians 4:15 *usïddja af makidonai*, “when I departed from Macedonia”; see the glossary, **Af I 1**.

bb) **Fram** with the dative, properly indicating simply movement from a place: Matthew 8:11 *managai fram urrunsa jah saggqa qimand*, “many will come from east and west”; 27:55 *laistidedun afar ïesua fram galeilaia*, “they had followed Jesus from Galilee”; John 8:42 *ïk fram guþa urrann*, “I came forth from God”; see the glossary, **Fram I 1**.

“Note 1.—After verbs of receiving, hearing, seeing, and the like, the person from whom something is received, heard, or seen is sometimes construed with *at* (‘at, with’), so that something is said to be received, heard, or seen at that person’s place. Thus, just as John 8:40 has *sunja hausida fram guþa*, ‘truth heard from God,’ so *Skeireins* IV, d has *anafalh fulhsnja þoei gasaw jah gahausida at attin*, ‘he handed down the mystery which he saw and heard from the Father.’ Further, Mark 12:2 *ïnsandida skalk ei at þaim vaurstvjam nemi akranis*, ‘he sent a servant in order that he might receive fruit from the cultivators,’ where *niman af* more properly means ‘to take something from someone’ (Luke 6:29; 19:24; etc.). For other examples see the glossary, **At B 1(c)**; compare **Af I 1(b)**.”

“Note 2.—If *af* and *fram* are occasionally construed with the genitive—Matthew 27:57 *manna gabigs af areimaþaias*, ‘a rich man of Arimathea’; Mark 15:43; John 11:1 *lazarus af beþanias*, ‘Lazarus of Bethany’; Luke 8:49 *gaggiþ sums manne fram þis fauramaþleis*, ‘someone has come from the ruler of the synagogue’—in the former case this arises because the translator, misunderstanding, imitated the Greek form when he rendered John 12:21 *filippus sa fram beþsaeida*, ‘Philip who was from Bethsaida’; and in the latter there is an error, unless recourse is had to ellipsis; compare § 216, note 7.”

cc) **Us** with the dative, properly signifying movement from a higher place: Mark 1:11 *stibna qam us himina*, “a voice came from heaven”; John 6:23 *skipa qemun us tibairiadau*, “boats came from Tiberias”; Luke 4:22 *vaurda usgaggandona us munþa*, “words proceeding from [his] mouth”; 1:78 *urruns us hauhiþai*, “the rising from on high”; 74 *us handau fijande unsaraize galausidai*, “delivered from the hand of our enemies”; 6:44 *ni us þaurnum lisanda smakkans*, “figs are not gathered from thorns”; Matthew 27:64 *urrais us dauþaim*, “he will rise from the dead”; Nehemiah 5:17 *þai qimandans at unsis us þiudom ana biuda meinamma andnumanai vesun*, “those coming to us from the nations around us were at my table”; John 7:52 *þu us galeilaia ïs*, “you are from Galilee”; subscription to Romans: *du rumonim gameliþ ïst us kaurinþon*, “written from Corinth to the Romans”; John 8:44 *jus us attin diabaulau sijuþ*, “you are of your father, the devil.”

“Note 3.—In general, the three above-mentioned prepositions—*fram*, *af*, and *us*—when used metaphorically, signify the origin from which something proceeds; and *fram* in particular is joined with passive verbs to indicate the agent by whom something is done. If Germans use the preposition *von* after verbs of speaking or narrating, this too was already in use among the Goths, since along with the commonly used *bi* (§ 246, 3[c]) they also use *fram*; see the glossary under the relevant entries.”

Here also belong **utana** and **utaþro** with the genitive, “out of, outside of”: Mark 8:23 *ustauh þana blindan utana veihsis*, “he led the blind man out of the village”; 7:15 *ni vaihts ïst utaþro mans ïnngaggando ïn ïna þatei magi ïna gamainjan*, “there is nothing outside a person entering into him which can defile him.”

b) “Far from” is **fairra** with the dative: Matthew 7:23 *afleiþiþ fairra mis*, “depart from me”; Luke 2:37 *ni afïddja fairra alh*, “she did not depart from the temple”; see the glossary, **Fairra**.

c) “From beyond” is **hindana** with the genitive: Mark 3:7–8 *filu manageins us galeilaia laistidedun afar ïmma jah us ïudaia jah us ïairusaulymim jah hindana ïaurdanaus*, “a great multitude from Galilee followed him, and [also] from Judea, Jerusalem, and from beyond the Jordan.”

d) “Down from” is **and** with the accusative: Matthew 8:32 *run gavaurhtedun sis alla so hairda and driuson ïn marein*, “the whole herd rushed down and fell into the sea”; 2 Corinthians 11:33 *þairh augadauro ïn snorjon athahans vas and baurgsvaddjau*, “through a window, in a basket, I was lowered down the wall.”

§ 246. III. In answer to the question WHITHER?

1) There are only a few places in which the simple genitive is used: Mark 4:35 *usleiþam jainis stadis*, “let us cross to the other side”; Luke 15:15 *baurgja ïnsandida ïna haiþjos seinaizos haldan sveina*, “he sent him into his fields to tend swine”; 19:12 *gaggida landis*, “he went into a distant country”; 1 Timothy 1:3 *baþ þuk saljan ïn aifaison galeiþands makidonais*, “I urged you to remain at Ephesus when I was going into Macedonia.” It is especially noteworthy that, in forming this construction, Gothic wholly departs from Greek: in Luke 19:4, it renders *ἐκείνης ἤμελλε διέρχεσθαι* not by *jainis* but by *and þata*. Anyone attempting to explain this construction by translating “from this place, from this region” would be making a wholly gratuitous conjecture: on the one hand, the matter here is not movement from but movement toward; on the other, the genitive itself never expresses movement from.

2) Adverbs of place: Mark 9:25 *atgaggands ïnn habaida handu maujos*, “coming in, he took the child’s hand”; [Col. 1164] John 19:4 *attiuha ïzvis ïna ut*, “I bring him out to you”; Romans 10:6–7 *was ussteigiþ ïn himin, þatïst xristu dalaþ attiuhan. aiþþau was gasteigiþ ïn afgrundiþa, þatïst xristu us dauþaim ïup ustiuhan*, “who will ascend into heaven—that is, to bring Christ down? Or who will descend into the abyss—that is, to bring Christ up from the dead?”; John 8:14 *vait waþro qam jah waþ galeiþa*, “I know whence I came and whither I am going”; 7:35 *qeþun ïudaieis wadre sa skuli gaggan*, “the Jews said, ‘Where does this man intend to go?’”; Mark 11:3 *sunsaiv fulan ïnsandeiþ hidre*, “he will immediately send it here”; John 11:8 *aftra gaggis jaind*, “are you going there again?”; Luke 17:37 *þarei leik, jaindre galisand sik arans*, “where the body is, there the eagles will gather”; John 18:3 *ïudas nam hansa ïddjuh jaindvairþs*, “Judas took a cohort and went there”; **framis**, “before, forward,” is used in compounds in response to Greek *πρό*; see Mark 1:19; Romans 13:12.

3) Among prepositions and adverbs note:

a) To express movement “into,” “to” cities and regions, or “among” a multitude, **ïn** with the accusative: Matthew 9:7 *usliþa urreisands galaiþ ïn gard seinana*, “the paralytic arose and went to his house”; John 18:11 *lagei þana hairu ïn fodr*, “put the sword into its sheath”; Luke 2:39 *ïosef jah maria gavandidedun sik ïn galeilaian ïn baurg seina nazaraiþ*, “Joseph and Mary returned to Galilee, to their own city Nazareth”; 2 Corinthians 1:16 *vilda galeiþan ïn makidonja*, “I wished to go into Macedonia”; Luke 10:29 *manna galaiþ af ïairusalem ïn ïaireikon jah ïn vaidedjans frarann*, “a man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers”; see the glossary, **In A 1**.

Likewise the adverb **ïnna** with the genitive means “inward, within” with motion: Mark 15:16 *gadrauhteis gatauhun ïesu ïnnana gardis*, “the soldiers led Jesus inside the courtyard.”

Here belong verbs of moving toward and going to, with **ïn** and **ana** plus the accusative: Luke 14:21 *usgagg ïn gatvons jah staigos baurgs jah unledans attiuh hidre*, “go out into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring the poor here”; 6:12 *usïddja ïesus ïn fairguni bidjan*, “Jesus went out to the mountain to pray”; John 6:21 *skip varþ ana airþai, ana þoei ïddjedun*, “the boat came to land, to which they were going”; Luke 4:5 *ustauh ïesu diabulus ana fairguni hauhata*, “the devil led Jesus up onto a high mountain”; Matthew 10:34 *ni qam lagjan gavairþi ana airþa*, “I came not to bring peace upon the earth”; Mark 4:21 *lukarn qimiþ duþe ei ana lukarnastaþan satjaidau*, “a lamp comes in order that it may be placed upon a lampstand”; see the glossary, **Ana A 1**. Hence **ïn** also indicates a goal, and both **ïn** and **ana** metaphorically mean “toward, against, concerning”: *ïn* either favorably or unfavorably, *ana* only unfavorably; the latter is also construed with the dative. See the glossary under the relevant entries.

“Toward, beside” is expressed by **faur** with the accusative: Mark 1:16 *ïesus warbonds faur marein galeilaias gasaw seimonu*, “as Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon”; 2:13 *galaiþ aftra faur marein*, “he went again beside the sea”; 4:4 *fraiv gadraus faur vig*, “seed fell beside the road”; see the glossary, **Fram A(a)**. Conversely, **and** with the accusative: Luke 14:23 *usgagg and vigans jah faþos jah nauþei ïnnatgaggan*, “go out into the roads and hedges and compel [them] to come in.”

“Note 1.—It is characteristic of Gothic that the verb *qiman*, ‘to come,’ always has and is regarded as a verb of rest, and is always construed with *ïn* or *ana* followed by the dative: 2 Timothy 1:16 *qimands ïn rumai auneiseifaurus sokida mik*, ‘having come to Rome, he diligently sought me’; 1 Timothy 1:15 *ïesus qam ïn þamma fairwau fravaurhtans nasjan*, ‘Jesus came into the world to save sinners’; Ephesians 5:6 *þairh lausa vaurda qimiþ hatis guþs ana sunum ungalaubeinais*, ‘through empty words the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience.’ Only at John 6:14, 22; 11:27 does *ïn* occur with the accusative. Commonly *ïn* after *lagjan*, ‘to lay,’ *satjan*, ‘to set,’ and *briggan*, ‘to bring,’ is also construed with the dative: Matthew 27:60 *ïosef galagida leik ïesuis in niujamma seinamma hlaiva*, ‘Joseph laid Jesus’ body in his new tomb’; 1 Corinthians 12:18 *guþ gasatida liþuns ainwarjanoh ïn leika svasve vilda*, ‘God placed each of the members in the body as he wished’; *Skeireins* II, a *sa ïupa brigganda ïn þiudangardjai guþs vig*, ‘he who brings the way into the kingdom of God from above.’ And at times it is likewise so construed after other intransitive verbs; see the glossary under the relevant entry.”

[Col. 1165] “Note 2.—With the verb ‘to strike’ *bi* and the dative are used: Luke IV.11; VI.48; also *du*: Romans IX.32.”

b) **To**, *du* with the dative: Eph. IV.13 *garinnaima du vaira fullamma du mitaþ vahstaus fullons xristaus* (“that we may attain unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ”); Luke II.11 *gagg du garda þeinamma* (“go to thy house”); 1 Thess. III.11 *frauja unsar garaihtjai vig unsarana du ïzvis* (“may our Lord direct our way unto you”); Luke I.16 *managans sunive ïsraelis gavandeiþ du fraugin* (“he shall turn many of the children of Israel unto the Lord”); see Glossary, s.v. *Du*. Hence *du* also indicates purpose; moreover, it is used when one person speaks to another, because he is regarded as turning toward the person whom he addresses (in which case we often also find the simple dative used, § 224, 2). It accordingly means “to meet,” either in a hostile sense, “against,” or in a friendly sense, “to”; see Glossary, s.v. It follows *qiman*, *briggan*, and other verbs which govern *ïn* with the dative (see Note 1); yet here *at* with the dative (“to come to [at] someone”) may also be used: Matt. VII.15 *liugnapraufeteis qimand at ïzvis ïn vastjom lambe* (“false prophets come to you in sheep’s garments”); Mark IX.19 *bairiþ ïna du mis. jah brahtedun ïna at ïmma* (“bring him to me. And they brought him to him”), where after *bairan* [“to bear, bring”] *du* is always used, but after *briggan* [“to bring”] *at* is found; see Glossary, *Ana* B) 1) b).

**Near, beside** is rendered by *new* with the accusative: Luke XV.15 *atïddja new razn* (“he went near a house”); but after *qiman*, *newa* governs the dative (compare Note 1): John VI.19 *gasaiwand ïesu newa skipa qimandan* (“they see Jesus coming near the boat”); 23. **As far as** is expressed by *und* with the accusative: Luke IV.42 *manageins sokidedun ïesu jah qemun und ïna* (“the multitudes sought Jesus and came as far as him”); 29 *brahtedun ïesu und auhmisto þis fairgunjis* (“they led Jesus to the brow of the mountain”); Mark XIII.27 *sunus mans galisid gavalidans seinans af fidvor vindam fram andjam airþos und andi himinis* (“the Son of Man shall gather his elect from the four winds, from the end of the earth unto the end of heaven”); see Glossary, *Und* I. A) 1).

**To meet**, *viþra* with the accusative: Matt. VIII.34 *alla so baurgs usïddja viþra ïesu* (“the whole city went out to meet Jesus”); hence, like *ïn* (see above a), it means “against,” “toward,” “opposite to,” whether in a favorable or unfavorable sense; see Glossary, *Viþra* b).

c) **Around**, *bi* with the accusative. Mark III.32 *setun bi ïna managei* (“a multitude sat around him”); Matt. VIII.18 *gasaw ïesus managans hiuhmans bi sik* (“Jesus saw great multitudes around him”); see Glossary, *Bi* I. A) 1). Hence in a figurative sense it means “of,” “concerning,” “about” (*περί* with the accusative) after verbs of speaking; likewise “in regard to” (*περί* with the genitive and accusative), and “according to” (*κατά* with the accusative); see Glossary, s.v. In the latter sense it commonly governs the dative.

d) **Through**, *þairh* with the accusative: Mark IX.30 *ïddjedun þairh galeilaian* (“they went through Galilee”); Luke VI.1 *varþ gaggan ïmma þairh atisk* (“it came to pass that he went through the cornfields”); Mark XI.16 *ni lailot ei was þairhberi kas þairh þo alh* (“he would not allow anyone to carry a vessel through the temple”); 2 Cor. XI.33 *þairh augadauro ïn snorjon athahans vas* (“through a window I was let down in a basket”); 1 Cor. XIII.12 *saiwam nu þairh skuggvan* (“now we see through a shadow”); see Glossary, *þairh* I.1).

**Over, beyond**, *ufar* with the accusative: Luke IV.39 *atstandands ïesus ufar ïja gasok þizai brinnon* (“Jesus, standing over her, rebuked the fever”); Eph. IV.10 *usstaig ufar allans himinans* (“he ascended above all heavens”); John VI.1 *ïesus galaiþ ufar marein* (“Jesus went over the sea”); 17; X.40; XVIII.1. Compare f).

The opposite of the preceding, **under, beneath**, is *undar* and *uf* with the accusative; for the distinction between them see § 244, 2) d): Mark IV.21 *ïbai lukarn qimiþ duþe ei uf melan satjaidau aiþþau undar ligr?* (“Does a lamp come in order that it may be set upon a measure or under a bed?”); Matt. VIII.8 *ni ïm vairþs ei uf hrot mein ïnngaggais* (“I am not worthy that thou shouldest enter under my roof”); 1 Cor. XV.25 *skal ïs þiudanon und þatei galagjiþ guþ allans fijands ïs uf fotuns mma* (“he must reign until God has placed all his enemies under his feet”); see Glossary, *Uf* A) 1).

[Col. 1166] f) **Behind, backward**, *hindar* with the accusative: Mark VIII.33 *gagg hindar mik* (“go behind me”). The same word also means **across, beyond**: Mark VIII.13 *galeiþands ïin skip uslaiþ hindar* (*εἰς τὸ πέραν*, “having embarked in the boat, he crossed over beyond”) *marein* (“the sea”); Matt. VIII.34 *bedun ïesu ei usliþi hindar* (*ἀπό*, “they asked Jesus that he might depart beyond”) *markos ïze* (“their borders”); see Glossary, *Hindar* I. Compare above e).

## H. DETERMINATION OF TIME

§ 247. Just as with space, so also with time the object may be related in three ways, and the two sets of relations correspond to one another. Thus the questions concerning place, “where?”, “whence?”, “whither?”, correspond to the temporal questions, “when?”, “since when?”, “for how long?” Now, the properly temporal relation in Gothic is indicated by the genitive and dative, whose differing significance is difficult to apprehend. To these must further be added prepositions, by which time is more narrowly determined. “For how long?” is expressed by the accusative, and more precisely by prepositions; “since when?” is always expressed through prepositions.

### I. In the question WHEN?

1) Here temporal adverbs are especially to be noted: Matt. XXV.38 *wan* (“when”) *þuk sewum gast?* (“when did we see thee as a guest?”); VII.23 *þan* (“then”) *andhaita ïm* (“then I shall confess to them”); VIII.26 *þanuh* (“then”) *urreisands gasok vindam jah marein* (“then, rising, he rebuked the winds and the sea”); XXVI.65 *nu* (“now”) *gahausideduþ þo vajamerein* (“now ye have heard the blasphemy”); XXVII.57 *seiþu* (“late”) *varþ* (“it became late”). Likewise *air* “formerly,” *mane* “in the morning,” *faurþis* “previously,” *suns* “immediately,” *anaks* “straightway,” *simle* “once, formerly,” *suman* “on a certain day,” *ufta* “often,” *aftra* “again,” etc.

2) The temporal [construction], which is almost exclusively restricted to *nahts* (“night”) and *dagis* (“day”):

a) Is rarely expressed by the genitive: Luke II.8 *hairdjos vesun vitandans nahts* (*τῆς νυκτός*, “shepherds were keeping watch by night”); 1 Thess. V.7 *nahts* (*νυκτός*) *drugkanai vairþand* (“they become drunken by night”); Neh. V.17 *vas fraquman dagis wizuh* (*εἰς ἡμέραν μίαν*, “there came daily”) *stiur ains* (“one ox”); Matt. VI.30 *havi haiþjos himma daga visando jah gistradagis ïn auhn galagiþ* (“the grass of the field, which exists today and tomorrow is cast into the furnace”), where *gistradagis* [“tomorrow,” Greek *αὔρων*] is probably an adverb, like *framvigis*; Mark XVI.2 *filu air þis dagis afarsabbate atïddjedun du hlaiva* (“very early on the first day after the Sabbath they came to the tomb”); Luke XVIII.12 *fasta tvaim sinþam sabbataus* (*τοῦ σαββάτου*, “I fast twice in the week”). Rather, however, the genitive is partitive in Neh. VI.15 *usþauhana vaurþ baurgsvaddjus ·n· dage jah ·b·* (“the wall was finished in fifty-two days”); and it takes the place of nominal government in Luke I.7 *zakarias jah aileisabaiþ framaldra dage seinaize* (*ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις*, “Zechariah and Elizabeth were advanced in their days”). On *ïnvisandin(s) sabbate dagis*, see below, Note 4.

“Note 1.—Prepositions are also used with temporal expressions: Luke XVII.4 *sibun sinþam ana dag* (*τῆς ἡμέρας*, “seven times in a day”); I.18 *qens meina framaldrozei ïn dagam seinaim ïst* (“my wife is advanced in her days”).”

b) More frequently, however, by the dative:

aa) Mark XIII.18 *bidjaiþ ei ni vairþai þlauhs ïzvar vintrau* (*χειμῶνος*, “pray that your flight may not occur in winter”); I.35 *air uhtvon* (“before dawn,” *ἔννυχον*) *usstandands usïddja* (“rising, he went out”); II.24 *wa taujand siponjos þeinai sabbatim* (*τοῖς σάββασι*, “why do thy disciples on the sabbaths?”), and Luke VI.9 *wa skuld ïst sabbato dagam* (“what is lawful on the Sabbath day?”). Add the formulas *naht jah daga* and *nahtam jah dagam*, “night and day” (*νύκτα καὶ ἡμέραν* or *νυκτὸς καὶ ἡμέρας*), Mark IV.27; 2 Thess. [Col. 1167] III.8; 2 Tim. I.3; Mark V.5; Luke II.37; 1 Tim. V.5.

“Note 2.—In Luke XVIII.7 only *dagam jah nahtam* occurs. In arranging these two words the Goth followed the Greek before him; therefore, at least from the precedence of night over day one cannot infer that the ancient Germans ever reckoned time by nights.”

bb) Frequently with a determining attribute, where Greek also uses the dative: Luke XVII.34 *þizai naht* (“in that night”); conversely, one does not say *þamma daga*, but always *himma daga* (“this day,” for *σήμερον*, “today”), Matt. VI.11 etc.; see Glossary. But relatively: *þammei daga*, Luke XVII.29; Mark XIV.12 *frumistin daga* (“on the first day”); IX.31; Matt. XXVII.62 *ïftumin daga* (“on the following day”); Mark XI.12; John VI.22; XII.12 *þridjin daga* (“on the third day”); Mark X.34; Luke IX.22; XVIII.33; Neh. VI.15 *·e· jah ·k· daga menoþs ailulis* (“on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul”); Mark XIV.49 *daga wammeh* (*καθ᾽ ἡμέραν*, “daily”); Luke XVI.19; XVII.49; in place of which *daga jah daga* occurs at 2 Cor. IV.16, following the Greek *ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἡμέρᾳ*; Luke II.41 *jera wammeh* (*κατ᾽ ἔτος*, “yearly”). Especially with *mela* (“time”) and *weilai* (“hour”): Mark VI.21 *herodes mela gabaurþais seinaizos nahtamat vaurhta* (“Herod made a supper at the time of his birthday”); 2 Cor. VI.2 *mela andanemjamma andhausida þus* (“in an acceptable time I heard thee”); Tit. I.3 *atbairhtida mela svesamma vaurd sein* (“he manifested his word in his own times”); 1 Tim. II.6 *gaf sik silban audabaht faur allans veitvodein melam svesaim* (“he gave himself a ransom for all, a testimony in its own times”); Luke I.10 *hiuhma vas beidandans uta weilai þymiamins* (“the multitude was waiting outside at the hour of incense”); XIV.17 *ïnsandida skalk weilai nahtamahtis* (“he sent his servant at the hour of the supper”); II.38 *anna þizai weilai atstandandei andhaitait fraujin* (“at that very hour she came up and gave thanks to the Lord”).

cc) With a participle, a construction corresponding to the Latin ablative absolute or the Greek genitive: Mark I.32 *andanahtja vaurþanamma* (*ὀψίας γενομένης*, “when evening had come”) *berun du ïmma allans þans ubil habandans* (“they brought unto him all that were sick”); John VI.18 *marei vinda mikilamma vaiandin* (*ἀνέμου ... πνέοντος*, “the sea, while a great wind was blowing”) *urraisida vas* (“was rising”); Luke III.1 *raginondin puntiau peilatau* (*ἡγεμονεύοντος Ποντίου Πιλάτου*, “while Pontius Pilate was governor”) *ïudaia varþ vaurd guþs at ïohannen* (“the word of God came to John in Judaea”); Mark XIV.66 *visandin paitrau ïn rohsnai dalaþa jah atïddja aina þiujo* (“while Peter was below in the court, one maid came”); Luke VIII.4 *gaqumanaim hiuhmam managaim qaþ ïesus þairh gajukon* (“when great multitudes had assembled, Jesus spoke by a parable”); VII.42 *ni habandam* [scil. “when they had not”] *waþro usgebeina baim fragaf* (“when they had nothing to repay, he freely forgave them both”); Mark V.35 *nauhþan ïmma rodjandin qemun fram þamma synagogafada* (“while he was still speaking, people came from the ruler of the synagogue”); Rom. IX.1 *ni vaiht liuga miþveitvodjandein mis miþvissein meinai* (“I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness with me”); and likewise Mark V.35; VI.54; X.17, 46; XI.12, 27; Luke II.42, 43; VII.6, 42; VIII.4, 45, 49; IX.34, 37, 57; XIV.32; XVII.12; XIX.33, 36; John VIII.30; XII.37; XVIII.22; 1 Cor. V.4; 2 Cor. VII.4. Just as *ïn* must be supplied in Luke VII.42, so, following the Greek, *unsis* must be supplied in 2 Cor. IV.17, unless the Goth included *fairveitjandam* in the construction and referred it as a participle to *unsis*.

“Note 3.—Moreover, frequently in Matthew, always in the *Skeireins*, and generally in the Pauline epistles, the preposition *at* is joined to the dative: Matt. VIII.16 *at andanahtja vaurþanamma* (*ὀψίας γενομένης*, “when evening had come”) *atberun du ïmma daimonarjans* (“they brought demoniacs to him”); Mark IV.6 *at sunnin urrinnandin* (*ἡλίου ἀνατειλαντος*, “when the sun arose”) *ufbrann* (“it was scorched”); Luke IV.2 *at ustauhanaim þaim dagam* (*συντελεσθεισῶν τῶν ἡμερῶν*, “when those days had been completed”) *qaþ du ïmma* [Col. 1168] *diabulus* (“the devil said to him”); VI.48, *at garunjon vaurþanai bistagq awa bi razna* (“when the building had been completed, the river beat against the house”); II.2 *so gilstrameleins frumista varþ at raginondin saurim kyreinaiu* (“this first enrolment took place when Cyrenius was governor of Syria”); Mark XIV.43 *nauhþan at ïmma rodjandin qam ïudas* (“while he was still speaking, Judas came”); and likewise Matt. XI.7; Mark IV.35; VIII.1; XI.11; XV.42; XVI.2; Luke III.15, 21; VII.24; IX.43; XIX.11; XX.1, 45; Rom. VII.2, 3, 9; 2 Cor. I.11; V.20; X.15; Eph. II.20; 1 Thess. III.6; *Skeireins* II.d; III.a; VII.b; VIII.a, c. Compare below c) cc).”

“Note 4.—Once the accusative is used, Matt. XXVII.1 *at maurgin vaurþanana* (*πρωίας γενομένης*, ‘when morning had come’) *runa nemun gudjans* (‘the priests took counsel’); in Mark XVI.1 there is *ïnvisandin sabbate dagis* (*διαγενομένου τοῦ σαββάτου*, ‘when the Sabbath had passed’) *usbauhtedun aromata* (‘they bought spices’), which is undoubtedly a corrupt reading for *ïnvisandins* (see on that passage), the final *s* having been omitted because of the same following letter. For the genitive here is temporal (see above 2); if the Goth had wished to use the accusative, he ought at least to have written *ïnvisandin daga*. That this participial construction can also be paraphrased with *biþe*, *miþþanei*, *sve*, will be shown below when we discuss the compound sentence.”

c) Very frequently also with prepositions, especially:

aa) To determine the point of time at which something happens, *ïn* with the dative, wherever the simple dative might stand: John VII.50 *nikaudemus atïddja du ïesua ïn naht* (*νυκτός*, “Nicodemus came to Jesus by night”); Mark III.4 *ïn sabbatim* (*τοῖς σάββασι*, “on the sabbaths”) *þiuþ taujan* (“to do good”); Luke IV.16; especially where there is an attributive determination: Matt. VII.22 *ïn jainamma daga* (“on that day”); VIII.13 *ïn jainai weilai* (“in that hour”); Luke I.59 *ïn daga ahtudin* (“on the eighth day”); 26 *ïn menoþ saihstin* (“in the sixth month”); John VI.40 *ïn spedistin daga* (“on the last day”); *Skeireins* VI.c *ïn missaleikaim melam* (“at diverse times”); II.a *ïn mela þulainais* (“at the time of suffering”); Matt. XI.22 *ïn daga stauos* (“in the day of judgment”); Luke I.5 *ïn dagam herodis* (“in the days of Herod”). For other examples see Glossary, *Dags* 2) a). Here the accusative is conspicuous: Mark XIII.24 *ïn jainans dagans* (*ἐν ἐκείναις ταῖς ἡμέραις*, “in those days”) *sauïl riqizeiþ* (“the sun shall be darkened”); Eph. VI.18 *þairh allos bidos aihtrondans ïn alla mela* (*παντὶ καιρῷ*, “praying at every time”), although here the translator seems to have had duration of time in view (see § 249)—“through those days the sun is darkened”—as in Luke II.1 *varþ ïn dagans jainans urrann gagrefts* (“in those days a decree went out”) and John XI.9 *jabai was gaggiþ ïn dag* (*ἐν ἡμέρᾳ*, “if anyone walks in the day”) *ni gastiggqiþ* (“does he not stumble?”), perhaps influenced by the verbs of motion. Also *πρωΐ*, “in the morning,” is always rendered *ïn maurgin*, Mark XI.20; XV.1; XVI.9; to this construction 1 Cor. XV.32 *du maurgina* (*αὔριον*, “tomorrow”) *gasviltam* (“we shall die”) also corresponds.

More rarely there occur here:

*Ana* with the dative, indeed where the Greek absolute genitive is paraphrased: John VII.14 *ana midjai dulþ* (*τῆς ἑορτῆς μεσούσης*, “when the feast was half completed”) *usstaig ïesus ïn alh* (“Jesus went up into the temple”); VI.23 *matidedun hlaif ana þammei aviliudoda frauja* (*εὐχαριστήσαντος τοῦ κυρίου*, “they ate bread when the Lord had given thanks”);

*At* with the accusative: Matt. XXI.34 *ïnsandida du þaim vaurstvam at mel* (*τῷ καιρῷ*, “at the time”) *skalk* (“he sent a servant to the husbandmen”); Luke II.41 *vratodedun berusjos ïesuis jera wammeh ïn ïairusalem at dulþ paska* (*τῇ ἑορτῇ τοῦ π.*, “the parents of Jesus travelled yearly to Jerusalem at the feast of Passover”); Gal. VI.9 *at mel svesata* (*καιρῷ ἰδίῳ*, “in its proper season”) *sneiþam* (“we shall reap”);

*And* with the accusative: Matt. XXVII.15 *and dulþ warjanoh* (*καθ᾽ ἑορτήν*, “at every feast”) *biuhts vas sa kindins fraletan ainana bandjan* (“the governor was accustomed to release one prisoner”); Mark XV.6.

[Col. 1169] *Bi* with the accusative: 2 Tim. IV.1 *ïesus skal stojan qivans jah dauþans bi qum* (*κατὰ τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν*, “Jesus shall judge the living and the dead at his appearing”) *ïs*.

“Note 5.—The accusative in 1 Cor. XVI.2 *ainwarjanoh* (*κατὰ μίαν*, “on every first [day]”) *sabbato warjizuh ïzvara fram sis silbin taujai* (“let each of you lay aside for himself on every Sabbath”) is conspicuous, in place of *and* with the accusative or the simple dative (see above b) bb); but perhaps *and warjanoh* should be read here, although in Luke IX.23 *dag wanoh* (*καθ᾽ ἡμέραν*, “daily”) stands.”
