bb) **During**, *bi* with the accusative: Mark XV.29 *o sa gatairands þo alh jah bi þrins dagans* (*ἐν τρισὶν ἡμέραις*, “O thou that destroyest the temple and in three days”) *gatimrjands þo* (“buildest it”); XIV.58 *alh bi þrins dagans* (*διὰ τριῶν ἡμερῶν*, “a temple through three days”) *gatimrja* (“I shall build”); Gal. II.1 *bi fidvortaihun jera usïddja aftra ïn ïairusaulyma* (“after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem”); Neh. V.18 *bi* (*ἀνόμεσον*, “within”) *·i· dagans gaf sein allai þizai filusnai* (“during ten days he provided for all this multitude”).

cc) **Under, during**, *bi* with the dative: Gothic Calendar *gaminþi marytre þize bi verekan papan ana gutþiudai gabrannidaize* (“commemoration of the martyrs burned in the land of the Goths under *verekan papan* [uncertain]”); *at* with the dative: Luke III.2 *at auhmistam gudjam* (*ἐπὶ ἀρχιερέων*, “under the high priests”) *annin jah kajafin varþ vaurd guþs at ïohannen* (“Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John”); *uf* with the dative: Mark II.26 *daveid galaiþ ïn gard guþs uf abjaþara gudjin* (*ἐπὶ Ἀβιάθαρ τοῦ ἀρχιερέως*, “David entered the house of God under Abiathar the high priest”); Luke IV.27; 1 Tim. VI.13; compare Luke III.23.

dd) **About, toward**, *bi* with the accusative: Matt. XXVII.46 *bi weila niundon* (*περὶ τὴν ἐννάτην ὥραν*, “about the ninth hour”) *ufhropida ïesus stibnai mikilai* (“Jesus cried with a loud voice”).

cc) **Before**, *faur* with the accusative: Matt. VIII.29 *qamt her faur mel* (*πρὸ καιροῦ*, “hast thou come here before the time”) *balvjan unsis* (“to torment us?”); XXVI.75 *faur hanins hruk þrim sinþam afaikis mik* (“before the cock crows, thou wilt deny me three times”); 2 Tim. I.9 *ansts guþs gibana ïst unsis faur mela aiveina* (“the grace of God was given to us before eternal times”), etc.; see Glossary, *Faur* I.

The opposite of the preceding, **after**, is *afar* with the dative in general, and in particular with the accusative: John XIII.27 *afar þamma hlaiba* (*μετὰ τὸ ψωμίον*, “after the morsel”) *galaiþ in ïudan satana* (“Satan entered into Judas”); Matt. XXVII.63 *afar þrins dagans* (*μετὰ τρεῖς ἡμέρας*, “after three days”) *urreisa* (“I shall rise”); XXVI.2 *afar tvans dagans paska vairþiþ* (“after two days the Passover takes place”); 1 Cor. XI.25 *nam stikl afar nahtamat* (“he took the cup after supper”), etc.; adding the formulas *afar leitil* and *afar ni filu*, “after a little time,” *afar þata*, “after that”; see Glossary, *Afar* I.A).

§ 248. II. SINCE WHEN?

Here we have only to note the temporal relation “from,” “out of,” from which [an action proceeds]; and indeed:

1) Among temporal adverbs, *ïupana* (“again”) belongs here: Gal. IV.9 *stabim ïupana skalkinon vileiþ* (“do ye desire again to be in bondage?”).

2) Among prepositions: *af* with the dative: Mark X.6 *af anastodeinai* (*ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς*, “from the beginning”) *gaskaftais gumein jah qinein gatavida guþ* (“of the creation, God made them male and female”); 2 Cor. VIII.10 *taujan dugunnuþ af fairnin jera* (“ye began to do [this] from the previous year”); but more commonly *fram* with the dative: Matt. IX.22 *ganas qino fram þizai weilai jainai* (*ἀπὸ τῆς ὥρας ἐκείνης*, “the woman was healed from that hour”); Col. I.9 *fram þamma daga ei hausidedum ni weilaidedum faur ïzvis bidjandans* (“from the day on which we heard [it], we have not ceased praying for you”); 2 Cor. IX.2 *axaja gamanvida ïst fram fairnin jera* (“Achaia has been prepared since the previous year”); Luke I.48 *fram himma nu audagjand mik alla kunja* (“from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed”); Mark XIII.19 *fram anastodeinai* (“from the beginning”); Luke II.36 *fram magaþein* (“from her virginity”), etc.; see Glossary, s.v. 2); *us* with the dative: John VI.66 *us þamma mela* (*ἐκ τούτου*, “from this [time]”) *managai galiþun siponje ïs ïbukai* (“many of his disciples went back”); 64 *vissa us frumistja ïesus, was* [Col. 1170] *ïst saei galeiveiþ ïna* (“Jesus knew from the beginning who it was that believed him”); *Skeireins* I.c *us anastodeinai* (“from the beginning”); John IX.1 *us gabaurþai* (“from birth”); Mark IX.21 *us barniskja* (“from childhood”); 2 Tim. III.15; *us jundai*, Mark X.20; Luke XVIII.21.

§ 249. III. FOR HOW LONG?

1) This determination of time, which differs from the preceding in that it indicates not merely the time in which or from which an action occurred, but presents a definite span and epoch of time, is expressed by the accusative: 2 Cor. XI.25 *naht jah dag* (*νυχθήμερον*, “a night and a day”) *ïin diupiþai vas mareins* (“I was in the deep of the sea”); 1 Cor. XVI.6 *at ïzvis vaitei salja aiþþau vintru visa* (*παραχειμάσω*, “I may remain with you or spend the winter”); John XI.6 *salida ïn þammei vas stada dagans tvans* (*δύο ἡμέρας*, “he remained in the place where he was two days”); Mark VIII.2; Luke IV.2 *tauhans vas ïn auþidai dage fidvortiguns* (*ἡμέρας τεσσαράκοντα*, “being in the wilderness forty days”; see § 198, 5) b)) *fraisans fram diabulau* (“tempted by the devil”); I.24 *aileisabaiþ galaugnida sik menoþs fimf* (*μῆνας πέντε*, “Elizabeth concealed herself five months”); 56; II.36 *anna vas framaldra dage magaize libandei miþ abin jera sibun* (*ἔτη ἑπτά*, “she had lived with a husband seven years from her virginity”); VIII.43; Mark V.25; Matt. IX.20 *qino bloþarinnandei ·ib· vintruns* (*δώδεκα ἔτη*, “a woman having an issue of blood twelve years”) *attaitok skauta vastjos ïesuis* (“touched the hem of Jesus’ garment”); Luke V.5 *alla naht þairharbaidjandans* (*δι᾽ ὅλης τῆς νυκτὸς κοπιάσαντες*, “having labored all night”) *waht ni nemum* (“we caught nothing”); Rom. X.21 *allana dag* (*ὅλην τὴν ἡμέραν*, “all the day”) *usbraidida handuns meinos du managein ungalaubjandein* (“I stretched out my hands unto a disobedient people”); Luke I.75; XX.9 *aflaiþ jera ganoha* (*χρόνους ἱκανούς*, “he went away for many years”); VIII.29 *manag mel* (*πολλοῖς χρόνοις*, “for many times”) *fravalv ïna* (“it had seized him”); John XIII.33 *nauh leitil mel* (*μικρόν*, “yet a little time”) *miþ ïzvis ïm* (“I am with you”); VII.23 *leitila weila* (*μικρὸν χρόνον*, “a little while”); XIV.9 *svalaud melis* (*τοσοῦτον χρόνον*, “so long a time”; see § 202, IV.1) *miþ ïzvis vas* (“I have been with you”); Luke VIII.27 *vair habaida unhulþons mela lagga* (*ἐκ χρόνων ἱκανῶν*, “for a long time he had demons”); Rom. VII.1 *vitoþ fraujinoþ mann sva lagga weila sve* (*ἐφ᾽ ὅσον χρόνον*, “the law has dominion over a man for as long time as”) *libaiþ* (“he lives”); 1 Cor. XVI.7 *venja mik wo weilo* (*χρόνον τινά*, “I hope to remain some time”) *saljan at ïzvis* (“with you”); VII.5; XV.30 *duwe bireikjai sijum weilo woh* (*πᾶσαν ὥραν*, “why are we in peril every hour?”).

2) To express how long a time is to last, and especially the limits within which it is restricted, prepositions are used:

a) *Du* with the dative: Luke IV.25 *galuknoda himins du jeram þrim* (*ἐπὶ ἔτη τρία*, “the heaven was shut up for three years”); especially in the formulas *du aiva* (John XII.34; XIV.16; XV.16; 2 Cor. IX.9) and *du aivam* (Rom. XI.36; 2 Cor. XI.31; Gal. I.5), “for ever” (*εἰς αἰῶνα* and *εἰς αἰῶνας*); *du weilai* (John V.35; Philem. 15), “for an hour” (*πρὸς ὥραν*); *du mela* (Luke VIII.13), “for a time” (*πρὸς καιρόν*); and *du leitilai weilai* (2 Cor. VII.8; *Skeireins* VI.a), *du leitilamma mela* (*Skeireins* IV.b), *du mela weilos*, 1 Thess. II.17.

“Note.—In place of *du* with the dative, the simple dative also occurs here: Luke XVIII.4 *ni vilda laggai weilai* (*ἐπὶ χρόνον*, ‘he would not for a long time’); or the accusative: thus Luke IV.25 *du jeram þrim* and *menoþs saihs* are indiscriminately interchanged.”

b) *In* with the accusative: John XII.7 *ïn dag* (*εἰς τὴν ἡμέραν*, “for the day”) *gafilhis meinis fastaida þata* (“she has kept this for the day of my burial”); 2 Tim. I.12; Luke I.33 *guþ þiudanoþ ufar garda ïakobis ïn ajukduþ* (“God shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever,” *εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας*); John VI.51, 58; likewise *ïn aivins*, “for ever,” Matt. VI.13; and *ïn aldins alde* or *aive*, Luke I.50; Eph. III.21; 1 Tim. I.17. Yet *ïn* with the dative is also found here: Eph. IV.30 *ahmin veihamma gasiglidai sijuþ ïn daga* [Col. 1171] (*εἰς ἡμέραν*, “be sealed with the Holy Spirit for the day”) *uslauseinais* (“of redemption”); 1 Thess. IV.15 *þai bilaibidans ïn quma* (*εἰς τὴν παρουσίαν*, “those remaining unto the coming”) *fraujins* (“of the Lord”); compare John XII.25.

c) *Und* with the accusative: 1 Cor. XVI.8 *visa ïn aifaison und paintekusten* (*ἕως τῆς πεντηκοστῆς*, “I shall remain in Ephesus until Pentecost”); Luke IV.13 *ustiuhands all fraistobnjo diabulus afstoþ fairra ïesua und mel* (“having completed every temptation, the devil departed from Jesus until a time”); 2 Cor. I.13 *venja ei und andi* (“I hope that unto the end”) *ufkunnaiþ* (“ye shall acknowledge”); Luke I.55 *svasve rodida du attam unsaraim und aiv* (“as he spoke to our fathers, unto eternity”); 1 Tim. VI.14 *fastai þo anabusn und qum* (*μέχρι τῆς ἐπιφανείας*, “keep the commandment until the appearing”) *fraujins* (“of the Lord”); Matt. XXVII.45 *fram saihston weilai varþ riqis ufar allai airþai und weila niundon* (“from the sixth hour darkness came over all the earth until the ninth hour”); 64 *hait vitan hlaiva und þridjan dag* (“command that the tomb be guarded until the third day”); 8 *haitans varþ akrs jains akrs bloþis und hina dag* (“that field was called the field of blood unto this day”), etc.; see Glossary, *Und* 2).

## I. DETERMINATION OF MEASURE

§ 250. 1) In relation to time, and in answer to the question **HOW OLD?**, there is used:

a) After *visan*, “to be old,” the genitive: Mark V.42 *mavi vas jere tvalibe* (*ἐτῶν δώδεκα*, “the girl was twelve years old”); Luke VIII.42 *vintrice tvalibe* (“a girl of twelve years”); III.23 *vas ïesus sve jere þrijetigive uf gakunþai* (“Jesus was about thirty years old at the beginning [of his ministry]”). Hence Luke I.7 *ba framaldra dage seinaize vesun* (“they both were advanced in their days”), in place of which verse 18 has *ïn dagam seinaim* (“in my days”).

b) After *vairþan*, “to become old,” “to grow old,” the accusative: Luke II.42 *varþ tvalib vintruns* (*ἐτῶν [ἔτη] δώδεκα*, “he became twelve years old”).

“Note 1.—From Luke III.23 it is apparent that *sve* expresses Gothic ‘about,’ ‘approximately,’ ‘toward,’ without changing the construction. Compare Luke IX.14 *vesun sve fimf þusundjos vaire* (‘there were about five thousand men’), or John VI.10 *þaruh anakumbidedun vairos raþjon* (‘there the men sat down in number’) *sve fimf þusundjos* (‘about five thousand’).”

2) In relation to place, in answer to the question **HOW EXTENSIVE?**, there is used:

a) The accusative: Matt. V.41 *jabai was þuk ananauþjai rasta aina* (*μίλιον ἕν*, “if anyone compels thee one mile”) *gaggais miþ ïmma tvos* (“go with him two”); Luke II.44 *qemum dagis vig* (*ἡμέρας ὁδόν*, “they had gone a day’s journey”).

b) *Ana* with the dative: John XI.18 *beþania newa ïairusaulymiam svasve ana spaurdim fimftaihunim* (*ἀπὸ σταδίων δεκάπεντε*, “Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away”).

3) The price—what a thing costs—is expressed:

a) By the dative: 1 Cor. VII.23 *vairþa galaubamma* (“with a great price,” *τιμῆς*) *usbauhtai sijuþ* (“ye were bought”); Matt. X.29 *niu tvai sparvans assarjau* (*ἀσσαρίου*, “are not two sparrows [sold] for an assarion?”) *bugjanda?*; John VI.7 *tvaimhundam skatte* (*διακοσίων δηναρίων*, “two hundred denarii”) *hlaibos ni ganohai sind* (“bread is not sufficient”).

b) By *ïn* with the accusative: Mark XIV.5 *maht vesi þata balsan frabugjan ïn managizo* (“this ointment could have been sold for more than”) *þau þrijahunda skatte* (“three hundred denarii”); John XII.5 *duwe þata balsan ni frabauht vas ïn ·t· skatte* (“why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii,” *τριακοσίων δηναρίων?*).

Conversely, to give a price **for** acquiring something, *ἀντί* (German *um, für, gegen*; French *pour, contre*) is Gothic *und* with the dative: Matt. XXVII.10 *atgebun þrinstiguns silubreinaize und akra kasjins* (“they gave thirty pieces of silver for the potter’s field”). Hence Rom. XII.17 *ubil und ubilamma usgiban* (“rendering evil for evil”) and Matt. V.38 *augo und augin jah tunþu und tunþau* (“eye for eye and tooth for tooth”).

4) In comparatives:

[Col. 1172] a) The amount **by which** one object surpasses another is expressed:

aa) By the dative: 2 Cor. XI.5 *man ni vaihtai* (“I am in nothing,” “in no respect,” *μηδέν*) *minnizo gataujan þaim ufar mikil visandam apaustaulum* (“inferior to the exceedingly great apostles”); XII.11; Matt. V.47 *we managizo taujiþ* (“what more do ye do?”); Mark VII.36 *wan filu ïs ïm anabauþ, mais þamma meridedun* (“the more he commanded them, so much the more they proclaimed [it]”). Hence also the expression “forty, one lacking,” *fidvortigjus ainamma vanai* = 39; see § 198, 3; or

bb) By *filu*, *filaus*, and also *und* with the accusative; see § 197, 3.

b) The object with which another is compared, and whose reciprocal relation is rendered in German by *als*, but in Latin by *quam*, the Goth expresses either with *þau* in the construction, see § 197, 4; or, omitting *þau*, by the dative (just as Greek uses the genitive and Latin the ablative): Matt. V.37 *sijai vaurd ïzvar ja ja, ne ne, ïþ þata managizo þaim* (“let your word be Yea, yea; Nay, nay; but what is more than these,” *quam hoc, τούτων*) *us þamma ubilin ïst* (“is from evil”); VI.25 *niu saivala mais ïst fodeinai* (*τῆς τροφῆς*, “is not life more than food”) *jah leik vastjom* (*τοῦ ἐνδύματος*, “and the body than clothing?”); 26 *niu jus mais vulþrizans sijuþ þaim?* (“are ye not of much more value than they?”); X.31 *managaim sparvam batizans sijuþ* (“ye are better than many sparrows”); John XV.18 *so manaseds mik fruman ïzvis fijaida* (“if the world hated me before you”); Luke XVI.8 *þai sunjus þis aivis frodozans sunum liuhadis* (*φρονιμώτεροι ὑπὲρ τοὺς υἱούς*, “the children of this age [are] wiser than the children of light”); John V.36 *ïk haba veitvodiþa maizein þamma ïohanne* (“I have testimony greater than John’s”; properly it ought to be *þizai ïohannes*, although this brevity of expression is not foreign to the Greeks either; Matthiae, *Gr. gr.* § 453). So also Matt. III.11; X.31; XI.9, 11; XXVII.64; Mark I.7; XII.31, 33; Luke III.16; VII.26; IX.13; John VII.31; VIII.53; X.29; XIII.16; XIV.12; XV.13; 1 Cor. X.22; XV.10; 2 Cor. XI.5; XII.11; 1 Tim. V.8.

“Note 2.—For the object with which another is compared to be put in the dative, it is necessary that the preceding construction be in the nominative or accusative; apart from these cases this construction is not to be employed, but *þau* must be used, as Matt. V.20 *managizo vairþai ïzvaraizos garaihteins þau þize bokarje* (‘unless your righteousness exceed that of the scribes’); Luke X.14, etc.”

## OBSERVATIONS ON PREPOSITIONS

“§ 251. Note 1.—Prepositions by their nature precede, and indeed immediately, the cases which they govern; nor does this rule admit any exceptions, except when prepositions placed at the beginning of a sentence can be separated from their cases especially by enclitics: John XVIII.34 *abu* (for *af-u*, ‘from-thou’) *þus* (“from thyself”); XIX.12 *framuh þamma* (“from him”); Luke X.21 *ïnuh þizai weilai* (“in that hour”); likewise by particles which cannot stand at the beginning of a sentence, such as *þan*, *raihtis*, *auk*: *Skeireins* II.d *at raihtis mann* (“at once [a] man”); Matt. VIII.5 *afaruh þan þata* (“after then that”); Mark XVI.12; Luke I.24; X.1; XVIII.4; VII.21 *ïnuh þan þizai weilai* (“in then that hour”); X.7; VI.45 *uzuh* (for *usuh*) *allis ufarfullein* (“out of all fullness”); 2 Cor. X.13 *und jah* (“even unto”) *ïzvis* (“you”). That *du* with the infinitive has the same character, see § 254, Note 1. Indeed, a preposition may be separated even from compound verbs: Luke XVIII.8 *biugitai*; Matt. IX.28 *ga u laubjats*; Mark VIII.23 *gau wa sewi*; see on Matt. IX.28; John XVI.28 *uzuhïddja*; XI.41 *uzuhhof*; VI.22 *miþ ni qam*; [Col. 1173] Luke XX.25 *us nu gibiþ*; Mark XIV.44 *atuh þan gaf*; XVI.8 *dizuh þan sat.*

“Conversely, one also says: John V.46 *bi mik auk* (‘for concerning me’), although the Greek has *περὶ γὰρ ἐμοῦ*; 1 Cor. IX.9 *ïn vitoda auk mosezis* (‘for in the law of Moses’); *Skeireins* II.d *us saivalai raihtis jah leika* (‘out of soul and body alike’); 2 Cor. X.14 *unte jah und ïzvis* (‘for even unto you’); compare § 213, Note 1.

“Note 2.—Where the same preposition refers to two or more objects, it is put only once: Mark III.8 *þai bi tyra jah seidona* (*οἱ περὶ Τύρον καὶ Σειδῶνα*, ‘those around Tyre and Sidon’); *Skeireins* II.d *manna ussatiþs ïst us saivalai jah leika* (‘man is composed of soul and body’); 1 Cor. XIV.21 *ïn anþaraim razdom jah vairilom anþaraim rodja* (‘in other tongues and with other lips I shall speak’), whereas Greek has *ἐν ἑτερογλώσσοις καὶ ἐν χείλεσιν ἑτέροις*; Rom. VII.6 *skalkinom in niujiþai ahmins jah ni fairniþai bokos* (‘we serve in newness of spirit and not in oldness of letter’); 2 Tim. II.14 *vaurdam veihan du ni vaihtai daug niba usvalteinai* (‘to contend about words, useful for nothing except subversion’), etc. Likewise in apposition the preposition is omitted: Rom. XIII.9 *jabai wo anþaraizo anabusne ïn þamma vaurda usfulljanda, þamma* (that is, ‘in this [word],’ Greek *ἐν τῷ*) *frijos newundjan þeinana sve þuk silban* (‘thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself’). Hence probably the reason why, when a word compounded with a preposition is to be used twice in a sentence, the second occurrence is simply introduced in Gothic: Rom. XV.4 *sva fila sve fauragameliþ varþ* (*προεγράφη*, ‘as many things as were written before’) *du unsarai laiseinai gameliþ varþ* (*προεγράφη*, ‘were written for our instruction’); 1 Cor. XV.48, 49 *þai ufarhiminakundans* (*ἐπουράνιοι*, ‘the heavenly ones’)—*þis himinakundins* (*τοῦ ἐπουρανίου*, ‘of the heavenly [one]’), etc.; see on 1 Tim. VI.6.

“Yet sometimes the preposition, just as in the Greek text, is repeated in Gothic: Luke II.44 *sokidedun ïna ïn ganiþjam jah ïn kunþam* (‘they sought him among relatives and among acquaintances’), where the Goth probably read the second *ἐν* in his manuscript; likewise Mark VI.26 *ïn þize aiþe jah ïn þize miþanakumbjandane ni vilda ïzai ufbrikan* (‘because of the oaths and because of those reclining with him, he would not reject her’); Luke VIII.34 *gataihun ïn baurg jah ïn veihsa* (‘they reported [it] in the city and in the country’); Col. I.26 *runa gafulgina vas fram aivam jah fram aldim* (‘the mystery had been hidden from ages and from generations’); III.17 *ïn vaurda aiþþau ïn vaurstva* (‘in word or in deed’); 1 Thess. II.1, 9; 1 Tim. IV.16; also where no Greek text precedes: Mark V.16 *spillodedun waiva varþ bi þana vodan jah bi þo sveina* (‘they related what had happened concerning the possessed man and concerning the swine’), etc.; 2 Cor. V.12, Codex A has *þai ïn andvairþja wopandaus jan-ni ïn hairtin* (‘those who boast in appearance and not in heart’), where Codex B omits the second *ïn*. In apposition: *Skeireins* II.d *manna us missaleikom vistim ussatiþs ïst, us saivalai raihtis jah leika* (‘man is constituted from various substances, namely soul and body’). The repetition is regular when the preposition refers to more than two objects: John XVI.8 *gasakiþ þo manaseþ bi fravaurht jah bi garaihtiþa jah bi staua* (‘he shall convict the world concerning sin, and concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment’); Col. II.16 *ni manna ïzvis bidomjai ïn mata aiþþau ïn dragka aiþþau ïn dailai dagis* (‘let no one judge you in food, or in drink, or in respect of a feast day’); 1 Tim. II.1, 2. Yet even in this case the preposition is omitted the second time but repeated the third: Matt. VIII.9 *qiþa du þamma—jah anþaramma—jah du skalka* (‘I say to one—and to another—and to [my] servant’), although Greek uses the simple dative everywhere; likewise at the parallel Luke VII.8; Mark VI.56 *ïddja ïn haimos aiþþau baurgs aiþþau ïn veihsa* (‘he went into houses or cities or the countryside’), while the Greek text commonly has *εἰς* only once; Matt. V.45 *guþ sunnon seina urranneiþ ana ubilans jah godans, jah rigneiþ ana* [Col. 1174] *garaihtans jah ana ungaraihtans* (‘God makes his sun rise upon evil and good, and sends rain upon righteous and unrighteous’), Greek *ἐπὶ δικαιους καὶ ἀδίκους*.

“In this case the Goth also sometimes uses elsewhere synonymous prepositions: Col. IV.13 *aipafras habaiþ manag aljan bi ïzvis jah du þans* (*ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν καὶ τῶν*, ‘Epaphras has much labor for you and for those’) *þaiei sind ïn laudeikaia jah ïairaupaulein* (‘who are in Laodicea and Hierapolis’); 1 Thess. V.9 *ni satida uns guþ ïn hatis ak du gafreideinai* (*εἰς ὀργὴν, ἀλλ᾽ εἰς ἐπιποίησιν*, ‘God did not appoint us unto wrath but unto the obtaining’) *ganistais* (‘of salvation’); 2 Cor. VIII.7 *ïn allamma managniþ, galaubeinai jah vaurda jah kunþja jah ïn allai usdaudein jah ana þizai us ïzvis ïn uns friaþvai* (‘in all abundance—in faith and speech and knowledge and all diligence and in your love toward us’), though Greek has *ἐν* only once.

“Note 3.—While on the one hand the Goth sometimes seems to avoid compounding the verb, after Greek fashion, with the preposition that precedes the object, thus saying simply 2 Cor. VI.16 *baua ïn ïm* (‘I shall dwell in them’) for *ἐνοικήσω ἐν αὐτοῖς*; 2 Tim. I.5; Mark VI.14 *vaurkjand ïn ïmma* (‘they work in him’) for *ἐνέργουσιν ἐν αὐτῷ*; or 2 Cor. VIII.18 *miþsandidedun ïmma* (‘we sent with him’) for *συνεπέμψαμεν μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ*—on the other hand he very often falls into the same pleonasm: Matt. XXVII.53 *usgaggan us hlaivasnom* (*ἐξελθεῖν ἐκ τῶν μνημείων*, ‘to come out of the tombs’); Mark I.29; V.2, 30; IX.25; Luke IV.22; John VIII.59; X.39; 1 Cor. V.10; 2 Cor. V.8; VI.17; Eph. IV.29; Col. III.8; Matt. IX.15 *bruþfaþs afnimada af ïm* (*ἀπαρθῇ ἀπ᾽ αὐτῶν*, ‘the bridegroom be taken away from them’); Luke V.2, 13, 35; IX.5; XVI.3; Rom. XI.26; 2 Cor. XII.8; Luke XVII.11 *þairhïddja þairh midja samarian* (‘he went through the midst of Samaria’); IV.30; XVIII.35, where the Goth read *διελθεῖν*; Mark XI.16; Col. II.13 *miþgaqivida miþ ïmma* (‘he made [us] alive together with him’); John XIII.25 *anakumbida ana barma ïesuis* (‘he reclined upon Jesus’ breast’); Eph. II.20; Luke IV.14 *all gavi bisitande bi ïna* (‘all the region around him’); 1 Cor. XV.27 *ufhnaivida uf fotuns* (‘he subjected [all things] under [his] feet’); Eph. I.21; Luke I.76 *fauragaggis faur andvairþja* (‘thou shalt go before the face’). Likewise there are adverbs of the same sense: *ïnnatgaggan ïin*—(Matt. VIII.23), *usvairpan ut*—(Matt. XXVI.75), *usgaggan ut us*—(Mark I.25), etc.

“But the Goth also very often uses this pleonasm—which Greek more frequently displays—where nothing corresponds to it in the Greek: that is, where Greek either uses the preposition once only, or employs a simple verb and a preposition: Rom. XI.26 *urrinniþ us sion* (‘there shall come out of Zion’), Greek simply *ἥξει ἐκ Σιών*; John XVII.15 *ni bidja ei usnimais* (‘I pray not that thou shouldest take’) *ïns us þamma fairwau* (‘them out of the world’); Gal. V.4 *us anstai usdrusuþ* (‘ye have fallen out of grace’), Greek *χάριτος ἐξεπέσατε*; Luke VIII.18 *afnimada af ïmma* (‘it shall be taken away from him’), Greek *ἀρθήσεται ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ*; Mark II.23 *þairhïddja þairh atisk* (‘he went through the cornfields’), Greek *παραπορεύεται διά ...*; John XVIII.15 *miþïnngalaiþ miþ ïesua* (‘he entered in with Jesus’), Greek *συνεισῆλθε τῷ ...*; likewise Matt. VII.25; Mark V.10; Luke III.20; VI.48; VIII.2; IX.33; XIV.10; XVII.29; John XII.42; Rom. VIII.35, 39; 2 Cor. XI.25; Gal. I.6; Eph. IV.31; Phil. III.14; Col. II.14.

“Prepositions which are different but synonymous are also used in this way: Matt. VIII.16 *atberun du ïmma* (*προσηνεγκαν αὐτῷ*, ‘they brought [them] to him’); XXVII.15 *atgaggand du peilatau* (*προσελθὼν τῷ Πιλάτῳ*, ‘having come to Pilate’); John VIII.42 *ïk fram guþa urrann* (*ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐξῆλθον*, ‘I came forth from God’); Mark XVI.8 *usgaggandeins af hlaiva* (*ἐξελθοῦσαι ἀπό ...*, ‘having gone out from the tomb’) *gaþlauhun* (‘they fled’); Luke II.37 *ni afïddja fairra alh* [Col. 1175] (*ἀφίστατο ἀπό ...*, ‘she did not depart from the temple’); 2 Cor. XII.9 *ufarhleiþrjai ana mis* (*ἐπισκηνώσῃ ἐπ᾽ ἐμέ*, ‘may rest upon me’) *mahts xristaus* (‘the power of Christ’), etc.

“Note 4.—Besides certain prepositions which, as determinate forms, assume the form of adverbs, such as *ïnn* from *ïn*, *us*, there are others which, lacking that form, are nevertheless used as adverbs: Mark VIII.23 *atlagida ana handuns* (‘laying [his] hands upon [him]’) *imponens* [Latin: “placing”]—that is, “he laid hands upon him” (*ἐπιθεὶς τὰς χεῖρας*); XI.7; Luke XIX.28 *ïddja fram* (*ἐπορεύετο ἔμπροσθεν*, ‘he went before’); Mark VIII.6 *atgaf hlaibans siponjam ei atlagidedeina faur* (*παραθῶσι*, ‘he gave bread to the disciples that they might set [it] before [them]’); Luke XIX.4 *biþragjands faur* (*προδραμὼν ἔμπροσθεν*, ‘having run ahead before’) *usstaig ana bagm* (‘he climbed up into a tree’); VIII.44 *qino atgaggandei du* (*προσελθοῦσα*, ‘a woman having come unto [him]’) *attaitok skauta vastjos* (‘touched the hem of his garment’), instead of *duatgaggandei* (as in the Greek of Matt. IX.20) or *atgaggandei du ïmma* (as in the Greek of Luke IX.12); Mark X.13 *sipunjos sokun þaim bairandam du* (*τοῖς προσφέρουσι*, ‘the disciples rebuked those bringing [them] to [him]’); 2 Cor. VIII.11 *faura ïst muns* (‘there is willingness beforehand’); Phil. III.14 *þoei faura sind* (‘the things which are before’).”

## 2. VERBAL OBJECT

§ 252. Since the infinitive, which expresses the abstract idea of the action or state denoted by a verb, is nominal in nature (§ 189), it can therefore serve as an object.

Accordingly, it is placed after verbs:

1) Of wishing: Matt. 5:42, “from him who wishes to borrow from you, do not turn away”; Luke 15:28, “he would not go in”; 1 Tim. 1:6 f., “some, having turned aside to empty talk, wishing to be teachers of the law”; Luke 10:22; 20:46; John 6:67; 8:44; Rom. 9:22; 2 Cor. 11:32; 1 Cor. 7:12, “if a wife is willing to dwell with him, let him not leave the wife”; Phil. 1:23, “I have a desire to depart and to be with Christ”; Luke 15:16, “he desired to eat husks”; 17:22; 2 Cor. 5:2; 1 Thess. 3:6; 2 Tim. 1:4; Luke 19:4, “and he purposed [thought] to go”; 10:1; John 6:15; 14:22; John 6:6, “Jesus knew what he himself intended [had in his will] to do”; 71; 12:26; 2 Cor. 12:14, “I am ready to come to you.”

2) [After verbs] expressing an act of will, such as to attempt, seek, decide, give, permit, forbid, compel, ask, command, exhort, etc.: Gal. 2:10, “they urged [us] to do this very thing”; Eph. 4:3; Luke 6:19, “all the multitude sought to touch him”; 9:9; 17:33; 19:3, 47; John 7:1; 19:12; Rom. 10:3; Luke 6:42, “first cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to cast out the mote in your brother’s eye”; 1 Cor. 5:3, “I have determined that the one who has thus done this be delivered to Satan”; Mark 15:23, “they gave him wine mixed with myrrh to drink”; Rom. 15:5, “may God grant you to think the same among yourselves”; Eph. 3:16; 2 Tim. 1:18; Matt. 8:21, “allow me to go and bury my father”; Luke 8:32; 9:59; 1 Tim. 2:12; Luke 18:16, “allow the children to come to me”; 4:41; 8:51; Matt. 8:22; John 11:44; 18:8; Gal. 5:7, “who hindered you from obeying the truth?”; 1 Thess. 2:16, “the Jews forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles”; Gal. 6:12, “as many as wish to make a fair showing in the flesh, these compel you to be circumcised”; Luke 14:23; Gal. 2:14, “why do you compel the Gentiles to live as Jews?”; Luke 8:37, “all the people of the district asked him to depart from them”; 2 Cor. 5:20, “we ask on Christ’s behalf: be reconciled to God”; 1 Tim. 2:1, “I ask, first of all, that prayers be made”; Luke 8:41; 9:38; Rom. 12:1; 2 Cor. 2:8; Eph. 4:1; Phil. 4:2; 1 Thess. 4:10; 5:12; 1 Tim. 1:3; Luke 8:29, “Jesus commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man”; 8:55, “he commanded that food be given to her”; 8:31; 1 Cor. 7:10; Matt. 27:64, “command that the tomb be secured”; 2 Tim. 1:6, “I remind you to rekindle the gift of God.”

3) After verbs of saying, and many verbs expressing an intellectual action, such as to know, deny, learn, teach, understand, believe, think, etc.; moreover to hope, fear, be ashamed, attempt, etc.: 1 Tim. 2:10, “which is fitting for women professing reverence for God, through good works”; Tit. 1:16, “they profess to know God”; John 13:38, “to know [acknowledge] me after you have denied [me]”; Luke 3:7, “who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?”; *Skeireins* V.d, “not equal but like oaths, he teaches, are to be rendered by us”; 1 Tim. 5:4, “if any widow has children, let them learn to care first for their own household” (*doceant se*, that is, “let them teach themselves,” i.e. “learn”); 5:13; 1 Tim. 1:19, “Hymenaeus and Alexander I handed over to Satan, that they might be taught not to blaspheme”; 1 Cor. 4:6, “that in us you may learn not beyond what is written”; Phil. 4:12, “I have learned both to be humbled and to abound”; 1 Thess. 4:4, “that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in holiness”; Rom. 7:18, “I do not find [how] to perform the good”; 7:10; 2 Cor. 10:2, “I trust that I shall dare [to act] against some”; John 16:2, “everyone who kills you will think that he offers service to God”; Phil. 3:4; Rom. 14:2, “one believes that he may eat all things.”

Luke 6:34, “if you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what reward is there for you?” Phil. 2:23; 1 Tim. 3:14; 2 Cor. 10:15, “we have great hope concerning you”; Luke 9:45, “they feared to ask him about this saying”; 16:3, “I am ashamed to beg”; 2 Cor. 1:8; Luke 20:40, “they no longer dared to question him”; 1 Cor. 6:1; 2 Cor. 10:12; *Skeireins* IV.d, “they acknowledged the Father and the Son to be one another [i.e. mutually].”

4) After “begin,” “continue,” “love” (that is, “be accustomed”), “cease,” “complete”: Luke 14:29–30, “if he has laid a foundation and cannot finish, all who see [it] begin to mock him, saying, ‘This man began to build and could not finish’”; Mark 14:65; Luke 9:12, 18; 2 Cor. 3:1; 8:10; Luke 20:11, “again he sent another servant”; 20:12; Matt. 6:5, “they love to pray standing in the synagogues”; Luke 7:45, “since I entered, she has not ceased to kiss my feet”; 2 Cor. 8:11, “now also complete the doing [of it].”

5) After “ought,” “it is necessary,” “there is need,” “it is permitted”: John 3:30, “he must increase, but I must decrease”; 7:35, 39, etc.; see Glossary, s.v. *Skulan*. Gal. 5:3, “every man who is circumcised is bound to perform the whole law.” To express the passive, *skulds im* is used: Mark 8:31, “the Son of Man must be rejected by the elders”; see §177, note 4d. And where things are concerned, *skuld ist* is used: Luke 6:2, “why do you do what is not permitted to do on the Sabbath days?” 4:9; 15:32; 20:22; 2 Cor. 11:30; 2 Thess. 3:7; 1 Tim. 3:15; and also impersonally: Luke 6:4, “it is not permitted to eat the loaves of setting forth except for priests alone”; Luke 14:18, “I bought land and must go and see it”; 1 Thess. 4:9; Phil. 2:25, “I thought it necessary to send Epaphroditus to you”; 2 Cor. 9:5, “I considered it necessary to ask the brothers to go beforehand to you”; 12:1, “boasting is indeed not beneficial”; 1 Cor. 7:26, “it is good for a man to be thus”; Mark 9:45, “it is good for you to enter into life lame rather than, having two feet, to be cast into Gehenna”; 9:47; Luke 18:25; Luke 3:16, “one stronger than I is coming, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to untie”; 20:35; 2 Cor. 3:5; 2 Tim. 2:2.

6) After “be able,” “can,” “be easy,” “be difficult”: Matt. 5:36, “you cannot make one hair white or black”; 6:24, “no one can serve two masters”; 6:27; Mark 15:31, etc.; see Glossary, s.v. *Magan*. 2 Cor. 9:8, “God is able to make all grace abound toward you”; Rom. 8:39, “nor is any other creature able to separate us from the love of God”; Luke 14:31; Tit. 1:9; Luke 14:14, “they do not have [the means] to repay you”; Eph. 4:28; Matt. 9:6, “the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”; John 19:10, “I have authority to crucify you”; Luke 9:1, “Jesus gave the apostles power and authority to heal diseases”; 5:24; 10:19; John 10:18; Rom. 9:21; 1 Cor. 9:4; Mark 10:24–25, “how difficult it is for those trusting in riches to enter the kingdom of God. It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God”; Mark 2:23, “it happened that he passed through the cornfields.”

“Note 1.—But when the object (the infinitive) is expressed not by a special verb, but by *visan* or *vairþan* together with a noun, the noun, where its meaning (a state or quality) is referred to the subject itself, is put in the nominative: 1 Tim. 3:2, ‘a bishop must be blameless’; 2 Tim. 2:24, ‘the servant of the Lord must not quarrel but be gentle’; *Skeireins* I.d, ‘the preaching of the Gospel was destined to become the destruction of wisdom according to its own likeness’; 1 Cor. 12:22, ‘those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary’; subscription to 1 Corinthians, ‘to the Corinthians, the first, it is thought to have been written from Asia’; Gal. 2:9, ‘Peter and James and John were regarded as pillars’; Phil. 4:12, ‘I have learned to be content and hungry.’ Hence also 4:11, ‘I have taught myself to be content,’ because *galaisida mik* (“I taught myself”) is equivalent to *lais* (“I learned”).

“Conversely, 2 Cor. 7:11 reads, ‘you proved yourselves to be pure’; and naturally Luke 20:20, ‘they sent spies, pretending themselves to be righteous.’ But in 2 Cor. 5:8, ‘we are confident and prefer to depart from the body and to be at home with the Lord,’ the dative occurs because *unsis* must be supplied after *valjam*. Rom. 9:3, however, ‘I myself wished to be accursed from Christ for my brothers,’ is a Greek construction.”

“Note 2.—After the verbs listed under number 4, a participle is also used: Matt. 11:1, ‘Jesus finished instructing the twelve’; Luke 5:4, ‘when Jesus had finished speaking, he said to Simon’; Col. 1:9, ‘from the day on which we heard [it], we have not ceased to pray for you’; Gal. 6:9, ‘let us not grow weary while doing good.’ Conversely, after *sveiban* an infinitive is employed (Luke 7:45), while in Eph. 1:16 ‘not ceasing’ is rendered by a participle, *unsveibands* (οὐ παυόμενος), ‘giving thanks for you.’”

“Note 3.—After the above-mentioned verbs, *ei* or *þatei* also occurs in place of the infinitive; see §§276, 277.”

## §253. Verbal object

When, besides the infinitive, there is another object to which the action is ascribed, this must be put in the accusative, and the construction is called the accusative with infinitive. [Note: In German, a subordinate clause with *dass* and an infinitive must be formed. Translator.] But where the personal subject and object are the same person, Gothic stands midway between Greek and Latin construction: either the personal object, a pronoun, is omitted, or it is put in the accusative; the latter construction occurring only in the Epistles. The accusative with infinitive is used:

1) After verbs of perception: Phil. 2:26, “he was distressed because you heard him to be sick”; John 6:62, “you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before”; Mark 13:29.

2) After verbs of saying, commanding, writing, etc.: Luke 9:19, “whom do the crowds say that I am?” 20:27, “the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection”; 20:41; John 12:29; 2 Cor. 4:6; Matt. 8:18, “Jesus commanded the disciples to depart to the other side of the sea”; 1 Tim. 6:13 f., “I command you to keep the commandment”; 1 Cor. 5:11, “I wrote to you not to associate”: in the first instance *izwis* is dative, “I write to you”; in the second it is accusative, “that you should not associate yourselves” [not “be associated”]; Eph. 3:5 f., “it has been revealed to the apostles that the Gentiles are fellow-heirs, fellow-members, and fellow-partakers of the promise.”

3) After verbs expressing volition or any other operation of the mind, such as to wish, seek, think, believe, trust, hope, know, etc.: Mark 15:9, “do you wish [me] to release to you the king of the Jews?” 19:15, “we do not wish this man to reign over us”; 1:62; 1 Cor. 7:7, “I wish all people to be as I myself [am]”; 10:20; 11:3; Gal. 6:13; 1 Tim. 2:4, 8; 5:14; John 7:4, “no one does anything in secret while seeking himself to be publicly known” (αὐτὸς ἐν παρρησίᾳ εἶναι); Phil. 3:7–8, “what was gain to me, this I counted to be loss for Christ. Yet indeed I count all things to be loss because of the surpassing worth of the knowledge of Christ … and I count all things to be refuse”; *Skeireins* VIII.b, “they considered the Lord’s teaching to have been made known beforehand to all humankind”; 1 Cor. 7:26, “I consider this to be good”; 2 Cor. 11:5, “I consider myself in no respect inferior to the very eminent apostles” (λογίζομαι … ὑστερηκέναι); Phil. 1:16, “preaching Christ out of rivalry, thinking to add affliction to my bonds” (οἰόμενοι … ἐπιφέρειν); 3:13; Luke 2:44, “Joseph and Mary, thinking him to be in the company, came a day’s journey”; 1 Tim. 6:5; Luke 20:6, “all firmly believe John to be a prophet”; 2 Cor. 10:7, “if anyone trusts himself to be Christ’s” (πέποιθεν ἑαυτῷ … εἶναι); Luke 4:41, “they knew him to be the Christ”; 1 Cor. 16:7, “I hope to remain with you for some time” (ἐλπίζω … ἐπιμεῖναι); 2 Cor. 5:11.

4) After verbs of making, doing, preparing: Mark 1:17, “I will make you become fishers of people”; Luke 5:34; John 5:21; John 6:10, “make the people recline”; 2 Cor. 9:5, “to arrange beforehand that your blessing should be ready as a blessing and not as an exaction.”

5) After impersonal expressions and formulas—“it happens,” “it comes to pass,” “it is fitting,” “it is easy,” “it is better,” “it is time,” etc.: Luke 4:36, “all came to be amazed”; Col. 1:19, “in him all fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things”; *Skeireins* I.c, “it was fitting that those obeying the same deceiving devil should in turn be made subject to the same will by the Saviour’s teaching”; Luke 16:17, “it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of the law to fall”; John 18:14, “it is better that one man perish for the people”; Rom. 13:11, “it is time for us to arise from sleep.”

“Note 1.—After *varþ*, *aglu ist*, *azetizo ist*, and similar expressions, the simple infinitive is also used where a personal object is connected with these formulas and is in the dative; see §252.6. Likewise after *letan*, *bidjan*, and similar verbs; see ibid., 2), although, from the construction of the words in 2 Cor. 6:1, *bidjand ni svarei anst guþs niman izwis*—where in our translation ‘to you’ must be read—the accusative with infinitive might seem possible here as well.”

“Note 2.—After verbs of perception and those expressing an operation of the mind, a participle also occurs in place of the infinitive, after Greek usage: Luke 4:23, ‘all that we heard had happened’ (ὅσα ἠκούσαμεν γενόμενα) in Capernaum; 5:2; 18:36; Mark 12:28; 13:26; 14:58, 62, 67; John 7:32; 10:12; 2 Thess. 3:11; Mark 5:15, ‘they see the demon-possessed man sitting, clothed, and in his right mind’ (θεωροῦσι τὸν δαιμονιζόμενον καθήμενον); 2:16; 8:24; 9:1, 38; Luke 5:1, 27; 10:18; 18:24; John 6:19; 11:33; 1 Cor. 8:10; Luke 8:46, ‘power known [to have gone] out from me’ (ἐξελθοῦσαν); Mark 7:30, ‘he found the demon gone out’ (ἐξεληλυθός) ‘and the daughter lying’ (βεβλημένη) ‘on the bed’; Luke 8:35. Hence the passive nominative in *Skeireins* VIII.c, ‘found lying’; Phil. 4:9. After *viljan*, the two constructions are found joined: 1 Tim. 2:8–9, ‘I wish men to pray’ (προσεύχεσθαι) ‘… likewise women to adorn themselves in decent apparel’ (κοσμεῖν). After *vitan*, in 2 Cor. 12:2–3, a participle and *þatei* are introduced in turn: ‘I know a man in Christ, fourteen years ago, caught up’ (ἁρπαγέντα) ‘to the third heaven; and I know such a man, that he was caught up’ (ὅτι ἡρπάγη) ‘into paradise.’

“This construction after *qiþan* is unusual, and it does not occur after *vairþan*, except where the Gothic translator could not use another auxiliary verb, *visan*: 2 Tim. 2:18, ‘saying that the resurrection has already occurred’ (γεγονέναι); hence Rom. 15:8, ‘I say that Christ became a minister of circumcision’ (γεγενῆσθαι), ‘but [that] the Gentiles glorify God.’

“Note 3.—In Gothic too, as in German, the verbal object is often expressed periphrastically by *ei* or *þatei*; see §§275, 276.”

## §254. The supine and gerund

Gothic does not know the supine or the gerund, and expresses both by the infinitive, commonly preceded by *du*.

### I. To express the supine, there is used

1) The simple infinitive, especially after verbs of motion or indicating motion. [Note: In German, by *zu*, *um zu*, French *pour*, and the infinitive. Translator.] Luke 1:76, “you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways”; 1 Tim. 1:15, “Christ came into the world to save sinners”; 1 Thess. 2:17, “we eagerly desired to see your face”; 2 Tim. 4:9; Luke 1:79, “to shine upon those who sit in darkness”; 2:22, “they brought the child to Jerusalem to present [him] before the Lord”; and elsewhere: Eph. 6:19, “that utterance may be given to me, with boldness to make known the mystery of the Gospel”; 1:9–10.

2) More commonly, however, with *du* prefixed: Luke 4:18, “the Lord sent me to heal the broken-hearted, to proclaim release to the captives, to send the oppressed away in freedom, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.” Before the second infinitive *du* is absent, either because the construction changes, or because, where the preposition is related to several objects, we have seen that it is placed only once (§251.2). 1 Thess. 3:5; Luke 4:29, “they brought him to the brow of the hill to cast him down” (εἰς τὸ κατακρημνίσαι); 5:4, “let down the nets for a catch” (εἰς ἄγραν); Mark 4:3, “the sower went out to sow” (τοῦ σπεῖραι); Luke 8:5; Rom. 11:26; Matt. 11:1, “Jesus departed from there to teach and preach” (τοῦ διδάσκειν); 1 Thess. 4:17, “caught up in clouds to meet the Lord in the air” (εἰς ἀπάντησιν); Luke 5:1, “the crowd pressed upon Jesus to hear the word of God” (τοῦ ἀκούειν); Phil. 4:10, “your concern for me has at last flourished again” (τὸ φρονεῖν); Mark 10:46 and Luke 18:35, “a blind man sat by the way begging,” Greek προσαίτων, whereas in John 9:8 *sat aihtronds* (“sat begging”) occurs; similarly the expression *ausona haban du hausjan* (“to have ears to hear,” Luke 8:8) alternates freely with *hausjandona* (“hearing,” Mark 4:9; Luke 14:35), while Greek always uses the infinitive.

Luke 19:48, “the people hung upon him to hear him” (ἀκούειν); 4:18, “the Lord anointed me to preach good news to the poor” (κηρῦξαι); Mark 7:4, “there are many other things which they received to observe” (κρατεῖν); Luke 14:28, “sitting down, he calculates whether he has [enough] to complete [it]” (εἰς ἀπαρτισμόν).

1 Cor. 7:25, “I give my judgment as one having received mercy from the Lord to be faithful” (πιστὸς εἶναι); 2 Cor. 11:2, “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present [you] as a pure virgin to Christ” (παραστῆσαι); Phil. 3:10, “[righteousness] from God is on the basis of faith, to know him” (τοῦ γνῶναι); Luke 1:77; Col. 1:22, “having reconciled [you] through death, to present you holy before him”; 4:3, “pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ” (λαλῆσαι). Especially in rendering Greek εἰς τό: Mark 14:55, “the whole council sought testimony against Jesus in order to put him to death” (εἰς τὸ θανατῶσαι); 2 Thess. 2:2, “we ask you, brothers, not to be quickly shaken in mind”; Rom. 7:5; 11:11; 12:2–3; 15:8; 1 Cor. 8:10; 11:22; 2 Cor. 1:4; 7:3; 1 Thess. 2:12, 16; 3:5, 13; 4:9; 2 Thess. 1:5; 3:9; in rendering πρὸς τό: Matt. 5:28, “everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery”; 6:1; Mark 13:22; in rendering ἐπὶ τῷ: 1 Cor. 11:21, “each one takes his own meal beforehand for eating” (ἐπὶ τῷ φαγεῖν); in rendering ἕνεκα τοῦ: 2 Cor. 7:12, “I wrote not for the sake of the wrongdoer, nor for the sake of the wronged, but in order to make manifest” (ἕνεκεν τοῦ φανερωθῆναι) “our earnestness.” Likewise *Skeireins* IV.d: “Now the accusations were from John, not in order that he might make known the Lord’s greatness, but to rebuke and accuse the arrogance of the scribes and Pharisees.” In rendering ἵνα: Mark 3:14, “Jesus appointed twelve to be with him” (ἵνα ὦσι).

“Note 1.—Sometimes *du* is separated from its infinitive by an object dependent on it: Rom. 7:5, ‘to bear fruit’; 11:11, ‘to provoke [them] to jealousy’; Phil. 4:10, ‘to be concerned for me’; 1 Cor. 8:10; 2 Thess. 1:5; 2:2; *Skeireins* II.c.

“Note 2.—Sometimes *du* with the infinitive is employed instead of the simple infinitive (cf. §252), usually where Greek precedes with τό, τοῦ, or εἰς τό: Luke 4:10, ‘he will command his angels concerning you to guard you’ (τοῦ διαφυλάξαι); John 13:24, ‘Peter signalled to him to ask’ (πυθέσθαι); 1 Thess. 4:9, ‘you are taught by God to love one another’ (εἰς τὸ ἀγαπᾷν); John 12:4, ‘Judas intended to betray Jesus’ (παραδιδόναι); 2 Cor. 10:6, ‘being ready to punish every disobedience’ (ἐκδικῆσαι); Luke 9:51, ‘he set his face to go to Jerusalem’ (τοῦ πορεύεσθαι); frequently after *giban* and its compounds: Matt. 26:2; Luke 9:16; John 6:31, 52; Col. 1:25; Phil. 1:24, ‘to remain in the flesh is more necessary for you’ (τὸ ἐπιμένειν). For the difference between *azetizo ist qiþan* and *du qiþan*, see §208.4.

“Note 3.—Moreover, the supine is also expressed by a special clause with *ei*; see §276.”

### II. What is to be presented as possible, or even as already in progress (the gerund), is commonly expressed by *du* and the infinitive:

Luke 6:7, “they watched whether Jesus would heal on the Sabbath, that they might find [grounds] to accuse him” (κατηγορίαν αὐτοῦ); 1:57, “Elizabeth’s time to bear [a child] was fulfilled” (χρόνος τοῦ τεκεῖν); 2:6, 21; 1 Cor. 9:6, “do we not have authority not to work?” (τοῦ μὴ ἐργάζεσθαι); Mark 3:15; Luke 1:9, “the lot fell to him to offer incense” (ἔλαχε τοῦ θυμιᾶσαι); 5:17, “the power of the Lord was [present] to heal them” (εἰς τὸ ἰᾶσθαι); 2 Cor. 8:11, “there is readiness to will” (τοῦ θέλειν).

“Note 4.—Here too the simple infinitive is sometimes used with *valdufni haban*, *ven haban*, etc.; see §252.”

## Ellipses in objective relations

### §255.

1) The object is sometimes omitted, as in Luke 5:25, “lifting up [namely, the bed] on which he had lain, he departed.” But there is no ellipsis in Phil. 4:16 and 1 Thess. 2:18, *ainamma sinþa jah tvaim*, “once and twice,” where the plural *sinþam* is to be supplied from the singular *sinþa* with *tvaim*; nor in John 15:13, *maizein þizai friaþvai*, “greater than this love,” where *friaþva* (“love”) must be understood after *maizein*. Indeed, this passage should, in accordance with the Greek text (μείζονα ταύτης ἀγάπην), read *maizein þizai friaþva*. John 10:31, “they took up stones in order that they might cast [namely, stones; λιθάσωσι] at him”; Matt. 8:32, “the whole herd rushed down,” namely the swine of v. 31. In 1 Tim. 6:6, simply *gavaurki* occurs in place of *faihugavaurki* (“gain”), which occurs in v. 5. Hence likewise Luke 15:24, *dugunnun visan* (“they began to be”) for *vailavisan* (“to make merry”); see v. 23, *visan vaila*; and 19:6, *atstaig* (“came down”) for *dalaþ atstaig* (“came down hastily”); see v. 5. On ellipses of a noun governing the genitive, see §216, note 7, compared with §245, note 2.

2) Regarding ellipses of the verb, the expressions *wa uns* (“what [is] to us?”) and *þus* (“to you”) in Matt. 8:29; Mark 1:24; 5:7; Luke 4:34; 8:28 are to be noted; *wa mik*, “woe [is] to me,” namely *karist* (“I am distressed”), 1 Cor. 5:12; Matt. 5:38, “eye for eye and tooth for tooth,” namely “you shall give.” Further, 2 Cor. 9:6, *þatuþþan*, namely “I say” or “one says”; 8:15, “he who [gathered] much [had] no surplus, and he who [gathered] little [had] no lack,” where from Exod. 16:18 “he who had gathered … found” must be supplied; Gal. 2:9, “they gave the right hands of fellowship to me and Barnabas, that we [should go] to the Gentiles, but they to the circumcised,” namely *gaggaima* (“that we should go”) or something similar; Rom. 13:7, “render therefore to all their dues: to whom [you owe] tribute, tribute.” So there are many places where verbs may readily be supplied from the preceding verse or clause: 2 Cor. 1:6, “whether we are afflicted, [it is] for your consolation,” namely “we are afflicted”; “or whether we are comforted, [it is] for your consolation,” namely “we are comforted.” Likewise 5:13; 7:12; 2:10, “to whom you forgive anything, I also [forgive],” namely *fragiba*; John 15:4, “remain in me, and I [remain] in you,” namely *visa*; 3:30; Eph. 5:24, “as the church submits to Christ, so also wives [should submit] to their own husbands,” namely *ufhausjaina*; 2 Tim. 1:5, “which dwelt in your grandmother Lois, and, I am persuaded, also in you,” namely *bauaiþ* (“dwells”); Rom. 9:32, “Why? Because not from faith, but from works of law,” namely, “they pursued a law of righteousness” from “pursuing a law of righteousness” in v. 31; Luke 7:43, “I suppose [the one] to whom he forgave more,” namely “loved more” from v. 42; 2 Cor. 3:13, where from “as Moses put a veil upon his face” must be supplied “we put no veil upon [our] face”; Matt. 27:43, “let him deliver him, if he wishes him,” namely, “to deliver [him]”; likewise Mark 15:8, where “do” must be understood; cf. also Luke 7:14; 1 Cor. 9:25; 11:1; 1 Cor. 7:19, “circumcision is nothing, but keeping the commandments of God [is],” namely “what is [important].” The affirmative may be supplied from the negative, as in 1 Tim. 4:3, “forbidding to marry and [commanding] to abstain from foods.” But 2 Tim. 3:4, “lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God,” is not to be regarded as an ellipsis because of the Greek φιλήδονοι μᾶλλον ἢ φιλόθεοι.

## C. The compound sentence

[Col. 1183]

### §256.

Just as in the simple sentence, so also in the compound sentence, thoughts—or the forms in which they are expressed, namely the individual clauses—are connected among themselves. Clauses which mutually extend or limit one another are considered to have the same grammatical value and are called coordinated clauses. Those which merely complete and explain others are called subordinate clauses, or secondary clauses, as opposed to principal clauses, which contain the principal thought.

## I. Coordinated clauses

[Col. 1183]

### §257.

The various relations in which coordinated clauses may be constructed with one another are these: one may extend and amplify another, yielding a copulative clause; one may be opposed to another, yielding an adversative clause; one may be excluded by another, yielding a disjunctive clause; or, finally, one may explain or establish another, yielding an explanatory or epexegetical, and a causal, clause. But where the verb is the same in both clauses, they are combined by using it only once and are linked by the thought alone.

## 1. Copulative clauses

### §258.

Two clauses are joined:

1) Positively by the conjunctions *jah*, “and, also”; enclitic *-uh*, “-que, and”; *jah … jah*, “both … and” (French *aussi bien … que*), where both thoughts proceed equally; and *ni þatainei … ak jah*, “not only … but also,” where one of the two is brought into prominence: John 3:23, “there also came and were baptized”; Mark 1:39, “Jesus was preaching in their synagogues and casting out demons”; John 3:26, “behold, he baptizes, and all are going to him”; 3:4, “can a man, being old, enter again into his mother’s womb and be born?” Gal. 4:20, “I desired to come to you now and change my voice”; 4:22, “Abraham had two sons, one by the slave-woman and one by the free woman”; Matt. 9:6, Jesus said to the paralytic, “take up your bed and go to your house.” And he went to his house. Matt. 5:39, “if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also”; Eph. 5:28, “he who loves his own wife also loves himself”; Mark 2:11, “rise, take up your bed also [*nim-uh*, καὶ ἆρον], and go to your house”; 16:7, “go and tell [*qiþid-uh*, ὑπάγετε, εἴπατε]”; 14:13, “Jesus sent two of his disciples and said [*qaþ-uh*, καὶ λέγει] to them”; Luke 10:30, “a man went down to Jericho, and they robbed him and, having inflicted wounds, departed”; Matt. 10:28, “fear him who is able both to destroy soul and body”; for other examples see Glossary, s.v. *Jah*, 6); Rom. 9:24, “vessels of mercy, whom God called not only from Jews but also from Gentiles”; 2 Cor. 9:12, “the service of this ministry not only supplies the needs of the saints but also abounds through many thanksgivings to God”; Rom. 12:17; 13:5; 2 Cor. 7:7; 8:10, 21; Eph. 1:21.

“Note 1.—For when *jah* is assimilated to the initial consonant of the following word, see Glossary, s.v. *Jah*.

“Note 2.—‘And also,’ ‘and likewise,’ in Gothic is *jah sa* and *jah is*; see §202.I.1, note 2.

“Note 3.—The enclitic *uh* does not correspond to Greek τε. The Gothic translator sometimes renders this by *iþ* (John 6:18), sometimes disregards it altogether, as in Rom. 7:7, *unte lust* (τὴν τε ἐπιθυμίαν) *nih kunþedjau*, ‘nor would I have known desire.’ This is especially so where τε … καί occurs: Luke 2:16, *bigetun Mariam jah Iosef*, τήν τε Μαρίαν καὶ τὸν Ἰωσήφ; Rom. 10:12; 1 Cor. 1:24. Sometimes he uses it without necessity: Luke 15:26, ‘having called one of the servants, he asked’; 18:31, ‘but they said to him.’ It occurs most often with especially adversative and transitional particles; see §259, note 2. When attached to the first word of a clause, it may also be appended to prepositions: John 19:12, *fram-uh þamma*; Matt. 11:25, *in-uh jainamma mela*; Luke 6:45, *uz-uh allis ufarfullein*, etc. Indeed, in compound verbs it is often inserted between the root and the preposition: John 17:1, *uz-uh-iddja*; 7:32, *in-uh-sandidedun*; Luke 17:7, *an-uh-kumbei*.

“Concerning the form of attached *uh*, it should be observed that, where the word to which it is attached ends in a vowel, there is always a certain elision: (a) the *u* of the enclitic is elided where the attached word ends in a diphthong or long vowel: *sumaih, viljauh, sah, soh, bih, biþeh* for *sumai-uh, viljau-uh, sa-uh, so-uh, bi-uh, biþe-uh*; (b) but where the final vowel of the word is short, that final vowel is elided: *þatuh, qiþuh, anþaranuh* for *þata-uh, qiþa-uh, auþarana-uh*. On assimilated *h*, see Glossary, s.v. *Uh*.

“Note 4.—In place of Greek καί, certain other particles are also used, where the translator proceeds somewhat freely and especially arranges the individual clauses in relation to one another: *auk*, ‘for’: 1 Cor. 8:11, ‘and [*auk*, καὶ] the weak brother is destroyed through your knowledge’; *aþþan*, ‘but’: Luke 6:32, ‘and [*aþþan*, καὶ] if you love those who love you, what reward is there for you?’; *þan*, ‘then’: Luke 2:37, ‘and [*soh þan*, καὶ αὕτη] she was a widow eighty-four years’; *þanuh*, ‘but’: Mark 10:13, ‘and [*þanuh*, καὶ] they brought children to him’; 1 Cor. 14:25; *þaruh*, ‘but’: John 7:45, ‘and [*þaruh*, καὶ] those men said to them there’; 3:23; 9:2; *þaþroh* and *þaþroh þan*, ‘then,’ ‘then indeed’: Luke 4:9; 2 Cor. 8:5; *iþ*, ‘however’: Luke 1:63, ‘they signalled to his father what he wished him to be called. And [*iþ is*, καὶ] he, asking for a writing-tablet, wrote’; see Glossary, s.v. *Iþ*, 2).

“Instead of a copulative particle, the comparative *sve*, ‘as,’ is also used: 1 Tim. 4:7, ‘but reject profane and old-womanish myths as [*sve*, like Greek καί] well’; or the preposition *miþ*, ‘with’: 2 Cor. 6:14, ‘what partnership has righteousness with [*miþ*, Greek καί] unrighteousness?’—undoubtedly because of the balance of the former clause with the latter.

“In place of καί, *ju*, ‘already,’ is also used: Mark 9:13, ‘I say to you that Elijah also [*ju*, καί] came’; Gal. 5:21, ‘I tell you beforehand, as I also [*ju*, καί] told you before’; compare Luke 15:19, 21. Or *sva*, ‘so,’ after *svasve*: John 13:15, ‘as I did to you, so [*sva*, Greek καί] also you do’; 15:9; 17:18.

“Note 5.—Not infrequently Gothic uses a finite verb with a copulative particle in place of a Greek participle. This particle is *jah* in Luke, and in John both *jah* and *uh*: Luke 1:67, ‘Zechariah prophesied and said’ (λέγων); 5:14, ‘go and show yourself to the priest’ (ἀπελθών); 7:3, ‘he asked Jesus to come and heal his servant’ (ἐλθών); 8:8, 43; John 12:3, 36; 19:2; John 6:5, ‘Jesus lifted up his eyes and, seeing that a great crowd was coming to him, said to Philip’ (ἐπάρας … καὶ θεασάμενος … λέγει); 6:17, ‘they went up into the boat and set out across the sea’ (ἀναβάντες … ἤρχοντο); 6:25, ‘having found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him’ (εὑρόντες … εἶπον); 8:12; 9:35; 13:25; 18:3, 22.

“Note 6.—Sometimes a finite verb is likewise used in place of a participle, but the copulative particle is omitted, so that the clauses proceed unconnectedly (ἀσυνδέτως): 1 Cor. 12:11, ‘but the one and same Spirit works all these things, distributing’ (διαιροῦν) ‘to each one separately as he wills’; Matt. 9:13, ‘but go, learn’ (πορευθέντες μάθετε) ‘what this means’; Mark 4:1, ‘a very great crowd gathered to him, so that he entered into a boat and sat’ (ἐμβάντα εἰς τὸ πλοῖον καθῆσθαι) ‘on the sea’; 7:19, ‘it goes out into the latrine, cleansing’ (ἐκπορεύεται καθαρίζον) ‘all foods’; John 12:14; see also §186, note 6c, and Eph. 3:19, where Gothic does not render τε. Asyndeton also occurs, as in Ps. 53:3: ‘all have turned aside; together they have become unprofitable.’

“Conversely, the Goth avoids asyndeton in the Greek text either by inserting a copulative particle: 1 Cor. XVI.13 *vakaiþ standaiduh* (“keep watch, and stand firm”; Greek: “keep watch, stand firm”), see § 186, note 6 b); or by changing the construction: John IX.7 *gagg þvahan*, “go, wash”—that is, “go so that you may wash yourself” (Greek: “go, wash yourself”); see the same place, d).”

“Note 7.—Sometimes a copulative particle is also redundantly placed after a participle: Matt. VIII.14 *jah qimands ïesus ïn garda paitrus jah gasaw* (“and Jesus, having come into Peter’s house, saw”; Greek: “he saw”); *Skeir.* IV b, *fraujins laiseins anastodjandei af ïudaia jah und allana midjungard gaþaih* (“the Lord’s teaching, beginning from Judaea, went through all the world”); Mark XIV.66; John VI.45; compare Matt. VI.24; Mark VIII.1 *athaitands siponjans qaþuh du ïm* (“having called the disciples, he said to them”); Luke XV.26; John XI.31.

“Note 8.—The verbal form is changed in copulative clauses, as in Mark I.6, *vas ïohannes gavasiþs taglam ulbandaus jah matida þramsteins*, ‘John was clothed in camel’s hair and ate locusts,’ in place of ‘he was clothed and was eating’ (Greek: “he was clothed and eating”); Luke XVI.20–21, *lazarus atvaurpans vas du daura gabigins banjo fulls jah gairnida saþ ïtan drauhsno*, ‘Lazarus lay cast at the door, full of sores, and desired to eat crumbs,’ in place of ‘and desiring’; this altogether has the flavour of Gothic usage. Likewise the following departures from the exemplar have been corrected: Luke XIX.12 *gaggida franiman jah gavandida sik*, ‘he went to receive and returned,’ for Greek “he went to receive and, having returned”; John VI.50 *sa ïst hlaifs saei us himina atstaig, ei saei þis matjai ni gadauþnai*, ‘this is the bread which came down from heaven, so that whoever eats of it may not die,’ for Greek “so that someone may eat and not die”; IX.8 *niu sa ïst saei sat aihtronds?*, ‘Is this not the one who sat begging?’ for Greek “the one sitting and begging?”; v. 11 *ïk galaiþ jah biþvahands ussaw*, ‘I went and, having washed, saw,’ for Greek “having gone and washed, I received sight.” But John VI.45, *wazuh nu sa gahausjands at attin jah ganam gaggiþ du mis*, ‘therefore everyone who hears from the Father and learns comes to me,’ for *jah ganimands* (“and having learned”; Greek: “the one who has heard and learned comes”), is said contrary to grammar; nor is the alteration in Col. III.9–10, *ni liugaiþ ïzvis misso afslaupjandans ïzvis þana fairnjan mannan jah gahamoþ niujamma*, ‘do not lie to one another, having put off the old person and put on the new’ (Greek: “having put off and put on”), to be accepted.

“Note 9.—Instead of *ni þatainei—ak jah* (‘not only—but also’) there also occurs *ni þatainei—ak*: *Skeir.* IV b, *þo ïnsakana vesun fram ïohanne ni ïn þis þatainei, ei fraujins mikilein gakannidedi, ak du gatarhjan jah gasakan þo afgudon haifst sabailliaus jah markailliaus*, ‘those accusations were made by John not only in order that he might make known the greatness of the Lord, but to rebuke and condemn the impiety of Sabellius and Marcellus’; or *nih—ak jah*: *Skeir.* VII a, *nih stains ak jah andraias, saei qaþ: ïst magula her*, ‘not only a stone, but also Andrew, who said: “There is a boy here.”’

2) Negative coordination by *nih*, *jah ni*, *ni*—“neither, nor,” “nor even”—and *ni—nih*, *nih—nih*, “neither—nor”: Mark XI.33, *qeþun du ïesua: ni vitum. jah andhafjands ïesus qaþ du ïm: nih ïk ïzvis qiþa*, ‘they said to Jesus, “We do not know.” And Jesus, answering, said to them, “Neither will I tell you”’; Luke XX.36, *þaiei vairþai sind usstassais us dauþaim, ni liugand, ni liuganda, nih allis gasviltan þanaseiþs magun*, ‘those judged worthy of resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage; nor indeed can they die any more’; John V.22, *svasve atta urraiseiþ dauþans jah liban gataujiþ, sva jah sunus þanzei vili liban gataujiþ. nih þan atta ni stojiþ ainohun, ak staua alla atgaf sunau*, ‘as the Father raises the dead and makes them live, so the Son makes live whom he wills. For neither does the Father judge anyone, but he has given all judgment to the Son’; *Skeir.* IV d, *ni airþeins vas nih us airþai rodjands*, ‘he was neither earthly nor speaking from earth’; John XV.4, *sve sa veinatains ni mag akran bairan af sis silbin, niba ïst ana veinatriva, svah nih jus*, ‘as the branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it remains in the vine, neither can you’; *Skeir.* I b, *kunnands þatei* [Col. 1187] *svaleikamma valdufnja mahtais nauþs ustaiknida vesi jan-ni þanaseiþs fastaida garaihteins garaihsns*, ‘recognizing that a proof of such mighty power was necessary before the firmness of true righteousness had yet been established’; VII c, *ainwarjanoh sva filu sve vilda andniman ïs gatavida jan-ni ïn vaihtai vaninassu vairþan gatavida*, ‘he made each one capable of receiving as much as he wished, not yet having made him in any respect deficient’; Mark V.26, *qens manag gaþulandei fram lekjam jah fraqimandei allamma seinamma jah ni vaihtai botida*, ‘a woman who had suffered much from physicians and spent all that she had, and was in no way healed’; Luke IX.36, *bigitans varþ ïesus ains jah eis þahaidedun jah mann ni gataihun*, ‘Jesus was found alone; and they kept silent and told no one’; John VIII.20, *þo vaurda rodida ïn gazaufylakio laisjands ïn alh jah ainshun ni faifah ïna*, ‘he spoke these words while teaching in the treasury in the temple, and no one seized him’; Luke X.19, *atgaf ïzvis valdufni trudan ufaro vaurme jah skaurpjono jah vaihte ainohun ïzvis ni gaskaþjiþ*, ‘I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and nothing shall harm you’; Matt. VI.28, *gakunnaiþ blomans haiþjos, waiva vahsjand, nih arbaidjand nih spinnand*, ‘consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither labour nor spin’; VI.20, *huzdjaiþ ïzvis huzda ïn himina, þarei nih malo, nih nidva fravardeiþ, jah þarei þiubos ni ufgraband nih stiland*, ‘store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves neither break in nor steal’; Luke X.4, *ni bairaiþ pugg, nih matibalg nih gaskohe*, ‘carry neither purse, nor bag, nor shoes’; Mark VI.8, *ïesus faurbauþ ïm, ei vaiht ni nemeina ïn vig niba hrugga aina, nih matibalg, nih hlaif, nih ïn gairdos aiz*, ‘Jesus commanded them to take nothing for the journey except a staff only—neither bag, nor bread, nor money in their belts,’ etc.; see glossary V, *Nih* 4), and § 260, note 4.

“Note 10.—For the use of negation, especially its construction, see § 213.

“Note 11.—Although there is no essential difference between *jah ni* and *nih* (formed from *ni-uh*, and consequently corresponding to Greek *οὔτε*, *οὐδέ*, and Latin *neque*), the Goth nevertheless avoids ordinarily using the former, except where the negation qualifies an indefinite such as *ainshun*, *mann*, *wahts*, *þanaseiþs*, etc.; compare § 213, 3 d).

“Note 12.—In negative copulative clauses asyndeton seems to occur where the negation proceeds only by *ni*, as in Mark VI.11, *sva managai sve ni andnimaina ïzvis, ni hausjaina ïzvis, usgaggandans jainþro ushrisjaiþ mulda*, ‘wherever they do not receive you or listen to you, as you leave there shake off the dust’; Col. II.21, *ni teikais, ni atsnarpjais, ni kausjais*, ‘do not handle, do not taste, do not touch’; Luke XX.35, *ni liugand, ni liuganda*, ‘they neither marry nor are given in marriage,’ etc. See glossary V, *Nih* 4 b).”

## 2. ADVERSATIVE CLAUSE

§ 259. 1) Of all adversative particles, *þan* (Greek *δέ*) is the weakest. Properly, it indicates the transition from one clause to another and continuation of the phrase, and thus comes closer to a copulative particle. It cannot stand at the beginning of a clause, but follows the first word as closely as possible. It should, however, be noted that, since it cannot stand alone after a preposition, it is postponed to the word governed by the preposition or to that word’s attribute—unless the preposition takes enclitic *uh*. In general *þan* very often causes the enclisis of *uh* upon the first word of the clause, whether for euphony or in order to stand closer to the initial word.

Matt. V.34: *ïk qiþa ïzvis ni svaran allis ni bi himina, nih bi airþai, nih bi ïairusaulymai, nih bi haubida þeinamma svarais. Sijaiþ-þan* (for *sijai-uþ-þan*) *vaurd ïzvar ja ja, ne ne*: ‘I tell you not to swear at all—neither by heaven, nor by earth, nor by Jerusalem, nor shall you swear by your head. But let your word be “yes, yes; no, no.”’ VI.28: *bi vastjos wa saurgaiþ, gakunnaiþ blomans haiþjos waiva vahsjand, nih arbaidjand, ni spinnand, qiþuh þan ïzvis þatei nih saulaumon gavasida sik sve ains þize*: ‘and why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither labour nor spin; yet I tell you that not even Solomon clothed himself like one of these.’ VIII.19: *duatgaggands* [Col. 1188] *ains bokareis qaþ du ïmma: laisari, laistja þuk þiswaduh þadei gaggis.—anþaruh þan siponje ïs qaþ du ïmma: uslaubei mis gafilhan attan meinana*: ‘one scribe approaching said to him, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.” But another of his disciples said to him, “Permit me to go and bury my father.”’ IX.7: *usliþa urreisands galaiþ ïn gard seinana. gasaiwandeins þan manageins ohtedun sildaleikjandans*: ‘having risen, he went away into his own house. But when the crowds saw, they were afraid and glorified [God].’ V.31: *hausideduþ þatei qiþan ïst: ni horinos.—qiþanuh þan* (“moreover”) *ïst þatei wazuh saei afletai qen, gibai ïzai afstassais bokos*: ‘you have heard that it was said, “You shall not commit adultery.”—Moreover it was said that whoever divorces his wife should give her a certificate of divorce.’ VI.5–7: *þan bidjaiþ, ni sijaiþ svasve þai liutans, unte frijond ïn gaqumþim jah vaihstam plapjo standandans bidjan. bidjandans uþ-þan* (“moreover”) *ni filuvaurdjaiþ svasve þai þiudo*: ‘when you pray, do not be like the hypocrites, because they love to pray standing in assemblies and broad streets. Moreover, when praying, do not use many words like the nations’; and so frequently. See other examples in the glossary, *þan* III.1).

“Note 1.—For enclitic *uh* contracted with the word to which it is joined, and for *h* assimilated to *þ*, see § 258, note 3. Until Zahn investigated it, the connection *-uh þan* was wholly unknown, since the particle *uh*, instead of being regarded as enclitic, was regarded as proclitic to *þan*, whence the meaningless form *uhþan* or *uþþan* resulted.

“Note 2.—Concerning the use of this *uh* before *þan*, observe the following:

“a) It is not attached to words which acquire another meaning when formed with *uh*, as the interrogative *was*: Luke XVII.7, *was þan ïzvara*, ‘but which of you?’; *wasuh* would mean ‘each one.’ But when it is joined to an interrogative, the elision mentioned in § 258, note 3 has no place; hence 1 Cor. IV.7, *wa-uþ þan habais*; 2 Cor. VI.15, *wo-uh þan samaqisse*, where, however, *wah*, *woh* means ‘what?’

“b) Among nouns, hardly ever does a substantive take *uh*; hence Matt. XXVII.7 *garuni þan*; Mark I.31 *andanahtja þan*; Luke VII.2 *hundafade þan*; John XI.31 *ïudaieis þan*. But Luke III.1 *filippauzuh þan* is especially noteworthy, where the translator of Luke used *uh* before *þan* quite irregularly.

“c) Of pronouns, almost only *sa* (compare a) regularly takes enclitic *uh*—*sah*, *soh*, *þatuh*—even in oblique cases, as *Skeir.* II b *þammuh þan* and VIII c *þoh þan*. Nevertheless Luke VIII.8 and IX.34 also have *þata þan*.

“d) Of adjectives, only those which assume a vocalic form receive *uh*, as *þvairhaiþ-þan*, Eph. IV.26; especially often indefinite numerals: *sums*, Matt. XXVI.67; Mark VIII.28, XII.5; John VII.44, XI.46; 1 Cor. XI.21, XV.6; 2 Tim. II.20; *Skeir.* VI c; *manag*, Luke III.18; also *anþar*, Matt. VIII.21; Mark IV.5; *Skeir.* II d. It is rare, however, in oblique cases, as *sumaimuh*, 2 Cor. II.16; more frequent in the accusative, as *anþaranuh*, *Skeir.* V a. Mark XII.5 *sumansuh* should be noticed: it ought to be *sumanzuh*; see Eph. IV.11. Yet here too *uh* is absent: *managai þan*, Mark XI.8; *sumai þan*, Luke IX.8, 19; John XI.37; *Skeir.* VI d; *anþarai þan*, Mark VI.15; Luke IX.19; John VI.23. Words with consonantal forms, however, avoid it; hence Matt. XXVII.62 *ïftumin þan daga*; Luke IX.43 *usfilmans þan*.

“e) Participles do not take *uh*, presumably because they are in themselves copulative in clauses; hence always *gahausjands þan*, Matt. VIII.10; *qimandin þan*, IX.28, and everywhere else. In Matthew, however, VI.7 has once *bidjandansuþ-þan*, where *s* in place of *z* is still more conspicuous. What *bijandzuh* [Col. 1189] in Philemon 22 signifies is unknown. But Matt. V.31 *qiþanuh þan ïst* must not be cited here, since *qiþan ïst* must be joined together, so that both form a finite verb.

“f) Verbs only rarely in general adopt the enclitic; *vas* and *vesun*, however, admit it regularly, as does sometimes *qaþ* (e.g. Mark VII.20; Luke VI.39; VII.48; X.2; XIV.12; XV.11; XVI.1; John VI.7; XI.13). But only *qeþun þan* is said. There occur at times, moreover: *qiþuh*, Matt. VI.29; Luke IX.27; 1 Cor. XI.2 *hasjuþ-þan*; 3 *viljauþ-þan*; XVI.8 *visuh þan*; John XVIII.2 *vissuh þan*; VI.11 *namuh þan*; XVIII.5 *stoþuh þan*; XI.5 *frijoduh þan*; Matt. V.37 *sijaiþ-þan* (see this passage); IX.31 *vitumuh þan*; 1 Thess. V.14 *bidjamuþ-þan*; Matt. XXVII.16 *habaidedunuh þan*.

“g) Prepositions neither take *uh* nor allow *þan* immediately after them; rather, they require it to be placed after their governed noun: Matt. VIII.18 *at andanahtja þan vaur þanamma*, etc.; XXVII.15 *and dulþ þan warjanoh*; Luke III.1 *ïn jera þan fimftataihundan*; Matt. XXVII.45 *fram saihston þan weilai*; Mark VIII.1 *ïn jainaim þan dagam*; Matt. XXVI.73 *afar leitil þan*. Sometimes, however, *ïn*, *fram*, and *ufar* admit enclisis, and then permit *þan* immediately to follow: Luke IX.21 *ïnuh þan þizai weilai*; X.7 *ïnuh þan þamma garda*; Matt. XI.12 *framuh þan þaim dagam*; Luke I.24 *afaruh þan þans dagans*. And one always says *afaruh þan þata*, Matt. VIII.5; Mark XVI.12; Luke X.1; XVIII.4; *Skeir.* III c. Hence it happens that with verbs compounded with a preposition, *uh þan* is sometimes inserted between the preposition and root: Mark XVI.8 *dizuh þan sat* (for *dissat þan*, Luke VII.16); 1 Cor. XV.15 *biþ-þan gitanda* (for *bigitanda þan*, John XII.14); Gal. II.2 *uzuh þan ïddja* (for *usïddja þan*, Mark I.28; John VI.3); Mark XIV.44 *atuh þan gaf*; 1 Cor. XIV.23; Eph. IV.23 *anuþ-þan niujaiþ*.

“h) Adverbs and conjunctions properly do not receive the enclitic, and one always says *miþþanei þan*, Luke VIII.42; *sunsaiv þan*, IV.39; *dalaþ þan*, Matt. VIII.1; Mark VIII.9. Yet alongside *samaleiko þan*, Luke XX.31, there occurs *Skeir.* VII c *samaleikoh þan*; and especially *biþe þan*, Luke VII.1; XV.14; XIX.37, and also *biþeh þan*, Luke IV.42; V.4; VII.12; further, *maizuh þan*, Gal. IV.9; *wanuh þan*, Matt. XXV.38, 39; *nauhþanuh þan*, Luke XV.20.

“Note 3.—Joined with *jah*, *þan* means: a) *þan jah*, ‘but also’ (Greek *δέ καί*), Luke IV.41; V.10, 36; XVIII.1; XIX.19; 1 Tim. V.24; but once it is also used for simple *δέ* (Luke XVIII.3), or *καί* (‘and’: Matt. IX.17; 1 Thess. V.25; 1 Tim. V.25). b) *jah þan*, ‘and then’ (Greek *καί—δέ*), Mark IV.36; Luke II.35; John VI.51; VIII.17; XV.27; 1 Tim. III.10; 2 Tim. III.12; also for *δέ καί*, Luke VI.6; 2 Cor. VI.1; 2 Tim. II.5; for simple *δέ*, Luke XVII.3; John XI.42, etc.; and finally for *καί*, Mark III.6; Luke VII.8.

“Note 4.—Since *þan*, except for certain cases listed in note 2 g), must always occupy the second position in its clause, Luke XX.16 *gahausjandans qeþun þan* may with all the more reason be concluded to be incorrect, since the Greek has ‘having heard, they said’ [Col. 1190]. Perhaps *gahausjandans þan qeþun* should be read.”

2) Closest in meaning to *þan* are *þanuh* and *þaruh*: the former properly denotes time, the latter place, ‘then’; but both are used as transitional particles for Greek *δέ*. Similarly, *nu*, in the sense of *οὖν* (‘therefore’), is not infrequently interchangeable with *þanuh* and other adversative particles. *þaruh* and *þanuh* always occupy the first position in the clause, whereas *nu* occupies the second.

Matt. IX.25: *ïesus gasaiwands svigljans jah haurnjans haurnjandans jah managein auhjondein qaþ du ïm: afleiþiþ, unte ni gasvalt so mavi ak slepiþ. jah bihlohun ïna. þanuh þan usdribana varþ so managei, atgaggands ïnn habaida handu ïzos jah urrais so mavi*: ‘Jesus, seeing the flute-players and the crowd making a tumult, said to them, “Depart, for the girl has not died but sleeps.” And they laughed at him. Then, when the crowd had been put out, he went in, took her hand, and the girl arose.’ Luke IX.11: *ïesus rodida du ïm þo bi þiudangardja guþs jah þans þarbans leikinassaus gahailida. þanuh dags juþan dugann hneivan. atgaggandans þan du ïmma þai tvalif qeþun du ïmma:—þanuh qaþ du ïm: gibiþ ïm jus matjan*: ‘Jesus spoke to them about the kingdom of God and healed those needing healing. Then the day began to decline. The Twelve, coming to him, said to him:—then he said to them, “You give them food.”’ Luke VIII.51–53: *qimands þan ïn garda ni fralailot ainohun ïnngaggan alja paitru jah ïakobu jah ïohannen jah þana attan manjos jah aiþein. gaigrotun þan allai. þaruh qaþ: ni gretiþ, unte ni gasvalt ak slepiþ. jah bihlohun ïna. þanuh ïs usdreibands allans ut jah fairgreipands handu ïzos vopida qiþands: mavi urreis*: ‘when he came into the house, he allowed no one to enter except Peter, James, John, and the girl’s father and mother. All were weeping. Then he said, “Do not weep, for she has not died but sleeps.” And they laughed at him. Then, having put them all outside and taken her hand, he called out, saying, “Girl, arise.”’ Mark X.18: *ïesus qaþ du ïmma: wa mik qiþis þiuþeigana? ni washun þiuþeigs alja ains guþ. þos anabusnins kant: ni horinos, etc. þaruh andhafjands qaþ: þo alla gafastaida*: ‘Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. You know the commandments: “Do not commit adultery,” etc.” Then he answered, “I have kept all these.”’ John V.46–47: *jabai mose galaubidedeiþ, ga-þau-laubidedeiþ mis, bi mik auk jains gamelida. þande nu jainis melam ni galaubeiþ, waiva meinaim vaurdam galaubjaiþ*: ‘if you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?’ For further examples see glossary V, *þanuh* 2), *þaruh* 2), *Nu* 2). *þaruh þan* together is used for *δέ* in Luke VIII.23: *þaruh þan sve faridedun anasaislep*, ‘and as they sailed, he fell asleep.’

“Note 3.—Since the adversative particles so far mentioned approach copulative ones very closely in meaning, the copulative *jah* and *uh* may replace them: Matt. VI.30, *jah þande* (‘but if’) *þata havi haiþjos himma daga visando jah gistradagis ïn auhn galagiþ guþ sva vasjiþ, waiva mais ïzvis leitil galaubjandans*, ‘but if God thus clothes the grass of the field, which exists today and tomorrow is thrown into an oven, how much more you of little faith!’ Probably *þan* in v. 29 precedes because of this interchange. John X.20, *qeþun uh* (‘but they said’) *managai: unhulþon habaiþ*, ‘many said: “He has a demon.”’ For further examples see glossary V, *Jah* 4) and *Uh* 1 a β).”

§ 260. 3) But properly expressed opposition is indicated by *aþþan* and *ïþ*, both corresponding to Greek *δέ* and both able to stand at the front of a clause. They essentially differ in this: *aþþan* is more strongly adversative, implies or bears a negation, and especially opposes whole clauses to one another; *ïþ*, more commonly occurring as a relative, has a more copulative force, like *þan*, and rather sets in opposition the constituent members of a compound clause. Yet the Goth interchanges these particles indiscriminately, according to principles repeatedly set forth: namely, where they more closely suit Greek *δέ*, and perhaps also where one or the other is required by euphony (thus, for example, one says *ïþ ïs qaþ* or *qaþuh þan*, but not *aþþan ïs qaþ*). Moreover, these particles are interchanged even in [Col. 1191] parallel passages.

The standard passage in which the respective use of both particles appears is Matt. V.21–22: *hausideduþ þatei qiþan ïst þaim airizam: ni maurþrjais, ïþ saei maurþreiþ skula vairþiþ stauai. aþþan ïk qiþa ïzvis: þatei wazuh modags broþr seinamma svare skula vairþiþ stauai. ïþ saei qiþiþ broþr seinamma raka, skula vairþiþ gaqumþai. aþþan saei qiþiþ dvala, skula vairþiþ ïn gaiainnan funins*: ‘you have heard that it was said to those of old, “You shall not murder”; but whoever murders shall be liable to judgment. But I tell you: whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment. But whoever says to his brother, “Raca,” shall be liable to the council. But whoever says, “Fool,” shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna.’ Thus, just as one simply has in V.43ff., *hausideduþ þatei qiþan ïst: frijos nehwundjan þeinana jah fiais fiand þeinana. aþþan ïk qiþa ïzvis: frijoþ fijands ïzvarans*, ‘you have heard that it was said, “Love your neighbour and hate your enemy.” But I tell you, love your enemies’; so also in V.31ff. one has *qiþanuh þan ïst þatei wazuh saei afletai qen, gibai ïzai afstassais bokos. ïþ ïk qiþa ïzvis þatei wazuh saei afletiþ qen seina ïnuh fairina kalkinassaus, taujiþ þo horinon*, ‘moreover, it was said that whoever divorces his wife should give her a certificate of divorce. But I tell you that whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery.’
