There is indeed Mark VIII.27–29: *wana mik qiþand mans visan? ïþ eis andhofun: ïohannen þana daupjand, jah anþarai helian, sumaih þan ainana praufete. jah ïs qaþ du ïm: aþþan jus wana mik qiþiþ visan?* ‘Whom do people say that I am? They answered, “John the Baptist; and others, Elijah; but some, one of the prophets.” And he said to them, “But whom do you say that I am?”’ So also in the parallel Luke IX.19ff.; compare likewise Matt. IX.6 and Mark II.10; Mark XII.26 and Luke XX.37. But whereas Matt. IX.15 reads, *ïbai magun sunjus bruþfadis qainon und þata weilos þei miþ ïm ïst bruþfaþs? ïþ atgaggand dagos þan afnimada af ïm sa bruþfaþs, jah þan fastand*, ‘can the sons of the bridechamber mourn while the bridegroom is with them? But days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast,’ the parallel passages Mark II.20 and Luke III.35 have *aþþan atgaggand* (*aþþan qimand*), etc.; compare Mark VIII.35 and Luke IX.24. Likewise, in similar formulae, for example, the Synoptic Gospels have only *ïþ jabai*, but John also has *aþþan jabai*: Matt. VI.14ff., *jabai afletiþ mannam missadedins ïze, afletiþ jah ïzvis atta ïzvar sa ufar himinam. ïþ jabai ni afletiþ*, etc., ‘if you forgive people their trespasses, your Father who is in heaven will forgive you also. But if you do not forgive,’ etc.; John XI.9ff., *jabai was gaggiþ ïn dag, ni gastiggqiþ. aþþan jabai was gaggiþ ïn naht, gastiggqiþ*, ‘if anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble; but if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles.’

Luke VI.39: *ïbai mag blinds blindana tiuhan?—nist siponeis ufar laisari seinana, ïþ gamanvids warjizuh vairþai sve laisaris ïs. aþþan wa gaumeis gramsta ïn augin broþrs þeinis, ïþ anza ïn þeinamma augin ni gaumeis*: ‘Can a blind person lead a blind person?—A disciple is not above his teacher; but everyone fully trained will be like his teacher. But why do you observe the speck in your brother’s eye and do not observe the beam in your own eye?’ Mark II.9ff.: *waþar ïst azetizo du qiþan: afletanda fravaurhteis þeinos, þau qiþan: urreis jah nim badi þeinata jah gagg? aþþan ei viteiþ þatei valdufni habaiþ afletan fravaurhtins*, etc.: ‘which is easier to say: “Your sins are forgiven,” or to say: “Rise, take up your bed, and walk”? But so that you may know that [he] has authority to forgive sins,’ etc. Matt. X.29ff.: *niu tvai sparvans assarjau bugjanda, jah ains ïze ni gadriusiþ ana airþa ïnuh attins ïzvaris viljan. aþþan ïzvara jah tagla alla garaþana sind*: ‘are not two sparrows sold for an assarion? Yet not one of them falls to earth without your Father’s will. But even all the hairs of your head are numbered.’ John XV.6ff.: *niba saei visiþ ïn mis, usvairpada ut. aþþan jabai sijuþ ïn mis, jah vaurda meina ïn ïzvis sind*, ‘unless one remains in me, he is cast out. But if you remain in me and my words remain in you’; XVI.7, *jabai ïk ni galeiþa, parakletus ni qimiþ at ïzvis: aþþan jabai gagga, sandja ïna du ïzvis*, ‘if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I shall send him to you.’ For further examples of the use of *aþþan* and *ïþ*, see glossary V under these words.

“Note 1.—*Iþ* is sometimes also used for *jah* (‘and’), see § 258, note 4; hence, just as a Greek participle is resolved by a finite verb and *jah* (§ 258, note 5), it is also resolved by following *ïþ*: John IX.25, *blinds vas ïþ nu saiwa*, ‘I was blind, and now I see’ (Greek: ‘being blind, now I see’).

[Col. 1192] “Note 2.—Sometimes *ïþ* and *þan* are redundantly joined in Gothic fashion (§ 284.2); in that case the subject of the clause is inserted between the two: Luke XVII.15, *ïþ ains þan ïze gaumjands þammei hrains varþ, gavandida sik*, ‘but one of them, seeing that he had been healed, returned’; IX.21; John VIII.59. So also Luke V.24, *ïþ þan ei viteiþ*, ‘but that you may know,’ where the parallel Mark II.10 has *aþþan*. But one would have no basis for conjecturing that *aþþan* is generally derived from *ïþ þan*, since, etymologically speaking, both *ïþ* and *aþþan* wholly escape us.

“Note 3.—From what has been said concerning *þan*, *aþþan*, and *ïþ*, it is also apparent that in Greek clauses connected by *μέν—δέ*—particles which are rather copulative, or at least only very slightly adversative, and which more commonly contrast parts and members of the clause than the clauses themselves—*δέ* is rendered not so much by *aþþan* as by *ïþ* or *þan*, while *μέν*, on the other hand, is more often represented by *aþþan*. Hence the following cases generally occur:

“a) With *ïþ* in the latter member: regularly *raihtis—ïþ*: Matt. IX.37 *asans raihtis managa, ïþ vaurstvjans favai*, ‘the harvest indeed is plentiful, but the workers are few’; John XVI.9; Rom. XIV.2; 2 Cor. X.10; Gal. IV.24–26; *Skeir.* III c; IV b. *aþþan—ïþ*: Matt. III.11 *aþþan ïk ïn vatin ïzvis daupja: ïþ sa afar mis gagganda svinþoza mis ïst*, ‘I indeed baptize you in water, but he who comes after me is mightier than I’; Mark I.8; Rom. XI.22; 1 Cor. IX.25; Titus I.15. *þan—ïþ*: Gal. IV.23 *akei þan sa us þiujai bi leika gabaurans vas, ïþ sa us frijai bi gahaita*, ‘but the one from the slave-woman was born according to the flesh, whereas the one from the free woman was through promise’; 1 Cor. IV.10 *veis dvalai ïn xristaus, ïþ jus frodai. veizuþ-þan unmahteigai, ïþ jus svinþai. juzuþ-þan vulþagai, ïþ veis unsverai*, ‘we are fools for Christ, but you are wise; we are weak, but you are strong; you are honoured, but we are dishonoured’; compare Luke III.18 (Greek *μὲν οὖν*). *auk—ïþ*: John XVI.22 *jus auk nu saurga habaiþ, ïþ aftra saiwa ïzvis*, ‘you indeed now have sorrow, but I shall see you again’; 1 Cor. XV.51; *allis—ïþ*, Luke III.16; *sveþauh—ïþ*, Mark X.39; Phil. III.1, 14.

“b) With *þan* in the latter member: *raihtis—þan*: Mark IV.4 *sum raihtis gadraus faur vig. anþaruþ-þan gadraus ana stainahamma*, ‘some indeed fell beside the way; but other seed fell on stony ground’; Phil. I.5; *Skeir.* V a. *auk—þan*: 2 Cor. II.16.

“c) *Aþþan* in the latter member, occurring only in the linkage *raihtis—aþþan*: 2 Cor. VIII.17 *unte raihtis bida andnam. aþþan usdaudoza visands silba viljands galaiþ du ïzvis*, ‘for he indeed accepted the request; but, being more eager, he went to you of his own accord’; X.1.

“d) Greek *μέν* in the first member remains untranslated: 1 Cor. IX.24 *þai ïn spaurd rinnandans allai rinnand, ïþ ains nimiþ sigislaun*, ‘those running in a race all run, but one receives the prize’; XII.20 *ïþ nu managai liþjus, ïþ ains leik*, ‘but now there are many members, but one body’; 2 Cor. IX.4; 2 Tim. II.20.

“Likewise in distinct members of a divided clause—one—another, some—others, former—latter, etc.—when the particle is absent in the first member, *uh-þan* is used in the latter, though it is sometimes omitted: Mark XII.5 *afslohun managans auþarans, sumans usbliggvandans, sumansuh þan usqimandans*, ‘they killed many others, beating some and killing some’; Eph. IV.11 *silba gaf sumans apaustauluns, sumanzuþ-þan praufetuns, sumanzuþ-þan aivaggelistans, sumanzuþ-þan hairdjans jah laisarjans*, ‘he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, some as shepherds and teachers’; Mark VIII.28 *eis andhofun ïohannen þana daupjand, jah anþarai helian, sumaih þan ainana praufete*, ‘they answered, “John the Baptist; others, Elijah; and some, one of the prophets”’; John VII.12 *birodeins mikila vas ïn managein: sumaih qeþun þatei sunjeins ïst, anþarai qeþun: ne, ak airzeiþ þo managein*, ‘there was much discussion among the crowd: some said, “He is good”; others said, “No, he misleads the crowd”’; X.20 [Col. 1193] *qeþun managai ïze: unhulþon habaiþ, sumaih qeþun: þo vaurda ni sind unhulþon habandins*, ‘many of them said, “He has a demon”; some said, “These words are not those of one possessed by a demon”’; Luke XIX.16–20, *qam sa frumista—jah qam anþar—jah sums qam*, ‘the first came—and another came—and another came,’ etc.; see glossary V, *Sums* 2). Hence *partly—partly* and *now—now* behave in the same way: *Skeir.* VI c, *missaleiks jah ïn missaleikaim melam attins bi ïna varþ veitvodeins: suman þairh praufete vaurda, sumanuh þan þairh stibna us himina, sumanuh þan þairh taiknins*, ‘the Father bore witness concerning him in diverse and various ways: partly through prophetic words, partly through a voice from heaven, partly through signs.’ In this case, however, simple *suman—suman* is also used: 1 Cor. XIII.9 *suman kunnum, suman praufetjam*, ‘we know in part, we prophesy in part.’”

4) Opposition of an entire clause is expressed by *sveþauh*, “yet, nevertheless” (Greek *πλήν*, *μέντοι*), ordinarily placed at the beginning of the clause; sometimes *aþþan* is used as well: Luke X.13, *ïþ ïn tyrai jah seidonai vaurþeina mahteis þozei vaurþun ïn ïzvis, airis þaus gaïdreigodedeina. sveþauh tyrai jah seidonai sutizo vairþiþ ïn daga stauos þau ïzvis*, ‘but had the mighty works which occurred among you occurred long ago in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented. Yet it shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you’; VI.34, *jabai leiwid, fram þaimei veneid andniman, wa ïzvis laune ïst? sveþauh frijod þans fijands ïzvarans*, ‘if you lend to those from whom you expect to receive, what reward do you have? Rather, love your enemies’; John VII.12, *birodeins mikila vas ïn managein: sumaih qeþun þatei sunjeins ïst, anþarai qeþun: ne, ak airzeiþ þo managein. nih þan ainshun sveþauh balþaba rodida bi ïna ïn agisis ïudaie*, ‘there was much discussion among the crowd: some said, “He is good”; others said, “No, he misleads the crowd.” Yet no one spoke openly about him for fear of the Jews.’ For other examples see glossary V, *Sveþauh*. Luke VI.24, *fijand ïzvis mans—aþþan vai ïzvis þaim gabeigam*, ‘people hating you—but nevertheless, woe to you who are rich’; 2 Tim. II.19, *yminaius jah filetus qeþun usstass ju vaurþana jah galaubein sumaize usvaltidedun. aþþan tulgus grunduvaddjus guþs standiþ*, ‘Hymenaeus and Philetus say that the resurrection has already occurred and overthrow the faith of some. Yet the firm foundation of God stands.’

“Note 4.—The adversative particles *ïþ* or *aþþan* are also redundantly prefixed before *sveþauh*: Luke XVIII.8 *aþþan qiþa ïzvis þatei gavrikiþ ïns sprauto. ïþ sveþauh sunus mans qimands biugitai galaubein ana airþai?*, ‘but I tell you that he will vindicate them quickly. Yet when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?’ XIX.27 *aþþan sveþauh fijands meinans briggiþ her*, ‘but nevertheless bring my enemies here’; Phil. III.16; IV.14. Thus in Rom. IX.6 the Goth renders Greek *οὐχ οἷον δὲ ὅτι* briefly indeed but excellently by *aþþan sveþauh ni*: ‘but nevertheless not.’

“Note 5.—*Sveþauh* is also used for *μέν*, meaning ‘indeed,’ ‘at least,’ or making emphatic the word before which it stands: Mark IX.12 *helias sveþauh qimands faurþis aftra gaboteiþ*, ‘Elijah indeed, coming first, restores all things’; Gal. IV.8 *akei þan sveþauh ni kunnandans guþ þaim þoei vistai ni sind guþa skalkinodeduþ*, ‘but indeed, when you did not know God, you were enslaved to those which by nature are not gods.’ Also with following *ïþ* for *μέν—δέ*, see note 3 a).”

5) *Ak* and *akei*, both standing at the beginning of a clause, correspond to Greek *ἀλλά*. They essentially differ in that *ak*, after a preceding negative, means “but, rather”; while *akei*, even when what precedes is not negative, means “but, on the contrary.” Further, *akei* approaches *aþþan* in meaning: Matt. IX.18, *reiks ains qimands ïnvait ïna qiþands þatei dauhtar meina nu gasvalt. akei qimands atlagei handu þeina ana ïja jah libaiþ*, ‘one ruler came and worshipped him, saying, “My daughter has just died. But come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live”’; Rom. X.2, *aljan guþs haband, akei ni bi kunþja*, ‘they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge’; Mark I.44, *saiw ei mannhun ni qiþais vaiht, ak gagg þuk silban ataugjan gudjin*, ‘see that you say nothing to anyone; but go, show yourself to the priest’; 1 Cor. I.17, *ni ïnsandida mik xristus daupjan ak vailamerjan*, ‘Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel.’ For further examples see glossary V, *Ak* and *Akei*.

“Note 6.—Where the antecedent proceeds positively and the consequent negatively, *ni*, *jah ni*, or *ïþ ni* is used: Mark II.27, *sabbato ïn mans varþ gaskapans, ni manna ïn sabbato dagis*, ‘the Sabbath was made for humankind, not humankind for the Sabbath’; Matt. IX.13, *armahairtiþa wiljau jah ni hunsl*, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice’; Mark XIV.7, *sinteino unledans habaiþ miþ ïzvis, ïþ mik ni sinteino habaiþ*, ‘you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me.’ For other examples see glossary V, *Ni* 6 aa). In Mark X.27, however, *akei fram mannam unmahteig ïst, ni fram guþa*, the negation *ni* does not mean ‘but—not’; rather, in accordance with the Greek (“with human beings it is impossible, but not with God”), and with an altered word order, one should say: *fram mannam unmahteig ïst akei ni fram guþa*, ‘with human beings it is impossible, but not with God.’

“Note 7.—For Greek *ἀλλά* a), meaning ‘but,’ *aþþan* is also used: Phil. III.8 *akei þatei vas mis gavaurki, þatuh rahnida ïn xristaus sleiþa visan. aþþan sveþauh all domja sleiþa visan ïn ufarassaus xristaus*, ‘but whatever was gain to me, that I counted loss in Christ. But indeed I count all things loss because of the surpassing worth of Christ’; and more often; compare § 281. b) Meaning ‘but only,’ *alja* (‘besides’) is also used: Mark X.40 *þata du sitan af taihsvon meinai aiþþau af hleidumein nist mein du giban alja þaimei man viþ ïst*, ‘to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to give, but only to those for whom it has been prepared’; John VII.48 *sai jau ainshun þize reike galaubidedi* (‘would one of the rulers believe?’ that is, no one believes) *alja so managei*, ‘but only this crowd.’

“Note 8.—For *δέ*, *akei* occurs only in 1 Cor. XIV.20. But *ak* is often used for *akei*: Mark XI.31, *jabai qiþam: us himina, qiþiþ: aþþan duwe ni galaubideduþ ïmma? ak qiþam: us mannam, uhtedun þo managein*, ‘if we say, “From heaven,” he will say, “Then why did you not believe him?” But if we say, “From human beings,” they feared the crowd’; XIV.49; John VIII.56. But in Eph. IV.28 and 1 Tim. I.9 *ak* is used for *δέ*, meaning, after a preceding negation, ‘only, but.’”

## 3. DISJUNCTIVE CLAUSE

§ 261. 1) Disjunctive members of a clause are marked by simple *aiþþau*, “or,” or by *jabai—aiþþau*, *andizuh—aiþþau*, “either—or”: Matt. V.17, *ni qam gatairan vitoþ aiþþau praufetuns*, ‘I did not come to abolish the law or the prophets’; v. 18, *jota ains aiþþau ains striks ni usleiþiþ af vitoda*, ‘not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the law’; VI.31, *ni maurnaiþ nu qiþandans: wa matjam aiþþau wa drigkam aiþþau we vasjaima*, ‘do not be anxious, saying, “What shall we eat? Or what shall we drink? Or what shall we wear?”’; XXV.38, *wanuh þan þuk sewum gast jah galaþodedum aiþþau naqadana jah vasidedum?*, ‘when did we see you a stranger and receive you, or naked and clothe you?’ Mark VIII.36, *wa boteiþ mannan, jabai gageigaiþ þana fairwu allana jah gasleiþeiþ sik saivalai seinai. aiþþau wa gibiþ manna ïnmaidein saivalos seinaizos?*, ‘what profits a person if he gains the whole world and loses his own soul? Or what will one give in exchange for one’s soul?’ Rom. XI.34, *was ufkunþa fraþi fraujins aiþþau was ïmma ragineis vas aiþþau was ïmma fruma gaf?*, ‘who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor? Or who first gave to him?’ Matt. VI.24, *ni manna mag tvaim fraujam skalkinon, unte jabai fijaiþ ainana jah anþarana frijoþ, aiþþau ainamma ufhauseiþ, ïþ anþaramma frakann*, ‘no one can serve two masters, for either he will hate one and love the other, or he will hold to one and despise the other’; whereas the parallel Luke XVI.13 reads *andizuh ainana fijaiþ—aiþþau ainamma andtiloþ—*. In the first member the particle may also be absent: 2 Cor. I.13, *ni alja meljam ïzvis alja þoei anakunnaiþ, aiþþau jah ufkunnaiþ*, ‘we write to you nothing other than what you read or also understand.’ For other examples of simple *aiþþau*, see the glossary under this word.

2) In disjunctive questions, no particle is prefixed to the first member, particularly where there is an interrogative word or enclitic *-u* (§ 214.1 a and b), or where the question is negative with *ïbai* (see the same place, 2 c). To the latter member, however, *þau*, more rarely *aiþþau*, is prefixed; and at times the interrogative particle *-u* (also written *-uh*) is attached to the first word after *þau*: Matt. IX.5, *waþar ïst raihtis azetizo qiþan: afletanda þus fravaurhteis, þau qiþan: urreis*, ‘which is easier, to say, “Your sins are forgiven,” or to say, “Rise”?’; XXVII.17, *wana vileiþ ei fraletau ïzvis, barabban þau ïesu?*, ‘whom do you want me to release to you, Barabbas or Jesus?’; 1 Cor. XI.22, *ïbai gardins ni habaiþ du matjan jah drigkan, þau aikklesjon guþs frakunnuþ*, ‘do you not have houses in which to eat and drink, or do you despise the church of God?’; John IX.3, *was fravaurhta. sa-u þau fadrein ïs?*, ‘who sinned—this man or his parents?’; XVIII.34, *ab u þus silbin þu þata qiþis þau anþarai þus qeþun bi mik?*, ‘do you say this of yourself, or did others tell you about me?’ Mark III.4, *skuldu ïst ïn sabbatim þiuþ taujan aiþþau unþiuþ taujan* (‘is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do evil?’; the parallel Luke VI.9 has *þau*); Mark XII.14, *skuldu ïst kaisaragild giban kaisara þau niu gibaima?*, ‘is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or shall we not give it?’; Luke XX.22; Gal. III.5, *vaurkeiþ mahtins ïn ïzvis uzu vaurstvam vitodis þau uzu gahauseinai galaubeinais?*, ‘does he perform miracles among you by works of the law or by hearing with faith?’; Mark XI.30, *daupeins ïohannis uzuh himina vas þau uzuh mannam?*, ‘was John’s baptism from heaven or from human beings?’; Luke XX.4; Matt. XI.3, *þu ïs qimanda þau anþarizuh beidaima?*, ‘are you the one who is to come, or should we await another?’; or in the parallel Luke VII.19, *þau anþaranu venjaima*, ‘or should we expect another?’ For other examples see glossary V, *þau* 3).

## 4. CAUSAL AND CONSECUTIVE CLAUSE

§ 262. 1) A causal clause either proves the preceding proposition, in which case *unte*, *nam*, and *auk* (“for,” Greek *γάρ*) are used—the first in first position, the latter in second; or it merely explains, in which case *raihtis* and *allis*, “namely,” are used, both standing at the beginning of the clause, as is also *auk*: Luke I.30, *ni ogs þus, mariam, bigast auk anst fram guþa*, ‘do not fear, Mary, for you have found favour with God’; v. 76, *barnilo praufetus hauhistins haitaza, fauragaggis auk faura andvairþja fraujins manvjan vigans ïmma*, ‘child, you shall be called prophet of the Most High, for you will go before the Lord’s face to prepare his ways’; Mark I.16, *gasaw seimonu jah andraian vairpandans nati ïn marein, vesun auk fiskjans*, ‘he saw Simon and Andrew casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen’; Matt. VII.25, *razn ni gadraus, unte gasuliþ vas ana staina*, ‘the house did not fall, for it had been founded on the rock’; IX.24, *afleitiþ, unte ni gasvalt so mavi, ak slepiþ*, ‘depart, for the girl has not died but sleeps’; VI.14, *unte jabai afletiþ mannam missadedins ïze, afletiþ jah ïzvis atta ïzvar sa ufar himinam*, ‘for if you forgive people their trespasses, your Father in heaven will forgive you also,’ referring to v. 12; Rom. XIII.3, *þai auk reiks ni sind agis godamma vaurstva ak ubilamma. aþþan vileis, ei ni ogeis valdufni, þiuþ taujais jah habais hazein us þamma, unte guþs andbahts ïst þus ïn godamma, ïþ jabai ubil taujis, ogs, unte ni svare þana hairu bairiþ, guþs auk andbahts ïst*, ‘for rulers are not a terror to good conduct but to evil. But do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it; for it is God’s servant for your good. But if you do evil, be afraid, for it does not bear the sword without cause; for it is God’s servant’; Mark VI.7, *vaila praufetida esaïas bi ïzvis þans liutans, sve gameliþ ïst so managei vairilom mik sveraiþ, ïþ hairto ïze fairra habaiþ sik mis. afletandans raihtis anabusn guþs habaiþ þatei anafulhun mannans*, ‘Isaiah prophesied well concerning you hypocrites, as it is written: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. For, abandoning the commandment of God, they hold to human tradition”’; v. 25, *ni vilda vitan mannan jah ni mahta galaugnjan: gahausjandei raihtis qino bi ïna—qimandei draus du fotum ïs*, ‘she wished no one to know, and she could not remain concealed; for the woman, having heard about him, came and fell at his feet’; VIII.3, *jabai fraleta ïns lausqiþrans du garda ïze, ufligand ana viga, sumai raihtis ïze fairraþro qemun*, ‘if I send them away fasting to their homes, they will faint on the way; for some of them have come from far away’; Luke III.34, *sai, aiþei meina jah þai broþrjus meinai. saei allis vaurkeiþ wiljan guþs, sa jah broþar meins jah swistar jah aiþei ïst*, ‘behold, my mother and my brothers. For whoever does the will of God is my brother and sister and mother’; Luke I.43, *waþro mis þata ei qemi aiþei fraujins meinis at mis. sai allis, sunsei varþ stibna goleinais þeinaizos ïn ausam meinaim, lailaik* [Col. 1196] *þata barn ïn vambai meinai*, ‘and why has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? For behold, as soon as the sound of your greeting came into my ears, the child in my womb leaped.’ For further examples see glossary V under *Auk*, *Unte* 2 a), *Raihtis*, and *Allis*.

At times adversative particles are used in place of causal ones: Mark VII.3, ïþ fareisaieis (*for the Pharisees*) niba ufta þvahand handuns, ni matjand, “for the Pharisees do not eat unless they often wash their hands”; see Glossary, s.v. *Iþ* 4); 1 Tim. IV.7, þroþei þuk silban du gagudein, aþþan (*for*) leikeina usþroþeins du favamma ïst bruks, “exercise yourself toward godliness, for bodily exercise is useful for little”; see Glossary, s.v. *Aþþan* 3), this occurring only in the Epistles; Matt. VI.32, all auk þata þiudos sokjand, vaituh þan (*for*) atta ïzvar þatei þaurbuþ, “for all these things the nations seek; for your Father knows that you need them”; see Glossary, s.v. þan III, 5), always preceded by *-uh*; likewise *nu*: 1 Cor. VII.16, wa nu (*for*) kannt, ei aban ganasjais? “For what do you know, wife, whether you shall save [your] husband?”; 2 Cor. XI.4; Gal. V.17; and *þannu*: Mark XIV.6, letiþ þo, duwe ïzai usþriutiþ, þannu goþ vaurstv vaurhta bi mis, “let her alone; why do you trouble her? She has indeed done a good work in me.”

> Note 1.—*Auk* is sometimes placed after two words closely joined together, as Luke XVI.2, ni magt auk, “you cannot also”; Rom. IX.15, du mose auk, “to Moses also,” etc. That *unte* and *auk* do not differ otherwise in meaning is evident from the passage cited above, Rom. XIII.3, and from the variant readings of the two manuscripts at 2 Cor. VII.8, where A has *unte gasaiwa*, “for I see,” and B *gasaiwa auk*, “I see indeed.”
>
> Note 2.—Καὶ γάρ is normally rendered literally *jah auk*, “and indeed/for also,” Matt. VIII.9; XXVI.73, etc.; see Glossary, s.v. *Auk* 5 a); and *jah þan auk*, Luke VII.8. Sometimes, however, simply *unte* is used (2 Cor. III.10), and *aþþan* (2 Cor. XIII.4), just as *jah auk* also corresponds to simple γάρ, Rom. VII.2; 1 Cor. XV.18; and *-uh þan auk* is used for δέ in John XII.10. Conversely, *auk jah* has the force of δὲ καί: 1 Cor. I.16, ïk daupida auk jaþ-þans staifanaus gadaukans, “I also baptized the household of Stephanas”; 2 Cor. XIII.9. Redundantly, moreover, *auk raihtis* (*for indeed*) occurs in Mark VI.17; VII.16, and *auk allis* in Mark IX.41.
>
> Note 3.—Eph. V.6, ni manna ïzvis uslusto lausaim vaurdam, þairh þoei qimiþ hatis guþs, “let no one deceive you with empty words, through which the wrath of God comes”: *þairh þoei* (“through which”) corresponds to the Greek διὰ ταῦτα γάρ, “through which indeed.”
>
> Note 4.—Mark IX.34, eis slavaidedun, du sis misso (πρὸς ἀλλήλους γάρ) andrunnun, “they kept silent, for among themselves they had disputed”: the causal particle *auk* is lacking, because it would probably have stood too far from the beginning (*du sis misso auk*).

2) The proper consecutive particles are *nu*, “thus, therefore,” οὖν, and *þannu*, “therefore, consequently,” ἄρα. The former stands in the first position of the sentence, the latter in the second: Matt. V.48, sijaiþ nu (*therefore*) jus fullatojai svasve atta ïzvar sa ïn himinam fullatojis ïst, “therefore be ye perfect, as your Father who is in heaven is perfect”; VI.1 ff., atsaiwiþ armaion ïzvara ni taujan ïn andvairþja manne du saiwan ïm. þan nu taujais armaion, ni haurnjais faura þus, “take heed not to perform your alms before men in order to be seen by them. Therefore, when you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before yourself”; VI.9, bidjandans ni filuvaurdjaiþ svasve þai þiudo; sva nu bidjaiþ jus, “when praying, do not use many words like the Gentiles; pray therefore thus”; Luke XX.25, wis habaiþ skatts manleikan jah ufarmeli? andhafjandans þan qeþun: kaisaris. ïþ ïs qaþ du ïm: usnu- (*therefore*) gibiþ þo kaisaris kaisara, þo guþs guþa, etc., “Whose image and inscription does it bear? They answered: Caesar’s. And he said to them: therefore render to Caesar the things of Caesar, and to God the things of God”; see Glossary, s.v. *Nu* 2); Rom. X.16, esaïas qiþiþ: frauja, was galaubida hauseinai unsarai? þannu (*therefore*, consequently) galaubeins us gahauseinai, “Isaiah says: Lord, who has believed our report? Therefore faith comes from hearing”; [Col. 1197] 2 Cor. V.15, domjam þata þatei ains faur allans gasvalt, þannu allai gasvultun, “we judge this: that one died for all; therefore all died”; 1 Cor. IV.7, ushraineiþ þata fairnjo beist, ei sijaiþ niujis daigs. þannu (*thus, so that*, ὥστε) dulþjam ni ïn beista fairnjamma ak in unbeistein sunjos, “purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump. Thus let us keep the feast, not with old leaven but with the unleavened bread of sincerity”; for other examples see Glossary, s.v. *þannu*.

Further, the following also occur as consecutive particles:

*Eiþan*: John IX.41, ïþ blindai veseiþ, ni þau habaidedeiþ fravaurhtais. ïþ nu qiþiþ: þatei gasewum, eiþan (*therefore*) fravaurhts ïzvara þairhvisiþ, “if you were blind, you would not have sin. But now you say, ‘We see’; therefore your sin remains”; 1 Cor. XI.26, sva ufta sve matjaiþ þana hlaif jaþ-þana stikl drigkaiþ, dauþau fraujins gakannjaiþ, unte qimai. eiþan (*therefore, so that*) wazuh saei matjiþ—or drinks—unworthily of the Lord, skula vairþiþ leikis jah bloþis fraujins, “as often as you eat this bread or drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes. Therefore whoever eats—or drinks—unworthily of the Lord shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord”; *Skeireins* III.b; IV.a; V.d; VI.a.

*Aþþan*: 2 Cor. VII.12, aþþan (*therefore*) jabai melida, ni ïn þis anamahtjandins ni ïn þis anamahtidins, ak du gabairhtjan usdaudein unsara, “therefore, although I wrote, [it was] not for the sake of him who did wrong nor for the sake of him who suffered wrong, but in order to make our earnestness manifest”; Mark XI.31, jabai qiþam: us himina, qiþiþ: aþþan (*therefore*) duwe ni galaubideduþ ïmma? “If we say, ‘from heaven,’ he will say: why then did you not believe him?” For other examples see Glossary, s.v. *Aþþan* 5).

*þanuh*: 1 Cor. XV.17, jabai xristus ni urrais, svare jah so galaubeins ïzvara ïst; jan-nauh sijuþ ïn fravaurhtim ïzvaraim. þanuh (*therefore*) jaþ-þai gaslepandans ïn xristau fraqistnodedun, “if Christ has not risen, your faith is vain; you are still in your sins. Therefore those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished”; Mark XII.6, afslohun skalkans managans. þanuh (*therefore*) nauhþanuh ainana sunu aigands liubana sis ïnsandida jah þana du ïm, etc., “they killed many servants. Therefore, still having one beloved son, he sent him also to them,” etc.; see Glossary, s.v. *þanuh* 4).

> Note 5.—The doubled *nu* (*nunu*) is used [Col. 1198] where the sentence is prohibitive: Matt. X.26, ni nunu ogeiþ ïzvis, “do not therefore fear”; v. 31; Rom. XIV.15, 20; 2 Tim. I.8. It is always inserted between the negation and the imperative, whereas simple *nu* precedes the imperative: Matt. VI.8, ni galeikoþ nu, “do not therefore be like [them].” Sometimes *nu* also occupies the third position in the sentence, as Rom. IX.19, qiþis mi nu, “you say to me then,” etc.; see Glossary, s.v. *Nu* 2).
>
> Note 6.—In a question, *nuh* is used in place of *nu*: Mark XII.9, wa nuh taujai frauja? “What then shall the lord do?”; John XVIII.37, an nuh (οὐκοῦν) þiudans ïs þu? “Then are you a king?”; 1 Cor. VII.16, with assimilated *h*, wa nuk-kannt?
>
> Note 7.—Ἄρα οὖν is rendered in Gothic by *þannu þan*, Rom. VII.3; by *þannu nu*, Rom. IX.6, etc.; see Glossary, s.v. *þannu*; by *þannu nu jai*, Rom. IX.18; and by *sai nu*, Eph. II.19. Yet these combinations of particles are also used for a single Greek particle: *aþþan nu*, Rom. VII.12 (ὥστε), 1 Cor. IX.26 (τοίνυν); *þannu nu*, 1 Cor. IV.5 (ὥστε); *þannu nu jai*, Rom. IX.20 (μενοῦνγε); ïþ nu, *Skeireins* I.d.
>
> Note 8.—Where οὖν is merely a transitional particle (“now then,” French *et maintenant*), it is also rendered in Gothic by *þaþroh þan* (John III.25; XVIII.7), *þan* (Mark III.31), and *-uh* (John XVI.18); where ἄρα is a particle of affirmation (“indeed, certainly”), it is translated by *þau* (1 Cor. XV.14) or *aiþþau* (Gal. II.21). But the Gothic translator incorrectly rendered ἆρα in Gal. II.17 by *þannu*, confusing it here with ἄρα. Ἄρα in the interrogative τί ἄρα (“what then?”), Luke I.66, is not translated.

## II. SUBORDINATE CLAUSES

[Col. 1197]

§ 263. This type of compound sentence may be reduced to a simple sentence, provided that the secondary or subordinate clause is regarded as a periphrasis of an attribute or object of the simple sentence. A relative clause pertains to the periphrasis of an attribute; an objective clause especially, and also causal, modal, and temporal clauses, pertain to the periphrasis of an object.

### 1. ATTRIBUTIVE CLAUSE, RELATIVE CLAUSE

§ 264. 1) The relative pronoun *saei* (ὅς, ὅστις, ὃς ἄν, ὅσος), agreeing closely with the noun which it defines, agrees with it in number and gender. Exceptions, however, are collective nouns, discussed in § 209.3), and cases in which the relative refers to several nouns: in these, the rule laid down in § 209.4) b) applies. As regards case, it must be that required by the verb of the relative clause (except in attraction, § 266): *Skeireins* VII.a, ïst magula her, saei habaiþ ·e· hlaibans barizeinans jah tvans fiskans, “there is here a boy who has five barley loaves and two fishes”; Luke VIII.2, vesun miþ ïesua qinons, þozei vesun galeikinodos sauhte, jah marja, sei haitana vas magdalene, us þizai ei usïddjedun unhulþons sibun, “there were with Jesus women who had been healed of diseases, and Mary, who was called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out”; Mark XI.21, smakkabagms þanei fraqast, gaþaursnoda, “the fig tree which you cursed has withered”; XII.20, ïn þize gavalidane, þanzei gavalida, gamaurgida þans dagans, “for the elect whom he chose, he shortened the days”; VII.13, ni blauþjaiþ vaurd guþs anabusnai ïzvarai, þo ei anafulhuþ, “you make the word of God void by your tradition which you have handed down”; *Skeireins* IV.d, afguda haifsts sabailliaus jah markailliaus, þaiei ainana anananþidedun qiþan attan jah sunu, “the idolatrous heresy of Sabellius and Marcellus, who dared to call Father and Son one”; Col. II.23, bi anabusnim jah laiseinim manne þoei sind sveþauh vaurd habandona handugeins, “according to commandments and teachings of men, which indeed have a reputation for wisdom”; 1 Cor. XVI.19, goleiþ ïzvis akvila jah priska, at þaimei jah salja, “Aquila and Prisca greet you, with whom also is the church”; Rom. IX.23, gakannida guþ gabein vulþaus seinis bi kasam armaions, þoei (grammatically referring [to the vessels]) fauragamanvida du vulþau, þanzei (by sense referring [to persons]) jah laþoda uns, “God made known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared beforehand for glory, whom he also called, [namely] us”; *Skeireins* VIII.c, so managei þaiei ni kunnun vitod, “the multitude who do not know the law”; 2 Thess. III.17, so goleins meinai handau, þatei (that is, “my greeting by the hand of Paul, which”) ïst bandvo ana allaim aipistauleim meinaim, “this greeting in my own hand, which is a token in all my epistles”; Luke V.3, galaiþ ïn ain þïze skipe, þatei (πλοῖον ὅ) vas seimonis, “he entered one of the boats, which was Simon’s”; IX.50, ni ainshun ïst manne, saei (Vulgate: *nemo est qui*, “there is no one who”) etc.

> Note 1.—Sometimes the relative agrees in gender not with the noun to which it refers, but with the predicate of the relative clause: Mark XV.42, vas paraskaive, saei ïst fruma (that is, *dags*, “day”) sabbato, “it was the Preparation, which is the day before the Sabbath”; Eph. VI.17, nimaiþ meki ahmins, þatei ïst vaurd guþs, “take the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” Although the Gothic translator correctly rendered John XV.26, þan qimiþ parakletus, þanei ïk sandja ïzvis, ahman sunjos, etc., “when the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you, the Spirit of truth,” it is nevertheless doubtful whether he took *ahman* as an apposition to the relative clause rather than to *parakletus*, an opportunity being supplied by the Greek neuter πνεῦμα. In the notable passage 1 Tim. III.16, the Gothic translator reads, with the best manuscripts, unsahtaba mikils (?) ïst gagudeins runa, saei gabairhtiþs varþ ïn leika, “great (?) is the mystery of godliness, who was manifested in flesh”; probably so—see the note on this passage. If, however, the singular neuter refers to several preceding objects, as Col. II.16 f., ni manna ïzvis bidomjai ïn mata aiþþau ïn dragka, aiþþau ïn dailai dagis dulþais aiþþau fulliþe aiþþau sabbaþum, þatei ïst skadus þize anavairþane, “let no one judge you in food or drink, or concerning a feast-day, new moon, or sabbaths, which is a shadow of things to come,” this is done in Greek fashion, the singular neuter being used in place of the plural; see § 196, note 7.
>
> Note 2.—A relative clause is placed between an attribute and its noun: Luke I.4, melja þus ei gakunnais þize, bi þoei galaisiþs ïs, vaurde astaþ, “I write to you that you may know the certainty of the words concerning which you have been instructed.” Sometimes the relative clause is even placed before the noun to which it refers: John XVIII.9, þanzei atgaf mis atta, ni fraqistida ïze ainummehun, “of those whom the Father gave me I lost not one”; Rom. VII.15, þatei hatja, þata tauja, “what I hate, that I do.” In that case, an opposition, if there is one, is inflected in the case of the relative: Mark VI.16, þammei ïk haubid afmaimait, ïohanne, sa ïst, sah urrais us dauþaim, “John, whom I beheaded—this is he; he has risen from the dead”; John V.37, saei sandida mik, atta, sah veitvodeiþ bi mik, “the Father who sent me, he has testified concerning me”; XII.49. Or the corresponding demonstrative is lacking: John XVII.3, so ïst so aiveino libains, ei kunneina þuk ainana sunja guþ jah þane ïnsandides, ïesu xristn, “this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.” Or it must be supplied from what precedes: Col. IV.16, soei (see note on this passage) ïs us laudeikaion, jus ussiggvaid, namely, “the epistle which is from Laodicea, read ye also.” Or, after the relative clause, the demonstrative may also be supplied: John X.25, vaurstva, þoei ïk tauja ïn namin attins meinis, þo veitvodjand bi mik, “the works which I do in my Father’s name, these testify concerning me”; 1 Cor. VII.20, warjizuh ïn laþonai, ïn þizaiei laþoþs vas, ïn þizai sijai, “let each remain in the calling in which he was called”; John XII.48; XIV.10; XVIII.11; compare § 202 II.2) a).
>
> Note 3.—Both subject and object may likewise be expressed by a relative clause: Mark IX.31, saei allis (ὃς ἄν) gadragkjai ïzvis stikla vatins ïn namin meinamma ni fraqisteiþ mizdon seinai, “whoever gives you a cup of water in my name shall not lose his reward”; see § 203.1) b) and § 205, note 10, where the Gothic rendering of ὃς ἄν is discussed in particular.
>
> Note 4.—After the relative, the indicative is commonly used. The subjunctive is used only: (a) in negative clauses: Mark IV.22, nih allis ïst wa fulginis, þatei ni gabairhtjaidau, “for nothing is hidden which should not be made manifest”; Luke IX.50, ni ainshun ïst manne, saei ni gavaurkjai maht ïn namin meinamma, “there is no one who shall perform a miracle in my name,” XVIII.29, etc.; or (b) after an interrogative: 2 Cor. XII.13, wa ïst, þize vanai veseiþ? “What is it in which you have been inferior?” etc.; or (c) where the relative clause is the subject of the main clause (Note 3), as Mark IV.9, saei habai (ὁ ἔχων) ausona hausjandona, gahausjai, “he who has ears to hear, let him hear”; Luke III.11, 13; 2 Cor. II.2. Yet the indicative and subjunctive are not improperly used interchangeably, as Matt. V.31 f., wazuh saei afletai qen—wazuh saei afletiþ qen—, “whoever may put away a wife—whoever puts away a wife”; 2 Thess. III.3, triggvs frauja, saei gatulgeiþ ïzvis jah galausjai ïzvis af þamma ubilin, “faithful is the Lord, who shall establish you and deliver you from evil.” In the latter passage the subjunctive is all the more appropriate because the Greek employs the future, which, as we have already seen (§ 182 I), may be translated by either indicative or subjunctive. In the periphrasis Col. II.22, þairh þatei ïs brukjaidau, “for the use of which it is,” for τῇ ἀποχρήσει, [Col. 1200] Roman influence must be inferred; likewise Col. I.10, all þatei galeikai, “everything which is pleasing” (πᾶσα ἀρέσκεια).

2) Besides the aforementioned relative *saei*, the following also occur as relatives:

a) *Sah*, which, just as *saei* is formed from the demonstrative pronoun *sa* and the relative particle *ei*, is formed from *sa* and enclitic *-uh* (“and he”); see § 202 II.1) b).

b) The relative particle *ei* and ïzei; see § 203.3) b).

c) Where a relative refers to a personal pronoun, instead of this relative the personal pronoun is repeated with appended *ei*, e.g. ïk, ïkei, etc.; see § 203.2.

> Note 5.—Conversely, John VIII.40 says sokeiþ mik usqiman, mannan ïzei sunja ïzvis rodida, “you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken truth to you,” where ïzei refers to the apposition *mannan*, although, because of the first person in *rodida* (λελάληκα, “I have spoken”), properly ïkei, referring to *mik*, ought to occur.

d) *Ei* and *þei* are also interchanged with *saei* after indefinite *wazuh* and its compounds; see § 205, note 10.

e) The relative adverb *sve* (“as”): Mark XIV.72, gamunda paitrus þata vaurd, sve (ὡς) qaþ ïmma ïesus, “Peter remembered the word, as Jesus had said to him.”

f) The correlatives also belong here: *wileiks—svaleiks*, “what kind—such”; and *svaleiks*, ordinarily used absolutely, “a certain one—such as”; *svalauds—svalauds sve*, “so great, so much—as great, as much”; *sva filu—sva filu sve*, “so much—as much”; *sva manags—sva manags sve*, “so many—as many”; see the Glossary under these words. ὁσάκις, ὅσος, and οἷος are always rendered fully with a preceding demonstrative: *sva ufta sve* (“as often as”), *sva laggs sve* (“as long as; as long, how long”), *sva managai sve* (“as many as”), *sva filu sve*, *svaleiks sve* (οἷος). 1 Cor. XI.25, þata vaurkjaiþ, sva ufta sve drigkaiþ, du meinai gamundai, “do this, as often as you drink [it], in remembrance of me”; Mark II.19, sva lagga weila sve (ὅσον χρόνον) miþ sis haband bruþfad, ni magun fastan, “as long a time as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast”; III.10, sva managai sve (ὅσοι) habaidedun vundufnjos, þaih þan ïna gasewun, drusun du ïmma, “as many as had diseases, when they saw him, fell upon him”; vv. 28; VI.11, 30, 36; IX.3, 13; X.21; XIII.19; Luke IV.20; IX.5, 10; John VI.11, etc.

§ 265. Just as, in German (French, Latin, etc.), a Greek participle may sometimes be resolved into a finite verb with a relative, so this also occurs occasionally in Gothic, especially often with *saei*: Matt. VI.4, atta þeins saei saiwiþ (ὁ βλέπων) ïn fulhsnja usgibiþ þus ïn bairhtein, “your Father, who sees in secret, shall repay you openly”; XXVII.17, wana vileiþ ei fraletau ïzvis, barraban þau ïesu saei haitada (Ἰησοῦν τὸν λεγόμενον) xristus? “Whom do you wish me to release to you—Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?”; Mark V.15, gasaiwand fraþjandan þana saei habaida (τὸν ἐσχηκότα) laigaion, “they saw him who had had the legion sitting [there]”; XV.41, anþaros managos þozei miþïddjedun (αἱ συναναβᾶσαι) ïmma ïn ïairusalem, “many other women who had gone up with him to Jerusalem”; Col. I.23, ni afvagidai af venai aivaggeljons sei merida ïst (τοῦ κηρυχθέντος) ïn alla gaskaft, “not moved away from the hope of the gospel which has been preached in all creation”; 1 Thess. II.14, þata samo vunnuþ fram ïzvaraim ïnkunjam svasve jah veis fram ïudaium þaiei jah fraujin usqemun (τῶν ἀποκτεινάντων) ïesua, “you suffered the same things from your own countrymen as we also from the Jews who killed the Lord Jesus,” etc. In John and the Epistles other relatives are also used: John XVIII.26, qaþ sums þize skalke þis maistins gudjins, sah niþjis vas (συγγενὴς ὤν), þammei afmaimait paitrus auso, “one of the servants of the high priest, being a kinsman of him whose ear Peter cut off, said”; XII.4, qaþ ïudas simonis ïskariotes, ïzei skaftida sik (ὁ μέλλων) [Col. 1201] du galevjan ïna, “Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, who was about to betray him, said”; XI.37; XVI.2; XIX.12; 1 Cor. XV.27, 57; 2 Cor. V.21; VIII.16; Gal. I.1; VI.13; Eph. I.3; 1 Tim. I.16. The same applies where there is reference to personal pronouns in the manner described in § 264.2) c): Rom. XIV.4, þu was ïs þuei stojis (ὁ κρίνων) framaþjana skalk? “Who are you that judge another’s servant?”; Eph. II.13, nu sai ïn xristau ïesu jus juzei simle vesuþ (ὑμεῖς οἱ ... ὄντες) fairra vaurþuþ newa ïn bloþa xristaus, “but now in Christ Jesus you who formerly were far off have become near through the blood of Christ”; 1 Thess. II.13, vaurd guþs vaurkeiþ ïn ïzvis juzei galaubeiþ (ὑμῖν τοῖς πιστεύουσι), “the word of God works in you who believe”; 1 Tim. I.13, galaubjandan mik gahugida xristus gasatjands ïn andbahtja ïkei faura vas (τὸν ... ὄντα) vajamerjands, “Christ counted me faithful, appointing me to ministry, [I] who had formerly been a blasphemer.” The Gothic translator also uses periphrasis where a participle is subject or object, as Mark V.16, spillodedun ïm þaiei gasewun (οἱ ἰδόντες), “those who had seen [it] told them”; X.32, ïesus dugann þaim tvalif siponjam qiþan þoei habaidedun (τὰ μέλλοντα) ïna gadaban, “Jesus began to tell the twelve disciples what was about to happen to him.”

> Note 1.—Nouns too are periphrastically expressed in this manner, as Col. I.10, πᾶσα ἀρέσκεια, all þatei galeikai, “everything which is pleasing.” Here an interrogative also stands in place of a relative: Col. IV.8, ïnsandida ïna du ïzvis ei kannjai wa bi ïzvis ïst (τὰ περὶ ὑμῶν), “I sent him to you so that he might learn what concerns you”; Eph. VI.21–22.
>
> Note 2.—Conversely, participle and periphrasis are interchanged: John VI.45, wazuh sagahausjands (ὁ ἀκούσας) at attin jah ganam (μαθών) gaggiþ du mis, “everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me”; 2 Cor. II.2, was ïst saei gailjai mik niba sa gaurida us mis? “Who is he that makes me glad except the one made sorrowful by me?”; Luke III.11; John X.1–2; 2 Cor. X.17–18.
>
> Note 3.—Rom. IX.20, þu was ïs ei andvaurdjais (ὁ ἀνταποκρινόμενος) guþa, “who are you, replying against God?”: simple *ei* occurs instead of *þuei*.

## ATTRACTION

§ 266. Attraction consists in this: either a word from a subordinate clause is in effect brought back into the main clause; or a word of the subordinate clause is construed in the same manner as another word of the main clause; or finally a word of the main clause is absorbed by one of the subordinate clause, the absorbed word then taking the construction of the absorbing word. These constructions, perhaps originally borrowed from Greek, are also used independently by the Gothic translator.

1) The subject of the subordinate clause becomes the object of the main clause: Mark XI.32, allai habaidedun ïohannen þatei bi sunjai praufetes vas, “all held of John that he was truly a prophet”—for “they believed John to be …”; John VII.27, þana kunnum, waþro ïst, “we know this man, whence he is”; IX.8, 29; XIV.19; XVIII.2; Mark XII.34; 1 Cor. XVI.15; 2 Cor. XIII.5; 2 Cor. VII.11, saiw þata bi guþ saurgan ïzvis, welauda gatavida ïzvis usdaudein, “see what earnestness this godly grief produced in you.” Compare John IX.19, sau ïst sunus ïzvar, þanei qiþiþ þatei blinds gabaurans vaurþi, “is this your son, whom you say was born blind?”; VIII.54.

2) The relative agrees in case with the word to which it refers: Luke II.20, hazidedun guþ ïn allaize, þizeei (ἐπὶ πᾶσιν οἷς) gahausidedun, “they glorified God for all the things which they heard,” instead of “for all the things about which they heard”; XIX.37, hazidedun guþ ïn allaizo þoze sewun mahte (περὶ πασῶν ὧν εἶδον δυνάμεων), “they glorified God for all the mighty works which they saw”; similarly III.19; 2 Cor. XIII.10, þata aljaþro melja ei andvairþs harduba ni taujau bi valdufnja, þammei (κατὰ τὴν ἐξουσίαν ἥν) frauja fragaf mis, “therefore I write these things while absent, that when present I may not act severely, according to the authority which the Lord gave me.”

[Col. 1202]

3) The demonstrative is wholly absent; the relative referring to it assumes its case and requires the substantive of the demonstrative to follow it: Mark VI.22, bidei mik þiswizuh þei (ὃ ἐάν) vileis jah giba þus, “ask of me whatever you wish, and I shall give [it] to you,” literally, “ask me whatever you wish,” instead of “this which you wish”; XV.12, wa vileiþ ei taujau þammei (ὅν) qiþiþ þiudan ïudaie, “what do you wish me to do with him whom you call king of the Jews?”; Luke IX.36, mann ni gataihun ni vaiht þizei (ὧν) gasewun, “they told no one anything of what they had seen”; John VI.29, þat-ïst vaurstv guþs ei galaubjaiþ þammei (εἰς ὅν) ïnsandida jains, “this is the work of God: that you believe in him whom that one sent”; 2 Cor. XII.17, ïbai þairh wann þizeei (ὧν) ïnsandida du ïzvis, bifaihoda ïzvis? “Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you?”; Col. III.2, þaimei ïupa sind (τὰ ἄνω) fraþjaiþ ni þaim þoei ana airþai sind, “set your minds on the things above, not on those which are on earth” (where attraction and regular construction alternate); Mark VII.7, duwe þai siponjos þeinai ni gaggand bi þammei anafulhun þai sinistans (κατὰ τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν πρεσβυτέρων), “why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition which the elders handed down?”; Luke III.13, ni vaiht ufarþatei garaid sijai (παρὰ τὸ διατεταγμένον) ïzvis lausjaiþ, “exact nothing beyond what has been prescribed to you”; VI.34, leiwid fram þaimei (παρ’ ὧν) veneid andniman, “lend to those from whom you expect to receive”; XVII.27, etun jah drugkan und þanei dag (ἄχρι ἧς ἡμέρας) galaiþ nauel ïn arka, “they ate and drank until the day on which Noah entered the ark”; John XI.6, salida ïn þammei vas stada (ἐν ᾧ ἦν τόπῳ), “he remained in the place where he was”; 1 Cor. IV.6; XI.23; 2 Cor. II.3; VIII.11; XII.6; 2 Tim. III.14; Philemon 21.

> Note 1.—Yet the Gothic translator sometimes does not imitate attraction: (a) Mark XIII.19, fram anastodeinai gaskaftais, þoei (κτίσεως ἧς) gaskop guþ, “from the beginning of the creation which God created”; Luke XV.16, gairnida sad ïtan haurne, þoei (κερατίων ὧν) matidedun sveina, “he desired to fill himself with the husks which the swine ate”; John XV.20, gamuneiþ þis vaurdis, þatei (τοῦ λόγου οὗ) ïk qaþ du ïzvis, “remember this word which I spoke to you”; XVII.5, hauhei mik þamma vulþau, þanei (τῇ δόξῃ ᾗ) habaida at þus faurþizei sa fairwus vesi, “glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world was”; 2 Cor. I.4, gaþrafstjam þans þairh þo gaþlaiht, þizaiei (διὰ τῆς παρακλήσεως ἧς) gaþrafstidai sijum silbans fram guþa, “we comfort them through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God”; Eph. II.4, 10; Col. I.23; 2 Thess. I.4; 2 Tim. I.13; Neh. V.14, fram þamma daga ei (ἀπὸ ἡμέρας ἧς), “from the day on which”; (b) John XVII.9, bidja bi þans, þanzei (περὶ ὧν) atgaft mis, “I pray for those whom you gave me”; Luke I.20, sijais þahands jah ni magands rodjan und þana dag ei (ἄχρι ἧς ἡμέρας) vairþai þata, duþe ei (because of which, ἀνθ’ ὧν) ni galaubides vaurdam meinaim, “you shall be silent and unable to speak until the day when these things take place, because you did not believe my words”; XVII.30, þamma daga ei (ᾗ ἡμέρᾳ), “on the day on which.”
>
> Note 2.—Nor does he imitate the so-called inverse attraction except rarely, namely where the subject of the main clause is put in the case of the relative: Mark XII.10 and Luke XVII.20, λίθον, ὃν ἀπεδοκίμασαν … οὗτος, “the stone which the builders rejected—this,” rendered as stains þammei usvaurpun þai timrjans, sah varþ du haubida vaihstins, “the stone which the builders rejected became the head of the corner”; 1 Cor. X.16, τὸν ἄρτον ὃν κλῶμεν οὐχὶ κοινωνία, rendered hlaifs þanei brikam, niu gamainduþs leikis? “the bread which we break—is it not a communion of the body?” Some, moreover (Winer, p. 485), explain Luke I.72 f. in this way, where the Gothic translator renders μνησθῆναι διαθήκης ἁγίας αὐτοῦ, ὅρκον ὃν ὤμοσε κτλ. by gamunan triggvos veihaizos seinaizos. aiþis þanei svor, “to remember his holy covenant, the oath which he swore,” avoiding attraction again.
>
> Note 3.—This kind of attraction, by which the impersonal expression of the main clause is made personal so as to agree with the subject of the subordinate clause, may be used in Gothic especially with φανερόν and δῆλον εἶναι, although the impersonal construction is native to the language. Thus 2 Cor. III.3, φανερούμενοι ὅτι ἐστὲ ἐπιστολὴ Χριστοῦ, “it being evident that you are an epistle of Christ,” is translated in Germanic fashion as svikunþ þatei sijuþ aipistaule xristaus, “it is manifest that you are an epistle of Christ”; manuscript A, however, has svikunþai þatei sijuþ, following the Greek. This attraction is more frequent in rendering δοκεῖν, as in the subscription to 1 Corinthians: du kaurinþium frumei þugkeiþ melida visan us asiai, “the First [Epistle] to the Corinthians seems to have been written from Asia,” instead of “it seems that the First [Epistle] to the Corinthians was written from Asia”; likewise 2 Cor. X.9; Gal. II.9; *Skeireins* I.c; IV.c; VI.a. Here the impersonal “it seems to me” is often used for “I seem,” as in Matt. VI.7; Luke XIX.11; 2 Cor. XII.19; Gal. II.2, though this does not belong here. So too Luke III.23, svaei sunus munds vas ïosefis, “as was supposed, son of Joseph,” is rendered from the Latin source (*ut putatus est*). Conversely, this type of attraction is regularly used as an idiom of Gothic with *skulds visan* and *mahts visan*, so that instead of “it is necessary that I …,” “it is possible that you …,” etc., one says “I am obliged to …,” “you can …,” etc.; see § 176, note 4 d).

### 2. OBJECTIVE CLAUSE

§ 267. Four objective determinations of a simple sentence are chiefly expressed periphrastically by clauses of their own: namely, the proper object, expressed by oblique cases; and the causal, modal, and temporal [determinations].

### A. OBJECTIVE CLAUSE IN THE STRICT SENSE, OR ACCUSATIVE (ALSO DATIVE AND GENITIVE) CLAUSE

§ 268. Here three cases must be distinguished according to the different relations of the action of the main clause to the object of the subordinate clause. Either this object has almost no intimate connection (relation) with it, so that it is simply the object of the action expressed by the verb of the main clause; or it is included in the very action of the verb of the main clause as the ground from which it comes into being, and is thus its effect; or the object in question does not yet exist, but is to be produced by the action of the main clause and is intended by the agent (the end).

> [Note: [Col. 1203] In other words, the object is either simply governed by the verb of the main clause, or is the effect of the action, or the end of the action. Translator.]

Now the case in which the object is presented as the consequence of a certain degree, measure, or extent of the action belongs to effect (consecution); the case in which what the agent intends is specially expressed belongs to end (purpose). Where the verbs of the main clause are constructed in the passive, the objective clause becomes subjective.

§ 269. With regard to the sequence of tenses in these clauses, the following is to be observed:

1) The tense of the subordinate clause corresponds with that of the main clause in this way: where the present or past is used in the main clause, the present or past subjunctive is used in the subordinate clause: John XVII.15, ni bidja þuk, ei usnimais ïns us þamma fairwau, ak ei bairgais ïm faura þamma unseljin, “I ask you not to take them out of the world, but to keep them from the evil one”; Luke VII.36, baþ ïna sums fareisaie, ei matidedi miþ ïmma, “a certain Pharisee asked him to eat with him”; Mark VI.25, viljau, ei mis [Col. 1204] gibais haubid ïohannis, “I wish you to give me the head of John”; IX.30, ni vilda, ei was vissedi, “he did not wish anyone to know”; John XI.31, gaggiþ du hlaiva, ei greitai jainar, “she goes to the tomb in order to weep there”; v. 19, gaqemun bi marþan jah marjan, ei gaþrafstidedeina ïzos bi broþar ïzo, “they came to Martha and Mary in order to comfort them concerning their brother”; 1 Tim. V.20, fravaurhtans ïn andvairþja allaize gasak, ei jah þai anþarai agis habaina, “rebuke those who sin before all, that the others also may have fear”; Phil. I.22, wa þau valjau, ni kann, “what I shall choose, I do not know”; Luke XVIII.36, frah, wa vesi þata, “he asked what this might be.”

2) Since the passive has no preterite, either the present is substituted for it, or a periphrastic past form is employed: Rom. VIII.4, gavargida fravaurht ïn leika, ei garaihtei vitodis usfulljaidau ïn uns, “sin was condemned in the flesh, in order that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us”; 1 Cor. I.17, ni ïnsandida mik xristus daupjan ak vailamerjan, ni ïn suntrein vaurdis, ei ni lausjaidau galga xristaus, “Christ sent me not to baptize but to preach the gospel, not in wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ should be emptied [of force]”; 2 Cor. VII.9; XI.7, etc.; Luke II.3, ïddjedun allai, ei melidai veseina (ἀπογράφεσθαι), warjizuh ïn sainai baurg, “all went to be enrolled, each in his own city”; Eph. III.10, mis atgibana varþ ansts so ïn þiudom vailamerjan gabein xristaus, ei kanniþ vesi (γνωρισθῇ) reikjam jah valdufnjau handugei guþs, “to me grace was given to preach among the nations the riches of Christ, in order that the wisdom of God might be made known to principalities and powers”; 1 Thess. III.1, etc.

3) Since Gothic has only one past tense, it also uses this in the subordinate clause as a perfect where a present occurs in the main clause: John IX.19, sau ïst sa sunus ïzvar þanei qiþiþ, þatei blinds gabaurans vaurþi, “is this your son, whom you say was born blind?”; 2 Cor. XI.21, bi unsveriþai qiþa sve þatei veis siukai veseima, “I speak by way of reproach, as though we had been weak”; Gal. IV.11, og, ïbai svare arbaididedjau ïn ïzvis, “I fear lest I have laboured in vain for you.”

4) Where the past tense in the main clause has perfect force, the present follows in the subordinate clause when something future is declared: Mark IX.12, gameliþ-ïst bi sunu mans, ei manag vinnai jah frakunþs vairþai, “it is written concerning the Son of Man that he shall suffer much and be despised”; XII.19, moses gamelido (“he wrote,” and what was written remains valid) þatei jabai wis broþar gadauþnai jah bileiþai qenai jah barne ni bileiþai, ei nimai broþar ïs þo qen ïs, “Moses wrote that, if anyone’s brother dies and leaves a wife but leaves no child, his brother shall take his wife”; 1 Cor. IX.22, allaim vas (γέγονα, “I have become”) all, ei waiva sumans ganasjau, “I have become all things to all, that I might by all means save some”; 2 Cor. I.9; XII.7, etc.

Otherwise, especially in the translation of the Epistles, after a past tense in the main clause a present is used in the subordinate clause where the meaning is objective (that is, where it is stated that something must be done), while the past gives a subjective sense (when it is said that something can or could happen). In the Greek text, since the optative occurs only very rarely in the New Testament, the subjunctive always appears here: John IX.22, gaqeþun sis ïudaieis, ei jabai was ïna andhaihaiti xristu, utana synagogais vairþai, “the Jews had agreed among themselves that, if anyone should confess him to be Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue”; Luke XVI.4, andþahta mik wa taujau (ποιήσω), “I have resolved what I shall do”; Col. I.9, ni weilaidedum faur ïzvis bidjandans ei fullnaiþ (πληρωθῆτε) kunþjis viljins ïs, “we have not ceased praying for you that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will”; Luke I.4, galeikaida mis þus meljan, ei gakunnais (ἐπιγνῷς: “you may learn,” “you may be instructed”) þize vaurde astaþ, “it seemed good to me to write to you, that you might learn the certainty of the words”; *Skeireins* I.d, leik man andnam, ei laisareis uns vairþai þizos du guþa garaihteins, “he took human flesh in order that he might become for us a teacher of the righteousness toward God”; 1 Thess. [Col. 1205] III.2, ïnsandidedum teimauþaiu ei ïzvis gatulgjai jah bidjai (εἰς τὸ στηρίξαι καὶ παρακαλέσαι) bi galaubein ïzvava, “we sent Timothy in order that he might strengthen and exhort you concerning your faith”; Rom. IX.11; XI.32; 2 Cor. I.4; II.3–5, 9; IV.4; V.15; Gal. II.5, 10, 16, 19; Eph. I.4; II.7, 9, 10; VI.22; Phil. II.28; Col. IV.8.

> [Note: [Col. 1205] Here an error has entered the text, since *kunnjai* is not a correct form. If it is minimally corrected to *kunnjau*, it may readily be assumed that the Gothic translator read γνῶ (“that I may know”) instead of γνῷ (“that he may know”), while preserving the sense otherwise: “that I may know what concerns you”; conversely Eph. VI.22, ei kunneiþ wa biugk ïst, “that you may know how matters stand.”]

1 Thess. II.16; V.10; 1 Tim. I.3; Philemon 15; *Skeireins* V.a.

Conversely, 2 Cor. I.15, þizai trauainai vilda faurþis qiman at ïzvis, ei anþara anst habaidedeiþ (ἔχητε: “that you may have,” “that you may be able to have”), “in this confidence I wished first to come to you, that you might have a second grace”; III.13, moses lagida hulistr ana andavleizn duþe ei ni fairveitidedeina (“that they might be able to see”) sunjus ïsraelis ïn andi þis gataurnandins, “Moses put a veil over his face so that the sons of Israel might not be able to look upon the end of what was passing away”; 2 Thess. III.8, ni arvjo hlaib matidedum at wamma ak vinnandans arbaidai naht jah dag vaurkjandans, ei ni kauridedeima (“that we might be able to burden”) wana ïzvara, “we did not eat anyone’s bread without payment, but worked in labour night and day so that we might not burden any of you”; Eph. IV.10, usstaig ufar allans himinans, ei usfullidedi allata, “he ascended above all heavens in order that he might fill all things”; 2 Cor. IX.3; Gal. I.4; II.4; IV.3, 4; Eph. II.15, 16; V.26, 27; Phil. II.30; 1 Tim. I.16; Philemon 13, etc. Hence the translator of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians said in V.21, xristus faur uns gatavida fravaurht, ei veis vaurþeima (“that we might become”) garaihtei guþs ïn ïmma, “Christ was made sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in him”; conversely, VIII.9, ïn ïzvara gaunledida sik, ei jus þamma ïs unledja gabeigai vairþaiþ (“that you ought to become rich through his poverty”). Hence 1 Cor. IX.21, varþ ïudaium sve judaius ei judaiuns gageigaidedjau—ei gageiggau vitodalausans—gageiggau is incorrect, as is shown partly by the preceding and following past tenses, partly by the marginal gloss (*gavandidedjau*).

5) The Gothic translator imitates Greek only when, in indirect discourse and an indirect question, after a past tense in the main clause he uses the present of the subordinate clause—here in the subjunctive, there in the indicative: Mark I.27, sokidedun miþ sis misso qiþandans, wa sijai (ἐστί) þata, “they questioned among themselves, saying, ‘What is this?’”; Luke VIII.9, frehun ïna siponjos ïs qiþandans, wo sijai (εἴη? ἦν)? so gajuko, “his disciples asked him, saying, ‘What might this parable be?’”; Mark II.1, gafrehun, þatei ïn garda ïst (ἐστί), “they heard that he was in the house”; John XII.9; Mark XVI.4, ïnsaiwandeins gaumidedun þammei afvalviþs ïst (ἀποκεκύλισται) sa stains, “looking, they observed that the stone had been rolled away”; John XVIII.14, kajafa garaginoda ïudaium, þatei batizo ïst ainana mannan fraqistjan faur managein, “Caiaphas had advised the Jews that it was better for one man to perish for the people.”

§ 270. I. 1) Where the subordinate clause has no intimate connection with the action of the main clause, but is joined to it only externally—as is the case after verbs of sensation, speaking, thinking, and the like—its relation is commonly indicated by *þatei*, more rarely by *ei*, *þei*, or *unte* with the indicative: Matt. V.21, hausideduþ þatei qiþan ïst þaim airizam: ni maurþrjais, “you have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not murder’”; *Skeireins* II.c, nasjands þana anavairþan dom ïs gasaw jah þatei ïn galaubeinai þeihan habaida, “the Saviour saw his present judgment and that he had growth in faith”; Mark XII.35, waiva qiþand þai bokarjos, þatei xristus sunus ïst daveidis? “How do the scribes say that Christ is David’s son?”; 1 Tim. I.15, triggv þata vaurd þatei xristus qam ïn þamma fairwau, fravaurhtans nasjan, “trustworthy is the saying that Christ came into the world to save sinners”; 2 Cor. I.12, woftuli unsara so ïst veitvodei miþvisseins unsaraizos, [Col. 1206] þatei ïn ainfalþein jah hlutrein guþs usmetum ïn þamma fairwau, “this is our boast, the testimony of our conscience: that in simplicity and godly sincerity we have conducted ourselves in the world”; 1 Thess. III.6, teimauþaius gataih uns galaubein ïzvara jah þatei gaminþi unsar habaiþ goþ, “Timothy came to us [bringing] your faith and that you have good remembrance of us”; Luke XX.37, þatei urreisand dauþans jah moses bandvida ana aiwatundjai, “that the dead are raised, Moses also showed at the bush”; Gal. IV.22, gameliþ ïst þatei abraham tvans aihta sununs, “it is written that Abraham had two sons”; 1 Cor. XI.23, andnam at fraujin þatei, ïn þizaiei naht galevïþs vas, nam hlaif jah aviliudonds gabrak, “I received from the Lord that, in the night in which he was betrayed, he took bread and, having given thanks, broke it”; Rom. VII.16, jabai þatei ni viljau þata tauja, gaqiss ïm vitoda, þatei goþ (that is, “that it is good”), “if I do what I do not wish, I agree with the law that it is good”; Luke XIX.42, gafulgin ïst faura augam þeinaim, þatei qimand dagos ana þus jah bigraband fijands þeinai grabai þuk, “it has been hidden from your eyes that days shall come upon you and your enemies shall surround you with a rampart”; 1 Cor. XV.27, biþe qiþiþ alla ufhnaivida sind, bairht (that is, “it is evident”) þatei ïnu þana ïze ufhnaivida uf ïna þo alla, “when it says, ‘all things have been subjected,’ it is evident that [this excludes] him who subjected all things to him”; 2 Cor. III.3, svikunþ (ïst) þatei sijuþ aipistaule xristaus, “it is manifest that you are an epistle of Christ”; 1 Tim. VI.7, ni vaiht brahtedum ïn þamma fairwau, bi sunjai þatei ni usbairan wa magum, “we brought nothing into the world; certainly, [it is evident] that we can carry nothing out”; Mark XIII.28, þan smakkabagmis asts þlaqus vairþiþ, kunnuþ þatei newa ïst asans, “when the fig-tree’s branch becomes tender, you know that summer is near”; V.29, ufkunþa ana leika þatei gahailnoda, “she knew in her body that she had been healed”; Matt. XXVI.2, vituþ þatei afar tvans dagans paska vairþiþ, “you know that after two days the Passover comes”; John XII.16, gamundedun þatei þata was du þamma gameliþ, “they remembered that this had been written concerning him”; VIII.45, þatei sunja rodida, ni galaubeiþ mis, “because I speak truth, you do not believe me.” Likewise after *gatrauan* (“trust”), Rom. VIII.38; *ahjan* (“say”), Matt. X.34; *haban* (“have” in the sense “hold that”), Matt. XI.32; *domjan* (“judge”), 2 Cor. V.15; etc.; see Glossary, s.v. *þatei* a).

John 14:28 “You heard that I said to you”; 9:17 “What do you say concerning him, since he opened your eyes?” 15:18 “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you”; 17:7 “Now they have known that all things which you gave me are from you”; 11:23 “I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you”; 2 Thess. 3:4 “We have confidence in the Lord concerning you, that you both do and will do what we command you”; 2 Cor. 1:13 “I hope that you will understand even to the end”; 10:7 “If anyone trusts in himself that he is Christ’s, let him again consider this concerning himself, that as he is Christ’s, so also are we”; Mark 11:23 “Whatever he believes—that what he says will happen—it shall happen to him.” Hence elliptical forms: 2 Cor. 1:18 “God is faithful, that our word is not yes and no”; Gal. 1:20 “Behold, before God, that I do not lie.”

John 13:38 “Truly I say to you, that the cock shall not crow until you have denied me three times”; Matt. 6:26 “Look at the birds of heaven, that they neither sow nor reap”; John 13:35 “By this all will know that you are my disciples”; 1 Cor. 4:9 “For I think that God has displayed us apostles as men condemned to death”; Luke 1:58 “Her neighbours heard that the Lord had magnified his mercy toward her.”

2) A subjective clause is formed by *þatei* and *ei*, when the main verb is intransitive: Mark 2:16 “Why is it that you eat and drink with tax-collectors and sinners?” Elliptically, Luke 2:49 “Why is it that you sought me?” John 9:30 “It is a marvel that you do not know whence he is”; Mark 9:21 “How long is it since this happened to him?”

> Note 1.—That in this subjective clause the Goth does not forget that *þatei* is a relative pronoun is apparent from the fact that, where the verb of the principal clause governs a dative, he uses *þammei* in place of *þatei*: Phil. 2:24 “I trust in the Lord that I myself also shall come shortly”; Mark 16:4 “And looking up, they observed that the stone had been rolled away”; 7:18 “Do you not understand that everything entering a man from outside cannot defile him?” Luke 1:32; 17:5; John 6:5; 2 Tim. 1:12; and likewise after *faginon þammei*, Luke 15:6, and *niu kara þuk þizei*, Mark 4:38. Nevertheless, especially in the later period, *þatei* occurs not infrequently after *gaumjan* and *fraþjan*: *Skeireins* VII, d: “He caused others to remember that he was the same one who, in the desert, for forty years fed the fathers”; Mark 12:12 “They perceived that he had spoken the parable against them”; Luke 20:19; John 8:27; *Skeireins* VIII, d.

> Note 2.—The Goth also mixes the aforesaid particles in his own fashion where they occur together in the same phrase: John 9:24–25, “We know that this man is a sinner.” Then that man answered: “Whether he is a sinner, I do not know; one thing I know, that whereas I was blind, now I see”; 1 Cor. 15:3–4, “I received that Christ died for our sins, and that he was buried, and that he rose on the third day, and that he appeared to the eleven”; also after different verbs: 2 Cor. 13:6, “I hope that you shall know that we are not rejected.” Codex B instead reads, conversely, *venja þatei kunneiþ ei*, etc.

> Note 3.—For the occasional use here of the subjunctive after *þatei* and *ei*, see §271; for the infinitive following these verbs instead of the particles *þatei* and *ei*, see §§252, 253.

§ 271. In indirect discourse, where a speaker reports another’s words not as his own, but as an object of his thought, *þatei* and *ei* are used with the subjunctive; in this case Greek uses the indicative: John 9:19 “Is this your son, whom you say was born blind?” 10:36 “Do you say that I blaspheme, because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” 1 Cor. 1:15 “I thank God that I baptized none of you, lest anyone should say that I baptized in my own name”; 10:19 “What then do I say? That what is sacrificed to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything?” *Skeireins* VIII, c: “Finding them false, lest any king or ruler should believe in him.”

Hence also Luke 16:1, “A certain rich man had a steward; and he was accused to him that he was wasting his goods”; John 8:56, “Abraham rejoiced that he should see my day”; John 9:18, “The Jews did not believe concerning him that he had been blind and had received sight”; *Skeireins* I, b: “Knowing that necessity had been shown to be of such mighty power”; Mark 6:55, “They carried those who were ill where they heard that he was”; Luke 18:9, “They trusted in themselves that they were righteous”; Matt. 6:7, “They think that they shall be heard for their much speaking”; 5:17, “Do not think that I came to destroy the law”; Luke 19:11; John 11:13; 12:18, 34; 2 Cor. 12:19, etc.

> Note 1.—Only when Greek precedes him does the Goth use the present indicative even after a past-tense main clause; see §269, 5.

> Note 2.—*Þatei* and *ei* are also used in direct speech, but with the indicative, following Greek: Matt. 27:43 “He said that he is the Son of God”; Mark 1:40 “He said to him, ‘If you will, you can cleanse me’”; 6:16 “Herod said, ‘He whose head I cut off—he is the one who rose from the dead’”; 10:33 Jesus began to tell them what would happen to him: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem”; John 9:9, some said, “He is [the man]”; others, “He is like him”; but he said, “I am [he]”; Luke 8:20, “It was reported to him that your mother and your brothers are standing outside”; John 13:33, he said to the Jews, “Where I go, you cannot come”; Matt. 7:23; 26:72; Mark 2:1; 12:7; 14:72; Luke 4:21; 15:27; 19:42, etc. In Matt. 5:31, “It has been said that whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce,” the subjunctive is used for the imperative (*δότω*, “let him give”).

> Note 3.—To this construction of *þatei* may be compared cases in which Old Testament passages are cited through similar particles: Rom. 9:17, “The scripture says to Pharaoh, ‘For this reason I raised you up’”; 10:9.

> Note 4.—At times the Goth also varies the construction, using *þatei* before a clause for the first time but omitting it the second time: Luke 9:8, “Some said that John had risen from the dead; others said, ‘Elijah has appeared’; but others, ‘One of the prophets of old has risen’”; John 7:12, “Some said that he is good; others said, ‘No, but he deceives the multitude.’”

> Note 5.—Where an intervening parenthetical clause is inserted between the particle of citation and the principal clause of the speech, the corresponding particle is repeated after the parenthesis: John 13:29, “Some thought, because Judas had the purse, that Jesus was saying to him, ‘Buy …’”; 2 Cor. 5:1, “We know that, if our earthly house of this tent is destroyed, we have a building from God.”

§ 272. Just as clauses with *þatei*, *ei*, etc. may be used as object or subject, so also may they be used as an apposition in explanatory or epexegetical clauses: Luke 2:10, “I bring you great joy, which shall be for all the people, namely, that this day a Saviour has been born to you”; John 5:36, “The works which I do bear witness concerning me, that the Father sent me”; 2 Cor. 8:2, “I make known to you the grace of God given in the churches of Macedonia, that their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality”; 8:9; 10:11, “Let such a one reckon this, that such as we are in word by letters, such also are we in deed”; Luke 7:39, “If he were a prophet, he would know who and what kind of woman this is who touches him, namely, that she is a sinner”; Rom. 10:9, “The word of faith which we preach, that … you shall be saved.” Instead of *þatei*, *unte* also occurs (cf. §278): 2 Cor. 11:7, “Or did I commit sin by humbling myself, that you might be exalted, because I preached the gospel of God to you freely?” Luke 8:30, “What is your name?” And he said, “Legion,” because many demons had entered into him.

John 16:17 “What is this that he says to us?” Mark 1:27 “They questioned among themselves, ‘What is this? What new teaching is this, that he commands even the unclean spirits and they obey him?’” 6:2; Luke 4:36; 1:43, “Whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” Here *ei qemi* stands for *ei* or *þatei qimiþ*, through excessive imitation of Greek *ἵνα ἐλθῃ*, which can stand only for *τὸ ἐλθεῖν* (“the coming”) or *ὅτι ἦλθε* (“that she came”); likewise John 6:29, “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom God sent”; v. 50, “This is the bread which came down from heaven, that whoever eats of it may not die”; 15:13; 17:3.

§ 273. 1) Indirect questions also belong here. They may generally have the verb in the subjunctive, but also in the indicative where the question concerns the past: Matt. 6:25 “Do not be anxious for your life, what you shall eat and what you shall drink, nor for your body, what you shall put on”; Luke 8:9, the disciples asked what the parable might be; Mark 1:27; John 16:18; Luke 15:26, he asked what this was; 19:48, “They did not find what they might do”; 19:15; Luke 1:29, Mary considered what manner of greeting this might be; 9:46, “A dispute arose among them as to which of them might be greatest”; Col. 4:6, “Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each one”; Matt. 8:20, “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head”; 2 Cor. 13:5, “Test yourselves whether you are in the faith”; 2:9; Mark 10:2; 15:36; Luke 14:28; 15:44, Pilate asked the centurion whether Jesus had already died; Phil. 3:12, “I press on, if I may lay hold of that for which I was laid hold of by Christ”; Luke 6:7, “They watched whether he would heal on the Sabbath”; 3:15, all reasoned in their hearts concerning John whether perhaps he might be the Christ; Phil. 1:22, “What I shall choose, I do not know,” where *þau* is rendered elsewhere by Greek *ἄν*.

John 8:14, “I know whence I came and whither I go, but you do not know whence I come and whither I go”; Eph. 1:18, “May God give you the spirit of wisdom, that you may know what is the hope of his calling”; John 6:64, Jesus knew who they were that did not believe, and who it was that would betray him; 9:15, they asked him how he had received sight; v. 21, “How he now sees, we do not know; or who opened his eyes, we do not know”; 2 Cor. 1:17, “Did I then use lightness?” Gal. 3:2; Eph. 6:22. Indicative and subjunctive are used indiscriminately in John 7:17: “You shall know concerning the teaching whether it is from God, or whether I speak from myself.”

> Note.—The interrogative particle may also be omitted: Mark 3:2, “They watched him, whether he would heal on the Sabbath”; or the main clause must be supplied: Mark 11:13, “He came [that is, he sought, looked] to see whether perhaps he might find anything on it.” Conversely, Luke 18:8 presents a direct question: “Will the Son of Man, when he comes, perhaps find faith?” Instead of *ei*, *jabai* is also used: John 9:25, “Whether he is a sinner, I do not know.”

2) Among cases of indirect questions there should be noted in Gothic those which mean “I fear lest,” since the subordinate clause is connected with the principal by the interrogative *ïbai* or *ïbai aufto* with the subjunctive: 2 Cor. 12:20, “For I fear lest perhaps, when I come, I may not find you such as I wish, and I may be found by you such as you do not wish me; lest perhaps, when I come again, my God may humble me before you, and I may mourn for many who have previously sinned”; Gal. 4:11, “I fear for you, lest perhaps I have laboured among you in vain”; 2 Cor. 11:3, “But I fear lest perhaps your minds should be corrupted from simplicity.”

With *ogan* (“to fear”) understood: Matt. 27:64, “Command that the tomb be guarded [for we fear] lest perhaps his disciples come, steal him away, and say, ‘He rose’”; Mark 2:21, “No one sews a patch of new cloth on an old garment [he ought to fear], lest the new piece tear away from the old”; 2:22; Luke 14:29; Rom. 11:21; 2 Cor. 12:6; 1 Tim. 3:6, etc.

Hence also 2 Cor. 8:20, “Avoiding this, lest anyone should blame us”; Gal. 2:2, “I went up … lest perhaps I should be running, or had run, in vain”; 6:1, “Take heed to yourself, lest you also be tempted”; 5:15, “See lest you be consumed by one another.”

§ 274. II. RESULT, which is otherwise rendered by the accusative with infinitive (§253, 4; cf. §252, 6), can also be expressed by *ei*, namely:

1) With the subjunctive after *taujan*, *gataujan*, and *biuhti ïst*: John 11:37, “Could not Jesus have done [this], so that he also should not have died?” Col. 4:16, “See to it that the epistle be read in the church of Laodicea, and that you also read that from Laodicea”; John 18:39, “It is a custom among you that I should release one to you at Passover.”

2) With the indicative after *varþ*: John 14:22, “How did it happen that you will reveal yourself to us and not to the world?” Luke 6:12, “It came to pass in those days that Jesus went out into the mountain to pray”; 8:1, “It came to pass afterward that he went through cities and villages.”

> Note 1.—After *varþ*, a coordinate clause also follows in place of a subordinate clause, especially in Luke: 5:17, “It came to pass on one day, and he was teaching”; 8:22, “It came to pass on one of those days, and he went aboard”; 2:15, “It came to pass, when the angels had departed from them, and the shepherds said to one another”; 5:12, 35; 9:51; 17:11; also Neh. 6:16 and Matt. 9:10. Or a subordinate clause without a particle is connected with the main clause: Matt. 26:1, “It came to pass, when Jesus had finished all these sayings, he said to his disciples”; Mark 1:9; Luke 1:59.

> Note 2.—Mark 10:38 has “Are you able to drink the cup which I drink, and to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” either because the Goth wished to use another construction, or perhaps because he needed a passive infinitive.

§ 275. CONSEQUENCE is expressed:

1) By simple *ei* with the past indicative or the present subjunctive: John 9:2, “Who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” Rom. 7:3, “If the husband dies, the wife is free from the law, so that she is not an adulteress if she becomes another man’s wife”; 1 Cor. 9:24, “So run that you may obtain.”

2) Ordinarily by *svaei* or *sve* (*ὥστε*, “so that”), namely:

a) With the indicative: Gal. 2:13, “The other Jews dissembled with him, so that Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation”; 2 Thess. 1:3, “The love of every one of you toward one another increases, so that we ourselves boast of you”; Mark 1:27; 2:28; Rom. 13:2; 2 Cor. 5:16–17; Gal. 4:7, etc., where it often passes into a coordinating sense, “therefore,” “hence”; Luke 5:6–7, “They enclosed a great multitude of fish, so that their nets were breaking; and they filled both boats, so that they began to sink.”
