> Note.—In Gal. 4:16 *ὥστε* is rendered by *ïþ sve*, whence it is inferred that the Goth read *ὥς τε*; *ïþ* is also used in John 6:18 for *τε*.

b) With the subjunctive: 2 Cor. 3:7, “The ministry of death, engraved in letters upon stones, came in glory, so that the sons of Israel could not look steadily upon Moses’ face because of the glory of his face”; 8:5, “They gave themselves to us, as we had hoped,” etc.; *Skeireins* III, c: “John did the lesser thing, promising remission; but the Lord’s [namely, baptism or preaching] brings forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Holy Spirit—so that John’s baptism may stand between the two.”

c) With the infinitive, following Greek: 2 Cor. 2:6, “Sufficient for such a one is this punishment inflicted by the many, so that you should rather forgive and comfort him”; 2 Thess. 2:4, “The opponent and one exalting himself above every so-called god or object of worship, so as to sit in the temple of God”; Luke 9:52, “They entered a village of the Samaritans to make ready for him.”

§ 276. III. PURPOSE, “in order that,” is indeed expressed in Gothic by the infinitive (see §252), but also by *ei* when affirmative; where the purpose is negative, by *ei ni* with the subjunctive:

a) After verbs of willing: Matt. 27:17, “Whom will you that I release to you?” 1 Cor. 16:12, “It was not his will that Apollos should come”; John 6:40; 1 Thess. 4:3, etc.

b) Especially after verbs signifying some intention of the will, such as commanding, forbidding, asking, seeking, deciding, giving, etc.: Mark 8:7, Jesus, blessing the fish, commanded that they should set them before them; Eph. 4:17, “I say and testify in the Lord that you no longer walk in the vanity of [your] mind”; Mark 3:9; 9:18; Luke 4:3; Gal. 5:16; Mark 5:43, “He strictly commanded them that no one should know this”; John 13:34, “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another”; Mark 7:36; 9:9; John 15:12, 17; Mark 6:8, “He commanded them that they should take nothing for the way,” etc.; 3:12, “He sternly charged them that they should not make him known”; 10:47, many rebuked him that he should be silent; 15:11, the chief priests stirred up the crowd that he should release Barabbas to them; 9:12, “It is written concerning the Son of Man, that he should suffer many things and be despised”; 12:19; 6:12, going out they preached that men should repent; Luke 5:7, they beckoned to their partners in the other boat that they should come and help them; Mark 5:10, he begged him earnestly that he should not send them out of the country; Col. 4:12, Epaphras “strives for you in prayers, that you may stand perfect,” etc.; 1 Thess. 5:27, “I charge you by the Lord that the epistle be read to the brethren”; 2 Cor. 2:1, “I determined this for myself, that I would not again come to you in sorrow”; Rom. 14:13, “Determine this, that you do not put a stumbling-block before your brother”; John 9:22, the Jews agreed that, if anyone should confess Jesus as Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue; 1 Thess. 3:1, “We thought it good that we should be left at Athens alone”; Matt. 27:1, the chief priests took counsel concerning Jesus, that they might put him to death; Mark 3:6; John 12:10, the chief priests resolved that they might also kill Lazarus; Gal. 2:17, “Seeking to be justified in Christ, might we ourselves be found sinners?” Matt. 8:4, “See—i.e. take care—that you tell no one”; 9:30; Mark 1:44; 8:15; 1 Cor. 16:10; Col. 4:17; Mark 15:15, Pilate delivered Jesus, having scourged him, that he might be crucified; 10:37, “Grant us that we may sit, one at your right and one at your left”; 11:16, Jesus did not allow anyone to carry a vessel through the temple.

c) After verbs and formulas indicating need, necessity, or obligation: Matt. 3:11, “I am not worthy to untie the thong of his sandals”; 8:8, etc.; *Skeireins* I, c: “It was contrary to what was fitting that the Lord, when he came, should destroy him by divine power”; John 12:23, “The hour has come that the Son of Man should be glorified”; 16:30, “You have no need that anyone should ask you”; 1 Thess. 5:1.

d) After impersonals and formulas such as *ganah*, “sufficient,” *goþ ïst*, “it is good,” *ïn minnistin ïst*, “it is of least concern,” etc.: Matt. 10:25, “It is sufficient for the disciple that he become as his teacher”; Mark 9:42, “It is better for him that a millstone be put about his neck and he be cast into the sea”; Matt. 5:29, “It is better for you that one of your members perish, and not your whole body be cast into Gehenna”; v. 30; John 16:7; 1 Cor. 4:2, “It is of least concern to me that I should be examined by you.”

> Note 1.—Here the indicative is rarely used after *ei*, [Col. 1213] as: Mark 11:28, “Who gave you this authority, that you do these things?” John 16:2, “The hour comes when everyone who kills you thinks that he offers service to God”; v. 17, “A little while, and you do not see me.” In the last two cases *ei* is simply relative. Elsewhere *jah* also follows *leitil*: John 16:19, as always happens in Greek; cf. §274, note 1. Compare Luke 7:4, “He is worthy that you should grant him this.”

> Note 2.—Instead of *ei*, *þatei* occurs once: *Skeireins* III, c, “The Lord grants them that they may become sons of the kingdom.”

> Note 3.—For the construction of the formula “to fear lest,” see §273, 2.

e) After verbs of motion and whole clauses: John 12:9, “They came not for Jesus’ sake alone, but that they might also see Lazarus”; Matt. 27:42, “Let him come down from the cross, that we may see and believe him”; Mark 3:2, “They watched him whether he would heal on the Sabbath, that they might accuse him”; 10:17, “What shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?” 16:1, “They bought spices, that, coming, they might anoint Jesus”; John 12:42, “Because of the Pharisees they did not confess, lest they should be cast out of the synagogue”; 1 Cor. 1:15, “I thank God that I baptized none of you, lest anyone should say that I baptized in my own name,” etc.; see Glossary V, *Ei* 5 a). Here also belongs the formula *ei usfullnodedi þata gamelido*, “that the scripture might be fulfilled,” Matt. 8:17; Mark 14:49; John 12:38, etc.

> Note 4.—In John *þei* is sometimes substituted for *ei*: 6:12, “Gather the remaining fragments, that nothing may be lost”; 7; 13:34; 16:33.

> Note 5.—Once *ei* with the indicative occurs: John 14:3, “I will come again and receive you to myself, that where I am, there you also may be”; and *ni*, *ne*, for *ei ni*: *Skeireins* III, b, “And bodily purity was customary, while purity with respect to God was commanded—not thereafter to employ Jewish transgressions to put [people] to death.”

> Note 6.—*Ei* also permits *þau* (*ἄν*) after it: Luke 16:4, “I have considered what I shall do, that, when I am put out of the stewardship, they may receive me”; Mark 6:56.

> Note 7.—Since purpose is also expressed by *du* and the infinitive (§254 I, 2), the two constructions are sometimes mixed: Mark 3:14, Jesus appointed twelve “to be with him and that he might send them to preach”; Luke 2:22–24, they brought Jesus to Jerusalem “to present him before the Lord and to offer sacrifice for him”; *Skeireins* IV, d: “The accusations against John were not in this, that he should acknowledge the Lord’s greatness, but in refuting and condemning idolatrous hatred.”

> Note 8.—Greek *ἵνα μή* is often rendered by *ïbai*, which ordinarily, however, means “lest”; see §273, 2.

§ 277. Grammatically speaking, AIM is distinguished from purpose in the same manner as consequence from result (§[Col. 1214] 275); for then the conjunction (*ei*) of the subordinate clause is prepared by a demonstrative in the main clause. Mark 4:21, “Does a lamp come for this purpose—that it may be put under a measure or under a bed? Is it not for this—that it may be put on a lampstand?” Eph. 6:22, “I sent Tychicus to you for this purpose, that you may know how we are”; 3:4; 2 Cor. 3:13; John 18:37, “For this I was born and for this I came into the world, that I might bear witness to the truth”; Rom. 9:17, “For this reason I raised you up, that I might show my power in you.”

> Note: [Col. 1213] Greek has *εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο*, “for this very thing”; this is commonly translated in Gothic by *du þamma* (2 Cor. 5:5; Eph. 5:28). *Ïn þize*, on the other hand, means “because of which”; but the Goth agrees with the translators of the Septuagint, whose wording (*ἕνεκεν τούτου*, Exod. 9:16) is cited here.

Hence also *þeei*, “therefore, in order that”: John 6:38, “I came down from heaven not in order to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me”; 2 Cor. 2:4, “I wrote to you through many tears, not in order that you should grieve, but that you might know my love.”

### B. Causal Clause

§ 278. Causal subordinate clauses are indicated by *ei*, *þei*, *unte*, and *þatei*, “that, because” (*ὅτι*, *ἐπεί*), with the indicative. They occur:

1) After verbs which state a reason for something, such as rejoicing, wondering, showing mercy, giving thanks [Note: [Col. 1214] Or rather after verbs whose action requires a reason, motive, or cause in order to exist—for example, rejoicing, wondering, etc., concerning or on account of something. Translator.], cf. §239: Luke 10:20, “Do not rejoice in this, that the spirits obey you”; John 14:28, “If you loved me, you would rejoice that I go to the Father”; Mark 15:44, Pilate marvelled that Jesus had already died; Gal. 1:6; 1 Cor. 1:14, “I thank God that I baptized none of you”; 11:2, “I praise you because you remember me in all things.”

Luke 15:9, “Rejoice with me, because I found the drachma”; Phil. 4:10; Luke 1:47, “My spirit rejoiced in God, because he looked upon the lowliness of his servant”; Mark 8:2, “I have compassion on the multitude, because they have now been with me three days and have nothing to eat”; 1 Tim. 1:13, “I obtained mercy because I acted ignorantly in unbelief”; 4:10, “We toil because we have hoped in the living God”; John 7:23, “You hate me because I made the whole man well on the Sabbath”; Luke 16:8, the lord praised the unjust steward because he had acted prudently; 18:11, “I thank you because I am not like the other men”; John 11:41; 2 Cor. 8:17; Luke 17:9, “Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded?” Matt. 5:8, “Blessed are the pure in heart, because they shall see God.”

> Note.—The subjunctive is used here only very rarely, as in John 11:15, “I rejoice for your sake, that you may believe”; Phil. 2:2, “Complete my joy, that you think the same thing.” In the latter passage *ei* rather means “for this reason, that.”

2) After interrogatives *wileiks ïst*, *was ïst*, with an emphatic sense, “Who is he?” “What manner is he?” Matt. 8:27, “What manner of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?” In the parallel passage, Mark 4:41, *unte* occurs instead of *ei*; Luke 1:29, Mary considered what manner of greeting this was, because it was addressed to her in such a manner; 8:25, “Who is this, that he commands even winds and water?” Here also the subjunctive is used after *ei*: Rom. 9:20, “Who are you, that you answer back to God?” John 9:36.

[Col. 1215] 3) After entire clauses, *þatei* and *unte*, and likewise *þande* with the indicative, are used: John 10:33, “We do not stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy, and because you make yourself God”; 15:5, “He who abides in me and I in him bears much fruit, because without me you can do nothing”; 16:9; 17:8; Gal. 4:6, etc.; Matt. 5:34, “I say to you, do not swear at all: neither by heaven, because it is God’s throne; nor by earth, because it is his footstool; nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great king”; 27:6, “It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood,” etc.; see Glossary V, *Unte* 2 b); Luke 2:29, “Now release your servant in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation”; 16:3, “What shall I do, because my lord is taking the stewardship from me?” 1:34; John 5:38; 9:16; 1 Cor. 15:20; Phil. 1:18.

Here a demonstrative also prepares the causal clause: Luke 1:13, “Do not fear, because your prayer has been heard”; v. 35, “The power of the Highest shall overshadow you; therefore the holy one who is born shall be called the Son of God”; v. 20; 2:4; 1 Cor. 15:9. In John, *dute unte*: 8:47, “For this reason you do not hear, because you are not of God”; 15:19, “Because you are not of the world, therefore the world hates you”; 10:17; 15:19; John 16:19, “You seek among yourselves concerning this, that I said …” Here also belongs Luke 15:6, “Rejoice with me, because I found my sheep,” where *þammei* is used for *þamma ei* (“because of that which”); see §270, note 1. Compare 2 Cor. 11:11, “Why? Because I do not love you?”

4) The subjunctive is used in causal clauses where a negation precedes the causal particle: John 7:22, “For this reason Moses gave you circumcision—not because it is from Moses, but from the fathers”; 2 Cor. 3:5, “We have such confidence through Christ toward God, not because we are sufficient to reckon anything as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God”; 2 Thess. 3:9, “We did not eat bread without payment, not because we had no authority, but that we might make ourselves an example for you”; 2 Cor. 1:24; Phil. 3:12; 4:11, 17; *Skeireins* IV, b; John 12:6, “He said this not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief.” Yet after *ni unte* the indicative follows: 2 Cor. 7:9, “Now I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved unto repentance.”

### C. Modal Clause

§ 279. The modal clause of the simple sentence (§241) corresponds here to:

## I. Comparative Clause

Two things are compared:

1) Things presented as alike. In this case the correlative particles “as” (*ὡς*)—“so” (*οὕτως, οὕτως καί*) are used: *svasve*, or, commonly when single objects are compared, *sve*—*sva*, or *svah jah* and likewise *svah*: John 13:15, “I have given you an example, that as I did to you, so you also should do”; Rom. 12:4, “As we have many members in one body, so we, being many, are one body”; Mark 4:26, “Thus is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed upon the earth”; 2 Cor. 1:5, “As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so also through Christ our consolation abounds”; Eph. 5:24, “As the church is subject to Christ, so also wives [should be subject] to their own husbands”; Luke 17:26, “As it came to pass in the days of Noah, so shall it also be in the days of the Son of Man”; John 15:4, “As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it abides in the vine, so neither can you unless you abide in me.”

At times the demonstrative particle is also absent: 2 Cor. 8:6, “We urged Titus that, as he had previously begun, so he should also complete among you this grace”; “but as you abound in everything, in faith, and in all diligence, and in your love for us, so abound also in this grace”; Matt. 6:10, “May your will be done as in heaven”; 7:29; 2 Cor. 2:17; Matt. 6:12, “Forgive us what we owe, as we also forgive our debtors”; Luke 6:36; 9:54, “Do you wish us to say that fire should come down from heaven, as Elijah did?” 2 Cor. 11:3, “But I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by cunning, your minds should be corrupted from simplicity.”

> Note 1.—Instead of *svasve* or *sve*, *svaei* occurs once, Luke 3:23: Jesus was about thirty years old at the beginning, being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph.

> Note 2.—The same meaning is expressed by *samaleiko sve*: Luke 17:28, “They ate and drank; likewise, as it happened in the days of Lot.”

> Note 3.—In comparative clauses, unless another influence is operative, the verb is always in the indicative. The subjunctive is used only in Eph. 6:20: “For the gospel, an ambassador in chains, that therein I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak”; and 1 Cor. 4:7, “Why do you boast as though you had not received?” In the same manner *ὡς* with a participle is paraphrased in Luke 16:1: the steward “was accused that he was wasting his lord’s goods,” though *sve* and *svasve* may stand with the participle; see 2 Cor. 10:9, 14.

2) Or one thing surpasses another; in this case the comparative is used with following *þau*: Mark 10:25, “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God”; Luke 5:23, “Which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’?” 16:17, “It is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of the law to fall”; Rom. 13:11, “Now our salvation is nearer than when we believed”; Eph. 3:20, “Glory to him who is able to do exceedingly above all that we ask or think.” Compare §§197, 4 and 250, 4 b.

> Note 4.—In Mark 9:47, “It is good for you to enter into the kingdom of God one-eyed, rather than having two eyes to be cast into Gehenna,” *goþ* (“good”) is used instead of the comparative *batizo* (“better”). Compare Luke 15:7: “Thus, in relation to the preceding comparison, there shall be joy in heaven over one sinner repenting, rather than over ninety-nine righteous persons.”

## § 280. II. HYPOTHETICAL OR CONDITIONAL SENTENCE

In conditional sentences, the mood to be chosen depends not so much on the preceding Greek as rather on the different way in which the translator views the matter: he either thinks of things as actually existing, or regards them as merely possible. In the former case, namely where the hypothesis is viewed as real, the indicative is used; in the latter, where the hypothesis is held to be simply possible, the present subjunctive; but the past subjunctive is used where the hypothesis is regarded as non-real only. Moreover, in this last case the past subjunctive occurs both with *þau* and with *aiþþau*; in the two former cases there is the indicative or present subjunctive, or indeed the imperative. The hypothetical or conditional conjunctions are: *jabai* (εἰ, ἐάν), “if,” “whether,” and *jabai ni*, *niba* (*nibai*, εἰ μή), “unless”; sometimes also *þande* (*þandei*, εἰ). Where antecedent and consequent are constructed in the present subjunctive, the positive condition is indicated by *ïþ* (“if”), which may be placed after the word, and the negative by *nih* (“unless”).

1) Indicative in conditional clauses:

Rom. VII.3: “while the husband lives, the woman is called adulterous if she becomes another man’s wife; but if the husband dies, she is free from this law”; John XIII.17: “if you know these things, blessed are you if you do them”; 2 Cor. XI.4: “if he who comes preaches another Jesus, whom we did not preach, or if you receive another spirit, which you did not receive, you tolerate it well”; VII.14: “if I have boasted, I have not been put to shame”; Matt. VIII.31: “if you cast us out, permit us to go into the herd”; Col. III.1: “if you have risen with Christ, seek the things above”; Gal. II.14: “if you, being a Jew, live as a Gentile, why do you compel the Gentiles to live as Jews?”; 1 Cor. IV.7: “what do you have that you did not receive? Or if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?”; Matt. VI.30: “if God so clothes the grass of the field, how much more you?”; Rom. XI.21: “if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either” (for the future, φείσεται).

Mark VII.3: “the Jews do not eat unless they frequently wash their hands”; and “when they return from the market, they do not eat unless they wash”; John XV.4: “as the branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me”; 1 Cor. XV.2: “you must hold fast the Gospel, unless you believed in vain”; John VII.51: “does our law judge a man unless it first hears from him?”

2) Present subjunctive in conditional clauses:

John VIII.52: “if anyone keeps my word, he shall never taste death”; 2 Tim. II.21: “if anyone cleanse himself from these things, he shall be a vessel for honour” (in our translation *mundet* should be read instead of *mundat*); 1 Cor. XIII.2: “if I have prophecy and know all mysteries—but do not have love, I am nothing; and if I distribute all my possessions—but do not have love, I gain nothing”; Gal. V.11: “if I still preach circumcision, why am I still persecuted?” (in our translation *patiar* should be read instead of *patior*); Matt. V.29: “if your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it from you”; 1 Cor. VII.8: “it is good for them if they remain as I am; but if they cannot control themselves, let them marry.”

John X.37: “if I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, even if you do not believe me, believe the works.”

3) Past subjunctive in conditional and consequent clauses:

John V.46: “if you believed Moses, you would also believe me”; VIII.42: “if God were your Father, you would love me”; XIV.28: “if you loved me, you would rejoice because I go to the Father”; XV.49; 1 Cor. XI.31; Luke VII.39: “if this man were a prophet, he would know what sort of woman this is”; X.13: “woe to you, Chorazin! For if the mighty works done among you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented, sitting in sackcloth and ashes”; *Skeireins* V: “if one and the same person were under the accusation of a sabbath-breaking, how could the same person both stand and not stand?” John VIII.19; IX.41; XI.21, 32; XIV.7; XVIII.36; 1 Cor. XII.19.

John XIV.2: “if it were not so, I would have told you; I go to prepare a place for you”; XVIII.30: “unless this man were an evildoer, we would not have delivered him to you”; Rom. IX.29: “unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah.”

> Note 1.—Sometimes *þau* (ἄν) is also used with the indicative of the consequent clause, where the condition, and generally also the consequent, is negative: Matt. V.20: “unless your righteousness should exceed that of the Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven”; 1 Cor. XV.11: “if Christ has not risen, then our preaching is vain”; Matt. VI.15; Mark XI.26. It is also used with an imperative or subjunctive substituted for it (§ 186): 2 Cor. XI.16: “unless you think me foolish, yet receive me as foolish.” Conversely, *þau* is also omitted in the cases cited under 3): Gal. IV.15: “if it had been possible, you would have plucked out your eyes and given them to me”; *Skeireins* I.b; John VIII.39: “if you were Abraham’s children, you would do Abraham’s works”; XV.24; IX.33: “unless he were from God, he could do nothing”; XV.22; XIX.11; Rom. VII.7.

> Note 2.—Against the natural sequence of tenses, a past tense in the conditional clause and a present (future) in the consequent occur in the following cases: Rom. IX.27: “if the number of the children of Israel were as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved”; John VIII.55: “if I should say that I do not know the Father, I shall be like you”; IX.22: “the Jews had agreed that, if anyone should confess him to be Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue.” On the last passage see § 269.4; compare also Matt. XI.14.

> [Col. 1219] Note 3.—ELLIPSES IN HYPOTHETICAL SENTENCES.
>
> a) Sometimes the consequent clause is missing, either to be supplied from the context or silently omitted, as in the striking passage Mark VIII.12: “Truly I say to you, if a sign shall be given to this generation”; or IX.23: “if you are able to believe”—namely, from what precedes, “I would help you”; John VI.62: “Does this offend you? What then if you see the Son of Man ascending?”—namely, “how much more troubled will you be?” Compare VII.23. Or only the verb is wanting, as Luke XIX.42: “if you too had known, even on this day, the things belonging to your peace”—namely, “you would have acted [accordingly]”; compare Gal. III.4; 1 Tim. VI.3. To this class also belong the parenthetically inserted formulas *jabai mahteig sijai* (“if it be possible,” Mark XIII.22) and *jabai magi vairþan* (“if it can be done,” Rom. XII.18).
>
> b) Where the particle is used once in the same connection, it is sometimes subsequently omitted: Mark XI.34: “if we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ But shall we say …?” The latter means “but shall we say no” (correct German: *aber sagen wir*), for “if we say” ([ἐάν] εἴπωμεν).
>
> c) Where a sentence is presented as an alternative to the antecedent—where Greek uses ἐπεί or εἰ δὲ μήγε, “otherwise”—Gothic uses *aiþþau*, “or else,” whether with the indicative: Matt. VI.1: “take heed not to do your alms before people in order to be seen by them, otherwise you have no reward from God”; IX.17: “nor do they put new wine into old wineskins, otherwise the wineskins burst”; Luke V.36–37; 1 Cor. VII.14 (ἐπεὶ ἄρα); or with the subjunctive: Rom. IX.11: “when they were not yet born and had done neither good nor evil.” In Luke XIV.32 *eiþau* occurs instead of *aiþþau*, excellently explained by the gloss *jabai nist mahteigs*, “if he is not able.” Instead of *aiþþau*, *ïþ jabai ni* is also used where a positive conditional sentence precedes, as Luke X.6: “if a son of peace is there, your peace shall rest upon him; but if not, it shall return to you.” On εἰ δὲ μή wrongly understood in John XIV.11, see the note on that passage. Elsewhere too, with the sense preserved, εἰ δὲ μή in Mark II.21 is translated by *ïbai*. But in 1 Cor. V.11, “do not associate with a fornicator—for otherwise you would have to go out of the world,” the translator’s rendering, though intelligible, is inadequate.
>
> Note 4.—Where a conditional sentence is disjunctive, *jaþþe—jaþþe* (εἴτε—εἴτε), “whether—or,” is used: 1 Cor. X.31: “whether you eat, or drink, or do anything, do all to the glory of God”; 2 Cor. I.6: “whether we are afflicted, for your consolation; or comforted, for your consolation”; *Skeireins* IV.c: “a human witness was either a priest or a prophet,” etc.; see Glossary V, *Jaþþe*. Elliptical is 1 Cor. XIV.27: “whether anyone speaks in tongues, by two …” *Jah—jah*, “both—and,” is also used once, 1 Tim. V.10.
>
> Note 5.—When related to a negation or interrogative in the principal sentence, *niba* (*nibai*) means the Latin *nisi* in such expressions as “none—but,” “except,” “than,” “that” (εἰ μή): John X.10: “the thief does not come except to steal”; Mark II.26: “it is not lawful to eat the loaves of presentation except for priests alone”; VIII.14: “they had with them only one loaf”; II.7: “who can forgive sins except God alone?” Rom. XI.15: “what is their acceptance but life from the dead?” etc.; see Glossary V, *Niba* 2). But where the matter is not a simple object but an entire thought, *niba þatei*, “except that” (εἰ μὴ ὅτι), is used: 2 Cor. XII.13: “in what were you inferior to the other churches, except that I myself was not burdensome to you?” Eph. IV.9: “what does ‘he ascended’ mean except that he also descended into the lower regions of the earth?”
>
> Note 6.—The compound conditional particles εἴγε and εἴπερ, “although,” “even if,” are rendered in Gothic by *jabai sveþauh* (2 Cor. V.3; Eph. III.2; IV.21; Col. I.23) and *sveþauh jabai* (Rom. VIII.9); the latter is also used for ἐάντε in 2 Cor. X.8.

## § 281. III. CONCESSIVE SENTENCE

In this type of sentence, which generally occurs only rarely, the concessive clause, introduced by *þauhjabai*, *jah jabai*, *jabai*, *sveþauh ei*—“even though,” “even if”—and the opposing clause, introduced by the adversative particles *akei*, *aþþan*, *ïþ*—“but,” “yet,” “nevertheless”—are used with the indicative; or the latter remains without an adversative particle: *Skeireins* IV.c: “although Jesus came from heaven to earth, he was not therefore merely earthly”; 2 Cor. IV.16: “though our outward person is decaying, our inward person is renewed day by day”; *Skeireins* IV.c: “he who came from heaven, even if he was thought to be in flesh, is nevertheless above all”; 2 Cor. XI.6; XIII.4; 1 Cor. IX.2: “though I am not an apostle to others, yet I am to you”; Luke XVIII.4: “though I do not fear God and do not respect any person, yet because this widow troubles me, I shall vindicate her.”

> Note: [Col. 1219] *Aþþan* must here be read instead of *aiþþau*; see 2 Cor. IV.16. Nor can *aiþþau* be conjectured from Gal. II.21, since here no adversative particle is needed, as it is there after a negative clause. Conversely, in Rom. XI.22 *aiþþau* must be read instead of *aþþan*; see the note on that passage. It is nevertheless possible that in the later period, to which the translations of the Epistles belong, these two particles no longer differed in usage. [Col. 1220]

1 Cor. VII.21: “though you can become free, use it rather”; John XI.25: “he who believes in me, though he die, shall live”; 2 Tim. II.5: “even if anyone competes, he is not crowned unless he competes lawfully”; 2 Cor. VII.8; XI.12: “I was in no way inferior to the super-apostles, even though I am nothing”; XII.15: “I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls, though, loving you more abundantly, I am loved less.”

> Note.—The concessive sense, which is also properly expressed by a participle, is brought out more distinctly by *jah (þan)*, καίπερ; see Phil. III.4.

## D. TEMPORAL SENTENCE

### § 282

The various ways of determining time in the simple sentence (§ 247 ff.) correspond to, and are here to be considered together with, sentences which answer the questions “when?” and “how long?” Some are used with present propositions (“when”) and past propositions (“when,” “after,” “as soon as”), as well as to designate either time (“while,” “until,” “before”); others are again divided according as they express a span of time (“how long”) or a point in time (“until”).

1) “When” (ὅταν): *þan* and *biþe*, both synonymous (see Mark VIII.38 and Luke IX.26), are constructed with the indicative, but rarely with the subjunctive—namely only where a final clause is connected with their principal clause and is itself in the subjunctive:

Matt. IX.15: “days will come when the bridegroom is taken from them, and then they will fast”; Mark IV.31: “when the mustard seed is sown in the earth, it is the smallest of all seeds”; VIII.38: “whoever is ashamed of me, the Son of Man too will be ashamed of him when he comes in the glory of his Father”; Luke VI.22: “blessed are you when people hate you”; Mark IV.29: “as soon as the crop permits, he immediately sends in the sickle, because the harvest has come”; John VII.27: “but when Christ comes, no one knows where he is from”; 1 Cor. XV.27: “when he says, ‘All things are subjected,’” etc.; see Glossary V, *þan* II.1) and *þe* 2.a.β).

Matt. VI.2: “when you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you”; 5: “when you pray, do not be like the hypocrites. But when you pray, go into your chamber”; Mark XI.25: “when you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone”; Luke XIV.12–13; XVI.9; XVII.10; 1 Cor. XIV.26; Col. IV.16; 2 Tim. IV.3; Luke XIV.10: “when you are invited, go and recline in the lowest place, so that, when he who invited you comes, he may say to you: ‘Go up higher’”; XVI.4: “I have considered what I shall do, so that, when I am removed from stewardship, they may receive me into their houses”; John XIII.19; XIV.29; XVI.4; 1 Cor. XVI.2.

2) “When” (ὅτε, ἐπεί, ὡς): *þan*, *biþe* (though synonymous, for example Matt. XI.1 and XXVI.1, the latter especially means “after”), *sve*, “when” (also used for ἥνικα), and *sunsei*, properly “as soon as.” The last two occur only in John and Luke, while *sve* also occurs in Nehemiah. All are constructed with the indicative:

Matt. VIII.27: “and it happened, when Jesus had finished these sayings, that the crowds were astonished at his teaching”; Mark III.11: “whenever they saw him, they fell down before him”; Rom. VII.5: “when we were in the flesh, sinful passions worked in our members”; Matt. XI.1: “and it happened, after Jesus had finished instructing the twelve, that he departed from there”; Mark IV.10: “when he was alone, those around him asked him about the parables”; Gal. IV.4: “when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son”; Luke I.41: “and it happened, when Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, that the child leapt in her womb”; John VI.16: “but when evening came, the disciples went down to the sea”; Neh. VI.16: “and it happened, when all our enemies heard, that all the nations were afraid”; Luke I.44: “for behold, as soon as the sound of your greeting came into my ears, the child leapt in my womb”; XIX.41: “as soon as he was near, seeing the city, he wept over it”; John XI.20, 29, 32–33. [Col. 1222] For other examples see Glossary V, *þan* II.2), *þe* 2.a.β), *Sve* 3).

> Note 1.—Instead of *þan*, *þanuh* is sometimes used. Thus, if John XVI.25, ἔρχεται ὥρα, ὅτε λαλήσω, is rendered *qimiþ weila, þanuh rodja*, it means: “an hour comes; then I shall speak.” In Matt. IX.25, *þanuh þan* does not mean “when, however,” but “but when—.”
>
> Note 2.—Here the subjunctive is used only in indirect discourse: Mark IX.9: “Jesus commanded them to tell no one what they had seen, until the Son of Man should rise from the dead.”
>
> Note 3.—These conjunctions are also used to paraphrase the Greek genitive absolute: Matt. XXVII.57: “when evening had come, Joseph of Arimathea came”; IX.32: “when they had gone out, behold, they brought him a possessed man”; X.33; Mark I.42; IV.17; VI.2; XV.33; Luke IV.42; XIV.29; XV.14; XVIII.40; XIX.37; John XIII.30; Luke VIII.23: “while they were sailing, Jesus fell asleep.” *Biþe* also serves to paraphrase Greek ἐν τῷ with an infinitive: Mark II.15: “and it happened, while he was reclining in his house, that many tax collectors reclined with Jesus”; Luke III.21; XIX.15.
>
> Note 4.—The principal (consequent) clause sometimes also admits *þan* or *þanuh*, which may function as a correlative to the former particle: 2 Cor. XII.10: “when I am weak, then I am strong”; 1 Cor. XV.54: “when this corruptible has put on incorruption, then the word written shall come to pass.” The same occurs after *biþe*, John XII.16; 1 Cor. XV.28; compare Luke XVI.23. But *biþe*, instead of *þan*, also prefers *jah* after itself: Luke II.21: “and when eight days were completed for circumcising him, his name was called Jesus”; compare § 274, note 1. In Luke V.35, *jah þan* are joined.

3) “After,” sometimes rendered by the particles mentioned under 2), especially *biþe*, and sometimes literally by *afar þatei*: Mark I.14: “after John had been delivered up, Jesus came into Galilee.”

> Note 5.—The literal *afar þatei* in *Skeireins* VII.c—“after the crowd had been fed, twelve baskets full of fragments left over were gathered”—is incorrect, since *þo managein* should occur here.

4) “Before” (πρίν, πρὶν ἤ, πρὸ τοῦ with infinitive), *faur þizei*, is constructed with the subjunctive:

a) Present: Matt. VI.8: “your Father knows what you need before you ask him”; Mark XIV.72: “Peter remembered the word which Jesus had spoken to him: ‘before the cock crows twice, you will deny me three times.’”

b) Past: Luke II.26: “it had been revealed to him that he would not see death before he saw the Lord’s Christ”; John VIII.58: “truly, truly I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am”; Luke II.21; John XIII.19; XIV.29; XVII.5; Gal. II.12.

5) “Until,” “till” (ἕως, ἕως ὅτου, ἕως οὗ, ἄχρις οὗ, μέχρις οὗ), *unte*, is constructed:

a) With the indicative:

aa) Present: Matt. V.26: “you shall not come out from there until you have paid the last coin”; Mark XII.36: “sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet”; Matt. X.23; Mark IX.1; Luke IX.27; XV.4, 8; XX.43; John XIII.38; 1 Tim. IV.13.

bb) Past: Mark XIV.54: “Peter followed Jesus from afar until he came into the courtyard of the high priest”; John IX.18: “the Jews did not believe concerning him that he had been blind and had received sight until they called his parents.”

b) With the present subjunctive: Mark VI.10: “wherever you enter a house, remain there until you leave from there”; Luke XIX.13: “trade until I come”; 1 Cor. IV.5; XI.26; Gal. IV.19; Eph. IV.13.

> Note 6.—*Unte* and *und þatei* (“until”) are indiscriminately intermingled: Matt. V.18: “until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the law until all comes to pass.” *Und þatei* also occurs elsewhere instead of *unte* with the indicative: Matt. V.18, 25; 1 Cor. XV.25; and with the subjunctive: Rom. XI.23; Neh. VII.3.

6) “While,” *miþþanei* (ἥνικα, ἐν τῷ with infinitive, genitive absolute), is constructed with the indicative:

a) Present (ἥνικα): 2 Cor. III.15: “until this day, while Moses is read, a veil lies upon their hearts; but while one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.”

b) Past, corresponding to the Greek genitive absolute and especially to τῷ, ἐν τῷ with the infinitive: Matt. IX.18: “while he was saying these things, one ruler came and worshipped him”; Luke IV.40: “while the sun was setting, they brought the sick to him”; Matt. XXVII.12: “while he was being accused by the chief priests, he answered nothing”; Mark IV.4; Luke I.8. For other examples see Glossary V, *Miþþanei*.

> Note 7.—*Ïn þammei* too is used for ἐν τῷ: Luke IX.51: “it happened while the days of his reception were being fulfilled,” “while they were being fulfilled” (ἐν τῷ ἐμπληροῦσθαι).

7) “While,” “as long as” (ὡς), *unte* and *þande*, is constructed with the present indicative: Luke XVII.8: “serve me until I eat and drink”; John IX.4: “I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day”; John XII.35: “walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you”; Gal. VI.10: “therefore, while we have opportunity, let us do good to all.”

> Note 8.—For Luke V.34, “can the sons of the bridechamber make a fast while the bridegroom is with them?” the parallel Mark II.19 has *und þatei* (ἐν ᾧ), and Matt. IX.15 has *und þata weilos þei* (“as long as,” ἐφ’ ὅσον). Compare Mark IX.19, *und wa* (“how long?” ἕως πότε); Luke IX.41; John X.24; and note 6.

## ELLIPSES IN THE COMPOUND SENTENCE

### § 283

Ellipses occurring in the compound sentence have already been incidentally discussed where we dealt in passing with certain particles that are sometimes omitted; compare §§ 258, notes 6 and 12; 270.1); 280, note 3. Add that an entire subordinate clause may be supplied by a particle, for example by *aiþþau*; see § 280, note 3.c). Likewise, the particle itself sometimes needs the supplementation of a sentence, as is illustrated, for example, by *ïbai ne*, properly “it is to be feared that not”; see § 273.2.

## D. APPENDIX

[Col. 1223]

## PLEONASM

284. 1) Pleonasm consists in expressly adding an attribute or object whose notion already lies in the verb or noun: Matt. IX.23, *haurnjans haurnjandans*, “trumpeters trumpeting” (σαλπιγκτὰς [σαλπίζοντας]); Luke II.29, *fraujinond frauja*, “ruling Lord” (δεσπόζον, δεσπότα); 2 Tim. IV.9, *sniumei qiman sprauto*, “come quickly, speedily” (also in Greek); Matt. XXVI.72, *afaiaik miþ aiþa svarands*, “he denied with an oath, swearing” (μεθ’ ὅρκου); Mark I.40, “a leper came to him, beseeching him and falling on his knees” (γονυπετῶν; for which X.17 has simply *knussjaads*, “kneeling”); for other pleonasms with the instrumental see § 240, note; Matt. V.35, *fotubaurd fotive*, “a footstool for the feet” (also Greek); Mark XII.14, *kaisara-gild giban kaisara*, “give Caesar’s tribute to Caesar.”

2) From tautology rather, two particles of the same meaning are used, as Luke VIII.1, *varþ biþe afar þata*, “it happened after these things” (ἐν τῷ καθεξῆς); John XI.7, *þaþroh þan afar þata*, “then after these things” (ἔπειτα μετὰ ταῦτα), “he said to the disciples”; likewise Eph. II.12: “because you were then at that time” (ὅτι ἦτε ἐν τῷ καιρῷ ἐκείνῳ); Luke XV.19: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son”; XVI.2: “you can no longer be steward”; 1 Thess. III.1; Mark III.6, “and the Pharisees, going out, then immediately took counsel,” for καί; Luke I.66, “and then the hand of the Lord was with him,” for καί; Mark I.31, “and they then came,” for οὖν; Luke VI.6, “and it then happened,” for ἐγένετο δέ; VII.8; XVII.3; John XIV.3, 21 (XV.27); XVI.22; XVIII.18; Luke VIII.23, “and then, while they were sailing,” for δέ; I.26, “then indeed in the sixth month,” for δέ; Matt. IX.17, “but then the wine too is poured out,” for δέ; Matt. XXVII.46, “but then, about the ninth hour,” for δέ; Luke XVII.15, “but one of them,” for δέ; see § 260, note 2; Mark VI.17, “for indeed Herod had arrested John,” for γάρ; IX.41, “for whoever gives you a drink,” for γάρ; John VIII.42, “for indeed I did not come from myself,” for γάρ; XII.10; Luke XIX.27, “but nevertheless bring my enemies here,” for πλήν; see § 260, note 4; 2 Cor. XI.21, “I say as though we were weak,” for ὡς ὅτι. Especially frequent is *svaei nu* (“therefore,” ὥστε): 1 Cor. XIV.22; XV.58; 2 Cor. IV.12; Phil. IV.1; 1 Thess. IV.18. [Col. 1225]

3) Predicates, coordinating clauses, and the like are sometimes added, not so much pleonastically as to determine, complete, or amplify more general expressions of the Greek text: Matt. IX.8, *manageins ohtedun sildaleikjandans*, “the crowds feared, being astonished” (ἐφοβήθησαν); Mark I.27, *afslauþnodedun allai sildaleikjandans*, “all were amazed, being astonished” (ἐθαμβήθησαν); II.12, *usgeisnodedun allai jah hauhidedun mikiljandans guþ*, “all were beside themselves and glorified God, magnifying [him]” (ἐδόξαζον); John XII.18, *ïddjedun gamotjan ïmma managei*, “the crowd went to meet him” (ὑπήντησεν; elsewhere *gamotjan*, “meet,” occurs simply; see Glossary under this word); XIII.38, *þu mik afaikis kunnan*, “will you deny knowing me?” (ἀπαρνήσῃ; elsewhere simply *afaikan*, “deny,” occurs; see Glossary, *Aikan*); 1 Cor. IX.25, *wazuh saei haifstjan sniviþ, allis sik gaþarbiþ*, “everyone who is about to contend restrains himself in all things” (ὁ ἀγωνιζόμενος, where the Gothic translator appears to have thought of someone preparing himself for combat), as Horace, *Ars Poetica* 412:

> He who strives to reach by running the desired goal  
> has abstained from sex and wine.

Luke I.63: “Zechariah, asking for a tablet, took [one] and wrote” (Greek αἰτήσας πινακίδιον ἔγραψε), where the Gothic adds the taking between the asking and the writing; compare Luke XVI.6. 1 Cor. XV.10: *managizo ïm allaim arbaidida jah usaivida*, “I laboured more abundantly than all of them and persevered,” Greek ἐκοπίασα, where the Gothic intended to indicate persistence in labouring. Mark II.4: *ïnsailidedun jah fralailotun*, “they lowered by ropes and let down,” Greek χαλῶσι: by these words both the means of descent and the lowering itself are expressed (“they roped down and lowered”). Phil. III.16: *du þammei gasnevum, ei samo hugjaima jah samo fraþjaima*, “to what we have attained, that we may have the same mind and think the same thing,” where Greek has only τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν. Matt. IX.23: “Jesus, seeing pipers and trumpeters, said,” Greek only αὐλητάς. Mark XII.4: *þana stainam vairpandans gaaiviskodedun jah haubiþ vundan brahtedun*, “having thrown stones at him, they insulted him and brought him away wounded in the head”; the corresponding phrase is entirely absent from the Greek text. Nor is it improbable that this *gaaiviskodedun* was originally a gloss interpreting ἠτίμησαν, a variant reading for ἀπέστειλαν ἠτιμωμένον, and entered the text. Nor should Eph. I.7, *gabei vulþaus anstais*, be accepted for πλοῦτος χάριτος.

> Note.—These examples must not be confused with cases in which a scribe transferred glosses or other variant readings from the margin into the text, as, for example, Luke XIV.32, *jabai nist mahteigs*, a gloss on *eiþau*; II.3, *at visandin kindina syriais de raginondin saurim*, glossed from *ruling Quirinius*; 1 Cor. XV.6, *fifhundam de taihun tevjam*; see the note on that passage. On X.20 see above, § 205, note 3.

## ANACOLUTHON

### § 285

Anacolutha, or inconsequent constructions, occurring for the most part after parenthetical clauses, consist in the continuation of a sentence otherwise than its beginning had led one to expect. The Gothic frequently shares them with the Greek, for example John VIII.53: “are you greater than Abraham, who died, and than the prophets, who died?” for “and than the prophets, who died?”; 1 Cor. VII.13: “a woman who has an unbelieving husband, and he is willing to dwell with her, let her not leave her husband,” for “and willing,” or at least “and who is willing”; Rom. VIII.3: “the weakness of the law, in that it was weak through the flesh, God, sending his own Son … condemned sin in the flesh.” This anacoluthon will not be difficult for anyone to explain in his own way, once he recognizes the solecism whereby the translator wrote *siuks* (“weak”) for *siuk*, namely agreeing with *vitoþ*, “law.” Gal. II.4–5: “because of false brethren secretly brought in, who slipped in to spy out our freedom which we have in Christ, in order that they might enslave us, to whom we did not yield in submission”; compare verse 6; Eph. I.21; 2 Cor. V.6 and 8; Col. I.22, etc.

Anacoluthon occurs especially in participial constructions: 2 Cor. IX.10 ff., “he who supplies seed [may] make it grow and multiply the fruits of your righteousness, being enriched in everything,” for *gabignandane*; verse 13; Col. III.16; Eph. III.17 ff. There is a double anacoluthon in Eph. IV.2 ff., *usdaudjandans—usþulandans*. *Skeireins* VIII.d: “when those men were saying that none of the rulers and Pharisees had believed, not knowing that he was the righteous Pharisee … but they not enduring [it],” where the inconsequence of construction consists not only in the incorrect case of the participle *fraþjandans*, “knowing,” but also in the fact that the consequent does not suit the antecedent. Similarly *Skeireins* IV.a: “to the disciples, who were seeking the deception of the Jews and saying to him: ‘Rabbi …,’ still not knowing the Saviour in this teaching”; and, generally, *Skeireins* displays very many departures from the correct path of agreement, particularly of participles and apposition; compare II.d.

Conversely, there are places in the biblical translation where Gothic writes anacoluthically without having preceding Greek to excuse it, for example Luke IX.13: “there are no more than five loaves and two fish among us,” where, if he intended to alter the construction (compare § 286.6), he should at least have used *jah þau fiskos tvai*, “and two fish”; Mark III.17: “he appointed twelve to be with him … and he gave Simon the name Peter, and James, son of Zebedee, and John, James’s brother, and he gave them the name Boanerges.” Here *ïakobu* and *ïohannen* ought to have been written as dependent on *gavaurhta*, “appointed,” after which the text proceeds more correctly with Andrew, Philip, etc.

Sometimes the Gothic translators avoided anacolutha in the Greek text: 2 Cor. XII.17, “did I exploit you through any of those whom I sent to you?” more correctly than μή τινα—δι’ αὐτοῦ ἐπλεονέκτησα; Eph. III.18: “I bend my knees to God, that he may grant you … that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, so that, rooted and grounded in love, you may be able to comprehend with all the saints.” All manuscripts read ἐν ἀγάπῃ ἐρριζωμένοι καὶ τεθεμελιωμένοι, ἵνα ἐξισχύσητε, so that the participles are referred anacoluthically to what precedes, exactly as in 2 Cor. IX.10 ff.; but the Gothic translator read and connected the passage as Griesbach, Knapp, and Lachmann would wish to connect and read it; compare Winer, p. 497*. Col. I.26: “the mystery which had been hidden from the ages, but has now been revealed to his saints,” where he resolves the participle ἀποκεκρυμμένον relatively, enabling him to continue correctly with *ïþ*, “but.” Conversely, no less legitimately, he used a finite verb in place of a participle: John VI.22: “the crowd standing on the other side of the sea saw that …,” Greek ἰδών, where already many manuscripts and versions read εἶδον or εἶδεν indifferently.

## CHANGE IN EXPRESSION

### § 286

For those undertaking this part of Gothic grammar, ample material is supplied for investigating and examining the character of the Gothic translators. For, overstepping the limits which other languages generally observe in changing an expression, they enter an open field: altering not only constructions but also words where closely related words follow; not only words but also the inflectional class, form, and spelling of words where a double form exists.

1) Thus, then, they alter the spelling almost at will. Hence especially the double mode of writing verbal and nominal endings in þ, þs and d, ds; in au and u; in i and ei; in j and ï; etc. Thus we find: John XV.11, “These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you and that your joy may be fulfilled”; XVII.18, “As thou didst send me into the world, so I also sent them into the world”; and conversely XV.19, “If ye were of this world, the world would love its own. But because ye are not of the world, therefore the world hates you”; XIII.31, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God is glorified”; 1 Tim. III.16, “He who was manifested in the flesh, was justified in the Spirit, was seen by angels, was preached among the nations, was believed on in the world”; Luke X.20, “Do not rejoice because the spirits obey you, but rejoice,” etc.; IX.26, “For whoever is ashamed of me, of him shall the Son of Man be ashamed”; III.14, “Extort from no one, accuse no one falsely, and be content with your wages”; I.32, 35; John XI.25; XII.48; XIII.13, 35; XIV.12, 15, 21; XV.10; compare Gal. III.1, 3, *unfrodans*—*unfroþans* (“foolish”); 2 Cor. VIII.9, “Jesus impoverished himself, though he was rich, that ye through his poverty might become rich”; Luke XVIII.38 ff., “He cried out, saying, ‘Jesus, son of David, have mercy on me!’—but he cried out much more, ‘Son of David, have mercy on me!’” 1 Cor. XII.13, “We all were baptized into one body; we all were made to drink of one Spirit”; IX.20, “I became to the Jews as a Jew, that I might gain Jews.”

> Note 1.—Yet John XII.47 is also read: “I did not come in order that I might judge the world, but in order that I might save the world”; XI.26, “And everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die,” etc.

2) Forms are altered: Luke I.1–2, “Many began [Col. 1228] to set forth an account concerning the events fulfilled among us, as they delivered them to us, who from the beginning were eyewitnesses”; 1 Cor. XIII.7, “It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things”; Mark XI.29 ff., “I will ask you one question, and answer me: Was the baptism of John from heaven or from men? Answer me.” Indeed even the vocalic and consonantal forms of the adjective and passive participle are interchanged, although each elsewhere occurs only according to definite rules; for example Rom. IX.2, “I have great and unceasing sorrow”; Luke I.28, “Rejoice, thou who hast received grace; the Lord is with thee; blessed art thou among women”; V.31, “The healthy have no need of a physician, but the sick”; *Skeireins* I.a, “the Savior was neither equal nor like us in righteousness”; V.d, “to give an oath neither equal nor like”; yet compare concerning the latter passages §196, note 3.

> Note 2.—Cases such as Matt. VI.30 are not to be brought in here: “If God thus clothes the grass of the field, which exists today and tomorrow is cast into the furnace,” since an active participle, where it is neuter, can take no form other than the consonantal one; see §103.

3) Words of differing declension, formation, and class: John XVIII.28, “They led Jesus from Caiaphas into the praetorium; now it was morning, but they did not enter into the praetorium”; 16 ff., “He spoke to the doorkeeper and brought Peter in. Then that maid, the doorkeeper, said,” etc.; Matt. X.41, “He who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward”; Luke VI.38, “A good and overflowing measure shall be given into your bosom. For with the same measure,” etc.; John XIX.2, 5, “They wove a crown of thorns.—Jesus came out wearing the thorny crown”; 2 Cor. III.7, 13, “They could not look upon the face of Moses.—Moses placed a veil upon his face”; John XV.6 ff., *visiþ* (“abides”)—but “if ye abide” (*sijuþ*): a case most worthy of notice, since both verbs share the infinitive *visan*, while, when inflected differently, the anomalous form properly becomes merely a copula; see §134.5 and note; Luke II.12, 16, “Ye shall find a child lying in a manger”; 1 Cor. XIII.8, “Love never falls; but whether prophecies, they shall be abolished; whether tongues, they shall cease; whether knowledge, it shall be abolished”; Luke X.9, 11, “The kingdom of God has drawn near unto you.—It has drawn near,” etc.; 1 Cor. X.23, “All things are lawful, but not all things are beneficial; all things are lawful to me, but not all things build up”; Luke VI.36, “Become merciful, as your Father also is merciful”; John VII.4, 10, *ni manna ïn analaugnein* (“no one in secret”); compare §242, note 1a; Luke XIX.17, 19, “Thou shalt have authority over ten cities.—Thou shalt be over five cities”; Matt. V.18, “Until all things come to pass”; VII.29, “Jesus was teaching as one having authority, and not as the scribes”; Mark I.22; compare Mark V.4, “Often he had been bound with fetters on his feet and with iron chains; and he broke the chains from himself and shattered the iron fetters upon his feet”; Luke VII.41, both *dulgis skula* (“debtor”) and *dulgahaitja* (“creditor”) occur.

4) a) Compounds and simple words are used indiscriminately: John XVII.25, “The world did not know thee, but I knew thee, and these knew that thou didst send me”; IX.31, “We know that God does not hear sinners; but if anyone is a worshipper of God, him he hears”; XIX.6; Rom. XV.4; 1 Cor. XV.48 ff.; Luke X.24, “Many desired to see what ye see and did not see it, and to hear what ye hear and did not hear it”; John IX.7, “He said to the blind man, ‘Go, wash in the pool of Siloam’; he went and washed”; Matt. V.23 ff., 27 ff.; Mark III.24 ff.; Luke XIV.11; XIX.24, 26; 1 Cor. IV.7.

> Note 3.—Yet Matt. V.17, 19 has *gatairan* for both λύειν, “to loose,” and καταλύειν, “to destroy,” etc.

b) Different compounds are interchanged with one another: for ἀπογράφεσθαι, “to register,” Luke II.1, 3, 5 has *gameljan*—*meljan*—*anameljan*; for εὐφραίνεσθαι, “to rejoice,” Luke XV.23, 24, 29, 32 has *vaila visan*—*visan*—*bivisan*—*vaila visan*; for παρεστάναι, “to stand near,” Mark XIV.69 ff. has *faurastandan* and *atstandan*; for ἀφιέναι, “to forgive/release,” Luke VII.47 has *fraletan* and *afletan*.

5) Synonymous words are interchanged, namely:

a) Nouns: John IX.22 ff., “His parents said this—but his parents said”; Luke IX.60, “Let the dead bury their own dead”; XVII.33, “Whoever seeks to save his life shall lose it; and whoever loses it for my sake shall save it”; X.26, “Then he said to him, ‘What is written in the Law?’ But he, answering, said,” etc.; Mark IX.37, “Whoever receives one of such children in my name receives me, and whoever,” etc.; X.43 ff., “Whoever wishes to become great among you shall be your servant, and whoever wishes,” etc.; Matt. V.32, “Whoever”—“he who”; John VI.64, “Jesus knew who they were that did not believe and who it was that would betray him”; Eph. I.18, “That ye may know what is the hope of his calling, what the riches of the glory of his inheritance [are].” Compare §203, note 2.

> Note 4.—Matt. IX.32 ff.: “They brought to him a man mute [and] possessed by a demon; and when the demon had been cast out, the dumb man spoke.” Although the Greek has κωφόν, “deaf/mute,” twice, *bauds* cannot here be understood as “mute”; rather, the Gothic translator probably read “deaf,” or “mute and deaf,” in his manuscript, as did several versions.

b) Verbs: Matt. VI.2, 5, “They have received their reward.”—“They have their reward”; Luke XIX.31, 34, “The Lord has need of this.”—“The Lord’s need of this [Col. 1230] exists”; John VII.28, “You know me and know whence I am”; IX.29; XVI.27 ff., “You believed that I came forth from God. I came out from the Father”; Rom. X.13 ff., “Whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. How then shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” XI.22 ff., “Toward thyself, if thou continue; but (? or else) thou too shalt be cut off. And they, unless they continue in unbelief, shall be grafted in”; 1 Cor. XV.5 ff., “Christ was seen by Cephas; then he was seen by more than five hundred; then he appeared to James”; 50, “Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, neither does corruption inherit incorruption”; 2 Cor. VII.9, “I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved unto repentance; for ye were grieved according to God,” etc.; Matt. XXVI.70, 72, 75, “Peter denied—then again denied—before the cock crows, thou shalt deny me three times.” In place of this Ambrosian-codex reading, the Codex Argenteus reads *afaiaik*—*afaikis* in both places (for the former passage is lacking); Luke V.27–28, “Follow me.”—“He went after him”; concerning *ïddja*, the margin glosses *laistida*.

c) Particles: Luke IX.51, 53, “He set his face to go into Jerusalem.”—“His face was as of one going toward Jerusalem”; 2 Cor. IX.13, “They glorify God on account of the submission of your confession to the Gospel and [on account of] simplicity,” etc.; *Skeireins* VII.c, “He showed forth the abundance of his power not in the bread alone, but also in the fishes”; Mark IV.21, “Does a lamp come in order that it may be placed under a measure or under a bed?” John VII.22, “Moses gave you circumcision—not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers”; Mark IX.19 ff., “Bring him to me.” “And they brought him to him”; Luke XV.29, “So many years I have served thee and never transgressed thy commandment; yet thou hast never given me a kid”; 1 Cor. VII.16, “For what knowest thou, wife, whether thou shalt save thy husband? Or what knowest thou, husband, whether thou shalt save thy wife?” Mark IX.11, “They said, ‘Why do the scribes say that Elijah must come?’” John X.36; Luke XV.6, 9, “Rejoice with me because”—“Rejoice with me, for”; Mark IV.5–6, “Because it had no depth of earth.”—“Because it had no root”; Luke X.20, “Do not rejoice in this, that the spirits obey you; but rejoice because your names are written in heaven”; John XIV.28, “If ye loved me, then ye would rejoice because I go to the Father, for,” etc.; XIII.34, “I give you a new commandment, that ye love one another as I loved you, that ye also love one another”; Luke XIV.10, “When thou art invited, recline in the lowest place, that when [he] comes,” etc.; John XVI.21; John VIII.21–23 reads *þanuh*—*þan*—*nu*—*þaruh* for οὖν, “therefore.”

> Note 5.—Conversely, in order to produce greater elegance, the same Gothic words are used, although other synonyms are available, not only where the Greek employs the same words; for example Matt. V.25: “Be well disposed toward thine adversary quickly, while thou art in the way with him, lest the adversary deliver thee to the judge and the judge deliver thee to the officer,” etc.; but also where it employs different terms: Matt. VII.17, “A bad tree produces bad fruits.” Thus also the opposites ἀγαθόν—κακόν, “good—evil,” are rendered in Gothic by *þiuþ*—*unþiuþ*: Rom. IX.11; XII.21; 2 Cor. V.11; and consequently Mark III.4, ἀγαθοποιεῖν—κακοποιεῖν, “to do good—to do evil,” by *þiuþ taujan*—*unþiuþ taujan*. Likewise Matt. VII.25, 27, *bistigqan* for προσπίπτειν, “to fall upon,” and προσκόπτειν, “to strike against”; XI.7 ff., *saiwan* for θεάσασθαι, “to behold,” and ἰδεῖν, “to see”; Luke VII.24 ff.; Mark I.20 ff., *galeiþan* for ἀπέρχεσθαι, “to depart,” and εἰσπορεύεσθαι, “to enter”; Luke VIII.22, for διέρχεσθαι, “to go through,” and ἀναφέρεσθαι, “to go up”; Mark V.4 ff., *urreisan* for ἐγείρεσθαι, “to be raised,” and ἀνιστάναι, “to rise”; XII.19, *bileiþan* for καταλείπειν, “to leave behind,” and ἀφιέναι, “to release”; XIV.68, 71, *afaikan* for ἀρνεῖσθαι, “to deny,” and ἀναθεματίζειν, “to curse”; Luke VI.41, *gaumjan* for βλέπειν, “to see,” and κατανοεῖν, “to observe”; VII.41, *qaþ* and *qiþ* for φησί, “he says,” and εἰπέ, “say”; John VI.53 ff., *matjan* for φαγεῖν, “to eat,” and τρώγειν, “to chew/eat”; XII.40, 47, *ganasjan* for ἰᾶσθαι, “to heal,” and σώζειν, “to save”; Rom. VII.15, *taujan* for πράττειν, “to practise,” and ποιεῖν, “to do”; XIII.4 (but VII.19 has *vaurkjan*—*taujan*); 1 Cor. IV.5, *galiuhtjan* for φωτίζειν, “to illuminate,” and φανεροῦν, “to reveal”; 2 Cor. V.16, *kunnan* for εἰδέναι, “to know,” and γινώσκειν, “to know/recognize”; XIII.7, *þugkjan* for φαίνεσθαι, “to appear,” and εἶναι, “to be”; Mark I.2, *faura* for πρὸ προσώπου, “before [the face],” and ἔμπροσθεν, “before”; 9, “Jesus came from Nazareth and was baptized by John”; V.19, “Go into thy house to thy [own people]”; XII.26, “Have ye not read in the book of Moses concerning the bush?” John VI.21, *ana* for ἐπί, “upon,” and εἰς, “into”; VII.42, *us* for ἐκ, “out of,” and ἀπό, “from”; 2 Cor. X.13 ff., *und* for ἄχρι, “as far as,” and εἰς, “unto”; VI.14 ff., “What share has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement then has Christ with Belial? Or what share has a believer with an unbeliever? What agreement then has the temple of God with idols?” 2 Cor. IV.10 ff., *sinteino* for πάντοτε, “always,” and ἀεί, “always”; John XVI.30, “We know that thou knowest all things and hast no need that anyone should ask thee”; VII.39, “Those believing in him were to receive the Spirit; for the Holy Spirit was not yet upon them, because Jesus was not yet glorified”; 2 Cor. IX.2. Likewise 2 Cor. XI.18 ff., *unte* for ἐπεί, “since,” and γάρ, “for”; Mark X.42, *ïþ* for δέ, “but,” and καί, “and”; John IX.41, for εἰ, “if,” and δέ, “but”; XI.20, for οὖν, “therefore,” and δέ; XII.8, for γάρ, “for,” and δέ; Luke XVIII.11, *svasve* for ὥσπερ, “just as,” and ὡς, “as”; John VI.20 ff., *þaruh* for δέ and οὖν; Mark I.32, *þan* for δέ and ὅτε, “when,” etc.

6) Properly grammatical alteration, or variation in expression, consists in changing the construction. Expression is altered in a twofold way, according as the change of construction concerns a noun or a verb.

a) Change of construction with reference to the noun. Thus:

aa) The gender of a noun is changed, as in 2 Cor. V.1: “If our earthly house of this tent should be destroyed, we have from God a building, an eternal house not made with hands, in heaven”; and this alteration is customary with collective nouns, as Matt. IX.8, “When the crowds saw it, they were afraid, glorifying [God].”

bb) The number of a noun is changed: Matt. VIII.14, “Peter’s mother-in-law lay in a fever—and the fever left her”; compare §192.2; Luke X.25 ff., “Blessed [are] the eyes that see what ye see.—Many desired to see what ye see, and did not see it”; Mark XIV.13, 15, “Go into the city, and a man shall meet you two.—And he shall show you [plural] a large upper room”; but especially:

cc) The cases of nouns are changed: Luke XVII.27, 29, “The flood destroyed them all.—It rained sulphur and fire and destroyed all”; 1 Cor. VII.10 ff., “To the married I command: let not a wife depart from her husband—and let not a husband put away his wife”; Luke II.46 ff., “They found him hearing them—All who heard him were astonished”; John XV.19, “If ye were of the world, the world would love its own; but because ye are not of the world,” etc.; 2 Cor. II.16; VI.15, “What concord has Christ with Belial?—What agreement has the temple of God with idols?” Mark I.6, “John was clothed with camel’s hair and with a leather belt about his loins”; Eph. VI.14 ff., “Stand, having girded your loins with truth—having shod your feet with the preparation of the Gospel.” Likewise, Luke VII.21 changes after *gahailjan* from the genitive to *af* with the dative; Luke III.16 changes after *daupjan* from the instrumental to *ïn* with the dative; 2 Cor. XII.21 changes after *ïdreigon* from the causal case (genitive) to *ana* with the dative; the partitive and other cases are used in place of the regular construction in Mark XII.28; IV.5 ff.; XIV.17; Luke X.4; X.5, 8; I.7, 18; after *framaldrs*, from the genitive to *ïn* with the dative; Luke IV.25 changes the expression of time from the accusative to *du* with the dative; etc.

> Note 6.—Conversely, Luke I.55, “He spoke to Abraham and his seed,” has *fraiv*, which is erroneous for *fraiva*, since neither *du* is so construed nor *rodjan* takes an accusative.

b) Change of construction with reference to the verb. Here are altered:

aa) Number; for example Luke XIX.30, “Go [dual]—find [dual]—loose [plural]”; Mark XIV.14 ff.; John VII.20, “The crowd answered and said”; moreover,

bb) Tense; for example 1 Cor. VII.22, “He who was called in the Lord while a slave is the Lord’s freedman; likewise he who was called while free”; and particularly the preterite and historical present; see §180.3. To this also belongs 1 Cor. IX.20, 22, where *varþ* and *vas* are used for ἐγενόμην, “I became”; concerning *hauhiþs varþ* and *hauhiþs ïst*, John XIII.21, for ἐδοξάσθη, “was glorified,” see §181, note; above all,

cc) Mood, namely: α) imperative and subjunctive: Mark VII.14, “Hear me, all of you, and understand”; John X.37; β) indicative and subjunctive [Col. 1233] for the future: Luke I.31, “Thou shalt conceive in thy womb and bear a son, and shalt call his name Jesus”; see §182, note 1; in indirect questions: John XII.5, “Why was this ointment not sold and given to the poor?” 1 Cor. IX.7; after *jabai*: John XII.26, “If anyone serves me, let him follow me.—And if anyone serves me, the Father shall honour him”; VIII.51 ff.; after *ïbai*: Mark II.22, “No one puts new wine into old skins, lest the new wine burst the skins, and the wine be spilled and the skins perish”; Matt. V.25; Luke XIV.12; John III.4; after *ei waiva*: Rom. XI.14, “I magnify my ministry, if somehow I may provoke my flesh to jealousy and save some of them”; after a relative: Mark V.19, “Whoever loosens one of the least of these commandments and teaches thus shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven”; vv. 31–32; γ) imperative and infinitive after a command: Luke IX.3, “He said to them, ‘Take nothing for the journey: neither staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money; nor have two coats each’”; compare 1 Cor. IV.9, 11, and likewise often where direct speech passes into indirect speech; see §271, note 3; δ) infinitive and participle after verbs of saying; see §253, note 3; ε) participle with *sa* and finite verb with *saei*: John X.1, “He who does not enter through the door—but he who enters,” etc.; Luke III.11, “He who has two coats, let him give to him who has none; and he who has food, let him do likewise,” etc.

dd) The voice of the verb is changed: Rom. X.10, “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.”

7) Likewise, the expression passes from a final clause to a coordinate clause: Luke VI.36, “Do not judge, that ye may not be judged; do not condemn, and ye shall not be condemned”; John XVI.17, “A little while and ye do not see me, and again a little while and ye see me”; from infinitive and gerund to a final clause: Mark X.38, “Are ye able to drink the cup which I drink, and [to undergo] the baptism with which I am baptized, that ye may be baptized?” This is probably so because Gothic had no passive infinitive; hence also John III.4, “Can a man enter again into his mother’s womb and be born?” Mark III.14, “Jesus appointed twelve to be with him and that he might send them forth to preach”; see §§276, note 7, and 274, note 2; or the infinitive is replaced with the corresponding preposition, as a supine: Mark X.45, “The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve,” perhaps required by the lack of a passive infinitive.

8) The order of words also changes; for example John VIII.32, 36, “The truth shall make you free”—“If therefore the Son shall make you free”; reflexive pronoun with *silba*: 2 Cor. XIII.5, “Examine yourselves. Test yourselves” (§200, note 4); demonstrative pronoun before and after the noun, as Mark VIII.12, “Why does this generation seek a sign?”—“If a sign shall be given to this generation.”

## CONJUGATION OF WORDS

§287. Although the Gothic translator carefully strives to prevent similar words from occurring close together (§286), he nevertheless likes, in the same sentence, to use as object a word of the same stem as the governing verb. Words derived from a similar root are called *conjugata*, and this mode of speech is called the conjugation of words.

> Note.—[Col. 1233] Cicero, *Topics* 3: “Those are called conjugates which derive from words of the same class; and words are of the same class when, having arisen from one root, they are variously altered, as *sapiens*, ‘wise,’ *sapienter*, ‘wisely,’ and *sapientia*, ‘wisdom.’ This conjugation of words is called συζυγία, ‘yoking together.’”

Now the Gothic translator sometimes shares this manner of expression with the Greek: Matt. VI.19, “Lay up treasures”; Mark IV.41, “They feared a great fear,” or Luke II.9, “They feared with fear”; Mark VII.7, “In vain do they worship me, teaching teachings”; XIV.6, “She did a good work to me”; John VI.28; Mark XV.26, “There was an inscription inscribed”; John VII.24, “Judge righteous judgment”; 2 Cor. VIII.24, “Show a proof of love”; Eph. IV.8, “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive”; Mark IX.49, “Every sacrifice shall be salted with salt”; Luke VII.29, “The tax collectors justified God, having been baptized with John’s baptism”; John XII.33, “He said this, signifying by what kind of death he was about to die”; Eph. V.19, “Being filled with the Spirit, singing spiritual songs”; Col. II.19, “The body grows with the growth of God”; see further John VI.28; Rom. IX.32; 1 Cor. XVI.10; 2 Cor. VII.13; XI.2; Eph. I.3; 1 Tim. I.18; 2 Tim. I.9; *Skeireins* IV.d. Compare Eph. I.21, “He set him above every name that is named”; Matt. V.35, “A footstool for his feet”; Eph. I.23, “The fullness of him who fills all things.”

Often it also employs this conjugation independently: Matt. V.43, “Thou shalt hate thine enemy”; IX.35, “Jesus went about all cities and villages, healing every sickness”; Mark VII.35, “The bond of his tongue was loosed”; John VIII.41, “Ye do the works of your father”; 2 Tim. IV.5, “Do the work of an evangelist”; 1 Cor. X.3, “They all ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink”; Gal. II.8, Codex A, margin, “He worked a work”; Eph. III.4, “Ye may understand my understanding in the mystery of Christ”; Mark VII.10, “He who speaks evil of father or mother, let him die by death”; Luke IV.40, “They brought to him those sick with diverse diseases”; 2 Cor. X.2, “I beseech [you] that, when present, I may not be bold with the confidence”; Luke XIX.43, “Thine enemies shall surround thee with a trench”; John XIX.2, “They clothed him with a purple garment”; Luke VII.25; VIII.27; Mark VII.30, “He found the daughter lying upon a bed”; 1 Tim. II.9, “Women are to adorn themselves with decent apparel.” Compare 1 Cor. XIII.1, “A clanging cymbal”; John VII.31, “Many of the multitude”; Luke XVIII.12, “I give a tenth part.”

Likewise in a relative clause, where the relative is the object: Mark XIII.19 ff., “Those days shall be tribulation such as has not been from the beginning of the creation which God created. For the elect whom he chose, he shortened the days”; John XVII.26, “That the love wherewith thou lovedst me may be in them”; instead of which Eph. II.4 uses *ïn þizai frijoda*, “in that love”; Eph. I.6, “To the praise of his grace, in which he favoured us”; see further 2 Cor. X.13; Eph. IV.1. Compare Mark XII.23, “In the resurrection, when they rise.”

> Note.—At times, however, this manner of expression is not used where Greek employs it: Mark II.4, “They uncovered the roof”; Luke II.8, “Keeping watch”; VI.48, “Building a house”; 2 Cor. XII.4, “Unspeakable words”; Mark IV.30, “With what comparison shall we compare?” Here conjugation was not possible in Gothic; it was possible, however, at Mark III.28, where nevertheless [the text has] *naiteinos sva managos sve vajamerjand*; 1 Cor. X.16, *þiuþiqissais þanei gaveiham*; XI.2, *svasve anafalh, anabusnins*; 2 Cor. VII.7, *gaþlaihtai þizaiei gaþrafstiþs vas*, where *vajamereins* instead of *naiteinos*, *gaþiuþjam* instead of *gaveiham*, *anafilha* instead of *anabusnins*, and *gaþrafsteinai* instead of *gaþlaihtai* might have been said.

## CONSTRUCTION OF WORDS

> Note.—[Col. 1235] That is, the physical, not the grammatical, construction of words. —Translator.

§288. With respect to the construction of words, the Gothic language enjoys the freedom generally enjoyed by languages whose nouns have inflectional capacity. Thus the Gothic translator can follow the Greek so closely that, for example, if at Mark XII.1 he translates ἀμπελῶνα ἐφύτευσεν ἄνθρωπος, “a man planted a vineyard,” as *veinagard ussatida manna*, yet at Luke XX.9 he can likewise construct ἄνθρωπος ἐφύτευσεν ἀμπελῶνα, “a man planted a vineyard,” as *manna ussatida veinagard*. Thus he says, at will, both Luke XX.6, “All the multitude will stone us,” and John XI.8, “The Jews have just sought to stone thee.” Nevertheless, certain cases occur in which, the Greek construction being disregarded or a native construction being employed in paraphrase, some traces of specifically Germanic construction become evident.

[Col. 1236] 1) Now observe this concerning the substantive: a dependent genitive commonly follows its governing substantive. For although, following the Greek, it may also be placed before it (§ 216, note 5), and indeed is prefixed in paraphrasing compounds where the component expressed by a genitive occupies the first part of the word—as *barne gabaurþs* for τεκτογονία, “the begetting of children” (see § 173, 2 a bb)—it nevertheless follows where simple words are paraphrased in this manner, as *mel gabaurþais* for γενέσια, “a birthday festival”; compare *slahs lofin*, “a blow of the hand” (ῥάπισμα, “a slap”).

But where, in a paraphrase, the substantive as object stands close to the verb, it is placed before it, since the notion of the object lies in the root; for example: *naht þairhvakan*, “to keep watch through the night” (διανυκτερεύειν); *mat giban*, “to give food” (ψωμίζειν); *aivaggeljon merjan*, “to proclaim the Gospel” (εὐαγγελίζεσθαι); *lofam slahan*, “to strike with the palms” (ῥαπίζειν); *vandum usbliggvan*, “to scourge with rods” (ῥαβδίζειν); *ana armins niman*, “to take into the arms” (ἐναγκαλίζεσθαι); *ïn aljana briggan*, “to provoke to jealousy” (παραζηλοῦν), etc. (see § 173, 1, 2).

Yet one also finds: Luke XVIII, 12, *afdailja taihundon dail*, “I tithe a tenth part” (ἀποδεκατῶ); XVII, 6, *uslausei þuk us vaurtim*, “be rooted up from the roots” (ἐκριζώθητι); and so often. The accusative likewise commonly stands immediately next to the verb, while other objects are far removed from it: Luke XIX, 34, *airþai þuk gaïbnjand*, “they shall raze you to the ground” (ἐδαφιοῦσί σε); Romans X, 19, *ïn aljana ïzvis brigga*, “I will provoke you to jealousy” (παραζηλώσω ὑμᾶς); Colossians III, 21, *ni gramjaiþ barna ïzvara du þvairhein*, “do not provoke your children to discouragement” (μὴ ἐρεθίζετε τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν); Luke XIX, 34, *fraujin þaurfts þis ïst*, “its Lord has need of it” (ὁ κύριος αὐτοῦ χρείαν ἔχει); John VIII, 32, *sunja frijans ïzvis briggiþ*, “the truth shall make you free” (ἐλευθερώσει ὑμᾶς)—in place of which verse 36 offers something more Germanic: *jabai nu sunus ïzvis frijans briggiþ*, “if therefore the Son makes you free”; Luke X, 29, *ïs viljands usvaurhtana sik domjan*, “he, wishing to justify himself” (δικαιοῦν ἑαυτόν). Very well, too, Luke VII, 7: *mik silban vairþana rahnida*, “I considered myself worthy” (ἐμαυτὸν ἠξίωσα); Galatians V, 4: *juzei ïn vitoda garaihtans qiþiþ ïzvis*, “you who are justified in the law” (δικαιοῦσθε).

2) The adjective and participle are sometimes placed, after the Greek fashion, after their governing word (see § 215 I, 1), and sometimes, though more rarely, may precede it. Thus, for example, John XVII, 2, 3: *libain aiveinon*—*so aiveino libains*, “eternal life”; Luke VIII, 8 and 15: *ana airþai godai*—*ana þizai godon airþai*, “on good ground”; IX, 10 and 12: *ana staþ auþjana*—*ïn auþjamma stada*, “in a desert place,” etc.

In paraphrasing compounds they are regularly prefixed: *vilþeis alevabagms*, “a wild olive-tree”; *gods alevabagms*, “a good olive-tree”; *lausa hauheins*, “release from elevation”; *auhumists gudja*, “the chief priest.” In this case the components of the compound expressed by adjectives hold the first place in the word, although *iftumin daga*, “on the following day” (τῇ ἐπαύριον), is also found. And although both *manageins filu* and *filu manageins*, “a great multitude,” are read according as the Greek has ὄχλος πολύς, “a great crowd” (Mark IV, 1; Luke IX, 37; John VI, 2, etc.), or πολύς ὄχλος, “a great crowd” (Mark III, 7), nevertheless in Mark IX, 14 *filu manageins* occurs contrary to the Greek.

3) On the construction of the numeral, whether simple in relation to the substantive or compound, see § 198 II, 3 and 4.

4) The personal pronoun may occupy any position, so that the Goth may even construct *þatei gaþeihis þn* in 1 Timothy IV, 15 for ἡ προκοπή σου, “your progress.” The reflexive pronoun, however, is placed before the verb (§ 176, 4), and, like the personal pronouns, precedes *silba*, “self,” where it is connected with it [Col. 1237] (§ 200 II, 3). As to the possessive, it may be placed either before or after the substantive (§ 201); but a following position accords better with the Gothic character, and the translator chooses it not merely of his own accord—for example, 1 Corinthians XI, 6, *gahuljai haubiþ seïn*, “let her cover her head” (κατακαλυπτέσθω)—but even against the Greek: Matthew VI, 7, *salbo haubiþ þein*, “anoint your head,” for σοῦ τὴν κεφαλήν; VII, 24, 26; VIII, 8, etc. Yet he translates, for example, 2 Corinthians X, 4, ὅπλα τῆς στρατείας ἡμῶν, “the weapons of our warfare,” as *wepna uusaris drauhtinassaus*.

Of the demonstratives, *sa* and *his* are placed before, *jains* after, the substantive (§ 202 IV, b). The position which *sa* has as a demonstrative—before the substantive—it also has as an article; but it is used in Germanic fashion in Luke XVI, 15, *þata hauho ïn mannam*, “that which is exalted among men,” for τὸ ἐν ἀνθρώποις ὑψηλόν, and consequently also in 1 Timothy V, 6, *so vizondei ïn azetjam*, “she who lives in luxury” (ἡ σπαταλῶσα). The relative always occupies the first position in the clause unless it depends upon a preposition. Finally, the interrogative may also be postponed, as in Luke XIV, 28, *ïzvara was*, “which of you?”

5) In verbal phrases of subordination, where the Goth yields to his own linguistic character, the governing elements follow; hence John XII, 18, *ïddjedun gamotjan*, “they went to meet”; XIII, 38, *afaikis kunnan*, “can you deny?” But in XII, 26 one finds *visan habaiþ*, because here *habaiþ* is simply an auxiliary, as in *gameliþs ïst*, “it is written,” *hauhiþs vas*, “was raised,” *gadomiþs varþ*, “was judged,” etc. Indeed, only rarely is the auxiliary prefixed without any compelling reason (§ 213, 2), as in John VI, 45 and XII, 14, *ïst gameliþ*, “it is written,” this usage occurring in the answer in X, 34. If, however, in 1 Corinthians [Col. 1238] IX, 25 *haifstjan sniviþ*, “he exercises self-control,” occurs, this is due to the influence of the relative clause; for one also reads Mark VI, 16, *þammei ïk haubiþ afmaimait*, “he whom I beheaded,” although in verse 27 *afmaimait ïmma haubiþ*, “he cut off his head,” is found. Likewise: Colossians II, 22, *þairh þatei ïs brukjaidau*, “through use”; and 1 Timothy V, 5, *soei bi sunjai viduvo ïst*, “she who is truly a widow.”
