But if in verse 3 the construction *þozei bi sunjai sijaina viduvons*, “those who are truly widows,” occurs, the reason is that the subjunctive seems deliberately to have been removed from the end, as also John XVI, 24, *ei faheds ïzvara sijai usfullida*, “that your joy may be made full”; Luke XIV, 31, *siaiu mahteigs*, “whether he is able” (εἰ δυνατός ἐστι). Nevertheless, Matthew VI, 12 also has *þatei skulans sijaima*, “as we forgive our debtors.” Contrary to Germanic construction, by which the verb in relative clauses is relegated to the end, Luke VIII, 2 has *us þizaiei usïddjedun unhulþons sibun*, “from whom seven devils had gone out,” where the Greek too places the verb at the end. For the rest, see above, 1).

6) Adverbs are commonly placed before the verb which they determine, although, following the Greek, they may also be placed after it: 1 Timothy III, 14, *qiman at þus sprauto*, “to come to you quickly”; Matthew XXVII, 54, *ohtedun abraba*, “they feared exceedingly”; VIII, 28, *sleidjai filu*, “exceedingly fierce”; Mark XVI, 4, *mikils abraba*, “very great.” On the construction of negation, which is of such importance in Gothic and so unlike the Greek, see § 213.

7) On the construction of conjunctions, according as they occupy either the first or the second position in a clause, see the third of the major divisions, on the compound sentence, § 256 ff.

**THE GRAMMAR OF THE GOTHIC LANGUAGE IS COMPLETED.**

[Col. 1237]

# GLOSSARY OF THE GOTHIC LANGUAGE, TRANSLATED FROM GERMAN INTO LATIN BY F. TEMPESTINI.

## PREFACE.

The more numerous and varied the demands made of a glossary, the more numerous and varied are the principles upon which it may be undertaken. We have therefore judged it our duty briefly to set forth the principles which we followed in preparing this work.

With regard to its material, all indeed agree that a lexicon ought, so far as possible, to contain the complete treasury of the whole language. [Note: [Col. 1237] Gothic glossaries compiled up to the present day have been able to extend only to what was known to their authors: Junius’s *Gothic Glossary*, in which most of the words of the Silver Codex are explained, Dordrecht, 1664; Amsterdam, 1684; Stiernhielm’s *Ulfilan-Gothic Glossary*, Stockholm, 1670; *Saxon- and Gothic-Latin Dictionary*, by Edward Lye, edited by Owen [Col. 1238] Manning, London, 1772; Fulda’s glossary, revised by von Reinwald, appended to Zahn’s edition of Ulfilas; or they have been confined to particular works, such as, not to mention certain small glossaries, Castiglione’s glossary to the Epistles to the Corinthians and Massmann’s glossary to the *Skeireins*.] But in the present case the question to be resolved is how extensive this treasury is.

Now, besides the words found in the Ulfilan translation, we have taken care to admit those occurring in the remaining [Col. 1239] monuments of the Gothic language: namely, the *Skeireins*, [Note: [Col. 1239] *Skeireins Aivaggeljons þairh Iohannen*, an exposition of the Gospel of John in the Gothic language, edited from Roman and Milanese manuscripts by H. F. Massmann, Munich, 1834, quarto. Part of the sixth page had already been published in the *Specimen* (see note 3), prepared jointly by Mai and Castiglione; the fragments were collected and critically edited in cols. 871–878 of our edition.] the Gothic Calendar, [Note: [Col. 1239] The Gothic Calendar is found in the Milanese codex (codex A), and was published in the *Specimen of the Unpublished Portions of Ulfilas*, prepared jointly by Mai and Castiglione, Milan, 1819, quarto; it was more recently revised and corrected by Massmann, who republished it according to his revision. See cols. 877 ff. of our edition.] and the Neapolitan and Aretine documents [Note: [Col. 1239] Zahn, *Attempt at an Elucidation of the Gothic Linguistic Remains at Naples and Arezzo*, Brunswick, 1804; ibid., preface, pp. 76 ff.; Massmann, *Frabauhtabokos* [Col. 1240], or *the Gothic Documents of Naples and Arezzo*, Vienna, 1838, folio.]—but not the *Γοτθικόν* (“Gothic”), which is not Gothic. [Note: [Col. 1240] See the introduction to the grammar, § 7, cols. 892 f. Translator.] Here there is no room for hesitation.

Indeed, considering the aim which we have in view, we have further judged that words borrowed from Greek or Latin authors and given a Gothic form should not be neglected but included—for example, *Azdiggs, Ans, Gepanta, Bilageineis* (*Strava, Sihora*). We have, however, distinguished those which seemed to us insufficiently Gothic or of doubtful authority by marking them with a cross (+). But here we stopped; for we should have gone too far had we also admitted words borrowed at a later period by other languages—for example, modern Spanish or the dialects of the Taurians—in which some authors have already identified Gothic words: in Spanish, Adelung (*Mithridates* II, 535) and Keil (*Spanish Grammar*, 103; compare Mascov, *History of the Germans* II, note XXVI, 4, pp. 176 f.); in Taurian, among very many travellers, more recently Busbecq (see Knittel, in the edition of fragments of the Latin letter, p. 429; compare Zahn, *Ulfilas*, Introduction, pp. 14 ff.; Zeuss, *The Germans*, pp. 43 ff.).

Similarly, we judged that this glossary would become unduly extended if it admitted proper names which occur, such as *Friþareiks, Sunjaifriþas, Gudilubs*, [Note: [Col. 1240] Because of the reading *Gudilebus*, occurring in the Latin part of the Aretine document, Massmann prefers to read *Gudilaibs*; but we cannot know the genuine reading, since the Gothic itself has perished.] *Vereka, Merila*, [Note: [Col. 1240] This name, occurring in the Neapolitan document, must be supplied in its proper place in the glossary.] *Ufitahari, Viljariþ, Alamod, Batvins*—not, indeed, in the known monuments of the Gothic language, but only in writers of other peoples. For if certain names, such as *Gudila, Eisarna* (*Isarna*), *Alareiks* (*Alarich* [Alaric]), *þiudareiks* (*Theoderich* [Theodoric]), etc., plainly display a Gothic form, this form in very many others—such as *Ermanarich* (*Airmanareiks*, according to Grimm, *DM* 89), *Amala*, [Note: [Col. 1240] Jornandes does not explain this *Amala*. Those, therefore, who have attempted to derive it from Sanskrit and to translate it as “one ignorant of inflection” or “secret”—Schlegel, *Indian Library*, vol. I, p. 2, no. 5; Manso, *History of the Ostrogoths*, p. 11; Aschbach, *History of the Visigoths*, p. 22—have indulged their own arbitrary judgment.] *Thorismund* (Jornandes, p. 195, where you will find others), etc.—is highly doubtful. Moreover, the meaning of those names remains so uncertain that, unless one wishes to wander through the broad field of conjecture, they would bring very little benefit to a Gothic glossary; and all the less because, in Jornandes’ own judgment, the Goths frequently borrowed their names from the Huns. [Note: [Col. 1240] Jornandes, p. 90: “The Goths for the most part borrow the names of the Huns.” Compare Gothic Grammar § 5, col. 886. Translator.]

As for proper names which, though not actually Gothic, nevertheless occur in Gothic writings, especially in the biblical translation, we have judged that they should by no means be omitted, any more than names borrowed from a foreign language such as *aikklesjo, aivaggeljo, aiffaþa, apaustaulus, kavtsjo, laiktjo, praitoriaun, praufetus*, etc. Through these, indeed, the possible and correct Gothic pronunciation of letters—and, conversely, of Greek letters—at that period may now be known, and the sound-system established (compare *Gothic Grammar*, § 19). Moreover, from their comparison grammar obtains material for laying down definite rules concerning their often peculiar declension. But words which occur in earlier editions of the Ulfilan translation but rest upon false readings, since we have carefully corrected them in our text, we have also taken care to delete from the glossary; for example, *frajaiþan, taihundonda, þrussaba, blisson, fairainan, gahiv*. Those which we have corrected by mere conjecture, however, such as *hauiþ, ligïnon*, we have indeed retained, but refer their explanation to the place where the legitimate reading is found.

No one, surely, will fail to approve our following, in arranging the words, the order supplied by the Gothic alphabetic series borrowed from Greek (*Gothic Grammar*, § 11, cols. 898 f.). But besides alphabetical order, the present state of scholarship required of us that individual words be placed under their roots, so that both their kinship and their derivation might thereby become better known. Here, however, both excess and deficiency had to be avoided: that is, kinship must neither be accepted without evidence nor denied without reason. Now, while on the one hand we judged it more hazardous to call forth simple and wholly fictitious roots, as Graff did in his *Thesaurus* after the manner of the Indians, on the other hand we could not refrain from adducing certain, especially so-called strong-conjugation verbs (*Gothic Grammar*, § 114, col. 980), which, though in most cases their roots are lost to us, are nevertheless more readily conceived because many words appear to derive from them; nor could we refrain from accepting certain simple forms occurring only in compounds. These we have marked with an asterisk (*). Compounds, however, we have placed under their final component word, since that is regularly primary in meaning, while repeating them under the others only with a cross-reference. Certain particles, nevertheless—such as *ei, uh, hun, tigus*—which stand between the separated parts of a compound word and are formative syllables, we have deliberately excepted, placing words composed from them also under the first component.

[Col. 1241] Although the affinity of the Gothic language with the other languages of its family has long been recognized by almost everyone, we judged it all the less suitable to neglect it in this work because the better part of the Gothic vocabulary known in these modern times requires that affinity in order to be granted citizenship in the domain of the Germanic languages. Accordingly, under every root, and indeed under certain derivatives also wherever necessary, we have introduced cognate words from the other languages of the Germanic family; and, lest this comparison should occupy too much space when expanded, we have referred the reader to authors of established scholarly reputation: Bopp (*Comparative Grammar*), Grimm (*German Grammar* [Gr.], *Mythology* [DM.], *German Legal Antiquities* [DRA.]), Graff (*Old High German Prepositions* and *Lexical Treasury* [Gf.]), Schmeller (*Bavarian Dictionary*, *Glossary to the Heliand*), Richthofen (*Old Frisian Dictionary* [Rchth.]). Only in certain rare cases have we noted the affinity or derivation of a word with a brief explanation.

This same consideration—namely, economy of space—is the reason why we have not invoked in our comparisons certain languages of the Indo-Germanic stock, such as Sanskrit, Persian, Slavic, and Celtic, whose affinity with Germanic languages is otherwise long beyond doubt from the celebrated works of Bopp, Pott, and others. Yet we wish to warn the reader that certain Gothic words, for which one might look in vain for an origin or explanation within the Germanic domain, are fully illuminated by Slavic or Lithuanian: *dulgs*, Slavic *dolg, dluh*; *hnuto*, Slavic *knota, knut*; *mota*, Slavic *myto, mytar*; *plinsjan*, Slavic *plasac, plesati*; *smakka*, Slavic *smokva*; *tekan*, Slavic *tykati*; *staurran*, Lithuanian *storawoti*; *faþs*, Lithuanian *pats* (Sanskrit *patis*).

It is evident that the Goths had no native words for debt, tribute, dancing, and a whip, but borrowed these from the Slavs; and that they could express wealth only through their own *faihu* (“cattle”), agreeing in this respect with the Romans, who derived *pecunia* (“money”) from *pecus* (“cattle”). But where the Goth needs to speak of coinage, he either employs a foreign expression, such as *drakma, unkja, sikls*, or uses a general one, namely *skatts*, “treasure,” or *silubrein*, “silver [coin].” Yet the single word *kintus*, of rather obscure origin, appears to be inscribed upon the Goths’ own coins, unless it derives from some foreign language wholly unknown to us. Only in more recent times did the term *skilliggs*, still used today in all Germanic languages, first arise. But let this be said in passing. For we should stray too far from our purpose if we wished to examine the entire treasury of the Gothic language in this manner and here collect, for example, the words relating to agriculture, clothing, arms, chronology, and so forth, as Grimm has already done (*German Grammar* III, 344 ff.). Those investigating the degree of culture and civilization (French *degré de civilisation*) attained by the Gothic people either before or during the time of migration will, however, undertake this labour not without profit.

Moreover, although the affinity of Gothic with the other languages of the Germanic family is beyond doubt, this glossary nevertheless shows that no small portion of its vocabulary remains without analogy in cognate languages. Apart from certain words explained from Latin or Greek, such as *aistan, akeits, aurali, aurkeis*, or *hlifan, þragjan, liteins*, there are very many others concerning which the mind remains in suspense, doubting whether they belong to this family at all, either because their derivation from a monosyllabic root is in no way possible, as with *ahaks, astaþs, biari, ïbuks, ïnilo, riqiz, siponeis*, or because their form suggests a foreign source, as with *bnauan, gards, daddjan, qrammis, plapja, snaga*, etc. But whether these words—and which of them—are genuinely Gothic, or to which of the numerous peoples among whom the Goths mingled both before and during their migration they should be referred, is difficult to determine with any certainty.

We have carefully indicated to what part of grammar—or part of speech—each word belongs, adding for substantives only the gender, not the declension. We did not wish, on the one hand, to anticipate the grammar in this respect, [Note: [Col. 1241] We have already noted that, in the German edition, the glossary precedes the grammar: col. 884, note 3. Translator.] and on the other hand, because once the gender and termination are known, the declension regularly becomes known as well. Yet the declension had to be indicated for masculines ending in *-s* in the nominative singular and *-eis* in the nominative plural, so that they might be carefully distinguished from others forming their plural in *-os*. We have also briefly described the deviation from the rule in the inflection of certain irregular substantives. But we have omitted to note the declensions of adjectives, since the grammar explains them individually.

Furthermore, departing from Grimm—whose grounds we have given in the grammar [§§ 114]—we have recognized three conjugations in verbs. The first contains those verbs which Grimm arranged under the so-called strong conjugation: that is, verbs which form the preterite partly through reduplication, partly through paraphrase, and partly by both methods. To these verbs we have judged it necessary to append, besides the infinitive, the third person of the preterite singular and plural, and also the past participle, since other forms and derivative words are derived from them. Our second conjugation corresponds to Grimm’s weak conjugation; the third, finally, includes verbs ending in *-nan*, which have passive or middle meaning, derive from verbs of the first or second conjugations, and are classed by Grimm among the anomalies of Gothic conjugation.

Conversely, it would have been superfluous to append to each individual word all the forms and inflections which it can assume, as Graff and Richthofen have done. For not only is Gothic orthography more certain and at the same time [Col. 1243] more regular than that of Old Frisian and especially Old German, in which unrestrained caprice seems to have been the sole law, but grammar is also, as we have seen, a far more suitable place for developing grammatical forms.

As for the interpretation of words, we considered it desirable to append, with a brief explanation, every Greek word corresponding to a Gothic one in the Ulfilan translation. Since Ulfilas undoubtedly translated the sacred texts from Greek into Gothic, we could certainly offer no better interpreter of the Gothic than the Greek. Accordingly, prompted by the same reason, we have appended at the end of this Gothic-Latin-Greek glossary a Greek-Gothic glossary rather than a Latin-Gothic one. Now, besides the considerable benefit that will arise from this conjunction for examining the Gothic text, whether already known or someday discovered by fortunate chance—and we ourselves have more than once experienced this benefit in distinguishing genuine readings—it will further disclose, as it were at a single glance, Gothic synonyms, and demonstrate how great a treasury of words was available to the translator, so that he could render and paraphrase by different words Greek terms for which he did not find in his native idiom a perfectly equivalent expression in every case, taking account rather of the sense than of the word. On this matter, diligent reader, direct your attention especially to words such as δικκαιοῦν, “to justify,” ἡσυχία, “quietness,” περισσεύειν, “to abound,” etc.

Finally, in order to make this glossary as complete as possible, we did not shrink from appending to every word all the places in which it occurs. From this labour it will be evident that we have omitted no meaning of any word, and considerable assistance is further offered to those who might wish to survey at a glance the forms and connections of a word. We did this especially for prepositions and conjunctions, which we could not treat in this manner in the grammar. We have excepted, however, certain words such as *qiþan*, “to say,” *ïs*, “he,” and *jah*, “and,” from which we have excerpted only selected passages, preserving nevertheless their meanings and choosing especially those which appear to exhibit different forms and remote meanings. And surely no one will censure us because, in order to save space and not overburden the reader, we have not appended approximately a hundred passages to certain words.

# A. GOTHIC–LATIN GLOSSARY. [Character]

[Col. 1243]

# A
[Col. 1243] **AAI**, indeclinable proper name, *Aai*: Ezra II, 28.

**ABA** (cf. Old Norse *afi*, Gr. II, 43; DRA. 418, 949), masculine: man, especially in relation to marriage, ἀνήρ: Mark X, 12; Luke I, 27, 34; II, 36; Rom. VII, 2, 3; I Cor. VII, 10, 11, 13, 14, 16; XI, 3, 4; Gal. IV, 27; Eph. V, 22, 24; I Tim. III, 2, 12; V, 9; Tit. I, 6.

**ABBA** (a Hebrew word), ἀββᾷ, “Abba”: Gal. IV, 6.

**ABEILENI**, indeclinable proper name, Ἀβιληνή, *Abilene*: Luke III, 1.

**ABIA**, masculine proper name, Ἀβιά, *Abijah*: Luke I, 5.

**ABJAþAR**, masculine proper name, Ἀβιάθαρ, *Abiathar*: Mark II, 26.

**ABU**, see under **Af**.

**ABRAHAM**, masculine proper name, Ἀββραάμ, *Abraham*: Matt. VIII, 11; Mark XII, 26; Luke I, 55, 73; III, 8, 34; XVI, 23; John VIII, 37, 39, 52, 53, 56, 57; II Cor. XI, 22; Gal. III, 6.

**ABRS** (Old Norse *afl*, *abl*, Anglo-Saxon *abal*, Gr. II, 43; cf. Gf. I, 99), adjective: strong, robust, ἰσχυρός: Luke XV, 14.

**ABRABA**, adverb: very, exceedingly, σφόδρα: Matt. XXVII, 54; Mark XVI, 4; Neh. VI, 16.

**BI-ABRJAN**, to be terrified, ἐκπλήττεσθαι: Matt. VII, 28.

**AGAN** (Old Norse *aegia, ógn, óga*, Old Saxon *egiso*, Anglo-Saxon *oga*, Old High German *ekiso*, English *awe*, Gr. II, 11; Gf. I, 103), verb, conjugation I: *og, ogun, agans*, to fear, be afraid.

[Col. 1244]

**UN-AGANDS**, participle: fearless, free from fear, ἄφοβος: I Cor. XVI, 10; Phil. I, 14.

**AGIS**, neuter: fear, φόβος: Mark IV, 41; Luke I, 12, 65; II, 9; V, 26; VII, 16; VIII, 37; John VII, 13; Rom. XIII, 3, 7; II Cor. V, 11; VII, 1, 5, 11, 15; Eph. V, 21; I Tim. V, 20; Neh. V, 15; VI, 16.

**AF-AGJAN**, conjugation II: to intimidate, πτύρειν: Phil. I, 28; to unsettle, σαίνειν: I Thess. III, 3.

**ÏN-AGJAN**, to rebuke, threaten, ἐμβριμᾶσθαι: Matt. IX, 30.

**US-AGJAN**, to terrify greatly; *usagiþs*, passive participle, greatly terrified, ἔκφοβος: Mark IX, 6.

6. In contrasted statements, μὲν—δέ, it occurs:

*Aþþan* and *aiþþau* are sometimes used interchangeably in the manuscripts; see on Rom. XI, 22; II Cor. IV, 16 and XII, 12.

To the countless investigations concerning this most obscure word (see on Matt. V, 23), Grimm (DM, p. 25; Gr. I, 43, 63 [3rd edition]) and Ettmüller (*Hallesche Allgemeine Literatur-Zeitung*, 1838, no. 224) have recently added a new conjecture. But the word *tibr*, which they conjectured and from which they derive Anglo-Saxon *tiber*, appears to belong not to Gothic or the Germanic language, but rather to Gaelic; see Bosworth, *Dictionary of the Anglo-Saxon Language*, p. 75 ff.

V, 17, 18, 36; VI, 24, 31; VII, 16; X, 37; XXV, 38, 39, 44; Mark III, 4; IV, 17, 21, 30; VI, 11, 56; VII, 10, 11, 12; VIII, 37; X, 29, 40; XIII, 21; Luke II, 24; VI, 42; VIII, 16; IX, 25, 26; XIV, 12, 31; XV, 8; XVII, 7, 23; XVIII, 29; XX, 2; John VII, 48; VIII, 14; IX, 21; XIII, 29; Rom. IX, 11; X, 7, 14; XI, 34, 35; XIV, 4, 10, 13; I Cor. I, 13; IV, 3; V, 10, 11; VII, 11, 15, 16; IX, 8; X, 19; XI, 4, 5, 27; XII, 21; XIII, 1; XIV, 23, 24, 27; XVI, 6; II Cor. I, 17; III, 1; VI, 14, 15; IX, 7; X, 12; XI, 4, 7; XII, 6; Gal. II, 2; Eph. III, 20; V, 3, 4, 5, 27; Phil. II, 3; III, 12; Col. II, 16; III, 17; I Thess. II, 19; II Thess. II, 4; I Tim. II, 9; Ps. LIII, 2; Skeir. VIII, c; ἢ καί, “or also”: Luke XVIII, 11.

Repeated disjunction, “either—or,” ἤ—ἤ, is expressed not by *aiþþau* alone, but by *jabai—aiþþau*: Matt. VI, 24; or by *andizuh—aiþþau*: Luke XVI, 13; or the particle is omitted in the first member and only *aiþþau* remains in the second: II Cor. I, 13.

2. “Otherwise,” εἰ δὲ μήγε: Matt. VI, 1; IX, 17; Luke V, 36, 37; II Cor. XI, 16; ἐπεί: I Cor. XV, 29; ἐπεὶ ἄρα: I Cor. VII, 14; ἤ: Rom. IX, 11, beginning; see on Rom. XI, 22.

3. “But, if indeed,” in the second member of interrogative and conditional clauses in the following connection: *aiþþau jabai*, εἰ δέ: John XVIII, 23; I Cor. IV, 7.

4. In the consequent of hypothetical sentences, ἄν: Matt. XI, 23; Luke XVII, 6 (?); John XIV, 2, 7, 28; XV, 19; XVIII, 36; cf. *aiþþau jah*, ἄρα: Gal. II, 21.

5. “But certainly,” “yet nevertheless,” ἀλλάγε: I Cor. IX, 2.

For *aiþþau* and *aþþan* interchanged with one another in manuscripts, see **Aþþan**, at the end.

XXVII, 14; Mark V, 37; VI, 5; IX, 8; XI, 2; XII, 34; Luke I, 37, 61; IV, 24, 26, 27; V, 36, 37, 39; VII, 28; VIII, 43, 51; IX, 50; XIV, 24; XVI, 13; XVIII, 19, 29; XIX, 30; John III, 32; V, 22; VI, 65; VII, 13, 19, 30, 44; VIII, 15, 20; X, 29, 41; XIII, 28; XIV, 6; XV, 24; XVI, 5, 22, 29; XVII, 12; XVIII, 9, 31, 38; XIX, 4, 11; Rom. XII, 17; XIII, 8; I Cor. I, 14; X, 24; II Cor. V, 16; VI, 3; VII, 2; XI, 8; Gal. VI, 17; Phil. IV, 15; I Thess. III, 3; I Tim. VI, 16; II Tim. II, 4; Skeir. V, c; VII, c, d. *Vaihte ainohun ni*, “nothing,” οὐδέν: Luke X, 19. *Ni ainhun wa*, “nothing,” μηδέν: I Thess. IV, 12.

2. One, anyone whatever, πᾶς, also in negative sentences: Mark XIII, 20; Luke I, 37; Gal. II, 16; Eph. IV, 29.

VII, 7; VIII, 10, 21; IX, 12; Gal. I, 23; II, 10, 14; IV, 18; V, 13; Eph. I, 21; Phil. I, 29; II, 27; I Tim. V, 13; II Tim. II, 20; IV, 8; Skeir. **AF-AIRZJAN**, the same: John VII, 47; I Cor. XV, 33; ἀποπλανᾶν: Mark XIII, 22. Passive: to stray, be deceived, ἀστοχεῖν: I Tim. I, 6; ἀποπλανᾶσθαι: I Tim. VI, 10.

**AIRþA** (Old Norse *jörd*, Old Saxon *ertha*, Anglo-Saxon *eorðe*, Old High German *erda*, Old French *irthe*, English *earth*, Swedish and Danish *jord*, Modern High German *Erde*, Greek Ἔρα; Gr. II, 62; III, 352; DRA. 492; Gf. I, 415; Rchth. 854), feminine: earth, land, γῆ: Matt. V, 18, 35; VI, 10, 19; IX, 6, 26, 31; X, 29; XI, 24; XXVII, 45, 51; Mark IV, 5, 8, 20, 26, 28, 31; VIII, 6; IX, 3, 20; XIII, 27; Luke II, 14; IV, 25; V, 11, 24; VI, 49; VIII, 8, 15, 27; X, 21; XIV, 35; XVI, 17; XVII, 8; XVIII, 8; John VI, 21; XII, 24, 32; XVII, 4; Rom. IX, 17, 28; X, 18; I Cor. X, 26; XV, 47; Eph. I, 10; III, 15; IV, 9; Col. I, 16, 20; III, 2, 5; Skeir. **AIRþEINS**, adjective:

1. Earthen, ὀστράκινος: II Cor. IV, 7.

**\*AIV** (Anglo-Saxon *aevisc*): shame, confusion.

**AIVAGGELI** (a Greek word), neuter: gospel, εὐαγγέλιον: I Cor. IX, 23; XV, 1; Gal. I, 6, 7; Eph. I, 13; I Tim. I, 11.

II, 12; IV, 3, 4; VIII, 18; IX, 13; X, 14; XI, 4; Gal. II, 5, 7; Eph. VI, 13, 19; Phil. II, 22; Col. I, 23; I Thess. III, 2; II Tim. I, 8, 10; II, 7; Philem. 13; Skeir. I, d; III, b.

**AIVAGGELISTA**, masculine: evangelist, εὐαγγελιστής: Eph. IV, 11; II Tim. IV, 5; Skeir. III, a.

**AIVNEIKA**, feminine proper name, Εὐνίκη, *Eunice*: II Tim. I, 5.

**AIVS** (Old Norse *aefi*, Old Saxon *euuan*, Anglo-Saxon *á, ava*, Old High German *ewa*, Modern High German *ewig*, English *age*; Greek αἰών, ἀεί, Latin *aevum*; Gf. I, 305), masculine, possessing all the meanings which αἰών, *aevum*, bears in the New Testament; thus:

a. A particular time, a period of time: Mark X, 30; Luke XVI, 8; XVIII, 30; XX, 34, 35; Rom. XII, 2; I Cor. I, 20; II Cor. IV, 4; Gal. I, 4; Eph. I, 21; III, 11, 21; hence also for κόσμος, “world”: Eph. II, 2.

b. A long period: Luke I, 70; Eph. III, 9, 11; I Tim. I, 17; especially in the formulas *du aiva*, “unto the age,” εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα: John VIII, 35; XII, 34; XIV, 16; XV, 16; II Cor. IX, 9; *und aiv*, “until the age,” ἕως αἰῶνος: Luke I, 55; *ïn aivins*: Matt. VI, 13; *ïn aivam*: Rom. IX, 5; *du aivam*: Rom. XI, 36; II Cor. XI, 31; Gal. I, 5; for εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας; *fram aiva*, “from the age,” ἐκ τοῦ αἰῶνος: John IX, 32; *fram aivam*, “from the ages,” ἀπὸ τῶν αἰώνων: Eph. III, 9.

c. In negative statements the accusative *aiv* is used adverbially for εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, “for ever”: Mark III, 29; XI, 14; John X, 28; XI, 26; I Cor. VIII, 13. In its place also occurs *aiva dage*, “for ever”: John VIII, 51, 52; πώποτε, “ever”: Luke XIX, 30. More strictly joined to the negative, *ni aiv* or *aiv ni*, “never,” οὐδέποτε: Matt. IX, 33; Mark II, 12; Luke XV, 29; I Cor. XIII, 8; *aiv wanhun*, “ever,” πώποτε: John VIII, 33; *ni aiv wanhun*, “never,” μηδέποτε: II Tim. III, 7; *ni wanhun aiv*: John VII, 46.

**HALIS-AIV**, adverb: with difficulty, μόγις: Luke IX, 39.

**SUNS-AIV**, immediately, εὐθέως: Mark III, 6; V, 29, 30, 36; VI, 25, 54; VII, 35; VIII, 10; IX, 15, 20, 24; X, 52; XI, 2, 3; XIV, 43, 45; XV, 1; immediately, παραχρῆμα: Luke IV, 39; V, 25.

**AIVEINS**, adjective: eternal, αἰώνιος: Matt. XXV, 41, 46; Mark III, 29; X, 17, 30; Luke X, 25; XVI, 9; XVIII, 18, 30; John VI, 27, 40, 47, 54, 68; X, 28; XII, 25; XVII, 2, 3; Rom. VI, 23; II Cor. IV, 17, 18; XV, 1; Gal. VI, 8; II Thess. I, 9; II, 16; I Tim. I, 16; VI, 12; II Tim. I, 9; II, 10; Tit. I, 2; Philem. 15.

**US-AIVJAN**, conjugation II: to endure: I Cor. XV, 10.

**AJUKDUþS**, feminine: a long period, eternity; in the formula *ïn ajukduþ*, “unto the age,” εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα: John VI, 51, 58; “unto the ages,” εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας: Luke I, 33.

**AIVVA**, feminine proper name, Εὖα, *Eve*: II Cor. XI, 3; I Tim. II, 13.

**AIVXARISTIA** (a Greek word): thanksgiving, εὐχαριστία: II Cor. IX, 11.

**AIFAISO**, feminine proper name, Ἔφεσος, *Ephesus*: I Cor. XV, 32; XVI, 8; Eph. I, 1; I Tim. I, 3; II Tim. I, 18; IV, 12.

**AIFAISIUS**, masculine: Ἐφέσιοι, *Ephesians*: inscription to Ephesians.

**AIWA-TUNDI**, see under **Tundi**.

**AIODIA**, proper name, Εὐοδία, *Euodia*: Phil. IV, 2.

but, ἀλλά: Matt. 5:15, 17, 39; 6:13, 18; 7:21; 8:4, 8; 9:12, 13, 17, 24; 10:31; Mark 1:44, 45; 2:17, 22; 3:26, 29; 4:17, 22; 5:19, 26, 39; 6:9; 7:5, 15, 19; 8:33; 9:37; 10:8, 43, 45; 11:23; 12:14, 25, 27; 14:49; Luke 1:60; 4:4; 5:14, 31, 32, 38; 7:7; 8:16, 27, 52; 9:56; 14:10, 13; 17:8; 18:13; 20:21, 38; John 5:22; 6:22, 26, 27, 32, 38; 7:10, 12, 16, 24, 28; 8:12, 16, 28, 42, 49; 9:3, 31; 10:1, 5, 33; 11:4; 12:6, 9, 16, 30, 44, 47, 49; 13:18; 14:10, 24, 31; 15:16, 19, 21, 25; 16:13, 25; 17:9, 15, 20; 18:40; Rom. 7:7, 13, 15, 18, 19, 20; 9:7, 8, 10, 11, 16, 24, 32; 11:11, 18, 20; 12:3, 16, 17, 19, 21; 13:3, 5, 14; 14:13, 17; 1 Cor. 1:17; 5:8, 10; 7:19; 9:20, 21, 27; 10:20, 29, 33; 12:14, 22; 15:10; 2 Cor. 1:9, 12, 19, 24; 2:4, 6, 12, 17; 3:3, 5, 6, 14; 4:2, 5, 18; 5:4, 12, 15; 6:4; 7:5, 7, 9, 12, 14; 8:5, 8, 13, 19, 21; 9:12; 10:4, 12, 13, 18; 11:17; 12:14, 16; 13:3, 7, 8; Gal. 2:7; 4:14, 17, 31; 5:6, 13; 6:13, 15; Eph. 1:21; 2:8, 19; 4:29; 5:4, 17, 18, 27, 29; 6:12; Phil. 1:20, 29; 2:3, 4, 6, 27; 3:9; 4:6, 17; Col. 3:11, 22; 1 Thess. 4:8; 5:6, 9, 15; 2 Thess. 3:8; 1 Tim. 2:10, 12; 2:3; 4:12; 5:1, 13, 23; 6:2; 2 Tim. 1:7, 8, 9, 17; 2:20, 24; 4:3, 8, 16; Skeireins I a, b; III b; IV b, d; V c; VII a, b.

2) but, ἀλλά: Mark 2:32; 14:49; John 8:56; δέ, “but”: Eph. 4:28; 1 Tim. 1:9.

3) for, γάρ: John 16:27; Eph. 2:10.

**AKEI** (*ake*, Gal. 2:14)

1) but, ἀλλά: Matt. 9:18; 11:8, 9; Mark 9:13, 22; 10:27; 13:20, 24; 16:7; Luke 6:27; 7:25, 26; 16:21; John 6:9, 36, 64; 7:27, 44; 8:26, 37; 10:8, 26; 11:11, 15, 22, 42; 12:27, 42; 16:2, 4, 6, 7, 12, 20, 25, 33; Rom. 8:37; 10:2, 8, 16, 18, 19; 1 Cor. 4:3, 4; 7:7, 21; 10:23; 15:35; 2 Cor. 1:9; 3:15; 4:8, 9, 16; 5:16; 7:6, 11; 8:7; 11:1, 6; 12:1; 13:4; Gal. 2:3, 14; 4:2, 8, 23, 29, 30; Eph. 5:24; Phil. 1:18; 2:27; 3:7; 1 Tim. 1:13, 16; 2 Tim. 1:12; 2:9; 3:9; Skeireins I b; III a; VII c; δέ, “but”: 1 Cor. 14:20.

**AKAJA** (*Axaja*, 2 Cor. 9:2, codex B; *Akaija*, 2 Cor. 1:1, codex B), proper feminine name, Achaia, Ἀχαΐα: 2 Cor. 1:1; 9:2.

**AKEIT** (Old Saxon *ecid*, Anglo-Saxon *aeced*, Latin *acetum*; compare Greek ὄξος, Old Norse *edik*, Swedish *ättika*, Danish *edike*, Old High German *ezih*, New High German *Essig*; Grimm III, 466; Gabelentz and Loebe I, 541), neuter (or masculine *akeits*), vinegar, ὄξος: Matt. 27:48; Mark 15:36.

**AKRAN** (Old Norse *ákarn*, English *acorn*, Danish *agern*, New High German *Ecker*; Grimm III, 375), neuter, fruit, καρπός: Matt. 7:16, 17, 18, 19, 20; Mark 4:7, 8, 20, 28, 29; 11:14; 12:2; Luke 1:42; 3:8, 9; 6:43, 44; 8:8; 20:10; John 12:24; 15:2, 4, 5, 8, 16; 1 Cor. 9:7; Gal. 5:22; Eph. 5:9; Phil. 1:22; Col. 1:10; 2 Tim. 2:6; γέννημα, “produce”: 2 Cor. 9:10. *akran bairan*, to bear fruit, καρποφορεῖν: Mark 4:20, 28; Luke 8:15; Rom. 7:4, 5.

**AKRANA-LAUS**, see under **Liusan**.

**AKRS** (Old Norse *akr*, Old Saxon *accar*, Anglo-Saxon *æcer*, Old French *ekker*, Old High German *achar*, English *acre*, Swedish *åker*, Danish *ager*, New High German *Acker*, Greek ἀγρός, Latin *ager*; Grimm III, 395; Gabelentz and Loebe I, 133; Rachtmann 703), masculine, field, ἀγρός: Matt. 27:7, 8; Mark 15:21; Luke 15:25.

**AKVILA**, proper name, Aquila, Ἀκύλας: 1 Cor. 16:19.

**ALABALSTRAUN** (Greek word), indeclinable, alabaster, ἀλάβαστρος: Luke 7:37.

**ALAIKSANDRUS**, proper masculine name, Alexander, Ἀλέξανδρος: Mark 15:21; 1 Tim. 1:20; 2 Tim. 4:14.

**ALAKJO** (compare **Alls**), adverb, together, collectively. *allai alakjo*, “all,” πάντες: Mark 11:32; Luke 4:22. *managei alakjo*, “the whole people,” ὁ λαὸς ἅπας: Luke 19:48; and *alahjo managei*, “the entire multitude,” ἅπαν τὸ πλῆθος: Luke 19:37.

**ALAMOD**, proper name (?), Arezzo and Neapolitan documents.

**ALJAN**, class-II conjugation, to fatten; participle *aliþs*, “fattened,” σιτευτός: Luke 15:23, 27, 30.

**ALDS**, the same as **Alþs**.

**ALDOMO**, see under **Alþan**.

**ALEV** (Old Norse *olia*, Old Saxon *olig*, Anglo-Saxon *ele*, Old High German *olei*, Old French *olie*, English *oil*, Swedish *olja*, Danish *olie*, New High German *Öl*, Greek ἔλαιον, Latin *oleum*; Gabelentz and Loebe I, 233; Rachtmann 959), neuter, oil, ἔλαιον: Mark 6:13; Luke 7:46; 16:6.

**ALEVA-BAGMS**, see under **Bagms**.

**ALHS** (Old Saxon *alah*, Anglo-Saxon *alh*, Old High German *alah*; Grimm 46, 428; Diefenbach and Müller 39; Gabelentz and Loebe I, 235; Ih. on Luke 2; II, 446; III), anomalous feminine, temple, ναός: Matt. 27:5, 51; Mark 14:58; 15:29, 38; Luke 1:9, 21, 22; 2 Cor. 6:16; Eph. 2:21; 2 Thess. 2:4; ἱερόν, “temple precinct”: Mark 11:11, 15, 16, 27; 12:35; 14:49; Luke 2:27, 37, 46; 4:9; 18:10; 19:45, 47; 20:1; John 7:14, 28; 8:20, 59; 10:23.

**ALþAN** (Old Norse *eldri*, Old Saxon *ald, eldi*, Anglo-Saxon *eald*, Old High German *alten*, Old French *ald, old*, New High German *alt*, English *old*, Swedish *äldre, ålder*, Danish *ælde*; Grimm III, 617; Gabelentz and Loebe I, 292; Rachtmann 596), class-I conjugation: *aialþ, aialþun, alþans*, to grow old.

**US-ALþAN**, the same; passive participle *usalþans*, “senile,” γραώδης: 1 Tim. 4:7.

**ALþS**, feminine, age, αἰών: Eph. 2:2, 7; 1 Tim. 1:17; 2 Tim. 4:10; γενεά, “generation”: Luke 1:50; Eph. 3:5, 21; Col. 1:26; βίος, “life”: 2 Tim. 2:4.

**ALþEIS**, adjective, old: ἀρχαῖος: 2 Cor. 5:17; γέρων, “old man”: John 3:4; Gothic calendar (for from its *þize alþjanoine*, as it should stand there, *þize alþjane* in the nominative can rightly be inferred); comparative *alþiza*, “elder,” πρεσβύτερος: Luke 15:25.

**ALDOMO**, neuter, old age, γῆρας: Luke 1:36.

**FRAM-ALDRS**, adjective, advanced in age: *framaldrs dage seinaize*, “advanced in his days,” προβεβηκὼς ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις αὐτοῦ: Luke 1:8; *framaldra dage managaize*, “advanced in many days,” προβεβηκυῖα ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις πολλαῖς: Luke 2:36; comparative feminine *framaldrozei ïn dagam seinaim*, “advanced in her days,” προβεβηκυῖα ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις αὐτῆς: Luke 1:18.

**ALIS** (Old Norse *ella*, Old Saxon *eli …*, Anglo-Saxon *ele …*, Old High German *ali …*, Greek ἄλλος, Latin *alius*; Gabelentz and Loebe I, 223), adjective, other: ἄλλος: 2 Cor. 1:13; Gal. 5:10; Skeireins VII b; ἕτερος: 1 Tim. 1:10.

**ALJA**

I. Conjunction (Grimm III, 187), after a negation, unless, εἰ μή, ἐὰν μή: Mark 10:18; Luke 4:26, 27; 5:21; 8:51; 10:22; John 6:22; Rom. 13:1; Gal. 1:7; 2:16; Phil. 4:15; ἀλλά, “but”: Mark 10:40; John 7:49 (Mark 9:8; 2 Cor. 1:13).

II. Preposition with the dative, except, πλήν: Mark 12:32.

**ALJAR**, elsewhere; *aljar visands*, “being absent,” ἀπών: 2 Cor. 10:1, 11.

[Col. 1254]

**ALJAþ**, abroad; *afleiþan aljaþ*, to depart abroad, ἀποδημεῖν: Mark 12:1.

**ALJAþRO**, from elsewhere, ἀλλαχόθεν: John 10:1; “absent,” ἀπών: 2 Cor. 13:2, 10; Phil. 1:27.

**ALJA-KUNS**, see under **Kuni**.

**ALJA-LEIKOS** and **ALJA-LEIKAþS**, see under **Leiks**.

**ALLS** (Old Norse *allr*, Old Saxon *al, all*, Anglo-Saxon *eall*, Old High German *al*, Old French *al, ol*, English, Swedish, Danish, New High German *all*; Gabelentz and Loebe I, 203; Rachtmann 594), adjective:

1) every, each, πᾶς: Matt. 5:15, 18; 6:29; 8:16, 33; 9:35; 27:1; Mark 1:27, 32; 2:12; 3:28; 4:11, 32, 34; 5:20, 26, 40; 7:3, 23; 9:12; 10:44; 11:17, 24; 12:33; 13:23; 14:50, 64; Luke 1:3, 6, 48, 65, 66, 71, 75; 2:3, 18, 19, 20, 31, 38, 39, 51; 3:3, 5, 6, 15, 16, 19, 20; 4:4, 5, 7, 13, 37; 5:9, 17; 6:10, 19, 26; 7:1, 16, 17, 18, 29, 35; 8:37, 40, 45, 47, 52; 14:17, 18, 29, 33; 15:1, 14, 31; 16:14; 17:10, 27; 18:12, 21, 22, 28; 19:7, 37; 20:6, 32, 38; John 3:26, 31; 5:22, 23; 6:37, 45; 7:21; 10:8, 29; 14:26; 15:21; 16:13; 17:2, 7, 10, 21; 18:4, 40; Rom. 7:8; 9:5, 6; 10:4, 12; 11:32, 36; 12:3, 4, 17; 13:1, 7; 14:11; 15:11; 1 Cor. 9:22, 25; 10:17, 33; 11:2; 12:12, 19; 13:2; 15:7, 8, 19, 27, 28; 16:14; 2 Cor. 1:1, 3, 4; 2:9; 3:2, 18; 4:2, 8, 15; 5:17, 18; 6:4; 7:1, 5, 11, 16; 8:7, 18; 9:8; 11:6, 9; 12:12, 19; 13:1, 12; Gal. 1:2; 2:14; 4:1; 5:3; Eph. 1:3, 11, 15, 21, 22, 23; 2:21; 3:9, 21; 4:6, 10, 13; 5:24; 6:18, 21; Phil. 1:18, 20; 2:26, 29; 3:8, 21; 4:5, 6, 7, 8, 12; Col. 1:9, 10, 11, 15, 16, 20; 2:13; 3:8, 11, 16, 17, 20; 4:7, 9; 1 Thess. 2:15; 3:7, 13; 4:10; 5:14; 2 Thess. 1:3, 4, 11; 2:17; 3:6, 16; 1 Tim. 1:15, 16; 2:1, 4, 8; 4:8; 5:10; 2 Tim. 1:15; 2:21; 3:17; 4:8; Ps. 53:3; Neh. 5:16; 6:16; Skeireins I a, b; V a, c; VI b; VIII b; ἅπας, “all”: Luke 3:16; 5:26, 28; 15:13.

2) whole, πᾶς: Matt. 8:32, 34; Mark 1:5; 4:1; 5:32; Luke 1:10; 2:1, 10; 4:25; 6:17, 19; 7:29; 8:47; 9:13; John 5:22; Rom. 9:17; 10:18; 11:26; Gal. 5:14; Eph. 4:16; Phil. 3:18; Neh. 5:13, 18; ἅπας: Luke 3:21; 4:6; Eph. 6:13; ὅλος: Matt. 5:29, 30; 6:22, 23; 9:26, 31; Mark 1:33, 39; 8:36; 12:30, 33; 14:9, 55; 15:1, 33; Luke 1:65; 4:14; 5:5; 7:17; 8:39, 43; 9:25; 10:27; John 7:23; 9:34; Rom. 8:36; 10:21; 16:23; 1 Cor. 5:6; 12:17; 14:23; 2 Cor. 1:1; Gal. 5:3, 9; 1 Thess. 4:10; Titus 1:11; Skeireins IV b.

3) much, πολύς: Mark 12:37 (from a broader interpretation).

**ALLIS** (Anglo-Saxon *ealles*, Old High German and Old French *alles, elle*; Grimm III, 88, 281; Rachtmann 600, 703; Schmeller I, 42):

I. Adverb, altogether, entirely, ὅλως: Matt. 5:34; 1 Cor. 15:29.

II. Conjunction, always postpositive (except Mark 12:25, where it is preposed), for, γάρ: Mark 3:35; 4:22; 6:14; 8:35 (9:41); 12:25; 15:14; Luke 1:44, 48; 6:26, 45; 7:28; 9:24, 25, 26; 14:24; 18:25; 19:26; 20:36; John 5:46; 1 Tim. 4:10 (1 Cor. 15:29). *allis—ïþ*, μέν—δέ: Luke 3:16.

**ALLAþRO**, from every side, παντόθεν: Mark 1:45; Luke 19:43.

**ALL-ANDJO**, see under **Andeis**.

**ALL-BRUNSTS**, see under **Brinnan**.

**ALL-SVEREI**, see under **Svers**.

**ALL-VALDANDS**, see under **Valdan**.

**ALLA-VAURSTVA**, see under **Vaurkjan**.

**ALA-þARBS**, see under **þaurban**.

**ALA-MANS**, see under **Manna**.

**ALJA**, see under **Alis**.

**ALJAN** (Old Norse *elian*, Old Saxon *ellan*, Anglo-Saxon *ellean, ellen*, Old High German *ellan*; Grimm II, 8, 447; Gabelentz and Loebe I, 202), neuter, zeal, emulation, ζῆλος: Rom. 10:2; 13:13; 2 Cor. 7:7, 11; 9:2; 11:2; 12:20; Gal. 5:20; Phil. 3:6; Col. 4:13. *ïn aljana briggan*, to provoke to emulation, παραζηλοῦν: Rom. 10:19; 11:11, 14.

**ALJANON**, class-II conjugation, to be zealous, with the dative of the person or the accusative of the thing, ζηλοῦν: 1 Cor. 13:4; 2 Cor. 11:2; Gal. 4:17, 18.

[Col. 1255]

**ÏN-ALJANON**, to provoke to emulation, παραζηλοῦν: 1 Cor. 10:22.

**ALFAIUS**, proper masculine name, Alphaeus, Ἀλφαῖος: Mark 2:14; 3:18; Luke 6:15.

**AMEINADAB**, proper name, Amminadab, Ἀμιναδάβ: Luke 3:33.

**AMEN** (Hebrew word), amen, ἀμήν: Matt. 10:42; John 6:26, 47; 8:34; 2 Cor. 1:20; 13:13.

**AMMO**, proper name, Amos, Ἀμώς: Luke 3:25.

**AMSA** (Greek ὦμος, Latin *humerus*; Grimm III, 403), masculine, shoulder, ὦμος: Luke 15:5. Probably it is an error in the Codex Argenteus for *ahsa*, as is found in the cognate languages: Old Norse *öxl*, Old Saxon *ahsla*, Anglo-Saxon *eaxl*, Old High German *ahsala*, Old French *axle*, New High German *Achsel*, Latin *axilla*; Grimm III, 403; Gabelentz and Loebe I, 139; Rachtmann 616 ff.

**AN** (Latin *an*), interrogative particle, but, καί: Luke 10:29; 18:26; John 9:36; οὖν, “therefore” (?): Luke 3:10. *an nuh*, “then indeed,” οὐκοῦν: John 18:37.

**ANA** (Old Norse *a*, Old Saxon, Anglo-Saxon, Old French *an*, Old High German *ana*, Swedish *å*, English *on*, New High German *an*, Greek ἀνά; Grimm III, 252; Gabelentz and Loebe I, 273; Althof, *Prepositions*, 68 ff.; Rachtmann 602). A preposition governing the accusative and dative, corresponding to Greek ἐπί and properly indicating direction toward a definite place, so that a more or less close, at least proximate, relation thereby arises between that place and the subject or object. It therefore means “upon” (ἐπί), “to” (εἰς). It also has an adversative sense, “against” (κατά with the genitive), and a causal sense, “because of,” “on account of.” In relation to time and manner, this preposition occurs only rarely.

I. Preposition.

A. With the accusative:

1) To indicate place:

a) After verbs of motion: upon, into, to, ἐπί (with the accusative, more rarely with the dative), and εἰς after *gaggan*, John 6:21; *atgaggan*, Mark 1:10; Luke 1:35; 3:22; John 6:16; *usgaggan*, Matt. 11:7; Luke 8:27; 10:10; John 6:3; *afgaggan*, Luke 9:10; *galeiþan*, Mark 1:35; Luke 4:42; *afleiþan*, Luke 5:16; *briggan* (“to lead”), Luke 5:4; *ussteigan*, Luke 5:19; 19:4; *snivan*, 1 Thess. 2:16; *faursnivan*, 1 Tim. 1:18; *atnewjan*, Luke 10:9; *qiman*, Mark 8:10; Gal. 1:21; compare John 18:4. Likewise after *urrinnan*, Matt. 5:45, and *dissiggqan*, Eph. 4:26, of the sun; *driusan* and *gadriusan*, Matt. 10:29; Mark 3:10; 9:20; Luke 20:18; Rom. 15:3. Further, *ana* occurs in the formula “to fall upon one’s face,” *driusan ana andvairþi* or *andavleizn*: Luke 5:12; 17:16; 1 Cor. 14:25; and “to fall upon the neck,” *driusan ana hals*: Luke 15:20; compare Mark 9:42.

b) After transitive verbs: *gatiuhan*, Luke 5:11; *ustiuhan*, Mark 9:2; Luke 4:5; *attiuhan*, Mark 15:22; *draibjan*, Luke 8:29; *vairpan*, Mark 4:26; Luke 8:59; 10:31. Mark 15:24, *vairpan hlauta ana vastjos*, belongs here, because the lot is thrown upon the objects to be apportioned. Also *usvairpan*, Luke 19:35; *niman*, Mark 9:36; Luke 2:28—especially in *ana armins niman* or *andniman*, “to take into the arms” or “receive into the arms,” ἐναγκαλίζεσθαι or δέχεσθαι εἰς ἀγκάλας; *satjan*, Matt. 5:15; Mark 4:21; *lagjan*, Matt. 9:16; 10:34; 27:48; Luke 5:36; 2 Cor. 3:13; *atlagjan*, Mark 15:17; *galagjan*, Matt. 8:25; Mark 9:42; 15:56; John 9:15; 19:2; *uslagjan*, Luke 9:62; 15:5; *uslagjan handuns ana—*, “to lay hands on—,” χεῖρας ἐπιβάλλειν ἐπί—: Mark 14:46; Luke 20:19; John 7:30, 44; “to lay one’s hand upon someone,” χεῖρα ἐπιτιθέναι ἐπί τινα, *handu lagjan* or *analagjan ana—*: Matt. 9:18; Mark 5:23; 10:16; *vaurkjan anakumbjan*, Luke 9:14; *anaaukan*, Matt. 6:27; Luke 3:20; *saian*, Mark 4:31; *gasmeitan*, John 9:6; *siujan*, Mark 2:21; *nikan*, Rom. 12:20; *giban*, Luke 7:44; 15:22.

c) Further after *gasitan*, Mark 11:7; John 12:14; *gahaftnan*, Luke 10:11; *speivan*, Matt. 26:67; Mark 10:34; 14:65.

2) It refers to time only in Luke 17:4: *sibun sinþam ana dag fravaurkjan*, “to transgress seven times in a day” (τῆς ἡμέρας); in place of this Luke 18:12 has the genitive, after Greek usage.

3) Metaphorically: against, ἐπί (with accusative), after *usstandan*, Mark 3:26; *gaggan*, Luke 14:31; *qiman*, John 18:4; *gadaursan*, 2 Cor. 10:2; *ushof ana mik fairzna*, John 13:18; *veitvodiþa ana ïns*, Luke 9:5; κατά (with genitive), after *veitvodjan*, Matt. 27:13; Mark 14:56, 57, 60; 15:4; *veitvodiþa*, Mark 14:55; *vroh bairan*, John 18:29; *þos ana uns vadjabokos*, Col. 2:14; *valdufni aigan*, John 19:11; *ufblesans visan*, 1 Cor. 4:6; *wopan ana—* (“to boast against,” κατακαυχᾶσθαι), Rom. 11:18. Luke 7:30, *runa guþs fraqeþun ana sik*, “they rejected God’s counsel against themselves” (εἰς ἑαυτούς, to their own detriment), is to be explained in the same way.

4) The same particle occurs in 2 Cor. 10:1, *ana andaugi*, “face to face,” κατὰ πρόσωπον, rendered elsewhere by *ïn andvairþja* (Luke 2:31); Rom. 11:28, *liubai ana attans*, “beloved for the sake of the fathers,” ἀγαπητοὶ διὰ πατέρας, where *ïn* with the genitive is used instead.

B. With the dative:

1) To determine place: upon, in, ἐπί (with genitive and accusative), ἐν:

a) After verbs of rest: *visan*, Mark 1:45; 4:1, 31, 38; 10:32; Luke 1:80; 2:14, 25, 40; 15:25; 17:31; John 6:10; 7:39; 15:4; Col. 3:2, 5; *vairþan*, Matt. 6:10; Mark 15:33; Luke 17:34; *sitan*, Matt. 26:69; 27:19; Mark 11:2; Luke 5:27; 19:30; John 12:15; *ligan*, Matt. 9:2; Mark 2:4; 7:30; Luke 5:25; 2 Cor. 3:15; Skeireins III d; *ufligan*, Mark 8:3; *anakumbjan*, Mark 8:6; Luke 14:10; John 13:25; *standan*, Luke 6:17. Also 2 Cor. 13:1, *ana munþa tvaddje veitvode gastandai all vaurde*, “every word shall stand on the mouth of two witnesses”; *gaweilan sik*, Luke 10:6.

b) After verbs of motion, which also readily take the accusative with *ana* (see above, A b): *qiman*, Luke 19:5; Eph. 5:6; Col. 3:6; Skeireins IV c, d (where *airþai* must be read for *airþa*); *vairþan*, Luke 1:65; John 6:21; *gaggan*, John 6:19; *gadriusan*, Mark 4:5; Luke 8:6, 8.

c) After transitive verbs, such as *lagjan*, Mark 6:56; *satjan*, Luke 4:9; 6:48; 8:16; *saian*, Mark 4:16, 20; *straujan*, Mark 11:8; Luke 19:36; *gatimrjan*, Matt. 7:24, 26; Luke 4:29; 6:49; *anatimrjan*, Eph. 2:20; *ufarhleiþrjan*, 2 Cor. 12:9; *gasuljan*, Matt. 7:25; Luke 6:48; *ushulon*, Matt. 27:60; *ufhaban ana handum*, Luke 4:11; *andniman ana biuda*, Neh. 5:17; *gameliþ ist ana praufetum*, “it is written in the prophets,” John 6:45 (especially in the books of the prophets), as in 1 Cor. 5:9, *gamelida ïzvis ana aipistaulein*, “I wrote to you in the letter,” and Luke 20:37, *moses banvida ana aiwatundjai*, “Moses disclosed [it] at the burning bush” (especially in this passage of Scripture, where the history of the bush is narrated).

d) In very many instances where the participle of the preceding verb (*visands, ligands, sitands*, etc.) must be supplied, or where the relation of the preposition to the verb is more general: Mark 5:4, *þo ana fotum eisarna*, “the iron fetters on his feet”; Gothic calendar, *þize ana gutþiudai marvtre*, “of the martyrs in Gothia”; Matt. 10:27, *merjaiþ ana hrotam*, “proclaim upon the housetops”; Mark 6:26, *mis gibais ana mesa haubiþ ïohannis*, “you will give me on a platter the head of John.” So further: Matt. 6:19; 9:6; Mark 2:10; 5:29; 6:55; 8:4, 27; 9:3; 11:4, 13; 12:26; 14:51; Luke 4:18; 5:18, 24; 8:13, 15; 15:4; 18:8; 19:44; John 6:31; 9:3, 12, 34; 17:4; Rom. 9:28; 2 Cor. 4:10; 7:13; 9:14; Gal. 4:14, 18; 6:16, 17; Eph. 1:10; 2:15; 3:15; Col. 1:16, 20; 2 Thess. 3:17; Skeireins VII c; compare Phil. 2:27, *gaurein ana gaurein haban*, “to have grief upon grief,” ἐπὶ λύπην.

2) With reference to time, this preposition is found only in John, to paraphrase the Greek genitive absolute: John 7:14, *ana midjai dulþ*, “when the feast was at its middle” (τῆς ἑορτῆς μεσούσης); 6:23, *ana þammei aviliudoda frauja*, “after the Lord had given thanks” (εὐχαριστήσαντος τοῦ κυρίου).

3) With reference to manner: toward, to, ἀπό: John 11:18.

4) Metaphorically:

a) It indicates the circumstance in which someone is situated: in, ἐπί (with dative), ἐν: 2 Cor. 1:4, *guþ gaþrafstida uns ana allai aglon*, “God comforted us in all affliction”; 7:13; 1 Thess. 3:7, 9; compare 1 Cor. 8:11, *sa unmahteiga ana þeinamma vitubnja broþar*, “the weak brother through your knowledge.”

b) In a causal sense, concerning, over, ἐπί (with dative), after verbs of emotion and similar verbs: *sildaleikjan*, Mark 12:17; Luke 2:33; *usfilms vairþan*, Mark 1:22; Luke 9:43; *usgeisnan*, Luke 2:47; *biabrjan*, Matt. 7:28; *faginon*, 2 Cor. 7:13; *ïdreigon*, 2 Cor. 12:21; *gaþrafstjan*, 2 Cor. 7:7; *gatrauan*, 2 Thess. 3:4; *mikiljan*, 2 Cor. 9:13; *usbeidan*, Luke 18:7. Here belongs the formula *ana þammei*, “because of which,” ἐφ’ ᾧ: 2 Cor. 5:4; Phil. 4:10; and the phrase *ana namin andniman*, “to receive in [someone’s] name,” Mark 9:37; Luke 9:48; compare also Phil. 3:9, *garaihtei ana galaubeinai*, “righteousness through faith.”

c) In an adversative sense: against,

[Col. 1257]

ἐπί (with accusative): Luke 10:19; Rom. 11:22. Luke 18:3, *fraveit mik ana (an, ἀπό) andastaþja*, “vindicate me against my adversary,” also belongs here.

d) It is used in several expressions: 2 Cor. 8:7, *managnan ana friaþvai*, “to abound in love,” ἐν, where elsewhere the bare dative or *ïn* is used; 2 Cor. 1:23, *veitvod guþ anahaita ana saivalai*, “I call God as witness upon my soul,” ἐπί with accusative; Luke 9:49, *ana iesuis namin usdreiban unhulþons*, “to cast out demons in Jesus’ name,” ἐπί with dative; in Eph. 1:9, the margin of codex A reads *ana leikainai*, “according to,” for which *bi* is used elsewhere. *1 Thess. 5:15, ubil ana ubilamma* would mean “evil upon evil,” but the Greek text has κακὸν ἀντὶ κακοῦ, rendered *ubil und ubilamma*, “evil for evil.”

II. Adverbially: Mark 8:23, *atlagjands ana*, “laying [his hand] upon”; 2:7, *galagidedun ana*, “they laid [it] upon.”

III. In composition:

1) with verbs: *anaaukan, anabiuaan, anagaggan, anadrigkan, anaqiþan, anaqiman, anahaban, anahaitan, anahamon, anahneivan, anahnaivjan, anaþivan, anaþrafstjan, anakaurjan, anakumbjan, anakunnan, analatjan, analagjan, anamahtjan, anameljan, anananþjan, ananauþjan, ananiujan, anapraggan, anasilan, anaslavan, anaslepan, anastodjan, anatimrjan, anatrimpan, anavammjan, anafilhan, anaweilan*; compound formations: *miþanakumbjan, anaïnsakan*.

2) with participles: *anahabaiþs*.

3) with substantives: *anabusns, anaqal, anaqiss, anakunnains, analageins, analaugnei, anamahts, ananiujiþa, anastodeins, anaviljei, anafilh*.

4) with adjectives: *anahaims, analaugnis, anasiuns, anavairþs*.

5) with adverbs: *analeiko, analaugniba, ananasiuniba*.

**ANAþAIMA** (Greek word), anathema, ἀνάθεμα: Rom. 9:3; 1 Cor. 16:22.

**ANAþOþ**, proper masculine name, Anathoth, Ἀναθώθ: Ezra 2:23.

**ANAKS**, adverb, suddenly, immediately, ἐξάπινα: Mark 9:8; ἐξαίφνης: Luke 2:13; 9:39.

**ANAN** (Old Norse *önd*, Swedish *anda*, Danish *aand*; compare Greek ἄνεμος, Latin *anima*; Bopp 126; Gabelentz and Loebe I, 267), class-I conjugation: *on*, to breathe.

**US-ANAN** (preterite *uzon*), to expire, to breathe out the spirit, ἐκπνεῖν: Mark 15:37, 39.

**ANANEIAS** and **ANANIAS**, proper masculine name, Ananias, Ἀνανίας: Neh. 7:2.

**AND** (Old Norse and Anglo-Saxon *and …*, Old and New High German *ant …, ent …*, Old French *and, ande, anda, ond …, and …*; Gabelentz and Loebe I, 352; Rachtmann 961, 604), preposition governing the accusative. Of all cognate languages it occurs as a separate word only in Gothic and Old Frisian; its primary meanings are “in,” “along,” and “through.” It is used to indicate that an action is not restricted to a point or individual object, but is carried out throughout a whole collective. Hence it is prefixed to words denoting the world, land, region, locality, city, district, etc., to which the adjective *alls* is also generally prefixed.

I. Preposition:

1) In relation to place:

a) through, in, εἰς, after *usgaggan*, Luke 14:23; likewise *þairhgaggan and þata* (“to pass through that [region]”), Luke 19:4; and the formula *and þana laist* (properly, “in the tracks”), Skeireins II d; V a.

b) down, κατά with genitive, after *run gavaurkjan*, Matt. 8:32, or *rinnan*, Luke 8:33; διά with genitive, after *athahan*, 2 Cor. 11:33, and with the addition of this word in Luke 5:19.

c) to, through, in, when the object is comprehensive, εἰς, κατά (with accusative, rarely genitive), ἐν, or ἐπί with accusative:

α) commonly after verbs of motion whose subject is *meriþa*, *laiseins*, *vaurd*, and the like: after *urrinnan*, Luke 4:14; *usgaggan*, Matt. 9:26; Mark 1:28; Luke 4:37; 7:17; *galeiþan*, Rom. 10:18; *gaþeihan*, Skeireins IV b. Or where the subject is said to be going, coming, etc. for teaching—such as a teacher or preacher: *vraton*, Luke 8:1; *galeiþan*, 8:39; *þairhgaggan*, 9:6; *qiman*, 3:3; hence after *merjan*, Mark 1:39; 14:9; Matt. 11:1; *gateihan*, Rom. 9:17.

β) In several other cases: *huhrus varþ*, Luke 4:25; 15:14; *gasatjan and baurgs praizbytairein*, “to appoint elders in every city,” Titus 1:5; *leikinonds and all*, “healing everywhere,” Luke 9:6. Also belonging here are 2 Cor. 8:18, *þizei hazeins ïn aivaggeljons and allos aikklesjons*, “whose praise in the gospel is throughout all the churches,” διὰ πασῶν τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν; and Eph. 4:6, *saei ufar allaim jah and allans*

[Col. 1258]

“who is above all and through all,” διὰ πάντων, *jah ïn allaim uns*.

2) In relation to time, it means “at,” κατά with accusative, and always stands beside *warjizuh*: Matt. 27:15; Mark 15:6.

II. In composition:

1) with verbs: *andbahtjan, andbeitan, andbindan, andbundnan, andqiþan, andhaitan, andhamon, andhausjan, andhafjan, andhuljan, andhruskan, andþagkjan, andletnan, andniman, andrinnan, andsaiwan, andsakan, andsitan, andsatjan, andspeivan, andstaldan, andstandan, andstaurran, andtilon, andvasjan, andveihan*.

2) with participles: *unandsakans, unandhuliþs*.

3) with substantives: a) *andaugi, andbahts, andbahti, andhuleins, andstald, andvairþi*; b) *anda …*: *andabauhts, andabeit, andahait, andahafts, andaþahts, andalauni, andanahti, andanem, andanumts, andastaþjis, andastaua, andavaurd, andavaurdi, andavizn, andavleizns*.

4) with adjectives: a) *andvairþs*, and the compound *unandsoks*; b) *anda …*: *andaneiþs, andanems, andanemeigs, andasets*.

5) with adverbs: *andaugjo, andaugiba, andvairþis*.

**ANDIS** (Swedish *antingen*, Danish *enten*), adverb, whence **ANDIZUH**, or, ἤ; *andizuh—aiþþau*, either—or, ἤ γάρ—ἤ: Luke 16:13.

**ANDBAHTS**, see under **Bahts**.

**ANDEIS** (Old Norse, Old Saxon *endi*, Anglo-Saxon, Danish, Dutch, New High German *Ende*, Old High German *anti*, Old French *enda*, English *end*, Swedish *ände*; Grimm II, 447; Gabelentz and Loebe I, 354; Rachtmann 706), masculine, end, τέλος: Mark 3:26; Luke 1:33; 18:5; 1 Cor. 15:24; 2 Cor. 1:13; 3:13; 11:15; Phil. 3:19; 1 Thess. 2:16; 1 Tim. 1:5; Skeireins III a; ἄκρον, “end”: Mark 13:27.

**ANDS**, masculine (plural *andeis*), end, boundary, πέρας: Rom. 10:18.

**ANDI-LAUS**, see under **Liusan**.

**ALL-ANDJO**, adverb, wholly, entirely, ὁλοτελῶς: 1 Thess. 5:23.

**ANDIZUH**, see under **And**.

**ANDRAIAS** (*Andrias* in the Gothic calendar), proper masculine name, Andrew, Ἀνδρέας: Mark 1:16, 29; 3:18; Luke 6:14; John 6:8; 12:22; Skeireins VII a.

**ANþAR** (Old Norse *annar*, Old Saxon *othar, athar*, Anglo-Saxon *oðer*, Old High German *andar*, Old French *other*, English *other*, Swedish *annan*, Danish *anden*, Dutch and New High German *ander*; Bopp 20, 80; Grimm IV, 455; Gabelentz and Loebe I, 370; Rachtmann 972), adjective:

1) other, ἄλλος: Matt. 5:39; 8:9; 10:23; 26:71; 27:61; Mark 4:5, 36; 6:15; 7:4; 8:28; 10:11, 12; 12:4, 5, 32; 14:58; 15:31, 41; Luke 5:29; 6:10, 17, 29; 7:8, 19, 20; 8:3; 20:16; John 6:22, 23; 7:12; 10:16; 14:16; 15:24; 18:15, 16, 34; 1 Cor. 9:2, 27; 2 Cor. 8:12; 11:4, 8; Gal. 1:7; Phil. 3:4; Skeireins V c; VII d; ἕτερος: Matt. 6:24; 8:21; 11:3; Luke 3:18; 4:43; 5:7; 6:6; 7:41; 8:3; 9:29, 56, 59, 61; 10:1; 14:19, 31; 16:7, 13, 18; 17:34; 18:10; 19:18; 20:11; Rom. 7:3, 4, 23; 8:39; 13:9; 1 Cor. 4:6; 6:1; 10:24, 29; 14:21; 15:47; 2 Cor. 8:8; 11:4; Gal. 1:6; 6:4; Eph. 3:5; Phil. 2:4; 2 Tim. 2:2; Ezra 2:31.

2) In distributive expressions, *anþar—anþaruh*, “one—the other,” Skeireins II d; likewise *sa—anþaruh*, Skeireins V a, and *ains—anþar*, Skeireins IV d.

3) *anþar anþaris*, “one of another,” ἀλλήλων: Eph. 4:25; *anþar anþarana*, “one another,” ἀλλήλους: Phil. 2:3; also *ainwarjizuh anþar anþarana*, “each one [regarding] another,” εἷς τὸν ἕνα: 1 Thess. 5:11. Likewise Rom. 12:5 reads in full *ainwarjizuh anþar anþaris liþjus*, “each one members of one another,” καθ’ εἷς ἀλλήλων μέλη.

4) second, δεύτερος: Mark 12:21, 31; 14:72; Luke 19:18; 20:30; John 9:24; 1 Cor. 15:47; 2 Cor., superscription; 1:15; 13:2; subscription; 2 Thess., superscription; Neh. 5:14; Skeireins II b. *anþar fruma*, “second-first,” δευτερόπρωτος: Luke 6:1.

5) the rest, λοιπός: Matt. 27:49; Mark 4:19; Luke 8:10; 18:9, 11; 1 Cor. 7:12; 9:5; 2 Cor. 12:13; 13:2; Gal. 2:13; Eph. 2:3; 4:17; Phil. 4:3; 1 Thess. 4:13; 5:6; 1 Tim. 5:20. *þata anþar*, “as for the rest,” τὸ λοιπόν: 1 Cor. 1:16; 2 Cor. 13:11; Eph. 6:10; Phil. 3:1; 4:8; 2 Thess. 3:1.

**ANþAR-LEIKO** and **ANþAR-LEIKEI**, see under **Leiks**.

**ANNA**, proper feminine name, Anna, Ἄννα: Luke 2:36.

**ANNAS**, proper masculine name, Annas, Ἄννας: Luke 3:2; John 18:13, 24.

**ANNO** (see on Luke 3:14; compare Old Norse *önn*), feminine, wages, pay, ὀψώνιον: Luke 3:14; 1 Cor. 9:7.

**ANS** (Old Norse *âs*, Danish *aas*; Grimm III, 429; Gabelentz and Loebe I, 388; Schmeller I, 84), masculine, beam, δοκός: Luke 6:41, 42.

**+ ANS** (Old Norse *ás*; Grimm II, 263, 447; Gabelentz and Loebe I, 387 f.; Geijer, *History of Sweden*, I, p. 14, note 5, considers it the same word as the preceding), hero, demigod. Jordanes, p. 94, ed. Lind.: “They called their nobles, as men who excelled by fortune, not mere human beings but demigods, that is, *Anses*.”

**ANSTS** (Old Norse *ást*, Anglo-Saxon *est*, Old Saxon and Old High German *anst*, Old French *enst*, Swedish *ynnest*, Danish *yndest*, New High German *Gunst*; Bopp 86; Gabelentz and Loebe I, 269; Rachtmann 708), feminine, grace, χάρις: Luke 1:30; 2:40, 52; 4:22; Rom. 6:23; 12:3; 16:24; 1 Cor. 9:20; 10:30; 15:10; 16:3, 23; 2 Cor. 1:2, 12, 15, 24; 4:15; 6:1; 8:1, 4, 6, 7, 19; 9:8, 14; 12:9; 13:13; Gal. 1:6; 2:21; 5:4; 6:18; Eph. 1:2, 6, 7; 2:5, 7, 8; 3:2, 7, 8; 4:7, 29; 6:24; Col. 3:16; 4:6, 19; 1 Thess. 5:28; 2 Thess. 1:2, 12; 2:16; 3:18; 1 Tim. 1:2, 14; 2 Tim. 1:2, 9; 2:1; Titus 1:4; χάρισμα, “gift of grace”: Rom. 6:23; 1 Tim. 4:14; 2 Tim. 1:6. *anstai audahafts*, “full of grace,” κεχαριτωμένος: Luke 1:28.

**ANSTEIGS**, adjective, acceptable, pleasing; *ansteigs visan*, to make gracious or favored, χαριτοῦν: Eph. 1:6.

**ANTIAUKIA** (*Antiokja*, Gal. 2:11), proper feminine name, Antioch, Ἀντιόχεια: Gal. 2:11; 2 Tim. 3:11.

**ANO**, proper name, Ono, Ὠνώ: Ezra 2:33.

**AJUKDUþS**, see under **Aivs**.

**AUGO** (Old Norse *auga*, Old Saxon *oga*, Anglo-Saxon *ægh, eage*, Old High German *auga*, Old French *age, ach, oge*, English *eye*, Swedish *öga*, Danish *öje*, New High German *Auge*; Latin *oculus*, Greek ὄκος; Bopp 81; Grimm II, 550; III, 399; Gabelentz and Loebe I, 122; Rachtmann 592), neuter, eye, ὀφθαλμός: Matt. 5:29, 38; 6:22, 23; 9:29, 30; Mark 7:22; 8:18, 23, 25; 12:11; Luke 2:30; 4:20; 6:20, 41, 42; 10:23; 16:23; 18:13; 19:42; John 6:5; 9:6, 10, 14, 26; 10:21; 11:37, 41; 12:40; 17:1; 1 Cor. 12:16, 17, 21; 15:52; Gal. 3:1; 4:15; Eph. 1:18. For *in augam skalkinon*, see under **Skalkinon**.

**AUGA-DAURO**, see under **Daur**.

**AUGJAN**, class-II conjugation, to show, δεῖξαι: John 14:8, 9.

**AT-AUGJAN**

1) the same: Luke 4:5; John 10:32; ἐπιδεῖξαι, “to show”: Luke 20:24; ἐνδεῖξαι, “to demonstrate”: Eph. 2:7; ὑποδεῖξαι, “to point out”: Luke 6:47; Skeireins III a. *sik ataugjan*, “to show oneself,” ἑαυτὸν δεῖξαι: Matt. 8:4; Mark 1:44; Luke 5:14; ἑαυτὸν ἐπιδεῖξαι: Luke.

XVII, 14; “to appear,” φανῆναι: Luke IX, 8; “to be manifested,” ἐμφανισθῆναι: Matthew XXVII, 53; “to be seen,” ὁρᾶσθαι: I Corinthians XV, 7, 8; *ataugiþs vairþan*, “to be seen,” ὀφθῆναι: Mark IX, 4; I Timothy III, 16; *ataugiþs visan*, the same: I Corinthians XV, 5; 2) neuter, “to appear,” φαίνεσθαι: Mark XVI, 9; “to be manifested,” φανεροῦσθαι: II Corinthians V, 10; “to show oneself,” ἐνδείξασθαι: I Timothy I, 16.

**AND-AUGI**, neuter, “face,” πρόσωπον: II Corinthians X, 1; I Thessalonians II, 17.

**AND-AUGJO**, adverb, “openly, publicly,” φανερῶς: Mark I, 45; John VII, 10; “with frankness,” παῤῥησίᾳ: John XVIII, 20.

**AND-AUGIBA**, adverb, “openly,” παῤῥησίᾳ: John VII, 26; X, 24; XVI, 25, 29.

* **AUD** (Old Norse *audr*, Anglo-Saxon *ead*, Old High German *ot*, New High German [*klein-*] *od*; RA. 491; Gf. I, 148), “treasure, good, means.”

**AUDA-HAFTS**, see under **Haban**.

**AUDAGS**, adjective, “blessed,” μακάριος: Matthew V, 8; XI, 6; Luke I, 45; VI, 20, 21, 22; VII, 23; X, 23; XIV, 14, 15; John XIII, 17; I Timothy I, 11; VI, 15.

**AUDAGEI**, feminine, “blessedness,” μακαρισμός: Galatians IV, 15.

[Col. 1260]

**AUDAGJAN**, conjugation II, “to call blessed,” μακαρίζειν: Luke I, 48.

**AUHNS** (Old Norse *ofn*, Anglo-Saxon, New High German *Ofen*, Old High German *ofan, ovan*, Old French *oven*, English *oven*, Danish *ovn*, Swedish *ugn*, cognate Greek ἴπνος; Gr. III, 352; DM, 359; Gf. I, 176; Rchth. 973), masculine, “furnace,” κλίβανος: Matthew VI, 30.

**AUHJON** (cf. New High German *jauchzen, ächzen*; Wacht. Gloss., V. *achten*, p. 17), conjugation II, “to make a tumult,” θορυβεῖσθαι: Matthew IX, 23; Mark V, 39.

**AUHJODUS**, masculine, “tumult,” θόρυβος: Mark V, 38; “insurrection,” στάσις: Mark XV, 7.

**AUHUMA** (cf. Gr. III, 628), adjective, “high, higher,” ὑπερέχων: Philippians II, 3.

**AUHUMISTS** (*auhmists*, Luke III, 2; XIX, 47), superlative, “highest,” ἄκρος: Ephesians II, 20; *auhumists gudja*, “chief priest,” ἀρχιερεύς: Matthew XXVII, 62; Mark VIII, 31; XIV, 43, 47, 53, 54, 55, 60, 61, 63, 66; XV, 1, 10, 11, 31; Luke III, 2; XIX, 47; XX, 19; John VII, 32, 45; XI, 47; XVIII, 19; after *gudjane auhumists*, Mark XI, 18; *auhumists veiha*, the same, John XVIII, 13; *auhmisto*, neuter used substantively, “the summit, precipice,” ὀφρύς: Luke IV, 29.

**AUHSA** (Old Norse *ox, oxe*, Anglo-Saxon, Old French *oxa*, Old High German *ohso*, English *ox*, Swedish, Danish *oxe*, Dutch *os*, New High German *Ochs*; Gr. III, 325; Gf. I, 140; Rchth. 974), anomalous masculine, “ox,” βοῦς: Luke XIV, 19.

**AUHSUS**, masculine, the same: I Corinthians IX, 9; I Timothy V, 18.

**AUþS** (Old Norse *audr*, Old High German *odi*, Swedish, Danish, New High German *öde*; Gf. I, 150), adjective, “deserted, solitary,” ἔρημος: Mark I, 35, 45; Luke IV, 42; IX, 10, 12; Galatians IV, 27.

**AUþIDA**, feminine, “desert,” ἔρημος: Matthew XI, 7; Mark I, 3, 4, 12; Luke I, 80; III, 2, 4; IV, 1; V, 16; VII, 24; VIII, 29; XV, 4; John VI, 31; XLIX [uncertain citation]; “wilderness,” ἐρημία: Mark VIII, 4; II Corinthians XI, 26; *Skeir.* VII, d.

**AUK** (Old Norse *auk*, Anglo-Saxon *eac*, Old Saxon *ac, oc*, Old High German *auh*, Old French *ak, oke*; Gr. III, 272, 2; 281, 5; Gf. I, 120; Rchth. 594), a conjunction which cannot stand at the beginning of a phrase (except John IX, 30), but is placed after the first word, or even after several words, provided that they present a single idea (as also *batizo ïst auk*, Matthew V, 29; *nih vaiht auk*, I Corinthians IV, 4; and Matthew XI, 10; Luke XVI, 2; XIX, 21; XX, 6, 36; John XVIII, 13; Romans IX, 15; XI, 29; XIV, 11; XV, 4; I Corinthians X, 26; *Skeir.* VII, c). For it signifies:

1. “For,” γάρ: Matthew V, 18, 20, 46; VI, 7, 8, 16, 21, 32; VII, 12, 29; IX, 21; X, 23, 26, 35; XI, 10, 13; XXVII, 18, 43; Mark I, 16; II, 15; III, 10, 21; IV, 28; V, 42; VI, 18; VII, 21; VIII, 36; IX, 5, 39, 41, 49; X, 22, 27; XI, 13, 18, 32; XII, 12, 14, 23, 36; XIII, 19; XIV, 5, 7, 56, 70; XV, 10; XVI, 4, 8; Luke I, 15, 30, 76; III, 8; IV, 10; V, 9, 39; VI, 23, 38, 43, 44, 48; VII, 8; VIII, 17, 29, 40, 46; IX, 14, 51; X, 7, 24; XIV, 14; XVI, 2; XVII, 21; XVIII, 23, 32; XIX, 5, 10, 21, 48; XX, 6, 19, 33, 36, 38; John V, 21, 36, 46; VI, 27, 33, 55, 71; VII, 1, 4, 5; VIII, 24, 42; IX, 22, 30; XI, 39; XII, 43; XIII, 13; XVIII, 13; Romans VI, 23; VII, 1, 5, 14, 18, 22; VIII, 38; IX, 3, 6, 9, 15, 17, 28; X, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, 11, 12, 13, 16; XI, 13, 15, 23, 24, 25, 29, 32, 33; XII, 3, 19, 20; XIII, 3, 4, 6, 9; XIV, 3, 4, 10, 11, 17, 18; XV, 4, 8; I Corinthians I, 19, 21; IV, 4, 7, 9; VII, 9, 22; VIII, 10; IX, 9; X, 17, 26, 29; XI, 5, 26, 29; XV, 3, 9, 16, 21, 25, 26, 52, 53; XVI, 5, 7, 9, 11, 18; II Corinthians III, 9, 11; V, 1; VI, 2, 16; VII, 3, 8, 9, 11; VIII, 12, 13, 21; X, 3, 14; XI, 2, 5, 12, 13, 14; Galatians III, 27; IV, 15, 22, 24, 26; V, 13; VI, 5, 7; Ephesians II, 14; V, 5, 8, 29; Philippians I, 18; II, 6; Colossians III, 25; IV, 13; I Thessalonians II, 14, 19, 20; III, 3, 9; IV, 2, 3, 7; V, 18; II Thessalonians III, 2, 7, 11; I Timothy II, 13; IV, 5, 16; V, 4, 18; VI, 7; II Timothy II, 6; IV, 15; Philemon 15; *Skeir.* I, b, c, d; II, b, c; V, c; VI, b, d; VII, c; VIII, a, b.

2. “And,” καί: I Corinthians VIII, 11.

3. “But,” δέ: Romans VIII, 10; I Corinthians X, 20; XV, 50; Titus I, 12.

4. In the first clause of adversative sentences it corresponds to Greek μέν and is followed by *ïþ*: John XVI, 22; I Corinthians XV, 51; or by *þan*: II Corinthians II, 16.

5. Regarding its combination with other conjunctions, note especially:

   a. *jah auk*, “for indeed,” καὶ γάρ: Matthew VIII, 9; XXVI, 73; Mark VII, 28; X, 45; Luke VI, 32, 33, 34; Romans XI, 1; I Corinthians V, 7; XII, 13; II Corinthians V, 4; VII, 5; XIII, 4; Philippians II, 26; I Thessalonians III, 4; IV, 10; II Thessalonians III, 10; “for,” γάρ: Romans VII, 2; I Corinthians XV, 16.

   b. *---auk jak*, “but also,” δὲ καὶ: I Corinthians I, 16; II Corinthians XIII, 9.

   c. *---þan auk*, “but,” δέ: John XII, 10.

   d. *---auk raihtis*, “for,” γάρ: Mark VI, 17; VII, 10.

**AUKAN** (Old Norse *auka*, Old Saxon *ocan*, Anglo-Saxon *eacan*, Old High German *auhon*, Old French *aka*, English *eke*, Swedish *öka*, Danish *oge*, Greek αὔξειν, Latin *augere*; Gf. I, 119; Rchth. 594), conjugation I: *aiauk*, “to increase, multiply,” *Skeir.* IV, b.

**ANA-AUKAN**, “to add,” προςτιθέναι: Matthew VI, 27; Luke III, 20; XX, 11; *Skeir.* VI, d.

**BI-AUKAN**, the same: Mark IV, 24; Luke XVII, 5; XIX, 11.

**GA-AUKAN**, “to increase,” περισσεύειν: I Thessalonians IV, 1.

**AUKNAN**, conjugation III, “to grow,” ἐπιχορηγεῖσθαι: Colossians II, 19.

**BI-AUKNAN**, “to grow, increase,” περισσεύειν: Philippians I, 26; I Thessalonians IV, 10.

**AUNEISEIFAURUS**, masculine proper name, Onesiphorus, Ὀνησίφορος: II Timothy I, 16.

**AUNISIMUS**, masculine proper name, Onesimus, Ὀνήσιμος: Colossians IV, 9.

**AURAHI** (or *aurahjo*?; cf. Greek ὀρύσσειν), feminine, “tomb,” μνῆμα: Mark V, 2, 3, 5.

**AURALI** (a Latin word), neuter, “handkerchief, burial-cloth,” σουδάριον: John XI, 44.

**AURKEIS** (Anglo-Saxon *orc*, Old High German *urzal*; Gr. III, 458; Gf. I, 477), masculine, “jar,” ξέστης: Mark VII, 4, 8.

* **AURTS** (Old Norse, Danish *urt*, Anglo-Saxon *ort* …, Swedish *ört*; Gr. II, 62; III, 371; Gf. I, 1049), feminine, “herb, plant.”

**AURTI-GARDS**, see under **Gards**.

**AURTJA**, masculine, “gardener, cultivator,” γεωργός: Luke XX, 10, 14, 16.

**AUSO** (Old Norse *eyra*, Old Swedish *ora, ore*, Anglo-Saxon *eare*, Old High German *ora*, Old French *are, ar*, English *ear*, Swedish *öra*, Danish *øre*, Dutch *oor*, New High German *Ohr*, Greek οὖς, Latin *auris*; Gr. III, 399; Gf. I, 457; Rchth. 608), neuter, “ear,” οὖς: Matthew X, 27; XI, 15; Mark IV, 9, 23; VII, 16, 33; VIII, 18; Luke I, 44; VI, 21; VIII, 8, 22; IX, 44; XIV, 35; John XVIII, 10; I Corinthians XII, 16; Nehemiah VI, 16; “earlobe,” ὠτίον: Mark XIV, 47; John XVIII, 26.

**AUFTO**, adverb:

1. “Perhaps,” ἴσως: Luke XX, 13; τάχα: Philemon 15; II Corinthians XII, 16.

2. “Perhaps,” πάντως (“certainly, by all means”): Luke IV, 23; I Corinthians XVI, 12.

*Ei aufto*, “if perhaps,” εἰ ἄρα: Mark XI, 13; *niu aufto*, the same, μήποτε: Luke III, 15; *ïbai aufto* and *nibai aufto*, see **Ibai** and **Nibai**.

**APAULLO**, proper name, Apollos, Ἀπολλώς: I Corinthians I, 12; IV, 6; XVI, 12.

**APAUSTAULUS** (*apaustulus*, Luke VI, 13; Philippians II, 25), a Greek word, masculine, “apostle,” ἀπόστολος: Mark VI, 30; Luke VI, 13; IX, 1, 10; XVII, 5; John XIII, 16; Romans XI, 13; I Corinthians IV, 9; IX, 5; II Corinthians I, 1; VIII, 23; XI, 5, 13; XII, 11, 12; Ephesians II, 20; III, 5; IV, 11; Philippians II, 25; II Timothy I, 11; Titus I, 1; Gothic Calendar. **GALIUGA-APAUSTAULUS**, “false apostle,” ψευδαπόστολος: II Corinthians XI, 13.

**APAUSTAULEI**, feminine, “apostleship,” ἀποστολή: I Corinthians IX, 2; Galatians II, 8.

**ARA** (Old Norse, *ari, örn*, Anglo-Saxon *earn*, Old High German *aro*, Danish *ørn*, Dutch *arend*, New High German *Ar*, cf. Greek ὄρνις; Gr. III, 361; Gf. I, 432), masculine, “eagle,” ἀετός: Luke XVII, 37.

**ARABIA**, feminine proper name, Arabia, Ἀραβία: Galatians IV, 25.

**ARAITAS**, masculine proper name, Aretas, Ἀρέτας: II Corinthians XI, 32.

**ARAM**, masculine proper name, Aram, Ἀράμ: Luke III, 33.

**ARBAIþS** (Old Norse *arvidi*, Old Saxon *arbed*, Anglo-Saxon *earfoð*, Old High German *arabeit*, Old French *arbeid*, Danish *arbeide*, New High German *Arbeit*, cf. Latin *arvum*; Gr. II, 550; Gf. I, 407; Rchth. 607), feminine:

1. “Labour, toil,” κόπος: I Corinthians XV, 28; II Corinthians VI, 5; X, 15; XI, 23, 27; Galatians VI, 17; I Thessalonians III, 5; II Thessalonians III, 8. *ïn arbaidai briggan*, “to exalt oneself,” ἐπαίρεσθαι: II Corinthians XI, 20.

2. “Pressure, burden,” ἐπισύστασις: II Corinthians XI, 28.

3. “Measure, rule,” κανών: II Corinthians X, 16; see the note on this passage.

**ARBAIDJAN**, conjugation II:

1. “To labour,” κοπιᾶν: Matthew VI, 28; I Corinthians XV, 10; XVI, 16; Galatians IV, 11; Ephesians IV, 28; Colossians I, 29; I Thessalonians V, 12; I Timothy IV, 10; II Timothy II, 6. *samana arbaidjan*, “to strive together,” συναθλεῖν: Philippians I, 27.

2. “To suffer hardship,” κακοπαθεῖν: II Timothy II, 3, 9; IV, 5.

**BI-ARBAIDJAN**, “to make it one’s aim, endeavour,” φιλοτιμεῖσθαι: I Thessalonians IV, 11.

**þAIRH-ARBAIDJAN**, “to toil through,” κοπιᾷν: Luke V, 5.

**MIþ-ARBAIDJAN**, “to work together, share hardship,” συναθλεῖν: Philippians IV, 3; συγκακοπαθεῖν: II Timothy I, 8.

**ARBI** (Old Norse *arfi*, Old Saxon *erbi*, Anglo-Saxon *yrf*, Old High German *arbi*, Old French *erva*, Swedish *arf*, Danish *arv*, Dutch *erf*, New High German *Erbe*; DRA. 466 ff.; Gf. I, 405; Rchth. 714), neuter, “inheritance,” κληρονομία: Mark XII, 7; Luke XX, 14; Ephesians I, 14, 18; V, 5; Colossians III, 24. *arbi niman*, “to inherit, receive an inheritance,” κληρονομεῖν: Galatians IV, 30.

**ARBI-NUMJA**, see under **Niman**.

**ARBJA**, masculine, “heir,” κληρονόμος: Galatians III, 29; IV, 7. *arbja vairþan*, “to become an heir, inherit,” κληρονομεῖν: Mark X, 17; Luke X, 25; XVIII, 18; Galatians V, 21.

**GA-ARBJA**, “co-heir,” συγκληρονόμος: Ephesians III, 6.

**ARBJO**, feminine, “female heir.” *arbjo vairþan*, “to become a female heir, inherit,” κληρονομεῖν: I Corinthians XV, 50.

**AREIMAþAIA**, proper name, Arimathea, Ἀριμαθαία: Matthew XXVII, 57; Mark XV, 43.

**AREISTARKUS**, masculine proper name, Aristarchus, Ἀρίσταρχος: Colossians IV, 10.

**ARKA** (Old Norse *örk*, Anglo-Saxon *arc*, Old High German *archa*, Old French *erke*, English, Danish, Dutch *ark*, New High German *Arche*, Latin *arca*; Gf. I, 467; Rchth. 712), feminine, “ark, chest,” κιβωτός: Luke XVII, 27; “money-box,” γλωσσόκομον: John XII, 6; XIII, 29.

**ARKIPPUS**, masculine proper name, Archippus, Ἄρχιππος: Colossians IV, 17.

**ARMS** (Old Norse *armr*, Anglo-Saxon *earm*, Old French *erm*, Old Saxon, Old High German, Swiss, etc. *arm*, Latin *armus*; Gr. III, 403; Gf. I, 425; Rchth. 713), masculine (plural *armeis*), “arm,” βραχίων: Luke I, 51; John XII, 38; “embrace,” ἀγκάλη: Luke II, 28; whence *ana armins niman*, “to take into one’s arms,” ἐναγκαλίζεσθαι: Mark IX, 36.

**ARMS** (Old Norse *armr*, Old Saxon, Anglo-Saxon *earm*, Old High German *aram*, Old French *erm*, Swiss, etc. *arm*; Gr. II, 556; Gf. I, 420; Rchth. 713), adjective, superlative *armosta*, “wretched, pitiable,” ἐλεεινός: I Corinthians XV, 19.

**ARMAN**, conjugation II, with accusative, “to have mercy on,” ἐλεεῖν: Matthew IX, 27; Mark X, 47, 48; Luke XVII, 13; XVIII, 38, 39; Romans IX, 15, 16, 18; XII, 8; I Timothy I, 13, 16.

**GA-ARMAN**, the same: Mark V, 19; Romans IX, 15; XI, 30, 31, 32; I Corinthians VII, 25; II Corinthians IV, 1; Philippians II, 27.

**ARMA-HAIRTEI**, see under **Hairto**.

**ARMA-HAIRTIþA**, see under **Hairto**.

**ARMAIO**, feminine:

1. “Mercy,” ἔλεος: Romans IX, 23; XI, 31; Galatians VI, 16; I Timothy I, 2; II Timothy I, 2, 16.

2. “Alms,” ἐλεημοσύνη: Mark VI, 1, 2, 3.

* **ARNEIS** (cf. Anglo-Saxon *eornest*, Old High German *ernust*, English *earnest*, New High German *Ernst*; Gf. I, 429), adjective, “certain, careful.”

**ARNIBA**, adverb, “certainly, carefully,” ἀσφαλῶς: Mark XIV, 44.

**ARJAN** (Old Norse *eria*, Anglo-Saxon *erian*, Old High German *aran, erran*, Old French *era*, English *eare*, Greek ἀροῦν, Latin *arare*; Gr. II, 56; III, 415; Gf. I, 402; Rchth. 710), conjugation II, “to plough,” ἀροτριᾶν: Luke XVII, 7.

**ARTARKSAIRKSUS**, masculine proper name, Artaxerxes, Ἀρθασασθά: Nehemiah V, 14.

**ARVJO** (Old High German *arawun*; Gf. I, 429), adverb, “without payment,” δωρεάν:
