[Col. 1263]

**ARFAKSAD**, masculine proper name, Arphaxad, Ἀρφαξάδ: Luke III, 36.

**ARWAZNA** (Old Norse *ör*, Anglo-Saxon *arewa*, English *arrow*; Gr. III, 444), feminine, “arrow, missile,” βέλος: Ephesians VI, 16.

**AROMATA** (a Greek word), “spices,” ἀρώματα: Mark XVI, 1.

**ASANS** (cf. Anglo-Saxon *ar*, Old High German *aran*, Old French *ara, arn*; DM. 435; Gf. I, 479; Rchth. 607, 608; Schm. I, 108), feminine:

1. “Summer,” θέρος: Mark XIII, 28.

2. “Harvest,” θερισμός: Matthew IX, 37, 38; Mark IV, 29; Luke X, 2.

**ASAF**, masculine proper name, Asaph, Ἀσάφ: Ezra II, 41.

**ASGAD**, masculine proper name, Asgad, Ἀσγάδ: Ezra II, 12.

+ **ASDIGGS**, see **Azdiggs**.

**ASER**, masculine proper name, Asher, Ἀσήρ: Luke II, 36.

**ASIA**, feminine proper name, Asia, Ἀσία: I Corinthians XVI, 19; II Corinthians I, 8; II Timothy I, 15.

**ASILUS** (Old Norse *asni*, Anglo-Saxon *asal*, Old Saxon and Old High German *esil*, English *ass*, Danish *asen, aesel*, Swedish *åsna*, New High German *Esel*, Latin *asinus*; Gf. I, 486), common gender, “ass, donkey,” ὀνάριον: Luke XIX, 30; John XII, 14; ὄνος: John XII, 15.

**ASILU-QAIRNUS**, see under **Qairnus**.

**ASMOþ**, masculine proper name, Azmoth, Ἀζμώθ: Ezra II, 24.

**ASNEIS** (cf. *asans*, Old Norse *asnast*, Anglo-Saxon *esne* …, Old High German *asni*, Old French *esna*; DRA. 304; Gf. 478; Rchth. 716; Schmid, *Schwäbisches Wörterbuch*, 99), masculine, “hired servant,” μισθωτός: Mark I, 20; John X, 12, 13; “hired worker,” μίσθιος: Luke XV, 17, 19.

**ASSAUM**, masculine proper name, Assum, Ἀσούμ: Ezra II, 19.

**ASSARJUS** (a Latin word), masculine, “assarion,” ἀσσάριον: Matthew X, 29.

**ASTAþS**, feminine (?), “truth, certainty,” ἀσφάλεια: Luke I, 4.

**ASTS** (Old Norse *jastr*, Old High German *ast*, cf. Greek ὄζος; Gr. III, 411; Gf. I, 478), masculine (plural *astos*), “branch,” κλάδος: Mark IV, 32; XIII, 28; Romans XI, 16, 17, 18, 19, 21; “leafy branches,” στοιβάς: Mark XI, 8; “palm branch,” βαίον: John XII, 13.

**AT** (Old Norse, Old Saxon, Danish *at*, Anglo-Saxon *aet*, Old High German *azs*, Old French *et*, Swedish *åt*, Danish *ad*, cf. Latin *ad*; Gr. III, 253; Gf. I, 523; Alth. *Präpos.* 93; Rchth. 717), a preposition governing the accusative and dative, primarily meaning “at, by” (πρός), and indicating proximity to something.

I. As a preposition.

A. With the accusative, it refers only to time, meaning “at,” and corresponds to the Greek dative: Mark XII, 2; Luke II, 41; Galatians VI, 9; or to the genitive absolute: Matthew XXVII, 1, *at maurgin vaurþanana*, “when morning had come.”

B. With the dative:

1. It refers to place:

   a. “At, by,” πρός with dative and accusative, παρά with accusative, and ἐπί with accusative after verbs of rest, such as *sitan*, “sit,” Matthew IX, 9; Mark II, 4; *ligan*, “lie,” Luke III, 9; *standan*, “stand,” Luke V, 2; John XVIII, 16; *gastandan*, “stand fast,” I Corinthians VII, 24; Galatians II, 5; *saljan*, “remain,” I Corinthians XVI, 6, 7, 19; *saliþwos taujan*, “make one’s dwelling,” John XIV, 23; *þairhvisan*, “remain,” Philippians I, 25; *haldan*, “keep,” Mark V, 11; *usmitan*, “be cast,” II Corinthians I, 12; *gamotian*, “assemble,” Mark II, 2; *anahaims visan*, “be away from home,” II Corinthians V, 8; *newa visan*, “be near,” Mark XI, 1; Luke XIX, 37. Thus, rightly, also in Luke XIX, 29 *at* should be read instead of *af*. Further examples are *garunnans*, Mark I, 33, and *gabundans*, Mark XI, 4; *visan*, Mark VI, 3; IX, 19; XIV, 49; Luke IX, 41; John XIV, 25; I Corinthians XII, 15, 16; XVI, 10; II Corinthians XI, 8; Ephesians VI, 9; Colossians III, 25; I Thessalonians III, 4; II Thessalonians III, 10; and in many cases in which the participle of the preceding verb, especially *visands* (“being”), must be supplied: Mark IV, 1; XIV, 54; John XVII, 5; II Corinthians IX, 2; XII, 21; II Thessalonians III, 1, 8. It also follows adjectives, as *kunþs visan*, “be known,” Philippians IV, 6; *mahteigs* and *unmahteigs visan*, “be possible and impossible,” Luke XVIII, 27; *garaihts visan*, “be just,” II Thessalonians I, 6; *habaiþs visan*, “be prepared,” Mark III, 9; likewise *anstai gateihan at guþa*, “to advance in grace with God,” Luke II, 52; finally, after *bileiþan*, II Timothy IV, 13; *gahaban*, Philemon 13; and in the phrase *gastauan at sis*, “to be present with oneself,” II Corinthians II, 1.

   b. “To,” πρός with accusative only, after *briggan*, “bring,” Mark IX, 20; XI, 7; XV, 1; Luke IV, 40; and *qiman*, “come,” Matthew VII, 15; Mark I, 40; II, 3; III, 8; VII, 31; IX, 14; X, 50; XI, 13; Luke I, 43; VII, 4, 7, 20; VIII, 35; [Col. 1264] XV, 20; John VI, 44, 65; X, 41; XII, 12; XIV, 6, 18, 28; XVI, 7; XI, 45; I Corinthians XVI, 5, 11, 12; II Corinthians I, 15, 16; II, 1, 12, 14; XIII, 1; Galatians IV, 20; Colossians IV, 10; I Thessalonians II, 18; III, 6; I Timothy III, 14; II Timothy IV, 9; Nehemiah V, 17; *Skeir.* VIII, c. Hence Mark X, 45, *at andbahtjam qiman*, “to come to be served” (διακονηθῆναι ἦλθεν).

   c. “From, out of,” παρά with genitive and ἀπό (here too the primary sense “at, by” fundamentally underlies it), after *gasaiwan*, “see,” John VIII, 38; *hausjan*, “hear,” John VIII, 26; XV, 15; II Timothy I, 13; II, 2; *gahausjan*, “hear,” John VI, 45; *Skeir.* IV, d; *fiþan*, “receive,” Mark XV, 45; *bigitan*, “find,” II Timothy I, 18; *niman*, “receive,” Mark XII, 2; John X, 18; I Thessalonians II, 13; Nehemiah V, 15; *ganiman*, “receive,” Ephesians VI, 8; II Timothy III, 14; *andniman*, “receive,” I Corinthians XI, 23; I Thessalonians IV, 1; II Thessalonians III, 6.

   d. “By, from” in passive expressions: *Skeir.* VI, d, *at gawairbam frakunnan ni skuld*, “not guilty of known deeds”; VI, b, *warjatoh vaurde at mannam maht ïst anþarleikein ïnmaidjan*, “yet by a human word the equality may be denied”; I Thessalonians IV, 9, *at guþa uslaisiþs*, “taught by God” (θεοδίδακτος); I Timothy VI, 5, *at þaimei gatarniþ ïst sunja*, “deprived of the truth” (ἀπεστερημένοι τῆς ἀληθείας). Thus also Luke X, 7, *þo at ïm* (sc. *gibanona*), “the things given by them.”

2. In a temporal sense, “during, at,” ἐπί with genitive: Luke III, 2; elsewhere also corresponding to the Greek genitive absolute: Matthew VIII, 16; XI, 7; XXVII, 1; Mark IV, 6, 35; VIII, 1; XI, 11; XIV, 43; XV, 42; XVI, 2; Luke II, 2; III, 15, 21; IV, 2, 6, 48; VII, 24; IX, 34 at this passage, 43; XIX, 11; XX, 1, 45; Romans VII, 2, 3, 9; II Corinthians I, 11; II, 12; V, 20; X, 15; Ephesians II, 20; I Thessalonians III, 6; *Skeir.* II, d; III, a; VII, b; VIII, a, c, d.

3. In a metaphorical sense, “beside, because of,” with a slight inclination toward a causal meaning: only *Skeir.* III, c; V, a, c; VII, b.

II. In compounds:

1. With verbs: *ataugjan, atbairan, atbairhtjan, atgaggan, atgiban, atdriusan, athaban, athahan, athaitan, athafjan, atþinsan, atkunnan, atligan, atlagjan, atnewjan, atniman, atrinnan, atsaiwan, atsatjan, atsnarpjan, atstandan, atsteigan, attekan, attiuhan, atvairpan, atvalvjan, atvandjan, atvisan, atvopjan, atfarjan*; double compounds: *atgaraihtjan; ïnnatbairan, ïnnatgaggan, ïnnattiuhan* (*usatbairan*); *duatgaggan, duatrinnan, duatsnivan*.

2. With nouns: *ataþni, atgaggs, atvitains*.

3. With adjectives: *unatgahts*.

**ATAþNI**, see under **Aþn**.

**ATER** (*Ateir*, Ezra II, 16), proper name, Ater, Ἀτὴρ: Ezra II, 16, 41.

**ATISKS** (Old High German *ezisc*, New High German *Esch* [sown field], Gallic *un champ ensemencé*, “a sown field”; Gr. II, 25, 373; III, 416; Gf. I, 229), masculine (?), “sown field, cornfield,” τὰ σπόριμα: Mark II, 23; Luke VI, 1.

**ATJAN**, see under **Itan**.

**ATTA** (Old High German *atto*; Old French *atha, atta, ettha*; Greek ἄττα, Latin *atavus*; Gf. I, 145; Rchth. 613; Schm. I, 126), masculine, “father,” πατήρ: Matthew V, 16, 45; VI, 1, 4, 8, 9, 15, 26; X, 29; Mark V, 40; VII, 10, 11; IX, 21, 24; X, 7, 19, 29, 30; XI, 10; XV, 21; Luke I, 17, 32, 55, 59, 62, 67, 72, 73; II, 48, 49; III, 8; VI, 23, 26; VIII, 51; IX, 26, 42, 59; XIV, 26; XV, 12, 17, 18, 20, 21, 22, 27, 28, 29; XVIII, 20; John V, 45; VI, 31, 42, 49; VII, 22; VIII, 19, 38, 41, 42, 44; X, 15, 29, 30; Romans IX, 5; XI, 28; XV, 6, 8; I Corinthians X, 1; XV, 24; II Corinthians I, 2, 3; VI, 18; XI, 31; Galatians I, 4; IV, 2; Ephesians I, 2, 17; III, 14; IV, 6; V, 20; Philippians II, 8, 22; Colossians I, 12; III, 17; I Thessalonians II, 11; III, 11; II Thessalonians I, 1; I Timothy V, 1; Titus I, 4; *Skeir.* IV, d; V, a; VI, b, c; VII, d.

* **AVI** (Old Norse *á*, Anglo-Saxon *eovu, eoved, eovestre*, Old High German *awi, ewit, ewist*, English *ewe*, Dutch *ooi*, Greek ὄϊς, Latin *ovis*; Gr. II, 368; III, 327, 433, 475; Gf. I, 505; Schm. I, 1), feminine, “sheep.”

**AVEþI**, neuter, “flock,” ποίμνη: John X, 16; I Corinthians IX, 7.

**AVISTR**, neuter, “sheepfold,” αὐλή: John X, 16.

**AVILIUD** (*aviliuþ*, I Corinthians XV, 57; Old Saxon *alat, olat* [which Schmeller, *Glossarium Heliandense*, 68, refers to *latan* and explains as *Erlass*, “release, remission”]), neuter, “grace, thanks,” χάρις: I Corinthians XV, 57; II Corinthians II, 14; VIII, 16; IX, 15; “thanksgiving,” εὐχαριστία: II Corinthians IV, 15; IX, 12; Ephesians V, 4; [Col. 1265] Philippians IV, 6; Colossians IV, 2; I Thessalonians III, 9; I Timothy II, 1; IV, 3, 4.

**AVILIUDON**, conjugation II, “to give thanks,” εὐχαριστεῖν: Mark VIII, 6; Luke XVII, 16; XVIII, 11; John VI, 11, 23; XI, 41; Romans VII, 25; I Corinthians I, 14, 30; X, 30; XI, 24; II Corinthians I, 11; Ephesians I, 16; V, 20; Colossians I, 12; III, 17; I Thessalonians II, 13; V, 17; II Thessalonians I, 3; *Skeir.* VI, b; “to give thanks,” χάριν ἔχειν: I Timothy I, 12; II Timothy I, 3; “to glorify,” δοξάζειν: Luke XVIII, 43; participle *aviliudonds*, “thankful,” εὐχάριστος: Colossians III, 15.

**AVO** (Latin *avus, avia*), feminine, “grandmother,” μάμμα: II Timothy I, 5.

**AF** (and, with interrogative postfix *u*, *abu*, John XVIII, 34; Old Norse, Old Saxon, Swedish, Danish, Dutch *af*, Old High German *ab, aba*, Old French *af, ef, of*, Anglo-Saxon and English *of*, New High German *ab*, Greek ἀπό, Latin *ab*; Bopp 83; Gr. II, 50, 253; Gf. I, 72; Alth. *Präp.* 213; Rchth. 956), a preposition governing the dative. It primarily means “from” (ἀπό), is opposed to *ana* and *at*, and indicates both the departure and separation of two objects formerly near each other, and direction away from or down from something.

I. As a preposition:

1. In a local sense, “from, out of,” ἀπό, ἐκ:

   a. After intransitive verbs: *qiman*, “come,” Matthew XVII, 57; Mark III, 22; XV, 21; II Corinthians I, 16; XI, 9; *usgaggan*, “go out,” Mark XVI, 8; Luke IV, 41; VI, 19; VIII, 29, 33, 35, 38, 46; Philippians IV, 15; *atgaggan*, “come down,” Matthew VIII, 1; Mark IX, 9; Luke IX, 37; XVII, 7; *afgaggan*, “go away,” Luke V, 2; *afleiþan*, “depart,” Mark I, 42; Luke V, 13; *galeiþan*, “go away,” Mark VII, 31; Luke X, 30; *urinnan*, “run out,” Luke IV, 33; *anastodjan*, *Skeir.* IV, b; *atsteigan*, “come down,” Matthew XXVII, 42; Mark XV, 30, 32; I Thessalonians IV, 16; *driusan*, “fall,” Luke XVI, 21; *aflinnan*, “cease,” Luke IX, 39; *afstandan*, “withdraw,” II Corinthians XII, 8; II Timothy II, 19; *gasviltan*, “die,” Colossians II, 20; after *andhuleins*, “revelation,” II Thessalonians I, 7; *newa vas beþanijin af fairgunja*, Luke XIX, 29, where *af* has the same value as *at*.

   By ellipsis are to be explained such cases as II Corinthians III, 18, *af vulþau ïn vulþu*, “from glory into glory”; Mark VII, 4, *af maþla* (sc. *qimandans*), “from the marketplace [having come] they do not eat”; Luke VI, 17, *hansa mikila manageins af allamma ïudaias* (sc. *qimandeins*), “a great multitude from all Judaea [having come]”; likewise Galatians IV, 24, *aina triggva af fairgunja seinai* (sc. *qumana*), “one covenant [having come] from Mount Sinai”; likewise II Corinthians III, 18, *vulþus af ahmin*, “glory from the Spirit.” Otherwise, II Corinthians XI, 3, *og ïbai aufto þriurja vairþaina fraþja ïzvara af ainfalþein jah sviknein* (sc. *afleiþandona*), “but I fear lest your minds may perhaps be led away from the simplicity and purity [in Christ].” So also *af* before city names with Greek endings: *manna gabigs af areimaþaias*, “a rich man from Arimathea,” Matthew XXVII, 57; Mark XV, 43; *lazarus af beþanias*, “Lazarus from Bethany,” John XI, 1.

   b. After transitive verbs: *niman*, “take,” Luke VI, 29; XIX, 24; John XVI, 22; Colossians III, 24; and with this verb understood Luke V, 36, *þamma fairnjin ni gatimid þata af þamma niujin*, “from the new [garment] he does not fit a piece to the old.” *afniman*, “take away,” Matthew IX, 15, 16; Mark II, 20, 21; VII, 33; Luke V, 35; VIII, 18; XVI, 3; XIX, 26; *usniman*, “take away,” Luke VIII, 12; *ganiman*, “receive,” Colossians I, 7; compare Mark XIII, 28; *lisan*, “gather,” Matthew VII, 16; *galisan*, “gather,” Mark XIII, 27; *leiwan*, “lend,” Matthew V, 42; *afvandjan*, “turn away,” Romans XI, 26; Galatians I, 6; II Timothy I, 15; IV, 4; *afvagjan*, “remove,” Colossians I, 23; *afhrisjan*, “shake off,” Luke IX, 5; *afvalvjan*, “roll away,” Mark XVI, 3; *afskaidan*, “separate,” Luke IX, 33; Romans VIII, 35, 39; *gaskaidan*, “separate,” II Thessalonians III, 6. Romans IX, 3 belongs here: *usbida anaþaima visan af xristau*, “to be accursed, separated from Christ.” After *gadrausjan*, “cast down,” Luke I, 52; *vairpan*, “cast,” Matthew V, 29, 30; *afvairpan*, “put away,” Ephesians IV, 31; *usvairpan*, “cast out,” Mark XVI, 9; *ushauhjan*, “lift up,” John XII, 32; *gaainanan*, “be separated,” I Thessalonians II, 17; *gahaban sik*, “keep oneself,” I Thessalonians IV, 3; V, 32; *lausjan*, “deliver,” Matthew VI, 13; Luke VI, 30; *galausjan*, “release,” Mark V, 4; Romans VII, 2; II Thessalonians III, 3; *uslausjan*, “rescue,” II Thessalonians III, 2; *andbindan*, “release,” Romans VII, 6; *hrainjan*, “cleanse,” II Corinthians VII, 1; *gahailjan*, “heal,” Luke VII, 21; *gahailnan*, “be healed,” Mark V, 29; add after adjectives *laus*, “free,” Galatians V, 4; *hails*, “whole,” Mark V, 34.

   c. “From,” ἐκ, in the formulas *af taihsvon* and *af hleidumein*, after *sitan*, “sit”: Mark X, 37, 40; XII, 36; XIV, 62; Luke XX, 42; and *standan*, “stand”: Luke I, 11. Thus Mark XV, 27, *miþ ïmma ushramidedun tvans vaidedjans ainana af taihsvon jah ainana af hleidumein ïs*, “with him they crucified two robbers, one on his right and one on his left”; Matthew XXV, 41, *þai af hleidumein*, “those on the left.”

2. In a temporal sense, “from, since,” ἀπό: Mark X, 6; II Corinthians VIII, 10.

3. In a metaphorical sense:

   a. “From,” ἐκ, ἀπό, in the phrase *af sis silbin*, “from oneself,” after *qiþan*, “say,” John XVIII, 34; *rodjan*, “speak,” John XIV, 10; XVI, 13; *þagkjan*, “think,” II Corinthians III, 5; X, 7; *taujan*, “do,” John VIII, 28; *qiman*, “come,” John VII, 28; [Col. 1266] *akran bairan*, “bear fruit,” John XV, 4; *saivala lagjan*, “lay down one’s life,” John X, 18.

   b. After passive constructions, “by, from,” ὑπό with genitive, ἀπό: Luke VIII, 14; Romans XII, 21. Thus Galatians II, 6, *af þaim þngkjandam visan wa* (“from those reputed to be something”; the construction in the Greek text is interrupted by an intervening clause, whereas at v. 7 it should have continued with the passive); and Galatians I, 1, *paulus apaustaulus ni af mannam* (“Paul, an apostle not from men,” that is, made an apostle).

   c. With partitive force, “of, from,” ἀπό: Mark VII, 28, *hundos matjand af drauhsnom barne*, “dogs eat from the children’s crumbs”; Matthew V, 18, *striks ni usleiþiþ af witoda*, “not one stroke shall pass from the law”; I Timothy I, 6, *af þaimei sumai*, “from which certain persons [have turned away]” (ὧν τινές).

   d. Sometimes, where other prepositions occupy its place elsewhere, it has the sense “before, from,” ἀπό: Luke XVIII, 34, *vas vaurd gafulgin af ïm*, “the saying was hidden from them” (elsewhere *faura*).

II. In compounds:

1. With verbs: *afagjan, afaikan, afairzjan, afgaggan, afgiban, afdailjan, afdaubnan, afdobnan, afdauþjan, afdaujan, afdumbnan, afdrausjan, afdomjan, afqiþan, afhaban, afhamon, afhugjan, afhrainjan, afhrisjan, afholon, afþaursjan, afþliuhan, afþvahan, afhlaþan, afleiþan, aflifnan, afletan, aflagjan, aflinnan, afmaitan, afmarzjan, afniman, afsatjan, afskaidan, afskiuban, afslahan, afslauþjan, afslauþnan, afslaupjan, afstandan, afsvairban, afsvaggvjan, aftaurnan, aftiuhan, afvairpan, afvalvjan, afvandjan, affilhan, afwaþjan, afwapnan*.

2. With nouns: *afgudei, afgrundiþa, afdrugkja, afdomeins, afetja, aflet, aflageins, afmarzeins, afsateins, afstass*.

3. With adjectives: *afguds, afhaims, afmainds*.

**AFAR** (cf. Old Norse *afar* …; Old High German *afar*; Gr. III, 259; Gf. I, 177), a preposition governing the accusative and dative, generally meaning “after.”

I. As a preposition.

A. With the accusative, only in a temporal sense, “after,” μετά with accusative: Matthew XXVII, 53, 62, 63; XXVI, 2; Mark VIII, 31; IX, 2; XIII, 24; Luke I, 24; II, 46; IX, 28; XV, 13; XIX, 14; I Corinthians XI, 25; *Skeir.* II, a; διά: Mark II, 1. Especially in the expressions *afar leitil*, “after a little while, shortly afterwards,” μετὰ μικρόν: Matthew XXVI, 73; Mark XIV, 70; *afar ni filu* (?) *Skeir.* IV, a; *afar þata*, “after these things, afterwards,” μετὰ ταῦτα: Matthew VIII, 5; Mark XVI, 12; Luke V, 27; X, 1; XVIII, 4; John VI, 1; VII, 1; XI, 7, 11; I Corinthians XV, 5; “apart from,” παρεκτός: II Corinthians XI, 28; *biþe afar þata*, “immediately afterwards, in sequence,” ἐν τῷ καθεξῆς: Luke VIII, 1; *afar þatei*, “after,” μετὰ τό with infinitive: Mark I, 14; *Skeir.* VII, b.

B. With the dative:

1. In a local sense, “behind, after,” ὀπίσω: after *gaggan*, “go,” Luke IX, 23; XIV, 27; *laistjan*, “follow,” Matthew X, 28; Mark VIII, 34; *galeiþan*, “go away,” Mark I, 20; John XII, 19; *hirjats*, “come [after me],” Mark I, 17; *ïnsandjan*, “send,” Luke XIX, 14; especially as an equivalent of ἀκολουθεῖν, *gaggan afar*, “follow”: Matthew IX, 9, 19; Mark II, 14, 15; V, 24; XIV, 13; Luke V, 28; John XI, 31; and *laistjan afar*, “follow”: Matthew VIII, 1, 22; IX, 9, 27; XXVII, 55; Mark I, 18; III, 7; VI, 1; XIV, 51, 54; Luke V, 11, 27; IX, 11.

2. In a temporal sense, “after,” ὀπίσω: Matthew III, 11; Mark I, 7; μετά with accusative: John XIII, 26.

3. In a metaphorical sense:

   a. “After, in pursuit of,” ἐπί with accusative, after *gaggan*, Luke XV, 4, and *afargaggan*, Philippians III, 14, in order to seek or obtain something; compare Mark X, 24, *hunjan afar faihau*, “to trust in riches.”

   b. “According to,” κατά with accusative: I Corinthians XV, 3, 4, *xristus gasvalt afar bokom*, “Christ died according to the Scriptures”; “into,” εἰς: II Timothy II, 26, *gafahanai tiuhanda afar unhulþins wiljin*, “taken captive by him for the devil’s will”; “upon,” ἐπί with dative: Luke V, 5, *afar waurda þeinamma vairpam natja*, “at your word I shall let down the nets”; Luke I, 59, *haihaitun ïna afar namin attins*, “they were going to call him after his father’s name”; “according to,” πρός with accusative: II Corinthians V, 10, *ganimai warjizuh swesona leikis afar þaimei gatavida*, “that each may receive what is his according to what he has done in the body.”

II. As adverb or noun (Gr. II, 43), it occurs in Luke I, 5, *us afar für* ἐξ ἐφημερίας; it also seems to be used adverbially in *Skeir.* III, c. *Sa afar dags*, “the following day,” ἡ ἑξῆς: Luke VII, 11; and *dags afar sabbate*, “the first day of the week,” μία σαββάτων: Mark XVI, 2, are properly contracted into *afardags* and *afarsabbate*.

III. In compounds:

1. With verbs: *afargaggan, afarlaistjan*.

2. With nouns: *afardags, afarsabbatus*.

**AFTA** (Old Norse *aftan*, Old Saxon *aftar, eft*, Anglo-Saxon *aeft*, English, Old High German *after*, Old French *efta, efter*, Dutch *achter*, cf. **Afar**, Greek αὖθις; Gr. III, 628; [Col. 1267A] Rchth. 698), adverb, “afterwards, behind, back”; *þo afta*, “the things behind,” τὰ ὀπίσω: Philippians III, 14.

**AFTANA**, “behind” (French *par derrière*), ὤπισθεν: Mark V, 27.

**AFTARO**, the same: Matthew IX, 20; Luke VIII, 44; “behind,” ὀπίσω: Luke VII, 38.

**AFTRA**:

**BI** (Old Saxon, Old Frisian, Anglo-Saxon *bi, be*, Old High German *bi*, English *be* …, *by*, Dutch *be, bi*, Modern High German *bei*; Bopp 84; Gr. II, 110, 254; Gf. III, 5; AP. 100; Rchth. 630), a preposition governing the accusative and dative. Primarily it means “at, by”; not, however, restricted like *at* to a particular place, but extending somewhat more broadly, and thus it can mean “around” and be used for Greek περί. Very frequently, with a closely related sense, it corresponds either to Greek περί with the genitive, especially after verbs of stating, or to κατά with the accusative in all its functions.

I. Preposition.

A. With the accusative:

1. In a local sense:

   a. “Around,” περί with the accusative, after *sitan*: Mark III, 32, 34; also without a verb: Matthew VIII, 18; Mark IX, 14. Thus **þai bi ïna**, Mark III, 8; IV, 10; and probably also John XI, 19. **gaqemun at þaim bi marþan** must be read in place of the textually unintelligible **gaqemun bi marþan**. Further, Mark I, 6: **vas ïohannes gavasiþs gairda bi hup**, “John was clothed with a belt around his waist”; and V, 4: **eisarna bi fotuns gabugana**, “iron things bent around his feet,” for Greek πέδαι, “fetters.”

   b. “Upon,” ἐπί with the accusative, in the expressions **stautan bi kinnu**, Matthew V, 39; Luke VI, 29; “along,” κατά with the accusative, **bi vig goljan**, Luke X, 4.

   c. “To,” εἰς: Romans IX, 31, **bi vitoþ garaihteins gasnau**, “attained to a law of righteousness.”

2. In a temporal sense:

   a. “About,” περί with the accusative: Matthew XXVII, 46.

   b. “During, within,” ἐν: Mark XV, 29; διά with the genitive: Mark XIV, 58; Galatians II, 1; ἀνάμεσον, “between”: Nehemiah V, 18.

   c. “At,” κατά with the accusative: 2 Timothy IV, 1.

   d. “Among,” ἐπί with the genitive: **gaminþi marvtre þize hi verekan papan jah batvin bilaif gabrannidaize**, Gothic Calendar: “the commemoration of martyrs who were burned; the syntax of **hi verekan papan jah batvin bilaif** is uncertain in the supplied reading.” (Thus *bi* occurs in Old High German; see Graff, *Althochdeutsche Präpositionen*, pp. 102 ff.)

3. Attached to numerals, it is distributive: “by, apiece,” κατά with the accusative: 1 Corinthians XIV, 27, **bi tvans**, “two at a time.”

4. In a metaphorical sense:

   a. “Concerning, with reference to,” περί, regularly with the accusative, after verbs:

   aa. Of general meaning, such as **taujan**, Luke II, 27 (**ei tavidedeina bi ïna**, περί with the genitive); **vairþan**, Mark V, 16, 33 (in Greek the dative or ἐπί with the dative is also used).

   bb. Of particular meaning, such as **naqaþs vairþan** (“to suffer shipwreck, suffer loss”), 1 Timothy I, 19; **siukan**, VI, 4; **usviss usmitan**, 2 Timothy II, 18; **uskiusans**, III, 8; after **visan** in an emphatic sense, Philippians II, 23, **wa bi mik ïst**, “the things concerning me,” τὰ περὶ ἐμέ; II, 28; Ephesians VI, 22; Colossians IV, 7, τὰ κατ’ ἐμέ; also **þo bi ïna**, *Skeir.* VI, a; and after nouns: Mark IV, 19, **þai bi þata anþar lustjus**, “the desires concerning other things,” αἱ περὶ τὰ λοιπὰ ἐπιθυμίαι; Philippians II, 30, **gaidv bi mein andbahti**, “the deficiency in your service toward me,” ὑστέρημα τῆς πρὸς ἐμὲ λειτουργίας.

   b. “According to, after the manner of,” κατά with the accusative, after **þata samo fraþjan**, Romans XV, 5; **saurgan**, 2 Corinthians VII, 9; hence also **so bi guþ saurga**, 2 Corinthians VII, 10; **usgiban**, *Skeir.* V, d; after **laiseins**, 1 Timothy I, 11; VI, 3; **sunja**, Titus I, 1; **garehsns**, *Skeir.* III, a; IV, a; **hrainei**, *Skeir.* III, b; **bi mannan**, “in the manner of a human being, in human fashion,” κατὰ ἄνθρωπον: 1 Corinthians IX, 8; XV, 32; **bi reik**, “according to the ruler,” κατὰ τὸν ἄρχοντα: Ephesians II, 2.

   c. “According to,” κατά with the accusative after **ufhausjan**, Colossians III, 20, 22. Compare 2 Corinthians I, 14, **gakunnaideduþ uns bi sumata**, “you recognized us in part,” ἀπὸ μέρους.

   d. “Concerning,” περί with the genitive, after verbs of speaking and perceiving:

[Col. 1274] **qiþan**, Matthew XI, 7; Mark I, 30; VIII, 30; John VII, 39; IX, 17; X, 41; XI, 13; XIII, 22, 24; XVIII, 34; compare 2 Corinthians VIII, 23; **rodjan**, Luke II, 17, 33, 38; VII, 24; John VII, 13; VIII, 26; IX, 21; XII, 41; XIII, 18; **vailamerjan**, Luke IV, 43; **gateihan**, Luke VII, 18; John XVI, 25; Matthew VIII, 33; **gakannjan**, Luke II, 17; **bandvjan**, 1 Corinthians XVI, 12; **galaisjan**, Luke I, 4; **praufetjan**, Mark VII, 6; **gaþrafstjan**, John XI, 19; **veitvodjan**, John V, 36, 37; VII, 7; VIII, 13, 14, 18; X, 25; XV, 26; XVIII, 23; **fraihnan**, Mark VII, 17; X, 10; Luke IX, 45; John XVIII, 19; **sokjan**, John XVI, 19; **ufkunan**, John VII, 17; **gakunnan**, Mark XII, 26; **hausjan**, Mark V, 27; VII, 25; Luke VII, 3; IX, 9; Philippians I, 17; **meljan** and **gameljan**, Matthew XI, 10; Luke VII, 27; XVIII, 31; John V, 46; 2 Corinthians IX, 1; 1 Thessalonians IV, 9; V, 1; ἐπί with the accusative: Mark IX, 12, 13; **anabiudan**, Luke IV, 10; **garaidjan**, 1 Corinthians XVI, 1; **stiurjan**, 1 Timothy I, 7; **galaubjan**, John IX, 18; **unveis visan**, 2 Corinthians I, 8; 1 Thessalonians IV, 13; **þagkjan**, Luke III, 15; and after nouns: **vaurd**, Luke V, 15; VII, 17; **ïnsahts**, Luke I, 1; **sokeins**, John III, 25; *Skeir.* III, b; **ïnilo**, John XV, 22; **veitvodeins**, *Skeir.* VI, c; **anabusns**, 1 Corinthians VII, 25; **missaqiss**, John VII, 43 (διά with the accusative); **gaminþi**, 2 Timothy I, 3. This also includes Luke IX, 11, **rodida du ïm þo bi þiudangardja guþs**, “he spoke to them about the kingdom of God,” τὰ περὶ τῆς βασιλείας τοῦ Θεοῦ; Colossians IV, 8, **ei kunnjai wa bi ïzvis ïst**, “that he may know the things concerning you,” τὰ περὶ ὑμῶν; *Skeir.* IV, a, **unkunnands þo bi nasjand**, “not knowing the things concerning the Saviour.”

   e. “For,” περί or ὑπέρ with the genitive, after **aljan haban**, Colossians IV, 13; **aviliud usgildan**, 1 Thessalonians III, 9; especially after **bidjan**, Matthew V, 44; Luke IV, 38; John XVI, 26; XVII, 9, 20; Romans X, 1; 2 Corinthians I, 11; Colossians IV, 3; 1 Thessalonians III, 2; V, 25; 2 Thessalonians I, 11; III, 1; *Skeir.* V, d; and **usdaudjan ïn bidom**, Colossians IV, 12.

   f. “On account of, because of,” in a causal sense, usually περί with the genitive, also ἐπί with the dative, after **sildaleikjan**, Luke II, 18; IV, 22, 32; IX, 43; **saurgan**, Matthew VI, 28; **unverjan**, Mark X, 41; **birodjan**, John VI, 41; VII, 32; **gasakan**, Luke III, 19; John VIII, 46; XVI, 8, 9, 10, 11; **gavargjan**, Romans VIII, 3; **þulan**, 2 Timothy II, 10 (διά with the accusative); **wopan**, 2 Corinthians X, 8; **bidjan**, 2 Corinthians XII, 8 (ὑπέρ with the genitive); **gretan**, Luke XIX, 41; Romans IX, 27 (ὑπέρ with the genitive). In Luke XIX, 11, **bi þatei newa vas** is read for διὰ τὸ ἐγγὺς εἶναι, “because he was near.” Here also belongs **liban bi hlaib**, “to live by bread,” ἐπί with the dative: Luke IV, 4.

   g. “Against,” in a hostile sense, κατά with the genitive, after **haban wa**, Matthew V, 23; **veitvodjan**, 1 Corinthians XV, 15 (for **bi guþ**, **bi guþa** must be read); **runa niman**, Matthew XXVIII, 1; **garuni gataujan**, Mark III, 6; **vrohs**, 1 Timothy V, 19.

B. With the dative:

1. In a local sense:

   a. “To, toward,” πρός, after **gastagqjan**, Luke IV, 11, and **bistigqan**, Luke VI, 48.

   b. “By,” only in the phrase **undgreipan** or **fairgreipan bihandau**, Mark V, 41; IX, 27, “to take by the hand,” κρατεῖν τῆς χειρός.

   c. “Before,” κατά with the accusative: **þo bi andvairþja**, 2 Corinthians X, 7; elsewhere **ïn andvairþja** is read.

2. In a temporal sense:

   a. “According to,” κατά with the accusative: Romans IX, 9.

   b. “After,” especially in the compounds **biþe** and **biþeh**; see under *þata*.

5. In a metaphorical sense:

   a. “In,” ἐν, εἰς, ἐπί, ἀπό, κατά with the accusative, after **vaurkjan**, Mark XIV, 6; **gataujan**, John VI, 2; **gabairhtjan**, Romans IX, 17; **ataugjan**, Ephesians II, 7; **gakannjan**, Romans IX, 23; **kunnan**, Luke I, 18; **ufkunnan**, Matthew VII, 16, 20; John XIII, 35; **galaisjan sik**, *Skeir.* V, a; **galaubjan** (“to know something and believe in it”), John XVI, 30.

   b. “In,” ἐν; “through,” διά with the genitive; also with the simple accusative, after **svaran**, Matthew V, 34, 35, 36; **bisvaran**, Mark V, 7; **bidjan**, 2 Corinthians X, 1.

   c. “Because of,” in a causal sense: for example, **ni vaiht andsitan bi gahugdai**, “to take no account because of conscience,” διά with the accusative: 1 Corinthians X, 27; **gaþlahsnan bi ïnnagahtai**, “to be troubled because of the thought,” ἐπί with the dative: Luke I, 29; **bi filusnai andhuleino ufarhafnan**, “to be exalted because of the abundance of revelations,” dative: 2 Corinthians XII, 7. Romans IX, 12, **ïnahs bi sis**, παρά with the dative, may also be adduced here.

   d. “With,” μετά with the genitive, after **armahairtei**, Luke I, 58, 72, and after **usbeidan**, Romans IX, 22.

   e. “Through,” διά with the genitive: **ïnsandjan bi siponjam**, Matthew XI, 2; **niman bi attin**, *Skeir.* V, c; compare Graff, *Althochdeutsche Präpositionen*, p. 104; *Althochdeutsche Sprachschätze* III, 10.

   f. Most frequently, however, “according to, after the manner of,” κατά with the accusative, especially in set formulas: **bi sunjai**, see under *Sunja*; **bi biuhtja**, Luke I, 9; II, 27, 42;

[Col. 1275] IV, 16; **bi nauþai**, Philemon 17; *Skeir.* VI, a; **bi leika**, Romans VIII, 1, 4, 5; IX, 3, 5; 1 Corinthians X, 18; 2 Corinthians I, 17; V, 16; X, 2; XI, 18; Galatians IV, 23, 29; **bi vitoda**, Luke II, 22, 39; John XVIII, 31; XIX, 7; Philippians III, 5; **bi gavaleinai**, Romans IX, 11; XI, 28; **bi ïnsahtai**, subscription to 1 Corinthians; *Skeir.* V, b; **bi mahtai**, 2 Corinthians VIII, 3; Ephesians III, 20; Colossians I, 11; 2 Timothy I, 8; **bi vaurstva**, 2 Corinthians XI, 15; Ephesians I, 19; IV, 16; Colossians I, 29; Philippians III, 21; 2 Timothy I, 9; IV, 14; **bi mitaþ**, 2 Corinthians X, 13; Ephesians IV, 7; **bi viljin**, Galatians I, 4; Ephesians I, 9, 11.

Skeir. V, c; according to the promise, Gal. III, 29; IV, 28; Tim. II, I, 1; according to the good pleasure, Eph. I, 5; Tim. II, I, 9; according to the command, Tim. I, I, 1; Tit. I, 3; according to the ordinance, Skeir. III, d; VIII, c; according to revelation, Gal. II, 2; Eph. III, 3; according to the injunction, Thess. II, III, 6, in place of which Mc. VII, 5 has *bi þammei anafulhun* (“according to what they handed down”); according to appearance, Joan. VII, 24; according to name, Joan. X, 3; according to this, in this manner, Luc. VI, 23; XVII, 30; and further in many places, which for the most part occur as formulas: Mth. IX, 29; Luc. I, 38; II, 29; Rom. X, 2; XI, 24, 28; XIV, 15; Cor. I, VII, 6; Cor. II, IV, 13, 17; X, 15; XI, 21; XIII, 10; Eph. I, 7; II, 2; III, 7, 11, 16; IV, 22; Phlpp. I, 20; II, 3; III, 6, 14; Col. II, 22; III, 10; Thess. II, I, 12; Tim. I, I, 18; V, 21; Tim. II, II, 8; Tit. I, 1; also in reference to a person: according to the inward person, Rom. VII, 22; according to the Lord, Cor. II, XI, 17; according to God, Eph. IV, 24.

II. In compounds:

1. With verbs: *biabrjan, biaukan, biauknan, biarbaidjan, bibindan, bigairdan, bigitan, bigraban, bidomjan, biqimam, bihlahjan, biþagkjan, biþragjan, biþvahan, bikukjan, bilaigon, bilaikan, bileiþan, bilaibjan, bimaitan, bimaminjan, binahan, biniman, biniuhsjan, biraubon, birinnan, birodjan, bisaiwan, bisauljan, bisaulnan, bisitan, bisatjan, biskaban, biskeinan, bismeitan, bisnivan, bispeivan, bistandan, bistigqan, bisvairban, bisvaran, bitiuhan, bivaibjan, bivindan, bivandjan, bivison, bifaihon, biwairdan*; compounds of compounds: *faurbigaggan, faurbiþragjan, faurbisnivan*.

2. With participles: *unbilaistiþs, unbimaitans*.

3. With nouns: *bibaurgeins, bihait, bihaitja, bihlaifs, bimait, bireikei, birunains, birodeins, bisauleins, bistuggqs, bifaiho, bifaih; unbimait*.

4. With adjectives: *bireiks*.

**BIþE and BIþEH**, see under **þata**.

**BIARI** (Anglo-Saxon *bera*, English *bear*, Swedish *björn*, Dutch *beer*, Modern High German *Bär*, Greek φήρ, Latin *fera, bestia*), neuter: beast, wild animal, θηρίον: Tit. I, 12.

**BIDJAN** (*bidan*, Rom. IX, 3; Cor. I, VII, 5) (Old Norse *bidia*, Old Saxon *biddian*, Anglo-Saxon *biddan*, Old High German *bitjan*, Old Frisian *bidda, bidia*, Swedish *bedja*, Danish *bede*, Modern High German *bitten*, Latin *petere*; Gr. II, 25; DM. 19; Gf. III, 51; Rchth. 632), conjugation I: preterite *baþ* (*bad*, Luc. V, 12; VIII, 41; XV, 28), plural *bedun*, participle *bidans*.

1. To ask, entreat, with the accusative of the person and genitive of the thing, but also with a double accusative, or with an accusative of the thing, with the particles *fram*, *faur*, and *bi* (see these entries), meaning “from” or “for,” and *du* (see it), meaning “to,” prefixed to the person; αἰτεῖν (“ask”): Mth. V, 42; VI, 8, 9; XXVII, 58; Mc. VI, 22, 23, 24, 25; X, 35, 38; XI, 24; XV, 6, 8, 43; Luc. VI, 30; Joan. XI, 22; XIV, 13, 14; XV, 7, 16; XVI, 23, 24, 26; Cor. I, I, 22; Eph. III, 13, 20.

   παρακαλεῖν (“urge, entreat”): Mth. VIII, 5, 31, 34; Mc. I, 40; V, 10, 12, 17, 18, 23; VI, 56; VII, 32; VIII, 22; Luc. V, 8; VII, 4; VIII, 31, 32, 41; XV, 28; Rom. XII, 1; Cor. I, XVI, 12, 15; Cor. II, II, 8; V, 20; VI, 1; VIII, 6; IX, 5; X, 1, 12; VIII, 18; Eph. IV, 1; Phlpp. IV, 2; Thess. I, II, 11; III, 2; IV, 1, 10; V, 14; Thess. II, III, 12; Tim. I, I, 3; II, 1; Philem. 10.

   ἐπικαλεῖσθαι (“call upon”): Rom. X, 12, 14.

   δεῖσθαι (“request, beseech”): Mth. IX, 38; Luc. V, 12; VIII, 28, 38; IX, 38, 40; X, 2; Cor. II, V, 20; VIII, 4; X, 2; Gal. IV, 12; Thess. I, III, 10.

   ἐρωτᾶν (“ask, request”): Mc. I, 40 (?); VII, 26; Luc. IV, 38; VII, 3, 36; VIII, 37; XIV, 18, 19, 32; Joan. XII, 21; XIV, 16; XVI, 26; XVII, 9, 15, 20; Phlpp. IV, 3; Thess. I, V, 12; Thess. II, II, 1.

   ἐπερωτᾶν (“ask”): Mc. X, 17.

   ἐντυγχάνειν (“intercede”): Rom. VIII, 34.

   εὔχεσθαι (“pray”): Cor. II, XIII, 7, 9.

   προσεύχεσθαι (“pray”): Mth. V, 44; VI, 5, 6, 7, 9; Mc. I, 35; XI, 24, 25; XIII, 18; Luc. III, 21; V, 16; VI, 12, 28; IX, 18, 28, 29; XVIII, 1, 10, 11; Cor. I, VII, 5; XI, 4, 5; Col. I, 9; IV, 13; Thess. I, V, 17, 25; Thess. II, I, [Col. 1276] 11; III, 1; Tim. I, II, 8; Skeir. V, d.

2. To beg, ἐπαιτεῖν: Luc. XVI, 3.

**US-BIDJAN**, to pray, εὔχεσθαι: Rom. IX, 3.

**BIDA**, feminine:

1. That which is requested; a request, αἴτημα: Phlpp. IV, 6.

2. Prayers, entreaties; παράκλησις (“appeal, encouragement”): Cor. II, VIII, 17; δέησις (“supplication”): Luc. I, 13; II, 37; V, 33; IX, 43; Rom. X, 1; Cor. II, I, 11; IX, 14; Eph. VI, 18; Phlpp. I, 19; Tim. I, II, 1; V, 5; Tim. II, I, 3; προσευχή (“prayer”): Mc. IX, 29; Luc. VI, 12; Rom. XII, 12; Eph. I, 16; Phlpp. IV, 6; Col. IV, 2, 12; Philem. 42; ἔντευξις (“intercession”): Tim. I, IV, 5.

*Bidai anahaitan*, see under **Haitan**; *gards bido* or *razn bido*, “house of prayer,” οἶκος προσευχῆς: Mc. XI, 17; Luc. XIX, 46.

**BIDAGVA**, masculine: beggar, ὁ προσαίτων: Joan. IX, 8.

**BINDAN** (Old Norse, Old Frisian, Swedish *binda*; Old Saxon and Anglo-Saxon *bindan*; Old High German *bintan*; Danish *binde*; Modern High German *binden*; Bopp 84; Gr. II, 35; Gf. III, 132; Rchth. 640), conjugation I: *band, bundun, bundans*; to bind, be bound, δεσμεῖν: Luc. VIII, 29.

**AND-BINDAN**:

1. To loose, release, λύειν: Mth. III, 11; Mc. I, 7; XI, 2, 4; Luc. III, 16; XIX, 30, 31, 33; Joan. XI, 44; καταργεῖν (“render inoperative, abolish”): Rom. VII, 6.

2. To explain, solve a parable, ἐπιλύειν: Mc. IV, 34.

**AND-BUNDNAN**, conjugation III: to be loosed, λύεσθαι: Mc. VII, 35.

**BI-BINDAN**, to bind around, περιδεῖν: Joan. XI, 44.

**GA-BINDAN**, to bind, δέειν: Mth. XXVII, 2; Mc. III, 27; V, 3, 4; VI, 17; XI, 2, 4; XV, 1, 7; Luc. XIX, 30; Joan. XI, 44; XVIII, 12, 24; Rom. VII, 2; Cor. I, VII, 27; Col. IV, 3; Tim. II, II, 9.

**GA-BINDA**, feminine: bond, σύνδεσμος: Col. II, 19.

**GA-BINDI**, feminine: the same: Col. III, 14.

**BANDI**, feminine: bond, chain, δεσμός: Mc. VII, 35; Luc. VIII, 29; Phlpp. I, 14, 16; Col. IV, 19; Tim. II, II, 9; Philem. 13.

**EISARNA-BANDI**, the same; chain, ἅλυσις: Luc. VIII, 29.

**NAUDI-BANDI**, the same: Mc. V, 3, 4; Tim. II, I, 16.

**FOTU-BANDI**, fetter, πέδη: Luc. VIII, 29.

**BANDJA**, masculine: prisoner, person in bonds, δέσμιος: Mth. XXVII, 15, 16; Mc. XV, 6; Eph. III, 1; IV, 1; Tim. II, I, 8.

**GA-BUNDI**, feminine: bond, σύνδεσμος: Eph. IV, 3.

**BANDVA** (compare Old Norse *benda*, Old High German *band*; in Paul the Deacon, *Historia Longobardorum* I, 20, “a banner which they call *bandum*”; hence Modern High German *Banner, Panier*), feminine: sign, σημεῖον: Cor. I, XIV, 22.

**BANDVO**, feminine: the same, Thess. II, III, 17; signal agreed upon, σύσσημον: Mc. XIV, 44.

**BANDVJAN** (*banvjan?* Luc. XX, 37), conjugation II:

1. To make a sign, νεύειν: Joan. XIII, 24; κατανεύειν (“signal to”): Luc. V, 7; διανεύειν (“make signs”): Luc. I, 22.

2. To indicate, signify, σημαίνειν: Joan. XII, 33; XVIII, 32; Skeir. V, b, c; μηνύειν (“make known”): Luc. XX, 37; Cor. I, X, 28; δηλοῦν (“make clear”): Cor. I, XVI, 12 (Luc. XX, 37); δῆλον ποιεῖν (“make evident”): Mth. XXVI, 73.

**GA-BANDVJAN**, to make a sign, ἐννεύειν: Luc. I, 62; Skeir. VI, c.

**BIJANDS** (Gr. III, 127; IV, 794), see the note on Philem. 22.

**BIUGAN** (Old Norse *beygia*, Anglo-Saxon *bugan*, Old High German *biugan*, Old Frisian *beia*, English *bow*, Swedish *böja*, Danish *boie, bukke*, Dutch *buigen*, Modern High German *beugen*; Bopp 115; Gr. II, 23; Gf. III, 36; Rchth. 622), conjugation I: *baug, bugun, bugans*; to bend, κάμπτειν: Eph. III, 14; to bend oneself, κάμπτειν: Rom. XIV, 11.

**GA-BIUGAN**, to bend; *eisarna bi fotuns gabugana*, “iron things bent about the feet,” fetters, πέδαι: Mc. V, 4.

**BIUDAN** (Old Norse *bioda*, Old Saxon *biodan*, Anglo-Saxon *beodan*, Old High German *biutan*, English *bid*, Swedish *bjuda*, Danish *byde*, Dutch *bieden*, Modern High German *bieten*; Gr. II, 21; DM. 24; Gf. III, 68), conjugation I: *bauþ* (*baud*, Luc. V, 14; VIII, 29, 55, 56; Joan. XIV, 31), *budun, budans*; to offer.

**ANA-BIUDAN**, to prescribe, command, ἐπιτάσσειν: Mc. I, 27; IX, 25; Luc. IV, 36; VIII, 31; XIV, 22; προστάσσειν (“give an order”): Mth. VIII, 4; Mc. I, 44; Luc. V, 14; συντάσσειν (“direct, prescribe”): [Col. 1277] Mth. XXVII, 10; διατάσσειν (“give orders”): Mth. XI, 1; Luc. VIII, 55; XVII, 9, 10; Cor. I, VII, 17; παραγγέλλειν (“command, charge”): Mc. VIII, 6; Luc. VIII, 29; Cor. I, VII, 10; Thess. I, IV, 11; Thess. II, III, 4, 6, 10, 12; Tim. I, IV, 11; V, 7; VI, 13; ἐντέλλεσθαι (“give a command”): Mc. X, 3; XI, 6; Luc. IV, 10; Joan. XIV, 31; XV, 14, 17; Neh. V, 14; VII, 2; διαστέλλεσθαι (“give strict orders”): Mc. V, 43; VII, 36; IX, 9; Skeir. III, b.

**FAUR-BIUDAN**, to forbid, prohibit; ἐπιτάσσειν (“order”): Luc. VIII, 25; παραγγέλλειν (“instruct, charge”): Mc. VI, 8; Luc. V, 14; VIII, 56; IX, 21; Tim. I, I, 3; ἐπιτιμᾶν (“rebuke, charge sternly”): Mc. VIII, 30.

**ANA-BUSNS** (*anabuzns*, Mc. XII, 28), feminine: command, precept, ἐπιταγή: Cor. I, VII, 25; Tim. I, I, 1; Tit. I, 3; παραγγελία (“instruction, charge”): Thess. I, IV, 2; Tim. I, I, 5, 18; ἐντολή (“commandment”): Mth. V, 19; Mc. VII, 8, 9; X, 5, 19; XII, 28, 29, 30, 31; Luc. I, 6; XV, 29; XVIII, 20; Joan. X, 18; XII, 49; XIII, 34; XIV, 15, 21; XV, 10, 12; Rom. VII, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13; XIII, 9; Cor. I, VII, 19; Eph. II, 15; Col. IV, 10; Tim. I, VI, 14; Tit. I, 14; Skeir. I, c; V, a; ἔνταλμα (“ordinance”): Mc. VII, 7; Col. II, 22; παράδοσις (“tradition”): Mc. VII, 13; Cor. I, XI, 2.

**BIUDS** (Old Norse *biodr*, Old Saxon *biod*, Anglo-Saxon *beod*, Old High German *biut*; Gr. III, 432; DM. 24; Gf. III, 76), masculine: table, τράπεζα: Mc. VII, 28; Luc. XVI, 21; Cor. I, X, 21; Neh. V, 17.

**BIUHTS** (compare Gr. II, 23), adjective: accustomed; *biuhts visan*, “to be accustomed,” εἰωθέναι: Mth. XXVII, 15; Mc. X, 1.

**BIUHTI**, neuter: custom, ἔθος: Luc. I, 9; II, (27) 42; τὸ εἰθισμένον, “the customary thing,” Luc. II, 27; τὸ εἰωθός, “what was customary,” Luc. IV, 16; συνήθεια, “customary practice”: Joan. XVIII, 39; Skeir. II, b.

**BIREIKS** (*bireks*), see under **Rikan**.

**BIRUSEIS**, the same as **Beruseis**.

**BLANDAN** (Old Norse *blanda*, Old Saxon *blandan*, Anglo-Saxon *bland*, Old High German *blantan*, English *blend*, Swedish *blanda*, Danish *blande*, Modern High German *Blendling*; Gr. II, 59, 487; Gf. III, 254), conjugation II:

1. To dye, disturb.

2. To mix with, συναναμίγνυναι: Cor. I, V, 9, 11; Thess. II, III, 14.

**BLAUþJAN** (English *blot, blast*, Swedish *blotta*, Danish *blotter*, Modern High German *blössen*; compare Old High German *blodan*; Gf. III, 251), conjugation II: to diminish, weaken, annul, ἀκυροῦν: Mc. VII, 13.

**GA-BLAUþJAN**, the same; *gablauþjan bairhtaba*, “to triumph openly,” θριαμβεύειν: Col. II, 15.

**BLEIþS** (Old Norse *blidr*, Anglo-Saxon *bliðe*, Old High German *blidi*, English *blithe, bless*, Swedish *blid*, Danish *blid, blod*; Gf. III, 249), adjective: good, gentle, merciful, οἰκτίρμων: Luc. VI, 36; φιλἀγαθος, “loving what is good”: Tit. I, 8.

**BLEIþEI**, feminine: goodness, mercy; οἰκτιρμός (“compassion”): Rom. XII, 1; Cor. II, I, 3; Col. III, 12; ἀγαθωσύνη (“goodness”): Gal. V, 22.

**GA-BLEIþEI** (*gableiþeins?*), the same, οἰκτιρμός: Phlpp. II, 1.

**BLEIþJAN**, conjugation II: to be merciful, οἰκτίρμονα εἶναι: Luc. VI, 36.

**GA-BLEIþJAN**, the same, with accusative: to have compassion on, οἰκτείρειν: Rom. IX, 15; σπλαγχνίζεσθαι (“be moved with compassion”): Mc. IX, 22.

**BLESAN** (Old Norse *blasa*, Old High German *blasan*, Anglo-Saxon *blaesan*, English *blow*, Swedish *blåsa*, Danish *blaese*, Modern High German *blasen*, Latin *flare*; Gf. III, 236), conjugation I: *baiblos, blesans*; to blow.

**UF-BLESAN**, to puff up, φυσιοῦν: Cor. I, XIII, 4; Col. II, 18; *ufblesans visan*, “to be puffed up,” φυσιοῦσθαι: Cor. I, IV, 6.

**BLIGGVAN** (Old High German *bliuwan*, Swedish *plagg*, Dutch *blouwen*, Modern High German *bläuen*; Greek πληγή, Latin *plaga, fligere, flagellum*; DRA. 703; Gf. III, 257), conjugation I: *blaggv, bluggvun, bluggvans*; to strike, κατακόπτειν: Mc. V, 5; to scourge, μαστιγοῦν: Mc. X, 34; to beat, δέρειν: Luc. XX, 11; Cor. I, IX, 26. *Attans bliggvands, aiþeins bliggvands*: patricide, matricide, πατραλῴης, μητραλῴης: Tim. I, I, 9.

**US-BLIGGVAN**, the same: to scourge, μαστιγοῦν: Luc. XVIII, 33; Joan. XIX, 1; to beat, δέρειν: Mc. XII, 3; Luc. XX, 10; to flog, φραγελλοῦν: Mc. XV, 15. *Usbliggvan vandum*, “to flog with rods,” ῥαβδίζειν: Cor. II, XI, 25.

**BLINDS** (Old Norse *blindr*; Old Saxon, Anglo-Saxon, [Col. 1278] Old Frisian, English, Danish, Dutch, Swedish, Modern High German *blind*; Old High German *blint*; Gr. II, 59; Gf. III, 255; Rchth. 654), adjective: blind, τυφλός: Mth. IX, 27, 28; XI, 5; Mc. VIII, 22, 23; X, 46, 49, 51; Luc. IV, 18; VI, 39; VII, 21, 22; XIV, 13, 21; XVIII, 35; Joan. IX, 1, 2, 6, 13, 17, 18, 19, 20, 24, 25, 32, 39, 40, 41; X, 21; XI, 37.

**GA-BLINDJAN**, conjugation II: to blind, make blind, τυφλοῦν: Joan. XII, 40; Cor. II, IV, 4.

**GA-BLINDNAN**, conjugation III: to be blinded, πωροῦσθαι: Cor. II, III, 14, at this passage.

**BLOþ** (Old Norse *bloð*; Old Saxon, Anglo-Saxon, Old Frisian, Swedish and Danish *blod*; Old High German *blot*; English *blood*; Dutch *bloed*; Modern High German *Blut*; Gr. III, 398; Gf. III, 252; Rchth. 654), neuter: blood, αἷμα: Mth. XXVII, 4, 6, 8; Mc. V, 25, 29; Luc. VIII, 43, 44; Joan. VI, 53, 54, 55, 56; Cor. I, X, 16; XI, 25, 27; XV, 50; Eph. I, 7; II, 13; VI, 12; Col. I, 20.

**BLOþA-RINNAN**, see under **Rinnan**.

**BLOþAN**, see **Blotan**.

**BLOMA** (Old Norse *blomi*, Old Saxon *blomo*, Anglo-Saxon *blosma*, Old High German *blomo*, English *bloom*, Swedish and Danish *blomster*, Modern High German *Blume*; compare Greek φλόος, Latin *flos*; Gr. III, 375; Gf. III, 241), masculine: flower, lily, κρίνον: Mth. VI, 28.

**BLOTAN** (*bloþan*, Cor. II, VIII, 4, at this passage; Tim. I, II, 10) (Old Norse *blota*, Old High German *blozan*, Anglo-Saxon *blotan*, Swedish *blot*; DM. 22; Gf. III, 259), conjugation II: to offer sacrifice, worship; λατρεύειν (“render cultic service”): Luc. II, 37; σέβεσθαι (“venerate”): Mc. VII, 7. *Guþ blotan* (a substantive infinitive): divine worship—properly, worshipping God—θεοσέβεια: Tim. I, II, 10.

**BLOTINASSUS**, masculine: divine worship, adoration; λατρεία: Rom. XII, 1; θρησκεία (“religious worship”): Col. II, 18; σέβασμα (“object of worship”): Thess. II, II, 4.

**US-BLOTEINS**, feminine: entreaty, prayer, παράκλησις: Cor. II, VIII, 4, at this passage.

**GUþ-BLOSTREIS**, masculine: pious, worshipper of God, θεοσεβής: Joan. IX, 31.

**BNAUAN** (Gf. IV, 1125), conjugation II (?): to pluck, ψώχειν: Luc. VI, 1.

**BUGJAN** (Old Saxon *buggean*, Anglo-Saxon *bycgan*, English *buy*; Gr. II, 23; DRA. 606), anomalous conjugation, preterite *bauhta*, participle *bauhts*:

1. To buy, ἀγοράζειν: Mc. XI, 15; Luc. IX, 13; XIV, 18; XVII, 28; XIX, 45; Joan. VI, 5; XIII, 29; εὑρίσκειν (“procure”): Luc. IX, 12.

2. To sell, πωλεῖν: Mth. X, 29.

**US-BUGJAN**, to buy, ἐξαγοράζειν: Gal. IV, 5; Col. IV, 5; ἀγοράζειν: Mth. XXVII, 7; Mc. XV, 46; XVI, 1; Luc. XIV, 19; Cor. I, VII, 23.

**FRA-BUGJAN**, with accusative or dative: to sell, πωλεῖν: Mc. X, 21; XI, 15; Luc. XVII, 28; XVIII, 22; XIX, 45; Cor. I, X, 25; πιπράσκειν: Mc. XIV, 5; Joan. XII, 5; Rom. XII, 14.

**ANDA-BAUHTS**, feminine: ransom, redemption, ἀντίλυτρον: Tim. I, II, 6, at this passage.

**FAUR-BAUHTS**, redemption, ἀπολύτρωσις: Eph. I, 7, 14; Col. I, 14.

**BUNDNAN**, see under **Bindan**.

**BUSNS**, see under **Biudan**.

**BRAIDS** (Old Norse *breidr*; Old Saxon, Old Frisian *bred*; Anglo-Saxon *brad*; Old High German *breit*; English *broad*; Swedish and Danish *bred*; Dutch *breed*; Modern High German *breit*; Gr. II, 15; Gf. III, 294; Rchth. 665), adjective: broad, πλατύς: Mth. VII, 13.

**BRAIDEI**, feminine: breadth, πλάτος: Eph. III, 18.

**US-BRAIDJAN**, conjugation II: to spread out, ἐκπετάζειν: Rom. X, 21.

**BRAKJA**, see under **Brikan**.

**BRANNJAN**, see under **Brinnan**.

**BRAW** (Old Norse *bra, brun*; Old Saxon *braha*; Anglo-Saxon *braev*; Old High German *brawa*; Old Frisian *bre*; English *brow*; Modern High German *Braue*; Greek ὀφρύς; Bopp 80; Gr. III, 402; Gf. III, 315; Rchth. 665; Schm. I, 242), neuter: eyebrow; *braw augins*, “a blink of an eye,” ῥιπή ὀφθαλμοῦ: Cor. I, XV, 52.

**BRIGGAN** (*bringan*, Luc. XV, 22) (Anglo-Saxon and Old High German *bringan*, Old Saxon *brengian*, Old Frisian *branga, brenga*, English *bring*, Swedish *bringa*, Danish *bringe*, Dutch *brengen*, Modern High German *bringen*; Gf. III, 192; Rchth. 664), anomalous conjugation, preterite *brahta*:

1. To lead, bring, carry; ἄγειν: Mc. XI, 7; Luc. IV, 29, 40; XIX, 27; Joan. X, 16; Tim. II, IV, 11; ἀνάγειν (“lead up”): Luc. II, 22; Skeir. II, a; συνάγειν (“bring together”): Luc. III, 17, for which *samana briggan* also occurs, Luc. XV, 13; ἀπάγειν (“lead away”): Mth. VII, 13, 14; φέρειν (“bring, carry”): Mc. VI, 27; IX, 17, 20; Luc. XV, 23; εἰσφέρειν (“bring into”): Mth. VI, 13; Tim. I, VI, 7; ἐκφέρειν (“bring out”): Luc. XV, 22; ἀποφέρειν (“carry away”): Mc. XV, 1; Luc. XVI, 22; Cor. I, XVI, 3; κομίζειν (“bring”): Luc. VII, 37; ὁδηγεῖν (“lead, guide”): Joan. XVI, 13.

2. With *skip* understood, to steer a ship, ἐπανάγειν: Luc. V, 4.

3. To render, especially in translating Greek verbs ending in *-όω*: *briggan frijana*, “make free,” ἐλευθεροῦν: Joan. VIII, 32, 36; Rom. VIII, 2; Gal. V, 1; *briggan vairþana*, “make fit/sufficient,” ἱκανοῦν: Cor. II, III, 6; “deem worthy,” ἀξιοῦν: Thess. II, I, 11; “count worthy,” καταξιοῦν: Thess. II, I, 5; *briggan haubiþ vundan*, “sum up under a head,” κεφαλαιοῦν: Mc. XII, 4; *briggan gamainana*, “share in fellowship,” συγκοινωνεῖν: Phlpp. IV, 14; *briggan ïn aljana*, “bring into jealousy,” that is, provoke to jealousy, παραζηλοῦν: Rom. X, 19; XI, 11, 14; *briggan ïn þvairhein*, “bring into anger,” make angry, παροργίζειν: Rom. X, 19. *Briggan ïn arbaidai* occurs at Cor. II, XI, 20, is unintelligible, and stands for ἐπαίρεσθαι; see the note at that passage.

**BRIKAN** (Old Norse and Swedish *braka*; Old Saxon and Anglo-Saxon *brecan*; Old High German *brechan*; Old Frisian *breka*; English *break*; Danish *brække*; Dutch *breken*; Modern High German *brechen*; Greek ῥῆξαι; Latin *frango, fregi*; Bopp 80; Gr. II, 26; III, 462; Gf. III, 262; Rchth. 667), conjugation I: *brak, brekun, brukans*.

1. To break, κλᾶν: Cor. I, X, 16.

2. To destroy, annihilate, make void, πορθεῖν: Gal. I, 23.

3. To contend, fight, ἀθλεῖν: Tim. II, II, 5.

**GA-BRIKAN**, to break, κλᾷν: Mc. VIII, 6, 19; Cor. I, XI, 24; κατακλᾷν (“break in pieces”): Luc. IX, 16; συντρίβειν (“shatter”): Mc. V, 4; Luc. IX, 39; ῥήγνυναι (“break, burst”): Luc. IX, 42.

**UF-BRIKAN**, not to heed, reject, ἀθετεῖν, with dative: Mc. VI, 26; Luc. X, 16; Thess. I, IV, 8. Participle *ufbrikands*: insolent, ὑβριστής: Tim. I, I, 13.

**UNUF-BRIKANDS**, participle: without causing offence, blameless, ἀπρόσκοπος: Cor. I, X, 32.

**BRAKJA** (compare Old High German *widarpruht*, “opposition”):

1. Resistance, opposition.

2. Wrestling, πάλη: Eph. VI, 12.

**GA-BRUKA**, feminine: fight, breaking, fragment, κλάσμα: Mth. VIII, 8; XIX, 20; Luc. IX, 17; Joan. VI, 13.

**US-BRUKNAN**, conjugation III: to be broken off, ἐκκλᾶσθαι: Rom. XI, 17, 19, 20.

**BRINGAN**, the same as **Briggan**.

**BRINNAN** (Old Norse and Swedish *brenna*; Old Saxon *brinnan, brennian*; Anglo-Saxon *byrnan*; Old High German *brinnan*; Old Frisian *barna, berna*; English *burn*; Danish *brænde*; Modern High German *brennen*; Gr. II, 34; Gf. III, 305; Rchth. 619), conjugation I: *brann, brunnun, brunnans*; to burn, καίεσθαι: Joan. V, 35.

**UF-BRINNAN**:

1. To blaze up, intransitive.

2. To be scorched, καυματίζεσθαι: Mc. IV, 6.

**BRINNO**, feminine: fever, πυρετός: Mc. I, 31; Luc. IV, 38, 39. *Ligan ïn brinnon*: to lie sick with fever, to be feverish, κατακεῖσθαι πυρέσσοντα: Mc. I, 30.

**GA-BRANNJAN**, conjugation II: to burn up, transitive, καίειν: Cor. I, XIII, 3; Skeir. III, c; Gothic Calendar.

**ÏN-BRANNJAN**, the same: Joan. XV, 6, at this passage.

**BRUNSTS**, feminine: burning, fiery heat.

**ALL-BRUNSTS**, whole burnt offering, ὁλοκαύτωμα: Mc. XII, 33.

**BRUþS** (Old Norse *brudr*, Old Saxon *brud*, Anglo-Saxon *bryd*, Old High German *brut*, Old Frisian *breid*, English *bride*, Swedish and Danish *brud*, Dutch *bruid*, Modern High German *Braut*; Gr. III, 322; Gf. III, 293; Rchth. 667), feminine:

1. Bride.

2. Daughter-in-law; νύμφη: Mth. X, 35.

**BRUþ-FAþS**, see under **Faþs**.

**BRUKA**, see under **Brikan**.

**HRUKS** (Old Norse and Swedish, Old Frisian *bruka*; Old Saxon and Anglo-Saxon *brucan*; Old High German *bruhan*; Danish *brug*; [Col. 1280] Dutch *bruiken*; Modern High German *Brauch*; Bopp 80, 84; Gf. III, 279; Rchth. 672), adjective: useful, advantageous, ὠφέλιμος: Tim. I, IV, 8; εὔχρηστος (“serviceable”): Tim. II, II, 21; IV, 11; Philem. 11. *Bruks visan*, “to be useful,” συμφέρειν: Cor. I, X, 33; Skeir. IV, b.

**UN-BRUKS**, useless, unprofitable, ἀχρεῖος: Luc. XVII, 10; *unbruks vairþan*, “become useless,” ἀχρειοῦσθαι: Psalm. LIII, 3.

**BRUKJAN**, anomalous conjugation, preterite *bruhta*: to use, χρῆσθαι: Cor. I, VII, 21; Cor. II, I, 17; III, 12; Tim. I, I, 8; V, 23; Skeir. III, b; V, a, b; ἀποχρῆσθαι (“use up”): Col. II, 22; μετέχειν (“partake”): Cor. I, X, 17, 30, at this passage.

**BRUNNA** (Old Norse *brunnr*; Old High German, Old Saxon *brunno*; Anglo-Saxon *burne*; Old Frisian *burna*; Swedish *brun*; Danish *brond*; Dutch *born*; Modern High German *Born, Brunnen*; Gr. III, 387; Gf. III, 310; Rchth. 676), masculine: well, spring, πηγή: Mc. V, 29.

**BRUNJO** (Old Norse *brynia*, Anglo-Saxon *byrn*, Old Saxon *brunjo*, Old High German *brunja*, Swedish *brynia*, Danish *brynie*; Gr. II, 34, 451, 487; III, 446; Gf. III, 312), feminine: breastplate, θώραξ: Eph. VI, 14; Thess. I, V, 8.

**BRUNSTS**, see under **Brinnan**.

**BRUSTS** (Old Norse *brysti, briost*; Old Saxon and Anglo-Saxon *breost*; Old High German, Old Frisian, and Modern High German *brast*; English *breast*; Swedish *bröst*; Danish *bryst*; Dutch *borst*; Gr. II, 450; III, 406; Gf. III, 275; Rchth. 672), feminine, anomalous, plural only:

1. Breast, chest, στῆθος: Luc. XVIII, 13.

2. Heart, inward parts, figuratively, σπλάγχνα: Cor. II, VII, 15; Col. III, 12; Philem. 12, 20.

**BROþAR** (Old Norse *brodir*, Old Saxon *brothar*, Anglo-Saxon *broðor*, Old High German *brodar*, Old Frisian; English *brother*; Swedish and Danish *broðer*; Dutch *broeder*; Modern High German *Bruder*; compare Greek φρατρία, Latin *frater*; Bopp 80, 84; Gr. III, 321; Gf. III, 300; Rchth. 671), anomalous masculine: brother, ἀδελφός: Mth. V, 22, 23, 24; VI, 3; XXV, 40; Mc. I, 16; III, 17, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35; V, 37; VI, 17; X, 29, 30; XII, 19; Luc. [Col. 1281] G
[Col. 1281] **GA** (Old Saxon *gi...*, *ge...*; Anglo-Saxon *ge...*; Old Frisian *ie...*, *ge...*, *gi...*; Old High German *ga...*, *ka...*, etc.; Gr. II, 733 ff., 832 ff.; III, 255; Gf. IV, 10, 1018; Rchth. 838), an inseparable particle, compounded with nouns, adjectives, and adverbs, but especially with verbs. There it partly serves to modify the form of the verb (in particular the passive form, or even the active when used passively, such as the infinitive; likewise the participial form when employed for the future; and finally the preterite and passive participle forms), and partly determines the meaning more precisely. In the latter case it usually corresponds to the Greek prepositions σύν, “with,” κατά, “down/according to,” διά, “through,” and sometimes also ἀνά, “up,” ἐν, “in,” ἀπό, “from,” ὑπό, “under,” etc.; it sometimes conveys the sense of acting or existing together, sometimes that of loss or acquisition (German *ver-*, *er-*), and finally sometimes brings out the verbal meaning more strongly.

Now, for very many verbs compounded with *ga*, the simple forms are no longer found; for others, however, simple forms still occur. In the latter class it frequently happens that the compound has the same meaning as the simple verb; hence the same may be inferred even concerning simple verbs no longer found. Other compounds correspond very closely to Greek verbs compounded with prepositions.

1) Compounds of this particle with verbs:

a) whose simple forms are no longer found: *gaaggvjan, gabatnan, gabeistjan, gablindjan, gablindnan, gageigan, gadaban, gadaubjan, gadaursan, gadiupjan, gadraban, gaqiujan, gaqiunan, gahailnan, gahaftnan, gahardjan, gaþarban, gaþarbjan, gaþairsan, gaþaursnan, gaþlaihan, gaþlahsnan, gaþvastjan, gaïbnjan, gakaran, gasvikunþjan, gakroton, gaunledjan, galeikon, gamainjan, gamaurgjan, gamotan, gamotjan, ganagljan, ganohjan, ganohnan, ganaitjan, ganavistron, ganipnan, ganisan, gapaidon, garaþan, garaihtjan, gasoþjan, gasibjon, gaskaidnan, gaskapjan, gaskeirjan, gasleiþjan, gasmiþon, gasuljan, gasuqon, gastagqjan, gastoþan (an), gastaurknan, gatarhjan, gateihan, gatevjan, gatiman, gatamjan, gavaknan, gavargjan, gavigan, gavadjon, gaveison, gavundon, gavrisqan, gafahrjan, gafriþon, gafrisahtjan*;

b) whose simple forms are likewise no longer found, but which occur compounded with other prepositions: *gaainan (an), gabrannjan, gadrobnan, gadrausjan, gahamon, gaþivan, galeiþan, galukan, galuknan, ganahan, gananþjan, garedan, gasmeitan, gastaldan, gasvogjan, gatairan, gataurnan, gatilon, gavidan, gafaihon*;

c) whose simple forms still occur: *gaaistan, gaaiviskon, gaaukan, gaarman, gabaidjan, gabairan, gabairgan, gabairhtjan, gabandvjan, gabauan, gabotan, gabeidan, gabindan, gabiugan, gablauþjan, gableiþjan, gabrikan, gagaggan, gadailjan, gadauþjan, gadauþnan, gadragan, gadrigkan, gadragkjan, gadriusan, gadomjan, gaqiþan, gaqiman, gahaban, gahailjan, gahaitan, gahaunjan, gahausjan, gahilpan, gahnaivjan, gahuljan, gahrainjan, gahorinon, gaþahan, gaþeihan, gaþiuþjan, gaþliuhan, gaþreihan, gaþulan, gaþrafstjan, gaïdreigon, gakiusan, gakausjan, gakunnan, gakannjan, galaþon, galaisjan, galaistjan, galaubjan, galatjan, galeikinon, galeikan, galevjan, galagjan, galaugnjan, galiuhtjan, galausjan, galiugan, galisan, gamagan, gamanvjan, gamaudjan, gamarzjan, gamatjan, gameljan, gamikiljan, gamitan, gamunan, ganamnjan, ganiman, ganiutan, ganasjan, gajiukan, garahnjan, garaginon, garaidjan, garinnan, gasaiwan, gasakan, gasokjan, gasalbon, gasaljan, gasandjan, gasigqan, gasigljan, gasitan, gasatjan, gaskaþjan, gaskaidan, gaskaman, gaslavan, gaslepan, gasnivan, gasniumjan, gasunjon, gasupon, gaspeivan, gaspillon, gastandan, gasteigan, gastojan, gastigqan, gasveran*;
