**DIUS** (Old Norse and Danish *dyr*, Old Saxon *dier*, Anglo-Saxon *deor*, Old High German *tior*, Old French *diar*, Swedish *djur*, English *deer*, Dutch *dier*, Modern High German *Thier*; Greek θήρ; Gr. III, 359; Gf. V, 447; Rchth. 686), neuter: beast, θηρίον: Mc. I, 13; see the note on this passage; Cor. I, XV, 32.

**DIS** (Greek δια-, Latin *dis-*; Gr. II, 723, 861; Gf. V

[Col. 1297] 696), inseparable particle, which 1) sometimes chiefly intensifies the meaning of verbs of separating and dividing, for example: *disdailjan, dishniupan, dishnaupnan, disskaidan, disskreitan, disskritnan, distahjan, distaheins, distairan, distaurnan, disvilvan, disvinþjan, disviss*. Here *dis* generally corresponds to Greek verbs compounded with δια-, such as διαμερίζειν, διαιρεῖν, διαρρηγνύναι, διασκορπίζειν, etc., although Greek simple verbs sometimes bear the sense of compounds, while compounds are sometimes used in place of simple verbs; 2) sometimes adds to verbs the notion of encompassing or enclosing, as in *disdriusan* (ἐπιπίπτειν, “to fall upon”), *dissiggqan* (ἐπιδύειν, “to set”), *dishaban* (συνέχειν, περιέχειν, “to hold together, encompass”), *dishuljan* (καλύπτειν, “to cover”), *dissitan* (λαμβάνειν, ἔχειν, “to receive, have”), *disniman* (κατέχειν, “to hold fast”).

**DIVAN** (Old Norse *deyfa*, Old Saxon *dojan*, Old High German *towjan*, Swedish *döia*; Gf. V, 339; compare **Dauþs**), conjugation I, *dau, divun, divans*: to be feeble, weakened, dead; participle *divans*: mortal, θνητός: Cor. I, XV, 53; Cor. II, V, 4; φθαρτός, “perishable”: Cor. I, XV, 54.

**UN-DIVANS**: immortal, imperishable, ἄφθαρτος or ἀθάνατος: Tim. I, I, 17; see this passage.

**UN-DIVANEI**, feminine: immortality, ἀθανασία: Cor. I, XV, 53, 54; Tim. I, VI, 16.

**AF-DAUJAN** (Gr. I, 479 [3rd edition], according to the reading ἐσκυλμένοι, which one can scarcely believe the Gothic translator had, wrongly treats as certain the sense “to flay, to torment”), conjugation II: to weary, ἐκλύειν: Mth. IX, 36. Thus also Gal. VI, 9 should read *af dauïdai* instead of *afmaïndai* [see that passage].

**DU** (Old Saxon and Old French *to, te, ti*, Anglo-Saxon *to*, Old High German *zi, zuo*, English *to*, Dutch *toe, te*, Modern High German *zu*; Gr. III, 254; Gf. V, 572; Al, *h. Präp.* 241 ff.; Rchth. 1087), a preposition construed with the dative, but rarely with the accusative; it corresponds also to Greek πρός (with the accusative) and εἰς, and to Latin *ad, in*, and especially signifies movement toward, direction into.

I. With the dative:

1) Locally:

a) After verbs of coming and going: “to,” “into,” πρός, εἰς, and rarely ἐπί. Thus after *gaggan*: Mc. I, 38, 45; II, 11, 13; V, 19; X, 14, 32; XI, 15, 27; Luc. VI, 47; IX, 53; XIV, 26; XV, 18; XVIII, 16; Joan. III, 26; VI, 5, 35, 37, 45; VII, 33, 37; XI, 15, 29, 32, 38; XIV, 12, 28; XVI, 5, 10, 16, 28; XVII, 11, 13; Tim. II, II, 16; *atgaggan*: Mth. XXV, 39; XXVII, 28; Mc. V, 15; VI, 25; XII, 18; XIV, 45; XVI, 2; Luc. VIII, 19; IX, 12; XVIII, 3, 14; Joan. VI, 17; VII, 50; XII, 21; XVIII, 29; *gagaggan*: Mc. VI, 30; Luc. VIII, 4; *usgaggan*: Mc. I, 5; *gaqiman* and *gaqiman sik*: Mth. XXVII, 62; Mc. V, 21; VII, 1; X, 1; *galeiþan*: Mc. III, 13; VII, 30; XIV, 10; Luc. I, 23; Joan. VI, 68; VII, 45; XI, 46; XIV, 23; Cor. II, VIII, 17; IX, 5; Tim. II, IV, 10; *galeïþan ïnn*: Mc. XV, 43; Luc. I, 28; *galeiþan ut*: Joan. XVIII, 38; *afleiþan*: Mc. III, 7; *rinnan*: Cor. I, IX, 26; *garinnan*: Eph. IV, 13; *urrinnan*: Mc. XIV, 48. Compare also *fairrinnan du þaurftai* for Greek ἀνήκειν, “to be fitting”: Eph. V, 4; *gasnivan*: Phlpp. III, 16; *faurbisnivan*: Tim. I, V, 24; *gaþeihan*: Tim. II, III, 9; *vahsjan*: Eph. II, 21; Col. II, 19; *gavandjan sik*: Luc. I, 56; VII, 10, 44; VIII, 39; X, 6; *usvandjan (sik)*: Tim. I, I, 6; *galisan sik*: Mc. IV, 1; *athaban sik*: Mc. X, 35; after substantives: *vigs*: Thess. I, III, 11; *atgaggs*: Eph. II, 18; *qums*: Phlpp. I, 26; *gakumþs*: Thess. II, II, 1; also after *driusan*: Mc. III, 11; V, 33; Luc. VIII, 28, 4; and especially in the formulas *driusan du knivam*, “to fall to the knees,” Luc. V, 8, and *du fotum*, “at the feet,” Mc. V, 22; VII, 25; Joan. XI, 32; and after *bistiggqan*: Rom. IX, 32.

b) After transitive verbs conveying the idea of bearing, bringing, leading, drawing, and the like: after *gavandjan*: Luc. I, 16, 17; Cor. II, III, 16; Gal. IV, 9; Tim. II, IV, 4; *Skeir.* I, c. The participle of this verb must also be supplied in Cor. II, VII, 15 after *brusts ïs ufarassau du ïzvis sind*, “his heart is more abundantly inclined toward you”; *briggan*: Mc. IX, 17; *bairan*: Mth. V, 23; Mc. I, 32; VII, 32; VIII, 22; IX, 18; Luc. XVIII, 15; *atbairan*: Mth. VIII, 16; IX, 2; Mc. X, 13; *tiuhan*: Luc. XVIII, 40; Tim. II, III, 6; *Skeir.* IV, b. With this verb also understood, *Skeir.* I, c, *so du guþa (sc. tiuhandei) gareihtei*, “thus toward divine righteousness,” is to be explained.

[Col. 1298] *Gatiuhan*: Mc. XIV, 53; Joan. IX, 13; XVIII, 13. Accordingly, κατάκρίνειν in Mth. XXVII, 3 is not rendered word for word, but in the narrative is fittingly translated by *gatiuhan du stauai*, “to bring to judgment.” Conversely, Cor. II, X, 12, συγκρίνειν ἑαυτόν τινι, “to compare oneself with someone,” is correctly rendered by *gadomjan sik du ainamma*. *Atþinsan*: Joan. XII, 32; *atwairpan*: Luc. XVI, 20; *atvalvjan*: Mc. XV, 46; *laþon*: Gal. V, 13; Col. I, 12; Thess. I, II, 12; IV, 7 (for here *du* must be read in place of *ïn*); Tim. I, VI, 12; *vopjan*: Luc. XIX, 15; *franiman*: Joan. XIV, 3; *ïnsandjan*: Mth. XXVII, 19; Mc. III, 31; VIII, 26; XII, 2, 4, 6, 13; Luc. I, 27; IV, 26; VII, 3, 6, 19, 20; XX, 10; Joan. XI, 3; XVI, 7; XVIII, 24; Cor. II, XII, 17; Eph. VI, 22; Phlpp. II, 25; Col. IV, 8; Neh. VI, 17; *fraletan*: Mc. VIII, 3; *atlagjan*: Luc. XIX, 23.

c) Verbs denoting direction toward have this particle in the sense “toward,” “to,” “into,” regularly corresponding to Greek πρός, ἐπί: *usbraidjan handuns du managein*, “to stretch out hands toward the people” (πρός), Rom. X, 21; *du þaim faura sik ufþanjan*, “stretching forward toward those things before oneself” (τοῖς ἔμπροσθεν ἐπεκτείνεσθαι), Phlpp. III, 14; *du diuzam veihan*, “to fight with beasts” (θηριομαχεῖν), Cor. I, XV, 32; also after *gagavairþjan* (καταλλάττεσθαί τινι, “to be reconciled to someone”): Cor. I, VII, 11; *ussaiwan du himina*, “to look into heaven” (εἰς): Mc. VII, 34; *augona ushafjan du himina*, “to lift the eyes to heaven” (εἰς): Luc. XVIII, 13; Joan. XVII, 1; *atsaiwan du sis*, “to give heed to oneself” (ἐπέχειν ἑαυτῷ): Tim. I, IV, 16; after *fairveitjan* (εἰς), “to gaze”: Luc. IV, 20; Cor. II, III, 7; especially after *ïnsaiwan* (εἰς), “to look into”: Mth. VI, 26; Mc. X, 21, 27; XIV, 67; Luc. I, 48; IX, 16, 38; XX, 17; Joan. XIII, 22; further, after *biugan kniva*, “to bend the knee” (πρός): Eph. III, 14; after *bidjan*, “to pray to” (πρός): Mth. VI, 6; Cor. II, XIII, 7; *Skeir.* V, d, and after the noun *bida*, “prayer”: Rom. X, 1; after *hropjan*, “to cry to”: Luc. XVIII, 7; after verbs of fighting, *sokjan* (πρός): Mc. IX, 10; *Skeir.* IV, a; *andrinnan*: Mc. IX, 34; especially after verbs of speaking and saying, *qiþan, rodjan*, where Greek uses the simple dative: Mth. VIII, 7, 9, 10, 19, 20, 21, 22, 26, 32; IX, 2, 6, 9, 11, 12, 15, 18, 24, 28, 37; XI, 3, 4; XXV, 40; XXVI, 71, 75; XXVII, 11, 13, 64; Mc. I, 37, 38, 40, 44; II, 5, 8, 10, 14, 16, 17, 18, 24, 25; III, 3, 4, 5, 23, 32; IV, 13, 21, 24, 33, 35, 38, 39, 40, 41; V, 9, 19, 31, 34, 36, 39, 41; VI, 10, 18, 22, 24; VII, 6, 9, 18, 27, 28, 29, 33; VIII, 1, 17, 19, 21, 27, 29, 34; IX, 1, 5, 12, 23, 25, 29, 31, 35, 36; X, 5, 11, 14, 18, 20, 21, 26, 28, 37, 38, 39, 42, 49, 51, 52; XI, 1, 5, 6, 14, 17, 21, 22, 23, 28, 29, 33; XII, 7, 12, 14, 15, 16, 17, 24, 32, 34, 36, 38; XIV, 12, 13, 48, 61, 65, 70; XV, 2, 12, 14; XVI, 3, 6, 7; Luc. I, 13, 18, 19, 22, 28, 30, 34, 35, 55, 61; II, 10, 15, 17, 18, 20, 34, 48, 49, 50; III, 7, 12, 13, 14; IV, 3, 6, 9, 21, 23, 36, 43; V, 4, 5, 10, 20, 22, 24, 27, 30, 31, 33, 34, 36; VI, 2, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, 20, 42; VII, 6, 8, 9, 13, 14, 22, 24, 40, 43, 44, 48, 50; VIII, 21, 22, 25, 48, 49; IX, 3, 11, 12, 13, 14, 20, 23, 33, 44, 48, 50, 55, 57, 58, 59, 60, 62; X, 2, 9, 18, 22, 26, 28, 29; XIV, 10, 15, 21, 22, 25; XV, 3, 6, 12, 18, 22, 27, 29, 31; XVI, 1, 2, 6, 7, 14; XVII, 5, 7, 8, 14, 19, 22, 37; XVIII, 9, 19, 22, 29, 31, 42; XIX, 5, 8, 9, 13, 17, 19, 22, 24, 25, 31, 32, 33, 39, 40, 46; XX, 1, 3, 9, 19, 23, 25, 34, 41, 42, 45; Joan. VI, 5, 12, 28, 29, 30, 34, 35, 43, 53, 61, 67; VII, 3, 9, 21, 26, 35, 45, 50, 52; VIII, 12, 13, 14, 19, 21, 23, 25, 28, 31, 39, 42, 48, 52, 57; IX, 7, 10, 12, 17, 24, 29, 30, 34, 35, 40; X, 6, 7, 24; XI, 7, 8, 11, 14, 21, 24, 32, 34, 39, 44, 46; XII, 19, 22, 29, 35; XIII, 12, 27, 33, 37; XIV, 2, 23, 26; XV, 3, 20, 22; XVI, 7; XVIII, 11, 17, 21, 25, 30, 31; IX, 9, 10; Rom. IX, 15, 17, 20; X, 21; Cor. I, XII, 21; Gal. II, 14; Thess. I, II, 16.

Hence after the expressions *munþ usluknan*, “the mouth is opened,” Cor. II, VI, 11, and *vaurd varþ*, “a word came,” Joan. X, 35. In Cor. II, I, 18, *vaurd unsar þata du ïzvis*, “our word, this toward you,” and VII, 14, *woftuli unsara so du teitau*, “our boasting toward Titus” (in the latter place, “before Titus,” for ἐπί with genitive), a verb of speaking must be supplied. In the same elliptical manner it occurs in the inscription of Ephesians, *aipistaule du aifaisium*, “epistle to the Ephesians,” and in the subscription, *du aifaisium ustauh*, “written to the Ephesians,” and similarly in all the preserved inscriptions and subscriptions of the epistles.

2) In a temporal sense:

a) Generally, it indicates the time at which something occurs, approximately: Cor. I, XV,

[Col. 1299] 32, *du maurgina gasviltam*, “tomorrow we shall die” (αὔριον); Luc. XVII, 8, *du naht matjan*, “to eat at night,” i.e. to dine (δειπνεῖν).

b) More commonly it has the same force as “in,” “throughout,” εἰς, πρός, ἐπί with accusative, answering the question “for how long?” Thus Luc. IV, 25, *galuknoda himins du jeram þrim*, “the heaven was shut for three years”; Joan. VI, 27, *visan du libainai aiveinon*, “to endure unto eternal life”; and in the formulas *du aiva*, “for ever”: Joan. XII, 34; XIV, 16; XV, 16; Cor. II, IX, 9; *du aivam*, “for ever”: Rom. XI, 36; Cor. II, XI, 31; Gal. I, 5; *du weilai*, “for a while”: Joan. V, 35; Philem. 15; *du leitilai weilai*, “for a little while”: Cor. II, VII, 8; *Skeir.* VI, a; *du mela*, “for a time”: Luc. VIII, 13; *du leitilamma mela*, “for a short time”: *Skeir.* IV, b; *du mela weilos*, “for a period of time”: Thess. I, II, 17.

3) Metaphorically it is used wherever a verb fundamentally signifies some movement or direction toward or into. Thus:

a) Where purpose, end, determination, or result is expressed; in this case *du* corresponds to Greek εἰς, πρός, and ἐπί with accusative, and to Latin *in, ad*: Mth. VIII, 4; XXVII, 7; Mc. I, 4, 44; VI, 11; XIV, 8, 9; Luc. II, 32, 34; III, 3; V, 14; IX, 5; XIV, 31, see the note on this passage, 35; XVIII, 1; Joan. IX, 39; XI, 4; XIII, 29; XVII, 23; XVIII, 37; Rom. VII, 10; IX, 22, 23; X, 1, 4, 10; XIV, 1; XV, 4, 7; Cor. I, V, 5; X, 31; XI, 24, 25; XII, 13; XIV, 26; XV, 34; XVI, 15; Cor. II, I, 20; II, 16; IV, 6, 15; V, 5; VII, 3, 9, 10; VIII, 2, 14, 19; IX, 4; X, 4, 8, 15; XI, 8; XIII, 10; Gal. I, 6; II, 8; Eph. I, 5, 6, 10, 14; II, 10, 22; III, 19; IV, 12, 13, 14, 16, 29; V, 2; VI, 18; Phlpp. I, 17, 19, 25; Col. I, 29; II, 22, 23; III, 10, 21; Thess. I, III, 3; V, 9; Thess. II, I, 11; Tim. I, I, 16; IV, 3, 7, 8; Tim. II, II, 14, 20, 21, 25; III, 13, 15, 16, 17; IV, 11 (IV, 3 for Greek κατά); Neh. V, 16; *Skeir.* I, d; II, d; VIII, b, d. Here must also be counted *þata wa ïst du sva managaim* (εἰς), “what is this for so many?” Joan. VI, 9, which occurs only once elsewhere.

Also belonging here are *duþe* (*duþþe*), “to that [end], moreover,” and *duwe*, “to which”; see under **þata** and **Was**.

b) In predicative determinations, where it means “as” or “for,” and partly corresponds to Greek εἰς, partly, in the manner of Germanic languages, expresses the case of an attribute. Thus after *visan*, “to be”: Mc. X, 8; Cor. I, XIV, 22; Col. IV, 11. Hence the Gothic translator also renders ὠφελεῖν, “to profit,” by *du botai visan*, “to be for benefit,” Gal. V, 2; and ἀπόβλητός ἐστι, “it is to be rejected,” by *du usvaurpai ïst*, “it is for rejection,” Tim. I, IV, 4; after *vairþan*, “to become”: Mc. XII, 10; Luc. III, 5; XX, 17; Joan. XVI, 20; Cor. II, VI, 18; *nimam du qenai*, “I take as wife”: Neh. VI, 18; *aigan du qenai*, “to have as wife”: Mc. XII, 23; Luc. XX, 33; *haban du gamana*, “to have as a partner”: Philem. 17. Hence κερδεῖν, “to gain,” is rendered by *du gavaurkja haban*, “to have as gain,” Phlpp. III, 8; after *taujan*: Joan. VI, 15; X, 33; Rom. IX, 21; Gal. V, 13; *gataujan*: Mc. XI, 17; Luc. XIX, 46; Eph. II, 14; *gaskapjan*: Eph. II, 15; *gagaleikon*: Cor. II, XI, 13; *ïnmaidjan*: Phlpp. III, 21; *du ludjai gafrisahtnan*, “to be formed into likeness” (μορφοῦσθαι): Gal. IV, 19; see the note on this passage; *rahnjan*: Rom. IX, 8; *giban*: Thess. II, III, 9; *atgiban*: Joan. XIII, 15; *lagjan (du plata fanan)*, “to lay [for the spreading out of a banner]”: Mth. IX, 18.

But the fundamental idea becomes much more apparent in the following cases, which are nearly referable to I.c:

c) “Toward,” πρός, after *vrohjan*, “to accuse,” Joan. V, 45, and *fravrohjan*, “to accuse,” Luc. XVI, 1; *þagkjan du sis misso*, “to dispute among themselves,” Mc. XI, 31; likewise Cor. II, III, 1, *anafilhis boko du ïsvis þaurbum*, “do we need letters of recommendation to you?”—although “a letter to you [namely, written]” might be understood; compare above, 1.c, at the end; Cor. II, IV, 2, *ustaiknjan sik silban du allaim miþvisseim*, “to commend oneself to every conscience”; similarly *ustaikneins*, “commendation”: Luc. I, 80.

d) “With respect to,” “concerning,” ἐπί with dative and accusative, εἰς: Mc. X, 11, *horinoþ du þizai*, “he commits adultery against her” (which may also be explained according to f or g); Joan. XII, 16, *þata vas du þamma gameliþ*, “this had been written concerning him”; likewise Cor. II, IX, 1, *andbahti rahtoda du veihaim*, “I have written concerning the ministry for the saints”; X, 16, *ïn framaþjaim arbaidim du manvjaim wopan*, “to boast in another’s labors concerning things made ready”; XI, 6, *gabairhtida ïn allaim du ïsvis*, “made manifest in all things toward you.”

e) “In relation to,” “in comparison with,” “before,” πρός with accusative, in the expressions *gaggan gafehaba du þaim þaiei uta sind*, “to conduct oneself becomingly toward those outside,” Thess. I, IV, 12; *gaggan ïn handugein du þaim uta*, “to walk in wisdom toward those outside,” Col. IV, 5; *raihtaba gaggan du sunjai*, “to walk uprightly with respect to the truth,” Gal. II, 14.

f) “Against,” εἰς, insofar as the action is directed against the object of the preposition, after *fravaurkjan*, “to sin”: Luc. XVII, 4; Cor. I, VIII, 12; *fiands*, “hostile”: Rom. VIII, 7; *friaþva haban*, “to have love for”: Cor. II, II, 4; compare VII, 15; *gamainduþs*, “obedience”: Cor. II, IX, 13.

g) “Upon,” “in,” ἐπί with dative and accusative, εἰς, πρός, after verbs of emotion and the like: *ïnfeinan*, “to have compassion on”: Mc. VIII, 2; Luc. VII, 13; *svegnjan*, “to rejoice in”: Luc. I, 47; *venjan*, “to hope in”: Joan. V, 45; Rom. XV, 12; Cor. II, I, 10; Tim. I, IV, 10; V, 5; *trauan*, “to trust in”: Mth. XXVII, 43; Cor. II,

[Col. 1300] I, 9; and *trauains*, “trust”: Cor. II, III, 4; VII, 4; *galaubjan*, “to believe in”: Mc. IX, 42; Joan. VI, 35, 40, 47; VII, 38, 39; IX, 35, 36; X, 42; XI, 25, 26; XII, 36, 42, 44, 46; XIV, 1; XVI, 9; XVII, 20; Rom. IX, 33; X, 10, 11; Phlpp. I, 29.

—*) Less correctly, or at least less explicably in view of its regular use, *du* occurs in Mc. VIII, 11 in *sokjandans du ïmma taikn*, “seeking a sign from him” (παρά with genitive).

II. With the accusative: only Col. IV, 10, *du þanei nemuþ anabusnins*, “concerning whom you received instructions” (περί with genitive), and v. 13, *habaiþ manag aljan du þans*, “he has much labor for them” (ὑπέρ with genitive); where it is interchangeable with *bi*.

—* As to Joan. XVI, 32, *distahjada warjizuh du seina* (πρὸς τὰ ἴδια), “each was scattered to his own things,” it cannot be explained as an accusative, because in neither the Gospel nor in general does *du* occur with the accusative in the sense “to.” In the note on that passage we regarded *seina* as a genitive and explained it by ellipsis; perhaps it should be changed to *seinamma*, or, as Zahn conjectures, to *seinaim*.

III. Added to the infinitive, it is regularly placed immediately before it; in the Epistles and the *Skeireins*, however, it is separated from it by the predicate, object, or by another word determining the infinitive, as Cor. I, VII, 25, *du triggs visan*, “to be faithful”; IX, 6, *du ni vaurkjan*, “not to work”; Rom. VII, 5, *du akran bairan*, “to bear fruit”; Thess. II, I, 5; Rom. XI, 11, *du ïn aljana briggan*, “to bring into jealousy”; Phlpp. IV, 10; Thess. II, II, 2, *du ni sprauto vagjan*, “not to be quickly shaken”; Cor. I, VIII, 10, *du galiugagudam gasaliþ matjan*, “to eat meat in an idol-temple”; *Skeir.* II, c, d.

In this construction it is used both as subject and as object, and in either function may take the article: Mc. XII, 33, *þata du frijon guþ jah þata du frijon newundjan sve sik silban managizo ïst allaim þaim allbrunstim*, “to love God and to love one’s neighbor as oneself is greater than all the burnt offerings”; X, 40, *þata du sitan af taihsvon meinai nist mein du giban*, “to sit at my right hand is not mine to give.”

1) As subject, in place of Greek τό with infinitive: Cor. I, XI, 6, *agl ïst qinon du kapillon aiþþau skaban*, “it is shameful for a woman to cut her hair or be shaven”; Cor. II, IX, 1, *ufjo mis ïst du meljan ïzvis*, “it is superfluous for me to write to you”; Phlpp. I, 24, *du visan ïn leika þaurftizo (ïst) ïn ïzvara*, “to remain in the body is more necessary for your sake”; or in place of the simple infinitive: Mc. II, 9, *waþar azetizo ïst du qiþan*, “which is easier to say?”; X, 40, *nist mein du qiþan*, “it is not mine to say”; Thess. I, III, 4, *anavairþ vas uns du vinnan agliþos*, “it was beforehand known to us that we should suffer affliction” (but elsewhere Tim. I, I, 16, *anavairþai vesun du galaubjan ïmma*, “those who were afterward to believe in him”); *Skeir.* II, c, *gadob vas du garehsn daupeinais andniman*, “it was fitting to receive the purification of baptism.”

2) As object, namely where that toward which the action tends indicates determination, result, and especially purpose. It then depends on nouns, verbs, formulas, and even whole sentences, and is used:

a) in place of the Greek infinitive: Tim. I, I, 16, *anavairþai vesun du galaubjan*, “those who were afterward to believe”; Rom. XI, 26, *urrinniþ us Sion sa lausjands du afvandjan afgudein*, “there shall come from Zion the Deliverer, to turn away ungodliness”; Luc. IV, 18, *gasalboda mik du vailamerjan unledaim*, “he anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor.” *Ïnsandida*
to heal me; John 12:4 he gave himself over to believe in him; Luke 9:16 he gave the loaves to the disciples to set before the multitude; John 6:31 he gave them bread to eat; 6:52 to give his flesh to eat; Col. 1:25 the dispensation was given to me to fulfil the word; 2 Cor. 11:2 I betrothed you to one husband, a chaste virgin, to present to Christ; 1 Cor. 7:25 having obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful; Luke 19:48 the people hung upon hearing him; Col. 1:22 having reconciled [you] through death, to present you holy; Col. 4:3 may [God] open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery; Phil. 4:10 I rejoiced that you at last revived your care for me.

b) For **τοῦ** with the infinitive, generally denoting determination; thus after: *urrinnan*, “to go out,” Mark 4:3; Luke 8:5; *ushafjan sik*, “to set oneself,” Matt. 11:1; *anatrimpan*, Luke 5:1; add, constructed in the Greek manner, “his face he set steadfastly (to go)” Luke 9:51; *anabiudan*, Luke 4:10; *bandvjan*, John 13:24; after “the time was fulfilled,” Luke 1:57; “the days were fulfilled,” Luke 2:6, 21; “the lot fell,” Luke 1:9; “readiness of mind,” 2 Cor. 8:11; “to have authority,” Mark 3:15; 1 Cor. 9:6; “to have ears,” Luke 8:8; “to have readiness,” 2 Cor. 10:6; “to prepare a way,” Luke 1:77, 79. Luke 6:7 also belongs here, where *κατηγορία* is rendered by *til du vrohjan* (“capacity, opportunity for accusing”); Phil. 3:10 should be understood as still more purposive, since *du kunnan ina*, “to know him,” corresponds to *τῷ ïn ufarassaus kunþjis ïesuis* (“the surpassing knowledge of Jesus”) in verse 7; compare also *Skeireins* IV.d: “Now they were not accused for this, merely because they had acknowledged the greatness of the Lord; but [Col. 1301] you have begun to dispute about the Law.”

c) For **εἰς τό** with the infinitive: Matt. 26:2 “the Son of Man was delivered up to be crucified”; 2 Thess. 3:9 “that we might give ourselves to you as an example, for you to imitate us”; 1 Thess. 3:5 “I sent [someone] to ascertain your faith”; Luke 4:29 “they brought him to the brow of the hill, to throw him down”; Rom. 7:5 “the passions worked in the members to bear fruit”; 1 Thess. 3:13 “may he make love abound, to establish [your] hearts”; Luke 5:17 “the power of the Lord was present to heal”; Rom. 15:8 “Jesus became a servant of the circumcision, to confirm the promises”; 11:11 “salvation came to the Gentiles, to provoke them to jealousy”; 1 Thess. 2:16 “to save [them], to fill up their sins”; 1 Cor. 8:10 “his conscience will be built up to eat food sacrificed to idols”; 1 Thess. 4:9 “you are taught by God to love”; Rom. 12:2 “be transformed by the renewal of your mind, to discern”; 2 Thess. 2:2 “we beseech you, concerning the coming of the Lord, not to be quickly shaken”; 1 Thess. 2:12 “beseeching, exhorting, and testifying that you should walk worthily”; Mark 14:55 “they sought testimony to put him to death”; 1 Cor. 11:22 “do you have houses to eat and drink in?”; 2 Thess. 1:5 “a token of righteous judgment, that you may be counted worthy”; Rom. 12:3 “to think soberly”; 2 Cor. 7:3 “you are in our hearts, to die and live together”; *Skeireins* I.d, “he was obliged, in accordance with his wisdom, to call man back again.”

Cases must also be included here in which the Gothic uses an infinitive in place of a Greek noun: Luke 5:4, “let down the nets for a catch” (*εἰς ἄγραν*); 14:28, “does he have enough to finish?” (*εἰς ἀπαρτισμόν*); 1 Thess. 4:17, “to meet” (*εἰς ὑπάντησιν*). But Matt. 27:7, *du usfilhan* (*εἰς ταφήν*, “for burial”) is incorrect; *du usfilham* should be read; see the note on that passage.

d) For **πρὸς τό** with the infinitive: Matt. 5:28 “to look at a woman in order to desire her”; 6:1 “to perform alms before men in order to be seen by them”; Mark 13:22 “giving signs to lead astray.”

e) For **ἐπὶ τῷ** with the infinitive: 1 Cor. 11:21 “to eat beforehand.”

f) For **ἕνεκεν** with the infinitive: 2 Cor. 7:12 “I wrote in order to make manifest [your] diligence.”

g) For **ἵνα**: Mark 3:14 “he appointed twelve, that they might be with him”; John 17:4 “you gave me work to do, that I might accomplish it.”

h) For a Greek participle: Mark 10:46 and Luke 18:35, “a blind man sat by the way begging” (*προσαιτῶν*); perhaps the Goth also read Luke 19:48 as *ἐξεκρέματο ἀκούων*, “hung upon [him], hearing,” (*hahaida du hausjan*).

IV. As an adverb: only in Luke 8:44, *atgaggandei du*; but probably Mark 10:13 should likewise read *bairandam du*; see the note on that passage.

V. In composition:

1. *duþe* (*duhþe*, *duþþe*), see under **þata**; *duwe*, see under **Was**.

2. But it is actually compounded only with verbs: *duginnan*, *durinnan*, *dustodjan*, *duvakan*; doubly compounded: *duatgaggan*, *duatrinnan*, *duatsnivan*; *dugasaiwan*, *dugavindan*; *fauradustodjan*.

**4. DUBO** (compare Old Norse *dufa*; Old Saxon *duba*; Anglo-Saxon *duva*; Old High German *tuba*; Swedish *dufva*; Danish *due*; English *dove*; modern High German *Tauhe*; Gr. II, 412; III, 341; Gf. V, 350), feminine: dove, pigeon. **HRAIVA-DUBO**, raven, crow (see under **Hraiv**); turtledove, *τρυγών*: Luke 2:24.

**DUGAN** (Old Norse and Frisian *duga*; Old Saxon and Anglo-Saxon *dugan*; Old High German *tugan*; Swedish *duga*; Danish *due*; modern High German *taugen*; Gr. II, 23; Gf. V, 369; Rchth. 695), anomalous conjugation: *daug, dugun, duhta*: to be useful, profitable, *συμφέρειν*: 1 Cor. 10:23; to be useful, *χρήσιμον εἶναι*: 2 Tim. 2:14.

**DULGS**, masculine: debt, obligation, *χρέος*: Luke 7:41, where *dulgis skula* means “debtor,” *χρεωφειλέτης*.

**DULGA-HAITJA**, see under **Haitan**.

**DULþS** (Old High German *tuld*, Middle High German *dult*; Gr. III, 521; Gf. V, 421; Schm. I, 366 ff.), feminine—also masculine in Matt. 27:15, and anomalously feminine in John 7:14, dative *dulþ*: festival, feast, *ἑορτή*: Matt. 27:15; Mark 15:6; Luke 2:41, 42; John 6:4; 7:2, 8, 10, 11, 14, 37; 12:12, 20; 13:29; Col. 2:16.

**DULþJAN**, second conjugation: to celebrate a feast, *ἑορτάζειν*: 1 Cor. 5:8.

**DUMBS** (Old Norse *dumbi*; Anglo-Saxon *dumb*; Old Frisian *dumbe, dume*; Old High German *tumb*; English, Swedish [Col. 1302] *dumb*; Danish *dum*; modern High German *dumm*; Gr. II, 59; Gf. V, 425; Rchth. 695), adjective: mute, dumb, *κωφός*: Matt. 9:33; Luke 1:22.

**AF-DUMBNAN**, third conjugation: to become mute, *πεφιμῶσθαι*: Mark 4:39.

**\*DRABAN** (compare *dreiban*), first conjugation: *drof, drobun, drabans*: to strike, hew.

**GA-DRABAN**: to cut out, quarry, *λατομεῖν*: Mark 15:46.

**DRAGAN** (Old Norse *draga*; Old Saxon, Anglo-Saxon *dragan*; Old High German *tragan*; English *drag, draw*; Danish *drage*; Swedish *draga*; modern High German *tragen*; Latin *trahere*; Gr. II, 11; Gf. V, 492), first conjugation: *drog, drogun, dragans*: to draw, pull; *sis dragan*, “to heap up for oneself,” *ἐπισωρεύειν*: 2 Tim. 4:3.

**GA-DRAGAN**: the same: 2 Tim. 4:3; see that passage.

**DRAGGK**, see under **Drigkan**.

**DRAIBJAN**, see under **Dreiban**.

**DRAKMA** (a Greek word), masculine: drachma, *δραχμή*: Luke 15:8, 9.

**DRAUHSNA** (*drausna*, *Skeireins* VII.d; Gr. III, 462), feminine: crumb, morsel, *ψιχίον*: Mark 7:28; Luke 16:21; fragment, *κλάσμα*: John 6:12; *Skeireins* VII.d.

**DRAUHTS**, see under **Driugan**.

**DRAUSJAN**, see under **Driusan**.

**DREIBAN** (Old Norse *drepa, drifa*; Old Saxon *driban*; Anglo-Saxon *drifan*; Old High German *triban*; English, Danish *drive*; Swedish *drifva*; Dutch *dryven*; modern High German *treiben*; Gr. II, 13; Gf. V, 481), first conjugation: *draib, dribun, dribans*: to drive; *us gaqumþim dreiban*, “to drive out of the assemblies,” to make a person *ἀποσυνάγωγος* (“excluded from the synagogue”): John 16:2.

**US-DREIBAN**: to cast out, *ἐκβάλλειν*: Matt. 9:25, 33, 34; Mark 6:13; 9:18, 28, 38; Luke 8:54; 9:40, 43, 49; *ἀποστέλλειν*: Mark 5:10.

**DRAIBJAN**, second conjugation: to drive, compel, urge, *ἐλαύνειν*: Luke 8:29; to trouble, vex, *σκύλλειν*: Mark 5:35; Luke 8:49; *draibjan sik*, “to trouble oneself,” *σκύλλεσθαι*: Luke 7:6.

**DRIGKAN** (*driggkan*, Mark 10:38, 39; Luke 10:7 and regularly in John; *driggan*, Luke 5:39; Eph. 5:18; Old Norse *drecka*; Old Saxon *drincan, drencian*; Anglo-Saxon *drincan, drencan*; Old Frisian *drinka, drenka*; Old High German *trinkan, trinkjan*; English *drink*; Swedish *dricka*; Danish *drikke*; modern High German *trinken, tränken*; Gr. II, 36; III, 465; Gf. V, 533; Rchth. 692 f.), first conjugation: *dragk, drugkun, drugkans*: to drink, *πίνειν*: Matt. 6:25, 31; 11:18, 19; Mark 10:38, 39; 15:23; Luke 1:15; 5:30, 33, 39; 7:33, 34; 10:7; 17:8, 27, 28; John 6:53, 54, 56; 7:37; 18:11; 1 Cor. 9:4; 10:4, 21, 31; 11:22, 25–29; 15:32. *Vato drigkan*, “to drink water,” *ὑδροποτεῖν*: 1 Tim. 5:23. Passive participle *drugkans*: “drunk”; *drugkans visan*, “to be drunken,” *μεθύειν*: 1 Cor. 11:21; *drugkans vairþan*, “to become drunken,” *μεθύσκεσθαι*: 1 Thess. 5:7.

**ANA-DRIGKAN**: to become drunk; *anadrigkan sik*, “to make oneself drunk,” *μεθύσκεσθαι*: Eph. 5:18.

**GA-DRIGKAN**: to drink, *πίνειν*: Luke 17:8.

**DRAGK** (*draggk*, John 6:55), neuter: drink, beverage, *πόσις*: John 6:55; Rom. 14:17; Col. 2:16; *πόμα*: 1 Cor. 10:4.

**DRAGKJAN** (*draggkjan*, Matt. 27:48), second conjugation: to give drink, refresh with drink; *ποτίζειν*: Matt. 25:42; 27:48; Mark 15:36; Rom. 12:20; 1 Cor. 12:13.

**GA-DRAGKJAN**: the same: Matt. 10:42; Mark 9:41.

**DRUGKANEI**, feminine: drunkenness, *μέθη*: Rom. 13:13; Gal. 5:2; see the note on that passage.

**AF-DRUGKJA**, masculine: drunkard, habitual drinker, *μέθυσος*: 1 Cor. 5:11; wine-drinker, *οἰνοπότης*: Matt. 11:19; see the note on that passage.

**VEIN-DRUGKJA**: drinker of wine, *οἰνοπότης*: Luke 7:34.

**DRIUGAN** (Old Norse *drott*; Old Saxon *druht*; Anglo-Saxon *driht, dreogan, drohtnian*; Old Frisian *dracht, drecht*; modern High German *Tross*; Byzantine Greek *δροῦγγος, δρουγγάριος*; Gr. II, 452; III, 473; Gf. V, 517; Rchth. 691; Du Cange, *Glossarium mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, s.v. *Drungus*), first conjugation: *drauh, drugun, drugans*: to serve as a soldier, wage war, *στρατεύειν*: 1 Tim. 1:18.

**GA-DRAUHTS**: soldier, *στρατιώτης*: Matt. 8:9; Mark 15:16; Luke 7:8; John 19:2; 2 Tim. 2:3.

**DRAUHTINON**, second conjugation: to perform military service, campaign, *στρατεύεσθαι*: 1 Cor. 9:7; 2 Cor. 10:3; 2 Tim. 2:4. *Sa þammei drauhtino*: “he whom I serve,” *ὁ στρατολογῶν*: 2 Tim. 2:4.

**DRAUHTINASSUS**, masculine: military service, warfare, *στρατεία*: 2 Cor. 10:4.

**DRAUHTI-VITOþ**, see under **Vitan**.

**DRIUSAN** (Old Saxon *driosan*; Anglo-Saxon *dreosan*; Gr. II, 21; Gf. V, 545), first conjugation: *draus, drusun, drusans*: to fall, *πίπτειν*: Mark 9:20; Luke 5:12; 6:39; 8:41; 10:18; 16:20; 17:16; 20:18; John 11:32; Rom. 14:4; 1 Cor. 14:25; *ἐκπίπτειν*: Mark 13:25. *Driusan ana—*, “to fall upon,” *ἐπιπίπτειν*: Mark 3:10; Luke 15:20. *Driusan du—*, “to fall toward,” *προσπίπτειν*: Mark 3:11; 5:33; 7:25; Luke 5:8; 8:28.

**AT-DRIUSAN**: to fall down, fall, *προσπίπτειν*: Luke 8:47; *ἐπιπίπτειν*: Neh. 6:16; *ἐμπίπτειν*: 1 Tim. 3:6, 7; 6:9; *Skeireins* I.a; II.b.

**GA-DRIUSAN**: to fall, *πίπτειν*: Matt. 7:25, 27; 10:29; Mark 4:4, 5, 7, 8; 5:22; Luke 6:39, 49; 8:6; 7:8, 14; 16:17; John 12:24; 18:6; Rom. 11:11, 22; *ἐπιπίπτειν*: Rom. 15:3; *ἐκπίπτειν*: 1 Cor. 13:8; to be cast, *βάλλεσθαι*: Matt. 5:29, 30.

**DIS-DRIUSAN**: to fall upon, befall, *ἐπιπίπτειν*: Luke 1:12.

**US-DRIUSAN**: to fall out, be cast out, *ἐκπίπτειν*: Rom. 9:6; Gal. 5:4.

**DRIUSO**, feminine: precipice, steep place, *κρημνός*: Matt. 8:32; Mark 5:13; Luke 8:33.

**DRUS**, masculine: fall, downfall, *πτῶσις*: Matt. 7:27; Luke 2:34.

**US-DRUSTS**, feminine: roughness; a rough, uneven road, *τραχεῖα*: Luke 3:5.

**AF-DRAUSJAN**, second conjugation: to throw down a precipice, *κατακρημνίζειν*: Luke 4:29.

**GA-DRAUSJAN**: the same; to cast down, *καταβάλλειν*: 2 Cor. 4:9; to bring down, *καταβιβάζειν*: Luke 10:15; to cast down, *καθαιρεῖν*: Luke 1:52.

**DRUGKJA** and **DRUGKANEI**, see under **Drigkan**.

**DRUNJUS** (Dutch *dreunen*; modern High German *dröhnen*; DM. 125, 693), masculine: cry, voice, sound, *φθόγγος*: Rom. 10:18.

**DRUS**, see under **Driusan**.

**DRUSTS**, see under **Driusan**.

**DROBJAN** (Old Saxon *drobi, drobian, druban*; Anglo-Saxon *drof*; Old High German *trobi, trobjan*; modern High German *trüben*; Gf. V, 489), second conjugation: to disturb, throw into confusion, trouble, *ταράσσειν*: Gal. 1:7; 5:10; to unsettle, *ἀναστατοῦν*: Gal. 5:12. Participle *drobjands miþ …*: “raising a disturbance with …,” *συστασιαστής*: Mark 15:7.

[Col. 1304] **DROBNAN**, third conjugation: to frighten; *θροεῖσθαι*, “to be alarmed”: 2 Thess. 2:2; see that passage.

**GA-DROBNAN**: the same, *ταράσσεσθαι*: Luke 1:12; John 12:27.

**ÏN-DROBNAN**: the same: John 13:21; 14:1, 27.

**DROBNA**, masculine: disturbance, disorder, sedition, *ἀκαταστασία*: 2 Cor. 12:20.

**DVALS** (Old Norse *dvalinn, dvelia*; Old Saxon *biduelian*; Anglo-Saxon *dvelian, dvolian*; Old High German *twelan*; Old Frisian *dwila*; Danish *dvale*; Dutch *dvaelen*; Swedish *dål*; English *dull*; modern High German *toll*; Gr. II, 29; Gf. V, 548; Rchth. 697), adjective: foolish, stupid, *μωρός*: Matt. 5:22; 7:26; 1 Cor. 4:10; 2 Tim. 2:16, see that passage; 2:23. *Dvalana gataujan*, “to make foolish,” to render foolish, *μωραίνειν*: 1 Cor. 1:20.

**DVALIþA**, feminine: folly, foolishness, *μωρία*: 1 Cor. 1:18, 21, 23; *τὸ μωρόν*, “the foolish thing”: 1 Cor. 1:25.

**DVALA-VAURDEI**, see under **Vaurd**.

**DVALMON**, second conjugation: to be mad, *μαίνεσθαι*: John 10:20; 1 Cor. 14:23.

**DOBNAN**, see under **Daubs**.

**DOBS**, see under **Daban**.

**DOGS**, see under **Dag**.

**DOMS** (Old Norse *domr, daema*; Old Saxon *dom, deman, domian*; Anglo-Saxon *dom, deman*; Old High German *tom, tomjan*; Old Frisian *dom, dema, domia*; English *doom, deem*; Swedish *döma*; Danish *domme*; modern High German …*dammen*; Latin *damnare*; Gr. II, 41, 452; DRA. 749, 768; Rchth. 684, 690; Gf. V, 334 ff.), masculine: sentence, judgment; *Skeireins* II.b; VI.c.

**DOMJAN**, second conjugation: to judge, distinguish, examine, *κρίνειν*: 1 Cor. 10:15; 2 Cor. 5:15; to discern, *διακρίνειν*: 1 Cor. 11:29; to compare oneself, *ἐγκρίνειν*: 2 Cor. 10:12; to regard, consider, *ἡγεῖσθαι*: Phil. 3:8. *Usvaurhtana domjan* and *garaihtana domjan*, see under **Raihts** and **Vaurkjan**.

**AF-DOMJAN**:

1. To judge, pass judgment, *κρίνειν*: John 16:11; to condemn, *καταδικάζειν*: Luke 6:37.

2. To curse, imprecate, *καταθεματίζειν*: Matt. 26:74.

**BI-DOMJAN**: to judge, *κρίνειν*: Col. 2:16.

**GA-DOMJAN**: to judge concerning someone, compare, distinguish, *συγκρίνειν*: 2 Cor. 10:12; to condemn, *κατακρίνειν*: Mark 14:64. *Garaihtana* and *usvaurhtana gadomjan*, see under **Raihts** and **Vaurkjan**.

**AF-DOMEINS**, feminine: condemnation, *Skeireins* VIII.b.

**FAUR-DOMEINS**: prejudice, partiality, *πρόκριμα*: 1 Tim. 5:21.

**DOFS**, see under **Daban**.

[Col. 1303] E

[Col. 1303] **EI** (compare Old Norse *er*; *Gr.* III, 14, 163), relative particle, by which:

1. When suffixed:

   a. demonstratives and relative particles are formed: *saei*, who; *þatei*, which; *þeei*, which; *þadei*, whither; *þarei*, where; *þaþroei*, by which way; *miþþanei*, while; *svaei*, as; *sunsei*, as soon as; *ïn þizei*, for which reason; *faurþizei*, before; *þatainei*, only; see under *þata*, *þan*, *sva*, *suns*, etc.

   b. It is also attached to personal pronouns, so that it corresponds to a Greek relative referring back to the preceding personal pronoun: 2 Cor. 10:1, *ïk silba pavlus bidja ïzvis ïkei* (ὅς, “who”) *ana andaugi hauns ïm*; 1 Cor. 15:9; Rom. 14:4, *þu was ïs þuei stojis framaþjana skalk* (ὁ κατακρίνων, “you who judge another’s servant”; conversely, in Rom. 9:20, *þu was ïs ei andvaurdjais*, where *ei* is used for *þuei*); Mark 1:11, *þu ïs sunus meins sa liuba ïn þuzei* (ἐν ᾧ, “in whom”) *vaila galeikaida*; Luke 3:22; marginal reading of Mark 1:11, *þu ïs sunus meins sa liuba þukei* (“whom”) *vilda*; Luke 16:15, *jus sijuþ juzei garaihtans domeiþ ïzvis silbans* (οἱ δικαιοῦντες, “you who justify yourselves”); 2 Cor. 8:10; Eph. 2:13, 17; 1 Thess. 2:13; Gal. 3:1, *was izvis afhugida ïzvizei* (οἷς, “before whose eyes”) *xristus fauragameliþs vas*. But Gal. 5:4, *lausai sijuþ af xristau juzei* (οἵτινες, “whoever”) *garaihtans qiþiþ ïzvis*; and 1 Tim. 1:13, *aviliudo fraujin unte galaubjandan mik gahugida ïkei faura vas vajamerjands*: the preceding personal pronoun is absent.

2. It is also used independently, though joined with a preceding demonstrative so as to form a relative expression: Luke 1:[Col. 1304] 20, *und þana dag ei* (ἄχρι ἧς ἡμέρας, “until the day on which”) *vairþai þata*; 17:30, *þama daga ei* (ᾗ ἡμέρᾳ, “on the day on which”); Col. 1:9, *fram þamma daga ei* (ἀφ’ ἧς ἡμέρας, “from the day on which”); Neh. 5:14; 2 Tim. 3:8, *þamma haidau ei* (ὃν τρόπον, “in the manner in which”).

II. Interrogative particle, “whether,” “if,” εἰ, in indirect questions: Mark 11:13; 15:44; Rom. 11:14; 1 Cor. 1:16; 7:16; Phil. 3:12.

III. Conjunction construed with indicative and subjunctive: “that,” ὅτι; and *ei ni*, “lest,” ἵνα μή, also with the infinitive, in explanatory clauses and in those indicating aim or purpose:

1. After demonstrative and interrogative clauses: John 17:3, *soh ïst so aiveino libains, ei kunneina þuk*, “and this is eternal life, that they may know thee”; Matt. 8:7, *wileiks ïst sa ei vindos ufhausjand ïmma*, “I am willing to come and heal him”;” Mark 1:27; 6:2; Luke 1:43; 8:25; John 9:17, 36; 14:22; ὡς, Mark 9:21. Rom. 9:20 also belongs here; see above, I.1.b. Also John 8:22, *nibai usqimai sis silbin ei qiþiþ*, “will he perhaps kill himself, because he says …?”

2. After verbs of saying, declaring, and willing: after *qiþan*, “say,” Mark 3:9; 8:7; 9:18; 16:7; Luke 4:3; John 13:33; 18:9, 37; Gal. 5:16; Eph. 4:17; *gaqiþan sis*, “say to oneself,” John 9:22; *andhafjan*, “answer,” Luke 20:7; *gameljan*, “write,” Mark 9:12; 12:19; Luke 2:24; 20:18; *liugan*, “deny,” *Skeir.* VIII.c; *aviliudon*, “command,” 1 Cor. 1:14; *svaran*, “swear,” Luke 1:73; *bisvaran*, “adjure,” 1 Thess. 5:27; *bidjan*, “ask, entreat,” Mark 5:10, 18, 23; 6:56; 7:26, 32; 8:22; 13:18; Luke 7:36; 8:21, 31, 32, 38; 9:40; John 17:15, 21; [Col. 1305] 1 Cor. 16:12, 16; 2 Cor. 1:11; 8:6; 9:5; 10:2; 12:8; 13:7; Eph. 1:17; Col. 1:9; 4:3, 12; 1 Thess. 3:10; 4:1; 2 Thess. 1:11; 3:1, 12; *Skeir.* V.d. It also follows ὅφως in the Greek text: Matt. 8:34; 9:38; Luke 7:3; 10:2; and, moreover, after *anabiudan*, “command,” Mark 5:43; 7:36; 9:9; John 13:34; 15:17; 2 Thess. 3:6, 10; Neh. 5:14; *anabusns*, “commandment,” John 15:12; *bandvjan*, “signal,” Luke 5:7; *faurbiudan*, “forbid,” Mark 6:8; 8:30; Luke 5:14; 8:56; 9:21; 1 Tim. 1:3; *andbeitan*, “rebuke,” Mark 3:12; Luke 18:39; *wotjan*, “urge,” Mark 10:48; *ïnvagjan*, “instigate,” Mark 15:11; *merjan*, “proclaim,” Mark 6:12; *veitvodjan*, “testify,” Eph. 4:17; 1 Tim. 5:21; *veitvod anahaitan*, “call to witness,” 2 Cor. 1:23; *fravrohjan*, “accuse,” Luke 16:1 (ὡς with a participle); *gasvikunþjan*, “make known,” *Skeir.* II.a; *ataugjan*, “show,” *Skeir.* III.a; *atgiban*, “deliver,” 1 Cor. 15:3; *viljan*, “will,” Matt. 27:17; Mark 6:25; 9:30; 10:35, 51; 14:12; 15:12; Luke 6:31; 9:54; 18:41; John 6:40; 17:24; 18:39; Rom. 13:3; 1 Cor. 16:12; 1 Thess. 4:3, 4; *sokjan*, “seek,” 1 Cor. 4:2; Gal. 2:17; *gastauan at sis*, “resolve within oneself,” 2 Cor. 2:1; *munan*, “intend,” John 12:10; *runa niman*, “take counsel,” Matt. 27:1. Hence also after *letan*, “allow,” Matt. 27:49; Mark 11:16; 15:36; *fragiban*, “grant,” Mark 10:37; *taujan*, “do,” John 11:37; Col. 4:16; and after *þaurban*, “need,” John 16:30; 1 Thess. 5:1; *magan*, “be able,” Mark 10:38; *vairþs visan*, “be worthy,” Matt. 3:11; 8:8; Luke 7:6; 15:19, 21; 1 Cor. 15:9.

3. After verbs of perception and emotion: *hausjan*, “hear,” Mark 6:55; John 12:18; 14:28; *saiwan* (only in the figurative sense of seeing, “take care”), Matt. 8:4; 9:30; Mark 1:44; 8:15; 1 Cor. 16:10; Col. 4:17; *kunnan*, “know,” John 15:18; 2 Cor. 13:6; see the note on this passage; *ufkunnan*, “recognize,” John 17:7; *vitan*, “know,” John 9:25; 11:22; 16:30; compare 2 Cor. 5:1; *hugjan*, “think,” Matt. 5:17; *þagkjan*, “think,” 2 Cor. 10:7; *þugkjan*, “seem,” Matt. 6:7; Luke 19:11; 2 Cor. 12:19; *galaubjan*, “believe,” Mark 11:23; *trauan*, “trust,” Luke 18:9; *gatrauan*, “be confident,” 2 Thess. 3:4; *venjan*, “hope,” 2 Cor. 1:10, 13; 13:6; *faginon*, “rejoice,” Luke 10:20; John 11:15; 14:28; *faheds*, “joy,” Phil. 2:2; *sifan*, “rejoice,” John 8:56; *sildaleikjan*, “wonder,” Mark 15:44 (where the Greek text has εἰ); Gal. 1:6.

4. After impersonal expressions and certain formulas: *ganah*, “it is enough,” Matt. 10:25; *galeikaiþ*, “it pleases,” 1 Thess. 3:1; *goþ ïst*, “it is good,” Mark 9:42; *batizo ïst*, “it is better,” Matt. 5:29, 30; John 16:7; *leitil*, “a little,” John 16:17 (καί); *ïn minnistin ïst*, “it is a very small matter,” 1 Cor. 4:3; *gadob ïst*, “it is fitting,” *Skeir.* I.c; *varþ*, “it happened,” Luke 6:12; 8:1; see the note on these passages; *biuhti ïst*, “it is customary,” John 18:39; *aeeila qam*, “the hour came,” John 12:23; 16:2, 32. Elliptical cases also belong here: Gal. 1:20, *sai ïn andvairþja guþs ei ni liuga*, “behold, before God, I do not lie”; 2 Cor. 1:18, *triggs guþ ei þata vaurd unsar nist ja jah ne*, “God is faithful, that our word is not yes and no.”

5. After clauses denoting end or purpose:

   a. ἵνα: Matt. 9:6; 27:42; Mark 1:38; 2:10; 3:2, 10, 14; 4:12, 21, 22; 5:12, 23; 7:9; 8:6; 9:22; 10:13, 17; 11:25, 28; 12:2, 13, 15; 14:10, 12, 49; 15:15, 20, 21, 32; 16:1; Luke 1:4; 4:11; 5:24; 6:7, 34, 37; 8:10, 12, 16; 9:12, 45; 14:10, 23; 15:29; 16:4 (*ei þau*), 9; 18:15; 19:4, 15; 20:10, 14, 20; John 5:23, 36; 6:5, 15, 28, 29, 30, 50; 7:3, 23, 32; 8:59; 9:2, 3, 39; 10:10, 17, 31, 38; 11:4, 11, 16, 19, 31, 42; 12:9, 20, 25, 36, 38, 40, 42, 46, 47; 13:15, 18, 19, 29; 14:3, 13, 16, 29, 31; 15:2, 8, 11, 13, 16, 25; 16:1, 4, 24; 17:1, 2, 11, 12, 13, 19, 21, 22, 23, 24, 26; 18:9, 28, 32, 36, 37; 19:4; Rom. 7:4, 13; 8:4; 9:11, 23; 11:11, 19, 25, 31, 32; 14:13; [Col. 1306] 15:4, 6; 1 Cor. 1:15, 17; 4:6, 8; 5:5, 7; 7:5; 8:13; 9:19–25; 10:33; 13:3; 15:28; 16:2, 6, 11, 16; 2 Cor. 1:4, 9, 15, 17; 2:3–5, 9, 11; 4:7, 11, 15; 5:4, 10, 12, 15, 21; 6:3; 7:9; 8:7, 9, 13, 14; 10:9; 11:3, 4, 7, 8, 12, 16; 12:7, 9; 13:7, 10; Gal. 2:4, 5, 10, 16, 19; 4:5, 17; 5:17; 6:12, 13; Eph. 2:7, 9, 10, 15; 3:10, 16, 18, 19; 4:10, 14, 28, 29; 5:26, 27; 6:11, 13, 19, 21; Phil. 1:26, 27; 2:2, 27, 28, 30; 3:8, 16; Col. 1:18, 28; 3:21; 4:4, 8; 1 Thess. 2:16; 3:3; 4:12, 13; 5:4, 10; 2 Thess. 3:8, 14; 1 Tim. 1:16, 18, 20; 2:2; 3:7, 15; 4:15; 5:7, 29; 6:1; 2 Tim. 1:4; 2:4, 10; 3:17; Philem. 13, 15, 19; *Skeir.* I.a, d; II.d; IV.d; V.a.

   b. ὅπως: Matt. 5:16, 45; 6:2, 4, 15, 16, 18; 8:17; Mark 3:6; 5:23; Luke 2:35 (ὅπως ἄν); 7:3; Rom. 9:17; 2 Cor. 8:11, 14; Gal. 1:4; 2 Thess. 1:12.

   c. In place of a Greek infinitive: Luke 2:3; Eph. 1:4; 4:22; Col. 1:10; 4:6.

   d. τό with infinitive: Rom. 14:13; 1 Thess. 4:6.

   e. τοῦ with infinitive: Luke 2:27; 4:42; Rom. 7:3.

   f. εἰς τό with infinitive: Rom. 7:4; 2 Cor. 4:4; Eph. 1:12, 18; 6:11; 1 Thess. 3:2.

   g. πρὸς τό with infinitive: 2 Tim. 3:8.

6. In combination with other particles: *duþe ei*, “wherefore”; see under *þata*; *sveþauh ei*, see under *þau*; *ei waiva*, “if perhaps,” see under *Waiva*; *ei wan ni*, “whether perhaps,” see under *Wan*; *Skeir.* VIII.c has *ïn þamma ei*, or, as Massmann reads, *ïn þammei*, “because, since.”

**EISARN** (Old Norse *jarn, isarn*; Old Saxon *isarn*; Anglo-Saxon *iren, isern*; Old High German *isan, isarn*; Old Frisian *isern*; English *iron*; Swedish *järn*; Danish *joern*; Modern High German *eisen, eisern*; Latin *aes*; *Gr.* II, 46, 452; *Gf.* I, 488; *Rchth.* 855), neuter, iron; *eisarna bi fotuns gabugana* and *þo ana fotum eisarna*, fetters, πἐδαι: Mark 5:4.
