XI, 33, *þairh augadauro ïn snorjon athahans vas*, “I was let down through a window in a basket”; and 2 Cor. V, 7, *þairh galaubein gaggam nih þairh siun*, “we walk through faith, not through sight”; 1 Cor. XIII, 12, *saiwam nu þairh skuggvan ïn frisahtai*, “now we see through a mirror obscurely”; Luke I, 70, *rodida guþ þairh munþ praufete*, “God spoke through the mouth of the prophet.” Add also John XIV, 6: *ïk ïm sa vigs. ainshun ni qimiþ at attin niba þairh mik*, “I am the way. No one comes to the Father except through me.”

2) Means:

a) In relation to things: Mark VI, 2, *mahteis þairh handuns ïs vairþand*, “powers are wrought through his hands”; *Skeireins* VI, c: “the Father’s knowledge concerning him came in some cases through prophetic words, in others through a voice from heaven, and in others through signs”; 2 Tim. I, 6, *ansts guþs ïst ïn þus þairh analagein handive meinaizo*, “the grace of God is in you through the laying on of my hands”; *Skeireins* VI, b, “the Father knew through my works”; Gal. II, 21, *þairh vitoþ garaihtei*, “righteousness through the law”; Rom. VII, 5, *vinnons þairh vitoþ*, “working through the law”; X, 17.

Likewise the formulas *apaustaulus þairh viljan guþs*, “an apostle through the will of God,” 2 Cor. I, 1; Eph. I, 1; 2 Tim. I, 1; 2 Cor. VIII, 5; John XVII, 20, *galaubjands þairh vaurda ïze du mis*, “believers through their word unto me”; 1 Cor. XVI, 3, *þairh bokos þans sandja*, “by letters which I shall send”; 2 Cor. X, 9, *þlahsjan þairh bokos*, “to frighten by letters”; X, 11; 2 Thess. III, 14; Eph. VI, 18, *þairh aihtronins jah bidos aihtron*, “through every prayer and supplication”; III, 6, *gadailans gahaitis þairh aivaggeljon*, “partakers of the promise through the Gospel”; 2 Cor. IX, 12, *ufarassjan þairh managa aviliuda*, “abounding through many thanksgivings”; I, 4, *gaþrafstjan þairh gaþlaiht*, “to comfort through consolation”; 2 Tim. III, 15, *usfraivjan du ganistai þairh galaubein*, “to make wise unto salvation through faith”; *Skeireins* I, c, “to deceive through a lie”; V, d; Rom. VII, 7, 8, 11; XII, 1, 3; XV, 4; 1 Cor. I, 21; 2 Cor. IV, 15; VI, 7; IX, 13; Eph. I, 7; II, 8, 16; III, 12, 17; Phil. I, 19; III, 9; Col. I, 20, 22; 1 Tim. II, 10, 15; 2 Tim. II, 2.

After adjectives: Gal. V, 6, *galaubeins þairh friaþva vaurstveiga*, “faith working through love”; compare Rom. XIV, 14, *nï vaiht gavamm þairh sik silbo*, “nothing is unclean through itself,” i.e. in itself.

Very often, particularly after passives: John XI, 4, *ei hauhjaidau þairh þata*, “that [he] might be glorified through it”; 1 Tim. IV, 14, *ansts gibana varþ þairh praufetjans*, “the grace was given through prophecy”; 2 Tim. I, 10, *ansts gasvikunþida þairh gabairhtein ïesuis*, “grace was manifested through the appearing of Jesus”; 1 Tim. IV, 5, *gaveihada þairh vaurd guþs*, “sanctified through the word of God”; Rom. VII, 4; Eph. III, 10; IV, 16; Philem. 22. Here it also stands for ὑπό with the genitive: 1 Cor. X, 29, *frijei meina stojada þairh ungalaubjandins þuhtu*, “my freedom is judged by the conscience of an unbeliever.”

After intransitive verbs: Eph. III, 16, *gasvinþnan þairh ahman*, “to be strengthened through the Spirit”; 1 Cor. XV, 2, *þairh aivaggeljon ganisiþ*, “you are saved through the Gospel”; Col. II, 19, “the body increases through joints and bands”; *Skeireins* II, b, “another birth through the washing of regeneration”; Col. II, 12, “raised with [him] through faith”; Gal. II, 19, *þairh vitoþ vitoda gasvalt*, “through the law I died to the law”; Rom. VII, 4, *þairh anabusn usqam*, “we came out through the resurrection”; *Skeireins* III, a, “the discourse concerning him was approaching its end through Herod’s inquiry”; Rom. VIII, 3, “it was weak through the flesh”; Gal. II, 16, “a human being is justified through faith”; Rom. VII, 13, “sin became evident through that which is good.”

b) In relation to persons: Rom. XI, 36, *þairh guþ alla*, “all things [are] through God”; 1 Cor. XV, 21, “through a man came death, and through a man resurrection”; 2 Cor. I, 20, *þairh ïna amen*, “through him, Amen”; Gal. I, 1, “an apostle, not from human beings nor through a human being, but through [Col. 1328] Jesus Christ”; IV, 7, “a son and an heir of God through Christ.”

Likewise very frequently in the formula *þairh Xristu*, “through Christ”: Rom. VII, 25; VIII, 37; 1 Cor. XV, 57; 2 Cor. I, 5; III, 4; IV, 4; V, 18; Gal. VI, 14; Eph. I, 5; Col. III, 17; 1 Thess. IV, 2, 14; V, 9. Further: 2 Cor. II, 14, “making known through us”; V, 20, “God exhorts through us”; IX, 11, “simplicity working through us thanksgiving to God”; XII, 17, “perhaps I defrauded you through any one”; Eph. II, 18, “through him we have access to the Father”; Col. I, 20, “through him he made peace”; 2 Tim. I, 14, “keep the good deposit through the Holy Spirit.”

Frequently also after passives: Col. I, 16, “all things were created through him”; Matt. VIII, 17, “what was spoken through Isaiah”; likewise Luke XVIII, 31; and the superscriptions to Mark and Luke, with *gamelida* understood, should be explained: *aivaggeljo þairh Marku, þairh Lukan*, “Gospel through Mark, through Luke”; Matt. XXVII, 2, “what was spoken through Jeremiah was fulfilled”; 2 Cor. I, 19, “Christ was preached among you through us”; I, 11, “the gift [for which] thanks are given through many [persons].”

c) It also expresses the manner and method by which something happens: 2 Cor. II, 4, “I wrote to you through many tears”; Phil. I, 20, “Christ will be magnified in my body, whether through life or through death.” Thus 2 Cor. V, 7, cited above under 1), must be explained. Luke VIII, 4, *qaþ þairh gajukon*, “he spoke through a parable”; Gal. IV, 13, “through infirmity of the flesh I preached the Gospel to you”; 2 Cor. III, 11, *þata gataurnando þairh vulþu*, “that which was passing away was through glory,” i.e. glorious. Here may also be included the periphrasis Col. II, 22: *þata ïst du riurein þairh þatei ïs brukjaidau*, “which is for destruction through being used,” for ἀποχρήσει, “consumption.”

3) Properly, **þairh** does not have a causal sense corresponding to Greek διά with the accusative; this is expressed by *ïn* with the genitive. Yet in some cases the translator seems to follow the Greek wording and to care little about the construction: Luke I, 78, *aflet fravaurhte þairh ïnfeinandein armahairtein guþs unsaris*, “forgiveness of sins through the compassionate mercy of our God” (διὰ σπλάγχνα ἐλέους, “through bowels of mercy”); Eph. V, 6, *þairh þata qimiþ hatis guþs*, “because of these things the wrath of God comes” (διὰ ταῦτα ἔρχεται ἡ ὀργὴ τοῦ θεοῦ); likewise Col. III, 6, *þairh þoei qimiþ hatis guþs*, “because of which the wrath of God comes” (δι’ ἅ); *Skeireins* VII, a, *þairh þoei usbar qiþands*, that is, 4), “while he cried out speaking.”

Only very rarely does **þairh** determine time. Perhaps Phil. I, 26 may be explained thus: *ei woftuli ïzvara biauknai þairh meinana qum aftra du ïzvis*, “that your rejoicing may abound through my coming again to you”; compare also I, 20. Elsewhere the Goth joins the preposition to the verb and puts the principal noun in the accusative, as Luke V, 5: *alla naht þairharbaidjandans … vaxt ni nemum*, “having laboured through the whole night … we caught nothing” (διὰ ὅλης τῆς νυκτὸς κοπιάσαντες); compare VI, 12, *naht þairhvakands*, “spending the night awake,” διανυκτερεύων. Elsewhere Greek διά with the genitive in temporal determinations is rendered by *afar* (Mark II, 1) or *bi* (Gal. II, 1).

II. In composition it occurs only rarely, where it answers Greek δια-, and sometimes also παρα-, κατα-, etc.: *þairharbaidjan, þairhbairan, þairhgaggan, þairhleiþan, þairhsaiwan, þairhvakan, þairhvisan; þairhgaleikon*.

**þAIRKO** (Anglo-Saxon *þyrel*, Old High German *durhil*; Gf. V, 224; compare **þairh**), neuter: an opening, eye [of a needle], τρυμαλιά: Mark X, 25; Luke XVIII, 25.

An asterisk.

**þAIRSAN** (Old Norse *þerra, þyrsta*, Anglo-Saxon *þyrstan*, Old Saxon *thorron, thurstian*, Old High German *darrjan, dorrjan, durstjan*, English *thirst*, Danish *tør, tørst*, Swedish *törr, törsta*, Modern High German *dürr, darren, dursten*; Latin *torreo*, “parch”; Greek τέρσεσθαι, “to become dry”; Bopp 100; Gr. II, 39; Gf. V, 199), first conjugation; þars, þaursun, þaursans: to dry, parch.

**GA-þAIRSAN**, to wither; past participle *gaþaursans*, dry, ἐξηραμμένος: Mark III, 1, 3.

**þAURSUS**, adjective: dry, ξηρός: Luke VI, 6; ἐξηραμμένος, “withered”: Mark XI, 20.

**GA-þAURSNAN**, third conjugation: to dry up, be dried up, wither, ξηραίνεσθαι: Mark IV, 6; V, 29; XI, 21; Luke VIII, 6; John XV, 6.

**þAURSJAN**, second conjugation: to thirst, διψῆν. Impersonal only: *þaurseiþ mik*, “I thirst” (διψῶ): John VI, 35; VII, 37; Rom. XII, 20. Personal is *þaursiþs visan*, “to be thirsty”: 1 Cor. IV, 11.

**AF-þAURSJAN**, the same; *afþaursiþs visan*, “to thirst,” διψῆν: Matt. XXV, 42.

[Col. 1329] **þAURSTEI**, feminine: thirst, δίψος: 2 Cor. XI, 27.

**þAISSALAUNEIKA**, feminine proper name: Thessalonica, Θεσσαλονίκη: Phil. IV, 16; 2 Tim. IV, 10.

**þAISSALAUNEIKAIUS**, masculine: a Thessalonian, Θεσσαλονικεύς: 2 Thess., superscription; 1 Thess. I, 1; subscription.

**þAN** (Old Saxon *than*, Anglo-Saxon *þon, þonne*, Old High German *danne*, Old Frisian *tha*, English *then*, Modern High German *dann*; Latin *tunc*, “then”; Gr. III, 165, 280; Gf. V, 44; Rchth. 1067), a conjunction which, when demonstrative, always follows the first word of the sentence (only rarely several words, as Luke XVIII, 40, *biþe newa vas þan ïmma*; XX, 16, *gahausjandans qeþun þan*). It is inserted between a preposition and its governed noun only when that noun has enclitic *-uh*: Matt. XI, 21, *framuh þan þaim*; Mark XVI, 12; Luke I, 24; VII, 21; X, 1, 7; XVIII, 4; compare Mark XIV, 44; XVI, 8; 1 Cor. XIV, 23; XV, 15; Gal. II, 2; Eph. IV, 23. Conversely: Matt. XI, 7; *at þaim þan*, XXVI, 73; *afar leitil þan*, XXVII, 1, 15, 45; Mark IV, 6, 35; VIII, 1; Luke III, 1, 15; VI, 48; VII, 24; XIX, 11; XX, 45. It is also placed between article and substantive: Luke II, 2, *soh þan gilstrameleins*; 37; John VIII, 35; XVIII, 15; Rom. XII, 4; 1 Cor. XII, 12; *Skeireins* VIII, a; and between negation and the word negated: hence John XVIII, 30, *niþ-þan nauhþanuh*; Luke XX, 40, *niþ-þan þanaseiþs*; conversely Luke VII, 42, *ni habandam þan*. Hence the annotation made at Matt. IX, 2 is justified. But as a relative particle it begins the sentence.

I. Demonstrative: then, at that time, τότε: Matt. VII, 23; IX, 15; Mark II, 20; XIII, 21, 26, 27; Luke V, 35; VI, 42; John VII, 33; XIII, 37; 1 Cor. IV, 5; XIII, 12 (where *ïþ* must be repeated before the second *þan*; see the note on that passage); XVI, 2; 2 Cor. XII, 10; Gal. IV, 8, 29; VI, 4; Eph. II, 12; “behold,” ἰδού: Matt. XXVII, 51. It also occurs in the consequent clause, especially after a participial clause: Luke II, 42, *at venjandein allai managein— andhof þan ïohannes*, “when all the people were coming—then John answered”; XVI, 23; compare II, 42; John XIII, 31, where it corresponds to no Greek word.

II. Relative:

1) When, whenever, as long as, ὅταν: Matt. VI, 2, 5, 6; IX, 15; Mark II, 20; III, 11; IV, 15, 16, 31, 32; VIII, 38; XI, 25; XII, 23, 25; XIII, 28, 29; XIV, 7; Luke V, 35; VI, 22, 26; VIII, 13; XIV, 10, 12, 13; XVI, 9; XVII, 10; John VII, 31; VIII, 28, 44; IX, 5; X, 4; XV, 26; XVI, 13, 21; Rom. XI, 27; 1 Cor. XIV, 26; XV, 24, 54; XVI, 5; 2 Cor. X, 6; XII, 10; XIII, 9; Col. IV, 16; 1 Thess. V, 3; 2 Thess. I, 10.

2) When, ὅτε: Matt. VII, 28; IX, 25; Mark I, 32; II, 25; VI, 21; VII, 17; VIII, 19, 20; XIV, 12; XV, 41; Luke IV, 25; VI, 3 (ὁπότε, “whenever”?); XV, 30; XVII, 22; John VI, 24; IX, 14; XII, 17, 41; XIII, 31; XVII, 12; Rom. VII, 5; XIII, 11; 1 Cor. XIII, 11; Gal. II, 11; IV, 3; Phil. IV, 15; Col. III, 7; 1 Thess. III, 4; 2 Thess. III, 10; 2 Tim. IV, 3. To resolve the Greek genitive absolute: Matt. XXVII, 57, *þan seiþu varþ*, “when evening came,” for ὀψίας γενομένης.

III. Connective:

1) But, now, δέ: Matt. III, 11; V, 31, 37; VI, 7, 29; VIII, 1, 5; X, 16, 18, 21, 30; IX, 8, 28, 36; XI, 7, 12; XXV, 38, 39; XXVI, 67, 71, 73; XXVII, 1, 7, 15, 16, 19, 45, 55, 61, 62; Mark I, 6, 28, 32; II, 5, 6; III, 32; IV, 5, 6, 35; V, 6, 11, 13; VI, 4, 15, 16; VII, 20, 26; VIII, 1, 8, 9, 28, 29; IX, 9, 25, 38; X, 14, 32; XI, 4, 8; XII, 5; XIV, 44; XV, 7, 25, 36, 39, 40; XVI, 8, 9, 12; Luke I, 6, 8, 11, 13, 22, 24, 34, 38, 39, 56, 62, 64; II, 1, 2, 4, 6, 17, 47; III, 1, 7, 11, 12, 14, 15, 18, 21; IV, 21, 24, 38, 39, 42; V, 3, 4, 8, 15, 22; VI, 9, 30, 39, 48; VII, 1, 2, 9, 12, 16, 20, 21, 24, 36, 39, 42, 43, 48; VIII, 4, 8, 9, 19, 22, 24, 25, 27, 28, 30, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 38, 40, 42, 45, 47, 51, 52; IX, 1, 6, 7, 8, 12, 14, 16, 19, 20, 23, 27, 28, 32, 34, 37, 41, 42, 43, 44, 46, 49, 51, 54, 55, 57, 59, 60, 61, 62; X, 1, 2, 7, 17, 18, 30; XIV, 12, 15, 25; XV, 1, 3, 11, 14, 17, 20, 22, 25; XVI, 1, 3, 14, 22; XVII, 6, 7, 17, 20, 22; XVIII, 4, 6, 9, 15, 19, 22, 24, 26, 28, 31, 35, 36, 40; XIX, 8, 9, 11, 13, 16, 32, 33, 36, 37; XX, 3, 13, 14, 16, 23, 25, 27, 31, 39, 40, 41, 45.

John (where *þan* almost always has *-uh* preceding it): VI, (3), 4, 6, 10, 11, 23, 71; [Col. 1230] VII, 2, 9 (32), 39, 44; VIII, 35; IX, 14 (20), 31, 37; X, 22; XI, 1, 2, 5, 13, 18, 30, 37, 38, 46; XII, 6, 14, 16, 20, 33; XIII, 23, 25, 28, 30; XVII, 3; XVIII, 2, 5, 10, 14, 15, 40.

Romans (where, as always in the Epistles and in the *Skeireins*, *-uh* is placed before *þan*, except at 2 Cor. VIII, 22; *Skeireins* II, b; VI, d—unless *ïupaþroþ-þan* and *sumaiþ-þan* are to be read there): XII, 4; 1 Cor. IV, 7; VII, 6; IX, 23; X, 29; XI, 2, 3, 21; XII, 11, 12; XIV, 23; XV, 6, 15; XVI, 8; 2 Cor. II, 16; VI, 15, 16; VIII, 22; IX, 6; XII, 19; Gal. I, 22; II, 2; IV, 9; Eph. IV, 9, 11, 23, 26; 1 Thess. V, 14; 2 Tim. II, 20; Philem. 22; *Skeireins* II, b, d; III, a, b, c; V, a; VI, c, d; VII, a; VIII, a, b, c.

2) And, καί: Luke II, 37; 1 Cor. XV, 28 (Mark X, 28).

3) But also, δὲ καί: Mark XV, 40; Luke III, 12.

4) Therefore, οὖν: Matt. XXVII, 17; Luke (III, 18; VI, 9; X, 2) XIX, 12; John—where it occurs most frequently, yet in this ordinary sense it is not preceded by *-uh*—VI (3, 11), 43; VII, 16, 25, 28, 30, 32, 40, 45, 47; VIII, 19, 22, 28, 48; IX, 12, 15, 16, 18 (20), 24; XI, 3, 14, 17, 25, 31, 41, 47; XII, 4, 7; IX, 17, 28, 29, 35; XIII, 12, 24, 27; XIX, 1; Rom. VII, 3; 2 Cor. I, 17.

5) For, γάρ, always with preceding *-uh*: Matt. VI, 32; John V, 22; VI (40), 64; XII, 47; 2 Cor. IV, 15; Gal. VI, 13; 1 Thess. IV, 15; 1 Tim. II, 3.

6) Consequently, ἄρα: 1 Cor. V, 10 (XV, 14); for *þannu*, see under **Nu**.

7) Indeed, μέν: John XI, 6 (Luke III, 18); commonly with the adversative *ïþ, þan,* or *aþþan* (δέ): 1 Cor. XI, 21; Gal. IV, 23 (1 Cor. IV, 10), where it is solemnly placed before the word which it limits.

8) δὲ καί, “but also”: Mark XV, 40; Luke III, 12.

9) Combined with other particles:

a) *þan auk*: δέ, “but,” John XII, 10; γάρ, “for,” Luke VII, 8.

b) *auk þan*: “indeed,” *Skeireins* VI, d.

c) *nih þan* (*niþþan*): οὐδέ, οὐ δέ, μηδέ, “not even, nor”: Matt. IX, 17; Luke VI, 43, 44; IX, 3; John VII, 13; VIII, 42; 1 Cor. V, 8; XII, 21; 1 Tim. I, 4; *Skeireins* VII, c; οὐ γάρ, “for not”: Matt. IX, 13; John XII, 47; XVI, 13; 1 Cor. I, 17.

d) *þan jah*: δὲ καί, “but also”: Luke IV, 41; V, 10, 36; XVIII, 1; XIX, 19; 1 Tim. V, 24; δέ, “but”: Luke XVIII, 3; καί, “and”: Matt. IX, 17; 1 Thess. V, 25; 1 Tim. V, 25.

e) *jah þan*: καὶ γάρ, “for also”: Luke I, 66; 1 Cor. XII, 14; 2 Cor. II, 10 (in place of which Luke VII, 8 has *jah þan auk*); καὶ—δέ, “and—but”: Mark IV, 36; Luke II, 35; John VI, 51; VIII, 17; XV, 27; 1 Tim. III, 10; 2 Tim. III, 12; δὲ καί, “but also”: Luke VI, 6; 2 Cor. VI, 1; 2 Tim. II, 5; καὶ—οὖν, “and therefore”: John XVI, 22; καίπερ, “although”: Phil. III, 4; δέ, “but”: Luke XVII, 3; John XI, 42; XIV, 21; XVIII, 18; 1 Cor. XVI, 4; 2 Cor. VIII, 18 (XII, 1); γάρ, “for”: 2 Cor. XII, 1; καί, “and”: Mark III, 6; Luke VII, 8; XVII, 3; John VII, 33; XIV, 3, 7; οὖν, “therefore”: Mark III, 31.

f) *þanuh þan*, see under **þanuh**.

g) *ïþ þan*, see under **Iþ**.

**þANA-MAIS**, see under **Mais**.

**þANA-SEIþS**, see under **Seiþu**.

**þAN-NU**, see under **Nu**.

**þANUH** (before þ also *þanuþ-*), 1) then, τότε: Matt. VIII, 26; IX, 6; XIV, 25, 29, 37; XI, 20; XXV, 41, 44, 45; XXVI, 3, 67, 74; XXVII, 3, 9, 13, 58; Luke XIV, 10, 21; John VII, 10; VIII, 28; XII, 16; XVI, 25 (Greek ὅτε, “when”); 1 Cor. XV, 54; Col. III, 4; 1 Thess. V, 3.

2) But, δέ: Matt. IX, 25, 32; Mark IV, 29; Luke VIII, 54; IX, 12, 13; X, 28; XV, 28; John VI, 12; XVIII, 28; 1 Cor. XV, 28, 54.

3) And, καί: Mark X, 13; 1 Cor. XIV, 25; see the note on Matt. IX, 2.

4) Therefore, οὖν: Mark XII, 6; John VI, 13, 34, 52, 60, 68; VII, 3, 11, 32, 43; VIII, 13, 21, 31, 41, 52, 57, 59; IX, 8, 10, 25, 26, 28; X, 7, 19, 24; XI, 12, 16, 21, 33, 38, 45; XII, 19; XIII, 22, 36; XVIII, 24, 38; XIX, 13.

5) Thus, ἄρα: 1 Cor. XV, 18; see the note on Rom. VII, 3.

*þanuh þan* (*þanuþ-þan*): τότε οὖν, “then therefore,” John XI, 14; XIX, 1; τότε μέν, “then indeed,” John XI, 6; τότε καί, “then also,” 1 Cor. XV, 28; δέ, “but,” Luke I, 26 (καὶ οὕτω, “and thus,” 1 Cor. XIV, 25).

*þanuh þan sveþauh*: ὅμως μέντοι, “yet nevertheless”: John XII, 42.

**þANDE** (þandei Luke I, 34; XVI, 3; Rom. XI, 16, 21; Gal. VI, 10; Phil. I, 18):

1) If, εἰ: Matt. VI, 30; John V, 47; XIII, 17; 1 Cor. XV, 12; Gal. III, 29; Phil. I, 18 (πλήν, “only”); εἰ δέ, “but if”: John VIII, 46; Rom. XI, 16; Gal. IV, 7; εἰ γάρ, “for if”: Rom. XI, 21.

2) Because, that, ὅτι: [Col. 1331] Luke II, 30; XVI, 3; John V, 38; IX, 16; 1 Cor. XV, 20; Phil. I, 18; ἐπεί, “since”: Luke I, 34.

3) While, until, ἕως or ὡς: John XII, 35, 36; Gal. VI, 10.

**þAN-EI**, see the notes on Luke V, 24; Matt. XXV, 40.

**EI-þAN**, therefore, οὖν: John IX, 41; *Skeireins* III, b; IV, a; V, d; VI, a; ὥστε, “so that”: 1 Cor. XI, 27.

**MIþ-þAN**, sometimes, now: *Skeireins* II, a, b, c.

**MIþ-þANEI** (miþþane Luke II, 43), when, while, ἡνίκα: 2 Cor. III, 15, 16. It is ordinarily used in paraphrasing:

a) Participial constructions: Matt. IX, 18, *miþþanei ïs rodida þata*, “while he was speaking these things” (ταῦτα αὐτοῦ λαλοῦντος); Luke IV, 40.

b) The infinitive with ἐν: Matt. XXVII, 12, *miþþanei vrohiþs vas*, “while he was being accused” (ἐν τῷ κατηγορεῖσθαι αὐτόν); Mark IV, 4; Luke I, 8; II, 6, 27, 43; V, 1, 12; VIII, 5, 40, 42; IX, 18, 29, 33, 36; XVII, 11, 14; XVIII, 35.

**NAUH-þAN**, still, ἔτι: Luke I, 15; VIII, 49; IX, 42. *nauhuþ-þan*, “still also,” ἔτι δὲ καί: Luke XIV, 26.

**Ni—nauhþan**, not yet, οὔπω: John VI, 17.

**NAUH-þANUH**, still, ἔτι: Mark V, 35; XII, 6; XIV, 43; Luke XIV, 32; XV, 20; ἔσχατον, “lastly”: Neh. V, 15.

**Ni—nauhþanuh; nauhþanuh—ni**, not yet, οὔπω: John III, 24; XII, 39; XI, 30; VII, 30, 39; VIII, 20; Rom. IX, 11; οὐδέπω, “not yet at all”: John VII, 39 following.

**JU-þAN**, already, ἤδη: Mark IV, 37; XI, 11; XIII, 28; XV, 42, 44; Luke VII, 6; IX, 12; XIX, 37; John VI, 17; VII, 14; IX, 22; XI, 17, 39.

*Juþan—ni*, no longer, μηκέτι: Mark I, 45; II, 2.

**þANKJAN**, the same as **þagkjan**.

**þANKS**, the same as **þagks**.

**þANJAN**, see under **þinan**.

**þAU** (þauh Mark X, 15; XIII, 20; John XI, 32; 2 Cor. XIII, 5; compare Old Norse *þo*, Anglo-Saxon *þeah*, Old High German *doh*, Old Frisian *dach, thach*, English *though*, Swedish *dock*, Danish *dog*, Modern High German *doch*; Gr. III, 274; Gf. V, 68; Rchth. 1067):

1) Therefore, then, perhaps; used especially in questions, negative statements, or subordinate clauses. ἄρα, “then”: 1 Cor. XV, 14, *jabai Xristus ni urrais, svare þau jas-so mereins unsara*, “if Christ has not risen, then our preaching is vain”; ἄν, a conditional particle: Luke IX, 46, *galaiþ mitons ïn ïns þata, warjis þau ïze maists vesi*, “there arose a thought among them, who then might be greatest”; 1 Cor. VII, 5, μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε, “do not deprive [one another],” *ïzvara misso, niba þau us gaqissai*, “except perhaps by agreement”; καί, “also”: 1 Cor. XV, 29, 30, *jabai allis dauþans ni urreisand, duwe þau daupjand faur ïns. duwe þau veis bireikjai sijum*, “if the dead do not rise at all, why then are they baptized for them? Why then are we in danger?” κἄν, “even if”: 2 Cor. XI, 16, *ïbai was mik muni unfropana. aiþþau vaila þau sve unfrodana nimaiþ*, “if you think me foolish, then at least receive me as foolish”; Mark VI, 56, *bedun ïna ei þau skauta vastjos ïs attaitokeina*, “they begged him that they might perhaps touch the fringe of his garment.”

So also where the Greek uses no corresponding particle: Phil. III, 13, *broþrjus ïk mik silban ni þau man gatahan*, “brothers, I do not consider myself yet to have grasped [it]”; I, 22, *wa þau valjau, ni kann*, “but what I might choose, I do not know”; Luke XVI, 4, *andþahta mik wa taujau, ei þau, biþe afsatjaidau is fauragaggja, andnimaina mik*, “I have considered what I shall do, so that, when I am removed from the stewardship, they may receive me.”

2) In the consequent clause of hypothetical sentences, where it corresponds to Greek ἄν: Mark XIII, 20, *ni frauja gamaurgidedi þans dagans, ni þauh ganesi ainhun leike*, “unless the Lord had shortened those days, no flesh would be saved”; Luke VII, 39; X, 13; XVII, 6; John VII, 46; VIII, 19, 42; IX, 41; XI, 21, 32; XVIII, 30; Rom. IX, 29; 1 Cor. XI, 31; compare Matt. V, 20; Mark X, 15; XI, 26; *Skeireins* I, c.

3) In the second member of a double question: or, whether, ἤ: Matt. IX, 5, *waþar ïst raihtis azetizo qiþan, afletanda þus fravaurhteis, þau qiþan urreis*, “which is easier: to say, ‘your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘arise’?” Matt. XXVII, 17; Mark II, 9; Luke VI, 9; John IX, 2; XVIII, 34; Rom. VIII, 35; 1 Cor. X, 22; XI, 22. Sometimes interrogative *-uh* or *-u*, “or,” follows: Matt. XI, 3, *þu ïs sa qimanda þau anþarizuh beidaima*, “are you the coming one, or are we to await another?” Mark XI, 30; XII, 14; Luke VII, 19; XX, 4, 22; John VII, 17; Rom. IX, 21; 1 Cor. IX, 6; 2 Cor. XIII, 5; Gal. III, 2, 5.

4) After comparatives: than, ἤ: Matt. V, 20; XI, 24; Mark VI, 11; IX, 43, 45, 47; X, 25; XIV, 5; Luke V, 23; X, 12, 14; XVI, 17; XVIII, 14, 25; Rom. XIII, 11; 1 Cor. VII, 9; XI, 22; XV, 6; Gal. IV, 27; Eph. III, 20; 1 Tim. I, 4; 2 Tim. III, 4; also after οὕτω, “thus”: Luke XV, 7; ἤπερ, “rather than”: John XII, 43; παρ’ ὅ, “beyond what”: Rom. XII, 3, *ni mais fraþjan þau skuli fraþjan*, “not to think more highly than he ought to think,” μὴ ὑπερφρονεῖν παρ’ ὃ δεῖ φρονεῖν.

**EI-þAU**, see the note on Luke XIV, 32.

**SVE-þAUH** (see the note on Matt. VII, 15):

1) Nevertheless, πλὴν: [Col. 1332] Matt. XI, 22, 24; Luke VI, 35; X, 11, 14, 20; XVIII, 8; Gal. VI, 13; μέντοι, “yet, however”: John VII, 13; XII, 42.

2) Indeed, at least; or it otherwise gives emphasis to the word to which it belongs, μέν: Mark IX, 12; X, 39; Rom. VII, 19; Gal. IV, 8; Phil. III, 1, 4; Col. II, 13; compare 2 Cor. XII, 12. Hence:

3) It stands for enclitic:

a) -γε in *jabai sveþauh*, εἴγε, “if indeed”: 2 Cor. V, 3; Eph. III, 2; IV, 21; Col. I, 23.

b) -περ in *sveþauh jabai*, εἴπερ, “if indeed”: Rom. VIII, 9; see the note on 2 Thess. I, 6.

It also stands for:

c) -τε in *sveþauh jabai*, ἐάντε, “whether … or,” or ἐὰν καί, “even if”: 2 Cor. X, 8.

*Aþþan sveþauh*, nevertheless, πλὴν: Luke XIX, 27; Phil. III, 16; IV, 14; μὲν οὖν (μενοῦνγε), “indeed then / certainly”: Phil. III, 8.

*ïþ sveþauh*, nevertheless, πλὴν: Luke XVIII, 8.

*unte sveþauh*, because indeed, ὡς ὅτι: 2 Cor. V, 19.

*sveþauh ei*, although, though, even if, εἰ καί: 2 Cor. XII, 15.

*sveþauh ni*, “not as though,” οὐχ οἷον ὅτι: Rom. IX, 6.

**þAURBAN** (Old Norse and Old Saxon *þurfan*, Anglo-Saxon *þearfan*, Old High German *durfan, darben, bidarbi*, Old Frisian *thurva*, Danish *dor*, Dutch *derven*, Modern High German *(be-)dürfen, darben*; Gf. V, 205; Rchth. 1081), anomalous conjugation; þarf, þaurbun, þaurfta: to have need, χρείαν ἔχειν: Matt. VI, 8; IX, 12; XXVI, 65; Mark II, 17, 25; XIV, 63; Luke V, 31; XV, 7; John XIII, 29; XVI, 30; 1 Cor. XII, 21; Eph. IV, 28; 1 Thess. IV, 9, 12; V, 1; ἀνάγκην ἔχειν, “to have necessity”: Luke XIV, 18; χρῄζειν, “to need”: Matt. VI, 32.

**GA-þAURBS**, adjective: self-controlled, temperate, ἐγκρατής: Titus I, 8.

**þAURFTS**, adjective, comparative *þaurftiza*:

1) Necessary, ἀναγκαῖος: 1 Cor. XII, 22; Phil. I, 24.

2) Useful, ὠφέλιμος: 2 Tim. III, 16.

**NAUDI-þAURFTS**, needy, necessary, ἀναγκαῖος: 2 Cor. IX, 5; *Skeireins* II, c.

**þAURFTS**, feminine: need, necessity, χρεία: Phil. II, 25; *Skeireins* VII, b; ἀνάγκη: 1 Cor. VII, 26. *mis þaurft ïst* with the genitive, “I have need,” χρείαν ἔχω: Luke XIX, 34. *þaurft gataujan sis*, “to make advantage for oneself,” to profit, ὠφελεῖσθαι: Luke IX, 25. *du þaurftai fairrinnan*, “to be fitting,” ἀνήκειν: Eph. V, 4.

**þARBS**, adjective:

1) Necessary, ἀναγκαῖος: Phil. II, 25 (perhaps *þaurb* should be read here?).

2) Needy, χρείαν ἔχων, “having need”: Luke IX, 11.

**þARBA**, masculine: poor person, beggar, πτωχός: Mark X, 21; John XII, 5, 6.

**ALA-þARBA**, needy, destitute; *alaþarbavairþan*, “to be in want,” ὑστερεῖσθαι: Luke XV, 14.

**þARBA**, feminine: want, deficiency, ὑστέρημα: 2 Cor. VIII, 14; XI, 9; ὑστέρησις: Phil. IV, 11. *þarbos þulan*, “to be in want, suffer need,” ὑστερεῖσθαι: Phil. IV, 12.

**GA-þARBAN**, second conjugation: to refrain, abstain, ἀπέχεσθαι: 1 Tim. IV, 3.

**GA-þARBJAN**, second conjugation: to abstain; *gaþarbjan sik* with the genitive, “to exercise self-control,” ἐγκρατεύεσθαι: 1 Cor. IX, 25.

**þAURNUS** (Old Norse, Old Saxon, Anglo-Saxon, and Old Frisian *þorn*, Old and Modern High German *dorn*, English *thorn*, Danish *torn*, Swedish *torne*, Dutch *doorne, deurne*; Gr. III, 370; Gf. V, 226; Rchth. 1076), masculine: thorn, ἄκανθα: Matt. VII, 16; Mark IV, 7, 18; Luke VI, 44; VIII, 7, 14; John XIX, 2.

**þAURNEINS**, adjective: thorny, ἀκάνθινος: Mark XV, 17; John XIX, 5.

**þAURP** (Old Norse and Anglo-Saxon *þorp*, Old Saxon and Old Frisian *thorp*, Old and Modern High German *dorf*; Gr. III, 418; Gf. V, 224; Rchth. 1076), neuter: field, farm, ἀγρός: Neh. V, 16.

**þAURSUS**, see under **þairsan**.

**þAURSTEI**, see under **þairsan**.

**þAR**, see under **þata**.

**þARA**, masculine proper name: Terah, Θάρα: Luke III, 34.

**þARBS**, see under **þaurban**.

**þARIHS** (see the note on Matt. IX, 16), adjective: unfulled, new, ἄγναφος: Matt. IX, 16.

**þATA**, neuter; **sa**, masculine; **so**, feminine (Old Norse *þat, sa, su*, Old Saxon *that*, Anglo-Saxon *þæt, se, seo*, Old Frisian *thet*, Old High German *daz*, English *that*, Swedish and Danish *det*, Modern High German *das*; Greek τό; Bopp 80, 83; Gr. I, 790; Gf. V, 2; Rchth. 1069).

I. Demonstrative pronoun:

1) Substantively:

a) He, that one, αὐτός: Matt. V, 8, 32; VI, 8, 26; VII, 13, 14, 24; VIII, 17; IX, 22; X, 39; XI, 12, 14; XXV, 44; XXVI, 70, 73; XXVII, 6, 7; Mark I, 19, 31; II, 8, 21; IV, 5, 30; V, 12, 23; VI, 3, 17; VIII, 7, 35; IX, 7, 16 (where its use for αὑτούς, “themselves,” is incorrect; this error arose because the translator read αὐτούς, “them,” without the diacritical mark; compare Prolegomena, cols. 484 following), 25, 28, 43; X, 11, 14, 16; XII, 6, 17, 21, 22, 23; VIII, 28; XIV, 5, 13, 15, 44, 69, 70; XV, 24, 29; Luke I, 36; II, 6; III, 15; IV, 6; XXVI, 35, 38, 41; VI, 47; VII, 13, 42; VIII, 5, 7, 32, 52; IX, 24, 35, 43; X, 21; XIV, 18, 19; XV, 4; XVII, 31, 33; XVIII, 5, 16; XIX, 9, 23, 31, 33, 34, 41; XX, 30, 33; John V, 36; VI, 7, 50, 60; IX, 9, 15, 17, 27; X, 3, 12, 17, 18, 20, 27, 28, 29, 32; XII, 7, 11; XIII, 17; XIV, 10, 21; XVI, 4; XVII, 10, 21; XVIII, 11, 25, 38; Rom. VII, 11; VIII, 9 (see the note on that passage); IX, 26; X, 5; XIII, 3; 1 Cor. VII, 12, 13; IX, 7; Gal. IV, 24; Eph. II, 10, 14; IV, 10; V, 25, 26; VI, 18; Phil. IV, 3; Col. II, 14, 15; III, 7, 19; 1 Thess. IV, 10; 1 Tim. I, 18; IV, 16; 2 Tim. I, 15 (where all Greek manuscripts read ὧν, “of whom”; therefore *þizeei* should perhaps be read instead of *þizei*, likewise Phil. III, 19); II, 10; Philem. 17; Neh. VII, 2; *Skeireins* III, c; VI, b, d.

b) This, that, οὗτος: Matt. V, 37; VII, 12; VIII, 9, 27; IX, 3, 18, 28; XI, 10; XXV, 46; XXVI, 71; XXVII, 47, 54; Mark I, 27; II, 7, 8; III, 35; IV, 18, 20, 41; V, 32, 43; VI, 2, 3, 16; VII, 2; VIII, 4; IX, 7, 21; X, 7, 20; XI, 3, 28, 29, 33; XII, 7, 11, 30, 31; XIII, 29; XIV, 8, 9, 60, 69; XVI, 12; Luke I, 18, 19, 20, 34, 36, 43; II, 12, 34; III, 20; IV, 22, 48; V, 6, 21, 27; VI, 3, 23; VII, 4, 8, 9, 18, 27, 39, 49; VIII, 1, 8, 11, 13, 14, 15, 21, 25, 42; IX, 9, 21, 34, 35, 48; X, 1, 11, 20, 21, 28; XIV, 15, 21; XV, 2, 26; XVI, 1, 2, 14; XVII, 17, 30; XVIII, 4, 11, 14, 21, 22, 23, 34, 36; XIX, 11, 14, 19, 28, 40; XX, 2, 8, 12, 13, 14, 28, 30; John I, 29; III, 26, 32; VI, 1, 5, 9, 14, 42, 46, 50, 52, 58, 59, 61, 66, 71; VII, 1, 4, 15, 25, 26, 27, 31, 32, 40, 41; VIII, 26, 28, 30; IX, 2, 3, 6, 8, 9, 19, 20, 22, 23, 29, 30, 31, 33, 40; X, 25, 41; XI, 4, 7, 11, 26, 28, 37, 43; XII, 16, 21, 36, 41; XIII, 17, 21, 24, 35; XIV, 12, 13, 25; XV, 8, 11, 12, 13, 17, 21; XVI, 1, 3, 4, 6, 17, 18, 19, 25, 30, 33; XVII, 1, 11, 13, 20, 25; XVIII, 1, 8, 17, 21, 22, 30, 34, 37, 38; XIX, 12; Rom. VII, 15, 16, 20; VIII, 37; IX, 6; XI, 24, 27, 31; XII, 20; XII, 11; XIV, 13, 18; 1 Cor. IV, 4; V, 3; VII, 20, 24, 26; IX, 3, 8; XI, 22, 24, 25; XII, 11; XV, 50; XVI, 3, 17; 2 Cor. II, 16; V, 2, 15; VIII, 10, 20; IX, 5; X, 7, 11; XII, 14; XIII, 1, 10; Gal. II, 18; V, 17, 21; VI, 12; Eph. II, 8; III, 14; IV, 17; V, 5; VI, 8; Phil. I, 18, 19, 22, 25, 28; II, 5; III, 15; IV, 8, 9; Col. III, 20; IV, 4, 11; 1 Thess. II, 3; IV, 3; V, 18; 2 Thess. III, 10, 14; 1 Tim. III, 10, 14; IV, 6, 11, 15; V, 4, 7, 21; VI, 2, 11; 2 Tim. I, 12; II, 2; III, 1, 5, 6, 8; Philem. 18; *Skeireins* I, a, b; II, d; III, a; IV, c, d; V, a, d; VII, a, d; VIII, d.

c) This, that, ἐκεῖνος: Mark VII, 15, 20; XII, 4; Luke XIX, 4; John VI, 57; IX, 12, 28, 37; X, 16; XII, 48; XIII, 26; XIV, 21, 26; XV, 27; XVII, 24; Rom. XIV, 14.

d) In the preceding sense, where it is not expressed in Greek: Mark I, 42; VII, 36; X, 9; XI, 23; Luke I, 4; IV, 6; VII, 43; John XVIII, 13; XIX, 5; Gal. V, 10.

At John XVI, 9, *þata* must be deleted as destructive of the sense; see the note on that passage. The same [pronoun], immediately followed by the relative *saei* or *ïze*, see under **þatei**, B 1), and under **Ize**.

f) This very [thing], αὐτὸς οὗτος, in the formula *du þamma*, εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο, “for this very purpose”: 2 Cor. V, 5; Eph. VI, 18 (and probably also in the corrupt passage Rom. IX, 17, where *du þamma urraisida* should perhaps be read instead of *ïn þize jah raisida* [where no word has been corrected]).

g) Such, ὁ τοιοῦτος: Mark X, 14; see the note on that passage.

h) It is used for the relative ὅς: Luke.

IX.31, “two men were speaking with him, who were Moses and Elijah; who, appearing in glory, spoke of his departure”; Phil. III.19, “whose god is the belly”; 2 Tim. I.15, “all who are in Asia turned away from me.” “Among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes.” [Col. 1334] Perhaps in these latter two passages there is a scribal error for *þizeei*; and in the former passage the translator erred through the absence of a diacritical mark (οι); cf. Prolegomena, col. 484 ff.; i) the expressions *afar þata*, *ïn þis*, etc., see under **Afar** and **In** I.C.—2) As adjective:

a) “the same,” αὐτὸς ὁ: Luke II.38; VII.21; X.7, 21; XX.19; John V.36.

b) “this very,” ὁ αὐτός: John XIV.11.

c) “this,” οὗτος ὁ or ὁ οὗτος: Matt. V.19; VI.32; VII.28; IX.26; X.23, 42; XI.16; XXV.40, 45; Mark I.27; IV.13; VII.6, 23, 29; VIII.12; IX.29; X.5, 30; XI.23; XII.10, 16; XIV.9, 71; XV.39; Luke I.24, 29, 39, 61, 65, 66; II.15, 17, 19, 25, 52; IV.23, 36; VII.17, 31, 44; VIII.9, 13; IX.28, 44, 45, 48; X.5; XIV.30; XV.3; XVII.6, 25, 34; XVIII.5, 9, 11, 30, 34; XIX.9, 15, 41; XX.2, 9, 17, 19, 34; John III.29; VI.34, 51, 58, 60; VII.8, 36, 46; VIII.20, 23; IX.16, 24, 39; X.6, 16, 18, 19, 21; XI.4; XII.5, 18, 27, 30, 31; XVIII.17, 29, 36; XIX.8, 13; Rom. IX.9; XI.25; XII.2; XIII.9; 1 Cor. I.20; V.10; XI.25, 26, 27; XIV.21; XV.19, 53, 54; 2 Cor. I.15; III.10; IV.1, 4, 7; V.4; VII.1, 11; VIII.6, 7; IX.3, 4, 12, 13; XI.10, 17; XII.13; Gal. VI.16; Eph. I.21; II.2; III.8; VI.12; Col. I.27; IV.16; 1 Thess. III.3; IV.18; V.27; 1 Tim. I.18; Tit. I.13; Neh. V.13; VI.16; *Skeir.* VIII.a, c, d.

Sometimes, moreover, following the Greek, it is postponed: Mark VIII.12, *kunja þamma*, “that generation”; Luke III.8, *stainam þaim*, “those stones”; IV.21; VI.12; XX.16; John VII.8; Rom. VII.23; 1 Cor. XIV.21; 2 Cor. II.6; VII.11; Eph. III.8; VI.12; 2 Tim. II.19; and 2 Cor. I.12, *woftuli unsara so*, “our conduct, this” (where in our translation “this” must be changed to “these”). Luke II.7, *ïn stada þamma*, “in that place,” also belongs here: the Gothic translator understood the article (ἐν τῷ καταλύματι, “in the lodging”) demonstratively, as ἐν τῷ καταλύματι τούτῳ, “in this lodging.”

d) “that,” ἐκεῖνος ὁ or ὁ ἐκεῖνος: Matt. XXVII.19; Luke XIV.21; XX.18; John XVIII.13.

## II. The Article

The article, “this” (masculine, feminine, and neuter), corresponds to Greek ὁ, ἡ, τό. Yet it is not employed wherever the Greek uses it, but—having regard to its demonstrative character—only:

1) To define objects: namely, those previously mentioned or understood.

α) Where the object before which the article stands has already been mentioned: Matt. V.25; VI.23; VIII.8, 13, 15, 24, 33; IX.2, 6, 15, 16, 22, 23, 24, 25, 28; XXVII.3, 5, 11, 14, 15, 42, 44, 58, 59, 60, 61, 64, 66; Mark I.20, 29, 31, 34, 42; II.4, 5, 9, 10, 20, 22, 28; III.3, 5, 9, 27; IV.7, 10, 13, 15, 16, 17, 19, 20, 27, 28, 33, 36, 39; V.4, 8, 11, 12, 13, 14, 16, 33, 35, 38, 40, 41, 42; VI.26, 27; VII.17, 26, 30; VIII.2, 6, 23, 26; IX.7, 9, 17, 20, 24, 10, 14, 24, 49, 51; XI.5, 7, 16, 20; XII.2, 8, 9, 19, 22, 32; XIII.20; XIV.4, 5, 7, 52, 61; XV.20, 30, 32, 45, 46; XVI.2, 3, 4, 5, 8; Luke I.13, 18, 19, 21, 27, 28, 34, 35, 38, 44, 59, 80; II.10, 13, 15, 16, 17, 20, 40; IV.2, 6, 17, 20, 28, 33, 38, 39; V.2, 3, 11, 13, 20, 24, 30, 35, 37; VI.5, 42, 48, 49; VII.6, 12, 15, 36, 38, 44, 50; VIII.7, 11, 12, 13, 15, 23, 29, 32, 33, 35, 47, 49; IX.34, 35, 36, 38; XIV.21, 22, 23; XV.21, 22; XVI.3, 8; XVII.22; XVIII.11, 13, 16; XIX.15, 24, 35, 37, 47; XX.10, 14, 15, 16, 28, 32; John VI.11, 14, 21, 22, 26, 33, 51; VII.10, 11, 17, 19, 45, 46; VIII.32; IX.6, 10; XIV.21, 30; X.3, 4, 7, 8, 12, 13, 15, 38; XI.3, 38, 39, 41; XII.6; XIII.27, 30; XIV.6, 8, 9, 26; XVIII.11, 15, 16; Rom. VII.2, 3; XI.17, 18; 1 Cor. I.25; VII.12, 13, 19; IX.7; XI.27, 28; XII.15, 16; 2 Cor. III.16; V.4, 8; IX.4; X.10; Gal. IV.21, 30; V.13; VI.8; 1 Thess. V.4; Neh. V.16; VI.15; VII.1; *Skeir.* V.c; VII.b, c; VIII.d.

β) Where the object to which the article refers corresponds to a preceding synonym, or is a species of that synonym as genus, or a part of it as whole, etc.: Matt. VIII.16, *þans ahmans*, “the spirits,” and v. 31, *þo skohsla*, “the herds,” after *daimonarjos*, “demoniacs”; Matt. IX.33, *sa dumba*, “the mute man,” after *bauda*, “a mute person”; XXVII.6, *þans skattans*, “the treasury,” after *silubr*, “silver”; Mark I.10, *us þamma watin*, “out of the water,” namely the Jordan; V.29, *þamma slaha*, “the flow,” namely a flow of blood; VI.22, *þizai maujai*, “the girl,” after *dauhtar*, “daughter”; v. 25, *þamma þiudana*, “the king,” namely Herod; IX.24, *þis barnis*, “this child,” after v. 17, *sunus*, “son”; XI.2, *þo baurg*, “the town,” after *haim*, “village”; XIV.14, *þamma heiwafraujin*, “the master of the house,” after *þadei*—that is, *ïn þanei gard ïnngaggiþ*, “into which house you enter”; Luke IV.35; V.19; VII.20, 24; VIII.29, 33, 36; IX.42; X.20; XX.10; John VI.10; XII.8; XIV.4; XVI.21; XVIII.2, 12; 2 Cor. V.6 (in the preceding passage the body had been discussed figuratively).

γ) Where the substantive itself has not previously been named, but a word of the same root, or of the same sense as its root, has: Matt. XXVII.54, *þo reiron*, “the earthquake,” v. 51 having *airþa reiraida*, “the earth quaked”; Mark XII.7, *þata arbi*, “the inheritance,” after *arbinumja*, “heir”; XIV.56; Luke XX.14; John IX.6; XII.3; 1 Cor. I.21; VII.19; 2 Cor. XI.17. Mark VI.26, *þize aiþe*, “because of the oaths,” v. 23 having *svor*, “he swore”; Luke VI.49, *so usvalteins*, “the collapse,” after *gadraus*, “it fell”; John XIV.4–5, *þana wig*, “the way,” after *gaggan*, “to go”; VII.40, *þize vaurde*, “the words,” after *þatuh qaþ*, “he said”; and so often *þata vaurd*, “the word,” Mark I.45; VIII.32; IX.10, 32; X.22; Luke V.15.

b) [Objects] defined by what follows, namely:

α) By an attached relative clause: Mark II.4, *þata badi ana þammei lag*, “the bed on which he lay”; X.39, *þana stikl þanei ik driggka*, “the cup which I drink”; XII.33, *ïn þizai usstassai þan usstandand*, “in the resurrection, when they rise”; XIII.20; XIV.72; XVI.6; Luke II.17, 43, 50; IV.29; V.9; VII.39; VIII.38; John V.36; VI.23, 63; IX.24; X.40; XI.30; XII.38; XIV.10, 12, 24; XV.3, 20, 24; XVII.5, 8; XVIII.9; Rom. IX.26; 2 Cor. I.4; Eph. III.3, 4, 5 (*so runa—þatei* for *soei*); IV.1; Col. IV.17. Also Luke I.4, *þize bi þoei galaisiþs is vaurde*, “of the words concerning which you have been instructed.” Hence also Matt. IX.15, *und þata weilos þei*, “for as long a time as,” for ἐφ’ ὅσον.

β) In the formula *triggwa þata vaurd*, “trustworthy is the saying,” 1 Tim. I.15; III.1, 4, 9; 2 Tim. II.11, by which notable propositions are introduced, being defined only by what follows; likewise *Skeir.* V.d, *þata qiþlo habes*, “you have the saying.” Similarly Mark XIII.28, *þo gajukon*, “the fig tree,” where the comparison follows.

c) [Objects] more strictly defined by an addition to the phrase itself:

α) By adjectives and numerals: Matt. V.26, *þana minnistan kintu*, “the smallest coin”; VII.17; XXVII.46, 53, 61, 64; VIII.31; IX.37; XI.27; XIV.43, 54, 55, 60, 61, 63, 66; XV.1, 3, 10, 11, 31; Luke III.7; IV.36, 43; V.37; VII.10; VIII.15; IX.26; XIV.9, 10; XV.13; XVIII.11; XIX.30, 47; John VI.44, 54; VII.24; X.3; XI.24, 47; XII.10; XVIII.10, 19, 22, 26; XIX.5, 6; Rom. VII.22; XI.24; 1 Cor. V.7; VII.26; IX.5; XI.25; XV.47; 2 Cor. III.14; IV.16; Gal. II.4, 13; IV.9; Eph. II.4; III.5; IV.22, 24, 30; VI.13; Phil. III.2; Col. III.9; IV.15; 1 Thess. V.27; 1 Tim. I.10, 11; IV.18; VI.12; 2 Tim. I.14; II.16, 23; IV.8; Tit. II.1; *Skeir.* II.b, c, d; III.b; IV.c; VI.b. Mark VIII.6, *þans sibun hlaibans*, “the seven loaves”; XIX.20; Luke IX.1, 16, 32.

The constructions John XVIII.16, *sa siponeis anþar*, “the other disciple,” and Luke V.7, *ba þo skipa*, “both boats,” are not customary. Likewise, the substantive must be supplied from what precedes: Matt. V.39, *þo anþara*, “the other [cheek]”; Mark II.21, *sa niuja*, “the new [piece]”; XII.20; Luke V.36, 39; VI.6, 10; XV.4, 12; XIX.16; XX.19; John X.4, 14; 1 Cor. XV.48; 2 Cor. IV.16. Mark XII.22, *þai sibun*, “the seven,” that is, brothers; v. 23; Luke XV.4; XVII.17; XX.31, 33.

β) By participles: Mark XI.10, *so qimandei þiudangardi*, “the coming kingdom”; XV.7, *sa haitana Barabbas*, “the one called Barabbas”; Luke I.1, *þos gafullaveisidons waihtins*, “the things accomplished”; III.7; VII.9; John VI.12; Rom. VII.17; X.5; 2 Cor. XI.5; XIII.3; Gal. II.4; Eph. II.11; III.8; 1 Tim. IV.18; V.21; *Skeir.* I.c; II.a; VII.d. Also Mark V.3, *þo maht usgaggandein*, “the power going out”; v. 31, *þo managein þreihandein*, “the crowd pressing.” With the substantive supplied: Luke XV.4, *þamma fralusanin*, “the lost [sheep]”; Rom. XIII.1; 1 Tim. V.6.

γ) By adverbs, which in this construction have adjectival force: Mark I.38, *þaim bisunjane haimom*, “the neighbouring villages”; Luke IV.37; IX.12; Luke VII.11, *sa afar dags*, “the next day”; 1 Cor. IV.11, *þo nu weila*, “the present time”; 2 Cor. VIII.14; Gal. IV.25; 2 Tim. IV.10; Gal. IV.26, *so iupa Iairusalem*, “the Jerusalem above”; Phil. III.14; 1 Tim. IV.8, *libainais þizos nu*, “of the life now [present].”

δ) By prepositional phrases: Mark IV.19, *þai bi þata anþar lustjus*, “the other desires”; V.4, *þo ana fotum eisarna*, “the irons upon his feet”; Luke VI.17, *þize faur marein Tyre*, “of those from the region of Tyre”; Rom. X.6, *so us galaubeinai garaihtei*, “the righteousness from faith”; XI.21; 2 Cor. VII.10; VIII.7; IX.2; XII.11; Col. II.14; IV.12, 15; 1 Tim. IV.14; V.16; VI.3; *Skeir.* I.d; III.b; IV.a. *Skeir.* III.a, *so garehsus bi ina*, “the righteousness concerning him.”

ε) By genitives of substantives: Matt. VIII.12, *þai sunjus þiudangardjos*, “the sons of the kingdom”; VIII.31; XXVII.7, 58; Mark I.24; VI.21; VIII.15; XV.9, 26, 32, 43; Luke IV.22, 34; VIII.24, 44; IX.43, 47; XVI.8; XVIII.44; XIX.47; John VI.4; IX.11; XVIII.39; Rom. VI.23; IX.8; X.1; 2 Cor. I.18, 24; Eph. III.9; IV.30; Phil. III.18; Neh. VI.17.

The construction is rarer in 1 Cor. I.16, *þans staifanaus gadaukans*, “the household of Stephanas”; 2 Cor. VIII.8, *þizos anþaraize usdaudeins*, “the earnestness of others”; *Skeir.* II.d, *and þana þize laist*, “and the trace of these.” Combined with α): Mark XIV.12, *þamma frumistin daga azyme*, “on the first day of unleavened bread”; Eph. III.10, *so managfalþo handugei guþs*, “the manifold wisdom of God.” The genitive itself can also take the article: Luke VII.31, *þans mans þis kunjis*, “the people of this generation”; VIII.51; XX.13; John XII.31; XVI.11; XVIII.26; 1 Cor. I.21; 2 Cor. IX.4; XI.17; Eph. II.2; Eph. III.19, *þo mikilon þis kunþjis friaþwa*, “the great love of this knowledge.”

ζ) With possessive pronouns: *sa þiumagus meins*, “my servant,” Matt. VIII.8; Mark III.33, 34; Luke VII.7; XIV.24; XV.24; XIX.23; John I.29; VI.55; VII.16 (*so meina laiseins*, “my teaching”); VIII.14, 54; XII.26; XIV.24; Rom. IX.25; XVI.21; 2 Tim. I.12; *Skeir.* IV.a. Matt. V.24, *þo giba þeina*, “your gift”; VI.4; IX.6, 14; Mark II.9, 11, 18 (*þai þeinai siponjos*, “your disciples”; likewise Luke V.33); Mark III.5; V.34; VII.5; Luke II.48; V.14, 24; VI.10; IX.41; XV.30; XIX.20, 39, 42; John VIII.13; XVII.6; XVIII.35. Matt. VI.12, *þaim skulam unsaraim*, “our debts”; John XIX.7; 1 Cor. XV.14; 2 Cor. I.18; II.5; IV.16; Col. I.7. Matt. V.47, *þans frijonds izvarans*, “your friends”; IX.11; Mark VII.9, 13; XIII.18; Luke V.4; VI.35; X.11; John VIII.4; IX.19; XVI.20, 22; 1 Cor. XV.17; 2 Cor. VII.15 (*þo izwara ufhausein*, “your boasting”); IX.15. Matt. II.1, *þaim siponjam seinaim*, “his disciples”; Mark I.18; III.9; VIII.33; XIII.27; Luke I.70; VII.1; X.2; XV.13; XVIII.7; John XI.16; Eph. I.6.

η) Also with *is, þis, ize*, used as possessive pronouns: *is*, Matt. VIII.3, *þata þrutsfill*, “his leprosy”; v. 13, *sa þiumagus is*, “his servant”; IX.11, *þaim siponjam is*, “his disciples”; X.25; XI.20; XXVI.65; XXVII.64; Mark I.22; V.29; VI.28; VII.2; VIII.25; IX.21; X.13; XI.14; XIV.12; XVI.64; Luke I.60; II.41; IV.23; VI.10; VII.3; John III.32; VI.8, 60, 61; VII.5, 10; IX.18, 20, 22; XI.12; XII.4; XIII.23; XVI.4, 29; 1 Cor. XV.20; 2 Cor. VIII.9, *þamma is wulþja*, “his glory”; IX.15; Eph. III.5; Col. I.26; IV.15; 1 Thess. III.13; 2 Thess. I.10. Luke XIX.33, *þai fraujans þis*, “its owners”; John XVIII.25. Matt. IX.4, *þos mitonins ize*, “their thoughts”; Mark I.23; John XI.19; Rom. XI.11, *þizai ize missadedai*, “their transgression,” and v. 30, *þizai ize ungalaubeinai*, “their unbelief”; 2 Cor. VIII.2; Gal. II.13.

θ) Further, with *jains*, “that”: Matt. VIII.28, *þana wig jainana*, “that way”; IX.22; Mark III.24, 25; VI.11; XIII.19, 24; Luke IX.5; X.12; XVIII.3; 2 Cor. VII.8. Rarer, however, is the construction *jainai þai vaurstvjans*, “those workers,” Mark XII.7; Luke XIV.24; 1 Cor. X.28.

ι) Frequently with *alls*, “all”: Matt. V.15, *allaim þaim in þamma razna*, “all those in the house”; VIII.32, *alla so hairda*, “all the herd”; VIII.34; XXVI.1; Mark I.33; III.28; IV.1, 13, 31; V.12, 23; VI.55; VII.14; XII.33, 37; XIV.55; XV.1; Luke II.18, 47; VII.1; IX.2, 13; XIV.29; XV.31; XVII.10; XVIII.31; XX.6; Rom. IX.6; X.4, 12; 1 Cor. XVI.16; 2 Cor. I.1; VII.11; Eph. I.10, 15; III.8, 18; VI.18; 1 Thess. III.13; 2 Thess. I.10; 1 Tim. II.2; Neh. V.13, 16, 18. Mark VIII.36, *þana fairwu allana*, “the whole world”; Luke IV.6; IX.25; 1 Cor. XII.12; XIII.12; Gal. I.2.

κ) For *sa silba*, *sa sama*, *sa svaleiks*, and *wazuh sa* with a participle, see under **Silba**, **Sama**, **Svaleiks**, and **Wazuh**.

d) [Objects] whose definition depends on the context: Matt. V.15, *in þamma razna*, “in the house” (where the light is kindled); VIII.27, *þai mans*, “the men” (who were in the boat); XXVII.7, *þaim gastim*, “for strangers,” namely those who die here; Mark III.22, *þaim unhulþom*, “the demons,” namely those whom he casts out; VI.14, *þos mahteis*, “the mighty works,” which he had done. Luke VII.6, *þamma garda*, “the house” into which he wishes to enter; VIII.22–23, *þana marisaiv*, “the sea” on which they were then sailing; John XII.3, *sa gards*, “the house” where they were; likewise *ana þamma stada*, “at that place,” Luke XIX.5; John VI.10; *Skeir.* VII.b. John XIX.2, *þai gadrauhteis*, “the soldiers,” who bound him; XVIII.26, *þize skalke*, “the servants,” namely those speaking to him.

e) It has demonstrative force where, especially in conversation, the speaker defines more particularly the object which he has in mind: Matt. XVII.72; Mark V.35, 39; Luke VIII.22, 49; IX.37; John XIII.26; XVIII.17. Thus, δεικτικῶς, “demonstratively,” *þata leik*, “the body,” in John VI.63 can also be explained by its opposition to *ahma*, “spirit”; and similarly, often in the Epistles: Gal. V.8, *so gakunds*, “this, such persuasion”; 2 Thess. III.17, *so goleins*, “this greeting”; 1 Tim. VI.14, *þo anabusn*, “the commandment,” of which mention had already been made in another letter: Rom. XVI.22; 1 Cor. V.9 (where it is evident that the translator, like many ancient interpreters, believed there had been only one Epistle to the Corinthians); 2 Cor. VII.8; 2 Thess. III.14.

f) The article is also used with several words denoting persons or things which are everywhere presented in Holy Scripture as familiar, or are used in an emphatic sense. Thus:

α) *þai bokarjos*, “the scribes”: Matt. V.20; IX.3; Mark I.22; II.6, 16; VII.1, 5; IX.11, 16; XI.18; XII.28, 33; XV.31; Luke V.21; VI.7; XX.19, 39. *þai fareisaieis*, “the Pharisees”: Mark VII.5; XII.13; Luke XVI.14; John VII.32, 47; VIII.13; IX.15, 16, 40; XI.47; XII.19. *þai gudjans* and *ufargudjans*, “the priests” and “chief priests”: Matt. XXVII.6, 12; Mark VIII.31; X.33; XIV.10; Luke XX.1; John VII.32, 45; XI.47; XVIII.3. For *þai auhumistans gudans*, “the chief priests,” see above under c). *þai reiks*, “the rulers”: John VII.26, 48; XII.42. *þai synagogafadeis*, “the rulers of the synagogue”: Mark V.22. *þai fauramaþleis*, “the chief men”: Neh. V.17. *þai siponjos*, “the disciples,” are Jesus’ disciples: Matt. IX.11; XXVII.64; John VI.8, 60, 61; VII.3; XI.8; XII.4; XIII.22; XVI.17, 29. Likewise *so managei*, “the multitude,” is the great crowd mentioned above: Matt. IX.25, 36; XI.7; XXVII.15; Mark III.9; IV.36; VIII.34; XI.32; XII.12; XV.11, 15; Luke IX.11, 12, 18, 19, 39; XX.1; John VII.12, 20, 31, 32, 40, 43, 49; XII.17, 34; Neh. V.15, 18; *Skeir.* VII.c. So too *so filusna*, “the multitude,” *Skeir.* VII.b, c.

*Sa sunus mans*, “the Son of Man,” occurs formally in Matthew: IX.6; X.23; XI.19; XXVI.2; in Mark only XIV.62; and in Luke only V.24 and VI.5 (elsewhere in both without the article); John VI.53; VIII.28; XII.34. So *sa sunus fralustais*, “the son of perdition,” John XVII.12; and *þai sunjus þis aivis*, “the sons of this age,” Luke XVI.8; XX.34; but *sunus guþs*, “Son of God,” without the article.

Conversely, the Gothic translator seems to have had regard for the mythology of his own people when he translated 1 Cor. X.19–20 as *þo galiugaguda*, “the false gods,” and 1 Tim. III.16 as *þaim aggilum*, “the angels,” in which passages he did not use the article at all.

β) *þos anabusnins*, “the commandments,” Mark X.19 and Luke XVIII.20, are Mosaic ordinances; *þai praufeteis*, “the prophets,” Mark VI.15, are the prophets of the Hebrews; *so baurgs*, “the city,” is Jerusalem, Mark XI.19; XIV.13; Luke IV.29; VII.37; XIX.41; *so alhs*, “the temple,” is the temple of Jerusalem, Mark XV.29; Luke II.27; *so dulþs*, “the feast,” is the Passover feast, John XII.20; *so usstass*, “the resurrection,” is the resurrection of the dead, Luke XX.33; *sa sunus*, “the Son,” is the Son of God, John VI.40; *þata vaurd*, “the word,” is the Gospel, Luke I.2 and Rom. X.10, just as *so aiwaggeljo*, “the Gospel,” occurs in Mark VIII.35. Finally, 1 Cor. I.21, *so wailamereins*, “the preaching,” is the preaching of Christ; Eph. III.19, *þata kunþi*, “the knowledge,” is knowledge of faith; 2 Thess. I.11, *so laþons*, “the calling,” is the calling to salvation.

γ) *Sa fairwus*, “the world,” meaning “this world,” both for οὗτος ὁ κόσμος and for ὁ κόσμος: Mark VIII.36; John VIII.26; IX.5, 36; X.36; XI.9, 27; XII.25, 31, 46; XV.19; XVI.11, 28, 33; XVII.5, 11, 12, 14, 16, 18, 37; 1 Cor. I.20, 21; V.10; 2 Cor. I.12; VII.10; Gal. IV.3; Col. II.20; 1 Tim. I.15; VI.7. *So manaseþs*, “the world”: Luke IX.25; John I.29; VI.14, 33, 51; VII.4, 7; XII.19, 31; XIV.17, 19, 22, 27, 30, 31; XV.18, 19; XVI.8; XVII.9, 14, 18, 21, 23, 25; 1 Cor. IV.9; *Skeir.* I.a. Hence also Luke IV.5, *sa midjungards*, “the inhabited world.” Further: *sa libains*, “life,” in the sense of human life, Mark IV.19; Luke VIII.14; *þizos aldais*, “of this age,” that is, of the present age, 2 Tim. II.4; *þata þeihs*, “the time,” Rom. XIII.11; *þata mel*, “the time,” Col. IV.5; 1 Thess. V.1.

g) Further, in proverbs and general maxims: Mark XII.10, *stains þammei usvaurpun þai timrjans, sa hwarþ du haubida waihstins*, “the stone which the builders rejected, this became the head of the corner”; Luke V.9, *ju so aqizi at waurtim bagme ligiþ*, “already the axe lies at the roots of the trees”; 1 Tim. V.18, *wairþs sa waurstva mizdons is*, “the worker is worthy of his wage”; Rom. XIII.4, *þai reiks ni sind agis godamma waurstva. guþs andbahts ni swarē þana hairu bairiþ*, “rulers are not a terror to good conduct. God’s servant does not bear the sword in vain.”

h) With metaphorical expressions: Phil. III.2, *þans hundans*, “the dogs,” that is, unworthy persons; 2 Cor. V.1, *þizos hleiþros*, “of this tent,” that is, this earthly life.

2) Sometimes proper names and ethnics also take the article; cf. Mark XV.15: Mark XV.15, *þana Barabban*, “Barabbas”; XV.32, *sa Xristus*, “the Christ”; Luke IV.38, *þis Seimonis*, “Simon’s”; VI.41, *þamma Iesua*, “Jesus”; John V.36, *þamma Iohanne*, “John”; VI.71, *þana Iudan*, “Judas”; Luke III.1, *þis Galeilaias*, “Galilee”; *þis Ituraias, jah Trakauneitidaus-landis*, “Ituraea and the region of Trachonitis”; Mark III.6, *þaim Herodianum*, “the Herodians”; Luke VIII.37, *þize Gaddarene*, “the Gadarenes”; John VI.25, *þize Iairusaulymeite*, “the Jerusalemites”; VII.1, *þai Iudaieis*, “the Jews”; VII.35; VIII.48, 52, 57; X.31, 33; XI.36, 45.

3) The article changes abstracts into concretes:

a) Adjectives into substantives:

α) Personal: Matt. V.8, *þai hrainjahairtans*, “the pure in heart”; V.21, *þai airizans*, “the ancient ones”; VI.2, *þai liutans*, “the hypocrites”; V.16; VIII.22, *þans dauþans*, “the dead”; X.25; XI.11; XXV.46; XXVII.1, 49; Mark III.22; V.7, 15, 16; VI.21; VII.3, 5; IX.42; X.42; XIII.17; XIV.53, 61; XV.1; Luke I.36, 49; V.31; VI.24, 32, 33, 35; VII.28; VIII.10; IX.8, 11, 19, 60; X.9; XIV.18; XVI.10, 21, 22; XVII.18; XVIII.9; XX.1; John IX.17; X.5; XI.37, 39, 44; XII.6; XIII.29; Rom. IX.12; 1 Cor. I.19; V.5 (*sa svaleiks*, “such a person”); V.13; VII.10, 12; VIII.9, 11; IX.21, 22; X.17, 33; XV.6, 9; XVI.5; 2 Cor. VIII.4; IX.2, 12; XI.19; Gal. II.10; IV.27; Eph. I.1; II.3, 19; III.8, 10, 20; VI.12, 16; Phil. I.28; Col. II.17; III.28; 1 Thess. IV.13; V.6, 14; 1 Tim. V.20; VI.15; *Skeir.* V.a; VI.d.

β) Things: Matt. V.37, *þata managizo*, “what is more”; in the same passage, *þata ubilo*, “evil”; VI.13; V.39, *þata unseljo*, “evil”; Luke III.5, *þata vraiqo*, “the crooked”; XVI.11, 12, 15; XVIII.27; John XVI.13; XVII.15; XVIII.23; Rom. VII.13; VIII.3; IX.22, 25; 1 Cor. XIV.25; 2 Cor. II.7; III.10; IV.2, 17; V.4, 10, 17; XIII.7; Gal. II.7; IV.13; V.21; 2 Thess. III.3; 1 Tim. IV.7. Mark IV.19, *þata anþar*, “the other things”; 1 Cor. I.16; 2 Cor. XIII.11; Eph. VI.10; Phil. III.1; IV.8; 2 Thess. III.1; Luke XV.31, *þata mein*, “what is mine”; Luke XVI.12, *þata izwar*, “what is yours”; Phil. II.4, *þo seina*, “his own things”; John XV.21, *þata allata*, “all these things”; 1 Cor. XII.19, *þo alla*, “all things”; XV.27, 28; Eph. IV.15; Col. III.8; Gal. V.21, *þata svaleik*, “such things”; *Skeir.* I.c, *þata gadob*, “the fitting thing” (?).

b) Participles into substantives:

α) Present participle.

αα) As a personal substantive: Matt. III.11, *sa gagganda*, “the one coming” (this must be read instead of *sa gaggida*); V.40, *þamma wiljandin*, “the one wishing”; v. 42, *þamma bidjandin*, “the one asking”; v. 44, *þans wrikandans—þaim hatjandam—þans usþriutandans*, “those who persecute—those who hate—those who oppress [you]”; VII.13, 14, 21; VIII.10, 16, 33; IX.12; X.28, 40, 42; XI.3, 11, 12; XXVI.68, 73; XXVII.3, 54; Mark I.32; II.17, 26; III.34; IV.3, 14, 18, 24; V.14, 32; VI.14, 22, 24, 26, 55; VIII.9, 28; IX.1, 23, 37, 42; X.13, 23; XI.5, 9, 15; XIV.42, 44, 47, 69, 70; XV.7, 29, 35; XVI.10; Luke I.45, 50, 65, 66, 71, 79; II.38, 47; III.11, 14; VI.4, 27, 28, 29, 32, 33, 49; VII.14, 19, 20, 25, 28, 32, 33, 49; VIII.12, 16, 34, 36; IX.19, 27, 49; X.16; XIV.10, 12, 29, 31; XVIII.24, 26, 29; XIX.24, 26, 38, 45; John III.31 (*sa qimands* in *Skeireins*; *sa qimanda*, “the one coming,” must be read); VI.11, 13, 35, 37, 38, 40, 45, 64; VII.16, 18, 33, 39; VIII.31, 43, 47; IX.4, 8, 39, 40; X.2; XII.2, 13, 20, 44, 48; XIII.16, 20, 28; XV.21; XVI.5; XVII.20; XVIII.2, 21; XIX.11; Rom. VII.4; VIII.4, 5, 37; IX.11, 20, 33; X.5, 11, 15, 20; XI.26; XII.8, 14; XIII.2, 4; XIV.3, 14; XV.3, 12; XVI.22; 1 Cor. I.18, 21; V.3; VII.15; IX.3, 24; X.18, 27; XIV.22; XV.18, 28, 29; 2 Cor. I.21; II.15; IV.3, 4, 14; V.12, 15; VII.12; IX.10; X.12, 17; XI.4, 12; XII.21; XIII.2; Gal. I.6; II.6; IV.27; V.8, 10, 12, 15, 21; VI.6; Eph. I.22, 23; VI.12; Phil. III.17; IV.13; 1 Thess. II.10; III.5; IV.12, 13, 15; V.12; 2 Thess. I.6; II.4; 1 Tim. I.12, 18; II.6; III.13; 2 Tim. II.14, 22, 25; Tit. I.9; Neh. V.17; *Skeir.* I.c, d; III.c; V.a, b; VI.b, c.

ββ) As a thing: Mark VI.55, *þata utgaggando*, “what goes out”; VII.18, *þata inngaggando*, “what enters”; v. 20; Luke VIII.14; 2 Cor. III.11, 13; 1 Tim. V.25.

β) Perfect participle:

αα) As a personal substantive: Matt. XXVII.9, *þis wairþodins*, “the one valued”; Mark IV.16, 18, 20; XIII.20, 23; XV.32; Luke IV.18; VI.18; VII.10; XIV.14, 17; XIX.10, 32; 1 Cor. I.24; VII.8; XI.5; 2 Cor. II.2; VII.12; Gal. II.29; VI.6; Phil. III.2; *Skeir.* IV.b, c; V.a; VIII.d.

ββ) As a thing: Matt. VIII.17, *þata gamelido*, “what was spoken”; XXVII.9, *þata qiþano*, “what was said”; XXVII.54, *þo waurþanona*, “the things that happened”; Mark V.14; XV.28; Luke I.45; II.18; VIII.34, 35, 56; IX.7; X.8; XVII.10; XVIII.31, 34; John X.35; XII.6; XIII.18; XVII.12; Rom. IX.17; [Col. 1339] 2 Cor. IV.13, 18; Gal. IV.30; Col. I.16; *Skeir.* IV.c.

c) It changes numerals into substantives, especially in the formula *þai twalif*, “the twelve”: Mark IV.10; VI.7; IX.35; X.32; XI.11; XIV.10, 43; Luke VIII.1; IX.1, 12; XVIII.31; John VI.67, 71. *þaim ainlibim*, “the eleven,” excluding Judas Iscariot: 1 Cor. XV.5. *þai taihun*, “the ten,” excluding James and John: Mark X.41. *þai sibuntehund*, “the seventy”: Luke X.17. Further: *þans twans*, “the two,” Eph. II.15; *þans bans*, “both,” II.16; *þo twa*, “the two,” Mark X.8; Phil. I.23; *þo ba*, “the two,” Eph. II.14.

d) It changes adverbs into personal or impersonal substantives: Mark IV.11, *þaim uta*, “those outside”; Phil. III.14, *þaim afta*, “what is behind”; John VIII.23; 1 Cor. V.12; Col. IV.5; 1 Tim. III.7. Likewise 2 Cor. V.16, *þata nu*, “the now”; 2 Cor. I.17 and 20, *þata ja ja—þata ne ne*, “the ‘yes, yes’—the ‘no, no.’”

e) Likewise in prepositional phrases: Matt. V.15, *þaim in þamma razna*, “those in the house”; XXV.41, *þaim af hleidumein fairai*, “those at the left”; Mark I.7, *sa afar mis*, “the one after me”; I.36; II.25; III.8; IV.10, 15; V.40; Luke V.9, 36; VIII.12, 13, 15, 45; IX.11 (*þo bi þiudangardja guþs*, “the things concerning God’s kingdom”); IX.32; X.7; XVII.24; XIX.42; Rom. VIII.1; IX.6; 1 Cor. IX.20; XIII.10; 2 Cor. I.4; X.7; XI.28; Gal. II.3, 12; IV.5, 23; Eph. I.10; Col. I.20; Tit. I.10; *Skeir.* IV.a; VI.a.

f) Elliptically:

α) Where the genitive of a substantive follows a plural article: Mark VIII.33, *þo guþs—þo manne*, “the things of God—the things of men”; XII.17, *þo Kaisaris—þo guþs*, “the things of Caesar—the things of God”; Luke XX.25; Luke II.49, *þo attins*, “the things of my Father”; 2 Cor. XI.30, *þaim siukeins meinaiþos*, “the things of my weakness”; Phil. II.4, *þo anþaraize*, “the things of others”; 1 Cor. XV.23, *þai Xristaus*, “those of Christ.” Compare *þai þiudo*, “the nations,” Matt. V.46; VI.7.

β) Where such ideas as “son,” “sister,” etc. must be supplied: Matt. XXVII.56, *so Iakobis*, “the [mother] of James”; Mark I.19, *þana Zaibaidaiaus*, “the [son] of Zebedee”; II.14; III.18; VIII.27; XVI.1; Luke VI.15.

g) The article is prefixed to an entire sentence: Mark IX.10, *þata us dauþaim usstandan*, “the rising from the dead”; v. 23, *þata jabai mageis galaubjan*, “that you can believe, if you are able”; X.40, *þata du sitan af taihswon meinai*, “to sit at my right hand”; XII.33, *þata du frijon ina us allamma hairtin*, “to love him from the whole heart”; Luke I.62, *þata waiwa willedi haitan ina*, “what he wished to call him”; IX.46, *þata warjis þau ize maists wesi*, “which of them might be greatest”; Rom. XIII.9, *þata ni horinos—þata frijos nehwandjan þeinana swe þuk silban*, “You shall not commit adultery—You shall love your neighbour as yourself”; Gal. V.14.

4) The article is used in apposition: Matt. XXVII.3, *Iudas sa galeiwjands*, “Judas the betrayer”; Mark VI.3, *sa timrja sa sunus Marjins*, “the carpenter, the son of Mary”; XIV.67, *Iesus sa Nazorenus*, “Jesus the Nazarene”; XV.40, *Marja so Magdalene*, “Mary Magdalene”; v. 47; XVI.1, 9; Luke I.9; II.15; IV.27; VI.15, 24; IX.7; XVIII.24; John VI.4, 42; IX.6; XII.1, 4; XIV.22; XVIII.5, 17; Rom. XI.13; XVI.23; 1 Cor. XVI.12; Gal. II.3; VI.1; Eph. III.8; IV.22; VI.21; Col. IV.7, 9, 10; 2 Tim. IV.8; Philem. 23; *Skeir.* III.b. Also John VII.2, *dulþs Iudaie so hleiþrastakeins*, “the Jewish feast of Tabernacles”; XVIII.1, *rinnon þo Kaidron*, “the brook Kidron.”

5) The article is postponed in order to define a substantive more strictly:

a) With adjectives: Matt. V.29, *augo þein þata taihswo*, “your right eye”; VI.11, *hlaif unsarana þana sinteinan*, “our daily bread”; VIII.12, *in riqis þata hindumisto*, “into the outer darkness”; Mark I.11, *sunus meins sa liuba*, “my beloved Son”; I.26, 27; II.22; IV.20; V.7, 13; VIII.37; IX.7, 25, 43; X.30; XI.2; XIV.47; XV.40; Luke I.70; II.7; III.22; VI.6; VII.47; VIII.29; IX.35, 42; XV.22, 25; XX.13; John VI.13, 32; VII.37, 39; X.11, 14; XIV.26; XV.1; Rom. IX.3; 1 Cor. XII.12; 2 Cor. I.6; XI.31; Eph. I.13; III.9; Col. IV.14; 1 Tim. IV.8; 2 Tim. IV.7.

b) With a participle: Matt. VII.13–14, *wigs sa brigganda*, “the broad way”; XI.23, *mahteis þos waurþanons*, “the mighty works done”; Mark III.22; IV.15; XI.2; XIV.58; XVI.6; Luke I.9; II.15, 21; VIII.21; X.11; XIV.24; XV.6, 23, 27; XVI.21; XVIII.30; XX.20, 46; John VI.14, 27, 41; IX.18; XI.27, 31, 42, 45; XV.25; XVIII.2, 5; Rom. VII.23; IX.30; 1 Cor. VII.14; VIII.10; XI.24; XV.54; 2 Cor. I.1, 8, 9; II.14; III.7; V.18; VIII.1, 19, 20; X.2; Gal. I.7; II.9, 20; IV.27; Eph. I.11, 19; II.2, 7; III.7, 9, 20; IV.18; Col. III.10; 1 Thess. II.14; IV.17; 1 Tim. I.4; VI.13; 2 Tim. I.9; III.15; *Skeir.* VIII.b. Matt. XXVII.53, *þai waidedjans þai miþushramidans*, “the saints who had fallen asleep”; Mark III.3, *þamma mann þamma habandin*, “the man having [the withered hand]”; XV.28, 39; Luke IV.22; VI.8; IX.32; XVIII.7; John VI.27; Eph. I.1; IV.23; 1 Thess. IV.15, 17.

c) Matt. V.45, *attins izwaris þis in himinam*, “your Father who is in heaven”; v. 48; VI.1, 6, 14, 18, 23, 26; VII.21; Mark IV.31; VI.11; XI.25, 26; XII.25; XIII.25; [Col. 1340] Luke VI.42; John XII.21; Rom. VII.5; VIII.39; IX.30; 2 Cor. V.2; VII.14; IX.3; XI.3; Gal. I.22; Phil. III.9; Col. I.23; 1 Thess. IV.16 (where the Greek lacks the article); 1 Tim. I.14; III.13; 2 Tim. I.1; II.1; III.15; Neh. V.17; VI.16; *Skeir.* IV.a. 1 Cor. XVI.1, *gabaur þata þaim weiham*, “the collection for the saints”; 2 Cor. I.18, *þata waurd unsar þata du izwis*, “our word to you.”

d) John VI.1, *marein þo Galeilaie*, “the Sea of Galilee”; VII.23, *witoþ þata Mosezis*, “the law of Moses”; 1 Tim. VI.3, *hailaim waurdam þaim fraujins unsaris*, “the sound words of our Lord.”

6) The article attached to the predicate: Mark VI.3, *niu þata ist sa timrja*, “Is not this the carpenter?”; XII.7, *sa ist sa arbinumja*, “This is the heir”; Luke XX.14; John VI.48; VII.40; X.9; XI.25; XIV.6; XV.5; XVII.3; XVIII.40; 1 Cor. XI.25.

**ÞAT-AIN**, see under **Ains**.  
**ÞAT-AINEI**, see under **Ains**.  
**ÞAT IST**, “that is,” τοῦτο ἐστίν: Mark VII.2; John VI.29; Rom. VII.18; IX.8, 9; X.6, 8; 1 Cor. IX.3; Philem. 12.  
**ÞIS**, genitive, see above.  
**ÞIS-HUN**, adverb: especially, mostly, μάλιστα: Gal. VI.10; 1 Tim. IV.10; V.8; 2 Tim. IV.13; Tit. I.10.  
**ÞIS-WAH**, see under **Was**.  
**ÞIS-WADUH**, see under **Was**.  
**ÞIS WAHÞEI**, see under **Was**.  
**FAURÞIS**, see under **Faur**.

**ÞE**, an old dative or instrumental form (Old High German *thiu*; Bopp, 189; Grimm I, 790; III, 175 ff.; IV, 707; Gf. V, 28):

1) “By that, so much the more,” before a comparative: *Skeir.* IV.d.

2) “To this,” especially in combination:

a) With *bi*: *biþe* (and *biþeh* before *þan*; John XIII.12; Luke IV.42; V.4; VII.12—not, however, XV.14; XIX.37).

α) Demonstrative: “then, afterward,” ὕστερον: Luke IV.2; VIII.1; John XIII.36; “after these things,” μετὰ ταῦτα: Luke XVII.8; “then,” τότε: Matt. V.24; IX.17.

β) Relative: “after, when, whenever,” ὅτε: Matt. XI.1; XXVI.1; Mark IV.10; XI.1, 19; XV.20; Luke II.21, 22, 42; VI.13; John XII.16; XIII.12; XIX.6, 8; Gal. II.12, 14; IV.4. “Whenever,” ὅταν: Matt. VI.16; Mark IV.29; IX.9; Luke IX.26; XIV.10; XVI.4; John VII.27; XIII.19; XIV.29; XVI.4, 21; 1 Cor. XIII.10, 11; XV.27, 28; XVI.2, 3, 12. “As,” ὡς: Luke I.23; II.15, 39; V.4; VII.12; XIX.5, 28; John VI.12; VII.10; “as soon as,” ὡς ἄν: Phil. II.23; “after,” ἐπεί: Luke VII.1. It is used to paraphrase the Greek genitive absolute: Matt. IX.10, 32, 33; Mark I.42; IV.17; VI.2; XV.33; Luke IV.42; XIV.29; XV.14; XVIII.40; XIX.37; John XIII.30; and likewise Greek ἐν τῷ with an infinitive: Mark II.15; Luke III.21; XIX.15.

2) With *du*:

a) *duþe* (Mark I.38; IV.21; XII.24; Luke I.13, 20, 35; II.4; IV.43; XIV.20; John VI.65; VIII.47; 1 Cor. XV.9; 2 Cor. III.13; 1 Thess. II.13; 1 Tim. I.16; Philem. 15; also *duþei*, Luke VII.7), and in solemn form *duþ-þe*—by assimilation for *duhþe*, as also at John IX.23; X.17; XVI.15; XIX.11—mean “for this purpose, therefore, because of this,” εἰς τοῦτο: Mark I.38; Luke IV.43; 2 Cor. II.9; 1 Tim. IV.10; διό: Matt. XXVII.8; Luke VII.7; Rom. XIII.5; 2 Cor. I.20; Eph. II.11; διόπερ: 1 Cor. VIII.13; διά τοῦτο or διά ταῦτα: Matt. VI.25; Mark VI.14; XI.24; XII.24; Luke XIV.20; John VI.65; VII.22; VIII.47; IX.23; X.17; XII.18, 27, 39; XV.19; XVI.15; XIX.11; Rom. XV.9; 1 Cor. XI.30; 2 Cor. IV.1; XIII.10; Eph. I.15; V.17; VI.13; Col. I.9; 1 Thess. II.13; III.5; 1 Tim. I.16; Philem. 15; *Skeir.* II.d; εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο, Col. IV.8.

b) *duþe ei*, “because, since,” διότι: Luke I.13; 1 Cor. XV.9; διό: Luke I.35; ἀνθ’ ὧν, “because of the things for which”: Luke I.20; πρὸς ὅ, “with reference to which”: Eph. III.4; ἵνα, “in order that”: Mark IV.21; Eph. VI.22. It paraphrases Greek πρὸς τό with an infinitive, 2 Cor. III.13, or διά τό with an infinitive, Luke II.4.

**JAÞÞE—JAÞÞE**, “either—or,” εἴτε—εἴτε: 1 Cor. X.31; XII.13; XIII.8; XIV.27; XV.11; 2 Cor. I.6; V.9, 10, 13; VIII.23; XII.2, 3; Eph. VI.8; Phil. I.18, 20, 27; Col. I.16, 20; 1 Thess. V.10; *Skeir.* IV.c. The simple form occurs only at 1 Cor. XIV.27.

**ÞATUH**, neuter; **sah**, masculine; **soh**, feminine (cf. *-uh*):

1) Properly, “and this one too,” καὶ αὐτός: Luke XVII.16; XIX.2; cf. John XIV.8; “and this one,” καὶ οὗτος: Luke II.38.

2) “Who,” ὅς: Luke [Col. 1341] II.37; XVI.20; XVII.12; 1 Cor. XV.1; Philem. 12; cf. Matt. XXVII.57, *þizuh namo was*, “whose name was.”

3) “This, that,” αὐτός: Matt. III.11; V.19 and Mark III.11 (where it is absent from the Greek text); Mark VI.16; Luke III.16; John V.37; XII.49; XVIII.10 and 26 (absent from the Greek); *Skeir.* VI.c. “This,” οὗτος: Matt. XXVII.58; Mark XII.10; Luke II.37; IX.26; XX.17; John V.38; VI.6, 40; VII.9, 39; VIII.40; X.3; XII.6, 16, 33; XIII.28; XVII.3; 1 Cor. VII.6; IX.23; 2 Cor. I.17; IV.15; IX.6; XIII.9; Gal. VI.7; Phil. II.23; III.7; 1 Thess. IV.15; 1 Tim. II.3; IV.16; VI.8; *Skeir.* I.c; II.b; III.a, d; V.a; VI.d; VIII.c. “That,” ἐκεῖνος: Mark XVI.10; John X.1.

4) “This,” οὗτος ὁ: Luke II.2; *Skeir.* VIII.a, b; “that,” ὁ ἐκεῖνος: John XVIII.15; “the,” ὁ: John VIII.35; Rom. XII.4; 2 Cor. XII.19; Eph. IV.9; *Skeir.* V.d, at the end; “but the,” ὁ δέ: Matt. XXVII.44; 2 Thess. III.12.

**ÞATEI**, neuter of the relative pronoun; **saei**, masculine; **soei, sei**, feminine:

1) It means:

a) “Who, which, that,” referring to a preceding or following word, ὅς: Matt. VIII.4; X.26; XI.20; XXVII.9, 15, 56, 57, 60; Mark I.2, 7; II.4, 24, 26; III.17, 19; IV.16, 22, 31; V.41; VII.4, 11, 13, 15, 25, 34; IX.38, 39; X.29, 38, 39; XI.2, 21; XII.10; XIII.19, 20; XIV.71; XV.16, 22, 34, 40, 42, 43, 46; XVI.9; Luke I.25, 26, 27, 61, 73, 78; II.11, 25, 31; III.19; IV.29; V.3, 9, 10, 17, 18, 25, 29; VI.2, 3, 4, 13, 14, 16, 18, 48, 49; VII.2, 27, 49; VIII.2, 13, 14, 17, 27, 35, 38, 41; IX.9,

I, 4, 6, 10, 13; II, 4; IV, 4, 6; VII, 7; VIII, 18, 22; IX, 2; X, 2, 8, 13; XI, 4, 15; XII, 4, 13, 21; XIII, 3; Gal. I, 5, 7, 23; II, 2, 5, 10; IV, 9, 19; V, 21; VI, 14; Eph. I, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, 20; II, 2, 3, 4, 10, 21, 22; III, 5, 7, 11, 12, 15; IV, 1, 16, 30; V, 5, 18; VI, 16, 17, 20, 22; Phil. II, 5, 6; III, 8, 18, 19, 21; VI, 3, 10, 11; Col.
