VIII, 13; Gal. IV, 30; V, 16; I Thess. IV, 15; V, 3; see on this passage; compare below, *ni þau*.

β) But where the verbal idea is expressed by an auxiliary verb

[Col. 1403] (*vairþan* or *visan*) and a noun, the negation is placed:

αα) before the nominal element when that element is a participle: Luke XVII, 18 *ni bigitanai vaurþun*, “they were not found”; II Cor. VII, 14 *ni gaaiviskoþs varþ*, “I was not put to shame”; John XII, 42 *ei us synagogein ni usvaurpanai vaurþeina*, “lest they should become excluded from the synagogue”; XII, 5 *ni frabauht vas*, “it was not sold”; XVIII, 36 *ni galeviþs vesjau*, “that I might not be handed over”; Rom. IX, 11 *ni gabauranai vesun*, “they had not been born”; Matt. XXVII, 6 *ni skuld ïst*, “it is not lawful”; Mark II, 24, 26; VI, 18; Luke VI, 2, 4, 15; XIX, 21; John XVIII, 31; II Cor. XII, 4; Tit. I, 11; *Skeir.* VI, d; *ni mahts visan*, “not to be able,” “not to have power”: Luke VIII, 43; John X, 35; I Tim. V, 25; Eph. III, 5 *ni kunþ vas*, “it was not made known.”

Where the nominal element is an adjective, however, it stands before *vairþan* or *visan*: Luke XVIII, 1 *ni vairþan usgrudjans*, “not to lose heart”; II Cor. IV, 16; Gal. VI, 9; Eph. III, 13; II Thess. III, 13; Gal. II, 16 *ni vairþiþ garaihts*, “is not justified”; V, 6 *ni vairþaiþ airzjai*, “do not be deceived”; II Cor. IX, 3 *ei woftuli unsara ni vaurþi lausa*, “lest our boasting should be made void”; Col. III, 19 *ni sijaiþ baitrai*, “do not be embittered”; I Tim. IV, 14 *ni sijais unkarja*, “do not neglect”; II Cor. III, 10 *ni vas vulþag*, “was not glorified.”

The only exceptions are: I Tim. II, 14 *ni varþ uslutoþs*, “was not deceived”; John VI, 7 *ni ganohai sind*, “are not sufficient”; II Cor. XII, 1 *nï batizo ïst*, “it is not advantageous”; II Cor. II, 11 *ni sijum unvitandans munins ïs*, “we are not ignorant of his designs”; John VIII, 41 *ni sijum gabauranai*, “we were not born.”

ββ) Further, the negation is placed next to the word whose notion it negates or qualifies, and together with it forms an adversative clause or part of a clause:

a) John XIV, 22 *ïudas ni sa ïskariotes*, “Judas, not the Iscariot” (but the son of James); Rom. IX, 25, 26 *so ni managei meina*, “not my people”; Gal. IV, 27 *so ni fitandei*, “she who does not bear”; Rom. VIII, 4 *þaim ni bi leik gaggandam*, “those walking not according to the flesh”; Luke XV, 13 *afar ni managans*, “after not many [days]”; *Skeir.* VI, a *afar ni filu*, “after no long time”; John XIII, 11 *ni allai*, “not all”; 18; Rom. IX, 6; I Cor. X, 23; Rom. XII, 3 *ni mais*, “not more”; I Tim. V, 9 *ni mins*, “not less”; II Cor. I, 13 *ni alja*, “not other things”; Mark X, 43 *ni sva*, “not so”; II Cor. VIII, 13; Eph. IV, 20; John VI, 58; II Cor. III, 13; VIII, 5; Rom. IX, 10 *ni þatain*, “not only that”; II Cor. VIII, 19; Rom. XII, 4 *ni þata samo*, “not the same”; XIII, 4 *ni svare*, “not in vain”; II Cor. VI, 1; Phil. I, 16 *ni sviknaba*, “not in pretence”; II Thess. II, 2 *ni sprauto*, “not quickly”; Mark XII, 34 *ni fairra ïs*, “he is not far”; I Cor. V, 6 *ni goda (ïst) woftuli*, “the boasting is not good”; Rom. XII, 11 *ni latai*, “not slothful”; XIII, 13 *garedaba gaggaima ni gabauram jah drugkaneim, ni ligram jah aglaitjam*, “let us walk decently, not in revelry and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and licentiousness”; I Cor. I, 17; II Cor. VII, 3; VIII, 15; X, 2, 3, 15, 16; Gal. V, 8; Phil. III, 1; Col. II, 23; II Thess. I, 8; I Tim. III, 3, 11; Tit. I, 6. The governed word may also be supplied, as II Cor. VIII, 12 *ni* [sc. *andanem*], “not according to what one does not have.”

b) In adversative clauses:

aa) what is affirmed stands first, and what is opposed follows:

α) with simple *ni*: Mark II, 27 *sabbato in mans varþ gaskapans, ni manna in sabbato dagis*, “the sabbath was made for the human being, not the human being for the sabbath”; X, 27; XIV, 7; Rom. XIV, 1; I Cor. VII, 6, 12; IX, 26; II Cor. V, 3, 7; IX, 7; Col. III, 2, 23 (in Greek *kai ou*, “and not”); I Thess. II, 27; IV, 5; I Tim. II, 9; Tit. I, 14.

β) with *jah ni*, “and not”: Matt. V, 30 *ei fraqistnai ains liþive þeinaize jah ni allata leik þein gadriusai ïn gaiainnan*, “that one of your members may perish and not your whole body be thrown into Gehenna”; IX, 13 *armahairtiþa viljau jah ni hunsl*, “I desire mercy and not sacrifice”; VII, 29; Mark I, 22; Rom. VII, 6; II Cor. V, 12; IX, 5; X, 8; XIII, 10; Gal. II, 14–16; VI, 4; Phil. III, 3; II Thess. III, 6.

γ) with *akei ni*, “but not”: Rom. X, 2 *aljan guþs haband akei ni bi kunþja*, “having zeal for God, but not according to knowledge”; II Cor. IV, 8, 9; XI, 6.

δ) with *ïþ ni*, “but not”: Mark XIV, 7 *sinteino unledans habaiþ miþ ïzvis, ïþ mik ni sinteino habaiþ*, “you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me”; John XII, 8.

bb) What is negated first, and the positive adversative follows, with *ak*, “but”: Matt. VII, 21 *ni wazuh saei qiþiþ mis frauja frauja ïnngaleiþiþ ïn þiudangardja himine, ak sa taujands viljan attins meinis*, “not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the kingdom of heaven, but the one doing the will of my Father”; Mark IX, 37 *ni mik andnimiþ ak þana sandjandan mik*, “does not receive me, but the one who sent me”; Luke IV, 4; John VI, 26, 27, 32, 38; VII, 10, 22; XII, 9, 30; XV, 16; XVII, 9, 20; Rom. VII, 15, 17, 19, 20; IX, 8, 32; XII, 16, 19; XIV, 13; I Cor. VII, 10; X, 29; XIV, 22; XV, 10; II Cor. I, 12; III, 3, 6; IV, 5; V, 15; VII, 12; VIII, 8; X, 4, 18; Gal. IV, 17; Eph. II, 8, 9; Phil. II, 4 *ni þo seina warjizuh mitondans ak jah þo anþaraize warjizuh*, “not looking to one’s own interests, but also to those of others”; 6; III, 9; Col. III, 22; I Thess. II, 13; IV, 8; I Tim. II, 12; II Tim. I, 9; Philem.

[Col. 1404] 16; *Skeir.* V, d.

Except: John X, 33 *ïn godis vaurstvis ni stainjam þuk ak ïn vajamereins*, “we do not stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy”; XIV, 10 *þo vaurda, þoei ïk rodja ïzvis, af mis silbin ni rodja ak atta* [sc. *rodeiþ*], “the words which I speak to you I do not speak from myself, but the Father speaks”; Rom. VIII, 9 *jus ni sijuþ in leika ak ïn ahmin*, “you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit”; I Cor. IX, 2; II Cor. XI, 17, 29; Gal. II, 16; IV, 31; II Thess. III, 15, where the verb has attracted the negation to itself.

But the rule does not apply in cases where, between the negation and its governed word, one of the particles normally occupying second position in the sentence is inserted, for example *þan*: I Cor. XII, 21 *niþ-þan mag*, “but cannot”; *auk*: Mark IX, 6 *ni auk vissa*, “for he did not know”; XI, 13 *ni auk vas mel*, “for it was not the season”; XII, 14; Luke VI, 43; VIII, 17; John VII, 1; Rom. X, 12; XI, 25; II Cor. XIII, 8; I Thess. IV, 7; II Thess. III, 2; Rom. IX, 6 *ni auk allai*, “for not all”; Eph. V, 29 *ni auk manna*, “for no one”; *Skeir.* V, c *ni auk þatainei*, “for not only that.” Yet *auk* may sometimes retreat even after the verb, as Luke XVI, 2 *ni magt auk*; I Cor. XVI, 7 *ni viljau auk*; John VII, 4 *ni manna auk*. Compare **Auk**.

Still less does the rule apply where *ni þau* (*ni þauh*) occurs, whether it stands for *ou mē*, “certainly not,” as Matt. V, 20 *ni þau qimiþ*, “you shall certainly not enter”; Mark X, 15; whether for *oude*, “nor,” as Matt. VI, 15; Mark XI, 26; whether for *ou*, “not,” as Phil. III, 13; or for *ouk an*, “would not,” as Mark XIII, 20; John IX, 41; XI, 21, 32; XVIII, 30 *ni þau veis atgebeima þus*, “we would not have handed him over to you.” In this place the personal pronoun, not expressed in Greek, is inserted between the negation and verb, although *veis ni meridedum*, “we did not preach,” also occurs, II Cor. XI, 4. *Nunu* is always inserted between negation and imperative; see on II Tim. I, 8.

Finally, something explanatory may be inserted between negation and verb, as II Cor. X, 14 *ni auk, svasve ni fairrinnandans und ïzvis ufarassau, ufþanjam uns*, “for we do not overextend ourselves, as though we had not reached you”; John XIV, 27; I Cor. XVI, 2; Gal. V, 17. Where an exception is present, as Rom. XIV, 15 *ni mata þeinamma fraqistjais*, “do not destroy by your food,” I Cor. IV, 4, 6, the word separating the negation from the verb must at least be pronounced emphatically. With compounds, however, the negation stands between the verb and its compositional particle, as John VI, 22 *miþ ni qam*, “did not come with”; compare X, 1 *ïnn ni atgaggiþ*, “does not enter in through.”

b) The negation may be construed freely:

aa) with indefinites. Since Gothic expresses negative indefinites (*nullus*, “no one”; *nemo*, “nobody”; *nunquam*, “never”; *nusquam*, “nowhere”) only through circumlocutions, forming them by adding negation to positive terms, the negation may be removed from them and brought to the verb:

α) *ni vaiht*, “nothing”: Mark VI, 8 *ei vaiht ni nemeina*, “that they should take nothing”; IX, 29 *ïn vaihtai ni mag usgaggan*, “can come out by nothing”; Luke IV, 2 *jah ni matida vaiht*, “and he ate nothing”; compare below; John VI, 12 *þei vaihtai ni fraqistnai*, “that nothing may be lost”; 63; VII, 26; XII, 19; XVI, 23; XVIII, 20; II Cor. VII, 9, etc. Conversely: Matt. X, 26 *ni vaiht auk ïst gahuliþ*, “for nothing is hidden”; Mark V, 26 *jah ni vaihtai botida*, “and was helped in no way”; XI, 13 *ni vaiht bigat*, “he found nothing”; XV, 4 *niu andhafjis ni vaiht?*, “do you answer nothing?”; Luke IX, 3 *ni vaiht nimaiþ ïn vig*, “take nothing for the journey”; XVIII, 34; John VIII, 28, 34; XVI, 24; Rom. VIII, 1; IX, 1; XIV, 14; I Cor. VII, 19 *þata bimait ni vaihts ïst*, “circumcision is nothing”; X, 25, 27; XIII, 2, 3; II Cor. VI, 10; VII, 5; XI, 5; XII, 11; XIII, 7; Gal. II, 6; IV, 1 *ni und vaiht*, “not at all”; 12; V, 10; VI, 3, 14 *ïn ni vaihtai*, “into nothing”; Phil. I, 20, 28 *ni ïn vaihtai*, “in no respect”; II, 3; IV, 6; II Thess. III, 11; I Tim. V, 25; IV, 4; II Tim. II, 14 *du ni vaihtai*, “for nothing”; Tit. I, 15; Philem. 14; *Skeir.* VII, c *ni ïn vaihtai*.

β) *ni manna*, “no one”: Matt. IX, 30 *ei manna ni viti*, “let no one know”; Mark VII, 36 *ei mann ni qeþeina*, “that they should tell no one”; 24; Luke IX, 21, 36 *jah mann ni gataihun*, “and they told no one”; John XV, 13 *maizein þizai friaþvai manna ni habaiþ*, “no one has greater love than this.” Conversely: Matt. VI, 24 *ni manna mag tvaim fraujam skalkinon*, “no one can serve two masters”; Luke VIII, 16 *ni manna lukarn tandjands dishuljiþ ïta*, “no one who lights a lamp hides it”; IX, 62; John VI, 44; VII, 4, 27; IX, 4; Eph. V, 6 *ni manna ïzvis usluto*, “let no one deceive you”; 29 *ni auk manna*, “for no one”; Col. II, 16; I Tim. IV, 12; II Tim. IV, 16.

γ) *ni ainshun*, “no one”: Mark XI, 2 *ana þammei nauh ainshun manne ni sat*, “on which no person has yet sat”; Luke V, 39 *jah ainshun driggandane fairni ni suns vili jugg*, “and no one, after drinking old [wine], immediately wants new”; X, 19 *jah vaihte ainohun ïzvis ni gaskaþjiþ*, “and nothing shall in any way harm you”; John VIII, 20 *jah ainshun ni faifah ïna*, “and no one seized him”; XIII, 28 *þatuh ainshun ni vissa*, “but no one knew”; XIV, 6 *ainshun ni qimiþ*, “no one comes”; XV, 24; XVI, 5; XVII, 12; XVIII, 38; I Cor. I, 14; Eph.

[Col. 1405] IV, 29. Conversely: Luke IX, 50 *ni ainshun ïst manne*, “there is no one against you”; XIV, 24 *ni ainshun manne jainaize kauseiþ nahtamatis*, “not one of those persons shall taste my supper”; XVIII, 19 *ni ainshun þiuþeigs niba ains guþ*, “no one is good except one, God”; 29; XIX, 30 *ana þammei ni ainshun aiv manne sat*, “on which no person ever sat”; John III, 32; VI, 65; VII, 19, 30, 44; X, 41; XVI, 22; XIX, 4; Rom. XIII, 8; I Cor. X, 24; II Cor. V, 16; VI, 3; VII, 2; XI, 8; Gal. VI, 17; Phil. IV, 15; I Thess. III, 3; IV, 12; II Tim. II, 4; *Skeir.* VIII, c, d.

δ) *ni mannahun*, “to no one”: Mark VIII, 30 *ei mannhun ni qeþeina*, “that they should tell no one”; IX, 9 *ei mannhun ni spillodedeina*, “that they should report [it] to no one.” Conversely: Mark VIII, 26 *ni mannhun qiþais*, “tell no one”; IX, 39; John VIII, 33; I Tim. V, 22.

ε) *ni washun*, “no one”: John X, 28 *ni fravilviþ washun*, “no one shall snatch [them] away.” Conversely: Matt. IX, 16 *ni washun lagjiþ*, “no one puts”; Mark X, 18 *ni washun þiuþeigs*, “no one is good”; Luke X, 22; John X, 18; Col. II, 18; II Thess. II, 3.

ζ) *ni wan* and *ni wanhun*, “never”: Luke IV, 11 *ei wan ni gastagqjais*, “lest perhaps you strike”; John VI, 35 *ni þaurseiþ wanhun*, “shall never thirst.” Conversely: Matt. VII, 23 *ni wanhun kunþa*, “I never knew”; Luke XV, 29; John VII, 46.

η) *ni aiv*, “never”: Mark II, 12 *aiv sva ni gasewum*, “we never saw [anything] thus.” Conversely: Matt. IX, 33 *ni aiv sva uskunþvas*, “never was anything thus seen”; Luke XV, 29; John X, 29; II Tim. III, 7, etc.

bb) The same applies to *ni þanaseiþs*, *ni þanamais*, *ni ju*, *ni juþan* (“no longer”), and *ni nauh* (“not yet”); hence:

α) Mark IX, 25 *þanaseiþs ni galeiþais ïn ïna*, “enter into him no longer”; X, 8 *svasve þanaseiþs ni sind tva*, “so that they are no longer two”; XII, 34 *þanaseiþs ainshun ni gadaursta ïna fraihnan*, “after that no one dared question him”; Luke XV, 19, 21; John XIV, 30; Eph. IV, 17, 14, 28; Mark XV, 5 *þanamais ni andhof*, “he answered no longer”; I Thess. III, 1 *ni usþulandans þanamais*, “no longer enduring”; Rom. XIV, 15 *ju ni bi friaþvai gaggis*, “no longer walk according to love”; Eph. II, 19 *ju ni sijuþ gasteis*, “you are no longer strangers”; I Thess. III, 5 *ju ni uspulands*, “no longer enduring.” But also Mark IX, 8 *ni þanaseiþs ainohun gasewun*, “they no longer saw anyone”; John XIV, 19; XVI, 10, 21, 25; XVII, 11; Gal. II, 20; IV, 7; *Skeir.* I, b; III, b.

β) John VII, 30 *nauhþanuh ni atïddja weila ïs*, “his hour had not yet come”; 39; VIII, 57 *fimftiguns jere nauh ni habais*, “you are not yet fifty years old”; Rom. IX, 11. Conversely: Mark IV, 40 *waiva ni nauh habaiþ galaubein*, “why do you not yet have faith?”; VIII, 17, 21; John III, 24; VII, 6, 8, 39; Phil. III, 13; see on this passage; *Skeir.* III, a.

c) In formulae: *ni þatei*, “not because,” “not that”: John VI, 46; VII, 22; I Cor. X, 20; II Cor. I, 24; Phil. III, 12; IV, 11, 17; II Thess. III, 9; *Skeir.* IV, b; *ni þeei*, “not because”: John XII, 6; “not in order that”: II Cor. II, 4; *ni unte*, “not because”: II Cor. VII, 9; *ni ei*, where the Greek uses merely “not”: II Cor. V, 12; but I Cor. VII, 17, see on this passage. The reading can both be justified and understood if *kannt*, “you know,” is supplied after *ni* and the clause is treated as interrogative; but then it no longer corresponds to Greek “unless.” *Ni þatainei*, or *ni þatain*, “not only,” with following *ak jah*, “but also”; see *þatainei* under **Ains**; further, Gal. II, 14; Phil. I, 29; I Tim. V, 13; *Skeir.* I, d. *Ei ni*, “lest,” “so that not,” “that not”: see under **Ei**; *jah ni* (*jan-ni*), see under **Jah** and above.

d) On *ni* in progressive force, see under **Nih**.

e) Two negations in the same sentence do not cancel each other but rather intensify one another: Mark III, 20 *ni mahtedun nih hlaif matjan*, “they were not even able to eat bread”; Luke XVIII, 13 *motareis ni vilda nih augona seina ushafjan*, “the tax collector did not even wish to raise his eyes”; John VIII, 42 *nih þan fram mis silbin ni qam*, “nor did I come from myself”; XVI, 21 *ni þanaseiþs ni gaman aglons*, “she no longer remembers the distress”; II Cor. V, 16 *ni þanaseiþs ni kunnum ïna*, “we no longer know him”; Mark VII, 12 *ni fraletiþ ïna ni vaiht taujan*, “you no longer permit him to do anything”; Luke IX, 36; XX, 40; John V, 22; IX, 33; XV, 5; XVI, 24; Gal. VI, 14; Matt. XXVII, 14 *ni andhof ïmma viþra ni ainhun vaurde*, “he did not answer him, not even one word”; Mark XV, 4 *niu andhafjis ni vaiht?*, “do you answer nothing?”—in place of which Luke XIV, 60 has only *niu andhafjis vaiht*, “do you answer anything?” Thus usually under the influence of Greek; but Gothic very frequently uses a single negation despite the Greek, for example John VI, 63 *leik ni boteiþ vaiht*, “the flesh profits nothing”; see the grammar.

2) In place of the Greek privative alpha: Rom. VII, 1 *ni vitan*, “to be ignorant”; Mark XVI, 11; Rom. XI, 30, 31; II Tim. II, 13 *ni galaubjan*, “to disbelieve,” “to be disobedient”; I Tim. III, 3 *ni sakjis*, “not quarrelsome”; *ni faihufriks*, “not fond of money.”

3) “Neither, nor”: Matt. VIII, 10 *ni ïn ïsraela svalauda galaubein bigat*, “not even in Israel have I found such great faith”; XXV, 45; XXVII, 14; Mark V, 3 *ni naudibandjom eisarneinaim manna mahta ïna gabindan*, “no one was able to bind him even with iron chains”; VIII, 26; XII, 21; XIV, 59; Luke VII, 7, 9; XX,

[Col. 1406] 8; John VII, 5; Rom. XI, 21; I Cor. V, 11 end; XIV, 21; Gal. II, 5; II Thess. III, 10. Compare **Nih**, in place of which *ni þau* occurs, Mark XI, 26.

4) “Unless”: Mark XIII, 20, where elsewhere *nih* occurs; see **Nih**, 3.

5) Interrogative “not,” “is it not?”: Mark VII, 18 *ni fraþjiþ þammei all þata utaþro ïnngaggando ïn mannan ni mag ïna gamainjan?*, “Do you not understand that everything entering a person from outside cannot defile him?”; I Cor. I, 20; V, 6; VI, 1; IX, 1; “not even”: Luke VI, 3. Compare **Niu**.

6) “That not,” only *Skeir.* III, b: *so bi guþ hrainei anabudana vas, ni þanaseiþs judaiviskom ufarranneinim brukjan usdaudjaina*, “thus, concerning divine purity, it had been commanded that it should no longer be rendered void by Jewish transgressions.”

**NIBA** (*nibai*, Matt. V, 20; Mark IV, 12; V, 37; Luke VI, 4; IX, 43; John VI, 44, 46, 53, 65; VII, 35, 51; VIII, 22; X, 10; XII, 24; Rom. XI, 15; II Cor. II, 2; XIII, 5 h. l.; Old Saxon *neba*; Gr. I, 32), particle:

1) “If not,” “unless”: Matt. V, 20; Mark III, 27; VII, 3, 4; John III, 3, 5; VI, 44, 53, 65; VII, 51; X, 37, 38; XII, 24; XIV, 2; XV, 4, 6; Rom. X, 15; XI, 23; I Cor. XV, 2; II Tim. II, 5, 14 h. l.

2) “Except,” after negation and interrogation: Mark II, 7, 26; V, 37; VI, 4, 5, 8; VIII, 14; IX, 9, 29; XI, 13; Luke VI, 4; IX, 43; XVII, 18; XVIII, 19; John VI, 46; X, 10; XIV, 6; XVII, 12; Rom. XI, 15; XIV, 14; II Cor. II, 2; XII, 5; Gal. VI, 14; I Tim. V, 19; “except, if not”: I Cor. I, 14.

3) In a question, “perhaps?”: John VII, 35; “surely not?”: John VIII, 22. *Nibai þau*, “perhaps”: I Cor. VII, 5; *nibai aufto*, the same: II Cor. XIII, 5; see this passage; *nibai þatei*, “except that”: II Cor. XII, 13; Eph. IV, 9; “except to”: Rom. XIII, 8; *nibai þau þatei*, “unless perhaps”: Luke IX, 13; *nibai wan*, “lest perhaps,” in place of “lest”: Mark IV, 12 (although it does not correspond to the Greek word; in the Latin translation, “unless perhaps” must be read in place of “perhaps”).

**NIH** (Old Norse, Anglo-Saxon *ne*, Old Saxon *nec*, Old French, Modern High German *noch*, Old High German *noh*; Latin *nec*; Gf. II, 980), conjunctive negative particle, from enclitic *-uh* …
formed, is always placed at the beginning of the clause (except Rom. VIII, 7; Gal. II, 3; Tim. II, I, 12), and its *h* is often assimilated to the *þ* or *s* of the following word (*niþ-* Luc. XX, 40; Joan. XI, 30; Rom. IX, 7; Cor. I, I, 17; V, 8; XII, 21; Gal. VI, 13, here; Tim. I, I, 4; *nis-* Luc. XX, 16; Rom. IX, 15; XI, 1, 11; Gal. II, 17).

1. **And not, neither, nor** (*οὐδέ, μηδέ*): Mc. II, 2; III, 20; XI, 33; XII, 10; Luc. XX, 36; Joan. V, 22; XV, 4; Rom. VIII, 7; Cor. I, XII, 15; XV, 13, 16; Gal. II, 3, 5, here; IV, 27, here; VI, 13; Thess. II, III, 10, here; *Skeireins* I, b; IV, d; VII, a, c; **by no means** (*οὐ μή*): Mth. X, 34; Luc. XX, 40 (*niþþan þanaseiþs*, “but no longer,” *οὐκέτι δέ*); Joan. VI, 38; VII, 13 (*nih þan ainshun*, “and no one,” *οὐδείς*); XI, 30 (*niþþan nauhþanuh*, “but not yet,” *οὔπω δέ*); XII, 47; XVI, 13; Rom. VII, 7; Cor. I, I, 17; IV, 3 (*nih vaiht*, “and nothing,” *οὐδέν*); XII, 21 (*niþ-þan*, “but not,” *οὐ δέ*); Cor. II, I, 19 (codex A has *ni*); XII, 3; Tim. I, III, 3, 6; Tim. II, I, 12. Hence the formula *μὴ γένοιτο*, “may it not be,” appears in Gothic as *nis-sijai* (instead of *nih* or *ni sijai*) in Luc. XX, 16; Rom. IX, 15; XI, 1, 11; Gal. II, 17; yet *ni sijai* also occurs: see on Rom. VII, 7.

2. **Not even, neither** (*οὐδέ*): Mth. VI, 29; Mc. III, 20; Luc. XVIII, 13; Cor. I, IV, 3; Eph. V, 3.

3. **Not, unless** (*εἰ μή*): Joan. IX, 33; XV, 22; XVIII, 30; XIX, 11; Rom. VII, 7; IX, 29; compare Mc. XIII, 20.

4. Where negation continues through several clauses or members of a clause, whether conjunctively (“neither—nor,” *οὔτε—οὔτε*, *μήτε—μήτε*) or disjunctively (“not—but not,” *οὐ—οὐδέ*, *μή—μηδέ*), Gothic employs:

   a. Ordinarily *ni—nih*: Mth. VI, 20, *þarei þiubos ni ufgraband nih stiland*, “where thieves neither break in nor steal”; 25, *ni maurnaiþ saivalai ïzvarai nih leika ïzvaramma*, “do not be anxious for your life nor for your body”; VII, 18, *ni mag bagms þiuþeigs akrana ubila gataujan nih bagms ubils akrana þiuþeiga gataujan*, “a good tree cannot produce bad fruit, nor can a bad tree produce good fruit”; X, 24, *nist* (that is, *ni ïst*), “a disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his lord”; Mc. VIII, 17; XII, 24; Luc. VI, 43, 44; VIII, 17; XVII, 20, 21, 23; Joan. VI, 24; VIII, 19; XIII, 16; XIV, 17, 27; XVI, 3; Rom. IX, 6, 7; Cor. I, V, 8; XV, 50; Cor. II, IV, 2; Gal. I, 1; III, 28; Thess. I, IV, 6; Thess. II, III, 8, here; Tim. I, I, 3, 4; VI, 16; Tim. II, I, 8; *Skeireins* I, a; VII, a. Also Mth. VI, 26, *ni—nih—nih*; Luc. X, 4; Col. II, 21, here; Mth. V, 34–36, *ni—nih—nih—nih—nih*; Luc. XIV, 12.

   b. Also *ni—ni*: Mc. VI, 11, *sva managai sve ni andnimaina ïzvis, ni hausjaina ïzvis*, “wherever they do not receive you or listen to you”; VIII, 26; XII, 25; XIV, 68; Luc. III, [Col. 1407] 14; XX, 35; Rom. IX, 16; Cor. II, IV, 2, here; VII, 12; Gal. IV, 14; Eph. IV, 26, 27; Thess. I, V, 5; Thess. II, III, 8. Indeed Col. II, 21 has *ni—ni—ni*; Tit. I, 7, *ni—ni—ni—ni—ni—ni*.

   c. Also *nih—nih*: Mth. VI, 20, *þarei nih malo nih nidva fravardeiþ*, “where neither moth nor rust destroys”; 28 (XI, 28); Mc. IV, 22; Luc. VII, 33; Joan. V, 37; IX, 3; Gal. V, 6; Tim. I, I, 7; and further *nih—nih—nih*, Mc. VI, 8 (Thess. II, II, 2); Tim. I, I, 7, here; *nih—nih—nih—nih—nih þan*, Luc. IX, 3.

   d. Mixed cases, such as *nih—ni*, Luc. XIV, 35; Gal. VI, 15; compare Tim. I, III, 3, are rarer. Others—such as *nih—ni—nih*, Tim. I, III, 8; *ni—ni—ni—nih*, Rom. XIII, 9; *ni—ni—ni—ni—ni—nih—nih*, Cor. I, XIII, 5, 6; and *ni—nih—ni—ni—nih—nih—nih—nih—nih*, Rom. VIII, 38, 39—occur only once.

5. *Nih þan*: see under *þan* III, 9, c.

**NIU** (compare . . . *u*), interrogative word: “is it not?” “or?” (*οὐ*): Mth. VI, 26, *niu jus mais vulþrizans sijuþ þaim?*, “are you not much more valuable than they?”; VII, 22; XXVII, 13; Mc. IV, 21, 38; VI, 3; XI, 17; XII, 24, 26; XIV, 60; XV, 4; Luc. II, 49; IV, 22; IX, 55; XV, 4; Joan. VI, 42, 70; VII, 19, 25; VIII, 48; IX, 8; X, 34; XI, 37, 40; XIV, 10; XVIII, 26; XIX, 10; Cor. I, IX, 24; XIV, 23; Cor. II, XII, 18; XIII, 5; Gal. IV, 21; “surely not?” (*οὐχί*): Mth. V, 46; VI, 25; X, 29; Luc. XIV, 28, 31; XV, 8; XVII, 8, 17; Joan. VII, 42; XI, 9; Cor. I, V, 12; VIII, 10; X, 16, 18; Thess. I, II, 19; “certainly not” (*οὐ μή*): Joan. XVIII, 11; Luc. XVIII, 7; “not?” (*μή*): Joan. XVIII, 25.

In the latter member of a double question, *þau niu*, “or is it not? or not?” (*ἢ οὐ*): Mc. XII, 14; Luc. XX, 22; Rom. IX, 21; Cor. II, XIII, 5. Combined with *ni* (see *ni*, 5): Cor. I, IX, 1, *niu* (“not,” *οὐκ*) *ïm apaustaulus? ni* (“not,” *οὐκ*) *ïm freis? niu* (“surely not,” *οὐχί*) *ïesu xristau fraujan saw? niu* (“not,” *οὐ*) *vaurstv meinata jus sijuþ?*—“Am I not an apostle? Am I not free? Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? Are you not my work?”

*Niu aiv*, “never?” (*οὐδέποτε*): Mc. II, 25; *niu wan*, “perhaps?” (*μή ποτε*): Tim. II, II, 25; *niu aufto*, “lest perhaps” (*μήποτε*): Luc. V, 13; *niu ni* in Cor. I, I, 21 is erroneous.

**NIST**, see under *Visan*.

**NIDVA**, feminine (?), rust (*βρῶσις*): Mth. VI, 19, 20.

**NIH**, see under *Ni*.

**NIÞ**, the same as *Nih*.

**NIÞAN** (compare Old Norse *nad*, Anglo-Saxon *nit*; Gf. II, 1024), verb, class I, *naþ, neþun, niþans*: to help (*συλλαμβάνεσθαι*, “to assist”): Phlpp. IV, 3.

**NIÞJIS** (Old Norse *nidr, nefi, nift*; Anglo-Saxon *nefa, nift*; Old Frisian *neva, nift*; Old High German *nefo, nift*; English *nephew, niece*; Dutch *neef*; Modern High German *Neffe, Nichte*; Latin *nepos, neptis*; Gr. III, 321; Gf. II, 1052; Rchth. 949), masculine: cousin, kinsman (*συγγενής*): Luc. XIV, 12; Joan. XVIII, 26; Rom. XVI, 21.

**GA-NIÞJIS**, the same: Mc. VI, 4; Luc. I, 58; II, 44; XIV, 12.

**NIÞJO**, feminine: sister, kinswoman (*συγγενής*): Luc. I, 36.

**NIKAUDEMUS** (*Nekaudemus*, *Skeireins* II, b; *Nikaudaimus*, *Skeireins* VIII, c), masculine proper name: Nicodemus (*Νικόδημος*): Joan. VII, 50; *Skeireins* II, b; VIII, c.

**NIMAN** (Old Norse *nema*; Old Saxon, Anglo-Saxon *niman*; Old High German *neman*; Old Frisian *nima, nema*; English *nim*; Dutch *nemen*; Modern High German *nehmen*; Gr. II, 30; Gf. II, 1054; Rchth. 952), verb, class I, *nam, nemun, numans*:

1. To take, seize (*λαμβάνειν*): Mth. V, 40; X, 38; XXVII, 48, 59; Mc. VII, 27; VIII, 6; IX, 36; XII, 2, 19, 20, 21, 22; XV, 23; Luc. I, 63; IX, 3, 16, 23, 38; XX, 28, 29, 30, 31; Joan. VI, 11; X, 17, 18; XII, 3, 12; XIII, 12; XVI, 14, 15; XVIII, 3, 31; XIX, 1, 6; Rom. VII, 8, 11; XIII, 2; Cor. I, IV, 7; IX, 24, 25; XI, 23; Gal. II, 6, here; Phlpp. II, 7; Col. IV, 10; Neh. VI, 18; *Skeireins* VII, b; to take up (*ἀναλαμβάνειν*): Eph. VI, 13; to receive (*δέχεσθαι*): Luc. XVI, 6, 7; Eph. VI, 17; to lift, take away (*αἴρειν*): Mc. VI, 8; VIII, 34; X, 21; XV, 21, 24; Luc. VI, 29, 30; XVII, 31; XIX, 21, 24; Joan. X, 18; XVI, 22.

2. To take, receive (*λαμβάνειν*): Mc. IV, 16; Joan. III, 32; VI, 21; XIII, 20; XVII, 8; to receive (*δέχεσθαι*): Cor. II, XI, 16.

3. To raise, lift up, carry (*αἴρειν*): Mth. IX, 6; Mc. II, 9, 11; Joan. VIII, 59; to bear (*βαστάζειν*): Joan. X, 31.

4. To receive (*λαμβάνειν*): Mth. X, 41; XXVII, 6; Mc. XI, 24; XII, 1; Joan. VI, 7; VII, 23, 39; XIV, 17; XVI, 24; Cor. II, XI, 4, 8, 24; Gal. III, 2; to receive (*παραλαμβάνειν*): Thess. I, II, 13; [Col. 1408] to receive back (*ἀπολαμβάνειν*): Col. III, 24; to receive (*δέχεσθαι*): Cor. II, VI, 1.

5. To take (*λαμβάνειν*): Luc. V, 5; Cor. II, XII, 16.

6. Expressions: *runa* or *garuni niman*, to take counsel, enter into counsel (*συμβούλιον λαμβάνειν*): Mth. XXVII, 1, 7; *arbi niman*, *qen et du qenai niman*, *ana armins niman*: see under *Arbi*, *Qens*, and *Arms*.

**AND-NIMAN**:

1. To receive, welcome (*δέχεσθαι*): Mth. X, 40, 41; Mc. VI, 11; IX, 37; X, 15; Luc. II, 28; VIII, 13; IX, 5, 11, 48, 53; X, 8; XVI, 4, 9; XVIII, 17; XIX, 15; Joan. XII, 48; Cor. II, VII, 15; VIII, 17; XI, 4; Gal. IV, 14; Col. IV, 10; Thess. I, II, 13; to accept (*παραδέχεσθαι*): Mc. IV, 20; Tim. I, V, 19; to receive (*προσδέχεσθαι*): Luc. XV, 2; Phlpp. II, 29; to welcome (*ἀποδέχεσθαι*): Luc. VIII, 40; to receive as a guest (*ὑποδέχεσθαι*): Luc. XIX, 6; to receive into (*εἰσδέχεσθαι*): Cor. II, VI, 17; to receive (*λαμβάνειν*): Joan. XIII, 20, 30; Cor. I, IV, 7; Tim. I, IV, 4; to take along (*παραλαμβάνειν*): Mc. IV, 36; VII, 4; X, 32; Luc. IX, 10; Col. IV, 17; Thess. I, IV, 1; to receive (*προσλαμβάνειν*): Rom. XIV, 1, 3; XV, 7; Philem. 12; to take up (*ἀναλαμβάνειν*): Eph. VI, 16; Tim. I, III, 16; Tim. II, IV, 11 (Neh. V, 17); *Skeireins* I, d; II, d. *Gastins andniman*, to receive strangers, practise hospitality (*ξενοδοχεῖν*): Tim. I, V, 10.

2. To receive, obtain (*λαμβάνειν*): Mc. X, 30; Phlpp. III, 12; to receive (*παραλαμβάνειν*): Cor. I, XI, 23; XV, 1; Thess. II, III, 6; to receive back (*ἀπολαμβάνειν*): Luc. VI, 34; XV, 24; XVIII, 30; Gal. IV, 5; to partake (*μεταλαμβάνειν*): Tim. II, II, 6; participation (*μετάληψις*): Tim. I, IV, 3; to have in full (*ἀπέχειν*): Philem. 15; to share (*μετέχειν*): Cor. I, X, 30; to receive (*κομίζεσθαι*): Col. III, 25; *Skeireins* V, c; VII, c; Neapolitan and Aretine document.

3. In the perfect: “to have received,” hence “to have” (*ἀπέχειν*): Mth. VI, 2, 16.

**AT-NIMAN**, to receive, take up (*μεθιστάναι*, “transfer”): Col. I, 13.

**AF-NIMAN**, to take away, remove (*ἀφαιρεῖν*): Luc. I, 25; XVI, 3; Rom. XI, 27; to remove (*περιαιρεῖν*): Cor. II, III, 16; to take away (*ἀπαίρειν*): Mth. IX, 15; Mc. II, 20; Luc. V, 35; to take away (*αἴρειν*): Mth. IX, 16; Mc. II, 21; IV, 25; Luc. VIII, 18; XIX, 26; Joan. I, 29; XI, 39; to take aside (*ἀπολαμβάνειν*): Mc. VII, 33.

**BI-NIMAN**, to take, steal (*κλέπτειν*): Mth. XXVII, 64.

**GA-NIMAN**:

1. To take with oneself (*παραλαμβάνειν*): Mc. V, 40; IX, 2; Luc. IX, 28; XVIII, 31. *Ganiman miþ*, to take along with oneself (*συμπαραλαμβάνειν*): Gal. II, 1.

2. To receive (*κομίζεσθαι*): Cor. II, V, 10; Eph. VI, 8; to inherit (*κληρονομεῖν*): Cor. I, XV, 50; to conceive (*συλλαμβάνειν*, literally “take together”): Luc. I, 31; II, 21.

3. To receive, learn (*παραλαμβάνειν*): Phlpp. IV, 9; to learn (*μανθάνειν*): Mth. IX, 13; Mc. XIII, 28; Joan. VI, 45; Cor. I, IV, 6; Eph. IV, 20; Col. I, 7; Tim. II, III, 14.

**DIS-NIMAN**, to contain (*κατέχειν*): Cor. II, VI, 10.

**MIÞ-NIMAN**:

1. To receive with.

2. To receive (*δέχεσθαι*): Mth. XI, 14.

**US-NIMAN**:

1. To take away (*αἴρειν*): Mc. IV, 15; VI, 29; VIII, 8; Joan. XV, 2; XVII, 15; Col. II, 14; to remove (*ἐξαιρεῖν*): Cor. I, V, 13; to take down (*καθαιρεῖν*): Mc. XV, 46.

2. To take (*λαμβάνειν*): Mth. XXVII, 9; Luc. VI, 4; Cor. II, XI, 20.

3. To receive, take with oneself (*παραλαμβάνειν*): Luc. XVII, 34, 35.

4. To take upon oneself (*λαμβάνειν*): Mth. VIII, 17.

**FRA-NIMAN**, to take, receive (*λαμβάνειν*): Luc. XIX, 12; to receive (*παραλαμβάνειν*): Joan. XIV, 3.

**ANDA-NEMS**, adjective: acceptable (*δεκτός*): Luc. IV, 19, 24; Cor. II, VI, 2; acceptable (*ἀπόδεκτος*): Tim. I, II, 3; V, 1; *vaila andanems*, “well acceptable” (*εὐπρόσδεκτος*): Cor. II, VI, 2; VII, 12.

**ANDA-NEMS**, neuter: reception, receiving (*λῆψις*): Phlpp. IV, 15.

**ANDA-NEMEIGS**, adjective: caring for, preserving (*ἀντεχόμενος*, “holding fast”): Tit. I, 9.

**ANDA-NUMTS**, feminine: taking up, assumption (*ἀνάληψις*): Luc. IX, 51; reception (*πρόσληψις*): Rom. XI, 15; acceptance (*ἀποδοχή*): Tim. I, I, 15; IV, 9.

**ARBI-NUMJA**, masculine: heir (*κληρονόμος*): Mc. XII, 7; Luc. XX, 14; Gal. IV, 1.

**NIU**, see under *Ni*.

**\*NIUHSJAN** (Old Norse *niosna*; Old Saxon *niusian, niuson*; Anglo-Saxon *neosian*; Old High German *niusjan*; Gr. II, 22; Gf. II, 1104), verb, class II: to seek, investigate.

**BI-NIUHSJAN**, to inspect, spy out (*κατασκοπεῖν*): Gal. II, 4.

**NIUHSEINS**, feminine: inspection, visitation (*ἐπισκοπή*): Luc. XIX, 44.

**NIUN** (Old Norse *niu*; Anglo-Saxon *nigon*; Old High German *niun*; Old Saxon and Old Frisian *nigun*; English *nine*; Swedish *nio*; Danish *ni*; Dutch *negen*; Modern High German *neun*; Greek *ἐννέα*, “nine”; Latin *novem*; Gr. I, 762; Gf. II, 1091; Rchth. 951), numeral: nine: Luc. XV, 4, 7; XVII, 17.

[Col. 1409]

**NIUNDA**, ordinal numeral: ninth (*ἔνατος*): Mth. XXVII, 45; Mc. XV, 33, 34.

**NIUNTEHUND**, ninety (*ἐνενήκοντα*): Luc. XV, 4, 7; Esdr. II, 16.

**NIUN-HUNDA**, nine hundred (*ἐννεακόσιοι*): Esdr. II, 36.

**NIUJIS** (Old Norse *nyr*; Old Saxon *niuui*; Anglo-Saxon *niwe*; Old High German *niuwi*; Old Frisian *nie*; English *new*; Swedish and Danish *ny*; Dutch *nieuw*; Modern High German *neu*; Greek *νέος*, “new, young”; Latin *novus*; Bopp 71; Gr. III, 618; Gf. II, 1109; Rchth. 951), adjective:

1. New (*καινός*): Mth. IX, 17; XXVII, 60; Mc. I, 27; II, 21, 22; Luc. V, 36, 38; Joan. XIII, 34; Cor. I, XI, 25; Cor. II, III, 6; V, 17; Eph. II, 15; IV, 24; unfulled (*ἄγναφος*): Mc. II, 21. *Niuja satids*, newly converted, a neophyte (*νεόφυτος*): Tim. I, III, 6.

2. Young (*νέος*): Mth. IX, 17; Mc. II, 22; Luc. V, 37; Cor. I, V, 7; Col. III, 10.

**ANA-NIUJAN**, verb, class II: to renew (*ἀνακαινοῦν*): Cor. II, IV, 16; Col. III, 10; to renew (*ἀνανεοῦν*): Eph. IV, 23.

**NIUJIÞA**, feminine: newness (*καινότης*): Rom. VII, 6.

**ANA-NIUJIÞA**, renewal (*ἀνακαίνωσις*): Rom. XII, 2; see on this passage.

**ÏN-NIUJIÞA**:

1. Innovation.

2. Restoration, dedication (*ἐγκαίνια*): Joan. X, 22.

**NIU-KLAHS**, see under *Klahs*.

**NIUTAN** (Old Norse *niota*; Old Saxon and Anglo-Saxon *niotan*; Old High German *niozan*; Old Frisian *nieta, neta, neth*; Swedish *njuta*; Danish *nyde*; Dutch *genieten*; Modern High German *nützen, geniessen*; Gr. II, 19; Gf. II, 1118; Rchth. 948, 951), verb, class I, *naut, nutun, nutans*:

1. To obtain (*τυγχάνειν*): Luc. XX, 35.

2. To enjoy (*ὀνίνασθαι*): Philem. 20.

**GA-NIUTAN**, to take (*συλλαμβάνειν*): Luc. V, 9; to catch (*ἀγρεύειν*): Mc. XII, 13.

**NUTA**, masculine: catcher, fisherman (*ἁλιεύς*): Mc. I, 17; one who captures alive (*ζωγρῶν*): Luc. V, 10.

**\*NUTIS**, adjective: useful.

**UN-NUTIS**, useless (*ἀνόνητος*): Tim. I, VI, 9.

**\*NIPJAN** (Anglo-Saxon *nipan*; compare Danish *neppe*, “with difficulty,” and Old Norse *neppi* . . .), verb, class II: to trouble, disturb.

**GA-NIPNAN**, verb, class III: to be grieved, become gloomy (*στυγνάζειν*): Mc. X, 22.

**\*NISAN** (Old High German *ganesan*; Old Saxon *ginesan, nerian*; Anglo-Saxon *genesan*; Dutch *genezen*; Modern High German *genesen*; Gr. II, 26; Gf. II, 1098), verb, class I, *nas, nesun, nisans*: to be healed (German . . . *nesen*).

1. To be healed (*σώζεσθαι*): Mth. IX, 21, 22; Mc. V, 23, 28; VI, 56; Luc. VIII, 36.

2. To be saved, become safe (*σώζεσθαι*): Mc. X, 26; XIII, 20; Luc. VIII, 12; XVIII, 26; Joan. X, 9; Rom. IX, 27; X, 9, 13; XI, 26; Cor. I, I, 18; V, 5; X, 33; XV, 2; Cor. II, II, 15; Thess. I, II, 16; Tim. I, II, 4, 15.

**GA-NISTS**, feminine: salvation, deliverance (*σωτηρία*): Rom. X, 10; XI, 11; Cor. II, VII, 10; Eph. I, 13; Phlpp. I, 19, 28; Thess. I, V, 9; Tim. II, II, 10; III, 15; *Skeireins* I, b; acquisition, possession (*περιποίησις*): Eph. I, 14; see on this passage.

**NASJAN**, verb, class II: to save (*σώζειν*): Mth. VIII, 25; XXVII, 49; Mc. III, 4; XV, 30; Luc. IX, 24, 56; XIX, 10; Joan. XII, 27; Tim. I, I, 15; Tim. II, I, 9.

*Nasjands*, participle used substantivally: deliverer, saviour (*σωτήρ*): Luc. I, 47; II, 11; Eph. V, 23; Phlpp. III, 20; Tim. I, I, 1; II, 3; IV, 10; Tim. II, I, 10; Tit. I, 3, 4; *Skeireins* I, a, c; II, a, c; IV, a; V, d.

**GA-NASJAN**:

1. To deliver, save (*σώζειν*): Mth. IX, 22; Mc. VIII, 35; X, 52; XV, 31; Luc. VI, 9; VII, 50; VIII, 48, 50; IX, 24; XVII, 19, 33; Joan. XII, 47; Rom. XI, 14; Cor. I, I, 21; VII, 16; IX, 22; Eph. II, 5; Tim. I, IV, 16.

2. To heal (*ἰᾶσθαι*): Luc. IV, 18; VI, 19; Joan. XII, 40; to save (*σώζειν*): Mc. V, 34; Luc. XVIII, 42; to bring safely through (*διασώζειν*): Luc. VII, 3; to preserve alive (*ζωογονεῖν*): Luc. XVII, 33.

**NASEINS** (*Nasseins*, Thess. I, V, 8), feminine: salvation (*σωτηρία*): Luc. I, 69, 71, 77; II, 30; XIX, 9; Rom. X, 1; XIII, 11; Cor. II, I, 6; VI, 2; Thess. I, V, 8; salvation (*σωτήριον*): Luc. III, 6; Eph. VI, 17.

**NIST**, see under *Visan*.

[Col. 1410]

**NU** (Old Norse, Anglo-Saxon, Old Saxon, Old High German, Old Frisian, Swedish, Danish *nu*; English *now*; Modern High German *nun*; Greek *νύ, νῦν*, “now”; Latin *nunc*; Gf. II, 976; Rchth. 956):

1. Adverb: now (*νῦν*): Mth. XXVI, 65; XXVII, 42, 43; Mc. X, 30; XV, 32; Luc. II, 29; VI, 21, 25; XIX, 42; Joan. VIII, 40, 52; IX, 21, 41; XI, 8, 22; XII, 27, 31; XIII, 31, 36; XIV, 29; XV, 22, 24; XVI, 5, 22, 29, 30; XVII, 5, 7, 13; XVIII, 36; Rom. XI, 30, 31; XIII, 11; Cor. I, VII, 14; XII, 20; XVI, 12; Cor. II, VI, 2; VII, 9; XIII, 2; Gal. I, 23; II, 20; III, 3; IV, 9, 25, 29; Eph. II, 2; III, 5, 10; V, 8; Phlpp. I, 20, 30; III, 18; Col. I, 24; Tim. II, I, 10; now (*νυνί*): Rom. VII, 17; Cor. I, XII, 18; XV, 20; Col. I, 21, 26; III, 8; Philem. 11; just now (*ἄρτι*): Mth. IX, 18; Joan. IX, 19 (here), 25; XIII, 33, 37; XVI, 12, 31; Cor. I, XIII, 12; XVI, 7; Gal. IV, 20; Thess. I, III, 6.

   In this sense it is also used as a noun: Luc. I, 48, *himma nu*, “henceforth”; V, 10; *Skeireins* IV, b; *þamma nu*, “the present,” Cor. II, V, 16; Cor. I, IV, 11, *þo nu weila*, “until now”; Cor. II, VIII, 14, *in þamma nu mela*, “at the present time”; Tim. I, IV, 8, *þizos nu libainais*, “of the present life”; Tim. II, IV, 10, *þo nu ald*, “the present age.”

2. Transitional and consequential particle. Whereas in the preceding sense it may occupy any position in the sentence, here it is commonly placed after the first word, though it may occur further on: Rom. IX, 19, *qiþis mis nu*; Cor. II, V, 20, *faur xristu nu*; VII, 1, *þo habandans nu gahaita*; XII, 9, *filu gabaurjaba nu*; Gal. IV, 15, *wileika vas nu audagei*; Phlpp. II, 15, *sva managai nu sve*; *Skeireins* III, d, *bi garaihsnai nu*; and also Luc. XX, 33, *ïn þizai usstassai nu*. But where a negation begins the clause, the particle is always placed after the negated word, for example Mth. VI, 8, *ni galeikoþ nu*; 31; Eph. V, 7; Rom. XIV, 13, *ni þanamais nu*; Col. II, 16, *ni manna nu*; see on Tim. II, I, 8. “Now then, therefore” (*οὖν*): Mth. V, 19, 23, 48; VI, 2, 8, 9, 22, 23, 31; VII, 24; X, 32; XXVII, 64; Mc. X, 9; XV, 12; Luc. III, 8, 9; IV, 7; VII, 31, 42; VIII, 18; X, 2; XIV, 33; XVI, 11; XX, 15, 29, 33; Joan. III, 29; VI, 42, 45, 62; VIII, 24, 36; XIII, 14, 32; XVIII, 8, 39; Rom. VII, 7, 13, 25; IX, 14, 19, 30; X, 14; XI, 1, 19, 22; XII, 1; XIII, 7, 10, 12; XIV, 13; Cor. I, VII, 26; X, 19, 31; XIV, 26; XVI, 18; Cor. II, III, 12; V, 6, 11, 20; VII, 1, 16; IX, 5; XII, 9; Gal. III, 5; IV, 15; V, 1; Eph. IV, 1, 17; V, 1, 7; VI, 10, 14; Phlpp. II, 1, 23, 28, 29; III, 15; Col. II, 16; III, 1, 5; Tim. I, II, 1, 8; III, 2; V, 14; Tim. II, II, 1, 3; *Skeireins* I, a, d; III, d; IV, a, d; V, b, c; VI, a; “therefore” (*τοίνυν*): Luc. XX, 25; “therefore” (*ἄρα*): Rom. VII, 21; “but” (*δέ*): Joan. V, 47; Rom. VII, 20; Cor. I, XV, 12; Cor. II, IV, 13; Gal. V, 17; “for” (*γάρ*): Gal. V, 17 (?); compare Cor. I, VII, 16; “for indeed” (*μὲν γάρ*): Cor. II, XI, 4.

*Aþþan nu*, “so that” (*ὥστε*): Rom. VII, 12; “therefore” (*τοίνυν*): Cor. I, IX, 26; compare *ïþ—nu*, *Skeireins* I, d. *Nu sai* and *sai nu*, see under *Sai*; *svaei nu*, see under *Svaei*.

**NUH** (compare —*uh*; *nuk-* Cor. I, VII, 16), “for, therefore,” in a question (*οὖν*): Mc. XII, 9, *wa nuh taujai frauja?*, “what therefore will the lord do?”; Joan. XVIII, 37, *an nuh* (“then,” *οὐκοῦν*) *þiudans ïs þu?*, “then are you a king?”; “for” (*γάρ*): Cor. I, VII, 16, *wa nuk-kannt?*, “for what do you know?”

**ÞANNU**, therefore, thus (*ἄρα*): Rom. X, 17; Cor. II, V, 15; VI, 3 (absent in the Greek); Gal. III, 29; V, 11; also in questions: Mc. IV, 41; Gal. II, 17 (“then?” *ἆρα*); “perhaps then” (*ἄραγε*): Mth. VII, 30; “so that” (*ὥστε*): Cor. I, V, 8; “for” (*γάρ*): Mc. XIV, 6.

*Þannu nu*, “therefore then” (*ἄρα οὖν*): Rom. IX, 16; XIV, 12, 19; Gal. IV, 31 (for the Gothic reads *ἄρα οὖν* in place of *ἄρα*); VI, 10; Thess. I, V, 6; “therefore now” (*ἄρα νῦν*): Rom. VIII, 1; “so that” (*ὥστε*): Cor. I, IV, 5; “finally, therefore” (*λοιπὸν οὖν*): Thess. I, IV, 1. *Þannu nu jai*, “therefore then” (*ἄρα οὖν*): Rom. IX, 18; “indeed, rather” (*μενοῦνγε*): Rom. IX, 20. *Þannu þan*, “therefore then” (*ἄρα οὖν*): Rom. VII, 3.

**NUNU**, therefore, accordingly, thus, in prohibitory sentences—where it is placed between the negation and the imperative—(*οὖν*): Mth. X, 26, 31; Rom. XIV, 15, 20; Tim. II, I, 8.

*Nunu nu*, Phlpp. IV, 4, can scarcely be defended; the particle is absent in the Greek.

**NUMJA, NUMTS**, see under *Niman*.

**NUTA**, see under *Niutan*.

**NYMFA**, masculine proper name: Nympha (*Νυμφᾶ*): Col. IV, 15.

**NOHJAN**, see under *Nahan*.

**NOTA** (Gr. III, 784), masculine: stern of a ship (*πρύμνα*): Mc. IV, 38.

Among the passages cited above are also included such formulas as *svasve jah* (“just as also”) and correlations *svasve---sva jah* (οὕτω καί), *ni þatainei---ak jah* (ἀλλὰ καί). Cases are also to be included here in which *jah* is placed at the beginning of the following clause: Luke V.17, *jah varþ ïn ainamma dage jah ïs vas laisjands*, “and it came to pass on one day that he was teaching”; VIII.22. Hence also Luke II.15, *jah varþ biþe galiþun fairra ïm þai aggiljus, jah þai hairdjos qeþun du sis misso*, “and it came to pass, when the angels had departed from them, that the shepherds said to one another”; V.12, 35; IX.51; XVII.11; Neh. VI.16. Likewise Matt. VIII.14, *jah qimands ïesus ïn garda paitraus jah gasaw*, “and Jesus, coming into Peter’s house, saw”; Mark XIV.66, *jah visandin paitrau ïn rauhsnai dalaþa jah atïddja aina þiujo*, “and while Peter was in the lower courtyard, one servant-girl came”; John VI.45, *wazuh nu sa gahausjands at attin jah ganam*, “therefore everyone who has heard from the Father and learned,” although contrary to the Greek; *Skeir.* IV, b, *fraujins laiseins anastodjandei af ïudaia jah und allana midjungard gaþaih*, “the Lord’s teaching, beginning from Judaea, spread through the whole world.” In the passage of Mark, *dalaþa* may be referred to *atïddja* and *jah* explained as “also.” Compare also Matt. VI.24, *jabai fijaiþ ainana, jah anþarana frijoþ*, “he will either hate the one and love the other.”

3) but, however, δέ: Matt. VI.30; Mark XV.33; Luke V.1; VI.1, 12; VII.6; XIX.22; John VI.35; Rom. XI.17.

**JIULEIS** (Old Norse *jol*; Anglo-Saxon *geol*; Swedish and Danish *jul*), masculine: the month of July, Gothic Calendar. Indeed, *fruma jiuleis*, which, when it is joined to *naubaimbair* so as to designate November, corresponds to the Anglo-Saxons’ *ærra geola*; accordingly their *æftera geola*, December, was probably called in Gothic *sa afar jiuleis*. Compare Maresh., on the June issue of Ausg. des Ulfilas, pp. 519 ff.; Mone, *Geschichte des Nordischen Heidenthums*, II, pp. 106 f.; compare DM, p. XXI.

[Col. 1413] …**U** (…**uh**, see below; Gr. III, 753), an enclitic particle used for direct or indirect questioning: Mark 3:4 *skuldu ist* (“is it lawful?”); 10:2 (εἰ, “whether”); 12:14; Luke 20:22; Matt. 27:49 *qimaiu* (εἰ, “whether”); Mark 10:38 *magutsu*; 15:9 *vileidu*; 36 *qimaiu* (εἰ); Luke 9:54 *vileizu*; 14:28 *habaiu* (εἰ); 31 *siaiu* (εἰ); John 13:12 *vitudu*; 18:39 *vileidu*; 2 Cor. 2:9 *sijaidu* (εἰ); 13:5; John 9:2 *sau*; 19; 18:22 *svau*. It is also inserted between a preposition and a noun: John 18:34 *abu þus*; Gal. 3:2 *uzu vaurstvam*; 5; likewise between a compositional particle and a verb: Matt. 9:28 *gaulaubjats*; John 9:35; Luke 18:8 *biugitai* (ἆρα, “then?”). Further, Mark 8:23 *gau wa sewi*; compare Rom. 7:1 *niu vituþ* (where *ni-vitan* stands for ἀγνοεῖν, “to be ignorant,” and *u* for ἤ, “or”). Where there is a double question, *u* is used in the second member; see under *þau* 3), in which case *u* sometimes occurs in the form *uh*; see under …*uh*.

[Col. 1414] **NI-U**, see under *Ni*.

III, 604; Gf. I, 92; Rchth. 722), adjective: evil, wicked, worthless, πονηρός: Matt. 5:37, 45; 6:13; 7:17, 18; 9:4; Mark 7:23; Luke 3:19; 6:22, 45; 7:21; 8:2; John 7:7; Rom. 12:9; 1 Cor. 5:13; Gal. 1:4; Eph. 6:13; Col. 1:21; 1 Thess. 5:22; 2 Thess. 3:2, 3; 1 Tim. 6:4; 2 Tim. 3:13; κακός, “bad, evil”: Mark 7:21; Rom. 7:19, 21; 12:17; 13:3, 4, 10; 1 Cor. 13:5; 15:33; 2 Cor. 13:7; Phil. 3:2; Col. 3:5; 1 Thess. 5:15; 1 Tim. 6:10; Titus

[Col. 1415] 1:12; χείρων, “worse”: 2 Tim. 3:13, in this passage; σαπρός, “rotten, corrupt”: Matt. 7:17, 18; Luke 6:43; Eph. 4:29. For *ubil qiþan*, *ubil haban*, *ubil vaurdjan*, see under *Qiþan*, *Haban*, *Vaurd*.

**UBILABA**, adverb: badly, wickedly, κακῶς: Mark 2:17; John 18:23.

**UBIL-VAURDS**, see under *Vaurd*.

**UBUH**, see under *Uf*.

**UGK** (Old Norse *ockr*, Old Saxon *unk*, Anglo-Saxon *unc*, Old High German *unch*: Bopp 200; Gr. I, 780 ff.; Gf. I, 350), accusative of the first-person dual personal pronoun: “us two,” ἡμᾶς: Eph. 6:22.

**UGKIS** (*uggkis*, Matt. 9:27; Mark 10:35; John 17:21): 1) dative, “to us two,” ἡμῖν: Mark 10:35, 37; John 17:21; 1 Cor. 4:6; 2) accusative, “us two,” ἡμᾶς: Matt. 9:27; Luke 7:20.

**UZU** and **UZUH**, see under *Us*.

…**UH** (compare Latin *-ce*, *-que*; Gr. III, 23), an enclitic particle chiefly attached to verbal forms and likewise to pronouns (*þatuh*, see under *þata*; *wazuh*, *warjizuh*, see under *was*; *ïmmuh*, Rom. 11:36; *veiz-uh*, *juzuh*, 1 Cor. 4:10); to adjectival pronouns, such as *sums* (Matt. 26:67; Mark 8:28; 12:5; Luke 9:8; John 7:44; 11:46; Rom. 9:21; 1 Cor. 11:21; 15:6; Eph. 4:11; 2 Tim. 2:20; and see under 1, a, β), *anþar* (Matt. 8:21; 11:3; Mark 4:5), *all* (1 Cor. 15:26), *manag* (Luke 3:18); to prepositions (see below); adverbs (*maizuh*, Gal. 4:9; *Skeir.* VIII, b; *sumanuh*, *Skeir.* VI, c; *wanuh*, Matt. 25:38, 39; *samaleikoh*, Luke 5:10; *nauhuh*, Luke 14:26; otherwise see under 1, c and 3); and rarely to nouns (*þuhtuh*, 1 Cor. 10:29; *þvairhaih*, Eph. 4:26; *filippauzuh*, Luke 3:1). Thus, where a word ends in a consonant, it causes the consonant to be changed into another: namely, *f* into *b*, *þ* into *d*, *s* into *z* (*ubuh* for *uf-uh*, *vitaiduh* for *vitaiþ-uh*, *wazuh* for *was-uh*, *filippauz-uh* for *filippaus-uh*, etc.). But where it ends in a vowel, if the preceding vowel is *a*, that vowel is elided (*sumuh* for *suma-uh*, *ïddjuh* for *ïddja-uh*, *bandvidah* for *bandvida-uh*, *qiþuh* for *qiþa-uh*, etc.), except in the monosyllables *svah*, *sah*, and *wah* for *sva-uh*, *sa-uh*, and *wa-uh* respectively. Yet *wauh* occurs as an interrogative pronoun in 1 Cor. 4:7. Where there are other vowels or diphthongs, the particle’s own *u* is elided (*biþeh* for *biþe-uh*, *nih* for *ni-uh*, *duh* for *du-uh*, *samaleikoh* for *samaleiko-uh* [but *wouh* occurs as an interrogative pronoun, 2 Cor. 6:15, 16], *sumaih* for *sumai uh*, *viljauh* for *viljau-uh*, etc.). Where *þ* follows, the particle’s *h* is frequently assimilated to it, as in Matt. 5:37; 6:7; 26:67; Mark 1:6; 4:5; 5:13; 7:20, 26; 8:9; 10:32; 15:40; Luke 3:18; 8:32; 9:8; 10:1; 14:12, 26; 15:1, 11, 25; 16:1; 18:1, 3, 4; John 11:46; 12:6, 10, 16, 20, 33; and regularly in Codex A in the Epistles, for example Rom. 9:21; 1 Cor. 4:7, 10; 7:7; 9:23, etc. Other assimilations are rare: *dul-leitilai*, 2 Cor. 7:8; *nis-sijai*, see under *Ni*; *nuk-kant*, see under *Nu*.

But when *uh* is used as a conjunction, it follows the first word of the clause and separates a preposition not only from its governing word (Matt. 8:5 *afaruh þan þata*; Mark 16:12; Luke 1:24; 10:1; 18:4; John 19:12 *framuh þamma*; Matt. 11:12; John 7:17; Matt. 11:25 *ïnuh jainamma mela*; Mark 10:7; Luke 7:21; 10:7, 21; Rom. 13:6; 2 Cor. 2:8; 4:16; 5:9; 6:17; 7:13; 1 Thess. 4:8; 5:11; 1 Tim. 4:15; 2 Tim. 2:10; *Skeir.* I, a, d; II, a, b; III, d; IV, a, b; VI, c, d; Luke 6:45 *uzuh allis ufarfullein*; Mark 11:30; Luke 20:4; John 6:65; *Skeir.* V, a *anduh þana laist*), but also from the verb (Luke 17:7 *anuhkumbei*; Eph. 4:23; John 7:32 *ïnuhsandidedun*; Mark 14:44 *atuh þan gaf*, see on this passage; 1 Cor. 14:23; Mark 16:8 *dizuh þan sat*; John 16:28 *uzuhïddja*; 17:1; Gal. 2:2; 1 Cor. 15:15 *biþ-þan gitanda*). This also happens where another conjunction precedes, in which case another word intervenes (Eph. 4:8 *ushanþ hunþ jah atuhgaf gibos mannam*; Luke 18:38 *ïþ ïs ubuhvopida*; John 11:41 *ïþ ïesus uzuhhof augona*).

1) As a conjunction, like Latin *-que*, it is used either alone

[Col. 1416] or joined with other particles.

a) Alone:

α) Ordinarily it means “and.”

αα) καί: Mark 2:11; 14:13; Luke 2:38; 17:16; 19:2; John 7:32; 17:1; 18:33.

ββ) Hence it is used to join clauses where the Greek employs no conjunction: Matt. 27:65; Mark 16:7; 1 Cor. 16:13; 1 Tim. 4:15.

γγ) It is also placed at the beginning of a clause in order to link it to the preceding one: Matt. 11:25; Luke 10:21; John 6:66; 9:17; 16:28; 19:12; Rom. 11:36; especially in the formula *ïnuh þis*, see under *In*.

δδ) It is used where Greek participles have been expanded: Mark 5:41; Luke 17:7; John 6:5, 17, 25; 8:12; 9:35; 13:25; 18:3, 22.

εε) Pleonastically with a finite verb where a participle precedes: Mark 8:1; Luke 15:26; John 11:31.

ζζ) In place of a relative pronoun; see *þatuh* 2) under *þata*.

β) “Then,” “therefore,” οὖν: John 16:18; δέ, “but”: Matt. 27:44; John 10:20; Eph. 4:32; 2 Thess. 3:12; especially in correlative clauses after *sums*, δέ: John 9:9; 1 Cor. 12:10; μέν: John 7:12. It is also used where no corresponding particle occurs in the Greek text: John 7:41; 9:9, 16; 10:21.

γ) In one or both members of a double question: Matt. 11:3; Mark 11:30; Luke 20:4; John 7:17 (πότερον, “whether”); elsewhere simple …*u* occurs in its place; see *þau* 3).

δ) “Also,” καί: Luke 14:26; 2 Cor. 5:9; see on this passage.

b) With other conjunctions, having no fixed meaning:

α) Before *þan*: Matt. 5:31, 37; 6:7, 29, 32; 8:5, 21, 30; 11:12; 25:38, 39; 26:67; 27:16, 55, 61; Mark 1:6; 2:6; 4:5; 5:11, 13; 7:20, 26; 8:9, 28; 10:32; 12:5; 14:44; 15:7, 25, 40; 16:8, 12; Luke 1:6, 24; 2:2; 3:1, 18; 4:42; 5:4, 10, 36; 6:7, 39; 7:12, 21, 48; 8:32; 9:8, 27; 10:1, 2, 7; 14:12, 26; 15:1, 11, 25; 16:1; 18:1, 3, 4; John 6:4, 10, 11, 64, 71; 7:2, 25, 44; 8:28, 35; 9:14, 31; 11:1, 2, 5, 13, 18, 38, 46; 12:6, 10, 16, 20, 33; 13:12, 23, 24, 30; 18:2, 5, 14, 15; Rom. 9:21; 12:4; 1 Cor. 4:7, 10; 7:7; 9:23; 10:29; 11:2, 3, 21; 12:11; 14:23; 15:6, 15; 16:8; 2 Cor. 6:15, 16; 12:19; Gal. 1:22; 2:2; 4:9; Eph. 4:9, 11, 23, 26; 1 Thess. 5:14, 25; 2 Tim. 2:20; Titus 1:7; Philem. 22; *Skeir.* III, b, c; VI, c; VIII, a, b, c.

β) After *ïþ*: Mark 10:38, 39; 14:62; Luke 6:8; 7:6; 18:21, 29, 38; 20:25; John 9:17, 38; 11:41; 14:8; 16:19; 18:31.

γ) After *jah*: Eph. 4:8.

δ) Before *auk*: Matt. 9:21; Rom. 13:6; 1 Cor. 15:26.

ε) Before *allis*: Luke 6:45.

ζ) After *jabai*: 2 Cor. 7:8; see on this passage.

c) In similar formulas formed from other particles, for example *duhþe* (*duþþe*), *þaruh*, *þaþroh*, see under *þata*; *þauh*, *sveþauh*, see under *þau*; *þanuh*, *nauhþanuh*, see under *þan*; *nih*, see under *Ni*; *nuh*, see under *Nu*; *svah*, see under *Sva*.

2) Demonstrative particle, attached, like Latin *-ce*, to demonstratives: *sah*, *soh*, *þatuh*, *þaruh*; see under *þata*.

3) Indefinite particle, comparable with Latin *-que* when attached to interrogative pronouns or pronominal adverbs that make general affirmations: *wazuh*, *warjizuh*, *waþaruh*, *þiswaruh*, *þiswaduh*; see under *Was*.

**UHT** (Old Norse *otta*, Anglo-Saxon *uhte*, Old Saxon *uhta*, Old High German *uohta*; Gf. I, 138; Schmid 8): morning time; a suitable time.

**UHTEIGS**, adjective: at leisure; *uhteigs visan*, “to be at leisure,” σχολάζειν: 1 Cor. 7:5.

**UHTEIGO** (*ohteigo*), adverb: opportunely, εὐκαίρως: 2 Tim. 4:2.

**UN-UHTEIGO**, adverb: inopportunely, ἀκαίρως: 2 Tim. 4:2.

**UHTIUGS**, adjective: at leisure; *uhtiugs visan*, “to have leisure,” εὐκαιρεῖν: 1 Cor. 16:12.

**UHTVO**, feminine: the early-morning time, ἔννυχον: Mark 1:35.

**UHTEDUN**, the same as *ohtedun*, Mark 11:32; see under *Agan*.

**ULBANDUS** (Old Norse *ulfalldi*, Old Saxon *olvunt*, Anglo-Saxon *olfend*, Old High German *olpenta*; Gf. I, 244), masculine: elephant, camel, κάμηλος: Mark 1:6; 10:25; Luke 18:25.

[Col. 1417] **UN—** (Old Saxon, Anglo-Saxon, Old High German *un—*, Old French *un—, on—*, Old Norse and Swedish *o—*, Danish *u—*; Gr. II, 775; Gf. I, 302), an inseparable particle with privative and negative force.

1) Compounded with verbs only in *unþiuþjan*, *unsveran*, *unverjan*, *gaunledjan*; more frequently,

2) with participles: *unagands*, *unbairands*, *unbairandei*, *unhabands*, *unkunnands*, *unliugands*, *unrodjands*, *unsaiwands*, *unsveibands*, *unvitands*, *unvunands*, *unfraþjands*, *unwapnands*; *unbaurans*, *unbeistjoþs*, *undivans*, *unqeniþs*, *unþvahans*, *unkunþs*, *unliugaiþs*, *unsaltans*, *unhanduvaurhts*; double compounds: *ungalaubjands*, *ungahabands*, *ungafairinonds*, *ungakusans*, *ungasaiwans*, *ungastoþans*, *ungatevids*, *ungavagiþs*, *ungafairinoþs*; *unandhuliþs*, *unandsakans*; *unbilaistiþs*, *unbimaitans*; *unuslaisiþs*, *unusspilloþs*; *unfairlaistiþs*; *unufbrikands*; and

3) with adjectives: *unaivisks*, *unbarnahs*, *unbruks*, *unqeþs*, *unhails*, *unnunslags*, *unhrains*, *unkars* (*unkunþs*), *unsvikunþs*, *unleds*, *unliubs*, *unliuts*, *untilamalsks*, *unmanvus*, *unnutis*, *unmanariggvs*, *unriurs*, *unsels*, *unsibis*, *untals*, *unsvers*, *untriggvs*, *unvahs*, *unvaurstva*, *unvamms*, *unveis*, *unvis*, *unvits*, *unfagrs*, *unfairins*, *unfaurs*, *unfroþs*, *unweils*; double compounds: *unandsoks*; *unatgahts*; *ungalaubs*, *ungatass*, *ungawairbs*; *unhindarveis*; *unfaurveis*;

4) with adverbs: *unuhteigo*, *unsahtaba*, *unvairþaba*, *unveniggo*, *unfairinodaba*; *unanasiuniba*; *ungatassaba*;

5) with nouns: *unagei*, *unbeistei*, *undivanei*, *unhaili*, *unhulþa*, *unhulþo*, *unhrainei*, *unhrainiþa*, *unkaureins*, *unkunþi*, *unledi*, *unlustus*, *unmahts*, *unriurei*, *unselei*, *unsibja*, *unsuti*, *unsverei*, *unsverains*, *unsveriþa*, *unvammei*, *unvereins*, *unviti*, *unfreideins*, *unfrodei*; double compounds: *ungahobains*, *ungalaubeins*, *ungaraihtei*; *unbimait*.

**UND** (Old Norse *unst, unz*, Old Saxon *unti*, Anglo-Saxon *oð*, Old French *und, ont*, Old High German *unt*; Gf. I, 363; Alth. Präp. 268; Rchth. 966).

I. Preposition.

A. With the accusative:

1) To mark place: “up to,” “as far as,” ἕως. After *þairhgaggan*, Luke 2:15; *qiman*, 4:42; *briggan*, 4:29; *ushauhjan* and *gadrausjan*, Luke 12:15 (Matt. 11:23); *fravilvan*, 2 Cor. 12:2; *fairrinnan*, 2 Cor. 10:14 (εἰς, “into”), 13 (ἄχρι, “as far as”); Mark 13:37, *galisiþ gavalidans seinans af fidvor vindam, fram andjam airþos und andi himinis*, “he will gather his chosen ones from the four winds, from the end of the earth to the end of heaven.” Conversely, in *Skeir.* IV, b, *laiseins fraujins anastodjandei af ïudaia jah und allana midjungard gaþaih*, “the Lord’s teaching, beginning from Judaea and going through all the world,” *and* should be read in place of *und*; compare Rom. 9:17. Mark 6:23, *giba þus und halba þiudangardja meina*, “I will give you up to half of my kingdom.” Hence the formula *und dalaþ*, “down to the bottom,” ἕως κάτω: Matt. 27:51; Mark 15:38.

2) To mark time: “until,” “while,” “until such time as,” ἕως and ἄχρι: 1 Cor. 16:8, *visa ïn aifaison und paintekusten*, “I shall remain in Ephesus until Pentecost”; Matt. 11:13, *praufeteis jah vitoþ und ïohanne fauraqeþun*, “the prophets and the law prophesied until John” (Luke 16:16, *und ïohannen*); Luke 4:13, *und mel*, “until a time”; 2 Cor. 1:13, *und andi*, “until the end”; 1 Thess. 2:16; Luke 18:5 (εἰς, “to”); Luke 1:55, *und aiv*, “for ever”; 1 Tim. 6:14, *und qum fraujins*, “until the coming of the Lord” (μέχρι); Gal. 4:2, *und garehsn attins*, “until the date fixed by the father”; Phil. 2:8, *und dauþu*, “unto death” (μέχρι); 30; 2 Tim. 2:9, *und bandjos*, “as far as bonds” (μέχρι); Luke 1:80, *und dag ustaikneinais*, “until the day of his manifestation”; Matt. 27:64, *und þridjan dag*, “until the third day”; Matt. 27:8, *und hina dag*, “until this day”; 2 Cor. 3:14, 15; Luke 17:27, *und þanei dag*, “until the day on which”; 1:20, *und þana dag ei*, “until the day when”; Matt. 27:45, *und weila niundon*, “until the ninth hour”; Mark 15:33; 1 Cor. 4:11, *und þo weila*, “until this hour”; *Skeir.* IV, b, *und hita nu*, “until now”; Matt. 11:12, *und hita*, “until now”; Mark 13:19; John 16:24; Matt. 9:15, *und þata weilos þei*, “until such time as,” “so long as,” ἐφ᾽ ὅσον; *und þatei*, “as long as,” “while,” ἐν ᾧ: Mark 2:19; “until,” ἕως: Matt. 5:18; Neh. 7:3; ἕως ὅτου: Matt. 5:25; ἄχρις οὗ: Rom. 11:25; 1 Cor. 15:25; *und wa*, “how long?” ἕως πότε: Mark 9:19; Luke 9:41; John 10:24.

3) With *filu* and *vaíht* in comparison: *und filu*, “much more,” πολλῷ: Luke 18:39; 2 Cor. 3:9; Phil. 1:23; *und wan filu*, “how much?” πόσῳ: Matt. 10:25; *ni und vaiht*, “for nothing,” οὐδενί: Gal. 4:1.

B. With the dative: “for,” “in return for,” ἀντί: Matt. 5:38, *augo und augin jah tunþu und tunþau*, “eye for eye and tooth for tooth”; Rom. 12:17, *ubil und ubilamma usgiban*, “to render evil for evil.” And likewise, probably, in 1 Thess. 5:15, *ubil und ubilamma usgildai*, “repay evil for evil,” *ana* should be read instead.

[Col. 1418] εἰς, “into”: Matt. 27:10, *atgebun þrinstiguns silubreinaize und akra kasjins*, “they gave the thirty silver coins for the potter’s field.”

II. In composition, where it is also changed into *unþa…*, only with verbs: *undgreipan*, *undredan*, *undrinnan*, *unþaþliuhan*.

**UNDAR** (Old Norse *undir*, Anglo-Saxon *under*, Old Saxon *undar*, Old French *under, onder*, Old High German *untar*, English, Swedish, Danish *under*, modern High German *unter*; Gf. I, 380; Alth. Präp. 174; Rchth. 1101), preposition construed with the accusative: “under,” ὑπό with the accusative: Mark 4:21, *uf melan satjan aiþþau undar ligr*, “to put under a bed.”

**UNDARLEIJA** (?), adjective: lower, ἐλαχιστότερος: Eph. 3:8; see on this passage.

**UNþA**, see under *Und*.

**UNKJA** (a Latin word), masculine: an ounce; *docum*, Arezzo [uncertain].

I, 780; Gf. I, 388; Rchth. 1117), genitive plural of the first-person personal pronoun: “of us,” ἡμῶν: Mark 9:22; Rom. 14:12; Eph. 4:7.

**UNS**, the same: 1) accusative: Matt. 6:13; Rom. 8:37, 39; 9:24; 13:11; 14:13; 2 Cor. 1:4, 5, 8, 10, 11, 14, 19, 20, 22; 2:14; 3:1, 6; 4:2, 5; 5:5, 11, 12, 14, 20; 6:4; 7:6; 8:4, 7, 20; 10:2, 12, 14; 12:19; Gal. 1:4, 23; 5:1; Eph. 1:5, 8; 2:4, 5, 7; 5:2; 1 Thess. 2:18; 4:7; 5:9, 10, 25; 2 Thess. 1:6; 3:9; 2 Tim. 1:9; 2:12; *Skeir.* I, a; III, d; V, d; 2) dative: Matt. 6:11, 12; Mark 1:24; Luke 2:48; 17:5; 20:14, 28; 2 Cor. 1:8, 9; 3:3, 5; 4:12; 5:12, 18, 19; 6:12; 7:7; 8:5, 19, 20; Eph. 1:6, 19; 3:20; 4:6; Col. 1:8; 2:13, 14; 1 Thess. 2:13; 3:1, 4, 6; 4:1; 2 Thess. 1:7; 3:6; 2 Tim. 1:14; *Skeir.* I, d.
